# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
# A LETTER
->CONCERNING THE PHILOSOPHY OF THE GOSPEL.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial Q depicting a scholar or saint seated at a lectern with an open book, within a square frame decorated with architectural and floral motifs.</image-desc>
ALTHOUGH in divine matters the mortal intellect—however sharp it may otherwise be—is so frequently blinded that it is forced to cry out with the Apostle Paul. For even though Paul had been caught up into the third heaven and had heard things more hidden than he was permitted to reveal to souls still weighed down by mortal bodies, nevertheless, when writing to the Romans, as the progress of his discourse brought his thoughts closer to the entrance of the divine counsel, he immediately cried out in astonishment: *O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are His judgments, and His ways past finding out! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor?* And soon, submitting the weakness of human understanding to the majesty of the Divine Spirit—who dispenses everything for the best, even if the reason for His plan cannot be perceived by us—he says: *To Him be honor and glory forever and ever.* Thus, having reverently withdrawn from the majesty he adored, he transitions to the instruction of morals. *I beseech you,* he says, *brethren, by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice.* Likewise, the Prophet exclaims: *The judgments of the Lord are a great deep.*

Yet, there is a point to which the pious curiosity of Christians is permitted to proceed, provided that, following Paul's example, as soon as one feels the edge of the human mind cannot endure that "inaccessible light" where the Heavenly Father dwells, one yields in adoration. Having venerated the inscrutable mystery of the Divine Spirit, let a man acknowledge his own weakness and take care of those things instead <note>Erasmus quotes Homer’s Odyssey here to suggest focusing on practical ethics at home rather than celestial mysteries.</note> "whatever of evil or good has happened in your halls." <note>original: "ὅττι τοι ἐν μεγάροισι κακόν τ' ἀγαθόν τε τέτυκται"</note> 

But I do not know how it happens that human curiosity exerts all its intellectual nerves nowhere more intensely than in those matters which are furthest from mortal understanding and contribute least to a life of piety. Of this kind are almost all those things debated concerning the divine essence. Yet no mystery concerns us more than the ineffable plan by which God, through His Son, restored the human race. To one who frequently dwells on this contemplation, it has sometimes seemed to me worth investigating whether it was truly necessary for the Son of God Himself, having become man, to show us the way of salvation through His own teaching. For there must have been some immense value in it. 

And yet, there is scarcely anything handed down in the Gospel writings that was not handed down many centuries before in the volumes of the Old Testament, and some things even in the books of the Philosophers. That souls survive their bodies and are affected by either rewards or punishments according to the merits of their past life was taught by none other than the famous Socrates of Plato. He also teaches that no man is truly just who would not rather cease to be just than endure being thought unjust. He teaches that the soul must be led away from the love of visible things toward the pursuit of those things which truly and eternally exist. He teaches that death is not to be feared, but rather hoped for by one who has lived well. He teaches that no one ought to trust in his own deeds, yet he who has striven with all his might to live purely ought to have good hope in a merciful God. 

Do these things not agree with those Gospel doctrines? *And these shall go into eternal life, but those into eternal fire.* And *blessed shall you be when men reproach you*, and *blessed are you when they persecute you for righteousness' sake.* And *do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth.* And *work for the food that does not perish.* And *do not fear those who kill the body.* And *when you have done all things, say: We are unprofitable servants.* 

Indeed, that law of charity, which alone encompasses all laws—was it not clearly and diligently handed down in the Old Testament? *You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your mind, and with all your strength, and your neighbor as yourself.* What could be emphasized more diligently, or expressed more effectively? Furthermore, those Gospel precepts of charity, by which we are commanded to be merciful and kind toward the needy, are so emphasized in the volumes of the Prophets and the Old Testament that they could scarcely be stated more clearly or accurately. Isaiah cries out: *Help the oppressed, judge for the fatherless, defend the widow.* Again, elsewhere: *Let those who are broken go free, and break every burden. Share your bread with the hungry, and bring the needy and the wanderers into your house. When you see the naked, cover him.* Christ teaches: *Give to everyone who asks of you.* But the book of Deuteronomy says this even more effectively: *There shall be no needy person among you, so that the Lord your God may bless you.* For he who commands that care be taken so that no one *is* in need seems to require more than he who commands that it be given to one who asks. 

Even that which seems peculiar to the **Philosophy of the Gospel**—namely, in what things Christian happiness consists—one may hear in Isaiah. The Lord Jesus said: *Blessed are the poor, blessed are those who hunger, blessed are those who mourn.* How well Isaiah harmonizes with these: *Behold,* he says, *my servants shall eat, and you shall be hungry; and my servants shall drink, and you shall be thirsty. Behold, my servants shall rejoice, and you shall be confounded. Behold, my servants shall praise for joy of heart, and you shall cry for sorrow of heart.* Christ says: *Blessed shall you be when men hate you.* What does Isaiah say? *Do not fear the reproach of men,* he says, *and do not be diminished by their contempt.* Finally, regarding what seemed specifically to belong to Gospel perfection—that we should not return injury when harmed, that we should love our enemies and deserve well of those who treat us ill—did not Isaiah also teach this when he said: *Say, "You are our brothers," to those who hate you*? Again, when Zechariah commands that no one should remember the malice of his neighbor. Again, when the Lord cries through the Prophet: *Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.* Indeed, not even examples of Gospel perfection are lacking in the Old Testament...

<meta>catchword: li-</meta>

<summary>In this preface, Erasmus argues that the Gospels provide a living image of Christ more powerful than any relic. He demonstrates that while ancient philosophers and the Old Testament contained seeds of Christian morality, Christ’s teaching perfected them into a practical "Philosophy of the Gospel."</summary>
<keywords>Desiderius Erasmus, Paraclesis, Philosophy of Christ, Gospel vs Old Testament, Socrates, Isaiah, Christian education, biblical humanism, charity, beatitudes</keywords>

--- Page 23 ---
<meta>This page concludes Erasmus’s "Letter on the Evangelical Philosophy" (his introduction to the New Testament) and begins a list of "Solecisms"—grammatical errors he identified in the standard Latin Vulgate translation of the Bible. Erasmus is arguing that the Gospel is the perfection of nature and that the "newness" of Christ lies in his absolute example of virtue and the universality of his message.</meta>

...books. For even Moses asks to be blotted out from the book of God, if he would but forgive the sin of his rebellious people. And Aaron intercedes for those who conspired against him. Nor are there lacking examples of brave men who suffered the ultimate for justice, just as the **Martyrs of the Gospel** did.

If anyone seeks miracles, he will find the dead raised, a leper healed, a jar of oil increased, a vessel of flour that did not fail, fire sent down from heaven to consume the flesh of a sacrifice though it was drenched with much water, a spring brought forth from a rock at the strike of a rod, and bitter, poisonous waters made sweet and healthy by the casting in of wood—along with many other things too well-known to need repeating here. Nor is the mystery of the **Holy Trinity** <note>original: "sacrae Triadis"</note> silent in those books. Everything is full of the name of the Father; there is mention of the Son in several places (whom Augustine testifies he even found in the books of the Platonists); and the name and power of the Divine Spirit is not kept quiet. Job taught the resurrection of bodies, and even before Christ was born, the Pharisees believed in it. Since all these things, I say, had been handed down so many centuries ago, what was that "new thing" for whose sake the Son of God descended to earth, who proclaims himself the **Renovator of all things**?

Indeed, I will state my opinion, but in such a way that everyone’s judgment remains free, if anyone has something that is closer to the truth. Since the Old Testament was a shadow and, as it were, a preliminary exercise for the **Evangelical Philosophy** <term>Philosophia Evangelica: Erasmus’s term for the teachings of Jesus, which he saw as a practical way of life rather than a set of complex dogmas.</term>, and since the doctrine of the Gospel is both the restoration and the perfection of nature as it was first created in its purity, it should not seem strange if it was granted to certain Pagan philosophers to perceive through a kind of natural force things that agree with the doctrine of Christ. For, as Paul testifies, they happened to gather from the visible structures of the world those things which are understood not by the eyes but by the mind, even unto the eternal power and divinity of God. It was most fitting that Christ should bring nothing of which some shadow or spark had not preceded in the books of the Old Testament, so that everyone’s faith might be more inclined toward a matter that was not entirely sudden or unexpected. First, then, everything Christ performed was promised by the oracles of the holy Prophets, foreshadowed by figures, and even expressed in fragments—like sparks flashing out here and there—which portended that light that was to break forth upon the world.

What, then, does that **Renovator of all things** have that is so exceptional? Many things, truly. First, that the absolute precepts or examples of virtue, which had been handed down piecemeal by different people, he alone both taught and expressed in their entirety. Nor did he only teach them, but he fixed them, instilled them, and impressed them upon the minds of all through various parables so that they could not slip away. And he expressed them so through his character and deeds that his whole life is nothing else than a certain absolute model of absolute charity, modesty, tolerance, clemency, and gentleness. This harmony, this concert of all virtues, you will find in none of the saints except in Christ Jesus alone. For he was truly that "shortened word" <note>An allusion to Romans 9:28 and Isaiah 10:22-23, suggesting God’s revelation was distilled into the person of Christ.</note> and "reduced to a summary" which the Lord finally made upon the earth, in which he would recapitulate all things in heaven and on earth. Thus, whatever was previously sought from so many books and so many holy men could now be taken in summary from the one Christ, in a way that is far more expressive and more perfect. From him, the seeds and elements of piety are most rightly taken; from him, progress and growth; from him, perfection—he who is the **Alpha and Omega** of all things. Although the virtue that shone in the saints is itself a gift from Christ, yet nothing in them is so exceptional that it does not seem cold and obscure if compared to the teaching and deeds of Christ. And I need not mention that while the lives of others shone with some remarkable virtues, they were also obscured in some part by at least human failings; but no matter which part of Christ you contemplate, you will find nothing that is not absolute and eternal. For what mortal was ever endowed with such innocence, such power, famous for so many miracles, generous with so many benefits toward all, yet so humbled himself and bore the weakness, ingratitude, and perversity of men with such perpetual gentleness—even unto the lashes, the spitting, the insults, and the cross? Who taught all things so perfectly, and performed absolutely what he taught? He wins also on this title: that Jewish justice was circumscribed by narrow boundaries and did not extend beyond one nation, and a small one at that. "You shall lend without interest, but to your brother"; "Do not remember malice, but toward your brother"; "There shall be no needy person, but among you." But Christ willed his Philosophy to be common to all nations of the whole world: "Give to the one who asks of you"; "Do good to all, even to your enemies"; "Pray for all, even those who persecute you." Furthermore, he not only taught and instilled the resurrection of bodies, but he performed it himself by coming back to life.

Therefore, it is no wonder if the whole world—previously divided into various sects of philosophers and religions—embraced the **Evangelical Philosophy** with unanimous consent. Let us also embrace the monuments of our teacher and prince, and let us strive to see that his Philosophy is spread as widely as possible. That will happen if we commend it to all through innocence of life and mutual charity. By this commendation, in the past and in not so many years, the Philosophy of the Gospel was diffused through every region of the world, even while the world rebelled in vain. Just as the name of God is glorified by the holy character of Christians and is, in a way, dishonored and defamed by our vices, so by our character other mortals are either lured to the love of the Gospel or alienated from it. The world has long been at war with Christ. However, wherever there are desires for worldly things, there is "the world." The truth of the Gospel offends those who are subject to these things. These people, having conspired with devoted minds, continually rise up against the heavenly word, saying: "Come, let us oppress him, for he is contrary to our works." But let us strive against them with brave and unconquered minds—not with brawls, not with threats, not with arms, not with injuries, but with simple wisdom, with benefits, and with gentleness and tolerance. By this path, the truth of the Gospel triumphs. Christ still lives and reigns, who knows how to turn the tumults of the wicked and the afflictions of the good to his own glory. To him be honor and power for all ages, Amen.

# G R A M M A T I C A L  E R R O R S
<note>Erasmus uses the term "Soloecismi" (Solecisms) to refer to errors in grammar or usage found in the Vulgate, the standard Latin Bible used in his time.</note>

->COMMITTED BY THE TRANSLATOR, MANIFEST AND INEXCUSABLE,<-
->A FEW SELECTED FROM AMONG MANY.<-

MATTHEW, chapter V. 41. *Whoever compels you to go a thousand paces, go with him another two:* <note>original: "Quicunque te angariaverit mille passus..."</note> instead of what should have been said, *one mile, and another two.*

Chapter VI. 26. *You are much more worth.* <note>original: "Magis pluris estis vos"</note> While the Roman tongue does not accept doublings of comparatives of this kind, which Augustine, in his books
<margin>On the Locutions of the Old Testament, teaches comes from the specific property of the Hebrew language.</margin>

Chapter VII. 5. *You will see to cast out* <note>original: "Videbis ejicere"</note>, instead of, *you will bring it about that you cast out*, referring to one who sees the person casting out.

Chapter VIII. 29. *What to us and to you?* <note>original: "Quid nobis & tibi"</note> instead of what it should be:

<column-break/>

*What have you to do with us?* Again, the translator abandoned the proper usage of the Greek language. For we do not say, "What to me and the flute and another two," but "What have I to do with long flutes?" <note>original Greek: τί μοὶ καὶ σοῖς αὐλοῖς;</note>

Chapter XI. 1. *When he had finished commanding* <note>original: "Cum consummasset praecipiens"</note>, the translator spoke in a Greek way, instead of what should be, *he had made an end of commanding.*

In the same chapter, verse 5. *The poor are evangelized* <note>original: "Pauperes evangelizantur"</note>, he spoke in a Greek way. For it is no less of a grammatical error to say "the poor are evangelized" than "the poor are announced," since something is being announced *to* them.

Chapter XV. 1. *Then came to him from Jerusalem Scribes*, instead of, *the Jerusalemite Scribes*: whereas in Greek it is, *the from Jerusalem scribes* <note>original Greek: οἱ ἀπὸ Ἱεροσολύμων γραμματεῖς.</note>.

--- Page 24 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the general introduction of the "New Testament" to Erasmus's specific philological critiques. Erasmus is listing "solecisms"—grammatical errors or awkward constructions—found in the Latin Vulgate (the standard Bible of his time). He argues that the translator (traditionally identified as St. Jerome) often followed the Greek syntax too literally or made errors in gender and case, which can lead to theological misunderstandings.</meta>

# SOLECISMS ADMITTED BY THE TRANSLATOR.

**Chapter 20:25.** The princes of the nations lord it over *them* <note>original: "eorum"</note>: first he said *them* (masculine), instead of *them* (feminine), having abandoned the Greek gender. Next, he says *lord it over them* <note>original: "dominantur eorum"</note>, instead of *lord it over them* <note>original: "dominantur eis"</note>, having carelessly left the Greek case usage.

**In the same chapter, verse 28.** *The Son of Man came not to be ministered unto*. He used a Greek phrasing, but it is bad Latin; it should have been, *He came not so that he might be served*. Although even this phrase *came to minister*, instead of *for the purpose of ministering*, is not standard Latin.

**Chapter 22:10.** *The wedding was filled with of those reclining*: the drowsy Translator left the Greek genitive case <note>Erasmus is criticizing the use of "of those reclining" (discumbentium) where Latin grammar would normally require a dative "for those reclining."</note> instead of *the wedding was filled with guests*.

**In the same chapter, verse 30.** *Neither shall they marry, nor be married*. Who has ever heard of the word *nubentur* <note>original: "nubentur" - Erasmus argues this passive form of "to marry" is non-standard Latin</note>?

**Chapter 24:6.** He said *opinions of wars*, instead of *rumors of wars*.

Indeed, in this conjunction, he misuses *because* <note>original: "quia"</note>, or *when*, instead of *that* <note>original: "quod"</note>; or, when it is added according to the property of the Greek language, it is superfluous in Latin. For example, in John, chapter 1:20: *He confessed, because I am not the Christ*. For even if we grant that *because* carries the same weight as *that*, what else is being said here except that the Baptist confessed *that* the Evangelist was not the Christ? Again in the same book, chapter 4:17: *You have said rightly, because I have no husband*. What else did he express than the Samaritan woman saying *that* Christ did not have a husband? Likewise in Mark, chapter 12:6: *Saying because I am*. Again in Luke 1:61: *Because there is no one in your kindred*, etc. These instances of "because" are clearly redundant.

**Luke chapter 1:72.** He said *to remember* <note>original: "memorare"</note>, instead of *to call to mind*.

**Chapter 4:23.** He translates *how great things we have heard*, which should be, *whatever things we have heard*. Similarly in John chapter 12:37: He said *so great signs*, instead of *so many*, or *numerous*.

**Luke 19:23.** Having spoken of *money* <note>original: "pecunia," which is feminine in Latin</note>, he added, *I might have exacted it* <note>original: "illud," which is neuter</note>, dreaming that he was speaking Greek: for the word for silver <note>original: "ἀργύριον" (argyrios)</note>, which he translates here as *money*, is of the neuter gender for the Greeks.

Likewise **chapter 23:29.** *And the wombs which have not borne*: he used a masculine relative pronoun <note>original: "qui"</note> for a feminine noun, thinking he was speaking Greek, because <gloss>womb</gloss> <note>original: "koilia"</note> is of the feminine gender in Greek.

**John chapter 1:14.** *Glory as if of the only-begotten of the Father*: he used *as if* <note>original: "quasi"</note> in a dangerous solecism, instead of *just as* <note>original: "tanquam"</note>. For *as if* implies a simulation or pretense, not the truth. But Christ was truly the only-begotten of the Father.

**Chapter 4:9.** *The Jews do not use with the Samaritans* <note>original: "non coutuntur"</note>. Even if we grant it is correct to say "they use the Samaritans" to mean "they have dealings with them," who ever said *couti* <note>A fabricated Latin word intended to mirror a Greek compound verb</note> to mean "to have mutual dealings with one another"?

**Chapter 6:21.** *He was at the land*, instead of *he arrived at the land*.

**Chapter 7:14.** He said *the feast mediating* <note>original: "festo mediante"</note>, imitating a Greek expression, but more boldly than successfully, when he could have used a paraphrase: *when half the feast had passed*.

**Chapter 14:12.** *And greater of these things he shall do*, instead of *greater than these*, he said, forgetting he was speaking Latin.

**Chapter 15:2.** *That it may bring more fruit* <note>original: "fructum plus"</note>, instead of *more of fruit* <note>original: "plus fructus"</note>, or *more abundant fruit*. For the Greek is *pleiona karpon*.

**In the same verse, 6.** Although *branches* <note>original: "palmites" - masculine</note> had preceded it, he added: *and they shall gather them* <note>original: "ea" - neuter</note>, preserving the Greek gender because <term>branch</term> <note>original: "klēma"</note> is neuter in Greek. For the number was changeably tolerated among the Greeks because he had previously spoken collectively of *every branch*. Meanwhile, I will overlook the fact that a little earlier he twice added *him* <note>original: "eum"</note> following the idiom of the Hebrew language: *Every branch not bearing fruit, he will take him: and every one that bears fruit, he will prune him*. Yet the same fault of speech exists in the Greek.

**Acts chapter 2:12.** *Saying to each other* <note>original: "ad invicem"</note>, instead of *saying among themselves*. What Latin speaker ever said "to each other" in this way? No more than one would say "to mutually." And yet this phrasing is very frequent for this Translator.

**Chapter 3:19.** He said *Be repented* <note>original: "poenitemini"</note> therefore, using an unheard-of verb form for the Greek *metanoēsate*, when in Latin he could have said *return to your senses*.

**Chapter 5:4.** Having previously mentioned a *field*, forgetting he was speaking Latin, he translated *sold* <note>original: "venundatum" - neuter</note>, because the Greek words for <term>possession</term> or <term>land</term> are neuter.

<column-break/>

**Chapter 8:7.** *Many of those who had unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, went out*. What could be said more absurdly? Since the sense is: *That the spirits went out with a great cry from those who were held by them*.

**Chapter 10:16.** He said *through thrice*, instead of *thrice*, or *on three occasions*.

**Chapter 16:13.** *Outside the gate* <note>original: "foras portam"</note>, instead of *out from the gate*.

**Chapter 17:15.** He said *how quickly* <note>original: "quam celeriter"</note>, instead of *as quickly as possible*, when in Greek it is *hōs tachista*.

**Chapter 20:24.** *Neither do I make my soul more precious than me*. The Translator rendered neither the Greek words nor the sense, since the Greek is *nor do I hold my life dear to myself*.

**Chapter 20:32.** Although *word* <note>original: "verbum" - neuter</note> preceded it, he adds, *who is powerful* <note>original: "qui potens est" - masculine</note>, instead of *which is powerful*, because in Greek <term>word</term> <note>original: "logos"</note> is of the masculine gender.

**Chapter 22:14.** *And when we could not urge him* <note>original: "suadere"</note>, he says, when he had previously narrated that they had urged him. Clearly, he is misusing *urge* for *persuade*, though there is a great difference between them.

**Chapter 26:2-3.** *Regarding all things of which I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa, I reckon myself blessed before you, since I am about to defend myself today, especially as you know all things which are customs and questions among the Jews*. First, ignoring that he said *of which I am accused* for *concerning which I am accused*, and *reckon* for *consider*; the fact that he said *blessed before you, who am to defend myself*, is a crude solecism; and since *all things* <note>original: "omnia" - neuter plural</note> had preceded, he immediately adds *customs and questions* <note>feminine nouns</note>, not noticing that the Greek gender he left in *all things* should have been changed. For who ever heard of *all* (neuter) *customs* (feminine)? Let us go on then, and argue that the Translator never fell asleep at his work.

In the **Epistle of Paul to the Romans, chapter 2:15.** *Their conscience bearing witness to them, and between themselves mutually of thoughts accusing or defending*, when he turned the Greek genitive absolute into a Latin ablative, *with conscience bearing witness*, what kind of laziness was it to leave the other genitive standing, to the irritation of all grammarians?

**Chapter 10:16.** *Who has believed our hearing?* Who, speaking Latin, ever used *hearing* to mean *the speech of the one talking*?

**Chapter 12:9.** *Hating evil*, using a participle <note>original: "odientes"</note> instead of the proper phrase *holding in hatred*.

In the **Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 8:15.** He said *He did not minorate* <note>original: "minoravit"</note> instead of *he did not have less*.

In the **Epistle to the Philippians, chapter 4:10.** *You have reflourished to feel for me*, instead of what it should be: *your affection for me has flourished again*.

In the **Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 3:3.** *By how much more honor the house has, who built it*, when the sense is, *by how much more honor he who built the house has than the house itself*. And meanwhile we deny that it matters how we speak, even though because of this solecism Thomas <note>Refers to Thomas Aquinas</note> and the more recent scholars who followed him have fallen most foully into error.

**Chapter 6:16.** He said *By the greater of himself*, instead of *greater than himself*, not considering that he speaks to Latins, not Greeks.

In the **Epistle of James, chapter 1:13.** When he says: *God is a non-tempter of evils* <note>original: "intentator"</note>, has he not spoken irreligiously of God? Since an *intentator* would be one who inflicts something of evil. But he means that God neither tempts anyone with evils, nor is tempted.

In the **Apocalypse, chapter 1:4.** There is a strange and notable solecism in the Greek speech: *from him who is, and who was, and who is to come* <note>Erasmus points out that the Greek original breaks the rules of case agreement after a preposition</note>. For how does "he who is" connect with the preceding "from"? Then what does "he who was" sound like to anyone? Again, how does "he who is coming" fit with the "from"? Let those who think the Apocalypse was written by John deny, if they wish, that the Apostles ever spoke bad Greek. For some—the patrons of the Apostles—contend exactly that.

**Luke 21:38.** *And all the people early-morninged to him* <note>original: "manicabat"</note>. He imitated the Greek word *orthrize* with a Latin voice, but shamelessly. For who can tolerate *manicare* instead of *to come early in the morning*?

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s critique of the Latin Vulgate translation. Having previously listed "solecisms" (grammatical errors), he now moves to "obscure passages" where famous medieval and ancient commentators—such as Thomas Aquinas, Nicholas of Lyra, and even Saint Augustine—misunderstood the text because they relied on a flawed Latin translation rather than the original Greek.</meta>

# OBSCURE PASSAGES,
## AND THOSE IN WHICH INTERPRETERS OF GREAT REPUTATION
### HAVE ERRED; A FEW SELECTIONS PLUCKED FROM COUNTLESS EXAMPLES,
### SO THAT THERE MAY BE SOMETHING AT HAND TO ANSWER THOSE
### WHO CLAIM THAT OUR ANNOTATIONS
### EXPLAINED SUPERFLUOUS MATTERS.

**Matthew chapter 1, verse 19.** "To lead away" <note>original: "traducere"</note> was wrongly understood by the Master of Sentences <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1100–1160), a medieval theologian whose book of "Sentences" was the standard textbook for centuries.</note>.

**Chapter 11, verse 12.** *The kingdom of heaven suffers violence*. Most interpret this as the force used to restrain one's emotions, whereas Christ actually intends it to mean that Gentiles and sinners break in by the violence of their faith, since the Jews who were invited refused to enter.

**Luke chapter 1, verse 1.** *Of the things which have been completed among us*. Who would have understood the Latin here without consulting the Greek? For the Evangelist means that the things he is about to narrate are certain and of proven reliability. The Translator thought there was no difference between <term>pepleromenon</term> <note>original: "πεπληρωμένων" — things that have been filled or completed</note> and <term>peplerophoremenon</term> <note>original: "πεπληροφορημένων" — things that have been fully assured or made certain</note>.

**In the same chapter, verse 51.** *He has scattered the proud in the imagination of his heart*. The common crowd of Interpreters thinks the meaning is that God scattered the proud by the thought of His own heart; however, the true sense is that *the proud were scattered by God by means of their own plans and thoughts*. On this point, there is no hesitation among the Greeks, since they read <term>kardias auton</term> <note>original: "καρδίας αὐτῶν" — meaning "of their heart," referring back to the proud people themselves</note>.

**In the same chapter, verse 73.** *The oath, which he swore to Abraham our father, that he would give to us*. A formal division in the text—by which church choirs split these verses apart because the sentence is quite long, I believe—has caused many to fail to notice the true meaning, as we have indicated in that place. And soon after, in **verse 77**, *into remission* <note>original: "in remissionem"</note>, when it should be *in remission* <note>original: "in remissione"</note>, standing for *through remission*. And shortly after, in **verse 78**, *The Dayspring* <note>original: "Oriens"</note> is a substantive noun, though the common crowd thinks it is a participle <note>Erasmus means "The Rising Sun" is a title for Christ, not just a description of something rising.</note>. There are also other things in this song <note>The "Benedictus," a song of praise in Luke's Gospel.</note> which is sung daily in churches, yet is understood by few.

**Chapter 2, verse 35.** *A sword shall pierce through your own soul*. On the phrase "your own," Hugh of St. Cher <note>A 13th-century Dominican cardinal and biblical commentator.</note> and Nicholas of Lyra <note>A famous Franciscan scholar (c. 1270–1349) known for his literal interpretations.</note> have erred. On the word "shall pierce through," Augustine erred, thinking "pierce through" was said instead of "pass by," as it is found elsewhere; however, in Greek it is <term>dieleusesthai</term> <note>original: "διελεύσεσθαι" — to go through the middle or to pierce through</note>.

**Chapter 19, verse 42.** *If you had known, even you*. An obscure passage, and thus far understood by few.

**Chapter 22, verse 36.** Regarding the buying of a sword: the interpretation of Nicholas of Lyra and of recent commentators is rejected as being utterly foreign to Christ's mind.

**John chapter 12, verse 35.** *Yet a little light is in you*. The common crowd interprets this as *there is a tiny bit of light in the Apostles*, whereas the true sense is that *Christ, the light, would remain among them for only a short time*.

**In Acts chapter 20, verse 24.** *Neither do I make my soul more precious than myself*. Who could understand the sense when the Translator rendered it so poorly? But we have spoken of this in the section on Solecisms.

**In the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 2, verse 7.** *To those seeking life*, etc. The Translator rendered this in such a way that the meaning cannot be grasped.

**Chapter 3, verse 2.** *The oracles were credited to them*. Nicholas of Lyra interprets this to mean that the Jews had faith in the oracles, whereas the sense is that *the oracles of God were committed, or entrusted, to them*.

**Chapter 5, verse 16.** *For the judgment indeed from one*. The common crowd takes this to mean "from the one man Adam," whereas the sense is "from one single sin."

**Chapter 11, verse 11.** *That they might emulate them*. Thomas Aquinas introduced a fourfold sense, yet did not touch upon the true one, which is this: *that God might provoke them to jealousy (or emulation)*.

**Chapter 12, verse 1.** *Reasonable service*. They commonly interpret this as a moderate weakening of the flesh, whereas the sense is that a victim should be sacrificed to God that is not a mindless beast, but one participating in reason—that is, the human being himself.

<column-break/>

**Chapter 14, verse 5.** *One man judges day from day, another judges every day*. Augustine interpreted this in a way that seems far removed from Paul’s meaning. Even Ambrose twists this passage somewhat. For Paul is dealing with the superstitious observation of days according to the example of the Jews, whereas for the early Christians, all days were equally sacred.

**In the same chapter, verse 2.** *He who is weak, let him eat vegetables*. They commonly interpret this as if he were commanding the superstitious to eat vegetables. On the contrary, Paul would prefer that no one be superstitious. But he is showing what the strong man does, relying on his faith, and what the weak man does, obeying his superstition.

**In the same chapter, verse 5.** *Let him abound in his own sense*. To "abound in one's own sense" is characteristic of a stubborn person. Paul’s meaning is that in those things which can be done or not done without sin, each person's own mind should be satisfied.

**In the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 2, verse 2.** *Comparing spiritual things with spiritual*. They commonly take this to mean that holy things are suitable for holy men, whereas Paul means that a type of speech should be used that is appropriate for spiritual subjects.

**Chapter 3, verse 12.** *Wood, hay, stubble*. They interpret these as faulty actions and levels of sin, whereas Paul means the insincere doctrine of certain apostles, which would be rejected upon exact judgment; the work of both those who learned and those who taught things that ought to be unlearned would perish.

**Chapter 10, verse 22.** *Do we emulate the Lord?* instead of *Do we provoke Him to anger?*

**In the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 1, verse 11.** *From the persons of many faces*. This passage is extremely obscure, and has been explained by us in various ways.

**John chapter 18, verse 24.** *To Caiaphas*. Here, because of a corrupted text, Augustine goes entirely astray.

**Chapter 4, verse 7.** *That the excellence may be of the power of God*: when the sense is, *that the excellence of the power displayed through us may belong to God, and not come from ourselves*.

**Chapter 5, verse 17.** *If any new creature in Christ*. The sense is: *If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature*.

**Chapter 8, verse 19.** *Destined will*. Thomas Aquinas interprets this as "predestined from eternity," wandering far from Paul’s meaning, since Paul said <term>prothymian</term> <note>original: "προθυμίαν" — readiness of mind or eagerness</note>.

**In the same place, verse 23.** *The glory of Christ*. The passage is obscure and cannot be explained here in few words.

**Chapter 10, verse 12.** *But they in themselves*. An obscure passage and little understood by the common crowd. It too cannot be noted in a few words.

**In the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 1, verse 16.** *I did not acquiesce to flesh and blood*. Thomas and the common crowd of recent commentators interpret this as: *I did not yield to carnal vices*, whereas Paul is denying that he compared his Gospel with Peter and the other Apostles—men whom he calls "flesh and blood."

**In the Epistle to the Ephesians, chapter 1, verse 22.** The common crowd reads, *Over all the Church*, when the sense is that *Christ is the supreme head of his Church, set over all things, as one to whom all power has been given*.

**In the same place, chapter 2, verse 2.** *The power of the air*. A passage thus far understood by few.

**In the Epistle to the Philippians, chapter 1, verse 18.** *While in every way, or by occasion*. Although this cannot be noted in few words.

**Chapter 2, verse 7.** *Taking the form of a servant*, etc. Explained differently than the common crowd explains it.

**In the same place, verse 13.** *And to perform*. They think this means "to finish," when it is <term>energein</term> <note>original: "ἐνεργεῖν" — to work, to act, or to be effective</note>.

<summary>Erasmus catalogs various New Testament passages where prominent medieval theologians and the Latin Vulgate translator erred due to a lack of Greek philological knowledge. He argues that his own annotations are necessary to correct these long-standing theological and linguistic misunderstandings.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s list of "obscure passages" where the Latin Vulgate translation misled famous theologians. He focuses on instances where the Greek text reveals a different meaning than the one traditionally taught by medieval scholars like Thomas Aquinas.</meta>

->INDEX OF OBSCURE PASSAGES.<-

In the same chapter [Philippians 1], verse 17. *Upon the sacrifice.* This passage is to be understood far differently than they commonly explain it.

In the Epistle to the Colossians, chapter 2, verse 2. *The riches of fullness.* Since in Greek it is <term>plerophorias</term> <note>original: "πληροφορίας" — meaning full assurance or total conviction</note>, the sense cannot be anything other than Paul wishing them a most certain faith and persuasion of the mystery.

In the same place, verse 8. *Lest anyone deceive you,* he said, instead of *plunder you* <note>Erasmus notes the Greek "sylagogon" implies carrying someone off as booty or prey</note>; which is certainly a fault of the Translator.

In the same place, verse 14. *The handwriting of the decree.* A passage commonly understood by few.

In the same place, verse 15. *He led them away,* an interpretation examined by Augustine. In this passage, Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century philosopher and theologian</note> has miserably tripped up.

In the same place, verse 18. *Let no one seduce you,* instead of what it should be, *let no one cheat you of your prize.*

In the same verse, *Walking in those things which he has not seen.* A passage not understood by just anyone, in which Augustine also seems to have tripped.

In the same place, verse 20. *Why do you still decree,* as the Translator wrongly rendered it, so the common crowd incorrectly understands it. For Paul means that they should no longer be held by human decrees.

Chapter 3, verse 15. *He triumphs,* he translated <term>bebaio-o</term> <note>original: "βεβαιόω" — to confirm or establish</note>. And the more recent interpreters, following the Translator, are completely off track.

In the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 2, verse 7. *You made him a little lower than the Angels.* This passage is explained differently than the common crowd accepts it.

In the same place, verse 10. *For it was fitting.* What was said about the Father, they commonly refer to the Son, wrongly reading *to be perfected* <note>original: "consummari"</note> instead of *to perfect* <note>original: "consummare"</note>.

In the same place, verse 18. *And having been tempted.* A passage newly and truly explained, and the reading restored.

Chapter 3, verse 3. *Greater honor of the house.* We have found both an obviously corrupted reading and a sense not understood until now.

Chapter 5, verse 8. *And indeed although he was.* A very obscure passage, but explained.

In the same place, verse 11. *Interpretable to speak.* Thomas <note>Aquinas</note> is anxiously tormented because of the fault of the Translator, who should have translated it *difficult to narrate* or *to interpret.*

Chapter 11, verse 34. *They turned the camps.* Some interpret this as *they overturned,* when the meaning is *turned to flight.*

In the same place, verse 37. *In sheepskins.* Thomas in this place remarkably

<column-break/>

has hallucinated.

Chapter 13, verse 2. *Some have pleased Angels as guests.* Just as we commonly read it in a corrupted form, so we misunderstand it; the sense is that some, unknowingly, received Angels as guests, thinking they were men.

In the First Epistle of Peter, chapter 2, verse 2. *As newborn babes, reasonable milk, etc.* From a corrupted reading follows a corrupted sense, since Peter does not call the boys *reasonable* <note>The Latin text used "rationales," which commentators applied to the children</note>, but calls the milk of the mind—not of the body—*reasonable* <note>The Greek "logikon" describes the nature of the spiritual milk, not the infants</note>.

Chapter 2, verse 23. *But he delivered himself to him who judged him unjustly.* Just as we commonly read it in a corrupted way, so we explain it wrongly, since Peter means that Christ did not take vengeance for himself, but delivered it to the Father, who judges justly.

Chapter 3, verse 6. *Fearing any disturbance,* when the sense is *not being terrified by any fear.*

In the same place, verse 7. *Bestowing honor.* Although Peter is speaking about abstinence from sexual intercourse, more recent authors explain it as providing for the wife's dignity in terms of care and livelihood. Likewise, what follows about not interrupting prayers is interpreted to mean that prayers are not heard unless the man and woman are in concord.

In the same place, verse 8. *In faith* we read, instead of *in the end* or *in summary*; and from this comes a strange confusion among interpreters.

In the same place, verse 18. *Put to death indeed in the flesh.* Because of a corrupted reading, the modern interpreters err by the width of the whole sky.

Chapter 4, verse 7. *Be therefore prudent,* whereas Peter commands there that one should be sober.

In the Second Epistle of Peter, chapter 1, verse 19. *And we have a more sure word.* A passage little understood before now.

In the same place, chapter 2, verse 8. *For in sight and hearing.* A passage narrated far differently than it was understood before now.

In the same place, verse 10. *They do not fear sects, etc.* A passage newly explained.

In the First Epistle of John, chapter 5, verse 16. *I do not say that one should pray for that, etc.* A very difficult passage newly explained.

John in his Gospel, chapter 5, verse 2. *The sheep-pool.* They think these words go together, when *Probatica* <note>original: "προβατική"</note> is the name of the place in which the pool was located.

Chapter 11, verse 9. *Twelve hours of the day.* Explained differently than the common crowd accepts.

Acts, chapter 24, verse 14. *To the Father and God,* instead of *the ancestral god.* And from this comes a strange commotion among interpreters.

# MANIFESTLY CORRUPTED PASSAGES,
## BUT FROM COUNTLESS EXAMPLES, AS THEY OCCURRED,
### A FEW SELECTED.

<image-desc>Decorative initial M showing a landscape with figures and buildings.</image-desc>MATTHEW chapter 3, verse 2. *It will draw near,* instead of *it has drawn near*; but rather *it is drawing near,* a sin almost perpetually committed by the scribes.

Chapter 4, verse 6. *He gave orders to his angels,* instead of *he will give orders*; the scribe compensating for the error.

Chapter 8, verse 26. *He commanded the winds,* instead of *he rebuked.* They tripped on the same stone in Luke chapter 4, verse 39: *He commanded the fever,* instead of *he rebuked.*

Chapter 12, verse 31. *But the blasphemy of the Spirit,* instead of *blasphemy of the spirit.* In this place, a flaw in the reading foully deceives modern interpreters.

Chapter 22, verse 30. *They will marry and be given in marriage,* instead of *they marry and are given in marriage.*

Chapter 23, verse 25. *You who clean, etc. you are full,* we read erroneously instead of *they are full.*

Luke chapter 8, verse 49. *To the ruler of the synagogue,* instead of *from the ruler of the synagogue.*

Acts chapter 1, verse 15. *Moreover, there were of men,* instead of *of names.*

<column-break/>

Chapter 14, verse 24. *Italy,* instead of *Attalia.*

Mark chapter 8, verse 38. *Whoever has confessed me.* *Confessed* <note>original: "confessus"</note> is corrupted from *ashamed* <note>original: "confusus"</note>.

Luke chapter 1, verse 77. *Into remission,* instead of *in remission*; that is, instead of *the remission.*

Chapter 8, verse 19. *And they could not hear.* *Hear* <note>original: "audire"</note> we read in a corrupted form for *approach* <note>original: "adire"</note>.

In the same place, verse 23. *They were compelled,* instead of *they were filled up.*

Chapter 9, verse 4. *And do not depart from there,* instead of *and depart from there.*

Chapter 10, verse 1. *For seventy* we read *seventy-two.*

In the same verse, verse 30. *Moreover Jesus, looking up,* instead of *replying* <term>hypolabon</term> <note>original: ὑπολαβὼν</note>.

Chapter 12, verse 52. *And two shall be divided against three.* By a faulty distinction, we have corrupted the meaning.

Chapter 14, verse 12. *Neither neighbors nor the rich;* it should read *neither rich neighbors.* For there was no danger from poor neighbors that they might invite you back to a banquet.

<meta>This page continues the index of scriptural passages that Erasmus considers corrupted in the standard Latin Vulgate Bible. He is systematically listing errors where the Latin text differs from the original Greek or where scribal mistakes have crept into the Latin tradition over centuries.</meta>

### INDEX OF MANIFESTLY CORRUPTED PASSAGES.

In Greek it is *phagesi* <note>original: "φαγεσί" — likely referring to Luke 15:30 regarding the "devouring" of property</note>. This error has become established even in the oldest copies.
In the same place [Luke 15], verse 14. *He had finished* <note>original: "consummaset"</note> was written instead of *he had consumed* <note>original: "consumfisset"</note>.
In the same place, verse 30. *Devoured his substance* instead of *your substance*.
Chapter 16:22. *And he was buried in hell.* A faulty punctuation has corrupted the sense. For after the words *he was buried*, there is a colon among the Greeks. <note>This implies the rich man was buried, and then a new clause begins: "In hell, lifting up his eyes..."</note>
Chapter 23:40. *Who are in the same condemnation.* *Who* <note>original: "qui"</note> is corrupted for *because* <note>original: "quia"</note> or *that*.
John chapter 1:28. *These things were done in Bethany.* *Bethany* was written corruptly instead of *Bethabara*.
In the same place, verse 29. *Who takes away the sins of the world*, whereas it should be *the sin of the world*.
Chapter 5:2. *Bethsaida* instead of *Bethesda*.
Chapter 7:2. *He did not wish* <note>original: "non volebat"</note> instead of *he was not able* <note>original: "non valebat"</note>, that is, *he could not*.
Chapter 11:4. *That the Son of God might be glorified through him*, whereas it should read *through it*, namely, the infirmity.
Chapter 18:28. *To Caiaphas* instead of *from Caiaphas*. In this passage, Augustine slipped up.
Chapter 21:22. *So I wish him to remain* <note>original: "sic"</note> instead of *If I wish him to remain* <note>original: "si"</note>.
Acts chapter 15:16. *Broken* <note>original: "dirupta"</note> was written instead of *destroyed* <note>original: "diruta"</note>.
In the same place, shortly after: *Poured out* <note>original: "suffusa"</note> instead of *undermined* <note>original: "suffossa"</note>.
Chapter 16:1. *Widow* <note>original: "vidua"</note> was written instead of *Judas*.
Chapter 19:11. *And no small miracles* <note>original: "virtutesque non modicas"</note>. The scribe mixed together a double reading.
Chapter 24:14. *To my Father and God* instead of *to my ancestral God*.
Chapter 27:8. *The city of Thalassa* instead of *the city of Lassa*.
In the same verse 42. In the place *bithalassum* <note>where two seas meet</note> instead of *dithalassum*, that is, *between two seas*.
Chapter 28:11. *The sign of the Camps* <note>original: "Castrorum"</note> instead of *the sign of the Castors* <note>original: "Castorum"</note>, that is, of Castor and Pollux.
Epistle to the Romans, chapter 3:4. *Is* <note>original: "est"</note> instead of *let it be* <note>original: "esto"</note>.
Chapter 8:7. *The wisdom of the flesh is an enemy* instead of *is enmity*.
Chapter 9:10. *From one intercourse* instead of *having intercourse from one* <note>referring to Rebecca conceiving by Isaac</note>. Here, the corrupted sense follows the corrupted reading.
Chapter 10:5. *For Moses wrote.* A corrupted passage which cannot be explained in a few words.
Chapter 12:19. *Vengeance to me* <note>original: "mihi vindictam"</note> instead of *Vengeance is mine* <note>original: "mihi vindicta"</note>.
Chapter 13:12. *The night has passed* <note>original: "præcessit"</note> instead of *has advanced* <note>original: "processit"</note>, that is, *has moved forward*.
Chapter 14:22. *The faith which you have, you have in yourself* instead of *You have faith; have it in yourself*.
Chapter 16:6. *Asia* was written instead of *Achaia*.
In the same place, verse 14. *Asineretum* instead of *Asyncritum*.
First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 1:10. *In the same knowledge* <note>original: "scientia"</note> instead of *in the same judgment* <note>original: "sententia"</note>.
Chapter 2:8. *Never* <note>original: "nunquam"</note> instead of *by no means* <note>original: "nequaquam"</note>.
Chapter 8:10. *Idolotica* instead of *Idolothyta* <note>things sacrificed to idols</note>.
Chapter 11:24. *Which shall be delivered for you* instead of *which is broken for you*.
Chapter 12:3. *Says a curse to Jesus* instead of *calls Jesus a curse* <note>referring to the Greek "anathema Iesoun"</note>.
In the same verse 26. *He boasts* instead of *he is glorified* <note>original: "δοξάζεται" — doxazetai</note>.
Chapter 14:2. *The Spirit speaks* instead of *he speaks by the spirit*.

<column-break/>

In the same verse 16. *Who fills the place of the unlearned* <note>original: "quis", used as a question</note> instead of *he who fills* <note>original: "qui"</note>, etc. One letter added has corrupted both the punctuation and the sense.
In the same verse 23. *What are you insane* <note>original: "quid"</note> instead of *that you are insane* <note>original: "quod"</note>.
Chapter 15:26. *Lastly the enemy* <note>original: "novissime", an adverb</note> instead of *the last enemy* <note>original: "novissima", an adjective</note>.
In the same place, verse 31. *Because of your glory* instead of *by our glory*, as it is an oath. And here the faulty reading subverts the entire meaning.
Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 1:13. *You have read and known* instead of *you read and know*.
Chapter 5:13. *We exceed* <note>original: "excedimus"</note> instead of *we have fallen away* <note>original: "excidimus"</note>, since in Greek it is *exestemen* <note>original: "ἐξέστημεν" — to be out of one's mind or in ecstasy</note>.
Chapter 8:8. *Talent* <note>original: "ingenium"</note> instead of *nobility* <note>original: "ingenuum"</note>, that is, *sincerity*.
Chapter 12:16. *But let it be, I burdened you* instead of *let it be, I did not burden you*.
To the Galatians, chapter 2:11. *Because he was blameworthy* instead of *he was rebuked*.
Chapter 4:18. *But you zealously seek the good* <note>imperative</note> instead of *it is good to be zealously sought in a good thing* <note>infinitive</note>.
To the Ephesians, chapter 2:15. *Voiding by decrees* instead of *in decrees*. Here the omitted preposition subverts the whole meaning.
Chapter 6:13. *And to stand as perfect ones in all things* instead of *to stand perfectly*.
First Epistle to the Thessalonians, chapter 2:4. *That it might be believed by us*: the *by* <note>original: "a"</note> is redundant and vitiates the sense.
In the second [Thessalonians], chapter 1:6. *To repay retribution* instead of *to repay affliction*.
In the First Epistle to Timothy, chapter 4:6. *Having attained* <note>original: "assecutus"</note> instead of *having followed* <note>original: "assectatus"</note>.
In the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians, chapter 3:14. *Through this epistle* <note>feminine: "hanc"</note>: *this* <note>masculine: "hunc", referring to the man</note> should be read, not *this* <note>epistle</note>.
In the First Epistle to Timothy, chapter 2:15. *If he shall remain* instead of *if they shall remain*. Where the corrupted reading also destroys the whole sense.
Second Timothy, chapter 4:21. *And his brothers* instead of *and all the brothers*.
To the Hebrews, chapter 2:10. *For it was fitting to be perfected* <note>passive</note> is written erroneously instead of *to perfect* <note>active</note>.
Chapter 13:2. *They pleased angels received in hospitality*: of which we have also made mention before.
Epistle of James, chapter 3:12. *Of others* instead of *otherwise*.
Chapter 5:6. *You have brought* <note>original: "adduxistis"</note> instead of *you have condemned* <note>original: "addixistis"</note>.
First Epistle of Peter, chapter 2:5. *Spiritual houses* <note>plural</note> instead of *a spiritual house* <note>singular</note>.
Chapter 3:8. *In the end* <note>original: "in fine"</note> instead of *finally* or *in summary*.
In the same verse 18. *Put to death in the flesh* <note>plural</note> instead of *put to death in the flesh* <note>singular</note>.
Chapter 5:13. *Collected in Babylon* instead of *chosen together in Babylon*.
Epistle of Jude, verse 9. *May God command you* instead of *may God rebuke you*.
Matthew 1:18. *Mary the mother of Jesus* instead of *Mary his mother*.
Again, verse 23. *And his name shall be called* instead of *they shall call his name*.
Chapter 5:24. *To be reconciled to your brother* <note>passive</note> instead of *reconcile yourself* <note>active</note>.
Chapter 26:75. *What he had said* <note>original: "quod"</note> instead of *who had said* <note>original: "qui"</note>.
Mark 11:32. *We fear the people* instead of *they feared the people*.
Luke 1:9. *It went out by lot* <note>original: "sorte"</note> instead of *chance went out* <note>original: "fors"</note>.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of textual discrepancies in the New Testament. The author, likely Erasmus of Rotterdam, is identifying "corruptions"—places where the Latin Vulgate (the standard Bible of the time) either lacks words found in the original Greek or includes words that were added by later scribes. He supports these claims by citing Greek manuscripts and the writings of early Church Fathers like Jerome and Ambrose.</meta>

# TO APPEASE THOSE WHO THINK THAT IN THE SACRED BOOKS NOTHING EITHER REMAINS OVER OR IS MISSING, WE HAVE SELECTED CERTAIN PASSAGES WHICH ARE MORE CLEARLY CORRUPTED IN THIS MANNER THAN CAN BE DENIED.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' depicting a landscape with classical architecture and a figure.</image-desc>

MATTHEW chapter 2:18. *Wailing and loud lamentation* <note>original: "Ploratus & ululatus"</note>, whereas the Greek codices have *lamentation, wailing, and weeping* <note>original: "lamentatio, ploratus, ac fletus"</note>. And Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who produced the Latin Vulgate.</note> recites it this way, both according to the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> and according to the "Hebrew Verity" <note>A term used by Jerome for the original Hebrew text.</note>.
Chapter 3:10. *For now the axe*: it should read, according to the Greeks: *For now also the axe* <note>original: "Jam enim & securis"</note>.
Chapter 12:18. Jerome indicates that something was omitted in the prophecy of Isaiah.
Chapter 16:13. *Who do men say the son of man is?* <note>original: "Quem dicunt homines esse filium hominis?"</note> whereas in both Greek and ancient codices it is held as *who do they say I am* <note>original: "quem me dicunt esse"</note>, etc.
Chapter 27:43. *Let him deliver him if he wants*: it should read, *if he wants him* <note>original: "si vult eum"</note>.
Mark chapter 1:27. *Because in power he commands the spirits*: it should read, *And he commands the spirits* <note>original: "Et spiritibus imperat"</note>.
Luke chapter 4:21. *The scripture is fulfilled*: it should read, *this scripture* <note>original: "scriptura hæc"</note>.
Chapter 7:35. *By her children*: it should read, *By all her children* <note>original: "Ab omnibus filiis suis"</note>: according to the Greeks and Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose, the 4th-century Bishop of Milan.</note>, who also interprets it this way.
John 1:16. *And grace for grace*: *And* <note>original: "Et"</note> is redundant.
Chapter 3:31. *He who is of the earth, speaks of the earth*: it should read—

<column-break/>

—read: *He who is of the earth, is of the earth, and speaks of the earth* <note>original: "Qui de terra est, de terra est, & de terra loquitur"</note>.
Chapter 6:42. *Is this not the son of Joseph?* whereas according to the Greeks and Augustine <note>St. Augustine, the influential 5th-century North African bishop.</note> it should read: *Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph?*
Epistle to the Romans chapter 12:6. *Having gifts*: it should read: *Having then gifts* <note>original: "Habentes autem donationes"</note>. The omitted conjunction subverts the sense.
1 Epistle to the Corinthians chapter 7:35. *That which is honorable, and may provide the ability to pray to the Lord without impediment*. <note>Erasmus suggests the Latin phrasing here is clumsy or missing the precise nuance of the Greek.</note>
Chapter 9:10. *And he who threshes*. Certain things are missing in our [Latin] version.
Epistle to the Galatians chapter 3:17. *The testament confirmed by God, etc.* According to the Greeks and Ambrose, *in Christ* <note>original: "in Christum"</note> is missing.
1 Epistle to the Thessalonians chapter 3:2. *Minister of God*. According to the Greeks and Ambrose, *and our fellow-worker* <note>original: "& cooperarium nostrum"</note> is missing.
Epistle to Philemon verse 6. *In Christ Jesus, etc.* Before these words, *which is in us* is missing: according to the Greek codices, Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom, the "Golden-Mouthed" preacher and Archbishop of Constantinople.</note>, Ambrose, and Jerome.
1 Epistle of Peter chapter 4. Are certain things missing in our version compared to the Greeks?

## WHAT THINGS HAVE BEEN ADDED IN OUR COPIES.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting a landscape with a tree and a seated figure.</image-desc>

EPISTLE to the Ephesians, chapter 2:5. *And he quickened together*. *He quickened together* <note>original: "Convivificavit"</note> is neither in the Greek, nor in Jerome, nor Ambrose, nor in the most ancient codices.
In the same, chapter 3:14. *For this reason I bow my knees to the Father*. Jerome testifies that these words, *of our Lord Jesus Christ*, have been added.
1 Epistle of John chapter 2:16. *Which is not from the Father*. *Which* <note>original: "Quæ"</note> is redundant.
1 Epistle to Timothy chapter 2:6. *Whose testimony, etc.* *Whose* <note>original: "Cujus"</note> and *is confirmed* <note>original: "confirmatum est"</note> are not among the Greeks.
2 Epistle to Timothy chapter 2:22. *Faith, hope. Hope* <note>original: "Spem"</note> is neither in the Greek, nor in Ambrose, nor in ancient copies.
Chapter 3:8. *Who resist the truth*: *The truth* <note>original: "Veritati"</note> is redundant, according to the Greeks and Ambrose.
In the same place verse 3. *Blind* <note>original: "Cæci"</note> is redundant; it is not in the Greek, nor in the old Latin, nor in Chrysostom, nor in Ambrose.
Epistle to the Colossians, chapter 1:9. *All the fullness of divinity*. *Divinity* <note>original: "divinitatis"</note> is redundant: it is not added among the Greeks, nor in Ambrose. <note>In modern Bibles, this phrase is usually found in Colossians 2:9.</note>
Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 4:14. *The confession of our hope*. *Of our hope* <note>original: "spei nostræ"</note> is not among the Greeks, nor added in Chrysostom, nor in the most ancient copies.
Chapter 5:8. *Since he was the Son of God*: *Of God* <note>original: "Dei"</note> is redundant according to the Greek codices. Likewise according to Chrysostom and the interpreters of the Vulgate.
Epistle to the Romans chapter 8:38. *Neither things to come, nor strength, etc. Strength* <note>original: "fortitudo"</note> is not among the Greeks.

<column-break/>

Chapter 11:5. *They are made safe, etc.* Two words are redundant, *of God* and *safe*.
1 Epistle to the Corinthians chapter 6:20. *For you are bought with a great price. Great* <note>original: "Magno"</note> is redundant according to the Greeks, Chrysostom, and Ambrose.
Luke chapter 11:34. *The lamp of your body. Your* <note>original: "Tui"</note> has been added.
Chapter 13:21. *Three measures* <note>original: "Sata tria"</note> were added in Luke from Matthew.
Matthew chapter 5:44. *Love your enemies*: there is more in the Greek than in our [Latin] version.
Epistle to the Romans, chapter 11:36. *Honor and glory. Honor* is redundant.
Epistle to the Ephesians, chapter 2:22. *In the Holy Spirit. Holy* is redundant according to the Greek codices, Jerome, and Ambrose.
Matthew chapter 6:13. *For yours is the kingdom*. This "crown" <note>The doxology at the end of the Lord's Prayer.</note> in Matthew was added by the Greeks only.
Epistle to the Romans, chapter 12:17. *Providing good things*. Among the Greeks it is only *before all men*, not only *before God*—this was added; nor do Origen <note>A 3rd-century scholar and theologian.</note> or Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine commentator.</note> add these.
1 Epistle to the Corinthians chapter 7:14. *By a faithful woman*: several words have been added in our version.
Matthew chapter 6:22. *The lamp of your body. Your* is redundant.
1 Epistle to the Corinthians chapter 4:16. This particle, *as I also of Christ* <note>original: "sicut & ego Christi"</note>, is neither ascribed among the Greeks, nor in the Pauline codex, nor in Ambrose.
Epistle to the Philippians chapter 2:20. *So like-minded. So* <note>original: "Tam"</note> is redundant in our version.
Matthew chapter 6:25. *Of your soul. About drink* <note>original: "De potu"</note> is not added in Chrysostom, nor in Hilary <note>St. Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century bishop and theologian.</note>, nor in—

<meta>This page continues the systematic catalog of textual discrepancies in the New Testament. Having previously discussed omissions, the author now turns to "additions"—words or phrases found in the Latin Vulgate that do not appear in the original Greek manuscripts or the earliest Latin versions. He then begins a new section addressing "errors of the translator," where he critisizes the Latin translator's choice of vocabulary based on the underlying Greek verbs.</meta>

<sig>Vol. VI. ** WHERE</sig>

# WHAT HAS BEEN ADDED IN OUR COPIES.

among the Greeks, with few exceptions.
*1 Corinthians chapter 3:5. For you are still.* <note>original: "Adhuc enim estis"</note> The word "for" <note>original: "enim"</note> is redundant and hinders the sense.
*Matthew 9:25. And he said, girl, arise.* <note>original: "Et dixit, puella surge"</note> These four words are neither held among the Greeks, nor added by Jerome, nor do they exist in the ancient copies.
*2 Corinthians chapter 2:3. Sorrow upon sorrow.* <note>original: "Tristitiam super tristitiam"</note> "Upon sorrow" <note>original: "super tristitiam"</note> was added in our version from some other place, since neither Ambrose adds it, nor the Vulgate Translator.
*In the same place verse 5. Me* <note>original: "Me"</note> is redundant in our version.
*Matthew chapter 10:13. Saying, peace to this house.* <note>original: "Dicentes, pax huic domui"</note> These words are added in our version, though they are neither among the Greeks, nor in Jerome the translator, nor in Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine biblical exegete frequently cited by Erasmus.</note>.
*2 Corinthians chapter 2:16. And for these things who is so qualified.* <note>original: "Et ad hæc quis tam idoneus"</note> The word "so" <note>original: "tam"</note> is most clearly redundant, as even Origen does not add it.
*Matthew chapter 14:20. The disciples gave to the crowds.* <note>original: "Discipuli dederunt turbis"</note> "They gave" <note>original: "dederunt"</note> was added.
*Galatians chapter 3:1. Not to believe the truth.* <note>original: "Non credere veritati"</note> Jerome thinks this little part is an addition, and it was not added in the oldest Latin copies.
*In the same place verse 1. And crucified among you.* <note>original: "Et in vobis crucifixus"</note> "And" <note>original: "Et"</note> is added, and it hinders the sense.
*Matthew chapter 15:8. He honors me with his lips.* <note>original: "Labiis me honorat"</note> Here something is redundant among the Greeks, or certainly is missing in our version.
*In the same place verse 9. Doctrines and precepts.* <note>original: "Doctrinas & præcepta"</note> "And" <note>original: "Et"</note> is redundant, since it is spoken appositively <note>Meaning the words describe the same thing and don't need a conjunction.</note>.
*Chapter 16:20. Because he himself was Jesus Christ.* <note>original: "Quia ipse esset Jesus Christus"</note> "Jesus" is redundant.
*2 Corinthians chapter 6:13. But having the same recompense.* <note>original: "Eandem autem retributionem habentes"</note> "Having" <note>original: "habentes"</note> is extra in our version.
*Ephesians chapter 5:18. Be filled with the Holy Spirit.* <note>original: "Implemini Spiritu sancto"</note> "Holy" <note>original: "sancto"</note> is extra.
*In the same place verse 26. In the word of life.* <note>original: "In verbo vitæ"</note> "Of life" <note>original: "vitæ"</note> is extra.
*Matthew 21:37. They will perhaps reverence my son.* <note>original: "Verebuntur forte filium meum"</note> "Perhaps" <note>original: "forte"</note> was added by the Translator, not without inconvenience to the meaning.
*2 Corinthians chapter 11:3. They should fall away* <note>original: "Excidant"</note> was added in our version.
*Matthew 27:35. That it might be fulfilled which.* <note>original: "Ut impleretur quod"</note> The entire testimony of the Prophet was added.
*Galatians chapter 5:7. Not to believe the truth.* <note>original: "Non credere veritati"</note>
*In the same place verse 8. You should consent to no one.* <note>original: "Nemini consenseritis"</note> Jerome passes over this little part as an addition.
*In the same place, This persuasion of yours.* <note>original: "Persuasio hæc vestra"</note> "This of yours" <note>original: "hæc vestra"</note> is extra. It is only "persuasion."

<column-break/>

*In the same place verse 13. In the opportunity of the flesh given.* <note>original: "In occasione dati carni"</note> "Given" <note>original: "dati"</note> was added.
*Mark chapter 5. Also* <note>original: "Etiam"</note> the Evangelist added something of his own.
*John chapter 6:13. Twelve baskets, and with two fish.* <note>original: "Duodecim cophinos, & duobus piscibus"</note> These three words were added, which are not found in the old Latin copies.
*Mark chapter 8:29. You are the Christ.* <note>original: "Tu es Christus"</note> "The Son of the living God" <note>original: "Filius Dei vivi"</note> appears to have been added from elsewhere.
*Luke chapter 4:19. And the day of recompense.* <note>original: "Et diem retributionis"</note> These words are neither among the Greeks, nor added by Jerome.
*Ephesians chapter 1:7. Unto the remission of sins.* <note>original: "In remissionem peccatorum"</note> "Unto" <note>original: "In"</note> is redundant, and is not in Ambrose or Jerome.
*Luke chapter 11:34. The lamp of your body.* <note>original: "Lucerna corporis tui"</note> "Your" <note>original: "tui"</note> was added.
*Acts chapter 1:4. Which you heard, he says.* <note>original: "Quam audistis, inquit"</note> "He says" <note>original: "inquit"</note> was added by the Translator.
*Luke chapter 11:8. If he shall continue knocking.* <note>original: "Si perseveraverit pulsans"</note> Added from another Evangelist.
*Chapter 17:7. Or pasturing oxen.* <note>original: "Aut pascentem boves"</note> In Greek it is not "oxen."
*John chapter 6:41. Because he had said.* <note>original: "Quia dixisset"</note> Here "living" <note>original: "vivus"</note> was added.
*Chapter 7:29. I know him, etc.* <note>original: "Ego scio eum, &c."</note> Here some words were added from another place.
*In the same place verse 39. For the spirit was not yet given.* <note>original: "Nondum erat spiritus datus"</note> "Given" <note>original: "datus"</note> is redundant.
*Chapter 8:59. And he went out of the temple.* <note>original: "Et exivit de templo"</note> In the Greek codices certain things are redundant.
*Chapter 12:19. Behold the whole world goes after him.* <note>original: "Ecce totus mundus abit post eum"</note> "Whole" <note>original: "totus"</note> is undoubtedly redundant in our version.
*Romans chapter 1:3. Who was made for him.* <note>original: "Qui factus est ei"</note> "For him" <note>original: "ei"</note> was added by the Translator.
*Same verse 18. The truth of God.* <note>original: "Veritatem Dei"</note> "Of God" <note>original: "Dei"</note> was added.
*Same verse 32. Who, since the justice of God.* <note>original: "Qui cum justitiam Dei"</note> In this place these words were added: "they did not understand." <note>original: "non intellexerunt"</note>
*Chapter 5:2. In the hope of the children of God.* <note>original: "In spe filiorum Dei"</note> "Of the children" <note>original: "filiorum"</note> is redundant in our version, and "of glory" <note>original: "gloriæ"</note> is missing.
*Chapter 6:3. Do you not know.* <note>original: "An ignoratis"</note> "Brothers" <note>original: "fratres"</note> was added.
*Chapter 8:15. Of the spirit of adoption.* <note>original: "Spirituum adoptionis"</note> Here "of God" <note>original: "Dei"</note> is redundant.
*Chapter 9:25. And not having obtained mercy, etc.* <note>original: "Et non misericordiam consecutam, &c."</note> Jerome admits something is extra.
*Chapter 10:21. And speaking against me.* <note>original: "Et contradicentem mihi"</note> "To me" <note>original: "mihi"</note> was added.

# ERRORS COMMITTED
->BY THE TRANSLATOR.<-

From these things which we have noted so far, some were committed by the carelessness of scribes, some by the zeal of the half-learned, and very many by the either ignorance or negligence of the Translator, whoever he was. However, what follows cannot be attributed to anyone but the Translator.
*Luke chapter 3:13. Do nothing more than what is appointed for you.* <note>original: "Nihil amplius... faciatis"</note> Since in Greek it is <term>exact</term> <note>original: "πράσσετε"</note>, he did not notice that it should have been translated as "exact," especially since elsewhere he translated <term>exactors</term> <note>original: "πράκτορας"</note> as "collectors," and <term>I exacted</term> <note>original: "ἔπραξα"</note> as "I had exacted."
*Luke 16:26. In all these things* <note>original: "In his omnibus"</note>, which I think should have been translated as "above all these things."
*Acts chapter 18:10. And no one shall be set upon you* <note>original: "Et nemo apponetur tibi"</note>, for "shall invade" or "lay a hand on you." Since it is <term>he will set upon you</term> <note>original: "ἐπιθήσεται σοί"</note>.

<column-break/>

*Chapter 24:14. Did he not clearly doze off when he interprets a Latin word through a Greek one, but signifying the same thing? According to the sect which they call a heresy.* <note>original: "Secundum sectam quam dicunt hæresim"</note>
*1 Timothy chapter 4:6. <term>You have followed</term>* <note>original: "Παρηκολύθηκας"</note>, he translates as "attained" instead of "pursued." He did the same in the preface to the Gospel of Luke.
*1 Timothy chapter 1:2. <term>Legitimate</term>* <note>original: "Γνησίῳ"</note>, he translates as "beloved" instead of "true-born."
*1 Corinthians chapter 16:8. <term>Until the fiftieth</term>* <note>original: "Ἕως τῆς πεντηκοστῆς"</note>, meaning until the fiftieth day; he translates it as "until Pentecost."
*In the same place verse 12. But concerning brother Apollos*, the Translator added of his own: *I make known to you* <note>original: "notum vobis facio"</note>, so that the speech might be clearer.

# WHERE THE TRANSLATOR DARED
## TO CHANGE SOMETHING CONCERNING THE WORDS
## OF THE APOSTLES OR THE 
## EVANGELISTS.

MATTHEW chapter 16:22. Although in Greek it is <term>ἵλεώς σοι κύριε</term> <note>original: "hileōs soi kyrie"</note>, that is, *may [God] be merciful to you, Lord*, the Translator did not hesitate to render it, *far be it from you, Lord* <note>original: "absit a te domine"</note>. Just like that phrase, <term>μὴ γένοιτο</term> <note>original: "mē genoito"</note>, that is, *may it not happen*, he constantly renders as *far be it* <note>original: "absit"</note>, expressing the sense while departing from the literal words.
Luke chapter 1:48. Instead of <term>μακαριοῦσι</term> <note>original: "makariousi"</note>, that is, *they will call blessed*, he did not hesitate to render it *they shall say I am blessed* <note>original: "beatam dicent"</note>, explaining the matter through a periphrasis <note>A roundabout way of speaking or a paraphrase.</note>.
Acts chapter 1:4. *Which you have heard, he said*: the Translator added the word *he said* <note>original: "inquit"</note> on his own authority.

<column-break/>

To the Romans chapter 8:21. *That it [the creature] also shall be delivered*: he added *it* <note>original: "eam"</note> for the sake of clarifying the subject.
Chapter 10:7. <term>Καταγαγεῖν</term> <note>original: "Katagagein"</note>, *to lead down*, which the Translator rendered as *to bring back* <note>original: "revocare"</note>.
In the same place verse 8. He added *the scripture* <note>original: "scriptura"</note> on his own authority so that the speech would be more lucid.
To the 1st Corinthians chapter 10:4. *The rock following them*: the Translator added *them* <note>original: "eos"</note> on his own.
Chapter 11:24. <term>Τὸ κλώμενον</term> <note>original: "To klōmenon"</note>, *which is broken*, he rendered as *shall be delivered* <note>original: "tradetur"</note>; I believe he did this because the other word would have been too harsh for the ears, since it is written of Christ: *You shall not break a bone of him*.

# BY ULRICH ZASIUS
## ON THE NEW TESTAMENT
# TRANSLATED BY ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
### A SIX-LINE POEM.

**EXCELLENT** eloquence has earned distinguished praise,
Now the Sacred Page shines with elegant refinement,
The name of noble Erasmus is raised to the heavens,
He who has rendered Latin words well in place of the Greek,
Therefore, you who read the flowers of this fertile field,
Pay the thanks that are due to the Author.

<column-break/>

If the Divine Page could previously be called silver,
Now indeed it can be called gold:
The meaning is clearer, and the Latin speech is more so
Than it was before; your labor, Erasmus, shines bright.
Ah, let envy perish, and let it not bark against holy daring,
And let pure love possess our hearts.
