<meta>This page serves as the formal opening of Erasmus’s "Apologia" (Defense), following the technical list of translation corrections on the previous page. Here, he pivots from specific textual critiques to a broad defense of his scholarly mission, justifying the necessity of returning to original Greek and Hebrew sources to correct the Latin Vulgate.</meta>

# THE DEFENSE OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'N' containing a scene with several figures in a room with a tiled floor and arched window; a central figure appears to be seated at a desk or engaged in discussion with others standing nearby.</image-desc>NOW, to address in a few words this Defense to those who might protest: the Apostle Paul, as Luke records, declares himself fortunate that he was to plead his cause before Agrippa, because Agrippa, through his long-standing familiarity with the Jews, was exceptionally well-acquainted with and knowledgeable about all the matters under debate. I only wish I could congratulate myself on the same grounds, for my experience is entirely different from Paul's. Indeed, I would have no need for a Defense at all, were it not for those people who do not understand this entire business over which the controversy arises; they slander me for no other reason than that they do not understand. For among those who have tasted Latin, Greek, and Hebrew literature even modestly—those who are seriously engaged in tracking down the mysteries of Holy Scripture, and who have successfully and diligently immersed themselves in those ancient theologians <note>Refers to the Church Fathers, such as Augustine or Origen.</note> who are no less true than they are ancient—among such people, I have no doubt that I shall find great favor, even if I have not fully achieved everything I attempted.

Consequently, it is a strange thing: those for whom this work of ours is not strictly necessary, and who alone would be qualified to condemn certain parts because their skill in the humanities <note>original: "bonarum literarum"</note> allows them to judge, are the very ones who not only approve of our industry with their vote but even show us no common gratitude. Conversely, those who are in no way able to pass judgment on these matters—and who need the help of this labor all the more because they are so far removed from good literature—not only fail to embrace a work prepared for their own use, but even clamor against it, slander it, and condemn it. The first of these behaviors seems to be a mark of extreme ingratitude; the second, a mark of notable impudence. For what can be imagined more impudent than to condemn a book you have not even read? And even if you did read it, you could not pronounce judgment on it without a knowledge of the languages. Furthermore, what is more ungrateful than to repay with slander such immense sweat and midnight oil—labors undertaken solely with the intent of helping others, for which no equal thanks could ever be returned—and to have this come especially from those to whom the utility of the work should primarily flow? While ingratitude is foul everywhere, there are none to whom we should be more grateful than those who, at the expense of their money, the loss of their pleasures, and even some detriment to their health and life, devote themselves with all their might to benefit the world through the monuments of their intellect. Yet, I do not know if you will find a more ungrateful spirit anywhere among mortals; nor do I believe there is a truer saying than that which was spoken no less elegantly than weightily by <margin>* Seneca.</margin> *Seneca: "It is safer to have once remembered than to have earned merit." <note>original: "Tutius esse, quiddam olim meminisse quam demeruisse." A reflection on how people often resent those they are indebted to.</note> Nothing perishes so completely, he says, as that which is bestowed upon the ungrateful. But in my opinion, a service perishes even more when it is placed upon those who do not understand the service; and less gratitude returns from those who do not recognize a merit than from those who merely refuse to acknowledge it. For even if the latter pretend otherwise, they are still inwardy indebted and are sometimes forced by shame to acknowledge it. Finally, there is hope that they may eventually come to their senses. But the former interpret a benefit as an injury, and when aided by a service, they haul their benefactor into court. It is the duty of theologians, above all, to display not only gratitude but also integrity and gentleness. And it was for theologians especially that I performed this grueling labor—specifically for those theologians who either lacked the time or the opportunity to learn those languages without which Holy Scripture cannot be fully understood or dutifully handled. I have spent my zeal to assist their studies so that my industry might supply what their fortune denied them. And yet, if any are going to protest, I predict they will come from this very flock. Doctors embrace it; lawyers do not despise it; philosophers receive it if it contributes anything to the restoration of their profession. Let it not be that theologians alone stubbornly protest, envying our own good. Truly, it is very distressing to receive no thanks for a benefit kindly bestowed. It is even more distressing to receive slander instead of rewards from those you strive to serve, and to be forced to plead your case against these accusers from whom you could rightfully demand owed gratitude. Seneca thinks it the highest kind of liberality, and closest to divine beneficence, if someone not only does good for free but even knowingly wastes the benefit. Yet I think I shall surpass even this if I continue to deserve well even of those who repay a benefit with injury. And just as faithful doctors continue to help patients even when they protest and shout insults, so we shall crown our benefit with a further "bonus" <note>original: "auctario"</note>: making them understand the benefit they are receiving.

First, therefore, I earnestly exhort all theologians—those who have the time by virtue of their age or lack of other duties—to taste of Greek literature, and likewise Hebrew, if possible. Let them philosophize diligently in the very fountains of the secret Scriptures; let them carefully unroll the ancient theologians, whom both learning and holiness of life recommend. Then, if they wish, let them compare and weigh our work, and only then approve if we have advised anything correctly; or let them amend it in a friendly way if we, being human, have strayed from the truth and failed to reach what we so zealously pursued. If I obtain this, I have won my case, for I shall have patrons instead of accusers.

Furthermore, from those for whom I do not obtain this, let them at least grant me this one thing, even if as a favor: to believe that I undertook whatever this labor is with a simple and pious desire to help. If success was lacking in some place, it is an error, not a crime; I deserve to be corrected, not attacked. For I acknowledge nothing more than that I know nothing. Let others profess as many great things as they like; I, professing nothing in accordance with my insignificance, nevertheless provide what I can, being most ready to recant <note>original: "palinodiam"</note> wherever I have slipped in the manner of men, and I shall be my own censor as soon as I catch the mistake.

Moreover, Saint Jerome does not tolerate a critic who can condemn but cannot teach. The former is tyrannical; the latter is friendly and learned. Now, just as it is beyond controversy among the learned, so I believe even the unlearned have been persuaded by the books of many men that this edition of the New Testament is not Jerome's, as it was originally emended by him. Nevertheless, we do not in any way tear down or slander this edition, whatever it is or whoever it belongs to. We only restore what had been corrupted by the fault of time and scribes, indicating in passing those things which the Translator rendered either ambiguously or with too little attention. For I have a religious scruple against saying "incorrectly," even if Jerome did not fear to say so in several places. And we have done this, as the saying goes, neither with a light hand nor rashly, but first by the counsel of the canons <note>The rules of the Church or textual standards.</note>, according to the reliability of the Greek original, having examined the Latin copies—yet not trusting a few, nor just any we found.

Lorenzo Valla <note>An earlier humanist scholar who pioneered the linguistic critique of the Vulgate.</note> testifies that he followed seven reliable codices. In our first revision, we were aided by four Greek ones; in the second, five; in the third, there was added the Asulan edition <note>The Greek New Testament printed by the Aldine Press in 1518.</note>; in the fourth, the Spanish edition <note>The Complutensian Polyglot, printed in Spain.</note> was also at hand. Then, having consulted several Latin volumes, both ancient and corrected, and not content with this, we stretched out and explored the most approved Authors, observing with wide-awake eyes what they cited, what they read, what they emended, and how they interpreted.

And when all these things had been compared and weighed with all possible vigilance and certainly with the highest good faith, we followed what we judged best. We have offered this for the common good under this condition: that each person might nonetheless enjoy their own judgment.

Now, if there are any who fear that the authority of the Holy Scriptures might be called into doubt if anything varies anywhere, they ought to know this: for more than a thousand years, neither the Latin nor the Greek copies have agreed in all points. This is something that could not possibly happen, given not only the great crowd of scribes but also their ignorance, drowsiness, and rashness—not to mention how many things were changed by "little scholars" or certainly by those paying too little attention.

I find certain errors or additions introduced by factions, in whose turmoil everything was mixed up and down, especially in the Eastern Church, while each person varied the scripture to support their own side. Jerome clearly declares this to have happened in several places. A lighter kind of corruption occurs whenever...

He outlines his rigorous methodology, citing his use of multiple Greek manuscripts and earlier humanist scholarship to restore the text from centuries of scribal error.</summary>

--- Page 32 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s "Apologia," where he moves from defending his qualifications to discussing the history of textual variation in the Bible. He argues that the existence of different versions and scribal errors necessitates a return to the original Greek and Hebrew sources.</meta>

# OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

sometimes a reader adds from elsewhere what seemed to fit: more seriously, when a commentator <note>original: "scholiastes"</note> has annotated in the margin, the reader transfers it into the main text. What, then, has happened to the Christian religion, given that for so many centuries Jerome read one thing, Hilary another, Ambrose another, and Augustine yet another? Among these fathers you will occasionally find things not only different, but even conflicting, while they yet agree on the core of the Christian faith. What happened to the orthodox Greeks, who followed the translation of the **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Old Testament.</note> in such a way that they frequently made mention of Symmachus, Theodotion, and Aquila? <note>Three other early translators of the Old Testament into Greek.</note> What can you do, since even the editions of our own times do not agree with each other in all things? If anyone doubts this, he will be convinced by the printed books, even those with marginal notes that declare a variety of readings: and if that is not enough, he will understand the same from the commentaries of Bede, Rabanus, Thomas [Aquinas], Lyranus, and Hugh of Saint-Cher. Origen already complained back then of the inexplicable variety in the Gospel books. And publicly, Greece reads one thing, while the Church of the West reads another. And around the age of Jerome, some churches followed the translation of the Septuagint, while others embraced the new one handed down from the Hebrew sources. Even after that era, the Gallican churches <note>The churches of France.</note> read one thing, and the Roman Church another. Finally, if you examine the ancient hand-written manuscripts which they then used in public worship, you will hardly find two that agree with each other. It is certainly established that Augustine used manuscripts that were not free from errors. And yet, for so many centuries, the Scriptures have maintained their authority.

If a variety of manuscripts totally abolished faith in the Scriptures, then they vary among the Hebrews, the Greeks, and the Latins. I ask you, what danger followed when Saint Jerome restored the Old and New Testament for a world already growing old, according to the Hebrew and Greek truth? There was an outcry then from some, whom he satisfied abundantly in his own books: and the outcry was for no other reason, I believe, than that they did not know those languages. But has even the slightest disadvantage to the Christian religion arisen from this? Augustine confesses that he was helped in no small way by the very discord of the manuscripts, so that where one had spoken less aptly, another might express it more clearly and correctly—something that must happen, if only by chance. What did it take away from the majesty of the Gospels that Juvencus enclosed them in heroic verses? Or that Arator dared the same in the *Acts of the Apostles*? We have renewed a few passages, not so much to render them more elegantly as to make them more lucid and faithful. What danger would there be if we had renewed the entire speech in a **Paraphrase**? <note>A restatement of a text to clarify its meaning; Erasmus famously wrote Paraphrases for the New Testament.</note> This is almost exactly what Jerome did in the Old Testament. For those who are pleased with this current Edition <note>The Vulgate, the standard Latin Bible of the time.</note>—which I neither condemn nor change—their Edition remains theirs. Indeed, it is not harmed by our correction, but is rendered more illustrious, purer, and more improved. Let it be read in the schools, sung in the temples, and cited in sermons. No one stands in the way. But I promise this: whoever reads this version of ours at home will understand their own version more correctly. Therefore, if nothing offends except novelty, even that old version was once new, and this new one, if we allow it, will one day be old. It is the mark of an excessively unskilled man to value books by the number of their years, and not rather by a judgment of the things themselves.

I myself would wish that in the Holy Scriptures nothing were corrupted, nothing in disagreement. But while it is easy to wish for that, it never has been so, nor, I believe, will it ever be. Those who preach the inviolable authority of the Divine Scriptures, we favor with both thumbs. <note>An ancient Roman expression meaning to give full approval.</note> He who knowingly corrupts them does an insult to the Holy Spirit. We admit this. However, this majesty is in the sources themselves. Isaiah did not err, nor does anyone strive to change what he wrote. Matthew did not slip; no one corrects what he handed down. Our business is with the Translators, with the scribes, and with the corrupters. But if the entire authority wavers because of a few corrupted places, then the Holy Spirit ought to have assisted the copyists no less than the Prophets and Evangelists. The Holy Spirit is never absent, but He exerts His power in such a way that He leaves us a portion of the labor. That inviolable authority remained within the Prophets and the Apostles or Evangelists. Indeed, this is the highest praise of the Scriptures: that having been poured into so many languages so many times, so often mutilated or corrupted by heretics, and contaminated in so many ways by the carelessness of scribes, they nevertheless retain the eternal vigor of truth. Thus the Church stands, though tossed by all the storms of evils. Truly, he serves the Holy Spirit who, according to his strength, restores to its pristine integrity what has been corrupted by men. There are never lacking those who corrupt; therefore, one must never cease from the study of correcting. It is one thing, then, to speak of the Holy Scripture, and another to speak of what the Translators have turned awkwardly or the scribes have corrupted. Again, it is one thing to change the public reading, and another for a private person to either improve or illuminate the public reading. And yet some people, who seem to themselves quite logical, strangely confuse these things.

Nor do I refute what some say—that mysteries lie hidden in the very letters and strokes—provided they recognize the hyperbole. Otherwise, it would not be necessary to draw Scripture except from the sources. For he who translates into a foreign language is forced to depart far and wide from the letters and strokes. Concerning the names of God, especially the **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH.</note>, the Jews boast of wonders; and Christians boast of some concerning the name of Jesus; but these mysteries perish in translation. Indeed, that very name "Jesus" is written with far different characters among the Hebrews than among the Evangelists and Paul. If such a serious matter lies hidden in dots and strokes, why did the Apostles, who knew Hebrew, not hand down that most holy name to us in the same characters in which it is written among the Hebrews, since they insist upon it so often in their writings? When I pressed someone with this argument, he replied that the name of Jesus is written and read corruptly in all the books of the New Testament. If that were true, the Catholic Church would have been in the dark in such a notable error for so many centuries. Rather, it is more probable that the Greeks and Latins commonly adopted that name, and the Apostles used the accepted word, not being anxious about characters and strokes. Indeed, those same Evangelists and Apostles were not so superstitious in citing testimonies from the Scriptures, sometimes following the Septuagint edition, sometimes bringing them from Hebrew sources, at other times rendering the sense by their own judgment, agreeing in all things with neither these nor those.

Now, what is the point of refuting those who are accustomed to cry out—as unlearnedly as they do impudently—that it is an unbearable crime for anyone to correct the Gospels, to amend the *Song of Zechariah*, the *Magnificat*, or to change the *Lord's Prayer*? <note>Common liturgical texts from the New Testament.</note> O, a voice hardly worthy of a wagon-driver, let alone a Theologian. Let the Theological order not be angry with me because I name a "Theologian": let them rather be indignant at those who, although they were Theologians of the first rank, were crying this out most cheerfully, and still cry it out in their ordinary professions and sacred sermons. But to the point. Is it permitted for any scoundrel to corrupt the manuscripts of the Gospel, and shall it be a sin to restore what has been corrupted? Especially for a man—to say nothing too arrogant—who is neither negligent nor untrained in this kind of literature, and that with so many Greek and Latin volumes and so many most famous Authors called into counsel?

To me, by many arguments, it is vehemently probable that the entire New Testament was written in Greek, not Latin. Certainly, if one excepts the Gospel according to Matthew and the one Epistle to the Hebrews, there is no controversy about the rest. Therefore, let them rightly cry out against him who hesitates to change what was written by the Apostles and Evangelists: but not against him who, according to the decrees of the Popes, replaces with sincere faith from Greek sources and from the opinion of holy Translators what had been either spoiled by scribes or rendered poorly by a Translator in the Latin manuscripts, since the Apostles wrote in Greek. But why do I go on at length about this? Since Saint Jerome acts as the patron of this cause in several epistles—who himself, when he labored in a not dissimilar matter, was not without slander. If his emendation still existed, either we would not have had to take up this labor, or there would have been something for us to follow. And so I ask you, best of readers, when something renewed by us occurs, do not immediately reject and condemn it because of your taste for and familiarity with the usual reading, as if it were necessary for whatever is different to be bad—thus defrauding me of my praise and yourself of the utility of the work. But first, compare our work with the Greek; which, so that it might be done more readily, we have placed right alongside it. Weigh whether I have expressed it more faithfully, more clearly, or more significantly than the old Translator. And here again, let them not immediately drag me to court if word does not answer to word; which, however much you may try, cannot even be done. If they think it a sin to depart anywhere from letters and syllables, why did this Translator dare it everywhere, sometimes compelled by no necessity, nor invited by any utility, but as if playing and yawning in a trivial matter? But if it is permitted to depart from letters and syllables in some places—as it certainly is permitted—if you find that I have rendered the meanings with greater faith than he rendered them, do not condemn what is new, but embrace what is more correct. Now, if the comparison does not satisfy you, do not pronounce judgment immediately. Consult our **Annotations**, which will perhaps satisfy you, either by the authority of witnesses or by the reasons brought forward. It happens sometimes that the reading is diverse; it happens that several senses can be taken from the same words. We, first of all, propose only a single reading. For we could not do otherwise. However, in the Annota-

<summary>Erasmus defends his revision of the New Testament by citing historical precedents for textual variation among Church Fathers and early translations. He argues that the authority of Scripture lies in the original Greek and Hebrew sources, and that correcting scribal or translation errors in the Latin Vulgate is a service to the Holy Spirit rather than a sacrilege.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s defense of his editorial methods. Having previously established that various traditions and manuscripts exist, he now explains how he handles these discrepancies—sometimes choosing the best reading and sometimes leaving the choice to the reader—while justifying his corrections of even the most revered Church Fathers.</meta>

-># APOLOGIA<-
->### [DEFENSE]<-

# BY DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<page-num>3</page-num>

we report various interpretations of the mind, either indicating what seems best to us, or leaving it to the reader's judgment to follow what they prefer.

There are instances in which our Vulgate edition is more approved, or the reading of **Ambrose** <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397), an influential Bishop of Milan.</note>, than the Greek codices. And yet, when all the Greek copies agreed, since it was not permitted to change them, we adapted the Latin to match, lest they fail to correspond when added for this very purpose.

However, we disagree on this in the scholia <note>Explanatory notes or comments.</note>. I find certain things added among them by solemn custom, such as that **doxology** <note>original: "coronidem"</note> added to the **Lord’s Prayer** <note>The phrase "For thine is the kingdom..." which Erasmus noted was in Greek manuscripts but not the older Latin ones.</note>, just as among us the "Glory be to the Father" is added at the end of the Psalms. We did not cut those out from the context, but we do advise in the short commentaries that they were added. For that error carries less danger than what I frequently find happens: a reader scribbles in from other places what he finds in a similar sentence elsewhere.

Nevertheless, we have taken care to advise on that as well.

Therefore, we do not hand down this reading as if all things were certain and beyond doubt, but rather that by our correction, with the addition of notes, the watchful and attentive reader might be helped in no small way. There will be many things within that will seem to some as trivial and frivolous, to be despised. Truly, he who weighs, handles, and interprets the **Sacred Scriptures** will find for himself that in these small details there is no small amount of utility.

Furthermore, he will easily grant me pardon for pursuing such minutiae if he considers that authors of the highest reputation have stumbled over such difficulties—sometimes even falling into shameful error—namely **Hilary**, **Augustine**, **Ambrose**, and among more recent figures, the most learned **Thomas Aquinas**, not to mention the others.

In this business, it was sometimes necessary to disagree with them.

Indeed, just as I have always done this with integrity, so have I never done it insultingly—not even toward those provocative critics whose impudent rashness and insolent ignorance deserved little of this civility. Even if I had attacked them more freely, the learned would excuse me by that saying of **Plautus**: "To speak ill of the deserving is a blessing, not a curse." <note>original: "quod dignis maledicitur, benedictum est, non maledictum."</note>

Truly, I preferred to consider what was worthy of me, rather than what those men deserved.

My intention was to ignore their silliness entirely, were it not for the fact that the books of such blockheads were being handled everywhere and read and cited like oracles.

Nor was this done by me out of affectation, but in passing in several places, so that hereafter those men might trust them less—those who, whatever they find placed or added by such writers, would turn it into their own commentaries with a "white line," as they say <note>A Greek proverb "alba amussi," meaning to follow a rule blindly or without judgment.</note>. Or certainly, those for whom these authors are great will understand that due to ignorance of these matters we have indicated, even great authors have hallucinated remarkably and more than childishly.

Otherwise, if I had wanted to pursue everything in their volumes that could be laughed at or disapproved of, then truly an **Iliad of evils** <note>original: "Ἰλιὰς κακῶν"; a proverbial expression for a vast number of troubles or errors.</note> would have been born in my hands, as the Greek proverb goes, nor would one Iliad have sufficed to refute them.

As for the others, whom life and holiness of character adorn beyond the recommendation of their learning, I am so far from attacking them petulantly that I often seek out pretexts to either minimize, excuse, or cover their error.

Nor should they be angry with me if **Augustine** or **Thomas** slipped in any way.

When the matter itself is clearer than can be hidden, it is due to the impudent ignorance of languages, or the pretense of it, which was helpless in those centuries.

It was in the interest of students not to hide those things entirely.

Not because I think myself more keen-sighted than those supreme men, but because I have perhaps been more attentive in some places, and perhaps better equipped with the riches of languages—certainly more so than **Aquinas**, who knew only Latin, and that not very exactly, since he contends that "to revel" <note>original: "luxuriant"</note> pertains properly only to lust.

I trust that all of them, as they were always most studious of the truth, will be more favorable toward me, if only for the fact that I have occasionally rendered their books more pure.

What is smaller than a **punctuation mark**? <note>original: "hypostigma"; a mark used in ancient manuscripts to indicate a pause or distinction.</note> Yet such a tiny thing gives birth to a heretical sense, just as **Aurelius Augustine** teaches in the third book of *On Christian Doctrine*, citing for example that passage from John: "In the beginning was the Word with God, and God was [the Word]." And if a **comma** <note>original: "diastola"</note> is interposed, there follows: "This Word was in the beginning with God."

He calls this a heretical reading, namely of those who denied that the Word of God is God.

Likewise that which is in Paul's **Epistle to the Romans**: "Who shall bring a charge against the elect of God?" From this place, the things that follow, unless they are read as a question, produce a sense that is not only heretical but altogether blasphemous.

As if you were to answer the preceding: "It is God who justifies. Who is he that condemns?" To that you would answer again: "It is Christ Jesus who died."

It is the same in the ambiguity of Paul’s speech when he says: "The foolishness of God is wiser than men." <note>1 Corinthians 1:25.</note> He prefers it to be rendered: "The foolishness of God is wiser *than* men," which otherwise might have seemed uncertain—whether it was said in the dative case "to men," or the ablative.

And these things and others very similar to them that great man [Augustine] noted there with many words; things which would be no trouble to notice, even if no one warned us.

What if he had read so many portents of lies produced and removed by us? So many thick shadows discussed? So many meanings rendered not only ambiguously but perversely, now restored to their integrity? Would he not have embraced this labor of ours with both hands?

Some things, however, are noted with such brevity that unless you compare our little annotation to the place itself, you will not notice what I intended.

For the fact that the same things occur in several places was done intentionally, so that we might consult the reader who is perhaps forgetful or avoids the labor of searching.

And truly I fear not a little that just as the novelty will offend many, so on the other hand there may be those who are displeased by the very fact that anything agrees with the **Old Translator** <note>Jerome, the traditional author of the Latin Vulgate.</note>.

By some, nothing is approved unless it is different; to others, it seems unlearned if it does not fight and disagree in every respect.

Again, others are offended by speech that is a little too pure and Latin—namely those who judge nothing to be sharp unless it teems with monstrous **solecisms** <note>Grammatical errors or unidiomatic speech.</note>.

Others, by contrast, are disgusted by whatever does not reflect that **Ciceronian** <note>Referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero, the standard for "perfect" classical Latin.</note> brilliance.

As we have not affected eloquence in this work, so we have not rejected cleanliness of style where it was at hand.

God is not offended by solecisms, but neither is He delighted by them.

He hates proud eloquence, I confess; but much more does He hate supercilious and arrogant muttering <note>original: "infantiam"; literally "speechlessness" or "childishness."</note>.

We tolerate the stammering of those men; let them in turn bear our mediocrity of speech, such as it is.

But, to finally make an end: just as I freely confess there are many things that could have been handled more learnedly—as I do not deny that I have nodded off from exhaustion in several places—so the matter itself, unless I am mistaken, will show that I have followed **Lorenzo Valla** <note>An Italian humanist who pioneered the philological study of the New Testament.</note> (to whom good letters owe much in this regard) and **Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples** <note>original: "Jacobum Fabrum"; a French humanist and theologian.</note> (a master of all virtue and letters), and have engaged in this business not without cause, nor without fruit.

Farewell, friendly reader; and if you desire anything further, seek it from the Preface which I have placed before the Annotations.

<sig>** 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: CONCERNING</meta>

<summary>Erasmus concludes his general apology by defending the necessity of correcting the biblical text, even when it means disagreeing with revered Church Fathers like Augustine or Aquinas. He argues that linguistic accuracy is vital for theology, as even a misplaced comma can lead to heresy.</summary>

### ON THE TWO LATEST EDITIONS
#### THE FOURTH AND THE FIFTH

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
## SENDS GREETINGS TO THE DEVOUT READER

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'O' featuring leafy vines and scrolling patterns.</image-desc>
To respond to every single quibble from every person, best of readers, would not only be an endless task, but I see it would not be at all worthy of the dignity of this work, nor do I think it worth the effort. This is because those who mock and disparage this labor of ours generally do not read—or certainly do not understand—our Defenses <note>original: "Apologias"; Erasmus wrote several formal defenses of his work against theological critics.</note>. They have already been sufficiently answered in the two Defenses which we placed at the beginning of the first edition, like shields against their weapons. Furthermore, they are answered in the letter where we respond to **Martin Dorp** <note>A theologian at Leuven who initially criticized Erasmus’s project for fear it would undermine the Vulgate’s authority.</note>; in addition, in the letter to the distinguished theologian **Henry Bullock** <note>A Cambridge scholar and friend of Erasmus.</note>. Again, in the letter against a certain person whose name I have intentionally suppressed; and finally, in the Defense where I recently responded to **Petrus Sutor** <note>A Carthusian monk and vocal critic of Erasmus who argued that the Church's Latin Vulgate was perfect and required no correction.</note>. Just lately, I also responded to the quibbles of men in a reply to a certain boastful brawler. Therefore, I will merely note the main points of my arguments here for the busy or less sophisticated reader.

First, we testify—and wish it to be testified everywhere—that we do not wish to depart by a nail’s breadth or a finger’s width from the judgment of the Catholic Church. If anything of that sort should be found anywhere, spoken unintentionally rather than by design (for even humans produce "smoke"), we wish it to be considered retracted even now.

I do not wish to prejudice the judgment of the learned, nor the authority of the public schools. Each person’s judgment remains intact. We write Annotations, not laws; and we propose things to be weighed, not immediately to be taken as certainties.

Nor did we prepare these later editions with immense labor because we entirely distrusted the earlier ones. Rather, the work—which we then gave as best as we could for our strength and the time available—we now give much more corrected and much richer. Indeed, we promised we would do exactly this from the very first edition. The more often this is done, the more profit there will be for the reader.

What we did more sparingly in the first edition—fearing that some might not tolerate such novelty—we have now performed more abundantly, following the encouragement and emboldening of great and learned friends. This was done so that the entire language of the New Testament would be simple, yet truly Latin. I have made exceptions for several words and <term>idioms</term> <note>ways of speaking unique to a language</note> which I saw were too well-received to be changed, such as *faith* <note>original: "fides"</note> instead of *trust* <note>original: "fiducia"</note>, *faithful* instead of *trusting*, *blessed* instead of *praised* or *to be praised*, *in the name of Jesus* instead of *by the author Jesus* or *by trust in Jesus*, and *grace* instead of *gratuitous benefit*. To me, some people seem far too stubborn; they allow Logicians, Philosophers, Rhetoricians, Grammarians, Doctors, and Mathematicians to have their own peculiar terms—which outside the practice of their art either mean nothing or mean something else entirely—yet they permit no such thing in the Divine Scriptures.

We have also added quite a bit to the previous Annotations, and we have strengthened the earlier ones by naming the Authors we cited, on account of certain people who are more eager to slander than to learn.

But those who do not know Latin are offended; they demand the old <term>solecisms</term> <note>grammatical errors or "slips of the tongue" in speech or writing</note> to which they have become accustomed. They may keep their old edition, which I have left whole and untouched. I knew that very many people, because of the lack of skill—not to say the "filth"—of the language, were repelled by the sacred Volumes. These people should take it in good part if we wished to look out for their interests too, especially since they themselves lose nothing.

But they say it is unworthy for people to be disgusted by the sacred Scriptures because of the simplicity of the language. In the sacred Scriptures, we do not change even a dot; our business is with the translators and those who have corrupted the text. We do not remove simplicity; we restore it. Finally, it is pious and humane to first entice the weak with a certain allure.

They say God is not offended by solecisms. That is perhaps true, but He is not delighted by them either. **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine (354–430 AD), a foundational Latin Church Father.</note> excuses a fault in speech; he does not prefer it. And he excuses it in the unlearned, not in Theologians; finally, he tolerates it against his will. For he would prefer it were changed entirely if it were permitted. But if a solecism renders the meaning ambiguous, or even perverse—as we have pointed out in several places—Augustine detests the solecism. Indeed, God hates proud "solecists" who attack those speaking correctly, who do not want to learn better things themselves, and do not allow others to do so—acting like the dogs in the manger in the proverb.

Otherwise, I would ask them whether they embrace all solecisms, or only those to which they are accustomed. If they embrace any and all, why are boys beaten by them when they say "He was in your house" <note>original Latin: "Fuit in domo tuo" (wrong gender)</note> or "My body is cold" <note>original Latin: "Friget corpus meus" (wrong gender)</note>? Indeed, everyone would hiss them out of the churches if a Deacon read "Pillip" instead of "Philip." And yet, the things they themselves commit are often more absurd. If no solecisms please them except those they are used to, it is clear they are not guided by right judgment, but are flattering their own blemishes—imitating those who, while they shrink from the sores of others, are not offended by their own familiar itch. Furthermore, what will happen in the meantime to those who are *not* accustomed to solecisms?

Augustine allows a barbaric way of speaking: "The just man shall flourish <note>original: "floriet"</note> like a palm tree," instead of the correct "shall flourish" <note>original: "florebit"</note>. But he allows it among the unlearned common people—though he would still prefer it to be corrected by them. He allows the learned to say *osum* [bone] for *os*—whose genitive case is *ossis*—but only when they speak to the unlearned who would not understand otherwise. Now, since no one speaks Latin as a common language anymore, what Augustine writes about solecisms pertains to us no more than if he were advising a preacher speaking French among the French to use French words known to the public. Otherwise, why does Augustine himself not use solecisms in his own books, since he is often not understood even by the "little scholars"?

Augustine does not admit solecisms except among the unlearned, as has been said, and only for the purpose of making the meaning clear. But we have shown that in several places the entire meaning is subverted by the Translator’s solecisms, and that on these occasions, Translators of great name have fallen into error.

Furthermore, as for their objection that it is unworthy for Divine Scripture to be subjected to the rules of **Donatus** <note>Aelius Donatus, a 4th-century grammarian whose works were the standard textbooks for Latin grammar in the Middle Ages.</note>: just as this was said by a holy man, so was it said without due circumspection—if I may say so with his permission. First, the Translator’s speech is not Holy Scripture; Holy Scripture is what Moses, the Prophets, or the Apostles wrote. We correct the Translator’s speech and restore to Holy Scripture its own light. Second, if it is an insult to speak correctly about divine matters, then almost all the Ancients must be called to judgment, Greeks and Latins alike, who wrote not only elegantly, but even...

<summary>In this preface, Erasmus defends his revised Latin translation of the New Testament against critics who prefer the familiar errors of the Vulgate. He argues that correcting grammar and style does not insult God but rather restores clarity and dignity to the sacred text.</summary>

### CHAPTER: ARGUMENTS AGAINST CERTAIN SOUR AND UNLEARNED MEN

...they also treated mystical matters eloquently, and for this reason they have attained the highest praise throughout the entire Church.

It seems to me to belong to the propagation of Christ’s Gospel that it be handed down in chaste and pure speech, as far as is possible. The principle of speaking correctly is common to all: but barbarism <note>original: "barbaries"; referring to non-classical or ungrammatical Latin that Erasmus felt obscured the meaning of the text</note> is a varied thing and difficult to understand, since it departs from natural speech. Just as nothing is clearer than correct speech, so nothing is easier.

But if anyone denies that there are solecisms <term>solecism: a grammatical mistake or intentional breaking of the rules of syntax</term> in this [Vulgate] translation—not those drawn from Apostolic speech, but from the dregs of the common people—let him consult my index, and soon, I believe, he will change his mind.

There he will see in how many places even Translators of great name have erred, solely due to a fault of language. Let no one think there is no other disadvantage except that the speech is somewhat unclean.

Furthermore, although we do not deny that in the Greek speech of the Apostles and Evangelists there are some things contrary to grammatical reason, nevertheless there was no reason why we should add so many monstrous solecisms to it.

And perhaps what was useful in those times—that the Apostles' speech should be more unpolished—may now be appropriate to change: since Bishops today do not use Apostolic simplicity, but splendor has been added to the Church in all things. Once it was useful for the Apostles to use that speech which was most widely known and understood by the literate and illiterate alike, since it appears Christ even spoke in Aramaic <note>original: "Syriace"; Erasmus, like many of his time, uses 'Syriac' to refer to the Aramaic language of Roman Palestine</note>: now that reasoning has no place, so much so that those who have learned Latin must learn a new way of stammering because of the Translator's solecisms, not the Apostles'. Therefore, just as they once used the Apostolic language, which they found most common among the people: so now it would be beneficial for the Sacred Letters to be handed down in that speech which is common to all who are learned in Latin. For it is fitting that what is most correct should be most common. What has been said about Apostolic speech applies equally to the speech of the ancient Translators, when the Roman tongue was still common to the general crowd.

If for that reason it is beneficial for the divine Books to be translated skillfully so they can be understood by more people, they should especially be translated into French or German. As it is, some parts are so translated that sometimes they are understood neither by the learned nor by the unlearned.

If Christians are not allowed to speak correctly, why does Augustine, in his books *On Christian Doctrine*, place Grammar—the teacher of correct speaking—among the arts necessary for understanding the sacred Volumes? Why are all places full of so many schools of Grammarians? Why is that unrefined age of youth tortured with so many labors—is it so that they may learn to speak incorrectly?

Even if there were no other advantage, certainly elegance of speech has this good: that it is simple and natural; whereas there are six hundred kinds of speaking incorrectly.

Although in the speech of the Apostles—as we have already said frequently—we do not change even a syllable; rather, we restore their speech which has been corrupted by the fault of scribes or otherwise. Therefore, let no one cry out, "This man corrects the Gospel!" or "He amends the Lord's Prayer!" but rather, "He cleanses the codices of the Gospels from errors." I am no more to be rebuked than one who sweeps filth out of a temple with brooms. For not everything in a temple is immediately holy.

Now, if one wishes to ascribe whatever the Translator here rendered to the Holy Spirit, and for that reason deems it a crime to change anything, why does Jerome dare to criticize what is read in this version—now criticizing the words, now the meaning, now removing what he affirms was added? He does this not rarely, even in those books which he published long after the version of both Testaments was issued. Why do Cyprian, Ambrose, and Augustine dare to read differently? Why do the Churches throughout the world read one thing in solemn worship and sing another, especially in the Psalms?

Jerome, in his *Preface to Desiderius*, thinks there is a great difference between a Prophet and a Translator:
> *In the former*, he says, *the Spirit predicts things to come; in the latter, erudition and a wealth of words translate those things which he understands:*
and yet here Jerome is discussing the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>, whose authority was almost sacrosanct, and whom Jerome himself confesses were full of the Holy Spirit. But no one knows who this [Vulgate] Translator was: for Augustine testifies that there were innumerable ones, and that they were quite meagerly educated.

I judge that no more honor is due to this Translator than to the Seventy, whose edition even the Apostles often followed; yet the Church changed their translation as soon as it obtained a better one.

Do they wish this honor to be held for this one man alone, or for all Translators? If for this one alone, let them bring forward the reason why for him rather than the others; if it is owed to all, then certainly an injustice has been done to the others by making them obsolete.

The same honor is not due to the Translator and the Evangelist; otherwise, whoever arranges or copies a Gospel manuscript will claim this honor for himself. All are engaged in Gospel work, but with unequal functions. Indeed, Saint Jerome compares the work of a Translator, by which they have poured the sacred Books into another language for us, with the study of Marcus Tullius Cicero, by which he gave certain small works of Xenophon, Plato, and Demosthenes to the Latins.

If God, through Caiaphas <note>The High Priest who presided over the trial of Jesus; Erasmus refers to John 11:49-51 where Caiaphas unknowingly prophesies</note>, an evil man, issued a most true prophecy, what prevents the sacred Books from being correctly translated through a man skilled in languages, even if a unique inspiration of the Spirit is not present?

How often does Jerome, following the orthodox Greeks, cite the authority of Symmachus, Theodotion, and Aquila—heretics who favored Jewish interpretations? And yet we are begrudged if anyone points anything out. In the Book of Daniel, the edition of Theodotion was preferred to the translation of the Seventy: Jerome indicates this when explaining the fourth chapter of this Prophet.

But if, according to Jerome, the best Translator is he who best grasps the languages and the subject matter, I think I appear inferior to this Translator in neither respect—to say nothing boastful of myself. Although it seems this Translator erred more through thoughtlessness than ignorance, and adapted many things to the common crowd of uneducated people for whom those things were then written.

Furthermore, if they absolutely require the inspiration of the Holy Spirit in a Translator, what prevents the common Spirit of all Christians from being present in us as well—which is accustomed to help more abundantly those who have also applied their own hard work?

There are those who extol the sanctity, piety, and erudition of this Translator in wondrous ways, and place him almost above the Seraphic spirits; while in the meantime, if anyone were to ask whether he was a Gaul or a Russian, a Jew or a Christian, a man or a woman, they would have nothing to answer readily, since no one even knows the man’s name. Truly, they exaggerate these things to stir up hatred against me.

Let us grant that the Holy Spirit was present to him while translating, or to Jerome while amending this version. We believe the same Spirit was present to all doctors of the Church, and yet it is permissible to depart from their opinion if someone has found something better.

But it is necessary to believe in that unique inspiration of the Spirit only in the canonical Books, in which there is nothing that disagrees with the truth, even if it sometimes seems otherwise to human sense. Truly, here a distinction must be made between what the Prophet or Apostle wrote, and what the Translator translated or the scribe corrupted. Again, a distinction must be made between a fault of language and a fault of meaning. For there to be some fault of language in the writings of Paul is no more insulting to the Apostle than if it were said he wore a worn-out tunic.

<summary>Erasmus argues that the Latin Vulgate is not divinely perfect and that correcting its grammatical errors (solecisms) is a service to the Church rather than an attack on scripture. He distinguishes between the inspired original authors and the fallible human translators who followed them.</summary>

# HEADINGS OF ARGUMENTS AGAINST

Again, this honor and authority is not owed to the Prophets and Apostles, except in those volumes which the Church has received into the Canon <term>Canon: the official list of books recognized as genuine Holy Scripture</term>. For it is likely that Paul wrote letters on various matters which, if they were to come to light today, we would not immediately be compelled to embrace as the oracles of the Holy Spirit. How much less should this authority, which is owed to the Canonical Books alone, be granted to this unknown Translator <note>original: "ignoto Interpreti"; referring to the then-anonymous author of the Vulgate, traditionally attributed to St. Jerome but often questioned by Erasmus</note>, who is but one of the many whom Augustine admits were not very learned.

But some say the Roman Church has "received" this version. Even that is not simply true. Let anyone who wishes observe what the Roman Church actually reads in its liturgy; he will find many things that disagree with this version. This version seems to have been the one used by the Gauls <note>referring to the "Gallican" version of the Latin Bible</note>, which gained its place only because people were weary of the infinite variety of translations. Nor was it "received" in such a way that it is a sin to point out where it could be better rendered.

There are fairer critics who do not condemn my labor itself, but are indignant that the Translator, whom the Church has honored for so many years, has been treated by me somewhat "uncivilly" in places. In this regard, I acknowledge some fault, evidenced by the fact that in later editions I have moderated many things—as I would have done in the very first edition had I been warned. But what can you do with those people who think it an unbearable insolence if I happen to remark that the Translator "frolics in his abundance of words"? <note>original: "Interpretem lascivire copia"</note> I am merely imputing a human error to him; I do not charge him with falsehood or impiety, and I believe him to have been a good man.

They condemn the fact that by pointing out solecisms <term>solecism: a grammatical mistake or a breach of the rules of syntax</term> and awkwardly translated passages in various indexes and annotations, I have tried to bring him into contempt. Such a thought was never in my mind, but I was driven to this by the stupid and wicked shouts of many people. If anyone requires proof: in the first edition, no such index was added. I could have ignored their barking if they had kept themselves within their own walls, but they broke out into crowded gatherings of scholars, into sacred and public sermons, into the halls and tables of the highest Princes. Where did they not go? There was neither limit nor end. And those who played this part were not common people, but those wearing the tragic masks of "reverend" men: Dominicans, Franciscans, Carmelites, Carthusians—men who, beyond the majesty of religion, are also venerable to the unlearned multitude because of their titles as "Doctor." Some were even conspicuous by their bishop's miters. Therefore, if any word was spoken too freely in my Indexes, it should be blamed on their most wicked insolence rather than on me.

In some places, I said certain people had slipped "shamefully" <note>original: "turpiter"</note> or by a "shameful error." I could have said they slipped "significantly" or by a "manifest error." But these critics think that "shamefully" and "wickedly" always mean the same thing. I used "shamefully" to mean "unbecomingly"; and to me, every error in the Scriptures seems "shameful" in the sense of being regrettable. Otherwise, why does the blessed Jerome write that he "blushed" at his earlier commentaries on Obadiah, even while others were praising them? If an error committed through imprudence is not something to be ashamed of, Jerome had written those commentaries with diligence and a good heart.

The ancient doctors also saw solecisms in this Translator, whose version Jerome corrected only in the sense <note>meaning the theological meaning</note>, neglecting the faults of the speech. If it is a sacrilege to point out a solecism or an awkwardly rendered meaning, how much graver a crime will it be to do the same for the Old Testament? For as they themselves assert, Jerome handed down to us the whole—or nearly the whole—of it from Hebrew and Chaldean sources. Yet many have arisen who here criticize not only the words, but even meanings that are diametrically opposed to the original. No one calls them to court for it. To say nothing of Capnio <note>Johann Reuchlin, a famous Hebrew scholar</note>, Nicholas of Lyra and Paul of Burgos dared such things. And to come to living men: Paul, Bishop of Fossombrone; the Right Reverend Cardinal Thomas Cajetan in his work on both Testaments; Felix on the Psalter; Agostino Steuco on the Pentateuch. Countless places are brought forward by these men in which they freely disagree with Jerome's interpretation. And their labors are received with applause, as is fair. Yet against me, attempting much lighter things, the whole world has risen up. But this usually happens to everyone who opens a way to noble things. The first hisses of the hydra <note>original: "excetræ"; a multi-headed serpent from mythology</note> are terrifying.

I too could have ignored the solecisms; but to ignore a stumbling block over which the explainers of the Scriptures trip is not "politeness," but unfairness. The Translator is sufficiently excused for his solecisms by this defense: that he wrote these things not for scholars, but for the common crowd—for blacksmiths, weavers, and cloth-cleaners.

I hear that some are so superstitious that they allow nothing to be changed from the words of the Evangelists in translating. As if that were "translating," and not rather "perverting." Speech consists of two things: the words, which are like the body, and the meaning, which is like the soul. If both can be rendered, I do not object; if they cannot, it would be backward for a Translator, clinging to the words, to depart from the meaning.

If they utterly insist that word must be rendered by word, why does this Translator depart from the words so many times, occasionally invited to do so by no convenience of style? If it is permitted to change them, then a Translator must always look to this: that he expresses the meaning in good faith with the most fitting words possible.

It is neither certain nor probable that this edition which we commonly use was approved by the authority of that ancient Synod <note>referring to various early church councils</note>. Nor is it probable that the Fathers used this version alone in the Synods, for those councils consisted of Greeks, Latins, and "Barbarians" <note>non-Greeks/Romans</note>, where one would quote in Greek, another followed Ambrose, another Cyprian, or someone else; this version was merely received by public use.

Jerome does not fear to declare that the "Seventy" <term>the Septuagint: the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</term> translated things they did not understand with ambiguous words; in some places, he even calls their translation a "lie." In many places, he points out by name where they manifestly slipped in rendering the meaning of Scripture. Why then should we think it sacrilege if someone disagrees with this unknown translator?

As has been said, the Roman Church has used this version for some years; let us grant that, but it does not use it alone. For it also reads Jerome and Ambrose; and the church chants often differ from this edition. Nor does the Church use it in such a way as to decree that there is nothing in it that could be rendered better.

For a long time, the Church used the old translation of the Old Testament <note>the Vetus Latina</note>, which rendered word-for-word what the Seventy had translated into Greek, in a speech that was utterly absurd—as would be obvious to anyone who reads Augustine’s *On the Expressions of the Prophets* <note>original: "De loquutionibus"</note>. Yet the Church did not reject the more convenient interpretation which was substituted for the previous one—by Jerome, as they think, and in part that is true.

But if anyone should utterly insist that one must never disagree with the Translator: First, let him excuse those places in which we have shown that he was clearly nodding off, or slipped, or rendered the Greek so unskillfully that because of his awkward interpretation, the highest Theologians (who only knew Latin or did not consult the Greek manuscripts) have slipped significantly—for I no longer dare say "shamefully." If these things are too well known to be denied, let us admit that the Translator was a man, to say nothing more harsh.

Even if many such errors are of the kind that were likely introduced by the fault of scribes <note>original: "librariorum"</note>, then while the Church may approve the translation, it certainly does not approve the corruption of it.

Nor is everything that has been received into ecclesiastical use immediately "received" by a formal judgment. Some things creep in by chance, to which the Church turns a blind eye, especially if they do not seem to involve danger to faith or morals. Indeed, it is possible that in this category, the Church may be unaware of certain things for a time.

<summary>Erasmus defends his right to correct the Latin Vulgate, arguing that no translation—even one long used by the Church—is infallible or immune to grammatical and scribal errors. He highlights that even revered figures like St. Jerome corrected earlier versions and were themselves later corrected by other scholars.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s defense of his New Testament project. Having argued that the translation commonly used by the Church (the Vulgate) is not beyond critique, he now addresses those he deems "peevish and unlearned," explaining the necessity of correcting manuscript errors to preserve the true authority of the Holy Scriptures.</meta>

# TO CERTAIN PEEVISH AND UNLEARNED CRITICS.

When Pope Damasus gave Jerome the task of correcting the New Testament from Greek sources, the Church already had a version it was reading, and had perhaps been reading for several centuries. If that version was perfectly accurate, what need was there for Jerome’s correction? But if it was corrupted, it is obvious that the Church uses what is available only until it can be turned into something better. I say the same regarding the Old Testament.

The authority of Holy Scripture does not waver because errors <term>errors: Erasmus uses the word "mendae," referring specifically to scribal mistakes or faults in the physical copies</term> are removed from the manuscripts. On the contrary, it would waver more if it were certain that we were using corrupted copies—and that is a fact that certainly cannot be denied. If no one applied a remedy to this problem, since it is the nature of human affairs to always slip toward the worse, then the authority of the Scriptures would truly waver because of the confusion in the manuscripts.

It is to be hoped that no error remains in the sacred Books, and we must strive toward that goal as much as possible. However, that has not happened in thirteen hundred years, nor perhaps will it ever be fully achieved. It will go well for us if as few errors as possible remain.

Therefore, we do not claim that every single error has been removed by us, but we dare to claim that many have certainly been removed. We have brought the matter to the point where, from now on, one may use copies with the fewest possible faults, should anyone wish to follow this path and make further corrections under the authority of the Roman Pontiff.

For we do not present this edition with the intent that it be considered corrected in every single detail. Rather, where a reading is very common and most consistent among the Greeks, that is what we have translated, indicating where our work agrees or disagrees with the Greek, and what seems most correct to us.

Here, it happens to be worth noting in passing that there are certain Greek manuscripts of the New Testament that have been "corrected" to match the Latin copies. This was done during the time of the union <note>original: "fœdere"; referring to the Council of Florence (1431–1449) where the Greek and Roman churches briefly reconciled</note> of the Greeks with the Roman Church, a union witnessed by the decree known as the **GOLDEN BULL**. It seemed that this would also help to strengthen their concord. We ourselves once came across a manuscript of this kind, and such a copy is said to still be preserved in the Papal Library. However, to correct our Greek books from these is to apply a "Lesbian rule," as they say <note>A "Lesbian rule" was a flexible lead ruler used by masons on the island of Lesbos; Erasmus uses the idiom to describe a standard that is inconsistently bent to fit a desired outcome</note>. We should rather look at what the ancient Greeks read: Origen, Athanasius, Basil, Gregory Nazianzen, Chrysostom, Cyril, and Theophylact. I have seen fit to mention this because some people are now boasting that they have noted three hundred places in a manuscript from the Papal Library where it agrees with our common Latin edition <note>the Vulgate</note> but disagrees with mine. Yet if they pressure us with the authority of the Vatican Library, the manuscript which Cardinal Francisco <note>Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros, who produced the Complutensian Polyglot</note>, formerly of Toledo, followed in the New Testament was not only from that same library, but was even sent by Leo X so that he might imitate it as a model of good faith. And yet, that manuscript agrees with my edition in almost every respect, disagreeing with the one written in capital letters which some people are now throwing in our faces. For that manuscript must necessarily disagree with the Greek if it agrees with the common Latin edition.

I know that sacred matters must be handled reverently and religiously, and therefore, although we are engaged in a very humble role, we have used all the circumspection possible. We have compared the most ancient and approved manuscripts of both languages, and certainly not a few of them. We have examined the commentaries of both ancients and moderns, Greek as well as Latin. We have observed what different people read. We have weighed the meaning of the passage itself, and only then have we pronounced what we thought. Indeed, we have not even "pronounced" it, but have advised the reader, leaving each person’s judgment free.

*Bede*, *Rabanus*, *Thomas*, *Nicholas of Lyra*, and *Hugh of Saint-Cher*, and others more obscure than these, think it enough to note: *Another reading says this*; because they found it written that way in some manuscript, or perhaps found it corrupted. They are seen as performing a useful service. Why then is there an outcry against us, who restore the true reading with so many arguments and the authority of the greatest men?

If variety takes away faith in books, then copies were already varying in the time of *Origen*, in the time of *Jerome*, in the time of *Bede*, in the time of *Thomas*; finally, they vary even in our own times today, and yet the sacred Books still maintain their authority.

If certain corrupted places diminished the credit of the secret Volumes, this would have happened long ago in the time of *Origen*, who, in his *eighth Homily on Matthew*, complains about this matter in these words:
> *For we find a great difference between the copies, whether through the negligence of scribes, or from the rashness of certain people, or because of those who neglect to correct the scriptures, or because of those who add or take away what seems good to them in the corrected versions.*
Do you hear, reader, that the books were already varying back then? Do you hear that they were corrupted? Do you hear that things were added or subtracted?

And just as he did not dare, especially in the New Testament, to pronounce judgment using obelisks and asterisks <note>textual marks used to indicate suspected or missing text</note>, but only to warn the reader; so we have shown separately what seemed right to us and why it seemed so, by no means laying a hand on the "received" version <note>the Vulgate</note>, nor claiming to do anything other than render into Latin what is found in the Greek books used by the orthodox Fathers Basil, Chrysostom, Cyril, and Athanasius.

In this, perhaps, we surpass Origen: he had nothing to follow in the New Testament except the Greek manuscripts. We have compared the Greek with the Latin, and have been aided by the most approved Translators of both languages; whereas he was almost the first to write on the Divine Books.

If anyone contends that there is no error at all in the sacred Books, what will happen to those places that are so obviously corrupted that there is no room for evasion? If they admit some places are faulty, why do they not allow them to be corrected, whatever is seen to need correction?

But I hear some people speaking thus: *We embrace the project, but a stumbling block is given to the multitude if they sense that in the books we have followed until now, there is anything either corrupted or not understood.* First, these things are not written for the multitude, but for the learned, and especially for students of Theology. These men ought not to be offended. Nor do we call our labor a "Correction," but "Annotations." Nor are we troublesome to anyone who cites differently or follows the old or even corrupted edition. Rather, the stumbling block arises from those who—in public assemblies, in computations, in carriages and on ships—shout among the uneducated and the womenfolk that there are people who "correct" the sacred Books and the Lord’s Prayer.

Wretched indeed is the condition of the sacred Volumes if their authority depends on unlearned scribes (as they generally are) or drunken printers.

They do not shout against those by whom it is clear the sacred Books are corrupted daily, since those who dare this are most illiterate. They cry out against me, a man in this kind of study—which depends on skill in languages—who is, I believe, neither entirely unlearned nor unpracticed. It is permitted for those others to rashly corrupt according to their own whim; shall it not be permitted for me to restore the text based on the faith of ancient manuscripts and the authority of the most approved Interpreters?

In those men, they do not require authority—it is enough that it is smeared on the pages. In me, they require almost miracles. "Why," they ask, "should we believe Erasmus?" Indeed, if they distrust Erasmus, let them trust any Theologian you like. For if the authority of interpreting sacred Letters has been handed to me, do they wonder if I dare to open my mouth regarding a reading?

However, I do not demand that they believe me. Let them believe the ancient and corrected copies; let them believe the Greek truth, especially where the reading of these agrees with the interpretation of the orthodox Fathers. Finally, let them not even believe these, but let them weigh the matter for themselves, and if they have anything more correct, let them bring it forward; let them not bite the one giving advice. For the way to seek better things has been closed to no one by us; rather, it has been opened.
