<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s rebuttal to his critics. In the previous section, he argued that correcting the biblical text does not undermine its authority but rather preserves it from the inevitable decay of scribal transmission. Here, he addresses specific legalistic and traditionalist objections, such as the claim that only a Church Council can authorize changes to the Scripture.</meta>

# HEADINGS OF ARGUMENTS AGAINST [MY WORK]

Jerome, they say, was commissioned by Pope Damasus. He was indeed commissioned, but as a friend, not as the Supreme Pontiff. We read that he was commissioned; we do not read that his work was officially approved <note>Erasmus is distinguishing between a personal request for scholarship and a formal dogmatic decree of the Church.</note>. Finally, it is beyond dispute that Jerome’s correction does not survive in its entirety—a fact I have clearly proven elsewhere. And it is well known that the version we have was corrupted again, even if the house of Jerome had corrected it most thoroughly, though this is easy to refute with the most certain arguments.

Nothing, they say, should be attempted without the authority of a Council <term>Council: Erasmus uses the word "Synodus," referring to a formal gathering of Church leaders to decide on doctrine or law</term>. What could be more ridiculous to say? In order for me to be allowed to point out what seems to have been corrupted by a scribe, or what could have been better translated by the Interpreter—especially according to the opinion of the Ancients—must an entire Council be summoned? New commentaries on the Sacred Scriptures are written every day, pronouncements are made on the weightiest matters, and so many articles of faith are established, yet no Council is required.

What if I had translated the New Testament into verse, as Juvencus did, or explained it more clearly in a Paraphrase? Would they think a Council had to be proclaimed for that reason? Now I am merely translating what is in the Greek, sometimes not approving of what is read among them and preferring our own readings, although in the Greek manuscripts there is nothing beyond corruptions from which Christian doctrine might be endangered.

But if they judge it a sin for anything to exist that differs from this edition <note>Referring to the Vulgate, the standard Latin Bible of the time.</note>, then the commentaries of Ambrose would have to be abolished; Cyprian, Jerome, and Augustine would have to be suppressed; and one should not touch any of the Greek Interpreters, whom both the schools and the Christian churches read in translation. By that same logic, it will be held a sin to have published the New and Old Testaments in Greek, which recently came forth from the workshop of my friend Aldus <note>Aldus Manutius, the famous Venetian printer who published the first major Greek editions of many classics.</note>, and soon the same was provided by Francisco, Archbishop of Toledo <note>Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros, who organized the Complutensian Polyglot Bible.</note>, with the approval of the Roman Pontiff, who supplied the manuscript for the New Testament, with which our edition agrees in almost all points.

We have produced this work not so that it is forbidden to disagree with it, but because it greatly contributes to both the correction and the understanding of the Sacred Books. And just as we propose it, so Leo X, truly the Greatest Pontiff, approves it in his own writing, desiring that Christian religion be consulted in this area as well. I know that here the authority of the Roman Pontiff is treated as a light matter—the very authority they want to seem more than sacrosanct whenever a papal decree grants the right of absolution against the will of local pastors, or some other function that yields a significant harvest of money, or the right to hold multiple church offices. Truly, his authority ought to carry weight here, whereas in those other matters the Pope’s indulgence is sometimes bought or extorted. Here, his favor was bestowed freely, and not so much to the man as to the cause.

We have removed so many errors; we have explained so many poorly translated passages; we have cleared away so many monstrous solecisms <term>solecism: a grammatical mistake or intentional breaking of grammatical rules</term>; we have untangled so many knots in which even the Ancients were stuck. We have pointed out so many notable slips of authors, cut away so many ambiguities, and organized so many word reversals <note>original: "hyperbata," a figure of speech where the natural order of words is changed.</note>. To finish: we have illuminated so many meanings that were previously obscure and cloudy. We have offered such great utility for free—and yet some cry out against one who has served them well. If even a slight error occurs, they stir up "Tyrian seas," as the saying goes <note>A classical proverb meaning to cause a massive, unnecessary uproar.</note>; for good deeds, there is no gratitude.

Now, it is no secret to me that this bothers certain people because I disagree with writers of great name. Because they favor Augustine, they roar that I do not agree with him in everything. Those who are devoted to Thomas Aquinas are grieved that he is touched. The Franciscans do not want Lyranus or Scotus <note>Scholastic theologians: Nicholas of Lyra and Duns Scotus.</note> to be refuted. Yet if we accept this law, it will be permitted to disagree with absolutely no one, even though they themselves disagree among themselves. In this work, greater account had to be taken of the truth than of authority.

It is not insulting to disagree with even the most approved authors if you do so by bringing forth reasons. There is a difference: there are those with whom it is right to disagree reverently, such as Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine; there are others to whom this reverence is not owed. Perhaps it is owed to Thomas, but it is not owed to Lyranus or Hugo of Saint-Cher <note>original: "Carrensi."</note>, neither in the name of their learning nor their holiness. And it was important that these men be criticized in some places because I saw that they alone were being read everywhere with wonderful confidence but no judgment.

But perhaps I am nitpicking these men in one or two places. First, let it be blamed on those who wrote such ridiculous things, not on me. Second, if they are annoyed that I touch upon them sometimes, why do they not rather acknowledge my civility when I overlook so many things? I would by no means have passed those over if I had criticized them for the sake of malice. That I have touched on them sometimes was forced by the utility of the studies; that I do so rarely was a concession to Christian modesty.

And yet I would have been happy to conceal even this, if it had been allowed by those who were crying out that this labor would be entirely fruitless, as if it were childish and merely a matter of grammar. Now, it cannot be utterly despised as "childish" if it shows the points in which the highest doctors have slipped.

Truly, this very thing, unless I am mistaken, offends most of them: that they are being warned as if they have hitherto been ignorant of something in these letters in which they profess expertise. They are ashamed to admit that what they learned as beardless boys must be unlearned as old men. First, it would be too arrogant for anyone to profess that he knows everything; second, let them learn these things silently, and they will cease to be ignorant. In this way, they will best escape this disgrace. Now, by such outbursts, they translate their own ignorance even more.

But if novelty is so hated that it cannot be endured, then this edition we use now was also once new. It is most foolish to take the value of things from their years. By that estimation, drunkenness would be a noble thing, since it is most ancient and has been brought down from early ages to this time. Why do we not weigh the thing itself rather than its annals?

If novelty offends, we are restoring old things and excluding novelty. For the corruption of the text is more recent than the original edition. If there are any who cannot change the "saliva" they have drunk since childhood <note>An idiom for being stuck in one's old ways or early education.</note>, their old edition remains for them if they want it—both clearer and more corrected. If they don't want it, let it stay just as it is. If acorns obstinately please their palate, let them at least not envy those who prefer to eat wheat.

I ask you, is it permitted to investigate anything after the Ancients, or not? If it is not permitted, why did Alexander of Hales and Thomas, and after them many others, dare to change the whole face of Theology? If it is permitted, why do they clamor against our studies, especially since we do not prescribe anything by our own judgment but rely on the authority of the Ancients? For if it is permitted to introduce new things, it is much more permitted to recall the old.

If I had done nothing else than correct our manuscripts from the Greek copies, my industry ought to have been approved, since I attempted what Augustine commands to be done in more than one place. Now, not content with this, I seek the matter from the commentaries of the orthodox Fathers.

Even if we grant that there is no error in our books, nevertheless for many reasons it was necessary to flee to the sources: because of ambiguities, because of certain obscure additions, because of the figures of speech and the emphasis of the Greek phrasing (which often cannot be rendered in translation), and because of the grace of the idiom, which does not translate well.

Even if we grant that the Greek books are as corrupted as the Latin ones, the true reading is often caught by comparing corrupted copies. This is because it frequently happens that what is corrupted by chance here is found intact in another manuscript—or at least a conjecture of the true reading is given by certain traces.

Augustine, in his fifty-ninth Epistle, does not dare to answer when asked about the meaning of a certain verse from the Psalms until he has consulted the Greek books. He also compared the books of the Old and New Testaments with the Greek, clearly distrusting the common translation. Others may see how much utility that has in the Old Testament, but certainly
in...

He is specifically addressing critics who believe that the Latin Vulgate is sufficient and that returning to Greek or Hebrew sources is unnecessary or even dangerous. He moves from the authority of Councils to the practical necessity of linguistic accuracy.</meta>

### TO CERTAIN PEEVISH MEN AMONG THE UNLEARNED.

<note>original: "MOROSOS QVOSDAM AD INDOCTOS." The title suggests Erasmus is targeting critics who are stubborn (peevish) but lack the linguistic training to understand his work.</note>

**Tom. VI. *** 2**

...in the New [Testament] it is necessary. And indeed, do they not hesitate to pronounce judgment on all things, relying solely on common manuscripts? Jerome teaches in many places that the purity of a reading must be sought from the more ancient language: that is, from the language into which the book was first translated. For example, when one is stuck on the Old Testament, he orders that the Greek manuscripts be consulted, if one does not know Hebrew: because the Old Testament was turned into that language <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> before it was turned into Latin.

Jerome praises the diligence of German women who compared the Latin Psalter with the Greek, even though it flowed from the fountains of the Hebrews; and do these critics think it is absurd for the same to be done for the New Testament, which flowed entirely, or almost entirely, from the Greeks?

But I hear some who would completely abolish faith in the books of the Greeks, simply because they have separated themselves from the Roman Church <note>This refers to the Great Schism of 1054 between the Western/Catholic and Eastern/Orthodox churches.</note>. Yet by that same logic, we should not trust the books of the Hebrews, because they are most hostile not only to the Roman Pontiff, but to Christ and all Christians. And yet Jerome trusted them at a time when it would have been most opportune for them to corrupt the text, if they had wished to corrupt anything.

If the Greeks had intended to corrupt their manuscripts, they would have corrupted them in those specific places where they disagree with us—such as the procession of the Spirit <note>The *Filioque* clause, a major theological divide between East and West.</note>, the equality of the three Persons, the primacy of the Roman Pontiff, the rite of consecrating and delivering baptism and the eucharist, the marriage of Priests, or other things of that kind. But in these matters, they agree with us. Nor can any passage be brought forward that could be held suspect on this account.

Aristotle holds his own authority among us, even though he is more than a schismatic—indeed, he is entirely alienated from Christ. Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to university education.</note> carries weight even in the schools of the Theologians, a man who blasphemed against Christ. And shall there be no faith among us for the volumes of the Greeks? Just because some of them defected from the Roman Pontiff; for indeed, not all of them defected. And those who defected, and those who did not, agree in their readings.

If the manuscripts of the Greeks were corrupted long ago, they were still orthodox then. But if they were corrupted recently by the schism, how is it that their manuscripts agree with the books of the Ancients? Unless perhaps someone is so impudent as to say that all the manuscripts and the commentaries of the Interpreters were corrupted by the schismatics at the same time.

I suspect rather that if anything has been changed in the Greek books, it proceeded from Latin copies, after the Roman Church began to absorb Greece.

Nor is all of Greece torn away from us: Rhodes and Crete acknowledge Christ and acknowledge the Roman Pontiff; why do we distrust their books? And it is from these places especially that our copies come.

Long ago, Jerome laughed at Helvidius, who most foolishly persuaded himself that the Greek manuscripts were corrupt; Jerome thought the man's statement was too foolish even to be refuted by arguments. And yet even then, almost the entire East was seething with the heresies of the Arians and Origenists. One should have feared those copies more than the ones from the schismatics.

The Church condemned certain opinions of the Greeks, but it never condemned the manuscripts of the Greeks. And why do we condemn what the Church did not condemn? Rather, why do we not have faith in those things in which the Church wished faith to be held?

There are those who, having accepted Jerome's translation, deny that anything should be attributed to either the Hebrew or Greek volumes. They claim that what Augustine writes—that the truth of the New Testament must be sought from the Greeks, and the Old from the Hebrews—has now ceased to apply. If these Greek books are the same, why should they be rejected today, when they formerly held authority? And as I have shown, they agree in most parts. Furthermore, if what Augustine wrote was no longer valid after the reception of Jerome's translation, why, so many centuries after Augustine, did the Church receive that same rule into the decrees of the Pontiffs? If we estimate the weight of that statement from the age of Gratian <note>The 12th-century author of the *Decretum*, a foundational collection of Canon Law.</note>, Jerome’s translation was already most widely accepted.

I bypass for now what the learned gather from many conjectures: that today we possess neither the Old nor the New Testament in a pure state, whether from the version or the emendation of Jerome. First, the Church never received the Psalter translated from the Hebrew. The Preface that Jerome placed before his commentaries declares that Ecclesiastes is not of Jerome’s translation. Finally, the manuscripts that are circulated according to the translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint.</note> and according to the Hebrew truth disagree vehemently among themselves.

Some here offer us a "Lesbian rule" <note>A leaden ruler used by masons on the island of Lesbos that could be bent to fit the shape of a stone; Erasmus uses it to mean a flexible or biased standard of truth.</note>, suggesting that whatever is most commonly accepted by the crowd should be held as correct. Truly, human affairs have never been so well-ordered that the best thing is sought from the crowd. The most certain rule is the comparison of languages, translations, expositors, and manuscripts themselves, applying a sober judgment and excluding contention.

Now, as for the fact that this study of ours is despised by some as humble and childish—because I labor over syllables and words—it does not move me much. I consider anything that pertains to theology to be great. And since I am not ignorant of how much reverence is owed to the Sacred Books, I am conscious of my duty, even if something in it seems lowly.

Let this be called grammatical, let it be called childish, let it be called trivial, provided they admit it is necessary. Even if I teach nothing other than the correct reading, it is certainly shameful for great doctors to be ignorant of this very thing. And yet this is more manifest than can be denied: we see that Augustine slipped here, Bede slipped, Thomas [Aquinas] slipped, Lyra and Carrensis <note>Nicholas of Lyra and Hugo of Saint-Cher (known as Carrensis), famous medieval biblical commentators.</note> slipped. We frequently hear those who preach in the temples bringing forward even the theme they propose while misunderstanding it.

These pebbles are as small as you like, but "those who look at the sun" <note>original: *οἱ τὸν ἥλιον βλέποντες*. A Greek idiom for those who seek high truths but ignore the ground beneath them.</note> frequently stumble over them. If, according to Chrysostom and Augustine, the article *ho* <note>original: *ὁ*. The Greek definite article "the."</note>—that is, the tiniest element—added or omitted makes a sense orthodox or heretical; if a sub-comma <note>original: *hypostigme*. A mark of punctuation.</note> placed in the wrong spot does the same, why should we neglect these trifles which have so much importance?

Because in some places we point out the order and explain the twists of transpositions <note>term: *hyperbatorum*. A figure of speech where the natural order of words is changed.</note>, they cry out "grammarian!" Someone even said in a crowded assembly, "Let him teach how to construct a sentence; I learned that forty years ago." As if Origen, in his exposition of the Scriptures (in my opinion second to none), or as if Jerome did not frequently point out the construction, calling it "the order." And yet he who was shouting these things is the one who has the greatest need of someone to show him the construction.

Let them be much more learned than I; I do not mind. However, I do not think a man should be "counted as nothing among the Megarians" <note>An ancient Greek proverb meaning to be considered of no value or importance.</note> when he teaches the more learned in so many places what was important to know, and what was both unseemly and useless to be ignorant of.

Does not Augustine, whom these men also hold as the supreme doctor of the Church, distinguish a "search" from an "interrogation"? Does he not point out punctuation marks, arrange the clauses, phrases, and periods, and indicate the tropes of the grammarians?

Are not the "stargazers" <note>original: *μετέωροι*.</note> mocked, who, with eyes lifted to the sky, contemplate the stars in such a way that they smash their shins against a rock?

Apelles did not despise the method of grinding or mixing colors, nor the drawing of simple lines, which are the lowliest things in the art in which he excelled.

Nor does a skilled architect, occupied with the roof and the summit, neglect to carry rubble into the foundation. He who does not know these things is no architect; he who neglects them builds a collapsed work.

<summary>Erasmus defends the use of Greek and Hebrew manuscripts against critics who claim Greek texts are corrupted by schism. He argues that linguistic "minutiae" like punctuation and grammar are the essential foundation of sound theology.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s defense against his critics, specifically those who argue that a scholar should already know the basics of Greek and Hebrew and that returning to these "minute" details is beneath the dignity of a doctor of theology. Erasmus responds by showing that even the great Church Fathers like Augustine and Jerome engaged in this kind of detailed linguistic analysis.</meta>

# THE MAIN POINTS OF THE ARGUMENTS AGAINST ME

But, they say, "It is a shameful thing for doctors of theology to be learning these things." I confess: it was necessary to have learned them, not to be learning them now. But what will you do for those who did not have the opportunity, either because they lacked the spirit or because the chance to learn was never granted? Is it better to remain ignorant of what is necessary to know, than to learn it late in life?

And yet, no one is forced to learn these things, even though anyone is permitted; certainly, this labor of mine is aimed primarily at the young.

I do not doubt that an age is coming—and perhaps it is even now arising—when these works of mine will seem, for the most part, unnecessary. However, those who have already grown into tall and sturdy men do not despise the nurse who first gave them the breast, or who placed pre-chewed food into their mouths. Nor did those Wise Men, the lights of Greece, who were perfect in every branch of learning, feel any lack of gratitude toward those from whom they had learned to recognize, draw, and sound out the basic elements of letters. These things are so small that without them, no one can become truly great. Each person has their own gifts. We share what has been given to us.

Indeed, these things will seem less negligible if someone actually tries to see how much sweat these "minutiae" cost. Or if someone attempts to handle Divine Scripture and, as is proper, curiously pries into every single detail. Utility is felt through use, not through a hurried reading. Finally, anyone who weighs the entire Work—not just one or two annotations—will stop looking down on it. You, lounging and idle, weigh this or that passage and think to yourself that you could have handled it more abundantly or more learnedly. I could have, too, if there had been only ten spots to examine. In so many thousands, it is extremely difficult to maintain this level of diligence; it certainly was for me, and I will not envy someone more fortunate.

Augustine did not regret his labor when he made certain notes of this kind on the books of the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible.</note>, not from the fountains of the Hebrews, but from Greek volumes. He thought it a matter worth noting that in the Sacred Scriptures, a plural verb is sometimes added to a noun representing a single thing made of many parts. A phrase of this kind is: *Let my people go that they may serve me.* Likewise, *Let all the earth adore you.* Furthermore, there is this speech: *If Esau asks you, saying: To whom do you belong, and where are you going, and whose are these things that go before you? And you shall say: They belong to your servant Jacob.* In the last part, the conjunction "And" is redundant. Again, in this sermon, *But you shall keep my covenant,* "you shall keep" <note>original: *conservabis*</note> is placed in the position of "Keep" <note>original: *conserva*, the imperative command</note>. Again, regarding these words in Leviticus, "being unclean, he shall be unclean" <note>original: *ἀκάθαρτος ὤν, ἀκάθαρτος ἔσται*</note>, he thinks they can be translated in this way: *Unclean existing, he shall be unclean.* And yet, he notes the participle "existing" <note>original: *existens*</note> is not from "to exist" <note>original: *exsistere*</note> but from "to be" <note>original: *esse*</note>; since in Greek it is "being" <note>original: *ὤν*, pronounced 'on'</note>, as if you were to say "be-ing" <note>original: *essens*</note>. Furthermore, he teaches that a woman is called "woman" even if she is a virgin—though he did not know the Hebrew word upon which the question depended. Likewise, he notes that the Greek word *unripe* <note>original: *ἄωρος*</note> is poorly said in Latin as "late-ripening" <note>original: *serotinum*</note>. So great a Bishop was not burdened by descending to such "childish" things.

What about Jerome himself? Did he not note things that might seem frivolous, if anything at all in the Holy Books could be frivolous? In the fifth chapter of the Epistle to the Ephesians, on the words of Paul: *Because of this he shall leave father and mother, etc.* he noted that "instead of this" <note>original: *ἀντὶ τούτου*</note> was said for "on account of this" <note>original: *ἕνεκεν τούτου*</note>. Even though both phrases fit well and produce the same sense: *In place of a wife you leave father and mother,* or *For the sake of a wife you leave father and mother.* Likewise, in the Epistle to Philemon, he indicated that "lovable" <note>original: *ἀγαπητὸν*</note> sounds more like "worthy of being loved" than "beloved" <note>original: *ἠγαπημένος*</note>. Again, in the Epistle to the Romans, "all who are truly among you" <note>original: *πάντες τῷ ὄντι ἐν ὑμῖν*</note> was said for "All"; since both ways say the same thing: *Whoever is among you* and *To all who are among you.* Truly, why should I mention how many things of this kind Jerome noted in the little book he wrote to Sunia and Fretela <note>Two Gothic clerics who wrote to Jerome asking about discrepancies between the Latin and Greek Psalters.</note> regarding the correction of the Psalter? There are so many tiny details there that I would not even deign to include them in my Annotations, however grammatical they may be.

Therefore, let no one find fault if I respond to the argument I have taken up. It is abundantly enough for me if no one before me has provided more in this genre of writing. What others may be able to do, or will provide in the future, I do not know. Certainly, I would wish for very many to appear who completely overshadow me. Indeed, I will even rejoice to be criticized if someone, through their own industry, aids a matter so sacred that we have attempted in whatever way we could. Let there only be an absence of insolence, which even the Pagans <note>original: *Ethnici*</note> engaged in literary matters considered foul and unbecoming.

Let the man who prepares a criticism remember that he too is human, and no less able to slip while criticizing than the author of the Work was while writing. Although far more mercy is owed to the one who, studying to be useful, nodded off somewhere in a massive Work and did not achieve what he wished, than to the one who, desiring to seem clever regarding another's book, hunts for something to pick apart—and yet does even this incorrectly. While he attacks the false errors of others, he reveals his own true ones. Furthermore, no error is fouler than a spirit breathing envy and the lust for picking apart even the most correct things.

A reader ought to approach reading a book as a polite guest approaches a banquet. The host strives to satisfy everyone; and yet, if something is served that does not suit this or that person's palate, the guests either politely hide their distaste or even approve of it, so as not to sadden the host. For who could tolerate a guest who comes to the table with the sole intention of picking apart what is served, neither eating it himself nor letting others eat?

And yet, you may find people even more uncivil than these, who openly and without end damn and tear apart a Work they have never read. And certain men do this who profess themselves to be teachers of Christian piety and leaders of religion; though it is more than sycophantic <note>In Erasmus's time, a "sycophant" was a false accuser or slanderer.</note> to damn what you do not know.

They do not understand how far the tongue of the prophetic dog (which heals ulcers by licking) ought to be from the tongue of a viper or an asp, whose venom is incurable. Nor do they think how much difference there is between a hierophant <note>An interpreter of sacred mysteries.</note> and a sycophant.

Since the schools of the Theologians do not free Duns Scotus, Peter Lombard, William of Ockham, Thomas Aquinas, Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome, Hilary, Cyprian, John Chrysostom, John of Damascus, Origen, or even Peter the Apostle himself from error—and indeed, from the kind of error which, if you were to defend it, you would be a heretic—why do they read our work with such unfair judgment?

"But," they say, "this respect is owed to those great men of the city, but not to you." On the contrary: the more they excelled in dignity or learning, the less excuse they had for error. Nor do I think those critics count me among the so completely unlearned that I ought not to write anything at all.

The name of heresy is heavy and hateful to Christian ears; therefore, it is all the more shameful to thrust it upon someone rashly. But these men have nothing more ready to hand, nor do they hesitate to cry "heresy!" before they have even looked around at what is being discussed. And just as when one pig grunts, they all grunt, so at the shout of this or that person, all the members of the same faction cry out "heresy!"

They wish to seem so very Christian by being forcefully abusive toward a fellow Christian. And so that they may do this with more impunity, they favor the tyranny of Princes and flatter the Roman Pontiff beyond measure—while meanwhile thinking very poorly of him, though they should think nothing is dearer to him than what pertains to the glory of Christ and the safety of the flock.

They repeatedly hammer home the name of the Church while they are doing their own business; they have the Holy Spirit in their mouths, when...

...far different in mind. Let these things be said against certain people, who are worthy of the title of neither Theologian nor Monk, though not against all.

# ON CERTAIN CAPTIOUS AND UNLEARNED MEN.

He who simply errs should be warned in a brotherly way. He who has striven for nothing other than to be of use should be read with favor and candor. But it is marvelous how those men rage, with what pride and what a haughty brow they pass judgment, frequently in matters where they do not understand the issue. If it were pleasing, I could show that this has indeed happened. In such a case, what could be more shameful?

Origen, in writing against Celsus—who was more than a heretic, having torn apart the whole of Christ with the most unworthy insults—dealt with him through arguments, not insults. Augustine, when disputing with Pascentius <note>A 5th-century Arian official who challenged Augustine to a debate</note>, always calls him a "most illustrious man," even though Pascentius, following the dogma of the Arians, denied that the Son was of the same substance as the Father. With Pollentius, he disputes regarding divorce in such a way that there is no mention of heresy anywhere. To the idolaters of Madaura, he writes back honorably, calling them "dearest brothers" and "praiseworthy lords"; nor is he burdened by helping their cause when it is commended to him.

Inquisitors have been given this task: to be indicators, not judges; teachers, not sycophants; monitors, not calumniators; guardians of the faith, not those affecting a tyranny under the pretext of defending the faith.

Heresy does not exist where there is no ambition, where there is no malice, and where stubbornness is not the companion of arrogance. Nor is heresy found in just any error, but only in those things which properly belong to the Catholic faith and are expressly contrary to the Canonical Books.

How unjust it is to inflict such a great insult with impunity, while no reward or retribution is proposed for the accused who wins, except that he seems to have escaped. Those who falsely bring a charge of heresy take away the praise for their "zeal"; those who clear themselves of the slander depart as if marked by a "shoemaker’s stain" <note>original: *futorio atramento*; a figurative expression meaning they are cleared but still left with a lingering social stain or "blackened" reputation</note>.

Christ himself does not extinguish the smoking flax, nor does he break the bruised reed; yet we, because of a human slip—no, rather because of our own deed—alienate upright and successful minds.

Is it not most shameful that the *Conclusions* of Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a brilliant Renaissance philosopher whose 900 theses were initially condemned by the Church, though later partially cleared</note> were once condemned as impious and heretical by great theologians among the Italians, which are now read piously as Christian works by everyone, and not without the applause of theologians?

Now I perceive that there are some who hunt for fame by carping at the writings of others—a shortcut, indeed, but a most wicked one. Once, that famous flute-player showed a better way of suddenly acquiring a name: by proving himself to the learned and to those celebrated by the common people; for by their votes, it would happen that he would also be approved by the populace. But what evil genius showed these men this method? They thrust themselves sideways into another’s work and pluck at one or two places; and soon, the fame which another has acquired for himself through the vigils of many years, they match in a single day. Nor do they merely match it, but even surpass it; for he is held to be a "doctor" who is a "reprover" and a "censor."

What kind of ingratitude is this, to claim the praise of the whole work for oneself because of one or two corrected spots, while meanwhile concealing how much one was helped in so many other places? It is just as if someone, having been given six hundred gold pieces, were to cry out that one or two of them were <term>ἐμβόλιμον</term> <note>original: *embolimon*; meaning "intercalated" or "inserted fraudulently"</note> or <term>κίβδηλον</term> <note>original: *kibdelon*; meaning "counterfeit" or "spurious"</note>. Or if someone were to condemn an entire banquet because one dish served was saltier than it should be.

If it is a matter of detestable ingratitude to deny a benefit received, how will it appear to return an insult for a service rendered for free? And if he is considered ill-bred who "looks a gift horse in the mouth," how will he be regarded who seeks nothing in a necessary work except something to gnaw on?

If there were someone who was entirely <term>ἀναλφάβητος</term> <note>original: *analphabetos*; meaning "illiterate" or "unlearned"</note> and uneducated, who out of some pious zeal of the soul corrected or repaired the Gospel codices for free: would it not happen that everyone would embrace the piety of this man? Would they not inscribe this man’s memory in their records? And yet in this service, which brings far more utility and costs us not a little more, some people are so ungrateful.

If someone gives those men a new cloak, if someone receives them with a more sumptuous dinner, if someone bestows a few coins: they nearly adore him, they preach the man’s piety everywhere; they impart their own merits—of which they possess an abundance, of course—to him. But they were in greater need of this benefit of mine, yet they bark at the one who has served them well.

Furthermore, as for the fact that we have noted in passing certain things which seem to disagree with those things publicly received in the schools: we have done so neither without cause, nor yet in an offensive way. Perhaps it would be expedient for the Christian Commonwealth if more things were uprooted which are now taught publicly as oracles, even while people privately confess that they feel differently.

One man acts so that the world may be Thomist, another Scotist, another Occamite, another a Realist, another a Nominalist <note>These refer to the "Ways" or schools of Scholastic philosophy based on the teachings of Thomas Aquinas, Duns Scotus, and William of Ockham</note>. Why do we all not rather act so that the world may be Christian?

Now I hear some boasting that many things were passed over by me which would be worthy of note. First, I want the reader to be advised that I have not pursued everything in the New Testament that seemed to need noting, but only those things which pertain to the integrity of the reading. Indeed, even here we have prudently omitted many things, lest we burden the reader. But if anyone adds something to our work, I will even congratulate the public utility. Nay, if someone disagrees with us in some place, provided he does so with arguments and not with insults—as is worthy of a learned man—I shall not be offended in the least. Arguments can be honorably refuted by arguments; but to retaliate against insults with insults is shameful, even while it is painful to endure them. He who acts with reasons both takes up a simple task for himself and presents a simple task for the response. But he who disagrees insultingly takes up and creates a double task, and invites a twin evil, while he both harms another’s reputation and wins for himself the suspicion of being a slanderer.

Just as being of use is most beautiful, so it is most difficult. Just as causing harm is most easy, so it is most foul. Why does this latter part please most people more? Let those who desire fame among posterity declare themselves great in the other way—the way worthy of a Christian man.

If I had any incantation by which I could put this new kind of asps to sleep, I would not be burdened to use it. Now, since that is not granted: against the poisonous hissing of those men, I console myself with the favor of good people, as if with an antidote. They bark, but among the truly learned, almost none do so; those who do are of that genus of men who seem to have devoted themselves to the gods of the underworld if they can utterly extinguish good letters—that is, all the things they themselves have not learned. For I believe we should ignore the idiots from the dregs of the common crowd, along with the superstitious "old women" <note>A common Erasmian trope for the uncritical or overly traditionalist</note>, whom those men have either bribed to shout or have suborned. Against the malice of these, first of all, a right conscience consoles me, as does Christ our judge and superintendent; and then the judgments of so many men, some of whom are vindicated from contempt by their holiness of life, others by their distinguished learning, others by the splendor of their fortune, others by the dignity of their ecclesiastical office, and some by all these things at once. Their vote ought to have more weight because there is no one among them whose favor I have either earned by service or flattered out of them with prayers. In letters sent from every corner of the earth, they thank me daily because by my labors, such as they are, they have been inflamed toward a good mind and the study of Sacred Literature; and those who have never seen Erasmus nevertheless love him as known through his books. Not one of these was provoked by me, as I just said, nor is there any reason why they should flatter me. There is nothing they might fear from me, or hunt for from me. Proven utility and a grateful heart have won these votes for me. As I have labored for everyone in common, so all the candid and upright—of whatever nation, of whatever order—return thanks. I consider this a most beautiful reward, more than if the dignity of a Bishop had fallen to me. Italy recognizes my service, for I am compelled...

### HEADINGS OF ARGUMENTS AGAINST THE CRITICS

...to be more glorious, especially at Rome and Venice. So many Cardinals favor our labors, but especially that man most accomplished in the weightier branches of literature, Cardinal Domenico Grimani <note>A renowned Venetian humanist and patron of the arts</note> of the title of Saint Mark; and most laden with every kind of distinction, the Cardinal of the title of the Four Saints <note>Lorenzo Pucci, a powerful figure in the Roman Curia</note>; Matthew, Cardinal of Sion; Cardinal Lorenzo Campeggio; and before these, Raphael, Cardinal of Saint George <note>Raffaele Riario</note>, and Francesco, Cardinal of Volterra. Indeed, the very prince of the entire Christian Republic, Leo X, just as he encouraged me toward the first edition with most kindly written letters, so afterward he encouraged me again toward the later one. Meanwhile, I shall not recount the many Bishops and hundreds of learned men. After Leo came Adrian VI, a man who, besides the sanctity of his life, was endowed with singular erudition and the keenest judgment. Again, what favor does Clement VII not bestow upon our studies—and that without my soliciting or even wishing for it? Surely a man born from the very stock of ancestors destined to help the best disciplines, he bestows this favor upon studies and religion, not upon me. Nor did the favor of these men I have listed consist merely of words, letters, and common courtesies; it was declared by more certain proofs. 

Spain has recognized this even by this argument: that Francisco, Cardinal of Toledo <note>Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros, who produced the rival Complutensian Polyglot Bible</note>, once and again solicited me with rewards by no means to be despised to come to the Spanish lands. Furthermore, William de Croy, Cardinal and Archbishop of Toledo—into whose dignity and zeal toward me succeeded that exceptional light of the Spains, Alfonso Fonseca—it is too well known to most people with what spirit he always pursued me to need recording here. All Germany recognizes it, with the letters of the highest Prelates and Princes calling me to the most ample rewards, decorating and at the same time exciting our industry with gifts that are not common. Hungary recognizes it; Moravia and Poland recognize it, giving thanks to me through the letters of Bishops and leading men, and not without distinguished gifts. Chief among these are two brothers, Jan Turzo, formerly Bishop of Wrocław, and Stanisław, Bishop of Olomouc. Among the Sarmatians <note>A historical term Erasmus uses for the peoples of Poland and the surrounding regions</note> there is Piotr, Bishop of Kraków and Chancellor of the Kingdom; with him Andrzej Krzycki, Bishop of Płock; and Jan, Bishop of Chełm, as famous for his letters as for his miter. 

For what shall I say of Britain, where I have so many patrons? First among them is the most illustrious Baron William Mountjoy; next, William, Archbishop of Canterbury and Primate of all England <note>William Warham</note>; third, Thomas, Cardinal of York <note>Thomas Wolsey</note>, a man of the keenest judgment. The supreme King himself <note>Henry VIII</note>, flourishing no less in the goods of the mind than of fortune, both of whom by their own kindness voluntarily foster our leisure and, if it should please me, invite me to greater things. In this catalog, where votes are weighed rather than merely counted, I could count John Fisher, Bishop of Rochester, as one man standing for many. Then there is Cuthbert Tunstall, formerly Bishop of London, now of Durham. Into the office of William Warham succeeded Thomas Cranmer <note>Original: "Thomas Cromerus." Cranmer succeeded Warham in 1533</note>, a man who is a theologian not only by profession, but truly theological in mind and character, who in his favor toward me yields in no way to the man he succeeded. Add to these John Longland, Bishop of Lincoln, famous also for his published books. By the French—especially by that incomparable man Étienne Poncher, Bishop of Paris, and by the Most Christian King Francis I—I am now so often invited with promises that are not common. 

Finally, although sycophants prevail nowhere on earth more than among our own people, and nowhere is less honor given to good literature, nevertheless there are those here too who favor one laboring for the public good. Chief among these is that most prudent and at the same time most eagle-eyed man, Erard de la Marck, Bishop and Prince of Liège, now a Cardinal and first Counselor of the Imperial Court; and the most illustrious Philip of Burgundy, Bishop and Prince of Utrecht. Both of these voluntarily offer an ample fortune if I were to seek anything of the kind. Meanwhile, let me not fail to mention the Emperor Charles V and his brother Ferdinand. I have touched only upon the most prominent among the highest, since I am daily overwhelmed by letters in which celebrated Universities, men outstanding in doctrine, and those commendable in religion both congratulate me and give me thanks. 

I have recounted something of the "braggart soldier" from the Comedy <note>A reference to the character *Miles Gloriosus* from the plays of Plautus; Erasmus admits he sounds like he is boasting</note>; the wickedness of certain men drove me to this. And yet, I have lied so little that I have knowingly kept silent about many others. For there are those who prefer to favor me in secret, just as Nicodemus favored Jesus. Nor have I ambitiously proclaimed their praises, though I could have most truly done so; nor have I set before your eyes how great a difference there is between those who approve, favor, and help, and those who clamor, calumniate, and condemn. Both groups deserved to be painted in their true colors, but it was necessary to remember Christian modesty. Nor does it matter to weigh down the latter with greater hatred, since they have rendered themselves so hated by their own shouts and behaviors that the world has long been trying to shake them off. Therefore, relying on the minds and votes of so many and such great men, I bear more moderately the grunting of these most ungrateful sycophants.

It is indeed most happy to have pleased everyone. But, since that has happened to no one yet, the next best thing is to have pleased the best people.

To draw the whole case into a few words, then, against those who condemn this entire undertaking: I have taught that it is pious, and always will be, to either remove errors from the sacred Books or to add some light to them, and that whatever anyone brings to this task according to his own measure is pleasing to the Holy Spirit. If anyone constructs a calumny against my intent, I can do nothing else than make Christ my witness that I have looked to nothing other than His glory and the benefit of the Christian people. If anyone claims that the authority of the Scriptures is endangered, I have demonstrated that by this industry it is preserved, not destroyed. 

If anyone imagines a "commotion" from this novelty, we do not change the public reading by private authority—nay, we warn so many times that this should not be done. If there was any commotion, novelty did not give birth to it, but rather the untimely shouts of certain men before the unlearned multitude. If these critics were from the dregs of the common people, I could be blamed for imprudently giving this handle to the ignorant; but now, since this has been done by the "pillars of wisdom," I ought not to be accused if I suspected that no such thing would arise from such men. 

Against those who require public authority, I have taught that none is necessary in a work prepared for private reading. It is enough that what I bring forward is submitted to the judgment of the Church. If anyone finds me lacking in proper erudition, I think I have surpassed as many as have dealt with this subject until now. If they find me lacking in care—if anything was missing—we have stuffed the later editions with better things, as the proverb goes. If anyone blames this too, I shall say: "I am human," and I follow the example of the most approved men. 

If anyone denies that I am a Theologian, I have played the part of a Grammarian <note>A "Grammarian" in this context refers to a scholar of language and philology</note>. If they despise a Grammarian, a Caesar does not despise the office of a barber or a herald. If they cry out that this could only have been performed by a Theologian—then as the lowliest of Theologians, I have taken upon myself the lowliest function of Theology. If no one is a Theologian unless someone else is more learned than he, the world will have but one Theologian. And yet, everyone has his own gifts. If no one brings forth better things, the matter itself will speak: that I have not altogether wasted my labor. If someone does bring better things, a double grace will be owed to me: first, because I spurred them on by my example, and second, because I helped them by preparing the way. 

If anyone cries out that these matters are too trivial for a Theologian to turn his eyes toward them, the many notable slips of otherwise great Theologians cry out in return. If any are ashamed not to know these things, let them learn, and the shame will depart. If it shames or irks them to learn, pardon will be given to their shame, it will even be given to their laziness; but it will not be given to their malice if they roar against younger men who desire to learn these things. If it makes someone feel poorly that I have touched upon certain Theologians too freely, the cause seemed to me then to require it, though I have moderated this too in later editions. I have attacked no "order" <note>Referring to religious orders like the Franciscans or Dominicans</note> anywhere; I have drawn my pen against no one unless most virulently provoked, and even then, I was always superior in civility to the provoker. Nor has any Theologian or Monk yet raved against me, even if a few Rabbis <note>Erasmus uses "Rabbis" here as a derogatory term for legalistic Christian doctors of theology</note> and many cloaked men have done so. But I beseech you through Christ: if we continue in this manner to attack one another with our teeth, what remains but that by mutual...

<meta>This page concludes Erasmus’s defense against his critics before transitioning into the formal Preface for his famous "Annotations on the New Testament." In the previous section, he listed the high-ranking Church officials who supported his work to shield himself from accusations of heresy. ...are we to be worn down by your habits at last? How much more sensible it would have been if anyone who finds something lacking in my writings would either advise me privately, so that I might fix it myself, or refute it publicly—but with arguments, not scurrilous insults. In this way, the reader would not be infected by the poison of bitterness, and I would owe a great debt of gratitude. Let the elders kindly favor the progress of the younger men; let the younger men, in turn, not insult the elders. Thus the fairness and integrity of the seniors, combined with the modesty and respect of the juniors, will nourish harmony, exclude turmoil, diminish envy, protect the authority of professors, and preserve the dignity of the profession while increasing its usefulness. Come now, as many of us as wish to be true theologians, true monks, and indeed true Christians: let us embrace this counsel, and we shall not regret having obeyed. From these rabid contentions, what can be expected except an ending just as bitter as the introductions we have seen for a long time now? These words, I believe, will abundantly satisfy anyone who allows himself to be satisfied in any way. As for those who stop their ears so as not to know, and close their eyes so as not to see, this "fable is told in vain." <note>original: "frustra canitur hæc fabula." A classical idiom meaning to speak to someone who refuses to listen.</note> Therefore, let enough have been given to this business for now.

### TO CERTAIN SURLY AND UNLEARNED MEN.

# PREFACE TO THE ANNOTATIONS ON THE NEW TESTAMENT
## OF THE FIRST EDITION,

->which was in the year 1515; to which, however, certain things were<-
->added later, pertaining to a later time up to the years 1521,<-
->1527, and 1535. I did not want you to be ignorant of this,<-
->reader, lest you be offended by anything.<-

->**DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM**<-

->SENDS GREETINGS TO THE PIOUS READER.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a seated figure in a landscape or garden setting.</image-desc>

*ALTHOUGH* we have done our best in this regard at the very threshold of this work, it will nonetheless be worthwhile to remind the reader once more in a few words what they ought to expect in these little commentaries, and what, in turn, it is appropriate for the reader to provide to us. First, we have written "little annotations," not full commentaries, and only those which pertain to the integrity of the reading. We do this so that no one—like a rude dinner guest—demands a full feast in place of a light snack, or requires from us something that is foreign to the profession of the subject we have undertaken. We have taken up the task of performing this particular play for the present. Therefore, just as we have had to serve the subject matter, it is only fair that the fair-minded and courteous reader, like a well-behaved spectator, should favor the actors and accommodate themselves to the scene being presented. 

We have revised the "New Testament," as they call it, with all the diligence we could muster and with the faith that was proper, and we have done so first according to the Greek truth <note>original: "Græcam veritatem." Erasmus famously argued that the Greek text was the ultimate authority for correcting the Latin Bible.</note>. To this Greek text, as if to a fountainhead, we must flee if any doubt arises; this is not only suggested by the examples of illustrious theologians, but Jerome and Augustine warn of it repeatedly, and the very decrees of the Roman Pontiffs command it. Second, we followed the authority of the oldest Latin manuscripts, two of which were provided by that distinguished initiate of divine philosophy, John Colet <note>The Dean of St. Paul's Cathedral in London and a close friend of Erasmus</note>, Dean of the Pauline Church in London. These were in such ancient script that I had to learn to read all over again and become a child once more in recognizing the characters. 

A third manuscript was provided by the most illustrious noblewoman <note>original: "virago," here used in the classical sense of a woman with heroic, manly spirit.</note> Margaret, aunt of the Emperor Charles; in this third edition, we have frequently cited the testimony of this "Golden Codex," so named because it is entirely covered in gold and beautifully written in golden letters. Soon after, the very ancient and by far most celebrated College of Saint Donatian in Bruges provided several manuscripts of marvelous antiquity. For previously, the College of Corsendonk had provided a beautifully corrected manuscript, in addition to those which the most learned Amerbach brothers shared with us. 

Therefore, we have not corrected things according to the dreams of our own mind, but according to the authority of the manuscripts I have listed, and others like them which it is not necessary to mention here. Finally, we looked to the citations, corrections, or explanations of the most approved authors: namely Origen, Chrysostom, Cyril, Jerome, Ambrose, Hilary, Augustine, Theophylact, Basil, and Bede. We have brought forward their testimonies in several places so that when the prudent reader sees that our correction in certain places agrees with their judgment, they may also have faith in us in other places—where I do not know if it happened by chance that they noted nothing, or if they otherwise supported the reading. 

However, since I knew it is human nature for novelty to be offensive—especially in scholarly pursuits—and that most people look for that old taste and that familiar, well-known "flavor," as they say; and then, considering how much easier it is (especially in these times) to corrupt corrected books than to correct corrupted ones, I have attached these annotations like index-markers to the revised Sacred Books. This was done partly to satisfy the reader by giving the reason why and what was changed (or at least to appease them if something should offend them, since the minds and judgments of mortals vary so much), and partly to look out for the safety of the work, lest hereafter it be easy for anyone to ruin again what had been restored with such great labor. 

First, therefore, if we found anything corrupted by either the carelessness or ignorance of scribes, or by the injury of time, we have restored it to the genuine reading—not rashly, but by scenting out everything possible. If anything was said obscurely, we have illustrated it; if anything was said ambiguously or perplexingly, we have explained it. Wherever a variety of manuscripts, or a different punctuation, or the ambiguity of the language itself gives rise to various meanings, we have opened them up in such a way as to show what we prefer, while leaving the final judgment to the reader. And although we do not willingly disagree with the Translator <note>The traditional author of the Latin Vulgate, usually identified as St. Jerome</note>—whoever he was—because of the long-standing and accepted edition, nevertheless, wherever the facts themselves cry out openly that he was either drowsy or hallucinating, we have not feared to point this out to the reader, championing the truth in such a way that we are insulting to no one. 

We have removed evident and monstrous solecisms <note>grammatical errors</note>, and we have pursued elegance of language everywhere as much as possible, while ensuring the simplicity remained no less. Nor did we shrink from pointing out and revealing where the idiom or emphasis of the Greek language contains something pertaining to the nature of the mystery. Finally, we have compared and examined the testimonies of the Old Instrument <note>The Old Testament</note>—of which not a few are cited—either from the Translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> or from the Hebrew sources themselves, whenever their edition differs from the Hebrew origin. This, however, was "not walking straight," <note>original: "οὐκ ὀρθοποδεῖν" (ouk orthopodein). A Greek proverb used by Erasmus here to mean he is out of his depth or stepping outside his usual path.</note> as the Greek proverb has it: for nothing is further from my nature and habits than to sell myself with "borrowed feathers," like the crow in Aesop's fable. Therefore, in this part, when we first published this work, we were aided by the secondary labor of a man eminent not only for piety but also for his skill in the three languages—that is, a true theologian, Johannes Oecolampadius of Weinsberg—because I myself had not yet progressed far enough in Hebrew letters that I would take it upon myself to judge...*

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s introductory defense of his work on the New Testament. Having previously addressed his critics, he now explains the necessity of his "minute" linguistic labor—correcting the Latin text by returning to the original Greek—and argues that even the smallest grammatical details are vital for a true understanding of divine wisdom.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...authority. Indeed, I was well aware that these small details and, as it were, thorns, involve far more sweat than glory, and that little gratitude usually returns to the author from this kind of labor; moreover, it is of more use to the reader than pleasure. But if we have swallowed so much weariness out of respect for public utility, it is surely fair that the reader, for the sake of his own benefit, should likewise digest a bit of trouble, and show the same spirit toward himself and his own advantage that we have shown in helping others.

These things we are treating are very small, I admit, but they are of such a kind that those great matters could have been handled with almost less effort—the ones which sublime theologians, with high eyebrows and cheeks puffing with pride, are accustomed <term>to represent as a tragedy</term> <note>original: ἐκτραγῳδίζειν (ektragōdizein); to make a grand or exaggerated performance of something.</note>. Furthermore, they are of such a kind that, because of these very small "minutiae," even those greatest matters must sometimes be scrutinized. They are tiny things, it is true, but because of these tiny things, we see even the greatest theologians sometimes remarkably slip and hallucinate. As we have indicated in several places—not to attack anyone (a sickness which should be as far as possible from a Christian work, indeed, from the entire Christian life), but rather to prove our reliability to the reader by citing a few examples without insulting anyone, lest anyone despise these as mere trifles. For indeed, as the poet *Horace* said: "these trifles lead to serious matters." <note>original: "hæ nugæ seria ducunt." A quote from Horace's *Ars Poetica*.</note>

Why are we so fastidious in the preparation of food? Why are we offended by even the smallest flaws in our clothing? In financial matters, there is nothing so small that it is not taken into account. Why is it that in Divine Literature alone this diligence is disliked, and neglect is preferred? I will not even mention for the moment the majesty of the subject: no part of it can be so humble that it should be loathed by a pious man—rather, there is no part that should not be handled with reverence and religious care. "He crawls on the ground," they say; "he tortures himself over words and syllables." But why do we think his word is to be despised, when we worship and adore him under the title of "the Word"? Especially since he himself testified that not even the smallest <note>original: "iota," the smallest letter of the Greek alphabet.</note> or tiny mark <note>original: "apiculum," referring to the "tittle" or small stroke in writing.</note> would pass away in vain.

The "letter," as they call it, is the lowest part, but the mystical sense rests upon this as a foundation. These are ruins, but the majestic mass of that wonderful building is supported by these ruins. Saint *Jerome* <note>A 4th-century Church Father and translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> criticized several excellent Greek writers because, having despised the historical sense, they preferred to play with allegories according to their own whim; and he deplored himself because, while still hot with youth, he had interpreted the Prophet *Obadiah* allegorically when he did not know the history. Just as a precious pearl lies hidden in a very cheap shell, as a noble grain is covered under a worthless husk, and as a miraculous power of seed lies hidden under a dry and tiny skin: so in words that appear common—and finally in the very marks of the letters—the immense mysteries of divine Wisdom are hidden. Anyone who wonders why that divine Spirit wished to hide his riches in these wrappings should also wonder why Eternal Wisdom assumed the person of a poor, humble, despised, and condemned man.

So that he might know these small details, Saint *Jerome* did not look down on a Jewish teacher—and one who came by night—nor did he flee any labor. Because of these small details, Saint *Augustine*, already a Bishop and an old man, returned to the Greek letters he had loathed as a boy. Because of these, *Origen* <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) known for his textual criticism.</note>, already grey-haired and old, descended to the basic elements of the Hebrew language as if becoming a child again, surpassing even the famous Roman *Cato*. *Ambrose* gladly alludes to these small details, and *Hilary* stands by them. *Chrysostom*—who was "golden-mouthed" in more than just name—examines them everywhere and philosophizes on them with pious curiosity. And *Cyril*, following him, draws a great mystery from a Greek article—that is, from a single little letter, <term>the</term> <note>original: ὁ (ho); the Greek definite article.</note>—and from this he borrows a kind of inevitable weapon to hurl at heretics.

I will not mention, meanwhile, that while we take care of these things professionally, those larger matters are nonetheless opened up in passing. For just as those who explain the meanings of sentences are sometimes forced to explain the logic of the words, so we, while we are occupied in explaining words, are forced in the interim to reveal the force of the meanings as well. Finally, we are preparing these things for the more serious commentaries on *Paul* that we have already begun. In those, perhaps, it will appear whether I descended to these small details by judgment or by chance.

But come, let anyone who wishes imagine that I could provide nothing else—whether because of a slowness of wit and "cold blood around the heart," or because of a lack of learning—and that I took up this lowest province. Nevertheless, it is the mark of a Christian heart to think well of any duty, whatever it may be, that is performed with pious diligence. *Christ* praised the farthing cast into the treasury by the poor woman, valuing a thing worthless in itself by the spirit of the giver. In a truly magnificent enterprise, even the lowest function is splendid. In royal palaces, those who sweep and those who cook are considered honorable. Furthermore, in the house of God, what function can possibly seem loathsome?

We have brought together the rubble, but for the structure of the temple of God. Others, more wealthy, will add ivory, gold, marble, and gems. We have paved the way, which was previously troublesome with ruts and puddles, through our industry; but on this path, the great theologians will afterwards be carried more comfortably in their carriages and nags. We have leveled the ground of the arena, in which they may now display those magnificent processions of their wisdom with their strides. We have cleared with a hoe the fallow land, previously inconvenient with thorns and briers, so that they may more easily cultivate a happy crop. We have opened the field, removing the obstacles, so that those who wish hereafter to unfold the secret Letters may either play more freely or engage more readily. For those whom that ancient Theology more pleases, they have a great support to lean on as they struggle through. Again, for him who says, according to the Gospel parable, "the old wine is better," and in his zeal for this more recent theology neglects the old, he also has what he may enjoy, and may handle what he prefers more certainly and faithfully.

And even if no convenience should come from this, he will certainly lose nothing of his own if benefits come to those who prefer to draw the divine Letters from the purest fountains rather than from any kind of rivulets and pools, which have been poured from one place to another so many times—not to mention being disturbed by their own claws and those of asses. Just as a fruit is more pleasing which you have plucked with your own hands from the mother tree itself, just as water is sweeter which you have drawn as it bubbles from the vein itself, just as wine is more delightful which you have drawn from the very jar in which it was first stored: so the divine Letters have I know not what native fragrance; they breathe something of their own and something genuine if they are read in that language in which they were first written by those who partly drew them from that sacred and heavenly mouth, and partly delivered them to us, inspired by the same Spirit.

If the speeches of Christ were extant in Hebrew or Syriac, and if they were delivered in the very words in which he spoke, who would not have it in his heart to philosophize on them, and to examine not only the force and property of the words, but even every single mark? Certainly, we have what is closest to this, and we neglect it. If someone displays the garment of Christ, or the footprint of his foot, we fall down, we adore, we kiss it. And yet, though you might bring forth all his clothes and the entire furniture of his mother’s house, there is nothing that refers to, expresses, and represents Christ more vividly, effectively, and perfectly than the writings of the Evangelists and Apostles.

Accordingly, if anyone is either not permitted or does not wish to be occupied in these sacred delights, let him at least not make a noise, let him not disturb, let him not envy those who are attempting better things. Let them embrace what they love, let them have it, let them enjoy it. No one forbids it. We did not write these things for them. But there will be those on the other side to whom these things seem very few, and who would prefer nothing to agree with the Vulgate edition. Truly, we did not strive for this—that the speech should be more polished—but that it should be more corrected and clearer. Nor was a "knot to be sought in a bulrush," as they say. Rather, it is to be hoped by everyone that there should be nothing anywhere in the sacred Letters that requires this labor.

In the Gospels, because the tenor of the history flows in a simple and unaffected style, being clear in itself and almost self-explanatory, it was not even possible for either a translator or a scribe to corrupt very many things. Although these very things, if one weighs the sum, are even too many in a place where no doubt should have existed. However, in the Apostolic Epistles, because of the obscurity of the speech and the meanings alike, it was necessary to change more. Meanwhile, we have moderated our diligence in noting things so that we would appear neither troublesome through superstition nor diminished through negligence. We have indicated the whole matter in as few words as possible rather than explaining it, lest we add the weariness of loquacity to a task that is, by its own nature, not very pleasant.

The Work is pious; the Work is Christian. Accordingly, I ask you, best of readers, that you too, in turn, bring pious ears and a Christian heart to the reading. Let no one take this into his hands with the spirit in which he perhaps takes up the *Attic Nights* of Gellius or the *Miscellanies* of Angelo Poliziano—namely, to test the strength of wit, the force of eloquence, and recondite erudition as if against a Lydian stone. We are occupied in a sacred matter, and in that matter which was commended to the world primarily for its simplicity and purity. In this, it would be ridiculous to want to display human erudition, and impious to boast of human eloquence—which, even if it were perhaps present, it was proper to disguise, lest anyone might justly object: <term>whatever may appear foolish</term> <note>original: ὃ Φανῇ μῶρον (ho phanē mōron); a reference to the "foolishness" of the Gospel compared to worldly wisdom.</note>. We have delivered these things to Christian ears with a simple and pure zeal, so that hereafter more people might be occupied in this most holy Philosophy, and more willingly—and finally, that they might do so with less effort and greater fruit.

I pray that Christ himself—with whom as witness and helper I undertake these things—may be little favorable to me unless we hunt for so little profit from these labors that we even knowingly and...

He asserts that the written word of the Apostles is a more vivid representation of Christ than any physical relic.</summary>

# PREFACE TO THE ANNOTATIONS ON THE NEW TESTAMENT.

...we have received them willingly. Furthermore, far from being tickled by the sweetness of fame, we would not even have added our own name to this work, had we not feared that by this means the utility of the Work might be diminished: for an anonymous book is a suspect thing among all people. We are equally prepared for either outcome: to give an account if we have advised correctly, or to frankly confess our error wherever we are found to have slipped. We are but human, and we consider nothing human to be foreign to us <note>original: "Homines sumus, & humani nihil alienum à nobis esse ducimus"; a famous line from the Roman playwright Terence, used here by Erasmus to express humility regarding his own potential for mistakes.</note>. Therefore, since I have given these things with this mind, best Reader, see to it that you also receive them in a similar spirit. That will be for the benefit of both of us. For you will gain more utility if you receive what is given willingly and candidly, and I shall less regret my late-night labors if I learn they have been of use to good people. 

But if anyone should arise who is so stubborn and morose, or so harsh and unjust, that they cannot be charmed by any spells <note>Erasmus uses the metaphor of "incantamentis" (spells/charms) to suggest that no amount of reasoning can soften a truly bitter critic.</note>, I shall certainly strive to obtain from them, at least by prayers, that they grant at least that much fairness to these pious studies as the law courts grant to parricides and those guilty of sacrilege. In those places, it is judged a disgrace if the voting stones precede the investigation, and no sentence is pronounced until the case has been diligently examined. Let such a person first read and inspect, and then, if it seems right, let them condemn and reject. It is arrogant to pass judgment on a book you do not understand, and more arrogant still to judge one you have not even read. Farewell, Reader, whoever you are; I ask you again and again that if you gather any fruit from these late-night labors of ours, be mindful, as is worthy of a Christian, to commend me in turn to Christ with your pious prayers, from whom alone we expect the solid reward for this labor.

# THE SUBJECT OF THE CANONS
## FOR THE HARMONY OF THE EVANGELISTS.

->E U S E B I U S<-

->TO C A R P I A N U S<-

->HIS BELOVED BROTHER IN THE LORD,<-

->G R E E T I N G S.<-

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'A' within a square frame, embellished with intricate foliage, vines, and classical stylistic patterns.</image-desc>AMMONIUS the Alexandrian <note>A 3rd-century Christian scholar from Alexandria who created one of the first Gospel harmonies.</note>, having brought to the task much industry and zeal, as was fitting, left to us the "Gospel through Four" <term>Diatessaron; a harmony of the four Gospels woven into a single narrative</term>. He placed the corresponding sections of the other Evangelists alongside the Gospel according to Matthew, so that the continuous flow of the other three was necessarily broken, at least as far as the reading of the text is concerned. However, so that the entire body and sequence of the others might be preserved while you are still able to know the specific places in each Evangelist where they were moved by a love of truth to speak on the same subjects, I took my starting point from the work of the aforementioned man. Using a different method, I have drawn up for you ten tables, which are set out below. 

The first of these contains the numbers where all four have spoken similarly: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The second, where three have: Matthew, Mark, and Luke. The third, where three have: Matthew, Luke, and John. The fourth, where three have: Matthew, Mark, and John. The fifth, where two have: Matthew and Luke. The sixth, where two have: Matthew and Mark. The seventh, where two have: Matthew and John. The eighth, where two have: Luke and Mark. The ninth, where two have: Luke and John. The tenth, where each of them has recorded something unique to themselves. This, then, is the subject of the tables set out below. 

The clear explanation for using them is as follows: in each of the four Gospels, a number is placed by each section, starting from the first, then the second, third, and so on, proceeding through the whole until the end of the book. Next to each number, a notation is placed in black ink, indicating in which of the ten Canons <term>tables or rules</term> that number happens to be located. For example, if it is a 1 (Alpha), it is clearly in the first; if it is a 2 (Beta), it is in the second; and so on up to ten. 

Therefore, if you open any one of the four Gospels and wish to stop at a certain chapter to know who has said similar things and to find the corresponding places in each where they were moved by the same spirit, you may take the number assigned to the section you are holding. By looking for that number within the Canon indicated by the black ink notation, you will immediately know from the headings at the top of the Canons how many and which others have spoken similarly. Then, by looking at the numbers of the other Gospels contained within the same row of the Canon you are using, and searching for them in their respective places in each Gospel, you will find them saying similar things. Farewell in the Lord.
