<note>The following section is the commentary, which extends across the page width.</note>

...when I found it written in several copies: why, then, was there such a religious scrupulosity here to translate *the wife of Uriah*? <note>original: "uxorem Uriæ"</note> It should be noted why he preferred to mark Bathsheba with this label rather than her own name—either because the event itself was better known than the woman's name, or because it pertained to the mystery of Christ and the Church to recall the memory of that deed.

<margin>8</margin> **In the transmigration of Babylon]** <note>original: "In transmigratione Babylonis"</note> We certainly perceive the sense well enough, but for those who know from the annals of the Hebrews that the Jewish nation was led captive to Babylon by King Nebuchadnezzar, and restored again to their seats by Ezra. Otherwise, from these words, nothing else can be understood except that either Babylon itself migrated somewhere, or Babylon led others away, if you use *transmigration* in the active sense. Yet the use of speech is applied so that through it those to whom a matter was previously unknown may know and learn it, not so that we might merely recognize or guess what we already knew. Fabius <note>Quintilian, the Roman rhetorician</note> rightly warns that ambiguities are to be avoided as much as possible, even if the sense allows for nothing truly ambiguous: as if someone should say, *I see the Thracian’s fallen sword destroyed*. <note>original: "Video Thracum casum deletum ferru"</note> For there is no danger that the sword might "swallow" the Thracian’s fall. Therefore, this must be avoided much more whenever the meaning is rendered double, or absurd, or nonexistent. Augustine carefully warns about this in the third book of *On Christian Doctrine*. One could have said, *After there was a migration to Babylon*, and *When they had migrated to Babylon*, or *After they had been led to Babylon*: if anyone likes to use <term>metoikesian<gloss>migration/deportation</gloss></term> transitively, or *In the Babylonian migration*. Although it was even clearer to say *in the exile* or *Babylonian captivity*, and *after the exile or Babylonian captivity*. Indeed, the Evangelist tempered the bitterness of the thing with the gentleness of the word, calling captivity and exile a "migration" <note>original: "metoikesian"</note>, which also applies to those who change their seats and homes of their own accord. And Chrysostom <note>An early Church Father</note> thinks this time also, which was spent among the Babylonians, is counted in the reckoning of the genealogy. Furthermore, the verb "to transmigrate" is found in Suetonius in his life of *Tiberius Caesar*: although "to migrate" <note>original: "demigrare"</note> is more Latin, just as he said "transported" for "deported."

<margin>9</margin> **Jeconiah begat Shealtiel]** <note>original: "Jechonias genuit Salathiel"</note> Saint Jerome warns that if this Jeconiah is referred to the end of the previous "fourteen" <note>original: "τεσσαρεσκαίδεκα"</note>, there are not fourteen in the next set, but only thirteen: hence he thinks this Jeconiah, who is the father of Shealtiel, was not the son of Josiah (whom he listed as the second to last in the previous series), but the son of that other Jeconiah. However, he calls him Jeconiah, who is also called Jehoiachin: but the father is distinguished from the son by two letters. For that one is called <note>Hebrew: יְהוֹיָקִים</note> Jehoiakim with a *q* and *m* <note>the Hebrew letters Qoph and Mem</note>: this one <note>Hebrew: יְהוֹיָכִין</note> Jehoiachin with a *k* and *n* <note>the Hebrew letters Kaph and Nun</note>. Although he confesses that this difference in scripture is entirely confused among Greeks and Latins alike by the fault of scribes and the length of time: otherwise, one should even say <note>Hebrew: בַּת שֶׁבַע</note> *Bath-sheba* for *Bethsabee*, which we ourselves have not dared to change.

<margin>10</margin> **The husband of Mary]** <note>original: "τὸν ἄνδρα Μαρίας"</note> He could have said equally well in Latin, and I know not if more modestly, *the maritus of Mary*. Even if I am not unaware that *vir* <note>man/husband</note> is found among the Latins for *maritus* <note>husband/spouse</note>. For these are names of affinity, not of sexual intercourse. But if anyone shrinks from the word *maritus*, let him hear Augustine speaking thus in the twenty-third book against Faustus: *First,* he says, *because he had been her husband, the person is rather to be honored on account of the male sex. For he was not any less a husband because he was not joined in intercourse.* Furthermore, what Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a humanist critic</note> quibbles about in this place concerning "of Mary" and "Mary," I judged too minor to wish to burden the reader here. Especially since if any should inquire, they can seek it from his commentaries published by us long ago.

<margin>11</margin> **Of whom was born Jesus]** <note>original: "ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη"</note> Of whom Jesus was begotten. For it is the passive of that verb which he translates so many times as "begat" <note>original: "ἐγέννησε"</note>. For there is no reason for anyone to be moved by that scruple, that it is improperly said for a woman to beget, since Valla has declared with suitable arguments that both among the Greeks and the Latins, "to beget" <note>Greek: γεννᾷν</note> applies to a woman as much as to a man. Nor without reason does he laugh in this place at certain unlearned men who, as if pronouncing an oracle, distinguish between these two prepositions *ek* <note>ἐκ</note> and *ex* <note>ἐξ</note>: as if *ek* spoke of perpetual conception and *ex* of the flowing forth—"born from the Virgin Mary"—when among the Greeks it is the same preposition *ek*, which the Interpreter <note>the Vulgate translator</note> at his own discretion translated now this way, now however it seemed fit. Certainly, this passage openly refutes the frivolous and fabricated distinction of those men.

<margin>12</margin> **Who is called Christ]** <note>original: "ὁ λεγόμενος Χριστός"</note> Since among the Hebrews there were many of this name, such as Joshua the son of Nun, and Joshua the priest, he distinguished him from the others by adding a surname. Although I see several learned men are of the opinion that the name of our Savior Jesus is somewhat different from the name of the leader Joshua and the priest Joshua, which is written by the Hebrews as <note>Hebrew: יֵשׁוּעַ</note> *Yeshua*. However, they say the name of our Jesus is signed with the same letters with which the ineffable name of God <note>the Tetragrammaton</note> was once signed, with only one consonant *shin* <note>Hebrew: ש</note> interposed. I wish posterity could prove this with solid arguments, as it is a plausible saying and pleasing to Christian ears. I would certainly wish, for this one cause, that the Gospel of Matthew existed written in Hebrew words and letters. If it did, it would be no trouble to either refute or support this opinion about the name of Jesus. Furthermore, *Christ* in Greek means "anointed," by which word the Hebrews signify a king: because among them those who were to undertake the honor of the kingdom were accustomed to be anointed, and by this name the Hebrews call their long-expected one <note>Hebrew: מָשִׁיחַ</note> *Messiah*, explaining the dignity of both king and priest with one word. For anointing is common to both, and both dignities belong to Christ alone. Although it is a small thing, yet it will not be out of place to have warned in passing that the common crowd of clergy in the churches sound the first syllable of *Christ* thin—that is, through a *kappa* rather than a *chi* <note>note: Erasmus is criticizing a hard "K" sound like 'Krist' instead of the aspirated Greek 'Khristos'</note>—so that whenever they call upon Christ in the vocative case, they seem to be addressing "crests" <note>Latin: cristas</note>, not Christ. But he is not offended by barbarisms, I confess, yet he is not soothed by them either. Let pardon be given to those who err simply through ignorance, but those who rightly pay so much honor to this name of the Church that at its pronunciation they bow the body, uncover the head, and bend the knees—one who is of a pious mind will not, I think, be reluctant to take a little trouble to pronounce those most holy words, as far as he can, with integrity and correctness. And just as it is a mark of Christian gentleness not to bitterly attack or pursue with insults the lack of skill of those who err simply, nor to stir up fierce tragedies over such slight errors: so again, it is a mark of Christian simplicity to willingly obey the warnings of the more learned. Otherwise, if anyone, having been warned, obstinately persists in errors, and even laughs at and attacks the monitor to whom he owes thanks, and finally demands that others err with him—that is, that those who see should follow the blind man who wanders—rather than change the error himself, who does not understand how far this is from that Christian simplicity to which pardon is owed? And if God hates boastful skill, how much more do we believe he turns away from haughty and intractable ignorance? They themselves would not endure it if someone called Peter *Pheter*, or Philip *Pilippum*: and they would not endure it for no other reason than because they themselves are not used to speaking that way. <margin>* And an aspirated *phi* [φ] is placed for *pi* [π], which should not be mixed rashly, although they are sometimes confused.</margin> And yet in those matters where the slip is more foul, they do not allow themselves to be warned.

<margin>13</margin> **All generations]** <note>original: "πᾶσαι αἱ γενεαί"</note> The Greek word *pasai* is ambiguous between "all," "any," and "the whole," whence "the whole" or "universal" fits better here, since the sum of the matter is signified.

<margin>14</margin> **Fourteen generations]** Origen, in the commentaries he wrote on the Epistle to the Romans, and Saint Hilary, in his exposition of the canon on Matthew, indicate that from David until that time when they were led to Babylon, not fourteen, but seventeen generations are found: and that this was done neither by a lie nor by the fault of negligence, but deliberately, so that three generations in the middle were passed over. For according to Matthew, Joram begat Uzziah, whereas he is the fourth from him. Indeed, as is related in the fourth book of Kings, Joram begat Ahaziah, Ahaziah begat Joash, Joash begat Amaziah, and Amaziah begat Uzziah, whom they sometimes also call Azariah. Origen disregards the literal letter, and he does this in his own manner. Hilary thinks they were passed over because Joram had fathered Ahaziah from a gentile woman. Furthermore, because it had been predicted through the Prophet that he would not sit on the throne of the kingdom of Israel until the fourth generation, the Evangelist wished to abolish the stain of the ethnic race with silence. But these things do not properly pertain to the purpose, especially since the copies of all the Greeks and Latins agree. For as to what Hilary writes, that it is found in certain books, I believe he is referring to the books of Kings. But Saint Jerome treats this matter more diligently...

### ACCORDING TO MATTHEW. CHAPTER I.

For when his mother Mary was betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit. But Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not wishing to make her a public example, intended to send her away secretly. But as he was thinking on these things, behold, an Angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying: "Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife. For that which..." <note>original: οὕτως ἦν... πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν... ἐκ Πνεύματος ἁγίου</note>

**A** Let the diligent reader consider this error in its place. Let him weigh how the Evangelist was criticized by the impiety of some, even though before Ruth he had placed both the wife of Uriah and Rahab—women famous for their notoriety. <note>Erasmus is defending Matthew's inclusion of "sinful" women in the holy genealogy to show God's grace.</note>

15 *Now the birth of Christ*] <note>original: ἡ γέννησις</note> In my opinion, "nativity" was more accurate than "generation" <note>term: generatio (descent/ancestry)</note>, if only to avoid ambiguity—even if it is not ambiguous to us. Otherwise, "generation" refers not only to the one being born, but also to the one begetting. And it was more "Latin" to say it "was so," rather than "so it was," without changing the sense. It is a minor matter that in the Greek manuscripts we find "of Jesus Christ," but in others "of the Christ." I suspect "Jesus" was added either by a scribe or from the custom of church readings. For neither <term>Chrysostom</term> <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father</note> touches upon the name of Jesus when he mentions Christ (that is, the Messiah). And the added name of Jesus does not fit the context as well. For it says: "And from the migration to Babylon until the Christ are fourteen generations. Now the birth of Christ was thus." The word "Christ" is repeated from the immediate predecessor. He elegantly used this little "preamble" to stir the listener's mind, as he was about to narrate something unheard of and miraculous.

16 *When she was betrothed*] We are missing the conjunction "for" <note>original: γὰρ</note>. <note>original: Μνηστευθείσης γάρ</note>. Although it is of little weight, except that it connects the narrative with the preceding promise. Among the Greeks, the word is more suited and specific to the matter. For they call those who seek a girl’s hand in marriage "suitors" <note>original: μνηστεῦσαι</note>, whom the Latins call <term>proci</term>. And "to betroth" <note>original: μνηστεύειν</note> is to hand over the bride to the suitor.

**C** 17 *Mother of Jesus Mary*] In Greek it is "His mother." For he mentioned Christ just before, so as not to seem to start a discourse about someone else: <note>original: τῆς μητρὸς αὐτοῦ</note>. And it is read this way in very old Latin manuscripts, specifically in two which I had during my second revision, the <term>Pauline</term> and the <term>Corsendonck</term>. Likewise in the "Golden Code" of Margaret, with the agreement of four very old manuscripts provided to us by the College of St. Donatian at Bruges. <term>Origen</term> <note>an early Christian scholar</note> cites it in this way in a homily commonly read in church services, explaining the force of that pronoun "his" with various names. Nor does Chrysostom read it otherwise in his fourth homily on Matthew, nor <term>Theophylact</term> <note>a medieval Byzantine commentator</note>.

18 *Before they came together*] <note>original: πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν</note> He modestly signifies the union of husband and wife. Otherwise, "coming together" refers more to those who agree or are gathered in the same place. Yet we read "congress" and "to come together" for the custom of husband and wife. Although "to go together" <note>original: coire</note> was once a modest word, it later became less pure through common usage. As for those who take this passage as an excuse to rave—saying that Mary later bore children in the common manner of women—<term>Jerome</term> abundantly refutes them writing against <term>Helvidius</term> <note>Helvidius argued that Mary had other children after Jesus</note>, as does Chrysostom explaining this passage. Finally, <term>Lorenzo Valla</term> supports this with examples brought forth from the books of pagans as well. For this was added by the Evangelist not to signify what followed, but to open the miracle of an unusual thing. Just as if someone were to say, "the judges pronounced on the case before they knew the cause"—since by solemn custom judges hear before they pass sentence. He who speaks thus does not mean that the judges learned the cause *after* they passed sentence. Therefore, just as "before they knew the cause" means nothing else than "without the cause being known," so here "before they came together" means nothing else than "without marital union" or "apart from intercourse." Furthermore, the Evangelist narrates the thing as it happened, not as he himself knew it. Joseph did not yet understand the mystery; he saw she was pregnant; he knew no union had occurred, and therefore the Evangelist does not yet pronounce the conception to be virginal until he brings forward the Angel revealing it. For who among men would suspect that a woman had conceived a human fetus from a heavenly Spirit? But the speech would have been less offensive if he had translated it in the past tense, "Before they had come together," or as we translated, "Before they had united." For it is softer to say "Before they had known the cause, they condemned the guilty," than "Before they knew." In the latter, the knowledge seems more likely to follow.

**E** 19 *She was found having in the womb*] <note>original: εὑρέθη</note> Why was it not rather "she was discovered," or certainly "found out"? For we "find" <note>Latin: invenimus</note> what we seek. We "discover" <note>Latin: deprehendimus</note> what was hidden, especially in crimes. We "find out" <note>Latin: reperimus</note> things met by chance or offered beyond hope. Furthermore, the participle "having" <note>original: ἔχουσα</note> is used in place of an infinitive verb. She was discovered to "have," meaning she was discovered "to be having." Chrysostom also noted something on this word in his fourth homily, signifying that something is "found" which is discovered to be new, beyond hope and expectation. It is a wonder why the Latin translator preferred the paraphrase "Having in the womb" for "pregnant" or "with child"—since these not only mean the same thing, but are more modest. For the Latins say "to carry the womb." Although "to have in the womb" is said elegantly and commonly by the Greeks, it is not the same for the Latins. Thus <term>Martial</term>, or his Greek translator, elegantly said "having in the belly" <note>original: ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχουσα</note>. Since <term>Athenaeus</term> in the tenth book of the *Deipnosophistae* writes in this way about the mime Ischomachus: "When a certain poor woman had a pain in her belly, and a doctor asked if she 'had in the belly' [was pregnant], she replied, 'How can I, when I haven't eaten for three days?'" The joke

<column-break/>

fourteen generations, and from the Babylonian migration until the Christ, fourteen generations. <margin>J</margin> <margin>α</margin> 18 But 15 the birth of Christ is as follows. 16 For when his 17 mother Mary was betrothed to Joseph, 18 before they had united, 19 she was discovered pregnant 20 by the Holy Spirit. <margin>β</margin> Furthermore, Joseph 19 her husband, 21 because he was a just man, and 22 did not want to...

**B** lies in this: that while the doctor meant to ask if the woman was pregnant, she took the ambiguity as an excuse for joking. Likewise, <term>Herodotus</term> in his third book writes that King Cambyses of the Persians, "moved by anger, rushed upon his sister and wife when she 'had in the belly' [was pregnant], and she died after a miscarriage." But we shall say a few more things about this shortly.

20 *Of the Holy Spirit*] <note>original: ἐκ Πνεύματος ἁγίου</note>, that is, "from the Holy Spirit." For there is no reason for us to be moved by the artificial distinction of some, even though here the Holy Spirit is placed in the position of the husband. For the reader, hearing that she had not united with a husband and yet was "carrying a womb," was immediately going to think: "from what other man then?" Therefore he quickly excludes this thought, saying "not from a man, but from the Holy Spirit." I would like the prudent and watchful reader to consider this, for here is the place for the distinction made by Saint <term>Augustine</term> in the book *On the Nature of the Good*, which he wrote against the Manichaeans, chapter twenty-six. Anything is correctly said to be "from" <note>Latin: ex</note> someone if it is made by him, but not the other way around. For all things are "from" God as their author, but not "of" <note>Latin: de</note> God, because created things do not share in the divine substance. But that human fetus, insofar as it was human, will more appropriately be said to be "from" the Holy Spirit than "of" the Holy Spirit, according to the aforementioned distinction. Certainly, among the Greeks, the preposition is the same, which we sometimes translate as "of" and sometimes "from."

**D** 21 *Since he was a just man*] <note>original: δίκαιος ὤν</note>. Since the Greek expressed the thought through a participle, it left us free to add a conjunction that would most conveniently fit the sense. But the word "since" sometimes sounds like an opposition—as in, "since you are poor, yet you swell with pride." But here it brings forward the cause why he did not want to expose her: because he was just. As if he had said, "Joseph, because he was a just man, did not want to defame her." It is truly marvelous that he calls him "just" because he did not want to bring her to trial, nor punish what the law commands to be punished. But he calls him "just" not because of one virtue (which is the first among the four moral virtues), but because of a goodness absolute in all its parts. Thus <term>Aristotle</term> in his *Ethics* says, "Justice in itself embraces every virtue," and Sacred Scripture uses "unrighteousness" for any sin. Chrysostom noted this. For it was indeed a rare and extraordinary goodness, when he saw the swollen womb of his betrothed and the indubitable signs of conception, not to argue with his wife, nor complain to the relatives, nor be tortured by jealousy, nor go to law and drag her to punishment, but only to suppress his own turmoils within himself and only think in his mind of a secret divorce. He saw she was pregnant, and the mystery, as I said, he did not yet know, which he soon learns from the Angel.

**F** 22 *He would not lead her away*] <note>original: παραδειγματίσαι (to make a public example)</note>. It is worth stopping here to ask how it happened that the Latin translator, usually negligent of polished speech, thought of such an elegant word [traducere]. For the word should have been translated "to make an example of." Indeed, the elegant use of this word was the reason why several famous theologians stumbled here. Among their number is the not-to-be-despised theologian <term>Peter Lombard</term>, the "rhapsodist" of that work they call the *Sentences*—whom I truly believe was both an upright man and, as that age went, learned. And would that his labor had turned out as happily for the Christian world as it was undertaken by him with pious zeal. For it appears he did this so that, once the relevant points were collected, he might exclude all further questions. But that matter turned out quite the opposite. For we see from that work, as if from a source meant to end questions, not just swarms but oceans of them have erupted. In the fourth book of the *Sentences*, he once and again uses this word [traducere] as if the groom "leads away" the bride when he has "had a matter" [intercourse] with her. For he has it in the twenty-seventh distinction: "Some nevertheless assert that a true marriage is not contracted before the *traduction* and carnal copula, nor are any truly spouses unless a mixing of the sexes intervenes." Again, a little later: "But because she was not yet *traducta* [led away], nor had the wifely matter intervened," that is, marital intercourse. Now I think it is clear enough that Peter Lombard took "union" and interpreted it as such. Otherwise, if he meant "to lead away" as in bringing the bride into the groom’s house, intercourse can occur without this leading, nor is everyone who is led away immediately "known" [sexually]. The example is the mother of the Lord Jesus. And today when the bride is a mere girl, the custom is for the groom to live in one house for one year with the bride's parents. Yet I do not deny that "to lead away" [traducere] in its native sense is to lead from one place to another, just as Demea in <term>Terence</term> orders both the mother and the whole family to be "led over." But there Terence did not use a marital word, nor is it likely that this author imitated Terence; but because he only knew Latin, and that not exactly, what he had read in the Gospel—"he did not want to lead her away"—he interpreted as "he did not want to have a matter with her," because he was thinking of divorce. Nor does it escape me that some want to escape from this by saying *traduction* is taken here for the "consent to live together," which is somewhat even more absurd. It is as if someone, refuting a person who said "gourd" signifies the back of a donkey, should deny it signifies the back itself, but rather the saddles placed on the back. For if *traduction* is consent to live together, why is it separated from the remaining duties of spouses? Or what marriage will there be without the consent of domestic custom? Finally, since this consent is mutual, *traduction* would be attributed as much to the bride as to the groom. But who ever read...

<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of the Gospel of Matthew, Chapter 1. The translator, likely Erasmus, is focusing on the specific wording used to describe Joseph’s reaction to Mary’s pregnancy. He is particularly concerned with the Latin word *traducere* (to expose or lead across) and the Greek word *paradeigmatisai* (to make a public example). He argues against medieval interpretations that misunderstood the Greek linguistic context.</meta>

# THE GOSPEL CHAPTER I.

<margin>21</margin> ...that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. And she will bring forth a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he will save his people from their sins. <note>original: ἐν αὐτῇ γεννηθὲν ἐκ Πνεύματός ἐστιν ἁγίου... Ἰησοῦν</note>
<margin>22</margin> Now all this happened so that what was spoken by the Lord through the Prophet might be fulfilled, saying: <note>original: Τοῦτο δὲ ὅλον γέγονεν... διὰ τοῦ Προφήτου</note>

Who would read that a groom is "led across" (*traducere*)? <note>term: traducere (literally "to lead across," but here used to mean "to expose to public shame")</note> Where among legal experts treating marriage is "leading across" mentioned? Even if they contend a bride is "led across" when she is brought to the groom's house, Joseph and Mary were already living together in one house—indeed, Mary was living in the house of Joseph, her betrothed. Chrysostom clearly testifies to this in his fourth homily on Matthew, adding that it was an ancient custom for brides to be kept in the houses of their grooms. And a little further down in the same homily: *For he did not wish,* he says, *to expel her from the house, but to quietly dismiss her.* By "expelling from the house," he means "exposing her" (*traducere*), because that could not be done without bringing infamy upon the bride, especially since she was pregnant.

Therefore, the facts indicate well enough that Peter Lombard <note>A famous 12th-century theologian known as the "Master of Sentences."</note> (or another author whom he followed) took this passage <margin>B</margin> as an occasion for error, understanding that Joseph, due to suspicion of adultery, did not wish to "confirm the marriage by sexual union." This is a shameful slip, especially for those who profess to be teachers of the whole world, but it should be blamed on the age rather than the man. For what could be done in that century, when the Greek language was utterly extinct, the Latin largely so, and Hebrew letters more than buried? Almost all ancient writers had been obliterated. If something needed explaining, they fled to the Jews as if to a "sacred anchor." <note>A Greek idiom meaning a final resource or last resort.</note> Following this same path, the *Metropolis* is interpreted as coming from *metra* (measure) and *polis* (city) <note>This is a false etymology; Metropolis actually comes from the Greek for "mother city."</note>, whereas in Greek it is *metropolis*. Likewise, *Acolytes*—or, as I certainly think it should be read, *Atoluthos* <note>original: ἀκόλουθος (follower/attendant)</note>, for that is what the Greeks call servants of the body—are interpreted as "taper-bearers," and other similar things. I suspect these were fabricated by more recent writers, as is often the custom in this type of writing.

Indeed, I wonder who suggested to Nicholas of Lyra <note>A prominent medieval Bible commentator.</note> that "to lead across" (*traducere*) is the same as "to make public" (*propalare*). That is how he interprets it. And in the so-called *Ordinary Gloss*, someone adds: *The Greeks use "propalare" for "traducere"*—as if *propalare* were a Greek word! Hugo Cardinalis interprets *traducere* as "to lead into one’s own loss." Although one can gather from many arguments that most writers of those times were assisted by commentaries of the Greeks, which had been translated into Latin however they could be, as we shall show in their proper places. Otherwise, how could Thomas [Aquinas] divine from that translation what Aristotle felt—a translation which Aristotle himself would not have understood even if he had known Latin? I do not condemn them for being helped by the monuments of others. I only wonder why they seem to go out of their way to hide the names of those from whom they profited. Even more, I wonder why the books from which they plucked their ideas were suppressed. But more on this elsewhere.

The "Collector of Sentences" <note>Peter Lombard</note> seems to have hallucinated based on the words of Jerome, who, explaining the present passage, writes in this manner: *If anyone is joined to a fornicator, they become one body. And it is written in the Law that not only the guilty, but also those conscious of crimes, are liable to sin.* As if Joseph for that reason did not want to "expose" (*traducere*) Mary—that is, be joined with her—because he judged her an adulteress and did not want to become one body with her. Yet Jerome is not acting there concerning marital union, but is revealing the reason why Joseph, a just man, did not want to accuse her and make her a public story, as the things that soon follow openly testify. Namely these: *But this is the testimony of Mary: that Joseph, knowing her chastity and wondering at what had happened, hid it in silence, for he did not know the mystery of it.*

There are various uses of this word *traducere* among the Latins. While none is more elegant, none is rarer than when it signifies to "make someone known" and to bring them into the public talk of the common people. Thus Martial says:
> You are laughed at, and much more, Afer, you are traduced (*traduceris*),
> Than if you walked naked in the middle of the forum. <note>original: Rideris, multoque magis traduceris Afer, / Quam nudus medio si spatiere foro.</note>

And Petronius Arbiter: *Do not wish to traduce (*traducere*) the secret counsels of so many friends, which scarcely a thousand men know*—that is, do not wish to spread them to the common people. Seneca used this word appropriately in his hundredth letter to Lucilius: *I want luxury to be rebuked, lust to be traduced (*traduci*), and lack of self-control to be broken.* Since lust enjoys hiding places and flees the light and the sight of men, he wishes for this disease to be "exposed," so that it might be healed by the remedy of shame. The word is then applied to those who are conspicuous to all, being led through the most crowded parts of the city—a thing usually done for the sake of ignominy to the conquered or those condemned for some crime. Thus Livy in the second book *From the Founding of the City*: *You were a spectacle for all citizens and foreign peoples as you left; your wives and children were traduced (*traductos*) before the faces of men.* Suetonius uses it in the same sense in his life of Vespasian.

Saint Chrysostom, explaining this passage, most clearly indicates the force of this word when he says: *He not only did not want to condemn her, but not even to publish it.* For the translator of Chrysostom used this word where the original has *to punish* (*kolasai*) and *to make an example of* (*paradeigmatisai*). Again, the same word *traducere* is interpreted as "to drag into judgment," and likewise "to publish" and "to hand over for judgment." Hilary does not shrink much from this, thinking that *paradeigmatisai* is "to produce a legal example" against someone. For he says in the exposition of the canon he composed on Matthew: *Since he, being just, did not want the law to be decreed against her.* Indeed, in the book of Numbers, chapter 25, where our edition has: *Take all the leaders of the people and hang them against the sun on gallows*, Saint Augustine, following the edition of that region, reads it this way: *Display (*Ostenta*) the leaders of the people to the Lord against the sun.* Where he translated "Display," the Greek had translated *Paradeigmatison*—as in, "make an example of them," so that others may be terrified by this example. Augustine, citing this very passage in Letter 54, reads *to divulge* for *to traduce*. Even Saint Ambrose, explaining the Psalm *Blessed are the undefiled*, in his seventh sermon stands openly with us, writing in this manner: *because a just man would rather accuse his own suspicion than defame another.* Finally, concerning Joseph, *to whom Mary the mother of the Lord was betrothed, it is written that when he saw her heavy with child, since he was*

<column-break/>

# THE GOSPEL CHAPTER I.

just, he did not want to expose (*traducere*) her: <margin>23</margin> wishing to secretly turn away from her. <margin>20</margin> While he was turning these things over in his mind, behold, an Angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying: "Joseph, son of David, do not fear to join Mary your wife to you. For that which..." <margin>25</margin>

...infame her, he wished to secretly turn away from her. So that you might hear no oracle as of yet. Thus the character of a just man is alien not only from the atrocity of vengeance, but even from the severity of accusation; he prefers his own neglect to be accused (for not having reported it) than to prove the crime of another. Agreeing with all these is Theophylact, Bishop of Bulgaria, a Greek interpreter of the New Testament: *paradeigmatisai*, he says, *that is, to make public and to punish.* <note>original: φανερῶσαι καὶ κολάζεσθαι</note> Finally, the Latin word is indeed ambiguous, since sometimes *traduci* is used for one who leads to a different part—so Cicero and Suetonius have used it. But <margin>B</margin> the Greek word does not allow us to take refuge in that meaning. But because of certain cranky people, it must be proven from here, as the learned reader will tolerate.

The sense, therefore, is: Since Joseph was a man of integrity and saw his bride was pregnant, yet her character did not allow him to believe she had committed adultery, he thought he should hide what he wondered at. Although I find Theophylact is of the opinion that Joseph wanted to turn away secretly because he judged himself unworthy of the company of a spouse who had already conceived from the heavenly Spirit. But this interpretation is more forced. For if, by the embrace of the Law, "she was found" (doubtless by Joseph) "to have in her womb from the Holy Spirit"—if that is the sense—and it was already discovered by Joseph that his bride had conceived not from any man but from the Spirit, why then was there need for an Angel to warn him in a dream?

Furthermore, when he adds this reason why he should not fear—*For that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit*—it indicates well enough that Joseph’s fear proceeded not from reverence, but from suspicion (which Chrysostom did not fear to say) or certainly from wonder. Otherwise, from the speech of the Angel, he ought to have feared more, <margin>C</margin> having been made certain of the heavenly mystery. If it seems too harsh to anyone to say that Joseph doubted Mary’s chastity at all, let him hear Augustine speaking again in Letter 54 to Macedonius: *From which Joseph,* he says, *to whom the mother of the Lord had been betrothed, when he found she was pregnant, and knew he had not slept with her, and for this reason believed nothing other than that she was an adulteress, yet he did not want her to be punished, nor was he an approver of the disgrace.* Likewise Ambrose, on the institution of a virgin: *What, however,* he says, *does it prejudice Mary if Joseph did not understand the mystery of the heavenly counsel and thought she was not a virgin when he saw her pregnant?*

The Apostle Saint Paul used the word for "traducing" in two places. In the Epistle to the Colossians, chapter two: *And stripping the principalities and powers, he traduxit (*traduxit*) them confidently.* <note>original: Καὶ ἐκδυσάμενος τὰς ἀρχὰς καὶ τὰς ἐξουσίας ἐδειγμάτισεν ἐν παῤῥησίᾳ</note> This refers to how the defeated are usually led around in triumphs and openly shown to the people. And in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter six: *crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and traducing (*paradeigmatizontas*) him.* <note>original: ἀνασταυροῦντας ἑαυτοῖς τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ παραδειγματίζοντας</note> The translator in the first instance used "traduxit" (he traduced/exposed), but here he translates <margin>D</margin> "holding him up to mockery" (*ostentui habentes*). Although it seems to me there is some difference between *deigmatizein* and *paradeigmatizein*; for *deigmatizein* is simply to show for the sake of an example, while *paradeigmatizein*, because of the added preposition, has a negative sound. Even if both are derived from *deigma* (an example), and *deigma* is derived from *deiknyo* (to show).

23 **To dismiss her secretly**] <note>original: ἀπολῦσαι</note> To the Greeks, this is an ambiguous word. We "dismiss" a drawn-up army; the senate is "dismissed"; a gathering is "dismissed" when everyone is given the power to go where they wish. We also "dismiss" a friend who wants to depart. But in this place, it is more Latin and at the same time more open to say "to let go from oneself," or to repudiate, or to make a divorce from her (for that is what the Evangelist meant), and to do so "secretly," because it could not be done openly without danger and infamy for the wife. I am not unaware that in Suetonius, a woman who has been repudiated is said to be "dismissed." Nor is it right for anyone to be offended by the harsher word "repudiate," since Hilary—an author as learned as he was pious—did not fear to use "divorce." For he says this in explaining the canon of Matthew: <margin>E</margin> *Wishing to cast her away.* That, indeed, is more atrocious than "to repudiate."

**In dreams**] <note>original: κατ’ ὄναρ</note> That is, through a dream. Although the translator expressed the sense elegantly. For what appears in sleep must necessarily appear through a dream. It does not say in the Greek "appeared to Joseph," but "appeared to him." Certainly, "to him" is read in our more emended copies, specifically in the "Golden Codex." Let it be permitted to signify by this mark the book which we said is in the courtly library at Mechlin.

24 **To receive Mary his wife**] <note>original: παραλαβεῖν</note> That is, to join her in the custom of life. For he had already "received" her, but was meditating on a divorce. Again, the translator shrank from the word "wife," even though the Evangelist does not fear to call Joseph the father of Jesus. Certainly, Saint Jerome reads "wife," not "spouse." His interpretation also declares this. For he excuses the fact that in the Divine Scriptures those who are betrothed are sometimes called "wives." Otherwise, the Greeks call a bride <margin>F</margin> *nymphe*. Furthermore, *gyne* to the Greeks sometimes sounds like "wife," sometimes just "woman." Chrysostom, in his fifth homily on Matthew, indicates this name is not very fitting for a virgin, but it was nonetheless frequently attributed by the Evangelists to hide the mystery and ward off suspicions of illicit sex.

25 **For that which is born in her**] <note>original: τὸ γὰρ ἐν αὐτῇ γεννηθέν</note> That is, "begotten." For that is what he calls that which is conceived in the womb and not yet brought forth. For "born" is also said of that which in any way begins to be. However, we preferred to translate it as "conceived," lest the less common speech trouble anyone. Furthermore, that "born" is placed here for "conceived" is admitted and indicated by Saint Augustine in the first book of *Questions on Genesis*. And Tertullian in his book *On the Flesh of Christ*: *For from this place the insane Valentinus said Christ was born through a virgin, not from a virgin*, whereas a little earlier Matthew did not shrink from this preposition: *Joseph begat Jacob the husband of Mary, from whom (*ex qua*) was born Jesus.*

<summary>This page provides a detailed philological analysis of the words used to describe Joseph's reaction to Mary's pregnancy, arguing that Joseph intended to protect her from public shame rather than punish her. Erasmus critiques medieval scholars for their lack of Greek and Hebrew knowledge, which led to misunderstandings of the biblical text's legal and social nuances.</summary>

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>
Luke 2:1.
</margin>

1 Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea, in the days of Herod the king, behold, there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem,

<margin>
Numbers 24:17.
Psalm 72:10.
Isaiah 60:3.
</margin>

2 saying, "Where is he that is born King of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him."

---

**26 Of the Holy Spirit]** <unclear>is from the Holy Spirit</unclear> <note>Greek: ἐκ Πνευματός ἐστιν ἁγίου</note>. That is, it is "by" the Holy Spirit, or, as we translate it, "it proceeded from" the Holy Spirit: the preposition indicates the author. I have already mentioned that some more recent theologians want to find a great mystery in these prepositions "from" (*ex*) and "of" (*de*): whereas among the Greeks the preposition is the same <note>original: ek</note>, and for us it is different only because it pleased the Translator, who frequently affects variety where there is no need.

**27 She shall bring forth a son]** Chrysostom noted that it was not said "she shall bear *to thee* a son," as is usually said to women: and yet it is said, "you shall call his name Jesus," because the authority of imposing a name usually rests with the husband. Although this seems foreign to the matter at hand, it seemed worth advising because it appears to pertain to protecting the integrity of the reading.

**28 And you shall call his name Jesus]** Here even the madness of the Jews of our time can be refuted, who claim that Christ had a different name from the name of the leader Joshua <note>original: Josue</note> and Joshua the priest. For it is certain that <term>Yeshua</term> <note>Hebrew: ישוע</note>, or with two letters added <term>Yehoshua</term> <note>Hebrew: יהושוע</note> and <term>Yehoshua</term> <note>Hebrew: יהושע</note>, signifies "salvation" to the Hebrews. And the Angel, explaining the reason for the name, said, "for he himself shall save his people." This was also noted by Jerome. And Saint Chrysostom in his first homily testifies at the very beginning of the Gospel, **The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David**, that the surname "Christ" was added by the Evangelist's study so that he might be distinguished from the leader Joshua. Again "son of David" was added because that Joshua was not of the tribe of David. Furthermore, if the name were different, what point would there be in these notes to distinguish one name from the other? Otherwise, it was more Latin to say "from their sins" <note>original: a peccatis suis</note> rather than "of them" <note>original: eorum</note>. But the Translator, I believe, avoided ambiguity: yet while avoiding this inconvenience, he fell into another. Truly there was no danger that anyone would think Jesus had freed his own Jews from his own sins. The middle ground was "from their sins" <note>original: a peccatis ipsorum</note>.

<column-break/>

**29 Through the prophet saying]** The Greek speech can be taken two ways. One way is: "That it might be fulfilled, which was spoken by the Lord, who spoke through the Prophet." The other: "That it might be fulfilled, which was spoken by the Lord through the Prophet, whose words these were." This ambiguity arises for the Greeks because both prepositions <note>original: hypo and dia</note>, that is, "by" and "through," take the same noun case: <unclear>that which was spoken by the Lord through the Prophet saying</unclear>. Truly the latter sense is more approved by me, because we see this figure of speech is solemn in the Sacred Scriptures whenever they recite the words of another. This is what the Latins do with "he says" or "I say." Now, the word "fulfilled" <note>original: impleretur</note> for "completed" <note>original: perficeretur</note>, while it sounds strange to Latin ears unless we mean adding what was missing to finish a thing, is nevertheless left here according to the property of Hebrew speech. One may observe many such instances in the letters of the Apostles.

**30 Behold, a virgin]** <unclear>Behold, the virgin</unclear> <note>Greek: Ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος</unclear>. In the Hebrew Prophet, the noun is <term>bethula</term> <note>Hebrew: בתולה</note>, which properly signifies a virgin and one untouched by man; but <term>alma</term> <note>Hebrew: עלמה</note> or <term>alama</term> signifies a girl or a young woman. The latter is a name of age, the former of integrity. However, Jerome denies that the word *alma* is found anywhere in the Old Testament except concerning a virgin. Certainly, in Genesis 24, it calls Rebecca *alma* while she was still a virgin. And in Deuteronomy chapter 22, the Law punishes the ravisher of an *alma*, that is, a girl, no doubt meaning a virgin; Origen also brings up this passage against Celsus. Therefore, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint translators</note> interpreted this voice as <unclear>parthenos</unclear> <note>Greek: παρθένος</note>, that is, "virgin," though all others interpreted it as "girl." Although among the Hebrews the voice is ambiguous, as it signifies both a girl and one who is "hidden," because <term>alam</term> <note>Hebrew: עלם</note> sounds like "hidden" to the Hebrews. Hence, what is placed in the title of the ninth Psalm as <term>al muth</term> <note>Hebrew: על מות</note>, which other translators rendered "for youth," the Seventy rendered "for hidden things": so that *alma* signifies not just a virgin, but an "invited" hidden virgin, secluded from the sight of men. This custom almost remains today among the Italians. Even in the Punic language, which some believe originated from Hebrew, a virgin is called *alma*. As for Jerome's addition that for the Latins, that which is holy is called *almum* <note>meaning "nourishing" or "kind"</note>, he seems to have spoken more in jest than in earnest. For even if in so many thousands of words one or two happen to match by chance, it shouldn't immediately seem to have happened through a commerce of languages. Nor does the word *alma* apply to just any virgin—for she could be an old woman—but only to that virgin who is a girl, already of marriageable age, but not yet married, that is, known by a man. But if one were to argue with contentious people, although the force of *alma* implies a virgin, we cannot prove from these words alone that it was a virgin who conceived. For one might speak of an infant girl saying, "this one shall bear children," but she will not bear them while she is an infant. But since God promises it as a new sign, what would be new if she who was previously a virgin conceived and gave birth after meeting a man, if that is common to all? Finally, I do not think we should neglect that it is not said simply "a virgin," but "**the** virgin" <note>original: hē parthenos</note>: so it cannot be taken as just any virgin, which would be no miracle, but a specific one: denoting that notable virgin who was to give birth. Therefore, it should be translated: *Behold, that virgin shall conceive.* In this way, we have expressed the force of the articles. And the <term>He</term> <note>Hebrew letter ה</note> placed here among the Hebrews has the force of an article.

<column-break/>

<page-num>10</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER II.</header>

...that which is conceived in her, <gloss>26</gloss> proceeded from the Holy Spirit. <gloss>27</gloss> And she shall bear a son, <gloss>28</gloss> and you shall call his name Jesus. For he shall save his people from their sins. Furthermore, all this was done so that what had been spoken by the Lord through <gloss>29</gloss> the Prophet speaking thus might be completed. <gloss>30</gloss> Behold, a virgin <gloss>31</gloss> shall be pregnant, and shall bear a son, and <gloss>32</gloss> they shall call his name Emmanuel: which, if anyone interprets it, sounds like, "God with us." <gloss>33</gloss> And Joseph, being excited from sleep, did as the Angel of the Lord had enjoined him: <gloss>34</gloss> and he joined his wife to himself. And not...

---

**31 Shall have in her womb]** <unclear>shall have in her belly</unclear> <note>Greek: ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει</note>, instead of "she shall be heavy" or "pregnant." For in Isaiah chapter 7, from where this place is cited, the word is <term>harah</term> <note>Hebrew: הרה</note>, which Saint Jerome translates as "she shall conceive," although the Hebrew voice here seems to be in the present tense. However, Saint Jerome, explaining this passage, has "she has" <note>Latin: habet</note>. Although this word is in the present tense, it nevertheless corresponds to a verb of the past tense. For "she has in her womb" is no different than "she has conceived." Jerome shows something similar from Paul, who when bringing testimony from the sixty-seventh Psalm: **Ascending on high, he led captivity captive, he shall receive gifts among men**, turned "he shall receive" (a future tense verb) into "he gave." Yet I do not know if Jerome's excuse has a place here—that what the Prophets predicted as future, this narrator tells as done—since Matthew brings the Prophet himself speaking in his own words: **That it might be fulfilled, he says, what was spoken by the Lord through the Prophet speaking thus**. Finally, if the Evangelist is narrating what has happened, he should not have said "she has" in the womb, but "she had." For Mary had already ceased to be pregnant. I do not see how these knots can be untangled unless the property of Hebrew speech comes to the rescue; anyone who is ignorant of it will necessarily either get stuck or stumble in many places. This place also offers proof that this edition we commonly use was neither in use by Jerome nor corrected by him. For if he had used it, he would have read "she has" here; if he had corrected it, we would have what he approved and followed. But, if I may say so with Jerome's peace, why did he look more to "she shall have" than "she shall bear," where the future tense remains? Or what was accomplished for Paul after he changed "he shall receive" into "he gave," while "he led" (a past tense verb) remains? For if you look at the time of the Prophet writing, Christ had not yet ascended on high, nor led captivity captive. I thought it best to touch on these things to give the learned and studious some occasion for tracking them down. But in the meantime, it comes to mind that this place is also corrupted in the Commentaries on this passage. For some sciolist <note>term: sciolist (a person who pretends to be knowledgeable)</note>, hearing mention made of the future, changed "he received" to "he shall receive." **He shall receive gifts among men**, when both according to the Seventy it is <unclear>elaves</unclear> <note>Greek: ἔλαβες, "you received"</note>, and according to the Hebrew truth Jerome translated it similarly. Nor does he cite this place differently in the Epistle to the Ephesians, chapter four. He did not notice, however, that the reason for the future tense is not in the voice of the verb, but in the reality. For he who has received things to be distributed has not yet distributed them, just as she who has conceived has not yet given birth. A similar error drove someone to stir up a heavy tragedy for me in this place. I will not be burdened to indicate this also to the pious reader: this passage in Jerome's Commentaries, in all the copies I have seen, is held to be corrupted, even in this Basle edition, which was worked on as much as possible. The reading should be restored in this manner: **But the Prophet, because he predicts future things, signifies what is to come, and writes "he shall receive." The Evangelist, because he narrates history not of the future but of the past, changed "he shall receive" and put "she has." For she who has is by no means about to receive.** Certainly, from this clause, **For she who has is by no means about to receive**, it is clear Jerome read "she has," not "she shall have." The same error seems to be in the Commentaries where he explains the seventh chapter of Isaiah.

<column-break/>

**32 And his name shall be called]** <unclear>they shall call</unclear> <note>Greek: καλέσουσι</note>, that is, "they will call," not "he shall be called." And so it is found written in the most ancient and most emended Latin copies. Indeed, Jerome in the third book of his Commentaries on Isaiah also noted this: that the Evangelist changed nothing of the words of this prophecy; since for <term>karat</term> <note>Hebrew: קראת</note>, which to the Hebrews sounds like "and you shall call" in the masculine, or "she shall call" in the feminine (referring to the virgin who gave birth), he changed it to "they shall call." For Origen also reads "they shall call," using this testimony against Celsus. And Chrysostom most clearly testifies this is the reading in his fifth homily: **But they shall call, he says, Matthew putting it in the plural number with respect to the person of the people, whose voice this is: "God with us," clearly congratulating themselves on such a birth.** Theophylact, Bishop of Bulgaria—a Greek interpreter who, though more recent, is not to be despised—also mentions something about this. "Emmanuel" to the Hebrews sounds like "God with us." For <term>immanu</term> <note>Hebrew: עמנו</note> is "with us," <term>El</term> <note>Hebrew: אל</note> is "God," <term>Immanuel</term> <note>Hebrew: עמנואל</note> is "God with us." Otherwise, because the phrase "which is interpreted" is somewhat unusual and not without ambiguity, we preferred to render it by paraphrase: **which, if anyone interprets it, sounds like "God with us."**

**33 And Joseph rising up]** <unclear>being thoroughly awakened</unclear> <note>Greek: διεγερθεὶς</unclear>, that is, "woken up," or "aroused," or "excited." Although the use of this word is usually adapted to three things: to one who stands up, to one who comes back to life, and to one who wakes up.

**34 And he took his wife]** He joined her to himself. For the word <unclear>paralambanein</unclear> <note>Greek: παραλαμβάνειν, to take/receive</note> contrasts with <unclear>apolysai</unclear> <note>Greek: ἀπολῦσαι, to release/divorce</note>. Saint Paul used it in the same way writing to the Romans: <unclear>receive him who is weak in faith</unclear> <note>Greek: τὸν δὲ ἀσθενοῦντα πίστει προσλαμβάνεσθε</note>, that is, **do not reject him who is weak in faith, but admit him and join him to yourselves.**

# GOSPEL CHAPTER II.

<margin>3</margin> ...to worship him. But when King Herod heard this, he was
<margin>4</margin> troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. And gathering
together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he in-
<margin>5</margin> quired of them where the Christ was to be born. And they said

<margin>6</margin> the Prophet: 'And you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means the least 
among the rulers of Judah; for out of you shall come a
<margin>7</margin> ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.'" Then Her-

exact time the star appeared. And sending them to Beth-

<margin>9</margin> child; and when you have found him, bring back word to me, so that 
I too may come and worship him." And having heard the king...

<meta>catchword: ...they departed, B</meta>

---

<margin>B</margin> <margin>25</margin> **His firstborn son** <term>ton prototokon</term> <note>original Greek: τὸν πρωτότοκον</note>. The Greek article seems to favor the Helvidians <note>A group in the early Church who argued that Mary had other children after Jesus, based on the word "firstborn."</note>, who add it as if to distinguish this son from others; however, it should rather be taken interpretatively, standing for "he who is the firstborn." Thus, you should understand it as that same son of whom he spoke before, whom she had conceived by the Holy Spirit. For the same reason, he added **her** <term>autēs</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτῆς</note>, that is, *her own*. Otherwise, what woman gives birth to someone else's son? I will remain silent for now on the mystery hidden within the term "firstborn." Furthermore, regarding his saying *until she brought forth*, it would be more Latin to say *until she had brought forth*. From these words too, the Helvidians hunt for support for their error, not noticing the specific character of Hebrew speech. You read in the same way about the raven sent out in Genesis chapter 8, which went forth and did not return "until the waters were dried up from the earth," though it signifies the bird never returned at all. We have, however, touched on this matter somewhat above. Furthermore, since it is beyond controversy that **he knew [her]** <term>egignōsken</term> <note>original Greek: ἐγίγνωσκεν</note> is used here for the sake of modesty to refer to sexual intercourse, it is a forced and cold interpretation that some devise: that he did not "know" her great dignity before the birth, but after the birth, having seen the miracles, he "knew" her to be superior to the whole world.

<margin>1</margin> **When therefore he was born** The Greek manuscripts, however, have *not* "therefore" but "but." <term>Tou de Iēsou gennēthentos</term> <note>original Greek: Τοῦ δὲ Ἰησοῦ γεννηθέντος</note>, that is, *But when Jesus was born*, and Chrysostom reads it this way, although the ancient Latin copies disagree. It makes little difference to the meaning.

<margin>2</margin> **In Bethlehem of Judah** I believe it should be read as "of Judea," not "of Judah," as our most ancient copies support. Indeed, "Judah" is the name of a person, while "Judea" is the name of a region. <term>En Bethleem tēs Ioudaias</term> <note>original Greek: Ἐν Βηθλεὲμ τῆς Ἰουδαίας</note>. Moreover, he clarified the name of this obscure village by adding the name of the region so it might be better recognized. For Bethlehem is a small town located in the tribe of Judah (from which "Judea" is named), not far from Jerusalem. Authors usually add the name of the region for the sake of distinction, such as "Antioch of Palestine," because there is another of the same name in Asia; this applies here as well. Indeed, the book of Joshua indicates there is another Bethlehem in Galilee, as Jerome points out in his commentaries, and again when explaining the fifth chapter of Micah. For he writes as follows: *It is beautifully said "in Bethlehem of Judah" to distinguish it from that Bethlehem situated in Galilee*, just as I found in that same book of Joshua. Similarly corrupted is what follows shortly after: *In* <margin>C</margin> *Bethlehem of Judah instead of Judea*. Jerome, however, thinks it happened through a scribe's error that "Judea" was written for "Judah," since "Judah" is read in Micah. He uses this argument: that there is no other Bethlehem among other nations, but in Judea there are two—one in the tribe of Judah and the other in Galilee. The manuscripts I have seen, both Greek and Latin, agree with Jerome's opinion, though his argument could be refuted. He takes "Judea" to mean the entire region encompassing the twelve tribes, whereas "Judea" strictly speaking refers to the portion of Judah and Benjamin. If anyone contends that "Judea" is only used for the entire Jewish region, he is immediately refuted by the authority of Matthew himself, who writes a little later: *When he heard that Archelaus reigned in Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there; but being warned in a dream, he withdrew to the regions of Galilee.* For he who admits that he fled from Judea and went to Galilee knows that Galilee is also a part of "Judea" in the broader sense. Indeed, if Jerome is to be believed, the "Galilee of the Gentiles" was in the lot of the tribe of Naphtali, and another part in the tribe of Zebulun. Furthermore, Origen says in the fourth book of *On First Principles* <term>peri archōn</term> <note>original Greek: περὶ ἀρχῶν</note> that the whole nation was split into two parts by Jeroboam son of Nebat: the ten tribes over which he ruled were called "Israel," while the other two—Benjamin and that of Judah from which the royal line of David took its origin—were called "Judah." The tribe of Levi, from which the priests were chosen, was always joined to these. Whatever lands this nation had received from God was called "Judea" by a common name. While this may be true in a general sense, it certainly does not seem to be true in every instance. But these matters have very little weight regarding the Evangelist's meaning. Therefore, whether we read "Judah" or "Judea," there is no reason for anyone to fight over it, since the meaning is the same; and it is certain that "Judea" was also written in the common copies long ago. Certainly, in the Prophet's prophecy which will soon be cited, "Judah" is read, not "Judea," with great consensus among the codes, both Greek and Latin. To this, it is peculiar to the Hebrews to use a person's name for a people or a place. Furthermore, **Bethlehem** in Hebrew sounds like *House of Bread*, from <term>bayit</term> (house) and <term>lechem</term> (bread); **Judah** means *praising* or *confessing*—a name of which those who most stubbornly deny Christ are now unworthy. Bethlehem is called the "City of David" by Jerome in *On Hebrew Sites*, the same city called Ephrata. It is six miles from Aelia <note>The Roman name for Jerusalem, Aelia Capitolina.</note> toward the southern region. Explaining the fifth chapter of Micah, he calls it a small village, but only in comparison to other cities. For in the second chapter of Luke it is called a "city" <term>polis</term> <note>original Greek: πόλις</note>. I will add this: If Jerome had seen the Hebrew Gospel as it is believed to have been written by Matthew, he would not think "Judea" was read here corruptly for "Judah," but would pronounce it plainly based on that authority. 

<meta>catchword: ...authority</meta>

<column-break/>

He did not know her, until she brought forth <margin>25</margin> **her first-
born son**, and he called his name JESUS. <margin>1</margin>
**Now when Jesus was born** <margin>2</margin> **in the city of Beth-** <margin>II, 1</margin>
**lehem of Judea**, in the times of Herod the king, behold,

<meta>catchword: lehem</meta>

---

...authority. Furthermore, regarding the fact that they are called **Magi** [wise men]: let no one dream of the wicked arts that we commonly call "magic." For those whom the Greeks call **wise** <term>sophous</term> <note>original Greek: σοφοὺς</note> or philosophers, the Chaldeans call Magi, as Saint Jerome also testifies in his commentary on Daniel. A smaller point is that he translated <term>elthon</term> <note>original Greek: ἤλθομεν</note>—that is, "they arrived"—as "they came": *They came to Jerusalem*, saying. The name of the city is almost always pronounced in the neuter gender among the Greeks as <term>Hierosolyma</term> <note>original Greek: Ἱεροσόλυμα</note> and <term>Solyma</term> <note>original Greek: Σόλυμα</note>; the people themselves are called *Hierosolymites* in the masculine plural, just as the *Solymi* are. Only once, as far as I can remember, do I read "Hierosolyma" [as a feminine singular], and that is in Cornelius Tacitus, in book 21 of the *Augustan History*: "Most authors agree," he says, "that the Solymi, a race celebrated in Homer's poems, founded the city and named it Hierosolyma after themselves." Truly, I do not know if he used "Hierosolyma" here as an appositive, just as Juvenal does in his Satires: *An interpreter of the Solymian laws*. Suetonius writes in his life of Titus Vespasian: *Whose brief command, and being left to subdue Judea, in the final siege of the Hierosolymites*, etc. Although I consider this too trivial a matter for anyone to fight over, nevertheless, because I find it written this way by the Evangelists—just as it is frequently found in approved authors, especially in Tacitus in the book just cited—we have preferred to follow it. Sometimes a paraphrase was pleasing, being smoother and clearer, such as shortly after: *and the whole city of the Hierosolymites*.

<margin>D</margin> <margin>3</margin> **Who is born** <term>ho techtheis</term> <note>original Greek: ὁ τεχθείς</note>, not <term>gennētheis</term> <note>original Greek: γεννηθείς</note>. It is a participle from the verb <term>tiktō</term> (to bear/give birth), as if you were to say "the one brought forth." Desiring to express the force of the article, we translated: *Where is he who was born, or is, King of the Jews?* And again, regarding the star, he added the article, <term>autou ton astera</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτοῦ τὸν ἀστέρα</note>. This is so you understand a specific star, and not just any star, but an extraordinary one.

<margin>4</margin> **And we have come** *Venimus* [we have come] should be pronounced with the first syllable stressed, as it is in the past tense <term>ēlthomen</term> <note>original Greek: ἤλθομεν</note>. I would consider this too minor to mention, were it not that I hear many people everywhere both wavering and erring on this. Therefore, we translated it as *we arrived*. Furthermore:

<margin>5</margin> **We have come to worship** He spoke in a Greek manner rather than a Latin one; *we have come so that we might worship*, or *for the purpose of worshipping*. Another minor point: he translated the past participle <term>akousas</term> <note>original Greek: ἀκούσας</note> as "hearing" [present]. It was more correct to say *when he had heard*, or as we translated, *but when these things were heard by Herod*. Additionally, regarding the case of the pronoun here, the Greek copies vary; while some read "troubling them" <term>tarassomenous auton</term>, others read "to worship him" <term>proskunēsai auton</term>. This should not disturb anyone, as the verb <term>proskunein</term> (to worship) is found joined to either case [dative or accusative] among Greek authors. I would teach this with examples if it were not clear in itself. Moreover, that he said "all Jerusalem" [as a feminine singular] rather than "the whole of Jerusalem" is more a matter of historical style; nor is it without the vice of ambiguity, as if there were multiple Jerusalems. Again, what he did with "having heard," he also did with "having gathered." But since these are slight matters and do not have much weight regarding the meaning, I do not intend to point them out everywhere.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>6</margin> **Princes of the priests** <term>archiereis</term> <note>original Greek: ἀρχιερεῖς</note>, that is, the primary priests, whom elsewhere he often translates as "pontiffs": and we have followed this in some places, because we feared Christian ears would not endure it if I had said *pontifices maximos* [high priests] in the Roman fashion. Otherwise, a "prince of the priests" could be someone who is not himself a priest.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>7</margin> **And you Bethlehem** This testimony is taken from the fifth chapter of Micah. Saint Jerome frankly admits that what is reported by Matthew agrees neither with the Septuagint version nor with the Hebrew truth in all respects. This may be because the Evangelist wished to report it exactly as it was answered by them, to show the negligence of the Scribes and Pharisees in the Divine Scripture. Or, according to the opinion of some, because the Evangelists themselves did not take such testimonies from books but, trusting their memory, slipped up as often happens—since a certain diversity is sometimes detected in the meanings as well, as if the wise authors neglected the specific words. And here, lest anyone weaker or more fretful be offended, I will not be burdened to subscribe Jerome's own words from his commentaries on this place: *It is clear,* he says, *even without me saying it, that this testimony agrees with neither the Hebrew nor the Septuagint; and I think Matthew, wishing to rebuke the negligence of the Scribes and Priests regarding the reading of Divine Scripture, set it down just as it was said by them.* *There are those, however, who claim that in almost all testimonies taken from the Old Testament, there is an error of this sort—either the order is changed, or the words, and sometimes the sense itself is different—because the Apostles or Evangelists did not pluck testimonies from a book, but trusted their memory, which sometimes fails.* Thus far we have reviewed Jerome's words. It appears that in this place, that most learned man was in great conflict and distress, from which he could hardly extricate himself. For that first reason, which he reports in his own name—if I may say so with the peace of that holiest man—seems rather forced and affected. First, because what follows, *for so it is written by the Prophet*, can be applied no less conveniently to the person of the Evangelist than to the Pharisees. Second, nowhere can it be found that the Pharisees and Scribes were noted for ignoring the Law, but rather for their ambition and...

# ACCORDING TO MATTHEW. CHAPTER II.

<margin>B</margin> ...corrupted by greed, though seeing they might not see. For the lawyer, when asked by Christ, *What did he read concerning the great commandment?* <note>original: "Quid legeret de magno mandato?"</note> responds immediately: *You shall love the Lord your God, etc.* And he, approving of his response, said: *Do this and you shall live.* Furthermore, it was said to the Sadducees: *You err, not knowing the Scriptures.* I believe this is the same passage narrated in Luke chapter 10, Matthew 22, and Mark 12. In Luke, the lawyer responds to the Lord’s question; in Matthew, the Lord responds, as he also does in Mark. But Mark himself provides a way to resolve this dissonance; for in his account, the Scribe repeats and, approving the Lord’s response, interprets it as it were. In Matthew, however, mention is made of the Pharisees, who propose the question through a lawyer.

<margin>
Jerome.
Jerome's book to Pammachius.
</margin>
<margin>C</margin> Now, the second defense, which Jerome recounts in the name of others, is somewhat harder: namely, that the Evangelists, having suffered a lapse of memory, often disagree in words from the Hebrew, and sometimes even in sense. Jerome reports this opinion under the title of "others" in such a way that he does not attack it as impious. Jerome noted this place in his book to Pammachius on the best method of translating, clearly showing that the Evangelist not only disagrees in words with the words of the Prophet, but also that the sense is entirely contrary. For what is in the Hebrew, *You are a little one among the thousands of Judah*, and the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translated as, *You are small to be among the thousands of Judah*, the Evangelist said, *By no means are you the least among the thousands of Judah.* And yet Jerome seems to approve more of the Prophet’s sense, showing it to agree with the words of Saint Paul in <margin>1 Cor. 1.</margin> *God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong.* Jerome closes this passage thus: *I repeat these things, not to accuse the Evangelists of falsehood—for that is the work of the impious Celsus, Porphyry, and Julian—but to convict my critics of ignorance, and to obtain pardon from them, so that they might grant to me in a simple letter what they must grant to the Apostles in Holy Scripture, whether they like it or not.* Thus far Jerome. Certainly, Jerome does not ask for it to be granted to him that he might render a contrary sense, but that he might express the same meaning in different words. But in the case of the Evangelist, he admits the sense is entirely at odds with the sense of the Prophet. If this is granted to the Evangelist, much more should Jerome be forgiven. While he abominates the charge of falsehood in the Gospels, he does not feel the same about <term>a slip of memory</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ μνημονικὸν ἁμάρτημα</note>. For the authority of the entire Holy Scripture does not immediately waver if they vary somewhere, either in words or in sense, provided that the substance of those things being dealt with remains consistent, upon which the hinge of our salvation hangs. For just as that Divine Spirit, the moderator of the Apostolic minds, allowed his own to be ignorant of certain things, and to slip or err in judgment or affection in some places—not only with no disadvantage to the Gospel, but even turning this very error into an aid for our faith—so it could be that he so tempered the instrument of Apostolic memory that even if something had escaped them in the human manner, it would not only not detract from the faith of the Divine Scripture, but even gain trust among those who otherwise might have slandered the writing as if it were a pre-arranged conspiracy. This sort of thing occurs if one name is put for another, which Jerome admits happened in places; <margin>Jerome in the preface.</margin> or if something is not narrated in its proper order, a point on which ancient interpreters are often tormented. Jerome, in the preface to his Commentaries on Matthew, testifies that Mark related those things he heard from Peter according to the reliability of the events rather than in order. That heavenly Spirit moderated this entire mystery of our salvation with secret counsels and reasons hidden from human intellect. It is neither within our capacity nor Christian modesty to prescribe the ways in which he tempered his business. Christ alone is called the Truth; he alone was free from all error. The Divine Spirit was present to Saint Cyprian, <margin>Cyprian.</margin> as is probable, and yet some of his views are rejected by the Orthodox; he was present to Jerome, and some of his are rejected; he was present to Augustine, <margin>Augustine.</margin> and he himself recanted some of his own works. The primary authority is indeed owed to the Apostles and Evangelists; but it could be that Christ, by a counsel hidden from us, willed that something human should reside in them as well, perceiving that this very thing would lead to the restoration of the human race. He could have freed his own from all ignorance and all error at once, but according to Augustine, even after receiving the Holy Spirit, Peter fell into error, <margin>Paul.</margin> and fell so much that he deserved to be sharply rebuked by Paul. Paul disagrees with Barnabas, <margin>Barnabas.</margin> which could not happen unless one or the other was erring. If we think the authority of the whole Scripture is utterly undermined if even the slightest error exists anywhere, then it is more than probable that in all the copies the Catholic Church now uses, there is none so corrected that some error has not been sprinkled in either by chance or by someone's zeal. Now, if the above reasoning is accepted, either this must be clearly denied, or the universal faith in Divine Scripture will totter. I say these things, best Reader, not because I wish to be the author or patron of this opinion, but if there are those who think such knots, which Jerome ties, cannot be explained, let them not immediately interpret it as if the authority of all Holy Scripture must be undermined over one or two little words, being more unfair toward the Sacred Books than toward profane ones. Suetonius is a heavy authority, even if he is found to have slipped in one or two places...
