...lehem in the land of Judah, you are by no means the least among the rulers of Judah: for out of you shall come to me a leader, who is to govern my people Israel. Then Herod, having secretly called the Magi, accurately inquired of them at what time the star had appeared. And ordering them to go into Bethlehem, he said: Having set out for that place, accurately inquire concerning the child: but when you have found him, report back to me, so that I also may come and worship him. And having heard the king, they departed: and behold the star, which they had seen in the east, went before them, until having progressed it stood over the place where the child was. When they had seen the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. And entering the house, they found the child...

...when he is found to be in one. If this refuge is not accepted, I would rather believe that either in the Hebrew or in our copies the place has been corrupted, or if anything was changed, it was changed for the better by divine counsel: or finally, that the Scripture is indeed pure, but our weakness does not grasp the mystery. I will repeat this: if the Gospel of Matthew had been written in Hebrew for Jerome, he surely would have cited its testimony in this place. Although it might seem impudent for anyone to attempt to untie a knot that Jerome himself does not untie—though he undoubtedly would have if he could—nevertheless, I would like the pious and diligent Reader to consider whether one might emerge from these straits by saying that the person speaking suddenly changed in the middle of the speech, which we notice has happened elsewhere in the Sacred Letters. Let us imagine the Prophet’s words are recited, either by the Pharisees or by the Evangelist, in such a way that he mixes in something of his own, which nevertheless in no way opposes the sense of the prophecy. For although the Prophet felt that previously Bethlehem had been humble and despised compared to the other cities of Judah, yet it would come to pass that, with such a birth having occurred, it would surpass all in happiness and fame. What had been said by the Prophet, the Evangelist kept silent; what the Prophet felt, the Evangelist explained, not looking back to the time when the Prophet wrote these things, but to his own times, in which, once Jesus was born, Bethlehem ceased to be the least and began to be the greatest. It is as if he had said: What was once predicted by the Seer, that from being the smallest of all you would become the greatest of all, has now happened. I will add this as well, to provide the Reader with more abundant material for consideration. I wonder if it can be taken as spoken through hyperbole: *You are by no means the least among the rulers of Judah*, so that, however much he wanted it to be understood as humble, he denied it was even the least among rulers—just as we might deny a man of the lowest reputation is even in the number of men; just as Paul calls things that are not "contemptible beyond measure." <margin>D</margin> Saint Jerome also suggests something of this sort when explaining the passage from Micah: *And compared to such thousands,* he says, *you are hardly a small village.* It seemed right to bring these things forward, partly so the Reader may be free to follow what he thinks most worthy of approval, and partly so that from these things something better might perhaps occur, as one thing often brings another to the minds of the studious. The Seventy translated in this manner: <note>original Greek: Καὶ σὺ Βηθλεὲμ οἶκος Ἐφραθᾶ ὀλιγοστὸς εἶ τοῦ εἶναι ἐν χιλιάσιν Ἰούδα, ἐκ σοῦ μοι ἐξελεύσεται, τοῦ εἶναι εἰς ἄρχοντα τῷ Ἰσραήλ</note>, that is, *And you Bethlehem house of Ephrata, you are by no means the least, that you should be among the thousands of Judah. Out of you shall come forth to me one to be a ruler in Israel*, even if in the Aldine edition the word "not" <note>Greek: οὐκ or οὐδαμῶς</note> is missing, if Jerome reports correctly. Jerome translated the Hebrew in this manner: *And you Bethlehem Ephratha, you are a little one among the thousands of Judah: out of you shall come forth to me one who is to be the ruler in Israel.* However, what is called *parvulus* <note>little one/small</note> in Latin, is for the Hebrews <term>tza'ir</term> <note>Hebrew: צעיר</note>, which does not simply mean a little one, but a <term>youth</term> or <term>young man</term>. Whence also in the Psalm: *I am a youth and despised.* For "youth" the word is *tza'ir*. <margin>E</margin> Regarding this, Jerome notes that the same little city of Bethlehem, which is situated in the region of Ephrata, is claimed now for the tribe of Judah, now Simeon, now Benjamin. Furthermore, *Ephrata* <note>Hebrew: אפרתה</note> sounds to the Hebrews like *fertile* or <term>fruit-bearing</term> <note>Greek: καρποφόρον</note>, according to Jerome. Since those things are minor, it is enough to have pointed out that he said *in the rulers* for *among the rulers*, and *shall go out* instead of *shall come forth*. Likewise, for *leader* he used the word <term>hegoumenos</term> <note>Greek: ἡγούμενος</note>, a participle of the verb from which *leader* <note>Greek: ἡγεμών</note> is derived, which signifies a prince and a guide, and he had just translated it as prince. Whence perhaps he would have better translated, *he shall go out who leads for my people.*

<margin>F</margin> **8 Who shall rule my people**] <note>original Greek: ὅστις ποιμανεῖ</note>, that is, *who is to rule*, or *shall rule*, in the future tense, supported by old Latin copies, specifically the one provided by John Colet <note>A friend of Erasmus and Dean of St. Paul's Cathedral in London.</note>. This signifies not simply to rule, but to feed (as a shepherd), as he translated elsewhere, and to rule in the manner a shepherd rules a flock. Although the Greek voice does not correspond to the Hebrew, which in this place signifies *dominion* more. However, in the Psalm *Why have the nations raged*: *You shall rule them with a rod* <note>Greek: ποιμανεῖς</note>, which the Seventy translated, corresponds to the Hebrew, which is <term>tira'em</term> <note>Hebrew: תרעם</note>, about which Hilary also noted something when explaining this Psalm.

**9 Inquire diligently**] <note>original Greek: ἀκριβῶς</note>, that is, *exactly*, which signifies a certain absolute diligence. From this comes the verb <term>akriboo</term> <note>Greek: ἀκριβόω</note>, which he used soon after: *he learned diligently from them* <note>Greek: ἐπηκρίβωσε παρ’ αὐτῶν</note>. This signifies doing something with accurate and exact care, where every effort is applied. Nor is it "to ask," but *search out* or *examine* <note>Greek: ἐξετάσατε</note>. Indeed, he rendered that other part less conveniently, *the time of the star which appeared to them* <note>Greek: τὸν χρόνον τοῦ φαινομένου ἀστέρος</note>, *which had appeared*. We, so that the speech might be clearer, translated it in this way: *at what time the star had appeared.* Nor is "to them" added among the Greeks. However, the Translator added the pronoun so that the narration might be clearer.

**10 They found the child**] Those things are also minor, such as that in Greek it is not...

# THE GOSPEL CHAPTER II.

---

*...is [not "child"], but a diminutive of <term>paidion</term> <note>original: "παιδίου"</note>, as if you were to say "little boy" <note>original: "puellum"</note>: just as previously, "Inquire diligently concerning the boy" <note>original: "περὶ τοῦ παιδίου"</note>. But a little earlier, "it went before them" <note>original: "προῆγεν"</note>. This means to go before someone so as to be a guide of the way. Furthermore, "with great joy" <note>original: "χαρὰν μεγάλην"</note>, that is, "great joy," is spoken in the <term>Attic manner</term> <note>The dialect of ancient Athens, known for specific grammatical structures</note>, which the Translator nevertheless rendered into Latin. Even if Terence said, "to rejoice a solid joy," and Virgil, "to rage a rage." Likewise, "entering the house" <note>original: "ἐλθόντες εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν"</note> instead of "having entered the house." As for "falling down" <note>original: "πεσόντες"</note>, that is, "prostrate," he translated it as "falling forward," which he did almost by necessity, and it is softer. These and many other such small details I knowingly pass over, lest I become a source of boredom to the reader.*

<margin>11 And having received a response</margin> Someone might say: What "response" was given to those who had asked nothing? <term>Chrematismoi</term> <note>original: "χρηματισμοὶ"</note> are called "oracles," which are given by some Divinity, but usually to those seeking or flocking to them. Thus, it would have been more convenient to translate it as *warned by an oracle*, or *having received an oracle*. Unless perhaps, having lost the guidance of the star, they desired some sign of the divine will. Next, "lest they return," in Greek is <note>original: "μὴ ἀνακάμψαι"</note>, that is, "lest they bend back," if one may translate so strictly. It is a word suitable and peculiar to those making a journey by ship or horse. And soon after:

<margin>12 Appeared in sleep</margin> <note>original: "Φαίνεται κατ᾿ ὄναρ"</note>, that is, "he appears through a dream," using a verb in the present tense: although the Translator rendered it into Latin and properly. Again, that "Arise and take" <note>original: "Ἐγερθεὶς παράλαβε"</note>, that is, "Having been awakened, join to yourself," or "take as a companion." And soon after, "But he, having arisen," or "having been excited." Although we have already warned before that this word is common to one waking up, rising up, and coming back to life.

<margin>13 Out of Egypt I called my son</margin> From this testimony, which Matthew brought forward from Hosea chapter eleven, Julian <note>Julian the Apostate, a Roman Emperor who criticized Christianity</note> took an occasion for slandering the Christians, claiming that the Evangelist violently twisted toward Christ what was said about Israel. Julian was surely following the <term>Septuagint edition</term> <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, which translated this passage in this way: *Because Israel was a child, and I loved him, and from Egypt I called his sons.* As I called them, so they departed from my face. They sacrificed to Baalim, and burned incense to carvings. However, according to the <term>Hebrew truth</term> <note>The original Hebrew text as opposed to translations</note>, Saint Jerome translated it thus: *Because Israel was a child, and I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son. They called them, so they departed from their face. They sacrificed to Baalim, and made offerings to idols.* But concerning these matters—for we are not dealing with this at present—Jerome discusses at length while explaining this passage: and he published a specific treatise on questions of this kind: nor did he pass over this place in his book to Pammachius on the best kind of translating. He also indicates that it could seem to be taken from the book of Numbers, chapter twenty-four, where Balaam says: *God called him out of Egypt, his glory is like the glory of a unicorn.*

<margin>14 And sending</margin> <note>original: "καὶ ἀποστείλας"</note>, that is, "having sent executioners," or "servants," or "guards." For otherwise, the custom of the Latin language does not accept it. Although for the Greeks <term>epitellein</term> is used absolutely for one who sends a letter, and <term>apostellein</term> for one who sends a command or a messenger.

<margin>15 And in all its borders</margin> <note>original: "τοῖς ὁρίοις αὐτῆς"</note>. "Its" <note>original: "ejus"</note> does not refer to Herod, but to Bethlehem: which is certain in the Greek. To escape this ambiguity, we translated it as *in all the Bethlehemite borders*.

<margin>16 From two years old and under</margin> <note>original: "ἀπὸ διετοῦς καὶ κατωτέρω"</note>, that is, all who were two years old, or younger. For <term>dietes</term> <note>original: "διετής"</note> to the Greeks is a space of two years. Again, "he accurately inquired" <note>original: "ἠκρίβωσε"</note>, which above he translated as "diligently learned," here he translated as "had searched out."

Jeremiah chapter thirty-one. Although the Evangelist reported it neither according to the Hebrew nor according to the Septuagint edition. As Saint Jerome clearly admits, explaining the prophecy, lest anyone should be angry with me. Indeed, according to the Septuagint we read thus: *A voice was heard in Ramah of lamentation, and weeping, and mourning; Rachel weeping over her sons, and she would not be comforted, because they are not.* <note>Erasmus provides the Greek quote here.</note> The Aldine edition has it in this manner, even if they do not entirely correspond to the things Jerome reports: except that I suspect many of these things were corrupted in the Latin manuscripts. Indeed, the things attributed here to the Septuagint agree more with those Jerome translated from the Hebrew truth, unless perhaps 
<margin>D</margin> by the negligence of scribes these things were confused: *A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and weeping, and mourning, Rachel weeping for her sons, and she would not rest, because they are not.* According to the Hebrew truth, Jerome translates thus: *A voice was heard on high, of lamentation, and weeping, and mourning, Rachel weeping for her sons, and she would not be comforted over her sons, because they are not.* Jerome warns here that "Rachel" is placed not for the woman, but for the place itself, because Rachel, having given birth to Benjamin, was buried near Bethlehem. Therefore, because of the guest-house of her little body, the place took the name of the buried woman. Furthermore, "Ramah" is not the name of a place, as it seems: but <gloss>Rama</gloss> <note>original: "רמה"</note> to the Hebrews sounds like "high" <note>original: "excelsum"</note>, so that you may understand a clear voice of weeping sounding far and wide. Therefore, it is a wonder that the Translator, whoever he was—for Matthew is believed to have written in Hebrew—left the Hebrew word *Rama*, unless perhaps he translated it as a place name. For there is a place of this name in the tribe of Benjamin, near Gabaa.

<margin>E 18 Weeping and wailing</margin>] Instead of the two which we read, the Greek manuscripts have three: *lamentation, and weeping, and mourning* <note>original: "θρῆνος, καὶ κλαυθμός, καὶ ὀδυρμός"</note>. And Jerome reckons just as many, both according to the authority of the Septuagint and the Hebrew truth, although in his Commentary he reckons only two. Moreover, they are placed in the nominative case, whereas both the Septuagint and Saint Jerome translated them using the genitive. Furthermore, what follows, "she would not be comforted," for the sake of avoiding ambiguity, should rather have been translated, *she would not admit consolation*. "Because they are not": This suddenly seems to refer to the person of Rachel, she would not admit consolation from this, as if those who died were not, whereas they have gone on to a better life. Hilary suggests something like this in his *Canon*. Theophylact suggests something similar. To me, it seems simpler that we understand they are said "not to be" because they perished. Indeed, with these words, "they are not," the Prophet wished to explain the inconsolable 
<margin>F</margin> grief of Rachel and the most monstrous cruelty of Herod. It offended Hilary that those who are slaughtered for Christ should be said "not to be." That little point—that he translated "behold, he appears" <note>original: "ἰδοὺ φαίνεται"</note> as "behold, he appeared," changing the tense of the verb—is a slight matter. Using the present tense is appropriate for one narrating a thing as if it were now being done. For concerning this "having arisen, take," we warned above. Again, "hearing" <note>original: "Ἀκούσας δὲ"</note>, for "But when he had heard": a thing which the Translator neglects everywhere, yet not perpetually, so that you may understand it was accidental rather than a matter of judgment or ignorance. He rightly changed that "he reigned" <note>original: "regnaret"</note> for "that he reigns" <note>original: "ὅτι βασιλεύει"</note>: because the Greek Translator spoke more in a Hebrew than a Greek manner by saying "that he reigns." Furthermore, this Herod was the father of Archelaus; when he was banished to Lyon by Tiberius Caesar, his brother Herod was substituted into the kingdom, by whom Christ was mocked—the son of that one under whom he fled into Egypt. So says Jerome. Although Josephus, whom Jerome cites, reports different things: since...

# ACCORDING TO MATTHEW.

> <margin>4</margin> And his food was locusts and wild honey. Then Jerusalem went out to him, and all Judea, and all the region around the Jordan. <margin>6</margin> And they were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins. <margin>7</margin> † But seeing many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them: "Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? <margin>8, 9</margin> * Produce, therefore, fruits worthy of repentance. And do not think to say within yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.' For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. <margin>10</margin> Even now the axe lies at the root of the trees. Every tree, therefore, that does not produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. <margin>11</margin> I indeed baptize you in water for repentance; but he who comes after me is...
<meta>catchword: comes-</meta>

---

Indeed, in the seventeenth book of the *Antiquities of the Jews*, the last chapter, Josephus reports it thus: <note>original: "Cæsar autem, videlicet Cajus..."</note> *But Caesar—namely Gaius, the successor of Tiberius—having heard the case when Archelaus arrived and certain accusers were present, ordered Archelaus to be thrust into exile when he could poorly clear himself, assigning him a residence in Vienne, a town in Gaul. He ordered his wealth to be applied to the imperial treasury.* Regarding the brother of this Archelaus, Herod the Tetrarch, the same Josephus mentions in book eighteen, chapter sixteen: *Then Caesar, holding the accusation to be true, took away his Tetrarchy and joined it to the kingdom of Agrippa; he even handed over all his resources to Agrippa. He condemned Herod himself to eternal exile, establishing a residence for him in the city of Lyons in Gaul.* These are the words of Josephus. From this, it follows that either Jerome’s memory failed him, or the passage in his *Commentary* is corrupted, or the manuscripts of Josephus are not without error. We have previously noted that this name is used here for a part of the Judean region.

<margin>19</margin> **He feared to go there]** <term>ἐφοβήθη ἀπελθεῖν</term> <note>original Greek: ephobēthē apelthein</note>. "There" (*illo*) is an adverb, even though it is written as "there" (*ekei*) in the oldest manuscripts. Nor is it simply "to go" (*ire*), but "to go away" (*abire*), as indicated by the Greek <term>ἀπελθεῖν</term>.

<margin>20</margin> **And being warned]** <term>χρηματισθεὶς δὲ κατ’ ὄναρ</term> <note>original Greek: chrēmatistheis de kat’ onar</note>. It is a strange whim of this Translator <note>referring to the Vulgate translator</note> that he sometimes translates this as "a response having been received" and now as "having been warned." Saint Jerome thinks the Greek word <term>χρηματίζει</term> <note>chrēmatizei</note> is used whenever God responds directly. Furthermore, it is not "and a response having been received," but "but a response having been received," despite what the Latin copies might claim. However, we have translated this as "having set out, he dwelt" or "he came and dwelt," though in some manuscripts it is "having gone away."

<margin>21</margin> **Through the Prophets, that [he shall be called] a Nazarene]** <term>διὰ τῶν Προφητῶν</term> <note>original Greek: dia tōn Prophētōn</note>. Matthew is usually accustomed to citing the author of a prophecy by name; here he speaks in general, saying "through the Prophets." This is because the Hebrew word <term>נָזִיר</term> <note>Nazir</note> means "holy" or "consecrated" according to the Septuagint. Christ is called "holy" not just in one place but throughout, as it is written of him: *When the Holy of Holies comes, your anointing shall cease.* Symmachus translates it as "the chosen ones." Others interpret it as "flowering," for the Hebrew word <term>נֵצֶר</term> <note>Netzer</note> means a flower or sprout, as the Septuagint translated it. However, that Hebrew letter *tsade* is here written with a *zeta*. Looking to this, some—while trying to link this testimony to a specific place—think it is taken from the eleventh chapter of Isaiah: *And a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall ascend from his root.* Furthermore, the word <term>נֵצֶר</term>, which only the Septuagint translated as "root," was translated by Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion as <term>κόρμον</term> <note>kormon</note>, meaning a "trunk" or "stump." Jerome follows this opinion in his notes on this passage and in his booklet to Pammachius on the *Best Kind of Translating*. Chrysostom, in his ninth homily on Matthew, thinks this oracle was brought from one of the volumes that perished either through the negligence or impiety of the Jews, or through the injuries of time and war. I would add that the conjunction <term>ὅτι</term> <note>hoti</note>, meaning "because" or "that," should probably have been omitted in this place, unless one rendered it as: "that he should be called a Nazarene."

**Repent]** <term>Μετανοεῖτε</term> <note>original Greek: Metanoeite</note>. Which is usually translated as "Perform penance" (*Poenitentiam agite*). I suppose the words "Repent" (*Poenitete* or *Poenitemini*) seemed insufficiently Latin, though the translator uses them elsewhere. But our common people think "to do penance" means to pay for one's committed sins by some prescribed punishment. Among early Christians, those who had sinned publicly were cast out of the fellowship and were openly afflicted; that satisfaction or punishment began to be called "penance." From this circumstance, a significant error arose among certain theologians who took what Augustine wrote about "penance"—that is, public satisfaction—and twisted it to mean the grief of the mind, which they call "contrition." Otherwise, the word <term>μετάνοια</term> <note>metanoia</note> is derived from <term>μετανοεῖν</term> <note>metanoein</note>, which means "to understand afterward." It is when someone who has slipped realizes their error only after the deed is done. According to the Homeric proverb, this is "the wisdom of fools." Another proverb points to the same: "Second thoughts are better." Hence, where we read "it repents me that I made man," Augustine in *The City of God* (Book 15, Chapter 24) reads "he reconsidered" (*recogitavit*) instead of "he repented," following an ancient manuscript. From the same root comes <term>μεταμέλεια</term> <note>metameleia</note>, which occurs when we, having been sluggish in action, late in the day begin to be attentive, now warned by our own misfortunes. Tertullian noted the elegance of the Greek word in his second book against Marcion: *For even in the Greek sound,* he says, *the name for repentance is composed not from the confession of a crime, but from a change of mind.* In my judgment, it could be conveniently translated as "Return to your senses" (*Resipiscite*) or "Come to a right mind." For he returns to his senses who is displeased with his former life. However, as for "performing penance" (*poenitentiam agere*) to mean being affected by regret, while I would not go so far as to call it barbaric or a solecism, I do not recall reading it in the best authors. "An act of penance" (*Actus poenitentiæ*) appears once in Suetonius to mean regret. And in Pliny’s *Epistles*, one finds "he acted out the penance of his penance," but with the addition of the genitive case. He seems to have said "to perform penance" for "to repent," just as we say "to lead a life" for "to live." Valerius Maximus used it absolutely in his chapter on wise words and deeds: *He responded that whichever of these*

<column-break/>

# ACCORDING TO MATTHEW, CHAPTER III.

> <margin>19</margin> ...that he reigned in Judea in the place of his father Herod, he feared to go there: but being <margin>20</margin> warned by an oracle in a dream, he withdrew into the parts of Galilee. And having set out, he dwelt in a city which is called Nazareth: so that it might be fulfilled what was spoken by the <margin>21</margin> Prophets: "He shall be called a Nazarene." In those days, however, comes John the III. 1 Baptist, preaching in the desert of Judea, and saying: 2 † Repent: <margin>B</margin> for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. For this is he of whom 3 the Prophet Isaiah spoke, saying: <margin>C</margin> "The voice of one crying in the desert: prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight." Now John himself <margin>4</margin> had his clothing of camel’s hair, and a leathern belt around his loins. Furthermore, <margin>D</margin> his food was locusts and 

---

*you did, you would perform penance,* where it is clear from the preceding context what the regret refers to. Just as when we say, "I have taken a wife, but it repents me." Quintilian, in book nine, indicates that Sallust wrote "not about to repent" (*non poeniturum*) instead of "not about to perform penance." However, I was not particularly pleased with the paraphrases "Perform penance for your former life" or "Perform penance for your sins." And yet there were men, both religious and learned, who preferred a roundabout way of speaking, lest anyone should slanderously claim that—now that these new flowers and times are here—penance has been banished by the Gospel. Nevertheless, that wholesome satisfaction which accompanies a change of mind—and which, through tears and pious duties, wipes away and in a sense compensates for a fault—is not immediately banished if the Greek word is derived from a change of mind or a changed opinion, rather than from "punishment" (*poena*), as it seems to some. (Though it is perhaps more likely that "penance" (*poenitentia*) is derived from "holding back" (*pone tenendo*)). We have therefore translated it both ways to satisfy everyone as much as possible.

<margin>A</margin> **2. For it shall approach]** <term>ἤγγικε</term> <note>original Greek: ēngike</note>. There is no doubt that it happened through a scribe's error that the future tense is almost perpetually read instead of the perfect in this specific word, since it is "it has approached." And Chrysostom cites it thus in his fourteenth homily. This happens more frequently because some nations incorrectly pronounce "u" like "v" and vice-versa, like saying "vivere" for "bibere" <note>to live / to drink</note>. Though in words of this kind, the Greeks sometimes misuse the perfect tense in place of the present. It was smoother to say "it is urgent," or "it is present," or "it is near at hand" is the kingdom of God. For that is what "it approaches" means. Indeed, to the Jews still living in shadows and ceremonies, it was approaching, but from a distance. Certainly, I found "it has approached" written in the past tense in the oldest Latin manuscripts, which agree on this, and also in most of the more corrected printed editions. Origen also hinted in his first homily on Matthew that the word "approached" refers not to time, but to the action. In one Donatian manuscript, it was "it approaches."

<margin>B</margin> **3. The voice of one crying]** John the Baptist himself testifies in the Gospel of John that this was said of him. It is found in Isaiah, chapter 40, where the Hebrew truth agrees with the Septuagint Edition, except that the Septuagint does not repeat "in the solitude." The Greek reads: <term>Φωνὴ βοῶντος ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ, Ἑτοιμάσατε τὴν ὁδὸν κυρίου, εὐθείας ποιεῖτε τὰς τρίβους τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμῶν</term> <note>original: "The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make the paths of our God straight."</note>. Furthermore, what is in the Prophet as "of our God," the Evangelist—rendering the sense, not the exact words—put as "his." Moreover, "prepare," in Greek is <term>ἑτοιμάσατε</term> <note>hetoimasate</note>, which means "render it prompt, ready, and unencumbered." The Hebrew word <term>פָּנָה</term> <note>panah</note> has the specific property of signifying "to make a way open and conspicuous to the eyes of onlookers," from the verb <term>פָּנָה</term> which means "he looked back." For worldly affections stand in the way, preventing men from seeing Christ's coming; once these are removed, the coming salvation is seen as if the way of the Lord had been prepared.

<margin>C</margin> **4. Had a garment of hair]** <term>Ἔνδυμα αὐτοῦ</term> <note>original Greek: Endyma autou</note>, that is, "his indumentum" or clothing, and "of hair" rather than "from hairs"; then "of camel," not "of camels." Although these do not greatly affect the meaning, nonetheless, since the integrity of the Scripture should be preserved, we thought it not irrelevant to point it out. And he used the Greek word "zone" for "belt" <note>cingulo</note>, even though I know the word "zone" is accepted by Latin writers.

<margin>D</margin> **5. Moreover his food]** <term>τροφὴ</term> <note>trophē</note>, that is, food or nourishment, from <term>τρέφω</term> <note>trephō</note>, "to nourish." What the Translator renders as "locusts," are in Greek <term>ἀκρίδες</term> <note>akrides</note>, a word derived from the fact that this animal flies to the "tops" (*akra*) of the stalks to feed. For the etymology seems more forced which thinks <term>ἀκρίδας</term> are so named because they have a tiny head, as if they were "short-headed." Theophylact (whom some, deceived by a title, think is Athanasius) indicates that <term>ἀκρίδας</term> could be understood as a type of wild herb or shrub, not an animal. Those who do not want them to be animals think the word is derived from "peaks," I suppose, if the Evangelist meant a shrub. Hilary, however, and the more recent Rabanus and Lyranus, take it to be an animal. Those who deny they are animals think the word is derived from the Greek word for "bit" or "tip" with an added "a" and the verb "to eat," meaning a shrub or herb is called *akrides* because it is eaten by living things while still green. Although this etymology fits an animal that devastates crops more correctly, as we read in Exodus 10. But Aelius Dionysius denies that the Athenians call a herb *akris*, but rather *kradē*; though these are still far from *akrides*, nor does it pertain here that some record that *akrides* are little rags hanging from oats. But however these things may be, certainly among the old Latin writers, I do not recall reading "locust" (*locusta*) for a shrub or herb, but only for a living creature, which they mention as two-fold: terrestrial and marine. It is probably gathered from what antiquity has produced regarding locusts that they were not in all ways similar to ours. For those used to fly with four wings and sometimes migrated from Africa into Italy; our farmers do not complain of such things from our own locusts, nor do they fly off in swarms to a foreign region. If this seems strange to anyone, let him compare our pigeons with Italian pigeons; you would say they are of a different kind. A similar difference is found in fi...

<page-num>19</page-num>
# THE GOSPEL

<margin>A</margin> ...the one who comes after me is stronger than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry; he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. <margin>12</margin> Whose winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly clean his threshing floor, and gather his wheat into the storehouse, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire. <margin>13</margin> Then Jesus comes from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. <margin>14</margin> But John forbade him, saying, "I have need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?" <margin>15</margin> But Jesus answering said to him, "Suffer it to be so now; for thus it becomes us to fulfill all righteousness." Then he allowed him. <margin>16</margin> <margin>B</margin> And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water; and lo, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him. <margin>17</margin> And lo, a voice from heaven, saying, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." <margin>IV. 1</margin> Then was Jesus led up into the wilderness by the Spirit to be tempted by the devil.

---

<margin>C</margin> ...in bushes and on many trees. I am forced at this point to miss the prudence in several writers—among whose number is Nicolaus Perottus <note>Nicolaus Perottus (1429–1480) was a Renaissance humanist and grammarian</note>, a man who was beautifully learned, of varied reading, and who deserved great credit for his studies in his age—who refuse to believe that the *locust* in this passage is an animal. Instead, they imagine it is some kind of fruit or a delicate sprout, and they execrate the idea as a vehemently impious thing if John the Baptist were said to have fed on such "vile" food. And here (Immortal God!) how foolishly he rhetorizes with a certain <term>wearisome listlessness</term> <note>original: ἀκηδιαζομένην</note>, asking why, by the same logic, the "friend of God" did not eat flies and other monstrosities with which God afflicted his enemies, the Egyptians? Truly, they do not protest for that very reason that we are dearer to God because, for the love of piety, we despise the delicacies of food. First, if it seems absurd to them that a man should eat locusts, they ought to remember what has been recorded by famous authors: that not only the Parthians, but also other nations, lived by eating locusts. Indeed, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> in Book 11, Chapter 29, testifies that this animal—so "abominable" to these critics—was even considered a delicacy among the Parthians. The same author in Book 6, Chapter 30, reports that certain peoples of Ethiopia were accustomed to living on no other food than locusts, which they preserved for this use by smoking and salting them. Nor was this unknown to Perottus; he is simply offended by the "vileness" of the food. Those who have traveled through distant regions report that even today Egyptians commonly eat locusts. Therefore, they call it an "unclean animal" because it was common, vile, easily obtained, and the food of the poor. The Evangelist recorded this very thing in praise of this most holy man: that although as a youth he was the son of a high priest, and of great authority both among the people and the king, he preferred to live in the desert in the manner of wild beasts, on vile and easily obtained food. It was not that this holy man superstitiously sought out this kind of food, but partly because the wilderness supplied this food of its own accord—for I believe that when he was among the citizens or the king, he did not demand locusts—and partly so that, according to the prophecy of Isaiah and the testimony of Christ, he might resemble the Prophet Elijah. Furthermore, why are those who are offended by the vileness of the food not also offended by the camel's hair and the leather belt? As if it were more appropriate for the forerunner of the poor Christ, destined for the cross, to be fattened on cakes and Athenian sweets, to drink honey-wine and spiced wine instead of water, to be clothed in fine linen and pure silk instead of camel's hair, and to be girded with a golden-studded belt instead of a leather one. These things seem to be said with no less a "pagan" spirit than those of Platina <note>Bartolomeo Platina (1421–1481), a papal librarian</note>, a truly learned man, who defends Pope Gregory—the first of that name—against certain people who tried to obscure his glory with the slander that, while he adorned the city with temples, basilicas, monasteries, and hospitals, he demolished certain ancient structures. He argues his case using a certain logic: as if Gregory, being a Roman by birth, would have been vehemently impious toward his fatherland if he had demolished some columns, arches, and amphitheaters (the remains of old paganism) with the intent that visitors would not be lured away from temples and basilicas by such spectacles. Yet today we see that if any monuments of pagan antiquity remain, they are valued by many far more than sacred places. But to the point: if these critics are offended by the vileness, they disparage what the Evangelist commemorates for the highest praise. If they call it an unclean animal which it was unlawful for Jews to eat, they reveal how carelessly they have studied the Sacred Volumes. In the eleventh chapter of Leviticus, among the winged creatures, the "bruchus," "atacus," "ophiomachus," and "locusta" <note>Various types of locusts or grasshoppers</note> are specifically exempted. These are of related species and are counted among the clean because, although they have four feet, they leap upon the earth with their longer hind legs. Pliny in Book 11, Chapter 29, reporting that female locusts die soon after giving birth because a little worm grows around their throats, and that the males die at the same time, marvels that they die for such a trivial reason, since they can kill a snake whenever they please by seizing its throat in their jaws. This seems to be the kind of locust that others call the <term>snake-fighter</term> <note>original: ophiomachum</note>, which is hostile to serpents. Nor does Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a famous medieval commentator</note> correctly conclude from this that the "snake-fighter" feeds on serpents because Aristotle says animals fight for the sake of mating or food; for a spider kills a snake, yet it does not feed on it. Again, his claim is irrelevant that the "snake-fighter" is poor nourishment because it feeds on serpents, implying it should be counted among the unclean, whereas it is listed there among the clean. And if what feeds on things harmful to man is poor nourishment, then one would have to abstain from venison because deer eat serpents, and even from chickens because they delight in spiders and scorpions. I do not mention these things because I entirely deny that the word <term>locusts</term> <note>original: ἀκρίδας</note> could here be taken for a type of shrub or herb—though that is not yet sufficiently clear—since there is no controversy that locusts were used as food; otherwise, Leviticus would have ridiculously listed them among clean things not for sacrifices, but for human consumption. Rather, I say this to refute those who flatly deny it and think it absurd that "locust" refers to an animal in this passage, meanwhile accusing the translator who translated it thus...

<column-break/>

<page-num>20</page-num>
# CHAPTER III.

...wild honey. Then Jerusalem went out to him, and all Judea, <margin>5</margin> and all the region *bordering on every side* the Jordan. And they were baptized in the Jordan by him, <margin>6</margin> confessing their sins. But when he had seen many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, <margin>7</margin> he said to them, <margin>8</margin> "Offspring of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath? Produce therefore <margin>9</margin> fruits that befit repentance. And <margin>10</margin> do not be of such a mind as to say within yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.' For I tell you that God is able to make <margin>11</margin> children rise up for Abraham from these stones. <margin>12</margin> Even now the axe is placed at the root of the trees. Every tree, therefore, that does not produce good fruit, <margin>13</margin> is cut down and thrown into the fire. I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance: <margin>14</margin> but he who is to come after me is stronger than I, <margin>15</margin> whose sandals I am not fit to [carry]..."
<meta>catchword: carry-</meta>

---

<margin>A</margin> ...and Jerome, who did not correct it—unless they can show that "locust" is found among the Latins to mean a herb or shrub. Furthermore, although the wilderness produces many fruit-bearing trees (though perhaps with a harsher fruit) and many shrubs and vegetables upon which the sons of the Prophets once lived, it was a type of luxury to feed on only one kind of herb or to pluck the tops of greens, especially since when these failed during the winter, locusts dried by the heat of the sun were also useful in the winter months.

<margin>C</margin> <margin>6</margin> *And all the region around the Jordan*] <term>And all the surrounding region of the Jordan</term> <note>original: καὶ πᾶσα ἡ περίχωρος τοῦ Ἰορδάνου</note>, that is, *all the region bordering the Jordan on every side*. I pass over those trivial matters, such as *the same one came seeing*, instead of *when he had seen*. Or that he said <term>many of the Pharisees</term> <note>original: πολλοὺς τῶν Φαρισαίων</note>, more in the Greek manner than the Latin, instead of *many from the Pharisees* or *many Pharisees*.

<margin>7</margin> *Offspring of vipers*] <term>offspring of vipers</term> <note>original: γεννήματα τῶν ἐχιδνῶν</note>. This is the same as what is elsewhere translated as "brood of vipers," but it is poor Latin. For *progenies* (offspring) refers to those begotten by another, and the Greek word sounds the same. He could have said *sons* or *shoots*. I do not think the word "brood" <note>Latin: genimen</note> is found anywhere among approved authors. For *geno* instead of *gigno* (to beget), which Varro and Lucretius used (but in poetry), is an obsolete verb that no one would want to use today. And while that is found occasionally, "brood" is nowhere to be found. For my part, I would wish it were found and accepted.

<margin>D</margin> <margin>8</margin> *Who showed you*] In the ancient and more correct manuscripts, it is written "to you" <note>vobis</note>, not "you" <note>vos</note>, <term>showed to you</term> <note>original: ὑπέδειξεν ὑμῖν</note>. It means "suggested" or "warned" rather than "showed"—as if you were to say he secretly indicated and warned you to flee the imminent danger. For the phrase <term>from the coming wrath</term> <note>original: ἀπὸ τῆς μελλούσης ὀργῆς</note>, which is *from the future wrath*, he changed it correctly to *from the coming wrath*, except that it was more explicit to say "from the wrath that is to be," so that you might understand a certain wrath now pressing upon you. Certainly, "future" is read in the "Golden Manuscript."

<margin>9</margin> *Fruit worthy of repentance*] <term>fruits worthy of repentance</term> <note>original: καρποὺς ἀξίους τῆς μετανοίας</note>. Although it is ambiguous whether the genitive "of repentance" belongs to the noun "fruits" or to "worthy" (which is rarely joined to the genitive case among Latins). It is positioned such that it seems more likely to refer to the nearest word, "worthy." The sense would be: "If you truly repent, as you claim, then live in such a way that it appears you have come to your senses and that you hold a heart-felt repentance for your former life." Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, 4th-century Church Father</note> explains it in roughly this sense. We translate it as: *Produce fruits that befit repentance*, to avoid ambiguity or a somewhat absurd sense. For "fruits worthy of repentance" could mean those for which someone *ought* to repent. Nor would it displease me if "worthy" were taken absolutely to mean "legitimate" or "suitable," as it is not infrequently used among the Greeks, and sometimes among the Latins as well.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>10</margin> *And do not wish to say*] <term>And do not seem to say</term> <note>original: Καὶ μὴ δόξητε λέγειν</note>, that is, *Do not appear to say*. The sense is: "Do not live in such a way that you seem to have placed all your confidence in piety in the kinship of your fathers." Although it can also be taken this way: "Do not be of the opinion that you should say you are children of Abraham," as if that were sufficient for righteousness and being descended from holy men. And soon:

<margin>11</margin> *Since he is powerful*] The conjunction <term>since</term> <note>original: ὅτι</note> should either have been omitted or translated as *that*, not *since* or *because*.

<margin>12</margin> *Children of Abraham*] <term>children to Abraham</term> <note>original: τέκνα τῷ Ἀβραάμ</note>. The Greek article indicates that *Abraham* is in the dative case, not the genitive. It is as if he says Abraham will not lack children, even if these people were not born to him. Some add the pronoun "to himself" in this place, but the ambiguity will be removed if you read *to Abraham*.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>13</margin> *For now the axe*] <term>for now even the axe</term> <note>original: ἤδη γὰρ καὶ ἡ ἀξίνη</note>. This conjunction is not idle; it indicates with emphasis that the danger is pressing and near. For as long as there is hope for a remedy, the faults of trees are helped by fertilizing or pruning. But it is a sign of ultimate desperation whenever the axe is applied to the root. Saint Jerome repeatedly cites *to the roots* (plural), not *to the root* (singular), although the Greek manuscripts protest against this.

<margin>14</margin> *Is cut down, and is thrown into the fire*] Both verbs are in the present tense in Greek, <term>is being cut down</term> and <term>is being thrown</term> <note>original: ἐκκόπτεται & βάλλεται</note>. First, so that the statement is general; second, because the use of the present tense adds more emphasis to the danger immediately looming. Just as when the axe is moved to the roots, the tree is on the very verge of being cut down. That Cyprian <note>3rd-century Bishop of Carthage</note> read it this way can be conjectured from his own words in his *Exposition of the Lord's Prayer*: "For since every tree," he says, "not producing fruit, *is cut down* and *is thrown* into the fire, so surely also the word," etc. Otherwise, he would have said, "Since every tree *is to be cut down* and *is to be thrown* into the fire." A lighter point is that he translates <term>unto repentance</term> <note>original: εἰς μετάνοιαν</note> as "into repentance" instead of "to repentance."

<margin>15</margin> *But he who is coming after me*] <term>but the one coming after me</term> <note>original: ὁ δὲ ὀπίσω μου ἐρχόμενος</note>
<meta>catchword: who</meta>

<summary>Erasmus provides a philological defense of the literal "locust" as John the Baptist's diet, refuting humanists who found it "vile," and offers detailed grammatical corrections to the Latin translation of John's warning to the Pharisees.</summary>

<header>ACCORDING TO MATTHEW. CHAPTER IV.</header>

> 2 **And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry.** 3 **And when the tempter came to him, he said, "If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread."** 4 **But he answered and said, "It is written, 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God.'"** 5 **Then the devil takes him into the holy city, and sets him on the pinnacle of the temple,** 6 **and says to him, "If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down; for it is written, 'He shall give his angels charge concerning you, and in their hands they shall bear you up, lest at any time you dash your foot against a stone.'"** 7 **Jesus said to him, "It is also written, 'You shall not tempt the Lord your God.'"** 8 **Again, the devil takes him up into an exceedingly high mountain, and shows him all the kingdoms of the world and the glory of them.** 9 **And says to him, "All these things I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me."** 10 **Then Jesus says to him, "Get away, Satan! For it is written, 'You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.'"**

---

"the one who comes," <note>original: "qui venit"</note> in the present tense, or "the one who is to come." For this participle, like the verb itself, is *ambiguous* <note>Erasmus uses the Latin term "anceps," meaning it can be interpreted in two ways</note>, so that you may understand it as referring either to Christ being younger in age, or to him who would succeed to the office of preaching. This is a minor point.

16 **I am not worthy**] <note>original Greek: "ouk eimi hikanos"</note>, that is, *I am not fit*. The word "stronger" <note>original Greek: "ischyroteros"</note> refers to physical power, not greatness of soul—meaning *more valiant* or *more powerful* than I—whereas in the elegance of the Latin language, "fortitude" refers more to the mind than the body. Also, the Greek term for footwear <note>original: "hypodemata"</note> sounds more like "sandals" than "shoes"; the Greeks named them thus because they are *bound under the feet*.

<margin>C</margin> 17 **In the Holy Spirit**] What is added in our Latin copies, *and fire*, has been erased in several Greek manuscripts. This was perhaps due to the hatred of certain heretics who used branding in place of washing for baptism. Certainly Jerome reads, *in the spirit and fire*, as does Hilary, and with them Cyprian; it is also seen as an addition in some Greek codices. Yet Chrysostom, in his eleventh homily on Matthew, reads and interprets it as *in the spirit and fire*, though Theophylactus <note>A prominent Byzantine commentator</note> reads it otherwise. Furthermore, lest anyone think it was added to our books by chance, Jerome reads and interprets it this way. Now, the phrase *in the spirit and fire* can be understood in three ways: First, as referring to the Holy Spirit sent upon the disciples in the form of fiery tongues on the day of Pentecost, which the Lord himself calls a baptism in the first chapter of Acts: *John baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.* Second, it may pertain to the fire of afflictions and the cross; for the Lord also called this a baptism when responding to the sons of Zebedee: *Can you drink the cup that I drink, and be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?* Third, by "fire" one can understand the vigor of Gospel grace given within, whereas the Jewish rites were "cold"; for fire possesses the greatest agility among all elements, transforming all things into itself and carrying them upward. Nevertheless, the preposition "in" was added according to the idiom of the Hebrew language. This is similar to the phrasing in John, *in the Spirit of God I cast out demons*, which means the same as saying, *by the Spirit of God I cast out*. Augustine notes this as a serious matter in his eleventh homily on the words of the Lord from Matthew, citing similar forms such as, *they struck in the sword, they burned in the fire, and he took stone knives in which he might circumcise the sons of Israel*.

<margin>E</margin> 18 **Whose winnowing fan**] <note>original Greek: "ptyon"</note> is the instrument the Greeks use to clean grain from chaff. Augustine, explaining Psalm 92, reads "shovel" <note>Latin: "palam"</note> instead of "winnowing fan," because the same thing is usually done openly with a shovel.

19 **The wheat into his storehouse**] <note>original Greek: "ton siton autou"</note>, that is, *his wheat*. The word "his" belongs to the *wheat*, not to the *storehouse*. And so it is written, not only in all Greek manuscripts, but even in the corrected and ancient Latin codices—not only those written by hand <note>original: "calamo descriptis"</note>, but also those printed from type <note>original: "formulis excusis"</note>. Furthermore, the Greek says "the chaff," <note>original Greek: "to de achyron"</note> in the singular, even though our Latin copies protest. But this is of little consequence.

20 **I ought to be baptized by you**] It is not "I ought," but <note>original Greek: "chreian echo"</note>, that is, *I have need to be baptized by you*. Furthermore, regarding the word "baptize," although it is Greek, I have decided to use it consistently since the new rite itself has come down to us by that name. However, Cyprian, in his letter to Caecilius, dared to read it this way: *Teach all nations, dipping <note>Latin: "tingentes"</note> them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.*

<margin>F</margin> 21 **Suffer it now**] <note>original Greek: "Aphes arti"</note>. The translator here uses "suffer" <note>Latin: "sine"</note>, but shortly after translates the same word as "dismissed" <note>Latin: "dimisit"</note>, even though the verb is the same in both places. Yet "to suffer" and "to dismiss" are not the same thing. I ask, what is this playfulness with the Divine Letters? One should either say, "Omit now," so you understand that it is consistent—John having tried to prevent Jesus with a stayed hand—and then shortly after, "then he omitted him"; or, "Suffer now," and "then he suffers him." For the Greek verb <note>original: "aphiesi"</note> is in the present tense, not the past.

22 **And Jesus being baptized**] The name "Jesus" was not added in the "Golden Codex," <note>A famous lavishly decorated manuscript</note> nor in a certain Donatian codex. Indeed, when we were recently in Bruges—a city than which none today is more flourishing or more fertile in good minds—at a most famous gathering of countless princes, especially the ever-august Emperor Charles and the Reverend Lord Thomas, Cardinal of York <note>Thomas Wolsey</note>, we searched the library of the very ancient college commonly called Saint Donatian. This place even today retains many traces of ancient learning and discipline. There we found several codices of the Gospels, some of which even testified by their inscription that they were copied eight hundred years ago. One contained the entire New Testament; another was the oldest of all and most worn by use, but faulty and mutilated, containing nothing of the New Testament except Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, and the Epistles of James,

<column-break/>

**fire.** 17 **Whose winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will**
**cleanse his threshing floor, and gather** 18 **his wheat**

---

<margin>A</margin> Peter, John, and Jude. Access to these was granted to us by Marcus Laurinus, the dean of that college, a man excelling in every kind of virtue. That library held many other books of venerable antiquity which perished through the neglect of some—as is the current custom of priests, to lean over platters <note>original: "patinis," referring to food</note> more than pages <note>original: "paginis"</note>, and to take better care of coins than of volumes. I did not want you to be ignorant of this, Reader, because I shall frequently use the testimony of these codices in this work. And the word "immediately" <note>original Greek: "euthys"</note>, which appears here in the Greek, is not added in most Latin codices.

<margin>B</margin> 23 **Like a dove**] <note>original Greek: "hosei peristeran"</note>. The Translator rendered this somewhat obscurely. For he seems to say that the Holy Spirit descended in the *manner* of a dove, whereas the sense is that he descended in the *form* of a dove.

24 **And lighting upon him**] From the Greek text, it is not clear to whom the heavens were opened—to Christ or to John—nor which of them saw the dove descending. Yet from the words of the Evangelist, it seems to refer more to Christ than to John, except for what follows: <note>original Greek: "ep’ auton"</note>, which the Translator should have rendered "upon him" or "upon the man himself." Otherwise, if it were meant to be "upon himself" <note>referring back to the subject</note>, it would have said <note>original Greek: "eph' hauton"</note>. Furthermore, it was not necessary for Christ to see these things; they were done for the sake of the Jews, so they might understand by an evident sign that he was the Messiah, not John. To John, otherwise, the voice of the Father might have seemed to mean nothing unless the dove had publicly designated Jesus. But Mark, who condensed Matthew into a summary, makes it even more obscure; unless the reality spoke for itself and those two words <note>original: "ep’ auton"</note> stood in the way, we would certainly understand that Christ saw it, not John. Luke recounts it such that he does not reveal who saw it. Only John the Evangelist explicitly explains that John the Baptist saw it.

<margin>D</margin> 25 **In whom I am well pleased**] <note>original Greek: "en ho eudokesa"</note>. This is a word peculiar to the Divine Scriptures, by which they signify a leaning mind and a certain special affection. It sounds as if you were to say, *in whom I have a good opinion of myself*; and, so to speak, *I am pleased with myself*; or *in whom I have been well satisfied*. Augustine, in his sixty-third sermon, reads *in whom I have felt well*, following his beloved Cyprian, who likewise reads it in the first book of *Against the Jews*, chapter fourteen. Both seem to have followed Tertullian, who in the book *Against Praxeas* reads, *in whom I have felt well*, and he followed, I believe, Irenaeus, who frequently speaks this way. For that is what the Greek <note>original: "eudokein"</note> means to them. Hence, what they call "celebrated" and "magnificent" are called <note>original: "eudokeseis"</note>. As for the word "beloved" <note>original: "dilectus"</note> which preceded it, the Greeks use <note>original: "agapetos"</note>, which the translator usually renders as "dearest" <note>Latin: "carissimus"</note>. For it is a noun, not a participle, and indicates something more than merely "beloved." If "dearest" was ever to be said, it certainly should have been said here, since he is speaking of Christ the Son. And Jerome cites it this way several times.

# ###
### ->Then was he led<-

**T** *hen was he led*] <note>original Greek: "anechthe"</note>, that is, *was led up*, or *lifted up*, or *as if led away from the midst*. For he did not immediately begin to preach, but hid himself for several days. Furthermore, regarding the fact that he simply said "by the Spirit," <margin>E</margin> whereas he usually adds "Holy," it is clear he is speaking of the Spirit he had just mentioned, and for that reason he added the article: <note>original Greek: "hypo tou pneumatos"</note>. For whenever that article is added, Didymus teaches in his work *On the Holy Spirit* that we should generally understand it as the Holy Spirit. Also, "spirit" <note>original: "pneuma"</note> is used for any spirit, and sometimes even for an impulse of the mind; while "spirit" is found in the sacred writings as a synonym for "breath," as Augustine notes in the thirteenth book of *The City of God*. Again, the Translator everywhere left the name <margin>F</margin> "devil" <note>Latin: "diabolus"</note>, and several times in the Pauline Epistles, where it seems to signify not an "impious spirit," but simply an "informer" or "slanderer." For that is what *diabolos* means to the Greeks, from the verb <note>original Greek: "diaballesthai"</note>, which is *to inform*, *to betray*, or *to make infamous*. As for the fact that in Hilary "zabulos" <note>a medieval corruption of diabolus</note> is read instead of "devil," this should perhaps be ascribed to an error of the scribes. Yet the same word is read elsewhere in his works; and not only in his. But from wherever this practice grew, it is certainly established that the Evangelists call him "devil," not "zabulos" or "zabolos," as I have found written in the more corrected codices. Some think the "za" in *zabios* stands for "dia," which is very likely what the ancient Greeks did in some words, surely following the Aeolic property. But it is a wonder why more recent Latin writers affected such antiquity. For it is a frivolous idea that some think "zabulos" (with a long middle syllable) is composed of the syllable "za," which the Greeks sometimes use for emphasis (as in "very divine" <note>original: "zatheos"</note>), and "ballo" (to throw), because he abounds in schemes. For he is called the accuser of the brothers, the one who slanders <note>original Greek: "ho diaballon"</note>. To this, where he here translates "afterward," <margin>Volume VI.</margin> <margin>B 2</margin> it later comes as "finally"; it could be translated, "at last he was hungry," or "finally he was hungry," so that you understand he only then felt hunger.

# GOSPEL CHAPTER IV.

<margin>k 11</margin> Then the devil left him: and behold, angels came and ministered to him. <margin>l 12</margin> Now when Jesus heard that John had been delivered up, he withdrew into Galilee. And leaving Nazareth, he went and lived in Capernaum by the sea, in the regions of Zebulun and Naphtali. <margin>14</margin> This was to fulfill what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying: <margin>15</margin> "Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond <margin>16</margin> the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles. The people sitting in darkness saw a great Light, and for those sitting in the region and shadow of death, a Light has dawned upon them." From that time Jesus began <margin>k 17</margin> to preach and to say, "Repent; for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." <margin>m 18</margin> While Jesus was walking by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea (for <margin>n 19</margin> they were fishermen). And he said to them, "Follow me, and <margin>x 20</margin> I will make you fishers of men." And they immediately left their <margin>p 21</margin> nets and followed him. Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them. And they immediately left the boat and their <margin>s 22</margin> father, and followed him. And Jesus went about all <margin>t 23</margin> Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every infirmity among the people. <margin>24</margin> And his fame went out into all Syria; and they brought to him all who were sick, seized with various diseases and torments, and those possessed by demons, and those who were lunar-struck <note>epileptics</note>—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and finally, he was hungry. And when <margin>3</margin> the one who tempts approached him, he said, "If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become bread." But he answered and said, "It is <margin>4</margin> written, 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds through the mouth of God.'" Then <margin>5</margin> the devil took him into the holy city, and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple. And he said to <margin>6</margin> him, "If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down: for it is written, 'He shall give his angels charge over you, and with their hands they shall lift you up, lest you ever strike your foot against a stone.'" Jesus said to him, "Again it is <margin>7</margin> written, 'You shall not tempt the Lord your God.'" <margin>B</margin> Again the devil took him onto an <margin>8</margin> exceedingly high mountain, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them. And he said to him, "All these things <margin>9</margin> I will give to you, if you will fall down and worship me." Then Jesus said <margin>10</margin> to him, "Go away, Satan: for it is written, 'The Lord your God you shall worship, and him only shall you serve.'" Then the devil left him: and behold, <margin>11</margin> angels approached and ministered to him. Now when <margin>12</margin> Jesus had heard that John was delivered up, he withdrew into Galilee. And leaving Nazareth, he went and <margin>13</margin> lived in Capernaum, which is a seaside city, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali. So that <margin>14</margin> what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, saying: "Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, <margin>15</margin> near <margin>C</margin> the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. The people who sat in darkness saw a great <margin>16</margin> light, and those who sat in the region and shadow of death..."

---

<margin>D</margin> **2 The tempter approaching]** <note>original: "ὁ πειράζων"</note> (ho peirazōn), that is, "the one who tempts." In the same manner the Apostle Paul says, "lest by some means the tempter had tempted you," <note>original: "μή πως ἐπείρασεν ὑμᾶς ὁ πειράζων"</note> that is, "lest in some way he who tempts had tempted you," which refers to the one who is accustomed to tempting. However, the name "the tempter" <note>original: "πειραζών"</note> can be seen as a proper noun, as if for a deceiver.

**3 Not by bread alone]** This is a testimony from Deuteronomy, chapter eight, which Christ recounted almost word for word. "To show you that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord." Furthermore, in both Greek and Hebrew, "to live" is in the future tense: "he shall live" <note>original: "ζήσεται" / "יהיה"</note>.

**4 Then he takes him]** <note>original: "παραλαμβάνει"</note> (paralambanei), that is, he "took along," meaning he led him away as a companion. And again a little further down, the word "takes" <note>original: "παραλαμβάνει"</note> is in the present tense. Furthermore, "pinnacle" <note>original: "πτερύγιον"</note> (pterygion) is a diminutive of the word for "wing" <note>original: "πτέρυξ"</note> (pteryx), because it flutters in the manner of wings.

**5 He gave charge to his angels]** <note>original: "ἐντελεῖται"</note> (enteleitai), that is, "he shall command," in the future tense. And I found it written this way in the Corsendonc manuscript <note>A manuscript from a Priory in Belgium used by Erasmus</note>, with the agreement of three manuscripts from St. Donatian's. Similarly, among the Hebrews it is "he shall command" <note>original: "יצוה"</note>. And thus it is read in the ninetieth Psalm <note>Psalm 91 in modern numbering</note>, from which this passage is taken, and the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament</note> also agree: "For he shall give his angels charge over you." Jerome, however, accuses the "accuser" <note>the devil</note> in this place of falsely citing the testimony of Scripture, plucking out what was convenient and omitting what was obstructive. For he omitted this part: "that they may keep you in all your ways." Then he was silent about what follows immediately: "you shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk." Finally, what was said about any good man, the devil twisted to apply to Christ, since the whole Psalm cannot be adapted to him. But I think the devil should be called to account not because he cited Scripture unlearnedly, but because he did so maliciously and impiously. Regarding the phrase "lest perhaps" <note>original: "μή ποτε"</note>, which the translator rendered in his own way as "lest by chance," it would be more correctly "lest at any time."

<margin>E</margin> **6 Jesus said to him again]** The word "again" <note>original: "πάλιν"</note> (palin) is positioned so that it can refer to either part. "He said again," or, "Again it is written." Furthermore, that word sometimes sounds like repetition, and sometimes like contradiction. If it refers to "said," it signifies repetition: for he had answered once before. If it refers to the following word, it signifies contradiction, as if you were to say, "on the contrary" it is written, so that he opposes Scripture against the devil's use of Scripture. But soon after it undoubtedly signifies repetition: "again he takes him."

**Not tempt]** The passage is from Deuteronomy chapter six. In the Hebrew it is read in the plural number: "You [all] shall not tempt the Lord your God," according to how you tempted him in the place of temptation. And here Christ plucks out only as much as was convenient. For he left out what follows: "as you tempted him in the place of temptation," because that part was not suitable except for the Israelite people.

**8 If falling down]** <note>original: "εἰ πεσών"</note> (ei pesōn), that is, "if prostrate," or face-down, which is the gesture of one worshipping. He used the same verb regarding the Magi.

<margin>F</margin> **9 Go, Satan]** What is "go"? Does Christ send him somewhere, that he should say "go"? In Greek it is <note>original: "ὕπαγε"</note> (hypage), that is, "begone," or "depart." And there is added in the common Greek codices "behind me, Satan" <note>original: "ὀπίσω μου Σατανᾶ"</note>, that is, "go behind me, Satan," but erroneously, if we believe Origen. For he notes this difference in his first homily: to Peter it was said, "go behind me, Satan"; but to the devil it was only said, "begone," because the former is appropriate for a disciple—according to the phrase "come after me, I will make you become fishers of men"—while the latter fits one who is simply to be rejected, not invited to follow. Nor does Chrysostom add these words, "behind me," when explaining this passage in his 13th homily. On the other hand, in Theophylact they are added. Therefore, I think we should agree with our own manuscripts in this part, because I suspect those words were added here from another passage in Matthew by some scribe with a busy memory, as we have shown happened in several places. Augustine, in explaining the ninth Psalm, reads, "Get thee back, Satan." And it is read thus not only in many manuscripts printed by typographers, but also in a very ancient manuscript from the Pauline Library in London, though the Corsendonc manuscript disagrees. It appears "back" was put for "behind me," but to me, as I said, Origen’s note is approved, especially since I see Ambrose supporting this in several places where he cites this passage. Furthermore, in <term>Hebrew</term> <note>Satan</note> means "adversary," one who stands in the way and disturbs. But he who is at the back does not stand in the way. Therefore, to Peter, who was already trying to go before the Lord, rebuking him lest he should undergo death, it was said, "Follow me, acting as a disciple, not an adversary."

**10 The Lord your God]** The passage is from Deuteronomy chapter six, except that there, instead of "you shall worship," it is written "you shall fear" in the Vulgate Edition, nor did the Seventy translate it otherwise. However, he who worships, also reveres and fears because he worships. Moreover, as for what is added, "him only" <note>original: "αὐτῷ"</note>, the Hebrew expressed this through the particle "eth" <note>original: "את"</note>, "eth Jehovah," that is, "the Lord himself" <note>original: "וֹאֹתוֹ תַעֲבֹד"</note>, "and him specifically you shall serve," so that we understand no one else is to be worshipped, and no one else served. Furthermore, as for the distinctions regarding <term>Latria</term> <note>a technical term for worship due to God alone</note> which Laurentius <note>Laurentius Valla, a famous humanist critic</note> disputes against the theologians, let him who wishes seek it from him; we strive for brevity.

**11 Then he left him]** <note>original: "ἀφίησιν"</note> (aphiēsin), that is, "he leaves," in the present tense. It is the same verb which he translated above as "dismissed."

**12 In the city of Capernaum]** <note>original: "εἰς Καπερναούμ"</note> (eis Kapernaoum). We see it written thus in the Golden Codex, with several manuscripts from St. Donatian's agreeing. The Latin translator added "city" on his own. But it was more necessary to do that in the case of Nazareth, because of the Greek article attached: "the [town of] Nazareth" <note>original: "τῇ Ναζαρέτ"</note>.

**13 Way of the sea]** In Greek it is in the accusative case, <note>original: "ὁδὸν θαλάσσης"</note> (hodon thalassēs), that is, "the way of the sea." Theophylact, the Greek interpreter, thinks the preposition "along" or "beside" should be understood, that is, "near the way of the sea." For here he calls the sea the Lake of Gennesaret, on whose shore are situated Capernaum, Tiberias, Bethsaida, and Chorazin.

**14 Galilee of the Gentiles]** <note>original: "τῶν ἐθνῶν"</note> (tōn ethnōn); it was more expressive to say "of the nations," with the article attached. For there are two Galilees: one surnamed "of the Gentiles," in the portion of the Tribe of Naphtali, bordering the Tyrians, in which Solomon gave twenty cities to Hiram, king of the Tyrians. The other is in the tribe of Zebulun, opposite Tiberias and the pool of Gennesaret, according to Jerome. Although some distinguish it so that "of the Gentiles" refers not to Galilee, but to the people: "The people of the nations who sat in darkness."

**15 In the region of the shadow of death]** The Greeks read it differently, <note>original: "ἐν χώρᾳ καὶ σκιᾷ θανάτου"</note> (en chōra kai skia thanatou), that is, "in the region AND shadow of death." Even if according to the Hebrew truth Jerome translates it "to those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death." And in Hebrew there is a single word <note>original: "צַלְמָוֶת"</note> (tsalmaveth), composed of "shadow" <note>original: "צֵל"</note> and "death" <note>original: "מָוֶת"</note>, so that you understand an deepest darkness, such as exists among the dead. It should be noted that "dwelling" has been changed to "sitting," even if dwellings are called seats. Otherwise, why are those who sit the same as those who were just said to walk? Although "sitting" <note>original: "καθήμενος"</note> was also placed in for that "walking," as one manuscript of St. Donatian had. From this it is clear that either Matthew, or his interpreter, wished to render the meaning rather than count the words of the prophet. Jerome, explaining this passage in Isaiah, testifies that it is cited by Matthew according to the Hebrew truth, even if some words are omitted. For the Evangelist omits: "In the first time it was alleviated, and in the last time it was aggravated." This, however, differs marvelously in the Septuagint. Indeed, instead of what Jerome translates from the Hebrew truth, "In the first time the land was alleviated," they have "drink this first, do it quickly, do it quickly." For Tertullian cites it likewise—
