# ACCORDING TO MATTHEW. CHAPTER V.

...epileptics, and paralytics; and he healed them.
<margin>25</margin> And many crowds followed him from Galilee, and the Decapolis <note>A region of ten cities on the eastern frontier of the Roman Empire</note>, and Jerusalem, and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.
<margin>V. ch. 1</margin> And seeing the crowds, he went up onto the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him.
<margin>ch. 2</margin> And opening his mouth, he taught them, saying:
<margin>ch. 3</margin> **Blessed are the poor in spirit; for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.**
<margin>ch. 4</margin> **Blessed are those who mourn; for they shall be comforted.**
<margin>ch. 5</margin> **Blessed are the meek; for they shall inherit the earth.**
<margin>ch. 6</margin> **Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness; for they shall be satisfied.**
<margin>ch. 7</margin> **Blessed are the merciful; for they shall obtain mercy.**
<margin>8</margin> **Blessed are the pure in heart; for they shall see God.**
<margin>9</margin> **Blessed are the peacemakers; for they shall be called sons of God.**
<margin>10</margin> **Blessed are those who are persecuted for the sake of righteousness; for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.**
<margin>ch. 11</margin> **Blessed are you when people insult you and persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account.**
<margin>ch. 12</margin> **Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven; for in the same way they persecuted the prophets who were before you.**
<margin>ch. 13</margin> **You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt loses its flavor, with what shall it be salted? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by men.**
<margin>ch. 14</margin> **You are the light of the world; a city set on a hill cannot be hidden.**
<margin>15</margin> **Neither do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a lampstand, and it gives light to all who are in the house.**
<margin>16</margin> **In the same way, let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.**
<margin>ch. 17</margin> **Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I did not come to abolish, but to fulfill.**
<margin>18</margin> **For truly I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke of a letter shall pass from the Law until all things are accomplished.**
<margin>ch. 19</margin> **Whoever therefore breaks one of the least of these commandments, and teaches others to do so, shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does and teaches them, he—**

---

<margin>B</margin> ...in the fourth book of *Against Marcion*: "Drink this first, do it quickly." Jerome does not reject or attack this interpretation, which has no affinity with the Hebrew.
<margin>D</margin> 16 *Do penance* <note>Latin: "Poenitentiam agite"</note>] The Greek is *Metanoeite*, meaning "Return to a right mind" or "Repent." This was discussed above. And *eggiken*, meaning "has approached," or is pressing and present, or is near at hand.
17 *As Jesus was walking*] The word "Jesus" was not in the "golden code" <note>A reference to a high-quality manuscript, likely the Codex Aureus</note>. Although I believe it is sometimes added among the Greeks for the sake of narrative flow, especially when excerpts are recited from the Gospel books.
18 *Casting a net*] The Greek is *ballountas amphiblestron*. It is a specific type of net, much like a *sagena* <note>a large drag-net</note>, named because it surrounds from all sides. For the general word for "net" in Greek is *diktyon*.
19 *You shall become fishers*] The word "become" is redundant; in Greek, it is simply "I will make you fishers." Furthermore, "fishers of men" sounds softer in Greek: *halieis anthrōpōn*. For "piscator" (fisher) comes from "piscis" (fish), while *halieus* comes from the sea, as if you were to say "mariner" in the French tongue, because he works on the sea. Though this is a small point, much like the one a bit later, "leaving their nets and father," where the Greeks add "their own."
20 *And healing every infirmity*] The Greek is *therapeuōn*. The Translator often renders this as "curing": and generally *therapeuein* means to heal with medicine. Hence Galen calls his work on remedies for diseases *Therapeutike*. I am therefore surprised that the Translator of the Evangelist used this word incorrectly, as it seemed it should have been avoided. Although Mark used the same word in the first chapter, "and he cured many." Likewise, Luke in the fourth chapter, "he healed them." The same logic applies to the Latin word *curare* as to the Greek. In this place, the Latin Translator avoids it and translates "healing" <note>sanans</note> instead of "curing" <note>therapeuōn</note>. Yet in Mark and Luke, he did not avoid it. For those who are "treated" <note>curantur</note> are not immediately "healed" <note>sanantur</note>: and many are "healed" without being "treated." Next, the word *noson*, which clearly means a disease, he here mostly translates as "infirmity" <note>languorem</note>. Again, *malakian*, which literally sounds like "softness," he translates not badly as "weakness," though it is more correctly translated as "languor." For languor is a slight and slow disease that does not confine one to bed but nevertheless prevents us from being in good health. Finally, it was perhaps better to say "any disease" rather than "every disease." For he did not heal every sick person in existence, but every kind of disease: some diseases which doctors consider incurable. Unless, of course, some Latin writers use "every" <note>omnis</note> as a substitute for "any" <note>quivis</note>.
21 *His fame went out*] The Greek is *apēlthen hē akoē*, that is, "the hearing went out," to render it word for word. I do not deny that "opinion" can be found in place of "fame," but not all things fit in every place. We prefer to translate it as "his fame spread abroad," if only to avoid ambiguity.
22 *Seized by torments*] The Greek is *basanois sunechomenous*, that is, those who were constricted or drawn together by tortures or pains. He separated these from diseases whose violence contracts the whole body. I would prefer "pains" <note>terminibus</note> to avoid ambiguity, as there are also the "torments" of legal interrogations.
23 *Those who had a demon*] The Greek is *daimonizomenous*. It is a single word: those who were driven by demons. Similar is what follows, *selēniazomenous*, which the Translator renders as "lunatics": because their madness would return at certain intervals. Saint Jerome denies that these were truly affected

<column-break/>

<page-num>26</page-num>
<header>ACCORDING TO MATTHEW. CHAPTER V.</header>
<sig>Volume V. I. B 5</sig>

<margin>A</margin> ...on them, a light has dawned. From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, <margin>17</margin> Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. <margin>18</margin> And Jesus, walking by the sea of Galilee, saw two brothers, Simon who was called Peter, and Andrew his brother, <margin>19</margin> casting a net into the sea (for they were fishermen). And he <margin>20</margin> said to them, "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." And they immediately left their nets and followed him. <margin>21</margin> And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their Synagogues, and preaching the Gospel of the kingdom, and <margin>22</margin> healing every disease and every infirmity among the people. And <margin>23</margin> his fame spread throughout all Syria: and they brought to him all who were ill, afflicted with various diseases and torments, and <margin>24</margin> those possessed by demons, and lunatics, and paralytics: and he healed them. And many <margin>25</margin> crowds followed him from Galilee, and Decapolis, and Jerusalem, and Judea, and *from the regions* situated beyond the Jordan. And when he saw the crowds, he went up V. 1 into a mountain: and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him. And after he had opened his mouth, 2 he taught them, saying: <margin>3</margin> Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. <margin>4</margin> Blessed are those who mourn: for they shall receive consolation. <margin>5</margin> Blessed are the meek: for they shall receive the inheritance of the earth. <margin>6</margin> Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness: for they shall be satisfied. Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy. <margin>8</margin> Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God. <margin>9</margin> Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the sons of God. <margin>10</margin> Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness: for...

---

<margin>D</margin> by the power of the moon, since they were possessed by demons, but that it was done by the craft of demons to bring infamy upon God's creature <note>the moon</note>. I believe they were called "lunatics" because the madness was not constant, but recurred at certain intervals.
<margin>24</margin> *From beyond the Jordan*] The Greek is *kai peran tou Iordanou*. The Translator added "from." For such expressions are found used this way to signify movement from a place. As Quintilian says: "Public safety must be sought across the sea," meaning from transmarine regions. And, "he returned from abroad," meaning from a pilgrimage. But "from under the foot" or "from behind the statues" are phrases unheard of by Latin speakers. He could have explained it by a paraphrase: "from the regions situated beyond the Jordan."
<margin>V 1</margin> *But Jesus seeing*] The word "Jesus" is not added in this place, neither in the Greek nor in the ancient Latin codes; it is *idōn de tous ochlous*, that is, "But when he had seen the crowds."
<margin>2</margin> *Blessed are the poor in spirit*] I see that the common crowd of Theologians, among whom is Bede, interpret this as regarding the thinness of one's resources; and the person who wrote the *Imperfect Work* on this Evangelist notes that it was said *ptōchoi*, not *penetes*—that is, "beggars," not merely "needy"—to express the utmost destitution. However, it should rather be referred to the loftiness and pride of the mind. For the Greeks use the word *ptyein* <note>meaning to spit, but here Erasmus links it to "puffing up"</note> to refer to an elated and fierce spirit, such as is common in princes or those who seek a kingdom. And this is generally the source of all evils. This sense is supported by what is added: "for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Furthermore, he said "poor in spirit" because arrogance is familiar to the wealthy. Certainly, Saint Augustine openly interprets it in this sense in the first book of the Commentaries he published on this sermon of the Lord, and again when explaining the seventy-third Psalm. Jerome disagrees, writing: "He added 'in spirit' so that you would understand humility, not penury." Chrysostom interprets it the same way in the fifteenth homily on Matthew. And Theophylact agrees with this. Not otherwise does Saint Hilary in his Canon on Matthew. Therefore, it seems to me forced and foreign to introduce here a question about the profession of begging or voluntary poverty; rather, the Lord, through modesty <margin>F</margin> and submission of oneself, shows the way to true sublimity, for Adam was cast down from his kingdom into servitude through pride.
<margin>3</margin> *Blessed are those who mourn*] In the Greek codes, "those who mourn" comes first; afterward, "Blessed are the meek." I suspect that happened by chance, as scribes are occasionally prone to slip in such lists.
<margin>4</margin> *They shall obtain mercy*] The Greek is *eleēthēsontai*. Why did the Translator not dare to use a paraphrase here as he does elsewhere? Hilary used a longer but clearer circumlocution, saying, "because God will provide mercy to them." And Augustine: "because God will have mercy on them."
<margin>5</margin> *Blessed are the pure in heart*] The Greek is *katharoi tē kardia*, that is, clean in heart. For which Augustine, using a compound word, reads "clean-hearted" <note>mundicordes</note>, even though there are two words in the Greek. Perhaps "pure in heart" would fit well here, because "cleanliness" is more opposed to filth, while "pure" is properly said of that which is corrupted by no mixture; for he placed the heart in the stead of the eyes. And elsewhere he calls it a "single" <note>or simple</note> eye.
<margin>6</margin> *Blessed are the peacemakers*] The Greek is *eirēnopoioi*. So that you may understand it is not enough for Christians...

# 27 GOSPEL CH. V 28

<margin>20</margin> ...shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven. For I say to you, that unless your righteousness abounds more than that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall by no means enter into the kingdom <margin>21</margin> of heaven. You have heard that it was said to the ancients, "You shall not kill; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment." <margin>22</margin> But I say to you, that everyone who is angry with his brother without cause <note>original: εἰκῆ</note> shall be liable to judgment; and whoever says to his brother, "Raca," <note>An Aramaic term of contempt, roughly "empty-headed"</note> shall be liable to the council; and whoever says, "You fool," shall be liable to the Gehenna <margin>23</margin> of fire. If therefore you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother <margin>24</margin> has something against you; leave your gift there before the <margin>25</margin> altar, and go; first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift. Be well-disposed toward your adversary quickly, while you are on the way with him, lest the adversary deliver you to the judge, and the judge deliver <margin>26</margin> you to the officer, and you be cast into prison. Amen I say to you, you shall by no means come out from there until you have paid the last <margin>27</margin> quadrant <note>A small Roman coin of very little value</note>. You have heard that it was said to the ancients, "You shall not commit adultery." <margin>28</margin> But I say to you, that everyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. <margin>29</margin> And if your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you; for it is better for you that one of your members perish, than that your whole body be cast into Gehenna. <margin>30</margin> And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it from you; for it is better for you that one of your members <margin>31</margin> perish, than that your whole body be cast into Gehenna. It was said that whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of <margin>32</margin> divorce. But I say to you, that whoever divorces his wife, except for the reason of unchastity, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery. Again <margin>33</margin> you have heard that it was said to the ancients, "You shall not swear falsely, but..."

---

...pertains to him to be at peace, unless the zeal for reconciling the other's peace is also added. Chrysostom noted this carefully. But these things, as morals are nowadays, are sung to the deaf.

<margin>7</margin> **When men shall revile you**] "Men" is not in the Greek books, but either the Translator or, more likely, a scribe added this from his own head; although it was not greatly needed. I thought it best to warn of this, lest anyone philosophize in vain here on the word "men." It is like the passage in Paul, "if I yet pleased men."

<margin>8</margin> **And shall persecute you**] Not wrongly, the Translator repeats "you" on his own, because in Latin "to revile" <note>maledicere</note> and "to persecute" <note>persequi</note> do not take the same grammatical case as they do in Greek. He added "men" again, which is neither in the Greek nor in the "golden manuscript" <note>A high-quality biblical manuscript Erasmus consulted</note>.

<margin>9</margin> **Every evil**] Certain Greek manuscripts add, "every evil word" <note>original: πᾶν πονηρὸν ῥῆμα</note>. The copy sent by Pope Leo, which the Spanish followed, agrees, although Chrysostom, citing this place in Book III, Chapter XI of *On the Priesthood*, does not add "word," saying "and shall say every evil against you." For the fact that "much" <note>original: πολύς</note>, that is, many or copious rewards, follows soon after, makes sense. And these are the doctrines of that most holy philosophy which Christ delivered with such care and authority—not to the promiscuous crowd, but uniquely to his own, that is, to Priests and Bishops, indeed to all noble Christians—and not in just any place, but on a mountain. Nor did Matthew add without purpose, "opening his mouth." By these names, Truth itself, which neither deceives nor is deceived, promised us happiness. And yet it is a wonder how cold we all are toward these things. Indeed, some are not ashamed, while professing a washed religion, to elude these things as if they were ancient and obsolete. It is held almost impious not to establish one's affairs by any means necessary. War is even praised in churches by Bishops, by Theologians, by Monks. For I myself have known some who, by chanting the praises of war, emerged to the dignity of a Bishop. The decrees of Aristotle move us more than those of Christ. Yet this is the characteristic and peculiar teaching of that heavenly doctrine, which none of the Philosophers ever effectively delivered. I have heard some, who seemed to themselves to be great Theologians, wrinkling their noses in disgust at these things we ought to adore (if we are truly Christians), and abominating in every way those things which Christ weighs as the highest happiness. Nor did that best of men, Chrysostom, hesitate to interpret for each grade of beatitude that what Christ pronounced blessed is more blessed even in this life, such as it is, than what the world judges to be most blessed. We, who seem to ourselves to be "one-and-a-half-times Christian," do not even receive this with fair ears, even if someone simply accepts that the reward for those things Christ taught must be performed here is to be set aside by Him in the future. And while we permit ourselves to be impious and blasphemous with impunity in those things where the entire hinge of our religion turns, it is a wonder what tragedies we stir up if anyone dares to gape at the fabricated propositions of certain men. But perhaps another more convenient place will be given for deploring these things.

<margin>10</margin> **Salt has vanished**] <note>original: μωρανθῇ</note>. So that he may not argue about the type of salt, what is it "to have vanished"? It is the same word Paul uses for "made foolish." Here, since he speaks of salt, he should have said "became fatuous," or "tasteless," or certainly, as Valla prefers, "lost its savor." Since even Martial calls beets "fatuous" because they are tasteless. Furthermore, what Valla critiques—that it should be translated "city" <note>civitatem</note> rather than "town" <note>urbem</note>—is not only a minor point, but unfair. Of the same kind is the phrase "under a bushel," that is, <note>original: ὑπὸ μόδιον</note>,

<column-break/>

<margin>11</margin> **A** for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you, when they shall cast reproaches at you, and hunt you down, and say every evil word against you, lying, because of me.
<margin>12</margin> Rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven: for so they persecuted the Prophets, who were before you.
<margin>13</margin> You are the salt of the earth: but if the salt has become tasteless, with what shall it be salted? It is good for nothing further, except to be cast out, and trampled by men.
<margin>14</margin> You are the light of the world: a town situated upon a mountain cannot be hidden:
<margin>15</margin> neither do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, and it shines for all who are in the house.
<margin>16</margin> **B** So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your father who is in heaven.
<margin>17</margin> **C** Do not think that I have come to destroy the Law or the Prophets: indeed, I have not come to destroy, but to fulfill.
<margin>18</margin> **D** For Amen I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, one iota or one tittle shall not have passed from the Law, until all things are done.
<margin>19</margin> Whoever therefore shall loosen one of these least commandments, and shall so teach men, shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But whoever shall do and teach them, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.
<margin>20</margin> **E** For I say to you, unless your justice abounds more than that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven.
<margin>21</margin> You have heard what was said to the ancients, "You shall not kill: but whoever shall kill, shall be liable to judgment."
<margin>22</margin> **F** But I say to you, that whoever is angry with his brother rashly, shall be liable to judgment: but whoever shall say...

---

...since otherwise the Greek *modios* is a bushel. It should be noted that the Translator, or perhaps the Evangelist himself, used a Roman word, which he often does elsewhere, as we shall indicate in their proper places.

<margin>11</margin> **That it may shine**] <note>original: καὶ λάμπει</note>, that is, "and it shines." For he shows what follows, not what should be strived for. In the Pauline copy it was written, "and let it shine." For it refers to the lamp, which shines in this way if it has been placed on a lampstand.

<margin>12</margin> **Because I came to loosen**] <note>original: ὅτι ἦλθον</note>, that is, "that I came," or "that I should have come." Or, as the Latin has it, "lest you think I came": and "for the purpose of loosening" rather than just "to loosen." Although this word <note>original: καταλῦσαι</note> means "to destroy" and "to demolish" or "to abrogate" rather than "to loosen"; for a law is loosened in one way, a debt of money in another, a belt or a knot in yet another.

<margin>13</margin> **Amen I say to you**] *Amen*, which among the Hebrews sounds like "let it be" or "truly"; as a word peculiar to the Hebrews, no Latin translated it, nor any of the Evangelists writing in Greek. It is the voice of one confirming and asserting.

<margin>14</margin> **One iota or a tittle**] Since it is probable that Jesus spoke in Hebrew, there is no doubt that what he calls an "iota" here is that letter which the Hebrews call *Yod*, the smallest of all, which is sometimes added in such a way that it can seem almost superfluous. But what did he mean by a "tittle" <note>apex</note>? Since it was not the custom of even the oldest Greeks to use tittles, and it was late before the Hebrews adopted the writing of accent marks—which they still do not use today—unless perhaps he called the very top point of a letter a "tittle," or that mark which, added to some, creates the letters Tet, Aleph, or He. To me, this speech seems to be said hyperbolically. For there is no laboring over the points of letters, since it is certain that not a few volumes of the Old Testament have perished, whose names we still see in the canonical volumes, such as the *Books of the Wars of the Lord* (cited in Numbers 21) and the *Book of the Just* (cited in Joshua 10 and 2 Samuel 1), and others cited in the books of Kings and Chronicles. These must have been of the highest authority, as the Canonical Scripture uses their authority so often. Whether they were in the Hebrew Canon, I leave for others to examine. We are not, therefore, laboring over tittles, but it is asserted that nothing at all promised or produced in the Mosaic Law exists which the Gospel does not fulfill. Augustine, explaining the Lord's Sermon on the Mount, does not shrink from this sentiment.

<margin>15</margin> **You shall not enter**] <note>original: οὐ μὴ εἰσέλθητε</note>. It appears to be placed emphatically, because of the doubled negation. Even if I would not deny that these sometimes signify future time, especially with the doubled negation.

<margin>16</margin> **He shall be guilty**] <note>original: ἔνοχος ἔσται</note>, that is, he shall be liable. Although the "guilty" are also called "liable": such as one who is "guilty of a vow," who has bound himself to a vow and made himself a debtor.

<margin>17</margin> **Who is angry with his brother**] In some Greek manuscripts is added "rashly" <note>original: εἰκῇ</note>, that is, "temere" or "without cause." But Jerome, discussing this place, and likewise in his second dialogue against the Pelagians, denies that this is found in ancient and faithful manuscripts. And it seems to have been added by some bold person who wanted to mitigate what otherwise seemed a rather harsh saying. But why did he not add the same "rashly" to the other parts? "He who says Raca without cause," "he who says fatuously without cause." Therefore, Saint Jerome orders these two words, "without cause," to be erased. Although the former reading is more approved by Lorenzo [Valla]. And Chrysostom in his homily on Matthew...

# ACCORDING TO MATTHEW. CHAPTER V.

33 Again, you have heard that it was said to the ancients, "You shall not swear falsely, but shall perform your oaths to the Lord."
34 But I say to you, do not swear at all: neither by heaven, for it is God's throne;
35 nor by the earth, for it is his footstool; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King.
36 Neither shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black.
37 But let your word be, "Yes, yes; No, no"; for whatever is more than these comes from the evil one.
38 You have heard that it was said, "An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth."
39 But I say to you, do not resist the evil one; but whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn the other to him also.
40 And if anyone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well.
41 And whoever forces you to go one mile, go with him two.
42 Give to him who asks of you, and do not turn away from him who wants to borrow from you.
43 You have heard that it was said, "You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy."
44 But I say to you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who spitefully use you and persecute you.
45 So that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, for he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain—

---

...the sixteenth homily seems to read *without cause* <note>original: εικῆ</note>, distinguishing appropriate anger from untimely anger, and denying that the emotion is entirely removed from us, but rather only restrained and guided. Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator</note> writes in agreement with this. There was no need here to distinguish just anger from unjust anger, the anger of the flesh from the anger of the soul, or the anger with which we are angry at a person from that with which we are angry at a person’s vice, if we understand the Lord here to be speaking of common anger, which is a movement of the mind tending toward revenge for pain, undoubtedly the first step toward murder. <margin>A</margin> Otherwise, even a judge who punishes a guilty person with anger sins, or is certainly imperfect, whom Christ teaches perfect things. But to return to the small word *without cause* <note>original: εικῆ</note>, that is, "for no reason," which Saint Jerome denies is in the true copies—what will those bring forward here who contend that this translation was corrected by Jerome? What he condemns has been left in; what has been left in pertains to the sense, not to the words, which he seems to have neglected in some places. Augustine, in his book *Retractions* (Book 1, Chapter 19), testifies that in the Greek codices "without cause" is not added. For in the Sermon on the Mount, he wants it to be understood in the other two parts as well: "he who says Raca, without cause," "he who says 'you fool,' without cause." <margin>B</margin>

<margin>18</margin> *Who says to his brother, "Raca"*] Among the Hebrews, this is a word of insult, as if you were to say in Latin "brainless," or lacking a brain, or empty. In the fourth Psalm, "empty" <note>original: ρειϰ</note> is explained as vanity: *I shall fall deservedly empty from my enemies.* And Jerome is indeed of this opinion, who thinks *racha* is equivalent to saying in Greek *empty* <note>original: ϰενος</note>. Indeed, the Greeks call a man of nothing *rakas* <note>original: ραϰας</note>, an insult taken from worn-out and discarded clothing. Saint Augustine also indicates this in the first book of the Commentaries he published on this passage. But *racha* seems more to be the voice of someone indignant, like an interjection. Otherwise, what will be the difference between *racha* and "fool"? For it is fitting that Christ show certain degrees: the first is to be angry, the second to signify the movement of the mind by some uncertain sound, and the third to break out into manifest insult. And Augustine feels this way in the place I cited a little earlier, adding that he received this from a certain Jew: that *racha* is like an interjection for the Hebrews, and by it we signify nothing certain, but only the indignation of the mind. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father known for his preaching</note>, in his sixteenth homily, teaches that *racha* is not a word of a more serious or atrocious insult, but proceeds from the impatience and irritation of the speaker: in the way we sometimes speak to servants when irritated: "Go on, you," or "Tell him, you." Indeed, he brings forward the testimony of the Syriac language, in which *racha* is used for the word "you." For so we speak to servants and to those we despise. Theophylact agrees with Chrysostom. Some distinguish between *racha* and "fool" such that the difference of the sin is not in the words, but in the mind of the speaker. For the Lord, in his usual way tempering his doctrine to the capacity of the simple, proposed an example of light anger in this way, which has not yet decreed revenge, and of heavier anger through *racha*, and of the heaviest anger, which is closest to murder, through "fool." Otherwise, he who is angry in silence often sins more gravely than he who rages with insults. Nor are there those lacking who teach that *recha* should be read, not *racha*, which for the Chaldeans <note>Aramaic speakers</note> sounds like *rocho*. They do not want that word to be an interjection, but simply to signify *empty*. Nor is it an insult, or if it is, it is a lighter insult, which applies to him who lacks education, or another thing that anyone can acquire for himself by his own industry, whereas the insult "fool" pertains to impiety. Regarding the word *racha*, if *recha* is to be read, since there is the greatest consensus in the Greek and Latin codices, either the Evangelist is rebuked, if he wrote in Greek, or the Translator, who must have been very ancient, whoever he was—for some think it was John the Evangelist. Then, since the Lord used the common language, which was corrupted by Syrian and Chaldean speech, if the Chaldeans say *rocho* for *racha*, what wonder if the Lord said *racha* for *recha*? For it does not follow that because it is written thus in the volumes of the Old Testament, therefore Christ pronounced it thus, even though the Greeks have *racha*, not *recha*. Regarding the distinction of "fool," it is established that in Greek it is written *more* <note>original: μωρε</note>; what Matthew might have written in Hebrew is uncertain to us, but it is the word Paul used concerning the disciples of the Lord: "God chose the foolish things of the world." He certainly did not mean the impious, but the humble and unskilled according to the world; and Paul himself acknowledges the word "fool," not because he was truly a fool, but because it is the way of fools to preach magnificently about themselves, which is not, however, an act of impiety, but rather silly, provided they preach true things. Now, just as it is not an insult if someone—

<column-break/>

# 28 SECUNDUM MATTHÆUM. CAP. V.

<margin>19</margin> ...to his brother Raca, shall be liable to the council: <margin>19</margin>
but whoever shall say "fool," shall be liable to the <margin>20</margin>
fire of Gehenna. Therefore, if you offer your gift <margin>23</margin>
at the altar, and there remember that your brother
has something against you: Leave your gift there <margin>24</margin>
before the altar, and go; first be reconciled to <margin>21</margin>
your brother, and then coming, offer your gift. <margin>25</margin>
Have goodwill with your adversary quickly, while
you are on the way with him: lest perhaps the adversary deliver
you to the judge, and the judge deliver you to the officer, and you be
cast into prison. Amen I say to you, you shall not come out from there, <margin>26</margin>
until you have paid the last quadrant. You have heard <margin>27</margin>
that it was said to the ancients, "You shall not commit
adultery." But I say to you, that whoever looks <margin>28</margin>
at the wife of another to lust after her,
has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
But if your right eye should be an obstacle to you, <margin>29</margin>
pluck it out, and cast it from you: for it is profitable for you, that
one of your members perish, and not your whole
body be cast into Gehenna. And if <margin>30</margin>
your right hand stands in your way, cut it off, and—

---

—rebuking a slow man calls him "slow," so it is not an insult if someone desiring to correct an impious man calls him "fool." In each case, therefore, it must be understood: "if anyone, being angry, says Raca," "if anyone, being angry, says 'fool'." Those who philosophize too much on the word "brother," as if there are no brothers except those who acknowledge a common father—I think that by the name "brother" all people are understood here. <margin>C</margin> For since the Lord commands that we bless the impious who curse us, to whom does he allow saying "fool," except according to the sense we have indicated.

<margin>19</margin> *The Council*] It is not "council" <note>original: βουλη, meaning a general assembly</note>, but *synedrion* <note>original: συνεδριω</note>, which signifies a bench of judges, as was also indicated by Chrysostom. In assemblies of this kind, such as at Athens in the court of Mars <note>The Areopagus</note>, more serious cases are usually debated. For in a judgment, which is sometimes carried out by one person, there is much hope of escaping; a serious case is not brought except to a *synedrion*, and then it is not so much a deliberation about condemning the defendant as about the manner of punishment.

<margin>20</margin> *Hell fire*] <note>original: εις γεενναν του πυρος</note>, that is, "to the Gehenna of fire." But it is spoken more in a Hebrew than Greek or Latin way, "Gehenna of fire" for "the burning of Gehenna" or "burning Gehenna." Furthermore, among the Hebrews, Gehenna <note>original: γι ηνομ</note> sounds like "Valley of Hinnom," about which we will say more below in chapter ten.

<margin>21</margin> *To be reconciled to your brother*] It is clear here that the mood of the verb was changed by the error of scribes, *to be reconciled* [passive] instead of *reconcile* [active command], <note>original: διαλλαγηθι</note>. Hence we translate it "should be reconciled," lest the corruption be just as easy. Certainly, "to reconcile" is also read in very ancient Latin copies, such as in the Paulinus manuscript. And in the Cottonian manuscript, a trace of an erasure indicates that "to reconcile" had been written there. I will omit that *go* <note>original: υπαγε</note> should have been translated as "depart" rather than "go." Nor should it be "you will offer," but *offer* <note>original: προσφερε</note>, that is, "offer" or "bring."

<margin>22</margin> *Be consenting*] <note>original: ισθι ευνοων</note>, that is, "Be well-disposed," or, as Jerome adds, "kind," even if I do not see how "kind" corresponds to *well-disposed* <note>original: ευνοων</note>. Some translated it "harmonious," as Augustine indicates.

<margin>23</margin> *And to the adversary*] <note>original: αντιδιϰω</note>. It does not absolutely mean "adversary," but "adversary in a lawsuit." Indeed, it refers to the plaintiff who makes someone a defendant and drags them into court. Again, he translates "lest perhaps," when it would be more correct to say "lest anytime," or simply "lest." Furthermore, "officer" <note>original: υπηρετη</note>, which he translates here as "minister," he elsewhere translated as "executioner," and other times as "collector." He is, however, the one who carries out the judge's sentence. <margin>E</margin>

<margin>24</margin> *The last quadrant*] <note>original: εσχατον ϰοδραντην</note>. Why "last" rather than "extreme"? For it is not about the order of time, but the total sum. Next, it appears that here too a Roman word was used by foreigners, as happens in most cases, but corrupted. A *quadrans* is a small coin, the fourth part of an *as*, which Pliny calls a *triuncius* from three ounces. Guillaume Budé <note>A famous French humanist and expert on ancient coinage</note> was the immortal glory of his nation, a man not only the most learned of all whom France ever produced, but also the most diligent; he thinks it is the same as what Cicero calls *teruncius*. And that this coin was generally held in contempt as a trifle is also attested by a proverb, which we noted in our *Adages* <note>Erasmus's own famous collection of proverbs, the *Chiliades*</note>.

<margin>25</margin> *Has committed adultery with her*] Setting aside for now that he so often translates "because" for "that": even if we grant that "to commit adultery" [moechari] is accepted by the Latins (for Catullus and Terence used it), what Latin ever said "adulteried her"? Therefore, if "to commit adultery" in this place means to commit the act, it should have been translated in this manner: "Whoever sees a wife or matron to lust after her, has already committed adultery with her." But if "to commit adultery" is used for any illicit lying together, as is sometimes found, instead of "has committed adultery," one should say "has debauched her," or as Suetonius says, "adulterated her." <margin>F</margin>

<margin>26</margin> *Causes you to stumble*] It is strange that the Greek word <term>scandalizat</term> was so pleasing to the translator, when it could have been said "offended you," or "was an obstacle or stumbling block." For the fact that he translated *exele* <note>original: εξελε</note>, that is, "take out" or "extract," as "pluck out," cannot be blamed.

<margin>27</margin> *Than your whole body*] This kind of speech style is found among the Greeks, and among some Latins who imitate Greek. But that is when "than" <note>original: η</note> is added, so that you understand "rather" <note>original: μαλλον</note>. But here it is otherwise: "and not the whole" <note>original: ϰαι μη ολον</note>. And likewise in the next part. Therefore it is strange that the Translator affected Greek—

# GOSPEL CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Matthew 5</margin>
**46** <note>original: καὶ ἐὰν ἀγαπήσητε τοὺς ἀγαπῶντας ὑμᾶς, τίνα μισθὸν ἔχετε; οὐχὶ καὶ οἱ τελῶναι τὸ αὐτὸ ποιοῦσι;</note> And if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same?
<margin>47</margin> <note>original: Καὶ ἐὰν ἀσπάσησθε τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς ὑμῶν μόνον, τί περισσὸν ποιεῖτε; οὐχὶ καὶ οἱ τελῶναι οὕτω ποιοῦσι;</note> And if you greet your brothers only, what extra are you doing? Do not even the tax collectors do so?
<margin>48</margin> <note>original: Ἔσεσθε οὖν ὑμεῖς τέλειοι, ὥσπερ ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς τέλειός ἐστι.</note> Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father who is in heaven is perfect.
<margin>Matthew 6</margin>
**1** <note>original: Προσέχετε τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην ὑμῶν μὴ ποιεῖν ἔμπροσθεν τῶν ἀνθρώπων, πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι αὐτοῖς· εἰ δὲ μήγε, μισθὸν οὐκ ἔχετε παρὰ τῷ πατρὶ ὑμῶν τῷ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς.</note> Take care not to perform your charitable deeds before men, to be seen by them; otherwise, you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.
<margin>2</margin> <note>original: Ὅταν οὖν ποιῇς ἐλεημοσύνην, μὴ σαλπίσῃς ἔμπροσθέν σου, ὥσπερ οἱ ὑποκριταὶ ποιοῦσιν ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς καὶ ἐν ταῖς ῥύμαις, ὅπως δοξασθῶσιν ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων· ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ἀπέχουσι τὸν μισθὸν αὐτῶν.</note> Therefore, when you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be glorified by men; truly I say to you, they have received their reward.
<margin>3</margin> <note>original: Σοῦ δὲ ποιοῦντος ἐλεημοσύνην, μὴ γνώτω ἡ ἀριστερά σου τί ποιεῖ ἡ δεξιά σου.</note> But when you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing.
<margin>4</margin> <note>original: Ὅπως ᾖ σου ἡ ἐλεημοσύνη ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ· καὶ ὁ πατήρ σου ὁ βλέπων ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ, αὐτὸς ἀποδώσει σοι ἐν τῷ φανερῷ.</note> So that your almsgiving may be in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will himself reward you openly.
<margin>5</margin> <note>original: Καὶ ὅταν προσεύχῃ, οὐκ ἔσῃ ὥσπερ οἱ ὑποκριταί, ὅτι φιλοῦσιν ἐν ταῖς συναγωγαῖς καὶ ἐν ταῖς γωνίαις τῶν πλατειῶν ἑστῶτες προσεύχεσθαι, ὅπως ἂν φανῶσι τοῖς ἀνθρώποις· ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ὅτι ἀπέχουσι τὸν μισθὸν αὐτῶν.</note> And when you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites, for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the corners of the streets, so that they may be seen by men; truly I say to you, they have received their reward.
<margin>6</margin> <note>original: Σὺ δὲ ὅταν προσεύχῃ, εἴσελθε εἰς τὸ ταμιεῖόν σου, καὶ κλείσας τὴν θύραν σου, προσεύξαι τῷ πατρί σου τῷ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ· καὶ ὁ πατήρ σου ὁ βλέπων ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ, ἀποδώσει σοι ἐν τῷ φανερῷ.</note> But you, when you pray, go into your room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.
<margin>Matthew 7 <note>Note: Marginal reference likely intended for verse 7 of chapter 6</note></margin>
**7** <note>original: Προσευχόμενοι δὲ μὴ βαττολογήσητε, ὥσπερ οἱ ἐθνικοί· δοκοῦσι γὰρ ὅτι ἐν τῇ πολυλογίᾳ αὐτῶν εἰσακουσθήσονται.</note> But when you pray, do not babble like the heathens; for they think that they will be heard for their many words.

---

...a mechanical pattern that the Greek language did not possess. Nor is it "let him go into hell," but <note>original: βληθῇ</note>, that is, "let him be cast." Although the Greeks do speak this way—<note>original: βάλλ᾽ ἐς κόρακας</note>, "go to the crows"—they imply "yourself," as if you were to say, "cast yourself away," or "remove yourself."

**28** *A certificate of divorce*] What is said in Greek with a single word <note>original: ἀποστά-σιον</note>, as if you were to say, "a release," that is, a document of divorce. Chrysostom <note>An early Church Father and famed orator</note> noted in this place: *The precept regarding not leaving one's wife depends on what came before: "When you give alms," and he did not describe it before, nor does anyone cast out his wife unless she is an adulteress, nor does anyone receive another man's wife with injury to the former husband.* And he soon adds concerning swearing: *Which he forbade in such a way that he excluded nothing at all. And yet, as if this were not said seriously by Christ, we swear everywhere. Certainly, it is to be hoped by all prayers that Christians would be such that there is no need for divorce, nor for an oath.*

**29** *He who marries her who is divorced commits adultery*] <note>original: μοιχᾶται</note>. This is translated as "commits adultery," and finally he translates it as "adulterates." Although "to adulterate" is one thing, and "to commit adultery" is another whenever it is used absolutely. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo</note>, in his work *On Adulterous Marriages* addressed to Pollentius, indicates that this clause, *and whoever marries her who is divorced commits adultery*, was not written in some Greek and Latin manuscripts, because it follows sufficiently from the previous speech. However, I have found this in no one else, either written or noted.

<margin>A</margin>
**30** *again you have heard*] <note>original: πάλιν ἠκούσατε</note>, "again you heard." For it does not signify a repetition, but an order.

**31** *Neither by heaven*] <note>original: μήτε ἐν οὐρανῷ</note>, that is, "neither in heaven," yet I believe the Apostles frequently use this preposition instead of "by," following the property of Hebrew speech, as in "by the finger of God," and "in your name we have prophesied," just as we shall point out in their proper places.

<margin>B</margin>
**32** *It is, it is; no, no*] <note>original: ναὶ, ναὶ, οὐ, οὐ</note>. What is here translated is the Greek adverb for affirming, <note>original: ναὶ</note>, but it is also used by the Latins. The translator sometimes renders it as "even," which the unlearned commonly say as "so": as if "so" responds to the negation "no." And indeed, "so" is found in Terence <note>A Roman playwright</note>, but spoken by one responding impertinently. Of that kind is the phrase, *So it shall be.* Furthermore, let no one think the doubling refers to the same person, <margin>the first part refers to the questioner, the second to the respondent.</margin> unless you take it this way: if your speech affirms, let it truly affirm; if it denies, let it truly deny. It is otherwise with those who do not perform what they promise, and do what they say they will not do.

**33** *Is more than these*] <note>original: τὸ δὲ περισσὸν τούτων</note>, that is, what is added beyond these. Certain theologians twist this place marvelously. *It is from the evil one*, some interpret as "from the evil of the one distrusting," not "from the evil of the one swearing"; others as "from the evil of punishment," not "from the evil of fault." But I believe Christ simply meant that for the perfect (for he speaks of these), one must not swear at all for these worldly things over which the common people swear. Otherwise, in a cause of faith or piety, even Christ and the Apostles swear. For he wants his followers to be such that there is no need for any oath. For what point would there be in swearing if there were no one who wanted to circumvent anyone, even if he could do so with impunity, but each, judging another from his own heart, distrusted no one? For he who is truly Christian consults the benefit of others even to his own disadvantage; so far is he from wanting to deceive anyone. And charity believes all things so much, and distrusts so little, that it interprets even things that are hardly honorable as good, as far as it can. By this reasoning, the knots of many questions can be dissolved, if we understand that Christ did not simply forbid these things, but forbade them to be done in the manner in which they were done according to common human custom. Thus he forbade being angry, thus he forbade greeting anyone on the road, thus he forbade becoming rich, thus he forbade resisting evil, thus he forbade being called masters, thus he forbade calling anyone father on earth. But these things do not properly belong to this specific purpose.

<margin>34</margin>
**34** *A tooth for a tooth*] The Greeks add the conjunction "and" <note>original: καὶ ὀδόντα ἀντὶ ὀδόντος</note>. The same is added in ancient Latin manuscripts. It should be noted in passing that in speeches of this kind, the Greek article cannot even be applied: because any eye and any tooth is signified.

<column-break/>

cast it from you: for it is profitable for you that one of your members should perish, and not that your whole body should be cast into hell. Furthermore, it has been said, <margin>31</margin> whoever shall divorce his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce. But I say to you, that whoever <margin>32</margin> divorces his wife, except for the cause of fornication, makes her commit adultery: and whoever shall marry her who is divorced, commits adultery. <margin>33</margin> Again you have heard what was said to the ancients, "You shall not swear falsely, but shall perform to the Lord those things which you have sworn." But I say to you, do <margin>34</margin> not swear at all: neither by heaven, because it is the throne of God: nor by the earth, because it is the footstool of <margin>35</margin> his feet: nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great king: Neither shall you swear by your head, <margin>36</margin> because you cannot make one hair white or black. But your speech shall be, "Yes, yes; No, no": for what is added beyond these, proceeds <margin>37</margin> from the evil one. You have heard what was said, <margin>38</margin> "An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth." But <margin>39</margin> I say to you, do not resist evil: but whoever shall strike a blow on your right cheek, <margin>36</margin> turn to him the other also. And to him who wishes to drag you into <margin>40</margin> court and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. And whoever compels you to go <margin>38</margin> one mile, <margin>41</margin> go with him two. To him who asks of you, give, and to him <margin>42</margin> who wishes—

---

<margin>35</margin> *Not to resist evil*] <note>original: μὴ ἀντιστήναι τῷ πονηρῷ</note>. "Evil" can refer either to a thing or to a person; furthermore, the case could be an "instrumental ablative." *Do not resist anyone*, with evil—that is, with injury or cunning. This sense pleased Chrysostom, who says the man must be resisted not with evil, but with patience, for fire is not extinguished by fire, but by water. It is a wonder, however, what force the added article has here, <note>original: τῷ πονηρῷ</note>, as if it signifies a specific evil. Unless perhaps it is added appositively to the word: as if you were to say, "to him who is evil." Some interpret the name "evil" to signify the devil, among whom is Theophylact. But who speaks this way? I tell you "not to go away," instead of "I command that you do not go anywhere." Then, what will they do with this passage—those who approve of lawsuits and wars by every calculation among Christians? Christ absolutely forbade resisting evil—that is, in the common way, so that evil is repelled by evil, which is to say, insult with insult, wound with wound, war with war, slaughter with slaughter. Indeed, what excuse will they make, those who return a benefit with a grievance? There is that slight point, that <note>original: ὅσις</note> is translated as "if anyone," instead of "whoever": unless perhaps he read <note>original: εἴ τις</note>. Also, that <note>original: στρέψας</note>, that is, "turn" or "offer," he skipped over to "provide." Augustine in some places reads "prepare."

<margin>D</margin>
**36** *Offer also the other*] This <term>hyperbole</term> <note>an intentional exaggeration for emphasis</note> of Christ, in my opinion, teaches nothing other than the highest patience and moderation of the mind, and that we should be so far from the desire for revenge that we are voluntarily ready to admit another injury rather than weigh evil against evil. And this perhaps is what Augustine felt, when in other places, specifically in his booklet *On Lying* and in the twenty-second book *Against Faustus*, he writes that the preparation of the other cheek must be made in the heart, not in the body. For Christ did not mean that the left cheek must be turned to him who struck the right, but he wanted us to be of such gentleness that we are more ready to receive a second injury than to retaliate for the first. Nor indeed should everything that contains a hyperbole be seen as connected to a lie. Saint Augustine noted this and other examples in the divine scriptures, following Origen, Jerome, and Chrysostom. Such as that kind in the book of Judges: *Their camels were without number, as the sand which is on the seashore.* Again, that in the Psalms: *They mount up to the heavens, and they go down even into the abyss:* <margin>E</margin> namely, regarding the waves of the sea alternately lifting themselves and sinking. Certainly, Augustine openly noted this <term>figure of speech</term> in his fifth letter to Marcellinus, showing that if anyone rejects the trope of the speech, it is more fitting that the first blow be said to have been received on the left, because the force of the striker is carried more toward this than toward the right. He likewise warns that in Luke no mention of left or right is made: so that you may understand in this place that "left" and "right" are nothing other than "one" and "the other": just as in another certain parable he placed five talents for many gifts, two for moderate ones, and one for the smallest. Furthermore, it should be noticed how he suddenly changed the number: *But I say to you: but whoever shall strike you on the cheek, etc.* For no other reason than that this number is more suited to impressing upon the mind what is said, while each person thinks that what is said is being said to himself.

<margin>F</margin>
**37** *And the cloak*] <note>original: καὶ τὸ ἱμάτιον</note>. Here he correctly distinguished the type of garment. For <note>original: χιτὼν</note>, the tunic, is the inner garment; <note>original: ἱμάτιον</note> is the outer, which is the "toga" for the Romans and the "pallium" or cloak for the Greeks. Except that among the Greeks, <note>original: ἱμά-τιον</note> is sometimes used for any kind of garment. Whence Augustine rightly advises that this is the sense: *if anyone takes away any one garment, concede to him rather if you have any other garments than that you should contend.* Otherwise, the speech would be backwards. For the cloak, which is the outermost garment, is taken off first, and then the tunic.

<margin>38</margin>
**38** *A thousand paces*] <note>original: μίλιον ἓν</note>, that is, one mile. Otherwise, what follows does not correspond.

<margin>39</margin>
**39** *Two others*] Not even that, "two other [miles]." And here again the Greek has used a Latin word: although Hesychius made mention of this word. Nor is it "two others" for the Greeks, but <note>original: ὕπαγε μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ δύο</note>: so that you may understand that double ought to be conceded to one extorting a single thing: just as he taught regarding the cheek and the garment. <margin>A</margin> Augustine <note>A famous early church father and philosopher</note> engages in philosophical reflection here regarding the number three; Theophylact and Chrysostom <note>Important Greek-speaking biblical commentators</note> do not touch on it. For if the word "their" <note>original: αὐτῶν</note> is used, they might be able to do it; if it refers to the lowly person asking of you, he did rightly.

40 **Do not turn away** | <note>original: μὴ ἀποστραφῇς</note> do not turn your back, as Augustine reads it; that is, do not reject. Although "to be turned away" is also found as a passive-style verb, it is more commonly used in poetry, as in Boethius:
> *Alas, with what a deaf ear she turns away from the wretched!*
Just as "to be anticipated" is used.

41 **You shall love your neighbor** | The Greeks use the word for neighbor <note>original: τοῖς πλησίον</note> to call those who are family members and those with whom we have a close and domestic association, not only blood relatives. For they do not have a superlative degree for this word.

42 **And you shall hate your enemy** | Since this is not read in the literal text of the Old Testament, some interpret this to be an addition of the Pharisees, not the Scripture itself. They claim the same about other articles, as if Christ added nothing to the legal precepts but only explained them. Certainly Saint Augustine, in the first book where he explains this passage, relates it as if it were found in the Sacred Books, for he says: *Nor is what was said in the Law, 'you shall hate your enemy,' to be taken as the voice of one commanding a just man, but of one permitting it to a weak man.* Such, surely, was the Jewish common people. Moreover, just as we accept the impulse of anger, so also the acceptance of hatred explains the difficulty. Certainly Chrysostom admits that the Lord in ancient times did not demand from the weak what he commanded in his own time to those now better instructed.

43 **Love your enemies** | After these words, the Greek manuscripts (among which is Theophylact) add a small phrase which I do not find in our Latin edition: *bless those who curse you* <note>original: εὐλογεῖτε τοὺς καταρωμένους ὑμᾶς</note>. Indeed, neither Jerome nor Chrysostom adds it. Therefore, I do not know whether some studious person added it here because of the similarity of the sentiment from the Epistle of Paul to the Romans. For on this occasion, we find several passages have been changed.

<margin>E</margin> 44 **For those who persecute and slander** | <note>original: ἐπηρεαζόντων καὶ διωκόντων</note> both of which mean almost the same thing; for "malice" <note>original: ἐπήρεια</note> is properly called "unjust" by the Greeks in war, as if you said *epareia*, from *Ares* (the god of war). From this, the word *epereazo* appears to be derived, which means to harass, or to do violence with force. But the Greeks teach that this word sometimes has the same value as "to harm"; we translate it as "they injure."

45 **Who makes his sun** | <note>original: ὅτι τὸν ἥλιον</note> that is, "because his sun." This is allowed despite the Latin copies pulling back. It is possible that the Translator read *who* <note>original: ὃς</note> or *whosoever* instead of *because*. Though this matters nothing to the sense. And for the phrase "makes to rise" <note>original: ἀνατέλλει</note>, it is a correct circumlocution for "causing to rise" or "bringing forth." Likewise, for "it rains," the Greeks have *brechei*, meaning "it waters." Again:

46 **What reward will you have** | In Greek it is *echete* <note>original: ἔχετε</note>, that is, "you have," in the present tense, so that the meaning refers to the reality of the thing, not the time. Furthermore, he could have used "reward" for "grace."

47 **And the tax collectors** | <note>original: τελῶναι</note> that is, those who buy up the right to collect taxes, hence they are also called "contractors." This class of men was once infamous among the Jews, but now among Christians, they are considered especially honorable. This is no wonder, since shopkeepers and money-changers are preferred almost above all others by the leaders of both types of State—men whom neither Aristotle nor Cicero wanted to be held among honorable citizens. And it is not "they do this," but "they do the same" <note>original: τὸ αὐτὸ</note>. And for "you shall greet," it is *aspasesthe* <note>original: ἀσπάσησθε</note>, which is not simply to say hello, but to greet with a kiss and an embrace; this was once done by custom among friends, not only among the Jews, but also among the Greeks and Romans. Otherwise, it is a common duty to say "be well" to someone you meet.

48 **Your brothers** | Most Greek manuscripts have "your friends" <note>original: τοὺς φίλους ὑμῶν</note>. But the Jews call any relative whatsoever "brothers"; and Jerome reads it this way.

49 **What more do you do** | <note>original: τί περισσὸν</note> what extraordinary thing, or what above the rest.

50 **Do not even the heathens** | Again in this place, some Greek manuscripts have *telonai*, that is, "tax collectors." However, from the interpretation of Chrysostom, one can gather that he read "heathen," since

<margin>C</margin> he says: *For which reason he also here brings Gentiles and tax collectors into the midst, so that by comparing the Disciples to such persons, he may kindle them to virtue through shame.* Certainly Theophylact repeats "tax collectors" <note>original: τελῶναι</note> here. For "Ethnic" sounds like "Gentile," a Greek word with which the Translator seems pleased, because, I think, "gentile" signifies something else to Latin ears—namely, someone joined by family kinship. And again, it is not here "they do this," but "they do so" <note>original: οὕτως ποιοῦσιν</note>.

51 **You shall therefore be** | <note>original: ἔσεσθε</note> that is, "you will be." The Translator seems to have read *esesthe*. I omit the fact that "he who is in the heavens" <note>original: ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς</note>, which he usually translates as "who is in heaven," he has now changed to "heavenly." Furthermore, the conjunction "as," like "and [as your] father," is not added among the Greeks. It is simply, "just as your heavenly Father."

<margin>D</margin> **Regarding [your justice]** In the Greek it is **almsgiving** <note>original: ἐλεημοσύνην</note>, that is, charity, not "justice," so that it matches what follows: *When therefore you do alms.* This is how Chrysostom and Theophylact read and interpret it. Even though Jerome reads "justice," he interprets it as almsgiving. And likewise Augustine, in his second sermon on the words of the Lord from Matthew, similarly interprets it as he reads it. One should mention in passing that Latins, when using the Greek word *eleemosyna*, cheat it of one syllable, since among the Greeks it has six syllables.

2 **That you may be seen by them** | Augustine, in the place we cited, indicates that this phrase should be added to the previous speech in such a way that it signifies the *purpose* of the action, not just a *consequence*. For he does not forbid good deeds being seen, but he does not want them to be done with that intent. Among the Latins, this speech is ambiguous—"so that you are seen" could mean "in such a way that you are seen" or "with the mind that you are seen." However, for the Greeks there is no ambiguity: *toward the being seen* <note>original: πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι</note>. Again, in that which follows,

3 **You shall not have a reward** | He changed the tense of the verb: "you do not have" <note>original: οὐκ ἔχετε</note>.

4 **As the hypocrites** | These words are among those whose number the Translator seems to have enjoyed. Otherwise, *hypokrites* among the Greeks signifies a "stage-actor"—that is, one who acts out a story before the people in a false persona, whom we call "actors." Hence, what we call "delivery" or "acting," they call *hypokrisis*. Although anyone who simulates and pretends in any way can be called a hypocrite. Hence Paul says "love without hypocrisy," that is, love that is not feigned and knows not how to pretend. Furthermore, as far as acting gestures are concerned, what he had just said fits beautifully: *toward the being seen*, that is, so that they may be spectated—which is the business of actors, and from this we get the word "theater" <note>original: theatrum</note>. For who is less an actor than those who, with an empty movement of the lips and a noise of voices, want to be seen praying to God and talking with him? Or those who lie about holiness through Jewish ceremonies? Again, where he translates "in the synagogues," it was more open as "in the meeting places." For it signifies the little gatherings that usually happen in the squares and the marketplace or the crossroads. And understand "streets" <note>original: vicos</note> in this place not as those which are not towns, but into which a city is divided. For a little later he mentions "broad ways," which are properly called wider roads where the common people gather; some philosophize on this word, saying that the cities of the impious have "broad ways," while the way for neighbors is narrow. To these points:

5 **They have received reward** | <note>original: ἀπέχουσιν</note> that is, "they have," or "they carried off." For *apechein* sounds like something that is received from elsewhere.

6 **Let not your left hand know** | In Greek there are two words, *me gnoto*, "let it not know."

7 **Let not your left hand know what the right is doing** | This is not said without a figure of speech, but hyperbolically <note>as an exaggeration for effect</note>, as if you were to say: "you yourself shall not know what you will do, if it can be done," so far should you be from showing it to others. Chrysostom noted this figure in Homily 19, and Theophylact followed him. However, the Greeks add "in secret" <note>original: ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ</note>, that is, "in the hidden place," or "in the open." Yet Augustine says he did not find this in the Greek manuscripts, and therefore thinks it should not be explained. Theophylact even interprets "in the open" <note>original: ἐν φανερῷ</note> as being when all good and evil works will be made manifest. To me, the genuine reading seems to be that which Augustine approves.

28 *A bill of divorce*] Which in Greek is said in a single word, <term>apostasion</term> <note>original: ἀποστάσιον</note>, as if you were to say, a "divortial" document, that is, a bill of divorce. 
Chrysostom noted in this place: *That the command about not leaving one's wife depends on what came before: for among such people as he described a little earlier, no one would cast out a wife unless she were an adulteress, nor would anyone receive another man's wife to the injury of the former husband.* And
soon after he adds regarding swearing: *Which he forbade in such a way that he excepted nothing at all. And yet, as if this were not said by followers of Christ, we swear everywhere. Certainly, it is to be hoped by all prayers that Christians were such that there would be no need for divorce, nor for an oath.*

<margin>C</margin> 29 *He who marries a dismissed woman commits adultery*] <note>original: μοιχᾶται / moichatai</note>. Which the
translator had rendered as "acts as an adulterer," he finally translated as "adulterates." Although it is one thing to *adulterate* and another to *commit adultery*, whenever it is placed
absolutely. Augustine, in "On Adulterous Marriages" to Pollentius, indicates
that this clause, *& whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery*, was
not added in some Greek and Latin codices, because it follows sufficiently
from the previous speech. However, I have found this in no
one else, either written or annotated.

30 *Again you have heard*] <note>original: Πάλιν ἠκούσατε / Palin ēkousate</note>, *Again you have heard*. For it
does not signify a repetition, but a sequence <note>meaning "next in order"</note>.

31 *Neither by heaven*] <note>original: μήτε ἐν οὐρανῷ / mēte en ouranō</note>, that is, neither in heaven,
which preposition, I believe, according to the property of the Hebrew
language, the Apostles frequently used for *by*, as in "by the finger of God,"
and "in your name we have prophesied," as we shall point out in the appropriate
places of this work.

32 *It is, it is, no, no*] <note>original: ναὶ, ναὶ, οὐ, οὐ / nai, nai, ou, ou</note>. What he here translates as "it is,"
is to the Greeks the adverb of affirmation <unclear>yes</unclear>, but it is also used by
the Latins. The translator sometimes renders it "even," which the poorly
educated commonly say: as if it corresponds to the negation "no." And
indeed "so" is repeated in Terence, but spoken by one responding rather
wickedly. Of which kind is that: *So it shall be*. Furthermore, let no one
think the doubling belongs to the same person, <unclear>or</unclear> that the first part belongs to the
questioner, the latter to the responder. Unless you take it this way: If your speech affirms, let it truly affirm; if it denies, let it truly deny.
Which is otherwise among those who do not perform what they promise, and do
what they say they will not do.

33 *This is more abundant*] <note>original: τὸ δὲ περισσὸν τούτων / to de perisson toutōn</note>, that is, what
has been added beyond these. Certain theologians twist this place marvelously. From *it is of evil*, some interpret "from the evil of the one who distrusts," not from the
evil of the one who swears; others "from the evil of punishment," not "from the evil of fault." But
I think Christ simply meant that for the perfect (for he speaks of these)
there should be no swearing at all for these common things for which
the common people swear. Otherwise, in a cause of faith, or of piety, even
Christ and the Apostles swear. For he wants his followers to be such that there is no
need for an oath. For what point would there be in swearing, if there were no one
who wanted to deceive anyone, even if he could do so with impunity,
and each estimating the other by his own mind, distrusted no one? For
he who is truly a Christian consults the convenience of others even at his own disadvantage: he is so far from wanting to deceive anyone. And charity so
believes all things, and so does not distrust, that as far as it can, it interprets
even things that are not entirely honest for the good. By this reasoning, the knots
of many questions can be untied, if we understand that Christ
did not simply forbid these things, but forbade them to be done in the manner
in which they were done by the common custom of men. Thus he forbade being angry, thus he forbade
greeting anyone on the road, thus he forbade becoming rich, thus he forbade resisting
evil, thus he forbade being called masters, thus he forbade calling anyone father on
earth. But these things do not properly belong to this present purpose.

34 *A tooth for a tooth*] The Greeks add the conjunction "and" <note>original: καὶ / kai</note>, <note>original: καὶ ὀδόντα ἀντὶ ὀδόντος / kai odonta anti odontos</note>. The same is added in old Latin 
copies. It should be noted in passing that in speeches of this kind
the Greek article is not even applied: because any eye and
any tooth is signified.

---

35 *Not to resist evil*] <note>original: μὴ ἀντιστήναι τῷ πονηρῷ / mē antistēnai tō ponērō</note>. "Evil" can either
refer to a thing, or to a person; furthermore, it can be the abla-
tive of instrument. Do not *resist anyone* with evil, that is, with
injury, or with craftiness. This sense pleases Chrysostom, when
he says, a man must be resisted not with evil, but with patience, for fire is not
extinguished by fire, but by water. It is strange, however, what force the added article
has here, <note>original: τῷ πονηρῷ / tō ponērō</note>, as if it signifies a certain specific evil. Unless
perhaps it is joined to a common noun: as if you were to say, to him who is evil.
Some interpret the name of evil as signifying the devil, among
whom is Theophylact. But who speaks this way? "I tell you not
to go away," for "I command that you go nowhere." Then what
will they do with this place, those who approve of lawsuits and wars for all Christians?
Christ absolutely forbade resisting evil, surely in the
common way, so that evil is repelled by evil, that is, insult
by insult, wound by wound, war by war, slaughter by slaughter. Indeed, what will
they pretend, those who repay a benefit with an injury? It is a small matter
that the translator renders <note>original: ὁσός / hosos</note> as *if anyone*, instead of *whoever*: unless perhaps he read <note>original: εἴ τις / ei tis</note>.
Likewise, where he translates *exobet*, that is, *turns*, or *turn toward*, he rendered it as *offer*.
Augustine in some places reads *prepare*.

<margin>D</margin> 36 *Offer to him the other also*] This hyperbole of Christ, in my opinion,
teaches nothing other than the highest patience and moderation of soul,
and that we should be so far from the desire for revenge, that we are
willingly ready rather to admit a second injury, than to repay evil
with evil. And perhaps Augustine felt this, when elsewhere,
as well as in the book "On Lying," and in the twenty-second book against
Faustus, he writes that the preparation of the other cheek is to be
made in the heart, not in the body. For Christ did not mean that
the left cheek must be turned to him who struck the right, but he
wanted us to have such gentleness that we are more ready to receive a
second injury than to retaliate for the first. Nor indeed should whatever 
contains a hyperbole be seen as immediately connected with a lie.
Which Saint Augustine noted elsewhere in the divine scriptures, besides Origen, Jerome,
and Chrysostom. Such as that kind in the book of Judges: *Of their camels there was no number, and
they were as the sand which is on the seashore*. Again that in the 
Psalms: *They go up to the heavens, and go down even to the abyss*:
<margin>E</margin> namely, concerning the waves of the sea alternately raising themselves and sinking.
Certainly Augustine openly noted this figure of speech in the fifth epistle
to Marcellinus, showing that if anyone rejects the trope of speech,
it would be more appropriate for the first blow to be said to have been
received on the left, because the impulse of the striker falls more on this
than on the right. He likewise warns that in Luke no
mention of left or right is made: so that we may understand that in this place "left" and "right" are
nothing other than "one" and "the other": just as in another
parable he placed five talents for many gifts,
two for moderate ones, one for the smallest. Furthermore, it should be
observed how he suddenly changed the number, *But I say to
you* [plural]: but *whoever strikes you* [singular] *on the cheek, etc.* For no other reason
except that this number is more suited for fixing in the mind
what is said, while each person thinks what is said is being said to himself.

<margin>F</margin> 37 *And the cloak*] <note>original: καὶ τὸ ἱμάτιον / kai to himation</note>. Here he correctly distinguishes the
kind of garment. Since <term>chiton</term> <note>original: χιτών</note>, the tunic, is an inner garment, <term>himation</term> <note>original: ἱμάτιον</note> is an 
outer one, which to the Romans is the toga, and to the Greeks the <term>pallium</term> <note>cloak</note>. Except that 
<term>himation</term> among the Greeks is sometimes used for any
kind of garment. Hence Augustine rightly warns that this is the sense: if anyone takes
one garment, concede to him rather whatever other garment you have than
that you should contend. Otherwise the speech would be backwards. For the
cloak, which is the outermost garment, is taken off first, then
the tunic.

38 *A thousand paces*] <note>original: μίλιον ἕν / milion hen</note>, that is, one mile-marker. Otherwise
what follows does not correspond.

39 *Another two*] Not even that, "others two." And here again the
Greek used a Latin word <note>mille/milion</note>: although Hesychius makes mention of this word.
Nor is it "another two" for the Greeks, but *go with him two* <note>original: ὕπαγε μετ᾿ αὐτοῦ δύο / hypage met' autou dyo</note>:
so that you understand that double ought to be conceded to one extorting a single thing:
just as he taught concerning the cheek and the garment. Although Saint Au-
