*Augustine philosophizes here on the number three <note>original: "numero ternario"</note>, which Theophylact and Chrysostom do not touch upon. As for the phrase "if they praise something," that is, "they could themselves," he translates "to the one asking of you," and he has done so correctly.*

<margin>40</margin> *Do not turn away] <note>original: μὴ ἀποστραφῇς</note> "Do not be turned away," as Augustine reads it, that is, "do not reject." Although "I am turned away" <note>original: avertor</note> is also found as a deponent verb, it is more common in poetry, as in Boethius:*

->*Alas, with how deaf an ear she turns away from the wretched!*<-

*Just as "it is turned before."*

<margin>41</margin> *You shall love your neighbor] The Greeks call those "neighbors" <note>original: τοὺς πλησίον</note> who are close friends, and those with whom we have a tight and domestic familiarity, not just relatives. For they do not have a superlative degree for this word.*

<margin>42</margin> *And you shall hate your enemy] Since this is not read in the letters of the Old Testament <note>literally "the old Instrument"</note>, some interpret this to be an addition of the Pharisees, not Scripture. They preach the same about other articles, as if Christ added nothing to the legal precepts but only explained them. Certainly, Saint Augustine, in the first book where he narrates this passage, reports it as if it were found in the Sacred Books, for he says: "Nor should what was said in the Law, 'thou shalt hate thine enemy,' be taken as the voice of one commanding a righteous man, but as one permitting it to the weak." Such, clearly, was the common lot of the Jews. Moreover, just as we accept a figure of speech regarding anger, so too in the case of hatred, he unravels the knot of perspective. Certainly, Chrysostom confesses that the Lord once did not demand from the weak what he later commanded of those who were now instructors.*

<margin>43</margin> *Love your enemies] After the words of this place, the Greek codices add a small part, among which is Theophylact, which I do not find in our edition: <note>original: εὐλογεῖτε τοὺς καταρωμένους ὑμᾶς</note> that is, "bless those who curse you." Surely neither Jerome nor Chrysostom adds this. Hence, I do not know whether some studious person, on account of the similarity of the sentiment, added it here from Paul's Epistle to the Romans. For on such occasions, several passages have been changed.*

<margin>44</margin> *For those who persecute and slander you] <note>original: ἐπηρεαζόντων καὶ διωκόντων</note>: both of which mean nearly the same thing; for the first verb is properly said of injuries in war, as if you were to say <note>original: ἐπαρεία</note> from "Ares" or Mars; hence it appears the word "insult" or "abuse" is derived, which is to vex, or to act with force and attack. But since the Greeks teach that this verb never means the same as "to harm," we translate it as "they hurt."*

<margin>45</margin> *Who [makes] his sun] <note>original: ὅτι τὸν ἥλιον</note> that is, "because [he makes] his sun." This is permitted despite the resistance of the Latin copies. And it may be that the Translator read "who" <note>original: ὅς or ὅστις</note> instead of "because." Though this matters nothing to the sense. And for "he rises," he rightly used the circumlocution "he makes to rise," or "he brings forth." Likewise, for "he rains," the Greeks say "it still rains," meaning "he waters." Again:*

<margin>46</margin> *What reward will you have] In Greek it is "you have" <note>original: ἔχετε</note>, that is, in the present tense, so that it signifies the nature of the thing, not the time. Furthermore, he placed "reward" in place of "grace."*

<margin>47</margin> *And the publicans] <note>original: τελῶναι</note>, that is, those who buy up the taxes, from which they are also called "redeemers." A class of men once infamous among the Jews, but now among Christians considered especially honorable. And that is not surprising, since merchants and money-changers are preferred to almost everyone among the leaders of both Republics—men whom neither Aristotle nor Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> wished to be held among honorable citizens. Nor is it "they do this," but <note>original: τὸ αὐτὸ</note>, that is, "they do the same thing." And "you shall salute" is <note>original: ἀσπάσησθε</note>, which is not simply to greet, but to greet with a kiss and an embrace; which was once done by custom among friends, not only among the Jews, but also among the Greeks and Romans. Otherwise, it is a common duty to say "hello" to someone you meet.*

<margin>48</margin> *Your brothers] Most Greek codices have "your friends" <note>original: τοὺς φίλους ὑμῶν</note>. Truly, the Jews call relatives of any kind "brothers"; and so Jerome reads it.*

<margin>49</margin> *What more are you doing] <note>original: τί περισσὸν</note> "what extraordinary thing," or "what above the rest."*

<margin>50</margin> *Do not even the Heathens] Again in this place several Greek codices have "publicans" <note>original: τελῶναι</note>. However, from the interpretation of Chrysostom, one can gather that he read "Heathen," since*

<margin>C</margin> *he says: "For this reason he also brings forward here the Gentiles and the tax collectors into the midst, so that by comparing his Disciples to such persons, he might kindle them to virtue through shame." Certainly, Theophylact finds "tax collectors" <note>original: τελῶναι</note> here. For "Heathen" <note>original: Ethnicus</note> sounds like "Gentile," a Greek word which the Translator seems to have delighted in, because, I believe, "gentilis" means something else to Latin ears, namely, someone joined by family descent. And again, it is not "they do this," but "they do so" <note>original: οὕτω ποιοῦσι</note>.*

*51 Therefore you shall be] <note>original: ἔσεσθε</note>, that is, "you will be." The Translator seems to have read "be ye" <note>original: ἴστε</note>. I omit the fact that "he who is in the heavens," which he usually translates as "who is in the heavens," he has now changed to "heavenly." Furthermore, the conjunction "therefore," as well as "Father," is not added among the Greeks. It is simply, "as your heavenly Father."*

<margin>D</margin> **1** *And your righteousness] In Greek it is "almsgiving" <note>original: τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην</note>, that is, "alms," not "justice" or "righteousness," so that it matches what follows: "When therefore you do alms." Thus Chrysostom and Theophylact read and interpret it. Although Jerome reads "justice," he interprets it as "alms." And likewise Augustine, in his second sermon on the words of the Lord from Matthew, similarly interprets it as he reads it. It should be noted in passing that Latins, when using the Greek word "eleemosyna," defraud it of one syllable, since it has six syllables in Greek.*

*2 To be seen by them] Augustine, in the place we just cited, indicates that this little part should be added to the previous speech in such a way that the conjunction "so that" signifies the purpose, not the consequence. For he does not forbid good deeds from being seen, but he does not want them to be done with this intention. For in Latin this speech is ambiguous: "so that you may be seen," that is, "in such a way that you are seen," or "with the mind that you are seen." However, for the Greeks there is no ambiguity: <note>original: πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι, meaning "for the purpose of being gazed at"</note>. Again in that which follows,*

*3 You shall have no reward] He changed the tense of the verb: "you do not have" <note>original: οὐκ ἔχετε</note>.*

<margin>E</margin> *4 As the hypocrites] This too is among the number of words in which the Translator seems to have delighted. Otherwise, "hypocrite" <term>hypokritēs: a Greek term for a stage actor who plays a part behind a mask</term> for the Greeks signifies a stage-player: that is, one who acts out a story before the people in a feigned persona, whom we call "actors." Whence, what we call "delivery" or "action," they call "hypocrisis." Although anyone who simulates and feigns in any way can be called a hypocrite. Whence Paul says, "love without hypocrisy," that is, love not feigned, ignorant of the simulator. Moreover, as far as stage-playing gestures are concerned, what was just said fits beautifully: "to be seen," which is the business of actors, and from this comes "theater." For who is less—who is less an actor than those who, by the empty movement of lips and the noise of voices, wish to be seen praying to God and talking with him? Or those who lie about holiness with Jewish ceremonies? Again it comes here, "in the synagogues"; it was clearer as "in the assemblies." For it signifies small gatherings that are accustomed to be held in the streets, and the marketplace, or at crossroads. And understand "streets" <note>original: vicos</note> in this place not as those which are not towns, but those into which a city is divided. For a little later he mentions the "broad ways" <note>original: platearum</note>, which are properly called wider roads in which the gatherings of the common people are accustomed to occur; on which word some philosophize that the cities of the impious have broad ways, while the way of virtue is narrow. To these:*

*5 They have received their reward] <note>original: ἀπέχουσι</note>, that is, "they have," or "they have carried off." For the verb sounds like something received from elsewhere.*

*6 Let your left hand not know] In Greek there are two words: "let it not know" <note>original: μὴ γνώτω</note>.*

<margin>F</margin> *7 Let not your left hand know what your right is doing] This is not said without a figure of speech, but hyperbolically, as if you were to say, "may you yourself not know what you are doing, if it can be done," so far should it be from you showing it to others. Chrysostom noted the figure in his 19th homily, and Theophylact followed him. Moreover, the Greeks add "in the open" <note>original: ἐν τῷ φανερῷ</note>, that is, "in public" or "in the open." Which nevertheless Augustine denies he found in the Greek codices, and therefore thinks it should not be explained. Theophylact interprets it even as "in the open," when all good and evil works will be made manifest. Let the twin reading be dismissed, which Augustine approves.*

8 *He will reward you]* The Greek is <note>original: αὐτὸς ἀποδώσει σοι</note>, *that is, he himself*, or *the same one, will reward you*, which more clearly distinguishes the person of the Father from the person of those upon whom the benefit is bestowed.

9 *And when you pray]* <note>original: καὶ ὅταν προσεύχῃ</note>, *that is, when you (singular) pray*. For a little earlier he used the singular number, *when you do alms*. Even if "your" (plural) follows shortly. Nor is it:

10 *You shall not be (plural)]* <note>but original: οὐκ ἔσῃ</note>, *that is, you shall not be (singular)*. And in several Latin codices it is added, *like the gloomy hypocrites*, even though <insert>C</insert> this word <note>original: σκυθρωποὶ (skythrōpoi)</note> is found among the Greeks, it is not in our more corrected versions.

11 *Who love]* <note>original: φιλοῦσι (philousi)</note>. While this means *they love*, it is frequently used by the Greeks for *they are accustomed to*. In this place, *they are accustomed to* certainly fits better. Again:

12 *In the synagogues]* Which we translate as *in the assemblies*. And *corners* are called not <note>original: ῥύμαι (rhymai)</note> as the common people take it, but *corners of the streets, as if near crossroads and meeting-ways*.

13 *That they may be seen by men]* <note>original: ὅπως ἂν φανῶσι τοῖς ἀνθρώποις</note>, *that is, that they may be conspicuous to men*, or rather *so that they might be able to be conspicuous*. Furthermore:

14 *Into the chamber]* <note>original: Εἰς ταμεῖον (Eis tameion)</note>, which in Latin they call a *penu* or *cella* (storeroom), where things pertaining to domestic use are stored; we translate it as *inner room*. The translator of Origen—*whoever he was*, for the style proves it was not Jerome—in the twenty-third *homily* on Matthew, translates it as *pantry*: because the Greeks use the word <note>original: ταμιεῖα (tamieia)</note> for what we call *stewards* or *storeroom keepers*: Hesychius is witness that <note>original: ταμιεύεσθαι (tamieuesthai)</note> can mean both a *storeroom* or a *closet* or *bedroom*.

15 *With the door closed]* The Greeks add <note>original: σου (sou)</note>, *your*. And likewise the old Latin codices, because what happens in one’s own house is most hidden. Furthermore:

16 *Your Father in secret]* Some codices had <note>original: τῷ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ</note>, *that is, your Father who is in secret*, so that you may understand a certain Father, different from a physical one, and a singular mystery by which the heavenly Father is hidden, who is present everywhere but hidden from us. And again it is added:

17 *in the open]* <note>original: ἐν τῷ φανερῷ (en tō phanerō)</note>. And Chrysostom reads it this way in the sixteenth homily. Chrysostom also noted a figure of speech in this place. For Christ did not mean that Christians must not pray except in the pantry of the house, but rather that they should not strive for men to praise them while praying, any more than if they were praying alone hidden in the most remote part of the building.

18 *Do not speak much]* <note>original: μὴ βαττολογήσητε (mē battologēsēte)</note>. In Greek, this is a composite proverbial expression, from a certain poet named Battus, who composed hymns in which he repeatedly drummed in the same things: as has been explained more fully in our *Adages* <note>Erasmus's own work, the Chiliades Adagiorum</note>. Ovid alludes to this when he makes Battus the informant repeating the same thing:
> *...In those*
> *mountains, he said, they were, and they were in those mountains.*
Mercury ridiculously imitated this *battology* <note>meaning stuttering or vain repetition</note>:
> *...Treacherously you betray me to myself,*
> *me to myself you betray, he said.*
There are those who prefer that Battus was a certain stutterer with a hesitating mouth and an impeded tongue; for we see it is peculiar to that kind of person that when they cannot express what they want even once, they repeat the same words again and again. Hence what Christ teaches here <insert>F</insert> pertains not only to immoderately long prayers—since Paul orders us to pray without ceasing, and Christ himself is read to have prayed at great length—but also to those who superstitiously repeat the same little prayers without end. Indeed, some Christians are so far from being free of this disease that they place the highest peak of piety in it. Furthermore, regarding what we see today—priests burdened with I will not say what kind of prayers, but certainly excessively long ones, and prescribed ones at that, sometimes foolish and ridiculous, if not impious—what I think on this matter is better left untouched: partly because the matter cannot be explained in a few words, and partly because it might not be without danger: lest, while we try to cure this evil, we invite another more serious one, so that there might be those who seek patronage for their vices from anywhere. I will say this: it is not the part of a wise man to fight with his own century. And it is a mark of a good mind to willingly and simply obey the decrees of the elders. But again, it is the duty of those elders to determine with the greatest vigilance what is best and most consistent with the teachings of Christ. Jerome warns that the heresy of certain people arose from this passage, who rejected the prayers of Christians entirely as if they were superfluous. Opposite to these was the faction of the Psallians, or Euchites <note>A sect that believed constant prayer was the only necessity for salvation</note>, a name given from "praying," who spent whole days in idle—

But when praying <gloss>18</gloss> do not be talkative <insert>B</insert>, like the heathens: for they think that it will be <gloss>19</gloss> on account of their much speaking that they are heard. —ness, only murmuring so many stains with a wonderful volubility of tongue, such that Augustine wrote it was incredible. They forbade monks to work with their hands for the sake of sustaining life, lest they should ever be forced to interrupt their prayers. Would that whoever professes the philosophy of Christ would so shrink from this superstition that they might offer a pure and unblemished victim of prayer, pleasing to Christ! For there is everywhere more than enough of little songs, shouts, murmurs, and buzzing, if such things delight the Powers Above. It was abundantly enough to indulge the feelings of the unlearned and the foolish in this, so that each might be free to pray privately what he wanted, or as much as he wanted. However, public prayers ought to have been moderate: nor should anything be mixed into them that is not taken from the Sacred Scriptures, or at least proceeded from those men whose writings taste of the Apostolic spirit. Now, what kind of thing is it that priests are compelled by such great censorship to read the nonsense of a doting old man or a little woman mixed with the sacred rites? It might have seemed too trivial to be worth warning that among the Greeks there is no word *polyete* <note>speak much</note>, even if the Translator rendered it in Latin, had I not seen Augustine philosophizing in vain on this word, both elsewhere and in the book *On Grace and Free Will* to Valentinus, chapter 11. For reasoning that man stands by his own will in the Law of God, he adds these words: *Then so many commands, which in a certain way suit the warning to the will itself, such as, "be not overcome by evil."* And he relates many things of this form from the Sacred Volumes. I wanted this warned once, lest anyone should inadvertently strike against the same stone.

19 *As the Heathens do]* "Do" is not added either among the Greeks, nor in the golden codex, nor in the Donauian manuscripts.

20 *in much speaking]* Here it is not *battologia* <note>stuttering/repetition</note>, but he used the proper word *polylogia*: as if explaining what he meant by *battologein*.

21 *You ask him]* <note>original: πρὸ τοῦ ὑμᾶς αἰτῆσαι αὐτόν</note>. It would have been more Latin and clearer to say, *before you ask from him*. Then, <note>original: προσεύχεσθε ὑμεῖς</note>, *that is, pray ye, not you shall pray*. For there is greater emphasis in the pronoun placed at the end, by which he distinguishes them from the Heathens.

22 *Who art in heaven]* The Greek article distinguishes that Father from an earthly father, <note>original: ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς (ho en tois ouranois)</note>. Just as if they were saying: We know no father on earth, we hang from you alone, heavenly Father: from whom we must ask for everything we need for the true life.

23 *Hallowed be thy name]* <note>original: ἁγιασθήτω (hagiasthētō)</note>. A thing is called holy not only if it is pure and unpolluted, but also venerable and inviolate. And Augustine, explaining the figures of speech of the Old Testament in the fourth book, shows that *hallowed* is said here not for *let it be made holy*, but for *let it be declared holy*. Although in <insert>E</insert> Jeremiah, God complains that his name is polluted among the nations by the fault of his own people. No kind of disgrace is more intolerable to noble minds than the ignominy of parents. Indeed, it was most truly said by the Greek tragic poet:
> *For a man is a slave, even if he be bold-hearted,*
> *whenever he is conscious of the evils of his mother or father.*
On the other hand, nothing equally supports and cheers the minds of children as the glory of parents. For these affections, which the common crowd of men has toward physical parents, he transfers to God. Of which kind is also that which follows, *Thy kingdom come*. If fathers are promoted to great honors, the children also reign under their shadow, and they think whatever dignity or authority has increased for the father increases for themselves. Now, as for a kingdom, so also for a family: happiness is situated in this, that all are obedient to the authority of the father or king, nor is there any faction or disagreement, but all things depend on the will of one.

24 *Thy will be done]* Augustine also noted the novelty of this figure of speech. For our words are not "done" when what we ordered is completed, but when we order it. Nor does he "make" a speech who performs in reality what was said, but he who speaks. Nor are our vows "done" when what we hope for happens, but they are "done" by the act of hoping. Thus "our will is done" when the faculty of willing is given. But this form of speech, taken from the Hebrews, is so frequent in the Sacred Letters that it should not have been changed. Otherwise, it was more Latin to say, *let what you want be done also on earth, just as it is done in heaven*.

25 *As in heaven and on earth]* <note>original: ὡς ἐν οὐρανῷ καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς</note>, *that is, just as in heaven, so also on earth*. The Translator, while expressing the Greek figure, brought out the meaning more obscurely. The sense, however, is: So let what you want be done on earth—that is, in your heavenly people who still dwell in the body on earth—just as it is done in heaven, where no one resists your will.

26 *Our daily bread]* <note>original: τὸν ἄρτον ἡμῶν τὸν ἐπιούσιον (ton arton hēmōn ton epiousion)</note>. Which...

Having previously discussed the earlier verses of the Lord's Prayer, he now addresses the petition for forgiveness, the lead-us-not-into-temptation clause, and the concluding doxology. He notably defends his choice of "remit" (remitte) over the traditional "forgive/dismiss" (dimitte) and explains why the conclusion "For thine is the kingdom" is likely a later addition by the Greek Church rather than the original words of Jesus.</meta>

oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith? 
31 Therefore do not be anxious, saying, "What shall we eat?" or "What shall we drink?" or "What shall we wear?"

33 all these things. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things 
34 will be added to you. Therefore do not be anxious for tomorrow; for tomorrow will be anxious for itself; sufficient for the 
VII. 1 day is its own trouble. Judge not, that you be not judged. 
2 For with the judgment you judge, you will be judged, and with the measure you measure—

<margin>B</margin>
What is translated here as *supersubstantial*, literally sounds like *supersubstantial* <note>Erasmus is discussing the difficult word *epiousios* in the Lord’s Prayer, often translated as "daily."</note>. According to Jerome, the translators of the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> usually translate this as <term>περιούσιον</term> <note>original: periousion; meaning "special" or "chosen"</note>, for which the Hebrew uses <term>סגלה</term> <note>original: segulah; a "treasured possession"</note>. Symmachus translates this as <term>ἐξαίρετον</term> <note>original: exaireton</note>, that is, *excellent or extraordinary*, although in some places he translates it as *peculiar*. In the "Gospel according to the Hebrews," Jerome found <term>מחר</term> <note>original: mahar; "tomorrow"</note>, which means *of tomorrow*, in place of "supersubstantial" bread. While I reject none of these, the latter option appeals to me most. For I do not believe Christ speaks of this common bread in such a heavenly prayer, which even the Gentiles receive from their parents. And in Greek, <term>ἐπιούσιος</term> <note>original: epiousios</note> means "of the coming day." Indeed, Luke uses <term>ἐπιούσης</term> <note>original: epiousēs</note> in the *Acts of the Apostles*, chapter seven: <term>τῇ ἐπιούσῃ ἡμέρᾳ</term> <note>original: tē epiousē hēmera</note>, that is, *the following day*. Augustine indicates something similar in his twenty-eighth sermon, suggesting this sense: *Just as earthly fathers look out for bread for their children to nourish the body even for the following day, so you, who are our heavenly Father and the father of spirits, provide for us the heavenly bread, the food of the soul.* But we shall say more on this elsewhere.

27 *And forgive*] <term>ἄφες</term> <note>original: aphes; to let go or release</note>. Why not rather *remit*? For the Greek word has many meanings. I hear that some are offended because I translated *remit* instead of *forgive*. Why are they not likewise offended when <unclear>z</unclear> <margin>Psalm 35:1</margin> Pope Manasses prays thus: *I ask, requesting of you, Lord, remit to me, remit to me*? Or that in the Apostles' Creed, as it is called, we believe in the *remission of sins* rather than the *dismissal*? If I were the first of all to say *remit* instead of *forgive*, what would be the crime? Now, Saint Cyprian, in explaining this passage, repeats *remit* for *forgive* so many times in the volumes I edited that where *forgive* was occasionally left in, it was likely placed there by a scribe. He cites it the same way in his book to Quirinus, <term>Book III, chapter 22</term>, quoting from Mark: *Remit, if you have anything, so that your Father who is in heaven may remit it to you.* Likewise in chapter <term>XXVIII</term> of the same work. Again in the Psalms: *You have remitted the iniquity of my sin, and you have remitted the injustice of your people.* Furthermore, Augustine in his book to the Catechumens, <term>Book II, chapter 10</term>, how often he uses the verb *to remit*: *Trust in yourself, because your sins have been remitted to you.* Again: *And this profession of his faith, in which all sins are remitted, etc.* If we frequently find "forgive" instead of "remit" in his writings, it was either granted to common usage or corrupted by copyists. What point is there in examining how often this word occurs in other Ecclesiastical writers for *to pardon*, since it appears so many times in the Gospel and Apostolic letters? For example, Matthew <term>XII</term>: *Every blasphemy shall be remitted to men.* And Luke <term>VII</term>: *Many sins are remitted to her, because she loved much.* And John <term>XX</term>: *Whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them.* If they think it so holy to speak Latin poorly, I do not object to them enjoying their "forgive." Who, I ask, are these people? I modestly noted in two words what was correct; I never troubled anyone if "forgive" pleased them more. Yet these people, when correctly advised, scream in sermons before the unlearned common folk, inciting them to throw stones; they rave at banquets, bark in the schools, on ships, in carriages—where do they not? They cry out that the Christian religion is finished, and that theologians exist in vain, if someone was found who dared to "corrupt" the Lord’s Prayer. O tongues deserving to be cut out, unworthy of preaching the Gospel of Christ! They are infants and dullards when it comes to explaining the text, but eloquent and charming when it comes to tearing down the reputation of a well-deserving man; they act as sycophants while professing to be priests. What is more arrogant? We allow them to <term>σολοικίζειν</term> <note>original: soloikizein; to speak ungrammatically or commit a solecism</note> as much as they like—no one shouts them down—but will they not allow us to speak correctly? But it is better to continue what I started.

28 *Our debts*] <term>ὀφειλήματα</term> <note>original: opheilēmata</note>. Some argue here that the word for "debt" encompasses more than "sin," namely the punishment due for the fault; whether that is true I will not examine now. Certainly, Saint Augustine simply interprets *debts* as sins, and Luke in chapter eleven puts <term>ἁμαρτίας</term> <note>original: hamartias; sins</note> in place of "debts," and the Translator renders it *our sins*.

29 *As we also*] <term>ὡς καὶ ἡμεῖς</term> <note>original: hōs kai hēmeis</note>. In this place, it signifies a likeness, not a condition; Luke explains this more clearly. For he intends for one thing to happen among the children of the heavenly Father, and asks that the other happen. For they do not ask that they might grant pardon among themselves in return (which is within their power), but rather, just as they forgive each other’s mutual errors (as is fitting for children of the same family), so may that gracious Father also be favorable, and not wish to take vengeance if they have perhaps offended him.

30 *And lead us not*] <term>εἰσενέγκῃς</term> <note>original: eisenenkēs</note>. Augustine indicates that in some manuscripts it was written *do not suffer us to be led*, though he thinks it makes no difference to the sense. Yet it does matter, except that <term>εἰσενέγκῃς</term> sounds more like *impelling and leading by force* than being led like a willing friend. It is enough to have noted this for this purpose; let other things be sought from elsewhere.

31 *From evil*] <term>ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ</term> <note>original: apo tou ponērou</note>. This can refer to a thing, as if you said, *from malice*. But the added Article suggests it refers rather to the devil. For it is his role to tempt. And he is opposed to the Father, with whom the prayer began. So Chrysostom teaches, explaining this passage.

<margin>B</margin>
32 *For thine is the kingdom*] I find this concluding flourish <note>The "doxology"</note> added in all the Greek manuscripts: <term>ὅτι σου ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία, καὶ ἡ δύναμις, καὶ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας, ἀμήν</term> <note>original: hoti sou estin hē basileia, kai hē dynamis, kai hē doxa eis tous aiōnas, amēn</note>, that is, *because thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory forever, amen*. However, since I see it written in none of the Latin manuscripts, nor is it explained by Jerome or any Translator at all except Chrysostom (and his recent abbreviator Theophylact), it appears to have been added according to solemn custom, just as some have added to the Angelic Salutation <note>The "Hail Mary"</note> things neither said by the Angel nor by anyone else. For, *blessed are you among women* are the words of Elizabeth; and *who gave birth to the Savior of our souls* was said by no one. With similar zeal, the *Glory to the Father* <note>Gloria Patri</note> was added to the end of the Psalms. Therefore, there is no reason for Lorenzo Valla to be annoyed that a good part of the Lord's Prayer has been cut short. Rather, the rashness of those who did not fear to sew their own trifles onto such a divine prayer should have been more criticized. I might rightly call "trifles" compared to divine teaching whatever has proceeded from men—especially if what was attached by men is attributed to Christ the author. If anyone contends that this was added by Christ himself, he must admit that all our people and the entire Roman Church have hitherto lacked a good part of the Lord’s Prayer. And not even the African Church read it correctly. For Cyprian, explaining this passage of the Gospel in a special booklet, does not acknowledge this flourish by even a word. Furthermore, those who think it was added by the Evangelist because Chrysostom interprets it rely on a weak argument. Indeed, he interprets what the solemn usage of the Greek Church sounded every day; just as if someone explaining the Psalms were to interpret that solemn flourish, *Glory to the Father and the Son*. Nor is it surprising if Chrysostom deigned to do this, since in his homilies he diligently explains the hymn with which certain Monks were accustomed to consecrate their banquet. In the *Golden Chain* <note>A famous commentary collection by Thomas Aquinas</note>, Chrysostom is cited this way: *Because he did not want us to be separated from the memory of the unconquered, in what he had said, deliver us from evil, he again offers boldness through this, which is added in some books, for thine is the kingdom, etc.*—though where this was taken from, I do not know. For these words are not found in Chrysostom’s Commentaries. As for those who contend this flourish was written by the Evangelist and also confirm that this Edition is either Jerome’s or at least corrected by him, I would like them to explain to us why he dared to omit such a large part of the sacred prayer, when he made no mention of it even in his Commentaries. Although these things are too clear to need arguments, there were nonetheless those who constructed a grave calumny against me from this passage as well. As for *amen*, which Aquila interprets as "faithfully," it could appear to have been added here in a similar way. Jerome warns that it is the "seal" of the Lord’s Prayer.

33 *Their sins*] <term>παραπτώματα</term> <note>original: paraptōmata</note>, that is, *delicts*, as he soon translates, or *errors*, or *lapses*. Since the word is derived from <term>παραπίπτειν</term> <note>original: parapiptien; to fall away or stumble</note>. And in Latin *their* is also added: something the Translator consistently ignores. And again, *will remit* instead of *will forgive*.

<margin>E</margin>
34 *Gloomy hypocrites*] <term>σκυθρωποί</term> <note>original: skythrōpoi</note>, that is, *harsh/tetric and far from cheerful*. The Translator renders it in Latin, provided *gloomy* is understood not as one who grieves, but as one who has an unpleasant and severe face. For elsewhere, *my soul is gloomy* is translated for *grieving*, and *to make gloomy* for *to cause pain*, <term>λυπεῖσθαι</term> <note>original: lypeisthai</note>. I wonder that the Greek word *hypocrita* pleased Christian Latins so much, when *simulator* is the Latin word. I cannot restrain myself from recounting, for the sake of amusement, what is added in Lyra’s Commentaries; for I do not like to suspect that he was so foolish: *Hypocrite*, he says, *is said from "hypes," which is "under," and "crisis," "gold": because under gold or under the honesty of an exterior lifestyle he has the lead of falsehood hidden.* Let them go now and deny that it matters whether someone knows Greek or not!

<margin>F</margin>
35 *For they disfigure*] <term>ἀφανίζουσι</term> <note>original: aphanizousi</note>. Which Chrysostom interprets as *diaphthirousi kai apollyousi*, that is, *they corrupt and destroy*. He likely thinks this is hateful to the masks of actors. Since they merely cover their native face with a mask, while these people corrupt and destroy their own face, and perform a play without a mask. Those who interpret it this way seem to me to follow the fact that one who dies is also said to be "removed from the midst" in Greek. Saint Jerome thinks it should be translated *they demolish*, adding that the word *to exterminate* is frequently found in Sacred Scripture by the lack of skill of Translators, although it means something else than what they want it to mean. Indeed, *to exterminate* is to drive out from the borders and boundaries, just as *to eliminate* is to carry outside the threshold and out the door. Cicero used it this way in *On Duties*, Book III, and in other places besides. Hilary interprets <term>ἀφανίζειν</term> <note>original: aphanizein</note> in this place as *to finish off*, and not inelegantly. For it is *to obscure*, and as if to remove from sight: just as those who use cosmetics hide their face and cover it as if with a mask; so do those who simulate holiness with a feigned thinness and a gloomy paleness. For piety also has its own thinness, its own paleness, but one in which the cheerfulness of Christ shines back.

36 *That they may appear to men*] <term>ὅπως φανῶσι</term> <note>original: hopōs phanōsi</note>. What he just translated as *that they may be seen*, he now translates as *that they may appear*, playing strangely with his abundance of words. Furthermore, <term>νηστεύοντες</term> <note>original: nēsteuontes; fasting</note>, a participle, seems to be placed in the stead of an infinitive verb, after the Greek manner; whence we translated it so: *that they...*

<margin>D</margin> *so that it is apparent to men that they are fasting. For they are not rebuked for wanting to seem to fast when they were not fasting, but because they wanted the fast to be visible to everyone, when it should rather have been kept secret. Likewise soon after: "Lest you appear to men as one fasting, so that your fasting is not visible to men."*

37 *They have received their reward* ] <note>original: Ἀπέχουσι (apechousi)</note>, that is, *they have*, as we have noted before.

38 *He will reward you* ] And here the Greek codices add, <note>original: ἐν τῷ φανερῷ (en tō phanerō)</note>, that is, *in the open* <note>or "publicly"</note>, so that it is contrasted with that which is *in secret*. Furthermore, where the translator used *demolishes* <note>original: demolitur</note> for the Greek <note>original: ἀφανίζει (aphanizei)</note>, he follows the opinion of Jerome. However, I would prefer *corrupts* <note>original: corrumpit</note>, since he is speaking of moths and worms. For "to demolish" is rather to destroy a wall or a barrier. The word is derived from *moles* <note>a massive structure</note>.

39 *To treasure up* ] It is a wonder why the Greek word <note>original: θησαυρίζετε (thēsaurizete)</note> was so pleasing, when he could have said *repose, hide away, collect,* or *heap up*. For a "treasure" <note>original: thesaurus</note> is properly said of things set aside and hidden away for a long time, which the Persians call *gaza* <note>a royal treasure</note>. For it is established among the Greeks that *thesaurus* is named from <note>original: παρὰ τὸ εἰς αὔριον θέσειν (para to eis aurion thesein)</note>, that is, to put away for tomorrow or for the future. And it is not so much *digging out* as *digging through* <note>original: perfodiunt</note>, <note>original: διορύσσουσι (dioryssousi)</note>. Since thieves penetrate to the chests by digging through the wall.

40 *Neither rust nor moth* ] <note>original: οὔτε σὴς οὔτε βρῶσις (oute sēs oute brōsis)</note>. Cyprian, in his third book to Quirinus, reads: *neither moth nor consumption shall destroy*. This is:

41 *Your treasure* ] <note>original: ὁ θησαυρὸς ὑμῶν (ho thēsauros hymōn)</note>. Even if he soon changes the number to singular: *If your eye is simple*. And it is not "there with you," but *will be there*.

<margin>E</margin> 42 *The lamp of your body* ] The word *your* is not added in the Greek copies, but only *the body*, and the sentence has a bit more dignity if it is omitted, so that it becomes an absolute statement. What a lamp is in a house, the eye is in the body—not only in yours or mine, but in any body of a human or living creature. And so Saint Chrysostom reads in those homilies which we saw written in Greek at Basel, with Theophylact and the Spanish Edition agreeing, and so Jerome cites it when writing against the Luciferians. Finally, we found it written thus in very ancient Latin codices. For the comparison is taken from the eye of the body to the eye of the mind. What the eye is in the body of a living thing, the affection is in the soul; if it is pure, the whole soul will be sincere. Therefore, that first part, *The lamp of the body is the eye*, belongs to the thing from which the comparison is drawn. The latter part, *If your eye be simple*, etc., belongs to those things to which the likeness is applied: hence he adds *your*, you who are spiritual, and whose sincere eyes I require.

43 *If your eye be wicked* ] <note>original: πονηρός (ponēros)</note>, that is, *bad* or *perverse*. For the Greek word sounds more like *shrewd* or *malicious*, as it is opposed to *simple*. A simple eye is one defiled by nothing, with a pure lens, free from phlegm or disease. Otherwise, to those who speak correctly, a "wicked eye" sounds more like a lustful one than a *vitiated* one.

44 *How great is that darkness* ] <note>original: τὸ σκότος πόσον; (to skotos poson?)</note> By adding *ipsae* <note>the/that</note>, he correctly explained the force of the Greek article. However, the speech would be more elegant if he had not added *will be*, which is not added among the Greeks. It is simply: *how great the darkness?*

45 *He will hate the one* ] <note>original: τὸν ἕνα μισήσει (ton ena misēsei)</note>. The speech has some obscurity, even if the sense is clear. For he sets up two—say, Demea and Mitio <note>Characters from Terence's play *Adelphoe*, used here as placeholders for "Person A" and "Person B"</note>—to one of whom he must cling, for he cannot cling to both at once. Either Demea must be loved so that you hate Mitio, or Mitio loved so that you hate Demea. Therefore, in my opinion, he would have translated more correctly as *this one and that one* rather than *one and one*. Furthermore, the Greek article is not idle: for it signifies a certain person, as if pointing someone out: *the one, the other*. Although that *the one* should not be taken as if the first refers to God and the second to Mammon (otherwise he would say the same thing twice), but so that each *the one* pertains to either person: whichever you choose, *the other* is opposed to it. But if you take it here according to the usual manner of distribution, where the first *one* marks Demea and the second Mitio, the sense will be: he will hate Demea and love Mitio; or he will cling to Mitio and despise Demea. Thus you see he says the same thing twice, even though the conjunction usually signifies a difference. But the whole speech pertains to either person, and the conjunction does not change the person, but the circumstance. Chrysostom also noted something on this matter in his twenty-second homily.

<margin>F</margin> 46 *And Mammon* ] *Mammon* is neither a Greek word nor a Hebrew one, but Syriac, as Saint Jerome shows; it signifies the same thing among them as <note>original: πλοῦτος (ploutos)</note> among the Greeks, whom the poets make a God. For it is a word in the singular number, masculine gender. Saint Augustine indicates that the language of the Punic people <note>Carthaginians</note> has an affinity with the language of the Hebrews—something Jerome also admits somewhere—and that in the Punic language, profit is called *Mammon*. Furthermore, it is not surprising that he thought it was Hebrew when it is Syriac, since there is some kinship between Hebrew and Syriac.

47 *For your soul* ] <note>original: τῇ ψυχῇ (tē psychē)</note>. He used *soul* for *life*, just as elsewhere: *He who loses his soul*. Furthermore:

48 *What you shall drink* ] Although it is found added in some codices, it is superfluous, because drink is contained under the name of food, and the drinking of water is available to everyone. Certainly it is not added in Chrysostom, nor in Hilary. Jerome indicates it was written in some codices, but in explaining it, he ignores it. We allowed it to be added so that the Latin would not fail to correspond to the Greek. Certainly it is not written in the oldest copies, although a little further down mention is made: *Be not anxious, saying, what shall we eat, or what shall we drink*. And again:

49 *Is not the soul* ] It was clearer as: *is not the life*.

50 *Than food* ] <note>original: τῆς τροφῆς (tēs trophēs)</note>, that is, *food* or *nourishment*, so that it also embraces drink. Even if Aristotle denies that *drink* is what nourishes, as its function is to digest food into the limbs. Moreover, for *nourishment*, which sounds like "more" to the Greeks, it was correctly changed to *pluris* <note>of more value</note>, and Latinity was taken into account.

51 *Look at the birds* ] <note>original: Ἐμβλέψατε τὰ πετεινὰ (Emblepsate ta peteina)</note>, that is, *Gaze upon the birds*, to render word for word. Certainly, one who "looks back" <note>the literal sense of the Latin 'respicite'</note> turns his eyes behind him. Hence we preferred to use a longer phrase: *Turn your eyes to the birds of the air*.

52 *Which do not sow* ] For so it is read in most codices, <note>original: ὅτι (hoti)</note>, that is, *because they do not sow*. And Saint Jerome reads *since*. I would prefer *that*, taken <note>original: εἰδικῶς (eidikōs)</note> specifically. For it is that very thing which he wants us to look at: that birds do not perform sowing, and yet they live in the manner of men, and meanwhile are not distracted by any anxiety of preparing food.

53 *Are you not much more* ] <note>original: μᾶλλον διαφέρετε (mallon diapherete)</note>, that is, *you much excel*, or *stand out above them*. For <note>original: διαφέρειν (diapherein)</note> to the Greeks is not only "to differ," but also "to excel." Since the force of the comparative is in the verb itself: either the doubling has an emphasis of excellence, or *much* <note>original: μᾶλλον (mallon)</note> is put for "rather." Therefore we translated: *are you not far better than they?* For the Translator <note>The author of the Vulgate</note> seems even to have affected an absurdity of speech. Augustine, in "On the Tropes of the Old Testament," demonstrates that among the Hebrews an adverb of comparison is sometimes added superfluously. And it is possible that the Greek Translator also expressed this form of speech.

54 *Who of you by thinking* ] <note>original: μεριμνῶν (merimnōn)</note>. It is more than *thinking*, it is *anxiously and solicitously thinking*, a participle of that verb which he often translates as *to be anxious*. Furthermore, that which follows:

55 *To his stature* ] In Greek it is <note>original: ἡλικίαν (hēlikian)</note>, which also signifies *age*...

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>56</margin> **Lilies of the field** <note>original: "Lilia agri"</note>] In the field <note>original: "τῷ ἀγρῷ"</note>. Not without purpose did he add "of the field," because garden lilies might seem to owe something to human care: just as he had said before, "birds of the air," to distinguish them from farm-raised birds. Nor is it "considered," but *learn thoroughly* <note>original: "καταμάθετε," katamathete</note>, that is, "get to know," or "you know." For the Greek word can mean either. I should also mention that the translator again rendered *anti* as "since" instead of "because," although he omitted the preface. And again, "he was covered" instead of "he was clothed" or "dressed" <note>original: "περιεβάλετο," periebaleto</note>. Regarding this, instead of saying "one," it would have been more correct to translate "one of any of these."

<margin>57</margin> **How much more**] <note>original: "ἢ πολλῷ μᾶλλον"</note>, that is, "will he not much more." Here, I ask, what was the reason for the translator to vary the Greek phrasing? Furthermore,

<margin>58</margin> **Of little faith**] In Greek, this is a compound word *oligopistoi* <note>original: "ὀλιγόπιστοι"</note>, which in Luke is translated as "of puny faith." A person who is *axiopistos* is weighty and fit to be trusted; an *alogopistos* is one who is either little to be trusted or who trusts little. For there are some terms in the Sacred Scriptures that are too well-accepted to be moved from their place, one of which is "faith" <note>original: "fides"</note>, which for Latin speakers pertains more to the one who promises or performs than to the one who trusts: except when we say "to have faith" instead of "to believe." Therefore, "of tiny confidence" would fit better here than "of little faith": or, as we have translated it, "little-trusting."

<margin>59</margin> **For your father knows**] In this place, the Greeks add "the heavenly one" <note>original: "ὁ οὐράνιος"</note>. Nor is it in most copies, "will be anxious for itself," but "will have care for its own self" <note>original: "μεριμνήσει τὰ ἑαυτῆς"</note>, that is, it will take care of its own things. Augustine, in his book against Adimantus, reads: "Do not think about tomorrow, for the morrow itself will think for itself." Cyprian reads it the same way in his explanation of the Lord's Prayer. And some copies have, "will be anxious for its own."

<margin>60</margin> **Sufficient for the day is its own malice**] <note>original: "ἡ κακία," kakia</note>, meaning "evil." Just as with the Greek *kakon*, the Latin word "malum" <note>evil/bad</note> is ambiguous, referring both to affliction and to wickedness. But *kakia* is the opposite of virtue, which some Latin writers call "malice" and others "vice." However, *kakia* here sounds like "affliction," from the verb *kakoo*, which means "to afflict with evils." The translator therefore misused "malice" <note>original: "κακίᾳ"</note> for "affliction" <note>original: "κάκωσις," kakosis</note>, as Jerome indicates when explaining this passage. Furthermore, in his Commentaries on Ecclesiastes, and again in the Commentaries on Amos, and Chrysostom in the twenty-third homily. Time itself brings enough evils that we should not afflict ourselves with anxiety over future evils. Augustine brings this passage of the Evangelist to this meaning in his second commentary on the Sermon on the Mount, interpreting "malice" as the evil of punishment. Tertullian was the first of all to teach this in his second book against Marcion.

<column-break/>

<margin>D 1</margin> **D**o not condemn, and you will not be condemned] I have not found these words in any Greek copies, nor are they cited in Jerome, nor in Chrysostom, nor in Hilary, nor finally in the most ancient Latin codices. Hence they seem to have been brought into the main text from a marginal space. Someone interpreted what he said about "judging" in this place as being nothing other than "condemning": just as in Paul, "judgment" is sometimes put for "condemnation." Nor is it as it was shortly before:
<margin>2</margin> **And you shall not be judged**] but "lest you be judged" <note>original: "ἵνα μὴ κριθῆτε"</note>. And

in that same manner Hilary reads it, with the copies of Saint Donatian in agreement. Not to mention that for *krinete* and *krinesthe* <note>original: "κρίνετε, & κρίνεσθε"</note>, that is, "you judge" and "you are judged," he translated as "you shall have judged" and "you shall have measured," and that for "it shall be measured" <note>original: "μετρηθήσεται"</note> he translated "it shall be measured back to you," which goes against proper Latinity. For with the noun added, he could have said, "others will measure to you." Indeed, I do not know if "you are judged" <note>original: "judiciamini"</note> can be said in sufficiently good Latin. For I do not think a person is called "judged" <note>original: "judicatus"</note> of whom a sentence has been pronounced, but rather the matter is "judged" <note>original: "res judicata"</note> and the "cause is judged"; for a person, it is "appointed," unless you add "judged insane" in the sense of being "held to be." Therefore, in my opinion, Augustine’s reading is more tolerable: "Do not judge, lest it be judged concerning you: for with what judgment you shall have judged, it will be judged concerning you." It would be best, however, if we read: "Do not condemn, lest you be condemned."

<margin>3</margin> **And the log in your eye**] <note>original: "τὴν δὲ ἐν τῷ σῷ ὀφθαλμῷ δοκὸν οὐ κατανοεῖς"</note>, that is, "but the log which is in your eye, you do not notice." Furthermore, "brother, let me." "Brother" is neither added in the Greek nor in the ancient Latin copies, but only, "let me cast out" <note>original: "ἄφες ἐκβάλω"</note>, and the Golden Codex agrees. Again:

<margin>4</margin> **And behold the log is in the eye**] In Greek it is more festive, with the substantive verb being understood: "and behold the log in your eye" <note>original: "καὶ ἰδοὺ ἡ δοκὸς ἐν τῷ ὀφθαλμῷ σου"</note>. Additionally:

<margin>E 5</margin> **You will see to cast out**] He spoke too much in the Greek style, "you will look through to cast out" <note>original: "διαβλέψεις ἐκβαλεῖν"</note>, that is, "you will see clearly so that you may cast out."

<margin>6</margin> **Do not give the holy thing**] <note>original: "μὴ δῶτε"</note>, that is, "do not give." He constantly varies this in the same way. I point this out, not because the Translator translates badly, but so that no one should philosophize in vain over the words: as if "will" were also intended here. And it was more correct to say "cast" <note>original: "projiciatis"</note> rather than "send" <note>original: "mittatis"</note> <note>original: "βάλλητε"</note>. Not to mention that "lest ever" <note>original: "μήποτε"</note>, that is, "lest at some time," he translates as "lest perhaps," quite inappropriately, downplaying the danger which ought rather to have been emphasized. Nor is it "with their feet," but "among their feet" <note>original: "ἐν τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτῶν"</note>: unless one prefers *en* <note>in/among</note> used for *per* <note>through/by</note> in the Hebrew manner. "The holy thing" is put in the neuter gender for "a holy thing" <note>original: "τὰ ἅγια"</note>: we translate it as "that which is holy." The Jews called "holy" that which was set apart from the use of the profane common people and was to be handled with reverence by consecrated persons.

<column-break/>

<margin>F 7</margin> **And the dogs turning**] "Dogs" is not added in the Greek, nor is it touched upon by the translator Chrysostom, nor in the more corrected Latin copies, nor even in the Golden one. The trampling and the tearing can be referred equally to both the dogs and the swine. For wild boars also rage. The dog is a profane animal, and the swine an impure one, which particularly shrinks from perfumes. Furthermore, as for his saying "pearls" <note>original: "margaritis"</note>, Pliny is an abundant witness that they once held the highest value. Finally, regarding what he said, "turning" <note>original: "στραφέντες"</note>, the meaning was clearly "turning against you." Nor is it "break" <note>original: "dirumpant"</note>, but "tear" or "mangle" <note>original: "ῥήξωσιν," rexosin</note>.

<margin>8</margin> **Will he reach him a stone**] We have softened the harshness of this phrasing in our translation, though the sense remains, so that no one may falsely claim we have departed from the words.

<margin>9</margin> **Good gifts**] <note>original: "δόματα ἀγαθά," domata agatha</note>, that is, "good donations" or "good gifts." This is a figure of speech from the idiom of the Hebrew language: like that phrase in Numbers: "I have taken your brothers the Levites from the midst of the children of Israel, a gift given to the Lord." <margin>A</margin> They read <note>original: "doma didotai"</note>. For here *given* <note>original: "data"</note> is not a participle, but a *noun*. Otherwise, what is given, since it has already been given? And I would have preferred *gifts* <note>original: "dona"</note> rather than *data*: except that *dota* could rightly be said, in whatever way it is *given*, just as Physicians call their medicines *doses* <note>original: "doseis"</note>, whereas a *gift* <note>original: "donum"</note> is something free, which the Greeks call by the word *doron*. Again, there also:
<margin>10 He will give good things to those asking him]</margin> Which we have explained as *if you ask from him*, just as the Translator did above. Likewise, *so also you do to them*, he omitted the little word <note>original: "houto kai hymeis"</note>, that is, *so also you do*. And so Chrysostom reads. Augustine also in his second Commentary on this place. The same says it was written in the common <note>Vulgate</note> codices: *Everything which you want men to do good things to you, so also you do to them*. He thinks "good things" was added by the Latin Translator for the sake of explaining the matter, since it is not found in the Greek copies. Although that phrasing is also added in Cyprian's exposition of the Lord's Prayer. Again:
<margin>11 Which leads]</margin> <note>original: "apagousa"</note>, that is, *which leads away*. And soon:
<margin>12 How narrow the gate]</margin> <note>original: "hoti stene"</note>, that is, *because narrow is the gate*, although many Latin copies disagree. The Translator seems to have read <note>original: "hos stene"</note>. Certainly in the Pauline codex it was written in both places as *because*.
<margin>13 From false Prophets]</margin> <note>original: "pseudoprophetōn"</note>. In Greek it is a single word, just as *pseudo-Christs* and *pseud-Apostles*: but *pseudo* in Greek means a lie. And it sounds more like *false Prophets* than just "falsifiers." And soon, <note>original: "epignōsesthe"</note>, is *you will recognize* rather than "you will know." And:
<margin>14 Do they gather]</margin> Certain people have <note>original: "mē tinos"</note>, that is, *whether anyone*. Again:
<margin>15 Bad tree]</margin> <note>original: "sapron ei"</note>, not <note>original: "ponēron"</note>, which sounds more like *putrid* and spoiled by decay, or withered, than just *bad*, if we believe anything in Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek lexicographer</note>. Not to mention that he translates both verbs of the present tense through the future, *is cut down and is sent* <note>original: "ekkoptetai kai balletai"</note>, that is, *is cut out and is cast*. And so it is written in very ancient copies. For Christ is not predicting what will be in the future for bad trees, but he shows that what commonly happens to defective trees will likewise happen to unfruitful men.
<margin>16 Lord, Lord]</margin> <note>original: "Kyrie Kyrie"</note>. He not only recounted the babbling of those praying, but also rebuked it; he even expressed

<column-break/>

the property of the Hebrew speech: which, because it exaggerates, increases by doubling: a kind of thing found in Jeremiah chapter seven: <gloss>The Temple of the Lord, The Temple of the Lord, The Temple of the Lord.</gloss> Furthermore, these words:
<insert>17 He shall enter into the kingdom of heaven]</insert> In the Greek codices they are not added, nor are they found by Jerome, even though the Latin copies object. Nor is it:
<margin>18 In your name]</margin> but *through your name*, <note>original: "tō sō onomati"</note>, without the preposition *in* <note>original: "en"</note>, which he usually puts there, although that matters nothing to the sense.
<margin>19 Many miracles]</margin> <note>original: "dynameis"</note>, so that you understand *mighty deeds*, which demonstrate divine power. Likewise:
<margin>20 All you who work]</margin> "All" is not in the Greek codices, nor in the ancient Latin ones, but only, <note>original: "hoi ergazomenoi"</note>, that is, *you who work*. Again:
<margin>21 And they rushed in]</margin> <note>original: "kai prosekopsan"</note>, that is, *they beat against*, which is different from that which just preceded, *they fell upon*.
<margin>22 And they were wondering]</margin> In Greek it is more vehement, <note>original: "exeplēssonto"</note>, <margin>F</margin> that is, *they were stunned*, or *they were made astonished*, or *they were struck with stupor*.
<margin>23 As one having power]</margin> <note>original: "hōs exousian echōn"</note>. Even if I forgive that he translates "as if" as *just as*.
<margin>24 Power]</margin> It is not here <note>original: "dynamis"</note>, but <note>original: "exousia"</note>, which sounds more like *authority*, that is, *power and right to do something*. Not like the Scribes, who claimed authority for themselves. *For he does not say*, "Thus says the Lord," *but "I say to you"*: and in performing miracles he does not implore the help of the Father, but says, *"Young man, I say to you, arise."* Again in,
<margin>25 Scribes]</margin> "Their" is added among the Greeks, *their scribes*, and in this place there is no mention of the Pharisees in the Greek copies that I have seen.
<margin>1 When he had descended]</margin> "Jesus" is not added here among the Greeks: as with that little expression, *behold behold*, or *if you wish*, which he translated as *if you will*. And:
<margin>2 Extending the hand]</margin> For "with an extended hand," <note>original: "ekteinas tēn cheira"</note>.
<margin>3 I wish, be clean]</margin> <note>original: "katharisthēti"</note>. *Cleanse* <note>Erasmus notes the Latin passive infinitive "mundare" vs. the Greek imperative "be cleansed"</note> is a passive verb.

<summary>This page presents Erasmus's Greek and Latin versions of Matthew 7 and 8, accompanied by notes on linguistic nuances such as the meaning of "authority" and the use of repetition as a Hebraism. Erasmus emphasizes that Jesus's teaching style was distinct from the Scribes because he spoke from his own divine right rather than merely citing tradition.</summary>

<margin>F</margin> ...cleansed.
It is in the imperative mood. Therefore we translate, *I will, be clean*.
Furthermore, regarding the word <note>original: ἐκαθαρτίσθη (ekathartisthē)</note>, he whom he calls here a "centurion"—for so 
it sounds in Greek, one who presides over ten decuriae—is called a *tribune* by 
Hilary. And:
**4** *I begged him*] <note>original: παρακαλῶν (parakalōn)</note>, that is, beseeching. For this is 
more vehement, while that other word <note>original: ὁτόμενος (deomenos)</note> is more lowly.
**5** *My servant*] <note>original: ὁ παῖς μου (ho pais mou)</note>. This word signifies both age, and a son, 
and a servant. However, Luke calls him <note>original: δοῦλος (doulos)</note>, that is, a slave, 
using an unambiguous word. Nor is it simply *lies*, but *is prostrate* <note>original: βέβληται (beblētai)</note>, 
and a little later *having been prostrate* <note>original: βεβλημένην (beblēmēnēn)</note>, used where someone lies prostrate 
with their whole body, which happens in grave illnesses. And:
**6** *Is poorly tormented*] <note>original: ὑπὸ δεινῶς βασανιζόμενος (hypo deinōs basanizomenos)</note>, that is, is heavily 
or bitterly racked with pain. Not to mention that he translates *to another* as "alio" instead of "allō", 
disregarding Grammar.
<margin>E</margin> **7** *Placed under authority*] Someone added "placed" from their own mind, 
as it is not found in the more correct copies, nor in the golden one.
**8** *I have not found such faith*] <note>original: οὐδὲ ἐν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ (oude en tō Israēl)</note>, that is, not even 
in Israel. So that you may understand the centurion was not an Israelite, 
which Hilary and Jerome indicate. And likewise Chrysos-
tom in his twenty-seventh homily. He thinks this is the same cen-
turion as the one mentioned by Luke, although in some points it 
seems to differ from Matthew's narration.
**9** *Into the outer darkness*] The Greeks occasionally use comparatives 
in place of superlatives. Whence we translate, *the extreme darkness*. 
Yet it is not <note>original: ἐσχάτας (eschatas)</note>, but <note>original: ἐξωτέρας (exōteras)</note>, as if you were to say, *outermost*, 
so you may understand that there is light in the kingdom, and the further away someone is from it, 
the more they dwell in darkness.
**10** *In that hour*] After the words "the hour," I found written in several 
copies: *And the centurion, returning to his house in 
that hour, found his servant healthy*. <note>original: Καὶ ὑποστρέψας ὁ ἑκατόνταρχος εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ, ἐν τῇ ὥρᾳ ἐκείνῃ εὗρε τὸν παῖδα αὐτοῦ ὑγιαίνοντα</note>. We preferred to follow those that 
agree with our own.
**11** *Having demons*] <note>original: δαιμονιζομένους (daimonizomenous)</note>, that is, demoniacs, 
or those who were driven by demons. But the Greek codices add, 
as do the ancient Latin ones, *many*, that is, <note>original: πολλούς (pollous)</note>.
**12** *He took our infirmities*] Matthew brought this testimony 
from the fifty-third chapter of Isaiah, turning it slightly to 
his own purpose. For what was said there about the passion of Christ 
and the wicked sins of men, he here adapts to the sick 
being healed; although this healing served as a type of that one. 
In this manner, Chrysostom explains the Evangelist in his twenty-
eighth homily. The Seventy <note>The Septuagint</note> rendered it thus: *and he himself 
will carry away their sins*. Furthermore, as for what we read in our version, 
"and he carried our sicknesses," let the reader know that "our" in this place is neither

among the Greeks, nor in the golden codex, nor in other more correct 
copies, but it is repeated from the nearby passage. Likewise soon after: "And Jesus says to them." 
"Jesus" was added; it is not in the Greek, nor in the golden codex. 
Jerome rendered the Hebrew thus, *truly he himself has borne our infirmities*, 
*and carried our sorrows*. In place of "infirmities," the Seventy translated 
"sins."
**13** *He ordered his disciples to go*] The translator added "his disciples" 
for the sake of explaining the matter, <note>original: ἐκέλευσεν ἀπελθεῖν (ekeleusen apelthein)</note>. Nor did I find it added 
in the golden codex. For since he wished to escape the crowd, there is no 
doubt that he wanted the Disciples as companions, certainly a few 
from the crowd. It could have been translated by an impersonal verb, *he ordered a departure* or *a with-*
*drawal*. And what follows, *across the strait*, <note>original: εἰς τὸ πέραν (eis to peran)</note>, could also 
refer to a mountain, or something by a river, unless mention of 
the boat were made soon after. For it signifies the further shore of the lake.
<margin>E</margin> **14** *Foxes have dens*] <note>original: φωλεούς (phōleous)</note>. Perhaps *caverns* was more 
appropriate. And what is here translated as *nests*, in Greek is <note>original: κατασκηνώσεις (kataskēnōseis)</note>, 
which sounds more like *shelters*. Augustine, against Faustus, book 22, 
chapter 48, reads *lodgings*. In the same way Cyprian reports 
in his third book to Quirinus. For birds have their retreats in a 
storm besides nests, such as hollow tree trunks, or thick 
thickets, or leafy branches.
**15** *Son of Man*] <note>original: ὁ υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου (ho huios anthrōpou)</note>. Although Augustine draws 
nothing from these words, he thinks Christ is not called the son of Adam. And he 
twists toward this what was said in the Psalms: *I am a worm, and not* 
*a man*; both elsewhere and in his hundred and twentieth letter. Again, 
dealing against Faustus in book five, he brings up this passage, proving Christ 
was born of a woman. Truly, the solution to this little knot is 
not difficult. Indeed, Christ calls himself the son of Adam because he was 
born from his descendants, from whom all other mortals 
had also come forth. Saint Jerome, explaining the ninth chapter of Ecclesiasticus, 
advises that according to the property of Hebrew speech, 
the common people are called "son of man." For even in those places where we read *sons* <margin>F</margin> 
*of men*, in the Hebrew it is <note>original: בְּנֵי אָדָם (benei Adam)</note>, that is, *sons of man*, 
namely Adam.
**16** *Where he may lay his head*] The pronoun "his" is not added in the 
Greek codices, nor in Chrysostom or Theophylact, 
nor in the ancient Latin ones, not even in the golden or Donatian ones. And 
the speech is more absolute, so you may understand that there is not even a place where 
the whole body may rest, nor is there even where the head may lean. To say nothing 
of the fact that a little later *upon the boat* comes without "dismiss." Nor is it simply 
*dead*, but <note>original: τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεκρούς (tous heautōn nekrous)</note>, that is, *their own dead*.
**17** *And he ascending*] <note>original: ἐμβάντι αὐτῷ (embanti autō)</note>, that is, *having entered*, 
or when he had climbed into the ship. Nor is it *a little boat*, but *a ship*, 
<note>original: πλοῖον (ploion)</note>. Lest anyone should dream that some huge mystery underlies 
this, that the ship...

<margin>A</margin> <note>original: "naviculam"</note> He said "little boat," not "ship." To be sure, it was not the Evangelist who said "little boat," but some translator or other—I know not who—and it is uncertain what he was following. Certainly, the other Evangelists write <note>original: "tò ploîon"</note>, that is, "vessel" or "ship." It is the consensus of all that they wrote in Greek, even if we grant that the Gospel was written by Matthew in Hebrew—though that itself does not seem likely to me, since no one testifies with sufficiently suitable arguments to having seen any trace of that Hebrew volume. For that which they call the "Gospel of the Nazarenes," Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> testifies was written not in Hebrew but in Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note>, using only Hebrew letters, and it is considered among the apocrypha. Furthermore, Matthew's style clearly agrees with Mark's style, and does not differ much from the diction of John. Therefore, it seems more probable to me that this Gospel was written in the same language in which the other Evangelists wrote. I feel the same about the Epistle to the Hebrews, which seemed to some to have been first written in the Hebrew tongue for no other reason than that it was addressed to the Hebrews. As if, indeed, it were necessary that if I now publish a book against the Jews, I must have spoken in Jewish <note>Hebrew</note>, or if to the Scots, in Scottish! But let us grant, as I said, that Matthew wrote in Hebrew and not Greek; certainly in the other Evangelists we read <note>original: "ploîon"</note> in this place, not <note>original: "ploiárion"</note>, that is, "ship," not "little boat." And yet I think it arose from this that they now everywhere call it the "little boat" of Peter whenever they signify the Church. But it was more fitting for it to be a huge ship, which would receive the entire human race, and better correspond to the type of the Ark <note>Noah's Ark</note>, which is described as having been most spacious. In a similar way, they distinguish a "council" <note>concilium</note> from a "conventicle" <note>conciliabulo</note>, thinking that "conventicle" is a diminutive or a compound word, as if you were to say "the Council of the Devil," whereas in Jerome it is found used in a good sense for a council, such as in his *Epistle to Gerontia* where he calls them "the conventicles of Christ." But perhaps we should warn about these things at greater length than the matter itself requires, except that I see some people <margin>E</margin> miserably philosophizing—or rather dreaming—over trifles of this sort as if they were serious matters. It is no wonder if those ignorant of the Greek language slip in these things. For who would suspect this translator would so often say "little boat" for "ship" without reason? And yet, if one were to ask the Translator why he said "little boat" so many times, he would not have anything to respond, unless perhaps what Homer responds in Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata, a 2nd-century satirist</note> when asked why he began the Iliad with the word "wrath": "Because it just pleased me then." Shortly after, Rufus <note>Likely referring to Tyrannius Rufinus, a 4th-century monk and translator</note> translates "little boat" for "ship" quite unseasonably as <note>original: "en hypopodíō"</note> [at the footstool]. Likewise, instead of "waves" or "from the waves," <note>original: "eît’ apò kymátōn"</note>, and so Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), Archbishop of Constantinople</note> reads it: to say nothing of the fact that he added here some words of his own, just as he soon added "Jesus" purely of his own accord.

<margin>18 And his disciples approached him</margin> "His disciples" is not added in the Golden Manuscript <note>Codex Aureus, a high-status illuminated manuscript</note>. In the Greek texts, however, I find "disciples."

<margin>19 He commanded the winds</margin> <note>original: "epetímēse"</note>, that is, "he rebuked." And I think it was written that way originally. However, someone offended by the dative case, "to the winds"—which, however, is the Greek custom to add here—changed it to "he commanded." Jerome, explaining this passage, <margin>F</margin> mentions both words, saying: "The creatures which he rebuked and which he commanded feel the one commanding." Anyone who interprets this must see that he indeed commands, but by threatening punishment if he is not obeyed. And that word "what sort of" is not <note>original: "poîos"</note>, with which we simply ask a question, but <note>original: "potapòs"</note>, which carries an emphasis of wonder. But then he wrongly omitted the Greek conjunction, for "the winds and the sea," <note>original: "hóti kaì hoi ánemoi kaì hē thálassa"</note>, because *even* the winds and the sea. The Golden Manuscript agrees with the Greek. Even the first conjunction not only connects but also amplifies: "Because the sea *also* and the winds obey him," who are accustomed to obey no one. Again:

<margin>20 And when Jesus had come</margin> <note>original: "Kaì elthónti autō"</note>, that is, "And when he had come," nor is "Jesus" added.

<margin>21 Exceedingly fierce</margin> <note>original: "chalepoì lían"</note>. Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD)</note> reads "dangerous" instead of "fierce." For in Greek the word <note>original: "chalepòs"</note> has many meanings: sometimes "fierce," sometimes "troublesome" and "difficult," sometimes "atrocious," and sometimes signifying "dangerous."

entered <margin>1</margin>

<margin>22 What to us and to you]</margin> Indeed, what does the Translator have to do with this Greek figure of speech? It should have been translated, if he wanted to speak in Latin, "What business have you with us?" And soon after:

<margin>23 Now there was not far off]</margin> The Greek has "far off," <note>original: "ēn dè makràn"</note>, with a great consensus of the manuscripts I have seen, but our manuscripts reclaim the opposite with an equally great consensus. From Chrysostom, it cannot be gathered with certainty what he read, nor even from Jerome; the same for Hilary. In Theophylact <note>11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator</note>, I find "it was far off" written: although from the interpretation it is not clear what he read, just as Chrysostom is turned. It is more probable, however, that the demons were banished far from Christ. The Spanish edition <note>The Complutensian Polyglot Bible</note> also agrees with the manuscripts we have seen. However, it makes no difference to the <margin>D</margin> meaning whether you read "far" or "not far." For if the herd is compared to those who were nearest to them wandering within, it "was far"; but if compared to other more remote places, it "was not far," because it was in view. For suppose the herd was three hundred paces away. Moreover, what the other Evangelists add, "there," does not prove the size of the interval. For these adverbs sometimes encompass an entire region. Nor is it:

<margin>24 If you cast us out from here]</margin> <note>original: "ē ei ekbálleis hēmâs"</note>, that is, "if you cast us out," with ancient Latin copies agreeing, and with these the Golden Manuscript and the Donatian ones. Nor do I see what the adverb "from here" achieves. Again, <note>original: "epítrepson hēmîn apelthen eis tēn agélēn"</note>, that is, "permit us to go into the herd of swine," he translates as "send us into the swine."

<margin>25 It went with great force]</margin> He has used three words to paraphrase a single Greek verb, <note>original: "hōrmēsen"</note>, that is, "it was carried" or "it rushed." For <note>original: "hormē"</note> entirely signifies force or impulse, and in the Golden Manuscript only "with force" is read— "great" is not added, with the Donatian codices agreeing. <margin>E</margin> And again:

<margin>26 in the waters]</margin> Hilary, in the Canon he published on the Gospel of Matthew, warns that it was written "in many waters," although I find nothing of this sort among the Latins or Greeks I have seen.

<margin>27 All these things]</margin> Someone added this pronoun of his own accord, which neither exists in the Greek manuscripts, nor in the older Latin ones, nor in the Golden Manuscript. And soon, <note>original: "kaì tà tōn daimonizoménōn"</note>, which could be conveniently translated, "and what had happened to the demon-possessed." And soon after:

<margin>28 And they begged him]</margin> Someone added "him." It is not added in the Golden Manuscript. And a little after, he said "from their borders" instead of "from his borders or their own borders."

<margin>1</margin> **A**nd Jesus ascending] "Jesus" is not found in this place, neither in the Greek nor in the ancient Latin manuscripts. Even if in the first edition, by I know not what chance, it had been added. <meta>catchword: Makes</meta>

---

<margin>*</margin> *Gergesenes*] The Greeks read <note>original: "Gergesēnōn"</note>, that is, "of the Gergesenes." Jerome, in his work on Hebrew places, handed down that even in his age a small village existed situated on a mountain, not far from the Lake of Tiberias, where they recalled the swine went headlong into the sea. Although in Mark this very place is called "of the Gadarenes," and by the same name in Luke: from which it may be gathered that for the same city, which gave the region its name, there were different names, and it was called both *Gerasa* and *Gadara*. Saint Jerome also indicates this in the Hebrew places, adding that mention is made of the *Gerasenes* in the Gospel. But the same man soon after, in *Gergesa*, reports that there the swine went headlong into the sea: so that it follows that either Gergesa is a small village in the region of the Gadarenes, or Gergesa and Gadara are the same. That which the Greeks call Gergesa, I think is called Gergaši by Jerome, which he says is a city across the Jordan, joined to Mount Gilead, which in his own time was called Gerasa, a distinguished city of Arabia. This city, as he reports, some thought to be the same as Gadara.

<margin>1</margin> And getting into a boat, he crossed over, and came into his own city. <margin>2</margin> And behold, they brought to him a paralytic lying on a bed: and when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, "Be of good cheer, son; your sins are forgiven you." <margin>3</margin> And behold, some of the scribes said within themselves, "This man blasphemes." <margin>4</margin> And when Jesus saw their thoughts, he said, "Why do you think evil in your hearts? <margin>5</margin> For which is easier, to say, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Arise and walk'? <margin>6</margin> But that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins," (then he said to the paralytic) "Arise, take up your bed, and go to your house." <margin>7</margin> And he arose, and went to his house. <margin>8</margin> But when the crowds saw it, they wondered and glorified God, who had given such power to men. <margin>9</margin> And as Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man sitting at the tax office, named Matthew: and he said to him, "Follow me." But the days will come when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then they will fast. <margin>16</margin> No one puts a patch of raw cloth on an old garment: for its filling pulls away from the garment, and a worse tear is made. <margin>17</margin> Nor do they put new wine...
