<margin>1</margin> <note>On verse 1</note> It would be redundant to repeat the name just mentioned, as if speaking of someone else. It is not "ascending," but "having entered," <note>original: "ingressus"</note> or "having boarded the boat," <note>original: "conscensa navi"</note> for which the text here uses "little boat" <note>original: "naviculam"</note> as if "boat" <note>original: "navis"</note> were not proper Latin. Furthermore, "crossed over" <note>original: "trajecit"</note> is more correct than "crossed the strait" <note>original: "transfretavit"</note>. For while a lake might be called a sea, I do not see how it can be called a strait. Not every sea is a strait; a sea narrowed by land is called a strait, though poets sometimes misuse these words by their own right.
<margin>2 Into his own city]</margin> <note>original: "eis tēn idian polin"</note>, that is, into his private city, namely Capernaum. Indeed, we read in Matthew chapter four that, having left Nazareth, he moved to Capernaum. And following that:
<margin>3 Lying]</margin> <note>original: "beblēmenon"</note>, cast down, about which we have advised previously.
<margin>4 Your sins are forgiven you]</margin> The word "your" <note>original: "tua"</note> is not added in the ancient Latin codices, nor is it found in several Greek ones, not even in the "Golden" one. The same occurs a little later in the repetition.
<margin>5 But Jesus seeing]</margin> <note>original: "kai idōn"</note>, that is, "but when he had seen." And presently, in his usual manner, he uses "dismissed" <note>original: "dimittuntur"</note> instead of "remitted" <note>original: "remittuntur"</note>.
<margin>6 Said within themselves]</margin> The Greek phrase is ambiguous: it can be taken to mean they murmured among themselves. But it is better to understand that they spoke thus in their silent minds, because of what follows: "Jesus knowing their thoughts." And a little later:
<margin>7 And when Jesus had seen]</margin> <note>original: "kai idōn"</note>. Chrysostom reads "and Jesus knowing" <note>original: "kai eidōs ho Iēsous"</note>. Theophylact reads "having seen." It matters very little to the sense. Furthermore:
<margin>8 To what purpose do you think]</margin> He omits "you," <note>original: "humeis"</note>—that is, "To what purpose do *you*." And:
<margin>9 What is easier]</margin> <note>original: "ti gar estin"</note>, that is, "for which is," with the ancient Latin copies also agreeing regarding the conjunction.
<margin>10 But that you may know]</margin> The sudden change of person makes the speech somewhat harsh: for there follows, "then he said to the paralytic."
<margin>11 The crowds feared]</margin> In the Greek it is "they wondered" <note>original: "ethaumasan"</note>, that is, they marveled. Thus Chrysostom reads in Homily 30, and Theophylact agrees with him. Even if Hilary reads "they feared." For he adds, "Admiration, not fear, ought to follow such a work." From this it appears that in some manuscripts it was written "they feared" <note>original: "ephobēthēsan"</note> instead of "they wondered" <note>original: "ethaumasan"</note>. There is a great similarity between these words.
<margin>12 In the tax office]</margin> <note>original: "epi to telōnion"</note>, that is, "at the tax booth." This is the place where the tax collector sits, who is the public official exacting the tribute, which in Greek is called <term>telos</term>. Not to mention those minor points, such as "Matthew by name" instead of "the one called Matthew" <note>original: "Matthaion legomenon"</note>. Or that in:
<margin>13 Behold many]</margin> he omitted the conjunction "and" <note>original: "kai"</note>. Or that he improperly translated "seeing." Or that he did not avoid the ambiguity of "There is no need for a doctor for the healthy," when he could have said, "Those who are well do not need a doctor."

<column-break/>

<margin>14 With publicans]</margin> Tertullian was noted by Jerome for thinking these called "publicans" were Gentiles. See the book to Damasus on the prodigal son.
<margin>15 I desire mercy]</margin> This passage is from Hosea chapter six. Jerome translated the Hebrew this way: "Because I desired mercy, and not sacrifice," with the Seventy <note>The Septuagint</note> agreeing in all respects: "Because I will mercy, and not sacrifice" <note>original: "Hoti eleos thelō, kai ou thusian"</note>. Lorenzo Valla is somewhat offended here that he translated "thusian" as "sacrifice" <note>original: "sacrificium"</note>, since he translated the same word in Luke as "host" <note>original: "hostiam"</note>. For "sacrifice" can refer to both incense and prayer, while "host" is properly a slaughtered beast, although that itself is called "thusia" because of the smell it gives off when burned. And a little after:
<margin>16 But sinners]</margin> The Greeks add "to repentance" <note>original: "eis metanoian"</note>, even if Jerome does not add it: yet I find it in Chrysostom. It is a trivial thing that he soon translates "they come" <note>original: "proserchontai"</note> as "they approached" <note>original: "accesserunt"</note>.
<margin>17 Sons of the bridegroom]</margin> <note>original: "huioi tou numphōnos"</note>, that is, "sons of the bridal chamber," which is more than "of the bridegroom"; that is, the sons of the bridegroom's household and those closest to him. He calls the Church the "bridal chamber," which he opposes to the Synagogue, which belongs to servants, not sons. And a bit later, "puts a patch" <note>original: "epiballei epiblēma"</note>, that is, to render it word for word, "puts on an imposition," or as he translates elsewhere, "sewed on a patch." Horace calls it a "scrap" <note>original: "pannus"</note>: "A scrap," he says, "is sewed on." The common people call it a "piece" <note>original: "petiam"</note>. And presently:
<margin>18 And a worse tear is made]</margin> <note>original: "schisma"</note>, which he could have translated "rupture." Sometimes he leaves the Greek word, as in John: "And there was a *schism* among them," when he could have said "dissension."
<margin>19 Of raw cloth]</note> <note>original: "rhakous agnaphou"</note>. What he just called "a patch" <note>original: "epiblēma"</note>, he here calls "a scrap" <note>original: "rhakos"</note>, which is a small piece of cloth; "agnaphon" is that which has not yet been prepared by the fullers, such as when cloth comes from the weaver. Although fullers also renew and clean old or soiled garments. And it is called "raw" because it is fresh. For thus he calls minds not yet infected by puny human traditions. It is worth seeing and laughing at how much Hugo the Cardinal <note>Hugo de Sancto Charo</note> fusses here, debating whether it can be gathered from this that fasting should not be enjoined on new converts. Indeed, he thinks these very things once pertained to Monks, who lured anyone at all into the snare of their institution. Finally, he even notes those who use multi-colored clothing. O, what a copious writer! This is how huge volumes are born.
<margin>20 Its fullness]</margin> <note>original: "to plērōma"</note>, that is, the "supplement" or "filling." For thus he calls the cloth added to the garment to mend the tear. For, offended by the dissimilarity of the new cloth, it later pulls away, and the tear becomes larger and uglier. Likewise:
<margin>21 New wine in new skins]</margin> "New" <note>original: "neon"</note> and "new" <note>original: "kainos"</note> do not correspond to the same word among the Greeks: for "new" is called "neon" when it properly corresponds to youth, and applies to things that experience age; "kainos" is opposed to what is worn out or ancient. Now, wine has its own certain age, but skins or cloth do not. Furthermore,

<margin>22 Lay your hand]</margin> The word "your" was not added in the "Golden Codex" <note>original: "aureo codice"; likely a reference to the Codex Aureus of Stockholm or a similar lavishly produced manuscript.</note>; though it is found among the Greeks.
<margin>23 Who suffered a flow of blood]</margin> In Greek it is a single word, *haimorrhoousa*, that is, laboring with a profluvy of blood, from *haima* (blood) and *rheos* (flow). I omit those smaller details, such as that he translated "within herself" instead of "within her very self"; or that he translated "he says" as "he said," "he says," or "he was saying"; or that he translated *opisthen* (that is, from behind) as "backwards." Furthermore, *tharsei*, which is poorly translated here as "trust" (confide), and which we have sometimes translated as "be of good heart," is read by Ambrose in his commentary on the Psalms as "Be constant, daughter."
<margin>24 And he said, Girl arise]</margin> These four words are found neither in the Greek copies, nor in the ancient Latin ones, nor are they added by Jerome. Finally, I did not find them in the Golden Codex, nor in the Donatian ones. And a little after,
<margin>25 And Jesus said to them]</margin> *kai legei*, that is, "and he says," in agreement with the ancient Latin codices.
<margin>26 Because I can do this for you]</margin> "For you" is not added among the Greeks. And *hoti* is wrongly translated as "because" instead of "that you are able" or "Do you believe that I am able?" And soon after, "certainly," which in Greek is *nai*, which he elsewhere translates as "even." For it is an adverb of affirmation. And a little after,
<margin>27 And he sternly warned them]</margin> The word is not *enetimēsato*, which sometimes translates as "to rebuke" and sometimes "to threaten," but *enebrimēsato*, which properly signifies to threaten sharply and as if angrily with authority, a word derived from *brimē* (a snorting or roaring). This makes what follows more evident: that they publicized everything. For thus, I believe, he would have more correctly translated *diephēmisan* than "they defamed." Certainly, he could have paraphrased it as "they spread his fame." Likewise,
<margin>28 Never appeared]</margin> He rightly omits "thus" (*outō*), which he usually likes to add. I will overlook that he translates *tas kōmas* as "castles" (castella), when elsewhere he frequently translates it as "villages" (vicos). Since villages lack walls, and castles are smaller towns but girded with walls. Also, that he used *languorem* (faintness) for "disease" (*noson*). For his translation of *malakian* as "infirmity" is tolerable. Since the Greeks also say "to have it softly" (*malakōs echein*) to mean being unwell.

<margin>29 He had pity on them]</margin> The Greek word *esplanchnisthē* has a bit more emphasis, that is, "he was touched with an affection of mercy." For the Hebrews call a vehement and pious affection "the bowels." And it was more correctly "toward them" than "on them." And soon after,
<margin>30 Because they were harassed]</margin> Saint Jerome reads and interprets it in this way, and likewise Hilary. Chrysostom also reads *eskylmenoi*, which sounds like "torn apart" and "harassed." Since grammarians want "to harass" (*vexare*) to be derived from "to carry" (*veho*). Some codices had *eklelymenoi*, that is, scattered or dissolved. One comes from *skyō*, the other from *skyllō*. Now, as for what follows immediately, *errimmenoi*, which is translated here as "lying," would have been more correctly translated as "dejected" or "scattered," from the verb *rhiptō*; Lucian used this participle when speaking of stars scattered here and there, randomly and in no order across the whole sky. Though *errimmenoi* can refer to the fleeces of sheep torn by brambles, and this latter *errimmenoi* to sheep scattered here and there: which usually happens when the shepherd is absent. For no animal is more destitute and more dependent on the protection of a shepherd than sheep; a fact also testified to by the proverb, "sheep-like manners" (*probateios ēthos*), meaning a foolish or helpless character.
<margin>31 That he might send laborers]</margin> *hopōs ekbalē*, that is, "that he might cast out." I found it written this way in very old codices, specifically in the Golden Codex and the Donatian ones, and the Translator rendered it thus a little earlier. We preferred "push out" (*extrudat*), so that we might understand that they are to be sent quickly, or even pushed out into the work of God against their will and hesitation; a point Jerome noted somewhere when citing this passage. Hilary, instead of "send," reads "cast out."

<margin>E</margin> **A**ND having called together the twelve] *Kai proskalesamenos*. He translates it almost this way, not entirely wrongly, yet not aptly, since the Greek word sounds like "called to himself." Therefore we translated it, "having summoned the twelve." And the added Greek article *tous* indicates that it cannot be taken as just any twelve, but as specific ones, namely those whom Jesus had chosen.

A reed shaken by the wind? <margin>8</margin> But what did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold...

---

As long as the book is free from error, I do not find the preposition added, nor is it in Theophylact <note>A 11th-century Byzantine biblical exegete</note>. Otherwise, the *power* of the spirits could be understood as the power which they themselves possess. Except that in Greek, *power* is *exousia* <note>original: ἐξουσία</note>, that is, right or authority over someone. Therefore Hilary, troubled by the ambiguity, reads, *the power of casting out unclean spirits.* Although the Evangelist added this soon after: *Immediately thereafter, every sickness.* For sickness he translates *noson* <note>original: νόσον</note>, concerning which we have already spoken.

**3 First, Simon]** Saint Jerome indicates that the Apostles are not listed in the same order by the other Evangelists as they are by Matthew; lest anyone should make Peter the first of all simply because he is placed in the first position here. For the others, in their pairings, place Matthew before Thomas, while Matthew himself puts Thomas first for the sake of modesty. But in the Epistle to the Galatians, Paul lists James in the first place: *James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars.* And Jerome believes it belongs to Him to

<column-break/>

distribute the order and merits of the individual Apostles who chose them, implying, as it seems, that the authority was equal among all the Apostles regarding the discharge of the Apostolic office. Certainly, one cannot effectively conclude from the order of the list who is to be preferred over another. Indeed, where many are numbered, someone must necessarily be first. Furthermore, the order which exists in our volumes differs somewhat from the Greek: yet the Greeks agree with Jerome, who arranges the number of Apostles by pairs, so that in the first place he joins Peter and Andrew; next James the son of Zebedee and John his brother; third Philip and Bartholomew; fourth Thomas and Matthew; fifth James the son of Alphaeus and Lebbaeus, surnamed Thaddaeus; sixth Simon the Cananaean and Judas Iscariot. He distinguishes Simon by the surname of Peter from Simon the Cananaean, and James the son of Zebedee from James the son of Alphaeus. In which, by the way, it should be noted that <term>ho tou Zebedaiou</term> <note>original: ὁ τοῦ Ζεβεδαίου - the [son] of Zebedee</note>, the Greek article should have been translated into that noun which is understood in the article, namely *son*, just as in <term>ho tou Alphaiou</term> <note>original: ὁ τοῦ Ἀλφαίου - the [son] of Alphaeus</note>. Moreover, since there was only one Matthew, so that there was no need for a mark by which he might be distinguished—and even if there had been a need, he had another name, namely Levi—yet he added *telones* <note>original: τελώνης - tax collector</note>, either to humble himself or to show that the way to Christ lies open to all. Even if the Greek article allows it to be translated as *who had been a publican*, or *that former publican*. Furthermore, he added a surname to Judas the traitor, either to distinguish him from Judas the brother of James (who is also called Thaddaeus and Lebbaeus, as he had three names), or to signify by the surname that he was born for that crime, because <term>Isachar</term> <note>original: שכר</note> sounds like *reward* <note>mercedem</note> to the Hebrews; and the name seems to be derived from the tribe from which he originated. Although there are some who prefer the surname to be derived from a village. Not *Scharioth*, as it is found in our codices, but *Iscariotes*. For we Latins do the same with the surname of Judas as the Greek Ecclesiastical writers do with Spain, pronouncing it *Spanias* <note>original: Σπανίαν</note>, though, as Pliny testifies, it is a land of remarkable fertility. I think this originated from the people of Praeneste, for whom, as Plautus says, *Conia* is *Ciconia* <note>stork</note>. In Chrysostom, it is read as *Iscariotes*. To these points:

**4 Lebbaeus surnamed]** In the Latin copies this is not read, but only *Thaddaeus*. However, Jerome declares that he read it thus, because in the Hebrew names in Matthew he mentions *Lebbaeus*, interpreting it as *little heart* <note>corculum</note>.

**5 Jesus sent]** <term>apesteilen</term> <note>original: ἀπέστειλεν</note>, that is, he sent out, or rather sent away with a commission. For that is properly <term>apostellein</term>, to send out with instructions, from which word the *Apostles* are named. Nor is it,

**6 into the cities of the Samaritans]** but *into a city*, <term>eis polin</term> <note>original: εἰς πόλιν</note>: which is more emphatic, so that you understand they are not to go into any city of theirs. Although it can not improperly be understood as the city which holds the name of the region, as a metropolis. Again:

<page-break/>

# CHAPTER XI.

The names of the Apostles are these: <margin>3</margin> first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew, who had been a publican; James the son of Alphaeus, and Lebbaeus surnamed Thaddaeus; <margin>4</margin> Simon the Cananaean, and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him. These twelve in number Jesus sent out, having commanded them, saying, “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and <margin>6</margin> do not enter into a city of the Samaritans. But rather go <margin>7</margin> to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. And as you go, preach, saying, ‘The kingdom of heaven has approached.’ Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, raise the dead, cast out demons; freely you have received, freely give. <margin>8</margin> Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor copper in your belts. Nor a pouch for the journey, <margin>9</margin> nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff; for the worker is worthy of his food. But into whatever city or village you enter, <margin>10</margin> inquire who in it is worthy, and stay there <margin>11</margin> until you leave. And when you enter a house, <margin>12</margin> greet it. And if indeed the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it; but if it is not worthy, <margin>13</margin> let your peace <margin>14</margin> return to you. And whoever does not receive you, nor hear your words, as you leave <margin>15</margin> from that house or city, shake the dust off your feet. Amen I say...

---

<margin>A</margin> **7 To the sheep which perished]** <term>pros ta probata apololota</term> <note>original: πρὸς τὰ πρόβατα ἀπολωλότα</note>, that is, to the lost sheep: as Jerome frequently cites this passage. Not to mention that for <term>hoti engiken</term> <note>original: ὅτι ἤγγικεν</note>, the Greek conjunction should have been omitted first: then *has approached* in Greek is not of the future tense, but the past, and should be translated as *is present*, or *is at hand*, or *is nearby*. We have already given warning about this matter.

<margin>B</margin> **8 Do not possess]** <term>Me ktesesthe</term> <note>original: Μὴ κτήσησθε</note>. This signifies *to prepare* or *acquire* rather than *to possess*. So that these three things are referred together to what follows: *in your belts*. For from these three materials money is usually struck: which was first copper and iron—for <term>chalkos</term> <note>original: χαλκός</note> signifies both—then silver, and finally gold. So that the opposite has happened to money and the morals of men, which have degenerated from gold into iron lead. The Translator turned the word as *money* <note>pecuniam</note>, as if gold and silver were not money. Certainly in Mark 6, he translates <term>chalkon</term> as *copper* <note>aes</note>; furthermore, as for what John said, <term>eis tas zonas</term> <note>original: εἰς τὰς ζώνας</note>, that is, *in your belts*, he spoke according to the custom of the ancients: according to which soldiers, if they had any copper, carried it in their belts. Hence that proverb in Horace: *He lost his belt*, said of one who had no money, as is explained more fully in our *Adages*. We have translated it *in your pouches* <note>crumenis</note>, not because it was more elegant, but because it signified the same thing more clearly.

<margin>C</margin> **9 Nor two tunics]** <term>duo chitonas</term> <note>original: δύο χιτῶνας</note>. It was more Latin to say *nor a pair of tunics* <note>binas tunicas</note>. For the Greeks do not know this elegance, which nevertheless should not have been neglected by a Latin Translator.

**10 Inquire]** <term>exetasate</term> <note>original: ἐξετάσατε</note>, that is, search out. And he placed <term>axios</term> <note>original: ἄξιος</note> (worthy) absolutely for *suitable*, which some Latins wrongly imitate.

<column-break/>

<margin>D</margin> **11 Until you leave]** <term>heos exelthete</term> <note>original: ἕως ἐξέλθητε</note>. This pertains to that which immediately preceded, *inquire*, and both refer to the city. For the precept aims at this: that they should not change their lodging frequently, nor go around seeking where they might stay; nor again should they rashly rush into any house which must be changed shortly after. So says Ambrose and Chrysostom.

**12 Saying, peace to this house]** There is nothing of these words in the Greek copies, nor are they added by Jerome. It is simply *greet it*. Indeed, when Jerome says that he secretly expressed the greeting of the Hebrew and Syrian speech, he indicates that the greeting was not spelled out, but is gathered from this which follows: *your peace will come upon it*. In a certain very ancient Latin copy, I found written in the margin, *First say, peace to this house.* From which I conjecture, as often happens, that this was added here from other Gospels. Although, to hide nothing, it is added in Hilary in the Canon, and in Chrysostom’s thirty-third Homily (but translated into Latin), whereas it is not added in the Greek Commentaries. Again, in Theophylact it is not added. Furthermore, let no one think this new kind of greeting was first invented by Christ: who used all very common things in such a way that he drew them to a far different purpose; just as they say *Xairein* <note>original: Χαίρειν - Rejoice/Greetings</note> in the solemn manner, or the Latins say *salve*, so the Hebrews or Syrians say <term>fcholom lecho</term> <note>original: שׁלם לך</note>, that is, *peace to you*. Now the Bishops claim that greeting for themselves as their own peculiar right—though it is little fitting for those who not only wage war themselves but also incite others to wars. Moreover, in,

**13 That house]** The Translator added *that* <note>illa</note> on his own, since it is not in the Greek codices, nor in the ancient Latin ones.

<margin>F</margin> **14 Let your peace come]** <term>eltheto</term> <note>original: ἐλθέτω</note>, that is, let it come. Nor is it *it will return*, but *let it return*, <term>epistrapheto</term> <note>original: ἐπιστραφήτω</note>. Supported also by the most ancient Latin codices. And a little after,

**15 From the house or city]** The Greeks add *ekeines* <note>original: ἐκείνης</note>, that is, *that*.

It is like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling to their companions, <margin>17</margin> and saying: “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we mourned for you, and you did not beat your breasts.” <margin>18</margin> For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, “He has a demon.” <margin>19</margin> The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, “Look, a glutton and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!” But wisdom is justified by her children. <margin>rv ε 20</margin> Then he began to rebuke the cities in which most of his mighty works had been done, because they did not repent: <margin>rv β 21</margin> “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works which were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. <margin>22</margin> But I say to you, it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the day of judgment than for you. And you, Capernaum, <margin>23</margin> who are exalted to heaven, will be brought down to Hades; for if the mighty works which were done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. <margin>24</margin> But I say to you,

---

<margin>16 *And simple*</margin> The Greek is not *haploi* <note>original: ἁπλοῖ, meaning single or simple</note>, but *akeraioi* <note>original: ἀκέραιοι</note>, which elsewhere he translates as "sincere" or "pure." Christ marvelously painted with this simile the simple prudence and prudent simplicity of truly Christian men. The dove is an innocent animal, whose entire defense for safety is placed in the swiftness of its wings; for this bird is of very rapid flight. And the serpent protects its own safety more by skill than by strength. For thus far the comparison holds.

<margin>17 *But beware of men*</margin> In Greek, *apo tōn anthrōpōn* <note>original: ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων</note>, that is, "from *those* men," as indicated by the article. For he does not warn them to watch out for all men, but for the evil ones, of whom he had just spoken and speaks of shortly after.

<margin>18 *In councils*</margin> In Greek, *eis synedria* <note>original: εἰς συνέδρια</note>, that is, in councils, meaning the assemblies of senators and judges. And again, he would have more correctly translated *synagogas* as "meeting places" or "assemblies." For he is not only speaking of the temples of the Jews.

<margin>19 *To governors*</margin> In Greek, *epi hegemonas* <note>original: ἐπὶ ἡγεμόνας</note>. This altogether signifies a *governor* or *prefect* of a province in several places. Furthermore, on that point:

<margin>20 *Do not think*</margin> In Greek it is *mē merimnēsēte* <note>original: μὴ μεριμνήσητε</note>, that is, "do not be anxious" or "solicitous." The Lord does not command us to cast away thought, but anxiety. And again:

<margin>21 *You will be hated*</margin> In Greek, *misoumenoi hypo pantōn* <note>original: μισούμενοι ὑπὸ πάντων</note>, that is, "being hated by all"; he varied the phrasing, but correctly. The word "men" is not added among the Greeks, not even in the "golden manuscript" <note>Erasmus often refers to a high-quality ancient manuscript as the 'aureo codice'.</note>.

<margin>22 *You will not finish the cities*</margin> In Greek, *ou telesēte* <note>original: οὐ τελέσητε</note>. What does "you will not finish" mean? Will they be building cities? Why was the translator afraid to depart slightly from the literal words here, when he does the same thing elsewhere for no reason? For the sense is that the Son of Man will come quickly, even before they can travel through all the cities of Israel. Therefore, we have explained it with a paraphrase, "you will not have wandered through" all the cities, etc., to render the emphasis of the Greek word *telesēte*. So it is written in the "golden manuscript." And again, "until, etc.," is placed more harshly than at the beginning of this Gospel. In addition to this, "a teacher is not above the lord" <note>original: οὐκ ἔστι διδάσκαλος, ὑπὲρ τὸν κύριον</note>. Why not rather "above the instructor, above the lord," or "superior or more powerful than the lord"?

<margin>23 *Beelzebub*</margin> It is strange why the Greeks constantly change *b* to *l* in this word, writing *Beelzebul* instead of *Beelzebub*, since neither element is a final letter for them <note>The letters Beta (β) and Lambda (λ) do not typically end words in Greek.</note>. Otherwise, this could have seemed the reason: especially since there is no affinity between the words or the shapes of the letters such that it could be seen as an error of the ears or of the scribes. Saint Jerome <note>original: Divus Hieronymus</note> indicates that *Beel* and *Baal* are the same, and sound like "idol" to the Hebrews, having come from the Sidonians to the Jews, or from the Babylonians. *Zebul* <note>original: זבול</note> means "idol," and *Zebub* <note>original: זבוב</note> means "fly," as if you were to say "fly-idol"; and by this name it was the most filthy idol of the Ekronites, who are indeed in the region of Judea, but are impious. From this, the Hebrews called the prince of demons *Beelzebub*.

<margin>24 *That will not be revealed*</margin> In Greek, *apokalypthesetai* <note>original: ἀποκαλυφθήσεται</note>, that is, "it will be revealed," and thus Hilary reads it. Even if the affinity between the Greek words *kekalymmenon* and *apokalypthesetai*—that is, "covered" and "will be uncovered"—is not yet rendered. And again, *gnōsthēsetai* <note>original: γνωσθήσεται</note>, that is, "it will be known," not "it may be known."

<margin>25 *Preach*</margin> In Greek, *kēryxate* <note>original: κηρύξατε</note>. This is proper to heralds and those publicly proclaiming something with their voice among the people. Jerome denies that the word "Gehenna" is found in ancient books, but says it was first brought forth by Christ. It is a place in the tribe of Benjamin, but possessed by the impious, in which they devoted their sons, consumed by fire, and sacrificed them to the demon Moloch, just as some pagans did to Saturn. It was called *Tophet*, located in the valley of the son of <meta>catchword: Ennon,</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment than for that city. <margin>16</margin> Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves; be therefore as prudent as serpents, and as simple as doves. <margin>17</margin> But beware of those men: for they will deliver you up to councils, and they will scourge you in their meeting places. <margin>18</margin> And you will even be led before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the nations. <margin>19</margin> But when they deliver you up, do not be anxious how or what you should speak: for it will be given to you in that hour what you should speak. <margin>20</margin> For it is not you who are speaking, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. <margin>21</margin> Now brother will deliver up brother to death, and a father his child, and children will rise up against parents and put them to death. <margin>22</margin> And you will be hated by all for my name’s sake: but he who endures to the end will be saved. <margin>23</margin> When they persecute you in this city, flee to another: for truly I say to you, you will not have traveled through all the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes. <margin>24</margin> A disciple is not above his instructor, nor a servant above his lord. <margin>25</margin> It is enough for the disciple to be like his instructor, and for the servant to be like his lord: if they have called the master of the house <margin>B</margin> Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household? <margin>26</margin> Therefore do not fear them: for there is nothing covered that will not be uncovered, and nothing hidden that will not be known. <margin>27</margin> What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light, and what you hear in the ear, <margin>25</margin> preach

---

Ennon, as you read in the fourth book of Kings, chapter twenty-three: where you read in this manner: *He also defiled Tophet, which is in the valley of the son of Ennon, so that no one might consecrate his son or daughter by fire to Moloch.* Likewise in Chronicles [Paralipomenon] XXVIII, we read concerning Ahaz: *he himself burned incense in the valley of Ennon, and purified his sons in fire according to the ritual of the nations, whom the Lord had destroyed.* Furthermore, *ge* <note>original: גיא</note> signifies "valley" to the Hebrews. And the Lord, in Jeremiah chapter seven, threatens that he will change the name <margin>D</margin> of the place, so that it is no longer called the valley of Tophet or Baal, nor the valley of Ennon, but *polyandrion* <note>original: πολυάνδριον</note>, that is, a tomb of many corpses. Hence the place was held as execrable among the Jews, just as among the Greeks was the *kyadan* <note>a pit for criminals</note>, about which I have spoken in my *Adages* <note>original: Chiliadibus</note>. Among the Evangelists, it is used for the place in which the impious are tortured. In Jeremiah, however, you read in chapter seven: *They built the high places, or the altar of Tophet, which is in the valley of the son of Ennon, to burn their sons and daughters with fire, etc.* And shortly after: *And it shall no longer be called Tophet, and the valley of the son of Ennon, but the valley of slaughter, and they shall bury in Tophet because there is no other place, etc.* Again in chapter nineteen: *That place shall no longer be called Tophet, and the valley of the son of Ennon, but the valley of killing.* For *Tophet*, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament</note> translated it as *polyandrion*. Again in chapter thirty-two: *And they built the high places of Baal, which are in the valley of the son of Ennon, to initiate their sons and daughters to Moloch, etc.* I have recounted these things, reader, so that I might incidentally point out the rabid harassment of a certain slanderer, who nevertheless is considered very learned by the judgment of many—he is clearly a God to himself—except that envy and hatred strip all judgment even from the learned. <margin>E</margin> For he writes that I have included almost as many lies in this place as there are words. He makes the first lie out to be that in the places I cite from the book of Kings IV, chapter XXIII, and Jeremiah VII, these two words, *ge* and *ennon*, are not read joined together, but one has *gia hennon*, that is, the valley of Ennon, and the other *gia ben hennon*, that is, the valley of the sons of Ennon. I ask, what lie is there here, since I am not speaking of joined or disjoined words, but indicating in which places mention is made of the thing from which this name is taken, by which we signify the underworld? If there were no mention of *Tophet* there, where they initiated and even killed their sons for the idol Moloch, he would rightly charge me with a lie. For I claimed nothing else. Now hear the second lie, not placed by me, but written against me. I say *Tophet* is in the tribe of Benjamin. This, he says, is not found in the places you commemorate. What? Had I promised it was found in the places I cite? Jerome indicates in those places that *Tophet* is in the suburbs of Jerusalem, and Jerusalem was in the lot of Benjamin, <margin>F</margin> just as Jerome testifies in those same places. That man brings forth for us the chapter of Joshua XVIII. There, he says, you will find both. What both? *Gehennon* as a single word. Who was denying this? And that the place is in the lot of Benjamin. This is what I taught, although without citing the specific verse, except that I profess Jerome as the author. And yet he objects to this very thing with great insult, that I rely on this author in Hebrew matters. But I am not ashamed to follow that man as an author anywhere, whose interpretation the Church has embraced and whom it holds among its chief Doctors. He even charges Jerome with a lie because he said the word "Gehenna" is not found in the ancient books but was first produced by Christ for the underworld, whereas it is found in the book of Habakkuk—as if Saint Jerome were dreaming there of the apocryphal books of the Jews and not rather dealing with the Volumes of the Old Testament. Again, he strikes at me because I wrote that children were usually sacrificed there by their parents, while Jerome only said they "initiated" them. On the contrary, Jerome, explaining this place, says, "and they burned or initiated their sons." Explaining the same place <meta>catchword: with</meta>

### ACCORDING TO MATTHEW. CHAPTER XI.

...for you, that it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom in the day of judgment than for you.
<margin>25</margin> At that time, Jesus answered and said: I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to babes.
<margin>26</margin> Yes, Father, for such was your good pleasure.
<margin>27</margin> All things have been delivered to me by my Father; and no one knows the Son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.
<margin>28</margin> Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
<margin>29</margin> Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.
<margin>30</margin> For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
<margin>1</margin> At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath; and his disciples were hungry, and began to pluck heads of grain and eat.
<margin>2</margin> But when the Pharisees saw it, they said to him: Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath.
<margin>3</margin> But he said to them: Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him?
<margin>4</margin> How he entered the house of God and ate the showbread <note>Bread traditionally set out in the Temple as an offering</note>, which was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those with him, but only for the priests?
<margin>5</margin> Or have you not read in the law that on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are blameless?
<margin>6</margin> But I say to you that something greater than the temple is here.
<margin>7</margin> But if you had known what this means, "I desire mercy and not sacrifice," you would not have condemned the blameless.
<margin>8</margin> For the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.
<margin>9</margin> And departing from there, he went into their synagogue.
<margin>10</margin> And behold, there was a man who had a withered hand; and they asked him, saying: Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath? — so that they might accuse him.
<margin>11</margin> And he said to them: What man shall there be...

<column-break/>

...preach on the rooftops. And do not fear those who <margin>28</margin> kill the body but cannot kill the soul; but rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna <note>original: "gehennam"; a term for hell or a place of punishment</note>. Are not <margin>29</margin> two small sparrows sold for a tiny copper coin? <note>original: "asse"; the 'as' was a Roman coin of very low value</note> And not one of them falls to the ground without your Father. <margin>30</margin> Indeed, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Do <margin>31</margin> not fear, therefore: you are of more value than many sparrows. Every one, therefore, who confesses me <margin>32</margin> before men, I also will confess him before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever <margin>33</margin> denies me before men, I also will deny him before my Father who is in heaven. Do not think <margin>34</margin> <margin>B</margin> that I have come to bring peace to the earth: I did not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I have come <margin>35</margin> to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a bride against her mother-in-law. And a man’s enemies will be <margin>36</margin> those of his own household. He who loves father <margin>37</margin> or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and he who loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. And he who does not take up his cross and follow <margin>38</margin> me is not worthy of me. He who finds his life <margin>39</margin> will lose it; and he who loses his life for my sake will find it. He who receives <margin>40</margin> you receives me; and he who receives me receives him who sent me. He who receives a prophet <margin>41</margin> <margin>C</margin> in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and he who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward. And whoever gives even <margin>42</margin> a cup of cold water to one of these little ones...

<column-break/>

---

<margin>D</margin> ...when in Jeremiah it speaks thus: *They consecrated their sons in the fire to idols, or offered them as a burnt offering.* My critic also grumbles at this: that while Jerome wrote that Tophet was a place of delights, I said it was an abominable name to the Jews, just as <term>syromarges</term> <note>original: "συνομαργὲς"; a Greek term for a place of filth or a sewer</note> is among the Greeks. Truly "wonderful delights," to burn one's sons for an idol! And yet, the place which previously attracted people with its beauty later became something to be loathed, namely a dumping ground for human corpses, as Holy Scripture teaches. Therefore, the name remained abominable to the Jews because the souls of many perished there in detestable superstition, as did the bodies of their sons. He attacks me for saying I do not see the difference between *racha* <note>An Aramaic term of contempt</note> and *fool*, and from this, the "logical" fellow concludes that I attribute injustice to Christ. On the contrary, I say this: *If it is true, as Jerome writes, that 'racha' means 'empty-headed,' you do not see what the difference is between racha and fool.* It is more atrocious to lack a brain than to be called a fool. He objects that I cited only one passage from the Psalms where *racha* is used for "empty," arguing from this that I have only read one or two Psalms—as if what he himself did would be difficult even for a dictionary-maker to do, if it pertained to my purpose. He objects that while others doubt the meaning of *racha*, I alone affirm it. On the contrary, Jerome affirms it, and likewise Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople</note>; I alone doubt it, denying that I see a distinction if Jerome's opinion is true. And he himself rejects Jerome's opinion, thereby agreeing with me. In passing, he mixes in the charge that I have detracted from the perpetual integrity of the Virgin Mother and from Christ’s divinity, lying with a bold face; and further, that I have taught the Germans contempt for the Roman See. The man blathers many other similar things, appearing to be saved by fate for the purpose of propping up the Church of God, shouting that it is most impudent for anyone in this century to write books while such a genius lives. But what can he show us but smoke, so many boasts, and so many insults? He says we should read *recha*, not *racha*, and that *rheca* can be said of one who nonetheless abounds in divine gifts—and from where does he teach this? From the books of the Jews, which the Christian Church does not recognize. Then he says he read *Gehenna* as a compound word in the book of Judges, and that *Gehenna* is found for the underworld in the books of the *Abot* <note>Jewish wisdom literature</note>, intending to bring forth similar mysteries, unless he fears casting what is holy to dogs and pearls before swine. Surely if the Roman Church sends us such writers, they will make it favored by all. Indeed, unless the Roman See provides or expects something else, it would not have fallen into such public hatred throughout the world. We deal with humble matters, surely according to the nature of the argument we have undertaken, standing in no one's way to prevent them from bringing forth more sublime things. Indeed, unless these humble matters had come first, perhaps there would be no one who would either desire or be able to learn those sublime things.

<margin>F</margin> 26 *Two sparrows* <term>dyo strouthia</term> <note>original: "δύο στρουθία"</note>, that is, two little sparrows; the diminutive form adds emphasis. And shortly after again, <term>annariou</term> <note>original: "ἀνναρίου"</note>, "for a penny," is a diminutive, as if you were to say "for a tiny farthing." Although either the translator or the Evangelist fashioned the word after the Roman term. For the *as* or *assis*, also called a *libella*, was a coin of such smallness that its worthlessness is attested even in a proverb. Catullus says: *Let us value them all as worth a single penny.* It is a wonder that Hilary repeatedly used the neuter *one* instead of the masculine *one* because <term>strouthion</term> in Greek is of the neuter gender, unless perhaps we prefer to blame the scribes. Cyprian cites it as neuter because mention had been made of two things. It is curious why Chrysostom reads, *and not one of them shall fall into a snare without your Father*. Origen reads it exactly the same way in his thirty-second Homily on Luke. For even if that work is not by Origen, it is the work of a learned man. Theophylactus reads with us: *upon the ground*. From this it is probable that Chrysostom had a manuscript in which <term>eis pagida</term> <note>original: "εἰς παγίδα", meaning "into a trap"</note> was written instead of <term>epi ten gen</term> <note>original: "ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν", meaning "upon the earth"</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>27 But yours</margin> *Yours* in this place is a primary pronoun rather than a derivative one, as if he says, "concerning you." For the Greeks lack this distinction. Moreover, it signifies the most worthless part of a man. The translator, or a scribe, omitted the Greek conjunctions *and* or *but*. *And the hairs*, or rather the individual bristles, which nonetheless adds to the emphasis, as it is felt that we are not so neglected by the heavenly Father that he does not even have our hairs numbered. And a little later,

28 *You are better*] <term>diapherete</term> <note>original: "διαφέρετε"</note>, that is, you excel, which elsewhere he translates as *you are worth more*. Nor is it,

29 *Will confess me*] but <term>en emoi</term> <note>original: "ἐν ἐμοί"</note>, *in me*. That is, *in my name*. Likewise, *I will confess in him*, <term>en auto</term>. Chrysostom also reads it this way. Although I suspect this speech is of a Hebrew idiom.

30 *To separate a man against, etc.*] <term>dichasai</term> <note>original: "διχάσαι"</note>, which means to draw apart into two things that were previously joined, which Chrysostom also seems to have noted in explaining this passage. Hence the Greeks use <term>dichostasis</term> to mean contending among themselves through sedition, and call sedition <term>dichostasia</term> whenever the uncertain common people are split into contrary pursuits. The passage, however, is in Micah, chapter seven, according to the Hebrew truth: *From her who sleeps in your bosom, guard the doors of your mouth, because a son brings shame to his father, and a daughter rises up against her mother, a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, a man's enemies are the members of his own household.* The Greek word <term>nymphe</term> <note>original: "νύμφη"</note> is ambiguous: if it refers to a husband, it means *bride*; if to the parents of the groom, *daughter-in-law*.

<margin>E</margin> 31 *He who finds*] <term>ho heuron</term> <note>original: "ὁ εὑρὼν"</note>, he who shall have found. For it is in the past tense, as is that <term>ho apolesas</term>, he who shall have lost: so a little later:

32 *In the name of a Prophet*] I know that some refer these phrases *in the name of a righteous man, and in the name of a Prophet* to Christ, who is truly righteous and a Prophet. Although it seems to me this is the sense: *He who receives a righteous man, not because he is a kinsman, or an in-law, or rich, or powerful, but because he is righteous, shall himself receive a righteous man's reward for his righteousness.* And we have left it as "in the name," because sometimes the Hebrew idiom is sufficiently explained neither by "under the name," nor "through the name," nor by "name" with the preposition omitted. And to me, those seem far too irritable who never allow the Gospel writings their own peculiar vocabulary, even though in works on Rhetoric they tolerate words like "status" and "constitution" signifying something far different to Latin ears, and "end" for "definition," and "superlation"—a word unheard of by Latins—for what the Greeks call "hyperbole."

33 *Shall receive a Prophet's reward*] Neither for "Prophet" nor "righteous man" is the article <term>tou</term> added in Greek, from which it cannot be understood as a specific Prophet or righteous man, but of any one at all—not of the one who is received. So the sense would be that he who receives a Prophet becomes a Prophet himself, and he who receives a righteous man becomes righteous himself. For this sense usually appeals to John Colet <note>Erasmus's friend and Dean of St. Paul's Cathedral in London</note>. Though Chrysostom seems to interpret it otherwise.

34 *Of these least ones*] <term>ton mikron touton</term> <note>original: "τῶν μικρῶν τούτων"</note>, that is, from these very small or little ones, lest certain people who call themselves "The Least" <note>The Minims, a religious order</note> please themselves in vain, while others have already occupied the name "The Minor." Though Hilary reads and interprets it as "the least." From Jerome’s and Chrysostom’s interpretation, it is not clear what they read. And in the twenty-fifth chapter of this same Evangelist, the word for "least" is used, although the form is "from these least," etc. But soon,

35 *A cup of cold water*] In Greek it is <term>poterion psychrou</term> <note>original: "ποτήριον ψυχροῦ"</note>, that is, *a cup of cold*, so that *water* must be understood. For even the Latins speak this way: "she washes in cold"; and, "he asked for cold." Furthermore...

->59 THE GOSPEL<-

<margin>11</margin> "What man among you, who has one sheep, and if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? <margin>12</margin> How much more valuable, then, is a man than a sheep? Therefore, it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath." <margin>13</margin> Then he said to the man, "Stretch out your hand." And he stretched it out, and it was restored to health, as sound as the other. <margin>14</margin> But the Pharisees went out and took counsel <margin>44 15</margin> against him, how they might destroy him. But when Jesus knew this, he withdrew from there. And great crowds followed him, and he healed them all. <margin>16</margin> And he warned them that they should not make him known. <margin>17</margin> This was to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah, saying: <margin>18</margin> "Behold my servant, whom I have chosen; my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my spirit upon him, and he will declare judgment to the nations. <margin>19</margin> He will not quarrel, nor cry out; nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets. <margin>20</margin> A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoking wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory. <margin>21</margin> And in his name the nations will hope." <margin>42 22</margin> Then a demon-possessed man, who was blind and mute, was brought to him; and he healed him, so that the blind and mute man both spoke and saw. <margin>42 23</margin> And all the crowds were amazed, and said, "Can this be the Son of David?" <margin>24</margin> But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, "This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, the prince of demons." <margin>102 25</margin> But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said to them, "Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation, and every city or house divided against itself will not stand. <margin>26</margin> And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself; how then will his kingdom stand? <margin>27</margin> And if <meta>catchword: if</meta>

1 <gloss>in the name of a disciple</gloss> <note>original: "nomine discipuli"</note>, that is, only as much as follows immediately, can be referred either to what precedes—meaning if anyone gives even just cold water—or to what follows, so you understand that anything is sufficient, provided it is done as if for a disciple of Christ.
2 **When he had finished instructing** <note>original: "Cum consummasset præcipiens"</note>] The Translator <note>Erasmus refers to the author of the Vulgate</note> poorly rendered the Greek figure of speech. For according to the specific properties of the language, a participle is placed in the stead of an infinitive verb: <note>original: "ἐτέλεσε διατάσσων"</note> instead of "to instruct" <note>original: "διατάττειν"</note>. Just as in "I remember having seen" <note>original: "μέμνημαι ἰδὼν"</note>, that is, I remember that I came, instead of I remember to come. Therefore, we have translated it: *When Jesus had made an end of commanding*, or instructing.
2 <gloss>in chains</gloss> <note>original: "in vinculis"</note>] <note>original: "ἐν δεσμωτηρίῳ"</note>, that is, in prison. The noun is derived from "to be bound" <note>original: "ὁ δεσμοὺς vinciri"</note>. For "custody" <note>original: "φυλακὴ"</note> is something else, derived from guarding. And shortly after, regarding **the works** <note>original: "τὰ ἔργα"</note>, why not "deeds" <note>original: "facta"</note> rather than "works" <note>original: "opera"</note>? For a "work" is something that stands, like a house. Though in these small details we often turn a blind eye. Not to mention that he translated "having sent" <note>original: "πέμψας"</note> as "sending" <note>original: "mittens"</note>, instead of *having sent two*, failing to observe the proper tense.
3 <gloss>You are the one who is to come</gloss> <note>original: "Tu es qui venturus es"</note>] <note>original: "Σὺ εἶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος"</note>, that is, "You are that coming one" or "one about to come." For the Greek word is ambiguous as to either time. A matter of greater weight is that he translates "what you hear and see" <note>original: "ἃ ἀκούετε καὶ βλέπετε"</note> as "what you hear and have seen" <note>original: "quæ auditis &amp; vidistis"</note>. The sense is fuller if it is understood to mean all the things that Jesus was doing.
4 <gloss>The blind see</gloss> <note>original: "Cæci vident"</note>] <note>original: "ἀναβλέπουσι"</note>. In Greek, it is more expressive, as if you were to say "they see again" or "they recover their sight."
5 <gloss>The poor have the gospel preached to them</gloss> <note>original: "Pauperes evangelizantur"</note>] <note>original: "εὐαγγελίζονται"</note>. The Translator spoke plainly in the manner of the Greeks, who say "I do good to you" <note>original: "εὐεργετῶ σε"</note>, and use the passive forms of these verbs proportionately: "I am well-treated by you." For they speak in both ways: "I bring good news to you" <note>original: "εὐαγγελίζω σοι"</note> and "I evangelize you" <note>original: "εὐαγγελίζω σε"</note>, as Theodulus indicates in *On Rhetorical Diction*. Therefore, we translate: *the poor receive the joyful message of the Gospel*. For he alluded to the words of the Prophet, "He has sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor."
6 <gloss>these are trivial matters, such as translating</gloss> <note>original: "σαλευόμενον"</note> <gloss>as</gloss> **agitated**, instead of that which is "shaken or moved," but back and forth like the waves. Whence Hilary, observing the sense of time, translates it: *a reed moved by the wind*.
7 <gloss>And that</gloss> <note>original: "τὰ μαλακὰ ἠμφιεσμένους"</note> <gloss>he translates as "those who</gloss> **are clothed in soft things**," instead of *those wearing soft things*, where you should understand "garments."
8 <gloss>Indeed I say to you</gloss> <note>original: "Etiam dico vobis"</note>] <note>original: "ναὶ"</note>, that is, certainly. An adverb of confirmation, which he translated just above as "verily." For having denied the other options, he confirms this last one.
9 <gloss>And more than a prophet</gloss>] He translates well if you read "more" <note>original: "περισσότερον"</note> in the neuter gender; but if it were masculine, it would sound like *one more excellent than a prophet*. Nor would it be permitted here to add the article, "the prophet" <note>original: "τῇ προφήτου"</note>, because it cannot be adjusted to any one specific prophet, since he places him before all of them.
10 <gloss>But what did you go out to see</gloss>] From this point, the punctuation has some ambiguity: in Origen we find this distinction: "But why did you go out? To see a prophet?" <note>original: "ἀλλὰ τί ἐξεληλύθατε, ἰδεῖν προφήτην"</note>.
11 <gloss>Among those born of women</gloss> <note>original: "Inter natos mulierum"</note>] <note>original: "ἐν γεννητοῖς γυναικῶν"</note>. He spoke absolutely, so that it pertains to all things that can be born of women. For I think "born" <note>original: "γεννητοῖς"</note> is placed in the neuter gender. Not that he intends things other than humans, but that the pattern of speech has a certain intensity <note>term: epitasis (a rhetorical increase in emphasis)</note>. For it is more vehement to say "no animal is more wicked than this" than "no man is more wicked." Now, although Jerome reasons piously that Christ is not held by this formula because he was born of a virgin, yet to refute a contentious person, this would not have enough weight: since elsewhere Christ himself, speaking to Mary, says <note>original: "γύναι"</note>, that is, *woman*. Furthermore, with what boldness does Paul write to the Galatians, that he was *made*

<margin>1</margin> in the name of a disciple, amen I say to you, he shall not lose his reward. ¶ And it happened when <margin>XI. 1</margin> Jesus had finished commanding his twelve disciples, he departed from there to teach and preach in their cities. Now when John had <margin>2</margin> heard <insert>a</insert> in prison the works of Christ, having sent two of his disciples, he said to him, <margin>3</margin> Are you the one who is to come <insert>b</insert>, or do we look for another? And Jesus answering <margin>4</margin> said to them, Go, and report to John those things which you hear and see: <margin>5</margin> The blind receive sight, and the lame <insert>c</insert> walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor receive the joyful message of the Gospel. And blessed is he who is not <margin>6</margin> <margin>B</margin> offended by me. And as they departed, <margin>7</margin> Jesus began to say to the crowds concerning John, What did you go out into the desert to see? A reed <insert>d</insert> that is shaken by the wind? Come, what did you go out to see? <margin>8</margin> A man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft things are in the houses of kings. <margin>9</margin> But what did you go out to see? A prophet? <insert>e</insert> Certainly I say to you, <margin>10</margin> and one more excellent than a prophet. For this is he of whom it is written, Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who shall prepare your way before you. Moreover, from the days of <margin>12</margin> John the Baptist until this day, the kingdom of hea- <meta>catchword: hea-</meta>

---

<margin>A</margin> <gloss>from a woman, if Christ was not born of a woman? It is true that "woman" <note>original: mulier</note> among the Latins sometimes signifies one who is defiled, and yet this did not stop the Translator from addressing the Virgin Mary by the name of "woman." But if a grown virgin is called a "woman" in Latin and Greek, it is much less absurd for a married woman and mother to be called a "woman." Then what need was there for him to soon except himself, if he was not held by this formula? For he says of himself: "but he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he." Augustine, both elsewhere and against the adversary of the Law and the Prophets (Book 11, Chapter 5), argues about the distinction, that this phrase "in the kingdom of heaven" can be referred to either side: <gloss>He who is minor—namely in time—is greater in the kingdom of heaven. Or, he who is least in the kingdom of heaven, is greater than he.</gloss> These things will seem childish, but they pertain to the present purpose.</gloss>
<margin>B</margin> 12 <gloss>No one greater has arisen</gloss>] Jerome noted this: that John is not preferred above all the Prophets and Patriarchs, but is made equal to them; for it does not follow that if Peter is not greater than John, then John is immediately greater than Peter.
<margin>C</margin> 13 <gloss>Suffers violence</gloss>] <note>original: "βιάζεται"</note>, that is, it is invaded by force, or occupied, either because of the crowd rushing in and attempting to break in by force, so greatly did the time of the Gospel now press. Although it does not escape me that Jerome, Augustine, and many others with them, interpret this place differently. Truly, let it be permitted to disagree somewhere even with the most approved Authors: since they were not only men, but they sometimes allowed themselves in their figurative interpretations <note>original: "tropologia"</note> to misuse the testimonies of Scripture. First, it is clear, I think, that in this place "the kingdom of heaven" refers to the new doctrine of the Gospel, toward which the crowd was already flocking of its own accord, as if weary of the Law. For the doctrine of Christ does not suffer violence in this, nor is it snatched by force if we apply force to our own affections, but rather it *exerts* force. To this, he soon explains what he himself intended: "for all the Prophets and the Law were until John," namely giving the reason why it began to break in thus, since the time of the Mosaic Law had now passed. Thus Chrysostom connects the sequence of the discourse in his thirty-eighth Homily. Theophylact agrees with this. Nor does Hilary differ much from our opinion, interpreting the kingdom of heaven as something owed to the Jews by covenant, but to be occupied by the Gentiles through the violence of faith. If anyone seeks his words, I will write them below: <gloss>As the nature of things exists, he says, the more powerful brings force, and the one to whom force is brought will be the lesser. What it is, therefore, that is plundering, and what suffers violence, must be considered. The Lord observes the infidelity of John's disciples: he had also understood the crowd's opinion of his messenger, in whose stumbling a great danger to faith was felt; he had rather ordered the Apostles to go to the lost sheep of Israel. They ought to have been established in the kingdom, and retained in the family of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But all this preaching brought progress to tax collectors and sinners. For from these come those now believing, from these now the people, from these now the kingdom of heaven. Otherwise, John is not believed by the common people, and they do not merit the authority of Christ's works. The future Cross was to be a stumbling block; now prophecy ceases, now the Law is fulfilled, now all preaching is enclosed, now the spirit of Elijah is sent ahead in the voice of John. Christ is preached to some, and recognized by others. He is born for some, and loved by others. His own reject him, strangers receive him. His own kin pursue him, enemies embrace him. Adoption seeks the inheritance, the family rejects it. The sons repudiate the Testament, the servants acknowledge it. Therefore the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those bringing force plunder it. Because the glory of Israel owed to the Fathers, announced by the Prophets, offered by Christ, is occupied and snatched away by the faith of the Gentiles.</gloss> Thus far we have reported the words of Hilary. By this speech the Lord excludes the murmur of the Jews, who were indignant that he would receive anyone at all into the promised grace of the Gospel; "rather," he says, "I do not receive them, but they themselves break in while you are hesitating."

<summary>This page covers Jesus's defense of healing on the Sabbath and his tribute to John the Baptist. Erasmus uses the text to argue for a more nuanced understanding of the transition from the Old Testament Law to the Gospel, emphasizing that the "violence" mentioned in the text refers to the eagerness of the Gentiles to embrace faith.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the bilingual presentation and scholarly critique of the Gospel of Matthew. The left column contains the Greek text of Matthew 12:28–41, where Jesus defends his miracles against the Pharisees and speaks of the "sign of Jonah." The right column and the surrounding commentary provide Erasmus’s Latin translation and his extensive philological notes on Matthew 11 and 12, where he justifies his departures from the traditional Vulgate translation by appealing to Greek grammar, musical theory, and the writings of Church Fathers like Jerome and Augustine.</meta>

<margin>30</margin> Or how can someone enter the house of a strong man and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? And then he will plunder his house.

<margin>14 They take it by force</margin> It is more fitting as it is read both in other ancient manuscripts and in the "Golden Codex": *And the violent plunder it.* <note>Erasmus is refining the translation of Matthew 11:12 regarding the "violence" the Kingdom of Heaven suffers.</note> The metaphor is taken from a fortress that is plundered when enemies break in.

<margin>15 He is Elijah</margin> The passage is at the end of the Prophet Malachi: *Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes.*

<margin>16 Elijah who is to come</margin> It was more gentle to say, *who was to come.* For in what way is he "to come" if he had already completed his preaching? It is well known, however, that present participles also pertain to the meaning of the imperfect past.

<margin>17 I will liken</margin> <gloss>homoiōsō</gloss> <note>original: "ὁμοιώσω"</note>, that is, *I will assimilate*, or as is more idiomatic in Latin, *I will say it is similar to*.

<margin>18 Jerome</margin> noted here that in Greek it is <gloss>en agorais</gloss> <note>original: "ἐν ἀγοραῖς"</note>, that is, *in the marketplaces or outdoors*. For in Latin, a *forum* is also a place where legal cases are tried. However, <gloss>agora</gloss> <note>original: "ἀγορὰ"</note> for the Greeks is properly a marketplace for selling things. From this comes the verb <gloss>agorazō</gloss> <note>original: "ἀγοράζω"</note>, that is, *I buy*. It is not <gloss>enō</gloss> <note>original: "ενω"</note>.

<margin>19 Crying out</margin> But <gloss>prosphōnousi</gloss> <note>original: "προσφωνοῦσι"</note>, that is, *calling out to, or addressing*. Again, it is not <gloss>eno</gloss>.

<margin>20 To their equals</margin> But <gloss>hetairois</gloss> <note>original: "ἑταίροις"</note>, that is, *to their companions*. Hilary has, *and crying out to each other*, from which I gather he read <gloss>etairos</gloss> for <gloss>etairos</gloss>. And it is not simply <gloss>eno</gloss>.

<margin>21 We have piped</margin> But <gloss>ēulēsamen</gloss> <note>original: "ηὐλήσαμεν"</note>, that is, *we have played the flute for you*. Saint Augustine cites it exactly this way in the second book of *Evangelical Questions*, chapter eleven: *We played the flutes for you, and you did not dance*; and so he translates this same word in the seventh chapter of Luke.

<margin>22 But who ever said "we have lamented"?</margin> <gloss>ethrēnēsamen</gloss> <note>original: "ἐθρηνήσαμεν"</note>, that is, *we have mourned, or we have grieved*, or to express the sense more clearly, *we have sung dirges*. Indeed, the ancients moved various emotions through different musical modes, which they called *Phrygian, Dorian, and Lydian*; they incited cheerfulness with flutes. And we read <gloss>athatō melos</gloss> for a *mournful song*. The meaning, therefore, is: we have tried to stir you by various means, yet you could not be moved in any way.

<margin>23 Furthermore, you beat your breasts</margin>, in Greek is <gloss>ekopsasthe</gloss> <note>original: "ἐκόψασε"</note>, which is said because in olden times those in mourning would strike themselves with their hands, which is properly called *planctus* (wailing). It appears, moreover, that this was a common little song that children would sing among themselves. Just as Pittacus sent his advisor to the children playing with hoops so that he might hear "drive your own," <note>original: "τὴν κατὰ σαυτὸν ἔλα"</note> as is discussed more extensively in our *Chiliads* <note>Erasmus's *Adagia*, a massive collection of Greek and Latin proverbs.</note>.

<margin>24 He has a demon</margin> In some manuscripts it was written, <gloss>hoti pneuma echei</gloss> <note>original: "ὅτι πνεῦμα ἔχει"</note>, that is, *that he is a spirit*. But all others disagree. Moreover, this was also one of the charges against Socrates: that he had a peculiar Genius, which was called the *Daemon* of Socrates.

<margin>25 The Son of Man came</margin> <gloss>tou anthrōpou</gloss> <note>original: "τοῦ ἀνθρώπου"</note>, so that it cannot be referred to Mary, since the article is of the masculine gender, lest anyone here philosophize in vain about the "Son of Man," as Augustine does in some places.

<margin>26 A gluttonous man</margin> In Greek it is <gloss>phagos</gloss> <note>original: "φάγος"</note>, which sounds more like *an eater or a glutton*. Then what follows,

<margin>27 A drinker of wine</margin> Among the Greeks, it is more pleasant because of the compound word <gloss>oinopotēs</gloss> <note>original: "οἰνοπότης"</note>, as if you were to say *wine-bibber*, which is contrasted with <gloss>hydropotēs</gloss> <note>original: "ὑδροπότης"</note>, *water-bibber*. Augustine, in the sixteenth book against Faustus, chapter twenty-one, reports *vinarius* (of wine) instead of *oinopotēs*, a word, unless I am mistaken, corrupted from *vini-bibus*, from draining wine. And from this come the compound verbs, <gloss>oinopoteō, hydropoteō</gloss>. Horace says: *Songs written by water-drinkers.* And again,

<margin>28 Very many miracles</margin> <gloss>dynameis</gloss> <note>original: "δυνάμεις"</note> is a word signifying divine power, about which we have already given warning.

<margin>29 Nor is it</margin> *Corazam* among the Greeks, but <gloss>Chōrazin</gloss> <note>original: "Χωραζίν"</note>, that is, *Chorazin*. Moreover, *Bethsaida and Chorazin* are towns of Galilee.

<margin>30 Likewise</margin> <gloss>anektoteron</gloss> <note>original: "ἀνεκτότερον"</note>, *more remissly*, which he had previously translated as *more tolerable*.

<margin>31 Because they had not repented</margin> What is here once and again <gloss>metenoēsan</gloss> <note>original: "μετενόησαν"</note>, could not be just as conveniently rendered by "they came to their senses"; therefore, we have expressed the matter through a paraphrase.

<margin>32 Will you be exalted even to heaven?</margin> The translator seems to have read <gloss>ē</gloss> <note>original: "ἦ"</note>, that is, *the conjunction instead of the article*; and Saint Jerome ->D<- warns that this place is found two ways in the manuscripts. In those which we have seen, it is written thus: <gloss>hē heōs tou ouranou hypsōtheisa, heōs tou hadou katabibasthēsē</gloss> <note>original: "ἡ ἕως τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ὑψωθεῖσα, ἕως τοῦ ᾅδου καταβιβασηθήσῃ"</note>, that is, *you who are exalted or lifted up even to heaven, shall be brought down even to hell*. And so Chrysostom cites it in his twenty-second Homily on John, and again in the thirty-eighth on Matthew, and Theophylact agrees with this.

<margin>33 Perhaps they would have remained</margin> <gloss>emeinan an</gloss> <note>original: "ἔμειναν ἄν"</note>. What need was there for *perhaps* here, except that the Translator seems to have utterly misused *perhaps* everywhere in place of an expletive conjunction. A little above, he had omitted the same in "they would have repented in sackcloth and ashes." And what he now wants to be doubtful, elsewhere he makes certain, as in the Epistle to the Hebrews: *For if that first one had been faultless, surely a second place would not be sought.* Valla, in many places, cleverly brings the Translator's inconsistency into the light. I ask, what is the meaning of this greedy affectation of variety, even to the disadvantage of the sense? For here the matter itself required confirmation rather than doubt.

->E<- <margin>34</margin> Furthermore, it must be examined how Jesus is written to have *answered*, when no one asked him anything: unless perhaps it is called an *answer* because it is added to the previous discourse. Others prefer this to be an idiom of the ancient Hebrew language, where *to answer* is put for *to speak*. And a little after,

<margin>35 Because you have hidden</margin> It was more correct to say, *that you have hidden*.

<margin>36 And I said confess</margin>, according to the property of Hebrew speech, for *I praise, or I give thanks*: hence we have also translated it so, that the sense might be clearer. For he who gives thanks confesses and acknowledges a benefit. And presently,

<margin>37 To little ones</margin> It is <gloss>nēpiois</gloss> <note>original: "νηπίοις"</note>, which signifies both *a fool* and *an infant*, that is, one who does not yet know wisdom due to the fault of age. For he did not say <gloss>mōrois</gloss> <note>original: "μωροῖς"</note>, which Chrysostom also noted. But here *fools* fits better, as it is opposed to the *wise*. Nor is there anything that should offend anyone in the name "fool," since Paul says openly, *God chose the things that are foolish to the world*. For he does not here ->F<- call *wise* those who are truly wise, but those who seem wise to the world. So he calls *fools*, not those who are truly fools, but those who are fools to the world. And yet in this matter, we have preferred the sense of certain others to our own judgment.

<margin>38 From the wise and prudent</margin> <gloss>sophois</gloss> <note>original: "σοφοῖς"</note>, who are sometimes called "the learned" by the Greeks, and <gloss>synetois</gloss> <note>original: "συνετοῖς"</note>, which sounds more like *the intelligent*. For it is not <gloss>phronimoi</gloss> <note>original: "φρόνιμοι"</note>. To these two words he opposes one, <gloss>nēpiois</gloss> <note>original: "νηπίοις"</note>, as if you were to say *simple infants*, who because of age neither excel in learning nor are wise in the experience of things.

<margin>39 Yes, Father</margin> <gloss>Nai ho Patēr</gloss> <note>original: "Ναὶ ὁ Πατήρ"</note>. Which he elsewhere translates as *even*, elsewhere as *certainly*, now he translates as *yes*. Moreover, "Father" is in the nominative case, not the vocative: which nevertheless, I know not why, they misuse in the Divine Scriptures, such as *my God*, <gloss>ho Theos mou</gloss> <note>original: "ὁ Θεός μου"</note>. Furthermore,

<margin>40 So it was</margin> He correctly omitted the conjunction <gloss>hoti</gloss> <note>original: "ὅτι"</note>. Although some have, *because so it was*.

<margin>41 And it was pleasing</margin> <gloss>egeneto eudokia</gloss> <note>original: "ἐγένετο εὐδοκία"</note>, that is, *it was a good will, or a well-pleasing*. And,

<margin>42 Before you</margin> <gloss>emprosthen sou</gloss> <note>original: "ἔμπροσθέν σου"</note>, that is, *in your presence, or in your eyes*.
