<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, specifically focusing on the end of chapter 11 and the beginning of chapter 12. Erasmus is comparing the Greek text with the Latin Vulgate, arguing that the "yoke of Christ" should be understood as gentle and kind, in contrast to the burdensome human regulations that he feels have cluttered the Church of his day.</meta>

# 63 THE GOSPEL

<margin>41 etc.</margin> The men of Nineveh will rise up in the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.
<margin>42</margin> The Queen of the South will rise up in the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and behold, something greater than Solomon is here.
<margin>43</margin> When the unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he wanders through waterless places, seeking rest, and finds none.
<margin>44</margin> Then he says, "I will return to my house..."

...with your [blessings]. By this particular word, the Sacred Scriptures signify the favor and benevolence of the Divine Will, not granted because of our merits, but proceeding from His own free goodness. Again, that phrase:

<margin>43</margin> <margin>A</margin> **I will refresh you**] <note>original: "Reficiam vos"</note> is the Greek *anapausō*, that is, *I will revive* or *recreate*. For it should not be referred to food, but to a remedy for weariness: since the noun that follows, **rest** <note>original: "anapausin"</note>, is derived from this verb, which the Psalms translate as **refreshment**: *Beside the waters of refreshment* <note>original: "ana-pauseōs"</note>. Furthermore:

<margin>44</margin> **My yoke is sweet**] <note>original: "Jugum meum suave"</note> the Greek *chrēston* sounds more like **easy**, **convenient**, **kind**, or **mild**, rather than "sweet," which is elsewhere translated as **good** or **goodness**, as we shall demonstrate in its proper place. For by "yoke" He means His authority, which He wants to be understood as mild, gentle, not at all harsh, and not at all severe. It is a wonder what Augustine was following when he quoted this passage in the first book of *Questions to Simplician*: *For my yoke is light, and my burden is sweet*; unless perhaps it was inverted by the carelessness of scribes. In his Letters, specifically number 45, the true reading appears: *calling the yoke mild and the burden light*. Ambrose, explaining the Psalm *Blessed are the undefiled*, noted the property of this word, translating *chrēston* as **sweet**. But in the Psalm, where we read "goodness," he reads "delight." Cyprian, in the second book against the Jews, chapter 13, reads: *my yoke is good*. It is established that *chrēstos* is said to be derived from *chrēsthai*, that is, *from using*, from which comes *chrēstotēs*: the ease and convenience of manners in the conduct of life. And those who were mild in words rather than kind in deeds were called *chrēstologoi* <note>smooth-talkers</note>.

Saint Jerome raises a question at this point: how can the yoke of the Evangelical law be called lighter and softer than the Mosaic Law, since the latter only punishes the deed, while our law punishes the will as well, and does not lower its standards? Certainly, Peter in the Acts of the Apostles openly calls the Mosaic Law—imposed for a time on a superstitious and rebellious people—**a hard and heavy burden, which neither they nor their ancestors were able to bear**. Nor can it be doubted that what Truth itself pronounced is true. Truly, the yoke of Christ is mild and the burden light, if, besides what He Himself imposed on us, nothing else were imposed by human constitutions. He commanded nothing except mutual charity; nor is anything so bitter that charity does not season and sweeten it. Whatever is according to nature is easily endured. Now, nothing agrees more with human nature than the **philosophy of Christ** <note>Erasmus uses "philosophy" here to mean a way of life based on the Gospel</note>, which does almost nothing else but restore fallen nature to its innocence and sincerity.

But just as human constitutions aggravated the Law among the Jews—which was troublesome enough on its own—so we must be careful again and again that the additions of human constitutions and dogmas do not make the Law of Christ, which is mild and light in itself, heavy and harsh. This happens first when things creep in, either neglected as tiny matters or willingly embraced by men who are more pious than prudent because they are recommended under the appearance of piety. Once received, they gradually spread and increase until, having grown to an immense size, they press upon and overwhelm the unwilling—either by the protection of custom, whose tyranny is violent, or by the authority of Princes, who use what was rashly received for their own profit and hold onto it tooth and nail.

How pure, how simple is the faith handed down to us by Christ! How similar to this is the Creed <note>symbolum</note> produced either by the Apostles themselves or by Apostolic men? To this, the Church later added much, provoked and vexed by the disagreements of heretics. While some of these additions could have been omitted without loss of faith, many still seemed relevant to the matter. Now there are as many creeds as there are men, and a sign of good faith is no better than when a matter is handled in contracts with many wordy legal documents; which, although used to exclude trickery, usually generate more trickery the more carefully they are written.

Finally, the matter has been gradually brought to the point where some of the decrees of the **Scholastics** <note>Theologians of the medieval universities</note>, which they call "Articles," or certain new ideas or dreams of little men inventing things for the sake of pride, are almost equated with the Articles of the Apostolic faith. And in these matters, neither different schools nor the initiates of the same school agree among themselves; nor are they permanent among them, but are changed according to the times. And yet they first crept in such that they were held only as probable opinions in the Schools. Soon, having left the walls of the Schools, they broke out into books and even into public sermons. And it often happens that what the rashness of defining once produced, the stubbornness of defending confirms and increases. Moreover, most things of this kind are such that it is impious for a man to define them—such as the things they philosophize about regarding the nature of the Divine essence and the distinction of Persons. If these are used only to lead our minds away from foul thoughts toward higher things, the study is not to be condemned. But if we pronounce with arrogance on these things, which far surpass the grasp of human wit, and boast before the people of our knowledge of things that even the Angels do not fully understand, it seems to me neither pious nor useful. Closest to these are the things we pronounce about the nature of the mysteries, as if we had learned them from heaven; whereas it would be more for piety to extract from them what leads to the holiness of life. But this rashness of pronouncing, which began with the Ancients, has now progressed further than can be borne. There are those who weave for us a cold syllogism and, from a poorly understood passage or from a man’s tiny regulation, give birth to an Article of Faith.

<column-break/>

# CAP. XI. 64

<margin>27</margin> ...good will with you. All things have been delivered to me by my Father: and no one knows the Son except the Father: nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.
<margin>28</margin> Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.
<margin>29</margin> Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am mild and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.
<margin>30</margin> For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.

<margin>B</margin> And by these things we are judged as Christians or non-Christians, though they do not pertain to Christian piety in the slightest. How popular, how ready was the doctrine of Christ, the Apostles, and the Apostolic Fathers! How hindered, thorny—not to say dark—it has now become, partly by the mixing in of human laws and disciplines, partly by the dreams and little inventions of ambitious men, since the profession of sacred Theology began to be a sort of scenic and theatrical thing. A man’s whole lifespan is not enough for the little questions and the labyrinths of useless subtleties. Amidst these, when will there be a study of the Christian life, if by the age of eighty we have only learned how to doubt?

For what is the point of speaking about the burden of human constitutions, when long ago Saint Augustine, in a letter to Januarius, was annoyed and deplored that the Church of Christ was so pressed that the condition of the Jews was almost more tolerable than that of Christians? And yet he was annoyed over certain frivolous things like "barefootedness" or whatever. What if he could see that free people of Christ entangled in so many laws, so many ceremonies, so many snares? And oppressed not by a simple tyranny of men? First of the seculars, then of Bishops, Cardinals, and Popes? And most of all, by their satellites <note>Erasmus likely refers to the mendicant orders or friars here</note>, who, masked with the image of religion, act for the sake of their bellies? We—certain of us—misuse the very sacraments instituted for the salvation of men for our own gain, pride, and tyranny, and to oppress the common people.

No kind of clothing was forbidden to the Jews, except that which was woven of linen and wool. Now, how many constitutions are there about dress, what great superstition regarding colors and garments! By such trifles—which in themselves have neither honor nor shame, but are changed according to the time and the opinion of mortals—are Christians judged, things of which Christ never made mention. The fasts of the Jews were few, and yet no one said it was a capital crime if someone had not fasted on those specific days. We are burdened by how many starvations? To which we are not invited, but compelled under pain of, as they say, eternal damnation. Certain kinds of fish and other animals were forbidden to the Jews, but they were not particularly desirable to eat. We waste away eating fish for a good part of the year, and are burst by hunger. No help is given to age or illness, unless a relaxation of the law is bought with coins.

Also, among the Hebrews, the number of feasts was moderate. In the age of Jerome, he knew very few feasts besides the Lord’s Day. Now there is neither end nor limit to holidays, which, though a few were originally instituted for the leisure of piety, should now be removed for the exclusion of crimes—unless the greed of the Priests looked rather to their own affairs than even to true Religion. What shall I say of the tangled and inextricable bonds of vows, some of which can be redeemed, but for an immense amount of money, while others cannot be redeemed at all. And we urge these things more and more every day, lest our profit perish.

Now, how much more convenient was the condition of marriage for the Jews than for us? In how many snares, how many intricacies have we involved marriage, lest a Scholastic dogma perish for us? In what ways have we narrowed the sacrament of Penance and Confession, and rendered it hindered by how many decrees of men? To say nothing meanwhile of the burden of prayers, which are aggravated by daily additions. To these things, as if there were not enough Laws and Decretal Constitutions, swarms of new Constitutions break out daily. Indeed, as if this too were not enough, they want us to be burdened by some "law of custom," which, having first proceeded from two crazy people, gradually gains strength. The lightning bolt of excommunication is everywhere ready and threatened; "irregularities" and "anathematizations" occur on all sides. Certain people so abuse the sacrosanct authority of the Roman Pontiff—which ought to be effective only for relieving the affairs of the Church—in absolutions, in dispensations, in pardons, and in executions, that there are many things which the truly pious cannot behold without a groan.

The matter of priesthoods is so tangled that you could learn all of Aristotelian philosophy sooner than the practice of priesthoods. In the churches, there is hardly time to interpret the Gospel. A good part of the sermon must be spent at the whim of the Commissioners. Sometimes even the sacrosanct doctrine of Christ must be suppressed or twisted to their advantage. To these things, those who are modestly pious groan silently to themselves. Those who are fed by the evils of the people, and whose interest it is that the flock of Christ—which He made free by His blood—should be as much a slave and subservient as possible, not only do not cry out against it, but exaggerate it in every way. They join those who either seek some reward for obedience or fear the punishment for freedom. Thus, while no one brings help, the matter gradually slides to the point where there is now almost no shame. And charity indeed, according to Paul, endures all things. I admit it. But these evils are much milder whenever they are inflicted by the enemies of the Christian flock. Once the impious Tyrant raged, the Heretic raged. The Bishops brought comfort. They encouraged one another with mutual exhortations. The title of the suffering was a part of the solace. In short, it was not heavy, because they suffered in the name of Christ. But it is intolerable, as Augustine says, when the body of the Church suffers these same things from its own members, or rather, from the governors of the Church. The snares are cast chiefly by those from whom it was right that the entangled should be helped. For healing these evils, one "sacred anchor" <note>a last resort</note> usually remains: a General Council. But now these very things are turned against the head of the State. Nor does any hope of healing remain, unless Christ Himself turns, or certainly stirs up, the minds of the Pontiff and the Princes toward those things which are of true piety: or if the Theologians and Preachers, not with seditious cries, but with...

# 65 ACCORDING TO MATTHEW. CHAPTER XII. 66

...to my house, from where I came out. And having come, he finds it unoccupied,
<margin>45</margin> swept, and put in order. Then he goes, and takes with himself seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and entering, they dwell there; and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first.
<margin>137 46</margin> Thus it shall also be for this wicked generation. While he was still speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother and brothers 
<margin>47</margin> stood outside, seeking to speak to him. Someone said to him, "Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, 
<margin>48</margin> seeking to speak to you." But answering, he said to the one who told him, "Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?" 
<margin>49</margin> And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, 
<margin>50</margin> he said, "Behold, my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, 
<margin>XIII. 1</margin> he is my brother, and sister, and mother." On that

<margin>2</margin> by the sea. And many crowds were gathered to him, so that he entered into a boat to sit down; and 
<margin>3</margin> the whole crowd stood on the shore. And he spoke to them many things in parables, saying, "Behold, a sower went out 
<margin>4</margin> to sow. And as he sowed, some fell by the path; and the birds came and devoured them. 
<margin>5</margin> Others fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, because they had no depth

<margin>8</margin> Others fell on good soil and yielded fruit; some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. He who has

<margin>139 12</margin> of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given. For whoever has, to him more will be given, and he will have an abundance; but whoever 
<margin>133 13</margin> does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him. For this reason I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see..."

---

<margin>D</margin> ...should soberly and calmly teach and emphasize those things which are worthy of Christ with great consensus. For as for a Turk, or some Tyrant, restoring the Christian state by opportunity after subverting the order of things through riot—I do not believe any pious person should wish for that. I certainly abhor it. One thing especially we must all be reminded of again and again: that according to Paul’s teaching, we should embrace the liberty given by Christ in such a way that we do not give occasion to the flesh, and under the pretext of liberty, serve vices more basely. Instead, let us shake off the heavy yoke of men so that we are truly pressed by the mild yoke of Christ. Evangelical charity commands less, but it obtains more. Tumult is to be avoided everywhere; and it is better to endure impious Princes than to bring about a heavier evil by revolutionary changes. But nevertheless, Christ must be continuously knocked upon with burning prayers, that he might inspire in his Vicars a mind worthy of their position, so that, setting aside the pursuit of their own glory, their own pleasure, and their own gain, they may strive for the glory and gain of Christ, and prefer that Christ reign widely by Evangelical laws, rather than that they themselves hold a narrow tyranny by human decrees. Truly, I see that I have discussed these matters at greater length than I had proposed, or than was fitting for the continuation of these Annotations.

<margin>A</margin> <insert>Jesus went</insert> <note>original: "eporeuthē"</note>. Why not rather "walked," or "passed through"? He translates it the same way in the first Psalm: *He went not in the counsel of the ungodly.*

<margin>2</margin> <insert>Nor is it 'on the sabbath,' but 'on the sabbaths'</insert> <note>original: "sabbasin"</note>, as Hilary also reads. Indeed, that entire period of seven days was called a *sabbatum* <note>Sabbath</note>, as were the individual Sabbath days. And shortly after he inverts it, <note>original: "en sabbatō"</note>, that is, *on the sabbath*, translating it as *on the sabbaths*: although many cases of this kind are usually permitted. Chrysostom <note>An early Church Father and famed orator</note> reminds us that this is the Sabbath which Luke calls the "second-first" <note>original: "deuteroprōton"</note>: regarding which more will be said in its proper place. Next,

<margin>3</margin> <insert>Which is not lawful for them</insert>] The Translator, or perhaps a Scribe, added "for them" on his own. For the absolute sense is simply, *it is not lawful*. And soon he made them equal.

<margin>4</margin> <insert>David was hungry</insert>] <note>original: "hopisō autos"</note>, that is, *he himself: he himself and those who were with him*.

<margin>5</margin> <insert>They violate the sabbath</insert>] <note>original: "bebelousin"</note>, that is, *they profane*. Indeed, the <note>original: "bebēloi"</note> are called the *profane*.

<margin>6</margin> <insert>Priests in the temple</insert>] A pleasant wordplay between the terms has perished for us, <note>original: "hiereis en tō hierō"</note>: as if you were to say, *the Sacrificers in the Sacred place*, which was preserved in "sabbaths" and "sabbath." Likewise,

<margin>7</margin> <insert>And are free of crime</insert>] <note>original: "anaitioi ōsin"</note>, that is, *they are blameless*, or nothing is imputed to them: or, as we translate, *they are vacant of crime*. Although in that which the Translator uses here, *without crime*, is better than what Jerome cites elsewhere, *they are without fault*, since <note>original: "anaitios"</note> refers to "crime" rather than "fault." Even so, I am not unaware that among the Greeks <note>original: "anaitios"</note> is sometimes taken for *harmless*, or *innocent*, just as he translates shortly after, *you would by no means have condemned the innocent*, <note>original: "anaitious"</note>.

<margin>8</margin> <insert>Because something greater than the temple is here</insert>] <note>original: "hōde"</note>, here, in this place, is a demonstrative adverb, not a pronoun: a point Jerome also noted, so that you might understand that place to be holier than the temple which held the Lord of the temple. Some Greek manuscripts had <note>original: "meizon"</note> (something greater) instead of <note>original: "meizōn"</note> (one who is greater), which would be more complete: so the sense is, *there is in this place that which is greater than the temple.*

<column-break/>

<margin>A XII. 1</margin> At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the sabbaths. His disciples were hungry, and began to pluck heads of grain, and to eat. But the Pharisees <margin>2</margin> when they saw it said to him, "Behold, your disciples are doing what it is not lawful to do on the sabbath." But he <margin>3</margin> said to them, "Have you not read what David did, when he was hungry, himself and those who were with him? How <margin>4</margin> he entered into the house of God, and ate the bread of presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those who were with him, but for the priests alone? Or have you not <margin>5</margin> read in the law, that on the sabbaths the priests in the temple profane the sabbath, and are free of crime? But I say to you, that something greater than the temple <margin>6</margin> <margin>B</margin> is here in this place. But if you knew what this means, 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,' you would by no means have condemned the innocent. For the Son of Man is lord even of the sabbath." And having moved on from there, he came into their synagogue, and behold, there was a man having a <margin>10</margin> withered hand, and they questioned him saying, "Is it lawful to heal on the sabbaths?" so that they might accuse him. But he said <margin>11</margin> to them, "Who among you will be the man who has one sheep, and if it falls into a pit on the sabbaths, will he not take hold of it and lift it out? <margin>12</margin> How much more valuable then is a man than a sheep? Therefore it is <margin>12</margin> lawful to do good on the sabbaths." Then he says to the <margin>13</margin> <margin>C</margin> man, "Stretch out your hand." And he stretched it out: and it was restored to health like the other. Then the Pharisees <margin>14</margin> went out and took counsel against him, how they might destroy him. But Jesus, when he knew it, <margin>16 15</margin> withdrew from there, and many crowds followed him, and he healed them all. And he warned them <margin>16</margin> not to make him known. So that there might be fulfilled <margin>17</margin> what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, who says: "Behold my son, whom I have chosen, my beloved, in <margin>18</margin> whom my soul is well pleased: I will put my spirit upon him, and he shall announce judgment to the nations. <margin>19</margin>

---

<margin>9</margin> <insert>And if it shall fall</insert>] <note>original: "empesē"</note>, that is, *fallen into*. Nor is it <margin>10</margin> <insert>may have</insert>] but *shall have*, <note>original: "exei"</note>.

<margin>11</margin> <insert>Will he not hold and raise it</insert>] <note>original: "kratēsei kai egerei"</note>, that is, *will take hold and lift out*. For this kind of sheep-nature is such that it remains prostrate by a blow or otherwise, unless it is lifted by the shepherd, it perishes. And soon,

<margin>12</margin> <insert>How much more better</insert>] <note>original: "posō oun diapherei anthrōpos"</note>, that is, *how much more does a man excel, or is more excellent*. What was the need here to affect such absurdity of speech? <note>original: "diapherei"</note> is said for *to excel*. And a little after,

<margin>13</margin> <insert>It was restored to health</insert>] <note>original: "hygiēs"</note>, that is, *healthy*. Although the Translator certainly translated this well.

<margin>14</margin> <insert>Then he says to the man</insert>] In the Gospel which the Nazarenes and Ebionites formerly used <note>Refers to the apocryphal "Gospel of the Hebrews"</note>, and which is cited in several places by Jerome, and which he testifies was translated by him from the Hebrew language into Greek—nor were there lacking those who thought it was Matthew’s own authentic work—it was written that this man was a *stonemason*, and implored Jesus's help <margin>E</margin> with these words: *I was a stonemason, seeking a living with my hands; I pray you, Jesus, that you restore my health to me, lest I shamefully beg for food.*

<margin>15</margin> <insert>They were making a plan</insert>] <note>original: "elabon"</note>, that is, *they took*: and <note>original: "symboulion"</note> *counsel*, that is, *consultation among themselves*. And,

<margin>16</margin> <insert>He withdrew</insert>] <note>original: "anechōrēsen"</note>. Lorenzo <note>likely Lorenzo Valla, the humanist scholar</note> prefers *secessit* (withdrew), which is more fitting for one removing himself. From which also those who withdraw are called *Anchorites* <note>Hermits</note>. And,

<margin>17</margin> <insert>Many followed him</insert>] The Greeks add <note>original: "ochloi"</note>, that is, *many crowds*.

<margin>18</margin> <insert>Lest they make him manifest</insert>] In better Latin it would be *lest they make himself*, or *him manifest*. Lorenzo argues something here, namely <note>original: "syniē ta sympanta praxai"</note>, that Christ warned them not to betray him for the reason that he had fled from the Pharisees, as if he feared lest they be seized by them. There is another mystery in these things. For we read of this being done by Christ more than once, by which he fled the suspicion of seeking glory, and by which he might provide us an example of modesty. Conversely, we read that he commanded that they tell <margin>F</margin> everyone what had happened, to teach us that the glory of God is not to be hidden.

<margin>19</margin> <insert>Behold my servant</insert>] The testimony is in Isaiah chapter forty-two. Although Matthew cites it somewhat differently than it is read in the Septuagint, or among the Hebrews. For Saint Jerome rendered the Hebrew in this manner: *Behold my servant, I will uphold him. My chosen one, my soul is well pleased in him. I have given my spirit upon him. He shall bring forth judgment to the nations. He shall not cry out, nor accept persons, nor shall his voice be heard outside. A bruised reed he shall not break, and a smoking flax he shall not quench. In truth he shall bring forth judgment. He shall not be sad, nor turbulent, until he sets judgment in the earth, and the islands shall wait for his law.* The Septuagint translates it this way: *Behold Jacob my servant, I will take him. Israel my chosen, my soul has accepted him. I have given my spirit upon him, he shall bring forth judgment to the nations. He shall not cry out, nor give up, nor shall he be heard outside...*

<margin>D</margin> *his voice outside. A bruised reed he will not break, and smoking flax he will not extinguish, but in truth he will bring forth judgment. He will shine, and he will not be broken, until he places judgment upon the earth, and in his name the nations will hope. Moreover, regarding the fact that one part of the prophecy was omitted in the middle—"he will not be sad, nor turbulent, until he places judgment on the earth," or according to the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, "He will shine and not be crushed, until he places judgment upon the earth"—Jerome thinks this happened through a scribe's error, who (as often happens) forgot and omitted the words that fell between the word "judgment" and "judgment." But anyone who wishes to be more fully instructed on this matter should read Jerome's explanation of this passage of the Prophet; in addition, his little book to Algasia, second question. I wonder what came into Lyranus's <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a prominent medieval commentator.</note> mind, that he should write that this testimony was cited by Matthew according to the translation of the Seventy, when it agrees far more with the Hebrew Truth <note>The Hebrew text of the Bible.</note>, even if it also differs somewhat from this, but in words rather than in sense. It should be noted in passing that although Jerome, in explaining this passage of the Prophet, refers us to his Commentaries on Matthew, in which he discussed this matter more fully, yet in those Commentaries he barely touches the matter with the "tips of his fingers" (as they say). I am led to the conjecture—as I have often suspected—that those Commentaries were shortened by some distasteful Reader, who omitted things in the middle that he did not understand. Although Jerome himself admits they are neither exhaustive nor full, yet compared to others he wrote fully on the Prophets and some Epistles of Paul, they hardly deserve to be called "Little Commentaries." I believe the same happened to the Commentaries he wrote on the Psalms: although on these, whoever it was, he raged with a double injury. First, because he omitted what he pleased. Second, because in many places he stitched in his own trifles like a "purple patch." For the commentary we have on Mark has nothing of Jerome except the title. Furthermore, the Commentaries on Luke, which he himself cites in several places, have entirely perished. It seemed good to show the Reader in passing how Cyprian cites this passage in the Book he wrote against the Jews:*

Furthermore, regarding what we translated as "son" where others use "boy," the Seventy used* παῖδα <note>original: "paida"</note>, *that is, "servant," as the word* παῖς <note>original: "pais"</note> *and "boy" are ambiguous in Greek and Latin, and likewise in Hebrew* <unclear>עֶבֶד</unclear> <note>original: "ebed" (servant)</note>. *But if it was ever appropriate to translate* παῖδα *as "son," it certainly fit here, since he is speaking of Christ. Nor were there lacking among the Greeks those who were afraid to attribute the word "servant" to the Son of God. <margin>D</margin> 20 *Blind and mute]* τυφλὸς καὶ κωφὸς <note>original: "typhlos kai kōphos"</note>, that is, blind and mute. Although *kōphos* in Greek also signifies "deaf," because, I suppose, those who are deaf by nature must also be mute. And presently,
21 *so that he spoke and saw]* Here the Greek codices <note>Manuscripts.</note> repeat "blind and mute." In some, the conjunction is doubled, "both to speak and to see," in some it is not doubled. It should have been rendered: "so that he who was blind and mute both spoke and saw."
22 *Is this not...]* Here some Greek codices add "the Christ," that is, "Is this not that Christ, the son of David?" Although here too the added article "the" <note>Referring to the Greek article *ho*.</note> makes it so that it cannot be understood as just any son of David, but a specific one—namely, the one who was expected as promised by the oracles of the Prophets. And,
23 *divided in itself]* καθ’ ἑαυτῆς <note>original: "kath' heautēs"</note>. It would have been rendered more faithfully and clearly as "divided against itself," as he translates it shortly after, "against himself."

<margin>E</margin> 24 *But the blasphemy of the Spirit]* This is certainly clearly corrupted by the fault of Scribes, which has nonetheless taken root in almost all manuscripts. For in the Greek it is: "but the blasphemy of the Spirit," that is, the curse that is made *against* the Spirit. According to the sincere and genuine reading, Saint Hilary cites this passage in the Canon where he explains Matthew. Likewise Augustine in his Sermon on the words of the Lord from the eleventh chapter of the Gospel of Matthew: and he does so again and again, lest anyone should claim it was an accident, arguing only this: that "blasphemy" is not taken for just any curse, nor "Spirit" for just any spirit. But what he said here more confusedly as "the blasphemy of the Spirit," is expressed more clearly elsewhere: "he who shall have blasphemed against the Holy Spirit." Although I do not deny there is an ambiguity in the Greek words: that it could be understood as an insult proceeding *from* the Spirit itself. Currensis <note>A reference to a contemporary or medieval commentator.</note>, explaining this passage, says: "What then is the blasphemy of the Spirit, other than the affectation and desire for divine reproach? The blasphemy of the Spirit breathes toward hatred of God: the Holy Spirit breathes toward the love of God." But lest anyone impudently despise the authority of the Greek codices, the ancient Latin examples agree with the Greeks: especially the Golden Codex <note>A famous 6th-century manuscript with purple parchment and gold/silver ink.</note>, and among the printed editions, the Edition of Mainz with the *Glossa Ordinaria*.
25 *But he who says a word against the Spirit]* The word "word" is not actually placed here, but is understood from the context. The Golden Codex also supports the Greeks.
26 Again there is *sapron* <note>original: "σαπρὸν" (rotten/corrupt)</note>, which we have spoken of before.
27 And *gennēmata* <note>original: "γεννήματα" (offspring)</note>, which elsewhere he translates as "offspring," here he correctly translates as "progeny."
28 And *ekballei* <note>original: "ἐκβάλλει" (throws out)</note>, which here he translates as "brings forth," elsewhere he translates as "casts out," elsewhere "sends out." We have translated it as "brings forth" and "draws out."

29 *In three days & three nights*] Although the Latin expresses this through the ablative case <note>indicating a point in time</note>, the Greek uses the accusative <note>indicating duration of time</note>: so that it cannot be taken as a specific moment of time, but a span of time: <gloss>three days and three nights</gloss> <note>original Greek: τρεῖς ἡμέρας καὶ τρεῖς νύκτας</note>. Accordingly, Saint Jerome explains the problem through a figure of speech, which Grammarians call <term>Synecdoche: a figure where a part is used to represent the whole, or vice versa</term>. For since only one day of this three-day period was complete—namely the Sabbath with its preceding night—and Christ was not in the tomb except from the evening of the Preparation until the dawn of the Lord's Day on which he rose, he is nevertheless written to have spent three days in the tomb. Saint Augustine explains it by the same reasoning in his first book on Gospel questions, question seven. Even if Faber <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, a rival scholar</note> loathes Synecdoche so much in his book on the three days of Christ—out of hatred, I suspect, for Grammar, with which he is poorly acquainted, as the facts themselves indicate—lest he should seem to anyone to be insufficiently a Philosopher.

30 *Something greater than Jonah is here*] also,
31 *Something greater than Solomon is here*] In both places the word is <gloss>here</gloss> <note>original: ὧδε</note>, an adverb, not a pronoun <note>referring to "this man"</note>, as we have shown before. Ancient orthographers used to distinguish these, writing the pronoun with a simple "i" (*hic*), and the adverb with the Greek diphthong "ei" (*heic*). Valla testifies that he discovered this in several very ancient marble inscriptions.

32 *Through dry places*] <gloss>Through dry places</gloss> <note>original: δι' ἀνύδρων</note>, that is, lacking water and parched. For places of this kind are generally sterile and therefore desolate. Hence the daughter of Caleb asked for a field irrigated above and below.

<margin>E</margin> ...codes vary—in the Homily of the same number, he attributes this imperious importunity primarily to the brothers, sparing the mother. But the same author, in expounding the Gospel of John regarding the miracle at the wedding <note>the wedding at Cana</note>, even more clearly attributes to Mary some desire for ambition and human glory: *For she desired,* he says, *to win favor with men already, and that her son's favor might become more famous; and perhaps she was affected by some human feeling: just as his brothers were, when they said, "Show yourself to the world," desiring to acquire fame for themselves through his miracles.* And a little later on the same matter: *Since they did not yet have the proper opinion of him, but in the manner of mothers, Mary thought she might rightfully command her son in everything, when it was proper to worship and revere him as Lord.* Thus far we have reviewed the words of Chrysostom. Augustine seems to attribute to her some small amount of doubt. We make her entirely immune from original sin, but here he seems to attribute some "actual sin," as they call it—unless perhaps that affection he attributes to her is free from all fault. And I believe it should rather be understood in this way. For just as a certain ignorance can exist without fault, so too doubt and maternal affection can be free from fault. Christ in Luke's account also responds to his parents with little sweetness: *Why is it that you were looking for me? Did you not know that I must be about my Father's business?* The Evangelist immediately adds: *And they did not understand the word.* Again, to the one praising his mother's blessed womb and the breasts that nursed him, he says: *Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God.* Again, on the cross he calls her "woman" and hands her over to John. From these things the Manichaeans <note>a dualistic sect deemed heretical</note> very foolishly concluded that Mary was not the mother of Jesus, except in the opinion of the common people, clearly denying that he was human. We can indeed piously conclude that <margin>F</margin> whenever the business of the Commonwealth is at hand, and whenever the business of Religion is at hand, the affection of bodily kinship ought not to have much power over us. Jerome tries to escape this by saying that the one who reported this to Christ did so insidiously, testing whether he would interrupt his duty of preaching because of affection for his own family. And for that reason, Christ responded more sharply. On this matter, I do not interpose my own opinion; I only hate the diligence of certain people who exaggerate everything in the saints to an immense degree; let them instead turn to the zeal of emulating what truly made them blessed. <margin>D</margin> A word <note>original: "secus," meaning "alongside" or "by"</note> devised by the Translator, which he uses so frequently. Pliny used it in book 24, chapter 15: "Chameleuce," he says, "which among us they call *Faranum* or *fariugium*: it grows *secus* <note>alongside</note> rivers, with a leaf like a poplar." Quintilian, in his book *Institutes*, book 8, chapter 2, dealing with "unintelligible things," brings forward this example: "A blind man was hired to stand *secus viam* <note>alongside the road</note>." Nor do I doubt that it can be found in many other places. If someone wished to be more pedantic, perhaps someone will be corrected that it is not quite as aptly said "he sits *secus viam*" as it is "it grows *secus* rivers" or "it grazes *secus* the bank," because in these latter cases we imagine a certain movement of the thing following along. For it is apparent that *secus* and *secundum* <note>according to/following</note> have a kinship with the verb *sequor* <note>to follow</note>. Therefore, of a plant it is more correctly said "it grows *secus* rivers," just as "willows *secus* the bank," because in these a certain sequence is understood. Of a single man sitting, it is not the same.

2 **He who sows went out]** <note>original: "εξηλθεν ὁ σπειρων"</note>, that is, "he was going out who was sowing," or "the sower." For participles of this kind adapt themselves to the verbs to which they are joined.

3 **To sow his seed]** "His seed" is neither in the Greek nor in the Golden Code <note>an ancient manuscript of the Gospels</note>.

4 **For that is correct,** and "while he sowed" in <note>original: "τω σπειρειν"</note>, that is, "during the sowing."

5 **And shortly after,** he has translated "height" for "depth" <note>original: "altitudinem pro profunditate"</note>.

6 **And,** <note>original: "εκαυματισθη"</note>, "they were scorched," for "they were burnt out" or "they perished from the heat."

7 **And again,** <note>original: "εξηρανθη"</note>, "they dried up," he translated as "they became parched."

8 **Likewise,** <note>original: "ανεβησαν"</note>, "they rose up," which elsewhere he translates as "they ascended." More softly "they grew up," or "they increased," or "the thorns emerged."

9 **And they gave fruit]** Here the Translator preferred to consult Latinity rather than to render the Greek words. Otherwise, it should have been translated word-for-word thus: "And they gave fruit, this one indeed a hundred, that one sixty, that one thirty." <note>original: "καὶ εδιδου καρπὸν, ὃ μὲν εκατὸν, ὃ δὲ εξήκοντα, ὃ δὲ τριάκοντα"</note>. Although it could be translated: "this one indeed a hundredfold, that one sixtyfold, another thirtyfold." Or, "one hundred-bearing, another sixty-bearing, another thirty-bearing," as one might understand "grains." For the Greeks lack distributives of this kind. He has misused the post-positive articles in this place in stead of pre-positives, which nevertheless often happens elsewhere.

10 **To you it is given to know the mysteries]** <note>original: "μυστήρια"</note>, that is, "the secret," although it is mostly used for sacred things.

11 **That it might be fulfilled in them]** Some manuscripts had <note>original: "καὶ αναπληρωθειται εν αὐτοῖς"</note>, "and it is fulfilled." Thus Saint Chrysostom reads: and I found it written so in the Corfendoncensian copy. Furthermore, "in them" was not held in most Greek copies, nor in the older Latin ones: but "to them" only. Nor is it "of the one saying," but <note>original: "λέγων"</note>, that is, "saying." Both the Golden Code and the Donatianic ones agree, or "which says." For he makes the Scripture itself the speaker.

12 **By hearing you shall hear]** The testimony which he brings forward is found in Isaiah, chapter six. However, the Hebrew truth differs in this place also from the Septuagint Edition. For the Septuagint hands down this passage as if God had predicted it would happen that those hearing would not 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> 3 ...many things in parables, saying, Behold ^2 the sower went out ^3 to sow, ^4 And when he sowed, ^4 some indeed fell by the way side, and the birds came and devoured them. Others truly fell ^5 on rocky places, where they did not have much earth, and immediately they sprang up, because they did not have 
5 depth of earth: But when the ^6 sun had risen, ^6 they were scorched: and because they did not have a root, 
7 they withered. Others again fell among thorns, and the thorns rose up, and ^7 choked them. Others ^8 truly fell on good ground, ^9 and gave fruit: one indeed a hundredfold, another truly 
<margin>B</margin> sixtyfold, another truly thirtyfold. He who ^9 has ears to hear, let him hear. And the disciples approaching ^10 said to him, Why do you speak to them in parables? But he answering said to them, ^10 To you it is given ^11 to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it is not given. For whoever has, it shall be given to him, and ^12 he shall have more abundance: but whoever has not, even that which he has shall be taken from him. Therefore ^13 I speak to them in parables: because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear nor understand. ^11 And the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled in them, which says, ^12 ^14 By hearing you shall hear, and shall not understand: and seeing you shall see, and shall not perceive. For the ^15 
<margin>C</margin> heart of this people is grown fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have closed their eyes, lest at any time they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them. But blessed are your ^16 eyes, because they see: and your ears, because they hear. For amen I say to you, that many prophets and ^17 righteous men have desired to see what you see, and have not seen, and to hear what you hear, and have not heard. 
You therefore hear the parable of the sower. When ^18 ^19 anyone hears the word of the kingdom, and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away that which was sown in the heart...

---

...hear, and those seeing would not see. But the Hebrew truth indicates this was commanded by the Lord, so that those seeing should not see, and those hearing should not hear. Luke cites according to the Septuagint—being more learned in Greek than in Hebrew—in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter twenty-eight: <note>original: "Πορεύθητι, καὶ εἰπὲ τῷ λαῷ τούτῳ... ἰάσωμαι αὐτούς." Erasmus quotes the Greek of Acts 28:26-27</note>. That is: "Go to this people, and say: With the ear you shall hear, and you shall not understand, and seeing you shall see, and you shall not perceive: For the heart of this people is hardened, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and they have shut their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn themselves, and I should heal them." On the other hand, Jerome rendered the Hebrew thus: "In hearing hear, and do not understand; and see in sight, and do not know. Blind the heart of this people, and make heavy their ears, and close their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and they understand with their heart, and be converted and healed." 

It appears, therefore, that the Septuagint deliberately changed the Hebrew Scripture, lest an occasion for blasphemy be given to the impious, as if God were for us the author of evils. But since there are many such places in the Divine Letters, like those: "God hardened the heart of Pharaoh," and "Let their table be a snare," etc., one ought not to be offended by this one, but rather recognize the idiom of divine speech, which by this figure threatens and terrifies the impious, as if commanding them to do that which they are going to do by their own malice: just as it was said to Judas, "What you do, do quickly." It is a wonder that, since Jerome says in more than one place that the Apostles were accustomed to cite testimonies of the Old Instrument <note>Old Testament</note> according to the Hebrew truth and not according to the Septuagint, Matthew does not do the same in this place—especially since he himself is believed to have written his Gospel in the Hebrew language. For he excuses Luke, I know not how conveniently, because he was more skilled in Greek letters than in Hebrew. Otherwise, it is most likely that Paul, a Hebrew, when dealing with Hebrews, would have brought forward the testimony of Isaiah according to the Hebrew truth. This excuse will not be admitted, I think, by those who want everything in the Apostles to be a peculiar gift of the Divine Spirit, especially the gift of tongues. And Jerome testifies that the Epistle to the Hebrews was not received by some for this reason—I think because it brings forward testimonies of the Old Instrument which are not held in the volumes of the Hebrews. Because when explaining this very place, he makes no mention of this matter, as if concealing, I think, what could not be explained. Unless perhaps those whom this very thing offended (which offended the Septuagint) changed this place, especially since it is so brought forward in the Acts of the Apostles. And we frequently find a passage changed from another passage: while the reader either thinks that which he remembers reading elsewhere is better, or suspects that what is different is corrupted. Furthermore, as to what Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a humanist scholar</note> thinks should be read—"you shall hear and not understand, you shall see and not perceive"—so that it is the voice of one cursing, not one paying attention to man: because it is found that these words are frequently used for the future, certainly among the Evangelists, especially with the double negation added, <note>original: "οὐ μὴ," a strong "not ever"</note>.

<margin>13</margin> *He who was sown by the way*] <term>ho spareis</term> <note>original Greek: "the one having been sown"</note>. The seed is sown, and the earth is sown. Just as moisture is sprinkled, and a garment is sprinkled with moisture. Thus he says here that the man is sown, just as we say the "earth is planted" and the "field is sown." Although he could have avoided this harshness of speech if he had said, *that person into whom the seed fell by the way*.

<margin>14</margin> *This is he who hears the word of God*] The word "God" is not added among the Greeks, nor in the Golden Codex, nor in the Donatian manuscripts, but the added article, <term>ton logon</term> <note>the word</note>, indicates which word he is speaking about. For the time being, we should not overlook that "word" is used in place of "speech" or "discourse."

<margin>15</margin> *But he is temporary*] <term>alla proskairos</term> <note>but for a time</note>. Expressed more clearly in Greek, as if you were to say, "for a season," and not perpetual, nor constant in himself, but changeable according to the occasion that arises. And soon after,

<margin>16</margin> *And the deceitfulness of riches*] <term>hē apatē tou ploutou</term> <note>the deception of wealth</note>. The Greek voice indicates "deceitful riches," not because they deceive—that is, frustrate a man—but because they lead him off the path: for that is properly what <term>apataō</term> <note>to deceive or mislead</note> means. Indeed, <term>apatos</term> refers to a well-trodden path <note>meaning the deception leads one away from the true path</note>.

<margin>17</margin> *This is he who hears the word, etc.*] It is not simply "and <term>brings forth fruit</term>," but <term>hos dē</term> <note>who indeed</note>, that is, "who finally," so that you may understand that while all others are unfruitful, this one at last yields fruit. Furthermore, the Greek article, <term>ho men, ho de</term> <note>the one, the other</note>, can refer either to the word or to the man: because <term>logos</term> (word) is masculine in gender among the Greeks. Although that it should be referred to the "word" is argued by the fact that he previously attributed the same thing to the "sown" seed that he does here to the word: for the word is the seed.

<margin>18</margin> *One a hundredfold, another sixtyfold*] In Greek it is held as <term>hekaton, hexēkonta, triakonta</term> <note>one hundred, sixty, thirty</note>, and likewise in the Golden Codex. This is because, as I have said, that language lacks distributive names for numbers. For it means that from individual grains many others came forth: from this one a hundred, from another sixty, from another again thirty. It was not clear to me for a long time whether "hundredth" was found among reliable authors in place of "a hundredfold." However, Pliny seems to have used it in this sense in Book 5, Chapter 4: *Thus*, he says, *it is called an extraordinary fertility, when the earth returns interest to the farmers with a hundredfold crop*. Again in Book 18, Chapter 10: *The fields of Leontini in Sicily yield a hundredfold*. Furthermore, Jerome labors here, referring the hundredfold yield to virgins, the sixtyfold to widows and the continent, and the thirtyfold to the married; while others have assigned the first yield to martyrdom, the second to virgins, and the third to widows, leaving no place for honorable marriage. Augustine, in the ninth question of his *Questions on the Gospels*, gives the first place to martyrs, the second to widows, and the third to the married. Theophylact refers the hundredfold to the Anchorites <note>hermits</note>, as it appears, who have achieved perfect poverty and are devoted only to divine things; the sixtyfold to the Cenobites <note>monks living in community</note>, who still labor for their living; and the thirtyfold to the married. As for me, while I do not disapprove of this pious diligence and holy curiosity

in Divine Letters, I think it simpler to understand that Christ, for the sake of teaching, set the hundredfold for the highest, the thirtyfold for the lowest, and the sixtyfold for the middle: just as he did with the ten, five, and one talents. And I would certainly wish to be advised of this, so that no one’s opinion is prejudiced by us. In Luke, there is no mention of degrees; he mentions only a hundredfold fruit. Augustine, in the twenty-first book of *The City of God*, testifies that some have foolishly twisted this passage to say that the wicked are to be liberated from eternal punishment by the saints—some thirty, some sixty, some a hundred—in proportion to their merits. But since the prescribed number is certain, if we neglect to become better through this confidence, there is a danger that the number of saints will not <margin>E</margin> correspond to such a great multitude of evil-doers.

<margin>19</margin> *He sowed over*] <term>kai espeire</term> <note>and he sowed</note>, that is, he sowed. It appears that the Translator read <term>epespere</term> <note>he sowed upon/over</note>. And a little later,

<margin>20</margin> *When the blade had grown*] <term>hote de eblastēsen ho chortos</term> <note>when the grass/blade sprouted</note>, that is, when the blade had germinated or budded. For <term>chortos</term> is sometimes translated as "herb," sometimes "hay," and occasionally "grass." Likewise,

<margin>21</margin> *Do you wish that we go and gather*] <term>theleis oun apelthontes syllexōmen</term> <note>do you wish then that going out we should gather?</note>, "Do you wish therefore that we go and gather them?" And again,

<margin>22</margin> *Lest*] comes from <term>mēpote</term> <note>not ever/lest</note>, "perhaps," in place of "lest at any time."

<margin>23</margin> *Let both grow*] <term>aphete synauxanesthai amphotera</term> <note>let both grow together</note>, "let both grow together equally." Again,

<margin>24</margin> *For burning*] The Greek codices add <term>auta</term> <note>them</note>, that is, "to burn them": which is consistent with the old Latin copies; however, it was rightly omitted by the Translator.

<margin>25</margin> *Which indeed is less than all seeds*] Some raise a scruple here, thinking that the seed of the poppy and the rue are smaller <margin>F</margin> than the mustard seed, as if the poppy seed were always and everywhere of the same size. It is enough that what the Lord says is true in a general sense. Indeed, it should be considered that here the mustard seed is not simply compared with any seeds whatever—otherwise the tall cypress tree would win, whose seed is so small it escapes the sight—but with the seeds of garden herbs, <term>lachanōn</term> <note>vegetables/herbs</note>. Now, the poppy is not counted among garden herbs, nor is the rue, because both herbs have use in medicine rather than in the kitchen. For as for <term>mikroteron</term> <note>smaller</note>, which the Translator rendered as "minimum" (smallest), he did so rightly. But why did he not do the same for "is greater than all," to say "is the greatest of all"? And soon after,

<margin>26</margin> *And they dwelt*] <term>kai kataskēnoun</term> <note>and to nest/dwell</note>, that is, "they nest." Since <term>kataskēnōsis</term> also translates as "nests." Again,

<margin>27</margin> *Which having been taken*] <term>ho labousa</term> <note>which [the woman] having taken</note>. He rightly changed the gender of the word: provided we understand that the woman herself took the leaven.

<margin>28</margin> *In three measures of flour*] <term>sata tria</term> <note>three seahs</note>. "Sata" is not a participle here from the verb "to bear," but is a Hebrew or certainly a Syrian word, signifying a type of measure which holds a modius and a half <note>about 1.5 pecks or 13 liters</note>, according to the custom of the province.

31 And immediately Jesus, stretching out his hand, took hold of him and said to him, “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” 32 And when they got into the boat, the wind ceased. <margin>44 6</margin> 33 Then those in the boat came and worshiped him, saying, <margin>44 7</margin> “Truly you are the Son of God.” 34 And having crossed over, they came to the land of Gennesaret. 35 And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent word into all that surrounding region and brought to him all who were sick. 36 And they begged him that they might only touch the edge of his garment; and as many as touched it were made well. ### XV.

<margin>44 8</margin> 1 —to Jesus scribes and Pharisees from Jerusalem, saying: 2 “Why do your disciples transgress the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread.” 3 But he answered and said to them: “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God because of your tradition? 4 For God commanded, saying: ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and ‘He who speaks evil of father or mother, let him die the death.’ 5 But you say: ‘Whoever says to his father or mother, “Whatever profit you might have received from me is a gift devoted to God,” 6 he need not honor his father or his mother.’ And you have nullified the commandment of God because of your tradition. 7 You hypocrites! Well did Isaiah prophesy about you, saying: 8 ‘This people draws near to me with their mouth and honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. 9 But in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.’” 10 And having called the crowd to him, he said to them: “Hear and understand. 11 It is not what enters into the mouth that defiles a man; but what comes out of the mouth, this defiles a man.” <margin>187 7</margin> 12 Then his disciples came and said to him: “Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?” 13 But he answered and said: “Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be uprooted. <margin>182 8</margin> 14 Let them alone; they are blind leaders of the blind. And if the blind leads the blind, both will fall into a pit.” 15 And Peter answered and said to him: “Explain this parable to us.” 16 And Jesus said: “Are you also still without understanding? 17 Do you not yet perceive that whatever enters into the mouth goes into the stomach and is cast out into the sewer? 18 But those things which proceed out of the mouth come from the heart, <margin>otherwise 'murders'</margin> 19 and they defile the man. For out of the—

---

...of Palestine, according to Jerome. Of this kind are also those terms, *cabus* and *batus* <note>Hebrew measures of capacity: the Kab and the Bat</note>. In the eighteenth chapter of Genesis, what is read in Hebrew as *qemaḥ se'im* <note>three seahs of flour</note>, our edition has as *sata* <note>original Latin: sata, from the Greek 'saton'</note>, which is the same name it elsewhere translates as "measures." And so Saint Hilary also reads in this place: *She hid it in three measures of flour*. Although this word "measure" is common to both the Hebrews and the Latins, just like *nugas* <note>trifles</note> and several others, as Jerome testifies in the commentaries he published on Isaiah. Furthermore, he added "three" to show the vast quantity of flour, all of which is nevertheless affected by a little leaven. And Chrysostom thinks "three" is put for "many." Jerome refers it more to the mystery of the Trinity, delighting in the number of the philosophers.

<margin>A</margin> 29 **I will open my mouth in parables**] Saint Jerome warns in this place that in most manuscripts it was written, *through Isaiah the Prophet*. Then, since this could nowhere be found in Isaiah, the name of the Prophet was removed by prudent men. However, he conjectures that it was first written by the Evangelist, *not Isaiah, but Asaph*: then it happened that a scribe, not recognizing the name *Asaph* and thinking the word had been introduced by a copyist's error, changed *Asaph* into *Isaiah*, as a name that was both better known and frequently cited by Matthew. For the seventy-sixth Psalm <note>Psalm 78 in modern numbering</note>, from which this testimony is borrowed, is inscribed with the name *Asaph*. Moreover, not only David, but all others who wrote Psalms are called Prophets, lest we think this title applies only to the twelve <note>The Minor Prophets</note>. Although even here the Evangelist did not scrupulously care to render the Hebrew words exactly, being content to explain the meaning. For where the Seventy <note>The Septuagint</note> translated "I will speak" <note>original Greek: phthegxomai</note>, he here renders "I will pour out" <note>original Greek: ereuxomai, literally 'to belch' or 'to overflow'</note>: where they have "problems" <note>original Greek: problēmata</note>, or as we read, "propositions," he here has "hidden things" <note>original Greek: kekryummena</note>. For Jerome translates the Hebrew thus: *I will open my mouth in a parable, I will speak ancient enigmas*.

<margin>B</margin> 30 **From the foundation of the world**] <note>original Greek: katabolēs</note>, which takes its name from the verb meaning "to cast down" <note>original Greek: kataballō</note>, evidently because a foundation is cast at the bottom; as if you were to say, *from the founding of the world*, or *from the casting of the world's foundations*. And somewhat lower,

31 **Explain to us**] <note>original Greek: Phrason hēmin</note>, that is, *explain*. Although the most ancient manuscripts have "double-explain" <note>original Greek: diphrason</note>, not just "explain." Now, "double-explain" is altogether something more than simply "speak." In this place, it occurs to me to warn that some impostor or other has not only published his own mixed-up ideas under the name of Jerome, but has even interspersed his trifles in the middle of Jerome's commentaries; something he undoubtedly did in this Psalm which I just cited. He stole the matter from Jerome, but the silliness of the speech, the ridiculous reasonings <note>original Greek: dialogismoi</note>, the babbling <note>original Greek: battologia</note>, the solecisms, and other such "delights" of his will become evident, as we shall expose more clearly elsewhere.

32 **Children of the wicked**] <note>original Greek: hyioi tou ponērou</note>. I ask, who from these Latin words could perceive what the Greek means? For "wicked" <note>original Latin: nequam</note> is in the genitive case for the Greeks: and it seems to pertain to the devil, because of the added article *tou*: so that the ungodly are called *sons of the devil*; whom he also designates by this name in the prayer <note>The Lord's Prayer: "deliver us from the evil one"</note>. Unless you prefer "the evil" <note>original Greek: ponērou</note> to be taken as a neuter noun, so that you understand *sons of malice*.

33 **Which he who finds**] <note>original Greek: hon heurōn</note>. It is in the past tense, *who had found*.

34 **He hid**] Likewise in the past tense, <note>original Greek: ekrypse</note>. I knowingly and prudently pass over many tiny details, lest I be too troublesome to the reader.

35 **Good pearls**] <note>original Greek: kalas</note>. This signifies not only "good," but more frequently "beautiful." Indeed, in these things, beauty increases the price.

<margin>E</margin> 36 **A net cast**] He left the Greek word <note>sagena / dragnet</note> as it was, although he previously rendered it by its general class as "a casting net" <note>original Greek: amphiblēstron</note>. It is a type of net which Laurentius <note>Laurentius Valla, a humanist scholar</note> thinks is called a *verriculum* in Latin, named from "sweeping" <note>Latin: verrendo</note> the sea, because a huge one is drawn around with very long ropes: he would have translated *sagena* more correctly as "thrown" <note>Latin: jacta</note> rather than "sent" <note>Latin: missa</note>.

37 **From every kind**] "Of fish" is not added among the Greeks. It is simply, *from every kind* <note>original Greek: ek pantos genous</note>, even if "of fish" is understood. From the interpretation of Jerome and Chrysostom, it is not clear enough whether they added it or not. Certainly, in Origen it is not added, though he repeats this passage so many times during his narration. Next, "drawing together" <note>original Latin: contrahenti</note> was more correct for the Greek <note>original Greek: synagagousē</note> than "gathering together" <note>original Latin: congreganti</note>. And presently,

<margin>F</margin> 38 **Bringing out, or rather: sitting on the shore**, etc.] The Greek is somewhat different, <note>original Greek: anabibasantes epi ton aigialon, kathisantes synelexan ta kala eis aggeia</note>, that is, *when they had drawn it onto the shore, sitting down they gathered what was good into vessels*. For the word "their" is not added, not even in the golden manuscript. Even if in some copies it is found written, *and when they had sat down* <note>original Greek: kai kathisantes</note>, for it indicates that this is done at leisure. Nor is it "the good ones" (masculine), but absolutely "the good things" (neuter), referring back to the "kinds" of fish he mentioned before. For I do not think it necessary to mention here that other things are sometimes pulled up by nets—as happened to that character in Plautus <note>A Roman playwright</note> who, having cast his net, caught a traveling bag <note>Latin: Vidulum</note>. And presently,

39 **Bad**] <note>original Greek: sapra</note>, that is, "bad," which we indicated above sounds more like "rotten" or "spoiled."

40 **Have you understood these**] In the Greek, this speech is immediately preceded by *Jesus says to them*, <note>original Greek: Legei autois ho Iēsous</note>. And,

41 **Yes**] Again, it is *nai*, an adverb of confirmation. And a little after,

42 **Master of the house**] <note>original Greek: oikodespotēs</note>, that is, the lord of the house: so that we take it to mean not someone who has children, but one who has legal authority over his household. And presently,

<margin>D</margin> **43 Instructed in the kingdom of God]** This is not "educated" <note>original: πεπαιδευμενος</note>, but "having been discipled" <note>original: μαθητευθεις</note>, so that you may understand that a teacher is made from a disciple. For as no one rightly commands unless he has first obeyed a command himself, according to the proverb, so no one acts well as a master unless he has first acted as a good disciple. Nor is it "in the kingdom," but "to the kingdom" <note>original: εις την βασιλειαν</note>, so that you may understand a type of long instruction and institution. Origen, repeating these words so many times during his narration, constantly reads "kingdoms" <note>original: βασιλεια</note>, that is, instructed in the kingdoms themselves, so that the sense is the same: instructed for the kingdom and instructed into the kingdom, as if you were to say, prepared for the kingdom—that is, for spiritual doctrine—by a more basic doctrine. Again, regarding what follows as "powers" <note>original: εις δυναμεις</note>, of which we have already spoken often.

**44 The carpenter's son]** <note>original: τεκτονος</note>. Valla thinks that in Greek a *tekton* is a worker in wood: even though Suidas clearly indicates the word is common to both stonemasons and woodworkers. For it appears the word is derived from *teucho* <note>meaning to build or craft</note>. And when we were at Puteoli, we saw the names of *tektonon* <note>builders</note> inscribed on the very ancient stones of the Temple, surely the Greek voice in Latin letters, because that part of Italy once spoke Greek: which the ancient monuments indicate. Furthermore, in another Evangelist, Christ himself is called a carpenter, so it is consistent that he labored with his hands for some time. Moreover, the mother of Jesus is "Mariam" in this place, according to Hebrew speech.

<margin>E</margin> **45 And his brothers]** According to the custom of the Hebrews, he calls them "brothers," not those who had parents in common, but those who had a common stock and race: concerning which matter Jerome disputed both most learnedly and most copiously in his book against Helvidius. But I wonder in passing why the same man, narrating this place, wrote: "Do you wonder if they err regarding the brothers, when they err regarding the father?" For they truly erred regarding the father, thinking Jesus to be the son of Joseph, whom Mary had married. But who was erring regarding the brothers, unless perhaps those were relatives of Joseph, not Mary, so that their affinity had nothing to do with Christ; truly to the extent that his relatives could be called brothers of this one. Though in the same work in which he refutes Helvidius, Saint Jerome admits those were called brothers of Jesus in no other way than Jesus himself was called the son of Joseph. But if they were falsely believed to be brothers, just as Joseph was falsely believed to be the father, how does it stand that he wrote a little before that they were called brothers by kinship? But to examine these things to the quick is not the purpose of this work.

<margin>F</margin> **46 And Joseph]** <note>original: Ιωση</note>, that is, Joses, which some inflect as Jojetis. Whenever that name occurs, they corrupt it into Joseph. But Jerome, citing this place against Helvidius, reads Joses and Jojetis, not Joseph. Likewise,

**47 Without honor]** <note>original: ατιμος</note>, vile, or neglected, or despised. The opposite of which is "held in honor" <note>original: εντιμος</note>, dear, or held in value. For I have already warned quite often about "powers" <note>referring to miracles</note>.

**1 To his servants]** <note>original: παισιν αυτου</note>, that is, to his ministers or servants. Although the Greek word encompasses male servants, female servants, children, and finally all domestics, except the father of the family and mother of the family. And thereafter,

**2 The powers are at work]** <note>original: δυναμεις ενεργουσι</note>. It is not "they work" <note>original: εργαζονται</note>, which means they labor: but by this word a certain effective force is signified, as we have indicated elsewhere. For it is not the same verb as elsewhere: "My Father works even until now."

<margin>D</margin> <gloss>having seized</gloss> <note>original: κρατηϲαϲ</note> is more "he caught" than "he held" or "laid a hand upon." And in some copies it was held <gloss>in prison</gloss> <note>original: εν φυλακη</note>, while in others again <gloss>into prison</gloss> <note>original: ειϲ φυλακην</note>.

**4 Herodias]** This has the form of a patronymic, or certainly a diminutive name. Jerome reports that she was the daughter of King Aretas, though I do not know if it is the one Paul mentions. He had cast her off to Philip the Tetrarch of Iturea and Trachonitis. Later, after a grudge arose between himself and his son-in-law, the daughter was taken away from him and joined to Herod, the brother but an enemy, in order to burn him all the more. Moreover, this Herod is reported to be the son of Herod of Ascalon, the one under whom Christ fled to Egypt, and the brother of the one under whom he suffered. However, it is nearer the truth that it was the same Herod who beheaded John and under whom the Lord suffered. Much obscurity has been brought to the history by the ambition of certain Kings, who change names in places, and either wanted their memory to survive in posterity by their given name, which happened with the Ptolemies, or they usurped the names of famous Princes for themselves, or distinguished a successor by a small change, like Constans, Constantius, Constantinus.

**5 On his birthday]** <gloss>while birthdays were being conducted</gloss> <note>original: γενεϲιων δε αγομενων</note>, that is, "But when birthdays were being celebrated." And thus the translator of Chrysostom reads. And presently,

**5 The daughter danced]** <note>original: ωρχηϲατο</note>. She did not merely jump up, as the common people think, but as they gesticulate in choral dances. For that is what "to dance" properly sounds like to the Latins, and <gloss>to dance</gloss> <note>original: ορχειϲθαι</note> to the Greeks. And a little after,

**7 Had requested from him]** "From him" <note>Latin: ab eo</note>, besides being added barbarously and not being found in the Greek copies, should have been said "from himself" <note>Latin: ab ipso</note>. And again,

**8 Forewarned by her mother]** <note>original: προϐιϐαϲθειϲα</note>, that is, previously instructed: which they commonly call "informed."

**9 On a dish]** <note>original: εν πινακι</note>, which elsewhere he translates as "platter": even if in Greek it sounds more like a "table." Since food is placed on square tablets. For it appears this was done for the sake of mockery, as if this too were some mixed dish of that festive and birthday banquet. And a little after,

**10 And he sent]** <note>original: και πεμψαϲ</note>. He would have more conveniently supplied, "having sent an executioner" or "a servant": which he does elsewhere. Certainly Mark expressed what was to be understood here, <gloss>and the king, having sent a scout/executioner</gloss> <note>original: και αποϲτειλαϲ ο βαϲιλευϲ ϲπεκουλατορα</note>.

**11 Furthermore, what he translates here as "beheaded,"** is <note>original: απεκεφαλιϲε</note> in Greek, which word-for-word sounds like "decapitated." Although Seneca used the word "beheading" <note>decollanti</note> in his satire on the death of Claudius: but he could be seen to have used it for the sake of mockery, were the same word not found in Suetonius in *Caligula Caesar*. Indeed, in the same Seneca, in his book *On Anger* to Novatus. It should be noted why it said that those sent by Herod cut off John's head, yet presently adds that he himself cut it off. For he who commands, does.

**12 And she brought to her mother]** "she" <note>Latin: illa</note> was added for the sake of explanation, otherwise...

...otherwise it is found neither in the Greek nor in the older Latin codices; finally, it is neither in the "Golden" codex, nor in the Constantinopolitan one, and yet I <term>approve</term> of it being added. And again,
<margin>A 13</margin> *he was moved with compassion*] <note>original: "ἐσπλαγχνίσθη"</note>, regarding which we have already warned. And soon after,
14 *And he cured the weak*] <note>original: "ἐθεράπευσε τοὺς ἀῤῥώστους"</note>, that is, *he healed those who were unwell*, or those who were in <term>bad health</term>. For it is strange how much the Translator was delighted by this word <term>languor</term> <note>Latin: "languoris," implying a state of weakness or illness</note>.
15 *To pass over those minor things for now*, such as his translating "to be released" <note>original: "ἀπολυθῆναι"</note> as "to go away" instead of "to depart."
16 *Because "but he having said"*, that is, "but he said" <note>original: "ὁ δὲ εἰπὼν"</note>, he translates as *who said*; which he also does elsewhere.
17 *That he uses "crowd"* <note>original: "ὄχλους"</note> in the singular instead of "crowds" in the plural.
<margin>B 18</margin> *That "upon the grass"*, that is, *upon the herbs* or *the turf* <note>original: "ἐπὶ χόρτως"</note>, he translated as *upon the hay*, although he previously translated it as <term>herb</term>.

20 *For "having broken, he gave"*, that is, *he broke and gave* <note>original: "κλάσας ἔδωκε"</note>, is more tolerable; although it was clearer to say, *when he had broken it, he gave it*. Finally, that,
21 *The disciples gave to the crowds*] He added the verb "gave" on his own, which is neither added by the Greeks, nor found in the old codices of the Latins. Nor was there a need to add it.
22 *And they took up the remains*] The Greek text has it thus: <note>original: "καὶ ἦραν τὸ περισσεῦον τῶν κλασμάτων δώδεκα κοφίνους πλήρεις"</note>, and *they took up what had remained of the fragments, twelve full baskets*. Now, the <term>Cophinus</term> was a <term>type of measure</term> for the Ancients, on the authority of Julius Pollux; although here it clearly stands for *baskets*, which Luke calls <note>original: "σπυρίδας"</note>, that is, *small hand-baskets*.
23 *Now of those who ate, etc.*] <note>original: "οἱ ἐσθίοντες ἦσαν ἄνδρες ὡσεὶ πεντακισχίλιοι χωρὶς γυναικῶν καὶ παιδίων"</note>, that is, *now those who had eaten were about five thousand, besides women and children*. Truly, here it is merely an injury to the Latin style.
<margin>E</margin> 24 *Furthermore, that he used "ordered"* instead of <term>compelled</term>, whether that was done by the Translator or by a scribe, it is joined with an injury to the meaning. For in Greek it is more than <term>ordered</term>; it is <note>original: "ἠνάγκασεν"</note>, that is, *he forced* or *compelled*. Thus we may understand that they departed from their teacher unwillingly, whom they loved so much that they could not be away for even a moment of time. As Saint Jerome also noted, who reads <term>compelled</term>, not <term>ordered</term>. Theophylact noted the same. And Origen, older than all these, repeatedly iterates this word and even interprets it. Certainly, the "Golden" codex also has "compelled." The word <term>compelling</term> offends someone who is foolishly merciful...

<margin>A</margin> ...he departed from there in a boat to a deserted place apart. And when the crowds had heard of it, they followed him on foot, having left their cities. He truly <margin>18</margin> said, "Bring them here to me." <margin>B</margin> And having ordered the crowds <margin>19</margin> to recline upon the grass, and having taken the five loaves and the two fish, with his eyes raised to heaven, he gave a blessing; and when he had broken them, he gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. And they <margin>20</margin> all ate and were satisfied; and they took up what had remained of the fragments, twelve full baskets. <margin>21</margin> Now those who had eaten were about five thousand men, besides women and children.
