<margin>A</margin> *they went into it.* <note>Latin: "gressi illis"</note> For he speaks of Jesus and Peter entering the boat together. And soon after, the Greek text uses a word for a small boat <note>Greek: "αὐτοῖς αὐ" [likely referring to πλοιάριον]</note> rather than a ship, though the standard word is *ship* <note>Greek: "πλοῖον"</note>. Nor is it,
<margin>39</margin> *Into the land of Genezar*] But *Gennezareth.* Although it appears that among them both names refer to the same lake. For he perceived the region neighboring that lake. With great consensus, however, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father known for his preaching.</note> and Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century bishop and theologian.</note> read *Genezar*, supported by ancient manuscript verses. Furthermore, Jerome <note>The primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> writes on this passage in this manner: *If we knew what Gennezareth echoed in our own language, we would understand how Jesus, through the type of the Apostles and the ship, might lead the Church—freed from the shipwreck of persecutions—to the shore and make it rest in a most tranquil harbor.* These are Jerome's words. First, why does he call it "his language"? I do not think he means the language of the Syrians, among whom he was living at that time; if he were proficient in it, a Latin word would not have failed him to express the Syrian. Then, when he says, *if we knew*, he seems to admit the interpretation of that name is unknown. In the common collections of Hebrew names, we read that *Genezar* signifies *the beginning of the garden* or *the start of birth*, and that *Gennezareth* signifies nothing other than *Genezar*. Although I do not see what Jerome's words have to do with this interpretation.
<margin>40</margin> *When they had recognized*] <note>Greek: "ἐπιγνόντες"</note>, that is, when they had fully acknowledged. For it is common for many to have been there who had seen Jesus before; Jerome does not shrink from this opinion. And soon after,
<margin>41</margin> *of this kind*] <note>Greek: "αὐτῶν"</note>. Why is it not his intention to add *all*? Nor is it, *into the whole region*, but <note>Greek: "εἰς τὴν ὅλην περίχωρον"</note>, *into the whole surrounding neighboring region.* For that phrase,
<margin>42</margin> *That even the hem*] He translates elegantly, since in Greek it is <note>Greek: "κἀν μόνον ἅψωνται"</note>, that is, that they might at least touch. And what is *of the garment*, for the Greeks is *cloak*: which is sometimes translated as a mantle. For it signifies the outermost garment, just as "clothing" <note>Greek: "αἱ ἐσθῆται"</note> does.
<margin>D</margin> <margin>1</margin> *Then approached*] <note>Greek: "Τότε προσέρχονται"</note>, that is, Then they approach. And soon after,
<margin>2</margin> *Scribes from Jerusalem*] <note>Greek: "οἱ ἀπὸ Ἱεροσολύμων Γραμματεῖς"</note>. The Greek article implies it should have been translated as "the Scribes who had come from Jerusalem," or "the Jerusalemite Scribes." Chrysostom indicates the same in explaining this passage, for there were Scribes from other cities as well. Nor is it,
<margin>3</margin> *Traditions*] But *tradition* <note>Greek: "παράδοσιν"</note>, as the oldest Latin manuscript and even the one from Constantinople admit. We could translate it as *institutions* or *ordinance*. For they do not complain about all traditions, but about one only: namely, regarding the not washing of hands.
<margin>4</margin> *For God said*] In Greek it is <note>Greek: "ἐντείλατο λέγων"</note>, that is, he commanded saying. This responds to what preceded, "commandment" <note>Greek: "ἐντολὴν"</note>, or as I would prefer, "precept." Furthermore,
<margin>5</margin> *Honor*] In Greek it is <note>Greek: "τίμα"</note>, which means to hold in honor. But, according to the custom of Scriptural language, it pertains more to support <note>term: "subsidium" — financial or material aid</note> than to mere honor. For God commands that which is also provided for by the laws of the Gentiles: that children should help their parents when they are failing in age, laboring in poverty, or otherwise afflicted—and as the Greeks say, "to act like a stork" <note>Greek: "ἀντιπελαργῶσι" — an ancient belief that young storks cared for their parents</note>. Today, some who do not understand this almost worship their parents, and parents demand such honor from their children, thinking the duty of piety is thus abundantly fulfilled. Paul used the same mode of speech when writing to Timothy: *Honor widows who are truly widows.* And again: *The Elders are worthy of double honor.* Indeed, even among the Romans, *honor* is used for a reward or favor given for merit. And among the Greeks, the word for honor <note>Greek: "τιμὴ"</note> is derived from a word <note>Greek: "τιῦ"</note> which, whenever it is taken in a positive sense, means to pay out or discharge a debt.
<margin>6</margin> *Whatever gift there is*] <note>Greek: "δῶρον ὃ ἐὰν ἐξ ἐμοῦ ὠφεληθῇς"</note>, that is, whatever gift having proceeded from me you might be helped by. However, the sense of the words is somewhat obscure, which is why it is explained by everyone in many different ways. For some attribute these words to the son, who speaks thus to his father: "The gift which was to come from me into the *corban* <note>term: "Corban" — a Hebrew/Syriac term for an offering dedicated to God</note>—for Mark used the Syrian word—that is, into the treasu-"

### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>B</margin> <margin>1</margin> Then there approach Jesus Scribes and Pharisees who had come from Jerusalem, saying,
<margin>2</margin> "Why do your disciples transgress the tradition of the Elders? for they do not wash their hands when they eat bread."
<margin>3</margin> But he answering said to them, "Why do you also transgress the precept of God because of your tradition?
<margin>4</margin> For God commanded, saying: 'Honor your father and mother,' and 'He who curses father or mother, let him die the death.'
<margin>5</margin> But you say: 'Whoever shall say to father or mother: Whatever gift was to proceed from me is turned to your advantage,'
<margin>6</margin> and he shall not honor his father or his mother. And you have made the precept of God void because of your tradition.
<margin>7</margin> <margin>C</margin> Hypocrites, rightly did Isaiah prophesy of you, saying,
<margin>8</margin> "This people approaches me..."

---

<margin>C</margin> ...-ry <note>Continuing from "treasury" across the column break</note> of the Temple, that whole amount is consumed for your uses, and is spent on helping you, surely defrauding the Temple." And so, under the pretext of piety, they were violating piety: first by deserting parents, as if for the sake of God; then they were mocking God, not sacrificing what they pretended was sacrificed, as Chrysostom says. For example, if a father asked for a sheep or something similar from his son, so that a pretext for refusal would not be lacking, the son would pretend that sheep was destined for the Temple. And the Scribes wanted it to seem a sin to bring to private uses what had been dedicated to the Temple: as if God were being defrauded of his right. And would that this disease of the Pharisees were absent from the customs of Christians! Everything is full of these kinds of traps. Anything that is kept for the luxury of Priests and Monks, or for the plunder of some Prince, is called "the property of Christ or Mary." It is considered sacrilege to help the needy from these funds. By these snares, wills are transferred to nourish the idleness and luxury of certain people professing religion by title and dress, while their duties and children are defrauded and excluded: as if whatever is given to children or relatives is somehow being delivered to the Devil. Furthermore, he said to the Pharisees, *But you say*, not because these are their words, but because they themselves taught children to speak to a father in this manner: so that parents, while abstaining from these things which seemed destined for the Temple out of fear of sacrilege, might be finished off by poverty; and thus, what God had ordered to be spent on supporting parents turned into the profit of the Priests. Others refer this to the Pharisees who would terrify a debtor with such words when he was burdened by returning what he owed. For the Pharisees acted with such craft that if anyone was a debtor from whom nothing could be extorted either due to poverty or power, the creditor would consecrate that money as *corban*. Then the right of demanding it passed to those who terrified the debtor in this way: "Do you keep for yourself money dedicated to God, and consume for profane uses what is consecrated to the Temple?" And so the creditor was defrauded of his money. But I do not see what these things have to do with honoring parents, even though Jerome and Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine biblical commentator.</note> also mention this sense. It is more to the point that a son says, "whatever I dedicate to the Temple is spent on my father," namely on God, and thus leaves his mocked father destitute. For this is how they interpreted the Divine Law, which provided that parents laboring under disease, age, or poverty should not lack support, *Honor your father and mother, honor the father*, that is, God the father of all, and the Synagogue the mother. For Chrysostom also rejects that interpretation—if the translator does not deceive us (since he has supplied the Greek manuscript thus far)—whereby he says to his father, "I owe you no honor, but only if something is spent on the house." Since this does not pertain to the Pharisees, under what title the son performs his duty to the father. The obscurity of the passage was the reason why translators guessed one thing after another. However, what Aurelius Augustine brings forward in the first book of *Questions on the Gospels*, sixteenth question—that by these words adult sons deny they are grateful for the gifts parents offer for them, after they have reached an age where they can offer gifts for themselves—whether that fits the sense of the Gospel, I leave for others to weigh. It certainly does not greatly please me. But Origen explains this passage somewhat more clearly in a fragment which we have translated. Furthermore, in the phrase *that by which from me* <note>Greek: "ὃ ἐὰν ἐξ ἐμοῦ"</note>, something must absolutely be understood, so that from the inner force of the Greek article, one is free to supply what is appropriate to the meaning—*is*, or *shall be*, or something similar. Then, *you might be helped* <note>Greek: "ὠφεληθῇς"</note>, it seems it should rather be read as *you might help* <note>Greek: "ὠφελήσῃ"</note>. "Thus you are helped by every gift which I was going to give to the Temple." Since Christ mentions this as an example of the insult by which children, taught by the Pharisees, treat their parents, unless the conjunction *that* <note>Greek: "ἵνα"</note> is also referred to the verb *you might be helped*, so that it is taken in a sense of giving, that is, you shall have helped or you will be able to be helped. Then, <margin>F</margin> the word *he shall honor* <note>Greek: "τιμήσῃ"</note>, if written with an *eta*, sounds as *he shall honor*; if with an *ei*, *he will honor*. Our common Translation <note>The Vulgate</note> neither matches the Greek well enough, nor explains any clear meaning. Therefore, as far as was permitted in such a variety of opinions, following what we judged best, we translated in this way: *Whatever gift was to proceed from me is turned to your advantage*, and *he shall not honor his father, or...*

...his mother, namely a son so instructed by you. And yet, 
whatever the sense will be, the composition of the speech is quite harsh, because for 
these particles—"whoever shall say to his father and mother"—there is 
no answer unless one understands "he does well," or something similar, which 
no one has pointed out except the *Gloss* <note>The Glossa Ordinaria, a standard medieval biblical commentary</note> cited by the *Catena Aurea* <note>A commentary on the Gospels compiled by Thomas Aquinas</note>. 
It is strange that Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a prominent medieval exegete</note> writes on this place as if he had not 
read any of the ancient Interpreters. For it is not worth 
addressing what someone argued in one place against Lyranus,

7 **Honors me with their lips**] In the Greek, there are a few more words: 
*This people draws near to me with their mouth, and honors me with their lips*, <note>original: "Ἐγγίζει μοι ὁ λαὸς οὗτος τῷ στόματι αὐτῶν, καὶ τοῖς χείλεσί με τιμᾷ"</note>. 
Truly, someone added a little who wanted to make the 
prophet's testimony complete, whereas Jerome, explaining 
this passage of the Prophet, indicates that the Evangelist plucked 
what was convenient for him, and did not report it entirely 
as it is written in Hebrew, nor as it was translated by the Septuagint. 
The passage is in Isaiah, chapter twenty-nine. Jerome renders the 
Hebrew thus: *Because this people draws near with its mouth, 
8 and glorifies me with its lips: but its heart is far from me, and 
they have feared me by the mandate and doctrines of men.* The Septuagint 
translated it in this way: *This people draws near to me in their mouth, 
and they honor me with their lips; but their heart is far 
from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching the 
precepts and doctrines of men.* <note>original: "Ἐγγίζει μοι ὁ λαὸς οὗτος... διδασκαλίας"</note> Therefore, the matter itself 
indicates that this testimony is not read by the Greeks as it was 
brought in by the Evangelist, but as it was left by some studious person: 
who, when he had found the place in the Prophet, thinking it was mutilated, 
filled it in—and that not from the Hebrew books, which he did not know, but 
from the Septuagint Edition, which the Greeks follow. Furthermore, 
what in this place the Interpreter (I know not who) translates as,

8 **Without cause**] In Greek it is *matēn*, <note>original: "μάτην"</note> that is, "in vain," or "without fruit," 
rather than "without cause." And so it is read in the Septuagint translation. 
Finally, "is far" is *apechei* <note>original: "ἀπέχει"</note> in Greek, which means "is absent." 
Nor is it,

9 **Doctrines & mandates of men**] For among the Greeks in this 
place, no conjunction is added. Rather, *doctrines, mandates 
of men*, <note>original: "διδασκαλίας, ἐντάλματα ἀνθρώπων"</note> so that they are read appositively as "doctrines which 
are the mandates of men," not of God. And 
I have found this in those most ancient Latin copies which 
I have already cited in several places; lastly, in the Golden Code and in 
the copy which was at hand when we were preparing this fourth 
edition, the Constance manuscript. And the Hebrew agrees: 
*commandments of men taught [by rote]*, <note>original: "מצות אנשים מלומדה" (mitzvot anashim melumada)</note> which word-for-word 
may be rendered as "the mandates of men [are] doctrines." Nor is it so much 
"they worship" as "they revere," *sebontas*, <note>original: "sebontas"</note> which comes even 
closer to the Hebrew truth, *tarihi*.

10 **Calling the crowds**] *proskalesamenos ton ochlon*, <note>original: "προσκαλεσάμενος τὸν ὄχλον"</note> that is, having 
called, or summoned the crowd to himself. He almost 
always translates it this way. However,

11 **Defiles**] In Greek it is *koinoi*, <note>original: "κοινοῖ"</note> that is, "makes common": 
or, as Augustine reads in his sixteenth book against Faustus, 
chapter thirty-one, "communicates." For the Jews call 
<margin>D</margin> that which is not holy and pure "common," which the Latins call 
profane, impure, or unspeakable. For pure things are called holy and 
not at all profane. Whence we translate, "they make impure." 
And shortly after, "it makes the man impure." Origen noted this, 
or rather Origen's interpreter, explaining the fourteenth chapter 
of the Epistle to the Romans, indicating that in some Latin 
copies it was written "they communicate," and in some "they defile."

12 **But what proceeds**] The interpreter lost the grace of the *prosopopoeia* 
<note>Giving a voice to something inanimate</note> and likewise the *enantiōsis* <note>Rhetorical contrast</note> in these words: *that which enters* and *that which goes out*. <note>original: "τὸ εἰσερχόμενον" and "τὸ ἐξερχόμενον"</note> And a little later,

13 **You know that**] <note>original: "Οἶδας ὅτι"</note> that is, "You know," and because it should have been 
translated as "that": or certainly the sense should have been rendered 
by an infinitive verb. In addition, for *having heard this word*, <note>original: "ἀκούσαντες τὸν λόγον τοῦτον"</note> it would have 
been better to translate "speech": since the Greek word signifies "speech" 
more than "word," or certainly a "saying." Not to mention that "scandalized" 
was put for "offended."

<margin>E</margin> 14 **They are blind leaders of the blind**] The Greek speech is more festive: 
*guides are they, blind ones of the blind*, <note>original: "ὁδηγοί εἰσι τυφλοὶ τυφλῶν"</note>. For 
*hodēgoi* <note>original: "ὁδηγοὶ"</note> is properly said of those who show the way, from *hodos* "way," and 
*agō* "I lead," or *hēgeomai* "I go before." And soon,

15 **Explain**] <note>original: "Φράσον"</note> "Declare" or "Set forth," about which we advised 
above, although it is not disapproved by me. Nor is it,

16 **You do not understand**] But *oupō*, <note>original: "οὕτω" (likely intended "οὔπω")</note> that is, "not yet," as it responds 
to *akmēn*, <note>original: "ἀκμὴν"</note> that is, "even now," which however is something 
more vehement than "still" (*eti*).

17 **Evil thoughts, murders**] In some Greek copies, 
it was written *phthonoi*, <note>original: "φθόνοι"</note> that is, "envies." And indeed 
the Aldine edition <note>A famous early printed Greek Bible from Venice</note> has it so. The word *phonoi*, <note>original: "φόνοι"</note> that is, "slaughters" 
or "murders," is very similar to this. It is not clear from 
Chrysostom nor Jerome what they read.

18 **Badly tormented**] *kakōs daimonizetai*, <note>original: "κακῶς δαιμονίζεται"</note> that is, "miserably." 
Although "badly" is also used by Latins for "miserably." And again,

<margin>F</margin> 19 **But he**] <note>original: "Ὁ δὲ"</note> that is, "But he said," he translates as "who says," as if 
affecting dissonance, though that is not of great importance. Likewise,

20 **Did not answer him a word**] *logon*. <note>original: "λόγον"</note> Again, why "word" 
rather than "speech"? For the sense is, "he did not answer him anything." 
For it is not the same trope in the Greek speech as it is in the 
Latin: just as we say, "he did not write back a letter," for 
"he wrote back nothing at all." Furthermore,

21 **They were asking**] <note>original: "Ἠρώτων"</note> that is, "they were questioning," a word he 
nevertheless seems to have misused sometimes for "I beg." For this word is 
ambiguous to the Latins. Likewise,

22 **Dismiss her**] *apolyson*, <note>original: "ἀπόλυσον"</note> that is, "release her": either so 
that having obtained what she came for, she may leave, or so that she is satisfied 
in some way. We translate "send away" (*amitte*) for "dismiss." 
For Terence used the verb "to send away" (*amittendi*) as an opposite to 
"to retain." For "to send away" is not always the same as "to lose."

23 **To the sheep which perished**] *ta apolōlota*, <note>original: "τὰ ἀπολωλότα"</note> that is, "the lost," 
as Jerome almost always translates. Furthermore, the article indicates that 
not all sheep are meant, but those which perished. And,

24 **Help**] *boēthei*, <note>original: "βοήθει"</note> more correctly "succor." For we help those who

<margin>F</margin> <insert>38 **Into the region of Magedan**] <note>original: "εἰς τὰ ὅρια Μαγδαλά"</note>, that is, into the borders of Magdala. Indeed, Jerome mentions Magdala in his description of places. However, in this passage he reads "Magedam" not "Magdalam," using these words: *Magedam, to whose borders Matthew the Evangelist wrote the Lord arrived, but Mark also records the same.* Now, however, the region is called Macera, opposite Jesura. Again, interpreting the Hebrew words in Matthew, he mentions Mageda. But "one witness," as they say, "is not believed, not even if it were Cato." Mark has Dalmanutha instead of Magedan, and they think the place had two names.</insert>

<margin>6 *Among themselves* <note>original: "Inter se"</note>] The Greek is "in themselves" <note>original: "ἐν ἑαυτοῖς"</note>, meaning between each other, or within themselves. The Golden Codex <note>A famous 9th-century manuscript</note> has "within themselves," so that you may understand a silent thought. For the Greek word "reasoning" <note>original: "διαλογίζονται"</note> is ambiguous, applying to both disputing and thinking. And shortly after, "among yourselves," that is, between you or within you.</margin>

<margin>7 *Of the five loaves, and five thousand* <note>original: "Quinque panum, & quinque millia"</note>] Why not rather "of the five thousand"? Although the accusative "loaves" was more convenient due to the crowd of genitives. Certain Latin codices had "of five loaves and of five thousand," some "of five loaves into five thousand," while the more corrected ones read with the Greek "of the five loaves of the five thousand," so that it is not an omission of a conjunction, but the loaves are said to belong to those who ate them. Or certainly, using the Greek genitive absolute, "there being five thousand." A similar variation exists in the next passage: "of seven loaves and four thousand," or "into four thousand"; the older ones had "of seven loaves of four thousand." Furthermore, the added article <note>Greek grammar often uses articles to point to specific previous mentions</note> causes us to understand specific loaves and specific men: "those five loaves" and "those five thousand." Perhaps the latter genitive could be translated absolutely: "when there were five thousand men." And a little after, "of the four thousand."</margin>

<margin>8 *Why do you not understand* <note>original: "Quare non intelligitis"</note>] The Greek is "How do you not perceive?" <note>original: "πῶς οὐ νοεῖτε"</note>, that is, "In what way do you not understand?", which is the tone of someone rebuking, meaning, "How does it happen that you do not understand?"</margin>

<margin>9 *Of Caesarea Philippi* <note>original: "Cæsareæ Philippi"</note>] The Greek is "Caesarea of Philip" <note>original: "Καισαρείας τῆς Φιλίππου"</note>. It was clearer to say "of that Caesarea which is named for Philip." Indeed, the added article distinguishes this Caesarea, which has the surname of Philip, from that which is called Caesarea without a surname. That is the one which Herod the Great, King of the Jews, restored in honor of Augustus Caesar, which was previously called the Tower of Strato. However, Caesarea Philippi is the one built by his son Philip, Tetrarch of Iturea and Trachonitis, in honor of Tiberius Caesar, which, with a changed name, was later called Paneas, in the province of Phoenicia at the roots of Lebanon, where the Jordan rises from two springs, "Jor" and "Dan," according to Jerome.</margin>

<margin>10 *Whom do men say* <note>original: "Quem dicunt homines"</note>] The Greek is "Whom do they say me to be?" <note>original: "Τίνα με λέγουσιν"</note>, and I found it written thus even in the oldest Latin codices, specifically in the Pauline copy. The oldest of all, Irenaeus (Book III, Chapter 11), added the pronoun, "Whom do they say me to be?" In some Greek copies, it was only "Whom do they say the Son of Man is?" Although Jerome in his Commentaries denies that Christ asked about himself arrogantly by saying "Whom do they say I am?", but rather "Whom do they say the Son of Man is?", even if it can be understood as an argument for modesty not in the omitted pronoun, but in the added phrase, "the Son of Man." It is not sufficiently clear from Origen or Chrysostom whether "me" was added. In Theophylact, it is clear that it was added.</margin>

<margin>11 *Son of man* <note>original: "Filius hominis"</note>] The Greek includes the article: "the Son of the man" <note>original: "τὸν Υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου"</note>. It expresses both articles, as neither is idle. For it signifies a certain son, and a certain man, namely Adam, who among the Hebrews is called "Adam" <note>original: "אדם"</note>, that is, "Man." Therefore, the commentary of those who think Christ is called the Son of Man because he was born only of a mother is frivolous, since here a masculine article is placed before "man." Likewise in what follows:</margin>

<margin>12 *You are the Christ* <note>original: "Tu es Christus"</note>] The Greek has the article <note>original: "ὁ Χριστὸς"</note>, meaning, "You are that Christ," and "You are that Son of God." Even to the participle "living" <note>original: "ζῶντος"</note> an article is added among the Greeks, and not without reason, which Origen suggests, citing the passage, "As I live, says the Lord." The Son, not of just any God (for the Gentiles also had their gods), but the Son of that God who alone has immortality, and who is the source and parent of all life. It is a minor matter that a little before, "Jesus says to them," the name Jesus was added, though it is absent in the Greek and the Golden Codex.</margin>

<margin>13 *Simon Bar-Jonah* <note>original: "Simon Barjona"</note>] It is strange why both translators preferred this in another language rather than Greek or Latin. For elsewhere he translates it, as in John chapter 1, "You are Simon son of John," and again in chapter 21, "Simon of John, do you love me more than these?" Unless perhaps he alluded to the mystery of revelation. For "Bar" <note>original: "Bar"</note> sounds like "son," and "Jona" <note>original: "יונה"</note> like "dove." With the element "n" <note>original: "נ"</note> added, it sounds like "John." Furthermore, "Jonah" is interpreted as "the grace of the Lord." Jerome thinks "Bar-Johanna" was corrupted into "Bar-Jonah."</margin>

<margin>D</margin> <margin>14 *Because you are* <note>original: "Quia tu es"</note>] The Greek is "that" <note>original: "ὅτι"</note>, not "because"; that is, "I tell you that you are Peter." Now "Petrus" among the Greeks signifies a rock <note>original: "πέτρορος"</note>: just as "Cephas" in the Syrian language (not Hebrew, as Jerome testifies) sounds like solidity. For he calls him a rock because he is solid in the confession of faith, and does not waver here and there with the lightness of common opinions. And "upon this rock," that is, this solid profession of faith, "I will build my Church," on which foundation if it stands, even the gates of hell will not be able to prevail against it, let alone men. Theophylact and Chrysostom (whom the *Golden Chain* cites) follow this opinion. Even if Saint Augustine, in a sermon on this passage, loosely fits the words "upon this rock" to Christ himself, not to Peter: "You are Peter," he says, "and upon this rock which you have confessed, upon this rock which you have recognized, saying: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God, I will build my Church," that is, "upon myself, the Son of the living God, I will build my Church. I will build you upon me, not me upon you." For men wishing to be built upon men said, "I am of Paul, I of Apollos, but I of Cephas" (who is Peter). And others who did not want to be built upon Peter, but upon the rock, said, "But I am of Christ." The same Augustine in his book of *Retractions* (Book 1, Chapter 21) reviews both opinions, yet is more inclined toward the one where Peter, by confessing Christ the Son of the living God, represents a type of the Church to which the keys are handed. However, he leaves the reader free to choose whichever they wish. Therefore, I wonder that there are those who twist this passage to the Roman Pontiff, to whom it undoubtedly applies primarily as the prince of the Christian faith. But not to him alone, but to all Christians, which Origen elegantly indicates in his first homily of those we have. But there are those for whom nothing is enough unless it is excessive. Thus some, even to the point of causing resentment, extol Francis with prodigious praises, whom it was more appropriate to imitate than to lift up immensely. For perhaps too much cannot be ascribed to the Virgin Mother of God and to Christ. Although here too I would wish all were as inflamed with the zeal of imitation as we see some are diligent in exaggerating praises. Saint Cyprian, in the third letter of his first book, seems to accept that the Church was founded upon Peter, saying, "Peter, however, upon whom the Church had been founded by the same Lord." Unless perhaps Cyprian is to be excused because he took Peter here not for that man, but for a type, which the following words almost indicate: "speaking one for all, and responding with the voice of the Church, he said, 'Lord, to whom shall we go?'" Similarly, those passages can be excused in which St. Jerome in his letters seems to say the Church of Christ was founded upon Peter. Therefore, Peter the "rock-man" represents the solid faith of the Church. Otherwise, our interpretation differs from the Augustinian one only in words, which we introduced because his seemed more strained, but toward which he preferred to turn rather than run into the other rock—namely, placing the foundation of the Church in a man.</margin>

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
<margin>C</margin> <margin>15 *Shall not prevail against it* <note>original: "Non prævalebunt adversus eam"</note>] Origen noted the ambiguity of this speech, because the pronoun "it" <note>original: "eam"</note> can refer either to the "rock" or the "Church." Truly, it matters little to the meaning. Furthermore, he used "the lower ones" <note>original: "inferi"</note> for "hell" <note>original: "inferno"</note>. Although even that is not quite proper Latin; in Greek it is "Hades" <note>original: "ἅδης"</note>, that is, Tartarus or Orcus. Lactantius, however, used it thus in a poem: 
> *The lower one shall open his hollow throat insatiably.*

# ACCORDING TO MATTHEW. CHAPTER [XVIII/XVII]

<margin>22</margin> I say to you, not up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.
<margin>123</margin> <margin>23</margin> Therefore, the kingdom of heaven is likened to a man who was a king, who wished to settle accounts with his servants.
<margin>24</margin> When he began to settle accounts, one was brought to him who owed
<margin>25</margin> ten thousand talents. But since he did not have the means to repay, his lord ordered him to be sold, along with his wife and children and all that he had, and payment to be made.
<margin>26</margin> So the servant fell down and prostrated himself before him, saying, "Lord, have patience with me, and I will repay you everything."
<margin>27</margin> Moved with compassion, the lord of that servant released him and forgave him the debt.
<margin>28</margin> But that servant went out and found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii; and seizing him, he began to choke him, saying, "Pay me what you owe."
<margin>29</margin> So his fellow servant fell at his feet and pleaded with him, saying, "Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything."
<margin>30</margin> But he would not; instead, he went and threw him into prison until he should pay what was owed.
<margin>31</margin> When his fellow servants saw what had happened, they were deeply grieved, and they went and explained to their lord all that had occurred.
<margin>32</margin> Then his lord, having summoned him, said to him, "You wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt because you pleaded with me.
<margin>33</margin> Should you not also have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had mercy on you?"
<margin>34</margin> And in anger, his lord handed him over to the torturers until he should pay all that was owed to him.
<margin>35</margin> So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts for their transgressions.
<margin>XIX. 1</margin> <margin>2</margin> And it happened when Jesus had finished these words, he departed from Galilee and came into the borders of Judea beyond the Jordan.
<margin>2</margin> And great crowds followed him, and he healed them there.
<margin>3</margin> And the Pharisees came to him, testing him...

---

**16 Will be bound and in heaven]** The conjunction "and" <note>Latin: *et*</note> is redundant; it is not added among the Greeks, nor in the ancient manuscripts. In the same way, *loosed in heaven* should be read instead of *loosed and in heaven*. And a little later.

**17 He commanded his disciples]** <unclear>diesteilato</unclear>. This word is translated as "distinguished" in the Psalms. It would be more correctly rendered as "he proclaimed" <note>Latin: *edicat*</note>. For from this, it seems the word "Edict" is derived, which is usually sent to all. And again.

**18 Because he himself was Jesus Christ]** The word "that" <note>Greek: ὅτι</note> should have been translated as "through which." And "Jesus" is not added, neither in the Greek manuscripts nor in our own corrected ones. Although in the Pauline text it was written *Jesus* <margin>D</margin> *Christ*, in another, it said that he himself was *Christ Jesus*. Origen, in his first Homily on Matthew, frequently brings up this passage according to our opinion: *Let us see then,* he says, *if he wanted those already doing the works of the Apostles to also preach that he was the Christ. And if he wanted it, it is worthy to ask why he now commands his disciples to tell no one that he is the Christ.* Likewise somewhat later: *Therefore the Savior, sending the Apostles, wanted them to tell no one openly that he was the Christ.* In the same way, he repeats this once and again in the following parts, distinguishing the time in which it was enough to preach Jesus, and the time in which the Christ <note>the Messiah</note> was to be preached. And it obstructs the meaning if you add "Jesus." For it was no great thing to be "Jesus," which was a man’s proper name, shared without doubt by six hundred people at that time; but to be the "Messiah" was a great thing. Otherwise, it would be as if you read, *that they should tell no one that they themselves were Jesus Christ*. For to prevent us from resorting to the excuse that it could be understood as "they should not tell anyone *that* Jesus was the Christ," we are blocked first by the pronoun "himself," and then by the very order of the speech. For no one speaks this way: "no one believes that was Plato a Christian," but rather, "no one believes that Plato was a Christian." Though this is certainly somewhat softer than what we read in this passage. I do not know whether "Jesus" is placed here not as a man's proper name, but as "Savior," so that we understand he forbade them from saying he was the "Savior Messiah." For I do not think "Jesus" or "Joshua" simply means "Savior" to the Hebrews, but is named from "salvation." And soon after.

**19 That it is necessary to go]** ὅτι, that he should depart, or *that he must go*.

**20 From the elders]** πρεσβυτέρων <note>presbyterōn</note>. I wonder if it would be more correct to leave the Greek word, *from the presbyters*, as he did before. Since this is a title of honor rather than <margin>E</margin> age. And a little lower.

**21 And taking him aside]** καὶ προσλαβόμενος, *and apprehending him*, essentially <unclear>epispasato</unclear> <note>drew him to himself</note>.

**22 to rebuke him]** The same word that he translates several times as "to threaten," namely <unclear>epetima</unclear>.

**23 Far be it from you, Lord]** Jerome noted that what is read by the Greeks is more significant: ἵλεώς σοί, Κύριε <note>hileōs soi, Kyrie</note>, that is, *Mercy to you, Lord*, as an expression of confidence or prayer. The translator shows that Origen read it this way in his first Homily on Matthew, and Chrysostom followed him in his fifty-fifth and eighty-third homilies. Theophylactus does not disagree. And the omission of the verb itself adds to the emotion of Peter, who vehemently detested what had been said. It is a way of speaking to show abomination, peculiar to the Hebrews. It seems to me "God be [merciful] to you" is better understood than "Be [merciful] to yourself," although Jerome thought so. Augustine, in the thirty-fourth Psalm, reads *Be merciful to yourself*, this shall not happen. Likewise in the Sermon on the words of the Lord from Matthew 17. Again in the book against Faustus, book 16, chapter 17. And soon after.

<column-break/>

# XVII.

<margin>16 A</margin> you bind on earth, will be bound in heaven: and whatever you loose on earth, will be loosed in heaven. <margin>17</margin> Then he commanded his disciples that they should tell no one <margin>18 20</margin> <margin>39</margin> that he himself was Jesus Christ. From that time, Jesus began <margin>21</margin> to show his disciples that it was necessary for him to go to Jerusalem, and to suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and to be killed, and on the third day be raised. <margin>21</margin> And when Peter had <margin>22</margin> led him aside, he began to rebuke him, saying, <margin>23</margin> "May you be spared, Lord; this shall by no means happen to you." But he, turning, said to Peter, <margin>24 23</margin> "Get behind me, Satan! <margin>B</margin> You are an obstacle to me: because you do not mind the things of God, but the things of men." Then Jesus said to his disciples, "If any man <margin>24</margin> <margin>B</margin> wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever wishes <margin>25</margin> to save his life will lose it; again, whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, <margin>26</margin> but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul? For it is to happen that <margin>27</margin> the Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each one according to his deeds. Amen I say to you, <margin>27</margin> there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the <margin>28</margin> Son of Man coming in his kingdom." <margin>XVII. 1</margin> And after <margin>C</margin> six days, Jesus takes Peter and James and John his brother, and leads them up into a high mountain apart. And he was transformed before <margin>2</margin> them: <margin>4</margin> and his face shone like the sun: his garments, however, became white as light.

---

**24 Go back, Satan]** Ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου Σατανᾶ, that is, *Depart behind my back, Satan*. <note>Hebrew: שָׂטָן</note> *Satan* means "adversary" to the Hebrews. Hence he calls Peter "Satan," not meaning the Devil, but because he was opposing the divine counsel with human affection. But he repels Peter now with almost the same words with which he previously repelled the tempting Devil. Origen indicated that "Go after me" is said to Peter here. However, in this same Matthew, chapter four, he says only "Go" <note>Greek: Ὕπαγε</note> to the Devil, and does not add "after me," which is proper for obedience following Christ. That applies to the Apostles, not to the Devil, as we also noted there, although this difference is not consistently observed in either the Greek or our Latin codices, perhaps through the negligence of scribes.

**25 You are a scandal to me]** It is remarkable how this Greek word *scandalum* also pleased Christians; it means to us an "obstacle" or "impediment," as Jerome also testifies in the Dialogue against the Pelagians. *Skalon* and *skandalon* are named from "ruin," because it is an occasion for falling if something blocks one's way, and for <unclear>the limping</unclear>, because a lame person bending over seems to tend toward ruin. He could have translated it, *you are an obstacle to me*, even though in Greek it is *emou* <note>of me</note> not *moi* <note>to me</note>.

**26 What exchange will a man give]** ἢ τί δώσει ἄνθρωπος ἀντάλλαγμα τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ; Here he calls *antallagma* that which is given to redeem something, according to the commerce of the ancients, which consisted not of money as it does today, but of the mutual exchange of things. Therefore the sense is that the loss of all things should be suffered sooner than the loss of life. If that had once perished, nothing is so dear that you could redeem it by exchange, whatever you abandon. Accordingly, we have translated, *or what will a man give by which he may redeem his soul?* Indeed, he calls "life" the "soul." Just as Horace says, *And Paul, prodigal of his great soul [life]:* and Origen certainly interprets it in this sense. For a comparison is taken from the life of the body, which is dearest to everyone, to the life of the soul, which ought to be much dearer.

**27 From those standing here]** Some Greek codices have τῶν ὧδε ἑστώτων, that is, *there are some among those who are here standing*, or *there are some of those present standing*. So that the article *tōn* refers to the adverb *hōde*, just as we say "those now" or "those of old." Origen, in his third Homily, philosophizes somewhat about "those standing," as if not everyone stood, but only those who were fixed upon Christ, and as if not everyone were going to see the kingdom of God.

**1 And after six days]** Regarding the number of days, Mark <margin>F</margin> agrees with Matthew, while Luke records that about eight days intervened. Chrysostom explains this by saying that Matthew and Mark counted only those days which passed in the middle between the speech being held and the mountain being reached; whereas Luke also included the two end points: namely, the day on which the previous speech was held, and the day on which they climbed the mountain.

**2 Jesus took]** παραλαμβάνει, that is, *he assumes* or *takes*, in the present tense. Likewise a little later.

**3 He led them]** ἀναφέρει αὐτοὺς, that is, *he leads them up*, or *he withdraws them*. And it is not.

**4 It shone]** but ἔλαμψεν, that is, *it flashed* or *shone*, not *annulavit* <note>an obscure technical or scribal point regarding Latin variants</note>. In addition, in all the Greek copies that I have seen, it was written "not."

**5 Like snow]** but ὡς τὸ φῶς, that is, *like light*, with even the Spanish Edition agreeing. Hence it could appear that "light" was changed to "snow" by a scribe's error, were it not for such great consensus among the Latin codices.

<columns>2</columns>
18 **It does not go out**] <note>original: "Non egreditur"</note> but the Greek says <term>ἐκπορεύεται</term> <note>ekporeuetai</note>, which means "it does not come out." The Translator <note>Erasmus refers to the author of the standard Vulgate Latin Bible as "the Translator."</note> seems to have read <term>ἐκβάλλεται</term> <note>ekballetai, meaning "is cast out"</note>; however, it makes little difference to the overall sense. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in prayer and fasting," <note>original: "in προσευχῇ καὶ νηστείᾳ"</note> which he translated as "by prayer and fasting," he rightly changed the Hebrew figure of speech. For the Hebrews use the letter <term>ב</term> <note>Beth</note>, meaning "in"—as in "in a strong hand" <note>original: "בְּיָד חֲזָקָה"</note> or "in the Lord" <note>original: "בַּיהוָה"</note>—to mean "through" or "by," as I have noted before.

19 **Those who receive the didrachma**] <note>original: "Qui didrachma accipiunt"</note> We err twice in this single word: first, because we write it with a 'g' when it should be written with 'ch' <note>referring to the spelling "didragma" vs "didrachma"</note>; and second, because we use a singular feminine form for a word that is actually neuter and plural. This word is read correctly in the "Golden Manuscript," as well as in the volumes of Donatianus and the Constance manuscript. In Greek, it is <term>τὰ δίδραχμα</term> <note>ta didrachma, the "two-drachma" coins</note>. Indeed, the text says "those who collect" <note>original: "ἀποδιδόντες"</note>; you should understand that they were accustomed to receiving it from individuals, and therefore he used the plural number. To the Greeks, a <term>δραχμὴ</term> <note>drachma</note> is a type of coin containing six obols, the hundredth part of an Attic mina. From this comes the name <term>didrachmum</term> for double a drachma, as well as <term>tridrachmum</term> (triple) and <term>tetradrachmum</term> (quadruple). Julius Pollux mentions all of these in his ninth book on vocabulary. And as for what follows immediately,

20 **Does he not pay the didrachma?**] <note>original: "Non solvis didrachma"</note> The verb "he pays" is in the present tense, <term>τελεῖ</term> <note>telei</note>. We should understand that the tax collector was not asking whether Jesus had *already* paid the tax, but whether he *was paying* it—that is, whether he owed it or was expected to pay it. Otherwise, Peter would have been lying when he replied <term>Ναὶ</term> <note>Nai</note>, that is, "Yes." As for the nonsense Nicholas of Lyra prattles about in this passage regarding the didrachma, citing Isidore and Papias—who could read it without laughing? <note>Erasmus frequently criticized Nicholas of Lyra, a 14th-century commentator, for relying on outdated medieval etymologies rather than Greek sources.</note>

<column-break/>

21 **Jesus anticipated him**] <note>original: "Prævenit illum Jesus"</note> <term>προέφθασεν αὐτόν</term> <note>proephthasen auton</note>, that is, he anticipated or spoke before him. It indicates that Peter was about to speak on the matter, but Jesus, not waiting for Peter's speech, spoke first. Nor is it,

22 **Tribute**] <note>original: "Tributum"</note> but "tributes," <term>τέλη</term> <note>tele</note>. For when he adds "the census," <note>original: "κῆνσον"</note> Matthew (or his Translator) used a Latin word, likely because this was a Roman administrative matter; foreign things or those brought from elsewhere often bring the vocabulary of their own nation with them. Furthermore,

23 **A stater**] <note>original: "Staterem"</note> Although this is also a measure of weight which the Hebrews call a <term>סֶלַע</term> <note>selah</note>, in this passage it surely signifies a coin that contained four drachmas. Since the "didrachma" (two-drachmas) was required from each person, Jesus ordered a stater to be given for two people: himself and Peter. From this event, a dispute soon arose among the disciples about who would hold the first place in the kingdom of heaven, because Peter seemed to be placed above the others by being paired with Christ. I thought it worth noting in passing—even if it does not strictly belong to this point—that I do not fully understand what Jerome means when he writes on this passage: *"Our Lord, according to the flesh and according to the spirit, was the son of a king, either born of the line of David or the Word of the Almighty Father. Therefore, as the son of Kings, he did not owe tribute; but he who had assumed the humility of the flesh had to fulfill all righteousness."* We are unfortunate, we who are called by the name of Christ and do nothing worthy of such majesty! He, out of exceptional love for us, both endured the cross and paid tributes; yet for his honor, we do not pay tributes, claiming we are exempt from taxes as if we were sons of the King. Indeed, Jerome seems to grant this arrogantly, as the clergy are reluctant to pay taxes to Princes, when today it is considered the highest piety to fight in every way for the immunity of the Clergy. Christ, while testifying that he did not owe it, paid anyway—not for all his followers, but only for himself and Peter—simultaneously refusing the obligation while complying with their greed. Perhaps he was teaching that one should not give what is not owed, and yet, where the situation demands it, a potential offense should be redeemed at some financial cost.

<columns>2</columns>
...offense. Jerome's words can also be taken this way: Christ, being so great, submitted himself for us, and we, who boast in Christ’s name and enjoy immunity from taxes, do not respond to his love for us. Augustine, in his twenty-third question on Matthew, concludes from this passage the immunity of Christians: *"Because he said, 'Therefore the children are free,' it is to be understood in every kingdom that the children are free, that is, they are not subject to taxes. Therefore, the children of that kingdom under which are all the kingdoms of the earth ought to be much more free in any earthly kingdom."* Thus far Augustine. If we accept this, no Christians should owe tax to their Princes, since all are children of that kingdom. Yet I do not know if, when the kingdom changed, the type of tax should have changed as well, and whether Augustine is discussing the tribute we owe to Christ the Prince.

1 **Who do you think**] <note>original: "Τὶς ἄρα μείζων"</note> The Translator used "Who do you think" <note>original: "putas"</note> in place of an explanatory conjunction. And <term>μείζων</term> <note>meizōn</note>, the comparative form, is clearly used here as a superlative, meaning "the greatest." Certainly, Saint Augustine reads it this way in the Homilies he published on Matthew. And soon,

2 **Calling a little one**] <note>original: "Advocans parvulum"</note> <term>προσκαλεσάμενος</term> <note>proskalesamenos</note>. The word "calling" has appeared so often now that I will not argue about the change in the participle's tense. Nor is it "a little one" <note>original: "parvulum"</note>, but <term>παιδίον</term> <note>paidion</note>, which is "a little boy," a diminutive of "boy." Although I am not unaware that this diminutive is sometimes used for a grown boy, in this place the diminutive was certainly not used pointlessly. It adds emphasis: he is not just inviting them to imitate any boy, but a very small boy. I do not see why the word "little boy" <note>original: "puellus"</note> seems too "soft" to some, since Prudentius did not fear to call Christ a "little lad" <note>original: "pusionem"</note>, and Jerome did not shrink from the word "little one" <note>original: "pusilli"</note>. Why would "little boy" <note>original: "puellus"</note> be obscene, while "little girl" <note>original: "puella"</note> is not? And again,

<column-break/>

3 **Like little ones**] <note>original: "Sicut parvuli"</note> <term>ὡς τὰ παιδία</term> <note>hōs ta paidia</note>, that is, "like little boys." And so the cited Saint Jerome translates it when explaining Isaiah. And again,

4 **Like this little one**] <note>original: "Sicut parvulus iste"</note> <term>ὡς τὸ παιδίον</term> <note>hōs to paidion</note>, that is, "as the little boy," or "tiny boy," for this is also found in approved Authors. It is surprising that the Translator, who usually strives for a variety of words, did not change "little one" <note>original: "parvulum"</note> here. Especially since the word "little one" does not quite capture Christ's meaning. For a "little one" could be someone of great age who is small in stature, like Dwarfs and Pygmies, who get their name from being only a cubit high. But here, he wanted to imply the innocence and simplicity with which the earliest age of childhood is endowed. However, certain words of this kind were accepted at that time. Nor does he add "this" <note>original: "iste"</note> in many Greek manuscripts, except that the article <term>τὸ</term> <note>to</note> achieves almost the same effect. He would have translated it more clearly this way: *"Unless one makes himself humble, as this little boy is—that is, as small as this boy is,"* and humbles himself to this child's measure. Furthermore, Jesus hints at <term>ταπεινοφροσύνην</term> <note>tapeinophrosynēn</note>, that is, modesty of mind, through the humility of the body, and signifies an elated mind through physical height.

5 **This is the greater in the kingdom**] <note>original: "Hic major est in regno"</note> <term>μείζων</term> <note>meizōn</note>, that is, "the greatest," as we indicated a little earlier. For there are those, including Origen, who think this refers to Christ himself: as nothing was humbler than him, so nothing is greater. The addition of the article <term>ὁ μείζων</term> <note>ho meizōn</note> does not seem pointless, as if to say "that greatest one": whoever approaches him more closely will be greater in the kingdom of heaven. Though anyway, the article indicates that "greatest" person about whom the Apostles were disputing.

6 **Of these little ones**] <note>original: "De pusillis istis"</note> <term>τῶν μικρῶν</term> <note>tōn mikrōn</note>. This is not the same word in Greek as was just used for "little ones" (<term>παιδίων</term>). And only in this place does Origen (or rather his Translator) read "tiny ones" or "little ones," while in the preceding parts he reads "boy." And a little later,

7 **A donkey-millstone**] <note>original: "Mola asinaria"</note> <term>μύλος ὀνικός</term> <note>mylos onikos</note>. It signifies a massive stone. Since...

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, the stone in a mill that is placed underneath to support the other that is turned around is called <term>ὄνος</term> <note>onos</note> by the Greeks, which means "donkey." From this comes the proverb, *A man is a donkey*, as we noted in the *Chiliades* <note>Erasmus's collection of Greek and Latin proverbs</note>. Yet it is not absurd, as Hilary followed, to take it as a "donkey-mill" <note>original: "mola asinaria"</note>, which a little donkey would turn. For lighter mills, which they call "hand-mills," are turned by human hands.

<margin>E</margin> However, heavier ones are driven in a circle by pack animals whose eyes are covered. Moreover, he expressed a type of punishment peculiar to the Palestinians, as Jerome indicates, which is usually demanded for enormous crimes. Therefore, from the atrocity of the punishment, he demonstrates the magnitude of the fault to a dull-witted people. Furthermore,

<margin>8</margin> *In the depth of the sea*] In Greek it is <term>εἰς τὸ πέλαγος τῆς θαλάσσης</term> <note>eis to pelagos tēs thalassēs</note>, that is, in the open sea, instead of saying in the middle of the sea. For usually, the further from the shore, the deeper it is. Since those who pass down Greek etymologies think *pelagus* <note>the sea</note> was so named because it is <term>πέλας τῆς γῆς</term> <note>pelas tēs gēs</note>, that is, "far from the land," as if it were *pelagur*. Therefore, he signifies certain destruction by two things: the size of the stone and the depth of the sea.

<margin>9</margin> *Woe to the man through whom*] Most Greek codices add <term>ἐκεῖνον</term> <note>ekeinon</note>, that is, "that" [man]. And,

<margin>10</margin> *Cut it off*] Some codices had <term>αὐτά</term> <note>auta</note>, that is, "them," so that it refers to both [hand and foot] which preceded. And,

<margin>11</margin> *Crippled*] This is <term>κυλλὸν</term> <note>kyllon</note>, of which we have already spoken. For it does not just mean weak in any way, but someone whose hand has been cut off or is otherwise mangled.

<margin>F</margin> And again,

<margin>12</margin> *With one eye*] In Greek the word is a compound, <term>μονόφθαλμον</term> <note>monophthalmon</note>, which could be called "one-eyed," or "squint-eyed," as it is translated elsewhere.

<margin>13</margin> *For the Son of Man came to save that which was lost*] In some Greek copies these words are not added, nor is there any mention of them in Jerome’s commentaries; even Origen does not touch upon this phrase. Conversely, they are found in some, such as in Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Hilary. And,

<margin>14</margin> *Which wandered*] In Greek it is <term>τὸ πλανώμενον</term> <note>to planōmenon</note>, that is, "the wandering one." Nor is it,

<margin>15</margin> *Because he rejoices*] But <term>ὅτι χαίρει</term> <note>hoti chairei</note>, that is, "that he rejoices," or "that he should rejoice." And a little later,

<margin>17</margin> *You will have gained*] But <term>ἐκέρδησας</term> <note>ekerdēsas</note>, that is, "you gained," or "you shall have gained." Since the use of this tense is specific.

<margin>18</margin> *But if he does not hear*] <term>Ἐὰν δὲ παρακούσῃ</term> <note>ean de parakousē</note>, that is, "but if he should neglect to hear," and the same word is repeated shortly after. Although in some it was "hear" in the first place and "neglect to hear" in the second. And soon after,

<margin>19</margin> *They shall be loosed also in heaven*] The Translator added the conjunction <note>"also"</note> on his own, as was indicated above. Moreover, in this matter Origen philosophizes wonderfully: that here it is said "in heaven" <note>singular</note>, whereas when the keys of the kingdom of heaven are delivered to Peter, whatever he looses or binds on earth is said to be loosed or bound "in the heavens" <note>plural</note>, not "in heaven."

<margin>20</margin> *And again I say to you*] <term>Πάλιν λέγω ὑμῖν</term> <note>palin legō hymin</note>, that is, "Again, truly I say." For he did not say the same thing twice, but it is the beginning of another parable. "Again" <note>original: "Rursus"</note> is ambiguous among the Latins, just as <term>πάλιν</term> <note>palin</note> is among the Greeks. But "again" <note>original: "iterum"</note> is not the same for us.

<margin>21</margin> *Up to seventy times seven*] <term>ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά</term> <note>heōs hebdomēkontakis hepta</note>, that is, "up to seventy times seven," for so the Greek can be rendered word for word, with "sins" or "faults" or something similar understood. Nor should the number be taken as only seventy-seven, but as four hundred and ninety: since seventy times seven makes this sum, according to the interpretation of Theophylact and also Jerome. For he placed a huge number for an infinite one, a figure of speech which Chrysostom clearly pointed out, as it is not probable that anyone would repeat an offense so many times. We speak in the same way when we say "bring in three hundred" for countless things, or "I have heard it a thousand times." Hilary seems to have been of the same opinion when he says: *How much more does he show it is necessary that forgiveness be rendered by us without measure or number*, etc. And yet seventy-seven is an infinite number. Moreover, the Lord alluded to the passage in the fourth chapter of Genesis: where God threatens a sevenfold punishment for whoever kills Cain. Lamech, however, says that whoever killed him would pay seventy-sevenfold. Which number the Hebrews think does not exceed seventy-seven. In the same place Origen, or certainly his translator in the same sixth homily, seems to take it simply as seventy-seven errors. A larger number fits well in forgiving, but not so in taking revenge.

<margin>22</margin> *To settle an account*] <term>συνᾶραι λόγον</term> <note>synarai logon</note>, that is, to compare, and at the same time to subtract, or to take up a calculation. For that is what "account" means in this place. This was done by moving pebbles <note>calculi</note>, or certainly by unfolding or folding the fingers. Whence Terence also spoke of "an account having been subtracted." For as to why,

—pass that when Jesus had finished these sayings, <margin>C</margin> he departed from Galilee and came into the borders of Judea across the Jordan. 2 And great crowds followed him, and he healed them there. 3 And the Pharisees came to him, testing him and saying to him, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any cause?” 4 He answered and said to them, “Have you not read that he—

---

<margin>D</margin> 23 **Ten thousand talents** <note>original: "Decem millia talenta"</note>] He said this instead of "of talents" (*talentorum*); it is merely a slight injury to Latin grammar while the sense remains intact. And soon after:
24 **He did not have the means to pay** <note>original: "Non haberet unde redderet"</note>] <note>original Greek: "μὴ ἔχοντος δὲ αὐτοῦ ἀποδοῦναι"</note>, that is, "since he was not able to pay." Indeed, the word *echo* ("to have") added to infinitive verbs often signifies "I am able." In Latin he would have said, "since he was not solvent." And a little after:
25 **He begged him saying** <note>original: "Rogabat eum dicens"</note>] The most ancient Latin codices had written "he prayed" (*orabat*). Most Greek texts have <note>original: "προσεκύνει"</note>, "he worshipped" (*adorabat*), used here to mean he acted as a suppliant. Suppliants were said to "worship" when they touched the knees or cheeks of the person they were begging, calling upon the divine power that protects suppliants. Some texts have <note>original: "παρεκάλει"</note>, that is, "he besought."
26 **And have patience** <note>original: "Et patientiam habe"</note>] In Greek <note>original: "καὶ μακροθύμησον"</note>, that is, "be long-suffering," or "be of a gentle mind," for which many read "magnanimous," and for "long-suffering" (*macrothymia*), they read "magnanimity." For by nature these are connected: to be of a "great mind" and a "gentle" one, since a desire for revenge proves a small mind.
27 **And he forgave the debt** <note>original: "Et debitum dimisit"</note>] <note>original Greek: "τὸ δάνειον ἀφῆκεν"</note>, that is, "he released the loan," or "remitted the debt." And a little after:
28 **And he choked him** <note>original: "Et suffocabat eum"</note>] It was clearer and more faithful to say, <note>original Greek: "κρατήσας αὐτὸν, ἔπνιγε"</note>, that is, "**having laid hands on him, he dragged him by a twisted neck**." For that is what "to seize" (*kratein*) and "to choke" (*pnigein*) mean in this place. The Evangelists use "to seize" elsewhere for "laying on a hand." Furthermore, what he adds, <margin>E</margin> "he choked," refers to someone dragging another by force, either to prison or to a judge. Likewise:
29 **They shall tell** <note>original: "Narrabunt"</note>] <note>original Greek: "διεσάφησαν"</note>, that is, "they indicated," or "opened up," or "betrayed." Again:
30 **Wicked servant** <note>original: "Serve nequam"</note>] <note>original Greek: "πονηρὲ"</note>, that is, "evil," or "villainous." Truly, I pass over many things of this sort knowing that I might be annoying to the reader with over-fussy diligence. And soon:
31 **I forgave you all that debt** <note>original: "Omnis debitum remisi tibi"</note>] <note>original Greek: "πᾶσαν τὴν ὀφειλὴν ἐκείνην ἀφῆκά"</note>, that is, "I released that whole debt." And subsequently:
32 **From your hearts** <note>original: "De cordibus vestris"</note>] Here the Greeks add <note>original: "τὰ παραπτώματα αὐτῶν"</note>, that is, "**their errors**," which I suspect was added for the sake of explanation, since it is not added in Jerome’s text. Even if it is added in Chrysostom and Theophylact.

<margin>F</margin> 1 **Is it lawful** <note>original: "Licet"</note>] For "is it not lawful," he spoke more in a Greek style than a Latin one. And <note>original: "ἀπολῦσαι"</note> means "to repudiate," or "to cast away."
2 **For any cause** <note>original: "Quacunque ex causa"</note>] <note>original Greek: "κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν"</note>, that is, "for whatever reason." Surely they felt there were some just causes for divorce, as Origen indicates. Indeed, Moses permitted so much right to husbands that the law seems unfair toward wives, who were allowed to depart from a husband for no reason, while husbands had the power to cast away wives for any slight foulness, merely with a written bill of repudiation. For so we read in Deuteronomy chapter 24: *If a man takes a wife and possesses her, and she finds no grace in his eyes because of some foulness, he shall write a bill of repudiation, and give it in her hand, and send her from his house. And when she has departed and married another husband, and he also hates her and gives her a bill of repudiation... the first husband cannot take her back as a wife.* Therefore the Pharisees test Christ: if he approved the Jews' licentious repudiations, he would seem to pronounce against natural equity, which was also favored

<column-break/>

by the Pagans, among whom there was a right of mutual divorce, though not for just any cause; if otherwise, he would seem insulting to the Mosaic Law. They thought it was permitted to them to cast away a wife for any cause as often as they pleased; Christ restricts this, excepting only a single cause, namely adultery. Someone—whoever it was whose 38 Homilies exist among the mixed titles of Chrysostom—noted this word "continually." Origen, explaining this passage, thinks that other crimes, either equal to adultery or even more serious, such as poisoning or parricide <note>The killing of a parent or close relative.</note>, dissolve a marriage. Augustine, in the cause of divorce, equates idolatry to adultery: because the worship of idols is a wretched adultery with foul spirits. But by this reasoning, every sin that alienates us from God would dissolve a marriage. I think adultery was excepted because it fights diametrically with the nature of marriage. Nor is the sacrament of marriage immediately abolished if, in a few cases where the couple were badly joined, they are well separated: certainly no more than by the adulteries that are now frequent everywhere, or the divorce which we have indulged for those who are badly matched. Although no one of the Ancients, as far as I know, brought up this reasoning regarding the sacrament, even though there is frequent and long dispute over these things, especially in Augustine and Jerome. Nor does a man immediately separate what God has joined; rather, what the devil joins badly through pimps and madams, through drunkenness, through folly and thoughtlessness, that God rightly separates through the authors and Ministers of the Church. And would that all marriages among Christians came together so that they ought rightly to be called begun with God as the author: or that we were all such that there was no need for any divorce: and there was no "hardness of heart" <note>original: "σκληροκαρδία"</note> among us, because of which it was formerly permitted to the Jews to cast away a wife. Augustine, writing to Pollentius, twists the exception only to the first part, making it a "clumsy argument" <note>original: "μακίαν"</note>: so that the exception only means that he who repudiates a wife is not free from the marriage, but only that he does not seem to make her an adulteress when he repudiates one who is already an adulteress. Furthermore, whoever marries her, whether she was repudiated for adultery or any other cause, commits adultery. Whether this commentary of Augustine agrees with truth and nature as much as it is clever, I leave to the learned to weigh. Certainly, this place is full of difficulties, such that the Doctors of the Church have not felt the same about it: since Ambrose, explaining the First Epistle to the Corinthians, grants the husband the right of repudiating, and Origen feels no differently. Hence we are forced to induce a certain other kind of divorce, which so dissolves domestic custom that the bond of marriage remains nonetheless. Indeed, this kind of divorce—or rather, merely the *name* of divorce—since it was invented by us, it is clear that the Jews (to whom this was entirely unknown) were not inquiring about this. Furthermore, what they everywhere babble in the Schools today, that marriage is contracted by consent alone, would that it were as well-proven as it is accepted. Nor do I demand that the Church diminish anything here from the ancient constitution of the Fathers, if that has never been done before. But if it is to be done in some other things, it is desirable that it be done here too, if it pertains to the salvation of men. If it cannot be done, certainly the wish proceeds from piety: and charity often wishes, not what *can* be done, but what it *wants* to be done. But concerning these things, as we touched on them somewhat before, they will be spoken of more copiously in the Pauline Epistles, 1 Corinthians 7. Although I would wish these things themselves to be accepted not as if I were asserting them, but as things I propose to the learned to be examined. And soon,

3 ***Male and female***] <note>original: "arrhen kai thēly"</note>, of the neuter gender among the Greeks.

4 ***And he said, For this cause a man shall leave***] It was uncertain whether God the Creator spoke this long ago, or whether Christ spoke these words and added the phrase, “for this cause a man shall leave father and mother.” Augustine, in his second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter four, takes it as if God had spoken: *Which nevertheless*, he says, *the Lord Jesus in the Gospel commemorates God as having said, because God certainly spoke through the man what the man predicted by prophesying*. Although in Genesis chapter two, from where these words are taken, they are reported in such a way that they could seem to have been spoken by Adam, or by the one who wove the history of the world’s creation, or by God himself. *Shall leave father and mother*, <note>original: "kai kataleipsei"</note>. He shall leave or rather desert, rather than dismiss: we “dismiss” one who is departing; we “desert” one whom we fail in a time of danger.

5 ***And shall cleave to his wife***] <note>original: "proskollēthēsetai"</note>, that is, he shall be glued to her. A metaphor taken from those things which are so joined with glue that you would think they were one. Chrysostom noted the emphasis of the word in Homily sixty-three. And presently,

6 ***Two in one flesh***] <note>original: "duo eis sarka mian"</note>, that is, into one flesh; this means, from two shall become one (masculine) or one (neuter): since “male and female” are neuter in Greek. Augustine noted this form of Hebrew speech in the seventh book of his work on this argument. Of this kind are also those words in the book of Judges, *And he shall be to us for a head to all the inhabitants of Gilead*. Likewise in the Psalms, *Be to me for a protecting God*. Not even the article seems redundant, <note>original: "kai esontai hoi duo"</note>, that is, those who were two shall be into one flesh. For he calls the whole man “flesh,” just as elsewhere Divine Scripture calls the whole man a “soul.” Saint Augustine also supports us in the fourteenth book of *The City of God*. Of this kind is also that passage of Paul to the Romans, *By the works of the law all flesh shall not be justified*. For what is “all flesh” but all men? And, *The Word was made flesh*, that is, the Divine Speech was made man. Furthermore, I have demonstrated from Jerome in our Scholia, with which we illustrated him, that it should be read "into flesh," not "in flesh," where he explains Matthew’s words thus: *He said into one, not into two*. And Cyprian, in the eighth letter of his second book, says, *They shall be two into one flesh*. And Tertullian, in his third book against Marcion: *And it was for the Ephesians what was proclaimed from the beginning concerning man, who would leave father and mother, and the two would be into one flesh, that is, into Christ and the Church*. Again in the book *On Monogamy*: *And the two shall be into one flesh, not three nor more*. I thought it right to give this warning, lest anyone here vainly imagine something obscene, or dream of that which is in the Greek manuscripts: <note>original: "amphō en sarki ēsan" - "both were in the flesh"</note>. Although in Genesis, from where this passage is taken, it does not say "the two shall be," but only "they shall be," <note>original Hebrew: "ve-hayu le-vasar echad"</note>. The Evangelist added it for the sake of explanation, or certainly the Greek translator added it, if Matthew wrote in Hebrew, which does not seem likely to me. And presently,

7 ***Therefore they are no longer two***] <note>original: "hōste ouketi eisi duo"</note>, that is, even if they are two: namely, after the marriage has begun. They had been created as two, not one, certainly male and female. Again, the bond of marriage rendered one out of two. The fable of Aristophanes, which he brings forward in Plato’s *Symposium*, does not differ entirely from this sentiment, though it is more obscene.

8 ***What God has joined***] <note>original: "synezeugxen"</note>, that is, yoked together, and joined with the same yoke. A metaphor taken from oxen pulling the same yoke together. We have translated it as "coupled" or "joined." And,

9 ***To the hardness of heart***] In Greek, it is a single word, <note>original: "sklērokardian"</note>.

10 ***It is not expedient to marry***] <note>original: "gamēsai"</note>, that is, *to lead a wife*, or certainly *to contract marriage* or *to have contracted* it. For among the Latins a man is not said "to veil himself" [marry] unless he serves his wife, as if she becomes the man rather than he. Also Festus Pompeius indicates that "to veil" <note>term: "nubere" - specifically the bride's action of wearing a veil</note> was once a common verb for Latin men as well, just as <note>original: "gamein"</note> is for the Greeks. But among the Hebrews, as has been said, there was no mutual right of divorce as there was among the Romans, but it was lawful for the husband alone to divorce. To which jealousy the wife was even forced to submit by a foul and horrific example.
<margin>D</margin> 11 ***Not all receive***] <note>original: "chōrousi"</note>. In this place, "we receive" does not mean the same as "they understand" or "they apprehend," as Lyra seems to have thought, who added as a commentary: *Because it is a high state, to which the weak cannot ascend*. But "they receive," that is, *they are capable*: in the way we call a "place capable" if it is so spacious that it can receive what is brought in. Thus Paul wants the Corinthians to be widened, so that they may "receive" him. For it is easy to understand what was said, but that saying does not descend into the souls of all, because they are occupied with other affections, so that there is no place there for divine counsel. And the same word is used in what follows: *He who can receive it, let him receive it*. <note>original: "Ho dunamenos chōrein, chōreitō"</note>.
<margin>E</margin> 12 ***Who were made***] <note>original: "hoitines eunouchisthēsan"</note>, those who were castrated, or those who were made eunuchs. For "eunuchs" had to be repeated. And he soon translates the same word himself as "castrated." Furthermore, <note>original: "eunouchos"</note> in Greek sounds like "guardian of the bed," because barbarians are accustomed to entrust their wives to be guarded by portents of this kind. Furthermore, those cut by force are called <note>original: "spadones"</note>. Peter Comestor interprets eunuchs as *well-conquering*, from <note>original: "eu"</note>, "well," and <note>original: "nikē"</note>, "victory," because it is the *highest victory*: as if it were not harder to conquer vain glory, or even a river of money, or anger. But "eunuch" is said from <note>original: "eunō"</note>, a bed, and <note>original: "echō"</note>, just as "torch-bearer" <note>original: "dadouchos"</note> and "wisdom-keeper" <note>original: "sophouchos"</note>. He likewise interprets "spadones" as being named from <note>original: "apo tou spaō"</note> (to drag/tear away): following which etymology all Germans think a "spado" is so called. And Hugo Cardinal follows this commentary. Since theologians once embraced such writers, some now cannot bear Erasmus. Indeed, for Hugo, the "castrated" <note>term: "castrati"</note> are so called as if they were "chastened" <note>term: "castinati"</note>. The Lord had distinguished three kinds of eunuchs. One of those who by nature cannot or do not desire to copulate with a woman. A second of those who are castrated by force. A third, who willingly restrain themselves for the sake of the kingdom of God. In which class shall we place those who, either by craft or fear, are thrust into celibacy, so that they may be allowed to commit fornication, but not allowed to marry a wife: to such an extent that if they openly keep a concubine, they are Catholic priests, but if they prefer to be said to have a wife, they are thrown into the fire. In my opinion, parents would treat their children more mercifully if, having destined them for celibacy, they took care to have the boys castrated while still young, rather than throwing them, whole and unwilling or ignorant, into this fire of lust. And again,

13 ***Little ones were brought to him***] <note>original: "ta paidia"</note>, that is, little boys.
<margin>F</margin> 14 ***Why do you ask me about the good***] Most Greek codices have, <note>original: "Ti me legeis agathon?"</note>, that is, *Why do you call me good?* but wrongly, if I am not mistaken, with the words translated here from another Gospel. Although Theophylact and Hilary read it in that way. But Jerome, Origen (Homily 8), and Chrysostom (Homily 64) read it otherwise. It appears that an inattentive reader was offended because Christ's response, *Only God is good*, did not seem to fit as well. But it does fit. For he does not rebuke him here because he called him good—although "Good" is added in Hilary's version—but because, being a man, he inquired about "the good," when there is nothing of good in men. Furthermore, he is good who does good. But if there is nothing truly good in human deeds, no one is called good. For whatever good is in us, is of the divine gift. But even if we read, *Why do you call me good*, there is no necessity that we receive the interpretation of the Heretics, who think the title of "good" belongs to...
