<margin>A</margin> ...applies properly to the one Father. Indeed, Christ hints that he is God, and for this reason—according to some interpretations—he rebukes the man for giving him the title of "good" when the man did not yet believe he was God; for I do not know if any of the Apostles yet believed this perfectly. In this passage, Origen <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) known for his prolific commentaries.</note> must be read cautiously; otherwise, his speech tastes of something Arian <note>Arianism was a 4th-century heresy that denied the full divinity of Christ.</note>, as if not even the Son should be called "good" in the proper sense, and as if the Son's goodness differs from human goodness only because the Son is closer to the Father in all good things than others are to the Son. However, just as he confesses that no man is properly called good in comparison to divine goodness, so they think no work of man is called good if it is compared to divine justice. And he wishes to disturb...

<margin>D</margin> **15 One is good, God]** <note>original Greek: οὐδεὶς ἀγαθὸς, εἰ μὴ εἷς ὁ Θεὸς</note>, that is, *none is good, except one, namely God*, so that the Greek article *ho* serves as an explanatory pointer.

<margin>E</margin> **16 You shall love your neighbor as yourself]** Origen, explaining this passage in his eighth published Homily, testifies that it seems to him these words were added and were not written by Matthew himself, and he gathers this from two arguments. First, that in Mark and Luke nothing of this sort is added, although the same event is otherwise reported. Second, since Paul in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter thirteen, testifies with these words, *You shall love your neighbor as yourself*, that the sum of the whole Law is contained therein: how is it fitting that something should be said to be still lacking for one who proclaims he has performed all these things? And in that place, he deplores that through the carelessness of scribes and the fault of correctors, the copies of the New Testament have been so corrupted that it is most difficult to restore them. Although, because of contentious people, he somehow excluded this difficulty by citing the apocryphal *Gospel of the Hebrews*. In which this matter concerning the young man is set forth in this manner: *The other of the rich men said to him, "Master, what good thing shall I do that I may live?" He said to him, "Man, perform the law and the prophets." He answered him, "I have done so." He said to him, "Go, sell all that you possess, and distribute to the poor, and come, follow me." But the rich man began to scratch his head, and it did not please him. And the Lord said to him, "How can you say, 'I have performed the law and the prophets,' since it is written in the law, 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself'? And behold, many of your brothers, sons of Abraham, are covered in filth, dying of hunger, and your house is full of many good things, and nothing at all goes out of it to them."* And turning, he said to Simon his disciple, who was sitting by him, *"Simon, son of Joanna, it is easier for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man into the kingdom of heaven."* From these things Origen reasons that, even if we grant it was written by the Evangelist just as we read it, the difficulty of the question can be explained this way: we should understand that Christ refuted the young man, who believed he had fulfilled the law, when he had bypassed the very head of the law, allowing the poor to perish in want while he himself was rich. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> also adds this: that he was conceited, that he was a liar, and that he asked the question in a testing spirit. But this does not fit what we read in Mark: *And Jesus loved (or kissed) him.* To me it seems simpler to understand the young man as being good in his own way, but due to weakness, not yet capable of Evangelical perfection.

<margin>F</margin> **17 Sell all that you have]** <note>original Greek: Σὺ πάντα σοῦ τὰ ὑπάρχοντα</note>, that is, *sell yours, or your possessions.* Nor is "all" added in Jerome's version. Nor is it in the "Golden Code," <note>Likely referring to a high-quality illuminated manuscript.</note> nor is the conjunction "and" added among the Greeks. It is simply, *go, sell*; and this <term>asyndeton</term> <note>A rhetorical figure where conjunctions are omitted for emphasis.</note> is not without its own grace.

<column-break/>

# CHAPTER XIX.

<margin>A</margin> do you call me good? <margin>17</margin> No one is good, except one, namely God. But if you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. He said to him, "Which?" And Jesus said, <margin>18</margin> "You shall not commit murder; You shall not commit adultery; You shall not commit theft; You shall not bear false witness; Honor your father and mother; <margin>19</margin> 16 and, You shall love your neighbor as yourself." The young man said to him, <margin>20</margin> "All these I have kept from my youth; what do I still lack?" Jesus said to him, "If you wish to be perfect, <margin>21</margin> go, 17 sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me." But when the young man had heard that word, <margin>22</margin> 18 he went away sad; for he had many <margin>B</margin> possessions. And Jesus said to his disciples, "Truly I say <margin>23</margin> to you, a rich man shall hardly enter into the kingdom of heaven. 19 And again I say to you, 20 it is easier for a camel <margin>24</margin> to pass through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man 21 to enter into the kingdom of God." When they heard these things, the disciples <margin>25</margin> were greatly astonished, saying, 22 "Who then can be saved?" But Jesus, looking at them, said to them, <margin>26</margin> "With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible." Then Peter answering said to him, "Behold, <margin>27</margin> we have left all and followed you; what then shall there be for us?" And Jesus said to them, "Truly I say <margin>28</margin> to you, that you who have followed me in the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit 23 on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes <margin>C</margin> of Israel. And everyone who has left houses, or brothers, <margin>29</margin> or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands for my name's sake, 24 shall receive a hundredfold, 25 and shall inherit eternal life."

---

**18 And he went away sad]** It is more like *grieving, or mournful* <note>original Greek: λυπούμενος</note>. And several manuscripts had this.

**19 And again]** <note>original Greek: Καὶ πάλιν</note> But in more corrected copies it is written *But again* <note>original Greek: Πάλιν δὲ</note>, or *Nay, again I say to you.* For he corrects what he had said before; though spoken softly, it had offended the disciples, so he repeats it more harshly.

**20 It is easier for a camel]** Saint Jerome undoubtedly took "camel" to mean the animal, following, I believe, Origen. Theophylactus <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator.</note> disagrees, wishing in this place to signify a nautical rope <note>Erasmus is discussing a famous linguistic debate: whether the Greek word is "kamelos" (camel) or "kamilos" (rope).</note>, and that indeed fits more naturally with the "eye of a needle." And in Suidas alone I find <term>kamelos</term> used with that meaning: after him, Camers says <term>kamelon</term> is a rope, but cites no author. Julius Pollux does not mention it among nautical instruments. And in this matter, I agree more with Jerome. For regarding what offends those who turn the camel into a nautical rope—namely, that it seems absurd for a camel to be led through the eye of a needle—this very point supports our side: for Christ proposed this example as an <term>adynaton</term> <note>A rhetorical figure expressing an impossibility.</note>. He wants it to appear completely impossible for a camel, a huge and lumpy animal, to pass through the eye of a needle. If the comparison seems somewhat absurd, let it be remembered that elsewhere the Lord rebukes one who prepares to cast a speck out of a brother's eye while he himself does not see the beam in his own eye. What is more absurd than a man carrying a beam in his eye? Truly, this absurdity of speech contributes to the emphasis. Nor is there any reason here to invent "old wives' tales" about there being a gate in Jerusalem named "The Needle," or that we should interpret "impossible" as "difficult." Indeed, if we interpret "rich" as "one trusting in his riches"—which the common crowd almost divinely does—only then can they unravel this knot. And Mark revealed this sense to us in chapter ten: *Children,* he said, *how difficult it is for those trusting in money to enter the kingdom of God.* If it is true that large nautical ropes are called <term>camels</term> by the Greeks, it appears they were named from a similarity to the animal's thickness; unless perhaps because among them nautical ropes were woven from camel hair. Nor does it entirely satisfy my mind what Jerome noted: that it was not said by Christ, "it is impossible for a rich man to enter," but "difficult." Where "difficult" is placed, he says, it shows not that it is hard, but demonstrates rarity; yet soon after he confesses the same thing was called "impossible" by the same person. For having brought in the comparison of the camel going through the eye of a needle, by this saying, he says, it is shown not to be difficult, but impossible. In the first dialogue against the Pelagians, he explains himself by a different reasoning, denying that those who were rich for others rather than themselves are truly "rich." Furthermore, the phrase "through the eye of a needle" can be taken two ways: either for the hole an actual needle has, or for a hole made by a needle. Finally, it is not.

**21 Into the kingdom of heaven]** But "into the kingdom of God" <note>original Greek: εἰς βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ</note>. Although what I read in Chrysostom and Jerome, "kingdom of heaven," is more approved by me. For he felt that the rich are not suited for the Evangelical doctrine, which he generally calls the kingdom of heaven.

**22 Who then can]** <note>original Greek: Τὶς ἄρα δύναται</note>, that is, *Who indeed can*, similar to what was above, *Who do you think.* And a little after,

**23 On the throne of majesty]** <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ θρόνου δόξης</note>, that is, *on the throne of glory.*

**24 Shall receive a hundredfold]** <note>original Greek: ἑκατονταπλασίονα</note>, as if you said *each thing multiplied a hundred times.* For it is a number of great multitude. And,

**25 Shall possess eternal life]** <note>original Greek: κληρονομήσει</note>, which literally [means to inherit].

1 **The kingdom is like** <note>original: "Simile est regnum"</note>] <note>original: "Ὁμοία γάρ ἐστιν"</note>, that is, *For the kingdom is like*. For it connects with the preceding sentence.
2 *From early morning* <note>original: "Ex primo mane"</note>] <note>original: "ἅμα πρωΐ"</note>, that is, at the very first light of dawn, or at the very break of day, or as soon as it grew light. And a little after:
3 *For a daily denarius* <note>original: "Ex denario diurno"</note>] <note>original: "ἐν δηναρίῳ τὴν ἡμέραν"</note>. First, there was no need to add the Greek preposition *ek* <note>from</note>, since Latin speakers say *hired for a denarius*. Secondly, this denarius is a type of Roman coin, worth three and a half shillings <note>term: "shillings" here refers to the *solidus*, a late Roman gold coin</note>, as Guillaume Budé <note>A famous French humanist and expert on ancient coinage</note> believes, a man who is exceptionally diligent and most learned in every matter. Nor is it "daily" in the sense of a quality, but "for each day," or "of the day." Hence it could be translated: *having agreed with the workers for a denarius for each day*.
4 *Go you also into my vineyard* <note>original: "Ite & vos in vineam meam"</note>] "My" is not found among the Greeks, nor in the "Golden Manuscript" <note>likely an ancient codex Erasmus consulted</note>. Again, concerning the phrase "whatever is right": <note>original: "καὶ ὃ ἐὰν"</note>, that is, *whatsoever* or *whatever*. And soon after, regarding those hired at the eleventh hour:
5 *Go you also into the vineyard*] In the common Greek copies "my" is not added, nor in the works of Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine commentator</note>, nor does it appear that Jerome added it. Nor did I find it added in the Constance manuscript, except that the pronoun explains the force of the article "the vineyard." Furthermore, the Greeks add here what is not found in our copies: <note>original: "καὶ ὃ ἐὰν ᾖ δίκαιον λήψεσθε"</note>, that is, *whatever is right you shall receive*. But since this is not added in Jerome's text, it may seem to have been repeated from the earlier passage. Likewise:
6 *They received a denarius each* <note>original: "Acceperunt singulos denarios"</note>] <note>original: "ἀνὰ δηνάριον"</note>, that is, *denarius-wise*, so to speak, and *each* rather than *individual denarii*.
7 *These last worked one hour* <note>original: "Hi novissimi una hora fecerunt"</note>] <note>original: "μίαν ὥραν ἐποίησαν"</note>, that is, *they did one hour*. It is uncertain whether "one hour" is a direct object or a measurement of time—that is, whether we should understand them as having "done an hour" (completed a period of time at work) or as having "done the work within an hour's space."
8 *Of the day and the heat* <note>original: "Diei & æstus"</note>] It is not "of the heat" (genitive), but "the heat" (accusative): <note>original: "βάρος τῆς ἡμέρας καὶ τὸν καύσωνα"</note>, that is, *the burden of the day and the heat*. Indeed, in the Greek copies there is a great consensus not only for "the heat," but also the article is added—*the* heat—so that you may understand the sense is twofold: the first part refers to the duration of the labor, the second to the difficulty of the weather. apply the allegory to the Jews called first and the Gentiles later, or to those called as youths and those as old men, the "burden of the day" fits, because the Jews were called to the Gospel after a long observation of the Law; the Gentiles were admitted suddenly to the same grace. Furthermore, "the heat of the day" is that under the Law concupiscence burned more fiercely, and in youths the fire of lust and anger is heavier; whereas in old age, which is the evening of life, these things are more relaxed. Therefore, this is not a pointless distinction, even if an error crept into the Latin manuscripts. Certainly, Augustine in Sermon 70, *On the Words of the Lord in the Gospel of John*, reads "the heat" <note>accusative</note>, not "of the heat" <note>genitive</note>. Next:
9 *I wish also to give to this one* <note>original: "Volo autem & huic"</note>] The "also" is redundant; <note>original: "θέλω δὲ τούτῳ"</note>, *I wish to give to this one*. Again:
10 *Or is it not lawful for me to do what I wish*] The Greeks add <note>original: "ἐν τοῖς ἐμοῖς"</note>, that is, *with my own things*, although it could also refer to people. Augustine, in the place I just mentioned, reads "of my own" following the Greeks. And soon:
11 *Is your eye wicked, etc.*] It appears the text varied due to an error of the ears, because <note>original: "εἰ"</note> (if) and <note>original: "ᾖ"</note> (is/be) sound the same to the Greeks. If you read "is," the sentence can depend on the previous part, so the sense is: *Is it therefore less lawful for me to act kindly with my goods as I wish, if your eye should have malice and envy?* since I certainly cannot help but be good. If you read "if," should it be translated "or not," so the sense is: *Does my kindness toward others torture your eyes?* Since his envy was born from the other's generosity, not from any injustice by the giver of what was agreed upon. Certainly, the "Golden" and Constance manuscripts have "or." Although I neither ignore nor deny that <note>original: "εἰ"</note> sometimes has the force of an inquiry among the Greeks; nor do I object if the old translation pleases anyone more.
12 *Many are called* <note>original: "Multi funt vocati"</note>] <note>original: "Πολλοὶ γὰρ"</note>, that is, *For many*. And "called" and "chosen" are nouns in this place, not participles—*klētoi*, *eklektoi*—which nonetheless seem to be used almost in place of participles. And a little later:
13 *Privately and said* <note>original: "Secreto & dixit"</note>] A few words are missing in our text: <note>original: "κατ’ ἰδίαν ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ"</note>, that is, *privately on the road*. Although here "alone" <note>original: "solos"</note> was more appropriate, as he translates it sometimes. For he did not want any companions on the journey except the disciples. And a little further down:

*...on the left is euonymon.* <note>original: "ἐωνύμων"</note> For the Greeks, for the sake of a good omen, call the left side of the body *euonymon*, which means *of good omen*: just as 
poets call the Furies the *Eumenides* <note>meaning "The Gracious Ones," a euphemism to avoid their wrath</note>, and as in the Book of Job, "to bless" is used 
to mean "to curse." <note>This is an example of antiphrasis, where a word is used to mean its opposite to avoid bad luck or offense.</note>

<margin>15</margin> *Are you able to drink the cup]* *potērion* <note>original: "ποτήριον"</note>, that is, a *drinking vessel*, which 
[the Vulgate] nevertheless always translates as *calix* [chalice], even though *poculum* [cup] expresses the 
Greek word precisely. For a *poculum* is any vessel from which one drinks, like a 
*potērion*, and is *itself named from drinking*. But *calix* is a specific type of cup, 
which the Greeks call *kylix* <note>original: "κύλιξ"</note>. Moreover, the phrase is a pro-
verb, "to drink from the same cup," meaning to be a partner in 
misfortune, as I have explained more fully in my *Adages* <note>original: "Chiliadibus"</note>. And 
in the more correct Greek manuscripts, it does not read *mellō pinein*, that is, "I am about to 
drink," but *pinō*, that is, "I drink," as a present 
narrative of what was imminent. And Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father</note> reads it this way. Furthermore, 
after these things, there is added in the Greek:

<margin>16</margin> *And the baptism with which I am baptized, to be baptized with]* <note>original: "Καὶ βάπτισμα, ὃ ἐγὼ βαπτίζομαι, βαπτισθῆναι"</note> that is, 
*with the baptism with which I am baptized, to be baptized;* For these words are 
added in Mark. And in this manner the same things are soon repeated: *You shall indeed 
drink my cup, and be baptized with the baptism with which I am bap-
tized.* But I do not know whether these have been brought over into this place from Mark; 
which is something that often happens, especially since I do not find them added 
in Jerome’s <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note> version. Although they are added 
in Origen, Chrysostom, and Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine commentator</note>. Next,

<margin>17</margin> *It is not mine to give to you]* Someone added "to you" on their own; 
in the Greek it is simply *ouk estin emon dounai* <note>original: "οὐκ ἔστιν ἐμὸν δοῦναι"</note>, that is, *it is not 
mine to give,* so that it is absolute, and you may understand that this whole matter is referred to the 
Father; and Chrysostom reads it this way, with the agreement of Theophylact. 
However, <unclear>un-</unclear> <note>The text likely meant "they added"</note> "to you" because of what follows: 
*but to those for whom it is prepared.* Yet that phrase is "headless" <note>lacking a clear grammatical subject</note>; for one must 
understand, *to those it will happen for whom it was prepared by my 
Father.* Nor would I conceal that Jerome interprets it this way, 
but you might almost suspect that he read it as we commonly read it, 
although he also includes the mention of the Father.

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>18</margin> *Princes of the nations lord it over them]* *archontes tōn ethnōn 
katakyrieuousin autōn* <note>original: "ἄρχοντες τῶν ἐθνῶν κατακυριεύουσιν αὐτῶν"</note>. Since he used the word *nations* [gentium], why does he not 
repeat *them* [earum, feminine], or rather, why not *to them* [eis]? And shortly after, "against them" [in eas] rather than 
"against them" [in eos]? For *ethnos* [nation] is of the neuter gender. Nor is it simply "to lord it over," 
but *katakyrieuousin*, *to lord it over them*, or *against them*. 
For frequently that preposition [kata-] suggests a bad sense, because tyrants 
exercise their rule to the harm of the people. Nor is it,

<margin>19</margin> *Those who are greater]* but *hoi megaloi* <note>original: "οἱ μεγάλοι"</note>, that is, *the great ones or the 
magnates*. Indeed, that was the specific title of the King of the Per-
sians, which is why Alexander was called *the Great*. And again,

<margin>20</margin> *They exercise power]* *katexousiazousin autōn* <note>original: "κατεξουσιάζουσιν αὐτῶν"</note>, that is, *they 
exercise authority by right*. And the preposition similarly suggests a 
bad sense, indicating that the power is tyrannical and 
joined with the harm of those obeying. Hence, in some manuscripts, it has 
been wrongly changed to *among them* instead of *against them*. Furthermore, what is here in-

<margin>D</margin>
-terpreted as a paraphrase of the Greek word, *could also have been done in the earlier 
part: they exercise dominion over them.* And a little later,

<margin>21</margin> *Whoever wants to become greater]* *megas genesthai* <note>original: "μέγας γενέσθαι"</note>, that is, 
*to become great.* And Jerome cites it this way when explaining a 
chapter of Ezekiel 45. Let no one argue that the Greek was written more loosely.

<margin>22</margin> *He did not come to be ministered unto]* Who ever said that a person 
"is ministered" [in the passive] when service is shown to him? No more, by Hercules, than 
"to be blessed" could mean to be someone spoken well of, or "to be announced" 
someone to whom something is announced. And yet the Greeks speak this way, 
though it is entirely unheard of to Latin ears. He could have translated it 
conveniently in this way: *He did not come so that he might be ministered to, but so that he himself might minister to others,* *dia-
konēthēnai, alla diakonēsai* <note>original: "διακονηθῆναι, ἀλλὰ διακονῆσαι"</note>. Again, here he calls the *anima* "life," 
not that part which is the other half of a human being. Again,

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>23</margin> *For many]* *anti pollōn* <note>original: "ἀντὶ πολλῶν"</note>. This sounds somewhat different to the Greeks 
than to the Latins: for us, it is merely opposed to "few"; for them, 
it suggests a multitude of people, almost what the Latins call the *vulgus* [the common people]. 
And *redemption*, in Greek is *lytron* <note>original: "λύτρον"</note>, which properly signifies the price 
by which captives or slaves are redeemed, which the French call 
*rançon* [ransom], from the verb *lyō* <note>original: "λύω"</note>, which is *to loose*. Next,

<margin>24</margin> *And immediately they saw]* The Greeks add a few words, 
*aneblepsan autōn hoi ophthalmoi* <note>original: "ἀνέβλεψαν αὐτῶν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ"</note>, that is, *their eyes 
received sight*, because mention had already been made of the eyes.

<margin>A</margin> *To the mountain of the olive grove]* it is *elaiōn* <note>original: "ἐλαιῶν"</note>, that is, *of the olives*. Only 
once in the Acts of the Apostles do we read of the mountain that 
was called *Elaiōn* <note>original: "Ἐλαιών"</note>, that is, *Olivetum* [Olive Grove], if the writing does not 
deceive. For the same word, if the last syllable has an acute accent, signifies *olive grove*, 
but if it has a circumflex, it signifies *of the olives*. Here it is certainly *of the olives*, because of the 
added article *tōn* <note>original: "τῶν"</note>. And a little later,

<margin>2</margin> *Into the village]* *eis tēn kōmēn* <note>original: "εἰς τὴν κώμην"</note>. It suggests a village or a small town, lest 
anyone should think it is a fortress or a magnificent palace, as Hugh of Saint-Cher <note>original: "Carrensis"</note> 
seems to think.

<margin>3</margin> *And immediately he sends]* In some Greek manuscripts it is 
*apostellei* <note>original: "ἀποστέλλει"</note>, in the present tense, as if it refers to the disciples. 
But why was it necessary to repeat, *And he will send them*, when he had already said, 
*Go into the village*? Hence it seems to me it should be read *apostelei* <note>original: "ἀποστελεῖ"</note>, that is, 
*he will send*, so that it refers to the pack animals, just as it is read 
in Mark, chapter eleven. And Chrysostom, 
Theophylact, and Jerome read it this way, with the agreement of the ancient 
Latin manuscripts; nor does Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers, a 4th-century bishop</note> interpret it otherwise. It is possible, however, 
that Matthew or his translator preferred the present tense to signify 
speed. Next, some had,

<margin>4</margin> *This was done]* Some, *All this was done*. It does not matter 
much. Chrysostom does not add "all," if we believe the 
translator; for Theophylact adds it.

<margin>5</margin> *Say to the daughter of Zion]* This testimony is taken from 
Zechariah, chapter nine. Although the Evangelist 
does not exactly agree with the Hebrew truth, nor with the 
Septuagint. For "say" is neither in the Hebrew, nor in the Septuagint. 
Again, what he says here...

<margin>6 He comes to you meek]</margin> In Hebrew it is *ani* <note>original: "ani"</note>, that is, poor. For the same word, if written with the letter *Ayin*, means "poor"; if with *Yod*, it means "meek." Jerome rendered the Hebrew thus: *Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout, daughter of Jerusalem; behold, your King will come to you, righteous and a savior, he is poor and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt, the son of an ass.* According to the Septuagint <note>The standard Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> it is read thus: *Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion, proclaim, daughter of Jerusalem, behold your king comes to you righteous and saving, he himself is meek, and mounted upon a beast of burden and a young colt.* That is, *Rejoice vehemently daughter of Zion, preach daughter of Jerusalem: behold your King comes to you righteous and he himself saving, meek, and ascending upon a yoked beast and a new colt.* The translator seems to have read *autos* <note>original: "αὐτὸς", meaning "he himself"</note>, whereas the Aldine edition <note>A famous printed edition of Greek texts from the Renaissance.</note> has *autós*. Furthermore, where the word "Savior" appears here, in Hebrew it is *nosha* <note>original: "נושע"</note>, alluding to the name of Jesus; hence the Jews, following the historical record, refer this passage to the Christ. Likewise:
<margin>7 Sitting upon an ass]</margin> *Epibebēkōs* <note>original: "ἐπιβεβηκώς"</note>, that is, having mounted the ass. And again,
<margin>8 Garments]</margin> It refers more specifically to robes or cloaks, *ta himatia* <note>original: "τὰ ἱμάτια"</note>, that is, the outer garments.
<margin>9 Hosanna to the son of David]</margin> Not without reason did Matthew, or his Translator, leave the Hebrew word as it was; I believe because it is a peculiar acclamation of that nation, much like *io triumphe* <note>A ritual shout of victory used in Roman triumphs.</note> was among the Romans. Truly, there are various opinions among translators regarding this word. Whoever wishes to be more fully informed on this should read Jerome’s little book to Pope Damasus, in which he notes that Hilary, due to his ignorance of the Hebrew language, interpreted *Hosanna* as "the redemption of the house of David." Though Ambrose interpreted it in almost the same way. And indeed Hilary interpreted it exactly so in the Commentary he wrote on Matthew: "For *osanna*," he says, "signifies in the Hebrew tongue the redemption of the house of David." This was surely a remarkable slip, since among the Hebrews it is well established that *purkana* <note>original: "פורקנא"</note> means redemption, and only then *d'vid* <note>original: "דביד"</note> means "of David." Furthermore, since the word "David" is the same among Hebrews as it is among Greeks and Latins, even someone entirely ignorant of the Hebrew language could have perceived the error, if only he had paid attention. But I suspect that Saint Hilary, when he was stuck on that word, inquired of some Jew what *osanna* meant to them; and that man, in order to mock the Christian, replied with whatever came to his mouth: "the redemption of the house of David." See what it is to see with others' eyes and walk with others' feet! Yet the same man, in his exposition of the second Psalm, does not approve of any interpretation of the Old Testament except the one called the Septuagint, because *Bresith* <note>original: "בראשית", the first word of Genesis</note>, which is the first word of the book of Genesis, signifies three things among the Hebrews: *in the beginning, in the son, and in the head*. Truly such is the human mind: each person approves only of as much as he trusts he can achieve himself. Hilary knew Greek to some extent. For Jerome recorded that he had only tasted a small breeze of Greek literature. And for that reason, he gladly adorns his Commentaries with Greek flourishes. But since he was utterly ignorant of Hebrew letters, he wanted nothing to be added to the Septuagint translation. Furthermore, Saint Augustine—since even he did not fully know Greek—did not approve of Jerome’s labor in either translating or emending the New Testament from Greek sources. Although he thought this was tolerable to some extent, because after comparing manuscripts, he had discovered Jerome’s faithfulness in that matter. For Augustine had tasted Greek literature as a boy, and was forced to return to it as an old man, since he even imitated Epiphanius’s Greek book on heresies as best he could. However, since he was entirely ignorant of the Hebrew tongue, he did not think it should be allowed for Jerome to change anything from the Hebrew sources, especially since he had already verified the man’s faithfulness in the New Testament. And yet this very man, who forbids Jerome—who was exceptionally skilled in the three languages—from innovating anything in the Sacred Books, noted many passages in his own volumes

of the Old Testament, and certainly not from Hebrew copies, but from Latin and Greek ones. For example, in that passage cited from the book of Numbers: *And all the multitude of women who have not known the couch of a male, keep alive.* Soon he adds: *Nowhere in the Hebrew reading does it appear that women are also usually called virgins.* But how does that appear unless he produces the Hebrew word? If Augustine had possessed the skill in languages that Jerome had, he would not have hesitated to do what he forbids Jerome from doing. But today, certain great Theologians (as they see themselves), though they do not even know Latin and are ignorant of all ancient and good literature—and for that reason are its enemies—want nothing to be mixed into Divine Letters except what they themselves can understand. But just as the Hebrew letters neglected by Hilary took their revenge for his contempt in the word *osanna*, so in these times good literature everywhere takes revenge for its neglect; for [these theologians] constantly stumble, get stuck everywhere, slip everywhere, and provoke either laughter or pity from learned men. These things are by no means said as an insult to the Theological Order, but against certain men little worthy of that Order. But to return to the matter: Jerome indicates this passage is taken from Psalm 117 [Psalm 118], in which, among other things clearly spoken of Christ, we also read: *O Lord, save now; O Lord, send now prosperity; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.* Furthermore, for what is found in the Septuagint as "O Lord, save me," the Hebrew reads *Ana Yehovah hoshia na* <note>original: "אנא יהוה הושיעה נא"</note>, which Symmachus <note>An ancient translator of the Old Testament into Greek.</note> interpreted more clearly, saying: "I beseech you, Lord, save me, I beseech you." Since *hoshia na* signifies "save," and *na* is an interjection among the Hebrews used by one demanding or entreating.
<margin>10 Blessed is he who comes]</margin> *Eulogēmenos* <note>original: "εὐλογημένος"</note>. This word occurs everywhere in the sacred scriptures, though it is foreign to Latin speech; yet there is no other word we can substitute for it, unless we prefer to say "one to be praised" or "the praised one." To the Greeks, "to speak well" (*to legein*) <note>original: "τὸ λέγειν"</note> means to bless someone of whom one speaks well, and he is "blessed" who has an honorable reputation. Just as one "does well" to someone on whom he confers a benefit. And one is said to be "well-treated" who has been helped by a benefit. What has been said of "to bless" and "blessed," consider the same said of "to curse" and "cursed." If it is a Christian practice to receive a foreign idiom in these matters, disregarding the custom of the Latin tongue, and to fashion as it were a new speech peculiar to Christians, why is it not done in all other cases? For what is right and done with judgment ought to be done consistently. Now, if the Translator acted randomly and however it struck his mind—sometimes avoiding the property of a foreign tongue, sometimes receiving it—what forbids other learned men from restoring certain things for the better? Indeed, I think it belongs to this pattern that Augustine, in noting the tropes of the Old Testament, cites from the eleventh chapter of Deuteronomy: *He who made the virtue of the Egyptians.* And he thinks that *virtutem* <note>In Latin, this can mean "virtue" or "power/strength."</note> is wrongly translated by the Latins as "virtue" when the sense is: "The power of the Egyptians was reduced to nothing." Clearly, he did not notice the idiom of the Greek language; whether it agrees with the Hebrew, I am not sufficiently certain. It is strange, however, why he did not recognize the idiom of the language here, whether Greek or Hebrew, yet soon in his sixth book he brings forward an example where it is said: "That you might make your handmaid" instead of "for your handmaid."
<margin>11 He who comes in the name of the Lord]</margin> *Ho erchomenos* <note>original: "ὁ ἐρχόμενος"</note>, he who was to come, or is coming. For it can be of the future tense, and thus it is read in the "golden codex," with the support of the Donatians as well.
<margin>11 The prophet from Nazareth]</margin> *Ho apo Nazareth* <note>original: "ὁ ἀπὸ Ναζαρέθ"</note>, that is, the Nazarene. And what he adds a little later,
<margin>14 The tables of the money changers]</margin> *Kollybistōn* <note>original: "κολλυβιστῶν"</note>, who are called the same as *trapezitai* <note>Bankers or money-changers.</note>. Furthermore, the testimony he brings forward is taken from the fifty-sixth chapter of Isaiah: *For my house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations.* The Septuagint also agrees.
<margin>14 Out of the mouth of nurslings and infants]</margin> This is taken from the eighth Psalm.

<margin>v. 5</margin> They do all their deeds to be seen by others; for they make their phylacteries <note>Small leather boxes containing Torah verses, worn on the forehead or arm.</note> broad <margin>6</margin> and the tassels of their garments long. They love the place of honor at feasts and the <margin>7</margin> best seats in the synagogues, and greetings in the marketplaces, and being called <margin>v. 8</margin> "Rabbi, Rabbi" by others. But you are not to be called Rabbi; for one is your teacher, the Christ; and you are <margin>9</margin> all brothers. And call no man your father on earth; for one is your Father, who is in <margin>10</margin> heaven. Neither be called teachers; for one is your <margin>v. 11</margin> teacher, the Christ. The greatest among you shall be <margin>12</margin> your servant. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, <margin>v. 13</margin> and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. But woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people's faces; for you neither enter yourselves nor allow those who are entering <margin>v. 14</margin> to go in. Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers; therefore you will receive a greater <margin>15</margin> judgment. Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you travel across sea and land to make a single convert; and when he becomes one, you <margin>16</margin> make him twice as much a son of hell as yourselves. Woe to you, blind guides, who say, "If anyone swears by the temple, it is nothing; but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath." <margin>17</margin> You blind fools! For which is greater, the gold or the <margin>18</margin> temple that has made the gold sacred? And, "If anyone swears by the altar, it is nothing; but if anyone swears by the gift that is on it, he is bound by his oath." <margin>19</margin> You blind fools! For which is greater, the gift or the altar that <margin>20</margin> makes the gift sacred? So whoever swears by the altar, <margin>21</margin> swears by it and by everything on it. And whoever swears by the temple, swears by it and by him who dwells <margin>22</margin> in it. And whoever swears by heaven, swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it. <margin>v. 23</margin> Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done,

eighth. Furthermore, where it here translates *infants* <note>original Latin: "infantium"</note>, the Greek is *nepiōn* <note>original: "νηπίων"</note>, which has until now been translated as *little ones*.

15 *He went forth outside the city*] <note>original Greek: "ἐξῆλθεν ἔξω τῆς πόλεως"</note>. What need was there for "outside"? "He departed from the city" was enough, or "he went out from the city." And immediately following:

16 *And I remained there*] <note>original Greek: "ηὐλίσθη" (ēulisthē)</note>, as if you were to say, "he was stabled," that is, "he lodged." From which comes that phrase in the Acts of the Apostles, "lodging together," which we shall discuss in its proper place. And a little after:

17 *A fig tree*] <note>original Greek: "συκῆν μίαν" (sykēn mian)</note>, that is, "a certain fig tree." Since the Hebrews use "one" for "a certain." The translator added "tree" lest we should take it for the fruit, for which reason elsewhere and even shortly hereafter he translates it as "ficulneam" <note>a Latin term for a fig tree</note>, a word not quite approved among Latin speakers, since "ficulnus" is the adjective from "ficus" <note>fig</note>, just as "quernus" is from "quercus" <note>oak</note>. Nor is it:

18 *Beside the way*] <note>original Greek: "ἐπὶ τῆς ὁδοῦ" (epi tēs hodou)</note>, that is, "in the way." This is that fig tree with whose leaves some cover their own ignorance: although it signifies more those who display holiness through dress, titles, and splendid words, when their life does not correspond. But these people are carefully on guard lest they touch anything of good literature; and they speak as insipidly as they can, lest they have any affinity with this fig tree. Yet by this very reasoning, they fall most especially into the category of the fig tree. I hear a rude and dirty speech, and I expect a simple and innocent life—that is, the fruit which the appearance of the speech (the leaves) promised. When one comes closer, I find Sardanapaluses <note>Sardanapalus was a legendary Assyrian king known for extreme luxury and decadence.</note>, I find Midases and Satraps <note>Midas refers to greed; Satraps refer to tyrannical local rulers.</note>: everything is tyrannical; only their talk recalls the Apostles. This is that fig tree which Christ hates and curses: if he thinks so little of lofty learning and haughty eloquence, how much more will he hate arrogant and supercilious ignorance, and an infancy disguised with the paint of holiness? But let us set these things aside as side-issues.

19 *How it withered immediately*] In common Greek manuscripts "the fig tree" is found, but it was added by scribes, in my opinion, since it is not found in the ancient copies, nor in Jerome.

27 *I go, Lord*] In the Greek it is read "Egō, Kyrie" <note>original: "Ἐγὼ Κύριε"</note>, not "eī" <note>you</note>. This is the speech of one offering himself ready and prompt for anything. Thus the boy Samuel, when he believed himself called by Eli, said, "Behold, I," for which the Latins say "Eccum" or "I am here." Origen reads "Nai Kyrie" <note>original: "Ναὶ Κύριε"</note>, that is, "Yes, Lord." In some Greek copies, however, I find "pro egō hypagō," that is, "I go forth, but, as I believe, corrected according to the Latin copies."

Except that in that place "the last" was written, by a slip of memory unless I am mistaken, unless we prefer to attribute it to the scribe who thought "the last" should be written there because mention was made of "the last" above in the parable of the vineyard. Yet I have found "the last" written in the copy which he exhibited at Constantine, so that it cannot seem to have happened by chance. From which it is gathered either that the order of the narrative was different in those books which Augustine had, or "the last" was said of the one who was mentioned first. For he is "the last" from the present place, that is, the furthest. Just as to one counting a genealogy upward from the father, the great-great-great-grandfather is the "last," so he who was first in the proposal is "last" in the response. Jerome mentions both readings, but he approves more of this one which we use, which it is clear he followed from his own interpretation, so that we may understand the Jews to be refuted by their own response. And yet, if any like the other reading, he explains the manner thus: that the Jews responded perversely because they understood they were being trapped by a little question. But why would they avoid a trap here when in the next parable they respond, "He will miserably destroy those wicked men"? Incidentally, this should also be noted: since this passage is cited from Jerome in the *Catena Aurea* <note>The "Golden Chain," a famous collection of Bible commentaries compiled by Thomas Aquinas.</note>, yet is not found in those commentaries of his which we possess, nor elsewhere in his writings—certainly as far as I can remember—it is an argument that these works have been shortened, a suspicion I have indicated elsewhere. **30 And he dug a winepress in it]** <term>Lēnon</term> <note>Greek: ληνὸν</note>. For in old times, fresh-pressed wine was caught in excavated pits. Thus, elsewhere he <term>translates it as a lake</term>. From this, the god Bacchus <term>is called "Leneus" by the Poets</term>. And a little after: 

**31 They will perhaps respect my son]** The word <term>Perhaps</term> <note>Latin: "Forte"</note> is not found among the Greeks, nor in the ancient Latin copies, nor in the Golden Codex, nor even in the Constance manuscript—which was the last to come into my hands—nor in the works of Jerome. It appears to have been added by someone who was afraid that God might seem to have either lied (by saying something would happen that did not) or been ignorant of the future. As if it were necessary that parables should match reality in every detail, or "by the ruler's edge," as they say. Some things are mixed in just to complete the order of the narrative, as Augustine testifies in his work *On Christian Doctrine*. This passage has been attacked with serious false accusations by two people who claim the Evangelists wrote "perhaps they will respect"; specifically Matthew here and Mark in chapter 12. They claim the word was removed by some forgers, especially since in Luke chapter 20 the word <term>īsōs</term> <note>Greek: ἴσως, meaning "perhaps" or "likely"</note> is added without controversy. 

First, I do not think anyone should require of me that whatever is found more or less in one Evangelist must immediately be transferred to the others. Furthermore, the consensus of all Greek manuscripts supports me. Added to this is the consensus of nearly all Latin manuscripts I have seen, especially the more corrected ones. The Basel Edition also agrees, which the Amerbach brothers <note>Famous printers in Basel and friends of Erasmus</note> gave to us with the greatest faithfulness from the most ancient copies. Not even Jerome, in explaining this passage, ever includes the adverb <term>perhaps</term>. I will say more on this shortly. 

Certainly Origen, in explaining this passage in Matthew, declares throughout his entire commentary that he read what we read. Indeed, in his 19th Homily, he raises this very question: Since God, the householder, said "They will respect my son," and the outcome shows they did not respect him, it appears God did not know what was going to happen. He solves this knot by saying that the general statement "They will respect my son" refers to those individuals who did embrace Christ and did not kill him, but respected him. Truly, Origen is dealing with the problem that if God predicted a future event that did not happen, He would either be ignorant or a liar. And since throughout his treatment he repeatedly cites the Evangelist's words, he never once adds <term>perhaps</term>, so it cannot be seen as an accident. 

Jerome enters into this question no differently than Origen: "Furthermore," he says, "that which is joined, 'They will respect my son,' does not come from ignorance. For what could the householder—who in this place is understood to be God the Father—not know?" From these luminaries, it is clear Jerome is showing that the outcome was different than what the householder had predicted would happen. But what is read in the same place in Jerome supports us even more clearly: <term>Let us ask Arius and Eunomius</term> <note>Early Christian heretics who argued that the Son was inferior to the Father; Jerome is using this text to argue against them.</note>: <term>Behold, the Father is said to be ignorant, and he tempers his sentence, and as far as it lies in you, he is proven to have lied.</term> If Jerome had read <term>perhaps they will respect my son</term> here, God might have seemed unaware of the future, but he could not have seemed to be a liar. For someone who says, "Tomorrow the King will perhaps arrive," cannot be called a liar if the King does not arrive, since he pronounced nothing as certain. 

What then does it mean to <term>temper a sentence</term>? It means to leave room for repentance, while signaling through his speech that some hope remains. But that does not seem to go against us, because Jerome mentions "doubting": but, he says, "God is always said to doubt." For someone who says something will happen with the intent to give courage or offer hope does indeed seem to doubt. For this is how we pray for those about to be beaten: "In the future, he will be of good worth." And when we give courage, we say: "In the future you will not commit this, so that anyone surpasses you in duty," or "You will take care to make up for this slip with a great effort." In the same way God, although he foreknew the Jews would kill his Son, nevertheless, to warn them of what they ought to do, speaks as if there were hope that they would finally repent and respect the Son, they who had so often killed the Prophets. 

And yet, on the opposing side, Chrysostom seems to stand in his 69th Homily. For they object to this. To this I answer: first, it is possible that here a translator added it on his own. It is possible that Chrysostom referred

Finally, as far as the meaning is concerned, there is nothing in Chrysostom that forces the addition of "perhaps." For when he says: *Certainly not from ignorance, far be it, but wanting to show the magnitude of the sin for which they could never show any satisfaction,* the one who predicts a future that will not happen seems more "ignorant" than the one who says, "Perhaps it will happen." Likewise, the one who says something will happen that absolutely ought to happen shows the magnitude of the sin more than the one who says, "Perhaps they will do it." 

It is probable, therefore, that "perhaps" is not added in the Greek of Chrysostom, since it is not added in Theophylact <note>A Byzantine archbishop and prominent biblical commentator.</note> either. Furthermore, in similar passages brought from the Prophets—"if perhaps they might hear" and "if perhaps they might rest"—the Greek is not <term>īsōs</term>, but <term>ean ara</term> <note>Greek: ἐὰν ἄρα, meaning "if then" or "if indeed."</note>. What it is in Hebrew, I do not know. Moreover, as for what Jerome adds in his Commentaries—that something similar is held in the Gospel, *perhaps they will respect my son*—there is no doubt that he cited it from Luke, referring to the sense rather than the exact words. I have seen fit to write these things down, not because I think it would be absurd if what Luke adds were also added here, but to defend the integrity of the reading and our hard work from false accusations. I will not omit this: what we read in Jerome’s Commentaries, where he explains this place: *But God is always said to doubt,* I suspect that by a scribe's error, "always" (*semper*) was changed from "often" (*saepe*). For God does not always speak this way in Holy Scripture.

<margin>A</margin> ...made by God. Now, what Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> may have translated from the Hebrew is not entirely clear, since it is well known that most of his volumes have been corrupted by half-learned scribes, and the volumes themselves do not agree with one another. Therefore, it is possible that he restored from his own memory the phrase: "that thing was done, and it is marvelous." But even if we grant that it was translated this way by Jerome, "that thing" can still refer to the "head" [of the corner], that is, to Christ. It is not necessary for it to refer to the whole preceding sentence. Certainly, Jerome, in explaining Psalm 117, reads and explains it in this way: *And he is marvelous in our eyes.* Not in the eyes of those who rejected him, but in ours, who received him by believing. So says Jerome. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian theologian.</note> makes it masculine in gender, although the passage is not without error, if I am not mistaken. The very flow of the speech teaches that it should be read thus: *the cornerstone was made by the Lord.* Even if we read "it was done," the words that follow prove what he meant. For these follow: *Although he would not have been made this, unless he had suffered, yet he was not made this by those at whose hands he suffered.* Indeed, Arnobius <note>Likely Arnobius the Younger, a 5th-century priest and commentator.</note> refers "marvelous" to the stone, not to the whole sentence: *And they confess,* he says, *that they have that marvelous stone in their eyes,* etc. Furthermore, whether you refer it to the stone, or the head, or the corner, the meaning is the same, and it pertains to Christ. 

Since I followed so many weighty authors in my annotation, and since the sense fits our reading perfectly, there has nevertheless appeared a certain person who, with tragic words, exaggerated my "inextricable error" here, seeking a solution from the idiom of the Hebrew language: "The Hebrews," he says, "since they lack a neuter gender, misuse the feminine." He claims this is the case in the third verse of this chapter: *In this [feminine] you shall know*, where in Hebrew it would be *In this.* And in Psalm 11, *In this I have known*, for *In this.* Furthermore, in Psalm 26, the translator even left the Hebrew gender: *One thing [feminine] I have asked of the Lord, this [feminine] I will seek.* He argued almost to this effect. Even if we grant these things to be entirely true, they achieve nothing else except that we understand it *can* be read and translated as the Vulgate Edition has it. It does not follow, however, that it *must* be so, especially since it is a more convenient sense for it to be referred to the "head" or "corner," that is, to Christ, as the most proven interpreters do. Where then is that "inextricable and dangerous error," unless this "new Hebrew" had come to the rescue? I will add something ridiculous: this passage was attacked by two people, as I said; the first confessed that the Hebrew is as I had noted, while the second asserts it is the opposite. Both profess to know Hebrew, and both published their opinions in writing, and meanwhile Erasmus is called "intractable" because he distrusts such monitors. Indeed, I have hardly ever seen two people who agree in a Hebrew matter, whether the fault lies in the language or the men. Furthermore, this testimony is compounded from two places: the first part from Psalm 117, the second from Isaiah chapter 28. Namely, that which follows: *He who falls on this stone,* etc. Not that the Lord is repeating the Prophet's words exactly, but that he is interpreting them while alluding to them. For the Prophet speaks thus, according to the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translation: *He who believes will not be put to shame.* From which the contrary sense is gathered: *He who does not believe will be put to shame.* To not believe is to stumble, and to be put to shame is to be crushed.

Again he sent other servants, <margin>4</margin> saying, 'Tell those invited, Behold, I have prepared my banquet, my bulls and <margin>1 fattened birds</margin> fattened birds are slaughtered, and everything is ready: come to the wedding.' But they neglected it <margin>5</margin> and went away; one <margin>2 to his farm</margin> to his farm, another to his business. The rest seized his <margin>6</margin> servants, and having treated them shamefully, killed them. But when the king <margin>7</margin> heard, he was angry, and sending his armies, he destroyed those murderers and burned their city. Then he said to his servants, 'The wedding <margin>8</margin> feast is indeed ready, but those who were invited were not worthy. Go therefore to the crossroads, and as <margin>9</margin> many as you find, invite to the wedding.' <margin>3 And going out</margin> And those <margin>10</margin> servants going out into the ways, gathered all <margin>4 as many as they found,</margin> as many as they found, <margin>5 bad and good alike: </margin> bad and good alike: <margin>6 and the wedding was filled</margin> and the wedding was filled with guests. But when the king entered <margin>11</margin> to see the guests, he saw there a man not dressed in a wedding garment, and said to him, 'Friend, <margin>12</margin> how did you enter here, not having a wedding garment?' But he was speechless. Then the king said to the <margin>13</margin> ministers, <margin>7 Having bound his feet and hands,</margin> 'Having bound his feet and hands, cast him into the outer darkness: there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.' <margin>8 For many are called, but few are chosen.</margin> For many are called, but few are chosen. <margin>14</margin>

---

<margin>38 Because it will be taken]</margin> <gloss>original: ὅτι</gloss> "because." Which the Translator <note>Refers to the traditional translator of the Vulgate.</note> correctly omitted in several places, but here added without cause; this is more a matter of stubbornness than ignorance or superstition. For if it was a religious duty not to omit anything, why omit it elsewhere? If he omitted it by judgment, why put it here? Likewise,
<margin>39 Producing its fruits]</margin> "Its" refers to the kingdom, not to God: <gloss>original: αὐτῆς</gloss> "of it," which is clear to those reading the Greek. And a little later,
<margin>40 To hold]</margin> <gloss>original: κρατῆσαι</gloss>, which is better rendered as "to seize" or "to lay hands on." And,
<margin>41 As a prophet]</margin> It was more convenient to say "as if a prophet" or "like a prophet." In a very old manuscript, namely the Corsendonk codex, I found it written "they have," using a present tense verb. Although in this place it is somewhat harsh, and another codex (from the Pauline Library) disagrees. Certainly, the Greek is <gloss>original: εἶχον</gloss> "they held."
<margin>1 Fattened birds]</margin> <gloss>original: καὶ τὰ σιτιστά</gloss>. The Latin word *Gravis* would respond nicely. For just as *altilia* [fattened birds] are named from *alendo* [nourishing], so *sitista* comes from *sitos*, which is food or nourishment. Irenaeus, or his translator, elsewhere renders it as "fatted." Furthermore, "killed" is poorly rendered; for <gloss>original: τεθυμένα</gloss> sounds more like "immolated" or certainly "slaughtered," as they were used to holding feasts for sacred weddings. Furthermore,
<margin>2 to his farm]</margin> Not very inconveniently, <gloss>original: εἰς τὸν ἴδιον ἀγρόν</gloss>, that is, "into his own field," to give word for word, or "into his countryside," to express the sense more. Furthermore, a *villa* is a house in the field. And a little further down,
<margin>3 And those servants going out]</margin> <gloss>original: ἐκεῖνοι</gloss>, that is, "those," not "his." Nor is it,
<margin>4 whom they found]</margin> but <gloss>original: ὅσους</gloss>, that is, "as many as they found." Additionally,
<margin>5 bad and good]</margin> In Greek it is <gloss>original: πονηρούς τε καὶ ἀγαθούς</gloss>, that is, "both bad and good," if one wants a word-for-word rendering. Or if in Latin, "whether bad or good," so that you understand no choice was made. For the sense here is that "good" pertains to the Jews, who seem good to themselves even today, and "bad" to the Gentiles. For Christ spoke according to the perspective of the Jews, although both were bad. And soon,
<margin>6 And the wedding was filled with guests]</margin> The Translator, nodding off, left the Greek genitive [possessive form] when he ought to have said "by the guests." For it is not likely that he affected the style of Virgil:
->They are filled with old wine and fat venison.<- <note>A quote from Virgil's Aeneid (1.215), where a genitive is used after a verb of filling.</note>
Now, although one may find "they are filled with old wine," or "he filled all Sicily with his name," or "he filled the allies with hope," you will hardly find "the house is filled of men," unless you disregard the ambiguity. In short, I would allow that the Translator wanted to speak in the manner of Livy here, except that elsewhere he stumbles on the same stone so often that there is no excuse.
<margin>7 from the outer darkness</margin> has already been discussed. In some Greek codices it is read: *Having bound his feet and hands, take him, cast him out into the darkness,* etc. And again,
<margin>8 Called and chosen]</margin> these are nouns in Greek, not participles: <gloss>original: κλητοί</gloss> [called].

...chosen ones and the elect, whereas a little before it was: "Tell those who are invited" <note>original: "Dicite invitatis"</note>.

9 **To entrap him**] <note>original: "παγιδεύσωσιν" (*pagideusōsin*)</note>, that is, to ensnare: like how we catch a wild beast or a bird. Furthermore, 10 **Herodians**] he calls the soldiers of Herod this. This Herod was the son of Antipater, a foreigner and a convert whom Augustus had placed over the Jews after granting him the kingdom, so that he might collect taxes in the name of the Roman Emperor. I see that Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> was of this opinion, whoever he was; I do not agree with the one who treated this passage as slanderous. Theophylact <note>A prominent Byzantine cathedral archdeacon and biblical commentator</note> thinks they were called Herodians not because they were his ministers, but because they were a certain faction of Jews claiming that Herod was the Christ, because a non-Jew was reigning over the Jews for the first time—namely the son of Antipater—which Jerome thinks is ridiculous. In truth, the Pharisees contended that the Jewish people, who paid tithes and were dedicated to God, ought not to pay tribute to Caesar nor obey profane laws. The Herodians, on the other hand, acted on behalf of their Prince. Therefore, they approached Christ together, both groups setting a trap in unison, so that whatever he answered, he would be liable to one of the two factions. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an early Church Father known for his preaching</note> thinks that Theudas and Judas, mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles, died for this reason: because they denied that tribute ought to be paid to Caesar. The author of this doctrine was a certain Judas the Galilean, who added a fourth sect to the Essenes, Sadducees, and Pharisees. See Josephus in the *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 18, chapter 1.

11 **Jesus, knowing their wickedness**] <note>original: "πονηρίαν" (*ponērian*)</note>, that is, malice or craftiness. For *poneria* pertains more to a malicious intent.

12 **Next, why did he not say "inscription" rather than "superscription"?** Since in Greek it is <note>original: "ἐπιγραφὴ" (*epigraphē*)</note>. And a little later,

13 **Render therefore to Caesar**] Christ tempered his response wonderfully: asked insidiously about a worldly matter, he orders a coin to be shown, as if it were unknown to him. Once shown, he acts as if he does not recognize the image or the inscription. When he learned it from them, he did not say absolutely, "Render the things of Caesar to Caesar," but "Render *therefore*." It is as if he said: "If what you say is certain, that these belong to Caesar, pay to him what is his." For not everything that has an image of Caesar is immediately owed to Caesar or the Prince. Perhaps it would not be out of place to mention that the Greek word <note>original: "ἀπόδοτε" (*apodote*)</note> is ambiguous, as it can be taken for "give back" or "you give back," so we may understand that Christ took the opportunity to note the fault of those who, while worried about what was owed to Caesar, did not care more for what was owed to God. You give back to Caesar what has his image; give back also to God what has God's inscription and image—namely, the soul.

14 **If a man dies, having no son**] All the Latin manuscripts I have been able to see agree on this, even the ancient hand-written ones, while the Greek consistently has <note>original: "μὴ ἔχων τέκνα" (*mē echōn tekna*)</note>, that is, "having no children." In Deuteronomy 25, "seed" is used for children, meaning posterity. Perhaps among the Hebrews the name did not pass to descendants except through males, and therefore for the Greeks *tekna* refers to a daughter as much as a son. Even among the Latins, a "parent of children" <note>original: "liberorum parens"</note> is someone who has even a single offspring. For whoever is not childless is called a parent of children. In Mark—

<margin>D</margin> 15 **They will neither marry, nor be given in marriage**] Neither the sense of time nor Latinity has been preserved here. For in Greek it is <note>original: "οὔτε γαμοῦσιν, οὔτε ἐκγαμίζονται" (*oute gamousin, oute ekgamizontai*)</note>, that is, they neither take wives nor are they given in marriage: so that "to marry" <note>original: "γαμεῖν" (*gamein*)</note> pertains to the grooms, and "to be given in marriage" <note>original: "ἐκγαμίζεσθαι" (*ekgamizesthai*)</note> to the girls. For who has ever heard of the Latin word "nubentur"? Although meanwhile the grace of the figure of speech is lost, it could have been preserved as: "they neither take wives, nor are they taken." Augustine, in his *Commentary on the Sermon on the Mount*, first reads: "they will neither marry, nor take wives." But I think the passage has been corrupted by scribes. Again, in his first *Sermon on the words of the Apostle*, except that here, by the inconsistency of the corrupter, "they marry" <note>original: "nubent"</note> is read, not "they will be married" <note>original: "nubentur"</note>, since "they take" follows, following the Greeks. He would have corrupted this <margin>E</margin> passage too, if he had been paying attention. Ambrose likewise cites this passage in his *Exposition of Psalm 118*, eleventh sermon: "they neither marry, nor take wives." For he does not designate a time, but expresses a way of life.

16 **But they will be like the angels of God**] <note>original: "ἀλλ᾿ ὡς ἄγγελοι Θεοῦ εἰσι" (*all' hōs angeloi Theou eisi*)</note>, that is, "but as the angels of God they are." And I found it written in that same way in the ancient Latin copies, specifically in the "Golden Codex," and in a very ancient one which the Church of St. Paul in London provided for this purpose. Also in the one provided by the Canons of the College of Corsendonck in Brabant. Finally, in the one offered by the College of Constance. From which it is sufficiently clear, I think, that in the earlier words the tense was changed by a scribe's error. It shows that some reader thought the resurrection had not yet happened, and for that reason the future tense was more fitting. But Christ indicates that the time of the resurrection is already present. For thus he calls those destined for resurrection "the resurrection," just as he calls those following the Gospel teaching "the kingdom of heaven." The resurrection will appear in us later, but meanwhile <margin>F</margin> the work of resurrection is carried out within us. Indeed, the translator of Origen turns it this way in the twenty-second Homily: "in the resurrection they neither marry, nor take wives, but are like angels in heaven." Therefore, a little later he repeats it, lest anyone should claim it was an accident.

17 **Is not the God of the dead**] In the copies I was able to see, this word "God" was repeated: <note>original: "οὐκ ἔστιν ὁ Θεὸς, Θεὸς νεκρῶν"</note>, that is, "God is not the God, the God of the dead." But I do not find the same in that Translator. From which it is to be conjectured that what was to be understood was added by someone, except that Theophylact, as he reads it, so he repeats it: "God, God."

...legal, <note>original: "legalis"</note> it sounds literally like "legal" or "legitimate," even if I do not condemn what the Translator <note>Erasmus refers to the author of the Vulgate, traditionally St. Jerome</note> rendered. Nor is it,
<margin>20</margin> **With all your heart** ] but "in the whole heart," <note>Greek: "en hole te kardia"</note>. Even if the preposition is superfluous for the Greeks and Latins. And again it is not,
<margin>21</margin> **This is the greatest and first** ] <note>Greek: "proton kai megale"</note>, that is, "first and great," although here "first" meant "foremost." Hilary reads: "which is great and first."
<margin>22</margin> **As yourself** ] <note>Greek: "hos seauton"</note>. For the Greeks, there is a single adverb *hos*, which we Latins barely render with twelve different words. Therefore, those who think this signifies not an equal measure of love but merely a similarity—that we should love our neighbor not as much as ourselves, but with a similar *kind* of love—are quibbling in vain. Their arguments can be shut out if it is translated: "your neighbor just as much as yourself." For this is not the place to refute those who, too much like Aristotle, introduce "orders of charity." I am more pleased by Paul’s analogy of the parts of the body, in which we show even more honor to those parts that are inherently inferior. Furthermore, where the Translator renders "neighbor," the Greek is *ton plesion*. Lest anyone despise this term as un-Latin, since it is frequently encountered in the Sacred Scriptures, it is found in Suetonius’s *Life of Otho*: *They say he pretended to have a high fever, and entrusted that excuse to his neighbors (proximis)*; except that among the Greeks, only intimate friends are called *hoi plesion* <note>meaning "those nearby"</note>. For it is the nature of intimacy to cling to one's side. Nor is it,
<margin>23</margin> **The whole law** ] But "entirely the law," <note>Greek: "olos o nomos"</note>.
<margin>1</margin> **Upon the seat of Moses** ] <note>Greek: "epi tes Moseos kathedras"</note>, that is, in the chair of Moses. Furthermore, for "they have sat," it would be more correctly said "they sit," or "they have taken their seat together," as Augustine cites against Faustus, book 16, chapter 29. In these words, we use the past tense in such a way that we understand the action is still remaining, just as in "they have wept" and "he has approached." Some twist this passage as if one must obey everything that Bishops or superiors—even impious ones—command because of the authority of their office: whereas Christ is speaking of those who were teaching the Mosaic Law correctly, not those who would ensnare men with their own petty little constitutions <note>original: "constitutioniculis"</note>. Thus now, perhaps, a Bishop who teaches the Gospel correctly should be heard, even if he himself lives in a way that is hardly Evangelical. But who could endure those who, for their own profit, exercise mere tyranny over the people with laws fixed and then un-fixed, measuring everything by their own gain and majesty? Those who ensnare the people with little constitutions devised for profit and tyranny do not sit in the Evangelical seat, but in the seat of Simon Magus, or of Caiaphas. And let this be said of bad Bishops—who, I hope, are nowhere to be found—so that the authority of good ones is in no way diminished. It was unnecessary to add this, except that in this age, there is nothing that malice does not gnaw upon.
<margin>2</margin> **Whatever they tell you, observe** ] Among the Greeks, one word is added, "whatever they tell you to keep, keep," <note>Greek: "hosa an eiposi hymin terein, tereite"</note>. However, "tell" is placed according to Greek custom for "commanded."
<margin>3</margin> **To be seen by men** ] <note>Greek: "pros to theathenai tois anthropois"</note>, that is, for the purpose of being watched by men, which is to say, to be a spectacle for men, or to be conspicuous. For the word "spectacle" fits actors <note>Erasmus uses the word "histrionibus," suggesting the Pharisees are like stage performers</note>, as was indicated above. Moreover,
<margin>4</margin> **Phylacteries** ] *Phylacterium* is a Greek word; for Latins, it is "conservatory," because in these the memory of the Law is preserved, from the verb *phylatto* <note>to guard/keep</note>, as if they were performing what God commanded through Moses: that His precepts be kept. For they seem to have taken the occasion for this superstition partly from Deuteronomy, chapter 6: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one Lord. You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength." Then these words: "which I command you today, in your heart, and...

...you shall tell them to your children, and you shall meditate on them sitting in your house, and walking on the journey, sleeping, and rising up. And you shall bind them as a sign on your hand. And they shall be and shall move between your eyes, and you shall write them on the threshold and the doors of your house." Consequently the Pharisees, so that they might seem exceedingly observant of the Law, wrote the Decalogue on parchments, as if in two volumes, one of which they wrapped around their forehead like a crown, and the other on their arm; so that whether they reached out their hand, it was in sight, or if they moved their head, it was before their eyes. Thus, like masked actors, they sold themselves to the eyes of the common people and simple women. Jerome testifies that this custom lasted until his own age among the Jews, Persians, and Babylonians, and that those who did it were regarded among them as religious. Just as today
<margin>D</margin> among us, those are held in high regard who profess holiness to the common people through various and new forms and colors of worship, even though not all of them live up to their outward dress. Partly from Numbers chapter 15, we read there in this manner: *"Speak to the children of Israel, and tell them to make for themselves fringes on the four corners of their cloaks, putting on them ribbons of hyacinth blue, so that when they see them they may remember all the commandments of the Lord."* Indeed, from this, the hypocrites, hunting for popular favor and pursuing profits from simple women, made large fringes, and tied very sharp thorns in them, so that while walking or sitting they would occasionally be pricked, and never be allowed to forget the laws. And whoever carried around the largest fringes was considered more religious among the superstitious and simple. And would that this tribe of actors <note>meaning hypocrites</note> were not so widespread among Christians, compared to whom the Pharisees seem sincere and simple. Not that one should not profess piety even by dress or simplicity of life and cleanliness, but that superstition and ostentation ought everywhere to be absent, and the chief part of piety should be placed in the soul and in character. Jerome condemns in this place the superstition of certain simple women, who did then with little Gospels, and with the wood of the cross, and other 
<margin>F</margin> things of this kind, what the Pharisees once did with phylacteries: *"who have," he says, "a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel."* If that most holy man felt this about simple women, whose weakness was somewhat to be forgiven, what would he say if he were to see today the "Milk of Mary" displayed everywhere for profit, which they honor almost as much as the consecrated body of Christ? Prodigious oil, fragments of the wood of the cross—so many, that if they were collected into a heap, a single cargo ship could hardly carry them; here is displayed the cowl of Francis, there the inner garment of the Virgin Mary, elsewhere the comb of Anne, elsewhere the boot of Joseph, elsewhere the shoe of Thomas of Canterbury, elsewhere the foreskin of Christ: which, though it be an uncertain thing, they adore more religiously than the whole of Christ. Nor are these things brought forward as if some "manufactured" Bishops were leading the way, lest religion seem to have no power anywhere unless they approve them with diplomas and adorn them with their pardons, with such gravity that whenever no approval of theirs is read, I believe it less than they believed before. In which matters, unless there were a grave loss of true piety involved, Christ would not have inveighed so sharply against this kind of men, since he is otherwise gentle toward sinners.
