XXV. 1 Then the kingdom of heaven shall be likened to ten virgins, who took <margin>tza 1</margin> their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom. 2 Now five of them were wise, and five were foolish. 3 Those who were foolish took their lamps but took no oil with them. 4 But the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps. 5 But while the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and slept. 6 And at midnight a cry was heard: "Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him!" 7 Then all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps. 8 And the foolish said to the wise, "Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out." 9 But the wise answered, saying, "No, lest there should not be enough for us and you; but go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves." 10 And while they went to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the wedding; and <margin>e 11</margin> the door was shut. 11 Afterward the other virgins came also, saying, "Lord, Lord, open to us!" 12 But he answered and said, "Truly I say to you, I do not know you." 13 Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour <margin>tzb 14</margin> in which the Son of Man is coming. 14 For it is as a man traveling to a far country, who called his own servants and delivered his goods to 15 them. 15 And to one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, to each according to his own ability; and immediately he went on his journey. 16 Then he who had received the five talents went and traded with them, and made...

---

<margin>γ Do not be called Rabbi]</margin> In several Greek copies, the word "Rabbi" is doubled—*Rabbi Rabbi* <note>original: Ῥαββὶ Ῥαββὶ</note>. In the same way, Judas salutes the Lord: "Rabbi, Rabbi." It seems this doubling carries a sense of honor among the Hebrews; expressing this custom, Christ says, "Not everyone who says to me 'Lord, Lord,' shall enter," etc. Even today, for the sake of honor, we address Priests and Bishops as "Lord" twice. Although I find no certain trace of this in Jerome, Origen, Chrysostom, or Theophylact. Augustine, in his *Annotations on the figures of the Old Testament*, demonstrates that speech is doubled in various ways among the Hebrews; sometimes to signify a multitude or distribution: like that passage in Exodus, according to the old Edition, "And they gathered heaps heaps," as if to say "in heaps." Sometimes it indicates intensity: like that in Jeremiah, "figs good good, and figs bad bad." Occasionally it has a general meaning: like that in Leviticus, "Man man if he curses God, he shall receive his sin," meaning "Whosoever the man may be." Likewise in Numbers, "Men men, if his wife goes astray." Related to this figure is what the Latins also use everywhere, such as *is prontiunque* <note>whosoever</note>, *ubirubi* for *ubicunque* <note>wherever</note>, *qualis qualis* for *qualis-sicunque* <note>of whatever sort</note>. Likewise when they call someone "thrice blessed," they mean "greatly blessed." Now, regarding the figure of speech itself, it should be understood not as a total prohibition on being called teachers, but as a warning against seeking the title out of pride; Augustine discusses this carefully and at length in his *Sermon on the words of the Lord from Matthew 11*.

<margin>δ For one is your teacher]</margin> The Greeks add *the Christ* <note>original: ὁ Χριστός</note>. The same phrase is repeated a little later: "Neither be called masters." If "Rabbi" sounds the same as "Masters," he seems to have said the same thing twice, having said just above: "Do not be called Rabbi." Unless perhaps "Rabbi" is the title for a preceptor, namely one who teaches: which is why among the Hebrews the word refers to a multitude of sciences. Some Greek codices do not repeat the same word in both places; in the first place they have *didaskalos* <note>original: διδάσκαλος</note>, which sounds like "doctor" or "teacher" and corresponds to the word Rabbi. In the second place is put *kathegetes* <note>original: καθηγητής</note>, which signifies a governor or moderator of life.

<margin>9 Who shut]</margin> <note>original: ὅτι κλείετε</note> that is, "because you shut," not "who," as supported by both the Pauline Latin codex and the one followed by the Amerbach brothers. In a correction found in the Constance manuscript, it was declared that "because" had been written. And soon after, "who travel around the sea," <note>original: ὅτι περιάγετε</note> that is, "because you travel around," just as above, "because you devour" <note>original: ὅτι κατεσθίετε</note>: it appears this was done in both places by the error of scribes, though it matters little to the sense.

<margin>10 Long, extended prayers]</margin> In Greek it is <note>original: καὶ προφάσει μακρὰ προσευχόμενοι</note>, that is, to render it word for word, "and by pretext praying long," that is, under the pretext of a long prayer, by which they hunted for a reputation of holiness. For so it is translated in Mark, "under the cover of a long prayer." And in Luke, "feigning a long prayer." The translator of Origen renders it "praying with a long opportunity." He, however, seems to have read it differently. Nor is it...

<column-break/>

7 [They love] to sit in the first place in assemblies, and greetings in the marketplace, and to be called by men Rabbi <gloss>γ</gloss>. 8 But you, do not be called Rabbi: for one is your teacher, namely Christ <gloss>δ</gloss>: and you are all brothers. And call no man your father on earth: for one 9 is your Father, who is in heaven. Neither be 10 called masters: for one is your master, namely Christ. He who is greatest among you shall be 11 your servant. Whoever exalts himself shall be 12 humbled: and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted. But woe to you Scribes and Pharisees, 13 hypocrites, because you shut <gloss>ε</gloss> the kingdom of heaven before men: for you do not enter, nor do you permit those arriving <gloss>D</gloss> to enter. Woe 14 to you Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you devour the houses of widows <gloss>ζ</gloss>, and that under the pretext of a long prayer: because of this you will be punished more severely. Woe 15 to you Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you travel around sea and dry land <gloss>11</gloss> to make one proselyte: and when he has been made, you make him a son of Gehenna twice as much as you are <gloss>12</gloss>. Woe to you 16 blind guides, because you say, "Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing: but whoever swears by the gold of the temple, he is a debtor" <gloss>13</gloss>. 17 Fools and blind: for which is 17 greater? The gold, or the temple that sanctifies the gold? And "whoever swears by the altar, it is 18 nothing: but whoever swears by the gift that is upon it, he is a debtor." Fools and blind, for which 19 is greater? The gift, or the altar that sanctifies the gift? He therefore who swears by the altar, swears 20 by it and by all things that are upon it. And he 21 who swears by the temple, swears by it and by him who dwells in it. And he who swears by heaven, 22 swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it. Woe to you Scribes and Pharisees, hypo- 23 crites, because you tithe mint and anise and cumin, and have left behind the weightier things of the Law: judgment and mercy and faith. These you ought to have done, and not to omit the others.

---

<margin>D</margin> The conjunction "and" <note>original: καὶ</note> is not idle here. For he feels they are to be punished more severely because they not only fill their bellies with the wealth of widows, whose poverty they ought rather to have helped, but they also do an impious thing under the pretext of piety—a point which Chrysostom also carefully noted. For let that passage correct certain people today, who by a similar craft devour houses, not only of widows, but of wives, virgins, old men, youths, peasants, and even Princes; and they do not just devour them, but also contaminate and infect them. Chrysostom in this place taxes these "bellies" who are a pestilence to the world.

<margin>11 Sea and dry land]</margin> In the Hebrew manner, he calls the land "the dry" <note>original: τὴν ξηράν</note>. And "proselyte" is a Greek word <note>original: προσήλυτος</note>, meaning a newcomer to us. For so the Hebrews called one whom they had received from a foreign nation into the fellowship of their law. And next,

<margin>12 And you make him a son of Gehenna twice as much as you]</margin> In Greek it is *diploteron hymon* <note>original: διπλότερον ὑμῶν</note>, that is, "more doubly than you are." As if both are sons of Gehenna for a double reason, but this newcomer more than they. Thus Augustine cites it in the second book *Against the Letters of Petilian*, chapter 72: "You make him a son of Gehenna more doubly than yourselves." For that is what the Greek speech sounds like: even if everyone else interprets it differently: namely, that we should understand those men to be evil on only one account, because they did not keep the Law in which they were born; but the newcomer on a double account: first because he was a Pagan and idolater, and next because he is not even an honest Jew, while he slides back into his former life, and from a bad Pagan becomes a worse Jew. Perhaps this also pertains to our customs, we who think it a great thing to have enticed a Jew to baptism. Not that this is not to be hoped for by all of us, that all Jews should repent: but that some seek their own glory from that business, and do not entice them by the proper way, and do not teach the one enticed those things which are truly of Christianity. For how can it be that we make others Christians, unless we ourselves have first been Christians? It happens, therefore, sometimes, that for one wicked Jew we have a more wicked Christian—a thing to which even Spain can bear witness. And there are those who, by a new example, make Christians by arms, under the pretext of expanding religion, looking out for their own wealth and their own dominion. Nothing will be achieved by these things, unless the business is undertaken with a purely Christian mind. To this is related what some Monks do, who partly by craft, partly by a zeal for piety but without judgment, entice whomever they can into their own way of life, especially those they predict will be of use to them; and with marvelous tricks they lay snares for those of a raw and simple age, which does not yet know itself, nor true Religion.

<margin>13 He is a debtor]</margin> <note>original: ὀφείλει</note> he owes, that is, he is guilty, and a debtor to punishment: because the Law forbids swearing by the name of God. This whole passage pertains to those who, while they keep silent before the people about the head of all religion, insist on things that pertain less to the matter: such as the power of the Pope, pardons, and the opinions of the Thomists or Scotists.

<margin>14 Fools and blind]</margin> In the Greek, this is repeated in the second place as well: *Moroi kai typhloi* <note>original: Μωροὶ καὶ τυφλοί</note>.

<margin>D</margin> 15 **Who clean** <note>original: "Qui mundatis"</note>] <note>original: "ὅτι καθαριζετε"</note>, that is, "because you clean." This agrees with our emendations, especially the "Golden" manuscript. Furthermore, regarding the phrase **the inside of the cup and the outside**: what is said elegantly in Greek is rendered somewhat clumsily in Latin as "the outside and the inside" <note>original: "τὸ ἔξωθεν καὶ τὸ ἐντὸς"</note>. It could have been translated as "the exterior part of the cup" and "that which is inside." It is not there.

16 **You are full** <note>original: "Pleni estis"</note>] Rather, "they are full" <note>original: "γέμουσιν"</note>, so that it refers not to the Pharisees, but to the cup and the plate. The ancient Latin codices agree with the Greek copies. In the Constance manuscript, the true reading had been erased by a corrupt one. For the sense is: **the cups and plates of the Pharisees are clean and polished on the outside, but the wine and food within them are unclean, being obtained through robbery and fraud.** It is this internal uncleanness that should be avoided by those who wish to appear truly clean. Since some did not understand this, they translated "of injustice" <note>original: "ἀδικίας"</note> as "of uncleanness." However, in several copies I find "of intemperance" <note>original: "ἀκρασίας"</note>, which Origen seems to have read. Our translator seems to have read "of impurity" <note>original: "ἀκαθαρσίας"</note>. In short, this passage seems to have been recorded differently by Chrysostom and other ancients. Augustine, in his thirty-seventh sermon, says "You are full of guile and robbery," but I believe he was explaining Luke. Furthermore, a *paropsis* <note>original: "παροψὶς"</note> is a small dish or bowl to the Greeks, used for serving food or seasoning. Since among the Italians each person is served their own small dish with the meal distributed into portions, it was parsimony that invented the common platter. The word *paropsis* is read in the same sense in Suidas; the term clearly comes from its roundness and curvature.

17 **Because you are like**] The genuine reading remains with us, I know not by what chance, while "who clean" was corrupted in many. And **whitewashed** <note>original: "dealbatis"</note> is <note>original: "κεκονιαμένοις"</note>, that is, "plastered," which is called "white-work." For they are plastered with gypsum or lime. And,

18 **You appear** <note>original: "Φαίνεσθε"</note>] Why not rather use "you are seen" or "you seem"?

<margin>F</margin> 19 **Who build**] <note>original: "ὅτι οἰκοδομεῖτε"</note>, that is, "because you build." To be clear,

20 **If we had been, we would not have been**] For "If we had been, we would not have been," the same verb is repeated in Greek <note>original: "ἤμεν, οὐκ ἤμεν"</note>, or as written in some, <note>original: "ἤμεθα"</note>. Origen rightly raises a question here: why does He curse the Pharisees on this account? For they are not to be cursed because they built monuments for the Prophets, nor because they were descended from the murderers of the Prophets; for the former is a duty, and the latter is not in our power—where we are born. But they are rebuked because they built the monuments of the saints to simulate holiness, while falsely denying they would have consented to their slaughter had they lived in those times, when in fact they showed they would be even more cruel to the Prophets by preparing to kill Christ himself. Chrysostom adds that they built the monuments not out of zeal for the Prophets, but so that a trophy of [their ancestors' crime might remain]...

...[so that others would be deterred] from the freedom of rebuking them. Furthermore, concerning Zacharias son of Barachias, the question is more difficult and has not yet been fully explained by anyone. Some bring up a story from apocryphal books: that there was a certain designated place in the temple where virgins sat during the performance of sacred rites. While Mary, the mother of Jesus, stood there—it being already known she had given birth, though the common people did not understand she had conceived by divine power—the people took offense. Here, when she was defended by Zacharias, the father of John, he was killed during a riot between the inner sanctuary and the altar. This is roughly Origen's view, and Jerome says much the same, except he varies by saying Zacharias the father of John the Baptist was killed because he preached the coming of Christ. Others refer it to Zacharias the son of Barachias, who is the eleventh among the twelve Prophets. However, although the father's <margin>E</margin> name agrees in this case, it is not very likely, since nothing of this sort is found in the divine histories regarding Zacharias the Prophet. Moreover, at that time there were hardly any ruins of the temple. A third opinion is more likely: that we understand it as Zacharias the son of Jehoiada, whom King Joash killed between the altar and the temple, as recorded in the books of Kings and Chronicles. The event and the name agree, only the father's name stands in the way, as he is written as the son of Jehoiada, not Barachias. They escape this latter difficulty in two ways: Jerome testifies that in the "Gospel of the Nazarenes," when this story is told, Zacharias is called the son of Jehoiada, not Barachias—suggesting that "Barachias" was written for "Jehoiada" by a scribal error in the codices. Chrysostom opens another window: that the man Barachias was also called Jehoiada.

21 **Offspring of vipers**] <note>original: "γεννήματα"</note>, which he had correctly translated earlier as "progeny."

22 **Who kills the prophets**] <note>original: "ἡ ἀποκτεινουσα"</note>. Since the present participle is used, and Christ’s speech looks toward both times, the act can be understood without a specific time frame—as if you were to say, "the murderess of prophets," who has killed, is killing, and will kill. I mention this because I see Origen is greatly tormented in explaining the historical logic, since we nowhere read of many Prophets being killed or stoned in Jerusalem. I believe that by the name "Jerusalem," which was the capital of Judea, the entire region is understood.

23 **And under its wings**] Someone added "its own" <note>original: "suas"</note> of their own accord. It is not in the Greek, nor in the golden codex, nor in the Constance manuscript. It is not there.

24 **Behold, it is left**] Not in the future tense, but the present, <note>original: "ἀφίεται"</note>, that is, "it is left," supported by ancient Latin copies.

1 **But he responding said**] In the Greek, there is no "he" nor "responding," for the disciples asked nothing; rather, "But Jesus said to them." It is not there.

2 **You see these things**] But "Do you not see these things?" <note>original: "Οὐ βλεπετε ταυτα"</note>. This is how Theophylact also reads it. And,

<margin>A</margin> 3 **There shall not be left here a stone** <note>Matthew 24:2</note>] "Here" in this place is an adverb, 
*hode* <note>original: "ωδε"</note>, that is, in this structure. Indeed, the disciples 
were showing him the structures of the temple with the intention that Christ, moved by the 
magnificence of the work, might change his mind and not allow to happen what he had 
previously predicted would occur; or certainly they felt the work was too 
great or too fortified for anyone to be able to demolish it.
4 **unto the Mount of Olives**] *elaion* <note>original: "ελαιών"</note>, that is, of olives. And 
shortly after,
5 **Secretly**] *kat’ idian* <note>original: "κατ' ιδίαν"</note>, that is, apart, or privately: that is, 
with the crowds removed. And a little further down,
6 **Wars and opinions of wars** <note>The Vulgate uses "opiniones" (opinions) where modern Bibles say "rumors."</note>] *polemous kai akoas polemon* <note>original: "πολέμους και ακοάς πολέμων"</note>, 
that is, wars and rumors, or the fame of wars. In-
deed, *akoas* literally sounds like "hearings." The Translator makes no 
distinction between a battle and a war. Furthermore, "opinion" is sometimes 
found used for "fame," but only when it refers to a person, 
not to a thing. Otherwise, an "opinion of war" exists whenever a war is thought to exist 
when it does not. However, a rumor of war is sometimes more grim 
than the war itself.

<column-break/>

7 **For these things must happen**] In place of "these," the Greeks read *ta panta* <note>original: "τα πάντα"</note>, 
that is, "all things."
8 **But the end is not yet**] Several manuscripts have *estai* <note>original: "ήται"</note>, 
that is, the end "will be."
9 **Pestilence and fames**] The Latin 
Translator could not render the pleasant similarity of the sounds in *limoi* and *loimoi* <note>original: "λιμοι, & λοιμοί"</note>, which 
can be distinguished more by spelling than by pronunciation. Furthermore, there is a grace 
in the similar word endings across three terms: *limoi, loimoi, seismoi* (famines, plagues, earthquakes). 
And the word "shall be heard" adds to the harmony. And,
10 **False prophet**] This is a single compound word, which the uneducated 
common folk divide: *pseudoprophetai* <note>original: "ψευδοπροφήται"</note>. It does not mean a 
lying prophet, but one who is called a prophet by a false name, when 
he is not: just like "false apostles," who claim that title 
falsely for themselves.
11 **Because iniquity shall abound**] *dia to plethynthenai ten anomian psygesetai he agape ton pollon* <note>original: "δια το πληθυνθήναι την ανομίαν ψυγήσεται η αγάπη των πολλών"</note>. 
The infinitive verb of the past tense, because it is attached to a verb of the future tense, passes 
into the force of the future itself. Although it would have been more conveniently translated 
using a participle in this manner: "With iniquity multiplied, the charity of 
many will grow cold," as Saint Jerome cites in several places. Except 
that here the force of the preposition is not rendered, *dia to* <note>original: "δια το"</note>, which makes us 
understand that the coldness of charity proceeds from nowhere else than from the 
magnitude of iniquity.
12 **And then shall the consummation come**] *telos* <note>original: "τέλος"</note>, which he has translated 
as "end" up to this point. And both a little above and here he adds the article, *to telos* <note>original: "το τέλος"</note>, 
as if you were to say, "that end which was expected." For the article makes 
you understand a certain specific end.
13 **By Daniel**] *dia Daniel* <note>original: "δια Δανιηλ"</note>, that is, through Daniel. Moreover, 
there is a passage in this Prophet at the end of the ninth chapter: "He shall confirm 
the covenant with many for one week, and in the half of the week 
the victim and the sacrifice shall fail, and there shall be in the temple the abomi-
nation of desolation, and even until the consummation and the end shall 

<page-num>124</page-num>
# CHAPTER XXIV.

<margin>D</margin> **desolation continue.** Furthermore, what the Greek calls *bdelygma* <note>original: "βδέλυγμα"</note>, that is, 
an abomination or a curse, is understood in this place as an idol, 
according to the interpretation of Jerome. And some interpret this regarding the statue of Hadrian Caesar, 
which had stood until the age of Jerome in that 
place where the Holy of Holies had previously been, and for that reason he adds 
"of desolation," because the temple had been destroyed. And some manuscripts 
had *ta ek ton oikias* <note>original: "τα εκ των οικίας"</note>, that is, domestic things, or 
household furniture.
14 **On the roof**] *epi tou domatos* <note>original: "επι τω δώματος"</note>, he understands either an upper room, or 
the roof itself, upon which the Ancients used to walk. However, it is not 
simply,
15 **Let him not return**] but *me epistrepsato opiso* <note>original: "μη επιστρεψάτω οπίσω"</note>, that is, let 
him not turn back, which is both more Latin and clearer: let him not return again. 
Nor is it,
16 **To take his coat**] but *ta himatia* <note>original: "τα ιμάτια"</note>, that is, garments, 
or cloaks—that is, the outer clothing. Although Hilary reads "coat."
17 **To those with child and those giving suck**] He rightly changed "those with child" 
and expressed it more in the Latin style than if he had rendered the Greek as it is, *tais en 
gastri echousais* <note>original: "ταίς εν γαστρί εχούσαις"</note>, that is, "to those having in the womb," as he is otherwise 
accustomed to translate. Furthermore, regarding "giving suck," the Greek is more specific, *thelazousais* <note>original: "θηλαζούσαις"</note>, 
meaning "those lactating," or "nourishing from the breast," because it signifies the 
nipple of the female breast. Hence Augustine, explaining 
Psalm thirty-nine, used "breast-feeding" instead of "nourishing." 
He likewise cites this in the 15th book of *On the Trinity*, chapter 15, according to the reliability of the ancient 
handwritten copies. Nor is it,
18 **In winter or of the sabbath**] but *cheimonos mede en sabbato* <note>original: "χειμώνος μηδέ εν σαββάτω"</note>, that is, 
"neither in winter nor on the sabbath." Winter is inconvenient for making a journey. 
And on the sabbaths it was a sin for the Jews to make a journey, except for a few furlongs. 
For Christ perceives that they must flee very quickly and far away, and therefore 
warns that nothing should stand in the way of the speed of flight. A large part of the Gospel 
understanding is situated in figures of speech.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> "Amen I say to you, there shall not be left here one stone

shall say...

---

<margin>19</margin> **Until now**] *mechri tou nyn* <note>original: "μέχρι του νυν"</note>, that is, up to the present time, 
or what was clearer, "until now," even if this is somewhat poor Latin.
<margin>20</margin> **Nor shall be**] *oude me genetai* <note>original: "ουδέ μη γένηται"</note>, that is, "nor may it happen," so as to be 
the expression of one who detests the idea. Although I see that they sometimes 
misuse these words for the future, if a double negative *ou me* precedes. Furthermore, the 
accumulation of three negatives has an emphasis of denial.
<margin>21</margin> **Unless they had been shortened**] *ekolobothesan* <note>original: "εκολοβώθησαν"</note>, that is, they had been 
cut short, as when something is amputated and clipped. Hence for the Greeks *koloboi* 
are those who pronounce words truncated and halved. 
Nor is it,
<margin>22</margin> **Would be saved**] but *ouk an esothe* <note>original: "ουκ αν εσώθη"</note>, that is, "by no means would have been 
saved," or "in no way would all flesh have been unharmed." And 
again, according to the Hebrew custom, he used "flesh" for "man," although 
"flesh" has a certain more absolute quality: just as when the Latins say 
"all mortals" for "all men." For there are mortals who are not men: 
and there is flesh which is not of a man. Whether that ought to be 
mentioned, I do not know.

# ACCORDING TO MATTHEW. CHAPTER 24 / 26.

<margin>A</margin> 8 ...on his head as he reclined at the table. But seeing this, his disciples were indignant, saying: "To what purpose is this waste? 9 For this ointment could have been sold for much, and given to the poor." 10 But Jesus, knowing this, said to them: "Why do you trouble the woman? For she has done a good work for me. 11 For you always have the poor with you; <margin>12</margin> 12 but me you do not always have. For in pouring this ointment on my body, she did it for my burial. 13 Truly I say to you, wherever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, what she has done shall also be told as a memorial of her." <margin>14</margin> 14 Then one of the twelve, called Judas Iscariot, went to the <margin>B</margin> chief priests, 15 and said: "What will you give me, and I will deliver him to you?" And they appointed for him thirty pieces of silver. 16 And from then on he sought an opportunity to betray him. 17 Now on the first day of unleavened bread, the disciples came to Jesus, saying to him: "Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?" <margin>18</margin> 18 And he said: "Go into the city to a certain man, and say to him: 'The Teacher says, My time is near; I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples.'" 19 And the disciples did as Jesus had commanded them; and they prepared <margin>20</margin> the Passover. 20 Now when evening had come, he reclined with the <margin>21</margin> twelve. 21 And as they were eating, he said: "Truly I say to you, that one of you will betray me." <margin>22</margin> 22 And they, being exceedingly sorrowful, began each of them to say to him: "Is it I, Lord?" <margin>23</margin> <margin>C</margin> 23 And answering, he said: "He who dips his hand with me in the dish, he will betray me."

---

> **23 Behold, here is Christ]** This is an adverb, not a pronoun, <note>original: "ὧδε" (hōde)</note>: and "the Christ," <note>original: "ὁ Χριστὸς"</note>, that Christ, so that you understand a specific person. The speech is more elegant without the addition of the verb "is" <note>original: "ἐστὶ"</note>, which is not added in the "golden manuscript." In Constantinople, some interloper had written "is" <note>original: "ἐστὶ"</note> in a barbaric hand. For it does not mean just any "anointed one" among many, but that unique one who was expected by everyone. St. Augustine, in explaining this passage in his *Evangelical Questions*, rightly interprets that these words exclude the schisms of Heretics, but we must take care that they do not also apply to us, who seem to ourselves to be Orthodox. We hear Monks everywhere shouting (I speak of the superstitious, not the pious), *Behold, here is Christ*, yet these men do not even agree among themselves. The Observants say, "Christ is not among the Coeletans or Conventuals, but here he is." The Jacobites cry, "Here is Christ," and say he is not among the Augustinians. Again, the Benedictines cry, "Here is Christ," and not among the Mendicants. Finally, this whole class of people cries out, "Here is Christ," and says that among the Priests who do not wear the cowl, "Christ is not." And from every side the voices of those crying out are deafening, "Here is Christ." But what does Christ himself say? Do not believe them. Christ is not divided; he is not in physical things. Christ is nowhere absent, wherever there are dispositions worthy of Christ. He wishes to be common to all, he who is the Sun of the world. He does not deign to be circumscribed by a place, nor included by human titles, or by worship and ceremonies. Finally, he does not wish to be pointed out with a finger, but wishes to be expressed through our affections. Here I must testify again that I do not condemn ceremonies which lead to piety; I condemn discord and superstitious confidence. I wish that the piety of all would progress so far that these words of mine might seem to have been said without cause, or at least be spoken with as much fruit as they are spoken by us with a sincere heart.
> **24 False Christs]** This is a single word, <note>original: "ψευδόχριστοι" (pseudochristoi)</note>, lest anyone should divide it—that is, those with a false name of Christ, which we just indicated. Likewise, for the phrase "so as to deceive" <note>original: "ὥστε πλανᾶσθαι"</note>, I would have preferred to translate it as *so that they are to be deceived*, because of the future tense words to which these refer.
> **25 If it can be done]** <note>original: "εἰ δυνατόν" (ei dynaton)</note>. Why not rather, *if it might be possible*?
> **26 If in the secret chambers]** In Greek it is <note>original: "ἐν τοῖς ταμείοις" (en tois tamieiois)</note>, which was previously translated as *in the bedrooms*. For *tamieia* are hidden and more inner places in houses, in which we store things we want to be safe. From this, the Latin *penitus* (inwardly) and *penus* (pantry) are derived.
> **27 As lightning]** <note>original: "ὥσπερ ἀστραπή" (hōsper astrapē)</note>. Nothing is swifter than lightning, and although lightning does not actually stretch from the East all the way to the West, it seems so to us. Certainly, in a very short time it covers an immense space. This cannot be understood as the "lightning" of the sun; for the sun rises gradually, and its arrival is felt long before it appears. Finally, *astrapē* means nothing other than lightning. Nor does lightning truly flash from the highest heaven, but from the region of the clouds; and the Lord does not say that lightning reaches from the East to the West, but that flashing from the East it suddenly appears in a different part of the sky. Luke says it flashes from under heaven to the things under heaven. But if someone says Christ is not speaking in the manner of Poets about appearances, but about truths, it must be said that to express the sudden and unexpected but universally conspicuous arrival of Christ, it is sufficient to adapt what appears to our eyes. Thunder is expected once lightning is seen, but when lightning is about to break forth, it is signaled by no indicator; before you expect it, it has already flashed and gone.
> **28 Wherever the body shall be]** For the Greeks it is <note>original: "πτῶμα" (ptōma)</note>, that is, a carcass, named by them from "falling" <note>original: "πίπτειν"</note>, just as *cadaver* (carcass) is named by the Latins from "falling" <note>original: "cadere"</note>. For he is speaking of the body of a dead living thing. And Origen frequently cites this passage this way in his thirtieth Homily. Although Jerome, frequently citing this passage, reads "body" <note>original: "corpus"</note> not "carcass" <note>original: "cadaver"</note>, he nevertheless notes that "carcass" is said more significantly.

believe it. For 24 false Christs and false prophets <margin>24</margin>
will arise, and will give great signs and wonders,
so that they might be led into error, 25 if it were possible, even <margin>25</margin>

wh— <margin>42</margin>

---

<margin>A</margin> Chrysostom, in his seventieth Homily, reads "body" <note>original: "σῶμα"</note> not "carcass" <note>original: "πτῶμα"</note>, if indeed the Translator is not mistaken. For Theophylact reads *ptōma*, not *sōma*. Likewise, the one who wrote the Homilies on Luke, which we have under the name of Origen, in the sixteenth Homily, reads "carcass." Nor do the Greeks add the conjunction **and** *eagles*, but simply "the eagles" <note>original: "οἱ ἀετοὶ"</note>. For eagles, and especially vultures, fly together to the carcasses of living things.
<margin>B</margin> **29 Will wail]** <note>original: "κόψονται" (kopsontai)</note>, so that you understand an uncontrolled mourning: which occurs when someone, out of the impatience of grief, beats and tears their own body.
<margin>C</margin> **30 With much power and majesty]** <note>original: "μετὰ δυνάμεως καὶ δόξης πολλῆς"</note>, that is, *with much power and glory*. Jerome certainly reads "glory," citing this passage in his Commentaries on Zechariah. Again,
<margin>D</margin> **31 Will send out]** is more than just "will send," <note>original: "ἀποστελεῖ"</note>. Nor is it,
**32 With a trumpet and a great voice]** but <note>original: "μετὰ σάλπιγγος φωνῆς μεγάλης"</note>, that is, *with a trumpet of a great voice*, so that you understand a vocal and far-sounding trumpet; or *with a trumpet in a great voice*: for the Greek speech is ambiguous.
**33 From the heights of the heavens]** <note>original: "ἀπ’ ἄκρων οὐρανῶν"</note>, that is, from the highest heavens, or from the highest summits of the heavens. And what he translates here as *to their ends*, in Greek is <note>original: "ἕως ἄκρων αὐτῶν"</note>, that is, *even to the summits of the same*, or *even to their highest parts*, so that you understand two "heights," the uppermost and the lowermost.
**34 From the fig tree]** The Greek is <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς συκῆς"</note>, from the fig. But because the Latin word is ambiguous [could mean the fruit], he rendered it well by paraphrase [the tree]. And soon after,
<margin>E</margin> **35 Learn the parable]** Here it was certainly more appropriate to speak in Latin as *Learn the similitude, or the comparison*, lest anyone should dream that the fig tree is actually speaking parables.
**36 Should be tender]** He means the bud in the forks of the branches, from which the leaves break out. Nor is it "born" <note>original: "nata"</note>, but "sprouted forth" <note>original: "ἐκφυῇ"</note>.
**37 And know]** <note>original: "γινώσκετε"</note>. This is an ambiguous verb, which he just translated as "you know." I will omit that he skipped over the word "so" <note>original: "ita"</note> because it was not in its place. And,
**38 In the doors]** It was more correct to say *at the doors* <note>original: "in foribus"</note>, or *to the doors*. For this is a proverbial way of speaking by which we signify that something is very near.
**39 This generation]** <note>original: "ἡ γενεὰ αὕτη"</note>. It should be noted in passing that among the Greeks *genea* is sometimes used not for the nation or race itself, but for what the Latins call an "age" <note>original: "ætatem"</note>, sometimes "memory," and sometimes a "century." Whence Nestor is read to have lived for three "generations" <note>original: "γενεὰς"</note>, because he had lasted for three human lifetimes. It seems to be taken in this way in this passage.
<margin>F</margin> **40 Until all things happen]** <note>original: "ταῦτα πάντα"</note>, that is, *all these things*.
**41 Shall not pass away]** <note>original: "παρελεύσονται"</note>. And a little earlier, <note>original: "οὐ μὴ παρέλθῃ"</note>. He seems to misuse these words, especially with the "not" <note>original: "μὴ"</note>: in some places it sounds more like *they may not pass away*, or *they cannot pass away* (in a potential sense).
**42 Nor the angels of the heavens]** It was more expressive to say *not even the angels*. Furthermore, in Mark there is added <note>original: "μηδὲ ὁ Υἱὸς"</note>, that is, *nor the Son*. And St. Jerome admits that this was also added in Matthew in some Latin manuscripts, but is not found in the Greek, especially in the copies of Adamantius and Pierius. Yet from the homilies of Origen, which he wrote on Matthew, it appears that he added the Son, whose words are these: *They did not know concerning that day and hour, neither the angels of the heavens, nor the Son. For the Son prepares the knowledge of that day and hour for the co-heirs of that promise, since he emptied himself.* And a little later: *And preparing everyone whom he wishes to know that day and hour with the holy angels, and with our Lord Jesus Christ himself.* Augustine reads it in the same way in the Homilies he published on Matthew, Sermon 21.

# THE GOSPEL
## CHAPTER 25 / 26

<margin>A</margin> <margin>Section 282, 2</margin> 24 "The Son of Man goes, just as it is written about him; but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if <margin>281, 7</margin> he had not been born." Then Judas, who was betraying him, answered and said, "Is it I, Rabbi?" <margin>281, 7</margin> He said to him, "You have said it." And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and having blessed it, he broke it and gave it to the disciples, and said, "Take, eat; this is <margin>282, 3</margin> my body." And taking the cup, and having given thanks, he gave it to them, saying, "Drink from it, all of you; 28 For this is my blood, the blood of the new covenant, <margin>283, 3</margin> which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. But I say to you, I will not drink from now on of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom." 30 And having sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of <margin>284, 2</margin> Olives. Then Jesus said to them, "All of you will be scandalized <note>offended or stumble in faith</note> because of me this night; for it is written, 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.' 32 But after I have been raised <margin>B</margin> <margin>286, 3</margin> up, I will go before you into Galilee." Peter answered and said to him, "Even if everyone else is scandalized because of you, I will never be scandalized." 34 Jesus said to him, "Truly I say to you, that this night, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times." <margin>C</margin> <margin>288, 2</margin> Peter said to him, "Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you." Likewise also said all the disciples. <margin>289, 3</margin> Then Jesus came with them to a place called Gethsemane, and said to the disciples, <margin>290, 5</margin> "Sit here, while I go over there and pray."

***

<margin>XVI.</margin> ...not only reads it, but also interprets it. Hilary does the same in his exposition of the Canon, saying that the day is unknown to everyone—not only to the angels but also to the Son, ascribing ignorance to him. Chrysostom reads and interprets it in the same way. In the text of Theophylact, by some chance, the phrase about the Son's ignorance is not added, though he interprets it. Finally, Jerome himself follows this reading in the course of his narrative. And since Mark wrote <term>historically</term> <note>original: ἱστορικῶς; meaning as a factual chronicle</note> following Matthew, it is likely he did not add this on his own. Therefore, I suspect this phrase was removed by some to prevent the Arians <note>A 4th-century group who believed Jesus was a created being, lesser than God the Father</note> from having a pretext to claim the Son is lesser than the Father because he shared our ignorance. But if that were the case, it should have been erased from Mark as well, where it is clearly read. It is not appropriate to remove the "occasions of heretics" in this way; otherwise, a good part of the Gospels would have to be erased—especially the verse, "The Father is greater than I." This evil should have been cured by interpretation, not by erasure; with the pen, not the scalpel.

<margin>43 Just as in the days of Noah</margin>
Even if it makes no difference to the sense, the text does not actually say "in the days of Noah," but <term>just as the days of Noah were</term> <note>original: ὥσπερ αἱ ἡμέραι τοῦ Νῶε</note>, that is, "just as those days of Noah," etc.

<margin>44 Marrying and giving in marriage</margin>
<term>Marrying and giving away in marriage</term> <note>original: γαμοῦντες καὶ ἐκγαμίζοντες</note>. Again, he applied "marrying" to the men. He could have said, "taking wives and giving daughters in marriage," so that one refers to the men (or rather both the groom and bride) and the other to the fathers-in-law and mothers-in-law.

<margin>45 One will be taken</margin>
The Latin translator used "one... and one," where he should have translated it "one... and another." Then a scribe, I think, changed the tense of the verbs. For in the Greek it is <term>is left</term> and <term>is taken</term> <note>original: ἀφίεται & παραλαμβάνεται</note>, in the present tense. This "misuse" of tense is not useless; it indicates that the event is certain to happen soon. Christ wanted his followers to be of the opinion that they should always expect that final day of judgment, prepared as if it were coming soon—not because he wanted them to be wrong, but because it truly comes "soon" in the eyes of eternity, even if it comes after several thousand years. Because it is known for certain to be coming, and it is not known when, it is always expected as if it were imminent. We see that Peter, Paul, Jerome, Gregory, and countless others held this opinion. "Two in a bed, one will be taken, and one will be left." The Greek manuscripts do not add this phrase here, nor is it read or explained in Theophylact. Chrysostom, however, explains it; I do not know if it was brought in from elsewhere. It seems to have been added here from Luke chapter 17. Two manuscripts, from St. Donatian and Constance, support the Greek reading. Also, it is not,

<margin>46 If he knew</margin>
but <term>if he had known</term> <note>original: εἰ ᾔδει</note>.

<margin>47 In what hour the thief would come</margin>
Some Greek manuscripts had written <term>in what watch</term> <note>original: ποίᾳ φυλακῇ</note>. This is how Origen reads it in his Homilies. Furthermore, he called the time of the guards a "watch." The ancients divided the night into several shifts, which he elsewhere calls "watches." He presents two characters: the householder on guard and the thief lying in wait. Also, it is not,

<margin>48 He would permit</margin>
but <term>he would have permitted</term> <note>original: εἴασε</note>, or "he would have allowed." He imagines a householder staying awake so his house wouldn't be broken into by thieves, which he wouldn't allow if he knew the time of night the thieves would attack. Furthermore, he wants the "thief" to be understood as that final day, and the "householder" as any one of us. Therefore, since that day tries to creep up like a thief, and the time is uncertain, we must watch continually so it doesn't overwhelm us while we are drowsy. Thus, I wonder why Hilary interprets this "thief" as the devil; although he followed Origen as his source, Origen often interprets the Sacred Scriptures in a rather forced way.

<column-break/>

36 ...[nor the angels] of heaven, but my Father only. <margin>But just as the days of Noah were, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. For just as they were in the days before the</margin> 37 <margin>38</margin> flood, eating and drinking, <margin>contracting marriages and giving in marriage, until that day when Noah entered the ark; and they did not know,</margin> 44 <margin>39</margin> until the flood came and took them all away: so will be the coming of the Son of Man. Then two will be <margin>40</margin> in the field: <margin>45</margin> one is taken, and the other is left. Two women grinding at the mill: one is taken, and the other <margin>41</margin> is left. Watch therefore, for you do not know at what hour <margin>42</margin> your Lord is coming. But know this: <margin>46 43</margin> if the householder had known <margin>47</margin> in what hour the thief would have come, he would surely have watched, and would not <margin>48</margin> have allowed his house to be broken into. Therefore you also be ready: <margin>49</margin> because <margin>44</margin> in the hour you do not think, the Son of Man is coming. <margin>D</margin> <margin>50</margin> Who then is the faithful and wise servant, <margin>51 45</margin> whom the lord has placed <margin>52</margin> over his household, to give them food in due season? Blessed is that servant, whom, <margin>46</margin> when his lord comes, <margin>53</margin> he finds so doing. Truly I say to you, <margin>54</margin> he will appoint him over all his goods. But if that evil servant says in <margin>48</margin> his heart, <margin>55</margin> "My lord delays his coming," and begins to beat his fellow servants, <margin>56</margin> and even to eat and drink with drunkards: The lord of that servant will come <margin>57</margin> on a day when he does not expect him, and at an hour he does not know, <margin>58</margin> and will cut him in two, and place his portion with the hypocrites: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then <margin>XXV. 1</margin> the kingdom of heaven shall be likened to ten virgins, who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom.

***

For there is nothing that should offend us in the dissimilarity of the things or persons being compared. It is enough that the similarity holds for the purpose it is used. A thief creeps in unexpectedly; that fact makes the householder always watch. So that day will overwhelm those not expecting it, unless we are always on guard.

<margin>49 For you do not know at what hour the Son of Man will come</margin>
The Greek reads thus: <term>because in the hour you do not think, the Son of Man comes</term> <note>original: ὅτι ᾗ ὥρᾳ οὐ δοκεῖτε, υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἔρχεται</note>. This is how Chrysostom reads it, or his translator, even if Theophylact (the Greek copy we had) reads it differently.

<margin>50 Who do you think</margin>
<term>Who then</term> <note>original: τίς ἄρα</note>; that is, "who indeed." For Lorenzo Valla prefers this.

<margin>51 Whom he appointed</margin>
<term>He appointed</term> <note>original: κατέστησεν</note> is in the past tense. For he presents what happened as a parable.

<margin>52 His family</margin>
<term>His domestic staff</term> <note>original: θεραπείας</note>, that is, his household, so it is understood he was placed over the servants. To note a difference:

<margin>53 Him</margin>
It would be better to say "should find" or "shall find" when he has come.

<margin>54 Over all his goods</margin>
<term>Over all his possessions</term> <note>original: ἐπὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ὑπάρχουσιν αὐτοῦ</note>; or, as Jerome quotes in some places, "over his entire substance," coming closer to expressing the Greek phrasing. Even so, the translator did not translate it badly.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>55 My lord makes a delay in coming</margin>
<term>He tarries in coming</term> <note>original: χρονίζει ἐλθεῖν</note>, that is, he hesitates to return, or delays his return. And the word "his" is not added; it is simply "fellow servants."

<margin>56 Let him eat and drink</margin>
<term>To eat and to drink</term> <note>original: ἐσθίῃ τε καὶ πίνῃ</note>, so that it depends on the verb "he began." Though in some copies it is "but he eats."

<margin>57 In which he does not hope</margin>
<term>On a day which he does not expect</term> <note>original: ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ᾗ οὐ προσδοκᾷ</note>. It is strange why the Translator chose "not hoping" here, preferring "hope" over "expect," since the Greek is "expect."

<margin>58 And he will divide him</margin>
<term>And he will cut him in two</term> <note>original: καὶ διχοτομήσει</note>; from <term>to cut in two</term> <note>original: διχὰ τέμνειν</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>F</margin> **To meet the bridegroom and the bride]** "And the bride" is not added in the Greek manuscripts. Nor is any mention made of the bride in Chrysostom or Hilary. In Chrysostom's 79th Homily, where he explains this passage, the bride is not named regarding the "meeting," neither in the context usually provided nor in the entire commentary. The same is true for Theophylact. However, in Origen's 32nd Homily, in the title of the Gospel History, someone or other added it, though Origen himself makes no mention of the bride when discussing it—or rather, he mentions it in a way that shows he read only "the bridegroom," not "the bridegroom and the bride." For he explains it this way: "All these senses take their lamps, that is, their natural organs, whether wanting to use them according to the word of God or against the will of God; yet they take them when they receive that the bridegroom is the Church, the word of God, and the Son of God. And they go out from the world and from the errors of many Gods; and they come to meet the Savior, who is always ready to come to those virgins, so that they may enter together with those worthy of them to the blessed bride, the Church." Thus far Origen. From this it is clear that they go out to meet the bridegroom who is going *to* the bride, to lead him to the bride's house. For the bride sits at home, waiting for the bridegroom. She does not go out, as if she were greedy for a man. Likewise in the rest. When the delay of the bridegroom is repeated, and the cry of the assembly "Behold, the bridegroom comes," the bride is silent. In only one place does Origen seem to refer the "meeting" to the bride as well, when he says it is necessary to go out to meet the Bridegroom-Word and the immaculate Church. Yet where he speaks of the cry by which all are called...

<margin>A</margin> Regarding the duty of meeting, it is clear that no mention of a bride is made. For he says, *Behold, the bridegroom comes, go out to meet him*. Nor does it immediately follow that if the commentary mentions a bride, the bride was explicitly mentioned by the Evangelist. For in relative terms, one is understood from the other. No one can conceive of a bridegroom in the mind unless he simultaneously thinks of a bride. For this reason, it could be resolved that Hilary mentions the *bride*, interpreting the bridegroom and bride in the one person of Christ—taking the bridegroom as the divine nature and the bride as the human nature—unless Hilary himself had indicated that he read *to the bridegroom and the bride* <note>original: "sponso & sponsae"</note> with these words: *Finally, at the sounding of the trumpet, they went out to meet only the bridegroom. For both were now one, because the humility of the flesh had passed into spiritual glory*. From these words, it appears that Hilary read *to the bridegroom and the bride* in the first instance, but only *to the bridegroom* in the second. Nor does Jerome make any mention of the bride in his commentary on this passage. Although there is no reason for anyone to contend over this matter. But if anyone finds *the bride* added elsewhere, let them understand that the bride also sometimes meets the bridegroom, so that the companions of the bridegroom may rightly be said to have met both. The bridegroom is Christ, and this whole parable looks to him, so that we may go to meet him as he arrives through faith and pious deeds. No part of the parable pertains to a bride; rather, those very ones who meet him well are the bride, even if it does not escape me that in Augustine, the mention of the *bride* is added in the one hundred and twentieth Epistle. But again, in the twenty-second Sermon on the words of the Lord from Matthew, explaining this passage, he neither reads nor comments on the word "bride."

<margin>B</margin> 2 *They did not take* <note>original: "Non sumpserunt"</note> ] <gloss>ouk elabon</gloss>. It was more fitting to say *they had not taken* <note>original: "sumpserant"</note>. For in these cases, we misuse the imperfect past or the second indefinite in place of the pluperfect.
3 *Lest perhaps they do not suffice* <note>original: "Ne forte non sufficiant"</note> ] <gloss>mepote</gloss>, that is, *lest they do not suffice*: or if you prefer to express the completion of the conjunction, *lest at any time it not be enough*. And it is not simply "no."
4 *Buy for yourselves* <note>original: "Emite vobis"</note> ] <gloss>poreuesthe mallon</gloss>, that is, *go, buy for yourselves*. Moreover, it is an incomplete sentence, unless you understand *we fear*, or *there is a danger*, or *we will not do it*. For it is understood, though not explained, that the prudent virgins denied them the oil.
5 *While they went to buy* <note>original: "Dum irent emere"</note> ] <gloss>aperchomenon de auton agorasai</gloss>, that is, *while they were going away to buy, the bridegroom came*, etc.
6 *Lastly* <note>original: "Novissime"</note> ] <gloss>Hysteron</gloss>, that is, *Then, or Later*. While this might be tolerable elsewhere, it certainly does not fit here, since he is speaking of two orders of virgins. Truly, it is not added in the Greek, nor in the Golden Codex, nor even in the Constantian one, except that here too someone had added "truly" with a different hand.
7 *Watch therefore* <note>original: "Vigilate itaque"</note> ] Some add *and pray*, which is found neither in the Greek nor in our more corrected copies. Indeed, Theophylact, in his commentary, neither reads nor touches upon this entire little section, just as neither Origen nor Hilary do; although Jerome both reads and interprets it quite diligently. Similarly Chrysostom. If it is an addition, it seems it could have been transcribed from Mark chapter 13.
8 *Because you know neither the day nor the hour* <note>original: "Quia nescitis diem neque horam"</note> ] In this place, the Greek codices repeat what was added above, *in which the Son of man will come* <note>original: "en hei ho Huios tou anthropou erchetai"</note>.
9 *His goods* <note>original: "Bona sua"</note> ] <gloss>ta hyparchonta</gloss>, *his resources, or his substance*, as we noted above.
10 *Proper ability* <note>original: "Propriam virtutem"</note> ] <gloss>dynamin</gloss>, that is, *faculty, or power: so that it pertains to strength, not to moral uprightness*.
11 *And he gained* <note>original: "Et lucratus est"</note> ] <gloss>kai ekerdese</gloss>, that is, *he made or produced*. And more in the Latin style,

13 *He came, & he settled* <note>original: "Venit, & posuit"</note> ] Both are in the present tense, <gloss>erchetai, kai synairei</gloss>, that is, *he comes, and he subducts (draws up the account)*. And a little after,

And a little before the servant speaks thus, *you reap where you did not sow*, which words the lord throws back at the servant. And it is not,

Although the Translator rendered the sense well. And I found *to send* <note>original: "mittere"</note> in the Golden Codex. # 131 GOSPEL CHAPTER XXVI. 132

<margin>51</margin> [One of those with Jesus] stretched out his hand, drew his sword, and striking the servant of the High Priest, cut off his <margin>ear 52</margin> ear. Then Jesus says to him, "Return your sword to its place; for all who take up the <margin>53</margin> sword shall perish by the sword. Or do you think that I cannot now call upon my Father, and he will provide for me more than twelve legions of angels? <margin>54</margin> How then would the scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen this way?" <margin>55 In</margin> In that hour, Jesus said to the crowds, "Have you come out as against a robber with swords and clubs to seize me? Daily I sat with you teaching in the <margin>temple 56</margin> temple, and you did not arrest me. But all this has happened so that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled." Then all the <margin>disciples 57</margin> disciples deserted him and fled. Those who had seized Jesus led him away to Caiaphas the High Priest, <margin>where 58</margin> where the Scribes and the Elders were gathered. But Peter followed him from a distance as far as the courtyard of the High Priest; and going inside, he sat with the <margin>servants 59</margin> servants to see the end. Now the High Priests and the Elders and the whole council sought false testimony against Jesus, so that they might put him to death. <margin>60</margin> And they found none; even though many false witnesses came forward, they found <margin>none 61</margin> none. But finally two false witnesses came forward and said, “This man said: ‘I am able to destroy the temple of <margin>62</margin> God, and build it in three days.’” And standing up, the High Priest said to him, “Do you answer nothing? What is it <margin>these</margin> these men testify against you?” But Jesus remained silent. And answering, the High Priest said to him, “I adjure you by the living God, that you tell us if you are the Christ, <margin>64</margin> the Son of God.” Jesus says to him, “You have said it. Nevertheless, I say to you, from now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of power, and coming <margin>65</margin> on the clouds of heaven.” Then the High Priest tore his robes, saying, “He has blasphemed! What further need have we of witnesses? Look, now you have heard his <margin>blasphemy 66</margin> blasphemy. What do you think?” And they answering <margin>67</margin> said, “He is guilty of death.” Then they spat in his face and struck him with their fists; others slapped him, saying, “Prophesy to us, Christ, who is <margin>who hit 68</margin> the one who hit you?” Now Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard; and a servant girl came to him, saying, “You also were [with Jesus]...”

<margin>A</margin> to put or cast. The Greeks use the word *katabalein* <note>original: "Καταβαλεῖν"</note> for those who count out ready money, and the word for purse, *balantion* <note>original: "βαλάντιον"</note>, seems to be derived from the fact that money is "cast" into it.

<margin>21 And what he seems to have]</margin> *and that which he has* <note>original: "καὶ ὃ ἔχει"</note>. Hilary also reads it this way, from which it appears this was transcribed here from the other Evangelist, as it seemed absurd to take anything away from one who has nothing.

<margin>22 Of his majesty]</margin> *of his glory* <note>original: "δόξης"</note>. For the translator frequently delights in rendering it this way.

<margin>23 And he shall separate them from one another]</margin> Although the word "nations" preceded it, the translator used the masculine "them," which cannot be blamed on the translator since it is found this way in the Greek. However, "from one another" *could certainly have been rendered more Latinately as "he will separate them, some from others, or the ones from the others," since he is speaking of two ranks, one of the godly and the other of the ungodly.* Furthermore,

<margin>B</margin> <margin>24 You gathered]</margin> He beautifully translates *synagagete* <note>original: "Συναγάγετε"</note> as "you have collected" or "received into hospitality" a <gloss>wandering</gloss> guest.

<margin>25 Then the king will say also to those on the left]</margin> "King" is not added in the Greek, nor in the Golden Codex.

<margin>26 You cursed]</margin> *katēramenoi* <note>original: "κατηραμένοι"</note>, that is, *execrated or devoted to destruction*.

<margin>27 Thirsty]</margin> *or thirsty* <note>original: "ἢ διψῶντα"</note>, in agreement with the ancient Latin codices.

<margin>28 To the least of my brothers]</margin> *the smallest* <note>original: "ἐλαχίστων"</note>. It is strange what came into the translator's mind that he would translate the same word a little later using the comparative *smaller* when he is speaking of the same people. And yet, I think it is from this passage that certain members of the Franciscan family took their name of *Minors* <note>The "Friars Minor" or Franciscans.</note>.

---

<margin>C</margin> <margin>1</margin> **T**he Passover happens] *it happens and is delivered* <note>original: "γίνεται, καὶ παραδίδοται"</note>. Both are in the present tense in the Greek.

<margin>2 Caiaphas]</margin> The Greeks write it *Kaiaphas* <note>original: "Καιάφας"</note> with four syllables.

<margin>3 Lest perhaps a tumult should occur]</margin> *lest a tumult happen* <note>original: "ἵνα μὴ θόρυβος γένηται"</note>, so that it refers to the Pharisees speaking among themselves: *let us not attempt anything on the feast day, lest a tumult arise among the common people by occasion of the feast day.* For the translator added "perhaps" on his own.

<margin>4 Alabaster]</margin> *alabastron* <note>original: "ἀλάβαστρον"</note>, a delicate glass ointment jar, so named from *labein* <note>original: "λαβεῖν"</note> to grasp, and the privative particle *a* <note>original: "α"</note>, with a redundant *ph* <note>original: "φ"</note> added, because due to its smoothness it cannot be grasped. So also Horace: *A small onyx jar of nard.* And, of great price, *eubareias* <note>original: "εὐβαρείας"</note>, as if you were to say, of heavy weight, because in old times bronze was weighed out, not counted.

<margin>5 Why this waste?]</margin> It is not *hina ti* <note>original: "ἵνα τί"</note> here, but *eis ti* <note>original: "εἰς τί"</note>, that is, *to what end or for what purpose*.

<margin>6 For much]</margin> It is indeed *pollō* <note>original: "πολλῷ"</note> in Greek, yet I think it would be more Latinate to say "for a great price."

<column-break/>

<margin>30</margin> even that which he has shall be taken away from him. And cast the useless servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. But when the Son of Man comes in his glory, <margin>31</margin> and all the holy angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne <gloss>22</gloss> of his glory, and all nations will be <margin>32</margin> gathered before him, <gloss>23</gloss> and he will separate them from one another, just as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats: He will set the sheep on his right hand, but the <margin>33</margin> goats on the left. Then the king will say to those who will be on his right, "Come, you blessed of my Father, possess <margin>34</margin> the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world. For I was hungry, <margin>35</margin> and you gave me to eat. I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink. I was a stranger, <gloss>24</gloss> and you took me in. Naked, <margin>36</margin> and you clothed me. I was sick, and you visited me. I was in prison, and you came to me." Then the righteous <margin>37</margin> will answer him, saying, "Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you? or thirsty and give you drink? Or when did we see you a <margin>38</margin> stranger and take you in? or naked and clothe you? Or when did we see you sick, or in <margin>39</margin> prison, and come to you?" And the king answering says <margin>40</margin> to them, "Truly I say to you, insofar as you did it to one of these my least brothers, you did it to me." <gloss>25</gloss> Then <margin>41</margin> he will say also to those who will be on the left, "Depart from me, <margin>26</margin> you cursed, into eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you gave me <margin>42</margin> no food. I was thirsty, and you gave me no drink. I was a stranger, and you did not take me in. Naked, and <margin>43</margin> you did not clothe me. I was sick and in prison, and you did not visit me." Then they also will answer, <margin>44</margin> saying, "Lord, when did we see you hungry, <gloss>27</gloss> or thirsty, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister to you?" Then he will answer them, saying, "Truly I say to <margin>45</margin> you, insofar as you did it not to one of <gloss>28</gloss> these least ones, neither did you do it to me." And these will go into eternal punishment, <margin>46</margin> but the righteous into eternal life. And it came to pass **XXVI.** when Jesus had finished all these sayings, he said to his disciples: "You know that after two days the Passover <margin>1</margin> happens, and the Son of Man is delivered to be crucified." Then <margin>2</margin> the chief priests and the scribes and the <margin>3</margin> elders of the people gathered in the palace of the high priest, who was called <gloss>2</gloss> Caiaphas: And they took counsel together, that they <margin>4</margin> might seize Jesus by guile and kill him. But they said, "Not on the feast day, <gloss>3</gloss> lest a tumult happen among the people." <margin>5</margin> Now when Jesus was in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, there came to him a woman having <gloss>4</gloss> an alabaster jar <margin>6</margin> of precious ointment, and poured it upon the head of him <margin>7</margin> as he sat at meat. But when the disciples saw it, they were indignant, saying, <gloss>5</gloss> "To what purpose is this waste? <margin>8</margin> For this ointment could have been sold for a <gloss>6</gloss> great price, <margin>9</margin> and given to the poor." When Jesus understood it, he said to them, <gloss>7</gloss> <margin>10</margin> "Why are you troublesome to the woman? <gloss>8</gloss> For she has wrought a good work upon me. For you always have the poor <margin>11</margin> with you, <gloss>9</gloss> but me you do not always have. <margin>12</margin> For in that she has poured this ointment upon my body, she did it for my burial. Truly I say to <margin>13</margin> you, wherever this Gospel shall be preached in the whole world, <gloss>11</gloss> this also that she has done shall be told <gloss>12</gloss> in memory of her." ---

<margin>D</margin> <margin>7 Why are you troublesome]</margin> *Ti kopous parechete* <note>original: "Τί κόπους παρέχετε"</note>, that is, *Why do you present difficulties, or Why do you cause trouble?* Although the translator renders it correctly.

<margin>8 A good work]</margin> *ergon kalon* <note>original: "ἔργον καλόν"</note>, which does not mean simply good, but excellent and beautiful. And,

<margin>9 But me you will not always have]</margin> In both places in the Greek it is *echete* <note>original: "ἔχετε"</note>, that is, *you have*, in the present tense. Nor is it "always" in the sense of *aei* or *dia pantos*, but "at any time," *pantote*, because the word *pas*, from which it is composed, can also be understood in this way.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>10 For pouring]</margin> *balousa* <note>original: "βαλῦσα"</note> is in the past tense, so it would be more fully expressed as: *For in that she poured this ointment on my body, she did it for my burial*, to signify that he was soon to die.

<margin>11 It shall be said what she]</margin> *lalēthēsetai kai ho epoiēsen hautē* <note>original: "λαληθήσεται καὶ ὃ ἐποίησεν αὕτη"</note>, that is, *it shall be told also that which she did*. For the "that" in this place is not a conjunction, but a relative pronoun.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>12 In her memory]</margin> *eis mnēmosynon autēs* <note>original: "εἰς μνημόσυνον αὐτῆς"</note>. "Her" is of the feminine gender, referring to the woman herself: "of her own self" would be more fitting. Furthermore, *mnēmosynon* does not simply mean memory, but some pledge or monument that a friend leaves with a friend.
