# ACCORDING TO MATTHEW. CHAPTER XXVI.

<margin>70</margin> [Peter] denied it before them all, saying, "I do not know what you are talking about." <margin>v.71</margin> When he had gone out to the gateway, another woman saw him; and she said to those who were there, "This man also was with Jesus the Nazarene." <margin>71</margin> <margin>72</margin> And again he denied it with an oath: "I do not know the man!" <margin>73</margin> After a little while, those standing by came up and said to Peter, "Truly you also are one of them; for even your accent makes you known." <margin>74</margin> Then he began to invoke curses and to swear, "I do not know the man!" <margin>v.75</margin> And immediately a rooster crowed. <margin>75</margin> And Peter remembered the word of Jesus, who had said to him, "Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times." And he went out and wept bitterly. <margin>XXVII.</margin> When morning came, all the Chief Priests and the Elders of the people took counsel <margin>v.1</margin> against Jesus, so as to put him to death. <margin>1</margin> And having bound him, they led him away and handed him over to Pontius <margin>v.2</margin> Pilate the governor. <margin>2</margin> <margin>v.3</margin> Then Judas, who had betrayed him, seeing that he had been condemned, felt remorse and returned the thirty pieces of silver to the Chief Priests and the Elders, <margin>3</margin> <margin>4</margin> saying, "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood." But they said, "What is that to us? You see to it." <margin>5</margin> And throwing the silver pieces into the sanctuary, he departed, and went away and hanged himself. <margin>6</margin> But the Chief Priests, taking the silver pieces, said, "It is not lawful to put them into the treasury <note>original: 'korbanan', refers to the temple fund</note>, since it is the price of blood." <margin>7</margin> And having taken counsel, they bought with them the potter's field, for the burial of strangers. <margin>8</margin> For this reason, that field has been called the Field of Blood to this day. <margin>9</margin> Then [was fulfilled what was spoken...]

<meta>catchword: fulfilled</meta>

---

<margin>13 Judas Iscariot]</margin> [Iscariotes] <note>original: "Ἰσκαριώτης"</note>, that is, *Iscariot*: about which we have already given warning.
<margin>14 On the first day]</margin> The word "day" is understood among the Greeks, not explicitly stated: just as in the phrase *on the first of the sabbath*. Here it says, [On the first of the unleavened] <note>original: "Τῇ δὲ πρώτῃ τῶν ἀζύμων"</note>, that is, to translate word for word, *On the first of the unfermented things*, so that as many nouns are understood as there are articles: *On the first day of the unfermented breads*.
<margin>15 To a certain man]</margin> It is not [to someone] <note>original: "πρός τινα"</note>, but [to such-and-such a man] <note>original: "πρὸς τὸν δεῖνα"</note>, that is, *to that specific person*. The Greeks speak this way when they mean a specific person whom they nevertheless do not name. From this it appears that Christ gave a name, but the Evangelist kept it silent. This detail greatly troubled Augustine in the book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, chapter 80.
<margin>16 He who dips with me]</margin> [the one having dipped] <note>original: "ὁ ἐμβάψας"</note>, that is, *he who dipped*. For if he had said, while the man was dipping his hand, "He who dips with me here will betray me," it would have been an indubitable and manifest sign. But now he wished to leave room for Judas to repent. Nevertheless, he gave a closer clue, indicating that the man was not only present at the feast, but was even dipping his hand into the same dish, into the same sauce—which is a sign of intimate friendship. As Origen also noted in his thirty-fifth Homily, explaining this passage so that Christ's speech further highlights the remarkable malice of Judas, whom even the intimacy of a shared table (which even pagans usually hold as sacred) could not pull back from his intended crime.
<margin>17 In the dish]</margin> [in the bowl] <note>original: "ἐν τρυβλίῳ"</note>, that is, *in the platter or dish*. It is strange why it pleased the translator to render one Greek word with another Greek word <note>Erasmus notes the Latin Vulgate used 'paropside', another Greek loanword, instead of a native Latin one</note>.
<margin>18 By whom the Son of Man is betrayed]</margin> [is betrayed] <note>original: "παραδίδοται"</note>, that is, *is being handed over*, a verb in the present tense. For it was already happening, the money having been agreed upon. And soon after:
<margin>19 Who betrayed him]</margin> [the one betraying him] <note>original: "ὁ παραδιδοὺς αὐτόν"</note>, that is, *he who was betraying*, or *his betrayer*.
<margin>20 While they were dining]</margin> [of them eating] <note>original: "ἐσθιόντων"</note>, that is, *while they were eating or feeding*.
<margin>21 Take and eat]</margin> [Take, eat] <note>original: "λάβετε, φάγετε"</note>, without a connecting word. And here Chrysostom, in his commentary, repeats those words from Paul: *which is broken for you*. Or rather from Luke chapter 22, where we read: *which is given for you*, that is, *is distributed*: just as he had said of the cup, *divide it among yourselves*, so the bread is distributed by breaking. Theophylact <note>a Byzantine commentator</note> reminds us that it is the true body, not a figure of the body, because the bread is transformed in an ineffable way.
<margin>22 And taking the cup]</margin> [and having taken the cup, and having given thanks, he gave to them] <note>original: "καὶ λαβὼν τὸ ποτήριον, καὶ εὐχαριστήσας, ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς"</note>.
<margin>23 For this is my blood]</margin> The word *For* is not in several Greek manuscripts, nor was it in the consecration of the body just before.
<margin>24 Of the New Testament]</margin> The added article makes the speech more significant to the Greeks: [that of the new covenant] <note>original: "τὸ τῆς καινῆς διαθήκης"</note>, that is, *which is of the New Testament*. Now, *Testament* here means the will that those about to die establish.
<margin>25 Which is poured out for many]</margin> [that which is being poured out concerning many] <note>original: "τὸ περὶ πολλῶν ἐκχυνόμενον"</note>. Although I find this is sometimes put for the future, like *of those who are strong*: except that Paul expressed both with a present participle: [that being broken] <note>original: "τὸ κλώμενον"</note> and [that being poured out] <note>original: "τὸ ἐκχυνόμενον"</note>, that is, *what is broken, what is poured out*, as we shall note in its proper place. The translator of Origen also reads *is poured out* in his thirty-fifth Homily.
<margin>26 And when they had said a hymn]</margin> [And having sung a hymn] <note>original: "Καὶ ὑμνήσαντες"</note>, that is, *when they had spoken or sung praises*, so that you understand the Apostles sang the hymns, not only Christ.

<column-break/>

# 134 ACCORDING TO MATTHEW. CHAPTER XXVI.

<margin>A</margin> <margin>14</margin> [Then one] of the twelve, who was called <gloss>13</gloss> Judas Iscariot, [went] to the <margin>15</margin> Chief Priests, and said to them, "What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you?" And they settled on thirty pieces of silver for him. <margin>16</margin> And from that time he sought an opportunity to betray him. <margin>17</margin> Now <margin>14</margin> on the first day of unleavened bread, the disciples came to Jesus, saying to him, "Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?" <margin>18</margin> And he said, "Go into the city to <gloss>15</gloss> a certain man, and say to him: 'The Master says, My time is near; at your house I am keeping the Passover with my disciples.'" <margin>19</margin> And the disciples did as Jesus had directed them, and they prepared the Passover. <margin>20</margin> Now when evening <margin>B</margin> came, he sat down with the twelve: <margin>21</margin> And <gloss>20</gloss> while they were eating, he said, "Amen I say to you, that one of you is going to betray me." <margin>22</margin> And they were greatly saddened, and each began to say to him, "Is it I, Lord?" <margin>23</margin> But he answering said, <gloss>16</gloss> "He who has dipped his hand with me <gloss>17</gloss> into the dish, this man is going to betray me." <margin>24</margin> The Son of man indeed goes as it is written of him: but woe to that man <gloss>18</gloss> by whom the Son of man is betrayed: it would have been better for that man if he had not been born. <margin>25</margin> Then Judas, <gloss>19</gloss> who betrayed him, answering said, "Is it I, Rabbi?" He said to him, "You have said it." <margin>26</margin> <gloss>20</gloss> Now as they were eating, Jesus took bread, <margin>C</margin> and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, <gloss>21</gloss> "Take, eat: this is my body." <margin>27</margin> And <gloss>22</gloss> having taken the cup, and given thanks, he gave it to them, saying, "Drink from this, all of you: <margin>28</margin> <gloss>23</gloss> For this is my blood, which is of the <gloss>24</gloss> new testament, <gloss>25</gloss> which is poured out for many for the remission of sins." <margin>29</margin> "But I say to you, I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom." <margin>30</margin> <gloss>26</gloss> And when they had sung a hymn, they went out into the mount of <gloss>27</gloss> olives. <margin>31</margin> Then Jesus says to them, "All of you will suffer an offense because of me on this night: for it is written, <gloss>28</gloss> I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered." <margin>32</margin> "But after I have risen again, I will go before you into Galilee." <margin>D</margin> <margin>33</margin> But Peter answering said to him, "Even if all suffer an offense because of you, I yet will never suffer an offense." <margin>34</margin> Jesus said to him, "Amen..."

---

[The commentator] leaves [the phrase] as something that reminds us of her. Therefore, he could have translated it appropriately as *in her monument*. However, this particle, *in memory of her*, does not refer to the nearer verb *she has done*, but to the earlier *it shall be told*.

<margin>27 Of the olive grove]</margin> Again [of the olives] <note>original: "ἐλαιῶν"</note>, that is, *of the olives*, which has already occurred so many times.

<margin>28 I will strike the shepherd]</margin> This is a prophecy in the Prophet Zechariah, chapter thirteen. The Septuagint Edition agrees with the Hebrew truth, except that for what Jerome translated as *upon the man clinging to me*, the Septuagint translated as [upon the man his citizen] <note>original: "ἐπὶ ἄνδρα πολίτην αὐτοῦ"</note>. Jerome thinks this happened because of the ambiguity of a single letter, the Yod <term>י</term>, which does not differ from the Vav <term>ו</term> except by size alone: if it is read as Yod, it means *my*; if Vav, *his*. The Septuagint translated it this way: [Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered] <note>original: "Πάταξον τὸν ποιμένα, καὶ διασκορπισθήσονται τὰ πρόβατα"</note>. From the Greek [strike] <term>πάταξον</term> (an imperative) the Evangelist made [I will strike] <term>πατάξω</term>, and from [they shall be scattered] he kept [they shall be scattered] <term>διασκορπισθήσονται</term>.

<column-break/>

<margin>E</margin> Furthermore, what was said there in the persona of the Prophet asking that God strike the shepherd, the Evangelist adapted to the persona of God himself. For Jerome pointed this out in his book *On the Best Kind of Translating* to Pammachius: and he repeats almost the same things when explaining this passage of the Prophet. And yet, in this matter, either I am utterly hallucinating, or Jerome has slipped. While I confess he was a man of the highest learning, equal eloquence, and incomparable holiness, I cannot deny that he was also a human being. For if anyone examines that passage of the Prophet more carefully, he will find that there is no necessity—indeed, it is only with hardship—that these words are adapted to the persona of the Prophet. To make this more conspicuous, I will write the words themselves: *Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is my companion, says the Lord of hosts.* These are certainly plainly said in the persona of God, since he added, *says the Lord of hosts*. And immediately it follows: *Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.* These also are the words of God addressing his own sword. If anyone wishes to twist this elsewhere, certainly <margin>F</margin> what follows will not allow it: *And I will turn my hand to the little ones.* And even more clearly, what is immediately joined to it cries out against it: *And they shall be in all the earth, says the Lord.* 

A certain person has also slandered this passage with great theatrics—who, if he were as well-instructed for teaching what is right as he seems animated for slandering the works of others, would be worthy of being numbered among famous writers. Since no one attributes more to Jerome than I, and since certain people have even accused me in published books of preferring Jerome to Augustine (as I know some do), this man cries out that I have chosen Jerome alone out of everyone to engage in a duel with, and he sings a cold eulogy of Jerome, as if I had not praised him with greater spirit before. Although this very praise which he attributes to Jerome here seems to have been borrowed from my own writings. And this turbulent man stirs up these riots because I have disagreed with Jerome in a matter that is not at all dangerous, yet with the highest preface of honor—especially since Jerome is consistent with himself. I, who would easily say Jerome was a man...

**EVANGELIUM**

...that which was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled, saying: “And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him who was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value; and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord commanded me.” <note>original: ἐπληρώθη τὸ ῥηθὲν... This refers to Matthew 27:9-10. Historically, this prophecy is found in Zechariah 11:12-13, but the Gospel attributes it to Jeremiah, a point of much historical debate.</note> And Jesus stood before the governor; and the governor asked him, saying, “Are you the King of the Jews?” And Jesus said to him, “You say so.” And when he was accused by the chief priests and the elders, he answered nothing. Then Pilate said to him, “Do you not hear how many things they testify against—” <note>The Greek text breaks off mid-word: καταμαρ[τυροῦσιν].</note>

<margin>A</margin>
...to be a man. But what could be said more mildly? And it was a matter of Jerome's honor, as if that stone had taken up the man’s defense with such great spirit. But, to set aside quibbles and reveal the matter to the upright reader in a few words: in his book *On the Best Kind of Translating*, when Jerome was dealing with this specifically to show that certain things among the Hebrews differ from the translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> or from the citations of the Apostles, he also brought forward this passage from Zechariah, distinguishing the persons in such a way as to suit the argument that fit this place.

<margin>B</margin>
However, in the *Commentaries* in which he explains this passage of the Evangelist, he tempers his opinion so much that he seems almost to retract what he had written in the book *On the Best Kind of Translating*. He says: **"This is written in other words in the prophet Zechariah, and if I am not mistaken, it is said to God from the person of the prophet: 'Strike the shepherd.'"** <note>original: *Percute pastorem* from Zechariah 13:7.</note> Furthermore, because he confirms this sense by the agreement of the sixtieth Psalm: **"For they have persecuted him whom you have struck,"** <note>Psalm 69:26 in modern numbering; 68:27 in the Vulgate.</note> even if we grant that the Psalmist felt what Jerome interprets, it does not force the person of the speaker to be changed. For since it is certain that the first part of the prophecy, **"Sword, awake against my shepherd,"** pertains to God the Father, if what follows immediately is referred to the same—**"Strike the shepherd,"** etc.—the sense remains the same: that Christ was struck by the Father, who commanded with his own sword that he should be struck. **"For He struck"** the one whom He handed over to be struck.

<margin>C</margin>
Furthermore, Jerome, in explaining the Prophet himself, disagrees even more with himself, and accommodates the entire speech to the Father. So that this may be more clear, I will subjoin his own words: **"Nor should it be thought that the testimony was taken from another place, because in the Gospel God says the shepherd was struck by Himself, and in the present place the sword and blade are commanded: 'Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.'"** Thus far Jerome. You see clearly that the voice of the Father commanding His blade is **"Strike the shepherd,"** and not the words of a supplicating Prophet. You see there is no mention of that matter which he had placed in the book *On the Best Kind of Translating*, even though it would have been most timely to insist on it here. What, then, is different in Matthew? The words are different, but the matter is the same. For whoever says to his sword, **"Strike,"** signifies that he himself wishes to strike, and therefore Matthew, setting aside the words, expressed the sense: **"I will strike the shepherd."** Indeed, Matthew even omitted the pronoun that is in the Prophet: **"against *my* shepherd."** This itself also invites us to accommodate the speech to the Father instead.

<margin>D</margin>
For He calls "His own" that unique one worthy of Himself, since for others there are other shepherds, some of whom are such that the flock is better off when they are struck. But the slanderer <note>Erasmus likely refers here to one of his contemporary critics, such as Edward Lee or Stunica.</note> exults, teaching us that persons in the Divine Scriptures are sometimes suddenly changed. There was no need for us to learn this from that man, which we have testified so many times in our own books. Truly, nothing here forced a change of person. And it appears that Jerome regretted his own opinion. And this is that "excellent doctor" who, equipped with all things, approached the handling of Sacred Scripture—which I began to touch "yesterday or the day before." <note>A sarcastic remark; Erasmus is mocking his critic's claim that Erasmus is a newcomer to theology.</note> Though I wrote the *Enchiridion* twenty years ago, and in this hurried work—upon which I cannot linger—I cite more from various authors than the nature of the work requires. That man merely wanders among the things cited by us, hunting for something to gnaw on. And not even this succeeds happily for him, even though he does it not hurriedly, but at his leisure. But to let this "stone" go, I think Jerome in this part is fairer to his own Antimachus than to such a Symmachus. <note>Erasmus uses "Antimachus" and "Symmachus" as literary types for fierce opponents or specific rivals.</note>

<margin>39 And he came again]</margin> <note>original: Καὶ ἐλθὼν εὗρεν αὐτοὺς πάλιν καθεύδοντας</note>, that is, *And when he had come, he found them sleeping again.*

<margin>40 Then he came to the disciples]</margin> Here "he comes" <insert>original: ἔρχεται</insert> is used; both are in the present tense <insert>original: ἔρχεται καὶ λέγει - "he comes and says"</insert>.

<margin>41 Sleep now and take your rest]</margin> There was doubt whether it should be read as a command, *Sleep and rest*, or as a question, *Are you sleeping and resting?*, if he had not added *behold*, that is, *hereafter*, or "for the rest," for which the Translator put *now* [jam]; and certainly not badly. Lorenzo Valla <note>An Italian humanist and critic (1407–1457) whom Erasmus admired.</note> quibbles about something or other in this place, saying it is not fitting that he who a little before rebuked his own for sleeping should now command them to sleep: especially since he immediately adds, *Rise, let us go from here*. Although Origen, Chrysostom, Hilary, and Jerome inter-

<margin>E</margin>
pret this in the sense that Christ commanded them to sleep, and they explain the matter with allegories. But, saving the judgment of others, the speech of Christ can have some irony: *"Up to now you could not obtain your wish to watch with me for a little while; now the event itself will rouse you, when you see my punishment and your danger."* And thus the things that follow fit perfectly: *Rise, behold he approaches.* And this opinion of mine began to displease me less after I discovered that Theophylact, on Mark, insists on it with many words.

<margin>42 Behold, it has approached]</margin> <note>original: ἰδοὺ ἤγγικεν</note>, that is, *behold it has approached*, in the past tense, or "it is present," or "it is near."

<margin>43 And the Son of Man is betrayed]</margin> "Is betrayed" is in Greek the present tense <insert>original: παραδίδοται</insert>.

<margin>44 Behold, he who betrays me has approached]</margin> <note>original: ἤγγικεν ὁ παραδιδούς με</note>, that is, *he who betrays me has approached.*

<margin>45 With swords and clubs]</margin> <note>original: καὶ ξύλων</note>, that is, "with woods." And he translates it thus elsewhere.

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>46 Sent by the priests]</margin> The Translator added "Sent" for the sake of explanation, although he did not maintain the logic of the gender, since "crowd" [turba] preceded it; so it should rather have been said "sent [feminine - missa]."

<margin>47 For what have you come]</margin> <note>original: ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάρει</note>, that is, *for what are you present, or for what do you arrive.* Nor can it be taken to mean "into what evils have you come," but "for the sake of what thing have you come," since the article is in the dative case. Even if in some copies I find it written as <note>original: ἐφ᾽ ὅ</note>. Though the relative pronoun is altogether used here in place of "who" or "what."

<margin>48 Cut off]</margin> <note>original: ἀφειλεν</note>, that is, *took away.*

<margin>49 Shall perish by the sword]</margin> In Greek it is "In the sword," although the Translator rightly omitted the preposition. Nor is it "shall perish" in some copies, but "shall die" <note>original: ἀποθανοῦνται</note>. And Augustine reads it thus.

<margin>C</margin> ...in the second Commentary, where he explains Christ’s sermon held on the mount. This passage somewhat distorted Saint Augustine, because this saying—that those who take up the sword will perish by the sword—could be openly refuted, since it is certain that some robbers do not perish by the sword. Therefore, he interprets it as the soul of the one who strikes with the sword being slaughtered by the sword of sin. But if that is true, what need was there for the future tense "shall die"? For the soul of the striker is already dead even before he brandishes the sword at his neighbor. Therefore, in my opinion, it will be simpler if we say that Christ felt, in a general sense, that it is not Apostolic to use this kind of defense—to repel iron with iron, and to retaliate injury with injury. For evil is not avoided in that way; rather, it causes evil to be propagated without end through small exchanges of injuries. Otherwise, if we push this saying to the quick—indeed, if we take it literally—what shall we do with a Judge and a Magistrate who carries a sword? What of the Emperor, who even by a solemn rite receives a sword from the Vicar of Christ? There are many such sayings of Christ in which it is proper to look at the essence of the meaning.

50 *And he will provide me now*] <note>original: "Et exhibebit mihi modo"</note> The word "now" has been moved to a place not its own, when it should have been joined to the verb "to ask," <note>original Greek: ὅτι οὐ δύναμαι ἄρτι παρακαλέσαι</note>, that is, "because I cannot now ask." The Golden Codex <note>An ancient manuscript reference.</note> also supports this. In the erasure of Constantine, it revealed the zeal of a corrupter.

51 *Legions*] <margin>D</margin> Here too the Greek used a Latin word, <term>legiones</term> <note>original Greek: λεγεῶνας</note>.

52 *Because it must thus happen*] <note>original: "Quia sic oportet fieri"</note> If the Greek word for "knowing" <note>original Greek: εἰδωσὶ</note> is accepted, something must be supplied for the sense, such as "the Scriptures which say" that it must thus happen.

53 *That they might be fulfilled*] <note>original Greek: πληρωθῶσιν</note> "That they may be filled up," so that it refers to the person of Christ speaking. Though it can also be referred to the person of the Apostle writing.

54 *Even into the courtyard*] <note>original Greek: ἕως τῆς αὐλῆς</note>, that is, all the way to the hall, or as far as the courtyard.

55 *To deliver him to death*] <note>original Greek: ὥς, sive ὅπως θανατώσωσιν</note>, that is, <margin>E</margin> so that they might kill him: or if a <term>periphrasis</term> <note>A roundabout way of speaking.</note> is preferred, "to affect him with death": although Virgil said, "give over to death."

56 *And they found not*] In the Greek codices it is placed twice: "and they found not," or "they were not finding." <note>original Greek: Καὶ οὐχ εὗρον. Καὶ πολλῶν ψευδομαρτύρων προσελθόντων οὐχ εὗρον</note>, that is, "And they found not. And when many false witnesses had approached, they found not." The Translator of Origen’s thirty-fifth Homily reads it in this way. Nor is it an idle repetition. Theophylact <note>A Byzantine biblical commentator.</note> reads it likewise.

57 *Lastly*] <note>original Greek: ὕστερον</note>, that is, afterward, or later: which he has already translated this way quite often. Perhaps a comparative put for a superlative.

58 *And after three days rebuild it*] <note>original Greek: καὶ διὰ τριῶν ἡμερῶν οἰκοδομῆσαι αὐτό</note>, that is, through three days, or to build it in a three-day period. For so they soon reproach him: "You who destroy the temple of God, and build it in three days, do not rebuild it."

59 *To those things which these men testify against you*] <note>original Greek: τί οὗτοι σου καταμαρτυρᾶσι</note>, <margin>F</margin> that is, "what" or "why" do these men give testimony against you?

60 *I adjure you*] <note>original Greek: Ἐξορκίζω</note>, "Exorcize." The same word we use in the consecration of holy water and in casting out unclean spirits. But where is he now—that fellow Calepinus—who grandly instructs us, shouting that <term>exorcize</term> is a barbarous word, and that our <term>solecisms</term> <note>Grammatical mistakes.</note> are laughed at by unclean spirits whenever we read "I exorcize you," when we should say "I exorgize you"? And he proves this quite dialectically: Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia.</note>, he says, writes that "exorgize" means "to throw into anger." This is just as if someone were to say, the word *eape* signifies a herb, therefore "I have often seen" (*sape vidi*) is not said in proper Latin. And yet there are those who are indignant at me because I dare to disagree with this.

61 *If you are the Christ the Son of the living God*] "Living" is neither in the Greek nor in the Golden Codex.

<margin>E</margin> 62 *Jesus said to him*] It is "He says" both in the Greek and in the ancient Latin copies.

63 *He has blasphemed*] <note>original Greek: ἐβλασφήμησε</note>, that is, "because he blasphemed." Although the word "that" or "because," being superfluous, was rightly omitted. For as it has a force of affirmation for the Greeks, so for the Latins it spoils the purity of speech. Furthermore, I know the word <term>blasphemia</term> is not Latin, but I have left it nonetheless, because it sounds like something more atrocious to us than "insult," namely an insult against God.

64 *What yet*] <note>original Greek: τί ἔτι</note>, "what besides," or "what further."

65 *You have heard the blasphemy*] The Greeks add <note>original Greek: αὐτοῦ</note>, that is, "of him," or "his."

66 *They gave palms to his face*] In Greek there is a single word <note>original Greek: ἐρράπισαν</note>, that is, they struck with slaps. I do not find fault, however, with the fact that the periphrasis expresses the indignity of the thing.

67 *A certain servant girl*] <note>original Greek: παιδίσκη</note>. It can be taken to mean a young girl. For it is a diminutive of "child" <note>original Greek: παῖς</note>.

68 *And as he was going out*] In Greek it is an accusative, <note>original Greek: ἐξελθόντα δὲ αὐτόν</note>, that is, <margin>F</margin> "but him having gone out." Nor is it "into the door," but into the porch/vestibule, <note>original Greek: πυλῶνα</note>, or in the entryway.

69 *Another servant girl*] The Translator added "servant girl," for the Greek says <note>original Greek: εἶδεν αὐτὸν ἄλλη</note>, "another [female] saw him."

70 *To curse*] <note>original Greek: καταναθεματίζειν</note>, that is, to devote to destruction, or to curse, or as it is read in some, <note>original Greek: καταθεματίζειν</note>, which is more serious than "to anathematize."

71 *Because he had not known*] <note>original Greek: ὅτι οὐκ οἶδα</note>, that is, "that I do not know." Although the conjunction <note>original Greek: ὅτι</note> does not correspond to the Latin "because" (*quia*): and the Translator rightly changed the Hebrew figure of speech. Yet elsewhere, I know not by what superstition, he does not dare to do so: as in that place, "and he confessed, because I am not the Christ."

72 *The cock crowed*] <note>original Greek: ἐφώνησε</note>, that is, "cried out" or "sounded." Though "song" (*cantus*) or "the cock's crowing" is rightly said of cocks.

73 *Which Jesus had said*] The Greeks add <note>original Greek: αὐτῷ</note>, that is, "to him" or "to himself." And "who" is to be read, not "which," <note>original Greek: τοῦ ῥήματος</note>, that is, "of the word [of him] who had spoken." for that which he said, "he came," or "of one saying": for the sense is that he had said it would be so. For a participle of this kind serves both tenses: the preterite perfect <note>past completed</note> and the preterite pluperfect <note>further past</note>. The same Interpreter <note>likely referring to the Vulgate translator</note> for the Greek word *autō* <note>to him</note> translates "to himself." Let no one entirely despise this point, as noted by us.

<margin>1</margin>**To the Chief Priests and the Elders of the people**] In this place, "of the people" is not added in the Greek, nor in the golden codex, but it is understood from the passage that immediately precedes it.

<margin>2</margin>**Righteous blood**] *athōon* <note>original: ἀθῶον</note>, that is, guiltless or innocent. Thus he translates shortly after, *I am innocent of this righteous blood*.

<margin>3</margin>**You see to it**] *sy opsei* <note>original: σὺ ὄψει</note>, that is, "you will see," or "you see to it," with the first syllable sharpened <note>referring to the Greek accent</note>, so that it is the future of the subjunctive verb from *videro*. Nor do I see how the logic of the speech stands, unless we either say the indicative mood is used for the imperative, or we imagine from the future *opsomai* a present *opsō*: from which comes the imperative *opsei*, just as *poiei* <note>do/make</note> comes from *poieō*.

<margin>4</margin>**He hanged himself with a noose**] *apēnxato* <note>original: ἀπήγξατο</note>. He has explained one word with three, and rightly so. For that expression is as strong as if you said, "he strangled himself with a noose." Concerning the *corbona* <note>temple treasury</note>, it has been said elsewhere that they otherwise call it the *gazophylacium* <note>the treasury chest</note>.

<margin>5</margin>**That field Acheldemah**] The Greek codices do not have the Hebrew word, but only, "that field was called the Field of Blood." Saint Jerome also noted this passage in his book titled *On the Best Kind of Interpreting*, denying that what Matthew cites here from Jeremiah actually exists anywhere in Jeremiah. Rather, it is in the prophet Zechariah, but as the Evangelist reported it, it corresponds poorly to the Hebrew truth, and much less to the common Septuagint edition: for although he feels the same, the words are inverted, indeed almost different. On account of the slanderous, I will subscribe Jerome’s own words: "Again in Matthew, when the thirty pieces of silver were returned by Judas the traitor and the potter's field was bought with them, it is written: *Then was fulfilled what was written through Jeremiah the prophet saying: And they took, etc.* This is not found in Jeremiah at all, but in Zechariah in much different words and a completely different order. For the common Edition <note>the Septuagint</note> has it thus: *And I will say to them, If it is good in your sight, give me my price, or refuse it. And they weighed out my price, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me, Put them in the furnace, and see if it is approved, as I was approved by them. And I took the thirty pieces of silver and put them in the house of the Lord in the furnace.*" It is clear how far the Septuagint translation differs from the Evangelist's testimony. But even in the Hebrew, though the sense is the same, the words are rearranged and almost different. *And he said*, it says, *to them, If it is good in your eyes, bring my price, and if not, be quiet. And they weighed my price, thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me, Cast it to the statuary <note>or potter</note>, the handsome price at which I was valued by them. And I took the thirty pieces of silver and cast them in the house of the Lord to the statuary.* Let them accuse the Apostle of falsehood, because he agrees neither with the Hebrew nor with the Septuagint translators, and what is greater than these, he errs in the name, putting Jeremiah instead of Zechariah. But far be it from saying this of the follower of Christ, whose care was not to hunt for words or syllables, but to set down the meanings of the teachings. Thus far we have related Jerome’s words. He can easily be excused because, being busy with other things here, he did not explain the manner of the proposed question. It is more a wonder why he neither explains the passage of the prophet itself nor, in narrating Matthew, washes away what he confesses is even greater than a discrepancy in words and order: that Jeremiah was put for Zechariah; especially since the same man, in the thirteenth chapter of this Evangelist, where something is cited from Isaiah which is actually from Asaph, says it happened by the fault of a scribe. Origen, frankly confessing that what is cited here from Jeremiah is read nowhere in Jeremiah—not even among the Hebrews—opens a double reason for solving the question. For either the name was changed by the fault of the scribes, especially since there is some affinity between the names; or the testimony was taken from the book titled *Apocrypha* <note>hidden</note>, that is, the *Secret Books of Jeremiah*, which Jerome confesses he had read; though he does not approve of this passage being referred to the authority of the apocrypha. Nor indeed is it approved by me, especially since it is brought forward not for the sake of warning, arguing, or exhorting—for which things they sometimes use even the testimonies of the Gentiles—but as a sequence of oracles by which the mystery of the Passion is explained. Origen, less hostile to the apocrypha than Jerome, thinks this could be sought from the apocryphal books: just as that which Paul brings forward in the first Epistle to the Corinthians, "What...

<column-break/>

# CHAPTER 27.

<margin>A</margin>**Having gone** outside, he wept bitterly. But when morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death. And they bound him and led him away and delivered him to Pontius Pilate the governor. Then Judas, who had betrayed him, seeing that he was condemned, was moved by repentance and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and the elders. Saying, "I have sinned, betraying innocent blood." But they said, "What is that to us? You see to it." And throwing the pieces of silver into the temple, he departed, and going away, he hanged himself with a noose. But the chief priests, having taken the silver pieces, said, "It is not lawful to put them into the treasury <note>original: corbonam</note>, because it is the price of blood." <margin>B</margin> Having taken counsel, they bought with them the potter's field for the burial of strangers: for which reason that field has been called the "Field of Blood" even to this day. Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet saying, "And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one valued, whom they valued from the sons of Israel, and they gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord appointed to me." But Jesus stood before the governor, and questioned...

---

<margin>C</margin>*eye has not seen*, etc. is thought to be taken from the apocrypha of Elijah. Likewise in the second Epistle to Timothy, chapter three, regarding *Jannes and Mambres* <note>the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses</note>, who resisted Moses, since there is no mention of these in Exodus, they seem to be taken from an apocryphal book titled *Jannes and Mambres*. Nor were there those who, for this reason, contended that this Epistle to Timothy was not Paul’s, but in vain: since no one has criticized the first to the Corinthians by the same name. Chrysostom, however, in explaining the Epistle to Timothy, indicates two other ways of explaining the question of the name: one of which is that the Jews had certain things which they passed down by mouth without written records, which they called *agrapha* <note>unwritten</note>, or traditions. It is possible that passages of this kind were drawn from them. <margin>D</margin> The other is what they say was Paul’s: that although these things were not written, nor did he hear them from others, yet the Apostle learned them by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. To me, however, it seems most likely that among the Greeks the name was changed by an error of the scribes: and from there the Latin Interpreter was deceived and passed down to us what he had read. I certainly believe there is nothing of this kind in the Gospels. <margin>E</margin> The Gloss, which they call "ordinary," I do not know from where it drew what it indicates: that in some codices the name of *Jeremiah* is not held, but only "through the Prophet." It adds another way of escape: Since the prophets wrote inspired by the same Spirit, it would not be absurd to attribute to one what is said by another; and it was not by forgetfulness that the name *Jeremiah* occurred to Matthew instead of the name *Zechariah*, but by the moderation of the divine Spirit. It opens yet another crack: that something of this prophecy is in Jeremiah, chapter thirty-two, namely about the bought field. But these words, "which they valued," are neither in Jeremiah nor in Zechariah, but were added under the person of the Evangelist. I bring these things into the open, leaving the judgment to the reader. However, even if there had been a lapse of memory only in the name, I do not think anyone ought to be so peevish that for that reason the authority of the whole Scripture should waver, especially since Augustine, in the third book of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, chapter seven, attributes it to the boldness of ignorance that in some codices *Zechariah* is found written for *Jeremiah*: but he thinks the double and apostolic scripture is that of Jeremiah. He attributes the error of the name to a lapse of memory, in which one name occurred to him for another, the Holy Spirit thus moderating the minds of the writers for hidden reasons. The same man in many places in this work seems to attribute to the Evangelists a certain forgetfulness and recollection, either while that which had been done much earlier came to their minds later, and from this he distinguishes the order of record from the order of events: or while they express the same meaning in different words, as when one says, "I am not worthy to carry his sandals," another, "I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal": since both declare the supreme excellence of Christ. Likewise in the *Questions*, chapter fifteen, he speaks thus of the Evangelist: "For he did not organize the narrative he began entirely according to the order of events, but according to each one's faculty of his own memory." It is not my purpose to defend or refute these words of Augustine: for me, against certain people who slander everything, it is enough that a pious man commemorates many such things, not to weaken the authority of the Gospels, but to beat back the impudence of those who were thrusting vanity upon the Evangelists. I will add from myself a fifth reason for untying the question. If we say that *Zechariah* had two names, just as was said a little before about Zechariah son of Barachiah, who is said to be the same as *Jehoiada*: Jerome reports that an apocryphal Jeremiah was shown to him by a certain Jew of the Nazarene sect, in which these things were held word-for-word as they are cited by the Evangelist. But, as I said, he does not approve that the Apostle should have brought testimony from apocrypha: especially since it is the custom of the Evangelists and Apostles that, neglecting words, they render the sense in whatever way when citing testimonies. Furthermore, to the Syrians <term>Aceldamah</term> is the <term>field of blood</term>. <margin>F</margin> Jerome testifies that even in his time the place existed in Jerusalem on the southern side of Mount Zion, where even then the corpses of the poor and weak were partly buried in the earth, and partly rotted under the open sky.

<margin>7</margin>**Which they valued**] *hon etimēsanto* <note>original: ὃν ἐτιμήσαντο</note>, that is, which they appreciated, which is to say, which they estimated by price.

<margin>7 You are the king]</margin> <note>original: "ὁ βασιλεύς"</note>, that is, *the king*: so that you might understand it refers to that king who was then expected by the Jews.
<margin>8 To any word]</margin> <note>original: "πρὸς οὐδὲ ἓν ῥῆμα"</note>. The Greek phrasing is ambiguous. For the sense can be, *He did not answer him a word regarding anything*, or, *He did not answer him even to one word*.
<margin>9 But on the feast day]</margin> <note>original: "Κατὰ δὲ ἑορτήν"</note>, that is, *actually during the festival*. There was no need for a long-winded explanation.
<margin>10 To release to the people]</margin> <note>original: "τῷ ὄχλῳ"</note>, that is, to the *crowd*, or the *multitude*.
<margin>11 He had then one prisoner]</margin> *One* is not in the Greek, nor in the ancient Latin manuscripts. Nor is *prisoner* <note>original: "vinctum"</note> a participle among the Greeks, but a noun, <note>original: "δέσμιον"</note>.
<margin>12 Before the judgment seat]</margin> <note>original: "ἐπὶ βήματος"</note>, that is, *on the tribunal* <note term="bema">The raised platform where a Roman magistrate sat to deliver judgments</note>. Although the Latin Translator <note>the Vulgate</note> translates it here more elegantly than is his usual custom: the reader should be warned here so as not to be deceived.
<margin>13 Nothing between you and that just man]</margin> It certainly would have been more Latin to say, *Let there be no business between you and that just man*. Just as Christ’s innocence earned testimony from all sides: from Judas, Pilate, this man's wife, Annas, the witnesses, the thief, the guards sent to arrest him, the Magi, the Canaanites, the Samaritans, and the centurions. But this happened to Him alone so it would be more certain that all he suffered was paid on our behalf.
<margin>14 Through a vision]</margin> <note>original: "κατ’ ὄναρ"</note>, that is, *in dreams*. For he translates it this way at the beginning of this Gospel, and correctly so. Lorenzo Valla <note>A famous 15th-century humanist scholar</note> discusses this at length; he thinks <note>original: "ὄραμα"</note>, that is, *vision*, belongs to those who are awake, while <note>original: "ὄναρ"</note> is a *dream*, and that which appears in sleep is called <note>original: "ἐνύπνιον"</note> by the Greeks.
<margin>15 They persuaded the peoples]</margin> And here again it is "crowds" <note>original: "ὄχλοις"</note>, not "peoples."
<margin>16 What then shall I do with Jesus]</margin> The preposition "with" <note>Latin: "de"</note> is not in the Greek. <note>original: "Τί οὖν ποιήσω Ἰησοῦν τὸν λεγόμενον Χριστόν;"</note>. Furthermore, the Greeks misuse the accusative case here instead of the dative when they mean doing something well or poorly to someone. Hence it should have been translated, *What shall I do to Jesus, who is called Christ?*
<margin>17 They all say]</margin> <note>original: "Λέγουσιν αὐτῷ"</note>, that is, *They say to him*: although the Greek manuscripts vary here.
<margin>18 He said to them]</margin> "To them" is not in the Greek. <note>original: "Ὁ δὲ ἡγεμὼν ἔφη"</note>, *But the governor said*.
<margin>19 He washed]</margin> <note>original: "ἀπενίψατο"</note>, that is, *he rinsed off*. And, *Having taken water* <note>original: "λαβὼν"</note>, that is, *when he had accepted* or *taken* it.
<margin>20 Innocent]</margin> This is the same word that he had translated a little earlier as *just*, <note>original: "ἀθῷος"</note>, that is, *guiltless* and *harmless*.
<margin>21 You see to it]</margin> <note>original: "ὑμεῖς ὄψεσθε"</note>, that is, *you will see*. Just as before, *you see to it*, so that it is a middle-voice verb with an active meaning in the future tense.
<margin>22 Scourged]</margin> <note>original: "φραγελλώσας"</note>. And here, writing in Greek, he used a Roman word <note>derived from the Latin 'flagellum'</note> by changing one letter: because it was the Roman custom to beat those condemned to the ultimate punishment with rods.
<margin>23 He delivered to them]</margin> "To them" is not in the more corrected Greek manuscripts, and it hinders the sense somewhat. For he did not deliver Jesus to the Jews, but to his own soldiers, the ministers of punishment. Even if I do not know by what chance it was added in our first edition. That Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note> read it as we have indicated is testified by his commentary on this passage.
<margin>24 Taking]</margin> <note>original: "παραλαβόντες"</note>, that is, *receiving*, or rather *having received*: as he often changes the type of verb elsewhere to match the tense.
<margin>25 Cohort]</margin> <note>original: "τὴν σπεῖραν"</note>, which also means *rope* in Greek. For a "cohort" is a rustic band of soldiers.
<margin>26 Scarlet]</margin> <note>original: "κοκκίνην"</note>, more like *dyed red with grain*. For *coccus* or *coccum* is a *grain* <note>Actually a scale insect used to make red dye, though historically thought to be a grain or seed</note>. And they are commonly called grains, with which certain reds are dyed because they add brightness to the color: see Pliny, Book 9, Chapter 41. Furthermore, a *chlamys* is a military cloak: so that both the color and form are that of military dress, making the mockery even greater, when the Holy One wore the clothing of the wicked.
<margin>27 Weaving a crown]</margin> <note>original: "πλέξαντες"</note>, that is, *having woven* or *fashioned*, to suit the timing.
<margin>28 They put it on his head]</margin> <note>original: "ἐπέθηκαν"</note>, that is, *they placed*. In some manuscripts it was held as "they put."
<margin>29 Spitting on him]</margin> <note>original: "καὶ ἐμπτύσαντες εἰς αὐτὸν"</note>, that is, *when they had spat on him*.

---

<margin>30 And after they mocked]</margin> <note>original: "καὶ ὅτε ἐνέπαιξαν"</note>, that is, *when they had finished mocking*.
<margin>31 To crucify him]</margin> <note>original: "εἰς τὸ σταυρῶσαι"</note>, that is, *for the purpose of crucifying*. And a little before, *his clothes*: it would be more fitting to say *their clothes* <note>referring back to Jesus's own garments</note>.
<margin>32 They compelled him]</margin> It is strange why this foreign word <note term="angariaverunt">A Latinized version of a Greek word meaning to press into service</note> was pleasing here, since he could have said *forced* or *compelled*. Indeed, Suidas indicates the word is Persian, because among them royal messengers were called <note>original: "ἄγγαροι"</note>. Because they hand over letters to be carried in turn, those whom they called <note>original: "ἀγγάρους"</note> are said to be *angari*. Finally, the word was transferred to anyone who carried burdens in the manner of slaves or beasts of burden. Perhaps that word was already usurped by soldiers, just as they had their own camp jargon.
<margin>33 which is called Golgotha]</margin> Jerome, in the book where he explains the Hebrew words in Matthew, warns that *Golgotha* is a Syrian word, not Hebrew, and sounds like *place of the bald* or *of the skull*. There are those who prefer it to be Chaldean, and to be pronounced *Golgotha* with a second Lambda added. For my part, I do not think it worth the effort to contend so vehemently over a barbaric little word, and I prefer to follow the consensus of the Latins and Greeks in this. In whatever language it belongs, the place in Aelia <note>Jerusalem, renamed Aelia Capitolina by the Romans</note> was so named on the northern part of Mount Zion because the heads of condemned men lay there. For as to what some say, that Adam was buried there and hence the name was given to the place, Jerome rejects that fable, since Adam is read to have been buried in Arba near Hebron.
<margin>34 They gave him wine]</margin> Certain Greek manuscripts did not have *wine*, but *vinegar mixed with gall*. Just as Jerome reads and interprets it. Although Hilary reads *wine*, and Chrysostom reads *vinegar*. Yet there is not much difference between *vinegar* and *sour wine*. Certainly, a little later mention is made of *vinegar*, not *wine*, nor *gall*. *You filled a sponge with vinegar*. Origen noted that Matthew had said *vinegar mixed with gall*, Mark said *wine flavored with myrrh*, and John said *vinegar with gall*, from which it is clear that Origen also read *vinegar*, not *wine*. And it agrees more with the Prophet, who says, *they gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink* <note>Psalm 69:21</note>. The Reader should be warned that the same drink does not seem to have been given here to Christ as that which is given while hanging on the cross. For it appears it was given twice: once before he was raised onto the cross according to custom, if I am not mistaken (which is still observed today); and again on the cross.

->to the one asking from the cross, for so Matthew narrates: *And they came to the place called Golgotha, which is the place of the skull, and they gave him wine to drink mixed with gall.* <note>original: "Et venerunt in locum, qui dicitur Golgotha, quod est calvariæ locus, & dederunt ei vinum bibere cum felle mixtum."</note> Mark records it in this manner: *And they brought him to the place Golgotha, which is translated "place of the skull"; and they gave him wine mixed with myrrh to drink, and he did not take it: and crucifying him, etc.* <note>original: "Et perducunt illum in Golgotha locum, quod est interpretatum calvariæ locus; & dabant illi bibere myrrhatum vinum, & non accepit: & crucifigentes eum, &c."</note> However, the opinion held by some that the chronological order is inverted in this narrative is quite harsh, especially since the same Evangelist soon follows with: *And immediately one of them running took a sponge and filled it with vinegar and put it on a reed and gave him to drink,* <note>original: "Et continuo currens unus ex eis acceptam spongiam implevit aceto & imposuit arundini & dabat illi bibere,"</note> particularly because in the first instance it is called wine mixed with gall, and in the second, vinegar—a distinction Mark also makes. It is more conducive to piety that we do not ignore this specific part of the Lord's cross. Augustine also mentions in the third book of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists* the separate drink offered before the crucifixion. Theophylact <note>A prominent Byzantine commentator on the Bible</note> thinks the vinegar was offered here so that he might die more quickly before Elijah could come. For they suspected he was imploring Elijah when he said *Eli, Eli*. Yet others said, *Wait, let us see if Elijah comes.*<-

<margin>35</margin> *That it might be fulfilled which]* This testimony of the Prophet <note>referencing Psalm 22:18</note> is not cited in most Greek manuscripts. Jerome, in his commentary on this passage, makes no mention of it at all. Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a 14th-century Franciscan scholar</note> adds that, according to Jerome, this testimony was not placed here by Matthew, but only by John, and is not found in the ancient copies. Certainly, it was not included in one very ancient manuscript from Dijon, nor in the one from Constance, nor in another ancient printed edition that I have in my possession. Nevertheless, the passage is found in the twenty-first <note>modern Psalm 22</note> Psalm.

<margin>36</margin> *It is a trivial thing that the Translator added on his own]* "to themselves" <note>Latin: "sibi"</note>, since this pronoun is neither in the Greek nor in the "Golden Codex," <note>likely referring to a prestigious illuminated manuscript</note> where it simply says *they divided my garments*.

<margin>37</margin> *Upon my vesture]* <note>Greek: "καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν ἱματισμόν μου"</note>. This sounds more like "clothing" than a single "garment." Thus, those who argue from this that Christ had five garments are not achieving much. It is established from the Gospel that there were two. It seems more like a repetition of the same or a similar word, as is characteristic of prophetic speech. For it is well established that one seamless garment was divided into four parts.

<margin>38</margin> *And sitting they watched him]* The Greeks add *there* <note>Greek: "ἐκεῖ"</note>.

<margin>39</margin> *Above his head]* <note>Greek: "ἐπάνω τῆς κεφαλῆς"</note>, that is, over the head. For the title was not *on* his head.

<margin>40</margin> *Cause]* <note>Greek: "αἰτίαν"</note>, a word which among the Greeks signifies both the "cause" and the "accusation" or "crime."

<margin>41</margin> *Then were crucified]* <note>Greek: "Τότε σταυροῦνται"</note>, that is, "Then they are crucified," in the present tense; it is told in the historical style as if the event is happening right now.

<margin>42</margin> *Aha, you who destroy]* The interjection *Aha* <note>Greek: "οὐὰ"</note> is not added in Matthew, but in Mark; it seems to have been added here from there. In the Constance manuscript, an erasure testified to this corruption. And the article *the* <note>Greek: "ὁ"</note> has some emphasis, as if to say, *You, that destroyer of the temple*.

<margin>43</margin> *Rebuild]* <note>Greek: "οἰκοδομῶν"</note>, that is, "building," as I warned above. Origen's translator rendered it, *who were destroying and who were building*. In some old copies, it was written "destroys and rebuilds" in the third person. The Constance manuscript agreed.

<margin>44</margin> *And we will believe him]* <note>Greek: "καὶ πιστεύσομεν ἐπ’ αὐτῷ"</note>, that is, *and we will believe in him*. Although a little further down the word *into* <note>Greek: "εἰς"</note> is used, so it makes no difference which you read.

<margin>45</margin> *He trusts]* <note>Greek: "Πέποιθεν"</note>, that is, "He has trusted," or "He has confidence in God"; since in these matters, as has been said, they use the tenses interchangeably.

<margin>46</margin> *Let him deliver him now if he wants him]* The Greeks add another pronoun, <note>Greek: "εἰ θέλει αὐτὸν"</note>, that is, *if he wants him*. For they seem to allude to that part of the Psalm: *He hoped in the Lord, let him deliver him, let him save him, because he wants him.* Otherwise, the insult seemed to fall not only on Christ but also on God.

<margin>47</margin> *They reviled him]* <note>Greek: "ὠνείδιζον αὐτῷ"</note>, that is, they reproached him, or said the same insults against him. Augustine, explaining the figures of speech in Exodus, in his third book of *Annotations*, thinks there is an "exchange" <note>Greek: "ἐναλλαγὴν"</note> here, where the plural number is used for the singular, because in the other Evangelists only one of the robbers says insults against Christ. Hence it is a wonder why Jerome in his *Commentaries* calls it a "synecdoche," acknowledging the figure of speech but suggesting another reason why a figure of speech is not needed: namely, that at first both

And immediately one of them running, when he had taken a <gloss>53</gloss> sponge and filled it with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave him to drink. But the others said, Wait, let us see if Elijah <margin>D</margin> comes <margin>54</margin>.

Cardinal Hugo <note>Hugo of Saint-Cher, a medieval theologian</note>, as if he had read neither, says, *This seems false.* Thus politely does he raise a question about the faith of the Evangelists. And soon, he says, *regarding this, it is said that it might have been said amidst the drinking.* <note>impliying the mockery was drunken rambling</note> O, what a theologian, treating the Sacred Letters so soberly and reverently! And some people are quick to charge me because I do not hold this man as a God, since he was of the Dominican Order.

<margin>A D</margin> <margin>48</margin> *And darkness was made from the sixth hour]* Therefore he had already hung on the cross for three hours, since Mark testifies that he was crucified at the third hour. Although there was formerly variation in the reading of that passage, as we shall demonstrate in its place.

<margin>49</margin> *Darkness was made over the whole land]* <note>Greek: "ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν"</note>, that is, "into the whole land," or "upon the whole land." For that darkness did not occupy the entire globe of the earth, as Origen correctly judges in my opinion, but only Judea, or the land of Jerusalem, though Theophylact disagrees. Otherwise, historians of worldly events would have mentioned this miracle, even by chance. Just as the "whole world" is said to be described in Luke, when it is understood that only the Roman world was described. Origen indicates that in some manuscripts it was added, *Darkness was made over the whole land, the sun failing*, as if an eclipse of the sun had brought on those darknesses. And indeed the Epistle which circulates under the name of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite</note>—which seems to me a forged title—records it thus. But Origen rejects this opinion far away and disapproves of the altered Scripture.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>50</margin> *The Greeks write the Hebrew words in this manner*, <note>Greek: "Ἠλὶ, Ἠλὶ, λαμὰ σαβαχθανὶ"</note>, that is, *Heli, Heli, lama sabachthani*. And it is no wonder if the Greeks and Latins write and pronounce words of a foreign language corruptly. However, in their own language they are written in this manner: <gloss>אֵלִי אֵלִי לָמָה עֲזַבְתָּנִי</gloss> <note>Hebrew: Eli, Eli, lamah azabtani</note>, that is, *My God, my God, why have you deserted me?* For it is the first verse of the twenty-first Psalm, in the translating of which it is a wonder why the Seventy <note>The Septuagint translators</note> mixed in three words of their own, removing one word. For they rendered it thus: *God, my God, look upon me, why have you deserted me?* But Matthew reported it as it is held among the Hebrews. Furthermore, the Hebrew words are to be distinguished in this manner: <gloss>אֵלִי</gloss> <note>Eli</note>, that is, *my God*, <gloss>אֵלִי</gloss> <note>Eli</note>, that is, *my God*, <gloss>לָמָה</gloss> <note>lamah</note>, "to what end" or "why," <gloss>עֲזַבְתָּנִי</gloss> <note>azabtani</note>, "you have forsaken me." Indeed, it is probable that Christ pronounced the words of the Psalm as they were described by the Psalmist himself. Otherwise, he could have been seen to use the Chaldean language <note>Aramaic</note>, who pronounce it *sabachthani*, where the Hebrews say *azabthani*. I have seen fit to note this so that, since these words are publicly recited in churches, they may be pronounced less corruptly hereafter. Nor is it simply *abandoned* <note>Greek: "κατέλιπες"</note> among the Greeks, but *deserted in a crisis* <note>Greek: "ἐγκατέλιπες"</note>, which properly signifies to desert in a moment of danger; as if someone were to desert a man stuck in the mud, to speak thus for the sake of teaching.

<margin>51</margin> *This man calls for Elijah]* <note>Greek: "φωνεῖ"</note>, which he would have rendered more expressively as, *calls out to, or invokes*.

<margin>52</margin> *And filled it with vinegar]* Here mention is openly made of vinegar. Furthermore, we read in Plutarch’s *Life of Mark Antony* that wine was given to Antony, as it seems, so that he might die more quickly, because the substance accelerates death. For wine and vinegar have a similar power of penetration; and Jerome indicates this in passing when he explains this passage, saying *so that they might lull him to sleep:* just as we noted a little before from Theophylact.

<margin>53</margin> *Saving him]* <note>Greek: "σώσων αὐτὸν"</note>, that is, *to save him*. Some manuscripts had <note>Greek: "ρύσων αὐτὸν"</note>, *about to deliver him*. The Translator seems to read *saving*.

54 *Crying out with a loud voice*] <note>original Greek: "κράξας" (kraxas)</note>, that is, when he had cried out: let no one think that he cried out and expired at the very same moment. Although this itself is marvelous, and quite unlike the common habit of men, to die immediately after a great shout.

55 *And many bodies which had slept*] The Greeks punctuate this so that it appears they rose immediately when Christ died: but they did not come out of the monuments, nor did they appear, until after Christ had risen. Hence they rose finally after his rising. Jerome indicates this clearly enough, writing on this passage: *Just as the dead Lazarus rose, so also many bodies of the saints rose, to show the Lord rising.* And yet, although the monuments were opened, they did not rise before the Lord rose, so that he might be the firstborn from the dead. Chrysostom indicates the same when he says: *At Christ's death voices were raised to wake the dead, who afterwards, when Christ rose, came out together.* Origen openly declares this when explaining this passage. But Theophylact hardly accepts this opinion, thinking that those who rose then later died again: just as Lazarus and the others whom we read were raised by the Lord or by the Apostles died twice. Augustine, in Letter 99, thinks it was said through anticipation that they rose, when they actually rose a little while later.

56 *There were also women here*] Certain Greek manuscripts had <note>original: "καὶ γυναῖκες" (kai gynaikes)</note>, that is, *and women*. And in the Greek it does not only say *from afar*, but watching from a distance, <note>original: "ἀπὸ μακρόθεν θεωροῦσαι" (apo makrothen theorousai)</note>. Indeed, Origen reads and interprets it thus, bringing in that prophecy from Isaiah, *Women, come to the spectacle*. For it is not a people having wisdom.

57 *And Joseph*] In Greek it is *Jose*, different from *Joseph*, about which I warned before. Though Origen does not seem to distinguish this *Joseph* or *Jose* from that *Joseph* the son of the Patriarch Jacob, the suppliant of his brother. For he says, *And Joseph the mother, according to the name of the Patriarch Jacob the suppliant of his brother, and Joseph over whom the mother said at birth, May the Lord add to me another son.*

58 *When it was made late*] <note>original: "ὀψίας" (opsias)</note>. Why not rather *evening* than *late*?

59 *A certain man*] "A certain" is not found among the Greeks, but only *a man*.

60 *Of Joseph*] Here the Greek has <note>original: "Ἰωσὴφ" (Ioseph)</note>, that is, *Joseph*.

61 *He had been a disciple of Jesus*] <note>original: "ἐμαθήτευσεν τῷ Ἰησοῦ" (ematheteusen tō Iēsou)</note>, that is, he had offered himself as a disciple to Jesus. A word he used elsewhere transitively, *make disciples for the kingdom*. And again in the next chapter, *Make disciples of all nations*, that is, *Teach all nations*.

62 *Mary Magdalene*] He has now placed Mary Magdalene twice, with the Hebrew pronunciation, whereas he called the other Marys "Maria" <note>the Latin 'Maria' vs the Greek/Hebrew 'Mariam'</note>, although here the Greek manuscripts vary.

63 *On the other day*] <note>original: "Τῇ δὲ ἐπαύριον" (Tē de epaurion)</note>, that is, *On the following day*, or *The day after*.

64 *Because that seducer*] <note>original: "ὁ πλάνος" (ho planos)</note>, *planus*, that is, *impostor*. For so Augustine translates in the thirty-sixth Homily of the fifty: *Lord, we heard that that planus*, that is, *impostor*. Furthermore, the Translator rightly added *that* <note>Latin: "ille"</note>, expressing the force of the Greek article. Moreover, as for what they say, *after three days*, although I do not deny it can be rejected on the grounds that this is said not by the Evangelist but by the Pharisees, yet it may also be understood in this way—in my opinion at least—that something is said to have happened after three days which began on the third day, using the figure of speech called synecdoche <note>a part representing the whole</note>. For why should we fear to accept a figure of speech regarding the third day, when we must accept one regarding the first? But we shall say a bit more on this matter in the Gospel of Mark.

65 *After three days I rise*] <note>original: "ἐγείρομαι" (egeiromai)</note>, that is, *I rise*, in the present tense.

65 *Lest perhaps*] <note>original: "μήποτε" (mēpote)</note>. Which he [the translator] so delights in translating. And certain manuscripts add *here "noctu"*, that is, *at night*.

67 *You have a guard*] <note>original: "Ἔχετε κουστωδίαν" (Echete koustōdian)</note>. It is uncertain whether it is *have* as an imperative command, or *you have* as a statement of fact. And the Greeks were already using the Latin word *custodia* <note>meaning guard or custody</note>. Suidas also mentions it.

68 *Go, guard*] <note>original: "ὑπάγετε, ἀσφαλίσασθε" (hypagete, asphalisasthe)</note>, that is, *go away, make secure*. For *asphalisasthai* is to make a thing safe. Just as he translates a moment later, *they secured*. Though he translated it as *guard* above.

69 *With the guards*] <note>original: "μετὰ τῆς κουστωδίας" (meta tēs koustōdias)</note>, *with the guard*. Although in this place he used *guard* for the flock and crowd of guards. It appears that it was a kind of group of men almost like the four hundred in Paris designated for the public guarding of the city.

V. **In the evening of the Sabbath**] <note>original: "Ὀψὲ δὲ σαββάτων" (Opse de sabbatōn)</note>, that is, *Late on the Sabbaths*. And he should have said "that which" <note>masculine/neuter</note> dawns, not "she who" <note>feminine</note>, as if it referred to *vesperum* [evening], unless you read *Vespera* [evening, feminine].

2 *On the first day of the week*] <note>original: "εἰς μίαν σαββάτων" (eis mian sabbatōn)</note>, that is, *on one of the Sabbaths*, so that you understand one day out of seven. For he means, unless I am mistaken, the twilight of the final day of the preceding week, dawning into the following day, which was the first of the succeeding Sabbath. Unless perhaps according to the property of Hebrew speech *one* is said for that which is *first*, just as we say "the other" for that which is "the second."

3 *He rolled back the stone*] The Greeks add <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς θύρας" (apo tēs thyras)</note>, that is, *from the door*.

4 *Upon it*] <note>original: "ἐπάνω αὐτοῦ" (epanō autou)</note>, that is, *above it*.

5 *His appearance*] <note>original: "ἰδέα αὐτοῦ" (idea autou)</note>, that is, *his appearance*, or *form*.

6 *And the garments*] Both the Greek and the ancient Latin manuscripts have *garment* [singular], and the Greeks add *white as snow*.

7 *The guards*] <note>original: "οἱ τηροῦντες" (hoi tērountes)</note>, that is, *those who were keeping watch*.

8 *But the Angel answering*] <note>original: "ἀποκριθείς" (apokritheis)</note>. For he misused that word, since they had asked nothing, unless it be that he responds to their thoughts.

9 *Come and see*] This is not in the Greek, <gloss>but *deute, idete* <note>original: δεῦτε, ἴδετε</note>, "come, see."</gloss>

<margin>A</margin> 7 [He] is [not] here: for he has risen, just as he said: come, see the place where the Lord was placed. And go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead: and behold 10 he precedes you into Galilee: there you will see him: 11 behold I have told you. And departing quickly from the monument with fear and great joy, they ran to report it to his disciples. But as they went to report to his disciples, 12 behold Jesus met them, saying, "Greetings." And they approached and took hold of his feet, and worshiped him. Then 13 Jesus said to them, "Do not be afraid: go, report to my brothers that they should go to Galilee, 15 and there they will see me."
<margin>B</margin> When they had gone, behold some of the guards came into the city, and reported to the chief priests all things that had happened. And having gathered with the Elders, after holding a council, they gave a large sum of money to the soldiers, saying, 14 "Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while we were sleeping. And if this 15 is heard under the governor, 16 we will persuade him, 17 and we will make you secure." And taking the money they did as they were taught: and this word was spread among the Jews even until this day. But the eleven <margin>C</margin> 18 disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them. And when they had seen him, they worshiped him: but some doubted. And Jesus, approaching, spoke to them, saying, "All power is given to me in heaven and on earth. 18 Go therefore and teach all nations: baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you. And behold I am with you always, even to the end of the world."

## BY DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
## ANNOTATIONS ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW

<margin>D</margin> <gloss>I advise, or I persuade. The sense therefore required that it say "we will persuade" rather than "we will advise," or "we will appease him."</gloss>
17 *And make you secure*] <gloss>*amerimnous* <note>original: ἀμερίμνους</note>, that is, we will render you secure, or we will free you from all worry: for that is what "amerimnos" sounds like, which is more than rendering them *akindunous* <note>original: ἀκινδύνους</note>, that is, free from danger.</gloss>
18 *Go therefore*] I do not find "therefore" in the Greek codices; in some codices I find "but" instead of "therefore." I do not know by what chance it happened that neither Origen nor Chrysostom, though they wrote commentaries on the rest, published anything on this single chapter, unless perhaps they failed to speak before the people because these things pertain to the resurrection. Theophylact, however, explains it, and the *Golden Chain* <note>A famous collection of commentary snippets compiled by Thomas Aquinas</note> frequently cites Chrysostom on this chapter, just as in the others. Anianus, in the preface to his version, testifies that Chrysostom wrote ninety-one "logoi" <note>discourses/homilies</note> on Matthew, whereas in the Vulgate Edition we have only 89. From this it is probable that two Homilies have been lost.

# M A R K
### ACCORDING TO SOPHRONIUS.

Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, after hearing Peter’s explanations, was requested by the brothers in Rome to compose a brief Gospel. When Peter encountered this work, he approved it and authorized it to be read in the church, as recorded by Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, an early Christian theologian</note> in the sixth book of his *Outlines* <note>original: "Hypotyposes"</note>. Papias, the Bishop of Hierapolis, also makes mention of this Mark. Furthermore, Peter mentions him in his first epistle, using the name "Babylon" to figuratively signify Rome, where he says: "She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you greetings; and so does my son, Mark." 

Taking the Gospel which he himself had composed, Mark then traveled to Egypt. He was the first to preach Jesus Christ in Alexandria, where he established a church. He was so distinguished by his teaching and his endurance in life that he persuaded all followers of Christ to adopt a rigorous way of living. On account of this, Philo—the most learned of the Jews—seeing the first church in Alexandria still following Jewish customs, wrote a book about their way of life as if in praise of his own nation. Just as Luke narrates that those who believed in Jerusalem held all things in common, so too did Philo record what he saw happening in Alexandria under Mark the teacher. Mark died in the eighth year of the reign of Nero and was laid to rest in Alexandria, succeeded by Annianus.

---

# A R G U M E N T
->for the<-
# GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK
### 
->by Theophylact, as it appears.<-

The Gospel according to Mark was written in Rome ten years after the Ascension of Christ. Mark was a disciple of Peter, whom Peter calls his "spiritual son." He was also certainly called John, was the cousin of Barnabas, and was a traveling companion of Paul. For a long time, he stayed mostly with Peter and was with him in Rome. The believers in Rome asked him not only to preach orally but also to set down the account of Christ’s deeds in writing. He was persuaded to compose it only with difficulty. It was revealed to Peter by God that Mark had written the Gospel; therefore, having seen it and confirmed it as true, Peter then sent Mark as a Bishop to Egypt. There, by preaching in Alexandria and establishing a church, he enlightened everyone in the southern regions. 

The character of this Gospel is clear and contains nothing convoluted. This Evangelist runs almost entirely parallel to Matthew, except that Matthew is more extensive. While Matthew mentions the birth of the Lord according to the flesh at the beginning, Mark begins with the Prophet John. For this reason, some have suggested a certain symbolic meaning regarding the Evangelists (though it may seem a bit curious): God, who sits upon the Cherubim—whom Scripture describes as having four faces—delivered to us a fourfold Gospel held together by a single Spirit. 

Just as each of the Cherubim had one face like a lion, another like a man, another like an eagle, and another like a calf, so too is the character of the Gospel preaching. The Gospel according to John has the **face of a lion**, for the lion is kingly and authoritative; likewise, John began from the kingly and lordly dignity of the Divinity of the Word, saying, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God." The Gospel according to Matthew has the **face of a man**, for he began from the birth according to the flesh and the incarnation of the Word. The Gospel according to Mark is likened to an **eagle**, for he began from the Prophet John. Prophetic grace, being far-seeing and gazing sharply at things far off, is like an eagle; for they say the eagle is the most sharp-sighted of creatures, so much so that it alone among animals can gaze at the sun without blinking. The Gospel according to Luke is like a **calf**, because he began from the priesthood of Zechariah, who offered incense for the sins of the people; and at that time, a calf was the animal of sacrifice. Mark, therefore, begins his Gospel from the lifestyle and appearance of the Forerunner <note>John the Baptist</note>. Listen, then, to what he says.
