SINCE we discovered that this work was growing to a size far greater than expected—for these notes were being written by us and printed by the typesetters at the same time—it seemed best to employ the same brevity in our annotations that Mark himself showed in shortening the Gospel of Matthew. In this way, we might cure both the reader’s boredom and our own intolerable weariness, and ensure the course of this work is completed within its allotted time. For we have "borrowed" (to speak more truly than "obtained") a few short months for this labor from our service to the most illustrious Charles, Prince of the Burgundians <note>The future Holy Roman Emperor Charles V</note>, into whose household we have recently been admitted; and I call Jesus to witness that this was not done without heavy personal financial loss. 

However, that loss moves me but little. Money matters can either be repaired or ignored. Furthermore, just as it is the mark of a good man not to fail in his duty, so it is the mark of an honest and modest man not to allow anyone to think he has forgotten his obligations. I remember how much I owe to that great Philip <note>Philip the Handsome</note>, son of Maximilian, not only as a Prince—and a most excellent one at that—but also as a man of magnificent merit. Whatever I owed to my country, to that excellent Prince, and to his merit, I must now pour out entirely upon Charles, since it has seemed best that I should look upon him rather than merely enjoy his favor. I would sooner forget my own name than that of my most kind patron <term>Maecenas</term> <note>A Roman name used here to mean a generous patron of the arts</note>, William Warham, Archbishop of Canterbury. He has deserved so well of honest and learned men that he ought to be celebrated by all who cherish integrity and literature. Indeed, he has advanced me with such great honors and overwhelmed me with such kindness that I must hold everything I own ready whenever the call of duty bids me obey his will. 

Therefore, since we owe much to both countries—born in one and adopted into the other—and since we owe much to both Princes—bound to one by many great favors and invited by the other most humanely to honors we neither deserve nor seek—it was not possible for me to extend this work any further, so that I might fulfill my promise to both in a timely manner. We have moderated the work such that we have added some new things while also shortening its overall length. Yet we have done this in a way that practiced a thrift of words rather than a thrift of substance, so that we might satisfy both the work and our duty as far as possible. Moreover, I truly hope that the brevity which was necessary for us will also be convenient and pleasing to the reader. For who has such a patient stomach that he could dwell for long on these small details without disgust? 

And yet, how small a portion of this trouble actually reaches the reader? While we are running back and forth among so many Greek, Latin, and Hebrew manuscripts—searching, as they say, for a needle in a haystack—while we are examining what one man translated, what another read, what has been corrupted here, what is interpreted there, what another corrected, what we ourselves have noted, where the Latin manuscripts disagree or agree with the Greek and the Hebrew; and finally, what the conflict or harmony is among manuscripts of the same language—while, I say, we are being stretched and tortured among these thorns, not for an hour or two, but for nearly six months, think, I beg you, dear reader, how much boredom we swallow for the sake of the public good. 

Nor will it bother me if, in future leisure, I happen to seek out other things that could make this work either richer or more corrected, and add those to the common use as well. We had a great deal of help with Matthew from the commentaries of the Ancients, since many wrote on him: Origen, Chrysostom, and Jerome. On this Gospel <note>Mark</note>, we have nothing ancient that I know of. For Theophylact is <term>neoteric</term> <note>A more recent/modern writer (11th century)</note>; and those commentaries circulated under the title of Jerome, though not to be entirely rejected, no more taste of Jerome than a service-berry tastes of a fig <note>A proverb meaning the two things are nothing alike</note>. As to why so few have written on Mark, I believe the reason is that they thought once Matthew was explained, Mark was explained as well. Now, I would not want it to be hidden from you, reader, that what we have prefaced here regarding Mark pertains to the first edition of this work, since this is now the fifth edition, with which we have decided to be content. This is not because any work is so perfect that nothing could be added or improved, but because I see that with "Sycophants" <note>harsh critics or detractors</note> reigning everywhere now, one must give way. To spend excessive diligence on such a humble and unrewarding argument would be rightly criticized.

---

<margin>1</margin> **The beginning of the Gospel**] Here, following the Hebrew custom, he has begun with the title of the work itself, just as Matthew did, whose Gospel Mark abridged, according to Augustine.

<margin>2</margin> 2 **In Isaiah the Prophet**] In the Greek manuscripts that I have seen, the name of Isaiah is not expressed, but only "in the Prophets" <note>original: "en Prophetais"</note>. However, it appears this was intentionally changed by learned men who noticed that this testimony was woven together from two different Prophets, as Jerome indicates in his book *On the Best Kind of Translating*. For the first part—namely, *Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who shall prepare your way before you*—is found in Malachi, chapter three. In that passage, it should be noted in passing that Jerome seems to have suffered a lapse of memory in the work we just cited, when he says this testimony is found at the end of Malachi. For since the entire prophecy of this Prophet is completed in four chapters, and this passage is right at the start of the third chapter, it is actually in the middle rather than the end. But I suspect what tripped up Jerome’s memory: a similar prophecy is found at the very end, which they also interpret as being about John: *Behold, I will send you Elijah the Prophet before the day of the Lord comes*. I am not satisfied by the excuse of a certain person who thinks it can be called "the end" because it is a little below the middle. Some indicate that there is a Greek manuscript in the Vatican Library written in capital letters which agrees with the Latin Edition. Is it any wonder it agrees if it was corrected according to Latin copies? Still, I believe this <note>the Latin reading "Isaiah"</note> is the genuine reading. Beda brings up a different point, following Augustine if I am not mistaken, suggesting it could have happened that while Mark was writing, one name occurred to him instead of another, but even after being warned, he did not think it should be corrected. He believed the Holy Spirit did not permit the wrong name to occur to the writer's mind without reason. Even colder is the solution that says because the Prophets predicted the same things in different ways by the same Spirit, everything belongs to everyone. If we accept that, it doesn't matter whose name is cited for anything in the Sacred Volumes. It is certain that here—

<column-break/>

<margin>E</margin> —the second part of the prophecy is found in Isaiah. But one could ask why, when bringing forward a twin prophecy, he names only one Prophet. As far as the meaning is concerned, it is truly one prophecy. But in Matthew 11:10, whom Mark follows, only Isaiah is named, and only his words are cited. Mark prefixed the prophecy of Malachi to the prophecy of Isaiah, content to name only the most famous Prophet. Furthermore, although the main point of the meaning agrees, the words of the Evangelist differ somewhat from both the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> and the "Hebrew Verity" <note>The original Hebrew text</note>. Indeed, Jerome rendered the Hebrew thus: *Behold, I send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before my face*, with the Septuagint agreeing in all points, except they turned "I send" into the future "I will send," in which Mark agrees with the Hebrew. However, he added "your" when it is simply "the way." And again, where it says there "before my face," he says here "before your face," changing the person speaking. For in the Prophet, these words seem to be Christ speaking about himself, even if he soon speaks of himself as if of another: *And the Lord shall suddenly come to his temple*. <margin>F</margin> In contrast, in the Evangelist, these are the words of the Father speaking to the Son: *who shall prepare your way before you*. Now the second part, *The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare the way of the Lord*, etc., is in Isaiah chapter forty. Jerome translates the Hebrew thus: *The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight the paths of our God*. The Septuagint does not differ from the Hebrew here. The Evangelists do differ somewhat here as well, but only in words. For where the others said *make his paths straight*, John said *direct the way of the Lord*. Then, where the Hebrew Verity and the Septuagint translated *make straight the paths of our God*, Matthew, Mark, and Luke put *his paths*. I suppose this is because the Evangelists, knowing Hebrew, did not need the Septuagint translation; further, since they did not transcribe what was written from the Hebrew books right in front of them, but wrote what memory suggested, they sometimes differ in words while agreeing in meaning—a point Saint Jerome noted in many places. Finally, since it is known even to those who do not know Greek that "angel" <note>original: "angelos"</note> signifies "messenger," I do not think I need to give a warning. Perhaps it would be better to translate it as "messenger" <note>original: "nuncium"</note> here. Then, he did not say...

<margin>A</margin> 4 *simply an angel, but with the article added*, <note>original: "ton angelon"</note> the messenger, *so that you may understand a certain specific messenger or herald is designated; since all the Prophets were in some way messengers of the coming Christ. But this man was that unique and preeminent messenger, who not only announced the coming of the Lord from a distance, but who, running ahead himself, prepared the way for him as he was already arriving. Furthermore, where it says*,
*before your face*] *In the Greek it is not* <note>original: "emprosthen sou"</note> *or* <note>original: "enopion sou"</note>, *which he sometimes translates as "in your presence" or "in your sight," but* <note>original: "pro prosopou sou"</note>, *so that you may understand this messenger precedes him and clears the obstacles from the path, so that the face of the arriving Lord can already be seen and appear. Shortly thereafter*,
4 *who shall prepare your way before you*] *In Greek it is* <note>original: "emprosthen sou"</note>, *as if you were to say, "from your front": so that you understand the Christ who was being announced is already present. For it is said differently: "Before Cicero, Caso said this," meaning before Cicero spoke.*
5 *was in the desert*] *Some, troubled by the word order <term>hyperbaton: a transposition of words from their natural order</term>, read it this way: "John baptizing in the desert was the beginning of the Gospel." However, it seems to me not absurd that these words, "The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, etc.," serve as a title, which is the custom of the Prophets, and also of Herodotus, and indeed that entire nation. Furthermore, regarding the fact that Valla prefers "existed" for "was," and argues some point I know not what about "John was baptizing," it pertains very little to the theological matter. For it was an idiom of the Hebrew language, which you will nevertheless find among the Attic Greeks as well. "He was baptizing," that is, he baptized.* <note>original: "etyngchane baptizon"</note> *The Greek did not add the article to "baptizing," hence it can be taken as if you said, "he began to baptize,"* <note>original: "egeneto baptizon"</note>, *he became a baptizer, or he began to baptize. He was in the desert. In the Greek, the word order is different: "John was baptizing in the desert." And this was more accurate than "he was."*
<margin>B</margin> 6 *unto the remission of sins*] *here "unto" signifies preparation, not the final effect; for John’s baptism prepared the way for Christ’s baptism, by which sins were truly remitted. Perhaps it should also be noted that the Apostles are commanded first to teach, then to baptize. John is said first to baptize, then to preach baptism. The Jew is led to knowledge through ceremonies; the Christian learns first—unless you prefer to understand this as the baptism of Christ, which John preached after his own baptism. For it follows: "I indeed baptized you in water, but he will baptize you, etc." From this it appears that he preached to those baptized by him that the baptism of Christ would soon follow, lest they should place their trust in his own baptism.*
7 *the region of Judea*] <note>original: "he Ioudaia chora"</note>, *that is, the Judean region, so that the two nouns are connected.*
8 *And all the inhabitants of Jerusalem*] *The Greeks punctuate this differently:* <note>original: "kai hoi Hierosolymitai kai ebaptizonto pantes"</note>, *that is, "both the Jerusalemites and they were all baptized." For not every single inhabitant of Jerusalem came, but all those who had come from all Judea and Jerusalem were baptized. For he said "all Judea" to mean from all parts of Judea. Nor is it* "into" <note>original: "eis"</note>,
9 *in the river Jordan*] *but* <note>original: "en Iordane potamo"</note>, *or in the river Jordan. He added this because the word "Jordan" was unknown to many.*
10 *And he was*] <note>original: "En de"</note>, *that is, "But he was." Clothed*, <note>original: "endedymenos"</note>, *that is, dressed. And with camel’s hair. It is "of a camel" in the Greek, and likewise in the Golden Codex <note>A famous 9th-century manuscript</note>, and likewise in the one from Constantinople. Although this changes nothing in the meaning. For "camel" here denotes the species of animal, not one specific individual of that kind. The volumes of Saint Donatian supported the Golden Codex. He expressed the species of the animal to show the roughness of the garment, according to the Lord’s testimony that those who are clothed in soft garments are in the houses of kings. Painters weigh John down with a camel's skin, just as the Greeks dress Hercules in a lion's skin. On the contrary, the garment was woven not from British wool, or the fleeces of the Silk-people <note>Ancient term for the Chinese</note>, or Dutch linen, but from the hairs of camels. A leather belt cinching his loins increased the roughness.*
<margin>C</margin> 11 *And a leather belt*] <note>original: "kai zonen dermatinen"</note>. *It is in the ablative case for us, not the nominative, and refers to the participle "clothed," just like the ablative "hair." And it should have been said "his loins," not "his."*

<column-break/>

...in the desert, <margin>5</margin> preaching the baptism of repentance <margin>6</margin> for the forgiveness of sins. And there went out to him the whole region of Judea, <margin>8</margin> and those of Jerusalem: and they were all baptized by him <margin>9</margin> in the river Jordan, confessing their sins. <margin>10</margin> Now John was clothed with camel's hair <margin>11</margin> and a leather belt around his loins, <margin>12</margin> and he ate locusts and wild honey: and <margin>A</margin> he preached, saying, <margin>13</margin> "There comes one mightier than I after me, <margin>14</margin> for whom I am not fit to stoop down and loosen the strap <margin>15</margin> of his sandals. <margin>16</margin> I indeed baptized you with water: but he will baptize you <margin>17</margin> with the Holy Spirit." And it happened in those days, Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee, and was baptized by John in the Jordan. And immediately <margin>18</margin> as he came up out of the <margin>B</margin> water, he saw the heavens torn apart, <margin>19</margin> and the Spirit, like a dove, <margin>20</margin> descending upon him. And a voice was made from the heavens, "You are that Son of mine, <margin>21</margin> the beloved, <margin>22</margin> in whom I am well pleased." And immediately the Spirit <margin>23</margin> drives him out into the desert. <margin>24</margin> And he was there in the desert for forty days, and was tempted by Satan, and was with the wild beasts: and the Angels ministered to him. <margin>C</margin> But after John had been arrested, Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom of God, and saying, <margin>25</margin> "The time is fulfilled, <margin>26</margin> and the kingdom of God is at hand: <margin>27</margin> repent, and believe the Gospel."
<margin>28</margin> When

<margin>D</margin> 12 *He ate wild honey*] <note>original: "esthion"</note>, *that is, eating, so that it belongs to the verb that preceded, "was." Although he varied this correctly, except that "he fed upon" was more appropriate than "he ate," or certainly "he lived on," since he was speaking about a type of food.*
13 *Comes*] <note>original: "erchetai"</note>, *comes—in Greek it is either in the present tense or the future. In the book of Donatian it was held as "will come." And the article is to be noted*, <note>original: "ho ischyroteros"</note>, *that is, "that one who is stronger and more powerful than I."*
14 *I am not worthy*] <note>original: "ouk eimi hikanos"</note>, *that is, I am not fit, or sufficient, as they commonly say.*
15 *And of his sandals*] *He added "his" in the Hebrew manner; it is not the custom for Latins to speak this way.*
16 *I baptized*] <note>original: "Ego men"</note>. *In the past tense he omitted the conjunction "indeed," which opposes this part to the Spirit.*
17 *With the Holy Spirit*] *In the Greek it is "In the Holy Spirit," even though the Translator rightly omitted the preposition. A certain Greek manuscript also added in this place "and with fire,"* <note>original: "kai pyri"</note>, *from Matthew, as I guess, although Theophylact does not add it.*
<margin>E</margin> 18 *Ascending he saw*] *The Greek speech is ambiguous as to whether John saw it, or Christ. He saw the heavens opened, he saw* <note>original: "schizomenous tous ouranous"</note>, *that is, he saw the heavens being split or torn apart. For it is a passive participle of the present tense, which should be translated not by "he had known," as it seemed to Lorenzo [Valla], but through the verb "was." He would have translated more elegantly as "the heavens being drawn apart" or "split."*
19 *And the Holy Spirit*] *"Holy" is not added, neither in the Greek, nor in the oldest Latin manuscripts, nor in the Golden Codex, nor even in the Constantian one. Furthermore, the added article indicates it should be understood as the Holy Spirit, which he mentioned a little before. Similarly, a little later, it says "immediately the Spirit drove him out," so that you take it to be the same Spirit.*
20 *Descending and remaining*] *"And remaining" is not added in the Greek; it seems to have been written in from the Gospel of John. From the Greek speech, nothing else can be understood except that the Spirit descending was seen by Christ, although the matter requires more that it be understood to have been seen descending by John and the others. Then, if we accept that Christ saw it, it should have been said* <note>original: "eph' hauton"</note>, *that is, "upon himself," not* <note>original: "ep' auton"</note>, *that is, "upon him." Yet I do not see how the matter can be explained unless we say* <note>original: "anabainon"</note> *in the nominative case was placed in the stead of the parenthetical* <note>original: "anabainontos"</note>, *that is, "when Jesus was ascending from the water, he saw, etc." Unless we accept that John descended into the river together with Jesus to dip him, and thus we read, "John ascending from the water, saw, etc."*
<margin>F</margin> 21 *Beloved*] <note>original: "ho agapetos"</note>. *The article does not lack emphasis, as if you were to say, "that beloved one." The same is added to the Son*, <note>original: "ho Huios"</note>: *there are many sons, many beloved, but this is that preeminent and uniquely beloved one. Secondly, the word here is a noun, not a participle, "the beloved," which he usually translates as "most dear."*
22 *I am well pleased*] <note>original: "eudokesa"</note>, *as if you were to say, "I have a good opinion," or "it is well pleasing to me."*
23 *He drove out*] <note>original: "ekballei"</note>, *that is, he sends out, in the present tense. Although* <note>original: "ekballo"</note> *is sometimes to eject or thrust out. Moreover, it signifies the force of the spirit seizing a man wherever it wishes. Theophylact and Chrysostom, cited in the Chain <note>A catena, or collection of patristic commentaries</note>, warn that this signifies one must not commit oneself to throw oneself into the danger of temptation, but if one falls into it by God's will, one must act bravely.*
24 *And he was in the desert*] *A certain Greek manuscript had only "And he was there." Another moreover adds "in the desert." But why was it necessary to repeat "desert" when it had just preceded? "Forty days"—in the Greek, "and forty nights" is not added.*
25 *Because it is fulfilled*] <note>original: "hoti"</note> *in this place should have been omitted by the Translator.*
26 *Has approached*] <note>original: "engiken"</note>. *"And has approached," or "is approaching," as in verbs of this kind the Greeks sometimes use the past tense in place of the present, as we have already pointed out more than once.*
27 *Repent*] <note>original: "Metanoeite"</note>, *that is, "Repent you," which usually...*
<sig>K 3</sig> <meta>catchword: has been</meta>

# THE GOSPEL, CHAPTER I.

16 And passing by the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew his brother, casting <margin>i. b 17</margin> a net into the sea; for they were fishermen. And Jesus said to them, "Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men." And immediately leaving <margin>ia e 19</margin> their nets, they followed him. And going on from there a little further, he saw James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, who were also in the boat mending the nets. And immediately he called them; and leaving their father Zebedee in the boat <margin>ib e 21</margin> with the hired servants, they went after him. And they entered into Capernaum; and immediately on the Sabbath, entering into the synagogue, he taught. <margin>ig b 22</margin> And they were astonished at his teaching; for he was teaching them as one having authority, and not as the Scribes. And there was in <margin>id e 23</margin> their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit, and he cried out, saying, "Ah! What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, the Holy One of God." And Jesus rebuked him, saying, "Be silent, and come out of him." And the unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him. And they were all amazed, so that they debated among themselves, saying, "What is this? What is this new teaching, that with authority he commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him?" And his fame spread immediately into the whole surrounding region <margin>ie k 29</margin> of Galilee. And immediately coming out of the synagogue, they entered into the house of Simon and Andrew with James and John. Now Simon's mother-in-law lay sick with a fever; and immediately they spoke to him about her. And coming to her, he raised her up, taking her by the hand; and the fever left her immediately, and she served them. When evening came, when the sun had set, they brought to him all who were sick and those possessed by demons. And the whole city was gathered together at <margin>is k 34</margin> the door. And he healed many who were sick with various diseases; and he cast out many demons, and he did not permit <margin>iz k 35</margin> the demons to speak, because they knew him. And in the morning...

<margin>16</margin> It would have been possible to translate as, "Do penance," or as I would prefer, "Return to a right mind" <note>original: *Resipiscite*</note>. And believe in the Gospel <note>Greek: *en Euangelio*</note>, that is, "in the Gospel," although this is a characteristic of the Hebrew language. <term>Theophylact</term> <note>A Bulgarian archbishop and influential biblical commentator</note> thinks that the observance of the Law is abolished here when he says, "believe in the Gospel," as if to say, "Let the shadows cease, the light is here." This matches what precedes it: "the time is fulfilled." Therefore, Christ did not teach exactly the same thing at the beginning as John did.

<margin>28</margin> **28 And passing by]** "Passing by the sea," that is, "Walking indeed at the sea, or near the sea." However, another manuscript had, "And passing along by the sea." Furthermore, he calls the lake a "sea."

<margin>29</margin> **29 His brother]** In Greek, it is "Simon’s" <note>Greek: *Simonos*</note>. Some repeat both: "his, that is Simon’s," which I think was added by someone who wanted to avoid ambiguity, lest we understand it to be Christ's own brother. Nor is the word for "nets" here the same as the word used a little later <note>Greek: *diktya*</note>, but rather a "casting-net" <note>Greek: *amphiblestron*</note>, a specific type of net mentioned by <term>Julius Pollux</term> <note>A 2nd-century Greek grammarian and rhetorician</note>.

<margin>30</margin> **30 Mending nets]** <note>Greek: *katartizontas*</note>, that is, repairing or refitting.

<margin>31</margin> **31 They followed him]** <note>Greek: *apelthon opiso autou*</note>, that is, "they went away after him," to render word for word. What for others is the common expression, "go behind me," here means "follow me." <term>Theophylact</term> thinks this records a second calling, because the narrative in Luke chapter 5 differs from the narrative in Matthew and Mark. However, regarding the addition that Peter and Andrew were disciples of <term>John the Baptist</term>, who began to trust because of his expert testimony about Christ but returned to their former trade after John was thrown into prison—whence they were called again and immediately followed—since this rests on no scriptural authority, I judge it should be considered a human conjecture.

<margin>32</margin> **32 As one having authority]** "As" <note>Greek: *hos*</note>, that is, "as if." Although this "as if," and what follows soon after, respond to the same Greek word, he could have translated it in both places as "as." Furthermore, we have spoken about "authority" <note>Greek: *exousia*</note> in Matthew.

<margin>33</margin> **33 In an unclean spirit]** What phrasing could be harsher to both Latin and Greek ears? It could have been said, "subject to an unclean spirit."

<margin>34</margin> **34 What to us and to you?]** <note>Greek: *Ea, ti hemin kai soi?*</note>, that is, "Let be, what to us and to you?" Although "Ah" <note>Greek: *ia*</note> is more correctly understood as a Greek adverb, for us it is an interjection of one exclaiming; in Latin one might have translated, "What business have we with you?" or, as it could also be, "What business do you have with us?"

<margin>35</margin> **35 Have you come before the time to destroy us?]** "Before the time" is not added in the Greek, nor in the Golden Codex, nor even in the Constance manuscript. It seems to have been added here from the eighth chapter of Matthew.

<margin>36</margin> **36 I know that you are]** <note>Greek: *oida se tis ei*</note>, that is, "I know you, who you are," and so our ancient manuscripts have "who you are," not "that you are," or "I recognize you, who you are," to express it more literally.

<margin>37</margin> **37 The Holy One of God]** <note>Greek: *ho hagios tou Theou*</note>. Nor is this article added without reason, as has often been indicated elsewhere. For he is not simply "holy," but "The Holy One," so that you understand a certain and distinguished person—

<column-break/>

<margin>16</margin> Now as he walked by the sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew his brother, casting nets into the sea; for they were fishermen. <margin>17</margin> And Jesus said to them, "Follow me, and I will cause you to be made fishers of men." <margin>18</margin> And immediately, having left their nets, they followed him. <margin>19</margin> And having gone forward a little from there, he saw James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, who themselves were in the boat refitting their nets. <margin>20</margin> And immediately he called them: and they, having left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men, followed him. <margin>21</margin> And they enter Capernaum: and immediately on the Sabbaths, having entered into the synagogue, he taught. <margin>22</margin> And they were amazed at his doctrine: for he was teaching them as one endowed with authority, and not like the Scribes. <margin>23</margin> And there was in their synagogue a man subject to an unclean spirit, and he cried out, <margin>24</margin> Saying, "Ah, what business have we with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, namely that Holy One of God." <margin>25</margin> And Jesus rebuked him, saying, "Be silent, and go out of the man." <margin>26</margin> And when the unclean spirit had convulsed him and had cried out with a loud voice, it went out of him. <margin>27</margin> And they were all astonished, so that they questioned among themselves, saying, "What is this? What new doctrine is this, that with authority he commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him?" <margin>28</margin> And his fame went out immediately into the whole surrounding region of Galilee. <margin>29</margin> And immediately, having gone out of the synagogue, they came into the house of Simon and Andrew with James and John. <margin>30</margin> Now Simon's mother-in-law lay sick with a fever: and immediately they tell him about her. <margin>31</margin> And approaching, he raised her up, having taken her hand: and the fever left her instantly, and she served them. <margin>32</margin> But in the evening, when the sun had set, they brought to him all who were unwell, and those who were driven by demons. <margin>33</margin> And the whole city was gathered at the door. <margin>34</margin> And he healed many who were sick with various diseases: and he cast out many demons: and he did not allow the demons to speak, because they knew him. And <margin>35</margin> in the morning...

—namely that one truly holy person, and the source of all human sanctity. Therefore, it was clearer to say, "I know you, who you are, namely that Holy One of God."

<margin>38</margin> **38 And he was threatened]** <note>Greek: *Epetimesen*</note>, that is, "And he rebuked."

<margin>39</margin> **39 From the man]** In the Greek it is "from him" <note>Greek: *ex autou*</note>.

<margin>40</margin> **40 And tearing him, and crying out]** Both participles in Greek are in the past tense <note>Greek: *sparaxan* and *kraxan*</note>, as if to say, "that one having been convulsed, and a cry having been sent forth."

<margin>41</margin> **41 What ever is this?]** <note>Greek: *Ti esti touto?*</note> The translator added the particle "ever" <note>Latin: *nam*</note> on his own, though elsewhere he neglects to express it, perhaps making pairs in this way. And again,

<margin>42</margin> **42 What ever doctrine?]** <note>Greek: *tis he didache*</note>. For "what doctrine," he added "ever" on his own.

<margin>43</margin> **43 Because in power he also commands spirits]** "Because in power and spirits" is found both in the Greek and in the ancient Latin, as if the conjunction adds emphasis. However, the Greek manuscripts punctuate the passage in two ways. Some read it thus: "What is this doctrine, for it is according to power," understanding "is" to be implied. Others join these with what follows: "What is this doctrine, that with authority he commands even the unclean spirits."

<margin>44</margin> **44 And it went forth]** <note>Greek: *Exelthen*</note>, that is, "And it went out, or it spread." "His rumor" <note>Greek: *he akoe autou*</note>, that is, his fame, which in some places is translated as "opinion." However, while we speak of a man's fame, we do not say "a man's rumor" in the same sense. For "rumor" refers more to an event, like a rumor of war. "Fame" is a general name.

<margin>45</margin> **45 Region]** <note>Greek: *perichoron*</note>, that is, "the whole surrounding region bordering Galilee," so that we understand Jesus's fame to have progressed even beyond the borders of Galilee.

<margin>46</margin> **46 He was reclining]** <note>Greek: *katekeito*</note>, that is, "he was lying down," as the ancient manuscripts also have, and with them that Golden Codex, and even the Constance one. For one "reclines" <note>Latin: *recumbit*</note> when resting on one's back. One "takes a place" <note>Latin: *accumbitur*</note> at a banquet. A sick person "lies down" <note>Latin: *decumbit*</note> confined to a bed.

<margin>47</margin> **47 Having taken her hand]** <note>Greek: *kratesas*</note>, which he so often translates as "he held," as in the case of Jesus being "captured" or "they held him," where it was more appropriate to say "they seized him." And why did he not use "left" rather than "sent away" <note>Greek: *apheken*</note>; unless perhaps the fever departed having said goodbye.

<margin>48</margin> **48 The whole city]** <note>Greek: *he polis hole*</note>, that is, "the whole city," though you might understand it as "several cities."

<margin>49</margin> **49 Who were troubled]** <note>Greek: *kakos echontas*</note>, that is, "those having it badly," or "badly affected." "With various illnesses" <note>Greek: *poikilais nosois*</note>, that is, with various diseases; which, however, he almost always translates this way.

<margin>50</margin> **50 Because they knew him]** In Greek it is thus: "that they knew him to be the Christ." For these two words are added in some Greek copies, as in Theophylact; in ours it is only, "because they knew him." The Greek phrasing, however, is ambiguous; it does not allow for this prologue that they recognized Jesus; or, he did not permit them to speak at all because they recognized him to be the Christ the Messiah, lest they blurt it out before the time. In the former sense, "himself" was more appropriate than "him."

# ACCORDING TO MARK. CHAPTER II.

<margin>E</margin> <note>original: "ne multa adhuc nocte" — while it was still deep night. This is what the Greek *ennuchon* signifies, when a significant part of the night remains.</note>
<note>52 original: "Dixerunt" — they said. The Greek is *legousi*, which means "they say." And shortly after, "Because all," the conjunction *hoti* (that/because) should have been omitted in the translation.</note>
<note>53 original: "In proximos" — into the next [places]. The Greek *eis tas echomenas* means "adjacent" or "neighboring." For "villages and cities," the Greeks have a compound word, *kōmopoleis*, which some interpret as municipalities. It signifies rural towns that could be seen as either villages or towns, as the Greek word is composed of *kōmē* (village) and *polis* (city).</note>
<note>54 original: "Ut ibi prædicem" — that I may preach there. In Greek it is *hina kai ekei*, "that I may preach *also* there." This is consistent in our ancient manuscripts. And for "in this," it was clearer to say "to this end" or "for this sake," from the Greek *eis touto*.</note>
<note>55 original: "Et in omni Galilæa" — and in all Galilee. The word "And" is not in the Greek; rather it says "in their synagogues throughout all Galilee."</note>
<note>56 original: "Si vis" — if you will. In this place, the Translator correctly omitted the word *hoti* (that); it is a wonder why he does not do the same everywhere when the flow of speech requires it.</note>
<note>57 original: "Volo, mundare" — I will, be clean. "Mundare" (be clean) here is in the passive, imperative mood: *Thelō, katharisthēti*, just as it is in Matthew.</note>
<note>58 original: "Et comminatus est" — and he strictly warned. The Greek *Kai embrimēsamenos autō, eutheōs exebalen* means "And having strictly warned him, he immediately sent him away." That is, he sternly threatened him not to tell anyone. He used "sent away" (*exebalen*) instead of "dismissed," perhaps because it was done quickly or because the man was unwilling to leave.</note>
<note>59 original: "Vide nemini" — see [you tell] no one. *Hora mēdeni*, that is, "See that you tell no one."</note>
<note>60 original: "Ostende te" — show yourself. The Greek *heauton deixon* means "show yourself." Although the Translator usually renders these compound pronouns as simple ones. And where our codices read "to the high priest," the Greek is "to the priest" (*tō hierei*), unless the article *to* suggests it refers to the High Priest.</note>
<note>61 original: "Cœpit prædicare" — he began to preach. The Greeks add *polla*, meaning "much" or "many things."</note>
<note>62 original: "Diffamare" — to spread the news. In Greek, *diaphēmizein* does not have a negative connotation [like "defame"]. It could be translated as "to scatter" or "to divulge."</note>
<note>63 original: "Ita ut iam non posset jam" — so that he could no longer. From the Greek words, it is clear this refers to Jesus. Lest the reader be confused here, we have substituted the name "Jesus" for the pronoun "him" (*auton*). Let no one immediately "correct" this as if it were a reckless change.</note>
<note>64 original: "In desertis locis esse" — to be in desert places. The Greek says "was" (*ēn*), not "to be."</note>
<note>65 original: "Et veniebant" — and they were coming. The Greek *kai ērchonto* means "and they were coming."</note>

<note>original: "Post dies" — after days. The Greek is *di' hēmerōn*, that is, "through days." One should not add "eight," which is found in some Latin codices. Certainly, in the Paulinus manuscript it had "after days," while in the Corfendonsian one "eight" had been added by a recent hand. But it was clearer to say "after some days" or "after several days." For "after days" in Latin means nothing on its own.</note>
<note>2 original: "Et convenerunt" — and they came together. The Greek *Kai eutheōs sunēchthēsan* means "And immediately they came together," or "were collected."</note>
<note>3 original: "Nec ad januam" — not even at the door. The Greek says *hōste mēketi chōrein mēde ta pros tēn thuran*, which means "so that there was no longer room, not even in the parts near the door," so that you understand the house was so crammed that even the vestibule and the areas close to the entrance could not hold the crowd. The Golden Codex had "it did not hold," as did the Constantian one and my own old printed edition: so that the verb "hold" refers to the house, and it is a double negative—that neither the house nor the places near the door (the vestibule) could hold them.</note>
<note>4 original: "Et veniunt" — and they come. The Greek *Kai erchontai* means "And they come."</note>
<note>5 original: "Nudaverunt tectum" — they stripped the roof. The Greek *apestegasan tēn stegēn* means "they uncovered the covering." For *apostegazein* is as if you were to say, "they un-tiled the tiles."</note>
<note>6 original: "Et patefacientes" — and opening it up. The Greek *kai exoruxantes* means "when they had dug it out," so we understand that the roof was actually broken through from above.</note>
<note>7 original: "Submiserunt" — they let down. The Greek *chalōsi* means "they lower," specifically with ropes, just as an anchor is lowered or something is let down by a line.</note>
<note>8 original: "In quo paralyticus jacebat" — in which the paralytic was lying. The Greek *katekeito* means "he was lying down," which had been slightly corrupted in older versions to "recumbent."</note>
<note>9 original: "Quid hic sic loquitur, blasphemias" — Why does he speak thus, blasphemies? In Greek it is *blasphemias*, he speaks blasphemies.</note>
<note>10 original: "Nisi solus Deus" — but God alone. The Greek *ei mē heis ho Theos* means "except the one who is God." In most of our codices it reads "except God alone," and it is used this way. <note>Erasmus enters a technical grammatical debate here about the Greek word *apheōntai* (forgiven).</note> It seems to be an Attic past tense for *aphōntai*. The active root is *aphiēmi*, the passive *aphiemai*. This is what the grammarian Herodian teaches. Perhaps the Translator read *aphientai* with an 'e' micron, derived from the verb *iō*. In our previous edition, we put "are forgiven"; this was because a man remarkably learned in Greek and of no small authority, when consulted on this passage, ordered that I should translate it "are forgiven" at his own risk. I complied, and was wrong. Though this has happened to me more than once, I am told I am stubborn and yield to no one.</note>
<note>12 original: "Ut mirarentur" — so that they wondered. The Greek says more: *hōste existasthai*, that is, "so that they were astonished," or as if outside themselves. For from this verb comes the word *ekstasis* (ecstasy), which is a seizing of the mind.</note>

---

<margin>13</margin> *They might honor*] <note>original: "δοξάζειν" (doxazein)</note>, that is, they might glorify.
<margin>14</margin> *Levi of Alphaeus*] <note>original: "τὸν τοῦ Ἀλφαίου"</note>, that is, the son of Alphaeus.
<margin>15</margin> *At the tax booth*] He retains the Greek word, <term>telonium <gloss>tax-collection office</gloss></term>, which is the table or place of the publicans where they collect the tax, which in Greek is called *telos*.
<margin>16</margin> *Seeing that he ate*] <note>original: "ἰδόντες αὐτὸν ἐσθίοντα"</note>, that is, when they had seen him eating. It is a wonder why this grammatical error [solecism] was preferred here, since the Greek language offered no occasion for it.
<margin>17</margin> *Why*] <note>original: "Τί ὅτι"</note>, that is, "What that," which means, "What is it that..." *Your Master*. Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo Valla, a pioneer of New Testament textual criticism.</note> denies that these words were added in the manuscripts he used. In some, however, he found them added, although Theophylact does not add them. In the Constance manuscript, it was erased.
<margin>18</margin> *They do not have necessity*] <note>original: "ἡ χρείαν ἔχουσι"</note>, that is, they have no need. *Healthy*, <note>original: "ἰσχύοντες"</note>, that is, those who are strong or those who are well.
<margin>19</margin> *To call the righteous*] The Greeks add <note>original: "εἰς μετάνοιαν"</note>, that is, to repentance. Although I suspect this was added by someone later. For it is not found in our most ancient codices, nor in the Constance one, nor in my old printed edition, even if it is added in Theophylact.
<margin>20</margin> *And the Pharisees*] A certain Greek codex had <note>original: "καὶ οἱ τῶν Φαρισαίων"</note>, that is, "and those *of* the Pharisees," so that "disciples" is understood, just as it is a little later; unless you prefer "those who are of the Pharisees," that is, of the Pharisaic faction.
<margin>21</margin> *Could they*] <note>original: "Μὴ δύνανται"</note>, that is, "Are they able?" or "Can they?"
<margin>22</margin> *Children of the marriage*] The Greek is slightly different: <note>original: "οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ νυμφῶνος, ἐν ᾧ ὁ νυμφίος μετ᾿ αὐτῶν ἐστι, νηστεύειν"</note>, that is, "the sons of the bridal chamber in which the bridegroom is with them, to fast." For *nymphōn* signifies the bridal bedchamber, according to the interpreter Suidas. Then immediately he answers himself: "As long a time as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast."
<margin>23</margin> *A patch*] <note>original: "ἐπίβλημα"</note>, which he had previously translated as a "joining" in Matthew 9 and Luke 5, literally means an "insertion." However, the Translator has translated clearly. *Of raw cloth*, <note>original: "ῥάκους ἀγνάφου"</note>, that is, of cloth not yet treated by a fuller <note>A person who cleans and thickens raw cloth.</note>. For the Translator calls this "raw." Indeed, *gnaphos* signifies a fuller.
<margin>24</margin> *Pulls away the new addition*] The Greek added "of it," as the Latin version by Cabaudias shows. What he translates here as "addition" <note>Latin: *supplementum*</note>, he elsewhere translated as "fullness," <note>original: "πλήρωμα" (plērōma)</note>, as in Matthew 9. Moreover, he calls the "fullness" that little piece of cloth with which a torn garment is patched and filled. I pass over many things wisely, because they have already been discussed regarding Matthew.
<margin>25</margin> *New wine into new skins*] For the Greeks, there is not the same distinction, since they have both *neos* and *kainos*, the former of which is more aptly said of things that feel age <note>i.e., new as in "recent" vs. new as in "unused".</note>.
<margin>26</margin> *They began to proceed*] <note>original: "ἤρξαντο οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ ὁδὸν ποιεῖν"</note>, that is, the disciples began to make a journey. For where the Greek speech has *erxanto*, that is, "they began," the Translator referred this to the person: just as when it is said "he began to speak," it is not someone who starts to talk after having been silent, but one who is first and begins to speak before others, and for that reason he translates it as "to proceed." Doubtless, he was shown the absurdity of the speech, because since it had been said just before that Jesus made a journey through the fields, now the same thing is added about the disciples, that they had begun to enter upon a journey. But here neither the beginning of a journey is meant, nor the order of walking, but the beginning of plucking. For already, while going, they began to pluck ears of grain. *And to pluck ears*, <note>original: "τίλλοντες"</note>, that is, plucking, or by plucking.
<margin>27</margin> *Behold what your disciples do on the Sabbath*] Just as "your master" was not added slightly above, so here "your disciples" is not added among the Greeks. For what was the point of naming them, since they were pointing them out with a finger, "behold"?
<margin>F</margin>
<margin>28</margin> *Under Abiathar the high priest*] Saint Jerome, in his booklet *On the Best Kind of Translating*, indicates that the name Abiathar is put for Ahimelech, because in the first book of Kings [1 Samuel], chapter 22, where the history of this matter is recounted, no mention is made of Abiathar, but only of Ahimelech; whether this happened by the fault of scribes, or because Abiathar and Ahimelech are names for the same man. For Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a famous medieval commentator.</note> thinks this Abiathar was the son of Ahimelech, who performed his father's duty under his father, and in that event, by Saul's command, was a companion of David's flight. Jerome ties the knot but does not untie it. Theophylact opens another crack, suggesting we should accept that there was another Ahimelech, who in the book of Kings is called only "priest" <note>original: "ἱερεὺς"</note>, while here Abiathar is called "High Priest" <note>original: "Ἀρχιερεὺς"</note>. It is strange, since Latin codices constantly have Ahimelech, why in the Greek Gospels it is always Abimelech, except that Suidas warns in the entry "anagrapsai" that the same man is designated by both names.
<margin>29</margin> *Except only*] "Only" is not added among the Greeks, nor was it in the Constance manuscript.
<margin>30</margin> *And he gave to them*] The Greeks add "also," "also to those who were with him." It would have been better translated: "who were with him; and he gave to those who were with him."

<margin>Other 22 31 lawful 32 2</margin> And the Scribes who had come down from Jerusalem were saying, "He has Beelzebub," and "By the prince of demons he casts out demons."

---

1 **To do good**] <note>original: "ἀγαθοποιῆσαι" (agathopoiēsai)</note>, or to do harm; this does not simply mean to do a bad or good thing, but to affect someone with good or evil, as if you were to say, *Is it right to benefit someone on the Sabbath, or to injure them?*
2 **Or to destroy**] <note>original: "ἢ ἀποκτεῖναι" (ē apokteinai)</note>, that is, *or to kill?*
3 **And looking around**] <note>original: "περιβλεψάμενος" (periblepsamenos)</note>, that is, *when he had looked around*. It is not just "looking," but a deliberate gaze.
4 **Being grieved**] <note>original: "συλλυπούμενος" (syllypoumenos)</note>, that is, *grieving with them or pitying their condition*. <note>Erasmus notes the Greek implies a shared or deep sorrow rather than just "condolescing."</note>
5 **And his hand was restored**] In Greek it is, <note>original: "καὶ ἀποκατεστάθη ἡ χεὶρ αὐτοῦ ὑγιής, ὡς ἡ ἄλλη"</note>, that is, *and his hand was restored healthy, like the other*. Truly, I do not know if some words were added here from Matthew.
6 **That a small boat should serve him**] <note>original: "ἵνα πλοιάριον προσκαρτερῇ αὐτῷ"</note>, that is, *so that a boat would wait on him*, meaning, *so that a boat would be for his use, or placed at his service*. For <term>proskarterein</term> <note>original: "προσκαρτερεῖν"</note> often elsewhere means *to assist, or to persist in attendance*.
7 **They might not crush him**] <note>original: "μὴ θλίβωσιν αὐτόν"</note>, that is, *lest they press upon him*. The first [Latin translation] is more Latinate, the second more adapted to the Greek phrasing.
8 **Afflictions**] <note>original: "μάστιγας" (mastigas)</note>, that is, *scourges* or *whips*. For this is what he calls the affliction with which God corrects men.
9 **They cried out, saying**] <note>original: "ἔκραζον, λέγοντα"</note>, this refers to the spirits themselves, because that word in Greek is of the neuter gender.
10 **He strictly warned**] <note>original: "ἐπετίμα" (epetima)</note>, that is, *he rebuked*. Although in this place, *he threatened* or *interdicted* was more tolerable.
11 **And ascending the mountain he called**] In Greek it is <note>original: "ἀνέβη καὶ προσκαλεῖται"</note>, that is, *he ascended & calls*, as the latter verb is in the present tense.
12 **And he made twelve**] The Greek copies differ somewhat: *And he made twelve, whom he also named Apostles, so that they might be with him*. Although that is not written in the more corrected Greek manuscripts: and it better suits the brevity of Mark that it be omitted. And here also I prudently ignore many things, either because they are trivial, or because they have already been noted in Matthew.
13 **And he gave**] <note>original: "καὶ ἔχειν"</note>, that is, *and to have, or so that they might have*. For it depends on what came before, *that they might be with him, and have power: or certainly it is to be connected with the next verb, he sent them to preach and to have power*.
14 **And he imposed on Simon**] Before these words, some Greek codices have <note>original: "πρῶτον Σίμωνα"</note>, that is, *first Simon*. Truly, this is not found in the more corrected and ancient copies, and it seems to be taken from Matthew. Certainly, I did not find it in Theophylact, nor in the Aldine Edition. *And he imposed the name Peter on Simon*. In Greek indeed it is <note>original: "ἔθηκε Πέτρον"</note>. But *Peter*, or *to Peter*, is more Latinate, if I am not mistaken, unless a paraphrase is more pleasing.
15 **Boanerges**] For in Hebrew <note>original: "בני רגש" (Beni Reges)</note> sounds like sons of <note>original: "רגש" (Reges)</note>, which is thunder or

<margin>4</margin> [Rise] up, stand in the middle. And he says to them, "Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good, or to do evil? to save a soul, or to kill?" But they were silent.
<margin>5</margin> And when he had looked around at them with anger, grieving over the blindness of their hearts, he says to the man, "Stretch out your hand." And he stretched it: and his hand was restored healthy, like the other.
<margin>6</margin> But the Pharisees, having gone out, immediately took counsel with the Herodians against him, so that they might destroy him.
<margin>7</margin> But Jesus with his disciples withdrew to the sea: and a huge multitude from Galilee followed him, and from Judea,
<margin>8</margin> And from Jerusalem, and from Idumea, and from across the Jordan: and those who lived around Tyre and Sidon, a great multitude of people, when they had heard what he was doing, came to him.
<margin>9</margin> And he commanded his disciples that a small boat should wait on him because of the crowd, lest they should press upon him.
<margin>10</margin> For he had healed many, so that they rushed upon him, so that they might touch him, as many as were afflicted.
<margin>11</margin> And the unclean spirits, when they saw him, fell down before him, and cried out, saying, "You are the Son of God."
<margin>12</margin> And he vehemently threatened them, that they should not make him known.
<margin>13</margin> And he ascended the mountain, and called to himself whom he himself wanted: and they came to him.
<margin>14</margin> And he made it so that twelve were with him, and that he might send them out to preach,
<margin>15</margin> And that they might have the power of healing diseases, and of casting out demons.
<margin>16</margin> And he imposed on Simon the name Peter:
<margin>17</margin> And James the son of Zebedee, and John the brother of James, and he imposed on them the names Boanerges, which is, sons of thunder:
<margin>18</margin> And Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddeus, and Simon the Canaanite,
<margin>19</margin> And Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him.
<margin>20</margin> And they come into a house: and the crowd gathers again, so that it was not permitted for them even to eat bread.
<margin>21</margin> And when those who belonged to him had heard, they went out to lay hands on him: for they were saying, "He has turned into a fury."
<margin>22</margin> And the Scribes, who had come down from Jerusalem, were saying, "He has Beelzebul," and "by the prince of demons he casts them out."

---

rumbling, so we are taught by a little book on the interpretation of Hebrew names, of uncertain title. Nevertheless, Jerome thinks the word is corrupted, and that it should be read as *Banereem*: for <note>original: "רעם" (Raam)</note> to the Hebrews sounds like *rumbling, unless you prefer "sons of commotion" or "tumult"*, for not rarely did the Seventy <note>The "Seventy" refers to the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> pronounce the letter <term>Ayin</term> <note>original: "ע"</note> as a "g," as can be seen in the word *Gomorrah*. Although "rumbling" is very close to *thunder*. Since Homer calls Jove <term>the high-thunderer</term> <note>original: "ὑψιβρεμέτην"</note> and <term>loud-crashing</term> <note>original: "ἐρίγδουπον"</note>, for no other reason than for *thunder*. Furthermore, why does Jerome call it corrupt? Perhaps because it was deflected from the Syrian or Chaldean language. The Evangelists frequently use words of this kind. Indeed, Christ seems to have spoken in this language, which was then most familiar to the common people. But if the Evangelist "corrupted" it, he did not do so carelessly, nor should what the Evangelist wrote—having been uttered by Christ—be held as corrupt by us, especially since he deigned to interpret it for us in Greek. Therefore, there was no reason why a certain person should rage against me, because I preferred to follow the authority of the Evangelist here rather than Jerome: especially since Jerome, in matters of this kind, sometimes either overlooks things or is inconsistent, and it is not to be doubted that he is mistaken in some places.
16 **And Matthew**] The Greek codex adds something here: <note>original: "τὸν τελώνην"</note>, that is, *the tax collector*. Although I do not find that in the more corrected and ancient copies.
17 **And the crowd gathers again**] <note>original: "καὶ συνέρχεται πάλιν"</note>. "Gathers" <note>original: "Convenit"</note> is in the present tense, so that the first syllable should be pronounced with an acute accent. Even though this is a tiny detail, I nevertheless judged it not unworthy to be indicated, because in so sacred a matter it is a sin to neglect even the smallest things.
18 **So that they could not**] In the Greek there are two negatives, <note>original: "ὥστε μὴ δύνασθαι αὐτοὺς μήτε ἄρτον φαγεῖν"</note>. This could be rendered in Latin in two ways: *So great a crowd gathered again, that they were not able to even eat bread. Or thus, so that they were not able even to eat bread*. For it means the multitude was so great that not only was there no side-dish left over, but there was not even enough bread for food. Or certainly, the influx was so great that the disciples had no leisure for taking food, so far were they from having leisure for other things: which latter sense, in my judgment, is more true.
19 **And when his own heard it**] <note>original: "οἱ παρ’ αὐτοῦ"</note>, those who belonged to him, and were of his family or kinship. Likewise, a little further down he translates "those things of his" as *his own*. For it means his relatives and kinsmen.
20 **They went out to hold him**] <note>original: "κρατῆσαι αὐτόν"</note>, that is, *that they might seize him, or lay hands on him*. For that is the duty of kinsmen, if anyone should begin to be disturbed in mind.
21 **He has turned into a fury**] that is, <note>original: "ἐξέστη"</note>, he is captured in mind, or, as it is read in some places, <note>original: "ἐξέστη"</note> [he is beside himself].
22 **Beelzebub**] <note>original: "Βεελζεβοὺλ"</note>, that is, Beelzebub, about whom we spoke in Matthew.
23 **Because in the prince**] Here the word <note>original: "ὅτι"</note> [that/because] was to be omitted or translated differently.

### GOSPEL CHAPTER IV.

24 **Against itself** <note>Latin: *In se*</note>] <note>original: "ἐφ' ἑαυτὴν"</note>, that is, into itself, or against itself.

25 **May be divided** <note>Latin: *Dispertiatur*</note>] The same word that he just translated as "be divided" <note>original: "μερισθῇ"</note>.

26 **It is divided** <note>Latin: *Dispertitus est*</note>] The Greek reads thus: <note>original: "Καὶ εἰ ὁ Σατανᾶς ἀνέστη ἑαυτὸν καὶ μεμέρισται, οὐ δύναται σταθῆναι"</note>, that is, "And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand."

27 **By which they have blasphemed** <note>Latin: *Quibus blasphemaverunt*</note>] <note>original: "ὅσας ἂν βλασφημήσωσι"</note>, that is, "whatever things they might blaspheme." For this is how the Attics <note>the standard dialect of classical Greek</note> speak: "they insult with insults," and "they flee with a flight."

28 **He shall not have forgiveness** <note>Latin: *Non habebit remissionem*</note>] <note>original: "οὐκ ἔχει"</note>, that is, "he does not have." Thus the "Golden Manuscript" <note>the *Codex Aureus*, likely a luxury 8th-9th century manuscript</note> reads, and also the *Coislinianus* manuscript.

29 **Of eternal sin** <note>Latin: *Aeterni delicti*</note>] <note>original: "αἰωνίου κρίσεως"</note>, that is, of eternal judgment, or eternal damnation. Although this matters nothing to the sense. For through <term>Synecdoche</term> <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole or vice versa</note> one thing is understood from the other.

<margin>E</margin> 30 **And looking around** <note>Latin: *Et circumspiciens*</note>] <note>original: "Καὶ περιβλεψάμενος τοὺς κύκλῳ περὶ αὐτὸν μαθητὰς καθημένους"</note>, that is, "And when he had looked around in a circle at the disciples sitting around him." Although in certain copies the word "disciples" <note>original: "μαθητὰς"</note> is not added, and there is a different order: "looking around in a circle at those sitting about him." In the first reading, the sense is that the disciples sat around the Lord on all sides; in the latter, we understand that the Lord cast his eyes around through the listeners, so that none sat behind Jesus' back.

1 **Beside the road** <note>Latin: *Secus viam*</note>] Here we have left the preposition "beside" <note>Latin: *secus*</note>, because there is a certain movement in the progress of the seed as it lies there. For we have taught elsewhere that this is a Latin word.

2 **Burning up** <note>Latin: *Exaestunans*</note>] <note>original: "ἐκαυματίσθη"</note>, that is, it was parched, or it perished by the heat.

3 **Ascending** <note>Latin: *Adscendentem*</note>] <note>original: "ἀναβαίνοντα καὶ αὐξάνοντα"</note>. The first word pertains to the plant emerging from the earth, the latter to the plant growing large and maturing.

4 **One a hundred-fold** <note>Latin: *Unum centesimum*</note>] <note>original: "καὶ ἔφερεν ἓν τριάκοντα, καὶ ἓν ἑξήκοντα, καὶ ἓν ἑκατὸν"</note>, that is, "it brought forth one thirty, and one sixty, and one a hundred." <term>Lorenzo Valla</term> <note>a 15th-century humanist scholar</note> declares that he read the preposition "in" <note>original: "ἐν"</note>, not the noun for "one" <note>original: "ἓν"</note>. And I myself have found it written thus in the more corrected books: specifically in a very ancient manuscript which contained the *Commentaries of Theophylact* <note>an 11th-century Byzantine exegete</note>, although the Aldine edition <note>the famous printed edition by Aldus Manutius</note> reads differently. If we read it that way, it can be rendered literally thus: "And it brought forth *in* thirty and *in* sixty and *in* a hundred," as if the preposition *en* were placed for *ana*, as if you said "by thirty, by sixty, by a hundred," which however could be conveniently translated: "and it brought forth thirty-fold, and sixty-fold, and hundred-fold," so that from single grains such a number of grains is understood to have grown. Although a little further down the same passage occurs, likewise written with the preposition. Furthermore, since a scribe could easily slip up in this matter, I leave the thing to the reader’s judgment, especially since the other reading can also be properly defended. Except that in the latter passage, when the Lord explains the parable to the disciples, it is said somewhat harshly as "one and one" when he speaks of people, not of seeds. Therefore we have used a paraphrase.

5 **When he was alone** <note>Latin: *Cum esset singularis*</note>] <note>original: "Ὅτε δὲ ἐγένετο καταμόνας"</note>, that is, "But when he had begun to be alone," or "solitary." For he translates it "alone" in Luke: "But when he was praying alone."

6 **Those who were with him, the twelve**] Here the Greek manuscripts vary: for Valla's manuscript had <note>original: "οἱ περὶ αὐτὸν σὺν τοῖς δώδεκα"</note>, that is, "those who were around him with the twelve." And indeed, it was written thus in the book which contained the *Commentaries of Theophylact*, with the Spanish Edition and the Aldine in agreement. My own had: <note>original: "ἐπηρώτησαν αὐτὸν οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ"</note>, that is, "his disciples questioned him." <margin>F</margin>

7 **Mystery of the kingdom**] <note>original: "μυστήριον"</note>, that is, a secret, or something hidden, not to be communicated to the profane, which he sometimes translates as "sacrament."

8 **But to those who are outside**] <note>original: "τοῖς ἔξω"</note>. He would have translated it more correctly by an adjective, that is, "to those exterior," "to strangers," or "external," or "exotic."

9 **Seeing, and they may not see**] The Greek has changed the verb <note>original: "ἵνα βλέποντες βλέπωσι, καὶ μὴ ἴδωσι"</note>, that is, "so that discerning they may discern, but not see." As if it were more to "see" than to "discern." For we look at certain things which we nevertheless do not "see," because the mind is doing something else. Although the Latin manuscripts resist this with great consensus, nor...

One may <unclear>detect</unclear> this reading from the exposition of Theophylact <note>A 12th-century Bulgarian archbishop and influential biblical commentator.</note> himself.
10 **And the cares** ] <note>original: "καὶ αἱ μέριμναι"</note>, that is, anxieties.
11 **These however are they who &c.** ] It seems <term>Demonstrative Pronouns<note>The author is discussing the Greek usage of "οὗτοί" (these) versus "οἱ" (the).</note></term> are used once and again; as if one were to point out these and those, which we are accustomed to do for the sake of teaching and represent with a gesture. And "to be sown" <note>original: "seminari"</note> is said of the seed that is cast, and likewise the field into which it is cast, just as water is sprinkled and a man is sprinkled. Laurentius <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous Renaissance humanist scholar.</note> notes that the translator said *sown* <note>original: "seminatum"</note> for *seed*, whereas *sowing* <note>original: "sementis"</note> is the act itself, and *seed* is that which is cast. In Latin one says "to make a sowing," but "to make a seed" is not said.
12 **The thirtieth verse** ] *Thirty, sixty, a hundred*, as I advised a little earlier, agreeing with the very ancient Latin codices, of which we spoke more fully on Matthew.
13 **Does it come** ] In Greek it is, "Is the lamp lit <note>original: "καίεται"</note> so that it may be placed under a bushel?"; that is, *See, is a lamp set on fire, so that it may be placed under a bushel?* Although I do not find that word "see" written in many Greek codices, as in Theophylact. In the Aldine Edition <note>The famous 1518 Greek Bible printed by Aldus Manutius in Venice.</note> it is written "comes" <note>original: "ἔρχεται"</note> for "is lit," just as in Theophylact.
14 **For there is not** ] <note>original: "Οὐ γάρ ἐστί τι κρυπτὸν, εἰ μὴ ἵνα φανερωθῇ"</note>, that is, *For there is not anything hidden, except that it may be manifested.* Although the manuscripts differ here. Theophylact reads, *For there is nothing hidden, which shall not be manifested.*
15 **Neither has it become** ] <note>original: "οὐδὲ ἐγένετο ἀπόκρυφον, ἀλλ᾽ ἵνα εἰς φανερὸν ἔλθῃ"</note>, that is, *neither was it made hidden, but that it should come into the open.* Although it can be read, *neither was it hidden.* However, in our speech <note>referring to Latin</note> the sentence seems a little incomplete; it should be supplied in this manner: *Neither was it made hidden, that it should remain hidden, but that it might come into the open.* This sentiment fits beautifully with Evangelical doctrine. Some things were hidden, not so they would always be concealed, but so they might be brought to light in their own time.
16 **See what you hear** ] Here too the Greek copies differ, although the Latin copies agree more than the Greek ones, *See what you hear, and it shall be added to you who hear. For whoever has, it shall be given to him, and whoever has not, even what he has shall be taken from him.* The codex of Donatianus supported the Greek reading. Then follows, *in what measure you measure, it shall be measured—*

to you, and it shall be added to you. Theophylact reads it thus, *See what you hear, in the measure you measure, it shall be measured to you who hear. For whoever has, to him it shall be given, and he who has not, even what he has shall be taken from him.* The Golden Codex <note>A famous illuminated manuscript, likely the Codex Aureus of Stockholm or a similar prestigious text.</note> and likewise the Codex of Constance agreed with this reading.
<margin>23 [OUT]</margin>
17 **Night and day** ] Some think both verbs, *sleeps and rises*, should refer to the one who cast the seed: so that we understand him to sleep at night and rise by day: and indeed Theophylact interprets it in this sense. I rather judge that the latter verb refers to the seed, which, with no one cultivating it, progresses by silent actions both night and day until maturity. For he is said to "sleep" who is at rest and no longer labors. This sense was followed by whoever wrote the *Scholia on Mark* <note>Brief explanatory notes often found in manuscript margins.</note>, which are attributed to Jerome. For he speaks thus: *The man casting seed is the Son of Man, the seed is the word of life, the earth is human hearts: the sleeping of the man is the death of the Savior: the seed rises night and day*, etc.
18 **And it grows while he knows not** ] The Greek speech is ambiguous, <note>original: "καὶ ὁ σπόρος βλαστάνῃ καὶ μηκύνηται ὡς οὐκ οἶδεν αὐτός"</note>. For it can be taken as the seed arising and springing up by the power of nature, while it itself <note>the seed</note> does not know this, because "seed" <note>original: "σπόρος"</note> is of the masculine gender.
19 **By what parable shall we compare** ] <note>original: "ἢ ἐν τίνι παραβολῇ αὐτὴν θῶμεν"</note>, that is, *or in what parable shall we place or set it.* Although some codices have "let us compare" <note>original: "παραβάλωμεν"</note> instead of "let us set" <note>original: "θῶμεν"</note>, that is, *by what comparison shall we compare it.* Since Cicero translates "parable" as "comparison" <note>original: "collationem"</note>. And the Hebrews use the preposition "in" for "by." In others, "in what kind" <note>original: "ἐν ποίᾳ"</note> is written for "to what." Truly I considered these things too minute to be noted.
20 **And when it is born** ] In the Greek this is repeated, <note>original: "καὶ ὅταν σπαρῇ"</note>, that is, "when it is sown," supported also by the Golden Codex, the Codex of Constance, and many others. It offends the reader because it seems absurd that the same thing is repeated: "and when it is sown."
21 **It ascends into a tree** ] <note>original: "ἀναβαίνει"</note>, that is, it rises. Furthermore, that "into a tree" is neither added among the Greeks, nor in our ancient codices, nor in the Golden one. It appears to have been added from the thirteenth chapter of Luke and Matthew.
22 **To dwell** ] <note>original: "κατασκηνουν"</note>, which elsewhere he translates as "to nest," a word derived from <note>original: "σκηνὴ"</note> meaning a booth or scene.

<margin>V. 1</margin> <margin>B</margin> And they came to the other side of the sea, into the region of the Gadarenes. <margin>2</margin> And when he had stepped out of the boat, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit, <margin>3</margin> who had his dwelling among the tombs; and no one could bind him anymore, not even with chains. <margin>4</margin> For he had often been bound with shackles and chains, but the chains were pulled apart by him, and the shackles were broken in pieces; and no one had the strength to subdue him. <margin>5</margin> And always, night and day, among the mountains and in the tombs, he was crying out and cutting himself with stones. <margin>6</margin> But seeing Jesus from a distance, he ran and fell down before him. <margin>7</margin> And crying out <margin>C</margin> with a loud voice, he said: "What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me." <margin>8</margin> For he had been saying to him: "Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!" <margin>9</margin> And he asked him: "What is your name?" And he answered, saying: "Legion is my name; for we are many." <margin>10</margin> And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country. <margin>11</margin> Now a great herd of pigs was feeding there near the mountain. <margin>12</margin> And all the demons begged him, saying: "Send us into the pigs, so that we may enter them." <margin>13</margin> And Jesus immediately gave them permission. And the unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs; and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea (they were about two thousand) and <margin>D</margin> were drowned in the sea. <margin>14</margin> And those who fed the pigs fled and reported it in the city and in the country. <margin>15</margin> And they went out to see what it was that had happened. And they came to Jesus, and saw the demon-possessed man sitting there, clothed and in his right mind—the one who had the legion—and they were afraid. <margin>16</margin> And those who had seen it described to them how it had happened to the demon-possessed man, and about the pigs. <margin>17</margin> And they began to beg him to depart from their region.

---

23 *He was explaining* <note>original: "Differebat"</note>] In Greek, this is *epilyon*, that is, he was dissolving or explaining: or as it is used elsewhere, he was setting forth. For riddles and things that are obscure and knotted, as it were, are "untied" or solved.
24 *Let us cross over*] That is, let us go across to the further part: or, as it has often appeared now, across the strait.
25 *And there arose*] That is, it happens or it springs up, describing the event as it unfolds.
26 *Was casting into the boat*] That is, it was rushing into the boat; the verb acts as a neutral one regarding its meaning.
27 *Sleeping on a pillow*] The Greek word *proskephalaion* is named for being moved toward the head. Ezekiel curses those who sew pillows under every elbow and cushions under every head. What Jesus displayed then is still happening among us today. How perilously do certain Prelates and Popes of these times sleep on such pillows and cushions! The whole population is in danger, yet there is no one to wake Christ, who is sleeping most deeply within them. Indeed, they do not wish to be awakened, and they have those who cherish this most pestilential sleep, singing "Bravo, bravo!" into their ears with a flattering whisper. Awake at last, O best Jesus, lest we perish.
28 *Does it not concern you*] That is, "is it not a care to you?" For it is one thing for something to *pertain* to us, and another for it to be a *care*. Indeed, many things pertain to us greatly which are of very little care to us.
29 *Because we perish*] The word *hoti* here means "that," specifically in this context.
30 *Rising, he rebuked*] That is, having been awakened, he scolded.
31 *Be silent*] The Greek *pephimōso*. The added prefix also indicates speed: as if you were to say, "be silent immediately."
32 *Why are you fearful*] That is, "Why are you so timid?" Others had it as "Why are you timid so?"
33 *Do you not yet have*] The Greek *pōs* here means "not yet." Others had it as "How is it that you do not have faith?" And they refer these words to the preceding part of the speech. Laurentius joined it to the following part: "Do you thus not yet have faith?" Furthermore, he rendered *pōs* into Latin poorly; it should have been translated as "how does it happen that you do not have faith?" For it is the word of one rebuking, not merely questioning.

34 *To one another*] That is, "among themselves." I have warned of this frequently now. Truly the Translator constantly errs regarding this word, as if on purpose.
35 *Who do you think*] In Greek *Tis ara*. Better "who then," or certainly "who." For in this place, the Latin language hardly has a word that responds to *ara*.
<margin>E</margin> 1 **Across the strait**] That is, to the further side. Although in Matthew he frequently translates it as "across the strait." As I said, they call the lake a "sea"; however, the same words could be used even if crossing a river, or a mound, or a mountain. But a "strait" is not the same as a "sea," even if every strait is called a sea.
2 *Of the Gerasenes*] That is, of the Gadarenes. We read the same in Luke, while Matthew calls them "Gergesenes," which we touched upon somewhat in Matthew chapter eight.
3 *Legion is my name*] The Greek writer used a Latin word here (*legio*), although the grammatical gender was changed.
4 *Feeding in the fields*] "In the fields" is added here neither by the Greeks, nor in the Golden Codex, nor in the Donatian or Constantinian manuscripts.
<margin>F</margin> 5 *And with great impetus*] That is, "and the herd was carried by impetus headlong into the sea." The Translator added "great" on his own.
6 *About two thousand*] That is, there were roughly two thousand, or twice a thousand: and "pigs" must be understood, not "spirits": because "spirit" in Greek is of the neuter gender, and "two thousand" is masculine, so it cannot refer to the spirits.
7 *What had been done*] That is, "what it was that had been done, or what had happened." Although the Translator did not translate this badly.
8 *And they came*] That is, "And they come," in the present tense. And the more corrected Latin codices have it this way.
9 *And of sound mind*] After these words the Greek codices add (which is not held in the Latin): "the one who had the legion." This was erased because it seemed redundant, since mention had just been made of the demoniac. But it is repeated for the emphasis of the miracle: that he was now of sound mind, who had not only been subject to a demon, but even to a legion of demons.
