10 *And as he was getting in*] <note>original: "Καὶ ἐμβάντος αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸ πλοῖον"</note>, that is, *with him having entered the ship, or the ship having been boarded.*
11 *Did not admit*] <note>original: "οὐκ ἀφῆκεν"</note>, that is, *did not permit, or did not suffer.*
12 *How great things*] <note>original: "ὅσα"</note>, which frequently signifies *whatever things.* Here the Translator seems to have read <note>original: "πόσα"</note> [how many], not <note>original: "ὅσα"</note> [how great/as many].
13 *And has had mercy on you*] This connects rather harshly with what precedes, *how great things God has done for you.* It should have been translated, *the things God did for you, and by which he had mercy on you*, or, *how greatly he has had mercy on you.*

-> F <-

14 *And there comes a certain man*] <note>original: "καὶ ἔρχεται εἷς"</note>, that is, *and one comes.* But I wish the Translator had changed the Hebrew figure of speech here—as he did elsewhere—so far be it from me to rebuke it. And "Jairus" should be pronounced with the second-to-last syllable sharp by the Latins, because of the diphthong <note>original: "ει"</note>.
15 *Because the daughter*] Even in the Greek there is no <note>original: "ὅτι"</note> [because/that], which nevertheless should have been omitted if it were there. Here he added it from some source of his own. *My daughter* <note>original: "θυγάτριόν"</note>, that is, *little daughter.* For it is a diminutive in Greek. *Is in extremes* <note>original: "ἐσχάτως ἔχει"</note>, literally sounds like, *it has extremely*, which is the same as saying, *she is in a very bad way, or is at the highest crisis of life.*
16 *That she may be saved and live*] <note>original: "ὅπως σωθῇ, καὶ ζήσεται"</note>, that is, *so that she may be made safe, and she will live.* So that the latter verb is in the future tense. Otherwise, what else is it for a sick person to be saved than to live? For the sense is, *lay hands on her so that she may be saved: and if you do not find it troublesome to do so, it will come to pass that she lives.* For it can happen that someone lays hands on a sick person so that they may be healed, and yet the sick person dies. However, this did not happen by the fault of the Translator, but of the Scribes. As I see it, they attribute an imperfect faith to this ruler of the synagogue. He did not believe a dead girl could be raised; he believed a sick girl could be healed, if only the Lord deigned to lay hands on her. My annotation supports this understanding.
17 *And she felt in her body*] <note>original: "καὶ ἔγνω τῷ σώματι"</note>, that is, *she knew in her body*, which the Translator not unsuitably rendered as *felt.* For the sense is: she knew this from the very feeling of her body, which was now free from torment and the flow.
18 *Because she was healed from the plague*] <note>original: "μάστιγος"</note>, that is, *scourge* <note>original: "flagello"</note>, as was indicated above. And *because* should have been translated as *that.*
19 *Knowing the power that had gone out*] <note>original: "ἐπιγνοὺς ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὴν ἐξ αὑτοῦ δύναμιν ἐξελθοῦσαν"</note>. I ask, what is this disgrace of speech?

-> E <-

For what power was unknown to him? Therefore the participle should have been translated into an infinitive verb: *But Jesus, as he recognized, or felt in himself, that power had gone out from himself.* For in this place, "from out of himself" <note>original: "ex sese"</note> is not to be tolerated for "from him" <note>original: "ex se"</note>, which our Edition has.
20 *The whole truth*] <note>original: "ἐπιγνοῦσα πᾶσαν τὴν αἰτίαν αὐτῆς"</note>, that is, *before everyone her whole cause*, even if that *before everyone* is not found written in all the Greek copies. And in some, instead of *cause* <note>original: "αἰτίαν"</note>, *truth* <note>original: "ἀλήθεια"</note> was written. We have preferred to follow this, if only because it agrees with the Latin copies. Furthermore, Luke has *cause*.
21 *Messengers come*] Some person or other added "Messengers," though not badly. Certainly it was not in the codices of Donatianus, nor even in the Constantian one. Nor is it "to the ruler of the synagogue," but "from the ruler of the synagogue," by a great consensus of the Greek codices, so that you understand they came from his house to report the death of the daughter. But not noticing—whether it be the Reader or the Translator—this figure of speaking, *Let us go to me, for that which is, to my house*, and *it goes out from you, that is, from your house*, he thought it could not be avoided that they came *to* the ruler of the synagogue; since he was already with Jesus. But they both came *from* him and *to* him, that is, from his house to his person. I found the genuine writing agreeing with the Greeks in the Constantian codex. Although the Greek speech can be seen as spoken by ellipsis, just as they say "in Hades" [meaning in the house of Hades], and "we come to Vesta's" [meaning her temple]. So "they come from the ruler of the synagogue's," understand "house."
22 *Jesus however*] The Greeks add <note>original: "εὐθέως"</note>, that is, *immediately.*
23 *Admitted*] <note>original: "ἀφῆκεν"</note>, that is, *permitted, or suffered.* For who would say, "he admitted to follow." He plays remarkably with his abundance of words, when the simple verb is to translate it as "let go" or "dismissed."
24 *And he saw*] <note>original: "καὶ θεωρεῖ"</note>, that is, *and he sees*, in the present tense.
25 *And wailing*] <note>original: "ἀλαλάζοντας"</note>, which in the Psalms he translates as "to shout for joy" <note>original: "jubilare"</note>. For <note>original: "ἀλαλάζειν"</note> is to wail, a voice not much different from that one. Although Valla, on the authority of Varro, shows that "jubilation" was the cry of peasants, while "quiritatus" was that of city-dwellers. Certainly Chrysostom, in his first Homily against the Jews, says shepherds <note>original: "ἀλαλάζειν"</note>—shout—to frighten the wolf away from the sheepfold.
26 *Why are you troubled*] <note>original: "Τί θορυβεῖσθε"</note>, that is, *Why do you make a commotion*, from the same word which he had just translated as "tumult" <note>original: "θόρυβος"</note>.
27 *And they laughed at him*] Some Greeks add, *knowing that she was dead.*

<margin>A</margin> <unclear>lying</unclear>, <note>original: "ἀνακείμενον"</note> that is, "knowing that she was dead," or "since they knew she was dead." Indeed, I suspect this was added here from Matthew’s account.
<margin>28</margin> *Who were with him*] It should be read as "and those who were with him," <note>original: "καὶ τοὺς μετ’ αὐτοῦ"</note> so that you understand those few whom he had allowed to follow, namely the disciples whom he listed by name.
<margin>29</margin> *Tabitha kumi*] The Greeks write *Tabitha* with a <term>lambda</term> <note>Erasmus is correcting the spelling to "Talitha" (ταλιθά)</note>, not *Tabitha* with a <term>beta</term>, supported by the oldest "Donationic" <note>likely referring to manuscripts from a specific gift or collection</note> Greek readings, and likewise the Constantinopolitan. Furthermore,
<margin>30</margin> *Girl, I say to you*] He added "I say to you" on his own—whether it was the Evangelist or someone else—to make the meaning more expressive, capturing both the feeling of the one calling and the authority of the one commanding. This is attested by Jerome in his letter to Pammachius, in the booklet titled *On the Best Method of Translating*. Mark himself, who undoubtedly wrote the Gospel in Greek, translates these Hebrew words for us as *Girl, arise*. Saint Jerome, in the booklet where he collects the Hebrew words of the Gospels, notes that this phrase, *Tabitha cumi* (for so it is written there), is, I believe, corrupted, and is Syriac, not Hebrew. <margin>H</margin> In Syriac, it signifies a girl. But the same Jerome, in the book *On the Best Method of Translating*, admits it is Hebrew: "The Evangelist," he says, "is accused of a lie for adding 'I say to you,' when in Hebrew it is only 'Girl, arise,' unless perhaps what is Chaldean or Syriac can be called Hebrew; not the opposite, because the speech of the Chaldeans or Syrians is nothing other than Hebrew, just corrupted in a different way, except for a few words which they adopted from elsewhere." Unless it seems more probable that the Hebrews, after they had migrated into Syria, learned the language of that nation, and in that language the Sacred Books, which had been lost, were restored through Ezra. Furthermore, it is clear in any language of this age that common speech never remains the same for long. Such is the volatility of human affairs. Nor does it seem unlikely to me that Christ used the popular speech, which was in common use among the multitude, especially when he spoke to the people. Those who profess expertise in this type of literature say that *Talitha*, as we read with great consensus in the Greek codices, sounds like "girl" to the Chaldeans. And it is possible that the word is common to both.
<margin>F</margin> 1 *The carpenter, the son of Mary*] Some ancient codices have "the son of the carpenter and of Mary," <note>original: "ὁ τοῦ τέκτονος υἱὸς καὶ Μαρίας"</note> supported also by the Greeks. But in others it was written, "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" <note>original: "Ὁὐχ οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ τέκτων ὁ υἱὸς Μαρίας"</note> and we find this wording also in old Latin copies, specifically in the Corbie manuscript. Next, it should be noted that the Greek article is applied in both places: "the carpenter, the son of Mary." Moreover, from this passage one can gather that it makes no difference whether you say *Mariam* in the Hebrew manner or *Maria* in the Greek manner, a matter Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla (1407–1457), a humanist scholar known for his philological critiques</note> disputes at great length. Finally, note this too: in Matthew, Christ is not called "the carpenter," but "the son of the carpenter." From this we understand that he also practiced the trade of his legal father. For why would the Son of God have refused this for our sake, he who did not even refuse the cross? Nor was the Apostle Paul ashamed to prepare things by manual labor to make a living. Though I do not deny that in Greek words a slip is very easy between "son of the carpenter" and "the carpenter, the son," except that it fits poorly with "of Mary." Thus, care was taken by the Holy Spirit that not many things about the external affairs of the Lord Jesus were committed to writing—such as his physical form, his food, or his clothes—lest an occasion be given to human minds prone to superstition. For from this fact, that the Evangelists pass down that Jesus was the son of a carpenter and a carpenter himself, there has arisen a group of men who wish to be called <term>Jesuits</term> <note>Erasmus is likely referring to a contemporary lay or monastic group, not the Society of Jesus (founded later)</note> because they practice the craft of a builder in monasteries and carry a hammer as their badge, even though it is uncertain what kind of building Joseph and the Lord practiced. For there are smiths of copper, silver, and iron, as well as wood-workers and stone-masons. There is no lesser group who wear unshorn hair, or who wear a seamless tunic. The Lord did not invite us to imitate these things, in which he bore himself as any one

2 *And Joses*] <note>original: "Ἰωσῆ"</note> that is, *Jose*, Lorenzo Valla reads. Some codices had *Joannes*, that is, *of John*, according to the Greek inflection.
<margin>3</margin> *Because there is not*] He added "Because" on his own, though there is no need. *Without honor*, <term>atimos</term> <note>original: "ἄτιμος"</note>, that is, unhonored or despised. The opposite is <term>entimos</term> or <term>timios</term>, that is, held in high value.
<margin>4</margin> *And in the house*] <note>original: "ἐν συγγενέσι [καὶ]"</note> The most general is the "country," then the "kinship," and closest is the "house and family." Then it is added, *and in his own kinship*, <note>original: "καὶ ἐν τοῖς συγγενέσι"</note> that is, <margin>D</margin> among his relatives.
5 *Except a few sick people*] The rules of Latin required that he add "except that." Next, "sick people" in Greek is <term>arrhostous</term> <note>original: "ἀῤῥώστους"</note>, that is, those suffering from ill health.
6 *And he called together*] <note>original: "προσκαλεῖται"</note> that is, he calls to himself, or summons, in the present tense. Perhaps some grumpy person will complain while we pursue such trifles: "Why 'summons' rather than 'calls together,' and why 'summons' rather than 'summoned'?" To whom I will respond with just as many words: "Why 'called together' rather than 'called,' and why 'called' rather than 'calls'?" Since the latter is more elegant, it was thus written by the Evangelist.
<margin>E</margin> 7 *Two by two*] <note>original: "δύο δύο"</note> The Latin translator expressed this elegantly, whereas in Greek it is "two two," that is, in pairs or in yokes, so that you understand all twelve were sent, but in six pairs. Since Matthew also, listing the names of the twelve Apostles, coupled them in twos.
8 *Authority over unclean spirits*] To avoid ambiguity, we have translated it as "authority *against* unclean spirits." For "authority" is used both for the one who possesses it and for the thing over which we are powerful.
<margin>F</margin> 9 *Shod with sandals*] <term>Sandalion</term> to the Greeks is a type of footwear, suitable for women, which protects only the flat part of the feet from injury, bound above with certain loops or cords. But <term>hypodemata</term>, which is frequently translated here as "shoes," take their name from being bound under the feet. Thus it is probable that the Evangelists made no distinction between "shoes" and "sandals," especially since here he joins the two: "shod with sandals." However, what are called "sandals" here in the Greek are translated by the interpreter as "boots" in Acts chapter 12: "put on your sandals." The ancients did not know this type of boot <note>caligae</note> which now covers <margin>F</margin> even the groin, but this was also a type of footwear. Thus the nickname *Caligula* <note>meaning "Little Boot"</note> was given to Emperor Gaius as a military joke, and the boot of Maximinus became a proverb in camp jokes, because his shoe proved he had feet of excessive length. The authors are Suetonius, Ausonius, and Julius Capitolinus. Finally, Pliny mentions the shoeing of horses, though only soles are added to them. Therefore, in my judgment, some people argue here in vain whether sandals are included under the name of shoes, and whether Christ used shoes, and about the double type of footwear—one worn on the feet and another carried on the back—concluding from this that Christ was barefoot, because at the banquet of the sinful woman she anointed Jesus's feet and wiped them with her hair moistened with tears. It is probable that Christ sometimes used footwear and sometimes did not, clearly as the current situation required. Otherwise, the Baptist would not have declared himself unworthy to untie the strap of Jesus’s shoes. Nor was it a great thing to walk unshod in warm regions in the past. In Horace’s last satire of the second book, Nasidienus, who was already reclining at the table, ran back and forth while preparing to return to the kitchen...

### ACCORDING TO MARK. CHAPTER VI.

---

<margin>A</margin> ...when he was getting ready, he asked for his sandals. And as Pliny the Younger relates in a Letter to Tacitus: <note>original: "Avunculus quum absque soleis flutaret..." This refers to Pliny the Elder observing the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 AD.</note> *While my uncle was wandering about without his sandals, about to observe the place from which the fire of Mount Vesuvius could be seen, he asked for his sandals.* Moreover, in Plato’s *Symposium*, Aristodemus (if I am not mistaken) wonders that Socrates went to Agathon’s banquet wearing sandals, since he was usually barefoot, and was polished everywhere in his reclining at the table. Among the ancients, the manner of reclining at banquets was different than how we recline today. To this, it seems it was once a matter of hospitality to wash the feet of a guest or visitor before they reclined. 

There remains a difficulty regarding the disagreement with Matthew 10, where the Lord forbids those about to go out and preach the Gospel from wearing footwear, while Mark writes the opposite. To this, some respond quite reasonably that the Apostles were not forbidden from wearing footwear on their feet, but from carrying extra pairs in their baggage. We see even today that it is the custom, especially among the Spaniards, for a servant to carry one finely folded cloak for his master, in case rain should break out. Thus, the Baptist quite reasonably declared himself unworthy to carry the footwear of Jesus. <note>original: "indignum qui bajularet calceamenta Jesu"</note> 

But it is simpler to say that Christ, speaking in a plain manner to his still unrefined disciples, wanted to persuade them to undertake the business of preaching without small bags and impediments, nor to be anxious about anything except announcing the kingdom of heaven. I do not think it would have been a difficulty for Christ if one of the Apostles—either because of the roughness of the road or a foot injury—had used shoes. In the same sense comes the command not to greet anyone on the road, signifying through <term>hyperbole</term> (exaggeration for effect) the greatest zeal for hurrying the business along. Thus, in <margin>2 Kings 4</margin> Elisha, sending his servant with his staff, forbids him from greeting anyone he meets—not meaning that he should not say "hello" to anyone, but that he should hurry as much as possible. 

Therefore, to urge these things literally tends toward superstition. Paul, that distinguished herald of the Gospel, in <margin>2 Timothy 4</margin> orders that the cloak he left at Troas be sent back to him, as well as the books, especially those written on parchment. This is more than having a change of footwear. It is not, therefore, a mark of Gospel perfection to anxiously mimic Christ in external matters. He did not come into the world to teach us how we ought to be shod or dressed. With a similar zeal by which they make Christ barefoot, they would also make him a beggar. Poverty is fitting for Christ, but <term>mendicancy</term> (begging) detracts from his dignity. For nothing excuses begging except unavoidable necessity. And for this reason, it is provided in the constitutions of the Popes that no one should be received into the rank of Priest unless a means of living is prepared for him. For what reason? Lest they be driven by want to begging, which detracts from the dignity of a Priest. Indeed, it would be a foolish constitution if begging were part of Gospel perfection. 

Paul, so that he would not beg among the Corinthians, worked with his hands at night in inns and on ships; rather than asking anything from anyone, he sewed skins at night for the use of tents. Christ was kind toward the needy, but he was so far from begging himself that he sometimes sent the Apostles to buy food. Nor is it unlike the truth that the Lord had something of his own from his paternal or maternal goods, or even from his trade. Otherwise, how is it read that he moved from Nazareth to Capernaum and had a home there, if he had neither a house nor furniture? Indeed, it is also probable that Christ wore respectable and decent clothing. Otherwise, the soldiers would not have divided his garments among themselves if they were mere torn rags. Furthermore, what was freely given by wealthy friends or pious women is far removed from begging. 

Nor is it a compelling point that he himself says the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. For this speech does not properly pertain to poverty, but to all those things in which the minds of men devoted to the world find rest. This, however, is located in the affections, not in external things. Moreover, the desire for glory is more dangerous than the desire for riches. As for those who, by this very fact, wish to be seen as "Apostolic men" and of "Gospel perfection" because they beg privately and publicly—let them see to it themselves. Certainly, we nowhere read that the Lord begged; for what they bring up regarding the Samaritan woman is frivolous. In that way, any king could be said to beg. Nor is it even certain that the Lord drank, but he sought an occasion to suggest to the woman who he was. Nor do we ever read that the Apostles begged, nor that they were ever ordered by the Lord to do so. 

Not even poverty is a virtue in itself, just as wealth is not a vice. But there is a twofold poverty: one which provides a frugal living, having nothing superfluous. This fits beautifully with Gospel philosophy. There is another which burdens and oppresses, and frequently tempts one toward graver crimes than riches do. Hence Solomon in <margin>Proverbs 30</margin> prays against both equally: riches, because they sometimes give birth to forgetfulness of God; and poverty, because it tempts one to steal and to swear falsely by the name of God, which is surely a type of blasphemy. Truly, want draws one toward many other things which Solomon does not mention: to sacrileges, poisonings, pimping, robbery, and parricide. Therefore, those who rightly use riches sought without fraud are to be praised; and those who bear forced poverty patiently and cheerfully are to be praised. Nor do I think those who embrace voluntary poverty should be blamed, provided that it is conducive to propagating the kingdom of God; but it should be rejected

<margin>B</margin> if it hinders it. There are likewise those who do not want Christ to have practiced his father's trade, because such labors draw the attention of the mind away from those things which lead more directly to the kingdom of God—such as the study of Theology, the contemplation of heavenly things, or pure prayer. Truly, there was no danger to Christ from this hindrance, nor did sewing leather call Paul away from the business of the Gospel. Yet I confess that leisure is rightly granted to those who prepare themselves with their whole heart for preaching the word of God. But whether those who do nothing but sing deserve this leisure, let that be the judgment of others. Among the ancients, singing belonged to the <term>laity</term> (non-clergy), whereas now it is the highest religious duty of Priests. 

Finally, there are those who contend that the Apostles took vows, namely those three "substantial" vows <note>poverty, chastity, and obedience</note>. Into whose hands? There is no doubt but into the hands of Christ, the supreme Abbot of all. Would that we rather studied to <margin>C</margin> emulate those things in Christ, the imitation of which makes one blessed, and in which the Apostles, imitating the Lord, were truly great, and in which blessed Paul professes himself an imitator of Jesus Christ. 

What does it profit not to carry copper in your belt if you carry it in a cloth, or if you have it deposited with receivers? Moreover, what great thing is it if, instead of sandals, you have shoes with windows cut in the top? <note>original: "calceos superne fenestratos" – likely referring to ornate or "slashed" shoes common in the translator's era</note> Furthermore, how great is the number of those who profess poverty for the very purpose of escaping poverty? Or even so that, by the pact of an Abbey, they may possess the finest riches? The profession of three vows does not bring Gospel perfection, but the imitation of Christ does. For so the young man hears who is ordered to sell all and give to the poor, and "come follow me." Moreover, Paul exhorts the Corinthians to imitate him, just as he himself imitates Christ. But in what things? He expressed this a little earlier: *"To this very hour,"* he says, *"we hunger and thirst, we are naked, we are beaten, we are homeless, and we labor, working with our own hands. We are cursed and we bless, <margin>D</margin> we suffer persecution and we endure it, we are blasphemed and we entreat; we have been made like the refuse of this world, the offscouring of all things, for his sake until now."* Similarly, the Apostle Peter, exhorting to the imitation of Christ, does not mention food, clothes, or unshod feet. But what? *"Who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. Who, when he was cursed, did not curse in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, etc."* But concerning these things, I think I have said enough and more. 

There is another puzzle regarding the staff, which the Lord in Matthew 10 and Luke 9 forbids to be taken, but here he allows it. Augustine, to escape from the narrowness of the question, flees to allegory: that we should understand the "forbidden staff" as that which is carried by travelers for bodily defense, but the "allowed staff" as the power of living from the Gospel. This invention is worth this much: that it seems to provide some answer rather than none. And yet it is harsh, when the other things are taken simply and without allegory, to suddenly take "staff" for "Gospel power." Then, what was the need to grant under the riddle of a <margin>E</margin> staff what he granted in open words—namely, that they should eat and drink what was provided by those to whom they announced the Gospel? 

It is better, in my opinion, to accept a <term>trope</term> (figure of speech) in all these things, so that we understand those things were not simply forbidden—otherwise it would not be lawful for clergy today to take any of these things on the road—but that the Lord wanted his Apostles to be free and unburdened in their Gospel embassy from all the anxiety that twists others about to go on a journey. People provide for themselves with supplies, arm themselves with shoes and clothes against the injury of the weather, with a staff against the violence of men, and equip themselves with travel money lest anything be lacking; that is surely the "copper in the belts," the "provisions in the pouch," the "footwear and second tunic in the baggage," and the "staff prepared for a fight." But sandals are allowed on the feet, which neither hinder the journey nor add anything to the baggage; and a staff is allowed—not that heavy one which is carried for a fight, but that which supports the one walking and refreshes the weary. Perhaps it would not have been a sin if one of the Apostles had happened to have a few small coins in his purse, but the Lord in Matthew forbids these things to be "possessed"—that is, to be prepared with anxious foresight as if necessary for the preaching of the Gospel. Just as they would not have violated the Lord's command if they had happened to say "hail" to someone they met, without any loss to the embassy they had undertaken. Therefore, by these figures of speech, anxiety of mind is taken away from the Apostles rather than the things themselves being forbidden.

<margin>F</margin> 10 *as a testimony to them*] The Greek codices add in this place—whether rightly I do not know—*"Truly I say to you, it will be more tolerable for Sodom or Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city,"* that is, *Amen dico vobis, tolerabilius erit Sodomis aut Gomorrhis in die judicii, quam civitati illi.* Truly, I do not know whether that was transcribed here from Matthew. This happens quite frequently in Mark, who generally agrees with Matthew except that he narrates more briefly. Nevertheless, it is in the majority of the Greek copies that I have happened to see.
11 *And they anointed with oil*] It appears that from here was born the practice today of anointing those struggling in danger with holy oil—not so much that they might recover, as that they might depart more safely; a matter which James also mentions. <note>Referring to the Sacrament of Extreme Unction or Anointing of the Sick.</note>
12 *And King Herod heard*] Some Greek codices add *τὴν ἀκοὴν Ἰησοῦ*, that is, *the fame of Jesus*, which, if I am not mistaken, was added from elsewhere.

13 *Herod however feared* ] For the Greeks read "For" <note>Greek: *gar*</note>, not "However," which is consistent with the ancient manuscripts. Indeed, he was succeeded by his son Archelaus, who was wretchedly extinguished; after ten years, when he was driven from his kingdom, his younger brother Herod succeeded him, who is mentioned here, with the kingdom divided into Tetrarchies between him, Philip, and Lysanias. Dismiss them, that they may go into the surrounding farms and villages and buy bread for themselves: for they have nothing to eat.” <margin>34</margin> But he answering said to them, **F** “You give them something to eat.” And they said to him, “Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give them something to eat?” <margin>36</margin> But he said to them, “How many loaves do you have? Go and see.”

-ever, but *athetesai*, that is, "to reject" or "to repel," which makes me wonder why Laurentius <note>Likely referring to the scholar Lorenzo Valla.</note> thought it meant "to cheat" or "to frustrate" in his translation.

21 *Sent an executioner* ] *Kai eutheos aposteilas ho basileus spekoulatora*. The Evangelist used a Latin word <note>The Greek *spekoulatora* is a transliteration of the Latin *speculator*.</note>, changing a vowel, even though the first syllable of *speculator* is long. And soon,

22 *And they took his body* ] *ptoma auto*, that is, "the corpse." The translator seems to have read *soma* <note>Meaning "body" generally, whereas *ptoma* specifically means a fallen body or corpse.</note>.

23 *What they had done and taught* ] The Greek speech doubles the conjunction, *kai hosa epoiesan, kai hosa edidaxan*, that is, "both what they had done and what they had taught."

24 *Come aside* ] *Deute hymeis autoi kat’ idian*, that is, "Come you yourselves aside." Furthermore, "yourselves" <note>Greek: *autoi*</note> is placed here for "alone," that is, after the others have been dismissed: just as one is said to be "by himself" when he is alone and without witnesses.

25 *And they saw them departing* ] In Greek it is, *Kai eidon autous upagontas hoi ochloi, kai epegnosan auton*, that is, "And the crowds saw them departing, and they recognized *him*": so that the first pronoun refers to all of them together, and the second to Christ alone.

26 *And when it was already a late hour* ] The sense of the Greek speech is: "When it was now quite the appropriate time to take food." For it appears from the other Evangelists that the evening of the day was already approaching.

27 *Into the nearest villages* ] *eis tas kuklo agrous*, that is, into the surrounding fields. And since nothing is bought from fields unless there are farmhouses, he translated it as "villages." For villages are houses in a field.

28 *Buy themselves food* ] *agorasosin heautois artous*, that is, "buy bread for themselves." For the Hebrews include all food under the name of bread.

29 *Which they may eat* ] For this the Greek has, *ti gar phagosin ouk echousin*, that is, "for they have nothing that they might eat." Here "what" <note>Greek: *ti*</note> is used in an unusual way.

30 *Give them to eat* ] The Greeks add "you," *Dote autois hymeis phagein*. And so the ancient Latin codices have, *Give them to eat, you.*

31 *And shall we give* ] *kai domen*, that is, "let us give."

> 32 **According to the companies** <note>original: "Secundum contubernia"</note>] <note>original: "symposia symposia"</note>, that is, "banquet by banquet," which means with the groups distributed, as he said before, "two by two." Laurentius would prefer "by handfuls" <note>original: "manipulatim"</note>.
> 33 **Upon the green hay** <note>original: "Super viride foenum"</note>] <note>original: "epi to chloro chorto"</note>, that is, on the green herb.
> 34 **And they sat down in parts** <note>original: "Et discubuerunt in partes"</note>] <note>original: "Kai anepesan prasiai prasiai"</note>, that is, they sat down "garden bed by garden bed." Now <note>original: "prasiai"</note> are called herb-beds, such as the small plots in gardens; for <note>original: "prasion"</note> means green. Moreover, both this phrase "garden bed by garden bed" and that one "banquet by banquet" are spoken according to the property of Hebrew speech. Saint Augustine noted many things regarding this form in the books he wrote on the figures of speech in the Old Testament, such as: "A tenth, a tenth for one lamb for seven lambs." And "a thousand from a tribe and a thousand from a tribe," for that which is "a thousand from each individual tribe."
> 35 **By hundreds and fifties** <note>original: "Per centenos & quinquagenos"</note>] <note>original: "ana hekaton kai ana pentekonta"</note>, to render it word for word, that is, by a hundred and by fifty. So that you may understand the places were distinct by a furrow or a similar interval: and according to the size, hundreds sat in some, fifties in others.
> 36 **Gazing into heaven** <note>original: "Intuens in coelum"</note>] <note>original: "anablepsas"</note>, that is, looking up, or with eyes lifted.
> 37 **And they took up** <note>original: "Et sustulerunt"</note>] <note>original: "Kai eran klasmaton dodeka kophinous plereis"</note>, that is, "And they took up twelve baskets full of fragments." The genitive case can refer either to "full" or to "baskets."
> 38 **And immediately he compelled** <note>original: "Et statim coegit"</note>] <note>original: "enankase"</note>, the same word that in Matthew had been translated as "ordered," but wrongly, as we indicated there.
> 39 **And when he had dismissed them** <note>original: "Et cum dimississet eos"</note>] <note>original: "Kai apotaxamenos autois"</note>. It is not the same word as a little above, "until he dismissed" <note>original: "eos apoluse"</note>, but another, which does not simply mean to send away, but to "dismiss by saying farewell" or with the instructions you wish to leave: just as we are accustomed to dismiss acquaintances and friends. He translates the same voice in Acts chapter eighteen as "saying farewell." Similarly in 2 Corinthians 11, the Greek voice sounds as if you were saying "to send away."
> 40 **And he saw them laboring** <note>original: "Et vidit eos laborantes"</note>] <note>original: "basanizomenous"</note>, in Matthew it translates as "vexed," elsewhere "tossed." **In rowing**, <note>original: "en to elaunein"</note>, which means to drive or manage either a ship, or a horse, or a chariot, or anything similar. For to row is properly called <note>original: "erettein"</note> by the Greeks; <note>original: "elaunein"</note> is a general word.
> 41 **And more greatly** <note>original: "Et plus magis"</note>] <note>original: "kai lian ek perissou"</note>, that is, "exceedingly from abundance," or "greatly beyond measure." Again here is <note>original: "existanto"</note>, which signifies a vehement wonder, such that a man is not himself on account of his admiration; and yet in the Greek codices it is added **and they wondered** <note>original: "kai ethaumazon"</note>,

42 **And they recognized him** <note>original: "Et cognoverunt eum"</note>] The Greeks add, <note>original: "hoi andres tou topou"</note>, that is, "the men of that place." Although this is not found in most manuscripts.
43 **Where they heard he was** <note>original: "Ubi audiebant eum esse"</note>] <note>original: "hopou ekouon hoti ekei esti"</note>, that is, as soon as they had heard that he was there, so that you may understand those who had recognized Jesus announced his presence to the others.

1 **They found fault** <note>original: "Incusaverunt"</note>] <note>original: "emempsanto"</note>, that is, they accused, or were blaming, or complained.
2 **Unless they wash their hands with the fist** <note>original: "Nisi crebro laverint manus"</note>] <note>original: "ean me pugme nipson-tai tas cheiras"</note>. Theophylact interprets "with the fist" <note>original: "pugme"</note> as an adverb, standing for "up to the elbow," or as someone else interpreted, "cubit-wise," because by the institution of the Pharisees they were accustomed to wash their hands up to the elbow before food, something the Law did not command. I find among Greek etymologists that <note>original: "pugme"</note> signifies two things: a "fist," that is, a folded hand, from the word <note>original: "ptysso"</note> which is "to fold" (whence "pugme," as if you said "ptugme"), and a "cubit" <note>original: "pechyn"</note>, for in this part the arm is foldable. Hence they think the Pygmy people mentioned by Homer are so named because they are a cubit in height. But I do not find <note>original: "pugme"</note> used as an adverb among the Greeks, and I am not sure if similar forms come from nouns, just as from "all" <note>original: "pas"</note> comes "everywhere" <note>original: "pante"</note>. If it were so, "from the cubit" <note>original: "pugmethen"</note> would fit better than "with the fist" <note>original: "pugme" </note>. Furthermore, I see no reason why this fable about elbow-washing should be brought in here. For if it were established that this was prescribed by Law, it might seem probable. But the Lord testifies that nothing of the sort is commanded by Law, saying "to eat with unwashed hands does not defile a man." Whence it is probable that in older manuscripts it was written not <note>original: "pugme"</note>, but "frequently" <note>original: "pyknos"</note> or "often," which means "repeatedly." However, I leave this for the learned to weigh.
3 **And coming from the market** <note>original: "Et a foro venientes"</note>] If "coming" was not added badly, it will not be in the Greek codices. And "from the market" is the same name that he just now translated as "street," <note>original: "agoras"</note>.
4 **Which were delivered to them** <note>original: "Qua tradita sunt illis"</note>] The sense entirely agrees, yet in Greek it is, "which they received to hold" <note>original: "ha parelabon terein"</note>, or as some manuscripts have it, <sig>Vol. VI. M</sig><meta>catchword: kra-</meta>

# GOSPEL CHAPTER VII.

<margin>4</margin> ...to hold onto, which they received to observe or maintain: namely the washing of cups, <margin>5</margin> and pitchers, and copper vessels, and couches. Then the Pharisees and Scribes ask him, "Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition handed down by the elders, but eat bread with unwashed hands?" <margin>6</margin> But he answering said to them, "Isaiah prophesied well about you hypocrites, as it is written: *This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.* <margin>7 8 9</margin> *In vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the precepts of men.* For leaving the commandment of God, <margin>10</margin> you hold onto the constitution of men—the washing of pitchers and cups; and you do many other such similar things." And he said to them, "You well reject the commandment of God, <margin>11</margin> so that you may keep your own constitution. For Moses <margin>12</margin> said, *Honor your father and your mother*; and, *He who speaks evil of father or mother, let him die the death.* <margin>11</margin> But you say, 'If a man says to his father or mother: Korban <note>original: "Κορβᾶν"</note> (which is, a gift), whatever of mine might have been to your benefit, [it is now dedicated to God].' And furthermore, you do not allow him to do anything for his father or his mother; <margin>13</margin> and you make void the word of God through your constitution, which you have handed down; and you do many such similar things." And when he had called the whole crowd to him, he said to them, <margin>14</margin> "Hear me, all of you, and understand. There is nothing outside <margin>15</margin> a man entering into him that can defile him; but the things which proceed from a man, those are the things that defile a man. <margin>16</margin> If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear." And when he had entered a house away from <margin>17</margin> the crowd, his disciples asked him about the parable. And he said to them, "Are you also so lacking in intelligence? Do you not yet understand that everything entering into a man from the outside cannot defile him? <margin>19</margin> Because it does not enter into his heart, but into the stomach; and it goes out into the latrine, <margin>18</margin> purifying all foods." And he said that what goes out from a man, <margin>20</margin> that is what defiles the man. For from within, <margin>21</margin> out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders, thefts, avarice, <margin>22</margin> frauds, deceit, lewdness, an evil eye, <margin>19</margin> slanders, pride, foolishness. All these evil things proceed from within, and they defile the man. And rising from there, <margin>24</margin> he went away to the borders of Tyre and Sidon; and entering a house, he wanted no one to know, but he could not remain hidden. <margin>25</margin> For a woman, as soon as she heard of him, whose little daughter had an unclean spirit, came and fell at his feet (for the woman was a Greek, a Syrophoenician by race) <margin>26</margin> and she begged him that he would cast the demon out of her daughter. ---

<margin>4</margin> <term>to hold onto</term> <note>original: "κρατεῖν"</note>: things which they received to be kept or held. However, since "to receive" <note>original: "παραλαμβάνειν"</note> seems to mean receiving what is handed down by another, the Translator has attempted to express the meaning more clearly.

<margin>5</margin> **Washing** <note>original: "Baptismata"</note>: I wonder why the Translator preferred to use the Greek word rather than the Latin *lotiones* (washings) or *ablutiones*, since ordinary washing is mentioned here.

<margin>6</margin> **Of pitchers** <note>original: "Ex urceorum"</note>: <note>original: "ξεστῶν"</note>. It appears wooden vessels should be understood, because he follows with "copper vessels." He called them *xestōn* because they are polished on a lathe, or because they are decorated with carvings—a type of cup still found today among the Swiss. Furthermore, he calls the "couches" <note>original: "lectos"</note> the benches on which they reclined while taking food, not just those used for sleeping.

<margin>7</margin> **And they asked** <note>original: "Et interrogabant"</note>: <note>original: "Ἔπειτα ἐπερωτῶσιν"</note>, "Then they ask."

<margin>8</margin> **Isaiah prophesied well about you hypocrites, as it is written**: Although the Greek matches, I do not know by what chance I found it written in the "Golden Codex" as: *Isaiah prophesied well of you, saying.*

<margin>9</margin> **Doctrines and precepts**: The conjunction "and" should be removed; <note>original: "διδασκαλίας ἐντάλματα"</note>, that is, "doctrines [which are] commandments," by apposition, as was noted in Matthew. The true reading still survives in the Constance Codex.

<margin>10</margin> **Commandments of God**: <note>original: "ἐντολὴν"</note>, that is, "commandment" [singular], just as "tradition" <note>original: "παραδόσιν"</note> is singular. For the Lord proposes an example using one precept and one tradition.

<margin>11</margin> **You make void**: <note>original: "ἀθετεῖτε"</note>, that is, you make of no effect. This is consistent with our ancient codices, including the Golden one. Though "you reject" <note>original: "rejicitis"</note> would be better, which is how Cyprian reads it.

<margin>12</margin> **If a man says**: Here he explains what was more obscure in Matthew—that some were taught by the Pharisees to neglect their parents in order to contribute money to the Temple treasury. Although the speech seems incomplete, we should understand "it is enough," or something similar.

<margin>13</margin> **Rescinding the word of God**: <note>original: "ἀκυροῦντες τὸν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note>, that is, making it of no effect, or abrogating it, or rendering it obsolete. For—

<column-break/>

<margin>14</margin> **Again the crowds**: <note>original: "πάντα τὸν ὄχλον"</note>, that is, "the whole crowd."

<margin>15</margin> **Nothing is outside a man**: <note>original: "Οὐδέν ἐστιν ἔξω τοῦ ἀνθρώπου εἰσπορευόμενον εἰς αὐτὸν"</note>, that is, nothing which enters into him from somewhere other than the man himself. As if you were to say, "from the outside," as he translates shortly after: "everything entering from without" <note>original: "τὸ ἔξωθεν εἰσπορευόμενον"</note>.

<margin>16</margin> **Parable**: <note>original: "περὶ παραβολῆς"</note>, that is, "concerning the parable," or "concerning the comparison."

<margin>17</margin> **Imprudent**: <note>original: "ἀσύνετοί"</note>, that is, without understanding, as he had translated before; or "void of intelligence." It would have been better as, "Are you also thus without [understanding]," rather than "so also you."

<margin>18</margin> **Purifying**: <note>original: "ἐκκαθαρίζον"</note>, that is, "purging out," literally.

<margin>19</margin> **Evil eye**: <note>original: "ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρός"</note>. Why did he not say "wicked eye" here as in Matthew, *Is your eye wicked because I am good?* For the Greek words are the same in both places. It refers not to a simple and pure eye, but to one that is casting a spell <note>a "fascinator"</note>, envious, and unjust.

<margin>20</margin> **Into the borders of Tyre**: <note>original: "μεθόρια"</note>, that is, the boundaries; meaning the regions neighboring Tyre, or those lying between Tyre and Sidon. Though a little later he uses the simple word for "borders" <note>original: "ὁρίων"</note> with the same meaning.

<margin>21</margin> **At his feet**: In this place follows: "Now the woman was a Greek, a Syrophoenician by race." Other codices had "Syrian Phoenician," but erroneously; for if she were Syrian and from the region of Phoenicia (which is undoubtedly Jewish), how could she be Greek by nation? Furthermore, when he says "race" <note>original: "genere"</note>, the Greek is not "nation" <note>original: "ἔθνους"</note>, but "Greek" <note>original: "Ἑλληνὶς"</note>, so that you should not understand her homeland to be designated, but rather to declare she was not Jewish by religion. Since she was of the Canaanite race, not Greek, she is called "Greek" according to the Hebrew custom, because she was a stranger to the religion of the Mosaic Law. For the Translator frequently renders "Greek" <note>original: "Ἕλληνα"</note> as "Gentile." There is, however, one part of Syria called Syrophoenice, in which Damascus is located, as Tertullian indicates in his third book against Marcion.

<margin>22</margin> **Yes Lord**: In the codices I have seen so far, nothing...

### VIII.
1 In those days, when there was a very great crowd and they had nothing to eat, Jesus called his disciples to him and said to them,
2 "I have compassion on the crowd, because they have now remained with me three days and have nothing to eat.
3 And if I send them away fasting to their own houses, they will faint on the way; for some of them have come from far away."
4 And his disciples answered him, "From where can anyone satisfy these people with bread here in the wilderness?"
5 And he asked them, "How many loaves do you have?" And they said, "Seven."
6 And he commanded the crowd to sit down on the ground; and taking the seven loaves, having given thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples to set before them; and they set them before the crowd.
7 And they had a few small fish; and having blessed them, he commanded these to be set before them also.
8 So they ate and were satisfied; and they took up seven large baskets of the fragments that were left over.

### VIII.
1 In those days, since the crowd was quite large and they did not have anything to eat, Jesus called his disciples to him and said to them,
2 "I am moved with mercy for the crowd, because they have now stayed with me for three days, and they do not have anything to eat.
3 And if I send them away hungry to their house, they will fail on the way: for some of them have come from a long distance."
4 And his disciples answered him, "From where will anyone be able to satisfy these people with bread here in the wilderness?"
5 And he asked them, "How many loaves do you have?" They truly said, "Seven."
6 And he commanded the crowd to sit down upon the ground: and having taken the seven loaves, when he had given thanks, he broke them, and gave them to his disciples to set out: and they set them out for the crowd.
7 And they had a few small fish: 8 and when he had blessed them, he ordered these also to be set out.
8 Moreover, they ate and were filled: and they took up what was left over, seven baskets of fragments.
9 Now those who had eaten were nearly four thousand: and he dismissed them.
10 And soon, entering into a boat with his disciples, he came into the regions of Dalmanutha.
11 And the Pharisees came out and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven, testing him.
12 And when he had groaned in his spirit, he said, "Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly I say to you, if a sign will be given to this generation." <note>original: "si dabitur generationi huic signum" - this reflects a Hebrew idiom where "if" implies a strong negative oath: "it shall certainly not be given."</note>
13 And having left them, entering again into the boat, he went away after crossing the lake.
14 And they had forgotten to take...

---

There was nothing in that place like "certainly," but only "Lord," and "the puppies," that is, *Lord, and puppies*; although afterwards I found it in some [copies].

23 **For also the puppies**] The Greeks have the same word for *dogs* and *puppies*: although in both places the diminutive used by them is *kunaria* <note>original: "κυνάρια"</note>, as we have advised. To this, he would have more correctly translated "of the children" <note>original: "filiorum"</note> rather than "of the boys" <note>original: "puerorum"</note>, since "children" <note>original: "τέκνων"</note> preceded it.

24 **He found the girl lying upon the bed, and the demon gone out**] In the common Greek manuscripts, the order of the sentence is inverted. For there, it says he found the demon gone out, and the girl lying on the bed; and "upon the bed" in Latin was *epi klinēs* <note>original: "ἐπὶ κλίνης"</note>.

25 **Borders of Decapolis**] *Decapolis* <note>original: "Δεκαπόλεως"</note>. This is a region of ten cities across the Jordan: from which it also has its name among the Greeks, around Hippos, Pella, and Gadara, as Jerome testifies in his work on Hebrew places.

26 **Deaf and mute**] *kōphon mogilalon* <note>original: "κωφὸν μογιλάλον"</note>, that is, *deaf with an impeded tongue*, or a stutterer, a word composed from *mogis* (scarcely) and *lalein* (to speak). Moreover, this defect is almost perpetual in the insane, or the melancholic, or those naturally foolish, as Aristotle testifies.

27 **To open up**] "To open," *Ephphata*. He adds the Hebrew <note>Actually Aramaic</note> word here as well, just as he did earlier with "Eli," except this is one of that kind of words which the Hebrews call "heavy" <note>referring to the intensive or passive verbal stems like Hithpael</note>, and which have a transitive force, as if you were to say, "Offer yourself opened," or "Be made open." Nor does it please me to mention here the ridiculous difference between "to open" and "to open up," which Laurentius <note>Lorenzo Valla, a Renaissance humanist scholar</note> mocks more sharply than befits a serious man, even if he does so deservedly. Certainly, in the Evangelist, there is no difference, since the verb is the same in both places, *dianoichthete* and *dianoichthesan* <note>original: "διανοίχθητε & δινοίχθησαν"</note>, one of which he translates "to open up," the other "were opened": as if it were a crime for Latins to repeat the same word.

28 **So much more the more**] Indeed, the Greek manuscripts distinguish it so that "more" refers not to the command, because *hison* <note>original: "ἴσον"</note> preceded it, not *hōtō* or *hosō*, but to the same verb it refers to—namely, they proclaimed it "more" <note>original: "plus"</note>: although the Greeks seem to use *hoson* sometimes adverbially. But *perissoteron* <note>original: "περισσότερον"</note> could be translated as "vehemently" or "greatly," as a comparative used in place of a positive: or *mallon* <note>original: "μᾶλλον"</note> should have been translated as "rather," so it does not have the force of comparing, but of correcting: as if you were to say, "They were so far from doing what they were commanded, that they rather proclaimed all the more what they were forbidden."

29 **And makes the deaf to hear**] Lest anyone complain about the integrity of Latin speech—because to Roman ears "makes to speak" and "makes to run" sounds like something else—it would have been more correct to say, "he brings it about that they hear, and the mute speak." The Translator, or certainly the Scribe, also changed the tense of the verb. For it is *poiei* <note>original: "ποιεῖ"</note>, that is, "he makes," and that is in the absolute [present]. Laurentius testifies that in some copies the Latin...

1 In those days, since the crowd was quite large and they did not have anything to eat, Jesus called his disciples to him and said to them, "I am moved with mercy for the crowd, because they have now stayed with me for three days, and they do not have anything to eat. ---

...the Latin had the conjunction doubled, *and he makes the deaf to hear, and the mute to speak*. "And the mute to speak," *alalous lalein* <note>original: "ἀλάλους λαλεῖν"</note>. The Translator was not able to render the charm of the wordplay, as if you were to say, *the speechless speak, or the speechless find speech*.

1 **Since the crowd was many**] In Greek *eis pampollou* <note>original: "εἴς παμπολλοῦ"</note>, that is, *quite many*, or *very many*. It is not added "with Jesus," neither among the Greeks, nor in the old manuscripts, nor in the Golden [codex], nor finally in the Constantinopolitan [codex].

2 **They sustain me**] *prosminousi moi* <note>original: "προσμένουσί μοι"</note>, that is, *they remain with me*.

3 **From where these**] "from where" <note>original: "unde"</note>, which the Greeks use in a negation in place of "how" or "in what way."

4 **And he himself blessed**] *kai auta eulogēsas* <note>original: "καὶ αὐτὰ εὐλογήσας"</note>, that is, *and when he had blessed these*. Although in some manuscripts it was held thus: *kai eulogēsas, eipe parathenai kai auta* <note>original: "καὶ εὐλογήσας, εἶπε παραθεῖναι καὶ αὐτὰ"</note>, that is, *and when he had blessed [them], he ordered these also to be set out*.

5 **As if four thousand**] *hōs* <note>original: "ὡς"</note>, that is, *nearly*, or *about four thousand*.

<column-break/>

6 **Into the parts of Dalmanutha**] A certain Greek manuscript had "Magdala," which Matthew mentions, or, as some read, "Magedan." Nor have I yet found a description of this place in anyone, except that in the collections of Hebrew words I find this also explained, but in such a way that it pertains to nothing in this passage. Augustine, in *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, thinks that there are several names for the same region, adding that in this place also some manuscripts had "Mageda."

7 **To inquire with him**] The Laurentian manuscript, as it seems, had it differently. Mine in this manner: *ērxanto syzētein par' autou sēmeion* <note>original: "ἤρξαντο συζητεῖν παρ’ αὐτοῦ σημεῖον"</note>, that is, *they began to seek a sign from him together*. Although later I obtained [copies] in which I found it written thus: *kai ērxanto syzētein autō, kai zētein par' autou sēmeion* <note>original: "καὶ ἤρξαντο συζητεῖν αὐτῷ, καὶ ζητεῖν παρ’ αὐτοῦ σημεῖον"</note>, that is, *and they began to dispute with him, and to require a sign from him*. In some, instead of "and to seek," it was "seeking."

8 **Groaning in spirit**] The Greeks add "his," *Kai anastenaxas tō pneumati autou* <note>original: "Καὶ ἀναστενάξας τῷ πνεύματι αὐτοῦ"</note>.

9 **If a sign will be given to this generation**] "If" in place of a strong denial, just as in that place, "If they shall enter into my rest" <note>referring to Psalm 95/Hebrews 3, meaning "They shall NOT enter"</note>. The Latins add "let them not," "let them despair," or something similar. He wondered at the arrogance of the Pharisees, who wanted to be seen as having commerce with heaven, though they were most wicked. But Christ promises them from the bottom of his heart a sign of the earth quite different from what they were demanding.

10 **And they forgot to take bread**] A certain Greek manuscript added, "his disciples": it pleases me more that it not be added.

<margin>11 See and beware]</margin> <note>original: "Ὁρᾶτε, βλέπετε"</note> "See, look." These are two words in Greek that signify the same thing, placed together without a conjunction, as if you were to say, "See, discern," or "Beware, flee," in order to express a more diligent caution.
<margin>12 From the leaven of Herod]</margin> <note>original: "Ἡρωδιανῶν"</note> "Of the Herodians"—that is, some manuscripts had "of the Herodians" instead of "of Herod." In Matthew, mention is made of the Herodians as a certain faction that attacked Christ together with the Pharisees.
<margin>13 And looking up]</margin> <note>original: "ἀναβλέψας"</note> "Having looked up," that is, with his sight restored.
<margin>14 I see men]</margin> <note>original: "Βλέπω τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, ὅτι ὡς δένδρα ὁρῶ περιπατοῦντας"</note> That is, "I see men, because I see them walking like trees." In Greek, the word "walking" <note>peripatountas</note> can only refer to the men, because for them "trees" <note>dendra</note> is a neuter noun <note>Grammatically, the masculine plural "walking" must agree with the masculine "men" rather than the neuter "trees."</note>.
<margin>15 And he made him see]</margin> <note>original: "καὶ ἐποίησεν αὐτὸν ἀναβλέψαι"</note> That is, "and he made him see again." For he received his sight twice: first somewhat unclearly, then distinctly.
<margin>16 And he was restored]</margin> Before this, the Greek codex adds, <note>original: "καὶ διέβλεψεν"</note> "and he saw clearly." It is not "all things," but <note>original: "ἅπαντας"</note> "all people"; though this is a very easy slip in writing.
<margin>17 And if you enter the village]</margin> It is clear that the Greek copies differ here and there. For the Laurentian codex had: "Neither enter the village, nor tell anyone in the village." But my copy had: "And if you should enter the town, tell no one, not even in the town." However, I later found a copy that agreed with the Laurentian codex, and I preferred to follow that, especially since Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Bulgarian archbishop and biblical commentator.</note> reads it that way.
<margin>18 Into the villages]</margin> <note>original: "εἰς κώμας"</note> The same word which he so often translates as "village."
<margin>19 But others as if]</margin> <note>original: "Ὡσαὶ"</note> "As if" is not added in the Greek.
<margin>20 You are the Christ]</margin> I believe "the Son of the living God" was added from another place; it is not added in Mark in the more corrected Latin copies, but it is found in Matthew.
<margin>21 And he threatened them]</margin> <note>original: "ἐπετίμησεν"</note> That is, "he rebuked" or "charged." Although "he strictly charged" could be tolerated here, as we forbid something by adding threats. Concerning "about him," <note>original: "περὶ αὐτοῦ"</note> it means "about himself."
<margin>22 And he began]</margin> <note>original: "Καὶ ἀπὸ τότε ἤρξατο"</note> That is, "from then," or "from that time he began," as was held in certain copies. "Because," <note>original: "ὅτι"</note> that is, "that."
<margin>23 After three days]</margin> In a few manuscripts I found written "on the third day"; but it appears the text was changed on purpose because it might seem false at first glance that Christ rose "after three days" when he rose "on the third day." This is especially so since the most corrected Greek copies agree with our Edition. Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>A French humanist and theologian known for his biblical commentaries.</note> discussed this matter diligently in the booklet he titled *On the Magdalenes and the Three Days of Christ*, leaving no stone unturned to explain this difficulty—now adding some hours to the day on which Christ revived (taken from the previous night), now sending him to the underworld before that day when he was weary and grieving in the garden, now adding two nights to one day (namely, the day of preparation). For my part, it is not necessary to reveal what I think about every part of that dispute. Certainly, I do not see

why he thought Bede should be criticized for trying to explain the mystery of the three days through <term>synecdoche</term> <note>A figure of speech where a part is used to represent the whole; here, a portion of a day counting as a full day.</note>, which is surely a grammatical figure. As if we do not owe the entire Gospel history to grammatical figures, or as if all the Ancients, both Greek and Latin, did not explain this question through synecdoche—among whom is also Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, in his commentary on the fifteenth chapter of the first Epistle to the Corinthians. How often do the holy Doctors explain the sense of the Divine Volumes through <term>hyperbole</term>, <term>enallage</term> <note>A substitution of one grammatical form for another.</note>, and similar tropes? Indeed, are not allegory, parable, and words found everywhere in the sacred scriptures the schemes of Grammarians? Why is it that we now drive away Grammarians from sacred matters, when they have deserved somewhat better of the Divine Letters than certain narrow and meager Dialecticians, not to say Sophists. Indeed, with what axe did Faber himself cut this Gordian knot: was it not one offered by Apollonius <note>Apollonius Dyscolus, a famous Greek grammarian.</note>, first a Pagan, and then nothing other than a Grammarian? If he had not come to the rescue, the whole world would still be in error, reading in Mark that Christ would rise "after three days." For he argues thus: He who rises on the third day does not rise after three days; but it is established that Christ rose on the third day. Therefore, whoever says Christ rose after three days opposes the Gospels, opposes the articles of faith, and opposes all truth. And yet, for so many centuries now, with great consensus, the Church has read, sung, and written this in both Greek and Latin. Nor has any mortal until now noticed such an impious error, nor was there any hope of escape, unless Apollonius, most skilled in literary matters, had pointed out that <note>original: "μετὰ"</note> "after" is sometimes used by the Greeks in place of <note>original: "ἐκ"</note> "from" or <note>original: "διὰ"</note> "through." Such is the weight of the single testimony of one Grammarian, whenever it pleases us. Although even this example which Faber produced from Apollonius does not seem to correspond to the Gospel discourse. For "having in hand" <note>original: "μετὰ χεῖρας ἔχειν"</note> and "after days" <note>original: "μετὰ ἡμέρας"</note> is not similar to what Mark says, "after three days" <note>original: "μετὰ τρεῖς ἡμέρας"</note>. Indeed, in Apollonius, <note>original: "μετὰ"</note> seems to be placed for "between," or certainly for "according to." Yet one may not abuse the word in this way if you add a specific number. Now it is established that "after" is frequently used by the Evangelists in this manner, and nothing else is meant but "after." For instance, in Matthew chapter twenty-six, "after two days the Passover will happen," <note>original: "μετὰ δύο ἡμέρας"</note>. Likewise in Luke, "after eight days." In Mark, "after six days." In Acts, "not after many of these days." And in many other places. But to leave these things aside and explain what I feel in a few words, I see no reason why we should stir up a tragedy of this kind here, or why we should flee to such a forced and violent interpretation, when the knot can be untied in two ways with little trouble. First, if we count the third day not from the death of the Savior, but from the whole passion, which began on the day before the preparation, when the plan was already being made for seizing Jesus, when he was sold, when he was weary and grieving. Indeed, Mark himself seems to embrace the sum of the passion in his own words: "And he began," he says, "to teach them that it was necessary for the Son of Man to suffer many things, and be rejected by the Elders and the chief Priests and the Scribes, and be killed, and after three days rise again." For he recounted it in such a way that "after three days" can be referred to the whole discourse that preceded it, not just to the last part, "be killed." Just as in the next chapter he recounted, "the Son of Man is delivered into the hands of men, and they shall kill—"...

<margin>8</margin> And as they were coming down from the mountain, he commanded them that they should tell no one the things they had seen, except when the Son of Man had risen from the dead. <margin>88 9</margin> And they kept the word to themselves, questioning <margin>D</margin> what "rising from the dead" meant. <margin>89 10</margin> And they asked him, saying, "Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?" <margin>11</margin> And he answered and said to them, "Elijah, having come first, restores all things; and how it is written of the Son of Man, that he must suffer many things and be treated with contempt. <margin>12</margin> But I say to you that Elijah has also come, and they did to him whatever they wished, just as it was written..."

<margin>A</margin> *They will kill him, and having been killed, he will rise on the third day.* Since he counts three days from the killing, he said *on the third day*, not *after three days.* Another way to look at it is if we understand it through <term>Synecdoche</term> <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole; here, meaning any part of the third day counts as the day itself</note>, that it happened "after three days" because it happened after the dawning of the third day. This is just like how we commonly say, "from that day he began to hate me," even if he began to hate on that very day. Or "after that day he stopped loving," even if he stopped on that same day. These explanations, if I am not mistaken, are certainly less forced than those produced with such effort by Stapulensis <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, a French humanist and theologian</note>. But if anyone brings forward better points than these, we will not be reluctant to follow.

24 *And openly*] <note>original: "καὶ παρῥησίᾳ"</note> that is, *freely and boldly.* For he did not say this except to his own followers, but he said it clearly and without concealment, as is his custom; even though this discourse was very harsh.

25 *He rebuked Peter*] This is a strange whim of the translator, who elsewhere translates this as *to rebuke*, but here translates it as *to threaten*, even though *to threaten* does not fit the meaning. For what follows,

26 *Get behind me, Satan*] is surely the voice of one rebuking, not threatening. Finally, while we read "to threaten" in the sense of *to forbid*, I do not recall reading it in this same sense here. Furthermore, "behind me" is <note>original: "ὀπίσω μου"</note>, which we noted in Matthew.

27 *Or what will a man give in exchange*] <note>original: "τί ἀντάλλαγμα"</note> that is, *what substitution*: we indicated what our view was on this in Matthew.

<margin>B</margin> 28 *For whoever has confessed me*] Ancient manuscripts with great consensus had *has been ashamed* and *will be ashamed* <note>original: "confusus fuerit & confundetur"</note> instead of "has confessed" and "will confess." This is supported by the "golden manuscript" and my own from an old printing house. In the erasure at Constance, the work of a corruptor was revealed. And so the Greek has it: <note>original: "Ὃς γὰρ ἂν ἐπαισχυνθῇ με καὶ τοὺς ἐμοὺς λόγους"</note>, that is, *For whoever shall have blushed for me and my words.* And a little after: <note>original: "καὶ ὁ Υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐπαισχυνθήσεται αὐτὸν"</note>, that is, *and the Son of Man will blush for him*, or *the Son of Man will be ashamed of him.* The interpretation of Theophylact supports us. In Bede, the text indeed reads "confessed" and "will confess," but the commentary itself, which mentions shame, declares that he read "ashamed" and "will be ashamed." The same is clear from the words of Gregory cited in the *Catena* <note>A "chain" of verse-by-verse biblical commentaries from the Church Fathers</note>. Saint Augustine read it in the same sense when refuting Adimantus the Manichean: *Everyone who has been ashamed of me in this adulterous and sinful people, the Son of Man also will be ashamed of him when he comes in the glory of his Father.* Indeed, Irenaeus in the third book, chapter twenty, uses it the same way.

*shamed and to be shamed.* It appears sufficiently here that the words "confessed and will confess" were substituted by some bold fellow. Otherwise, whether we speak correctly in Latin saying *I am shamed by you* <note>original: "confundor te"</note> instead of "I am ashamed of you," the men of letters can decide.

29 *The kingdom of God coming*] <note>original: "ἐληλυθυῖαν"</note>, that is, *to have come.* For it is a perfect participle, which had to be translated by an infinitive because of the poverty of the Latin language.

---

2 *And he led*] <note>original: "καὶ ἀναφέρει"</note>, that is, *he leads up*, in the present tense, as is also "he takes," <note>original: "παραλαμβάνει"</note>.

<margin>C</margin> 3 *Separately by themselves*] So the most ancient manuscript had it, <note>original: "κατ' ἰδίαν μόνους"</note>, that is, *separately alone.* The old Latin versions agreed on "separately," but the Pauline one had "alone," agreeing with itself. Likewise the one from Constance. Someone, offended by the <term>perisology</term> <note>Use of redundant words</note>, left out one of the words as superfluous. But in this way, the Evangelist wanted to signify a profoundly secret withdrawal.

4 *And he was transfigured*] In Greek it is, <note>original: "καὶ ἐν τῷ προσεύχεσθαι αὐτὸν, μετεμορφώθη"</note>, that is, *and while he was praying, he was transfigured.* Although that part, "while he was praying," is not added in most Greek manuscripts, nor has it been added by us. It appears to have been transcribed here from Luke chapter nine; since Theophylact neither reads nor touches upon this small part.

<margin>F</margin> 5 *Shining and white*] The conjunction is absent in the Greek, <note>original: "σίλβοντα, λευκὰ λίαν"</note>, so that you understand they were reflecting light from their remarkable whiteness. I thought it right to advise on this so it seems less absurd that the Greeks read in Matthew "as light," not "as snow."

6 *Like a launderer*] One could avoid the absurdity of the speech if one translated it as an adverb: "so white as a launderer cannot make them."

7 *And let us make*] <note>original: "καὶ ποιήσωμεν"</note>, that is, *do you want us to make.* Although most Greek copies agree with our Vulgate edition.

2 *Dearest*] <note>original: "ἀγαπητός"</note>, that is, *beloved* or *dear*, except that the added article indicates he is uniquely beloved, *the* beloved.

<margin>D</margin> 9 *Why then do they say*] <note>original: "πῶς οὖν λέγουσι"</note>, that is, *how then do they say.* Although corrected manuscripts had, <note>original: "Ὅτι λέγουσι"</note>, that is, "because they say." And soon after,

10 *First he restores all things*] <note>original: "ἀποκαθιστᾷ"</note>, that is, *he restores*, in the present tense...

<note>The following sections are Erasmus’s philological notes on the Greek text and Latin translation.</note>

<margin>11</margin> **What are you disputing among yourselves]** <note>original: "Καὶ ἐπηρώτησε τοὺς Γραμματεῖς, Τί συζητεῖτε πρὸς αὐτούς."</note> This sense can also be taken as: "And he asked the Scribes, 'What are you inquiring or disputing against them, or with them?'" It appears the Translator read <note>original: "πρὸς ἑαυτοὺς"</note> or <note>original: "πρὸς αὐτούς"</note>, meaning "among yourselves." But we have elsewhere warned that this rule of orthography is frequently neglected in Greek manuscripts.

<margin>12</margin> **The spirit convulsed him]** In Greek it is <note>original: "εὐθέως τὸ πνεῦμα ἐσπάραξε τὸ παιδίον"</note>, that is, "immediately the spirit tore the boy." I suspect the Translator read <note>original: "ἐτάραξε"</note> (disturbed), and perhaps more correctly. Although in most copies it was not "the boy" <note>original: "παιδίον"</note> but "him" <note>original: "αὐτόν"</note>; for it appears he was no longer a small child, since the father responds that this happened to him "from a boy," even if a little later the father of the boy calls him a "child."

<margin>13</margin> **Falling on the ground]** <note>original: "καὶ πεσὼν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς"</note>, that is, "and having slipped onto the earth."

<margin>14</margin> **From childhood]** <note>original: "παιδιόθεν"</note>, that is, "from a boy." But the Translator changed it correctly, unless he preferred to say "from earliest childhood"; for he was already a boy when he was healed. And "into the water," in Greek is "into the waters" <note>original: "εἰς ὕδατα"</note>, agreeing with the ancient copies, specifically the one from Constantinople.

<margin>15</margin> **If you can believe]** <note>original: "Τὸ εἰ δύνασαι πιστεῦσαι."</note> He added the article <note>original: "Τὸ"</note>, which however can be referred to what precedes, as if responding: "That 'if you can' that you said," or to what follows: "This 'if you can' means to believe." Just as it is said in Greek, <note>original: "τὸ μηδὲν ἄγαν, ἄγαν με τέρπει"</note> <note>This refers to the proverb "Nothing in excess," meaning "The phrase 'nothing in excess' pleases me excessively."</note>. For the article is not idle here, as it is found by great consensus in the Greek manuscripts.

<margin>16</margin> **They passed through Galilee]** <note>original: "παρεπορεύοντο διὰ τῆς Γαλιλαίας."</note> The preposition <note>original: "παρὰ"</note> makes you understand that they made their way through Galilee secretly, or quickly and in passing, as if by the way, so that they did not reveal themselves anywhere nor linger. They could seem to have avoided Galilee in their departure, were it not for the preposition <note>original: "διὰ"</note> (through), which makes it impossible to accept anything other than that their journey was made through Galilee.

<margin>17</margin> **The Son of Man is delivered]** <note>original: "παραδίδοται"</note>, that is, "is being delivered," so that you understand it is about to happen soon.

<margin>18</margin> **And they did not understand the word, and were afraid to ask him]** These words are not found in the Aldine edition. Whether this happened by chance, I do not know. It could seem to have been done by someone who was eager to make the Gospel of Mark more complete by adding fragments from elsewhere; for these words are found in Luke, unless the Latin manuscripts agreed with the Greek.

<margin>19</margin> **When he was in the house]** <note>original: "καὶ ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ γενόμενος"</note>, that is, "and having been in the house," or in a building, not necessarily his own.

<margin>20</margin> **Which of them was greater]** In Greek it is only <note>original: "τίς μείζων"</note>, that is, "who was greater." The rest was added for the sake of explaining the matter.

<margin>21</margin> **When he had embraced him]** <note>original: "καὶ ἐναγκαλισάμενος"</note>, that is, "and having taken him into his arms," as we are accustomed to do with infants. For we "embrace" <note>Latin: "complectimur"</note> even those whom we do not take up in our arms.

<margin>22</margin> **Does not receive me]** <note>original: "οὐκ ἐμὲ δέχεται μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸν ἀποστείλαντά με"</note>, that is, "receives not me only, but also him who sent me." Some Greek manuscripts had it this way, but the other reading is more approved by me. For here the negation does not remove, but rather corrects: as if to say, "he does not receive me so much as he receives him who sent me."

<margin>23</margin> **And we forbade him]** After this, in the Greek copies, there is a repetition of <note>original: "ὅτι οὐκ ἀκολουθεῖ ἡμῖν"</note>, that is, "because he was not following us." It is probable that someone, offended by the repetition, removed the latter part.
