---

<margin>24 A cup of cold water]</margin> <note>original: "Calicem aqua frigidæ"</note> The word "cold" is not added in the Greek copies, nor especially in the edition of Jerome from Basel, nor in the oldest copies, specifically the Paulinus, the Corfendonensis, the Constantiensis, or the Golden Manuscript.

<margin>25 He shall not lose his measure]</margin> <note>original: "Non perdet mensuram suam"</note> "Reward" <note>original: "mercedem"</note> should be read instead of "measure." This is how it is written in the more corrected Latin copies.

<margin>26 A donkey's millstone]</margin> <note>original: "Mola asinaria"</note> The Greeks read "a millstone," <note>original: "lithos mylikos"</note> that is, a molar stone. In Matthew, however, it is "a donkey's millstone."

<margin>27 Maimed]</margin> <note>original: "Debilem," Greek: "kyllon"</note> Among the Greeks, the word *kyllos* is properly used for one who has one hand truncated or crippled. For "debility" pertains to all limbs, just as "lame" <note>original: "cholos"</note> properly pertains to the feet.

<margin>28 Where their worm]</margin> <note>original: "Ubi vermis," Greek: "Hopou ho skolex"</note> Elsewhere the translator renders this as "rust," which he here calls "worm." Furthermore, "dies" and "is extinguished" are both in the present tense in the Greek, though some Latin codices have begun to corrupt them into the future tense ("will die," "will be extinguished"). Those who argue from this passage that the fire in the underworld is material must also admit that the worm there is material; but if they admit a figure of speech here, interpreting the worm as the remorse of conscience, they could also understand the fire as the perpetual torment of the soul. Theophylact interprets the passage in this sense.

<margin>29 One-eyed]</margin> <note>original: "Luscum," Greek: "monophthalmon"</note> that is, "single-eyed." Yet he translates this elegantly in this place. For among the Latins, *luscus* refers not to one with crossed or distorted eyes, but to one who lacks one of his eyes.

<margin>30 For every man shall be salted with fire]</margin> To make the speech smoother, I have added of my own "every man."

<margin>31 If the salt becomes unsalted]</margin> He rendered the Greek <note>original: "anartymon, analas analos"</note> as "if the salt lacked salt."

<margin>32 By which it shall be seasoned]</margin> I read "you will season" <note>original: "condietis," Greek: "artysete"</note> in old codices. For it seems he who translated it this way read it so. And "it" <note>original: "ipsum"</note> was more fitting than "that thing" <note>original: "illud"</note>.

<margin>33 Have in yourselves]</margin> He used "salt" here in the masculine gender, following, I think, nothing other than the pleasantness of the sound of the word <note>term: "euphony"</note>.

<margin>1</margin> **B**EYOND the Jordan] <note>original: "dia tou peran tou Iordanou"</note> which sounds more like "through the region" or "the bank" which is beyond the Jordan. The Translator expressed the sense.

<margin>2 And they shall be two]</margin> <note>original: "hoi dyo"</note> those who were two, so that we may understand that from two people, as it were, one is made. It is not "in one flesh" <note>original: "in carne una"</note>. Some interpret this vulgarly regarding sexual intercourse, but it means "one," as I have indicated elsewhere.

<margin>3 What God joined]</margin> <note>original: "synezeugxen"</note> that is, "yoked together," if one prefers to render it word-for-word.

<margin>4 Commits adultery]</margin> The Greek uses the same word that was just translated as "commits adultery" <note>original: "moichatai"</note>. But what does "upon her" <note>original: "ep' auten"</note> mean? Why not rather "against her," or "unto her," that is, to her injury?

<margin>5 They offered him little ones]</margin> <note>original: "paidia"</note> that is, boys or little children.

<margin>6 They threatened them]</margin> <note>original: "comminabantur," Greek: "epetimon"</note> that is, they "rebuked" them. It is strange why the Translator usually delights in rendering this word as "threatened," even when it goes against the meaning.

<margin>7 Suffer the little ones]</margin> <note>original: "ta paidia"</note> that is, little children, as was just said. The Greek did not add the conjunction "and do not forbid." For it is more vivid as "Suffer them, do not forbid them." The repetition of the sentiment <note>term: "anadiplosis"</note> adds emphasis.

<margin>8 Shall not enter]</margin> <note>original: "ou me eiselthe"</note> The doubled negation adds the force of the future tense, or certainly of the potential mood.

<margin>9 And embracing]</margin> <note>original: "kai enagkalisamenos auta"</note> that is, "And taking them into his arms," as was said a little before.

10 **Running forward**] <note>Greek: "prosdramon"</note>, that is, running to. The translator, unless he was nodding off, seems to have read <term>prodromos</term>, that is, running ahead.
11 **Receive eternal life**] <note>Greek: "kleronomeso"</note>, which elsewhere is translated as "shall inherit."
12 **Except one, God**] <note>Greek: "ei me heis ho Theos"</note>, that is, except one, who is God, or indeed God, so that the <term>article</term> <note>the word "the" in Greek</note> has the force of an interpreter, as it were, explaining who that one is.
13 **Do not defraud**] <note>Greek: "Me apostereses"</note>, that is, Do not cheat. For we defraud someone when we deprive them of something owed to them; although he who plunders also <term>defrauds</term> <note>Greek: "aposterei"</note> according to the Greeks.
14 **And Jesus looking at him, loved him**] <note>Greek: "agapesen auton"</note>. Origen seems to have read <term>ephilesen</term> <note>a word often implying a kiss or friendly affection</note> rather than <term>agapesen</term> <note>a word for deep, divine, or selfless love</note>. The evidence is that his Homily on Matthew, citing this passage, reads it as "he loved him," or "he kissed him." For I do not think <term>agapesen</term> can relate to the meaning of a kiss. Furthermore, regarding this "loving," there is no mention of it in either Matthew or Luke. It is possible that someone, offended either by the ambiguity of the word or by the kissing of the youth, changed <term>ephilesen</term> to <term>agapesen</term>: although in Greek lexicons I also find <term>agapazomai</term> meaning "to embrace," but as we embrace what we approve, just as we "embrace" good literature.
15 **And come, follow me**] The Greek codices add here: <term>aras ton stauron</term>, that is, "having taken up the cross," although this is not found in the ancient codices, nor is it found in the other Evangelists, so it may seem to have been added here from elsewhere.

a diminutive <note>a word ending that makes something sound small or endearing</note>, like that in Paul's letter to the Galatians, <term>Teknia mou</term> ("My little children").
17 **Trusting in money**] <note>Greek: "pepoithotas"</note>, relying on or trusting in. For although "confiding" is the same as "trusting," yet "a confident person" does not mean the same thing, as Marcus Tullius <note>the Roman orator Cicero</note> pointed out. Nor does it seem to be a participle, but a noun, and therefore it is placed absolutely: a "confident man," not "confiding in me." Here he sufficiently reveals whom he called "rich"—not those to whom riches happened to come, but those who, like the common crowd of wealthy people, attribute much to their wealth.
18 **Who were more amazed**] <note>Greek: "exeplessonto"</note>, that is, they were stunned. The Greek verb is more forceful.
19 **Or father, or mother**] In this place the Greek codices add <term>e gynaika</term>, that is, "or wife." However, that this was added erroneously by someone can be inferred from the fact that shortly after, when he repeats the things left behind, he does not add "wives." It is likely that the name of "wife" was added here from Matthew and Luke. Truly Mark, being studious of brevity, judged that the name of the "house" included the wife.
20 **Or children**] <note>Greek: "tekna"</note>, that is, offspring, so that you might include both sexes.
21 **At my right hand or at my left**] So that the sense is the same, the Latin is "to sit for me at the right" and "to sit for me at the left." It is not in the Greek "to give to you," but only "it is not mine to give." The Constance codex <note>an ancient manuscript from Constance</note> agreed with the Greek codices.
22 **But for whom it is prepared**] To the somewhat incomplete sentence we have added two words. For it is understood: "but they shall sit at the right and left for me, for whom etc."

->And<-

23 *And hearing it, the ten were indignant*] <note>original: "Et audientes decem indignari sunt"</note> *ἤρξαντο ἀγανακτεῖν* <note>original: "erxanto aganaktein"</note>, that is, they began to be indignant. And our ancient manuscripts have it this way.
24 *And the princes*] <note>original: "Et principes"</note> *καὶ οἱ μεγάλοι αὐτῶν* <note>original: "kai hoi megaloi auton"</note>, that is, their great ones. This is not badly translated, unless you prefer it to be said, *and those who are great among them*, or *their magnates*.
25 *To become greater*] <note>original: "Fieri major"</note> *μέγας* <note>original: "megas"</note>, that is, great, and Jerome frequently cites it in this manner. Christ alludes to the common life of men, among whom the magnates and the elite look down from on high at the lowly, and do not consider them as men, though nothing is more abject than themselves if we wish to judge a man by his virtues.
26 *And as he was proceeding*] <note>original: "Et proficiscente eo"</note> *καὶ ἐκπορευομένου αὐτοῦ* <note>original: "kai ekporeuomenou autou"</note>, *and as he was going out*.
27 *Bartimaeus*] Son of Timaeus. This seems to have been added for the sake of interpretation. For that is what Bartimaeus means. For to the Hebrews *bar* is son, and then Timaeus: just as Bartholomew is the son of Ptolemy, formed from words of different languages, and corrupted, unless I am mistaken, by one or two letters. Furthermore, concerning what we said about Bartimaeus, someone <note>Likely a critic of Erasmus</note> pursues it with a strange mockery in his Annotations, even though I drew this from Jerome’s Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 4. Let him therefore turn his mockery toward Jerome, not toward me.
28 *And they threatened him*] <note>original: "Et comminabantur"</note> *Καὶ ἐπετίμων* <note>original: "Kai epetimon"</note>, that is, *and they rebuked*.
29 *Be of more level mind*] <note>original: "Animéquior esto"</note> *Θάρσει* <note>original: "Tharsei"</note>, that is, *Be of good heart*, or *Trust*. For it is not a comparative, but a positive; and it is one thing *to trust*, that is, *θαῤῥεῖν* <note>original: "tharrein"</note>, and another *to be of a level mind*. He is of a level mind who considers a thing well and endures it. He trusts who has a certain hope.
30 *Leaping up, he came*] <note>original: "Exsiliens venit"</note> In Greek it is not *ἐξαλλούμενος* <note>original: "exalloumenos"</note>, but *ἀναστὰς* <note>original: "anastas"</note>, that is, *rising*. For a little before he was said to be sitting by the road. In Acts chapter three, it is read of the lame man *ἐξαλλόμενος* <note>original: "exallomenos"</note>, that is, leaping up, for that word serves to declare the greatness of the miracle, because he who was healed was so lame that he was carried by porters. Here the miracle is in the eyes, not in the feet.
31 *Rabboni, that I may see*] <note>original: "Rabboni, ut videam"</note> Rufus <note>Rufinus of Aquileia</note> could have changed the Jerome-style word slightly in pronunciation, as elsewhere it becomes Rabbi, which is corrupted by the interaction of the Hebrew, Chaldean, and Syrian languages: just as today the Jews call a Master "Rabeni," but one who is distinguished and eminent. *That I may see*, *ἵνα ἀναβλέψω* <note>original: "hina anablepso"</note>, that is, *that I may recover sight*.
32 *And immediately he saw*] <note>original: "Et confestim vidit"</note> *ἀνέβλεψε* <note>original: "aneblepse"</note>, that is, *he recovered sight*.

1 *And when they approached Jerusalem*] Here the Greek manuscript adds Bethphage, so that there are three places: Jerusalem, Bethphage, and Bethany. Indeed, the Mount of Olives is two miles away from Jerusalem, on the side of which is Bethany, while Bethphage is situated on the mount itself.
2 *What are you doing*] <note>original: "Quid facitis"</note> *Τί ποιεῖτε τοῦτο* <note>original: "Ti poieite touto"</note>, that is, *Why are you doing this*.
3 *And he sat upon him*] <note>original: "Et fedit super eum"</note> Some Greek manuscripts have *ἐπ᾿ αὐτόν* <note>original: "ep auton"</note>, referring to the donkey, or certainly the foal of a donkey. Some have *ἐπ᾿ αὐτῶν* <note>original: "ep auton"</note>, that is, "upon them" <note>the garments</note>, or referring to a female donkey. The latter agrees with Matthew.
4 *When the hour was evening*] <note>original: "Cum vespera esset hora"</note> *ὀψίας ἤδη οὔσης τῆς ὥρας* <note>original: "opsias ede ouses tes horas"</note>, that is, when it was already evening time. For the Greek speaker used "hour" for "time."
5 *And on another day*] <note>original: "Et alia die"</note> *Καὶ τῇ ἐπαύριον* <note>original: "Kai te epaurion"</note>, that is, *On the next day, or The following day*.
6 *If perhaps*] <note>original: "Si quid forte"</note> *εἰ ἄρα εὑρήσει τὶ* <note>original: "ei ara heuresei ti"</note>, that is, *if he was going to find anything*. He translates an expletive conjunction as "perhaps" <note>original: "forte"</note>, and that according to his custom.

7 **Which you cursed**] <margin>to which you cursed</margin>, that is, which you devoted to destruction, or which you execrated, or upon which you called down evil. <note>original: "ᾗ κατηράσω" — explaining the Greek verb for cursing.</note>
8 **Have faith in God**] The translator rendered the Greek <margin>faith of God</margin> in good faith. Otherwise, it signifies trust toward God. <note>original: "πίστιν Θεοῦ" — discussing the genitive case in Greek, which can mean "faith in God" or "God's faith."</note>
9 **To be lifted and cast**] <margin>Be lifted and be cast</margin> are in the passive imperative mood. <note>original: "Ἄρθητι καὶ βλήθητι"</note>
10 **When you stand to pray**] <margin>And when you stand praying</margin>, that is, when you have stood up to offer prayer. From this, it appears that in ancient times they were accustomed to pray while standing.
11 **Your sins**] Augustine, in the twenty-first book of *The City of God*, chapter twenty-seven, noted the force and emphasis of this pronoun <term>your</term> <note>original: "vestra"</note>. For he understands not just any sins, or any grave ones, but those kinds without which even the upright do not live, such as the Apostles were to whom these things were said. <insert>If you do not forgive. 13 **The baptism of John**] <margin>baptism</margin>, that is, *baptisma* or *baptismus*. Since we have received both <term>baptisma</term> (neuter) and <term>baptismus</term> (masculine) from the Greeks, what was the need to devise the barbaric word <term>baptisatum</term>? Some think it matters nothing how they speak. Lorenzo Valla fumes about this sort of thing in this passage not without cause, although he was unaware, it seems, that Augustine speaks this way frequently—so frequently that it cannot be excused as a scribe's error. For so he speaks in the fourth tractate on John, regarding the first chapter: *and so the baptism <note>original: "baptismum"</note> of John did not last.* Again, in the next tractate: *for him there was no baptism* [etc].

And soon after: *since John had therefore received a baptism, which was properly called John's.* Again, a little lower: *Such was the baptism <note>original: "baptisimum"</note> of John.* Nor is it rare to find him doing the same elsewhere. Even if we find it placed this way once or twice in the Homilies of Origen. And in Irenaeus, so that it appears learned men followed this custom of the people's ignorance.
14 **We fear the people**] <margin>they feared the people</margin>, that is, they were afraid of the people. And so the oldest Latin manuscripts have it, specifically the Paulinus and Constance copies. In the Corsendoncensis copy, a trace of an erasure could still be seen. However, a corrector was offended by the harsh and sudden change of person, as if this were something new in the Gospels. That awkwardness could have been avoided by changing the figure of speech to "the people are to be feared by us," or by changing the person of the other verb, as we have done: *But if they had said from men.*

**Planted**] <margin>planted</margin>, that is, he set it in the ground. The word is derived from <term>pastinum</term> <note>a two-pronged gardening tool</note>, which designates the forked instrument with which plants are fixed in the ground; hence, when barren vines are dug up, they are said to be <term>repastinari</term> <note>to be re-trenched or replanted</note>.
2 **And had dug a pit**] <margin>under-vat</margin> <note>original: "ὑπολήνιον"</note>, into which the liquid of the grapes is received.
3 **Wounded in the head**] <margin>having stoned him, they headed him</margin>, that is, to render it literally, they struck him on the head, which is to say, they crushed his head. But because the Translator saw that he returned alive, he translated it as <term>wounded</term>, lest he be thought to have been killed.
4 **And they affected him with insults**] <margin>and they sent him away dishonored</margin>, that is, and sent him back affected by contumely or rather ignominy. For "contumely" consists more in words.

<columns>2</columns>

5 **Dearest** <note>original: "Chariffimum"</note> The Greek is <note>original: "ἀγαπητὸν"</note>, that is, "beloved."
6 **Because they will respect** <note>original: "Quia reverebuntur"</note> The Greek says "perhaps they will respect" <note>original: "ἴσως ἐντραπήσονται"</note>. Although some Greek manuscripts had "that" <note>original: "ὅτι"</note> instead of "perhaps." This is how Theophylactus and the Spanish Edition <note>The Complutensian Polyglot</note> read it. Certainly, the old Latin manuscripts have "because" instead of "perhaps." I prefer this reading. For it is not consistent for someone sending an only son to be uncertain. And although the Greek word <note>original: "ὅτι"</note> cannot be rendered as "because" in Latin in this spot, among the Greeks it has a confirming force.
7 **This was done by the Lord** <note>original: "A Domino factum est istud"</note> "This" should refer to the "head" or certainly to the "corner," as the Greek speech indicates: "of the head of the corner: by the Lord this was done." That is, into the head of the corner: this was done by the Lord—understand "head," unless you prefer "corner," as mentioned in Matthew. It is beyond controversy that for Theophylactus "this" refers to the "corner," which he interprets as the Church, because it connects both peoples (Jews and Gentiles) in the faith of Christ. Jerome, explaining Psalm 118 from which this testimony is taken, reads "this one was made," so that it refers to the stone and Christ.
8 **Wonderful** <note>original: "Mirabile"</note> Greek <note>original: "θαυμαστή"</note>. This also refers to the "head" or the "corner," just as "this was done" does.
9 **That they might catch him** <note>original: "Ut eum caperent"</note> Greek <note>original: "ἀγρεύσωσι"</note>, that is, to snare or hunt. And why not rather "in discourse" than "in a word," since the Greek word signifies "discourse" more than a single "word"?
10 **You do not care for anyone** <note>original: "Non curas quemquam"</note> Greek <note>original: "οὐ μέλει σοι περὶ οὐδενός"</note>, that is, you have no care about anyone. Although to the Greeks this can refer either to a person or to a thing. That is, you do not care for any person, or you do not care for any matter; although what follows indicates it refers more to a person, as others rejected the truth so as not to offend certain people.
11 **In the face of men** <note>original: "In faciem hominum"</note> Greek <note>original: "εἰς πρόσωπον τῶν ἀνθρώπων"</note>, that is, to the "person" of men. Although in Greek the word <note>original: "πρόσωπον"</note> signifies both "face" and "person," in this place "person" was softer than "face"; and thus the same expression was translated in Matthew chapter 22.
12 **It is lawful to give tribute** <note>original: "Licet dare tributum"</note> The Greek is <note>original: "κῆνσον"</note>, that is, "census" <term>census: a Roman poll tax</term>, which is a Latin word, as we have already indicated.
13 **Should we not give** <note>original: "An non dabimus"</note> The Greek is: "Is it lawful to give census to Caesar, or not? Should we give, or should we not give?" 

<column-break/>

They press for an answer with this repetition, as if to say, if he answers it should not be given, they will not give, but if it should, they will. Here the Spanish manuscript agrees with Theophylactus, though Theophylactus does not touch on this reading in his Commentary. I think the Latin is truer here. Otherwise, the same thing is asked twice in the first part: "is it lawful to give" and "shall we give." Whoever corrupted the passage did not notice that "should we not give" <note>original: "μὴ δῶμεν"</note> has a potential force, as if you said "ought we not to give," so that it responds to "is it lawful to give." The Greeks allowed themselves too much liberty in the Sacred Books, especially in Mark and the Acts of the Apostles; though this is chiefly to be blamed on the scribes, who took what some studious person had noted in his own manuscript and moved it into the main text.
14 **Who knowing their craftiness** <note>original: "Qui sciens versutiam"</note> Greek <note>original: "εἰδὼς τὴν ὑπόκρισιν"</note>, that is, "hypocrisy" or "simulation." I wonder why the Interpreter chose to change this, unless perhaps he read "villainy" <note>original: "πανουργίαν"</note>.
15 **What is God's to God** <note>original: "Quæ sunt Dei Deo"</note> I do not know if it happened by chance or on purpose that he added the article twice to "God" but not at all to "Caesar" <note>original: "τὰ Καίσαρος Καίσαρι, τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ τῷ Θεῷ"</note>. It is as if he names Caesar as someone uncertain and unknown, because there are many of that name, but designates God as certain and unique.
16 **And they came upon him** <note>original: "Et venerunt super eum"</note> Greek <note>original: "Καὶ ἔρχονται πρὸς αὐτὸν"</note>, that is, "And they come to him."
17 **And left no sons** <note>original: "Et filios non reliquerit"</note> Greek <note>original: "τέκνα"</note>, "children," for the Greek word also encompasses daughters. In Matthew chapter 22, although the Greeks read "children" with great consensus, the Latin manuscripts have "son," not "sons," though it matters nothing to the sense which you read.
18 **Raise up seed for his brother** <note>original: "Suscitet semen fratris sui"</note> But rather "to his brother," in the dative case <note>original: "ἀδελφῷ αὐτοῦ"</note>. For he calls posterity or offspring "seed," which a brother raises up for his brother, not for himself, because that which is born passes into the name of the dead man. In this way, children were in a certain manner adopted by the dead.
19 **Do you not therefore err** <note>original: "Nonne ideo erratis"</note> Greek <note>original: "Οὐ διὰ τοῦτο πλανᾶσθε;"</note> "Is it not for this reason you err?" so that it refers to what follows, and the sense is that they err because they did not understand the Scriptures. Indeed, the Pharisees erred not because they were ignorant of the Scriptures, but because they were blinded by greed and ambition. The Sadducees fell because of their lack of skill in the Scriptures.
20 **Neither shall they be married** <note>original: "Neque nubentur"</note> The Greek <note>original: "γαμίζονται"</note> is a common verb, used for both man and woman. But this was discussed in Matthew.

<margin>21 *Disputing*]</margin> <note>original: "συζητούντων"</note>, that is, disputing together.
<margin>22 *From all your strength*]</margin> <note>original: "ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ἰσχύος σου"</note>, that is, from your entire vigor. For he himself soon translates it as "fortitude." "Virtue" <note>original: "virtus"</note> is an ambiguous word among the Latins.
<margin>23 *Is like it*]</margin> In Greek it is: "And the second is like that." <note>original: "Καὶ δευτέρα ὁμοία αὐτῇ"</note>. The first commandment is, *You shall love the Lord your God.* And the other is like it, namely this, *You shall love your neighbor, etc.* The translator seems to have read <note>original: "ταύτῃ"</note> instead of <note>original: "αὕτῃ"</note>.
<margin>24 *That he had answered wisely*]</margin> <note>original: "νουνεχῶς"</note>. This is a compound word from "having a mind" <note>original: "νοῦν ἔχειν"</note>, which is a Greek phrase meaning to be wise or sensible, which we translate as "wisely" <note>original: "cordate"</note>.
<margin>25 *And Jesus answering said, teaching*]</margin> <note>original: "Καὶ ἀποκριθείς"</note>. You will find this participle placed in several spots where the sense rather requires "interrogating" <note>original: "ἀνακρινόμενος"</note>. Unless you prefer to understand from this that the speech of others preceded it, which the Evangelist did not record.
<margin>26 *And the first places at table*]</margin> The Translator ought to have been consistent with himself after he began to turn nouns into verbs; for thus it is in Greek: <note>original: "τῶν θελόντων ἐν στολαῖς περιπατεῖν, καὶ ἀσπασμοὺς ἐν ἀγοραῖς, καὶ πρωτοκαθεδρίας ἐν συναγωγαῖς, καὶ πρωτοκλισίας ἐν τοῖς δείπνοις"</note>, that is: wishing to walk in robes, and [wishing] greetings in the forums, and presidencies in the synagogues, and the first places at dinners: or, those who desire to walk in robes, and to be greeted in the forums, and to hold the first chairs in the synagogues, and to recline in the first place at dinners.
<margin>27 *Who devour houses etc.*]</margin> The Greek reads thus: <note>original: "Οἱ κατεσθίοντες τὰς οἰκίας τῶν χηρῶν, καὶ προφάσει μακρὰ προσευχόμενοι"</note>, that is, Devouring the houses of widows, and by a pretext they make long prayers, or under a pretext praying at length.
<margin>28 *More extensively*]</margin> <note>original: "περισσότερον"</note>, that is, more abundantly, or more judgment. Furthermore, he calls condemnation "judgment," as it is frequently understood in the sacred writings. Saint Augustine also noted this fact in his book *On the Christian Struggle*, chapter twenty-seven.
<margin>29 *Should throw*]</margin> <note>original: "βάλλει"</note>, that is, should send, or should cast. For they send these sorts of things by a throw.
<margin>30 *Which is a quadrans*]</margin> Writing in Greek, he misused the Latin word <note>original: "κοδράντης"</note>, albeit in a corrupted form.
<margin>31 *And calling together*]</margin> <note>original: "προσκαλεσάμενος"</note>, that is, summoning, or when he had called them to himself.

<image-desc>Initial letter Q contains a small illustration of a man sitting at a desk writing, likely representing one of the Evangelists.</image-desc>
**Q** *What manner of stones*] <note>original: "ποταποὶ"</note>. I wonder why Laurentius <note>referring to the scholar Lorenzo Valla</note> thought "what manner" <note>original: "quales"</note> should be changed to "how great" <note>original: "quantos"</note>: for <note>original: "ποταπὸς"</note> sounds like "of what sort," but in a way that does not hold a simple question, like <note>original: "ποῖος"</note>, but rather admiration in a positive sense. For instance, if speaking of an unknown happiness, you would correctly say "what sort is this" <note>original: "ποῖος οὗτος"</note>, but you would not correctly use <note>original: "ποταπὸς"</note>.
2 *See all these*] <note>original: "Βλέπεις"</note>, that is, He sees. In some versions it was <note>original: "Βλέπετε"</note>, that is, See [plural].
3 *Saying that I am*] <note>original: "Ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι"</note>. "That" <note>original: "Quia"</note> in this place only affirms, and for that reason it should have been omitted. The phrasing corresponds neither to Greek nor Roman custom. It can, however, be taken two ways: Saying, "I am," so that you understand "the Christ." Or, Saying, that they are the one who "I am." The awkwardness could have been avoided if he had translated it, "Saying, I am the Christ."

<margin>4 And reports]</margin> <note>original: ἀκοὰς (akoas)</note>, that is, rumors. For literally it sounds like "hearings."
<margin>5 And kingdom against kingdom]</margin> Why not rather, "against" the kingdom? Just as he had just translated. For the Greek preposition is the same, <note>original: ἐπὶ (epi)</note>.
<margin>6 Watch yourselves]</margin> The Greek codices indeed agree, but the figure of the Greek speech should have been changed in this place: "Beware for yourselves." Nor is the addition of the pronoun idle, as the disciples are distinguished from others. And I do not know whether it was written by Mark as <note>original: ἑαυτοῖς (heautois)</note>.
<margin>7 In councils]</margin> It was more correct to say, "into councils," <note>original: εἰς συνέδρια (eis synedria)</note>.
<margin>8 And before governors]</margin> <note>original: καὶ ἐπὶ ἡγεμόνων καὶ βασιλέων ἀχθήσεσθε</note>, that is, "and you shall be led before governors and kings," so that you understand they are being led to judges.
<margin>9 Do not premeditate]</margin> <note>original: μὴ προμεριμνᾶτε (mē promerimnate)</note>, that is, do not be anxious beforehand, or do not think ahead with worry, as those who are about to plead a case before Princes usually do.

<margin>14 Where it ought not]</margin> <note>original: ὅπου οὐ δεῖ (hopou ou dei)</note>, where it is not proper.
<margin>15 And to the nurses]</margin> <note>original: καὶ θηλαζούσαις (kai thēlazousais)</note>, that is, those who are nursing.
<margin>16 Tribulations]</margin> <note>original: θλίψις (thlipsis)</note>, that is, tribulation, such as has not been: as it becomes an apposition making an emphasis, since he calls calamitous days "calamity."
<margin>17 Of creature]</margin> <note>original: κτίσεως (ktiseōs)</note>. As it is a verbal noun. Although we find this word to be ambiguous in the Sacred Letters. Sometimes it is used for the act of creation itself, sometimes for the things created.
<margin>18 Nor shall happen]</margin> <note>original: οὐδὲ μὴ γένηται</note>, that is, nor should it happen. By some great part of the prior measure. For this is "to shorten" <note>original: κολοβοῦν (koloboun)</note>, as we noted in Matthew. <margin>F</margin>
<margin>20 Behold here he is]</margin> <note>original: ἰδοὺ ὧδε ὁ Χριστὸς</note>, that is, "Behold here is Christ." And here it is an adverb, not a noun.
<margin>21 Nor the angels in heaven]</margin> <note>original: οἱ ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ</note>, that is, those who are in heaven. In Matthew there is no mention of the Son.
<margin>22 Power of each work]</margin> In Greek it is <note>original: ἑκάστῳ τὸ ἔργον αὐτοῦ</note>, that is, "to each his own work." Furthermore, in some Greek codices "the authority" <note>original: τὴν ἐξουσίαν</note> was held to mean substance, in others "the authority" to mean power. The former reading agrees more with the parable which is in Matthew concerning goods distributed among servants.

# GOSPEL CHAPTER XIV.

<margin>23 Or at the cock-crow</margin> <note>original: "alektorophōnias"</note>, that is, at cock-crowing. For it is a compound word for the Greeks, just like that other one, <note>original: "mesonyktion"</note>, as if you were to say "mid-nighting."

<margin>1</margin> **Passover & Unleavened Bread**] <note>original: "Azyma"</note> is plural in number, just as we say *Lupercalia* or *Saturnalia* <note>ancient Roman festivals</note>; hence it could be translated "the time of unleavened bread," during which they abstained from fermented things.

<margin>2 They might hold him by craft</margin>] <note>original: "en dolō kratēsantes apokteinōsin"</note>, that is, that having captured or seized him through craft, they might kill him. For the preposition "in" is used for "through" by the Hebrews.

<margin>3 For they were saying</margin>] <note>original: "Elegon de"</note>, "But they were saying." Although that matters very little.

<margin>4 Lest perhaps a tumult</margin>] <note>original: "mēpote"</note>, that is, "lest," or "lest ever," about which we have already warned more than once.

<margin>5 Of pistic nard</margin>] It should be read as *pisticæ*, because nard is of the feminine gender. Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous 15th-century humanist scholar</note> thinks it is called *pistica*, meaning "proven and esteemed," arguing against the "divine Christian" <note>likely a reference to a specific commentator</note> who thinks it is named after a place. However, there is an allusion to the Christian faith, which in Greek is called <note>original: "pistis"</note>. The translator rendered it *pisticam*, because a certain kind of nard is called *ipica*, or *spicum nardi* <note>spikenard</note>. Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Greek archbishop and Bible commentator</note>, although more recent, is uncertain whether it is called *pistica* as a species of nard of that name, or "proven," such as <note>original: "adolos"</note>, that is, genuine, corrupted by no art. But Dioscorides <note>an ancient Greek physician and botanist</note>, recording many kinds of nard whose names are added from places, made no mention of *pistica*, nor did Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the 'Natural History'</note>. He whose Commentaries on Mark exist under the name of Jerome (but falsely) interprets *pistica* clearly and expeditiously as "mystical." Hugh of Saint-Cher <note>a 13th-century cardinal and theologian</note> interprets it as "mixed ointment," which is composed not only from the leaves and root, but also from the spikes of the nard—as if indeed that which is made from the leaves were not by far the best. For Pliny, in book twelve, chapter twelve, relates that the leaf of the nard holds the primary place in ointments. In that place, it will be permitted to learn more about the kinds of nard, if anyone has the time. There, mention is made of "false nard" growing everywhere: I think this herb is what we commonly call "lavender," with a thicker and looser leaf, as he says, and a faint color turning toward white. But he depicts true nard in these words: *It is a heavy shrub with a thick root, but short and black and brittle, though oily, smelling of mold like cyperus, with a harsh taste and a small, dense leaf. The tops spread out into spikes; therefore they celebrate the spikes and leaves with a double gift of nard.* However, it could have happened that Mark, speaking in a common way, used a corrupted Latin word, calling it *pisticam* instead of *spicatam* <note>spiked</note>. For it is surprising how corruptly the Greeks

<column-break/>

use the names of the Latins. The same author <note>Pliny</note> mentions the alabaster stone in book thirty-six, chapter seven. For when he had mentioned onyx in the previous chapter, he continues thus: *Some call this stone 'alabastrite,' which they hollow out for ointment vessels, since it is said to preserve them uncorrupted best.* These things agree with what Horace writes in the Odes:
-> A small onyx of nard will draw forth the jar. <-
Bede <note>the Venerable Bede, an 8th-century English monk and scholar</note> reports on nard and alabaster from these two passages of Pliny which I have indicated, with some words changed, strangely concealing the author, as if Pliny were an author to be ashamed of, especially when dealing with natural things. Although it could have happened that Bede noted Pliny in the margin space, just as he testifies in his preface that he noted the titles of those from whom he had drawn what he reports. But the laziness of scribes omitted these. The same thing happened in the Commentaries he published on the Gospel of Luke, since he himself beseeches the Reader or Scribe not to omit these names. Thomas Aquinas acted more cautiously, for in his *Catena* <note>the 'Catena Aurea,' a collection of patristic commentary</note> he mixed the titles of the authors into the context itself. From the *Catena*, it seems that Theophylact was also translated at that time, so much do the things reported there in the name of Theophylact agree. Indeed, it is also a wonder that, since it appears so many monuments of the Greeks in both Sacred Letters and philosophy were translated, they have perished so that they exist nowhere. It can hardly seem that this happened by chance. Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a 14th-century Franciscan biblicist</note> torments himself over whether the nard is an herb, or a shrub, or a very small tree.

<margin>6 To what purpose</margin>] <note>original: "eis ti"</note>, that is, "for what."

<margin>7 She came beforehand to anoint my body</margin>] It is not <note>original: "chrisai"</note>, which is to anoint with any smearing, but <note>original: "myrisai"</note>, which is properly to anoint with ointments and perfumes.

<margin>8 In memory of her</margin>] <note>original: "eis mnēmosynon autēs"</note>, that is, as a monument to her (understand "of the woman"), which we noted in Matthew.

<margin>9 A pitcher</margin>] <note>original: "keramion"</note>, that is, a clay vessel, or a clay water-jug, except that "water-jar" or "water-jug" is added harshly to "water." It will be smoother if you say "full of water," for a "water-jug" is such even when empty.

<margin>10 Where is the guest-chamber</margin>] <note>original: "katalyma"</note>. Lorenzo prefers "inn," as he translates in Luke, although the Greek word signifies both.

<margin>11 An upper room</margin>] <note>original: "anōgeon"</note>, he understands a dining room, but with couches spread out on which they used to recline in the old days. Now, it was called <note>original: "anōgeon"</note> by the Greeks because it was raised from the ground, because the Ancients used to dine in the upper part of the house.

<margin>12 Layered</margin>] After this, in the Greek codices, is added <note>original: "hetoimon"</note>, that is, "ready," but if I am not mistaken, it was transcribed here from elsewhere.

19 "Is it I?" and another, "Is it I?" But he answering said to them,
20 "It is one of the twelve who dips with me in the dish."
21 "The Son of Man indeed goes, as it is written of him: but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed: it were better for him if that man had not been born."
22 And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and when he had blessed it, he broke it, and gave it to them, and said, "Take, eat; this is my body."
23 And taking the cup, when he had given thanks, he gave it to them: and they all drank from it.
24 And he said to them, "This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many."
25 "Truly I say to you, that henceforth I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God."
26 And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
27 And Jesus said to them, "You will all suffer a stumbling-block because of me this night: for it is written: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered."
28 "But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee."
29 But Peter said to him, "Even if all shall find a stumbling-block, yet not I."
30 And Jesus said to him, "Truly I say to you, that today, in this night, before the cock crows twice, you shall deny me three times."
31 But he spoke more vehemently, "Even if I should die together with you, I will not deny you." And likewise also said they all.
32 And they came into a place whose name is Gethsemane. And he said to his disciples, "Sit here, until I have gone and prayed."
33 And he took Peter and James and John with him, and began to be terrified and distressed.
34 And he said to them, "My soul is affected with grief even unto death: stay here, and watch."
35 And going forward a little, he prostrated himself on the ground, and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him.
36 And he said, "Abba, Father, all things are possible to you, take this cup from me: nevertheless not what I would, but what you would."
37 And he came, and found them sleeping, and said to Peter, "Simon, are you sleeping? Could you not watch for one hour?"
38 "Watch and pray, lest you come into temptation: the spirit indeed is ready, but the flesh is weak."
39 And again having gone away he prayed, and spoke the same words.
40 And having returned he found them again sleeping (for their eyes were heavy) nor did they know what they should answer him.

---

19 **Is it I?**] The Greek texts have it as, <note>original: "Mēti egō; kai allos, Mēti egō"</note>, that is, *Is it I? and another, Is it I?* But to me, it truly seems that this was added from some commentary. For when he had already said, "one by one," what was the necessity of adding, *and another*, and then another? Especially since Mark wrote little else than a compendium of Matthew.

20 **who dips his hand**] <note>original: "ho embaptomenos"</note>, that is, *who dips*. The Translator <note>referring to the Vulgate translator</note> added *hand* on his own. And the most ancient manuscripts have it this way: although in Matthew it was <note>original: "embapsas"</note>, that is, *who has dipped*. Nor is it necessary here to take an exact account of the tense. For he did not express what Judas was doing at that exact moment, but indicated by these words to what great intimacy he had been admitted—one who sought a morsel from the same dish with Christ.

21 **The Son of Man shall be delivered**] <note>original: "paradidotai"</note>, that is, *is betrayed* <note>or "is being delivered"</note>, in the present tense, but used in place of the future. There are those who raise a scruple about the word *betray* <note>Latin: "trado"</note>, which they think has no place unless when a thing is given into a hand or passed down to posterity; whereas *to betray* <note>Latin: "prodere"</note> is sometimes to reveal, sometimes to desert, and sometimes to give into a hand, but in a bad sense.

22 **And blessing he broke**] <note>original: "kai eulogēsas eklase"</note>, that is, *when he had blessed he broke*, for he did not bless and break at the same time. And *to bless* is not to form the sign of the cross with a gesture of the hand, but to sing praises to God and to speak words of good omen.

22 **Take, this is**] The Greeks add <note>original: "labete, phagete"</note>, that is, *Take, eat*, just as it was in Matthew.

24 **Which shall be shed for many**] <note>original: "to peri pollōn ekchunnomenon"</note>, that is, *which is being shed for many*. For he was already representing that which would happen a little later. Those who take so much delight in arguing over which words Christ used to consecrate <note>the Eucharist</note>, since it is nowhere expressly read, should take note of this passage, in which the matter is narrated as if Christ offered the cup, then when they had drunk, only then did he say, *This is the chalice*, etc. For the words of the Evangelist are: *And having taken the chalice giving thanks, he gave it to them: and they all drank from it. And he said to them, This is my blood etc.* Although I would not want to be stubbornly contentious in this matter, as the passage can be excused by the figure of <term>hysteron proteron</term> <note>a figure of speech where the natural order of events is reversed</note>.

25 **that now**] <note>original: "hoti ouk eti"</note>. *Now* can stand for *hereafter*, and not badly, though it is somewhat obscure.

25 **Of this offspring**] <note>original: "ek tou gennēmatos"</note>. "Genime" is a Greek word that can truly be translated as *fruit* or *offspring*. And *this*, the pronoun, is neither added in the Greek manuscripts nor in the ancient Latin ones, so that the sense is, *he would taste no wine thereafter*. Hence, even on the cross, he rejected the wine mixed with myrrh moved to his mouth: except that the article "the" has some emphasis.

26 **And a hymn being said**] <note>original: "Kai hymnēsantes"</note>, that is, *After they had spoken praises, so that you may understand the praises were sung by all*.

30 **Shall have given a voice twice**] What was ambiguous in Matthew, Mark explains clearly, so that *twice* refers to the singing of the cock. For the Ancients divided the night thus: when the sun set it was called *evening*; from this time the *first torch*; then *bedtime* <note>Latin: "concubia"</note>; and *the dead of night* <note>Latin: "intempesta"</note>, which is the middle of the night. Soon the *inclination of the night*; then the *cock-crow* <note>Latin: "gallicinium"</note>; then the *time of silence* <note>Latin: "conticinium"</note>, when even the cocks had grown silent and men were still resting. After these, *the dawn* <note>Latin: "diluculum"</note>, when the darkness thins. Then *clear morning*. Thus Juvenal says:
> *But now at the second cock-crow he does that,*
> *the nearby innkeeper will know before daybreak.*

31 **But he said more vehemently**] <note>original: "Ho de ek perissou elege mallon"</note>. He doubled the comparative again, wishing to express the vehement assertion of Peter. Unless one prefers to separate "more" <note>Greek: "mallon"</note> by punctuation from what precedes and attach it to what follows: *Rather, if it behooves me etc.* And soon the doubled negative, <note>original: "ou mē"</note>, does not lack the emphasis of a constant assertion, as if you were to say *never ever*.

32 **into a farm**] <note>original: "eis chōrion"</note>, which is elsewhere translated as *field* or *villa*, but it signifies a *place*. Moreover, *Gethsemane* is a place at the roots of Mount Olivet. Concerning which we gave a reminder in Matthew.

33 **To fear and to be weary**] <note>original: "ekthambeisthai kai adēmonein"</note>, that is, *to be struck with terror and to be anxious*. For this latter is to be powerlessly distressed in soul and to be sick beyond measure: the kind of affection that seizes a man at the first sight of great danger, so that for a while he is not himself.

36 **Abba Father**] The Evangelist set down the Syriac word, and interprets it as it were, adding <note>original: "ho Patēr"</note>. Augustine in his 178th Letter thinks *Abba* is a Greek word, unless perhaps the writing has been corrupted. For in *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*, Book III, Chapter IV, he says *Abba* is a Hebrew word. But we shall touch on this matter somewhat in the Epistle of Paul to the Romans, Chapter VIII.

36 **Not what I**] In Greek it is, <note>original: "all’ ou ti egō, alla ti sy"</note>, that is, *not what I, but what you*. Although here the Greek manuscripts vary; some have, <note>original: "all’ ouch hōs egō thelō, alla hōs sy"</note>, that is, *not as I will, but as you*. In others it was thus, <note>original: "all’ ou ti egō thelō, alla ti sy"</note>, that is, *not what I might will, but what you*. For the speech is altogether involved.

37 **And he comes, and finds**] Both are in the present tense, <note>original: "erchetai, kai heuriskei"</note>. He comes <note>Latin: "venit"</note> with the first syllable circumflexed, and he finds <note>Latin: "invenit"</note> with the first acute, lest anyone here unseemly either hesitate or err.

40 **And returning home**] Once again among the Greeks it refers to the sleepers, not to the returning, <note>original: "heuren autous palin katheudontas"</note>. Certainly the speech among the Greeks is ambiguous.

->### GOSPEL CHAPTER XIV.<-

<margin>41</margin> ...they were heavy) and they did not know what they should answer him. And he comes the third time and says to them, "Sleep on now and take your rest; it is enough, the hour has come; behold, the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of <margin>42</margin> sinners. Rise up, let us go; behold, he who betrays <margin>181 43</margin> me is at hand." And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas arrives, being one of the twelve, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, from the Chief Priests and the Scribes and the <margin>182 44</margin> Elders. Now he who betrayed him had given them a common signal, saying, "Whomever I shall kiss, that is he; seize him, <margin>45</margin> and lead him away safely." And when he had come, immediately approaching him, he says to him, "Rabbi, Rabbi," and he kissed <margin>46</margin> him. Then they laid their hands on him and <margin>183 47</margin> seized him. But a certain one of those standing by, drawing his sword, struck the servant of the High Priest <margin>184 48</margin> and cut off his ear. ***

<margin>30 It is enough] <note>original: "ἀπέχει τὸ τέλος"</note></margin> Although "the end" <note>original: "τὸ τέλος"</note> is not found in some codices, it did not seem right to us to add it. Furthermore, we noted in Matthew that this speech of Christ is more of a reproach than a command.

<margin>31 And the Son of Man is betrayed]</margin> "He is betrayed" is found in both the Greek and the ancient Latin copies <note>original: "παραδίδοται"</note>.

<margin>32 He who betrays me] <note>original: "ὁ παραδιδούς με"</note></margin>, that is, he who betrays me. "Is near" <note>original: "ἤγγικε"</note>, that is, has approached, or is present. Here the Translator rightly changed the tense of the verb.

<margin>33 Signal] <note>original: "σύσσημον"</note></margin>, which sounds like a "common signal" given by agreement, such as those which soldiers call "symbols" <note>passwords/signals</note>, some of which are vocal, and others silent.

<margin>34 And lead him away carefully] <note>original: "ἀπαγάγετε ἀσφαλῶς"</note></margin>, that is, lead him away safely, or surely; that is, with a strict guard, lest he should be able to slip away.

<margin>35 Rabbi] The Greeks double it, <note>original: "Ῥαββί Ῥαββί"</note></margin>, Rabbi Rabbi; whether correctly, I do not know.

<margin>36 But that the scriptures may be fulfilled]</margin> The speech is abrupt; for it must be understood: "These things happen, that they may be fulfilled," etc.

<margin>37 And they held him]</margin> Some Greek codices had it this way, which we also followed—though I do not know if erroneously—<note>original: "καὶ κρατοῦσιν αὐτὸν οἱ νεανίσκοι"</note>, that is, "and the young men hold him," or they seize him, or they lay hands on him, as they might have laid a hand on a youth. Some divine that this young man was from the household where the Lord had eaten the Passover. Others think it was James the brother of the Lord, to whom the surname "the Just" is added. Gregory suspects it was John the Evangelist. However, Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator</note> reads the word "young men" <note>original: "νεανίσκοι"</note>, but does not touch upon it in his explanation. It is also added in the Spanish Edition <note>The Complutensian Polyglot Bible</note>.

<margin>38 And he was warming himself at the light] <note>original: "καὶ θερμαινόμενος πρὸς τὸ φῶς"</note>.</margin> That phrase, "at the light," should be referred to "sitting," not to "warming himself." For it was the light that betrayed him.

<margin>39 They were not consistent] <note>original: "καὶ ἴσαι αἱ μαρτυρίαι οὐκ ἦσαν"</note></margin>, that is, and the testimonies were not equal. He called them "equal," I think, meaning "sufficiently suitable," or "consistent" <note>original: "ἴσα"</note>, because they did not agree with one another. For it is by this evidence that false testimonies are first refuted.

<margin>40 This temple made with hands]</margin> In Greek, these are compound words: "made with hands" <note>original: "χειροποίητον"</note>, and "not made with hands" <note>original: "ἀχειροποίητον"</note>. Otherwise, who is said to be about to build something that is "made with hands"? The Greek words sound as if you were to say a temple of "manual work" and an "artifice not manual."

<margin>41 After three days] <note>original: "διὰ τριῶν ἡμερῶν"</note></margin>, that is, through three days, or in a three-day period, not "after three days" <note>original: "μετὰ τρεῖς ἡμέρας"</note>. The Golden Codex, and the copies of Saint Donatian, and finally the Constance copy, support the Greek reading, in which it is held as "through a three-day period."

<margin>42 And there was no consistency] <note>original: "Καὶ οὐδὲ οὕτως, ἰδὲ ἴση"</note></margin>, "And not even so." For their testimonies had already been rejected once.

<margin>43 Which are objected against you] In Greek it is, <note>original: "Τί οὗτοί σου καταμαρτυροῦσιν"</note></margin>, that is, "What," or "Why do these testify against you?"

<margin>44 Why do we still desire witnesses] <note>original: "Τί ἔτι χρείαν ἔχομεν μαρτύρων"</note></margin>, that is, "What further need have we of witnesses?" And indeed properly...

<margin>69</margin> ...the porch; and a rooster crowed. ---

<margin>A</margin> The translator renders this elegantly as *we desire*, instead of *we require*. Truly, I do not know if the reader expects so much.
<margin>45</margin> *Before the atrium*] <note>original: "εἰς τὸ προαύλιον"</note>, that is, *into the vestibule of the courtyard*, or the place which was before the courtyard.
<margin>46</margin> *For you are a Galilean*] The Greek manuscripts add here, <note>original: "καὶ ἡ λαλιά σου ὁμοιάζει"</note>, that is, *and your speech is similar*, or agrees: added to this place from Matthew, if I am not mistaken.
<margin>47</margin> *To anathematize*] What he translates as *to vow* in the Acts of the Apostles, and *to detest* in Matthew, he has left here as *to curse*.
<margin>48</margin> *And again the rooster crowed*] <note>original: "ἐφώνησε"</note>, the same word as before, although he had used a different word <note>original: "φωνῆσαι"</note> for the sound previously. Since the matter is repeated in the narrative, it was more fitting to repeat the same word. Therefore, this variation was not intended at the time.
<margin>49</margin> *And he began to weep*] <note>original: "καὶ ἐπιβαλὼν ἔκλαιε"</note>, *and bursting out, or suddenly he wept, or broke into weeping.* Since <term>epiballein</term> <note>a Greek verb with many meanings, here suggesting a sudden onset of action</note> among its various meanings sometimes declares *to attack*, or *to take up with force* to do something, hence <term>epibole</term> for *impulse*. Thus with this word Mark studied to express the vehement and sudden change in Peter.

<margin>1 E</margin> **A** ND the whole council] Although "council" is said here twice, the Greek words are different. The first is <note>original: "συμβούλιον"</note> *a small council*, the second is <note>original: "συνέδριον"</note>, that is, *an assembly or convention.*
<margin>2</margin> *And when the crowd had shouted*] <note>original: "Καὶ ἀναβοήσας ὁ ὄχλος"</note>, that is, *And when the crowd had shouted.* Because the Greek copies differ constantly from the Latin, I suspect that something else was written than what we read; I think they read <note>original: "ἀναβάς"</note> *going up*, instead of *shouting*. Even though Theophylact <note>an 11th-century biblical exegete</note> reads "shouting," agreeing with the Spanish edition, it is not clear from his interpretation what he actually read.
<margin>3</margin> *Began to ask*] <note>original: "ἤρξατο αἰτεῖσθαι"</note>, that is, *began to seek or demand.* For he had just translated it thus, <note>original: "ὅνπερ ᾐτοῦντο"</note>, that is, *whomever they had asked for.*
<margin>4</margin> *As he always did for them*] To make the sentence complete, one must supply: *That he might do as he had always done for them.*

<column-break/>

<margin>69</margin> "I neither know nor understand what you are saying." And he went out into the vestibule; and the rooster crowed. And when the servant girl saw him, she began to say again to those standing by, "This is one of them." <margin>70</margin> But he denied it again. And a little later, those standing by said again to Peter, "Truly you are one of them: for you are also a Galilean, and your speech matches." <margin>71</margin> But he began to curse and to swear, "I do not know this man of whom you speak." <margin>72</margin> And again the rooster crowed: and Peter remembered the word that Jesus had spoken to him, "Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times": and he began to weep. And immediately at dawn, after holding a consultation, the <margin>XV. 1</margin> chief priests with the elders and scribes and the whole assembly led Jesus away bound, and delivered him to Pilate. And Pilate questioned him, "Are you the king <margin>2</margin> of the Jews?" But he answering said to him, "You say so." And the chief priests accused him of many things. <margin>3, 4</margin> Pilate then questioned him again, saying, "Do you answer nothing? See how many things they testify against you." But Jesus thereafter answered nothing, so that <margin>5</margin> Pilate wondered. Now at the festival he used to release <margin>6</margin> one prisoner to them, whomever they asked for. There was <margin>7</margin> a man called Barabbas, who was bound with the authors of sedition, who had committed murder during the rebellion. And when the crowd had shouted, they began to demand <margin>8</margin> that he do as he had always done for them. Pilate answered them, saying, "Do you want me to release <margin>9</margin> to you that king of the Jews?" For he knew that <margin>10</margin> the chief priests had delivered him up because of envy. But the chief priests stirred up the <margin>11</margin> crowd, so that he should rather release Barabbas to them. And Pilate <margin>12</margin> answering said to them again, "What then do you want me to do to him whom you call the king of the Jews?" But they <margin>13</margin> cried out again, "Crucify him." And Pilate <margin>14</margin> said to them, "For what evil has he done?" But they cried out more vehemently, "Crucify him." And Pilate, <margin>15</margin> wishing to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas to them, and delivered Jesus, having been scourged, to be crucified. The soldiers <margin>16</margin> then led him away inside into the courtyard, which is the praetorium, and they call together the whole cohort. And they <margin>17</margin> clothe him in purple, and they place around him a crown woven of thorns. And they began to salute him, "Hail, king <margin>18</margin> of the Jews." And they struck his head with a reed, and <margin>19</margin> spat upon him, and falling on their knees, they worshiped him. And when they had mocked him, they took the purple off him, <margin>20</margin> and clothed him in his own garments: and they lead him out to crucify him. And they compelled a certain passerby, <margin>21</margin> Simon of Cyrene, who was coming from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to take up his cross. And they lead him to the place Golgotha, which is, <margin>22</margin> if you interpret it, the Place of the Skull. And they gave him <margin>23</margin> to drink...

---

<margin>5</margin> *But the High Priests*] Where it just said *Chief Priests*, it now uses *Pontiffs*. For in Greek, it is the same word: <note>original: "Ἀρχιερεῖς"</note>.
<margin>6</margin> *They stirred up the crowd*] <note>original: "ἀνέσεισαν"</note>. Some Greek manuscripts had <note>original: "ἀνέπεισαν"</note>, that is, *they persuaded*, or *drew them back* to this opinion.
<margin>7</margin> *But Pilate said to them, "What evil has he done?"* Saint Augustine, in the third book of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, chapter 13, noted a serious matter: that the Evangelist said here, "Pilate was saying," not "Pilate says," specifically indicating that this was not said by the Governor just once, but that much time was spent in this conversation. And in the Greek it is indeed <note>original: "ἔλεγεν"</note> <note>the imperfect tense, suggesting ongoing or repeated action</note>. Yet in Matthew, the word is in the same tense <note>original: "εἶπεν"</note>, where the translator renders it *he said*, not *he was saying*. He did the same in Luke. I have noted this only to show how we seize upon even the smallest things to support our case whenever we are constrained by difficulties.
<margin>8</margin> *In the courtyard of the praetorium*] <note>original: "ἔσω τῆς αὐλῆς, ὅ ἐστι πραιτώριον"</note>, that is, *inside the courtyard, which is the praetorium.* And here, writing in Greek, he used a Roman word <note>Praetorium is a Latin loanword in the Greek text</note>.
<margin>9</margin> *Father of Alexander and Rufus*] <note>original: "πατέρα Ἀλεξάνδρου καὶ Ῥούφου"</note>, that is, *the father of Alexander and Rufus, or the son of Rufus.* Some Greek manuscripts agreed with our Edition: that we should understand Simon as having two sons. For Theophylact interprets it thus, the names of the sons being added so that the truth of the narrative might be more certain. The same reading is followed by the one who wrote the scholia <note>brief explanatory notes</note> on Mark, which are attributed to Jerome, who thinks that Alexander and Rufus were disciples of the Lord whose father was from Cyrene, and Cyrene is a city of Libya. Thus already the Jewish religion had propagated so far. Indeed, in Acts, among the various nations who were amazed by the miracle of tongues, are mentioned *those who inhabited the parts of Libya around Cyrene.* Again, in chapter 6 of the same work, among those who disputed with Stephen, is mentioned the *Synagogue of the Freedmen, of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians.* Likewise, in chapter 11, mention is made of certain Cypriots and Cyrenians, and even Jews.

It is not *they compelled*, but *they are compelling* <note>original Greek: ἀγγαρεύουσι</note>, a word about which we have spoken elsewhere.
<margin>10</margin> *And crucifying him*] <note>original: Καὶ σταυρώσαντες αὐτὸν</note>, that is, *When they had crucified him*.
<margin>11</margin> *It was now the third hour*] At this point, Peter Comestor <note>a 12th-century theologian</note> advises, on the authority of Saint Jerome, that in Mark it was originally written that the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour. However, Greek scribes likely made an error due to the similarity of characters. Instead of the mark for the number six <note>original: ϛ</note>—which is not a letter for the Greeks but a composite numeral sign used after the letter epsilon (5) and before zeta (7)—they painted the letter gamma <note>original: γ</note>, which signifies three. This passage is found in Jerome’s exposition of Psalm 77. The same point was cited a bit earlier from the "Greater Breviary," a work we do not recognize, unless perhaps he means the *Commentaries on the Psalms*, just as the "Lesser Breviary" might refer to the *Commentary on Matthew*. If we accept Jerome's opinion, this question is easily resolved, a matter over which Augustine struggles greatly in Book III of his *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*. The knot is untied in the same way in the book *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, question 65. Let anyone who wishes seek it there; we have added what we have found.
<margin>12</margin> *Who rebuildest*] The Greek phrasing is ambiguous because of the participles. But Jerome, in his commentary on Isaiah, cites it in the third person: *Vah! he who destroys the temple and in three days restores it*. I found it written this way in the Codex of St. Donatian and likewise in the Constantian codex. It should be noted that in the Greek codices, the word "of God" is not added; it is simply "the temple," supported by the books of St. Donatian and the Constantian. In some of our Latin copies, "rebuildest" has been wrongly changed from "buildest."
<margin>13</margin> *Eloi, Eloi, lamma sabachthani*] There is no doubt that the Evangelist correctly rendered these Hebrew or Syriac words, however they sound to us, as we discussed in the notes on Matthew.
<margin>14</margin> *My God*] In the Greek copies, I believe through the carelessness of scribes, the pronoun "my" is not repeated, even though it is repeated in the Hebrew: *My God, my God*. Therefore, we did not hesitate to include it, especially relying on the fact that we see it included in Matthew. Later we found it added in some Greek texts, such as the Spanish one, though it was not added in the very ancient codex of Theophylact, nor in the Aldine edition, which I think happened through scribe negligence. Since the Hebrew says *Eloi, Eloi*, that is, *My God, My God*, it is appropriate that the Evangelist's interpretation does not differ from this.
<margin>15</margin> *To what end*] <note>original: εἰς τί</note>, that is, *for what purpose* or *why*.
<margin>16</margin> *And placing it around a reed*] A little further up, the translator rendered

"reed" as *arundinem*. Now having forgotten, I believe, he left the Greek word: he did the same in the Psalm: *Sending out crystal like a morsel*, when instead of <note>original: κρύσταλλο</note> he should have translated it as *ice*; for it is rightly said of snow and of cold.
<margin>17</margin> *But the centurion seeing*] Here too the Evangelist used a Roman word, <note>original: κεντυρίων / centurion</note>, whom elsewhere he calls a <note>original: ἑκατοντάρχην / hekatontarchos</note> in the Greek tongue. And the word "and" is not present.
<margin>18</margin> *Crying out, he expired*] <note>original: ὅτι οὕτως</note>, that is, *a cry having been sent forth*, or *when he had cried out*, for he expired immediately after the cry.
<margin>19</margin> *Of James the less*] <note>original: τοῦ μικροῦ</note>. In Greek this is the simple form "the small"; it is not the comparative "the less." It appears to have been a surname. And *Joseph*, <note>original: Ἰωσῆ</note>, that is, *Joses*.
<margin>20</margin> *Which is before the Sabbath*] In Greek this is one word, <note>original: προσάββατον</note>, as if you were to say *pre-Sabbath*, that is, the *start of the Sabbath*.
<margin>21</margin> *Joseph from Arimathea came*] It cannot be understood merely that he came from that place, since the article <note>original: ὁ ἀπὸ Ἀριμαθαίας</note> intervenes, meaning *the Arimathean*, indicating his homeland. Jerome, in the *Directory of Places*, indicates it was called *Arimatha Jophim*, the city of Elkanah and Samuel in the region of Thamnitica, near Diospolis, the homeland of the Joseph mentioned here.
<margin>22</margin> *A noble decurion*] <note>original: εὐσχήμων βουλευτής</note>, that is, *an honorable senator*. Lorenzo Valla advises that *Decurion* here should be understood as a *municipal senator*.
<margin>23</margin> *Boldly he entered*] <note>original: τολμήσας</note>, that is, *having taken courage*, although the Translator rendered it correctly. Let no one think I am mocking him because we translated it differently. Furthermore, "boldness" is not always the opposite of "good counsel," but often refers to danger. For the Evangelist means that the Senator dared to do this not without risk, out of love for Jesus.
<margin>24</margin> *If he were already dead*] <note>original: εἰ πάλαι ἀπέθανε</note>, that is, *if he had been dead for some time* or *long ago*. Even though some codices have "already" <note>original: ἤδη</note> instead of "long ago" <note>original: πάλαι</note>. I later found it this way in the Aldine edition, agreeing with the Spanish one and also Theophylact. Therefore, I do not agree with certain learned men who think that <term>why</term> <note>original: τί</note> here has the same value as the conjunction <term>that</term>. Indeed, the things that follow indicate that Pilate still doubted: *so that the matter might be known from the centurion*. Furthermore, the form of the speech should offend no one, since Terence speaks thus: *I wondered if he would get away like that*. From this passage, Origen concludes that the soul of Christ did not leave his body in the common manner of dying men, but departed from the body of his own will when he saw fit. For according to nature, he would not have left a youthful body so early, especially since his legs were not broken, which usually happens to others to hasten death.

<margin>5</margin> <gloss>Lastly, as they were reclining</gloss> Augustine, in his *Harmony of the Evangelists*, Book III, struggles with the question of how Mark says Jesus appeared "lastly" here, when John reports that he appeared later to his followers at the Sea of Tiberias. He unties this knot by explaining that "lastly" refers not to the total number of appearances, but specifically to the appearances made on that first day. Yet, since the Greek says *hysteron*, which sounds like "later" or "afterwards," there was no reason to raise the question if he had consulted the Greek manuscripts—though I should not hide that comparatives are sometimes used in place of superlatives. Because he had said "first," the Translator here preferred to say "last."
<margin>6 F</margin> <gloss>To those eleven</gloss> <note>original Greek: *autois tois hendeka*</note>. Saint Augustine, from the added pronoun "those" and the Greek article, concludes that this passage can only be understood as referring to the Apostles. However, the Greek does not say "to those very ones" <note>original Greek: *ekeinois autois*</note>. If taken relatively, it sounds as if Jesus appeared to the same twelve Apostles he appeared to before. If taken distinctly, the meaning will be that Jesus appeared not to the women or any random disciples mentioned earlier, but to the eleven themselves, namely the Apostles, who had not believed the reports. Mark weaves the text as if this were the sense: First he appeared to Mary Magdalene. *Afterward* to the two walking to the village. *Lastly* to the eleven reclining. This sense is not contradicted if he had already appeared to one or another of the Apostles; certainly, he had not yet appeared to the eleven dining together.

saw that he had risen. They perhaps read "those who had seen him *rising*," as this Translator frequently turns past participles into present participles. Saint Jerome, in his *Letter to Hedibia*, question three, indicates that this final chapter of Mark was not received by many, because it was found in few Latin manuscripts and almost no Greek ones, especially since it seems to narrate things clearly at odds with the other Gospels. For example, it reports that the Lord rose early on the first day of the week, while Matthew records that he rose on the evening of the Sabbath "which dawns into the first day of the week." Now, "evening" and "morning" conflict with each other. Jerome offers a twofold solution to this difficulty, the first being: "Either," he says, "we do not accept Mark’s testimony, which is found in few Gospels, since almost all the books of Greece do not have this chapter at the end." This would be an impious solution if this chapter had the same authority at that time as the rest of Mark’s Gospel. Jerome also suggests that a sub-distinction <note>a minor punctuation mark or pause</note> should be made before the word "early": so that we understand Christ rose in the *evening*, and then on the *first day of the week* appeared to Mary, reading it this way: "when Jesus had risen," and here inserting a pause <note>original: *hypostigme*</note>, followed by "early on the first day of the week he appeared first to Mary." Theophylact also points out this distinction. To make the speech clearer, for *anastas* <note>rising</note>, which the Translator rendered as "rising," we have translated "when he had risen." For it is a past participle, which should be rendered with a circumlocution. The same Jerome, in his second *Dialogue against Pelagius*, mentions that at the end of the Gospel according to Mark, in some copies, especially Greek ones, a concluding statement <note>original: *coronidem*</note> was added to these words of Mark: "Afterward, when the eleven had sat down, Jesus appeared to them and rebuked their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed many who had seen him rising. Here it was added: And they made satisfaction, saying: This age of iniquity and unbelief is the substance which, through unclean spirits, does not allow the true power of God to be apprehended. Therefore, reveal your justice even now." However, as this final chapter of Mark is held today in all the Greek manuscripts I have seen, which Theophylact also explains: so this conclusion from the apocrypha...

<margin>A</margin> It appears that this was added from some apocryphal Gospel by a reader who was far too bold. For Jerome <note>Hieronymus, a 4th-century Church Father and translator of the Vulgate</note> testifies that the *Gospel of the Hebrews*—which was then read by the Nazarenes and Essenes, written in Hebrew letters but in the Chaldaic <note>Aramaic</note> tongue—was translated by him into the Greek language; he brings forth several testimonies from it, in which certain things not unlike these are read. However, this addition, since it possesses nothing of Gospel-like weight but rather reeks of the Manichaean <note>A dualistic religious movement often labeled as heresy by the early Church</note> doctrine, was deservedly trimmed away and rejected by both the Greeks and the Latins. Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, an 8th-century English monk and scholar</note> testifies that the holy Ambrose wrote accurately on this Evangelist <note>Mark</note>, from whose commentaries he confesses to have plucked many things. This work has been lost to us, unless perhaps Bede felt that the com-

<column-break/>

-mentaries on Mark, which circulate under the name of Jerome, are actually by Ambrose. This I neither refute nor assert. For they seem to be the work of a man who is neither speechless nor unlearned, who certainly has this in common with Ambrose: that he is much given to allegories and emotions. However, the booksellers seem to have added an inept and unlearned preface, so that they might entice a buyer with the charm of a famous name. I will add this: that Jerome refers to this passage in different words than those held in the Latin Edition <note>The Vulgate</note> of Mark, even though he wrote against the Pelagians as a very old man. From this, one may guess either that this Edition is not Jerome’s, or that he himself neglected what he had handed down. For what I am pointing out here is quite frequent for him in that work.

## DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

### ANNOTATIONS ON THE GOSPEL OF MARK

# F I N I S .

---

## THE LIFE

### OF

# L U K E

### ACCORDING TO SOPHRONIUS. <note>Sophronius was a 7th-century Patriarch of Jerusalem, though this text is often associated with Jerome's "De Viris Illustribus."</note>

Luke, a physician of Antioch, as his writings declare, was not unskilled in Greek learning. A traveling companion of the Apostle Paul and a follower of all his travels abroad, he composed a gospel, concerning which Paul himself says: "We have sent with him the brother whose praise is in the gospel throughout all the churches." <note>original: *Apeisteilamen... ton adelphon*, quoting 2 Corinthians 8:18</note> And to the Colossians: "Luke, the beloved physician, greets you." <note>Colossians 4:14</note> And to Timothy: "Only Luke is with me." <note>2 Timothy 4:11</note> He also issued another excellent volume titled the *Acts of the Apostles*, whose history extends until the two-year period of Paul's stay in Rome—that is, until the fourth year of Nero. From this, we are persuaded that the book was composed in that same city. For the *Travels of Paul and Thecla* <note>An early Christian apocryphal story</note> and the whole myth regarding a baptized lion <note>original: *leontos baptisthentos*; an legendary tale of a lion converted and baptized by Paul</note> shall be judged among the apocryphal writings. For it was not possible that the inseparable companion of the Apostle should be ignorant of this among his other deeds. But even Tertullian <note>A 2nd-century North African theologian</note> reports from those times that a certain elder in Asia, a devotee of the Apostle Paul, was convicted before John of having composed the book; he confessed he had done it out of love for Paul. Therefore, some suppose he was removed from office. Whenever Paul says in his own epistles, "According to my gospel," <note>original: *kata to euangelion mou*</note> it is clear that he signifies the volume according to Luke. And that Luke alone learned the gospel from the Apostle Paul, as he was not with the Lord in the body at that time, but also from the rest of the apostles, as he himself clearly says at the beginning of his own composition: "Just as those who were eyewitnesses from the beginning delivered them to us." <note>Luke 1:2</note> Therefore, he wrote the gospel as he heard it. But the Acts of the Apostles he composed as he himself had witnessed. His remains were brought and laid to rest in Constantinople, to which city, in the twentieth year of Constantine, his body was transferred along with the remains of the Apostle Andrew.

## INTRODUCTION

### TO THE

# GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE

### BY THEOPHYLACT. <note>Theophylact of Ohrid was an 11th-century Byzantine Archbishop and prominent Bible commentator.</note>

The divine Luke was an Antiochene and a physician; he was well-versed in external <note>secular/Greek</note> wisdom, but moreover, he practiced Hebrew education, having visited Jerusalem when our Lord was teaching. Thus, some say he was one of the seventy apostles, and that he met Christ after he rose from the dead along with Cleopas. <note>A reference to the Road to Emmaus in Luke 24</note> After the Lord’s ascension, having believed in Paul, he became his traveling companion. I mean he joined Paul and indeed composed the gospel with all accuracy—as his own preface shows—fifteen years after the ascension of Christ. He writes to Theophilus, who was of the senatorial rank and perhaps a ruler. For the term "most excellent" <note>original: *kratistos*</note> was used for rulers and governors, just as Paul says to the governor Festus, "Most Excellent Festus." <note>Acts 26:25</note> Furthermore, every man who is a "lover of God" <note>A pun on the name Theophilus, which means "God-lover" in Greek</note> and has taken up power over his passions is a "most excellent Theophilus," who is truly worthy to hear the gospel.
