<margin>1</margin> SINCE many have undertaken to set in order a narrative concerning the matters that have been fully accomplished among us, <note>original: "ΕΠΕΙΔΗΠΕΡ πολλοὶ ἐπεχείρησαν..." Luke 1:1</note>
<margin>2</margin> Just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and became ministers of the word delivered them to us, <note>Luke 1:2</note>
<margin>3</margin> It seemed good to me also, having followed all things accurately from the beginning, to write to you in order, most ex- <note>Luke 1:3</note>

1 <gloss>Since indeed</gloss> ] Luke alone both prefaces his work and mentions his books by name. Although he is purer and more lucid in his speech than the others—owing to his skill in Greek literature, which Jerome <note>Hieronymus, a 4th-century scholar and translator of the Vulgate</note> attributes to him in his *Catalog of Writers*—he nevertheless mixes in much from the idiom of the Hebrew language. Furthermore, as to why he translates <term>ἐπεχείρησαν</term> <note>epicheirēsan; original: "undertook" or "attempted"</note> as "since indeed," I do not know if "since indeed" is found at the start of a sentence among those who speak correctly. I would have preferred "since," or "after," or "inasmuch as." Yet he does not translate <term>ἐπεχείρησαν</term> entirely poorly as <term>conati sunt</term> ("they attempted"): so that we may understand that those people wished for the task more than they performed it, and tried the matter more truly than they achieved it. For at that time, it was not only the Gospel of Matthew or Mark that existed, but many Gospels were being circulated: those of the Nazarenes, of Thomas, of Matthias, one according to the Egyptians, one according to the Twelve, one of Nicodemus, and likewise of others, which the Church later rejected as apocryphal. Furthermore, <term>ἐπιχειρεῖν</term> <note>epicheirein</note> properly means to take something into one's hands and approach it.

2 <gloss>To set in order a narrative</gloss> ] <term>ἀνατάξασθαι</term> <note>anataxasthai</note>. I would have translated this as "to digest" or "to weave together": for that is to arrange in order what others might have produced piecemeal, or not according to a continuous series of events. Indeed, even Matthew himself, although he is fuller than the others and begins in a historical manner from the very birth of Christ, nevertheless passed over almost the entire childhood and youth of Christ. Furthermore, Mark’s Gospel might seem an epitome <note>a summary</note> of that which was produced by Matthew, passing over many things and beginning the Gospel history from the preaching of John. John touches on certain things piecemeal, as if they had been omitted by others. Accordingly, Ambrose <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Milan and influential theologian</note> attributes a historical style to Luke as his own particular trait. For when he had attributed specific qualities to each, he said:
> But truly Saint Luke held to a certain historical order, and revealed to us more miracles of the Lord's deeds: yet in such a way that the history of this Gospel embraced all the virtues of wisdom.
The same author says a little later:
> For that reason we said this book of the Gospel was "digested" <note>organized</note> by his pen. Finally, we see a more abundant zeal spent on describing events than on expressing precepts, in comparison to the others.
And the Evangelist himself began the narrative in a historical manner: "There was," he says, "in the days of Herod, King of Judea, a certain priest named Zacharias," and he follows that history with a full arrangement.

3 <gloss>Of the things which have been completed in us</gloss> ] I ask, who could perceive from this translation what the Evangelist felt? For it should not be taken simply that the things he is about to narrate "happened," but that they have been discovered with the most certain faith and persuaded by indubitable arguments. For that is what the Greek <term>πεπληροφορημένων</term> <note>peplērophorēmenōn</note> sounds like, from the verb <term>πληροφορέω</term> <note>plērophoreō</note>, which is "I make full faith" <note>I give full assurance</note>. From this comes <term>πληροφορία</term> <note>plērophoria</note>, a certain faith which is made by arguments or by the thing being shown: and they call <term>πληροφορηθῆναι</term> <note>plērophorēthēnai</note> what we commonly call "to be certified." And he is called <term>πεπληροφορημένος</term> <note>peplērophorēmenos</note> to whom a certain faith in a matter is made, so that he no longer doubts at all: hence it is a compound word, because those things are brought forward which are usually required for the full proof of a matter. Accordingly, in Paul's Epistle to the Romans, chapter four, for <term>πληροφορηθείς</term> <note>plērophorētheis</note>, the Translator <note>the Vulgate author</note> renders it "most fully knowing." And again in the same, chapter fourteen, "Let every man abound in his own sense," the Greek is <term>πληροφορείσθω</term> <note>plērophoreisthō</note>, that is, "Let each man's own mind satisfy him," and let him rest in that. Paul uses the same verb in quite a few other places: and so does Luke himself in the Acts of the Apostles, which we shall point out in its proper place. Indeed, the translator of Origen <note>A 3rd-century Alexandrian scholar</note> translates it in this manner:
> Which have been most manifesty shown in us:
and he adds the same, that <term>πεπληροφορημένων</term> is something the Latin tongue does not explain in a single word: for he had known it by certain faith and reason. Although from these words one may gather that this writer was either a paraphraser of Origen, not a translator, or added something of his own so the matter would be clearer. Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator</note>, a more recent Greek interpreter but by no means a bad one in my opinion, interprets it with the same meaning. For he says: <term>Res autem gestas dixit πεπληροφορημένας...</term> <note>original Greek translated by Erasmus: "He called the deeds 'peplērophorēmenas'; for the deeds of Christ were not simply handed down in a common way, but they stand firm and true, with all certainty."</note> That is, "He called the deeds *peplērophorēmenas*: for the deeds of Christ were not handed down simply and in a common manner, but they stand firm and true, with all certainty. But come, tell us Luke, from where does that certainty of things come? Just as they delivered them to us who from the beginning were themselves onlookers and ministers of the things they narrate." Ambrose also indicates something of this sort, though more obscurely, writing in this manner:
> Which are completed in us, or which abound in us. For that which abounds lacks for no one: no one doubts concerning the completed, since the effect adds faith and the outcome proves it.
And soon after:
> Therefore, he who is founded on the rock, and who has taken up all the ful-

<column-break/>

# LUKE.

<margin>1</margin> SINCE several have attempted to weave together a narrative of those things which, among us, are of most certain faith,
<margin>2</margin> Just as they were delivered to us by those who from the beginning saw them with their own eyes and were some part of those things they were narrating:
<margin>3</margin> It seemed good to me also,

<margin>A</margin> -ness and the firmament of constancy, rightly says, "Which are completed in us." Ambrose played cleverly with words here, but in the meantime, being knowledgeable in the Greek language, he indicates well enough the force of the Greek word <term>πεπληροφορημένων</term>. I do not know if it is worthwhile to add that this voice is accommodated both to the thing and to the person. For he who is persuaded is called <term>πεπληροφορηθείς</term>, and the things of which faith has been made are called <margin>B</margin> <term>πεπληροφορημένα</term>, just as faith is made to a person, and we create faith in a thing. Suetonius <note>A Roman historian</note>, referring to a Greek expression in his own style, wrote in *Tiberius*: "Most persuasively full that all things are ruled by fate," as if expressing the Greek word <term>πεπληροφορηθείς</term>.

4 <gloss>Just as they delivered</gloss> ] Even from this it is clear that Luke writes his Gospel from things heard from others. For that which is poured out by narration from some to others is "delivered." Unless we prefer to take it this way: "Just as they delivered to us" is said absolutely: so that Luke himself is among the number of those who delivered it, and "to us" refers to all who learned of Christ from the preaching of the Apostles. Truly, as this has been said by no one, it is more forced, in my opinion at least. Why is there a need to labor here over proofs, when Saint Jerome in the *Catalog of Ecclesiastical Writers* frankly confesses that Luke followed only those things which he had received from others, but from men of the most certain faith—that is, not from just anyone, but from those who were present at everything they narrated. I will subscribe Jerome’s words on this matter, if anyone should require them:
> And Luke, he says, learned the Gospel not only from the Apostle Paul, who had not been with the Lord in the flesh, <margin>C</margin> but from the other Apostles. Which he himself also declares at the beginning of his volume: "Just as they delivered to us who from the beginning saw it themselves, and were ministers of the word."
Therefore he wrote the Gospel just as he had heard it. Let him see who composed the Acts of the Apostles. And even more clearly in the Preface which he placed before the Commentaries on Matthew:
> Third, he says, is Luke, a physician, Syrian by nation, an Antiochene, whose praise is in the Gospel, who was himself a disciple of the Apostle Paul; he composed a volume in the regions of Achaia and Boeotia, repeating certain things more deeply, and as he himself confesses in the proem <note>introduction</note>, describing things heard rather than seen.
Thus far Jerome. Truly, concerning this we shall say a few more things shortly, on the occasion of other words. It could be doubted to which part this little phrase "Just as they delivered to us" should be referred: to the preceding, so that the sense is that the certainty of persuasion comes from this, that they had related it; they were not only present themselves as witnesses and spectators of the deeds, but had themselves also performed a part of the deeds; or to the following, so that the sense is that he also wishes to weave together the life of Christ in good faith, the whole of which he had learned fully from the weightiest authors.

<margin>D</margin> 5 <gloss>Who from the beginning saw it themselves</gloss> ] What the translator expressed with a circumlocution, "who saw it themselves," is a single word for the Greeks: <term>αὐτόπται</term> <note>autoptas; eyewitnesses</note>, from the pronoun <term>αὐτὸς</term> (self) and <term>ὄπτω</term> (I see). For an eyewitness is held to be the most certain witness, as they say. By this evidence also one may gather that Luke did not see the things he writes in this book: since he confesses himself to be the writer, borrowing authority and faith from those "eyewitnesses," not from himself. Furthermore, he calls those who were some part of the deeds <term>ὑπηρέτας</term> <note>hypēretas</note>, that is, "ministers." For he who helps in carrying out a matter serves: they were <term>αὐτόπται</term> (eyewitnesses) when they saw him casting out a demon; they were <term>ὑπηρέται</term> (ministers) when they untied Lazarus, when they themselves performed miracles at the Lord's command, and when they were endangered for his sake. Greek men of letters think the word is derived from <term>ὑπὸ</term> (under) and <term>ἐρέσσειν</term> (to row), that is, from rowing under, because the rowers serve the ship's master. Furthermore, since it seemed harsh to the Latins to say "minister of a business" for one who was not just an executor but who had himself played a part and suffered, we preferred to render it thus: "and were some part of those things they were narrating." Thus Virgil’s Aeneas wins faith for himself:
> Which most miserable things I saw,
> And of which I was a great part. ------ <note>Aeneid, Book II</note>

<margin>E</margin> Jerome, in the Preface which he published for all the Gospels, reads it a little differently:
> Just as they delivered to us, who from the beginning themselves saw the word, and ministered to it.
Nor does it matter at all that Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a humanist scholar who preceded Erasmus in critiquing the Vulgate</note> is argued with here, that <term>λόγον</term> <note>logon</note> should have been translated as "Word" rather than "speech," so that it might more conveniently be referred to Christ. Since in this place he calls <term>λόγον</term> the deeds themselves which are narrated. This type of expression is by no means new in the Sacred Books. It is of the same kind as in the Third Book of Kings <note>1 Kings</note>, chapter 15:
> He did not turn aside from all that he had commanded him all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite. <note>original: "excepto sermone Uriæ"</note>
For Uriah is not said to have spoken anything here, but he wished the wicked crime to be understood, which David had committed against him, the rumor of which had now reached many. Nor do I think that what we read in this same Evangelist is dissimilar:
> Let us see this word which has been made to us. <note>Luke 2:15</note>
For they feel that they wish to experience what they had heard the Angels announcing. Nor is it unpolished what Origen and Ambrose philosophize here: how the "word," which is perceived more by hearing than by the eyes, is here said to be [seen]...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on the first chapter of Luke. # THE GOSPEL CHAPTER I.

<margin>1.</margin> 4 ...most excellent Theophilus; That you may know the certainty of the words in which you were instructed. 5 There was in the days of Herod, the king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah; and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. 6 And they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless. 7 And they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in their days. 8 And it came to pass, while he was serving as priest in the order of his division before <meta>God</meta>

---

it seems to be seen, because he says, "Let us see," and here we have **eyewitnesses of the word**. <note>original: "αὐτόπτας τοῦ λόγου" (autoptas tou logou)</note> Nor is the distinction of the "substantial word," as they call it—which was made flesh—from the "word" that reaches the ears by a strike of the air, a false one. <note>Erasmus is distinguishing between Christ as the eternal 'Word' (Logos) and the spoken 'word' of the Gospel.</note> Nor is it untrue that what you have known by understanding and intended in your mind must be demonstrated by deeds. For they twist that phrase, "ministers of the word," toward this. But nonetheless, in this place, such conjectures do not seem very timely. Where an allegory admits no such guesses, I would not mind the reader's mind being called forth by similar little commentaries, lest he stop reading in despair or shrink back offended by the absurdity of the historical sense. In other matters, I would prefer the simplest sense, and the one least distorted, in the Sacred Letters. Now, as for Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a 15th-century humanist scholar whose work Erasmus edited</note> denying that Christ is ever called *Sermo* (Speech/Discourse) in mystical literature, but only *Verbum* (Word), it is easy to refute him, since it is found everywhere—not only in Lactantius, whom he makes the sole exception, but also in Cyprian, Hilary, Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, Prudentius, and more recent writers like Bede, Anselm, and Remigius: as we have sufficiently declared in the apology we wrote on this matter, and as we will touch upon in passing in the Gospel according to John.

6 **Having followed all things**] <note>original: "παρακολουθηκότι" (parakolouthēkoti)</note> "Having followed" is not to be understood here as the Latins use it, by whom one is said to have "followed/attained all things" who was frustrated in nothing—which the Greeks call "to happen upon" <note>original: "τυχεῖν" (tychein)</note>, the opposite of which is "to fail" <note>original: "ἀτυχεῖν" (atychein)</note>. Rather, *parakolouthein* means to accompany, to be present, and to follow after rather than to overtake. For just as one is said to "sit by" a letter who never departs from it, so he is said to "follow along" who, wherever you turn, is present and follows as an inseparable companion. Indeed, there are those who take the opportunity of this word to interpret it as meaning that Luke was present from the beginning for everything he writes. For this, I believe, was the view of whoever wrote the *Commentaries on Luke* under the title of Adamantius <note>A name often associated with Origen</note>. But this interpretation is openly contradicted by what precedes in this very discourse of Luke; no matter how much you twist them, I ask you, was Luke present for everything he narrates? Was he at the conversation of Mary with the Angel? Was he at the spectacle of the transfigured Jesus? However, if anyone weighs Origen's discourse more carefully, they will feel that he does not affirm that Luke was present at all the things he wove into the history, but rather denies that he knew them piecemeal or from rumor—that is, from a doubtful and uncertain author—but knew the whole matter in order from the weightiest and most certain witnesses. I will subscribe his own words: "It seemed good to me also, having followed from the beginning." He impresses and repeats this because he did not know the things he was about to write by rumor, but had himself followed them from the beginning. Whence he is also deservedly praised by the Apostle, saying: "Whose praise is in the Gospel through all the Churches." Thus far Origen. Certainly Luke, traveling through all the Churches, did not see the things Christ did, but knew and learned from the Disciples and Apostles themselves what He had done and taught. And that they were not unreliable authors, their life and miracles declared. Yet I do not mean that "all things" <note>original: "πᾶσιν" (pasin)</note> refers to a person, as if we should understand Luke was present with all the Apostles, but to the matter, so that the sense is that he pursued everything in order, and thus knew everything from those who remembered what they had seen, so that he omitted nothing pertaining to the series of the history. Augustine, in book four, chapter eight of *The Harmony of the Gospels*, reads "having followed all things from the beginning," preserving the Greek construction. Moreover, he wrote not "all things," but "from all things," as Ambrose noted. Furthermore, lest anyone distrust us, Demosthenes used this word in his speech *On the False Embassy*: "So that each of you, knowing his deeds and having followed them all, may accuse him with the greatest indulgence." He means not that he was a spectator and witness to what Aeschines had done, but that he had investigated everything. The same elsewhere: "For you are able to follow those who are speaking." For the thought of a judge follows the order of the one reporting. And in Galen we read "to follow a certain theory," because the contemplation of the mind follows the speech: which those do not do who pay little attention to what is being said. Paul also used this word several times in his Epistles in almost the same sense, as to Timothy in chapter four: "If you put these things before the brothers, you will be a good minister of Jesus Christ, nourished in the words of faith and the good doctrine which you have followed." <note>1 Timothy 4:6</note> That is, if you remind the brothers of these things, you will be a good minister of Jesus Christ, nourished in the words of faith and the good doctrine, which you have followed throughout. For I do not agree with those who think *parakolouthein* is the same as "to reach back" or "to make one's own" for the Greeks. Indeed, we "attain" <note>Latin: "assequumur"</note> things sought after and difficult. We "accompany" and "follow along" <note>original: "παρακολουθῦμεν" (parakolouthoumen)</note> things from which we do not depart. We will say more on this in the passage of Paul we just cited. Now, as for his saying "from the beginning" <note>original: "ἄνωθεν" (anōthen)</note>, it must be understood either as "from the start and in order," so that we understand nothing was omitted, or "anew and from the start," so that what others narrated either piecemeal or with little certain faith, he himself weaves a history anew with full and most certain faith concerning those same matters. For this word *anōthen* among the Greeks declares three things: from above (i.e., from the heavens), from the start (or anew), and from the beginning all the way to the end (or from the top to the bottom).

7 **Most excellent Theophilus**] I wonder where Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a 14th-century biblical exegete</note> got the suspicion that Theophilus was some grandee or prince because Luke

<column-break/>

seemed good to me, having investigated all things accurately from the beginning, to write to you in order, 7 most excellent Theophilus:
<margin>1.</margin> 4 That you may recognize the 10 certainty of those things 8 in which you were instructed. 11 There was in the days of Herod king of Judea a certain priest named Zechariah, 12 of the division of Abijah: and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. 6 And they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and justifications of the Lord 13 blameless. And they had no offspring, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were now of advanced age. 14 And it happened, 15 while he was performing the priestly office... <meta>tur</meta>

---

added the title "most excellent." Is it so that we only call the elites "excellent," or is it peculiar to them to be "excellent"? Truly Lyranus had read that in some gloss, which while he could read it, he could not understand it due to ignorance of the Greek language. For among the Greeks, *kratistos* sounds of strength or power. And *kratein* is to conquer or to be master, whence Paul in the Acts of the Apostles calls the governor "most excellent," <note>Acts 26:25</note> as if you were to say "illustrious and powerful." This is also attested by the Interpreters: Origen, Theophylact, and Ambrose. Although *kratistos* signifies not only the more powerful and superior (to which *kreittōn* corresponds), but also the better and more valuable, for which *kratistos* acts as the superlative. He who translated Origen’s Homilies on Luke noted that *kratistos* signifies "best" or "most powerful." Furthermore, "Theophilus" sounds like "lover of God" or "dear to God"; whether this is a proper name or an epithet for a pious reader, others may dispute. I think it is a man's proper name.

<margin>C</margin> 8 **That you may recognize**] <note>original: "Ἵνα ἐπιγνῷς" (Hina epignōs)</note> Theophylact also notes this, that it was not said "that you may know" (i.e., learn), but "recognize" (*epignōs*). For we "know" things we learn that were previously unknown to us. We "recognize" things we previously knew in some way, just as we recognize a face seen some years before. St. Jerome also points out this elegance of the two words, both elsewhere and in his apologies against Rufinus.

<margin>D</margin> 9 **In which you were instructed**] <note>original: "περὶ ὧν κατηχήθης" (peri hōn katēchēthēs)</note> Formerly, those who were candidates for baptism had the mysteries of the Christian faith handed down to them, but by living voice, without writing, just as was the custom among the early theologians among the Egyptians and the Druids among the Gauls. That was to be initiated into the mysteries, which Paul and Luke call *katēcheisthai*: for *ēchos* is to sound with the voice. Thence *katēchein* means to instruct with the voice, which commits nothing to writing. Whence those who were taught in that manner were called Catechumens (*katēchoumenoi*), and those who taught were called Catechists, whom the Dionysian interpreter calls "sponsors" (*suscéptores*), I believe; they are commonly called "godparents." Lucian used this word in *The Ass*: "He handed me over to a certain freedman among his young men, and he was instructed <note>original: "κατηχήθη"</note> what he should do so that I might especially be able to entertain him." Lucian ridiculously makes a boy the "catechist" of an ass. Although in the Acts of the Apostles Luke used *katēcheisthai* for "having found out" or "been informed," not acting on the mysteries of the faith, but regarding a warned prefect. Truly the Church has so made this word its own that they call them "Catechumens" even if they do not understand what a Catechumen is. The sense here, therefore, in my judgment at least, is that those things which you once learned as a catechumen by the living voice, you may now know more fully and certainly by writing. For he opposes these to each other as if they were contrasting: "to write" (*graphein*) and "to be orally instructed" (*katēcheisthai*). Although, as I said, in Acts he used this word once or twice for "it was heard," simply.

<margin>E</margin> 10 **Instructed the truth**] In Greek it is not "the truth" (*tēn alētheian*), but "certainty/security" (*asphaleian*). For truth and faith were consistent even in those things he had learned in the catechism. But *asphalés* is said of what is certain and safe, and in which there is no danger of slipping or error. For the Greek word is derived from "to stumble" (*sphallesthai*) and a privative particle. For we know more certainly those things which we have known by writing and in order, especially if we have heard the same things before from others, or even the same things from the same people. Inasmuch as the very constancy of the narrative claims trust for the matters.

<margin>F</margin> 11 **It was in the days**] <note>original: "Ἐγένετο" (Egeneto)</note> "There was" rather.
12 **Of the division of Abijah**] <note>original: "ἐξ ἐφημερίας" (ex ephēmerias)</note> The Greek word is more evident, indicating that certain days were prescribed in which certain orders of priests would minister. Nor is it "the wife to him" in the dative case, but "his" (*autou*), and thus it is also read in emended Latin codices. Though it matters nothing to the sense.
13 **Without query**] <note>Luke 1:6; Vulgate: "sine querela"</note> In Greek it is a single word, "blameless" (*amemptoi*), which sounds as if you would say "of such a kind that no one can complain about them." He could have said "unblamed" or "irreproachable." For Valla's change to "innocent" or "guiltless" is not as approved by me. For it seems to be a greater praise to be "blameless" than "innocent." For it is a very great thing to so temper one's character and whole life that you satisfy even the judgment of men, so that you please even the wicked as far as it lies in you. Furthermore, where he translates "they had proceeded," etc. (*probebēkotes*), we more usefully say "of advanced age."
14 **It happened however**] This form of speech is frequent in Luke, as if you were to say, "it was done that Peter visited me," instead of "it happened that he visited me."
15 **When Zechariah performed the priestly office**] In Greek, instead of "Zechariah" it is "he" (*auton*), which nonetheless matters nothing to the sense. Nor is it added in the golden codex, nor in the Donatian ones, nor in the Constance one. The pronoun could be rendered elsewhere as "when he performed the priestly office." And in "the order of the division," it is again *ephēmerias*. Furthermore, where it follows "according to the custom of the priesthood," it is not "of the priesthood" (*hierōsynēs*) in Greek, but "of the priestly service" (*hierateias*), a name from that word which he just now better translated as "performing the priestly office." He could, therefore, also have translated here "according to the priestly custom."

# ACCORDING TO LUKE. CHAPTER I.

->221<- ->222<-

9 According to the custom of the priesthood, it fell to him by lot to burn incense, having entered the temple of the Lord. 10 And the whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense. 11 And there appeared to him an Angel of the Lord, standing at the right side of the altar of incense. 12 And Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him. 13 But the Angel said to him, "Do not be afraid, Zechariah; for your prayer has been heard; and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. 14 And you will have joy and gladness, 15 and many will rejoice at his birth. For he will be great in the sight of the Lord, and he shall drink neither wine nor strong drink; and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb. 16 And he will turn many of the sons of Israel to the Lord their God. 17 And he will go before Him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous, to prepare for the Lord a people made ready." 18 And Zechariah said to the Angel, "By what shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days." 19 And the Angel answering said to him, "I am Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God; and I was sent to speak to you, and to bring you these glad tidings. 20 And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day these things happen, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their season." 21 And the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they wondered that he lingered in the temple. 22 But when he came out, he could not speak to them; and they perceived that he had seen a vision in the temple; for he kept making signs to them and remained mute. 23 And it happened, when the days of his service were completed, he departed to his own house. 24 Now after those days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and she hid herself for five months, saying, 25 "Thus the Lord has dealt with me in the days when He looked upon me, to take away my reproach among men."

<meta>Catchword: an-</meta>

---

16 **The lot went out** <note>original: "Sorte exiit"</note>] In the Greek it is *elache* <note>original: "ἔλαχε"</note>, that is, "he obtained by lot." The previous translators, if I am not mistaken, wishing to make the phrase clearer, turned it into "the lot went out," because when lots are cast into an urn, the lot for this or that person <margin>D</margin> is said to "go out." Someone corrupted this into **it happened by chance** <note>original: "forte exiit"</note>, therefore we have corrected it to **it fell to him by lot**. Otherwise, Zechariah entered; he did not "go out." Ambrose suggests this: *He was chosen by lot,* he says, *so that the Priest might enter the temple.* The speech sounds as if a drawing of lots was made among the priests to see who would enter to offer the incense. Yet some, including Bede, think his priesthood itself had previously fallen to him by lot; whether that is true, I leave for others to judge. For it is possible that among several high-ranking priests, the lot chose the one to enter during the actual service.

17 **To place the incense** <note>original: "Ut incensum poneret"</note>] *tou thumiasai* <note>original: "τοῦ θυμιᾶσαι"</note>, that is, to burn incense, or to set fragrant spices on fire. For the word **incense** <note>original: "incensum"</note> is not approved by Laurentius <note>Laurentius Valla, a humanist scholar whom Erasmus greatly admired</note> because that word does not correspond in all respects to this matter; the Latins call it **fumigation** <note>original: "suffitum"</note>. Although soon after he also translates "the hour of incense" <note>original: "horam incensi"</note>, and a little later, "at the right of the altar of incense."

18 **But there appeared** <note>original: "Apparuit autem"</note>] It is not *ōphthē* <note>original: "ὤφθη"</note>, but *ōphthē*, that is, "he was seen," or "he was beheld." For things that do not exist can also "appear"; though I do not blame the Translator for how he rendered it. Augustine, in his 112th Letter, following Ambrose, philosophizes about this word **appeared**, which is not entirely relevant to the matter.

19 **Many will rejoice at his birth** <note>original: "Multi in nativitate ejus gaudebunt"</note>] *epi tē gennēsei autou* <note>original: "ἐπὶ τῇ γεννήσει αὐτοῦ"</note>, that is, "concerning his birth," or "over his birth."

20 **Wine and strong drink** <note>original: "Vinum & siceram"</note>] **Sicera** <term>sicera: a fermented drink other than wine</term> should be written with an *s*, not a *c*. For it is not named after *cicer* (the chickpea), but is a Hebrew word written with the letter *sin*, from the verb *shakar* <note>original: "שכר"</note>, which means to be intoxicated. Hence, among them, every artificial drink that can intoxicate is called *sicera*. Furthermore, Diodorus Siculus in the first book of his History testifies that the Egyptians used artificial wine, which they called *zythum* in their own language—or as it is found in some places, corrupted I believe, as *citum*. This is what the Gauls used to call *cervisia* (beer) and the Spaniards *caelia*, according to Pliny. Dioscorides also mentions it in his second book, teaching that it is made mostly from barley, but also from wheat, which the Western nations of Ireland and Britain are accustomed to use. However, he strongly disapproves of this kind of drink, as it is harmful in many ways.

21 **Even from the womb** <note>original: "Adhuc ex utero"</note>] *eti ek koilias* <note>original: "ἔτι ἐκ κοιλίας"</note>. He translated the words faithfully enough. However, it would have been expressed more purely and in better Latin as: **right from his mother’s womb**; for in this way we signify a beginning traced far back. <margin>F</margin>

22 **And in the power of Elijah** <note>original: "Et virtute Heliae"</note>] *en dunamei* <note>original: "ἐν δυνάμει"</note>. You should understand this as the power of miracles, not just moral uprightness, as we have noted in some books; although it is not stated in writing that John performed miracles, he nevertheless possessed a strength of faith that went even to the contempt of life. This agrees with the prophecy of Malachi, who predicted Elijah would come before the great day of the Lord, as we indicated in Matthew. But neither Luke, nor the Angel whose words he reports, cites Malachi's testimony word-for-word. For we read this according to the Hebrew truth, as translated by Jerome: **And he shall turn the heart to the fathers, to the children.**

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...was serving in the order of his shift before God, according to the custom of the priestly function, 10 **it fell to him by lot**, 17 **to burn the fragrances**, having entered the temple of the Lord. And the whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the time of the incense. 11 **But there was seen by him** an Angel of the Lord, standing at the right of the altar on which fragrances are usually burned. 12 And Zechariah was troubled at the sight, and fear rushed upon him. But the 13 Angel said to him, "Do not fear, Zechariah: because your prayer has been heard: and your wife Elizabeth shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name John: And there shall be joy 14 to you and exultation, 15 and many **over his birth** shall rejoice. For he shall be great before the Lord, <margin>B</margin> 16 and wine and **strong drink** he shall not drink: and he shall be filled with the Holy Spirit 21 **right from his mother's womb**: And many 16 of the sons of Israel he shall turn to the Lord their God. And he shall go before him with the spirit 22 and 17 **power of Elijah**, that he may turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, 23 and the **disobedient** to the wisdom of the righteous, 25 to **prepare** for the Lord 26 **a people made ready**. And Zechariah said to the Angel, "By what proof shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is of advanced age." And the Angel answering said to him, "I am Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you, and to announce these happy things to you. And behold, it shall happen that you will be silent, nor can you speak until that day in which these things happen, because you did not believe my words, <margin>C</margin> which will be fulfilled in their time. And the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they wondered 27 **that he lingered** in the temple. But when he came out he could not speak to them: and they knew that he had seen a vision in the temple: and he was making signs to them, 28 **and remained mute**. And it happened, when the 29 **days of his service** were completed, 23 he went to his house. After these days 24 Elizabeth his wife conceived, and she hid herself for five months, saying, 30 **Thus** the Lord has done for me in the days 25 in which 31 **he looked upon me**, to take away my shame among...
<meta>Catchword: men</meta>

---

...and the heart of the children to their fathers. In place of this, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> read: *who shall restore the heart of the father to the son, and the heart of a man to his neighbor.* <margin>E</margin>

23 **And the incredulous** <note>original: "Et incredulis"</note>] "Incredulous" in Greek is *apeitheis* <note>original: "ἀπειθεῖς"</note>, which he sometimes translates as **disobedient**; here perhaps it fit better, since mention was made of fathers and children. For **unbelievable** <note>original: "incredibiles"</note> instead of **unbelieving** <note>original: "incredulos"</note>—which Valla seems to have read—I have never found written anywhere, except in two old copies, and finally in the one from Constance.

24 **To the wisdom of the righteous** <note>original: "Ad prudentiam justorum"</note>] I do not know if Luke misused the preposition *en* <note>original: "ἐν"</note> instead of *eis* <note>original: "εἰς"</note>, as he did in chapter 28: *when he comes in his kingdom*. Certainly, it is **in the wisdom of the righteous**. And yet the other reading is smoother. Otherwise, the sense could be: he will lead them, not by force, but by the wisdom of the righteous; for the righteous do not take revenge, but persuade through sobriety.

25 **To prepare for the Lord** <note>original: "Parare Domino"</note>] Laurentius rightly rebukes the Translator because, either being drowsy or affecting variety, he turned one infinitive into a finite mood and left the other as it was: **that he may turn the hearts of the fathers** and **to prepare for the Lord**; when with the same effort he could have said, **that he may turn and prepare**. Yet he does this so frequently that he seems to have done it on purpose. If that is true, I wonder why he affected what should have been avoided. Likewise in the Psalms: *he lies in wait that he may catch the poor man, to catch the poor man while he draws him in.* When in both places it is *harpasai* <note>original: "ἁρπάσαι"</note>. And a little later, **To perform mercy** with our fathers, and **to remember** his testament, when in Greek it is *poiēsai* <note>original: "ποιῆσαι"</note> and *mnēsthēnai* <note>original: "μνησθῆναι"</note>. And again, **to shine upon** those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, **to guide** our feet, when it is *epiphanai* <note>original: "ἐπιφᾶναι"</note> and *kateuthunai* <note>original: "κατευθῦναι"</note>, both words being infinitives.

26 **A people made ready** <note>original: "Plebem perfectam"</note>] *kateskeuasmenon* <note>original: "κατεσκευασμένον"</note>. This sounds more like **instructed** and **adorned** or **prepared**. For in this John was the precursor: that by his baptism, preaching, and testimony about Christ, he might make the minds of the Jews teachable for Gospel philosophy, which Theophylact explains diligently. Our Translator seems to have read *katērtismenon* <note>original: "κατηρτισμένον"</note>.

27 **That he lingered in the temple** <note>original: "Quod tardaret ipse in templo"</note>] *en tō chronizein auton* <note>original: "ἐν τῷ χρονίζειν αὐτὸν"</note>. The word **himself** <note>original: "ipse"</note> should not have been rendered here if he wanted to speak in good Latin; however, he has elsewhere dared to omit it more than once in a similar type of speech.

28 **And he remained mute** <note>original: "Et permansit mutus"</note>] It is a wonder why "mute" offends Laurentius, as if *kōphos* <note>original: "κωφὸς"</note> only signifies "deaf." Where then does that proverb come from, *Kōphon prosōpon* <note>original: "Κωφὸν πρόσωπον"</note>, that is, **A mute person**? He who collected the etymologies of Greek words, citing authors, teaches that *kōphos* is said by the Greeks not only of one who is deaf, but also of one who is mute, whom they call *alalon* <note>original: "ἄλαλον"</note>; and there is no difference, except that *alalos* is said of one who cannot speak due to age, like infants, while *kōphos* is one who has no voice at all.

29 **Days of his service** <note>original: "Dies officii"</note>] *leitourgias* <note>original: "λειτουργίας"</note>, that is, **ministry**, which is usually understood as sacred ministry.

30 **Because he did thus** <note>original: "Quia sic fecit"</note>] The conjunction *hoti* <note>original: "Ὅτι"</note> should have been omitted by one translating into Latin, although he has ventured it elsewhere.

31 **And he looked to take away** <note>original: "Et respexit auferre" </note>] *epeiden aphelein* <note>original: "ἐπεῖδεν ἀφελεῖν"</note>: that is, he looked...

# GOSPEL CHAPTER I.

26 among men. And in the sixth month the Angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee, named 27 Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David, and the name 28 of the virgin was Mary. And the Angel having entered into her presence, said: "Greetings, favored one, the Lord is with you; blessed are 29 you among women." But she, having seen him, was troubled at his word, and considered what kind of greeting this might be. 30 And the Angel said to her, "Do not fear, Mary; for you have found 31 favor with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear 32 a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give him 33 the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of 34 his kingdom there will be no end." But Mary said to the Angel, "How will this be, since I do not know a man?" 35 And answering, the Angel said to her, "The Holy Spirit 

---

...hear me, do not take away, etc. That is, "He has taken away my wretchedness and my reproach."

32 ***Betrothed to a man***] I find both "betrothed" and "promised" used among reputable authors. In Greek it is <term>μεμνηστευμένην</term> <note>original: memnēsteumenēn</note>, which properly means to deliver a bride to a suitor. For already, as it appears, the girl was living with her betrothed, even if sexual union had not occurred.

33 ***To a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David***] Chrysostom, in his second Homily on Matthew, indicates that this place should read "of the house and family," <term>ἐξ οἴκου καὶ πατριᾶς</term> <note>original: ex oikou kai patrias</note>. He takes this as if the designation "house" is broader, while "family" pertains to a smaller group. However, we do not read it this way in Ambrose, nor in the most ancient manuscripts. Truly, the name "family" is added in the next chapter: *And Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David.* Our manuscripts agree here with the Greek. Therefore, it is possible that Chrysostom’s memory slipped, especially since he cites this passage differently than it is found in Luke; for he added it in this manner: *Hear Gabriel speaking to the Lord: Go to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name is Joseph, from the family and house of David.* Although Chrysostom could establish the same point from the other passage that he wished to establish from this one. For he does not contend here that "of the house and family of David" refers to the virgin, but to Joseph; nevertheless, it is gathered from this that Mary was of the same tribe. But if "house and family" was dealt with in both places, it is a wonder why Chrysostom did not cite both. Certainly, Theophylact makes no mention of "family" in this place.

34 ***And the name of the virgin was Mary***] <term>Μαριάμ</term> <note>original: Mariam</note> with the Hebrew sound and accent. Although we have shown that this is not observed perpetually—whether that happens through the negligence of scribes, or because it makes no difference.

35 ***Hail, full of grace***] <term>Χαῖρε κεχαριτωμένη</term> <note>original: Chaire kecharitōmenē</note>. The same word <term>χαίρειν</term> <note>original: chairein</note> among the Greeks signifies three things: *to rejoice, to be well, and to be strong.* Thus, it mattered nothing whether "hail" or "greetings" was used. Nor is it "full of grace," but rather, if I may translate it word-for-word, "favored" or "made dear." Paul uses the verb from which this participle is derived in the first chapter of the Epistle to the Ephesians: *He has favored us in his beloved Son,* <term>ἐχαρίτωσεν</term> <note>original: echaritōsen</note>, that is, he made us pleasing and dear. Although Homer used the participle, which has the same power, for someone uniquely beloved: "favored in my soul," that is, dear to my heart. For one can be "dear" who has commended himself to us by his services. But one is not called <term>κεχαριτωμένος</term> <note>original: kecharitōmenos</note> except for one whom we embrace with a certain gratuitous favor of the mind. Furthermore, "grace" is what Latins call those who are favored with a certain inclined zeal of the mind. It is a word like one announcing someone’s love toward the virgin, because it sounds like something flattering. Whence the troubled virgin thought about what kind of greeting this was. Origen also noted that this form of speaking appears nowhere else in the Sacred Books, neither addressed to any man nor any woman. Therefore, the novelty itself increased the virgin's amazement. This is supported by the fact that in Greek it is not "to you," but simply "favored one," so that you may understand it as a remarkable and wonderful greeting. For the solemn greeting of the Jews wished for peace. Moreover, it was most fitting that she should be greeted with a word of joy who was to conceive the Author of true pleasure; and addressed with the word "grace" who was to give birth to Jesus, the end of cold ceremonies and the chief Author of saving grace. I see certain Theologians, men otherwise learned and pious, among whom is Bernard, who have philosophized marvelously on these words, "full of grace," as if this uniquely applies to Mary, to be called full of grace; even though Luke did not say "full of grace" in this place, and that phrasing is found attributed to many people indiscriminately in the secret scriptures. Indeed, we read of John the Baptist: *And he shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb.* Again, of Elizabeth: *She was filled with the Holy Spirit.* And soon: *Zechariah is read as being filled with the Holy Spirit.* And in the Acts of the Apostles, those who had gathered are read as being filled with the Holy Spirit. And Stephen is said to be full of the Holy Spirit, and full of grace and power. These things should not seem negligible to anyone. For just as it is elegant to philosophize aptly on the secret scriptures in these kinds of small details, so it is foul to trifle outside the matter. Therefore, lest anyone trip over the same stone, we speak for the sake of truth.

36 ***Blessed are you***] <term>εὐλογημένη</term> <note>original: eulogēmenē</note>, which sounds like "praised" or "of excellent fame," of whom everyone speaks well. Although "blessed" and "cursed" are not found in place of "praised" and "unpraised" among Latin authors, nevertheless, whether we like it or not, we must wink at certain things of this sort, which are too well-received to be changed without an uproar. And, "in women," <term>ἐν γυναιξὶν</term> <note>original: en gynaixin</note>, that is, "among women": which he himself a little later translated in that manner, and so Saint Ambrose reads it. Although I am not unaware that "in" is sometimes used for "among" in Latin authors as well.

In the sixth month the Angel Gabriel was sent by God into a city of Galilee, named 27 Nazareth, to a virgin 27 betrothed to a 33 man, whose name was Joseph, of the house of David, 34 and the name of the virgin was Mary. But Mary said to the Angel, "How will this be, since 42 I do not know a man?" 34 And answering, the Angel said to her, "The 35 Spirit

---

37 ***When she had heard***] The Greeks have it differently, <term>Ἡ δὲ ἰδοῦσα</term> <note>original: Hē de idousa</note>, that is, "But she, when she had seen." Valla attests that it was written thus in some ancient manuscripts. In the Constance manuscript, some eraser had made "heard" out of "seen." And lest anyone chatter in protest, Saint Ambrose reads it this way. Although in his work, she is not troubled by the speech, but by the entrance. For he reads it in this manner: *but she, as she saw him, was moved at his entrance.* And lest anyone protest that the writing was changed by chance, he adds an interpretation of what he read: *It is the nature of virgins to tremble, and to be afraid at every entrance of a man, and to dread all addresses of a man.* Unless perhaps Ambrose changed a little of his own here.
<margin>C</margin> Nevertheless, he says things consistent with this in the first book of *On Duties*, chapter eighteen: *that being greeted by the Angel she is silent and moved at his entrance, because the sight of a virgin is troubled by the appearance of the male sex.* Now also in the *Catena Aurea* (Golden Chain), the words of some Greek author are cited, from which it is clear that he too read "when she had seen," not "when she had heard." They go like this: *Since she was accustomed to these visions, the Evangelist attributed the trouble not to the vision, but to the reports, saying, "She was troubled in his speech," etc.* And a little later, *and she thought what kind of greeting this was, not what kind of conception: for she was still ignorant of the immensity of the mystery, but the greeting, whether it was lustful, as from a man to a virgin, or divine, while he made mention of God, saying, "The Lord is with you."* These are the words of that Greek. When I had noted in three words that the Angel's greeting bore something of love and suitors about it, and because of that Mary was initially troubled, immortal God! what tragedies someone stirred up here, and renewed them from the start, 
<margin>D</margin> though Saint Thomas Aquinas cited these things in his *Catena*, by no means intending to cite them if they were blasphemous and impious. I had said "something amatory" and "something of suitors," intending both, but here he interpreted it as more or less a range of lust. Yet Theophylact agrees with these views so closely that his own words could seem to be cited in the *Catena*; I will write his words below: <term>Διελογίζετο δὲ περὶ τοῦ ἀσπασμοῦ, ποταπὸς εἴη οὗτος, μὴ ἄρα ἀπατηλός τις καὶ πορνικὸς, ὡς ἐξ ἀνδρὸς πρὸς κόρην, ἢ θεῖος, ἐπειδὴ καὶ Θεοῦ μνήμην ποιεῖται τῷ ἀσπασμῷ, τὸ ὁ Κύριος μετὰ σοῦ.</term> <note>original Greek: "She pondered the salutation, what kind it might be, whether perhaps it were some deceitful and whorish thing, as from a man to a girl, or divine, since mention of God is made in the greeting, 'the Lord is with you.'"</note> That is, *She thought about the greeting, what kind it might be, whether it was some absurd and wanton thing, as if coming from a man to a girl, or divine, since the mention of God is mixed into the greeting.* In this which you say, "The Lord is with you." These are the words of Theophylact. I mentioned "suitors" only, and the word for "suitor" <note>Latin: procus</note> is no less honorable than "betrothed," and I said "amatory," which is not an obscene word—for a betrothed man writes "amatory" letters to his betrothed—and they cry out that the matter is full of blasphemy: yet here he mentions "lust" and "whorishness." What is blinder than the judgment of these men? Now I do not weigh the quality of what that earlier Greek said, that the virgin was not troubled by the sight but by the speech because she was accustomed to the vision of Angels: for first, it is not established whether the virgin was so accustomed that she would not be troubled at the first sight; and if she recognized the Angel, why did she fear the speech, or why does she doubt whether the greeting is lustful or from God? It is enough for me that he read, "when she had seen." Otherwise, it was frivolous to note that the virgin was troubled by the speech and not by the sight, unless mention had been made of the sight and the vision at the same time. Therefore, I judge it pious to believe that the modest virgin was initially troubled both by the sight of the young man and by the flattering and novel form of greeting. Furthermore, regarding what Laurentius Valla hints at in this place—something rather subtle, saying, "I do not wish to dispute now why it is better 'When she had seen' than 'When she had heard,' lest I seem to doubt the faith of the Scripture"—to speak frankly, I do not sufficiently understand what he means. For I myself think the Evangelist spoke thus to show that the virgin was troubled on a double account: first, because she saw a young man entering to her, and then because she heard a greeting that was new and unusually flattering. And the more chaste the virgin was, the more she feared for her modesty—lest anyone cry out that it is unworthy to attribute this fear to the virgin, which Ambrose praised in her.

38 ***What kind of***] Again here is, as I said, <term>ποταπὸς</term> <note>original: potapos</note>, which Laurentius in Mark wanted to translate as "how great." And it was more apt.

39 ***You have found***] Or "you have obtained" grace, rather than "you found," that is, it happened to you to be favored by God. For among the Greeks <term>εὑρεῖν</term> <note>original: heurein, to find</note> has many meanings. Whence those who philosophize here—that nothing is "found" except what was lost—discuss the matter more cleverly than appositely.

40 ***And the Son of the Highest***] <term>Ὑψίστου</term> <note>original: Hypsistou</note>, which someone reads as "of the supreme." The same word which elsewhere he translates as "in the highest," <term>ἐν ὑψίστοις</term> <note>original: en hypsistois</note>.

41 ***David his father***] In better Latin it would be "his own father," and it is read thus in some manuscripts. And for "forever" it is <term>εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας</term> <note>original: eis tous aiōnas</note>, that is, "into the ages." For as to "how will this be," that is, *how will it be, come to pass, happen*, the Translator did not err.

42 ***I do not know a man***] Since here the Latin agrees with the Greek

# ACCORDING TO LUKE. CHAPTER I.

->225<- ->226<-

...the Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore also that holy thing which shall be born shall be called the Son of God. 
36 And behold, your kinswoman Elizabeth, she also has conceived a son in her old age; and this is the sixth month for her 
37 who was called barren; for with God no word <note>original: ῥῆμα (rhēma)</note> shall be impossible. 
38 And Mary said, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word." And the 
39 angel departed from her. And Mary, rising up in those days, went into the hill country with haste, into a city of 
40 Judah, and entered into the house of Zacharias, and greeted 
41 Elizabeth. And it happened, when Elizabeth heard the greeting of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb; and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit, 
42 and she cried out with a loud voice, and said, "Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of 
43 your womb. And why is this granted to me, that the mother of my 
44 Lord should come to me? For behold, as the voice of your greeting reached my ears, the babe leaped for joy 
45 in my womb. And blessed is she who believed, for there shall be a fulfillment of those things which were spoken to her from the Lord." And 
47 Mary said, "My soul magnifies the Lord. And my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior, 
48 for he has looked upon the lowly estate <note>original: ταπείνωσιν (tapeinōsin)</note> of his handmaid; for behold...

<margin>43</margin> In ancient copies, it is strange that Ambrose alone reads *I have known* <note>original: cognovi</note> instead of *I know* <note>original: non cognosco</note>, unless perhaps this was introduced by a scribal error, where *novi* was turned into *cognovi*. Indeed, the present tense of the verb better explains the Virgin’s intent.

<margin>43</margin> **Which shall be born of you** <note>original: Quod nascetur ex te</note>] The Greek is <term>τὸ γεννώμενον</term> (to gennōmenon), that is, *that which shall have been born*. Furthermore, I have not found those two words, *of you* <note>original: ex te</note>, added in any Greek copies, not even in Theophylact, nor in the ancient Latin codices, except for one, in which someone or other had added it in the margin. Therefore, I wonder how they slipped into the first edition of this work. The speech is more complete if they are not added. For the subject here is not the person conceiving, but the new manner of conceiving and the excellence of the offspring. It appears to have been added by some commentator; although I found it added in the Aldine edition.

<margin>44</margin> **Because it will not be impossible**] The Greek uses the compound verb <term>ἀδυνατήσει</term> (adynatēsei). The sense is that nothing is promised by God so new or great that He Himself cannot perform it. And here he clearly used "word" <note>original: verbum</note> for "matter" or "sentence," <term>ῥῆμα</term> (rhēma). And a little later, *Let it be to me according to your word*, <term>ῥῆμά σου</term> (rhēma sou). Unless perhaps one may use *rhēma* in its native sense, by which we call a "speech" a <term>ῥῆσιν</term> (rhēsin).

<margin>45</margin> **Into the hill country**] In Greek <term>εἰς ὀρεινήν</term> (eis oreinēn), that is, into the mountainous area, so that you understand "region." The same word appears a little lower: *And fear came upon all the hill country of Judea*, <term>ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ ὀρεινῇ</term>. However, the Translator has rendered the sense correctly; let no one think he is being rebuked by me.

<margin>46</margin> **The greeting of Mary**] Here he certainly pronounced "Mary" with a Greek inflection, not according to the Hebrew custom.

<margin>47</margin> **Leaped**] The Greek is <term>ἐσκίρτησε</term> (eskirtēse), he jumped or bounded; it is the same a little later, *leaped in joy*. It is not "with joy" <note>original: χαρᾷ</note>, but "in exultation" <note>original: ἀγαλλιάσει</note>, which suggests the physical gesture of one rejoicing rather than the joy itself. Hence in the Psalms, he translates <term>ἀγαλλιάσεσθε</term> as "let us exult." Since "in" was placed for "through," we translated it "for joy."

<margin>48</margin> **And blessed are you who believed**] Since in Greek it is a participle, <term>ἡ πιστεύσασα</term> (hē pisteusasas), it could also refer to the person joined to God, as the Translator did. It would be *even more convenient* if the word "to her" <note>original: αὐτῇ</note> that follows had the aspiration <term>αὑτῇ</term>, so that it would mean *for herself*. Nor am I unaware, nor do I fail to testify elsewhere, that this difference is not observed in the Sacred Books, for what reason is uncertain. We therefore translated it in the third person, not because we condemn what the Translator rendered, but because this speech seems to have something prophetic about it. Certainly, either person renders the same sense. And in some old copies it is found written, *Blessed is she who believed*, as in my copy of old typography and similarly in the Constance copy.

<margin>49</margin> **Which were told to you by the Lord**] In Greek <term>παρὰ Κυρίῳ</term> (para Kyriō). This sounds not as if the Lord spoke them directly, but as if they were spoken to her in the name of the Lord and in His words, as we say, "Give him greetings from me." It can also be ordered thus: *they shall be perfected by the Lord*.

<margin>50</margin> **And Mary said**] In the written Homilies on Luke, which we read under the title of Origen, it is indicated that in some codices it was written "she prophesied" instead of "she said." And this canticle tastes of something prophetic. For Origen calls it a prophecy.

<margin>51</margin> **My soul magnifies**] The Greek is <term>μεγαλύνει</term> (megalynei). "Does magnify" was more appropriate than "magnifies." Although "magnifies" is used for "extols and brings forth with praise," just as we say "to beatify" for "to proclaim as blessed."

<margin>52</margin> **In my Savior**] In Greek <term>ἐπὶ σωτῆρί μου</term> (epi sōtēri mou), that is, *in my Savior*, or, as the Latins prefer to say, *in my Preserver*. The Translator seems to have read <term>σωτηρίᾳ</term> (sōtēria, "salvation").

<margin>53</margin> **The humility of his handmaid**] The Greek is <term>ταπείνωσιν</term> (tapeinōsin). You should understand this as "smallness" or "lowly estate," not the virtue of the mind, which the Greeks call by its own name <term>ταπεινοφροσύνην</term> (tapeinophrosynēn, "humility of mind"). Nor is it "he respected her humility," but "he looked toward her lowly estate," <term>ἐπέβλεψεν ἐπὶ τὴν ταπείνωσιν</term>, so that it is the opposite of "to turn away from." The sense is: "Even though I am the lowest handmaid, yet he has not turned away from me." Let whoever wishes laugh at these grammatical annotations, provided they admit that theologians stumble in these matters three or four times over. It would be tolerable if they merely stumbled, if they did not join the impudence of slandering to their fall. For indeed, while they were adorning this Edition, which...

<margin>A</margin> ...the Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you: wherefore also that holy thing which shall be born shall be called the Son of God. And the Angel departed from her. 39 And Mary rising up in these days, went into the hill country with haste into a city of Judah, and entered into the house of Zacharias, and greeted Elizabeth. And it happened, as Elizabeth heard the 41 greeting of Mary, 41 the infant leaped in her womb: and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit, <margin>B</margin> and she cried out with a loud voice, and said, "Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. And why is this granted to me, that the mother of my 43 Lord should come to me? For behold, as the voice of your greeting reached my ears, the infant leaped for joy 45 in my womb. 45 And blessed is she who believed, because those things 46 which were told to her from the Lord shall be perfected." 50 And 46 Mary said, 51 "My soul magnifies the Lord. And 47 my spirit has rejoiced in God 52 my Savior, because 48 he has looked 53 toward the lowly estate of his handmaid: for behold..."
<margin>54 from</margin>

<margin>C</margin> ...which we are producing, a certain Parisian Theologian <note>Likely referring to Noël Béda, a frequent critic of Erasmus.</note>, who considers himself the chief Atlas of the tottering Church, proves from this passage that Mary deserved to become the mother of God by the virtue of humility. He accused me of "Lutheranism" because, in explaining the Angel's speech "you have found grace" and "highly favored" <note>original: κεχαριτωμένη (kecharitōmenē)</note>, I wrote that it was not of my merit, but of divine favor. Certainly, insofar as it was of grace, it was not of merit. Otherwise, I have not denied that there were merits. But what I found written in the Gospel, I interpreted as a Paraphrast; what I did not find, I had no need to invent. But if we grant that *tapeinōsin* <note>lowly estate</note> is taken for the virtue, which is called *tapeinophrosynē* in Greek and *modestia* in Latin; if we grant it to be true that Mary deserved such great happiness by her modesty of mind; how does it fit that Mary, who began by professing herself a handmaid to magnify the Lord, should soon extol herself, saying that by her own virtue she deserved such dignity as for a virgin to give birth to God? Therefore, it could not be proven from this passage that the Virgin deserved what she received by the virtue of modesty. If she deserved it, where is the grace that the Angel proclaims? If she deserved it by her own <margin>D</margin> virtue, how does it hold together: *For behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed*? For no one is called "blessed" <note>meaning "fortunate" or "happy"</note> because of things they prepared for themselves by their own virtue. Furthermore, how does it fit: *because he has done great things for me*? She did not say, "he has rewarded me magnificently." Nor does she add, "because he is Just," but "because he is powerful" and "merciful." For it follows, *and his mercy is from generation to generation*. These points are not intended to detract from the merit of the most holy Virgin, but to argue that these things, which the "Atlantic" Theologian brought against my interpretation, are more contrary to the opinion he tries to defend. Now, I am well aware that there are those who, on the occasion of this word "humility," preach much about modesty, especially the one who wrote the Homilies on Luke under the name of Origen, which is not at all suspected. But I will not allow myself to be pressed by the authority of this author, whom no one knows, unless someone approves all things contained in those homilies. For there are very many things there that are condemned by Theologians. If they allow themselves to disagree with this work in many points, it is fair that they grant me pardon if in one place I prefer to follow the opinion of others which seems to me <margin>E</margin> more probable. Lest I pursue all the opinions of everyone, I will bring forward at least one, Theophylact, whose words are cited in the *Catena* of Thomas [Aquinas], but in a truncated way. This is what he wrote in Greek: *The Virgin, having been most perfectly informed, glorifies God, ascribing the gift to Him as the one who is sufficient. She was saying, he says: "My soul magnifies the Lord, because I looked up before seeing. For she hoped that I myself stretched out. And from now on all generations shall call me blessed, as the mother spoke, but also the generations of those who believed. But why blessedness? Is it then because of my virtue? No; but because the Powerful one has done great things with me. And she called Him powerful, so that you might learn not to lack faith in the things being said, realizing that the Lord is able to do these things. And she said His name is holy, showing that the most pure one is not defiled even when being conceived in the womb of a woman, but remains holy. Moreover, His mercy is not upon me alone, but upon all who fear Him."* Which we will not be burdened to translate for those ignorant of the Greek tongue: *The Virgin*, <margin>F</margin> he says, *being more fully taught, glorifies God, ascribing the miracle to Him as the sufficient one. For He, she says, looked toward me, a lowly one; I did not look up at Him. He had mercy on me; I did not seek Him. And from this time all generations shall call me blessed, not only Elizabeth, but all generations of believers. But for what reason shall they call me blessed? Is it because of my virtue? Not at all: but because He who is powerful has done magnificent things with me. For she called Him powerful, lest anyone lack faith in those things that are told, indeed considering that the Lord can do these things. Furthermore, she said His name is holy, declaring that He, being most pure, is not polluted even when conceived in a woman's womb, but remains holy. However, His mercy is not on me alone, but on all who fear Him.* These many things agreeing among themselves sufficiently declare that Mary is not proclaiming her own modesty, by which she deserved to become the mother of God, but is extolling the grace and mercy of God toward herself and toward all. How much better it would be for the theological task if those who profess absolute theology would kindly receive from linguists and grammarians what they contribute to the common good, each according to their portion; and if they, in turn, acknowledged those more sublime mysteries...

<summary>This page contains Erasmus's commentary on the Annunciation and the Magnificat, where he argues that Mary's "humility" refers to her social lowliness and God's grace, rather than a personal merit that earned her the role of Mother of God. He defends this using philological analysis and citations from church fathers like Theophylact to counter his contemporary critics.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s annotations and his revised Latin translation of the first chapter of the Gospel of Luke. It covers the Magnificat (the Song of Mary) and the birth and naming of John the Baptist. Of particular historical note is Erasmus’s aggressive defense in Note 66 against monks who accused him of heresy regarding the Latin word for "seed."</meta>

# THE GOSPEL

->227<-

...for behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed.
<margin>A</margin> 49 For he who is powerful has done great things for me, and holy is his name. 50 And his mercy is from generation to generation to those who fear him. 51 He has shown strength with his arm; 52 he has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts. 53 He has put down the mighty from their thrones, and exalted the lowly. He has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty. 54 He has helped Israel his servant, in remembrance of his mercy 55 (even as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham, and to his seed) forever. 56 And Mary remained with her about three months, and returned to her own house. 57 Now for Elizabeth, the time was fulfilled that she should give birth, and she bore a son. 58 And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had magnified his mercy toward her, and they rejoiced with her. 59 And it happened, on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child, and they were calling him by the name of his father, Zacharias. 60 And his mother answering said, "No; but he shall be called John." 61 And they said to her, "There is no one in your family who is called by this name." 62 And they made signs to his father, what he would want him to be called. 63 And asking for a writing tablet, he wrote, saying, "John is his name." And they all wondered.

<margin>A</margin> ...they might communicate, with all the more modesty as they have more deeply entered into the inner sanctums of that philosophy, which un-teaches all falsehood and haughtiness, and teaches the greatest tolerance toward the weak. <note>This marginal note appears to be a philosophical reflection on the character of the Apostles or early Christians.</note>

***

54 **From this [now]** ] <term>ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν</term> <note>original: apo tou nyn</note>, that is, "hereafter," or literally, "from this now," a phrase the Translator <note>Erasmus refers to the author of the Vulgate as "the Translator."</note> does not hesitate to translate this way elsewhere. Yet the Translator does not speak poor Latin here, provided that Suetonius wrote Latin in his life of *Claudius Caesar*: "And from then [ex eo] he never failed to give his opinion last among the Consulars in the Senate."

55 **Will call me blessed** ] <term>μακαριοῦσί με</term> <note>original: makariousi me</note>, that is, "they will beatify," which among the Greeks means to judge someone happy, just as it can mean to extol with praises. It is like the word <term>εὐδαιμονίζειν</term> <note>original: eudaimonizein</note>, meaning to call someone fortunate or judge them happy.

56 **Great things he who is powerful** ] <term>μεγαλεῖα</term> <note>original: megaleia</note>, which elsewhere he translates as "wonders" <note>original: magnalia</note>. And "he who is powerful," <term>ὁ δυνατός</term> <note>original: ho dynatos</note>, that is, the Powerful One, or he who is able.

57 **And holy is his name** ] Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (672–735 AD), an English monk and scholar.</note> refers this small part to the preceding phrase "he who is powerful," explaining what the Greek word <term>ἅγιος</term> <note>original: hagios</note> sounds like, as if it were <term>ἄγειος</term> <note>original: ageios</note>, meaning "far from the earth," so that you may understand divine power. Others think the Greeks derive "holy" [<term>ἅγιον</term>] from <term>ἄζομαι</term> <note>original: hazomai</note>, which means to revere religiously, as if you were saying "venerable." To me, it seems it should rather be referred to the things above it, and to "his mercy." For he called "holy" that which is "glorious." For the name of God is glorified when nothing is attributed to our merits, but everything is granted to his mercy.

<margin>D</margin> 58 **From progeny to progeny** ] <term>εἰς γενεὰν καὶ γενεάν</term> <note>original: eis genean kai genean</note>, that is, "into generation and generation." Lorenzo Valla <note>An Italian humanist who critiqued the Vulgate before Erasmus.</note> read in his copies, "into generations of generations," meaning innumerable ages. And certainly whoever was the author of the *Homilies on Luke*—which we read under the title of Origen, specifically the eighth homily—read it that way. I myself found it written thus in only one copy. This shows that the scripture was varied even in our own manuscripts. In two of the very oldest, it was written "unto progenies and progenies," which means the same as saying "unto countless progenies," in the Hebrew manner.

59 **He showed strength** ] <term>κράτος</term> <note>original: kratos</note>, "might" or "dominion." For the word indicates both. And "with his arm" is said in the Hebrew manner for "that which is through his arm."

60 **Of their heart** ] <term>καρδίας αὐτῶν</term> <note>original: kardias autōn</note>. The Greek voice indicates that "their" should not be referred to God, but to the proud. Nor is it strictly "in the mind," but <term>διανοίᾳ</term> <note>original: dianoia</note>, "in the thought," so that you understand the proud are scattered by their own very counsels.

61 **He put down the powerful** ] <term>Καθεῖλεν δυνάστας</term> <note>original: Katheilen dynastas</note>, that is, "He dragged down the leaders," or "magistrates." For a <term>δυνάστης</term> <note>original: dynastēs</note> is properly one who performs public power in a city, like those who are in command. Nor is it "from the seat" [singular], but <term>ἀπὸ θρόνων</term> <note>original: apo thronōn</note>, that is, "from their thrones" [plural].

62 **He sent away** ] This is not "he permitted" here, but "he sent out from himself," <term>ἐξαπέστειλε</term> <note>original: exapesteile</note>, as if they were frustrated. Furthermore, the Translator would have more conveniently translated the Greek participles as verbs: "those who were hungry he filled with good things, and those who were rich he sent away empty."

63 **He took up Israel** ] <term>ἀντελάβετο</term> <note>original: antelabeto</note>. This properly refers to someone bringing help and stretching out a hand.

64 **To be mindful** ] <term>μνησθῆναι</term> <note>original: mnēsthēnai</note>, that is, "so that he might be mindful." First, the Translator misused the mood of the verb. Second, I do not know if "to be mentioned" <note>original: memorari</note> is ever read for "to remember" <note>original: recordari</note>. Yet the church choir today sings, "Remembering his mercy." Nor is "his" added among the Greeks, but it is only "of mercy," even though all the Latin copies I have seen protest against this.

65 **As he spoke** ] <term>ἐλάλησεν</term> <note>original: elalēsen</note>. Since the verb is in the past tense, but indefinite <note>the Aorist tense</note>, it would have been more correctly translated here as "as he had spoken." For it has the significance of a double past tense.

66 **Abraham, and to his seed** ] Even though "Abraham" is indeclinable in Latin, the Greek article placed next to it indicates it is in the dative case, <term>τῷ Ἀβραάμ</term> <note>original: tō Abraam</note>, that is, "to Abraham himself," so that he speaks clearly rather than strictly in Latin. Certainly, "Abrahamo" was both Latin and free of ambiguity. Furthermore, what Lorenzo Valla disputes—that one should say "among our fathers" rather than "to our fathers"—is a dream. Did God speak "among" the fathers of the Jews in the same way we speak "before" a judge or
