# CHAPTER I.

<margin>A</margin> ...from now 55 all generations will call me blessed: Because 56 he who is powerful has done magnificent things for me, 57 and holy is his name. And his mercy is 58 from progeny to progeny to those who fear him. 59 He provided strength through his arm: he scattered the proud in the thought 60 of their own heart. 61 He dragged the powerful from their thrones, 62 and lifted up the humble. The hungry he filled with good things, and the rich 62 he sent away empty. 63 He took up Israel his servant, 64 so that he might be mindful of mercy 65 (As he had spoken to our fathers, namely 66 to Abraham, and to his seed) 67 forever. 68 And Mary remained with her about three months, and returned to her own house. But for Elizabeth, the time of giving birth was fulfilled, and she bore a son. And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had magnificently used his mercy toward her, <margin>B</margin> 69 and they congratulated her. And it happened, on the eighth day 70 they came to circumcise the boy, and they were calling him by the name of his father, Zacharias. And his mother answering said, "By no means: but he shall be called John." And they said to her, 71 "There is no one in your family who is called by that name." And they made signs to his father, 72 what he wanted him to be called. 73 And he, having requested tablets, 74 wrote, saying, "John is his name." And they all wondered.

<margin>A</margin> a prince? Even if in some places <term>πρὸς</term> <note>original: pros</note> sounds like "with" or "at," as in "the Word was with God," it is not necessary to demand the same thing everywhere. On the contrary, just as in Latin we say, "I write to you" [scribo tibi] and "I write toward you" [scribo ad te], so do the Greeks. Therefore, since it was permitted to say it either way, Luke varied the figure of speech. Mary senses that God has now provided to the human race what he once promised to our ancestors. To which ancestors? Surely to Abraham, to whom God spoke: "And in your seed shall all the nations be blessed." Then to the "seed," that is, to his descendants, namely David, to whom it was promised: "From the fruit of your body I will set upon your throne." 

And certain monks had most impudently slandered me regarding this passage before the Cardinal of Sion <note>Matthäus Schiner (c. 1465–1522), a powerful Swiss cardinal and diplomat.</note>. They had persuaded him that I had changed "seed" [semini] to "seeds" [seminibus], and they wanted this to smack of heresy because it would conflict with the words of Paul, who wrote: "Not in seeds," as if many, but in one "seed," which is Jesus Christ. That man [the Cardinal] warned me seriously about this matter when we were passing the time with literary stories after lunch; he was concerned for my safety out of his devotion to me. I have never heard anything more impudent than this slander. I would not have believed it of anyone, had I not found six hundred similar instances of their behavior. By such things, they achieve nothing except that they are regarded not as Theologians, but as buffoons among the wise; they are not even believed when they tell the truth. First, it was an impudent lie that I had changed it, for I had not. Second, even if the Greeks did read "seeds" [plural], they would do nothing against the words of Paul cited above. For while Paul is dealing there with Christ, through whom alone Gospel salvation was promised to us, here Mary is not speaking of Christ, but of Abraham and the descendants of Abraham, to whom the Savior Jesus was promised. Although this was not part of my original plan, I wanted to point this out in passing so that posterity may know what beasts [belluas] this age has had: men who, while they serve their own bellies, disrupt the industry of others with such foolish sycophancy. These men, through a false reputation for learning and a deceptive appearance of holiness—things they acquire for themselves among the simple and ignorant with titles and tragic garb—are held to be the bases and columns of the Catholic Church, when they are truly its abscesses [vomicae] rather than its members.

***

67 **forever** ] <term>εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα</term> <note>original: eis ton aiōna</note>, that is, "into the age." Although in a certain copy I read <term>τοὺς αἰῶνας</term> <note>original: tous aiōnas</note>, that is, "even unto the ages."

68 **As if for [three] months** ] <term>ὡσεὶ</term> <note>original: hōsei</note>, that is, "almost," or "about," or "more or less."

<margin>E</margin> 69 **And they congratulated** ] <term>συνέχαιρον</term> <note>original: synechairon</note>, that is, to render it literally, "they rejoiced with," which the Latins usually call "to congratulate." Although one can "rejoice with" someone without "congratulating" them, since the former is of the soul, while the latter is a vocal testimony of joy.

70 **They came to circumcise** ] There are those who think this also pertains to Mary—that she was present at the circumcision of John—and they excuse with a trope the fact that she was said earlier to have returned to her own house. Truly, I do not see how these things pertain to the matter, no more, by Hercules, than the way Jean Gerson <note>A famous French scholar and chancellor of the University of Paris (1363–1429).</note> twists himself over how many years old Joseph was when he married Mary, and at what time the wedding celebration took place. Gerson thinks it happened after he discovered his wife was pregnant; for he twists the phrase "before they came together" as if "coming together" here meant something other than "having sexual intercourse." Likewise the phrase, "do not fear to take Mary as your wife," contrary to the interpretation of all the Ancients, and whether the Angel who appeared to Mary was the same as the one who appeared to Joseph.

<margin>F</margin> 71 **Because no one is** ] <term>ὅτι</term> <note>original: hoti</note> should have been completely omitted here, since Latin speech rejects this kind of phrasing <note>In Greek, *hoti* often introduces direct speech like a quotation mark, which Erasmus finds clunky if translated literally into Latin.</note>.

72 **What he would want him to be called** ] <term>τί ἂν θέλοι καλεῖσθαι</term> <note>original: ti an theloi kaleisthai</note>, that is, "what he would want him to be called," meaning by what name.

73 **And requesting a writing tablet** ] How did he write on the tablets if he was only just "requesting" that they be brought? Therefore, the Greek past participle should have been translated as "and the tablet having been requested" [postulata tabella]. For it refers to a wax tablet, which he calls a <term>πινακίδιον</term> <note>original: pinakidion</note>, as these were used for writing in the past.

74 **He wrote, saying** ] If he "said" it, what need was there to write? Thus "saying" in this place must refer not to Zacharias speaking, but to the writing "speaking." Or, to speak more clearly, to Zacharias...

<margin>73</margin> **73** *Who do you think*] <note>original: Τίς ἄρα</note>, that is, *Who then*. For the word <note>original: ἄρα</note> is a completing conjunction. Most manuscripts had <note>original: Τί ἄρα</note>, that is, *What then*. For the word *Child in Greek* is of the neuter gender, <note>original: παιδίον</note>. This is certainly what Augustine reads in the second book of *The Harmony of the Gospels*.

<margin>76</margin> **76** *Of his people*] <note>original: τῷ λαῷ αὐτοῦ</note>, that is, to his people, which agrees with the ancient Latin manuscripts, in which it is *to his folk* <note>original: plebi suae</note>. Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo Valla, a humanist critic</note>, who is most observant of Latinity, prefers *people* <note>original: populo</note> rather than *folk* <note>original: plebi</note>, because "people" encompasses all ranks of a city, while "folk" refers to the lowest part.

<margin>77</margin> **77** *Of his prophets*] In Latin it should have been said "Of their own" <note>original: suorum</note>, and "who were from the beginning" rather than simply "who were."

<margin>78</margin> **78** *Salvation from enemies*] <note>original: σωτηρίαν</note>. This sounds more like *preservation* or *safety*. For a *Savior* <note>original: Σωτὴρ</note> is a preserver or protector, hence *salvation*. Although the same word was used above, *He raised a horn of salvation*, and shortly after, *To give knowledge of salvation to his people*. Furthermore, the following verses depend on what preceded: *As he spoke*. What did he speak? He spoke of *salvation from enemies*, that he would show mercy, and be mindful of the covenant; he spoke that he would fulfill the oath: and he spoke that he would grant to us that we, without fear, etc. Therefore, we have explained these things more freely in our translation, so that no one may find fault if something seems discordant at first glance.

<margin>79</margin> **79** *To perform... to remember*] In Greek, both are infinitives, <note>original: ποιῆσαι, μνησθῆναι</note>, that is, so that he might do and might be mindful.

<margin>80</margin> **80** *That he would give*] <note>original: δοῦναι ἡμῖν</note>, that is, to give to us. Although the Greek words mean something slightly different than how we take them: <note>original: τῷ δοῦναι ἡμῖν ἀφόβως ἐκ χειρὸς τῶν ἐχθρῶν ἡμῶν ῥυσθέντας λατρεύειν αὐτῷ</note>, that is, "to grant to us, being delivered without fear from the hands of our enemies, to serve him."

<margin>81</margin> **81** *To prepare his ways*] <note>original: ἑτοιμάσαι</note>, that is, for the purpose of preparing.

<margin>82</margin> **82** *To give knowledge of salvation*] Although he just used the infinitive <note>original: ἑτοιμάσαι</note>, he now turns to the gerund <note>original: τοῦ δοῦναι</note>, *for giving*. And these things can also be properly referred to the child, whom he addresses: *For you shall go before the face of the Lord, to prepare his ways*, and *you shall give knowledge of salvation to his people for the remission of sins*. For John's preaching caused them to understand that salvation was near, which would happen in the remission—that is, through the remission—of sins. For in Greek it is not "into remission" but "in remission" <note>original: ἐν ἀφέσει</note>. Not that John himself remitted sins, but that by his baptism he prepared them for repentance. Otherwise, that the remission of sins was not from John is clearly proven by what follows immediately: *through the tender mercy*. Certainly, Theophylact and Ambrose and others interpret this as referring to John regarding the first part.

<margin>83</margin> **83** *in the remission of sins*] This is how it is read in Greek and in the ancient Latin manuscripts. However, since it makes no difference to the sense, we prefer *his* or *its* to avoid awkward phrasing.

<margin>84</margin> **84** *in which*] This is said instead of *through which* tender mercy. *Rising sun* <note>original: Oriens</note> is not a participle here, but a substantive noun, <note>original: ἀνατολή</note>. This word signifies the rising of the sun, or the region from which it rises. Therefore, he calls Christ himself the rising Sun. This was diligently noted by Theophylact. Add to this *from on high* <note>original: ἐξ ὕψους</note>, that is, from altitude or loftiness, to distinguish him from the physical sun, which

---

appears to us rising from below and moving upward; this Sun, by contrast, having arisen from on high, descends to us to give us light.

<margin>85</margin> **85** *to enlighten*] <note>original: ἐπιφᾶναι</note>, that is, to illustrate, or to shine upon, or to arise. Although I prefer it to be an infinitive of the verb, which nevertheless had to be translated in another mood: *the Rising Sun from on high has visited us, so that he might shine upon those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death*, or upon us who were sitting, and *might direct our feet*. Otherwise, the person would have to be changed, since up to this point the third person has been used in reference to John. Theophylact agrees with us and reads it conjunctively.

<margin>86</margin> **86** *And was strengthened*] <note>original: ἐκραταιοῦτο</note>, that is, he became robust and powerful, not only in body like the common people, but in spirit. For age gradually adds strength and power to the body, which he here transfers to the soul. Nor is it simply *he grew*, but <note>original: ηὔξανε</note>, which is a term specifically used for plants and living things. Furthermore, it would have been more appropriately said here that *he came of age*.

<margin>87</margin> **87** *He was shown to Israel*] <note>original: ἕως ἡμέρας ἀναδείξεως αὐτοῦ πρὸς τὸν Ἰσραήλ</note>. The sense of these words is: until he should be brought forth and shown again among the people of Israel, as if he were [newly revealed]. For in the meantime he remained hidden, destined to come forth at his proper time.

<margin>1</margin> **1** The Translator changed this. We have translated it as *decree* <note>original: decretum</note>, not correcting what he translated, but explaining it.

<margin>2</margin> **2** *Cyrenius*] <note>original: Κυρηνίῳ</note>, that is, Cyrenius. Although there are those who think this word was corrupted by the Evangelist—as the Greeks often pronounce Latin names, saying <note>original: Κυρηνίον</note> for *Quirinus*—especially since Josephus in the eighteenth book of *Jewish Antiquities* calls this man appointed to conduct the census "Cyrenius," not "Quirinius." While I do not intend to strongly oppose this opinion, I would more willingly accept it if the Evangelist had not replaced *s* with *r*, and then turned *s* into *n*. Furthermore, if Rufinus had translated it, he would have said *Quirinus*, not *Cyrenius*. And it is not "by the governor," but <note>original: ἡγεμονεύοντος</note>, that is, while he was acting as governor, or while he was governor. Furthermore, *first* can refer to the governor Cyrenius, so that you do not take it simply as "the first registration," but the first *under him as judge*.

<margin>3</margin> **3** *To be registered*] <note>original: ἀπογράφεσθαι</note>. The same word that he has translated as "to be described" until now. However, the same thing, when it concerns military matters, is called *giving one's name*; when it concerns the valuation of resources and counting heads, it is called a *census*. For as Ulpian says, *When new declarations are issued, the flaws of previous censuses vanish*. Therefore, the Magistrate *conducts the census* <note>original: censet</note>, and the people *declare themselves* <note>original: profitetur</note>. And it would have been more Latin to translate "should be taxed" <note>original: censeretur</note> above than "should be described." And "declaration" <note>original: professio</note> is more correct than "description." Ambrose also declares in this passage that a *declaration* is nothing other than a *census*. This "declaration," he says, is of faith; it is a *census* of souls. Furthermore, regarding what he said, *the whole world*, Ambrose prefers to take this allegorically, since Augustus at that time ruled neither the Armenians nor the Goths. But so that the history may also retain its credibility, "the whole world" must be understood either by synecdoche <note>a part representing the whole</note>, meaning the greatest part of the world, or the whole Roman world. For from this passage some conclude that the empire of the whole world belongs to the Emperor, though Luke does not intend this, nor did Augustus himself hold empire over the entire world. While I would not disapprove if one person possessed empire over the whole world—provided that as he predominated in authority, he likewise excelled in both wisdom and integrity—I think it most foolish to dream of something that never was, and which, even in the form it did exist, has long since vanished from human life. Indeed, such a dream is most cruel.

...to pursue such artificial titles amidst such a great tumult of all things and such a great loss of blood. Finally, it is by no means suitable for human affairs to commit such great power to the whim of a single man, who might turn out to be the worst and even the most foolish of men. Nor do I see where this will end, except that tyranny will grow for the miserable common people.

<margin>4</margin> *Into his own city* <note>Latin: "In suam civitatem"</note>] Here one could translate, *in his own city*, that is, *each in his own city*, unless you refer it to the verb *they went*.

<margin>5</margin> *Into the city of Judea*] The Greek reads: <note>original: "εἰς τὴν Ἰουδαίαν, εἰς πόλιν Δαυΐδ"</note>—into Judea, into the city of David. The preposition "in" is missing before "city" <note>Erasmus is noting a grammatical omission in the Latin Vulgate compared to the Greek</note>. For he first placed the name of the region, then the city.

<margin>6</margin> *And lineage*] The Greek is <note>original: "καὶ πατριᾶς"</note>. This is the same word that in the Pauline Epistles is translated as *paternity*: "From whom all paternity in heaven and on earth is named," but we will note something about this matter in the next chapter.

<margin>7</margin> *With his pregnant wife*] The translator <note>the Vulgate</note> renders it such that Joseph seems to have married Mary while she was already pregnant before the marriage was initiated, whereas the Greek is <note>original: "οὔσῃ ἐγκύῳ"</note>; that is, *who was pregnant*, or *who was carrying a womb*. The order of the sentence has some ambiguity, as it could be arranged this way: *Joseph went up with his pregnant wife*, or *he went up to be registered with his pregnant wife*. However, Peter Comestor <note>a 12th-century theologian</note> noted this before us, lest we deprive anyone of their due credit.

<margin>8</margin> *Firstborn*] In Greek, <note>original: "πρωτότοκον"</note>. Even among the Pagans, a firstborn is one before whom no one was born, even if no one follows. He added the name of the firstborn because that birth was holy according to the Law, and because first births are more difficult than others.

<margin>9</margin> *And wrapped him in swaddling cloths*] The Greek is <note>original: "ἐσπαργάνωσεν"</note>. Literally, it means *he swaddled him*, that is, wrapped him in bands, lest anyone imagine torn rags. For I believe Mary's poverty was clean. Furthermore, what Suidas <note>a Greek lexicographer</note> says—that the word properly means "rags"—it is not necessary to understand as old, torn rags, since in Matthew a "new cloth" <note>original: "ῥάκος ἄγραφος"</note> is called a raw and fresh cloth.

<margin>10</margin> *There was no room for them*] "Them" in Greek is <note>original: "αὐτοῖς"</note>, so that you understand it refers to both of them. Moreover, it is fitting that there was no room in the inn, though I suppose the manger was part of the inn: except that elsewhere the word *inn* <note>original: "κατάλυμα"</note> is translated as *guest chamber* or *upper room*. It was not a suitable place for one giving birth, who requires solitude.

<margin>11</margin> *Vigilant* <note>or "staying in the fields"</note>] The Greek is <note>original: "ἀγραυλοῦντες"</note>, that is, living in the fields, or stabling. For this Greek word is composed of "field" <note>original: "ἀγρὸς"</note> and "stable" <note>original: "αὐλὴ"</note>. Flocks are kept in folds at night because of the attack of wolves, but those folds are in the fields.

<margin>12</margin> *And keeping watch*] The Greek <note>original: "φυλάσσοντες φυλακὰς"</note> literally means *guarding guards*, or keeping vigils.

<margin>13</margin> *Stood by them*] The Greek <note>original: "ἐπέστη αὐτοῖς"</note> signifies more that the Angel hovered from above them than stood next to them. We are content to leave this as the Translator rendered it, because the Greek preposition is ambiguous. It could be that the one who first announced it stood by them.

<margin>14</margin> *And brightness*] The Greek <note>original: "καὶ δόξα"</note> means *glory*, which is sometimes translated as *majesty*.

<margin>15</margin> *Wrapped in swaddling cloths*] This is a participle of the verb mentioned before, meaning wrapped in infant bands, lest we again imagine the rags of beggars. For while we gladly attribute thinness and poverty to the parents of Jesus, we keep filth and beggary far away. Poverty has its own cleanliness. It was not poverty that prevented Mary from giving birth in a room, but the crowd of travelers. Otherwise, if beggary had pleased Christ so much, as some think, he could have been born in a poorhouse <note>original: "ptochodochio"</note>. Now, under the name of "Mendicants" <note>a jab at the Mendicant orders of monks</note>, even those who possess the wealth of Lords at home sell themselves as such. I do not attack the institution of those who truly live by begging, but I think they would do better if those who are able—and many are—would work with their hands to provide for themselves and other needy people.

<margin>16</margin> *To men of good will*] The Greek says: <note>original: "καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς εἰρήνη, ἐν ἀνθρώποις εὐδοκία"</note>, that is: *and on earth peace, in men good will*. You should understand these three things as distributed: glory is given to the one God *in the highest*; peace to the earth; and to men, "good will" <note>original: "εὐδοκίαν"</note>, which elsewhere is translated as *good pleasure*. Indeed, he places men as a third group between heaven and earth. Nor should it be understood, I think, as if men themselves had

And suddenly there was with the Angel a multitude <margin>13</margin> of the heavenly host, praising God, and saying, "Glory in the highest to God, and on earth peace, in <margin>14</margin> men..."

---

...good will, but so that they may understand this glory and this peace were not exhibited to the world because of human merits, but solely from the *good pleasure* of God, to whom it seemed fit to favor men. And indeed Chrysostom interprets it this way in his commentaries on the Epistle to the Colossians. Furthermore, since this is consistently held in all Greek copies, and both Chrysostom and <margin>C</margin> Theophylact explain it in this manner, it is a wonder that this reading is found nowhere—not in Jerome, nor in Ambrose, nor in Augustine. It is easy for anyone to look at Theophylact, who clearly reads <note>original: "ἐν ἀνθρώποις εὐδοκία"</note>, distinguishing this part from the one above, interpreting *eudokia* in men as the rest and satisfaction of God in men, which he had not found in them before. Thus it is clear that *good will* does not pertain to men, as if they were those who had good will, but to God, who became favorable to men through his Son. I will provide his words, because the one who recently translated them seems to have rendered the meaning obscurely: <note>Greek quote omitted in this translation for brevity; it argues that human nature was previously at enmity with God, but now God is reconciled and "rests" or finds pleasure in humanity</note>. <margin>D</margin> This certainly works for us here, in that he refers *good will* not to men, but to God, and refers peace to God's good will toward us—that is, a tranquil mind, if I may put it that way, with his anger set aside and being lovingly disposed toward us. Wherever that conjunction "and" crept in here, it stands in the way of the sense; it is not in the Latin manuscripts, nor in the more correct Greek ones. Furthermore, Chrysostom <margin>E</margin> uses these words in the Epistle to the Colossians: <note>Greek quote: "Therefore giving thanks we say, Glory to God in the highest... Behold, he says, even men are shown to be favored. Finally, what is 'good will'? reconciliation."</note> From these things it is clear that he both distinguishes the phrase as the Greek manuscripts do and interprets it as we have suggested. For the fact that we are reconciled to God did not happen from our merits, but from his free benevolence toward us. Moreover, in the books we have translated from Chrysostom, this reading is found, specifically in the *Homilies on the Life of Monks*. In some Greek manuscripts, I find the preposition "in" is not added, <margin>F</margin> so it is *to men good will*, though the case remains the same. Now, from the words of Origen, which are cited in the *Golden Chain* <note>a medieval commentary</note>, it can be gathered that he agrees with us: "But the diligent reader should inquire how the Savior says, 'I did not come to send peace on earth,' yet now the Angels sing of his birth, 'on earth peace to men,' but the fact that it is said to be 'peace in men of good will' solves the question. For the peace which the Lord does not give on earth is not the peace of good will." Here it is evident that *good will* is not referred to men, but to the peace; furthermore, the conjunction "and" is not added, and the preposition "in" is added, which is not added in the common Latin manuscripts. For the manuscript which the College of Constance recently showed us had the preposition added by an ancient hand. The Greek word *eudokia* almost compels us to this view. For if he had said "good thinking" <note>original: "ἀγαθὴ δόκησις"</note>, it could fit a man, but now it does not.

# 233 ACCORDING TO LUKE. CH. II. 234

you might aptly say "good will" <term>eudokia</term> <note>original Greek: ευδοκια</note> of man toward God. For this reason, I think the Ancients, who knew Greek, felt the same as what they translated. I see that I have caught what deceived others who were less attentive. Here, he calls "peace" reconciliation. Thus Christ is called "our peace" by Paul, that is, reconciliation; and He himself prays for His own "peace," that is, the remission of sins. Furthermore, this nominative case "good will" <term>eudokia</term> is related to "peace" by apposition <note>A grammatical structure where two nouns are placed side-by-side to define one another.</note>, as if the Angels, responding to one who asks, "What is this peace you announce?" answer: "It is not from your merits, but this peace is the godly affection of God toward men." For the speech should be arranged thus: "Peace on earth, which is the good will of God in men," that is, toward men. For this form of speech agrees with that phrase, "in whom I am well pleased" <term>en hō eudokēsa</term> <note>original Greek: εν ω ευδοκησα</note>. For just as it is said, "in whom I am well pleased," in place of saying "toward whom I have a good affection," so here it is said, "good pleasure in men," for "good affection toward men." Paul spoke similarly in 1 Corinthians 10: "But with most of them God was not well pleased" <note>original Greek: αλλ’ ουκ εν τοις πλειοσιν αυτων ευδοκησεν ο Θεος</note>, that is, God’s good pleasure was not in many of them. And in many other places in Scripture, "good will" <term>eudokia</term> is used to express the free and gratuitous benevolence of God, as in Chapter 10 of this Evangelist: "Even so, Father, for so it was your good pleasure before you" <note>original Greek: Ναι ο Πατερ, οτι ουτως εγενετο ευδοκια εμπροσθεν σου</note>. Furthermore, the Latin Translator turned the appositive nominative into a genitive <note>The possessive case: "of good will."</note>, just as we say "the city of Rome" instead of "the city Rome." Since, however, the genitive seems to refer to what is closest, namely to "men," the Latins were often given the opportunity to slip, whereas it actually refers back to "peace." Therefore, three particles—or rather two—pertain to the same thing. The Angels announce that the time has come in which God has determined, out of His free mercy, to save the human race: at which admirable goodness the Angels are struck with awe, and they sing glory to God in the highest, where there was no sin and therefore no need for reconciliation, but they announce peace to the earth, that is, the abolition of sins, which is given freely through faith: and for this reason, he calls this peace "good will" <term>eudokia</term>, that is, the friendly and benevolent affection of God toward men. Thus, there will be no difficulty if we read and punctuate in this manner: "Glory to God in the highest," and here, a period being placed, let it follow, "and on earth peace." Again, with a comma <note>original Latin: hypostigme</note> inserted, let there be added, "in men good will." Yet for the sense, it matters little if the genitive "of good will" is referred to men, provided we understand men to be called "of good will" just as they are called "children of grace," "children of charity," "children of election," and "children of wrath"—those whom God deigns to favor with His grace and charity, or whom He has chosen, or upon whom He exercises His wrath. Thus, let men be called "of good will" toward whom God bears good will, who has saved us not according to our righteousness, but according to His mercy. This sentiment agrees with the words of Blessed Paul in several places, specifically 2 Timothy 1: "not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace." What is called "good will" <term>eudokia</term> here, is there called "purpose and grace" <term>prothesin kai charin</term> <note>original Greek: προθεσιν και χαριν</note>. By this reasoning, this particle, "in men of good will," restricts the one that immediately preceded it, "peace on earth." Lest anyone think that peace pertained to every kind of living creature dwelling on earth, he added "in men." Again, lest we think that peace was to be given to all men indiscriminately, he added "of good will," so that we understand only the elect are designated, whom God, by His free will, deigns to grant Evangelical grace. Otherwise, a man’s good will is a gift of grace. I believe this will be enough for the candid reader. For I think I have caught what is true. The Song of the Angels, which is sung in churches today, was expanded by Telesphorus <note>A 2nd-century Pope traditionally credited with adding the "Gloria" to the Mass.</note>. I have mentioned this partly because Peter Comestor <note>A 12th-century theologian known for his "Ecclesiastical History."</note> indicates it is in the *Lives of the Popes*: and partly so you might understand in what ways the Mass has grown, by shortening those things that were principal and adding things that pertained less to the matter. For the things Telesphorus added—if indeed this is true—have more words than substance, and would that those human things he wove into the divine ones at least fit the theme of the Song better. This example has spread widely. In many churches, water is publicly consecrated, and a responsory is sung for the entrance of the Mass. The Psalm, which used to be sung in its entirety, has been shortened. Before the Gospel, "Proses" <note>Metrical hymns or sequences.</note> are sometimes sung by the unlearned, and the Creed is put forward. Before the Canon of the Mass, an expanded Preface is sung; during the consecration, the *Sanctus* is sung; when the mysteries are shown, a song is sung imploring the help of the Blessed Virgin, or St. Roch, and the Lord’s Prayer is suppressed. These things are not impious, but they depart from the gravity of the ancient worship, and if no one resists, they tend toward superstition.

---

17 <term>The shepherds spoke</term>] In most Greek codices it was written thus: <term>kai hoi anthrōpoi hoi poimenes eipon</term> <note>original Greek: και οι ανθρωποι οι ποιμενες ειπον</note>, that is, "And those men, the shepherds, were saying," so that the men are contrasted with the Angels. The Spanish Edition agreed here. Now, that phrase "to one another" instead of "among themselves" occurs too frequently for me to need to warn about it.
18 <term>Let us go across</term>] The Greek word <term>dē</term> <note>original Greek: δη</note> is an expletive conjunction, <term>dielthōmen dē</term> <note>original Greek: διελθωμεν δη</note>, which sometimes carries an urgent sense, so that here it has the emphasis of those hurrying and eager to depart.
19 <term>This word which has happened</term>] I do not object if anyone wishes to philosophize here about the "word being made," provided he knows that according to the property of Hebrew speech, a "word" <note>referring to the Hebrew concept of 'Davar'</note> can mean a new thing or event that is spread by rumor: and anyone who cares to observe will find it so. Augustine also noted this before us in his book on the idioms of the Old Testament, citing a passage from Joshua chapter 8: "Why have you done this word to us, that you did not call us?" However, the word here is not <term>logos</term> <note>original Greek: λογος</note>, by which the Son of God is sometimes designated, but <term>rēma</term> <note>original Greek: ρημα</note>. Nor is it "because the Lord [revealed]" but "for he made known" <term>dia to egnōrisen</term> <note>original Greek: δια το εγνωρισεν</note>, that is, he notified, or made manifest, or indicated and opened. For who else is said to have shown the word?
21 <term>And they found Mary</term>] One conjunction is missing, "and they found both Mary and Joseph" <note>original Greek: και ευρον την τε Μαριαμ και τον Ιωσηφ</note>. Although in this place the first conjunction was almost idle for the Latins, it is sometimes added by the Greeks in such a way that it seems to serve the elegance of the speech more than emphasis, a kind of speaking in which we see Ennius <note>An early Roman poet.</note> delighted.
22 <term>And they knew of the word</term>] That is <term>diegnōrisan</term> <note>original Greek: διεγνωρισαν</note>, that is, "when they had seen, they made it known" or "divulged it": so that you understand they preached what they had seen to others who had not seen it. For it is a compound verb from "to make known" <term>gnōrizō</term> <note>original Greek: γνωριζω</note>, which he just translated as "he showed to us." Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator.</note> supports this interpretation, explaining it in this sense: It would thus be the duty of spiritual shepherds to seek the heavenly bread, which when they have seen, they ought to preach it to others, just as the shepherds, who saw the infant, spoke of him to others. Lest I hide anything, however, the Greek word <term>diegnōrisan</term> is ambiguous, meaning either "to know" (or rather "to know thoroughly") or "to bring to the knowledge of others." Thus, "they knew thoroughly" fits well, because perfect knowledge comes from the eyes more than from the ears. That the shepherds divulged what they had seen can be gathered from what follows: "And all who heard, wondered."
23 <term>But Mary</term>] <term>Hē de Mariam</term> <note>original Greek: Η δε Μαριαμ</note>. It would have been more expressive if it had been "Mary herself," because of the added article, by which she is more distinguished from the others who were talking about these things while she remained silent.
24 <term>In all things</term>] <term>epi pasi</term> <note>original Greek: επι πασι</note>, that is, "upon all things" or "concerning all things."
25 <term>Just as it was said to them</term>] This clause should be referred only to the nearest verb, "and they had seen." For they had heard, and they saw what they had heard.
26 <term>Days of his purification</term>] One codex had "his" <term>autou</term> <note>original Greek: αυτου</note>, so that you refer the purification to Christ. The Spanish Edition had "her" <term>autēs</term> <note>original Greek: αυτης</note>, so it refers to Mary. A third had "their" <term>autōn</term> <note>original Greek: αυτων</note>, referring to both. And indeed Origen <note>A 3rd-century Alexandrian theologian.</note> (or whoever it was) reads and explains it thus in the fourteenth Homily, writing in this manner: "If it were written 'because of her purification,' that is, Mary’s, who had given birth, no question would arise, and we would boldly say that Mary, who was human, needed purification after birth. But now, in that it says 'the days of their purification,' it seems to signify not one, but another, or several." Again, in the eighteenth Homily, he refers to the offering made for the cleansing of Christ, not feeling that Christ was unclean, but that he was purified by the same rite as others who are usually subject to filth. Let no one here philosophize in vain about the purification of Mary. For he calls those ceremonies "purification" by which formerly both the woman in childbirth and the fetus were cleansed. Moreover, the word "purification" is used in the same sense by Suetonius <note>Roman historian.</note> in *Octavius Augustus*: "As if she had purified herself from the husband’s embrace." It seemed fit to mention this because of certain people who are more than enough pedantic in examining words.
27 <term>That they might present</term>] <term>parastēsai tō Kyriō</term> <note>original Greek: παραστησαι τω Κυριω</note>, that is, that they might exhibit or commend him to the Lord. For the Greek word signifies both.
28 <term>Opening the womb</term>] <term>dianoigon mētran</term> <note>original Greek: διανοιγον μητραν</note>, "opening the uterus": for so Laurentius <note>Laurentius Valla, a 15th-century humanist philologist.</note> preferred, a man of superstitious modesty, as if indeed "vulva" were an obscene word, or as if the words of this law...

24 ...and to offer a sacrifice according to what was said in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. 25 And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon; and this man was righteous and devout, looking for the consolation of Israel; and the Holy Spirit was upon him. 26 And it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ. 27 And he came in the Spirit into the temple; and when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law, 28 he also took him into his arms, and blessed God, and said: 29 "Now, Master, you are letting your servant depart in peace according to your word. 30 For my eyes have seen your salvation, 31 which you have prepared before the face of all peoples: 32 A light for revelation to the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel." 33 And his father and mother were marveling at those things which were spoken about him. 34 And Simeon blessed them, and said to Mary his mother: "Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign which shall be spoken against. 35 And a sword shall pierce through your own soul also, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed."

<meta>catchword: out of</meta>

---

...whether these things were said specifically of Mary, and not rather of all women who give birth. Indeed, "opening the womb" <note>original: "adaperiens vulvam"</note> is said according to the property of Hebrew speech for "being born." And whoever the author was of the 14th Homily, whose testimony we just cited, he thinks that Christ also opened his mother’s womb, but not at all in the manner of others. For the conception of others also opens the woman's womb, whereas Christ was conceived in the closed womb of the virgin, without the work of a man; there, the "power of the Most High" overshadowing from heaven took the place of an embrace, the Holy Spirit entering in place of masculine seed. Furthermore, in being born, He opened the womb, but in such a way that He did not tear the enclosures of virginal modesty. This is indeed that author's opinion, for which I have no intention to fight at present, even if it conflicts with what pious belief has long ago fixed in the minds of all: that Christ came forth from the closed womb of the virgin without stain, and without the straining and labor of one giving birth. While these things are certainly plausible and not irreverent to say, they cannot be taught by certain testimonies of the Holy Scriptures. Certainly, Saint Ambrose does not shrink from that opinion when explaining this passage; for he concludes his commentary with these words: *For He who sanctified another's womb so that a prophet might be born <note>Referring to John the Baptist</note>, this is He who opened His own mother's womb so that He might come forth immaculate.* For he thinks it can be understood religiously that He came forth from the closed womb of the virgin in such a way that He did not violate the enclosures of virginal modesty.

**29 And behold, there was a man ]** From these words, Theophylact <note>A prominent Byzantine commentator</note> concludes that Simeon was not a priest, but only a righteous man, so that Christ might have testimony from every class of men. Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a 14th-century theologian</note> affirms he was a priest, but by a clearly frivolous argument. He is commended by the name of justice and piety, not by the priesthood.

**30 And devout ]** <term>eulabēs</term> <note>original Greek: εὐλαβής</note>, that is, pious or religious. The word is derived from the fact that something is handled with reverence and circumspection.

**31 And he had received an answer ]** Here, "answer" should be understood as an oracle. "And it had been revealed to him" <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἦν αὐτῷ κεχρηματισμένον</note>, that is, "it had been promised to him by an oracle."

**32 His parents ]** "His" <note>original: "Ejus"</note> is not added among the Greeks: <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ εἰσαγαγεῖν τοὺς γονεῖς τὸ παιδίον Ἰησοῦν</note>, that is, "when the parents led in the boy Jesus."

**33 Now you let depart ]** <term>apolyeis</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπολύεις</note>. Augustine noted this passage in the fourth book of *Tropes of the Old Instrument*, saying it is rarely found used in reference to death. For a wife who is divorced is "released" <note>original Greek: ἀπολύουσι</note>. He brings up a passage in the book of Numbers, "And all the congregation saw that Aaron was released," for which our edition has: "But all the multitude seeing that Aaron had died wept," etc.

**34 Before the face of all ]** <term>kata prosōpon</term> <note>original Greek: κατὰ πρόσωπον</note>. Which sounds more like "in the sight of."

**35 And his father and mother were ]** In several Greek manuscripts, I read "Joseph" instead of "father." I think this was changed by someone who feared to call Joseph the father of Jesus, even though later Mary herself calls him the father of Jesus. Certainly, Augustine, in his book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists* (Book 2, Chapter 1), cites this passage according to our reading.

**36 And he blessed them ]** Since mention of the father, mother, and son immediately preceded, it can be referred by others to all of them. Nor is it absurd if someone is said to "bless" Christ, whether we wish Him glory or proclaim His praises. In praying, we say to the Father, "Hallowed be Thy name." And in the Psalms, "Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord." Those who are offended by the word "to bless" imagine that Simeon’s blessing was like that of Bishops today, where the greater blesses the lesser. In ancient times, parents blessed their children. What is absurd if Simeon, an old man, blesses the boy as a father would, wishing him success in the task for which he was sent? This blessing is a prayer/vow. Furthermore, the distinction that some bring between "I bless you" <note>original: "benedico te"</note> and "I bless to you" <note>original: "benedico tibi"</note> is clearly ridiculous, since in this very passage the same Greek verb <term>eulogēsen</term> <note>original Greek: εὐλόγησεν</note> is used, and in both places the accusative case is added—first "God" <note>original: "ton Theon"</note> and then "them" <note>original: "autous"</note>—and also when the Church sings "Bless the Lord, you heavens." And yet, a certain "thrice-greatest" Parisian Rabbi <note>A sarcastic reference to Noël Beda, Erasmus's critic</note> taught this obscure distinction with many insults—though I would wish this to be said without insult to his order, as I would never have mentioned it if he had not boasted in a published book that he had taught this.

**37 Which shall be spoken against ]** <term>antilegomenon</term> <note>original Greek: ἀντιλεγόμενον</note>, that is, "which is spoken against," to be understood absolutely. And thus Augustine cites it in various places, especially when explaining Psalm 88. And it is also frequently cited by...

...Origen in the Homilies in which he explains this Evangelist, if
<margin>C</margin> the title of the work is truthful. Likewise, Tertullian in his book *On the Flesh of Christ* says, "And for a sign which is spoken against." And shortly after, he says: "We recognize, therefore, the sign of contradiction: the conception and birth from a Virgin."

**38 And your own soul ]** <note>original Greek: Καὶ σοῦ δὲ αὐτῆς τὴν ψυχὴν διελεύσεται</note>, that is, "And through your own soul also it shall pass." The conjunction "but/and" <note>original: "de"</note> is not idle here; it signifies a change of person, as if the beginning of a new sorrow. I do not care to report here the various interpretations that Lyranus and Hugh of Saint-Cher heap upon this passage—the latter even cites Chrysostom as the author of the opinion that Simeon said "your own soul," meaning "the soul of your son," whom you love as your own soul. However, he draws this very fiction from Peter Comestor. It is certain that "her/own" <note>original: "ipsius"</note> cannot refer to anyone but Mary, since it is <term>autēs</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτῆς</note>. There is no reason
<margin>D</margin> to devise monstrous interpretations here, since the sense is straightforward: that as Christ is rejected, a certain portion of sorrow would return to his mother. Furthermore, "your own soul" <note>original: "suam ipsius"</note> offended those who are more accustomed to refined speech as being more elegantly said than their ears were used to. Although "it shall pass through" <note>original: "pertransibit"</note> was more beautiful than "it shall pass through" <note>Erasmus is comparing two Latin forms of the word</note>, even because that which passes by also passes through. And from here Augustine seems to have drawn his opinion in his *Book of Questions on the Old and New Testaments* (Question 73), when he writes that Mary, the mother of Jesus, also wavered somewhat in faith when she saw her son dead, but only until he rose from the dead; and for that reason the "sword passed through," because this doubt did not settle in her soul, but merely passed through. Since these things were said contrary to the common opinion of theologians, lest anyone summon me to court, I will provide his own words: *"But what he added, saying, 'And a sword shall pierce your own soul, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed,' certainly signified this: that even Mary, through whom the mystery of the Savior's incarnation was carried out, would doubt at the death of the Lord; yet in such a way that she would be strengthened in the resurrection, though all would doubt with a certain stupor at the Lord's death. For who would not hesitate, seeing him who called himself the Son of God humbled so far as to descend into death? And because, as I said, all ambiguity was to recede at the Lord’s resurrection, he said the sword would 'pass through,' not 'fall upon' or 'strike' a passing limb. So that just as a sword thrust, passing near a man, creates fear but does not strike, so also doubt would create sadness, but not kill, because it did not sit in the soul but passed through as if touching the hearts of the disciples like a shadow."* Thus far Augustine. Theophylact indicates it can be understood either as the sorrow of the Passion or as a somewhat doubtful thought when she saw a son born in such a way and famous for so many miracles dying on the cross. Nor do I think Chrysostom shrank from this opinion, for he attributes to Mary some of the emotion that the common crowd of mothers has toward their sons, from whose deeds they claim some glory for themselves: *"Consider," he says, "the importunity of both the mother and the brothers; for when they ought to have entered and listened along with the crowds, or at least waited outside for the end of the discourse and then approached, moved by a certain ambition and ostentation, they called him out in the presence of everyone,"* etc.
<margin>F</margin> Explaining the second chapter of John’s Gospel in the twentieth Homily, he attributes a similar emotion to Mary: *"For she hoped," he says, "that he would now win the favor of men, and perhaps she was moved by some human emotion, just as his brothers were when they said, 'Show yourself to the world.' And a little later: 'Since they did not yet have a proper opinion of him, but in the manner of mothers, Mary thought she would rightly command her son in all things, when it was proper to worship and revere him as Lord.'"* To these things, whoever it was who wrote the Homilies on Luke—which we have from the edition of a certain Merlin, attributed to Origen—teaches even more clearly that the sword of scandal touched Mary’s breast: *"What do we think," he says, "that while the Apostles were scandalized, the mother of the Lord was immune from scandals? If she did not suffer scandal in the Lord's passion, Jesus did not die for her. But if all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, being justified by his grace and redeemed, surely even Mary was scandalized at that time."* And shortly after in the same place: *"The sword of infidelity shall pass through, and you shall be struck by the blade of ambiguity, and your thoughts shall tear you in different directions,"* etc. Likewise, in the twentieth Homily, regarding Joseph and Mary...

36 [And there was] out of many hearts, their thoughts. And there was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. ---

<margin>D</margin> ...bestows a faith that is not yet perfect, as they lead the boy away from the temple with a reprimand. I shall leave the judgment of others' opinions to themselves. For my part, while I would not wish to fight to the death <note>original: "gladiari"</note> for this particular view, neither do I approve of the audacity or stubbornness of certain people who can imagine anything they like and attribute it to Mary. They defend these ideas as if they were a Gospel oracle, shouting "heretic!" if anyone dares to doubt them. Moreover, since Christ wished to redeem the human race by an ineffable and new counsel, it seems a matter of impious audacity for anyone to contend that they can prescribe the methods by which he did so—especially in matters like these, which cannot be known by us with certainty. 

Certainly, regarding the current task, the Greek words for "to talk throughout" <note>original: "dialalein"</note> and "to talk alongside" <note>original: "parelalein"</note> are quite different; the latter means to pass over or omit. But Luke says, "it was spoken of throughout" <note>original: "dielaleito"</note>, which means it shall go through the middle and cut the heart in two. Let us go now and mock the knowledge of the Greek language as if it were a superfluous thing, when we see from this example that it happened to a most distinguished Doctor of the Church <note>Erasmus likely refers to Jerome or another Latin Father here</note> because he either knew too little Greek or did not consult it. No one should interpret this as a slight against such a holy Doctor, but rather as an encouragement for the studies of virtuous young men. For there are some so devoted to certain authors that they immediately cry out that it is an intolerable insult if anyone disagrees with them by even a hair's breadth. A Franciscan will not suffer any departure from the judgment of Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a famous 14th-century biblical commentator</note>; a Dominican <note>original: "Praedicator"</note> will not tolerate anything being plucked from the decrees of Thomas Aquinas or Cajetan; an Augustinian will not allow disagreement with Augustine. Yet if we accept this—that everyone must hold tooth and nail to their own author—it will eventually happen that we are allowed to disagree with no one at all, since the authors themselves do not agree with each other; indeed, they sometimes even disagree with themselves. A person who deals in the truth ought to be devoted to no man's authority, nor is it right to grant this to any human, as they do not even claim it for themselves—and if they did claim it, it should be granted all the less.

<margin>37 And she was a widow up to]</margin> "And she was a widow of about eighty-four years." The Translator <note>the author of the Vulgate</note> seems to have read "until" <note>original: "heos"</note> instead of "about" <note>original: "hos"</note>. However, this should be understood such that the number of years refers not to the woman's age, but to the duration of her widowhood, in which she had persevered for so many years. Ambrose shows this plainly, saying: "It was not without purpose that he expressed eighty-four years of widowhood." Thus says Ambrose, even if it is somewhat hard to believe that so many years had passed since her marriage, unless she was extremely old or married quite young.

<margin>40 With prayers]</margin> <note>original: "deesesi"</note>. I wonder why "prayers" or "supplications" displeased the Translator, since "obsecration" <note>original: "obsecratio"</note> signifies something else—namely, whenever we entreat through a sacred thing, which the Greeks call an <term>orkismon</term> <note>a solemn oath or adjuration</note>. "Serving with fastings and obsecrations." It is uncertain whether these Greek dative forms refer to the object or the instrument; for example, whether you say "I serve profit" or "I serve with my body"—that is, to understand that she served God, or that she worshipped Him with such sacrifices as fastings and supplications.

<margin>41 At this very hour]</margin> "at the same hour." It would have been clearer to say "at that same hour."

<margin>42 Coming up]</margin> <note>original: "epistasa"</note>, that is, "standing by." What Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a humanist critic whom Erasmus admired</note> suggests is trivial; for one can "come upon" a scene while these things are happening, even if one is already present in some part of the temple.

<margin>43 She gave thanks to the Lord]</margin> <note>original: "anthomologeito"</note>. This is not simply "she confessed," but "she responded in turn," so that it refers back to the confession of Simeon and others, to whose testimony she was responding.

<margin>44 Redemption of Israel]</margin> "Israel" is not in the Greek, but rather "Jerusalem."

But thinking that he was in the company, they came a day’s journey, and sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintances. <margin>45</margin> And when they had not found him, they returned to Jerusalem, seeking him. <margin>46</margin> And it happened after three days, they found him in the temple sitting in the midst of the teachers, both hearing them and questioning them. <margin>47</margin> And all who heard him were amazed at his intelligence and his answers: <margin>48</margin> and seeing him, they wondered. Did you not know that I must be in those things which are my Father’s?" <margin>50</margin> And they did not...

---

<margin>E</margin> ...rusalem, which is *Ierousalem*. The oldest manuscripts have *Hierusalem* without a preposition. And Saint Irenaeus reads it this way. Likewise Augustine in *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*, Book 2, Chapter 5; and Bede reads it no differently.

<margin>45 And he was strengthened]</margin> The Greek codices add <term>pneumati</term>, "in spirit." Furthermore, what follows, "full," is not the noun <term>pleres</term>, but the participle <term>pleroumenos</term>, which indicates that he was already being filled as he grew in age; not that he progressed in the manner of ordinary men as he aged, but that divine grace gradually shone forth in him, lest the matter seem monstrously miraculous before its time. This is how Theophylact <note>a medieval Byzantine commentator</note> interprets it, agreeing with me regarding the emphasis of the participle. However, it is hardly for men to define how and to what extent the divine nature communicated itself to the human nature in Christ.

<margin>46 Through every year]</margin> <note>original: "kat' etos"</note>, that is, "annually," or "in individual years," or "yearly."

<margin>47 On the solemn day of the Passover]</margin> "at the feast of the Passover." Why was this roundabout phrasing used? And a little later:

<margin>48 As they returned]</margin> It would have been clearer if he had added "they." Because of what follows immediately, "the boy Jesus remained." And in Greek it is, "while they were returning." This pronoun, though sometimes omitted elsewhere without trouble, was appropriate to add here for clarity.

<margin>49 And his parents did not know]</margin> The Greek codices have, "And Joseph and his mother did not know," which I suspect was changed, especially since in some copies it is different, namely, "his parents," just as it was a little earlier.

<margin>50 In the company]</margin> <note>original: "en synodia"</note>. This properly signifies companions and associates on the same journey.

<margin>51 They were amazed]</margin> <note>original: "existanto"</note>, which signifies violent wonder, or fear, so that one is not oneself; similar to the word he uses next, "they were astonished," as if you were to say, "they were struck thunderstruck."

<margin>52 And they themselves did not understand the word]</margin> In this place, <term>rhema</term> is certainly used for "speech" or "saying." Now, what will those people do with this passage—those who, with more zeal than caution, attribute almost as much blessedness to the Virgin from the very beginning as she possesses now? Certainly Christ did not speak obscurely, and yet the Evangelist adds that what Jesus said was not understood by them. Indeed, that also

<margin>F</margin> should be noted: when the boy was rebuked, he did not respond gently to his parents; rather, he almost rebukes the rebukers. For Ambrose was not afraid to say this; he writes thus on this passage: <quote>"There are two generations in Christ: one is of the father, the other of the mother. The father’s is more divine, the mother’s is that which descended into our labor and use. And therefore those things which happen above nature, above age, above custom, are not to be assigned to human virtues, but referred to divine powers. Elsewhere, when the mother urges him toward a mystery, here the mother is rebuked because she still demands what is human."</quote> However, in what follows, I suspect a mistake lies beneath. <quote>"But when," he says, "he is described as twelve years old here, and there he is said to have a disciple, the mother seems to have learned from the son to demand a mystery from a stronger one, she who was amazed at the miracle in a younger one."</quote> For in more corrected books it is read: <quote>"You see that the mother learned from the son to demand a miracle from a stronger one, she who was amazed at the mystery in a younger one."</quote> For she had first been stunned when she found him in the midst of the Doctors. Thus Luke says, "seeing him they were astonished." From this, she conceived the confidence to demand a miracle at the wedding [at Cana]. But in the first place, the mother urges him toward a mystery...

## III.

1 Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, while Pontius Pilate was presiding over Judea, and Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, and Philip his brother was tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias was tetrarch of Abilene,

<margin>a</margin> [Regarding the word "subject"]: There is no doubt that it should be read as "for service," that is, for obedience; for it is read, *And he was subject to them*. They were amazed at the mystery in the youth because it is read, *And they themselves did not understand the word*: the mystery is hidden. Therefore, the obedience of the son as a boy taught the mother to require service from him when he was older, as at the wedding <note>the wedding at Cana</note>. Thus Christ wished his business, which depended entirely on heaven, to be pure from human affections, nor did he allow any human authority to be mixed in here. So also he immediately rejected Peter when he advised him not to go to Jerusalem, saying, *Get behind me, Satan*. Nowadays, everything is conducted by human desires, though we wish them to appear heavenly above all. Then, while teaching, when interrupted by his mother and brothers, he responds somewhat bluntly: *Who is my mother?* Similarly, when addressed at the wedding regarding the wine running out. This rebuke belongs to the one interrupting; that he obeys despite not being understood belongs to his obedience, which was appropriate for that age and yielded to the weakness of his parents. Some attribute the parents' fear solely to Joseph, and similarly the son’s obedience. Finally, there is the point, *And they did not understand the word*, as if none of this applied to the Virgin, who might not have been as worried about what might happen to her son as she was about what they might have neglected through oversight. While I admit it is a pious sentiment for those who delight in attributing the most perfect gifts to the most holy Virgin, it is not far from the danger of rashness to define, beyond the authority of the Scriptures, by what steps Christ raised his mother to a perfect knowledge of himself.

<margin>b</margin> 51 *And he was subject to them*] <note>original Greek: ὑποτασσόμενος</note> *subjectabatur*, that is, he was compliant. For one who is compliant is not immediately "lesser." A father complies with a son, a master with a servant, not out of necessity, but out of humanity. It is a harsh claim made by some that Christ owed obedience to his mother even in his Gospel business, since one who administers a commonwealth is not bound by a father's authority. For it is not a father’s place to prescribe to a Bishop how he should administer Gospel doctrine. But it is much harsher what the same people teach: that the Blessed Virgin can even now command Christ as a human being, and that this is what the Church sings: *Show yourself to be a mother, let him receive prayer through you* <note>A line from the hymn "Ave Maris Stella"</note>, etc., that is, "order your son to hear us." If this is true, the mother should be implored rather than the son, and not all power has been handed to Christ even according to his human nature if he is bound by a mother’s command. Nor has she yet surrendered her maternal right to the son, though the Father has handed all power in heaven and earth to the Son. Civil law usually grants freedom to children through emancipation, yet Christ is still under his mother’s power? Now, how does it fit that they deny children are held by the power of parents in entering marriage, or similarly in the profession of monastic life, yet the Virgin Mother had the right to prescribe to her son in the business of the Gospel? A son obeys his parents chiefly because an imprudent age needs the counsel of others. Yet parents do not have a perpetual right to act as judges and prescribe whatever they wish to their children. The Lord did not need his mother's advice, yet for the sake of example, he showed supreme obedience not only to his mother but also to Joseph, who was not his father. The phrase "he owed obedience" seems a harsh word to me when applied to Christ. He who "owes" sins if he does not perform. They usually cry out, "these things offend pious ears." But these things certainly offend *my* ears. But let us let this <unclear>dispute</unclear> pass.

<margin>c</margin> 52 *And Jesus advanced etc.*] It does not escape me by what reasoning the Interpreters explain this passage: that Christ "advanced" not because anything was added to him from the time he was conceived in his mother's womb, but because he more and more displayed and exercised his gifts, with which he was most abundantly filled, both among men (whose salvation he consulted) and before God (whose glory he illustrated). Again, there are those who explain it by saying that Christ acquired these same gifts differently: what he previously held by divine inspiration, he soon acquired through human use and study. I do not refute their opinion; I would only want the reader to consider whether it can be held while keeping the sincerity of faith intact. It is beyond controversy that all the gifts with which Jesus was endowed as a man were from divine beneficence, and the Deity imparted them to the assumed human nature through certain degrees—especially since we read this twice in the same chapter of Luke. For he says a little earlier: *The boy grew and became strong, full of wisdom.* For that which is "strengthened" seems to be supported by an increase of strength. And again, more clearly in this place: *And Jesus advanced in wisdom, and age, and grace before God and before men.* Since he joins three things—*wisdom, age, and grace*—just as he truly advanced by the addition of age, so he seems to have truly advanced by the increments of his gifts. For as for the claim made by some that Jesus was 
<meta>The catchword "qua" at the bottom of the column indicates the first syllable of the next page's first word.</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>from</margin> the beginning full of grace, this does not hinder progress, since the same is said of John and of others, to whom we nevertheless attribute degrees and additions of virtues. Nor should it move us if this conflicts with some decree of the Scholastics <note>medieval university theologians</note> or the opinion of any man; but rather whether what Luke clearly wrote is contrary to the sincerity of faith, which must always be adhered to in every way. And I have proposed this very point, whatever it may be, with no other intent than that the reader may first and more learnedly weigh it with himself. Now it must also be examined why he placed "age" in the middle between wisdom and grace, since "age," as the lightest part, might seem to deserve the first place—unless perhaps the word "age" <note>Latin: aetate</note> here encompasses all the gifts that adolescent years usually bring. Again, the Greek word is ambiguous: does it mean he advanced in gifts divinely implanted, or that he became more "gracious" through the commendation of the virtues showing themselves in him? Furthermore, regarding "age" here, it is the same word in Greek <note>original: ἡλικίαν</note> which they translate as *stature* in the sixth chapter of Matthew. Likewise, in the nineteenth chapter of this same Evangelist, because *he was small in stature*.

<margin>d</margin> 1 *While Pontius [governed]*] The translator delighted in variety, now translating as "governing" <note>procurante</note> what he had just translated as "presiding" <note>praefide</note>; <note>original Greek: ἡγεμονεύοντος</note>, that is, "acting as governor."

<margin>e</margin> 2 *But as tetrarch*] These too are participles in the Greek placed absolutely, <note>original Greek: τετραρχοῦντος</note>, that is, "acting as tetrarch." There was Herod the elder, the son of Antipater of Ascalon and Cypros the Arabian woman. He, a foreigner, received the kingdom of Judea through the favor of Octavius Augustus Caesar and the Senate, through whom the priesthood was both profaned and transferred to foreigners according to prophecy. Under him, the Redeemer of the world was born; under him, he fled into Egypt. This Herod, having reigned a long time, died of a skin disease, leaving four sons: Archelaus, Herod the younger, Philip, and Lysanias—though there is some doubt whether Lysanias was a son of Herod. Bede, explaining this passage, says Lysanias, Herod the younger, and Philip were the sons of the Herod under whom the Lord was born. The *Glossa Ordinaria* followed this, as did the *Golden Chain* <note>the Catena Aurea by Thomas Aquinas</note>. However, Lyra adds that this was put forward by no heavy [reliable] author. Theophylactus seems to have felt what Bede wrote, writing thus on this passage: *the tetrarchy of Herod of Ascalon's sons held etc.* distinguishing Lysanias from Herod and Philip with no mark. Josephus, in the fourteenth book of *Jewish Antiquities*, chapter 21, mentions a Lysanias who succeeded his father Ptolemy son of Mennaeus to the kingdom, with his mother being Alexandra, daughter of Aristobulus. Peter the Censor, following Josephus I believe, says he lived below Lebanon. Archelaus, however, was banished to Vienne, a city in Gaul, in the tenth year of his rule due to his cruelty. The Romans, in order to break the power of the kingdom, distributed the tetrarchies among the brothers, the sons of Herod, so that Herod (whom I believe was surnamed Antipas) administered Galilee; for Pontius Pilate the governor administered Judea; while Philip administered Ituraea and Trachonitis, which Jerome lists as if it were the same region with two names, saying: *The region of Trachonitis, or Ituraea, of which Philip was tetrarch, in which is Caesarea Philippi*, also called Paneas. Lysanias held Abilene, which is between Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon, which Ptolemy calls Lysania. I think touching on these things from the historians is sufficient for this passage and this purpose.

<margin>f</margin> 3 *Into all the region*] <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν περίχωρον τοῦ Ἰορδάνου</note>, into all the region around the Jordan, or the neighboring, or the surrounding area of the Jordan.

<margin>g</margin> 4 *Make his paths straight*] And here, instead of "of our God," which is in the Hebrew and the Septuagint, he changed it to "his," which we noted above. Except that Luke followed the testimony of Isaiah further, in which he agrees with the Hebrew truth as well as the Septuagint; for instead of what the Hebrew truth has, *And all flesh shall see together that the mouth of the Lord has spoken*, here, as if interpreting with the Septuagint, he said, <note>original Greek: τὸ σωτήριον τοῦ Θεοῦ</note>, that is, *the salvation of God*. Furthermore, Jerome rendered the Hebrew thus: *Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be humbled, and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places into plain ways, and the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see together that the mouth of the Lord has spoken.*

<margin>h</margin> 5 *The crooked into straight*] <note>original Greek: τὰ σκολιὰ εἰς εὐθείας</note>, that is, the slanted into the straight, so that "way" is understood. For here the translator used "crooked" <note>prava</note> not for "evil things," but for "distorted things." It was a Hebrew figure of speech by which they speak thus: *he shall be to me into a father, two shall be into one flesh*, instead of *he shall be my father, and two shall be one flesh.*

A significant portion of this section is dedicated to correcting the translation of how tax collectors and soldiers should behave, which Erasmus uses as a platform to discuss his views on social justice and his famous critiques of war and military service.</meta>

# ACCORDING TO LUKE. CHAPTER III.

<margin>5</margin> ...straight, and the rough into smooth ways; <margin>6</margin> And all flesh shall see the salvation of God. <margin>7</margin> He said therefore to the crowds that came out to be baptized by him, "Offspring of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? <margin>8</margin> Produce therefore fruits worthy of repentance; and do not begin to say within yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father'; for I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. <margin>9</margin> And already the ax is laid to the root of the trees; every tree therefore not producing good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire." <margin>10</margin> And the crowds were asking him, saying, "What then shall we do?" <margin>11</margin> And answering he says to them, "He who has two tunics, let him share with the one who has none; and <margin>12</margin> he who has food, let him do likewise." And tax collectors also came to be baptized, and they said to him, "Teacher, what <margin>13</margin> shall we do?" And he said to them, "Exact nothing more than what is commanded you." <margin>14</margin> And soldiers also were asking him, saying, "And what shall we do?" And he said to them, "Do not shake anyone down, nor accuse falsely, and be content with your wages." <margin>15</margin> And while the people were in expectation, and all were wondering in their hearts about <margin>16</margin> John, whether he himself might be the Christ; John answered, saying to all, "I indeed baptize you with water; but one stronger than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to loose; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire. <margin>17</margin> Whose winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly clean...

<meta>catchword: his</meta>

---

<margin>6</margin> **And the rough into ways...]** <note>original: καὶ τραχεῖαι</note>, that is, *and the rough*, so that "ways" is understood. And "smooth," in Greek <note>original: εἰς λείας</note>, *leveled*, which, with the first syllable lengthened, is the opposite of "rough."

<margin>7</margin> **Offspring of vipers]** <note>original: γεννήματα</note>, which elsewhere he translates as *progeny*, a point we have remarked upon more than once.

<margin>8</margin> **Who showed]** <note>original: τίς ὑπέδειξεν</note>, which more specifically means *hinted* or *indicated secretly*, in the way we usually point something out when danger is imminent.

<margin>9</margin> **Worthy of repentance]** <note>original: ἀξίους τῆς μετανοίας</note>. It can also be taken as *worthy by repentance*. For among the Greeks, "worthy" takes the genitive case. However, we have already noted this in the commentary on Matthew.

<margin>10</margin> **Do not begin to say]** What was said in Matthew as "do not think" <note>original: μὴ δόξητε</note>, is said here as "do not begin" <note>original: μὴ ἄρξησθε</note>. The Greeks add here <note>original: ἐν ἑαυτοῖς</note>, that is, *in yourselves*, or *within you*, meaning *in your mind*.

<margin>11</margin> **And children of Abraham]** "Abraham" is in the Greek dative case <note>original: τῷ Ἀβραάμ</note>, that is, "to Abraham himself."

<margin>12</margin> **For now the ax]** The Greeks add a conjunction, *and the ax* <note>original: καὶ ἀξίνη</note>, which is certainly not useless; for it signifies the present danger if they do not repent.

<margin>13</margin> **To the root of the tree]** It is *of the trees* <note>original: τῶν δένδρων</note> both in the Greek and in our most ancient codices. For he is thinking of all men, and this is how Ambrose reads it.

<margin>14</margin> **Will be cut down]** In Greek, it is *is cut down and is thrown* <note>original: ἐκκόπτεται καὶ βάλλεται</note>, just as in Matthew.

<margin>15</margin> **Let him give to the one not having]** <note>original: μεταδότω</note>, that is, *let him share*, or *impart*. For he does not command that two tunics be given away, but one out of the two. For that is what it means to share.

<margin>16</margin> **Than what is commanded you to do]** I wonder that it was not noticed, either by Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo Valla, a pioneer of New Testament criticism</note>, or anyone else, not even Bede, that the Greek <note>original: πράσσετε</note> should have been translated here not as *do*, but as *exact*: since he is speaking of publicans, that is, those who farm the public taxes. Among such men, then as now, it is the custom to extort from the common people not just what the Ruler has ordered (which is often unjust enough in itself), but as much as they possibly can. The Greek word signifies both. Hence <note>original: πράκτορες</note> means *exacters*. And a little later, the translator twice renders it as *exacters*, and in chapter nineteen, he translates <note>original: ἔπραξα</note> as *I should have exacted*. And this is certainly how Ambrose reads and understands it, rendering the sense of this passage in these words: *Saint John the Baptist gave a suitable answer to each class of men: one for all, so to the publicans, that they should not exact beyond what is prescribed; to the soldiers, that they should not commit false accusation nor seek plunder.* Similarly, Augustine, in his sermon on the words of the Lord from Matthew 19, reads and interprets: *Exact nothing more than what is appointed for you.* Theophylact <note>A prominent Byzantine commentator</note> also explains the Greek word with another Greek word <note>original: εἰσπράττετε</note>, to demand from outside, that is, to exact, which is to demand. For it is said both ways.

<margin>17</margin> **Do not commit calumny]** <note>original: συκοφαντήσητε</note>. Among the Greeks, this term is not defined in only one way, but for the most part, to play the "sycophant" is to *bring a false charge*, and to pin a crime on someone by design so that some gain may be extorted from the accused. He wishes two things to be absent from soldiers: the violence with which they oppressed the provincials, and the false accusation with which they terrified them before their governors, so that they might plunder them not by force, but no less destructively. Sometimes men plunder ships or villages, and then claim they were just dealing with the remains of an enemy, or some other invented offense. I heard of a certain commander who warned his men to take whatever they could, whether it was the property of enemies or friends; for if things went badly, they might be forced to make restitution, but in the meantime, some portion of the loot would stick to the hands of the thief. I am not at all convinced by those who try to use this passage to justify war, as if John had said these things to Christians, and not rather to Pagans, or at least to the most worldly Jews—though these Jews
