<margin>A</margin> ...the crooked things are made straight, and the rough shall be turned into smooth ways: And all flesh shall see the salvation of God. He said therefore to the <margin>6 7</margin> crowds, which came out to be baptized by him, "Offspring of vipers, who suggested to you that you should flee from the coming wrath? Produce therefore fruits worthy of <margin>8</margin> repentance: and do not begin to say within yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father': for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. For now also the ax is placed at the root of the <margin>9</margin> trees: every tree therefore, not producing good fruit, is cut down, and is cast into the fire." And the crowds <margin>10</margin> were questioning him, saying, "What then shall we do?" But answering he says to them, "He who has two tunics, let him <margin>11</margin> impart to the one not having: and he who has food, let him <margin>B</margin> do likewise." But there came also tax collectors to be baptized, <margin>12</margin> and said to him, "Master, what shall we do?" But he <margin>13</margin> said to them, "Exact nothing more than what has been appointed for you." But there were questioning him <margin>14</margin> also soldiers, saying, "And what shall we do?" And he said to them, "Do not shake anyone down, nor bring false charges, and be content with your wages." While the <margin>15</margin> people were in expectation, and all were thinking in their hearts about John, whether he himself might be that Christ; John answered, saying to all, "I indeed <margin>16</margin> baptize you with water: but one stronger than I will come, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to loose, he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire. <margin>C</margin> Whose winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will purge his threshing-floor, and will gather... <margin>17</margin>

<meta>catchword: gather</meta>

---

never served under the Pagans; or as if he intended to prescribe how soldiers ought to be, and not rather that those who were the worst of men might begin to be less evil. Theophylact notes this elegantly: *He exhorts the crowds,* he says, *to do something good, that is, to share their own; but the publicans and soldiers to desist from evils, for they were not capable of doing anything good, but it was enough for them not to do evil.* Thus Theophylact. For a soldier who plunders unjustly is not even a good soldier, let alone a good man. Thus he was preparing the way of the Lord on every side. Otherwise, how could John have abolished military service for them, when Christ did not even abolish the ceremonies and superstitions of the Mosaic Law and the petty constitutions of men for the Jews? Who denies that war was permitted to the Jews? But it was permitted to the same people to whom it was permitted to hate an enemy. We read that the Jews fought legally; we do not read that they earned wages under foreign leaders. The Jews fought, but by the command of the Divine. Because of this, do we want Christians to wage war against the command of Christ? Indeed, to have iron and slaughter for sale? Gregory places trade among those activities to which it is not lawful to return after baptism; yet we take criminal men, who fly to war and the slaughter of Christians enticed by various rewards—even breaking out of their own accord if a recruiter is lacking—and we count them among Christians and defend them with Gospel sponsorship? It does not escape me what Augustine disputes here, both elsewhere and against Faustus: but it is right to prefer the pure doctrine of Christ and the Apostles to the opinion of Augustine. Nor does he approve of this kind of war by which we are endlessly shattered. For the sake of protecting the public peace of Christians, he grants arms to Caesar and Caesar's prefects. But this is not the purest part of the body of Christ. In those days, an Emperor was "religious" if he merely did not oppress the Church and occasionally favored it. Now, Bishops wage war, and they do almost nothing else but wage war. Ambrose, in his book on widows, openly declares with what arms he wants Priests and pure Christians to be equipped. *The arms of the Church,* he says, *is faith: the arms of the Church is prayer, which conquers the adversary.* And in the same place: *But the Church does not conquer opposing powers with secular arms, but with spiritual arms, which are powerful to God.* So then, war may be seen as among necessary evils, if only it be legal. It is not necessary that we derive this right from the prescriptions of the Gospel. But another place will be given for speaking on these matters.

<margin>18</margin> **With your wages]** <note>original: ὀψωνίοις ὑμῶν</note>, a word Terence used for *finer foods*. Although Paul also used this word once or twice for a stipend or military enlistment pay. It appropriately expresses the reward of base men with a base word. Indeed, <term>opsonion</term> <note>original: ὀψώνιον; literally 'provisions' or 'rations'</note> is a reward for the belly, worthy of those who fight for their bellies.

<margin>19</margin> **While they were thinking]** <note>original: Προσδοκῶντος δὲ</note>, that is, *while expecting*, or *hoping*, as if one were about to judge from the outcome. Ambrose reads "Estimating," and does not add "while all were thinking," but only "while the people were estimating and thinking." Unless, through interpretation, one can almost scent that Ambrose read *Expecting*. For he says, among other things: *For it was he who was expected, and surely it was he who was expected, not someone unexpected, who arrived.* Since, however, the oldest codices agree with the Vulgate Edition, I cannot quite guess what the Translator read, unless perhaps instead of <note>original: προσδοκῶντος</note> he read <note>original: δοκοῦντος</note> ("it seemed").

<margin>20</margin> **Lest perhaps]** <note>original: μή ποτε</note>. I would prefer *Whether* rather than *Lest*. For here "lest perhaps" is clearly an expletive conjunction.

<margin>21</margin> **Of whom I am not worthy]** Ambrose seems to read in this place, *of whom I am not worthy to carry the sandals*, just as we read in Matthew.

<margin>22</margin> **Whose winnowing fan]** <note>original: οὗ τὸ πτύον</note>: so called because it separates the chaff from the grains. For <note>original: πτύω</note> means to spit out, as if rejecting and thrusting away.

23 **Into his granary**] <note>original: εἰς τὴν ἀποθήκην αὐτοῦ</note>. It is uncertain whether the pronoun "his" refers to the wheat or to Christ, but I am more of the opinion that it refers to the wheat, as indicated in the previous sections.

24 **He added also above all this**] The order of words was corrupted by a scribe's error. It should be read, "He added this also above all," just as I find it written in the more corrected Latin manuscripts.

25 **Now it happened**] The Greek could have been more suitably rendered: "It happened while all the people were being baptized, that Jesus also having been baptized and praying, heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form like a dove upon him, and a voice went forth from heaven, which said..."

26 **As a dove**] <note>original: ὡσεὶ περιστεράν</note>. Lorenzo Valla prefers "as if a dove," because otherwise the sense might seem to be that a literal dove descended upon Jesus. In truth, it means the Holy Spirit descended, but in the appearance of a dove.

27 **You are my Son**] <note>original: Σὺ εἶ ὁ Υἱός μου</note>, that is, "You are *that* Son of mine," on account of the Greek article <note>the word 'ho'</note>, the force of which is not idle in this place.

28 **About [thirty] years**] <note>original: ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα</note>, that is, around thirty years of age. Although some manuscripts had it this way: "And Jesus himself was thirty years old when he began, as he was supposed to be the son of Joseph." The sense of these words is: "And Jesus himself had entered his thirtieth year, as he was thought to be the son of Joseph"; or certainly in this manner: "And Jesus himself was approaching his thirtieth year," so that we understand him to have begun to spend his thirtieth year, or to have already reached that age. Furthermore, the participle of the substantive verb "being" <note>original: ὢν</note> is placed so that it can refer either to what precedes it or what follows. Origen—if the attribution is not false—in his 28th Homily on Luke, openly advises that only in Luke is the word "beginning" used, drawing an allegory that from baptism we begin to be as if reborn. But who would place him as the son of Joseph if he only "seemed" to be and was not? Hence the matter itself compels us to refer it to what precedes, and we should take the participle used in place of an infinitive verb, "beginning" for "to be," he who began to be, which is certainly not infrequent among the Greeks.

29 **Who was of Heli**] <note>original: τοῦ Ἡλὶ</note>, that is, who was the son of Heli. In Greek, these names are connected by articles. Therefore, our word "who" should not be referred to Joseph, nor to Christ, but to the next name, except for the first, which pertains to the nearest Joseph. Thus we understand Joseph to have been the son of Heli, and Heli in turn to have been the son of Matthat, and likewise for the rest. However, Augustine, in his *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, question 56, denies that Heli was the father of Joseph. For he wants Christ to be called the son of Heli in the same way he is called the son of David. For Joseph and Heli were sons of brothers. In the listing of names, there is a marvelous confusion in the Greek manuscripts, and even the Latin ones do not agree among themselves; in some places names are missing, in others there are extras, and many are inverted and corrupted, which we have restored by the most diligent collation possible. 

Furthermore, as to why Matthew differs from Luke in recording the genealogy of Christ—the latter tracing the line through Nathan to David, and the former through Solomon—it would take a long time to delve deeply into the disputes of certain theologians on this matter. Some of them claim this Nathan was not the son of David but the prophet, whom David adopted in place of a son, namely his own rebuker; and lest they be refuted by the timeline, they claim Nathan was "exceptionally long-lived" <note>original: μακροβιώτατον</note> and the others who reigned before him from Solomon were "supposititious" <note>original: ὑποβολιμαίους - substituted or fake</note>, to use a Homeric word. And I see that Saint Jerome, Ambrose, and before them Origen, were almost of this opinion. For Augustine "sings a palinode" <note>recants</note> of his own opinion, both elsewhere and in his *Retractions*, book 2, chapter 16, with these words: "Likewise where I said, 'Luke truly ascends through David himself to Nathan, through which prophet God expiated his sin,' I should have said 'through the prophet of that name,' lest it be thought he was the same man, when he was another, though he too was called by this name." 

However, there was no need to turn to these refuges if they had weighed the fact that among the Hebrews sons are spoken of in two ways: according to law, and according to nature. The law was that if anyone died without children, his brother should restore the offspring of the deceased. Thus, one born in this way had two fathers: one natural, from whom he was born, and the other legal, into whose name and lineage he succeeded, namely the deceased. In this manner, when the line of Solomon failed in Ahaziah, from Simeon (nicknamed Joash), who was born from the line of Nathan the son of David, the Solomonic line was restored, as we shall soon teach more extensively. 

This is clearly argued by that Preface (I know not by whom) which is placed before Luke’s Gospel. For it is so far from the style of Jerome that it cannot seem to belong to any Latin author at all, but rather to some Greek, albeit a learned and eloquent one. Some attribute it to Isidore, but nothing fits less. In it we read: "Therefore to him, after the baptism of the Son of God, the power of human birth was permitted to be repeated from the beginning, so that he might demonstrate to seekers in whom he was taking hold through Nathan the son of David, the entry of the generation returning into God being admitted, the inseparable God, so that preaching his Christ to men, he might make the work of the perfect man return into himself through the son, who through David the father provided a path for those coming in Christ." I ask you, who would ascribe this speech to Jerome? 

But to the point: this author, whoever he is, openly asserts that the Davidic line was cut off, and the sequence of the race was restored through Nathan the son of David. Gregory Nazianzen also supports this view in his genealogical poem, counting two "Davids," that is, sons of David: Solomon and Nathan, making no mention of adoption. In the work attributed to Augustine, *On the Questions of the Old and New Testaments*, question 56, these words are found: "Heli, however, the son of Matthat, holds his order from David through Nathan, the son of the same David." He repeats and emphasizes this for the whole chapter. Nor does it matter that this work is not by Augustine, since the matter indicates it belongs to someone more practiced in Holy Scripture than Augustine was. Moreover, in the first book of Chronicles, chapter 3, among the sons whom David fathered from Bathsheba in Jerusalem, Nathan is explicitly listed by name, prior in order to Solomon. Furthermore, any excuse for adoption is openly excluded because it is added: "Sons of David from Bathsheba." 

Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>Erasmus calls him 'Jacobus Faber Stapulensis', a famous French humanist</note>, that great leader of good literature, explained this matter more accurately in his Commentaries on the Epistle to the Hebrews. Johannes Annius also reports many things from Philo. And although they are quite probable, nevertheless, because he does not cite as certainly as I would like, especially in a controversial matter, and because we did not have a copy of the Greek Philo, we judged it should be touched upon in few words, and only so far as to provide the diligent reader a handle for investigating the rest, especially since these things are almost "peripheral tasks" <note>original: πάρεργα</note> to this project. 

Now, since most are deceived here because some are namesake <note>having the same name</note>, some are two-named or even three-named, and sometimes added surnames are mixed with the names themselves, we will review a few things which, once known, may decrease the chance of error. First, Heli. He is the same as "Jehoiakim," whom they corruptly call "Joachim," the natural father of the Virgin Mary and the grandfather of Jesus Christ according to the flesh. Jerome also testifies to this. And from this it is possible to gather that Luke followed the natural line of the Christian genealogy, not the legal one, at least as far as Christ is concerned; if you refer it to Joseph, it will be the opposite. For Matthew comes to Joseph through the line of nature, which is the legal line for reaching Christ.

30 **Next, of Jannai**] Both this man and the Janus who preceded him, along with those who come between these two, Philo testifies performed the leadership of Israel. They are listed marked by these surnames: "Jannaeus II, Hyrcanus, Joseph Junior, Arsei, Mattathias, Silas, Amos, Sirach, Nahum, Maslot, Hepli, Aglai, Nagid, Artaxas, Maath, Aser, Elih, Mattathias, Semei, Abner, Joseph I, Judas I, Hyrcanus, Jana, Jannaeus I."

31 **Furthermore, Zerubbabel**] Also called "Barachias," he had two sons: one named "Rhesa," with the surname "Meshullam," as you read in Nehemiah—Luke relates his lineage; the other was "Abiud," with the surname "Hananiah," whose line Matthew follows. From the lineage of these men descend both those subsequently referred to in Luke and in Matthew.

32 **To these, Shealtiel**] More correctly, if I am not mistaken, called <note>Hebrew: שאלتیאל</note> "Shealthiel," if we wish to render the Hebrew voice; he is called by another name, "Mesebbel," and "Zerubbabel" is recorded in both Luke and Matthew: so that one might conjecture these arose from Nathan.

33 **And now Neri**] He is the same who is called "Jeconiah" in Matthew. That surname was attributed to him by the people after he was rescued from prison and held in high esteem by Evil-Merodach, because the lamp of the Davidic line, which seemed destined to be extinguished, was relighted in him. He then fathered Shealtiel. Therefore, Julian the Apostate <note>Roman Emperor who opposed Christianity</note> acts in vain...

**D** Julian <note>referring to Julian the Apostate, the 4th-century Roman emperor who wrote against Christianity</note> constructs a slander against the Evangelists, as if they attribute two fathers to one son, when in fact *Neri* and *Jechonias* are the same person, just as the other kings who preceded him were <term>polyonymoi <note>original: "πολυώνυμοι" — "of many names"</note></term>, up until *Joas*, who is called *Simeon* in Luke. He was certainly not from the line of Solomon, which had already been cut off in the generation of *Ahaziah*, but from the line of *Nathan*, whose descendants had the right to succeed to the kingdom up to that point. Furthermore, it will not seem so strange that the number of people listed in Luke does not match those in Matthew, if one considers first what Jerome pointed out, and Origen before him: that several names in the genealogical sequence were omitted, and this was done deliberately, as we noted in our commentary on *Matthew*. Although *Joas* is not listed anywhere either. If you add these names to the others, you will find the number agrees. Moreover, *Jechonias* is the same as the one called *Neri*. His father *Joachim*, omitted in Matthew, is the same as *Melchi*, before whom *Jehoahaz* reigned for three months—whom Matthew did not mention either. And I do not know if *Addi* corresponds to him.

<margin>34</margin> *Again Josiah, Amon, Manasseh, Hezekiah, and Ahaz* are designated here by the surnames *Cosam, Elmodam, Er, Joshua, Eliezer*, which surnames Philo <note>Erasmus likely refers to the "Biblical Antiquities" attributed to Philo, though now known as Pseudo-Philo</note> also mentions.

<margin>35</margin> *Then Jothan, Azariah, Amaziah, Joas* are called by these names which appear in Luke: *Joram, Matthat, Levi, Simeon*, of whom Matthew makes no mention at all. *Even Simeon*, who is in Luke, had three names, being called *Simeon, Heli, and Joas*. This man was the first to arise from the "helpers" of the Davidic line, whom the Hebrews call <term>Achefarim <note>original: "אביהעפרים" — likely a corruption of "abi-ha-opherim," understood here as royal restorers</note></term>, as if they were helpers of the kingdom, since the lineage of Solomon had failed in *Ahaziah*. And not only this line, but the *Achefarim* family itself [was nearly lost], for all were killed by *Athaliah*, with only this one surviving because *Jehosheba*, the sister of *Ahaziah*, had saved him while he was still in the cradle. For that *Joas* was not the son of *Ahaziah* by birth, but only by succession, according to the right of the *Achefarim*. Although in the fourth book of Kings <note>Modern 2 Kings 11</note> he is called the son of *Ahaziah*. Philo, however, openly declares that he was not a son by birth, but, as just said, by the right of succession. Therefore, from this point, all remaining descendants belong to *Nathan*, as the one from whom he drew his line, even if he is placed in the portion of Solomon. For if the royal line failed in *Zedekiah*, as appears from the fourth book of Kings, last chapter, and Jeremiah chapter 22, it does not immediately follow that it had not failed before then. Furthermore, this *Nathan*, of whom we began to speak at the start, was the son of *David*, the brother of Solomon by *Bathsheba*, as you read in the first book of Chronicles, chapter three. He, as I said, was neither a prophet nor adopted by David as a legal son, but the right of the kingdom remained with his descendants, and this by the edict of David, if ever the line of Solomon should fail—which Philo teaches as cited by Annius <note>Annius of Viterbo, a 15th-century scholar known for "recovering" (and likely forging) ancient texts</note>. One can gather almost the same from the third book of Kings <note>Modern 1 Kings 4</note>: namely, that *Nathan Achifar* was established, that is, as the restorer of the royal line. For he is called there the son of *Nathan*, whom Luke calls <term>the priest <note>original: "הכהן" (ha-kohen)</note></term> Nathan. His duty was to manage the entire royal family: and for this reason they were called by the Hebrews <term>Achefarim</term>, that is, those granted the right to succeed, and <term>brothers of the princes <note>original: "אחי־השרים" (achi-hasarim)</note></term>, because they were held in equal honor with the sons of kings. To these belonged the tribe of Benjamin, while to the line of Solomon belonged only the house of Judah. We have touched upon these few points out of many, lest we provide no light to those eager to investigate these matters more exactly, especially since they contribute to the credibility of the history.

<column-break/>

On the other hand, I would not approve of being anxiously tormented or fighting contentiously over questions of this kind: in which I see not much more fruit than in that famous battle of the theologians concerning the conception of the Virgin Mother of God <note>A reference to the fierce contemporary debate over the Immaculate Conception</note>. And Paul warns in more than one place that pious men should avoid such genealogies and never-ending questions, because they not only contribute nothing to piety, but even give birth to strifes and contentions, the plague of Christian harmony.

**E** <margin>1</margin> *Returned from the Jordan*] It should be read as "He returned," <term>hypestrepsen <note>original: "ὑπέστρεψε"</note></term>, meaning he went back, or has returned. Certainly "returned" is more consistently found in the ancient manuscripts.

<margin>2</margin> *And was led*] <term>kai ēgeto <note>original: "καὶ ἤγετο"</note></term>, that is, he was led, or driven, although elsewhere it says he was "expelled" by the Spirit.

<margin>3</margin> *In the wilderness*] <term>eis tēn erēmon <note>original: "εἰς τὴν ἔρημον"</note></term>, that is, into the wilderness, using the grammatical case indicating movement into a place.

<margin>4</margin> *For forty days*] <term>Hēmeras tessarakonta peirazomenos <note>original: "Ἡμέρας τεσσαράκοντα πειραζόμενος"</note></term>, that is, "For forty days being tempted." For "forty days" is placed so that it can apply either to what comes before or what follows, but it is smoother if it belongs to what follows: not that he was tempted by the devil for that entire time, but during some part of this time. Certainly Origen, or whoever else it was, in the twenty-ninth Homily, reads it in such a way that he feels Jesus was tempted throughout the forty days. Nor is this view inconsistent with what Mark writes in chapter one: *And immediately the Spirit drove him into the wilderness, and he was in the wilderness forty days and forty nights, and was tempted by Satan*. But the Greek phrasing, which uses <term>peirazomenos <note>the present participle "being tempted"</note></term>, supports this sense even more. Matthew in chapter four tells it as if he were tempted after the fortieth day, or only on the fortieth day, though it is possible he was tempted on other days for other reasons.

<margin>5</margin> *Man shall live*] In the Greek it is <term>zēsetai <note>original: "ζήσεται"</note></term>, that is, he will live, or shall live, a verb in the future tense. This is agreed upon by the old Latin copies, specifically the Consonensian manuscript. In the Constantian manuscript, a corrector had changed the "e" to an "i" <note>likely changing the future "vivet" (he shall live) to the present "vivit" (he lives)</note>.

<margin>6</margin> *In a moment of time*] <term>en stigmē chronou <note>original: "ἐν στιγμῇ χρόνου"</note></term>, that is, in a point of time, a proverbial figure by which the Greeks indicate the briefest moment. It is taken from the concept of a mathematical point.

<margin>7</margin> *And to whom I wish*] <term>kai hō ean thelō <note>original: "καὶ ᾧ ἐὰν θέλω"</note></term>, that is, "and to whomsoever I wish," or "might wish."

<margin>8</margin> *If falling down you worship*] <term>Sy oun ean proskynēsēs enōpion mou <note>original: "Σὺ οὖν ἐὰν προσκυνήσῃς ἐνώπιόν μου"</note></term>, **F** that is, "You therefore if you worship before me." And indeed it is read thus in the old Latin manuscripts, specifically in the Consonensian, and likewise the Golden and Constantian manuscripts, and my own ancient printed copy, though Paulinus disagrees. Therefore, whoever added the word "falling down" made the matter clearer. For <term>proskynein <note>original: "προσκυνεῖν"</note></term> is "to worship," but specifically with a gesture of the body; the word is said by the Greeks to come either from "moving the hat" or from "kissing [ the hand]."

<margin>9</margin> *It is written*] Here the Greek manuscripts add, <term>Hypage opisō mou Satana <note>original: "Ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου Σατανᾶ"</note></term>, that is, "Get behind me, Satan." For it was so in Matthew, though spoken to Peter; the devil only heard <term>hypage <note>"go away"</note></term>. But it appears this was added here from that other passage: a zeal which caused a strange corruption to creep into the Holy Books, since nothing of this kind is read in Ambrose, nor in Origen, under whose name we have the Homilies on this Evangelist. Indeed, Origen noted that "get behind me" is not added when the devil is commanded to depart. Among Theophylact's writings, however, "Get behind me, Satan" is added, contrary to Origen’s note: and the Spanish Edition <note>The Complutensian Polyglot Bible</note> agreed with Theophylact. In the Latin manuscripts, none of these words appear.

<margin>10</margin> *You shall serve*] <term>latreuseis <note>original: "λατρεύσεις"</note></term>. Which mostly pertains to divine worship, from which the term <term>Latreia <note>The highest form of worship due to God alone</note></term> is derived.

11 **He commanded concerning you** <note>original: "Mandavit de te"</note>] The Greek *enteleitai* means "he will command," in the future tense, as we have indicated elsewhere.
12 **Lest perhaps** <note>original: "Ne forte"</note>] The Greek *mepote* means "lest at any time," or simply "lest." Why was the word "perhaps" <note>the Latin *forte*</note> necessary here?
13 **Through the whole region** <note>original: "Per universam regionem"</note>] The Greek *kath’ holes tes perichorou* means through the entire neighboring region, or through every region on all sides.
14 **And he was magnified** <note>original: "Et magnificabatur"</note>] The Greek *doxazomenos* means "he was glorified." I do not quite see why Lawrence <note>referring to the humanist scholar Laurentius Valla</note> ought to have shown a conjunction here. For he prefers: "he taught in their synagogues, with everyone glorifying him."
15 **On the Sabbath day** <note>original: "In die sabbati"</note>] The Greek *sabbaton* is plural, meaning "of the Sabbaths."
16 **And he unrolled the book** <note>original: "Et revolvit librum"</note>] I would have preferred to translate this as "and having opened the book," for he himself soon translates "when he had closed the book" <note>original: "cum plicuisset librum"</note> from the Greek *ptyxas*.
17 **The Spirit of the Lord is upon me** <note>original: "Spiritus Domini super me"</note>] This passage is in Isaiah, chapter sixty-one. Although in this place Luke’s citation agrees more with the Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> than with the Hebrew volumes, even if it differs from both. Indeed, Jerome translates the Hebrew in this manner: "The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me. To announce to the meek he has sent me, that I might heal the contrite of heart, and proclaim indulgence to the captives, and an opening to those shut up, and announce the year of the Lord’s favor." Furthermore, according to the Septuagint, we read: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me, to preach the gospel to the poor he has sent me, to heal the brokenhearted, to preach release to the captives, and sight to the blind, to call the acceptable year of the Lord."
18 **Because he has anointed me** <note>original: "Eo quod unxit me"</note>] The Greek *hou heineken echrise me* means "on account of which..."

**Because he has anointed me.** <note>original: "quod unxit me"</note> And so it is read in the most ancient Latin copies, but rendered more according to the Greek word for word than with elegance.
19 **And sight to the blind** <note>original: "Et cæcis visum"</note>] The Greek is *kai typhlois anablepsin*. Which perhaps is more literally rendered as "recovery of sight" than just "sight," as if one were to say, a restoration of life. **And the day of retribution.** These words are not added in the Greek volumes, nor are they added by Jerome, who cites this place from Luke while explaining the prophet Isaiah. Likewise, that other phrase does not fit, "to dismiss the broken in release."
20 **The scripture is fulfilled** <note>original: "Impleta est scriptura"</note>] This should be added, and so it is read in the more corrected books: "fulfilled *by* this scripture."
21 **Surely you will say** <note>original: "Utique dicetis"</note>] The Greek is *Pantôs ereite*, that is, "Doubtless you will say." For it is an adverb of confirmation.
22 **How great things we have heard** <note>original: "Quanta audivimus"</note>] The Greek *hosa* means "which," or "whatever." <margin>F</margin> And so the author of the Homilies on Luke reads it, which the common people read under the title of Origen.
23 **In truth I say to you** <note>original: "In veritate dico vobis"</note>] The Greeks add a conjunction that is not idle: "But in truth I say to you." For this part stands in opposition to the upper part which mentions contempt. And so the order is to be arranged: "You despise me because I am present, but it is not given to all to have such a one as I am."
24 **Because his word was in power** <note>original: "Quia in potestate erat sermo ipsius"</note>] No one is ignorant of what it means to be "in power." And here, according to the property of the Hebrew speech, it means the speech of Jesus was joined with authority and power. Thus elsewhere, "he will come in virtue" is said for "he will come with virtue."
25 **Let be** <note>original: "Sine"</note>] The Greek *Ea*. Which nevertheless is sometimes an adverb of one exclaiming. Concerning the figure of speech, "what to you and to me," it has already been discussed more than once.
26 **I know you who you are** <note>original: "Scio te quis sis"</note>] The Greek *oida se tis ei*, that is, "I know who you are, namely that Holy One of God."
27 **And fear was made** <note>original: "Et factus est pavor"</note>] The Greek *thambos*, which often translates as "stupor" or "amazement." It is...

28 <note>original: "Divulgabatur fama"</note> **The report was spread]** <note>original: "ἐξεπορεύετο ἦχος αὐτοῦ"</note> "A sound concerning him went out." The noun comes from the verb *echein*, which means to resonate, from which "Echo" is also named, who returns the voice she receives; because fame rings out, and for one voice it returns many. From the same root is composed the word *Catechumen* <note>A person receiving basic instruction in the Christian faith; literally "one being sounded into" or "instructed".</note>.

29 <note>original: "Magnis febribus"</note> **With great fevers]** <note>original: "πυρετῷ μεγάλῳ"</note> that is, with a high fever. You might ask, Reader, what difference it makes whether you read "great fevers" (plural) or "a great fever" (singular). Let no one philosophize here without cause by treating this with an allegorical sense, as if many fevers held the same woman. Nor is it a "fourth-day" fever <note>a recurring fever characteristic of malaria</note>, but a "continuous" one, which elsewhere is translated as "to be constrained." Nevertheless, the Latin Translator rendered the *sense* rather than the literal word.

30 <note>original: "Et stans super illam"</note> **And standing over her]** <note>original: "Καὶ ἐπιστὰς ἐπάνω αὐτῆς"</note>. The Translator’s phrasing sounds just as if Jesus had stepped on the woman with his foot. Whether this is true, I do not know; it seems more probable that he stood near and, with a bowed body, leaned over her, like one calling to a sleeper.

31 <note>original: "imperavit febri"</note> **He commanded the fever]** <note>original: "ἐπετίμησε"</note>, that is, he rebuked. Perhaps it was originally written "he rebuked the fever," following the Greek style. And being offended by the novelty of the construction, the translator changed "rebuked" to "commanded"—something we have detected happening elsewhere, and we will point it out in its proper place. Furthermore, regarding what follows, **and he dismissed her**, I would have preferred it be rendered **and he left her**, lest Christ seem to have discarded the woman, if I may put it that way.

32 <note>original: "Et surgens ministrabat illis"</note> **And rising she served them]** Rendered somewhat awkwardly, since it should have been said, "having been raised, she served them," or "she rose and served them."

33 <note>original: "Cum autem sol occidisset"</note> **Now when the sun had set]** <note>original: "Δύνοντος δὲ τοῦ ἡλίου"</note>, that is, "while the sun was setting," or "with the sun indeed setting." It is likely they hurried more because night was looming.

34 <note>original: "Quia sciebant"</note> **Because they knew]** <note>original: "ὅτι ᾔδεισαν τὸν Χριστὸν αὐτὸν εἶναι"</note>. And the sense here can be that they knew themselves, or him, to be the Christ. So that

35 <note>original: "Quia & aliis civitatibus"</note> **Because also to other cities]** Here, Hugo Cardinalis noted that the conjunction is redundant, writing that it is a pleonasm <note>The use of more words than necessary</note> from the idiom of the Hebrew language.

1 <note>original: "Venerunt in eum"</note> **They came upon him]** <note>original: "ἐν τῷ τὸν ὄχλον ἐπικεῖσθαι αὐτῷ"</note>, that is, "when the crowd rushed upon him," or "urged him."

2 <note>original: "Præceptor"</note> **Master]** <note>original: "Ἐπιστάτα"</note>. It is not *didaskale* <note>teacher</note>, nor *kathegeta* <note>guide/instructor</note>, but a third thing, which sounds like "overseer" or "prefect."

3 <note>original: "Venirent & adjuvarent eos"</note> **They should come and help them]** It should have been said this way; it is not "and in the other ship" rather than "another."

4 <note>original: "Ita ut pene mergerentur"</note> **So that they almost sank]** "Almost" is not added in the Greek, nor in the ancient manuscripts, specifically in the "Golden" one. But some Reader, not wanting the Apostles to perish there, added "almost."

<insert>F</insert> 5 <note>original: "In captura piscium"</note> **In the catch of fish]** This part is not to be referred to the verb "they were," but to the phrase "amazement possessed," so that you understand they were stupefied because of such a great catch of fish.

6 <note>original: "Ex hoc jam"</note> **From this moment now]** <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν"</note>, that is, "hereafter."

7 <note>original: "Eris capiens"</note> **You will be catching]** <note>original: "ζωγρῶν"</note>. Now *zogrein* is properly to catch alive, as is done in war—a word composed of *zoos* (alive) and *agreyo* (I hunt, or catch by hunting). Nowadays, those who invade the Turks to slaughter and despoil them prefer to take them dead rather than alive. Indeed, we hunt for the money of the Turks rather than the Turks themselves.

8 <note>original: "Volo, mundare"</note> **I will, be cleansed]** "Cleanse" is passive and in the imperative mood: <note>original: "καθαρίσθητι"</note> "be made clean."

9 <note>original: "Sed vade, ostende"</note> **But go, show]** Here nothing was to be added, specifically, "he said." *But go, show yourself to the priest.* Lest anyone think he did not do this with religious intent, he did the same in the Acts of the Apostles, saying, "when he had heard," he said, "through my mouth."

---

...it succeeded the carnal Sabbath of the Law; first, because it was preferred over that Sabbath which it succeeded, just as the second Adam <note>A theological title for Jesus</note> was preferred over the first Adam. Bede follows this and gathers almost similar points. Saint Jerome, in his Letter to Rusticus the Monk, relates that when he was staying with Gregory Nazianzen, he proposed this question to him: what did the "second-first" Sabbath <note>original: "sabbatum δευτερόπρωτον" (deuteroproton). This is a famously difficult term in Luke 6:1 found in some ancient manuscripts.</note> mean in Luke? But Gregory—as he did not, I believe, have a ready answer—evaded it with a joke: "I will tell you," he said, "before the people, where with everyone shouting and applauding, you will be forced, willing or not, to agree with us." Nicholas of Lyra <note>A 14th-century biblical exegete</note> leaps over this difficulty entirely. Hugh of Saint-Cher <note>A 13th-century cardinal and commentator</note> adds that it is called "second-first" because it is the one immediately following the previous one. Yet by this logic, all Sabbaths would be "second-first," except the one that was the first of all. The same diligent man reminds us that "second-first" is two words, lest even an unwary person might easily err: so that, just as among the Greeks a single compound word is made from two, so too among the Latins he would make one, and say "second-first" <note>original: "secundoprimo"</note>, just as Plautus said "Tragicocomedy," and we say "Gallo-Greece."

For my part, I have found nothing yet among the authors on this matter that is satisfactory. However, let us record here what Theophylactus, the Greek interpreter (though more recent), produced on this passage, and indeed in his own words: <note>original Greek: "Οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι πᾶσαν ἑορτὴν σάββατον ὠνόμαζον... [etc.]"</note> "The Jews," he says, "called every feast a Sabbath; for 'Sabbath' means rest. Often, therefore, a festival fell on the Day of Preparation <note>The day before the Sabbath</note>, and they called the preparation 'Sabbath' because of the festival. Therefore, that which was properly the Sabbath they named 'second-first,' as it was the second from another preceding festival and Sabbath." So far Theophylactus. John Chrysostom, in his fortieth Homily on Matthew, indicates that this is the Sabbath mentioned in the twelfth chapter: adding that it is called "second-first" when the rest and leisure were doubled, as much for the Lord's Sabbath as for another solemnity following it. It is truly a pitiful thing to say how soon Peter Comestor <note>A 12th-century theological writer</note> twists himself in this place, trying to explain what "first-second" is, turning himself every which way and not even escaping thus. Nor does Hugh of Saint-Cher do much better. It would have been simpler to say, "I do not know." Nor do I care to examine what Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville</note> divines here, or others like him. This could be explained better by a Jew, if they could bring anything relevant to the matter. Recently a certain Monk, and likewise a Professor of Theology, was asked at a banquet by an errand scholar (one of a different branch of study) what the "second-first" Sabbath in Luke meant; he denied that any such thing was found anywhere in the Gospels, which he otherwise claimed to know thoroughly. When the other man asserted it was in Luke, this "bold warrior" challenged him to a wager: "I will stake this habit <note>original: "cappa" (the hooded cloak of a monk)</note> of mine," he said, "if Luke wrote any such thing anywhere."

2 **I will ask you**] <note>original: "Ἐπερωτήσω"</note> that is, I shall question.

3 **Is it lawful on the Sabbath**] <note>original: "τί ἔξεστι"</note> that is, what is allowed, or whether it is allowed, since he is asking about two options. The translator read "if" <note>original: "εἰ"</note> instead of "what" <note>original: "τί"</note>.

4 **His hand was restored**] The Greek manuscript adds "healthy as the other" <note>original: "ὑγιὴς ὡς ἡ ἄλλη"</note>. Truly, I do not know if this was added here from elsewhere.

5 **They were filled with madness**] <note>original: "ἀνοίας"</note> that is, with dementia or folly.

6 **Simon, whom he named**] <note>original: "ὃν καὶ ὠνόμασε Πέτρον"</note> that is, whom he also named Peter; or whom he named the same, that you may understand him as having two names, although elsewhere he calls it a surname.

7 **James of Alphaeus**] Understand "son"; although the translator ought to have added what is understood in the Greek article.

8 **And the seacoast of Tyre**] <note>original: "καὶ τῆς παραλίου Τύρου"</note> that is, and the maritime region of Tyre. Formerly Tyre was an island, later made a peninsula by Alexander the Great acting with royal madness. "Maritime" can be taken as a noun, like the "suburbs" or "region," just as he previously spoke of the "hill country" of Judea. In the Constance manuscript, a correction had changed the place; it seemed to have been written "the maritime parts of Tyre and Sidon," for both cities are markets on the seashore.

9 **And Sidon**] It is a wonder why he left the Greek genitive case here, unless, as I said, he thought both should be left, as if to understand "region," in this manner: "from the maritime part of Tyre and Sidon," that is, from the extreme part which faces the sea.

10 **Blessed are the poor**] Here that heavenly Doctor <note>Jesus</note> opens his secret philosophy, which he descended from heaven to earth to deliver to his own. We allow this to be abandoned by the common crowd of Christians and to grow obsolete while we busy ourselves with other trifles, even though these things should be especially impressed upon the minds of all. If this were done, we would not everywhere be fighting so much over frivolous things, for a little money, for the vainest titles of power, or for any slight injury. These are the things that truly make Christians, not the cleverness of the Sophists or the followers of Ockham <note>Nominalist philosophers</note>, or the cold regulations of men.

11 **They revile you**] <note>original: "ὀνειδίσωσι"</note> that is, they affect you with reproaches.

<margin>A</margin> <margin>12</margin> *Woe when all men speak well of you*] Or, as it is read in the ancient manuscripts, *when they have spoken well of you*. *For in the same way their fathers did to the prophets*. The Greeks read not "prophets," but *pseudoprophetais* <note>original: ψευδοπροφήταις</note>, that is, "false prophets," which agrees with several more corrected Latin manuscripts, though Paulinus objects. In the Corseiendonfensi manuscript, "false" (*pseudo*) was added by a more recent hand, just as in the Constantiensi. From this, a suspicion arises in me that the copies of both languages varied. I do not know if the genuine reading is "prophets." However, since the sentence at first sight seems harsher, I think some minor scholar was offended and changed the writing. In my judgment, it fits well that we read "prophets" here too: in the former case they cast out the prophets because they spoke the truth; here they did so to the prophets because they demanded flattery rather than truth from them. But if another reading pleases someone more, I would not strongly fight it. For above, He spoke the same words concerning the prophets. But here, He speaks concerning the flattery of prophets. There, "they did" meant "they afflicted"; here, "they did" means "they presented themselves and were soothed by their flattery." From Ambrose it cannot be gathered what he read. Certainly, Bede reads and interprets it as "prophets." Irenaeus has "false prophets." Theophylactus reads "prophets," but in his commentary, he does not touch upon this word.

<margin>13</margin> *And he who strikes you*] The sudden change in number <note>from plural to singular</note> serves to emphasize the precept, so that each person should hear it as if it were said to him alone. And a little later it returns to the plural, *and as you want them to do*.

<margin>14</margin> *Takes away your cloak*] *himation* <note>original: ἱμάτιον</note>, that is, a cloak, which is the outer garment. For the tunic is beneath the cloak. Hence that saying of Plautus: "The tunic is closer than the cloak."

<margin>15</margin> *And if you do good to those who love you*] *And if you do good to those who do good*, that is, *if you benefit those who benefit you*: the ancient Latin manuscripts agree. The translator seems to have read "those who love."

<margin>16</margin> *Since even sinners do this*] *do the same thing*.

<margin>17</margin> *Sinners lend to sinners*] *daneizousin* <note>original: δανείζουσιν</note>, that is, they give a loan. For it is the same word He used above. However, the translator, understanding "lending" <note>original: fenerari</note> as a vice <note>usury</note>, did not dare to use that word when speaking of upright things. Therefore, there he said "to give a loan," and here "to lend," although in Greek the word is the same in both places, which is nevertheless ambiguous for them. For both he who gives a loan without interest "lends" <note>daneizei</note>, and he who gives at interest "lends." But here it should have been translated consistently as "to give a loan." For He is not discussing the profit of usurers, but the mutual duties of friends among themselves. Even among the impious you will find someone who trusts his money as a loan to a friend. If the disciples of Christ do the same, they do nothing great. For Christ devalues—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> will be and will weep. <margin>26</margin> 12 Woe to you, when all <margin>26</margin> men have praised you: for in this way their fathers did to the false prophets. But I say to you who hear, <margin>27</margin> Love your enemies: do good to those who hate you. Bless those who curse you, and pray for <margin>28</margin> those who slander you. <margin>13</margin> To him who strikes you on the cheek <margin>29</margin> offer the other also: and from him who <margin>14</margin> takes away your cloak, do not withhold the tunic either. To everyone who demands <margin>30</margin> from you, give; and from him who takes away what is yours, do not ask it back. And just as you want men to do to you, you <margin>31</margin> also do to them likewise. And if you love those who <margin>32</margin> love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those by whom they are loved. <margin>B</margin> 15 And if you do good to those <margin>33</margin> who do good to you, what credit is that to you? <margin>16</margin> for even sinners do this. And if you lend to <margin>34</margin> those from whom you hope you will receive back, what credit is that to you? For even 17 sinners lend to sinners, so that they may receive back equal amounts. <margin>18</margin> Rather, love your enemies, <margin>35</margin> and do good, and lend, 19 hoping for nothing from it: and your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High: 20 because He himself is kind toward the ungrateful and the evil. Be therefore merciful, just as your Father <margin>36</margin> is merciful. Do not judge, and you will not be judged. <margin>37</margin> Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. 21 Forgive, and it will be forgiven you. Give, and it will be given to you. A <margin>38</margin> <margin>C</margin> good measure, 22 pressed down, and shaken together, 23 and overflowing, they will give into your lap. For with the same measure by which you measure, it will be measured back to you. And He spoke <margin>39</margin> a comparison to them: Can the blind lead the blind? Will they not both fall into the pit? The <margin>40</margin> disciple is not above his teacher: but everyone will be perfect 24 like his teacher. Why do you see <margin>41</margin> the speck in your brother's eye, 25 but the beam that is in your own eye, you do not notice? Or how <margin>42</margin> can you say to your brother, Brother, let me cast out the speck that is in your eye, while you yourself do not see the beam in your eye? Hypocrite, first cast out the beam from your eye, <margin>D</margin> and then you will succeed in casting out the speck that is in the eye of your brother. For there is no good tree that makes <margin>43</margin> bad fruit: nor a bad tree, making good fruit. For every tree is known by its own fruit: <margin>44</margin>

---

Christ devalues common favors, as they are shared with Heathens and evil men, so that He may call us to those things that are peculiar to Christians, that there might be something in which they excel the rest. But things have returned to such a point that, if you remove the title and the ceremonies, by this mark you can scarcely distinguish a Christian from a Heathen. I speak of the common crowd of Christians, not of everyone.

<margin>18</margin> *But nevertheless*] *Plēn* <note>original: Πλήν</note>, that is, "Rather" or "Indeed."
<margin>19</margin> *Hoping for nothing from it*] *medēn apelpizontes* <note>original: μηδὲν ἀπελπίζοντες</note>. In Greek it is a compound word, *apelpizein*, to hope for something back from a thing. For it refers, I think, to the interest that returns from a loan. For the Ancients interpret it in this sense. <margin>E</margin>

<margin>20</margin> *because He himself is kind*] *chrēstos* <note>original: χρηστός</note>, which he frequently translates as "good." But it sounds like convenient, and humane, and easy to gratify, which "kind" also nearly declares; a matter spoken of and to be spoken of in many places.

<margin>21</margin> *Forgive, and it will be forgiven you*] In better Latin it was, "Release, and it will be released." It can hardly be believed what tragedies certain sycophants, masked in cowls, have stirred up among the unlearned common people because in the Lord's Prayer they preferred "Release to us our debts, as we also release," as if an atrocious insult were done to Christ if someone prefers to say "release" rather than "dismiss" <note>original: remitte vs dimitte</note>. And yet Saint Augustine, in his book of fifty Homilies, Homily twenty-nine, citing this place, reads: "Release, and it will be released": why do they not cry out against him equally?

<margin>D</margin> <margin>22</margin> *Pressed down and shaken together*] *pepiesmenon* <note>original: πεπιεσμένον</note>, which sounds like "pressed." For this is done in dry goods, so that the measure may hold more. And "shaken together" is *sesaleumenon* <note>original: σεσαλευμένον</note>, that is, "concussed." For in this way too, it happens that the vessel with which we measure holds more. For Christ delights in using comparisons of these things, which are very well known to the senses of all.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>23</margin> *And overflowing*] *hyperekchynomenon* <note>original: ὑπερεκχυνόμενον</note>. The translator sufficiently expressed the Greek word, which is said because that which the measure cannot hold is poured out from above.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>24</margin> *If he be as his teacher*] The Greek has it differently, namely in this manner: *katērtismenos de pas estai hōs ho didaskalos autou* <note>original: κατηρτισμένος δὲ πᾶς ἔσται ὡς ὁ διδάσκαλος αὑτοῦ</note>, that is, "but everyone will be perfect like his teacher." For Christ does not forbid the disciple from being perfect, but He does not want the disciple to claim for himself what the teacher did not claim, nor to try to go before him: but he will be perfect in this way, if he imitates his teacher in all things. And in this sense Theophylactus reads and interprets. Irenaeus also cites this near the end of his work. Christ did not claim the riches and honors of this world; if the vicar of Christ strives for these, he seems to claim something more for himself than Christ claimed.

<margin>25</margin> *But the beam, which is in your eye*] *en tō idiō ophthalmō* <note>original: ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ ὀφθαλμῷ</note>, that is, in your very own eye, or in your own eye.

<margin>26</margin> *Who dug deep*] He translates the sense correctly; otherwise in Greek it is <note>original: ὃς ἔσκαψε καὶ ἐβάθυνε</note>, that is, to render it word-for-word, *who dug and deepened*.

<margin>27</margin> *Building his house*] <note>original: οἰκοδομήσαντι</note>, that is, "who built," in the past tense. Nor is it *upon the rock*, which the Greeks say <note>original: ἐπὶ τὴν πέτραν</note>, but *upon the earth*, or *on the ground*.

C <margin>1</margin> *While he was announcing*] From this passage, it is clear that what Matthew calls a <term>child</term><note>original: παῖδα</note> was not a son, but a servant: for <note>original: δοῦλος</note> signifies nothing other than a slave or a domestic servant. And as it is translated here,

<margin>2</margin> *He was about to die*] <note>original: ἔμελλε τελευτᾷν</note>, could be translated as *he was giving up the ghost*, or *he was in danger of death*, or certainly *he was beginning to die*. For he translates it this way several times. Furthermore,

<margin>3</margin> *Who was precious to him*] He has spoken in a new way. For *Dear* pertains both to a thing and to a person. *Precious* pertains only to a thing, unless used metaphorically. Therefore, <note>original: ἔντιμος</note> should have been translated as *dear*, or *held in high regard*.

F *earnestly*, and *assiduously*. And because the conjunction *was* should be omitted. It should be noted how Jewish this commendation is, which Luke did not record without reason: *He loves, they say, our nation, and he himself built our synagogue for us*. In the same way today, some people, while pretending piety, flatter the rich. "He gives generously to the Brothers," "he built part of the Monastery for us," "he favors our Order," "he bequeathed so much," even though his own children were defrauded. As if what is given to them, perhaps for luxury, is given to God; but what is left to children or needy relatives is not given to God. These remarks do not aim to condemn generosity, especially toward pious Monks, but to warn those who do nothing else but try to capture the wealth of the rich.

<margin>5</margin> *Not even in Israel have I found such great faith*] Ambrose showed long ago that in the Latin manuscripts this was the reading: *In no one have I found such great faith in Israel*, whereas according to the Greeks it should read, *Not even in Israel have I found such great faith*.

<margin>6</margin> *His disciples*] The Greeks add <note>original: ἱκανοὶ</note>, that is, *many*.

<margin>7</margin> *In that very hour*] <note>original: Ἐν αὐτῇ δὲ τῇ ὥρᾳ</note>. In the same hour: although in this place it signifies a general time rather than a specific sixty-minute hour.

8 **The poor have the good news preached to them]** I wonder what happened 
to Laurentius <note>original: "Laurentio," referring to the scholar Lorenzo Valla</note> 
when he preferred the active "they preach the Gospel" rather than the passive 
"the Gospel is preached to them" in this place. As if the meaning were that the 
poor preached the Gospel, and not rather that they received the Gospel. 
For just as the Greeks say, *I evangelize you* <note>original: "evangelizo te"</note> 
for "I bring you good news," so they say *he is evangelized* 
<note>original: "evangelizatur"</note> for "he received the joyful news," as 
we have indicated elsewhere. Although that could apply to the Apostles, 
nevertheless, the proof that the Messiah had come was not that the 
Apostles were preaching the Gospel, but that the humble and unlearned 
were being received into the grace of the Gospel. Moreover, the Lord alludes to the 
prophecy: "He has sent me to preach the good news to the poor." By this evidence, 
he signifies that he is the Christ. Furthermore, he calls the meek or gentle 
"poor" in the Hebrew manner, for whom the word <term>עני</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Ani," meaning poor or afflicted</note> 
is translated as "poor" by Jerome and as "meek" by the Seventy <note>The Septuagint</note>, 
because ferocity usually accompanies riches, and ferocity is unteachable.

9 **What did you go out]** In some ancient manuscripts, this passage is 
punctuated differently: *What did you go out into the desert? To see a reed 
shaken by the wind? But what did you go out? To see a prophet?* The same 
distinction could exist in the Greek, even if it does not change the 
meaning.

10 **Shaken by the wind]** <note>original Greek: "σαλευόμενον" (saleuomenon)</note>, 
that is, that which is driven or wavering. For it is a present passive participle. 
Accordingly, Ambrose reads "a reed to be moved by the wind," changing the 
participle into a verb so that the sense of time would be consistent. And 
it is indeed read this way in the "Golden Codex," in the Constance Codex, 
and many others.

11 **In precious clothing]** <note>original Greek: "ἐνδόξῳ" (endoxo)</note>, 
that is, glorious or splendid. For it is not the word for "honorable" or "costly." 
But if he had wanted to speak in pure Latin, the form of the Greek speech 
would have had to be changed. For the Greeks say "the one in purple," 
meaning the one dressed in purple. It should therefore have been translated 
this way: *those who use splendid clothing and live in luxury are in 
royal places, or in the palaces of kings.* For the Greeks use the term 
"in the royal [places]" <note>original Greek: "ἐν τοῖς βασιλείοις" (en tois basileiois)</note>.

12 **Certainly I say]** <note>original Greek: "Ναὶ" (Nai)</note>, 
which is an affirmative.

13 **They rejected against themselves]** <note>original Greek: "ἠθέτησαν εἰς ἑαυτοὺς" (ethetesan eis heautous)</note>, 
that is, they were spattered against themselves. For he means that 
those [the people] received it for their own good, while these [the Pharisees] 
rejected it to their own harm. Ambrose reads "in themselves." The word *into* 
<note>original Greek: "εἰς" (eis)</note> can also be taken in place of *in* 
<note>original Greek: "ἐν" (en)</note>, and thus the sense would be *within themselves*, 
that is, in their hearts, since they did not dare to openly condemn what 
so greatly pleased the people.

14 **And speaking to one another]** <note>original Greek: "καὶ προσφωνοῦσιν ἀλλήλοις" (kai prosphonousin allelois)</note>, 
that is, and calling out among themselves. We have spoken of the 
other things that follow in the commentary on Matthew.

15 **But he came]** <note>original Greek: "Ἐλήλυθε γὰρ" (Eleluthe gar)</note>, 
that is, "For he came," supported also by ancient manuscripts. 
And the word is not "devourer," but "glutton" <term>phagos</term>.

16 **And drinking wine]** <term>oinopotes</term> <note>original Greek: "οἰνοπότης"</note>, 
that is, a wine-drinker or wine-bibber, a word of insult.

17 **Wisdom by all her children]** In Luke, "all" is added, so that 
we may understand that the doctrine of Christ pleased all who were 
the children of wisdom. And thus Ambrose reads, and not only reads 
it, but also interprets it: and likewise it is written in the more 
corrected books, both Greek and Latin.
<margin>E</margin>
18 **Behold a woman, who was a sinner in the city]** 
<note>original Greek: "Καὶ ἰδοὺ γυνὴ ἐν τῇ πόλει, ἥτις ἦν ἁμαρτωλός"</note>, 
that is, "And behold a woman in the city, who was a sinner," or 
"who had been a sinner."

19 **She began to wet with tears]** The translator omitted the word 
"weeping" <term>klaiousa</term> <note>original Greek: "κλαίουσα"</note>, though 
I do not know if it was added by some over-zealous person. Since 
it is almost understood by itself that she wept abundantly, she 
who wet his feet with tears. "And standing near his feet from 
behind, weeping, she began to wet..." that is, standing by his feet... 
Moreover, one can gather that the dining room was on an elevated 
platform according to the custom of the ancients, so that she, 
standing, touched his feet from behind the open couches on which 
they reclined.

20 **Who and what sort]** Again there is the word <term>potape</term> 
<note>original Greek: "ποταπὴ"</note>, which elsewhere Laurentius 
wanted to be translated as "how great," which certainly could 
not be done here unless he had said "how great a sinner." 
Certainly, the word carries a sense of wonder.

21 **To a certain moneylender]** <term>daneiste</term> 
<note>original Greek: "δανειστῇ"</note>, which sounds not only like 
a moneylender <note>fenerator</note> but also a creditor; it is a noun 
derived from the verb "to lend" <term>daneizo</term>, about which we 
spoke above. In this place, "creditor" certainly fits better, 
since he is speaking of a duty. Otherwise, who ever heard of a 
moneylender forgiving anyone a debt?

22 **One owed denarii]** One should say "one and the other," 
not "another," or "the other and the other," if he had studied 
speaking in pure Latin.

23 **He gave to both]** <term>echarisato</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐχαρίσατο"</note>, 
it was better here to say "forgave."

24 **Which therefore will love more]** The Greeks have: 
"Which of them therefore, tell me, will love him more?"

25 **I suppose]** <term>Upolambano</term> <note>original Greek: "Ὑπολαμβάνω"</note>, 
that is, "I think," or "I estimate."

<margin>26 My feet</margin> "Upon my feet" <note>original: ἐπὶ τοὺς πόδας μου</note>, that is, *on my feet*, as the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> rendered it, and afterwards, *over my feet*.
<margin>27 Did not cease to kiss</margin> <note>original: οὐ διέλιπε καταφιλοῦσα</note>. The author elegantly changed the participle into an infinitive verb. For in Greek it is, *she did not fail while kissing*.
<margin>28 To whom less is forgiven</margin> In Greek it is *little* <note>original: ὀλίγον</note>, that is, *small or a tiny amount, not "less"*.
<margin>29 Within themselves</margin> The Greek phrase is ambiguous; it can be taken as *within themselves, so that they merely thought it, or among themselves, so that they spoke together*.
<margin>1 Through cities and villages</margin> Ancient manuscripts have *through city and village*, in the singular number, truly rendered word-for-word from the Greek <note>original: κατὰ πόλιν καὶ κώμην</note>. But in Greek, this is just as valid as saying *city-by-city and village-by-village*, that is, *through individual cities and villages*. Hence the Translator changed the number not entirely wrongly.
<margin>2 From the cities</margin> <note>original: καὶ τῶν κατὰ πόλιν ἐπιπορευομένων</note>, that is, *and of those who were approaching city-by-city, that is, from individual cities*.
<margin>3 Among the thorns</margin> <note>original: ἐν μέσῳ ἀκανθῶν</note>, that is, *in the middle of thorns*. Yet the Translator changed this correctly.
<margin>4 And the thorns grew up</margin> <note>original: καὶ συμφυεῖσαι αἱ ἄκανθαι</note>, that is, *and the thorns having sprouted together*, which is to say, alongside the stalks of the crop.
<margin>5 For those on the rock</margin> <note>original: Οἱ δὲ ἐπὶ τῆς πέτρας, οἳ ὅταν ἀκούσωσι</note>, that is, *Those indeed on the rock, who when they have heard, as substances, are women, or they received the seed*.
<margin>6 Because they believe for a time</margin> The Greek is *who* <note>original: οἳ</note>, not *because* <note>original: ὅτι</note>: this is supported even by the ancient copies.
<margin>7 Going they are choked</margin> Instead of *going* <note>Latin: euntes</note>, the Greek is *traveling* <note>original: πορευόμενοι</note>. It appears this participle is not used as a deponent verb <note>a verb with passive form but active meaning</note>, but as a passive from the word meaning "to provide." While that word certainly means *to do* or *to lead*, I suspect it might also mean *to bring abundance*. For that is...

---

...to provide, so that we may arrange it in this manner: *they are choked while being overwhelmed by cares, and riches, and pleasures*. However, I leave this to the judgment of the learned reader. For it can be understood as the abundance of riches increasing over the progress of time. What if *traveling* <note>original: πορευόμενοι</note> was said instead of *engaging in business*, so that it pertains to merchants?

<margin>8 They do not bring back fruit</margin> <note>original: τελεσφοροῦσι</note>. He rendered a single Greek word with two. The Greek voice, however, sounds not only of "fruit," but of bringing forth fruit that is perfect and complete in its own time. For even those seeds sprout, but they do not produce the fruit which the farmer expects. Just as the word *End* <note>original: Τέλος</note> signifies "conclusion" to the Greeks, so also it signifies "tax" or "profit" which is taken from any thing. Euripides felt this when he said, "it seems some people farm the 'profit' of the vines." From a bad tree, bad fruit comes. The word *bearing* <note>original: φόρος</note> sounds the same to the Greeks, from bringing forth, just as *end* <note>original: τέλος</note> is from the conclusion, because the fruits finally come forth in their own time. Hence the composite word *to bring fruit to maturity* <note>original: τελεσφορεῖν</note>.

<margin>9 Good and best</margin> <note>original: ἐν καρδίᾳ καλῇ καὶ ἀγαθῇ</note>, that is, *in a heart honest and good*; both are in the positive degree. But the doubling serves for emphasis, as if you were to say, "extraordinarily good." In this place in certain books, I found the phrase added: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear."

<margin>10 And under a bed</margin> Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous Renaissance humanist scholar</note> rightly changes the adverb *under* <note>Latin: subter</note> into the preposition *under*.

<margin>11 Which not manifest</margin> In the Greek, both verbs are in the future tense: *it will become manifest* and *it will be known*. Therefore, by merely changing the mood of the verb, he would have conveniently rendered it thus: *For nothing is hidden, which will not become manifest; nothing secret, which will not be known and come into the open.*

12 *Into the open*] <note>original: "In palam"</note> *eis phaneron*, that is, *into public view, or into the courtyard.* The Translator did not speak in pure Latin, nor did he render the Greek words accurately.
13 *See then how you hear*] <note>original: "pōs akouete"</note>, that is, *in what manner you listen.*
14 *For he who has*] <note>original: "hos gar an echē"</note>, that is, *for whosoever has, or shall have had.*
15 *What he thinks he has*] <note>original: "ho dokei echein"</note>, that is, *what he seems to have.* Although the Greek phrase has a double meaning: *he seems to himself to have*, and *he seems to others to have.*
16 *And they could not approach*] "To approach" <note>original: "Adire"</note> is the reading to be used, supported by ancient manuscripts. For in Greek it is *ouk ēdynanto syntychein autō*, that is, *and they were not able to meet with him.* Truly, this error happened not through the fault of the Translator, but the Scribes.
17 *Into a boat*] <note>original: "eis ploion"</note>, that is, *into a ship*; for this author is pleased by nothing except diminutives.
18 *We cross over the lake*] <note>original: "Di-elthōmen eis to peran tēs limnēs"</note>, that is, *Let us cross into the further parts of the lake.* Then, *and they set sail* <note>original: "anēchthēsan"</note>, is rather *they loosened [the cables]*, that is, *they departed from the shore having been launched.* I am not sure if it is aptly said *to cross the lake* <note>original: "transfretari stagnum"</note>, since a "fretum" <note>strait</note> is rapid, while a "stagnum" <note>lake/pool</note> takes its name from "standing" <note>standing water</note>, just as the Greeks think *limnē* <note>lake</note> is named from "remaining too much" <note>original: "lian menein"</note>. Although in Homer even the ocean is called a *limnē*, as in the Iliad:
->The Dove shall loose the winds from the woolly lake.<- <note>original: "Peleios d’ anemous lysei perimallia limnēn"</note>
And here the Lake of Tiberias is in some places called a "sea" in the Gospels. Indeed, Jerome indicates this is a lake in his *Hebraic Places*: *Gergesa,* he says, *where the Savior restored to health those vexed by demons, is demonstrated today as a village above the mountain next to the Lake of Tiberias, into which the swine were precipitated.*
19 *They were being filled*] I know this was corrupted by Scribes, yet because it comes so close to the true reading, lest the error prevail, I thought it necessary to warn that *complebantur* <note>they were filling up</note> is the reading, as agreed by the oldest Latin copies, namely...

<column-break/>

18 and will come into the open. 13 See therefore how you hear: 14 for whoever has, to him it shall be given, and whoever has not, even 15 what he thinks he has, shall be taken from him. Then his mother 19 and his brothers came to him, 16 and they could not approach him because of the crowd. And it was told to him and said, "Your mother and your brothers stand outside, wishing to see you." He answering 21 said to them, "My mother and my brothers are these who hear the word of God and do it." Now it happened on a certain day, that he went 17 into a ship, and his disciples, and he said to them, 18 "Let us cross to the further shore of the lake": and they set sail. But as they were sailing, he fell asleep, and a storm of wind fell upon the lake, and 19 they were being filled and were in danger. And coming to him, they woke him, saying, 20 "Master, Master, we are perishing!" 21 But he, having awakened, rebuked the wind and the storm of water: and they ceased, and a calm occurred. And he said to them, "Where is your 25 faith?" But they, being afraid, wondered, saying among themselves, "Who do you think this is, that he commands even the winds and the water, and they obey him?" And they sailed to the region of the 22 26 Gadarenes, which is opposite Galilee. And when he had 27 gone out from the ship to the land, there met him 23 a certain man from the city, who had a demon now for many times, and did not wear a garment, nor stay in a house, but in the tombs. When he saw Jesus, and 28 cried out, he fell down before him, and with a loud voice said, "What business have I with you, Jesus, Son of the most high God? I pray you, do not torment me." For he was commanding the unclean spirit to come out of the man: for frequently it 24 had seized him, and he was bound with chains, 25 and kept in shackles, and having broken the bonds, he was driven by the demon into the deserts. Now 32 there was there a herd of many swine feeding on the mountain: and they begged him that he would permit them to enter into them: and he permitted them. Therefore the demons went out from 33 the man, and entered into the swine, and with an impulse the herd went headlong into the lake, and was suffocated. Furthermore, when 34 those who were feeding them saw what had happened, they fled, and told the news in the city and the villages. And they went out to see what was done: and they came to Jesus, and found the man sitting, from whom the demons had gone out, clothed, and in a sound mind, at the feet of Jesus, and they were afraid. <margin>B</margin> <margin>C</margin> <margin>D</margin> <margin>E</margin> <margin>F</margin> ...being filled <note>original: "syneplyrounto"</note>. A certain Latin manuscript adds *with waves.*
20 *Master*] In Greek it is *Epistata, epistata*, that is, *Master, master*, so that you may understand both that Jesus had fallen into a deep sleep, and the disciples were calling out urgently.
21 *But he rising*] <note>original: "Ho de egertheis"</note>, that is, *But he, having been awakened.*
22 *Of the Gerasenes*] <note>original: "tōn Gadarēnōn"</note>, that is, *of the Gadarenes*, which we have already discussed more than once before.
23 *A certain man*] The Greeks add *ek tēs poleōs*, that is, *from the city*, which I find nowhere added among the Latins: nor was it possible to gather from Ambrose's Commentaries that he read it so. I find it in the Greek of Theophylact. Although it should rather have been translated *from that city*, so that you understand the demoniac came out of the city of Gadara.
24 *It snatched him*] <note>original: "synērpakei auton"</note>, that is, *it had seized him.*
25 *And kept in shackles*] <note>original: "kai pedais phylassomenos, kai diarrēssōn ta desma ēlauneto"</note>, that is, *and he was being served in shackles, and breaking the bonds he was driven, etc.* This could have been translated more smoothly in this way: *and though he was being kept in shackles, yet breaking the bonds he was carried by the spirit into desert places.*
26 *In the desert*] <note>original: "eis tas erēmous"</note>, that is, *into the deserts*, so that *places* is understood. And so it is read in the more corrected Latin manuscripts.
27 *Into the abyss*] This is a Greek word; in Latin it is called a *vorago* <note>a deep pit or chasm</note>.
28 *Headlong*] <note>original: "kata tou krēmnou"</note>, that is, *through the precipice*, or *through the steep place.* And the oldest Latin manuscripts have it so.
29 *By a legion*] <note>original: "ho daimonistheis"</note>, that is, *he who was vexed by a demon, or agitated by demons.*
30 *The multitude of the region of the Gerasenes*] <note>original: "hapan to plēthos tēs perichōrou tōn Gadarēnōn"</note>, that is, *the entire multitude of the region everywhere neighboring the Gadarenes.* Ambrose either read *Gerasenes*, or thought the *Gerasenes and Gadarenes* were the same, when a little later he says, *He had left the Gerasenes* <unclear>although</unclear> *Christ etc.*

# ACCORDING TO LUKE. CHAPTER IX.

<margin>38</margin> ...having entered the boat, he returned. Now the man from whom the demons had gone out begged him that he might be with him; <margin>39</margin> but Jesus sent him away, saying, "Return to your own house, and tell what great things God has done for you." And he went away through the whole city, proclaiming what great things Jesus had done for <margin>40</margin> him. And it happened, when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him; for they were all <margin>41</margin> waiting for him. And behold, there came a man named Jairus, and he was a ruler of the synagogue; and falling at the feet of Jesus, he begged him to enter into <margin>42</margin> his house. For he had an only daughter about twelve years old, and she was dying. But as he went, <margin>43</margin> the crowds pressed against him. And a woman who had a flow of blood for twelve years, who had spent her whole living on physicians and could not be <margin>44</margin> healed by anyone, came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately the flow of <margin>45</margin> her blood stopped. And Jesus said, "Who is the one who touched me?" When all denied it, Peter and those with him said, "Master, the crowds surround you and press against <margin>46</margin> you, and you say, 'Who touched me?'" But Jesus said, "Someone touched me; for I perceived power going <margin>47</margin> out from me." When the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him, she declared to him in the presence of all the people for what reason she had touched him, and <margin>48</margin> how she was healed immediately. And he said to her, "Take heart, daughter, your faith has saved you; go in peace." <margin>49</margin> While he was still speaking, someone came from the ruler of the synagogue’s house, saying to him, "Your daughter is dead; do not trouble <margin>50</margin> the teacher." But Jesus, hearing it, answered him, <margin>51</margin> saying, "Do not fear, only believe, and she will be saved." And her spirit returned, and she rose up immediately; and <margin>56</margin> he commanded that something be given to her to eat. And her parents were amazed.
