And having called together the twelve, he gave them power and authority over all the <margin>2</margin> demons, and to heal diseases. And he sent them to preach the kingdom of God, and to heal those who were <margin>3</margin> sick. And he said to them, "Take nothing for the journey, neither staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money, <margin>4</margin> nor have two tunics each." And into whatever house...

<margin>31</margin> *But Jesus sent him away, saying*] Since the Translator <note>The "Translator" refers to the author of the Latin Vulgate, St. Jerome.</note> elsewhere uses <term>sent away</term> <note>original: "dimisit"</note> to mean "allowed" or "permitted," the reader should know that the Greek word here is <term>apelyse</term> <note>original: "ἀπέλυσε"</note>, which is to say: *he did not allow him to be with him, but sent him away.*

<margin>32</margin> *And she was dying*] <term>apethnesken</term> <note>original: "ἀπέθνησκεν"</note>. It could also be translated as *and she had died*, so that we might understand the girl had already breathed her last even then, although the father (who had left her while she was still clinging to life) did not yet know it. Indeed, I do not know if this word can be used otherwise.

<margin>33</margin> *And it happened while he went*] Although it has no impact on the meaning, the phrase <term>and it happened</term> <note>original: "καὶ ἐγένετο"</note> is not added in the Greek manuscripts I have seen.

<margin>34</margin> *By the crowds he was pressed*] <term>hoi ochloi syneppnigon auton</term> <note>original: "οἱ ὄχλοι συνέπνιγον αὐτὸν"</note>, that is, *the crowds were suffocating him*, which is to say, *they were constricting and squeezing him*. This is a different word from the one he soon translates as "press."

<margin>35</margin> *Which she had spent on physicians*] <term>hetis eis iatrous prosanalosasa holon ton bion, ouk ischysen hyp' oudenos therapeuthēnai</term> <note>original: "ἥτις εἰς ἰατροὺς προσαναλώσασα ὅλον τὸν βίον, οὐκ ἴσχυσεν ὑπ᾿ οὐδενὸς θεραπευθῆναι"</note>, that is, *who, because she had consumed her whole substance on physicians, could not be cured by anyone*. And a little later.

<margin>36</margin> *The crowds press and afflict you*] <term>synechousi se kai apothlibousi</term> <note>original: "συνέχουσί σε καὶ ἀποθλίβουσι"</note>. I would prefer: *they hem you in, or they squeeze you and harass you.*

<margin>37</margin> *For I also perceived*] In the Greek it is simply *for I perceived* <note>original: "nam ego novi"</note>, which agrees with the Pauline manuscript, though it disagrees with the <term>Confessionensian</term> <note>A reference to a specific manuscript used by Erasmus.</note>. Ambrose agrees with the Pauline.

<margin>38</margin> *That power went out from me*] <term>exelthousan ap' emou</term> <note>original: "ἐξελθοῦσαν ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ"</note>. The Translator rightly turned the participle into an infinitive verb here, though he did not do so in Matthew and Mark.

<margin>39</margin> *Go in peace*] <term>eis eirēnēn</term> <note>original: "εἰς εἰρήνην"</note>, that is, *into peace*: though the Greek preposition can be read both ways.

<margin>40</margin> *Someone came to the ruler of the synagogue*] This is how the Latin codices, even the ancient ones, consistently have it. It is not clear from Ambrose what he read. However, in Greek it is <term>para tō archisynagōgō legōn autō</term> <note>original: "παρὰ τῷ ἀρχισυναγώγῳ λέγων αὐτῷ"</note>, that is, *from the ruler of the synagogue, saying to him*. Truly, someone, offended by the absurdity that the speech presents at first glance, changed "from the ruler" to "to the ruler." Yet "from the house" was meant to be understood, as is common in such phrasing. But this was discussed more fully above regarding the fifth chapter of Mark.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>41</margin> *But he himself*] Here the Greeks add, <term>ekbalōn exō pantas</term> <note>original: "ἐκβαλὼν ἔξω πάντας"</note>, that is, *all having been put outside*: a detail which is added in the other Gospels. Although I do not find it added in Ambrose, and I do not know if it was transcribed here from elsewhere. It is argued that it would be vain or unfitting for only the parents to be astonished if that whole crowd, mentioned before, were present. Furthermore, he asks, what was the point of forbidding them to tell anyone if the deed was done with so many witnesses? Because of these things, it was thought necessary to add these words, which indeed seem consistently written in the Greek codices: *having put everyone out*. To me, as I said, they seem added from Mark and Matthew, both of whom testify that the crowd was put out. Matthew in chapter nine relates the crowd was put out, saying the same as Mark in chapter five, who reported that everyone had been put out except both parents of the girl and the disciples he had with him—namely three: James, Peter, and John, whom he had ordered to follow him alone a little before. Nor was there a reason why it should be added here, *all having been put outside*, since Luke testified a little before that Jesus did not allow anyone to enter where the girl lay, except the father and mother and the three disciples just mentioned. If we understand them to have been put out, how are they said to have been astonished? Nor was there a danger that the matter could not be concealed, since it was done with so few witnesses. Therefore, there is nothing for Laurentius <note>Laurentius Valla, a humanist scholar known for his critiques of the Vulgate.</note> to quibble about here. Only one
<margin>F</margin> difficulty remains: If, according to Luke, Jesus did not allow the crowd to enter, how is the "girl" spoken of? But it could have been that the crowd stayed in the vestibule or the courtyard, while the body was placed in the inner parts of the house.

<margin>42</margin> *And her spirit returned*] <term>epestrepse</term> <note>original: "ἐπέστρεψε"</note>. "Turned back" rather than "returned": unless perhaps the Translator read <term>anestrepse</term> <note>original: "ἀνέστρεψε"</note>.

<margin>1</margin> *For the journey*] <term>eis tēn hodon</term> <note>original: "εἰς τὴν ὁδὸν"</note>, that is, *on the way*. And "take" <note>original: "tuleritis"</note> is not from the word for "bearing" but from "carrying off." Do not carry anything away on the road or for the journey; that is, do not carry it along with you.

<margin>2</margin> *Nor two tunics*] <term>mēte ana dyo chitōnas</term> <note>original: "μήτε ἀνὰ δύο χιτῶνας"</note>, that is, *neither two tunics each*, meaning each person should not have two. Furthermore, <term>echein</term> <note>original: "ἔχειν", to have</note>, an infinitive verb, is used here in place of an imperative, in the Greek manner. Moreover, he said "tunic" not for just any garment, but for a specific type of garment, so you may understand that one is worn and the other is carried in a pack as a change of clothes.

### [Translator's Annotations]

3 **And from there do not depart** <note>original Latin: "Et inde ne exeatid"</note>] The Greek is different: *and from there go out* <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐκεῖθεν ἐξέρχεσθε</note>. He means that they should use only one house: that they should not leave for another place until they leave the city, so they do not appear unstable to anyone. Theophylact <note>An 11th-century archbishop and biblical commentator.</note> not only reads it this way but also interprets it so. It is clear this was changed not by the translator's fault but by a scribal error.

4 **In testimony upon them**] <note>original Greek: ἐπ᾿ αὐτούς</note>. I ask why it shouldn't be *against them* rather than *upon them*? Was there a deliberate effort to speak incorrectly?

5 **And he hesitated**] <note>original Greek: διηπόρει</note>. While this means *to hesitate*, it also means *to be perplexed, of two minds, and doubtful in spirit.* For he was afraid if the one he had killed had risen.

6 **Which is Bethsaida**] <note>original Greek: εἰς τόπον ἔρημον πόλεως καλουμένης Βηθσαϊδά</note>, that is, into a solitary place of a city which is called Bethsaida. In ancient copies I read "which is Bethsaida," so that you understand the desert near Bethsaida.

7 **Who needed care**] <note>original Greek: θεραπείας</note>. Why not rather "healing" <note>original Latin: curatione</note>, since he is speaking of diseases? It is more Latin and more fitting to express the Greek word.

8 **And the villages which are around**] <note>original Greek: εἰς τὰς κύκλῳ κώμας</note>, that is, into the surrounding villages or small towns. And again, he translates "fields" as "villas" <note>In this context, small farming settlements.</note>, which is not bad as long as it is understood correctly.

9 **Find food**] <note>original Greek: ἐπισιτισμόν</note>, that is, provisions: for *episitismos* means to furnish with food.

<meta>Catchword: about</meta>

<margin>A</margin> 4 And into whatever house you enter, stay there, and depart from there. 5 And whoever does not receive you, departing from that city, shake off even the dust from your feet as a testimony against them. 6 And having set out, they went around through the towns, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere. 7 Now Herod the tetrarch heard all that was done by him, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had risen from the dead; 8 by some, that Elijah had appeared; by others, that some prophet from the ancients had risen. 9 And Herod said, "John I have beheaded: but who is this, of whom I hear such things?" And he sought <margin>B</margin> to see him. 10 And the Apostles, having returned, told him whatever they had done. And taking them, he withdrew aside into a deserted place of a city called Bethsaida. 11 When the crowds knew this, they followed him: and he received them, and spoke to them of the kingdom of God, and those who had need of healing, he cured. 12 Now the day began to decline, and the twelve approaching said to him, "Dismiss the crowds, so that going into the towns and neighboring villages they may find lodging and food, because we are here in a deserted place." 13 But he said to them, "You give them something to eat." <margin>C</margin> But they said, "We have no more than five loaves and two fish, unless we should go and buy food for all this people." For there were about five thousand men. But he said to his disciples, "Make them sit down in each group fifty at a time." 15 And they did so, and made everyone sit down. 16 And taking the five loaves and the two fish, looking up to heaven, he blessed them, and broke them, and distributed to the disciples to set before the crowd. 17 And they all ate and were satisfied: and what remained of the fragments was picked up, twelve baskets. 18 And it happened when he was praying alone, his disciples were with him, and he questioned them, saying, "Who <margin>D</margin> do the crowds say that I am?" 19 And they answered and said, "John the Baptist, others Elijah, and others that some prophet from the ancients has risen." 20 He said to them, "But who do you say that I am?" Peter answering said, "The Christ of God." 21 But he, strictly charging them, commanded that they should tell this to no one: 22 Saying, "The Son of Man must suffer many things, and be rejected by the Elders and the chiefs of the Priests and the Scribes, and be killed, and on the third day rise again." 23 And he said to all, "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me. 24 For whoever wishes to make his life safe will lose it: but he who loses his life for my sake, he will make it safe. 25 For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, but loses himself, or causes his own destruction? <margin>E</margin> 26 For whoever is ashamed of me and my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his majesty, and the Father's, and the holy Angels'. 27 But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God." 28 And it happened after these words about eight days, and taking...

### [Translator's Annotations continued]

10 **By groups**] <note>original Greek: κλισίας ἀνὰ πεντήκοντα</note>, that is, in each single seating, fifty. For that is what the Translator understands by "groups." For it is not here *symposia* <note>a drinking party or banquet</note> as in Matthew, but *klisiai*, which means a place to lie down or sit at a meal.

11 **And they all sat down**] <note>original Greek: καὶ κατέκλιναν ἅπαντας</note>, that is, they made them all sit down, as is also read in the golden manuscript. The Translator seems to have read *anepeson* <note>meaning "they reclined"</note>, assuming it meant "they sat themselves down." Otherwise, he seems to have said the same thing twice: *And they did so, and they made all sit down.*

12 **But he rebuking them**] Before this, the translator almost always translated *epitiman* as "to threaten" <note>original Latin: comminari</note>, which if ever needed elsewhere, was certainly needed here. For why would Christ rebuke the disciples for this answer, for which Peter was so greatly praised according to the other Evangelists? Therefore it should have been translated: *he forbade them, or strictly charging them, he commanded them not to tell anyone.*

13 **Saying, because it is necessary for the Son of Man**] Either the Translator should have omitted the conjunction *that* <note>original Greek: ὅτι</note>, or it should have been translated, "that it would be necessary, etc."

14 **Take up his cross daily**] "Daily" was not added in some Greek manuscripts, but it is supported by the oldest Latin ones.

15 **For he who shall lose**] <note>original Greek: ὃς δ᾿ ἂν ἀπολέσῃ</note>, "whoever indeed shall lose," unless "for" is used in place of "but."

16 **For he who shall blush at me**] Whether this is proper Latin I do not know; certainly in Quintus Curtius we read, "he blushed to confess," and "blushing fortune."

> *face.* For among those who speak more precisely, the word *to grow red* <note>original: rubescere</note> is almost an obsolete verb. Certainly, it ought to be a Latin word that a translator can use, nor would he himself be offended by such things, unless my ears were more delicate. Yet this is more tolerable than what we noted elsewhere: "he who *will have been confused* by me."
>
> 23 <insert>In the greatness of God</insert> <note>original: ἐπὶ τῇ μεγαλειότητι</note>, that is, in magnificence or majesty. For it is derived from that noun which is usually translated as *mighty works* <note>original: magnalia, μεγαλεῖα</note>.
>
> 17 <insert>The appearance of his face was altered</insert> ] <note>original: τὸ εἶδος τοῦ προσώπου αὐτοῦ ἕτερον</note>. I would have preferred to render it thus: *the appearance of his look was another*, or different: or, if one may depart from the literal words, *the appearance of his face was changed*.
>
> 24 <insert>Put these words into your ears</insert> ] In Greek it is, *into your ears* <note>original: εἰς τὰ ὦτα ὑμῶν</note>, that is, listen diligently to what I am about to say. For it refers to what follows. Furthermore, he said "in your ears" rather than "in your hearts" because they were not going to understand. For it follows immediately, *But they did not know this word*.
>
> 18 <insert>And his clothing was white and gleaming</insert> ] <note>original: ἐξαστράπτων</note>. As if you were to say, sending out lightning from itself, or flashing forth. This agrees with what we noted in Matthew, "like light" instead of "like snow." Then that which immediately precedes,
>
> 25 <insert>Veiled before them</insert> ] <note>original: παρακεκαλυμμένον ἀπ' αὐτῶν</note>, that is, hidden from them.
>
> 19 <insert>In majesty</insert> ] <note>original: ἐν δόξῃ</note>, that is, in glory, just as it was translated a little earlier by Paul.
>
> 26 <insert>A thought entered</insert> ] <note>original: εἰσῆλθε</note>, that is, it occurred to them. *Thought* <note>original: διαλογισμὸς</note>, that is, a dispute. Although the Greek word is ambiguous. However, it is clear from the other Evangelists that there was a debate among them on this matter, and the thing did not remain a silent thought within the mind. But in that which follows immediately,
>
> 20 <insert>His departure</insert> ] By *departure* <note>original: excessum</note> he means death. For in Greek it is *exodos* <note>original: ἔξοδον</note>, that is, exit, not "a sight." Since both *excessus* and *exitus* are used for death, Laurentius teaches this with several examples for anyone who might doubt it. We aim for brevity.
>
> 27 <insert>But Jesus seeing the thought of the heart</insert> ] indicates that he is speaking about their inner thought. For the same word is used here, *thought* <note>original: διαλογισμόν</note>. However, there is a great diversity among the Evangelists in this place, which nevertheless can be brought into harmony without great difficulty. Now the Greek article, which Luke adds, *the* <note>original: τό</note>, "who might be the greater," could be rendered thus: *concerning this, who would be the greater*, or the greatest.
>
> 21 <insert>Tearing him</insert> ] <note>original: καὶ μόγις ἀποχωρεῖ ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ συντρῖβον αὐτὸν</note>, that is, "and it scarcely departs from him, shattering him," so that you understand the boy scarcely escapes from the spirit. Although the Greek manuscripts vary in this place. Some have *shattering* <note>original: συντρῖβον</note>, that is, breaking into pieces or tearing apart, which reading I prefer, so that you take it to mean the spirit tears the boy.
>
> 28 <insert>This one is greater</insert> ] In Greek it has it thus: <note>original: ὁ γὰρ μικρότερος ἐν πᾶσιν ὑμῖν ὑπάρχων, οὗτος ἔσται μέγας</note>, that is, "for he who is the lesser among you all, this one shall be great." It has already been shown before that "great" refers to a person of high rank, and "lesser" to one of low rank.
>
> 22 <note>Note: The OCR says "Elisit" in the margin but the annotation text says "Elisit eum dæmonium"</note> <insert>The demon shattered him, and tore him</insert> ] <note>original: ἔῤῥηξεν αὐτὸν τὸ δαιμόνιον, καὶ συνεσπάραξεν</note>, that is, the demon tore him and pulled him apart. The translator seems to have read *threw down* <note>original: ἔῤῥιψεν</note> instead of *tore* <note>original: ἔῤῥηξεν</note>, for which he rendered *shattered* <note>original: elisit</note>. I do not dislike this reading.
>
> 29 <insert>Into a city</insert> ] <note>original: εἰς κώμην</note>, that is, into a village or small town. For he usually translates it this way, even though some manuscripts have "city" <note>original: πόλιν</note>. And so the translator seems to have read it. For a little later, "into another village" <note>original: εἰς ἑτέραν κώμην</note>, he translates as *into another small town* <note>original: castellum</note>.

# THE GOSPEL [OF LUKE] CHAPTER X.

<margin>54</margin> ...was heading toward Jerusalem. And when his disciples, James and John, saw this, they said, "Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them, <margin>55</margin> just as Elijah did?" But Jesus turned and rebuked them, and said, "You do not know what kind of spirit you are of. <margin>56</margin> For the Son of Man did not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them." <margin>57</margin> And they went on to another village. And it happened that as they were going along the road, someone said to him, "I will follow you wherever you go." <margin>58</margin> And Jesus said to him, "Foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." <margin>59</margin> And he said to another, "Follow me." But he said, "Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father." <margin>60</margin> Jesus said to him, "Let the dead bury their own dead; but as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God." <margin>61</margin> And another also said, "I will follow you, Lord; but first permit me to say farewell to those who are at my house." <margin>62</margin> Jesus said to him, "No one, having put his hand to the plow and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God." <margin>1</margin> After these things, the Lord appointed seventy others also, and sent them out two by two ahead of him into every city and place where he himself was about to come. <margin>2</margin> Therefore he said to them, "The harvest truly is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore pray to the Lord of the harvest that he may send out laborers into his harvest. <margin>3</margin> Go your way; behold, I send you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. <margin>4</margin> Carry neither money bag, nor knapsack, nor sandals, and greet no one along the road. <margin>5</margin> But whatever house you enter, first say, 'Peace to this house.' <margin>6</margin> And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, it will return to you. <margin>7</margin> And remain in that same house, eating and drinking such things as they give; for the laborer is worthy of his wages."

---

<margin>30 his face was that of one going]</margin> <note>original Greek: τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ἦν πορευόμενον</note>, that is, *his face was going*. Although this makes no difference to the meaning. It is more common and frequent for an Evangelist to render the sense rather than the literal words. For just as eyes are said to "speak" when they signal what someone wants said, so a face is said to "go" when it shows a journey intended for elsewhere.
<margin>31 Do you wish us to say]</margin> <note>original Greek: θέλεις εἴπωμεν</note>, that is, *do you want us to speak*.
<margin>32 And consume them]</margin> <note>original Greek: ὡς καὶ Ἠλίας ἐποίησε</note>, that is, *just as Elijah did*. I find this addition in all the Greek codices <note>Erasmus uses "codex" to mean a handwritten manuscript book.</note> that I have seen. However, I am not sure if it was added here by someone explaining the passage. For I have not found it in any of our ancient Latin copies, even though Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and Bible commentator.</note> reads it this way.
<margin>33 He did not come to destroy souls, but to save them]</margin> In the Greek codices I remember seeing, "of men" is added, but many reliable and even common copies reject this, and it does not change the meaning. Indeed, Theophylact does not touch upon this entire phrase, "The Son of Man did not come to destroy souls, but to save them," neither reading nor interpreting it; whether this happened by chance is uncertain, but it seems to have been skipped through carelessness. Otherwise, it might seem to have been added here from Matthew chapter 18.
<margin>34 Wherever you go]</margin> <note>original Greek: ὅπου ἂν ἀπέρχῃ</note>, that is, *anywhere*.
<margin>35 Where he may lay his head]</margin> We have noted elsewhere that the word "his" was added among the Latins.
<margin>36 To renounce those things which are at home]</margin> From the Greek, it is not clear whether we should read "those things which are at home" or "those people who are at home." Except that a very ancient codex had <margin>τοῖς</margin> <note>the masculine plural article</note> "those who are at home," in the masculine gender, which agrees with the copy of Consentius, surely referring to people. However, Luke uses the same word in the fourteenth chapter of this Gospel to refer to things: "Unless one renounces, etc." Just as we bid a person "farewell" <note>original Latin: valere</note>, we also bid "farewell" to pleasures. Therefore, it could also be understood here as *to renounce domestic affairs*. What the Translator here renders as "renounce," he elsewhere renders as "bid farewell": as in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter two, <margin>ἀλλ’ ἀποταξάμενος αὐτοῖς</margin>, "but bidding them farewell." Again in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter twenty: "And having exhorted him, he said farewell." For there the Translator seems to have read "having greeted," although our codices have "having said farewell." Again in chapter eighteen of the same work: "Bidding farewell to the brothers, he sailed for Syria" <note>original Greek: τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς ἀποταξάμενος</note>. Properly, however, <term>apotaxasthai</term> means to dismiss someone with whatever instructions you wish. Whether the word "renounce" <note>original Latin: renunciare</note> has the same force is not entirely clear to me. I find "renounce" used sometimes to report what has been done, and sometimes to forbid by a sent message, as in Cicero, "he renounced his hospitality," and in Suetonius's *Caligula*, "he renounced his friendship" for one who had decided to die. To make the speech clearer, we have translated it as "bid farewell" instead of "renounce."
<margin>37 No one putting his hand]</margin> <note>original Greek: ἐπιβαλών, καὶ βλέπων</note>. One participle is in the past tense, the other in the present. These could be aptly rendered: "No one, who, after he has moved his hand to the plow, looks back at his rear, is suitable for the kingdom of God."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...his face was that of one going to Jerusalem. But when his disciples, James and John, had seen this, they said, "Lord, <margin>31</margin> do you want us to say that fire should descend from heaven <margin>32</margin> and consume them, just as Elijah did?" <margin>55</margin> But Jesus turned and rebuked them, saying, "You do not know of what spirit you are. For the Son of Man <margin>56</margin> did not come to destroy the souls of men, but to save them." And they went away into another village. <margin>57</margin> And it happened as they were walking on the road, a certain man said to him, "I will follow you <margin>34</margin> wherever you go." <margin>58</margin> Jesus said to him, "Foxes have dens, and the birds of heaven have nests: but the Son of Man has not <margin>35</margin> where he may lay his head." <margin>59</margin> And he said to another, "Follow me." But he said, "Lord, permit me first to go away and bury my father." <margin>60</margin> But Jesus said to him, "Let the dead bury <margin>B</margin> their own dead: but you, go and announce the kingdom of God." And another said, "I will follow you, Lord, <margin>36</margin> but permit me first <margin>36</margin> to say farewell to those who are at my house." <margin>62</margin> Jesus said to him, <margin>37</margin> "No one who, with his hand moved to the plow, looks behind his back, is fit for the kingdom of God." <margin>1 X,</margin> After these things, however, the Lord appointed seventy others also, and sent them two by two before his face into every city and place where he himself was about to come. <margin>2</margin> He said to them, therefore, "The harvest indeed is great, but the laborers are few: <margin>2</margin> pray therefore to the Lord of the harvest, that he may thrust out laborers into his harvest. Go, behold I send you as lambs <margin>3</margin> among wolves. <margin>4</margin> Do not carry a small bag, nor a knapsack, nor shoes, and greet no one along the road. <margin>5</margin> Into <margin>C</margin> whatever house you enter, first say, 'Peace to this house.' And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; if not, it will return to you. <margin>6</margin> But stay in that same house, eating and drinking <margin>6</margin> what is given by them: for the laborer is worthy of his reward."

---

<margin>D</margin> ...of which there were thirty-five, three were chosen, making the number one hundred and five; whether this be true or not, I do not think it much concerns this passage. Certainly, it is probable. It is strange that some made seventy-two out of the seventy disciples: as if the same thing ought to have happened with the Disciples as happened with the Seventy Translators <note>Referring to the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, traditionally translated by 72 scholars.</note>, even though the Apostle chose twelve, but not one from each of the individual tribes. Otherwise, the Greek codices agree on "seventy." And Saint Ambrose seems to have read it this way too, for when explaining this passage, "Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves," he says, "He says this to the seventy disciples." The type <note>A symbolic foreshadowing.</note> of the Old Testament also supports us, where twelve springs and seventy palm trees found in the desert prefigure the twelve Apostles and the seventy Disciples. Theophylact carefully noted this, and Cyril, who is cited in the *Catena* <note>A "chain" of verse-by-verse biblical commentary from various Church Fathers.</note>, agrees; in addition to the twelve springs and seventy palms, he also mentions those seventy Judges whom Moses chose by the Lord's command, and who were filled with the Holy Spirit. And lest anyone argue that only the Greeks read it this way, Saint Jerome, in his sixth stay [of the Israelites] to Fabiola, writes as follows: "Never before did the purest springs appear, except where the mastery of teaching burst forth; nor is there any doubt that the discourse is about the twelve Apostles, from whose springs the derived waters irrigate the dryness of the whole world. Near these waters, seventy palms had grown, whom we also understand to be teachers of the second rank." Luke the Evangelist testifies that there were twelve Apostles and seventy Disciples of a lower degree, whom the Lord sent two by two ahead of himself. From these things, it is clear that Augustine had a faulty codex, as we shall demonstrate in other places as well. A single codex from the Papal Library is thrown at us, as if we did not know that after the Greeks were brought into harmony with the Roman See, their codices were corrected to match the Latin copies. From many arguments, I gather that the codex written in capital letters was one of that number. For if the authority of the Papal Library moves us, even that codex which the Roman Pontiff sent to Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros of Toledo was from the same library. The reason that Bede brings forward, concerning the twelve tribes of Israel and the seventy-two nations of the rest of the world, is weak. Nor is the one Augustine brings forward much more solid, regarding three times twenty-four hours, which number makes seventy-two. Furthermore, the martyr Dorotheus, in his compendium of Apostolic and Prophetic history, listing the Disciples by name, makes them only seventy, not seventy-two. And Irenaeus, who is older than these, reads 70, not 72, both elsewhere and in Book III, chapter 23. Finally, Eusebius, in the first book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter twelve, reports that only seventy were chosen. And yet a little lower in the common copies, "seventy-two" is repeated: "But the seventy-two returned with joy," making it appear that this was done not by chance, but by design. And in this, the Latin copies strangely agree.
<margin>2 But pray]</margin> It should be read "Pray therefore," <note>original Greek: δεήθητε οὖν</note>.
<margin>3 That he may send laborers]</margin> <note>original Greek: ὅπως ἐκβάλῃ</note>, that is, *that he may thrust out* or *cast out*: so that we may understand that they are either to be sent out against their will, or to be thrust out quickly, as was noted in earlier sections.
<margin>4 Among wolves]</margin> <note>original Greek: ἐν μέσῳ λύκων</note>, that is, *in the midst of wolves*. And Valla prefers "as if sheep" rather than "just like sheep."
<margin>5 But if not]</margin> <note>original Greek: εἰ δὲ μήγε</note>, that is, *otherwise*, this is, *if a son of peace is not there*. And it is not.
<margin>6 Which are with them]</margin> <note>original Greek: τὰ παρ’ αὐτῶν</note>, that is, *those things which are offered by them*; otherwise he would have said, <note>original Greek: τὰ παρ’ αὐτοῖς</note>.

---

<margin>7 They would repent] <term>metanoōsi</term>.</margin> Why not rather *they should have repented*, since it refers to past time? Indeed, Nonius Marcellus cites the poet Pacuvius using this verb in a personal sense. For others, a paraphrase is more pleasing: *they would have performed repentance for their crimes*: which fits this place quite aptly, because mention is made of sackcloth and ashes. And although pain follows the one who changes his mind regarding things that preceded, nevertheless for the Greeks <term>metanoia</term> <note>repentance</note> is not derived from "punishment" <note>original: poena</note>, nor for the Latins, I think, is *poenitere* <note>to repent</note>, but rather from *pene tenus* <note>almost to the limit</note>, because after the fact we grasp and understand our error. Finally, he who changes his mind does not immediately recover from crimes, but sometimes from ignorance or simple error.

<margin>8 He who rejects you, rejects me] Jerome in some places translates this as, *he who reprobates you, reprobates me*.</margin> For the Greek verb is <term>athetei</term>, which means *he rejects* or *turns away from*; and so Cyprian reads it in his Letter to his brother Cornelius. And people distort this passage toward our modern tyranny. "He rejects Christ who rejects a Bishop, who rejects the Pope." This is true, but only for an Apostolic bishop, one doing Christ's business: he who rejects *such* a man rejects me. Indeed, let both sides take care to remember their duty: let the Priests strive to be such as the Apostles were, and let us receive them as Christ himself and obey them. Otherwise, where a Priest acts as a tyrant and pursues the business of his belly rather than Christ’s, I do not know if it is timely to cite, *he who rejects you, rejects me*. I know, however, that even the wicked must be obeyed at times to avoid causing a rift, provided they do not compel us to impiety.

<margin>9 But seventy-two returned]</margin> Again [the Latin] has added *two*, while in the Greek manuscripts there are only *seventy*.

<margin>10 I saw Satan]</margin> <term>Etheōroun</term> <note>I was beholding</note>; in a certain Latin manuscript I found "they saw," for the Greek voice has an ambiguity. Although all interpreters take it as the first person. From this, Theophylact introduces a new meaning, namely this: "It is no wonder that demons are subject to you, since their prince has already fallen and been cast down."

<margin>11 Behold I have given] <term>idou didōmi</term>, that is, Behold I give.</margin>

<margin>12 He rejoiced in the Holy Spirit] <term>en autē tē hōra ēgalliasato tō pneumati ho Iēsous</term>,</margin> that is, *in the same hour Jesus exulted in the Spirit*. The word <term>holy</term> is not added, nor the preposition *in*, except where old Latin manuscripts resist. In those [Latin copies], just as the epithet <term>holy</term> is added, so the name of *Jesus* is not added. Certainly, the [Greek] article makes it so that we understand it as the *Holy Spirit*.

<margin>13 To little ones] <term>nēpiois</term>.</margin> In this place, it truly should have been translated more as *to the foolish* or *to the unwise*, so that it might be opposed to that which precedes, *the wise*, unless the speech seemed a bit harsh. Although this has been discussed elsewhere.

<margin>14 Even so, Father] <term>nai</term>.</margin> Which previously occurred as "certainly." It is an adverb of one who is confirming.

<margin>15 Since it so pleased before you] <term>hoti outōs egeneto eudokia emprosthen sou</term>,</margin> that is, *because such was the good will before you*. For this is how Jerome translates it. It is the same word used by the Angels announcing peace on earth to men of *good will*, by which is signified the free benevolence and favor of the divine power toward mortals.

<margin>16 All things delivered to me] Before these words, several Greek manuscripts add, *And turning to the disciples he said*,</margin> that is, <term>Kai strapheis pros tous mathētas eipe</term>. Then follows, *All things have been delivered to me*. And the error arose from this: that the same phrase follows shortly after.

<margin>17 And turning to his disciples] But here the Greek manuscript adds, <term>kat' idian</term>,</margin> that is, *privately* or *separately*: likewise it is separated from the above, even though the Latin copies cry out against it.

<margin>18 But Jesus, looking up] <term>Hypolabōn de ho Iēsous</term>,</margin> that is, *Jesus, taking it up*. And so it is read in the oldest Latin manuscripts. Moreover, *looking up* <note>suspiciens</note> is placed for *taking up* or *succeeding* in the turn of responding. In the same manner, Virgil says:
> *Ascanius takes it up [excipit]. — —*
And Xenophon, "And Cyrus taking it up <note>original: hypolabōn</note> said," that is, *And Cyrus*

---

*...said of the fortunate*. <note>original: feliçium dixit</note> That error was not even the fault of the Translator, but of some half-learned person to whom it seemed that "looking upon" <note>original: peripiens</note> signified nothing in this place, and so changed it to "being wise," <note>original: sapiscient</note> as if Jesus, about to answer the man, had looked up to heaven. We have translated it as *looking back* <note>original: respiciens</note>, lest the reader stumble again on the same stone.

<margin>19</margin> *Half-dead*] <note>original: ἀφέντες ἡμιθανῆ</note>, that is, *leaving him half-dead*. Jerome, in his *Epitaph on Paula*, translates this as "half-extinguished." However, that change carries no weight regarding the meaning.

<margin>20</margin> *Into an inn*] <note>original: εἰς πανδοχεῖον</note>, that is, *into a lodging-place*. For the Greek word is derived from the fact that it receives everyone; what the Latins call a "lodging for hire" <note>original: diversorium meritorium</note>. Nor did the Translator intend a stable for beasts of burden, but a place where one stays; hence those who keep such a place are called "stablars" <note>original: stabularii</note>.

<margin>21</margin> *And on the other day*] <note>original: Καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν αὔριον</note>, that is, *And on the following day*.

<margin>22</margin> *To the innkeeper*] <note>original: πανδοχεῖ</note>, that is, *to the host, but one who charges for stay*.

<margin>23</margin> *Into a certain castle*] <note>original: εἰς κώμην τινὰ</note>, that is, *into a little town*, or *a certain village*, lest anyone imagine a powerful fortress similar to those which are now commonly called "castles."

<margin>25</margin> *She was busy*] <note>original: περιεσπᾶτο</note>, that is, *she was distracted, or drawn away*. Although the Translator rendered this more elegantly than a simple reader might notice; for *satagere* <note>to be busy/agitated</note> properly means to be anxiously tormented by the difficulty of completing a task. But the Greek word fits more aptly with what follows, "furthermore, one thing is necessary." For "being distracted" and "being intent" on one thing are opposites.

<margin>25</margin> *About frequent ministry*] <note>original: περὶ πολλὴν διακονίαν</note>, that is, *about much serving*.

<margin>26</margin> *Toward very many things*] <note>original: περὶ πολλά</note>, that is, *about many things*, or *more things*: supported also by some very ancient books. And I am not sure if the Translator wrote *more* <note>plura</note> instead of *many* <note>multis</note>. Someone may have translated this as *very many* <note>plurima</note>, just as we read in the solemn prayers "of very many martyrs" <note>plurimorum martyrum</note> instead of "of several" <note>plurium</note>.

<margin>27</margin> *Furthermore, one thing is necessary*] <note>original: Ἑνὸς δέ ἐστι χρεία</note>, that is, *There is need of one*, so that it is opposed to "many," which is the word that precedes it. Regarding the historical sense, the Lord seems to rebuke Martha, not because a feast is being prepared, but because it is too varied and elaborate. For Luke said before "much serving," as if you were to say "varied administration," whereas for a simple preparation, a few things suffice. This is why Jesus, denying the need for many things, says "one thing is necessary." Theophylactus also touches upon this meaning.

<margin>28</margin> *The best part*] <note>original: τὴν ἀγαθὴν μερίδα</note>, that is, *the good part*: except that the added article clarifies the matter, namely that specific part which is truly good. Augustine, in his *Sermon on Luke XXVI*, does not read "best" but "better": saying, "She chose the *better* part; not that yours is bad, but hers is better." Ambrose seems to have read it no differently, adding in his commentaries: "Yet Martha is not rebuked for the good of her service, but Mary is preferred because she chose the *better* part for herself." There are those who are pleased

5 And he said to them, "Which of you shall have a friend, and shall go to him at midnight, and say to him, 'Friend, 4 lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has come from a journey to me, and—'"

by the property of Hebrew speech, where the positive is placed in the stead of the comparative or superlative, because that language lacks words of that kind. While this interpretation does not entirely displease me, I do not see why it should carry more weight here than in three hundred other places.

<margin>1</margin> *To us today*] Here the Greek codices vary. In some it was written, <note>original: δὸς ἡμῖν τὸ καθ’ ἡμέραν</note>, that is, *give us daily*. And so it was written in the "Golden Codex," and likewise the "Constance Codex." The reader is offended by the same word being repeated: "daily bread daily." Yet it is not "daily" in Greek, but *epiousion* <note>original: ἐπιούσιον</note>, which sounds more like "for the morrow." For they do not ask for provisions for many years, but only for the next day. And he who prays in the evening for food for the following day, what else does he seek but *daily* food? I point this out lest anyone think there is much difference in the sense. Although this was discussed elsewhere somewhat more fully.

<margin>2</margin> *Forgive us our sins*] <note>original: τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν</note>. There are those who think there is a difference between "debts," that is, <note>original: ὀφειλήματα</note>, and "sins," because the name "debt" encompasses not only the fault but also the obligation to make satisfaction. But Luke did not think there was any difference. Nor did Augustine in *On the Words of the Lord*: "But what is a debt," he says, "if not a sin?"

<margin>3</margin> *But deliver us from evil*] This is not added in some Latin copies of Luke, just like several other things which seem to have been added from the other Gospels lest they appear to disagree. This happened by conjecture in several other places as well. Indeed, in Luke this Prayer encompasses much less than in the others, in this manner: "Father, hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come. Our daily bread give us today. And forgive us our sins, since we also forgive everyone owing to us. And lead us not into temptation." For so it was found written in the most ancient codices, which at that time the Amerbach, Paulinus, and Corsendonck collections showed us, and finally the Constance one as well. The others do not differ greatly from this, nor do they entirely agree, even among themselves. In the Greek codices, the Lord's Prayer was reported as complete, except for the conclusion <note>The doxology: "For thine is the kingdom..."</note>, which we have indicated elsewhere was added. Even from this, it is clear how the Evangelists were not superstitious about words. A certain Bishop had not prescribed this form of prayer, nor a Roman Pontiff, but Christ himself; and yet in such a small prayer, Luke omitted so great a part. And certainly, it is consistent with the truth that he prayed in such a way as to hand down to us the form of praying with Christ as the author. Where are those meanwhile who wretchedly tremble whenever a little syllable has been omitted from human prayers? Yet those same people are strong and intrepid whenever they tear apart the reputation of their brothers with a poisonous tongue. I do not say this so that we should be less attentive in prayers, but so that we should not be given over to preposterous superstition.

<margin>4</margin> *Lend*] <note>original: χρῆσον</note>, that is, *give as a loan*, or *give a loan*. Although...

# ACCORDING TO LUKE. CHAPTER XI.

<margin>7</margin> And he from within answering might say, "Do not cause me trouble; the door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot get up and give to you."
<margin>8</margin> I tell you, even if he will not get up and give to him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence <note>original: "ἀναίδειαν" (anaideian) - literally "shamelessness" or "boldness."</note> he will get up and give him as much as he needs.

---

...just as the Greek word <note>original: "χρῆσον" (chreson)</note> is ambiguous, applying to a thing consumed by use and to one that is not. For he who asks for bread says, <term>lend me bread</term> <note>original: "χρῆσόν μοι ἄρτον"</note>, and he who asks for a bowl says, <term>lend me a bowl</term> <note>original: "χρῆσόν μοι μάκτραν"</note>. To the Latins, however, the words are different, though among those same people "money" has a specific word, <term>dænari</term> <note>A reference to lending money for interest/debt.</note>. Among the Latins, a <term>commodatus</term> <note>A "loan for use" where the specific object (like a horse or clothing) must be returned.</note> is something whose use is provided for a time, like a horse, clothing, or a plate. A <term>mutuum</term> <note>A "loan for consumption" where the item is used up (like oil or grain) and an equivalent is returned.</note> is given which is consumed by use, which the Legal Scholars call a *mutuum*, such as oil or wheat, where the same item is not returned. 

*If he continues knocking*: I did not find these words in most Greek manuscripts, and the very ancient Latin manuscript held in the Library of St. Paul's Church in London agrees with this omission, though the one from Constance disagrees.

<margin>5</margin> *Because of his persistence*] <term>on account of his impudence</term> <note>original: "διά γε τὴν ἀναίδειαν"</note>, that is, because of his shamelessness. The Translator <note>Likely referring to the author of the Vulgate, Jerome.</note> translated this elegantly, provided it is understood correctly. For just as a "probity" means "good," so "improbity" <note>In Latin, *improbitas* can mean wickedness, but also relentless persistence.</note> means "bad"; yet one who urges and does not stop is sometimes called "improbus," occasionally even in a good sense; as Virgil wrote:
-> *Unrelenting labor conquers all.* <-
-> *Persistent labor. [Georgics 1.145]* <-

<margin>6</margin> *Which of you a father*] The Greek texts differ slightly. <term>Which of you a father shall his son ask for bread</term>, that is, <term>Which father among you will a son ask for bread?</term>. We have rendered it in this way: <term>But which of you is a father, from whom if a son asks for bread, will he give him a stone?</term> Although this phrasing is a bit harsh, I believe it comes from the idiom of the Hebrew language. It seems, moreover, to allude to a common joke, in which people hold out a stone to someone expecting bread, according to that line from Platina <note>Bartolomeo Platina (1421–1481), a Renaissance humanist.</note>:
-> *In one hand he carries a stone, in the other he shows bread.* <-
Likewise, they hold out a scorpion hidden in an empty eggshell. In the same way, the *displades* <note>Likely referring to a type of deceptive lizard or spider mentioned in natural histories.</note> deceive by hiding themselves in the empty shells of ostriches.

<margin>7</margin> *Good gifts*] <term>good givings</term> <note>original: "ἀγαθὰ δόματα"</note>, that is, "good dations," if it is permitted to speak thus.

<margin>8</margin> *Will give the good Spirit*] The Greek manuscripts that were available then had <term>Holy Spirit</term> <note>original: "Πνεῦμα ἅγιον"</note>, but the Latin copies—even the ancient ones—protested with great consensus, to which...

<margin>7</margin> ...and I have nothing to set before him. And he from within answering may say, "Do not be troublesome to me, the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give to you."
<margin>8</margin> I say to you, even if he will not give to him by rising because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence he will rise and give him as many as he has need of.
<margin>9</margin> And I say to you: Ask, and it shall be given to you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you.
<margin>10</margin> For everyone who asks, receives; and he who seeks, finds; and to him who knocks, it shall be opened. <insert>B</insert>
<margin>11</margin> But which of you is a father, from whom if a son asks for bread, will he give him a stone? Or if a fish, will he give him a serpent instead of a fish?
<margin>12</margin> Or if he asks for an egg, will he reach him a scorpion?
<margin>13</margin> If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those asking Him?
<margin>14</margin> And He was casting out a demon, and it was mute; and when He had cast out the demon, the mute man spoke, and the crowds marveled.
<margin>15</margin> But some of them said, "By Beelzebub, the prince of demons, He casts out demons."
<margin>16</margin> And others, testing Him, sought a sign from heaven from Him.
<margin>17</margin> But He, since He knew their thoughts, said to them, "Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation, and house falls upon house."
<margin>18</margin> But if Satan also is divided against himself, how shall his kingdom stand? Because you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebub.
<margin>19</margin> But if I by Beelzebub cast out demons, by whose help do your sons cast them out? Therefore they shall be your judges.
<margin>20</margin> Moreover, if by the finger of God I cast out demons, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you.
<margin>21</margin> When a strong man, armed, guards his palace, the things he possesses are in peace.

<margin>23</margin> He who is not with Me is against Me; and he who does not gather with Me, scatters.
<margin>24</margin> When the unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he walks through dry places, seeking rest; and not finding it, he says, "I will return to my house, from which I came out."
<margin>25</margin> And when he has come, he finds it swept with brooms and decorated.
<margin>26</margin> Then he goes and takes seven other spirits more harmful than himself, and entering in they dwell there: and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first.
<margin>27</margin> And it happened, as He said these things, a certain woman from the crowd, lifting up her voice, said to Him, "Blessed is the womb that bore You, and the breasts which You sucked."
<margin>28</margin> But He said, "Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it."
<margin>29</margin> And as the crowds were flocking together, He began to say, "This nation is evil: it seeks a sign, and a sign shall not be given to it..."

---

...I certainly agree more. From Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose (c. 340–397), Bishop of Milan.</note>, nothing can be elicited because he treats these matters only in passing.

<margin>9</margin> *And it was mute*] Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla (1407–1457), a humanist critic of the Vulgate.</note> is hallucinating again in this place regarding the words <term>mute</term> and <term>dumb</term> <note>original: "κωφόν" and "κωφός"</note>, thinking that in both cases "deaf" should have been translated, not "mute"—either not understanding or certainly not noticing that both sound like <term>kophos</term> to the Greeks. Likewise shortly after, *Every kingdom divided against itself*, he prefers "in itself" or "upon itself," though it is *against itself*: because to the Greeks this preposition is ambiguous, as almost all of them are.

<margin>10</margin> *Is desolated*] <term>ἐρημοῦται</term>, that is, it "is desolated" [present tense]. And a little later, <term>πίπτει</term>, that is, "falls," not "will fall," supported by the most ancient Latin manuscripts.

<margin>11</margin> *In peace are all the things he possesses*] <term>τὰ ὑπάρχοντα</term>, that is, <term>those things which he possesses</term>, as the Golden Manuscript <note>Likely the *Codex Aureus*, a sumptuously illuminated gospel book.</note> agrees.

<margin>12</margin> *All armor*] <term>τὴν πανοπλίαν</term> [panoplia]. By this word, the Greeks declare whatever pertains to the proper equipment of an armed man.

<margin>13</margin> *He takes away*] <term>αἴρει</term>, that is, "you take away," and <term>distributes</term> <note>original: "διαδίδωσιν"</note>, so that they are in the present tense, not the future. For He is not prophesying what will be, but proposing what is usually done, making a comparison.

<margin>14</margin> *Finds it swept with brooms*] <term>εὑρίσκει</term>, that is, he "finds" [present tense], with the first syllable accented. *Swept with brooms*. The Greek manuscripts add, <term>and decorated</term> <note>original: "καὶ κεκοσμημένον"</note>, which I suspect might have been added here from the other Evangelists. Furthermore, that phrase *swept with brooms* is a single word in Greek: <term>σεσαρωμένον</term>, that is, "turned," from the verb <term>σαρόω</term>, not "I sweep."

<margin>15</margin> *Rather*] <term>Μενοῦνγε</term> [Menounge]. This conjunction neither denies what was said, nor rejects it, but introduces what is more certain. Augustine, in his book *On Holy Virginity* chapter 3, reads <term>imo</term> <note>Latin for "nay rather" or "on the contrary."</note> for "rather," as is common for someone correcting. Moreover, here too Christ seems like Himself, not attributing much to the affection of kinship.

<margin>16</margin> *As the crowds were flocking together*] <term>ἐπαθροιζομένων</term>, that is, *crowding together, massing, or packing themselves in*, or *when the crowds were flowing in more densely*. For in Greek <term>epathroizomai</term> is used when everything is gathered together into one place.

# THE GOSPEL, CHAPTER XI.

30 of the Prophet. For as Jonah became a sign to the Ninevites, so also will the Son of Man be to this generation. 31 The Queen of the South will rise up in the judgment with the men of this generation and will condemn them, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. 32 The men of Nineveh will rise up in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.
<margin>Psalm 133, otherwise called 'The Light', Psalm 134</margin> 33 No one, after lighting a lamp, puts it in a hidden place, nor under a basket, but on a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light. 34 The lamp of the body is the eye; therefore, when your eye is clear, your whole body is full of light; but when it is evil, your body is full of darkness. 35 See to it, then, that the light which is in you is not darkness. 36 If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be entirely bright, as when a lamp illuminates you with its radiance. 37 While He was speaking, a certain Pharisee asked Him to dine with him; so He went in and reclined at the table. 38 But the Pharisee, seeing this, wondered why He had not first washed <note>original: "ἐβαπτίσθη" (ebaptisthē) – literally "baptized" or "immersed," here referring to ritual washing.</note> before the meal. 39 But the Lord said to him, "Now you Pharisees clean the outside of the cup and the platter, but your inside is full of greed and wickedness. 40 You fools, did not He who made the outside also make the inside? 41 But give alms from what is within, and behold, all things are clean for you. 42 But woe to you Pharisees, for you tithe mint and rue and every herb, yet you bypass justice and the love of God; these things you ought to have done, without neglecting the others."
<margin>Psalm 43</margin> 43 Woe to you Pharisees, because you love the seat of honor in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces.

---

17 **Something greater than Solomon is here**] <gloss>original: "ὧδε" (hōde)</gloss>. This word "here" is an adverb of place, not a pronoun. The same applies a little further down to "greater than Jonah here," so that Christ may be understood as greater than the Temple, Solomon, and Jonah.

18 **The lamp of your body**] The word "your" is not added by the Greeks, and the meaning fits better if it is removed. It becomes a universal statement, as we indicated above.

19 **Lest the light which is in you**] <gloss>original: "μὴ τὸ φῶς" (mē to phōs)</gloss>. This could be understood as "Is the light which is in you...?" etc. because the adverb "not" <note>original: "μὴ" (mē)</note> is suited to both meanings: that of a question and that of a prohibition.

20 **And as a lamp**] <gloss>original: "ὡς ὅταν ὁ λύχνος τῇ ἀστραπῇ φωτίζῃ σε" (hōs hotan ho lychnos tē astrapē phōtizē se)</gloss>, meaning "as when a lamp illuminates you with its flash." The sense is: your body will be no more bright with a pure eye than your house is bright for you when a lamp is lit. It is not "will illuminate," but "illuminates." Otherwise, the speech might seem repetitive—if the whole is bright, then the whole will be bright. Therefore, we have added "so" on our own accord to better show the comparison of the sentence.

21 **Had been washed**] <gloss>original: "ἐβαπτίσθη" (ebaptisthē)</gloss>. Why not rather "had been bathed," since it refers to a simple washing of the hands? <note>The author questions why the translator used a word related to baptism for a simple hand-washing ritual.</note>

22 **Of the dish**] <gloss>original: "τοῦ πίνακος" (tou pinakos)</gloss>. This signifies not only a "dish" or "platter," but also a "square board" or a "tablet."

23 **Your interior**] Lorenzo Valla <note>A famous Italian humanist and scholar who criticized the Latin Vulgate translation.</note> prefers "of you" <note>original: "vestri"</note> so that it is the genitive of the personal pronoun. Thus it refers not to the furniture (the dishes), but to the Pharisees themselves. What was said ambiguously in Matthew 23, Luke explains by adding the pronoun "your" <note>original: "ὑμῶν" (hymōn)</note>. For some interpret that place to mean that what was contained in the dishes and cups was unclean because it was gained by fraud and violence. Luke, however, seems to compare the whole man to wooden or earthenware vessels; although these are outside the man, they thought that some religious duty rested in cleaning them. Similarly, in the washings of bodies—which is the external part of a man, namely the dwelling-place of the soul—they allowed the mind itself to be utterly defiled with the filth of vices. He mentions two vices which lie deeper in the soul, *avarice* and *malice*, which Theophylact <note>A late 11th-century Archbishop of Bulgaria known for his biblical commentaries.</note> interprets as *envy*. For the Greek is not "wickedness" <note>kakia</note> or "lawlessness" <note>anomia</note>, which usually translates as "iniquity," but "perversity" <note>ponēria</note>, which signifies a twisted mind. Therefore the Lord shows the remedy most opposed to avarice and envy: *almsgiving*. He who gives away his own is far from stealing others' goods; and he who feels pity and grieves at others' misfortunes is far from envy, which rejoices in others' troubles and is tormented by their successes. Yet that meaning which I mentioned first does not contradict this comparison; for it can be understood thus: "You Pharisees, by a backwards judgment, value external things more than internal ones; you clean the outside of cups and bowls, but you do not take care that your food and drink is clean. For in God's eyes, whatever is gained by fraud is unclean." Likewise, with frequent washings, you care for the cleanliness of your bodies while you have unwashed minds. Ambrose and Theophylact write in agreement with this interpretation.

24 **What remains**] <gloss>original: "τὰ ἐνόντα" (ta enonta)</gloss>. This is a different word from the more frequent and common "the rest" <note>ta loipa</note>. However, where our translator has rendered "what remains," Theophylact interprets it far differently. I will add his words: <note>original Greek quote: "τὰ ἐνόντα ταῦτ’ ἐστὶ, τὰ ὑπάρχοντα ὑμῖν... κ.τ.λ."</note> That is: *"The things that are inside, therefore, are the things that belong to you. He spoke rightly*

<column-break/>

A except the sign of Jonah the Prophet. For just as Jonah was to the Ninevites, so will the Son of Man be to this nation. 31 The queen of the south shall rise in judgment with the men of this nation, and shall condemn them: because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon: and behold, 32 something greater than Solomon is in this place. The men of Nineveh shall rise in judgment with this nation, and shall condemn it: because they were brought to repentance by the preaching of Jonah: and behold, something greater than Jonah is in this place. B 33 No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, nor under a basket, but upon a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light. 34 The lamp of the body is the eye: when therefore your eye is simple, your whole body also will be bright: but if it is evil, your body also will be dark. 35 Look to it therefore, lest the light which is in you be darkness. 36 If therefore your whole body is entirely bright, having no part dark, it will be bright throughout, as when a lamp illuminates you with its radiance. 37 And while he was speaking, a certain Pharisee asked him to dine with him: and Jesus went in and sat down. 38 But the Pharisee, when he saw it, wondered why he had not first 21 washed before the meal. C 39 And the Lord said to him, "Now you Pharisees clean the outside of the cup and 22 the dish, but what is 23 inside of you is full of plunder and malice. 40 Fools, did not he who made what is outside also make that which is inside? 41 Nevertheless 24 give as alms what remains, and behold, all things are clean to you. 42 But woe to you Pharisees, 26 because you tithe mint, and rue, and every herb, and pass over judgment and the love of God. These things you ought to have done, and not to have omitted the others. 43 Woe to you

---

*when he said 'the things that are inside' and did not say 'the things that are,' because money sits inside the heart of the greedy man, and settles into it. Therefore David also warns that the heart must not be attached to riches."* Theophylact seems to take it so that "the things that are inside" and "almsgiving" are joined in apposition: "give your possessions as alms." But it can also be taken as if the word "according to" <note>original: "κατά" (kata)</note> is understood: "according to the things you have, give alms." The translator seems to have understood "according to those things that are in you." But what has passed is not "in us," and because of that, he translated it as "what remains." Although it perhaps sounds like "it is allowed," from which "the things in our power" can be named. Some interpret "what remains" to mean "what is left over," but poorly. Let the learned reader consider whether "the things that are inside" <note>original: "τὰ ἐνόντα" (ta enonta)</note> is placed absolutely for "the things that are," so that you understand that things already done cannot be undone, and that what remains in our power is to balance out plunder with almsgiving. Bede touches on this meaning. It should be noted that, although He just mentioned plunder, He does not mention restitution in the remedy; He only promises that "alms having been given, all things will be clean." But he who is ordered to give to those to whom he owes nothing, is much more ordered to give back if he owes anything to someone. Furthermore, the Lord calls avarice "plunder"; so that what the Pharisees collected from tithes, though legally, was nonetheless plunder because they served their own greed under the pretext of observing the Law. Finally, it is plunder when a rich man possesses what was legally contracted if he does not share it with a needy neighbor. In these cases, restitution is not demanded, but it is enough to redeem the vice of the soul with alms.

25 **Give alms**] <gloss>original: "δότε ἐλεημοσύνην" (dote eleēmosynēn)</gloss>. It is ambiguous whether it means "give" (a command) or "you give" (a statement of fact). According to the latter reading, the sense would be: "Do you think you are freed from all plunder by giving alms, if you spend a tiny bit of it on the poor?" Indeed, He elsewhere reproaches the Pharisees because they did their almsgiving before men. According to the former reading (the command), the meaning is manifest. Yet this exhortation fits somewhat harshly with what precedes and follows, which sound more like a reproach than an admonition. Otherwise, how does it follow that He would wish those whom He just called so wicked to be seen as clean in every way just by giving alms?

26 **Who tithe**] In Greek it is "because" <note>original: "ὅτι" (hoti)</note>, as the Golden Manuscript also agrees in other places. **Mint**, <gloss>original: "ἡδύοσμον" (hēdyosmon)</gloss>. The word is named for the grace of its scent. He names two cheap herbs, not especially necessary for human life. And He said "every herb" for "any kind of herb," that is, no matter how contemptible, noting their remarkable avarice. Even if Saint Ambrose seems to take "you tithe" to mean "you give tithes." For he writes: *"Briefly He touches upon their many vices, who exert all their zeal in contributing tithes of the cheapest fruits."* Theophylact and Cyril interpret it no differently. This sense fits better with what follows: "and you pass over judgment and the love of God." The judgment of men is when someone is judged pious from little observations like these: if someone fasts frequently, if someone says many little prayers, if someone dresses poorly. The judgment of God is when a man's piety is estimated by the affection of his soul. The charity of men is when someone is helped by a tiny benefit, which was sometimes provided just so as not to be a nuisance. The charity of God is when a person is helped in those things that pertain to his eternal salvation, and when this affection is shown even to enemies. And I do not know whether this speech of Christ might apply to those who increase the wealth of monasteries or colleges, or perhaps even the riches of Popes who already have more than enough, while passing over the needy—sometimes even their own relatives or children.

# XII.
<margin>144 1</margin> Meanwhile, when the crowds had gathered in the tens of thousands, so that they were trampling one another, He began to say to His disciples, "First, guard yourselves against the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy."

---

> 27 *Which they cannot carry*] <note>original: "δυσβάστακτα" (dysbastakta)</note>, that is, difficult to be carried.

> 28 *You do not touch the packs*] <note>original: "τοῖς φορτίοις" (tois phortiois)</note>. The same word that he just translated as *burdens*. The word "attingitis" (you reach for/touch upon) was more significant and more appropriate to the Greek term than just "tangitis" (you touch). This passage applies to those who ensnare the common people with human regulations, looking for nothing other than the convenience of those who institute them.

> 29 *That you consent*] <note>original: "συνευδοκεῖτε" (syneudokeite)</note>, that is, you approve or find it acceptable.

> 30 *From the generation*] <note>original: "γενεά" (genea)</note>, which Holy Scripture often uses to mean an "age." This is not the same word Matthew uses in the genealogy of Christ.

> 31 *Between the altar and the sanctuary*] <note>original: "καὶ τοῦ οἴκου" (kai tou oikou)</note>, that is, the house, but he understands it as a specific part of the temple.

> 32 *So I say to you*] "So" is not used here as a conjunction like "wherefore" <note>original: "ὥστε" (hōste)</note>, but "Yes" <note>original: "ναὶ" (nai)</note>, which sometimes translates as "even" or "certainly," an adverb of one making a strong affirmation. It could have been translated as "assuredly" or "certainly."

> 33 *You have taken the key*] <note>original: "ἤρατε" (ērate)</note>. From *tollo*, that is, you took it upon yourselves. For we "take up" a sword to kill, and we "take" what we snatch from others.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...from these Pharisees, because you love the first seats in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplace. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like tombs that do not appear, and people walking over them do not know it. Then one of the experts in the Law answering said to Him: "Master, saying these things you affect us also with insult." But He said: "And woe to you experts in the Law, because you load people with burdens <sup>27</sup> which they cannot carry, and you yourselves <sup>28</sup> do not touch the packs with one of your fingers. Woe to you, because you build the monuments of the prophets, but your fathers killed them. Assuredly you testify <sup>29</sup> that you approve the deeds of your fathers, because they indeed killed them, but you build their sepulchers. Therefore also the wisdom of God said: I will send to them prophets and apostles, and from them they will kill and persecute. That the blood of all the prophets, which is shed from the constitution of the world <sup>30</sup> by this nation, may be required; from the blood of Abel even to the blood of Zechariah, who perished <sup>31</sup> between the altar and the sanctuary: <sup>32</sup> certainly I say to you, it shall be required from this nation. Woe to you experts in the Law, because <sup>33</sup> you have taken the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and those who were entering, you forbade. While He was saying these things to them, the scribes and Pharisees began to <sup>34</sup> insist harshly, <sup>35</sup> and to question Him captiously about many things, laying traps for Him and seeking to hunt something from His mouth, that they might accuse Him. Meanwhile, when a multitude of countless crowds had assembled, so that they trampled each other, He began to say to His disciples: 'First, beware for yourselves of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.'"

<margin>A</margin> <note>Notes on the text following markers A, B, C, D, I, F</note>
These things and those that follow make it clear: *For seeking, he says, to hunt something from His mouth.* For what he had just called *apostomatizein* <note>to force speech</note>, he now calls *to hunt something from His mouth.* Thus far Theophylact. <note>Theophylact was an 11th-century Byzantine archbishop known for his biblical commentaries.</note> Furthermore, not even Laurentius <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous humanist scholar</note> was attentive enough in this passage; he thinks that *apostomatizein* (or *apostomatizesthai*, for I find both) could have been rendered by a single word: *to interrupt*, *to rebuke*, or *to speak against*. And yet he reads it as *epistomatizein* <note>to silence</note>, not *apostomatizein*. Personally, I do not remember reading this word in other authors except for a few, namely Athenaeus in the eighth book of the *Philosophers at Dinner* <note>The Deipnosophistae</note>, where it stands for reciting from memory without the help of a book—what is commonly called "to speak by mouth." I will write down his words: "And Plutarch used to say there were some Rhodian stories, which he could not *apostomatizein* <note>recite from memory</note> at the present moment, because he had come across the book containing them a very long time ago." Hesychius also adds: *apostomatizein* means to want to speak from memory without a partner. Although the same author soon interprets *apostomatizōn* as *phrazōn*, that is, stopping up or closing the mouth. This latter meaning certainly comes closer to the sense of the Evangelist. Truly, I do not know if *epistomizein* should be read instead of *apostomatizein*. Athenaeus used that word a little further down in the same book: "For while you strive to *epistomizein* <note>close the mouth of</note> everyone, you do not condemn others for ignorance, but you show yourself to be emptier than a Lampridas." Paul used it in a similar way in the first chapter of the Epistle to Titus: "whose mouths must be stopped" <note>original: "οὓς δεῖ ἐπιστομίζειν"</note>, where Jerome translates it as "imposing silence." I have corrected the translator of Theophylact. Julius Pollux mentions this word in Book 11, explaining *epistomizein* as "to restrain the speaker." He also indicates that *apostomatizesthai* is found in Plato, who wrote somewhere that "the boys were being *apostomatizesthai*" whenever, at the demand of their teachers, the boys recite from memory what was taught. Indeed, even that which is recited is called *apostomatizesthai*, whether it refers to the matter or the person. We certainly found it in Aristotle's *On Sophistical Refutations* in a similar sense. This fits this passage well. For teachers, when they examine students, are accustomed to interrupt frequently with little questions, testing whether they understand what they are pronouncing, so that if they err, they may correct them. Thus these men, as Cyril interprets, were interrupting the Lord with many little questions, so that if He did not answer, He would seem unlearned; if He answered poorly, He would be refuted; or if He answered well, it would still provide a handle for criticism from so many angles. I have brought forward what I found in reliable authors regarding this word, leaving the choice to the prudent reader.

> 34 *To insist*] <note>original: "ἐνέχειν" (enechein)</note>, that is, to hold back. But more corrected manuscripts had *enischein*, that is, to press upon or urge, and it is likely the Translator read it that way.

> 35 *And to oppress his mouth*] <note>original: "ἀποστοματίζειν"</note>. The Translator seems to have read *epistomizein*, which means "to stop the mouth" and not allow speech. But the Greek manuscripts have *apostomatizein*, which signifies more "to hang from the mouth" and observe what is being said. And that fits much more correctly with those things that precede and follow: "they were lying in wait for him," and "seeking to catch something from his mouth." For these things do not fit one who closes the mouth of the speaker. Finally, the Greek interpreters explain it in this way. If anyone lacks faith in me, I will write down the words of Theophylact himself regarding this passage: "And they began to *apostomatizein* him, that is, to ask him bitterly and to be at a loss. For <margin>F</margin> *apostomatizein* happens when several people ask one person about various different arguments; for then, when he cannot respond, he gives the appearance of a fool because he is stuck. This was indeed what those cursed men were then devising against Christ. For many questioning one person seemed to *apostomatizein* him and lead him into difficulty, as one unable to answer, which would likely have happened. For how could one respond to many asking different things? However, *apostomatizein* can also be understood this way, as ensnaring him and catching him by the mouth. For when someone is caught by what he says, he is seen to be *apostomatized*, that is, caught and condemned by his own mouth." The following words also show this: "Seeking, it says, to hunt something from his mouth." So what I called *apostomatizein* a little before, he now calls "to hunt something from his mouth." I will not find it troublesome to translate these things for the sake of those who do not know Greek. Indeed, they also explain *apostomatizein* as "to interrogate him frequently and render him perplexed."

<margin>M</margin> *Many crowds*] <note>original: "τῶν μυριάδων τοῦ ὄχλου"</note>, that is, the myriads of the crowd. Now *myrias* in Greek means ten thousand. However, they use that word loosely for an innumerable multitude. Hence it could be translated as "a countless crowd of people." And it is not "running together," but *episynachtheisōn*, that is, gathered together at once. Ancient manuscripts had "standing around."

2 *To the disciples*] Here the Greeks add *prōton*, that is, "first" or "at first." Although the adverb is placed so that it could refer to either: "He first said to the disciples," or "First, pay attention." Then also,

3 *Pay attention*] <note>original: "προσέχετε ἑαυτοῖς"</note>.

<margin>4 Revealed]</margin> In the Greek, it is "will be revealed" (*ἀποκαλυφθήσεται*) and "will be known" (*γνωσθήσεται*), rather than "is revealed" and "is known."
<margin>5 In the inner rooms]</margin> *en tois tameiois*, that is, in the inner chambers or the most private parts of the house.
<margin>6 Yes, I say to you]</margin> Here again is the word *nai* <note>original: "ναὶ" — an adverb of affirmation.</note>, which I just warned about, an adverb used for affirming.
<margin>7 Two pennies]</margin> The translator explained what he was translating. For in Greek it is "two assaria" (*assarion duo*), which means two pennies. Although the Greek word is a diminutive, just like "little sparrows" (*passerculi*).
<margin>8 In oblivion]</margin> *epilelēsmenon*. You might say this in the passive sense as "forgotten."
<margin>9 Confessed me]</margin> The Greek says *en emoi*, that is, "in me." Thus it is not simply "confess him," but "in him." This does not change the sense at all; it is merely a Hebrew idiom.
<margin>10 How or what you will answer]</margin> *ti apologēsēsthe*, that is, what you are going to answer, specifically to an accuser. This refers to the ways you will form your words, the logic you will use for your defense, or what evidence you will bring forward to defend your case—just as common defendants do, who usually face danger in two ways: either by not knowing the proper form of legal action or by being poorly prepared to refute what is being charged against them.
<margin>11 From all greed]</margin> "All" is not added in the Greek codices. Nor is it simply "avarice" (which is more often called *philargyria*, or love of money), but it is *pleonexia*, a name derived from "having more," which Saint Paul used frequently. It refers to when someone, by defrauding others, takes more for himself than is fair.
<margin>12 Be merry]</margin> *euphrainou*, that is, rejoice. For there was no need to repeat "feast" since it had already been said, "eat, drink." Furthermore, the word *euphrainestai* is used because it goes well with the soul; it encompasses all the pleasures of life with which the soul delights itself. Thus in the *Psalms*, "And wine gladdens the heart of man," the Greek uses *euphrainei*. But here [the Vulgate] consistently translates it as "to feast." For a little later—
