rest, eat, drink, be glad.' 20 But God said to him, 'Fool, this night they demand your soul back from you: and the things you have prepared, to whom will they go?' 21 So is he who stores up for himself, and is not rich toward God." <margin>D</margin> 22 And He said to his disciples: "Therefore I say to you, do not be anxious for your soul, what you shall eat, nor for your body, what you shall put on. 23 The soul is more than food, and the body more than clothing. 24 Consider the ravens, for they do not sow, nor do they reap, for whom there is no pantry nor barn, 25 and God feeds them: how much more do you excel the birds? 26 But which of you by his anxiety can add one cubit to his stature? 27 If therefore you cannot do even that which is least, why are you anxious about the rest? <margin>E</margin> —namely in chapter 15: "Bring the fatted calf and kill it, and let us eat and be merry, *euphranthōmen*." And again, "And they began to be merry, *euphrainestai*." They did this, I think, because "to feast" (*epulari*) is not simply to have a dinner, but to eat in a jovial and sumptuous manner.
<margin>13 Demanding back]</margin> *apaitousin*, that is, they demand back or they reclaim. Jerome also cites it this way frequently, so that it is in the present tense: and this figure of speech is more suited to signify the danger immediately looming. Cyprian, in his work on the Lord’s Prayer, brings it up with these words: "Fool, this night your soul is called for." And the Constance manuscript had "they demand back."
<margin>14 Whose will they be]</margin> *tini estai*, that is, to whom will they belong? This means, to whom will they pass, and who will happen to be their master? This same figure of speech is found in Paul: "if she should be to another man," that is, with another man.
<margin>15 So is he who [stores up] for himself]</margin> The word "is" is not added in the Greek copies, so that one is free to understand whatever is most convenient.
<margin>16 For whom there is no cellar]</margin> For "cellar" the Greek has the same word that has already been translated several times as "inner room," *tameion*. This is properly a place in the house in which food and drink are stored, from *tameuein*, which is to dispense provisions, and *tamias*, a steward or butler. Furthermore, when Laurentius <note>Likely Laurentius Valla, a famous humanist critic of the Vulgate whom Erasmus often cited.</note> quibbles that a "cellar" should only be understood as a wine-cellar, and that ravens are water-drinkers, he has erred twice. For first, "cellar" (*cella*), named from "hiding" (*celando*), is not only a storage place for wine. Second, if ravens do not drink wine, this actually supports the Gospel's meaning: they are content with whatever drink nature provides everywhere for everyone, and they do not need wine cellars.
<margin>17 You are of more value than them]</margin> *diapherete tōn peteinōn*, that is, you excel the birds. For *diapherein*, although it means "to differ," is nevertheless frequently used to mean "to surpass" or "to excel." Paul used it in this sense to the Philippians in the first chapter, and also to the Romans in the second chapter.

The Greek is a participle, as if you said <italic>caring</italic>, <italic>or thinking anxiously</italic>.

<margin>E</margin>
19 <italic>If however the hay</italic>] <note>original: "τὸν χόρτον" (ton chorton)</note>. Why not rather "grass" or "herb," as it is translated elsewhere? Unless perhaps there is no difference between hay and grass. For the comparison is used so that we might understand that God will not neglect us, since he cares for even the grass, which is green on the same day, and having failed, withers on the same day, especially in hot regions.
20 <italic>How much more you of little faith</italic>] "You" is brought forward in the accusative case, <note>original: "ὑμᾶς"</note>, so that you may understand <italic>he will clothe</italic>. And <italic>of little faith</italic> is a compound word in Greek, <note>original: "ὀλιγόπιστοι"</note>, which sounds like <italic>little-trusting</italic>. For <term>fides</term> <note>Latin: faith</note> is excellence, and faith is <term>fidentia</term> <note>Latin: confidence/trust</note>. For this is how we Christians use the term.
21 <italic>Do not be lifted up on high</italic>] <note>original: "μὴ μετεωρίζεσθε"</note>. This does not properly pertain to pride, which the Greeks call <note>original: "μεγάλην φρονῆσιν"</note> (high-mindedness), but rather that we should not worry about those things that are above us: for those things are called <note>original: "μετέωρα"</note> (meteora) which are in the clouds and in the high region of the air; about which Aristotle wrote his <term>Meteorologica</term> <note>Aristotle's treatise on natural phenomena and atmospheric science.</note>. That Socratic saying agrees with the doctrine of Christ: <italic>What is above us, is nothing to us</italic>. Nor do I see how this little part fits with the preceding and following verses, unless it is felt to refer to those who consult the stars far into the future, which is almost the death of divine and princely things. Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and Bible commentator.</note> and other Greeks interpret <note>original: "μετεωρίζεσθαι"</note> as one who is not content with present things, but always gapes for greater ones, which is surely the nature of human desires. And in a way, he raises himself above the condition of man who heaps up riches for the far future, ignorant of whether he will be alive the next day. <italic>And all these things</italic>. These words are not added in this Evangelist, neither in the Greek nor in the old Latin copies, but truly were transferred here from another place. And indeed the addition <italic>first</italic> is not used. The Golden Codex <note>An illuminated manuscript of the Gospels, possibly the Codex Aureus of Stockholm.</note> agrees with the Greek reading, as do the Donatian manuscripts, and finally the Complutensian <note>The first printed polyglot edition of the entire Bible (1514-1517).</note>. In which I found it written, <italic>Seek the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added, etc.</italic> Truly, what seems to be missing in Luke, some studious person added from the sixth chapter of Matthew.
22 <italic>If the master of the house had known</italic>] Luke used words of the past tense: <italic>if he had known, he would have watched, and would not have allowed</italic>, <note>original: "ᾔδει, ἐγρηγόρησεν, ἀφῆκε"</note>.

For he sets it forth as a parable of someone whose house was broken into.

<margin>F</margin>
23 <italic>Over the household</italic>] <note>original: "ἐπὶ τῆς θεραπείας"</note>, that is, <italic>over the body of servants</italic>, so that you understand he is appointed only over the servants, not also over the children. Which kind of servants they call the <term>colamen familiae</term> <note>Latin: the 'sifter' or 'protector' of the family—the chief slave.</note>. Now that phrase, <note>original: "τίς ἄρα"</note>, "Who then," comes in his own style, for <italic>who</italic>, or <italic>whoever</italic>. And it is not "he set," in the present tense, but <note>original: "καταστήσει"</note>, "he will set," in the future tense, as the Pauline copies mark it, though in Matthew it is "he set."
24 <italic>A measure of wheat</italic>] <note>original: "σιτομέτριον"</note>. It can refer to all food. That which in Latin they call <term>demensum</term> <note>A slave's monthly allowance or ration of grain.</note>, either because it is granted in a certain measure, or because it was returned in individual months, as Donatus prefers. So Terence in his play <italic>Phormio</italic>: <italic>Which that poor wretch hardly saved ounce by ounce from his own ration [demenso], defrauding his own spirit</italic>. And Plautus in <italic>Stichus</italic>: <italic>You remember how many Calends [months] you sought your measured food [demensum]</italic>. Furthermore, for the Greeks, the word is a compound <note>original: "σιτομέτριον"</note>, from "corn" and "measure," not just from "wheat." Although sometimes for the Greeks "corn" signifies wheat, and sometimes by a change of genus it signifies any food. For servants were not nourished by wheat alone. And that word <note>original: "διχοτομήσει"</note>, is "to cut in two," that is, <italic>he will divide into two parts</italic>, or <italic>he will dissect</italic>.
25 <italic>With the unfaithful</italic>] <note>original: "μετὰ τῶν ἀπίστων"</note>, that is, <italic>with the untrustworthy</italic>, for which Matthew said, <italic>with the hypocrites</italic>. For he who is faithful does not pretend, nor does he dissemble.
26 <italic>Will be beaten many</italic>] And a little after <italic>will be beaten with stripes</italic>. Why did he not add "stripes" in both places, or omit it in both? Since among the Greeks "stripes" <note>original: "πληγάς" (plegas)</note> is understood in both places. But we have corrupted this by our punctuation: for the <italic>ablative stripes</italic>, which we refer to "few," should have been referred to "worthy," <note>original: "ἄξια πληγῶν"</note> (worthy of stripes), and thus in both places "stripes" <note>original: "πληγάς"</note> should be understood for "many" <note>original: "πολλάς"</note> and "few" <note>original: "ὀλίγας"</note>. For so the Greeks distinguish: <italic>But he who did not know, yet did things worthy of stripes, will be beaten [with] few [stripes].</italic> Indeed, he used the form <italic>to be beaten many stripes</italic> in the same way we say in the Attic manner <italic>to rejoice a joy</italic> and <italic>to grieve a grief</italic>. Augustine, in his book to Valentinus <italic>On Grace and Free Will</italic> chapter 3, following I know not what, reads: <italic>he will be beaten few, and he will be beaten many.</italic>

### THE GOSPEL, CHAPTER XIII.

<column-break/>

<margin>50</margin> <margin>A</margin> 27 And what do I desire, if it is already kindled? But I have a baptism to be baptized with: and how I am distressed until it is accomplished!
<margin>51</margin> Do you think that I came to bring peace to the earth? No, I tell you, but rather division.
<margin>52</margin> For from now on, there will be five in one house divided, 28 three against two, and two against three.
<margin>53</margin> The father will be divided against the son, and the son against the father; the mother against the daughter, and the daughter against the mother; the mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law, and the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.
<margin>54</margin> He also said to the crowds: When you see a cloud rising from the west, immediately you say, "A rain shower is coming," and so it happens.
<margin>55</margin> And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, "There will be heat," and it happens.
<margin>56</margin> <margin>B</margin> Hypocrites, you know how to discern the face of the sky and the earth; but how is it that you do not discern this time?
<margin>57</margin> 31 And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?
<margin>58</margin> 32 For when you are going with your adversary to the magistrate on the way, make an effort to be released from him, lest 34 he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer throw you into prison.
<margin>59</margin> I tell you, you will not get out of there until you have paid the very last cent <note>original: "λεπτόν" (lepton), the smallest Greek copper coin.</note>.
<margin>XIII. 1</margin> There were some present at that very time reporting to him about the Galileans, whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices.
<margin>2</margin> And answering, Jesus said to them, <margin>C</margin> Do you think that these Galileans were sinners above all other Galileans because they suffered such things?
<margin>3</margin> No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.
<margin>4</margin> Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them—do you think they were debtors <note>In this context, "debtors" is used as a metaphor for "sinners" or those owing a spiritual debt to God.</note> beyond all the men living in Jerusalem?
<margin>5</margin> No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.
<margin>6</margin> And he spoke this parable: A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none.
<margin>7</margin> And he said to the vine-dresser: Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and I find none; cut it down. Why 3 should it even occupy the ground?
<margin>8</margin> <margin>D</margin> But answering, he said to him: Lord, leave it alone this year also, until I dig around it 5 and put in manure.
<margin>9</margin> And if indeed it produces fruit, [well]; but if not, in the future you shall cut it down.
<margin>10</margin> Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath.
<margin>11</margin> And behold, there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years; she was bent over and was not able—
<meta>catchword: —to straighten up</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>27</margin> **And what do I desire, unless it burns?** <note>original: "Et quid volo, nisi ut ardeat?"</note> The Greek is <note>original: "καὶ τί θέλω, εἰ ἤδη ἀνήφθη"</note>, which means, "and what do I want, if it is already kindled?" Hilary alluded to it this way in his *Commentary on the Song of Ascents*. Ambrose and Jerome also read it this way, the latter of whom cites the passage thus: *I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I wish but that it burn.* Truly, I suspect that *quam* [than/but] was corrupted into *quum* [when], for in other places I find *quum*. It appears the Translator read <note>original: "καὶ τί θέλω εἰ μὴ ἤδη ἀνήφθη"</note>, that is, "and what do I want unless it be kindled." Or certainly, what is closer to the truth, <note>original: "τι θέλω, ἢ ἤδη ἀνήφθη"</note>, that is, "what do I want, except that it be kindled." Since in Greek, "if" <note>original: "εἰ"</note> is joined even to positive statements with "but" being understood, just as the Latins add "when" to positives with "after" or some such word understood. For example: "on the third day since (when) you departed from me." Theophylact not only reads but also interprets according to our Edition. For "what I want" is placed there for what was "I want nothing else; and if it is already kindled," it carries an emphasis of speed: and in the "if" there lies a sacred expression of a wish.

<margin>28</margin> **For they shall be from now on** <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν"</note>, that is, "hereafter" or "from this point," as some say, rendering the Greek form.

<margin>29</margin> **And two shall be divided against three** This passage has been corrupted by the scribes with faulty punctuation, as they referred the verb "will be divided" to the previous part, and to make it fit, they changed the singular "will be divided" to the plural. But what was the need to repeat "will be divided" in this part, when it was already said, "There will be five in one house divided"? Thus, it should have been punctuated this way: "The father shall be divided against the son, etc." Since "being divided" refers to having a disagreement. Therefore, it would have been better to translate "against the son" <note>original: "adversus filium"</note> than "into the son" <note>original: "in filium"</note>, since the Greek preposition is added. If anyone is moved by this, Luke changed the case in the same place: though he began by adding the dative <note>original: "ἐπὶ υἱῷ"</note>, he soon adds the accusative <note>original: "ἐπὶ τὴν νύμφην"</note>.

<margin>30</margin> **And so it happens** It should be read as "It happens" <note>original: "Fit"</note>. And Laurentius prefers "rain shower" <note>original: "imbrem"</note> over "cloud" <note>original: "nimbum"</note>, since the Greek is <note>original: "ὄμβρος"</note>.

<margin>31</margin> **Why even of yourselves** <note>original: "Τί δὲ καὶ ἀφ' ἑαυτῶν"</note>. It would be clearer as: "Moreover, why do you not also judge from yourselves what is just?" The sense being: You seek arguments from elsewhere to guess about things outside of yourselves, but regarding those things within you—for which arguments can be gathered from yourselves—you make no conjecture.

<margin>32</margin> **When however you go** For the Greek "however" <note>original: "γάρ"</note> is here instead of "but" <note>original: "autem"</note>. For it connects with what precedes, so they may understand that the time for repentance is at hand; unless they do so, things will go harder for them in the future if they neglect such obvious divine mercy.

<margin>33</margin> **To the ruler on the way** <note>original: "ἐπ' ἄρχοντα"</note>. Which Ambrose translated not

<column-break/>

badly as "to the magistrate." And "on the way" refers more correctly to what follows: "on the way, give effort."

<margin>34</margin> **Drag you to the judge** I wonder what Ambrose read, for in place of "drag" <note>original: "trahat"</note> he has "condemn" <note>original: "condemnet"</note>; unless perhaps he read <note>original: "κατακρίνῃ"</note> (condemn) instead of <note>original: "κατασύρῃ"</note> (drag). And the sense certainly fits better. For the judge does not seem to be anyone other than the one he just called the "ruler." For he wants the matter to be settled with the adversary while walking, so that there is no need to reach the judge. Origen, or whoever it was, in the 25th Homily on Luke, notes that there is an ambiguity in "drag," as it could mean either "drag you" or "the adversary drags you."

<margin>35</margin> **Hand you over to the officer** <note>original: "πράκτορι"</note>, from the verb <note>original: "πράττω"</note> meaning "to exact" [a debt], which he previously translated incorrectly as "to do," as we noted in Matthew.

<margin>1</margin> **In Siloam** <note>original: "ἐν τῷ Σιλωάμ"</note>. The Hebrews pronounce it *Siloah*. I believe this is the city where the Tabernacle first resided, which Psalm 77 mentions: *And he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh*, where the Greek reads <note>original: "Σιλὼμ"</note>. Likewise Jeremiah chapter 7. Since the article <note>original: "τῷ"</note> is added here, it seems to signify the river (or pool) of Siloam, which supplies the city with water, though it is neither permanent nor abundant. In the oldest Latin manuscripts, it was written *Siloa* in some places and *Siloam* in others.

<margin>2</margin> **In the fig tree** <note>original: "ἐν τῇ συκῇ"</note>, that is, "in the fig." It is the same word he just translated as "a tree of fig," an excessive seeker of variety, not to say an untimely one.

<margin>3</margin> **Occupies the ground** <note>original: "καταργεῖ"</note>, that is, "burdens," but with a useless burden, for this is what <note>original: "καταργεῖν"</note> properly means. And regarding "also the ground," I certainly would have preferred to translate it as "why does it even occupy the ground?", so that we understand it is unfruitful, and not only unworthy of manuring and cultivation, but even of the space it occupies.

<margin>4</margin> **And I will put in dung** <note>original: "κοπρίαν"</note>, that is, "manuring," or rather "manure"; later he translates it as "dung-pit." For the Greek word sounds more like "the act of manuring" than "the dung" itself. And manuring is not only done from the excrement of animals, but also from straw, stalks, or the marrow of the earth, which the Britons call *merga* [marl], according to Pliny. Ambrose reads "a basket of dung."

<margin>5</margin> **But if not** <note>original: "εἰ δὲ μήγε"</note>, that is, "but if otherwise" or "if not so." "And if indeed it produces fruit," the speech is incomplete <term>ellipsis/aposiopesis: a rhetorical device where a sentence is left unfinished for effect</term>, so that "we will leave it" or some other benefit is understood. For there is an ellipsis or aposiopesis, as our friend Budé prefers, <note>original: "ἀποσιώπησις"</note>, who brings forth one or two examples of this form from Aristophanes and Cicero in the Annotations he wrote on the Pandects of the Law. Nor should anyone be defrauded of their own praise. Furthermore, where this Translator renders it "but if not" <note>original: "sin autem"</note> in somewhat poor Latin, he at other times translates it more tolerably as "otherwise" <note>original: "alioqui"</note>.

<margin>6 Not at all</margin> <note>original Greek: "εἰς τὸ παντελές"</note>. This is elsewhere translated as "forever." She was not just "inclined," but "bent over" <note>original: "συγκύπτουσα"</note>, that is, with her whole body bent down toward the ground and contracted. *The opposite of this is what follows, "to lift up" <note>original: "ἀνακύψαι"</note>, which is translated as looking upward, that is, to straighten oneself up.* For the text does not strictly mean "looking," but refers to the posture of the body used by those who desire to look up. Similarly, the term "peering" <note>original: "παρακύψαι"</note> is properly used when someone looks out a window with a tilted head.

<margin>7 Called to him</margin> <note>original Greek: "προσεφώνησε"</note>. This can be understood as "he addressed her" or "spoke to her." The phrase "to himself" is not added in the Greek.

<margin>8 Each one of you</margin> <note>original Greek: "ἕκαστος ὑμῶν"</note>. Which he sometimes translates as "each one," and other times as "to inhabit."

<margin>9 Three measures</margin> <margin>F</margin> <note>original Greek: "σάτα τρία"</note>. We advised above that "satum" is not a Latin word, but a Syrian one <note>scholars today identify it as Hebrew/Aramaic</note>, which among them indicates a type of measure holding one and a half *modii*. In the writings of Ambrose, "three measures" is not added. It simply says, "hid it in flour until the whole was leavened." In his interpretation, he indicates this was transcribed here from Matthew, saying: "And because in Matthew the leaven is said to be hidden in three measures, etc." Why would he cite Matthew if he had read the same in Luke? But this sort of thing in the Gospel volumes should not seem new, nor should it greatly disturb anyone, since it does not hinder godly character or the sincerity of faith.

<margin>10 If few are those who are saved</margin> The word "if" <note>original: "Si"</note> is not ambiguous in Latin as the word "if" <note>original: "εἰ"</note> is in Greek; therefore it should have been translated as "whether," since they are asking a question.

<margin>11 Strive to enter</margin> <note>original Greek: "Ἀγωνίζεσθε"</note>, that is, "Compete" or "Labor." Although the Translator <note>referring to the Vulgate translator</note> translates it aptly, if only we understand it correctly. For he "contends" who exerts himself sharply.

<margin>12 Who will be the last</margin> It should be read "will be" <note>original: "ἔσονται"</note> in both places. "There are those who are last who *will be* first, and there are those who are first who *will be* last." For he is speaking of the reversal of order between those who were there then, and those who were to succeed in the Gospel.

<margin>13 Go and tell</margin> "Having gone" <note>original: "πορευθέντες"</note>, tell. In ancient books it is read as "having gone, speak."

<margin>14 On the third day I am finished</margin> It should be read "I am finished" <note>original Latin: "consummor"</note> with a double 'm'. The Greek is "I am perfected" <note>original: "τελειοῦμαι"</note>. Since this is a middle-voice verb, it was better to translate it actively, so we understand that he would finish his work on the third day. Though that finishing was his death and resurrection.

<margin>15 Because it does not contain</margin> <note>original Greek: "ἐνδέχεται"</note>. Matthew used "apart from" <note>original Greek: "χωρίς"</note>. It is used here almost impersonally, as if you were to say, "the very nature of things does not allow it." A little later he says "it is impossible" <note>original: "ἀνένδεκτόν ἐστι"</note> for that which is "not possible." Tertullian speaks in this manner repeatedly, using "it contains" <note>original: "capit"</note> for "it is fitting" or "it is proper," and "it does not contain" for "it is not fitting."

<margin>16 Who are sent to you</margin> <note>original Greek: "πρὸς αὐτήν"</note>, that is, "to itself," in the third person, unless it is joined with another pronoun. The speech sounds like this to the Greeks: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, she who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her." Then he suddenly changes the person. Thus we also mixed the third person with the first. "You, that stoner of prophets." And yet if the second person pleases someone more, I do not intend to fight over this, because of the pronoun used above, which some think fits every person. Certainly, regarding the sense, there is no ambiguity.

<margin>17 Just as a bird</margin> <note>original Greek: "ὄρνις"</note>, which can mean either a bird in general or a hen. For there is a gentle love in birds for brooding over their chicks, but especially in hens. Augustine, in *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*, Book II, Chapter 75, reads "bird."

<margin>18 Behold, it is left</margin> <note>original Greek: "ἀφίεται"</note>, that is, "it is abandoned," as we have noted before.

Then the master of the house, becoming angry, said to his servant, 'Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor and crippled and lame and blind.' <margin>22</margin> And the servant said, 'Sir, what you commanded has been done, and there is still room.' <margin>23</margin> And the master said to the servant, 'Go out into the roads and hedges and compel them to come in, so that my house may be filled. <margin>24</margin> For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my dinner.'" <margin>25</margin> Now great crowds were traveling with him, and turning to them, he said, <margin>26</margin> "If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. <margin>27</margin> And whoever does not carry his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple. <margin>28</margin> For which of you, wanting to build a tower...

"I tell you, you will not see me until the time comes when you say, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.'" <margin>XIV. 1</margin> And it happened, when he entered the house of one of the leaders of the Pharisees on the Sabbath to eat bread, they were watching him. <margin>2</margin> And behold, a certain man with dropsy was before him. <margin>3</margin> And answering, Jesus spoke to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, "Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?" <margin>4</margin> But they kept silent. The first said to him, 'I have bought a farm, and I must go out and see it; I ask you, hold me excused.' <margin>19</margin> And another said, 'I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to test them; I ask you, hold me excused.' <margin>20</margin> And another said, 'I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come.' <margin>21</margin> And the servant, returning, reported these things to his master. <margin>1</margin> *And it happened* ] Regarding this form of speech <note>original: "Et factum est"</note> peculiar to Luke, we have already given warning.

<margin>2</margin> *He also said to those invited* ] The conjunction "and" is not added in the Greek, nor in the ancient manuscripts.

<margin>3</margin> *More honorable* ] is *entimoteros* <note>original: "ἐντιμότερος"</note>. This signifies both "dearer" and "held in higher value."

<margin>4</margin> *Neither neighbors, nor rich* ] <note>original: "μηδὲ γείτονας πλουσίους"</note>, that is, "nor rich neighbors." In the Antellan and our most ancient manuscripts, including the Golden Codex and the Constance manuscript. Indeed, Christ’s parable pertains to this: that a benefit should be conferred freely, without hope of returning interest. This occurs if it is provided to the needy, who do not have the ability to return the favor.

<margin>5</margin> *Lest perhaps* ] <note>original: "μή ποτε"</note>, that is, "lest," or "lest ever." And what follows, *and they invite you in return*. It could be more suitably translated as "they invite you back in turn." For "to reinvite" is Latin; one "reinvites" who invites again someone already called once. In Greek it is *antakalesōsi* <note>original: "ἀντικαλέσωσι"</note>.

<margin>6</margin> *They do not have to repay* ] <note>original: "οὐκ ἔχουσιν ἀνταποδοῦναι"</note>, that is, "they are not able to repay." For "to have" <note>original: "ἔχω"</note> is frequently understood in this way when it is attached to infinitive verbs. In the Golden Codex it was written, "they do not have whence they might repay." and shortly after, instead of "in the resurrection," it was written "in the retribution." I found the same in two ancient manuscripts of St. Donatian. But the Greek texts disagree.

<column-break/>

<margin>7</margin> *Who will eat bread* ] Some codices have *ariston* <note>original: "ἄριστον"</note>, that is, "lunch," instead of *arton* <note>original: "ἄρτον"</note>, "bread," but the ancient Latin manuscripts disagree. "He who will eat" <note>original: "ὃς φάγεται"</note> can be understood as "he who eats" or rather "is eating" in the present tense. For in these three verbs—to eat, to devour, and to drink—the future middle does not differ from the present. But this matters very little for the sense.

<margin>8</margin> *That they might come* ] <note>original: "Ἔρχεσθε"</note>, that is, "Come." The translator perhaps read *erchesthai* <note>original: "ἐρχέσθαι"</note>, "to come."

<margin>9</margin> *All together to excuse* ] <note>original: "παραιτεῖσθαι"</note>, that is, "to refuse." Although the translator elegantly used the word "to excuse" <note>original: "excusare"</note>. Provided the reader notices that he "excuses" who refuses what is asked by bringing forward a cause.

<margin>10</margin> *Shall taste my dinner* ] In this place, the Greek books add, "for many are called, but few are chosen" <note>original: "πολλοὶ γὰρ εἰσι κλητοὶ, ὀλίγοι δὲ ἐκλεκτοὶ"</note>. Although this is not found in all manuscripts. I suspect it was written in here from elsewhere.

<margin>11</margin> *Not first* ] <note>original: "οὐχὶ"</note>, that is, "not." Although even this is sometimes placed for "is it not?" "Sitting, he calculates" <note>original: "καθίσας ψηφίζει"</note>, that is, he draws a reckoning with pebbles <term>psēphizei: to count using small stones, implying a very precise and careful calculation</term>, so that you may understand a diligent and exact computation. And a little after, "lest perhaps," he finally ceased to translate as "lest by chance" instead of "lest ever."

<margin>28</margin>...to build a tower, does he not first sit down and calculate the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it? <margin>29</margin> Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it will begin to mock him, <margin>30</margin> saying, "This man began to build and <margin>31</margin> was not able to finish." And he divided his property <note>original: "his life/livelihood"</note> between them. <margin>13</margin> Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living. <margin>14</margin> And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. <margin>15</margin> So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. <margin>16</margin> And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything. <margin>17</margin> But when he came to himself, he said, 'How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! <margin>18</margin> I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, "Father, I have sinned against heaven..."

<margin>12 Going to engage in battle]</margin> <note>original: "ἀνερχόμενος συμβαλεῖν εἰς πόλεμον"</note>, that is, he went away to clash, or to meet in war; although "in battle" <note>original: "praelio"</note> would have been more Latin.
<margin>13 Not sitting]</margin> This is the same word which he had just translated as "not," <note>original: "οὐχὶ"</note>.
<margin>14 With ten thousand]</margin> <note>original: "ἐν δέκα χιλιάσιν"</note>. The translator did not do badly to change the Greek preposition "in" <note>original: "en"</note>—placed there because of a Hebrew idiom—into "with" ten thousand. Although it would have been purer to omit it entirely, since it has no use among us and makes the speech inelegant. Such is the kind of phrasing found in Deuteronomy, "And burning the city in fire." Likewise, "And you shall stone them in stones." Augustine reviewed many such examples in his *Annotations on Hebrew Speech*.
<margin>15 To himself]</margin> <note>original: "ἐπ᾿ αὐτόν"</note>. Why not rather "against him" or "towards him"?
<margin>16 Otherwise while he is still far off]</margin> <note>original: "Εἰ δὲ μή γε"</note>. What he previously translated as "but if," incorrectly, he here correctly translates as "otherwise." "Being far off" <note>original: "πόῤῥω αὐτοῦ ὄντος"</note>, that is, when he is at a distance, or is far away.
<margin>17 Who does not renounce]</margin> <note>original: "ὃς οὐκ ἀποτάσσεται"</note>. Which elsewhere means to say farewell or to dismiss.
<margin>18 Becomes tasteless]</margin> <note>original: "μωρανθῇ"</note>, that is, it is rendered foolish. Indeed, not only humans but other things are called "foolish" <note>original: "fatua"</note> when they have no flavor. Just as Martial calls beets "foolish" <note>meaning tasteless</note>.
<margin>19 It is useful]</margin> <note>original: "εὔθετον"</note>, that is, suitable; previously translated as "fit." Nor was I anxious about the gender of this word, as I well know it is found in the neuter, though more frequently and among more approved authors in the masculine.

<margin>1 Congratulate me]</margin> <note>original: "Συγχάρητέ"</note>, that is, "Rejoice with me." Or if that seems insufficiently Latin to anyone, "Gaudete mecum."
<margin>2 Does she not light]</margin> <note>original: "οὐχὶ"</note>; But "Does she not" or "Whether she does not" was no more fitting here, even if this speech suffers from the same inconvenience as the one we noted before: "Which of you, a father, if a son asks for bread," etc.
<margin>3 Sweeps]</margin> <note>original: "σαροῖ"</note>, that is, she sweeps, which is to say, she cleans with a broom. Perhaps the Translator had written *everrit* <note>sweeps</note>, and some wicked and pseudo-learned person, not understanding it, changed the writing to *everrit* <note>overturns</note>. It is truly a wonder how it was so corrupted and not noticed. This error has grown into all Latin copies, even the oldest ones. The translator Carrensis also felt some trouble here, interpreting it as "she overturns the whole house," that is, those things which are in the house. And morally, to overturn the house is to disturb the consciences of sinners. Theophylact translates "sweeps" as *perisaroī*, and Gregory of Nyssa, who is cited in the *Catena* <note>a chain of commentary</note>, follows the same sense; although Pope Gregory, deceived by the wine <note>perhaps "flaw" or "mistake"</note> of the manuscript, interprets "overturns" as "shaking the conscience."
<margin>4 Which falls to me]</margin> <note>original: "τὸ ἐπιβάλλον"</note>, that is, which returns to me.
<margin>5 Substance]</margin> There are two words among the Greeks, "substance" and "means of living" <note>original: "οὐσίας καὶ βίον"</note>. Although among the Greeks *bios* signifies both life itself and the resources by which one lives.
<margin>6 Living luxuriously]</margin> <note>original: "ζῶν ἀσώτως"</note>, that is, living in a profligate manner. From this, Paul calls luxury *asōtian*: "Wine in which there is luxury." However, this does not pertain to lust alone.
<margin>7 And after he had consumed all]</margin> <note>original: "Δαπανήσαντος δὲ αὐτοῦ πάντα"</note>, that is, when he had consumed or used up everything. Indeed, I think this was corrupted by the fault of scribes, though it is less so by the consensus of our copies. Ambrose indicates that he read it in the Greek manner when he writes in his *Commentaries*: "he therefore living luxuriously consumed all the ornaments of nature. Hence you, who received the image of God, who have his likeness, do not consume it in irrational filthiness."
<margin>8 How many hired servants]</margin> Why not rather "How many," <note>original: "πόσοι"</note>? Neither "in the house" is added, nor is it in the Greek, nor in the old...

<note>Erasmus’s Commentary on the Text</note>

In the Donatian manuscripts, there is only <unclear>this much</unclear>. *How many hired servants of my father have bread enough and to spare, etc.* This agreed with the Constantinian manuscript. For the contrast is between the hired servant and the son. And some minor scribe added *in the house*, so that there would be something to answer to the adverb *here*.

9 *While he was still far off*] <note>original: μακρὰν ἀπέχοντος</note>, that is, when you were at a distance.

10 *Bring forth quickly*] "Quickly" is not added in the Greek manuscripts. Budé <note>Guillaume Budé, a famous French humanist</note> thinks that here also the force of the article should have been expressed: <note>original: τὴν στολὴν τὴν πρώτην</note>, that is, "that first robe." Moreover, it is a type of garment that hangs down to the ankles, so that we understand it is not meant to be just any robe, but a certain and excellent one. For the Greek article is not placed before the rings and shoes. But again, he added a double article to the calf so you would know: <note>original: τὸν μόσχον τὸν σιτευτὸν</note>, that is, "that fatted calf," so that we understand a specific and notable calf is designated. Furthermore, in what follows, when this calf is often repeated, the articles are always added, whereas just now no article was added, because it is not any notable thing being designated, but anyone from the flock. Now, they interpret the calf as the very body of Christ sacrificed for us.

11 *And let us feast*] <note>original: εὐφρανθῶμεν</note>, that is, "let us rejoice," as Valla prefers.

12 *And they began to feast*] Again it is <note>original: εὐφραίνειν</note>, concerning which we have already given warning above.

13 *Music and dancing*] <note>original: συμφωνίας καὶ χορῶν</note>, that is, "harmony and choirs," which means dances. For that is what "choirs" means in this place.

14 *He began to entreat him*] In the Greek it is <note>original: παρεκάλει αὐτόν</note>. This signifies not only to ask, but also to invite and to exhort.

15 *I might feast with my friends*] Again it is <note>original: εὐφρανθῶ</note>. Likewise a little later, *But to feast*, <note>original: Εὐφρανθῆναι δὲ</note>.

16 *He devoured your substance*] The Greeks with great consensus read "your," so that it might be more hateful: <note>original: ὁ καταφαγών σου τὸν βίον</note>. And it is possible to gather that Ambrose read it thus from these words of his: "Envious one," he says, "who accuses your brother because he squandered your father’s substance on harlots." For he did not say *his* substance, but *your father's*.

I *Who had a steward*] <note>original: οἰκονόμον</note>, that is, a manager, which is to say an *oeconomus*, from <note>original: οἶκος</note> "house," and <note>original: νέμω</note> "to distribute," because he manages those things which per-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> to him, "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you: I am 19 no longer worthy to be called your son: make me as one of your hired servants." And rising, he came to his father. 20 But while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with mercy, and running, he fell on his neck and kissed him. And the son said 21 to him, "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; nor henceforth am I worthy to be called your son." But the 22 father said to his servants, "Bring out the first robe and clothe him, and put a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet. And bring that 23 fatted calf and kill it, and taking our fill of the feast, let us <margin>B</margin> rejoice: Because this my son was dead and has come back to life, 24 he had perished and is found." And they began to rejoice. Now 25 his older son was in the field: and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. And he called 26 one of his servants and asked what those things were. And he said to him, "Your brother has come, 27 and your father has killed that fatted calf, because he has received him back safe and sound." But he was indignant, 28 and would not go in. Therefore his father went out and entreated him. But he answering said to the father, "Lo, so many 29 years I have served you, nor have I ever transgressed your command, nor did you ever give me a kid, that <margin>C</margin> I might rejoice with my friends. But after this son of yours 30 came, who devoured your substance with harlots, you killed for him that fatted calf." But he said to him, "Son, you are always with me, and all 31 mine is yours. But it was fitting to rejoice and be glad, 32 because this your brother was dead and has come back to life, he had perished and is found." And he said also to 1 XVI. his disciples, "There was a certain rich man who had a manager <term>dispensatorem: manager or steward</term>, and this man was accused before him as one who was wasting his goods. And he called him and said to him, 2 'What is this I hear about you? Give an account of your management: for you can no longer manage.' But 3 the manager said within himself, 'What shall I do, since my <margin>D</margin> lord takes away the management from me? I am not 4 strong enough to dig, I am ashamed to beg. I know what I will do, so that when I have been removed from the management, they may receive me into their houses.' Therefore, having called together the individual debtors 5 of his lord, he said to the first, 'How much do you owe my lord?' And he said, 'A hundred baths of oil.' And 6 he said to him, 'Take your bond, and sit down quickly and write fifty.' Then he said to another, 'But you, 7 how much do you owe?' Who said, 'A hundred kors of wheat.' And he says <meta>catchword: to him,</meta>

***

tain to the domestic estate. *Villicus* <note>a farm bailiff</note> (as Varro says in his books *On Agriculture*) is one appointed for the sake of tilling the field, named from *villa* <note>country house/farm</note>, because the fruits are carried into it by him and carried out when they have arrived. And Saint Jerome himself distinguishes a *villicus* from an *oeconomus*. "A *villicus*," he says, "is properly the governor of a villa; he took the name *villicus* from *villa*: an *oeconomus* is the governor not only of the crops, but of all things which the master possesses." Hence the most beautiful book of Xenophon is the *Oeconomicus*, which signifies not the government of a villa, but the management of the entire house, according to Cicero's interpretation. Therefore, in this place, *oeconomus* or *dispensator* <note>manager</note> was more fitting than *villicus*. Furthermore, in those things which soon follow—"give an account of your stewardship" and "you can no longer be steward"—it is in Greek <note>original: οἰκονομίας</note> and <note>original: οἰκονομεῖν</note>, that is, "of management" and "to manage." And thus Saint Jerome cites it, explaining this passage in his *Letter to Algasia*: "Give an account of your management, for you can no longer manage." But as for what follows here...

2 *He was accused*] In the Greek it is <note>original: διεβλήθη</note>, which sounds more like "he was reported" or "denounced," from <note>original: διαβάλλεσθαι</note>, whence comes *diabolos* <note>the devil/slanderer</note> or *diabole* <note>slander</note>. Though there is this difference: a slanderer reports falsely, but even one who is justly accused is reported. Nor is it "as if," <note>original: ὑπὸ διασκορπίζων</note>, "as if wasting," or "as one who would waste," for surely he was reported on this account: that he was wasting the man's goods.

3 *I am ashamed to beg*] <note>original: ἐπαιτεῖν</note>, for which he used <note>original: προσαιτεῖν</note> elsewhere.

4 *Having called together the individuals*] <note>original: προσκαλεσάμενος</note>, that is, called to himself, or summoned.

5 *A hundred baths*] <note>original: ἑκατὸν βάτους</note>, that is, a hundred baths, not casks. For *bath* is a Hebrew word, signifying for them a measure of liquids, as Josephus teaches in the eighth book of *Jewish Antiquities*. It contained seventy-two *sextarii* <note>approx. 1 pint each</note>: just like that which follows soon after, *kors*. That measure of dry goods contained forty-one Attic *medimni*, as the same author testifies in the third book.

6 *Take your bond*] <note>original: τὸ γράμμα</note>. The same word that he soon translates as "letters," and that not in good Latin. For "letters" in the plural number signifies an epistle. Either, therefore, he ought to have translated it "bond" in both places, since in both it is *gramma*, which sounds like "letter," or "writing," or "contract," or "notepads," or "little books," or something of this sort.

# ACCORDING TO LUKE. CHAPTER XVI.

<margin>8</margin> ...your bill, and write eighty. And the lord praised the steward of unrighteousness, because he had acted prudently; for the sons of this age are more prudent than the sons of light in their own generation. And I say to you: Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of unrighteousness <note>The word "mammon" refers to wealth or profit, often with a negative connotation of greed.</note>, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings. <margin>10</margin> He who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much; and he who is unrighteous in a very little is also unrighteous in much. <margin>11</margin> If therefore you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will entrust to you the true wealth? <margin>12</margin> And if you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own? <margin>v. 13</margin> No servant can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and mammon. <margin>v. 14</margin> Now the Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they derided him. <margin>15</margin> And he said to them: You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts; for what is exalted among men is an abomination before God. <margin>v. 16</margin> The Law and the Prophets were until John; from that time the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces their way into it. <margin>17</margin> But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of a letter of the Law to fail. <margin>v. 18</margin> Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery; and everyone who marries her who is divorced from a husband commits adultery. <margin>v. 19</margin> There was a certain rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen, feasting sumptuously every day. <margin>20</margin> And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, who lay at his gate full of sores, <margin>21</margin> and desiring to be filled with the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table; moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores. <margin>22</margin> And it happened that the beggar died and was carried by the angels to Abraham’s bosom; and the rich man also died and was buried. <margin>23</margin> And in Hades, lifting up his eyes, being in torments, he saw Abraham from afar and Lazarus in his bosom. <margin>24</margin> And he cried out and said: Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame. <margin>25</margin> But Abraham said...

<margin>7 Steward of iniquity]</margin> Following the idiom of the Hebrew language, he said *steward of iniquity* <note>original: "villicum iniquitatis"</note> instead of *unjust or unrighteous manager*, which is not unlike what follows shortly after: *from the mammon of iniquity*.
<margin>8 And in the greater]</margin> In the Greek <note>original: "ἐν πολλῷ"</note>, that is, in much.
<margin>9 In the lesser]</margin> In the Greek <note>original: "ἐν ἐλαχίστῳ"</note>, that is, in the least. But the Translator <note>referring to the Vulgate</note> loves to vary his terms. Here it is not "in the greater," but *in much*, as above.
<margin>10 Who will entrust to you what is yours?]</margin> In the Greek <note>original: "τὸ ἀληθινὸν"</note>, that is, what is *true*. This was corrupted in several manuscripts, undoubtedly by the fault of scribes. Since in the more corrected Latin copies we read *true* [verum], not *yours* [vestrum]. He opposes *true* to *unrighteous*. For true riches are those prepared without fraud. And in this place, *entrust* [credet] is used for *commit*. Furthermore, he who commits to you surely commits what belongs to another, not to you. But in the next clause, he opposes *yours* to *another's*. And what is true is not "trusted," what is ours is not "given."
<margin>11 For either he will hate one]</margin> Since this is said in so many words in Matthew, let whoever wishes seek from there what we have noted on this passage.
<margin>12 Now the Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things and derided him]</margin> The Greeks punctuate this differently <note>original: "Ἤκουον δὲ ταῦτα πάντα, καὶ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι φιλάργυροι ὑπάρχοντες ἐξεμυκτήριζον αὐτόν"</note>. That is, *Now they heard all these things, and the Pharisees who were lovers of money derided him*. This implies that everyone else heard these things too, but only the Pharisees were offended, whose greed he had touched upon, even though some copies added the conjunction again: *and they derided him*.
<margin>13 They derided]</margin> In the Greek <note>original: "ἐξεμυκτήριζον"</note>. Now, to *mykterizein* is what the Latins call *to hang from the nose* <note>to turn up one's nose at something</note>. For of old, the nose was dedicated to mockery. *Mykter* in Greek means nose, hence *mykterizein* means to sneer or scoff. Cicero used the term *antimykterizein*, to mock in return.
<margin>14 From that time]</margin> In the Greek <note>original: "ἀπὸ τότε"</note>, that is, *from then*, as it is translated elsewhere, as in the Psalm: *Thy throne is prepared from then* [from of old]. It would be more Latin to say *from that time* or *since that time*.
<margin>15 And everyone forces their way into it]</margin> He rendered the Greek words indeed; but it would have been more Latin, without losing the sense, to say *and all*, as Ambrose reads, or *anyone into it. For by now even the Gentiles were attempting to break in indiscriminately*.
<margin>16 Purple and fine linen]</margin> It is a wonder why Augustine, in his commentary on the forty-eighth Psalm, reads *silk* instead of *purple*.
<margin>17 He feasted]</margin> In the Greek <note>original: "εὐφραινόμενος"</note>, which in other places he translates as "rejoiced." For the Greek word signifies both: joy of the mind and a cheerful banquet.
<margin>18 Named Lazarus]</margin> To the Hebrews this sounds like *helped by the Lord*, so that the very name fits the parable: he was destitute of men, but had God as a helper. Indeed <note>original Hebrew: "עזר"</note> means *help*, and <note>original Hebrew: "אל"</note> means *God*. This seems to have been the view of the one who collected the "forest of Hebrew names" from all the Sacred Books. Furthermore, he whose collection of names exists for each Evangelist interprets *Lazarus as helped*.

<margin>D</margin> [Lazarus] sounds like *help*, and *El* is *God*. This seems to be the meaning of the one who compiled the "forest of Hebrew names" from all the Sacred Books. Moreover, he whose collection of names for each Evangelist is extant, interprets *Lazarus as helped*.
<margin>19 Who lay]</margin> In the Greek <note>original: "ἐβέβλητο"</note>, that is, he had been cast down. This verb is usually used for one who is violently ill and confined to bed. Nor is it simply a *door* [janua], but <note>original: "πυλῶνα"</note>, which sounds like a vestibule, or the gate of the wealthy. The name is derived from *pyle*, a gate. Nor is it,
<margin>20 Full of ulcers]</margin> but <note>original: "ἡλκωμένος"</note>, that is, *ulcerated*, or *ulcerous*, similar to the word *kecharitomene*, that is, gracious, or full of grace. "And no one gave to him." I do not find this phrase added in the Greek codices, not even in those provided to us by the Library of Saint Donatian and that of Constance. Indeed, Bede himself neither reads nor interprets it. From the Ambrosian Commentaries, one might sooner conclude that crumbs *were* given than that they were not. For the rich man is not rebuked on this account—that he shared nothing with the poor—but because he chose to live in luxury while he saw his brother tortured by so many evils, yet neither took him in as he lay there, nor deemed him worthy of his table, nor cared for his sores, when even the dogs were more humane than he; nor shared anything except those things which fell from his expensive table, to be picked up by dogs.
<margin>21 And he was buried in hell]</margin> The Greek is different: *and he was buried. And in hell lifting up his eyes* <note>original: "καὶ ἐτάφη. Καὶ ἐν τῷ ᾅδῃ ἐπάρας τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς"</note>. So the sense is that the rich man also, who had placed his happiness in his wealth and luxuries, similarly died and was buried, just as that poor man did. But his soul, which had been carried down to the lower world, saw Abraham when he lifted his eyes. Otherwise, how could he lift his eyes while buried? Theophylact clearly distinguishes it in this way, making a new chapter beginning from that place, *And in hell lifting up his eyes*, with a commentary interposed in the middle. Augustine similarly distinguishes in the Sermon where he explains this verse: *To you the poor man is left: and see, he says, the departure of both. For it happens that that destitute man dies and is taken by Angels into Abraham's bosom. The rich man also died, and was buried, for perhaps the poor man was not buried* etc. Again, in Homily fifty-seven, he follows the distinction of the Greeks. Hence it is a wonder that Bede, a compiler of Augustine, follows a different reading. Those things cited in the *Golden Chain* from Chrysostom have two words corrupted; if they were absent, they would agree with us entirely. For they philosophize on this: that only the rich man is read to be "buried," and there is no mention of servants or friends standing by him as he died, because everyone usually deserts a rich man when the end of life has come. He is said only to be buried—now twice buried—whose soul was previously buried in his body. Chrysostom is mostly of this opinion.

# THE GOSPEL CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>25</margin> "Child, remember that you received your good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise the bad; but now here he is comforted, and you are in agony. <margin>24</margin> <note>Though the margin says 24, this corresponds to verse 26.</note> And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, so that those who want to cross from here to you cannot, nor can those from there <margin>27</margin> cross over to us." <margin>1</margin> Then He said to the disciples, "It is impossible for stumbling blocks not to come; but woe to him through whom they come. <margin>2</margin> It would be better for him if a donkey-millstone <note>A large millstone turned by a beast of burden, rather than a small hand-mill.</note> were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea, than that he should cause one of these little ones <margin>3</margin> to stumble. Take heed to yourselves. If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive <margin>4</margin> him. And if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turns back to you, saying, 'I repent,' you shall forgive him." <margin>5</margin> And the Apostles said to the Lord, "Increase our <margin>6</margin> faith." So the Lord said, "If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this sycamine tree, 'Be uprooted and planted in the sea,' <margin>7</margin> and it would obey you. And which of you, having a servant plowing or tending sheep, will say to him when he has come in from the field, 'Come at once and sit down to eat'? <margin>8</margin> Will he not rather say to him, 'Prepare something for my supper, and gird yourself and serve me until I have eaten and drunk, and after <margin>9</margin> that you will eat and drink'? Does he thank that servant because he did the things that were commanded him? I <margin>10</margin> think not. So you also, when you have done all the things commanded you, say, 'We are unprofitable servants; we have done <margin>11</margin> what we were duty-bound to do.'" And it happened, while He was going to Jerusalem, that He passed through the <margin>12</margin> midst of Samaria and Galilee. And as He entered a certain village, ten men who were lepers met Him, <margin>13</margin> who stood at a distance. And they lifted up their voices, saying, "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us." <margin>14</margin> And when He saw them, He said to them, "Go, show yourselves to the priests." <margin>15</margin> And it happened that as they went, they were cleansed. And one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice. <margin>16</margin> And he fell on his face at His feet, giving Him thanks; and he was a Samaritan. <margin>17</margin> So Jesus answered and said, "Were not ten cleansed?"

Then he said to the disciples, <margin>XVII.</margin> <margin>B</margin> <margin>1</margin> "It cannot be but that stumbling blocks will come; yet woe to him through whom they come. It is better for him if a donkey <margin>2</margin> millstone be placed around his neck and he be cast into the sea, rather than that he be a stumbling block to one of these little ones. So also you, <margin>10</margin> when you have done all that has been commanded of you, say, 'We are useless servants, for we have done what we ought to have done.'" And it happened while he went to Jerusalem, and <margin>11</margin> he himself passed through the middle of Samaria and Galilee. And when he entered a certain village, there met <margin>12</margin> him ten men who were lepers, who stood far off, and with a <margin>13</margin> strained voice said, "Jesus teacher, have mercy on us." When he saw them, he said to them, "Go, show yourselves to the priests." <margin>14</margin> <margin>D</margin> And it happened that as they went they were cleansed. But one of them, when he saw that he was cleansed, <margin>15</margin> returned, with a great voice glorifying God. And he fell on his face at his feet, giving thanks to him; <margin>16</margin> and this man was a Samaritan. But Jesus answering <margin>17</margin> said, "Were not ten cleansed? But where are those nine?"

---

<margin>22</margin> *You received good things*] The Greeks add "your" <term>σου</term>, <term>τὰ ἀγαθά σου</term> <note>original: sou, ta agatha sou</note>, so that He might distinguish that man's false goods from the true goods of the other. And for *bad*, likewise "your bad" <term>κακά σου</term> <note>original: kaka sou</note>, implying "your," not because they were simply bad things, but because they were his misfortunes.

<margin>23</margin> *But now here he is comforted*] <term>παρακαλεῖται</term> <note>original: parakaleitai</note>, in the passive voice, that is, "he enjoys solace," or "he has comfort," or "he is affected by solace," and thus it avoids ambiguity.

<margin>24</margin> *And in all these things*] <term>Καὶ ἐπὶ πᾶσι τούτοις</term> <note>original: Kai epi pasi toutois</note>. This sense can also be taken here, namely, "above all these things," or "besides all these things." So we may understand this as adding to the rich man's unhappiness, that because of the yawning abyss lying between them, he cannot be helped.

<margin>25</margin> *A great chaos has been established*] It is a wonder what came into the Translator's <note>Referring to the author of the Latin Vulgate.</note> mind, to render a Greek word with another Greek word, and certainly one not signifying the same thing. For in Greek it is <term>χάσμα</term> <note>original: chasma</note>, which signifies a "hiatus" or opening of the earth, such as often happens in an earthquake, which Aristotle in his book *On the Universe* calls a "chasmatia" <term>chaſmatias</term>, from which an earthquake is called <term>χασματίας</term> <note>original: chasmatias</note>. Some call it a "vorago" [abyss], because a fissure in the earth sinks to an immense depth. But *Chaos* signifies "confusion," this being named from the word "to pour" <term>χέω</term> <note>original: cheo</note>, whereas the former is from "to gape" <term>χαίνω</term> <note>original: chaino</note>. Our colleague Guillaume Budé noted this passage, adding something to the annotation of Laurentius Valla. I thought this should be mentioned, partly so as not to defraud anyone of their due honor, and partly so that those who wish to know these things more diligently and exactly might seek them from his annotations on the *Pandects of Law*. For we everywhere strive for brevity, lest we be a weariness to the reader.

<margin>26</margin> *Neither from there*] <term>μηδὲ οἱ ἐκεῖθεν</term> <note>original: mede hoi ekeithen</note>, that is, "nor those from that place." For the Greeks lack this specific property of adverbs, whereas among the Latins *hinc* refers to the first person (the speaker), *istinc* to the second, and *illinc* or *inde* to the third. 

<margin>27</margin> *To cross over*] is not the word, but rather <term>διαπερῶσιν</term> <note>original: diaperosin</note>, that is, "lest they cross over," in the subjunctive mood. 

<margin>28</margin> *Testament*] is not the word, but rather <term>τῆς βασάνου</term> <note>original: tes basanou</note>, "of torment" or "of torture."

<margin>1</margin> *Millstone*] <term>μύλος ὀνικός</term> <note>original: mulos onikos</note>, that is, a "donkey-mill." For the Greeks call the bottom stone in a mill, which receives the grain, an "onos" <term>ὄνον</term> <note>meaning "donkey"</note>, about which we spoke in Matthew.

<margin>2</margin> *If he does penance*] <term>εἰ μετανοήσῃ</term> <note>original: ei metanoese</note>, that is, "if he repents" or "if he comes to his senses." We should not take this to mean "satisfaction and punishment" <note>Erasmus is distinguishing between the interior change of heart (repentance) and the external Catholic sacrament of Penance.</note> as it is properly called. To say nothing of how he used "dismiss" <note>dimittes</note> so many times for "forgive" <note>remittes</note>. <margin>F</margin>

<margin>3</margin> *And he be turned*] In some Greek manuscripts "to you" <term>ἐπὶ σὲ</term> <note>original: epi se</note> was added, in others it was not. It is added in the works of Saint Ambrose.

<column-break/>

<margin>4</margin> *If you have*] <term>Εἰ εἴχετε</term> <note>original: Ei eichete</note>, that is, "If you had," which would have been correctly translated as *Si haberetis*.

<margin>5</margin> *Like a grain of mustard*] I do not know if the Translator used <term>κόκκον</term> <note>grain/berry</note> in the neuter gender. Nor would the sense, in my opinion, be absurd if you wished to have faith like "kermes" <note>A red dye made from insects, also called *coccum*</note>, which appears humble and low, and does not show its strength until provoked by rubbing. So elsewhere He calls us to the example of sparrows and lilies. But if it is preferred that <term>κόκκον</term> <note>grain</note> is placed here in the masculine gender, as <term>κόκκον</term> <note>original: kokkon</note>, it will have the same force as saying "faith similar to a grain."

<margin>6</margin> *You will say to this*] <term>ἐλέγετε ἄν</term> <note>original: elegete an</note>, that is, "you would have said." Ancient manuscripts have *diceretis* [you would say], not *dicetis* [you will say], which comes closer to the Greek truth.

<margin>7</margin> *To the mulberry tree*] <term>συκαμίνῳ</term> <note>original: sykamino</note>. It is a tree of its own kind, peculiar to Syria, as Jerome indicates. Hesychius adds that it is called *moron* [mulberry] by some, a common word, I guess. More will be said about this in Chapter 19. Furthermore, where he adds "transplant," he expressed the sense more than the word. For it is not "re-plant" <term>μεταφυτεύθητι</term>, but "be planted" <term>φυτεύθητι</term> <note>original: phytethetis</note>.

<margin>8</margin> *And it will obey*] <term>καὶ ὑπήκουσεν ἄν</term> <note>original: kai hypekousen an</note>, that is, "it would have obeyed." An ancient manuscript had *obediret* [it would obey], corresponding to "you would say." Although the mood makes it potential, perhaps the future tense was more tolerable for that reason.

<margin>9</margin> *Or feeding oxen*] In Greek it is not "oxen," but only "tending/feeding." The oldest Latin copies also agree: <term>ποιμαίνοντα</term> <note>original: poimainonta</note>. However, it should be understood more as a shepherd of sheep than of oxen. Accordingly, in the Corsendonk manuscript, "sheep" was written between the lines; and I suspect Saint Ambrose read it thus, although they also translated "sheep" as "oxen" there.

<margin>10</margin> *Magnifying God*] <term>δοξάζων</term> <note>original: doxazon</note>, that is, "glorifying": which he translates thus now and then, so that he may be more varied.

<margin>11</margin> *Where are the nine?*] It is more elegant among the Greeks with the verb omitted: <term>οἱ δὲ ἐννέα ποῦ</term> <note>original: hoi de ennea pou</note>, that is, "but those nine, where?" For I add "those" in place of the Greek article.

<margin>12 *Was not found*</margin> <note>original: "Non est inventus"</note> "None were found returning to give glory to God," that is, *They were not discovered having returned to give glory to God*, to translate it word for word. Furthermore, the Greeks use the word "to be found" for something that happens or that has been established as a fact.
<margin>13 *When you desire*</margin> <note>original: "Quando desideretis"</note> *when you shall desire*, that is, *at the time you will desire*. Although it can be read as a subjunctive "might desire": I believe the Translator read it this way.
<margin>14 *From under heaven*</margin> <note>original: "De sub cælo"</note> From the <term>sub</term> (under) the <term>un</term> (the) heaven; thus "the [region] under heaven," that is, *from the region which is under heaven, into that which is under heaven*, which means from one quarter of the sky to the other. For so it appears to the eyes of men. A similar expression is in Deuteronomy chapter 4: *From the highest part of heaven even to the furthest part of it*. Moreover, this comparison signifies that the coming of the kingdom of God is sudden and unexpected, not only regarding the time it occurs, but also regarding the place, just as lightning suddenly breaks out, now here, now there, which you see before you expect it to come.
<margin>15 *First it is necessary*</margin> <note>original: "Primus autem oportet"</note> The word "first" is placed beforehand. It will indeed come like lightning, but it will not come yet; rather, it is necessary first for him to suffer many things, etc.
<margin>16 *They took wives*</margin> <note>original: "Uxores ducebant"</note> They were marrying, they were being given in marriage. Where previously in Matthew it says "they marry," here it says "they take wives"; where it says there "they are married," here "they were given to nuptials." *Two in the field*. This part is not added among the Greeks in Luke, even if Saint Ambrose mentions the field. Indeed, in the Pauline manuscript there was no mention except of the bed. Theophylact reads only two instances: the bed and the millstone; the third regarding the field seems to have been added here from Matthew chapter 24. Furthermore, Ambrose, instead of what is in the Greek "in the same place," reads "in the mill," perhaps referring to the opinion of another Evangelist.
<margin>17 *Wherever the body shall be*</margin> <note>original: "Ubicunque fuerit corpus"</note> In Greek it is, *Where the body is, there also the eagles will be gathered*, that is, *Where the body [is], there the eagles will be gathered*. 

---

Although some manuscripts have <term>ptōma</term>, that is, a "corpse," which the Greeks call "that which has fallen." And Jerome seems to more greatly approve this reading.

<margin>1</margin> **H**ow it is necessary] *toward the necessity of always praying*, that is, in the fact that one ought always to pray. Furthermore, the word "to lose heart" <note>original: "ekkakien"</note> sounds like becoming sluggish, that is, to be worn out, which he calls here "to fail": for in Greek they sometimes call the lazy and cowardly by this name.
<margin>2 *For a long time*</margin> <note>original: "Per multum tempus"</note> *for a time*, that is, "to a time," or "for a while." Then "at the end," which he translates as "at the last," he would have more correctly translated as "finally."
<margin>3 *Bruises me*</margin> <note>original: "Sugillet me"</note> <note>original: "hypōpiazē"</note> that is, "reproaches" or "disparages." For "to bruise" <note>original: "sugillare"</note> means that, a word taken from boxers, who "bruise" from above, marking the cheeks with livid color, and "supplant" from below, pushing the antagonist to ruin. <note>Erasmus is explaining that the widow's persistence is described by the judge as a physical assault on his reputation.</note>
<margin>4 *And he will have patience in them*</margin> <note>original: "Et patientiam habebit in illis"</note> The Greek differs somewhat: "crying to him day and night, and being long-suffering over them," that is, *crying to him night and day, and bearing them with a gentle mind*. But another manuscript had: "And I say, being long-suffering over them he will do justice," that is, "also I say, long-suffering over them he will do justice": so that we may understand he will certainly avenge, even if later. Although Theophylact reads it otherwise, and more correctly if I am not mistaken, because there follows "quickly," that is, "speedily," which conflicts with that "long-suffering." Chrysostom also, in his sermon on praying to God, reads "he is long-suffering," which the Translator seems to have read.
<margin>5 *Do you think he will find*</margin> <note>original: "Putas inveniet"</note> It is not "certainly" <note>original: "ara"</note> in Greek, but a particle <note>original: "ara"</note> meaning "perhaps" or "whether."
<margin>6 *As if righteous*</margin> <note>original: "Tanquam justi"</note> "righteous in themselves," that is, *because they were righteous*: although it could be translated as "toward themselves," as if they were righteous. For he means that they attributed righteousness to themselves, and relying on this opinion, they looked down on others.

# THE GOSPEL, CHAPTER XVIII.

<margin>7</margin> *The rest of men* <note>original: "Ceteri hominum"</note>] In the Greek, it is expressed this way, although in Latin one should say "men" <note>original: "homines"</note>: since the Greeks in these instances use the genitive case in place of any other case.

<margin>8</margin> *Just as also* <note>original: "Velut etiam"</note>] The Greek is [ἢ καὶ ὡς οὗτος], that is, "or even as this man." Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo Valla was a famous 15th-century Italian humanist who first applied critical scholarship to the New Testament text.</note> seems to suspect that it was written as "or as" <note>original: "vel ἢ ὡς"</note>. Furthermore, the complaint he makes about the changed conjunction is a trivial matter, pertaining more to the elegance of the language than to a theological issue.

<margin>9</margin> *He was not willing nor his eyes* <note>original: "Nolebat nec oculos"</note>] Perhaps these two negatives applied to a single verb will trouble the logicians. Therefore, one could translate it as: "nor was he willing to lift his eyes to heaven." Indeed, Cyprian <note>A 3rd-century bishop and influential Early Christian writer.</note> cites it this way in his exposition on the Lord's Prayer.

<margin>10</margin> *Justified in his house from that one* <note>original: "Iustificatus in domum suam ab illo"</note>] Some Greek manuscripts had [κατέβη οὗτος δεδικαιωμένος εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ, ἢ γὰρ ἐκεῖνος], that is: "this man went down to his house justified, more certainly indeed than that one," or "certainly more than him." But in most manuscripts, I do not find the word "for" <note>original: "γὰρ"</note>. Therefore, it should be translated as "rather than him," or "more than him." I am not unaware that Gellius <note>A 2nd-century Roman author known for his work "Attic Nights."</note> speaks this way somewhere—"he is cold from/compared to that one"—meaning "he is cold compared to him." However, I preferred the usage that is more common among reliable authors. And lest anyone think our interpretation should be rejected, Saint Jerome <note>The 4th-century scholar who produced the Vulgate, the standard Latin Bible.</note>, in his work against the Pelagians, cites it as: "Justified more than that one." And Augustine <note>Saint Augustine, the 5th-century North African theologian.</note>, in Letter 86 to Casulanus, writes: "He did not say: 'besides that Pharisee,' but he said the tax collector was 'more justified.'"

<meta>catchword: And-</meta>

<column-break/>

I fast twice a week; I give tithes <margin>12</margin> of all that I possess." And it happened <margin>33</margin> <margin>34</margin> that as he approached Jericho, a certain blind man <margin>35</margin> <margin>E</margin> was sitting by the road, begging. And when he heard the crowd passing by, he asked what this was. <margin>36</margin> They told him that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by. <margin>37</margin> And he cried out, saying, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" <margin>38</margin> And those who went in front rebuked him, that he should be quiet; <margin>39</margin> but he cried out all the more, "Son of David, have mercy on me!" Then Jesus stood and ordered him to be brought to him; and <margin>40</margin> when he had come near, he asked him, saying, <margin>41</margin> "What...

---

<margin>11</margin> *Calling them* <note>original: "Convocans illos"</note>] The Greek is [προσκαλεσάμενος], that is, "advocating" or rather, "having called them to himself." The word [αὐτὰ] (them) is in the neuter gender and refers to the children <note>original: "παιδία"</note>, since the girls were also called: he spoke, no doubt, while others were trying to prevent them.

<margin>12</margin> *Like a child* <note>original: "Sicut puer"</note>] This offended Valla, who prefers "just as a child" <note>original: "velut puer"</note> or "as if a child" <note>original: "tanquam puer"</note>, so that we understand an imitation of the person's character, not just an imitation of the act of receiving. "Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God, having become like a child, will not enter"—this is the imitation of the person. "Whoever does not receive as a child receives"—this would be the imitation of the act.

<margin>13</margin> *Why do you call me good* <note>original: "Quid me dicis bonum"</note>] This differs somewhat from Matthew. For in that Gospel, Jesus is offended that he was asked about what "good thing" he should do. For there the young man hears, "Why do you ask me about what is good?" Mark agrees with Luke. Nevertheless, both readings tend toward the same point: namely, that it is not fitting for a man to claim any goodness for himself. He is speaking to Christ, to be sure, but only as a man. And as a man, he had no goodness that he could claim for himself, as if it originated from his own self.

<margin>14</margin> *To pass through the eye of a needle* <note>original: "Per foramen acus transire"</note>] In both places in the Greek, the word is [εἰσελθεῖν], to "enter" through the eye of a needle, and to "go into" the kingdom. Nevertheless, the Translator rendered the meaning well.

<margin>15</margin> *Concerning the Son of Man* <note>original: "De Filio hominis"</note>] The word "but" <note>original: "δὲ"</note> is not added in the Greek: [τῷ Υἱῷ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου], that is, "to the Son of Man."
