<margin>16</margin> **That I may see, and look up]** The word is the same in Greek, *ἵνα ἀναβλέψω*, which means *to recover sight*. It is a wonder why the Translator <note>The "Translator" usually refers to the author of the Latin Vulgate bible</note> changed it shortly thereafter.

<margin>S 1</margin> **He was small in stature]** What he translates here as *stature*, he translates elsewhere as *age*. In Greek it is *ἡλικίᾳ* <note>The Greek word can mean either physical height or the span of one's life/age</note>.

<margin>2</margin> **Into a sycamore tree]** Luke used *sycomoream*, which those who know such things say is the same as what they call the *sycomorus*, and which he called the *sycaminum* in the seventeenth chapter. Celsius calls it *morofrycon*, that is, the *fatuous fig* <note>original: "fatuam ficum"</note>, and indicates in his work that the *sycomorus* and *sycaminum* are the same tree. This is called the "Egyptian fig" by Pliny and Theophrastus, because they believe it only grows there; though Jerome, explaining the seventh chapter of the Prophet Amos, testifies that there were those who thought this was a genus of tree familiar to Palestine, thriving in flat places and bearing wild figs which, unless they are nipped <note>ancient farmers would puncture or "scarify" the fruit to make it ripen</note>, produce very bitter dried figs, and the fruit is ruined by gnats. Although Jerome does not agree with their opinion, denying that any tree of this kind grows in that wilderness where Amos lived; he prefers the Prophet's words to be understood as the wild mulberries that grow on brambles, so that shepherds might console their hunger and poverty with them. Dioscorides, in the first book of *On Medical Materials*, chapter 162, teaches that this tree, as has been said, is called by three names: *sycomorus*, *sycominus*, and *Egyptian fig*, adding that the name was given to the offspring because it has a dull flavor. The same was written by Theophrastus, who indicates that the sycamore also grows in Cyprus, but is of a different species from the Egyptian one. Indeed, the Egyptian one has leaves resembling our mulberry, and fruit like our fig, except it does not produce them on branches but from the trunk itself, not ripening unless it is scratched with iron claws. The Cyprian one, however, has leaves not unlike an elm and produces fruit equal in size to a plum, but sweeter. Furthermore, as to why Luke names the *sycomoream* for the *sycomoro*, no one should be disturbed, since the Greeks call *morias* what the Romans call *morum* <note>the mulberry</note>, if we believe Dioscorides. By many arguments it could seem to be a type of wild fig, or because its sharp juice resembles the offspring of a wild fig, as Theophrastus teaches (translated by Gaza): so much so that, as Plutarch relates, a certain witty Athenian insultingly called Sylla <note>The Roman dictator Sulla, known for his blotchy red and white complexion</note> a *sycomorus sprinkled with meal*, because the redness in his face seemed scattered over the whiteness. Otherwise, it might seem to come from proven "folly," if *sycomorus* were written through *mōros* <note>A pun on the Greek word "mōros" meaning foolish</note>. Thus Plutarch roughly writes in his *Life*, as far as the reason for the insult goes. Nor do I deny it is consistently written by authors with the "o" of *mōros* <note>meaning "foolish"</note>, and...

...I doubt whether correctly or corruptly: especially since the mulberry tree, to which the sycamore is related by the similarity of the leaves, has the middle syllable long in the poetry of Naso <note>Ovid</note> and Pastadias. Athenaeus in book 11 reports that *sycomoros* is the common name, but only the Alexandrians call it *mōron* or *morean*. But I think enough has been said about the sycamore for our current purpose. But if anyone thinks the power and form of this tree is more exactly relevant to the <margin>E</margin> spiritual mystery, we have indicated the authors from whom he can seek it.

<margin>3</margin> **Because thence]** *ἐκείνης*, that is, *by that way*, for it is not *ἐκεῖθεν* <note>The commentator is distinguishing between "by that route" and "from that place"</note>. Ambrose reads *in that part* for *by that way*.

<margin>4</margin> **To stay with a man who was a sinner]** *εἰσελθεῖν καταλῦσαι*, that is, he entered to lodge at his house.

<margin>5</margin> **And if I have in anything defrauded anyone]** *ἐσυκοφάντησα*, which properly means to extort something by false accusations; he uses it here for any kind of fraud.

<margin>6</margin> **Because even he is a son of Abraham]** It is a bit harsh that these things are pronounced by Christ in the third person, especially since it is not written to others in the surrounding verses. Therefore, I suspect that what is said in Greek, *son of Abraham*, does not refer to Zacchaeus, but to the *house*, which for the Greeks is of the masculine gender <note>Original: "οἶκος" (house) is masculine in Greek, whereas "domus" is feminine in Latin</note>. For just as we would call a "Christian house," so he called the house a *son of Abraham*, because it imitated the father Abraham in faith. Under this reading, however, the same sense remains as that brought by ancient interpreters: for by "house" the fatherhood is understood. Yet it is fuller for the house <margin>F</margin> to be called a *son of Abraham*, because a family is usually of the same character as the *head of the household*. Theophylact reads and interprets that the house itself is called a *son*, but by the house, the inhabitant *Zacchaeus* is understood. Furthermore, an inconsistency of gender created an opportunity for error, which exists among the Latins but not among the Greeks. If Zacchaeus is designated by the "house," the leader of the house is called a "son"; it would be harsher to call Zacchaeus a "daughter."

<margin>7</margin> **A certain noble man]** *εὐγενὴς*, that is, *illustrious*, and born of an illustrious family. For *nobilis* <note>noble</note> is anyone who is merely known to the common people.

<margin>8</margin> **Ten minas]** The Latins interpolate an *i*, saying *minas*. In most Greek manuscripts, I find *μνᾶς* [mnas], in the nominative case *ὁ μνᾶς* [ho mnas]; whether this was done by error or by intent, I am uncertain.

<margin>9</margin> **How much each]** *τί τί*, that is, *what what*, in the form: "Behold again and again whom you commend to whom." And, "What you give to whom, What you trust to whom." And,

<margin>10</margin> **Well done, good servant]** that is, *Rightly, good servant*. For he highly praises the servant who was holy in his duty.

<margin>D</margin> *11 I should have collected it* <note>original: "Exegissem illud"</note> ] It should have been said as "illam" <note>feminine</note>, as I found it written in two codices of Saint Donatian. But the word for "money" <note>original: "ἀργύριον"</note> among the Greeks is of the neuter gender. And the Translator, forgetting that he had translated it as *pecuniam* <note>Latin feminine for money</note> and not *argentum* <note>Latin neuter for silver/money</note>, left it as *illud* <note>neuter</note>. To this, what he here translates as "I might have collected," is *epraxa* in Greek, the same verb he ought to have translated the same way earlier when speaking of tax collectors: "Do nothing more than what is appointed to you."
*12 To every one who has, it shall be given and he shall abound* ] "And he shall abound" is neither in the Greek codices, nor in the Golden one, nor in the Constantian. I suspect it was added here from another Evangelist.
*13 And what he has shall be taken from him* ] "From him" was added from the Hebrew idiom of speech, lest someone might think it was omitted by you and try to replace it.
*14 He preceded, going up* ] *eporeueto emprosthen anabainon*, that is, "he went forward, that is, he continued to go, or to ascend."
*15 Into the castle which is against you* ] *eis ten katenanti komen*, that is, "into the village which is on the opposite side." For it was as much against Christ as against the Apostles. In the Golden codex it was only held as "which is against"; likewise in the Constantian, and in my own of old typography.
<margin>†</margin> *16 The colt of an ass* ] In the Greek codices "of an ass" is not added; it is only *polon* <note>colt</note>, and yet by some error I found it added in the second edition. From the commentaries of Ambrose it can be sufficiently gathered that he read it as the Greeks do. For he says: "And therefore according to Matthew we read 'the ass and the colt,' etc."
*17 On which no one ever* ] It should be read "on which never," *eph' hon*. This is supported by the most ancient copies and Origen, although the Translator turned it correctly.
<margin>E</margin> *18 Because the Lord* ] *Hoti* <note>Greek: because/that</note>. In this place, the conjunction should either be omitted by the Translator or translated as "that." Likewise in the next place, "he desires its use" <note>original: "autou chreian echei"</note>, that is, "he has need of it."
*19 Just as he had said to them, the colt standing* ] The Greek codices do not add "the colt standing." It appears to have been added by some Latin to make the speech clearer. But the speech is more complete if "the colt standing" is not added: so that you understand they found whatever the Lord had predicted.
*20 Because the Lord has him as necessary* ] These Greek words differ nothing from the previous ones, where he translates "the Lord desires his work," since in both places it is *autou chreian echei*, that is, "he has need of him."
*21 And casting* ] *kai epirripsantes heauton ta himatia*, that is, "and their garments being cast on, or their cloaks."
*22 All the crowds of those descending* ] *hapan to plethos ton matheton*, that is, "the whole multitude of disciples." For shortly he is commanded to rebuke the disciples. It is probable that the Translator translated it "of those learning" <note>original: "discentium"</note>, and it is still seen written that way in some very old codices. In the Constantian, a trace of an erasure appeared.
*23 Glory in the highest* ] *en hypsistois*, that is, "in the highest places."
*24 The stones will cry out* ] *kekraxontai*, which the Greeks call <term>met' oligon mellon</term> <note>the "shortly-to-be" future tense</note>, that is, a "little-after future," and it has something urgent and vehement about it. Therefore you should render it, "presently the stones will cry out."
*25 Because if you had known even you* ] The conjunction "because" <note>oti</note> was to be omitted, which from the idiom of the Greek language is sometimes added for the sake of affirmation. Saint Jerome in his commentaries on Isaiah cites this place more than once, but with the sense somewhat changed: "If you knew even you what things are for your peace." Then he adds from himself: "Which because she did not receive, he brought in, 'Now however the days will come upon you etc.'" He similarly brings in and explains this place while expounding the second chapter of Micah. This interpretation, while it sounds far and wide different from the interpretation of recent theologians, yet strongly agrees with the truth of the Greek and the interpretation of Theophylact. For the Greeks have it thus: "If you knew even you indeed in this your day, the things toward your peace," that is, "If you knew, you would surely seek," and that is the sense. This day is yours, in which the Redeemer visits you: but if you understood how much good is offered to you, at least you would care for those things which belong to your peace, that is, you would believe and obey me. Saint Jerome seems to have read it in this manner. Moreover, in most codices it is written thus: "If you had known even you, at least in this your day, the things which belong to your peace, you would care." Nor is the repetition of the conjunctions "and" and "and indeed" <note>kai and kai ge</note> idle, because the first refers to the person of the city, the second to the day. So that we may understand the coming belongs peculiarly to the city of Jerusalem, especially on that day on which he was now arriving to die. Although the second conjunction is not added in Origen, or whoever the author is, in Homily 38. Furthermore, what the more recent interpreters interpret, "If you knew the evils imminent upon you, you also would weep etc.," does not cohere with what follows, "but now they are hidden from your eyes." For Christ repeats what he had said, "If you had known," surely indicating they do not recognize the day of their salvation. And I have said these things without prejudicing anyone's opinion. Certainly Cyril, who is cited in the *Catena*, refers "If you had known" not to the imminent evils, but to the understanding of the prophecies concerning Christ’s coming. And Eusebius, cited in the same place, does not refer "peace" to the delights of this world, as Gregory does, but to the reconciliation of the human race, lest anyone believe what we have brought forward is entirely a dream.
<margin>26</margin> *They shall throw down to the ground* ] *kai edaphiousi*: *edaphos* means the ground or the pavement.

<note>Notes at bottom of page 311 and 312</note>

<note>original: "qui negant ullam esse resurrectionem"</note> Rather, it should have been translated as "those who deny there is any resurrection." There is a resurrection of bodies, and there is one of souls. Then there are those who admit the Lord rose with a few, while denying the universal resurrection.

31 *And he died without sons*] <unclear>childless</unclear>, that is, bereaved, or without offspring. For the term "children" also includes daughters.

35 *Neither do they marry, nor are they given in marriage*] <unclear>oute gamousin, oute ekgamiskontai</unclear>, that is, they neither take wives nor are given in marriage. Cyprian, in the third book to Quirinus, translates this as *marry*, although the Greek word <term>gamein<gloss>to marry</gloss></term> is ambiguous. Elsewhere he certainly translates it as "they take wives," even a little earlier in this very book of Luke. The first word <term>gamousin</term> can pertain to men taking wives and to women marrying; <term>ekgamiskontai</term> to parents giving them away.

36 *For they are equal to angels*] <unclear>isaggeloi</unclear>, a compound word, that is, similar or equal to angels. Just as Homer calls distinguished men <unclear>isotheos</unclear> <note>original: "god-like"</note> and <unclear>Theō epieikelos</unclear> <note>original: "comparable to a god"</note>, to be equated with the gods.

37 *But because the dead rise*] <unclear>Hoti de egeirontai</unclear>. Although the Greek conjunction is ambiguous, in this place it should have been said, "But that the dead rise," or, "But the rising of the dead."

47 *Pretending a long prayer*] and <unclear>prophasei makra proseuchontai</unclear>, that is, and *they pray under a long pretext*. In some manuscripts it was held as <unclear>prophasei makra</unclear>, with the last syllable sharp, not circumflexed, meaning "praying many things under a pretext." For what does a "long pretext" mean? We have rendered the sense rather than the words: *pretending long prayers*. For they do not truly pray who pray for human praise or profit.

<column-break/>

13 *A greater damnation*] <unclear>perissoteron krima</unclear>, that is, a greater judgment. The translator explains the meaning, not just the word. For here <term>krima</term> is used several times for "condemnation."

R <insert>Looking up then] To look back is to look with eyes turned behind. But here it is <unclear>anablepsas</unclear>, which sometimes means to recover sight, and sometimes to lift up the eyes for the sake of seeing, either because the treasury was in a high place, or because he had been looking down before and then raised his eyes to those who were further away.</insert>

2 *From their abundance*] <unclear>ek tou perisseuontos autois</unclear>, that is, *from that which is left over for them*.

3 *From what is lacking*] <unclear>ek tou hysterematos</unclear>, that is, *from a defect*, which is to say, *from penury*.

4 *All her living*] <unclear>bion</unclear>, which elsewhere he translates as *substance*.

5 *And with gifts*] <unclear>anathemasi</unclear>. Those things are called gifts which are hung as sacred items for the gods on the walls and columns of the temple: the kind of which are now seen especially near the monuments of the Saints—silver statues, golden horses, jeweled cups—named from <unclear>anatithesthai</unclear>, that is, from setting aside or hanging up. From which also <unclear>anathema</unclear> is said.

6 *When they begin to happen*] <unclear>mellei tauta ginesthai</unclear>, *these things are to be*. But he expresses <unclear>mello</unclear> here and elsewhere using a verb of beginning.

7 *Saying that 'I am'*] <unclear>Hoti ego eimi</unclear>, that is, *That I am [he]*, which is to say, *they will say that they are the Christ, who I myself am*. And so our translator did it more clearly than word-for-word. Let no one think this was done by error.

8 *Not immediately*] <unclear>ouk eutheos</unclear>, that is, *not at once*.

# ACCORDING TO LUKE. CHAPTER XXI.

<margin>a 11</margin> 11 There shall be terrors, and great signs from heaven. <margin>b 12</margin> 12 But before all these things, they will lay their hands upon you and persecute you, delivering you up to synagogues and prisons, being brought before kings and governors for the sake of my name. <margin>13</margin> 13 And it shall happen to you as a testimony. <margin>14</margin> 14 Therefore, settle it in your hearts <margin>14</margin> not to meditate beforehand on your defense. 15 For I myself will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all those who oppose you will not be able to contradict or resist. <margin>16</margin> 16 And you shall be delivered up even by parents and brothers and kinsmen and friends, and they will put some of you to death. <margin>17</margin> 17 And you will be hated by all because of my name. <margin>18</margin> 18 And yet, a hair from your head shall not perish. <margin>19</margin> 19 By your patience <margin>19</margin> possess your souls. <margin>20 b</margin> 20 But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation is at hand. <margin>21 b</margin> 21 Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and those who are in her midst depart, and those who are in the country, let them not enter into her. <margin>22</margin> 22 For these are the days of vengeance, so that all things which are written may be fulfilled. <margin>23 b</margin> 23 But woe to those who are pregnant <margin>16</margin> and to those nursing at the breast in those days: for there shall be great distress <margin>17</margin> upon the land, and wrath upon this people. <margin>24</margin> 24 And they shall fall by the <margin>18</margin> edge of the sword, and shall be led captive into all nations. And Jerusalem shall be trodden down by the nations, until the <margin>19</margin> times of the nations are fulfilled. <margin>25 b</margin> 25 And there shall be signs in the sun and moon and stars, and upon the earth anxiety of nations <margin>20</margin> through despair, <margin>21</margin> as the sea and the waves roar, <margin>22</margin> with men fainting from fear and the expectation of those things which are coming upon the whole world: for the powers of the heavens shall be moved. <margin>26</margin> 26 <margin>27 c</margin> 27 And then they shall see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. <margin>28</margin> 28 But when these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near. <margin>29</margin> 29 And he spoke to them a parable, <margin>23</margin> "Look at the fig tree and all the trees. 30 <margin>24</margin> When they already put forth their buds, seeing them for yourselves, you know that summer is now near. 31 So also you, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near. 32 Amen I say to you, <margin>D</margin> this generation shall not pass away before all things are done. 33 Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away. <margin>34</margin> 34 But take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with carousing and drunkenness and <margin>25</margin> the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly. 35 For like a snare it shall come upon all who sit upon the face of the whole earth. 36 Watch therefore at all times, praying, <margin>26</margin> that you may be worthy to escape all these things that are to come, and to stand before the Son of Man." 37 And during the day he was teaching in the temple, but at night he went out and stayed on the mountain called the Mount of Olives.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> 9 **Pestilences and famines** <note>original: "Pestilentiæ & fames"</note>] We have already noted elsewhere the wordplay between "famines" <note>Greek: limoi</note> and "plagues" <note>Greek: loimoi</note>. And soon after:
10 **Terror [and from heaven]** <note>original: "Terrore[que de cælo]"</note>] <note>original: "phobētra te"</note>, that is, "terrifying things." For "terror" is one thing, and a "monster" or "omen" that strikes terror is another.
11 **Not to meditate beforehand how you might answer** <note>original: "Non præmeditari quemadmodum respondeatis"</note>] <note>original: "mē promeletān apologēthēnai"</note>, that is, "defense is not to be practiced beforehand." This is what other defendants do, who work by the lamp to craft a speech to sway the judge. <term>Cyprian</term> <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage and influential Latin writer.</note> in the final letter of his third book cites this passage thus: "Set it in your hearts not to meditate beforehand to excuse yourselves." Furthermore, "to meditate" is said of that for which we prepare ourselves with care.
12 **All your adversaries** <note>original: "Omnes adversarii vestri"</note>] <note>original: "antikeimenoi hymin"</note>, that is, "those opposing you." And a little later:
14 **A hair from your head shall not perish** <note>original: "Capillus de capite vestro non peribit"</note>] <note>original: "apolētai"</note>, that is, "perishes." The <term>aorist</term> tense <note>a Greek verb tense usually indicating a completed action</note> has something more certain and comforting about it.
15 **You shall possess** <note>original: "Possidebitis"</note>] <note>original: "ktēsasthe"</note>, that is, "possess" or "obtain." It appears the Translator read <note>original: "ktēsesthe"</note> <note>a future tense</note>, although the Greek codices that I have seen consistently have <note>original: "ktēsasthe"</note> <note>an imperative or command</note>.
16 **And to those nursing** <note>original: "Et nutrientibus"</note>] <note>original: "thēlazousais"</note>, that is, "suckling" and "feeding at the breast," as indicated above. And <term>Ambrose</term> <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Milan.</note> reads for "nursing," "those who give the breast." <term>Augustine</term> <note>The famous 5th-century theologian from Hippo.</note> in some places reads "breast-feeding."
17 **Distress** <note>original: "Pressura"</note>] <note>original: "synochē"</note>, that is, "confinement" or "anxiety." Some codices had <note>original: "anankē"</note>, which sounds like "necessity" or "forced violence." Nor is it:
18 **In the mouth of the sword** <note>original: "In ore gladii"</note>] But "by the edge of the sword," <note>original: "stomati machairas"</note>, which would have been more correctly translated as "by the sharpness of the sword." Since the Greeks call the "edge" of a sword the "mouth" <note>original: "stoma"</note>, because it bites in that part, and a "double-mouthed" sword is one that cuts on both sides.
19 **Times of the nations** <note>original: "Tempora nationum"</note>] <note>original: "ethnōn"</note>, "of the Gentiles." The same noun as

<column-break/>

<margin>E</margin> preceded it. The Translator strangely avoided repeating the same word, even though the Evangelist does not avoid it.
20 **Before confusion** <note>original: "Præ confusione"</note>] <note>original: "en aporia"</note>, that is, "in perplexity" or "despair." Although both genitives can be read absolutely, so that the sense is, "because of the roar of the sea and the waves in despair," and "men withering away."
21 **The sound of the sea** <note>original: "Sonitus maris"</note>] <note>original: "ēchousēs thalassēs"</note>, that is, "of the resounding sea."
22 **Men withering away** <note>original: "Arescentibus hominibus"</note>] <note>original: "apopsychontōn"</note>, which sounds like "being breathless with grief" or "fainting away."
23 **See** <note>original: "Videte"</note>] The Greek word <note>original: "idete"</note> is ambiguous, whether it means "You see" or "Look!"
24 **When they now produce fruit from themselves** <note>original: "Cum producant jam ex se fructum"</note>] In Greek it is simply <note>original: "probalōsin ēdē"</note>, which I would have translated as "they have burst forth." For it does not refer to the fruit, but to the buds and foliage breaking out, which is clear from the other Evangelists. Certainly from Mark chapter 13, which mentions the tender branch and the foliage breaking forth. For first the branch becomes tender so that the buds can be pushed out. However, this is peculiar to the fig tree, that it immediately pushes out the early figs without any preceding flowers. Although other trees also push out buds. For Luke adds "and all trees" besides the fig. Although in other ways the 
<margin>F</margin> Greek differs from our version, <note>original: "blepontes aph' heautōn ginōskete"</note>, that is, "looking for yourselves, you recognize," meaning that when you see the buds and leaves pushed out on the trees, even if no one warns you, you nevertheless understand from the thing itself that summer is near. And a little later, he again translates <note>original: "mēpōpote"</note> as "lest perhaps," as if this were a matter of their luck, and not rather of their care.
25 **With the cares of this life** <note>original: "Curis hujus vitæ"</note>] <note>original: "merimnais biōtikais"</note>, which in Paul he translates as "worldly things" <note>original: "biōtika"</note>. It signifies those cares which pertain to providing food and the use of life.
26 **That you may be counted worthy** <note>original: "Ut digni habeamini"</note>] <note>original: "kataxiōthēte ekphygein tauta panta"</note>, that is, "that you may be rendered worthy, so that you are able to escape all these things." The sense, however, is that they should pray for this very thing, that they might be able to escape.
27 **He stayed on the mountain** <note>original: "Morabatur in monte"</note>] <note>original: "ēulizeto"</note>, which he had previously translated as "to be stabled."

# 215 THE GOSPEL

<margin>38</margin> And all the people came early in the morning to him in the temple to hear him. <margin>XXII</margin> Now the feast of unleavened bread drew near, which is called the Passover. <margin>2</margin> And the chief priests and the scribes sought how they might kill him; for they feared the people. <margin>3</margin> Then Satan entered into Judas, surnamed Iscariot, being of the number of the twelve. <margin>4</margin> And he went his way and communed with the chief priests and captains, how he might betray him to them. <margin>5</margin> And they were glad, and agreed to give him money. <margin>6</margin> And he promised, and sought an opportunity to betray him to them without a crowd. <margin>7</margin> Then came the day of unleavened bread, when the Passover must be killed. <margin>8</margin> And he sent Peter and John, saying, "Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat." <margin>9</margin> And they said to him, "Where do you want us to prepare it?" <margin>10</margin> And he said to them, "Behold, when you have entered into the city, a man shall meet you bearing a pitcher of water; follow him into the house where he enters. <margin>11</margin> And you shall say to the master of the house, 'The teacher says to you, Where is the guest chamber, where I shall eat the Passover with my disciples?' <margin>12</margin> And he shall show you a large upper room furnished; there make ready." <margin>13</margin> And they went and found as he had said to them, and they prepared the Passover. <margin>14</margin> And when the hour was come, he sat down, and the twelve apostles with him. <margin>15</margin> And he said to them, "With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. <margin>16</margin> For I say to you, I will not any more eat of it, until it be fulfilled in the kingdom of God." <margin>17</margin> And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and said, "Take this, and divide it among yourselves. <margin>18</margin> For I say to you, I will not drink of the fruit of the vine, until the kingdom of God shall come." <margin>19</margin> And he took bread, and gave thanks, and broke it, and gave to them, saying, "This is my body which is given for you; this do in remembrance of me." <margin>20</margin> Likewise also the cup after supper, saying, "This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you. <margin>21</margin> But behold, the hand of him that betrays me is with me on the table. <margin>22</margin> And truly the Son of man goes, as it was determined; but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed!" <margin>23</margin> And they began to inquire among themselves, which of them it was that should do this thing. <margin>24</margin> And there was also a strife among them, which of them should be accounted the greatest. <margin>25</margin> And he said to them, "The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and those who exercise authority upon them are called benefactors. <margin>26</margin> But you shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that serves. <margin>27</margin> For who is greater..."

---

<margin>28</margin> *And all the people remained]* <note>original: "Et omnis populus maniebat"</note> The Translator has imitated the Greek word *orthrize* <note>original: "ὤρθριζε" - meaning to rise early</note>. It is the same word that in the Psalms he translates as "I watch for the light" <note>original: "de luce vigilo"</note>. A very ancient Latin manuscript had "came frequently at dawn." It is therefore a wonder from where this word "maniebat" <note>stayed/remained</note>—entirely unheard of by Latin speakers—crept in, which even Augustine’s ears could not endure. For they note this in the book of Judges, in the forty-seventh question, indicating that some interpreted it as "he matured," because that word was derived from "morning" <note>matutino</note>. There are those who guess that "manicabat" <note>to do something early in the morning</note> was corrupted into "maniebat." But they are merely guessing. Augustine indicated the varied readings of his time in the book of Judges, and the word there from the Septuagint translation is the same as here: "he rises early and extends" <note>original: "ὀρθρίζει καὶ ἐκτενεῖς"</note>, which Jerome rendered: "And early in the morning as the sun rose he rushed upon the city." However, neither the word "manicandi" nor "maturandi" pleases Augustine; he denies the former is found in approved authors, and he does not quite approve of the etymology of the latter—for "to hasten" is one thing, and "to come in the morning" is another: for often he who comes in the morning comes late. Furthermore, the Commentaries of Bede in the context have it mistakenly as "he remained to him," but in the exposition he reads "he did it early in the morning."

<margin>1</margin> **O** *the twelve]* <note>original: "E duodecim"</note> *onta ek tou arithmou ton dodeka*, that is, "being of the number of the twelve."

<margin>2</margin> *And the magistrates]* And the leaders, or the commanders of the army. For it is *strategois* <note>original: "στρατηγοῖς"</note>, whom elsewhere, if I am not mistaken, he means as the prefects for guarding the temple; no other judges should be understood here. Theophylact mentions other opinions besides this one.

<margin>3</margin> *Without crowds]* <note>original: "Sine turbis"</note> *ater ochlou*, that is, without a crowd, which means without a riot. For *ochlos* signifies both, just as "turba" in Latin means "crowd," "multitude," and "tumult."

<margin>4</margin> *The Passover to be killed]* <note>original: "Occidi Pascha"</note> *thuesthai*, that is, to be sacrificed.

<margin>5</margin> *A certain man]* "Certain" <note>original: "quiddam"</note> is not added among the Greeks, but the Latin Translator added it on his own to make the speech smoother.

<margin>6</margin> *A pitcher]* <note>original: "Amphoram"</note> *keramion*, which signifies an earthenware vessel. I noted this because it seems to me to pertain to a mystery if one examines what "earthenware water-pot" <note>original: "hydria fictilis"</note> means, which is broken in Ecclesiastes when the golden bowl is crushed. It is the same word which elsewhere he translates as "flagon" <note>original: "lagenam"</note>.

<margin>7</margin> *From this]* <note>original: "Ex hoc"</note> *ex autou*, that is, "from it," namely the Passover, lest anyone refer it to time.

<margin>8</margin> *Take and divide]* <note>original: "Accipite & dividite"</note> *Labete touto*, that is, "Take this." It has been noted by the ancients that in Luke the mention of the cup occurs twice. For first he took the cup, and after giving thanks and the blessing, he said, "Take this and divide it among yourselves." Soon, after the bread is consecrated, there follows: "Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying..."

<margin>9</margin> *In my remembrance]* <note>original: "In meam commemorationem"</note> *eis ten emen anamnesin*, which would be expressed more clearly as "for the renewing of my memory."

<margin>10</margin> *In my blood]* "In" appears to be used for "through" <note>original: "per"</note>. Just as the Old Testament was confirmed and dedicated by the people being sprinkled with the blood of a beast, so Christ dedicated the New Testament through his own blood, which the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews elegantly explains. I do not see why religious scrupulousness should prevent us from rendering the sense more clearly here, since priests today do not use these exact words for consecration.

<margin>11</margin> *Which is poured for you]* <note>original: "Qui pro vobis fundetur"</note> *to hyper hymon ekchynnomenon*, that is, "which is being shed for you." Since he said just a little earlier "is given" in the present tense, why do we fear to say "is shed" here? Certainly "is given" is found in our copies.

<margin>12</margin> *Through whom he is betrayed]* <note>original: "Per quem traditur"</note> *paradidotai*, that is, "is betrayed," as it is in the present tense.

<margin>13</margin> *Rule over them]* It should have been translated as "of them" <note>feminine</note>, or "over them." For "nation" among the Greeks is of the neuter gender. Therefore in *auton* <note>original: "αὐτῶν"</note>, the Translator, forgetting himself, used the Greek gender.

<margin>14</margin> *As the younger]* <note>original: "Sicut minor"</note> *os ho neoteros*, that is, "as the younger," or "the minor by birth." The oldest manuscripts have "junior," not "minor." Although in this place it signifies contempt rather than age. For just as they called them "presbyters" <note>elders</note> as a title of honor, so they called the despised "juniors": as in that phrase in the Psalms: "I am a youth and despised." For to the Hebrews, *na'ar* <note>original: "נער"</note> sounds like "youth" and someone of no authority.

<margin>15</margin> *And he who is the leader]* <note>original: "Et qui praeest est"</note> *ho hegoumenos*, that is, "the leader or rector." For the Greek word also signifies this, and it fits better with what follows. For it is a conflict to be both a "presiding officer" and a "servant."
<margin>16</margin> *He says*

# ACCORDING TO LUKE. CHAPTER XXII.

<note>original Greek: "ζῶν, ὁ ἀνακείμενος..."</note> ...living, the one reclining at table, or the one serving? Is it not the one reclining? But I am in your midst as one who serves. You are those who have stayed with me in my trials. And I assign to you, just as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and you will sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And the Lord said, "Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has asked for you, to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, when once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers." And he said to him, "Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death." And he said, "I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow today before you deny three times that you know me." And he said to them, "When I sent you without a money bag and knapsack and sandals, did you lack anything?" And they said, "Nothing." He said therefore to them, "But now, he who has a...

<margin>A</margin>
16 **And the Lord said to Simon]** The Greek copies read: <note>original: "Εἶπε δὲ ὁ Κύριος, Σίμων, Σίμων, ἰδοὺ, etc."</note>, that is, *And the Lord said, Simon, Simon, behold, etc.* Furthermore, the repetition of the name serves to show affection. Saint Jerome cites it this way in his *Dialogues against the Pelagians* <note>Jerome was a 4th-century scholar; Pelagians were followers of a belief system Jerome and others considered heretical</note>. Nor does Bede report it otherwise in his *Commentaries*, lest anyone should think it happened by chance.

17 **Has sought you out]** <note>original: "ἐξῃτήσατο"</note>, which more strongly sounds like "demanded for punishment." For those who are sought for punishment are "demanded": just as Satan demanded this, that he might crush them, even as Satan demanded Job and obtained him, though within prescribed limits. Ambrose, in the first book of *On the Calling of All Nations*, the last chapter, brings this passage forward thus: *Simon, Simon, behold Satan has demanded that he might discern <note>or "sift"</note> you like wheat.* Indeed, the word for "sieve" seems to be derived from "discerning." In Greek, it is <note>original: "ἐπὶ σινιάσαι"</note> [to sift].

<margin>B</margin>
18 **Shall not crow]** <note>original: "οὐ μὴ φωνήσει"</note>, that is, shall not sound, or shall not give forth a voice.

19 **But now he who has a money bag]** I ask you, Christian reader, who is so witless <note>original Greek: "ἀγύλατος", likely a typo for "ἀναίσθητος" (senseless)</note> that he can restrain himself from laughter, considering how ridiculous the things some more recent writers have written on this passage. Who is such a lover of truth <note>original Greek: "Φιλάγγελος", likely "Philalethes"</note> that he would not be indignant that this heavenly teaching is trifled with by such interpretations? For that fellow Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a 14th-century theologian</note>, an approved Doctor in the eyes of many, twists Christ's words here as if he were advising the Apostles that, when the storm of persecution broke, they should arm themselves with two things: namely, provisions and the protection of weapons, lest they lack food or be overwhelmed by persecutors. And Hugo of Saint-Cher <note>A 13th-century Cardinal and commentator</note>, or whoever it was, insists on the same thing even more shamelessly, citing Chrysostom as the author. But these recent writers report his words in a mangled and corrupt way. For Chrysostom plainly rejects the invention concerning the literal sword, however much he moderates his interpretation of the money bag. His words on Matthew chapter 26 are: *So that they might more easily believe he was being betrayed, for that reason he said to them, "Buy swords." Not so that they should strike souls, but so that he might place the prediction of this event before their eyes.* These are his words. But what he meant by "prediction" is explained by his words cited in the *Golden Chain* of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas's collection of commentary from Church Fathers</note>: *What is this? He who had said, "If someone strikes you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also," now arms his disciples, but only with a sword. For if he intended to arm them fully, it was necessary to possess not only a sword, but also shields and helmets. But how could eleven men, raised by lakes and rivers, procure such weapons against so many insults and snares of peoples, tyrants, cities, and nations, if they did not tremble at the mere sight of troops? Therefore, let us not think he commanded them to possess swords, but through "swords" he hinted at the looming plots of the Jews. Whence it follows: "For I say to you, that this which is written must still be fulfilled in me: And he was counted among the wicked."* Again, a little further down: *Indeed, if he wanted them to use human help, not even a hundred swords would suffice; but if he did not want them to use human aid, even two are superfluous.* The words of Basil and Theophylact (whom I think is cited as "Theophylus" by mistake) are reported there to the same effect, and finally those of Bede. If it is established that we should take "the knapsack" in a simple sense, why should we seek a figurative interpretation for "the sword"—one that opens up a meaning conflicting with the words? For if the Lord commanded that things pertaining to food and defense be prepared, does clothing not pertain to the necessities of life? And yet he commands this to be sold. Therefore, just as by these words he prepared the minds of the Apostles to bravely endure the cruelty of persecutors, so by the mention of taking a money bag he prepared them for the endurance of hunger and all the inconveniences that usually happen in wars. By the prediction of evils, he does not exhort them to provide supplies and fortifications, but to the endurance of evils, which more quickly prostrate a person if they arrive unforeseen. Because the Lord, as long as he was present as a mortal, had supplied them abundantly without care and kept them safe from the incursion of evils, they were weak—still contending for primacy even at the very time of the Lord’s death, and not sufficiently instructed against the storms of evils that were imminent. He warns them of evils, therefore, not so they may trust in their own strength, but so they may be vigilant against the encroaching tempest of afflictions. How should they be vigilant? Surely as he himself taught by example as well as by warnings: *Watch and pray that you enter not into temptation.* Nor do we read that they did anything other than what they had learned from the Lord after they received the Holy Spirit. He wanted them to depend on him, not as infants, as they had done before, but as men who join their own industry with heavenly help. This is what Chrysostom felt, this is what Theophylact felt, this is what Basil felt, who also noted that in many manuscripts it is not *written: "let him take, let him lift, or let him buy," but "he shall take and he shall buy," so that the speech is that of one predicting imminent affliction, not of one exhorting them to prepare provisions or armor.* Some interpret

<margin>C</margin>
this speech as belonging not only to the Apostles but to all the Jews, over whom such a storm of war was looming that they would be concerned neither with food nor clothing, but only with protecting their lives; this being signified by the trope <note>a figure of speech</note> by which he commands the sword to be bought after selling the tunic and knapsack. To what purpose, then, do the words of Chrysostom pertain: *Teaching the boys now to be men, he commands them to use their own wings?* Does it mean to prepare spears, helmets, shields, and cannons? <note>Erasmus uses "bombardas," an anachronism to mock the idea of Apostles using modern weaponry</note> What then is the difference between a common mercenary soldier and an Apostolic man? But, they say, when times change, it is permissible to change the way of life. In time of peace, weapons are forbidden; in time of war, they are permitted. As if indeed persecution were ever lacking for good men. Did Christ then, just as he was about to die, sing a recantation of all those teachings of his—about not resisting evil, about loving and helping enemies, about praying for those who curse us, about the blessedness of the mild and those suffering for the sake of justice, about offering the other cheek if someone strikes one, and many other such things—and now rouses his followers to provide supplies and prepare weapons? Has he also forgotten those things he said just a little before: *In your patience you shall possess your souls?* And yet there he speaks truly of persecution, and makes no mention of defenses. Indeed, when he places the entire tragedy of persecutions before our eyes in Matthew, I ask, is there anywhere any mention of defense? Where is that one thing he commands the Apostles to learn from him, that he was mild and humble of heart? Where is that severe voice: *You know not of what spirit you are,* by which he recalls his disciples from an impulse of vengeance? Where is that voice by which he denies he recognizes a disciple who does not follow him after taking up his cross? Does he here change the cross into a sword? Furthermore, what does Christ teach his own by way of an image, if he commanded that which pirates and robbers do of their own accord? Is this that heavenly doctrine which he descended to earth from heaven to impart to us? Moreover, if he taught what those people want, why does he himself not perform what he teaches? When did he prepare provisions for himself? When did he fortify himself with swords or machines against the force of persecutors? They do not see how these things clash with the prophecy Isaiah gave concerning him: *Like a sheep before its shearer, he was silent.* Meanwhile, I will remain silent so as not to seem to dwell on their invention. For let us imagine this was Christ’s mind, that he wanted his Apostles to prepare an iron sword, such as robbers use, and provisions, such as army leaders prepare; by what logic will they explain the fact that he commands the sword to be bought after the tunic is sold? Since they choose to press the letters and syllables of the speech. Does he send them into war girded only with naked blades? A new kind of troop indeed! To this, when he said: *But now he who has a money bag, let him take it, and likewise a knapsack,* how does that which immediately follows fit: *And he who has not, let him sell his tunic and buy a sword?* Is it not evident enough from this that he was not commanding them to carry a money bag and knapsack with them, but to take them to be sold, and with the price to redeem <note>buy</note> a sword? If none of these were available, they should sell their tunic rather than be without a sword. Even if they twist it as much as possible, he does not command them to prepare a money bag or knapsack, but permits it as something to be tolerated, if someone happens to possess one. But he commands the sword to be bought even with the tunic sold. Therefore, to look out for food is merely permitted, but we are commanded to defend ourselves with the sword so much that we must clash with the enemy even naked, as if the height of piety were placed in this! Yet they do not even come to their senses from what follows immediately in the other Evangelists. He rebukes Peter menacingly and severely for using the sword, and commands it to be put away, adding that those who fight by the sword perish by the sword, and that many legions of aid from the Father would not be lacking to him if he had wished to defend himself by force. Furthermore, when did we ever read that the Apostles did what Christ so strongly commands to be done here? We read they were beaten, we read they answered, but we nowhere read they wore a breastplate or a sword, and they did not even fight back with their fingernails, let alone swords. Finally, why do they dare in all their Epistles to discord from the teaching of their master? With one voice they all teach endurance; they command that enemies be overwhelmed with benefits and that coals of fire be heaped upon their heads. Paul commands that evil be overcome with good; he boasts of the calamities he endured, he does not boast of prostrated or routed enemies. That man arms the Christian recruit with the Evangelical panoply <note>full armor</note>: the helmet of salvation, the shield of faith, the sword of the spirit. Where among these is the mention of this literal sword which we are imagining? In more trivial matters, which could be ignored without the expense of Evangelical philosophy, they pour forth <note>original: "ἐπαναβλύζουσιν"</note> accusations of heresy and blasphemy. To many, no heresy seems more pernicious, no blasphemy more wicked, than if someone—following the example of the Philistines—should fill the wells of the Evangelical field (which have a vein of living water from Christ springing up into eternal life) with earth, and turn the spiritual sense into a carnal one, corrupt heavenly doctrine into earthly doctrine, and twist the most holy dogmas of Christ, indeed corrupt them, and that in the face of all his precepts, in the face of his whole life, in the face of Apostolic doctrine, and against so many thousands of mar- <note>The word "mar-" is a catchword for "martyrum" (martyrs) on the next page.</note>

<summary>Erasmus provides a detailed commentary on Luke 22, arguing forcefully against medieval scholars who interpreted Jesus's command to "buy a sword" literally, instead identifying it as a spiritual metaphor for enduring future persecution.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on Luke 22, specifically focusing on the "two swords" passage. On the previous page, Erasmus began debating whether Jesus intended his disciples to arm themselves literally. Here, he marshals the authority of the Church Fathers—Ambrose, Origen, and Augustine—to argue that the "sword" is a spiritual metaphor for fortitude and the Word of God, rather than a justification for physical warfare.</meta>

# GOSPEL CH. XXII.

<column-break/>

**[Page 319]**

<margin>35 36</margin> "But now, let him who has a money-bag take it, and likewise a knapsack; and let him who has none sell his garment and buy a <margin>37</margin> sword. For I tell you, that this which is written must still be fulfilled in me: 'And he was reckoned among the lawless'; for indeed the things <margin>38</margin> concerning me are reaching their end." And they said, "Lord, behold, here are two swords." And he said to them, "It is enough." <margin>39</margin> And going out, he went according to his custom to the Mount of Olives; and his disciples also followed <margin>40</margin> him. And when he had come to the place, he said to them,

---

...[modern interpreters] who resist the ancient Interpreters. Nor do they notice how Ambrose interprets this here—though in a matter so clear, what need is there for an Interpreter? "Why," he asks, "do you order a sword to be bought, you who forbid me to strike? Why do you command me to have what you forbid me to draw? *Unless perhaps a defense is prepared, not a necessary revenge, so that I might appear to have been able to be vindicated, but unwilling.*" Then, resolving what could be objected from the letters of the Old Instrument <note>The Old Testament</note>—that war was permitted—he says: "*The Law* indeed *does not forbid me to strike back*," <margin>B</margin> and therefore perhaps to Peter offering two swords, he says: "*It is enough*": as if it were permitted up to the time of the Gospel; so that in the Law there is instruction in equity, but in the Gospel the perfection of goodness. Soon he opposes those who protest with these words: "*To many this seems unjust, but the Lord is not unjust, who, though he could avenge himself, preferred instead to be sacrificed.*" Finally, at the end, he adds this, interpreting the two swords as the knowledge of the Old and New Testaments: "*As if nothing is lacking to him whom the doctrine of both Testaments has fortified.*" Origen, without controversy the most learned of the ancient theologians, in his *Seventh Homily on Matthew*, pronounces this discourse of Christ to be pernicious <note>original: "pestiferum"</note> if it is taken literally. After reciting it, Erasmus <note>Referring to himself in the third person or citing his own previous notes</note> adds in this manner: "*If anyone, therefore, wishing to look at the letter and not understanding the intent of the words, sells his physical garment and buys such a sword, receiving his word against the will of Christ, he will perish—perhaps he will even perish by the sword.*" But concerning which sword he speaks, this is not the place to explain. <margin>C</margin> The same author, in his second book *Against Celsus*, pronounces that war was abolished by Christ alone, as if this were peculiar to him. All the writings of all men, all the books of the Saints, agree with this opinion, recommending tolerance to us, not decreeing armor. It must be tolerated somehow, if only they distorted one single place of the heavenly philosophy <term>philosophia caelestis</term> <note>Erasmus's term for the simple, lived teachings of Christ in the Gospel</note> in this corrupt way. There is almost no dogma of Christ which certain people do not subvert with comments and distinctions of this kind. And these things are read and approved by the highest Theologians, as they commonly seem; these are cited as if produced by an oracle; these are taught publicly; Princes hear these, and by these are animated to war, as if indeed they were not insane enough of their own accord. Because of these things, it has come to pass that among Christians there is almost more insane rioting, litigation, and fighting—for property, for dominion, for revenge—than anywhere among the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicos"</note>. But the grief of the soul must be moderated, however justified; especially since the unworthiness of the matter can scarcely be explained, as is fitting, in a huge volume. Nor do those move me even a little who do not want the right of war to be taken away from Princes. <margin>D</margin> How Princes wage war now, I do not care to remember; nor is it necessary to teach them this, which they do only too sharply from the womb: if indeed this is "waging war," and not rather conspiring among themselves for the destruction of the people, and using the pretext of wars to establish their own tyranny. This I do not endure: that we refer dogmas of this kind to Christ as their author. If the necessity of human life has anything—as it has many "necessary evils," as that man says—if anything is granted to worldly coarseness, what does this have to do with the heavenly philosophy of Christ? He came from heaven to teach heavenly things; these coarse things he either was as if ignorant of, or rejected, or neglected. He did not recognize Caesar's coins until they were shown to him, and then he commanded that the things which are Caesar's be cast away. He rejects the man by whom he was asked to be the arbiter of a divided inheritance. He neither absolves nor condemns the adulterous woman. <margin>E</margin> Nor indeed does it escape me that Saint Augustine brings forward this passage against Faustus the Manichaean in his twenty-second book, who detested war even among the Jews. But he brings it forward in such a way that he still does not want the Apostles to wage war, nor even Emperors, unless they are clearly sons of piety, unless for a just cause, unless against the sacrilegious and worshipers of demons, and unless for public tranquility. Nor does he disagree with us regarding the taking of a knapsack and staff on the road: in this alone he differs, that he wants Peter to have been rebuked because he unjustly entered the fight, having been commanded indeed to carry a sword, but not to strike with the sword. How much weight this comment has, I leave to others to examine, lest I seem to say anything too harsh against such a great Doctor of the Church. For there are those who immediately interpret it as an insult if anyone differs from received authors, though they themselves did not demand this honor. On the contrary, it would be insulting, I think, if anyone tried to defend them against the truth when they have slipped in the manner of men. For what kind of thing is it, I ask, to burden the disciples with a useless sword by such a trivial precept, which one may not draw even when it is most needed? Just as if someone were to command: "Make sure you have a shovel ready, but beware that you never dig." "Carry sandals around, but always walk with bare feet." The interpretation was more tolerable if we understand it in this way: even if at some time the faculty of defending oneself is present, nevertheless abstain from defense; defend yourselves with the sword of the divine word alone. Here certain people bring forward a very cold distinction: he commanded them to have a sword for defense, but forbade it to be drawn for revenge. Now it must be seen whether Augustine is consistent with himself regarding war: he who in so many places detests war in a Christian manner, now against the Manichaeans and Donatists <note>The Donatists were a schismatic Christian sect in North Africa whom Augustine eventually supported suppressing via state force</note> seems to be a patron of war. Indeed, he, expounding the thirty-seventh Psalm, writes: "*One must pray for enemies, not that they be killed, but that they be corrected*"; if it is not permitted to pray to God that enemies be restrained by a just punishment, much less is it permitted for us to kill them. The same man, in Letter 48, writes that the passions of the saints are contaminated if the enemies are killed in turn. Again, in his fifth letter, how many things he discusses against war. Furthermore, in how many places does he plead with the Caesarean prefects, lest the Donatists—not only heretics, but also those attacking the Orthodox with a horrible kind of brigandage—should be killed...

**[Page 320]**

...lest there be no one who could be corrected, but that they should be restrained only so far that, the goods of the Church having been transferred elsewhere, they might be forced to follow. Finally, when the Donatists laid ambushes for Augustine so many times, when is he read to have gathered an armed hand against their violence? But with what face would he do this himself, he who so strenuously intercedes and protests lest it be done by the Caesarean prefects? But it usually happens this way, that in conflict with adversaries, everyone twists Holy Scripture to his own cause. And it is true what they say: that heretics have benefited the Christian Religion in some part, while they stimulate the Orthodox to the investigation of the divine volumes. Yet to this benefit is joined that disadvantage: that while we force the testimonies of the Scriptures to serve victory, not rarely is there a deflection from the genuine and true meaning. <margin>B</margin> Now, if what those people interpret is true, what did those think who believe this was said ironically—"it is enough"—namely, against such a great multitude? Nor does Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine commentator</note> reject this opinion: but he adds another, which likewise works for us: "*Since*," he says, "*they did not understand what he was saying, he left them, so as not to be troublesome.*" Certainly the Apostles were understanding according to the flesh; therefore the Lord was not speaking according to the flesh. Therefore it seems simpler to me that Christ, gradually trying to remove common affections from the minds of his followers—since he had previously freed them from the care of provisions—now wished to free them also from the fear of punishments and death. <margin>C</margin> He knew what would come into the minds of those who were still unrefined in that tumult, and therefore he allowed them to err for a time concerning the swords, so that he might more effectively remove from their affections the desire for revenge. If he had been silent about the sword, defense might have seemed permitted whenever the danger of life pressed upon the Apostolic men. Now he so tempered the matter and the discourse that no one can doubt but that he interdicted the use of iron to his own. He had sent them a little earlier to give a specimen of themselves and to take a certain taste of the Evangelical duty, but only within the borders of Judea. And since here human anxiety might require provisions and some travel funds, he ordered his followers to set out without a knapsack, without a staff; and yet nothing had been lacking, since good men voluntarily supplied necessary things. But since it was going to be that the peak and the final hand of the Evangelical preaching would be martyrdom, and nothing is more formidable than death: he wanted his followers to be instructed against this struggle as well, not only by the example of his own death, but also by admonition. Therefore, so that from those things which they had already experienced, they might have faith in those things which were to follow later, he reminds them of their former preaching. <margin>D</margin> "When I sent you without a money-bag, and knapsack, and sandals, did anything lack to you?" And when they had responded that nothing at all was lacking, he calls them to perfection: "You see that until now nothing was lacking to you though you were naked; let no anxiety trouble you from this. But just as there is no reason for anxiety to distress you concerning provisions and the supports of life, so there is no reason for you to be anxious about defense, if ever a persecutor threatens tortures or death. You will conquer tyrants with the same protections by which I conquer. Indeed, the more you are destitute of all human protections, the more you will be equipped for this war." <margin>E</margin> So much so that if someone happens to have a tunic or a knapsack, let him cast these away so that he may be more unencumbered. "There is no need except for my sword, which so cuts away and plucks out all carnal affections that, girt with it, one fears neither torments nor death—far be it from him to fear hunger or nakedness." Nor indeed, when I say these things, do I take away the right of waging war from Princes, provided it is waged in a Christian manner. Caesars are also praised by Ambrose, who opposed themselves like a wall for the protection of Christian tranquility against the Barbarians; and yet the same man denies that this belongs to the Evangelical purity, which Christ teaches his followers here. But what is this to us, we Priests who ourselves wage war without end, and that for empire, for plunder, for worldly glory? What is this to Christian Princes, who through ambition, anger, avarice, or some other private affection endlessly mix the world in the tumults of wars? What to these wars, which are waged with such great injustice—not to say cruelty—that frequently there is less evil from the enemy than from the defender? But a place will be given elsewhere for discussing these things more at length. Theophylact differs somewhat from this interpretation, since he interprets the taking up of the knapsack and money-bag just as he does the sword: not that he wants them to be anxious about providing for these things in the manner of men, but lest they could totally depend on the protection of Christ, who until now had care for them just like children; but that they themselves also for the future should prepare their minds against want, against hunger, against death—and that this was signified by the knapsack, money-bag, and sword. But if anyone should press me to pronounce whether I think war is entirely forbidden to Christians or not, I will first ask the questioner to answer me: what did Saint Martin mean when he said, "Let your [officer] take your bounty if he is going to serve as a soldier; I am a Christian, it is not permitted for me to fight." Then, what did Saint Jerome say, besides other ancient Orthodox writers, who so often condemns war among Christians? But if they do not deign to respond, I will say that war does not suit Apostolic men, nor is the Christian Religion to be propagated only by arms, nor is any war to be undertaken by a Prince that can be avoided by any means, and once undertaken, it must be waged with the least possible loss of blood, and ended as quickly as possible. Finally, that this very sanction <note>The right to war</note> does not belong to Evangelical purity, nor is this right to be sought from Evangelical precepts. Many things are conceded which the Gospel does not teach, such as oaths and forensic litigation. Among the Pagans the right of the sword is not disapproved; let them offer laws...

<summary>In this commentary on the "two swords" of Luke 22, Erasmus argues against a literal interpretation of Jesus's command to buy a sword, instead viewing it as a spiritual metaphor for fortitude and the Word of God. He uses the writings of the Church Fathers to condemn the warmongering of contemporary priests and princes, asserting that true "Evangelical purity" is inherently pacifist.</summary>

And as it became light, <margin>29</margin> there gathered <margin>66</margin> the Elders of the people and the chief Priests and Scribes, and they led him into their council, Saying, <margin>67</margin> "Are you that Christ? tell us." And he said to them, "If I tell you, you will not believe. And if I also question you, you will not <margin>68</margin> [answer]"

<margin>E</margin> ...truly, which [signifies] an urging and heavy crisis. We have translated it as we could: *And being seized with anguish*.

<margin>22 Drops of blood running down to the earth</margin>] Here the Greek manuscripts vary, but in such a way that it does not affect the sense; and the slip of the Scribes is easy in such a narrow difference between *falling down* <note>original: "katabainontes" - masculine, referring to the "drops"</note> and *falling down* <note>original: "katabainousas" - feminine, referring to the "drops"</note>. Jerome, in his second book *Against the Pelagians*, and before him Hilary in the tenth book *On the Trinity*, indicates that in many Greek and Latin manuscripts no mention is made either of the bloody sweat or of the Angel comforting him. But it seems to have been erased by those who feared to attribute such significant marks of human weakness to Christ, even though Hilary even tries to take away from him the sensation of pain.

<margin>23 Shall we strike</margin>] *ei pataxomen* <note>original Greek: εἰ πατάξομεν</note>, that is, *should we strike?* The Translator used "if" <note>Latin: "si"</note> for "whether" <note>Latin: "an"</note>.

<margin>24 Permit thus far</margin>] *Eate heos toutou* <note>original Greek: Ἐᾶτε ἕως τούτου</note>, that is, "Let it go this far." This sounds to the Greeks as if one were saying, "Do not resist any further," whereas the Evangelist has another meaning.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>25 And magistrates of the temple</margin>] *strategous* <note>original Greek: στρατηγοὺς</note>, *leaders*. For there were also soldiers appointed to guard the temple, whose commanders he calls here *strategous* <note>term: strategoi — usually translated as "generals," but here referring to the captains of the Temple Guard</note>.

<margin>26 And when she had fixed her gaze</margin>] *kai atenisasa auto* <note>original Greek: καὶ ἀτενίσασα αὐτῷ</note>, that is, *and with her eyes fixed on him*. For *atenizein* <note>original Greek: ἀτενίζειν</note> is something more than merely looking; namely, to behold with unmoving eyes.

<margin>27 About an hour</margin>] *hosei* <note>original Greek: ὡσεὶ</note>, that is, *roughly* or *nearly*. Although Suetonius also used *quasi* in this manner.

<margin>28 As he had said</margin>] *hos eipen auto* <note>original Greek: ὡς εἶπεν αὐτῷ</note>, in what manner, or as he had said to him. For this very thing came into his mind: that Christ had told him it would happen that he would deny him.

<margin>29 The elders gathered</margin>] *synechthe to presbyterion* <note>original Greek: συνήχθη τὸ πρεσβυτέριον</note>, that is, the order of the Elders came together.

"perverting" rather than "subverting," <note>original Greek: διαστρέφοντα</note>.
2 "Are you the king of the Jews?" <note>original Greek: Σὺ εἶ ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων</note>, that is,
"Are you *that* king of the Jews?" so that you understand him to be that one and only
King promised and expected by the Jews.
3 "I find no cause" ] <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν αἴτιον</note>, that is, no harm, or
no crime that ought to be imputed. Indeed, a fault is called *noxia* [harm],
while *noxa* is rather the punishment.
4 "He stirs up the people" ] <note>original Greek: ἀνασείει</note>, that is, he excites, he stirs up, in the

<margin>14</margin> *Blessed are the barren, and the wombs which*] It should have been said, *the wombs which did not give birth*. It appears the Translator hallucinated <note>meaning he made a grammatical slip</note> because the Greek word for *wombs* (koiliai) is of the feminine gender. But soon the Greek speech certainly refers to *breasts*, which are <note>original: "mastoi oi ouk ethēlasan"</note>, *and the breasts which did not nurse*. Here, "which did not <gloss>nurse</gloss>" refers to the <gloss>breasts</gloss>, not to the *women*. Otherwise, there would be a point where someone could somehow try to evade the meaning.

<margin>15</margin> *In the green [wood]*] <note>original: "en tō hygrō"</note>, that is, *in the moist*, just as Hilary cites it according to the Greek reading when explaining the first Psalm; and thus it corresponds better to what follows, *the dry*. For *moist and green* belong together, although the Translator expressed the general sense.

<margin>16</margin> *Two wicked ones*] <note>original: "dyo kakourgoi"</note>, that is, two evildoers, or criminals.

<margin>17</margin> *And robbers*] <note>original: "kai kakourgous"</note>. He now translates this as "robbers," though he just translated it as "wicked," being a man of many words <note>The author is critiquing the inconsistency of the Vulgate translator</note>.

<margin>18</margin> *They know not what they do*] Whether the Latins speak this way, I do not know; perhaps it was more correct to say, *they know not that which they do*. For if you say, *they know not what they do*, you fall into another inconvenience, namely ambiguity of meaning.

<margin>19</margin> *The people stood waiting*] <note>original: "heistēkei"</note>, that is, *he stood, looking on*: supported by our ancient copies. Truly there is no doubt that this happened by the error of the scribes.

<margin>20</margin> *And they derided him*] <note>original: "exemyktērizon"</note>, that is, *they turned up their noses at him*. This is the same word which, as indicated above, means *to hang by the nose*, or to attack with scoffs.

<margin>21</margin> *If you are King*] <note>original: "ho basileus"</note>, that is, *the king*. And a little before <note>original: "ho Christos"</note>, that is, *the Christ*. And again <note>original: "ho tou Theou eklektos"</note>, that is, *the chosen one of God*. For the Greek article is not idle <note>meaningless</note> in these cases.

<margin>22</margin> *There was also a superscript*] <note>original: "epigraphē"</note>. Why not rather *inscription* than *superscription*?

<margin>23</margin> *In Greek, and Hebrew, and Latin*] The order is different in Greek: <note>original: "Hellēnikois, kai Rōmaïkois, kai Hebraïkois"</note>, that is, *Greeklike, and Roman, and Hebraic*. Truly these three languages ought to be commended to all Christians for this reason alone: that on the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, these alone of all were chosen. At least it was fitting for this title to be depicted everywhere in its own forms, which John sets down in this form:

->JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS<- <note>Hebrew: Yeshua HaNazri Melekh HaYehudim</note>
->JESUS THE NAZARENE THE KING OF THE JEWS.<- <note>Greek: IESOUS O NAZŌRAIOS O BASILEUS TŌN IOUDAIŌN</note>
->JESUS NAZARENE KING OF THE JEWS.<- <note>Latin: JESUS NAZARENUS REX JUDÆORUM</note>

<margin>24</margin> *Who hung with the robbers*] <note>original: "kakourgōn"</note>, which he just translated as "wicked."

<margin>25</margin> *Nor do you fear God*] The silent force of the conjunction "neither" (neque) can refer to three things unless the composition prevents it: to "fear," to "you," and to "God." If to God, the sense will be: "Not only do you not fear men, but you do not even fear God." If to "you," it is: "It is a small thing if those men despise God, unless you also despise him." If to "fear," the sense will be: "Not only do you not love God, but you do not even fear him, though you are set in punishment." But the composition of the speech among the Greeks is such that it can only be taken in this sense, which I reviewed in the last place: <note>original: "Oude phobē sy ton Theon"</note>, that is, *You do not even fear God*, or, *Do you not at least fear God?*

<margin>26</margin> *Who are in the same condemnation*] In the Greek it is not *in*, but *under* (epi), with the ancient copies of the Latins also agreeing. Indeed, in the Pauline codex it was "that not," agreeing with "Finishing"; in the Corbeian it was "who," except that "a" seemed erased, but with a clear trace testifying to the corruption. And likewise in the golden codex it was written "because." Furthermore, we have spoken of the ambiguity of the sense elsewhere.

<margin>27</margin> *Nothing of evil*] <note>original: "ouden atopon"</note>, that is, *nothing absurd* or *nothing out of place*.

<margin>28</margin> *Amen I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise*] Theophylact shows here that some people punctuate the speech differently. For they want the adverb *today* to be referred to the preceding words: *Amen I say to you today*, then after placing a comma they add, *you shall be with me in paradise*. The matter itself shows that this is a cold <note>weak/forced</note> invention; they fled to it to escape the question of how what the Lord promised could be true—*today you shall be with me in paradise*—since on that day and also the following, his body was in the tomb and his soul descended into hell. But just as the Lord elsewhere calls extreme unhappiness "Gehenna," so here he calls the highest rest and pleasure "Paradise." Although Theophylact, disputing more at length on this passage, mixes in some things that do not quite agree with the decrees of the Scholastic theologians of this time.

<margin>29</margin> *Into your hands I commend*] In Greek it is <note>original: "parathēsomai"</note>, that is, *I will commend*, or *I will deposit*, in the future tense. And this is according to the Hebrew truth, which has it in this manner: <note>original: "B’yadkha afkid ruchi"</note>. Indeed, the word "afkid" from the verb "pakad" indicates the future tense. And so indeed Saint Jerome and the Seventy <note>the Septuagint</note> translated it. Even if it were possible that Christ changed the tense, nonetheless the consensus of the Greek codices that I have seen holds this. The passage is taken from the thirty-first Psalm, which it is probable the Lord recited on the cross up to that point, and there raised his voice. In the Gallic Psalter, which Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples published, it is held as *I will commend*, just as the Seventy translated it. Here again, that blessed codex of the Pontifical Library is brought forward. The Lord added "Father" from his own, since neither among the Hebrews nor in the Seventy does the name of "Father" or "Lord" appear in this place. Nor does the future tense verb fit badly, first because he is reciting a Psalm, then because he predicts that he is about to die before he actually dies. Moreover, *to commend* (parathesthai) is to commit something as a deposit to be kept and returned in its own time. For Ambrose alluded to this when he said, "The Spirit is therefore a good pledge, a good deposit."

<margin>46</margin> "I will commend my spirit." And having said this, he breathed his last. <margin>47</margin> When the centurion saw what had happened, he glorified God, saying, "Truly this man was righteous." <margin>48</margin> And all the crowds who had gathered for this spectacle, when they saw what had happened, struck their breasts and began to return home. <margin>49</margin> But all his acquaintances stood at a distance, as did the women who had followed him from Galilee, watching these things. <margin>50</margin> And behold, there was a man named Joseph, a member of the council, <note>original: bouleutes</note> a good and righteous man. <margin>51</margin> This man had not consented to their council and deed; he was from Arimathea, a city of the Jews, and he himself was waiting for the kingdom of God. <margin>52</margin> This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. <margin>53</margin> And taking it down, he wrapped it in a linen shroud and laid <margin>B</margin> it in a tomb hewn from rock, where no one had ever yet been laid. <margin>54</margin> And it was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was beginning to dawn. <margin>55</margin> The women who had come with him from Galilee followed after, and they saw the tomb and how his body was laid. <margin>56</margin> Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments.
