<margin>50</margin> *Who was more secure*] <note>original: bouleutēs</note>. This is a title of dignity, not a military office; it sounds essentially like a <term>senator</term> or <term>councilor</term>, about which something has been said elsewhere.

<margin>51</margin> *In counsel and acts*] <note>original: tē boulē kai tē praxei</note>, that is, <term>in plan and deed</term>. The translator seems to have read it as "deeds" (plural).

<margin>52</margin> *And he placed him in a tomb*] It should be read "And he placed **it**" <note>referring to the body</note>. For this refers to the <term>body</term> <note>original: auto</note>. And for that reason, in the more corrected Latin codices it is written <term>illud</term> (it), not <term>illum</term> (him), so that it is clearly a mistake of the scribes, not the translator. Similarly, regarding the participle <term>deposited</term> <note>original: kathelōn auto</note>, which actually sounds more like <term>taken down</term> than <term>deposited</term>. Just as in the Song of Mary, *He has put down the mighty* <note>original: katheilen</note>, meaning <term>he dragged down</term>. For *katheilen* is said of something that hangs suspended on high, such as a shield or a flask.

<margin>53</margin> *In a tomb hewn out*] <note>original: laxeutō</note>. So that we may understand it was solid rock, not joined together or built up, but carved out in its own natural place.

<margin>54</margin> *On the Sabbath they were silent*] <note>original: hēsychasan</note>, that is, they rested, for *hēsychazein* signifies both.

<margin>1</margin> *On the first day of the week*] It is "on one of the Sabbaths" in Greek, where you must understand the word <term>day</term>.

<margin>2</margin> *Very early in the morning*] <note>original: orthrou batheos</note>, that is, in the "deep dawn," which is when much of the night still remains. For after the turning of the night comes the cock-crow, then the hushed time of night, then the dawn when the night begins to thin, then the morning, and finally the day when the sun has risen.

<margin>3</margin> *To the tomb*] Here the Greek codices add, <term>and certain ones with them</term>. This is ambiguous, however, as to whether it refers to men or women, because the word *tines* (certain ones) is of common gender.

<margin>4</margin> *They were dismayed in mind*] <note>original: en tō diaporeisthai</note>, that is, while they were stuck, perplexed, and uncertain in spirit.

<margin>5</margin> *In flashing garments*] <note>original: astraptousais</note>. This sounds more like <term>lightning-bright</term> or <term>shining like a bolt of lightning</term>.

<column-break/>

<margin>46</margin> "...I commend my spirit." And when he had said this, <margin>47</margin> he expired. Now when the centurion saw what had happened, he glorified God, saying, "Truly this man <margin>48</margin> was righteous." And all the crowds of those who had come together to this spectacle, and saw the things that were happening, striking their breasts, began to return. <margin>49</margin> But all his acquaintances stood far off, as did the women who <margin>50</margin> had followed him from Galilee, seeing these things. And behold, <margin>b</margin> a man named Joseph, a <term>decurio</term> <note>A Latin term for a member of a municipal council.</note>, who was a good and <margin>51</margin> righteous man—he had not consented to their counsel and deed—being from Arimathea, a city of the Jews, <margin>52</margin> who also himself was waiting for the kingdom of God: this man went to <margin>d</margin> Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. And taking it down, <margin>B</margin> <margin>53</margin> he wrapped it in linen and placed it in a tomb <margin>e</margin> that was hewn in stone, in which no one had yet been placed. <margin>54</margin> And it was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was beginning to shine. <margin>55</margin> The women who <margin>f</margin> had come with him from Galilee followed after and saw the tomb, and how his body was placed. <margin>g</margin> Returning, they prepared spices and ointments, and <margin>56</margin> on the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment. <margin>h</margin>
<margin>XXIV. 1</margin> But on the first day of the week, in the deep dawn, they <margin>a</margin> came to the tomb, carrying the spices they had prepared, and some others with them. They found the <margin>2</margin> stone rolled away from the tomb. And entering, they did <margin>3</margin> not find the body of the Lord Jesus. And it happened while <margin>4</margin> they were dismayed in mind about this, behold, two men <margin>b</margin> stood near them in flashing garments. <margin>5</margin> When they were terrified and turned their faces toward the earth, <margin>c</margin> the men said to them, "Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen. Remember how <margin>6</margin> he spoke to you while he was still in Galilee, saying <margin>d</margin> <margin>7</margin> that it was necessary for the Son of Man to be delivered into the hands <margin>e</margin> of sinful men, and to be crucified, and on the third day to rise again." And they remembered his words. And returning <margin>8</margin> from the tomb, they announced all these things to those <margin>f</margin> eleven, and to all the rest. Now it was Mary <margin>10</margin> Magdalene, and Joanna, and Mary the mother of James, and the others <margin>d</margin> who were with them, who told these things to the Apostles. And <margin>11</margin> their words seemed to them like a "delirious tale" <note>original: deliramentum</note>, nor did they believe them. But Peter, rising, ran <margin>12</margin> to the tomb; and peering in, he saw the linen <margin>k</margin> cloths placed alone, and he went away, wondering <margin>i</margin> to himself at what had happened. And behold, two of them were going that <margin>13</margin> same day to a village that was a distance of sixty <margin>l</margin> stadia from Jerusalem, named Emmaus. And <margin>m</margin> <margin>14</margin> they were talking among themselves about all these things that had <margin>n</margin> happened. And it happened while they were talking and <margin>15</margin> debating, Jesus himself, approaching, went along with <margin>o</margin> them. But their eyes were held, so that they did not <margin>16</margin> recognize him. And he said to them, "What are these speeches <margin>17</margin> that..." <margin>E</margin>

---

<margin>6</margin> *While they were afraid*] The Evangelist said more than the translator: <note>original: Emphobōn de genomenōn, kai klinousōn to prosōpon eis tēn gēn</note>, that is, "While they were struck with terror and turning their faces toward the ground." It appears the translator read *emphobōn* (in fear), which is found in some Greek codices.

<margin>7</margin> *Remember how he said*] The Greek <note>original: Mnēsthēte</note> is ambiguous, just as "Remember" is for us, as to whether it is in the imperative or indicative mood; except that the things following argue for the imperative mood, namely, "And they remembered his words," etc. It would be more Latin to say "how he said" rather than "in what manner he spoke." Laurentius prefers "that he said."

<margin>8</margin> *Because it is necessary*] Either *hoti* (that/because) should have been omitted, or translated as "that," with the mood of the verb changed to "that it would be necessary," etc.

<margin>9</margin> *And leaning forward he saw*] <note>original: parakypsas</note>, which is to look forward with the head tilted; as if someone were to look through a window with their head thrust in. From this comes the proverb "concerning the peering-in." And it is not "he saw," but "he sees" <note>original: blepei</note>.

<margin>10</margin> *And the linen cloths placed alone*] <note>original: keimena</note>. I would have preferred "lying" rather than "placed."

<margin>11</margin> *And he went away, wondering with himself*] "With himself" should be referred to the participle "wondering." "And he went away, wondering within himself," <note>original: kai apēlthe, pros heauton thaumazōn</note>, unless you prefer this sense: "he went away to his own home wondering."

<margin>12</margin> *Named Emmaus*] The Greeks write <note>original: Emmaous</note> with a double 'm,' making it a three-syllable word, and it is inflected *Emmauntis*, *ti*, *tem*, like *Piryus, Piryuntis*. The name of Emmaus was changed later; it was called <term>Nicopolis</term>.

<margin>13</margin> *They were speaking to each other*] <note>original: hōmiloun pros allēlous</note>, that is, they were talking together or conversing among themselves. For the same verb is soon translated as "they were talking."

<margin>14</margin> *And they were seeking with themselves*] I cannot quite guess what the translator read. For in Greek it is simply <note>original: syzētein</note>, that is, they were seeking together, or disputing, or deliberating.

15 **And are you sad** <note>original: "Et estis tristes"</note>] *skythrōpoi* <note>Greek: σκυθρωποί</note>, that is, with a face that is not very cheerful, referring to the outward appearance of the face, not just the inner mind.

16 **Are you a stranger** <note>original: "Peregrinus es"</note>] *paroikeis* <note>Greek: παροικεῖς</note>, that is, you are a newcomer. This has a double meaning: "Are you the only guest in Jerusalem who is ignorant of these things which no one fails to know, however much a newcomer?" Or, "Are you so much of a stranger that you do not know these things?"

17 **Into condemnation** <note>original: "In damnationem"</note>] I have elsewhere noted that *krisin* <note>Greek: κρίσιν</note> and *krima* <note>Greek: κρίμα</note> are often placed for *katakrisin* <note>Greek: κατάκρισιν</note>; the simple word used for the compound.

18 **Because he was the one who would redeem Israel** <note>original: "Quia ipse esset redempturus Israel"</note>] "We were hoping <note>Greek: ἐλπίζομεν</note> that he was the one destined to redeem Israel."

19 **And now besides all this** <note>original: "Et nunc super hæc omnia"</note>] "But yet <note>Greek: ἀλλά γε</note> with all these things, he/it keeps this third day today." <note>Note: This refers to the passing of time since the event.</note> Luke spoke in a novel way, unless perhaps it was written "upon all these things." It is not "and now above," but *alla ge*, that is, "but" or "nevertheless." Nor is "is" <note>original: "est"</note> present in the Greek.

20 **Certain women from our own** <note>original: "Mulieres quædam ex nostris"</note>] but "from us" <note>Greek: ἐξ ἡμῶν</note>, that is, of our flock. Furthermore, it is more than just "they terrified us"; *exestēsan* <note>Greek: ἐξέστησαν</note> means they rendered us astonished. For this pertains more to an ecstasy of wonder than of fear.

21 **Certain of our own** <note>original: "Quidam ex nostris"</note>] "certain of those who were with us." And soon after:

<column-break/>

<margin>F</margin> 22 **And to enter** <note>original: "Et intrare"</note>] This is somewhat redundant, but it was added for the sake of explaining the speech.

23 **He vanished from their eyes** <note>original: "Evanuit ex oculis eorum"</note>] *aphantos egeneto ap’ autōn* <note>Greek: ἄφαντος ἐγένετο ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν</note>, he became invisible from them. Except that the Translator expressed the force of the noun "invisible" (*aphantos*). Otherwise, it was more fitting here to say, "he ceased to be visible to them." We appropriately use the word "vanish" for smoke and ghosts; here mention is made not of a ghost, but of a true body. There were Heretics who attributed a "phantom body" to Christ. No handle for this error should have been given to them.

24 **It is I, do not fear** <note>original: "Ego sum, nolite timere"</note>] In the Greek copies there is only, "Peace be to you," the rest seems to be added. Nor does it quite hang together with what follows, in which he removes their terror—though these words are present in Ambrose, but I believe they were mixed in from another Evangelist. They were terrified at the voice of the one greeting them. The Lord removes that terror afterward, saying, "Why are you troubled?" It appears this was transcribed here from the Gospel of John.

25 **Something to be eaten** <note>original: "Aliquid quod manducetur"</note>] *brōsimon* <note>Greek: βρώσιμον</note>, that is, edible, or a piece of food. And soon after.

26 **Honeycomb** <note>original: "Favum mellis"</note>] *apo melissiou kēriou* <note>Greek: ἀπὸ μελισσίου κηρίου</note>, that is, from a bee-made honeycomb. For certain other insects also have honey and comb.

27 **And when he had eaten before them** <note>original: "Et cum manduclasset coram eis"</note>] The Greek differs slightly: "and taking [it] in their presence, he ate." Taking it...

<meta>This page concludes the Gospel of Luke and Erasmus's scholarly annotations on it. It follows the narrative from the previous page where Jesus appeared to the disciples in Jerusalem and now focuses on his final instructions and the Ascension.</meta>

### THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE. CHAPTER XXIV.

<margin>A</margin> 47 ...and from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. 48 And you are witnesses of these things. 49 And behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you; but stay in the city of Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high. 50 And he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands, he blessed them. 51 And it happened while he was blessing them, he departed from them and was carried up into heaven. <margin>B</margin> 52 And they, having worshiped him, returned to Jerusalem with great joy. 53 And they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God. Amen.

->THE END OF THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE<-

<note>Erasmus notes that a phrase about Jesus eating remains of a fish, often found in Latin versions, is missing in the Greek.</note> He ate before them and said to them. For what is read among us—"he gave them the remains"—is not found among the Greeks.

<margin>C</margin> **28 Beginning]** <note>original: "ἀρξάμενοι" (arxamenoi)</note>. It appears the Translator <note>The "Translator" usually refers to the author of the Vulgate, traditionally St. Jerome.</note> read "beginning" as a plural, so that it refers to the disciples. And I believe this is the genuine reading, even though the Greek manuscripts and the edition recently produced from the workshop of Asulanus <note>Andreas Asulanus, who ran the famous Aldine Press in Venice.</note> object. But if we read "beginning" as a singular <note>original: "ἀρξάμενον" (arxamenon)</note>, so that it refers to Christ, it should not have said "in his name" but "in my name," in this manner: "It was necessary for Christ to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and remission of sins to be preached in his name, he himself having made a beginning from Jerusalem." But this reading is contradicted by the fact that Christ did not begin from Jerusalem, but the Apostles did. Furthermore, what follows fits better with this reading: *But you are witnesses of these things*, although it is ambiguous whether we should read "you are" or "you shall be," and both fit well enough.

<column-break/>

47 ...rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins be preached in his name among all nations, 28 beginning 29 from Jerusalem. 48 And you are witnesses of these things. 49 And behold, I send the promise <note>original: "promissum"</note> of my Father upon you: but stay in the city of Jerusalem, until you be clothed with power from on high. 50 And he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands, he blessed them. 51 And it came to pass while he blessed them, he departed from them, and was carried into heaven. 31 And they, having worshiped him, returned to Jerusalem with great joy. 53 And they were always in the temple, praising and blessing God. Amen.

->THE END OF THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE<-

**29 From Jerusalem]** <note>original: "Ab Hierofolyma"</note>. Laurentius <note>Laurentius Valla, a pioneer of New Testament scholarship whom Erasmus admired.</note> warns that "Jerusalem" is not found in the feminine gender, but he is mistaken. Suetonius, in his *Life of Julius Caesar Augustus*, writes: "And he commended his grandson Caius because, while traveling through Judea, he had not offered prayers at Jerusalem."

**30 The promise of my Father]** <note>original: "ἐπαγγελίαν" (epangelian)</note>. Be aware that "promise" here is a noun, not a participle.

**31 And they, worshiping]** <note>original: "προσκυνήσαντες αὐτὸν ὑπέστρεψαν" (proskynēsantes auton hypestrepsan)</note>, that is, having worshiped him, they returned. For they worshiped him as he was departing into heaven, and then they betook themselves to Jerusalem. The Acts of the Apostles should have been placed immediately after this point. For Luke composed his history in two books, both of which he wrote to the same Theophilus. Indeed, he begins the second book by connecting it with the former. Therefore, the Acts are clearly a part of the Gospel history. However, so as not to seem to separate John from the other Evangelists, we have divided Luke’s two books and placed the Acts in the next position <note>Erasmus is explaining why the Book of Acts doesn't follow Luke immediately in his edition—he wanted to keep the four Gospels together as a group.</note>.

---

<meta>This page transitions from the end of the Gospel of Luke into the introductory material for the Gospel of John. It contains two traditional biographical and theological prefaces commonly found in Byzantine manuscript traditions: one attributed to Sophronius and another to Theophylact.</meta>

# THE LIFE
->of<-
## JOHN
### FROM SOPHRONIUS.
<note>Sophronius was a 7th-century Patriarch of Jerusalem, though this biographical sketch is a traditional text often circulating under his name in Greek Bibles.</note>

John, whom Jesus loved very much, was the son of Zebedee and the brother of James, who was beheaded by Herod after the Passion of the Lord. He was the last of all to write a Gospel, having been requested to do so by the bishops of Asia against Cerinthus and other heretics—especially at that time when the doctrine of the Ebionites <note>The Ebionites were an early Jewish Christian sect that emphasized Jewish law and often denied the divinity or pre-existence of Christ.</note> was emerging, who claimed that Christ did not exist before Mary. For this reason, he was compelled to declare His divine generation. Another reason is also given for his writing: after reading the volumes of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, he approved the style of their histories and confirmed that they had spoken the truth. However, they had only composed the history of the single year in which He suffered, following the imprisonment of John the Baptist. Therefore, passing over that year whose deeds had been set forth by the three, he set forth the actions of the earlier time, before John was cast into prison. This can be made clear to those who carefully read the four Gospels; this also resolves the apparent disagreement between John and the others. 

He also wrote one Epistle, which begins: "That which was from the beginning," which is approved by all churchmen and learned men. The other two, which begin, the first: "The Elder to the elect lady," and the second: "The Elder to Gaius the beloved," are said to be by John the Elder, for whose memory there is still another tomb at Ephesus today. Some believe that both tombs belong to John the Evangelist; we shall explain this when we come in order to Papias, who was a student of these men. 

Therefore, in the fourteenth year of the reign of Domitian—who stirred up the second persecution after Nero—John was exiled to the island of Patmos, where he composed the Revelation, which Justin Martyr and Irenaeus interpreted. After Domitian was slain and his acts were annulled by the Senate because of his great cruelty, John returned to Ephesus during the reign of Nerva. Remaining there until the reign of the Emperor Trajan, he founded and built all the churches of Asia. Having reached extreme old age, he died in the sixty-eighth year after the Passion of the Lord, and was granted rest near the aforementioned city <note>Ephesus</note>.

***

# PREFACE
->to the<-
## GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN
->from Theophylact.<-
<note>Theophylact of Ohrid was a prominent 11th-century Byzantine archbishop whose commentaries were widely used in the Renaissance.</note>

The power of the Spirit is perfected in weakness, just as it is written and as we believe—weakness not only of the body, but also in speech and in the wisdom of the tongue. This is clear from many things, but especially from what concerns the great "Theologian" <note>A traditional title for St. John in the East, meaning "one who speaks of God."</note> and brother of Christ by grace. For he was a fisherman by trade, following his father's craft; he was not only unlearned in Greek and Indian education, but was entirely illiterate, as the most divine Luke witnesses concerning him in the Acts. Furthermore, his homeland was most humble and obscure—a place suited for fishing, not for the art of logic; for he came from a place called Bethsaida. 

Yet, see what kind of Spirit this illiterate, obscure man, who possessed nothing remarkable, was granted: so that those things which none of the other Evangelists taught us, he himself thundered forth. Since the others occupied themselves with the physical life of Christ, and said nothing clearly or plainly regarding His existence before the ages, there was a fear that some earthly-minded people, unable to conceive of anything lofty, might think that Christ first came into existence when He was born of Mary, and was not begotten of the Father before the ages—a view which Paul of Samosata <note>A 3rd-century bishop later declared a heretic for teaching that Jesus was a mere man who became divine.</note> certainly fell into. For this reason, the great John treats the birth from above. Yet he does not leave the incarnation unmentioned in his account. For he says, "And the Word became flesh." 

Some say that the orthodox bishops urged him to write about the birth from above because certain heretics had appeared in those days who dogmatized that Jesus was a mere man. It is said that when the saint had read the works of the other Evangelists, he marveled at them for their truthful narrative of all things, and he approved them as being sound and noted that the Apostles had spoken without seeking favor. However, those things which they did not say clearly, or omitted entirely, he decided to unfold and clarify, adding them to his own Gospel. He wrote this while living as an exile on the island of Patmos, thirty-two years after the Ascension of Christ. 

John was loved by the Lord more than all the disciples because he was simple, most gentle, most kind, and pure in heart, remaining a virgin. From this gift, he was entrusted with "Theology," delighting in mysteries invisible to the many. For He says, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." He was also a kinsman to the Lord—and listen to how. Joseph, the betrothed of the all-pure Mother of God, had seven children from a previous wife: four males and three females, Martha, Esther, and Salome. This John was the son of that Salome. Thus the Lord is found to be his uncle; for since Joseph was the father of the Lord <note>legally</note>, and Salome was the daughter of this Joseph, she is considered the sister of the Lord; thus through her, John is the nephew of the Lord. 

It is perhaps not out of place to explain the names of both his mother and the Evangelist himself. His mother, called Salome, is interpreted as "Peaceful," and John means "Grace of her." Let every soul know, therefore, that peace—both toward other men and within the soul regarding the passions—becomes the mother of divine grace and generates it within us. For a troubled soul still at war with other men and itself is not likely to be deemed worthy of divine grace. We have also noted something even more wonderful occurring regarding this holy Evangelist: he alone is revealed as having three mothers: Salome, the Mother of God (for He said, "Behold your mother"), and "Thunder"—for he is a "Son of Thunder" because of the great voice of his Gospel. But since these things have been said as an introduction, we must now begin the explanation of the text itself.

<meta>The previous page concluded a biographical summary of John the Evangelist attributed to Sophronius, discussing the dating of his Gospel and his motives for writing—specifically to combat the Ebionite heresy and to provide an account of Christ’s ministry prior to the imprisonment of John the Baptist. # THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN.

->The Beginning<-

<margin>v. 1. In the beginning was the Speech, and the Speech was with God, <note>original: ἘΝ ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν Θεόν</note></margin>
<margin>A</margin>
<margin>1</margin>
**IN** the beginning was the Word] <note>Latin: *In principio erat Verbum*</note> It should first be noted, as Chrysostom also indicated, that John does not begin in the manner of Matthew or Mark, nor after the example of Luke. Instead, he entered into the Gospel history with the very same words with which Moses entered into the Genesis of the world. However, the interpretation some give there—that "In the beginning" refers to "in the Son"—certainly has no place here.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>2 *Was the Word*] *Logos* <note>original: λόγος</note> in Greek has various meanings: *word, speech, discourse, reason, manner, calculation*; sometimes it is even used for a book, derived from the verb *lego* <note>original: λέγω</note>, which means "I say" or "I gather." Saint Jerome thinks most of these meanings apply in some way to the Son of God. I wonder, however, why *verbum* <note>Latin for "word"</note> pleased the Latins more than *sermo* <note>Latin for "speech" or "discourse"</note>. We saw that the term *sermo* better expresses the Greek word *logos* used by the Evangelist; yet, in the first edition, out of a certain superstitious fear, we did not change the word the translator had used, lest we give any handle to those who find occasion to slander anything. We merely testified elsewhere that the Son of God is not infrequently designated by the name *sermo* in the Sacred Volumes. Later, when we discovered this was done so widely and that the Church itself once read this very passage as "In the beginning was the Speech" <note>Latin: *In principio erat Sermo*</note>, and that it is cited as such in the books of Cyprian and Augustine, we did not think anyone would be offended. This is especially true since this volume is to be read in libraries <note>literally "Museums," referring to places of study</note>, not in churches. For what sacrilege was it if, in a book read privately, I say *speech* or *utterance* or *discourse* or *voice* instead of *word*, or another term of equal weight? No more, I think, than if I call the *Father* the *begetter, the sower, or the parent*, or any other word that represents the author of a race to Latin ears. Since there would have been no reason to rebuke me even if the term *speech* had never been attributed to the Son of God in the Sacred Books, I now deserve it even less. *Speech* expresses the Greek word more correctly and aptly than *word* for many reasons; it was used frequently by recent authors against the Orthodox; it is still used today in public ecclesiastical practice; and the Church once read it publicly exactly as we have translated it. If anyone wishes to know about this more precisely, let him read our *Apology*, in which we beat back the stupid barks of certain critics. For now, it will suffice to extract a few points to satisfy the reader’s mind if he is troubled. First, *speech* explains what the Evangelist set down as *logos* more conveniently because, among Latin speakers, *word* <note>verbum</note> does not sound like a whole discourse, but just a single term; rarely is a short saying, like a maxim or old proverb, called a *verbum*. But Christ is called *Logos* because whatever the Father speaks, He speaks through the Son. Furthermore, the harmony of gender makes the phrasing smoother when we say "The Speech of God was made flesh" <note>Latin: *Sermo Dei factus est caro* (both masculine)</note> rather than "The Word of God was made flesh" <note>Latin: *Verbum Dei factum est caro* (neuter and masculine mixture)</note>. Otherwise, nothing rendered the emphasis of the Greek *logos* better than *discourse* <note>oratio</note>.

<margin>C</margin>
Now Cyprian, renowned on so many counts—first for a truly theological eloquence, then for an Apostolic holiness, and finally for martyrdom—in the work he wrote *Against the Jews*, in the fifth chapter of the second book, relates this passage of the Evangelist exactly as we have translated it: "In the beginning," he says, "was the speech, and the speech was with God, and God was the speech." And in the third chapter of the same book, the title of which is *That Christ is the same Speech of God*, he brings this up among several passages of Holy Scripture where he teaches that the Son of God is called *speech*. In this case, a half-learned scribe had perversely changed *speech* into *word* in the manuscripts, not noticing what the title promised—which undoubtedly belongs to Cyprian, not the scribe. In addition, Augustine, explaining this passage from John 18, "Your speech is truth," openly teaches that it makes no difference whether you say *speech* <note>sermonem</note> or *word* <note>verbum</note>. He also teaches that in this place most manuscripts have "In the beginning was the speech, and the speech was with God, and God was the speech." Indeed, in many places he interprets the term *speech* in the Sacred Books as referring to the Son of God, which need not be repeated here. If those who wish to be seen as doctors of the Church do not read those things, they certainly could not have missed what the Church sings every year from the Book of Wisdom: "Your almighty speech, Lord, leaping down from heaven from the royal throne." <note>A reference to Wisdom 18:15, traditionally applied to the Incarnation.</note> These and other similar passages are interpreted as referring to the Son of God not only by the Ancients, but also by Thomas Aquinas, Hugh of St. Cher, the *Glossa Ordinaria*, Bede, Remigius, and Anselm, finding no lack in the term *word* nor any offense in the word *speech*.

<margin>D</margin>
Saint Hilary, in his second book *On the Trinity*, calls the Son of God sometimes *word* and sometimes *speech*. For when he says, "The speech of thought is eternal, He who thinks is eternal," does he not openly call Christ the eternal speech proceeding from the eternal mind of the Father without time? And shortly after, when he says, "Had you not heard in God, so as to receive the speech of hidden thought?"—does he not grant Christ the title of *speech*? Somewhat later, he disputes at length about the difference between human and divine speech, never shrinking from attributing the term *speech* to Christ.

<margin>E</margin>
Furthermore, Ambrose, in the second chapter of his book *On the Faith* against the Arians, calls Christ sometimes *word* and sometimes *speech*. Jerome does the same in several other places: in the first chapter of the Epistle to the Ephesians, he says, "Not that the assumed man is one and the speech who assumed him is another," etc., using *speech* for the Son of God. Again in the same chapter: "So that as

<column-break/>

<meta>catchword: cis</meta>
<margin>A</margin>
<margin>1. In the beginning was the Speech, and the Speech was with God, and God was the Speech. <note>original interlinear: ἦν erat Sermo, καὶ & Sermo erat πρὸς apud Θεὸν Deum, καὶ & Deus erat ὁ λόγος Sermo.</note></margin>
our Lord *Jesus Christ* is speech, wisdom, and truth." And Lactantius, in the eighth chapter of his fourth book, calls the Son of God *speech*. Likewise in the next chapter, more than once. Claudian dared to say "voice": "The voice of the supreme mind of God"; he said "voice" for *speech*, and "mind" for *wisdom*. Prudentius in his *Hymns* is granted so much by the Church that they are solemnly chanted in the sacred liturgies. In these, the Church hears without offense: "Be present, supreme Father, Whom no one has ever seen, and Christ the speech of the Father, and the kindly Spirit." But it might seem foolish for me to pursue these things which, if one were to examine the Sacred Writers, have no end—were it not for certain people who noisily protest so impudently. Thus the Church once read, thus it sings today, thus the ancient Orthodox often spoke, and thus the more recent; yet some are as offended by the term *speech* as if it had never been read or heard among Christians.

<margin>B</margin>
But "novelty" offends them, they say. Whom, exactly? The very ones who slander? But for those who wish to be seen as most learned in Theology, it ought not to be "new" when it is so frequently encountered in the Sacred Authors. The unlearned? But unknown things would not have moved them at all, had not certain people seditiously cried out to the public, adding vanity to their malice. "It is all over for the Christian cause," they say, "now that we have a 'New Gospel'." What is more stupid than this cry? Is the Gospel "made new" because *speech* is said instead of *words*? By Hercules, no more than a man named Nicholas is "made new" if he puts off a white garment and puts on a dark one. I know that much must be granted to long-standing custom. But often a performance is put on for the people. It is accepted that when we baptize, we speak half-Greek: "I baptize thee" <note>baptizo te</note>. I would not want to say to the unlearned, "I dip thee" <note>tingo te</note>, even though it makes no difference to God. As things now stand, I would not want to recite in churches, "In the beginning was the speech," if I reasonably suspected there were those who would be violently offended, especially since the current reading is sound and the other is tolerable. But if a received reading were clearly faulty, and there were those among the listeners who preferred the old error without judgment, while others preferred what is correct with judgment, and it could not be avoided that one side be offended, which side would I be ordered to obey? I would prefer to be pleasing <note>original Greek: ἀρεστὸς</note> to everyone. Perhaps first I would obey the unskilled, because they are more prone to ferocity, and later I would appease the learned.

<margin>C</margin>
Yet, in the meantime, the unskilled must be warned not to start a riot through their ignorance against those whom they ought rather to obey. Just as Paul, out of charity, wants us to abstain from food sacrificed to idols so that a weak brother is not offended, he nevertheless warns and rebukes the weak who judge a brother who gives thanks without cause. I admit that things which have been wrongly accepted by the public should be abolished gradually, just as Paul abolished the Mosaic Law, yet they must be made obsolete. I know the story from Augustine which tells of some minor bishop in Africa who was nearly abandoned by his people because of one little word from Jerome's translation <note>The "gourd" vs. "ivy" controversy in the Book of Jonah.</note> that was read differently than the people were used to. But Jerome, a holy and learned man, strongly mocked those "gourd-headed" Africans. If it had pleased everyone to grant everything to the unlearned, we would not have so many things restored by the ancient Orthodox. For those who think we should have varied less from what was received bring forward nothing of weight. First, since men's judgments are various, who will provide the rule by which I should moderate the variety? For I know that what happened to Jove in the poets has happened to me: he could please no one, whether he brought rain or clear skies.

<margin>D</margin>
Next, what they say might perhaps have some weight if my translation were to push out the publicly accepted one. But in this project of mine, the greater the variety, the more fruit there is. Since these new things are applied not so that the old is made obsolete, but so that it might be both clearer and more refined, it was expedient that even individual words be varied if anyone wished. Indeed, Augustine confesses in more than one place that he received the most light in the Sacred Volumes from the variety of manuscripts. For who does not approve the work of scholars who, in the grammar schools, interpret individual words of Virgil or Horace with various different terms—not doing this so that those authors seem to have spoken incorrectly, but so that what they spoke might be understood? Furthermore, this pertains more closely to our purpose: the Greek does not simply say *logos*, but adds the article, *ho logos* <note>original: ὁ λόγος</note>, so that it cannot be understood as just any word, but as one certain and pre-eminent Word. For the article has this force, which we have rendered in Latin by adding the pronoun *ille* <note>"that" or "the specific"</note>. For instance, when Aristotle speaks of "good" in general, he calls it *agathon* <note>original: ἀγαθὸν</note>.

<margin>E</margin>
But when he wants the "one and highest good" to be understood, he adds the article, *to agathon* <note>original: τ’ ἀγαθὸν</note>. Likewise, philosophers call "beautiful" <note>kalon</note> whatever is in any way fair; but *to kalon* is that excellent and truly beautiful or honorable thing that proceeds from virtue. Likewise they call "god" <note>theos</note> whatever is in any way divine; but that true and absolute Whole which truly embraces all things, they call not simply *theos*, but *ho theos* <note>original: ὁ θεὸς</note>. Similarly in Holy Scripture, when they call the friends of God "gods," the article is not added, but only "Ye are gods" <note>original: Θέοι ἴστε</note>. Or when the gods of the nations are meant, as in Paul’s first Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter eight: "Even if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, just as there are many gods and many lords." For here no Greek article is attached: "For even if there are those called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, as there are many gods and many lords." <note>original: Καὶ γὰρ εἴπερ εἰσὶ λεγόμενοι Θεοί, εἴτε ἐν οὐρανῷ, εἴτε ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, ὥσπερ εἰσὶ Θεοὶ πολλοί, καὶ Κύριοι πολλοί</note> Augustine, in the *Questions* he wrote on Genesis, brings another example from Genesis chapter 33, in which Jacob says he saw the face of Esau as if someone saw the face of God, noting that in the Greek...

<summary>This page features Erasmus's famous defense of translating the Greek 'Logos' as 'Sermo' (Speech/Discourse) rather than 'Verbum' (Word), citing numerous Church Fathers to justify the philological and theological accuracy of his choice. He argues that his translation is intended for scholars and private study, aiming for clarity rather than the disruption of liturgical tradition.</summary>

--- Page 237 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous page, the author is providing a detailed linguistic and theological analysis of the Prologue of John's Gospel, specifically focusing on the translation of "Logos" as "Speech" or "Word" and its relationship to the Godhead.</meta>

# ACCORDING TO JOHN. CHAPTER I.

2 <note>Greek: οὗτος ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν θεόν</note> He was in the beginning with God. 3 All things were made through him, and without him was made not even one thing that was made. 4 In him was life, and the life was the light of men. 5 And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it.
<margin>Ephesians</margin>

---

<margin>A</margin> written in the [Greek] copies as <note>original: πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν</note> "with God," using the article, rather than <note>original: πρὸς Θεὸν</note> "with God" without the article. For whenever the true and only God is signified, the article <note>original: ὁ</note> "the" is always added, <note>original: ὁ Θεός</note> "the God," unless some peculiar reason stands in the way. Similarly, whenever Christ wishes to be understood not merely as a Son of God in any sense, but as the Son by nature and truth, he is called <note>original: ὁ Υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ</note> "the Son of the God." Conversely, when he masks his Divinity, he calls himself the Son of Man, but attaches the article to both nouns, <note>original: ὁ Υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου</note> "the Son of the man," as if he were not just any son of Adam, but that eminent Son of Man, the restorer of the human race. Again, <note>original: ὁ ἀμνὸς</note> "the lamb"—though there are many lambs—refers to that unique lamb whose sacrifice takes away the sins of the world. And <note>original: ὁ Προφήτης</note> "the Prophet" refers to that unique Prophet promised through Moses. And when that light is designated from which all our light flows, it is called <note>original: τὸ φῶς</note> "the light," with the article added. And when the good shepherd is mentioned, meaning Christ that unique shepherd, it is <note>original: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλὸς</note> "I am the shepherd, the good [one]," with a doubled article. And <note>original: ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα</note> "I am the door," where not just any door, but that unique one is denoted. And a little further down, "we have found the Messiah," <note>original: τὸν Μεσσίαν</note> that unique Messiah. And "You are the King of Israel," <note>original: ὁ βασιλεὺς</note> "the King." Didymus <note>a 4th-century Alexandrian theologian</note>, in his book on the Spirit which Jerome translated into Latin, also carefully noted this: whenever mention is made of the Divine Spirit in Holy Scripture, the article is attached, <note>original: τὸ Πνεῦμα</note> "the Spirit," and he confirms this with many passages of Sacred Scripture brought forward for this purpose. By this argument especially, he teaches that it was the same Spirit who inspired the Prophets and whom the Apostles received. Athanasius noted the same in his book on the Holy Spirit to Serapion, proving his opinion with many testimonies from the Scriptures. It is clearly of such great importance in this passage to omit or add articles that Chrysostom and Cyril use this very argument to reject the heresy of those who denied that Christ was that Word which was with the Father from the beginning, claiming instead that there was some other interior Word in the Father from which another Word was born, which was Christ.

<margin>B</margin> 3 **And the Word was with God**] Again he added the article, not only to "Word" but also to "God," so that we might understand that unique and true Word of which he had spoken before, and the Father as truly God, not some other god.

<margin>C</margin> 4 **And the Word was God**] In this place, the article is not added to "God," even though it signifies God by truth and nature; he does this by necessity. Otherwise, he could not simultaneously explain the Divine Essence common to the three Persons. For if he had added the article to both—"and the God was the Word"—he would have confused the properties of the Persons. The meaning then would have been: *and that God, namely the Father, was that Word, namely the Son.* Conversely, if he had added the article to "God" but not to "Word"—"and the God was a Word"—it would have signified two Words, and the sense would have been: *and that God, namely the Father, was himself also a certain Word,* and if not the same Word as the Son, then some other Word. Some of the ancients held this view, making two Words: the begetting and the begotten, as was mentioned slightly above. Indeed, Prudentius himself might seem to have felt something of this sort when he writes in his Iambic Hymn on the Birth of Christ: *Born from the Father's mouth, and brought forth by the Word;* unless we prefer to interpret "by the word" as "by the speaking of the word." Now, because he added the article to "Word" and does not add it to "God," <note>original: καὶ Θεὸς ἦν ὁ Λόγος</note> "and God was the Word," he expresses the Christian view so that it cannot be twisted elsewhere, namely this: *And that same Word, which I just said was in the beginning with God, was God—that is, a participant in the Divine Essence,* or as I might better say in Greek, <note>term: ὁμούσιος τῷ Πατρί (homoousios to Patri)</note> "of the same substance with the Father." For it would not be permitted for the Greeks to speak thus: "the fir is the tree" or "the lyre is the wood," if the article were attached [to both]. That these things are as we have said, anyone even moderately skilled in Greek will easily prove. Although we have changed things more sparingly in this beginning out of reverence for the ineffable mystery, I nevertheless thought it necessary to give warning, so that our theologians might better understand that it makes a difference whether you drink the mystical writings from their own springs or from stagnant pools.

<margin>D</margin> 5 **All things were made through him**] Since mention is made here also of the Word, of whom he has just spoken, it would have been more correctly translated as "All things were made through *it*" (the Speech), so as to repeat the reference to the Word, or "All things were made through the *same*," just as a little earlier, "This was in the beginning." Unless you prefer the pronoun "him" <note>Latin: *ipsum*</note> to refer to God the Father, who immediately preceded. Truly, the preposition <note>term: διὰ (dia)</note> "through" somewhat opposes this sense, as it does not fit as well with the nature of the paternal principle—unless you prefer to use Hilary's term "authority"—and harmonizes more with the words of Paul, who says, "through whom he also made the ages," so that we understand all things were created by the Father through the Son. But now the Latin has rendered the meaning ambiguous, because the pronoun "him" could be applied to either. Although the speech is also ambiguous to the Greeks, all the Greeks interpret it so that "through him" refers to the Word, not the Father. Indeed, from this the Orthodox prove the Son existed from eternity: "In the beginning God created." If this creation was made through the Son, it follows that he existed before created things and is not numbered among created things. From these same words the Arians seized an opportunity, dreaming that the Father used the Son as a tool in creating things, whereas the Father created all things through the Son in such a way that the Son nonetheless created all things with the Father. Ambrose wants these words, "Let there be light," to be the Father's to the Son; "And light was made" was surely from the authority of the Father through the Son. Moreover, Chrysostom refutes those who argue from the preposition that the Son is less than the Father, showing that this preposition is sometimes attributed to the Father in Holy Scripture. Therefore, both the opinion of the Orthodox and the slander of the Heretics declare that "through him" refers to the Son, not the Father.

6 **And without him nothing was made**] They distinguish this passage in two ways. Chrysostom in his fourth Homily, followed by Theophylact, reads it together: "All things through him"—understand the Word—

<sig>Volume V.</sig>

with God, 2 & the Word was that Speech. This was in the beginning with God. 3 All things through him were made, & without him nothing was made, which was made. 4 In him was life, & life was the light of men. 5 And the light in the darkness shines, & the darkness did not grasp it.

<margin>7 Was</margin>
<margin>E</margin> were made, and without him nothing was made that was made, so that you understand nothing at all was created which was not created by the Father through the Son. Chrysostom writes, however, that certain Heretics distinguish it in this way: "All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made." And here, interposing a <note>term: diastole</note> pause, they add: "that which was made, in him was life," interpreting the Holy Spirit—whom they make a creature—to be understood in that which is called "that which was made." And yet Cyril the Greek and Augustine the Latin distinguish it in this way, though with a different sense. For Augustine understands every creature to be "life" in God, not willingly <note>original: πλανώμενος</note> wandering in his usual manner. Cyril, however, interprets it so that we understand all things were created through the Son, both visible and invisible, and whatever was created, in him that Word is life: so that he is not only the author of their origin with the Father, but also allows all things there, as it were, to be protected and preserved by life. Hilary follows this distinction, not differing much from Cyril's view. Gregory Nazianzenus also follows it in his work on the Holy Spirit, rejecting the Heretics by saying this passage should be taken as referring to things that were made, so that it cannot be applied to the Son or the Holy Spirit. Moreover, as for those who interpret "nothing" as sin or malice—because those things alone exist which are natural, and for that reason good, while sin is merely privative—that is more Sophistical than Theological. Saint Jerome, narrating Micah chapter 11, reports that some interpret "nothing" in this place as malice, and consequently the Devil; an opinion he does not approve. Blessed Augustine, explaining this passage, seems to grant to the Manichaeans that [sin] is not a nature, but corrupted by malice. Thus sin is "nothing," and a man becoming a sinner becomes "nothing," and the Devil is "nothing." God created the Angel, not the Devil; and he created man, not the sinner; and God created the tree, not the idol. But here again a question arises: whether sin or malice is only a privation, or something "positive," as they call it, and whether a viper can be called evil by nature. Furthermore, what Augustine says about a sinner becoming "nothing," and an idol according to Paul being "nothing," is not to be taken simply. Otherwise, what was the point of denying it was made by God if it is "nothing" and for that reason can be made by no one? But "nothing" sometimes sounds like that which is not in the nature of things at all, that is, what is neither substance nor accident. Sometimes it refers to what is considered as nothing; occasionally to what is nothing by comparison, just as a man compared to God is nothing, and man's wisdom compared to divine wisdom is foolishness. Here, therefore, it is simply denied: *Nothing was made without him, that is,* whatever subsists in created things was made by God. He interprets it thus in the book *On the Nature of the Good against the Manichaeans*, chapter 25: "Without him nothing was made" has no other value than if you say, "Whatever was made, was not made without him." But there are those who again distinguish this distinction, who denied this sense could be rendered unless it were pronounced in this order: "Nothing without him was made." However, if you pronounce it, "Without him was made nothing," "nothing" is now taken for that which is something and was made. Although Augustine mocks this with many words, the Sophists nonetheless think it makes a great difference whenever a word is transferred to another place. Even if this were true elsewhere, it certainly had no place here. For elsewhere the Lord speaks thus: "I have spoken openly to you, and in secret I have spoken nothing." Besides, what difference does it make whether you say, "I saw no one more foolish than this man," or "Than this man, I saw no one more foolish." Some fellow cavils here, in whose name some Homilies on John exist under the title of Origen, but most falsely. Even if I were silent, the thing itself screams it, since there is nothing there that tastes of any vein of Origen in any part. And yet matters have come to the point that printers add these sorts of trifles even to prudent and deliberate works, so that by increasing the volume, the profit becomes richer. If it is permitted for them to publish whatever they want under any name, and it is not lawful for us to resist once a title has cheated the pages, the condition of scholars will truly be beautiful if they are forced to embrace the trifles of a scoundrel or an impostor as oracles. But these things are <note>original: παρέργως</note> incidental. To return to the matter. That person, whoever he is, or whoever they are, whether men or Gods, is refuted—I know not what is said more significantly in Greek—for that which we say, "And without him was made nothing." For among them it is "outside," not "without." Truly, what this means I do not sufficiently understand, except that in all the Greek copies we have seen, I find written <note>original: χωρὶς αὐτοῦ</note> "apart from him." And the same Greek preposition is in John chapter 15: "Without me you can do nothing," <note>original: χωρὶς ἐμοῦ</note>. But he wants it to be read in both places as "outside," not "without." Unless perhaps that person, whoever he was, read <note>original: ἔκτος</note> "outside" instead of <note>original: χωρὶς</note> "apart from." Or unless he thinks <note>original: χωρὶς</note> should be translated "outside, before, without." <margin>F</margin> It contributes somewhat to Cyril's opinion that when he said "all things" twice, he did not add the article the first time, but added it the second. In that which was created, that Word was a certain "life," while it imparts safety to the created nature. And soon he calls that Word itself "life" in a peculiar way, and "the life was the light of men," adding the article, signifying that true and ineffable life, <note>original: ἡ ἦν ζωὴ ἦν τὸ φῶς τῶν ἀνθρώπων</note>. Augustine indicates a distinction here also, for he teaches it should be read, "What was made," so that here, with a silence interposed, there is added, "In him was life," so that you do not take life to be in any created thing, according to the Manichaeans—otherwise stones would have life—but that the creature was in the creator who is life, clearly thinking of the [Platonic] Ideas. For the Manichaeans distinguish it thus: "Without him was made nothing. That which was made in him, was life," reasoning in this way, or rather irrationally raving: "Nothing was not made in him, that is, through him; therefore whatever was created is life, that is, it lives." And Augustine, joining this particle "in him" with those things that follow,

# THE GOSPEL CHAPTER I.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
6 There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. 7 This man came for a testimony, to bear witness of the Light, that all men through him might believe. 8 He was not that Light, but was sent to bear witness of that Light. 9 That was the true Light, which lightens every man that comes into the world. 10 He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not. 11 He came unto his own, and his own received him not. 12 But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name: 13 Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. 14 And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only-

---

<margin>B</margin>
when it says, *life was*, it takes whatever has been created to live, not in itself—since all things by their own nature neither feel nor live—but in Him who created them, in whose eternal mind all things live, even before they were created. It seems to me the true reading, which the Latin usage follows to this day, is: *that which was made, in him was life*. <note>Erasmus is discussing the punctuation of John 1:3-4, specifically whether "that which was made" belongs to the previous sentence or the start of the next.</note> For it agrees with the peculiar style of this Evangelist to almost always begin the following clause from the end of the preceding one. *Nothing was made* is the end of the upper member. *That which was made* is the beginning of the next. Of this form are also those: *In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.* The diction ending the first part begins the next. In the fourth part it finds the beginning of the first, *this was in the beginning*, and thus completes the period. Again, in what follows: *What was made, in him was life, and the life was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.* The next step is always taken from the closest member. Hilary distinguishes it otherwise: *what was made in him*; so that they are distinguished thus, then *the light shines itself, life was*. Lest this be doubtful to anyone, *those things which follow*: This therefore is not without him, which was made in him. For what was made in him, was also made through him. Although he distinguishes it similarly to the Manichaeans <note>A dualistic religious movement that the early Church fought as heretical.</note>, he does not, however, hold the same opinion as they do.

**7 There was a man sent]** <note>original: Ἐγένετο</note>. The same word that he just translated as *were made*. Consequently, Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a pioneering Renaissance humanist and critic.</note> preferred *there appeared* in this place, rather than *was*. But I would prefer, *There was a man sent*, since a little lower it follows, *He was not that light*. It should be noted that here the article is not placed before "man," to indicate only the nature of the man, and to separate John by this mark from Christ, who was at once both God and man; to correspond to this, "God" also stands here without the article, <note>original: παρὰ Θεοῦ</note> "from God." It was a man who was sent to announce Christ to men. But lest anyone think lightly of this man’s testimony, he was sent by God, not by man. And I do not know if it is otherwise a constant rule in the sacred writings that when the article is added to "God," either a certain Person is denoted among the divine Hypostases <note>The distinct persons of the Trinity.</note>, or that true and unique God is distinguished from the remaining gods of the nations, though one should not rashly add or remove the article.

**8 Whose name was John]** <note>original: Ὄνομα αὐτῷ Ἰωάννης</note>, that is, "the name to him was John." The Latin Translator changed this somewhat and added of his own, and that compelled by no necessity. Let no one be angry with us if we perhaps change something somewhere, either driven by necessity or invited by convenience. Nor is he simply "sent," but <note>original: ἀπεσταλμένος</note>, a participle of that verb from which the "Apostles" and "Evangelists" are named. For to the Greeks, <note>original: βάλλειν</note> refers to one who throws an inanimate thing like a stone; <note>original: πίπτειν</note> to one who in any way moves hands or something similar; <note>original: ἐνστέλλειν</note> to one who sends a letter; <note>original: ἀποστέλλειν</note> to one who sends someone out with mandates.

**9 That all might believe through him]** Among the Greeks it is uncertain whether *through him* refers to John: so that we understand that by his testifying all ought to have believed in Christ; or whether all ought to have believed in the Father through that light, to which John bore witness: because <note>original: αὐτῷ</note> ("him/it") can be taken as masculine or neuter. But if learned Teachers refer it to John, then *himself* would fit better here than *it*.

**9 He was not that light]** First, the Reader must be advised that the Latin Translator here sometimes renders it as *lumen* and sometimes as *lux*, though in Greek it is the same word, <note>original: φῶς</note> "phos." Lest anyone ignorant of the Greek language dream that some mystery lies beneath the changed Latin word. In the more corrected copies of Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential 4th-century theologian.</note>, it reads: *He was not that light [lumen], but that he might bear witness of the light [lumine]*. Moreover, it is asked not without reason by the learned: since Christ in Matthew chapter 5 calls his Apostles the *light of the world*, and since John the Baptist was specifically called a *burning and shining lamp*, why does he here deny that he is the light? Indeed, the added article complicates this knot of ambiguity: whenever it signifies that true light, luminous by its own nature, he adds the article, <note>original: τὸ φῶς</note> and <note>original: τοῦ φωτός</note>. Here likewise, when he denies that John is the light, he did not say, <note>original: Οὐκ ἦν ἐκεῖνος φῶς</note>, that is, "He was not light," but, <note>original: Οὐκ ἦν ἐκεῖνος τὸ φῶς</note>, that is, "He was not *the* light." He was not that true light. Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a major Greek Church Father.</note> noted these things, if our authority is light to anyone, as did Theophylact. Just as God alone is called wise and immortal, so Christ alone is called the Light. John was "light" [phos], but he was not "the Light" [to phos]. Or take it thus: He was not the light of which I just spoke when I was saying, but that he might testify of the light. For the article also has this function, to refer to a thing of which there was prior speech. We add this because in Matthew, where Christ calls his own the light of the world, the Greek article is added in both places. Furthermore, why was the paraphrase *that he might bear witness of the light* more pleasing than *he might testify*, when in Greek it is <note>original: μαρτυρήσῃ</note>? Although this speech seems to have some ellipsis, which could be supplied thus: *He was not that light, but was sent that he might testify of the light.*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
6 There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. 7 This man came for testifying, to bear witness of the light, that all might believe through him. 8 He was not that light, but was sent to bear witness of the light. 9 That was the true light, which illuminates every man coming into the world. 10 He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world knew him not. 11 He came unto his own things, and his own people received him not. 12 But as many as received him, he gave them power to become the sons of God, namely to those who should believe in his name: 13 Who were born, not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. 14 And that Speech <note>original: Sermo</note> was made flesh, and dwelt among us: and we beheld his glory,

---

<margin>C</margin>
**11 And the true light]** I have already warned that *lux* and *lumen* are the same noun to the Greeks: lest anyone err regarding "lux" and "lumen," thinking there is some distinction. But this pertains more to the matter: where ought one to refer "was," if not to the *Word*? For the sense itself prevents it from being referred to John. Indeed, I think it should not be referred to the Word, but to the light itself which follows immediately, because the article is placed before both nouns, "light" and "true," <note>original: τὸ φῶς τὸ ἀληθινόν</note>, so that we read it in this manner: John was not that light of which I speak, but was only sent into this world to testify of the light. For this light of which I speak was the true light which illuminates every man; that is, it was the fountain of light, from which light flowed even to John himself.

**12 Coming into this world]** <note>original: εἰς τὸν κόσμον</note>, that is, "into the world." For the Greeks do not add "this" <note>original: hunc</note>: except that the Translator use it so frequently, desiring, I think, to express the force of the article. But why did he add "this" more here than in those things that follow? *He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world knew him not*, each of which is uttered with its own article. And "coming" <note>original: ἐρχόμενον</note> is so placed that it could also pertain to the light coming into the world; Augustine indicates in his book *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, chapter 25, that some followed this reading. An added article, <note>original: τὸν ἐρχόμενον</note>, would have removed the ambiguity.

<margin>D</margin>
**13 And the world knew him not]** It seems discordant to refer this to the "Word" <note>original: Verbum</note>, which in Greek is of the masculine gender <note>Logos</note>. However, for the Latin Translator, it should have been rendered in the neuter: *And the world knew it [illud] not*. The same must be thought of those things that soon follow: *and his own received him not. But as many as received him*. Certainly, this inconvenience could have been avoided if *Speech* <note>original: Sermo</note> had pleased the Translators instead of *Word* <note>original: Verbo</note>. Furthermore, *He came unto his own [propria]*, and *his own [sui] received him not*; in Greek, it is the same word: <note>original: ἴδια</note> and <note>original: ἴδιοι</note>, "he came unto his own things," and "his own people received him not." And it appears that Saint Augustine read it thus, since we see written in his works, *he came into his own proper things*. But if the Greek codices had <note>original: αὐτὸ</note> [neuter] instead of <note>original: αὐτὸν</note> [masculine], the meaning would have fit beautifully: the light came into the world, not created like the sun and moon, but by whom the world was founded, and yet the world, blinded by vices, did not recognize that light. So says Cyril.

**14 Who not of bloods]** Saint Augustine confesses that "bloods" <note>original: sanguinibus</note> is not used in Latin in the plural number, but the Translator abused the number to declare that in the common generation of man, not only the seed of the man, but also of the woman concurs. He also warns that in this place "flesh" is called "woman."

<margin>E</margin>
**15 Of the will of the flesh]** It should be noted that neither to "flesh," nor to "man," nor to "God," is its own article appended, so that you understand the species of flesh or man is designated, not this or that flesh or man. And against these three—"bloods," "flesh," and "man"—God is opposed, also without the article. But Lorenzo [Valla] prefers *begotten* in this place, rather than *born*, <note>original: ἐγεννήθησαν</note>. Moreover, it is not "in his name," but "into the name," <note>original: εἰς τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ</note>. Although the Evangelists use these promiscuously: "to believe him," and "to believe into him," and "in him"; "to be judged him," and "to confess in him"; "to be baptized into the name of Christ," and "to be baptized in the name of Christ." Valla disputes this matter in many words, if anyone perhaps requires it.

**16 And the word was made flesh]** <note>original: Καὶ ὁ λόγος</note>, that is, "And that word," namely, of which we have said such sublime things. And Augustine rightly warned in several places that "flesh" is placed here for "man," partly to exclude the error of the Apollinarists <note>Followers of Apollinaris of Laodicea, who argued Christ had a human body but a divine mind/soul.</note>, who denied that Christ had a human soul; partly so that the miracle would be evident in the word joined with flesh, which is the densest part of man. And this was said according to the idiom of the Hebrew language, which notes the whole man now by the name of "soul," now of "flesh." Moreover, since the Greek speech is ambiguous, *he dwelt among us* <note>original: inter nos</note> was more suitable than *in us* <note>original: in nobis</note>, <note>original: ἐν ἡμῖν</note>. Even if Chrysostom <margin>F</margin> follows a different interpretation, and Theophylact sings along with him. For they feel the Divine Nature in the Hypostasis of Christ as if confined to a human body, which is the tabernacle of the soul. Although the Divine Nature dwelt in the soul and body of Christ equally, not enclosed, but united. But the other reading, besides being simpler, fits more aptly with what follows: *And we saw his glory*. Some explain it as *we saw on Mount Tabor* <note>The site of the Transfiguration.</note>. But in my opinion, it is simpler: we see from his words and deeds while he lived among us.

**17 And the word dwelt]** <note>original: ἐσκήνωσεν</note>, is derived from "tabernacles," which elsewhere he translates as "to nest," so that you understand a temporary habitation among us. This must also be noted: "dwelt" <note>original: habitavit</note> in Latin might sound as if he ceased to dwell, whereas in Greek <note>original: ἐσκήνωσεν</note> sounds like "he made a habitation or domicile in us": so that we understand he began to dwell in us and has not ceased.

**18 And we saw]** <note>original: ἐθεασάμεθα</note>, that is, we gazed upon, or beheld, as a new and wonderful spectacle.

He argues for precise translations that distinguish the eternal nature of Christ from the temporal ministry of John the Baptist.</summary>
