341 ACCORDING TO JOHN. CHAPTER I. 342

<margin>14</margin> <note>original: "μονογενὴς παρὰ Πατρὸς, πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας"</note> ...the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.
<margin>15</margin> <note>original: "Ἰωάννης μαρτυρεῖ περὶ αὐτοῦ..."</note> John bears witness of him, and cried out, saying, "This was he of whom I spoke: He who comes after me is preferred before me, for he was before me." <margin>16</margin> And of his fullness have we all received, and grace for grace. <margin>17</margin> For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ. <margin>18</margin> No man has seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him.

19 ***Glory as of the only begotten***] Laurentius <note>Laurentius Valla (1407–1457), an influential Italian humanist and philologist whom Erasmus admired.</note> prefers "just as the only begotten," as if he were truly the only begotten. On this word, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), a famous preacher and Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> and Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine commentator whose works Erasmus often used.</note> engage in a bit of philosophy, interpreting the Greek word <term>ὡς</term> <note>original: "hos" (as/like)</note> as it is used by the Greeks; here, it does not suggest a mere comparison or likeness, but rather the reality of the appearance shown. It is like saying, after describing a royal procession, "he walked as a King," meaning he appeared with actual royal majesty. Furthermore, "only begotten" here is not a participle but a noun, <term>μονογενοῦς</term> <note>original: "monogenous" (only-begotten)</note>, meaning the "unique" or "only" one. Thus, what follows—"from the Father"—pertains more to the "glory" than to the "only begotten." We beheld his glory, a glory, I say, not just of any kind, but a glory displayed by the Father which declared him to be the unique Son. I believe he is thinking of the baptism of Jesus and the Transfiguration, when the voice of the Father was heard: *This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him.* Truly, the glory of the only begotten shone forth from more than just these events. Moses had glory as a servant from a master; Christ as the unique Son from God the Father.

20 ***Full of grace and truth***] "Full" here is in the nominative case, not the accusative, <term>πλήρης</term> <note>original: "pleres" (full)</note>, and it refers back to the "Word" (<term>λόγος</term>), which in Greek is masculine. Thus the sense is: "That Word was made flesh, full of grace and truth." Otherwise, these words might seem to connect more with John, who follows, as if we should read: "John, full of grace and truth, bears witness of him." This would mean John is being commended by this little preface to give his testimony more weight. However, almost all interpreters agree that this refers to Christ, not to John. Yet, because it connects somewhat awkwardly with what precedes it, I thought the reader should be advised to weigh the matter. I would want the reader to take this as a suggestion from one pointing it out, rather than from an author of a fixed dogma. For what follows—"of his fullness we have all received"—supports the common view. Even if the Evangelist were calling the Baptist "full of grace and truth," John himself confesses here that his own grace, of which he is said to be full, flowed from that same source. Nor is it new in the Holy Scriptures for other saints to be called "full of grace" and "perfect," lest anyone think this is attributed to Christ alone. We read in Acts that Stephen was "full of the Holy Spirit," Zechariah is read to be "filled with the Holy Spirit," and the Baptist is said to be "filled with the Holy Spirit" from his mother's womb. Again, in the Acts of the Apostles, all who had gathered were said to be "filled with the Holy Spirit." In the same work, Paul is read as "full of the Holy Spirit," and he himself commands that we be "filled with the Holy Spirit." Truly, as I said, I define nothing on this matter; let everyone follow what they find more probable. Certainly, Theophylact refers these words—"of his fullness we have all received"—not to the Evangelist, but to John speaking of Christ. In his commentary, he suddenly changed the tense of the verb <term>μαρτυρεῖ</term> and <term>κέκραγε</term> <note>original: "martyrei" (witnesses) and "kekrage" (has cried out)</note>, that is, "he witnesses" and "he cried out"—unless perhaps the past tense is used in place of the present. For so the translator of Cyril reads it: "he witnesses and cries out." But he who translated Chrysostom reads: "he offers testimony and was crying out."

21 ***He who comes after me is preferred before me***] <term>Ὁ ὀπίσω μου ἐρχόμενος ἔμπροσθέν μου γέγονε</term>. The participle "coming" (<term>ἐρχόμενος</term>) is from the verb "to come" (<term>ἔρχομαι</term>), which is often adapted to both the present and future tense. Although in this place, if the present tense is preferred, it should be translated as a past-perfect because it is attached to a past-tense verb, "has become" (<term>γέγονε</term>), in this manner: "He who, though he came after me, has been made before me." We are to understand that Christ was both born later and began to preach later than John, but nevertheless surpassed him in authority. This is what happens to industrious runners: though they leave the starting line later, they catch up to and overtake the one who departed long before. Both Cyril and Theophylact explain it in roughly this sense: Christ was born six months after John, and John held the highest authority among the Jews while Jesus was still unknown; this is what "comes after me" means. What is "is preferred before me"? He who is later in time has become prior in glory. Why? Because greater miracles preceded him: Angels singing at his birth, then the Magi worshipping him, the Holy Spirit descending upon him, and the Father testifying from the clouds. Therefore, he began to be "first" among men. Why was he considered first? Because in reality, he was first in dignity. It was only right that he should be held as greater by everyone, who was in every way greater. Chrysostom does not want the phrase "comes after me" to refer to the birth of Christ, but to the start of his preaching. Even if he had spoken of his birth, he says he would not have used the word "coming" (<term>ἐρχόμενος</term>) in the future or present tense, but "having come" (<term>ἐλθὼν</term>) in the past tense. But there is no difficulty here if you refer "coming" to the whole arrival of Christ, which encompasses his birth, circumcision, youth, and all the steps of our redemption up to the cross. This was the end of the race, for which John was the forerunner; just as John entered the stadium first, so he finished his course first. Furthermore, from the phrase "was made before me," the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who believed that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father.</note> concluded that the Word of God was created, not noticing how great an absurdity would exist here: "Christ is before me—that is, before I was born—because he was prior to me." For what is more foolish than to speak thus? God created him before me, because he was prior to me—since that which is created does not exist before it is created. But rather, it was a matter of verbal order: "because this one is prior to me"—that is, established before me—"therefore he was before me." Chrysostom discusses similar points, but the passage is so obscure, whether by the fault of the translator or the scribes, that unless Theophylact had said the same things more clearly, I would hardly have

<column-break/>

14 ...the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, 20 full of grace and truth. John bears witness of him, and cries out, 15 saying, "This was he of whom I spoke, 21 who, though he followed me, excels me, 22 because he was before me. 23 And of his fullness have we all received, and grace for grace: Because the law was given through Moses, grace and truth 24 arose through Jesus Christ. 25 No man has ever seen God: the only begotten Son, who is...

understood it. However, "before" (<term>ἔμπροσθεν</term>) here is "has been made" (in Greek <term>γέγονε</term>), a word that can mean both "to become" and "to be." For what we read earlier, "there was a man sent from God," used the word <term>ἐγένετο</term> <note>original: "egeneto" (happened/became)</note>. Therefore, "was made" does not mean the same as "was fashioned" (<term>πεποίηται</term>) or "created" (<term>κτισθείς</term>), but "was made" is used for that which "began to be." "He who was coming after me began to be before me," that is, he who was following has now moved ahead. For Christ is never simply called "made" in the Holy Scriptures, although he is called "made man" or "made better known to men." Just as we say, "daily he becomes more foolish," while the same man remains; so John was made "later," who had been "first," and conversely Christ was made "first," who had been "later." If you take one word (namely "later") as referring to his arrival or preaching, and the other (namely "first") to his authority and glory, there is no difficulty. Or if you prefer to take both as referring to glory and authority, there would be nothing absurd, provided you estimate "before" and "after" not by nature, but by the knowledge of men. Even if the point Chrysostom brings up is not absurd—that "was made" is used for "will be," following the custom of the Prophets—it is not entirely necessary to flee to this explanation, since many miracles and testimonies had already preceded concerning Christ, as I said, which surpassed the virtue of John, even if Christ was not yet as well known to the multitude. Additionally, "before" in Greek is <term>ἔμπροσθεν</term> <note>meaning "in front of"</note>, not <term>πρὸ</term> <note>meaning "prior to in time"</note>, so that you understand one who precedes in rank. This is also what Saint Augustine noted.

22 ***Because he was before me***] "Prior" stands for "superior" or "more powerful" or "more famous"; although in Greek it is <term>πρῶτος</term> <note>original: "protos" (first)</note>, a superlative used instead of a positive. But if he was prior, how was he "made" prior? Because what he already was, he also began to be recognized as. Again, since John was better known than Christ at that time, how is he said to have been "made prior" already? Chrysostom thinks that, in the manner of the Prophets, the past tense is used for the future—that is, "was made" for "shall be made." Now, as for "because he was before me," Saint Augustine seems to refer this to time when he says, "He was before me because in the beginning was the Word." To me, it seems to pertain to dignity, by which Christ, even as a man, was greater than John. His authority obscured John's by its own majesty. Again, he refers "comes after me" to birth, whereas according to Chrysostom it relates more to the time of preaching. For John did not relate birth to authority, even if John was three or four months "heavier" <note>older</note> than Christ.

23 ***Of his fullness have we all received, and grace for grace***] Augustine advises that, based on the authority of the Greek manuscripts, a **conjunction** should be added here: "We have all received, **and** grace for grace." And I have found it written this way in very ancient copies: one of which was held by the Library of Saint Paul's in London, the other by the College of the Canons of Corsendonk, near the famous Antwerp in Brabant. A manuscript from Constance also agreed. However, Chrysostom interprets this as if the conjunction <term>καὶ</term> <note>original: "kai" (and)</note> does not join two things here, but interprets and explains. The Mosaic Law had some grace, but it did not have fullness. But from Christ's fullness we have all received, namely the Evangelical grace, in place of the grace of nature and the Mosaic Law. Nor do I think we should omit what Chrysostom notes in his 13th Homily: that these words—"of his fullness we have all received, and grace for grace"—should be referred not just to the person of the Baptist, but to the Evangelist. For he writes: "And the Baptist joins his testimony to his own." For this little part—"of his fullness we have all received"—is not the word of the forerunner, but of the disciple. This is made clearer by the pronoun "we" added in the Greek. For those to whom John the Baptist spoke had not yet received of his fullness. Cyril agrees. Theophylact, however, refers it to the person of the Baptist, so that the sense is: "Whatever we Prophets have, we have drawn from him," so that "we" refers not to the listeners but to the prophetic order. But what follows—"No man has ever seen God"—seems to contradict this opinion, as those words clearly seem to be the Evangelist's.

24 ***Was made through Jesus Christ***] Lest anyone idly dream of a mystery in the phrase "was made," it is the same word used first: "all things were made," and "it was made," then "there was a man," and again "was made before me." Therefore "was made" in this place means rather "began to be" or "arose," or, the word that Valla preferred, "existed." However, it was rightly noted by the Ancients that the Law is said to be **given** through Moses, who was not the author of the Law, but grace **was made** through Jesus, as through the author and fountain of grace. For even under the Mosaic Law, grace flowed to pious men from no other source than this fountain. I wonder what Augustine was following when, in several places and especially in his book against Faustus (Book 22, Chapter 10), he reads it this way: "The Law given through Moses, but grace and truth were made through Jesus Christ," as if the Evangelist meant that the Law which Moses brought became that same grace through Christ. Augustine is subtle indeed, even if the Greek does not express this meaning.

25 ***No man has seen God at any time***] Perhaps someone will wonder why the Greek article is not added here: <term>Θεὸν οὐδεὶς ἑώρακε πώποτε</term>. But I believe it was omitted because "God" here is not used in a way to distinguish him from other gods, nor for a specific person, but rather for the Deity itself, as Saint Augustine also used this word, or for the Divine Nature. In the same way, a little earlier, "but were born of God" (<term>θεοῦ ἐγεννήθησαν</term>). For it signifies a certain divine generation distinct from the human.

26 ***He has declared him***] <note>original: "Ipse enarravit"</note> Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), a prominent Greek Church Father known for his eloquent preaching.</note> also noted this word, by which a more certain and expressive doctrine is declared. In Greek, the word is *exegesato* <note>original: "ἐξηγήσατο"</note>. Indeed, *exegemata* <note>original: "ἐξηγήματα"</note> is the term for "Commentaries," in which obscure sayings are explained more fully and clearly. For what the Father had spoken more hiddenly through the oracles of the Prophets, the Son has explained; and this also pertains to that "fullness" mentioned just before. However, where the Latin translates "he" <note>original: "ipse"</note>, the Greek does not use *autos* <note>original: "αὐτός"</note>, but *ekeinos* <note>original: "ἐκεῖνος"</note>, suggesting something must be understood: *No one has ever seen God, but the only-begotten who is in the bosom of the Father sees him; he, therefore, who has seen, has declared him.* This is roughly what the commentary of Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine biblical scholar whose commentaries were highly regarded in the Renaissance.</note> indicates. Furthermore, the word "declared" <note>original: "ἐξηγήσατο"</note> carries weight not only because Christ declared what he saw more clearly than Moses or the Prophets—for we declare more lucidly those things we have seen—but also because, while the Law spoke only to the Jews, Christ through the Gospel has set forth the grace of God to all nations of the world.

27 ***Because I am not the Christ***] <note>original: "Quia non sum ego Christus"</note> Either it should have been translated by omitting the conjunction—*I am not the Christ*—or by changing the person of the pronoun: *he confessed that he was not the Christ.* Or, as we have translated it: *he confessed, saying, "I am not the Christ,"* because the Baptist's own words, recited as if spoken by himself, seem to add some emphasis to his faith. Otherwise, what else was expressed by these words, *and he confessed, because I am not the Christ*, except that the Baptist confessed that John the Evangelist was not the Christ? <note>The author is critiquing a literal Latin translation of the Greek grammar which, if read strictly in Latin, suggests the speaker is talking about someone else.</note> And yet, for the time being, we grant that the conjunction can be taken causally <note>original: "αἰτιολογικῶς"</note>, meaning "that." If this is not granted, the sense would be that the Baptist confessed because the Evangelist was not the Christ. There is no reason for the Fathers to protest here. We understood the meaning regardless of the words used; whose job was it to point this out? We understood it, not because we knew Latin, but because we were accustomed to these most fortunate blunders. Yet how much simpler it is to render the Evangelist’s meaning so that there is no need to learn a new way of babbling, but so that anyone who knows Latin may understand it immediately. But I often knowingly and prudently wink at such trifles, so as not to cause the reader nausea.

28 ***Make straight the way of the Lord***] <note>original: "Dirigite viam Domini"</note> The Greek *euthynate* <note>original: "Εὐθύνατε"</note> is elsewhere rendered "Make right," which other Evangelists expressed as *hetoimasate* <note>original: "ἑτοιμάσατε"</note>, that is, "prepare." For a bend in the road prevents you from seeing one who is approaching. In Hebrew, the word is *tam*, which is not inconsistent with John's word. For he commands the removal of the obstacles of evil desires, which prevent people from being able to perceive the approaching Christ.

29 ***If you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet***] For "the Christ," the Greek article is added—*ho Christos* <note>original: "ὁ Χριστός"</note>—to express that unique individual. For Elijah, it is not added here or above, because there was only one Elijah, whom some thought would live again and announce the coming of Christ, according to what is read in Malachi, chapter four: *Behold, I will send you Elijah the Prophet before the day of the Lord comes.* Therefore, an article would have been redundant since there was nothing to distinguish. But one might ask: why did he not place the article before "Prophet" here, while just a moment ago he added it in "Are you the Prophet?" <note>original: "Ὁ Προφήτης εἶ σύ;"</note> The solution is at hand. For when they ask, "Are you the Prophet?", they are not asking simply if he is *any* prophet, but *the* prophet whom Moses promised as pre-eminent in Deuteronomy 18: *The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your own people.* Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444), a central figure in early Christological debates.</note> noted this before me. Here, by saying *the Prophet*, they seem to feel that John is in no way a prophet. Previously, those jealous of Christ's glory were inquiring; now, turned to anger, they threaten him, saying, "By what authority do you do these things," if you are not the Christ, nor his precursor Elijah, nor even a prophet at all. But John does not deny being a prophet; rather, he denies being *that* Prophet whom Moses had promised. To deny being the Prophet promised by Isaiah would be different, even if the article is added in both places in some Greek manuscripts. And it appears Chrysostom read it this way, for although he noted elsewhere that *ho prophetes* was said with the article, he raised no scruple about the article being omitted shortly after. Theophylact clearly states that he added the article here, arguing the ignorance of the Pharisees, who thought that the Proph-

-et whom Moses promised was someone other than the Christ, when in fact the Messiah promised by the Prophets and the Prophet promised by Moses are the same person. They also erred in thinking that Elijah would be the precursor of the first coming, when the prophecy speaks of the second coming.

<margin>B</margin> 30 ***But he stood in your midst***] It is better read, as Saint Jerome <note>The primary translator of the Latin Vulgate (c. 347–420).</note> cites in Haggai: *But he stands in your midst.* Frequently in these verbs that signify a lasting action, such as *gignotha* or *esteka*, the past tense is used for the present, as we have already advised in several places. It is even clearer <margin>C</margin> in what Cyprian <note>Bishop of Carthage (c. 210–258), an early Christian writer and martyr.</note> reads in the second book against the Jews, chapter 18: *He stands in your midst.*

31 ***It is he who is to come after me***] He repeats in so many words what he had placed above, about which we have already advised.

32 ***Of whom I am not worthy***] The "of whom" <note>original: "ejus"</note> is repeated redundantly, according to the characteristic of Hebrew speech.

33 ***These things were done in Bethany***] Chrysostom, and his emulator Theophylact, also point out that in the older and more corrected manuscripts, one does not read *Bethany*, but *Bethabara*, because Bethany is not across the Jordan, nor in the desert, but near the Jordan, close to Jerusalem. Origen <note>An early and influential Greek scholar and theologian (c. 184–253).</note>, cited in the *Catena* <note>A "chain" of interpretations or a commentary made up of excerpts from earlier Church Fathers.</note>, reads it this way as well. Suidas <note>The author of a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedic lexicon.</note>, or whoever that person was (human or divine), corrects this passage and substitutes *Thabara* <note>original: "Θαβαρά"</note> for *Bethany*. From the *Hebrew Places* of Saint Jerome, it was not possible to extract anything certain, because through the fault of copyists, everything is corrupted in all the <margin>D</margin> good authors. Nonetheless, he mentions in the same order the village of *Bethany*, which is two thousand paces from *Aelia* (that is, Jerusalem), on the side of the Mount of Olives, where Christ called his friend Lazarus back to life; and immediately after he mentions *Bethabara*, which was across the Jordan, where John baptized for repentance. From this, it appears that even in Jerome's time the custom endured that those desiring to be reborn in Christ were washed in that life-giving pool at that location. I do not think it is at all unlikely that this is the place John designates, however the name of the place has varied—especially since it can be immediately proved that Bethany is not across the Jordan, nor in the desert. A certain Gloss <note>A marginal or interlinear note in a medieval manuscript.</note> suggests there were perhaps two Bethanys; I would not deny that this could be possible. Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100), the Jewish historian.</note>, in the seventeenth book of the *Antiquities*, chapter ten, mentions *Bethania* (spelled with an *alpha* in both places) when speaking of the testament of Herod the Great, who designated Gaulanitis, Trachonitis, *Bathania*, and Paneas for his son Philip. He mentions this name and matter in chapter sixteen (or seventeen in some codices) of the same book. I believe this *Bathania* is across the Jordan. If someone objects that the location of these events is irrelevant, let them know that the Evangelist felt otherwise; he thought the testimony of the place was relevant to the verification of the narrative.

<margin>E</margin> 34 ***But on another day***] <note>original: "Τῇ ἐπαύριον"</note>, that is, *the next day*, or *the day after*: so that you understand the very next day. And it is not "he saw," but *he sees* <note>original: "βλέπει"</note>, in the present tense. This "exchange of tenses" <note>original: "ἐναλλαγὴ"</note> has a wonderful grace in storytelling, as we imagine what we are narrating is happening right now. I would not point out these minor things so often if I did not see that this diligence would ensure that the Sacred Codices cannot be easily corrupted hereafter, or if they are corrupted, they can be restored by these aids.

35 ***The Lamb of God***] <note>original: "ὁ ἀμνός"</note>, that is, *the* lamb: so that we understand it as the one and distinguished lamb of whom Isaiah said, *As a lamb before the shearer he was silent.* Chrysostom and Theo-<margin>F</margin>phylact indicated this as well. The article has emphasis not only of dignity, as we said, but also of reference. This is *that* lamb of whom Isaiah prophesied. So also a little later, "This is the *Son of God*," the Greek article *ho Huios* <note>original: "ὁ Υἱός"</note> is added, signifying that he is not called the Son of God by the general title of the pious, but by a certain peculiar and distinguished reason.

36 ***The sins of the world***] <note>original: "τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τοῦ κόσμου"</note>, that is, *the sin of the world*, in the singular number. And it expresses something more than if he had said "sins." This lamb is innocence itself. And he alone takes away sin from us—that is, the very tyranny and power of all sins, so that there is no longer any sin in them. For just as the same John in his Epistle calls the sum of all impiety (and as it were a world of all vices) "wickedness," when he writes

<meta>This page continues the detailed scholarly commentary on the first chapter of the Gospel of John. The translator/author is weighing various interpretations from the Church Fathers (Augustine, Chrysostom, Cyril, etc.) regarding the baptism of Jesus and the specific Greek wording used by the Evangelist. # ACCORDING TO JOHN. CHAPTER I. #

...he was before me. 31 And I did not know him, but so that he might be revealed to Israel, for this reason I came baptizing in water. <margin>v. 1, 32.</margin> 32 And John gave testimony, saying: I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it—

---

<margin>A</margin> [John] writes that the world is set in wickedness; so here he calls the "sin of the world" a collection of all vices. Two very ancient codices—whose testimony we have cited more than once—agree with the Greek copies, as does the Council of Constance. Finally, Origen cites this passage in his tenth *Homily on Numbers*. Again, in the twenty-fourth Homily of the same work. Likewise, Augustine in his book *Against Faustus*, book 11, chapter 30, following the faith of the ancient codices. Again, in his book to Boniface, book 3; even in the printed volumes the full reading remains. Indeed, even Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, in order to prove that there is one original sin in man and not many, brings forward this passage from John. It has been noted by the learned that he said <term>αἴρει</term> <note>original Greek: αἴρει</note>, that is, "takes away" or "lifts," not "remits": either because he removes it entirely, which John could not do, or because he took it upon himself. For we "take up" the burdens that we impose upon ourselves. Chrysostom also noted the logic of the tense: it was not said "he took" or "you will take," but "he takes," using the present tense. This indicates that every purging of crimes always proceeds from him, just as one might say, "Hellebore purges the brain," meaning that it possesses a perpetual and native power for purging the head. I have pointed this out all the more willingly because "he takes" <note>Latin: tollit</note> could easily have been changed to "he will take" <note>Latin: tollet</note> through a scribal error.

<margin>37 After me comes a man]</margin> "Comes" is in the present tense, or certainly the future, <note>original Greek: ἔρχεται</note>. What he had previously said through a participle—"he who comes after me"—he expressed here through a verb. Although the significance of the tense is ambiguous in both, the Translator <note>the Vulgate translator</note> rendered it there with a future tense verb and here with a present tense verb, even if the sense remains almost the same. For Jesus had already begun to follow in the preaching of the Baptist, and once the Baptist was gone, he was destined to succeed him entirely. Thus, he who previously followed is now said to have overtaken him, since he had been commended by such a remarkable testimony from the Father.

<margin>38 I did not know him]</margin> I would prefer to translate this as: "And I had not known him," especially since the Greek sounds like this: <note>original Greek: Κἀγὼ οὐκ ἤδειν αὐτὸν</note>. This reading is more suitable for explaining the question raised by this passage. For it is remarkable how Saint Augustine tortures himself here while trying to explain how it stands that, since John said shortly before the baptism, "I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?", he now says he did not know who he was until the Spirit, descending in the form of a dove, pointed Christ out. He certainly understood him to be the Messiah, from whom he confessed he must request the gift of baptism. Augustine tries to escape this difficulty by saying that John knew Christ even before this, but nevertheless learned something from the sign of the Spirit that he previously did not know—namely, that Christ had reserved the authority of baptizing to himself. This is gathered from what follows: "This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit." And indeed, I think this interpretation seemed appropriate at that time for refuting heretics, especially among the uneducated, who contended that those who had been baptized by "bad" bishops had to be baptized again. For if Christ is the author of baptism and the priest is nothing other than a minister, it is not right for the benefit of a good author to be invalidated by the vice of a minister. 

However, to speak frankly (but with peace toward such a great man), this interpretation seems rather forced and violent, and one that common sense does not easily embrace, unless perhaps my own judgment deceives me. First, if baptism is not attributed to a mere man because the power of baptism flows from Christ himself, by this logic no Sacrament should be attributed to man, since Christ is in all of them, bestowing power and efficacy, while the priest is nothing other than the administrator of another's generosity. Nor has any heretic ever been so crudely delirious as to take upon himself the authority of baptizing in his own name; rather, following the Gospel prescription, they too dipped "In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." It is strange, therefore, that this one thing was hidden from John—which is known even to bad men—when he knew everything else that Augustine mentions: that he was the Lord, that he was the Christ, that he was Jesus, that he was born of a virgin, and that he was both after him and before him. Was it for this one reason that the Holy Spirit descended from heaven: so that he would no longer be ignorant of this? 

Now, as for the fact that nowhere in Holy Scripture is any man read to have called baptism "his own," whereas Paul calls the Gospel "his" (for Augustine also brings forward this argument), it can be answered that it is proved and received by the public custom of the Church that the one who baptizes says these words: "I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." If <term>Baptismos</term> <note>original Greek: Βαπτισμός</note> is the same to the Greeks as "baptizing" or "dipping" is to the Latins, then surely the baptizing belongs to the one who baptizes, just as the writing belongs to the one who writes. Who forbids calling it a man's baptism in some way—not as the author, but as the minister? Otherwise, with what face does a priest say "I baptize" in order to baptize? But Paul calls the Gospel "his" in some places, yet elsewhere calls it the "Gospel of God" and the "Gospel of Jesus Christ"—of God as the author, of Christ because he first preached it and was himself the author for Paul, who had undertaken the functioning of this duty delegated by Christ. In the same way, he commanded the turns of preaching and baptizing to the other Apostles, that they should go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Thus, baptism can be called that of the man administering it, and yet be denied to be the man's, just as Christ in John denies that his speech is his own. Otherwise, not even John’s baptism should have been called John’s, since it had God as its author. It is true that in the Sacred Letters after John, no one's baptism is mentioned except Christ's; and perhaps Augustine felt this, for although he acts somewhat obscurely, he treats this in the present passage: not to show simply that Christ is the sole author of baptism rather than man, but to prove that baptism given by anyone in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit is valid and not to be repeated, even if given wickedly by a wicked man. For he reasons thus: If Christ—

<column-break/>

### 346 GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN. CAP. I. ###

<margin>A</margin> [For, After me] comes a man who has been preferred before me, because he was before me. <margin>31</margin> And I did not know him; 39 but so that he might be made manifest to Israel, therefore I came baptizing with water. <margin>32</margin> And John bore witness, saying: I saw the Spirit—

---

<margin>B</margin> is the author of baptism and has not handed this authority over to any mortal, the gift cannot be corrupted by the vice of a minister, however impure. The Holy Spirit allowed John to be ignorant of this for a while, so that after being warned, he might render certain to others what he had learned privately. Even if in this whole dispute he seems to me somewhat forced, and something was granted to the needs of that time and to the ears of the common people. <margin>C</margin> Chrysostom frankly confesses that Christ was unknown to John for a long time, because it is probable that he, who had not yet become known to the public by any miracles, was not known to John, who had spent most of his life in the desert. For the miracles that are circulated regarding the childhood of Christ are fables. He explains the manner by this reasoning: he says that what was said—"And I did not know him"—is not to be referred to the immediate time when Jesus came to be baptized, but to a more distant time when Jesus had not yet become famous through miracles. But that distance of time is more correctly explained, I think, by the pluperfect tense: "And I had not known him." Theophylact comes closer to Augustine's commentary: He knew he was the Messiah, but he did not know he was the one who would baptize with the Holy Spirit. Although not even this interpretation satisfies me in all respects, because the very series of the speech plainly declares that Christ was unknown to John until he was made certain by the sign of the dove. For we read: "And I did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize in water, he said to me: Upon whom you see the Spirit descending." It is not the purpose of this work, nor is it within my meager ability, to untie such knots. 

Nevertheless, it is right to advise the Reader to consider whether it might be simpler to say that it happened by divine plan that Christ became known to John by certain degrees, so that his testimony concerning Christ might be more certain and more thoroughly tested. In the same way, he allowed the Apostles to believe somewhat slowly so that they might make the faith more certain for us, regarding things they themselves had not believed rashly. When John said, "I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?", he recognized a certain great and exceptional man who did not need his baptism, but perhaps he was not yet certain that this was the Son of God. Therefore, "I did not know him" insofar as he did not yet have it confirmed, the sign not yet having been given by which the Father willed it to be certain; once it was brought forth, he freely and openly confessed the Son of God. He knew the Messiah had come or was about to come; whether this was the one, he had not known by investigation. And he repeats immediately, "And I did not know him." Partly so that he himself might finally be understood to have recognized by a most certain argument the one he previously did not know; and partly so that John’s testimony might have no less weight if it seemed he had given it to a relative or an acquaintance. Now it is given to one not even known by face, nor known otherwise than by the indication of a heavenly symbol. 

Cyril extricates himself from this question differently: "I did not know of myself, but I knew from the inspiration of the Spirit indicating the Father to me." This opinion <margin>D</margin> would be softer if one were to translate <note>original Greek: ἤδειν</note> as "I would not have known" unless the Father had warned me. Consider, Reader, whether it can be taken thus: "I did not know him," that is, I had not received the right to bring him into the knowledge of all. I knew him for myself, but not for others, just as the Son of God is said not to have known the final day. Augustine explains it thus: John knew him, because he held many things concerning him; he did not know him, because he was ignorant of certain things about him. Some, as indicated, explain it thus: "I did not know him," namely by face; I knew by the Spirit that the Messiah had come, but I did not know for certain who he was, nor did I dare to pronounce it openly until he was demonstrated divinely. 

Furthermore, as for the fact that John, exulting in the womb, recognized Christ: this pertains more to the mothers and to us than to John; unless perhaps we contend that when the rocks were split at the Lord's death, sense was given to the rocks. Nor does it escape me that those will immediately cry out <margin>E</margin> here whose sole desire is to extol the gifts of the Saints to an immense degree, as if it were unworthy if John, who while not yet born felt the not-yet-born Christ through a prophetic spirit, should be ignorant of him now that he is grown. But those people must look again and again, lest while they exaggerate the praises of the Saints too much, they do not have enough regard for the wisdom and counsel of God, who so tempered the whole business of the incarnation and redemption that it could not have been done more effectively in any other way. And it will be borne more moderately to say this of John if one remembers that something similar is attributed by Chrysostom to the Virgin Mother, who spoke to her Son with a certain human affection: "They have no wine." But it is better to subscribe his own words; they are in his twentieth *Homily on John*: "For she desired," he says, "that he should now gain the favor of men, and the grace of the Son might be made more famous through her, and perhaps she was moved by some human affection, just as his brothers were when they said, 'Show yourself to the world,' desiring to acquire fame for themselves by his miracles. Therefore he answered rather harshly: 'What is that to me and <margin>F</margin> to you, woman?'" And a little further down: "Inasmuch as they did not yet have the due opinion of him, but Mary, in the manner of mothers, thought she had the right to command everything to her Son, when it was right to worship and revere him as Lord." 

If we want nothing to have been hidden from John, by the authority of Augustine, how did he not know what was most important in Christ? For since Christ was the fountain and author of salvation, and baptism is the door to salvation, how can one who knows Christ be ignorant that Christ is the author of true baptism? It would be as if someone knew God but did not know whether He was supremely wise. And yet, by the consensus of Jerome and Gregory, John doubted whether Christ would descend to the underworld when he sent his disciples to ask: "Are you the one who is to come, or do we look for another?" Truly, I pronounce nothing on this matter. I only supply material for the learned Reader to think upon, being ready to embrace gladly whatever the Spirit of Christ suggests more correctly.

<margin>39 But so that he may be manifest in Israel]</margin> The preposition "in" <note>original Greek: ἐν</note> is absent from the Greek "Israel." And it appears that Chrysostom read it this way from his twentieth Homily.

40 **On another day** ] Again <note>original: ἐπαύριον</note>, that is, *on the next day*, as we just noted.

41 **And looking back at Jesus** ] <note>original: ἐμβλέψας</note>, that is, having gazed upon, as he himself translates elsewhere and soon after: *But Jesus, gazing upon him, said*. For strictly speaking, one "looks back" <note>original: respicit</note> who turns his face toward his back to see.

42 **Where do you dwell** ] <note>original: ποῦ μένεις</note>, that is, where are you staying. It is the same verb which in the same place he soon translates as *to stay*, now as *to dwell*.

43 **And they saw where he was staying** ] <note>original: ποῦ μένει</note>. And again, *they stayed with him* <note>original: παρ’ αὐτῷ ἔμειναν</note>. It seemed necessary to point this out, lest anyone wishing to philosophize over the words might fall into error.

44 **Now it was about the tenth hour** ] Some do not approve of using "quasi" for *about* or *nearly* <note>original: ferme</note>, and consider it a less common usage among authors who speak correctly. Even if Suetonius speaks this way in some places, though other newly-coined sayings are found in his work as well. Furthermore, naming the hour not only adds to the credibility of the narrative but also explains the eagerness of the Apostles, who, even though it was evening, still went about to speak privately with Christ; and it shows the wonderful kindness of Christ, who did not bid them return to him the next day, using the imminent night as an excuse. For since the Jews count the hours from sunrise, the *sixth* is noon, and the *tenth* is verging toward evening <note>roughly 4:00 PM</note>.

45 **You are Simon son of John** ] <note>original: ὁ υἱὸς Ἰωνᾶ</note>, that is, son of Jonah, which in Hebrew is <note>original: יוחנן bar Jona</note>, which elsewhere he translates as *son of John*. In one very ancient codex I found written, *son of Jonah*, not *John*, according to the Greek reading. The Constance manuscript agreed. Nor is the article added here idly; for it does not simply mean he is *a son of Jonah*, but from the mystical meaning of the paternal name, it declares his extraordinary happiness.

46 **You shall be called Cephas, which etc.** ] Jerome, in his work on Hebrew names, denies that *Cephas* is a Hebrew word, but says it is Syrian, and among them it sounds like *solid*. Hence those who hand down the etymologies of Greek names want *petra* <note>rock</note> to be named from this, because it is not easily moved.

47 **on the morrow** ] <note>original: ἐπαύριον</note>. What he twice translated above as *on another day*, he finally changed to *on the morrow*, but even that is not quite Latin enough or convenient, since it should have been said, *on the following day*, or *the day after*.

48 **From the city of Bethsaida** ] In Greek it is <note>original: ἀπὸ Βηθσαϊδὰ ἐκ τῆς πόλεως</note>, that is, from Bethsaida from the city, as if Bethsaida were a region in which a city is located. Although Saint Jerome, in his *Hebrew Places*, shows that *Bethsaida* is a city of Galilee, near the lake—

<column-break/>

—of Gennesaret, the homeland of three Apostles: Andrew, Peter, and Philip. Hence the preposition *from* <note>original: ἐκ</note> seems to be redundant, especially since the word is added neither in Chrysostom nor in Cyril, nor in the ancient Latin copies. Unless perhaps John said this in his own way, as every writer has something peculiar to his style. For in the next chapter he used a similar form: <note>original: Ὅτε δὲ ἦν ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις ἐν τῷ Πάσχα ἐν τῇ ἑορτῇ</note>, that is, *When he was in Jerusalem at the Passover at the feast*. Although *Passover* and *feast* belong together by apposition, like genus and species, he nevertheless repeated the preposition, just as if one were to say, *I received letters from the teacher from Philip*, instead of *from the teacher Philip*. And in the Greek Theophylact, I find the preposition added.

49 **Philip finds Nathanael** ] *Finds* should be pronounced with the first syllable sharp <note>accented</note>, for it is in the present tense. Although the Latin translator reports it as *he had seen* him, as if he happened upon him. And a little earlier, *we have found the Messiah*. Even if Chrysostom approves a different sense when he says, "for finding belongs to one who seeks." But let the judgment of this matter remain with the reader. Here the same Chrysostom notes that the article was added, <note>original: τὸν Μεσσίαν</note>, because he wanted that unique Christ, promised to and expected by the Jews, to be understood. Otherwise, all kings and priests, indeed all those sacred to God, are called "Messiahs" and "Christs."

50 **the son of Joseph from Nazareth** ] Was Joseph a Nazarene, or Christ? For the Latin speech is altogether ambiguous, while the Greek is clear and certain: <note>original: τὸν ἀπὸ Ναζαρέτ</note>, that is, the Nazarene, or *originating from Nazareth*. The article placed before the preposition ensures this cannot be doubted.

51 **From Nazareth can anything...** ] In some Greek manuscripts it was written as a declaration, though it can also be taken as a question, as Saint Augustine also noted; he thinks that what follows fits both pronunciations equally. Yet what he denies, he confirms more persuasively: that it should be read as a question, because it seems like an answer to one questioning, *Come and see*. And in this way Chrysostom reads it, indicating that this question belongs to one hesitating about the name of the place, since prophecy had promised that Christ would come forth from Bethlehem.

I **In Cana of Galilee** ] Jerome indicates there are two Canas, the greater near Sidon, and the lesser in the tribe of Asher. Therefore, *of Galilee* <note>original: τῆς Γαλιλαίας</note> was added to distinguish it from the other. For it is a town of the Gentiles in Galilee, which Jerome, in *Hebrew Places*, testifies still existed in his own time.

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>2 *What to me and to you*]</margin> He rendered it from the Greek. For in Latin it should have been said, *What have I to do with you?* <note>original: *Quid mihi tecum?*</note> based on the Greek *Ti emoi kai soi*.
<margin>3 *Water jars*]</margin> This is a Greek word <note>original: *hydriae*</note>, for Plautus calls it a water-pot <note>original: *aqualem*</note>, since *hydria* is named by the Greeks from *hydor* meaning water.
<margin>4 *Two measures*]</margin> that is, *cadi* <note>large jars</note>: although both words are Greek, the Latin authors used the same, as in Horace: "A small onyx jar of nard will draw out a *cadum*." And in Pliny. *Metreta* is found in Cato and Columella. A *cadus* or *metreta* is a measure of ten *congii* <note>about 9 gallons</note>, as our most learned Budé teaches in his fifth book *On the As*, if anyone should happen to desire more.
<margin>5 *Master of the feast*]</margin> This is a Greek word <note>original: *architriclinus*</note>, it signifies the one who is in charge of preparing the banquet. A *triclinium* is a place spread with three couches for reclining at a meal.
<margin>6 *Until now*]</margin> *Heos arti*, that is, until now, or up to this time.
<margin>F</margin>
<margin>7 *The money-changers sitting*]</margin> He said *kermatistas*, not *trapezitas* <note>bankers</note>. *Kermata* are small copper coins, hence *kermatistai* are those who exchange larger coins for small bits not without profit, a custom which lasts even today among the Italians.
<margin>8 *And when he had made as it were a whip*]</margin> "As it were" <note>original: *quasi*</note> is not added in the Greek codices. "And having made a whip" <note>original: *poiēsas phragellion*</note>, that is, "And making [it] with a whip." He pronounced the Latin word corruptly according to common usage.
<margin>9 *Sheep also and oxen*]</margin> There is no "also" in the Greek, but *te*, "both the sheep and the oxen."
<margin>10 *Zeal for your house has eaten me up*]</margin> This testimony is issued from the sixty-eighth Psalm.
<margin>11 *Destroy this temple etc.*]</margin> *Lysate*. The Greek word is ambiguous regarding that which is "raising up one lying down, sleeping, or dead," and "raising up a building," that is, to construct. For we find "to raise" used in this sense in Suetonius's *Life of Caligula*: "And as a sign of victory he raised an extremely high tower."
<margin>12 *Forty-six years*]</margin> Although it is outside our primary purpose, it seemed right to remind the reader—as I know Augustine indicated more than once—that this number is found in the name *Adam*, if written in Greek letters Ἀδάμ. The double *alpha* denotes *two*, *delta* four, and *my* forty. This is a common interpretation, although discovered and produced by others as he himself testifies; I wonder, however, that it pleased such a grave man so much, when (to say nothing else) Jerome mocks Greek allegory in Hebrew names. Perhaps it would have been something if this number were signaled by these letters among the Hebrews. Very similar to this is what he noted: that the four letters with which *Adam* is written designate the four quarters of the world: *anatole* (east), *dysis* (west), *arktos* (north), and *mesembria* (south). Saint Cyprian also noted this before him, but both were only human.
<margin>14 *Because he knew all men*]</margin> It is "all things" in Greek, *ta panta*, in some manuscripts, but otherwise in others. Augustine reads, "he knew all [people]."

<margin>1</margin> **That you have come from God as a teacher**] "Teacher" <note>original: *magister*</note> is in the nominative case, not the vocative; God sent you as a teacher, not man. For it is "you have come" <note>original: *elēlythas*</note>, though you may find "master" used for "teacher."
<margin>2 *Unless one is born again*]</margin> *Gennēthē*, that is, has been begotten or born. And in the most ancient Latin codices it is "born," not "born again." Thus Augustine cites it in the 24th book against Faustum, chapter 1. So it is written in the Golden Codex. Valla prefers "begotten," because someone is also begotten from the living, whereas we are "born" from a woman.
<margin>3 *How can a man be born again*]</margin> *Gennēthēnai*, that is, to be born or begotten, is more concordant and preferred by the ancients. Likewise in the following verses it is "to be born," not "to be born again."

<margin>4 From water and the Holy Spirit</margin> In the Greek copies, the word "Holy" <note>original: *Sancto*</note> is not added, nor is it found in Augustine, who cites this passage in his book *Against Faustus*, book 24, chapter 1. For in order to distinguish the heavenly birth from the earthly and physical one, he proposed two fluid elements: water and air. Indeed, even in the "golden codex" <note>An ancient, prestigious manuscript written in gold ink</note> the word "Holy" is not added.

<margin>5 And to be born again, *anothen* <note>original Greek: ἄνωθεν</note></margin> This is the same adverb used by Luke in the preface of his Gospel, which we translate as "from the beginning" <note>original: *ab integro*</note>. Chrysostom <note>An influential 4th-century preacher known as "Golden-Mouthed"</note> noted that the Greek word is ambiguous. For it can mean "again" <note>original: *palin*</note>, referring to a past time, or "from above" <note>original: *ano tou ouranou*</note>, meaning from the heavens. It is used in this second sense in John chapter 19: "You would have no power over me at all, unless it were given to you *from above*." Cyril follows this latter meaning, interpreting it as being born as if from heaven, referring to one who is reborn through the Holy Spirit. Origen was the first to note this when explaining the sixth chapter of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, though in that place Origen's translator added *something extra* of his own.

<margin>8 the spirit/wind blows where it wills</margin> Here "where" is an adverb of place, not time. Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous Renaissance humanist and critic</note> prefers "blows *to wherever* it wills"; for shortly after it describes the spirit <note>original: *to pneuma*</note> as "where it may go." It is a simile about a breeze—a thing that is invisible but nonetheless effective. And here he seems to take "spirit" to mean the blowing of the air, so that you may understand the comparison drawn from this physical wind (a most powerful thing despite being unseen) to the force of that divine Spirit. Chrysostom interprets it exactly this way in his 25th Homily, as do Cyril, Theophylact, and Augustine in his book *On Questions of the Old and New Testament*, Question 59, most clearly testifying that the example of the wind's force was used for the sake of teaching, so that no one might cry out that this interpretation is merely my own dream.

<margin>7 You are that teacher in Israel] *to Israel* <note>original Greek: τὸ Ἰσραὴλ</note></margin>, "Israel" is in the genitive case, so that you understand he is the teacher of that nation. Nor is the article absent here: *ho didaskalos* <note>original Greek: ὁ διδάσκαλος</note>, that is, "the famous teacher" about whom there is such a high opinion. To express this better, we have translated it as: "You are *the* teacher of Israel."

<margin>8 And I have told you earthly things, and you do not believe</margin> Here the Greek manuscripts vary: some have "you did not believe" <note>original: *non credidistis*</note>. Others, again, have "you do not believe" <note>original: *non creditis*</note>. There was no reason, therefore, to immediately erase the writing, especially since in verbs of this kind the past tense is often used for the present. <margin>E</margin> <margin>9 And no one has ascended into heaven</margin> "Ascended" in the Greek is in the past tense <note>original: οὐδεὶς ἀναβέβηκεν</note>, so that no one should think it refers to a future ascension. Indeed, his point is that he alone speaks of the heavenly rebirth because he alone of all people has descended from the heavens.

<margin>10 Who is in heaven, *ho on en to ourano* <note>original Greek: ὁ ὢν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ</note></margin> The participle could be translated as the past imperfect: "who was in heaven," namely, before he descended. For the Son of Man is said to have been in heaven just as he is said to dwell in the heavens, much as the "Lord of Glory" is said to have been crucified, because the two natures are joined in one Person <note>term: Hypostasis — the union of Christ’s human and divine natures in one individual existence</note>.

I did not wish to change it, as the word itself does not seem out of place—especially since it is found in Seneca (certainly not a bad author, in my opinion) and even in Columella <note>A 1st-century writer on agriculture</note>.

<margin>12 For God so loved the world</margin> From this point, it could be seen as the words of the Evangelist himself, following up and explaining the discourse that Jesus had begun with Nicodemus. For it does not continue with how Nicodemus departed, or what he replied to these wonderful things. We pointed out something similar in the first chapter regarding "from his fullness we have all received." A similar case seems to happen to Paul in the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 2, where he does not conclude the speech begun with <margin>F</margin> Peter, but follows it up as if providing an interpretation.

<margin>13 For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world</margin> "Judge" <note>original: *judicet*</note> is used here in place of "condemn," as is frequently found in Paul and others, so that it may be contrasted with what follows: "that the world might be saved through him." The same should be understood in the following passages:

<margin>14 He who believes in him is not judged. And, he is already judged. And shortly after,</margin>

<margin>15 Now this is the judgment</margin> "Judgment" <note>original: *judicium*</note> is used here to mean condemnation.

<margin>16 For everyone who does evil, *ho phaula prasson* <note>original Greek: ὁ φαῦλα πράσσων</note></margin>, that is, he who does bad things. The sense is the same, except that "to do evil" <note>original: *male agere*</note> is also said of someone who is in a bad state or afflicted by evils.

IV. <margin>1</margin> When therefore the Lord knew that the Pharisees heard that Jesus made and baptized more disciples than John, <margin>2</margin> (Although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples,) <margin>3</margin> He left Judea, and went again into Galilee. <margin>4</margin> But it was necessary for him to pass <gloss>e</gloss> through Samaria. <margin>5</margin> He came therefore into a city of Samaria, which is called Sychar, near the estate which Jacob gave to Joseph his son. <margin>6</margin> Now the fountain of Jacob was there. Jesus therefore, fatigued from the journey, <gloss>f</gloss> sat thus upon the fountain: it was about the sixth hour. <margin>7</margin> There came a Samaritan woman to draw water. Jesus says to her, Give me something to drink. <margin>8</margin> For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food. <margin>9</margin> That Samaritan woman therefore says to him, How is it that you, although you are a Jew, ask a drink from me, who am a Samaritan woman? <gloss>g</gloss> for Jews have no commerce with Samaritans. <margin>10</margin> Jesus answered, and said to her, If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, Give me something to drink, <gloss>h</gloss> you would have asked of him, and he would have given you living water. <margin>11</margin> The woman says to him, Lord, <gloss>i</gloss> you have nothing with which you may draw, and the well is <gloss>k</gloss> deep, from where then do you have that living water? <margin>12</margin> Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well, and he himself drank from it, and his sons, <gloss>l</gloss> and his cattle? <margin>13</margin> Jesus answered, and said to her, Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again.

---

<margin>17</margin> <gloss>a</gloss> *He who is of the earth, speaks of the earth*] In the Greek copies some words are added: <note>original: "ὁ ὢν ἐκ τῆς γῆς, ἐκ τῆς γῆς ἐστι, καὶ ἐκ τῆς γῆς λαλεῖ"</note> that is, "he who is of the earth, is of the earth, and speaks of the earth." It is just as if you were to say, "he who has proceeded from the earth is earthly, and speaks earthly things." For he does not speak "about" the earth (which would be <note>original: "περὶ τῆς γῆς"</note>), but "from" the earth (that is, <note>original: "ἐκ τῆς γῆς"</note>), meaning humble things. And so Chrysostom reads it, as does Theophylact, and with these Cyril and Hilary in the preface to the Commentaries which he wrote on the mystical Psalms. In the same way, I find it written in the oldest Latin copies: *he who is of the earth, is of the earth, and speaks of the earth*. The Constance manuscript agreed, as did my own from an old printing; although in the Cosemdoncensian manuscript, very clear traces testified that this second part, *is of the earth*, had been erased. Augustine reads, *he who is of the earth, is earth, and speaks of the earth*: this is confirmed by what follows: for if he were not enlightened, he says, "earth would speak earth." However, a less attentive reader changed the text because the repetition *is of the earth, is of the earth* seemed redundant. But he did not notice that each part is opposed to its counterpart: He who comes from heaven is heavenly—that is, he is above all, and speaks heavenly things, and does heavenly things, baptizing with the Spirit. He who has proceeded from the earth is humble and earthly, and speaks from the place where he is from—that is, a humble person speaks humble things, and both reflect their origin. It would have been clearer, however, if he had added the article to the final part: "speaks the things of the earth" <note>original: "τὰ ἐκ τῆς γῆς λαλεῖ"</note>.

<margin>18</margin> *And he who comes from heaven*] "Comes" is in the present tense, <note>original: "ὁ ἐρχόμενος"</note>, except that these participles serve two tenses, the present and the imperfect past. And so it should have been translated even as "was," meaning "he who was from the earth was earthly, but he who had proceeded from heaven is above all."

<margin>19</margin> *Sealed*] <note>original: "ἐσφράγισεν"</note>, that is, he has sealed up, which means he has confirmed by a sign. For a seal added to a thing makes it certain.

<margin>20</margin> *For God does not give the Spirit by measure*] The Evangelist omitted the pronoun "to him" <note>original: "αὐτῷ"</note>, because it would be clear enough from what precedes and follows of whom he was speaking. This happens more frequently among the Greeks than among the Latins. We, therefore, lest anything should offend the reader, have added the pronoun from our own store, but only in the version. Moreover, it is said in a proverbial figure, *he gives by measure*, for that which is done sparingly or moderately. He who gives bountifully and profusely does not measure what he gives or count it, but pours it out in heaps. Otherwise, grace in Christ, insofar as he was man, could be called finite. And here the Evangelist seems to have attached his own discourse to the discourse of John. For he does not finish what happened to the disciples.

<margin>21</margin> *And has given all things into his hand*] It is uncertain whether, by using the preposition, he meant that all things were handed over to the Son "into his hand," or whether all things are given to us "through his hand," because according to the property of Hebrew speech the preposition *in* can have the significance of an instrument: but the Greek interpreters follow the former sense, and it is more pleasing to me.

---

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>1</margin> <gloss>e</gloss> *Through the middle of Samaria*] "Middle" is not added, neither in the Greek codices, nor in the ancient Latin copies which largely agree, nor even in the "Golden" one, which says simply <note>original: "διὰ τῆς Σαμαρείας"</note>, "through Samaria." And so Chrysostom reads it. Whence it can seem a marvel where this crept into the common copies, unless perhaps someone interpreted "through Samaria" as "through the middle of Samaria," and someone else transferred that into the text—an occasion by which we detect many faults have crept in.

<margin>2</margin> <gloss>f</gloss> *Sat thus upon the fountain*] "Thus" <note>original: "οὕτως"</note> adds a sense of modesty, so that it expresses the gesture of a weary man, or "here," namely because he was fatigued. And this expression is found used in a similar way in Terence and other approved authors. Chrysostom suggests "having the fountain," for so it was held in common copies, although in the ancient ones it is read *super* (upon), not *supra* (above). He specified the sixth hour so that we might understand the Lord was fatigued not only by the labor of the journey but also by the midday heat.

<margin>9</margin> <gloss>g</gloss> *For they do not use*] <note>original: "συγχρῶνται"</note>. A Latin voice has more easily rendered the Greek word. For who ever said "they use," or who would understand it to mean "to have commerce and the custom of shared life" at a meal? For also to the Latins, "use" (usus) signifies familiarity. And we "use" those with whom we keep company. Otherwise, *coeni* and *conjua* are unheard-of words.

<margin>10</margin> <gloss>h</gloss> *You perhaps would have asked*] <note>original: "σὺ ἂν ᾔτησας"</note>, "you would have asked." The translator, for the expletive conjunction *an*, placed an adverb of doubting ("perhaps"), when it is actually more affirmative. Furthermore, since in the Evangelist the conjunction *an* is added to both verbs—"you would have asked" and "he would have given"—in the former he translates it as "perhaps," and in the latter he does not translate it at all. Yet it should either have been omitted in both places or added in both.

<margin>11</margin> <gloss>i</gloss> *Nor in which you may draw*] <note>original: "ἄντλημα"</note>, that is, a drawing-vessel. For Lucretius used that word, since Valla’s "haustorium" seems insufficiently polished. And it was more Latin to say "with which you may draw" than "in which you may draw."

<margin>11</margin> <gloss>k</gloss> *High*] <note>original: "βαθὺ"</note>, that is, deep. For "high" (altus) is an ambiguous word <note>note: in Latin 'altus' can mean both high and deep</note>.

<margin>12</margin> <gloss>l</gloss> *And his cattle*] <note>original: "θρέμματα"</note>. This word embraces every kind of living creature, named from "nourishing," like "grazing animals."

8 **Forever** <note>original: "In aeternum"</note>] <note>original Greek: εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα</note>, that is, *unto the age*.
9 **Because I have no husband** <note>original: "quia non habeo virum"</note>] I ask you, what can be understood from these words, except that the woman said that Christ did not have a husband? <note>The scholar is criticizing a literal translation of the Greek "oti" (that/because). If translated too literally into Latin, it sounds like the woman is saying Jesus has no husband, rather than stating she herself has none.</note> We are so careless in how we speak, or what the reader will hear. Therefore, the conjunction <note>original Greek: ὅτι</note> (because/that) should have been omitted here, as it is elsewhere, or the mood of the verb should be changed to translate it this way: *You have well said that you do not have a husband*, or *you have well said, you have no husband*. If the Translator had never omitted the Greek conjunction, it might seem to have been done out of superstition. But since he is found to have omitted it elsewhere, it is a wonder why he thought it should be added here.
10 **Who worship him** <note>original: "Qui adorent eum"</note>] <note>original Greek: τοὺς προσκυνοῦντας αὐτὸν</note>, that is, *those worshipping him*, or *who may worship him*. It appears the Translator avoided the ambiguity of the reciprocal pronoun, which could be taken to mean they were worshipping themselves. This could have been avoided if he had said, *who may worship him [ipsum]*.
11 **That Messiah is coming** <note>original: "Quia Meffias venit"</note>] <note>original Greek: ἔρχεται</note>. Which the Greeks sometimes use for the future, even though it is a present tense word. In this place, *shall have come* was more fitting, because of what follows: *when therefore he shall have come*. And *he will come* is read in the ancient and corrected Latin codices.
12 **And immediately** <note>original: "Et continuo"</note>] <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἐπὶ τούτῳ</note>, that is, *at this*, or *meanwhile*, specifically while these things were being said.
13 **That he was speaking with a woman** <note>original: "quod cum muliere loqueretur" </note>] <note>original Greek: ὅτι μετὰ γυναικὸς ἐλάλει</note>, that is, *that he was speaking with a woman*, or *had spoken*. The Translator seems to have read <note>original Greek: τι</note> (something) instead of <note>original Greek: ὅτι</note> (that). For they were not wondering *what* it was that he had discussed with her, but rather they were marvelling at this: that Christ was speaking so familiarly with a poor Samaritan woman. Furthermore, <note>original Greek: μήτι</note> is placed for <note>original Greek: ὅτι</note>, as we sometimes use a pronoun

in place of a conjunction. For it was not a new or suspicious thing to the Apostles that Christ should speak with a woman. What we have said can be gathered almost from the interpretation of Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an early Church Father known for his eloquent preaching and biblical commentary.</note>. The reliability of the ancient manuscripts also supports us, in which it is written, *and they wondered, because he was speaking with a woman*, that is, *they wondered that he was conversing with a woman*. For what follows, *you who speak with her*, should rather be translated, *why do you speak with her*, specifically with a Samaritan. For the Jews shrank from commerce with the Samaritans. Indeed, the disciples seem to have wanted to break off Christ's conversation with the woman, but they did not dare to do so.
14 **And says to those men** <note>original: "Et dicit illis hominibus"</note>] The Translator added "those" <note>original: "illis"</note> on his own, and not at all inappropriately; in Greek it is only <note>original Greek: τοῖς ἀνθρώποις</note> (to the men/people). And again, "men" is said instead of "them."
15 **Has anyone** <note>original: "Nunquid aliquis"</note>] <note>original Greek: Μή τις</note>, that is, *Has anyone*.
<margin>F</margin> 16 **That I may finish his work** <note>original: "Ut perficiam opus ejus"</note>] In Greek it is read, <note>original Greek: καὶ τελειώσω</note>, *and I may finish*, and so Chrysostom has it. Although this matters little to the sense. And in this part "that" <note>original: "ἵνα"</note> can be repeated, as if you were to say, *even until I finish his work*. And.
17 **That yet** <note>original: "Quod adhuc"</note>] The conjunction "that" <note>original: "ὅτι"</note> should not have been translated, since it reports their own words. "Four months," in Greek is a single word, <note>original Greek: τετράμηνος</note>, that is, *four-monthly*.
18 **And the harvest comes** <note>original: "Et messis venit"</note>] <note>original Greek: ἔρχεται</note>. It could also be *and is about to come*.
19 **For in this is the word true** <note>original: "In hoc enim est verbum verum"</note>] <note>original Greek: ὁ λόγος</note>, with the article, so that you understand it refers to that speech which he had just spoken. Furthermore, he prefaced it as being true, since he adds a new and incredible thing.
20 **Because of his word** <note>original: "Propter sermonem ejus"</note>] "His" <note>original: "ejus"</note> must be referred to Christ, not to the woman; <note>original Greek: αὐτὸς</note>, from which "of him himself" <note>original: "ipsius"</note> was better.

---

> 21 **Savior of the world** <note>original: "Salvator mundi"</note>] The Greeks add *Christ*, "the Savior of the world, the Christ."
> 
> 22 **A certain royal official** <note>original: "Quidam regulus"</note>] A *basilikos*, that is, a certain royal person. Although I think it should be read *basiliskos* <note>a diminutive form, perhaps implying a petty official</note>, even if the Greek manuscripts consistently disagree. Indeed, the Interpreters who write on this Gospel say he was called "basilicus" either because he was of royal stock or because he held a royal office or duty. Chrysostom <note>a 4th-century Church Father known for his preaching</note> is mostly of this opinion, except that I read "regulus" <note>petty king</note> there, not "regalis" <note>royal</note>, though I do not know if this is the fault of the Translator or the Scribe. Certainly Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine archbishop</note> reads *basilikos* without controversy, that is, "royal." And Jerome <note>the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> in his commentary on Isaiah chapter 59 reminds us he was from the royal court, whom we might more rightly call a Palatine <note>a high-ranking palace official</note>. And a little later:
> 
> 23 **for he began to die** <note>original: "incipiebat enim mori"</note>] The Greek says "he was about to die," or "he was giving up the ghost," that is, he was heading toward death; yet the translator here has rendered it this way several times on purpose.
> 
> 24 **He was doing better** <note>original: "Melius habuerit"</note>] The Greek is "he had himself more elegantly," that is, he was better or more comfortable.
> 
> 25 **This again [the second]**] It might seem he meant Jesus did two "second" signs, and another word remains, even if the Greek reads this way. Chrysostom felt the awkwardness of this—and what did he not feel?—and thinks "second" was added deliberately to further emphasize the unbelief of the Galileans. Having seen the first miracle at the wedding and now this one regarding the healed boy, they nonetheless persisted in distrusting Christ.
> 
> <margin>E</margin> **E Now there is at Jerusalem near the sheep [gate]**] The Greek text means "Now there is in Jerusalem at the sheep pool," that is, *Est autem Hierosolymis super probaticam, sive ad probaticam piscina*. For in Greek "probatica" <note>sheep-related</note> is in the dative case and "pool" is the nominative. And indeed one can see this in the "Golden Codex" <note>a luxury manuscript</note>, "above the sheep [pool]," with the manuscripts of St. Donatian agreeing. In the Constance manuscript, some amateur had erased the preposition "above." The word "probatica" sounds like you are saying "of sheep" or "cattle," as Jerome translates it. Although from Chrysostom or Cyril one cannot determine the certain reading of this place. And "pool" <note>piscina</note> in this place does not mean a pond for fish, but one in which one swims, as the Greek word itself testifies, being called *kolymbethra*, which comes from "swimming."
> 
> 2 **which is named in Hebrew Bethesda**] In Greek it is *Bethesda*. Although this same word was corrupted even in the works of Saint Jerome. This can be gathered from the fact that while he previously named "Bethsaida" as a city of Galilee (the home of three Apostles: Andrew, Peter, and Philip) near the lake of Gennesaret, a little later he again adds "Bethsaida" as a pool that was in Jerusalem, nicknamed "probatica," which we can interpret as "cattle-related." This pool once had five porches. Twin lakes are shown, one of which is usually filled by winter rains, the other is wondrously red—as if the waters were bloody—testifying to the signs of the ancient work within it. For they say the priests used to wash the sacrificial victims in it, from which it took its name. This is roughly Jerome's account. Furthermore, what he says about the name being given from this refers not only to the Greek word *probatica*, which means "cattle" or "sheep," but also to the Hebrew *Bethesda*. For to the Hebrews *Beth* means "house" and *tseda* means "flock" or "cattle." It appears, therefore, the whole place was called the sheep-pool, in which some part was reserved for natural uses. Hugo of Saint-Cher <note>a 13th-century Cardinal and biblical commentator</note> suggests the pool was named through "antiphrasis" <note>a figure of speech where a word is used as its opposite</note>, because it had very few fish. Just as the Fates <note>Parcae</note> are called the sisters of the Devil because they spare <note>parcant</note> no one. Truly, this etymology is very similar to the one he brought for the sycamore: he says *Sycomorus* is called such as if it were a *siccus morus* <note>dry mulberry</note>, because it is similar to a mulberry. In this manner, it is no great feat to build huge volumes if one is allowed to contaminate wretched papers with such silly trifles <note>original: "naeniis"</note>. Let no one think these things are said by me out of a disease of slander. Rather, I thought it best to consult the studies of those who read this writer and others like him as if they were enslaved to them, without any discernment—some because he was a Cardinal, others because he was of the Dominican Order. But while I hear that Hugo was admitted into the number of Cardinals, I do not read that he was enrolled in the number of Saints. Even if that were the case, reverence is owed to holy men only to the extent that if they erred—for even saints err—we may champion the truth without personal insult. Though one should speak more sparingly of others than the matter itself deserves, so that our rebuke of them might seem given for the public good, and our moderation for Christian modesty.
> 
> <margin>F</margin> 3 **And the water was moved**] Ancient manuscripts have "and he moved the water," that is, "and he stirred the water." Although others again had "the water was stirred"; the article "the" was the occasion of the error, since the same syllable could be the end of the verb. Chrysostom interprets this place so that you can understand the water was accustomed to be stirred by an Angel. Certainly Theophylact reads "he stirred the water," that is, "he troubled that water."
> 
> 4 **And whoever first**] Ancient manuscripts, with the Greek copies agreeing, have "whoever then first having entered," that is, whoever was therefore the first to go in.
> 
> 5 **descended into the pool**] "Into the pool" in this place is neither in the ancient nor the Greek copies; rather, someone added this for the sake of explaining, repeating from the nearby passage what the Evangelist preferred to be understood.
> 
> 6 **After the motion of the water**] "After the stirring," that is, after the disturbance. Which he previously called "he stirred the water."
> 
> 7 **Had known that he already had a long time**] When we perform the duty of a grammarian, we will not be burdened to remind you that "in his infirmity" should be understood here from what immediately precedes.

For <margin>44</margin> Jesus himself testified that a Prophet in his own country has no honor. When therefore he had come into Galilee, <margin>45</margin> the Galileans received him, since they had seen all the things he had done in Jerusalem on the feast day; for they also had come to the feast day. Jesus therefore came again into <margin>46</margin> Cana of Galilee, where he had made wine from water. And there was <margin>B</margin> 22 a certain royal official, whose son was sick in Capernaum. This man, when he heard that Jesus had come from <margin>47</margin> Judea into Galilee, went to him and asked him that he would come down and heal his son; 23 for he was at the point of death. <margin>7</margin> ...the pool; but while I am coming, another <margin>8</margin> goes down before me. Jesus says to him, "Rise, take up <margin>9</margin> your bed, and walk." He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him. <margin>24</margin> Truly, truly, I say to you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life. <margin>25</margin> Truly, truly, I say to you, that an hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live. <margin>26</margin> For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself, <margin>27</margin> and he gave him authority also to execute judgment, <margin>28</margin> because he is the Son of Man.
