## CHAPTER V. ##

...puts me into the pool: <margin>8</margin> but meanwhile, while I am coming, another descends before me. Jesus says to him, "Rise, <margin>9</margin> take up your bed and walk." And immediately that man was made whole, and he took up his bed and walked. He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him. <margin>24</margin> Truly I say to you, he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and shall not come into condemnation, but has passed from death to life. <margin>25</margin> Truly, truly I say to you, that the hour comes, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear shall live. <margin>26</margin> For as the Father has life in himself, so he has also given to the Son to have life in himself, <margin>27</margin> and he has given him power to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of Man. <margin>28</margin> Marvel not at this, for the hour comes in which all who are in the graves...

---

<margin>8 While I am coming</margin>] <note>original: "ἐν ᾧ δὲ ἔρχομαι ἐγὼ"</note>, "in which [time] moreover I am coming," to translate it literally. However, it should have been translated as "but," "meanwhile," while I am coming, *another descends before me*.

<margin>9 Take up your bed</margin>] It is strange why the Greeks write <term>krabbaton<gloss>a small bed or cot</gloss></term> with a double 'b', since Martial <note>A Roman poet</note> shortens the first syllable of this word in his Epigram: *But lest the hearth buy anything, lest the weighted frame of the bed give.* <note>original: "Sed ne focus ecquid emat, ne det sponda gravata."</note> Furthermore, since Peter <note>likely Petrus Crinitus or similar scholar</note> seeks the etymology of the word from the Greeks, for he thinks it is called *krabaton* as if it were *kamabaton*, from *kama* (head) and *baton* (passable). Whether this is more true or not, I do not dispute at present. Certainly, it is a type of small bed, or rather a litter; in the Great Greek Etymological Dictionary <note>the Etymologicum Magnum</note>, I find *krabaton* said to be from "suspending the feet" <note>original: "παρὰ τὸ κρεμαῖν τὰς βάσεις"</note>, that is, because they were carried in litters in such a way that their feet did not touch the ground.

<margin>10 That man</margin>] The word "that" <note>original: "ille"</note> is not in the Greek, but the translator expressed the force of the article, *the man* <note>original: "ὁ ἄνθρωπος"</note>.

<margin>13 For Jesus slipped away from the crowd</margin>] <note>original: "ἐξένευσεν"</note>. It is uncertain whether it comes from the verb *anne* or *exneuo*. Hesychius <note>a Greek grammarian</note> indicates that *ekneuo* is the same as "to swim out" <note>original: "enatare"</note>, from the verb *neo* (to swim), when he writes it thus: "having slipped away" <note>original: "ἐκνεύσας"</note>, "having swam out." But it is not so.

<margin>13 From the crowd gathered in that place</margin>] Otherwise he would have added the article, "from the crowd that was in the place," but Jesus withdrew himself *since there was a crowd in the place*, because among many people it is easy for any one person to be hidden, whom you would then not recognize. Hence it seems more likely to be said that "he slipped away," as if becoming a stranger and unknown. Not to mention that "healthy" <note>original: "ὑγιής"</note> pertains more to the wholeness of limbs than to a disease like a fever. For good health is the opposite of disease; weakness is the opposite of a bodily defect.

<margin>13 For Jesus</margin>] <note>original: "μέλλει"</note>, that is, "hereafter." Although the Translator <note>referring to the Vulgate</note> correctly translates it for those who are skilled in the Latin language, among whom "now" has the same force as "hereafter."

<margin>14 Therefore the Jews persecuted Jesus, because he did these things on the Sabbath</margin>] In the Greek codices, I find added, *and they sought to kill him* <note>original: "καὶ ἐζήτουν αὐτὸν ἀποκτεῖναι"</note>, perhaps because it follows: *Therefore they sought all the more to kill him*, etc., but the Latin codices reclaim this with great consensus.

<margin>14 My Father until now</margin>] <note>original: "ὁ Πατήρ μου"</note>. Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria</note> notes that by adding the article to "Father," he is not declaring just any Father, but God, that is, that He is truly the Father.

<margin>16 Unless he sees the Father</margin>] <note>original: "ἐὰν μή τι βλέπῃ"</note>, that is, "unless anything" he sees, or certainly "unless he sees." For "anything" <note>original: "τὶ"</note> is frequently added as a property of the Greek speech.

<column-break/>

<margin>17 And greater than these</margin>] <note>original: "καὶ μείζονα τούτων"</note>. Why did the Translator dare here what he did not dare in the fourteenth chapter of this same Evangelist, *and greater of these things he shall do*? Where it is written in exactly the same words, "greater than these" <note>original: "μείζονα τούτων"</note>.

<margin>18 For neither does the Father judge anyone</margin>] Cyprian <note>early Christian bishop and writer</note> seems to have read "approached" instead of "judges." For he reports it thus: *The Father judges nothing*. In the same manner he cites it in the third book to Quirinus, chapter thirty-three.

<margin>19 But he shall pass over</margin>] <note>original: "ἀλλὰ μεταβέβηκεν"</note>, that is, "he has passed," in the past tense, not the future. For "he passed" <note>original: "transiit"</note> was easily corrupted into "he shall pass" <note>original: "transiet"</note>. Theophylact <note>Byzantine archbishop and commentator</note> reads "he passed," citing it in Luke chapter 23. His commentary supports the reading: *Into punishment, he says, he does not come, but he lives eternal life. Furthermore, he who lives, has already passed into life.* In the golden codex transcribed in Constantinople, it was written "he passed."

<margin>20 And the Father gave him power to do judgment</margin>] The "and" <note>original: "καὶ"</note> is a dotted conjunction in common copies, though it is found standing in old ones. Therefore we have restored "also" <note>original: "quoque"</note>, so that we may understand this also was added to his authority: that he might be allowed to act in the persona of a judge, as a partner in his father’s kingdom.

<margin>21 Because he is the Son of Man</margin>] It is strange here that the Greek article is not prepended to either word: *because he is Son of man* <note>original: "ὅτι Υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου ἐστί"</note>. As to why it was omitted here, I will bring forward my conjecture. For I think this phrase "because he is the Son of Man" means nothing else than "because he is human," and for expressing that sentiment, articles are superfluous. And here Saint Augustine agrees with me, who suggests that the power of judging, which always belonged to Christ, was in turn handed over to him by the Father as a man. Even if Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, known for his eloquence</note> does not approve of the distinction of the reading followed by Augustine, showing that this reading followed by the common people belongs to a certain heretic, Paul of Samosata, and he does not think the sense holds at all, since Christ did not receive the power of judging simply because he was human. For if he had received it for that reason, it would be given to all humans. Therefore he orders it to be punctuated in this way: *And he gave him power of doing judgment also*, and let a colon come between here. Then let there be added: *Because he is the Son of Man, do not marvel at this*: so that the sense is: What I said about the power of giving eternal life, and what about the power of judging, let it not seem incredible to you because I...

---

<margin>E</margin> ...you might see that I am a man. Indeed, from the interpretation of Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century theologian</note> itself, it can be gathered that he agrees with Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an early Church Father known for his preaching</note>. Although the translator confused the distinction. Truly, regarding the method of distinguishing the speech, I leave the judgment to each person. Everyone in this part acts for me, because "Son of man" is placed simply for "man." For Chrysostom writes thus: *For he did not receive judgment for this reason, because he is a man. For nothing would have prohibited all men from being judges.* Likewise Cyril: *Do not, he says, wonder if, since you see me to be a man, I nevertheless promise that I will raise the dead.* Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator</note> similarly distinguishes it, so that this little part does not depend on the previous words, but refers to what follows: *Because he is the Son of man, do not wonder.* He denies it is to be wondered at that such great authority was given to him who was the son of man, since he was the same Son of God; for he declares the divine nature from the general resurrection of the dead, which is reserved for the Son of God alone.

**22 And they will hear the voice of the Son of God**] In the Greek codex it was written, *and they will hear his voice*, because a little before he called himself the Son of God. And therefore it seems harsh to repeat "Son of God" here. The copies of Saint Donatian, and with these the Constantinopolitan one, supported the Greek reading.

**23 And they will proceed, those who have done good**] There is some importance in the distinction, that after the word "proceed" you add a comma <note>original: *hypodiastolen*</note>, so that we understand not only the good will proceed, but everyone whoever hears the voice. <margin>F</margin> Then let two parts be subjoined, one of the good, the other of the evil. If anyone reads Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo</note> carefully explaining this, he will feel that he noted this. I know what I am about to say is a bit crude, but nevertheless, since this work is prepared for the less experienced, it will not be a burden to remind them that "will proceed" is in Greek <term>ἐκπορεύσονται</term> <note>original: *ekporeusontai*</note>, that is, "they will go out," or "come forth." For he speaks of those who are to come forth from the tombs at the voice of the Angel sounding the trumpet. Otherwise "proceed" means that which goes well or is moved forward.

**24 His testimony is true, which he bears of me**] The pronoun "his" is neither added among the Greeks, nor in the ancient codices.

**25 But I have a testimony greater than John**] The translator rendered the Greek in good faith. For if he had wanted to express it more clearly, "I have testimony greater than the testimony of John," he would have added another feminine article, <term>τὴν μαρτυρίαν μείζω τῆς τοῦ Ἰωάννη</term> <note>original: *tēn martyrian meizō tēs tou Iōannē*</note>. And yet there is no doubt that this is the sense of the Evangelist. For he does not compare the testimony with John, but the testimony of the Father with the testimony of the Baptist.

**26 Those very things**] <term>Those</term> refers to the preceding, <term>very things</term> to the following. For the works which the Father gave me, *that I might complete them, those very works, etc.* This distinction remains even now in very old Latin copies. "Them" was added from the property of the Hebrew language. "Very things" <note>original: *ipsa*</note> is placed for "further" or "by themselves." The works which I do testify further who I am, even if no man were to testify. Furthermore, the repetition of "works" serves for emphasis.

**27 Search the Scriptures**] <term>Ἐρευνᾶτε</term> <note>original: *Ereunate*</note>. It is no less uncertain for the Greeks than for us whether "Search" was said in the imperative mood (a command) or the indicative (a statement). And either sense is tolerable, except that Cyril thinks it was said in the indicative mood, *You search the Scriptures*, and those same people, in that which is most important, do not believe the Scriptures. Chrysostom, in his preface, seems to seize upon the imperative mood, noting that he did not say *Read*, but *Search*: though in explaining the indicative mood, he says, *Do you not admire the Scriptures? For they would not search unless they admired.*

**28 You think**] <term>ὑμεῖς δοκεῖτε</term> <note>original: *hymeis dokeite*</note>. The Greek speech is ambiguous, and can be taken as "you seem" or "you seem to yourselves."

**29 Brightness**] <term>δόξαν</term> <note>original: *doxan*</note>. I wonder why he did not prefer "glory" in this place. However, *doxa* is not ambiguous toward brightness, but toward glory and opinion.

**30 You do not receive**] <term>οὐ λαμβάνετε</term> <note>original: *ou lambanete*</note>, that is, "you do not receive," using a verb in the present tense.

**31 In whom you hope**] <term>ἐλπίκατε</term> <note>original: *elpikate*</note>, that is, "you have hoped," although the translator renders it well, that is, "you have placed hope."

**32 For if you believed, etc.**] <term>Εἰ γὰρ ἐπιστεύετε Μωσῇ, ἐπιστεύετε ἄν ἐμοί.</term> That is, "if in your soul you had believed Moses, you would certainly have believed me." Again, for <term>ἂν</term> <note>a Greek particle denoting potentiality</note> he placed "perhaps," which is certainly not in the right place, since the translator calls into doubt that which Christ affirms.

19 So when they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia <note>A stadium was roughly 600 feet; thirty stadia is about 3.5 miles</note>, they saw Jesus walking on the sea <gloss>16</gloss> and drawing near to the boat, and they were afraid. 20 But he said to them, "It is I, do not be afraid." 21 Then they were willing to receive him into the boat, and immediately the boat <gloss>17</gloss> reached the land <gloss>18</gloss> to which they were going. 22 On the next day, the crowd that stood on the other side of the sea saw <gloss>20</gloss> that there was no other small boat there except that one into which his disciples had entered, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but his disciples had gone away alone. 23 But other small boats arrived <gloss>21</gloss> from Tiberias near the place where they had eaten the bread <gloss>21</gloss> after the Lord had given thanks. 24 When the crowd therefore saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they also got into the small boats and came to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.
<margin>D</margin>
25 And when they had found him across the sea, they said to him, "Rabbi, <gloss>22</gloss> when did you come here?" 26 Jesus answered them and said, "Truly, truly I say to you, you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled. 27 Work not for the food that perishes, but for the food that remains for eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you: for <gloss>23</gloss> God the Father has sealed him." 28 They said therefore to him,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
9 Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, says, "There is one lad here who has five barley loaves <gloss>1</gloss> and two small fish; but <gloss>2</gloss> what are these for so many?" 10 Jesus said, "Make the men sit down." <gloss>3</gloss> Now there was much grass in that place. So the men sat down, in number about five thousand. 11 Jesus took the loaves, and having given thanks, <gloss>6</gloss> distributed them to the disciples, and the disciples to those sitting; likewise also <gloss>7</gloss> of the fish, as much as they wanted. 12 When they were filled, he said to his disciples, "Gather the fragments that remained, <gloss>8</gloss> so that nothing is lost." 13 So they gathered them, and filled <gloss>9</gloss> twelve baskets with fragments <gloss>10</gloss> from the five barley loaves, which remained for those who had eaten.
<margin>B</margin>
14 Then those men, when they saw the sign Jesus had done, said, <gloss>11</gloss> "This is truly that Prophet who is coming into the world." 15 Jesus therefore, knowing they were about to come <gloss>12</gloss> and take him by force to make him king, <gloss>13</gloss> withdrew again to the mountain himself alone. 16 When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea: 17 And having entered a boat, they came across the sea to Capernaum: and it was now dark, and Jesus had not come to them.
<margin>C</margin>
18 The sea was being stirred up by a great wind blowing. 19 When they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia, they saw Jesus walking on the sea <gloss>16</gloss> and drawing near the boat, and they were afraid. 20 But he says to them, "It is I, do not be afraid." 21 Then they were willing to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going. 22 The next day, the crowd standing on the other side of the sea, seeing that there was no other small boat there except that one into which his disciples had entered, and that Jesus had not gone into the small boat with his disciples, but his disciples had gone away alone. 23 But other small boats came from Tiberias near the place where they ate the bread, after the Lord had given thanks. 24 When the crowd therefore saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they also got into the small boats and came to Capernaum, seeking Jesus. 25 And finding him on the other side of the sea, they said to him, "Rabbi, when did you get here?" 26 Jesus answered them and said, "Truly, truly I say to you, you seek me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled. 27 Work not for the food that perishes, but for the food that remains for eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you: for God the Father has sealed him." They said...

---

...is not observed by chance in the Ecclesiastical books among the Greeks.
<gloss>1</gloss> **And two small fish**] <note>original: καὶ δύο ὀψάρια</note>. Even in Terence’s play *The Brothers*, **fish** are called **side dishes** <note>original: *obsonium*</note>. For the Greeks call **relish** <note>original: ὄψον</note> any food that is added to bread, especially if it is cooked: hence **to eat sumptuously** <note>original: ὀψωνάρε</note> and **gourmets** <note>original: ὀψωφάγοι</note> or "side-dish eaters" used to have a bad reputation; **small fish** <note>original: ὀψάριον</note> is a diminutive of **relish**.
<gloss>2</gloss> **What are these among so many**] <note>original: εἰς τοσούτους</note>, that is, **among so many**, or **among such a great number**. He is speaking of the number of people, not their physical size.
<gloss>3</gloss> **Now there was hay**] <note>original: χόρτος</note>, herbs, or grass.
<gloss>6</gloss> **He distributed to those sitting**] The Greek texts differ slightly: <note>original: καὶ εὐχαριστήσας διέδωκε τοῖς μαθηταῖς, οἱ δὲ μαθηταὶ τοῖς ἀνακειμένοις</note>, that is, **and when he had given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to those sitting**. For the other Evangelists report it in roughly that manner—that he did not give to the crowd himself, but to the disciples, and then the disciples distributed to the multitude. However, the Latin manuscripts argue against this with great consensus. This suggests that something was added here from the other Gospels. From Chrysostom and Theophylact, it could not be guessed what they read in the context. Theophylact has what is in the Greek manuscripts, but in Chrysostom, there was what is found in the Latin manuscripts.
<margin>E</margin>
<gloss>7</gloss> **Of the fish as much as they wanted**] <note>original: ὅσον ἤθελον</note>, that is, as much as he wanted—namely, Jesus—not as much as that multitude wanted. For he was the one who, by his own will, increased that otherwise meager supply. And so Cyril reads it. Although from Chrysostom it cannot be certainly gathered what he read. Moreover, it was a change of a single little letter: **they wanted** <note>original: ἤθελον</note> versus **he wanted** <note>original: ἤθελεν</note>, as is read in Theophylact and in some other copies. Augustine reads "as much as was sufficient." Unless perhaps Augustine there explained the sense of the Evangelist in his own words, as he did a little before: **But the Lord Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks, ordered the loaves to be broken and placed before those sitting**. The Aldine edition does not agree with our reading, for it has **they wanted**, not **he wanted**.
<gloss>8</gloss> **Lest they perish**] <note>original: μή τι ἀπόληται</note>, that is, **lest anything perish**; unless you prefer "lest any bit remain."
<gloss>9</gloss> **Twelve baskets of fragments**] It could also be read "with fragments," relating to the verb **they filled**.
<gloss>10</gloss> **From the five barley loaves and two fish**] This phrase, **and two fish**, is not added in the Greek manuscripts, and both of the very old Latin copies support this; the edition of the Amerbach brothers also supported it, based on very old and most faithful copies. Finally, the Golden Codex and the Constance Codex support it.
<margin>E</margin>
<gloss>11</gloss> **Because this is truly the Prophet**] The word **Because** should have been omitted. And it should not have been translated simply as **Prophet**, but **that Prophet** <note>original: ὁ Προφήτης</note>. For Elijah, or one like him, was expected based on Malachi's prophecy. Likewise based on the promise of Moses.
<gloss>12</gloss> **That they might seize him, and make him**] In both places, one should say **himself** <note>original: *se* or *ipsum*</note>, not just **him** <note>original: *eum*</note>.
<gloss>13</gloss> **He fled again**] <note>original: ἀνεχώρησε</note>, that is, **he withdrew, or he removed himself**. It is strange why the Translator chose to depart from the Greek word here.
<gloss>14</gloss> **But when it was late**] <note>original: ὀψία</note>. He always uses "late" for "evening." We read in Livy "the late of the day" for the later part of the day. We do not find "late" used except as an adverb.
<gloss>15</gloss> **When they had climbed into the boat**] <note>original: εἰς τὸ πλοῖον</note>. Why did he forget the "small boat" <note>original: *navicula*</note> here? Nor is it **they had climbed**, but <note>original: ἐμβάντες εἰς τὸ πλοῖον</note>, that is, **having entered the boat, or certainly having boarded the boat**.
<gloss>16</gloss> **And to become near the boat**] To be sure, he translates the Greek <note>original: καὶ ἐγγὺς τοῦ πλοίου γινόμενον</note>, which is **to approach the boat, or to come toward the boat**.
<gloss>17</gloss> **It was at the land**] <note>original: ἐγένετο ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς</note>, **it was made on the land**, or **it reached the land**.
<margin>F</margin>
<gloss>18</gloss> **To which they were going**] <note>original: εἰς ἣν ὑπῆγον</note>, that is, **to which they were going**, namely the Apostles.
<gloss>19</gloss> **On the other day**] <note>original: Τῇ ἐπαύριον</note>, that is, **On the next day**. Which, however, the Translator rendered correctly.
<gloss>20</gloss> **Because another small boat**] <note>original: πλοιάριον</note>. Here the noun is truly a diminutive.
<gloss>21</gloss> **Giving thanks to God**] These words were not found in one copy; in the other, they were different: <note>original: ὅπου ἔφαγον τὸν ἄρτον, εὐχαριστήσαντος τοῦ Κυρίου</note>, that is, **where they had eaten the bread, when the Lord had given thanks**. Although the old manuscripts agree with our Edition, with Augustine also testifying to it. For what Chrysostom and Cyril read was not very clear from their interpretation.
<gloss>22</gloss> **When did you come here**] <note>original: πότε ὧδε γέγονας</note>. Here he translates **you have become** <note>original: γέγονας</note> as **you came**. Why not also a little before **it was made on the land**, meaning **it came to the land**?
<gloss>23</gloss> **The Father sealed**] <note>original: ἐσφράγισεν</note>. So that you may understand he was approved by the authority and testimony of the Father, as we have noted elsewhere.

-># ACCORDING TO JOHN. CHAPTER VI.<-

<column-break/>

<margin>28</margin> They said therefore to him, "What shall we do, that we may work the works <margin>28</margin> <margin>29</margin> of God?" Jesus answered and said to them, "This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent." <margin>30</margin> They said therefore to him, "What sign then do you perform, that we may see and believe you? What work do you do? <margin>31</margin> Our fathers ate manna in the desert, as it is written: He gave them bread from heaven to eat." <margin>32</margin> Jesus then said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, <margin>24</margin> it was not Moses who gave you that bread from heaven, but <margin>25</margin> my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. <margin>26</margin> For the bread of God is he who <margin>33</margin> comes down from heaven and gives life to the world." <margin>34</margin> They said therefore to him, "Lord, always give us this bread." <margin>35</margin> And Jesus said to them, "I am that bread of life: he who comes to me shall not hunger, and <margin>27</margin> he who believes in me shall never thirst. <margin>36</margin> But I said to you, that you have also seen me, and you do not believe. <margin>37</margin> All that the Father gives me shall come to me; and him who comes to me I will not cast out. <margin>38</margin> For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me. <margin>39</margin> And this is the will of the Father who sent me, that of all which he has given me I should lose nothing, but should raise it up on the last day. <margin>40</margin> And this is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have everlasting life, and I will raise him up on the last day." <margin>41</margin> The Jews then murmured about him, <margin>28</margin> because he had said, "I am that bread which came down from heaven." <margin>42</margin> And they said, <margin>29</margin> "Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then does he say, 'I have come down from heaven'?" <margin>43</margin> Jesus therefore answered and said to them, "Do not murmur <margin>30</margin> among yourselves. <margin>44</margin> No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him; and I will raise him up on the last day. <margin>45</margin> It is written in the Prophets: And they shall all be <margin>31</margin> taught by God. Everyone therefore who has heard from the Father and has learned comes to me. <margin>46</margin> Not that anyone has seen the Father, except him who is from God; he has seen the Father. <margin>47</margin> Truly, truly, I say to you, he who trusts in me has everlasting life. <margin>48</margin> I am that bread of life. <margin>49</margin> Your fathers ate manna in the desert and are dead. <margin>50</margin> <margin>32</margin> This is the bread coming down from heaven, <margin>33</margin> so that someone may eat of it and not die. <margin>51</margin> I am the living bread that came down from heaven; <margin>34</margin> if anyone eats of this bread, he shall live forever; and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world." <margin>52</margin> <margin>35</margin> The Jews therefore disputed among themselves, saying, "How can <margin>36</margin> this man give us that flesh of his to eat?" <margin>53</margin> Jesus therefore said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless..."

<column-break/>

<margin>24 He did not give you the bread]</margin> <note>original: "Non dedit vobis panem"</note> In the Greek, there is a specific article used with "bread," meaning *that* particular bread. He does not deny that some bread was given through Moses, but rather that it was not that excellent, heavenly bread intended by the Divine Scripture. Likewise a little later: "For it is the bread of God."

<margin>25 My Father gives you]</margin> <note>original: "Pater meus dat vobis"</note> Many Latin manuscripts had "was giving" <note>Latin: *dabat*</note> instead of "gives" <note>Latin: *dat*</note>, but this was in error. Here, "gives" does not refer to a specific time, but to power. For He gives who alone is able to give. In Greek, it is *didōsin* [gives], not *edōke* [gave].

<margin>26 For it is true bread]</margin> <note>original: "Panis enim verus est"</note> The Greek reads, "For it is the bread of God," which agrees with the most ancient copies, including the "Golden Manuscript" and the Constance manuscript.

<margin>27 He who believes in me will never thirst]</margin> <note>original: "Qui credit in me non sitiet in æternum"</note> The Greek is *pōpote*, which means "at any time" or "ever." The Golden Manuscript says the same.

<margin>28 Because he had said, I am the living bread]</margin> <note>original: "Quia dixisset, Ego sum panis vivus"</note> Here, the word "living" is not added in the Greek, but only: *Egō eimi ho artos ho katabas ex ouranou*, that is, "I am that bread which descended from heaven." Both very ancient manuscripts agree with the Greek here, as does the Donatian manuscript. A little earlier, "bread of life" is read, and not "living bread."

<margin>29 Is this not the son of Joseph]</margin> <note>original: "Nonne hic est filius Joseph"</note> The Greek is *Ouch houtos estin Iēsous, ho huios Iōsēph?* That is: "Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph?" The oldest Latin copies agree, supported also by Augustine. I wonder, then, by what reasoning the name "Jesus" was removed from the common copies. In this place, the name of Jesus is added as if he were a common man, used in contempt—just as today the common people call a man of no dignity by his given name alone.

<margin>30 Among yourselves]</margin> <note>original: "In vicem"</note> The Greek is *met’ allēlōn*, meaning "reciprocally" or "among yourselves."

<margin>31 Taught by God]</margin> <note>original: "Doctibiles"</note> The Greek is *didaktoi tou Theou*, that is, "taught of God," which we should understand in a passive sense <note>meaning they are the recipients of the teaching</note>. This testimony is found in Isaiah, chapter fifty-four: "And all your children shall be taught by the Lord." Saint Jerome indicates that John took the sentiment from there. But why then did he not say "in Isaiah," but "in the Prophets"? Jerome cites a similar sentiment from Jeremiah, chapter thirty-one. Furthermore, while Jerome translated it according to the Hebrew truth as "taught by God," the Seventy <note>the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated it as *didaktous Theou*, to be understood passively. Lorenzo <note>likely Lorenzo Valla</note> indicates that in some copies it was written *didaktikos* [fit to teach] and in others *didaktous* [taught], and he approves of the latter reading. I subscribe to this same opinion: for *didaktikos* refers to someone who is <unclear>suited</unclear> for teaching, according to Jerome's interpretation. This is why Paul, in—

<column-break/>

—listing other gifts, wants a Bishop to be *didaktikos*, that is, fit to teach, as we shall show in the proper place. However, *docilis* [teachable] is one who learns easily. The word *docibilis* [the word used in some older Latin Bibles] is unheard of to Latin ears. Paul, in the Epistle to the Thessalonians, expressed this with a compound word that John divided: *autoi gar hymeis theodidaktoi este*, that is, "for you yourselves are taught by God." Although this word for "taught" is not a participle in Greek but a noun, the translator strove to render noun for noun with a similar compound. Homer calls a harper *autodidaktos* [self-taught], one who does not play by art but by the inspiration of a deity:

> *I am self-taught. A god has implanted in my mind*
> *ways of song of every kind ———*

Therefore, in this passage, it should not have been translated as "the teachables of God," but "taught by God." This agrees with what precedes: "unless the Father who sent me draws him." This is surely what it means to be *theodidaktos* [taught by God]: to be drawn by the inspiration of the Father.

<margin>32 This is the bread coming down from heaven]</margin> <note>original: "Hic est panis de cœlo descendens"</note> The Greek uses *ho katabainōn*. Here he used the present participle, indicating no specific time; for he means that no bread is coming down or has come down from heaven except himself. For even the manna was a "true" thing <note>in a symbolic sense</note>. But because what the manna prefigured had now been shown, he later changes the tense of the participle to *ho katabas* [the one who came down].

<margin>33 So that someone may eat of it]</margin> <note>original: "Ut si quis ex ipfo manducaverit"</note> In Greek: *hina tis ex autou phagē kai mē apothanē*, "so that someone may eat of it and not die." Though this does not change the meaning much.

<margin>34 If anyone eats of this bread]</margin> <note>original: "Si quis manducaverit ex hoc pane"</note> It is strange what Hilary did in the tenth book *On the Trinity*; he refers to this passage from the old copies thus: "If anyone eats of my bread he shall live forever," implying that in this is the mystery of the divine nature assuming the human—that while he affirms he is the bread that descended from heaven, he nevertheless calls that same bread "his own." However, the Ancients interpret this passage as referring to heavenly doctrine: for he called it "his bread" just as he frequently called it "his word."

<margin>35 Therefore they disputed]</margin> <note>original: "Litigabant ergo"</note> The Greek is *Emachonto*, which means they were fighting or contending.

<margin>36 Give his flesh to be eaten]</margin> <note>original: "Carnem suam dare ad manducandum"</note> In the Greek, "his" <note>Latin: *suam*</note> is not added, but the translator expressed the force of the article, *tēn sarka* [the flesh], wanting it to be understood as *that* flesh of which Jesus had previously spoken.

<summary>In this passage, Jesus identifies himself as the "Bread of Life" to a skeptical crowd, contrasting himself with the manna eaten by their ancestors. The accompanying scholarly notes provide a rigorous linguistic comparison between Greek and Latin manuscripts, particularly debating the correct translation of being "taught by God."</summary>

<margin>37 **You will not have**] <note>original: "οὐκ ἔχετε"</note>, that is, *you do not have*, in the present tense. Although it may appear to be a misuse of tense <note>term: catachresis — a grammatical term for using a word in a way that departs from strict usage.</note>.</margin>

<margin>38 **As the living Father sent me, and I live**] The Translator needed to add a small word that corresponds to "as," so that the sentence would be clearer: *Just as the Father who lives sent me, so also I live because of the Father*. Regarding the phrase "he who eats me" <note>original: "ὁ τρώγων με"</note>, the participle should have been matched to the verb it is attached to, "he will live" <note>original: "ζήσεται"</note>: *he who eats me, he too shall live because of me*. The speech can also be divided so that it is woven from two parts, each of which consists of two members: *Just as the living Father sent me, and just as I live because of the Father, so he who eats me, he too shall live because of me*. This distinction agrees with the interpretation of Saint Augustine; for he labors over how the comparison stands. For we do not live because of the Son of God in the same way that he lives because of the Father. Moreover, there seems to be a misuse of the preposition "because of" <note>original: "διὰ"</note>, to which he added an accusative case instead of the genitive case.</margin>

<margin>39 **Who came down from heaven**] <note>original: "καταβάς"</note> The "descending" is in the past tense.</margin>

<margin>40 **If therefore you should see the Son of man**] Something is to be understood here to make the sentence complete. *What therefore if you should see?* <note>original: "Ἐὰν οὖν θεωρῆτε"</note>, signifying that something even more wonderful is going to happen—namely, that he should return to heaven, from whence he came.</margin>

<margin>41 **From this**] <note>original: "Ἐκ τούτου"</note>, that is, "from that," as "time" is understood.</margin>

<margin>42 **Is a devil**] I wonder why the Greek word <note>term: diabolus</note> was preferred here; he could have said, "he is an informer," or "he is a slanderer." For thus he designates Judas the betrayer. And yet we have left the word "devil," because we saw that Chrysostom interprets "devil" almost as "Satan."</margin>

<margin>1 **In Galilee, for he did not wish to [walk] in Judea**] The Evangelist wrote "in Galilee" and "in Judea." For "to walk" is used in place of "to stay." It is like the expression, "walk with good men," meaning "have companionship with good men." In what follows, Chrysostom agrees with us. For he does not read, "he did not wish to walk in Judea," but "he was not able to walk in Judea." To make this clearer, I will add his own words: *After this Jesus walked in Galilee: for he did not have the power in Judea.* And as it becomes clear that Chrysostom is reviewing the Evangelist's words, he had first stated what the Evangelist signifies by these words, and soon adds: *what does blessed John say, "for he did not have the power to walk in Judea," he who can do all things that he wishes? etc.* And soon: *When he says he did not have power, he speaks as if of a man who worked in a human way. From these things it is clear that Chrysostom did not read "he wished" <note>original: "ἤθελεν"</note>, but "he had authority" <note>original: "εἶχεν ἐξουσίαν"</note>.* And someone, offended by the sentiment because it seemed absurd that Jesus—who slipped away from the hands of those lying in wait whenever he pleased—could not stay there, changed "he had authority" into "he wished." Indeed, a slip was easier in the Latin words. This error might have seemed to originate from us, were it not for the great consensus of the seventy [translators]. Although Cyril agrees with Chrysostom, who, in explaining this passage, speaks thus: *He walked, that is, he stayed in Galilee, which was done not voluntarily nor willingly, but by necessity, as the added cause shows. Therefore, he says, he was in Galilee with foreigners for a long time, because the Jews sought to kill him. For in saying that he stayed in Galilee against his will, he signifies that it was not permitted for him to stay in Judea.* Therefore, we leave the matter to the Reader's judgment, although the authority of Chrysostom and Cyril ought to be weighty. In Theophylact, "he wished" <note>original: "ἔθελεν"</note> is read, even if the interpretation of what he read is not clear enough; indeed, one might suspect that Augustine also read "he wished," when he says, *he himself had not lost power, but he was consoling our weakness.* We have therefore three authors of no small weight who read "he did not wish." Theophylact was more recent, and I do not know if he was after the Greeks were allied with the Roman Church. If it were permitted to change Scripture because of such scruples, the passage in Mark chapter six would have to be changed: *And he could not do any miracle there, except that he healed a few sick people by laying his hands on them, and he wondered at their unbelief.* Likewise that in the same author, chapter one: *So that he could not openly enter the city.* In these, the words are not to be changed, but the sense of the words is to be sought. In Judea he "could not" stay, because he did not wish the time of his passion to be brought forward. In Mark, he "could not" perform many miracles, because the unbelief of men stood in the way. Moreover, he calls "Judea" here not the whole region of the Jews, in which Galilee also was, but that part which encompasses the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin.</margin>

<margin>2 **Scenopegia**] <note>original: "Σκηνοπηγία"</note> Scenopegia. This compound Greek word is named from the "fixing of tents." Our people wrongly add an aspiration <note>note: an "h" sound</note> which the Greek word rejects.</margin>

<margin>3 **And he himself seeks to be in public**] <note>original: "καὶ ζητεῖ αὐτὸς ἐν παῤῥησίᾳ εἶναι"</note>, that is, *and he seeks to be in liberty, that is, to speak freely and boldly*. Although according to Chrysostom's interpretation, "in public" <note>original: "παῤῥησίᾳ"</note> seems less clearly used for "being famous," because his kinsmen judged that it would lead to his glory if he revealed himself to the world. Furthermore, whether the phrase "in public" <note>original: "in palam"</note> is found among approved authors, just as "in presence" <note>original: "in coram"</note>, I leave for others to examine.</margin>

<summary>This page concludes Jesus' "Bread of Life" discourse, noting the departure of many disciples, and begins Chapter 7 where Jesus remains in Galilee to avoid threats in Judea. The extensive scholarly notes debate whether Jesus "did not wish" or "was not able" to stay in Judea, analyzing the nuance of divine power versus human action.</summary>

<margin>4</margin> *For I shall not go up]* <note>original: "ἐγὼ οὔπω ἀναβαίνω"</note>, that is, *I am not yet going up*. Otherwise, he might have seemed to have lied, having denied he would go up, yet he went anyway. <term>Chrysostom</term> <note>An influential 4th-century preacher and theologian</note> clearly pointed this out, lest our authority seem trivial to anyone. <term>Cyril</term> <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century bishop</note> reads, *I do not go up*, explaining that by this speech he signified the ceremonies of the Law were to be abolished, but only gradually. He went up, therefore, and yet did not "go up" in the sense of appearing publicly. In the manuscripts of Donianus it was written, *For I shall not yet go up*. Again, in an ancient manuscript held at Louvain in the College of the Martinensian Canons, the Constance codex agreed.
<margin>5</margin> *Much murmuring]* <note>original: "γογγυσμὸς πολύς"</note>, that is, *much grumbling*, or *much murmur*, as <term>Augustine</term> <note>The famous 4th-century Latin philosopher and theologian</note> reads it.

<note>The following notes are scholarly annotations regarding the textual variants and interpretations of the preceding verses.</note>

...you may think these words were transcribed here by some scholar comparing passages, and soon after brought into the main text by a careless person, since neither Augustine nor Chrysostom touch upon this fragment in their Commentaries.

<margin>15</margin> *Is he about to go into the dispersion of the nations*] <term>Ἑλλήνων</term> <note>original: Hellēnōn</note>, that is, *of the Greeks*, though he sometimes uses it for any nations whatsoever. As a little later, *to teach the Nations*, <term>ταὶς Ἕλληνας</term> <note>original: tais Hellēnas</note>, that is, the *Greeks*.

<margin>16</margin> *He who believes in me, as the Scripture says*] John Chrysostom <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his preaching</note> punctuates this so that "as the Scripture says" refers to the phrase "believes in me," and that which follows—"rivers of living water shall flow from his belly"—are the words of Christ, and not from the Scripture. Thus the sense is: "The Scripture warns that I should be believed in, for it testifies concerning me. Therefore, he who believes in me, according to what the Scripture warns, it shall be that he, having conceived by my Spirit, shall pour forth rivers of effective doctrine." Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine biblical exegete</note> relates this even more clearly, advising that we distinguish it thus: "he who believes in me," as the Scripture says; and with a period placed there, let "rivers from his belly etc." follow. It is as if he warns that he must be believed because the Scriptures command this, rather than because of miracles. Chrysostom fled to this distinction because those words which follow are nowhere read in the Divine Letters. Although Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a 14th-century Franciscan teacher</note> thinks they are quoted from Solomon, following, I believe, the authority of Jerome, who in his prologue to the Pentateuch indicates this place is not in the books translated from the Seventy <note>The Septuagint</note>, but must be sought from the Hebrew fountains. He openly affirms the same in the prologue to Chronicles. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> guesses the place is in Proverbs chapter five: *Let your fountains be derived abroad, and divide your waters in the streets*. Truly, the facts themselves refute this guess. For since the translation of the Seventy differs nothing here from our Church Edition <note>The Vulgate</note>, it follows that either this is not the place Jerome had in mind, or the translation used by the Church does not correspond to the Hebrew truth. For the Greeks read thus: <note>original: Ὑπερεκχεῖσθω σοι τὰ ὕδατα ἐκ τῆς σῆς πηγῆς, εἰς δὲ τὰς πλατείας διαπορευέσθω τὰ σὰ ὕδατα</note>, that is, *Let the waters from your source be poured out for you, and let your waters be channeled into the streets*. Therefore, one must either agree with Chrysostom or seek another passage. Indeed, even Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo</note> so explains this passage as to attribute these words to Christ: "he who believes in me." For he writes in this manner: >Whence the Lord said, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink, and he who believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly," the Evangelist consequently explained, saying...
Augustine makes the Lord the speaker; there is no mention of quoted Scripture. Furthermore, as for Carrensis <note>Hugo de Sancto Caro</note> wishing to change "living water" into "living boundary" <note>original: finitem vivum</note> on the authority of Chrysostom, he himself should see what he means by that. For you will find nothing of this sort in Chrysostom; rather, he quotes from another place: *It shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life*. Finally, it is beyond controversy that this part, "rivers from his belly," does not pertain to Christ, but to the believing man. Otherwise the speech would be incomplete.

<margin>17</margin> *The Spirit was not yet given*] For "given" <note>original: datus</note>, the Greek has "holy" <note>original: sanctus</note>, and "given" is not added. Furthermore, someone showed at the first face of the speech, as if the Holy Spirit at one time did not exist, and made "given" instead of "holy." And yet there was no danger. For he does not deal with the substance of the Holy Spirit, but with that gift and inspiration by which the Apostles were suddenly changed into other men. And that can almost be

<column-break/>

<margin>D</margin> gathered from Chrysostom's words. Although in his work "Spirit given" is found once or twice, as it is in Theophylact, agreeing with even the oldest Latin copies. Therefore, I pronounce nothing on this matter, except that in the Greek codices it is constantly written, *for the Holy Spirit was not yet*. Certainly Theophylact, whose copy is held by the Preachers at Basel, clearly reads *Holy Spirit*, and interprets it as "was not, that is, was not given." Indeed, if anyone reads Augustine's Commentary more attentively, he will find that he himself read just as we find written in the Greek volumes. Even if the Scribe repeatedly mixes in "given." For he raises the question thus: >But what is this that he says, "The Spirit was not given, because Jesus was not yet glorified"? The understanding is evident. For it was not that the Spirit of God was not with God, but he was not yet in those who had believed in Jesus. For the Lord Jesus so arranged not to give them this Spirit of which we speak except after his resurrection, and this not without cause.
And soon he raises another question: how can it be denied that the Spirit of God was in the Saints, when we read that the Prophets, Simeon, and the widow Anna were not lacking the Holy Spirit; that Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit; and that the <margin>E</margin> Holy Spirit descended upon the Virgin Mother. To which he responds that it was indeed the same Spirit, but the manner of giving was different. If Augustine had read "given," there would have been no room for the first question. Nor does Origen <note>A 3rd-century scholar and theologian</note> seem to have read otherwise. For he writes: >For the Holy Spirit had not yet come upon any of those believing in Jesus, as John testifies.
You hear "Holy Spirit"; there is no mention of "given." 
Indeed, Saint Jerome in his letter to Hebidia, question 9, cites this place such that "given" is superfluous; for he says, adding: *not that there was no Holy Spirit, etc.* If "given" had been added, there would be no need to address the question. I think the first writing had neither "given" nor "holy," but "holy" was added by the Greeks and "given" by our people. In the Latin Constance codex, "given" was written by a more recent hand in the space between the lines. Chrysostom, in his Homilies on the Acts of the Apostles, reads, *for the Spirit was not yet*. It should also be noted that among the Greeks the article is not added here, but it is <greek>Πνεῦμα ἅγιον</greek> <note>Pneuma hagion</note>, which, as I said, speaks not of the nature of the Spirit, but of the Spirit's power, and thus sounds like "Spirit was not," that is, the disciples were still carnal.

<margin>18</margin> *From that crowd therefore*] <greek>Πολλοὶ οὖν ἐκ τοῦ ὄχλου ἀκούσαντες</greek> <note>original: Polloi oun ek tou ochlou akousantes</note>, that is, *Many therefore of the crowd having heard*.

<margin>19</margin> *They are cursed*] <greek>ἐπικατάρατοι</greek> <note>original: epikataratoi</note>, that is, *devoted to destruction or accursed*.

<margin>20</margin> *Search the Scriptures*] "The Scriptures" is not added among the Greeks, <margin>F</margin> nor even in Chrysostom, although it is not entirely wrongly added. However, the same thing can be sought by other conjectures besides the Scriptures. It is only <greek>ἐρεύνησον</greek> <note>ereunēson - "search"</note>. The Greek reading is supported by the holy codices of Donatian and Constance.

<margin>21</margin> *From Galilee a Prophet does not rise*] <greek>οὐκ ἐγήγερται</greek> <note>original: ouk egēgertai</note>, that is, *has not arisen*, or *has come forth*, so that you understand no one has come forth. And so Chrysostom reads. For they gather from the past what will be in the future. In Augustine's Commentaries "will rise" is read, but there is added, *But the Lord of the Prophets rose from there, as if he himself read "rose."* I believe, however, the genuine reading is that which the Translator follows.

<margin>22</margin> *And each one returned to his own house*] This clause is not...

<margin>This is not added in the works of Chrysostom, nor even in those of Theophylact.</margin>

<margin>n, 1</margin> **T**he Scribes and Pharisees bring a woman] This story of the adulterous woman is not found in most Greek copies. In some, it was added at the end. Furthermore, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a famous 4th-century preacher</note> makes no mention of this, discussing the Gospel of John and reading this sequence: *Search and see, for a prophet does not rise from Galilee.* Then immediately: *Again Jesus spoke to them, saying, "I am the light of the world," etc.* Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator</note> reads it in the same way, even though he wrote a continuous commentary on the whole Gospel of John. Thus, it is strange that Chrysostom elsewhere—specifically in Homily 60—mentions this story. He writes among other things: *As when they asked whether it was lawful to give tribute to Caesar, and whether the adulteress should be stoned.* Unless, perhaps, we should think that the other instance was added by some studious person. Nevertheless, Saint Augustine both explains this passage in his commentaries and frequently cites it in his works. Moreover, Saint Jerome, in his second dialogue against the Pelagians, though he strongly needed the testimony of this passage (in which case he is even accustomed to bring testimony from the apocrypha), yet in alleging this story, he frankly admits it is not found in all manuscripts: *In the Gospel according to John,* he says, *it is found in many Greek and Latin manuscripts concerning the adulterous woman who was accused before the Lord.* Eusebius of Caesarea, in the third book of his Church History, indicates that this story of the adulterous woman brought before the Lord was added to the Gospel of John from the Gospel which is titled "According to the Hebrews." I believe Eusebius means the apocryphal Gospel of the Nazarenes. Otherwise, if this story were found in the Gospel believed to have been written by Matthew, it should rather have been restored to the place from which it was plucked. Nor would Jerome have ignored such a significant matter. But it could have happened that what was lost from John's Gospel survived in an apocryphal one, or that John added this part to his Gospel later. Thus it came to be that it was held in some manuscripts and not in others. Finally, it is possible that many true things are reported in apocryphal writings. This story, then, was added from true reports and now holds authority—not because it was written in apocrypha, but because Papias heard it from his teacher, and because the Church has approved it as worthy of the Gospel. Therefore, since it is now accepted everywhere, especially among the Latins, we did not wish to move it from its place, especially as we ourselves found this part written in one particular Greek manuscript. And it is clear enough that in the manuscripts used by Lorenzo <note>Likely Lorenzo Valla, the humanist scholar</note>, it was not absent, proved by the fact that he discusses one or two points of this story.

---

<margin>E</margin> —that I am he, you will die in your sins." On the matter of apocryphal texts, many truths may be recorded in them. From such truths, then, this history was added, which now has authority: not because it was written in apocrypha, but because Papias <note>An early 2nd-century bishop and author</note> heard it from his teacher, and because the Church, by consensus, has validated it as worthy of the Gospel. Accordingly, since it is now everywhere received, especially among the Latins, we were unwilling to move it from its place, particularly since we found this part transcribed in one Greek manuscript. It is also clear enough that it was not absent from the manuscripts used by Lorenzo Valla, at least by this argument: that he discusses one or two points of this history.

<margin>z, 2</margin> *Caught in adultery*] <note>original: "κατειλήφθη ἐπ' αὐτοφώρῳ μοιχευομένη"</note>, that is, she was caught in the very act while she was committing adultery. For *phora* <note>original: "Φωρά"</note> means to catch someone in the crime itself. And he calls this kind of catching *autophoron* <note>original: "αὐτόφωρον"</note>.

<margin>s, 3</margin> *Is without sin*] <note>original: "ἀναμάρτητος"</note>. This does not only signify one who has not sinned, but one who *cannot* sin, as Jerome indicated in his dialogues against Pelagius.

<margin>t, 4</margin> *But hearing these things, one after another*] The Greek copies differ: <note>original: "οἱ δὲ ἀκούσαντες, καὶ ὑπὸ τῆς συνειδήσεως ἐλεγχόμενοι, ἐξήρχοντο εἷς καθ' εἷς"</note>, that is: "But when they had heard, and were being convicted by their conscience, they went out one by one." Although Valla reads it differently, and the Aldine Edition <note>A famous early printed edition of the Greek text from Venice</note> has it otherwise.

<margin>s, 5</margin> *From the elders*] Certain Greek manuscripts add here <note>original: "ἕως τῶν ἐσχάτων"</note>, that is, "even to the last ones."

<margin>6</margin> *And remained alone*] <note>original: "κατελείφθη"</note>, that is, he was left behind, or deserted. It is strange why anyone thought they should deviate from the Greek word.

<margin>7</margin> *Perhaps also my Father*] Again, he turned the conjunction *an* <note>original: "αν"</note> into "perhaps," whereas Christ is affirming it rather than calling it into doubt. Augustine, offended by the adverb, warns that "perhaps" here is not the word of one doubting, but of one rebuking.

<margin>8</margin> *You are from below*] <note>original: "ἐκ τῶν κάτω"</note>, that is, from the depths, or from those things that are beneath. Ancient books have: "You are from below." And shortly after: <note>original: "ἐκ τῶν ἄνω"</note>, that is, from the heights, because the article added to the adverb has the force of an adjective.

### GOSPEL CHAPTER VIII

...I told you, therefore, that you will die in your sins. <page-num>25</page-num> They said therefore to him, "Who are you?" And Jesus said to them, "Even what I speak to you from the beginning." <page-num>26</page-num> I have many things to speak and to judge concerning you; but he who sent me is true; and what I heard from him, these things I speak to the world. <page-num>27 28</page-num> They did not understand that he spoke to them of the Father. Jesus therefore said to them, "When you lift up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing from myself, but as my Father taught me, these things I speak. <page-num>29</page-num> And he who sent me is with me; the Father has not left me alone, because I always do the things pleasing to him." <page-num>30 31</page-num> As he spoke these things, many believed in him. Jesus therefore said to the Jews who had believed him, "If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples; <page-num>32</page-num> And you will know the truth, and the truth—
->shall set you free.<-

---

<margin>A</margin>
*9 The beginning, who also speaks]* <note>original: "Principium qui & loquor"</note> "Beginning" is not in the nominative case here <note>the grammatical case for a subject</note>, as if Christ were saying that he himself *is* the Beginning. Nor is it in the accusative case as the divine Augustine thinks—his interpretation doesn't quite fit with the preceding words. Rather, it is an adverb. For the Greeks use the term <term>τὴν ἀρχήν</term> <note>tēn archēn; literally "the beginning"</note> to mean "at first" or "from the start," just as they use <term>τέλος</term> <note>telos</note> to mean "finally" or "lastly" in an adverbial sense, as if the preposition <term>κατὰ</term> <note>kata; meaning "according to" or "at"</note> were understood.

Furthermore, the Greek word is not "who" (<term>ὅς</term>), but <term>ὅτι</term> <note>hoti</note>, which means "because" or "that." Even knowing this, the sense in the Greek remains somewhat ambiguous. The meaning could be that when Jesus was asked who he was, he replied: "I will say this first: I am the one speaking with you. For you are unworthy to hear the rest about me." 

Alternatively, if you read <term>ὅτι</term> as "that," as the Greek manuscripts consistently have it—supported by some Latin copies which read, "The beginning, because I also speak to you"—the sense could be: "I am primarily that which I am telling you. I do not explain everything I am to those who are unworthy; I say first that I am sent by the Father and am a herald of life, which I have been telling you for a long time." Indeed, the Greek word <term>ὅτι</term> is versatile; it can be a relative pronoun if you add a punctuation mark (the hypodiastole, <term>ὅ, τι</term>) or a conjunction if you write it as one word (<term>ὅτι</term>). 

In this way, it refers back to what came before: "unless you believe that I am he." For this phrase "I am" is unique to God. Elsewhere he said, "before Abraham was, I am." To those asking "Who are you?", he rightly signaled he was God, responding that "from the start, I am this which I have been telling you all along," however many times he says "I am." 

A third sense can be taken where these words connect to what follows: "I have many things to say of you; primarily because I am even speaking to you at all, a benefit of which you show yourselves unworthy." "I have many things to say of you"—that is, many things for which to accuse and condemn you—and I would have even more to say if I told you who I am, namely both God and man. For that would have only increased their impiety, since the things they had already heard had inflamed them with the plan to kill him. John Chrysostom explains it mostly in this sense, and Theophylact follows him. Both take it to mean that Christ did not deign to answer their question, "Who are you?", as they were more worthy to hear what they themselves were—namely impious, rebellious, and wicked—than to hear who Christ was, whom they were insulting. 

To make this clearer to the reader, I will include Chrysostom's words: "The beginning, because I also speak to you; that is, you are certainly unworthy to hear my words and to understand who I am. You always speak to test me, but you do not pay attention to me. And I can now rebuke you in all things." For this is what "I have many things to speak and judge of you" signifies. 

Consider, reader, if it can also be understood this way: that the part "From the beginning, that which I also speak to you" belongs to what preceded: "you will die in your sins," etc. Primarily because of this very fact that I am speaking to you. As for what the manuscripts support, I see it read conveniently this way: <term>Τὴν ἀρχὴν ὅτι καὶ λαλῶ ὑμῖν</term>, so the sense is: "From the beginning I am he who also speaks to you." I do not wish to be the author of a new reading, but only to advise the reader in case they find something in reliable manuscripts. Furthermore, the addition of "In the beginning," as if he were about to add more, relates to what follows: "I have many things to say and judge concerning you."

However, the divine Augustine twists this passage to mean that the words "Who are you?" are the same as if they had said, "Who do you say you are?" or "Who do we believe you are?" And as if they had asked this, Christ replied: "The Beginning, because I also speak to you." Do you want to know what you should believe? Believe that I am the Beginning. I wish this interpretation were as fitting as the frequency with which he insists upon and repeats it, softening with his assertion what was rather harsh in reality. Although he certainly realized that "beginning" in this place was in the feminine gender and the accusative case. If he had realized this, without any stumbling block, he would have immediately pronounced that to "Who are you?", the answer was: "I am the beginning." 

Yet it does not escape me that Ambrose cites this passage according to Augustine's opinion in his book *On the Six Days of Creation*, chapter two: "As," he says, "in the Gospel the Son of God, to those saying to him, 'Who are you?', replied, 'The Beginning, who also speaks to you.'" And again I ask: "And that in the Gospel especially, where the Lord, being asked who he was, replied, 'The Beginning, which I also speak to you.'" Likewise in *On the Faith*, book three, chapter four: "Nor does any question remain regarding the 'beginning,' since when asked in the flesh, 'Who are you?', he replied, 'The Beginning, who also speaks to you.'" Ambrose did not consult the Greek, and therefore felt no hesitation. Augustine, because he did consult it, is troubled; but to seek the accusative case here is plainly difficult, and noted by none of the Greeks. It seems even more forced what he adds: "who also speaks to you." For I gather from the sense that he who read this, read it as "because" rather than "who." For he says: "And he added: Because I also speak to you; that is, because having become humble for your sake, I descend to these words. For if the Beginning remained with the Father as it is, and did not take the form of a servant, and a man did not speak to men, how would they believe him, since—

<column-break/>

—if you do not believe that I am he, you will die in your sins." <page-num>25</page-num> They said therefore to him, "Who are you?" And Jesus says to them, "In the first place, that which I also speak to you." <page-num>26</page-num> I have many things to speak and judge concerning you; but he who sent me is true; and what I heard from him, these things I speak in the world. <page-num>27</page-num> They did not know that he had spoken to them of the Father. <page-num>28</page-num> Jesus therefore said to them, "When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing from myself, but just as the Father taught me, these things I speak. <page-num>29</page-num> And he who sent me is with me; the Father has not left me alone, because I always do what is pleasing to him." <page-num>30</page-num> While he was speaking these things, many believed in him. <page-num>31</page-num> Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him, "If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples; <page-num>32</page-num> And you will know the truth, and the truth—
->shall set you free.<-

---

<margin>C</margin>
—weak hearts cannot hear the intelligible Word without a sensible voice? Therefore," he says, "believe that I am the beginning, because so that you might believe, I not only am, but I also speak to you." From these words it is clear enough that Augustine read "because" <note>Latin: quia</note> and not "who" <note>Latin: qui</note>; especially since he relates this in the book *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* in this way: "The Beginning, which I also speak to you," as we just cited from Ambrose. 

Truly, if it is permissible to disagree with such great men, neither interpretation is proven to me. Ambrose, while occupied with other matters, cites this passage. Augustine diligently brought forward what then came to his mind; he would have changed his opinion, if I am not mistaken, if he had looked closer at the matter, or if he had searched through the Greek commentaries. Although he cites this passage of John for that opinion elsewhere frequently, as in the third chapter of the book against the adversary of the law <unclear>nomou</unclear>: gathering and demonstrating from here that Christ is rightly called "the beginning." 

And it seems to me that Augustine is sometimes a little more persistent in defending things he has said once than the matter requires. If Greek letters had been as sweet to this boy as Roman ones were, and if he had not later as an old man deplored his youthful distaste for them, he would have handled the Divine Letters more successfully, aided by Greek books. I wonder more at Ambrose, who knew Greek beautifully, and who usually draws his interpretation of the Sacred Volumes from the Greek commentaries, yet here consents with Augustine, and teaches from this passage that Christ is rightly called "the beginning," both elsewhere and in the third book of *On the Faith*, chapter four. 

Indeed, it should also be noted that neither Chrysostom nor Theophylact found anything offensive in this passage, whereas Augustine was troubled; I suppose because the Greeks recognized the form of the Greek speech and knew that <term>τὴν ἀρχὴν</term> was placed in the role of an adverb, just as <term>πρὸ ἀρχῆς</term> <note>pro archēs</note> means "by no means," and <term>τέλος</term> <note>telos</note> means "finally." Furthermore, as Chrysostom's authority is heavy for me, so his interpretation seems—

<margin>D</margin>
—less forced. One hesitation could still remain: whether <term>τέλος</term> or <term>ἀρχήν</term>, whenever they have the force of an adverb, are usually used by authors with the article placed before them. But Gregory Nazianzen used it in this manner in his *Sermon on Easter*: "You shall not swear falsely, like him: but you, do not even swear at all [from the beginning]." And Galen in his booklet *On the Best Way of Teaching*: "But I do not think they would even wish to be taught at all [from the beginning]." 

Now Augustine also labors over how Christ is called the "beginning," since being from another <note>i.e., being begotten by the Father</note> conflicts with the logic of being a "beginning." For the Father is called the Beginning simply and absolutely. I say absolutely, not perfectly, since this title applies perfectly to the Son as well, but in such a way that nothing can be named of which he is not the beginning. For the Father is the beginning of all things, both created and uncreated. The Son certainly cannot be called the beginning in part, nor of the whole Deity, as Augustine realized. 

<margin>E</margin>
Although Paul in the *Epistle to the Colossians* calls him "the beginning" absolutely, he adds "the firstborn from the dead," and a little earlier he had said "the firstborn of all creation." As for what is said in the *Apocalypse* <note>the Book of Revelation</note>, "the beginning and the end," it is established that this must be understood as Christ being the start and the consummation of the Church, which he established at his first coming and will perfect at his second. This passage was the source of fierce slanders. Since we have answered these abundantly, if I am not mistaken, in a booklet published once and again, and the matter cannot be repeated in a few words, I would not wish to burden this volume further. Let anyone who wishes to know more precisely seek it there.

<margin>F</margin>
*10 Because he called his Father God]* Ancient manuscripts have: "because he told them of the Father." For in the Constance manuscript, some unknown person had added "God" with a recent hand, even though it was not in the text. The Greeks have it thus: <term>ὅτι τὸν Πατέρα αὐτοῖς ἔλεγεν</term>, "that he spoke to them of the Father," and "God" is not added. The sense seems to be this: the Jews did not understand, when Jesus spoke of the Father, what he was calling the Father; for it seemed to signify something other than what is commonly called Father. Nor could they have been ignorant that he was speaking of the Father, since a little earlier he speaks clearly of his Father. Indeed, this interpretation, being the simplest, will perhaps be most approved by the learned: that we take it as Christ telling them that the Father is God, in place of what it was, that he was speaking concerning God the Father. Chrysostom seems to have understood it in this way: "While he said many things about his Father, they did not understand that he was speaking of the Heavenly Father, since they held him to be a simple man." For this color of speech is also accepted: "I say this one," for "I speak concerning this one."

*11 You will truly be my disciples]* The Greeks read <term>ἐστε</term> <note>este</note>, that is, "you are"; the translator seems to have read <term>ἔσεσθε</term> <note>esesthe</note>, "you will be." Just as it is read in several copies today. And likewise a little later, "you will truly be free," <term>ὄντως ἐλεύθεροι ἔστε</term>, that is, "you are truly free."

*12 And the truth shall set you free]* <term>ἐλευθερώσει</term> <note>eleutherōsei</note>, that is, "shall make you free." Divine Augustine also noted the emphasis of the Greek word in this place. For in Latin, those are said to be "liberated" who are withdrawn from danger or disease, but the Greek word pertains to "liberty," which is opposed to—
<meta>catchword: slavery.</meta>

<summary>This page analyzes Jesus’s response to the Jews regarding his identity in John 8:25-32, debating whether the Greek "tēn archēn" describes Christ as "the Beginning" or simply refers to him speaking "from the start." Erasmus critiques Augustine and Ambrose for their reliance on Latin translations over original Greek grammar, arguing for a more contextual, adverbial reading.</summary>

...[set free]. Likewise, for the Latins, a man is called "free" <note>original: "liber"</note> if he has escaped danger, but the Greek word <note>original: "eleutheros"</note> suggests one who is noble-born and subject to no servitude. The resentment of the Jews, saying "we have never served anyone," shows this to be the case.
<margin>13</margin> **My word has no place in you** [οὐ χωρεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν], that is, it finds no room in you because you are not capable of receiving it.
<margin>14</margin> **And you do what you have seen with your father**] Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Church Father</note>, cited in the *Catena Aurea* <note>A "Golden Chain" of coordinated commentaries by Church Fathers</note>, reads "do" as a command [do it!] instead of a statement of fact [you are doing it], because the Greek word **ποιεῖτε** can mean either. Yet it is not clear that Chrysostom intended this from his own interpretation, which is as ambiguous as the text itself. It cannot be certain what Augustine read.
<margin>15</margin> **If you were the children of Abraham**] <note>original: "Εἰ τέκνα τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ ἦτε, τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Ἀβρααμ ἐποιεῖτε"</note> that is, "If you were sons of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham," so that it connects with what follows, *But now you seek to kill me*. A very ancient manuscript had "you do" [indicative] not "do" [imperative]. I believe this was the original reading. For the Lord reasons from reciprocal signs—or as the logicians say, "convertible" terms. "If it is an animal, it feels; if it feels, it is an animal." He sets this definition: A son is one who imitates the father. If you are sons of Abraham, you certainly do his works; if you do them, you are sons; but you do not do them, therefore you are not.

the Devil, but to the **lie** [ψεῦδος]. Chrysostom and Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine commentator</note> interpret it this way, as does Saint Jerome in his explanations of Isaiah, and also Saint Augustine. Thus, while "every man is a liar," the Devil is the father of the lie, as he was the first of all to produce a lie: *You shall be as gods* <note>quoting the Serpent in Genesis 3:5</note>. The Manicheans <note>followers of a dualistic religion that saw the world as a struggle between light and dark</note> surely drew their error from this passage, believing the Devil himself had a father—I suppose a "principle of evil"—as Saint Augustine notes. Now, while Augustine rightly exposes their folly, our interpretation faces a slight obstacle because the Greek adds the article **ὁ πατὴρ** [the father], which points more to a specific person than an abstract concept. Whatever the case, I leave this for the learned reader to discuss.
<margin>18</margin> **Convicts me of sin**] The oldest manuscripts have "convicts" [present tense]. Likewise the Greek, **ἐλέγχει**, so that "convicts" is used for "could convict me"; and he used "convict" to mean "to prove guilty by evidence," not merely "to accuse." For that is what the Greek word means.
<margin>19</margin> **Treated with ignominy**] In some copies it was **ἀτιμάζετε** [you are dishonoring], not the past tense, meaning "you are currently treating me with insult." The ancient versions have "you dishonor," which agrees with certain Greek texts.
<margin>20</margin> **I shall be a liar like you**] From here was transcribed the phrase we noted as added above. For Chrysostom also reads and interprets it in this place.
<margin>21</margin> **Fifty years**] Chrysostom reads "forty," adding as a commentary that Jesus was already nearly approaching that age. That reading would be more convincing to me if only the manuscript were free from error, as I suspect it was corrupted by scribes—especially since Theophylact clearly reads "fifty," adding that it is a matter of curiosity why the Jews preferred to say "fifty" rather than "forty." ### GOSPEL CHAPTER IX.

...indeed occurred to the Jews. For they were not looking so much at the age of Christ as at the length of time that had passed from Abraham until Christ. Nor is there any reason for us to imagine Christ had a weary face due to his labors <note>suggesting he looked older than he was</note>. This is an opinion mentioned by Hugo of Saint-Cher <note>original: "Carrensis", a 13th-century biblical commentator</note>. But, as I said, it is possible that in Chrysostom the scribes of the manuscripts agreed. Saint Irenaeus <note>Bishop of Lugdunum, 2nd century</note>, in Book II, chapters 39 and 40, reads **fifty**, but asserts that the Lord preached the Gospel when he was older than forty; he confirms this partly by the authority of this passage, and partly from those who said they had heard it from the Evangelist John himself. However, Eusebius <note>the "Father of Church History"</note>, in Book III, chapter 39, notes that Papias <note>an early Christian author</note>, a disciple of John the Evangelist, passed down certain things from the Apostle's words because they were not sufficiently understood, which gave others a handle for error. And among these he numbers Irenaeus. He adds that it is clear from Papias's books that the man was of slender wit <note>original: "exigui ingenii"</note>.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>22 Before Abraham was made</margin> <note>original Greek: πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι, "prin Abraam genesthai"</note>, that is, before Abraham was, or had been. Perhaps the Translator had rendered it "had been," which by a scribe's error was changed to "was made." We have translated it, **before Abraham was born**, so that we might distinguish the manner in which Abraham exists from that in which Christ always is. For in this place Augustine "philosophizes" <note>interprets deeply</note> that Abraham is said to be "made" <note>factus</note>, while Christ simply "is" <note>esse</note>. Yet Chrysostom does not philosophize on that point, but only on the fact that regarding **Abraham** he used a verb of the past tense, while regarding **Christ**, he used the present. In this way God speaks of Himself: **I am who I am**.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>23 He hid himself</margin> <note>original Greek: ἐκρύβη, "ekrybe"</note>, that is, he was concealed. Although the Translator expresses the sense correctly, he also avoided ambiguity.

<margin>24 And went out of the temple</margin> After these words, some Greek codices had: *passing through the midst of them, and so passed by* <note>original Greek: "διελθὼν διὰ μέσου αὐτῶν, καὶ παρῆγεν οὕτως"</note>. Since I find these words neither in Chrysostom, nor in Augustine, nor in the ancient Latin copies, I suspect they were added by some studious person from the fourth chapter of Luke: where Jesus escapes the hands of the Jews in a similar way. Someone, therefore, comparing neighboring passages, added to one what was abundant in the other. Then, so that he might connect what follows with the preceding narrative, he interposed *and passed by*, namely slipping away among those who were plotting against his life, followed by *and passing by*. Therefore, we have not feared to
