<margin>1 And Jesus passing by]</margin> *Jesus* is not added in the ancient Latin copies.
<margin>2 This man or his parents]</margin> One should have said "or" <note>original: "an"</note> his parents, not "or" <note>original: "aut"</note>. For *aut* separates, while *an* asks a question, and so Saint Augustine reads it. Furthermore, the Greek word <note>original: ἤ, "e"</note> covers both.
<margin>3 And he smeared]</margin> <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐπέχρησε, "kai epechrese"</note>, that is, he spread it on, or anointed it.
<margin>4 In the swimming-place]</margin> <note>original Greek: εἰς κολυμβήθραν, "eis kolymbethran"</note>, that is, into the pool. For so he had translated it before. However, it sounds like "swimming-place" <note>original: "natatorium"</note>, as we warned before.
<margin>5 Which is interpreted sent]</margin> *Shalach* <note>original Hebrew: שׁלח</note> means to send for the Hebrews, hence *Shiloach* <note>original Hebrew: שׁלוח</note>.
<margin>6 Neighbors who had seen]</margin> The conjunction **and** must be added, *and those who had seen*, according to the ancient and Greek copies. Those who were not neighbors had also seen him.
<margin>7 Because he was a beggar]</margin> <note>original Greek: ὅτι τυφλὸς ἦν, "hoti typhlos en"</note>, that is, because he was blind. Although Augustine reads "beggar" <note>original: "mendicus"</note>, not "blind," and all the very ancient Latin codices I have seen agree. Thus, "beggar" <note>original: "ptochos"</note> pleases me more than "blind" <note>original: "typhlos"</note>, especially since it fits the context. For he was known for that—not just because he was blind, but because he was a public beggar; and Theophylact also reads "beggar."
<margin>8 And he went and I washed]</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἀπελθὼν δὲ καὶ νιψάμενος ἀνέβλεψα</note>, that is: "When I had gone and washed, I received sight."
<margin>9 And I see]</margin> <note>original Greek: καὶ ἀνέβλεψα</note>, that is, and I received sight. And soon after,
<margin>10 How he saw]</margin> <note>original Greek: πῶς ἀνέβλεψεν</note>, that is, how he had received sight.
<margin>11 There was a schism]</margin> *Schisma* <note>original: σχίσμα</note> is a Greek word; he could have translated it as **dissension**. For this is what *schisma* means, whether division or discord. A little later he translates it as "dissension," elsewhere as "tearing" <note>original: "scissura"</note>.
<margin>12 Concerning him who opened thy eyes]</margin> In Greek it is: *because he opened* <note>original: ὅτι ἤνοιξεν</note>, so the sense is: "Who do you think he is, based on the fact that, as you say, he opened your eyes?"
<margin>13 Let him speak for himself]</margin> <note>original Greek: λαλήσει</note>, that is, he will speak, in the future tense.

<header>ACCORDING TO JOHN. CHAPTER X.</header>

14 **To be put out of the synagogue** <note>original Latin: "Extra synagogam fieri"</note>] *Aposynagogos* <note>Greek: ἀποσυνάγωγος</note>, that is, **estranged from the congregation, which people now commonly call excommunicated.**
15 **They spoke evil to him therefore**] This does not mean they prayed for a bad outcome, but *eloidoresan* <note>Greek: ἐλοιδόρησαν</note>, that is, **they reviled or insulted him.**
16 **God does not hear sinners**] Where the translator here used "hear" <note>Latin: "audit"</note>, he soon after translates as "hear favorably" <note>Latin: "exaudit"</note> in the phrase: "if anyone is a worshiper of God and does His will, He hears him favorably." I thought it necessary to point this out so that no one ignorant of the Greek language might think some deep mystery is hidden here, which would lead to ridiculous confusion in trying to explain it. In truth, the Translator chose to play with words, even in a matter more than serious.
17 **He could not do anything**] *Ouk edynato* <note>Greek: οὐκ ἠδύνατο</note>, that is, **he would not have been able**, or **could not.** For "not" he adds "anything," necessarily departing from the Greek words. Otherwise, he who "cannot do nothing" would be able to do something <note>a grammatical note on double negatives in Latin versus Greek</note>.
18 **Your sin remains**] "Therefore" is missing; *he hamartia* <note>Greek: ἡ ἁμαρτία</note>, that is, **your sin therefore**, surely because of the fact that although you are blind, you nevertheless seem to yourselves to be sighted.

—the word *aulen* <note>Greek: αὐλὴ</note> can also apply to other livestock. For *aulen* sometimes signifies a courtyard, sometimes a dwelling, and at other times an enclosure.
2 **This proverb** <note>original Latin: "Hoc proverbium"</note>] *paroimian* <note>Greek: παροιμίαν</note>. "Proverb" seems to be used here in place of "parable," because most proverbs contain an inherent metaphor.
3 **What things he was saying to them**] This passage would have three variations among the Greeks: "they did not understand what he was speaking to them"; or, "they did not know any of the things he was speaking to them." In some manuscripts it was written, *ouk egnosan, tina en ha elalei autois*, that is, **they did not know what things they were which he had spoken to them.**
4 **As many as came**] The Greeks add *pro emou*, that is, **before me.** Yet this might seem to have been added by an interpreter wishing to explain this passage.
5 **I am the good shepherd**] *ho poimen ho kalos* <note>Greek: ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός</note>. Each noun has its own article added: **I am the shepherd, the good one**, or the excellent one.
6 **And it does not pertain to him regarding the sheep** <note>original Latin: "Et non pertinet ad eum de ovibus"</note>] *kai ou melei auto peri ton probaton*, that is, **he does not care for the sheep**, or **the care of the sheep is not his.** For something can "pertain" to us that we nevertheless do not care about.
7 **I am known by mine**] *ginoskomai hypo ton emon* <note>Greek: γινώσκομαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἐμῶν</note>, that is, **I am known by my own**, although I praise what the Translator did <note>Erasmus likely refers to the Latin "a meis," which captures the sense well</note>.

<margin>A</margin> **It behooves me to lead** <note>original: "Oportet me adducere"</note>] *Agagein* <note>Greek: ἀγαγεῖν</note>, that is, **to lead**, which Theophylact interprets as **to gather**; for both flocks were lacking a shepherd.
**There shall be one fold and one shepherd**] First, the ancient beauty of the Greek phrasing has been lost for us, which rested on the words *poimne* and *poimen* <note>Greek: ποιμήνη & ποιμήν</note>, that is, **flock and shepherd**, however it might be rendered, **one flock and one herder**, though for the Greeks *poimne* is more a **flock** than a **fold** <note>enclosed pen</note>, according to Valla. And in some Greek copies the conjunction "and" is not added; it is simply **there shall be one flock, one shepherd**. Although "behold, one shepherd" might seem added, as Chrysostom does not touch on this when explaining the passage, nor even Augustine, though the latter does touch on it in his *Sermon on the words of the Lord according to John XLIX* and the following *L*. Indeed, since he designated one shepherd, nothing remained except for there to be one flock, with Gentiles and Jews conspiring into one religion. Theophylact, however, reads it as we do, **one flock and one shepherd**, and also interprets it so.
19 **A dissension again occurred**] And here the word is *schisma* <note>Greek: σχίσμα</note>.
22 **The Dedication took place**] <note>original: *Encaenia*</note> that is, **the initiation**, to translate word for word, from *kainos* <note>Greek: καίνος</note>, **new**, and *enkainizo* <note>Greek: ἐγκαινίζω</note>, **I renew, I initiate, I dedicate.** A holy day among the Jews in memory of the restored temple, after the long captivity in Persia. It should be written *Encaenia* with the *ae* diphthong, because *kainos* with an *e* <note>epsilon</note> sounds empty to the Greeks. Although I am reluctant to occupy the Reader and fill pages with such trifles, I cannot restrain myself from relating, for interest's sake, what a "beautiful" etymology Hugo of Saint-Cher offers for this word. This pleasant fellow wants the second-to-last syllable written with an *e*, *En-cenia*, which he says is composed of *en*, meaning **in**, and *ness*, meaning **new**, and *ce*, which is an **intensive addition**. It is no wonder some are ignorant of these things. What is a wonder is finding people so impudent that they do not fear to teach with such authority what they do not understand at all.
<margin>B</margin> **You take away our soul** <note>original: "Animam nostram tollis"</note>] Since the Greek is *aireis* <note>Greek: αἴρεις</note>, I wonder why the translator of Chrysostom turned **you take away** into **you destroy**, unless it means **you keep in suspense** here. Only Alcuin in his *Catena* seems to follow the proper sense; for he says, **he might hold [them] in suspense and uncertainty while being admitted, he who came to save souls.**
25 **Tell us plainly** <note>original: "palam"</note>] *Parrhesia* <note>Greek: παῤῥησίᾳ</note>, that is, **freely**, or **candidly.** Though "sincerely" does not translate it badly in this place.
34 **I speak to you**] *Eipon hymin* <note>Greek: Εἶπον ὑμῖν</note>, that is, **I said to you.**
26 **Because you are not of my sheep**] Here the Greeks add, **just as I told you**, *kathos eipon hymin* <note>Greek: καθὼς εἶπον ὑμῖν</note>, although the Latin copies resist this with great consensus. It appears to have been added by some studious person because the same thing had been said a little earlier.

<column-break/>

<margin>C</margin> 28 **They shall not perish**] *kai ou me apolontai* <note>Greek: καὶ οὐ μὴ ἀπόλωνται</note>, that is, **and they may not perish except [if]**, because *apolontai* seems to be placed in the potential mood <note>subjunctive</note>, as can be seen elsewhere: *ei me* <note>Greek: εἰ μὴ</note> doubled and joined to a subjunctive creates a potential mood, or adds the meaning of the future tense.
<margin>D</margin> 29 **What the Father gave me**] The Greek text is different: **My Father who gave to me is greater than all**, *Ho Pater mou hos dedoke moi meizon panton esti* <note>Greek: Ὁ Πατήρ μου ὃς δέδωκέ μοι μείζων πάντων ἐστὶ</note>, or **is the greatest of all.** Indeed, by this argument he proves there is no one who can snatch the sheep from the Father's hands, because he is more powerful to save than the adversary is to snatch away. Chrysostom reads it this way, and Theophylact agrees with him. However, Augustine follows a different reading. And it is an easy slip between the Greek words *meizon* <note>greater, masculine</note> and *meizon* <note>greater, neuter</note>, and *ho* <note>which, neuter</note> and *hos* <note>who, masculine</note>. According to Augustine's reading, it can be understood as referring to the Church, whose adversaries are many, but that little flock is greater in virtue—not of itself, but because the Father gave it to the Son.
<margin>E</margin> 31 **They took up stones therefore**] The Greeks add *palin* <note>Greek: πάλιν</note>, that is, **again.**
35 **And the Scripture cannot be broken**] That which is destroyed is "broken" <note>or dissolved/loosened</note>, and that which is explained is "broken." However, the entire speech is somewhat obscure and confused. Therefore, it could be rendered more clearly thus: **If he called those gods to whom the word of God was made, and the Scripture cannot be broken?**—so that this is a question. Then let us add: **Of me, whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, do you say that I blaspheme, because I said, I am the Son of God?** Or in this way: **And the Scripture cannot be broken**, understand, **concerning him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world.** Then, with a second beginning, let it follow: **Do you say that I blaspheme, because I said, I am the Son of God?** It can also be understood in this manner: **Is it not written in your Law, I said, You are gods, and the Scripture cannot be broken?** so the sense is: if this is written in the Law, and what is written must be true, etc. Hilary certainly refers it to this sense in his commentary on Psalm 82. Again, in book 4 on the Trinity, section 7: **For since,** he says, **the Law assigned the naming of this name to holy men, and the word of God confirmed it as indissoluble to impart this profession of the name.** Likewise in the Psalm: **But the Lord,** he says, **has freed us from the error of this naming in the Gospels, saying: I said, You are gods, and you are all sons of the Most High.** And he adds: **If therefore he called them gods to whom the words of God were made, and the Scripture cannot be broken—the word of God is indissoluble—he named men as gods.** Thus the speech is to be ordered: **If he called those gods to whom the word of God was made, and because what is written cannot be proven false, how do you say to me, whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, that I blaspheme, because I said I am the Son of God.** Certain codices add the conjunction **and**, and...

<note>Erasmus's Commentary</note>
...you say, it disturbs the sense, and it is not found among the Greeks, nor in the old Latin codices. Cyprian, citing this passage in his fifth book *Against the Jews*, does not add "the Scripture."

<margin>20</margin> *They sought to seize him*] Here too they add <unclear>pàlin</unclear>, that is, "again," because they had attempted the same thing before.

1 **A**ND LAZARUS FROM BETHANY] In Latin it was "the Bethanian," even if the article is not added among the Greeks, "the [one] from Bethany."

2 *And of Martha his sister*] *autēs* <note>Greek: "her"</note>, so that it refers back to Mary, not to Lazarus. Although Lazarus was also their brother. Some codices had "of the sisters," but the Greek and even our older Latin ones disagree.

3 *That the Son of God may be glorified through him*] *di’ autou*, that is, "through it," so that it pertains to the infirmity <note>the sickness</note>, not to Lazarus. And this is how it is read in the more corrected Latin codices, specifically in the Corbeian and Constantian copies. In the Golden Codex it was written "Son of Man" instead of "Son of God," which the Constantian copy agreed with.

4 *Are there not twelve hours*] Although I see this is outside the scope of this work, yet, since it has come up, I wish to point out that the interpretation of the Ancients seems a bit forced to me in this passage, when the natural sense is readily available. Augustine interprets Christ as the Day and the twelve hours as the Apostles. Chrysostom explains it in two ways: either that nothing is to be feared by those who are conscious of no crime; or that nothing is to be feared in the light, much less by those who adhered to Christ, who was the light of the world. And while there is nothing absurd in these interpretations, it seems simpler to me to take it that Christ said there was no danger yet, for the time of his death was not yet present. Just as in Luke 13, he replied to the Pharisees who warned him that Herod wanted to kill him: "I perform cures today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am finished." And he calls the time of his passion "the power of darkness" and "the hour of the wicked." The day has its own hours, and it does not become shorter or longer by our will; I too have a prescribed time in which I must

<note>Commentary continued</note>
...carry out the business of redeeming the world. The malice of the Jews cannot anticipate that, therefore there is nothing for you to fear for me. Furthermore, he calls that time of his "the day" elsewhere: "Abraham desired to see my day; he saw it and was glad." Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator</note> is not far from this opinion, calling the "day" the time that preceded the passion, and the "night" the time when he was captured. And for us, only the equinoctial day has exactly twelve hours; at other times it has either more or fewer. But as I said before, I think the hours among the Jews were unequal <note>temporal hours</note>; yet twelve hours always passed between sunrise and sunset, and the night—whether at its longest or shortest—was divided into the same number of hours. Among us, who have equal hours, a day might sometimes have only eight hours, and sometimes sixteen. Nor are days and nights of the same length in all regions. Furthermore, those who used unequal hours took their certainty from midday, which is the fixed point <note>status</note>, corresponding to the Greek *mesēmbria* <note>noon</note>. I call them unequal hours not because the hours of the day are unequal to the hours of the night, but because they are unequal to themselves day by day. For example, today's hours will be longer tomorrow until the summer solstice, and the night hours shorter. From midday, then, which is the fixed point, the dimension is taken (rather than the start of the day), so that the morning parts are divided into six parts, and the afternoon into the same. Likewise from the middle of the night.

5 *And let us die*] "that we may die" <note>Latin: *ut moriamur*; Greek: *hina apothanōmen*</note>, as the ancient copies agree.

6 *Many of the Jews had come to Martha*] <note>Greek: *tas peri Marthan kai Marian*</note>. Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a humanist scholar</note> did not recognize the form of the Greek idiom here, where they say "those around Plato" to mean Plato himself, or "those around Epicurus" for Epicurus himself. For they were not visiting those who were *around* them, but the women themselves in their constant mourning, which the following words clearly prove: "to console *them* concerning their brother." Luke used a similar form of speech in Chapter 13 of the Acts of the Apostles.

7 *Certainly Lord*] <note>Greek: *Nai Kyrie*</note>, which elsewhere he translates as "even so."

8 *I believe that you are*] We have frequently reminded that in words of this kind pertaining to emotion, the past tense is often used...

->...in place of the present, <note>original: γίγνεται</note>, *I have rejoiced* <note>original: gavisi sum</note> instead of *I rejoice* <note>original: gaudeo</note>, <note>original: δεδείκει</note>, *I have feared* <note>original: metui</note> instead of *I fear* <note>original: metuo</note>, <note>original: ἤλπικα</note>, *I have hoped* <note>original: speravi</note> instead of *I hope* <note>original: spero</note>. Therefore we did not fear [to use] *I believed* <note>original: credidi</note> for *you believe* [or] *he who is coming* <note>original: ventore credis</note>.<-

9 **Who into this world** ] "This" <note>original: hunc</note> is not added in the Greek, <note>original: εἰς τὸν κόσμον</note>, that is, *into the world*. Nor is it <insert>F</insert> *had come* <note>original: venisset</note>, but *the one coming* <note>original: ὁ ἐρχόμενος</note>, that is, *coming*, or *who comes*, or, *that Christ who was to come into the world*.

10 **Saying in silence** ] How could one call while silent? In Greek it is <note>original: λάθρα</note>, that is, *secretly* <note>original: clanculum</note>.

11 **She, as she heard, rose** ] <note>original: ἐγείρεται</note>, *she rises*; and so we see it written in the ancient Latin codices. And the verb in the present tense is more graceful.

12 **And came** ] Likewise in the present tense, <note>original: ἔρχεται</note>, *she comes*. And "castle" <note>original: castellum</note> here signifies a *small town* or *village*, lest anyone imagine a palace or a tyrant's fortress.

13 **He already stinks** ] <note>original: ἤδη ὄζει</note>, that is, *he already smells*. This word is ambiguous among the Greeks, and "smells" <note>original: olet</note> is more modest than "stinks" <note>original: foetet</note>.

14 **Bound hands and feet with bands** ] This is a synecdoche <note>rhetorical device where a part represents the whole</note> in Greek. And "bands" <note>original: instritis</note> is <note>original: κειρίαις</note> in Greek, which are burial bonds.

15 **With a sudarium** ] The Evangelist, writing in Greek, used a Latin word <note>sudarium: a sweat-cloth or handkerchief</note>, which he also does elsewhere.

16 **Therefore the High Priests and Pharisees gathered a council** ] In this place, in some Greek codices, we see added <note>original: κατὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ</note>, that is, *against Jesus*, but I suspect that was added from another Evangelist.

17 **Since he was High Priest** ] <note>original: Ἀρχιερεὺς</note>, that is, *Summus Sacerdos* <note>Highest Priest</note>. And again, *but since he was High Priest*, <note>original: Ἀρχιερεύς ὤν</note>.

18 **They thought to kill him** ] <note>original: συνεβουλεύσαντο</note>, that is, *they were consulting*, or *they were entering into a plan among themselves*.

19 **Among the Jews** ] <note>original: ἐν τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις</note>, that is, *among the Jews*.

20 **Which is called Ephraim** ] The Greeks read <note>original: Ἐφραΐμ</note>. And so Jerome reports in *Hebrew Places*. In Chrysostom, however, by some chance, <note>original: Ἐθραΐα</note> is read instead of <note>original: Ἐφραΐμ</note>, unless perhaps the name of that place is pronounced in various ways. For Jerome also, in the entry for *Ephren*, seems to indicate that Ephraim and Ephron are the same.

<note>The following notes provide a scholarly commentary on the translation and linguistic choices of the Greek and Latin texts.</note>

1 *A pound of ointment*] <note>original: "libram unguenti"</note> The Greek word used is *litra*. It might seem that the Evangelist turned a Latin word into a Greek one, were it not that Julius Pollux <note>A 2nd-century scholar of Greek vocabulary</note> testifies that the word was used by ancient Greek writers; it is thus more likely that the Latins borrowed the word from the Greeks, changing a single letter.

2 *Of genuine spikenard*] <note>original: "nardi pisticae"</note> This was discussed in the notes on Mark, for both writers use the same words.

3 *Not that he cared about the needy*] <note>original: "ὅτι περὶ τῶν πτωχῶν ἔμελεν αὐτῷ"</note> Meaning "not that he had a concern for the poor." This is similar to the phrase we pointed out a little earlier: "he does not care about the sheep."

4 *And having the money box*] <note>original: "τὸ γλωσσόκομον εἶχε"</note> That is, a *purse*, or rather a *casket* in which money is stored. I believe it was named after *glossa* (tongue), perhaps because such items were shaped like a tongue.

5 *Let her alone*] <note>original: "Ἄφες αὐτὴν"</note> Our oldest manuscripts agree on this. This was said specifically to Judas alone, not to all of them, since it was he who was likely to stop her.

6 *She has kept this for the day of my burial*] The Greek manuscripts differ: <note>original: "εἰς τὴν ἡμέραν τοῦ ἐνταφιασμοῦ μου τετήρηκεν αὐτὸ"</note>, meaning "she has kept this for the day of my burial." She was already anticipating the burial of Christ. Although for "has kept," John Chrysostom <note>An early Church Father and famed orator</note> reads "she will keep," if the translator is not mistaken; for Greek codices were not plentiful. Otherwise, he seems to have read *teresē* (future) instead of *tetērēken* (perfect).

7 *But me you do not always have*] Both verbs are in the present tense: "The poor you always have with you, but me you do not always have," *echete*, *echete*.

<note>E</note> 8 *On the next day*] <note>original: "ἐπαύριον"</note> Which is sometimes translated as "on the other day." It should have been translated as "the day after" or "the following day."

9 *Branches of palms*] <note>original: "τὰ βαΐα τῶν φοινίκων"</note> Properly, *baion* is a palm branch, named because it is not easily plucked, as this tree by nature pushes upward against the hand trying to pull it down. Some illiterate people think this "palm" is the same as the *boxwood* tree, which the common people also call "palm."

10 *Jesus found a young donkey*] <note>original: "Εὑρὼν δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὀνάριον"</note> This could be translated as "Jesus obtained a young donkey." In Greek, the diminutive is neuter in gender, which can be applied to either sex.

<note>F</note> 11 *Behold your king*] This passage is found in Zechariah, chapter nine. However, the Evangelist selected from the prophecy only those things pertaining to this event. For the prophecy first mentions a "female ass": "Behold your king comes to you, righteous and a savior, himself poor, and riding upon an ass and a colt, the foal of an ass." Matthew also relates that Christ sat upon a "female ass." I think the prophecy was not concerned with the sex of the animal, but only wanted it understood that the Messiah's coming would be gentle and humble according to the world. And perhaps, just as daughters are included in the name of "children," female donkeys are included in the name of "colts." We touched upon these matters in the notes on Matthew; "Hosanna" was also discussed elsewhere.

12 *Behold, the whole world has gone after him*] "Whole" <note>original: "totus"</note> is not added in the Greek. Furthermore, in Augustine it is indeed added, but one can guess from his own interpretation that he read it otherwise, for Augustine writes: "Why does the blind crowd envy, because the world goes after him, through whom the world was made?" And Chrysostom says, "He calls the crowd 'the world' in this place." Theophylact <note>A Byzantine biblical commentator</note> says similar things, reading "the world," not "the whole world."

13 *Certain Gentiles*] <note>original: "Ἕλληνες"</note> That is, "Greeks," which is frequently translated as "Gentiles," although Gentiles are usually called *Ethnikoi*.

# GOSPEL CHAP. XIII.

These things Jesus spoke, and departing, he hid himself from them. <margin>37</margin> But although he had done so many signs before them, they did not believe in him, <margin>38</margin> so that the word of Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, which he spoke: "Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" <margin>102 103 39</margin> For this reason they could not believe, because Isaiah said again, <margin>104 40</margin> "He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they should see with their eyes and understand with their heart, and turn, and I should heal them." <margin>105 41</margin> Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke of him. <margin>42</margin> Nevertheless, even among the rulers many believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they did not confess it, lest they should be put out of the synagogue. <margin>43</margin> For they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God. <margin>106 44</margin> Then Jesus cried out and said, "He who believes in me, believes not in me but in Him who sent me. <margin>45</margin> And he who sees me sees Him who sent me. <margin>46</margin> I have come as a Light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me should not remain in darkness. <margin>47</margin> And if anyone hears my words and does not believe, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world. <margin>48</margin> He who rejects me and does not receive my words has that which judges him; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day. <margin>49</margin> For I have not spoken on my own authority; but the Father who sent me gave me a command, what I should say and what I should speak. <margin>50</margin> And I know that His command is everlasting life. Therefore, whatever I speak, just as the Father has told me, so I speak." <margin>XIII. 1</margin> Now before the Feast of the Passover, Jesus knowing that his hour had come that he should depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world...

<meta>catchword: the</meta>

---

<margin>24 Clarify]</margin> *glorify*, that is, make glorious. Likewise in the following: *And I have glorified, and will glorify*, or rather, *And I have illumined, and again I will illumine.*
<margin>25 I will draw all things]</margin> <note>original Greek: "pantas helkysō"</note>, that is, I will draw all people. The Greek manuscripts consistently hold to this form; and **Chrysostom** <note>a 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople</note> interprets it in this sense, that it is understood only regarding men, and the meaning is that not only Jews, but even Greeks and barbarians are to be drawn. However, **Saint Augustine** <note>the 5th-century North African theologian</note> specifically warns that we should read *all things* <note>Latin: "omnia"</note>, not *all people* <note>Latin: "omnes"</note>; for he argues thus: *He did not say "all people," but "all things." For faith is not for all.* Therefore, he did not refer this to the whole of mankind, but to the integrity of creation—that is, spirit, soul, and body, both that which we understand and that which we live, and that which is visible and observable about us. And soon after: *Or if by "all things" we must understand men themselves, we can say "all things predestined for salvation," of which nothing shall perish, as when he speaks of his sheep. Or certainly all types of men, whether in all languages, all ages, all ranks of honor, all professions of arts and letters, or whatever else can be said according to innumerable differences, etc.* **Theophylact** <note>an 11th-century Byzantine commentator</note> agrees with Chrysostom. But to return to the matter at hand: there is a very slight difference in the Greek words *pantas* [all people] and *panta* [all things], and it does not matter much for the meaning, especially since Christ calls every kind of man "all creatures."
<margin>26 Yet a little light]</margin> <note>original Greek: "Eti mikron chronon to phōs meth’ hymōn esti"</note>, that is, "For a little while longer the light is with you," or "for a brief time." So that you do not understand that a "tiny amount of light" remains in them, but rather that Christ, who was the light of the world, would soon withdraw himself; Chrysostom interprets it in this sense, followed by Theophylact. Augustine seems to follow a different reading, interpreting this as the "modicum light" which they understood in their conscience...

<column-break/>

...my servant shall be: if anyone serves me, the Father will honor him. Now my soul is troubled. And <margin>27</margin> what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But for this reason I came into this hour. Father, † illumine <margin>A 24</margin> <margin>28</margin> your name. Then a voice came from heaven, saying, "I have illumined it, and I will illumine it again." The crowd, therefore, which stood <margin>29</margin> and had heard it, said it had been thunder. Others said, "An angel spoke to him." Jesus answered and <margin>30</margin> said, "Not for my sake did this voice come, but for yours. Now is the judgment of this world: now the <margin>31</margin> prince of this world shall be cast out. And I, if I am exalted <margin>32</margin> from the earth, † will draw all things <note>commentary note 25 discusses "all people" vs "all things"</note> to myself." <margin>B 25</margin> <margin>33</margin> Now he said this, signifying by what death he was to die. The crowd answered him, "We have heard from the law <margin>34</margin> that Christ remains forever: and how do you say, the Son of Man must be exalted? Who is this Son of Man?" Jesus therefore said to them, † "Yet for <margin>C 26</margin> <margin>35</margin> a short time the light is with you: walk while you have the light, lest darkness seize you: and he who walks in darkness knows not where he goes. While you <margin>36</margin> have the light, believe in the light, that you may be sons of light." These things Jesus spoke, and departing he hid himself from them. But though † he had done so many signs before them, <margin>D 27</margin> <margin>37</margin> they did not believe in him: that the word of Isaiah the prophet <margin>38</margin> might be fulfilled, which he said, † "Lord, who has believed our <margin>E 28</margin> report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" Therefore they could not believe, because again said <margin>39</margin> Isaiah, "He blinded their eyes, † and hardened their heart, <margin>F 29</margin> <margin>40</margin> lest they see with eyes, and understand with heart, and be converted, and I heal them." Isaiah said these things <margin>41</margin> when he saw his glory, and spoke of him. Jesus however <margin>44</margin> cried out and said, "He who believes in me, believes not in me, but in him who sent me. And he who sees me, sees him <margin>45</margin> who sent me. I have come as a light into the world, so that everyone <margin>46</margin> who believes in me may not remain in darkness. And if anyone <margin>47</margin> hears my words, † and has not believed, I do not <margin>31</margin> judge him. For I did not come to judge the world, but to save the world. † He who rejects me and does not receive <margin>32</margin> <margin>48</margin> my words, has one who judges him. The word that I have spoken, that will judge him on the last day. Because <margin>49</margin> I have not spoken from myself: but he who sent me, the Father, he gave me a command, what I should say and what I should speak. Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus knowing <margin>XIII. 1</margin> that his hour had come, to pass from this world to the Father, when he had loved his own who were in the world...

<meta>catchword: to</meta>

---

...regarding what he said about being "lifted up from the earth," since they already had it in mind to lift him onto a cross, or because they understood that Christ remains forever. Nor is it "in you," but <note>original Greek: "meth' hymōn"</note>, that is, "with you," so that he might be understood as departing shortly. Although, to speak frankly, I think "time" <note>original Greek: "chronon"</note> was added by someone among the Greeks who wanted to make the passage an explanation, especially since the same John speaks in a similar way in the next chapter: *Yet a little while and you see me no more.* And hence surely is the handle of the error, because he did not add "time"; otherwise there would have been no room for a slip. And yet the article <note>original Greek: "to phōs"</note> prevented "little" from being applied to the light; if he had meant "a little bit of light," he would have said *mikron phōs* [without the article].
<margin>27 So many signs]</margin> <note>original Greek: "tosauta"</note>. The sense can be "so many signs," or "so great."
<margin>28 Lord, who has believed our report]</margin> The testimony is found in Isaiah chapter 53, but he cites it according to the **Septuagint** <note>the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> rather than the Hebrew truth. For he added from them "Lord," just as Paul does in his Epistles when bringing forward this same passage. For in the Hebrew it is thus, according to the translator **Jerome**: *Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?* Furthermore, the next testimony, which he brought from the sixth chapter of the same prophet, corresponds neither to the Hebrew nor to the Septuagint edition; the Evangelist merely touched upon the sense. But we have noted something of this elsewhere.
<margin>29 And he hardened their heart]</margin> <note>original Greek: "kai pepōrōken autōn tēn kardian"</note>, that is, "and he blinded their heart." The translator seems to have read *epērōsen*.
<margin>30 Lest they be cast out of the synagogue]</margin> <note>original Greek: "aposynagōgoi genōntai"</note>. Concerning which we advised a little earlier.
<margin>31 And has not kept]</margin> <note>original Greek: "kai mē phylaxē"</note>, that is, "and has not believed." Others seem to have read *kai mē tērēsē*. It matters very little to the sense.
<margin>32 He who scorns me]</margin> <note>original Greek: "athetōn"</note>, "he who rejects"; **Cyprian** <note>a 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage</note> reads it this way.

<meta>This page continues the Gospel of John, transitioning from the end of Jesus' public ministry into the private setting of the Last Supper in Chapter 13. # ACCORDING TO JOHN CHAP. XIII.

<margin>102 1</margin> Before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass out of this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. And during supper, the devil having already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him, <margin>103 3</margin> Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going to God, <margin>104 4</margin> rose from supper and laid aside his garments, and taking a towel, he tied it around his waist. 5 Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples' feet and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded. 6 So he came to Simon Peter, and Peter said to him, "Lord, do you wash my feet?" 7 Jesus answered and said to him, "What I am doing you do not understand now, but you will know after these things." 8 Peter said to him, "You shall never wash my feet!" Jesus answered him, "If I do not wash you, you have no part with me." 9 Simon Peter said to him, "Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head." 10 Jesus said to him, "He who has bathed has no need except to wash his feet, but is entirely clean. And you are clean, but not all of you." 11 For he knew the one who was betraying him; for this reason he said, "Not all of you are clean." 12 So when he had washed their feet and taken his garments and reclined again, <margin>105 13</margin> he said to them again, "Do you know what I have done to you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and you say well, for so I am. <margin>106 14</margin> If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet. 15 For I have given you an example, that <margin>107 16</margin> just as I have done to you, you also should do. Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is an apostle <note>or "one who is sent"</note> greater than the one who sent him. 17 If you know these things, <margin>108 18</margin> blessed are you if you do them. I do not speak concerning all of you; I know whom I have chosen; but that the scripture may be fulfilled, 'He who eats bread with me has lifted up his heel against me.' 19 From now on I tell you before it happens, <margin>109 20</margin> so that when it does happen, you may believe that I am he. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever receives anyone I send receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me." <margin>110 21</margin> When Jesus had said these things, he was troubled in spirit and testified, saying, "Truly, truly, I say to you, that one of you will betray me." <margin>111 22</margin> The disciples looked at one another, <margin>111 23</margin> uncertain of whom he spoke. Now there was reclining at the table one of his disciples in the bosom of Jesus, whom Jesus loved. 24 So Simon Peter gestured to this one to ask who it might be of whom he spoke. 25 That one, leaning back against the chest of Jesus, said to him, "Lord, who is it?" 26 Jesus answered, "It is he to whom I shall give the piece of bread after I have dipped it." <margin>112 27</margin> And having dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas Iscariot, son of Simon.

---

<margin>1</margin> **Supper being ended** <note>Latin: *Coena facta*; Greek: *deipnou genomenou*</note>] Saint Augustine thinks that "ended" or "made" should be understood here as *begun* or *prepared*, just as in the Holy Scriptures a day is said to be "made" when the sun has risen, not when the day is finished. For later we read that he reclined and handed the morsel to Judas. Furthermore, in ancient times those about to dine would wash, unless perhaps what was done later is seen to pertain to the second course <note>the dessert or final portion of the meal</note>.

<margin>2</margin> **The Father gave all things to him**] Why "to him" rather than "to himself," and "gave" <note>past tense</note> rather than "had given"?

<margin>3</margin> **And he puts aside his garments** <note>Greek: *ta himatia*</note>] He means the outer garments, lest anyone think Jesus was completely naked when he washed the disciples' feet. The same word appears in chapter nineteen in the same way, "carrying the crown of thorns and the purple garment" <note>Greek: *to porphyroun himation*</note>, where here it undoubtedly signifies the royal cloak.

<margin>4</margin> **When he had taken a towel** <note>Greek: *labōn lention*</note>] That is, "and having taken a linen cloth." It is a marvel whence this Latin word <note>*linteum*</note> flowed down to the Jews or Greeks. However, the Evangelists do this frequently.

<margin>5</margin> **And he began to wash** <note>Greek: *ērxato niptein*</note>] Since it is said he "began," and shortly after follows, "When he therefore came to Peter," Chrysostom suspects he started with Judas himself, the more to call him back from his intended crime by this honor. But Augustine disagrees, not enduring that anyone should be preferred before the prince of the Apostles. To me, however, Chrysostom’s suspicion is more pleasing. For I do not think Christ observed this "primacy" in ceremonies of this kind, especially since at that time he was acting to tear out all desire for ambition from the souls of his followers. Theophylact agrees with Chrysostom. Origen, who is cited in the *Catena* <note>a "chain" of patristic commentaries</note>, thinks Christ came to Peter only after all others were washed. Chrysostom thinks it happened by Judas's impudence that he was washed first, but after him, Jesus came to Peter; he argues this by the fact that only Peter refused, and surely the others would have refused too, had they not been terrified by the example of Peter's rebuke. But Origen attributes this to Peter’s fervor, that he alone shuddered at the washing.

<margin>6</margin> **You shall have no part** <note>Greek: *ouk echeis*</note>] That is, "you do not have," using a verb in the present tense.

<column-break/>

[This column contains the Latin translation of John 13:1-27, which corresponds to the English narrative provided above.]

---

<margin>7</margin> **Teacher and Lord**] In the Gospels, these are in the nominative case used as a vocative <note>direct address</note>: *ho Didaskalos kai Kyrios*. For they even called him this when he was absent, as John says, "It is the Lord." Therefore, there would be no harm in translating it "the Teacher and the Lord," and the sense would be fuller.

<margin>8</margin> **Wash one another's**] In Greek *allēlōn*, that is, "mutually" or "one of the others." Although this could also be defended according to Laurentius <note>Valla</note>, the censor of language.

<margin>9</margin> **Nor is an apostle greater than he who sent him**] There is no wordplay in the Evangelist's Greek words, but in the concepts. For "Apostle" <note>Greek: *apostolos*</note> is derived from the verb "to send" <note>Greek: *apostellein*</note>, which specifically means to send with mandates, whereas *pempein* means to send in any manner. One could translate it "messenger" <note>Latin: *proxeneciam*</note>; a legate is not greater than the one who delegated him.

<margin>10</margin> **He will lift up against me**] It is "He lifted up" both in the Greek and in our most ancient manuscripts <note>Greek: *epēren*</note>, making it a verb in the past tense. "He lifted his heel against me." It is taken from the fortieth Psalm <note>Psalm 41 in modern numbering</note>; he does not take care to cite it word-for-word. For the Hebrew has it thus, according to Jerome's translation: "But even my man of peace, in whom I had trust, who ate my bread, lifted his heel against me." The Septuagint translated it in this manner: "For even the man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who eats my breads, magnified the supplanting against me."

<margin>11</margin> **From now on** <note>Greek: *ap’ arti*</note>] "After this," or rather "From this time," unless the adverb "from now on" may be referred to the following words "it happens" and "you may believe."

<margin>12</margin> **He testified** <note>Greek: *emartyrese*</note>] That is, he bore witness.

<margin>13</margin> **Simon Peter therefore gestured to this one**] The Greek says: "Simon Peter gestured to this one to ask who it might be of whom he spoke." "Gestured" <note>Greek: *neuei*</note> is in the present tense.

<margin>14</margin> **Dipped bread** <note>Greek: *psōmion*</note>] That is, a morsel or a small bite.

<margin>15</margin> **He gave to Judas**] He gives <note>present tense</note>, *didōsin*, and "having dipped" <note>Greek: *embapsas*</note>, so that you understand Christ himself did the dipping. "Judas son of Simon Iscariot" <note>Greek: *Iouda Simōnos Iskariōtē*</note>, so that "Iscariot" is in the dative case matching Judas, and Judas is understood as the son of Simon.

Erasmus's commentary explores the order in which the disciples were washed and analyzes the Greek etymology of "apostle" and the use of Latin loanwords like "linteum" in the New Testament.</summary>

# THE GOSPEL

<margin>27</margin> And after the morsel, Satan entered into him. Then Jesus said to him, “What you are going to do, do quickly.” <margin>28</margin> But no one reclining at the table knew why he said this to him. <margin>29</margin> For some thought, since Judas had the money box, that Jesus was saying to him, “Buy what we need for the feast,” or that he should give something to the poor. <margin>30</margin> Having taken the morsel, he immediately went out. And it was night. <margin>31</margin> When he had gone out, Jesus said, “Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him. <margin>32</margin> If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and will glorify him at once. <margin>33</margin> Little children, I am with you only a little longer. You will seek me; and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come,’ so now I say to you. <margin>34</margin> A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another; even as I have loved you, that you also love one another. <margin>35</margin> By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” <margin>36</margin> Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered him, “Where I am going you cannot follow me now; but you will follow afterward.” <margin>37</margin> Peter said to him, “Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.” <margin>38</margin> Jesus answered him, “Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow until you have denied me three times.”

<margin>XIV. 1</margin> And he said to his disciples, “Let not your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me. <margin>2</margin> In my Father’s house are many rooms; if it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you? <margin>3</margin> And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, so that where I am, you may be also. <margin>4</margin> And where I am going, you know, and the way you know.” <margin>5</margin> Thomas said to him, “Lord, we do not know where you are going, and how can we know the way?” <margin>6</margin> Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me. <margin>7</margin> If you had known me, you would have known my Father also; and from now on you do know him and have seen him.” <margin>8</margin> Philip said to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.” <margin>9</margin> Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you so long, and yet you do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father; how can you say, ‘Show us the Father’?”

---

<margin>A</margin> **16** *After the morsel*] <note>original: "Post buccellam"</note> Where the translator previously used the word "bread" twice, he now uses "morsel" <note>buccellam</note>, so that no one should think there is a different word in the Greek. The Greek word <term>psomion</term> <note>ψωμίον</note> properly means a small piece of bread dipped in sauce.

**17** *God will glorify him in himself*] <note>original: "Deus clarificabit eum in semetipso"</note> In Greek: <term>en autō</term> <note>ἐν αὑτῷ</note>. The scripture would have been more accurate if it said *in him* <note>is αὐτῷ</note>, referring to the Father, though I know this distinction is not always observed in the Sacred Books. I suspect the preposition "in" is used here according to the custom of Hebrew speech instead of "through."

<margin>B</margin> **18** *Little children*] <note>original: "Filioli"</note> Some manuscripts had *Teknia* <note>Greek for "children"</note>, while others had the diminutive *Teknia* <note>Greek for "little children"</note>. Cyril seems to have read it as the diminutive. *A little while longer*: in Greek <term>epi mikron</term> <note>ἐπὶ μικρόν</note>, meaning for a short time, which I have noted above.

**19** *By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you love, etc.*] <note>original: "In hoc cognoscent omnes..."</note> This is the wondrous mark by which a Christian is distinguished from others. He did not say: "if you are called by this or that title," "if you wear these or those clothes," "if you eat certain foods," "if you observe such and such ceremonies," or "if you pour out so many prayers," but rather *if you love one another*—and not just in any common way, but *as I have loved you*. Since Christ himself puts this forward as the single and certain mark, is it not inevitable that by our own fault the name of Christ sounds bad among the Pagans? For when they read or hear these things, they see instead that for so many centuries, Christian Prince has fought with Prince, kingdom with kingdom, and city with city in continuous wars—to say nothing of the insane lawsuits before judges and the sharp stabbings of everyone against each other over the most frivolous causes. And while we do these things, we still think ourselves Christians because of our titles and some ceremonies or other.

<margin>C</margin> <insert>**1** *And he said to his disciples*] <note>original: "Et ait discipulis suis"</note> These words were not added in the ancient manuscripts, nor even in all the Greek ones. They seem to have been added by some learned person to smooth out the flow of the speech.</insert>

**2** *You believe in God*] <note>original: "Creditis in Deum"</note> In both instances, the Greek word <term>pisteuete</term> <note>πιστεύετε</note> is ambiguous: it could mean "you believe" <note>indicative</note> or "believe!" <note>imperative</note>. Thus, it can be read in four ways:
1. *You believe in God, and you believe in me* (as a statement of fact). Chrysostom seems to have read it this way, as if the faith they already had would be a defense against the coming storm.
2. *Believe in God, and believe in me* (as a double command to prevent them from being troubled). Hilary cites it this way.
3. *You believe in God [already], so now believe in me* (to move from being Jews to being Christians).
4. *Believe in God, and [by doing so] you believe in me*.
Cyril interprets both as commands. However, in this place, it would be more significant to say *have trust* or *have confidence in me*.

<column-break/>

# CHAPTER XIV.

<margin>27</margin> <margin>A</margin> <margin>28</margin> <margin>29</margin> <margin>30</margin> <margin>31</margin> <margin>32</margin> <margin>33</margin> <margin>34</margin> <margin>35</margin> <margin>B</margin> <margin>36</margin> <margin>37</margin> <margin>38</margin> <margin>XIV. 1</margin> <margin>C</margin> <margin>2</margin> <margin>3</margin> <margin>4</margin> <margin>5</margin> <margin>6</margin> <margin>7</margin> <margin>8</margin> <margin>9</margin> <margin>D</margin> <margin>E</margin> <margin>F</margin> And after the morsel, Satan entered into him. Jesus therefore said to him, “What you do, do more quickly.” But no one of those reclining understood why he said this to him. For some thought, since Judas had the money bags, that Jesus had said to him, “Buy those things which we need for the feast day,” or that he should give something to the needy. When he had received the morsel, he went out immediately: and it was night. Therefore when he had gone out, Jesus said, “Now is the Son of man glorified, and God is glorified through him. If God is glorified through him, God will also glorify him through himself, and will glorify him immediately. Little children, I am with you yet a little while: you will seek me, and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I go, you cannot come,’ so I say to you now. A new commandment I give you, that you love one another, as I have loved you, so that you also love one another. In this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have mutual love between you.” Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered him, “Where I go, you cannot follow me now: but you will follow later.” Peter said to him, “Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.” Jesus answered him, “Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly I say to you, the rooster will not crow until you have denied me three times.” And he said to his disciples, “Let not your heart be troubled: you believe in God, and believe in me. In my Father’s house are many rooms: if it were otherwise, I would have told you, I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go away to prepare a place for you, I will come again, and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be. And where I go, you know, and the way you know.” Thomas said to him, “Lord, we do not know where you are going, and how can we know the way?” Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me. If you had known me, you would certainly have known my Father also: and now you know him, and have seen him.” Philip said to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.” Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you for so long a time, and you have not known me? Philip, he who sees me, sees the Father: and how do you say, ‘Show us the Father’?”

---

<margin>D</margin> **3** *If not*] <note>original: "Si quo minus"</note> <term>ei de mē</term> <note>εἰ δὲ μή</note>, that is, "if less so," or "otherwise."

**4** *Because I go to prepare*] <note>original: "Quia vado parare"</note> The word "because" <note>ὅτι ἐγὼ</note> is not in certain Greek manuscripts, though it is added superfluously unless it is a causal conjunction. Therefore, even if it were present, it shouldn't be translated as "because," but rather: *In my Father’s house are many rooms; if it were otherwise, I would have told you: I go to prepare a place for you*, or, *if I were going to prepare a place for you*. Furthermore, I do not agree with Lorenzo [Valla] on this part, who wants "otherwise I would have told you" to be the end of the first sentence, and then the next to follow: "I go to prepare a place for you." For these two are entirely connected, the sense being: In my Father's house many rooms are *already* prepared, so that there is a place not just for me alone, but for all my people; if it were not so, I would have said I was going now to prepare those rooms. But now there is no need, since they are ready and waiting for you to follow soon. Furthermore, as for my leaving, I will be gone for a short time, and I do not go to prepare rooms that are already ready, but to open the way to heaven for you by my death. For before this, the way was impassable. When he says, *I come again* instead of *I will come*, it either indicates the speed of his return or the certain reliability of the promise.

<margin>E</margin> **5** *I am the way, truth, and life*] It should be noted that the article is placed before each of these names: *the* way, *the* truth, and *the* life <note>ἡ ὁδὸς, ἡ ἀλήθεια, καὶ ἡ ζωή</note>, so that we understand it is not just *any* way or truth, but that true and unique one.

**6** *And you would have known my Father also*] <note>original: "Et Patrem meum utique cognovissetis"</note> In Greek: <term>egnōkeite an</term> <note>ἐγνώκειτε ἄν</note>. The translator rendered *an* <note>ἄν</note> as "certainly" <note>utique</note>, which elsewhere he translates as "perhaps," though the former is for confirming and the latter for doubting.

**7** *And from now on you will know*] <note>original: "Et a modo cognoscetis"</note> <term>ginōskete</term> <note>γινώσκετε</note>, that is, "you [already] know," which is supported by ancient copies, making it a verb in the present tense. This is also agreed upon by the interpretations of Cyril and Augustine, if one considers them. And "from now on" <note>ἀπ' ἄρτι</note>, which in Greek is "just now," he used once or twice for "now." It would have been more clearly translated as: *and already now you know him*. So says Cyril.

<margin>F</margin> **8** *And you have not known*] <note>original: "Et non cognovisti"</note> <term>egnōkas</term> <note>ἔγνωκάς</note>, that is, "you have known me, Philip." For Chrysostom reads it this way, so that Philip is the occasion for this speech, and he says to this one man, "you have not known me." Hilary reads it no differently in the seventh book of *On the Trinity*. For there follows, "Do you not believe?" <note>singular</note>. Soon after it says, "Do you all not believe?" <note>plural</note>, changing the number. And Saint Augustine noted the change of number here, since at first only Philip was being rebuked.

**9** *He who sees me*] <note>original: "Qui vidit me"</note> In Greek: "He who has seen me, has seen the Father." The conjunction "and" is not added in the Greek, and both verbs are in the past tense. Certain ancient Latin manuscripts agree with all the Greek copies, specifically the oldest of all from the Library of Saint Paul in London.

10 **Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father is in me?**] Augustine reads it exactly this way. However, Cyril and Chrysostom do not add the word "that" <note>Greek: *hoti*</note>, because just before this he rebuked Philip with a question of this sort. Furthermore, he commands everyone to believe, saying: *Believe, that I am in the Father, etc.*

11 **Otherwise because of the works.**] <note>Greek: *ei de mē*</note>. Where the translator just before rendered this "if otherwise," here he translates it tolerably as "otherwise," that is: even if you do not believe other things, be moved to believe by the deeds themselves—though that is almost not believing at all. For we do not strictly "believe" what we see, but rather we experience it.

12 **And greater than these.**] <note>Greek: *kai meizona toutōn*</note>, that is, *greater than these*. But the Translator, through forgetfulness, left the Greek genitive structure <note>Erasmus means the Latin reflects the Greek "greater of these" rather than the more natural Latin "greater than these"</note> when there was no need.

13 **And whatever you shall ask the Father.**] "The Father" is not added in the Greek, nor in the ancient manuscripts, nor in the interpretation of Augustine. When Augustine repeats these same words so many times during his discussion, he makes no mention of the Father, except when the occasion of those words arises: *so that the Father may be glorified in the Son*. Nor should it have been translated "whatsoever" <note>Latin: *quodcunque*</note>, but "whatever" <note>Latin: *quidquid*</note> <note>Greek: *hoti an*</note>, or as others have it, <note>Greek: *ho ean*</note>. And shortly after, it is not the same Greek expression, but *If you ask anything* <note>Greek: *Ean ti aitēsēte*</note>. In some very old manuscripts it was held: *Whatever you ask me in my name*. I found that pronoun "me" added in the Aldine Edition when I was preparing my third edition. Cyril and Theophylact do not add it, and it is more conveniently omitted. For Christ constantly yields authority to the Father; he more rightly indicates his own Divine nature when he promises that he himself will provide whatever they might ask of the Father in the name of the Son. For he was the Advocate, to whom the Father denied nothing.

14 **And another Paraclete.**] It is now too well known to need warning that *Paraclete* should be written with an *e* in the second-to-last syllable, and that syllable should be lengthened, since in Greek it is <note>Greek: *Paraklētos*</note> with an *eta*. But in this place, it was more convenient to translate it as "Consoler" or "Advocate," lest anyone imagine there are two different types of Paracletes. For what he has spoken so far, he has spoken for the sake of consoling. Thus, Christ was the "Paraclete" <note>Advocate</note>. He promises that he will send another Consoler, namely the Spirit of truth. Paul calls Christ our Advocate with God, and he writes the same of the Spirit, that he intercedes for us with unutterable groanings.

15 **Because it does not see him.**] <note>Greek: *hoti theōrei*</note>, that is, "it does not see," in the present tense, just as it is in the more corrected Latin copies. And following that:

16 **He will remain with you.**] "He remains" <note>Greek: *esti*</note>, unless we read it with a changed accent as "he will remain."

17 **I will not leave you as orphans.**] *Orphans* is a Greek word, but it has been adopted by Latin speakers. I do not care to include the etymology that the Greeks provide, because it seems rather foolish to me; but *orphan* sounds like one bereaved of parents and destitute of the protection of friends.

18 **But you shall see.**] <note>Greek: *theōreite*</note>, that is, "you see," which agrees with the ancient manuscripts.

19 **And I will manifest myself to him.**] <note>Greek: *emphanisō*</note>, which more specifically means to indicate something silently and secretly. From this comes the word *emphasis*, because it has a silent power. This better fits with the "breathing" or inspiration by which God introduces himself into the souls of his people.

20 **Lord, what has happened.**] <note>Greek: *ti gegonen*</note>, that is, "what has occurred?" This is a proverbial way of speaking about a sudden or new thing. Indeed, Martial used "what has happened" in the same sense: 
> *I ask, what has happened, that has happened so suddenly?*

21 **And (the word which you have heard) is not mine.**] Not without reason does Valla wonder what came into the Translator's mind, who affected this type of phrasing in prose, which is hardly tolerated even by poets in verse—especially since in the Greek it is not "the word" <note>Latin: *sermonem*, accusative</note> but "the word" <note>Greek: *ho logos*, nominative</note>. Certainly, Saint Augustine reads: "the word which you heard," not "the word [it] which you heard." Thus, I plainly suspect this passage was changed by a scribe's error. Nor is it "you hear" in the Greek, but <note>Greek: *akouete*</note>, "you are hearing," although our Latin copies protest. From Chrysostom’s interpretation, one cannot tell what he read. Certainly, Theophylact reads "you hear." The same is indicated by Cyril, who says in his explanation: *For he who spoke through me to the ancients, he even now speaks to you through me*. Even if a slip between <note>Greek: *akouete* and *akousate*</note> is easy. Therefore, I do not think one should fight over this matter, especially since the sense remains nearly the same.

22 **The Paraclete however the Holy Spirit.**] Two substantive nouns are joined here rather harshly, especially since the first is masculine and the second is neuter: <note>Greek: *ho Paraklētos* and *to Pneuma*</note>. Therefore, it would have been more conveniently rendered this way: *However, that Counselor who is the Holy Spirit, which Spirit the Father is going to send in my name*. For the Greek articles "the" <note>Greek: *ho* and *to*</note> are added in both places. And the relative pronoun "which" <note>Greek: *ho*</note> in Greek can only refer to the Spirit. Furthermore, because the accent of this word *Paracletus* offended Valla, it can cause some worry to those who are more superstitious than religious—those who think the hinge, indeed the very "stern and prow" of Christian piety, consists in whether they have rightly and legitimately performed those prayers which they call the "Hours." For while many other things are required, this is foremost: that every single word be uttered fully and clearly. But those who pronounce *Paraclitus* with a short second-to-last syllable, every time they do so, they defraud God—if not of a whole syllable, certainly of one unit of time. According to the laws of Grammarians, a long syllable has two units of time, a short one only one. Nor should we listen to those who say "the tiny duration of a syllable is a small matter," since one should look at *whom* you are defrauding rather than by *how much*. However, to help their case a little as far as is permitted, I see that the ancient Romans, when adopting Greek words, changed the vowel length according to the logic of the Latin accent; Prudentius did this with the word "idol," a man who should be counted among the learned in any age. But it is much harsher that in the *Lord have mercy* <note>original: "Kyrie eleyson"</note>, words they repeat so many times every day, they defraud the divine ears of two syllables, turning the eight-syllable <note>Greek: *eleēson*</note> into a two-syllable word, and making a four-footed "have mercy" into a three-footed one. Now, since this disgrace is committed perhaps a hundred times a day, if one were to calculate the sum over forty or fifty years, I do not know if a person could ever make it up, even if they repeated nothing but "Lord have mercy" with the correct seven syllables for a whole year. For it is fair, I think, that what we have defrauded God of should be restored. Even the laws of the marketplace take care that a man repays a man if even a tiny coin was taken. If it is sacrilege to take a little gold from a sacred place, how much more serious a sacrilege is it to take from the Author of all things himself, in a matter so much more sacred...

<summary>In this passage from John 14, Jesus promises the coming of the Holy Spirit as "another Counselor." Erasmus provides a deep philological analysis of the Greek text, critiquing the Latin Vulgate's grammar and engaging in a famous digression on the importance of correct pronunciation in liturgy.</summary>
