# GOSPEL CHAPTER XV.

...all things to you. Peace I leave with you, my peace I give to you; not as the world gives, do I give to you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
28 You heard that I said to you, I go away and I am coming to you. If you loved me, you would have rejoiced that I said, I go to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.
29 And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it does happen, you may believe. I will no longer talk much with you; for the ruler of this world is coming, and in me he has nothing.
30 But so that the world may know that I love the Father, and just as the Father commanded me, so I do. Arise, let <margin>XV. 1</margin> us go from here. I am the true vine, and 2 my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away; and every branch that bears 3 fruit he prunes <note>original Greek: "kathairei," which also means "cleanses"</note>, so that it may bear more fruit. You are already 4 clean because of the word which I have spoken to you. Abide in me, and I in you; just as the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can 5 you, unless you remain in me. I am the vine, you are the branches; he who remains in me, and I in him...

<meta>catchword: ...this [man]</meta>

<column-break/>

...to defraud? Now indeed, it seems not only easy, but even insulting and blasphemous, that they constantly make **Cristus** out of <term>Christus</term> <note>The author is criticizing those who drop the 'h' sound in Christ's name</note>, and address their King by no other name than that which would be used for the <term>crests</term> <note>Latin: "cristae"</note> of helmets or roosters. Would the greatest and best Christ endure this insult, if he were as irritable as these men are superstitious toward others, or if God were as unjust toward men as these men are unjust toward their fellow man? You do not dare, when speaking in the presence of a king who is a mere mortal, to say <term>Ferdinand</term> for **Ferdinando**, nor <term>Philip</term> for **Philippo**, and yet you do not fear in those sacred mysteries, where it is a sin to distort even a jot, to say <term>Criste</term> instead of **Christe**. Meanwhile, why should I cavil about the accent being wrongly transferred from the last syllable to the first? Since that matter carries such weight that by a sudden metamorphosis you might turn a "way" into a "little song" if you pronounce <term>law</term> <note>original: "nómos"</note> as <term>pasture</term> <note>original: "nomós"</note>, or a "necklace" out of a "harbor" if you say <term>necklace</term> <note>original: "hormós"</note> instead of <term>harbor</term> <note>original: "hórmos"</note>, or a "lazy man" out of an "opulent city" if you say <term>lazy</term> <note>original: "argòs"</note> instead of <term>shining/swift</term> <note>original: "árgos"</note>. It is not fitting for those men to laugh at these things as jokes, who in other matters far lighter than these are as anxious as the Jews. Indeed, I would gladly <margin>D</margin> excuse them from capital guilt, lest I seem too harsh to anyone, as long as they erred through ignorance. However, after they have been lovingly warned by those who are wise in these matters, since they are able with the same effort to pronounce correctly what they have pronounced wrongly—if they afterwards persist in their bad habits, and having rejected and scorned the advice of the learned, they continue to err knowingly—I truly do not see how they can be excused from a grave crime. Nor will the crowd of others erring in the same way support them. For God as a judge is neither corrupted nor overwhelmed. Now truly, what do we think should be said of those who, having erred so dangerously for more than fifty years, and having erred not only in these things, do not repent when warned, nor give thanks to the monitor, but even hiss and hoot him away with a certain **Sardonic laughter** <note>A bitter or cynical grin</note>, treating a well-deserving man as an enemy, hounding him with insults, and shouting "heretic"? And yet, wondrous to say, those who are so strong here are actually weak—or certainly wish to seem so—in the things they have persuaded themselves of. They call us proud if we should suggest any such thing even kindly or by occasion: they think themselves healthy and modest, who prefer to persist in an admitted error lest they seem to have been ignorant of anything, and would rather stain a well-deserving brother with the mark of heresy than acknowledge their own slip. And I would gladly ask of them: if whenever it occurred in the Canon of the Mass, someone pronounced <term>phuter</term> for **puer** <note>boy</note>, or <term>phillum</term> for **filium** <note>son</note>, would they tolerate it? I think not. Rather, they would swiftly demand punishment with lashes. And yet, remove custom, and it is even more serious in itself to make **Cristum** out of <term>Christum</term>, or **Kyrgelayson** out of <term>Kyrie eleison</term> <note>Lord have mercy</note>, and to sin in so many ways in such few words that there are more errors than syllables. Since, however, the school of letters has always belonged to the care of the Church, it should also have been provided that boys imbibe the genuine and true pronunciation of the Latin language, since it seemed best to the Fathers that the sacred rites be performed in the churches only in Latin. Now there is such negligence in this matter that an Italian does not understand a German pronouncing Latin, nor a German a Frenchman; indeed, not even a man of Lower Germany understands the speech of one from Upper Germany. To such an extent is the whole pronunciation sought not from the rules of Grammar, but from the custom of the common people. The same thing has happened among the Greeks, among whom the sounds of <term>i, ē, y, ei, oi, yi</term> <note>Greek: ι, η, υ, ει, οι, υι</note> all sound the same. Nor is there a distinction between <term>o</term> and <term>ō</term> <note>omicron and omega</note>. And after a sharp accent, a syllable that is long often seems short, such as <term>humiliation</term> <note>original: "tapeinōsis"</note>. Again, the same accent often makes a short syllable seem long, such as <term>theologian</term> <note>original: "theológos"</note>. Yet anciently, even the common people would hiss an actor off the stage if he faked a long syllable for a short one. It would be very difficult to restore all these things, yet some can be restored from common pronunciation. Among the French, you may still hear the diphthongs <term>oi & ai, au & eu</term>, in the words for <term>faith, deed, lightning</term> or <term>dust, and two</term>. Likewise in our language—I mean the **Dutch language**—in the words for <term>hay, tenacious, fine, lie</term>. Indeed, they have a manifest distinction of quantity whenever a consonant follows a vowel. Now when they want to signify a long vowel, and the accent cannot indicate it, they either write a double vowel or write a diphthong with an added vowel. The Greeks sound the word for <term>indeed</term> <note>original: "men"</note> as sharp and short, but the Dutch pronounce it long and circumflex, in the same way I think the Ancients pronounced it, as if they were saying the diphthong <term>meein</term>. Likewise when they say "white," they sound a short <term>i</term>, but when "bed," a long <term>i</term>; when they say "loosened," they sound a short and sharp <term>u</term>, but when "clever," they sound a long and circumflex <term>u</term>. It would be very easy to imitate this in words that end in a consonant: as in <term>beautiful</term> and <term>beautifully</term> <note>original: "kalos" and "kalōs"</note>, as in...

<meta>catchword: as in...</meta>

---

# GOSPEL CHAPTER XV.

...he will teach you all things, 23 and will suggest to you 24 all things whatsoever I have said to you. 25 Peace I leave with you, my peace 27 I give to you: not as the world gives, do I give to you: let not your heart be troubled, 26 nor let it be afraid. You heard that I said to you, 27 I go away and I am coming to 28 you. If you loved me, 28 you would surely rejoice that I said, I go to the Father, 29 because the Father is greater than I. And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it has 29 happened, you may believe. Hereafter I will not speak much with you: 30 for the prince of this world comes, and in me he has nothing. But so that the world may know 30 that I love the Father, and as the Father gave me commandment, so I do. Arise, let us go from here. I am the true vine, <margin>XV. 1</margin> and my Father is the vinedresser. 1 Every branch 2 in me not bearing fruit he takes away, and every one that bears fruit 2 he prunes, so that it may bring forth more abundant fruit. Now you are clean because of the word which I have spoken 3 to you. Abide in me, and I in you: just as the 4 branch cannot bear fruit of itself, unless it remains in the vine: so neither can you, unless you remain in me. I 5 am...

<meta>catchword: ...am</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> 23 **and he will suggest to you**] <term>hypomnēsei</term>, that is, he will remind, or put you in mind, to express it more literally. He placed two things: <term>didaxei</term>, **he will teach**, and <term>hypomnēsei</term>, **he will remind**. We are taught things we did not know; we are reminded of those things that had already slipped away. And soon,
24 **All things whatsoever I shall have said to you**] In the Greek it is <term>eipon</term>, **I have said**, or certainly **I might have said**. For "I shall have said" is in the future tense.
<margin>B</margin> 25 **Peace I leave**] **Augustine** noted this: that in the first part he did not add "my," but in the second he did. Since this pertains to the integrity of the reading, it seemed necessary to warn, lest any scribe corrupt it.
<margin>E</margin> 26 **Nor let it be afraid**] <term>deiliatō</term>. Which properly means to shrink back out of cowardice, and to decline danger, and to be of a fearful mind.
27 **I go away and I am coming to you**] <term>Hypagō kai erchomai pros hymas</term>, that is, **I depart and I am about to come to you**, that is, I leave soon to return, even if the latter verb is ambiguous.
28 **You would surely rejoice**] **Lorenzo** <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous 15th-century philologist</note> is offended that the translator rendered <term>an</term> as **surely**, because that conjunction is expletive, although even these are not entirely without use.
29 **Because the Father is greater than I**] According to **Hilary**, the Father is greater than the Son in authority, that is, by reason of origin, because the Son is from the Father, not the reverse; which interpretation **Cyril** also approves in the *Thesaurus*, book 11. However, when Hilary says the Father is greater than the Son, but the Son is nonetheless not lesser, it must be understood that the Father is the beginning of the Son, who by nature is nevertheless equal to the Father, because the nature of the Father and the Son is the same. In the Divine Persons there is indeed an order, but there is no inequality: just as there is distinction, there is no diversity.
30 **For the prince comes**] <term>erchetai gar ho tou kosmou toutou archōn</term>, <margin>F</margin> that is, for that prince of this world comes, because of the added article, so that we understand the **Devil**. The pronoun **this** <note>Latin: "toutou"</note> was also added, lest we understand the entire universe. Although Cyril, in his commentary, does not add "this." Furthermore, "he comes" can be "he will come" in the future tense, because of the imminent passion and accusation. **Jerome**, in his *Commentary on Hosea*, cites it as "he will come." Certainly, it cannot be in the past tense.

<margin>I</margin> **Every branch in me not bearing fruit he will take away**]
In Greek it is <term>airei</term>, that is, **he takes away**, in the present tense: in the Constance manuscript, someone had made an <term>e</term> out of an <term>i</term>, with a curved top: and <term>e</term> was added, according to the property of the Hebrew language. And soon,
2 **He will prune him**] <term>kathairei</term>, **he prunes**, to declare the action and function of the Father without regard to time.
3 **more fruit**] <term>hina pleiona karpon</term>, that is, so that more fruit, or more abundant fruit. This is what might seem corrupted by a scribe, unless the translator was nodding off.

<meta>catchword: 4 so that</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>C</margin> ...it is held as if it were a genitive **...** This distinction will become more obscure in the middle syllables, and yet here too it can be preserved, so that **malum**, for a "wicked man," has the first syllable sharp and short, while **malum**, for a "type of fruit" <note>an apple</note>, has the same syllable long and circumflex, as if you were saying **maalum**. And just as we distinguish by accent and the lengthening of the syllable a "cross" <note>crucem</note> from a "wise man," so in Latin **vis** <note>force</note> and **lis** <note>lawsuit</note> can be distinguished from **his** <note>these</note>. Similarly **fax** <note>torch</note> and **lex** <note>law</note> from **nex** <note>death</note>. Just as the French sharpen all final syllables, so they also lengthen them. They sound **Iesus** well, but **animus** or **Christus** not well. But in these slips, the public custom of everyone offers some defense. In this, however, I warn, that teachers should gradually correct what usage has corrupted. In words like <term>paracletes</term>, <term>idols</term>, and the like, they unfairly pardon themselves, who are so irritable toward others if they happen to pronounce something differently than they do, even if it were more correct. And I have warned of these things in passing, not looking to my own resentment—for I am not even slightly moved by the errors of others—but looking to their own well-being. For if it is proud not to endure someone erring badly in divine matters, it is much more proud not to endure someone advising well in those same matters. Now let the mind return to what we have undertaken, but only after I have first warned of this one thing: in Greek words received by us, just as it is simpler and easier, so it is also more correct if we follow the Latin accent, because the Greek accent, according to the laws of that language, repeatedly shifts elsewhere, such as **Iákōbos** and **Iakōbou** <note>James</note>, while the Latin does not. Therefore, he who in the nominative case sounds **Paracletus** with the second syllable sharp, correctly pronounces it according to the Greeks; but if he does the same in the genitive and dative cases, he will then be pronouncing it neither in Greek nor in Latin.

5 **You are the branches** <note>original Greek: "klēmata"</note>] Augustine, in the first book against the letters of Petilianus, chapter five, reads "withes" <note>original Latin: "vimentis"</note> instead of "branches" <note>original Latin: "palmitibus"</note>.
6 **He shall be cast out** <note>original Latin: "mittetur foras"</note>] The Greek says <note>eblēthē exō</note>, that is, "he was cast out," or rather "he has been cast out." This agrees with what follows, "and he withers."
Likewise,
6 **And he withers** <note>original Latin: "et arescit"</note>] The Greek is <note>exēranthē</note>, that is, "he has withered." In this passage, ancient manuscripts support this reading, although that "scraper" <note>Erasmus's term for a scribe who erased or altered texts</note> had been at work in the Constance manuscript. Hence it is probable that "shall be cast" was substituted for "is cast" by the errors of scribes, especially since "and he burns" follows. For he shows through a simile what is accustomed to happen, so that through it we may understand what will happen to us if we do not remain in the vine.
7 **And they shall gather them** <note>original Latin: "et colligent ea"</note>] The Greek is <note>kai synagousin auta</note>, that is, "and they gather them," so that "branches" is understood. The oldest Latin manuscript has "gather them" <note>original Latin: "colligent eos"</note>, as "branches" in Greek is of the neuter gender; and it says "they burn," not "it burns." There were two occasions for error here: one, because the number suddenly changes from singular "branch" to plural "branches"; the other, because even in Greek there is a singular verb, <note>kaietai</note>. Truly, in the former, one ought to remember that in things signifying a kind or species, the number is often changed. For it makes no difference whether you say, "The elephant gives birth after ten years," or "Elephants give birth." Here he distinguished the species of the branch from the trunk. In the latter, he did not notice that in Greek, a singular verb is added to neuter plural nouns.
<margin>F</margin>
And lest the Greeks alone seem to read it thus, in the Constance manuscript there was an erasure at "is and they burn," so you may recognize it was written "is and they burn." From Chrysostom it is not clear what he read. Theophylact agrees with us. Nor is it clear from Cyril, except that he mentions the example, by which he indicates these things are said of the vine and branches.
8 **They shall cast** <note>original Latin: "mittent"</note>] The Greek is <note>ballousi</note>, that is, "they cast," and very ancient copies support this; although "they hurl" <note>original Latin: "conjiciunt"</note> was more fitting.
9 **Much fruit** <note>original Latin: "fructum plurimum"</note>] The Greek is <note>karpon polyn</note>, that is, "much fruit," or, as translated elsewhere, "abundant."
10 **Than that [he lay down] his life** <note>original Latin: "quam ut animam"</note>] The Greek is <note>hina tis tēn psychēn</note>, that is, "that one [lay down] his life." <gloss>For</gloss> the word "than" <note>original: "quam"</note> is not added, nor should it be. For if you add "than," you suggest this specific charity is greater than that which Christ had—if someone spends his life for his friends. Certainly the Golden Manuscript does not add it, nor does the Constance manuscript.

11 **Now I will not call** <note>original Latin: "jam non dicam"</note>] The Greek is <note>Ouk eti legō</note>, that is, "now I do not say," or "Henceforth I do not say." The Golden Manuscript supports the Greek reading.
12 **Know that me** <note>original Latin: "scitote quia me"</note>] The Greek word <note>ginōskete</note> is ambiguous, meaning both "know!" <note>imperative</note> and "you know" <note>indicative</note>. "Me prior to you" <note>emē prōton hymōn</note>, that is, "me who am before you," or "me before you." For the Greek speech is ambiguous toward either sense, though the latter is more approved, so that "first" <note>prōtos</note> is an adverb, or a superlative used in place of a comparative.
13 **Remember my word** <note>original Latin: "mementote sermonis mei"</note>] "My" is not in the Greek manuscripts, but the translator expressed the emphasis of the Greek article, "the word" <note>tō logō</note>.
14 **But now they have no excuse** <note>original Latin: "nunc autem excusationem non habent"</note>] The Greek word is <note>prophasin</note>, meaning "pretext." He said something more than if he had said "excuse." For even those who do not have a just excuse nevertheless offer some pretext; from these people, every evasion was taken away.
15 **They hated me without cause** <note>original Latin: "odio habuerunt me gratis"</note>] This is a prophecy from Psalm 68, according to our numbering <note>modern Psalm 69:4</note>.
16 **But when the Comforter comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth**] Because "the Spirit" <note>to Pneuma</note> is of the neuter gender in Greek, it is uncertain which case it is: nominative or accusative. However, the nominative "Spirit" was more suitable. For he is explaining who that Comforter is, namely, the Spirit of truth. For he does not become the Spirit by being sent, but he who is already the Spirit is sent.
17 **Who proceeds from the Father** <note>original Latin: "qui a Patre procedit"</note>] The Greek is <note>ekporeuetai</note>. This could have been elegantly translated as "sets out" <note>original: "proficiscitur"</note>, if the word "procession" had not already occupied everyone's ears. Yet properly, he "proceeds" who comes forth in a certain public ceremony, as a bridegroom or bride proceeds. As Virgil said:
*At last he advances.*
18 **And you shall bear witness** <note>original Latin: "et vos testimonium perhibebitis"</note>] In Greek it is <note>martyreite</note>, that is, "bear witness!", so that it is the imperative mood, or "you bear witness" <note>indicative</note>. And I suspect it was written this way by the Translator. Indeed, Cyril's translator renders it "bear witness!", following his own copy, not our edition. Although it seems more appropriate to me as "you bear witness," that is, you yourselves are witnesses, and he soon adds the cause: "because you have been with me from the beginning." In the Constance manuscript it was "you bear witness."

<margin>1</margin> **Excluded from the synagogues** <note>original: "Absque synagogis"</note>] In Greek the word is a compound, *aposynagōgous* <note>original: "ἀποσυναγώγους"</note>, as if you were to say "someone away from the synagogue," and they will interdict the **synagogue** to you.
<margin>2</margin> **But the hour comes** <note>original: "Sed venit hora"</note>] *erchetai* <note>original: "ἔρχεται"</note>, "comes," is either in the present tense or the future. Here it should rather be translated as **will come**, or **is at hand**. And "time" <note>original: "tempus"</note> rather than "hour."
<margin>3</margin> **May think he offers service** <note>original: "Arbitretur obsequium se praestare"</note>] *doxē latreian prospherein tō Theō* <note>original: "δόξῃ λατρείαν προσφέρειν τῷ Θεῷ"</note>, that is, he may seem to exhibit worship to God and offer a sacrifice. Among the Latins, "service" <note>original: "obsequium"</note> sounds like something far different.
<margin>4</margin> **You may remember** <note>original: "Reminiscamini"</note>] *mnēmoneuēte* <note>original: "μνημονεύητε"</note>, that is, you should be mindful, or you might remember. For we properly "recollect" <note>original: "reminiscimur"</note> things that had slipped away from us.
<margin>5</margin> **And now you will not see** <note>original: "Et iam non videbitis"</note>] *kai ouk eti theōreite* <note>original: "καὶ οὐκ ἔτι θεωρεῖτε"</note>, that is, you see no longer. Although it appears he is abusing the tense <note>using present for future</note>. Likewise *eit’ an ite*, that is, **afterward**, or **then**.
<margin>6</margin> **That Spirit** <note>original: "Ille Spiritus"</note>] "That" <note>original: "ille"</note> does not refer to "Spirit" in terms of grammatical agreement, but to the *Paraclete*, that is, the **Comforter**, *ekeinos to Pneuma* <note>original: "ἐκεῖνος τὸ Πνεῦμα"</note>, that is, "he who is the Spirit." For "Spirit," as we have said, is of the neuter gender among the Greeks.
<margin>7</margin> **He will teach you all** <note>original: "Docebit vos omnem"</note>] In Greek it is not "he will teach," but **he will lead**, *hodēgēsei* <note>original: "ὁδηγήσει" — term: hodegeo, to show the way or guide a traveler</note>, and **into all truth**.
<margin>8</margin> **A modicum, and you will not see** <note>original: "Modicum, & non videbitis"</note>] *theōreite* <note>original: "θεωρεῖτε"</note>, that is, "you see," as supported even by ancient Latin manuscripts. Although, as I said, he seems to abuse the tense, since it is followed by the changed word *opsesthe* <note>original: "ὄψεσθε"</note>, **you will see**. Furthermore, in using *modicum* for **a little while** <note>original: "pusillo"</note>, he follows his own custom, since among the Latins *modicum* usually means "moderate," derived from "measure" <note>original: "modus"</note>. Here, *mikron* <note>original: "μικρὸν"</note> refers to time.
<margin>9</margin> **You will weep and cry** <note>original: "Plorabitis & flebitis"</note>] *klausete kai thrēnēsete* <note>original: "κλαύσετε καὶ θρηνήσετε"</note>, that is, **you will weep and lament**, or **you will mourn**.
<margin>10</margin> **No one takes from you** <note>original: "Nemo tollet a vobis"</note>] *oudeis airei* <note>original: "οὐδεὶς αἴρει"</note>, that is, **no one takes**, using a verb in the present tense, meaning **no one is able to take**.
<margin>11</margin> **In my name** <note>original: "In nomine meo"</note>] Among the Hebrews, something is said to be done "in someone's name" which is done by the authority and power of someone. I do not see how that can be expressed in Latin. Indeed, "in my name" <note>original: "in nomine meo"</note> is not of Roman elegance. "Under my name" does not express exactly the same thing. "In my name" <note>original: "nomine meo"</note> is certainly ambiguous. Therefore, it might be better to count this speech among those which must be allowed to the peculiar language of the Sacred Scriptures.
<margin>12</margin> **For the Father himself** <note>original: "Ipse enim Pater"</note>] *Autos* <note>original: "Αὐτὸς"</note> among the Greeks has a certain quality which I am not sure exists among the Latins, signifying something done of one's own accord. For the sense is: I do not say I will ask for you, so that he may favor you, for he already loves you of his own accord, even with no one asking. Whence they also call things *automata* <note>original: "αὐτόματα" — term: acting of one's own will</note>.

---

<margin>12</margin> **Behold the hour comes, and has now come** <note>original: "Ecce venit hora, & jam venit"</note>] The first "comes" is in the present tense, <term>erchetai</term> <note>original: "ἔρχεται"</note>, which the Greeks sometimes use with the meaning of the future. In the Greek, the words for "comes" and "has come" are different; the latter being <term>elelythen</term> <note>original: "ἐλήλυθεν"</note>. Hence it would be more correctly translated as "the hour is imminent, and is now present."

<margin>14</margin> **in the world you shall have pressure** <note>original: "in mundo pressuram habebitis"</note>] The Greek is <term>echete</term> <note>original: "ἔχετε"</note>, in the present tense: "you have."

**Power over all flesh**] He calls "mankind" <term>flesh</term>.

<margin>2</margin> **And all that you have given him, he may give them eternal life**] I suspect this form of speaking is taken from the Hebrews <note>Erasmus often notes where Greek grammar reflects Hebrew thought patterns</note>, and therefore the sense should have been rendered rather than just the literal words.

<margin>3</margin> **Thee the only true God** <note>original: "Te solum verum Deum"</note>] The Greek is <term>se ton monon alēthinon Theon</term> <note>original: "σὲ τὸν μόνον ἀληθινὸν Θεὸν"</note>, that is, "you who alone are the true God." This passage, more than others, gave the <term>Arians</term> <note>A group in the early Church who argued that Jesus was a created being and not equal to God the Father</note> an opportunity for error, so that they said only the Father is truly and properly God. However, the word "only" does not exclude the Son, but separates the true God from the false gods of the nations. Cyprian, in the second book against the Jews, chapter one, reads "Lord" instead of "God," unless we prefer to attribute this to the scribes. Saint Augustine in several places repels the Arians by a different punctuation, arranging it thus: "that they may know you, and him whom you have sent, Jesus Christ, as the only true God." While this distinction is harsh in Latin, it is even harsher in Greek because of the added article <term>tō</term> <note>original: "τῷ"</note>, even if the meaning Augustine brings forward is most true. But before the mystery of the Passion, Christ revealed his divine nature by signs in such a way that it was not clearly understood until after the Resurrection. We should not grant so much to the heretics that we twist the Scripture out of hatred for them. Here I know some will cry out that I am criticizing the holy Doctors of the Church <note>The influential early Christian theologians</note> because they sometimes twisted Scripture to achieve a victory in debate. These pleasant men themselves admit that there are many opinions in those holy Doctors which, if anyone were to defend them today, he would be thrown onto the pyre. Yet they cry out to heaven and earth against me for pointing out that in one or two places they adapted Scripture for victory—either because they convinced themselves it should be interpreted that way, or because they allowed themselves this in conflict with the ungodly.

<margin>4</margin> **Clarify me** <note>original: "Clarifica me"</note>] The verb for "to clarify" repeated so often here is <term>glorify</term> in Greek, <term>doxazein</term> <note>original: "δοξάζειν"</note>. And "clarity" <note>original: "claritate"</note> is <term>doxē</term> <note>original: "δόξῃ"</note>, that is, "glory."

<margin>5</margin> **Before the world was made**] In Greek it is <term>pro tou ton kosmon einai para soi</term> <note>original: "πρὸ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι παρὰ σοὶ"</note>, that is, "before the world was with you." The translator seems to have read "become/be made" <note>original: "γενέσθαι"</note> instead of "to be" <note>original: "εἶναι"</note>. Jerome, citing this place to Fretela, reads "was" <note>Latin: "esset"</note> and in Greek reads <term>einai</term>.

<margin>6</margin> **Except the son of perdition**] This too is a figure of speech peculiar to the Hebrews, who add a noun in the genitive case as an epithet: "God of peace," "God of patience," "law of death" (a deadly law), "sons of disobedience" (disobedient sons). Otherwise, what is a "son of perdition" except one whom perdition has brought forth?

<margin>7</margin> **As you sent me into the world, so also I sent them into the world**] The sense could also be this, if we read them together: "As you sent me into the world, and as I sent them into the world, so for them I sanctify myself," so that just as I holily preach your truth, they also may preach what they have learned from me. If this reading is preferred, the adverb "so" <note>original: "ita"</note> should be omitted. In the <term>golden manuscript</term> <note>A reference to a high-quality, likely Carolingian, biblical manuscript Erasmus consulted</note> the word "so" is not added.

**1** **A** *cross the brook of the Cedars* ] <note>original: "tōn Kedrōn"</note>. The addition of the article indicates that "Cedron" is not a Hebrew name here, but means "of the Cedars." There is an opinion that the brook was so named because it had cedars on both sides, just as the Mount of Olives was named. Saint Jerome mentions this name in his *Hebrew Places*, indicating that the brook and the valley of that name are on the eastern side of the city of Jerusalem. And yet, I do not know whether the name was given to the place because of its location, since he also testifies in that same work that <margin>Face of the East <note>Hebrew: פני קדים</note></margin>, which is found in Ezekiel, was translated by Aquila and Symmachus as "the East." Even our Caspion might argue it was named by the Hebrews for its "obscurity" <note>likely referring to the word "Qidron" meaning dark or turbid</note>, and that the word *Cedron* is Hebrew, not Greek, since the Hebrews call cedars <margin>Cedar <note>Hebrew: ארז</note></margin>. Mention of this brook is made in the second book of Kings, chapter fifteen <note>2 Samuel 15 in modern bibles</note>, which David crossed while fleeing from Absalom. Again, in the third book of Kings, chapter fifteen <note>1 Kings 15</note>, Asa burned the idol of Priapus at the brook *Cedron*. Likewise, in the fourth book of Kings, chapter twenty-three <note>2 Kings 23</note>, King Josiah burned the profane grove that was in the house of the Lord in the valley of *Cedron*. From the first passage, it is not entirely clear what the translators thought of *Cedron*. For we read: "and the king crossed the brook Kedron." In the second passage, the article seems to be added: "and he burned it by the brook of the Cedars." Again, in the third passage, *Kedron* is placed twice without the article. Nor is it read differently in the third book of Kings, chapter two, although the order of the narrative here in the Greek codices differs from our Latin copies. Yet, I would not deny that all these variations could have been committed through the fault of scribes who knew Greek but were ignorant of Hebrew. Therefore, I not unwillingly subscribe to the opinion of Cajetan <note>Cardinal Cajetan, a contemporary theologian and commentator</note>. For the Lord delivers himself to the power of darkness.

**2** *Let these go their way* ] I confess this is somewhat far from my natural instinct to mention, but since the opportunity arises, I wish to give a warning. I know a certain theologian of great name who twisted these words of Christ to defend the "immunity of the clergy," as if Christ had commanded Princes not to burden Priests with taxes or tyranny. I strongly approve of the sentiment—for it would be better for Princes if they were content with their own pay. But to gather that from this passage is, in my opinion, ridiculous. Here Christ acts in the person of the True Shepherd, and the disciples represent the Christian people. He teaches, therefore, that whenever a storm of persecution rushes in, a Bishop should expose his own head to danger for the safety of his people and consult for them as much as he can. This is quite different from how the common crowd of Princes and Popes sometimes act, thinking it right that for the sake of protecting one person’s head, the entire people—nay, so many nations—should lose themselves, their families, and their property.

**3** *The cohort and the tribune* ] "Cohort" in Greek is *speira*, which means a "rope" or a "crowd," and "tribune" is *chiliarchos*, which means a "commander over a thousand men." Saint Augustine and several others labor over this point, trying to bring the Gospel narratives of Peter's denial into harmony. This is because John, in chapter XVIII, seems to disagree with all the others, and this dissonance rings out not only

## CHAPTER XVIII.

...my glory, which you gave me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world. <margin>25</margin> Righteous Father, the world has not known you: but I have known you, and these have known that you sent me. <margin>26</margin> And I have made known your name to them, and will make it known, so that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them. When Jesus had said these things, <margin>1 XVIII.</margin> he went out with his disciples across the brook Cedron, where there was a garden, into which he and his disciples entered. <margin>2</margin> Now Judas, who was betraying him, also knew the place, because Jesus had frequently met there with his disciples. Judas therefore, having received a cohort, <margin>3</margin> and officers from the Chief Priests and Pharisees, came there with lanterns and torches and weapons. Jesus says to them, "I am he." And Judas, who was betraying him, was also standing with them. When therefore <margin>6</margin> he said to them, "I am he," they went backward and fell to the ground. Then he asked them again, "Whom do you seek?" <margin>7</margin> But they said, "Jesus the Nazarene." ---

in the Latin books, but also in the Greek ones. It is all the more remarkable that Chrysostom was not bothered by this discrepancy. For John reports it thus: Jesus was seized and <margin>D</margin> bound, and first led away to Annas; Peter followed him there, and there first denied Jesus. Then, after many things, he adds that Jesus was sent by Annas to Caiaphas, where Peter denied him twice more. From this narrative, it appears that the first denial took place at the house of Annas, and the remaining two at Caiaphas’s, while the other Evangelists, with great consensus, report that all of Peter’s denials took place in the house of Caiaphas. Jean Gerson <note>a famous 15th-century French scholar</note> felt some hesitation here, testifying that various people have felt differently about this matter; he adds that it seems to him Augustine was of the opinion that all the denials were made in the house of Annas. However, this entire difficulty seems to be explained by the commentaries of Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria</note>, who, in reading and interpreting, makes it clear enough that in both the Greek and our own Latin codices, certain words were perhaps omitted through the negligence of scribes. For the Greek reads: *The cohort then, and the tribune, and the officers of the Jews seized Jesus and bound him, and led <margin>E</margin> him to Annas first; for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was the High Priest of that year. And Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas the High Priest.* Our consistent translation has it this way: *The cohort, and the tribune, and the officers of the Jews seized Jesus and bound him, and led him to Annas first; for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was the High Priest of that year; now Caiaphas was the one who had given counsel to the Jews, etc.* But Cyril, as the Latin version has it, reads it this way: *The cohort therefore and the tribune and the officers of the Jews seized Jesus and bound him, and led him to Annas first; for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was the High Priest of that year. And, with the commentary interjected, he adds: they sent him to Caiaphas the High Priest; now Caiaphas was the one who gave counsel to the Jews, that it is expedient for one man to die for the people. Peter followed Jesus.* From this it is clear that between these words, *who was High Priest of that year*, and these, *Now Caiaphas was he who had given counsel*, these words were omitted: *And they sent him bound to Caiaphas the High Priest*, so that there follows: *Now Caiaphas was he who had given counsel to the Jews*. By this order of reading, all the denials are understood to have been made in the house of Caiaphas, after he was sent from Annas. What Gerson meant, however, I do not quite understand, since nothing of the sort can be gathered from Augustine's words, nor is there any hesitation in the other Evangelists, except that they all omit the part of the story about Jesus being led to Annas; for Matthew reports that as soon as he was captured, he was led to the house of Caiaphas. Mark and Luke say the same, except they do not mention the name, merely calling him the Prince of Priests. The rest agree. Therefore, the only hesitation remains in John, who alone tells that he was first led to Annas because he, as Cyril interprets, had made the pact with Judas. Once he was satisfied, Jesus was led without delay, bound, to Caiaphas, as the one preeminent in authority. What happened at the house of Annas...

...ceeded to the Praetorium of the Governor, and by his own decision had left the Son of those listening; or in the house of Caiaphas, Pilate had taken up the Praetorium, and the house was so large that it could hold its master living in one part, and the judge in another. And soon after, <gloss>They did not enter, he says, the Praetorium</gloss>, that is, into that part of the house which Pilate held, if it was indeed the house of Caiaphas. Furthermore, although in the common printed editions of the publishers it is held as <gloss>from Caiaphas</gloss> <note>original: "a Caipha"</note>, not <gloss>to Caiaphas</gloss>, it is clear from the interpretation itself that Augustine read it this way, since he asks: "but if to Caiaphas, why into the Praetorium?" Otherwise, there was no reason why Augustine should cast himself into these difficulties, unless he forced the High Priest and the Governor—as two endowed with the highest magistracy, from two very different religions and nations—to live under the same roof. The matter itself is clear; the whole error arose from the faults of the scribe which twisted Augustine’s view. And yet, since he was so stuck that he did not satisfy even himself, it is a wonder that he did not consult the Greek codices, or at least more corrected Latin ones. First Jesus was led to Annas, who <margin>F</margin> sent him bound to Caiaphas his son-in-law; from there, when he had answered nothing all night, in the morning he was led down to the house of the Governor. The occasion for the corruption was born here, because the reader did not recognize the figure of speech <note>original: "tropum"</note> by which we say "to us" <note>original: "ad nos"</note> for "to our house," and "from you" <note>original: "a vobis"</note> for "from your house." We indicated a similar error in Mark chapter five, regarding the <gloss>synagogue leader</gloss> <note>original: "archisynagogo"</note>. This trope is a type of Synecdoche, by which we indicate the possessor by the name of the thing possessed. Such is that line of Virgil: <gloss>Already neighboring Ucalegon is burning</gloss> <note>From the Aeneid, meaning Ucalegon's house is on fire</note>. Likewise that from the *Eunuch* <note>A play by Terence</note>: <gloss>Let us go to me</gloss>, that is, <gloss>to my house.</gloss>

<margin>36 My servants would surely fight]</margin> Since the Greek confirms it is <gloss>ēgōnizonto</gloss> <note>meaning to struggle, fight, or contend</note>, it is a wonder that Cyprian, following the second book *Against the Jews*, chapter twenty-eight, read, <gloss>my servants will be troubled.</gloss>

1 <gloss>*And they said, Hail]* In Latin manuscripts, there is an addition here: *And they came to him*, and said, "Hail." This is not in the Greek, nor do I see how it fits, unless perhaps some were striking him while others were mocking him with greetings.</gloss>
2 <gloss>*And from then on]* <note>original: "Ek toutou"</note>, that is, "From that time," so that the time is understood.</gloss>
3 <gloss>*Lithostrotos]* <note>original: "Lithostrōtos"</note>. In Greek it sounds like you would say "laid with stone." And so it is read in the ancient Latin copies as *lithostrotos*. Although I am quite unwilling to waste time on such trifles, it is worth hearing how beautifully two writers of great name, Nicolaus Lyranus and Hugh of Saint-Cher, interpret the Greek word *lithostrōtos*. For the former says, "*Lithostrosus* is a Greek word, and it is said from *lithos* (stone) and *stratus* (which is a pavement or a layer)." The latter, however, says, "*Lithostratos* in Greek is 'judgment' or 'judicial'." I ask you, honest reader, what can those do who draw whatever learning they have from such writers—from dictionaries, from compilers of summaries, from remains gathered more than ten times over? And this from those who, if they happen to find something learned in good authors, either pass it over because they do not understand it, or if they touch it, they defile and contaminate it by their handling. Nothing is so fortunate that these men do not somehow make it worse, and yet we read their nonsense as if it were oracles and grow old in them. Consequently, we ourselves become just like those in whose writings we are constantly occupied. However, to return to the matter: <term>lithos</term> <note>original: "λίθος"</note>, not *lithus*, is "stone" to the Greeks; and <term>strounuo</term> <note>original: "στρώννυμι"</note> means to spread out, and from that is said whatever is laid down in any way, and <term>stroma</term> <note>original: "στρῶμα"</note> is that which is spread over something. In the "Golden Code" <note>a famous luxury manuscript</note>, *lithostrotos* was written correctly, just as it was in the Constance manuscript. Furthermore, "Gabbatha" signifies a high place to the Hebrews. From this it appears the place was an elevated area suitable for judgment.</gloss>
4 <gloss>*We have no king but Caesar]* "Caesar" in this place signifies the Roman Emperor. For although that name did not originate with Julius, yet from this usurper of the empire, it was derived to the successors of his tyranny. Furthermore, as to why he is called "King" <note>original: "basilea"</note> and not "Emperor" <note>original: "autokratora"</note>, it should be known that the Roman Emperor is also called "King" <note>original: "basilea"</note> by the Greeks.</gloss>
5 <gloss>*And bearing the cross for himself]* The Greeks read "his own cross" <note>original: "ton stauron autou"</note>. Although this makes no difference to the sense, yet I wanted the reader to be advised, lest he should immediately strike it out.</gloss>
6 <gloss>*And Pilate a title]* The Evangelist used a Latin word, *titulus* (title), just as above with *linteo* (linen) and *praetorio* (praetorium). Matthew called it a <term>aitian</term> <note>a cause or accusation</note>. He could have said <term>epigraphēn</term> <note>an inscription</note>, as Luke said.</gloss>

<margin>4</margin> The two were running together, and...

<margin>7 Into his own]</margin> <note>original: "eis ta idia"</note>, that is, *into his own possession*, as the most ancient volumes agree, meaning *into his own right*. This is also how Ambrose interprets it in his booklet to the virgin.
<margin>8 A vessel full of vinegar]</margin> Although the Greek reads this way, Hilary, citing this passage in his Commentary on Psalm LXVIII, reads *concha* <note>a shell-shaped vessel</note> instead of *vas* <note>vessel</note>, as if expressing a specific type of container.
<margin>9 He gave up his spirit]</margin> Cyril adds a comment here and interprets the tearing of the temple veil, which is found added neither in the Latin codices nor the Greek ones; and yet he assigns a specific chapter to this small detail, so that no one should think it happened by chance.
<margin>10 Pierced his side with a spear]</margin> <note>original: "enyxe"</note>, that is, *he dug or pricked*. The translator seems to have read <note>original: "enoixe"</note>, which means *he opened*. It is a wonder where that fable originated which boasts that much different things were written about the piercing of Christ's side—namely, that the Lord's side was pierced with a spear before he gave up his spirit—since John narrates that it was done after he had expired. Yet, since that reading is found nowhere in Matthew, nor in the Greek books, nor in the Latin books, nor does anyone at all make any mention of this thing among the many who have tried to bring into harmony the places in the Evangelists that seem discordant, it is likely that this is a fabrication of the Glossographers <note>commentators who added notes to legal or biblical texts</note>. These men, as the facts show, were no less impudent toward the learned than they were in the *Pandects* <note>a compendium of Roman law</note>; when they had nothing to say regarding the exchange of Diomedes and Glaucus, they devised a ridiculous fable from themselves. Thus, the man who wrote the glosses on the first of the *Clementines* <note>decrees of Pope Clement V</note>, not understanding why Clement V or John XXIII (who published the *Clementines*) declared that the Evangelist John followed the correct order of narrative when he tells of Christ's side being pierced while lifeless, falsely claimed that the opposite is read in some copies of Matthew, and added that the passage was removed from Matthew's Gospel by Pope John. Yet there are many places in which the speech of the Evangelists seems to conflict with one another, and we do not cure such scruples with erasures or patches, but with explanation. From the fragments of that *Clementine* decree, it can more probably be gathered that there were Scholastic Doctors who felt that John narrated later what had happened earlier. For he first narrated that Jesus, after tasting the vinegar and bowing his head, gave up his spirit; then he continues with how they broke the legs of the two thieves to hasten the death of the condemned. Soon they came to Jesus to do the same, but they found that he was already dead. *They did not break his legs,* he says, *but one of the soldiers struck his side with a spear.* They seem to have understood it in this way.

<margin>A</margin> ...Jesus, seeing his mother and the disciple standing by whom he loved, says to his mother, "Woman, behold your son." Then <margin>27</margin> he says to the disciple, "Behold your mother." And from that hour the disciple took her <gloss>7</gloss> into his own. After this, Jesus, knowing <margin>28</margin> that all things were now finished, so that the scripture might be completed, says, "I thirst." <margin>B</margin> A vessel was therefore <margin>29</margin> placed there full of vinegar; but they filled a sponge with vinegar and hyssop, and having placed it, they moved it to his mouth. When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, "It is <margin>30</margin> finished," and with his head bowed, <gloss>9</gloss> he gave up his spirit. The Jews therefore, since it was the Preparation, so that the <margin>31</margin> bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that was a great Sabbath day), asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and they be taken away. But when they <margin>33</margin> came to Jesus, as they saw him already dead, they did not break his legs. But one of the soldiers <gloss>10</gloss> pierced his side <margin>34</margin> with a spear, and immediately there came out blood and water. And <margin>35</margin> he who saw it has given testimony, and his testimony is true; <gloss>11</gloss> and he knows that he tells true things, so that you also may believe. For these things were done so that the scripture would <margin>36</margin> be fulfilled: "You shall not break a bone of him." And again another <margin>37</margin> <margin>C</margin> scripture says, <gloss>12</gloss> "They shall look on him whom they have pierced." After <margin>38</margin> these things, Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but a secret one for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate that he might take the body of Jesus, and Pilate permitted it. Nicodemus also came, who had come to <margin>39</margin> Jesus first by night, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes of about a hundred pounds. They took the body <margin>40</margin> of Jesus therefore, <gloss>13</gloss> and bound it in linen cloths with spices, as is the custom for the Jews to bury. Now there was in <margin>41</margin> that place where he was crucified a garden, and in the garden a new tomb, in which no one had yet been placed. There, therefore, because of the Preparation of the <margin>42</margin> Jews, because the tomb was nearby, they placed Jesus.
But on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene comes <margin>1 XX.</margin> <margin>D</margin> early, while it was still dark, to the tomb, and sees the stone taken away from the tomb. Peter therefore went out, and that <margin>3</margin> other disciple, and they came to the tomb. They were <margin>4</margin> running...

...as if that soldier had opened the side while the Lord was alive, before the legs were broken of the thieves, and as if the Lord died from that wound, so that there was no need to break his legs. The Greek word is <note>original: "enyxe"</note> in the indefinite tense <note>the aorist</note>, which if one were to translate as *had pierced* <note>pluperfect</note>, the sense they wanted would be held. But this opinion is condemned by this <margin>E</margin> *Clementine* decree writing to the School of Bologna, that the matter should be accepted as having been done in the order the Evangelist narrates it. Moreover, that the soldier pierced the side of Jesus was not out of cruelty, but as one testing whether death was certain. Just as in a slaughter of enemies, if it is doubted whether one lies dead or still breathes, they strike the foot or shin with a dagger. At such a blow, he who is not yet fully dead usually moves. None of these things happened by chance, but all by the providence of the Divine Power, so that no one should boast that Christ had not been truly dead. There is this slight point, that the Greek speech is ambiguous, because *autou* can refer to the spear: "he struck the side *with his own* spear." The translator renders it "his side" <note>original: "autou ten pleuran"</note>, so that *autou* marks Christ. There would be no ambiguity if the difference were preserved which the Grammarians hand down between *hautou* with the first syllable aspirated <note>meaning "his own"</note>, and *autou* with the first syllable smooth <note>meaning simply "his"</note>.
<margin>F</margin> 11 *And he knows that he tells true things*] The sense is ambiguous even to the Greeks, whether Christ knows that the Evangelist narrates true things, or whether John himself is conscious that he speaks the truth. For he speaks of himself as if in the third person.
12 *They shall look on him whom they have pierced*] This is found in Zechariah, chapter twelve. According to the Septuagint Edition it is read in this manner: "And they shall look toward me, because they have mocked/danced," <note>original: "Kai epiblepsontai pros me, anth' hon orchēsanto"</note>. The Hebrew truth has it thus, according to the translator Jerome: "And they shall look toward me whom they have pierced." Saint Jerome indicates the Septuagint slipped due to the similarity of a letter. For if it is read *dqru* <note>דקרו</note>, it sounds like *exekentēsan* <note>pierced</note>. But if in the opposite order with the letters switched it is read *rqdu* <note>רקדו</note>, it sounds like *orchēsanto* <note>danced/leaped</note>. Therefore John did not show greater respect for what the Septuagint saw, and took more care to weigh the sense from the Hebrew than to count the words. Jerome cites this same place in his booklet to Pammachius on the best kind of interpreting.
13 *And they bound him*] <note>original: "edēsan"</note>, that is, *it*, namely the body. And so Augustine reads it.
<margin>G</margin> *She runs therefore*] <note>original: "trechei"</note>, that is, *she runs*, a verb in the present tense.

<margin>2 And the handkerchief ]</margin> He used a Latin word while writing in Greek <note>original: "sudarium"</note>. For they call it a *soudarion*, as Pollux testifies. 
<margin>3 wrapped in one place ]</margin> In one place, although the Greek preposition is ambiguous. 
<margin>4 The disciples therefore went away again to themselves ]</margin> What does it mean to "go away again"? Had they already gone away once? Therefore "back" should have been said, not "again." And "to themselves" he said, meaning "to their own home." 
<margin>5 And she saw two Angels ]</margin> In Greek *theorei*, that is, she perceives or sees, in the present tense. "Two Angels in white." The translator rendered the Greek figure of speech, just as they call a man in purple "purpurated"; hence we translate it "clothed in white." 
<margin>6 She turned back and saw ]</margin> Again it is *theorei*, that is, she sees, in the present tense. 
<margin>7 I ascend to my Father ]</margin> In this speech, the article is added only once: *to the Father of me and Father of you, and God of me and God of you.* Either because the preceding article serves the remaining parts, or because in this way what Christ felt is more clearly expressed: that he was approaching him who was a Father common to himself and the disciples, and the same God common to him and them. So also Paul says in one place, *the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.* Indeed, if he had said "the God of me," he would have seemed to call one person his Father and another his God. 
<margin>8 Because she saw the Lord, and he said these things ]</margin> *that she had seen the Lord, and he had said these things to her.* That is, that she had seen the Lord, and he had spoken these things to her. The translator seems to have read "he was saying," but it makes no difference to the meaning. 
<margin>9 He said to them again, Peace be with you ]</margin> You see how Christ emphasized nothing more to his own than peace. He does not say "be in agreement," but "be one," and he added the notable example of the highest consensus: *Just as you and I are one.* Here again, not content with having said once, "Peace be with you," he repeats "Peace be with you," and does it not shame the Christian people today that they do nothing other than wage war? It might be tolerated somehow if only the common people were so mad, but many Princes hunt for nothing else; indeed, what is more foul, not only do the Priests incite them to these things, but they themselves wage war. They who profess the Gospel of peace exhort the common folk to wars: and they whose job it was to inflame people to piety, here sound the trumpet, and with the Sacred Scriptures distorted for this purpose, they make that peaceful and most gentle Christ the author of war. If he were to return in this age, he would see that he might be treated more harshly by this race of Pharisees than he was once received by those of old. But these are side-issues <note>original: "parerga"</note>. Note also that, having prayed for peace once and again, he then breathed upon them with his spirit and said, "Whose sins you remit, etc." Those who from these latter words raise their crests <note>meaning to act proudly/arrogantly</note> and claim a certain tyranny for themselves, why do they not remember those things which immediately preceded? Everything is full of dissension, lawsuits, and wars. We all rise up with a worldly spirit, and yet we please ourselves with the authority committed to us of remitting or retaining sins. Protect the authority, but see to it that the spirit is present through which he granted the authority. 
<margin>10 The mark of the nails ]</margin> *typon*, that is, the figure or form; and so it is read in certain Latin codices. Certainly, in the Corbie manuscript, a clear trace of an erasure declared that "figure" <note>original: "figuram"</note> had been written first, not "mark/fixure" <note>original: "fixuram"</note>. The Constance manuscript had "figure" without erasure; yet neither word completely pleases me. For it means the trace of the wound impressed by the nails. Augustine, explaining the Epistle of John, translates it "scars" <note>original: "cicatrices"</note>. But just as for the Latins there is a slight difference between *fixuram* and *figuram*, so for the Greeks between *typon* and *topon* <note>meaning "mark" versus "place"</note>. In Irenaeus I read "figures."

<margin>28 *Unbelieving, but faithful*] <note>original: "ἄπιστος, ἀλλὰ πιστός"</note> that is, unfaithful but faithful, or incredulous but believing, or a believer, lest the <unclear>title/appellation</unclear> be lost. For as Valla writes, the word *faithful* <note>Latin: "fidelem"</note> sounds to Latin ears more like a man of "good faith" than a "believer"—that is, not one who has faith in another, but one who keeps his word. Truly he speaks correctly, but that word has now been used in this [religious] sense by all Christian writers.</margin>

<margin>29 *My Lord & my God*] This is one place in which the Evangelist openly attributes the title of God to Christ. Otherwise, although there are innumerable arguments in the books of the New Testament by which it is clearly evident to pious minds that Christ was equally God and man, it is nevertheless infrequent for him to be called God openly. This is because such a heavenly mystery seemed scarcely ready for the ears of many in that age. Regarding this matter, we shall speak a little more fully in the *Annotations* which we shall write on the first chapter of the First Epistle to Timothy. Nor is there any reason for a Heretic to quibble that this was said by a disciple; Christ acknowledged it, and surely would have rejected it if he had been falsely called God, especially with the other disciples listening.</margin>

<margin>30 *Those who have not seen & have believed*] <note>original: "οἱ μὴ ἰδόντες καὶ πιστεύσαντες"</note>. Augustine, in the passage we cited just before, translates this as "and believe" <note>Latin: "et credunt"</note>, which is not rare among the Greeks regarding verbs of affection, especially those noting a continuous act. For he who has believed does not cease to believe, just as he who has dined ceases to dine.</margin>

<margin>1 *And in that night they caught nothing*] And again: *Bring some of the fish which you have [just] caught*. In some versions it was *captured* or *took*. In Greek it is <note>original: "ἐπίασαν"</note> and <note>original: "ἐπιάσατε"</note>, except that <note>original: "πιάζομαι"</note> is more properly used for "seizing" things that are fleeing. For we "take" <note>Latin: "capimus"</note> things in any manner whatsoever.</margin>

<margin>3 *Do you have any fish?*] <note>original: "προσφάγιον"</note>, which he soon calls <note>original: "ὀψάριον"</note>, so named because it is added to bread; for what else should it be called, or certainly a <term>morsel</term> of relish.</margin>

[The notes continue:]
...that the Greek words *opson* and *opsarion* (a diminutive of that name) are taken for "fish," since it is derived from *edein*, which means "to eat."
<margin>6 *And when so many*] <note>original: "τοσούτων ὄντων"</note>, that is, "since there were so many." He is speaking of the number, not the size.</margin>
<margin>7 *He takes the bread & was giving it to them*] "He comes, he takes, and he gives"—these are all in the present tense in Greek: <note>original: "ἔρχεται, λαμβάνει, δίδωσι"</note>. The Golden Manuscript supports this Greek reading.</margin>
<margin>8 *This already the third*] <note>original: "τοῦτο ἤδη τρίτον"</note>, that is, "This now for the third time." It was "the third" in Latin.</margin>
<margin>9 *Simon of John*] <note>original: "Σίμων Ἰωνᾶ"</note>, that is, "Simon son of Jonah." Although
<margin>E</margin> in some versions it was <term>John</term> <note>Greek: "Ioannou"</note>, just as it is in Luke.</margin>
<margin>10 *Do you love me more than these*] Why did the translator not avoid the ambiguity: "do you love me more than these [men do]?" Otherwise, "do you love me more than these" could be understood as "do you love me more than [you love] these [things/fish]."</margin>
<margin>11 *You know that I love you*] Where just now it was "cherish" <note>Latin: "diligit"</note>, he now changes it to "love" <note>Latin: "amo"</note>. Indeed, the Evangelist also varied the Greek word; the first is <note>original: "ἀγαπᾷς"</note> [agapas], the latter is <note>original: "φιλῶ"</note> [philo], yet he used them with a distinction. Augustine also pointed this out in the fourteenth book of *The City of God*, lest anyone think there is a hidden mystery in this variety or philosophize in vain. Among the Latins, "to love" <note>Latin: "amo"</note> is more vehement than "to cherish" <note>Latin: "diligo"</note>.</margin>
<margin>12 *Feed my lambs*] Twice he had said <note>original: "βόσκε"</note>, that is, "Feed" or "Nourish," and once <note>original: "ποίμαινε"</note>, that is, "Rule," as a shepherd rules a flock. Nor is it "lambs" everywhere, but twice <note>original: "ἀρνία"</note>, that is, "sheep," and once <note>original: "ἀρνία"</note> <note>note: Erasmus seems to be comparing different Greek diminutives for sheep/lambs here</note>. Nor do I think there is any difference in these. One thing should be noted in passing: those who boast from this passage that the flock of the Lord has been committed to them must first remember that love for Christ was demanded of Peter three times—and not just any love, but one more ardent <margin>F</margin> than the others. Then, three times the care of the flock was committed to him. This undoubtedly signifies that no one is fit for the priesthood unless, having neglected all else, he loves nothing but Christ—that is, truth, innocence, and piety. To these things, nothing ought to be more important to him than the safety of the flock entrusted to him. Therefore, I ask: what nerve do those have who enter [the church] through profane, even wicked obedience to Princes, or through money—those who think the priesthood is nothing other than profit and tyranny? Do they not remember how attentively and by what laws Christ committed his sheep to Peter? He did not commit them to be devoured, but to be fed. Fed by the example of a pious life, fed by the food of Gospel doctrine (whether they desire milk or solid food), and fed even by the support of one's resources, if the situation demands it.</margin>

13 **Where you do not want** ] <note>original: "ὅπου οὐ θέλεις" (hopou ou theleis)</note>. But why did the same phrasing not appear above as "where you wanted," since the Greek adverb is the same? Although I would prefer in both places: "where you want," "where you wanted," and "they will lead you where you do not want."

14 **Who will betray** ] <note>original: "ὁ παραδιδούς" (ho paradidous)</note>, that is, *the one who is giving up* or *betraying*.

15 **So I want him to remain** ] Since all the Greek manuscripts consistently have written, <term>if I want him to remain</term> <note>original: "ἐὰν αὐτὸν θέλω μένειν"</note>, there can be no doubt that the conjunction <term>if</term> <note>original: "si"</note> was changed into the adverb <term>so</term> <note>original: "sic"</note>, and this was not by the fault of the Translator, but by the error of a Scribe. Indeed, among the Latins, it is an easy and prone slip from *si* to *sic* because of the similarity of the words. However, among the Greeks, there is nothing similar between <term>if</term> <note>original: "ἐὰν" (ean)</note> and <term>so/thus</term> <note>original: "οὕτως" (houtos)</note>, such that the Translator could be seen to have slipped on this occasion. Nor do only the Greek manuscripts agree, but also the Interpreters: Cyril, Chrysostom, and Theophylact. Although in these volumes of Chrysostom recently printed, it had been <unclear>changed</unclear> <note>Latin: "immutatum"</note> into *sic* by some unlearned person. Truly, the interpretation itself clearly proves that Chrysostom read *if*. He says two things on this point: that Christ did not wish to answer Peter regarding what He was going to do with John, but wished to blunt Peter’s rash and curious questioning. He would not have done this if He had simply answered that John was going to remain. Furthermore, Saint Jerome, in his first book against Jovinian, cites this passage according to the "Greek truth" <note>A common Erasmian phrase referring to the original Greek text as the ultimate authority</note>. And even though all things of this kind are usually corrupted to match a once publicly received error, I do not know by what chance it happened that this passage has remained uncorrupted in the common manuscripts of Jerome. Even if it had been greatly corrupted, the very tenor of the dispute proves that Jerome read *if*, not *so*. And although such a great consensus of all Greek codices was enough to prove the matter, nevertheless, in the manuscript which the Library of the Canons of Corfendonck made available to us, it is clearly written, <term>If I want him</term>, not <term>So I want him</term>. Nor do I doubt that it was written the same way in the Pauline codex, except that the last page failed us. In an ancient codex which we saw in the Library of the College at Bruges, dedicated to Saint Donatian, both were written, <term>If so</term>, nor was the place free from erasure. The most ancient codices support us, whose authority the Amerbach brothers followed in Basel. Likewise, the Gospel codex preserved as a miracle of antiquity in the Library of the College of Constance—of which Joannes Botzernus, a Canon of that fellowship and a man of very pure heart, gave us the opportunity to inspect—had <term>If him</term> twice without any trace of erasure. Among the older writers, only Augustine seems to some to have read, <term>So I want him to remain</term>. That man was indeed—as cannot be denied—holy, upright, and endowed with a sharp mind; yet, because of the simplicity of his nature, he was excessively credulous, and not similarly protected by the defense of languages. Even if he was not entirely ignorant of Greek literature, he was not so learned as to be able to readily unfold the Greek Interpreters. Add to this that he came late to the profession of the Christian name, and as a young man was soon snatched away to the Episcopal office, so that he was forced to learn what he taught by teaching it, and to learn what he wrote by writing it, as he himself confesses somewhere. Therefore, even if he slipped in some way, though otherwise a very great man, he was not to be attacked with insults, as Valla did too sharply in this place. Valla says, "Augustine, not even here consulting the Greek truth, hopes to find the truth among falsehoods." And a little later, more hatefully: <term>Now in such a matter, whether Evangelical or pertaining to the Gospel, having omitted the truth of the Greek fountain, he demands that we believe him, etc.</term> On the contrary, if someone examines Augustine's exposition more attentively, they will find that he too read <term>If him</term>, not <term>So him</term>, and that "so" was corrupted by some unlearned person. For when he admits that it could be objected that the Lord did not actually say John would not die, but nevertheless hinted at it, does he not sufficiently reveal what he read? For if someone asked how he wants the bed made, and he answers, <term>If I want it to remain</term>, he does not mean that he wants the tool to remain, but he explains it clearly. But if he answers, <term>What if I want it to remain so</term>, he implies he does not want it done, but in such a way that he leaves what he wants in doubt. Just as in a Legal Agreement, someone who speaks thus: <term>What if I do not want to sell it to you, will you force me?</term>, does not deny that he wants to sell, but indicates that he is free to sell or not to sell. And I have said these things not because I think it impious to disagree with Augustine in some places, but because I do not want him to be rebuked without cause. Furthermore, although these things do not make one a heretic—if you read *so* for *if*—nevertheless, such a manifest error must not be concealed in the Gospel writings. And as I admit that one who slips thus should not be attacked with insults, so I say he should be pitied and assisted. He who through ignorance of letters baptized with these words, <term>In the name of the Father, and of the Daughter, and of the Holy Spirit</term> <note>Latin: "In nomine Patri, et Filia, et Spiritu Sancta" (incorrect grammar)</note>, is excused. Yet no one who knows better would tolerate such a baptizer. Indeed, Augustine himself did not approve of the people singing in churches, <term>But upon him it shall flour</term>, instead of <term>flourish</term> <note>Latin: "floriet" for "florebit"</note>, even though he knew God is not offended by grammatical errors. How much less should it be ignored if so foul a mistake has crept into the Gospel writings? But if the Latin

B Interpreter had translated the indicative mood into the subjunctive mood, the slip would not have been so slippery: <term>If I should wish him to remain until I come</term>. Not to repeat in the meantime that the very context of the speech refutes that reading. For it follows, <term>And Jesus did not say that that disciple would not die</term>. If we read above, <term>So I want him to remain</term>, he plainly said he would not die until He came, which John denies was said. Nor does John doubt that Christ spoke of "remaining," not "not dying," but he denies it was said affirmatively; rather, He left it in ambiguity, so that the matter did not concern Peter. Now, since there is the highest consensus in all the Greek codices, and since in so many ancient Latin books the writing is found agreeing with the Greeks, and since the translation of Cyril by George of Trebizond contains the genuine reading (which is indeed repeated more than once and was printed in Paris by the authority of the Theologians, as the preface indicates), and since the same integrity of reading remains in Jerome—furthermore, since the interpretation of Jerome, Chrysostom, Cyril, and I do not doubt Theophylact (for here the last page had fallen away) does not allow anything to be read other than <term>If I want him</term>—nevertheless, a certain Carthusian theologian, in a published book, strongly asserts that *sic* <note>so/thus</note> must be read on the authority of all Greeks and Latins. He relies on two arguments: first, that a codex of Chrysostom translated into Latin and poorly printed has it so; second, because *sic* is recited in the Church today. For he prescribes this law for us: that we should hold that writing as genuine which common usage has obtained. And yet the codices declare that three hundred or four hundred years ago, public use had <term>if</term>. Therefore, this was then the genuine reading according to his own prescription. But because now, the passage having been corrupted, public use has *sic*, what was previously the genuine reading is now spurious. Usage has such power that the same thing can be both a vice and a gem. But I will add Cyril's words, by which he declares what he read: <term>Here, therefore, he says, when Peter looked back at the one so beloved by the Lord, he immediately asked what end of life was imminent for him. But since the inquiry into other people's affairs is more curious than useful, He answers indeed, but in such a way as to lead the mind of the questioner to other things. He does not say John will be exempt from death, but "If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?" That is: Peter, you have heard what pertains to you; why do you seek after other people's things? Why do you pry into the secrets of divine justice? For even if I willed that he should not die at all, what profit or what consolation would you ever obtain? It is not for a prudent man to be curious if someone else is to suffer, or whether others undergo the same things or not, since one's own dangers are not mitigated by the calamity of others. Although it commonly seems just to men to hope, if they are to undergo some danger, that they are not alone, but that others also either appear to suffer similar things, or at least to hear that they have endured them, or will suffer the same altogether.</term> Indeed, even in the *Catena* <note>A commentary composed of "chains" of quotes from Church Fathers</note> where many are cited in fragments, some good chance preserved the integral reading in those parts which, I believe, are cited from Theophylact: <term>Attend to and finish the work committed to you; but if I should want this man to remain here, what is that to you?</term> Augustine alone among the Ancients can be seen to have read, <term>So I want him to remain</term>, deceived by a fault in the codex; and being offended by the absurdity of the speech, he twists the sense with various interpretations. But so that you may understand that this was done by the rashness of Scribes: in the first place, a Reader offended by this speech, <term>Jesus said to him, If I want him to remain until I come</term>—not noticing that "if" <note>si</note> was placed for "whether" <note>an</note> or "what if," and that this part refers to what follows, "what is that to you"—turned <term>if</term> into <term>so</term>, and separated the particle <term>what to you</term> from the preceding words. Soon, where he saw it repeated, <term>If I want him to remain</term>, and *if* no longer seemed to fit if you separate *what to you* from the preceding, he left *if*, yet he was loath to restore what he had changed before. Thus it happened that in some codices the first instance has *so*, and the second has *if*. Then, with the writing varying, since in some *so* and in others *if* was found, someone wrote the other in the margin; finally, both were brought into the main text. We frequently encounter this kind of corruption in Jerome and Cyprian. Whenever a Scripture was cited by them differently than it is commonly read, a "learned" scribe, being offended, changed what was cited from his own memory according to the Vulgate edition. Later, when he saw the same things repeated more often, he realized it was not a slip of the Scribes and ceased to change it. And so the reading varied in the beginnings and in the excerpts or at the end. But after the matter has been made clear by so many arguments, if someone in the common codices had erred superfluously, or immediately pronounced, <term>if I want him to remain</term>, he was not to be carped at, but imitated, provided he gave the reason for the changed reading. Now, I am not the author of scraping out text, nor of pronouncing it otherwise in the churches; I only point out the genuine reading from the faith of the codices of both languages, and from the interpretation of the more probable Doctors of the Church. Thus, he who does not believe the demonstrated truth might perhaps be called stubborn; he who cries out against it, impudent; he who neglects the one pointing it out, ungrateful; and he who does not grasp such evident things, slow. However, he who teaches what is right in place of an inveterate error does not thrust in new things, but...
