<header>ACCORDING TO JOHN CHAPTER XXI.</header>

<margin>A</margin> ...until I come, what is that to you? You follow me. This saying therefore went out among the brothers, that this disciple would not die; yet Jesus did not say to him, "He will not die," but, "If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?" This is the disciple who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things, and we know that his testimony is true. And there are also many other things that Jesus did, which if they were written one by one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that would be written. <note>original Greek: "ἔρχομαι, τί πρός σε; ... οὐδὲ αὐτὸν οἶμαι τὸν κόσμον χωρῆσαι τὰ γραφόμενα βιβλία."</note>

# THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN
## T H E  E N D.

But if someone restores ancient things, and if another person seditiously cries out that he is a forger and incites the world against him with furious writings, I ask, by what name does he deserve to be called? Though I remain silent, the matter speaks for itself. And yet these men boast that they are absolute theologians, and they seem to themselves no less pious than learned, thinking it an abominable crime if they eat mutton instead of sturgeon, <note>Erasmus uses the "scaro" (a prized fish) versus "ovilla" (mutton) to mock the misplaced priorities of his critics who focus on dietary laws while attacking scholarship.</note> and they lead others to believe it is pure religion if they thus calumniate one who gives good advice. Such a race of "saints" is produced for us by linen and wool, leather and cloth, fish and beans, blackness and whiteness, names and titles. <note>These refer to the various habits and dietary restrictions of different monastic orders.</note> May the Lord stir up His Spirit in all people.

<margin>C</margin> <margin>16 Until I come</margin> Here Christ, if I may put it this way, deceives his disciples in the phrase *until I come*. For they were expecting the kingdom of Israel to come soon. To "follow" was to die a violent death, and to "remain" does not simply mean not to die, but not to die according to the example of Christ.

<margin>17 The word went out among the brothers</margin> How did it "go out" if it was already "among" the brothers? Nevertheless, Suetonius used this word in his life of Nero: "The opinion," he says, "went out after the theatrical crowns." <note>original: "Exiit... opinio."</note> Therefore, it would be clearer and more Latin to say: "The rumor spread among the brothers," <note>original: "Permanavit rumor inter fratres."</note> that is, to the rest of the Christians; and what was said there to a few listeners crept out to the many as the rumor was made public.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...if I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me. 17 Therefore the saying went out among the brothers, that that disciple would not die: and Jesus had not said to him, 18 "He does not die," but, "If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?" This is that disciple, who provides testimony concerning these things, and wrote these things: and we know, that his testimony is true. There are also many other things which Jesus did, which if they were written individually, 19 I suppose that not even the world itself would contain the books that would be written.

<margin>B</margin>
# OF THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN
## T H E  E N D.

<margin>18 That he does not die</margin> It would be more correct to say, "that he would not die." <note>original: "quod non moreretur."</note> Although it was more convenient to omit the conjunction, because of what follows: "but, If I want him to remain." For "He said to him" does not refer to John, but to Peter. I thought to add this in passing, because a certain learned man thought in this place that the conjunction could not be omitted without disadvantage.

<margin>19 I do not think the world itself could contain</margin> Here Augustine, offended by the hyperbole, refers "to contain" not to the space of a location, but to the mind. <note>Augustine argued that the "world" (mankind) could not mentally grasp or understand the full extent of Christ's deeds.</note> But in the same way, the world could not contain even one page of divine wisdom. Chrysostom and Cyril say nothing of the sort; they frankly admit it is a hyperbole. It suggests an incredible power and multitude of books. For the Greek word is <term>χωρῆσαι</term> <note>chōrēsai: to have room for, to contain, or to give way.</note>, which is properly said of the space of a location, as we noted on that passage, "Not all contain this word." <note>Matthew 19:11.</note> Nor does the Greek say "to be able to contain," but only <term>χωρῆσαι</term>, that is, "to contain" or "being about to contain." Certainly, in the "Golden Codex," the word "to be able" is not added. Not even in the Constance manuscript. Finally, regarding "which are to be written," it was better to say, "which would have to be written."

<meta>This page serves as a historical and biographical appendix following the conclusion of the Gospel of John. It departs from Erasmus’s commentary to provide a traditional Greek account of the life, travels, and eventual martyrdom of the Apostle Paul, likely included as a reference for the subsequent Pauline Epistles. The text relies heavily on the Acts of the Apostles and the chronological frameworks established by early church historians like Eusebius.</meta>

423 THE JOURNEYS OF 424

# THE APOSTLE PAUL.

He began from Damascus and went up to Jerusalem, from there to Tarsus, and from there to Antioch; then again to Jerusalem, and again to Antioch. From there he was sent with Barnabas on his mission; he went down to Seleucia, then to Cyprus, where he also began to be called Paul. Then to Perga, then to Antioch in Pisidia, then to Iconium, then to Lystra and Derbe of Lycaonia, then to Pamphylia, then back to Perga, then to Attalia, then for a third time to Antioch in Syria, and then for a third time to Jerusalem because of the matter of circumcision. Then for a fourth time to Antioch; then he passed through Syria and Cilicia. Then for a second time to Derbe and Lystra, where he circumcised Timothy. Then to the region of Phrygia and Galatia, then to Mysia, then to Troas. From there to Neapolis, then to Philippi in Macedonia. Then, having passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, he came to Thessalonica, then to Berea, then to Athens, then to Corinth, then to Ephesus, then to Caesarea. Then for a second time to Antioch in Pisidia, then to the Galatian region and Phrygia. Then for a second time to Ephesus, then having passed through Macedonia, he came to Greece. From there, having passed through Macedonia, he came for a second time to Philippi, and from Philippi back to Troas, where he raised Eutychus after he had fallen. <note>original: "ἔγειρε πεσόντα" — refers to the miracle in Acts 20 where a young man falls from a window during Paul's preaching.</note> Then to Assos, then to Mitylene, then opposite Chios, then to Samos, and from there to Miletus. From there, having sent for those in Ephesus, he spoke with them. Then to Cos, then to Rhodes; from there to Patara, from there to Tyre, then to Ptolemais, and from there to Caesarea. From there he went up for a fourth time to Jerusalem. From there he was sent to Caesarea, and finally as a prisoner to Rome. Thus, from Caesarea he came to Sidon, and from there to Myra in Lycia; then to Cnidus, and from there, after suffering much, he came to the island <note>Malta</note> where the viper fastened onto his hand, but he remained unharmed. Then to Syracuse, then to Rhegium in Calabria, then to Puteoli, and from there he went on foot up to Rome, with the brothers meeting him at the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns. Finally, having entered Rome and having taught for a sufficient time, he later suffered martyrdom in Rome itself, having fought the good fight there. <note>original: "τὸν καλὸν ἀγῶνα ἀγωνισάμενος" — a reference to 2 Timothy 4:7.</note> The Romans, having placed these remains in magnificent houses and palaces, celebrate a day of memory for him on the third day before the Kalends of July, <note>June 29th</note> celebrating in this sixth of the total months of martyrdoms. The blessed man had already given many exhortations regarding life and virtue before that time, and had introduced many things to men concerning what must be done; furthermore, through the sight of these fourteen epistles, he described the entire way of life for all people.

I considered it necessary to briefly note the time of Paul's preaching, making a summary from the *Chronological Canons* of Eusebius Pamphili. <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian known as the "Father of Church History."</note> Having taken that book into my hands and opened it, I find the Passion of our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ occurred in the eighteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, as well as his three-day resurrection and his ascension into heaven in Christ. A few days later, I saw there the Apostles appointing to service the namesake of the crown, Stephen, and those with him. Later, I find him among all the Jews again, as we said before, with Stephen contending there and Paul consenting to the murder. A little later, Paul appeared before the high priests of the Jews and received letters to the Jews in Damascus against the disciples. In the middle of the road, his calling by God occurred, so that that year was nearly spent. When the nineteenth year of Tiberius Caesar began, history says Paul was joined to the preaching and ran through the whole world evangelizing piety in Christ until the thirteenth year of Claudius Caesar, when Felix was governor of Judea, before whom Paul, being accused by the Jews, made his defense. Felix confined the Apostle in the prison at Caesarea for two years. After him, Porcius Festus succeeded to the rule and immediately set out to examine the Apostle, wishing to grant a great favor to the Jews. Then the blessed man, thinking there was no other way to escape the plot than by appealing to Caesar, perhaps appealed to Caesar at the judgment seat; and he was sent away to Rome to Nero Caesar. Aristarchus was with him, whom he reasonably calls a "fellow prisoner" in the epistles, and Luke, who handed down the *Acts of the Apostles* in writing. There, Paul was kept under guard by the Romans for two whole years. For Luke records these things up to that point in the *Acts of the Apostles*, having composed the book at that time. Knowing the rest that followed, he thus placed the martyrdom in the book; for leaving him there, both Luke and Aristarchus departed. 

Eusebius, having accurately investigated the subsequent times, also related the martyrdom to us in the second volume of his *Ecclesiastical History*, and says that Paul spent time at liberty and preached the word of God without hindrance. At that time, after Paul made his defense before Nero, the story goes that he was sent out again for the ministry of preaching, having been released by Caesar, and evangelized for another ten years. But when Nero reached the height of madness, he first killed his own mother Agrippina, then his father's sister, and Octavia his own wife, and countless others related to him by blood. Afterward, he stirred up a general persecution against the Christians, and thus was led to the slaughter of the Apostles; for having summoned Paul again, he presented him at the judgment seat. Luke was with him again. There it happened that Paul suffered martyrdom in the thirty-sixth year after the Savior's Passion, and in the thirteenth year of Nero, being beheaded with a sword. Therefore, from the nineteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when he began to preach the Gospel, until the twenty-second year is four years; and the years of Gaius <note>Emperor Caligula</note> are likewise four years; then again the years of Claudius are a little less than fourteen; whom Nero succeeded, and in the thirteenth year of his own reign, he killed the Apostle. Therefore, the same Apostle Paul writes to Timothy concerning his first defense, saying this: "At my first defense no one stood with me, but everyone deserted me—may it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fully accomplished, and all the Gentiles might hear; and I was rescued from the lion's mouth," <note>2 Timothy 4:16-17</note> saying that this "lion" was Nero. Concerning the second defense, in which he was perfected by his martyrdom, he says, "you will fulfill your good ministry; for I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come." <note>2 Timothy 4:5-6</note> And because Luke was with him again, a little further in the letter he writes, "Luke, who is with me, greets you." Thus, the entire time of Paul's preaching was twenty-one years; and two other years which he spent in the prison at Caesarea; in addition to these, the first two years in Rome, and the final ten years, so that the total years from his <term>new birth</term> <note>His conversion on the road to Damascus</note> until his completion were thirty-five.

## THE MARTYRDOM OF THE

# APOSTLE PAUL.

Under Nero, the Caesar of the Romans, the Apostle Paul suffered martyrdom there, being beheaded with a sword in the thirty-sixth year after the Savior’s Passion, having fought the good fight in Rome on the fifth day of the month of Panemos, which among the Romans would be called the third day before the Kalends of July. On this day the holy Apostle was perfected by his martyrdom, in the sixty-ninth year of the <term>presence</term> <note>referring to the Incarnation/Birth</note> of our Savior Jesus Christ.

# THE PILGRIMAGE OF THE APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL,
## WITH A CHRONOLOGICAL ACCOUNT
### BY
### DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'E' featuring ornate vine and foliage patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

FROM THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, it is not clear that Peter changed his location frequently, except that after the death of Stephen, he set out together with his colleague John for the city of Samaria—which was later renamed *Sebaste* <note>original: "Sebaste" — the Greek name given to the city of Samaria by Herod the Great in honor of Emperor Augustus</note>, from which the entire region of Samaria takes its name—in order to confirm with his own authority and complete what had been begun there by Philip the Deacon. Afterwards, he seems to have traveled through most parts of Samaria. For we read this in the eighth chapter: *And they preached the gospel in many regions of the Samaritans.* Now, Samaria lies between Judea and Galilee. Furthermore, the ninth chapter testifies that he traveled through various regions of Palestine before he came to Lydda and Joppa. For it says:

<margin>*And it happened that as Peter went through all parts, he also came down to the saints who dwelt in Lydda.*</margin>
For Lydda is in Palestine, not far from the coastal city of Joppa. Again, he is recorded as having set out from Joppa to Caesarea, a maritime city of Palestine which was previously called the *Tower of Strato*. Here he baptized Cornelius the centurion. From here he returned to Jerusalem. However, as to when he set out for Antioch (where he is believed to have presided) or when he moved to Rome, and which regions he traveled through, I will not labor to pursue these details since they are recorded only in human histories <note>Erasmus distinguishes between "divine" history (the Bible) and "human" history (church traditions and secular records).</note>. For Eusebius, who thinks that Peter preached the Gospel among the people of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, drew this conjecture from no other source than the fact that Peter mentions these nations in his first Epistle. It was fitting, however, that the chief of the Apostles should reside for several years in that city from which the Lord Jesus willed that the Evangelical doctrine should be propagated: first into all regions of Judea, and soon into the whole world. Regarding what the record—which they call Ecclesiastical History—hands down, namely that the primary care of affairs was entrusted by Christ to Peter, James, and John, they gather this from the fact that these men are mentioned by name several times, while nothing is narrated about what the others said or did, except that they stood by Peter as witnesses while he spoke. Now, there were two named James: one the son of Zebedee and brother of John, whom Herod killed; and this very fact proves that he was a leader among the Apostles. The other was the son of Alphaeus. Frequent mention is made in the Acts of a third James, who was called the "Brother of the Lord," with the surname "the Just," the son (as Jerome believes) of Mary, who was the sister of the Lord’s mother. To this James they attribute the Epistle which is read among the catholic <note>In this context, "catholic" means "universal" or "general" epistles, not specifically the Roman Catholic Church.</note> letters. Although he was not among the number of the twelve Apostles, nevertheless, immediately after the death of Christ, the Apostles designated him as the Bishop of Jerusalem. After Paul had appealed to Caesarea, this James was cast down from the pinnacle of the temple, and while being stoned, he died after being struck by a fuller's club <note>A "fuller" was someone who cleaned and thickened cloth; their heavy wooden clubs became a traditional symbol of James's martyrdom.</note>. Jerome, in other places as well as when explaining the seventeenth chapter of Isaiah, denies that this man was of the number of the twelve Apostles. And yet, how great his authority was is declared by this: that when the Council was treating the matter of not burdening the Gentiles with the Law of Moses, he pronounced the sentence with authority after Peter, saying, "I judge" <note>original: "ἐγὼ κρίνω" (ego krino) — James’s decisive words in Acts 15:19.</note>. This same man later advised Paul to join himself with four men who had bound themselves by a vow, and to be purified with them in the temple according to the Jewish rite; Paul complied with his counsel. Indeed, upon entering the city, Paul greeted him first, as if he held the primary place there. And in the Epistle to the Galatians, Paul names him as a principal figure: *I saw none of the other Apostles,* he says, *except James the brother of the Lord.* Furthermore, Paul declares in the same Epistle that Peter was at Antioch, narrating how he rebuked him for his pretense. Now, Dionysius, Bishop of the Corinthians, a very ancient writer cited in Eusebius, recorded in writing that Peter and Paul earned the palm of martyrdom on the same day in Rome by the order of Nero. Moreover, that Peter was the primate even among the chief Apostles is shown by the fact that in all the Evangelists, and also in the Acts, he is always listed in the first place in the catalog of the twelve. Secondly, he was almost always the first to speak at the beginning. For even before the Holy Spirit was sent, when the disciples were gathered in the upper room, he proposed the substitution of someone in the place of Judas. Again, when there was a tumult among the people because of the miracle of tongues, Peter alone began the Gospel sermon. He was the first of all to perform a miracle in the name of Jesus, healing the lame man before the temple gates. And soon, for this reason, when a crowd gathered in Solomon’s Portico, Peter preached to the people. There, John, Peter’s companion, also seems to have said something that is not recorded. For Luke says, *And as they were speaking to the people:* unless one prefers to understand that both said what Peter said in the name of both. For a similar passage follows soon in the same third chapter: *But Peter and John, answering, said to them.* Again, in the fourth chapter: *But Peter and the Apostles, answering, said.* This suggests Peter spoke with the voice of all. Again, when dealing with the creation of Deacons, Peter alone spoke. He alone pronounced the sentence upon Ananias. Indeed, this also proves Peter’s dignity among the Apostles: that he was the first led into prison and beaten with rods; although from Luke’s narrative it appears that all the Apostles were beaten with rods at the same time as Peter, when he was thrown into prison a second time.

Now let us speak of Paul, who, like a vigorous leader, flew through all lands and seas to bring all nations under the yoke of Christ. First, he set out from Jerusalem for Damascus. That is a city of Coele-Syria, or Syrophoenicia, which was formerly assigned to Arabia, as Tertullian asserts in his third book against Marcion: the capital of all Syria, situated between Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon. Here Paul was baptized and began the preaching of the Gospel. But fleeing secretly from here, it is not sufficiently clear from the Acts whether he went away into Arabia and returned from there to Damascus, and only after three years finally returned to Jerusalem to see Peter (as he himself relates in the Epistle to the Galatians), or whether he withdrew to Jerusalem immediately. Indeed, it is not even clear whether he was endangered by the snares of the governor during his first preaching or his second. From Luke’s narrative, it seems that as soon as he had fled from Damascus, he withdrew to Jerusalem; because those who a little while before had seen him set out with a hostile mind against the disciples were unwilling to receive him into their fellowship. If he had preached for so many years, it could hardly have happened that they would not have known by rumor that he had been changed. Again, as a fugitive from Jerusalem, he was led to Caesarea Philippi, which Ptolemy calls *Panea* and Eusebius *Paneas*; it is in Phoenicia at the foot of Mount Lebanon, where the springs of the Jordan are. From Caesarea he was sent to Tarsus. That is the metropolis of Cilicia, Paul's homeland, through which the river Cydnus flows. From Tarsus, he was brought back to Antioch by Barnabas, the metropolis of Phoenicia <note>Antioch on the Orontes, the capital of the Roman province of Syria.</note>, from which the region next to Cilicia also takes its name. It sits above the Orontes river. From here he set out...

<meta>This page continues the chronological account of the Apostles' travels. ### THE PILGRIMAGE OF PETER AND PAUL
#### (Continued)

...he [Paul] was led back again to Jerusalem, so that he might present the collected money for the relief of the poor. Having done this, he returned to Antioch, from where he had come. Here, having been granted the title of Apostle, he set out for Seleucia. This is located on the headland of Antioch in Syria, lying in the path of anyone wishing to travel from the city of Antioch to Cyprus. From Seleucia he sailed to Cyprus, an island opposite Cilicia, which is in Asia Minor. He landed at Salamis, which is the first city of Cyprus one encounters to the East, and reached Paphos, which is at the extreme West; from this we understand that he traversed the entire island. It is here that some believe his name was changed from *Saul* to *Paulus* after Sergius Paulus, the Proconsul of that island; however, it is more fitting that parents and patrons bestow their names upon children and freedmen, rather than borrowing names from them.

Setting sail from Paphos, he landed at Perga. That is a city in Pamphylia. From there he went to Antioch in Pisidia <note>original: "Antiochiam Pisidiæ" — not to be confused with the more famous Antioch in Syria; this was a major Roman colony in the highlands of Asia Minor</note>. From there to Iconium: then to Lystra, which is a city of Lycaonia. It was here that Paul was stoned. From Lystra he set out for Derbe, which is also in Lycaonia. From here, retracing the path by which he had come, he returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch in Pisidia, so that he might confirm what had been begun. And likewise, having traversed the rest of Pisidia, they returned to Pamphylia, as far as Perga, where they had first landed from Cyprus. From there they went to Attalia. This is a coastal city of Pamphylia, regarding which a scribe once wrote *Italy* <note>original: "Italiam" — Erasmus is noting a common copyist error where "Attaliam" was mistaken for "Italiam" due to the similar spelling</note>.

Setting sail from Attalia, they sailed to Antioch in Syria, where this journey had first been inaugurated. From here they went again to Jerusalem, to prove to the rest of the Apostles what he had accomplished in Asia Minor; but in the meantime, he preached the Gospel in Phoenicia and Samaria, through which his journey lay. This completed, he returned to Antioch, from where he had come. Here, having separated from Barnabas, he traveled through Syria, and soon through Cilicia. From there he revisited Derbe and Lystra once more, where he circumcised Timothy. From Lystra he made his way through Phrygia and Galatia. From here they came into Mysia, and soon to Troas.

And here a certain "scruple" <note>term: "scruple" — a scholarly or moral hesitation or difficulty in interpretation</note> arises. For if one considers Phrygia, in which Troas is located, Galatia is encountered before Phrygia when coming from Lycaonia. And yet Luke, in the sixteenth chapter, reports it thus: *And passing through Phrygia and the region of Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia.* Nor can it seem certain whether "Asia" here is understood as that part of Asia Minor which is simply called *Asia* <note>original: "Asia" — referring to the Roman Province of Asia, the westernmost part of modern Turkey</note>, or as the whole of Asia Minor, in which he had already preached in many places. Since Galatia is situated to the North—that is, toward the Euxine Sea <note>original: "Pontum Euxinum" — the Black Sea</note>—it has Cappadocia to the East, Bithynia to the West, and Pisidia and Lycaonia to the South. Furthermore, Greater Mysia is very close to Asia properly so-called. Lesser Mysia is above Phrygia. Therefore, the difficulty can be explained such that in these two names, *Phrygia* and *Galatia*, the order is reversed; you will find the correct order in the description of the same journey in the eighteenth chapter. We should understand that he came from Lycaonia straight into Galatia, then into Phrygia, and from Phrygia he wished to seek Bithynia through Mysia, had the Spirit not forbidden it. Moreover, this part of Asia borders Phrygia to the East and South. Therefore, Paul, forbidden to go here, turned his journey toward Mysia, if I am not mistaken, through which the path leads to Bithynia, which was once called *Bebrycia* and *Mygdonia*; it has that part of Asia properly called *Pontus* closest to the North and the East. Again, when the Spirit forbade him to go there, he turned his journey back toward the West, and having traversed Lesser Mysia, he returned through the middle of Phrygia as far as Troas. Troas is on the coast of Phrygia; it was also called *Antigonia*, and it sits opposite the Chersonese, from where the nearest crossing is into Europe from Asia Minor.

From Troas they set sail, and by a straight course reached the island of Samothrace, opposite Thrace, which lies to its North. From there they went to Neapolis. That city is on the coast, at the border of Macedonia and Thrace. From there to Philippi, which Luke reminds us is a colonial city in the first part of Macedonia. Paul wrote one Epistle to these people. Here he was beaten with rods and cast into prison with Silas. After this, passing through Amphipolis—which is not far from the river Strymon—and Apollonia—which is very close to Thessalonica—they came to Thessalonica. That city is the metropolis of Macedonia. Paul also wrote an Epistle to these people. Here, after a riot arose, he was sent away secretly to Berea, which is separated from Thessalonica by Pella, the birthplace of Alexander the Great. Here he found teachable listeners. Furthermore, Berea is not so far from the sea. Thus, when a riot was stirred up, he was led down to the sea, and from there he reached Athens by ship, if I am not mistaken, because Luke mentions that he was sent away to go to the sea. There is also another conjecture: that since the journey from Berea all the way to Attica is long, no mention is made of the regions or cities that would have been encountered by those traveling on foot.

Here he converted Dionysius: whether he was a Jew or a Philosopher is not entirely clear, since Luke only calls him the *Areopagite* <note>original: "Areopagitam" — a member of the Areopagus, the high court of Athens</note>. I believe, however, that all those who inhabited that part of the city of Athens were called *Areopagites*. I wonder, though, why Bede <note>original: "Beda" — the Venerable Bede (c. 673–735), an English monk and historian</note> makes him the Bishop of the Corinthians, since in Eusebius <note>original: "Eusebium" — Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339), often called the "Father of Church History"</note>, a certain Dionysius, Bishop of the Corinthians, teaches that Dionysius the Areopagite was ordained Bishop at Athens by Paul himself. Indeed, it is more probable that Dionysius the Areopagite left no writings at all, since in Eusebius the books of Dionysius, Bishop of the Corinthians, are so diligently cataloged, yet no mention is ever made of any monuments by the Areopagite.

From Attica he came to Corinth. That is the metropolis of Achaia. From here he had decided to sail for Syria, and having undertaken a vow in Cenchreae—which is the Corinthian port looking toward Attica—he shaved his head. From here, therefore, setting sail, he reached Ephesus. That is on the coast of Asia Minor, in the part called *Ionia*. It was here at that time that he left Priscilla and Aquila. Setting sail from Ephesus, he came to Caesarea, and then to Antioch. I do not doubt that Bede, following some ancient source, intends this to be Caesarea in Cappadocia, not in Syria; and the Greeks maintain that this Antioch is the one in Pisidia, which he mentioned twice above. Although, for those departing from Ephesus, Pisidia is encountered before Cappadocia. Furthermore, the Greek manuscripts contain more in this place than ours do. Specifically, in this manner:

> But when they asked him to stay with them for a longer time, he did not consent, but said farewell to them, saying, *I must by all means keep the coming feast in Jerusalem.*

By those who approve this reading, it is preferred that Paul sailed straight from the coast of Ephesus to Caesarea in Palestine, then sought Jerusalem and greeted the brothers, and after this returned to Antioch in Syria, and from here again revisited Asia Minor. This opinion is supported by what is read: *Going down to Caesarea, he went up and greeted the Church.* It shows where he "went down" but does not specify where he "went up." Yet in the Gospel writings, those who seek Jerusalem are said to "go up" <note>original: "adscendere" — a technical biblical term because Jerusalem is geographically elevated</note>, from which they conjecture that he went up from Caesarea in Palestine to Jerusalem, where he had said the feast day must be kept, and from here he "went down" again, seeking Antioch. We have followed this opinion as probable in this Paraphrase, though we will easily yield if someone brings forward a more probable one. It is also read that he stayed in Antioch for some time. Now, Paul was accustomed to staying gladly in Antioch of Syria. From here, then, having revisited Asia and traveled through the middle regions where he had previously taught, he came to Galatia: from there again to Phrygia, everywhere confirming the disciples. From there, since Apollos had already set out for Corinth, he himself set out for Ephesus—whether by a land route or by sailing is not quite clear, except that it is more probable that he made the journey by land, because Luke adds: *having traveled through the upper regions.* Here Paul had proposed to revisit Jerusalem, but first having traveled through Macedonia and Achaia; understanding through the Spirit that he must go to Rome after visiting Jerusalem. Therefore, he sent Timothy and Erastus ahead into Macedonia, while he himself stayed for some time in Asia Minor. After the riot stirred up by Demetrius, he followed those whom he had sent ahead. Having traveled through the upper parts, he came down into that part which is properly called *Greece*, in which are Attica and Achaia. Here Luke does not name Athens or Corinth, but it is conjectured from the circumstances that, just as he had done before, he came from Attica into Achaia,

# PAUL ACCORDING TO ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Achaia, in which Corinth is located: from there he prepared to set sail from Cenchreae for Syria. However, because he sensed that an ambush had been prepared for him there by those who would be sailing, he changed his plan. Retracing the path by which he had come, he returned to Macedonia, traveling by land (as it appears), since the ambush was being prepared for him if he traveled by sea. While he was staying in Macedonia, he sent some of his companions—of whom he then had many from Macedonia—ahead to Troas, which is in Phrygia. Paul followed after, and he seems to have celebrated the Passover at Philippi, because Luke writes: *We sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread.* <note>original: "Navigavimus post diem azymorum a Philippis"</note> Thus, he set sail from Philippi for Troas, where his companions had gone ahead, as we mentioned. Here he restored to life a young man <note>referring to Eutychus</note> who had died in a fall. 

From Troas he reached Assos by a journey on foot, while his companions had gone ahead by ship at Paul's command. Assos is a coastal city not far below Troas, also called *Apollonia*. Setting sail from Assos, they arrived at Mitylene. That is the city of the island of Lesbos, which lies in the path of those sailing from Assos toward Chios. Coasting along the shores of Asia from Mitylene, they reached a point where they had the island of Chios on their right. Chios is located opposite Clazomenae on the coast of Asia, midway between Lesbos and Samos, to which (Samos) they later sailed. Samos is situated opposite the Trogyllium promontory of Asia. Setting sail from Samos, they reached Trogyllium, as is noted in the Greek manuscripts—although the Greek author who wrote of Paul's pilgrimage does not mention Trogyllium. 

From Trogyllium they went to Miletus. That is a coastal city of Caria. They could have easily landed at Ephesus from Chios, but they deliberately sailed past it so that Paul would not be delayed in Asia. Since they had celebrated the Passover at Philippi, they had decided to celebrate Pentecost in Jerusalem. Therefore, after Paul had summoned the elders from Ephesus to Miletus and commanded what he wished, they set sail from there and arrived at Cos by a direct course. That is an island between Samos and Cnidus, a city on the promontory of Asia. From Cos they came to Rhodes. That is an island opposite Lycia. Now, as they sail, they begin to have Asia to the North, whereas previously they had it to the East. From Rhodes they came to Patara. That is a coastal city of the province of Lycia. Here, having found a ship heading straight for Phoenicia in Syria, they began to head there by a direct course. Leaving the island of Cyprus on their left, they landed at Tyre. That is on the coast of Phoenicia, below Sidon. 

From Tyre they went to Ptolemais. This is also a coastal city between Tyre and Mount Carmel. From here they landed at Caesarea in Palestine, where Paul stayed with Philip. From there he finally reached Jerusalem by a journey on foot. From Jerusalem, by order of the tribune Lysias, he was led away in chains to Antipatris, which lies halfway between Jerusalem and Caesarea. From there he was led by horsemen to Caesarea in Palestine, and then, by order of the governor Festus (who had succeeded Felix), he was led in chains to Rome, following this itinerary: 

First, placed on a ship, he went from Caesarea to Sidon, which (as we said) is above Tyre. From there they reached Cyprus, leaving it on their left in a roundabout course, for the contrary winds drove them that way. Thus, coasting along the shores of Cilicia and Pamphylia, they arrived at Myra, which scribes had mistakenly turned into "Lystra." Myra is in Lycia, not far from the shore. From here, by a difficult and long navigation, they advanced until they had the promontory of Cnidus on their right. But because the wind was blowing against them, they turned their course toward Crete, which was then on their left. They came to a port named Salmone. I believe Luke used the name that the common people happened to use then. For I think this is the place which Pliny and Strabo call *Sammonium*. This promontory of Crete faces East. 

From here, because of adverse winds, they were barely able to coast along the shores of Crete, keeping the island on their right, until they came to a place in Crete near the city of Lasea, which is called the Good or Fair Havens <note>original: "Boni seu Pulchri Portus"</note>, a name not found among ancient geographers. It appears to have been a name used in that time. Furthermore, that it was on the southern side of Crete is shown by the fact that they were trying to head from there toward Phoenix, which is a promontory of Crete facing the Southwest and Northwest winds. The Southwest wind <note>original: "Africus"</note> blows from the winter sunset, and the Northwest wind <note>original: "Chorus"</note> from the summer sunset. Since the harbor there seemed suitable, they had decided to winter there. 

Meanwhile, when the South wind—a fairly favorable wind blowing from due South—began to blow, they set sail from Assos (this is a city on the coast of Crete) and coasted along the shore of Crete to reach the aforementioned Phoenix. But suddenly the wind changed to the opposite direction; instead of the South wind, there began to blow a "Typhonic" wind <note>a hurricane-force wind</note>, violent and terrifying to sailors, also called the *Euraquilo* <note>a Northeast wind</note>, which blows between the North and the East. By the force of the storm, they were driven to the island called Clauda, which faces Crete between the West and South—the direction in which the Euraquilo, blowing from the opposite quarter of the sky, was most able to drive them. Because of this, they feared even more the danger of being driven into the *Syrtes* <note>dangerous sandbanks off the coast of Africa</note>. 

Finally, in a desperate situation, they ran the ship aground at an island called Melite <note>modern Malta</note>. It lies between Epirus and Italy, facing Sicily to the North. Here Paul shook off a viper without being harmed. Having found another ship there (for the first had been lost), they landed at Syracuse, which is in Sicily, not far from the Pachynus promontory. Coasting along its shores, they came to Rhegium, a town at the extreme edge of the territory of the Bruttii, where Italy is closest to Sicily. From Rhegium, by a direct course, they were carried to Puteoli, a promontory in Campania, not far from Naples. From here they reached the Forum of Appius by a land journey, at a place called Three Taverns <note>original: "Tres Tabernæ"</note>, and here Paul was met by disciples from Rome. The Forum of Appius is a day's journey from the city. From there, they finally reached Rome. 

It is established, therefore, from the *Acts of the Apostles* that he traveled through all of Asia Minor, then crossed into Europe, and traveled through all of Greece, from the northern part where Macedonia is, as far as Illyricum. For Illyricum is the furthest part of Macedonia to the North and West. He himself reports this in the fifteenth chapter of the *Epistle to the Romans*: *so that from Jerusalem and round about even unto Illyricum, I have fully preached the Gospel.* However, we nowhere read that he preached in Crete, where he landed only because he was forced by the storm and held in chains. Nor is it read that he stayed there, though he himself thought they should winter there. And yet, he left Titus in Crete to ordain elders in every city and to correct what remained to be corrected, as he himself testifies in his Epistle; from these words it appears that he did preach in Crete as well. Neither does Luke record what Paul did in Arabia. 

So much for the places he traversed. Now let us briefly touch upon the calculation of the dates.

The sum of the events contained in the *Book of Acts* took place under four Roman Emperors: Tiberius, who succeeded Octavian; Gaius Caligula; Claudius Drusus; and Claudius Nero. Of these, Tiberius held power for twenty-three years; Caligula for four years, except for two months; Claudius for thirteen years and nearly ten months; and Nero for fourteen years and almost eight months. Therefore, everything that occurred from the death of Christ until Paul was brought to Rome spans six years of Tiberius, four of Caligula, and fourteen of Claudius. 

It is believed that Peter arrived in Rome at the beginning of this reign [Claudius's], and in its fourth year, the famine mentioned by Luke occurred. Again, in its ninth year, as Josephus and Eusebius attest, the Jews were expelled from Rome, an event Luke mentions in the eighteenth chapter. Then there are four years of Nero. Meanwhile, the governors of Judea were Pontius Pilate, who died in the third year of Caligula. He was succeeded by Felix, before whom Paul pleaded his case; Claudius, in the eleventh year of his reign, had appointed him procurator of the entire province, including Samaria, Galilee, and the region called Perea. Paul declared himself fortunate for this reason: that he was to plead his case before one who, having been in that province for a long time, was well-acquainted with Jewish affairs. Nero gave him a successor, Porcius Festus. After Paul had pleaded his case before him in the presence of Agrippa, because he appealed to Caesar, he was sent in chains to Rome in the third or sec- <note>The text cuts off mid-word "secun-", likely intended to be "secundo" (second).</note>

->### THE TRAVELS OF PETER AND PAUL BY ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM<-

secondly. Furthermore, these were the leaders of the Jews: King Herod, Philip, and Lysanias; they presided for six years. King Herod <note>Herod Agrippa I</note>, who died struck down by an Angel at Caesarea, presided for seven years. Agrippa his son <note>Herod Agrippa II</note>, by whose counsel Paul was sent to Rome, presided for twelve years, which pertains to the history of the Acts. Although the father was also called by the surname Agrippa, the son is simply called Agrippa in the Acts. And so, the Lord Jesus was killed, returned to life, and ascended into heaven, and sent the Holy Spirit in the eighteenth year of Tiberius. And in the following year, or (as some would have it) in the same year, soon after he was ordained among the Deacons, Stephen was stoned, with Paul standing by and guarding the clothes of the witnesses who were stoning him. Paul himself was struck down and converted near Damascus shortly thereafter, in the nineteenth year of Tiberius. He traveled through various regions, everywhere spreading the Gospel, until the thirteenth year of Claudius. For in this year, Paul was thrown into chains in Jerusalem by Lysias the tribune <note>a Roman military commander</note>, by whom he was sent bound to Caesarea to be heard before Felix, where he was detained in chains for two years; and he was handed over by Felix, still bound, to Porcius Festus, by whom he was sent to Rome. There he spent two whole years in chains—that is, until the fifth year of Nero. 

Luke does not follow the history any further. Other writers, not lacking in merit, seem to have added the rest from various conjectures: namely, that Paul was first acquitted at his trial before Nero, and freely preached the Gospel wherever he wished for ten years. Finally, when Nero’s cruelty had already advanced into madness, he was called back to his tribunal and beheaded. They take the evidence for this conjecture from the Second Epistle of Paul to Timothy. In this, he mentions his first defense, in which he was deserted by everyone, and yet was freed by the protection of God. And from this, they conclude that he returned to preaching because of what he adds immediately after: *But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled, and all nations might hear.* <note>original: "Dominus autem mihi adstitit & confortavit me, ut per me prædicatio impleatur, & audiant omnes gentes."</note> Furthermore, that he was in danger during his second defense is proved by what he writes in the same place: *For I am now being sacrificed, and the time of my departure is at hand* <note>original: "Ego enim jam delibor, & tempus meæ resolutionis instat"</note>, and so forth. 

Therefore, they believe he was crowned with martyrdom in the thirteenth year of Nero, thirty-six years after the death of Christ, or according to the *Chronological Directory*, thirty-eight years. Furthermore, they conclude that Luke left Paul at the first defense because he ended his narration of the things he had seen there. On the other hand, Paul testifies in the same Epistle that Luke was present at the second defense, saying: *Luke is with me alone.* <note>original: "Lucas est mecum solus."</note> From these things, one may conclude that Paul was engaged in the business of the Gospel for twenty-one years, in addition to those two years he was held in chains at Caesarea; and again, the other two years he spent in chains at Rome living in a rented house, to which, as the Histories record, ten years were added. Thus you will find that from the baptism of Paul until his death, there were thirty-five years, or, as some calculate, thirty-seven. 

Because these things seemed likely to bring some light to the reading, I chose to place them at the beginning of this work. Although I am not unaware that a chronological account can hardly be rendered perfectly <note>original: "ad unguem," an idiom meaning "to the fingernail" or with extreme precision</note>, since in these matters not only do different writers disagree among themselves, but even the same writers differ from themselves. For instance, Bede, in his *Commentaries* on the eighteenth chapter, writes on the authority of Josephus that the Jews were expelled from Rome in the ninth year of Claudius. In the annotation of times which he placed at the beginning of his work, he says it happened in the eighth year. So too in Eusebius, you will sometimes find one year in his *History* and another in his *Chronicles*, where it is left in doubt whether Tiberius reigned for twenty-one years or twenty-three. 

Farewell, Reader, and prepare yourself to read the Acts with good omens <note>original: "bonis avibus," literally "with good birds," a Roman expression for good luck</note>.

# THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES

<margin>L</margin>
The <gloss>1</gloss> first account I composed, O Theophilus, concerning all things that Jesus began both to do and to teach, <gloss>2</gloss> Until the day, <gloss>3</gloss> after he had given commands to the Apostles, <gloss>4</gloss> through the Holy Spirit, <gloss>5</gloss> whom he had chosen, he was taken up; <gloss>6</gloss> To whom also he presented <gloss>7</gloss> himself alive after his suffering by many proofs, being seen by them for forty days, and speaking the things concerning the kingdom of God. 

->And<-

***

<margin>1</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'A' featuring floral and foliage motifs.</image-desc>
**The ACTS of the Apostles**] <note>original: "Πράξεις" (Praxeis)</note>. What Cyprian translates as *Acta* (Acts), Jerome sometimes calls *Actiones* (Actions) and other times *Acta*. Furthermore, the word *actus* is indeed found in the masculine gender, but usually in poetry, as in Lucan: "Though he broke off his great acts." <note>original: "Licet ingentes abruperit actus"</note> But that term more commonly refers to things transacted in legal courts, wills, or similar manners. Therefore, I would prefer the term *Gesta* (Deeds) rather than *Acta*, if both were equally available for use.

<margin>2</margin>
**The first account indeed**] <note>original: "Primum quidem sermonem"</note> I truly wished to join this book of Luke’s with his previous one. Since he encompassed the Gospel histories in two volumes, both of which he wrote to the same Theophilus, he makes mention of the first when beginning the second. However, I feared it would seem intolerable to separate the Gospels from one another. Yet what else is this History but a part of the Gospel, and in my judgment, no small part? For in the Gospel is described the grain of wheat buried in the soil; here is described that grain sprouted, gradually opening and bringing forth its riches. If we had not learned through Luke in what ways Christ left the earth, where, in what place, and in what ways that promised Spirit arrived, with what beginnings the Church started, by what things it grew strong, and by what methods it increased, would we not be ignorant of a good part of the Gospel? And I wish that holy Luke, just as he began this narration, had followed it further and touched upon the deeds of the other Apostles as well. For this reason, I wonder all the more why this Book is found in such variety among the Greeks, and why no one among the ancient Latin writers existed who would illustrate such a distinguished work—entirely of both Gospel majesty and faith—with their own Commentaries. Nothing exists, as far as I know, on this book except for the names of some places that Jerome noted; but those are not only few, they are very few—if indeed this small work is even to be considered Jerome's. Certainly, it is the work of a learned man and not unworthy of Jerome, except for the fact that Jerome is cited within it. The Epistle to the Hebrews was accepted late. There was some doubt about the Epistle of James. Italy was slow to accept the Apocalypse <note>the Book of Revelation</note>, and Greece does not even now sufficiently approve of it. However, regarding the Acts, there was never any doubt. For the fact that this Book was not accepted by the Manichaeans <note>a dualistic religious sect considered heretical by the early church</note>, as Augustine indicated in the book where he refutes Adamantius the Manichaean, should carry even more weight among the Orthodox, if it displeased heretics who were no less ridiculous than they were impious. And it is fitting that Christians study the cradle of their own nation with greater zeal: so that after they have learned by what things it grew, they may understand that fallen Religion must be restored by those same means. While I was preparing this fourth Edition, I happened upon Greek Commentaries under the title of John Chrysostom <note>a famous 4th-century preacher</note>—whether truly his or falsely attributed, I do not yet declare. From these, I have included certain things in this third Edition which were supplied by friends. In his introduction, he testifies that this work was so little known among the Greeks that not only was the author unknown to most, but it was not even known whether this Book on the deeds of the Apostles existed. I believe he was speaking of the common people, not the learned. Furthermore, the manuscripts show that this Book was not as well-worn among the Greeks as the Epistles of Paul. For in no volume (of the sacred writings) was there a greater variety of readings. From the fragments which are cited piecemeal in the so-called *Ordinary Gloss* <note>a standard medieval collection of biblical commentaries</note>, it appears that there once existed commentaries on this work that were by no means unlearned; I suspect these were suppressed by those compilers so that their own collections would be more highly valued. I suspect the same regarding the ancient writers we see cited in the *Golden Chain* <note>the Catena Aurea, a commentary by Thomas Aquinas</note>. For what occasion would have extinguished so many volumes so completely that not a single one survived, even by the benefit of chance? For my part, there is no doubt that the Holy Spirit willed this work to survive for the certainty of our faith, but did not want the history of deeds to be extended further—partly so that the "toys" <note>the infancy or early stages</note> of the Church would not be uncertain to us, and partly so that we would not gradually slide away from Christ toward human affairs through a variety of narratives. The inviolable authority of the Scriptures had to be finalized once and for all, lest it be diminished by a crowd of volumes. Indeed, if you read those things which outsiders—who were said to be close to the times of the Apostles—have committed to writing, either as they supposedly heard them themselves or received them from those who had seen them, you will seem to be reading fables, so to speak, if you compare them with the gravity and faith of this History. And it is established that among these writers are those who, as often happens in dialogues, wove together fictional narratives from things contained in the Sacred Books, or certainly mixed the false with the true; and again, those who, either because of slowness of mind or weakness of memory, handed down things they had neither heard nor understood. I think the writings of Clement and Papias, and perhaps Dionysius, are of this sort. Certainly, Eusebius notes Papias in his *Ecclesiastical History*—

<column-break/>

In the <gloss>1</gloss> FORMER volume we spoke, Theophilus, <gloss>2</gloss> of all things which Jesus began both to do and to teach, <gloss>3</gloss> Until that day, in which, after he had imparted the Holy Spirit for this very purpose, <gloss>4</gloss> and had given commands <gloss>5</gloss> to the Apostles whom he had chosen, <gloss>6</gloss> he was taken up: <gloss>7</gloss> To whom also he had presented himself living, after he had suffered his punishment, and that by many proofs, while for [forty] days 

->days<-

***

—as one who did not grasp with his intellect the things he had heard from John, and thus provided an occasion for error to many through his writings. They were men, and subject to human failings. If, even among those who lived with the Apostles, a suspicion of either error or vanity was immediately found, what do you think would have happened if the authority of such narratives or writings had passed down to posterity through a long line of succession? Eusebius of Caesarea wove together the *Ecclesiastical History* with the greatest care and equal faith. But how many things are reported there that have no ecclesiastical weight?

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>3</margin>
**The first indeed**] <note>original: "Primum quidem"</note> We have frequently pointed out that among the Greeks, "first" (πρῶτον) is used in place of the comparative. "First" for "former" or "previous." For without doubt, he calls the Gospel Book a "discourse" <note>original: "sermonem"</note>: for he had not just spoken those things, but had written them. And Isocrates calls his small books "discourses" <note>original: "λόγους" (logous)</note>. Furthermore, I do not know if it is sufficiently idiomatic in Latin to say "to make a discourse" <note>original: "facere sermonem"</note> for "to speak words." Hence we, so that the sense might be clearer, have not feared to translate it in this way: *In the former volume we spoke, Theophilus, of all things which Jesus began both to do and to teach.* It could also be: *both to do and to teach, or either to do or to teach.* For the construction "to do-que and to teach" is poetic among the Latins, though it is the standard "to do and also to teach" <note>original: "ποιεῑν τε καὶ διδάσκειν"</note> among the Greeks. He has divided all of Christ's life into two parts: deeds and doctrine. He did wonderful things, but he taught things no less amazing. The deeds consist of miracles, the doctrine of decrees. Furthermore, as some point out here, that "doing" comes before "teaching," that is more clever than it is relevant. And yet, for the sake of exhortation, such a clever point is not useless.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>4</margin>
**Concerning all things**] <note>original: "De omnibus"</note> Chrysostom also noted this: that he did not say "all things," but "concerning all things," surely indicating the order and series of events rather than suggesting that nothing was omitted. Otherwise, he would disagree with John, who says the world could not contain the volumes if every single thing the Lord said or did were written. That he speaks of order is proved by what follows: *until that day*. He began from the birth of the Forerunner <note>John the Baptist</note> and followed the narrative until the Ascension of the Lord. Since Ambrose attributes the title of historian to Luke, many of Luke’s transitions are of this sort—like a joining of parts—which refresh the reader's memory by repeating a few things that were said and make the listener more teachable for what remains by proposing what is to be said. *I have followed the Gospel History from the beginning,* he says, *up to the time of the ascension: what remains, I shall complete in this book.* Chrysostom also noted this: that for the sake of modesty, Luke calls his work a "discourse" <note>sermonem</note>, not a "gospel."

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
<margin>5</margin>
**Commanding the Apostles through the Holy Spirit**] <note>original: "Ἐντειλάμενος" (Enteilamenos)</note>. It is in the past tense, that is, "when he had commanded." And this passage, because it otherwise seemed somewhat obscure, we have explained a little more fully in this manner: *Until that day, in which, after he had imparted the Holy Spirit for this very purpose and had given commands to the Apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up.* Bede also felt some difficulty here, for he mentions a transposition of words <note>hyperbaton</note>. Furthermore, the phrase *through the Holy Spirit* is placed so that it is ambiguous whether it refers to what precedes it or what follows. But the sense requires it to refer to what precedes: for he imparted the Holy Spirit to them after the resurrection, and thus commanded the office of preaching. Unless we prefer to take it that Christ himself at his baptism received the Holy Spirit descending upon him, after which he later chose the Apostles. However, the first reading pleases me more. Especially since Chrysostom agrees with this, saying "commanding through the Spirit," that is, "he breathed spiritual things upon them, breathing into everything." For the addition "through the Holy Spirit" does not please me as much if it implies the commands were the Spirit's. Chrysostom also proposes this sense. And what he says about "commanding," Chrysostom does not refer to what follows ("that they should not depart from Jerusalem"), but rather to "Go and teach all nations" etc., so that we might understand that doctrine is not Mosaic, nor worldly, but spiritual and heavenly. I thought it necessary to point this out because I see Latin interpreters are somewhat tortured and vary in this place.

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>6</margin>
**Whom he chose**] <note>original: "Οὓς ἐξελέξατο" (Hous exelexato)</note>. He inserts this so that it appears Christ did not give commands to everyone, but only to those whom he had chosen for this office, namely the twelve Apostles and the seventy Disciples.

<margin>7</margin>
**He was taken up**] <note>original: "Ἀνελήφθη" (Anelēphthē)</note>, which more specifically sounds like "he was received," namely into heaven, from whence he had come. For a person is said to be "assumed" who is joined into a fellowship, which the Greeks call *paralambanein* in the first chapter of Matthew, and *proslambanesthai* in Romans 14. And this very word *anclēphthē* is translated as "was received" in the tenth chapter of Acts.

# 435 ACTS CHAPTER I.

<margin>4</margin> And being assembled together with them, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, you have heard from me.
<margin>5</margin> For John truly baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.
<margin>6</margin> Therefore, when they had come together, they asked him, saying, "Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?"
<margin>7</margin> And he said to them, "It is not for you to know the times or the seasons which the Father has put in his own power.
<margin>8</margin> But you shall receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you shall be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth."
<margin>9</margin> And when he had spoken these things, while they watched, he was taken up, and a cloud received him out of their sight.
<margin>10</margin> And while they looked steadfastly toward heaven as he went up, behold, two men stood by them in white apparel,
<margin>11</margin> Who also said, "Men of Galilee, why do you stand gazing up into heaven? This same Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will so come in like manner as you saw him go—"

***

<margin>4</margin> **In many proofs**] <term>τεκμηρίοις</term> <note>original: "tekmeriois"</note>. Here the author calls a "proof" any sign through which faith is produced regarding a doubtful matter. By saying "in many," he follows a Hebrew idiom meaning *through many proofs*. Furthermore, as for the word that follows, <term>ὀπτανόμενος</term> <note>appearing; original: "optanomenos"</note>, it is a passive present participle. Therefore, while the Translator <note>The Vulgate translator</note> attempts to express the sense of the tense—which he does not usually do—the word he used was less than successful. Indeed, that which is not real can also "appear." We have therefore preferred to *rephrase* it as *while he was seen*.

<margin>9</margin> **This is consistent with the instructions**] <note>Erasmus is discussing the phrase "eating together" or "assembling" in verse 4</note> Lorenzo Valla thinks it is an error in the Latin manuscripts to read *convescens* <note>eating with</note>, suggesting instead it was written as *conversans* <note>living/staying with</note>. He does not hide the fact that some Greek manuscripts have <term>συναλιζόμενος</term> <note>synalizomenos</note>, while others have <term>συναλισκόμενος</term> <note>synaliskomenos</note>. He interprets the former as *staying with* and the latter as *gathering together* or *joining himself with them*, though he maintains both words have the same force. It is clear enough that <term>συναλίζεσθαι</term> <note>synalizesthai</note> is derived from <term>ἅλς</term> <note>hals - salt</note>, which suggests a symbol of hospitality or a lodging place. However, the exact origin of "being assembled" is not quite as clear, except that Hesychius interprets it as "having been brought together" and "having been gathered," that is, *congregated* and *crowded together*; the writings of Suidas point in the same direction. Although Suidas adds "having lodged together," "having gathered," and "having assembled," and a little later interprets "having lodged together" as "having been brought together." 

Now, while it follows that those living under the same roof might sometimes take food together, this cannot be proven from the logic of the word itself, nor from the Greek authors I have cited. Furthermore, in the heap of vocabulary pertaining to banquets collected by Pollux, there is no mention of this word. Even so, I do not deny that Jerome, in his seventh question to Hedibia, seems to have read it as *eating with them*, when he writes: *In the other case there was such familiarity and persistence that he ate with them as an equal*. From this, the Apostle Paul also reports that he appeared to five hundred disciples at once. And in John we read that he stood on the shore while the Apostles were fishing and ate a piece of roasted fish and a honeycomb, which are signs of a true resurrection. And Chrysostom, in the commentaries attributed to him on this book, openly interprets this as taking food. I will include his words: <note>Erasmus quotes Chrysostom in Greek</note> "For this reason he remained with them for forty days after the resurrection, providing proof through a long period of visibility in their homes, so they would not think what was seen was a ghost. And even this was not enough, but he also added a table; for thus says Luke, 'And eating with them.' The Apostles themselves always made this a proof of the resurrection, saying, 'We who ate and drank with him.'" 

If these arguments satisfy anyone, as they do not entirely dissatisfy me, let them consider whether <term>συναλίζεσθαι</term> might be derived from the sharing of salt, according to the proverb: *do not pass by the salt and the table*. Otherwise, it is not clear from this passage that there was a banquet between Christ and the Apostles. Certainly, Cyril, in the work where he explains the vocabulary of Holy Scripture, interprets "being assembled" as "gathering together," from the word <term>ἅλις</term> <note>halis</note> or <term>ἅλιος</term> <note>halios</note>, which signifies a council or congregation. Thus Herodotus in his first book says: "Cyrus, having written in a book what he wanted, made an assembly of the Persians." In the same author, one frequently encounters "being assembled" meaning *to gather*. I do not doubt that the other word was derived from *salt*, according to the saying, *Do not pass by the salt and the table*. The Etymologicon indicates that <term>ἅλιος</term> refers to the vessel in which salt is poured or stored. 

Again, even the punctuation of the sentence varies. For some refer this participle to what comes before, so that they count his domestic and long-term companionship among the proofs of the resurrection. For that, if I am not mistaken, is what "living together" means. Others refer it to what follows, so that while staying under the same roof with them, he is understood to have commanded them not to leave Jerusalem. This is the view I approve of regarding the punctuation. Otherwise, the things that follow would hang rather loosely from what precedes. Furthermore, if we read "being assembled" according to Valla—that is, *gathering himself with them* or *gathering them into the same place*—it fits better 

<column-break/>

# 436 ACTS CHAPTER I.

<margin>A</margin> <margin>4</margin> for forty days he was seen by them, and spoke to them about the kingdom of God. And gathering them into the same place, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, <gloss>10</gloss> about which (he said) you have heard from me, <margin>5</margin> because John indeed baptized with water, but you <gloss>11</gloss> will be baptized with the Holy Spirit after these not many days. <margin>6</margin> Therefore, when they had convened, they questioned him, saying, "Lord, <gloss>12</gloss> is it at this time that <gloss>13</gloss> you will restore the kingdom to Israel?" <margin>7</margin> But he said to them, "It is not for you to know <gloss>14</gloss> the times and the moments of time, <gloss>15</gloss> which the Father has established in his own power: <margin>8</margin> but <gloss>16</gloss> you will receive power after the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my <margin>B</margin> <gloss>17</gloss> witnesses not only in Jerusalem, but also in all Judea and Samaria, and finally even to the ends of the earth." <margin>9</margin> And when he had spoken these things, while they were watching, he was lifted up on high, and a cloud withdrew him from their eyes. <margin>10</margin> And while their eyes were fixed on heaven as he went, <gloss>19</gloss> behold, two men stood by them clothed in white garments, <margin>11</margin> who also said, "Men of Galilee, why do you stand gazing into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up—"

***

with what follows a little later: *Therefore, when they had convened, they questioned him, saying, "Lord," etc.* For he appeared to them sometimes to a few, sometimes to many. However, for the eating together <margin>C</margin> before the Ascension, he wanted all to be present, so that he might give his final commands. Augustine in several places reads it as *having lived among them*.

<gloss>10</gloss> **Which you heard, he says, through my mouth**] <note>original: "ἣν ἠκούσατέ μου"</note>, that is, *which you heard from me*. Hilary, citing this passage in the eighth book of *On the Trinity*, does not add "he says." However, the Translator did not do badly to add "he says" on his own, so that the speech would not be confusing due to the sudden change in the person speaking. And where are they now, those who cry out that it is a sacrilege to add even an iota to the Sacred Volumes?

<gloss>11</gloss> **You will be baptized in the Holy Spirit**] <note>original: "ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ"</note>, that is, *in the Holy Spirit*, which means *through the Holy Spirit*. The Translator was right, therefore, to omit the preposition. Augustine, in his 108th Epistle, mentions that in some Latin manuscripts it was written "you will begin to be baptized" instead of "you will be baptized." But he rejects this reading as faulty, based on the authority of the Greek manuscripts, although this Translator has occasionally turned phrases in a similar way.

<margin>D</margin> <gloss>12</gloss> **If at this time**] The word "If" (<term>Εἰ</term>) among the Greeks is frequently used for a question. It would have been more correctly translated as *whether at this time* or *is it at this time*.

<gloss>13</gloss> **Restore the kingdom to Israel**] <note>original: "τὴν βασιλείαν"</note>, that is, *to Israel*. For this is what they call the Jewish nation. They were still dreaming of some kind of Hebrew kingdom.

<gloss>14</gloss> **Times or moments**] <note>original: "χρόνους ἢ καιρούς"</note>, that is, *times and articles* or *opportunities*. Although among the Greeks <term>καιρός</term> <note>kairos</note> is sometimes used for <term>χρόνος</term> <note>chronos</note>, the reverse is not true. *Chronos* is "time" when we deal with the general category or a long duration of time, such as an age, a year, a month, a day, or an hour; but *kairos* is when we perceive the opportunity for doing something. For both are listed by the Rhetoricians among circumstantial arguments. Saint Augustine also notes this difference of words in Epistle 78 to Hesychius. Indeed, among the Greeks, *Kairos* is a god, whom Ausonius translates as *Opportunity*. Nor is *kairos* a species of the genus *chronos*, as Valla indicates; it is more a distinct thing than a part. And altogether, *kairos* is something more than "time"—it is the specific moment and point, as they say, in which <margin>E</margin> a thing must be done. Hence it is sometimes translated as "article" <note>as in "an article of time"</note>. I do not doubt that Terence’s phrase, "just as he was crushed in the very article," would be *kairos* in Greek. For two Greek words, there is only one Latin word: *tempus* (time). Augustine had cited this passage this way: "No one can know the times which the Father has put in his own power." But Hesychius, on the authority of ancient copies, reads with us: "It is not for you."

<gloss>15</gloss> **Which the Father has put in his power**] <note>original: "ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐξουσίᾳ"</note>, that is, *in his own or his very own power*.

<gloss>16</gloss> **You shall receive power**] <term>δύναμιν</term> <note>dynamin</note>, that is, *strength and fortitude*, lest anyone mistake it for "virtue," which is moral goodness as opposed to vice. And "of the Spirit coming upon you" (<term>ἐπελθόντος</term>) is a past participle, but one that is attached to a future tense verb. It could be translated as *having glided into you*, or as we translated it, *after the Holy Spirit has come upon you*. For it is also ambiguous in the Greek whether the genitive case is used absolutely; thus Hilary reports it in his books *On the Trinity*: *with the Holy Spirit coming upon you*.

<margin>F</margin> <gloss>17</gloss> **Witnesses in Jerusalem**] There is a double conjunction in the Greek: *both in Jerusalem and in all Judea*. However, because he joined "Judea" to "Jerusalem"—the whole to the part—it could not be rendered perfectly with the double "both/and." Therefore we rendered it: *not only in Jerusalem, but also in all Judea*. For here I think "Judea" is placed not for the entire region of the Jewish people, which encompasses the twelve tribes, but for that province whose capital is Jerusalem, even though Jerusalem itself is in the tribe of Benjamin. For the Gospel was propagated by these steps: from Jerusalem, as if from a fountain, it flowed to all parts of Judea, then to the Samaritans (who were half-Pagan and half-Jewish), soon into Syria, from there into all of Asia Minor, from there into Greece, later into Italy, and finally into the whole world.

<gloss>18</gloss> **And while they were gazing into heaven**] <note>original: "Καὶ ὡς ἀτενίζοντες ἦσαν εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν"</note>, that is, *when they were with eyes intent or fixed upon heaven*. For that is what <term>ἀτενίζειν</term> <note>atenizein</note> means to the Greeks: *to look with fixed and motionless eyes, in the manner of lovers*. Moreover, "into heaven" is positioned so that either

<margin>A</margin> 12 as you saw him going into heaven. Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount which is called Olivet, which is away from Jerusalem <gloss>21</gloss> a Sabbath’s journey.
