---

could be referred to either those watching or to the one going. Except that he soon explains, as it were, *Why do you stand looking into heaven?* Someone or other had noted this in the "Ordinary Gloss" <note>A standard medieval commentary on the Bible.</note>. For the fact that he translates *in white clothing* as "white garments" matters little to the sense. 

19 **Behold two men**] <note>original: "καὶ ἰδού" (kai idou)</note>. We have noted that it is a peculiarity of Luke to add the conjunction "and" superfluously. Therefore, the translators rightly omitted it. 

20 **In the same way**] <note>original: "ὃν τρόπον" (hon tropon)</note>, meaning "in the manner that"; there are three words. 

<margin>C</margin> 21 **A Sabbath day’s journey**] <note>original: "σαββάτου ἔχον ὁδόν" (sabbatou echon hodon)</note>. This means a distance of two thousand paces <note>About 1,000 yards or 1 kilometer.</note>. It was not permitted for Jews to make a longer journey on the Sabbath. Jerome indicates this when writing to Algasia in the tenth question, namely that it was religiously observed by the Jews not to walk more than two thousand paces on the Sabbath, based on the teaching of the Rabbis Barachiba, Simeon, and Hillel, whom they were accustomed to call "our masters," as Jerome teaches there. Furthermore, in John chapter eleven, Bethany was about fifteen stadia away from Jerusalem. That makes a little less than two thousand paces. Moreover, Bethany was on the side of the Mount of Olives. Chrysostom testifies to this same thing when describing the banquet of Simon the Leper. Therefore, I wonder why we read in Lyra and other more recent interpreters that a Sabbath journey does not have more than a thousand paces—unless perhaps this happened through a fault of the scribes. Therefore, we translated it: *is away from Jerusalem a Sabbath's journey*. 

22 **Into the upper room**] <note>original: "εἰς τὸ ὑπερῷον" (eis to hyperōon)</note>. Here "dining room" <note>Latin: "coenaculum"</note> does not mean the place where one dines, but the upper part of the house. This is what the Greek word indicates: they went up into the upper room, <note>original: "ἀνέβησαν εἰς τὸ ὑπερῷον"</note>. That is, having entered the city, they climbed to the upper room. Our reading sounds as if, having entered the dining room, they climbed to where Peter was staying. Lyra thinks it is <unclear>pithomeron</unclear>. In the Ordinary Gloss, someone or other warns about the Greek reading. Although in the Latin reading there was no need for that figure of speech. Since the subjection added to the word "had entered" excludes ambiguity. In some manuscripts of our language, it was written, *they went up into the higher parts, where Peter was staying.* And it is possible that there was a higher place above the dining room, which in the tenth chapter of this work he calls the "roof" <note>original: "δῶμα" (dōma)</note>, where Peter went up to pray. 

23 **Peter and John**] I suspect it happened through the carelessness of the scribes that the pairs of Apostles are not consistently distinguished here. However, we have dared to change nothing, since neither the manuscripts nor suitable interpreters supported it. Not even the order agrees sufficiently. For with us <note>In the Latin Vulgate</note> *Peter* is coupled with *John*, among the Greeks with *James*. With us, *James* and *Andrew*, among the Greeks, *John* and *Andrew*. 

24 **Persevering**] <note>original: "προσκαρτεροῦντες" (proskarterountes)</note>, that is, enduring, which Augustine somewhere translates as "serving." "In prayer" is missing in the Latin manuscripts, <note>original: "καὶ τῇ δεήσει" (kai tē deēsei)</note>, that is, "and in supplication." Paul also doubles these terms in the same manner. 

25 **With the women**] <note>original: "σὺν γυναιξὶ" (syn gynaixi)</note>. It can also be understood as "with their wives," because he separated Mary from the women. And again, 

26 **With his brothers**] "His" refers to Jesus, not to Mary: <note>original: "αὐτοῦ" (autou)</note>. The Ordinary Gloss also noted this. It is cited under the name of Bede, although nothing of the sort is found in his commentaries. Since I have found this to be true in several other places, I suspect that these books which Badius gave us have been shortened. 

27 **In those days**] <note>original: "ταύταις" (tautais)</note>, that is, "these," for it is not <note>original: "ἐκείναις" (ekeinais)</note>. It is a historical style to report a matter as if it were currently happening. 

28 **In the midst of the brothers**] <note>original: "μαθητῶν" (mathētōn)</note>, that is, "of the disciples." And at once, <note>original: "ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ" (epi to auto)</note>, that is, gathered or congregated in the same place. 

29 **Now there was of men**] <note>original: "ἦν τε ὄχλος ὀνομάτων" (ēn te ochlos onomatōn)</note>, that is, "and there was a crowd of names." It is clear that this did not happen through the fault of the translator, but was corrupted by some bold person who thought "of names" meant nothing in this place, but "of men" fit perfectly. Thus is the judge of ignorance headlong. Furthermore, he said "of names" because men are usually counted by name whenever a number is sought. This part of the speech, since it is inserted as a parenthesis, should be separated by its own marks on both sides; however, it will be more fitting if we read <note>original: "ἐν δὲ" (en de)</note>. 

30 **It must be fulfilled**] <note>original: "ἔδει" (edei)</note>, that is, "it was necessary," or "it behooved"; <margin>D</margin> he speaks of a completed matter. 

31 **Which he foretold**] <note>original: "ταύτην ἣν προεῖπε" (tautēn hēn proeipe)</note>, that is, "this [scripture] which he foretold." 

32 **Who was the guide**] <note>original: "ὁδηγῷ" (hodēgō)</note>. This is properly said of one who shows the way: lest someone understand a "leader of an army," for whom the Greeks have another name, <note>original: "στρατηγός" (stratēgos)</note>. 

33 **In us**] <note>original: "σὺν ἡμῖν" (syn hēmin)</note>, that is, "with us." And, "Who was numbered," <note>original: "ὅτι" (hoti)</note>, "because," not "who." 

34 **And he possessed a field**] <note>original: "ἐκτήσατο" (ektēsato)</note>, which could also be translated as "prepared." For Judas did not possess this field, but that field was prepared with that money. Furthermore, concerning the "reward of iniquity," he alludes, if I am not mistaken, to the surname Iscariot, which for the Hebrews <gloss>אישקריא</gloss> <note>Hebrew: "Ish-Karya," though Erasmus likely means a play on "sheqel" or "sachar" (reward/hire).</note> sounds like "reward." 

35 **And being hanged he burst**] <note>original: "καὶ πρηνὴς γενόμενος" (kai prēnēs genomenos)</note>, that is, "and <margin>E</margin> having become prone," or "sloping downwards": for <note>original: "πρηνὴς" (prēnēs)</note> is said by the Greeks of one whose face is cast down to the ground. It expresses the gesture and condition of one suffocated by a noose. Otherwise, from this place alone it could not be understood that Judas hanged himself. Augustine, in the first book against Felix the Manichean, chapters four and five, citing this passage, reads: *And being cast down on his face, he was burst in the middle.* 

36 **And it was made known**] Although Peter is speaking these things both in Jerusalem and in Hebrew, nevertheless Luke's words sound as if Peter were speaking to others in a different language. For he who says "their," seems to speak of absent people, and he who says "their language," namely Hebrew, seems to speak in a language other than Hebrew. Therefore, some have wanted this whole part of the speech, *And it was made known*, up to, *For it is written*, to have been interwoven by Luke writing in Greek as his own. There are those who refer "their language" to the difference between the Galilean and Jerusalem dialects, which varied so much that Peter was recognized by this. But in my opinion, it is simpler for us to understand that Luke, writing in Greek, added the Hebrew word for greater credibility of the matter, and that this particle, "their language," should be referred to the persona of Theophilus and Luke, one of whom would write in Greek, the other would read. For it is probable that this very Hebrew name for the field became known to men of different languages, just as some names for exotic things and even some proverbs migrate from their own language to foreigners. 

37 **Akeldama**] The Greeks write <note>original: "Ἀκελδαμὰ" (Akeldama)</note>, coming closer to the Hebrew word than we do. For the Hebrews <gloss>חלג</gloss> <note>Helegh</note> is a plot or property, and <gloss>דם</gloss> <note>Dam</note> is blood, even though Saint Jerome indicates the name is Syrian. 

38 **Let his dwelling become**] <note>original: "ἔπαυλις" (epaulis)</note>. A compound from the same word from which <note>original: "εὐνουχισθῆναι" (eunouchisthēnai)</note> comes, about which we spoke a little before. Augustine, in that place I just cited, reads: *Let his villa become deserted.* Moreover, "bishopric" <note>office of oversight</note> is <note>original: "ἐπισκοπὴν" (episkopēn)</note>, which for the Hebrews is <gloss>פקרה</gloss> <note>Pekudah</note>. Among other things, this also signifies a prefecture. The Greek word is derived from "looking into." I heard a certain Hebrew who affirmed that what the Greek and Latin translator turns into "bishopric" sounds to the Hebrews like a "singularly dear wife," who was held in delight as a woman apart, not for the sake of bearing children, but for the sake of the mind <note>i.e., for companionship or pleasure</note>. Whether this is true, I do not know. This testimony is taken from two Psalms: *Let their dwelling become deserted*, and *in their tabernacles*.

# ACTS CHAPTER II.

<margin>21</margin> ...time, in which the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, <margin>22</margin> Beginning from the baptism of John until the day he was taken up from us, one of these must become a witness with us of his resurrection. <margin>23</margin> And they put forward two, Joseph called <margin>24</margin> Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias. And they prayed, saying, "You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen <margin>25, 43</margin> to take the lot <note>original: "klēron"</note> of this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas turned aside to go <margin>26, 44</margin> to his own place." And they gave lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and <margin>II 1.</margin> he was numbered with the eleven Apostles. And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all together in one place.

---

*Let their habitation be desolate*, is taken from Psalm 68 <note>Modern Psalm 69:25</note>. *And let another take his office*, is taken from Psalm 108 <note>Modern Psalm 109:8</note>. The first testimony, which pertained to all the Jews who persecuted Christ, Peter applied to Judas. Furthermore, since both Psalms are inscribed to David himself, either it is not true what some note concerning the titles, or these Psalms were not written by David. And yet Peter says the Holy Spirit spoke through the mouth of David. 

Moreover, as for Bede's <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 672–735), an English monk and scholar</note> claim that through the ignorance of readers the context of the Psalms has been corrupted, today we find no such thing in our manuscripts. For the question is whether the first part of the testimony, which exists in Psalm 68, was added to Psalm 108. On this matter, neither Augustine nor Jerome complains in their commentaries. And yet it is probable that Bede drew this from elsewhere. For these verses are added in the Psalter called the "Roman." 

But while I am investigating these things, I have fallen into others. I have elsewhere warned that the commentaries we have under the title of Jerome on the Psalms seem to me to be cut short in some places, and conversely expanded in some places with "sewn-on patches." For what was added as a commentary on this verse, *And let another take his office*, might be believed to be Jerome’s, but it is of this sort: *This is also more clearly interpreted in the Acts of the Apostles*. What follows is ambiguous: *Not only was it said of Judas at that time, but it is said even today and even until the day of judgment.* (Understand "it is said.") What does it matter if it is said? What matters is what happens. Furthermore: *If Judas himself lost his Apostleship, let Priests and Bishops guard themselves, lest they also lose their priesthood. If an Apostle fell, a Monk can more easily fall.* 

Thus he writes. To avoid exaggerating the ineptitude of the language here, which is completely uncharacteristic of Jerome—*even today it is said, and until the day of judgment*—what do the things that follow mean? *If an Apostle fell, a Monk can more easily fall.* Is an Apostle and a Monk the same thing? "A wine-jar was intended; as the wheel runs round, why does a water-pitcher come out?" <note>A quote from Horace’s *Ars Poetica*, meaning a project that started as something grand but ended up as something trivial.</note> To these he adds things that cohere poorly: *Virtue does not give birth; though a man may fall and perish, yet the Lord places his coins under interest. If that man has not doubled it, his money is taken and given to the one who has. The Lord's money cannot be idle.* 

Who does not see that these are not the words of Jerome, but of a foolishly talkative man who has contaminated this entire Psalm with similar "ornaments"—and if only it were this one alone! Those who wish to appear as guardians of the Divine Scripture tolerate these things calmly, and are indignant at those who point them out, yet they would not show the same leniency if someone cheated them in a similar way regarding wine or cloth; if a monitor there exposed the fraud, they would be very grateful. 

And *another*, ἕτερος <note>Greek: heteros</note>, would more rightly be "one of two." For the Greeks frequently use *heteros* for *allos* <note>Erasmus is distinguishing between "another of a different kind" and "another of the same kind."</note>. However, the fact that some refer *another* to the two designated for election, one of whom would succeed to Judas's place, is a bit forced.

<margin>39</margin> **He went in and out]** This means he had a constant habit of life with them. It is spoken as a proverbial figure. However, this whole discourse had a bit of obscurity, not only in the Latin language but also in the Greek; therefore, as much as we could, we have tried to translate it more clearly.

<margin>40</margin> **He was surnamed Justus]** *Justus* is a Roman name. This surname was once given to Aristides among the Athenians. The *Ordinary Gloss* <note>A standard medieval collection of biblical commentaries</note> doubts whether it is Latin or Hebrew, and interprets it as if it were Hebrew—as if it were a new thing for Jews to be designated by Greek and Roman surnames! *Andrew* is Greek, just as *Bartholomew*, *Mark*, and *Luke* are Latin names. *Nicodemus* is Greek. And this is cited under the name of Bede, although it is not found in Bede's commentaries. A little before, the opinion of someone is cited who thought these two, for whom lots were cast, were from the number of the seventy disciples, though Bede counts seventy-two. And yet here a "B." was written, indicating I know not what.

<margin>41</margin> **You who know the hearts]** In Greek it is a single compound word, καρδιογνῶστα <note>original: "kardiognōsta"</note>, a knower of hearts. And soon after,

<margin>42</margin> **Show]** It is ἀνάδειξον <note>original: "anadeixon"</note>, that is, designate. For he translates it thus: *Jesus designated seventy others*.

<margin>43</margin> **To take the place]** λαβεῖν τὸν κλῆρον <note>original: "labein ton klēron"</note>, that is, so that he might receive the lot, or inheritance, or succession.

<margin>44</margin> **That he might go to his own place]** ἴδιον <note>original: "idion"</note>, that is, his own proper place, as if he had previously occupied someone else's.

<margin>45</margin> **And they gave their lots]** Καὶ ἔδωκαν κλήρους αὐτῶν <note>original: "Kai edōkan klērous autōn"</note>, that is, and they gave the lots *of them*, namely of the two for whom they were casting lots. For a lot is said to be "his" in whose name it is cast.

<margin>46</margin> **And he was numbered with]** καὶ συγκατεψηφίσθη <note>original: "synkatepsēphisthē"</note>, that is, he was added by votes or pebbles. Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla (1407–1457), a humanist whose work inspired Erasmus</note> prefers "he was co-opted," which certainly does not displease me. Earlier there was a different word for this, "numbered with us" <note>original: "katērithmēmenos syn hēmin"</note>. Augustine recites this whole chapter and a good part of the next in the book which... <meta>catchword: which</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...all the time that the Lord Jesus <margin>39</margin> lived a constant life among us, <margin>22</margin> Beginning from the baptism of John until that day on which he was taken up from us, one should be appointed who may be with us a witness of his resurrection. <margin>23</margin> And they appointed two: Joseph who is called Barsabas, <margin>41</margin> who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias. <margin>24</margin> And when prayer was made, they said: "You, Lord, <margin>42</margin> who know the hearts of all, show which of these two you have chosen, <margin>43</margin> to receive <margin>25</margin> the lot of this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas by transgression fell away, <margin>44</margin> that he might go to his own place." <margin>45</margin> <margin>B</margin> <margin>26</margin> And they gave their lots, and the lot fell upon Matthias, <margin>46</margin> and he was co-opted into the number of the eleven Apostles. And when the <margin>II 1.</margin> day of Pentecost was fulfilled, <margin>1</margin> <margin>2</margin> they were all with one accord in the same place.

...we mentioned a little while ago, namely *Against Felix the Manichaean* <note>The Manichaeans were a religious group that the Church Father Augustine debated</note>, Book I, chapters 4 and 5. But some things are different than how we read them; for those who think it worth the effort to know them, so that they may more conveniently compare them, we have written them here as he recited them from the Acts of the Apostles:

And how he conversed with them. And he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, you heard from my mouth. For John indeed baptized with water, but you will begin to be baptized with the Holy Spirit, whom you are to receive not many days hence, even until Pentecost."* 

So when they had come together, they asked him, saying, *"Lord, will you at this time present the kingdom to <margin>C</margin> Israel?"* But he said, *"No one can know the time which the Father has placed in his own power, but you will receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and even unto the whole earth."* 

When he had said these things, a cloud received him, and he was taken up from them. For it is written in the book of Psalms: Let his villa be deserted, and let there be no one to live in it, and let another take his office."*

<margin>1</margin> **The day of Pentecost]** "Day" is in the singular number: therefore "it was being completed" <note>Latin: "compleretur"</note> is the reading to be used. Although commonly this whole time is called the Fortieth and the Fiftieth.

# OF THE APOSTLES. CHAPTER II.

2 And suddenly there came a sound from heaven, as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. 3 And there appeared to them divided tongues, as of fire, and one sat upon each of them. 4 And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance. 5 And there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men, from every nation under heaven. 6 And when this sound occurred, the multitude came together, and were confused, because every man heard them speaking in his own language. 7 And they were all amazed and wondered, saying to one another, "Look, are not all these who speak Galileans? 8 And how is it that we hear, each in our own language in which we were born? 9 Parthians and Medes and Elamites, and those dwelling in Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, 10 Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene, and visitors from Rome, both Jews and Proselytes, 11 Cretans and Arabs—we hear them speaking in our own tongues the wonderful works of God." 12 And they were all amazed and were perplexed, saying to one another, 13 "What could this mean?" Others mocking said, "They are full of new wine." 14 But Peter, standing up with the eleven, raised his voice and addressed them, "Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and heed my words. 15 For these are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day. 16 But this—

---

<meta>catchword: ta-</meta>

...as he translated a little before, *persevering with one accord in prayer*. The Latin translator seems to have read <unclear>homothym</unclear> <note>original Greek: ὁμοθυμαδόν, meaning "with one mind"</note>, which reading I suspect is the true one. Someone interpreted it as "with one accord," and since that word was more pleasing, it prevailed. Augustine, in his writing *Against the Epistle of Manichaeus*, reads it as *with the same animation*.

3 *The arrival of the spirit*] A rushing wind <note>original Greek: Φερομένης πνοῆς</note>, that is, *a breath which is carried*, which is characteristic of a wind moving with a swift impulse. Augustine expresses this almost exactly in the first book of *On the Origin of the Soul to Renatus*: *Suddenly there was a sound from heaven, as if a violent breath were being carried*. Likewise in his 102nd Letter to Evodius. Again in the sixth Sermon on the words of the Apostle. Again in the first book of *Against Felix*, chapter 5. Also in *Against the Epistle of Manichaeus*, chapter 9. The Greeks call an impulse *phoran*. "Violent" <note>original: βιαίας</note> has more the force of something "forceful."

4 *And there appeared to them*] <note>original Greek: Καὶ ὤφθησαν αὐτοῖς</note>, that is, *And they were seen by them*, or rather *beheld*. *Divided tongues* <note>original: διαμεριζόμεναι</note>, in the present tense, that is, tongues that were being distributed. However, a double meaning can be understood: either we take it that the tongues themselves were cloven, or we understand that they descended from heaven and were distributed among the individual disciples.

5 *As if of fire*] <note>original Greek: ὡσεὶ πυρός</note> is in the genitive case, not the nominative; that is, as if from fire. We translated it as "fiery" to avoid ambiguity.

6 *In various tongues*] <note>original Greek: ἑτέραις γλώσσαις</note>, that is, in others. Jerome also cites it this way in his *Questions to Hedibia*, according to the ancient manuscripts, so that it matches that Gospel passage: *they shall speak with new tongues*. For that which is "other" is the same as that which is "new."

7 *From every nation which is under*] <note>original Greek: τῶν ὑπὸ τὸν οὐρανὸν</note>, that is, of those who are under heaven, or of those [people] who are under heaven. I would gladly ask those who do not accept hyperbole <note>Exaggeration for emphasis</note> in the Holy Volumes whether there were also English or Scots in this gathering.

8 *And when this voice occurred*] <note>original Greek: Γενομένης δὲ τῆς φωνῆς ταύτης</note>. Some interpret this as the sound of the wind; some as the voice with which the Apostles began to speak, which does not displease me. To me, "voice" seems to mean the rumor or report spreading what had happened, just as we have elsewhere indicated that "speech" or "word" is used for a thing done which is spread by rumor. Augustine does not add the pronoun "this," but the Translator seems to have expressed the article.

9 *And the mind was confused*] I do not read "in the mind" in the Greek manuscripts. It is simply <note>original Greek: συνεχύθη</note>, *was confused*; Augustine reads it this way. However, this refers to disturbance or wonder, not to shame, which is how this word is usually translated here.

10 *And they wondered, saying*] The Greeks add <note>original Greek: πρὸς ἀλλήλους</note>, that is, *one to another*, or *among themselves*: Augustine reads "to one another."

11 *And how have we heard*] <note>original Greek: ἀκούομεν</note>, *we hear*, in the present tense, which has been corrupted by the scribes. Instead of "we hear," Augustine reads "we recognize."

12 *Our own tongue*] <note>original Greek: ἰδίᾳ διαλέκτῳ</note>, that is, *in their own tongue*, or *speech*, so that we understand, *them speaking*. To the Greeks, a *dialect* <note>original: διαλέκτος</note> is a specific property or type of language; for example, among the Greeks, although there is one language, there are nevertheless five dialects. Thus, one who is skilled in Greek can soon recognize whether the speaker is Attic or Doric, Ionic or Lacedaemonian. It is more probable, however, that the Apostles spoke in their own language, and by a miracle it happened that everyone understood, just as if each had heard his own language. Nor do we ever read of this miracle happening elsewhere, except perhaps once or twice. For instance, in Acts 10 concerning the household of Cornelius: *They heard them speaking in tongues*. And Paul, writing to the Corinthians, boasts that he spoke in the tongues of all of them. It should not be doubted that there were different speak-

-ings in tongues whenever the business of the Gospel required it. But for the same man to speak in different languages at the exact same time implies a contradiction. That difficulty remains: whether the Cretans and Medes and others far removed from the Jews knew Syriac, or only their own language. For now, Jews living in Germany have their own language besides the common tongue. Likewise those who inhabit Spain and Italy. Furthermore, that word <note>original Greek: ὁμοῦ, meaning "together"</note> could not be conveniently rendered in Latin.

13 *And they who dwell*] <note>original Greek: καὶ κατοικοῦντες</note>, that is, *dwelling*. Otherwise, if one chose to translate with a verb, it should have been said, *we who dwell*, because of the verb that preceded, *we hear*.

<margin>D</margin> 14 *And the parts of Libya*] instead of *Libya*, Augustine reads *Africa*. Nor is *around Cyrene* added thoughtlessly. Jerome, in his works on geography, indicates that there are two provinces of Libya: one is Cyrenaica, which Luke means here near Cyrene. This, he says, is the gateway to Egypt in the first part of Africa; it gave its name to the Libyan sea. The other he places after this, *Ethiopian Libya* <note>original: Αἰθιοπικην</note>, which reaches all the way to the southern Ocean.

15 *Roman strangers*] It is not <unclear>epidēmountes</unclear>, which he uses elsewhere, but <unclear>epidēmountes</unclear> <note>Erasmus is likely distinguishing between permanent residents and temporary visitors</note>, that is, those staying there. Furthermore, the Hebrews called those *Proselytes* <note>original: προσήλυτος</note> who, born of a different group, were received into the law of the Mosaic Code. Here he means those who were Jews by religion, but had their home in Rome.

16 *Jews also*] <note>original Greek: Ἰουδαῖοί τε καὶ Προσήλυτοι</note>, that is, *both Jews and Proselytes*, so that there is a double conjunction. These two small words seem to refer to what preceded, "Romans"—Romans who were either Jews by birth or Proselytes, that is, from the Gentiles, but Jews by adoption. Again, what follows, *Cretans and Arabs*, is uncertain whether it refers back to the general division of nations, or only to the Proselytes, some of whom were Cretans and others Arabs. Bede thinks that in this place *Judea* is not taken for the whole region of the Jews, but only for that which encompasses the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. But that is not likely. For he would have added Galileans and Samaritans and those of the Decapolis; now he mentions none of these, but other regions into which the Jews, driven from their own borders, had fled for refuge. Furthermore, because he repeats at the end, *both Jews and Proselytes*, they are called Jews not by nation but by religion and origin, from whom he distinguishes the Proselytes, who are Pagans by nation but made Jews by religion. However, *Cretans and Arabs* were added in such a way that they can refer to the prior list, so that we understand that Proselytes also came from foreign nations mixed with the Jews. Truly, many Jews came from Crete and Arabia, because they would not have fled there, but only Proselytes. The Translator preferred to say *Cretes* in the Greek manner rather than *Cretenses*.

17 *We have heard them*] Again <note>original Greek: ἀκούομεν</note>, that is, *we hear*, as we noted above.

18 *And they were all stunned and wondered*] <note>original Greek: καὶ διηπόρουν</note>. That word signifies that they were hesitating in their minds and perplexed. He used this word regarding Herod, when he believed John had come back to life, <note>original: διηπόρει</note>, which is translated there as *he was hesitant*. And Augustine here reads *they were hesitant* instead of *they wondered*. However, someone changed this place based on the previous one, though I think it is corrupt: "they were amazed and wondered" <note>original: ἐξίσταντο δὲ καὶ ἐθαύμαζον</note>, because that former expression is stronger than this latter one.

19 *Saying to one another*] <note>original Greek: ἄλλος πρὸς ἄλλον λέγοντες</note>, that is, *saying one to another*, or *saying among themselves*.

20 *Full of new wine*] <note>original Greek: μεμεστωμένοι</note>, that is, *they have been filled*. Augustine reads, *they are burdened with new wine*. "Full are these men." "These men" is redundant. Nor is it found in the more corrected Latin copies.

21 *Since it is the third hour of the day*] It was the time of Pentecost, when the sun rises before five, if I am not mistaken. Therefore, what Peter calls the third hour would be our eighth hour <note>approx. 8:00 or 9:00 AM</note>. Yet it would be no miracle among certain nations for a man to be drunk at the eighth hour. 25 For David says concerning him: 'I saw the Lord before me always, for he is at my right hand, so that I may not be moved.
26 Therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; moreover, my flesh also will rest in hope.

<margin>C</margin>
29 Brothers, I may speak freely <note>original: 'μετὰ παῤῥησίας', with boldness or openness</note> to you concerning the patriarch David, that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day."

---

22 **Through the Prophet Joel**] The testimony he cites is found in that Prophet, chapter 2. It wonderfully declares the abundance of the divine gift, which previously seemed owed only to the Jews, but is now overflowing unto all the nations of the world. However, Luke differs somewhat from both the Hebrew and the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, which are mostly in agreement here. In the Hebrew, it does not say "in the last days," but "after these things."

23 **And the Lord says**] Luke, or certainly Peter, adds this "on his own," because that clause ought to be applied to all prophets. Then, "from my Spirit" follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew has "my Spirit." Furthermore, regarding the fact that he placed "young men" first and then "old men," while the order is reversed in both the Hebrew and Septuagint, I suspect this happened through a scribal error. Moreover, where the Latin translator rendered it "and indeed upon my servants," he seems to have read the Greek particles <term>kaige</term> <note>original: 'καί γε', meaning 'and even' or 'and indeed'</note>. Jerome translates it "but also upon my servants." Again, after these words, "in those days I will pour out my Spirit," Luke added from himself "and they shall prophesy." This is neither in the Hebrew nor the Septuagint, if they are faithfully reviewed in Jerome’s translations of them. But just as this was transferred here from the beginning of this prophecy, so those words "in the days" were transferred from this place to the beginning—unless perhaps we prefer to blame the reader for this. And soon after: "They shall show wonders in the heaven above, and signs on the earth below." "Above," "below," and "signs"—Luke added these three words himself; they are not in the Hebrew or the Septuagint. Finally:

24 **The great and horrible day of the Lord**] Instead of "horrible," Luke used "illustrious" <note>original: 'ἐπιφανὴς', meaning manifest, notable, or glorious</note>, while the Hebrew is "horrible." From this we may understand, as I have frequently advised, that the Apostles and Evangelists were not anxious about rendering the exact words of the prophecies, but rather rendered the actual sense in good faith. Although it can occasionally happen that a learned reader might corrupt something while trying to "correct" it against the Septuagint Edition. However, so that the reader may more easily compare these himself, Jerome translates the Hebrew thus: *And it shall be after these things that I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions. But also upon my servants and my handmaids in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and I will give wonders in heaven and on earth, blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and horrible day of the Lord comes. And it shall be that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved.* According to the Septuagint, we read it this way: [Erasmus provides the Greek text of Joel 2:28-32]. That is: *And it shall be after these things, I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy, and your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions. And upon my servants and upon my handmaids in those days I will pour out from my Spirit, and they shall prophesy. And they shall give wonders in heaven, and on the earth blood, fire, and vapor of smoke. The sun shall be turned...*
<meta>catchword: into darkness</meta>

<column-break/>

17 ...is through the Prophet Joel: "And it shall be in the last days," says God, "I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your elders shall dream dreams.
18 And indeed upon my servants and upon my handmaids in those days I will pour out of my Spirit, and they shall prophesy.
19 And I will show wonders in heaven above, and signs on the earth below, blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke.
20 The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and illustrious day of the Lord comes.
21 And it shall come to pass, that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved."
22 "Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man exhibited <note>or 'vouched for'</note> by God toward you by miracles and wonders and signs, which God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves also know,
23 Him, being delivered by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, when you had taken him by the hands of the wicked, you killed by crucifying him,
24 Whom God raised up, having loosed the pains of death, because it was impossible for him to be held by it.
25 For David says concerning him: 'I foresaw the Lord before me always, because he is at my right hand, that I may not be moved.'
26 For this reason my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced: moreover, my flesh also shall rest in hope,
27 Because you will not leave my soul in hell, nor will you allow your Holy One to see corruption.
28 You have made known to me the ways of life, you will fill me with joy with your face.'
29 Brothers, let it be permitted to speak freely among you concerning the patriarch David, that he is both dead and buried, and his tomb is among us unto this day."

---

...into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and illustrious day of the Lord comes. And it shall be that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. It should be noted in passing that in Jerome's version "and they shall prophesy" is not recorded, yet it is found in this edition which the workshop of Asulanus <note>A famous Venetian printing house</note> recently gave us. And where it is rendered there as "I will give," the Greeks read "I will give" <note>original: 'δώσω'</note>, whereas Luke has "he will give." Jerome noted this word "I will pour out" <note>original: 'ἐκχεῶ'</note>, which the Septuagint translated as "I will pour out." For we pour out, not that which we dispense and give sparingly, but that which we bestow amply, profusely, and bountifully.

<margin>D</margin>
25 **A man approved**] The translator seems to have read "approved" <note>original: 'ἀποδεδειγμένον'</note>, from the verb meaning "to demonstrate," which sometimes means "I approve." Our manuscripts had "demonstrated," that is, shown, declared, or exhibited. Both readings are acceptable. Peter's prudence is praised here; speaking to an unrefined multitude, he praises Christ magnificently but calls him only a "man," so that from his deeds they might gradually recognize his Divinity.

26 **Delivered by the foreknowledge of God**] Here the Greek manuscripts differ from ours: "taking him delivered" <note>original: 'ἔκδοτον λαβόντες'</note>. Rabanus <note>Rabanus Maurus, a Carolingian scholar</note> also noted this. Furthermore, the phrasing is not without ambiguity <note>term: 'amphibologia', a phrase that can be interpreted in two ways</note>. For it can be understood that God delivered the Son, or it can be taken that the wicked delivered him. The former sense pleases me more. For it agrees with the words of Paul: "He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all." Moreover, the adverb "somehow" <note>original: 'πως'</note> is not added in the Greek manuscripts we see today, though it is not without emphasis: He was delivered just as it had been foreknown and decreed by God. By these words, Peter shows that nothing in Christ was done at random, but all things were done by the unchangeable counsel of God; at the same time, he mitigates the crime of the Jews, who, though acting ignorantly, served the Divine plan. In a similar form of speech, Luke said in chapter 27 of this work: "and lowering the gear, they were thus driven."

<margin>E</margin>
27 **Nailing him, you killed him**] Since the Greek is "having affixed" <note>original: 'προσπήξαντες'</note>, there can be no doubt that the translator rendered it "nailing." This is how Irenaeus cites it, and the original writing still exists in ancient copies.

28 **Having loosed the pains**] <note>original: 'ὠδῖνας'</note>. From which it is necessary to understand that God loosed the pains. Furthermore, as Bede <note>The Venerable Bede</note> notes, the Greek manuscripts have "loosing through him," but "through him" is not added in our manuscripts. "The pains of hell": the translator seems to have read "of hell" <note>original: 'ᾅδου'</note>, whereas our manuscripts have "of death" <note>original: 'θανάτου'</note>. Hence "by it" [feminine in Latin, referring to death] should be translated, not "by him."

29 **According to what**] <note>original: 'καθ᾽ ὅτι'</note>, that is, "insofar as," or "because."

30 **To be held by it**] "To be held" is <term>krateisthai</term> in Greek, which means "to be conquered" or "to be captured." "From it" refers to death, not "from him."

<margin>F</margin>
31 **Lest I be moved**] <note>original: 'ἵνα μὴ σαλευθῶ'</note>. Which properly means "to be moved from one's place."

32 **Let it be permitted to speak boldly**] <note>original: 'ἐξὸν εἰπεῖν μετὰ παῤῥησίας'</note>, that is, "it being permitted to speak freely." It is an impersonal participle placed absolutely in the nominative case, which sometimes happens in the genitive among the Greeks. But the translator judged the speech would be insufficiently harmonious unless he changed the participle into a verb. For Peter softens his speech with this introduction, as it would have been harsher to the ears of the Jews if he had said plainly that this was not predicted of David, but of Christ. This is certainly how Chrysostom interpreted it, praising Peter's modesty; he did not openly deny that this was said of David, but rather, having first shown great honor to the Prophet David, he softened his speech so they would not be offended by the freedom of his discourse.

33 **Since he died**] "That he also died" in Greek is <note>original: 'ὅτι καὶ ἐτελεύτησε'</note>.
<meta>catchword: 34 Ju-</meta>

<header>ACTS OF THE APOSTLES. CHAPTER III.</header>

30 [Therefore, David] being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn to him with an oath that from the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up the Christ to sit upon his throne, 31 foreseeing this, he spoke concerning the resurrection of the Christ, that his soul was not abandoned to Hades, 32 nor did his flesh see corruption. This Jesus God raised up, of which we all are witnesses. 33 Therefore, being exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he poured out this which you now see and hear. 34 For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says, "The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, 35 until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." 36 Therefore let all the house of Israel know for certain that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ. 37 When they heard this, they were pierced to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the Apostles, "What shall we do, brothers?" 38 Peter said to them, "Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. 39 For the promise is for you and your children, and for all who are far off, as many as the Lord our God shall call." 40 And with many other words he testified and exhorted them, saying, "Save yourselves from this crooked generation." 41 Those who gladly accepted his word were baptized, and about three thousand souls were added that day. 42 And they were persevering in the teaching of the Apostles, and in fellowship, and in the breaking of bread, and in prayers. 43 And fear came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were done through the Apostles. 44 And all who believed were together and had all things in common; 45 and they sold their possessions and goods and distributed them to all, as anyone had need. 46 And day by day, persevering with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, they took their food with gladness and sincerity of heart, 47 praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to the church daily those who were being saved.

---

### III. 1
Now Peter and John were going up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. And a certain man who was lame from his mother's womb was being carried,

---

34 **By an oath &c.** <note>original: "Jurejurando &c"</note>] The Greek text contains more than the Latin: "that God had sworn to him with an oath, that from the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up the Christ to sit on the throne" <note>original: "ὅτι ὅρκῳ ὤμοσεν αὐτῷ ὁ Θεὸς, ἐκ καρποῦ τῆς ὀσφύος αὐτοῦ τὸ κατὰ σάρκα ἀναστήσειν τὸν Χριστόν, καθίσαι ἐπὶ τοῦ θρόνου"</note>. This means that God had sworn to him by an oath that from the fruit of his loins, as far as the flesh is concerned, he would raise up the Christ to sit on the throne, although the Greek manuscripts vary in this place. I suspect this was added by some minor scholar to whom the speech otherwise seemed insufficiently complete. Furthermore, in these words, "swore with an oath" <note>original: "ὤμοσεν ὅρκῳ"</note>, there is not that affinity of words in Greek as there is in the Latin. Additionally, regarding the phrase "to sit from the fruit of his loins," one must supply a subject <note>such as "someone" or "the Christ"</note>.

35 **Of the fruit of his loins** <note>original: "De fructu lumbi ejus"</note>] The Greek has more than our <note>Latin</note> versions: "from the fruit of his loins to sit upon his throne, to raise up the Christ according to the flesh" <note>original: "ἐκ καρποῦ τῆς ὀσφύος αὐτοῦ καθίσαι ἐπὶ τοῦ θρόνου αὐτοῦ, τὸ κατὰ σάρκα ἀναστήσειν τὸν Χριστόν"</note>. Again, the sense in the Greek words is ambiguous. For "to sit" <note>original: "καθίσαι"</note> can mean both to sit down and to cause to sit, and "to raise up" <note>original: "ἀναστῆσαι"</note> can mean to wake up or to rise again. An active sense better fits the prophecy, which promises that God would raise him up and place him on the throne of David. This is the throne of the Gospel kingdom.

36 **Foreseeing** <note>original: "Providens"</note>] The Greek is "Proidon" <note>original: "Προϊδών"</note>, that is, "Foreseeing." Although in some manuscripts it was "Prosidon" <note>original: "Προσίδών"</note>, that is, "Present."

37 **Neither was he left in hell** <note>original: "Neque derelictus est in inferno"</note>] "That his soul was not left behind" <note>original: "ὅτι οὐκ ἐγκατελείφθη ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτοῦ"</note>, that is, because his soul was not abandoned.

38 **Poured out this** <note>original: "Effudit hunc"</note>] "He poured out this" <note>original: "ἐξέχεε τοῦτο"</note>. The Greek speech is two-sided <note>ambiguous</note>; for it can be understood as having poured out "this Spirit," because "Spirit" <note>original: "πνεῦμα"</note> in Greek is of the neuter gender. As for what the *Ordinary Gloss* <note>a standard medieval Bible commentary</note> mentions—that the Greek says "this gift"—I do not find "gift" <note>original: "δῶρον"</note> in the Greek codices.

39 **Most certainly know** <note>original: "Certiffime scias"</note>] "Therefore safely" <note>original: "Ἀσφαλῶς οὖν"</note>, that is, "Therefore certainly."

40 **Now having heard these things** <note>original: "His autem auditis"</note>] "But they, having heard" <note>original: "Ἀκούσαντες δὲ"</note>, that is, "But when they had heard." I praise the Translator, however, who successfully moved away from the literal words when no necessity compelled him.

41 **Do penance** <note>original: "Paenitentiam agite"</note>] "Metanoesate" <note>original: "Μετανοήσατε"</note>, that is, "Let it repent you," or "Return to a right mind."

42 **For the promise is to you** <note>original: "Vobis enim est promissio"</note>] One should add "made," or "unto you."

43 **Also to others** <note>original: "Aliis etiam"</note>] "Eterois te" <note>original: "Ἑτέροις τε"</note>, that is, "And to others."

44 **Those therefore who received** <note>original: "Qui ergo receperunt"</note>] "They therefore, having gladly accepted" <note>original: "Οἱ μὲν οὖν ἀσμένως ἀποδεξάμενοι"</note>, that is, those who therefore received willingly.

45 **On that day** <note>original: "In die illo"</note>] "On that day" <note>original: "τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ"</note>, that is, to that day, unless you understand the preposition "in" <note>original: "ἐν"</note>.

46 **In the breaking of bread** <note>original: "Fractione panis"</note>] "And in the breaking of the bread" <note>original: "καὶ τῇ κλάσει τοῦ ἄρτου"</note>, that is, so that there are four things: doctrine, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayers. The Greek codices consistently have it this way, and so John Chrysostom <note>an influential 4th-century Church Father</note> interprets it. Perhaps he calls "fellowship" the sharing of resources. It should be noted that he placed doctrine first—but Gospel doctrine—next, mutual charity, which made everything common among them; thirdly, that sacred symbol of Christian conspiracy <note>union</note>; and fourthly, prayers. Our <note>Latin</note> reading lists only three: doctrine, the breaking of bread (which it calls fellowship), and prayers. This <note>fourfold practice</note> lasted a long time among the Ancients, where bishops or some serious guests would first pray with the Bishop, then take a part of the broken bread, and finally converse. Thus they were said to be of the same "communion," because heretics were not admitted to that fellowship. It is uncertain whether he speaks here of the consecrated bread, since no mention is made of the chalice. **In Jerusalem.** I do not find these two words in the Greek manuscript. Nor are they cited by Chrysostom.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
30 Therefore, since he was a prophet, and knew that God had sworn to him with an oath that from the fruit of his loins, as far as the flesh is concerned, Christ would arise and sit upon his throne, 31 foreseeing this, he spoke of the resurrection of Christ, 37 that his soul was not left in hell, nor did his flesh see corruption. This Jesus God raised up, of which we are all witnesses. Being therefore exalted by the right hand of God, and having received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, 33 he poured out this which you now see and hear. David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says: "The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make 
<margin>B</margin>
your enemies a footstool for your feet." 36 Therefore let the whole house of Israel know for certain that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ. 40 Now when they heard these things, they were pierced to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the Apostles, "What shall we do, men and brothers?" Peter said to them, "Do penance 41 for your sins, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. 42 For the promise is made to you and to your children, and to all who are far off, whomsoever the Lord our God shall call." 43 And with many other words he testified and exhorted them, saying, "Save yourselves from this wicked generation." 44 Those therefore who willingly received his word were baptized; and there were added 
<margin>C</margin>
on that day about three thousand souls. And they were persevering in the doctrine of the Apostles, and in fellowship, 46 and in the breaking of bread, and in prayers. 47 And fear came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were performed through the Apostles. 48 And all who believed 49 were joined together, and had all things in common. 50 They sold their possessions and substance, and divided them among all, as each had need. And daily continuing with one accord in the temple, and breaking 51 bread from house to house, 52 they took their food in turn, with exultation and simplicity of heart, praising God, and having favor 53 with all the people. 54 And the Lord added daily to the congregation those who were being saved. 55 Now at the same time Peter and John were going up into the temple, for the ninth hour of prayer. And a certain man, who was lame from his mother's womb, was being carried, 
<margin>D</margin>
whom

---

47 **And there was great fear in all** <note>original: "Et metus erat magnus in universis"</note>] But I did not find these words written down <note>in the Greek</note>.

48 **All also** <note>original: "Omnes etiam"</note>] "But all" <note>original: "Πάντες δὲ"</note>, that is, "But all." I think the Translator read "Pantes te" <note>original: "Πάντες τε"</note>.

49 **Were together** <note>original: "Erant pariter"</note>] "Were in the same place" <note>original: "ἦσαν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ"</note>, which previously he translated as "in the same place."

50 **Possessions** <note>original: "Possessiones"</note>] In Greek it is "ktemata" <note>original: "κτήματα"</note>, which means both "possessions" and "resources," with a doubled conjunction: "both the possessions and the goods" <note>original: "καὶ τὰ κτήματα καὶ τὰς ὑπάρξεις"</note>.

51 **About the houses** <note>original: "Circa domos"</note>] "Kat' oikon" <note>original: "κατ' οἶκον"</note>, that is, through individual houses, or house-by-house. Just as "kata polin" <note>original: "κατὰ πόλιν"</note> and "kath' emeran" <note>original: "καθ' ἡμέραν"</note> mean town-by-town and daily.

52 **They took food** <note>original: "Sumebant cibum"</note>] "Metelambanon" <note>original: "μετελάμβανον"</note>. This means to take from another, and to be a participant. We translated it as "they took in turn." But again, "for a price."

53 **To all the people** <note>original: "Ad omnem plebem"</note>] He said "all" for "the whole," and "plebs" for "people" <note>original: "ὅλον τὸν λαόν"</note>.

54 **But the Lord increased** <note>original: "Dominus autem augebat"</note>] The Greek reads: "But the Lord added those who were being saved daily to the church" <note>original: "Ὁ δὲ Κύριος προσετίθει τοὺς σωζομένους καθ' ἡμέραν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ"</note>. I suspect the Translator wrote "added" <note>original: "addebat"</note>, and a scribe corrupted that into "increased" <note>original: "augebat"</note>. Someone also noted in the *Ordinary Gloss* that the Greek codices differ from ours, although by a ridiculous slip of the scribes, "ecce" <note>behold</note> was put for "ecclesia" <note>church</note>.

55 **Into the same** <note>original: "In idipsum"</note>] The Latins seem to refer this to the preceding text; by contrast, the Greeks refer it to what follows: "But at the same time Peter" <note>original: "Ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ δὲ Πέτρος"</note>, that is, "Now together Peter," so that "into the same" refers not only to place but also to time. Certainly Chrysostom begins a new chapter of his Commentaries with these words, "into the same." Someone noted the faulty punctuation in the *Ordinary Gloss*.

<meta>This page continues the narrative from the end of Acts chapter 2, moving from the communal life of the early believers into the first recorded miracle of the Apostles: the healing of the lame man at the Temple gate. The text provides a parallel comparison of the Greek source and a Latin translation, accompanied by scholarly notes on translation choices and manuscript variations.</meta>

<header>ACTS CHAPTER III.</header>

<margin>A</margin> 2 [a certain man, lame from his mother’s womb, was being carried], whom they placed daily at the gate of the temple called "Beautiful," to ask for alms from 3 those entering into the temple. Who, seeing Peter and John about to enter the temple, asked to 4 receive alms. But Peter, fixing his gaze on him along with 5 John, said, "Look at us." And he gave them his 6 attention, expecting to receive something from them. But Peter said, "Silver and gold I do not have, but what I 7 have, this I give to you: In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, rise up and walk." And taking him by the right hand, he raised him up; and immediately 8 his feet and ankles were made strong. And leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and entered with <margin>B</margin> them into the temple, walking and leaping and praising 9 God. And all the people saw him walking and 10 praising God. And they recognized him, that this was the one who used to sit for alms at the Beautiful Gate of the temple; and they were filled with wonder and amazement at what 11 had happened to him. And as the healed lame man held onto Peter and John, all the <margin>C</margin> people ran together to them at the portico called Solomon's, greatly amazed. 12 And seeing this, Peter answered the people, "Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as if by our own power or piety we made 13 him walk? The God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his servant Jesus, whom you handed over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him. 14 But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked 15 for a murderer to be granted to you; and the Author of Life you killed, whom God raised from the dead, 16 of which we are witnesses. And on the basis of faith in his name, his name has made strong this man, whom you see and know; and the faith which is through him has given him this perfect health in the presence of all of you. 17 And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, 18 just as your leaders did. But what God announced beforehand through the mouth of all his prophets, <margin>D</margin> 19 that the Christ would suffer, he has thus fulfilled. Repent therefore, and turn back, so that your sins may be wiped away, 20 so that times of refreshing may come from the presence [of the Lord]—

---

2 **At the gate** <note>original: "Ad portam"</note>] to the door <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὴν θύραν</note>, *that is, at the entrance*.
<margin>A</margin> **Beginning to enter** <note>original: "Incipientes introire"</note>] being about to enter <note>original Greek: μέλλοντας εἰσιέναι</note>, *that is, those about to go in*.
3 **He asked to receive alms** <note>original: "Rogavit ut eleemosynam acciperet"</note>] *The Greek only has "although he was asking for alms,"* <note>original: ἠρώτα ἐλεημοσύνην</note>. *In some manuscripts, however, "to receive"* <note>original Greek: λαβεῖν</note> *is added, so that they agree with our Latin versions*.
4 **Gazing** <note>original: "Intens"</note>] Gazing intently at him <note>original Greek: Ἀτενίσας εἰς αὐτὸν</note>, *that is, with eyes fixed upon him*.
5 **Look at us** <note>original: "Respice in nos"</note>] Look toward us <note>original Greek: Βλέψον εἰς ἡμᾶς</note>, *that is, Look at us, or Behold us*.
6 **And having taken his hand** <note>original: "Et apprehensa manu"</note>] And grasping him by the right hand <note>original Greek: Καὶ πιάσας αὐτὸν τῆς δεξιᾶς χειρὸς</note>. *Instead of "grasping"* <note>original Greek: πιάσας</note> *some manuscripts had "holding"* <note>original Greek: κρατήσας</note>, *that is, having taken his right hand*.
7 **His feet were made firm** <note>original: "Consolidata sunt bases"</note>] *The Translator left the Greek word* <note>original Greek: βάσεις, bases/steps</note> *as it was: the Ancients would put "steps" or "feet." Or because "ankles"* <note>original Greek: σφυρά</note> *follows, a word of almost the same weight, it means the soles and the ankles, so that the "basis" is the lowest part of the foot. Irenaeus reads "steps" instead of "bases."*
8 **Walking & leaping** <note>original: "Ambulans & exiliens"</note>] leaping <note>original Greek: ἁλλόμενος</note>, *that is, jumping, to signify not just walking in the common way, but also being joyful and exultant. Irenaeus records it thus. And a little before, the verb was a compound,* "And leaping up he stood" <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἐξαλλόμενος ἔστη</note>.
9 **He sat for alms** <note>original: "Ad eleemosynam sedebat"</note>] the one sitting for alms <note>original Greek: ὁ πρὸς τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην καθήμενος</note>, *that is, he who was sitting for alms, or he who had sat*.
10 **And in ecstasy** <note>original: "Et ecstasi"</note>] and of amazement <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐκστάσεως</note>. *Elsewhere he translates this as "stupor." But because he had already rendered "wonder"* <note>original Greek: θαμβος</note> *this way, he lacked a word for "ecstasy." He could have translated* <term>thambos</term> <note>original Greek: θαμβος</note> *as "admiration." For it is used this way in Homer:* "amazement seizes me as I look upon it" <note>original Greek: θάμβος μ' ἔχει εἰσορόωντα</note>. *They think it is derived from the verb* <term>thēpō</term> <note>original Greek: θήπω</note>, *which means "to wonder at."*
11 **When they saw, however, etc.** <note>original: "Cum viderent autem &c."</note>] *The Greek readings are different:* "But as the healed lame man held Peter and John, all the people ran to them" <note>original Greek: Κρατοῦντος δὲ τοῦ ἰαθέντος χωλοῦ τὸν Πέτρον καὶ Ἰωάννην, συνέδραμε πρὸς αὐτοὺς πᾶς ὁ λαὸς</note>. *Indeed, in several of our own codices, "held"* <note>original Latin: tenerent</note> *is seen written instead of "saw"* <note>original Latin: viderent</note>, *from which it is sufficiently clear that "held" was the original. Chrysostom interprets this as a proof of love toward the Apostles, from whom the one who had been lame could not be torn away.*
12 **To the portico** <note>original: "Ad porticum"</note>] at the portico <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ τῇ στοᾷ</note>, *that is, in the portico*.
13 **Seeing this, however** <note>original: "Videns autem"</note>] "Seeing" <note>original Greek: Ἰδὼν</note> *is a past participle; it could mean "when Peter had seen it," or "this having been seen by Peter."*
14 **By our own virtue or power** <note>original: "Nostra virtute aut potestate"</note>] by our own strength or religion, or piety <note>original Greek: ἰδίᾳ δυνάμει ἢ εὐσεβείᾳ</note>. *It appears the Translator read "authority"* <note>original Greek: ἐξουσίᾳ</note> *instead of "piety"* <note>original Greek: εὐσεβείᾳ</note>. *And that reading is certainly more approved by me. Irenaeus makes no mention of "piety." In the very ancient Constantinopolitan codex, it was "piety."*
15 **The God of Abraham, & the God of Isaac, & the God of Jacob** <note>original: "Deus Abraham, & Deus Isaac, & Deus Jacob"</note>] *The Greeks only put "God" once: "The God of Abraham and Isaac and Ja-"*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> [a certain man, lame from birth] whom they placed daily at the gate of the temple which is called Beautiful, so that he might ask for alms from those entering 3 into the temple. When he had seen Peter and John about to enter into the temple, he asked to 4 receive alms. But with his eyes fixed upon him, 5 Peter with John said, "Look at us." And he gave them his attention, hoping that he would receive something from them. 6 Peter, however, said, "Silver and gold is not mine, but what I have, this I give to you: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk." And having 7 grasped his right hand, he raised him up: and immediately his soles and ankles were made strong. 8 And leaping up he stood, and was walking, and entered with them into the temple, walking <margin>B</margin> and leaping and praising God. And all the people saw 9 him walking and praising God. And they 10 recognized him, that he was the very one who had sat for alms at the Beautiful gate of the temple: and they were filled with admiration and stupor over that which had happened to him. While the lame man who 11 had been healed held Peter and John, all the people ran to them in the portico which is called Solomon’s, <margin>C</margin> being astonished. Seeing this, Peter answered to the 12 people, "Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you gaze at us, as if by our own virtue or piety we had brought it about that this man should walk? The God of Abraham 13 and Isaac and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his son Jesus, whom you delivered up and denied in the sight of Pilate, when he had judged that he should be released. But you denied the Holy and Just One, 14 and requested that a man who was a murderer be granted to 15 you: but the Author of Life you killed, whom God raised from the dead, of which we are witnesses. And 16 through faith in his name, his name has strengthened this man, whom you see and know: and the faith which is through him has given him this perfect health in the sight of all of you. And now, brothers, I know that you did it 17 through ignorance, just as your leaders did. But 18 God, what he had announced beforehand through the mouth of all his <margin>D</margin> prophets, that Christ should suffer, he has thus fulfilled. Therefore, repent of your error and be converted, that 19 your sins may be wiped away, 20 so that when the times [of refreshing] come—

---

cob. <note>original: "...and Jacob"</note> *In Chrysostom, "the God"* <note>original Greek: ὁ Θεός</note> *is repeated four times. And indeed, he is frequently named thus in the Holy Scriptures. Some scholar, offended because it seemed that many Gods were being made out of one, removed "the God" twice.*
16 **When he had judged** <note>original: "Judicante illo"</note>] judging <note>original Greek: κρίναντος</note>, *in the past tense: when he had judged, or when he had determined to release him.*
17 **A man who was a murderer** <note>original: "Virum homicidam"</note>] *He has truly expressed that Apostolic majesty of style, which he is testified to have had in speaking, even by just one of his Epistles. He has related these opposites no less weightily than elegantly. A murderer takes away life; to this man the Jews granted life, while the Author of Life they dragged to death.*
<margin>E</margin> 18 **And in the faith of his name** <note>original: "Et in fide nominis ejus"</note>] And on the basis of faith in his name, his name has made strong this man whom you see and know <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἐπὶ τῇ πίστει τοῦ ὀνόματος αὐτοῦ τοῦτον, ὃν θεωρεῖτε καὶ οἴδατε, ἐστερέωσε τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ</note>. *The Greek speech has much ambiguity* <term>amphibologia</term>, *because it is uncertain what "his"* <note>original: αὐτοῦ</note> *refers to, and who is the subject of the verb "made strong"* <note>original: ἐστερέωσε</note>, *and whether "name"* <note>original: ὄνομα</note> *is in the nominative or accusative case. It seems to me Peter meant this: the God of our fathers has confirmed his own name through the faith regarding the name of Jesus, which this man has, whom you see and know. But if "name" is the nominative case, the sense will be: the name of Christ has strengthened this man whom you see and know through the faith of his name.*
19 **This man whom you have seen** <note>original: "Hunc quem vos vidistis"</note>] this man whom you see <note>original Greek: τοῦτον ὃν θεωρεῖτε</note>, *that is, a verb in the present tense.*
20 **His name & faith** <note>original: "Nomen ejus & fides"</note>] *In the Greek the punctuation is different; they refer "his name" to what came before, and "faith" to what follows.*
<margin>F</margin> 21 **And the faith which is through him** <note>original: "Et fides quæ per eum est"</note>] *Again it is uncertain whether "him"* <note>original: αὐτῷ</note> *refers to Christ or the name: through that man, or through that name.*
22 **Gave him perfect** <note>original: "Dedit integram"</note>] gave to him <note>original Greek: ἔωκεν αὐτῷ</note>, *that is, he gave to him. That perfect health,* <term>holoklērian tautēn</term> <note>original Greek: ὁλοκληρίαν ταύτην</note>, *that is, this integrity, to which "debility" is opposed, which properly signifies a defect of the limbs. Irenaeus reads "safety/soundness" instead of "integrity."*
23 **God however who** <note>original: "Deus autem qui"</note>] *It is not "who" in Greek, but "the things which"* <note>original Greek: ἃ</note>. *God, the things which he had previously announced, and that through the mouths of all the Prophets, he has fulfilled just as he predicted.*
24 **Repent therefore etc.** <note>original: "Pœnitemini igitur &c."</note>] Repent <note>original Greek: Μετανοήσατε</note>. *I wonder why he did not say "Do penance"* <note>original: Pœnitentiam agite</note> *according to his usual custom. It could have been translated as "Return to your senses"* <note>original Latin: Resipiscite</note>, *just as Tertullian reads in his book "On the Resurrection of the Flesh," although the first printed books had "Look back"* <note>original: Respicite</note> *instead of "Return to your senses," or "Let you repent of your former life," or something similar.*
25 **So that when the times come** <note>original: "Ut cum venerint tempora"</note>] *It appears this is an incomplete thought* <term>anapodoton</term>, *for he does not finish what he began. Therefore either something must be understood, such as "so that you may be saved," when the times of refreshing come etc. Or "so that"* <note>original Greek: ὅπως ἂν</note> *is put for "whenever," and thus it is to be taken as an expletive conjunction.*
