<meta>This page continues the text of the Acts of the Apostles, picking up in the middle of Peter's speech following the healing of the lame man. It transitions from Chapter 3 into the beginning of Chapter 4, where the apostles face their first opposition from the religious authorities in Jerusalem.</meta>

# OF THE APOSTLES. CHAPTER IV.

<margin>21</margin> ...of the Lord, and that he may send the one preached to you beforehand, Jesus Christ, whom heaven must indeed receive until the times of the restoration of all things, which God spoke of through the mouth of all his holy Prophets from the beginning of the age.
<margin>22</margin> For Moses said to the fathers: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a Prophet from your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him in everything, whatever he may speak to you."
<margin>23</margin> And it shall be that every soul who does not listen to that Prophet shall be destroyed from among the people.
<margin>24</margin> And indeed, all the Prophets from Samuel, and those who followed, as many as have spoken, have also announced these days.
<margin>25</margin> You are the sons of the Prophets and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying to Abraham: "And in your seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed."
<margin>26</margin> To you first, God, having raised up his servant Jesus, sent him blessing you, in turning each of you away from your wickednesses.

<margin>IV. 1</margin> And as they were speaking to the people, the Priests, and the Captain of the temple, and the Sadducees came upon them,
<margin>2</margin> being greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead.
<margin>3</margin> And they laid hands on them and put them in custody until the next day; for it was already evening.
<margin>4</margin> But many of those who heard the word believed, and the number of the men became about five thousand.
<margin>5</margin> And it happened on the next day that their Rulers and Elders and Scribes gathered in Jerusalem,
<margin>6</margin> along with Annas the High Priest, and Caiaphas, and John, and Alexander, and as many as were of the high-priestly family.
<margin>7</margin> And having stood them in the middle, they inquired: "By what power or in what name did you do this?"
<margin>8</margin> Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them: "Rulers of the people and Elders of Israel,
<margin>9</margin> if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a sick man, by what means this man has been healed,
<margin>10</margin> let it be known to all of you, and to all the people of Israel, that in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, by him this man stands before you healthy."

---

...filling out the sense, *However the times of refreshing may come.* <note>original: "Utcunque veniant tempora refrigerii"</note> For the Translator seems to have read the Greek as "so that," <note>original: "ὅπως ἂν"</note> otherwise it should have been rendered "as if the times of refreshing should come." Tertullian, in his book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, removes this difficulty by omitting the word "when," reading it as: "That times of refreshing may come upon you from the person of God." Irenaeus reads it no differently: "That your sins may be blotted out, and times of refreshing may come to you from the Lord." Furthermore, the phrase "from the face of the Lord" should be referred to the mention of "refreshing," so that you understand His appearance will be terrifying to the wicked, yet a refreshing to the pious. I thought it necessary to mention this, as I see more recent translators interpreting it otherwise.

<margin>26</margin> *Who was preached to you* <note>original: "Qui prædicatus est vobis"</note>] I suspect it happened through a scribe's error that in some Latin copies "he who is to preach" was written instead of "having been preached." In some Greek copies, instead of "preached beforehand," <note>original: "προκεκηρυγμένον"</note> it was written as "prepared beforehand," <note>original: "προκεχειρισμένον"</note> which means "appointed." For he uses this verb again around chapter 22. Nor is it simply "preached," but "preached *beforehand*."

<margin>27</margin> *Times of restoration* <note>original: "Tempora restitutionis"</note>] The Greek is *apokatastaseos*; I wonder why Irenaeus, following this, reads it as "disposition."

<margin>28</margin> *Through the mouth of holy ones* <note>original: "Per os sanctorum"</note>] The Greek codices here repeat the word "all," *pantōn*; just as it is added among us in the phrases that precede and follow.

<margin>29</margin> *Moses indeed said* <note>original: "Moyses quidem dixit"</note>] The Greek is "For Moses indeed said to the fathers." For he is explaining why he said "preached beforehand."

<margin>30</margin> *The Lord God will raise up a Prophet for you*] The testimony he brings forward is found in the eighteenth chapter of Deuteronomy. Peter gave the meaning, not the exact words.

<margin>31</margin> *Like unto myself* <note>original: "Tanquam meipsum"</note>] This phrase must be divided so that "me" refers to "will raise up" and "him" (implicit) refers to "you shall hear." For the Greek speech indicates this: "A Prophet he will raise up like me, him you shall hear." Furthermore, for "like myself," he says a little later "similar to you," *hōsper se*.

<margin>32</margin> *Shall be exterminated* <note>original: "Exterminabitur"</note>] The Greek is *exolothreuthēsetai*. The Greek word does not sound like a mere "casting out," but an "utter destruction," from *olethros* (ruin/death). But just as salvation comes from being joined to the Church, so destruction is found in departing from the Church.

<margin>33</margin> *And all the Prophets from Samuel and thereafter*] The Greeks add the conjunction "and" (*kai*), which makes the sentence incomplete; this is omitted among the Latins. But since we see such things frequently occurring in Peter’s speech, or rather in Luke's writing, I wonder if someone, being offended by it, removed it. Therefore, to whoever thinks it should be added, one must understand something implied, so the sense is: not only Moses, but *also* all the Prophets promised something of this kind, as many as etc. Nor is it simply "And all the Prophets," but "But also all," <note>original: "Καὶ πάντες δὲ"</note> so that it relates back to Moses, who went before.

<column-break/>

<margin>21</margin> <insert>A</insert> ...times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord, and he shall send him who was preached to you before, Jesus Christ, whom heaven must indeed receive until the times of the restoration of all things, which God has spoken by the mouth of all his holy Prophets since the world began.
<margin>22</margin> Moses indeed said to the fathers: "The Lord your God shall raise up a Prophet for you from your brothers, like me; you shall hear him according to all things whatsoever he shall speak to you."
<margin>23</margin> And it shall come to pass, that every soul which will not hear that Prophet shall be exterminated from among the people.
<margin>24</margin> <insert>B</insert> Yea, and all the Prophets from Samuel, and those that follow after, as many as have spoken, have likewise foretold these days.
<margin>25</margin> You are the children of the Prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying to Abraham: "And in your seed shall all the families of the earth obtain a blessing."
<margin>26</important> To you first, God, when he had raised up his son Jesus, sent him blessing you, so that every one of you should turn himself from his iniquities.

<margin>IV. 1</margin> And as they spoke to the people, the Priests and the Captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them,
<margin>2</margin> being grieved that they taught the people, and preached in the name of Jesus the resurrection from the dead.
<margin>3</margin> And they laid hands on them, and put them in custody until the next day: for it was now evening.
<margin>4</margin> But many of them which <insert>C</insert> heard the word believed; and the number of the men was about five thousand.
<margin>5</margin> And it came to pass on the morrow, that their Rulers, and Elders, and Scribes were gathered together in Jerusalem,
<margin>6</margin> and Annas the High Priest, and Caiaphas, and John, and Alexander, and as many as were of the kindred of the high priest.
<margin>7</margin> And when they had set them in the midst, they asked: "By what power, or by what name, have you done this?"
<margin>8</margin> Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them: "Ye rulers of the people, and elders of Israel,
<margin>9</margin> if we this day be examined of the good deed done to the impotent man, by what means he is made whole;
<margin>10</margin> be it known to you all, and to all the people of Israel, that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, even by him does this man stand here before you <insert>D</insert>

---

<margin>A</margin> 24 *All the families of the earth*] For "families," the Greek is *patriai*, which elsewhere is translated as "paternities." From which "all paternity in heaven and on earth is named." Elsewhere it is "families," as in "Of the house and family of David." In some copies, it was *phylai*, that is, "tribes."

<margin>B</margin> 25 *To you first God raising up*] The Greek *anastēsas* is in the past tense, "having been raised" or "brought forth"; for it refers to a "coming forth" or "arising," not specifically rising from the dead here. Peter is looking back to the words of Moses: "God will raise up a Prophet for you."

<margin>C</margin> 26 *From his wickedness*] The Greek is *apo tōn ponēriōn hymōn*, that is, "from your malices," although the Translator rightly changed the form of the speech, as the literal Greek was foreign to Latin ears. Even so, the Greek is not without ambiguity. For this sense can also be taken: "In this, that he might turn each one of you away from his vices." For he calls the favor and benefit of God a "blessing." This consisted in the fact that He called us away from sins toward innocence. Those who have more superstitiously cultivated the elegance of the Latin tongue teach that the word *nequitia* (wickedness) properly fits crimes committed through luxury and lust, though Seneca sometimes ignores this rule.

<margin>D</margin> 1 *The Captain of the temple*] The Greek is *kai ho stratēgos tou hierou*, that is, the prince or leader of the temple. For "magistrate" here is in the singular number and signifies a specific man to whom the protection of the temple was committed.

<margin>E</margin> 2 *Five thousand men*] Nearly five thousand, *hōsei chiliades pente*, which previously came as "about."

<margin>3</margin> *And Caiaphas*] The Greek is *kai Kaiaphan*, that is, "and Caiapham," with four syllables and a Hebrew ending, just like "Annan" (Annas).

<margin>4</margin> *And elders of Israel, hear*] "Hear" is not added among the Greeks, but someone added it on his own. In the Constance codex, neither "hear" nor "Israel" was present.

<margin>F</margin> 5 *In the good deed of the sick man, in which this man was made whole*] First, who ever said "the good deed" of the one who is helped by a benefit? Secondly, what is this: "in which this man was made whole"? Unless perhaps Peter asks this and then immediately answers himself. Indeed, the Greek says: "If we today are examined concerning a good deed to a sick man, by what [name/power] this man has been saved, let it be known to you all... that in the name of Jesus..." Which should have been rendered: "If we are examined today concerning this, that we have done a good deed to a sick man, or that a good deed was done to a sick man, in whom, or through whom, or because this man was made whole, let it be known to you all, and to the whole people of Israel, that in the name of Jesus the Nazarene etc." That is: If there is a question about this matter, and if you desire to know from us by whose power and by whose name this lame man was restored to health, know that it was done neither by magic art nor by our own strength, but in the name of the Lord Jesus.

<meta>This page continues the account of Peter and John before the Sanhedrin following the healing of a man who had been lame from birth. # 451 ACTS CHAPTER IV. 452

11. This is the stone that was treated with contempt by you, the builders, which has become the head of the corner. 12. And there is salvation in no other; for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved. 13. Now when they observed the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlettered and ordinary men, <note>original: "idiōtai," meaning private citizens or those without professional training</note> they were amazed; they also recognized them as having been with Jesus. 14. But seeing the man who had been healed standing with them, they had nothing to say in response. 15. So, having ordered them to go outside the Sanhedrin, they conferred with one another, 16. saying, "What shall we do with these men? For that a notable sign has occurred through them is manifest to all who inhabit Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it. 17. But so that it may not spread further among the people, let us threaten them with a threat to speak no longer to any human in this name." 18. And having called them, they commanded them not to speak at all, nor to teach, in the name of Jesus. 19. But Peter and John answered and said to them, "Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you judge. 20. For we cannot help speaking of what we have seen and heard." 21. After threatening them further, they released them, finding no way to punish them because of the people, for everyone was glorifying God for what had happened. 22. For the man on whom this sign of healing had occurred was more than forty years old. 23. Being released, they went to their own people and reported everything the Chief Priests and Elders had said to them. 24. When they heard it, they raised their voice to God with one accord and said, "Lord, you are God, who made the heaven, and the earth, and the sea, and everything in them, 25. who said through the mouth of David your servant: 'Why did the nations rage, and the peoples plot vain things? 26. The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers were gathered together into one place against the Lord and against his Christ.' 27. For truly they were gathered against your holy servant..."

<margin>A</margin> ...he stands before you healthy. This is that stone <note>indicated by the number 6</note> which was rejected by you builders, which has become the head of the corner. Nor is there salvation in any other; for there is no other name under heaven <note>indicated by the number 7</note> given among men, in which it is necessary for us to be saved. Observing, moreover, <note>indicated by the number 8</note> the freedom of Peter and John in speaking, and it being discovered that they were unlettered and ordinary men, they wondered, <note>indicated by the number 9</note> and they recognized them, that they had been with Jesus. <note>indicated by the number 10</note> But seeing the man standing with them, who had been healed, they could say nothing in contradiction. Having ordered them to withdraw from the council, they conferred among themselves, saying, "What shall we do to these men? <note>indicated by the number 11</note> For a conspicuous sign has been performed through them; it is manifest to all inhabitants of Jerusalem, nor can we deny it. <note>indicated by the number 12</note> But lest <margin>B</margin> it be spread further among the people, <note>indicated by the number 13</note> let us threaten them with menaces, so that they no longer speak <note>indicated by the number 14</note> in this name to any man." <note>indicated by the number 15</note> And having summoned them, they commanded, <note>indicated by the number 16</note> that they should not speak at all, nor teach in the name of Jesus. But Peter and John answering, said to them, <note>indicated by the number 17</note> "Whether it be just in the sight of God to listen to you rather than God, you judge. For we cannot not speak of the things <note>indicated by the number 18</note> which we have seen and heard." But they, having added threats, dismissed them, finding nothing—no reason—to punish them because of the people, because all <note>indicated by the number 19</note> were glorifying God over that which had happened. For the man was more than forty years old, in whom this sign of healing had been performed. Being dismissed, they came to their own people, and reported <note>indicated by the number 20</note> whatever <margin>C</margin> the chief Priests and Elders had said. When they had heard this, they with one accord lifted their voice to God, and said, <note>indicated by the number 21</note> "Lord, you are God, who made heaven, and earth, the sea, and all things that are in them, <note>indicated by the number 22</note> who through the mouth of David your servant said, <note>indicated by the number 23</note> 'Why have the nations roared, and the peoples meditated on vain things? The kings of the earth stood by, and the princes came together as one against the Lord and against his Christ.' For they came together <note>indicated by the number 24</note> truly against your holy son..."

---

<margin>D</margin> **6. Who was rejected**] <note>original: "exouthenētheis"</note> that is, who was held in contempt, or regarded as nothing.
**7. Given to men**] <note>original: "to dedomenon en anthrōpois"</note> that is, which was given among men, meaning, which happened to be heard among men. For *Jesus* is the name of a man. He adds "among men" on account of Moses, in whom the Jews trusted.
**8. Peter's constancy**] <note>original: "Petrou parrēsian"</note> that is, Peter's audacity or freedom in speaking.
**9. And they recognized them**] The Latin translator would have translated more aptly to express the Greek as "And they acknowledged," <note>original: "kai epeginōskon"</note>.
**10. Also the man**] The Greek says <note>original: "ton de anthrōpon"</note>, that is, "the man however." The translator seems to have read <note>original: "ton te anthrōpon"</note>.
**11. Since indeed a known sign has been done**] It would have been clearer if he had translated in this manner: "for it is plain to all inhabitants of Jerusalem that a manifest sign has been done through those men, nor can we deny it." For the word "manifest" refers to the sign, and "plain" to the fact that it occurred.
**12. Lest it be spread further among the people**] <note>original: "dianemēthē"</note>. I would have preferred "creep," and he translates it thus elsewhere, "as a cancer creeps" <note>original: "nomēn hexei"</note>, in 2 Timothy 2.
**13. Let us threaten them**] <note>original: "apeilē apeilēsōmetha"</note>, that is, let us threaten them by threatening. This is according to the Hebrew custom, by which they signify a vehement and sharp threat.
**14. In this name**] This phrasing is frequently met by us in the Sacred Books, and sometimes the preposition is not ineptly translated as "through," and sometimes it is better omitted. Here, since neither seemed to fit well enough, we have left it as it was, asking the reader to grant us the same indulgence here as we take in a few other cases. "Under the name" does not please some, because it seems to sound like a fiction, though that is not always the case.
**15. And calling them they denounced**] How do we denounce someone who is present? Therefore, <note>original: "parēngeilan"</note>, I would have preferred "they commanded." For it is well known that "parangelmata" are called commands. And thus he translates himself in the very next chapter, "by commanding we commanded."
**16. That they should not speak at all**] <note>original: "mē phthengesthai"</note>, which is more than "lest they speak," as if you were to say, lest they even open their mouths or utter any sound about Jesus.
**17. If it is just**] <note>original: "Ei dikaion esti"</note>, that is, "Whether it be just," or "Is it just." And shortly after,
**18. But they threatening**] <note>original: "prosapeilēsamenoi"</note>, that is, with threats added. For previously they had only commanded. When they made little progress by that route, they added threats of capital punishment if they did not obey.
**19. They glorified that which had been done**] <note>original: "edoxazon ton Theon epi tō gegonoti"</note>, that is, they were glorifying God over that which had been done. Otherwise, the same thing would seem to be said twice—that which had been done in that which had happened.
**20. How great**] <note>original: "hosa"</note>, that is, "whatever"; otherwise he would have said "posa."
**21. Lord you who made**] In the Greek it is a bit more: <note>original: "Despota sy ho Theos"</note>, that is, "Lord you who are God," or "you are that God." For unless you understand the substantive verb "to be," the speech <margin>E</margin> will not be complete. "You who made," <note>original: "sy ho poiēsas"</note>, that is, "You, the very God who made."
**22. Who by the Spirit**] In this place also the Greek differs somewhat. For they have it thus: <note>original: "Ho dia stomatos Dabid paidos sou"</note>, that is, "Who through the mouth of David your servant."
**23. Why did the nations rage**] He rendered these two verses word for word according to the Septuagint Edition. Furthermore, that word "gathered together" <note>original: "synēchthēsan"</note> is not simply to meet, but to be congregated in an assembly or council, and as if to conspire, which the Hebrew word also indicates <note>original: "nosdu"</note>. Likewise, that word "raged" <note>original: "ephryaxan"</note>, is to the Hebrews <note>original: "ragshu"</note>, which signifies they are gathered with tumult and roaring.
**24. Truly in this city**] "In this city" I do not find in the Greek codex, and it seems to have been added by some translator. "Against your holy servant <note>Latin: "puerum"</note> Jesus." Valla <note>referring to Lorenzo Valla, a famous 15th-century humanist</note> is angry in this place because the translator assigned the title of "servant" to Jesus, the Son of God. Although "puer" among the Latins can mean "child," it less frequently means "servant," but most frequently a name for one of tender age. But when Christ was bringing salvation, he was not a "puer" <note>child</note>. Indeed, he saved us by his death, of which he speaks here. And perhaps the name of "servant" does not fit him, even if he was obedient and subject to the Father according to his assumed humanity—but as a son, not as a servant. Therefore, "paida" <note>original Greek word</note> ought to have been translated here as "son," not "servant" or "boy." Although I am not unaware of what is in Paul, "taking the form of a servant," which is referred by some to the assumed human nature, so that he was almost a servant. But it is more approved by me that he be called "emptied," not because he was a man, but because he was treated as a servant—and a criminal servant—with whips and the cross. For when he calls David a "puer" <note>servant/boy</note> a little before, that is, a servant of God, he does so correctly. If the translator had never translated "paida" as "son," it might seem he held the opinion that it was not permitted to translate otherwise. Now, since he has translated it so many other times, and even shortly after this, it is a wonder why he varied in this place. Certainly Ambrose, citing this place in the second book of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, chapter five, reads "son," not "servant," lest anyone stir up a fierce tragedy against me. <margin>F</margin> Furthermore, Saint Hilary in his *Commentaries* on this Psalm reads "son," not "servant" or "boy." And again in the eleventh book of *On the Trinity*, and more recently than all these, Cassiodorus. And Chrysostom, explaining this place from the Epistle to the Hebrews, "Your throne O Lord," denies that the Son is called a "servant," since he called the Angels "ministers." Yet it does not escape me that Jerome contends in many places that the word "servant" applies to Christ. But meanwhile, I do not see why either he should labor in this, that Christ be called "servant" somewhere, or why others should shrink so much from the word "servant" being attributed to Jesus as a man. For if a servant is one who in good faith obeys the commands of the Lord, why should Christ as a man not be called a servant? But if a servant is one who, compelled by evil, does his duty, the name of servant does not apply to Christ. Here, although I reviewed Valla's opinion in the first edition, nevertheless this passage was sharply attacked by two people, because I responded to the other in a small book on this very matter. The other, not content to have struck at my ignorance of the Sacred Scriptures, fled— <meta>catchword: fled-</meta>

<margin>D</margin> He <note>Erasmus is likely referring to a critic like Edward Lee</note> snaps at me, as if I feel the same as Apollinaris, <note>Apollinaris of Laodicea (d. 390) was a bishop whose views on the nature of Christ were condemned as heresy because he argued Christ had a human body but a divine mind.</note> who would take something away from human nature. For I guess that is what he thinks. Now he gathers an even more bitter suspicion from these words of mine: *Even if he obeyed and was subject to the Father, but as a son, not as a servant, as if I felt with Arius <note>Arius (d. 336) taught that the Son of God was a created being, not co-eternal or co-equal with the Father.</note> that the Son is not equal to the Father.* What is more impudent than this calumny? Does he who confesses Christ to have been a man not confess him to be a man? Furthermore, he is called the Son of God, according to the nature of both. Nor do they deny that the Son of God is a servant in any other sense than that in which Christ denies that his disciples should be called <term>servants</term> <note>original: "servos"</note>, but rather <term>friends</term> <note>original: "amicos"</note>. If the title of servant is rightly taken away from the Apostles, is it heresy not to admit it in Christ? And are men not ashamed, who seem to themselves absolutely learned, to bring such trifles into the light, and from the vainest dreams to inflict a double heresy? And he promises that he will point out many such dangerous errors. If this plague holds the title of Theological literature, it is much better either to grow old in Poetic and Philosophical literature, or to weave a basket of hibiscus. Finally, the question here is not whether the nickname of *servant* can be attributed to Christ, but whether it is customarily attributed in the Sacred Scriptures.

<margin>E</margin> 25 *Herod & Pontius Pilate* ] <note>original: "Ἡρώδης τε καὶ Πάντιος Πιλάτος"</note> In the Greek, there is a double conjunction, [te] Herod [kai] Pontius Pilate, or, "Herod together with Pontius Pilate." Paul also seems to have been delighted by this doubling. And in every way there is no small affinity in the style of their speech between the two.

-brew word, <note>original: "υἱὸς παρακλήσεως"</note>, that is, *among other things it signifies to be refreshed and cooled and consoled*. Even if Jerome interprets it variously as *son of a prophet, son of one coming, or son of consolation*. The last of these signifies what has pleased most people. There is one who thinks this word in Paul is corrupted, and that instead of *Barnabas* one should read *Bar-nabion*, and that the word is Syriac, not Hebrew. Just as I do not dare to guess this in such a great consensus of manuscripts, so I have no intention to sharply refute it. However, he wished to have this honor for the piety of the one who sincerely offered his own things, in order to make the different example that follows more detestable. In some Greek manuscripts there was added <note>original: "μεθερμηνευόμενος"</note>, that is, *which is interpreted*, or, *if someone should interpret*.

<margin>T</margin> 1 *Sold a field* ] <note>original: "ἐπώλησε κτῆμα"</note>, that is, he sold a possession, which is to say, a house or a piece of land.

2 *And he cheated regarding the price* ] <note>original: "ἐνοσφίσατο"</note>, that is, he set aside and tore away, which nevertheless the Translator correctly rendered.

3 *Bringing a certain part* ] <note>original: "ἐνέγκας μέρος τι"</note>, that is, a certain part having been brought. To Ananias. These two words are neither found among the Greeks, nor in the ancient Latin manuscripts.

4 *Why did he tempt* ] <note>original: "διὰ τί ἐπλήρωσε"</note>, that is, "he filled." So Augustine reads in his little book *On the Time of the Barbarians*, chapter three. Someone or other in the *Glossa Ordinaria* <note>A standard medieval collection of biblical glosses</note> noted here a different reading among the Greeks. Chrysostom reads <note>original: "ἐπείρασεν"</note> ["he tempted"]. I suspect the Translator read *epeirasen*.

5 *That you should lie* ] Again he translates the Greek figure, "so that you should lie." *To the Holy Spirit*, in Greek it is "against the Holy Spirit," <note>original: "ψευσασθαί σε τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον"</note>. Either because the Greeks speak this way, "I lie you," just as "I evangelize you," and "I do good you," or because the sense is that he lies to the Holy Spirit who falsely feigns and imitates what others were doing by the instinct of the Holy Spirit. For not only does he lie who speaks what is false, but also he who feigns; as in, "Create feigned a face." And, "the brass lies to be gold." Augustine, in the book I just cited, reads *to lie in the presence of the Holy Spirit*, as if the Greek had been <note>original: "πρὸς τὸ Πνεῦμα"</note>. Chrysostom indeed reads it with us, but the ambiguity of the reading is not resolved by the interpretation.

6 *Remaining, it remained to you* ] Again, in the manner of the Hebrews, he expressed the emphasis by a doubling of the word, <note>original: "μένον ἔμενε"</note>, that is, "truly and altogether it remained," with no one compelling him in any way. Now Peter accuses him in two steps. First, it remained when no one compelled him to sell. Secondly, if he chose to sell, no one compelled him to take away the price.

7 *And once sold, it was in your power* ] <note>original: "καὶ πραθὲν"</note>. The Translator rendered different Greek expressions by the same Latin one. There it is *ktēma* (possession) and *chōrion* (estate or villa); here he translates both as *field* <note>original: "agrum"</note>: and yet, forgetting himself, he added the neuter *sold* <note>original: "venundatum"</note>, responding to the Greek word, but forgetting the Latin, since he ought to have said the masculine *sold* <note>original: "venundatus"</note> to match the masculine word for field.

8 *The space of three hours* ] <note>original: "διάστημα"</note>, that is, an interval.

I wish those who are entirely devoted to the comforts of this world would read these things attentively—those who either despise or even mock the poverty and humility of Christ. However, it is in a different manner. Nor does he share these things except with one who, having despised all else, has devoted himself to this kingdom with his whole heart. I myself watched, first at Bologna and then at Rome, Julius the Second, the Roman Pontiff of that name, leading the most magnificent triumphs, indeed such that they could be compared with the triumphs of Pompey or Caesar. ...consistent? <note>original: *convenient?* — This completes the word from the previous column's catchword</note>. And that same magnificence would follow the successors of the Apostles today, if they were equal in spirit.
<margin>13</margin> *They might cast out the sick*] <note original="ἐκφέρειν">to carry out</note>, that is, *they were bringing*, or *they were exporting*. Nor is the Greek word <note original="ἐκβάλλειν">to throw out</note>, such that the Translator should have been forced to translate it that way.
<margin>14</margin> *And on mats*] <note original="καὶ κραββάτων">and of beds</note>. It is a Greek word, yet accepted among the Latins, with two small letters changed.
<margin>15</margin> *So that they might come... of them*] More in the Latin style would be *any one*. And *they were delivered from their infirmities*. This is not in the Greek copies, but it appears to have been added by someone who wanted to provide an interpretation. The Greek reading is supported by the very ancient manuscripts of Saint Donatian.
<margin>16</margin> *And all the elders*] <note original="πᾶσαν τὴν γερουσίαν">all the senate</note>, that is, *the order of the elders*.
<margin>17</margin> *They were in doubt about them*] <note original="διηπόρουν">they were thoroughly perplexed</note>. He meant something more: *to be perplexed, and of a wavering mind, and lacking a plan*.
<margin>18</margin> *By commanding we commanded*] <note original="Οὐ παραγγελίᾳ παρηγγείλαμεν">Did we not with a command command</note>, that is, *Did we not command with a decree*, which is to say, we commanded sharply, just as he said before, *let us threaten with threats*.
<margin>19</margin> *It is necessary to obey God*] <note original="πειθαρχεῖν">to obey a ruler</note>. This properly means *to obey a Prince* or a *Magistrate*, a compound word from <note original="πείθεσθαι">to obey</note> and <note original="ἄρχων">prince/ruler</note>. And a little later, *to those obeying him* <note original="τοῖς πειθαρχοῦσιν αὐτῷ">to those obeying him</note>.
<margin>20</margin> *Whom you killed*] <note original="διεχειρίσασθε">you handled/killed with your hands</note>. This means *to kill with violent hands*. For the Greek word is derived from this. For a person is "killed" <note>original: *interimitur*</note> even when they are executed by law and merit.
<margin>21</margin> *Prince* (& *Savior*)] <note original="Ἀρχηγὸν">Archegon</note>, *leader* and *author*. Although I do not find fault with what the Translator rendered.

<margin>E</margin>
22 **And we [are witnesses]** The Greeks add the genitive <note original="αὐτοῦ">of him</note>, that is, "of him," which the Latin could have translated in the dative, "to him." Nor is it simply, **and the Holy Spirit**, but <note original="καὶ τὸ Πνεῦμα δὲ τὸ ἅγιον">and indeed the Holy Spirit</note>, that is, "but even the Holy Spirit," as if it were a correction of the previous statement. As if he were saying: we are not so much witnesses to him as the Holy Spirit himself is, by whose power these things are done.

23 **And they thought to kill them** <note original="ἐβουλεύοντο">they were deliberating</note>, that is, they were consulting how they might kill them. The translator read <note original="ἐβούλοντο">they were wishing</note>, or certainly formed it that way.

24 **That the men become** In Greek it is "the Apostles," not "the men." Nor is it "to become," but "to make" or "to put," <note original="ποιῆσαι">to do/make</note>, that is, to send them outside.

25 **Theudas rose up** He translates elegantly as **rose up**, <note original="ἀνέστη">stood up</note>, that is, he arose or appeared. The Greek manuscripts have <note original="Θευδᾶς">Theudas</note>, that is, **Theudas**, not **Theodas**. Chrysostom thinks these men were removed from the midst because they forbade the paying of tribute to Caesar, and that they were Pharisees. See Eusebius in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 2, Chapter 11.

26 **To whom he joined** <note original="προσεκολλήθη">was glued/joined to</note>. Which elsewhere he translates as "adhered"; it is more correctly translated that way here as well. For they did not only agree, but also conspired with him and taught the same things.

27 **In the days of the profession** <note original="ἀπογραφῆς">of the registration/census</note>. Which in the Gospel he translates as "the taxing" or "description."

28 **He turned away the people** The Greeks add <note original="ἱκανὸν">sufficient/many</note>, that is, **many**.

29 **This counsel or work** <note original="ἡ βουλὴ ἢ τὸ ἔργον τοῦτο">the counsel or the work this</note>, that is, "this counsel or work."

30 **Lest perhaps** <note original="μήποτε">lest ever</note>, that is, "lest at any time."

31 **And you be seen to fight against God** <note original="καὶ θεομάχοι εὑρεθῆτε">and God-fighters you be found</note>, <margin>F</margin> lest you be found to be those fighting with God. However, the translator renders it correctly, except that the Greek has more emphasis, signifying a state or character, not just an action—as if you were to say **enemies of God**, or **rebels against God**.

32 **They agreed with him** <note original="Ἐπείσθησαν">they were persuaded</note>, that is, "they obeyed" or "complied."

33 **Lest they speak at all** I do not find "at all" in the Greek manuscripts; it is simply <note original="μὴ λαλεῖν">not to speak</note>, that is, "that they should not speak." It was missing from the ancient manuscripts.

34 **And around the houses** <note original="κατ' οἶκον">according to house</note>, that is, through individual houses, or "domestically."

35 **Teaching** <note original="ἐπαύοντο διδάσκοντες καὶ εὐαγγελιζόμενοι">they ceased teaching and evangelizing</note>. It should have been translated, **they ceased to teach and to evangelize**, changing the participle into an infinitive.

him as a Prince and Savior God has exalted by his right hand, to give repentance to Israel, and the remission of sins.
<margin>32</margin> And we are witnesses to him of these things which we say, and furthermore also the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.
<margin>33</margin> When they had heard these things, they were cut asunder, and they consulted how they might kill them.
<margin>34</margin> But a certain Pharisee rising in the council, named Gamaliel, a doctor of the law held in honor among all the people, commanded that the Apostles be put outside for a little while.
<margin>35</margin> And he said to them: "Men of Israel, take heed to yourselves concerning these men, what you are about to do.
<margin>36</margin> For before these days Theudas rose up, saying that he was somebody, to whom joined a number of men about four hundred, who was slain; and all who believed him were scattered and brought to nothing.
<margin>37</margin> After him rose up Judas of Galilee in the days of the census, and turned away much people after him, and he himself perished; and all as many as had obeyed him were dispersed.
<margin>38</margin> And now I say to you: refrain from these men and let them alone; for if this counsel or this work is of men, it will be dissolved.
<margin>39</margin> But if it is of God, you cannot dissolve it, lest perhaps you be found even to fight against God."
<margin>40</margin> And they went along with his opinion. And when they had called the Apostles, having beaten them, they charged them that they should not speak in the name of Jesus, and they let them go.
<margin>41</margin> And they indeed went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were accounted worthy to suffer reproach for his name.
<margin>42</margin> And every day in the temple and in individual houses they did not cease to teach and to announce Jesus Christ.

**VI.** And in those days, the number of disciples increasing, there arose a murmuring of the Greeks against the Hebrews, because their widows were being despised in the daily ministry.
<margin>2</margin> But those twelve, when they had commanded the multitude of disciples to be present, said: "It is not pleasing that we, having left the word of God, should serve tables.
<margin>3</margin> Look out therefore, brothers, for seven men from among you of proven integrity, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, to whom we will delegate this business.
<margin>4</margin> But we will apply ourselves to prayer and to the administration of the word."
<margin>5</margin> And this speech pleased the whole multitude: and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolas, a proselyte of Antioch.
<margin>6</margin> These they placed in the sight of the Apostles.

---

1 **The number of disciples increasing** <note original="πληθυνόντων τῶν μαθητῶν">of the multiplying of the disciples</note>, that is, when the disciples became more numerous. Although I approve of the Translator's paraphrase.

2 **The murmur of the Greeks** It is not <note original="Ἑλλήνων">Hellenon</note>, but <note original="Ἑλληνιστῶν">Helleniston</note>, **Hellenists**. For the Jews call all pagans and those foreign to the Mosaic Law "Greeks." And it is probable that in this number there was not yet anyone from the gentiles; therefore he did not say "Greeks," but "Hellenists"—Jews who had been born or had lived among the gentiles, and spoke the language of the nation where they lived. Therefore, those who were born in the regions of the Jews called Jews born elsewhere and speaking another language "semi-pagans"; here he does not call them **Jews**, which was a name of religion, but **Hebrews**, which more indicates the race and nation.

3 **Because they were despised** Even here the sense is ambiguous: whether they seemed to be despised because they were not admitted to the ministry as if they were not true Judeans, or because they were burdened with the weight of a more menial ministry. And for this reason, the seven Deacons seem to have been chosen, not so that they themselves should serve everyone, but so that they might manage the turns and orders of serving, so that the Apostles would not be interrupted by similar complaints.

4 **Calling together the twelve** He explained this obscurely. For it can be taken as if the twelve disciples were called by others, which is why we translated it clearly. Now, regarding **we will be insistent**, why was a paraphrase necessary? Again in, **also a great crowd**, it is redundant, that is, there is nothing else to which "also" responds.

5 **It is not right** <note original="Οὐκ ἀρεστόν ἐστι">it is not pleasing/fit</note>, that is, **it is not pleasing**, or **it is not agreeable**, or **it is not of such a kind that it ought to please us**.

6 **Of good testimony** <note original="μαρτυρουμένους">witnessed</note>, as if you were to say, **testified of**. That is, of seen and proven integrity, about whom others testify well. Otherwise, one who gives testimony in good faith is said to be "of good testimony."

7 **Over this work** <note original="ἐπὶ τῆς χρείας ταύτης">over this need/use</note>, that is, in this use, or over this necessity; this is more pleasing to Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, an earlier humanist scholar</note>, but not so much to me, although "function" fits better.

8 **And Nicolas a newcomer** It is more correctly called a **proselyte**, as Valla notes, so that we may understand one received into the Mosaic Law—such as one who was an Antiochene by his father, but a Jew by religion. This man was later considered a Heresiarch <note>The leader of a heretical sect, specifically the Nicolaitans mentioned in Revelation</note>, although Clement, in Eusebius, diligently excuses him.

<header>ACTS CHAPTER VII.</header>
<sig>A</sig>

<margin>7</margin> They laid their hands on them. And the word of God increased, and the number of disciples in Jerusalem multiplied greatly; a large crowd of priests also became obedient to the faith. <margin>8</margin> Now Stephen, full of faith and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people. <margin>9</margin> But some rose up from the synagogue called "of the Freedmen" <note>original: Λιβερτίνων (Libertinōn). These were likely former slaves or their descendants who had gained Roman citizenship</note>, and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and those from Cilicia and Asia, debating <margin>10</margin> with Stephen. And they were not able to resist the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke. <margin>11</margin> Then they suborned men to say, "We have heard him speaking blasphemous words against Moses and God." <margin>12</margin> And they stirred up the people, the Elders, and the Scribes; and attacking him, they seized him and led him to the council <note>The Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish judicial body</note>. <margin>13</margin> They set up false witnesses who said, "This man does not stop speaking blasphemous words against this holy place and the law. <margin>14</margin> For we have heard him say that this Jesus the Nazarene will destroy this place and change the customs which Moses handed down to us." <margin>15</margin> And all who sat in the council, gazing at him, saw his face as if it were the face of an Angel. <margin>VII. 1</margin> Then the High Priest said, "Are these things so?" <margin>2</margin> And he said, "Men, brothers, and fathers, listen: The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Haran <note>original: Χαῤῥὰν (Charran)</note>, <margin>3</margin> and said to him, 'Go out from your land and from your kindred, and come into the land which I will show you.' <margin>4</margin> Then, going out from the land of the Chaldeans, he dwelt in Haran. And from there, after his father died, He moved him into this land in which you now dwell. <margin>5</margin> And He gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's breadth; yet He promised to give it to him for a possession, and to his seed after him, though he had no child. <margin>6</margin> And God spoke in this way: that his seed would be a sojourner in a foreign land, and they would enslave them and mistreat them for four hundred years. <margin>7</margin> 'And the nation which they shall serve, I will judge,' said God; 'and after these things they shall come out and serve me in this place.' <margin>8</margin> And He gave him the covenant of circumcision; and so he begot Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day; and Isaac begot Jacob, and Jacob the twelve Patriarchs. <margin>9</margin> And the Patriarchs, moved by jealousy against Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him, <margin>10</margin> and rescued him out of all his afflictions, and gave him grace and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt; and he appointed him governor over Egypt and over his whole house. <margin>11</margin> Now there came...

---

9 **And they laid hands on them**] <note>Acts 6:6</note> Rabanus <note>Rabanus Maurus, a 9th-century Carolingian scholar</note>, I believe, reminds us that this is the manner of conferring holy orders: that the people choose, and the Bishop ordains. This custom certainly persisted in the Church for a very long time, but was rightly changed due to popular disturbances.

10 **To the Spirit who spoke**] <note>Acts 6:10</note> *tō pneumati hō elalei*. This can be understood such that the meaning is: "They could not resist the Spirit who spoke." Although the other reading also holds well, where the relative pronoun *hō* is put for *hou* because of the preceding dative "to the wisdom" (*tē sophia*). Here in an ancient manuscript I found written: *on account of which they were refuted by him with all confidence*. The Spanish Edition <note>The Complutensian Polyglot, the first printed polyglot Bible</note> had the same, but it is not added in the Greek, nor in the Latin except in a few cases.

11 **Does not cease to speak words**] <note>Acts 6:13</note> *rhēmata blasphēma*, that is, blasphemous or abusive words. Although I suspect "blasphemous" was added later. For what need was there, since "against the holy place" follows? Certainly Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an early Church Father known for his preaching</note>, in explaining this passage, makes no mention of "blasphemies." Nor is it added anywhere in the older Latin manuscripts.

12 **And will change the traditions**] <note>Acts 6:14</note> *ta ethē*, that is, the customs or institutes.

1 **Are these things so?**] <note>Acts 7:1</note> *Ei ara tauta houtōs echei*, that is, "Whether these things happen to be so?"

2 **Who said**] <note>Acts 7:2</note> I ask you, what is this laziness in translating? How does "who said" connect with the preceding speech? For it preceded: "The prince of the Priests said, if these things were so." But in Greek it is *ho de ephē*, that is, "But he said."

3 **Before he lived in Haran**] <note>Acts 7:2</note> Stephen's narrative seemed to differ somewhat from the history in Genesis chapter 12, because there, mention is made of Terah, Abraham's father, and afterward it is reported that God spoke with him. Nor does the number of years quite agree. But on this matter Jerome in his *Hebrew Questions* and Augustine in *The City of God* (book 16, chapter 15) and again in *Questions on Genesis* (book 1) have untied the knot.

4 **Not a foot's breadth**] <note>Acts 7:5</note> *oude bēma podos*, that is, not even a footprint. For a "pace" (*passus*) encompasses several feet, and a pace cannot be of a single foot. Therefore, what Augustine reads in *Questions on Genesis* (book 1) is more tolerable: *not a foot's space*. Indeed, in that same place he raises the question of how it could be that he who is read to have previously bought a field near the oak of the oath now possessed not even a footprint there. He did not possess it, not even that little bit, from the divine gift, regarding the promise of which Stephen is treating there. For with money it was permitted to acquire fields anywhere.

<column-break/>

<margin>7</margin> ...of them, and when they had prayed, they also laid hands on them. And the word of God was growing, and the number of disciples in Jerusalem was multiplied greatly, and a great crowd of priests was obeying the faith. <margin>8</margin> Furthermore, Stephen, full of faith and strength, was performing great wonders and signs among the people. <margin>9</margin> But there arose certain ones from the synagogue which is called [the synagogue] of the Freedmen and the Cyrenians and the Alexandrians and those of Cilicia and Asia, disputing with Stephen. <margin>10</margin> And they were not able to resist the wisdom and the Spirit which was speaking. <margin>11</margin> Then they suborned men who said, "We heard him saying insulting words against Moses and God." <margin>12</margin> And they moved the common people and the Elders and the Scribes, and rushing upon him, they seized him and led him into the council. <margin>13</margin> And they set up false witnesses who said, "This man does not cease to speak insulting words against this holy place and the law. <margin>14</margin> For we heard him saying, 'This Jesus of Nazareth will demolish this place and will change the institutes which Moses handed down to us.'" <margin>15</margin> And gazing at him, all who sat in the council saw his face as the face of an Angel. Then the High Priest said, <margin>7:1</margin> "Are these things so?" <margin>2</margin> But he said, "Men, brothers, and fathers, listen: The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he stayed in Haran. <margin>3</margin> And he said to him, 'Go out from your land and from your kindred, and come into whatever land I shall show you.' <margin>4</margin> Then he went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. And from there, after his father was dead, He transferred him into this land in which you now dwell. <margin>5</margin> And He did not give him an inheritance in it, not even a footprint; and He promised that He would give it to him to be possessed, and to his seed after him, when he had no son. <margin>6</margin> But God spoke thus: That his seed would be a lodger in a foreign land, and that they would subject it to slavery and treat it badly for four hundred years. <margin>7</margin> 'And the nation, whichever they shall serve, I will judge,' said God: 'and after these things they shall go out and shall serve me in this place.' <margin>8</margin> And He gave him the covenant of circumcision, and so he begot Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day; and Isaac begot Jacob, and Jacob begot the <margin>D</margin> twelve Patriarchs. <margin>9</margin> And the Patriarchs, moved by envy, sold Joseph into Egypt: and God was with him, <margin>10</margin> and rescued him from all his afflictions, and gave him grace and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of the Egyptians, and appointed him governor over Egypt and over his entire house. But there came <margin>11</margin> ...

---

5 **But he spoke to him**] <note>Acts 7:6</note> *houtōs*, "But he spoke thus"; so in the Greek, and "to him" is added.

6 **Because his seed will be a neighbor**] <note>Acts 7:6</note> *Hoti estai to sperma autou paroikon*. Even if we overlook that "because" (*quia*) is misused for "that" (*quod*), and that "neighbor" (*accola*) can be of the neutral gender. Certainly "inhabitant" (*incola*) is different from "neighbor" (*accola*). For neighbors are called those nearby, like a "neighbor of the Rhine," but an inhabitant is one who is not indigenous (*autochthōn*). Although in Greek it is *paroikos*, one who, having set out from elsewhere, has a home in another place. We translate it as "lodger" (*inquilinum*), in this manner: "But God spoke thus, that his seed would be a lodger in a foreign land, and that they would subject it to slavery," etc. "An inhabitant among his descendants" was smoother. For he calls descendants "seed." Nor is it "the Lord says" in the concluding clause, but *eipen ho Theos*, that is, "God said."

7 **They will treat badly**] <note>Acts 7:6</note> *Kai kakōsousi*, that is, they will afflict or torment. **For four hundred years**. In a corrupted edition, it was read <margin>F</margin> "four hundred and thirty," and so Rabanus reads from the calculation of times. Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, 8th-century English monk and scholar</note> indicates a "Hyperbaton" <note>A figure of speech where words are transposed from their natural order</note>: he will be an inhabitant for four hundred years, so that what intervened in the middle—"and they shall subject them to slavery and treat them badly"—does not hinder the context of what precedes and follows. Although in my opinion, there is no need to resort to this Hyperbaton.

8 **And so he begot Isaac**] <note>Acts 7:8</note> The translator, unless it is a mistake, seems to have read *houtos* ("this man"), when in the Greek manuscripts it is *houtōs* ("thus," or "in this way"). If you read it as "thus," the sense is that he did not beget Isaac except as one circumcised, whereas he had fathered Ishmael uncircumcised. I suspect it happened that the Greeks, out of hatred for circumcision, changed *houtōs* ("thus") into *houtos* ("this man"). Nevertheless, the Greek manuscripts vary; Chrysostom and the Spanish Edition had *houtos*, but my manuscripts and the Aldine Edition <note>A famous early printed edition of the Greek classics and Bible from Venice</note> had *houtōs*.

9 **And Isaac Jacob**] <note>Acts 7:8</note> *ton Iakōb*, so that you understand "begot."

<header>OF THE APOSTLES. CHAPTER VII.</header>

<margin>A</margin> 11 Then a famine came over all the land of Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers found no sustenance. 12 But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent our fathers there first. 13 And on the second visit, Joseph was made known to his brothers, and Joseph’s race became known to Pharaoh. 14 Then Joseph sent and called for his father Jacob and all his relatives, seventy-five souls in all. 15 So Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, as did our fathers. 16 And they were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a price of silver from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem.

<margin>B</margin> 17 But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had sworn to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt, 18 until another king arose who did not know Joseph. 19 This king, dealing craftily with our race, oppressed our fathers, making them expose their infants so that they would not be kept alive. 20 At this time Moses was born, and he was beautiful in the sight of God; he was brought up for three months in his father’s house. 21 And when he was exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter took him up and nourished him as her own son. 22 And Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in his words and deeds.

<margin>C</margin> 23 When he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the sons of Israel. 24 And seeing one of them being wronged, he defended him and avenged the one who was oppressed by striking down the Egyptian. 25 For he supposed his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. 26 The next day he appeared to them as they were fighting and tried to reconcile them in peace, saying, "Men, you are brothers; why do you wrong one another?" 27 But the one who was wronging his neighbor pushed him away, saying, "Who appointed you a ruler and a judge over us? 28 Do you want to kill me the same way you killed the Egyptian yesterday?" 29 At this saying, Moses fled and became a stranger in the land of Midian, where he fathered two sons.

<margin>D</margin> 30 And when forty years were completed, an Angel of the Lord appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in the flame of a burning bush. 31 When Moses saw it, he wondered at the sight; and as he drew near to look, the voice of the Lord came to him, 32 saying, "I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." Moses trembled and did not dare to look. 33 Then the Lord said to him, "Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground. 34 I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send you into Egypt."

<margin>E</margin> 35 This Moses, whom they rejected, saying, "Who appointed you a ruler and a judge?"—this man God sent as both a ruler and a redeemer by the hand of the Angel who appeared to him in the bush. 36 He led them out, performing wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, and in the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years. 37 This is the Moses...

---

10 **They found no food** <note>original: *Non inveniebant cibos*</note>] The Greek word is *chortasmata* <note>original: χορτάσματα</note>. This word is derived from a term meaning "to satisfy or fatten" <note>often used for livestock fodder, emphasizing the severity of the famine where even basic sustenance was gone</note>.

11 **And on the second** <note>original: *Et in secundo*</note>] In the Greek, "And in the second" <note>original: Καὶ ἐν τῷ δευτέρῳ</note>. To render it word for word: "on the second occasion," or "when he had sent them a second time."

12 **Jacob went down with seventy-five souls** <note>original: *In septuaginta quinque animabus descendit Jacob*</note>] In Genesis chapter 46, Saint Jerome, following the Hebrew truth <note>the Masoretic Hebrew text</note>, translates it as only seventy. Nevertheless, Luke seems to have followed the authority of the Septuagint <note>the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, which was widely accepted everywhere then; either because five years were added by scribes among the Hebrews, or because he did not think the exact calculation of the number was relevant to the point being made at the time.

<margin>F</margin> 13 **Which Abraham bought for a price of silver from the sons of Hamor, the son of Shechem** <note>original: *Quod emit Abraham pretio argenti a filiis Emor filii Sychem*</note>] Jerome also noted this passage in his book to Pammachius regarding the best method of translating, as it is recorded differently in Genesis. There, we read that Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite, son of Zohar, near Hebron, for four hundred drachmas, a double cave and the field around it, and buried his wife Sarah there. In the same book, we read that later, when Jacob returned from Mesopotamia with his wives and children, he pitched his tent before Salem, a city of the Shechemites in the land of Canaan, and lived there, and bought a part of the field where he had his tents from Hamor, the father of Shechem, for a hundred lambs, and set up an altar there and called upon the God of Israel. Therefore, Abraham did not buy the cave from Hamor the father of Shechem, but from Ephron the son of Zohar; nor was he buried in Shechem, but in Hebron (which is corruptly called Arboch). Furthermore, the twelve Patriarchs

<margin>A</margin> 11 there was a famine in the whole land of Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers found no food. 12 But when Jacob heard there was grain in Egypt, he sent our fathers the first time. 13 And when he had sent them again, Joseph was recognized by his brothers, and Joseph’s lineage became known to Pharaoh. 14 Then Joseph, having sent a messenger, summoned his father Jacob and all his relatives, seventy-five souls in all. 15 And Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, as did our fathers. 16 And they were moved to Shechem and placed in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a price of silver from the sons of Hamor, the son of Shechem.

<margin>B</margin> 17 But when the time of the promise approached, which God had sworn to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt, 18 until another king arose who did not know Joseph. 19 This man, outwitting our race, oppressed our fathers so that they would expose their infants, lest they should survive. 20 At that same time Moses was born, and he was pleasing to God; he was nourished for three months in his father’s house. 21 When he was exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter took him up and nourished him for herself as a son. 22 And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was powerful in deeds and words.

<margin>C</margin> 23 But when a period of forty years was completed for him, it entered his heart to visit his brothers, the sons of Israel. 24 And when he saw one being treated unjustly, he defended him and avenged the one who was suffering by killing the Egyptian. 25 He thought his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation through his hand; but they did not understand. 26 And the following day he appeared to them while they were quarreling, and he tried to bring them to peace, saying, "Men, you are brothers; why do you hurt each other?" 27 But the one doing the injury to his neighbor pushed him away, saying, "Who appointed you a ruler and a judge over us? 28 Do you wish to kill me just as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?" 29 Moses fled at this word and became a sojourner in the land of Midian, where he fathered two sons.

<margin>D</margin> 30 And when forty years were finished, an Angel of the Lord appeared to him in the desert of Mount Sinai in the flaming fire of a bush. 31 When Moses saw it, he marveled at the vision; and as he approached to observe, the voice of the Lord came to him, 32 "I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." Moses, being terrified, did not dare to look. 33 Then the Lord said to him, "Take the sandals off your feet; for the place where you stand is holy ground. 34 I have seen, I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to rescue them."

<margin>E</margin> 35 "Now come, and I will send you into Egypt." This Moses, whom they denied, saying, "Who appointed you a ruler and a judge?"—this man, I say, God sent as a ruler and a redeemer by the hand of the Angel who appeared to him in the bush. 36 This man led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt, and in the Red Sea, and in the desert for forty years. 37 This is the Moses who said to the sons...

were not buried in Arboch <note>Hebron</note>, but in Shechem, in the field that was not bought by Abraham, but by Jacob. Jerome ties this "knot" <note>a theological or historical difficulty</note> there and does not solve it in this specific place, but he explains it elegantly in his *Hebrew Questions*.

14 **Which he had confessed** <note>original: *Quam confessus erat*</note>] In Greek, "which he had sworn" <note>original: ἧς ὤμοσεν (hēs ōmosen)</note>. The translator seems to have read "confessed" <note>original: ὁμολόγησεν (homologēsen)</note> instead.

15 **Who did not know** <note>original: *Qui non sciebat*</note>] In Greek, "who had no knowledge of" <note>original: ὃς οὐκ ᾔδει (hos ouk ēdei)</note>, meaning one who did not recognize him.

16 **Lest they be made alive** <note>original: *Ne vivificarentur*</note>] In Greek, "so that they would not be brought forth alive" <note>original: εἰς τὸ μὴ ζωογονεῖσθαι (eis to mē zōogoneisthai)</note>, meaning to the end that the newborns would not survive.

17 **Pleasing to God** <note>original: *Gratus Deo*</note>] In Greek, "beautiful to God" <note>original: ἀστεῖος τῷ Θεῷ (asteios tō Theō)</note>. Elsewhere, *asteios* means festive or sophisticated. Abulensis <note>Alonso Tostado, a 15th-century Spanish scholar</note> seems to take this word in place of *charitos*, which means graceful and also refined.

18 **He thought his brothers would understand** <note>original: *Existimabat autem intelligere fratres*</note>] Here he calls men of his own race "brothers," a term which was later transferred to Christians. Augustine, in his *Questions on Exodus*, wonders whether Moses’ act of homicide was merely a sign of his character or something to be praised, as it seems from Stephen’s speech that he did it by divine prompting.

19 **Quarreling** <note>original: *Litigantibus*</note>] In Greek it is "fighting" <note>original: μαχομένοις (machomenois)</note>. The translator rendered it correctly, nonetheless.

20 **In the fire of the flame of the bush** <note>original: *In igne flammæ rubi*</note>] The Greek has the reverse order: "in the flame of fire" <note>original: ἐν φλογὶ πυρὸς (en phlogi pyros)</note>. Regardless, the phrase persists longer than usual, not due to the nature of the Hebrew language.

21 **Seeing I have seen** <note>original: *Videns vidi*</note>] This is a Hebrew idiom <note>a figure of speech</note> meaning "I have seen attentively."

22 **And now come, I will send** <note>original: *Et nunc veni, mittam*</note>] In Greek, "And now come here" <note>original: καὶ νῦν δεῦρο (kai nyn deuro)</note>, meaning "and now come hither."

# ACTS CHAPTER VII.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>37</margin> This is the Moses who said to the sons of Israel, "The Lord your God will raise up for you a Prophet from your brothers, <note>original: "ὡς ἐμέ" — like me</note> **like me**; you shall listen to him." <margin>38</margin> This is he who was in the **assembly** in the wilderness with the Angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers; he is the one who received **living words** to give to us. <margin>39</margin> Our fathers did not wish to be obedient to him, but they rejected him, and in their hearts they turned back to Egypt, <margin>40</margin> Saying to Aaron, "Make us gods who will go before us; for this Moses, who led us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him." <margin>41</margin> And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol, and <margin>B</margin> rejoiced in the works of their own hands. <margin>42</margin> But God turned away and gave them over to worship the **host of heaven**; <note>The "host of heaven" refers to the sun, moon, and stars, which were often worshipped as deities by surrounding cultures.</note> as it is written in the book of the Prophets: "Did you offer me victims and sacrifices for forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? <margin>43</margin> You even took up the tent of **Moloch**, <note>An Ammonite god associated with child sacrifice.</note> and the star of your god **Remphan**, <note>Likely an Egyptian or Babylonian name for the planet Saturn.</note> the figures which you made to worship; and I will carry you away beyond Babylon." <margin>44</margin> The tabernacle of witness was with our fathers in the wilderness, just as He who spoke to Moses directed him to make it according to the pattern he had seen. <margin>45</margin> Our fathers, having received it in turn, brought it in with **Joshua** <note>The Greek and Latin texts use the name "Jesus," which is the same as "Joshua" in those languages. In this context, it refers to the leader who succeeded Moses.</note> into the possession of the nations, whom God drove out from the face of our fathers, until the <margin>C</margin> days of David, <margin>46</margin> Who found favor before God and asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. <margin>47</margin> But **Solomon** built a house for Him. <margin>48</margin> Yet the Most High does not dwell in temples made with hands, as the Prophet says: <margin>49</margin> "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest? <margin>50</margin> Did not my hand make all these things?" <margin>51</margin> **Stiff-necked** and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you. <margin>52</margin> Which of the Prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold the coming of the Just One, <margin>D</margin> whose betrayers and murderers you have now become. <margin>53</margin> You who received the law by the direction of Angels and did not keep it. <margin>54</margin> When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed their teeth at him. <margin>55</margin> But being full of the Holy Spirit, looking up to heaven, he saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. <margin>56</margin> And he said, "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God." <margin>57</margin> Then crying out with a loud voice, they stopped their ears and rushed at him with one accord. <margin>58</margin> And casting him out of the city, they stoned him; and the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named **Saul**. <note>This is the first mention of the man who would later become the Apostle Paul.</note> <margin>59</margin> And they stoned Stephen as he called out, saying, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." <margin>E</margin> <margin>60</margin> And falling on his knees, he cried out with a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them."

Come, or "be present now," as the verb is in the second person, not the first. For he commands Moses to be present.

23 *You shall hear as myself*] In several Greek copies, "You shall hear" <note>original: "Audietis"</note> is not written in this place. The Donatian manuscripts support the Greek reading, in which it was, "from your brothers like me." In Chrysostom, there is no mention of this clause either in the context or the commentary. Regarding the phrase "like me," Chrysostom explains it as being despised and targeted by plots; just as Herod plotted against the child Christ, so Pharaoh plotted against Moses in Egypt, and both escaped safely. It was shown above that the word "him" <note>original: "ipsum"</note> belongs to the verb "you shall hear," not to "me," which belongs to the verb "will raise up": "He will raise up for you a Prophet like me, that is, similar to me, and as if another me; you shall hear him." Though it appears the translator read "as of myself" <note>original: "ὡς ἐμαυτοῦ"</note>, unless, as is more probable, someone added this of their own.

24 *In the church*] [*in the wilderness*] In the Greek it is not "and," but "in the assembly, in the wilderness" <note>original: "ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ, ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ"</note>, that is, in the congregation, in the desert, without the conjunction, as the Latin emenders agree.

25 *To give you words of life*] Some manuscripts had "living speech" <note>original: "λόγος ζῶντα"</note>. Others had "living words" <note>original: "λόγια ζῶντα"</note>. For this is how he usually translates *logia*.

26 *Your fathers*] In both places in the Greek it is "our" <note>original: "ὑμῶν" corrected to "noſtri"</note>, that is, the first person.

27 *For to this Moses*] "For this Moses" <note>original: "ὁ γὰρ Μωσῆς οὗτος"</note>; and so the Constance manuscript has it. Though the Translator rightly changed this.

28 *Which you made to worship*] The Translator did not note the Greek figure of speech, "which you made so that you might worship them." But it is strange that the article is not added to the infinitive verb.

And he said, "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God." <margin>57</margin> But crying out with a loud voice, they stopped their ears and made an onset upon him with one accord. <margin>58</margin> And casting him out of the city, they stoned him, and the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man who was called Saul. <margin>59</margin> And they stoned Stephen as he was calling out and saying, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." <margin>60</margin> And falling on his knees, he cried out with a loud voice, "Lord, do not charge them with this [sin]."

29 *And I will transport you across Babylon*] In some copies I found "across" <note>original: "trans"</note> changed to "into" <note>original: "in"</note>. The passage is taken from the fifth chapter of the Prophet Amos. Although there, instead of "across Babylon," it reads "across Damascus," by the authority of the Hebrew truth and the Septuagint alike. Jerome excuses Stephen in this way, saying that he rendered the sense rather than the words, because the Jews were led across Damascus into Babylon, or beyond Babylon. There are those who prefer to admit that the scripture was corrupted, and "across Babylon" was written instead of "across Damascus."

30 *With the fathers*] The "with" <note>original: "cum"</note> is redundant.

31 *God speaking*] "He who was speaking" <note>original: "ὁ λαλῶν"</note>.

32 *Your fathers*] In Greek it is "our" <note>original: "ἡμῶν"</note>, as we just advised.

<margin>F</margin>
33 *But the most high not in things made by hand*] The Greek adds "temples" <note>original: "ναοῖς"</note>. And "made by hand" <note>original: "manu factis"</note> is a single word for them <note>original: "χειροποιήτοις"</note>.

34 *Stiff-necked*] In Greek this is a compound epithet, *sklerotrachēloi*, as if you were to say "hard-necked," as Pacuvius says in Quintilian, and Politian, imitating him, said "the incurve-necked cattle." Furthermore, it appears that Stephen's speech was interrupted by the shouts of the clamoring Jews. For otherwise this ending does not sufficiently respond to a beginning repeated from so far back, especially since there are many things in it which do not seem to pertain very much to what he had established.

35 *You resist*] "You fall against" <note>original: "ἀντιπίπτετε"</note>, that is, you resist.

36 *And homicides*] "Slayers" <note>original: "φονεῖς"</note>.

37 *In the disposition*] "Into dispositions" <note>original: "εἰς διαταγὰς"</note>, or "toward dispositions." Augustine, in the tenth book of *The City of God*, quotes several times "in the edicts of Angels" instead of what we read, "in the disposition of Angels."

38 *Of the power of God*] I do not find "power" <note>original: "virtutis"</note> in the Greek codex. It is only "at the right hand of God," which the older Latin versions also support.

<margin>VIII. 1</margin>
...their sin. And having said this, he fell asleep. <note>original: "ἐκοιμήθη" — a common New Testament metaphor for the death of a believer.</note> Now Saul was consenting to his execution. And on that day a great persecution arose against the church in Jerusalem; and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except for the Apostles. <margin>2</margin> Devout men buried Stephen and made a great lamentation over him. But Saul was ravaging the church, entering house after house, and dragging off both men and women, he delivered them to prison. <margin>4</margin> Therefore, those who were scattered went about, preaching the word. Now Philip went down to a city of Samaria and proclaimed Christ to them. <margin>6</margin> And the crowds with one accord paid attention to the things spoken by Philip, as they heard him and saw the signs he was performing. For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them; and many who were paralyzed and lame were healed. <margin>8</margin> And there was great joy in that city. But there was a certain man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, claiming to be someone great. <margin>10</margin> Everyone, from the least to the greatest, paid attention to him, saying, "This man is the power of God that is called Great." They paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic arts. But when they believed Philip as he preached the good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized, he stayed constantly with Philip; and seeing the signs and great miracles being performed, he was amazed. <margin>14</margin> Now when the Apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. <margin>15</margin> When they arrived, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit. <margin>16</margin> For He had not yet fallen upon any of them; they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. <margin>17</margin> Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit. <margin>18</margin> Now when Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the Apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying, "Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit." <margin>20</margin> But Peter said to him, "May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have no part or portion in this matter, for your heart is not right before God. <margin>22</margin> Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to God, if perhaps the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond...
