<margin>VIII. 1 A</margin>
...this sin to them. And when he had said this, he fell asleep. But Saul had consented to his death. And on that day a great persecution was made against the church which was in Jerusalem, and all were dispersed through the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the Apostles. <margin>3</margin> Moreover, religious men took care of Stephen’s burial and made a great mourning over him. But Saul laid waste to the church, entering into every house and dragging away men and women, delivering them into custody. <margin>4 B</margin> Therefore, those who were dispersed wandered about, announcing the word of God. Philip, meanwhile, went down to a city of Samaria and preached Christ to them. <margin>6</margin> And the multitudes attended to those things which were said by Philip, hearing with one mind and seeing the signs which he performed. For unclean spirits went out from many who were possessed by them, crying with a loud voice; <margin>8</margin> and many paralytics and lame people were healed. And there was great joy in that city. Now there was a <margin>9</margin> certain man named Simon, who previously in that city had practiced the magic art and had driven the people of Samaria out of their minds, saying that he was someone great. <margin>10</margin> To him they all listened, from the least to the greatest, saying, "This is the power of God, which is called great." And they listened to him because for a long <margin>11</margin> time he had driven them out of their minds with his magic arts. <margin>12</margin> But when they believed Philip, who brought the good news of the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, men and women alike were baptized. Then Simon himself also believed, <margin>13</margin> <margin>C</margin> and when he had been baptized, he clung to Philip; and seeing signs and wonders being done, he was struck with admiration. Now when the Apostles who were in Jerusalem heard <margin>14</margin> that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. And when they had <margin>15</margin> descended, they prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit. <margin>16</margin> For He had not yet fallen upon any of <margin>17</margin> them, but they were only baptized in the name of Christ Jesus. Then they laid hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit. Now <margin>18</margin> when Simon saw that through the imposition of the hands of the Apostles the Holy Spirit was given, he offered them money, saying, "Give also to me <margin>19</margin> this power, so that on whomever I lay hands, he may receive the Holy Spirit." But Peter said to him, "May your <margin>20</margin> <margin>D</margin> money be with you unto perdition, because you thought the gift of God could be prepared with money. You have no part nor <margin>21</margin> lot in this reason: for your heart is not right before God. Repent therefore from this malice <margin>22</margin> of yours, and ask God, if by chance the thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see you are in the gall of bitterness and... <margin>23</margin>

<meta>Catchword: and</meta>

---

<margin>*</margin> *He fell asleep in the Lord*] "In the Lord" is not added in the Greek copy; it only says *he fell asleep*. This is supported by the ancient Latin copies.
<margin>1</margin> *In the church*] <note>original: "ἐπὶ τὴν ἐκκλησίαν"</note>, that is, *against the church*, or *toward the church*.
<margin>2</margin> *They took care of Stephen*] <note>original: "Συνεκόμισαν δὲ"</note>, that is, *they together took care of*.
<margin>3</margin> *God-fearing men*] <note>original: "εὐλαβεῖς"</note>, that is, *religious* or *pious*.
<margin>4</margin> *Entering through the houses*] <note>original: "κατ’ οἴκους"</note>, that is, *house by house*, so to speak, or *through individual houses*, to show his immense zeal for destruction.
<margin>5</margin> *Therefore those who were scattered*] <note>original: "Οἱ μὲν οὖν διασπαρέντες"</note>, that is, *Therefore those indeed having been scattered*. For they were already being dispersed.
<margin>6</margin> *Into a city of Samaria*] It seems to be spoken appositively, "the city of Samaria," so that Samaria is the name not of the region, but of the city from which the whole region takes its name. This same city was called Sebaste.
<margin>7</margin> *Many of those who had unclean spirits crying with a loud voice went out*] I ask, who was it that went out? Surely not the men themselves? The Latin version did not render the Greek as it is, nor did it translate it in a way that can be understood. This is like that phrase sung in the praises of the Virgin Mother of God, "Whose humility the Lord regarding, by the Angel's announcement she conceived the Redeemer of the world." From these words, what else would a Latin-speaker understand except that the Lord became pregnant? To such an extent they think it matters nothing how we speak, provided we ourselves understand what we say. But as pertains to this passage, the Greek reads: <note>original: "Πολλῶν γὰρ τῶν ἐχόντων πνεύματα ἀκάθαρτα, βοῶντα μεγάλῃ φωνῇ ἐξήρχετο"</note>. Since these could not be rendered word-for-word, we have expressed the sense in this manner: *For unclean spirits from many who were held by them, crying with a loud voice, went out*. In two codices of the Donatians <note>Referring to manuscripts from the Donatian library or collection.</note>, this small part was not added; I think the scribe omitted it, offended by the absurdity of the language. For the Greek codices agree.
<margin>8</margin> *A magician in the city*] <note>original: "ἐν τῇ πόλει μαγεύων"</note>, that is, *practicing the magic art*.
<margin>9</margin> *To whom they listened*] This word "listened" and what follows shortly, "attended," are the same word in Greek: <note>original: "προσείχον"</note>.
<margin>10</margin> *Which is called great*] "Which is called" is not added in the Greek copy; it is simply <note>original: "ἡ δύναμις τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡ μεγάλη"</note>, that is, *the great power of God*. The translator strived to explain the force of the Greek article "the" (the great one).
<margin>11</margin> *Because that*] <note>original: "διὰ τὸ"</note>, that is, *on account of the fact that*: and yet I see this form of speech was familiar to ancient Christians, even though it signifies something quite different.
<margin>12</margin> *By his magic arts*] <note>original: "ταῖς μαγείαις"</note>, that is, *magically*, or *by magic arts*.
<margin>13</margin> *He had amazed*] <note>original: "ἐξεστακέναι αὐτοὺς"</note>, that is, *they were stunned*, and as if alienated from their minds.
<margin>14</margin> *Of the kingdom of God in the name of Jesus*] In Greek it is, *by the name*.
<margin>15</margin> *Being stunned, he wondered*] <note>original: "ἐξίστατο"</note>. The translator rendered one Greek word with two Latin ones. Laurentius <note>Laurentius Valla (1407–1457), a humanist scholar known for his philological critiques of the New Testament.</note> is somewhat annoyed at this passage, and not entirely without cause, that the translator allowed himself so much as to render the same Greek diction differently in the same passage. For what he translated a little earlier as "seducing" is <note>original: "ἐξιστῶν"</note> in Greek. What he translated as "demented" is <note>original: "ἐξεστακέναι"</note>. What he translated as "being stunned he wondered" is <note>original: "ἐξίστατο"</note>.
<margin>16</margin> *And they prayed for them*] It is doubtful whether the Apostles themselves prayed to God for them, or whether Philip and those who were with him asked the Apostles. The translators seem to follow the latter sense, although in Greek it is <note>original: "προσηύξαντο"</note>, a word the Scripture usually uses for a prayer addressed to God.
<margin>17</margin> *Upon anyone of them he had come*] <note>original: "ἦν ἐπιπεπτωκός"</note>, that is, *had slipped down*, or *fallen down*.
<margin>18</margin> *The hands of the Apostles*] <note>original: "χειρῶν"</note>, that is, *of the hands*. But the translator, offended by the repeated sound of the genitive case, varied the wording.
<margin>19</margin> *If perhaps*] <note>original: "εἴ ἄρα"</note>. He translated the expletive conjunction in his usual way as *if perhaps*.
<margin>20</margin> *In the gall of bitterness*] <note>original: "Εἰς χολὴν πικρίας"</note>, that is, *in the bile of bitterness*, meaning in bitter bile. The Magician was not angry, but the writer expressed a corrupted soul through the bitterness of bile.
<margin>21</margin> *And in the bond*] <note>original: "καὶ συνδέσμῳ"</note>, that is, *in a binding*, which is to say, in chains.

<margin>24</margin> "In the bond of iniquity I see you are." Simon answered and said, "Pray to the Lord for me, <margin>25</margin> so that nothing you have said may come upon me." And he arose and went; and behold, an Ethiopian man, a eunuch, a high official of Candace, the queen of the Ethiopians, who was over all her <margin>28</margin> treasury, who had come to worship in Jerusalem, was returning, and sitting in his chariot, <margin>29</margin> he was reading the Prophet Isaiah. And the Spirit said to Philip, "Go near, and join yourself to <margin>30</margin> this chariot." Running up, Philip heard him reading the Prophet Isaiah, and said, <margin>31</margin> "Do you understand what you are reading?" And he said, "How could I, unless someone guides me?" And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. <margin>32</margin> Now the passage of scripture which he was reading was this: "As a sheep led to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he does not open his <margin>33</margin> mouth. In his humiliation his judgment was taken away; who will describe his generation? For his life is taken from the <margin>34</margin> earth." The eunuch answered Philip and said, "I beg you, about whom does the Prophet say <margin>35</margin> this, about himself, or about someone else?" And opening his mouth, and beginning from this <margin>36</margin> scripture, Philip preached Jesus to him. As they were going along the road, they came to some water; and the eunuch says, "Look, water! What prevents me from being <margin>37</margin> baptized?" <margin>22</margin> *Which you have said* <note>original: "Quæ dixistis"</note>] *of which you have said* <note>original Greek: ὧν εἰρήκατε</note>. The relative pronoun agrees with the case of the preceding word, distinguishing it from its own verb. It should be noted that while responding to Peter alone, he uses the plural verb, *you all have said* <note>original: "εἶρήκατε"</note>. From this it is probable that what Peter warned, the others warned as well.
<margin>23</margin> *And in many regions* <note>original: "Et multis regionibus"</note>] *many villages* <note>original Greek: πολλάς τε κώμας</note>, meaning villages or rural districts. It appears the Translator read *chōras* <note>original: "χώρας" — regions</note>.
<margin>24</margin> *Against the south* <note>original: "Contra meridianam"</note>] *toward the south* <note>original Greek: κατὰ μεσημβρίαν</note>, that is, toward the midday sun, or to the south.
<margin>25</margin> *Which descends to Jerusalem* <note>original: "Quæ descendit ad Hierusalem"</note>] *descending* <note>original: "καταβαίνουσαν"</note>. This refers to how the city of Jerusalem is situated in part on Mount Zion. Some manuscripts had *Phousan*, meaning "which leads."
<margin>26</margin> *Gaza*] This is a notable city of Palestine, assigned by lot to the tribe of Judah, though it could not be held. He adds *deserted* because that old Gaza, of which Zephaniah spoke—"Gaza shall be destroyed"—was so demolished that scarcely a trace of the city remains; another was built in its place, but not on the same spot.
<margin>27</margin> *And behold a man a eunuch* <note>original: "Et ecce vir eunuchus"</note>] Jerome noted that he is called a "man" even though he is a eunuch, though these terms "to be a man" and "to be a eunuch" conflict with each other, which is why they are called "unmanned." Truly in Christ there is neither sex nor condition, but a new creation.
<margin>28</margin> *A powerful eunuch* <note>original: "Eunuchus potens"</note>] *dynast* <note>original Greek: δυνάστης</note>, that is, a magistrate or prefect. Cicero also used the Greek term, *Tetrarch and Dynast*; for he is not called the queen's eunuch, but the queen's prefect, specifically a <term>treasurer <note>original: "gazophylax"</note></term>.
<margin>29</margin> *Of Candace* <note>original: "Candacis"</note>] *Candaces* <note>original Greek: Κανδάκης</note>, that is, Candace, from the nominative Candace. This name seems to have been common to queens, on account of a certain queen of Ethiopia named Candace who was highly distinguished among that nation, just as Pharaoh and Ptolemy were for the Egyptian kings.
<margin>30</margin> *Had come to worship* <note>original: "Venerat adorare"</note>] *about to worship* <note>original Greek: προσκυνήσων</note>.
<margin>31</margin> *Do you think you understand* <note>original: "Putas ne intelligis"</note>] *Indeed* <note>original Greek: Ἆρά γε</note>. Does he, or does he not, understand what he reads?
<margin>32</margin> *And how* <note>original: "Et quomodo"</note>] "And" is not in the Greek, but only *For how could I* <note>original Greek: Πῶς γὰρ ἂν δυναίμην</note>, or *How indeed can I*. For a negation is understood: "I do not understand."
<margin>33</margin> *Should show me* <note>original: "Oſtenderet mihi"</note>] *should guide me* <note>original Greek: ὁδηγήσῃ με</note>, that is, should have led me.
<margin>34</margin> *The place of the scripture* <note>original: "Locus autem ſcripturæ"</note>] *The passage* <note>original Greek: Ἡ δὲ περιοχή</note>. Which you might call the content; we translate it as the "argument," though it could also be called the "sentence."
<margin>35</margin> *Like a sheep to the slaughter* <note>original: "Tanquam ovis ad occiſionem"</note>] This passage is in Isaiah chapter 53. Indeed, it appears this eunuch read not from a Hebrew book, but from a Greek one, because everything agrees exactly with the <term>Septuagint Edition <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note></term>. And Egypt was Greek-speaking at that time

<margin>A</margin> <margin>24</margin> "and in the bond of iniquity I see you are." Simon answering said, "Pray you for me to the Lord, that nothing of these things which you have said may happen to me." <margin>25</margin> And they indeed, having testified and spoken the word of God, returned to Jerusalem, and in many towns of the Samaritans they preached the gospel. <margin>26</margin> But an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, "Rise, and go toward the south, to the road that descends from the city of Jerusalem to the city of <margin>27</margin> Gaza: this is a desert." Philip said, <margin>37</margin> "If you believe with all your heart, it is permitted." And answering <margin>38</margin> he said, "I believe Jesus Christ to be the Son of God." <margin>E</margin> because of commerce with the Romans and, before this, with Alexander. For Jerome translates the Hebrew thus: *as a sheep he shall be led to the slaughter, and as a lamb before his shearer he shall be silent, and shall not open his mouth. From distress and from judgment he was taken away, his generation who shall describe, because he was cut off from the land of the living.* According to the Septuagint, we read in this manner: *As a sheep to the slaughter he was led, and as a lamb before its shearer is voiceless, so he does not open his mouth. In his humiliation his judgment was taken away. His generation who will tell, because his life is taken from the earth.* That is, "As a sheep to the victim he was led, and as a lamb before the shearer is mute, so he does not open his mouth. In humility his judgment was taken away. His generation who will tell, because his life is taken from the earth." Furthermore, for "is taken" <note>original: "αἴρεται"</note>, our manuscripts wrongly have "shall be taken" <note>original: "tollétur"</note>, a future tense verb, just as we read "will open" <note>original: "aperuet"</note> instead of "opens."
<margin>36</margin> *Says this* <note>original: "Dicit hoc"</note>] *he says this* <note>original Greek: λέγει τοῦτο</note>, as if he were speaking now to you, whose writings you read.
<margin>37</margin> *Who prohibits* <note>original: "Quis prohibet"</note>] *what prevents* <note>original Greek: τί κωλύει</note>, that is, what prohibits, or rather, what forbids, or what stands in the way of my being baptized.
<margin>38</margin> *Philip said | If you believe etc.* down to that place, *And he ordered the chariot to stand*, I did not find in the Greek manuscript. Although I think it was omitted by the negligence of scribes. For I found these things written in a certain Greek manuscript, but in the margin. However, in the translator Chrysostom, these are not added. Nor in the Spanish Edition. In Alcala it was added. <note>This refers to the famous textual variant of Acts 8:37, which is missing from the oldest Greek manuscripts but present in the Latin Vulgate and some later Greek texts.</note>
<margin>F</margin> <margin>39</margin> *Each* <note>original: "Uterque"</note>] *both* <note>original Greek: ἀμφότεροι</note>.
<margin>40</margin> *Philip and the eunuch*] *both Philip and the eunuch* <note>original Greek: ὅ τε Φίλιππος καὶ εὐνοῦχος</note>, with the conjunction doubled.
<margin>41</margin> *The Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip*] Rabanus in the Ordinary Gloss seems to have noted a different reading, as if the Spirit were said to have rushed upon the eunuch, and snatched Philip, but I find nothing of this kind in either the Greek or Latin manuscripts.
<margin>42</margin> *He was found in Azotus*] Who was seeking him, that he was "found" there? *He appeared* was more tolerable. For the sense is that Philip was suddenly at Azotus. This is a city of Palestine, one of the five cities of the Philistines <note>original: "Allophylorum"</note>, called by the Hebrews <term>Ashdod <note>original Hebrew: אַשְׁדּוֹד</note></term>.

### IX.
<margin>1</margin> **A** *Still breathing* <note>original: "Dhuc ſpirans"</note>] *breathing into/upon* <note>original Greek: ἐμπνέων</note>. Perhaps *ek* was changed for *eti*. In others, both are held, *still breathing into* <note>original Greek: ἔτι ἐμπνέων</note>, that is, even now breathing. But whence "of threats"? For we do not say, "he desires you," and "he is desiring of you," nor can one say "the voice does not sound human," and "the voice is not sounding of a human," and "it tastes of wine," and "it is tasting of wine." Therefore, in my judgment, it should have been translated, *breathing threats* and slaughter. And,

<margin>A</margin> <margin>2</margin> [Saul, breathing threats and murder] against the disciples of the Lord, went to the High Priest, and asked him for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way <note>original: "τῆς ὁδοῦ" (tēs hodou). And <margin>20</margin> immediately in the synagogues he preached Christ, that he was the Son of God. But all who heard <margin>21</margin> him were amazed, and said, "Is this not he who attacked those in Jerusalem who invoked this name? and did he come here for this, that he might lead them bound to the High Priests?" Saul, however, much more <margin>22</margin> increased in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived <margin>E</margin> at Damascus, affirming that this was the Christ. But when <margin>23</margin> [many days] were completed...

---

<margin>2 *against the disciples of the Lord*]</margin> It was more clearly "against the disciples of the Lord" in the original.
<margin>3 *men of this way*]</margin> "being of the way" <note>original: "τῆς ὁδοῦ ὄντας"</note>, that is, who were of that sect. For the article functions in place of a pronoun in this passage. And instead of "any" <note>original: "τινας"</note> many manuscripts had "a certain one" <note>original: "τινὰ"</note>.
<margin>4 *Men and women*]</margin> "both men and women" <note>original: "ἄνδρας τε καὶ γυναῖκας"</note>, that is, and men and women, or whether men or women.
<margin>5 *shone around*]</margin> "flashed around" <note>original: "περιήστραψεν"</note>, that is, it lightened all around, if one may speak thus. For he calls a sudden light "lightning."
<margin>6 *Saul Saul*]</margin> "Saul Saul" <note>original: "Σαούλ Σαούλ"</note>. Although Luke elsewhere calls him Saul and Paul, here he left the Hebrew voice intact, because Christ addressed him in Hebrew, as he himself later testifies. And likewise Ananias says, "Brother Saul" <note>original: "Σαοὺλ ἀδελφέ"</note>, about which we shall touch upon somewhat in the Pauline Epistles.
<margin>7 *It is hard for you*]</margin> In most Greek manuscripts this is not added in this place, since "rise" follows soon after, but rather a little lower down when this event is narrated again. It happens not infrequently that a more learned scribe adds something in the margins from elsewhere, which later a less learned one moves into the main text. Certainly Chrysostom <note>An early Christian Church Father and famous orator.</note> makes no mention of this small part in this place. However, it is also a proverb among the Pagans "to kick against the goads" <note>original: "πρὸς τὰ κέντρα λακτίζειν"</note>. It is a metaphor taken from oxen or other beasts of burden who are provoked by a goad, just as horses might kick back. In the older manuscripts, not even these words were held: "He, trembling and stunned, said, 'Lord what do you wish me to do? And the Lord said to him,'" instead it is only: "it is hard for you to kick against the goads. I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting, rise and enter, etc."
<margin>8 *who accompanied him on that journey*]</margin> "those journeying with him" <note>original: "οἱ συνοδεύοντες αὐτῷ"</note>, that is, those who were making the journey with him, or companions of the journey. The translator neither spoke in pure Latin nor matched the Greek word perfectly.
<margin>9 *They stood stupified*]</margin> "speechless" <note>original: "ἐννεοὶ"</note>, a Greek word formed from the idea that the novelty of a thing renders a man astonished.
<margin>10 *He saw nothing*]</margin> "he saw no one" <note>original: "οὐδένα ἔβλεπε"</note>, that is, he beheld no person. It appears the Translator read "seeing nothing" <note>original: "οὐδὲν βλέπων"</note>.
<margin>11 *But pulling him by the hands*]</margin> "leading him by the hand" <note>original: "χειραγωγοῦντες δὲ αὐτὸν"</note>. For why was there a need for "pulling" him, since he went willingly? And thus he translates it himself a little later: "But led by the hand by his companions."
<margin>12 *into the street called Straight*]</margin> "onto the street" <note>original: "ἐπὶ τὴν ῥύμην"</note>. "Street" <term>vicus</term> in this place is not a village or a small town, lest anyone err in this, for that is "village" <note>original: "κώμη"</note> to the Greeks, but a part of a city. For a city is divided into districts, districts into streets, and streets into houses.
<margin>13 *how many evils he has done to the saints*]</margin> "how many" <note>original: "ὅσα"</note>, that is, how many or whatsoever. Likewise a little later, "how much he must suffer for my name."
<margin>14 *And he has here*]</margin> "Here" <note>original: "ὧδε"</note> in this place is an adverb, not a pronoun, meaning "in this city."
<margin>15 *vessel of election*]</margin> "vessel" <note>original: "σκεῦος"</note>. I would have preferred "chosen instrument" <term>organum electum</term>. Although among the Ancients, all furniture was called "vessels."
<margin>16 *Brother Saul*]</margin> "Saul brother" <note>original: "Σαοὺλ ἀδελφέ"</note>, which suggests Ananias was speaking in Hebrew to his kinsman.
<margin>17 *That you may see*]</margin> "that you might receive sight" <note>original: "ὡς ἀναβλέψῃς"</note>. For he had translated the same word thus a little before.
<margin>18 *They fell from his eyes*]</margin> "fell down" <note>original: "ἀπέπεσον"</note>, they fell away.
<margin>19 *Who attacked*]</margin> In Greek a military word is used; for to the Greeks "having attacked" <note>original: "πορθήσας"</note> means to destroy and pillage a city.
<margin>20 *that he might lead them bound*]</margin> "that he might lead" <note>original: "ὡς ἀγάγῃ"</note>, that is, lead or drag away, which is what Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a Renaissance humanist and critic.</note> prefers.
<margin>21 *And he confounded*]</margin> This is not "he put to shame," as it is usually used elsewhere, but "he threw into confusion" <note>original: "συνέχυνε"</note>, that is, he stirred up and disturbed them, confirming: "that Jesus is the Christ."

This transition bridges the mission from the Samaritans to the "ends of the earth," concluding with the introduction of Saul of Tarsus, the future Apostle Paul.</meta>

<margin>A</margin> 24 <note>Greek text</note> [Simon] answered and said, "Pray to the Lord for me, so that nothing of what you have said may happen to me." 25 They, then, having testified and spoken the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem, and preached the gospel in many villages of the Samaritans. 26 An angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, "Arise and go toward the south, onto the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza; this is a desert road." 27 And he arose and went; and behold, an Ethiopian man, a eunuch, a high official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was over all her treasury, who had come to Jerusalem to worship, 28 was returning and sitting in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. 29 Then the Spirit said to Philip, "Go near and join yourself to this chariot." 30 So Philip ran to him and heard him reading the prophet Isaiah, and said, "Do you actually understand what you are reading?" 31 And he said, "How could I, unless someone guides me?" <margin>22 Which you said]</margin> <note>original: ὧν εἴρηκας (hōn eirēkas)</note>. The relative pronoun matches the case of the preceding word, even though it is distant from its verb. We have noted that while they respond to Peter alone, he uses a plural verb, "disciples." From this, it is probable that what Peter advised, the others also agreed to.

<margin>23 And many regions]</margin> <note>original: πολλὰς τε κώμας (pollas te kōmas)</note>, villages or rural districts. It appears the Translator read "villages."

<margin>24 Toward the south]</margin> <note>original: κατὰ μεσημβρίαν (kata mesēmbrian)</note>, that is, toward the midday sun, or to the south.

<margin>25 Which descends from Jerusalem]</margin> <note>original: καταβαίνουσαν (katabainousan)</note>. Because the city of Jerusalem is situated in part on Mount Sion. Some manuscripts had "Philip," that is, "he who speaks."

<margin>26 Gaza]</margin> This is a famous city of Palestine, assigned as the lot of the tribe of Judah, though it could not be held. He adds "desert," because that ancient Gaza, of which Zephaniah spoke saying "Gaza shall be forsaken," was so destroyed that hardly a trace of the city remains; another was built near it, but not in the same place.

<margin>27 And behold an Ethiopian man]</margin> Jerome noted that he is called a "man" who is a "eunuch," though these terms conflict with each other—being a man and being a eunuch—which is why they are called "un-manned." Truly, in Christ there is neither sex nor condition, but a new creature.

<margin>28 A powerful eunuch]</margin> <note>original: δυνάστης (dynastēs)</note>, that is, a magistrate or prefect. Cicero also used this Greek word, "Tetrarchs and Dynasts." For he is not called the Queen's eunuch, but the Queen's prefect, surely the treasurer <note>original: gazophylax</note>.

<margin>29 Candace's]</margin> <note>original: Κανδάκης (Kandakēs)</note>, that is, Candace, from the nominative Candace. This name seems to have been common to their queens, because of a certain Queen Candace of Ethiopia who served that nation very well; just as among the Egyptians, "Pharaoh" and "Ptolemy" were used for kings.

<margin>30 Had come to worship]</margin> <note>original: προσκυνήσων (proskynēsōn)</note>, that is, about to worship.

<margin>31 Do you think you understand]</margin> <note>original: Ἆρά γε (Ara ge)</note>. "Do you indeed," or "Can it be," or "Do you perhaps understand what you read?"

<margin>32 And how]</margin> The word "yet" is not in the Greek, but only "How indeed could I?" <note>original: Πῶς γὰρ ἂν δυναίμην (Pōs gar an dynaimēn)</note>. The negation is understood: "I do not understand."

<margin>33 Show me]</margin> <note>original: ὁδηγήσῃ με (hodēgēsē me)</note>, that is, "led me."

<margin>34 The passage of scripture]</margin> <note>original: Ἡ δὲ περιοχὴ (Hē de periochē)</note>. Which you could call the "contents": we translated it as "the theme" <note>original: argumentum</note>, but it could also be called the "sentence."

<margin>35 As a sheep to the slaughter]</margin> This passage is in Isaiah chapter 53. Indeed, it appears this eunuch was not reading from a Hebrew book, but from a Greek one, because everything agrees exactly with the Septuagint Edition <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>. And Egypt at that time was becoming "Hellenized" <note>Greek-speaking</note> due to trade with the Romans, and before that with Alexander.
<column-break/>
For in Hebrew, Jerome translates it this way: "As a sheep to the slaughter he shall be led, and like a lamb before its shearer he shall be silent, and shall not open his mouth. From distress and from judgment he was taken away; his generation who shall tell, because he was cut off from the land of the living?" According to the Septuagint, we read it in this manner: <note>original Greek: Ὡς πρόβατον... ἡ ζωὴ αὐτοῦ</note>. That is: "As a sheep to the slaughter he was led, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. In his humility his judgment was taken away. His generation who shall declare, because his life is taken from the earth." Furthermore, for "is taken" <note>original: αἴρεται (airetai)</note>, our manuscripts wrongly have "shall be taken," a future tense verb, just as we read "shall open" for "opens."

<margin>36 Says this]</margin> <note>original: λέγει τοῦτο (legei touto)</note>, that is, "speaks this," as if he is speaking now to you, whose writings you read.

<margin>37 Who prohibits]</margin> <note>original: τί κωλύει (ti kōlyei)</note>, that is, "what prohibits," or rather, "what forbids," or "what stands in the way of me being baptized."

<margin>38 Philip said]</margin> "If you believe," etc., up to that place, "And he ordered the chariot to stand," I did not find in the Greek manuscript. Although I think it was omitted by the negligence of scribes. For I found these things written in a certain Greek manuscript, but in the margin. Otherwise, these are not added in the translator Chrysostom. Nor in the Spanish Edition. It was added in the Alcine edition.

<margin>39 Both]</margin> <note>original: ἀμφότεροι (amphoteroi)</note>, that is, "both."

<margin>40 Philip and the eunuch]</margin> <note>original: ὅ τε Φίλιππος καὶ εὐνοῦχος (ho te Philippos kai eunouchos)</note>, that is, "both Philip and the eunuch," with the conjunction doubled.

<margin>41 The Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip]</margin> Rabanus in the *Ordinary Gloss* seems to have noted a different reading, as if the Spirit was said to have rushed upon the eunuch, and snatched Philip; but I find nothing of this kind in either the Greek or Latin manuscripts.

<margin>42 Was found in Azotus]</margin> Who was looking for him, that he should be "found" there? "He appeared" or "He was discovered" would be more tolerable. For the sense is that Philip was suddenly at Azotus. That is a city of Palestine, one of the five cities of the "foreigners" <note>Philistines</note>, called by the Hebrews <term>Ashdod</term> <note>original: אשדוד</note>.

Still breathing] <note>original: ἐμπνέων (empneōn)</note>. Perhaps the prefix "en" was changed from "epi." In others, it is "under-breathing" or "breathing in," that is, still breathing. But why "of threats"? For we do not say "he desires of you" and "he is desiring of you," nor can we say "the voice does not sound of a man," and "the voice is not sounding of a man," and "it tastes of wine," and "it is tasting of wine." Therefore, in my judgment, it should have been translated, "breathing threats and slaughter." And,

<meta>This page continues the narrative from the previous chapter, moving from Philip’s encounter with the Ethiopian official to the pivotal transformation of Saul of Tarsus. While the previous page ended with Philip's ministry, we now transition to the famous "Damascus Road" experience, where the primary persecutor of the early Church becomes its most famous apostle.</meta>

### THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES. CHAPTER IX.

<margin>A</margin>
2 ...[Saul, still breathing threats and murder against] the disciples of the Lord, went to the High Priest 3 and asked him for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, whether men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. As he journeyed, it happened that he was approaching Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him. 4 And falling to the earth, he heard a voice saying to him, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" 5 He said, "Who are you, Lord?" And the Lord said, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting; it is hard for you to kick against the goads." 6 Trembling and astonished, he said, "Lord, what do you want me to do?" And the Lord said to him, "Arise, and enter the city, and it will be told to you what you must
<margin>B</margin>
7 do." The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. 8 Saul rose from the ground; and though his eyes were open, he saw no one; so, leading him by the hand, they brought him into Damascus. 9 For three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank. 10 Now there was a certain disciple in Damascus named Ananias, and the Lord said to him in a vision, "Ananias." 11 And he said, "Here I am, Lord." And the Lord said to him, "Arise and go to the street called Straight, and look in the house of Judas for a man named Saul of Tarsus; for behold, he is praying." 12 And [Saul]
<margin>C</margin>
saw in a vision a man named Ananias coming in and laying a hand on him so that he might regain his sight. 13 But Ananias answered, "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints in Jerusalem. 14 And here he has authority from the High Priests to bind all who call upon your name." 15 But the Lord said to him, "Go, for this man is a chosen instrument <note>original: "vas electionis" / "skeuos ekloges"</note> of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel. 16 For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name." 17 So Ananias departed and entered the house, and laying his hands on him, he said, "Saul,
<margin>D</margin>
brother, the Lord has sent me—the one who appeared to you on the road as you were coming—so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit." 18 And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight; then he rose and was baptized. 19 And after taking food, he was strengthened. For several days Saul remained with the disciples who were in Damascus. 20 And immediately in the synagogues he preached Christ, that he is the Son of God. 21 All who heard him were amazed and said, "Is this not the man who ravaged those in Jerusalem who call upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the High Priests?" 22 But Saul grew even stronger and confounded the Jews who lived in
<margin>E</margin>
23 Damascus, proving that this man is the Christ. When many days had passed, they conspired—

<column-break/>

2 **Against the disciples of the Lord** <note>original: "In discipulos Domini"</note> It would be clearer to say *against* the disciples of the Lord.
3 **Men of this way** <note>original: "Hujus viae viros"</note> <gloss>Those who were of that sect.</gloss> The article here functions in place of a pronoun. Some other copies used the word "life" instead of "way."
4 **Men and women** <note>original: "Viros ac mulieres"</note> That is, both men and women, or whether men or women.
5 **Flashed around** <note>original: "Circumfulfit"</note> <gloss>Shone like lightning.</gloss> He calls the sudden light a "lightning flash."
6 **Saul, Saul** <note>original: "Saulo Saule"</note> Even though Luke calls him Saul or Paul elsewhere, he leaves the Hebrew voice intact here because Christ addressed him in Hebrew <note>specifically Aramaic, the common Hebrew dialect of the time</note>, as Paul himself later testifies. Ananias also says, "Saul, brother," a point we will touch upon in the Pauline Epistles.
7 **It is hard for you** <note>original: "Durum est tibi"</note> In most Greek manuscripts, this phrase is not added here but appears later when the story is retold. It often happens that scribes add more learned details in the margins which later copyists insert into the main text. Certainly, Chrysostom <note>an early Church Father</note> makes no mention of this part here. However, "To kick against the goads" was a common proverb even among the pagans. It is an image taken from oxen or other pack animals who, when poked with a sharp stick <term>goad: a spiked stick used to drive cattle</term>, kick back and only hurt themselves more. In older manuscripts, the text read: "And trembling and astonished he said, 'Lord, what do you want me to do?' and the Lord said to him only: 'I am Jesus whom you persecute, arise and enter...'"
8 **Who accompanied him** <note>original: "Qui comitabantur eum illo"</note> Those who made the journey with him. The translator <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate</note> neither spoke in good Latin nor matched the Greek word precisely.

---

9 **They stood stupefied** <note>original: "Stabant stupefacti"</note> The Greek word *enneoi* describes someone who is struck dumb by the novelty of an event.
10 **He saw nothing** <note>original: "Nihil videbat"</note> The Greek says *he saw no one*. It appears the previous translator misread "no one" as "nothing."
11 **Leading him by the hand** <note>original: "Ad manus autem illum trahentes"</note> Why would there be a need for "dragging" <note>the Latin word "trahentes" implies dragging</note> when he went willingly? Later, the same translator correctly uses "led by the hand."
12 **To the street called Straight** <note>original: "In vicum qui vocatur Rectus"</note> "Vicus" here does not mean a village or small town, but a "street" or "ward" within the city. A city is divided into districts, districts into streets, and streets into houses.
13 **How much evil he has done** <note>original: "Quanta mala fecerit"</note> Meaning "how many" or "whatever" evils.
14 **And here he has** <note>original: "Et hic habet"</note> In this context, the word *hic* is an adverb meaning "in this city," not a pronoun.
15 **Chosen vessel** <note>original: "Vas electionis"</note> I would have preferred "chosen instrument." Though the ancients used the word "vessel" for all sorts of equipment or tools.
16 **Saul, brother** <note>original: "Saule frater"</note> It is consistent that Ananias would have spoken in Hebrew.
17 **That you may see** <note>original: "Ut videas"</note> That is, "so that you may regain your sight." The translator used this same phrasing just a moment before.
18 **Fell from his eyes** <note>original: "Ceciderunt ab oculis ejus"</note> They dropped away.
19 **Who ravaged** <note>original: "Qui expugnabat"</note> The Greek uses a military term, *porthein*, which means to sack or depopulate a city.
20 **To bring them bound** <note>original: "Ut vinctos illos duceret"</note> Meaning to lead or drag them away.
21 **And he confounded** <note>original: "Et confundebat"</note> This doesn't mean "shamed" here, but rather "unsettled" or "thoroughly disturbed" the Jews by proving Jesus was the Messiah.

The annotations provide philological insights into the Greek text, particularly correcting the Latin Vulgate's phrasing regarding the "chosen instrument" and the proverb of "kicking against the goads."</summary>

the earth, and the sea, and everything in 
<margin>25</margin> them, Who by the mouth of your servant David said, 'Why 
<margin>26</margin> did the nations rage, and the peoples plot in vain? The

<margin>27</margin> For truly they were gathered together against your holy

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>6</margin> **Who was rejected** <note>original: "Qui reprobatus est"</note> The Greek term is *exouthenētheis*, which means one who was despised or held as nothing.
<margin>7</margin> **Given to men** <note>original: "Datum hominibus"</note> The Greek is *to dedomenon en anthrōpois*, meaning that which was given among men—that is, what happened to be heard among men. For "Jesus" is the name of a man. He adds "among men" because of Moses, in whom the Jews placed their trust.
<margin>8</margin> **Boldness of Peter** <note>original: "Petri constantiam"</note> The Greek is *Petrou parrēsian*, meaning Peter’s audacity or freedom in speaking.
<margin>9</margin> **And they recognized them** <note>original: "Et cognofcebant eos"</note> The Latin translator would have more aptly expressed the Greek by saying "they recognized" (*agnoverunt*) for the Greek *epeginnōskon*.
<margin>10</margin> **The man also** <note>original: "Hominem quoque"</note> The Greek is *ton de anthrōpon*, meaning "but the man." The translator seems to have read it as *ton te anthrōpon* ("and the man").
<margin>11</margin> **Since indeed a notable sign was done** <note>original: "Quoniam quidem notum signum factum est"</note> It would have been clearer if he had translated it this way: "For that a manifest sign has been done through them is plain to all dwelling in Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it." For "notable" (*gnōston*) refers to the "sign" (*sēmeion*), and "evident" (*phaneron*) refers to "all," and those things which follow.
<margin>12</margin> **Lest it be further spread among the people** <note>original: "Ne amplius divulgetur in populum"</note> The Greek is *dianemēthē*. I would have preferred "creep" <note>original: "serpat"</note>, as it is translated elsewhere: "that it may creep like a cancer" in 2 Timothy 2.
<margin>13</margin> **Let us threaten them** <note>original: "Comminemur eis"</note> The Greek is *apeilē apeilēsōmetha*, meaning "by threatening let us threaten them." This is done in the Hebrew manner <note>a "Hebraism," where a verb is doubled for emphasis</note>, by which they signify a vehement and sharp warning.
<margin>14</margin> **In this name** <note>original: "In nomine hoc"</note> This phrase is frequently encountered by us in the Sacred Books. Sometimes the preposition "in" is not unsuitably translated as "through," and sometimes it is better omitted. Here, since neither seemed to fit perfectly, we left it as it was, asking the reader to grant us the same indulgence we seek in a few other places. "Under the name" does not please some, because it seems to sound like a fiction, though that is not always the case.
<margin>15</margin> **And calling them, they denounced** <note>original: "Et vocantes eos denunciaverunt"</note> How do we "denounce" someone who is present? Therefore, for the Greek *parēngeilan*, I would have preferred "commanded." For it is well known that *parangeliamata* are called "commands." And so he translates it himself in the very next chapter: "by commanding we commanded."
<margin>16</margin> **Lest they should speak at all** <note>original: "Ne omnino loquerentur"</note> The Greek is *mē phthengesthai*, which is more than "not to speak"—it is as if you said, "not even to make a peep" or utter any sound concerning Jesus.
<margin>17</margin> **If it is just** <note>original: "Si justum est"</note> The Greek is *Ei dikaion esti*, meaning "whether it be just" or "is it just." And presently,
<margin>18</margin> **But they, threatening** <note>original: "At illi comminantes"</note> The Greek is *proshapeilēsamenoi*, meaning with threats added. For previously they had only given a command. Since they had made little progress that way, they added threats of capital punishment unless they obeyed.
<margin>19</margin> **They glorified that which had been done** <note>original: "Glorificabant id quod factum fuerat"</note> The Greek is *edoxazon ton Theon epi tō gegonoti*, that is, they glorified God for that which had been done. Otherwise, it seems the same thing is said twice: "that which had been done" in "that which had happened."
<margin>20</margin> **How many** <note>original: "Quanta"</note> The Greek is *hosa*, meaning "whatever"; some might have said *posa*.
<margin>C</margin>
<margin>21</margin> **Lord, you who made** <note>original: "Domine tu qui fecisti"</note> In the Greek it is a bit more: *Despota sy ho Theos*, meaning "Lord, you who are God," or "you are that God." For unless you understand the verb "to be," the speech

<margin>B</margin>
is not complete. "You who made" <note>original: "sy ho Theos ho poiēsas"</note> means "You are that God who made."
<margin>22</margin> **Who by the spirit** <note>original: "Qui spiritu"</note> In this place also the Greek differs somewhat. 
<margin>D</margin>
For they have it thus: *Ho dia stomatos Dauid paidos sou*, meaning "Who by the mouth of David your servant."
<margin>23</margin> **Why did the nations rage** <note>original: "Quare fremuerunt gentes"</note> These two verses he rendered word-for-word according to the Septuagint Edition. Furthermore, that word *synēchthēsan* is not simply "to come together," but to be gathered into an assembly or council, and as if to conspire, which the Hebrew word *nosdu* also indicates. Likewise, that word "raged" <note>original: "fremuerunt"</note>, Greek *ephryaxan*, is in Hebrew *ragshu*, which signifies that they were massed together with tumult and roaring.
<margin>24</margin> **Truly in this city** <note>original: "Vere in civitate ista"</note> I do not find "in this city" in the Greek manuscript, and it seems to have been added by some translator. **Against your holy servant Jesus.** Lorenzo Valla <note>a famous 15th-century humanist scholar</note> is angry in this place because the translator assigned the title of "servant" to Jesus, the Son of God. Although "puer" among the Latins can signify a son, it does so infrequently; more frequently it means a servant, and most frequently a person of young age. But when Christ brings salvation, he was not a "boy" <note>original: "puer"</note>. Indeed, he saved us by his death, of 
<margin>E</margin>
which he speaks here. And perhaps the title of "servant" does not fit him, even if he obeyed and was subject to the Father according to his assumed humanity—but as a son, not as a servant. Therefore, one should have feared to use "son" <note>Greek: *paida*</note> here, not "boy" or "servant." I am not unaware that he was "as a servant," and like a wicked servant was afflicted with whips and the cross. For as he called David a "servant" <note>original: *puerum*</note> just before, that is, a minister of God, he does so correctly. If the translator had never translated *paida* as "son," it might seem he held the opinion that it was not permitted to translate it otherwise. Now, since he has translated it that way many times elsewhere, and even shortly after this, it is a wonder why he varied it in this place. Certainly, Ambrose <note>4th-century Bishop of Milan</note>, citing this passage in the second book of *The Calling of the Nations*, chapter five, reads "son" <note>original: *filium*</note>, not "servant," lest anyone stir up a terrible tragedy against me. 
<margin>F</margin>
Furthermore, Saint Hilary <note>Bishop of Poitiers</note> in the *Commentaries* in which he explains this Psalm, reads "son," not "servant." And again in the eleventh book on the *Trinity*, and Cassiodorus, who is more recent than all these. And Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, the "Golden-Mouthed" preacher</note>, explaining this passage from the Epistle to the Hebrews, "Your throne, O Lord," denies that the Son is called a "servant," since he called the Angels "ministers." Nor does it escape me that Jerome <note>translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> contends in many places that the term "servant" is applicable to Christ. But in the meantime, I do not see why he labors so much in this, that Christ should somewhere be called "servant," or why those others shrink so much from the term "servant" being attributed to Jesus as a man. For if a servant is one who obeys the just commands of the Lord in good faith, why should Christ as a man not be called a "servant"? But if a servant is one who, compelled by evil, does his duty, the title of servant does not fit Christ. Although I reviewed Valla's opinion here in the first edition, nevertheless this passage was sharply attacked by two people, to one of whom he responded in a booklet published for this very purpose. The other, not content with having charged ignorance of the Sacred Scriptures, slandered...

<margin>E</margin> 1 *Sold a field]* <note>original: "ἐπώλησε κτῆμα"</note> *he sold a possession*, which means a house or an estate.
2 *And he defrauded from the price]* <note>original: "ἐνοσφίσατο"</note> that is, *he set aside and tore away*, which the Translator nevertheless correctly rendered.
3 *Bringing a certain part]* <note>original: "ἐνέγκας μέρος τι"</note> that is, *a certain part having been brought*. "To Ananias": these two words are found neither among the Greek texts nor in the ancient Latin manuscripts.
4 *Why did he tempt]* <note>original: "διὰ τί ἐπλήρωσεν"</note> that is, *he filled*. This is how Augustine reads it in his small book *On the Barbarian Time*, chapter three. Someone or other in the *Ordinary Gloss* <note>The standard medieval commentary on the Bible.</note> noted a different reading among the Greeks here. Chrysostom reads *filled*. I suspect the Translator read <note>original: "ἐπείρασεν"</note> *he tempted*.
5 *That you should lie]* Again, he translates the Greek figure, *that you should lie to the Holy Spirit*. In Greek, it is the Holy Spirit in the accusative. Either because the Greeks speak this way—"I lie you," just as they say "I evangelize you" and "I do you good"—or because the sense is that he lies to the Holy Spirit who falsely pretends and confesses that which others were doing by the instinct of the Holy Spirit. For one lies not only who speaks a falsehood, but also who feigns; as in the phrase, "Creusa having feigned her face," and "the brass lies to be gold." Augustine, in the book I just cited, reads *to lie before the Holy Spirit*, as if the Greek had been <note>original: "πρὸς τὸ Πνεῦμα"</note>. Chrysostom indeed reads it as we do, yet the ambiguity of the reading is not resolved by his interpretation.
6 *Remaining to you, did it not remain?]* Again, after the manner of the Hebrews, he expressed emphasis by doubling the word: <note>original: "μένον ἔμενε"</note>, that is, *it truly and entirely remained*, with no one compelling him in any way. Moreover, Peter accuses him in two stages. First, it remained when no one compelled him to sell. Secondly, if it pleased him to sell, no one compelled him to bring the price.
7 *And having been sold, it was in your power]* <note>original: "καὶ πραθέν"</note>. The Translator rendered different Greek words with the same Latin word. For them, <note>original: "κτῆμα"</note> is a possession, and <note>original: "χωρίου"</note> is an estate or a villa; here he translates both as "field." And yet, forgetting himself, he added the neuter *having been sold* <note>original: "venundatum"</note> to match the Greek word, forgetting the Latin grammar where he ought to have said the masculine *sold* <note>original: "venundatus"</note> to agree with "field."
8 *The space of three hours]* <note>original: "διάστημα"</note>, that is, *an interval*.

And now, Lord, look upon their threats, and grant to your servants that they may speak your word with all confidence, <margin>30</margin> by stretching out your hand for this: that healing and signs and wonders may be performed through the name of your holy <margin>31</margin> son Jesus. <margin>V. 1</margin> <margin>C</margin> But a certain man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, had sold a possession, <margin>2</margin> and defrauded from the price, his wife also being aware, and having brought a certain part, he placed it at the feet of the Apostles. But Peter said, "Ananias, <margin>3</margin> why has Satan filled your heart, that you should lie to the Holy Spirit, and defraud from the price of the field? <margin>4</margin> Did it not entirely remain to you, and when sold was it not in your power? Why have you set this thing in your heart? You have not lied to men, but to God." Hearing <margin>5</margin> these words, Ananias collapsed and expired: and great fear arose over all who heard these things. And the young men rising up removed him, and having carried <margin>6</margin> him out, they buried him. There intervened moreover a space of about <margin>7</margin> three hours, and his wife, not knowing what...

<margin>D</margin> [An opponent] mocks me as if I agree with Apollinaris <note>A 4th-century heretic who denied that Jesus had a human soul.</note>, who would take something away from human nature. For I guess that is what he feels. Now he gathers an even more atrocious suspicion from these words of mine: *Even if he obeyed and was subject to the Father, he was so as a son, not as a servant*, as if I agree with Arius <note>A 4th-century heretic who taught that the Son was not equal to the Father.</note> that the Son is not equal to the Father. What is more impudent than this slander? He who confesses the Son is subject to the Father, does he not confess the man? He is called purely the Son of God, according to both natures. Nor do they deny the Son of God is a servant in any other sense than that in which Christ denies his disciples should be called *servants*, but rather *friends*. If the third title is rightly taken away from the Apostles, is it a heresy not to admit it in Christ? And are men not ashamed, who seem to themselves absolutely learned, to produce such nonsense in writing, and to inflict a twin heresy out of the most vain dreams? And he promises that he will point out very many such dangerous errors. If this is how he treats theological writings, it is much better to grow old in Poetry or Philosophy, or to waste time playing a pipe with a stick. Finally, the issue here is not whether the name of "servant" *can* be attributed to Christ, but whether it *is* customarily attributed in the Holy Scriptures.

<margin>25 Herod & Pontius Pilate]</margin> <note>original: "Ἡρώδης τε καὶ Πόντιος Πιλᾶτος"</note>. To the Greeks, there is a double conjunction: *both Herod and Pontius Pilate*, or *Herod together with Pontius Pilate*. Paul also seems to delight in this doubling. And altogether there is some affinity in the style of speech in both.
<margin>26 And to the peoples of Israel]</margin> Some manuscripts had <note>original: "καὶ λαοῖς"</note>, *and to the peoples*; *and peoples* is more approved. For in interpreting the Psalm, he refers the "nations" to the cohorts of Herod and Pilate, and the "peoples" to the Jews.
<margin>27 To do what your hand]</margin> The Translator rendered the Greek figure, which he would have avoided if he had said *that they might do*.
<margin>28 Decreed to be done]</margin> <note>original: "προώρισε γενέσθαι"</note>, that is, *he had pre-established that they should happen*, or *had pre-defined future things*.
<margin>29 In that you extend your hand]</margin> <note>original: "Ἐν τῷ τὴν χεῖρά σου ἐκτείνειν σε"</note>, that is, *in extending your hand*. For the sense is to be thus: that they may speak the word of God freely and fearlessly among the people, if He stretches out His hand and helps the speakers, with the power of signs added.
<margin>30 To healings]</margin> <note>original: "εἰς ἴασιν"</note>, that is, *to healing*.
<margin>31 Of your son Jesus]</margin> <note>original: "παιδός σου"</note>. The Greek word is the same as when he just translated "child," I know not by what plan he affects this variety.
<margin>32 With boldness]</margin> <note>original: "μετὰ παῤῥησίας"</note>, that is, *boldly* and *freely*.
<margin>33 Moreover of the multitude of believers]</margin> <note>original: "τῶν πιστευσάντων"</note>, that is, *of those who had believed*. Augustine, bringing up this passage in the eighth Letter to Letus, adds two words: "It is said," he says, "There was for them in God one heart and one soul," though the style of this Letter tastes more of Paulinus than of Augustine.
<margin>34 Before the feet]</margin> <note>original: "παρὰ τοὺς πόδας"</note>, that is, *beside the feet*.
<margin>35 Joses]</note> <note>original: "Ἰωσῆς"</note>, that is, *Joses*.
<margin>36 Which is son of consolation]</margin> Barnabas. For it is a Hebrew word, <margin>D</margin> <gloss>filius [son] is "Bar", and besides other things, "Naba" signifies to be refreshed and cooled and consoled. Even if Jerome interprets it variously as "son of the prophet," "son of the coming one," or "son of consolation." This last one means it has pleased more people. There is one who thinks this word was corrupted in Paul, and that one should read "Bar-nabum" for Barnabas, and that the word is Syrian, not Hebrew. Since I do not dare to guess this in such a consensus of manuscripts, I have no intention to sharply refute it. However, he wanted to have this honor for the piety of that man, who sincerely offered his own, so that he might make more detestable the example of the division that follows. In some Greek manuscripts, there was added <unclear>translated</unclear>, that is, *which is interpreted*, or, *he who interprets*.</gloss>

9 <note>Peter answered her] original: "'Απεκρίθη δὲ αὐτῇ" (Respondit autem ei). That is, "He responded," even though no question had been asked of him. I have found it written this way in several of the older Latin manuscripts.</note>
10 <note>You agreed] original: "Τί ὅτι συνεφωνήθη" (Convenit vobis). That is, "Why was it conspired by you?" and "You consented in this to test the Spirit of the Lord," or "Why was there this conspiracy among you?"</note>
11 <note>Beside her husband] original: "πρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα" (Ad virum suum). Why not rather "next to" the husband?</note>
12 <note>More however was the number of believers in the Lord increased] The Greek is slightly different: original: "Μᾶλλον δὲ προσετίθεντο πιστεύοντες τῷ Κυρίῳ, πλήθη ἀνδρῶν τε καὶ γυναικῶν" (Magis autem apponebantur credentes Domino, multitudines virorumque & mulierum). To translate word for word: "More believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women." Furthermore, the phrase "So that they carried out the sick into the streets" connects somewhat roughly with what precedes, unless we understand that the fame of the Apostles grew along with the crowd. I wish those who are entirely addicted to the comforts of this world—who either despise or even mock the poverty and humility of Christ—would read these things attentively. What kingdom, what wealth, what power can compare with this glory of the Apostles? Everything in Christ was far more splendid than this world can provide. Yet it is given in another way, and no one shares in it unless they have devoted themselves to this kingdom with their whole heart, despising all other things. I myself witnessed first at Bologna, and then at Rome, the Roman Pontiff Julius II, the second of that name, leading most splendid triumphs—triumphs exactly like those of Pompey or Caesar. But what were those compared to the majesty of Peter? He converted the whole world into a miracle of himself, not by arms, not by troops, not by machines, not by gold, but by faith alone. And that same magnificence would follow the successors of the Apostles today, if they were equal in spirit.</note>

<column-break/>

13 <note>They carried out the sick] original: "ἐκφέρειν" (Exierent infirmos). That is, "to lead out" or "to export." For it is inhumane to "eject" or "cast out" (ejicere). The Greek word is not *ekballein*, which would have forced such a translation.</note>
14 <note>On mats] original: "καὶ κραββάτων" (In grabatis). This is a Greek word, though it has been adopted among the Latins with two letters changed.</note>
15 <note>Any of them] original: "τινὰ αὐτῶν" (Quemquam illorum). More correctly in Latin: "aliquem." And "they were freed from their infirmities." This is not in the Greek manuscripts, but appears to have been added by someone who wished to provide an interpretation. The oldest codices of Saint Donatian <note>A famous manuscript from Bruges consulted by Erasmus</note> support the Greek reading.</note>
16 <note>And all the elders] original: "πᾶν γερουσίαν" (Et omnes feniores). That is, the order or senate of the elders.</note>
17 <note>They were perplexed about them] original: "διηπόρουν" (Ambigebant de illis). This word says something more: to be completely perplexed, of an uncertain mind, and helpless in the face of conflict.</note>
18 <note>By commanding we commanded] original: "Οὐ παραγγελίᾳ παρηγγείλαμεν" (Præcipiendo præcepimus). That is, "Did we not command with a command?" This means to command sharply, as was said before, "to threaten with threats."</note>
19 <note>It is necessary to obey God] original: "πειθαρχεῖν" (Obedire oportet Deo). This word properly means to obey a Prince or a Magistrate; it is a compound word from "to obey" <note>peitho</note> and "prince" <note>archon</note>. And a little later: "to those obeying him."</note>
20 <note>Whom you killed] original: "διεχειρίσασθε" (Quem vos interemistis). Which means to kill with violent hands. For the Greek word is derived from this. We are "done away with" (interemimur) even when we are punished justly and deservedly.</note>
21 <note>Prince and Savior] original: "Ἀρχηγὸν" (Principem & Salvatorem). A leader and an author. Although I do not find fault with what the Translator rendered.</note>

<margin>22 And we are witnesses]</margin> The Greeks add "of him" <note>original: "αὐτοῦ"</note>, which the Latin could have translated in the dative as "to him." Nor is it simply "and the Holy Spirit," but "and indeed the Holy Spirit" <note>original: "καὶ τὸ Πνεῦμα δὲ τὸ ἅγιον"</note>, which acts as a correction of the previous statement. It is as if he were saying: we are not so much witnesses to him as the Holy Spirit himself is, by whose power these things are done.
<margin>23 And they thought to kill them]</margin> "They consulted" <note>original: "ἐβουλεύοντο"</note>, that is, they deliberated on how to kill them. The translator read "they wanted" <note>original: "βούλοντο"</note>, or certainly dreamed it.
<margin>24 Men of Israel]</margin> In Greek, it refers to the Apostles, not "men." Nor is it "to be done," but "to do" or "to put" <note>original: "ποιῆσαι"</note>, meaning to send them outside.
<margin>25 Theudas arose]</margin> He translates this elegantly as "exstitit" <note>stepped forth</note> for "arose" <note>original: "ἀνέστη"</note>. The Greek codices have "Theudas" <note>original: "Θευδᾶς"</note>, not "Theodas." Chrysostom <note>a 4th-century Church Father</note> thinks he was removed because he forbade the census to be given to Caesar and that he was a Pharisee. See Eusebius in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 2, Chapter 11.
<margin>26 Whom he consented to]</margin> "Joined" <note>original: "προσεκολλήθη"</note>. Where elsewhere it is translated "adhered," it should have been translated that way here too. For they did not just consent, but conspired with him and taught the same things.
<margin>27 In the days of the profession]</margin> "The registration/census" <note>original: "ἀπογραφῆς"</note>. Which in the Gospel is translated as "the enrollment."
<margin>28 He turned away the people]</margin> The Greeks add "many" <note>original: "ἱκανὸν"</note>, meaning a great number.
<margin>29 This plan or work]</margin> "This counsel or work" <note>original: "βουλὴ ἢ τὸ ἔργον τοῦτο"</note>.
<margin>30 Lest perhaps]</margin> "Lest at any time" <note>original: "μήποτε"</note>.
<margin>31 And you be seen to fight against God]</margin> "And you be found fighting against God" <note>original: "καὶ Θεομάχοι εὑρεθῆτε"</note>. In Greek, this is a compound word derived from the verb "to fight against God" <note>original: "θεομαχεῖν"</note>. Otherwise, the translator renders it correctly, except that the Greek has more emphasis, signifying a state or character (like being "enemies of God") rather than just an action.
<margin>32 They consented to him]</margin> "They were persuaded" <note>original: "Ἐπείσθησαν"</note>, meaning they obeyed or complied.
<margin>33 Not to speak at all]</margin> I do not find "at all" <note>Latin: "omnino"</note> in the Greek codices; it is simply "not to speak" <note>original: "μὴ λαλεῖν"</note>. The old codices were being shortened.
<margin>34 And about the houses]</margin> "From house to house" <note>original: "κατ' οἶκον"</note>, meaning through individual houses, or domestic ministry.
<margin>35 Teaching]</margin> "They did not cease teaching and preaching" <note>original: "ἐπαύοντο διδάσκοντες καὶ εὐαγγελιζόμενοι"</note>. It should have been translated "they ceased to teach and preach," changing the participle into an infinitive.

And this speech pleased the whole multitude: and they <margin>5</margin> chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, <margin>8</margin> and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. These they stood in the sight of the Apostles... <margin>6</margin>
<meta>catchword: word</meta>

---

<margin>1</margin> **A**s the number of disciples was increasing] "While the disciples were multiplying" <note>original: "πληθυνόντων τῶν μαθητῶν"</note>, meaning as more disciples were being made. However, I approve of the translator's phrasing.
<margin>2</margin> Murmuring of the Greeks] It is not "Greeks" <note>original: "Ἑλλήνων" - Hellenon</note>, but "Hellenists" <note>original: "Ἑλληνιστῶν" - Helleniston</note>. For the Jews called all pagans and those foreign to the Mosaic Law "Greeks." It is probable that in this number there was not yet anyone from the gentiles; therefore he did not say "Greeks," but "Hellenists"—Jews who had been born or lived among the gentiles and spoke the language of the nation where they lived. Thus, those born in the regions of the Jews considered Jews born elsewhere and speaking other languages as semi-pagans. He does not call them Jews here, which was a religious name, but Hebrews, which more specifically indicates the race and nation.
<margin>3</margin> Because they were looked down upon] This sense has been accepted: whether they seemed to be looked down upon because they were not admitted to the ministry (as if they were not truly Judean), or because they were burdened with the weight of more menial service. Thus the seven Deacons seem to have been elected, not to serve everyone themselves, but to manage the shifts and orders of service so the Apostles would not be interrupted by endless complaints.
<margin>4</margin> But the twelve calling together] He explained this obscurely. For it could be taken as if the twelve disciples had been summoned by others, which is why we translated it clearly. Now, in "we will be persistent," why was a paraphrase necessary? Again, in "even a great crowd," the "even" is redundant; there is nothing else for it to respond to.
<margin>5</margin> It is not right] "It is not pleasing" <note>original: "Οὐκ ἀρεστόν ἐστι"</note>, meaning it is not a matter of grace, or not the sort of thing that ought to please us.
<margin>6</margin> Of good testimony] "Being witnessed for" <note>original: "μαρτυρουμένους"</note>, as if you were to say "of proven character." That is, of established and proven integrity, of whom others testify well. Otherwise, "of good testimony" could seem to refer to someone who gives testimony in good faith.
<margin>7</margin> Over this work] "For this use" <note>original: "ἐπὶ τῆς χρείας ταύτης"</note>, or "for this necessity," which appeals more to Valla <note>a fellow humanist scholar</note>, though not as much to me, although "task" fits better here.
<margin>8</margin> And Nicolaus a newcomer] He more correctly distinguished "proselyte," as Valla notes, so we understand him as one received into the Mosaic Law, being Antiochene by birth but Jewish by religion. He was later regarded as a leader of a heresy, though Clement (quoted in Eusebius) diligently excuses him.

---

9 *And they laid hands on them*] Rabanus <note>Rabanus Maurus (c. 780–856), a Benedictine monk and influential theologian of the Carolingian era.</note>, I believe, reminds us that this is the manner in conferring holy orders: that the people choose, and the Bishop ordains. Certainly, this custom persisted in the Church for a very long time, but on account of popular riots, it was rightly changed.
10 *To the Spirit who spoke*] <note>original Greek: "ᾧ ἐλάλει"</note>. This can be understood such that the meaning is: They were not able to resist the spirit with which he was speaking. Although the other reading is also sound, where the Greek word for "which" is used in place of "who" because of the preceding word for "Spirit" being in the dative case. Here, in an ancient manuscript, I found written: *because they were refuted by him with all confidence*. The Spanish Edition <note>The Complutensian Polyglot Bible, the first printed polyglot of the entire Bible, produced in Spain.</note> had the same, but it is not added in the Greek, nor in the Latin except for a few.
11 *He does not cease to speak words*] <note>original Greek: "ῥήματα βλάσφημα"</note>, that is, blasphemous or abusive words. However, I think "blasphemous" was added. For what need was there for it, since "speaking against the holy place" follows? Certainly Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an important Early Church Father known for his preaching.</note>, in explaining this passage, makes no mention of "blasphemous." Nor is it added anywhere in the older Latin manuscripts.
12 *And he will change the traditions*] <note>original Greek: "τὰ ἔθη"</note>, that is, the customs or institutions.

1 *Are these things so?*] <note>original Greek: "Εἰ ἄρα ταῦτα οὕτως ἔχει"</note>, that is, "Do these things truly stand this way?"
2 *Who said*] I ask you, what is this indifference <note>Erasmus uses the word "supinitas" to describe a lazy or careless style of translation in the Vulgate.</note> in translating? How does "who said" connect with the previous speech? For it preceded: "The prince of the Priests said, if these things were so." But in Greek it is "But he said" <note>original Greek: "Ὁ δὲ ἔφη"</note>.
3 *Before he lived in Haran*] Stephen’s narrative seemed to differ somewhat from the history in Genesis chapter 12, because there, after mention is made of Terah the father of Abraham, it is later recorded that God spoke with him. Nor does the number of years quite agree. But Jerome <note>The translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> in *Hebrew Questions* and Augustine in *City of God* (book 16, chapter 15) have untied this knot. Again in *Questions on Genesis* (book one).
4 *Not a foot's breadth*] <note>original Greek: "οὐδὲ βῆμα ποδός"</note>, that is, not even a footprint. For a "pace" <note>the Latin term "passus"</note> encompasses several feet, and there cannot be a

---

pace of only one foot. It is more tolerable, therefore, what Augustine reads in *Questions on Genesis* (book one): *not even a foot's breadth*. In that place, he simultaneously examines how it could be that he who is previously read to have bought a field near the well of the oath, now possessed not even a footprint there. He did not possess it, not even that small amount, by divine gift, about whose promise Stephen is dealing here. For with money it was permitted to acquire fields anywhere.
5 *But He spoke to him*] <note>original Greek: "ᾧ λαλήσει"</note>, "But He spoke thus" in the Greek, and "to him" is not added.
6 *Because his seed would be a sojourner*] <note>original Greek: "Ὅτι ἔσται τὸ σπέρμα αὐτοῦ πάροικον"</note>. It is more fitting that "quia" <note>because/that</note> is used for "quod" <note>that</note>, and "accola" <note>neighbor/sojourner</note> can be used in the neuter gender. Certainly an "incola" <note>inhabitant</note> is different from an "accola" <note>neighbor</note>. Indeed, those who are bordering are called "accola," like the neighbors of the Rhine; an "incola" is one who is not native <note>original term: "αὐτόχθων" (autochthon)</note>. Although in Greek it is "paroikos" <note>πάροικος</note>, one who, having set out from elsewhere, has a home in another place. We translate it as "inquilinus" <note>tenant/lodger</note>, in this manner: "But God spoke thus, that his seed would be a tenant in a foreign land, and that they would subject it to slavery, etc." It was smoother to say "his descendants were inhabitants," for he calls descendants "seed." Nor is the phrase "says the Lord" in the conclusion, but "God said" <note>original Greek: "εἶπεν ὁ Θεός"</note>.
7 *They will treat poorly*] <note>original Greek: "καὶ κακώσουσι"</note>, that is, they will afflict or torment. *For four hundred years*. In a very old edition, it was read *four hundred and thirty*, and so Rabanus reads from the calculation of times. Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (672–735), an English monk and scholar.</note> indicates a transposition <note>term: "Hyperbaton" — a figure of speech where the natural order of words is disrupted.</note>: "he will be an inhabitant for four hundred years," so that what comes in the middle—"and they will subject them to slavery and treat them poorly"—does not hinder the context of what precedes and follows. Although in my opinion there is no need to flee to this transposition.
8 *And so he begat Isaac*] The translator, unless it is an error, seems to have read "thus" <note>original Greek: "οὕτως"</note>, while in the Greek manuscripts it is "this man" <note>original Greek: "οὗτος"</note>. If you read "this man," the sense is that he did not beget Isaac except as a circumcised man, whereas he had fathered Ishmael while uncircumcised. I suspect it happened that the Greeks, out of hatred for circumcision, changed "this man" to "thus." However, the Greek manuscripts varied; Chrysostom and the Spanish Edition had "this man," while my manuscripts and the Aldine Edition <note>The first printed Greek New Testament, published by Aldus Manutius in Venice.</note> had "thus."
9 *And Isaac Jacob*] <note>original Greek: "τὸν Ἰακώβ"</note>, so that you should understand "begat" <note>the verb is implied</note>.

10 **They could not find food** <note>original: "Non inveniebant cibos"</note>] In Greek, *χορτάσματα*. This is a word derived from "to satisfy" or "to fill."

11 **And at the second time** <note>original: "Et in secundo"</note>] In Greek, *Καὶ ἐν τῷ δευτέρῳ*. This translates word for word as "And in the second," meaning "On the second visit" or "When he had sent them again."

12 **Jacob went down with seventy-five souls** <note>original: "In septuaginta quinque animabus descendit Jacob"</note>] In Genesis chapter 46, Saint Jerome, following the <term>Hebrew Truth</term> <note>The Hebrew text of the Old Testament.</note>, translates this as only seventy. However, Luke seems to have followed the authority of the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, which was widely accepted at the time—either because five years were added by Hebrew scribes, or because he did not think the exact calculation of the number was relevant to the point being made.

13 **Which Abraham bought for a price of silver from the sons of Hamor, the son of Shechem** <note>original: "Quod emit Abraham pretio argenti a filiis Emor filii Sichem"</note>] Jerome also noted this passage in his book to Pammachius regarding the best style of interpretation. It is recorded differently in Genesis, where we read that Abraham bought the double cave and the field around it from Ephron the Hittite, son of Zohar, near Hebron, for four hundred drachmas, and buried his wife Sarah there. In that same book, we read that later, upon returning from Mesopotamia with his wives and sons, Jacob pitched his tent before Salem, a city of the Shechemites in the land of Canaan, lived there, and bought the part of the field where he had his tents from Hamor, the father of Shechem, for a hundred lambs; he set up an altar there and called upon the God of Israel. Therefore, Abraham did not buy the cave from Hamor, the father of Shechem, but from Ephron, the son of Zohar; nor was he buried in Shechem, but in Hebron (which is sometimes corruptly called Arboch). Furthermore, the twelve Patriarchs

<column-break/>

<margin>F</margin> were not buried in Arboch, but in Shechem; and that field was not bought by Abraham, but by Jacob. Jerome ties this "knot" there and does not truly unravel it in that place, but he explains it elegantly in his *Hebrew Questions*.

14 **Which he had sworn** <note>original: "Quam confessus erat"</note>] In Greek, *ἧς ὤμοσεν*, that is, "which he had sworn." The translator seems to have read *ὁμολογήσατο* (confessed/acknowledged).

15 **Who did not know** <note>original: "Qui non sciebat"</note>] In Greek, *ὃς οὐκ ἤδει*, that is, "who did not recognize/know."

16 **Lest they should be kept alive** <note>original: "Ne vivificarentur"</note>] In Greek, *εἰς τὸ μὴ ζωογονεῖσθαι*, that is, "to the end that the offspring should not be viable."

17 **Fair in the sight of God** <note>original: "Gratus Deo"</note>] In Greek, *ἀστεῖος τῷ Θεῷ*. The word *ἀστεῖος* otherwise sounds like "festive" or "urbane." It seems he used this word in place of *χάριτος*, which signifies "pleasing" or "graceful," and also "urbane."

18 **He thought his brothers would understand** <note>original: "Existimabat autem intelligere fratres"</note>] Here he calls men of his own nation "brothers," a term that was later transferred to Christians. Augustine, in his *Questions on Exodus*, wonders whether Moses' act of homicide was merely a sign of his natural character or something to be praised, as it seems from this speech of Stephen that he did it by divine prompting.

19 **Quarreling** <note>original: "Litigantibus"</note>] In Greek, *ἐπὶ μαχομένοις*, which is to say "fighting." The translator rendered this correctly.

20 **In the fire of a flaming bush** <note>original: "In igne flammæ rubi"</note>] The Greek has the reverse order: *ἐν φλογὶ πυρὸς*, that is, "in a flame of fire." This phrasing is somewhat harsh to us because of the properties of the Hebrew language.

21 **Seeing I have seen** <note>original: "Videns vidi"</note>] This is a Hebrew figure of speech <note>A double verb used for emphasis.</note> meaning "I have seen attentively."

22 **And now come, I will send** <note>original: "Et nunc veni, & mittam"</note>] In Greek, *καὶ νῦν δεῦρο, καὶ ἀποστελῶ*, "and now come,"
