23 *Like myself you shall hear]* "You shall hear" is not written in this place in some Greek copies. The manuscripts of the Donation support the Greek reading, in which it was: *from your brothers like me*. In Chrysostom, there is no mention of this clause in the text or the commentary. Regarding the phrase *like me*, Chrysostom explains it as being despised and sought after with plots, because just as Herod plotted against the child Christ, so Pharaoh plotted against Moses in Egypt, and both escaped safely. It was demonstrated above that *him* belongs to the verb *you shall hear*, not to *me*, which belongs to the verb *will raise up*: *He will raise up for you a Prophet like me, that is, similar to me, and as if another me; him you shall hear.* Although it appears the Translator read "like myself" <note>original: "ὡς ἐμαυτόν"</note>, unless, as is more probable, someone added this of their own accord.

24 *In the church in the solitude]* In the Greek, "and" is not there, but it is "in the congregation, in the desert," without a conjunction, which agrees with the more corrected Latin versions.

25 *He might give you words of life]* Some manuscripts had "living speech" <note>original: "λόγον ζῶντα"</note>. Some had "living oracles" <note>original: "λόγια ζῶντα"</note>. For he was accustomed to translate *logia* as "oracles" or "divine utterances."

26 *Your fathers]* In both places in the Greek it is "our," that is, of the first person.

27 *For to this Moses]* "For that Moses," and so the Constance manuscript has it. Although the Translator correctly changed it.

28 *Which you made to adore]* The Translator did not note the Greek figure of speech, "which you made to worship them." But it is strange that the article is not added to the infinitive verb.

<column-break/>

<margin>F</margin> 29 *And I will transport you beyond Babylon]* In some copies, "beyond" <note>original: "trans"</note> is found changed to "into" <note>original: "in"</note>. The passage is taken from the fifth chapter of the Prophet Amos. Although there, instead of *beyond Babylon*, it reads *beyond Damascus*, based on the authority of the Hebrew truth as well as the Septuagint. Jerome excuses Stephen by saying he rendered the sense rather than the words, because the Jews were led *beyond Damascus* into Babylon, or *beyond Babylon*. There are those who prefer to admit the scripture was corrupted, and *beyond Babylon* was written instead of *beyond Damascus*.

30 *With fathers]* "With" is redundant here.

31 *God speaking]* "The one who speaks," that is, the one who was speaking.

32 *Your fathers]* In Greek it is "our," as we just pointed out.

33 *But not the Most High in things made by hand]* The Greek adds "temples" <note>original: "ναοῖς"</note>. And "made-by-hand" is a single word for them.

34 *Stiff-necked]* In Greek, the epithet is a compound, "hard-necked" <note>original: "σκληροτράχηλοι"</note>, as if you were to say "stiff-necked," as Pacuvius used in Quintilian; and following him, Politian said "the bent-necked herd." Furthermore, it appears that Stephen's speech was interrupted by the shouting of the clamoring Jews. Otherwise, this ending would not quite correspond to a beginning repeated from so far back, especially since there are many things in it which do not seem to pertain very much to the point he established.

35 *You resist]* "You fall against," that is, you resist.

36 *And homicides]* "Murderers," that is, slayers.

37 *In the disposition]* "In the arrangements," or "at the arrangements": from the word meaning "I ordain." Augustine, in the tenth book of *The City of God*, quotes several times "in the edicts of Angels," instead of what we read, "in the disposition of Angels."

38 *Of the power of God]* I do not find "power" in the Greek manuscript. It is only "at the right hand of God," which is also supported by the older Latin versions.

## VIII.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...this sin against them. And when he had said this, <margin>39</margin> he fell asleep. Now Saul had consented to his death. And <margin>1</margin> on <margin>VIII.</margin> that day a great persecution arose against the church that was in Jerusalem, and all were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except for the Apostles. <margin>2</margin> Devout men <margin>2</margin> <margin>3</margin> cared for Stephen's burial and made great lamentation over him. But Saul was ravaging the church, <margin>3</margin> entering into every <margin>4</margin> house; dragging off both men and women, he committed them to prison. <margin>4</margin> Therefore, those who were scattered went about <margin>5</margin> preaching the word of God. And Philip went down <margin>5</margin> <margin>6</margin> into a city of Samaria and preached Christ to them. The crowds <margin>6</margin> paid attention with one mind to the things spoken by Philip, hearing and seeing the signs he performed. <margin>7</margin> For unclean spirits came out <margin>7</margin> of many who were possessed by them, crying out with a <margin>B</margin> loud voice; many who were paralyzed and lame were healed. And there was great joy in that city. But a 8 9 certain man named Simon, who previously <margin>8</margin> had practiced magic in that city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he was someone great, <margin>9</margin> to whom they all listened, from the least to the greatest, 10 saying, "This man is the power of God, <margin>10</margin> which is called Great." And they listened to him <margin>11</margin> because for a long 11 time he had <margin>13</margin> amazed them <margin>12</margin> with his magic arts. But 12 when they believed Philip, as he preached <margin>14</margin> concerning the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, <margin>C</margin> both men and women. Then Simon himself also believed, 13 and when he was baptized, he kept close to Philip; seeing the signs and great miracles being done, <margin>15</margin> he was filled with wonder. Now when the Apostles who were in 14 Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they had 15 come down, <margin>16</margin> they prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit. For he had not yet <margin>17</margin> fallen upon 16 any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid hands on 17 them, and they received the Holy Spirit. And when <margin>18</margin> Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying <margin>18</margin> on of the Apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying, "Give me <margin>19</margin> this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the <margin>D</margin> Holy Spirit." But Peter said to him, "May your 20 money perish with you, because you thought the gift of God could be purchased with money. You have no part 21 or lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God. Repent, therefore, of this your wickedness <margin>22</margin> and pray to God, <margin>19</margin> if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you. <margin>20</margin> For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness <margin>21</margin> 23 and...

---

39 **He fell asleep in the Lord]** In the Lord <note>original: "in Domino"</note> is not added in the Greek manuscript; it simply says *he fell asleep* <note>original: "εἰπ᾿ ἐκοιμήθη" (eip' ekoimēthē)</note>. This is supported by the ancient Latin manuscripts.

1 **In the church]** <note>original: "ἐπὶ τὴν ἐκκλησίαν" (epi tēn ekklēsian)</note>, that is, *against the church* or *toward the church*.

2 **They cared for Stephen]** <note>original: "Συνεκόμισαν δὲ" (Synekomisan de)</note>, meaning *they together took care of him*.

3 **Devout men]** <note>original: "εὐλαβεῖς" (eulabeis)</note>, meaning *religious* or *pious* men.

4 **Entering through the houses]** <note>original: "κατ᾿ οἴκους" (kat’ oikous)</note>, that is, *from house to house*, so to speak, to show his great zeal for destruction.

5 **Therefore those who were scattered]** <note>original: "Οἱ μὲν οὖν διασπαρέντες" (Hoi men oun diasparentes)</note>, that is, *therefore those indeed having been scattered*. For they were already being dispersed.

6 **Into a city of Samaria]** This seems to be said descriptively, "the city of Samaria," so that Samaria is the name not of the region, but of the city from which the whole region takes its name. This city was also called Sebaste.

7 **Unclean spirits came out of many who had them, crying with a loud voice]** I ask, who exactly was coming out? Surely not the men themselves? The previous translator neither rendered the Greek as it stands, nor translated it so that the sense could be perceived. It is like that phrase sung in the praises of the Virgin Mother of God: "Whose humility the Lord beholding, with the Angel announcing, he conceived the Redeemer of the world." <note>The author is mocking a grammatical error in a popular hymn where, strictly speaking, the Latin suggests the *Lord* got pregnant rather than Mary.</note> From these words, what Latin speaker would understand anything, unless they thought the Lord had become pregnant? They seem to think it does not matter how we speak, as long as we understand what we mean. But as for this passage, the Greek reads: <note>original: "Πολλῶν γὰρ τῶν ἐχόντων πνεύματα ἀκάθαρτα, βοῶντα μεγάλῃ φωνῇ, ἐξήρχετο" (Pollōn gar tōn echontōn pneumata akatharta, boōnta megalē phōnē, exērcheto)</note>. Since these could not be rendered word-for-word, we expressed the sense this way: *For unclean spirits from many, who were held by them, crying with a loud voice, went out.* In two of the Donatist manuscripts, this part was not added; I suspect the scribe omitted it because he was offended by the absurdity of the phrasing. Yet the Greek manuscripts agree.

8 **In the city a magus]** <note>original: "ἐν τῇ πόλει μαγεύων" (en tē polei mageuōn)</note>, meaning *practicing the magic art*.

9 **To whom they listened]** This word "listened" and the one that follows, "attended," are the same word in Greek: <note>original: "προσείχον" (proseichon)</note>.

10 **Which is called Great]** <note>original: "ἥτις καλεῖται" (hētis kaleitai)</note> is not added in the Greek manuscript; it is simply <note>original: "ἡ δύναμις τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡ μεγάλη" (hē dynamis tou Theou hē megalē)</note>, that is, *the great power of God*. The translator tried to explain the force of the Greek article *the* <note>original: "ἡ" (hē)</note>.

<margin>E</margin> 11 **Because of which]** <note>original: "διὰ τὸ" (dia to)</note>, meaning *on account of the fact that*; and yet I see this form of speech was familiar to the early Christians, even though it means something quite different.

12 **With his magics]** <note>original: "ταῖς μαγείαις" (tais mageiais)</note>, meaning *by magic* or *by magic arts*.

13 **He had amazed]** <note>original: "ἐξεστακέναι αὐτοὺς" (exestakenai autous)</note>, meaning *they were stupefied and, as it were, alienated from their minds*.

14 **Concerning the kingdom of God in the name of Jesus]** In Greek it is *and* the name.

15 **Stupefied, he wondered]** <note>original: "ἐξίστατο" (existato)</note>. The translator rendered one Greek word with two Latin ones. Laurentius <note>Likely referring to the scholar Lorenzo Valla, a pioneer of New Testament textual criticism.</note> is quite annoyed at this point, and not without reason, that the translator allowed himself so much freedom as to render the same Greek word in three different ways in the same passage. For what he translated just before as *seducing* is <note>original: "ἐξιστῶν" (existōn)</note> in Greek; what he called *amazed* is <note>original: "ἐξεστακέναι" (exestakenai)</note>; and what he calls *stupefied he wondered* is <note>original: "ἐξίστατο" (existato)</note>.

<margin>F</margin> 16 **And they prayed for them]** It is doubtful whether the Apostles themselves prayed to God for them, or whether Philip and those with him prayed to the Apostles. The translators seem to follow the latter sense, but in Greek it is <note>original: "προσηύξαντο" (prosēuxanto)</note>, a word the Scripture usually uses for a prayer addressed to God.

17 **It had come upon any of them]** <note>original: "ἐπιπεπτωκὸς" (epipeptōkos)</note>, meaning *it had slipped in* or *fallen down upon*.

18 **The hands of the Apostles]** <note>original: "χειρῶν" (cheirōn)</note>, meaning *of hands*. But the translator, offended by a sequence of genitives, varied the phrasing.

19 **If perhaps]** <note>original: "εἰ ἄρα" (ei ara)</note>. He translates an emphatic conjunction, according to his custom, as *perhaps*.

20 **In the gall of bitterness]** <note>original: "Εἰς χολὴν πικρίας" (Eis cholēn pikrias)</note>, meaning *in the bile of bitterness*, that is, *in bitter bile*. The Sorcerer was not literally angry, but his mental vice is expressed through the bitterness of bile.

21 **And in the bond]** <note>original: "καὶ συνδέσμῳ" (kai syndesmō)</note>, that is, *in the binding together*, meaning *in chains*.

### THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES CHAPTER IX.

<column-break/>

24 <margin>A</margin> and the bond of iniquity. And Simon answering said, "Pray to the Lord for me, so that nothing <gloss>22</gloss> of these things you have said may happen to me." 25 And they, having testified and spoken the word of God, returned to Jerusalem, <gloss>23</gloss> and they preached the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans. 26 But an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, "Arise and go <gloss>24</gloss> toward the south, to the road <gloss>25</gloss> that descends from the city of Jerusalem to the city of <gloss>26</gloss> Gaza; this is a desert road." 27 And arising he went: <gloss>27</gloss> and behold, an Ethiopian man, <gloss>28</gloss> a eunuch, an official of <gloss>29</gloss> Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all <margin>B</margin> her treasure, <gloss>30</gloss> had come to Jerusalem to worship. 28 And he was returning, sitting upon his chariot, and was reading the prophet Isaiah. 29 And the Spirit said to Philip, "Go near, and join yourself to this chariot." 30 Philip, running up, heard him reading the prophet Isaiah, and said, <gloss>31</gloss> "Do you understand what you are reading?" 31 And he said, <gloss>32</gloss> "For how can I, unless someone <gloss>33</gloss> acts as a guide to me?" And he asked Philip to come up and sit with him. 32 <gloss>34</gloss> Now the passage of scripture he was reading was this: <gloss>35</gloss> "Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and as a lamb is silent before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth. 33 In his humiliation his judgment was taken away; <margin>C</margin> but who shall describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth." 34 The eunuch, answering Philip, said, "I beseech you, about whom <gloss>36</gloss> does the prophet say this? About himself, or about someone else?" 35 Then Philip, opening his mouth and beginning from this very scripture, preached Jesus to him. 36 And as they went along the road, they came to some water; and the eunuch said, "See, here is water; <gloss>37</gloss> what prevents me from being baptized?" 37 <gloss>38</gloss> And Philip said, "If you believe with all your heart, you may." And he answering said, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God." 38 And he commanded the chariot to stop; and <gloss>39</gloss> both went down into the water, <gloss>40</gloss> both Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. 39 When they had come up out of the water, <gloss>41</gloss> the Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more; for he went on his way rejoicing. 40 But Philip <margin>D</margin> <gloss>42</gloss> was found at Azotus, and passing through, he preached the gospel to all the cities, until he came to Caesarea. **IX. 1.** But Saul, <gloss>1</gloss> still breathing threats and murder <margin>IX. 1.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>22</margin> *Of these things you have said*] <note>original: ὧν εἰρήκατε</note>. The relative pronoun agrees with the case of the preceding word, even though it differs from its own verb. It should be noted that where Peter responds, the eunuch uses the plural verb, *you all have said*. From this, it is probable that when Peter gave the warning, the others present also gave warnings.

<margin>23</margin> *And in many regions*] <note>original: πολλάς τε κώμας</note>, meaning villages or hamlets. It appears the Translator may have read <note>original: χώρας</note> (regions).

<margin>24</margin> *Toward the south*] <note>original: κατὰ μεσημβρίαν</note>, that is, toward the midday sun, or to the south.

<margin>25</margin> *Which descends from Jerusalem*] <note>original: καταβαίνουσαν</note>. Because the city of Jerusalem is situated in part on Mount Zion. Some manuscripts had the word *desert*, referring to the path.

<margin>26</margin> *Gaza*] This is a distinguished city of Palestine, assigned as a portion to the tribe of Judah, though it could not be held. He adds *desert* because that old Gaza, of which Zephaniah said "Gaza shall be destroyed," was so demolished that scarcely a trace of the city remains; another city was built in its place, but not on the same site.

<margin>27</margin> *And behold, a man, a eunuch*] Jerome noted that it is strange to call a man a eunuch, since being a "man" and being a "eunuch" seem to contradict each other (the latter being "un-manned"). But in Christ, there is neither sex nor condition, but a new creation.

<margin>28</margin> *A powerful eunuch*] <note>original: δυνάστης</note>, that is, a magistrate or prefect. Cicero also used this Greek word, *Tetrarch and Dynast*. For he is not called the Queen's eunuch, but the Queen's prefect—certainly her treasurer <note>original: gazophylax</note>.

<margin>29</margin> *Of Candace*] <note>original: Κανδάκης</note>, that is, *Candace*, from the nominative form *Candace*. This name seems to have been common to queens there, perhaps because of a certain Queen Candace of Ethiopia who served that nation exceptionally well, just as *Pharaoh and Ptolemy* were names for the kings of the Egyptians.

<margin>30</margin> *Had come to worship*] <note>original: προσκυνήσων</note>, that is, intending to worship.

<margin>31</margin> *Do you think you understand?*] <note>original: Ꮌρά γε</note>. Whether, or indeed, or "Do you at all understand what you read?"

<margin>32</margin> *If how*] The word "If" is not present in the Greek, which reads only <note>original: Πῶς γὰρ ἂν δυναίμην</note>, "For how could I?" or "How indeed could I?" For a negative is implied: "I do not understand."

<margin>33</margin> *Show me*] <note>original: ὁδηγήσῃ με</note>, that is, should guide me.

<margin>34</margin> *The place of scripture*] <note>original: Ἡ δὲ περιοχή</note>. Which you could call the contents; we have translated it as "argument," but it could also be called the "sentence" or "theme."

<margin>35</margin> *As a sheep to the slaughter*] This passage is found in Isaiah, chapter 53. But it appears this eunuch was reading these things not from a Hebrew book, but from a Greek one, because everything agrees perfectly with the Septuagint Edition. And Egypt was "Greeky" <note>Hellenized</note> at that time 

<column-break/>

due to trade with the Romans and, before that, with Alexander. For Jerome translated the Hebrew as: *As a sheep he shall be led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he shall be mute, and he shall not open his mouth.* Regarding his distress and judgment, he was taken away; who shall tell of his generation, for he was cut off from the land of the living? According to the Septuagint, we read it this way: <note>original: Ὡς πρόβατον ἐπὶ σφαγὴν ἤχθη...</note> <margin>E</margin> That is: *As a sheep he was led to the victim, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth. In his humiliation his judgment was taken away. Who shall tell of his generation, because his life is taken from the earth.* Furthermore, in our [Latin] manuscripts, "is taken away" is incorrectly written as a future tense verb, just as we read "opened" instead of "opens."

<margin>36</margin> *Says this*] <note>original: λέγει τοῦτο</note>, that is, "he says this," as if he were speaking to you now, whose writings you are reading.

<margin>37</margin> *Who prohibits*] <note>original: τί κωλύει</note>, that is, what prohibits, or rather, what forbids, or what stands in the way of me being baptized.

<margin>38</margin> *Philip said*] The section from "If you believe etc." up to the point "And he commanded the chariot to stop," I did not find in the Greek manuscript. Although I suspect it was omitted through the negligence of scribes. For I found these things written in a certain Greek manuscript, but in the margin. Otherwise, these are not added in the work of the interpreter Chrysostom. Nor are they in the Spanish Edition. They were, however, added in the Aldine edition.

<margin>39</margin> *Each of the two*] <note>original: ἀμφότεροι</note>, that is, both.

<margin>40</margin> *Philip and the eunuch*] <note>original: ὅ τε Φίλιππος καὶ εὐνοῦχος</note>, that is, both Philip and the eunuch, using a doubled conjunction.

<margin>41</margin> *The Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip*] Rabanus, in the Ordinary Gloss, <margin>F</margin> seems to have noted a different reading, as if the Spirit were said to have rushed upon the eunuch, and snatched Philip away; however, I find nothing of this kind in either the Greek or Latin manuscripts.

<margin>42</margin> *He was found in Azotus*] Who was looking for him, that he might be "found" there? "He appeared" would have been more tolerable. For the sense is that Philip was suddenly at Azotus. That is a city of Palestine, one of the five cities of the Philistines, called Ashdod by the Hebrews.

<margin>IX. 1</margin> **S** *till breathing*] <note>original: ἐμπνέων</note>. Perhaps the prefix *em-* was changed from *eti* (still). In others, both are present, "even still breathing." But why "breathing of threats"? Just as we say someone "desires you" and is "desirous of you," one cannot say "the voice does not sound like a man" and "the voice is not sounding of a man," or "it tastes like wine" and "it is tasting of wine." Therefore, in my judgment, it should have been translated as *breathing threats and slaughter*.

### THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES. CHAPTER IX.

<margin>2</margin> [Saul, still breathing threats against] the disciples of the Lord, went to the High Priest, and asked him for letters to Damascus to the synagogues, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, whether men <margin>3</margin> or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. <margin>2</margin> *Against the disciples of the Lord* <note>original: "In discipulos Domini"</note>] It would have been clearer to say *against* the disciples of the Lord.
<margin>3</margin> *Men of this way* <note>original: "Hujus viae viros"</note>] <note>original: "tēs hodou ontas"</note>, that is, those who were of that sect. For in this place, the article functions in place of a pronoun. And instead of *viri* (men), many manuscripts had *vitae* (of life).
<margin>4</margin> *Men and women* <note>original: "Viros ac mulieres"</note>] <note>original: "andras te kai gynaikas"</note>, that is, both men and women, or *whether men or women*.
<margin>5</margin> *Flashed around* <note>original: "Circumfulfit"</note>] <note>original: "periēstrapsen"</note>, that is, it lightened around him, specifically to speak. For he calls a sudden light "lightning."
<margin>6</margin> *Saul Saul* <note>original: "Saule Saule"</note>] <note>original: "Saoul Saoul"</note>, that is, Saul Saul. While Luke elsewhere calls him *Saulus* and *Paulus*, here he left the Hebrew voice intact because Christ addressed him in Hebrew, as Paul himself later testifies. And likewise Ananias says, <note>original: "Saoul adelphe"</note>, that is, "Brother Saul," a matter we will touch upon in the Pauline Epistles.
<margin>7</margin> *It is hard for you* <note>original: "Durum est tibi"</note>] In most Greek manuscripts, this is not added in this place (since *arise* follows shortly), but a bit further down where this event is recounted. It is not uncommon for a learned scribe to add something in the margins from elsewhere, which a later, unlearned scribe then moves into the main text. Certainly, Chrysostom makes no mention of this phrase in this location. Moreover, it is a proverb even among the pagans <note>original: "hēmas to kentron laktizein"</note>, that is, *To kick against the goad*. This is a metaphor taken from oxen or other beasts of burden who are urged on with a goad, just as horses might kick back. In the older manuscripts, even these words were not found: *And trembling and astonished he said, Lord what do you want me to do? And the Lord to him, it is enough, it is hard for you to kick against the goad. I am Jesus, whom you persecute, arise & enter etc.*
<margin>8</margin> *Who accompanied him* <note>original: "Qui comitabantur cum illo"</note>] <note>original: "hoi sydeuontes autō"</note>, that is, those who were making the journey with him, or his travel companions. The translator did not speak in good Latin, nor did he respond accurately to the Greek verb.

And when [the days] were fulfilled...

---

<margin>9</margin> *They stood astonished* <note>original: "Stabant stupefacti"</note>] <note>original: "enneoi"</note>. The Greek word is formed from the idea that the novelty of a thing renders a person stunned.
<margin>10</margin> *He saw nothing* <note>original: "Nihil videbat"</note>] <note>original: "oudena eblepen"</note>, that is, he saw *no one*. It appears the Translator read <note>original: "ouden eblepen"</note> (nothing).
<margin>11</margin> *Dragging him by the hands* <note>original: "Ad manus autem illum trahentes"</note>] <note>original: "cheiragōgountes de auton"</note>, that is, leading him by the hand. For what was the need for "dragging," since he went of his own accord? And so he translates it himself a little later: *Led by the hand by his companions*.
<margin>12</margin> *Into the street called Straight* <note>original: "In vicum qui vocatur Rectus"</note>] <note>original: "epi tēn rhymēn"</note>. In this place, "vicus" is not a village or a small town—lest anyone err in this—for the Greeks call that a <note>original: "kōmē"</note>, but rather a part of a city. For a city is divided into districts <note>original: "vici"</note>, districts into streets, and streets into houses.
<margin>13</margin> *How many evils he has done to the saints* <note>original: "Quanta mala fecerit sanctis"</note>] <note>original: "hosa"</note>, that is, "which," or "whatever." Likewise a little later, *how many things he must suffer for my name*.
<margin>14</margin> *And here he has* <note>original: "Et hic habet"</note>] "Hic" in this place is an adverb, not the pronoun <note>original: "hōde"</note>; that is, "in this city."
<margin>15</margin> *Vessel of election* <note>original: "Vas electionis"</note>] <note>original: "skeuos eklogēs"</note>. I would have preferred *chosen instrument*. Although among the ancients, "vessels" referred to all kinds of equipment or furniture.
<margin>16</margin> *Brother Saul* <note>original: "Saule frater"</note>] <note>original: "Saoul adelphe"</note>, that is, Saul brother, for it is consistent that Ananias would have spoken in Hebrew.
<margin>17</margin> *That you may see* <note>original: "Ut videas"</note>] <note>original: "hōs anablepsēs"</note>, that is, so that you may regain your sight. For he had translated the same verb that way just a moment before.
<margin>18</margin> *Fell from his eyes* <note>original: "Ceciderunt ab oculis ejus"</note>] <note>original: "apepeson"</note>, they fell down.
<margin>19</margin> *Who destroyed* <note>original: "Qui expugnabat"</note>] In Greek, a military term is used; <note>original: "porthēsas"</note> for the Greeks means to tear down or depopulate a city.
<margin>20</margin> *That he might lead them bound* <note>original: "Ut vinctos illos duceret"</note>] <note>original: "hōs agagē"</note>, that is, might lead or drag away, which is what Valla prefers.
<margin>21</margin> *And he confounded* <note>original: "Et confundebat"</note>] This does not mean "he put to shame," as it is used elsewhere, but <note>original: "synechyne"</note>, that is, he stirred up and threw into confusion, by confirming that Jesus is the Christ.

### THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, CHAPTER IX.

<margin>A</margin> After many days had passed, <gloss>22</gloss> the Jews plotted together to kill him. But their plot became known to Saul. They were even watching the gates day and night in order to kill him.
25 Then the disciples took him by night and let him down through the wall, <gloss>23</gloss> lowering him in a basket.
26 When Saul had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples; but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was truly a disciple.
27 But Barnabas took him and brought him to the Apostles, and described to them how he had seen the Lord on the road, and that He had spoken to him, and how in Damascus he had acted boldly in the name of Jesus.
28 So he stayed with them, <gloss>24</gloss> moving about freely in Jerusalem, <gloss>25</gloss> speaking with confidence in the name of the Lord Jesus. 
<margin>B</margin> He spoke <gloss>26</gloss> and disputed against the Greeks; but they <gloss>27</gloss> sought to kill him.
30 When the brothers learned of this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
31 <gloss>28</gloss> So the churches throughout all Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace and were being built up. Walking in the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Holy Spirit, they multiplied.
32 Now it happened that as Peter <gloss>29</gloss> traveled through all those regions, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda.
33 There he found a certain man named <gloss>31</gloss> Aeneas, who had been bedridden for eight years, for he was paralyzed.
34 Peter said to him, "Aeneas, <gloss>30</gloss> Jesus Christ heals you; get up and make your bed." And immediately he stood up.
35 And all who lived in <gloss>31</gloss> Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
<margin>C</margin> <gloss>32</gloss> Now in Joppa there was a certain disciple named Tabitha, which in translation is called Dorcas <note>meaning "Gazelle"</note>. She was full of good works and acts of charity, which she continually performed.
37 It happened in those days that she became ill and died. <gloss>33</gloss> When they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
38 Since Lydda was near Joppa, and the disciples had heard that Peter was there, <gloss>34</gloss> they sent two men to him, urging him, <gloss>35</gloss> "Please do not delay in coming to us."
39 So Peter got up and went with them. When he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood around him weeping, showing him the tunics and cloaks <gloss>36</gloss> that Dorcas had made while she was with them.
<margin>D</margin> Peter sent them all outside, knelt down and prayed; then turning toward the body, he said, "Tabitha, arise." She opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter, she sat up.
41 Giving her his hand, he raised her up. Then calling the saints and the widows, he presented her alive.
42 This became known throughout all Joppa, <gloss>37</gloss> and many believed in the Lord.

<column-break/>

---

22 **They took counsel together** <note>original Latin: *Consilium fecerunt in unum*</note>] I do not find "together" in the Greek books that I have seen; it is simply "they plotted together" <note>original Greek: συνεβουλεύσαντο</note>. Unless perhaps the translator wished to express the force of the prefix *syn-* <note>meaning "with" or "together"</note>.

23 **Lowering in a basket** <note>original Latin: *Submittentes in sporta*</note>] From the Greek *chalantes*. This means to lower something suspended by ropes from a height, as we have indicated elsewhere.

24 **Moving about** <note>original Latin: *intrans & exiens*, literally "entering and exiting"</note>] In the Greek copies I find only "entering and exiting" <note>original Greek: εἰσπορευόμενος καὶ ἐκπορευόμενος</note>; I do not find "in Jerusalem." However, "entering and exiting" is a Hebrew figure of speech for "to live" or "to be active," much like the Latins say "at home and abroad" <note>original Latin: *domi ac foris*</note>. Therefore, from the Commentaries read under the name of Chrysostom, I added "and exiting," although this has very little impact on the meaning. I believe, however, that the other reading is the original.

25 **Acting confidently** <note>original Latin: *Fiducialiter agens*</note>] From the Greek *parrhesiazomenos*, that is, speaking or acting freely or with confidence; but it pertains more to speech, which is how the Greek word is composed.

26 **And disputed with the Greeks**] *To dispute against the Hellenists* <note>original Greek: συζητεῖν πρὸς τοὺς Ἑλληνιστάς</note>. Again, he uses the word "Hellenists," which refers to Jews born in Greek lands. For it was not yet the time for disputing with the Gentiles. Furthermore, that which preceded—"with the Gentiles"—I do not find in the Greek codices, nor even in the older Latin ones. And presently:

<margin>E</margin> 27 **They sought to kill him**] In Greek it is *epecheiroun*, which means "they were attempting" or "they were attacking."

28 **The church indeed**] From the Greek *Ai men oun ekklesiai*, which is "Therefore the churches," in the plural number. At that time, all the scattered congregations of Christians were called "The Church," yet they all fall back into the one Church.

29 **While he passed through all**] Some add the word "borders" <note>or regions</note> in this place, but erroneously, since Luke was thinking of the people, not the places.

30 **The Lord heals you**] *Iatai*. It could be understood as "you are healed," as a statement of fact rather than a command.

31 **Lydda and Sharon**] *Lyddan kai ton Assarona*. I am not sure if this is the place we read as "Accaron" <note>Ekron</note> in the corrupted Hebrew names, which some think is Strato's Tower, later called Caesarea. It is very likely that this is the region which Jerome, in his names of places, calls "Sarona," which to the Hebrews means "a flat or plain region." It stretches from Caesarea in Palestine all the way to the town of Joppa. He testifies that even in his own time, the land there was suitable for pasturing flocks. Furthermore, Joppa was not far from Lydda. There is, however, another region of the same name between Mount Tabor and the Lake of Tiberias, which Isaiah mentions, saying "Sharon is turned into marshes." But Jerome indicates that the first one was the one Luke meant here.

<margin>F</margin> 32 **By the name Tabitha**] In this place, Tabitha certainly cannot be a verb. Johannes Reuchlin <note>referred to as "Capnion"</note> thinks it should be read as "Thabia," for it is an Assyrian word that signifies "a she-goat" or "gazelle" to them. Certainly, those skilled in Hebrew letters admit that this name for a girl has some relationship to the verb "to see," which they call *Tzvi*. Similarly, in Greek, *dorcas* (gazelle) is derived from *derkomai* (to see), because that animal is thought to have very sharp eyesight. From this, those with sharp eyes are called *oxyderkeis*. However, Lorenzo Valla preferred that the Latin word *capream* (gazelle) be used by the translator. For Luke interprets it as "Dorcas," but he was writing in Greek.

33 **When they had washed her**] The *Glossa Ordinaria* <note>a standard medieval commentary</note> mentions that in some codices it was written "they washed her with ointments." But according to the custom of the Ancients, they first washed the body and then anointed it. However, it is not probable that such great expense was spent here on Dorcas.

34 **They sent two men**] In most Greek codices, it simply says *apestellan*, "they sent." In one I found "two men" added, but only in the margin.

35 **Do not delay**] For no reason the translator changed the person of the verb. It should be "do not delay to pass through to them" or "to themselves."

36 **Which Dorcas made for them**] *hosa epoiei met' auton ousa he Dorkas*, that is, "which Dorcas made while living with them," or "which she made while she was with them."

37 **And many believed in the Lord**] *epi ton Kyrion*, that is, "into the Lord." From this, it appears that it mattered nothing to the Translator whether you say "believe the Lord" or "believe in the Lord."

43 ...of Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. <margin>A</margin> 1 And it happened that he stayed many days in Joppa with a certain <margin>X. 1</margin> Simon, a tanner. But while they were preparing it, a trance fell upon him. 11 And he sees heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending to him like a <margin>11</margin> great sheet, bound at the four corners, being let down from heaven to the earth, <margin>C</margin> 12 in which were all the four-footed animals of the earth, and beasts, and <margin>12</margin> creeping things, and birds of the air. 13 And a voice came to him, "Rise, Peter, kill and eat." 14 But Peter said, "By no means, Lord, for <margin>14</margin> I have never eaten anything common or unclean." 15 And the voice spoke again a second time to him, "What God has cleansed, you must not call common." 16 This <margin>16</margin> happened three times, and again the vessel was taken up into heaven. 17 Now while Peter was doubting within himself what the vision he had seen might be, behold, the men who were sent from Cornelius, having asked for Simon's house, stood at the gate. 18 And having called out, they asked whether Simon, <margin>18</margin> who was called Peter, was a guest there. 19 While Peter was thinking about the vision, the Spirit said to him, "Behold, men are looking for you. 20 Rise therefore and <margin>D</margin> go down, and go with them, doubting nothing, for I have sent them." 21 Peter, going down to the men who were sent from <margin>21</margin> Cornelius to him, said, "Behold, I am the one you seek; what is the reason for which you have come?" 22 And they said, "Cornelius the centurion, a righteous man and one who fears God, and well spoken of <margin>22</margin> by the whole nation of the Jews, was warned by an oracle..."

38 *With Simon the tanner* ] <term>βυρσεῖ</term> <note>original: "byrsei"</note>. This trade was considered not only common, but even filthy. Oh, how great a guest, and the prince of the Apostolic height, to stay with such a host! Now the riches of the Church have grown immensely. We should congratulate this success, provided that the success of the Church truly lies in this, and if piety corresponds to that success.

<column-break/>

<margin>C</margin> 1 *Centurion of the cohort* ] It was less ambiguous in the phrase "from the cohort." For he was not the leader of the entire cohort, which contains about a thousand soldiers, but one from that cohort. And so it is in the Greek, <term>ἐκ σπείρης</term> <note>original: "ek speirēs"</note>. Moreover, Chrysostom, or whoever it was, interprets <term>Spira</term> as <term>νέμερον</term> <note>original: "nemeron" (a Latinism for "numerus" or unit)</note>, and here speaking in Latin.

2 *What is it, Lord?* ] <term>Τί ἐστι Κύριε</term> <note>original: "Ti esti Kyrie"</note>, that is, "What is it, Lord?", which means, "What is the matter?". And even the response of the Angel itself argues for this reading: "Your prayers, etc."

3 *He will tell you what you must do* ] This was not contained in the Spanish Edition, and it seems to have been added from the chapter that immediately preceded, and it is repeated shortly below in this very one.

4 *Two servants* ] <term>δύο τῶν οἰκετῶν</term> <note>original: "dyo tōn oiketōn"</note>, that is, "two of the household servants."

5 *And a soldier who feared the Lord* ] <term>στρατιώτην εὐσεβῆ</term> <note>original: "stratiōtēn eusebē"</note>, that is, a "pious soldier." Why was there a need for a paraphrase here? Lest the reader be offended that Cornelius used a soldier for a matter of piety, he added "pious."

6 *Who obeyed him* ] <term>τῶν προσκαρτερώντων αὐτῷ</term> <note>original: "tōn proskarterountōn autō"</note>, that is, "those who were at his side," or, as he translates elsewhere, "who served him." The other soldiers also obeyed, but these were always present for the sake of service.

7 *To the higher parts* ] <term>ἐπὶ τὸ δῶμα</term> <note>original: "epi to dōma"</note>. Which in the Gospels he translates as "roof." For it appears Peter climbed onto the roof, where some were accustomed to walk, so that he might pray under the open sky, as if closer to God, and also more removed from the noise of men.

8 *And he saw* ] Καὶ <term>θεωρεῖ</term> <note>original: "Kai theōrei"</note>, that is, "And he sees," in the present tense.

9 *A certain vessel like a sheet* ] Jerome, in his commentary on Isaiah, cites it as "a certain vessel of linen," nor does he do so in only one place; thus we should understand that the sheet itself was the vessel, and so he calls it such shortly after without the word "like."

10 *By the four corners [let down]* ] The Greeks read, "bound by the four corners and let down from heaven," <term>τέσσαρσιν ἀρχαῖς δεδεμένον καὶ καθιέμενον</term> <note>original: "tessarsin archais dedemenon kai kathiemenon"</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>E</margin> 11 *Four-footed animals, etc.* ] In Greek it has it thus: <term>τετράποδα τῆς γῆς, καὶ τὰ θηρία, καὶ τὰ ἑρπετὰ</term> <note>original: "tetrapoda tēs gēs, kai ta thēria, kai ta herpeta"</note>, that is, "four-footed animals of the earth, and beasts, and reptiles." Furthermore, <term>θηρία</term> <note>original: "thēria"</note> properly signifies a harmful beast to the Greeks, such as a viper or a wolf.

12 *Kill and eat* ] <term>θῦσον καὶ φάγε</term> <note>original: "thyson kai phage"</note>, that is, "sacrifice, or slaughter, and eat."

13 *Far be it, Lord* ] <term>Μηδαμῶς</term> <note>original: "Mēdamōs"</note>, that is, "By no means."

14 *Again a second time* ] <term>πάλιν ἐκ δευτέρου</term> <note>original: "palin ek deuterou"</note>, "again a second time."

15 *You shall not call common* ] It should have been translated "common things." Although in Greek the verb is <term>μὴ κοίνου</term> <note>original: "mē koinou"</note>, that is, "do not make common," which means, "do not treat as common." For this is what the Hebrews call things that are impure and forbidden.

16 *Three times* ] <term>ἐπὶ τρίς</term> <note>original: "epi tris"</note>, that is, "up to three times," although it was enough to say "thrice." The Translator has devised a new "beauty" of speech. Someone defended this place from being a grammatical error (solecism) on the grounds that the Translator rendered the Greek form. But one should have said "thrice." And the Latins say "around the Kalends of January" for an approximate time. However, to render a Greek figure into Latin is frequently to commit a grammatical error. And yet, from this error, I believe, was born a story which is commonly told and not without humor. A certain priest, a rather rustic shepherd of a rustic flock, when he was first about to baptize an infant, came across a note in the margin of the book from which he was pronouncing the solemn words: "Jump thrice" <note>original Latin: "Salta per ter"</note>. By these words, the scribe had intended to warn him that three pages were to be turned back <note>The Latin "Salta per ter" was meant as "Skip over three [pages]" but the priest read it literally as "Jump across three [times]"</note>. He immediately ordered the sexton to bring the pole on which the cross is carried. Having received it, he said, "This is good; I have never tried this before, but the matter demands it." Leaning on the pole, he jumped over the stone arch three times, and having thus returned to the book, he finished the rest.

17 *And immediately it was received back* ] <term>καὶ πάλιν ἀνελήφθη</term> <note>original: "kai palin anelēphthē"</note> that is, "and again it was taken up," presumably back to where it had come from.

18 *Peter, going down to the men* ] After these words, in several Greek manuscripts, there was added: <term>τοὺς ἀπεσταλμένους ἀπὸ τοῦ Κορνηλίου πρὸς αὐτὸν</term> <note>original: "tous apestalmenous apo tou Cornēliou pros auton"</note>, that is, "who had been sent by Cornelius to him."

# THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES. CHAPTER X.

...instructed by a holy Angel to summon you to his house, and to hear words from you. Therefore, having called them in, he received them as guests. On the following day, Peter set out with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him. 24 And on the next day they entered Caesarea; moreover, Cornelius was waiting for them, having called together his relatives and close friends. 25 As it happened that Peter entered, Cornelius met him, and falling at his feet, he worshiped him. 26 But Peter raised him up, saying, "Rise, I myself am also a man." 27 And talking with him, he entered, and found many who had gathered. 28 And he said to them, "You know that it is not lawful for a Jewish man to join with or approach a foreigner; but God has shown me not to call any man common or unclean. 29 For which reason I came without hesitation when I was summoned. I ask therefore, for what reason have you summoned me?" 30 And Cornelius said, "From four days ago until this hour I was fasting, and at the ninth hour I was praying in my house, and behold, a man stood before me in shining clothing, 31 And said, 'Cornelius, your prayer has been heard, and your alms have been remembered in the sight of God. 32 Send therefore to Joppa, and summon Simon, who is surnamed Peter; he is staying in the house of Simon the tanner by the sea; who, when he arrives, will speak to you.' 33 Immediately therefore I sent to you, and you have done well to come. Now therefore we are all present, with God as our witness, to hear all things whatever have been commanded to you by God." 34 Then Peter, opening his mouth, said, "In truth I perceive that there is no respect of persons with God, 35 But in every nation, he who fears Him and works righteousness is accepted by Him. 36 The word which God sent to the children of Israel, preaching peace through Jesus Christ (He is Lord of all). 37 You yourselves know the report that was spread throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee, after the baptism which John preached, 38 How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and power, who went about doing good..."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...was instructed by a holy Angel, 19 to summon you into his house, and to hear words from you. 20 Therefore, having called them in, he received them as guests. On the following day, Peter set out with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him. On the next day, 24 they entered Caesarea: moreover, Cornelius was waiting for them, having called together his relatives and close friends. As it happened that Peter entered, Cornelius came forward to meet him, and falling at his feet, he worshiped him. But Peter raised him up, saying, "Rise, I myself 26 am also a man." And talking with him, he entered, and 27 found many who had gathered, and he said to them, 28
<margin>B</margin> "You know, 21 it is not right for a Jewish man 22 to join with or approach a foreigner: but God has shown me not to call any man common or unclean. For which reason 23 I came without hesitation when I was summoned. I ask therefore for what cause you have summoned me?" And 30 Cornelius said, 24 "Four days ago until this hour I was fasting, and at the ninth hour I was praying in my house, and behold, a man stood before me 25 in shining clothing, and said, 'Cornelius, your prayer has been heard, 31 and 26 your alms have been remembered in the sight of God. Send therefore those who may go to Joppa, and summon 32 Simon, who is surnamed Peter; he is staying in the house of 27 Simon the tanner by the sea; who, as soon as he arrives, will speak to you.' Immediately therefore I sent to 33 you, and you have done well to have arrived. Now therefore we all, 28 with God as witness, 29 are present, to hear all things whatever have been commanded to you by God." Peter, opening his mouth, said, "In truth I find that there is no respect of persons with God, 30 But in 35 every nation, he who fears him and works righteousness is accepted by him. 31 The word which God sent 36 to the children of Israel, announcing peace through Jesus Christ—He is Lord of all. You yourselves know the report 37 that was spread throughout all Judea, 32 with the rumor first beginning from Galilee, after the baptism which John preached, 33 How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth 38 with the Holy Spirit and power, who went about doing good..."

---

<margin>E</margin> 19 **To summon you** <note>original: "Accersire te"</note>] Here again is a Greek grammatical structure. In Latin, it would have been said, "that he might summon you" <note>original: "ut accerseres te"</note>.
20 **Therefore, having called them in** <note>original: "Introvocatos ergo"</note>] In Greek, *Eiskalesamenos*, which means called in or invited.
21 **How it is abominable** <note>original: "Quomodo abominatum est"</note>] The Greek is *os athemiton est*, meaning "as it is not right" <note>original: "ut nefas est"</note>. For it would be hardly civil for Peter to say to a Gentile that it was "abominable" to speak with them. Rather, he says that according to the custom of his nation, it is not lawful to associate with him. And soon after,
22 **To join with** <note>original: "Conjungis"</note>] In Greek this is *kollasthai*, to cling to, or to be glued to.
23 **Without doubt** <note>original: "Sine dubitatione"</note>] The Greek is *anantirrhetos*, that is, without contradiction, or without hesitation.
24 **Four days ago, etc.** <note>original: "Nudius quartus die, &c."</note>] "From the fourth day until this hour I was fasting, and at the ninth hour praying," that is, "Four days from now until this hour I sat fasting, and at the ninth hour praying." From the words of the Translator, it appears Cornelius fasted and prayed for the entire four days. However, the sense is that he fasted and prayed on a certain day, which was the fourth day before the one on which he spoke with Peter. Indeed, he used the word "I was" <note>original: "emen"</note> for the condition of the hour, for "up to this time," and for "I was," some read it as "I sat" <note>original: "emen"</note>, with the first vowel shortened.
25 **In white clothing** <note>original: "In veste candida"</note>] The Greek is *lampra*, which means shining or splendid.
26 **Your alms were commemorated** <note>original: "Eleemosynae tuae commemoratae sunt"</note>] *Emnesthesan*, that is, were held in memory; for what is recounted is remembered.
27 **Of Simon the tanner by the sea** <note>original: "Simonis coriarii juxta mare"</note>] Following this, the Greek manuscripts add—*which is not found in our Latin versions at all*—"who, having arrived, will speak to you" <note>original: "hos paragenomenos lalese soi"</note>.
28 **In your sight** <note>original: "In conspectu tuo"</note>] The Greeks read "in the sight of God" <note>original: "enopion tou Theou"</note>. This is the speech of one confirming the simplicity of his mind, making God his witness. The *Glossa Ordinaria* <note>a standard medieval commentary</note> also notes something here.
29 **We are present to hear** <note>original: "Adsumus audire"</note>] He rendered the Greek form of speech, "we are present to hear" <note>original: "paresmen akousai"</note>, for that which is, "we are present so that we may hear," or "for the purpose of hearing."
30 **But in every nation** <note>original: "Sed in omni gente"</note>] In Greek *en panti ethnei*, that is, in whatever nation.
31 **The word he sent to the children** <note>original: "Verbum misit filiis"</note>] *Ton logon hon apesteile*, that is, "The word which he sent." The reader, offended by the incomplete sentence, pauses at "which." But indeed, the speech is an <term>anapodoton</term> <note>a sentence that lacks a grammatical conclusion</note>, or he has misused the accusative case instead of the nominative—that is, "the word which he sent to the children of Israel." Or, which I most approve of, this accusative "word" <note>original: "logon"</note> should be referred to the verb that follows, "you know" <note>original: "oidate"</note>. Then, because a <term>hyperbaton</term> <note>a transposition of words</note> and a parenthesis intervene, he repeats what he had previously called "word" <note>original: "logon"</note> with another term, "report" <note>original: "rhema"</note>, so that we might read it in this way: "The word which he sent to the children of Israel, announcing peace through Jesus Christ; (then the parenthesis is inserted: He is Lord of all) and immediately there follows: you yourselves know the word—I say—which was made throughout all Judea."
32 **For beginning** <note>original: "Incipiens enim"</note>] Someone added "for" <note>original: "enim"</note> on their own, as it is not in the Greek copies. And "beginning," *arxamenos*, in this place is of the neuter

<column-break/>

<margin>F</margin> gender, so that it refers back to "the word." Furthermore, "word" <note>original: "verbum"</note> in this place means nothing other than a matter tossed about in popular speech. He says that rumor arose from Galilee after the baptism of John. Then he sets down the subject of the rumor, namely, concerning Jesus of Nazareth.
33 **How he anointed him** <note>original: "Quomodo unxit eum"</note>] Some manuscripts had, "how he anointed him" <note>original: "hos echrisen auton"</note>. Some had, "whom he anointed" <note>original: "hos echrisen auton"</note>. However, that pronoun "him" <note>original: "eum"</note> should have been omitted by the Translator, as it is from the idiom of the Hebrew language. It is uncertain whether Peter said these things in Hebrew or in Greek. Nevertheless, even when the Apostles write in Greek, they bring much from the property of their own language. Just as today, those who speak Latin but are little educated, mix in something from their mother tongue, even unintentionally—for instance, a Frenchman from the French language, a Briton from the British, a German from the German. For the Apostles did not learn their Greek from the orations of Demosthenes, but from the conversation of the common people. For thus it seemed good to Divine Wisdom, to draw the world to its own opinion with no supports of mortal eloquence. Nor indeed was it necessary for that gift of tongues to be perpetual. It was enough for it to be present as often as use required. Just as they did not always raise the dead, nor always heal the sick, but only then when it pertained to the business of Religion and the Gospel. We read only once that the Apostles speaking in new tongues was a miracle. And in Chapter 19 of this volume, it is told of those who, having been baptized and receiving the Holy Spirit, spoke in tongues and prophesied; though it is more likely the Apostles at that time spoke in a single language, and it was done by divine power that they were understood equally by everyone. Nor is it necessary, I think, to immediately attribute to a miracle whatever was in the Apostles. They were men; they were ignorant of some things; they erred in some things. Even after receiving the Holy Spirit, Peter is rebuked and taught by Paul. Paul disagrees with Barnabas, even to the point of separation. And I do not know whether this more befitted the Gospel of Christ: that it be delivered to the common people in simple and unpolished speech, and that the speech of the Apostles be such as their clothing, their food, and their whole life—except for those things which pertain to piety and the soul—lest the arrogance of human eloquence should claim anything for itself in this business. Christ often left his disciples to human strengths; they hungered, they thirsted, they were exhausted by the labors of the body and the cares of the soul; they felt the weight of increasing age and other inconveniences of human fragility. But the same Lord was present whenever He wanted His majesty to be known to the world. And so He tempered the instruments of His own, whom He used for the propagation of the Gospel, insofar as He understood it to lead most to the reason of the divine counsel and to the salvation of mortals. Nor indeed is it a wonder if—since Egypt, Syria, Cilicia, and nearly all of Asia Minor commonly spoke Greek, first due to the empire of Alexander and soon that of the Romans—the Apostles knew Greek without a miracle, especially since they later lived for so many years among Greek speakers. For the Gospel was not written down by them immediately. Those who lived among...

<summary>This page contains Acts 10:22-38 in Greek and Latin, alongside Erasmus's extensive notes explaining Peter's visit to Cornelius. Erasmus famously argues that the Apostles' Greek was influenced by their native tongues and that their linguistic abilities were not always miraculous, but often natural products of their environment.</summary>

The scholarly commentary below the scripture text addresses a controversial debate: whether the Apostles were miraculously granted perfect, polished Greek, or if they spoke a more common, "unpolished" version of the language.</meta>

# THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES. CHAPTER XI.

<margin>A</margin> <margin>38</margin> ...doing good and healing all those who were oppressed <note>Greek: katadynasteuomenous, implying those under the tyranny of a ruler</note> by the devil, because God was with him. <margin>39</margin> And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the region of the Jews and in Jerusalem; whom they killed by hanging him on a tree. <margin>40</margin> This man God raised on the third day, and allowed him to become manifest, <margin>41</margin> Not to all the people, but to witnesses previously chosen by God—namely us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. <margin>42</margin> And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead. <margin>43</margin> To him all the Prophets bear witness, that through his name everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins. <margin>B</margin> <margin>44</margin> While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell upon all those who heard the word. <margin>45</margin> And the believers from the circumcision <note>Meaning Jewish converts to Christianity who still adhered to the law of circumcision</note>—as many as had come with Peter—were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even upon the Gentiles. <margin>46</margin> For they heard them speaking in tongues and magnifying God. <margin>47</margin> Then Peter answered, "Can anyone withhold the water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?" <margin>48</margin> And he ordered them to be baptized in the name of the Lord. Then they asked him to stay for some days. <margin>XI. 1</margin> <margin>C</margin> Now the Apostles and the brothers who were in Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God. <margin>2</margin> And when Peter went up to Jerusalem, those of the circumcision contended with him, <margin>3</margin> Saying, "You went in to men who have foreskins <note>Uncircumcised Gentiles</note> and ate with them." <margin>4</margin> But Peter began and explained it to them in order, saying: <margin>5</margin> "I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision: a certain vessel descending like a great linen sheet, let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came right to me."

---

<margin>D</margin> If someone lives among the Gauls <note>The French</note>, within a single year he speaks French, even if he previously knew nothing of that language. Are we then to wonder that the Apostles, over so many years, acquired a moderate facility in speech? Now, I am well aware that Paul mentions "kinds of tongues" and "interpretation of languages" among the gifts of the Spirit. He even boasts that he speaks in tongues more than all the others. However, what the nature of that gift was is perhaps not the subject for this place. But even if we grant that the gift was similar to what happened when the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the Apostles, we should add this: they did not attain a polished and exact mastery of languages through this gift, but only insofar as was most necessary for the business of the Gospel. 

Just as a person who received the gift of prophecy might be able to explain this or that passage, yet could not immediately explain any passage of Scripture at any time—because God imparts these gifts to individuals according to the "measure of faith," as Paul testifies—so it seems that if someone received a facility in languages for a specific occasion, they could not necessarily do the same before any audience on any subject. Indeed, we believe that the gift of prophecy was present in Augustine for explaining Holy Scripture, and yet in some places he does not grasp the literal sense of the text. Nor was the gift of languages lacking, I believe, in Jerome; and yet those who profess Hebrew letters disagree with him on several points. 

If someone should stubbornly contend that a mastery of all languages was divinely infused into the Apostles and that this gift was permanent—arguing, as Chrysostom does, that things done by divine power are more perfect than those done by the order of nature or human industry—how then is it that the speech of the Apostles is not only unpolished and unformed, but even imperfect, disordered, and at times plainly contains solecisms <note>Grammatical errors or non-standard usage</note>? For this cannot be denied; the reality of the text cries it out. It pleased the Holy Spirit to use simplicity of speech, yet speech that was pure, intact, and free from those defects that usually hinder the understanding of listeners. 

Greek interpreters, for whom Demosthenes and Plato were easy and clear, struggle everywhere with these texts. How often does Origen find the integrity of the Greek language lacking in Paul? How often is he offended by hyperbaton <note>inverted word order</note>, anapodosis <note>incomplete sentences</note>, and ambiguities? Chrysostom does not deny this, and Jerome admits it in many places, openly attributing to Paul a lack of skill in the Greek language. Jerome attributes more skill in Greek letters to Luke than to the others, for no other reason than that he was better trained in them, being from Antioch. He also admits Paul was more eloquent in the Hebrew language than in Greek, because he was born to the former and merely trained in the latter. Again, in one place, noting that the second Epistle of Peter differs in style from the first, he suggests the reason is that Peter used a different translator for it. But why would they need a translator if the Holy Spirit gave them perfect mastery of all languages? Especially since it is beyond dispute that all the Apostles wrote only in Greek, except for Matthew, according to the opinion of some. 

Why have interpreters dared to suggest that Paul missed Titus because Titus was more fluent in the faculty of Greek speech? These suggestions are not far from blasphemy if one holds tooth-and-nail to the idea that the gift of tongues provided total mastery. And yet, the most approved Doctors of the Church did not fear to set these things down in their books. I have discussed these matters at length because the subject of my annotations demanded it, lest anyone think I spoke impiously or rashly in saying the Apostles learned the Greek language not from the orations of Demosthenes, but from common conversation. For not from orations...

<margin>E</margin> ...but the authority of the Apostles must be measured by the quality of their minds. A pious person should no more be offended by the unrefined speech of the Apostles than by an unwashed body or a common garment. Indeed, Christ himself, as can be gathered from many conjectures, used the most common and popular speech, speaking in Syriac <note>Aramaic</note>, and perhaps sometimes in Chaldaic, and I do not know if he perhaps spoke in Greek occasionally; as was the speech of the people at that time, corrupted by various languages. Likewise, the Apostles, though writing in Greek, use many Roman words. The facts themselves persuade us of this opinion regarding the Apostles' speech, even if the authority of the greatest men did not support it. However, I have no intention of fighting for this or any other view if the Church thinks otherwise. We are admonishing the reader, not issuing oracles; we are always ready to yield to better arguments. 

I will add something ridiculous. When I wrote elsewhere that the language used by the Lord was not pure Hebrew, but corrupted by the Syriac and Chaldaic tongues, a certain "thrice-greatest" theologian from the Sorbonne shouted in a published book, "You beat the air in vain!" <note>Greek: matēn trachēlas</note>, because I had said the speech of the Lord and the Apostles was "corrupt." This same man would cry out, I suppose, if I had written that the Lord did not drink pure wine, but wine diluted with water. This is what the judgments of certain "Rabbis" <note>Here used sarcastically for rigid theologians</note> have come to.

**34 All those oppressed**] *katadynasteuomenous*. The translator renders this correctly, provided we understand "oppressed" here to mean those crushed by the tyranny and power of someone, for that is what the Greek word sounds like.
**35 In the region of the Jews**] *en te tē chōra tōn Ioudaiōn*, that is, "and in the region of the Jews," using a copulative conjunction.
**36 Preordained by God**] *prokecheirotonēmenois*: which sounds more like "chosen," as is done by voting. The Greek word is derived from extending the fingers, a gesture by which the people used to vote in ancient times.
**37 Who ate and drank**] The *Glossa Ordinaria* <note>A standard medieval collection of biblical commentaries</note> warns that in some Greek copies it was written "who for forty days," etc., although that is not found in our manuscripts.
**38 To receive remission of sins**] *aphesin hamartiōn labein*, that is, to obtain the remission of sins, or "that he would receive the remission of sins."
**39 All who believe**] *panta ton pisteuonta*, that is, "every one who believes," or "whoever should believe."
**40 From the circumcision**] *hoi ek peritomēs*, that is, those who were of the circumcision.
**41 And upon the nations**] *kai epi ta ethnē*, that is, "And upon the Gentiles." And the word is not *charis* (grace), but *dōrea* (gift). And because it says "it was poured out," it is used instead of "that it had been poured out."
**42 Can anyone [forbid] water**] The Greeks read it in this way: "Can anyone forbid the water, so that these should not be baptized?" And it appears this is the sense: Can anyone forbid that these people—who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have—should be baptized with water? As if the Spirit were greater than the water, and since the former has happened, it is no great thing if the latter follows. 
**43 Why did you enter**] "That you entered in to men having foreskins." For the word *hoti* (that) in this place is used for confirmation. They are not asking a question, but making an accusation, or at least a demand for explanation. The translator seems to have read *ti* (why) instead of *hoti* (that).

### XII.
<margin>XII.</margin> 1. And at the same time, Herod the king stretched forth his hands, to afflict some of the church. <margin>2</margin> 2. And he killed 

---

<margin>2</margin> *By no means, Lord]* <term>Medamos</term>; the same word that he had previously translated as "far be it." 

<margin>3</margin> *Gave repentance]* The Greek manuscripts add, "unto life" <note>Greek: eis zoen</note>. 

<margin>4</margin> *Under Stephen]* <term>epi Stephano</term>, that is, "in the time of Stephen," or "against Stephen." For a matter is said to be carried out "under" one who holds power. But in such cases, the Greeks add the genitive case. 

<margin>5</margin> *Spoke also to the Greeks]* Again, it is not "Hellenas" <note>Gentile Greeks</note>, but <term>Hellenistas</term>, which signifies those who are Jews by religion and origin but born elsewhere, who had not yet believed the Gospel. Otherwise, it might seem that the example of the baptized Cornelius had added so much courage to the Christians that they already dared to preach Christ even to the Gentiles. 

<margin>6</margin> *To remain in the Lord]* The Greek has a little more here, thus: "to adhere to the Lord with the purpose of the heart," <note>Greek: prosmenein te kardia prosmenein to Kyrio</note>, that is, "to adhere to the Lord with a steadfast heart." The Latins added the preposition "in" to this. What he said, "with purpose of heart," is the same as if he said from the soul and of free will, not out of fear or human shame. 

<margin>7</margin> *so that they were named]* "It happened that for a whole year they were gathered in the church and taught a great crowd, and first in Antioch the disciples were called Christians." <note>Latin translation of Acts 11:26</note>. That is, it happened that for a whole year they held fellowship with the congregation, and taught—

<column-break/>

<margin>F</margin> —a great multitude, and first in Antioch they called the disciples "Christians." For they <note>the outsiders</note> called them "Christians," but Luke calls them "disciples." Church history explains the sense. It says there that the disciples were first called Christians, as if taking the name from an ever-flowing fountain. <note>original Greek: "Hote ei tinon nomo chrematizein pro onomazesthai"</note>, a term Paul used in the seventh chapter of the Epistle to the Romans. The word seems to have been used because a surname is usually added based on the office we perform; just as "publicans" are so named because they collect public taxes, so "Christians" because they profess Christ. Furthermore, where he seems to misuse an active verb for a passive one, it is similar to what the Latins say, "the doctor is heard," instead of "he is called a doctor." 

<margin>8</margin> *To send in ministry]* <term>eis diakonian</term>. He calls the relief or supply a "ministry." For he "ministers" who supplies necessary things. Paul also uses the term in this way.

**M** *This Herod the king]* <term>epebalen</term>, that is, "he laid hands upon," or "he was laying hands upon." The one whom Luke calls "Herod" here, Josephus calls "Agrippa," and he is called "the Elder" to distinguish him from his son Agrippa. The name Herod seems to have been common to many, such as Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, and Philip, the brother of this Herod. This Herod Agrippa was the brother of Herodias, who was the wife of Herod the Tetrarch, and son of Aristo—

### Annotations

1 **Aristobulus**, who was the son of the elder Herod <note>Herod the Great</note>, and brother of Alexander, both of whom their father killed. Tiberius Caesar had thrown this <term>Agrippa</term> <note>Herod Agrippa I</note> into chains because in a splendid banquet, where he was receiving Gaius Germanicus <note>the future Emperor Caligula</note>, he openly prayed that Tiberius would soon pass away so he might see Gaius as Emperor. He was in prison for six months until the death of Tiberius. Gaius, who was given the surname Caligula, not only freed him but also granted him three tetrarchies <note>regions ruled by a local prince</note>—those of Philip, Lysanias, and the younger Herod who was exiled to Lyon—and further granted him the honor of the royal title. This is essentially how Josephus tells it in the second book of the <term>Jewish War</term>, chapter 8, and the <term>Jewish Antiquities</term>, chapter 9.

2 <gloss>Because it would please</gloss>] <note>original: "ὅτι ἀρεστόν ἐστι"</note>, that is, it was pleasing or agreeable. This is the same word that was previously translated as <term>fair</term> or <term>right</term> in: "It is not <term>right</term> to leave the word of God and serve tables."

3 <gloss>To seize</gloss>] <note>original: "συλλαβεῖν"</note>, that is, to <term>apprehend</term>.

4 <gloss>Now it was the days</gloss>] <note>original: "ἦσαν"</note>, in the plural number.

5 <gloss>Without ceasing</gloss>] <note>original: "ἐκτενὴς"</note>, that is, prolonged or intense, as it is translated in the Gospel, or <term>earnest</term>.

6 <gloss>And shoe yourself with your boots</gloss>] <note>original: "καὶ ὑπόδησαι τὰ σανδάλιά σου"</note>, that is, <term>tie on your sandals</term>.

7 <gloss>And considering</gloss>] <note>original: "Συνιδών τε"</note>, that is, <term>the matter having been weighed</term>, unless you prefer to refer it to recognizing the house.

8 <gloss>At the door</gloss>] The "at" is redundant. It means of the gate, <note>original: "πυλῶνος"</note>, not just a door <note>original: "θύρας"</note>. For since he says <term>the door of the gateway</term>, either the vestibule of the house had a door, as we see today in many buildings, or he meant the gate of the vestibule; he mentioned first the door that was exposed to the vestibule.

9 <gloss>To see</gloss>] <note>original: "ὑπακοῦσαι"</note>, that is, <term>to listen</term> or <term>to eavesdrop</term>. For it follows: "And having recognized Peter's voice."

<column-break/>

10 <gloss>Beckoning however</gloss>] <note>original: "Κατασείσας δὲ"</note>, <term>beckoning with the hand</term>.

11 <gloss>What had become of Peter</gloss>] <note>original: "τί ἄρα ὁ Πέτρος ἐγένετο"</note>, that is, what Peter had been made into; either because Luke allows himself to speak this way (as the Greeks say "he makes him" for "he does to him"), using a passive verb to ask what had happened; or because they suspected he had been changed by a metamorphosis into something else, according to the foolishness of the common people who believe men are turned into birds or spirits by magical arts.

12 <gloss>Ordered them to be led away</gloss>] <note>original: "ἐκέλευσεν ἀπαχθῆναι"</note>. It is not entirely clear whether Luke used the Roman custom of saying <term>to be led</term> for those who are led to execution, or simply to be led away from him into prison.

13 <gloss>Now Herod was angry with the Tyrians</gloss>] <note>original: "θυμομαχῶν"</note>. Laurentius <note>Laurentius Valla, a humanist scholar</note> thinks this should be translated as "fighting angrily or bitterly." Although I do not entirely agree with him here, for the Greek word is composed of <note>original: "θυμὸς"</note> (spirit/anger) and <note>original: "μάχεσθαι"</note> (to fight). It means he had not yet declared war, but was already meditating on war in his mind, unless they appeased his anger.

14 <gloss>Because their regions were nourished by him</gloss>] <note>original: "διὰ τὸ τρέφεσθαι αὐτῶν τὴν χώραν ἀπὸ τῆς βασιλικῆς"</note>, that is, because their region was nourished by the royal [supply]—you may understand this as grain, money, or food—whether this is understood as the commerce of the Jewish nation or the royal treasury.

15 <gloss>Voices of God</gloss>] <note>original: "Θεοῦ φωνή"</note>, that is, the Voice of God. The translator seems to have read "voices" <note>original: "φωναί"</note> in the plural. Although the Greek manuscripts consistently have the singular "voice," someone argues it should be read as "to the voice of God," as in a cry we shout to God, not to a man. But since Luke records that Herod was making a speech, it is more correct that they shouted by way of flattery that it was a [divine] voice, not a human one.

<margin>D</margin> **16 Honor to God]** <note>original: δόξαν</note>, that is, glory.
**17 And consumed by worms]** <note>original: καὶ γενόμενος σκωληκόβρωτος</note>, that is, having become susceptible to a disease where those who suffer from it are eaten by worms. There is an opinion that this is the same disease that physicians call the "louse disease" <note>pediculosis</note>, from which Lucius Sulla also died—certainly not a "lucky" end for him there.
**18 They returned from Jerusalem]** <note>original: εἰς Ἱερουσαλήμ</note>, that is, *into* Jerusalem. This is how the Greeks read it. Truly, I am not sure if it is a mistake, even though the Aldine Edition agrees.
**1 Simon who was called Niger]** It is remarkable that a Latin word <note>"Niger" means "Black" in Latin</note> was placed here by the Evangelist, even in its Latin form. For names of this type among us ending in *er* usually decline into *po*. Additionally, in place of "Simon," "Simeon" was written in some Greek copies as a three-syllable word.
**2 Brought up with]** <note>original: σύντροφος</note>, that is, educated together with him at the same time; although we know the term "collectaneus" is used by legal experts in the *Digest*, specifically in the well-known title regarding those set free by the rod <note>manumissis vindicta</note> from Law 3.
**3 As they were ministering]** <note>original: Λειτουργούντων</note>. This term is specific to those performing sacred rites. However, no sacrifice is more pleasing to God than the sharing of Evangelical doctrine.
**4 Set apart for me Saul]** The translator omitted the word "now" <note>original: δὴ</note>, in the phrase "Separate *now* for me."
**5 Called for]** <note>original: προσκαλεσάμενος</note>, that is, summoned or sent for.
**6 They went to Seleucia]** If you take this to mean the region, it would be more correct to say "into Seleucia." But if it refers to the city of that name, named after Seleucus, it is stated correctly. There are two Seleucias: one on the headland of Coele-Syria (which is called Syria-Antioch), the other in Pisidia; he speaks here of the former.
**7 And when they had come to Salamis]** In Greek, "And when they were in Salamis." This is a city in Cyprus, later called Constantia according to Jerome, which the Jews utterly destroyed in the time of Emperor Trajan, killing all the inhabitants.
**8 As far as Paphos]** This is a city in Cyprus once sacred to Venus. Just as Salamis is on the eastern edge of Cyprus, so Paphos is on the western edge, so that you may understand the whole island was traversed. Jerome reports that it was once noble, but in his time it had collapsed from frequent earthquakes so that only ruins showed what it had once been.
**9 Bar-Jesus]** The Greeks read <note>original: Βαριησοῦ</note>, which sounds like "Son of Jesus," though it is a compound word. It appears that the phrase "whose name was" <note>original: ᾧ ὄνομα</note> was not written by Luke, as that phrase would explain not the man's own name, but only his father's; his own name is added shortly after. But why did he add "is interpreted," as if indicating a translation? To what does this interpretation refer? To Bar-Jesus? It cannot be, since that sounds like "Son of Jesus." "Elymas" is the same as "one who causes straying," or, as Lyranus interprets it, "the measure of my God," or "the wealth of my God." For *El* means God...
