And immediately there fell on him a mist and darkness, and going about he sought someone to lead him by the hand. <margin>12</margin> Then the proconsul, when he had seen what happened, believed, wondering at the doctrine of the Lord. <margin>13</margin> And when Paul and those who were with him had set sail from Paphos, they came to Perga in Pamphylia: but John, departing from them, returned to Jerusalem. <margin>14</margin> But they, having traveled through the regions...

---

...my God, *El* wealth, from which there are some who think the "Mass" <note>original: Missam</note> was derived as the Christian sacrifice; to me, this does not seem likely. Does the interpretation refer to a different language? He was a Jew, and "Elymas" is neither Greek nor Latin. Why then does he say "Elymas is interpreted"? Unless perhaps he was called Bar-Jesus by his parents, and then, on account of his life's deeds, the name Elymas was given to him. Bede indicates that this word Bar-Jesus or "Barien" is corruptly written for "Barieu." He suspects the writing was corrupted because if you place a horizontal abbreviation mark over "Bar-Jesus" <note>original: Βαριησοῦ</note>, it signifies the same as "Royal" <note>original: Βασιλικὸς</note> when written out. However, he does not allow this holy name to be placed on a magician. As if that magician did not already have a name in common with the Apostle Peter, being called Simon <note>referring to Simon Magus</note>.
<margin>A</margin> **17 Digression]** <unclear>p...</unclear>
**10 But he resisted him]** The Greeks read "resisted *them*," so that it refers to Barnabas and Paul. For "him" in the Latin refers to the Word of God.
**11 But Saul, who is also Paul]** Lorenzo <note>Valla</note> disputes the name of Paul in this place, which we will touch upon briefly when we come to the Pauline Epistles. He who wishes to know Lorenzo's views should seek them from his own books. Certainly, before this he was always called Saul. Here is the first mention of the name Paul.
**12 And all deceit]** <note>original: ῥᾳδιουργίας</note>. He said "deceived" before; here something different should have been added. The Greek word signifies a propensity for committing any crime, from *rhadion* (easy) and *ergazomai* (I work). Although Hesychius considers the word to be many-valued, meaning the same as "faking," "shorthand writing," "evil," "scheming," "crafty"—that is, deceptive, or even writing quickly, shrewd, an artisan, or a shifter of shapes. Nor is it properly "to subvert," but <note>original: διαστρέφειν</note>, that is, to turn inside out, to deprave, to make the straight crooked.
**13 Those who might give him a hand]** <note>original: χειραγωγούς</note>, that is, hand-guides, to render it word for word, or those who might lead him by the hand.
**14 Paul and those who were with him]** <note>original: οἱ περὶ τὸν Παῦλον</note>. Word for word it sounds like "those around Paul," but according to the property of the Greek language, it simply means "Paul." Truly, lest he should seem to go unaccompanied, the translator rendered both senses: "Paul and those who were with him." For I think the phrase "those around Paul" is used here by the same figure of speech with which the Greeks say "those around Plato," meaning Plato himself.
**15 They came to Perga in Pamphylia]** He added the name of the province not for the sake of distinction, since there is only one Perge, but because the name of the town was not as well known to everyone as the province. But a little further down, for the sake of distinction, he added the name of the province "Antioch of Pisidia," because there are two Antiochs. One is in Coele-Syria according to Jerome, in which the Apostles Barnabas and Paul were ordained, the other in Pisidia, in which they preached.
**16 Passing through Perga they came to Antioch]** The Greek differs slightly: "But they, having passed through from Perga, arrived at Antioch." That is, they themselves, having left Perga, came to Antioch. Indeed, "they themselves" distinguishes them from John, who returned straight to Jerusalem, while they, having traveled through the towns in between, arrived at Antioch.
**17 And...**

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Paul and Barnabas's first missionary journey. Having left Cyprus and reached the mainland of Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), they travel from the coast at Perga up to Antioch in Pisidia. The text provides a transcript of Paul's major sermon delivered in the synagogue there, where he connects Jewish history to the arrival and resurrection of Jesus.</meta>

### THE APOSTLE. CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>14</margin> <margin>A</margin> They, passing through from Perga, came to Antioch of Pisidia; and entering into the synagogue on the day of the Sabbath, they sat down.

17 ***And signaling for silence with his hand***] <note>original Greek: "kai kataseisas tē cheiri"</note>. This is the same participle used here as was translated above as "beckoning with the hand." It literally means "with a movement of the hand." For by this gesture, those about to speak in an assembly used to demand silence. Persius says: "Silence was made by the majesty of the hand of the crowd."

18 ***Of the people of Israel***] <note>original Greek: "tou laou toutou"</note>, that is, "of this people."

19 ***He bore their manners***] <note>original Greek: "etropophorēsen autous"</note>. In Greek, this is a single word made of two parts, *trophophorein*, which is to bear or tolerate someone's character.

20 ***As if after & etc.***] The Greek differs somewhat from our Latin version. <note>original Greek: "Kai meta tauta hōs etesi tetrakosiois kai pentēkonta edōke kritas"</note>, that is, "And after these things, in about four hundred and fifty years, he gave judges."

21 ***Brought to Israel a savior***] <note>original Greek: "ēgage tō Israēl sōtēra"</note>, that is, "he led salvation to Israel." Israel in this place is in the dative case. The translator seems to have read "salvation" <note>original Greek: "sōtērion" or "sōtērian"</note>.

22 <margin>F</margin> ***Jesus***] The name "Jesus" <note>original: "Iēsoun"</note> is not added in the Greek in several copies, but only "Savior." Perhaps it was not yet the time to explain the name to those quite ignorant of this discourse. Although it seems probable to me that among the Greeks this was a scribal error from their notes. Perhaps from a lack of attention, a scribe made "salvation" <note>original: "sōtērian"</note>. Be that as it may, Chrysostom the Interpreter certainly does not add it, reading it this way: "From this man's seed, God, according to the promise, raised up a savior for Israel."

23 ***John preaching***] <note>original Greek: "Prokēryxantos Iōannou"</note>, that is, "John having previously preached."

24 ***Who do you think I am? I am not***] Either Luke misused the particle for "if," or it should be punctuated differently: "Who do you think I am?" so that there is an interrogation here. Then he responds, "I am not he," etc. For in Greek it is <note>original: "Tina me hyponoeite;"</note>. The common commentary, called the *Glossa Ordinaria*, also suggests it can be read as a question: "Who do you say that I am?"

25 ***And those among you who fear***] He has mixed two persons together so that they cannot be separated: "to you" and "who fear."

26 ***That they might kill him***] This can be understood as Pilate killing him. For the Greek phrase is ambiguous.

27 ***Fulfilled for your children***] <note>original Greek: "tois teknois autōn"</note>, that is, "for their children," meaning the children of the fathers.

28 ***As it is written in the second Psalm***] Some manuscripts had "in the second Psalm," some just "in the Psalm," omitting the number. But Jerome, explaining this Psalm, openly testifies that in the Acts this Psalm, which is second for us, is cited under the title of the first. From this he takes an argument: either that first Psalm, "Blessed is the man," was added as a preface, or that it and the next, "Why do the nations rage," are the same Psalm. Hilary reports the same thing, ingenuously confessing that this is cited as the first by Paul. Even Saint Augustine in his commentaries indicates this is "one" rather than the "first." Therefore, on the authority of these men, we have restored the original reading.

29 ***To the will of God***] <note>original Greek: "tē boulē"</note>, that is, "by the counsel." The sense in Greek has some ambiguity: "For David indeed, having served his own generation, by the counsel of God fell asleep."

41 Look, you scoffers, and marvel, and vanish; for I am working a work in your days, which you will not believe, even if someone explains it to you. 42 As they were going out of the synagogue of the Jews, the Gentiles <note>The Greek text here mentions "the nations" or Gentiles, though some manuscripts differ on the specific group requesting the speech.</note> entreated that these words be spoken to them on the following Sabbath. 43 When the congregation was dismissed, many of the Jews and devout converts followed Paul and Barnabas; who, speaking to them, persuaded them to continue in the grace of God. 44 On the following Sabbath, almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of God. 45 But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy, and they spoke against the things said by Paul, contradicting and blaspheming. 46 Then Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly and said, "It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first; but since you thrust it away and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. 47 For so the Lord has commanded us: 'I have set you as a light for the nations, that you should be for salvation to the ends of the earth.'" 48 Hearing this, the Gentiles rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. 49 And the word of the Lord was spread through the whole region. 50 But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, and they stirred up a persecution against Paul and Barnabas and expelled them from their borders. 51 But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and came to Iconium. 52 And the disciples were—

30 *That which was said in the Prophets*] He used the plural number <note>original: "numero primiero" [likely a typo for "plurali" or referring to the category of 'Prophets']</note>, although this is found in Habakkuk chapter one. Paul also followed the wording of the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> here. For Jerome, following the Hebrew truth, translates it thus: *Behold among the nations, and see, and wonder, and be astonished; for a work is done in your days, which no one will believe when it is told.*

31 *And you vanish*] <note>original: "καὶ ἀφανίσητε" (kai aphanisthete)</note>, that is, and disappear. It means to be taken out of the way so as to appear nowhere. For this, Jerome translates "be astonished."

32 *As they were going out*] In this place the Greek manuscripts differ somewhat: *As they were going out of the synagogue of the Jews, the Gentiles entreated that [these words] be spoken on the intervening Sabbath,* that is, as the Jews left the synagogue, the Gentiles asked them to speak the following Sabbath. Some add *the words to them* <note>original: "αὐτοῖς τὰ ῥήματα"</note>. However, the Greek phrasing is ambiguous; it can be taken either way: that the Jews left the assembly, or the Apostles left the assembly of the Jews.

33 *And of those worshiping God*] <note>original: "σεβομένων" (sebomenon)</note>, that is, of the religious. Of the strangers <note>original: "προσηλύτων" (proseluton)</note>, that is, proselytes. For so he translates it several times.

34 *Contradicted those things said by Paul, blaspheming*] The Greeks add one word, I know not if correctly: *contradicting and blaspheming* <note>original: "ἀντέλεγον τις καὶ βλασφημοῦντες"</note>.

35 *Boldly*] <note>original: "παρρησιασάμενοι" (parrhesiasamenoi)</note>, that is, having taken up confidence or audacity.

36 *Preordained*] <note>original: "τεταγμένοι εἰς ζωὴν" (tetagmenoi eis zoen)</note>, that is, ordained to life.

37 *The word was spread*] <note>original: "Διεφέρετο" (diephereto)</note>, that is, it was carried through, it was scattered. It appears the Translator read "Διεσπείρετο" <note>meaning "sown" or "dispersed"</note>.

38 *Religious women*] <note>original: "σεβομένας" (sebomenas)</note>. The same participle he just translated as "worshiping God," for the sake of variety.

39 *And honorable*] <note>original: "καὶ εὐσχήμονας" (kai euschemonas)</note>. This refers to a decorous manner and dress of the body, worthy of upright people.

**F** *It happened, moreover, in Iconium*] Since Iconium is the name of a city, not a region, one should say "at Iconium" <note>using the locative case "Iconii"</note>, not "in Iconium." The Constance manuscript had "at Iconium." There are two cities

41 'Take care, therefore, lest that which was spoken in the Prophets come upon you: See, you scoffers, and marvel, and vanish, for I work a work in your days, which you will not believe, if anyone tells it to you. 42 As they left the assembly of the Jews, the Gentiles asked that they might speak these words to them on the following Sabbath. 43 When the assembly was dissolved, many Jews and religious proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas, who, speaking to them, persuaded them to persevere in the grace of God. 44 On the following Sabbath, almost the entire city gathered to hear the word of God. 45 But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy, and they contradicted those things said by Paul, contradicting and speaking blasphemies. 46 Then, having taken confidence, Paul and Barnabas said: "It was necessary to speak the word of God to you first, but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. 47 For so the Lord commanded us: I have set you as a light for the nations, that you may be salvation unto the end of the earth." 48 Hearing this, the nations rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed. 49 Moreover, the word of the Lord was published throughout the entire region. 50 But the Jews incited the religious and honorable women, and the leading men of the city, and stirred up a persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and cast them out of their borders. 51 But they, having shaken the dust of their feet against them, came to Iconium. 52 Furthermore, the disciples were filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.

<margin>XIV.</margin> 1 It happened moreover at Iconium that they entered together into the synagogue of the Jews, and spoke in such a way that a vast multitude of both Jews and Greeks believed. 2 But the Jews who were unbelieving stirred up and corrupted the minds of the Gentiles against the brothers. 3 Therefore they stayed for a long time acting boldly by the support of the Lord, who gave testimony to the word of his grace, and granted that signs and wonders be done by their hands. 4 But the multitude of the city was divided; and some indeed stood with the Jews, but some with the Apostles. 5 <margin>D</margin> When an assault was made by the Gentiles as well as the Jews with their rulers, to treat them with violence and stone them, 6 having understood the matter, they fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe, and the surrounding region on every side. 7 And there they were preaching the Gospel. 8 <margin>F</margin> And a certain man at Lystra sat, weak in his feet, lame from his mother’s womb, who had never walked.

of this name: one in Lycaonia at Mount Taurus, the other in Cilicia. He speaks here of the former, unless I am mistaken.

2 *They stirred up to wrath [and] incited*] <note>original: "ἐπήγειραν καὶ ἐκάκωσαν"</note>, that is, they stirred up and corrupted. For "afflicted" <note>the Latin "afflixerunt"</note> did not fit here.

3 *That they might treat them with insults*] <note>original: "ὑβρίσαι" (hybrisai)</note>. In this place it means rather "to do violence." For they were not so afraid of mere insults. Furthermore, what follows about stoning explains the preceding word *hybrisai*.

4 *Understanding, they fled to the cities of Lycaonia*] <note>original: "Συνιδόντες" (Synidontes)</note>. It was more fitting to say, "The matter being understood," or "When they had observed this."

5 *And the whole region in the circuit*] <note>original: "καὶ τὴν περίχωρον"</note>, that is, and the surrounding region. What was the point of adding "the whole"? In this place, the Latin codices have more than the Greek ones. Namely this: *And the whole multitude was moved by their teaching; but Paul and Barnabas stayed at Lystra.* Bede, if I am not mistaken, admits in the *Glossa Ordinaria* <note>A standard medieval collection of biblical commentaries</note> that these words are not found in some Latin codices, and certainly they are not in this context. Nor does Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a prominent medieval commentator</note> touch upon these, although he writes a continuous commentary. However, in the edition to which the commentaries of Hugh of Saint-Cher <note>Caryensis</note> are added, we see it added in the marginal space: otherwise it does not have it, but it is in the Greek. Not even Chrysostom, in his diligent exposition of this passage, touches upon any of these words. Furthermore, a little earlier, after these words, *and the whole region in the circuit*, Bede notes that there is more in the Greek codices: *But God made peace, which is not found in some of ours.* Although today we see it in neither the Greek nor the Latin. Nor does Chrysostom touch upon what we indicated was missing. *Rise upright on your feet.* Here too, Bede in the *Glossa Ordinaria* indicates that it is held differently in Greek books. Namely in this manner: *He said with a loud voice, I say to you in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, rise upright on your feet.* And it is possible that such a thing was found in some Greek codex, as they vary wonderfully in the Acts. Certainly, in those I have seen, nothing here differs from our reading. I later found it added in the Spanish Edition: *I say to you in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.* It was not added in the Aldine edition.

6 *Lystra*] A city of Lycaonia, as well as Derbe, as Jerome records.

# THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES. CHAPTER XV.

<margin>8</margin> And there sat a certain man at Lystra, disabled in his feet, being a cripple from his mother's womb, who never had walked. <margin>9</margin> This man heard Paul speaking: who, looking steadfastly at him, and seeing that he had faith to <margin>10</margin> be healed, said with a loud voice, "Stand upright on your feet." And he leaped up and walked. <margin>11</margin> And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices in the Lycaonian language, saying, "The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men." <margin>12</margin> And they called Barnabas, Jupiter; and Paul, Mercury, because he <margin>13</margin> was the chief speaker. Then the priest of Jupiter, whose temple was before their city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates, and would have offered sacrifice with the crowds. <margin>14</margin> But when the Apostles, Barnabas and Paul, heard of this, they tore their clothes and ran in among the crowd, <margin>15</margin> crying out and saying, "Sirs, why are you doing these things? We also are men of like nature with you, preaching to you that you should turn from these vanities to the living God, who made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are in them: <margin>16</margin> Who in times past suffered all nations <margin>17</margin> to walk in their own ways. Nevertheless, He did not leave Himself without witness, in that He did good, and gave us rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and <margin>18</margin> gladness." And with these sayings, <margin>19</margin> they scarcely restrained the crowds from sacrificing to them. And there they stayed a long time with the disciples.

---

<margin>4 By the Apostles and Elders]</margin> Laurentius <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous 15th-century humanist scholar</note> discusses this passage at length, arguing that whenever a title of dignity is meant, the Greek word "Presbyter" should be used. For, according to Saint Jerome in more than one place, this is what Bishops were once called. Whenever it refers to age, the Latin word "Seniores" <note>Elders</note> should be used. Now the Translator, at his own whim—not to say without care—calls them sometimes "Presbyters" and sometimes "Elders."

<margin>5 And who knows the hearts]</margin> Again, we have a compound word <term>kardiognostes</term>, which means "one who knows the heart."

<margin>6 Purifying by faith]</term> <term>katharisas</term> is in the past tense; that is, "since he has purified their hearts with faith." For he is speaking of those who had already believed.

<margin>7 Simon related how]</term> <term>Symeon</term>. I do not know if this was written incorrectly by error, or if there is no difference between Simon and Symeon—except perhaps that Symeon is the Hebrew form and Simon the Greek inflection, much like Saul and Paul. At least, that is Valla's guess.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>8 And its ruins]</margin> <term>kateskammena</term>, which means "ruins" or "things torn down"; and so it is read in the more corrected Latin copies. Furthermore, the testimony he brings forward is from Amos, Chapter 9. However, James cites the sense of the prophecy in such a way that he does not exactly use the words of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, nor does it correspond in all respects to the Hebrew reading. For the Hebrew (according to Jerome's translation) says: <quote>On that day I will raise up the tabernacle of David that has fallen, and I will rebuild the gaps in its walls, and I will restore those things that collapsed, and I will rebuild it as in the ancient days, so that they may possess the remnants of Edom and all the nations, because my name has been called over them, says the Lord who does these things.</quote> Furthermore, according to the edition of the Seventy, we read it this way: <quote>On that day I will raise up the fallen tabernacle of David, and I will rebuild its fallen parts, and I will raise up its ruins <note>Greek: kateskammena</note>, and I will rebuild it as in the days of old, so that the rest of men may seek me, and all the nations upon whom my name has been called, says the Lord who does all these things.</quote> First, instead of "on that day," he put "after these things"; and he adds "and I will return" on his own. Furthermore, in the phrase "that the rest of men may seek me," he followed the Seventy, not the Hebrew books. Finally, where we cited "torn down" <note>Latin: suffossa</note>, the common copies have <term>physeso</term> <note>I will blow</note>, but that is an error. It should correspond to the Greek <term>kataskammena</term>, from the verb meaning "to demolish by digging under."

<margin>F</margin> <margin>9 Upon whom my name is called]</margin> The Translator correctly omitted "upon them" <note>Greek: ep’ autous</note>, which was added as a Hebrew idiom, even though it is not added in the Seventy.

<margin>10 Known from eternity]</margin> In Greek it is <term>gnosta</term>, a plural, meaning "His works are known to God," and "all" <note>Greek: panta</note> is added.

<margin>11 I judge]</margin> <term>ego krino</term>. It would be more appropriate to say "I am of the opinion." Next, "not to be troubled": where the Greek has <term>me parenochlein</term>, it would have been better translated as "not to be disturbed" or "not to have trouble added to them." For that is what the preposition <term>para</term> implies.

<margin>12 From ancient times]</margin> <term>ek geneon archaion</term>, that is, "from ancient generations," if he had wanted to translate word-for-word. We have already noted several times that "generations" is used to mean an "age."

<margin>13 Leading men among the brothers]</margin> <term>andras hegoumenous</term>, meaning those who go before or are prominent; that is, "foremost men" rather than just "first men."

<margin>14 Antioch and Syria and Cilicia]</margin> <term>kata ten Antiocheian kai Syrian kai Kilikian</term>. I believe that "Antioch" here refers to the region, not the city, because it is joined with Syria and Cilicia, which are certainly regions. Therefore, the preposition should have been added: "who are in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia." The Translator neither rendered the Greek nor the Latin... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence.</note>

# OF THE APOSTLES. CHAPTER XVI.

[...telling them] to be circumcised, and to keep the law, <margin>A</margin> to whom we gave no such command: It seemed good to us, <margin>25</margin> being assembled with one accord, to send chosen men to you, with our beloved Barnabas and Paul, men who <margin>26</margin> have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will also report the same things <margin>27</margin> by word of mouth. For it seemed good to the Holy <margin>28</margin> Spirit and to us to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things: namely, that you abstain <margin>29</margin> from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what is strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these things, you will do well. Farewell. So when they were dismissed, they <margin>30</margin> came to Antioch; and when they had gathered the multitude together, they delivered the letter. When they had read it, they rejoiced <margin>31</margin> <margin>B</margin> over its encouragement. And Judas and Silas, being <margin>32</margin> prophets themselves, exhorted the brothers <margin>18</margin> with many words <margin>19</margin> and strengthened them. And after staying <margin>33</margin> there for some time, they were sent off in peace by the brothers <margin>20</margin> to the Apostles. But it seemed good to Silas <margin>34</margin> <margin>21</margin> to remain there. Paul and Barnabas also remained <margin>35</margin> in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also. After <margin>36</margin> some days, Paul said to Barnabas, "Let us now return and visit our brothers in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing." <margin>22</margin> Now Barnabas advised <margin>37</margin> taking with them John, called Mark. <margin>23</margin> But Paul did not want to take along the one who had deserted them <margin>38</margin> <margin>C</margin> in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work. <margin>24</margin> And the disagreement was so sharp between them that they separated from each other; and Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus. But Paul <margin>40</margin> chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of God. And he went through Syria and Cilicia, <margin>41</margin> strengthening the churches. Then he came to Derbe and <margin>1</margin> XVI. Lystra, and behold, a certain disciple was there, named Timothy, <margin>1</margin> the son of a certain faithful Jewish woman, but his father was a Greek. The brothers who were at Lystra and Iconium spoke well <margin>2</margin> of him. Paul wanted this man to go with him, and he took <margin>3</margin> and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, <margin>D</margin> for they all knew that his father was a Greek. As they went through the cities, they delivered to them <margin>4</margin> for their observance the <margin>2</margin> decrees that had been ordained by the Apostles and Elders at Jerusalem. So the <margin>5</margin> churches were strengthened in the faith and increased in number daily. Now when they had gone through Phrygia and <margin>6</margin> the region of Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit <margin>3</margin> to speak the word in Asia. After they had come to Mysia, <margin>7</margin> they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit did not permit them.

<column-break/>

<margin>E</margin> ...he took account of the situation. For if it is repeated elsewhere, he said *Gallia* instead of *in Gallia* <note>meaning "in Gaul"</note>; certainly it is an unusual and harsh way of speaking.

<margin>25</margin> *To whom we gave no command*] Before these words, the Greek manuscripts add, <note>original Greek: λέγοντες περιτέμνεσθαι καὶ τηρεῖν τὸν νόμον</note>, that is, *commanding you to be circumcised and to keep the law.* Bede pointed this out.

<margin>26</margin> *Gathered together in one*] <note>original Greek: γενομένοις ὁμοθυμαδόν</note>, that is, *being of one mind, or by common consent of spirits.*

<margin>27</margin> *From those sacrificed to idols*] <note>original Greek: τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων</note>, that is, *from things offered to images.* I suspect the Translator <note>referring to the author of the Latin Vulgate</note> wrote *from things sacrificed to images.* For Ambrose frequently uses this word. Although Irenaeus refers to this passage several times, he does not mention "strangled things," but only "things sacrificed to idols, blood, and fornication."

<margin>28</margin> *With many words*] <note>original Greek: διὰ λόγου πολλοῦ</note>, that is, *with much speech*, or in many words. But why use the superlative "plurimo" <note>very many</note>? What was the point of turning a simple positive word into a superlative?

<margin>29</margin> *The brothers were cared for and they confirmed them*] <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐπεστήριξαν</note>, that is, they added further confirmation to those who were already confirmed by the letter itself: such is the force of the prefix *epi-*.

<margin>30</margin> *To those who had sent them*] <note>original Greek: πρὸς τοὺς Ἀποστόλους</note>, that is, *to the Apostles*. It appears the Translator read <note>original Greek: πρὸς τοὺς ἀποστείλαντας</note> <note>meaning "to those who sent [them]"</note>.

<margin>31</margin> *To remain there*] <note>original Greek: ἐπιμεῖναι αὐτοῦ</note>, that is, *to stay in that very place.* However, after these words, the phrase that follows in our Latin copies—*But Judas went back alone to Jerusalem*—I do not find in the Greek. In fact, I did not even find the phrase *But it seemed good to Silas to stay there* except in one single manuscript, and even there it was added in the margin. It seems this might have happened through a scribe's error.

<margin>32</margin> *But Barnabas wanted*] <note>original Greek: ἐβουλεύσατο</note>, that is, *he advised, or he was thinking.* The Translator seems to have read *ebouleto* <note>a simpler word for "wanted"</note>.

<margin>33</margin> *But Paul asked*] The Translator seems to have wanted to soften the suspicion of a rift; for in Greek it is <note>original Greek: ἠξίου</note>, that is, *he judged or deemed it fair.* Nor is it simply that Mark had "departed," but <note>original Greek: τὸν ἀποστάντα</note>, that is, *one who had revolted or defected*, a participle of the word from which we get *apostate*, a deserter or defector.

<column-break/>

<margin>24</margin> *And a disagreement arose*] Again, the Translator sought to soften the Greek word, which is *paroxysmos* <term>paroxysm: a sudden attack or violent expression of emotion</term>, which signifies more than just a "disagreement." For the root word means *to irritate, provoke, or embitter.* It signifies, therefore, that they disagreed in this matter even to the point of agitation, and so much so that they were torn apart. They were Apostles, yet they were still human. Origen candidly admits that disagreements of this kind occur even among the best of men, while each abounds in his own sense of judgment; yet these do not proceed so far that Christian charity is severed or the religion of Christ is weakened. Furthermore, it is foolish to try to heal this "inconvenience" in the text by ignoring the consensus of the Greek manuscripts. We have translated it: *So sharp was the dispute between them.* Regarding the phrase *instructing them to keep the precepts of the Apostles and Elders*, I do not find these words in the Greek manuscripts. They seem to have been moved here from the following chapter, where it says *they delivered to them the decrees to keep.*

<margin>F</margin> <margin>1</margin> *The son of a certain faithful widow*] In the Greek we read it thus: <note>original Greek: υἱὸς γυναικός τινος Ἰουδαίας πιστῆς</note>, that is, *the son of a certain faithful Jewish woman.* And the phrase that follows corresponds to this reading: *but with a Greek father.* For he contrasts the Greek father with the Jewish mother. But a scribe, perhaps not paying attention, turned "Jewish" (*Judaeae*) into "widow" (*viduae*) by rearranging a few letters. Indeed, Rabanus also noted in the "Ordinary Gloss" <note>a standard medieval Bible commentary</note> that in some books it was written "Jewish." Furthermore, the word here is not "Gentile" (*Ethnicus*), but "Greek" (*Hellēn*), a word the Translator renders variously, sometimes as *Greek*, sometimes as *Gentile*.

<margin>2</margin> *The dogmas which were decreed*] <note>original Greek: κεκριμένα</note>, that is, *judged; he rightly translates this as "decreed."* Furthermore, *dogmata* is a Greek word signifying decrees or formal decisions, not "doctrine" as the common people think. The Translator elsewhere renders *dogma* as "decree" or "edict."

<margin>3</margin> *To speak the word in Asia*] He means that part of Asia—not the entire region commonly called Asia Minor, which is surrounded by sea on all sides except the East and includes Phrygia, Pamphylia, Lycaonia, Cilicia, and Galatia—but specifically that province which...

And when she was baptized, and her household, she pleaded with us, saying, "If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay." And she persuaded us. <margin>16</margin> 16. Now it happened, as we went to prayer, that a certain girl having a spirit of divination <note>Greek: *Pythonos*, referring to the Pythian spirit of the Delphic oracle</note> met us, who brought much profit to her masters by fortune-telling. <margin>17</margin> 17. She followed Paul and us and cried out, saying, "These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to us the way of salvation." <margin>18</margin> 18. And this she did for many days. But Paul, being greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, "I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her." <margin>19</margin> 19. And it came out that same hour. But when her masters saw that the hope of their profit was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace to <margin>20</margin> the rulers. 20. And bringing them to the magistrates, they said, "These men, being Jews, are troubling our city; <margin>21</margin> 21. and they proclaim customs which are not lawful for us to receive or observe, being Romans." <margin>22</margin> 22. And the crowd rose up together against them; and the magistrates, having their clothes torn off, commanded them to be beaten with rods. <margin>23</margin> 23. And when they had laid many stripes on them, they threw them into prison, commanding the jailer to keep them safely. <margin>24</margin> 24. Who, having received such a command, threw them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the <margin>25</margin> stocks. 25. But at midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them. <margin>26</margin> 26. Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s chains were loosed. <margin>27</margin> 27. And the jailer, waking out of sleep and seeing the prison doors open, drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing the prisoners had escaped.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the Spirit. <note>original: "ritus"</note> But when they had passed through Mysia, they <margin>8</margin> went down to Troas. And a vision was seen by Paul <margin>9</margin> during the night. A certain man of Macedonia was standing, and entreating him, and saying, "Set out for Macedonia, help us." But when he saw the vision, immediately we sought to <margin>10</margin> set out for Macedonia, being assured that the Lord had called us to evangelize them. When we had set sail <margin>11</margin> therefore from Troas, by a straight course we came to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, <margin>12</margin> which is the first city of that part of Macedonia, a colony: we were moreover in the same city for some days, <margin>B</margin> staying. And on the day of the sabbaths we went out from the city <margin>13</margin> near the river, where there used to be prayer, and sitting, we spoke to the women who had come together. And <margin>14</margin> a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purples of the city of Thyatira, worshiping God, heard, whose heart the Lord opened, so that she might attend to these things which were said by Paul. But when she was baptized, and <margin>15</margin> her house, she entreated, saying, "If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, enter into my house, and remain": and she compelled us. But it happened as we were going <margin>16</margin> to prayer, that a certain girl having a spirit of Python met us, who provided a great gain to her masters by divining. This girl, <margin>17</margin> following Paul and us, was crying out, saying, "These men are servants of the most high God, who announce to you <margin>C</margin> the way of salvation." But this she did for many days: but <margin>18</margin> Paul taking it ill, and turning, said to the spirit, "I command you by the name of Jesus Christ, that you go out from her." And it went out in the same hour. But her masters seeing <margin>19</margin> that the hope of their gain had gone away, having seized Paul and Silas, they dragged them into the forum to the leaders, and <margin>20</margin> offering them to the magistrates, they said, "These men disturb our city, since they are Jews, and <margin>21</margin> they announce institutes which it is not permitted for us to receive, nor to keep, since we are Romans." And the <margin>22</margin> crowd ran together against them: and the magistrates, with their garments torn off, commanded them to be beaten with rods. <margin>D</margin> And when they had imposed many blows on them, they <margin>23</margin> threw them into prison, commanding the guardian of the prison, that he should diligently guard them. Who, when he had received such a precept, <margin>24</margin> threw them into the interior prison, and their feet he bound in the wood <note>meaning the stocks</note>. But at midnight Paul and Silas <margin>25</margin> praying were praising God: moreover those who were bound were listening to them. But suddenly a great earthquake <margin>26</margin> was made, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and the bonds of all were loosed. But the guardian of the prison, having been <margin>27</margin> awakened, when he saw the gates of the prison open, with his sword drawn was about to kill himself, thinking the prisoners had fled.

---

<margin>E</margin> ...which is very close to Ephesus; for this is properly called Asia Minor, which he seems to mean here.
<margin>4</margin> *They went down to Troas*] For that city is on the coast of Asia, also called *Antigonia*.
<margin>5</margin> *We came by a straight course*] One Greek word <note>original: "εὐθυδρομήσαμεν"</note> is a circumlocution for three Latin ones, that is, "we hastened by a direct route." For "course" <note>original: "cursus"</note> is also properly said of those sailing. We came to *Samothrace*. That is an island in the Pagasetic Gulf, in the region of Thrace, with a name composed from *Samiri* and *Thracians*.
<margin>6</margin> *Neapolis*] It is not the one which the Spanish now hold in Italy <note>Naples</note>, but another in Caria in Asia. Jerome seems to have felt this while collecting names of places in the Acts of the Apostles, but I think he was mistaken. There are those who prefer *Neapolis* to be in Thrace or Macedonia according to Ptolemy, not far from Philippi. And this opinion is more probable: for there are many of this name. Philippi is a city in the first part of Macedonia.
<margin>7</margin> *City colony*] <note>original: "κολώνια"</note> Luke used the Latin word, as it appears it was then used by the Greeks. For he added "colony" because that city was inhabited by those led from elsewhere.
<margin>8</margin> *Staying some days*] The *Glossa Ordinaria* <note>a standard medieval Bible commentary</note> indicates that in some books it was "conferring" instead of "staying." For <note>original: "διατρίβοντες"</note> means those who stay, and <note>original: "διατρίβονται"</note> those who confer and dispute; hence the Greeks call Scholastic disputes *diatribes*. "Staying" <note>original: "διατρίβοντες"</note> sounds more like "dwelling."
<margin>9</margin> *Outside the gate*] <note>original: "ἔξω τῆς πόλεως"</note> that is, "out of the city," or with the preposition omitted, "we left the city." Which is a common figure of speech, "out the gate."
<margin>10</margin> *Where prayer seemed to be*] <note>original: "οὗ ἐνομίζετο προσευχὴ εἶναι"</note> that is, where it was thought there would be prayer, or certainly, as I would prefer, where prayer was *accustomed* to be: since *nomos* <note>law/custom</note> sometimes also sounds like custom, and *nomizesthai* means "to be accustomed."
<margin>11</margin> *Lydia a seller of purple*] <note>original: "πορφυρόπωλις"</note> that is, a female seller of purples, from the name *porphyra* (purple) and *polein* (to sell). For "purple-sellers" <note>original: "purpurarii"</note> seem more to be called those who collect the purples, that is, divers, or those who dye. Jerome interprets it as "a seller of purple" in the entry for *Thyatira*, which is a word expressed in the plural number and neuter gender; it is a city of Lydia in Asia. Whence, because she is called "Lydia," it did not seem to be the girl's name but the name of the region, unless "by name Lydia" had been added.
<margin>12</margin> *And she compelled us*] <note>original: "καὶ παρεβιάσατο ἡμᾶς"</note> It is more "she urged us" than "she forced us."
<margin>13</margin> *A certain girl*] <note>original: "παιδίσκην τινά"</note> that is, a certain handmaid, because mention is soon made of her masters, so that we may understand her condition is being explained, not the age of the woman.
<margin>14</margin> *Having a spirit of Python*] The Greeks read <note>original: "Πύθωνος"</note>, that is, of Python. That was the name of the dragon which Apollo finished off with his arrows, whence he himself was called "Pythian." Then that spirit, by which those inspired predicted the future, began to be called "Pytho."
<margin>15</margin> *But Paul grieving*] <note>original: "διαπονηθείς"</note> which elsewhere he translates as "to take it ill."
<margin>16</margin> *Magistrates*] <note>original: "τοῖς στρατηγοῖς"</note> which sounds more like "chiefs of the <margin>F</margin> army," although it is accepted for a magistrate who once used the attendance and service of soldiers.
<margin>17</margin> *A custom which is not lawful*] <note>original: "ἔθη"</note> that is, "customs," but he correctly changed the number, because "customs" sounds like something else than "a custom." He could have said, "other traditions," or "other institutes," not to mention for now that in his custom he translates *himatia* <note>garments</note> as "tunics."
<margin>18</margin> *Their tunics being torn*] The Greek speech is such that it is uncertain whether the magistrates tore the Apostles' tunics or their own.
<margin>19</margin> *Worshiping they praised God*] <note>original: "προσευχόμενοι ὕμνουν"</note> Why "adoring" <note>original: "adorantes"</note> rather than "praying"? Since the Greek word <note>original: "προσεύχομαι"</note> signifies both, indeed "to pray" rather than "to adore," by the witness also of Augustine. "And they praised" <note>original: "ὕμνουν"</note> that is, they were singing and praising with hymns.

<margin>21</margin> *He rushed in* ] <note>original: *introgressus est* / *eise-pēdēse*</note> This means he leaped in, or flew in, or rushed in, or broke in, so that you express the force and speed of his entry, just as the Greek word does.
<margin>22</margin> *He fell at the feet of Paul and Silas* ] The translator added "at the feet" on his own. In Greek it is simply, "he fell before Paul." But the translator added it rightly to avoid ambiguity.
<margin>23</margin> *And all his house* ] <note>original: *kai hoi autou*</note> That is, "and his family members, or those of his household."
<margin>24</margin> *With his whole household* ] <note>original: *panoicí*</note> The translator used three words for this Greek adverb. However, it is more fitting that "with the whole household" refers to the following participle "having believed." Nor is it simply that he was "glad," but "he exulted" <note>original: *ēgalliatō*</note>. For he usually translates it this way.
<margin>25</margin> *The magistrates sent officers* ] <note>original: *rhabdouchous*</note>, named from carrying rods. We translate this as "sergeants" <note>original: *viatores*</note>, because it is their custom also to carry rods. For these are properly the ones through whom magistrates announce what they want.
<margin>26</margin> *Do they now cast us out* ] A little before, "they cast us out secretly" was in the Greek; here a different verb is used, "let them lead us out" <note>original: *exagagetōsan*</note>. For the former was suitable for those being pushed out secretly, while this suits those being led out openly, not without a formal apology.
<margin>27</margin> *They entered to Lydia* ] It is uncertain whether this refers to the woman Lydia who was recently converted, or to the region; but the first sense is more likely to me. For Lydia is in Asia Minor, and soon they arrive at Amphipolis and Apollonia, which are very close to Philippi. I do not think there is any difficulty here, except that the Greek preposition "into" <note>original: *eis*</note> does not seem to fit a person as well as "toward" <note>original: *pros*</note>, unless we take "Lydia" to mean "the house of Lydia." <margin>F</margin>

the scriptures. For from these he brought forward testimonies. But I wonder
what the translator followed when he put *insinuating* <note>original: *insinuans*</note> in this place, since it is preceded by *opening*. For *to insinuate* is to introduce a fight secretly, which conflicts with the word *opening*; unless perhaps he read "expounding" <note>original: *hypotithemenos*</note> for "setting forth," so that he expounded the Scriptures to the Jews, but in passing, where the occasion allowed, made mention of Christ, whom they were not going to believe unless they were charmed by the exposition of the Scriptures.
<margin>4</margin> *Whom I announce to you* ] Since the person speaking has suddenly changed,
why does he not also add "he said" here? As he did at the beginning of this work, "Whom you heard," *he says*, "through my mouth."
<margin>5</margin> *And of the worshipping Gentiles* ] <note>original: *tōn te sebomenōn Hellēnōn polü plēthos*</note>, that is, "a great multitude of the religious Greeks."
Who understood that "worshipping" means the pious and religious? I
have already warned more than once that "Greek" in the letters of the Apostles is sometimes
put for the *nation*, and sometimes for the *heathen*.
<margin>6</margin> *The jealous Jews* ] The Greek adds some words here:
"But the Jews who did not believe, moved with jealousy, and taking some men of the marketplace," that is, "With zeal indeed those Jews who did not believe were moved, and having taken some marketplace-loafers." For in Greek it is *agoraiōn*, which the translator rendered as "of the common people." Although the Greek manuscripts vary somewhat in this place.
<margin>7</margin> *And standing by the house* ] What do I hear? Were they blockading the house
of Jason? It is actually *epistantes*, that is, "having attacked," or "pressing upon and
looming over."
<margin>8</margin> *And certain brothers* ] Whenever he uses "brothers" on its own, he understands
Christians, whom he also sometimes calls "disciples." Here Bede,
who is cited in the Ordinary Gloss, notes that the Greek has "and
certain *other* brothers," concluding from this that Jason was also a
Christian. But I have not found "others" <note>original: *allous*</note> among the Greeks.
<margin>9</margin> *These who stir up the world* ] "The world" should undoubtedly be read,
*tēn oikoumenēn*, which he frequently translates as "the orb of the lands." Nor is it
"stir up," but *anastatōsantes*, that is, "they have moved," or "overturned," that is,
those who have thrown the state of things into confusion, which usually happens with revolutionary acts. The sense is: what they have done everywhere, they are here to do also.
<margin>10</margin> *Whom Jason received* ] <note>original: *hypodedektai*</note>, that is, received secretly or
stealthily, because of the preposition *hypo*.
<margin>11</margin> *Against the decrees of Caesar* ] <note>original: *tōn dogmatōn*</note>. Which a little before he expressed as "dogmas" just as it was in the Greek.

# THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES. CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>8</margin> And they troubled the crowd and the city rulers <note>Greek: *politarchas*</note> who heard these things. <margin>9</margin> And when they had taken security from Jason and the rest, they released them. <margin>10</margin> And the brothers immediately sent away both Paul and Silas by night to Beroea; who, when they arrived, went into the synagogue of the Jews. <margin>11</margin> Now these were more noble <note>Greek: *eugenesteroi*</note> than those in Thessalonica, for they received the word with all readiness, examining the scriptures daily to see if these things were so. <margin>12</margin> Many of them therefore believed, as well as not a few of the honorable Greek women and men. <margin>13</margin> But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was also proclaimed by Paul in Beroea, they came <margin>B</margin> <margin>14</margin> there also, stirring up the crowds. Then the brothers immediately sent Paul away to go <gloss>b</gloss> as far as the sea; but both Silas and Timothy remained there. <margin>15</margin> And those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens; and having received a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as quickly as possible, they departed. <margin>16</margin> Now while Paul was waiting for them in Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. <margin>17</margin> So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there. <margin>18</margin> Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him; and some said, "What does this babbler <note>Greek: *spermologos*, literally 'seed-picker'</note> wish to say?" Others said, "He seems to be a proclaimer of foreign demons <note>Greek: *daimonion*, here meaning gods or spiritual beings</note>," because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection to them. <margin>C</margin> <margin>19</margin> And taking hold of him, they brought him to the Areopagus <note>The "Hill of Ares," the high court of Athens</note>, saying, "May we be able..."
<meta>catchword: ...able</meta>

---

<margin>12 They dismissed Paul and Silas]</margin> <term>sent away both Paul and Silas <note>original: "ἐξέπεμψαν τὸν τε Παῦλον καὶ τὸν Σίλαν"</note></term>, that is, *they sent out both Paul and Silas*. And presently, *some write Berrhoea*, although Stephanus calls it <term>Beroia <note>original: "Βέροιαν"</note></term> and <term>Beroe <note>original: "Βερόην"</note></term>, that is, *Beroea*. It is a city of Macedonia, not far from Pella, the birthplace of Alexander the Great.
<margin>13 Who when they had come into the synagogue of the Jews entered]</margin>
The word order is different among the Greeks, <term>who having arrived, went away into the synagogue of the Jews <note>original: "οἵτινες παραγενόμενοι εἰς τὴν συναγωγὴν ἀπῄεσαν τῶν Ἰουδαίων"</note></term>, that is, *who after they had arrived, went off into the synagogue of the Jews*. So that the first part refers to the city, the next to the assembly. Then, he would have more correctly translated <term>nobler</term> as <term>most noble</term>, although I see Catullus, and Pliny, <margin>D</margin> and with them Quintus Curtius, occasionally following the Greek custom of using the comparative in place of the superlative, <term>more noble than those in Thessalonica <note>original: "εὐγενέστεροι τῶν ἐν Θεσσαλονίκῃ"</note></term>, that is, *born of the highest rank among those who were in Thessalonica*. Although the sense of the Greek speech is quite ambiguous, it seems more likely here to be, *these, however, were of more generous character than the Thessalonians*, meaning that this "nobility" refers to a mind that is more ready and more teachable.
<margin>14 With all eagerness]</margin> <term>of readiness <note>original: "προθυμίας"</note></term>, that is, *with promptness of mind*, or willingly, or with inclined souls. And presently, *if these things were so*, it should have been translated as *whether*.
<margin>15 Of the Gentile women]</margin> <term>of the Greeks <note>original: "Ἑλληνίδων"</note></term>, that is, *Greek women*. And presently, *honorable*, is <term>of good form <note>original: "εὐσχημόνων"</note></term>, which, as we have said, pertains to the dignity of one's habit, dress, and gait.
<margin>16 In Thessalonica Jews]</margin> <term>the Jews from Thessalonica <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς Θεσσαλονίκης Ἰουδαῖοι"</note></term>, that is, *Thessalonian Jews*.
<margin>17 Stirring up and troubling]</margin> <term>shaking the crowds <note>original: "σαλεύοντες τοὺς ὄχλους"</note></term>, that is, *stirring up the mobs*. I have not found "troubling" in the Greek manuscripts, except in one Greek codex, and that was written in the margin: <term>shaking and troubling the crowds <note>original: "σαλεύοντες καὶ ταράσσοντες τοὺς ὄχλους"</note></term>. I suspect it was added by someone who wanted to explain the word with a similar one.
<margin>E</margin>
<margin>18 That he might go as far as the sea]</margin> <term>as if toward the sea <note>original: "ὡς ἐπὶ τὴν θάλασσαν"</note></term>, that is, *as though to the sea*. The translator seems to have read <term>until to the sea <note>original: "ἕως ἐπὶ τὴν θάλασσαν"</note></term>. It is uncertain, however, whether Paul reached Athens by ship or by a journey on foot. Except that it is more probable he sailed, either because it is reported he was led down to the sea, or because there is no mention of what Paul did on the journey, though he would have had to pass through so many cities; and he is not accustomed to pass through any city in silence, unless perhaps he was silent because he was alone and deprived of his colleagues.
<margin>19 Having received a command to them]</margin> <term>receiving a command to them <note>original: "λαβόντες ἐντολὴν πρὸς αὐτοὺς"</note></term>, that is, *when they had received a command to Silas*.
<margin>20 That as quickly as]</margin> It was more Latin and more congruent with the Greek speech to say, *as most quickly*. For in Greek it is <term>as most quickly <note>original: "ὡς τάχιστα"</note></term>, that is, *as rapidly as possible*.
<margin>21 His spirit was incited]</margin> <term>it was provoked <note>original: "παρωξύνετο"</note></term>, that is, *it was irritated*, just as Augustine reads in the first book against Cresconius, chapter 12. He was irritated by the Holy Spirit within him. It is the same word from which the noun <term>paroxysm <note>original: "παροξυσμός"</note></term> is derived, which a little earlier he translated as *dissension*. In this place, he certainly rendered it better.
<margin>F</margin>
<margin>22 Seeing in it]</margin> In the Greek it is <term>to him seeing <note>original: "θεωροῦντι"</note></term>, that is, *to the one seeing, or when he saw*. For Paul was seeing, and then as he saw, his mind was moved. The translator either read, or certainly dreamed, <term>the one seeing <note>original: "θεωροῦντι"</note></term> in place of "devoted to idolatry." He paraphrased <term>full of idols <note>original: "κατείδωλον"</note></term> not badly, as if you said *subject to images*, because the preposition <term>kata <note>original: "κατὰ"</note></term> sounds like subjection.
<margin>23 And to those worshipping]</margin> <term>to those being reverent <note>original: "τοῖς σεβομένοις"</note></term>, that is, *to the religious and those devoted to divine worship*.

<margin>24 To those who had approached]</margin> <term>to those happening to be present <note>original: "πρὸς τοὺς παρατυγχάνοντας"</note></term>, that is, *to those who by chance were approaching*. It is obvious that this is not the fault of the translator, but of a scribe, who made "had approached" out of "had gone to."
<margin>25 Epicureans and Stoics]</margin> *Epicureans* from Epicurus. *Stoics* named from the Stoa
porch. Rabanus notes here, "Stoics," he says, "in Greek, in Latin 'elements'." What this might mean I clearly do not understand, unless I guess the cause of the error. Whoever it was, he had a Lexicon of Greek words poorly written in Greek letters: <term>stoichoi <note>original: "στοῖχοι"</note></term> was written as
*elements*: he made a <term>k <note>original: "κ"</note></term> out of a <term>ch <note>original: "χ"</note></term>, and so <term>stoichioi <note>original: "στοικιοὶ"</note></term> were turned into *elements*, now having become <term>stoikoi <note>original: "στοϊκοὶ"</note></term>.
<margin>26 They differed with him]</margin> <term>they engaged with him <note>original: "συνέβαλον αὐτῷ"</note></term>, that is, *they came together or joined battle with him*. It is the same word by which they signify
clashing hands in war.
<margin>D</margin>
<margin>27 Spermologus]</margin> For which Augustine cites, *sower of words*, and indeed it is seen written thus in some copies of our edition, <term>the spermologos <note>original: "ὁ σπερμολόγος"</note></term>. The translator fashioned a Greek-style compound. It is strange, however, why he preferred to do that in this one word more than in many others. But what, pray tell, does *seminiverbius* mean to Latins? Perhaps he would have fashioned it more happily if he had said *word-planter*, for one who scatters new rumors among the common people, or *scraps-gatherer*, for a talker and someone chattering for gain. Hesychius interprets <term>spermologos <note>original: "σπερμολόγος"</note></term> as <term>the trifler <note>original: "ὁ φλύαρος"</note></term>, that is, *a nugatory person, or one who collects seeds <note>original: "ὁ τὰ σπέρματα συλλέγων"</note></term>. And from this, a bird of the jackdaw kind was said to be a <term>spermologos <note>original: "σπερμολόγον"</note></term>. Athenaeus also mentions it in the second book of *The Deipnosophists*, but I find it written there as <term>spermatologos <note>original: "σπερματολόγος"</note></term>, namely <term>Sittakas and spermatologoi <note>original: "Σιττάκας τε σπερματολόγους"</note></term>, that is, *seed-picking parrots*. For I suspect the <term>tetrax</term>, or <term>tetrix</term>, as I find it written both ways, is the bird meant by <margin>E</margin> Athenaeus. He mentions the <term>spermologos <note>original: "σπερμολόγου"</note></term> bird again in the ninth book. Demosthenes also used this word in the speech *On the Crown*: <term>And why should I say much about what the Areopagus knows, when you brought this spermologos before them, a man in such misfortunes, and having arrested him you brought him to you... such a man would have escaped, and saying he was giving justice, the spermologos would have deceived you by night <note>original: Greek quote from Demosthenes</note></term>. He who interprets some small words selected from this says that this insult is usually said against a worthless man, of the least value and held for nothing, even doubting whether it applies to one who is not a sower, but feeds on another’s food. The metaphor is taken from the little bird we just mentioned. Moreover, Demosthenes calls Aeschines a <term>spermologos <note>original: "σπερμολόγον"</note></term>, an insulting term because he would say anything for profit, an insult we call *shyster* <note>Latin: "rabulas"</note>. Paul, still unknown, seemed like someone of this sort to certain Athenians. Hence also <term>to spermologize <note>original: "σπερμολογεῖν"</note></term> for *to trifle*. Leonardo Aretino translated *spermologon* as *rabula*, <margin>F</margin> that is, a man of intemperate and annoying loquacity. Furthermore, it cannot be taken as *sower of words*, which Augustine thinks, because the word is composed of <term>sperma <note>original: "σπέρμα"</note></term> (seed) and <term>lego <note>original: "λέγω"</note></term> meaning *to collect*, that is, *from collecting seeds*; <term>spermologos <note>original: "σπερμολόγος"</note></term> would more clearly express what Augustine thinks.
<margin>28 Of new demons]</margin> <term>of foreign demons <note>original: "ξένων δαιμονίων"</note></term>, that is, *of foreign gods*: especially since these are pagans speaking, who call *demons* gods. Furthermore <term>xenon <note>original: "ξένων"</note></term>, as it sounds like *foreign*, so it declares both *new and unheard of*, and sometimes *absurd*.
<margin>29 To the Areopagus]</margin> <term>to the Areopagus <note>original: "ἐπὶ τὸν Ἄρειον πάγον"</note></term>, that is, *to the Mars Hill*. For there are two words among the Greeks. It is, however, an elevated place, like the peak of a hill or a rock. I wonder, though, why Jerome in this place interpreted "pagus" as *villa*. If however this work is...

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Acts 17. Paul has arrived in Athens and has been brought to the Areopagus (the "Hill of Ares" or "Mars Hill"), a high court and place of public assembly, where the philosophers and citizens have asked him to explain his new teachings.</meta>

# THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES. CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>19</margin> ...May we know what this new doctrine is that you speak of? <margin>20</margin> For you bring certain strange things to our ears; we want to know, therefore, what these things mean. <margin>21</margin> Now all the Athenians, and the strangers visiting there, spent their time in nothing else but telling or hearing something new. <margin>22</margin> Then Paul, standing in the middle of the Areopagus <note>The high court of Athens</note>, said: "Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very <term>religious</term> <note>original: δεισιδαιμονεστέρους (*deisidaimonesterous*); often translated as "superstitious," but Paul likely used a polite term for their intense devotion to gods</note>. <margin>23</margin> For as I passed by and contemplated your objects of worship, I even found an altar on which was inscribed: TO AN UNKNOWN GOD. Therefore, what you worship in ignorance, this I proclaim to you. <margin>24</margin> The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made with hands; <margin>25</margin> neither is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all life and breath and all things. <margin>26</margin> And he made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on the entire face of the earth, having determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their habitation; <margin>27</margin> that they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might grope for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us. <margin>28</margin> For in him we live and move and have our being; as even some of your own poets have said: 'For we are also his offspring.' <margin>29</margin> Since then we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Divine Nature is like gold or silver or stone, an image carved by the art and imagination of man. <margin>30</margin> God, having overlooked the times of this ignorance, now commands all men everywhere to repent; <margin>31</margin> because he has appointed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by the man whom he has ordained, having provided proof to all by raising him from the dead..."

---

The word "district" <note>original: *vicum*</note> is Jerome’s. I would have preferred "district," since it is well known that there was a "Martian District" in Athens. And not everyone who lived there was a judge.
<margin>30 For certain new things</margin> <term>Xenizonta gar tina</term>. A participle of the verb derived from the noun for new or "foreign" things, <term>xenōn</term>.
<margin>31 And the visiting guests</margin> <term>kai epidēmountes xenoi</term>, that is, those who were staying there as guests or travelers.
<margin>32 They had leisure for nothing else</margin> <term>eukairoun</term>. He has rendered this well, as if they were busy with nothing else. But that phrase, *either to tell or to hear*, was translated too much in the Greek style for the ears of Lorenzo Valla <note>A famous humanist scholar who critiqued the Vulgate</note>; it would have been more correctly said as *for the purpose of telling or hearing something new*: even though the Greek says <term>kainoteron</term> ("something newer"), as if to suggest they had leisure for any new thing at all.
<margin>33 I see you are rather superstitious</margin> The Greek speech is a bit more polite, <term>hōs deisidaimonesterous</term>, which means "almost too religious." Certainly, the copies used by Donatus had "more superstitious," not merely "superstitious." Paul softened the harshness of the remark, first with the adverb <term>hōs</term> ("as it were") and then with the comparative form. This was his way of "becoming all things to all men" to win them all.
<margin>34 And seeing your images</margin> <term>anatheōrōn</term>, meaning considering and inspecting closely, like those who examine a thing not seen for a long time. Nor is "images" the word here for <term>sebasma</term>, which would be a more hateful term, but <term>sebasmata</term>, a word that encompasses everything we venerate—altars, shrines, statues, monuments—from the verb <term>sebomai</term>, which properly relates to religion. Jerome, citing this place in his Commentaries on the Epistle to Titus, translates <term>anatheōrōn</term> as "contemplating" and <term>sebasmata</term> as "cults" or "objects of worship."
<margin>35 To the Unknown God</margin> <margin>E</margin> Here Jerome indicates that Paul used a certain "pious craftiness," in that he changed the inscription slightly and omitted quite a bit so he could more easily pivot to preaching Christ. For the actual title, according to Jerome (whom I just cited), read: *To the Gods of Asia, Europe, and Africa; to the unknown and foreign gods.* From "unknown gods" (plural), Paul made it "Unknown God" (singular), and omitted mention of the others. I believe this civility should be imitated by those who wish to bring pagans, or princes corrupted by bad education, to piety; they should not immediately start with insults and aggravate those they wish to heal, but by overlooking many things, gradually lead them to a better mind. Perhaps it should not be criticized if good men act this way in the courts of Kings, gradually creeping into the affections of Princes, provided they do not author things that are clearly unjust, even if they reluctantly wink at certain things.
<margin>36 That which you therefore ignorantly [worship]</margin> <term>ho oun agnoountes eusebeite, touton egō katangellō</term>, that is: "Him, therefore, whom you worship without knowing, I announce." For he is speaking of the unknown God.
<margin>37 Is served by the hands of men</margin> <term>therapeuetai</term>, which Irenaeus <note>An early Church Father</note> reads as "is handled." For among the Greeks, both servants and doctors are said to "serve" or "treat" (<term>therapeuein</term>).
<margin>38 Life and inspiration</margin> <term>zōēn kai pnoēn</term>, that is, life and breath, as if explaining what makes up the life of a living thing; there is a pleasant harmony in the Greek words.
<margin>39 And made from one every race of men</margin> The Greeks read <term>ex henos haimatos</term>, that is, "from one blood," as Bede also pointed out. But I wonder if the text was changed by scribes in error. Furthermore, regarding what follows—"to dwell on the face of the earth"—the infinitive should have been changed to a gerund: "for the purpose of inhabiting the face of the earth." Otherwise, the sense would be that God brought it about that the whole human race lived

<column-break/>

<margin>19</margin> ...to know what this new doctrine is that you report? <margin>20</margin> <margin>A</margin> For you bring certain new things to our ears; we want to know therefore what these things mean. <margin>21</margin> Now all the Athenians, and the guests who stayed there, spent their time in nothing else but saying or hearing something new. But Paul, standing <margin>22</margin> in the middle of the Martian district <note>the Areopagus</note>, said: "Men of Athens, in almost all things <margin>23</margin> I see you are rather religious. For passing by <margin>24</margin> and contemplating your objects of worship, I also found an altar on which was inscribed: TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Him, therefore, whom you worship in ignorance, I announce to you. God, who made the world and all that is in it, <margin>24</margin> <margin>B</margin> since he is Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in man-made temples; neither is he served by human hands, <margin>25</margin> as if needing anything, since he himself gives to all life and breath in all things: <margin>26</margin> And he made from one blood every race of men, to inhabit the universal face of the earth, defining the pre-appointed times and fixing the limits of their habitation, so that they might seek God, <margin>27</margin> if perhaps they might feel after him and find him, although he is not far from each of us. For through him we live and move and ex- <margin>28</margin> ist, just as some of your own poets have said: <note>44</note> 'For we are even his offspring.' Since <margin>29</margin> we are therefore the offspring of God, <note>45</note> we ought not to think that the <margin>C</margin> divinity is like gold or silver or stone carved by art and the invention of man. And while God <margin>30</margin> has until now <note>47</note> overlooked the times of this ignorance, he now announces to men that all should repent everywhere, because he has appointed a day in which he is about to judge <margin>31</margin> the world with justice, <note>48</note> through that man whom he had ordained, <note>49</note> having provided faith to all by

---

living on the earth. Rather, he created all, and created them for this purpose: that they should live upon the lands.
<margin>40 Defining the appointed times</margin> <term>horisas protetagmenous kairous</term>, that is, when he had previously defined the appointed times. "Times" is not <term>chronous</term>, but <term>kairous</term> <note>specific seasons or moments of opportunity</note>, so we may understand that it was pre-defined by God what should happen in each age. <margin>D</margin> For he distinguished empires that would last for a certain time, exiles, and migrations. Likewise the law of nature, of Moses, and of the Gospel. For none of these things happened by chance, but each in its own time.
<margin>41 And the boundaries of their habitation</margin> <term>kai tas horothesias tēs katoikias autōn</term>, that is, he fixed the limits for their dwelling. For <term>horothesia</term> is the designation of boundaries.
<margin>42 If perhaps they might touch him</margin> <term>psēlaphēseian</term>, that is, "grope for," which is the action of blind people searching with their hands.
<margin>43 Some of your own</margin> <term>hōs kai tines tōn kath’ hymas</term>, that is, your own poets. Augustine, explaining some questions on the Epistle to the Romans, reads it as "just as some among you have said." Irenaeus reads it the same way, omitting the mention of "poet" entirely.
<margin>44 For we are also his offspring</margin> This is a heroic half-verse <note>A line of dactylic hexameter</note> from the *Phaenomena* of Aratus. And it is marvelous how what the poet said about Jupiter, Paul here twists to the true God. Saint Jerome is accustomed to use the defense of several of these passages against those who accused him of contaminating Holy Scripture with the filth of the Pagans. But Paul did this in only one or two places, and then only because the opportunity to preach the Gospel almost compelled it. What does this matter to those people who, by force and affectation, drag into the doctrine of Christ not only poets and orators, but all the writings of Sophists, Philosophers, Mathematicians, and even Magi—when that doctrine ought to be most simple and pure? In some Greek copies, it was written <term>touto gar kai genos esmen</term>, but incorrectly, unless I am mistaken, since in Aratus it is written <term>tou</term> in the poetic manner in place of <term>toutou</term> ("of him"). The commentator on Aratus reminds us that this was said in accordance with what is frequent in Hesiod and Homer: "father of both men and gods." We have rendered the half-verse as a half-verse: *For we are also his offspring.*
<margin>45 We ought not to estimate</margin> <term>nomizein</term>, that is, to judge or think. Next,
<margin>46 Or stone of the art of sculpture</margin> <margin>F</margin> "Sculpture" is in the dative case, and refers back to each of those three: "stone, silver, gold." We, therefore, so that the sense might be clearer, have translated it: *We ought not to think the divinity is like gold or silver or stone carved by art and the invention of man.*
<margin>47 God despising</margin> <term>hyperidōn</term>. The translator seems to have understood this as "looking down from on high," for that is what "despising" <note>original: *despiciens*</note> can mean. But <term>hyperidōn</term> is like "dissembling" or "overlooking"—when you see something but behave as if you do not see it. And the sense of time ought to have been preserved by the translator for <term>hyperidōn</term>, that is, *the times of ignorance having been overlooked*. For then he was silent; now he announces to all, no longer intending to overlook it. Let Nicholas of Lyra see for himself what he meant when he interpreted "despising" as God not wishing for them to endure any longer.
<margin>48 In the man in whom he appointed</margin> <term>en andri hō hōrise</term>, that is, in the man whom he had defined or appointed. For in Greek, the relative pronoun often agrees with the noun that precedes it, rather than responding to the following verb.
<margin>49 Offering faith to all</margin> These are two past-tense participles, neither of which he translated as was proper. The sense, however, is that God has already exhibited faith to all—that Christ is the one through whom he had decided [to judge].
<meta>Tom. VI. I i 2</meta>

...having raised him from the dead. And when they heard <margin>32</margin> of the resurrection of the dead, some indeed mocked, but others said, "We will hear you concerning this again." Thus <margin>33</margin> Paul departed from their midst. But certain men, <margin>34</margin> clinging to him, believed; among whom was also Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them. After this, Paul <margin>A</margin> departed from Athens and came to <margin>XVIII. 1</margin> Corinth. And because <margin>b</margin> he was of the same craft, <margin>3</margin> he stayed <margin>3</margin> with them and worked; <margin>c</margin> for their craft was weaving tents.
