<margin>A</margin> <gloss>Stepping away from Athens</gloss> <term>χωρισθεὶς ἐκ τῶν Ἀθηνῶν</term> <note>original: choristheis ek ton Athenon</note>, that is, having departed from Athens.
<margin>D</margin> <note>This note refers to a previous section regarding the resurrection</note> He was able to make the world new because he had raised him from the dead: this one thing happened to no other mortal, neither Moses nor the Prophet.
<margin>34 Among whom also Dionysius</margin> <gloss>etc.</gloss> Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo Valla, a 15th-century humanist scholar</note> in this place refutes the opinion of those who think this Areopagite was the author of those books we have regarding the *Celestial Hierarchy* and *Divine Names*, and that he is the same one who was crowned with martyrdom at Paris, making one out of three Dionysiuses, if I am not mistaken. First, the <term>Areopagites</term> were judges, not philosophers. But these people make Dionysius a supreme philosopher, who supposedly discerned from a solar eclipse that the nature of things was in danger—though it is not probable that those darknesses reached all the way to Athens. For when the Evangelist says darkness was made over the whole earth, he understood the land of that region, as Saint Jerome agrees and Origen asserts in his homilies on Matthew: where he plainly denies that those darknesses happened from an eclipse of the sun, but rather either from intervening clouds or otherwise from the density of the air being compressed. For if these darknesses had happened over such a great distance throughout the whole world, surely some Greek writer among six hundred would have remembered the event. Lorenzo has already provided a letter on this matter, forged as if in the name of Dionysius. To me, it does not seem that in those early times there were as many ceremonies for Christians as that author describes. Furthermore, it is a wonder if he was such an ancient author and wrote so much, why he was cited by none of the ancients, whether Greek or Latin—not by Origen, not by Chrysostom, not even by Jerome, who left nothing unexamined. Indeed, even Gregory himself, a man of good faith, citing his letters, does not indicate that he was Dionysius the Areopagite. Moreover, since in *Ecclesiastical History* much mention is made of the books of Dionysius, Bishop of the Corinthians, it is not probable that Eusebius would have been silent about such works. There are most learned men who have judged those books to belong to Apollinaris. Although Jerome mentions two of that name, one the Bishop of Hierapolis who flourished under Marcus Antoninus II, the other the Bishop of Laodicea in Syria. Yet he attributes no such works to either. Nor do I think these should be attributed to the heretic Apollinaris. Several years ago, as I remember, the incomparable William Grocyn <note>A famous English scholar and friend of Erasmus</note>—who was a supreme theologian and exquisitely learned in every discipline—began a lecture in St. Paul’s Cathedral in London on the *Celestial Hierarchy*. In his prepared preface, he strongly asserted that this work was by Dionysius the Areopagite, vehemently venting his anger at the impudence of those who disagreed. But before he had finished half the work, when he had tasted it more closely, he frankly confessed to the audience that, having changed his mind, he did not believe the work was by Dionysius the Areopagite. I wonder why Bede thinks this Dionysius was made Bishop of the Corinthians, when *Ecclesiastical History* plainly shows there was another Dionysius, Bishop of the Corinthians, who wrote many things. And his authority is cited there, who in a certain letter he wrote to the Athenians, showed that Dionysius the Areopagite, converted by Paul, was the first Bishop at Athens, appointed by the same Apostle. Nothing else is found among ancient writers concerning Dionysius the Areopagite. But it will be enough to have pointed these things out as a few <term>side-notes</term> <note>original: πάρεργα (parerga)</note>.

<margin>2 A native of Pontus</margin> <gloss>For Pontus is a part of Asia Minor; he is not called "Pontic" from the sea <note>The Black Sea/Pontus Euxinus</note>. Paul greets this man in the Epistle to the Romans, except that there the wife is called Prisca instead of Priscilla, as Origen notes. A vision occurred to me while writing this: in the volumes of Origen first printed by our friend Badius, someone or other corrupted the text. "After these things Paul departed from Athens and came to Corinth, and having found a certain Jew named Aquila, from the Pontic people <note>Latin: de Ponticis gente</note>," instead of what it should be, "a native of Pontus" <note>Latin: de Pontico genere</note>. Offended, I suppose, because he thought it absurd to call someone "of the Pontic race" who was a Jew. As if at that time Jews were not living scattered through almost every region! Certainly Peter specifically writes to the Jews who lived in Galatia, Bithynia, and Pontus. But we will touch on this matter somewhat in the Epistle to the Romans.</gloss>
<margin>3 He was of the same craft</margin> They are called <term>Homotechnoi</term> by the Greeks, <gloss>of the same craft or workmanship: just as a painter is to a painter, a smith to a smith, a cobbler to a cobbler, or a sailor to a sailor, he is <term>of the same craft</term>.</gloss>
<margin>4 Of the craft of tent-making</margin> <term>ἦσαν γὰρ σκηνοποιοὶ τὴν τέχνην</term> <note>original: esan gar skenopoioi ten technen</note>, that is, they were artisans of weaving hangings or tents. The translator of Origen, explaining Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, interprets <term>skenopoios</term> as artisans of tents, that is, cobblers <note>Latin: sutores</note>: for this reason, I suppose, because tents among the ancients were made from skins. Even now in Spain, <term>hangings</term> <note>Latin: aulaea</note> are made this way. The seventeenth Homily on Numbers testifies to the same. <margin>E</margin> Truly, to have been so great in gifts! We do not wish to be seen as great through a bodyguard, troops, wealth, or threats. <gloss>And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, interposing the name of the Lord Jesus: and he persuaded the Jews and Greeks.</gloss> This whole part is not held in certain manuscripts, even printed ones. One manuscript of Donatianus agreed with the Greek: which, while they have the rest, do not add "interposing the name of the <term>Lord Jesus</term>."
<margin>§ Paul was insistent on the word, testifying</margin> <gloss>The Greeks read quite differently than we do: <term>συνείχετο τῷ πνεύματι ὁ Παῦλος, διαμαρτυρόμενος τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις</term> <note>original: syneicheto to pneumati ho Paulos...</note>, that is, Paul was constrained in spirit, testifying to the Jews; so that you may understand he did it unwillingly and with a reluctant mind, as if he had sensed beforehand that he would be wasting his effort.</gloss>
<margin>6 Titius Justus</margin> <gloss>I do not find "Titius" in the Greek manuscripts: but only "Justus." But I suppose it was omitted through the negligence of scribes. Since Jerome, or whoever that author was, mentions this Titius in the names of Holy Scripture. Although even there, there is no mention of the surname Justus.</gloss>

12 **Persuades men** <note>original: "Persuadet hominibus"</note>] *anapeithei* <note>Greek: ἀναπείθει</note>; this suggests urging or coaxing rather than successfully persuading. It might even mean "misleads," as Paul was calling people away from the ancient worship of the gods.
13 **While Paul was beginning** <note>original: "Incipiente autem Paulo"</note>] *When Paul was about to open his mouth* <note>Greek: Μέλλοντος δὲ τοῦ Παύλου ἀνοίγειν τὸ στόμα</note>. The Translator <note>Erasmus refers to the Vulgate translator here</note> occasionally renders this phrase with specific intent, and not at all incorrectly.
14 **Some injustice or crime** <note>original: "Iniquum aliquid aut facinus"</note>] *adikēma* <note>Greek: ἀδίκημα</note>, which more strongly implies an injury or a specific legal wrong. Furthermore, why does the one who here translates *rhadiourgēma* <note>Greek: ῥᾳδιούργημα</note> as "crime" translate its relative *rhadiourgia* earlier as "deceit"? It is not "the worst," but simply "bad" (*ponēron*). Nor is "I would sustain you" quite right; it should be "according to reason" (*kata logon*), meaning "reasonably" or "deservedly."
15 **Of the word and names of your law** <note>original: "De verbo & nominibus legis vestrae"</note>] Our version lacks the conjunction "and"; the Greek reads *of the word AND names AND your law*. Paul opposed "words" to "actions." Furthermore, the author calls questions about common or uncommon things and genealogies **names**. He calls the Mosaic ceremonies **the law**.
16 **And you shall see** <note>original: "Et videritis"</note>] This is in the future tense, *opsesthe* <note>Greek: ὄψεσθε</note>, just as in the Gospel.
17 **And he drove them** <note>original: "Et minavit eos"</note>] *apēlasen* <note>Greek: ἀπήλασεν</note>. Why not rather "drove away" or "pushed back"? For *minare* <note>a Latin word for driving cattle</note> is surely an unusual word to Latin ears.
18 **Saying farewell to the brothers** <note>original: "Fratribus vale faciens"</note>] *apotaxamenos* <note>Greek: ἀποταξάμενος</note>, that is, having dismissed the brothers or having said goodbye. It is not "he sailed," but *exeplei* <note>Greek: ἐξέπλει</note>, meaning "he sailed away."
19 **Who had shaved his head** <note>original: "Qui sibi totonderat caput"</note>] From the Greek text itself, it is not clear who shaved his head, Paul or Aquila. Additionally, the participle is in the past tense: *having shaved his head*. For he was first shaved in the port, then he sailed. And for **Cenchreae**, it should be read as a three-syllable name *Cenchrees*, like Athens. It is the port of the Corinthians.
20 **I will return to you again** <note>original: "Iterum revertar ad vos"</note>] There is more in the Greek manuscripts than in ours: *I must by all means keep the coming feast in Jerusalem, but I will return to you again*. That is, "It behooves...

21 **He set out from Ephesus** <note>original: "Profectus est ab Epheso"</note>] *kai anēchthē apo tēs Ephesou* <note>Greek: καὶ ἀνήχθη ἀπὸ τῆς Ἐφέσου</note>. I would have preferred, *and he set sail from Ephesus*.
22 **Named Apollos** <note>original: "Apollos nomine"</note>] *Apollos* <note>Greek: Ἀπολλὼς</note>, whose genitive is *Apollo*, not *Apollinis*. Paul mentions him in his Epistles.
23 **A learned man** <note>original: "Vir eloquens"</note>] *logios* <note>Greek: λόγιος</note>, which suggests both one who is well-read and one who is prudent.
24 **He had been taught** <note>original: "Hic erat edoctus"</note>] *katēchēmenos* <note>Greek: κατηχημένος</note>, a participle from the same verb from which the word **catechumen** is derived. He had not yet been fully taught the "way of the Lord," which he soon learns from Priscilla and Aquila, but he was somehow instructed in the baptism of John.
25 **When he wished to go to Achaia** <note>original: "Quum autem vellet ire Achajam"</note>] Since the Greek includes the preposition *into Achaia* <note>Greek: εἰς τὴν Ἀχαΐαν</note>, it is strange why the Translator omitted the preposition, which goes against the rules of grammar, as Achaia is the name of a region, not a city.
26 **He helped much those who believed** <note>original: "Contulit multum his qui crediderunt"</note>] Here the Greek codices add, **through grace** (*dia tēs charitos*). This was added <margin>F</margin> so we might understand it was a divine gift that benefited the Christians. Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, an 8th-century scholar</note> notes that in some codices, "he profited" was written instead of "he helped." And "vehemently" (*eutonōs*), meaning sharply. "In public" could refer to either; I think it refers to the former, for it was by grace that he dared to publicly refute the Jews.
27 **That Jesus was the Christ** <note>original: "Esse Christum Jesum"</note>] *einai ton Christon Iēsoun* <note>Greek: εἶναι τὸν Χριστόν Ἰησοῦν</note>. The Jews did not deny that Jesus existed, but they denied that he was the Messiah (*the Christ*) whom they were expecting. Therefore, the Greek uses the article *ton Christon*, meaning **that** Christ, showing either that "Jesus was the Christ" or "Jesus is the Messiah."

2 **If the Holy Spirit is**] instead of what it should be: **whether there is a Holy Spirit**.

<margin>E</margin>
<gloss>3 in the school of a certain Tyrannus]</gloss> <note>original: "in schola tyranni cujusdam"</note> Translators are divided here as to whether "Tyrannus" in this place signifies a ruler or powerful man, or if it is the proper name of a person. But what would a school have to do with a tyrant? Furthermore, if it is a proper name, why did he add "a certain" <note>original: "τινὸς"</note>? Therefore, I suspect it was the private chapel of some Nobleman, in which he was accustomed to spend his leisure, since "schola" <note>original: "σχολὴ"</note> among the Greeks sounds like leisure. Jerome, alluding to the words more than the sense, twists this elsewhere to call it the "school of a tyrant" where matters are not settled by arguments but by authority and force. This also displeased Augustine, who does not wish heretics to be coerced unless they are taught. Now we judge it sufficient to say, "This is an error, recant it: this is heresy, deny it." Because heresies weaken others, they themselves cannot wander.

<gloss>4 Jews and Gentiles]</gloss> <note>original: "Ἰουδαίους τε καὶ Ἕλληνας"</note> That is, both Jews and Greeks, whom the translator here renders as Gentiles.

<gloss>5 And virtues not modest of any kind]</gloss> <note>original: "Virtutesque non modicas quaelibet"</note> I found it written this way in several Latin manuscripts. However, the matter itself sufficiently indicates that this happened through the fault of the scribes, who took the word "modest" <note>original: "modicas"</note>—which someone had added as a kind of interpretation—and put it back into the text as if omitted by the writer. The Greek says "extraordinary miracles" <note>original: "δυνάμεις τε οὐ τὰς τυχούσας"</note>, that is, virtues not of the common sort, or not vulgar; literally, "not happening by chance." In other copies it was written "any virtues," with the negation omitted. Cerrensis thinks both can be read, but the Greek language cries out against it.

<gloss>6 Handkerchiefs & aprons]</gloss> He used the Latin terms for both, <term>sudaria</term> <note>handkerchiefs for wiping sweat</note> and <term>semicinthia</term> <note>narrow aprons or loincloths worn by workers</note>.

<gloss>7 a very evil demon]</gloss> <note>original: "τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ πονηρὸν"</note> That is, an evil spirit. Furthermore, in what follows immediately, "he leaped" <note>original: "ἐφάλλετο"</note>, some Greek codices had "having mastered" <note>original: "κατακυριεύσας"</note>, so that it refers to the demon's dominion. Some had "mastering" <note>original: "κατακυριεύσαν"</note>, so that it pertains to the man in whom the demon was. Furthermore, since our copies have "of both," the Translator seems to have read "of them" <note>original: "αὐτῶν"</note> instead of "to them" <note>original: "αὐτοῖς"</note>.

<gloss>8 Confessing & announcing their deeds]</gloss> Even from this, it can be gathered that in ancient times there was some form of confession for a life poorly lived...

<column-break/>

5 ...in Christ Jesus. Having heard these things, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.

<gloss>9 Those who had been of a curious sect]</gloss> <note>original: "τὰ περίεργα πραξάντων"</note> That is, those who practiced curious arts. For so he calls the magic arts.

<gloss>10 Money of five thousand denarii]</gloss> <note>original: "ἀργυρίου μυριάδας πέντε"</note> That is, fifty thousand pieces of money.

<gloss>11 No small disturbance]</gloss> <note>original: "τάραχος οὐκ ὀλίγος"</note> That is, no slight disturbance. And a little later, "not a modest gain" <note>original: "ἐργασίαν οὐκ ὀλίγην"</note>, that is, no small gain.

<gloss>12 Concerning the way of the Lord]</gloss> <note>original: "περὶ τῆς ὁδοῦ"</note> That is, concerning the way, or concerning *this* way. For the added article makes us understand a specific way. Furthermore, they added "of the Lord" so that the matter might be clearer, or certainly more gentle.

<margin>F</margin>
<gloss>13 A certain Demetrius by name, a silversmith]</gloss> "Silversmith" <note>original: "argentarius"</note> elsewhere in Latin signifies both a banker and a money-changer; but in this place it sounds like a worker and sculptor of silver, whom we call a goldsmith or silver-worker, since whoever hammers gold, the same also hammers silver. He is an <term>argyrokopos</term> <note>original: "ἀργυροκόπος"</note>, named from the working of silver: unless you prefer to derive it from "to strike" <note>original: "κόπτειν"</note>, from which the Greeks also call a coin a "piece" <note>original: "κόμμα"</note>, as in "a bad piece."

<gloss>14 Silver houses]</gloss> <note>original: "ναοὺς"</note> That is, temples. For he means small shrines, or cases, in the likeness of a temple, in which statues were placed. We translate it as "shrines" <note>original: "delubra"</note>.

<gloss>15 From this craft is our acquisition]</gloss> <note>original: "ἐκ ταύτης τῆς ἐργασίας ἡ εὐπορία ἡμῶν ἐστιν"</note> What he just now translated as "gain," he now translates as "craft," and for "abundance" <note>original: "εὐπορίαν"</note>, "acquisition." From this gain, a plenty of things is supplied to us.

<gloss>16 Not only at Ephesus]</gloss> It is not "in Ephesus" <note>original: "ἐν Ἐφέσῳ"</note>, but "Ephesus" <note>original: "Ἔφεσον"</note>, so that it refers to the great crowd. Hence, since the ambiguity offended some, instead of "at Ephesus" we translated it "in the Ephesine city."

<gloss>17 Not</gloss>

17 *Not only will this be in danger* <note>original Latin: "Non solum autem haec periclitabitur"</note>] The Greek is *kindyneuei* <note>original: "κινδυνεύει"</note>, that is, *it is in danger* [present tense]. However, this entire speech is not very conveniently rendered by the Latin Translator: "And not only is this part, or this business of ours, in danger for us, lest it be rejected, or lest we be rejected, but also lest the temple of the great Diana be held for nothing: furthermore, lest it happen that her majesty also be destroyed, she whom all Asia and the world worship."

18 *And her majesty will begin to be destroyed*] The Translator seems to have read *mellein te* <note>original: "μέλλειν τε"</note>, as it was written in many Greek books. In others the reading was *mellei de* <note>original: "μέλλει δὲ"</note>, <gloss>moreover</gloss>: "but," as if it were a correction, as though it were the most serious thing of all that would happen if her majesty and divine power should perish among the common people. Jerome, in the preface to his Commentaries on the Epistle to the Ephesians, indicates that this Diana of the Ephesians was not that huntress, but was named *polymathon* <note>original: "πολυμαστόν"</note>, that is, *many-breasted*: because they wanted her to be considered the nourisher of all living things.

19 *Companions of Paul*] *synekdemous* <note>original: "συνεκδήμους"</note>, that is, partners in travel, who are also called companions.

20 *For the church was confused*] Since he is speaking about a promiscuous multitude, it was more appropriate to say *gathering* or *assembly* [Latin: *concionem*], rather than *church* [Latin: *ecclesiam*].

21 *They drew out Alexander*] *proebibasan* <note>original: "προεβίβασαν"</note>, that is, they instructed him beforehand. For that is what *probibazein* means. We "instruct" a patron who is about to argue our case. The Translator, unless I am mistaken, read *probibasan* [having brought forward]: even if *proballonton* is used of one who is forced to come forward and is pushed out.

22 *Having beckoned for silence with his hand*] The Translator plays with a strange variety in rendering this phrase, *kataseisas ten cheira* <note>original: "κατασείσας τὴν χεῖρα"</note>, that is, *with the hand moved*. As Persius says:
> ...... having made silence for the heated crowd
> By the majesty of the hand ......

23 *And when the Scribe had quieted the crowd*] *Katasteilas de ho Grammateus ton ochlon* <note>original: "Καταστείλας δὲ ὁ Γραμματεὺς τὸν ὄχλον"</note>, that is, *But when the Scribe had settled the crowd*. Truly, from the Greek words it is not quite clear which of the two spoke after the crowd was quieted, Alexander or the Scribe.

24 *To be a worshiper of the great Diana*] He used a peculiar word, *neokoron* <note>original: "νεωκόρον"</note>: which is a word composed of *neos* <note>original: "νεὼς"</note>, which in Attic means a temple, and *koro* <note>original: "κορῶ"</note> I clean or I sweep, according to the authorities Hesychius, Etymologus, and Suidas; hence the second to last syllable is long omega [ω]. Those who are more intensely devoted to some Goddess are accustomed to honor her altar with various kinds of ornaments,

just as Psyche does in the works of Apuleius.

25 *And of the offspring of Jupiter*] The Greek reads quite differently, *kai tou Diopetous* <note>original: "καὶ τοῦ Διοπετοῦς"</note>. "Of Artemis and of the *Diopetes*," that is, "of that great Diana and of the [object] fallen from heaven," so that an "image" or "statue" is understood. Indeed, the article *tou* <note>original: "τοῦ"</note> prevents *Diopetous* from referring to Diana [feminine], but rather to *agalma* <note>original: "ἄγαλμα"</note>, that is, the statue of Diana [neuter]: for *Diopetes* is said by the Greeks of something that has fallen from Jove or come from heaven. Furthermore, the makers of images, so that the superstition of the common people might be greater, used to pretend that they had fallen from the sky, that is, "images fallen from Zeus" <note>original Greek: "εἴδελα Διοπετῆ"</note>. The same was commonly believed regarding the image of Diana of the Ephesians, as Suidas also testifies under the word *Diopetes*. The conjunction *kai* [and] also supports our view, because it would have been superfluous if *Diopetous* referred to Diana herself. The sense, therefore, is: that there was a temple of Diana among the Ephesians, and an image of her which was thought to have fallen from heaven. Numa persuaded the Romans of the same thing regarding the sacred shields [ancilia]. Homer attributes this title to Kings, as if they proceeded from Jove. The Translator seems to have followed this, whose book perhaps did not have the article *tou* added.

26 *It cannot be contradicted*] *Anantirrheton onton* <note>original: "Ἀναντιῤῥήτων ὄντων"</note>. It could be taken as, "Since no one contradicts these things."

27 *Court sessions*] He added *sessions* [Latin: *conventus*] for the sake of explaining the matter, since in Greek it is only *agoraioi agontai* <note>original: "ἀγοραῖοι ἄγονται"</note>, that is, "forensic [days] are being held": so that "trials" or "lawsuits" must be understood.

28 *In a lawful church it can be settled*] Since he is speaking about a secular and promiscuous gathering of men, it should have been called an *assembly* [Latin: *concio*] rather than a *church* [Latin: *ecclesia*]. And so presently, "he dismissed the church," instead of "the assembly." Then, *lawful* is *ennomo* <note>original: "ἐννόμῳ"</note>, that is, one which is summoned not by riot, but by lawful custom. Nor is it "could be settled," but "will be settled," *epilythesetai* <note>original: "ἐπιλυθήσεται"</note>.

29 *Since no one is liable*] *medenis aitiou hyparchontos* <note>original: "μηδενὸς αἰτίου ὑπάρχοντος"</note>, that is, "since no one is at fault," or "since no one was the author of this gathering." For that phrase, "concerning which we will be able to give an account," is inserted as a parenthesis. Although in some copies I find it written, "concerning which we will *not* be able to give an account," that is, because we are not going to defend it. Finally, it is uncertain whether "since no one is at fault" refers to a person (as masculine) or to a thing (as neuter). Thus the sense would be: "Since no cause underlies this, through which we will be able to defend this gathering of the people."

**1** *Having exhorted them, he said farewell*] The Greek differs from the Latin: *proskalesamenos ho Paulos tous mathetas, kai aspasamenos exelthe* <note>original: "προσκαλεσάμενος ὁ Παῦλος τοὺς μαθητὰς, καὶ ἀσπασάμενος ἐξῆλθε"</note>, that is, "Paul, having called the disciples to him and having embraced them, departed." The Translator seems to have read *parakalesamenos* [having exhorted] instead of *proskalesamenos* [having called to]. And that indeed seems more probable to me.

<summary>This page analyzes the climax and resolution of the Ephesian riot in Acts 19, focusing on the Greek term 'Diopetes' (fallen from Zeus) and arguing for more precise Latin translations of 'ecclesia' and 'concio' in a secular context.</summary>

---

<margin>2</margin> *But there accompanied him Sopater, son of Pyrrhus, of Berea]* <term>of Pyrrhus</term> <note>original: "Pyrrhi"</note> is not added in the Greek copies. But while this is missing, the words *as far as Asia* are present, which I do not find in the Latin versions. <note>original: "Συνείπετο δὲ αὐτῷ ἄχρι τῆς Ἀσίας Σώπατρος Βεροιαῖος"</note>, that is, *But Sopater of Berea followed him as far as Asia*. For the Greeks have *Sopater*, not *Sosipater*. Bede suggests that in ancient Latin copies it was written *Sosipater, son of Pyrrhus*, as if the son were better known by his father.
<margin>3</margin> *They sustained us]* <note>original: "ἔμενον ἡμᾶς"</note>, that is, *they expected us*, or, literally, *they were waiting for us*.
<margin>4</margin> *On the first of the sabbath]* <note>original: "σαββάτων"</note>, that is, *on the first day of the week*. One word appears in place of "first."
<margin>5</margin> *Paul disputed with them]* <note>original: "διελέγετο αὐτοῖς"</note>, that is, *he discoursed to them*, or *conversed with them*. For he was not arguing with those who had come to break bread; rather, Paul delivered a sermon there among them. As for the phrase *the disciples having gathered* <note>original: "συνηγμένων τῶν μαθητῶν"</note>, which he translates as *when the disciples had convened*, it is acceptable.
<margin>6</margin> *Intending to set out on the morrow]* <note>original: "μέλλων ἐξιέναι τῇ ἐπαύριον"</note>, that is, *about to depart or leave the next day*. For we call "tomorrow" the day that immediately follows the one in which we are currently speaking. Furthermore, when referring to some past or future day, one should not say "yesterday" or "tomorrow," but "the day before" or "the day after."
<margin>7</margin> *When he was sunk in sleep]* <note>original: "καταφερόμενος"</note>, that is, *when he was being drawn downward*, which happens to one who falls into a heavy sleep while sitting. Yet this is not a "heavy" sleep <note>Latin: "gravis"</note>, but <note>Greek: "βαθύς"</note>, that is, *deep* or *profound*. The translator seems to have read <note>Greek: "βαρύς"</note>, which means "heavy."
<margin>8</margin> *Paul disputing]* And here I would prefer *discoursing*. Lest anyone imagine there was a sophistical dispute among those pure Christians.
<margin>9</margin> *Led by sleep he fell]* <note>original: "κατενεχθεὶς"</note>, that is, *drawn downward, or oppressed, or overcome*. And perhaps the Translator had written *downward*. Furthermore, that phrase *furthermore* <note>original: "ἐπὶ πλεῖον"</note>, which the Translator applied to what preceded, is placed in the middle by the Greeks so that it can be applied to either: to Paul discoursing longer, or to the boy being even more overcome by sleep. In my opinion, it is better to refer it to the following part. For first he was nodding with his body inclining downward, then, being more overcome, he fell.
<margin>10</margin> *From the third dining room]* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ τριστέγου"</note>, could be translated *from the third story*. For Luke added this so we would understand the fall was fatal, specifically from such a high place. The word is derived from *tris*, "three," and *stegos*, "roof." Immortal God! What nonsense the author of the <term>Catholicon</term> <note>A popular medieval Latin dictionary by John Balbi, often criticized by Renaissance humanists for its lack of classical precision</note> brings forward regarding this word *Tristegum*. O, what a wretched age that was! When from such books, as if from hidden shrines, the oracles of literature were sought. However, the floor of the first story is the roof of the lowest part of the house. Again, the floor of the second is the roof of the first. Likewise, the floor of the third is the roof of the second.
<margin>11</margin> *And they were comforted not a little]* <note>original: "οὐ μετρίως"</note>, that is, *not mo-*

<column-break/>

<sig>A</sig> traveled through *Macedonia*. <margin>2</margin> And there accompanied him as far as *Asia, Sopater of Berea*; and of the *Thessalonians, Aristarchus* and *Secundus*; and *Gaius of Derbe*, and *Timothy*; and of *Asia, Tychicus* and *Trophimus*. These, having gone ahead, waited for us <margin>5</margin> at *Troas*. But we sailed away after the days of *Unleavened Bread* from *Philippi*, and came to them at *Troas* within five days, where we stayed seven days. <margin>6</margin> <margin>7</margin> And on the first day of the week, when the disciples had gathered to break bread, *Paul* discoursed with them, intending to depart the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. And there were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered. But a certain young man named *Eutychus*, sitting in a window, <margin>7</margin> since he was weighed down by a deep sleep, <sig>B</sig> while Paul discoursed at length, <margin>9</margin> being more overcome by sleep, fell down from the third story, and was taken up dead. But when *Paul* had gone down, he lay upon him, and embracing him, said, "Do not be troubled; for his life is in him." When he had come up, and had bro- <margin>10</margin> ken bread and tasted it, and talked a long while even until dawn, he finally departed. And they brought the boy alive, <margin>11</margin> and were comforted <margin>12</margin> not a little. But we, having boarded the ship, <margin>13</margin> *set sail for Assos*, intending to take *Paul* on board there; for so he had arranged, <sig>C</sig> intending himself to travel by land. And when we had met at *Assos*, having taken him on board, we came to *Mitylene*. And sailing from there, the following day <margin>14</margin> <margin>15</margin> we came opposite *Chios*. But the next day we arrived at *Samos*, and staying at *Trogyllium*, the next day we came to *Miletus*. For *Paul* had proposed to sail past *Ephesus*, lest he should waste time in *Asia*; <margin>16</margin> for he was hurrying, if it were possible for him, to spend the day of *Pentecost* in *Jerusalem*. And from *Miletus*, having sent <margin>17</margin> messengers to *Ephesus*, he summoned the *Elders* of the church. When they had come to him, he said to them, "You <margin>18</margin> know from the first day that I entered *Asia*, how I have been with you at all times, Serving <margin>19</margin> the *Lord* with all humility, and with many

---

<sig>D</sig> *derately*. I truly wonder why the Translator thought this should be changed.
<margin>12</margin> *We sailed to Assos]* Some copies had *Thassos* instead of *Assos*. For there is also an island *Thassos* opposite Thrace, from which the proverb arose, "Thassian goods" <note>original: "Θάσιος ἀγαθά" — meaning excellent things</note>. However, there are several cities by the name of *Assos*: one in Lycia, situated on a precipice; another in Aeolis; a third in Mysia; a fourth in Lydia; a fifth in Lesser Epirus, the homeland of *Cleanthes*. Saint Jerome places this one in Asia, which is said to be the same as *Apollonia*, supported also by Pliny in book five, chapter thirty. We are left free to choose whether we prefer *Assos* to be an island or a city.
<margin>13</margin> *Intending himself to go by land]* <note>original: "οὕτως γὰρ ἦν διατεταγμένος, μέλλων αὐτὸς πεζεύειν"</note>, for so he had ordered, intending himself to come by a pedestrian journey, or to travel on foot. The Translator seems to have avoided this, lest anyone should think Paul came there not on horses or vehicles, but on foot. Yet this very thing added to Paul's glory, that he preferred the more laborious journey, provided it was with greater fruit.
<sig>E</sig> <margin>14</margin> *Mitylene]* This is a coastal city of Lesbos, encountered on the right by those sailing toward the island of Chios. *Samos* is an island in the region of Caria. *Miletus* is a coastal town of Caria.
<margin>15</margin> *And the next day we came opposite Chios]* In this place, the Greek differs from what we read: <note>original: "τῇ ἐπιούσῃ κατηντήσαμεν ἀντικρὺ Χίου· τῇ δὲ ἑτέρα παρεβάλομεν εἰς Σάμον, καὶ μείναντες ἐν Τρωγυλλίῳ, τῇ ἐχομένῃ ἤλθομεν εἰς Μίλητον"</note>, that is, *the next day we arrived opposite Chios; but on the other day we arrived at Samos, and having stayed at Trogyllium, on the following day we came to Miletus*. Moreover, *Trogyllium* is a promontory in the region of Samos, according to Ptolemy and Strabo, although there are others of the same name.
<sig>F</sig> <margin>16</margin> *To sail past Ephesus]* <note>original: "παραπλεῦσαι τὴν Ἔφεσον"</note>, that is, *to sail past or be carried past Ephesus*. For what does it mean to "sail across" a city, unless the ship is carried in the clouds? Ephesus, a coastal city, was encountered sooner than *Trogyllium*.
<margin>17</margin> *Lest any delay happen to him]* <note>original: "μὴ γένηται αὐτῷ χρονοτριβῆσαι ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ"</note>, that is, *lest it happen to him to waste time in Asia*. The Translator rendered this more elegantly than truly. For Paul did not fear just any delay, but he dreaded a longer one, as he was hurrying to Jerusalem.
<margin>18</margin> *Elders]* <note>original: "πρεσβυτέρους"</note>: whom he sometimes calls seniors, sometimes presbyters by the Greek word, and sometimes elders by birth: although in this place the Greek word fits better, indicating honor rather than age. For here he understands Bishops and leaders of the Churches, who were sometimes young men, such as Timothy.
<margin>19</margin> *With all humility]* <note>original: "ταπεινοφροσύνης"</note>. Which is a modesty of mind, feeling nothing high of itself. O, a voice truly worthy of a great Bishop!

### THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES. CHAPTER XXI.

<margin>A</margin> ...dangers and trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews; how I did not shrink from anything that was profitable, failing not to announce it to you and to teach you 21 **publicly and from house to house**, testifying both to Jews and to Greeks repentance toward God and faith toward 22 our Lord Jesus. And now, look, bound by the spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing the things that will happen to me 23 there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies in every city, saying that 24 **chains and tribulations await me**. But I make no account of anything, nor do I hold my life precious to myself, so that I may **finish my course with joy**, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to 25 the Gospel of the grace of God. And now, look, I know that you all, among whom I have gone about preaching the kingdom of 26 <margin>B</margin> God, will see my face no more. Therefore I testify to you this day that I am clean from the blood of all men. For 27 I did not shrink from announcing to you **the whole counsel of God**. 28 Take heed therefore to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops <note>original: "episkopous"</note> **to rule the church of God**, which he purchased with his own blood. 29 For I know this, that after my departure **heavy wolves** will enter among 30 you, not sparing the flock. And from among your own selves will arise **men speaking perverse things**, to 31 <margin>C</margin> draw away the disciples after them. Therefore watch, remembering that for three years, night and day, I did not cease 32 to warn each one with tears. And now I commend you, brothers, to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and give 33 you an inheritance among all those who are sanctified. **I have coveted no one’s silver, or gold, or clothing.** 34 You yourselves know that these hands have served my needs and those who 35 were with me. I have shown you all things, that by so laboring **it is necessary to support the weak**, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, for he himself said, **“It is more blessed to give than to receive.”** 36 And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed 37 <margin>D</margin> with them all. And there was much weeping by all, and falling on Paul’s neck, they kissed him, 38 grieving most of all over the word he had spoken, that they would see his face no more; and they accompanied him XXI. 1 to the ship. And when it happened that we had put to sea, having torn ourselves away from them, we ran a straight course and came to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. 2 And having found a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, we went aboard...

---

20 **That I have withheld nothing from you** <note>original: "Ut nihil subtraxerim vobis"</note>] Now he seems to say this: that he has withheld no good things from them, which is to say, he cheated them of nothing. On the contrary, Paul feels that he has shrunk from no danger or labor that might pertain to their benefit. A little later he used the same verb as "to shrink back" <note>original: "subterfugi"</note> in "For I have not shrunk back," etc.

21 **publicly and through houses** <note>original: "publice & per domos"</note>] In Greek: *demōsiai kai kat’ oikous*, that is, publicly and domestically, or through individual houses, which seems to correspond to what the Latins call "privately." Jerome, in the preface to his Commentaries on the Epistle to the Ephesians, translates this as "publicly and domestically."

22 **Chains and tribulations await me** <note>original: "Vincula & tribulationes me manent"</note>] The Greek word *menousi* is the same verb which a little earlier was translated as "stayed."

23 **I fear none of these things** <note>original: "Nihil horum vereor"</note>] In Greek: *All’ oudenos logon poioumai*, that is, "I care for nothing," or "Nothing moves me." How could he not fear when he knew they were coming? Rather, he held them in contempt.

<margin>E</margin> 24 **Nor do I make my soul more precious than myself** <note>original: "Nec facio animam pretiosiorem quam me"</note>] What moved the Translator so that he neither expressed the sense nor rendered the words of Luke? The Greek is *oude echō tēn psychēn mou timian emautō*, that is, "neither do I have or hold my life as precious to myself." Augustine, in his commentary on Psalm 36, reads: "I do not make my soul precious to me." Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a 14th-century biblical exegete</note> interprets this as the "intellectual soul." But Paul meant that he despised his life for the love of the Gospel.

25 **Provided I may finish my course** <note>original: "Dummodo consummem cursum meam"</note>] The Greek adds *meta charas*, that is, "with joy."

26 **The whole counsel of God** <note>original: "Omne consilium Dei"</note>] It is strange what Irenaeus follows here; for "counsel of God," he reads "sentence": for in Greek it is *boulēn*, not *gnōmēn*.

27 **To rule the church of God** <note>original: "Regere ecclesiam Dei"</note>] The Greek is *poimainein*, which is to govern and care for a flock in the manner of shepherds; for he immediately mentions wolves.

28 **Ravening wolves** <note>original: "Lupi rapaces"</note>] The Greek is *Bareis*, that is, "heavy" or "burdensome," not "ravening." One manuscript from Donatianus supported this. Irenaeus reports this passage no differently in his third book, chapter fourteen.

29 **Men speaking perverse things** <note>original: "Viri loquentes perversa"</note>] The Greek is *diestrammena*, that is, distorted and crooked; that is, not at all simple and not at all sincere. For, as the Tragic poet says, "the speech of truth is simple."

<column-break/>

...with tears and trials, which happened to me from the plots of the Jews: 20 That I have not shrunk from anything that was for your benefit, but that I should announce it to you, and teach you 21 publicly and through individual houses, testifying to Jews and Greeks alike, the repentance which is toward God, and the faith which is toward our Lord Jesus. And now behold, I, bound in the spirit, 22 set out for Jerusalem, not knowing what things shall happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit in 23 every city testifies, saying that chains and afflictions await me. But 24 nothing moves me, nor is my life dear to myself, 25 so that I may finish my course with joy, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the Gospel of the grace of God. And now behold, I know that 25 hereafter you shall not see my face, all you through whom I have passed, preaching the kingdom of God. Wherefore 26 I call you to witness this day, that I am clean from the blood of all. For I did not shrink back from announcing 26 the whole counsel of God to you. Take 28 heed therefore to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to rule the church of God, which he acquired by his own blood. For I 29 know this, that after my departure heavy wolves shall enter among you, not sparing the flock. And from 30 among your own selves shall arise men, speaking perverse things, to lead away disciples after them. Because of which, watch, 31 being mindful that for three years, night and day, I 30 did not cease to warn each one with tears. And now I commend you, brothers, to God and to the word of his 31 grace, who is powerful to build up and to give you an inheritance among all the sanctified. Silver, or gold, or clothing of no man have I coveted. Yea, 34 you yourselves know that for my needs and for those who are with me, these hands have provided. I have shown all things to 35 you, that thus laboring it behooves you to support the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, for he himself said, 33 It is more blessed to give rather than to receive. And 36 when he had said these things, having knelt down, he prayed with all of them. And a great weeping arose from 37 all, and falling on Paul’s neck, they kissed him, grieving most of all for the word which he had said, that 38 they were to see his face no more: and they escorted him to the ship. And when it happened that we had XXI. set sail, having torn ourselves from them, by a straight course we came to Cos, and the following day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. And having 2 found a ship which was crossing to Phoenicia, having gone aboard, we set sail—

---

30 **I did not cease warning** <note>original: "Non cessavi monens"</note>] Here too the participle should have been translated as an infinitive: "I did not cease to warn."

31 **Who is powerful** <note>original: "Qui potens est"</note>] It should rather be "because he who," since "who" refers to God. However, because in Greek the gender is masculine, this surprisingly tripped up the Translator. Nor is it simply "to build" <note>original: "aedificare"</note>, but *epoikodomēsai*, that is, to build upon, evidently upon those foundations which Paul had laid.

32 **It behooves us to support the weak** <note>original: "Oportet suscipere infirmos"</note>] The Greek is *antilambanesthai*, which properly means to hold back someone who is about to fall or depart by stretching out a hand. Paul, lest he should suffer the loss of anyone at all, was careful not to offer any handle to the weak or to those who might be alienated from Christ because they did not wish to be burdened by the expense of his support. I wish those would take delight in this example who, while they demand tithes from the people in such an unsacerdotal manner, completely forget their own duty: not that I deny those tithes are owed, but that the other Apostles only accepted what was offered. Paul did not even accept what was offered, although he labored more than all of them.

33 **It is blessed to give more than to receive** <note>original: "Beatum est dare magis quam accipere"</note>] Neither the logic of Latin grammar required the comparative, nor did the Greek speech have it. It is strange, therefore, what came into the Translator's mind, for the Greek is *Makariōn esti didonai mallon ē lambanein*, that is, "It is more blessed to give than to receive." Moreover, they say this testimony is nowhere found to have been spoken by the Lord <note>Erasmus notes this is an "agraphon," a saying of Jesus not recorded in the four Gospels</note>. I wish, however, that the preachers of our time would imitate this spirit of Paul, so lofty and abhorring every appearance of profit. There was one who forbade himself the eating of meat for his whole life, and some are found who imitate him; there was one who always walked with bare feet, and he has imitators; there was one who girded himself with a rope, and there are those who zealously emulate him; there was one who always walked dressed in mourning, and he finds emulators. Only this most beautiful example of Paul has no emulators.

<margin>F</margin> 1 **We came to Cos** <note>original: "Venimus Coum"</note>] Some manuscripts have *Kō*, some *Kōn*: Stephanus admits it is pronounced both ways, and that it was once called *Koō*: whence Pliny also advises it was called *Ceum* and *Koō*. The island is too well known to need explanation.

2 **And from there to Patara** <note>original: "Et inde Pataram"</note>] The Greeks pronounce *Patara* in the neuter gender and plural number, although I find names of this sort used in both ways, such as *Lystra* and *Lystram*, *Phyra* and *Phyram*.

<margin>E</margin>
3 **When we had sighted Cyprus** ] I suspect the Translator rendered this as "When we had opened Cyprus" <note>original: "Quum aperuiffemus autem Cyprum"</note>; for the Greek is *Ἀναφανάντες δὲ τὴν Κύπρον*. Furthermore, sailors are said to "open" or "hide" this or that land when it begins to be in sight, or otherwise. Therefore we have translated it, "When Cyprus began to appear to us." Virgil used a similar figure of speech:
-> the lands and cities recede. <-
In the codex of Saint Donatian, the word *apparuiſſemus* ("we had appeared") was corrupted; but "Cyprus" remained, indicating the true reading should have been, "When we had sighted Cyprus."
4 **We came to Tyre** ] This is a maritime city, the metropolis of Phoenicia. It was once an island separated from the mainland by seven hundred paces of very deep sea, but it was joined to the mainland by Alexander the Great using mounds of earth brought together with incredible labor. It is in the tribe of Naphtali, twenty miles from Caesarea Philippi.
5 **We said farewell to each other** ] *ἀσπασάμενοι ἀλλήλους*, that is, having embraced one another, or with a mutual greeting having been made. It appears the Translator read *ἀσπαζάμενοι*.
6 **We came to Caesarea** ] This is Caesarea of Palestine, a coastal city, first called the Tower of Straton; later it was restored by Herod in honor of Caesar Augustus and named Caesarea. There is another Caesarea Philippi at the foot of Mount Lebanon, named Caesarea in honor of Tiberius Caesar. There is a third in Cappadocia, where Jerome claims Paul greeted the Church after being brought from Ephesus.
7 **For several days** ] *ἡμέρας πλείους*, that is, many days.
8 **We and those who were of that place** ] *ἡμεῖς τε καὶ οἱ ἐντόπιοι*, that is, both us and those who were residents of that place.
9 **And since we could not persuade him** ] What is this? Had he not just said they *tried* to persuade him? Indeed, the Translator misused "urge" <note>Latin: "suadere"</note> for "persuade" <note>Latin: "persuadere"</note>. For he who gives counsel urges, but he who leads a man where he wishes persuades. The Greek word is ambiguous for either: *πειθο-*

But we, having finished the voyage from 7 Tyre, came down to Ptolemais, and having greeted the brothers, we stayed one day with them. Now he had 9 four virgin daughters, who prophesied. And while we 10 remained for several days, there came from Judea a certain prophet named Agabus. When he had come to 11 us, he took Paul's belt, and binding his own feet and hands, he said, "Thus says the Holy Spirit: The man whose belt this is, so shall the Jews bind him in Jerusalem, and they shall deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles." And when 12 we had heard these things, both we and the others who were of that place entreated him not to go up to Jerusalem. Then 13 Paul answered and said, "What are you doing, weeping and afflicting my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus." And when he would not be persuaded, 14 we grew quiet, saying, "The will of the Lord be done." After 15 these days, having taken up our baggage, we went up to 16 Jerusalem. And there came also some of the disciples from Caesarea with us, bringing with them the one with whom we were to lodge, a certain Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple. And when we had come to 17 Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. And on the 18 following day, Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders assembled. When he 19 had greeted them, he related one by one what things God had done among the nations through his ministry. And when they 20 heard it, they glorified the Lord, and said to him, "You see, brother, how many thousands there are of Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous followers of the law. 21 Now they have heard about you, that you teach a falling away from Moses to all the Jews who are among the Gentiles, saying that they ought not to circumcise their sons, nor live according to the customs. What is it then? It is 22 entirely necessary for the multitude to come together: for they will hear that you have come. Do therefore this, which we say to you. We have 23 four men who have a vow upon them. Having taken these, 24 purify yourself with them, and pay for them, so that they may shave their heads: and all may know that the things they heard...

<meta>catchword: ...concerning you</meta>

---

...*μένου δὲ αὐτοῦ* <note>original: "me-nou de autou"</note> applies not only to the one urging, but also to the one complying. *Μὴ πειθομένου δὲ αὐτοῦ, ἡσυχάσαμεν* ("Since he was not persuaded, we were silent"). Otherwise, "Since he could not be persuaded," or "since he would not comply," we rested.
10 **Prepared, we went up** ] *ἀποσκευασάμενοι*, which I think should be translated, "having taken up our baggage" <note>original: "sublatis farcinis"</note>.
11 **A certain Jason** ] The Greeks read, *Μνάσωνί τινι*, that is, "a certain Mnason." Although in Chrysostom's commentary on the last chapter of the Epistle to the Romans it is read as "Jason"; nevertheless, scribes are prone to corrupt many such things. I will pass over the fact that he translated *ἐδόξαζον* as "they magnified" <note>original: "magnificabant"</note> instead of "they glorified" <note>original: "glorificabant"</note>.
12 **They have heard about you** ] *κατηχήθησαν*. This is the same word from which we said "Catechumens" is derived. He uses the same word a little later: "of which they have been informed." It does not mean "discord," but *ἀποστασίαν*, that is, "apostasy" or "falling away."
<margin>F</margin>
13 **Of those Jews who are among the Gentiles** ] *τοὺς κατὰ τὰ ἔθνη πάντας Ἰουδαίους*, that is, "all those Jews who are in the nations." The Translator was misled by the double accusative added to the verb of teaching.
14 **Nor to walk according to the custom** ] *μηδὲ τοῖς ἔθεσι περιπατεῖν*, "nor to walk according to the customs." For he calls "living" "walking," and the "customs" are the institutes and manners of that nation. Nor is it "they are false," but *εἰσὶν ἐν*, that is, "they are nothing." And indeed from this passage James seems at that time still to have been of the opinion that the Mosaic Law should be observed to some extent by the Jews, even though Peter and Paul are read to have lived after the manner of the Gentiles. Not that he thought it necessary for salvation, but useful for avoiding the stumbling block of the weak, whereas Paul thought it was already time to cast off that superstition, as it was leaning toward a great danger to the Gospel doctrine.
15 **Sanctify yourself** ] It is not this, but *ἁγνίσθητι*, that is, "purify yourself." And a little later, "having been purified," *ἁγνισθείς*.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>16 From things sacrificed to idols, etc.]</margin> We have four [prohibitions], just as the Greeks do. Augustine, in his *Speculum*, mentions only three: *things sacrificed to idols, blood, and fornication*. And lest anyone interpret this as an accident, he adds that some have seized upon the occasion for error from these words of Luke, saying there are only three deadly crimes.
<margin>17 They stirred up all]</margin> *synecheon* <note>original: "συνέχεον"</note>, that is, they were confusing or disturbing. And it is better to say "the whole" rather than "all." Nor is it "the people," but *ochlon* <note>original: "ὄχλον"</note>, "the crowd" or "the multitude." And "help" is better than "assist," *boētheite* <note>original: "βοηθεῖτε"</note>: for one assists who is a partner in a work. And, "this is the man," *ho anthrōpos* <note>original: "ὁ ἄνθρωπος"</note>, that is, that specific man.
<margin>18 Teaches everyone everywhere]</margin> The grace of the literary figure is lost in our language: *pantas pantachou* <note>original: "πάντας πανταχοῦ"</note>, that is, all people in every place. Nor is it "he violated this holy place," but *kekoinōke* <note>original: "κεκοίνωκε"</note>, that is, "he profaned," or, as the Hebrews would say, "he made it common."
<margin>19 Know the truth for certain]</margin> *to asphales* <note>original: "τὸ ἀσφαλές"</note>. This is quite correctly translated. But why did the translator not likewise translate it in the preface of the Gospel, *tēn asphaleian*, as "certainty"?
<margin>20 Ordered him to be led into the barracks]</margin> *eis tēn parembolēn* <note>original: "εἰς τὴν παρεμβολήν"</note>. This is what he calls a fortified place. However, some have turned "barracks" into "prison": and for that reason we have noted it, lest the error creep further.
<margin>21 Are you not the Egyptian]</margin> Egyptians had a bad reputation in ancient times, as if they were the authors of evil arts. Juvenal and Lucian indicate this in several places. Indeed, the character of this nation is noted in several proverbs which we have reviewed in our *Chiliades* <note>Erasmus's own collection of Greek and Latin adages.</note>.
<margin>22 And of the Assassins]</margin> Writing in Greek, he used a Latin word <note>original: "σικαρίων" (sikariōn) from the Latin "sicarius"</note>, which can no longer seem new, since it is encountered so often.
<margin>23 From Tarsus of Cilicia]</margin> *Tarseus tēs Kilikias* <note>original: "Ταρσεὺς τῆς Κιλικίας"</note>, that is, a man of Tarsus, which is a city of Cilicia. It is the metropolis of that region. Nor

<column-break/>

is it unknown, but *asēmos* <note>original: "ἄσημος"</note>, that is, "obscure" <note>Erasmus is correcting the translation here, noting that Paul says he is from a city that is *not* obscure.</note>, except that Horace called unknown men "obscure" and "ignoble." Stephanus testifies the same regarding the names of cities, calling this one "most notable" <note>original: "ἐπισημοτάτην"</note>, that is, primary and distinguished above others; it was once called *Iersan*, with an epsilon, either because it was the first dry land to appear after the flood, or because Pegasus, having fallen there, broke his ankle—which they call *tarson* <note>original: "ταρσόν"</note>—and developed a limp. Furthermore, however celebrated it was by other names, it is distinguished by none more than the fact that we owe Paul to it. He was so exceptional a herald and champion of Christian philosophy that if he had not been granted to us by divine gift, there would have been a danger that all Christians might have slipped back into that slavish and humble Law of Moses. Although even now we differ from them more by reason than by the number of ceremonies: that is how far Christ has receded over time. There is another city of the same name in Bithynia. Again, another somewhere in India, as Jerome indicates in the commentaries he wrote on Jonah. Josephus thinks that Tarsus of Cilicia is the place to which Jonah fled. Furthermore, some read "citizen-soldier" <note>original: "municeps"</note>, some "citizen" <note>original: "civis"</note>; in Greek it is *politēs* <note>original: "πολίτης"</note>, that is, "citizen." But I think the translator was bothered by the similarity of the words "city" and "citizen," though it is the same in the Greek tongue, *poleōs, politēs* <note>original: "πόλεως, πολίτης"</note>. There is also some ambiguity, for "not obscure" <note>original: "ἄσημος"</note> seems to be joined to "Cilicia" as an appositive, whereas it belongs to "Tarsus."

<margin>1</margin> **I gave an account]** *apologias* <note>original: "ἀπολογίας"</note>, which means both a "defense" and an "excuse."

<margin>2</margin> **According to the truth of the paternal law]** *kat' akribeian tou patrōou nomou* <note>original: "κατ᾿ ἀκρίβειαν τοῦ πατρῴου νόμου"</note>, that is, "according to the exact reasoning of the fatherland's law," or "according to the vigor of the ancestral law." And "ancestral" <note>original: "patriæ"</note> is better than "paternal" <note>original: "paternæ"</note>, since he is not thinking of his own father, but of all his ancestors.

<margin>3</margin> **Zealot for the law]** *zēlōtēs tou Theou* <note>original: "ζηλωτὴς τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note>, that is, "zealot for God," as we read among the Greeks.

# ACTS OF THE APOSTLES CHAPTER XXII.

<margin>5</margin> <margin>A</margin> "As the High Priest also bears me witness, and the whole council of elders, from whom I also received letters to the brothers and was traveling to Damascus, to bring those who were there also as prisoners to Jerusalem, so that they might be <margin>6</margin> punished. But it happened to me as I was traveling and drawing near to Damascus about noon, that suddenly from heaven a great light flashed around <margin>7</margin> me. And I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?' <margin>8</margin> And I answered, 'Who are you, Lord?' and He said to me, 'I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are <margin>9</margin> persecuting.' Those who were with me saw the light indeed and became terrified, but they did not hear the voice of the one <margin>10</margin> speaking to me. And I said, 'What shall I do, Lord?' And the Lord said to me, 'Arise and go into Damascus, and there it will be told to you concerning all the things <margin>11</margin> which have been appointed for you to do.' <margin>B</margin> And since I could not see because of the glory of that light, being led by the hand by those who <margin>12</margin> were with me, I came into Damascus. Then a certain Ananias, a pious man according to the Law, well-spoken of by <margin>13</margin> all the Jews dwelling there, came to me and standing by, said to me, 'Brother Saul, receive your sight.' <margin>14</margin> And in that very hour I looked up at him. And he said, 'The God of our fathers has appointed you to know His will, and to see the Just One, and to <margin>15</margin> hear a voice from His mouth; for you will be a witness for Him to all men of what you have seen and <margin>16</margin> heard. And now why do you delay? Arise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on the <margin>17</margin> name of the Lord.' Then it happened to me, having returned to Jerusalem, and while I was praying in the temple, that I fell into a <margin>18</margin> trance, and saw Him saying to me, 'Hurry and go out quickly from Jerusalem, because [they will not receive your testimony]...'" <meta>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</meta>

---

<margin>A</margin> 5 *Just as the High Priest* <note>original: "Sicut princeps Sacerdotum"</note>] The Greek says: "As also the High Priest bears me witness," that is, *In the same manner as the Pontiff is my witness.*
5 *All the elders* <note>original: "Omnes majores natu"</note>] The Greek uses *pan to presbyterion*, that is, *the entire order of Presbyters.* For I think this refers to a rank of dignity, not merely to age.
6 *To the brothers* <note>original: "Ad fratres"</note>] Greek: *pros tous adelphous*. Either he calls the Jews "brothers" here, or the word *pros* is more correctly translated as "against," if he is referring to the Christians as brothers.
7 *To bring them bound from there* <note>original: "Ut adducerem inde vinctos"</note>] Greek: "about to bring also those who were there bound to Jerusalem."
8 *A great light flashed around me* <note>original: "Circumfulsit me lux copiosa"</note>] Greek: *periastrapsai peri eme*. This means *to flash around like lightning* rather than merely *to shine around*, as was noted previously.
9 *And falling to the ground* <note>original: "Et decidens in terram"</note>] Greek: "And I fell into the soil." For the word *edaphos* means the ground or floor, even if it were made of stone or wood.
10 *Saul, Saul*] The Greeks read this as *Saul, Saul*, in the Hebrew manner. For Christ spoke to him in the Hebrew language, as Paul himself testifies later.
<margin>B</margin> 11 *And those who were with me saw the light*] To this, the Greek adds, "and they were terrified." Then it is added, "but they did not hear the voice of the one speaking to me." Truly, I cannot help but strongly praise the diligence of Lorenzo Valla <note>A famous 15th-century Italian humanist who critiqued the Latin Vulgate using Greek manuscripts.</note>. Although he was a man of Rhetoric (as the common people think) and certainly did not profess to be a theologian, he nevertheless investigated with such vigilance what was discordant, consistent, or corrupted in the Holy Scriptures. Today, I dare say there are thousands of theologians who are so far from this skill of comparing and discerning that they do not even know in which language the Apostles wrote. When they happen to hear that Mark, Luke, Paul, Peter, and John wrote in Greek, they are stunned as if hearing something unheard of and incredible. One thinks they wrote nothing but Hebrew, because they were Hebrews. Another believes that the texts we commonly read are the originals they published; such is the laziness in so necessary a matter. 

Valla asks how it can be reconciled that Luke wrote earlier in chapter nine that Paul's companions "heard the voice but saw no one," while here he says they "did not hear the voice" of the speaker, but only saw the light. Furthermore, how does it fit that there they are said to have "stood speechless," yet shortly after (in chapter twenty-six), when Paul explains this same event to Agrippa, he says "all had fallen to the ground"—whereas here he says only he fell? There he says: "At midday, O King, I saw on the way a light from heaven above the brightness of the sun flashing around me and those who were with me; and when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice speaking to me in the Hebrew tongue, 'Saul, Saul.'" 

How is it that Luke wrote conflicting things? In his own narrative he says the companions heard the voice, yet here Paul denies that the voice was heard by anyone but himself? As for the difference between standing and falling, it is not a great matter to resolve: it is possible that they fell at the first shock and then quickly stood up, while Paul remained lying down. Regarding the voice being heard and not heard, the knot is harder to untie. Some explain it away by saying the "voice" (the sound of words) was heard, but the "words" were understood only by Paul; thus the voice was heard and yet not heard. Valla rather suspects the earlier passage where Luke recounts the story in his own person has been corrupted, with two Greek words—*Phos* (Light) and *Phone* (Voice)—being swapped, which are not very different in Greek. He thinks Luke originally wrote: "seeing the light, but hearing no one." Let others judge how much weight to give this opinion. Peter Comestor <note>A 12th-century theological writer.</note> escapes through another crack: he says in chapter nine they heard the voice of Paul responding, not the voice of Christ calling. Here, when Paul says they did not hear the voice, he means the voice of Christ.

<column-break/>

<margin>5</margin> <margin>A</margin> "As even the High Priest is my witness, and the entire Council of Elders, from whom I also received letters <margin>6</margin> to the brothers and was going to Damascus, to bring those who were there also as prisoners to Jerusalem, that they might be punished. But it happened to me while making the journey and approaching <margin>6</margin> Damascus about noon, that suddenly from heaven a great light flashed around me, <margin>7</margin> and I fell into the <margin>9</margin> soil, and heard a voice saying to me, <margin>10</margin> 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?' But I answered, 'Who <margin>8</margin> are you, Lord?' And He said to me, 'I am that Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting.' <margin>11</margin> And those who <margin>9</margin> were with me saw the light indeed, and were terrified, but they did not hear the voice of the one who was speaking with me. And I was saying, 'What shall I do, Lord?' And the <margin>10</margin> Lord said to me, 'Arise and go to Damascus, and there it will be told to you concerning all things <margin>12</margin> which have been ordained for you to do.' <margin>13</margin> And since I could not see because of the glory <margin>11</margin> of that light, being led by the hand by the companions who were with me, I came to Damascus. <margin>14</margin> But a certain Ananias, a pious man according to the law, proven by the testimony <margin>15</margin> of all the Jews dwelling there, <margin>13</margin> coming to me and standing by, said to me, 'Brother Saul, <margin>16</margin> receive your sight.' And in that same hour, having received my sight, I saw him. But he said, 'The God of our fathers has <margin>17</margin> prepared you, so that you might know His will, <margin>18</margin> and see that which is just, and hear a voice from His mouth: because you will be a witness for Him before all men of those things <margin>15</margin> which you have seen and heard. And now why do you delay? <margin>16</margin> <margin>C</margin> Arise and be baptized and wash away your sins, having called upon the name of the Lord. And it happened when I had <margin>17</margin> returned to Jerusalem, and was praying in the temple, that I was caught out of myself, and I saw Him saying to me, <margin>18</margin> 'Hurry...'"

---

<margin>C</margin> [Referring to the previous column's discussion on Luke's narrative.]

<margin>D</margin> 12 *What you ought to do* <note>original: "Quae te oporteat facere"</note>] In some manuscripts it was held as: "concerning all things which have been ordained for you to do." In others again there was only: "what it behooves you to do."
13 *Since I could not see for the brightness of the light* <note>original: "Quum non viderem prae claritate luminis"</note>] Greek: *apo tes doxes tou Photos ekeinou*, that is, *because of the glory of that light.*
14 *Ananias, a certain man according to the law having testimony* <note>original: "Ananias quidam vir secundum legem testimonium habens"</note>] The Greek codices add a bit more: "A certain Ananias, a pious or religious man, according to the law, being witnessed to by all the Jews dwelling there." Valla indicates that he found in one Latin manuscript an addition corresponding to the Greek: "Ananias a certain god-fearing man." For he uses "god-fearing" for "religious." Furthermore, instead of *eusebes* (pious), some copies had *eulabes*, which means *devout.* And what is translated here as "according to the law," could also be "in the law." That particle can refer to both parts: to what precedes, meaning "religious or pious in the law (meaning according to the Jewish law, not the Gospel)"; or to what follows, meaning "proven by the testimony of all in the law."
<margin>E</margin> 15 *By all the cohabiting Jews* <note>original: "Ab omnibus cohabitantibus Judaeis"</note>] "Inhabiting" or "dwelling" is *katoikounton*. And a certain Greek manuscript had written in the space between lines, "in Damascus," meaning *by all the Jews dwelling in Damascus.*
16 *Look up* <note>original: "Respice"</note>] Greek: *anablepson*, that is, *receive sight* or *lift up your eyes.* As it says shortly after, "And I looked up," Greek: *Kago aneblepsa*.
17 *He has preordained you* <note>original: "Praeordinavit te"</note>] Greek: *proecheirisato se*, that is, *He has prepared you* or *prepared you beforehand*; unless one prefers "He previously determined." However, that [the specific Latin word *praeordinavit*] was not in any of the Greek manuscripts. Ananias here is not discussing divine predestination, but rather Paul’s downfall and blindness—the means by which Christ was already acting and approaching him, so that by this occasion he might know the faith of the Gospel. My annotation does not exclude predestination, but explains the specific property of the Greek word. Chrysostom <note>An early Church Father.</note>, in explaining this passage, makes no mention of predestination.
<margin>F</margin> 18 *That you might see the just one* <note>original: "Ut videres justum"</note>] Greek: *ton dikaion*, that is, *justice* or *that which is just*: meaning you may discern that which you did not see before, being blinded by zeal for the law. Again, in others it was held as "that Just One," meaning Christ: and that agrees with what follows, "and hear a voice from His mouth." For he seems to be referring to the light he had seen and the voice of Jesus he had heard; although he also narrates shortly after how he saw and heard the Lord in the temple.
19 *Which you have seen and heard* <note>original: "Quae vidisti & audisti"</note>] Greek: *hon heorakas*. The relative article, according to the Greek idiom, agrees with the preceding pronoun which is understood—*eorum* (of those things)—even though it differs from its own verb. The translator did well to add "of those things" on his own.

<margin>20 I was standing and consenting</margin> Here the Greeks add two words, <note>original: "τῇ ἀναιρέσει αὐτοῦ"</note> that is, "to his death": "and I myself was standing by and approving of his killing."

<margin>21 Take such a one from the earth</margin> <note>original: "τοιοῦτον"</note>, that is, "such a man": referring to Paul. Hence it would not have been bad to add "this kind of man." And shortly after,

<margin>22 It is not lawful</margin>] possibly <note>original: "καθῆκον"</note>, that is, "it is not fitting" or "it is not becoming."

<margin>24 To be beaten with whips and tortured</margin>] The tribune ordered him to be led into the barracks, giving the command that they should examine him with whips. That nothing else was ordered is indicated by what follows, even if I momentarily set aside the fact that if he called him a Roman man, it was a matter of honor: since he did it so consistently that he seemed to do it by his own right.

<margin>28 A great sum</margin>] <note>original: "πολλοῦ κεφαλαίου"</note>. This is what the Greeks call a calculation brought to a total. In some versions we read "this state" <note>Latin: *civitatem*</note>, in others "citizenship" <note>Latin: *civilitatem*</note>, in Greek *politeian*. Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo Valla, a humanist scholar</note> prefers "citizenship," but I prefer "state" (or the right of citizenship). For among the Latins, those to whom the right of the state was granted are said to be gifted with "citizenship" <note>civitate</note>; and just as from *politēs* (citizen) comes *politeia* for the Greeks, so for us from *civis* (citizen) comes *civitas* (state/citizenship). Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, an 8th-century monk</note> notes that in some manuscripts the speech was clearer, written as: "The tribune said, 'You say so easily that you are a Roman citizen. For I know at what a price I possessed that citizenship.'" The word used is not "attained," but "acquired" <note>original: "ἐκτησάμην"</note>, which appeared earlier when someone "purchased a field with the reward of iniquity."

<margin>29 Wishing to know more diligently</margin>] <note>original: "τὸ ἀσφαλές"</note>, that is, "the certain fact": just as earlier he translated it "more certainly," he now translates it "more diligently."

---

<margin>E</margin> ...curse: unless perhaps one who, with a moved soul, predicts what will happen is said to curse. Although it is easy to explain regarding the "banquet," since a banquet is often prepared at a "whitewashed wall" <note>Erasmus explores various metaphors for the term "whitewashed wall," including the hypocrisy of a clean exterior hiding a dirty interior</note>. But how could it be that Paul did not recognize the primary Priest, perhaps even from his attire, especially being a man of the law who was familiar with every place? Then why does he retract his statement—not because he cursed a man, but because he cursed a Ruler of the people? Yet he surely knew he was a judge even when he spoke the insult: "You," he said, "sit judging me according to the law." Is it permitted to insult others, but not the Ruler alone? Yet Christ did not want anyone to be cursed at all. Saint Jerome, bringing up this passage in his dialogues against Pelagius, indeed excuses Paul, yet confesses that he did not display that same gentleness which Christ displayed. But Jerome wrote this before he fully defended the cause, and even in Christ he suggests some trace of imperfect piety. Nor does he himself hide that it is one thing to gather arguments against an adversary, and another to teach a disciple. He who fights does one thing; he who exhorts another; he who deters yet another. Furthermore, as there are diverse and infinite human temperaments, so too are there diverse opinions. But we, having no regard for these matters, have plucked three words from any corner of any work, and from there, having woven a syllogism, we issue a new oracle. Indeed, I do not deny that Paul was not entirely free from human emotions, since he himself mentions the "thorn in the flesh," and a certain disagreement existed between Barnabas and himself, indeed between two very good men. However, in this place, it is consistent that Paul was not ignorant of the High Priest, nor did he pray evil upon him with that mind which the irritated common folk usually have, but he burned with Apostolic spirit against one who, while holding the place of the best of men, did not offer even the appearance of equity which even the Heathens provided. So Peter burned against Ananias and Sapphira. So Paul himself against Elymas the sorcerer. What is it then that he excuses himself for, saying "I did not know he was the High Priest"? Surely he meant to speak of the "tumult," and he says he did not recognize as High Priest 
<margin>F</margin> one who showed himself by his deeds not to be a High Priest, but a tyrant. Therefore, under a double name he grants these trifles: first, by recognizing that he is the High Priest who in reality was nothing but a whitewashed wall; second, he does not deny that it was an insult, which seemed an insult to them, though it was not an insult but a free rebuke. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father</note> indicates that to some this seems to have been said through irony: "I did not know that he was the High Priest." But he himself firmly asserts that Paul truly did not know, either because he had been away from the customs of the Jews for a long time, or because he did not recognize Ananias in the crowd of many people. Bede, not disagreeing with Chrysostom, adds an interpretation more clever than true: "I did not know he was the High Priest," because through the Gospel the Mosaic priesthood had already ceased; and yet he corrects himself as if he had sinned, to teach others that reverence is owed to those in whose power we are. Furthermore, the testimony he brings forward is found in Exodus, chapter twenty-two: "You shall not disparage the gods <note>referring to judges</note>, and you shall not curse the Ruler of your people." Indeed, they call those judges and magistrates "gods."
