---

<margin>E</margin>
<note>2</note> **I did not know, brothers, that he is the ruler** | The word "that" [original: *quia*] is redundant in Latin; among the Greeks, it is sometimes added for the sake of affirmation. Augustine also noted in the first book of *On the Expressions of Genesis* that it often occurs redundantly in the Sacred Books, such as in the passage: *And he said, that he is the Lord*, or here: *but I was ignorant*.

<note>3</note> **And the multitude was divided** | The Greek is *eschisthē*, that is, it was split into sects. The [Latin] translators seem to have read *ilythē* [loosened].

<note>4</note> **But if a spirit has spoken to him or an angel** | The Greek reads differently: *if a spirit has spoken to him, or an angel, let us not fight against God* [original: *mē theomachōmen*]; this is the same word Gamaliel used previously. This clause, "lest we fight against God," was not found in our Latin copies; it appears to have been added from the earlier passages.

<note>5</note> **They bound themselves by a curse** | The Greek is *anematizsan*; however, the Translator renders it elegantly. I wonder indeed who pointed out to Carranza <note>Bartolomé Carranza (1503–1576), a Spanish theologian</note> that the Greek here says "they anathematized." And shortly after:

<note>6</note> **By a curse we have bound ourselves** | *Anathemati anethematisamen*, that is, to curse oneself, or to devote oneself to the "spirits of the dead" [original: *Diis manibus*], as the Pagans say.

<note>7</note> **Make it known to the tribune** | The Greek is somewhat different from our versions: *Now therefore you notify the tribune and the council, so that tomorrow he might lead him down to you, as if you were going to investigate more accurately the things concerning him.* With this reading, Chrysostom and the Aldine Edition agree, although some Greek codices almost agree with our copies, in which it is "to you" [original: *ymas*] instead of "to us" [original: *ēmas*], and "about to [be]" [original: *mellontes*] instead of "intending to [do]" [original: *mellontas*]. Thus the sense would be: "We have clearly decided to kill Paul at any risk; you help us, so that he is merely brought out to the people, using this pretext as if you wished to dispute more exactly about the cause." Otherwise, they knew the tribune would not bring Paul out if he knew of the ambush. Yet Carranza explains it as if they wanted this very thing reported to the tribune and the council—that they intended to kill Paul during a riot. Furthermore, it appears Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a Franciscan teacher</note> read it as, *Now you make it known to the tribune with the council*, as it is read in some Greek copies. Since this means the same thing, he interprets and orders it thus: "You," he says, "with the council," meaning you Pharisees and Sadducees joined together, lest your dissension hinder Paul's death. Let us go now and deny that it matters which Greek text one considers, such as whether *intending to* should be translated through a specific verb form. For he feigns that this will happen, and therefore the word *as if* [original: *hōs*] is added. Nor have I ever found *mallon* [rather] used this way, except when the unlearned say "he wants to come" or "he ought to come" instead of "he is coming."

<column-break/>

<margin>F</margin>
<note>8</note> **As if about to know something more certain of him** | If "to inquire" [original: *pynthesthai*] refers to the tribune and the council, perhaps "about to hear" was more appropriate. For the Greek voice is ambiguous, especially since "to investigate" [original: *diaginōskein*] preceded it, which seems to pertain more to a judge than a plaintiff. And so in the first part, one should read *mellontes* [nominative], not *mellontas* [accusative]; the nominative case should be taken for the genitive absolute, although the Greeks sometimes use the accusative case absolutely as well. Now, whether one should read *pros hymas* [to you] or *pros hēmas* [to us] must be weighed.

<note>9</note> **That you have indicated these things to me** | The Translator did well to change the second person into the third; for in Greek it is: *commanding him to tell no one that you have indicated these things to me*, which means, "he ordered that he should not report to anyone that he [the boy] had indicated these things to me [the tribune]." Unless you prefer the infinitive mood placed in stead of the imperative, as we translated: *tell no one* [original: *mēdeni eklalēsai*], "do not reveal it to anyone."

<margin>A</margin> And calling two of the centurions, he said: "Prepare two hundred soldiers to go as far as Caesarea, along with seventy horsemen and two hundred <margin>24</margin> light-armed troops <note>original: δεξιολάβους (*dexiolabous*), literally 'right-hand takers,' likely meaning spearmen or guards</note> from the third hour of the night. But the tribune Lysias came and with great force took him out of our hands, <margin>8</margin> ordering his accusers to come before you."

10 **And two hundred light-armed troops** <note>original: *Et lancearios ducentos*</note>] The Greek word is *dexiolabous*, because they threw spears with the right hand. Or, as it is read in others, *dexiobolous*: for in old times they almost always used such soldiers. And shortly after,
11 **And provide beasts of burden**] He used the infinitive for the imperative here. He feared that the Jews might seize and kill Paul, and that he himself would later face a false accusation as if he had accepted a bribe. Everything I have reviewed so far is missing in the Greek manuscripts that I have happened to see. Nor did this passage offend Laurentius Valla <note>a famous 15th-century Italian humanist and critic</note>: from which it appears that either his manuscript had these things, or he did not notice. Certainly Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a medieval biblical commentator</note> denies these are found in the more correct books; rather, he thinks this was a marginal note <note>original: *glossoma*</note> that someone ignorantly moved into the main text. It is certain, however, that Lyranus did not dream this up. Even Chrysostom <note>an influential early church father</note>, when explaining this passage, does not read or explain the things we have shown to be missing in the Greek.
12 **To the most excellent governor**] The Greek word *kratistō* is more suitable for a powerful man than a "good" man, as was said in the preface of Luke to his Gospel.
13 **Through the night to Antipatris**] There was no need to add a preposition, since *Antipatris* is the name of a city in Palestine, named after Antipater, the father of Herod.
14 **From what province he was**] The Translator rendered this quite elegantly from the Greek *eparchias*.
<margin>F</margin> 1 **As they went to the governor**] The sense is rendered correctly: they approached the judge to bring charges against the accused. However, the Greek *emphanizein* sounds like "they made known," unless "themselves" is understood. Some mistakenly read "approached" where they should have read "appeared."
2 **And many reforms are made through your foresight**] In Greek it is *katorthōmatōn*, which signifies a deed done with virtue and praise—what Cicero <note>the Roman orator</note> calls "duty" <note>original: *officium*</note>. The meaning is: "Since through your foresight we enjoy much peace, and you perform many duties for this people."
3 **We acknowledge, most excellent Felix**] We translate this as "most distinguished." As I said, the Greek *kratiste* sounds more like "most powerful."
4 **Lest I detain you longer**] Meaning "hinder" or "delay." And for "your clemency," the Greek is *epieikeia*, which some translate as "humanity" and others as "fairness."
5 **This pestilent man**] In Greek, it is not an adjective like "pestilent," but a <meta>continued on next page</meta>

This man was seized by the Jews, and when he was already about to be killed <margin>B</margin> by them, I came upon them with the army and rescued him, having learned he was a Roman. And wanting to know the cause for <margin>27</margin> which they accused him, I led him into their council. I found him to be accused concerning questions of <margin>28</margin> their law, having no crime worthy of death or bonds. And when it was reported to me regarding the <margin>29</margin> plot they had prepared against him, I immediately sent him to you, giving word also to his accusers that they should say before you what they have against him. Farewell." <margin>30</margin> The soldiers indeed, according to what was enjoined upon them, took Paul and led him <margin>13</margin> through the night to Antipatris. On the <margin>31</margin> following day, having sent the horsemen to go with him, they returned to the camp. When they had come to Caesarea and delivered <margin>32</margin> the letter to the governor, they also presented Paul before him. When the governor <margin>33</margin> had read it and asked <margin>14</margin> from what province he was, and learned he was from Cilicia, he said: "I will hear you when your accusers <margin>34</margin> have also arrived," and he ordered him to be guarded in Herod's palace. After five days, the <margin>XXIV. 1</margin> High Priest Ananias descended with the Elders and a certain orator named Tertullus, who approached the governor against Paul. And when Paul was summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: "Since we live in great peace through you, <margin>2</margin> and many things are managed rightly in this nation through your foresight, we always and everywhere <margin>3</margin> approve, <margin>C</margin> most excellent Felix, with all thanksgiving. <margin>D</margin> But lest I detain you any longer, I pray you to hear us <margin>4</margin> briefly in your humanity. For we have found <margin>5</margin> this pestilent man, stirring up sedition among all the Jews in the whole world, <margin>6</margin> and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes, <margin>7</margin> who even attempted to profane the temple, whom we also seized and wanted to judge according to our law. But the <margin>7</margin> tribune Lysias, coming upon us with great force, snatched him from our hands, ordering his accusers to come to you." <margin>8</margin>

---

noun, that is, "the pest." Just as they call a deadly thing *olethron*, meaning "destruction." Also, it is not "the man," but "the way."
6 **And a leader of the sedition of the sect**] "Sedition" is absent in the Greek codices; it reads "the ringleader of the sect or faction called the Nazarenes."
7 **Even attempted to violate the temple**] The Greek means to "profane." This was added so that no one would imagine Paul was being accused of using physical violence against the temple building itself.
8 **Whom we seized and wanted to judge... But the tribune Lysias...**] All of these phrases were missing in many Greek manuscripts. I found them added in only one, but in very tiny handwriting and in the margin. Therefore, we have added them here. Furthermore, Beda <note>The Venerable Bede, an 8th-century English monk and scholar</note>, if I am not mistaken, indicates in the "Ordinary Glosses" that several verses were missing in the Latin books which are read in the Greek to this effect: "Whom we apprehended," etc. It is easy to believe that Bede had access to some commentaries of learned men that are no longer available to us. In his preface, he admits he was aided by the commentaries of certain writers, though he names none except Arator <note>a 6th-century Christian poet</note>. It is strange that these verses, once noted as missing in Latin books, are now constantly found in them but are missing in most Greek books. In a very ancient manuscript shown to us at Constance, these same things were missing. It is possible someone added them from the narrative of the previous chapter or from the Letter of Lysias. However, if these are removed, the flow of the speech still holds together. For it could be read: "whom we seized... from whom you yourself will be able to learn about all these things." Instead of "coming upon us," some Latin books had "interceding."
9 **From whom you yourself will be able to learn, judging**] Since the Greek is *anakrinas*, the word "interrogating" or "having made an inquiry" would be more fitting here.

# THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES. CH. XXIV.

<margin>8</margin> ...from whom you will be able, by examining him yourself, to learn the truth of all these things of which we accuse <margin>9</margin> him." And the Jews also joined in the charge, asserting that these things were so.
<margin>10</margin> Then Paul, after the governor had beckoned for him to speak, answered: "Knowing that for many years you have been a judge to this nation, I cheerfully make my defense concerning <margin>11</margin> myself. As you are able to understand, it has been no more than twelve days since I went up <margin>12</margin> to worship in Jerusalem. And they did not find me disputing with anyone in the temple, or inciting a crowd to riot, neither in the synagogues nor throughout the city. <margin>13</margin> Nor can they prove the things of which they now <margin>14</margin> accuse me. But I confess this to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect <note>original: αἵρεσιν (*hairesin*), often translated as 'heresy'</note>, so I worship the God of my fathers, believing all things written in the Law and in the <margin>15</margin> Prophets. I have a hope in God, which these men themselves also look for, that there will be a <margin>16</margin> resurrection of the dead, both of the just and the unjust. In this I myself strive to always have a clear conscience toward God and <margin>17</margin> toward men. Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and <margin>18</margin> offerings. In the midst of these they found me purified in the temple, <margin>19</margin> neither with a crowd nor with a disturbance. But there were certain Jews from Asia who ought to be present before you <margin>20</margin> and accuse me, if they have anything against me. Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found in me when I stood before <margin>21</margin> the council, except concerning this one statement which I cried out while standing among them: 'Concerning the resurrection of the <margin>22</margin> dead I am being judged by you today.'" When Felix heard these things, having more accurate knowledge concerning...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...from whom you will be able, after an inquiry is made, to learn of all these things of which we accuse him. <margin>9</margin> Furthermore, the Jews also added their agreement, saying these things were so. Then Paul answered, <margin>10</margin> when the governor himself had nodded for him to speak: "With a more tranquil mind I plead my cause for myself, since I know you have been a judge for this nation for many years. You can learn that there <margin>11</margin> are no more than twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem to worship. And they did not <margin>12</margin> find me in the temple disputing with anyone, or making a gathering of a crowd, nor in the synagogues, nor <margin>B</margin> in the city. <margin>13</margin> Neither can they prove the things of which they <margin>14</margin> accuse me. But I confess this to you: that <gloss>according to the way</gloss> which they call a heresy, so <margin>14</margin> I worship the God of my fathers, believing all things that are written in the Law and the Prophets, having a hope in God—which they themselves also expect—that there will be <margin>15</margin> a resurrection of the dead, of the just and unjust alike. Indeed, in this I also strive <margin>15</margin> to have a conscience <margin>16</margin> without offense toward God and toward men always. After many years I arrived to show <margin>17</margin> alms to my nation, and offerings, in which they found me purified in the <margin>18</margin> temple, not with a crowd, nor with a tumult. <margin>16</margin> <margin>19</margin> But certain Jews from Asia, who ought to be here before you and accuse me, if they had anything against <margin>C</margin> me: Or let these men themselves say if they discovered <margin>20</margin> any iniquity in me when I stood in the council, <margin>17</margin> except for this <margin>21</margin> one statement, which I cried out while standing among them: 'Concerning the resurrection of the dead I am judged today by you.' But <margin>22</margin> Felix, hearing these things, adjourned them, <margin>18</margin> knowing certainly the things which...

---

<margin>10</margin> *The governor nodding to him* ] <note>original: νεύσαντος αὐτῷ τοῦ ἡγεμόνος (*neusantos autō tou hēgemonos*)</note>, that is, <gloss>when the governor himself had nodded.</gloss> The Translator seems to have read "of him" <note>original: αὐτοῦ (*autou*)</note>; but it does not matter much.
<margin>11</margin> *With a good mind I shall satisfy for myself* ] <note>original: εὐθυμότερον τὰ περὶ ἐμαυτοῦ... ἀπολογοῦμαι (*euthymoteron ta peri emautou... apologoumai*)</note>, that is, <gloss>with a more tranquil mind I answer the cause for myself.</gloss> For "I make a defense" <note>original: ἀπολογοῦμαι (*apologoumai*)</note> is in the present tense, which the Translator renders in various ways. Properly, an <term>apology</term> is a speech by which a defendant protects himself before a judge.
<margin>12</margin> *Neither can they prove to you the things of which they now accuse me* ] <note>original: Οὔτε παραστήσασαί με δύνανται (*Oute parastēsasai me dynantai*)</note>, that is, <gloss>nor are they able to present me in those things of which they accuse me.</gloss> He said <term>to present</term> <note>Latin: exhibere</note> in the sense of <term>to convict</term>.
<margin>13</margin> *According to the sect, which they call heresy* ] Since <term>heresy</term> among the Greeks is nothing other than a <term>sect</term>, what was in the Translator's mind to interpret a Latin word using a Greek one that signifies the same thing? Was he afraid that someone might not understand the word <term>sect</term>, and for that reason explained it with the Greek term as if it were better known? Therefore, let the Reader know that in this place the Greek does not use "sect"—otherwise he would have had to say "sect and sect" twice—but "the way" <note>original: ὁδὸν (*hodon*)</note>, that is, <gloss>according to the Way, which they call heresy, or a sect.</gloss> For Paul explains what he meant by "the way," that is, a way of life, which they call a <term>sect</term> by a better-known word. For I think he felt it referred to the <term>sect</term> of the Pharisees, which excelled the others in learning. This is gathered from what he adds: <gloss>believing all things which are written in the Law and the Prophets, having a hope in God, which they themselves also expect, the resurrection of the just and the wicked.</gloss> The Apostle conceals the hateful name of the <term>Nazarenes</term>, which the accuser Tertullus had pushed upon him. He used a similar prudence in the previous chapter, crying out, <gloss>"Men and brothers, I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee; concerning the hope and resurrection I am being judged."</gloss> Furthermore, among the Ancients, "heresy" was not such a hateful word as it is today among Christians. Since the greatest harmony is required of Christians, as members of the same body, the word <term>sect</term> is rightly hated, as it <gloss>sounds like division.</gloss> As for what he mentions regarding <term>the Way and heresy</term>, we later found it noted by Bede in his Scholarly notes on this work. It is also mentioned in the Standard Gloss. Although what he adds is not entirely foreign: <gloss>that it is called heresy by the unbelieving, since in that age the word "heresy" was not yet infamous; rather, he explains with a word born of common usage what he had said in a Hebrew rather than Greek manner as "The Way."</gloss> For in these words of Paul, <gloss>which they call heresy</gloss>, the name <term>Nazarenes</term> is understood, which truly was a <term>heresy</term> of those mixing the Law with the Gospel. Paul was not of this sect, for he taught that circumcision along with the other ceremonies of the Law were made obsolete by the Gospel. However, he professes himself a Pharisee because there were many Pharisees among his accusers, and that title did not suffer from the same envy as that of the <term>Nazarenes</term>. That the word <term>heresies</term> was not once as hateful as it is now can be gathered from many arguments. First, because Josephus, in recounting the sects of the Jews, counts the <term>Pharisees</term> among the <term>Essenes and Sadducees</term>, to which he adds a fourth, the <term>Herodians</term>. Yet no error was charged against the Pharisees. Indeed, Paul himself in the twenty-third chapter of this work speaks in this manner: <gloss>According to the most certain sect of our religion, I lived as a Pharisee in Jerusalem.</gloss> What the Translator here renders as <term>sect</term> is "heresy" in Greek, without controversy in a good sense. Among the Jews, therefore, the word <term>sect</term> was no more hateful than it was among the Greeks to be called a <term>Platonist</term>, a <term>Stoic</term>, or a <term>Peripatetic</term>. And if we examine the words themselves, the word <term>sect</term>—which comes from "cutting"—is more hateful than <term>heresy</term>, which the Greeks say comes from "choosing." Moreover, a "sect" is properly called one way out of many. Thus says Titus Columella in his second book:

<column-break/>

> Which, as if it were a sect and a law in the initial plowing of fields, the farmers follow.

<margin>D</margin> <margin>14</margin> *I serve the Father (and my God)* ] First, "I serve" is <note>original: λατρεύω (*latreuō*)</note>, which is <gloss>to offer worship</gloss>, from which verb the <term>theologians' term "latria"</term> is derived. In this place, I do not know what Hugh of Saint-Cher intended, excusing Paul because he allegedly equaled himself to the Prophets here, when nothing of the sort can be perceived from Paul's words. Secondly, it is not "the Father and God," but <note>original: πατρῴῳ τῷ Θεῷ (*patrōō tō Theō*)</note>, <gloss>the God of my fathers.</gloss> This did not happen through the fault of the Translator, however, but by an error of the scribes. Nor was Hugh of Saint-Cher asleep in this place, adding that Paul called God "the Father" so that he might be shown as a son, not a servant. As if Paul were more accustomed to boast in that title than in being a servant of God and Jesus Christ. He never calls himself a son except when he speaks of everyone in general, as in: <gloss>"that we are the sons of God."</gloss> Furthermore, he calls him <term>the God of his fathers</term> because He was the same one whose worship he had received from his ancestors, so that he would not seem to be abolishing the religion of the Jews; it is as if he had said, <gloss>"the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob."</gloss>
<margin>15</margin> *A conscience without offense* ] <note>original: ἀπρόσκοπον συνείδησιν (*aproskopon syneidēsin*)</note>, as if <gloss>you were to say, an unoffended conscience, or one free of offense</gloss>: that is, one which stumbles nowhere. And "they seized me, crying out and saying, 'Away with our enemy.'" These words were not added in two very ancient copies from St. Donatian, nor even in the Constance copy; with these words removed along with the conjunction, something from Asia is referred back to "they found me."
<margin>16</margin> <margin>E</margin> *But certain Jews from Asia* ] The speech is not complete unless you understand something to be missing. And, to my surprise, Hugh of Saint-Cher noticed this and thinks the phrase <gloss>"they saw me in the temple"</gloss> should be supplied. As if it matters at all to the defense of this case if he was seen by Asian Jews in the temple. I think the missing part should be repaired from the context; for since he just said <gloss>he had been purified in the temple, but without a tumult,</gloss> he adds: <gloss>"But certain Asian Jews (understand: they stirred up that tumult, not I)."</gloss> This conjecture is supported by what we read in chapter twenty-one: <gloss>"But when the seven days were almost over, the Jews who were from Asia, when they saw him in the temple, stirred up all the people and laid hands on him."</gloss> Chrysostom, in the Greek Commentaries, does not add the conjunction "but" <note>original: δὲ (*de*)</note>, nor was it in the Spanish Edition. It can also be taken as if Paul, being asked who those people were by whom he had been found in the temple (because he had only said "they found," without designating the person), answered: <gloss>"Certain Jews from Asia: and it was necessary for them to be present."</gloss> It can also be understood that not all were Asian Jews, but some of them: who could more conveniently be present because they were Asians, just as Paul was.
<margin>F</margin> <margin>17</margin> *Except concerning this one statement alone* ] The Translator seems to have read "unless" <note>original: εἰ μὴ (*ei mē*)</note> instead of "or" <note>original: ἢ (*ē*)</note>. But what then? Does Paul acknowledge this one crime, that he stirred up a sedition with that voice? I think not, unless perhaps he mixed this in on purpose so that he might again set the Jews against one another and turn them away from himself. Rabanus, in the Gloss they call <term>Standard</term>, indicates that this was said <gloss>by way of contradiction</gloss>, as if Paul felt this statement could not be seen as a cause for sedition, nor should he be accused of a crime by the Asians, by which he testified that he preached the same thing they believed. Certainly, the Greeks read it thus: <note>original: Ἢ περὶ μιᾶς ταύτης φωνῆς, ἧς ἐκέκραξα ἑστὼς ἐν αὐτοῖς (*Ē peri mias tautēs phōnēs, hēs ekekraxas hestōs en autois*)</note>, that is, <gloss>Or concerning this one statement, which I cried out standing among them, so that the sense is: If they have nothing else, let them even object to this crime.</gloss> It can also be taken for "than," with which "except" sometimes has the same force: as in, <gloss>"They have nothing else except words: nothing other than words."</gloss> And then indeed it is necessary to supply what seems to follow naturally from what has been said: <gloss>"Or let these men themselves say if they found any iniquity in me. But they have nothing to object to, except concerning this one statement only."</gloss>
<margin>18</margin> *Knowing most certainly* ] <gloss>Knowing more accurately the things concerning the Way,</gloss> that is, when...

# THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES. CH. XXV.

<margin>23</margin> ...concerning that Way, saying: "When Lysias the tribune <note>original: χιλίαρχος (*chiliarchos*), a commander of a thousand men</note> comes down, I will decide your case." He ordered the <margin>23</margin> centurion to keep Paul in custody, but to allow him some liberty, and not to forbid any of his friends from serving him or visiting him.

<margin>24</margin> After some days, Felix arrived with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish. He sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ. <margin>25</margin> But as Paul discussed justice, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became afraid and answered: "For now, go your way; when I find a convenient time, I will summon you." <margin>26</margin> At the same time, he was hoping that money would be given to him by Paul so that he might release him; for this reason, he sent for him quite often and talked with him.

<margin>27</margin> When two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. Wishing to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.

**CHAPTER XXV.**

<margin>1</margin> Now when Festus had entered the province, after three days he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea. <margin>2</margin> The chief priest and the leaders of the Jews informed him of the charges against Paul and urged him, <margin>3</margin> asking for a favor against Paul: that he would have him brought to Jerusalem. They were planning an ambush to kill him on the road. <margin>4</margin> Festus answered that Paul should be kept at Caesarea, and that he himself would be going there shortly. <margin>5</margin> "Therefore," he said, "let those among you who are powerful <note>original: δυνατοὶ (*dynatoi*), meaning influential or leading men</note> come down with me, and if there is any crime in this man, let them accuse him."

<margin>6</margin> After staying among them more than ten days, he went down to Caesarea. The next day, sitting on the judgment seat, he ordered Paul to be brought in. <margin>7</margin> When he arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many serious charges against Paul which they could not prove. <margin>8</margin> Paul defended himself, saying: "Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense."

<margin>9</margin> But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, answered Paul and said: "Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and there be judged before me concerning these things?" <margin>10</margin> Paul said: "I am standing before Caesar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be judged. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you also know very well. <margin>11</margin> For if I am a wrongdoer and have done anything worthy of death, I do not refuse to die; but if there is nothing in these things of which they accuse me, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar." <margin>12</margin> Then Festus, having conferred with his council, answered: "You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you shall go."

<margin>13</margin> After some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea to greet Festus. <margin>14</margin> Since they were staying there for many days, Festus laid Paul's case before the king, saying: "There is a certain man left in prison by Felix, <margin>15</margin> about whom, when I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews informed me, asking for a sentence against him. <margin>16</margin> I answered them that it is not the Roman custom to give up any man to destruction before the accused meets the accusers face to face and has an opportunity to defend himself against the charge. <margin>17</margin> Therefore, when they had come together here, without any delay, on the next day I sat on the judgment seat and ordered the man to be brought in. <margin>18</margin> When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge against him of the kind I was expecting..."

<column-break/>

*As if he knew that way exactly.* The author used the comparative form in place of the positive, unless you refer it back to the tribune Lysias, so we might understand that Felix was more familiar with the nature of that sect than Lysias was, because he had served as a magistrate among the Jews for a longer time.
<margin>19</margin> *That he might have rest*] <gloss>anesin</gloss>, that is, relaxation: meaning that he should not be held too harshly or strictly. And soon after:
<margin>20</margin> *Nor anyone of his own*] <gloss>and to forbid no one of his own to serve him, or to visit him</gloss>, that is, <gloss>that he should not forbid any of his family or friends from serving or visiting him</gloss>: for he calls Paul's friends, companions, servants, or disciples <term>idios</term> <note>original: ἰδίων (*idion*), 'one's own'</note>. In some Greek manuscripts, <gloss>Ioudaion</gloss> (Jews) was written instead of <gloss>idion</gloss>. But I prefer the other reading for this reason: it agrees with our Edition.

<margin>1</margin> And the chief priests went to him] <gloss>Enephanisan de auto</gloss>, that is, *And they informed him*: and this was done privately. Previously he translated this as *to make known*, and soon after as *to go to*. The translator seems to have read <gloss>enetuchon</gloss> <note>meaning 'met with' or 'petitioned'</note>. I do not dislike this, especially since a little later when the matter is told to Agrippa, the Old Edition again has *they went to*.
<margin>2</margin> *Asking for a favor against*] <gloss>aitoumenoi charin</gloss>. In this place, he calls the judge's favor "grace." And soon after:
<margin>3</margin> *The powerful*] <gloss>dynatoi</gloss>, that is, those who are able and for whom it is convenient to follow us.

<margin>4</margin> *Days not more than eight or ten*] The Greek reads <gloss>pleious e deka</gloss>, that is, *more than ten*.
<margin>5</margin> *For if I have done harm or anything worthy*] <gloss>Ei men gar adiko</gloss>, that is, *If I am doing wrong*, or *If I commit an injury*. He suddenly changed the tense. For <gloss>pepracha</gloss> <note>'I have done'</note> follows: thus <term>adiko</term> here seems to sound like an <term>imminent</term> act: *If I am being injurious, or am in a state of guilt.*
<margin>6</margin> *Asking for condemnation against him*] <gloss>diken</gloss>, which signifies a cause, a dispute, or a right, and sometimes a penalty. We have translated it as <term>sentence</term>; it could have been translated as <term>legal inquiry</term>. For who asks for a condemnation from a judge before a case is heard? But they were asking that, under the false appearance of an inquiry, Paul might seem to be justly condemned. Indeed, the words of Festus indicate this: *It is not the custom for Romans to give up any man, etc.* And yet those who prefer <gloss>diken</gloss> to be translated as "penalty" or "condemnation" will disagree with us more on the word than on the meaning. For they were asking for an inquiry for no other purpose than that he might be condemned under a false pretext of law. Therefore, for their sake, we have put <term>sentence</term> instead of <term>inquiry</term>.
<margin>7</margin> *To give up anyone before*] In some copies it was written <term>to condemn</term> instead of <term>to give up</term> <note>original: 'donare' (to give/grant/sacrifice)</note>: because it followed the request for condemnation. However, in Greek it is <gloss>charizesthai tis anthropon</gloss>, that is, *to grant a man to destruction or to death*. Moreover, <gloss>charizesthai</gloss> means *to give as a favor to someone*.

<meta>This page continues the account of Paul’s legal proceedings in Caesarea. Festus, the new Roman governor, is summarizing Paul's case to King Agrippa II and his sister Bernice. Paul then begins his formal defense before the King, highlighting his background as a Pharisee and his hope in the resurrection.</meta>

# THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES

<margin>19</margin> ...as I was saying. But they had certain questions against him regarding their own religion <note>original: δεισιδαιμονίας (*deisidaimonias*); Festus uses a word that can mean either "religion" or "superstition," reflecting a characteristically detached Roman view of Jewish debates</note>, and about a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul affirmed to be alive. <margin>20</margin> Being at a loss as to how to investigate such matters, I asked whether he was willing to go to Jerusalem and there be judged concerning these things. <margin>21</margin> But when Paul appealed to be kept in custody for the decision of the Emperor <note>original: Σεβαστοῦ (*Sebastou*), the Greek title for Augustus</note>, I ordered him to be held until I could send him to Caesar. <margin>22</margin> Then Agrippa said to Festus, "I would also like to hear the man myself." "Tomorrow," he said, "you shall hear him." <margin>23</margin> So on the next day, when Agrippa and Bernice arrived with great pomp <note>original: φαντασίας (*phantasias*), suggesting a grand, theatrical procession</note>, and entered the auditorium with the commanders and the prominent men of the city, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. <margin>24</margin> And Festus said: "King Agrippa, and all you men present with us, you see this man about whom the whole multitude of the Jews petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer. <margin>25</margin> But when I found that he had done nothing worthy of death, and since he himself appealed to the Emperor, I decided to send him. <margin>26</margin> I have nothing certain to write to my lord <note>original: τῷ κυρίῳ (*tō kyriō*), referring to the Emperor</note> about him. Therefore I have brought him before you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after this examination has taken place, I may have something to write. <margin>27</margin> For it seems unreasonable to me to send a prisoner without also specifying the charges against him." <margin>xxvi. 1</margin> Then Agrippa said to Paul: "You are permitted to speak for yourself." Then Paul stretched out his hand and began his defense: <margin>2</margin> "Concerning all the things of which I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa, I consider myself fortunate that I am to make my defense before you today, <margin>3</margin> especially because you are an expert in all the customs and questions among the Jews; therefore I beg you to hear me patiently. <margin>4</margin> My manner of life from my youth, which was spent from the beginning among my own nation at Jerusalem, all the Jews know. <margin>5</margin> They have known me for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest sect of our religion I lived as a Pharisee. <margin>6</margin> And now I stand on trial for the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers, <margin>7</margin> to which our twelve tribes, earnestly serving God night and day, hope to attain. For this hope’s sake, King Agrippa, I am accused by the Jews. <margin>8</margin> Why is it considered incredible among you if God raises the dead? <margin>9</margin> Indeed, I myself thought that I must do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth. <margin>10</margin> And this I did in Jerusalem; I shut up many of the saints in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests; and when they were being put to death, I cast my vote against them. <margin>11</margin> And punishing them often in every synagogue, I tried to force <note>The Greek text breaks off here with the word ἠνάγκα- ("I was compelling/forcing"), continued on the next page.</note>

---

<margin>8</margin> <note>original: "Nullum causam defenderet..."</note> *He should defend no cause of those things which I suspected of evil*] This passage is somewhat corrupted among the Latin versions, whereas it is held more purely in the Greek, <unclear>μηδεμίαν αἰτίαν ἐπιφέρειν ὧν ὑπενόουν ἐγώ</unclear>, that is, *they brought no charge regarding the things of which I was suspecting*. For Festus suspected they would accuse Paul of other matters [criminal acts] rather than questions of the Law, which the Romans neglected as superstitious.

<margin>9</margin> <note>original: "Cum multa ambitione"</note> *With much ambition*] <unclear>μετὰ πολλῆς φαντασίας</unclear>, that is, *with much ostentation*. We might say with a "din" or "great apparatus." Bede noted this before us.

<margin>10</margin> <note>original: "Interpellavit me"</note> *He petitioned/interpellated me*] <unclear>ἐνέτυχόν μοι</unclear>, that is, *approached or convened before me*. Although the Translator [of the Vulgate] rendered this correctly enough.

<margin>11</margin> <note>original: "Adduxi eum ad vos"</note> *I brought him to you*] <unclear>ἐφ᾽ ὑμῶν</unclear>, and especially <unclear>ἐπὶ σοῦ</unclear>: which sounds more to the Greeks like, *to your knowledge or judgment, rather than simply to you or to y'all*.

<margin>12</margin> <note>original: "Sine ratione mihi videtur"</note> *It seems without reason to me*] <unclear>Ἄλογον</unclear> (*Alogon*), that is, *Iniquitous, or what is commonly called irrational*.

<margin>1</margin> **A** <note>original: "Estimo me beatum"</note> *I consider myself blessed*] Why should we complain that it says "I consider," when in Greek it is <unclear>ἥγημαι</unclear> (*hēgēmai*), which since I am [the one] defending, for which I am now to defend. Furthermore, <unclear>ἐπὶ σοῦ</unclear>, *before you*, he translates beautifully: though previously he translated it *to you*. Now since *before you* has preceded, see how elegantly it coheres with, *You especially knowing*. But that which follows is the sweetest of all, *all things which are among them, customs and questions*: as if it were right to speak thus, "all customs and questions." Yet Jerome, in the Preface he wrote to Pammachius on the best style of translation, citing this passage, translated it this way: *Concerning all things of which I am accused by the Jews, O King Agrippa, I consider myself blessed, since I am to be defended before you today, who especially know all the customs and questions which are in the Jews*. And Bede remembers this place as restored by Jerome. We translate it in this manner: *Concerning all things of which I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa, I consider myself blessed, who am about to speak my cause today before you, because you are most knowledgeable of those things which are among the Jews and questions and customs*. The Greek has it thus: <unclear>Περὶ πάντων ὧν ἐγκαλοῦμαι...</unclear> [Quotes Greek text]. Although <unclear>ὄντα σε</unclear> fits harshly, unless perhaps it should have been written <unclear>ὄντος σου</unclear>: or unless it pleases the accusative case to be placed absolutely for the genitive. Here Bede refers to another Edition, which would have had it thus: *I consider myself blessed before you, beginning to give an account today*. I would gladly ask those who contend that this translation is Jerome’s, and produced by the breath of the Holy Spirit, and that whatever differs from it is heretical: why did Jerome dare to change it? Or if he amended it after these things, why was he delighted by a useless solecism [grammatical error], especially since the Greek speech has nothing of the sort. In the word <unclear>ἔρη</unclear> the Greek codices agree, nor do I see a solution, unless we understand <unclear>εἰδώς</unclear>, that is, *knowing*.

<margin>2</margin> <note>original: "Quae ab initio fuit in gente mea"</note> *Which from the beginning was in my nation*] Twice in this place is the word <unclear>ἄνωθεν</unclear> (*anōthen*), which the Translator renders *from the beginning*. However, it signifies the series of life from the start even to the end.

<margin>3</margin> <note>original: "Secundum certissimam sectam"</note> *According to the most certain sect*] <unclear>κατὰ τὴν ἀκριβεστάτην αἵρεσιν</unclear>. He called the sect of the Pharisees a "heresy," doubtless because it was meant in a good sense <note>The word 'heresy' at this time simply meant a 'school of thought' or 'sect'</note>. Then, where it translates *most certain*, in Greek it is <unclear>ἀκριβεστάτην</unclear> (*akribestatēn*), that is, *most exact* and *most diligent*: because it was more learned and vigilant than that of the Sadducees, and approached most closely to the truth.

<margin>4</margin> <note>original: "Et nunc in spe quae ad patres"</note> *And now in the hope which [was made] to the fathers*] <unclear>ἐπ᾽ ἐλπίδι</unclear>, it was better *concerning the hope*, or *on account of the hope*. And soon,

<margin>5</margin> <note>original: "Duodecim tribus"</note> *Twelve tribes*] <unclear>τὸ δωδεκάφυλον</unclear> (*to dōdekaphyton*). In Greek it is a single word, which does not signify one or another sect, but the entire nation of the Jews distinct in twelve tribes: to which the participle <unclear>λατρεῦον</unclear> (*latreuon*) responds, which, as we have often said, signifies the worship of the Divinity: whence we translate, *worshipping God*. However, in our version [the Vulgate] two words are missing, <unclear>ἐν ἐκτενείᾳ</unclear>, that is, *sharply or assidiously*: so that you read, *the twelve tribes instantly night and day we have served*.

<margin>6</margin> <note>original: "Detuli sententiam"</note> *I brought the sentence*] <unclear>κατήνεγκα ψῆφον</unclear> (*katēnenka psēphon*). It is uncertain whether he brought the sentence as a decree made by the synagogue, or whether he himself also condemned the Christians by his own vote. <margin>12</margin> I compelled them to blaspheme; and being exceedingly mad against them, I persecuted them even unto foreign cities. <margin>13</margin> While I was occupied in these things and journeying to Damascus with authority and commission from the chief priests, at midday, O king, along the road I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and those who journeyed with me. <margin>14</margin> And when we had all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice speaking to me and saying in the Hebrew tongue, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads." <note>original: πρὸς κέντρα λακτίζειν (*pros kentra laktizein*); a common proverb in antiquity referring to an ox kicking against the sharpened sticks used by a driver—resisting a higher power only causes more pain</note> <margin>15</margin> And I said, "Who are you, Lord?" <margin>A</margin> *...might minister, or carry out. Nicholas of Lyra <note>A 14th-century Franciscan teacher and influential biblical commentator</note> holds the latter opinion; Rabanus Maurus <note>A 9th-century Benedictine abbot and scholar</note> holds the former.*
<margin>7 In which things while I went]</margin> *In the Greek, "In which things journeying," that is, being occupied in these matters and doing this: a figure of speech he used once before.*
<margin>8 That I may appoint you a minister]</margin> *The Greek word is "procheirisasthai," meaning to prepare or appoint: which we have rendered in various ways previously.*
<margin>9 Delivering you from the people and nations, into which]</margin> *The Greek says "from the people," meaning the Jews. Some Greek manuscripts even have "from the Jews" instead of "people." He repeats this shortly after: "to the people and to the nations." However, in the Greek it does not say "into which" (responding to nations), but "to whom" (referring to the purpose rather than the grammatical gender).*
<margin>10 Works worthy of repentance]</margin> *If you take "worthy" in an absolute sense, the speech is well-formed; otherwise, they are works worthy of penance, which one rightfully repents of—a matter we discussed in Matthew chapter three.*
<margin>11 Wanting to kill]</margin> *The Greek word is "diacheirisasthai," which signifies to violate with an impious hand rather than simply to kill.*
<margin>12 If the Christ was to suffer]</margin> *That is, "Whether it was necessary for Christ to suffer." For he argued from the Prophets to show their predictions were fulfilled in Christ. These things refer to the prediction of the Prophets, not merely to the fact that Christ suffered; otherwise, it would not follow well that he was "to announce light to the people."*
<margin>13 For none of these things was done in a corner]</margin> *What the Translator reads is not difficult, yet the Greek has it slightly differently: "for this thing was not performed in a corner."*

<margin>14 in a little you persuade]</margin> *In the Greek, "En oligō me peitheis." First, the Translator uses "modicum" (a little) for "paulo" (by a little) according to his custom. Secondly, he perceives no difference between "suadere" (to urge) and "persuadere" (to thoroughly persuade) among the Latins, even though in Greek a single verb corresponds to our two. Furthermore, it was not easy to translate this passage conveniently. Lorenzo Valla <note>A famous 15th-century Italian humanist and critic</note> thinks it could be rendered: "It is not far off that you persuade me to become a Christian." To which Paul said, "I would pray to God, whether it was a little or a lot distant..." <margin>F</margin> I think it could also be rendered: "You somewhat persuade me to become a Christian." And Paul said, "I would pray to God, that not only somewhat, but even much..." For I do not think Agrippa meant that he was "almost" desiring to become a Christian, but rather that he was somewhat moved by Paul's speech.*

<margin>U</margin>> **As** it was judged...] <gloss>The Greek "ekrithē" means it was decreed or decided. This does not refer to Paul, but to the King and Governor, who had so decided after hearing Paul.</gloss>
<margin>2 And they delivered Paul with the other prisoners]</margin> *The Greek says, "They handed over both Paul and certain other bound ones."*
<margin>3 A ship of Adramyttium]</margin> *The commentator Hugo of Saint-Cher interprets this as a ship from Adramyttium heading for Rome. However, Adramyttium is a city in Mysia <note>In modern-day Turkey</note> according to Stephanus. There is also an island called Adramyttis in Lycia, and Adrumetum is a city in Africa from which the Lesser Syrtis is named; some say Adrumetum, others Adramyttium.*

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Paul’s journey to Rome as a prisoner. Following his hearing before King Agrippa, he has been handed over to a centurion named Julius to be transported by sea.</meta>

# THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES. CHAPTER XXVII.

<margin>2</margin> We set sail, destined for the ports along the coast of Asia, with Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, accompanying us. <margin>3</margin> The next day we landed at Sidon; and Julius, treating Paul with kindness <note>original: φιλανθρώπως (*philanthrōpōs*); literally "with love for humanity," a term often used for the hospitable treatment of guests</note>, permitted him to go to his friends to receive their care. <margin>4</margin> Putting out to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus because the winds were against us. <margin>5</margin> When we had sailed across the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia. <margin>6</margin> There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship bound for Italy and put us on board. <margin>7</margin> We sailed slowly for many days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus. Since the wind did not allow us to go further, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone. <margin>8</margin> Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasaea. <margin>9</margin> Since much time had passed and sailing was now dangerous because even the Fast <note>original: τὴν νηστείαν (*tēn nēsteian*); referring to the Jewish Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur), which occurred in late September or early October, marking the end of the safe sailing season in the Mediterranean</note> was already over, Paul advised them, <margin>10</margin> saying to them, **"Men, I perceive that this voyage will be attended with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives."** <margin>11</margin> But the centurion paid more attention to the pilot and the owner of the ship than to what Paul said. <margin>12</margin> Since the harbor was not suitable to winter in, the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that they might reach Phoenix, a harbor in Crete facing southwest and northwest, and winter there. <margin>13</margin> When a gentle south wind began to blow, thinking they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed close along the shore of Crete. <margin>14</margin> But not long after, a violent wind struck down from the island...

---

<margin>3</margin> *to Adrumetinas*: <note>original: "cendum erat Adrumetinas"</note> although the manuscripts vary on this. For Jerome, or whoever was the author of the *Catalogue of Places* in this work, indicates that *Adrumetum* is a city in the Byzacium region of Africa. Pliny calls *Adrumetum* a neuter noun. In the Greek manuscripts, we read *Adramyttinam* <note>original: Ἀδραμυττινήν (*Adramyttinēn*)</note>. And Stephanus derives *Adramyttenum* from the town of *Adramyttium*.

<margin>4</margin> *They come to Lystra which is in Lycia*: <note>original: "Veniunt Lystram quæ est Lyciæ"</note> the Greek says "we came down to Myra in Lycia," that is, we arrived at Myra, which is in Lycia, or the city of Lycia. It is pronounced in two ways, both in the neuter and feminine gender. Strabo mentions this in his fourteenth book. However, *Lystra* is in Lycaonia, not Lycia. An alert reader should be warned that the Greek text here has *Myra*, but Jerome writes *Myrra*. Furthermore, in the list of locations for this work, he mentions *Smyrna in Lycia*: noting that in some copies it was written, "we came to Lystra which is in Cilicia"; and at that point someone patched in their own text. Moreover, Jerome, in his books on Hebrew names, lists *Smyrna* and interprets it as "bitter." But we shall discuss these locations more accurately in the account of Saint Paul’s travels.

<margin>5</margin> *We sailed slowly*: <note>original: "Tarde navigaremus"</note> In Greek, this is the compound word *bradyploountes* <note>original: βραδυπλοοῦντες</note>.

<margin>6</margin> *Cnidus*: <note>original: "Cnidum"</note> Cnidus is an island opposite Asia, looking toward the province of Caria, and there is a town of the same name on the island of Calymnia, according to Jerome in the booklet attributed to him, which Bede followed. But Pomponius Mela shows that Cnidus is a town on the horn of the Carian peninsula; and Ptolemy supports this view in his first map of Asia. It is certain that they were then hugging the shores of Asia Minor, where Caria is located. Strabo also records this in his fourteenth book, calling it an island, though it had previously been joined to the mainland. He says its circumference is seven stadia and it has two ports, so that the site itself is displayed as if for a spectacle, making the island appear to have two cities—that is, a "double-city" <note>original: διπολίς (*dipolis*)</note>. Horace in his *Odes* indicates that Venus was worshiped in this place:
> O Venus, queen of Cnidus and Paphos.
Bede indicates that in some manuscripts *Chios* was written instead of *Cnidus*, but he rejects this.

<margin>7</margin> *Near Salmone*: <note>original: "Juxta Salmonem"</note> Salmone is a maritime city on the island of Crete, according to Jerome.

<margin>8</margin> *Which is called Fair Havens*: <note>original: "Qui vocatur Boni portus"</note> "Fair Havens" is plural in number, *Kalous limenas* <note>original: Καλοὺς λιμένας</note>, although he said "Beautiful ports" rather than "good" ones. He is referring, if I am not mistaken, to the Cretan city named "Fair Shore" <note>original: Καληὴ ἀκτή (*Kalē aktē*)</note>, which Stephanus mentions.

<margin>9</margin> *Near which was the city of Thalassa*: <note>original: "Cui juxta erat civitas Thalassa"</note> Saint Jerome also indicates that this name is corruptly read as *Thalassa*. However, the word he suggests as a correction was itself corrupted in the common manuscripts; for it was written *Layset*. The Greeks read *Lasaea* <note>original: Λασαία</note>, which is also a coastal city of Crete, not far from Fair Havens. Some printed copies had *Thessala* instead of *Thalassa*.

<margin>10</margin> *Because the fast had already passed*: <note>original: "Eo quod jejunium jam præteriisset"</note> *dia to kai tēn nēsteian ēdē parelēlythenai* <note>original: διὰ τὸ καὶ τὴν νηστείαν ἤδη παρεληλυθέναι</note>. It does not escape me that for some people "the fast" here refers to a specific time when the Jews were accustomed to fast. But first, what does the centurion and the sailors have to do with such fasts? Secondly, if the fast had already passed, sailing ought to have been more convenient. Burgensis indicates that the principal fast among the Jews usually occurs around the Autumn Equinox, at which time sailing becomes more difficult. There was not just one time for fasting for the Jews, and around the Autumn Equinox sailing can be favorable.

<column-break/>

<margin>2</margin> **W**e set sail, with Aristarchus the Macedonian of Thessalonica remaining with us. <margin>3</margin> The following day we arrived at Sidon: and Julius, having treated Paul humanely, permitted him to go to his friends and be cared for by them. <margin>4</margin> And having set sail from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were contrary. <margin>5</margin> And having crossed the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, <margin>6</margin> we reached Myra in Lycia. And there the centurion, finding an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy, put us on it. <margin>7</margin> And when we had sailed slowly for many days, and had difficulty reaching Cnidus, the wind preventing us, we sailed toward Crete off Salmone. <margin>8</margin> And coasting along it with difficulty, we reached a certain place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasaea. <margin>9</margin> Much time having passed, and when sailing was now dangerous, because the time of the fast had also now passed, Paul warned them, <margin>10</margin> saying to them, **"Men, I see that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives."** <margin>11</margin> But the centurion trusted the pilot and the shipmaster more than those things said by Paul. <margin>12</margin> And since the harbor was not suitable for wintering, the majority took counsel to sail from there, if by any means they might reach Phoenix to winter there; it is a harbor of Crete looking toward the Southwest and the Northwest. <margin>13</margin> When a gentle South wind blew, thinking they had achieved their purpose, they set sail from Assos and coasted along Crete. <margin>14</margin> But not much later...

---

Burgensis contends that the Jewish fast was the most important of all, celebrated on the feast of expiation <note>The Day of Atonement or Yom Kippur</note>. That feast fell on the tenth day of the seventh month, which month roughly corresponds with September. A long voyage remained, and October and November were imminent—months not at all suitable for sailing in the past, though today our sailors fly through every sea even in the middle of winter. The author whose Greek commentaries on this work exist under the name of Chrysostom wants "the fast" to be understood not as the hunger of the sailors, but as the season of the year, agreeing with Burgensis. There is also the argument that he calls this fast *nēsteian* <note>original: νηστείαν</note>, a word almost always used for a religious fast; he calls the hunger of sailors *asitia* <note>original: ἀσιτίαν</note>. Although both words have the same etymology from the deprivation of food. This opinion is supported by the addition of the article, "the fast," which designates not just any fast, but one known and celebrated by us. But we must ask <margin>D</margin> what the conjunction "and" <note>original: καὶ (*kai*)</note> means there: "because *also* the time of the fast had now passed." The conjunction indicates that the voyage was becoming dangerous for two reasons: both because the storm was pressing, and because the season was approaching which by its nature makes sailing difficult. Previously, we had followed the opinion of Lyranus, who thinks that although they had provisions, they did not have the opportunity to take food due to worry and grief. And therefore, Paul persuades them to eat so that they might restore their bodies. Indeed, it might seem a wonder how sailors, a gluttonous race of men, lasted fourteen days "fasting" <note>original: ἄσιτοι (*asitoi*)</note>, that is, unfed; unless perhaps they are said not to have taken food because they did not have a proper meal in leisure, as sailors are accustomed to do in a calm sea.

<margin>E</margin> *And Paul comforted them*: <note>original: "Et Consolabatur eos Paulus"</note> What had happened to them that they needed a comforter? For the Greek is *parēnei* <note>original: παρῄνει</note>, which means he "exhorted" or "warned" them not to go further; although Paul’s speech, which is added immediately, sufficiently proves that he was not comforting them, but giving advice.

<margin>12</margin> *The voyage is about to be*: <note>original: "Incipis efse navigatio"</note> *mellein esesthai ton ploun* <note>original: μέλλειν ἔσεσθαι τὸν πλοῦν</note>, that is, the voyage would be; which he nevertheless frequently translates in this manner.

<margin>13</margin> *Arriving at Phoenix to winter*: <note>original: "Devenientes Phœnicem hybernare"</note> *Phoenix* here is the accusative of *Phoenix*, which in Greek means "palm tree"; from which it appears the part of Syria called *Phoenicia* was also named. Luke himself indicates it is a harbor of Crete of this name.

<margin>14</margin> *Toward the Southwest and the Northwest*: <note>original: "Ad Africum & ad Chorum"</note> These are the names of winds. He names two because the harbor faced toward both. Someone might say: why was it necessary to mention this, which everyone knew? Indeed, why did it matter that Hugo of Saint-Cher, a theologian of that time, wrote in his commentaries that "Chorus" was an island or a city in Crete? It mattered so little that it did not matter whether he built a new island or founded a new city in a very ancient one.

<margin>15</margin> <margin>F</margin> *When they had weighed anchor from Assos*: <note>original: "Quum fustulissent de Asson"</note> *arantea Asson* <note>original: ἄραντες Ἄσσον</note>, that is, when they had lifted from Assos. It is uncertain whether they landed there and, setting sail again, passed Crete, or whether, having passed Assos, they thought they were now in safety. For *Assos* is a maritime city of Lycia, situated on a high promontory, so that it is not very safe to approach. Hence the joke of Nicostratus the Cithara-player: "Go to Assos, so that you may reach the ends of destruction more quickly." Jerome places *Assos* in Asia, a maritime city, which is also said to be called Apollonia: Pliny also testifies to this in book five, chapter thirty. However, I think Luke is referring to *Assos*, a small town in Crete: from which Jupiter was also called "Asius." For they were still hugging the shores of Crete.

The accompanying commentary provides a deep philological and geographical analysis of the Mediterranean locations and the timing of the dangerous sailing season.</summary>

# THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES. CHAPTER XXVII.

<margin>14</margin> ...against the ship there arose a tempestuous wind, called a Northeaster <note>original: Εὐροκλύδων (*Euroklydōn*), often interpreted as a "typhonic" or "whirlwind" wind from the East-North-East</note>. <margin>15</margin> When the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along. <margin>16</margin> Running under the lee of a small island called Clauda, we were scarcely able to get control of the skiff <note>original: σκάφης (*skaphēs*); the small boat or dinghy towed behind the main vessel</note>. <margin>17</margin> After hoisting it up, they used supports to undergird the ship; and fearing they would run aground on the Syrtis <note>referring to the Syrtis Sands, dangerous shallows off the coast of North Africa</note>, they lowered the gear and were thus driven along. <margin>18</margin> Since we were being violently tossed by the storm, the next day they began to throw the cargo overboard. <margin>19</margin> On the third day, they threw out the ship’s tackle with their own hands. <margin>20</margin> When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small storm kept raging, all hope of our being saved was finally abandoned. <margin>21</margin> Since they had been without food for a long time, Paul then stood up among them and said, "Men, you should have listened to me and not set sail from Crete, and so avoided this injury and loss. <margin>22</margin> And now I urge you to take heart; for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. <margin>23</margin> For this very night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve stood by me, <margin>24</margin> saying, 'Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar; and behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.' <margin>25</margin> Therefore, take heart, men; for I believe God, that it will be exactly as I have been told. <margin>26</margin> But we must run aground on some island." <margin>27</margin> When the fourteenth night had come, as we were being driven across the Adriatic, about midnight the sailors suspected they were nearing some land. <margin>28</margin> So they took soundings and found twenty fathoms; and a little further on, they took soundings again and found fifteen fathoms. <margin>29</margin> Fearing that we might run aground on rocky places, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for daybreak. <margin>30</margin> When the sailors were seeking to escape from the ship and had lowered the skiff into the sea under the pretext of intending to lay out anchors from the bow, <margin>31</margin> Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, "Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved." <margin>32</margin> Then the soldiers cut the ropes of the skiff and let it fall away. <margin>33</margin> Until day was about to break, Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, "Today is the fourteenth day that you have been in suspense and remained without eating—"

---

<margin>16 *A Typhonic Wind* ]</margin> This is one of the sudden and unexpected winds named Typhon. All these winds have this in common: they arise from the earth's exhalations, are trapped within dense clouds, and burst forth in various ways. Wandering and rushing like mountain torrents, they produce thunder and lightning. Furthermore, if they are carried with greater weight and curve, and if they burst a dry cloud with their blast, they produce a storm which the Greeks call *typhōs* <note>original: τυφώς</note>. But if a downward pressure of the cloud, rotating more tightly, breaks out without fire (that is, without lightning), they create a whirlwind which is called *typhōn* <note>original: τύφων</note>, which is a *vibrating cloud-storm* <note>original: *vibratus ecnephias*</note>. It brings something broken off from a cold cloud down with it, rolling and turning, aggravating its own ruin with that weight, and changing from place to place with a rapid spinning. <margin>E</margin> If the cloud erupts from a larger opening but lower than a typical storm, and not without a loud noise, it is called a *turbo* (whirlwind), flattening everything near it. If it is more fiery and ignited, it is called a *prester* <note>a "burning" whirlwind</note>, scorching whatever it touches as it tramples it. Furthermore, Pliny calls the Typhon the primary plague of sailors, as it breaks not only the yardarms but even the vessels themselves by twisting them. However, he writes that such a great evil can be met with a slight remedy: if vinegar—whose nature is extremely cold—is poured out against the approaching wind. The wind is struck back by it and carried back up into the sky, swallowed into the heights. It is named Typhon from the Greek word *typhō* <note>original: τύφω</note>, which means "to inflame." Rabanus, in the *Glossa Ordinaria*, writes regarding the word *Typhonic*: another translation calls it a *tempestivus* (timely) wind. Sulpicot notes that someone added *tempestuosus* (tempestuous) wind as a commentary.

<margin>17 *Which is called Euroaquilo* ]</margin> The Greeks read *Euroclydon* <note>original: Εὐροκλύδων</note> instead of Euroaquilo: a word named because it stirs up huge waves. <margin>F</margin> However, I do not know whether Luke, even though writing in Greek, fashioned our Latin term by saying *Euroaquilo*, just as he makes the name Paul similar to *Apollyon*. He adds the surname of "Typhon" only to express the danger, and also to show from where it erupted: so that we might understand the disadvantage of this name, as it was not suited to the intended course, whereas the South wind (*Notus*) is favorable for those sailing from Syria to Italy.

<margin>18 *Could not face the wind* ]</margin> *antophthalmein* <note>original: ἀντοφθαλμεῖν</note>, which to the Greeks means to "look in the eye," that is, to look at it from the opposite side. Furthermore, he who resists turns his eyes toward the source.

<margin>19 *Giving the ship to the winds* ]</margin> The Greeks have a single word, *epidontes* <note>original: ἐπιδόντες</note>, and it can refer to "the wind," so that the word placed in the middle responds to both "to resist" and "to give."

<margin>20 *Which is called Clauda* ]</margin> Ptolemy calls it *Claudos*, looking toward Crete between the South and the West; it is quite consistent that they were driven here by the blast of the Northeaster. Although someone notes that in the Greek manuscript of the Papal Library the name is written *Kanda*, that is, *Cauda*. And Suidas indicates an island near Crete called *Kaudo*, memorable for the fact that giant wild asses are born there.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...there arose against it <margin>16</margin> a Typhonic wind, <margin>17</margin> which is called Euroaquilo. And when the <margin>15</margin> ship was caught <margin>15</margin> and could not face the wind, <margin>19</margin> we were driven along, giving the ship to the winds. And having been carried down to a certain island <margin>16</margin> <margin>20</margin> called Clauda, we were scarcely able to obtain the skiff. When it was hoisted up, they used supports, <margin>17</margin> undergirding the ship; fearing they would fall into the Syrtis, they lowered the gear and were thus driven along. And as we were being tossed by a violent <margin>18</margin> storm, the following day they made a jettison. And on the third day, <margin>21</margin> with our own hands, <margin>19</margin> we threw out the ship's tackle. Furthermore, neither the sun nor the stars <margin>20</margin> <margin>B</margin> appearing for many days, and with no small storm threatening, all hope of our safety was now taken away. And since there had <margin>22</margin> now been much fasting, <margin>21</margin> then Paul, standing in the middle of them, said: "Men, you should indeed have <margin>23</margin> listened to me <margin>24</margin> and not loosened from Crete, nor <margin>25</margin> brought upon us this injury and loss. And now <margin>26</margin> I exhort you to be of good courage: for there will <margin>22</margin> be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. For there stood by me this night <margin>27</margin> an Angel of the God whose <margin>23</margin> I am and whom I serve, saying, 'Fear not, Paul; <margin>24</margin> you must be presented before Caesar: and behold, God has given you all who sail with you.' Therefore, men, be of good <margin>25</margin> <margin>C</margin> courage: for I believe God, that it shall be just as it was told to me. But we must be cast away on a certain <margin>26</margin> island." But after the fourteenth night came, <margin>27</margin> as we were sailing in the Adriatic about midnight, the sailors suspected that some region <margin>28</margin> was appearing to them. And <margin>29</margin> having lowered the sounding lead, <margin>28</margin> they found twenty fathoms; and having gone a little further, and again having lowered the lead, they found fifteen fathoms. And fearing lest they should fall into rough places, <margin>29</margin> having thrown out four anchors from the stern, they wished for day to break. But while the sailors <margin>30</margin> were seeking to flee from the ship, <margin>30</margin> when they had lowered the skiff into the sea under the pretext as if they were <margin>31</margin> about to extend anchors from the prow, Paul said to the centurion and the <margin>31</margin> <margin>D</margin> soldiers, "Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved." Then the soldiers cut the ropes of the skiff and <margin>32</margin> allowed it to fall away. And when the day began to <margin>33</margin> appear, Paul exhorted everyone to take food, saying, "This is the fourteenth day that you have been waiting, fasting—"

---

<margin>21 *With our own hands we threw out the ship's tackle* ]</margin> *autocheires tēn skeuēn tou ploiou erripsamen* <note>original: αὐτόχειρες τὴν σκευὴν τοῦ πλοίου ἐῤῥίψαμεν</note>, that is, with our very own hands we threw out the ship's equipment. It appears the Translator read "we threw out" (*erripsamen*), and there is very little difference in the meaning.

<margin>22 *There had now been much fasting* ]</margin> *asitia* <note>original: ἀσιτία</note>, that is, lack of food.

<margin>23 *Having listened to me* ]</margin> *peitharchēsantas moi* <note>original: πειθαρχήσαντάς μοι</note>, that is, having obeyed me, although I do not see why Valla notes the Translator here. For he who obeys, listens. Justin would have noted that *peitharchein* is properly said by the Greeks of those who obey princes or magistrates.

<margin>24 *Not to loosen from Crete* ]</margin> In Greek it is *mē anagesthai apo tēs Krētēs* <note>original: μὴ ἀνάγεσθαι ἀπὸ τῆς Κρήτης</note>, that is, not to set sail from Crete.

<margin>25 *And to make a gain of injury* ]</margin> *kerdēsai* <note>original: κερδῆσαι</note>, that is, to bring upon oneself without cause. For that is what "to gain" means in this context. And *hybrin* <note>original: ὕβριν</note>, that is, injury, refers to the inclemency of the weather and the violence of the sea.

<margin>26 *I advise* ]</margin> *kai parainō* <note>original: καὶ παραινῶ</note>, that is, I exhort.

<margin>27 *The Angel of God, whose I am* ]</margin> It was uncertain whether "whose" refers to God or the Angel, unless he had added *hō kai latreuō* <note>original: ᾧ καὶ λατρεύω</note>, that is, "whom I also worship, or whom I also serve."

<margin>28 *To appear to them* ]</margin> *prosagein* <note>original: προσάγειν</note>, which more specifically means "to approach," unless perhaps the Translator read *prosaygein* <note>original: προσαυγεῖν</note>, that is, "to shine forth."

<margin>29 *Submitting the sounding lead* ]</margin> A *bolis* <note>original: βολὶς</note> is named from *ballō*, which means "to throw": that is, a weight attached to a small cord, which sailors throw down to explore the depth of the sea. Sometimes they do the same with a very long spear or pole lowered into the water. According to Hesychius, a soldier's spear is also called a *bolis* by the Greeks. However, Luke spoke with a single word, which the Translator rendered with two: *bolisantes* <note>original: βολίσαντες</note> (having sounded).

<margin>30 *They let down the skiff* ]</margin> *Skaphē* <note>original: Σκάφη</note> signifies two things to the Greeks: a bowl, and a type of lighter vessel, from the word *skaptō* (to dig): for a bowl is a digging instrument, and skiffs are made from a hollowed-out trunk, a type we still see on the Rhine. Bede thinks skiffs are made of wicker covered in leather. He adds that a skiff is also called a *catascopus* <note>literally "scout" or "observer"</note> by the Greeks, from "contemplating." This is the source of error for those who compiled the *Glossa Ordinaria*, thinking a skiff is named from "contemplating." *Kataskopos* in Greek means "scout"; that name was given to the skiff because when it is sent out, sailors explore the depth along the shore or other dangers of the sea.

<margin>31 *They began to extend the anchors* ]</margin> *mellontōn ekteinein* <note>original: μελλόντων ἐκτείνειν</note>, that is, being about to extend: a phrasing the Translator often used. But here it was a bit more archaic. And a little later: *achri de hou emellen hēmera ginesthai* <note>original: Ἄχρι δὲ οὗ ἔμελλεν ἡμέρα γίνεσθαι</note>, that is, "when the day was about to be," meaning, "when the day was pressing and was not far off."
