# THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES. CHAPTER XXVIII.

<margin>A</margin> <margin>34</margin> "Therefore I urge you to take some food; for this is for your survival; for not a hair shall fall from the head of any of you." <note>original: οὐδενὸς γὰρ ὑμῶν θρὶξ ἐκ τῆς κεφαλῆς πεσεῖται — a common Hebraic idiom meaning total protection</note> <margin>35</margin> And when he had said these things, he took bread and gave thanks to God in the presence of all; and when he had broken it, he began to eat. <margin>36</margin> Then they all became encouraged and took food themselves. <margin>37</margin> We were in all two hundred and seventy-six souls in the ship. <margin>38</margin> And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing the wheat into the sea. <margin>39</margin> When day came, they did not recognize the land; but they noticed a certain bay with a beach, upon which they planned, if possible, to <margin>B</margin> drive the ship ashore. <margin>40</margin> So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes of the rudders; and hoisting the foresail <note>original: ἀρτέμονα (artemona); a small sail used for maneuvering toward the shore</note> to the wind, they made for the beach. <margin>41</margin> But striking a place where two seas met, they ran the vessel aground; and the bow stuck fast and remained immovable, but the stern was being broken up by the violence of the waves. <margin>42</margin> The soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. <margin>43</margin> But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from their purpose; he ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and get to land, <margin>44</margin> and the rest on planks or on some pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land. <margin>C</margin> <margin>XXVIII. 1</margin> After we were brought safely through, we then learned that the island was called Malta <note>original: Μελίτη (Melitē)</note>. <margin>2</margin> The natives <note>original: βάρβαροι (barbaroi); meaning non-Greek speakers, not necessarily "uncivilized"</note> showed us unusual kindness; for they kindled a fire and welcomed us all, because of the rain that had set in and because of the cold. <margin>3</margin> When Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand. <margin>4</margin> When the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, "No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he has escaped from the sea, Justice <note>original: ἡ δίκη (hē dikē); likely referring to the goddess of Vengeance or Divine Justice</note> has not allowed to live." <margin>5</margin> He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm. <margin>6</margin> They were waiting for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But after they had waited a long time and saw nothing unusual happen to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god. <margin>7</margin> In the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and entertained us hospitably for three days. <margin>8</margin> It happened that the father of Publius lay sick with fever and dysentery; Paul visited him and prayed, and putting his hands on him, healed him. <margin>9</margin> When this had taken place, the rest of the people on the island who had diseases also came and were cured. <margin>10</margin> They also honored us with many marks of respect, and when we were setting sail, they provided us with the things we needed. <margin>11</margin> After three months we set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island, a ship of Alexandria, with the Twin Brothers <note>original: Διοσκούροις (Dioskourois); referring to Castor and Pollux, patrons of sailors</note> as its figurehead. <margin>12</margin> Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there for three days. From there...

---

<margin>E</margin> 32 *They became more encouraged*] <note>original: Εὔθυμοι (Euthymoi)</note> That is, "Of good spirit," or "With spirits now refreshed." It is a simple state of being, not a comparative degree.

39 *A beach, into which they intended*] <note>original: ἔχοντα αἰγιαλὸν (echonta aigialon)</note> That is: why is it "the beach" rather than "into which"? Since among the Greeks, "beach" <note>original: αἰγιαλὸς</note> is masculine, just like "bay" <note>original: Κόλπος</note>. For they were, I believe, looking for land. There are many shores among the Geographers which are called "Beaches" by their proper name, such as those between Sicyon and Baptisia. There is another bordering the Black Sea, after the promontory of Carambis, which Homer mentions. Again, there is one in Thrace near the river Strymon. Finally, there is a "Beach" nicknamed "the Wanderer" <note>original: migans</note> between Egypt and Ethiopia. Jerome, citing this passage, mentions "Agall."

34 <note>referring to verse 40</note> *Hoisting the foresail*] <note>original: ἐπάραντες τὸν ἀρτέμονα (eparantes ton artemona)</note> That is, with the "artemon" raised. And "to the blowing wind," which the Translator renders "according to the blast of the breeze," I think should be referred to the wind itself: so that we understand the sails were set against the gusts, with the yardarm raised high, so that it might be carried toward the shore more by the will of the wind. Furthermore, "artemon" seems here to be used for a type of sail; Bede also indicated this in the *Ordinary Gloss*. It takes its name from <term>sustaining</term> <note>Latin: sustinendo</note> or from <term>sewing</term> <note>Latin: assuendo</note>. For a certain part is usually attached to the bottom of sails so they catch more wind. There are some who prefer it to be written as "autonomen" instead of "artemon."

35 <note>referring to verse 41</note> *Into a place where two seas met*] The Translator did not explain the Greek word, nor have we kept it uncorrupted, reading <term>bithalassum</term> instead of <term>dithalasson</term>. For Luke wrote <note>original: εἰς τόπον διθάλασσον</note>, that is, "into a place between two seas." For thus Horace says in his Odes:
> *--or of Corinth situated*
> *between two seas.*
This is because it is an isthmus, and is washed by the sea on both sides. They were striving to drive the ship into the bay if they could. But that did not happen, as the winds drove them onto some isthmus projecting into the sea.

<column-break/>

<margin>34</margin> ...you continue fasting, taking nothing. Because of this I exhort you to take food: for this pertains to your safety: because not a hair of the head of any of you shall perish.
<margin>35</margin> And when he had said these things, having taken bread he gave thanks to God in the sight of all, and when he had broken it, he began to eat.
<margin>36</margin> Furthermore, the spirits of all being now refreshed, they themselves also took food.
<margin>37</margin> We were in truth all the souls in the ship, two hundred seventy-six.
<margin>38</margin> And being satisfied with food, they lightened the ship, casting the wheat into the sea.
<margin>39</margin> But when it was day, they did not recognize the land: but they noticed a certain bay having a beach, into which they intended, if they could, to drive the ship.
<margin>40</margin> And when they had taken up the anchors, they committed themselves to the sea, at the same time loosening the lashings of the rudders, and having raised the foresail to the breeze, they made for the beach.
<margin>41</margin> And when they had fallen into a place between two seas, they ran the ship aground: and the prow indeed remained fixed and immovable: but the stern was being broken by the force of the waves.
<margin>42</margin> Now the counsel of the soldiers was that they should kill the prisoners, lest any, when he had swum out, should escape.
<margin>43</margin> But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, restrained them from their purpose: and he ordered that those who could swim should cast themselves first and get out to land,
<margin>44</margin> And the rest, some on planks, some on certain fragments of the ship: and so it happened that all escaped safe to land.
<margin>XXVIII. 1</margin> And when they had escaped, then they knew that the island was called Malta. The barbarians indeed showed 
<margin>2</margin> no common kindness to us: for having kindled a fire, they received us all, because of the rain which was imminent, and because of the cold.
<margin>3</margin> But when Paul had gathered a multitude of twigs, and had laid them on the fire, a viper creeping out from the heat, attacked his hand.
<margin>4</margin> But as the barbarians saw the beast hanging from his hand, they said among themselves, "Altogether this man is a murderer, whom, though saved from the sea, vengeance does not allow to live."
<margin>5</margin> And he indeed, having shaken off the viper into the fire, suffered no evil.
<margin>6</margin> But they thought that he would be turned into a swelling, or suddenly fall down dead. But when they had expected for a long time, and saw no evil happen to him, changing their minds they said he was a God.
<margin>7</margin> <margin>D</margin> Now in those places were the estates of the chief man of the island, named Publius, who, having received us, treated us kindly with hospitality for three days.
<margin>8</margin> And it happened that the father of Publius lay sick, troubled with fevers and dysentery: to whom Paul entered, and when he had prayed, and laid his hands upon him, he healed him.
<margin>9</margin> This therefore having been done, the others also, who had infirmities in the island, came and were healed:
<margin>10</margin> Who also honored us with many honors, and to us setting sail they laid on things which were necessary.
<margin>11</margin> But after three months we sailed in an Alexandrian ship, which had wintered in the island, whose sign was Castor and Pollux.
<margin>12</margin> And when we had come to Syracuse, we stayed for three days.
<margin>13</margin> From there...

<margin>D</margin> 1 *Which was called the island of Malta*] Hugo of St. Cher <note>original: Hugo Carrensis; a 13th-century biblical commentator</note> leaves it to us whether we prefer to read "Meliten" or "Mileten": even if there are those who read more corruptly "Mytilene." The Greeks read "Melite." It is an island between Africa and Sicily; from which the "Melitean" dogs, kept as pets, were named. Strabo mentions this in book six. Ptolemy in book four of his *Geography* lists "Melita" among the islands of Africa. Pliny in book three, chapter eight, places it among the islands of the Sicilian sea. Although there is a "Miletus," a city of Cappadocia, he calls it an island here.

2 *They were refreshing us all*] <note>original: προσελάβοντο (proselabonto)</note>, that is, they were receiving us.

3 *To be turned into a swelling*] <note>original: μέλλειν πίμπρασθαι (mellein pimprasthai)</note>, that is, to be inflamed or set on fire, although a swelling accompanies inflammation.

<margin>F</margin> 4 <note>referring to verse 7</note> *He kindly kept us for three days*] <note>original: Φιλοφρόνως ἐξένισεν (Philophronōs exenisen)</note>, that is, he treated us as a friend, or, if it were permitted to say so, "he hosted us." Furthermore, I wonder how such an elegant verb came into the Translator's mind, so far be it from me to criticize that he translated it "held" instead of "treated."

5 <note>referring to verse 11</note> *Whose sign was the Castors*] That "Castors" <note>the plural of Castor, referring to the twins Castor and Pollux</note> should be read is indicated even by more recent authors, Lyra and Hugo of St. Cher. For in Greek it is <note>original: Διοσκούροις (Dioskourois)</note>: for that is the name for Castor and Pollux, the sons of Jupiter and Leda. For Bede also, in the gloss they call "ordinary," indicates that in some manuscripts it was written, "for the Castors, the sons of Jupiter." Antiquity believed them to be gods who brought safety to those sailing if they appeared together; they appear in the form of fire, sitting on the mast or yardarms <note>a reference to St. Elmo's Fire</note>; but they were considered dire if they appeared singly or alone. Therefore, that ship had their sign. Therefore, if you wish to laugh, Reader, read what Hugo of St. Cher put forward in this place regarding the "sign of the camps" <note>Hugo apparently confused the name "Castorum" (of Castor) with "Castrorum" (of the camps)</note>, though someone eventually gives it a true and serious interpretation. It seems to me this whole work, which is attributed to Hugo, is by many...

# THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES. CHAPTER XXVIII.

<margin>13</margin> From there we cast off and arrived at Rhegium <note>Modern Reggio Calabria, at the "toe" of Italy.</note>, and after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli. <margin>14</margin> There we found brothers and were invited to stay with them for seven days, and so we went toward Rome. <margin>15</margin> And from there, when the brothers heard about us, they came to meet us as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage. <margin>16</margin> When we entered Rome, the centurion delivered the prisoners to the captain of the guard; but Paul was permitted to live by himself with the soldier who guarded him. <margin>17</margin> After three days, Paul called together the local leaders of the Jews. When they had gathered, he said to them: "Brothers, though I have done nothing against our people or the customs of our ancestors, I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans. <margin>18</margin> When they had examined me, they wanted to release me, because there was no basis for a death sentence in my case. <margin>19</margin> But because the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar—not that I had any accusation to bring against my own nation. <margin>20</margin> For this reason, I have asked to see you and speak with you; it is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain." <margin>21</margin> They said to him, "We have received no letters from Judea about you, nor have any of the brothers come here and reported or said anything evil about you. <margin>22</margin> But we desire to hear from you what your views are; for concerning this sect, we know that it is spoken against everywhere." <margin>23</margin> When they had set a day for him, many came to him at his lodging. From morning until evening, he explained the matter to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus from both the Law of Moses and the Prophets. <margin>24</margin> Some were convinced by what he said, but others did not believe. <margin>25</margin> So, disagreeing among themselves, they began to leave after Paul had made one final statement: "The Holy Spirit was right in saying through Isaiah the prophet to your ancestors: <margin>26</margin> 'Go to this people and say: You will indeed listen, but never understand; and you will indeed look, but never perceive. <margin>27</margin> For this people’s heart has grown dull, and their ears are hard of hearing, and they have shut their eyes; so that they might not look with their eyes, and listen with their ears, and understand with their heart and turn—and I would heal them.' <margin>28</margin> Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen." <margin>29</margin> And when he had said these things, the Jews departed, having much dispute among themselves. <margin>30</margin> Paul stayed two whole years in his own rented house and welcomed all who came to him, <margin>31</margin> preaching the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.

<column-break/>

<sig>A</sig> Sailing around, we reached Rhegium, and after one day with the South wind blowing, on the following day we came to Puteoli: Where, having found brothers, we were asked to remain with them <margin>14</margin> for seven days, and so we came to Rome. And from there, when <margin>15</margin> the brothers had heard about us, they came out to meet us as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns: whom when Paul had seen, giving thanks to God, he took courage. <sig>B</sig> When we had come to Rome, the centurion <margin>16</margin> delivered the prisoners to the prince of the army <note>original: principi exercitus; likely referring to the Praetorian Prefect</note>: but it was permitted to Paul that he might remain alone with the soldier guarding him. After the third day, Paul <margin>17</margin> called together the chiefs of the Jews: and when they had come, he said to them: "I, men and brothers, though I have done nothing against the people or the institutions of the elders, was delivered bound from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans: Who, <margin>18</margin> when they had examined me, wished to release me, because there was no cause of death in me. But with the <margin>19</margin> Jews speaking against it, I was forced to appeal to Caesar, not as if I have anything of which to accuse my nation. For this <margin>20</margin> cause, therefore, I called for you, that I might see and speak with you: for on account of the hope of Israel I am surrounded by this chain." But they said to him: "We neither <margin>21</margin> received letters about you from Judea, nor has any of the brothers coming here announced or spoken anything of evil concerning you. But we wish to hear from you what you think: for <margin>22</margin> <sig>C</sig> concerning this sect, it is known to us that it is everywhere spoken against." And when they had appointed a day for him, <margin>23</margin> many came to him at his lodging, to whom he set forth testifying the kingdom of God, and persuading them concerning Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets, from morning until evening. And some believed these things which were said, <margin>24</margin> but some did not believe. And when they <margin>25</margin> were not in agreement among themselves, they departed, after Paul had spoken one word: "Well did the Holy Spirit speak through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers, Saying: Go to <margin>26</margin> this people, and say: With hearing you shall hear, and shall not understand: and seeing you shall see, and shall not perceive. For the <margin>27</margin> heart of this people is grown fat, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and they have closed their eyes: lest <sig>D</sig> at any time they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them." Let it be <margin>28</margin> known therefore to you, that to the Gentiles is sent this salvation of God, and they will hear. And when he had said these things, the <margin>29</margin> Jews went out from him, having much debate among themselves. And Paul remained two whole years in his <margin>30</margin> rented house: and he received all who entered to him, Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching the things which are <margin>31</margin> concerning the Lord Jesus with all confidence without anyone prohibiting him.

-> ## THE END OF THE ACTS. <-
-> ## THE END OF THE ACTS. <-

<sig>E</sig> ...that it was put together by many. Nor indeed are the things he handed down about the Three Taverns any less festive. Furthermore, both are named and called Caesars, though only one of them held that name. We, lest the Reader err hereafter, have translated it as <term>Castor & Pollux</term> <note>original: Castor & Pollux; the twin sons of Zeus used as a figurehead for the ship</note>.

<margin>6 We reached Rhegium</margin> For that is a maritime city of Italy, twenty miles distant from the Pelorus promontory: the Greek name is drawn from a "rupture" <note>Greek: rhēgnymi (to break)</note>, because that part of Sicily, once clinging to the Bruttian field of Italy, was later torn away by the sea flowing between; a strait fifteen miles long and one thousand five hundred wide runs between. In it is the rock Scylla and the whirlpool Charybdis. Jerome says these things generally; regarding whom it is a wonder why he calls Rhegium a city of Sicily, since Geographers teach it is in the territory of the Bruttians, who are a people of Italy. Unless perhaps a scribe corrupted "of Italy" into "of Sicily." Regarding the distance, Strabo in his sixth book records that Rhegium is sixty stadia from Messana—which is a city on Pelorus—that is, roughly seven miles and fifty paces. Regarding the measurement of the strait, I suspect the passage in Jerome is corrupt. If, however, this work is by Jerome, since Jerome is cited within it.

<margin>7 As far as the Forum of Appius</margin> Since it was said before, <term>and so we came to Rome</term>, and afterward mention is made of the Forum of Appius, some think the Forum of Appius is within the city of Rome; and that is also read in the catalog of places which Saint Jerome indicated in the Acts of the Apostles. But just as I suspect many things were removed from there by compilers—whom this proverb born among drinks pleases tremendously: <term>Moderns delight in brevity</term>—so I see some things added by others, of which I believe this is one. Otherwise, it is well known that the town called <term>Appii Forum</term> is further away from Rome than Aricia is; a fact which Horace declares in the first book of his Satires, the fifth Satire:

> Having left great Rome, Aricia received me
> In a modest lodging; my companion was the rhetorician Heliodorus,
> By far the most learned of the Greeks; from there, to the Forum of Appius.

Therefore, when Luke said in summary that they went to Rome, he backtracks slightly to describe the meeting with the brothers at <term>Appii Forum</term> and <term>Three Taverns</term>. For so we read in the corrected Latin copies, whereas in some it is written <term>at Three Taverns</term>. Otherwise, if <term>Appii Forum</term> and <term>Three Taverns</term> are in Rome, what does he mean by <term>what he immediately adds</term>:

<margin>8 But when we had come to Rome</margin>, <term>it was permitted to Paul to stay</term>? Here the Greeks have more: <note>original: Ὅτε δὲ ἤλχομεν εἰς Ῥώμην... (When we had come to Rome, the centurion delivered the prisoners to the commander of the camp; but to Paul it was permitted...)</note>, that is, <term>when however we had come to Rome, the centurion delivered the prisoners to the leader of the army, or to the tribunes; but it was permitted to Paul</term>.

<sig>F</sig> <margin>9 They remained by themselves</margin> <note>original: μένειν καθ’ ἑαυτόν (to remain by himself)</note>, that is, <term>to stay at his own place</term>, which is <term>alone and without the rest of the captives</term>.

<margin>10 You shall hear with the ear</margin> <note>original: Ἀκοῇ ἀκούσετε (By hearing you shall hear)</note>, that is, <term>to render it word for word, By hearing you shall hear</term>, and so Jerome, the translator of Didymus, rendered it concerning the Holy Spirit. It is a Hebraic doubling, just as if you were to say, <term>Hearing you shall hear</term>, which is <term>You shall certainly hear</term>. Nor do I disapprove that he translates it here as <term>With the ear</term>, except that I would prefer <term>With the ears</term>. For thus the Latins speak: <term>I saw with these very eyes, I heard with these very ears</term>.

<margin>11 And when he had said these things, the Jews went out from him, having much dispute among themselves</margin> These words I did not find in several ancient codices.

<margin>12 Without hindrance</margin> <note>original: ἀκωλύτως (unhindered)</note>. Which can be taken in two ways: prohibited or forbidden by no one, or with such a spirit that he could be hindered by no one.

# OF THE BLESSED JOHN
## ARCHBISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE,
# C H R Y S O S T O M
### PROLOGUE TO ALL THE
# E P I S T L E S  O F  P A U L
->PROLOGUE<-

As I continuously hear the epistles of the blessed Paul being read—often twice, three, or four times each week whenever we celebrate the memories of the holy martyrs—I rejoice, enjoying that spiritual trumpet. I am roused and warmed with desire, recognizing my friend’s voice; I almost seem to imagine him present and see him conversing with me. Yet I am pained and grieved that not everyone knows this man as he ought to be known. Indeed, some are so ignorant of him that they do not even know the number of his epistles clearly. This happens not from a lack of natural intelligence, but from a lack of desire to converse continuously with this blessed man. For even what we know, we do not know by some innate talent or sharpness of mind, but because we hold onto the man continuously and are very well-disposed toward him. For those who love someone know their affairs better than anyone else, because they care for them. This is what the blessed one indicated when he said to the Philippians:
> Even as it is right for me to think this of you, because I have you in my heart, both in my bonds, and in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel. <note>Philippians 1:7</note>
If you would only attend to this reading with eagerness, you would need nothing else; for Christ’s word is true when He said:
> Seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. <note>Matthew 7:7</note>
But since most of us gathered here have taken on the raising of children, the care of a wife, and the management of a household, and for this reason cannot bear to give ourselves entirely to this labor, at least rouse yourselves to receive what has been gathered by others. Devote as much zeal to hearing what is said as you do to the collection of money. For although it is shameful to demand only that much from you, it would be a welcome thing if you gave at least that much. For from this—ignorance of the Scriptures—countless evils have sprung. From this the great plague of heresies has sprouted; from this, neglected lives; from this, fruitless labors. Just as those deprived of physical light cannot walk straight, so those who do not look toward the rays of the divine Scriptures are forced to sin many times and continuously, as they walk in a difficult darkness. Lest this happen, let us open our eyes to the brightness of the apostolic words. For the tongue of this man shone like the sun, and surpassed all others in the word of teaching. Since he labored more than they, he drew upon himself an abundance of the Spirit’s grace. I assert this not only from his epistles, but also from the Acts. For whenever there was a time for public speaking, they everywhere yielded to him; for this reason, he was thought by the unbelievers to be a priest <note>Original: ἱερεὺς. Likely a reference to Acts 14:12, where Paul was called "Hermes" because he was the chief speaker.</note>, because he prevailed in speaking.

As we are about to enter into this epistle, it is necessary to speak of the time in which it was written. For it is not, as many think, the first of all the others. It was written before all those sent from Rome, and before some of the others, though not all. For both epistles to the Corinthians were sent before this one. This is clear from what he wrote at the end of it, saying: 
> But now I go to Jerusalem to minister to the saints. For it pleased Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem. <note>Romans 15:25-26</note>
And when writing to the Corinthians he said: 
> If it be meet that I go also, they shall go with me <note>1 Corinthians 16:4</note>
referring to those who were carrying the money. From this it is clear that when he sent to the Corinthians, his journey there was still a matter of doubt. But when he wrote to the Romans, the journey had already been announced. From this it is admittedly clear that this epistle came after those. And the epistle to the Thessalonians seems to me to be earlier than the one to the Corinthians; for having sent to them first, and having moved them to the topic of almsgiving, when he said: "But as touching brotherly love, you need not that I write to you: for you yourselves are taught of God to love one another; and indeed you do it toward all the brethren," <note>1 Thessalonians 4:9-10</note> he then wrote to the Corinthians. This he makes clear by saying: 
> For I know the forwardness of your mind, for which I boast of you to them of Macedonia, that Achaia was ready a year ago; and your zeal has provoked very many. <note>2 Corinthians 9:2</note>
From this he showed that he had spoken to them first about this matter. Therefore, this epistle [to the Romans] is later than those to the Thessalonians. Of the ones written from Rome, it is the first; for he had not yet visited the Romans when he wrote this epistle. He makes this clear by saying: 
> For I long to see you, that I may impart unto you some spiritual gift. <note>Romans 1:11</note>
But he sent to the Philippians from Rome; thus he says: "All the saints of Italy salute you." <note>Cf. Hebrews 13:24/Philippians 4:22</note> And the epistle to Timothy he also sent from Rome while in bonds, which seems to me to be the very last of all the epistles, as is clear from the end: 
> For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand. <note>2 Timothy 4:6</note>
Moreover, that he ended his life there is evident to everyone. The epistle to Philemon is also one of the last, for he wrote it in extreme old age; thus he says: "As Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ." <note>Philemon 1:9</note> Yet it is earlier than the one to the Colossians; this is clear from the end. For writing to the Colossians he says: "Tychicus shall make known all things to you... whom I have sent with Onesimus, a faithful and beloved brother." <note>Colossians 4:7-9</note> This was the same Onesimus on whose behalf he composed the epistle to Philemon. And that this was not another of the same name is clear from Archippus; for the same man whom he took as a fellow-worker in the epistle to Philemon to intercede for Onesimus, he also rouses when writing to the Colossians, saying: 
> Say to Archippus, "Take heed to the ministry which you have received, that you fulfill it." <note>Colossians 4:17</note>
It also seems to me that the epistle to the Galatians is earlier than the one to the Romans. If it holds a different order in the books, it is no wonder; for even the Twelve Prophets are not in chronological order but are separated by much time, yet they lie in sequence in the arrangement of the books. For Amos, Zechariah, and Haggai prophesied after Ezekiel and Daniel. And again, after Jonah and Zephaniah, and all the others; yet they are joined to all of them, though they are not so close in time. Let no one think this labor is a side-matter, nor such an inquiry a superfluous curiosity. For the time of the epistles contributes not a little to our investigations. For when I see him writing to the Romans and Colossians on the same subjects, yet not in the same way—writing to the former with much condescension <note><term>condescension (synkatabasis)</term>: Chrysostom’s term for God or the Apostles adapting their language to the limited understanding of the audience.</note> when he says: 
> Him that is weak in the faith receive, but not to doubtful disputations. For one believes that he may eat all things; another, who is weak, eats herbs. <note>Romans 14:1-2</note>
But to the Colossians he speaks on the same subjects with greater boldness: "If you be dead with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, are you subject to ordinances? Touch not; taste not; handle not; which all are to perish with the using... not in any honor to the satisfying of the flesh." <note>Colossians 2:20-23</note> I find the cause of this difference is nothing other than the timing of the letters. In the beginning, it was necessary to be condescending, but after some time, it was no longer so. One might find him doing this in many places. Thus both a doctor and a teacher are accustomed to act. For a doctor does not use the same treatment for those just starting to be sick as he does for those approaching the end of recovery; nor does a teacher treat children who are just beginning to learn the same way as those needing more perfect lessons. Some epistles, however, were prompted by specific causes and circumstances, as he makes clear to the Corinthians, saying: "Now concerning the things whereof you wrote to me," <note>1 Corinthians 7:1</note> and similarly to the Galatians, as he shows in the prologue of the epistle itself. For what reason this—

<meta>catchword: and</meta>

<summary>In this prologue, John Chrysostom expresses his deep love for Paul's letters and explains that their order in the New Testament is based on pedagogical needs rather than chronology, which helps explain Paul's differing tone across different letters.</summary>
<keywords>John Chrysostom, Paul the Apostle, Biblical Exegesis, Chronology of Epistles, Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Condescension, Spiritual Trumpet</keywords>

<meta>The previous page introduced the "Prologue to the Epistles of Paul" by St. John Chrysostom, where he encourages the faithful to read Paul's letters with devotion, explaining that understanding comes from love and persistence rather than just raw intellect.</meta>

# CHRYSOSTOM’S PROLOGUE TO ALL THE EPISTLES OF PAUL.

And why? For he appears to bear witness to them, that they are "full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, and able to admonish one another." <note>Romans 15:14</note> For what reason, then, did he write to them? "Because of the grace," he says, "given to me by God, that I should be a minister of Jesus Christ." <note>Romans 15:15-16</note> This is why he said at the beginning, "I am a debtor... as much as is in me, I am ready to preach the gospel to you who are in Rome also." <note>Romans 1:14-15</note> For the things he said—such as that they are able to admonish others and similar remarks—are intended more as praise and encouragement; yet, the correction provided through his letters was also necessary for them. Since he had not yet arrived in person, he guides these men in a twofold way: by the benefit of his letters and by the expectation of his presence. For such was that holy soul: it embraced the whole world <note>original: "oikoumenē," the inhabited world</note> and carried everyone within itself. Considering the kinship according to God to be the greatest of all, and as if he were personally the father of all, he felt he owed this care. Rather, he displayed an affection greater than any natural father; for the grace of the Spirit surpasses the labor pains of the flesh and demonstrates a warmer desire. One can see this especially in the soul of Paul, who, having become like a winged bird through love, continuously encompassed everyone, never staying or standing still in one place. For since he heard Christ saying, "Peter, if you love me, feed my sheep," <note>John 21:16</note> and seeing this as the greatest labor of love, he displayed it to an extreme degree. Therefore, you too should emulate him; even if you cannot care for the whole world, nor for entire cities and nations, let each man at least guide his own house—his wife, his children, his friends, and his neighbors. And let no one say to me, "I am unskilled and a commoner." <note>original: "idiōtēs," meaning a layperson or one without formal training</note> You are no more unlearned than Peter, nor more of a commoner than Paul; even he himself admits this and is not ashamed, saying, "Even if I am unskilled in speech, yet I am not so in knowledge." <note>2 Corinthians 11:6</note> Yet this "unskilled" man and that "unlearned" one conquered ten thousand philosophers, silenced ten thousand orators, and accomplished everything through their own zeal and the grace of God. What defense shall we have, then, if we are not even useful to those who live with us? These excuses are merely pretexts and covers for laziness. For it is not ignorance or lack of education that hinders teaching, but lethargy and sleep. Shaking off this sleep, then, let us hold fast to our own members with all diligence, so that we may enjoy great peace here by guiding our households according to the fear of God, and there participate in ten thousand blessings by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power, now and always, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.

->THE ARGUMENT OF THE EPISTLE<-
->OF THE HOLY<-

# P A U L

->TO THE ROMANS.<-

**H**E sends this letter from Corinth, having not yet seen the Romans, but having heard about them and longing to see them. First, he accepts their faith, which was being proclaimed everywhere, as he loved them. Then he indicates that he had often intended to come because of his desire for them, but had been prevented until now. For the rest, he makes the epistle a work of teaching concerning the calling of the Gentiles, and that circumcision has ceased for a time and has now fully ended, and that through Christ the transgression of Adam is undone, and the shadow of the Law has passed away. He establishes that the calling of the Gentiles happened as a natural consequence, demonstrating that the law is innate in all men—that all are untaught by nature and can know God from creation itself. Therefore, he rightly blames the Greeks <note>used here to mean "Gentiles" or "pagans"</note> first, since God revealed the knowledge of Himself and His eternal power to them through His works in the world, in which and through which He made all things; yet they, having known from the created things that God is their creator, instead deified the works and worshipped the creation rather than Him. He also blames the Jews for not keeping the Law, but rather dishonoring God through their transgression of the Law. Thus, he shuts up both the greatest groups—Jews and Greeks—and convicts them of lawlessness, in order to show that all having become equal, all alike as guilty ones need a Redeemer. Since grace and redemption have come equally to the Jews and to the nations, the calling of the Gentiles followed logically. And with the calling of the Gentiles, circumcision and the shadow in the Law necessarily ceased. For Abraham, he says, was justified not in circumcision, but before circumcision; he was renamed Abraham because he was to be the father of many nations according to the faith he had while uncircumcised. He received circumcision in the flesh after being justified so that it might be a sign to those born of him according to the flesh, that circumcision would one day cease when the Gentiles became children of Abraham, beginning to live according to the faith of Abraham in which he was justified while still uncircumcised. For this reason, he was renamed Abraham. It is necessary that when the things signified arrive, the sign must cease. If you force the Gentiles to be circumcised, let them also cease using the name of Abraham and be called "Abram"; but if he was renamed "Abraham" by God, the Gentiles must not be circumcised, nor even the Jews according to the flesh anymore, so that the name may remain firm and he may be called the "father of many nations." For he has no further need of circumcision, being satisfied with the faith of Abraham, nor of the rest of the shadow in the Law; for it is not by these, but by faith that one is justified, just as Abraham was. Having established these points, he demonstrates again that redemption and grace would not otherwise come to Israel and the nations unless the ancient sin of Adam, which happened to all, were dissolved. He says it cannot be wiped out by anything else except through Christ the God; for it was not possible for another to undo the transgression, for through Him the curse also came from the beginning. Then he writes that this could not happen unless the Son of God wore a body and became man, so that by offering this for all, He might free all from death; just as through one man sin entered the world, so through one man grace might come. Finally, as a good steward, he comforts the Jews, saying, "You are not transgressors of the Law if you believe in Christ," and he warns those from the Gentiles not to be arrogant toward Israel, but to know that as branches they were grafted onto them as onto the root. After these things, an exhortation regarding morals concludes the epistle.

# ON THE EPISTLE OF PAUL
## TO THE ROMANS, AN ARGUMENT BY
### DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'J' at the beginning of the text, featuring ornate foliage and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>

**NOW**, so that the matter may be clearer, the argument <note>In this context, "argument" means the theme or introductory summary.</note> of the Epistle must be explained in a few words. To begin with the name itself, it does not escape me that Jerome—in the commentaries he wrote on the Epistle to Philemon—is of the opinion that the Apostle was first called Saul, and took the surname "Paul" as a kind of trophy from Sergius Paulus the proconsul <note>A Roman provincial governor.</note>, whom he won for Christ, as we read in the thirteenth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles. On the other hand, there are others who prefer the idea that he was called Saul while in Judaism, and changed his name at the same time he changed his religion. But the former view is made less probable by what Luke writes in the very chapter we just cited: *Saul, who is also Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit* <note>original: "Saulus qui & Paulus repletus Spiritu sancto"</note>; clearly declaring that he had two names before Sergius Paulus was converted. The second view is plainly refuted by the fact that in several other places, as well as in that same chapter, he is called Saul even while already preaching the Gospel of Christ: *The Holy Spirit said to them, "Set apart for me Saul and Barnabas."* <note>original: "Dixit illis Spiritus sanctus, Segregate mihi Saulum & Barnabam."</note> Therefore, the opinion of Origen seems truer to me: just as we find in several books of the Old Testament <note>original: "veteris Instrumenti," literally "the Old Instrument," a term Erasmus often used for the Old Testament.</note> people marked by different names—such as he who was called Jedidiah but elsewhere named Solomon, or Uzziah who is elsewhere Azariah—and likewise in the Gospel writings, he who is called Levi by Luke calls himself Matthew in his own Gospel; so Paul had a double name. However, he never calls himself Saul in his own Epistles, but everywhere Paul—perhaps because the name "Paul" was more familiar to the ears of the Greeks and Romans to whom he was writing. For "Saul" appears to be derived from the Hebrew name *Saul* in the same way the Greeks derived "Josephus" from "Joseph." To the Hebrews, "Paul" sounds like "wonderful," if indeed we think it acceptable to seek the etymology of a Roman or Greek name from a foreign language. Although Jerome elsewhere criticizes this practice in others, he allows it for himself here, I suppose, as a matter of no great seriousness. To the Greeks, it certainly sounds like "quiet," and to the Latins, "small." Among the Hebrews, Saul sounds like "requested," and if we believe Ambrose, "unrest" or "temptation." And so much for the reasoning behind the name, which is perhaps more than enough for an introduction.

Otherwise, he dictated this Epistle while Tertius took it down, as Tertius himself testifies at the end of the letter, adding: *I, Tertius, who wrote this epistle, greet you in the Lord.* <note>original: "Saluto vos ego Tertius, qui scripsi Epistolam in Domino." Romans 16:22</note> It appears it was sent from Corinth by Phoebe, a woman of Cenchreae. Now, Cenchreae is a port of the Corinthians, located not far from the city. If the time of writing is also required, it appears to have been written after both Epistles to the Corinthians; for this reason, they think the proofs of a now-matured and confirmed piety shine forth most clearly in this work. It was at the time when he had already traveled through Achaia <note>A Roman province in modern-day Greece.</note> (where Corinth is) and neighboring Macedonia as far as Illyricum <note>A region on the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea.</note>, and had not only preached the Gospel of Christ everywhere—specifically in those places where none of the other Apostles had preached—but also, following the advice of Peter, he had collected a sum of money from his people for the relief of the poor. He was preparing for a journey to Jerusalem so that, after delivering what he had received, he might set out from there for Spain, making his way through Rome. There, he intended to greet the Christians in passing, of whose faith and religion he had heard, though he had not yet seen them. For something had happened to them quite different from what happened to the Galatians. Indeed, the Galatians were first correctly instructed by Paul, but were later deceived by the trickery of false apostles and dragged back into Judaism. By contrast, the Romans were first poorly instructed by false apostles, but as soon as they perceived the fraud through their own wisdom, they came to their senses and persevered in what they recognized to be right. 

For in the beginnings of the nascent Church, there were those who thought that the grace of the Gospel—since it seemed promised specifically to the descendants of Abraham and the Jewish nation—should not be spread to the pagan nations <note>original: "profanas gentes," the profane or common nations.</note> who were devoted to the worship of idols and demons. It appears Peter himself held this opinion, as he had to be warned by a vision to admit the centurion Cornelius. On this account, trouble was soon brought against him in Jerusalem by those who had converted to Christ from Judaism, complaining that he had had dealings with the uncircumcised; and it is probable that some of the Apostles were among them. For so we read in the eleventh chapter of Acts: *Now the apostles and the brothers who were in Judea heard that the Gentiles also had received the word of God.* <note>original: "Audierunt autem Apostoli & fratres qui erant in Judæa, quoniam & gentes receperunt verbum Dei."</note> When Peter had gone up to Jerusalem, those of the circumcision contended against him, saying: *Why did you go to uncircumcised men and eat with them?* <note>original: "Quare introisti ad viros præputium habentes, & manducasti cum illis?"</note> Again, there were those who, while they did not think the Gentiles should be entirely barred from the fellowship of the Gospel, nevertheless held they should not be admitted unless they were circumcised according to the Jewish rite—just as if Christ needed the support of the Mosaic Law, and simultaneously so they might claim the glory of the Gospel for their own nation. And in the eleventh chapter of the Acts of the Apostles, it is recorded that those who had fled to Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch because of the persecution following Stephen's death preached Christ to no one but the Jews. Again, in the fifteenth chapter, certain Jews came to Antioch, openly preaching against Paul and Barnabas that there was no hope of salvation unless they were circumcised according to the prescription of Moses. Such a great tumult was stirred up by these men that, after a council was gathered, it was decreed that Paul and Barnabas, along with their adversaries, should go to Jerusalem, and the dispute should be settled by the judgment of the Apostles and Elders. And there again, with some resisting sharply—especially those Christians of the Pharisaic faction, to which Paul himself had belonged—a synod of the Apostles and Elders was convened. By the authority of Peter and James, it was decreed that the Gentiles should not be burdened with the Mosaic Law; they should only abstain from eating the meat of strangled animals, from blood, from meat sacrificed to idols, and from fornication. That this was granted to the invincible superstition of the Jews only for the needs of that time is proven by the fact that we see those first three restrictions have long since been removed and entirely abolished. 

From this same source arose that dispute between Paul and Peter at Antioch, when the Apostle to the Gentiles, seeing his people endangered by Peter’s pretense, publicly rebuked him, as he himself relates in the second chapter of the Epistle to the Galatians. Again, in Jerusalem, at the suggestion of James, in order to clear up a rumor already spreading among the Jews that he seemed to be withdrawing people from the Mosaic Law, he shaved his head along with others and, having been purified according to the Jewish rite, offered a gift in the temple, as Luke relates in the twenty-first chapter of Acts. From this passage, it seems that James, although he had previously freed the Gentiles from almost all the burden of the Mosaic Law, was nevertheless of the opinion that the observation of the Law should be demanded from the Jews, even if only to please those who had not yet progressed far enough in the truth of the Gospel to be able to completely despise their ancestral rites. For James speaks thus—as must be conjectured on behalf of the gathered multitude: *And all will know that what they heard about you is false, but that you yourself walk keeping the Law.* <note>original: "Et scient omnes, quia quæ de te audierunt, falsa sunt, sed ambulas & ipse custodiens Legem."</note> Nor for any other reason, I suppose...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s introduction (Argumentum) to the Epistle to the Romans. The previous page discussed the naming of Paul and his background; this page focuses on the historical context of the Roman church—composed of both Jews and Gentiles—and the central themes of the Epistle, such as the transition from the Mosaic Law to faith in Christ.</meta>

# THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS BY DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<margin>A defense of the Jewish Antiquities.</margin>
I believe he shaved his head at Cenchreae according to a vow, as told in the eighteenth chapter <note>Acts 18:18</note>. Out of a similar necessity, he circumcised Timothy, as told in the sixteenth chapter <note>Acts 16:3</note>, since Timothy was born of a Jewish mother but a Greek father. It was a task of such great difficulty <note>original: "Tantæ molis erat"</note> to make a Christian out of a Jew. For that nation has a certain unique stubbornness, and no people was ever more tenacious of its own religion, as Josephus elegantly teaches in his defense of the *Jewish Antiquities* <note>Erasmus likely refers to Josephus’s work *Against Apion*, which defends the ancient heritage of the Jews.</note>. In addition to this, just as the Jewish nation was then uniquely hated by all the nations of the world, so in turn they detested everyone else as impure, profane, and impious—to the point that they did not even deign to meet with them, and believed their Temple was polluted if any uncircumcised person happened to enter. Such was the haughty arrogance <note>original: "supercilium," literally a raised eyebrow</note> of that cut-away scrap of skin. 

Therefore, since there was no hope that the Greeks and Romans would accept the hated Mosaic Law, and since the Jews would reclaim it with incredible stubbornness, Paul understood the danger: that through such a deadly disagreement, the fruit of the Gospel might largely perish, and the glory of Christ might be obscured by the mixing-in of the name of Moses. Because of this, he makes it his primary goal everywhere to abrogate <note>To formally abolish a law.</note> and render obsolete the ceremonies of the Law, transferring all confidence in attaining salvation to Christ alone. Just as he rebukes the Galatians sharply, though still lovingly, because they had been led back into Judaism, so he fortifies and instructs the Romans—lest they be ensnared through lack of caution by the "False Apostles" whom he knew never ceased their work—so that they might persist in the right doctrine they had begun to embrace. For there was a huge number of Jews in Rome, whether moved there by Pompey <note>The Roman general who conquered Jerusalem in 63 BCE.</note> or because Judea was by then a Roman province; their superstition is frequently noted in the writings of Juvenal, Horace, and Seneca <note>Famous Roman poets and a philosopher who often mocked Jewish customs like the Sabbath.</note>. The final chapter of the *Acts of the Apostles* testifies that Paul had much business with these people after he arrived in Rome.

And with marvelous planning, like a singular craftsman, Paul tempers his speech in this Epistle between the Jews and the Gentiles. He strives to draw all people by all means to Christ, and he does not wish, if it were possible, for any mortal man to perish from the leader under whom he served as a soldier. Thus, now he rebukes these, now those; then again, he lifts them up and relieves them. He strikes down the superciliousness of the Gentiles, showing that neither the law of nature nor philosophy (of whose profession they were so proud) had been of any use in preventing them from falling into every disgrace of crime. Conversely, he restrains the arrogance of the Jews, who, through their reliance on the Law, had lost the very head of the whole Law: faith in Jesus Christ. 

He teaches that the ceremonies of the Law have been made obsolete, now that the Gospel of Christ is shining forth—that Christ whom the shadows of the Law had only sketched out. He teaches that the idleness of Sabbaths is now abolished, as is the <term>injury of circumcision</term> <note>original: "circumcisionis injuriam." Erasmus likely refers to the physical "mark" or the "offense" of the ritual in a Gentile context.</note>, the recurrence of the new moons, the festivals returning three times a year, the choice of foods, the washings that would only need to be repeated daily, the slaughter of innocent cattle, and the religious devotion of a temple constantly defiled by slaughter. He shows that these shadows of things vanish when the light of truth flashes forth. 

He argues that the true sons of Abraham are those who reflect the faith of Abraham; the true Jews are those who profess Christ; the truly circumcised are those who have a mind cleansed of foul desires. True justice and perfect salvation are bestowed equally upon everyone through the Gospel and through faith alone in Christ, without the assistance of the Law. Although that salvation was once promised uniquely to the Jews, it was promised in such a way that the Prophets were not silent about the fact that, should the Jews reject it, the preaching of Christ would be spread to the Gentiles. Through the Mosaic Law, true justice comes to no one, but rather through faith; he proves this both by the example of Abraham and by various testimonies of the Law itself. And in this manner, having stripped away the arrogance from both sides and removed their self-confidence, he makes everyone equal in the business of the Gospel faith. He congratulates the Gentiles on their salvation in such a way that he also deplores the blindness of his own nation with a father’s affection, even though he experienced them everywhere as most stubbornly hostile. This harsh reality he mitigates by saying that not all of them are blinded, and that the Jewish nation will eventually return to its senses, provoked by the faith of the Gentiles. 

And here, in passing, he treats various and manifold doctrines regarding those "preordained" or "predestined," those "foreknown," and those "called"; he discusses grace and merit, free will, the divine counsel which is inscrutable to us, the law of nature, the law of Moses, and the law of sin.

He also employs various sources of allegory, as when he creates two "Adams": one by whom we are born mortal according to the flesh, and the other by whom we are reborn to be immortal. He describes two "men": the internal and the external. The internal man obeys the spirit and reason; the external man is subject to desires and passions. The former he sometimes calls the *Spirit*; the latter he sometimes calls the *body or members*, sometimes the *flesh*, and several times the *law of sin*. He describes a double death: of the body and of the soul; and a third death, by which we die to sin and to the urges of sinning. Likewise, a triple life: that by which we live in the body, that in the soul, and that by which we live for justice and sin. He describes a double servitude or liberty: where we either serve innocence, having been emancipated from sins, or we serve sins, being "free" from justice. 

There is a double Judaism; a double circumcision; twin descendants of Abraham; two parts of the Mosaic Law: the carnal (which is like the body) and the spiritual (which is like the soul of the Law). There is a double baptism: the one by which we are first washed from our former sins in the holy font, and the one by which we die together with Christ, having renounced the passions of the world. There is a double burial: the physical one, in which Christ was buried for three days, and the spiritual one, in which we, removed from the vices of the world, rest in Him. There is a double resurrection: the one which occurred first in Christ and will follow in us, and the other by which we, revived from our former sins, move forward from virtue to virtue, meditating in this life (as far as we are able) on our future immortality. There is a double justice: that of God and that of men. A double judgment: God’s and men’s. A double glory or praise: before God and before men.

Having discussed these things, he moves to the moral section: first exhorting them to mutual harmony, using the example of the members of a body. And since peace cannot stand where there is pride or envy, he begs that they nourish and foster mutual love through mutual service. He asks the Romans to bear with the weakness of the Jews that remains from their long habituation to the Law; conversely, he warns the Jews not to envy the Gentiles who have been admitted into the fellowship of the Gospel, but rather to emulate their faith and liberty. Since there is one God for all, one Christ, one grace, and one reward, all should grow together into one body, and no one should claim anything for himself. Rather, if anyone excels in some gift, he should apply it to the help of his brother. 

He treats this topic in various ways, teaching how they ought to behave toward unbelieving Jews, toward the more superstitious Christians (whom he calls "the weak"), toward superiors, toward inferiors, toward equals, and toward the Gentile Princes and Magistrates (so long as they are performing their duty). He teaches how to act in prosperity and in adversity. Then, once again with praise for the Romans, he softens the bitterness of his admonition and commends his own authority to them, reminding them how much more he has advanced the Gospel of Christ than others. He declares how great a desire he has to see them and offers hope of his arrival. He explains why he is forced to delay it, praising the spontaneous generosity of the Macedonians and Corinthians toward the "holy poor" <note>The poor Christians in Jerusalem.</note>, quietly and modestly provoking the Romans to emulate them. 

He occupies the final chapter almost entirely with greetings—not just a cold list of many names, but each with a marvelous little eulogy <note>A short tribute or statement of praise.</note> added. Finally, because he knew well both the wicked craftiness of the False Apostles and the simplicity and easy-going nature of the Romans, he warns them again and again to be careful lest they be deceived by their smooth talking. 

Now, although most of these things pertain more specifically to that age—in which the still-unrefined Church was gradually sprouting, mixed with Jews and Gentiles and subject to Gentile Princes—nevertheless, there is nothing here from which some part of wholesome doctrine cannot be adapted even to these present times: such as the need to flee superstition (which is the seed-bed of disagreements, and which wears the mask of piety so well that nothing is more contrary to true piety); regarding the foolish confidence in worldly philosophy; regarding the merit of faith; regarding the avoidance of pride; regarding the need to tolerate, in some places, the weakness of the less learned or the superstitious; and regarding the nurturing of harmony through mutual service.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s introductory "Argumentum" (Introduction) to the Epistle to the Romans. Having previously discussed the background of Paul and the cultural friction between Jews and Greeks, Erasmus now transitions into the practical moral teachings of the letter and the technical linguistic difficulties he encountered while translating it.</meta>

### INTRODUCTION TO THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS.

...discipline: concerning the bearing of bad Princes and impious Bishops for a time, so that the order of the public state is not disturbed; on overcoming evil deeds with kindness; on not judging what does not pertain to you; on interpreting favorably whatever can be done with a right mind; on guarding against treacherous smooth-talking; and other things of that sort, in which the common life of men is still involved today.

But the difficulty of this Epistle equals and almost surpasses its utility; and this seems to me to happen for three main reasons. First, because nowhere else is the order of speech more confused, nowhere is the oratory more gapped with *hyperbatons* <term>hyperbaton: a transposition of words from their natural grammatical order for emphasis</term>, nowhere more frequently incomplete with *anantapodota* <term>anantapodoton: a figure of speech where a grammatical sequence is started but the concluding part is omitted</term>. On this point, the interpreter Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 185–253 AD)</note> repeatedly complains, struggling and laboring throughout these kinds of difficulties. Whether this should be attributed to the translator, or to the scribe Tertius <note>The person who physically wrote down the letter as Paul dictated it, mentioned in Romans 16:22</note>, or to Paul himself, let it be the judgment of others. He certainly acknowledges his lack of skill in speech, although he pleads against a lack of knowledge in matters. 

Again, he so little sought after a speech composed by human art, that he even thought he should avoid it, lest anything should detract from the glory of the cross. Because of this, Origen thinks it is superfluous to look for formal composition of speech in him. Jerome <note>The 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> sometimes attributes oratorical artifice to him and at other times takes it away, frankly confessing that he drew some flaw from the corrupt speech of the Cilicians <note>The region in modern-day Turkey where Paul's hometown of Tarsus was located</note>. Augustine even draws the ornaments and flourishes of the Rhetoricians from his Epistles. Indeed, in the Acts of the Apostles, he is the leader of the word, and in the first Epistle to the Corinthians, he speaks in tongues above all others. For although, as Jerome testifies, at that time the whole East spoke Greek, just as it is consistent that among the Celts there was not the same purity of the Roman speech as there was in Rome, so it is likely there was no small difference between a Cilician speaking Greek and an Athenian <note>original: "Atticum"</note>. To these disadvantages of oratory was added *Hebraism* <term>Hebraism: a Hebrew idiom or grammatical structure used in another language</term>, the idioms of which he brings in everywhere, speaking Greek in such a way that you nevertheless recognize the Hebrew in the meantime. 

I think the second cause of difficulty is that, because of the obscurity of inexplicable matters, no other Epistle is hindered by more frequent rough patches or interrupted by deeper abysses, so much so that he himself, having abandoned what he had begun, is forced to exclaim: *O the depth of the riches* <note>Romans 11:33</note>. What about the fact that he touches on certain mysteries so prudently that he shows them only as if through a lattice-window <note>original: "per transennam"</note>, according to the capacity of those times and the understanding of those to whom he writes, tempering his speech accordingly. He had known and seen certain things which it would be unlawful for a man to speak, and he knew how far there was a need for milk, and how far for solid food. He knew the stages of age in Christ, and what should be applied to whom. With this plan, the Apostle Peter, when about to speak words about Christ to a raw [uneducated] crowd, calls him a *man*, and is silent about him being *God*. 

The third reason, I think, is the frequent and sudden change of persons, while he looks now to the Jews, now the Gentiles, now to both, sometimes believers, sometimes unbelievers, at times the weak, at times the strong, sometimes the pious, sometimes the impious—he takes on their persona. Because of these things, it happens that the reader, wandering as if in certain inexplicable labyrinths and *Meanders* <note>A reference to the winding Meander River in Turkey, symbolizing a complex or circuitous path</note>, does not see clearly where he entered, nor where the exit is. So it seems to me that Origen, no less truly than elegantly, makes Paul similar to one who leads a guest into the palace of some most wealthy Prince, a place tangled with various winding paths and the seclusions of chambers. He shows some things from a distance out of a most rich treasury of wealth, some things he brings closer, and some things he does not wish to be seen. Meanwhile, he often enters through one door and leaves from another, so that the guest himself wonders where he came from, where he is, or which way he must go out. The Apostle Peter also acknowledged this in his second Epistle, testifying that there are certain things in the Pauline Epistles difficult to understand, which the poorly learned and unstable distort to their own destruction. 

We have tried to the best of our ability to remove these difficulties, except that certain things are so peculiar to the Pauline language that at times they cannot be changed: such as these, *faith, grace, body, flesh, members, spirit, mind, sense, to build up*, and others of this kind, which as they absolutely ought not to have been changed, so we have studied to soften them as far as was permitted.

<summary>Erasmus discusses the extreme difficulty of translating Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, citing Paul's complex grammar, Hebrew-influenced Greek, and sudden shifts in perspective as major challenges. He justifies his translation choices by comparing Paul's writing style to a vast, winding palace where some mysteries are revealed while others are hidden.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the general introduction of the Epistle to the Romans into the specific verse-by-verse commentary and translation. # THE EPISTLE OF PAUL THE APOSTLE TO THE ROMANS.

<margin>I. 1</margin> PAUL, A SERVANT of Jesus Christ, called to be an Apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, <margin>2</margin> which he had promised beforehand through his Prophets in the holy scriptures, <margin>3</margin> concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, <margin>4</margin> who was declared— <note>original: ΠΑΥΛΟΣ ΔΟΥΛΟΣ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ... (Paul, a servant...)</note>

**1 PAUL**] There are those who think the name was changed from Saul at the time of his conversion; among these is Ambrose. However, Saint Jerome, in his commentary on the Epistle to Philemon, thinks he began to be called Paul because of the proconsul Sergius Paulus, whom this Apostle won for Christ as the very first of the Gentiles, as we read in the thirteenth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles. Chrysostom thinks his name was changed by divine authority, just like the leader of the Apostles, who was called Cephas, or Peter, instead of Simon. Again, there are those who think he had two names from the start, which in my opinion is closer to the truth. Although I suspect that as a Hebrew, the Hebrew name Saul was first given to him. For Christ addresses him by this name on the road: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" <note>original: Σαὺλ Σαὺλ τί με διώκεις;</note> Then, since Egypt, Cilicia, and the neighboring part of Syria were already using the Greek language due to the empire of Alexander the Great and later Roman administration, the Hebrew word was bent into a Greek form. Because the Greeks have no vowels ending in "l," *Saul* became *Saulon* <note>original: σαυλὸν</note>; just as today Latin speakers turn *Adam* into *Adamus*, *Abraham* into *Abrahamum*, and *Joseph* into *Josephum*. Finally, because the name Paul was familiar to both Greeks and Romans, *Saul* was turned into *Paul* so that those whose teacher he professed to be would recognize the name more gladly—here too, he became all things to all people. He certainly used this name constantly in his writings. *Saul* <note>Hebrew: שאול (*Sha'ul*)</note> sounds like "asked for" to the Hebrews, a passive form of "to ask" <note>Hebrew: שאל (*sha'al*)</note>, because he was called to the Apostolic office. Ambrose indicates that *Saul* means "temptation" or "restlessness." They add other interpretations of these Hebrew names that have only a slight allusion to the sounds; since this is not my purpose here, I will not discuss them anxiously. However, to the Greeks, the word *saulos* <note>original: σαῦλος</note> (with only the "u" removed) specifically sounds like the commotion and tumult of the sea and waves, *salos* <note>original: σάλος</note>. But *Paulus* sounds like "quiet" to the Greeks, from the verb *pauō* <note>original: παύω, meaning "to cease" or "rest"</note>, hence they call rest *paula*. To the Romans, it sounds like "small" <note>Latin: *paulus*</note>. As for Jerome's reminder that *Paul* sounds like "wonderful" to the Hebrews, I wonder that he commits the very error he elsewhere criticizes in others—seeking the etymology of words from a different language. For since it is certain that *Paul* is either a Roman or a Greek word, it was not appropriate to borrow its etymology from the Hebrews. I mention these things in passing so that readers may more easily understand what holy interpreters touch upon or allude to regarding the meaning of names in their commentaries.

**2 Called an Apostle**] <note>Greek: κλητὸς Ἀπόστολος</note>. "Called" in this place is not a participle meaning "named" or "labeled," as many now commonly write out of modesty, "the called Bishop," signifying—not so much modestly as truthfully—that they are Bishops more in name than in reality. Even Saint Bernard, a man otherwise Christianly learned, holily eloquent, and piously witty, fell into this affectation when styling his own name as "the called Abbot." But here, the word is a substantive, like "Apostle by call," not "having been called." Just as a little further down we see "the called of Jesus Christ" <note>original: κλητοί</note>, and "called to be saints" <note>original: κλητοῖς ἁγίοις</note>. Furthermore, the name "called" is absolute; just as among the Romans those who were summoned as friends to war were called *evocati* <note>meaning "the summoned ones"</note>, and today among the French some are called "the elect" <note>French: *élus*</note> who are closest to Senatorial dignity. It essentially means as if you said, "an Apostle by vocation," or "a saint by vocation." For right in the beginning, Paul conducts his business and establishes his own credit and authority. First, with his very name, he displays a renewed way of life. Next, when he calls himself a "servant," he indicates he is not doing his own business, but the business of the one who sent him. To this, when he adds "of Jesus Christ," he excludes Moses, who was so fixed in the minds of the Jews that there was a danger the Gentiles might also be led away into the slavery of the Mosaic Law. It clearly would have happened, had Paul not resisted most fiercely with hands and feet, so that through this "athlete," the Gospel of Christ might seem reborn. After this, he adds "Apostolic," which means an envoy or one sent by another. And because at that time there were many "Pseudo-apostles" <note>False apostles</note> who thrust themselves into this office for the sake of fame or profit, he added "called" <note>original: κλητὸς</note>, which has a double meaning: either that he was called to this office by Christ himself (that is, summoned), and did not claim the Apostolic function for himself nor receive this duty from man but from Christ; or that by this word he excludes the merit and works of the Law and asserts the grace of the Gospel, which is given to all—not from the ceremonies of the Mosaic Law in which the Jews trusted, nor from human wisdom on which the Greeks relied, but from the calling of the Divine. For Saint Paul’s primary aim in this Epistle is to lower the pride of both sides: to take away the Jews' confidence in the Mosaic Law and the Greeks' reliance on philosophy, and thus to join both equally in Christ. The Apostles have certain peculiar words of their own: grace, calling, election, foreknowledge, destination, and
