<margin>A</margin> <margin>1. I.</margin> **PAUL, A SERVANT** of Jesus Christ, called to the Apostolic office, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised before through <margin>2</margin> his Prophets in the holy scriptures, concerning his Son, who was <margin>3</margin> begotten from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was <margin>4</margin> de-

predestination, which are almost always opposed to the confidence in the Law, because the greatest danger seemed to loom from there. I am well aware that some, following Origen, argue from this word about those who are "called" but fail to produce the fruit of the office—an argument certainly clever and learned, which I do not intend to reject. However, those things in Holy Scripture that are simplest and least forced appeal to me more. Although I would not deny that this word "called" <note>original: κλητὸς</note> is sometimes used in a way not far from the nature of a participle, as in Matthew: "Many are called, but few are chosen" <note>original: ἔκλεκτοι and κλητοί</note>. This word is a favorite of Paul’s, who is eager to strip away everyone’s confidence in human works and transfer all glory to the God who calls—for he who listens to the caller is saved. Thus Paul, called from heaven, obeyed immediately.

<margin>B</margin> **3 Set apart for the Gospel of God**] <note>Greek: ἀφωρισμένος (*aphorismenos*)</note>. With a wonderful emphasis, he commends his office: he was not only called to perform the Apostolic duty, but like a "chosen vessel," he was set aside and separated for the duty of preaching the Gospel. For *aphorizein* <note>the Greek verb</note> means not just to separate, but to set aside and distinguish by judgment. This is why physicians call laws pronounced briefly and with finality "aphorisms," just as the sayings of the wise are called "aphorisms." Nor is this word a simple impulse. First, he wards off the charge of inconstancy, as he seemed to be deserting the Mosaic Law: "called," he says, and "set apart"—like a special and chosen instrument, as Christ himself testified: "He is a chosen vessel for me, to carry my name before the Gentiles." Next, he alludes to his former faction which he followed in Judaism. For the Jewish people, although they embraced the same Law, were divided into various sects; Josephus, in the eighteenth book of the *Antiquities*, chapter two, lists the Essenes, Sadducees, and Pharisees. Paul belonged to the Pharisaic heresy; it is so named from the Hebrew word *pharas* <note>Hebrew: פרש</note>, because due to their remarkable holiness of life and excellent learning, they wished to seem set apart and separated from the common people. Paul, therefore, began to be in the Gospel what he had been in Judaism, but in a different way. There, it was a title of pride; here, he was marvelously separated from Moses for Christ, from the letter to the spirit, from confidence in works to grace.

<margin>D</margin> **4 Who was made, etc.**] <note>Greek: τοῦ γενομένου (*tou genomenou*)</note>. Lorenzo Valla prefers "begotten" or "born" rather than "made"; I neither approve nor disapprove of his opinion at present. Certainly, it would be "begotten" if it had been written *gennētheis* <note>Greek: γεννηθεὶς</note>. Augustine, in the eleventh book against Faustus, chapter four, testifies that in some Latin manuscripts "born" <note>Latin: *natus*</note> was written instead of "made" <note>Latin: *factus*</note>. And yet elsewhere, the same man gives a reason why the Apostle preferred to say "was made" rather than "was born": namely, because he was conceived and born not from male seed, but by the workmanship of the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, this reason does not prevent him from being called "born" elsewhere. Furthermore, the pronoun "to him," which is added in the Latin manuscripts, is found in none of the Greek. But because the speech seemed somewhat awkward if it said "who was made from the seed of David," the "to him" was added for the sake of explanation. However, the addition of this pronoun does so little for the sense that it actually hinders it. For Paul’s point here is not to show to whom Christ was born, but to make clear that the one for whose Gospel he had been set apart was the true God, and likewise truly man. Man, from the fact that he was born of the seed of David according to the flesh; God, from the fact that his divine power was declared through the Spirit of holiness and the resurrection from the dead. If it were relevant to define for whom he was born or made, he was born for *us* rather than for the Father, as it was our business that was being dealt with. If "born" does not please someone, and they prefer what the Vulgate edition has—"made"—I will not fight it much, provided they understand that "made" is said here in the sense of "having begun to be." This is like the phrase: "He who comes after me was made before me"—that is, he who was following me began to be first and preceded me, as I indicated in my *Evangelical Annotations*. For he who never began to be God nevertheless began to be man.

<margin>E</margin> **5 Who was predestined**] With great consensus, the Greek manuscripts have *horisthentos* <note>original: ὁρισθέντος</note>, that is, "who was finished" or "defined"—which, according to the interpretation of the Greek scholia, means "certainly pronounced, demonstrated, and declared." Chrysostom and Theophylact read it this way, and Origen specifically warns it should be read so when explaining this passage. In this, it occurs to me to wonder in passing how Origen cites the Latin copies in that place, admitting that in most of them *praedestinatus* ("predestined") is found instead of *destinatus* ("destined")—unless perhaps the translator added something of his own, or Origen, who investigated the Hebrew sources with such zeal, not content with so many editions, also surveyed the Latin manuscripts. It is remarkable how much Thomas Aquinas twists himself in this place, a man otherwise great not only in his own century. For in my mind, no recent theologian is equal to him in diligence, sounder in judgment, or more fortunate in learning; he clearly deserved to have the mastery of languages and the rest of the equipment of good literature, seeing how skillfully he used those things which were available in that time of scarcity. How—

<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of Romans 1:4, focusing on the Greek word 'horisthentos' and whether it should be translated as 'predestined' or 'declared.' The author explores the theological implications of these terms regarding the divinity and humanity of Christ, citing early Church Fathers such as Origen, Jerome, and Chrysostom.</meta>

-># THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER I.<-

<margin>the one declared Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord— <note>original: ὁρισθέντος Υἱοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν δυνάμει, κατὰ Πνεῦμα ἁγιωσύνης, ἐξ ἀναστάσεως νεκρῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ Κυ-</note></margin>
Even if great writers sometimes hesitate in the Pauline Epistles, it is partly due to the impurity of the language and the obscurity of the meanings, and partly to the misfortune of the times, in which good literature had almost entirely perished. An alert and ingenious man, therefore, moves every stone in this place, and like a Proteus, turns himself into all shapes to see if he can escape. Sometimes he follows the reading of Origen, sometimes he retreats to ours; at one moment he interprets "to define" as "to send," at another "to ordain," again as "to predestine," then "to foreknow," or he wants it to be something else entirely, offering various relations between the ideas of designation and predestination. Yet Origen indeed defines predestination and designation quite clearly, pronouncing it thus: **He who already is, is defined; he who is not yet, is predestined.** <note>original: Definari eum qui jam est, praedestinari qui nondum sit.</note> From this, Saint Jerome notes—commenting on the first chapter of the Epistle to the Ephesians and following, I believe, this same opinion—that Paul does not use the word <term>pro-oristheis</term> <note>original: προορισθείς; having been predestined</note> except when speaking of us. He openly advises that in this passage concerning the Son, the word used is <term>horisthentos</term> <note>original: ὁρισθέντος; having been defined or declared</note>, not <term>pro-oristhentos</term>; that is, "designated" or "determined," not "predestined." Furthermore, if it offends us that "to predestine" refers to something that does not yet exist because of the added prefix of "preceding," the same difficulty remains with the simple verb. For "to define" does not mean "to send," as the unlettered common people think, but to prefix a certain thing in the mind; indeed, by its very nature, the word carries the meaning of a future thing, just like the words "to hope," "to fear," "to decree," "to deliberate," or "to establish." None of these occur unless they refer to something in the future. Again, if you prefer to derive this reference to the future from something other than the nature of the Son of God himself—so that He, who was the Son of God begotten from eternity, was designated and ordained to do this or that—then the prefix "pre" (*pro*) no longer stands in the way. For in this manner, nothing prevents us from calling the Son of God "predestined" for that which happened later. <margin><term>horizomenon</term> <note>original: ὁριζόμενον; being defined/determined</note></margin> Unless, perhaps, we prefer what Origen seems to have felt: that in "pre-defining" there is a double reference to the future, whereas in "defining" there is only one. For if I "define" a bride for a son already born to me, the person to whom I designate her pertains to the present time, while the thing I designate pertains to the future. However, if I determine in my mind to dedicate the first son who shall be born to me to the study of Theology, both the person and the thing pertain to the future; and Origen wanted the word "predestination" to belong to this kind of situation. But whether you read "designated" or "predestined," and wherever you refer that future reasoning, what follows remains constant: **Son of God according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead.** For if you make the designation eternal—that he was always destined to be the Son of God—how does that connect with "through the Spirit of sanctification" and "from the resurrection of the dead"? What do these have to do with that eternal designation? Thus Ambrose, struggling in these straits, adds (I know not from where) two words: **so that he might be manifested as the Son of God.** And Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> reminds us that sometimes in Divine Scripture a thing is said "to be made" when it is understood to be made known or to become famous. And when they say these things, they are, as it were, divining our own sentiment. Though there was no need to seek from elsewhere what is already in Paul's own words. For the Greek word <term>horizein</term> <note>original: ὁρίζειν</note> not only means "to define" and "to decree," but also "to pronounce certainly" and "to promulgate what you have decreed." This is why they call a certain judgment on the nature of a thing a <term>horos</term> <note>original: ὅρον; a definition or boundary</note>. And the Grammarians call the indicative mood <term>horistikon</term> <note>original: ὁριστικὸν</note> because it indicates and declares something certain. <margin><term>pro-oristhentos</term> <note>original: προορισθέντος; having been predestined</note></margin> Therefore, if instead of "is pre-defined" you read "is declared," the whole sentence will fit perfectly on all sides, and no rough patch will be encountered anywhere. That Christ was a man is evidenced by the fact that he was born of the seed of David; this was proved to the senses themselves. But it had to be declared that he was the same Son of God that he had always been, though he was unknown to the world. He who was clearly a man was declared to be the Son of God. The flesh declared the man; the power and the Spirit of sanctification declare the Son of God and God himself. And this was declared in other ways, namely by the prophecies of the Prophets and by innumerable signs, but then most especially "by the resurrection of the dead." In this manner, as has been said, the Greek scholia <note>ancient commentaries</note> interpret it, from which I will subscribe the words themselves so that no one distrusts us: **<term>horisthentos</term>, <term>tout’ esti apodeichthentos, apophanthentos, dia te tōn prophētōn, dia te tōn ginomenōn thaumatōn, dia te tēs anastaseōs</term>, that is,** ***Defined, that is demonstrated, declared, both through the prophets, and through so many signs of divinity, and through the resurrection itself.*** So far the Greek scholia. Theophylact does not disagree with these; indeed, he brings forward no other interpretation than this, explaining <term>horisthentos Hyiou tou Theou</term> <note>Son of God having been defined</note> as "known to be the Son of God," then "shown," "confirmed," "indicated." For these are the words used by the Translator of the work falsely attributed to Athanasius; since we soon discovered, by comparing the Greek and Latin, that it was actually the work of Theophylact. His words are these: <term>apodeichthentos, bebaiōthentos, krithentos</term>, that is, ***demonstrated or declared, confirmed, judged,*** or decreed. Chrysostom explains it with these words: <term>deichthentos, apophanthentos, krithentos, homologēthentos</term>, that is, ***demonstrated, declared, judged, confessed.*** He had always been the Son of God, but known to few, namely to the Jews, and even to few of them. But afterward, he was declared as such to the whole world. So that it may be more clear that no mention of eternal predestination is made here, Chrysostom adds: ***Judged by the vote of all, from the Prophets, from the wonderful birth according to the flesh, from the power of signs, from the Spirit of sanctification which he gave, and from the resurrection, through which he loosed the tyranny of death.*** These things sufficiently prove that <term>horisthentos</term> sounds different to the Greeks than how the Latins interpret it.
**in power.** <term>en dynamei</term> <note>original: ἐν δυνάμει</note>. He translates it correctly, provided we understand it correctly. For the Latin word *virtus* is ambiguous: sometimes it is understood as the opposite of vice, responding to the Greek <term>aretē</term> <note>original: ἀρετῇ; virtue</note>; sometimes it stands in contrast to weakness. Therefore, in some places, we have preferred to translate it as "potency" or "power," since <term>dynamis</term> <note>original: δύναμις</note> is derived from <term>dynamai</term> <note>margin: <term>epikritheis</term> (having been decided/judged)</note> <term>namai</term> <note>original: δύναμαι; to be able</note>. With wonderful skill, Paul opposed opposites to opposites. For first, he opposed "Paul" to "Saul," the ser-
<meta>catchword: ser-</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **he was declared the Son of God with power, and according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the fact that he rose**
-vant of Jesus Christ to the servitude of the Mosaic Law, so that he might defend his Apostleship to those who were intruding themselves; "set apart for the Gospel" from the Pharisaism he previously professed. Thus far he has commended himself and his office. What follows pertains to the commendation of Christ, who was promised, not by just anyone, but by God himself; and not through just anyone, but through his Prophets, that is, the true and divine ones; and not in just any instruments, but in the Holy Scriptures. Then, with wonderful verbal emphasis, he describes Christ's twin natures in the same person (*hypostasis*). Of the man, he says: ***he was made:*** so that you may understand something was added that was not there before. Of the divinity, he says: ***he was declared.*** There he adds, ***according to the flesh:*** whose companions are weakness and impurity; whence, "the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak." And the "lusts of the flesh" are what they call the impulses soliciting us toward vices. Therefore, he opposed the power of God and the Spirit of sanctification to the flesh; that is, <margin>B</margin> power to weakness, and sanctification to uncleanness. He took up our flesh, therefore, and showed his power; and he did this most especially by the fact that he rose from the dead by his own power, and received back the soul which he had willingly laid down in dying when it seemed best. And again, since mortality belongs to the flesh, he opposed this with the resurrection of the dead, which is immortality. One thing seemed worth noting: regarding <term>en dynamei</term>, that is, "in power" or "in virtue," this preposition in the Gospels and Apostolic writings is sometimes used as if it were almost the same as "through." Thus the sense would be, "in the power" of God, that is, ***through divine power,*** or "out of power," as Chrysostom interprets it: he received from David the ability to die, and from the Father the ability to make us immortal.
7 ***Through the Spirit of sanctification.*** Thomas indicates there were some who twisted these words to refer to the moment of the incarnation, specifically "who was made of the seed of David"—and that this happened not through the common union of bodies, but through the Spirit of sanctification, from which that ineffable offspring was conceived. But this opinion is too absurd even to deserve refutation; thus we shall not labor in exploding it, as Thomas himself <margin>C</margin> rejected it. The reader should be advised that these types of speech are peculiar to the Apostolic men: they say "sons of disobedience" for "disobedient sons," and "rock of scandal" for "a stone of stumbling." So here too, Paul said ***Spirit of sanctification*** for "Sanctifying Spirit." Furthermore, as for Origen's mention here of his division of flesh, soul, and spirit—although it was said beautifully in its own place—it is foreign and forced in this context.
8 ***By the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ.*** This passage can be read in many ways. We shall simply propose all the reasons, as is the purpose of this undertaking; it will be in the reader's hands both the right to judge and the power to choose. First, the ancients seem mostly to have followed the reading where the sense is that the divine power and the spirit of sanctification were declared by the fact that many bodies of the saints rose with Christ, as Matthew the Evangelist recounted. I do not strongly oppose this sentiment, especially as I see it did not displease Origen and even pleased Jerome; particularly since Paul, writing to the Colossians, calls Christ the ***firstborn from the dead,*** and in the first <margin>D</margin> Epistle to the Corinthians calls him the ***firstfruits of those who sleep.*** Above all, since the resurrection is the same for the head and the members, as Origen writes, Christ's glory is in some way not yet perfect unless the members of the whole body are gathered together; so his resurrection is not perfect unless the remaining members are also joined to their head. In Christ, therefore, the resurrection began, and hope was offered to the members; thus it can be understood that the resurrection of the dead belonging to Jesus Christ and his own resurrection are the same. Otherwise, what Paul writes to the Corinthians—"But now Christ has risen, the firstfruits of those who sleep"—would pertain not only to those few who rose when the tombs were opened then, but to all the members of Christ, in whom Paul constantly instills the hope of rising based on the fact that Christ himself rose. For it is not fitting that the head—and such a head—though he lives and reigns, would abandon his members. I think it is clear that Paul's goal is to persuade us that Christ was a man who sacrificed himself for us, and at the same time God, by whose power the work of sanctifying is finished and we attain immortality. <margin>E</margin> And in passing, he touches upon the chief arguments, namely the lineage of David, then the death (which must precede the resurrection), and then the resurrection from the dead, upon which the entire hinge of our faith depends. Furthermore, concerning these dead who rose with Christ, Paul makes mention of them nowhere else in his Epistles, even though he often tries to establish the resurrection of the dead. Indeed, not even one of the Evangelists mentions it except Matthew, who himself touches on it with few words and as if in passing, without explaining who those were who rose or to whom they appeared. I do not say this as if the faith of Matthew the narrator were less certain than if everyone had recorded the same thing in writing; for we do not test the reliability of the Evangelists and other historians on the same whetstone. But it is probable that if that matter specifically pertained to proving Christ's divinity, the other Evangelists would not have omitted a matter of such importance, <margin>F</margin> especially since they were never more diligent than in proving the arguments for the resurrection. Not to mention, meanwhile, that from Matthew's words, the resurrection of these people seems to have preceded Christ's own resurrection. For we read in his account: ***And Jesus crying out again gave up his spirit: and behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two parts from the top to the bottom, and the earth shook, and the rocks were split, and the monuments were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had slept arose, and coming out of the monuments after the resurrection they came into the holy city and appeared to many.*** And it appears more clearly from the Greek themselves, as we indicated in its proper place, that these words, ***after the resurrection,*** should be referred to the nearest thing, namely to this: ***they appeared to many,*** or certainly to what immediately preceded, ***having gone out from the monuments,*** so that you may understand the bodies of the dead revived immediately at the moment of death, but did not appear until after the resurrection of
<meta>catchword: Christi,</meta>

<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of Romans 1:4, moving into verses 5 and 6. Erasmus is debating the precise grammatical relationship between the "resurrection of the dead" and the title "Jesus Christ," while also beginning to define the terms "grace" and "apostleship."</meta>

5 <note>original: "Κυρίου ἡμῶν, Δι' οὗ ἐλάβομεν χάριν καὶ ἀποστολὴν, εἰς ὑπακοὴν πίστεως ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ἔθνεσιν, ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὀνόματος αὐτοῦ, 6 Ἐν οἷς ἐστε καὶ ὑμεῖς, κλητοὶ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ."</note> ...our Lord, through whom we have received grace and apostleship for the obedience of faith among all nations for his name's sake; 6 Among whom you also are, the called of Jesus Christ.

...of Christ, so that just as John [the Baptist] was a forerunner of the preaching and passion of Christ, so these others [who rose from their graves at the crucifixion] were **forerunners** <note>original: προδρόμοι (prodromoi)</note> of the resurrection. It is not unknown to me that Jerome and several other interpreters are of the opinion that the tombs were merely opened when Christ died, but that no one actually rose until after his own resurrection had been completed. I easily yield to such authority. However, if anyone weighs the words of Matthew themselves, he will find that this interpretation is somewhat distorted. Furthermore, if anyone is troubled by this—fearing that Christ might not be the *firstfruits of those who sleep*, as Paul wrote—what will he say about the fact that Lazarus and many others returned to life before Christ? But those others rose only to die again, while these rose to live forever; I admit there is a significant difference. Yet even if we grant that these others returned to life earlier, Christ will nonetheless be the "firstfruits of those who sleep," as he was the leader and author of all resurrection, through whom even those who returned to life before him were revived. But I will not fight over this matter. 

This point is closer to our purpose: since Paul wished to assert the divinity and power of Christ in passing, he ought to have brought forward Christ’s own resurrection rather than that of others, of whom I am not sure the Romans had even heard. Just as he set forth Christ's birth to declare him a man, so he should set forth his resurrection to declare him the Son of God. Therefore, this must be understood either as the entire resurrection which began in Christ, or specifically as the resurrection of Christ himself. The second reading, which I see pleased Lorenzo Valla—a man of truly sharp judgment—comes closest to this sense: that the Latin genitive, *of Jesus Christ*, should be changed to an ablative [meaning "by Jesus Christ"]. For among the Greeks, the genitive <note>original: Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (Iesou Christou)</note> can refer to either: the dead, or to what precedes it, <note>original: περὶ τοῦ Υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (peri tou Huiou autou Iesou Christou)</note> that is, *concerning his Son Jesus Christ*. Then, following the <term>hyperbaton</term> <note>a transposition of words for effect</note> which Paul frequently uses, it should be rendered *by Jesus Christ*. 

I do not disapprove of Valla's opinion; indeed, I wonder why it did not occur to Origen, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Augustine, or Ambrose, especially since the passage is so tortured. Augustine felt the awkwardness of it, for it seemed as if "of Jesus Christ" was added as if one person were the Son of God and another were Jesus Christ—a matter he discussed when explaining Psalm 67. We would escape this awkwardness if we embraced Valla’s reading. Others remedy it by saying this repetition is a Hebrew idiom, where they repeat the proper name instead of using a pronoun; an example is: *Moses did as the Lord commanded Moses*, instead of *as the Lord commanded him*. A third reading holds that *of Jesus Christ* is the "fatherly case" [genitive], but refers only to the resurrection, not to the other dead—not that we exclude them from the resurrection, but we are weighing what Paul is doing here. For the addition of the word *dead* does not force us to understand anyone other than Christ. But because the word for *resurrection* (Latin *resurrectio*, Greek <note>original: ἀναστάσεως (anastaseos)</note>) was ambiguous—since one who was sitting or lying down also "rises," and those about to give an opinion in the Senate "stand up" <note>original: ἀνίστανται (anistantai)</note>—he added *of the dead* so there would be no room for ambiguity. Therefore, these two words, *resurrection of the dead*, like a <term>periphrasis</term> [a roundabout way of speaking] explaining the same thing, refer collectively to *Jesus Christ*. 

The sense would be: he who was a man, born of David according to the flesh, was thus declared the Son of God in the power of God through the Spirit of sanctification. Declared, I say, by the fact that he rose from the dead, which is something belonging to God alone. Furthermore, if anyone is worried that, according to our view, the Greek preposition *from* <note>original: ἐξ (ex)</note> should have been added—*from the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ*—one can answer that the preceding preposition can easily be repeated, or was omitted for the sake of brevity. Prepositions are frequently omitted in Greek, especially *from, with, according to, into, through*. This is especially true here because "resurrection" (<term>anastasis</term>) carries the force of a preposition within itself, signifying movement from a place. In words of this kind, the Latins also frequently omit the preposition if they like, as in *he rose [from] the earth* or *he cast down [from] heaven*. Finally, if one takes *resurrection of the dead* collectively, as we showed before, there is no need for any preposition, since two words are used for a single concept. 

As for my translating it as *Jesus Christ* in the nominative case, it does not change Paul’s meaning, yet we avoid two inconveniences: the ambiguity of the language and the trouble of the transposed word order. Otherwise, it could be rendered word-for-word this way: *Concerning his Son born of the seed of David according to the flesh, declared the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification from the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord*. Indeed, I would like the diligent reader to consider whether *resurrection* <note>original: ἀνάστασις (anastasis)</note> can be taken transitively here, as if you were to say, *by the raising of the dead*. Chrysostom nearly suggested this, as did his imitator Theophylact, when he said: *Christ was the first of all and the only one who raised himself, and by this argument especially it is clear that he was the Son of God*. Augustine certainly pointed out correctly that *resurrection of the dead* should not refer to the words immediately preceding it, but to what came before: *who was predestined*. Yet that word *predestined* connects harshly with the resurrection, unless we interpret it as *declared*. The same Augustine interprets *predestined from the dead* as *predestined for this, that he should be the first to rise*, so that the preposition *from* pertains to the order of rising. However, Paul’s own words do not quite express this sense. To bring this long discussion to a summary, if we read *of Jesus Christ*, there are three variations: first, that *resurrection* be taken in an active-neutral sense, meaning either the Father raised the Son from the dead, or that the

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...Jesus Christ our Lord rose from the dead, 5 Through whom we have received 10 grace and the performance of the Apostolic office, 11 so that there may be obedience to the faith among all nations, 12 for the sake of his name, 13 Among whose number you also 6 are...

...Son raised himself; for both senses are pious. Second, that "resurrection" be spoken of passively, and we understand the dead are to be raised at the voice of the Son of God, just as he raised Lazarus among others. Although nothing prevents *resurrection* here from being taken as the universal resurrection of both the Head [Christ] and the whole mystical body [the Church]. Finally, this genitive *of the dead* refers to Jesus Christ, whose "dead" are those who die in the faith, so that you understand only the resurrection of the just is mentioned here. It can also be read collectively as *resurrection of the dead* in place of *resurrection from the dead*, so that *of Jesus Christ* pertains to the "resurrection," not to the "dead." However, if we read *by Jesus Christ*, it will pertain to what came before: *concerning his Son Jesus Christ, who was predestined*, etc. I have discussed these things somewhat wordily, perhaps as much as the nature of this project allows; but I did it deliberately, lest anyone shout that I have rashly changed the reading against the opinion of all my predecessors. For the rest, I have performed the office of a judge, deferring the final judgment to the reader.

<margin>A</margin> *Jesus Christ our Lord* ] The reader will find this also in Paul, as Ambrose noted, and likewise in the other Apostles: they almost always attribute the title *God* to the Father, and *Lord* to Christ, although both terms apply equally to both, because the Father and Son share the same lordship.

<margin>10</margin> <margin>C</margin> *Grace and Apostleship* ] <note>original: Χάριν καὶ ἀποστολὴν (Charin kai apostolen)</note>. "Grace" is also a characteristically Pauline word, which he gladly emphasizes, desiring to exclude carnal reliance on the Mosaic Law. Among the Greeks, *charis* sometimes signifies a benefit conferred freely—hence the verb *charizesthai*, meaning "to bestow" or "to give for free." Sometimes it means favor, as in *you have found grace with God*; sometimes the obligation for a benefit, as in *to have grace* (to be grateful). I see there have been some who were offended by the word *apostolatus* [apostleship], which is poorly approved by Latin ears, and they prefer the Greek word *apostolē*. I would easily agree with them if as many people understood *apostolen* as understood *apostolatum*. Furthermore, I see that Christian writers, forced I suppose by necessity, have accepted this form in many cases: *Clericatus* [clergy-state], *Diaconatus* [diaconate], *Episcopatus* [episcopacy]. We have translated it as *the discharge of the apostolic office*, lest anyone think Paul is merely signifying a title of dignity; for just as *episkopē* is the actual function of a bishop, so is *apostolē* the function of an apostle. He calls it "grace" here because he was called back from error—and not just called back, but delegated to this task: to call others with authority to the grace of the Gospel.

# TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER I.

<margin>11</margin> <margin>D</margin> *For the obeying of the faith* ] In Greek this is a noun, not an infinitive: <note>original: εἰς ὑπακοὴν πίστεως (eis hypakoen pisteos)</note>, that is, *unto the obedience of faith*. But because that phrasing was ambiguous in Latin, the [Vulgate] translator explained it using a gerund, while we used a verb: *so that there may be obedience to the faith*. He calls it "obedience of faith," as Chrysostom explains, because it is not accepted through curious reasoning, but through simple obedience and silent listening. This pertains to both peoples: the Jews, who required signs, and the Greeks, who demanded philosophical reasons—and perhaps today, it pertains to the inexplicable labyrinths of Scholastic questions concerning those things which are piously left unknown.

<margin>12</margin> <margin>E</margin> *For his name* ] <note>original: ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὀνόματος αὐτοῦ (hyper tou onomatos autou)</note>, that is, *concerning his name*, or *over his name*. For the Greek preposition has a double meaning, as do many of their words. The sense is: "We have received the Apostolic office for this, so that in all nations, not just among the Jews, there may be obedience to the faith which concerns the name of Jesus Christ." The Greek commentaries indicate the same, taking these words, *concerning his name*, to refer back to the obedience of faith. Theophylact explains *hyper* as "instead of." 

On this point, that distinguished man and our incomparable friend, Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, differed. Whenever I mention him, I do so with honor, for I greatly approve of his most ardent zeal in restoring good literature; I admire his varied and far-from-common learning; I love his rare kindness and approachability; and I even venerate and kiss the singular holiness of his life. But who was ever so learned or attentive that he did not hallucinate or drowse somewhere, especially when dealing with so many volumes and so many difficult matters? He himself would not doubt that upon re-reading his own work, he would do as Augustine did in his *Retractions*. Therefore, let no one interpret it as an insult if we disagree with him in a few places; I am defending the truth to the best of my ability. In turn, I will not only bear it calmly if the same is done to me, but I will consider it a great benefit, provided there is no insolence. 

In this place, Lefèvre’s opinion does not displease me: that *for his name* refers to what came before, *we have received the Apostleship*—that is, the apostolic function and this embassy which we perform. But concerning what matter? Namely, the preaching of the name of Jesus. Therefore, both readings fit perfectly, so that it is difficult to pronounce which should be preferred over the other. The translator Chrysostom seems to follow the latter view. For he explains: *I was not sent to reason, but to hand over what was entrusted to me*. The Greek says: *unto the obedience of faith; he did not say 'of faith and destruction,' but 'obedience,' for we were not sent, he says, to construct arguments, but to give back what was put into our hands*.

<margin>13</margin> *In which you are* ] <note>original: Ἐν οἷς (En hois)</note>, that is, *Among whom*, or *From the number of those*, meaning the called nations. This is the same usage as "among all nations" <note>original: ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ἔθνεσιν (en pasi tois ethnesin)</note>. I am well aware that Latin authors sometimes spoke this way following the Greek style. But we followed what was clearer. Chrysostom noted that Paul attributed nothing exceptional to the Romans, the masters of the world, but in the context of the Gospel, made them just one of the number of other nations.

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER I.

<margin>A</margin> **14 To all who are in Rome.]** <note>original: Πᾶσι τοῖς οὖσιν ἐν Ῥώμῃ (Pasi tois ousin en Rhōmē)</note> Since the Greek expresses this through a participle, it could be understood as either the third or second person: *To all who are*, or *To all of you who are*. Literally it sounds like, *To all the beings in Rome*, although that does not change the meaning. It is already a formal custom to write the name of the person we greet in a letter in the third person, such as "Pliny to his friend Tacitus, Greetings." Thus far the entire discourse has been considered quite broadly; now, finally, the main clause is completed and the second part is rendered. At this point, the error of those who think Paul wrote to the Romans in the Roman language <note>i.e., Latin</note>—just as he wrote to the Hebrews in Hebrew and the Greeks in Greek—must be refuted or rather laughed at. For he does not write only to the Romans, but to all who were living in Rome. By that time, almost all of Greece had flooded into the city, so much so that the poet Juvenal calls it a "Greek city." Certainly, the Greek language had been adopted not only by Italy but also by Syria, Egypt, Cilicia, and a good portion of the world. If he had written in Latin, Origen would have complained unfairly in his interpretation of this Epistle that the Greek phrasing was perplexed, obscured by exaggerations, and that certain non-Greek elements from the Cilician dialect <note>A regional Greek dialect associated with Paul’s hometown, Tarsus</note> tasted of foreignness.

**15 Beloved of God]** <note>original: ἀγαπητοῖς Θεοῦ (agapētois Theou)</note> This is the word they often translate as "most dear." To the Greeks, however, it is not a participle but a noun—as if you were to say "friend"—and for that reason, among them, it clings more softly to the name of God.

**16 Called saints]** <note>original: κλητοῖς ἁγίοις (klētois hagiois)</note> I noted above that "called" in this place is not a participle but a noun, and it has the same force as if you said, "those called to holiness." For the name of the "Gentiles" was hateful to the Jews, because they held them to be profane and estranged from God and Moses. Paul therefore removes this opinion when he says the Romans, as far as the law is concerned, are from the number of the Gentiles, but they are equal to the Jewish fathers in this: that they are loved by the same God and have been called by Him to the same holiness. In their own opinion, the Jews were born holy, descended from the holy and born into the Holy Law; but what lineage seemed to provide for the Jews, the favor and calling of God provided for the Gentiles. Now, he calls "grace" a gratuitous munificence. First he had said "beloved," then "called"; but since someone could be called and loved based on merit, he adds "grace." Grace, once given, produces the remission of sins, which in his custom he calls "peace." For sin creates enmity between God and men. He called us; we did not seek Him. He loved us first when we were enemies. He bestowed the gift of the Spirit on those who deserved punishment; and through the Spirit, He gave the pardon of sins and an abundance of spiritual gifts.

**17 From God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ]** The Greek phrasing is indeed ambiguous. It can be taken as *from our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ*, implying a Father common to us and Him; or as *from our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ*, to understand that the grace he prays for them proceeds simultaneously from the Father—whom, as just mentioned, he usually calls "God" as a specific title—and from the Son, whom he usually delights to call "Lord," and very rarely "God." Yet in this very Epistle, in the fifth chapter, he openly calls Him a man: *Much more has the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, abounded unto many.* And Peter, in the Acts of the Apostles, calls Him a man: *a man approved by God.* Likewise, Paul among the Athenians: *by the man whom He has appointed.* I approve of this latter reading more, especially since it was noted by both Ambrose and Didymus in the second book of *On the Holy Spirit*, yet in such a way that this form of speech neither takes away lordship from the Father nor deity from the Son. For by the same logic that the Father is Lord and the Son is God, so too the Holy Spirit is called Lord; for Didymus used these words. Indeed, this note aims at nothing other than indicating the custom of Apostolic speech. Tertullian noted the same in the book he wrote *Against Praxeas*. It is better to include his words here: *Therefore, I will not say "Gods" or "Lords" at all, but I follow the Apostle, so that if the Father and Son are to be named together, I call the Father "God" and Jesus Christ "Lord." However, I can call Christ alone "God," as the same Apostle says: "From whom is Christ, who is," he says, "God over all, blessed forever." For I will call a ray of the sun "the sun" when it is by itself; but when naming the sun, whose ray it is, I will not immediately call the ray "the sun." For although faith makes two, yet I will count both the sun and its ray as two things and two forms of one and indivisible substance, just as I count God and His Word as Father and Son.*

**18 First indeed I give thanks]** How much one admires Origen's diligence in examining the Sacred Scriptures! This too troubled the man: in what way Paul says "first" here, and which part corresponds to this as the "second." He doubts whether the answer is found in the phrase: *I would not have you ignorant, brothers.* But in the beginning of any argument, it is not absurd for a "first" point to be stated formally, even if you do not properly provide a second.

<margin>B</margin> **κόσμῳ, in the whole world,** <note>original: kosmō</note> and according to the Greek Interpreters it was said 
as *oikoumenē* <note>the inhabited world</note>, meaning in many parts of the world: why was it necessary for the Latin translator to exaggerate further, saying "in the entire universe"? For even though Origen, after pointing out the hyperbole, goes on to philosophize about the Angelic world and its relationship to our own, this is not inelegant. However, simple and genuine things delight us more—those that show the sense of the Apostle rather than showing off the ingenuity of the translator.

**20 For God is my witness]** <note>original: Μάρτυς γὰρ μοι ἐστὶν ὁ Θεὸς (Martys gar moi estin ho Theos)</note>, that is, "For God is my witness." Although the Translator rendered it nicely and served Latin ears better than expressing the Greek speech, unless he perhaps read "my" <note>original: μου (mou)</note> instead of "to me" <note>original: μοι (moi)</note>.

**21 Whom I serve]** <note>original: ᾧ λατρεύω (hō latreuō)</note>, that is, "whom I worship." This is different from the Greek word for "slave-service" <note>original: δουλεύω (douleuō)</note>; hence they call the worship offered to the Divine or God *latreia*. The Greeks think the word is derived from *la*, a particle signifying intensity, and *trein*, which is to tremble or fear. Although the Translator elsewhere sometimes renders *latreia* as <margin>C</margin> "compliance" or "servitude," it is more correctly translated as "worship." For Paul hints that the method of religion and worship must be renewed, as the Jews were urging that the Gentiles be dragged toward the ceremonies of the Mosaic Law. Therefore, although Paul himself had moved from Moses to Christ and no longer sacrificed cattle, he nevertheless worshipped the same God with a different ritual—namely, by preaching the Gospel of the Son, which is a spiritual worship, and for that reason far more pleasing to God. For when he says "in my spirit," he excludes bodily victims. Furthermore, we have frequently shown that in the phrase "in spirit," the preposition *in* was added to the dative of instrument or manner, according to the property of Hebrew speech.

**22 Mention of you]** <note>original: μνείαν ὑμῶν (mneian hymōn)</note>. Since the Greek word can be taken either way, and we do not say "I make memory" in Latin, he would have translated it more conveniently as "mention." Since praying is nothing other than conversing with God, no one should think it too harsh to say "I make mention of you."

**23 If somehow]** <note>original: εἴπως ἤδη ποτὲ (eipōs ēdē pote)</note>, that is, "if by any means now at <margin>D</margin> last," or "finally at some time." For *ēdē* among the Greeks sometimes has the force of urgency. Moreover, this heap of adverbs and conjunctions—*pōs, ēdē, pote*—expresses a certain wonderful and impatient desire and zeal for hurrying, as the Greek commentaries also point out.

**24 I may have a prosperous journey]** In Greek it is *euodōthēsomai*, a word composed of two parts: *eu* (well) and *hodos* (way): they use this word whenever a matter succeeds according to one's wish. It is also in the first Psalm: *And all things whatsoever he shall do, shall prosper* <note>original: εὐοδωθήσεται (euodōthēsetai)</note>. For Paul signifies that up until now it had not succeeded.

**25 In the will]** <note>original: ἐν τῷ θελήματι (en tō thelēmati)</note>. We have noted both elsewhere and just a little above that this preposition *en* is sometimes used for "through," a figure of speech taken, I believe, from the Hebrews. Therefore, expressing the sense more than the words, we translate it as "God willing." <margin>E</margin>

**26 Of coming to you]** <note>original: ἐλθεῖν (elthein)</note>. It was more correct to say "to come" or "that I may come," so that the infinitive verb refers back to the participle that preceded it shortly before: "requesting." *Praying that I may come to you, if it may happen to me by a sign, God willing, a prosperous journey.* For this is the meaning of the Greek words.

**27 I may impart some of grace]** <note>original: ἵνα τὶ μεταδῶ χάρισμα (hina ti metadō charisma)</note>, that is, "a gift," not "grace" <note>original: χάριν (charin)</note>. Although the Translator played with his own abundance in this word after his fashion. For in some places he translates it as "gift," as in: *but not as the offense, so also the gift* <note>original: ἀλλ’ οὐχ ὡς τὸ παράπτωμα, οὕτω καὶ τὸ χάρισμα (all’ ouch hōs to paraptōma, outō kai to charisma)</note>. Elsewhere he left the Greek word, as if there were no way to render it in Latin: as in, *Follow after the better charismata* <note>spiritual gifts</note>. Furthermore, what the difference is between *charin* and *charisma*, I leave to others to express. This much is certain: *charin* is placed for a benefit, and *charisma* is "I bestow a benefit" or "I do a favor"; from which the verbal noun *charisma* is derived. <margin>F</margin> Both are applicable when something is given for free or done well for someone.

**28 To be comforted together]** Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo Valla, a pioneer of New Testament philology</note> attacks the Translator here, and not entirely without reason. For what was the reason—since in Greek both verbs are infinitives, "to be established" and "to be comforted together"—that he would leave one as it was and render the other through a gerund? It appears that both pertain to the accusative "you," because it precedes them in order: so that the sense is, "that you may be confirmed, and at the same time you may receive mutual consolation among yourselves." Indeed, that "to be comforted together" seems to be added not to move to a different subject, but as if softening by explanation what he had said, "to confirm you." He did this so that the somewhat arrogant nature of the Romans would not be offended if they seemed to need "confirmation" as if they were wavering or nodding. But he interprets that confirmation as mutual consolation, speaking most modestly in his custom; although the Greek school refers the latter verb "to be comforted together" also to Paul, so that you understand they are to be confirmed and supported by the arrival of...

<summary>This page analyzes the greeting of the Epistle to the Romans, where Erasmus argues that Paul wrote in Greek to a city that had become effectively Greek-speaking. He provides deep philological dives into the terms for worship, grace, and spiritual gifts, emphasizing Paul's rhetorical modesty in seeking mutual encouragement with the Roman church.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed commentary on the first chapter of the Epistle to the Romans. Having previously discussed Paul's apostolic calling, he now moves into the heart of the introduction, examining Paul’s desire to visit Rome, his debt to all nations, and the defining thesis of the letter: that the Gospel is the power of God for salvation through faith.</meta>

# TO THE ROMANS. CAP. I.

<margin>12</margin> [that is, that I may be encouraged together] with you, through the faith we have in one another, both yours and mine.
<margin>13</margin> I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often intended to come to you—though I have been prevented until now—so that I might reap some fruit among you,
<margin>14</margin> just as I have among the rest of the nations. To both Greeks and barbarians, to both the wise and the foolish, I am a debtor.
<margin>15</margin> So, for my part, I am eager to preach the gospel also to you who are in Rome. <margin>16</margin> For I am not ashamed of the Gospel of Christ; for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew
<margin>17</margin> first and also to the Greek. For the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith; as it is—

---

<margin>A</margin> [Regarding] the arrival of Paul: Paul expected to receive mutual solace from their strengthened faith. If it please the reader, the first-person pronoun "we" or "us" <note>original: ἡμεῖς ἡμᾶς (hēmeis hēmas)</note>—meaning "me" or "us"—is to be understood here. Both Origen and Theophylact interpret the passage this way. This view is further proven to me by the addition of the conjunction "but" <note>original: δὲ (de)</note>, which clearly indicates that what follows softens or corrects what preceded it. This is similar to the phrasing, *This is a great mystery, but I speak in Christ and the Church.* Furthermore, if he had meant "among you," he would have more likely said *en hymin* <note>original: ἐν ὑμῖν</note>. Finally, what follows fits better: *through the faith we have in one another, both yours and mine.* Their faith was being proclaimed throughout the whole world, and Paul also possessed faith. Thus, by comparing their experiences, they would both be supported by each other in their shared faith. In the same way, whenever two people compare a matter they have heard from different sources, each believes more certainly what they had heard because of the mutual agreement of their accounts. I will add this, lest anything escape the Reader: the word *to be encouraged together* <note>original: συμπαρακληθῆναι (symparaklēthēnai)</note> can refer either to "mutual consolation" or to "mutual exhortation." Since he has just spoken of strengthening them, "mutual exhortation" fits better than "consolation." Theophylact notes that in this context, "consolation" could not ineptly be taken to mean "joy." Chrysostom refers it to the soothing of afflictions which the believers endured for the name of Christ, while also pointing out the steps by which the Apostle softened and tempered his speech. For when he had said "to be established," fearing that the arrogant Romans might say, "What? Are we wavering, that we must be propped up by your tongue?" he mitigated this and turned the word "establishing" into "consoling." Not content with this, he did not simply say "to be consoled" <note>original: παρακληθῆναι (paraklēthēnai)</note>, but "to be consoled *together*" <note>original: συμπαρακληθῆναι (symparaklēthēnai)</note>; as if he himself needed their consolation no less than they needed his. Finally, he joined their shared faith, laying aside the persona of the teacher and putting on that of the fellow disciple. Thus Paul becomes all things to all men, that he might win all. This is a pious cleverness, and a holy flattery, if I may put it that way. Theophylact's interpretation does not differ from Chrysostom's.

29 **I do not want you**] Origen points out a *hyperbaton* here—that is, a disordered arrangement of the sentence—thinking that something is even missing. But he believes the flow of the sentence can be restored in this way: *Just as I had fruit among the other nations (for I am a debtor to Greeks and Barbarians, to the wise and the ignorant), so as far as I am concerned, I am ready, if permitted, to preach the gospel even to you who are in Rome.* I have noted this in passing as it pertains to the punctuation of the Scripture.

30 **And I was hindered**] <note>original: ἐκωλύθην (ekōlythēn)</note>, which sounds more like "I was impeded" than "I was forbidden," doubtless by obstructing business, which the Greeks call *empodizein* <note>original: ἐμποδίζειν</note>. For one "forbids" properly who interdicts you from doing something; unless we believe Paul was forbidden by the Holy Spirit, just as in the sixteenth chapter of Acts, the Holy Spirit did not permit him when he wished to go into Bithynia. Chrysostom suggests something like this when he says: *By the will of God I was entrusted, but by the struggle I was cut off.* Even if Paul does not have the opportunity given to go to Rome, he religiously interprets it as the will of God.

31 **I might have among you**] <note>original: σχῶ καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν (schō kai en hymin)</note>, that is, "I might have even in you." The conjunction "even/also" <note>original: καὶ (kai)</note> is not without emphasis. Among all the Greeks he had gathered some fruit; he desires the same among the Romans. Again, "in you" is used for "among you."

32 **To Greeks and Barbarians**] In the Greek, there is a double conjunction: *To both Greeks and Barbarians.* And again, *To both the wise and the foolish.* This repetition of the conjunction is not idle; it signifies that Paul is equally a debtor to everyone without any selection of nation. He emphasizes this because of the Jews, who wanted to keep the preaching of the Gospel to themselves alone. Furthermore, here "wise" <note>original: σοφοῖς (sophois)</note> does not mean "wise" so much as "erudite" or "educated," and "foolish" <note>original: ἀνοήτοις (anoētois)</note> means "crass" and "unlearned" rather than "stupid." For the Greeks claimed "wisdom"—that is, erudition—for themselves. Moreover, he here opposes "Greeks" (whom you will sometimes find used for any nations at all) to "Barbarians," whom he calls "ignorant," as if they were unpolished in philosophy and unlearned.

33 **So what is ready in me**] Lorenzo <note>translator: Lorenzo Valla, a famous humanist scholar</note> advises that in this place, "ready" <note>original: promptum</note> should be taken substantively, for "readiness" itself. Just as the Greeks use the adjective "good" for "goodness" or "swift" for "swiftness," using adjectives in place of nouns, so the sense is: *Thus, according to my manly readiness, and the readiness of mind present in me, I am ready to preach the gospel even to you who are in Rome.* And indeed, Ambrose reads it this way: *Therefore, as far as I am concerned, I am ready,* etc. But there are those who prefer to link the infinitive "to preach the gospel" <note>original: εὐαγγελίσασθαι (euangelisasthai)</note> to the verbal noun "debtor," and to take the adverb "so" <note>original: οὕτως (houtōs)</note> not as a connector to the preceding parts, but as referring to the others to whom Paul had already preached: so that the sense is, *Just as I have already preached to other nations, since I owe it to everyone, so as far as the readiness of my mind is concerned, I owe it also to you—*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>12</margin> I may receive consolation among you, through our mutual faith, both yours and mine. <margin>13</margin> I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that I often proposed to come to you (though I have been hindered until this day), that I might have some fruit among you as well, just as among the rest of the nations. <margin>14</margin> To Greeks and barbarians alike, to the learned and the unlearned equally, I am a debtor: <margin>15</margin> So, as much as is in me, I am ready to preach the gospel to you who are at Rome also. <margin>16</margin> <margin>B</margin> For I am not ashamed of the Gospel of Christ: <margin>C</margin> for it is the power of God for salvation to every believer, <margin>D</margin> to the Jew first and also to the Greek. <margin>17</margin> For the righteousness of God is revealed through it <margin>E</margin> from faith <margin>F</margin> into faith:

---

—you who live in Rome, even though you are wise, powerful, and learned, to preach the Gospel of Christ. And that indeed fits beautifully with what follows immediately.

34 <margin>B</margin> **For I do not blush at the Gospel**] <note>original: Οὐ γὰρ ἐπαισχύνομαι τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον (Ou gar epaischynomai to Euangelion)</note>. The translator sometimes renders this as "I am confounded," sometimes "I blush," adding the accusative case. It would be more Latin to say, *For I am not ashamed of the Gospel.* Although I know that in Quintus Curtius one reads "to blush at fortune" <note>original: erubescere fortunam</note>; if that occurred frequently in good authors, I would not be reluctant to imitate it. Some Greek manuscripts add "of Christ," *the Gospel of Christ*; because the name of Christ was still held in contempt by many, especially those swollen with the persuasion of wisdom, among whom Plato, Pythagoras, Zeno, and Aristotle were held in high price. Although Chrysostom does not add "of Christ," the article indicates they are thinking of the Gospel he had spoken of before: "the Gospel of God."

35 <margin>C</margin> **For it is the power of God**] <note>original: δύναμις γὰρ Θεοῦ ἐστιν (dynamis gar Theou estin)</note>, that is, "for it is the potency of God." This is to show that even for the Romans, this thing is not to be looked down upon as if it were humble and ineffective. I have noted this because the word *virtus* [virtue/power] among the Latins is ambiguous: it is sometimes used to correspond to the Greek word *aretē* <note>original: ἀρετή</note> and is opposed to *kakia* <note>original: κακίᾳ</note> (vice); at other times it corresponds to the Greek *dynamis* <note>original: δύναμις</note> and is opposed to weakness or impotence. He added "of God," however, lest Christ be despised as a mere man by the weak and the unbelieving. The article is not added to "God," because God is placed here not as a specific person, but for the divine nature itself, to distinguish it from men.

36 **To everyone who believes**] <note>original: παντὶ τῷ πιστεύοντι (panti tō pisteuonti)</note>; it would be clearer to say, "to any believer whatsoever." For he does not want there to be a selection of nation or fortune, provided that the faith is shared.

37 <margin>D</margin> **To the Jew first and the Greek**] Here too the Greek has a double conjunction, *To both the Jew first and the Greek.* "First" in this place has the same value as if you said "especially": because Christ was promised to the Jews, from whom he also arose, and the Greeks excelled in wisdom. Furthermore, in this place he takes "Greek" to mean "Gentile," and he translates it thus in more than one place. Although above, in "Greeks and Barbarians," he used it for a specific nation.

38 <margin>E</margin> **From faith into faith**] Latin speech has no word that sufficiently corresponds to *pistis* <note>original: πιστει (pistei)</note>. For to the Latins, one is said "to have faith" <note>original: habere fidem</note> in someone when he believes their words; and he is said "to give faith" <note>original: dare fidem</note> who makes a solemn promise; and he "binds his faith" who obligates himself to someone. He "releases his faith" who performs what he promised. He "lacks faith" who is not believed (*There is no faith in his face*). He "violates faith" who does not perform what was agreed; hence he is called "perfidious," and it is called "perfidy." He "derogates faith" from someone who makes it so they are not believed. He "conciliates faith" who does the opposite. We "desire faith" in him who does not perform what he received. We "approve the faith" of him who did what he could diligently. And we "hand over into the faith" of someone what we commit to their trust. And one is called a "possessor in good faith" who began to possess without deceit. He who does the opposite is "in bad faith." We read much about the "faith of servants" toward their masters. And he "makes faith" who persuades, and he is called "faithful" <note>original: fidus</note> who conducts a matter in good faith; likewise "faithful" <note>original: fidelis</note>. Therefore, "faith" <note>original: fides</note> among the Latins is sometimes the quality of the one promising, sometimes of the one performing the promise, sometimes of the one believing, sometimes of the one who is believed; sometimes it is a general noun, as when we say "faith has been removed from the customs of men," meaning that no one performs what they promise, nor does anyone trust another. And in Greek, *pistis* sometimes sounds like the faith of the one performing or promising, and sometimes the proof through which we persuade. And *pistos* <note>original: πιστὸς</note> is said of one who does not deceive; *apistos* is unfaithful or distrusting; *pisteuei* is he who believes or trusts or commits; and *apistei* is he who does not trust. Among the Latins, *incredulus* [unbelieving] is he who distrusts. For "credulous" and "credulity" almost always sound like a vice; and "to believe" <note>original: credere</note> is varied. He "believes" who assents to words, and he "believes" who trusts; and he "believes [entrusts] his wife" to another who commits her. Now we use both "trusting" and "confidence" in a good sense, which exists only in the believer. Likewise "to trust" and "to rely" are in a good sense. "Confident" and "confidence" [boldness] are in a bad sense. <margin>F</margin> But the Sacred Letters frequently misuse these words: for they frequently employ "faith" for "confidence/trust" <note>original: fiducia</note> toward God, so that it does not differ much from "hope." Sometimes it is for "credulity" or "persuasion," by which we assent to those things which have been handed down to us about Him, in which even the Demons believe. Sometimes the word "faith" embraces all these things: that assent both in things narrated and in things promised, and the confidence conceived from His omnipotent goodness, not without hope—that is, the expectation of things promised. And so far, indeed, it is called the "faith of man." But it is also called the "faith of God," which He performs in His promises: whence God is called "trustworthy" or "faithful," that is, *pistos*, because He does not deceive. But a man is called "faithful" who believes the one promising—contrary to the usage of the Latin language, and yet the Sacred Letters frequently speak thus. For a "faithful steward" is said in Latin: but an "unfaithful" man is said not in Latin, but in the Scriptures, of one who distrusts; in Greek better *apistos* or *apeithēs*. Sometimes it is called the "faith of God," by which we trust Him rather than man; it is called His also because it is given by Him, not only because it tends toward Him. Sometimes it is of both, as—

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s philological and theological commentary on the first chapter of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans. # THE EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER I. 564

...it is written: 'The righteous shall live by faith.' 
18 For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who suppress the truth in unrighteousness; 
19 Because what may be known of God is manifest in them; for God has shown it to them. 
20 For since the creation of the world His invisible attributes are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made, even His eternal power and Godhead, so that they are without excuse; 
21 Because, although they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God, nor were they thankful, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish hearts were darkened. 
22 Professing to be wise, they became fools, 
23 and changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like corruptible man—and birds and four-footed...

<column-break/>

from faith to faith: as it is written, "The righteous shall live by faith." 40 For the wrath of God is made plain from heaven against all the impiety and injustice of men, who 41 hold back the truth in injustice: Because 42 that which can be known of God 43 is manifest among them: for God has disclosed it to them. For those things which are 20 invisible of Him, 44 from the creation of the world, while they are understood through His works, are clearly perceived, 45 both His eternal power and divinity, 46 so that they might be without excuse: Because although they had known God, they 21 did not glorify Him as God, nor were they grateful, 47 but they were frustrated by their own thoughts, and their senseless heart was darkened. 48 While they believed themselves 22 to be wise, 49 they were made fools: And they changed 23 the glory of the 50 immortal God 51 for an image, fashioned not only into the likeness of a mortal man, but...

---

<margin>A</margin>
38 **The righteous shall live by faith**: This refers to the faith of God, who does not fail in His promises, and the faith of man, who trusts in God. What is said here, *from faith to faith*, pertains to both. For just as God began to reveal His nature and fulfill His promises at appointed times, so too did knowledge and trust toward God grow by degrees in men. Few believed the prophets before the Lord presented to their eyes what the prophets had promised. Likewise, our faith regarding what was predicted about the final advent is confirmed by the things we have seen and continue to see.

39 **Lives by faith**: One should read "shall live" <note>original: vivet</note> in the future tense, as in the Greek `ὃς πίστεως ζήσεται` (hos pisteōs zēsetai). It is quoted this way both here, in the Epistle to the Galatians, and in the Epistle of Saint James. Chrysostom interprets it this way, explaining it as a reference to the future life, since one is meanwhile afflicted and killed in this life; thus it was said "he shall live," not "he lives." The passage Paul cites is from the Prophet Habakkuk in the second chapter, which the Seventy <note>The "Seventy" refers to the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translated as, `ὁ δέ δίκαιός μου ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται` (The righteous one of mine shall live by faith). Only Symmachus expressed it more significantly: `ὁ δὲ δίκαιος τῇ ἑαυτοῦ πίστει ζήσεται`, that is, *But the righteous shall live by his own faith*. Jerome thinks the Seventy erred due to the similarity of Hebrew characters, as they differ only by a tiny stroke. For in Hebrew, `אֱמוּנָתֹו` (emunato) sounds like "in his faith": because the letter *vau* <note>The Hebrew letter ו</note>, when added to the end of a word, has the force of the pronoun "his." However, the letter *Iod* <note>The Hebrew letter י</note> added has the force of "my": `אֱמוּנָתִי` (emunati), that is, "in my faith." Furthermore, that "shall live" is a future tense verb is indicated not only by the Greek edition Jerome cites and the common Greek manuscripts, but also by the Hebrew word `יִהְיֶה` (yihyeh), for the addition of the *y* at the beginning makes it the third person masculine future. I suspect Paul omitted both pronouns, perhaps because the Romans were familiar with the Septuagint and he did not want to deviate from it, nor introduce the Hebrew version which they did not know. Or perhaps such pronouns are commonly understood, or he wished to make the statement more absolute and universal: *He shall live by faith*. The preposition signifies the origin. For life has its beginning from this: that by submitting our human senses, we believe the divine words. This was spoken against the philosophers.

40 **Is revealed**: `Ἀποκαλύπτεται` (Apokalyptetai), that is, it is uncovered and opened, when that which was previously hidden becomes public. For before the Gospel of Christ was brought forth, the wrath of God seemed open and unlocked only against the Jews if they sinned. And for this reason he adds, *upon all ungodliness*, because the grace of the Gospel pertains equally to all. Now, I think it is understood even without a teacher that "wrath," according to the custom of Hebrew speech, is frequently used for vengeance and punishment.

41 **The truth of God**: "Of God" is not added in the Greek, nor in the old Latin copies, nor does Chrysostom mention it. For Paul means the truth known to the philosophers, which belongs to them rather than to God. For the truth of God bestows life, while the truth of the philosophers puffs them up. But the truth, from which they ought to have progressed to higher things, they held back in injustice.

42 **That which is known of God**: `τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ` (to gnōston tou Theou), that is, that which is "knowable" of God; this is what can be known or recognized about God, as the Interpreters agree. For there is that in God which no imagination of the human mind can reach in any way.

43 **Is manifest in them**: "In them" is used here in a new way for "among them" or "between them." For "in them" cannot refer to created things (which haven't been mentioned yet), but to the philosophers. Furthermore, he added "in them" to distinguish them from the Barbarians and the unlearned common people.

44 **From the creation of the world**: `Κτίσις` (Ktisis) is an ambiguous word among the Greeks, as it can signify either the act of creation itself—the act of founding—or the "creature" itself—the thing created. The Translator <note>Erasmus often refers to the Vulgate translator as "the Interpreter."</note> seems to refer *creation* to man, and "the things made" <note>original: τὰ ποιήματα (ta poiēmata)</note> to created things, so that you understand "from the creature," that is, it is perceived by the mind of created man, things which cannot be seen with physical eyes, and this through the created things in which traces of Divinity exist. Others, conversely, prefer to refer "creature" to the world's creation. Although the sense is the same either way: it seems to me both can be referred not absurdly to the founded world, so that you understand the invisible things of God are seen from the very creation of the world, while they are understood through His works, which display the power, wisdom, and goodness of God the founder. Thus the Greek dative `ποιήμασιν` (poiēmasin) pertains not to the verb "is seen," but to the participle "being understood," that is, things which are understood—through what? namely, "through the works," as if by an instrument. For the Greeks express the instrument in the dative case, just as we do in the ablative. Now, it is not so important to note that `νοούμενα` (nooumena), which he translates as "understood," is a present participle, not 

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin>
a past one. For they are not seen in such a way that they were understood previously, but they are seen at the moment they are understood from created things, as if explaining what he meant when he said "they are seen." For they are understood from created things as if you were seeing an image in a mirror, which is why the word `καθορᾶται` (kathoratai) <note>a Greek verb for "to see clearly" or "look down upon"</note> is used. Indeed, the pronoun "of them" <note>original: αὐτοῖς (autois)</note> can be referred to either: to "the invisible things," meaning the nature and virtues of God which cannot be seen; or to what follows immediately, "to His works," that is, by His creatures.

<margin>C</margin>
45 **Also eternal**: `ἥ τε ἀΐδιος αὐτοῦ δύναμις` (hē te aidios autou dynamis). In Greek, there is no "also" <note>original: quoque</note>, a conjunction they completely lack here, but rather `τε` (te). Although the Translator rendered it correctly, provided Origen's interpretation is true: that "invisible things" refers to invisible creatures, namely separate substances <note>A philosophical term for angels or disembodied souls</note>, and not to God Himself, whom he later adds separately. Origen's diligence, who is always philosophizing, does not displease me, but that other view, followed by Ambrose and Chrysostom, seems simpler to me.

<margin>D</margin>
46 **So that they are**: The word "so" <note>original: ita</note> is not only redundant but actually subverts the sense if it is added. The Greeks have it thus: `εἰς τὸ εἶναι αὐτοὺς ἀναπολογήτους` (eis to einai autous anapologētous), that is, *that they might be inexcusable*, or *to this end, that they might be inexcusable*. This is either because through the knowledge of God they were brought to the point that they cannot pretend ignorance when they sin, or because God granted them knowledge of Himself for this very purpose, so that they would later have nothing to use as a pretext for their unbelief if they rejected Christ. Even now, Theologians point out that Paul used this turn of phrase not to indicate the "final cause" (purpose), but the "consequent result," a style also found in the Psalm: *Against you only have I sinned... so that you may be justified in your words.* For he did not mean this in a good way—that he sinned *so that* God might appear righteous—but rather that this followed: while he did not cease to sin, the justice of God shines forth, who fulfills His promises to the sinner.

<margin>E</margin>
47 **But they became vain**: `ἐματαιώθησαν` (emataiothesan), that is, they were made empty or superfluous, or they were frustrated; for `μάτην` (matēn) means "in vain." From this comes `μάταιος` (mataios), meaning superfluous and of no use; hence "vanity" or "to be frustrated." Commonly, people call a boastful or proud person "vain," and Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a famous medieval commentator</note> explains it in that sense. Those who are skilled in Latin use "vain" for what is either untrue or what is frivolous and empty, having nothing solid. Furthermore, something is said to "vanish" <note>original: evanescere</note> when, after being presented to the eyes as a false image, it then ceases to appear, like smoke. But Paul means that they were frustrated by their own thoughts, that is, things turned out far otherwise than they thought. This is declared by what follows shortly after: *Claiming to be wise, they became fools*. For that is what it means to be frustrated: when you hoped for the highest wisdom, you fell into the highest folly; and when you dreamed of the brightest light, you were plunged into the deepest darkness; and when you set before yourself some rare glory among mortals, you slid into such shameful desires that even the nature of brute animals would shrink from them. Moreover, `διαλογισμὸς` (dialogismos) is not a simple thought, but the thought of one reasoning, weighing, and judging—which is entirely foreign to the faith of Christ to which Paul calls them. He is subtly criticizing the logical quibbles of the philosophers, relying on which they vainly claimed absolute wisdom for themselves and promised it to others.

<margin>F</margin>
48 **Claiming to be wise**: `Φάσκοντες εἶναι σοφοί` (Phaskontes einai sophoi). If nothing may be changed in the sacred letters, why did the Translator here dare to render a Greek figure of speech into Latin? Although even so, he did not fully express the meaning. For `Φάσκοντες εἶναι σοφοί` sounds more like, "Who, while they thought or professed themselves to be wise." Indeed, due to the affinity of the ideas, they often misuse the verb "to say" <note>original: φημὶ (phēmi)</note> for "to think" <note>original: οἴομαι (oiomai)</note>. Now, the conjunction "for" <note>original: enim</note>, which is added in many of our copies, is found neither in the Greek volumes nor in the ancient Latin ones, specifically those provided to us by the library of the College dedicated to Saint Donatian in Bruges.

49 **They were made fools**: In Greek, there is a single word, `ἐμωράνθησαν` (emōranthēsan), that is, they were infatuated or made into fools.

50 **Of the incorruptible God**: `ἀφθάρτου` (aphthartou), which elsewhere he translates as "immortal," as in First Timothy chapter one, "to the immortal God" <note>original: ἀφθάρτῳ Θεῷ (aphthartō Theō)</note>; and in this place it certainly fits better. For he contrasts the immortal God with the image of a mortal man, `φθαρτοῦ` (phthartou), except that "incorruptible" signifies something more than "immortal." For the souls of men are immortal, but by no means incorruptible.

51 **Into the likeness of an image**: `ἐν ὁμοιώματι εἰκόνος` (en homoiōmati eikonos), in the likeness of an image, or rather in the effigy or assimilation of an image. For he did not stop at saying they turned the glory of God into an image of a man, but that they thought otherwise of God than was proper, when they fashioned an image of a man for Him to whom nothing in bodily things is similar; and thus it is said "in likeness," as if you were to say, "through the assimilation of an image." In the same way a little later, *they changed His truth into a lie*, so that in both places the case is ablative, not accusative.

<summary>In this passage, Erasmus provides a linguistic analysis of Romans 1:17-23, arguing that the "righteous shall live by faith" refers to a growing trust in God's promises, while critiquing the pagan philosophers who ignored the clear evidence of God in creation.</summary>
<keywords>faith, Habakkuk, Septuagint, Greek grammar, Hebrew particles, wrath of God, invisible attributes, creation, vanity of philosophers, incorruptible God, idolatry, Erasmus, Romans 1</keywords>
