<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s philological and theological commentary on the first chapter of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans. Having established that the pagans are without excuse for failing to recognize God through His creation, Erasmus now examines the consequences: how God "handed them over" to their own vices. He pays particular attention to wordplay in the original Greek that is lost in the standard Latin translation.</meta>

# TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER I.

<margin>24</margin> <margin>A</margin> <term>erpetōn</term> <note>original: "ἐρπετῶν", meaning "creeping things"</note>. Therefore God also gave them up in the desires of their hearts to uncleanness, to dishonor their bodies among themselves;
<margin>25</margin> Who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever, Amen.
<margin>26</margin> For this cause God gave them up to vile passions; for even their women changed the natural use into that which is against nature;
<margin>27</margin> <margin>B</margin> And likewise also the men, leaving the natural use of the woman, burned in their lust one toward another; men with men working that which is unseemly, and receiving in themselves that recompense of their error which was meet.
<margin>28</margin> And even as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient;
<margin>29</margin> Being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wicked—

---

<margin>A</margin> For they did not change the truth of God into a lie in a literal sense, but while they themselves were occupied in a lie, they altered the truth of God for themselves, speaking of Him otherwise than He truly is. Certainly, a very ancient manuscript from the Library of Saint Donatian had the phrase *in a lie*. If they had worshipped a man instead of God, it would have been a great insult to the Creator, but the madness would have been lighter; as it is, he calls an idol a "lie," because it falsely takes the appearance of a man or another animal, though it neither lives nor feels. For a living monkey is more excellent than a statue of a man.

**52** *In the desires of the heart]* <term>en tais epithymiais tōn kardiōn autōn</term> <note>in the desires of their hearts</note>, that is, in the cravings of their hearts. It is not "heart" (singular), nor merely "into desires." In this place, it might seem like a misuse of a preposition (which he does elsewhere), unless it fits better to understand "handed over" as meaning "abandoned." For God did not drive them into foul cravings, but abandoned them as they went there by their own fault. It can also be understood as "by means of cravings." They fell into such great shames, enticed and pulled away by their own desires, with God permitting it. Nor is it without emphasis that "hearts" is used in the plural, so you may understand that the impulses of these waves are diverse; there is no single heart among them, nor any agreement.

**53** *Their bodies in themselves]* <term>en heautois</term> <note>among themselves</note>, that is, between one another. For it signifies, if I am not mistaken, the mutual sexual immorality of males among themselves, and likewise of females among themselves.

**54** *The truth of God]* <term>tēn alētheian autou</term> <note>His truth</note>, that is, the truth of Him—namely, of God. Otherwise, since "God" preceded it just before, it is a bit harsh to repeat it suddenly; though here the Greek manuscripts vary.

<margin>B</margin> **55** *And they worshipped]* <term>esebasthēsan</term>, that is, they felt reverence, which we properly say of those to whom we attribute something divine and majestic, which are also called <term>sebasma</term>, that is, *august things*. Regarding what follows, <term>elatreusan</term>, *they served*, we prefer to translate it as *worshipped*.

**56** *Rather than the creator]* <term>para ton ktisanta</term>, that is, *beyond Him*, or *above Him* who created; that is, they showed more honor to created things than to the one who had created them. Hilary, in the twelfth book of *On the Trinity*, says: "They served the creature, having passed over the Creator," beautifully expressing the sense.

**57** *Who is blessed]* <term>eulogētos</term>: which we, for the sake of the unlearned, would translate as *praiseworthy*. For <term>eulogein</term> to the Greeks is to speak honorably of someone, from which I believe the "blessings" of Bishops are named, because they pray well for the people and give good omens. Even so, this word is so widely accepted in Sacred Scripture that it is scarcely permissible to change it.

**58** *Into passions of ignominy]* <term>eis pathē atimias</term>. <term>Pathē</term> among the Greeks sometimes means "disturbances" of the soul, or "movements," or "diseases," or, as Quintilian most prefers, "affects." In such a great abundance of approved names, what need was there for the new and artificial word "passions" (*passiones*)? In this place, "diseases" fits best, since Horace also calls effeminate lust a disease:
> ->With a contaminated flock of men<-
> ->shameful with disease :<- <note>Horace, Odes 1.37.9-10</note>
Furthermore, what he adds, "of ignominy," appears to be taken from a Hebrew idiom, meaning "into disgraceful affects," or "insulting" and "ignominious" ones. Indeed, he calls lust an insult to the body, as he did a little earlier: "to the dishonoring of their bodies." And Peter, as interpreted by Jerome, calls a wife "the honor" of a husband if she is not contaminated by [illicit] intercourse. Truly, <term>atimia</term> <note>dishonor</note> is the opposite of honor.

<margin>C</margin> **59** *For even their women changed the natural use of the female]* The final word "female," <term>thēleias</term>, is added in some Greek manuscripts, but erroneously, if I am not mistaken—likely added here from the nearby passage.

**60** *In their desires]* <term>en tē orexei autōn</term>, that is, in their appetite, or, as I would prefer, "for each other": so that you understand the mutual appetite of the males among themselves.

<margin>D</margin> **61** *And the reward which]* In Greek it is more significant: <term>antimisthian</term>, as if you were to say a "counter-payment," or "repayment," and a retribution of a prize, or a reward corresponding to merits. For there are some outrages of such a kind that they are not only crimes themselves, but also the punishments for crimes. Augustine, in *Against Julian*, book 5, chapter 3, several times cites the "reward of error," as if expressing the force of the preposition <term>anti</term> <note>against/in return</note>: for <term>antapapologia</term> is called a "mutual accusation." Truly, this is not the constant meaning of that word; for sometimes it indicates only a "giving back," just as the Latins use *re-* in *respondere* (to respond) and *rependere* (to pay back). And yet it would not be absurdly called "mutual" if a reward were paid back for a reward, just as he "loves mutually" who responds in love:

<column-break/>

even of birds and four-footed animals and creeping things.
<margin>24</margin> Wherefore God gave them up **52** through the cravings of their hearts into uncleanness, so that they might affect with ignominy **53** their own bodies among themselves mutually: Who changed **54** His truth for a lie, and revered **55** and worshipped those things which were created **56** above Him who created them, **57** who is to be praised forever, amen.
<margin>26</margin> For which reason God gave them up **58** into ignominious cravings: for even their women changed the natural use into that which is against nature: And similarly also the males, having left the natural use of the female, burned **60** through an appetite for each other, one toward another, males upon males performing filthiness, **61** and receiving in themselves the prize, which was necessary, for their error.
<margin>28**52** And just as they did not approve **28** of acknowledging God, so God gave them up **63** into a reprobate mind, so that they did **64** what was not fitting: **65** Filled with all injustice, fornication, craftiness, **19** **66** avarice, **67** malice, full of **68** envy, murder, strife—

---

but here a punishment is paid back to the sinner, not a sin for a sin. It is much more absurd if you refer "mutual" to the persons mixing in obscene pleasure.

<margin>E</margin> **62** *And as they did not approve]* The sense is twofold, but both are rendered by the Greek words <term>Kai kathōs ouk edokimasan ton Theon echein en epignōsei</term>. For either you take this sense: "And even as they did not approve," that is, "they were unwilling to have God in their recognition." For here "recognition" (*agnitio*) is more than "knowledge" (*cognitio*), and though they had knowledge, they were unwilling to acknowledge Him; it would seem the article <term>to</term> is missing from "to have God." Or this sense: "And even as they did not approve that God should recognize them": as if, with Him knowing nothing, they were sinning freely. The accusative seems to be missing, which the verb "to have" required, to express what God should have in His notice. And although in some places they seem to use <term>epignōsin</term> for <term>gnōsei</term>, that is, "recognition" for "knowledge," nevertheless the difference between these names is noted both by our Jerome and by the Greek Interpreters. In this place, it fits "recognition" beautifully. For he said before that God was "known" (*cognitum*) by them, but here he denies He was "recognized" (*agnitum*). "To know" belongs to one who understands; "to acknowledge" belongs to one who is grateful and mindful. An ungrateful person knows a benefit, but while he pretends he does not owe it, he does not "acknowledge" it. Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator</note> advises here that *edokimasan* is put for *ekrinan*, that is, "it did not seem good to them," so that you understand it is not ignorance that is accused, but a perverse will. For the word "to prove" (*probandi*) is ambiguous to the Latins: he proves who "approves," he proves who "tests," he proves who "teaches" by arguments. The sense, therefore, according to the Greek Interpreters, is roughly this: "It did not seem good to them to acknowledge and worship God, whom they knew."

**63** *Into a reprobate sense]* <term>eis adokimon noun</term>. This is not "sense" as in "sensory" <note>Greek: aisthētikos</note>, like sight or hearing, but <term>nous</term>, that is, "mind." Thus it was clearer to say "into a reprobate mind." There is, moreover, a playful affinity of words in *edokimasan* (they approved) and *adokimon* (reprobate), that is, "they approved" and "disapproved." For here that which pleases is said to be "proved" (*dokimazetai*), and that which displeases everyone is "disapproved." Of this sort are these monsters of outrages he commemorates, which even the Pagans themselves curse.

**64** *Which were not fitting]* <term>ta mē kathēkonta</term>. The sense is: things unworthy of them, that is, which it was unbecoming for such men to do.

**65** *Filled]* The translator referred these accusatives back to the preceding verb, "handed over." But they are more conveniently referred to the infinitive verb "to do": which, after it has been changed into another mood, the accusatives were to be changed simultaneously into nominatives: "so that they did what was not fitting, being filled with all iniquity."

<margin>F</margin> **66** *Avarice]* <term>pleonexia</term>. Which he sometimes translates as "plunder," sometimes "fraud," and occasionally "avarice." But <term>pleonexia</term> is a compound word from <term>pleon echein</term>, that is, "from having more," which the Greeks use when someone usurps more for himself than is just, or occupies the better parts, with the rest even being cheated; whence come <term>pleonektēs</term> and <term>pleonektein</term>. To us, no one is greedy who is not also a cheater, but not even any man is rich who is not either unjust or the heir of an unjust man, if we believe the proverb. Furthermore, as often as a catalog of such names occurs, the copies disagree somewhat, whether the Greek ones are confused or the Latin; this happens through the forgetfulness of scribes, because it is difficult to remember things of this kind. Nor do I entirely approve of the over-anxious diligence of some in these matters, who think the number of words must also be observed in a gathered forest of names: as in some other places, and in the Epistle to the Galatians—what is the point of counting the fruits of the spirit, when the works of the flesh correspond neither in number nor in kind, and finally they add to the catalog "and things like these"?

**67** *Wickedness]* <term>kakia</term>. This word sometimes means "vice" to the Greeks and is opposed to <term>aretē</term> (virtue). Sometimes it means "cowardice," from which <term>kakōsis</term> means to fail or be weary; sometimes "affliction," though we more correctly call that <term>kakōsin</term>. In this place, we prefer to translate it as "malice," which is used simply for "vice" in Seneca; otherwise it sounds like perversity, when someone does evil on purpose. But he translates <term>ponērian</term> as "malice," a word which sometimes signifies not only malice but craftiness and cunning: whence "avarice" precedes it as its sister. "Wickedness" (*nequitia*) properly pertains to lust and luxury, because these vices declare a man lost and worth nothing, and those subject to them are usually despised by all. There is, however, to those reading Greek, a not-unpleasant affinity in <term>ponēria</term> <note>malice</note> and <term>porneia</term> <note>fornication</note>.

**68** *Envy, murders]* Among the Greeks there is a pleasant affinity of words in <term>phthonou</term> <note>envy</note> and <term>phonou</term> <note>murder</note>. Although "slaughter" (*cæde*) is better in the singular than "murders" (*homicidiis*).

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed philological analysis of the list of vices in Romans 1, specifically verses 29–32. Erasmus compares the Latin Vulgate translation with the original Greek and the writings of early Church Fathers like Origen, Chrysostom, and Theophylact. # THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER II.

...wickedness, greed, malice; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, maliciousness; whisperers, backbiters, haters of God, violent, proud, boastful, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents, witless, faithless, heartless, irreconcilable, unmerciful; who, knowing the righteous judgment of God, that those who practice such things are deserving of death, not only do the same but also approve of those who practice them. Therefore... <note>Erasmus provides the Greek text of Romans 1:29–31 here to set the stage for his linguistic corrections.</note>

---

<margin>A</margin>
69 *Malignity* <note>original: "κακοηθείας"</note>. This term more specifically suggests a harshness and difficulty of character. For among us, malignity is the opposite of kindness or candor; one who praises "malignantly" does so sparingly and almost enviously, and one who gives "malignantly" gives stingily.

70 *Backbiters* ] The Greek term <term>katalalous</term> <note>original: "καταλάλους"</note> is more expressive. A detractor is one who takes away deserved praise; a backbiter is one who speaks evil of another.

<margin>B</margin>
71 *Haters of God* ] This is a single word in Greek: <term>theostugeis</term> <note>original: "θεοστυγεῖς"</note>. It sounds more like those to whom God is hateful, rather than those whom God hates. This is how the Greek commentaries interpret it, although Theophylact allows for both meanings; Chrysostom does not address it. Cyprian, in the fourth epistle of his first book, reads it as *those who shrink from God*—undoubtedly of the sort who say to God, "depart from us, we do not want the knowledge of your ways." Julius Pollux, among the words used to express impiety, mentions this term and notes it is a tragic or poetic word.

72 *Violent* ] <note>original: "ὑβριστάς"</note>, that is, *ferocious* people who oppress others by force; you might call them "wrong-doers," which is why Paul immediately adds the related vice, *the proud*.

73 *Arrogant* ] <note>original: "ἀλαζόνας"</note>. Plautus translates this as *boastful*, which you might also correctly call "vainglorious." The Greeks derived the word from a phrase meaning "to live by wandering," because impostors of this kind often change locations so they can more easily deceive those to whom they are unknown. The *alazōn* (boaster) is different from what the Greeks call an <term>eirōn</term> <note>original: "εἴρωνα", an ironist or self-deprecator</note>. The former shows off what he is not; the latter hides what he is.

74 *Inventors of evil things* ] <note>original: "ἐφευρετὰς"</note>. Either because they mix some evil into things that are inherently good, or because they are always adding new evils to existing ones. For evil is always born from evil.

75 *Disobedient* ] <note>original: "ἀπειθεῖς"</note>, meaning *unruly*, disobedient, or unmanageable. There was no need for the Latin translator to use a long phrase here.

76 *Witless, faithless* ] Here again is a very pleasant similarity of sounds in the Greek—<term>asynetous, asynthetous</term> <note>original: "ἀσυνέτους, ἀσυνθέτους"</note>—which the Latin translator neither attempted nor was able to replicate. Theophylact interprets "faithless" as those who are "insipid" and fail to keep their agreements or are slippery in their promises. This is because to "agree" in Greek is *syntithesthai* and agreements are *synthēkai*. Furthermore, he calls them "witless" because they are not restrained by the reason that is unique to humans, without which a human ceases to be human.

77 *Heartless* ] <note>original: "ἀστόργους"</note>. I will not dwell for now on how the Translator misused the word *affectio* (disposition) for *affectus* (emotion), though there is a great difference. According to the Stoics, to be free of emotions is the highest praise; likewise, among us, to be free of *evil* emotions is considered praiseworthy. But <term>storgē</term> <note>original: "στοργὴ"</note> does not simply mean emotion, but rather that natural affection of piety or charity felt by parents toward children, children toward parents, or brother toward brother. Therefore, those who have advanced so far in vice that they have become deaf to these common affections and the very sense of nature are called *astorgous*. Such was the man described by the Satirist:
> *He neither loves, nor is he loved by anyone.* <note>Erasmus quotes Juvenal here to illustrate a total lack of human connection.</note>
Chrysostom connects these words—witless, faithless, heartless, unmerciful—explaining them thus: the first refers to the natural affection of all living things for their own kind (man for man, wolf for wolf); the second to civil treaties made by pact; the third to the affection of kinship; and the fourth to the emotion of mercy, by which we sometimes feel for the misfortunes of even our enemies. He emphasizes that their impiety made them deaf to all these natural feelings. Theophylact follows the same order, interpreting "faithless" as those who "trample on commercial agreements."

78 *Covenant-breakers* ] What does this fourth term, "without a treaty," mean? Does he condemn those who do not make treaties, or rather those who cannot be restrained by any treaty from doing whatever they please? Hence, he should have said *treaty-breakers*. Although elsewhere the Greeks call the irreconcilable <term>aspondous</term> <note>original: "ἀσπόνδους"</note>, as in an "irreconcilable war." It also signifies an unsociable person—one who is unmanageable, lives only for himself, and acknowledges no bonds of necessity toward anyone. This is a "congeries" <note>a heap or accumulation of words</note>, and he uses these terms to give force and vehemence to his speech. Such a list not only adds charm but also highlights the odiousness of the subject, much like saying of a blatant lie, "this was never written nor painted anywhere."

79 *Unmerciful* ] <term>aneleēmonas</term> <note>original: "ἀνελεήμονας"</note>, that is, *merciless*. It is strange why the Translator preferred a roundabout phrase here.

80 *Who, knowing the justice of God* ] In this place, the Greek manuscripts differ significantly from our Latin ones. For among the Greeks it reads: *Who, knowing the justice of God—namely, that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only do them, but also consent to those who do them.* This suggests it is a graver matter to approve of the misdeeds of others than to commit them oneself in silence. The confusion likely arose from the Greek words for "do" and "consent," which look similar to certain plural participles and verbs. First, he posits the "justice of God," then he explains what that justice is: namely,

<column-break/>

<page-num>568</page-num>
# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER II.

...guile, 69 endowed with evil habits, whisperers, 70 Backbiters, 71 God-haters, 72 violent, 73 arrogant, 74 inventors of evil, 75 disobedient to parents, 76 Witless, faithless, 77 heartless, 78 covenant-breakers, 79 unmerciful: 80 Who, knowing the justice of God—namely, that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only do them, but also approve of those who do them. <note>This is Erasmus's revised translation of Romans 1:29–32 based on the preceding notes.</note>

---

<margin>II. 1. Therefore</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
that *those who do such things are worthy of death*. However, I do not quite understand where these two words—*they did not understand*—came from in our Latin copies <note>Erasmus is noting that the Vulgate wrongly added "they did not understand," which is absent from the Greek.</note>. Even if they are added, the sense remains the same if you read it as a negative question, implying it was impossible for them *not* to have understood. Nothing certain can be gathered from Origen regarding this specific point, except I suspect his text was corrupted there. But the Greek commentaries indicate that some people used to read this passage differently, as if "doing" were more serious and "consenting" less so. But our translators, feeling something was missing to complete the sense, added those two words "they did not understand" on their own. However, the existing Greek manuscripts show with great consensus that Paul’s meaning is different: it is more serious to approve of the misdeeds of others than to slip into sin oneself. This is because sinning is often done by chance or weakness, whereas approving of sin is a sign of either pestilential flattery or the most wretched malice. It was the duty of the wise to restrain the unlearned common people from these vices; but these leaders not only did the same things but confirmed the madness of the people with their own authority. Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret it this way, though Cyprian and Ambrose disagree. However, for the sake of <term>syntonian</term> <note>original: "συντονίαν", intensity or vigor</note>, it is worth providing Chrysostom’s own words: <note>Erasmus provides a long Greek quote from Chrysostom's homily on Romans, which he then translates below.</note> "He dissolves two objections here: for what can you say? 'I did not know what should be done?' You certainly did know. You are at fault for abandoning the God who made Himself known through His works. Now he proves with many arguments that you sin knowingly and willingly. But passion drags you to sin. Why then do you both do these things and praise them? For they not only do them, but approve of those who do. He placed the more serious and inexcusable fault first to grab attention: for he who praises the sin of a transgressor is much more vehement in evil. Having said this first, he strikes them even more forcefully in what follows, saying: *Therefore you are inexcusable, O man.*" Theophylact says: "He showed that because they refused to acknowledge God, they were filled with all malice; he now shows that they are not even worthy of pardon. For they cannot say, 'we did not know what was honorable.' They knew the justice of God. Therefore they act willingly, and what is worse, they approve of those who act; for to consent to evil is to be incurably sick." The very flow of the speech supports this: *Therefore you are inexcusable, O man, etc.*

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>E</margin>
1 *Therefore ]* Origen points out the correct order of this entire Pauline disputation, which is somewhat complex because the word "handed over" is repeated three times, and several causes for this "handing over" are given, though they do not seem to correspond neatly to each individual instance. Therefore, Origen thinks it better to heap together all the causes of the "handing over" and then join the types of "handing over" together, so that we may order it in this way: Since men changed the glory of the immortal God into an image made like mortal man, birds, four-footed beasts, and serpents; and since they traded the truth of God for a lie and worshipped the creature rather than the creator; and since it did not please them to acknowledge God—let this be the pile of causes—then immediately join the types of evils into which He handed them over. For all these reasons, God handed them over to the desires of their hearts and to uncleanness, to dishonor their own bodies; and God handed them over to shameful passions, so that their women changed the natural use for that which is against nature, and likewise the men. And God also handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things that are not fitting, being filled with all iniquity, lust, fraud, greed, malice, and full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and the other evils he mentions. And who, knowing the justice of God to be such that those who do these things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to them. And therefore, for all these evils, they will be inexcusable while they judge and condemn others for the very things they commit themselves. For one pronounces judgment upon oneself when one punishes another for what he himself does. Origen indicated this order of reading. But meanwhile, we can guess from this that he read the text differently than the Greeks do today, not ending the sentence where we end the chapter, but connecting it with the beginning of the next...

He also discusses Origen's structural analysis of Paul's argument as it transitions into Chapter 2.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s philological examination of the Epistle to the Romans. On the previous page, he concluded Chapter 1 by discussing the list of pagan vices. Here, he begins Chapter 2, where Paul addresses those who judge others while being guilty of the same sins. Erasmus focuses heavily on the nuance of Greek terms for "kindness," "judgment," and "repentance," comparing the Greek original against the Latin Vulgate and the interpretations of the Church Fathers.</meta>

->### TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER II.<-

1 Therefore you are without excuse, O man, whoever you are who judges; for in that which you judge another, you condemn yourself; for you who judge practice the same things.
2 But we know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who practice such things.
3 And do you think this, O man, who judges those who practice such things and yet do them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God?
4 Or do you despise the riches of His goodness, and forbearance, and longsuffering, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?
5 But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are treasuring up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God,
6 who will render to each according to his works:
7 to those who by perseverance in good work seek glory and honor and immortality, eternal life;
8 but to those who are contentious, and

from the previous chapter, *Therefore you are inexcusable, O man.* And this sense would be perfectly clear if it could be drawn from the Greek words. It could be, however, by adding a single article, "the" <note>original: "ὁ"</note>, so that we read it this way: *therefore, you are the only one who does these things, yet you also approve of those who practice them* <note>original: "διὸ ὁ μόνος εἶ αὐτὰ ποιῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ συνευδοκεῖς τοῖς πράσσουσι"</note>. For it is not fitting, in my opinion, to attribute such a gross grammatical error <term>solecism|A grammatical mistake or intentional breaking of rules</term> to Paul, as if he used the dative case in place of the nominative—that is, *doing and approving* <note>original: "ποιῶν, & συνευδοκῶν"</note> instead of *to do and to approve* <note>original: "ποιῆσι & συνευδοκῆσι"</note>. Yet I am not sure if the Translator <note>Erasmus refers here to the author of the Latin Vulgate</note> changed the Greek reading. Certainly, in some places, he uses the freedom of a paraphraser.

<margin>A</margin> 2 **Every one who judges** ] *every one who judges* <note>original: "πᾶς ὁ κρίνων"</note>, that is, whoever you are who judges, or whoever you may be who acts as a judge.

3 **for in that [which you judge] another** ] *for in which* <note>original: "ἐν ᾧ γὰρ"</note>. The meaning is: by judging another, you condemn yourself; that is, by the very act of judging, you condemn yourself. This is a property of the Greek language. Likewise in 1 Peter, chapter 2: *in that which they speak against you* <note>original: "ἐν ᾧ καταλαλοῦσι"</note>. These things are properly said against magistrates and censors of morals: while you bring a sentence against another, you bring it against yourself—just as we read that David pronounced a sentence of death upon himself. There is something slightly awkward in the sudden change of number, between *in which* and *for you do the same things*. Furthermore, when he adds, *for you do the same things*, etc., he almost repeats the same sentiment, unless you read it according to our annotation.

4 **For the same things that you judge** ] *for the one who judges practices the same things* <note>original: "τὰ γὰρ αὐτὰ πράσσει ὁ κρίνων"</note>, that is, you do the same things, you who are judging, or you, that judge. Although this error has occupied even the ancient manuscripts—either because it is a very easy slip between "who" and "which" <note>Referring to the Latin "qui" and "que"</note>, or because some read *which you judge* <note>original: "ἃ κρίνεις"</note> instead of *the one who judges* <note>original: "ὁ κρίνων"</note>. Furthermore, it is not clear from the interpretations of Origen, Chrysostom, Theophylact, or Ambrose what they read in this specific part, except that the Greek constantly has *the one who judges* <note>original: "ὁ κρίνων"</note>. You judge, you condemn: *krineis, katakrineis* <note>original: "κρίνειϛ, κατακρίνειϛ"</note>. The pleasantness of the Greek figure could not be rendered by the Translator, because the <term>prosonomasia|A rhetorical device where words of similar sound but different meaning are placed together</term> does not correspond in Latin words.

5 **The riches of his goodness** ] *or the riches of his goodness* <note>original: "ἡ τῷ πλούτῳ τῆς χρηστότητος"</note>. Paul delighted in the word "riches," perhaps for this reason: he uses it more frequently whenever he wants a vast force and abundance of a thing to be understood. Furthermore, "goodness" here is not *agathotes* <note>original: "ἀγαθότης"</note>, which signifies the kind of goodness opposed to *poneria* (that is, malice), but *chrestotes* <note>original: "χρηστότης"</note>, which in Latin is called *benignitas* (benignity). Philosophers define it thus: Benignity is a virtue inclined toward doing good of its own accord; hence the Greek word is derived from "utility" <note>Greek *chrestos* means useful or good</note>. Although the same word is accepted for the convenience and sweetness of character by which we show ourselves easygoing in the conduct of life. Indeed, the Latins use "use" to mean familiarity or social custom. And the Greeks call those who are very companionable and charming in meeting others *chrestologous* <note>original: "χρηστολόγους"</note>. Nor is "goodness" far from "benignity." For when they call the Gods "good," they want them to be understood as "beneficent." But we preferred to follow that which, besides being certain, was also clearer and more suited to this passage. He calls God's leniency and mildness—and the fact that He is not at all austere—His *chrestoteta* <note>original: "χρηστότητα"</note>.

6 **you ignore** ] *ignoring* <note>original: "ἀγνοῶν"</note>, that is, being ignorant, as supported by the very ancient Donatian codex. It is a participle among the Greeks and depends on the preceding words. Jerome refers to it this way in his commentary on Ezekiel.

7 **That the goodness of God** ] *that the "good" [thing]* <note>original: "ὅτι τὸ χρηστὸν"</note>. He placed an adjective in the place of a noun; it is the same word we just explained.

8 **Leads you to repentance** ] *agei* <note>original: "ἄγει"</note>, that is, leads—which is to say, allures and invites. Jerome, in Ezekiel, translates it as "provokes." Otherwise, "to lead toward" <note>Latin: "adducere"</note> is the same as "to lead through" <note>Latin: "perducere"</note>.

9 **Impenitent heart** ] More significantly in Greek: *ametanoyton* <note>original: "ἀμετανόητον"</note>, as if you were to say, "un-repentable," which no amount of God's beneficence can lead to repentance. You would correctly translate *metanoia* <note>original: "μετάνοια"</note> as both "repentance" and "resipiscence" <note>A change of mind or coming to one's senses</note>, and *metanoein* as "to recover one's senses." For the word is named from the fact that after a crime has been committed, a person feels that he has sinned, from *meta* (after) and *noein* (to understand).

10 **You treasure up for yourself** ] *you treasure up for yourself* <note>original: "θησαυρίζεις σεαυτῷ"</note>, that is, "you treasure up for your own self." For here the compound pronoun is not idle; it signifies that he himself is the cause of such great evil, even while the goodness of God calls him elsewhere. I wonder, however, why the Greek word delighted the Translator so much, when he could have said "you collect," "you hide away," or "you store up." It signifies that divine wrath is heaped up little by little, so that finally the whole may be brought out in the manner of a treasure.

11 **Of the revelation of the righteous judgment** ] The Greeks divide this with an interposed conjunction: *of revelation AND of righteous judgment* <note>original: "ἀποκαλύψεως καὶ δικαιοκρισίας"</note>. Although for the Greeks, "righteous judgment" is a single word <note>dikaiokrisia</note>, and for that reason more elegant, as it distinguishes divine judgment from our human judgments by a newly coined word—judgments in which not rarely the guilty escape and the innocent are condemned. He marked that same day with three signs: *wrath*, because then there will be no place for mercy; *revelation*, because

<column-break/>

1 Therefore you are without excuse, O man, whoever you are who judges: for by this very thing that you judge another, you condemn yourself: for you who judge do the same things.
2 But we know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things.
3 But do you think this, O man who judges those who do such things and you do the same, that you will escape the judgment of God?
4 Or do you despise the riches of His goodness and patience and the mildness of His forbearance, not knowing that the goodness of God invites you to repentance?
5 But according to your hardness and a heart that does not know how to repent, you collect for your own self wrath in the day of wrath, in which the righteous judgment of God shall be made manifest,
6 Who will render to every man according to his deeds:
7 To those indeed, who by perseverance in well-doing seek glory and honor and immortality, eternal life:
8 But to those who are contentious, and who do not obey the truth, but obey injustice, there shall come

all things will be naked which are now hidden; and **righteous judgment**, because it is to be pronounced rightly according to each person's merits. And one who reads his interpretation more attentively will find that Theophylact read it this way. Certainly the context holds this way, both in his work and in Chrysostom's. Nevertheless, in some Greek manuscripts, the third conjunction is not added, so that the sense is: *In that day, in which the impious have experienced not the goodness of God, which they despised, but His wrath—that is, His justice and vengeance—and in which the divine judgment shall be opened, which meanwhile lies hidden among mortals.*

<margin>B</margin> 12 **According to his works** ] *according to his works* <note>original: "κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ"</note>, that is, according to his own deeds, not "his" [referring to someone else]; unless you prefer the <term>third [person pronoun]|tritou</term>, which pronoun comes very close to a reflexive nature.

<margin>C</margin> 13 **According to patience** ] *according to patience* <note>original: "καθ’ ὑπομονὴν"</note>, that is, perseverance or the endurance of a good work, meaning that one has persevered in good work.

<margin>D</margin> 14 **To those seeking life** ] This passage is rendered somewhat awkwardly, whereas the Greek reading, if one pays attention, is quite beautiful: *To those indeed who by perseverance in good work seek glory and honor and immortality, eternal life* <note>original: "Τοῖς μὲν καθ’ ὑπομονὴν ἔργου ἀγαθοῦ δόξαν καὶ τιμὴν καὶ ἀφθαρσίαν ζητοῦσι, ζωὴν αἰώνιον"</note>. This means: *He who will render to each according to his works: to those indeed, who through perseverance of good work seek glory and honor and immortality—or to those seeking—eternal life.* Thus, *eternal life* refers back to the verb **will render** <note>original: "ἀποδώσει"</note>, and the article *to those* <note>original: "τοῖς"</note> refers to the participle *seeking* <note>original: "ζητοῦσι"</note>. The sense is: to those who here seek that glory, honor, and immortality, persevering in good works through which those things are prepared, He will render eternal life—namely, that which they sought. On the contrary, to those who preferred to be contentious and did not obey the truth, wrath is coming to them, etc. Origen seems to have read it this way too, when he says: *To those, he says, seeking glory and honor and incorruption, eternal life will be given for the patience of good work.* And shortly after: *Now indeed let us seek glory and honor.* Theophylact, Archbishop of Bulgaria, reads and explains it in the same way, as do Chrysostom and the rest of the Greek commentaries; so that we understand this excellent reward is given, but only to those who have striven for it, and striven for it by right deeds. There is a great consensus among the manuscripts. The phrasing is the same in both. Theophylact, however, more clearly refers these accusatives—*glory and honor and incorruption*—to the participle *seeking* than Chrysostom does. I do not know what Rufinus was following in the third book of *On First Principles* <note>original: "περὶ ἀρχῶν"</note>, where he relates this passage thus: *to him indeed who according to the patience of a good work, glory and incorruption, who seek eternal life. But to those who are from contention, and who do not believe the truth but believe iniquity, wrath and indignation,* etc. In this case, the verb "shall be" would be understood in both parts. However, it is well known that Rufinus is a Translator of little good faith.

<margin>E</margin> And this version offers an opportunity for another reading, which will occur if a <term>hypostigme|An ancient punctuation mark similar to a comma, indicating a partial pause</term> is placed in the next spot, so that the primary accusatives—*glory, honor, and incorruption*—pertain to the preceding verb *will render*: and *eternal life* to the participle *seeking*. The order would be: *To those who, according to the patience of good work, seek eternal life, he will give glory, honor, etc.* Thus, a *hypostigme* is placed after "good work," and the verb "are" is understood, which the Translator expressed in the other part: *but to those who ARE from contention.* This reading seems to have been followed by Ambrose, and certainly by Rufinus in this place. This does not displease me, but the Translator expressed neither clearly, because he did not turn the participle into a verb, although he turned the article into a pronoun: *to those who seek*, so that it corresponds to the opposite part: *but to those who are from contention*, for he opposed "contention" to "patience." There is not much difference between the two meanings created by the different placement of the *hypostigme*. For it matters little whether eternal life is sought by good works, or glory, honor, and immortality, since God is all these things to us. Furthermore, let no one be offended that we translated "immortality" instead of "incorruption"; Ambrose translates it the same way in the first Epistle to Timothy, chapter one: *to the immortal God* <note>original: "ἀφθάρτῳ Θεῷ"</note>, and the Church reads it the same way. Indeed, that is the force of the Greek word. For whether "incorruption" <note>Latin: "incorruptio"</note> is a proper Latin word, I do not know.

<margin>F</margin> 15 **From contention** ] *to those from contention* <note>original: "τοῖς ἐξ ἐριθείας"</note>, that is, to the contentious, as Theophylact also noted, or those who are "of" contention. For the Greeks call people *those from something* <note>original: "τοὺς ἐκ τινος"</note>, and Paul calls the circumcised *those from the circumcision*.

16 **Do not acquiesce** ] In Greek, it is a single word and a participle: *apeithousi* <note>original: "ἀπειθοῦσι"</note>, that is, "to those not obeying" or "not complying." The pleasantness of the Greek phrasing is not rendered among us, which consists of the words *eritheias, apeithousi, and peithomenois*—that is, "not obeying" and "obeying."

<summary>Erasmus provides a detailed linguistic analysis of Romans 2:1-8, focusing on the Greek concepts of kindness, judgment, and the grammatical structure of Paul's sentences. He critiques the Latin Vulgate's translation choices and consults several Church Fathers to determine the most accurate reading of the text regarding divine judgment.</summary>

17 **Of the Jew first and also of the Greek** <note>original: "Judæi primùm & Græci"</note>] In these words there is also the doubling of the conjunction which we showed above, <note>original: "Ἰουδαίῳ τε πρῶτον καὶ Ἕλληνι"</note> "to the Jew first and to the Greek." However, I believe the adverb "first" refers to both nations, the Jews and the Greeks, so that we understand that just as the grace of Christ first went out to the Jews and the Greeks, so punishment is to be inflicted chiefly on them if they despise the gift being offered.

18 **Respect of persons** <note>original: "Acceptio personarum"</note>] <note>original: "προσωποληψία"</note>. This is a single word <term>prosopolepsia|A Greek compound meaning to 'receive the face,' referring to favoritism</term> that signifies "respect of a person," as when we favor one person over another, not because of the facts of the case, but because of a distinction in the person. To this is opposed what he said a little earlier, <note>original: "δικαιοκρισίαν"</note>, that is, "righteous judgment." "Acceptance of persons" signifies nothing to Latin ears, even though it is frequent in the Sacred Scriptures. A <note>original: "προσωπολήμπτης"</note> (respecter of persons) seems to refer more to those whom the favor of a person has captured than those who "receive" them, in the same way that contractors and those making agreements are described. Nor does this word pertain more to the "person" than to the "face." Certainly, in some places, it denies that God judges according to the face.

19 **Sinned without the law** <note>original: "Sine lege peccaverunt"</note>] The Greek phrasing is more elegant through the adverb <note>original: "ἀνόμως"</note> (anomōs), as if you were to say, "illegally" or "outside the law," which is used in both instances. For we read "outlaw" for <note>original: "ἀνόμῳ"</note>. Indeed, this whole speech is decorated with the repetition of the two terms and the comparison of opposites, and is paced with rhythmic members: "sinned without the law," "in the law," "through the law," "sinned, sinned," "will perish, will be judged."

20 **Without the law they shall perish** <note>original: "Sine lege peribunt"</note>] In the Greek it is <note>original: "καὶ ἀπολοῦνται"</note>, that is, "and they shall perish," so that you may understand a similarity is being rendered, and that their end will be such as their life was.

21 **But the doers of the law** <note>original: "Sed factores legis"</note>] <note>original: "οἱ ποιηταὶ τοῦ νόμου"</note>, that is, those who work and do the precepts of the law. Otherwise, those who "make" the law are those who establish it.

22 **Who do not have the law** <note>original: "Qui non habent legem"</note>] In the Greek it is <note>original: "νόμον"</note>, that is, twice, not "the law" in that specific sense. The translator seems to have read <note>original: "τὸν νόμον"</note> (the law) and does not refer back to the sense.

23 **Written in their hearts** <note>original: "Scriptum in cordibus"</note>] "Written" is a noun in the Greek, not a participle: <note>original: "γραπτόν"</note>, as if you were to say "scripted," so that it is opposed to that which the legal experts call <note>original: "νόμον τὸν γραπτὸν"</note>, "unwritten law."

24 **Their conscience bearing witness to them, etc.** <note>original: "Testimonium illis reddente &c."</note>] <note>original: "συμμαρτυρούσης αὐτῶν τῆς συνειδήσεως"</note>, that is, their conscience witnessing together. For "to them" is not in the Greek: so that you understand their conscience agrees with the judgment of God.

25 **Of thoughts accusing** <note>original: "Cogitationum accusantium"</note>] The Translator was wonderfully drowsy here, since in the second verse he left the Greek <term>genitive case|The 'of' case in grammar</term> as it was, while changing <note>original: "συμμαρτυρούσης"</note> into a Latin <term>ablative|A case typically used for 'by' or 'from'</term>. It should have been translated, "with thoughts mutually accusing or even defending." And Jerome lists it this way, explaining the sixteenth chapter of Ezekiel. Ambrose the Translator reads it in the same way. Augustine does so as well, both elsewhere frequently and in the twentieth book of *The City of God*, chapter 26. Although he cites it differently when explaining the Sermon on the Mount, if the manuscript is free of error. For scribes are accustomed to "correct" the citations of the Ancients to match this Vulgate edition. Nor does the translator of Origen on this Epistle read it otherwise, whoever he was. Those who do not want the Translator to have ever erred, and believe he translated with the Holy Spirit suggesting it, let them explain this one passage if they can. Yet the supine negligence and evident yawning of this one notable passage can be argument enough of how much he is to be trusted in other matters. I speak of the suitability of the language, not of the meanings. It is not necessary that we attribute everything to the Holy Spirit. Some try to refer these genitives...

against every soul of man who commits evil,
<note>17</note> to the Jew first and also to the Greek. But glory, 10

without the law, <note>20</note> shall also perish without the law; and as many

but those who express the law in deeds shall be held righteous.

do the things of the law, <note>22</note> these, not having the law, 
are a law unto themselves, who show the work of the law <note>23</note> written 15
in their hearts, <note>24</note> their conscience witnessing with them,

who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach

adultery, do you commit adultery? You who detest idols, do you

of God is <note>32</note> spoken ill of among the Gentiles because of you, 
just as it is written. For circumcision indeed 25
profits if you keep the law; but if you are a transgressor of the 
law, your circumcision has turned into uncircumcision. Therefore, if 26

<margin>D</margin> ...referring the genitives "of thoughts" to the word that preceded, "of conscience," resulting in "the conscience of thoughts." But that is extremely harsh. In my opinion, the Translator cannot be excused except by saying that at that time the common people were accustomed to speaking this way in imitation of the Greeks, and he was working for them rather than for the learned.

26 **But if** <note>original: "Si autem"</note>] The truer and older reading among the Greeks is <note>original: "Ἰδὲ σὺ"</note>, that is, "Behold you." But "If," is <note>original: "εὶ δὲ"</note>. Otherwise the order does not hang together well with what follows: "You then, who teach another." Although Ambrose reads <note>original: "Εἰ δὲ"</note> (If), if the books do not deceive, as do Origen and Theophylact. Nor is there any inconvenience regarding the sense, except that, as I just said, the following words hang together somewhat loosely: "You, therefore, who teach another, etc." Although this is not new in Paul, and is otherwise tolerable.

27 **You approve the more useful things** <note>original: "Probas utiliora"</note>] <note>original: "τὰ διαφέροντα"</note>, that is, the excellent or outstanding things. The Translator seems to have read <note>original: "τὰ συμφέροντα"</note>, that is, useful or conducive things. Finally, though, Theophylact wanted to interpret "excellent things" as "useful things," unless perhaps the Greeks speak in the manner of the Latins, so that they say it "makes a difference" <note>original: "interesse"</note> for "it is useful" <note>original: "συμφέρειν"</note>, because it pertains to the matter at hand. Furthermore, "you approve" in this place is <note>original: "δοκιμάζεις"</note>, that is, "you verify," which is to approve by judgment and as if having tested it.

28 **Instructed by the law** <note>original: "Instructus per legem"</note>] In Greek <note>original: "εἰς κατηχούμενος"</note>, that is, "erudite, or initiated, and instructed." This word is peculiar to Paul; it seems to be derived from the word by which mysteries were once handed down, which it was a sin to commit to books. His disciple Luke used the same in the preface of the Gospels, as was indicated there.

<margin>E</margin> 29 **Teacher of infants** <note>original: "Magistrum infantium"</note>] <note>original: "διδάσκαλον νηπίων"</note>. This name, as we have already warned in several places, signifies an "infant" when referred to age; when referred to the mind, it signifies someone little-educated, little-refined, and inexperienced in affairs. Here "of the foolish, or the witless, or of boys" would have been more timely. For who teaches infants? "Of little ones" would have been more tolerable, as he often translates elsewhere. For in this place, it is not a "master" who rules, but a <note>original: "διδάσκαλος"</note>, that is, one who teaches. Furthermore, the word that just preceded, <note>original: "παιδευτὴν"</note> (instructor), is an ambiguous noun, common both to one who instructs boys and one who chastises and corrects those who err. It appears here that Paul is quietly alluding to a passage in Isaiah chapter 38 <note>note: Erasmus likely means Isaiah 10 or 28, or perhaps a different citation</note>. Where it is written: "Where are those who weigh the words of the law? Where is the teacher of little ones?"

30 **Having the form** <note>original: "Habentem formam"</note>] <note>original: "μόρφωσιν"</note>, that is, "formation," as if you were to say, a method of instructing and forming which one prescribes to others, just as there are those today who profess that they can form the consciences of individuals. Likewise, the Jews were pleased with themselves because they prescribed a "form" of life to proselytes as if they were recruits. Theophylact also explains in this sense, but adding that there were those who interpreted "formation" in this place not as a form, but as a feigned and shadowed image of righteousness, since they were prescribing: "do not touch, do not taste, do not handle."

31 **You dishonor** <note>original: "Inhonoras"</note>] <note>original: "ἀτιμάζεις"</note>, that is, "you disgrace," or affect with ignominy.

<margin>F</margin> 32 **Is blasphemed** <note>original: "Blasphematur"</note>] In Greek the word is <note>original: "βλασφημεῖται"</note>, which in Latin you may translate as "is spoken ill of," or "is affected by curses." The testimony which Paul brings forward is referred by Origen to Isaiah, in whose law <note>note: referring to the book of Isaiah</note> chapter 52 it says: "Because my people are taken away for nothing, and those who rule over them act iniquitously, says the Lord, and continually all day my name is blasphemed." Furthermore, these two words, "among the Gentiles," were added from the Septuagint edition, which Paul seems to have made use of in this place.

<summary>Erasmus provides a detailed philological commentary on Romans 2:9-26, highlighting the nuances of Greek terms for "doers of the law," "conscience," and "respect of persons" while criticizing the Latin Vulgate's grammatical slips and word choices. He emphasizes Paul's critique of Jewish pride in the Law, noting that even those without the written Law have a moral compass in their conscience.</summary>

# TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTERS II & III.

<page-num>573</page-num>
<page-num>574</page-num>

...keeps the requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision <margin>27 his</margin> be counted as circumcision? And will not <margin>the uncircumcision which is by nature, if it fulfills the law, judge</margin> <margin>you, who through the letter and circumcision are a trans-</margin> <margin>28 gressor of the law? For he is not a Jew who is one out-</margin> <margin>wardly;</margin> <margin>neither is that circumcision which is outward in the</margin> <margin>29 flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly,</margin> <margin>and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the</margin> <margin>letter; whose praise is not from men, but</margin> <margin>III. 1 from God. What then is the advantage of the Jew? Or</margin> <margin>2 what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every</margin> <margin>way; for first, they were entrusted with the</margin> <margin>3 oracles of God. For what if some were unfaithful? Shall</margin> <margin>their unfaithfulness make the faithfulness of God of no</margin> <margin>4 effect? May it not be! Rather, let God be true,</margin> <margin>but every man a liar, as it is written: That</margin> <margin>you may be justified in your words, and over-</margin> <margin>5 come when you are judged. But if our unrighteousness</margin> <margin>demonstrates the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust who inflicts wrath? I speak according to</margin> human <note>Greek: *kata anthrōpon legō*. Erasmus notes this is a way of speaking using human logic to illustrate a divine point.</note> ways.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> uncircumcision has kept the justifications of the law, will not his uncircumcision be reckoned as circumcision? <margin>27</margin> And shall not that which is by nature uncircumcision, if it has kept the law, judge you who through the letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the law? <margin>28</margin> For he is not a Jew who is one in manifest <note>Visible or outward.</note>: nor is that circumcision which is manifest in the flesh: but he who was a Jew in <margin>29</margin> secret, he is a Jew: and the circumcision of the heart is circumcision, which consists in spirit, not in letter: whose praise is not from men, but from God. <margin>III. 1</margin> What therefore does the Jew have in which he excels? Or what is the utility of circumcision? <margin>2</margin> Much in every way: for first indeed, that the oracles of God were committed to them. For what if some were unbelieving? <margin>3</margin> Shall their unbelief <margin>B</margin> make the faith of God void? <margin>4</margin> Far be it: rather let God be true, but every man a liar, as it is written, <margin>7</margin> That you may be justified in your words, and overcome when you are judged. <margin>5</margin> But if our injustice commends the justice of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust, who brings on wrath?

***

<margin>24.</margin> ...been used. <note>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on the name of God being blasphemed.</note> Otherwise, the Hebrew truth <term>Hebrew truth</term><note>A common Renaissance term for the original Hebrew text of the Old Testament.</note> has: *And my name is continually blasphemed all day long.* Saint Jerome, explaining this passage in Isaiah, indicates it can also be referred to Ezekiel, in whose book at chapter 36 it says: *And they entered among the nations to which they went and polluted my holy name, when it was said of them, "This is the people of the Lord," yet they polluted my holy name.* Furthermore, as to what <term>Lyranus</term> <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a highly influential medieval biblical commentator known for his focus on the literal sense of scripture.</note> intended in this place, let him see to it himself. For our edition <note>The Latin Vulgate.</note> agrees with the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> and the Hebrew truth. Nor is there any discrepancy in this place, if any faith is to be had in the common manuscripts. Indeed, I wonder less about Lyranus. But <term>Aquinas</term> <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent scholastic theologian.</note>, who is far more diligent, for some reason introduces a double reading in this place; I will not be burdened to write down his words, so that it may be easier for the reader to judge or inquire about this matter. For when he had cited the passage in Isaiah, *Those who rule over them act wickedly, and my name is continually blasphemed all day long*, he adds from Jerome another testimony: "you were slaves twice." I ask, what is this other reading—or as they call it, the "letter"—which disagrees with the other? Search, inquire, you will find nothing of the sort. Therefore, I suspect Thomas, hurrying to another point, did not draw these from the sources themselves, but from the collections of others. For there are two places in Ezekiel in the same chapter with a similar meaning. The first is what we just cited, in which there is no conflict <margin>D</margin> between the Hebrew truth and the Septuagint Edition. The second, which follows after a short interval, repeating what had already been said and which Aquinas cites: *Not for your sake do I do this, O house of Israel, but for my holy name, which you have polluted among the nations to which you went.* And even here there is no discord between Jerome's translation and the Septuagint. If anyone distrusts us, let him compare both editions joined in the works of Jerome recently published at Basel. Now, what Paul warned the Jews about is much more to be avoided by us Christians: if our life differs in nothing from the life of the Heathen, except for the title of the Christian name and ceremonies—if in other matters it is equal or even more contaminated—there is a danger that the most holy name of Christ may be polluted and treated with insults among the enemies of the faith, the Jews and Turks, if they see us serving lust no less abjectly, gaping for profit no less immoderately, no less eager for revenge, no <margin>E</margin> less fearful of death and greedy for life, no less furiously warring, rioting, and sword-fighting for however slight causes. *By you it is blasphemed.* In Greek it is <note>original: *di’ hymas*</note>, that is, "because of you," so that you understand it is not the instrument, but the cause.

<margin>33 For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly]</margin> In this place, we have explained with several words the brevity which the prepositive articles provide to the Greeks, so that the sense might be clearer—but in such a way that we did not change the meaning even in the slightest—in this manner: "He is not a Jew who is one in the manifest: nor is that circumcision which is manifest in the flesh: but he who was a Jew in secret, he is a Jew: and the heart’s circumcision is circumcision, which consists in spirit, not in letter."

<margin>1 What then is the advantage]</margin> The Greek word <note>original: *perisson*</note> sometimes signifies "superfluous," sometimes "excellent," that is, <note>original: *exa構成reton*</note>. Here "excellent" is taken for excellence, for there follows <margin>F</margin> <note>original: *to Ioudaiou*</note>, that is, "in what the Jew excels."

<margin>2 Much]</margin> <note>original: *Poly*</note>. Thus it is also found among the Greeks with a "y." Although it seems it should be read as <note>original: *polla*</note>, with a double "l" and an "a," as an epithet for this noun "utility" (<note>original: *ōpheleia*</note>). "First" (<note>original: *prōton*</note>) here signifies the order of the discourse rather than "chiefly."

<margin>3 the oracles were entrusted to them]</margin> "To them" is not in the Greek, but the Translator added it necessarily: <note>original: *episteuthēsan ta logia tou Theou*</note>, that is, "the oracles were believed," meaning they were "entrusted" or "committed" to them. For the Greeks speak this way: "I was entrusted with this care," "this way of life is entrusted to me," that is, "this province was committed to me," "this knowledge was delegated to me," as if you said in Greek "he is credited this thing" and "I am committed this business"; just as the Latins say, "I am taught Grammar." Furthermore, what we read as "eloquia" [utterances/words], in Paul is <note>original: *logia*</note>; <term>Origen</term> <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD). Erasmus often critiques his commentators.</note> philosophizes somewhat on this word. However, he called the oracles *logia* because that people kept the oracles, which would be more profitable to others than to themselves, and they held them without understanding them; for thus <term>Hesychius</term> <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian and lexicographer.</note> interprets *logia* as "divine sayings," "prophecies," "fame," "oracles," that is, prophecy,

responses, predictions, rumors, oracles. And in this sense it is frequently repeated in Aristophanes' *The Knights*. Among the Latins, Juvenal sometimes used it for eloquence:

-> The eloquence and fame of Demosthenes... <-

<margin>4 Made void]</margin> In Greek it is the future tense <note>original: *katargēsei*</note>, that is, "will you abolish," "obliterate," "render void," or "make obsolete," a word which Saint Paul frequently uses. The Translator often renders it as "to destroy." <note>original: *Argos*</note> means "idle," hence <note>original: *katargein*</note> means to render "idle" and "superfluous."

<margin>5 Far be it]</margin> Frequently encountered in Paul. In Greek it is <note>original: *Mē genoito*</note>, that is, "let it not be," or "may it not happen," or "God avert or prohibit it." It is the speech of someone filled with loathing.

<margin>6 but let God be]</margin> In Greek it is <note>original: *ginesthō*</note>, "let God be" or "let God become true." Perhaps the Translator had rendered it as <note>original: *eiē*</note>, as the Translator of Theophylact (falsely inscribed as Athanasius until now) rendered it. But <note>original: *ginesthō*</note> is placed for "let it be declared," "let it be shown." For it cannot happen that God is not true, but it concerns us that men understand Him to be such. Although it can be used <note>original: *doxologikōs*</note> [in praise], just as we say, "Glory to you, O Lord."

<margin>7 That you may be justified in your words]</margin> The testimony is from the fiftieth Psalm [Psalm 51]: "that you may be justified." And "when you are judged," in Greek the verb is passive, <note>original: *en tō krinesthai se*</note>, or as others read, "to judge." However, for the Hebrews, <note>original: *yizkeh*</note> <margin>C</margin> is ambiguous, whether it speaks of God being judged or of Him judging. Jerome seems to interpret this place so that he understands God as having been judged, but while He is judged by the unbelieving, both His faithfulness in promises is declared and their vanity in judging. Thus "every man is a liar," either because he cannot perform what he promises whenever it is up to him, or because whoever distrusts God's promises is a liar, since He performs everything.

<margin>8 But if our iniquity commends the justice of God]</margin> <note>original: *synistēsi*</note>, that is, "establishes," which is to say "stabilizes" and "confirms" and "supports." Although "commends" also translates it correctly. For, if we believe Hesychius, <note>original: *synistēsin*</note> declares many things to the Greeks: "to praise," "to make manifest," "to confirm," "to present" or "to commend." Origen himself, explaining <margin>E</margin> that passage of Paul a little later, "But God commends his charity in us," indicates that "commends" has the same power as "confirms" or "makes lovable."

<margin>9 Is God unjust who inflicts wrath]</margin> Origen, explaining this passage—or if you prefer, Jerome or Ruffinus—shows that in some Greek codices it is read: "who inflicts wrath against man." Certainly, so that the phrase "I speak as a man" (<note>original: *anthrōpōn legō*</note>), that is, "I speak according to man," is written as "against man" (<note>original: *kat' anthrōpou*</note>), with the word "I speak" omitted. The Translator, I believe, added the other reading of Origen found in Latin manuscripts, and even in some Greek ones. Since he rejects neither reading, everyone will be free to follow whichever he prefers. Certainly Chrysostom and Theophylact read and interpret together "I speak according to man" (<note>original: *kata anthrōpon legō*</note>), that is, "I speak according to human sense," responding for God, as His judgments are inscrutable. Hitherto the title and the conclusion of Origen's commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans misled me into believing they were translated by Jerome, even though I <margin>F</margin> doubted the phrasing somewhat; yet here it seemed to me purer than in the other versions of <term>Ruffinus</term> <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410), a monk and translator known for his controversial translations of Origen.</note>. However, I was more offended by many additions, which partly could not be said by a Greek writer ignorant of the Roman tongue, and partly fight diametrically with Origen's dogmas. Jerome, moreover, is more scrupulous in translating than Ruffinus, who not only permits himself to interweave several of his own opinions but even omits entire books and substitutes his own in their place. Hence I almost entirely side with those who think this version is by Ruffinus. For it is probable the title was changed by a scribe to make the book more salable through the charm of a popular name. By the same trick, in the conclusion, Ruffinus's name was twice changed to Jerome's. However, enough was left behind to betray the deception. For he says he is urged by Gaudentius to finish [the translation of] Clement, which he had begun to translate. Now, it is well known that Clement was translated by Ruffinus and dedicated to Gaudentius. Ruffinus was heard by many as an "Origenist," and so he warns in the conclusion that, omitting the name of the Translator, the scribe should put the name of the Author.

<summary>Erasmus provides a detailed philological and theological commentary on Romans 2:26 through 3:5, emphasizing the internal nature of faith and critiquing historical translations and commentaries by Aquinas, Lyranus, and Ruffinus.</summary>

In the previous section, Erasmus explored the advantage of the Jewish people and the faithfulness of God. # THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER III.

<margin>D</margin> <margin>10 God will judge this world</margin> ] <note>original: τὸν κόσμον</note> *the world*, that is, the world, not *this* world, as if there were another world, except that the added article sometimes serves to designate a specific thing.
<margin>11 As we are slandered</margin> ] He used the Greek word βλασφημούμεθα <note>original: blasphēmoumetha</note>, that is, we are ill-reputed, or men speak poorly of us.
<margin>12 Let us do evil</margin> ] Not ineptly did he omit ὅτι <note>original: hoti, meaning "that"</note>, which he otherwise tends to add freely even when there is no need.
<margin>13 We excel them</margin> ] <note>original: προεχόμεθα / proechometha</note>. The word "them" is not added in the Greek, but it is simply "we surpass" or "we excel." Indeed, the Greeks place a distinction after these words, *what then?* Otherwise, it could be read together as, *In what then do we excel?*
<margin>14 We have charged</margin> ] <note>original: προῃτιασάμεθα / proēitiasametha</note>, that is, we have previously given the cause.
<margin>15 And all under sin</margin> ] And the conjunction is redundant.
<margin>16 Because there is no one righteous</margin> ] <note>original: ὅτι / hoti</note>. "Because" is redundant and should have been omitted in this place, just as he did a little before. *Anyone righteous*, <note>original: οὐδὲ εἷς / oude heis</note>, that is, not even one.
<margin>17 Seeking</margin> ] <note>original: ὁ ἐκζητῶν / ho ekzētōn</note>, that is, the one who seeks out. For we "require" (seek) not what we track down, but what we grieve to find missing; as we require loyalty in a friend.
<margin>18 Cursing</margin> ] <note>original: ἀρᾶς / aras</note>, that is, devotion to destruction, execration, or imprecation. Furthermore, I wish to advise the reader in passing that this testimony, which Paul took from the Old Testament, is woven together from various places and is, so to speak, "patched together." <note>Erasmus is noting that Paul is quoting several different scriptures in a row.</note> For the first part is taken from Psalm 13, but in such a way that the Apostle rendered the meaning more than the exact words. The next two verses, *Their throat is an open grave. With their tongues they dealt deceitfully*, are from the fifth Psalm. That which follows, *The poison of asps is under their lips*, is from Psalm 139. Again, what is annexed, *Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness*, is taken from the ninth Psalm. Furthermore, the three verses that follow, *Their feet are swift to shed blood. Ruin and unhappiness are in their ways. And the way of peace they have not known*, etc., are plucked from Isaiah. The last verse, *There is no fear of God before their eyes*, is at the beginning of the thirty-fifth Psalm. Some unknown person interwove these eight verses into Psalm 13 because they could not find a suitable place to refer to Paul’s testimony, as they are not found in the Hebrew manuscripts. Jerome pointed this out, explaining the cited passage of Isaiah, and again more fully in his preface to the sixteenth commentary. Moreover, the parts borrowed from Isaiah are found in that Prophet in chapter 59, according to the Hebrew truth, in this manner: *Their thoughts are useless thoughts, wasting and destruction are in their paths. They have not known the way of peace, and there is no judgment in their steps.*
<margin>E</margin> <margin>19 Subject</margin> ] <note>original: ὑπόδικος / hypodikos</note>. As if you were to say, liable and guilty. For *dikē* among the Greeks signifies both a crime, a cause, and vengeance or punishment—as one bound to punishment.

<margin>20 Knowledge of sin</margin> ] <note>original: ἐπίγνωσις / epignōsis</note>. "Recognition" <note>original: agnitio</note> was more elegant and significant than "knowledge" <note>original: cognitio</note>.
<margin>D</margin> <margin>21 But now without the law the righteousness of God is manifested</margin> ] Augustine, in *Against Pelagius and Celestius on the Grace of Christ*, book 1, chapter 8, indicates a distinction in this sentence: for it should be pronounced, *The righteousness of God without the law, is now manifested*. There would be something to what he says if the article had been placed before the adverb, <note>original: Νυνὶ δὲ ἡ χωρὶς νόμου δικαιοσύνη</note>. Since that was not done, it is to be understood that the righteousness of God has been promulgated to all, and will be profitable without the protection of the law. Although for the meaning, it matters very little how you distinguish it. I will subscribe Augustine's words: *How then*, he says, *is it manifested without the law, if it is testified by the law? It is not manifested "without the law" in that sense, but rather it is "righteousness without the law": which is the righteousness of God.* Thus Augustine. The scruple that moved Augustine is of no weight. The righteousness of God has been manifested through faith and grace by the coming of Christ, but the law had predicted that this would happen.
<margin>22 And they lack</margin> ] In Greek it is <note>original: ὑστεροῦνται / hysterountai</note>, that is, they lack or are destitute; literally it sounds like they "are left behind," as if not attaining what they desired. And *glory* among the Greeks is *grace* <note>Erasmus is debating the nuances of *doxa* (glory) and *charis* (grace)</note>, not "grace" as we read <margin>E</margin> even in the more corrected Latin manuscripts, <note>original: δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ / doxēs tou Theou</note>, *the glory of God*. For God is glorified in this, that out of his goodness he saves the human race.
<margin>23 Justified freely</margin> ] <note>original: Δικαιούμενοι / dikaioumenoi</note>. It is a passive participle, but in the present tense: whence we translated it, *Being justified*, having added a little conjunction of my own so that I might make the sense clearer.
<margin>24 Through redemption</margin> ] <note>original: διὰ τῆς ἀπολυτρώσεως / dia tēs apolytrōseōs</note>. Which is properly the redemption of a captive, once the price has been paid for his head, which the common folk of the Gauls call a *rançon* (ransom): *which is in Christ Jesus*, and here it seems to be put in place of "through," which redemption happens through Christ Jesus; for he repeats this so that he may again exclude the glory of human works.
<margin>25 Propitiator</margin> ] <note>original: ἱλαστήριον / hilastērion</note>, that is, propitiation, or rather "propitiatory" (mercy seat), so that, as Origen prefers, it may look back to the mercy seat of the Jews, a type of our Christ, just as he also mentions the blood. Theophylact explains it in the same way, <margin>F</margin> and before him Chrysostom; and finally Augustine in the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 13. Perhaps the translator takes the masculine gender *ton hilastērion*, just as *ton sōtērion* (the Savior).
<margin>26 On account of remission</margin> ] It is a marvel that Ambrose, following a particular copy, reads *on account of the purpose of preceding offenses*. For the Greeks have *paresin* (remission/passing over), not *prothesin* (purpose), unless by chance the Ambrosian codex is faulty. Although in his interpretation he adds, *God knowing the purpose of his kindness*, it suggests he read "purpose" and not "remission." Augustine reads it the same way in the place we just indicated.
<margin>27 In forbearance</margin> ] <note>original: ἐν τῇ ἀνοχῇ / en tē anochē</note>, that is, in patience and tolerance.
<margin>28 Where then is</margin> ] And the Translator added the word "therefore" <note>original: οὖν / oun</note>. For in Greek it is, *Where...* <unclear>pou</unclear>...

# TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER IV.
