*...it is, "How then was it credited?" That is to say, "Where then is the boasting?" In the same way, the matter is indeed settled. Such inquiries are very common in spoken discourse <note>Erasmus uses the term "achronon," meaning timeless or following the rhythm of speech</note>, especially when the matter has already been proved by arguments.*

*29 **We judge therefore**] <note>original: "Λογιζόμεθα οὖν"</note>. We reckon, or we conclude therefore. For Theophylact interprets this as "we conclude by reasoning," <note>original: "συλλογιζόμεθα"</note> as if Paul has now gathered this point through the process of argumentation.*

*30 **Indeed, also of the Gentiles**] In place of the Latin "parà," the Greek has "nai," <note>original: "ναὶ"</note> which is an adverb of affirmation, as if you were saying, "certainly, of the Gentiles as well."*

*31 **Who justifies**] <note>original: "δικαιώσει"</note>, he will justify, in the future tense. For he was looking toward those who were still in Judaism or Paganism. In the codex of Saint Donatian, it was written "justified" <note>original: "justificavit"</note>, with the letter 'b' changed to a consonant 'v', a mistake that scribes frequently make.*

*32 **Do we then destroy the law**] <note>original: "καταργοῦμεν"</note>, that is, we make it void, or we abolish it, as we showed a little earlier. Furthermore, regarding what follows, "we establish the law," the word "histamen" <note>original: "ἵσταμεν"</note> is used in the sense of propping up or stabilizing, making something stand that was wavering. Otherwise, "to establish" <note>original: "statuere"</note> sounds different to Latin ears, meaning "to decree."*

**1** ***What then shall we say, that Abraham our father according to the flesh has found?*** *It is uncertain where this little phrase "according to the flesh" refers: to "Abraham our father," or to the word "found." I know that in most Greek manuscripts the order is: "What then shall we say, that Abraham our father has found according to the flesh?" But Origen reads it differently, as does Ambrose, and it is found differently in the ancient Latin manuscripts—namely, with this distinction, that "our father" is joined directly to the phrase "according to the flesh." For Paul means that Abraham, according to his calling to faith, is the father of the Gentiles as well, but he is the father of the Jews only according to the flesh. Theophylact interprets it this way: "He calls him father according to the flesh," he says, "excluding them from spiritual kinship, or rather leading them back to the memory of his circumcision in all things." <note>original Greek: "Πατέρα δὲ... κατὰ πάντα."</note> That is, he calls him father according to the flesh, excluding them from spiritual relationship, or rather compelling them to imitate him in all things. Chrysostom says similar things: "He called him father according to the flesh, excluding them from the true kinship with him, and opening a way for the Gentiles to attain affinity with Abraham." <note>original Greek: "Πατέρα δὲ... ἀγχιστείαν."</note> And yet, the order of the Greek speech indicates another sense, which would require us to accept a transposition of words <term>hyperbaton: a figure of speech where the natural order of words is shifted for emphasis</term>; otherwise, it should have been read: "What then shall we say, that Abraham the father according to the flesh has found?" Therefore, we were not afraid to restore this speech to its original order. Although it does not escape me that Ambrose interprets this passage such that "according to the flesh" refers to "found": so that we understand the Mosaic Law is so incapable of providing salvation that not even Abraham himself obtained anything "according to the flesh"—that is, through circumcision—unless he had pleased God by the merit of faith.*

**2** ***He has glory***] <note>original: "ἀπόκριμα"</note> signifies "boasting" more than "glory," just as "kauchesis" <note>original: "καύχησις"</note> does; that is, he has something to boast about and to brag of.*

**3** ***Abraham believed***] Origen debates this somewhat, hesitating whether it is by a scribe's error that "Abraham" is read instead of "Abram"—that is, a three-syllable name instead of a two-syllable one—because at the time he believed God's promise, he was not yet Abraham, but Abram. Thus, it is consistent that among the Hebrews it is not "Abraham believed God," but "Abram believed." And the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated it as "Abram." I certainly praise the man’s diligence, and I am ashamed of our own laziness. However, in this place, if the speech refers to the one who wrote it—whether it was Moses, or Ezra, or someone else—he was certainly "Abraham" to them. Furthermore, where God is narrated to call him by name, he is called "Abram," not "Abraham," until his name was increased by the addition of a syllable. There are those who say that even in some faulty Latin manuscripts, "Abram" is read here instead of "Abraham."*

**4** ***And it was reputed***] <note>original: "ἐλογίσθη"</note>, that is, it was "imputed" or "credited" in this specific place. For the Greek word has multiple meanings. However, it is a very different thing*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the law of faith. <margin>29</margin> We judge therefore that <margin>28</margin>
a man is justified by faith without the works 
of the law. Is he the God of the Jews 
only? Is he not also the God of the Gentiles? <margin>30</margin>

we establish the law. <margin>IV. 1</margin> What then shall we 
say that Abraham our father according to the flesh <margin>IV.</margin>
has found? For if <margin>2</margin> Abraham was justified 
from works, he has something to boast about, 
but not before God. For what does the Scripture 
say? <margin>3</margin> Abraham believed God, and it was <margin>3</margin>

one who works, the <margin>4</margin> reward is not imputed 
according to grace, but according to 
debt. <margin>5</margin> Furthermore, to the one who does not work, 
but believes in <margin>B</margin> him who justifies the ungodly,

Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, <margin>7</margin> 
and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the <margin>8</margin> 
man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin. 
<margin>9</margin> Does this blessedness then come upon <margin>9</margin> 
the circumcision only, or also upon the 
uncircumcision? For we say that faith 
was imputed to Abraham for righteousness. 
How then was it imputed? When <margin>10</margin> 
he was in circumcision, or when he was in 
uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in 
uncircumcision. And he received a sign... <margin>11</margin>
<meta>catchword: received</meta>

---

<margin>C</margin> *...to "repute" than to "impute." To repute is to consider in the mind; to impute is to credit as received, or to add to an account, usually without blame. To "depute" is the same as to calculate or to estimate, whereas the Greek word is "polysemous" <note>having many meanings</note> for reputing, imputing, and estimating. "Ellogizesthai" <note>original: "ἐλλογίζεσθαι"</note> properly sounds like "to impute," a word the Apostle used elsewhere. Nor is it without cause that Valla <term>Lorenzo Valla: a Renaissance humanist who critiqued the Vulgate Bible</term> criticizes the childish affectation of variety in the Translator here, since he translates the same Greek word in the same passage sometimes as "reputed," sometimes as "accepted," and sometimes as "imputed," as if it were a sin to repeat the same word several times.*

<margin>E</margin> **5** ***To the one who does not work, but believes***] *Both are participles in the Greek, "to the one working" and "but believing." <note>original: "τῷ ἐργαζομένῳ, πιστεύοντι δὲ"</note> And again, "reputed" is used for "imputed." "According to the purpose of the grace of God": this clause is not in the Greek codices. Even if Ambrose reads and explains these words specifically. From this it appears that he used a different copy. In the very ancient codex provided by John Colet <note>Founder of St. Paul's School and friend of Erasmus</note> from the Pauline Library, they were not in the main text, but were added in the margin by a different and more recent hand.*

<margin>D</margin> **6** ***Accepted***] <note>original: "λογίζεται"</note>, that is, "he imputes" or "he accepts." To "accept as received" <term>acceptilatio: a Roman legal term for the formal discharging of a debt</term> means to treat as received what you have not actually received, which among legal experts, if I am not mistaken, is called "acceptilation."*

**7** ***Has not imputed***] <note>original: "λογίζεται"</note> is in the future tense, although it could be the aorist subjunctive if it were written with the letter "eta" <note>original: "λογίσηται"</note>, meaning "he might have imputed"; although these are also used for future tenses.*

**8** ***Remains only***] *I do not find "remains" among the Greeks. The Greek codices have it thus: "Is this blessedness then upon the circumcision, or upon the uncircumcision?" <note>original: "Ὁ μακαρισμὸς... ἀκροβυστίαν;"</note> That is, this happiness, or blessedness, or blessing—does it apply to the circumcision or the uncircumcision? You must understand a word like "comes," "belongs," or a similar verb; and so the Greek commentaries read and interpret it. Theophylact, in his explanation, instead of the verb "remains" provided by the Translator, substitutes "falls" <note>original: "πίπτει"</note>, that is, "falls to" or "belongs to": just as we say, "Anger does not fall upon <note>suit</note> a wise man." And indeed, I wonder if the Translator, desiring to explain Paul's mind, wrote "manat" (flows) into the circumcision, which was later changed into "manet" (remains). Otherwise, the preposition "epi" (upon) would be harshly joined to the accusative case. The verb can also be repeated from above: "David spoke of blessedness, etc." Was this blessedness therefore spoken only regarding the circumcision, or also regarding the uncircumcision? It should also be noted that in Origen and Ambrose the word "only" is added, which I do not find in the common Greek codices, nor even in the ancient Latin copies. Certainly, in that Pauline codex I find it written this way: "Is this blessedness then in circumcision, or also in uncircumcision?" Although I would not deny that the force of that adverb "only" lies hidden in the conjunction "kai" (and/also), "or *also* in uncircumcision," which they added to make it clearer. Nor do I think this should be neglected: "blessedness" <note>original: "μακαρισμὸν"</note> is taken here not for the quality of being blessed itself, but for the *proclamation* of blessedness, which David attributes to a man not from works, but from the grace of God through faith that does not impute sins. For among the Greeks, those who are proclaimed blessed—even falsely—are called "makarismoi." Moreover, he calls "righteousness" here not universal virtue, but the innocence that happens by the free pardon of sins. Furthermore, blessedness and righteousness are naturally linked: from which it follows that upon whomever the praise of righteousness falls, upon the same also falls the praise of blessedness. But the praise of righteousness is attributed to Abraham while not yet circumcised: therefore, upon him, and through him upon the uncircumcised nations, falls the praise of blessedness which David, who was circumcised, proclaims. Thus, uncircumcision not only shares a part with circumcision, but even excels in this: that it earned this praise before circumcision was ever born.*

<margin>F</margin> **9** ***in circumcision***] <note>original: "ἐν περιτομῇ ὄντι"</note>, that is, "while he was in circumcision," which is the same as if he had said "to the one circumcised," just as "in uncircumcision" is for one who was "uncircumcised." Besides the grace of the question, the addition of "being" <note>original: "ὄντι"</note> does much; by rejecting one side, it proves the other. For no type of argument is either more clear or more forceful.*

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s philological and theological examination of Romans Chapter 4. On the previous page, Erasmus began discussing Paul’s argument that Abraham’s righteousness was credited to him through faith before he was circumcised. This page explores the specific Greek terminology Paul uses to describe circumcision as a "seal" and investigates the textual variants in the Greek manuscripts regarding the relationship between Jews, Gentiles, and the faith of Abraham.</meta>

### EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER IV.

...he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had while still uncircumcised, so that he might be the father of all who believe while uncircumcised, so that righteousness might also be credited to them.

12 And the father of circumcision to those who are not only of the circumcision, but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith which our father Abraham had while still uncircumcised.

13 For the promise to Abraham or his offspring that he would be heir of the world was not through the law, but through the righteousness of faith.

14 For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith is made void,

15 and the promise is nullified. For the law brings about wrath; for where there is no law, there is no transgression.

16 Therefore it is by faith, so that it may be according to grace, in order that the promise may be certain to all the offspring—not only to those of the law, but also to those of the faith 

17 of Abraham, who is the father of us all (as it is written, "I have made you a father of many nations"), in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead, and 

<column-break/>

...he received the sign of circumcision, and a seal of the righteousness of faith, which had been in his uncircumcision, so that he might be the father of all believing through uncircumcision, so that righteousness might be imputed also to them,

12 And the father of circumcision to those who would not only derive their descent from circumcision, but would also walk in the footsteps of the faith, which was in the uncircumcision of our father Abraham.

13 For the promise did not happen to Abraham, or to his seed, through the law, that he should be the heir of the world, but through the righteousness of faith. For if those who belong to the law are heirs, faith is made empty, and the promise is made void. For the law works wrath: since where there is no law, there is no transgression.

16 Therefore the inheritance is given by faith, so that it may be according to grace, that the promise might be firm to all the seed, not only to that which is of the law, but also to that which is of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of all of us: As it is written, I have appointed you the father of many nations, namely after the example of God in whom he had believed, who restores the dead to life, and calls those things which are not, as—

---

10 <term>signaculum</term> <note>original: "seal"</note>] Paul uses two words: <term>σημεῖον</term> <note>original: "sign"</note> and <term>σφραγῖδα</term> <note>original: "seal"</note>. The latter is <term>signum</term> <note>original: "a sign"</note> and a mark pressed into something. For the sake of reliability, we usually seal what we want to be certain. In this way, we seal what we want to be set aside and hidden for a time, to be brought out in its proper place. Otherwise, Paul might seem to have said the same thing twice, having said "sign" just before repeating "seal." For the Greeks, a <term>σημεῖον</term> is a sign by which something else is signified. Indeed, that fleshly circumcision then bore the type of Christian circumcision, which does not remove a piece of skin, but cuts away all harmful desires from the heart. It was also a <term>signaculum</term> <note>original: "seal"</note> to cover the mystery for a time until it was opened—namely, the mystery of righteousness, which is conferred through faith. Someone can be a "sign" without being a "seal," just as a statue is a sign, but the symbol on a ring for another's contract is a <term>σφραγίς</term> <note>original: "seal"</note>. There is a specific phrasing here. The same thing is called a "sign" insofar as it declares righteousness from faith which was in Abraham before circumcision, and a "seal" insofar as, by Abraham's example, righteousness from faith without circumcision was promised to all believers. This was noted carefully by Origen <note>An influential early Christian theologian and scholar (c. 184–253 AD)</note>.

<margin>A</margin> 11 <term>Not to those only who are of the circumcision</term>] The Greek reads quite differently: <term>τοῖς οὐκ ἐκ περιτομῆς μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς στοιχοῦσι τοῖς ἴχνεσι</term>, that is, <term>who are not only of the circumcision, but also walk in the footsteps</term> etc. This is so you understand that for Jewish sons, this birth of righteousness does not make one a son of Abraham unless he walks in the same footsteps, which is the mark of true sons. Ambrose <note>The 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note> agrees with me, reading it this way: <term>That he might be the father of the circumcision of those who are not only of the circumcision, but also of those who follow the footsteps of faith</term>. Origen’s interpretation does not shrink from this reading, signifying that the Jews would only have Abraham as a father if they belonged to the faith, which had earned him the title of "righteous" before he was circumcised. Certainly, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), known for his eloquent preaching</note> agrees with me, even if Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and biblical commentator</note> explains it somewhat differently. In the manuscript I used, the scribe had negligently omitted "and" (<term>καὶ</term>). That little word was written into others in the wrong place, "not to those only," while Chrysostom reads "to those not only," and the statement should match the distinction. For he does not mean by these words that Abraham is the father of both Jews and Gentiles, but that he is not the father of the Jews unless they follow his footsteps. For he said before that he is the father of all nations—not simply all, but those who believe. He calls him the father of the Jews here so that they would not think it enough to be born from Abraham’s lineage; he shows that blood relation is useless unless they prove themselves his true sons by imitating his faith. The article being repeated against normal usage, <term>ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς</term> <note>original: "but also to those"</note>, is somewhat offensive. However, it is possible that the scribe added something to that syllable. Having obtained a Greek manuscript of Theophylact again, I inspected the passage more closely. He indeed repeats the same reading I indicated, with the "and" (<term>καὶ</term>) added above the line, noting how it should be read, although he does not disagree with Chrysostom in meaning. The one who translated Theophylact rendered the Greek in a way that I don't know if he fully understood; therefore, I will not be burdened to render this passage in good faith: <term>He dissolves the existing offering. For perhaps someone was going to say, if Abraham was justified while he was uncircumcised, for what grace was he circumcised? To this he answers, that he received circumcision as a sign in place of a seal, which would seal and proclaim that very justification from faith, which faith he had shown earlier while uncircumcised. Thus, since these two things are now considered in Abraham—uncircumcision and circumcision—through uncircumcision he is declared the father of the uncircumcised. But of which ones? Those who believed in the same way he had believed, so that faith might be credited to them for righteousness, that is, so they might become righteous. Through circumcision, on the other hand, he is declared the father of circumcision, that is, of the circumcised. But he is a father not only to those who have circumcision, but also to those who walk in the footsteps of his faith, which faith he had in uncircumcision.</term> Therefore, it must be read in this way: "And he would be the father of circumcision, not to those who resemble him in circumcision only, but also to those who walk in the footsteps of faith," that is, who believe in the same way he did in the resurrection of dead bodies, etc. The translator omitted certain words and added one. I suspect, however, that the passage in Theophylact is not without error. When he advises how it should be read, it is probable that he placed the reading which Chrysostom followed, since the rest of the commentary shows he follows the same opinion. But I believe I see the end of this difficulty, so that neither the repeated article nor the transposed negation causes offense.

<column-break/>

<margin>C</margin> ...the negation, as Chrysostom interprets it, but toward <term>ἐν περιτομῇ</term> <note>original: "in circumcision"</note>, so that we understand two ranks among the Jews: one who have nothing of Abraham except that they are circumcised (and he denies Abraham is their father), and the other of those who, besides circumcision, also imitate his faith; of these latter ones, he wants Abraham to be the father. Theophylact followed this sense and this reading, and it is not different from Chrysostom’s view. But here the conjunction "and" (<term>καὶ</term>) makes a noise, being placed in the wrong spot: <term>ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς</term> <note>original: "but also to those"</note>. If you read <term>ἀλλὰ τοῖς καί</term> <note>original: "but to those also"</note>, not even a tiny bit of doubt remains. It is probable that this happened through the carelessness of scribes. Both readings have a universal <note>original: "catholic"</note> and almost identical sense. In both, however, there is a small doubt: in the former about the repeated article <term>τοῖς</term>, in the latter about the transposed <term>καὶ</term>. The former, with the article removed, will be: <term>to those not only of circumcision, but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith which was in uncircumcision</term>. The latter is: <term>not to those who are nothing else but circumcised, but to those who also walk in the footsteps of faith</term>, so that the conjunction "also" repeats the circumcision. The latter is more approved by me. The translator rendered neither reading, though I suspect the place has been corrupted by copyists.

<margin>D</margin> 13 <term>For the promise to Abraham was not through the law</term>] <term>τὸ κληρονόμον αὐτὸν εἶναι τοῦ κόσμου</term> <note>original: "that he should be heir of the world"</note>. It would have been better to add here, <term>it happened that he was the heir of the world, or would be the heir of the world</term>.

13 <term>Was abolished</term>] <term>κατήργηται</term> <note>A Greek word meaning "to render useless" or "to nullify"</note>. Although he translated the same word in various ways, he did so correctly in this place: <term>it was made void, it was abolished, it was made obsolete</term>.

14 <term>Not only to him who is of the law</term>] Among the Greeks, "Abraham" seems to be in the dative case, so that it belongs to the pronoun <term>εἰ</term> <note>original: "if"</note>; otherwise he would have added: <term>to the Abraham or to the one in the law only, but also to the one from the faith of Abraham</term>. That is, not only to that Abraham who is peculiar to the Jews through the law, but also to the one who is common to all Gentiles through faith—as if you were to imagine two Abrahams in one. Although the other sense does not displease me, this latter one is more subtle. For just as he makes two Adams, the earthly and the heavenly, so he makes as if two Abrahams: the one justified in uncircumcision through faith, who is the spiritual father of the Gentiles; and the one justified through faith in circumcision, who is the father of believing Jews by a double title. Although I see most people follow a different opinion. But what we read, "not to him who is of the law only," was more fitting because "seed" had preceded it. He mentioned the "seed" later here, according to the characteristic of Hebrew speech.

<margin>E</margin> 15 <term>Because I have placed you as a father of many nations</term>] If it is not permitted to omit anything, why did he elsewhere omit the superfluous conjunction "that" (<term>ὅτι</term>)? If it is allowed anywhere, it certainly should have been omitted here. Thomas Aquinas <note>The famous 13th-century Scholastic philosopher and theologian</note> indicates that some manuscripts have "appointed" instead of "placed." He would have noted other things of greater importance if his skill in languages had permitted it. For he knew only one language, and even that not fully. However, among the Greeks, "to place" is frequently used for "to make." Furthermore, the passage is from Genesis 17. In that place, it should be noted in passing that in the prophetic manner, the past tense is used for the future: "I have appointed" for "I will appoint."

<margin>F</margin> 16 <term>In whom you believed</term>] In Greek it is <term>κατέναντι οὗ ἐπίστευσε Θεοῦ</term>, that is, <term>in the presence of the God in whom he believed</term>; so Augustine <note>The 5th-century Bishop of Hippo and Latin Father</note> says. Or, <term>after the example of the God in whom he believed</term>. For Paul referred this to his own person. He means that just as God is not the God of this or that nation only, but common to all, so Abraham would be the father of all believers. For Chrysostom, Theophylact, and the Greek scholia interpret it this way: <term>before God</term>, lest anyone should scatter it as our dream. For we reflect the pattern placed opposite us. Although Ambrose reads "invisurus," <note>original: "about to see"</note> that is, "in whom you believed," so that it refers to the Gentile whom he addresses. For he says: <term>In order to teach that there is one God of all, he addresses the Gentiles</term>. Nor is the singular number an obstacle, since this kind of <term>ἐπεργασία</term> <note>A rhetorical elaboration or additional explanation</note> is frequent in Paul. Origen likewise indicates that this clause, "before the God in whom you believed," was added from Paul's own person, but he reads "he believed," not "whom you believed."

17 <term>As though they are</term>] <term>ὡς ὄντα</term>, that is, <term>as if they are; for it is not 'as if they were'</term>. He said more than that it was dead; he said it "was not." And according to the Greek truth, Augustine brings this passage up while explaining Psalm 14: <term>For he called the famine, who calls those things which are not as though they are</term>. Nor did the Apostle say there, "who calls those things which are not *so that* they are," but "as though they *are*." For ancient writers also used to say things "were not" if they were of no weight. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero, the Roman statesman and orator</note> seems to call the will of a certain Minutius "nothing" <note>original: "nullum"</note> because it was "invalid" and rejected by law; and the Greeks call "invalid" laws <term>νόμους οὐκ ὄντας</term> <note>original: "laws that are not"</note>.

He critiques Thomas Aquinas’s lack of linguistic skill and uses classical authors like Cicero to explain Paul’s rhetorical style.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of the Epistle to the Romans, specifically concluding Chapter 4 and beginning the famous discourse on justification by faith in Chapter 5. Erasmus is comparing Greek manuscripts with the Latin Vulgate, focusing on the character of Abraham's faith and the theological shift from "having peace" to "let us have peace" with God.</meta>

-># TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER V.<-

<margin>18</margin> ...who calls things that are not as though they were. **Against hope, he believed in hope**, so that he might become the father of many nations, according to what had been said, "So shall your <margin>19</margin> offspring be." **And not being weak in faith**, he did not consider his own body, already dead (since he was about a hundred years <margin>20</margin> old), or the deadness of Sarah’s womb. **He did not waver at the promise of God through unbelief**, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, <margin>21</margin> **and being fully convinced that what He had promised He was <margin>22</margin> also able to perform. And therefore it was credited to him as <margin>23</margin> righteousness. Now it was not written for his sake alone that it was <margin>24</margin> credited to him, but also for us**, to whom it shall be credited, if we believe in Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead, <margin>25</margin> **who was delivered up for our trespasses, and was raised for our justification.** <margin>V. 1</margin> **Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, <margin>2</margin> through whom also we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and...**

***

<margin>A</margin> ...void and abolished. Saint Jerome, in the first chapter of Jeremiah, refers to this passage: *Who called those things which were not, as if they were;* <note>original: "Qui vocavit ea quæ non erant, quasi ea quæ essent"</note> he differs from us in words, but agrees in substance.

18 **Against [hope]** <note>original: "παρ' ἐλπίδα"</note>, that is, beyond hope or outside of hope; this means that even when there appeared to be nothing that could be hoped for, he nevertheless held the highest faith in God’s promise.

19 **In [faith]** <note>original: "ἐλπίδι ἐπίστευσεν"</note>, that is, he used hope, or he trusted in hope. Although some manuscripts have *in hope* <note>original: "in ἐλπίδι"</note> or *under hope*. This is a pleasant play on the same word, relating opposites to one another: as if you were to say, he hoped in hopeless things, and when there was no hope, he nevertheless hoped, distrusting himself and trusting God. For that faith is most pleasing to God which, whenever we are deprived of our own resources, hangs entirely upon God. Thus Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom was a 4th-century Archbishop famous for his preaching</note> neatly distinguishes it as **beyond human hope, in the hope of God** <note>original: "παρ' ἐλπίδα τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην, ἐπ' ἐλπίδι τῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note>. He calls "the hope of God" that which Abraham held in the promises of God.

20 **That he might become]** <note>original: "εἰς τὸ γενέσθαι αὐτὸν πατέρα"</note> it would have been better to say, **that he would be a father**. For that was what he hoped for beyond hope. It would also have been clearer to say "according to what had been said" rather than "as it was said." Otherwise, the Translator added the pronoun for the sake of explanation.

21 **As the stars of heaven, and the sand of the sea]** None of these words are found in the Greek manuscripts; it simply says, **So shall your offspring be**. The rest are not found in Chrysostom, nor in Theophylact, nor in Ambrose. Although learned men note that Theophylact was supplemented from the Vulgate edition. It appears these words were added by someone wishing to make the meaning clearer. For Paul was referring to God's words when showing the stars of heaven to Abraham, as we read in Genesis chapter fifteen: *Count the stars if you can, so shall your offspring be.* Here, however, the speech does not fit well: *So shall your offspring be as the sand of the sea etc.* It was enough to say, *Your offspring shall be as the stars of heaven.*

22 **He was not weakened in faith]** <note>original: "Μὴ ἀσθενήσας τῇ πίστει"</note> that is, not made infirm in faith, meaning not doubting for a moment, but firm and robust in faith. The preposition "in" is redundant in our Latin version.

23 **His own body]** <note>original: "ἑαυτοῦ σῶμα"</note> that is, his very own body. Although Paul, in his usual manner, freely uses the simple pronoun for the composite one, here it carries a certain emphasis.

24 **He was nearly a hundred years old]** <note>original: "ἑκατονταέτης που"</note>: the particle *pou* <note>a Greek word meaning "somewhere" or "about"</note> makes the years uncertain. For at that time Abraham was ninety-nine years old, as the Greek notes indicate and as it is written in Genesis.

25 **The deadness of the womb]** <note>original: "νέκρωσιν τῆς μήτρας"</note> that is, as you might say, the "mortification" of the womb. However, he calls "deadened" <note>original: "νενεκρωμένον"</note> that which is worn out or barren, lest anyone think he was already a corpse; rather, he was weakened by old age—not simply so, for later he is said to have fathered children by Keturah without any notable miracle—but "deadened" in the sense that without divine help he could not father a child from Sarah. For it is read that he took Keturah as a wife while she was still of a sound age. Augustine writes something similar in the first book of *Questions on Genesis*. Furthermore, he calls it the "womb" <note>original: "vulva"</note>, not the external female parts as the unlearned common people understand it, but the <term>matrix</term> <note>the internal womb where a fetus is conceived</note> which, when it lacks the power to attract and retain seed, makes a woman sterile.

26 **In the promise also of God]** <note>original: "Εἰς δὲ τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note> that is, "but regarding the promise of God." And this is how Ambrose reads it, so that this part contrasts with the preceding: *He was not weakened, he did not consider etc.* but he did not distrust at all, he did not hesitate at the promises of God, or rather "toward" the promises of God. For in Greek it is "unto the promise" <note>original: "εἰς ἐπαγγελίαν"</note>.

27 **He did not waver]** <note>original: "οὐ διεκρίθη"</note> that is, he did not judge between options or investigate too much, which is the mark of one who distrusts. For someone who does not fully trust finds it difficult to stop analyzing.

28 **He was strengthened]** <note>original: "ἐνεδυναμώθη"</note> that is, he grew strong and was made powerful, which corresponds to the earlier phrase, **not being weak in faith**. Here too the preposition "in" is not added, not even in the ancient Latin manuscripts, though it is contained within the compound Greek verb.

29 **Most fully knowing]** <note>original: "πληροφορηθεὶς"</note> that is, having been made certain and having accepted a certain persuasion; as if you said "certified," as we explained more fully in the preface to the Gospel of Luke.

30 **Whatever God promised]** <note>original: "ὅτι ὁ ἐπήγγελται, δυνατός ἐστι καὶ ποιῆσαι"</note> because what he promised, he is also able to do. The conjunction "because" <note>Latin: "quia"</note> is used here for the Greek *hoti*, which is used not to declare a cause, but to explain what he was persuaded of.

31 **Therefore it was credited to him]** Here, where the testimony of Genesis is repeated for the third time, the Latin manuscripts add **unto righteousness**. But the Greek manuscripts
<meta>catchword: as if</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>582</page-num>
-># TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER V.<-

...as if they are. Who <margin>18</margin> against hope believed in hope, <margin>18</margin> that he would be the father of many nations, according to that which was said, <margin>21</margin> "So shall your offspring be." And <margin>22</margin> not weakened <margin>19</margin> in faith, he did not consider <margin>23</margin> his very own body now deadened, <margin>24</margin> when he was about a hundred years old, nor the <margin>25</margin> deadness of Sarah’s womb: <margin>26</margin> But toward the promise <margin>20</margin> of God <margin>27</margin> he did not waver through unbelief, but <margin>28</margin> was made robust in faith, giving glory to God: <margin>29</margin> Having <margin>21</margin> conceived a certain persuasion, <margin>30</margin> that he who had promised was also powerful enough to perform it. <margin>31</margin> Therefore it was also <margin>22</margin> credited to him as righteousness. Now it was not written <margin>23</margin> for his sake alone, that it was credited to him; but <margin>24</margin> also for our sake, <margin>32</margin> to whom it shall be credited, believing in him <margin>33</margin> who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead, who was delivered up for our sins, and <margin>25</margin> was raised for our justification. Justified <margin>V. 1</margin> therefore by faith, <margin>1</margin> we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom <margin>2</margin> it has also happened for us, <margin>2</margin> that by faith we were led into this grace,

***

<margin>C</margin> only read, **therefore it was credited to him** <note>original: "διὸ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ"</note>. And that was enough. For it notes everything that was said above as if already concluded. And the most ancient manuscript I have seen, from the Library of Saint Paul, agrees with the Greek copies.

32 **To whom it shall be credited]** <note>original: "οἷς μέλλει λογίζεσθαι"</note> that is, "to whom it will be imputed." I wonder why Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>a French theologian and contemporary of Erasmus</note> in his examinations felt it should be "ought to be imputed." As if *mellei* in Greek carries the meaning of "ought" in this tense. It is as if "ought to be credited" and "will be credited" were the same thing, as the uneducated common people think. Unless perhaps he thought it better to speak this way for the sake of teaching.

33 **Who raised Jesus Christ]** "Christ" <note>original: "Χριστὸν"</note> is not added in the Greek.

<margin>D</margin> **L**et us have peace with God] In most Greek manuscripts it is written **we have** <note>original: "ἔχομεν"</note>, though the writing varies in others. For instance, in Theophylact the text has **we have** (indicative), but the explanation has **let us have** (subjunctive). In Chrysostom the text has **let us have**, and likewise the commentary, but that this was committed through the carelessness of scribes is indicated by what follows: **for we no longer sin** <note>original: "καὶ γὰρ, οὐκ ἐπὶ ἁμαρτήμασι"</note>. Now, I do not know if the first-person forms of these verbs agree with the indicative, just as the second-person "let us have/you have." Even if we grant that, the sense here does not allow for a command (the imperative mood). Since the Apostle is speaking here of those justified by faith, who *already* have peace with God; if he had wanted to deter them from sinning lest they lose the peace they received, he would have said instead, **let us keep the peace** <note>original: "τηρῶμεν τὴν εἰρήνην"</note>. He is not warning the justified here, but congratulating them on their happiness, because—not by their own merits, but by the grace of God’s kindness—they are free from sins and reconciled to Him whom they previously had as an enemy. This meaning is supported by what follows: about the confidence of approaching God, the hope of the glory of the children of God which perseveres even in the afflictions of this world, and the love of God, who reconciled the world by the death of His Only-begotten. It is clear that Ambrose read **we have**, not **let us have**, as these words prove: *Faith, he says, makes us have peace with God, not the law. For this reconciles us to God by taking away the sins that had made us God's enemies:* and because *the Lord Jesus is the minister of this grace, through him we are pacified toward God etc.* In Origen, we read **let us have** in the text, and he repeats it in the commentaries: *If we have cast away the weapons of the Devil and taken up the standard of Christ, we surely have peace with God:* and his explanation matches this reading. *Most clearly, he says, through these things which he understood—what it means to be justified by faith and not by works—he invites us to the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, in which the height of perfection consists.* Thus far Origen. Just as one who praises the tranquility of the monastic life or the virtues of virginity invites those who have not yet embraced it to that kind of life. It follows in the same Origen: *When we were enemies of God, we were reconciled to God etc.* Origen shows that it is a consequence: he who is freely reconciled to God should no longer think of things that were hostile to God. It is no wonder if, later speaking under that persona, he turns the indicative mood into an imperative, "let us have peace," so that there is no "yes and no" in us. For this exhortation, there is no need for a verb of commanding; the matter itself exhorts us that, having once been freed from sins and reconciled to God, we should not slide back into those things which tear apart the friendship between God and men. This is also the reasoning behind what Chrysostom writes, <margin>F</margin> and Theophylact, who borrowed his ideas. This kind of admonition is more consistent with Pauline modesty and courtesy. Nor is that figure of speech infrequent, where we say something *is* happening because we want it to be understood that it *ought* to happen, such as: *He who is born of God does not sin*, or *A mother cannot hate her son*, or *A Prince measures all things by the benefit of the Republic.* I have discussed these things in such a way that I do not entirely condemn the other reading. For this speech could pertain to those who are baptized but still weak in spirit and constantly falling back into sin, so that the Apostle, to soften his warning, included himself in the phrasing.

2 **Access]** <note>original: "προσαγωγὴν ἐσχήκαμεν"</note> that is, we have had an entrance, or we have obtained it. However, it is not hidden from me that the Greeks use the past tense for the present in certain verbs, especially those of the emotions, like "I have become," "I know," and in this which follows shortly after, **we have stood** <note>original: "ἑστήκαμεν"</note> for **we stand**. It should also be noted in the phrase **in which we stand**, it is uncertain whether the relative pronoun refers to "grace" or "faith." Ambrose seems to refer it to faith when he says: *standing because we previously lay prostrate, but by believing we are raised up, etc.*

Erasmus argues that "we have peace with God" is an indicative statement of the believer's new status rather than a command to seek peace.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of the Epistle to the Romans, specifically moving into the heart of Chapter 5. Erasmus is examining the Greek source for the famous "chain of virtues" (tribulation leads to patience, etc.) and discussing the nuances of how Christ’s death for the ungodly is described. He focuses heavily on the difference between Latin and Greek idioms, citing early Church Fathers like Origen, Ambrose, and Augustine to justify his translation choices.</meta>

# PAUL'S EPISTLE CHAPTER V.

<margin>2</margin> ...we boast in the hope of the glory of God. <margin>3</margin> And not only that, but we also boast in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience, <margin>4</margin> and patience produces character, and character produces hope. <margin>5</margin> And hope does not put us to shame, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us. <margin>6</margin> For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. <margin>7</margin> For scarcely for a righteous man will someone die; though perhaps for a good man someone might even dare to die. <margin>8</margin> But God demonstrates His own love toward us, <margin>B</margin> in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. <margin>9</margin> Much more then, having now been justified by His blood, we shall be saved through Him from the wrath. <margin>10</margin> For if while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son, much more, having been reconciled, we shall be saved by His life. <margin>11</margin> And not only that, but we also boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation. <margin>12</margin> Therefore, just as through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men—

---

<margin>C</margin> *3 In the hope of the sons of God]* The Greeks read <term>in the hope of the glory of God</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν ἐλπίδι τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ</note>. They do not add "of the sons." It is clear that Origen read "in the hope of the glory of God" based on his own commentary. No trace of the word "sons" can be found in the interpretation by Ambrose that would suggest he included it. Indeed, he writes: *But we who believe are uplifted, boasting in the hope of the brightness which God promised us*; this does not differ from Origen, who interprets it as *boasting in the hope of seeing the glory of God*. Theophylact interprets it as *in the hope of the good things that come to us, not by our merit, but so that God may be glorified*. Chrysostom reads it no differently.
*4 And not only so]* <note>original Greek: Οὐ μόνον δὲ</note>. Latin speech does not naturally recognize this phrasing; it would be smoother if a pronoun were added, such as "Neither this alone" or "Not only this." Indeed, Origen thinks this particle "not only" should refer not just to what was said immediately before—*we boast in the hope of the glory of God*—but also to the other things he taught we had obtained through Jesus Christ: namely, that we are justified by faith through him, that through him access has been given into this grace, and through him it happened that we may boast and hope for the glory of God. It seems to me it can be referred to the last of these without being ungraceful.
*5 Does not confound]* <term>does not put to shame</term> <note>original Greek: ἡ καταισχύνει</note>, that is, does not make one ashamed or affect one with shame. What Latin speaker would understand "confounds" as "makes ashamed"? Those who blush are said to be "suffused," and those whose minds are disturbed are said to be "confounded." To be sure, a powerful sense of shame sometimes produces this in a person, but "confound" and "make ashamed" do not mean the same thing, just as "to drink wine" is one thing and "to be drunk" is another. As for the passage in Acts where it says he *confounded* the Jews <note>original Greek: ἐσυνεχύνετο</note>, it is not the same as *put to shame* <note>original Greek: κατῄσχυνε</note>, but rather *poured out upon* <note>original Greek: κατέχεε</note>, that is, he disturbed them and rendered them at a loss for a plan. It is likely, however, that the common people spoke this way then, and the New Testament was originally delivered in the common tongue. Augustine, in the fourth book of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter seven, points out the rhetorical figures of this passage, one of which is called in Greek a <term>climax</term> <note>original: κλῖμαξ</note>, or in Latin a "gradation," which adds much to the pleasantness of the speech. This occurs whenever the following part picks up the last word of the preceding part, so that one arrives at the end through certain steps: as here, from tribulation patience, from patience character, from character hope are connected. He also points out the beauty of the composition, where a "period" (a full sentence) completes the speech modulated by "cola" and "commata" (phrases and clauses). The first part is: *since tribulation produces patience*; the second: *but patience produces character*; the third: *character indeed produces hope*. Then the period is added, itself consisting of three parts: the first of which is: *but hope does not confound*; the second: *because the love of God is poured out in our hearts*; the third: *through the Holy Spirit who was given to us*. These are roughly Augustine's points. Although in my opinion nothing prevents us from completing the first composition with four parts, so that the fourth is: *but hope does not confound*; for this is the end of the gradation. Then a period is added consisting of either one or two parts, *because the love of God is poured out in our hearts, through the Holy Spirit who was given to us*. Indeed, the higher phrases can be divided into two clauses: so that a clause is *since tribulation*, and after a brief breath there follows *produces patience*, and likewise for the rest. Saint Augustine admits these were by no means sought after by the Apostle, but that eloquence followed wisdom of its own accord as a companion, nor does wisdom despise such a companion.

<margin>E</margin> *6 Poured out]* <term>has been poured out</term> <note>original Greek: ἐκκέχυται</note>, that is, was shed forth or was poured out, so that you understand it was poured out abundantly.
*7 For why indeed]* In Greek it is different: <term>For while we were still weak, Christ</term> <note>original Greek: Ἔτι γὰρ Χριστὸς ὄντων ἡμῶν ἀσθενῶν</note>, that is, *For Christ, when we were yet weak*. It appears the manuscript which the Translator followed had <term>To what end?</term> <note>original Greek: Εἰς τί</note>, that is, *For what?* Both senses are tolerable. For "to what end?" implies "so that hope might be confounded." And Ambrose also reads "For why." Theophylact reads and interprets it as "Still" or "Yet."
*8 According to the time]* <term>at the right time</term> <note>original Greek: κατὰ καιρὸν</note>. If it refers to "the weak," it softens what was said, as if their weakness should be blamed on the time when the grace of the Gospel had not yet appeared. But if it refers to "he died," you will understand that he met death at a suitable time and one prescribed by the Father. And thus the Greek commentaries interpret it. Ambrose follows that opinion, writing: *If Christ gave himself over to death for a time for the unbelieving and enemies of God.* For

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...into this grace in which we stand and boast under the hope of the glory of God. <margin>*</margin> And not only that, but we even boast over afflictions, knowing that affliction <margin>4</margin> produces patience, and patience produces character, and character <margin>5</margin> hope. Moreover, hope does not make us ashamed, because the love of God <margin>*</margin> has been poured out in our hearts, through the Holy Spirit <margin>6</margin> who was given to us. <margin>†</margin> For Christ, when we were still weak, <margin>‡</margin> according to the reckoning of the time, died for the ungodly. <margin>7</margin> For scarcely <margin>§</margin> for a righteous man will anyone die: since for a good man perhaps someone even <margin>8</margin> sustains dying. But God commends his charity toward us, <margin>††</margin> because, while we were yet sinners, <margin>9</margin> Christ died for us. Much more therefore, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved through him <margin>10</margin> from wrath. For if when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more being <margin>11</margin> reconciled shall we be saved through his life. And not only this, <margin>††</margin> but even boasting in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now <margin>12</margin> obtained reconciliation. <margin>†‡</margin> Therefore, just as through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and so into all men—

---

<margin>D</margin> —he died "for a time" because he rose on the third day. And soon after: *Among men, therefore, that is, according to the time, he seemed to die.* Origen agrees, and Theophylact almost seconds him, interpreting *at the right time* as *at an opportune and destined time*. Though Ambrose refers it more to the brevity of the time than to its opportuneness. Chrysostom does not touch on this particle <note>original Greek: κατὰ καιρὸν</note> in his commentary. Origen seems to touch on both readings. For in the context the speech is distinguished thus: *When we were still weak according to the time, he also died for the ungodly.* Again, in his commentary when he says: *Who, according to that time in which he suffered, did not refuse to undergo death for the ungodly and unjust*: he seems to feel the same as what Ambrose expressed; a little later when he adds, especially if he understood that because while we were yet in the time of being ungodly and weak, he first died for us, he touches upon the other distinction. Both readings have a pious sense. He whose commentaries are circulated on the Epistles of Paul under Jerome’s name includes a triple sense: *weak according to the time*, when we were still weighed down by the sicknesses of sins and crimes; and *weak according to the time*, when justice had by then almost failed. He adds another: either because Christ suffered in the last time. He adds a third, which is peculiar to Ambrose: or that he died for the space of three days, as was foretold. Thomas [Aquinas] also touches on a different distinction.
*9 For a just man dies]* <term>will die</term> <note>original Greek: ἀποθανεῖται</note>, that is, he shall die. Furthermore, *just* and *good* in this place do not signify a specific person, but a thing, that is, justice and goodness itself, as they are in the neuter gender, not the masculine, as Saint Jerome thinks in the *Epistle to Algasia*, question seven. Origen explains it both ways: for a just man and for a just cause. Ambrose follows the first sense, referring the word "just" to a person.
*10 Dares to die]* And "dares," or even "might dare to die" <note>original Greek: καὶ τολμᾷ ἀποθανεῖν</note>. Although here he would have translated more correctly as *sustains* <note>Latin: sustinet</note>, a word Suetonius used in a similar sense.
*11 Since if]* It is different among the Greeks: <term>that while we were yet sinners</term> <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν</note>, that is, *because when we were still sinners*, so that this particle depends on the preceding words. Perhaps there will be one who dies for a good thing. Yet God’s love toward us is remarkable in this, and surpasses human life however great it may be: *that for the ungodly and unworthy He willed His only Son to die.* Then, after a clause is inserted, let it follow: *Much more therefore now justified, etc.* That distinction, if anyone distrusts me, exists in the Pauline manuscript which we have often mentioned. "But God commends his love in us," here after a comma is inserted, there follows: *Because when we were still sinners, Christ died for us.* Here, with a period mark placed between, what follows begins with a capital: *Much more therefore, etc.* Although some later person, wishing, I think, to emend what had been written, had added "if" in the space between the lines. *Because if while we were still sinners, etc.* My copy from the old printing press had the same distinction, and "if" is not added.

<margin>F</margin> *12 But also let us glory]* <term>but even boasting</term> <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ καὶ καυχώμενοι</note>, that is, *but also glorying*. Although it matters very little to the meaning. And in several Greek manuscripts I found <term>we boast</term> <note>original Greek: καυχώμεθα</note> written, such as in the one provided to us by the Monastery of the Preachers at Basel.
*13 Therefore as by one man]* Thus indeed it is among the Greeks, <term>for this reason as through one man</term> <note>original Greek: διὰ τοῦτο ὥσπερ δι᾿ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου</note>, but what follows does not correspond to the "as," unless "as" is read for "because," or unless you take "just as" for "like," or unless one prefers this also to be an <term>anapodoton</term> <note>a grammatical construction where the main clause is omitted</note>, of which Paul seems to have many. Origen reports two opinions. According to the first, he wants Paul to have left this part unfinished not from ignorance of the Greek language, but to have suspended it on purpose, because something had to be added, as he judged it more convenient for both to be understood than openly explained. For if he had added the part that corresponds to "just as, etc."—*So through one man justice came into the world, and through justice life passed into all men*—there was a danger that those who heard this would be rendered more secure and negligent, or would even now begin to expect what will happen later, or that they would think what we follow not without care and study falls to those who are yawning. Therefore, in the rest, he returns the other part with the tense changed through a verb of the future tense: *Just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive.*

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed philological and theological commentary on Romans 5:12. He is specifically investigating the phrase "in whom all sinned," which was a central proof-text for the doctrine of original sin. Erasmus contrasts the views of Augustine, who favored an inherited "mass" of sin, with others who see "sin" here as the act of imitating Adam’s disobedience.</meta>

# TO THE ROMANS. CH. V.

<margin>Until</margin>
...they shall be made alive. According to the latter view, he intends for the second part of the comparison to be provided later, albeit after a longer interval—specifically there, where he says: *But the gift is not like the offense.* <note>original: "Sed non sicut delictum, ita & donum"</note> For if by the offense of one many died, much more did the grace of God and the gift by the grace of one man, Jesus Christ, abound for many. To me, however, there seems to be another way to remedy this awkwardness of speech: if we understand the word "as" <note>Greek: "hos"</note> to be implied within the conjunction "and" <note>Greek: "kai"</note>, a common habit among the Greeks. You have an example of this in the Gospel: *as in heaven and on earth* <note>Greek: "hos en ourano kai epi tes ges"</note>, that is, *just as in heaven, so also on earth*; the word "so" <note>Greek: "hoste"</note> is understood. Here, then, the sense will be: *Wherefore, just as through one man sin entered into the world, so also through one man death entered*, so that you understand both proceeded to us from Adam. He sinned and, because of sin, fell into death. We likewise, because we sin by following him, fall into death; and thus it happened that both death and sin flowed down into all people.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>14 in whom all have sinned] <gloss>eph' ho pantes hemarton</gloss></margin>
In this phrase, "in whom," some refer the "whom" back to Adam, in whom—as if in a collective mass—his posterity lay hidden, and in him everyone sinned. Augustine thinks it can refer back to "sin," so that we understand that in one sin of Adam, everyone somehow sinned. However, this reading is not consistent with the Greek, since "sin" <note>Greek: "he hamartia"</note> is a feminine noun. Otherwise, it would hardly fit the meaning. Others interpret "in whom" <note>Latin: "in quo"</note> to mean "because" or "insofar as." Those who push the former meaning use this passage primarily to establish the doctrine of original sin <note>The inherited guilt or stain of sin from Adam</note>, of which Saint Augustine was the most fierce defender, especially after his conflict with Pelagius and Julian grew heated. Nor was Saint Ambrose averse to this opinion; following Origen as he usually does, he philosophizes on this point as well: that the Apostle did not say "in which" <note>Greek: "eph' he", feminine</note>, but "in whom" <note>Greek: "eph' ho", masculine</note>, that is, in the man, not the woman. He argues that the man is the primary author of posterity, even though the woman was the first to fall. To others, a better sense <margin>C</margin> appeals: taking the phrase absolutely, not referring to Eve or Adam, but to the matter itself—that is, "in that all have sinned." Yet this reading does not simply exclude original sin; for it can be understood that all sinned in Adam, in whom they also died before they were born. For this figure of speech <note>metaphor or trope</note> cannot be avoided. Otherwise, those who do nothing do not sin, nor do those who do not yet exist die. Furthermore, if Adam's sin deserved not only the death of the body but also the death of Gehenna <note>eternal punishment/hell</note>, then this sin did not pass to everyone, nor does that death pass to infants if they die without the washing of rebirth <note>baptism</note>—at least if we believe the theologians of our own time. From this, it is clear that the language does not lack tropes; if we exclude them, many absurdities follow. For if we wish to embrace either the definition of the theologians or common sense, sin is something said or done, and no such thing exists in newborn infants. But if "sin" is taken here as the removal of divine grace (which was in Adam before he sinned), or for a certain natural proneness to sin <margin>D</margin> which seems implanted in everyone—though I think this arises more from examples than from nature—these things are more truly the *punishment* of sin than sin itself. Therefore, those who say the entire posterity sinned in Adam as if in a mass seem to say nothing other than that Adam's sin harmed all his descendants and was a loss to them. If he had not violated God's command, he would have fathered descendants like himself: immortal, full of knowledge, fear, love, and faith, teachable and eager for every good thing; instead, he now fathers them subject to so many evils. Yet the Scholastics <note>medieval university theologians</note> do not allow these evils to be called "sin"; they do not even allow "concupiscence" <note>uncontrolled desire or lust</note> to be called sin, despite others protesting. And yet, baptism does not remove these evils from infants: the necessity of dying remains, as does a body subject to disease and a proclivity toward sinning, although both are turned to good for the pious. Other things they excuse through the "habits of infused grace." I will not enter deeper into this labyrinth here; I have touched on it only enough to demonstrate that this speech of the Apostle is not without tropes. Furthermore, I do not know if the Greek language accepts this sense—that all are said to have sinned "in Adam" <margin>E</margin> as if hiding inside him. For he does not say "in whom" <note>Greek: "en ho"</note>, but "upon whom" <note>Greek: "eph' ho"</note>. In Greek, one says "to have in the belly" <note>Greek: "en gastri echein"</note> for being pregnant; one does not say "upon the belly" <note>Greek: "epi gastri"</note>. And one says "in a place" <note>Greek: "en topo"</note> for what is contained by a place, rather than "upon a place" <note>Greek: "epi topo"</note>. Though one does say "at the house" <note>Greek: "ep' oiko"</note> and "at the home." For whenever the word "upon" <note>Greek: "epi"</note> declares "over" or "in," it is joined to the genitive case, as in "upon the table," "upon the earth," and "over all." Likewise, when it indicates time or condition, as in "in the time of Claudius Octavius," and in Acts 26: "about to defend myself before you." When it indicates cause or imminence, it is joined to the dative, as in "under penalty of death." Also, when it declares vicinity, "at the bridge." Again, when it indicates power, as "he rules over someone," that is, in the king's hand. Also, when it indicates an addition, "besides these things," that is, in addition to or after these things. Or when it indicates a condition, "he was bound by these terms," that is, he bound you by this law; and "on stated terms," that is, certain prescriptions. Finally, when it means "above," as "above the column"; very similar to that phrase, "on the threshold of old age." It takes the accusative case whenever movement to a place is signified. However, since the use of Greek prepositions is varied, I would not dare <margin>F</margin> to affirm that "upon" <note>Greek: "epi"</note> is never found joined to the dative case to declare that something is "in" another, just as a tree is in a seed. Certainly, I have not happened to find anything similar so far. For in Hebrews 7, when Paul says Levi was "in the loins of Abraham," he does not say "upon the loins" <note>Greek: "ep' osphui"</note>, but "in the loins" <note>Greek: "en osphui"</note>. Conversely, in 1 Corinthians 15, "Just as in Adam all die, so in Christ all shall be made alive," it is not "upon Adam" or "upon Christ," but "in Adam" <note>Greek: "en to Adam"</note> and "in Christ" <note>Greek: "en to Christo"</note>. Now, even if we grant it was written "in whom" <note>Greek: "en ho"</note>, what is more common in the Sacred Scriptures than for "in" to be used for "through"? So the sense could be: *Death passed to all through this, that all sinned*, or *because all sinned*. Furthermore, where the Translator <note>the Vulgate</note> renders "passed through" <note>Latin: "pertransiit"</note>, the Greek is "pervaded" <note>Greek: "dielthen"</note>, which we preferred to translate as "spread through" or "pervaded," both to avoid ambiguity and to express the speed and violence of the evil flowing into everyone. I did this especially when I noticed that Saint Augustine tripped on this occasion, thinking that "to pass through" was the same as "to pass by"; from this, he concluded that even the Virgin Mother doubted somewhat at the death of the Lord, but in such a way that the sword "passed through" her but did not "touch" her. The passage is in his *Book of Questions on the Old and New Testament*, question 73, as we noted in Luke chapter 2. I believe the words are naturally related: the one in Luke and the one here, which could best be rendered as "flowed through" or "was derived," unless one wished to express the force and power of evil leaping across everyone. Moreover, I doubted whether "pertransiit" would be found among those who speak correctly, since "pervading" is both an elegant word and suited to this sense. Besides, since there is only a single preposition in the Greek word, "transiit" <note>passed</note> was more appropriate than "pertransiit" <note>passed through</note>. "To pass" <note>transire</note> is indeed said of contagions that are propagated from some to others. Hence that line of Ovid:

> And many things harm by a bodily transition.

There is nothing here in the words, therefore, that cannot be adjusted to the "sin of imitation" <note>The idea that we sin because we follow Adam's example, rather than inheriting his guilt</note>. Only two syllables seemed to stand in the way: "upon whom" <note>Greek: "eph' ho"</note>, which I have shown hardly yields the sense that some want to be the only one. And even if it were "upon whom," it would not much obstruct the opinion of those who think Paul is speaking here of the sins of individuals committed in imitation of Adam. Nor am I the author of this interpretation, since whoever it was whose notes on all Paul’s Epistles are circulated under the name of Jerome explains this whole passage this way. For to these words, *Sin entered, and death through sin*, he adds this note: *by example or form*. Again, after these words, *So it passed into all men*, he adds, *while they sin in the same way, and die similarly*. And so that you may understand he is speaking of a capital crime and the death of the soul, he adds: *For it did not pass into Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, of whom the Lord says, "All those are living."* But here he says *all died* because in a multitude of sinners a few righteous ones are not excepted; just as it says elsewhere, *There is none who does good, not even one.* And, *Every man is a liar.* For as for what Origen philosophizes regarding the word "world"—as if sin only passed into the world, that is, into men of a worldly spirit—this seems more forced to me. Yet he also touches on this interpretation when he says, *Either it passed into all those who sin, not living in a heavenly manner*. Soon he adds, *For it passed also into all men who transgressed the natural law*. Now, to those words of the Apostle, "in whom all have sinned," he adds such a note: *that is, in that they all sin by the example of Adam*. So far his view. Thus, no ambiguity remains: whoever that author was, he interprets this whole passage as being about the sin of imitation and the death of the soul. I confess this work is not by Jerome, despite what the silly preface lies about; however, the thing itself cries out that it is the work of a learned man. And those who think faith should be held in all titles and reject our criticisms must certainly accept these as Jerome's. From Origen, however, who is usually slippery in argument—especially since we have this work in a loose translation with many things added, removed, and changed—it is not so easy to gather what he thought. First, he touched somewhat on the "mass" in which all sinned: *If therefore,* he says, *Levi, who was born in the fourth generation after Abraham, is said to have been in the loins of Abraham, much more were all men who are born and have been born in this world in the loins of Adam when he was still in paradise; and all men were expelled from paradise with him or in him when he was driven out from there. Through him, death, which came to him from transgression, consequently also passes into those who were held in his loins.* And a little later the Apostle says: *For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive.* Therefore, sin is said to have entered—and death through sin—not from the serpent who sinned before the woman, nor from the woman who was made to transgress before the man, but from Adam, from whom all mortals draw their origin. But here surely is the one man through whom sin entered, and death through sin, etc. With these words, he indeed seems to look toward original sin, though to a closer observer it appears otherwise. He only shows why Saint blessed Paul makes neither the Devil nor Eve the author of sin, although in truth by the envy of the Devil death entered into the world, and through the Devil it passed into Eve, and through Eve into Adam: and that the first author of sinning was the serpent, then Eve drew the man into sin. But because posterity is reckoned by the name of the father, he therefore says all sinned in Adam, who transmitted the example of sinning to his descendants and, being corrupt, fathered corrupt children. That Origen is not strictly speaking of original sin here is sufficiently argued by what he immediately subjoins: *since by the name of the father, having cast off the image of the earthly, we bear the image of the heavenly—that is, so that living according to the word of God we may be renewed and reformed according to the inner man into the image of God who created him, etc.* When he says "living," he indicates he is speaking of the sin of imitation. Again, in the same series of arguments a bit later: *having our conversation not in this world, but in heaven. And soon: he walks in the image of the earthly, and walks according to the image of the earthly, and thinks on the flesh, and does the things that are of the flesh, etc.* None of these things apply to infants. Here follow certain things, it seems, either about the fall of Satan or about souls which (according to Plato) sinned before they were sent into bodies, which the Translator passed over. Furthermore, while he touches on everything, he makes no mention at all of the sin of infants, to whom they want this passage specifically to belong. Then, when he brings Paul in to speak of the death of the soul, citing that of the Prophet, *The soul that sins, it shall die*, it is clear he is discussing personal sin. This is argued even more evidently by the fact that he moves to the question: *Why Christ suffered death, though he never sinned. He answers: Christ, because he was immune to sin, owed nothing to death, but for our sins he laid down his soul of his own accord.* Nor does he mention original sin here, but says "he committed no sin." Even more evident is what follows; for he approaches the very point which they press regarding the sin of infants. *But let us see,* he says, *how death passed into all men, "In whom all," in-*
<column-break/>

<summary>Erasmus provides a philological and patristic analysis of Romans 5:12, arguing that the Greek text (eph' ho) points toward "sin of imitation" or "because all sinned" rather than strictly "in Adam's person." He critiques Augustine’s reliance on a potential Latin mistranslation and cites "Pseudo-Jerome" and Origen to suggest that the passage refers to adult behavior rather than the inherited guilt of infants.</summary>
