<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s philological analysis of Romans 5:12. He is challenging the idea that this specific verse is the definitive proof-text for "original sin" (inherited guilt), suggesting instead that it may refer to "personal sins" committed by individuals following Adam's example. He continues to contrast the interpretations of Origen, Chrysostom, and Ambrose.</meta>

### EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER V.
### 587

...entered, they sinned. In a definitive judgment, the Apostle pronounced in that <margin>in whom [Greek: en hō]</margin> all men had passed into the death of sin, in that in which all have sinned. Here I suspect there is a textual error, and that it was originally written "in that" or "by which" all have sinned, so that "in whom" is understood causally <note>original: "aitiologicalos," meaning providing a reason or cause</note>. However, so you may understand that he is speaking of the sins of individuals, he says, *All have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God*: therefore, even if you speak of that first fall, no one can be excused, for *All* have sinned. He proceeds from Abel to Seth, from Seth to Enoch, from Enoch to Methuselah, from Methuselah to Noah, from Noah to Abraham, declaring with arguments that each one sinned by their own sins. But fearing to review the rest, lest he should offend anyone if he attributed sin to those whom the world holds in the highest veneration, he comes to Christ: to whom he says sin came—I believe when he was tempted by Satan—but was repelled by this one man: and thus death was conquered, whose sting is sin: whence it is written, *Where, O death, is your sting?* etc. From these points, I think it is clear enough that Origen interpreted this passage as the sin of imitation, just like that Scholiast: the former of whom, even when he examines individual words—such as when he distinguishes "the world" from "men," saying that sin entered into the world but does not say it left, yet passed into men, namely by repentance providing an exit—does not even touch upon the sin of infants with a single word, to whom this passage properly pertained. These things are not said by us to call into doubt whether there is such a thing as original sin, but to declare the opinion of those who say that I alone remembered this interpretation, and that this commentary has nothing uniquely in common with Pelagius <note>Pelagius was a 5th-century theologian declared a heretic for arguing that humans have the free will to achieve salvation without divine grace and that Adam's sin was merely a bad example, not an inherited stain.</note>. I condemn the opinion of Pelagius, and the consensus of the Ancients on this matter does not escape me: the dispute is only concerning the sense of *this passage*, whether it properly pertains to original sin. First, it is generally admitted that the starting point of this whole discussion proceeded from something other than original sin, and the summary of the discussion leads to a different conclusion. For in the first chapter, he reproaches the Gentiles because, contrary to the law of nature and philosophical knowledge, they degenerated into every kind of crime; in the second, he rebukes the Jews because they did not observe the law in which they boasted; in the third, he concludes that both Gentiles and Jews are equally liable and in need of the grace of God; in the fourth, he teaches that neither Gentiles nor Jews are saved by their own works, but through faith, and that the promise made to Abraham pertains to all who return it through faith; in the fifth, he teaches that the remission of sins and the gift of justice—that is, innocence—happens for all through the free love of God, who washes away the sins of all with the blood of his Only-begotten. Thus far, there is nothing that does not apply to personal sins, as the Scholastics call them. Moreover, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Greek Father known for his preaching.</note> advises that in the fifth chapter, Paul is addressing how those who have been justified by baptism ought to arrange their lives—that is, to abstain from sins in the future, lest we rescind the peace made with God. Nothing here yet concerning original sin. Soon after, what follows—*For until the law sin was in the world*, but sin was not imputed etc.—it is established that most doctors interpret this as the sin of imitation. For Saint Ambrose writes thus: *Until the law, sin was not even imputed; for men thought they could sin among men with impunity, though not before God: for the natural law had not entirely become numb, because they were not ignorant that they should not do to others what they did not wish to suffer themselves etc.* This discourse clearly testifies that Ambrose feels this passage speaks of personal commissions. Now, whether you read "in the likeness of Adam" or "not in the likeness," they refer both readings to the sin of imitation. Furthermore, that passage, *For if by the transgression of one many died etc.*, which seemed as if it could again be referred to original sin, they interpret thus: that is, if by the transgression of one many died by imitating his prevarication, much more the grace of God etc. And a little later: *Death, he says, did not reign over all, but over those who died by the fault of Adam, whom he says sinned in the likeness of Adam’s prevarication.* Again, upon these words, *For the judgment was from one unto condemnation*, he comments thus: *It is manifestly different, because by the one sin of Adam they were condemned who sinned in the likeness of his prevarication.* Again, these words, *As through the offense of one unto all men to condemnation etc.*, he explains thus: *that is, Just as through the offense of one all men deserved condemnation, by sinning similarly, so also by the justice of one all who believe are justified*: and he tempers the entire subsequent discussion so that you understand him to be speaking of the proper sins of individuals. But in the middle he writes: *It is manifest, therefore, that in Adam all have sinned as if in a mass: for he himself having been corrupted through sin, all whom he begot were born under sin: therefore from him all are sinners, because we are all from him.* And soon after: *Let there be also another death, he says, which is called the second in Gehenna <term>Gehenna: a historical valley in Jerusalem used as a metaphor for hell or eternal punishment</term>, which we do not suffer for the sin of Adam, but is acquired by our own sins on his occasion etc.* Here he distinguishes the sin of Adam from personal sins, and the death of the body from the death of hell. Truly, the question now is not whether Ambrose recognizes original sin—for it is clear he does so in many places—but whether it is necessary to take *this passage* as being about original sin. For if this discourse, *so death passed to all men, in whom all have sinned*, must necessarily be understood as original sin, it is necessary that what is annexed to this—*for until the law sin was in the world*—we must understand similarly, because this part gives the reason for the previous statement. But Ambrose interprets this part as being about sins committed by each person. How then will the tenor of the argument hold together, if both what precedes and what follows are taken as the commissions of individuals, yet in the middle, a sin of a different kind is suddenly mixed in—especially since the conjunction *for* [Latin: *enim*] so connects the lower parts with the upper that it appears the same matter is being discussed? Just as the conjunction *gar* <note>Greek: γὰρ, meaning "for"</note> glues that which follows with what precedes, so *dia touto*, that is, *therefore*, connects this particle with those things which preceded: and what had preceded was that Christ had died for enemies and sinners, by whose blood, having been freed from the wrath of God, we have obtained life instead of death, and the glory of children instead of ignominy. For it makes no difference, except that when we say "therefore," the cause preceded and the effect follows; when we use "for," it is the opposite. If Titius owed Actius a thousand coins under the name of a loan, and ten drachmas under the name of a deposit,

<column-break/>

### 588

<margin>A</margin> would this speech seem to hang together if he said, *I never had a more convenient creditor than Actius, to whom, since I owed a thousand coins from a loan and he saw me struggling with family financial difficulties, he voluntarily forgave that sum, and from being a debtor of debt, he made me a more bound debtor of his goodwill. For he has always embraced nothing past with singular benevolence, and thereby freed me from the obligation: for he could have sued me under the name of the loan, and if I did not pay, led me to prison, or seized my property as a pledge.* Here, since the first and last parts speak of the loan, who would suspect that those things in the middle—which free me from obligation—pertain to the deposit? And yet two conjunctions do this, "wherefore" and "for," so that this discourse hangs together much more harshly unless we take the whole as being about original sin, or the whole about personal sin, or the whole about both. But there are things which cannot be understood as original sin, and things which cannot be understood as both. Now Saint Chrysostom, in <margin>B</margin> this passage which they insist must be taken as original <margin>What is this, "in which all have sinned"? When he fell, even those who did not eat from the tree became mortal because of him. <note>original Greek: "Τί δέ ἐστιν, ἐφ᾿ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον; Εκείνου πεσόντος, καὶ οἱ μὴ φαγόντες ἀπὸ τοῦ ξύλου γεγόνασιν ἐξ ἐκείνου θνητοί."</note></margin> sin, comments on nothing else but this: *that is, What is this, in which all have sinned? When he fell, even those who did not eat from the tree became mortal because of him.* This discourse can pertain to both kinds of sin. Furthermore, the passage annexed to this he explains in two ways: I will write down his own words, rendered into Latin in good faith: *For until the law sin was in the world, but sin is not imputed when there is no law. That which he says "until the law," some think the Apostle meant concerning that time which was before the law was given, such as what was under Abel, Noah, and Abraham until the time Moses was born. What sin, therefore, was there then? Some say he speaks of that which was in paradise. For it was not yet dissolved, he says, when its fruit rather flourished. For that brought in the common death, which conquered and reigned. For what reason, therefore, does he add: But sin is not imputed where there is no law? Those who have discussed our side say the Apostle placed this speech under the person of Jews objecting: If there is no sin without the law, how is there death for all who were before the law? But to me it seems that what I am about to say is more probable, <margin>C</margin> and more agreeable to the Apostolic sense. What is this? When he says, sin was in the world until the law, he seems to me to be saying this: that once the law was given, sin abounded—namely that which was from transgression—and it abounded as long as the law existed. For sin cannot exist if there is no law. Therefore if this sin, he says, generated death from the transgression of the law, how did it happen that all who were before the law died? For if death drew its root from sin, but when there is no law sin is not imputed, how did death prevail? From this it is clear that it was not this sin of the violated law, but that one committed through the disobedience of Adam, which contaminated all things. What is the sign of this? The fact that even before the law, everyone died. For death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin etc.* In these words, Chrysostom attributes no sin to infants, but says the death of the body flowed into them, just as if they had eaten from the forbidden tree with Adam their progenitor; that is, they paid the penalty for another's sin. Moreover, when Theophylact <margin>D</margin> speaks thus: *For from the one falling, even those who ate nothing from the tree were made mortal by his crime, just as if they themselves were liable for the sin, because he preceded them:* does he not pronounce that infants are not liable for the sin? Although if we take this passage as being about the death of Gehenna, which Adam had deserved, infants are not punished by this; if about the death of the body, baptism does not free one from this. Seeing these things, Origen fled to the death of the soul, which separates God from it through sin. If we accept this death, this passage cannot be taken as original sin. But this passage, which Chrysostom seems to interpret as the transgression of Adam, Ambrose interprets as personal sin, as we have shown. Therefore, it is false what some boast, that all the Ancients, both Greek and Latin, interpreted this passage with great consensus as original sin, since Origen the Greek and the Latin Scholiast interpret it otherwise: and consequently it is false that this interpretation is peculiar to me along with Pelagius, since both Ambrose and the preceding and following parts interpret it as the sins of individuals, only appearing to touch upon the sin of Adam in the middle. <margin>E</margin> But it is even more false that this interpretation fights against the property of Pauline diction and the Greek reading, since I have declared that both the property of speech and the series and tenor of the argument fit more smoothly with that opinion which I show can stand. I will not now examine what is cited by others to drag this passage toward original sin; for they speak in ambiguous tropes: certainly none of them attribute sin to infants, but they say some part of the punishment passed to their descendants. There remains that quarrel, which I think belongs to the Pelagians, disarming the Church by wrenching away this weapon—the most powerful of all, as they say. First, I have taught that there are other more powerful weapons: second, how am I acting for the Pelagians, whose opinion I openly detest? But I indicate that both readings can stand. Even if I were silent, the matter itself cries out that the Scripture is more conveniently taken as the sin of individuals. One passage of Scripture was sufficient against Pelagius, and the Church was safe even <margin>F</margin> if destitute of this weapon. But "the whole Church interprets this passage thus." Is the whole Church three or four Doctors? The whole Church teaches that all descendants of Adam are born liable to punishment because of the sin of Adam: but the universal Church never teaches that this passage cannot be taken as anything except original sin. And yet this was the only thing I noted. But in the African Council—of Milevis, I believe—anathema is pronounced against those who would interpret this passage of Paul otherwise. On the contrary, anathema is pronounced there against those who said infants do not need baptism because they had no contagion from Adam: and after the anathema, it is added, *because it ought not to be understood otherwise.* I do not here examine how many anathematas are in those provincial Councils, which Hilary translated as best he could, nor do I think one is so strictly bound by Synods of that kind. Otherwise, if anyone urges that whatever was decreed in them must be kept, I will bring forth from them a dogma—

<summary>Erasmus argues that Romans 5:12 does not exclusively refer to inherited "original sin," but likely refers to individual "personal sins" committed in imitation of Adam. He uses the writings of Ambrose and Chrysostom to show that ancient consensus on the verse is not as unified as his critics claim, and defends himself against charges of Pelagianism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed philological and theological defense of his interpretation of Romans 5. He is addressing critics who claim that by suggesting this passage might refer to "imitation of sin" rather than "inherited original sin," he is undermining Church doctrine. Erasmus argues that scholarship requires looking at how the Greek Fathers (like Origen and Chrysostom) read the text, and he points out that even Saint Augustine’s interpretations have not always been followed by the Church in other matters.</meta>

# TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER V.
## 589 / 590

<margin>13</margin> For until the law, sin was in the world; but sin is not counted when there is no law. <margin>14</margin> Nevertheless death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin after the likeness of Adam’s transgression. <note>original Greek: Ἄχρι γὰρ νόμου ἁμαρτία ἦν ἐν κόσμῳ· ἁμαρτία δὲ οὐκ ἐλλογεῖται, μὴ ὄντος νόμου. Ἀλλ᾽ ἐβασίλευσεν ὁ θάνατος ἀπὸ Ἀδὰμ μέχρι Μωσέως, καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς μὴ ἁμαρτήσαντας ἐπὶ τῷ ὁμοιώματι τῆς παραβάσεως Ἀδὰμ.</note>

---

<margin>A</margin> I could bring forward certain practices which the Church now condemns as heretical; I could bring forward institutions which the Church nowhere preserves today; I could bring forward decrees from universal Synods that forbade this passage from being explained otherwise. Even if the Synod of Milevis <note>A North African council in 416 AD that condemned Pelagianism and affirmed the necessity of infant baptism for the remission of original sin.</note> condemned the <term>Pelagian</term> <note>Pelagianism was a 5th-century belief that human nature was not corrupted by original sin and that humans could achieve salvation through their own will and effort.</note> interpretation, that has nothing to do with me. My critic tries to remove this interpretation by asserting that because the Church disapproved of it, I am "disarming" the Church by showing this passage is not sufficiently effective for refuting the Pelagians. On the contrary, I am referring the debater to other passages that are more certain on this point. This is not taking a weapon away from the Church, but rather pointing out more reliable weapons in place of less reliable ones. Nor is it opening a gap for the enemy, but rather advising that we should not press the enemy in a place where he might be able to slip away. 

We admit the Church has the authority to interpret the Scriptures, but the Doctors of the Church, however famous, have hesitated on many passages, and have interpreted many things in various ways—some even incorrectly. No one contended that this passage could *not* be understood otherwise until Saint Augustine, after he fell into conflict with the Pelagians. If they do not permit us to disagree with Augustine here—at least so far as to allow this passage of Paul to be interpreted in two ways—why then is the same honor not given to everything that great man taught and asserted in this very dispute? For in this same work, he repeatedly insists that infants are baptized in vain unless they are given the body and blood of the Lord. He drew that opinion from the sixth chapter of John:
> **"Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you."** <note>John 6:53</note>
Regarding that passage, which the Ancients interpreted as referring to the teaching of Christ, later writers added a second sense regarding the taking of the <term>Eucharist</term> <note>The sacrament of Holy Communion.</note>. Yet now the Church neither practices nor allows what Augustine (and with him, likely the whole Western Church) judged necessary for salvation. It rejects his interpretation and would consider it heretical if someone were to defend it stubbornly today. 

In the same work, he insists that Christ alone was free from all sin, and he teaches this by the testimony of many; yet classes of theologians, especially those in Paris, condemn this opinion, frankly rejecting the dogma and scriptural interpretation of such men. In the same place, he cites Ambrose, who interprets the washing of the feet of the Apostles as referring to <term>original sin</term> <note>The inherited guilt or stain of sin from Adam.</note>, whereas today it is permitted to interpret it otherwise. For Peter, already circumcised, was not subject to that sin. There he cites Cyprian, who wrote that through baptism the sins of others are remitted to infants, whereas today the Church teaches that only that first and unique sin of Adam is imputed to the newborn, and even that not entirely. He also asserted from 1 Corinthians 15, to prove original sin:
> **"For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive"** <note>1 Corinthians 15:22</note>
Yet did not Chrysostom dare to interpret that passage as referring to the individual sins of each person? For he comments thus: 
> *Tell me then, did all die the death of sin in Adam?*
How then was Noah just in his generation? How was Abraham, how was Job, how were all the others, etc.? He mentions these in vain if the passage meant original sin, since none of them was immune from it. 

Yet Saint Augustine thinks this passage of Paul must be understood so strictly as referring to original sin that, because it pertains to the foundations of the faith, anyone who tries to interpret it otherwise is striving to take away everything we believe in Christ. They also bring forward against the Pelagians: *We were by nature children of wrath*. Why did Saint Jerome dare to interpret that passage otherwise than as original sin? Why did he dare to indicate it could be taken to mean "utterly" or "entirely"? Why does no one cry out here that a weapon has been snatched from the Church's defenders? Must we be crushed by this rule, that it is a crime for anyone to interpret any testimony of Scripture differently than the ancient Doctors of the Church did when they were fighting heretics? But what about those who, when they bring forward so many opinions and interpretations from those conflicts, find that modern theologians not only reject them but judge them impious and heretical? 

If the whole Church totters because I have noted this passage can be interpreted differently (without condemning the other explanation), why has no one until now protested against the *Scholia* circulated under Jerome’s name, which explain this whole passage as referring to sins committed by the will? It is certain that this whole discussion of Paul is full of obscurities, as Origen truly stated in his preface. It is certain that many things are said through <term>tropes</term> <note>Figures of speech or metaphorical language.</note>. We do not assert original sin only here, but in many places in my writings, and even in the Paraphrase itself, we embrace both senses, speaking thus: *For if that prince of sinning was so powerful that such a great number of men were subject to death because of the crimes of one...* And soon after: *Just as the loss of Adam turned into gain for us by the kindness of God.* Again: *Although through the one sin of Adam destruction was brought in, and through Christ the innocent one salvation was brought in, yet both are not equal to the other. Since the mixture arose in such a way that the sin of one was propagated to all descendants, and thus finally rendered all liable, etc.* And soon after: *But if the fault of one man was so powerful that it made all bound to the tyranny of death, etc.* 

What? Is this to exclude original sin? Now, regarding what we translated as "in that" or "inasmuch as," it can be accommodated to either sense or rather to both: that is, *death passed because all sinned*, namely, in Adam. What then are they afraid of? Will the Pelagians immediately come back to life if I have interpreted this one passage differently than Augustine did in the heat of battle, especially since there are many other passages by which heretics can be more effectively refuted? Truly, why should this be less permitted here than it was permitted for the Orthodox in other passages cited by the same author? Will they say I should have concealed the fact that this passage is explained in two ways? As if, even if I were silent, the heretics would not have seen it—indeed, as if they had not seen it a thousand years ago! If we place the defense of the faith in silence, what is the purpose of those many volumes of "Questions" with which modern theologians have filled the world, calling everything into doubt by proposing arguments—

<margin>B</margin> 13 *For until the law sin*) <note>original Greek: Ἄχρι γὰρ νόμου</note>. Origen interprets this as, *Until the end of the Mosaic law, that is, until Christ.* So also Augustine in his annotated opinions on the Epistle to the Romans.

<margin>C</margin> 16 *Was not counted*) <note>original Greek: ἐλλογεῖται</note>, that is, "is imputed" [counted]. It is in the present tense to make the statement more absolute. For "when there is no law" fits both times [past and present], as if you were saying in a general sense: "where there is no law, sin is not imputed." And Origen certainly reads it this way. He found it written thus in a very ancient and very correct Pauline codex. Here, some interpret *ellogeitai* not as "imputed" [to an account], but as "reputed," that is, "judged." Thus, you would understand that when no law has been passed, those who sin do not regard what they commit as sin, since they are not forbidden from doing it by any law. A certain learned man, in a published book, thinks the Greek reading is corrupted and that *ellogeito* [was being imputed] should be written instead of *ellogeitai*. As if it were not impudent to disagree with such a consensus of Greek volumes, or as if, should one require the imperfect past tense, one should say *ellogeito* and not rather *enelogeito*. And here is one who could claim wonderful erudition for himself if he incessantly boasts of knowing nothing at all. In the codex of Donatianus <note>A specific manuscript reference used by Erasmus.</note> it was written, *when the law is not*. From this, one might guess that "was imputed" is a corruption of "is imputed." *Elogeito* could be tolerated if it were said *elogeito* instead of *elogizeto*. *Elogeito* was written in the Commentaries of Chrysostom, and in Theophylact it is *elogeito*,

<margin>D</margin> but both are corruptions, if I am not mistaken. It should be noted in passing that Paul in this place uses these two words interchangeably: *hamartia* [sin] and *paraptoma* [trespass/fall], although Jerome thinks somewhere that *paraptoma* is lighter than *hamartia*.

<margin>17</margin> *In the likeness*) <note>original Greek: ἐν ὁμοιώματι τῆς παραβάσεως Ἀδὰμ</note>, that is, "in the likeness," not "into the likeness," of Adam's transgression. This particle "in the likeness" can be referred either to "prevailed, death reigned in the likeness," or to the closer part, "those who did not sin in the likeness." Origen and Ambrose, and even Augustine in the first book of *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, chapter eleven, and again in Letter 89, indicate a double reading of this passage. One is: *death reigned even over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam*. Origen seems to prefer this one, as he puts it in the first place, as does Ambrose. The other, which he indicates is found in some copies, is: *death reigned from Adam even over those who did not sin*. Of the first reading, in which the negation ["not"] is not added, this is the meaning:

<margin>E</margin> That death reigned not only in Adam, but over all who sinned according to his example. The second reading has a double sense. The first is that death reigned not only in Adam and those who sinned after his example, but even over those who either did not sin, or certainly had not sinned as gravely as he did. The second sense is that death reigned even over those who had not sinned [personally], but it reigned not because of their own crimes, but in the likeness of Adam's transgression—that is, just as if they themselves had transgressed exactly as Adam did. Now, since Paul has said elsewhere, *God has shut up all under sin*, and *all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God*, how does he now say that some have "not sinned"? Truly, they had not sinned "after his likeness"—that is, not so capitally, nor after receiving a mandate, which is properly called "transgression" [*praevaricatio*]. For sin was deservedly imputed to Adam, as to one who had been given a precept regarding what he should follow and what he should flee. But before the law of Moses, sin "was not imputed"—that is, it did not seem that it should be imputed, because there was no law that forbade the sin. It should be added that the word is not *homoiosis* [the act of becoming like], but *homoioma* [a copy or likeness], which sounds more like a "likeness" such that you understand those who sin refer back to their sinning parent in this respect. He used the same word a bit earlier: "in the likeness of the image of man." 

Furthermore, it does not escape me that some refer this whole passage to original sin. I do not greatly fight against them; nevertheless, it seemed right to indicate the other interpretation, which Ambrose did not entirely overlook and Origen follows almost exclusively. He whose scholia we read under the name of Jerome speaks similarly, saying: *For when he had explained that those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam are those who sinned before the law of Moses, he explains what he said with these words: These are those who sinned not according to the likeness of Adam's transgression, who transgressed through natural law, and not like Adam through a mandate.* And soon after he adds: *For just as Adam, who first transgressed the mandate of God, is an example for those wishing to imitate it.* But why do I pursue these things, since he, as was said, interprets the whole chapter as referring to the sins which men commit by imi-

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER V:
## 591, 592

<margin>15</margin> 15 Adam’s transgression, of whom he was a type of the one to come. But the gift is not like the offense; for if by the offense of the one, many died, much more did the grace of God and the gift in grace, which is of the one man Jesus Christ, abound unto the many. <note>original Greek: ἡ παράβασις Ἀδάμ, ἧς ἦν τύπος τοῦ μέλλοντος. Ἀλλ' οὐχ ὡς τὸ παράπτωμα, οὕτως καὶ τὸ χάρισμα· εἰ γὰρ τῷ τοῦ ἑνὸς παραπτώματι οἱ πολλοὶ ἀπέθανον, πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἡ χάρις τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ ἡ δωρεὰ ἐν χάριτι, τῇ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ εἰς τοὺς πολλοὺς ἐπερίσσευσε.</note>
<margin>16</margin> 16 And the gift is not as it was through the one who sinned; for the judgment was from one offense resulting in condemnation, but the gift is from many offenses resulting in justification. <note>original Greek: Καὶ οὐχ ὡς δι' ἑνὸς ἁμαρτήσαντος, τὸ δώρημα· τὸ μὲν γὰρ κρίμα ἐξ ἑνὸς εἰς κατάκριμα, τὸ δὲ χάρισμα ἐκ πολλῶν παραπτωμάτων εἰς δικαίωμα.</note>
<margin>17</margin> 17 For if by the offense of the one, death reigned through that one, much more those receiving the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness shall reign in life through the one, Jesus Christ. <note>original Greek: Εἰ γὰρ τῷ τοῦ ἑνὸς παραπτώματι ὁ θάνατος ἐβασίλευσσε διὰ τοῦ ἑνός, πολλῷ μᾶλλον οἱ τὴν περισσείαν τῆς χάριτος καὶ τῆς δωρεᾶς τῆς δικαιοσύνης λαμβάνοντες, ἐν ζωῇ βασιλεύσουσι διὰ τοῦ ἑνὸς Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.</note>
<margin>18</margin> 18 Therefore, as through one offense judgment came upon all men to condemnation, so also through one act of righteousness the gift came upon all men to the justification of life. <note>original Greek: Ἄρα οὖν ὡς δι' ἑνὸς παραπτώματος εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπους εἰς κατάκριμα, οὕτως καὶ δι' ἑνὸς δικαιώματος εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπους εἰς δικαίωσιν ζωῆς.</note>
<margin>19</margin> 19 For as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one the many shall be made righteous. <note>original Greek: Ἥσπερ γὰρ διὰ τῆς παρακοῆς τοῦ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου ἁμαρτωλοὶ κατεστάθησαν οἱ πολλοὶ, οὕτως καὶ διὰ τῆς ὑπακοῆς τοῦ ἑνὸς δίκαιοι κατασταθήσονται οἱ πολλοὶ.</note>
<margin>20</margin> 20 Moreover, the law entered that the offense might abound; but where sin abounded, grace did much more abound. <note>original Greek: Νόμος δὲ παρεισῆλθεν, ἵνα πλεονάσῃ τὸ παράπτωμα· οὗ δὲ ἐπλεόνασεν ἡ ἁμαρτία, ὑπερεπερίσσευσεν ἡ χάρις.</note>
<margin>21</margin> 21 That as sin reigned in death, so grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life through Jesus Christ. <note>original Greek: Ἵνα ὥσπερ ἐβασίλευσεν ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐν τῷ θανάτῳ, οὕτως καὶ ἡ χάρις βασιλεύσῃ διὰ δικαιοσύνης εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.</note>

---

...by the nature of the first parent. If someone should bring forward the example of the Virgin <note>Referring to Mary, the mother of Jesus; Erasmus notes the debate over her being born without sin.</note>, the ancient writers freed no one from sin entirely except Christ alone. If they bring forward infants—Paul does not seem to be dealing with them here, nor was that question being raised then, since it was not yet the custom to baptize infants. Furthermore, we must see to it that we do not hate the <term>Pelagians</term> <note>Followers of Pelagius, who denied original sin; Erasmus warns against over-reacting to them.</note> more than is proper. It is not that I don't want their opinion exploded—the one which denies there is any original sin—but that I don't want it to be mixed in by design where it is not needed. I do not want us to engage in overly clever arguments, or to act like <term>Astrologers</term> who invent <term>epicycles</term> <note>Small circles used in ancient astronomy to explain the complex movements of planets; Erasmus uses this as a metaphor for overly complicated theological explanations.</note> to rescue themselves from many difficulties, and thus resort to this <unclear>impoverished cycle</unclear> of questions at every turn. Unless, perhaps, we allow ourselves, when disputing with an adversary who needs to be conquered more than taught, to twist the words of Scripture in any way possible to secure our victory. This is what Jerome seems to do sometimes when fighting against Jovinian, and Augustine does it a few times, as does Ambrose. I say these things, I repeat, not because I favor those who deny original sin, but because I do not want, if possible, any violence to be done to the Divine Scriptures. Rather, let us carefully weigh the consequence of the argument itself, looking at where Paul begins and where he is heading, and whether it is consistent for him to have wanted to reveal this mystery to the Gentiles immediately—a mystery which today is still believed more than it is understood, as common sense cries out against it. In vain do some people falsely claim that in this annotation I seem to undermine original sin, which I sincerely profess and assert in so many places in my writings. Yet this passage seems to me more gently explained as referring to the personal sins of Adam's descendants, though I do so without prejudice to anyone else’s opinion.

<margin>18 Form of the future</margin> <note>original Greek: τύπος τοῦ μέλλοντος</note>, that is, the figure or type of the future, meaning the Christ who was to come. Thus the name "future" does not refer to the time when Paul was writing, but to Adam who preceded Christ, of whom he bore the type. Paul used this same kind of expression when writing to the Colossians about Sabbaths and New Moons, saying they are a "shadow of things to come." For to Paul, those things were no longer future, but present. It seems a bit forced to me (however clever you might call it) what Origen suggests, that it could refer to the light and the condition of the world to come. Therefore, Adam was a form and type of Christ. However, from the figure it falls into the opposite, and it is an analogy rather than a direct likeness. For as the former was the prince of sinning and dying, so the latter is the leader and author of innocence and immortality. Hence Origen wrote elegantly, and Ambrose followed him, saying that according to the "genus" there is a likeness of structure, but according to the "species" there is a contradiction. Just as something flowed from Adam into all, so also from Christ—this is the "genus." But from the former came death and sin, from the latter innocence and life—this is the "species." Furthermore, "form" in Greek is <term>typos</term> <note>original: τύπος</note>, which sounds like a "pattern" from which another similar thing is expressed. But "of the future" <note>original: τοῦ μέλλοντος</note> can also be taken absolutely in the neuter gender, so that it refers not to the later Adam, but to the sin itself of whoever imitates their parent Adam. For he was the example of sinning for his descendants. He shows what sense can be extracted from the Greek words; the prudent and wise reader will follow what he judges best. It must be added that the Translator in this place sometimes renders it "more" and sometimes "many"; in Greek it is the same word, <note>original: πολλοὶ</note>, which Origen thinks was put for "all," so that it might better correspond to the "one." For where there are "all," there are also "many."

<margin>19 And not as through one sin</margin> In the Greek it is more obscure: <note>original: Καὶ οὐχ ὡς δι' ἑνὸς ἁμαρτήσαντος τὸ δώρημα</note>, that is, "And not as through one who sinned, so is the gift." For one may translate it word-for-word this way, and it is necessary to understand several words as implied, as the Greek commentaries also advise. "And not as through one who sinned" (understand: "death entered"), "so through the one came the gift," that is, not in the same way. For from one sin we all die, but from many sins all are justified through one. And where the common manuscripts have "through one sin," Ambrose reads "through one sinning," not "sin," <note>original: δι' ἑνὸς ἁμαρτήσαντος</note>, that is, through one who sinned. And that Theophylact read it this way can be gathered from his own interpretation. Certainly Chrysostom reads it thus, although shortly after this is referred to the sin, "the judgment indeed from one to condemnation," because it follows, "but the gift from many..."

<column-break/>

**Column 2 (Page 592)**

<margin>A</margin> ...of the transgression of Adam, 18 who bears the type of the one to come.
<margin>15</margin> But not as the sin, so also the gift: for if by the offense of the one, many died, much more did the grace of God, and the gift through grace, which was of the one man Jesus Christ, overflow unto the many.
<margin>16</margin> 19 And not as death had come through one who had sinned, so is the gift: for the condemnation indeed arose from one offense resulting in condemnation, 21 but the gift arose from many offenses resulting in justification.
<margin>17</margin> For if by the offense of the one, death reigned through that one, much more those who <margin>B</margin> 22 receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness shall reign through life by the author, the one Jesus Christ.
<margin>18</margin> 23 Therefore, as through the offense of the one, evil was propagated into all men resulting in condemnation, so also through the justification of the one, good is propagated into all men resulting in the justification of life.
<margin>19</margin> 24 For just as through the disobedience of the one man we many were made sinners, so through the obedience of the one righteous man shall many be made righteous.
<margin>20</margin> Moreover, 25 the law entered by the way, so that the offense might abound: but where sin overflowed, there grace overflowed even more.
<margin>21</margin> 27 That just as sin reigned 28 in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life 29 through Jesus Christ.

---

<margin>C</margin> <margin>What</margin> ...offenses. When he says "one sin," he means the sin of Adam; when "many," he understands the other sins which each person adds for themselves.
<margin>20 For the judgment from one</margin> "From one" does not refer to the person of Adam, but to the sin, so that "offense" is understood, to which "from many" corresponds a little later. The sense is: "For the judgment indeed from one sin resulted in condemnation, but the gift from many sins resulted in justification." Although all the Interpreters agree here. Augustine, in the second book of *On Marriage and Concupiscence* to Valerius, chapter 27, and again in Letter 89, openly asserts: it must be understood as "from one sin," not "from one man," to correspond to what follows, "grace however from many offenses." Thus we understand that one sin was for the condemnation of the whole human race, but the one grace was for the blotting out of all sins. He affirms the same thing against Julian the Pelagian in the first book. Again in the first book of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 11. For there follows, "grace however from many offenses."
<margin>21 Grace from many offenses</margin> <note>original Greek: χάρισμα</note>. What he had just translated as "gift"—and rightly so—he now translates as "grace," which is hardly right, unless we think grace and gift are exactly the same thing.
<margin>D</margin> <margin>22 Receiving the abundance of grace and of donation and of righteousness</margin> It should be read as "the gift of righteousness," so that you understand righteousness to be the gift, <note>original: καὶ τῆς δωρεᾶς δικαιοσύνης</note>, with the conjunction removed. And then there will be no need for that distinction of Thomas [Aquinas], who explains the difference between grace, donation, and righteousness. Although Ambrose adds the conjunction in our manner, reading "and of righteousness," I think it is a flaw in the manuscript, since his commentary indicates no such thing. Certainly Chrysostom and Theophylact stand with us.
<margin>23 Therefore as through the offense of one into all men</margin> This speech is incomplete and requires words to be understood—namely, what was brought in by each one. Therefore, "just as through the offense of the one, sin crept in to condemnation, so through the righteousness of the one, salvation entered to the justification of all." This is almost how Theophylact explains it, supplying in his commentary what is missing from the speech. See Augustine, Letter 89.
<margin>E</margin> <margin>24 For as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners</margin> It makes no difference to the sense that in our texts the third person is used, "they were made," which was found in some Greek manuscripts <note>original: κατεστάθησαν</note>, while in most Greek texts it is "we were made" <note>original: κατεστάθημεν</note>, as it is in the Aldine edition.
<margin>25 Moreover [it entered by the way]</margin> <note>original Greek: παρεισῆλθεν</note>. As if you were to say "it crept in incidentally," because of the Greek preposition, which is almost always added in a negative sense.
<margin>26 Grace superabounded</margin> Here it is "grace" <note>original: χάρις</note>, not "gift" <note>original: χάρισμα</note>. Although the Greeks sometimes take *charis* (grace) to mean a benefit. Furthermore, where the Latin Translator said "superabounded," in Greek it is <note>original: ὑπερεπερίσσευσεν</note>, which does not mean that the liquid abounds so much that the excess is poured out, but rather that it abounds vehemently and beyond measure. For "hyper" <note>original: ὑπὲρ</note> increases the meaning among the Greeks just as "per" does among us. Hence some people, speaking in the Greek manner <margin>F</margin> but in poor Latin, say "super-blessed" for "exceedingly blessed," or "super-excellent" for "vehemently exalted."
<margin>27 That just as sin reigned in death</margin> Origen thinks that under the name of "death," the Devil can be understood, both here and in previous passages. This is softer in Greek, where "death" <note>original: θάνατος</note> is of the masculine gender. Ambrose thought the sense should be referred to the death of the soul. Origen also interprets it as bodily death, disputing about Enoch being snatched away from death. Furthermore, when he says "sin reigned in death," <note>original: ἐν τῷ θανάτῳ</note>, it appears that Paul used the preposition "in" <note>original: ἐν</note> for "into" <note>original: εἰς</note>. For this particle ought to match the one that follows, "that grace might reign through righteousness into eternal life," where he did not say "in eternal life" <note>original: ἐν ζωῇ αἰωνίῳ</note>, but "into eternal life" <note>original: εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον</note>.
<margin>28 into death</margin> <note>original: ἐν τῷ θανάτῳ</note>, that is, "in death," which means "through death," as we advised above.
<margin>29 Through Jesus Christ our Lord</margin> "Our Lord" is not added in this place among the Greeks, nor in the ancient Latin copies, even if it is added in Ambrose—though in such a way that it cannot be certain from his interpretation that he read it that way. Although in...

<summary>Erasmus provides a detailed philological analysis of Romans 5:15-21, comparing Greek manuscripts with the Latin Vulgate and the writings of the Church Fathers. He argues for a nuanced reading of "original sin," suggesting the text focuses on the contrast between Adam's singular offense and Christ's overwhelming gift of grace.</summary>

# TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER VI.
## 593, 594

### TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER VI.
**Pp**
<meta>Volume VI. catchword: dam; 18 Ser.</meta>

<margin>VI. 1</margin> What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, so that grace may abound? <margin>A</margin>
<margin>2</margin> By no means. We who have died to sin, how shall we still live in it?
<margin>3</margin> Or are you ignorant that as many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus, were baptized into his death?
<margin>4</margin> We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life.
<margin>5</margin> For if we have become united with him <note>original: σύμφυτοι, meaning grown together or grafted</note> in the likeness of his death, we shall certainly also be united in his resurrection.
<margin>6</margin> Knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, so that we should no longer be enslaved to sin. <margin>B</margin>
<margin>7</margin> For he who has died has been justified from sin.
<margin>8</margin> But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him.
<margin>9</margin> Knowing that Christ, having been raised from the dead, no longer dies; death no longer has dominion over him.
<margin>10</margin> For the death he died, he died to sin once for all;
<margin>11</margin> but the life he lives, he lives to God. So you also, reckon yourselves to be dead indeed to sin, but alive
<margin>12</margin> to God in Christ Jesus our Lord. Therefore, let not sin reign in your mortal body,
<margin>13</margin> so as to obey it in its lusts. Neither present your members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin, but present yourselves to God as those living from the dead, and your members as weapons of
<margin>14</margin> righteousness to God. For sin shall not have dominion over you;
<margin>15</margin> for you are not under law, but under grace. What then? Shall we sin because we are not under law, but under
<margin>16</margin> grace? By no means. Do you not know that to whom you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves to the one you obey, whether of sin leading to death, or of obedience leading to
<margin>17</margin> righteousness? But thanks be to God, that though you were slaves of sin, you obeyed from the heart that form
<margin>18</margin> of teaching to which you were delivered. And having been set free from
<margin>19</margin> sin, you became slaves to righteousness. I speak in human terms...

---

<margin>C</margin> In some Greek copies I have found *our Lord* <note>original: Dominum nostrum</note> added, by the same chance, I suppose, as in our Latin versions, where two words were transcribed here from elsewhere.
1 <margin>Q</margin>ui enim mortui sumus peccato <note>For we who have died to sin</note>.] The word *enim* <note>for</note> is redundant. The Greek says <gloss>whosoever</gloss> <note>original: Οἵτινες</note> to sin—that is, <gloss>Whosoever of us have died</gloss>, or <gloss>Who have died to sin</gloss>. And "to sin" is in the dative case <note>indicating the recipient of the action</note>, not the ablative, as if someone speaking to sin might say: *I am dead to you, but I live to Christ.*
2 *Vivimus in illo* <note>We live in him</note>] The Greek is *in it* <note>original: ἐν αὐτῇ</note>. *In it*, or "in the same," would have been more significant.
3 *An ignoratis fratres* <note>Or are you ignorant, brothers</note>] "Brothers" was added by the Translator or a Scribe. The Greek is <note>original: Ἢ ἀγνοεῖτε</note>, which means *Or are you ignorant*. And indeed, Origen and Ambrose read it this way, nor is it otherwise in the oldest handwritten Latin codices.
4 *baptizati sumus in Christo Jesu* <note>we were baptized in Christ Jesus</note>] In the Greek it is *into Christ Jesus* and *into death* <note>original: εἰς Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν & εἰς τὸν θάνατον</note>. Although that preposition has a specific nature among the Greeks, here *into Christ* was more fitting, because through baptism we are grafted into the mystical body of Christ.
5 *Si enim complantati facti sumus* <note>For if we have been planted together</note>] The word is <note>original: σύμφυτοι</note>, which means "grafted in" and <gloss>participants</gloss>. He alludes to the grafting of a plant, which corresponds to the communion of the body of Christ. Just as a shoot cut from its own tree becomes a partaker of the sap of the tree into which it is grafted, so those who are grafted into Christ's body through baptism become sharers in his goods. See also whether the preposition *sun* <note>with/together</note> pertains to the Jews and Gentiles being gathered together into the one Christ.
6 *Simul & resurrectionis* <note>At once and of the resurrection</note>] In the Greek it is <note>original: ἀλλὰ καὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως</note>, which is *therefore also of the resurrection*. The Translator seems to have read "at once" <note>original: ἅμα</note> instead of "but/rather" <note>original: ἀλλὰ</note>. However, *alla* is a conjunction of reasoning, which we translate as *surely*. And "we shall be of the resurrection" can be understood in two ways: *we shall be of the resurrection*, meaning we will belong to it, or we will be "grafted into the likeness of his resurrection." Following the former sense, we have translated it by adding a word: *we shall be partakers of the resurrection*.
7 *Quia simul etiam vivemus cum illo* <note>Because we shall also live together with him</note>] The Greek is <note>original: συζήσομεν αὐτῷ</note>, *we shall live with him*. Although the Translator rendered the sense well.
8 *Resurgens a mortuis* <note>Rising from the dead</note>] The Greek is <note>original: ἐγερθεὶς ἐκ νεκρῶν</note>, that is, "having been raised" or "he who rose from the dead." For it is a past-tense participle. Although in other places the Translator misuses participles of this kind.
9 *Ultra non dominatur* <note>No longer dominates</note>] The Greek is <note>original: οὐκ ἔτι κυριεύει</note>, meaning it no longer dominates, in the present tense, not the future, just like "he does not die." For he gives the reason why he does not die: because through him the dominion of death has been removed. These words pertain not only to Christ, but also to the mystical body of Christ, for which the present tense words are more fitting. And Theophylact reads it this way, nor is the commentary of Chrysostom different: "He does not die" is put for "he is immortal," and "death now does not dominate him" is put for "death has no right over him," who by dying gave birth to his own immortality.

<column-break/>

<margin>VI. 1</margin> What therefore shall we say? Shall we remain in sin, so that grace may abound? Far from it. 1 We who have died to sin, how
<margin>2</margin> shall we live in it hereafter? 2 Or are you ignorant,
<margin>3</margin> that whosoever of us 4 were baptized into Christ Jesus, were baptized into his death? We were therefore
<margin>4</margin> buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life. 5 For if we have become grafted
<margin>5</margin> to him through the likeness 6 of his death, surely we shall also be partakers of his resurrection. Knowing this, that our old
<margin>6</margin> man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be abolished, so that hereafter we might not serve sin. For he who
<margin>7</margin> has died has been justified from sin. But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also 7 live
<margin>8</margin> with him. Knowing that Christ, 8 raised from the dead, no longer dies: death 9 no longer
<margin>9</margin> dominates him. 10 For in that he died, he died to sin
<margin>10</margin> once: but in that he lives, he lives to God. So also
<margin>11</margin> you, 11 reckon yourselves to be dead indeed to sin, but living to God 12 through Christ Jesus
<margin>12</margin> our Lord. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, 13 so that you obey it through its lusts.
<margin>13</margin> 14 Neither offer your members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin, but offer yourselves to God, as those living from the dead, and your members as weapons of
<margin>14</margin> righteousness to God. For sin shall not dominate
<margin>15</margin> you: for you are not under law, but under grace. What then? Shall we sin, because we are not under law, but under
<margin>16</margin> grace? Far from it. Do you not know, that to whom you offer yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are the slaves of the one you obey, whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto
<margin>17</margin> righteousness? 15 But thanks be to God, that you were indeed slaves of sin, but you obey from the soul that form
<margin>18</margin> of doctrine into which you were handed over. Furthermore, having been set free from
<margin>19</margin> sin, 16 you have been made slaves of righteousness. 17 Something human...

---

<margin>D</margin> 10 *Quod enim mortuus est* <note>For that which he died</note>] The Greek is <note>original: Ὃ γὰρ ἀπέθανε</note>. Erasmus corrects this to *quod enim mortuum est* <note>for that which is dead</note>, in the neuter gender. For among the Greeks, the word *ho* <note>original: ὃ</note> is a relative pronoun, not a conjunction. And indeed, following the opinion of Laurentius [Valla], Hilary reads it this way in Book IX of *On the Trinity*, according to the trust of ancient codices, referring *mortuum* <note>the dead thing</note> to the human body or to the divine nature. But in my opinion, the word "died" <note>original: ἀπέθανε</note> is better referred simply to Christ, so that the sense is: this very thing, that Christ died, he died only once, and that to sin; but that he lives, etc. As if you were to say: the death that he died, he died to sin, and the life that he lives, he lives to God. According to the Greek punctuation, a comma should be placed after *Ho gar apethane* <note>For the death he died</note>, so that what follows, "he died once," refers to sin—which word here is in the dative case (to sin), just as "to God" is, not the ablative. He confirms this by what he said in the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 2: <note>original: ὃ δὲ νῦν ζῶ ἐν σαρκὶ, ἐν πίστει ζῶ</note>, that is, "that which I now live in the flesh, I live in faith." Besides, what sense is there if you read, "that which is dead, etc."? For Paul's point is rather that, just as Christ, having once died to sin, remains immortal forever, so we, having once died to sin through baptism and been reborn in him, should not afterward fall back into sin. By this reasoning, the Translator is cleared of a double error <note>term: soloecismo - a grammatical mistake or impropriety</note> which our friend from Étaples <note>Stapulensis</note> charged him with.
11 *Existimate vos mortuos* <note>Consider yourselves dead</note>] The Greek is *logizesthe* <note>original: λογίζεσθε</note>, meaning *yourselves*: a word which the Translator seems to have frequently neglected. And "consider" in Greek is *logizesthe*, a verb of thinking, as Origen also noted, because this matter depends mostly on thought. For as often as we think of ourselves as dead with Christ, the lusts of the flesh are suppressed and vanish. Hence *reputate* <note>reckon/repute</note> fits better, that is: consider, and have before your eyes.
12 *in Christo Jesu*] The Greeks add *our Lord*.
13 *ut obediatis concupiscentiis ejus* <note>so that you obey its lusts</note>] The Greek is <note>original: εἰς τὸ ὑπακούειν αὐτῇ ἐν ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις αὐτῇ</note>, that is, *to obey it in its lusts*: so that the pronoun "it" refers to sin, and "its" refers to the body. Understand this as obeying sin through the attractions of the body enticing one to sin.
14 <margin>F</margin> *Sed neque exhibeatis* <note>But neither exhibit</note>] The Greek is <note>original: Μηδὲ παριστάνετε</note>, meaning *Nor exhibit or offer*: but the "but" <note>sed</note> is redundant.
15 *Gratias autem Deo* <note>But thanks be to God</note>] The Greek is <note>original: Χάρις δὲ τῷ Θεῷ</note>, meaning *But grace be to God*, with "be" understood. Here someone gets angry, crying out that saying "grace to the Gods" is for Pagans, but for Christians it is "thanks to God." Truly, Christians used to speak this way in the past, but being unlearned in letters, they understood "we give" or "let us give." Yet Paul spoke differently; what point was there in departing from his speech into an affected grammatical error? The song "Thanks be to God" <note>Deo gratias</note> is most pleasing to God, not because of the grammar, but because of the singer's piety; nor would it be less pleasing if "Grace be to God" were pronounced with similar affection.
16 *Servi facti estis justitiæ* <note>You were made slaves of justice</note>] "Justice" is in the dative case <note>original: τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ</note>, meaning *to be captives and bound as slaves to justice*.
17 *Humanum dico* <note>I say a human thing</note>] The Greek is <note>original: Ἀνθρώπινον λέγω</note>. Paul is accustomed to softening his tone with this figure of speech if he seems to say something a bit harsh or inconsiderate: *I speak according to man*.

<summary>In this commentary on Romans 6, Erasmus uses grammatical analysis of the Greek text to explain the believer's union with Christ through baptism, famously comparing it to a branch being grafted into a tree. He also defends the use of the phrase "Grace to God" against critics who preferred the more common "Thanks to God," arguing that the heart's intent matters more than linguistic technicalities.</summary>

6 But now we have been released from the law, having died to that in which we were held, so that we serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.
7 What shall we say then? Is the law sin? Certainly not! On the contrary, I would not have known sin except through the law; for I would not have known covetousness unless the law had said: "You shall not

---

18 *To serve impurity*] In Greek the word is a noun, and more expressive: <note>original: δῶλα (doula)</note>, that is, "slaves," or "serving members," and as it were, "subject to."
19 *You were free of righteousness*] In this place, the Greek uses the genitive case for "sin" and the dative for "righteousness," meaning "free from righteousness." And it means "you used to be" rather than "you were," because it follows "since you were."
20 *The end, however, eternal life*] Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>Erasmus refers to his contemporary humanist rival, Faber Stapulensis</note> reads "unto eternal life." Truly, in corrected manuscripts, I find "eternal life" without the preposition, in agreement with both Greek and Latin copies, acting as an apposition. It seemed to me that the reader should know that in this place, as well as in what precedes—"the end of those things is death"—the word <note>original: τέλος (telos)</note> can be understood as a "tribute" or "tax" collected from the service of sin. For soon after follows "wages." Although Ambrose and Chrysostom interpret it otherwise. It seems that "wage" <note>original: ὀψώνιον (opsonion)</note> is what is given to feed a soldier, and "end" <note>original: τέλος (telos)</note> is the final reward by which he now lives for himself, having been granted a discharge. Chrysostom opposes this sense, noting that in the mention of sin, "wages" <note>military pay</note> are named, but in the mention of eternal life, "reward" is not named.
21 *For the wages of sin is death*] <note>original: Τὰ γὰρ ὀψώνια (Ta gar opsonia)</note>, that is, *Provisions*. For soldiers were lured by food and gifts, or enlistment pay, as they are the most wretched class of all men, seeing as they hold their lives for sale for the sake of food and the belly; yet in the past, almost all signs of dignity were bestowed upon them by the Roman Emperors. Ambrose reads "reward" and "gain." Seneca calls that which he first calls the "enlistment pay of vices" a "reward" shortly after.
22 *The grace of God, however*] <note>original: τὸ δὲ χάρισμα (to de charisma)</note>, that is, a *free gift*, so that it is contrasted with "wages," which is a vulgar word, while the former is noble.
1 *The law has dominion over a man as long as he lives*] To us, it is ambiguous whether it should be understood as "as long as the man lives" or "as long as the law lives." And the same ambiguity exists in the Greek words. To me, it seems the verb "lives" refers to the "law" rather than the "man"; and what follows soon after makes me prefer that. Furthermore, it was possible to avoid the ambiguity in this way: "The Law dominates the man as long as it shall have lived," or more elegantly, "so long as it remains in force." Suspecting this, I consulted Origen and found it carefully noted by him: in comparing the analogy, Paul placed the "law" in the role of the husband and the "man" in the role of the wife. Just as the wife is freed by the death of the husband, so the one previously subject to the law is freed by the law being made old. Moreover, he says the law "lives" as long as it is valid, and is "dead" after it has ceased to have force. Now <note>original: κυριεύει (kyrieuei)</note> for the Greeks is not only "dominates" but also "has right and authority." It should be noted in passing that the example is drawn from a woman, not a man, because among the Jews it was lawful for men to divorce their wives, while only death freed women from marital right. Nor is there reason to argue from this passage that divorce is forbidden to Christians in all ways; for when he adds, "for I speak to those who know the law," he plainly indicates he is not making a law for Christians concerning marriage, but drawing a comparison from the Mosaic law for the sake of teaching. Nor is it necessary that what is produced for the sake of a comparison should match in every detail: it is enough if it matches that which it is used to teach and prove. The coming of Christ in the Gospels is compared to a thief digging through a house at night; not because the comparison of a thief and Christ's coming matches everywhere, but only insofar as both arrive unexpectedly.
2 *Who is under a husband*] <note>original: ἡ γὰρ ὕπανδρος γυνή (he gar hypandros gyne)</note>, that is, "subject to a

our Lord. Or are you ignorant, brothers, for I speak to
1 those who know the law, that the law has dominion over a man only so long as it lives? For a woman subject to a
2 husband is bound by the law to her living husband: but if the husband has died, she is released from the law of the husband.
Therefore, while the husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she
3 joins herself to another man: but if the husband has died, she is free from the right of the husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is joined to another man. Therefore, my brothers, you also were
4 put to death to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might be joined to another, namely to him who rose from the dead, so that <margin>C</margin>
5 we might bear fruit for God. For when we were in the flesh, the affects of sins, which are through the law, were
vigorous in our members, to bear fruit for
death. But now we have been released from the law, having died to that
6 in which we were held, so that we serve through the newness of the spirit, and not through the oldness of the letter. What then
7 shall we say? Is the law sin? Far from it: but I did not know sin, except through the law: for I would not have known lust, unless the law had said: "You shall not

---

<margin>D</margin>
man," as if you said *subviralis*; and <note>original: γυνὴ (gyne)</note> signifies both "wife" and "woman."
3 *Bound by law to a living husband*] <note>original: τῷ ζῶντι ἀνδρὶ δέδεται νόμῳ</note>, that is, "she is bound by law to the living husband," that is, "through the law." For the Greeks also call marriage or the right of marriage "the law," as shortly after, "from the law of the husband."
4 *She will be called an adulteress*] <note>original: μοιχαλὶς (moichalis)</note>: which in Greek is <note>original: χρηματιεῖ (chrematisei)</note>, not *chrematisetai*; this is a property of the Greek language. For just as we say, "the father hears," or "the prince hears," referring to one who is called father and prince, so for the Greeks <note>original: χρηματίζει (chrematizei)</note> is said of an orator, one who professes to be an orator or is held as an orator. Luke used this word in Acts chapter 11.
5 *If she has been with another man*] <note>original: ἐὰν γένηται ἀνδρὶ ἑτέρῳ</note>, that is, "if she happens to another man," or "if she begins to be of another man," unless we prefer to understand the preposition "with" <note>original: σύν (syn)</note>. Augustine, pointing out the figures of speech in the Old Testament, also shows this from Leviticus chapter 21: "And the daughter of a priest, if she has been to a foreign man," in place of what it was, "if she has married a foreign man." And yet a certain person calumniated this passage in a published pamphlet, though Augustine interprets it thus: unless perhaps it is one thing to be joined to a man, and another to marry a man. Yet we read this form of speech in Terence’s *Hecyra*: "As will happen to another, if it does not happen to this one." Where the father is thinking of the marriage of his daughter, not of sexual intercourse.
<margin>E</margin> 6 *If however her husband has died*] "Her" is not added among the Greeks. Likewise later, "she is loosed from the law of the husband," "of the husband" is not found among the Greeks, nor does it pertain to the matter. For the article at the end indicates he is speaking of the law of which he spoke before, "a woman bound to a husband through the law." Although I find <note>original: τὸ ἀνδρὸς (to andros)</note> in certain manuscripts. Nor is it in Greek "she has been released," but "she is free," <note>original: ἐλευθέρα ἐστὶν ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου</note>. While this does not affect the sense at all, I do not see why it seemed best to depart from the Apostolic word. Although I suspect "liberata" <note>released</note> was made from "libera" <note>free</note> by scribes.
7 *Released from the law of the husband*] <note>original: κατήργηται ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου</note>. The verb <note>original: καταργεῖσθαι (katargeisthai)</note> signifies "a right abolished and made old," as also a little later, "now we have been released."
8 *That you may be of another*] He superfluously adds "you" in the translation, even if it is added among the Greeks. It was enough to say "that you may be of another"; although in Greek it is "to another," not "of another," that is, "that one may have you," and that you "may not be under your own right." The Greek speech takes no offense because of the impersonal verb, but in the Latin verb the first and second person is understood, unless it is expressed for the sake of emphasis or distinction. In the more correct Latin versions, "you" is not added, so that this should be imputed to the scribes rather than the Translator.
9 *That you may bear fruit for God*] <note>original: ἵνα καρποφορήσωμεν</note>, that is, "that we might bear fruit." It follows, "For when we were," in the same person, that is, "When we indeed were." Moreover, he alludes to the wife he just mentioned, who bears children for her husband.
10 *Passions of sins*] <note>original: παθήματα (pathemata)</note>, that is, "disease, desires, or affects, or disturbances."
11 *Which were through the law*] <note>original: τὰ διὰ τοῦ νόμου</note>. In this place, "which" does not refer to "sins," but to "passions," so that you understand the law excited the lust for sinning.
12 *They worked in the members*] <note>original: ἐνηργεῖτο (energito)</note>. Which more specifically means "they had power," or "they acted secretly." For hidden power is called <note>original: ἐνέργεια (energeia)</note>, as in a seed, and the power of the mind in a man.
13 *In which we were held*] "In which" refers to the law, not to death. For in most Greek texts it is not "of death," but "having died," <note>original: ἀποθανόντες (apothanontes)</note>. Origen testifies that both readings were known to him.
