# TO THE ROMANS. Chapter VII.
## 597, 598

### THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS. Chapter VII.

8 **...covetousness.** But sin, taking opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every kind of covetousness; 9 for apart from the law, sin is dead. I was once alive apart from the law; but when the commandment came, 10 sin revived; and I died; and the commandment which was intended for life was found to result in death for me. For 11 sin, taking opportunity through the commandment, deceived 12 me, and through it killed me. So then, the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and 13 good. Therefore, did that which is good become death to me? By no means! But it was sin; so that sin might be shown to be sin, working death in me through what is good, so that through the commandment sin might become sinful beyond measure. 14 For we know that the law is spiritual; but I am 15 carnal, sold under sin. For what I am working, I do not understand; for I do not do what I want, 16 but what I hate, this I do. But if I do what I do not 17 want, I agree with the law, that it is good. So now it is no longer I who work it, but the sin dwelling 18 in me. For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh; for the willing is present with me, but the working of what is good, 19 I do not find. For I do not do the good I want; but 20 the evil I do not want, this I practice. But if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who work it, 21 but the sin dwelling in me. I find then the law to be that for me who wants to do good, 22 evil is present with me. For I delight in the law of God 23 according to the inner man. But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and making me a captive to the law of sin, ...

---

...had been. But this reading, which we follow, he approves more. Ambrose follows a different one; yet both agree well enough with what follows. It is called the *law of death*, in place of *deadly law*. Furthermore, that phrase, *in which we were held*, can refer either to the *law*—so the sense is: We, now dead in Christ, are freed from the jurisdiction of the law in which we were held—or it can refer to the *dead*, implying the pronoun: *dead to that law in which we were held*. Saint Chrysostom has a third reading: <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου ἀποθανόντος"</note> "from the law having died." Lest anyone attribute this to the scribes, he interprets it, <note>original: "τουτέστιν δείξειν, ὁ δεσμὸς, δι᾿ οὗ κατειχόμεθα, ἐτελεύτησε καὶ διεῤῥύη"</note> "that is to say, to show that the bond by which we were held has died and wasted away."

14 *But opportunity being taken*] <note>original: "Ἀφορμὴν δὲ λαβοῦσα ἡ ἁμαρτία"</note> The translator has not inelegantly changed the gender of the participle and turned the active into the passive to fit the tense. For *labousa* [taking] is in the past tense. Nor do I see why Stapulensis <note>Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples, a contemporary humanist and theologian.</note> needed to be followed here.

15 *I, however, have died*] <note>original: "ἀπέθανον"</note> that is, I had died, or I was dead, as befits the past tense, to correspond with that phrase *revived*. For Paul, for the sake of teaching, transfers the matter to his own person and relates things that are in conflict with each other. For the life of sin is the death of man. Therefore, if sin revived, the death of man immediately followed.

16 *It seduced me*] <note>original: "ἐξηπάτησέ με"</note> that is, it deceived me and led me away from the path. For this is what *exapatan* properly signifies.

17 *But sin, that it might appear, etc.*] The punctuation of this passage varies. The Greeks punctuate it thus: "Has then what is good become death to me? By no means; but sin," so that one understands *it became death to me*. The Greek reads thus: <note>original: "Τὸ οὖν ἀγαθὸν, ἐμοὶ γέγονε θάνατος; μὴ γένοιτο, ἀλλὰ ἡ ἁμαρτία."</note>

18 *It worked in me*] <note>original: "κατεργαζομένη"</note> that is, working—a participle used in place of an infinite verb—that is, so that sin might be seen to work death in me through that which is good. It does not mean "by working," as Laurentius <note>Lorenzo Valla, the pioneer of New Testament textual criticism.</note> prefers. However, Laurentius's note will also stand if "that sin might be shown" is taken as an inserted parenthesis, in this manner: "Has then what is good become death to me? By no means; but sin, so that it might be rendered more evident how great an evil it is, became death to me, while through the most wholesome law it brought forth destruction for me, and turned the very remedy into an increase of the disease." For it must be a massive evil that turns the best thing into ruin. Origen, Chrysostom, and Theophylact follow this reading, except that Origen’s translator turns the participle into a verb. For Chrysostom and Theophylact read *working* [the participle], while the translator seems to have read *it was working* [the verb]; it makes little difference to the sense. Furthermore, what he adds, *so that it might become sinning sin beyond measure*, is an insistence and exaggeration of what preceded, namely *that sin might appear*. There is no need for us to take *so that it might become* to mean *so that it might appear*, since in fact sin was increased through the law, and concupiscence grew because of the opposing precepts, as if against barriers.

19 *Sinning sin beyond measure*] <note>original: "καθ᾿ ὑπερβολὴν ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ ἁμαρτία"</note> Which sounds as if you were to say, "a most criminal crime," or if one were to translate clearly rather than in proper Latin, "a sinful sin." For what he translates as *sinning* is not a participle in Greek, but an adjective. Origen (or his translator) noted carefully that Paul creates a kind of personification of sin, which in Greek is of the feminine gender, so that they may say "a sinning female-sin." If "sin" were masculine for us, so that one could say of it as of a man, "a vehemently sinner sin," the expression would be less harsh. Yet I do not see why Jerome...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> 14 But sin, taking the opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every kind of desire: since without the law, sin was dead. I was once living without the law: but when the commandment came, sin revived: 15 I, however, died: and that very commandment, which was established for life, was found to yield death for me. For sin, taking the opportunity through the commandment, 16 deceived me, and through it killed me. Therefore, the law itself is indeed holy, and 12 the commandment is holy and just and good. Therefore, did that which was good become death for me? By no means: 17 on the contrary, sin: so that sin might appear, through that which was good, 18 to produce death in me, so that it might become <margin>B</margin> a sinning sin in a greater way through the commandment. For we know that the law is spiritual: but I 14 am carnal, 20 sold under sin. For what I 15 do, I do not approve: 21 for I do not do what I want, but what I hate, that I do. But if I do what I do not want, 16 I agree with the law, that it is good. Now, 17 however, 22 it is no longer I who perform it, but the sin dwelling in me. For I know that good does not dwell in me, 18 that is, in my flesh: for the will is present with me, but how to perform the good, I do not find. For I 19 do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, this I do. Furthermore, if I do what I myself do not want, 20 it is no longer I who perform it, but the sin dwelling in me. 23 I find therefore through the law, for me wanting to 21 do good, that evil is joined to me. <margin>C</margin> For the law of God delights me according to the internal 22 man. But I see another law in my members, 23 24 rebelling against the law of my mind, and 25 rendering me a captive...

---

...says he would rather admit a flaw in the language than not express Paul's meaning with sufficient integrity. Indeed, in Greek, <note>original: "ἁμαρτωλὸς ἁμαρτία"</note> [sinful sin] is not a solecism, at least according to the Attic dialect. Furthermore, what Latin speaker would understand what a "sinner sin" is, in place of a notable and evident sin? Or why "sinner sin" [masculine] rather than "sin-ess sin" [feminine]? And yet Augustine reads it this way in the first book *To Simplician*, question one, except that in the published copies it is faultily read as "beyond measure sinner or sin," instead of what it should be, "beyond measure a sinner sin." He reads it the same way in his fourth sermon on the *Words of the Apostle*, which provides a probable conjecture that the author of the version Augustine followed there had read "a sinful sin beyond measure."

<margin>D</margin> 20 *Sold under sin*] <note>original: "πεπραμένος ὑπὸ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν"</note> that is, sold or handed over under sin, meaning into the slavery and yoke of sin. I do not see what obscurity here could have offended Faber <note>Lefèvre d'Étaples.</note>.

21 *For not what I want, the good*] The words *good* and *evil* are not in the Greek here: <note>original: "οὐ γὰρ ὃ θέλω τοῦτο πράσσω, ἀλλ᾿ ὃ μισῶ"</note> "for not what I want do I do, but what I hate." But a little further down in Paul, these two words, *good* and *evil*, are added. For I do not do what I want—namely, the good.

22 *Now not I*] <note>original: "οὐκ ἔτι ἐγώ"</note> Which, being elegantly and properly translated into Latin by the translator, I wonder why it would seem necessary for anyone to change it.

23 *I find then a law to me wanting to do good*] Origen, as he often does with Paul, finds a lack of linguistic integrity here; he thinks this speech is inconsistent, either because the conjunctions are superfluous or because they are not used as they ought to be. He thinks <margin>E</margin> this disadvantage can be removed in such an order: if we read in this way, "Therefore because evil lies near, I, wanting to do good, find the law of God and delight in it according to the inner man, etc." In my opinion, it can also be taken so that the conjunction *hoti* [that/because] is not causal here, as Origen takes it, but is used specifically, and the sense is: While I strive to obey the good law, and am dragged to evil by winning desire, I feel that evil is in me, not in the law. And this sense holds up well. But if we approve this, we must admit that Paul stammered in this speech and did not finish what he had started. For it appears he was going to say something like: "I find therefore the law, whenever I try to do good, effects this in me: that I understand the malice of sinning has its source in myself, not in the law." Theophylact restores it in this manner: "I find therefore the law acting for me, who wants to do what is good, but not doing it, because evil lies near me." He admits, however, that the speech is obscure because something seems to be missing. He also indicates that others <margin>F</margin> arrange it in this way: "I find therefore the law is for no one else except for me wanting to do good." For to the one who desires to act rightly, the law is finally the law, as it prescribes that which he desires to do. And this is the opinion of Chrysostom, with which what follows agrees: "For I delight in the law of God." Just as the law favors me when I want what is good, so I, desiring what is honorable, approve the law.

24 *Repugnant to the law*] <note>original: "ἀντιστρατευόμενον τῷ νόμῳ"</note> as if you were to say, "militating against" and "rebelling." For Paul delights in metaphors that savor of military service. Just as before he mentioned "wages" [stipends].

25 *Captivating me in the law of sin*] <note>original: "αἰχμαλωτίζοντά με τῷ νόμῳ τῆς ἁμαρτίας"</note> that is, who renders me a captive to the law of sin.

# EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER VIII.
## 599 600

<margin>24</margin> ...truly in my members. Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this <margin>25</margin> death? I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law <margin>VIII. 1</margin> of sin. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who walk not according to the flesh, but according <margin>2</margin> to the Spirit. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of <margin>3</margin> sin and death. For what was impossible for the law, in that it was weak through the flesh, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and as an offering for sin, he condemned sin in <margin>4</margin> the flesh, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh, but <margin>5</margin> according to the Spirit. For those who live according to the flesh [set their minds on] the things of the...

---

<margin>26</margin> **From the body of this death**] <note>original: "De corpore mortis hujus"</note> *from the body of this death*. The Greek phrasing sounds more as if "this" refers to the "body" rather than to "death," meaning *from this body of death*. For he calls it a "body of death" because the body is liable to the impulses of sinning. And he adds *from this body* because he has taken upon himself the persona of a man feeling these kinds of impulses. Indeed, this is like a single key to understanding Paul: if one notices the shifting of the personas of whom and to whom he speaks. Certainly, it is clear that Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine exegete who synthesized earlier Greek commentaries</note> feels the same as we have indicated, if one observes not what the Translator rendered, but what he himself interprets: for he adds, that is, *subject to death*. Origen <note>A 3rd-century scholar and one of the most influential early Christian theologians</note> interprets it no differently, interpreting "death" as "sin," and for that reason, it is called a "body of death" in which sin dwells. Most recent scholars subscribe to these views. For the explanation some give of the "torpor of death" regarding a crowd of encroaching evils is less clear.

<margin>27</margin> **The grace of God**] <note>original: "Gratia Dei"</note> *I thank God* <note>original: "Εὐχαριστῶ τῷ Θεῷ"</note>, that is, *I give thanks to God*. And so it is read in the corrected Latin manuscripts, so that the speech belongs to one showing through whom he has been delivered, namely, through the one to whom he gives thanks. Although Laurentius <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous Renaissance humanist and critic</note> indicates that in some copies it was written *Grace to God* <note>original: "Χάρις τῷ Θεῷ"</note>, which differs in words but is the same in meaning. From Origen’s interpretation, it is not clear what he read, but nonetheless, one may guess that he read what we have shown to be in the Greek, even from these words: *The response is truly to what he had said, 'Who will deliver me from the body of this death?' Now no longer by that person’s authority, but by Apostolic authority: the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.* From this, it appears that the Apostle describes all these things <margin>A</margin> to expose the evils that go on within us, so that in the end he might <term>teach</term> <note>Latin: doceres</note> from how many and how great evils Christ has snatched us. Thus far Origen, indicating that what has been said by Paul up to this point was said under the persona of one who is not yet a partaker of divine grace, still struggling with the impulses of the flesh, unequal to them. But the response to the exclamation is not under that same persona, but under the persona of one who has been delivered from that most miserable slavery, not through the law, but through the grace of Christ. Therefore, he refers the exclamation, *Infelix ego homo, quis me &c.* <note>translation: "Wretched man that I am, who me..."</note> to one persona, and the speech of the one giving thanks to God to another: just as Origen himself wants those many things which Paul mentions above regarding the law of death and the members, and the necessity of sinning, to be said under the persona of another. Ambrose <note>The 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note> likewise interprets from these words that the man is to be understood as having been delivered by the grace of God from the body of this death, not as one *to be* delivered. The words that follow shortly after support this: *For the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death.* Yet if he had read *Grace of God*, this particle would not fit Paul, who was not in need of being delivered, but had already been delivered; nor do the things Ambrose writes hold up. Therefore, it must be read as *Thanks to God* or *I give thanks*: by which words, having already been delivered, he gives thanks to God, through whose grace he has attained what neither nature, nor the law of Moses, nor conscience, nor works could provide. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, the "Golden-Mouthed" 4th-century preacher</note> without controversy reads and interprets *I give thanks* <note>original: "Εὐχαριστῶ"</note>. For he speaks thus: *For even if he gives thanks to the Father, yet he also does so to the Only-begotten; for the Son is also the cause of the same thing* <note>original: "Εἰ γὰρ καὶ τῷ Πατρὶ εὐχαριστεῖ, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ μονογενεῖ, ταὐτὸ γὰρ καὶ ὁ Υἱὸς αἴτιος"</note>. And in the rest of his commentary, "I give thanks" is repeated so many times that it cannot be seen as an error of the scribes. Theophylact follows Chrysostom in all things. Furthermore, Saint Jerome, in his eighth question to Algasia, reads *The grace of God*: and the commentary itself declares that he read it so, when he says: *The Apostle, having turned back to himself, or rather the man under whose persona the Apostle speaks, gives thanks to the Savior that he has been redeemed by his blood and has laid aside his filth in baptism. And shortly after: I give thanks to God through Jesus Christ our Lord, who has delivered me from the body of this death.* Nor does it matter that certain interpreters, citing this passage, mention the "grace of God" and remind us that he who delivers from the body of death is shown here; for anyone who gives thanks to God as one delivered indicates by this very fact through whom others also can be delivered. For the rest, since he gives thanks as one delivered, all apply this to the persona of Paul, though they vary regarding the exclamation: the older commentators do not want it to pertain to the Apostle’s persona, while Jerome thinks it is said under the persona of a righteous man. And yet, if we take "the body of death" to mean the proclivity toward sinning, as if you were to say "dying," nothing prevents all these things from fitting Paul even <term>according to</term> <note>Latin: juxta</note> the Latin reading. Certainly, Augustine argues this against two epistles of the Pelagians, in book one, chapter eight, and several following, so that this whole passage might apply to Paul—either as a child, or under the law of sin, or under grace—feeling the movements of the impulses, even if not consenting to them. But he twists many things so harshly that it is more fitting to say Paul takes upon himself the persona of the human race,

<column-break/>

leading me captive to the law of sin, which is in my members.
<margin>24</margin> Wretched man that I am, who will rescue me 26 from this body
<margin>25</margin> liable to death? 27 I give thanks to God through Jesus
Christ our Lord. And so I myself serve the law of God
with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin.
<margin>VIII. 1</margin> There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are
in Christ Jesus, who do not live according to the flesh, but
<margin>2</margin> according to the spirit. For the law of the spirit of life through
Christ Jesus has set me free from the jurisdiction of sin and
<margin>3</margin> death. For what the law could not provide,
in that part where it was weak through the flesh, this God
provided, having sent his own Son in the appearance of flesh liable to
sin; and concerning sin, he condemned
<margin>4</margin> sin through the flesh, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled
in us, who do not live according to the flesh, but
<margin>5</margin> according to the spirit. For those who are carnal, the things
of the flesh...

---

in which is the lawless Gentile, the carnal Jew under the law, and the spiritual man delivered through grace.

<margin>1</margin> **For the law of the spirit of life**] <margin>C</margin> *For the law of the spirit of life*: "spirit" in this place is in the genitive case, so that you understand the law, not of the flesh, which brings death, but of the spirit, which bestows life. *For the law of the spirit* <note>original: "Ὁ γὰρ νόμος τοῦ πνεύματος"</note>. Although the Greek is such that the sense could be: *the law of the spirit which is life* <note>original: "τοῦ πνεύματος τῆς ζωῆς"</note>, since the masculine article is placed before "life." "The law of the spirit," however, sounds as if you were to say "the spiritual law," according to the idiom of the Hebrew language. Furthermore, it did not escape Theophylact to refer two genitives to the same word: the law of the spirit, the law of life. For he refutes those who interpret the "law of life" as the law of Moses. Chrysostom discusses almost these same things.

<margin>2</margin> **The law of sin and death**] *from the law of sin and death* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου τῆς ἁμαρτίας καὶ τοῦ θανάτου"</note>. And here he would have translated more elegantly: *from the right* <note>or jurisdiction</note> *of sin*. Furthermore, the Greek phrasing is ambiguous. For it can be taken thus: "from the law of sin and of death," so that "law" refers to both equally; or "from the law of sin and from death," which is the companion of sin. Moreover, as for the fact that in Chrysostom *set you free* is read instead of *set me free*, it makes no difference to the sense.

<margin>3</margin> **For what was impossible for the law**] *For the impossibility of the law* <note>original: "Τὸ γὰρ ἀδύνατον τοῦ νόμου"</note>. In Greek, it is "of the law" in the genitive case, not "to the law" in the dative. And indeed, Ambrose reads it thus. But this phrasing has no small difficulty, since it could be understood as *the impossibility of the law*, or the weakness of the law, through which it was infirm and ineffective. But the things that follow do not fit unless we are willing to admit that Paul, either through forgetfulness or lack of skill or neglect of the Greek language, did not render the remaining part. For as I weigh this passage with all my strength, it seems to me that some words are missing to complete the thought, as if we should read it thus: *For <margin>D</margin> what the Mosaic law could not do according to the carnal part, according to which it was weak and ineffective, this God provided by sending His Son, who fulfilled the spiritual part of the law.* And the conjunction that follows makes me approve of this more: *and concerning sin he condemned sin.* For unless you understand the verb *provided*, or *effected*, or something similar, the conjunction seems redundant. Unless it pleases you that "impossible" <note>original: "ἀδύνατον"</note> is placed as a nominative absolutely instead of a genitive, so that the sense is: *Since it was impossible &c.* Otherwise, this part, *For what was impossible of the law*, in which it was weakened, would have to be referred to that which follows, *he condemned sin concerning sin*, which is the thing that the law could not do.

<margin>4</margin> **In which it was weakened**] *in which it was weak* <note>original: "ἐν ᾧ ἠσθένει"</note>. It can also be taken thus: "in that it was weak," that is, "insofar as it was weak," so that *in* <note>original: "ἐν"</note> is placed for *through* <note>original: "διὰ"</note>. Furthermore, he said "was weakened" for that which is invalid and not very effective. And lest he should seem to accuse the law, he added *through the flesh*, that is, through the carnal understanding of the law, <margin>E</margin> or the weakness of the flesh, which lacked evangelical grace.

<margin>5</margin> **In the likeness of sinful flesh**] *in the likeness* <note>original: "ἐν ὁμοιώματι"</note>, that is, in similarity: which, as indicated above, sounds more like assimilation and image. For that Christ assumed the persona of a guilty man was a kind of "hypocrisy" (let there be no offense at the word). So that this might be more evident, we have translated *under the appearance of flesh liable to sin*: for the word *appearance* <note>original: "species"</note> seems more suited to expressing a false similarity. Furthermore, according to the idiom of the Hebrew language, he said *flesh of sin* for "flesh liable to sin." And for this reason, Augustine warns in his thirty-first sermon on the words of the Apostle that it should be read as a compound: *Christ truly had flesh; he appeared to have the flesh of sin, although he did not have it.*

<margin>6</margin> **Concerning sin he condemned sin**] The translator of Origen indicated (for he added this of his own) that in the Greek it is not *concerning sin* <note>original: "de peccato"</note>, but *for sin* <note>original: "pro peccato"</note>: so that we may understand that sin was condemned regarding sin. For it cannot be understood as sin condemned *out of* sin, since it is *concerning sin* <note>original: "περὶ ἁμαρτίας"</note>: and yet they seem to interpret it thus. To me, it seems this sense can be taken not absurdly: *Christ, having been sent, even condemned sin regarding sin*: that is, he convicted and refuted sinners, so that those who before had deceived with a false image of justice, it might now be clear that they were impious; since they killed Christ, the end of the law, under the pretext of keeping the law. Others explain *concerning sin* as being taken for a "victim," which is usually sacrificed for a fault according to the rite of the Mosaic law. And that indeed fits Christ beautifully, except that the preposition *concerning* <note>original: "περὶ"</note> stands in the way. It would be smoother if it were *by* <note>original: "παρὰ"</note>. What Theophylact brings forward fits the Greek reading better: that sin, by a certain right of its own, had raged against sinners. But when it struck against the innocent Lord, it was then, in a certain way, caught in a sin. But the curious reader will weigh these things more exactly. In this argument, we chiefly pursue those things which contribute to the integrity of the reading.

7 <term>The things of the spirit, they savor]</term> <note>original: "φρονῶσι"</note> *they set their minds on*. This is not repeated among the Greeks. It is more accurately *they feel* or *they care for*, rather than *they savor* <note>Erasmus critiques the Latin word *sapiunt*, which can mean "to taste" or "to be wise," preferring a word for "inclination."</note>. It is strange why the Translator here affected a useless abundance of words, which even hinders understanding. For the same word, which just now was rendered *they savor*, he now translates as *they feel*. You might say, what does it matter? It matters a great deal if one wishes to philosophize on these matters.

8 <term>Because the wisdom of the flesh]</term> <note>original: "φρόνημα"</note> *mind* or *disposition*. This is the same word that he just several times translated as *they feel*. It is a noun derived from the verb that he just translated as *to savor* and *to feel*; rather, it signifies an affection of the mind: as in <note>original: "μίγμα φρονεῖν"</note> *to be of a high mind*, and <note>original: "ξηρὰ φρονεῖν"</note> *to care for human things*. Thus in this place, the word does not so much signify *wisdom* or *prudence* as it does *affection and care, or thought*. This is indicated by the words *to think* and *to be anxious*, which flow from the same source. In Latin, one is said to "savor the flesh" who is led by carnal affections; I have never found "wisdom" used to mean "affection." It is no wonder that Origen philosophizes in his own way about the carnal understanding of the law, since a coarse understanding is born from coarse affections, and vice versa. Saint Chrysostom also touches upon Origen’s commentary. And the word *and* is not found among the Greeks.

9 <term>Is an enemy to God]</term> But rather, it is *enmity against God*, <note>original: "ἔχθρα εἰς Θεόν"</note>. Saint Jerome cited it this way more than once against Jovinian. Likewise Augustine, both in several other places and when explaining certain passages of this Epistle, if I am not mistaken. For in the common manuscripts, this reading remains: *because the prudence of the flesh is an enemy unto God*; it is probable that *enemy* was substituted for *enmity*. Furthermore, the speech is more harmonious if an abstract noun responds to an abstract noun: for *Prudence of the flesh, death* preceded it; *but prudence of the spirit, life and peace*. What he had previously called "death," he exaggerates by repeating that it is "enmity against God"—as if he were saying it is something worse than death. So says Chrysostom. Yet for the Greeks, if the accent is moved to the last syllable, it will sound like "hostile" <note>original: "ἐχθρὰ"</note>. But the preceding neuter noun *mind* <note>original: "φρόνημα"</note> does not allow this, since it would more likely be *hostile* in the neuter <note>original: "ἐχθρὸν"</note>. Hence I wonder that some contend the reading "enemy" is correct, unless perhaps they think the scripture, which is consistent in all copies, should be changed. Now it is no wonder if some Latin authors in their narrations say *wisdom is an enemy to God*, since both readings declare nearly the same sense, except that *enmity* is more effective and more congruent with Paul's phrasing.

10 <term>If however the Spirit of God]</term> <note>original: "εἴπερ"</note> is the Greek word, which is equivalent to *surely* or *since*. Although in this place it does not seem to be the word of someone doubting, but of someone reasoning: as if you were to say, *since indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you*. Even though Origen and Ambrose read and explain it ambiguously. Yet it is more probable that Paul attributes the *Spirit* to those whom he addresses, for shortly after, speaking more harshly, he turns the discourse away from them, saying, *but if anyone does not have the spirit of Christ*. This was noted by both Theophylact and, before him, Chrysostom, who warns that *if indeed* <note>original: "εἴπερ"</note> in Paul's writing is frequently the word of one confirming, not doubting, as if you were to say *since* <note>original: "ἐπειδὴ"</note>. An example of this is in the first chapter of Second Thessalonians: *if indeed it is just for God to repay with affliction those who afflict you*. Theophylact noted here that *if indeed* does not sound like doubt, but confidence. Sometimes it is also the word of one entreating: *If I have deserved any good of you, or if anything of mine was ever sweet to you.* Since the Translator removed this ambiguity, why are those silent now who cry out that the breadth of meaning is being narrowed by me—as if the ignorance of a translator produces a "fruitful abundance" of scripture, or as if unskillfulness does not rather produce a false fertility. For that fertility is not to be praised which the legal experts describe as, *Say this, or say that, or say that.*

11 <term>The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit lives]</term> For *lives*, the Greeks have *is life*; and so Augustine cites it in explaining questions on this Epistle. And again, in explaining the seventy-fifth Psalm. Also in the thirteenth book of the *City of God*. And against Faustus in the twenty-fourth book, second chapter. Likewise Hilary in the eighth book on the *Trinity*. Similarly Athanasius in the booklet *On the Holy Spirit* to Serapion. And likewise Ambrose explaining this place, supported by old Latin handwritten manuscripts. Perhaps *is life* is more effective than *lives*. Indeed, it *is life* because it provides life. For he is treating, if I am not mistaken, of the Spirit of Christ, not our own spirit: which is almost indicated by what follows: *But if the Spirit of him, who raised Jesus from the dead, dwells in you.* There is, however, an easy slip between *life* and *lives* <note>original: "ζωή & ζῇ"</note>; and there is very little difference as far as the meaning is concerned, according to the property of Hebrew speech. It is no wonder if some Authors here mention *our spirit*; since just as the resurrected body of Christ promises resurrection to our bodies, so the immortal spirit of Christ confers life upon our spirit. Theophylact truly not only reads *life*, but also interprets it in this sense: "Not only," he says, "does he live himself, but he is able to give this to others." He also mentions there were those who understood "spirit" here to be Christ himself.

12 <term>Because of justification]</term> <note>original: "διὰ τὴν δικαιοσύνην"</note>, that is, *because of righteousness*: as he often translates elsewhere. For *justification* <note>original: "δικαίωσις"</note> sounds more like the act of being made just.

13 <term>Because of his Spirit dwelling in you]</term> Hilary, in his second book on the *Trinity*, reads *because of his Spirit who dwells in you*; as does the Latin version. Although this is too minute a point to be contended over. Certain Greek manuscripts varied here, D in most of which it was, <note>original: "διὰ τὸ ἐνοικοῦν αὐτοῦ Πνεῦμα ἐν ὑμῖν"</note>, that is, *because of his Spirit who dwells in you*. In some, <note>original: "διὰ τοῦ ἐνοικοῦντος αὐτοῦ Πνεύματος ἐν ὑμῖν"</note>, that is, *through his Spirit who dwells in you*. To the meaning it matters very little. For although the preposition *through* <note>original: "διὰ"</note> added to the genitive signifies the instrument, and joined to the accusative the cause, nevertheless nothing forbids the same thing from being both the cause and the instrument in some places.

14 <term>Again in fear]</term> <note>original: "εἰς φόβον"</note>, that is, *unto fear or terror*.

15 <term>The Spirit of adoption of the sons of God]</term> Instead of these three words, there is one among the Greeks, <note>original: "υἱοθεσίας"</note>, which signifies the adoption of sons. Indeed, the adoption of those who are not sons by nature into the place of sons. For even grandsons are adopted, though this is a very dear form of adoption. The Greek speech has no awkwardness; the Latin I do not see how it can stand. For if "adoption" is taken actively, as if the sons were adopting, the speech is absurd; but if passively, sons are not said to be adopted, since they come into a foreign family through adoption, just as a E Magistrate is said to be *created* or a Bishop *elected*, when he becomes a Magistrate or Bishop by votes. One does not say "adoption of sons" in the same way one says "creation of Magistrates"; rather, the sons of another are adopted by a person into the place of sons, and they are said to become the sons of the adopter through adoption, and the adopter or "arrogator" makes the sons or grandsons of another his own. A father or paternal uncle is said to "give into adoption." If we understand the "adoption of sons" who were previously sons of Satan, the scripture does not mean this. If we understand "to be adopted as sons of God," the Latin phrasing does not hold; it should rather have been said, *the Spirit of adoption into the sons of God*. Just as it is permitted for Paulus to adopt the son of Scipio into the place of his own grandson, so it is permitted to adopt the grandson of another to become his son. To avoid this awkwardness, some translated it *Spirit of adoption*: because adopting into the place of a son is the primary type of adoption; hence, when placed by itself, it is understood to refer to that which is excellent. Indeed, the very tenor of Apollonius’s speech declares that this is about those adopted into the right of sons. Furthermore, the genitive *of God* has been added, although it is not found in the Greek codices. For he does not here distinguish the sons of God from the sons of men, but F distinguishes the sons of grace from the servants of the law.

16 <term>Abba, Father]</term> <note>original: "אבא יהוה"</note> To the Hebrews, or rather the Syrians, as Jerome indicates, this sounds like *father*, a word composed of the first two letters, *aleph and beth*. But he left the Hebrew word as it was, to signify that there is something peculiar in that vocabulary, which both fathers listen to with pleasure and children learn to sound out first. For with this they immediately implore the father's help, just as among the Latins there is *pappus*, a word peculiar to infants. As for the fact that he added, *the Father* <note>original: "ὁ Πατὴρ"</note>, it is uncertain to the Greeks whether this is an interpretation of a foreign word for the sake of emotional emphasis, or an interpretation of a foreign word for the Romans, especially since it was added in the nominative case. Though it seems more likely to me that it was said by way of *anadiplosis* <note>repetition of a word</note>, since this style of speaking is almost peculiar to the Hebrews for the sake of intensity, sometimes repeating the same word, sometimes rendering the same word with another of the same power: as in, *Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord*: and, *God, my God*: and, *Good fig, good*: and, *Lord, Lor-*

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the eighth chapter of the Epistle to the Romans. Having established the believer’s transition from the law of sin to the life of the Spirit, the text now explores the intimate relationship between the believer and God through the cry of "Abba, Father" and the shared suffering and future glory of all creation.</meta>

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER VIII.
## 603 604

16 ...Abba, Father. The Spirit itself bears witness with 
17 our spirit that we are children of God. And if children, also heirs; heirs indeed of God, and joint-heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him, so that we 
18 may also be glorified with him. For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is 
19 to be revealed in us. For the eager expectation of the creation waits for the revealing of the sons of 
20 God. For the creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in 
21 hope. Because the creation itself also will be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the 22 glory of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation groans together and travails in pain together until now. 
23 And not only it, but we ourselves also, having the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves,

<margin>A</margin>
*not our Lord*. For in this last example, the Hebrews use different words: the first is the four-letter name of God, the Tetragrammaton <note>original: יהוה</note>, consisting of these letters: *he*, *vav*, *he*, *yod*, which they call "ineffable" <note>original: ἄῤῥητον</note>, that is, unspeakable. The latter is *Adonai* <note>original: אדני</note>: which is a common title and is frequently attributed even to men. However, these are the same words that Christ uses when praying to the Father in Mark chapter fourteen: "Abba, Father." Furthermore, I believe it happened through an error of copyists that Augustine writes in his 178th Epistle that *Abba* is a Greek word and *Pater* is Latin; since Paul was not writing in Latin to the Romans, and it is beyond controversy that *Abba* is a Syriac or Hebrew word. But I will subjoin Augustine’s words: *Paul, writing to the Romans, says: "in whom we cry Abba, Father." In one name he uses two languages; for he says Abba using the Greek word for Father, and then the Latin name for Father again.* Truly, I believe these words were falsely attributed to Augustine’s writings. Thomas Aquinas is better, for he says *Abba* is a Hebrew voice, while *Pater* is Greek or Latin; similarly, both Greeks and Latins call upon a "Father."

<margin>B</margin>
17 **Bears witness with** ] <note>original: συμμαρτυρεῖ</note>. This is rendered as "witnesses along with." It refers either to what is reported or what is owed. Thus, an account is "rendered" to reason. But for the Greeks, it is "to attest with," or to translate more literally, "to contest," so that you understand there is a double testimony of two spirits: ours, and God's. Furthermore, the testimony of our spirit is confirmed by the testimony of the Divine Spirit; just as those are called "allies" <note>original: symmachi</note> who bring help in battle. And we commonly say, "conscience is the witness." The human spirit's testimony is weak, especially in those who are imperfect, unless the testimony of the Divine Spirit is added. Nor does anything forbid us from saying there is a mutual love between God and man, which the love of God gives as a gift; so too there is a mutual testimony between God's Spirit and ours—not because our spirit confirms God, but because it is a witness to itself. Chrysostom suggests the Greek preposition refers to the vocal testimony that preceded it: "in which we cry Abba, Father." The vocal testimony is then confirmed by the secret testimony of the Divine Spirit, who confirms that voice by his gift. Theophylact does not disagree.

18 **If indeed we suffer with him** ] <note>original: εἴπερ</note>, that is, *provided that*. This could also be taken as a point of reasoning rather than doubt. Also, in this place, "to suffer with" is not what is commonly understood by those influenced by popular usage—"to be moved by another's misfortune"—but rather to be a partner, imitator, and rival of the afflictions of Christ.

19 **So that we may also be glorified** ] glorified together <note>original: συνδοξασθῶμεν</note>: so that you understand the glory is common to us and Christ.

20 **For I reckon** ] <note>original: Λογίζομαι</note>, that is, *I repute* or *I calculate*. For Paul does not "opine" this as if doubting, but certain that it is so, he weighs it in his mind. He is not speaking of faith—for which the word "think" is too harsh a term to describe such a trial, as it is frequently joined with doubt—but of the consideration of those things which he believed. Through this, he calculates the account, as it were, comparing the troubles of this life to be endured for the Gospel with the reward of eternal life, which Christ promised to all the pious. This comparison makes the things we suffer here seem light while we contemplate that eternal happiness in our minds. Indeed, I have not yet read "to reckon" <note>original: λογίζεσθαι</note> used for "to think/suppose" <note>original: οἴεσθαι, ἡγεῖσθαι, δοκεῖν, νομίζειν</note> in the way Greeks use those other terms. It would be more tolerable to say "to estimate" <note>original: æstimare</note>, which word fits with reasoning: we "estimate" that as dear which we think is of great price; but we "reckon" as dear that which we hold as dear through the induction of the mind. If the Greek term meant nothing other than our word "suppose," Paul spoke wrongly to the Philippians in the fourth chapter, "think on these things" <note>original: ταῦτα λογίζεσθε</note>; or certainly, the translator erred by rendering it "cogitate on these things" when he should have rendered it "estimate these things." And in Second Corinthians chapter ten, he translates "let him think this again" for the same Greek root. Paul used this word in the twelfth chapter of the same Epistle: "lest anyone should think more of me," that is, "lest anyone estimate me more highly." In the Epistle to the Romans, chapter two, he used it for "do you think this, O man?" In the sixth chapter of the same Epistle, "so also you reckon yourselves," he is not teaching what they ought to believe—which they had learned long ago—but what they should remember and turn over in their minds; where "estimate" was more fitting than "suppose." Again, in First Corinthians chapter four, "so let a man reckon us," "estimate" fit better than "suppose." For it would be strange if the Corinthians did not already suspect Paul was a steward of the mysteries of God. Again, in Second Corinthians chapter ten, "with that confidence wherewith I am reckoned to be bold against some," the Translator renders the Greek as "I am supposed," while Chrysostom explains it as "I think." For with this speech, he threatens certain people who were despising Paul as just any man. He does not yet say he has decided, but only that he is "thinking" about punishing them unless they repent. Theophylact interprets "reckon" as "to suspect and suppose."

<column-break/>

15 ...Father. The same Spirit 17 testifies together with our spirit, that we are children of God. But if children, therefore also heirs: heirs indeed of God, co-heirs however of Christ, 18 provided that we suffer together with him, 19 so that we may also be glorified together with him. 20 For I calculate that the afflictions of the present time are not equal to the glory, 21 which shall be revealed toward us. 22 For the anxious expectation of the creature waits for the sons of God to be made manifest. 23 For the creature was subjected to vanity, not of its own will, but because of him who subjected it under hope. Because the creature itself 25 shall be delivered from the servitude of corruption, into the liberty of the glory of the children of God. For we know that 26 every creature groans together and travails in birth together with us until this time. 27 And not only that, but even they who 28 have the firstfruits of the Spirit, 29 even we ourselves groan within ourselves.

One who "suspects" <note>original: λογίζομαι</note> he will do something has not yet formed a certain purpose of mind: and he who defines it still holds the spear in his hand, thinking <note>original: cogitans</note> at whom and how it is to be thrown. Furthermore, whoever taught that "to suppose/reckon" <note>original: existimare</note> refers to a certain opinion taught a clearly false thing. For "supposition" is nonetheless doubtful, since an opinion—indeed, an estimation—is often deceptive, as in the phrase: "he who thinks himself to be something," and "they supposed they saw a spirit."

<margin>C</margin>
21 **Which shall be revealed in us** ] There is doubt among the Greeks whether the word "to be revealed" <note>original: ἀποκαλυφθῆναι</note> should refer to the preposition "to/toward" <note>original: πρός</note> or to the participle "future" <note>original: μέλλουσαν</note>. For if it refers to the preposition, the sense will be, "to this end, that future glory may be revealed in us," and then the article "the" <note>original: τῆς</note> seems to be missing, which usually precedes infinite verbs. The Translator seems to have ordered it thus: "toward the glory that is going to be revealed," that is, "to the glory which will be revealed." And it is not "in us," but "into us," or rather "toward us": according to that saying, "We see now through a mirror and in a riddle, but then face to face." Since the preposition "into/to" <note>original: εἰς</note>, as I have often warned, is ambiguous for the Greeks, this reading also holds the sense of a pious soul.

<margin>D</margin>
22 **For the expectation of the creature** ] <note>original: Ἡ γὰρ ἀποκαραδοκία</note>. This does not signify expectation simply, but a vehement and anxious expectation: as both the Greek scholia testify, indicating the emphasis of the Greek voice when something is expected from the heart; hence we translate it "anxious expectation." The Greek word is composed of three parts: the preposition *apo*, and *kara* "head," and *dokein* "to seem/watch": because they vehemently desire to see something, they frequently look forward with their heads stretched out. Hence Ambrose explains it as a "frequent expectation" and Hilary as "distant," because with the head brought forward we look out further. Paul used the same word in the Epistle to the Philippians, chapter one. Aristophanes in *The Knights* used it without the preposition: "the bread-seller looked out for me" <note>original: Ἐκαραδόκησεν εἰς ἐμὲ ὁ βωλο πώλης</note>, that is, "they turned their eyes toward me, standing tall for the promise," to give the sense rather than just the words.

23 **For the creature was subjected to vanity** ] Vanity here does not sound like deceitfulness, but rather frustration <note>original: ματαιότητι</note>: because the creature meanwhile does not achieve what it strives in some way to effect. For example, while propagating one thing from another, with individuals falling and being reborn in turn, it protects the species so it does not perish, meditating on a certain immortality, but in vain.

<margin>E</margin>
24 **Who subjected it** ] "It" was added for the sake of explanation <note>original: διὰ τὸν ὑποτάξαντα</note>. And "in hope" <note>original: ἐπ᾽ ἐλπίδι</note> is more like "under the condition of hope." Furthermore, what follows—"Because the creature itself also shall be delivered," and the rest—could be connected to the previous words: "subjected it under hope: namely this, that it also is to be delivered from servitude," but the repetition of "creature" makes the speech a bit harsh.

25 **Shall be delivered from the servitude of corruption** ] <note>original: ἐλευθερωθήσεται ἀπὸ τῆς δουλείας τῆς φθορᾶς</note>, that is, "shall be rendered free," or "shall be vindicated into liberty." And "corruption" <note>original: φθορά</note> is also an ambiguous word for the Greeks: for it is said of vice, and of that which perishes; here it sounds of destruction. And thus Augustine reads it, explaining the Epistle to the Galatians. The sense is: the Creation, which is now subject to death, is to be brought into liberty, that is, into the glory of the children of God.

<margin>F</margin>
26 **Every creature groans and travails** ] More aptly in Greek <note>original: συστενάζει καὶ συνωδίνει</note>, that is, "groans together and travails together," or "condoles," so to speak. Jerome certainly cites "groans together" in the eighth book of his Commentaries on Isaiah; and Augustine, in the sixty-seventh of his *Eighty-Three Questions*, reads "groans together and grieves." For "grieves," Ambrose reads "travails": so that the preposition "with" <note>original: σὺν</note> refers either to us, indicating that even the mute elements in some way groan with us, or to the entire creation among itself, so that we may understand the whole world is to be changed for the better. Paul, using metaphors to better express the magnitude of the evils, imagines this whole world as one person: though it lacks sense, he nevertheless attributes sense to it, just as in the Psalms mountains are said to exult and rivers to clap. Origen also specifically notes that it is said "groans with," for that which is "groaning with another"; yet not hiding that the books vary: for in some, it was simply "groans."

27 **And not only that** ] "That" is not added among the Greeks <note>original: μόνον δέ</note>. But nevertheless, from those things which soon follow, it is clear it must be understood. What do they do here, who do not want even a tiny mark changed in the Sacred Letters? Origen frequently notes this form of expression in Paul.

28 **Having the firstfruits of the Spirit** ] <note>original: τὴν ἀπαρχήν</note>. It is a wonder what Ambrose was following when he read: "but even we who have the receptacle of the Spirit"; although it is not clear from his narration what he read, unless perhaps where he had written "inception" <note>original: inceptaculum</note>, a scribe changed it into "receptacle" <note>original: receptaculum</note>.

29 **We groan within ourselves** ] <note>original: ἐν ἑαυτοῖς στενάζομεν</note>, that is, we ourselves groan in ourselves, or within our very selves, that is, silently.

<summary>This page analyzes the profound Greek vocabulary used by Paul in Romans 8 to describe the shared destiny of humanity and nature. It highlights how the "joint-testimony" of the Spirit and the "anxious expectation" of creation point toward a universal redemption from corruption.</summary>
<keywords>Abba Father, Tetragrammaton, Adonai, joint-testimony, eager expectation, vanity, corruption, firstfruits of the Spirit, groaning of creation, philological analysis</keywords>

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>30 The adoption of the sons of God]</margin> <note>original: "υἱοθεσίαν"</note>, that is, *adoption*. But the Translator <note>the Latin Vulgate translator</note> added certain words for the sake of explaining the matter: and he does this constantly with this word. Augustine, in the third book against Faustus, chapter three, does not add "of sons," but only cites "adoption." For who adopts their own children? It is strangers who are adopted, not as children already, but into the place of children, as was said before.
<margin>31 The redemption of the body]</margin> <note>original: "ἀπολύτρωσιν"</note>, which is properly said when captives are redeemed by a price paid, as those taken by pirates or in war. "Of the body" is said instead of "from the body": so that we may be freed from this body, which he previously called the "body of death." However, this seems added as if he wanted to interpret "adoption" as being nothing other than our being freed from this body and receiving an immortal body.
<margin>32 What he hopes for]</margin> <note>original: "τί καὶ ἐλπίζει"</note>, what *also*, or what *further* does he hope for? The conjunction was not idle, signifying that it is in vain to hope for what you already see.
<margin>B</margin>
<margin>33 Likewise also the Spirit helps our infirmities]</margin> In the Greek it is in the plural number, "infirmities," or our "weaknesses" <note>original: "συναντιλαμβάνεται ταῖς ἀσθενείαις ἡμῶν"</note>. Now, the word "to help" <note>original: "συναντιλαμβάνεσθαι"</note> means to be present with assistance for one struggling in an undertaking, and therefore he added "likewise," that is, in a similar way. Just as we strive by waiting through patience, so also the Spirit applies his help to those who are failing, as if reaching out a hand to those in labor.
<margin>34 For what we should pray]</margin> <note>original: "τὸ γὰρ τί προσευξώμεθα"</note>. The Translator did not express the force of the article *to*, which refers to this whole phrase that follows: hence we translate it, *Indeed, this very thing, what we are to pray for as is fitting, we do not know*: that is, so far are we from being able to protect ourselves, that we do not even know what protections are needed.
<margin>35 The Spirit asks]</margin> <note>original: "ὑπερεντυγχάνει"</note>, which is sometimes translated as "asks," sometimes as "interpellates," or "intercedes." It occurs whenever someone approaches another regarding the business of a third party, just as if someone were to go to a Prince to recommend the cause of a friend. It should be noted that he does not simply say "intercedes" <note>original: "ἐντυγχάνει"</note>, but "intercedes excellently" <note>original: "ὑπερεντυγχάνει"</note>. For this prefix <note>original: "ὑπέρ"</note> usually signifies excellence in Greek. The sense here is, unless I am mistaken, that even if the spirit of a man sometimes asks for harmful things, nevertheless the Holy Spirit, by his breathing, corrects the minds of some regarding what was wrongly asked, acting as a supervisor over all petitions.
<margin>36 What the Spirit desires]</margin> <note>original: "τὸ φρόνημα"</note>, that is, the "sense," or what the Spirit "thinks," that is, the "affection" of the Spirit: which Terence translates as "sense," saying *I know his mind [sense] well*. It is the same Greek word which he has already translated so many times as "prudence." I do not know what he is thinking who considers "sense" and "affection" to be carnal words that do not suit the divine Spirit. Do we think Paul was not in his right mind when he wrote this? Or was it not said of God, "Who has known the mind [sense] of the Lord?" And is not "mercy" an affection, which is especially attributed to God? And if the Spirit of God is rightly said to desire, to long for, to groan, and to intercede, is it absurd to attribute "affection" to him? But in God there are no affections just as there are in us: truly, neither to be wise, nor to live, nor to have mercy, nor to love is in him just as it is in us, and yet Scripture uses human words of this kind everywhere when speaking of him.
<margin>37 Work together for good]</margin> The word "works together" <note>original: "Συνεργεῖ"</note> can refer in Greek either to the Spirit or to "all things": so that according to the first sense you understand that the Holy Spirit turns all things to good by his help; according to the second, you take it that all things, even bad things, are an aid to the saints toward happiness: and this sense pleases me more, and Chrysostom and Theophylact follow it. Nor should the singular verb "works together" move anyone, since "all things" <note>original: "πάντα"</note> is a neuter plural subject <note>In Greek, neuter plural subjects often take singular verbs</note>.
<margin>38 According to purpose]</margin> <note>original: "κατὰ πρόθεσιν"</note>, that is, according to the destination of the mind, so that the "purpose" refers not to the saint, or to a man of right purpose, but to the predestination of God. So say Origen and Thomas, even though Ambrose seems to touch upon both senses: although Origen, explaining a little further down who are called and not chosen, and who are called and chosen, disagrees somewhat with himself, interpreting "those called according to purpose" as those who, before they were called, were already inclined in mind toward divine worship, and whose ready will only lacked the calling—meaning that "purpose" pertains not to God who destines, but to the man who determines in his mind: unless perhaps the Translator added this from his own head. Augustine follows Ambrose in the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter seven: "They are the elect," he says, "who

are called according to purpose, but a purpose not their own, but God's." For Paul, in the next chapter of this Epistle, used "the purpose of God" in a similar sense; and again to the Ephesians, chapter one. Nor indeed is "of the saint" added among the Greeks; it is simply "the called." And that Origen read it thus is clear from his own interpretation, when he says: "It must be seen whether perhaps from this which he said, to those who are called according to purpose (whom he foreknew and whom he predestined, etc.)." Nor did Ambrose read it otherwise, for he rendered it thus: "to those who are called according to purpose, whom God foreknew as believers who would be fit for him, so that before they believed, they were known." Augustine read <margin>C</margin> the same in the book *On Rebuke and Grace*. Chrysostom and Theophylact follow this reading and sentiment, although Thomas and most of the ancient Latin manuscripts resist it. It appears that "saints" was added from other places in which these two words, "called saints," are frequently joined together.
<margin>39 Called saints]</margin> <note>original: "κλητοῖς οὖσι"</note>, those who are called. First, "saints," as has been said, is redundant: second, "called" here is not a participle, but a noun: as we indicated at the beginning, so that he may again exclude the works of the law, in which the Jews wrongly trusted, and show that true holiness comes from the calling of God.
<margin>40 Whom he foreknew]</margin> <note>original: "οὓς προέγνω"</note>, or, as it is read by some, *he fore-knows*. We have already noted above that among the Greeks this verb is sometimes taken for "he decided" or "he decreed," because knowledge is joined to deliberation: and it seems that these terms do not differ so much in kind or reason, but are connected as if distinct by certain steps and intervals, so that Paul might set the matter more clearly before the eyes. Thus "foreknowledge" <note>original: "πρόγνωσιν"</note> belongs to one deliberating and deciding, which nevertheless <margin>D</margin> might in some way be changed, to speak in the manner of men. Then "predestination" or "definition" <note>original: "προορισμὸν"</note>, because it is a decree of one now openly pronouncing what has been decided, which is not usually done unless something has been so decreed that it cannot be changed. Furthermore, when you have pronounced what you have decided, it remains that you exhibit and perform what you have promised. But he begins to exhibit who calls and invites. Then, lest he should seem to have called in vain, he also justifies those called, without which we are not capable of the promise. Finally, the reward is given to the justified. Therefore, God had "foreknowledge" from eternity of those whom he decided and established were to be called to immortality: "foreknowledge" of those about whom he has now pronounced through his Prophets, and much more through his Son, his decree having been promulgated. But he "called" through the preaching of Jesus; he "justified" through his death; he "glorified" through the resurrection and the reward of immortality. Or, he "called" through the Gospel doctrine; he "justified" through baptism; he "glorified" through the gifts of the Spirit. In this way, Paul, by certain <margin>E</margin> steps, proceeds from that which is first of all to that which is highest of all, so that the matter might be more firm and absolute. But if anyone should think it too harsh that I remove "foreknowledge" in the common sense from this place, let him know that Theophylact, the Greek interpreter, interpreted it in the same way, and—which some will believe more willingly—a recent scholar, who thinks this is the difference between "foreknowledge" and "predestination," that the former is less firm and the latter more firm: indeed, where Peter writes "foreknown before the foundation of the world," in which place "foreknown" should have been translated according to their sentiment, even Lyranus does not fear to explain it as "pre-ordained." And Thomas indicates there were those who interpreted "foreknowledge" in this place as something else, namely a preparation for grace, which in time God shows in the saints, lest forsooth there be no difference between foreknowing and predestining—whose commentary Thomas rightly rejects. Although Origen also does not approve in this place that we take "foreknowledge" in the common sense, according to which God also foreknew <margin>F</margin> sinners, so that it would then be false that whomever he foreknew, those he also predestined. Truly, just as Divine Scripture, according to the custom of its own speech, says those are "known" whom God embraces with affection ("I do not know you," and "The Lord knows the way of the righteous"), so here they are called "pre-known." Nor indeed is it hidden from me that some have sought from this place a field for exercising their wit, in which they might philosophize about the foreknowledge and predestination of God—namely Origen, Saint Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, and after all these the Schools of the theologians, whose industry I do not disapprove. But this sense, which we have shown, seems to me simpler and more genuine. But if a different sense pleases anyone, let each enjoy his own judgment by my leave. We advise, we do not lead; and we bring our things into the open in such a way that we do not prejudice the opinion of anyone at all.
<margin>41 Those he also magnified]</margin> In Greek it is <note>original: "ἐδόξασε"</note>, that is, *glorified*, namely through the gifts of the Spirit and the excellent adoption: and better...
<meta>catchword: ...better</meta>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Romans, Chapter 8. # THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>32</margin> He who did not spare even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not also with him freely give us all things?
<margin>33</margin> Who shall bring a charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies.
<margin>34</margin> Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died, or rather, who is also risen, who is even at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us.
<margin>35</margin> Who shall separate us from the love of God? <note>original: "ἀγάπης τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note> Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or the sword?
<margin>36</margin> As it is written: "For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter."
<margin>37</margin> But in all these things we are more than conquerors <note>original: "ὑπερνικῶμεν"</note> through him who loved us.

---

<margin>A</margin> *[his love] was toward him, than toward them.* <note>The author is likely citing a variant or a specific father's commentary here.</note> Ambrose reads "magnified." Origen, explaining this passage, reads "glorified," though he notes the context according to our *Vulgate* edition.
*Who also [did not spare] his own Son*] The word "own" <note>original: "suo"</note> is redundant in our version; for "Son" was sufficient to mean "his own" or "proper." Certainly, "own" was not present in the ancient manuscripts, nor in Augustine, who cites this passage in the fourth book of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter twenty. Indeed, Ambrose in several places cites this testimony according to the Greek reading. Hilary, in the sixth book of *On the Trinity*, also thought it should be noted that he said "his proper Son" <note>original: "proprio Filio"</note> rather than simply "his Son."

<margin>B</margin> *He gave us all things*] <note>original: "χαρίσεται"</note>, that is, "he will give," in the future tense. Ambrose and Chrysostom explain it this way, and Theophylact agrees, even if the ancient codices and citations of the Fathers might suggest otherwise. Therefore, I suspect a variation in the Greek manuscripts; in some, it was written as "he gave" <note>original: "ἐχαρίσατο"</note> instead of "he will give." Both senses work well. I suspect someone, seeing that it does not yet appear that all things have been given to us by God, changed the tense of the verb. But nothing prevents the gift from having already been completed—as it stands by decree—even if there is not yet full possession of what was given.

<margin>C</margin> *Who shall accuse against the elect of God?*] <note>original: "Τίς ἐγκαλέσει κατὰ ἐκλεκτῶν τοῦ Θεοῦ;"</note> that is, "Who will bring a charge, or who will intend a crime against God’s chosen ones?" Faber <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, a contemporary humanist scholar.</note> reads it as "Who would accuse on their behalf," that is, "Who would institute an accusation for the elect of God," in defense of the elect against enemies. However, in this place, Paul's meaning is clear if you understand the interrogation to function as a negation; the sense being that no one would dare to criminalize those whom God has not only called but also chosen. Consequently, the words that follow, up to the phrase "who shall separate us from love," should be read under the same interrogation, so that you understand them as a defense. Although we hear these passages read publicly in churches as statements <note>original: "pronuntiative"</note> rather than questions. For most common manuscripts have: *Who is he that condemns?* As if responding to this inquiry, the following are added: *Christ Jesus who died, nay rather who rose again, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us.* Augustine noted this passage in the third book of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter three. However, he distinguishes this speech somewhat differently than we commonly do. For when he had pointed out the difference between a "searching inquiry" <note>original: "percontationem"</note> and a "simple question" <note>original: "interrogationem"</note>—in that many things could be answered to an inquiry, but to a question only "yes" or "no"—he adds: "It shall be pronounced in such a way that after the inquiry, 'Who shall accuse against God's elect?', the part that follows is uttered with the sound of a question: 'Is it God who justifies?' so that it may be silently answered, 'No.' And again we inquire, 'Who is he that condemns?' and again we ask, 'Is it Christ Jesus who died? Nay, rather who rose again? Who is at the right hand of God? Who also intercedes for us?' so that everywhere it is silently answered, 'No.'" In the same manner, one can gather that Ambrose distinguishes it from his words explaining this place: "He denies that God, who justifies us, accuses us. Likewise, he says Christ cannot condemn us, because he loved us with such affection that he died for us, and rising again, he always pleads our cause with the Father." Origen seems to join these two particles in our manner: "God who justifies, who is he that condemns?" For "to justify" and "to condemn" are opposites. Then, "Christ Jesus who died, etc.," he does not seem to read as being spoken by one inquiring, but by one declaring; not as an answer to the previous question (which is already finished, with "None" being understood), but as a new heap of arguments. Thus the sense is: "It is God who justifies; who will be the one to condemn? It is Christ Jesus who died for us, nay rather who also rose, and sitting at the right hand of God the Father intercedes for us; who will accuse the elect or who will condemn them?" Thus, from so many arguments piled together, it follows equally that there will be no one to criminalize or condemn us. And to me, this reading seems more genuine, if only because some of these points seem too great to be gathered if it is concluded that the Father will not accuse the elect since he justifies, or that Christ will not condemn since he intercedes for us. It is more effective that, since we have God as a judge justifying us, and the Son of God dying and still interceding for us, there is nothing for us to fear from anyone's accusation. Neither Chrysostom nor Theophylact mention an inquiry here, but read these words—"Christ Jesus who died, etc."—declaratively, not disagreeing with Origen. This part could be connected with the following, "Who therefore shall separate us, etc." For it follows that him who loved us so much that he died for us, rose for us, and now sits at the Father's right hand and does not cease to plead our cause, we should constantly love in return, even if hard things must be borne for his sake. But I do not see that any interpreter has followed this distinction. Much light would have been added to the speech if the translator had added one syllable: "Is it God who justifies?" and "Is it Christ who died?" For among the Greeks,

<header>THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER VIII.</header>

<margin>32</margin> He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how is it possible that he would not also with him give us all things?
<margin>33</margin> Who will bring charges against God's elect? It is God who justifies.
<margin>34</margin> Who is the one who condemns? It is Christ who died, nay rather who was raised, who also is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us.
<margin>35</margin> Who shall separate us from the love of God? Shall affliction? Shall distress? Shall persecution? Shall famine? Shall nakedness? Shall peril? Shall the sword?
<margin>36</margin> Just as it is written: "For your sake we are delivered to death all day long; we are considered as sheep destined for slaughter."
<margin>37</margin> Truly in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.

---

the articles make the speech clear enough: <note>original: "Θεὸς ὁ δικαιῶν"</note> and <note>original: "ὁ κατακρίνων"</note>, "God is the one who justifies," "Who is the one who condemns?" <note>original: "Χριστὸς ὁ ἀποθανών"</note>, "Christ is the one who died, etc.," so that what preceded is repeated here: "Who is the one who condemns?"

<margin>D</margin> *Who therefore shall separate us?*] "Therefore" <note>Latin: "ergo"</note> was added by the Latin translators, and it is better adorned by it. For if you separate this speech from the preceding ones, Paul seems as if suddenly seized by emotion and to have broken out into this exclamation because of the great arguments of confidence that preceded. This is how it appears to Theophylact, following the opinion of Chrysostom, who separates it. But if you read it conjunctively, it would cohere better without the conjunction: since God and Christ are such toward us, who shall separate us from the love of Christ? "Love" here seems to be taken actively—namely, the love with which God loved us and provoked us to love him in return. It is of minor importance that Ambrose reads "from the love of Christ," while Origen reads "from the love of God." Augustine, in the fourth book of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter twenty, offers this entire passage as an example of a speech that joins vehemence—that is, *deinosis* <note>A rhetorical term for powerful, vivid, or indignant language meant to move an audience.</note>—with ornament. For the pleasantness of the speech lies partly in the gradations: *foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified*; partly in the similar endings and cadences; partly in the repetition of the same word (which they call "tradition"), as in the nearby example, *overcome, overcome*; then in opposites: *justifies* and *condemns*; death, life; things present, things to come; height, depth. For parallelisms and the lack of conjunctions <note>original: "asyndeta"</note> also contribute to vehemence, as does the use of questions. Indeed, this whole speech teems with inquiries and questions. If one distinguishes the sharpness or contention of a speech from "grandeur"—which is the third character of style among rhetoricians—a question that is more vehement than even a strong assertion contributes to sharpness. For it is more vehement to say, "how will he not also give us all things?" than if he had said, "Doubtless he will give us all things with him." By this confidence in the manifest truth, the listener is so pressed as if he has nothing to answer. Likewise, it is sharper to ask, "shall tribulation, shall distress, shall persecution, shall famine," than if he had simply denied it. Short clauses starting with the same word <note>original: "incisa"</note> contribute to the same effect, as I just mentioned, as does that part: "neither death, nor life, nor angels, etc." Those things properly make a speech "grand" because, as if by divine inspiration, it speaks of nothing lowly. It proposes magnificently: "We know that for those who love God all things, etc." Then the whole speech consists of magnificent things and persons: "death, life, strength, height; God, Christ, at the right hand of God, Angels, principalities, powers." Nay, even that is magnificent: "in all these things we are more than conquerors" <note>original: "ὑπερνικῶμεν"</note>; and, "For I am certain." What did Cicero ever say more grandiloquently?

<margin>E</margin> *As sheep of the slaughter*] This testimony is taken from Psalm 44. Furthermore, where the translator renders it "of the slaughter" <note>original: "occisionis"</note>, the Hebrew is *ha-tebach* <term>הַטֶּבַח</term>, which among them sounds more like "mactation" <note>The ritual preparation or slaughtering of an animal.</note>: that is when a butcher handles and examines a beast to see if it is fit to be killed. Indeed, there is something similar among the Latins in "mactatio," hence Horace says:
->*The slaughtered <note>original: "mactata"</note> victim will come more gently.*<-
Therefore, he said "sheep of slaughter" in place of "sheep destined for slaughter." Otherwise, in this place, the translator should have omitted the conjunction "that" <note>original: "ut/quia"</note>; for what does this speech mean to the Latins, "It is written because for your sake we are mortified," unless the Scripture was produced for the reason that we are mortified for God all day long? Among the Greeks, the force of this conjunction <note>original: "ὅτι"</note> is varied; among us, it is not. Whenever it has the force of confirming a statement, it was better to omit it if we wish to speak in proper Latin. I admit that ecclesiastical writers frequently use "since" and "because" in this way, either to confirm or to introduce a quotation, especially where they support opinions with testimonies from the Scriptures, but it is not for that reason called good Latin.

<margin>F</margin> *We overcome because of him*] <note>original: "ὑπερνικῶμεν"</note>, that is, "we are more than conquerors," so that you understand something more than simply "we win"; but we even win such great things easily, being superior to all those evils. Thus says Theophylact. Then, "through him who, etc.," not "on account of him" <note>original: "διὰ τό"</note>. Augustine, in the twenty-second book of *The City of God*, chapter twenty-three, reports it this way: "in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us." He cites it the same way in the fourth book of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter twenty. Origen likewise reads it this way, explaining: "And therefore, he says, in all these things we overcome, not by our own virtue, but through him who loved us." St. Basil, in his work to Amphilochius *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter eight, reports it thus: "Through him: so that if you read 'because of him,' his argument would collapse." Ambrose, however, reads "because of" <note>original: "propter"</note>, understanding that in such great afflictions we endure with an unbroken spirit out of love for Christ, who spent so much on us, in a way repaying him by dying in turn. These are the words of Ambrose himself, if anyone should ask: "And what wonder is it if servants die for a good master, when the master died for servants and evil ones? Therefore benefits overcome and exhort the mind to persevere because of him who..."

<vocab>Epistle of Paul, Romans, Origen, Ambrose, Augustine, Theophylact, Chrysostomus, justification, condemnation, God's elect, mactation, more than conquerors, hypernikōmen, ha-tebach</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final verses of Romans Chapter 8 and begins the transition into Chapter 9.
