# TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER IX.

<margin>38</margin> ...who loved us. For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, <margin>39</margin> nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

<margin>IX. 1</margin> I say the truth in Christ, I lie not, my conscience also bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, <margin>2</margin> That I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart. <margin>3</margin> For I could wish that myself were anathema <note>A term meaning "set apart" or "accurst."</note> from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh: <margin>4</margin> Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises; <margin>5</margin> Whose are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen.

<meta>catchword: who</meta>

---

<margin>A</margin> **Who loved us**] <note>original: "qui dilexit nos"</note> Chrysostom and Theophylact <note>Two significant Greek Church Fathers known for their commentaries.</note> agree with us, both as readers and interpreters, that it is no wonder if we emerge superior to such great evils when we have God as our defender. And I believe this to be the genuine reading. For since the Apostle had spoken certain magnificent things, in his usual manner he transfers all glory to Christ.

**For I am certain**] <note>original: "Certus sum enim"</note> The Greek is *Pepeismai gar*, that is, "I am persuaded," or "I trust," as Saint Jerome translates it in his ninth question to Algasia. Ambrose reads it the same way.

**Neither things to come, nor things present**] This phrase is said to be missing in some Greek copies, or at least it has nothing to which it corresponds, whereas "present things" <note>original: "instantia"</note> usually correspond to "future things," and "height" to "depth." Although in the place I just cited, Saint Jerome adds "fortitude," but omits "virtues," which he reads as the Greek *dynameis* <note>powers or miracles</note>; and to those, as it seems, he said "powers." In Ambrose, a reading somewhat different from this is found, counting only nine parts: *Neither death, nor life, nor angel, nor virtue, nor height, nor depth, nor presence, nor future, nor other creature*. His own interpretation clearly proves that Ambrose read it this way. From this it is clear that in place of "fortitude"—which in our version is not placed in its proper spot—he placed "virtue" next to "angels," which he relates to a miracle. Furthermore, he makes no mention of "principality," even if Origen, in the course of his explanation, touches somewhat on "principalities," though he is otherwise not anxious in this place about reciting the parts of this *synathroismos* <note>A rhetorical term for a gathering or enumeration of different things.</note>. Augustine, in explaining questions on this Epistle, lists several: *death, life, angel, principality, presence, future, virtue, height, depth, and another creature*. But it often happens that in a catalog of individual names like this, the manuscripts vary somewhere because the scribes' memories slip.

<margin>B</margin> **1** **My conscience bearing me witness**] Since the Greek is *symmartyrousēs*, it is understood either that the testimony of the conscience is added to other testimonies, or, according to a common figure of speech, the character of a person is attributed to the conscience—just as when we speak to our own soul, or say we are quarreling with our soul, when it is the soul itself speaking to itself. Or, perhaps the prefix *syn* <note>meaning "with" or "together"</note> simply emphasizes the act. Certainly, no ancient writer, as far as I know, has noted the force of this word in this specific place.

**2** **For I myself wished**] Among the Greeks, *Anathemata* refer to things dedicated to the gods and buried or set aside for this purpose. Look, Reader, whether the Greek *Euxomēn an* might be taken as "I would pray" instead of "I would wish"—even if the particle *an* is not added—so that you take it as "I would wish if it were possible." Furthermore, the phrase "from Christ" refers to the *anathema*; as if you were to say, something set aside and alienated from Christ. Indeed, *anathēmata* are called gifts dedicated to the deities in temples. From this, the ancients also used "sacred" in a negative sense, as Horace says:
-> —— *let him be sacred and untouchable.* <- <note>original: "sacer intestabilis esto"</note>
and Virgil:
-> *The sacred hunger for gold.* <- <note>original: "Auri sacra fames"</note>
Jerome, in his ninth question to Algasia, thinks *anathema* can be taken here for bodily killing, not for the destruction of the soul; but what follows, "from Christ," contradicts this. Accordingly, Chrysostom laughs at the trifles of certain people who wanted *anathema* to stand for *kephalaion*, that is, for a dear thing set aside, which we commonly call a "treasure" or "jewel." He also notes that Paul said "I myself," when the second pronoun seems redundant; but it has emphasis: "I, the very one who labored so much not to be separated from Christ." It also seems to have a sense of singularity: "I alone would wish to perish for so many, if it were allowed."

**3** **Whose is the adoption of sons**] The Greek is *hōn hē huiothesia*, that is, "whose is the adoption," as we have advised before. The translator wanted to explain the force of the Greek word, suggesting that even brothers are adopted as grandsons. Augustine does not add "of sons" in the third book of *Against Faustus*, chapter three; a matter discussed more fully above.

**4** **And the covenant**] The Greek is *kai diathēkai*, that is, "and the covenants." Augustine reports it this way in the twelfth book of *Against Faustus* and in handwritten books, and soon, discussing this passage, he repeats "covenants"; for the tablets of the covenant pertain to the sons. Jerome reads it thus in his ninth question to Algasia, interpreting one in the letter and the other in the spirit. And so it is written in the oldest Latin manuscripts, although Jerome thinks this word among the Hebrews, from whom it was taken by our people, sounds more like "pacts" than "testaments."

<margin>C</margin> **5** **Legislation**] <note>original: "Legislatio"</note> The Greek is *hē nomothesia*. For the Greeks, this is a single word that pertains to the making of all laws, not just one. Augustine, in the booklet he wrote against the adversary of the law, reads it as "the constitution of the law." For Paul feels that the glory of the Law established by God belonged to them.

<column-break/>

...we overcome, through him who loved us. <margin>38</margin> For I have persuaded myself that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, <margin>39</margin> nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

<margin>IX. 1</margin> I say the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience attesting to me at the same time, through the Holy Spirit, <margin>2</margin> That I have a great sorrow and continuous torment in my heart. <margin>3</margin> For I myself would wish to be anathema from Christ for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, <margin>4</margin> Who are Israelites, whose is the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the constitution of the law, and the worship, and the promises, <margin>5</margin> Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ, as far as pertains to the flesh, who is God over all, to be praised forever, amen.

<meta>catchword: amen.</meta>

---

**6** **And the service**] The Greek is *hē latreia*, that is, worship or religion; which elsewhere he translates as "servitude." However, he means the priestly duties and the rites and ceremonies of the sacred things, according to Origen’s interpretation. But what Latin speaker would understand any such thing by "obsequium" <note>the word used in some Latin versions</note>? For *obsequium* is said of someone complying with another's will, which often sounds negative. Certainly, no one speaking Latin has used it for the worship of a Deity; but the translator spoke in common speech.

**7** **And the promise**] The Greek is *epangeliai*, that is, "promises" or "things promised," as Ambrose reads.

<margin>D</margin> **8** **He is God over all**] This passage can be divided in three ways: First, so that this part, "who is over all" <note>original: "ho ōn epi pantōn"</note>, stays attached to what came before and is separated from what follows, like this: "From whom is Christ according to the flesh, which Christ is over all," or "who was over all." For lest anyone suspect Christ’s dignity was diminished by his assumed human nature, looking to his divinity, Paul added, "who is over all." This division attributes divinity to Christ, because nothing is "over all" except the one God. For it is placed there in stead of "he is." Then, after a colon, let there follow: "God blessed forever," so that this is an act of thanksgiving arising from the contemplation of such great charity toward the human race—that God willed His Son, who is God, to assume a human body for our sake. But in this reading, the article *ho* would be somewhat redundant in "the blessed God." The second reading holds that the whole speech hangs together: "From whom is Christ according to the flesh, who, since he is God over all, is blessed forever." This reading most evidently declares Christ to be God, though it would be smoother if *hos ōn* <note>who being</note> had been written instead of *ho ōn* <note>the one being</note>. The third reading has no inconvenience regarding the grammar: "From whom is Christ according to the flesh." Here the sentence ends. Then, from the consideration of such great goodness of God, an act of thanksgiving is added: *ho epi pantōn Theos, eulogētos eis tous aiōnas*, that is, "May the God who is over all be blessed forever." In this way, we understand that God, by an ineffable plan, provided all these things—the Law, the Covenant, the Prophets, and finally Christ sent in a human body—to restore the human race. And here, you may take "God" to mean the whole Trinity, which frequently happens in Holy Scripture—just as when we are commanded to adore God alone and serve him only, Christ is not excluded. But if "God" refers to the person of the Father (which is frequent in Paul, especially if Christ or the Spirit is mentioned in the same place), even though it is clear from other places of Scripture that Christ is no less truly called God than the Father or the Holy Spirit, nevertheless, this passage is not effective for refuting the Arians <note>A group in the early Church who believed Jesus was a created being, not fully equal to God the Father.</note>, since nothing prevents it from being referred to the person of the Father. Therefore, those who contend that it is clearly proven from this passage that Christ is openly called God either seem to trust too little in other testimonies of Scripture, or attribute no intelligence to the Arians, or <margin>E</margin> have contemplated the Apostle's speech with too little attention. There is a similar passage in the eleventh chapter of this Epistle, where he calls the Father "blessed forever": *The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever*. For there, among the Greeks, "blessed" can only be referred to the Father. Ambrose indicates that there were those who tried to twist these words toward the Father, especially since the mention of the Son preceded here. Whenever that happens, the Apostle usually uses the name of God to signify the person of the Father. But Ambrose, who contends that this passage cannot be understood except of the Son, seems to have thought they must produce another person to whom this speech applies; yet the matter itself shows that this is very easy to do. Those who came after the defeat of Arius argue with great contention that this cannot be understood as anything other than the Son; among these is Theophylact, who specifically warns that the impiety of the Arians is crushed in this place, as they wanted only the Father <margin>F</margin> to be truly and properly called God. It is surprising that similar points are discussed in the Commentaries of Origen, indicating that at that time there were those who did not dare to call Christ God, lest they seem to be making multiple gods. But it is likely that this passage was corrected in the Commentaries by Jerome (or whoever the translator was), or if at the beginning of the work he does not hide that he added certain things of his own, using such freedom that he occasionally compares Greek manuscripts with Latin ones. And Saint Jerome objects to Rufinus that in the books he translated from Origen, he left all his errors except those regarding the Divine Persons, because he knew such a notable blasphemy would be utterly intolerable to Roman ears. For Origen was taught that the Son was a creature, and the Holy Spirit was a servant of the creature. How then does Origen manage to fight against the Arian dogma, which they had drawn from his own books and for which they were condemned many years later? Someone might say Origen corrected himself here, having discussed the matter impiously in his books *On First Principles*. But Jerome, writing against Rufinus, denies that it is found in his writings where...

<meta>This page continues the detailed scholarly commentary on Romans Chapter 9. # PAUL’S EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER IX.

<margin>6</margin> 6 ... Not however that the word of God has failed <note>original: "οὐχ οἷον δὲ, ὅτι ἐκπέπτωκεν ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note>. For they are not all Israel who are of Is- <margin>7</margin> rael. Neither, because they are the seed of Abraham, are they all children, but: In Isaac shall your seed be called. That is, <margin>8</margin> it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, <margin>9</margin> but the children of the promise are counted as the seed. <margin>10</margin> For this is the word of promise: At this time <margin>11</margin> I will come, and Sarah shall have a son. And not only this, but also when Rebecca had conceived by one, our father Isaac. For when the children were not yet born, nor had done anything good or evil, so that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him who calls,

---

He speaks in a "catholic" <note>Meaning "orthodox" or "universal" in a theological context.</note> manner regarding the dogmas about which he wrote heretically in his books *On First Principles* <note>original: "περὶ ἀρχῶν"; this refers to Origen's famous and controversial theological treatise.</note>. Chrysostom, although he does not exclude the divinity of the Son, nevertheless does not use the weapon of this testimony against the Arians <note>A fourth-century heresy that denied the full divinity of Christ.</note>, which he is otherwise inclined to do quite willingly when the occasion arises. However, because he seems to interpret this passage somewhat obscurely, I will faithfully transcribe the commentary pertaining to this place: *For both the foreknowledge,* he says, *of God's grace, and the rainbow, and the promises, and the law—considering and weighing all these things in his mind, and how much zeal God applied through His Son to save the Jews, he cried out vehemently, saying: Who is blessed forever, amen; giving thanks for all these things to the only-begotten of God. For what, he says, if others speak evil? We, however, who know His secrets, and His ineffable wisdom, and His great providence, know for certain that He is worthy to be glorified, not to be attacked with insults, and so forth.* 

First, he interprets this passage as referring jointly to the Father and the Son, although in the context there is no mention of the Father, unless He is understood by the name of "God." Secondly, since he says that thanks are rendered step by step to the only-begotten of God for all the things he recounted, he signifies that these words, *blessed forever*, should be referred to the Son, whom the Jews were cursing because he had promised things to some but displayed the promise to others. And yet, by this phrase, *who is over all things, God*, nothing prevents those words from also being referred to him, as *who is over all things, God*. For I think some might perhaps devise a fourth reading, so that this phrase, *who is over all things, God*, is inserted into the context as a parenthesis, as if by a sudden rapture of the mind, as though from one admiring the depth of the divine counsel, which was pleased to redeem the human race in such a way. In the same way, Thomas the Apostle pronounced an incomplete sentence: *My Lord and my God.* Let the rest of the speech cohere: *from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is blessed forever.* 

From the Scripture, which is sometimes corrupted by scribes, a certain judgment cannot always be drawn. I found it punctuated this way in Chrysostom: *the promises, of whom are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh.* <note>original: "αἱ ἐπαγγελίαι, ὧν οἱ πατέρες, καὶ ἐξ ὧν ὁ Χριστὸς τὸ κατὰ σάρκα"</note> Here, after a colon, follows: *he who is over all things, God,* <note>original: "ὁ ὢν ἐπὶ πάντων Θεὸς"</note> and then after a minor pause <note>Erasmus uses the term "hypostignē," a Greek punctuation mark similar to a comma or semicolon.</note>, follows: *blessed unto the ages* <note>original: "εὐλογητὸς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας"</note>. This distinction renders the meaning, as has been said: "May he who is over all things, namely God, be blessed forever." The same was found in Theophylact, except that he did not add the pause after "God." Saint Cyprian, in his second book against the Jews, chapter five, cites this passage with the mention of "God" omitted. Likewise, Hilary when explaining Psalm 122; this might seem to have been omitted by the negligence of librarians. Even Chrysostom gives no sign that he read the word "God" in this place; a word that might seem to have been added by some studious person as if explaining who that "over all" was—namely, God. Nor is there any reason for people to shout that Christ is being robbed of his divinity, since the periphrasis <note>A roundabout way of speaking.</note> says the same thing as the name of God, just as if one were to say "the creator of heaven and earth" instead of "God." 

Therefore, let those people be quiet who, tickled by this zeal, stir up a tumult at every opportunity as if the Church were about to fall. Whether the word "God" is omitted here matters nothing to the meaning, since his own periphrasis stands in place of the name of God. For he recounted all these things—the adoption, glory, covenants, legislation, worship, and promises, and the fathers from whom Christ was born according to the flesh—to declare that they were not done by chance, but by the admirable providence of God, who provided for the salvation of the human race in so many ways. He did not simply say "God," but "He who rules and is over all," dispensing and moderating all things by His divine counsel, to whom praise is due forever for such remarkable love toward us, whom the Jews were cursing while they attacked His only Son with blasphemies. Therefore, nothing is taken away from the glory of God, even if this word is not added. Whether this passage refers to the entire Trinity, the Son is not excluded, nor is the Holy Spirit; or whether it properly refers to the Father, who promised and sent His Son to redeem the human race, the divine nature of Christ is abundantly demonstrated from other passages of Scripture. Nor do I think there is anyone today of the Christian profession whose ears would endure someone doubting this matter. 

Furthermore, if the Church teaches that this passage is to be interpreted in no other way than regarding the divinity of the Son, the Church must be obeyed. But this does nothing to refute heretics or those who listen to nothing but Scripture. If one says this passage cannot be explained otherwise according to the property of the Greek language, the facts themselves quickly refute this assertion. Now it is also admitted that "over all" <note>original: "ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων"</note> can be taken in two ways: "over all things" or "over all people." The translator of Origen touches on both readings; "over all things" is more absolute, but "over all people" is more properly suited to Christ, so that he is preferred over Patriarchs, Prophets, and Moses, just as an only son is over servants or even friends. There remains one variation of reading: "over all" can be referred to "blessed," so that we understand Christ is to be praised above all people or all things forever. Unless the article also seems significant in the phrase "according to the flesh" <note>original: "τῷ κατὰ σάρκα"</note>, which some see as superfluous; for it has a more expressive force of exception. Otherwise, Christ might have seemed simply born of the Jews and nothing more than a man; now the article as if excludes this thought, "that which is according to the flesh," that is,

<column-break/>

<margin>6</margin> Amen. 9 Not however that I speak these things as if the word <margin>7</margin> of God had failed: 10 for not all who are of Israel are Israel. Neither because they are the seed of Abraham are they all children, but: Through Isaac shall your seed be named. That is, not those who are children of the flesh are the children of God, but those who are the children of the promise are counted as the seed. 12 For this is the word of promise: 13 At this time I will come, and there shall be a son for Sarah. 14 And not only this, but also Rebecca had conceived by one, Isaac our father. For the boys being not yet born, when they had done neither anything good nor evil, so that the purpose of God might remain according to election, not from works, but from him who calls,

---

<margin>Distinction</margin> only as far as it pertains to the human body: for according to his better nature, he is God born of God, just as he is man born of the fathers.

<margin>B</margin> 9 **Not however as if the word of God had failed** [ *Οὐχ οἷον δὲ, ὅτι ἐκπέπτωκεν ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ* ]. Which he translates thus, *Not however as if the word of God had fallen away*: that is, what I so desire, as if despairing of them, is not such that I think the divine promises have been made void, since God promised salvation to Israel. The figure of speech has an omission <note>An ellipsis.</note>. "I do not say these things because..." and so forth. Thus also the Latins say, "not that," but the added conjunction makes the speech somewhat harsher.

10 **for not all from the circumcision**] "From the circumcision" is not in the Greek, but it is in this manner: *οὐ γὰρ πάντες οἱ ἐξ Ἰσραὴλ, οὗτοι Ἰσραήλ*. "For not all who are from Israel, these are Israel," so that "are" is understood. For in the second instance, he calls the nation itself "Israel." Not everyone born from the stock of Israel is a true Israelite. Nor is it rare in the Sacred Books for "Judah" to be used not for the man, but for the nation, and "Jacob" to be used for the Hebrews themselves. Furthermore, I see that the Ancients almost all agreed in the interpretation of this name—among whose number are Origen and Jerome—that they interpret *Israel* as *a man seeing God*. However, this interpretation of the word does not fit the passage <margin>C</margin> in Genesis chapter thirty-two, where Jacob's name is changed. *Your name shall by no means be called Jacob, but Israel, because if you have been strong against God, how much more shall you prevail against men?* For here it indicates the name was changed because he had prevailed against the Angel in wrestling. This is that force by which God rejoices that we break into the kingdom of heaven, and by faith and persistent prayers extort a blessing from Him which we do not deserve, and by which martyrs, while they are tested by various afflictions even to the contempt of life, persevere in the profession of the name of Jesus. 

Only Tertullian seems to me to touch upon the correct interpretation in his fourth book against Marcion: "And another," he says, "is inscribed in the name of Israel, for what is wiser and of an irreproachable confession than the name of a martyr growing strong with God, which is the interpretation of Israel?" Josephus was of this opinion; why Jerome rejects it I do not see, since he himself interprets it as, *If you have been a prince with God*. But to be a prince in wrestling with God is to prevail. Indeed, "with God" here has the same force as "against <margin>D</margin> God": just as we are said to fight *with him* against whom we fight. Only Theodoret translates it, *You have been strong with God*. Saint Jerome, in his *Hebrew Questions*, confesses that he is overwhelmed by the authority of famous authors who interpreted *Israel* as *a man or a mind seeing God*. That interpretation, although he follows it elsewhere, he strongly rejects here.

<margin>E</margin> 11 **Neither they who are the seed**] *Οὐδ᾽ ὅτι*, that is, "Neither that," or "Because": and thus Ambrose reads it. The most ancient manuscript of the Pauline Library agrees with this, from which this was corrupted by scribes. Otherwise, the Translator seems to have read *ὄντα* instead of *ὅτι*. *Neither therefore are they immediately the children of Abraham because they are the lineage drawn from him.*

12 **For the word of promise**] *ὁ λόγος*, "the word" or "the speech": for he does not put just one word.

13 **According to this time**] *κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τοῦτον*, that is, "in this time."

14 **Not only she**] *Οὐ μόνον*, the Translator added the pronoun "she" to soften the Greek figure; and that not wrongly, though elsewhere he did not dare to do so.

15 **From one intercourse**] *ἐξ ἑνὸς κοίτην ἔχουσα*, that is, "having a bed from one." It can be read two ways: "from one, Isaac," and thus the Greek genitive was to be translated into the Latin ablative, *patre nostro*, that is, "by our father"; or, "from one," understand "son"; then, "having a bed," that is, the marriage of our father Isaac, so that you understand the promise consisted of one offspring, namely Jacob: for Esau was rejected. Finally, unless you understand *ἐξ* as "she was having," the speech seems incomplete, unless you repeat what was above. He was counted in the number of the children of Abraham as far as children are concerned, since she had raised them equally from the same father: but he who was rejected was not held as a son, nor did it profit him to have been begotten of the same father. Furthermore, "having a bed" was said modestly for "she had conceived." 

Lorenzo Valla rightly refutes those who think in this passage that Rebecca conceived the twins from the same single act of intercourse, as if it pertained to this matter how many acts of intercourse it took to conceive <margin>F</margin> Jacob and Esau. Rather, Paul, to take away the confidence of parents, puts forward two brothers from the same father, the same mother, and born at the same time on the same day, one of whom was nevertheless rejected. What about the fact that it cannot even cohere as "one intercourse," since *κοίτη* <note>bed/intercourse</note> among the Greeks is of the feminine gender, while *ἑνὸς* <note>one</note> is masculine? Nor is it read as *κείτηται*, but *κοίτην*, that is, "a bed." Someone most impudently attacked my "impudence" because I placed this passage among those of more recent authors that are manifestly corrupted. Hear the man's boastful speech: *Truly, if the other things are such as Desiderius <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the author.</note> recounts in that catalogue of corrupted passages, and there are no other places more corrupted in the Latin edition, it may be said—not to say impudently—that it is less than modest to say this place is one of infinitely many that are manifestly corrupted.* These...

Thus he says. Yet he had undertaken to defend the Translator <note>Erasmus refers to the author of the Vulgate, whom he often critiques for linguistic inaccuracies.</note>, and he showed a way so that if anything occurred which could not be excused, it should be blamed on the scribes. Although he does this here, he nevertheless expresses great annoyance; and he does this all the more shamelessly because he himself could not polish this passage, which I have said was corrupted. "Who," he asks, "ever said to have a 'bed' <note>original: "cubile"</note> instead of 'to conceive'?" Indeed, who ever said "to have" instead of "to be pregnant"? Yet it must be understood this way here if we read "from one intercourse" <note>original: "ex uno concubitu"</note>. What would be so strange if, for the sake of modesty, we say "intercourse with a man" for one who had a matter with a man, just as Paul in Hebrews 13 calls the "undefiled bed" <term>torum immaculatum</term> the chaste use of marriage, and here had said "to have a bed" for "to conceive" or "to be pregnant." The Latins do not speak this way, I admit; but it is probable the Hebrews spoke thus, whose idioms the Apostle frequently expresses. "It is well enough," he says, "to say 'from one intercourse' if we translate our <term>ἐξ ἑνὸς κοίτης</term> <note>original Greek: "from one bed/conception"</note>." Has he not neatly untied the knot? I noted that the word was corrupted by scribes, "intercourse" <note>original: "concubitu"</note> for "conception" <note>original: "concubitum"</note>; he prefers to have the Apostle's speech considered corrupted, since no Greek manuscript has this, nor does any Greek interpret it in the same way. For Chrysostom and Theophylact mention the same parents and the same birth of twins, but by no means the same act of intercourse. Moreover, who knows whether twins are conceived from the same act? As for his saying that Theophylact seems to feel it was the same act, the very words he cites from Theophylact testify that they are obscure; Theophylact, following Chrysostom in his usual manner in this interpretation, distinguishes between the example of Isaac and Ishmael and the example of Esau and Jacob: the former had only a common father, while the latter had both parents in common, and were twins brought forth in a single birth. In the freely translated text of Origen, the words "from one intercourse" <term>ex uno concubitu</term> are indeed found; but in the commentary, there is not a single syllable declaring that he read it that way. The same applies to the words of Irenaeus. Nor does Ambrose touch upon anything regarding the "same intercourse." There remain two Latins who seem to have read "from one intercourse"; but, as must be guessed, they were deceived by a fault in the manuscripts. To the Scholiast, who is falsely called Jerome, I give no answer. Augustine is not infrequently deceived by corrupted scripture, especially when he does not consult the Greek copies. Where now, then, is that choir of Greeks and Latins who read "from one intercourse"? The Ambrosian text has, "having our father Isaac from one intercourse," but faultily, if I am not mistaken. For Rebecca did not give birth to Isaac, but from him received the twins Jacob and Esau. Nor is our reading much more troublesome. Accordingly, some, offended by words that signify nothing, were reading it with a few words added: "But also Rebecca, having twin sons from one intercourse," as Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a prominent medieval exegete.</note> indicates and rejects. And yet the translator of Theophylact turns it this way, though there is nothing of the sort in the Greek author. And it seems to me that this remaining difficulty can be removed if you take the nominative of the participle for the genitive absolute, <term>ἐξ ἑνὸς κοίτην ἔχουσα</term> <note>original Greek: "having a bed from one"</note>, which the Greeks sometimes do. But then the order will be: "Not only Sarah, but also when Rebecca was pregnant from one, namely our father." Then, as if inserted by parenthesis: "For when the children were not yet born, nor had done anything good or evil, so that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him who calls," to which follows the response, "It was said to her": and then, "The major shall serve the minor." Saint Augustine, in explaining several questions of this Epistle, reports it in this manner: "For of those not yet born nor having done anything good or evil." This is how people commonly spoke then, I think.

**17 I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy**] Among the Greeks it is otherwise: <term>Ἐλεήσω ὃν ἂν ἐλεῶ, καὶ οἰκτειρήσω ὃν ἂν οἰκτείρω</term>, that is, "I will have mercy on whomsoever I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whomsoever I have compassion," that is, whomever it has been decreed to pity. Certainly in the first part of this discourse, the Donatian manuscript <note>An ancient manuscript tradition Erasmus frequently consulted.</note> agreed with us, in which it was written: "I will have mercy on whom I am merciful." Here too the Translator, as usual, unsuccessfully strives for variety, turning <term>οἰκτειρήσω</term> (I will have compassion) into "I will show mercy" <note>original: "misericordiam præstabo"</note> and <term>οἰκτείρω</term> into "I have mercy" <note>original: "misereor"</note>. Furthermore, what follows is said in a new way: "Scripture says to Pharaoh," instead of what it was, "Scripture records what was said to Pharaoh."

18 *Therefore it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs*] Chrysostom calls this particle an "objection" <term>ἀντίρῥησιν</term>, as if it were being raised by an adversary, just like the phrase, "Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills." But where is the solution? "O man, who are you," and so on.
19 *Why does he still complain?*] <term>Τί ἔτι μέμφεται</term>, that is, "Why does he still complain, or accuse—God being understood." Even if Laurentius <note>Lorenzo Valla, the humanist scholar who pioneered New Testament textual criticism.</note> and Stapulensis <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, a French humanist and theologian.</note> disagree; of whom the latter wants "complains" to be taken impersonally, and the former passively. Although Laurentius adds our opinion, with which all Greek interpreters agree. First, I do not find <term>μέμφεται</term> (finds fault) positioned in such a way that the person is not added. Secondly, in my opinion, it fits perfectly with what follows: "O man, who are you to answer back to God?" Ruffinus, in the third book of *On First Principles*, renders the sense with changed words: "Why then are we still blamed?" The unrefined reader must only be warned that "complains" <note>original: "queritur"</note> here is said from the deponent verb *queror* (to complain), not from the active *quæro* (to seek). Let whoever wishes mock this "little grammatical note," provided he knows that Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> stumbled over this stone, except that he added a second sense but did not reject the first.
20 *O man, who are you, etc.*] <term>Μενοῦνγε ὦ ἄνθρωπε σὺ τίς εἶ</term>? But "O man, who are you?" Furthermore, the Translator renders it "And indeed" <note>original: "Et quidem"</note>, here he ignored the word <term>Μενοῦνγε</term> (Indeed/But rather). There is, however, a silent opposition <term>ἐναντίωσις</term> in the words "man" and "God"; moreover, an emphasis by no means idle, for man is nothing when compared to God.
<margin>
D
</margin>
21 *Who answers back to God*] <term>Ὁ ἀνταποκρινόμενος</term>, that is, "answering against"; as it is indeed cited by Origen in his fourth Homily on Exodus: or, "you who respond against God." Because he had said, "What then does he have to complain about, if he does what he wills?" And in my opinion, "you who answer back" was more correct than "he who answers back." For he had already made him a responder. He is not indignant that he responds, but that he responds impiously; nor does he deter him from responding, but rebukes him because he dared to respond thus. The translated Origen has "those who rebuke him who [responds]," but now the interpretation declares he read "you who answer back," indicating that silence is imposed for this reason: that he murmurs insolently against God. Just as the Lord in the Gospel did not deign to give any answer to those who petulantly questioned by what authority he did what he did, or from where he had received that power; but by posing a question which they did not dare to solve, he shut their mouths. Yet to those inquiring reverently, he everywhere answers calmly. In meaning there is no small difference, but the Greek word allows for that "you who answer back." Just as before, "who is he that judges" <term>τίς ὁ κρίνων</term> was not translated "everyone who might judge"; as in the fourteenth chapter of this Epistle, <term>σὺ τίς εἶ ὁ κρίνων ἀλλότριον οἰκέτην</term>, the translator renders, "Who are you who judges another's servant?" Neither the interpretation of Chrysostom, nor Theophylact, nor Ambrose, nor Augustine declares that one should read "he who answers" rather than "you who answer." It might aptly be said to a petulant person, "Who are you to answer back?" but to one rebuking him who has already answered insolently, "Who are you who answers back?" is more fitting. The metaphor is taken from bad servants who, when they murmur against the orders of their masters, are called "back-answerers" <note>original: "responfatores"</note>. Thus it is said in this place: "What are you doing, man, answering back to God?" Augustine treats this passage in the sixty-eighth of his *Eighty-Three Questions*, refuting the calumnies of Heretics who gathered from this that Paul had suddenly turned aside to reproaches because he could not explain the knot of the proposed question.
<margin>
E
</margin>

23 *From the same mass*] <term>ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ φυράματος</term> which Augustine cites "from the same lump of kneading." For it refers to clay soaked and tempered with moisture.

24 *One for honor*] <term>τιμὴν καὶ ἀτιμίαν</term>. Laurentius thinks it could be more correctly translated as "glory or disgrace" <note>original: "decus aut dedecus"</note>, especially because "insult" <note>original: "contumelia"</note> does not apply to vessels. And yet, since "insult" is derived from "despising" <note>original: "contemnendo"</note>, what prevents "insult" from fitting an inanimate thing, when it is both expected and despised? Even if it fit less well, the metaphor would still add charm: as if someone were to say that Bassus, receiving the burden of his belly in golden vessels in Martial's poetry, treats the gold with "insult." It is true that in "glory and disgrace" the pleasantness of the figure is restored, which perishes in "honor and insult."

Origen thinks the somewhat disorganized speech can be put together in this way: "God, wanting to show his wrath and make his power known, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, that he might make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy." which is followed by the opposite: *And I will have mercy on the house of Judah*. It
corresponds more correctly with what we read at the end of the second chapter:
*And I will have mercy on her who was without mercy*. Since, how-

*Without Mercy*, it is probable that here too there was a variation in the writing.
Therefore, some reader encountering a different reading thought

and added what he thought was missing. Augustine thinks it was taken from the same
passage of the Prophet that the Apostle Peter writes in the second chapter
of his first Epistle: *Who once were not a people, but now are*
*the people of God, on whom once he did not have mercy, but now he*
*has mercy*. Peter seems to differ from Paul in this, that he reads
*mercy* instead of *beloved*: but in the order he differs equally with the Prophet,

is followed by the son, whose name is *Not My People*. The order is the same in
the joining of the earlier names at the end of the second chapter: *And I*
*will have mercy on her who was without mercy, and I will say to "Not My People,"*
*you are my people*. Furthermore, what follows in Paul, *It shall be in the*
<margin>C</margin> *place where it was said to them, "not my people are you," there they shall be called sons*
*of the living God*, is taken from the first chapter. But what was said by the Pro-
phet concerning the Israelite people, Paul by way of comparison turned toward the Gentiles. In a very ancient manuscript of Donatianus, I found the other part
was omitted. For it read: *I will call not my people, 'my people,' and not having obtained mercy, 'having*
*obtained mercy.'*

31 *There they shall be called*] This was added by the Apostle, since it is not in the
Prophet, evidently so that he might speak more clearly.

32 *Of the living God*] <term>ζῶντος <note>original: "zōntos" — living.</note></term> is in Greek, <term>ζῶντος</term>.

33 *For Israel*] *Over Israel*, or *concerning Israel*, <term>ὑπὲρ <note>original: "hyper" — over or on behalf of.</note></term>: although
the preposition here is ambiguous.

34 *If the number shall be*] The testimony is in Isaiah, chapter ten,
in which, although the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> agree with the Hebrew truth, Paul
nevertheless differs somewhat, though more in words than in meaning. Indeed, the
Seventy translated it, <term>τὸ κατάλειμμα αὐτῶν σωθήσεται <note>original: "to kataleimma autōn sōthēsetai" — their remnant will be saved.</note></term>, that is, *the remnant will be converted*. But Jerome translates in
<margin>D</margin> this manner, *For if your people Israel shall be like the sand of the*
*sea, a remnant of them will be converted*.

35 *For the word completing*] "Word" <note>original: "Λόγον" — Logos.</note> is in the accusative case;
"completing and shortening" are in the masculine gender, implying *it is, name-*
*ly God*. <term>Λόγον γὰρ συντελῶν <note>original: "Logon gar syntelōn".</note></term>, that is, *For completing the word*.
Chrysostom and Theophylact clearly reveal this when
explaining this passage. Nor does it contradict this note that Ori-
gen and Ambrose interpret it concerning the *shortened* Word, since here
both are placed: *He who completes and shortens is the Father*,
he who is completed and shortened is either Christ or his doc-
trine. Although these also differ somewhat from the Hebrew
truth, according to which we read thus on the authority of Jerome, *For a con-*
*summation and an abbreviation the Lord God of hosts will*
*make in the midst of all the earth*. A similar passage of the same meaning is in
the same Prophet, chapter eight: *For a consummation and an*
<margin>E</margin> *abbreviation I heard from the Lord God of hosts over the universal*
*earth*. Furthermore, what he adds, *Isaiah predicted*, is not of one pro-
phesying about the future, but that this testimony preceded that which he
brought forward first, so it would be more fitting: *As Isaiah said above*.
Furthermore, the Apostle left the Hebrew word <term>κύριος Σαβαὼθ <note>original: "Kyrios Sabaōth" — Lord of Hosts.</note></term>, which
the Seventy are accustomed to translate in two ways, sometimes <term>παντοκράτωρ <note>original: "pantokratōr" — almighty.</note></term>,
that is, *almighty*: at other times <term>τῶν δυνάμεων <note>original: "tōn dynameōn" — of powers.</note></term>, that is, *of virtues*. Only
Aquila <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Old Testament into Greek.</note> translates it, <term>τῶν στρατευμάτων <note>original: "tōn strateumatōn" — of the armies.</note></term>, that is, *of the hosts*. Jer-
ome pointed this out when explaining the first chapter of Isaiah. Paul, as I said,
did not fear that the Hebrew word should be changed, I think because
some mystery lies hidden in it that could not be rendered in a foreign language.

36 *Had left to us*] <term>ἐγκατέλιπεν ἡμῖν <note>original: "enkatelipen hēmin" — left remaining in/for us.</note></term>, that is, *he had left in*
*us*. The testimony is taken from Isaiah chapter one.

37 *What then shall we say?*] What follows should be read declaratively,
<margin>F</margin> not interrogatively: *What then shall we say? Namely, we shall say this,*
*that the Gentiles through faith obtained righteousness, and so forth*. Augustine
also noted this passage in the third book of *On Christian Doctrine*. And
Theophylact explains it in this way.

38 *Has not reached*] <term>οὐκ ἔφθασε <note>original: "ouk ephthase".</note></term>, a word which is translated in various ways.
It is proper to one hurrying to occupy something: so that you may
understand that the Israelites also contended for it through the works of the Law, but the Gentiles,
having excluded them, occupied it.

39 *As if from works*] <term>ὡς ἐξ ἔργων <note>original: "hōs ex ergōn".</note></term>, that is, as if from works,
and the Greeks add <term>νόμου <note>original: "nomou" — of the law.</note></term>, that is, *of the law*, so that you may understand works
devoid of faith and charity; it is not added among the Latins. Chrys-
ostom noted, and Theophylact following him, the little word <term>ὡς <note>original: "hōs" — as, like.</note></term>,
as if to signify that the works of the Jews were not truly the works of the Law.
It seems to me it can also refer to imputation. For the Jews attributed their
salvation to their own works, excluding the grace of God.

40 *Rock of offense*] The Translators freely used this Greek word,
whereas they could have said, *stumbling, or offense, or obsta-*

# TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER X.

A 33 **A stone of stumbling.** <note>original: "Λίθῳ τῷ προσκόμματος"</note> As it is written, Behold, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.
<margin>v. 1.</margin>
1. Brothers, the goodwill of my heart, and my prayer to God for Israel, is for their salvation.
<margin>v. 2.</margin>
2. For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.
<margin>v. 3.</margin>
3. For being ignorant of God's righteousness, and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they did not submit to the righteousness of God.
<margin>v. 4.</margin>
4. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.
<margin>v. 5.</margin>
5. For Moses writes of the righteousness which is from the law, that the man who does these things shall live by them.
<margin>v. 6.</margin>
6. But the righteousness of faith speaks thus: Do not say in your heart, "Who will ascend into heaven?" (that is, to bring Christ down).
<margin>v. 7.</margin>
7. Or, "Who will descend into the abyss?" (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead).
<margin>v. 8.</margin>
8. But what does it say? "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart" (that is, the word of faith which we preach).
<margin>v. 9.</margin>
9. That if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
<margin>v. 10.</margin>
10. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made—

---

...of the world, although I am not unaware that a Hebrew idiom remains: "stone of stumbling" <note>original: "lapis offendiculi"</note> instead of "offensive stone," or a stone against which they stumble. Nor do I see why some are offended by the word <term>proskommati</term> <note>original: "προσκόμματι", meaning a stumble or obstacle</note>, which undoubtedly signifies "I strike against" or "I stumble." Furthermore, this testimony is joined together from two places in Isaiah. For the beginning—namely, *Behold, I place in Zion a stone*—and the end—namely, *And everyone who believes in him will not be confounded*—are taken from the twenty-eighth chapter of Isaiah. However, the part woven into the middle, *and a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense*, is taken from his eighth chapter. Yet in this place, too, Paul was more concerned with rendering the sense than the exact words. For while the "Hebrew truth" <note>Erasmus's term for the original Hebrew text.</note> has "he who believes shall not hasten," according to the edition of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, he said "he will not be confounded."

<margin>41 *Will not be confounded* or "kataischynthēsetai" [καταισχυνθήσεται], that is, will not be made ashamed.</margin>

1 **The goodwill indeed of my heart**] <term>hē men eudokia</term> <note>original: "ἡ μὲν εὐδοκία"</note>, which signifies something pleasing and acceptable to the mind. Aurelius Augustine, explaining various questions of this Epistle bit by bit, reads <margin>instead of eudokia,</margin> *good will*: just as the translator here had rendered it in Luke. For this Greek word, modeled after a Hebrew expression, the Roman tongue has no word that properly corresponds. For no one would be happy, I think, if one were to say, "the delight of my heart." However, it sounds like an inclined benevolence and a gratuitous favor which one bears toward another, such as God's favor toward us. Likewise, the things that follow do not match in every respect: for the Greeks have it thus, *and the prayer which is made to God, for Israel is unto salvation*. For he feels that he is providing for the Jews what he can: the inclined goodwill of his mind and prayers to God.

2 *That zeal indeed*] <term>hoti zēlon Theou</term> <note>original: "ὅτι ζῆλον Θεοῦ"</note>, that is, an emulation of God, certainly. For one who knows nothing but Latin, what sense is he to perceive from these words, *they have an emulation of God?* <margin>emulation</margin> "Emulation" in a good sense sounds like imitation; in a bad sense, envy. Neither fits here. Therefore we have translated it as *zeal* [studium], by which word the Latins signify a vehement favor of the mind. From *zēlō* [ζήλῳ] it thus sounds more like "according to knowledge," <term>kat’ epignōsin</term> <note>original: "κατ’ ἐπίγνωσιν"</note>. Zeal is present, but without judgment: like a persistence that urges on one whom it foolishly loves.

3 *And seeking to establish their own*] Here the Greeks repeat "righteousness." <margin>And their own</margin> For the speech is more elegant from the translation of the same word. There is also something underlying in the words "their own—to establish," [idiān-stēsai] and "God's": likewise in "to establish," and "they were not subject." For these things conflict with each other more in sense than in words. Moreover, *idiān* [ἰδίαν], that is, *one's own* [propriam], is more significant than just *suam*.

4 *For Christ is the end of the law*] <term>telos</term> <note>original: "τέλος"</note> in this place sounds like consummation and perfection, not destruction: as Augustine also indicated when explaining the fifth Psalm. Again, Priscillian and the Origenists <note>Followers of the early Christian scholar Origen.</note> noticed this in the seventh chapter. For the Greeks call that which is absolute and perfect in all things usually required, *teleion* [τέλειον]. The sum of the law, therefore, is Christ. And in the Psalms, whose title contains *unto the end*, they think something more hidden and secret must be tracked down. What he called *telos* here, he calls *plērōma* [πλήρωμα, fullness] elsewhere.

5 *For Moses wrote*] "Writes" is what the Greeks have. This passage is corrupted among us; among the Greeks it is correctly held thus: *For Moses writes the righteousness which is from the law, that the man who has done these things, shall live in them.* Moses indeed writes of the righteousness which is from the law, because he who has done these things, shall live in them. Lorenzo Valla argues in this place, but somewhat obscurely: sensing that the whole speech is not to be referred to Moses—namely this, *Since the man who does the righteousness which is from the law, shall live in it*—as if Moses wrote all this; rather, only this latter part: *The man who does these things, shall live in them*. For he cited words which are in the eighteenth chapter of Leviticus: *Keep my laws and judgments, which a man doing, shall live in them*. Likewise you read in the twentieth chapter of Ezekiel: *They cast away my judgments, which a man doing shall live in them*. Indeed, Paul, for the sake of teaching, makes a twin righteousness: one of Moses, which requires the works of the law; the other of the Gospel, which requires faith in Christ. Of the one, Moses says—or if you prefer, righteousness itself speaks—*He who does these things, shall live in them*. The other, which is from faith, speaks thus: *Do not say in your heart*. Chrysostom <note>An influential 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching.</note> interprets it in this manner: Moses, he says, shows us the righteousness which is from the law, of what kind it is and of how much weight. What kind is it then, and from where is it commended?

<column-break/>

B 33 **stone of stumbling.** As it is written, Behold, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense: and everyone who believes in him, shall not be made ashamed.
<margin>v. 1.</margin>
1. Brothers, the inclined goodwill of my heart indeed, and the prayer which is made to God, is for Israel unto salvation.
<margin>v. 2.</margin>
2. For I bear testimony to them, that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.
<margin>v. 3.</margin>
3. For being ignorant of God's righteousness, and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they were not subject to the righteousness of God.
<margin>v. 4.</margin>
4. For the perfection of the law is Christ, unto justification for everyone who believes.
<margin>v. 5.</margin>
5. For Moses writes concerning the righteousness which is from the law, that the man who has done those things, shall live through them.
<margin>v. 6.</margin>
6. Moreover, the righteousness which is from faith, speaks thus: Do not say in your heart, "Who shall ascend into heaven?" that is, to lead Christ down from on high.
<margin>v. 7.</margin>
7. Or, "Who shall descend into the abyss?" that is, to lead Christ back from the dead.
<margin>v. 8.</margin>
8. But what does it say? "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart": that is, the word of faith, which we preach.
<margin>v. 9.</margin>
9. Namely, if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
<margin>v. 10.</margin>
10. For with the heart it is believed unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made—

---

...by what it is commended? By the fact that he fulfills the precepts: *He who does them*, he says, *shall live in them*. But a little later, *But tell us, O Paul*, and *that other righteousness which is from grace, etc.* The reading of Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine commentator.</note> agrees with the reading of Chrysostom, nor does the explanation disagree. Ambrose reads and interprets according to the Greek codices: "For Moses wrote the righteousness which is from the law, because the man who does those things, shall live in them." The translator of Origen reads and interprets what our Vulgate Edition has. But his liberty makes it so that we cannot judge for certain from here what he read. A reader, offended by the absurd appearance of the speech, transferred the conjunction <term>hoti</term> [ὅτι, that/because], and having removed the pronoun <term>en</term> [ἐν, in], at the end he put *in* instead of *into*. *For Moses wrote, since the righteousness which is from the law, the man who does it, shall live in it*. At first it seemed harsh, "he writes righteousness," instead of what it was, "he describes righteousness," or "he writes about righteousness": then it seemed even longer, *he who has done those things shall live in them*, not noticing that the words of Scripture are being referred to under the persona of Moses, or of righteousness, so that *hoti* is taken "specifically" <note>original: "εἰδικῶς"</note>. *Moses described the righteousness which is from the law. Presently, as if to one asking what sort it was, he answered him in the words of Leviticus: "He who does them, shall live in them."* This can be taken in two ways: either he will have that life which the works of the Law provide for a time; or, he will not have life, because no one performs the works of the Law without the gift of faith. In our reading, however, the very disordered speech argues that the place was corrupted by a scribe. For "Moses wrote, since the righteousness which is from the law, he who does it, shall live in it." Not to mention anything about *en* being turned into "since" [quoniam].

6 *To lead down*] <term>katagagein</term> <note>original: "καταγαγεῖν"</note>, comes from leading down from on high: to which <term>anagagein</term> [ἀναγαγεῖν] corresponds, which the translator rendered as "to recall," although it is more significant to "lead back" from the depths to the heights. For it seems to me in this place, especially the Latin interpreters struggle greatly, even though the sense is clear. For he had said that only faith is required by the Gospel. Furthermore, faith does not demand a trial; it strives in the spirit, and the one who believes sees with certain eyes of his own: whereas he who distrusts also demands the sense of testimony, saying to himself that which is read in the thirtieth chapter of Deuteronomy, *Who shall ascend into heaven?* And that which was said of the Law, Paul interprets by adapting it to Christ. For that, he says, *is to drag Christ down from heaven*, so that either he is not believed to be there, or he is forced to return here, to show himself again to our senses. Or *who descends into the abyss?* That is, who would believe what is said of the underworld unless he had seen it? This is, he says, *to lead Christ back from the dead*, either as if he had not descended to the underworld, or as if they demand that he descend to the underworld again while they are watching—since arguments for these things need not be sought so far away if faith is present in the heart. Now that phrase, *But what does it say?*, can seem ambiguous as to what "it says" refers: to Moses, or to the righteousness of faith, which is Christ, whom he just made to be speaking, as Origen thinks, and even Chrysostom. Although elsewhere Paul also places "it says" in this same way, so that "the Scripture" is understood. Therefore the Translator not ineptly added words of his own for the sake of explaining the speech.

7 *The word is near*] <term>Engys sou to rhēma</term> <note>original: "Ἐγγύς σου τὸ ῥῆμα"</note>, *Near you is the word*, that is, there is no need to seek so far from heaven or the abyss, since it is within you. Moreover, the testimony, as I just said, is taken from the thirtieth chapter of Deuteronomy. Which Origen first indicated, then Augustine: except that the latter adds "greatly," *This word is very near in your mouth*. Just as it is also read in our Vulgate Edition. Although other things also differ somewhat in Paul's words from the Hebrew, indeed from our Edition, which has it in this manner: *This command, which I command you today, is not above you, nor placed far off, nor situated in heaven, so that you can say, "Which of us is able to climb to heaven, to bring it down to us, that we may hear it and fulfill it by work?": nor is it placed across the sea, so that you may make an excuse and say, "Who among us can cross the sea, and bring it even to us, so that we can hear and do that which is commanded?" But within you is the word, very much in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do it.* First, what is placed there—*who among us can cross the sea?*—Paul translates, *Who will descend into the abyss?* Furthermore, regarding what Augustine reads in the Questions on Deuteronomy, *This word is very near in your mouth and in your heart* and *in your hands* to do it—the last part, *and in your hands*, which he thinks was omitted by Paul—our Vulgate Edition certainly does not have it; whether it is among the Hebrews, let those more skilled in those letters see. It is possible that this place...

# PAUL'S EPISTLE, CHAPTER X.

<margin>11</margin> [leads] to salvation. For the Scripture says, "Everyone who 
<margin>12</margin> believes in him will not be put to shame." <note>original: "Πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων ἐπ᾽ αὐτῷ οὐ καταισχυνθήσεται"</note> For there 
is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the 
same Lord is Lord of all, enriching all those 
<margin>13</margin> who call upon him. For "everyone who calls

will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how

<margin>15</margin> without a preacher? And how will they preach unless

<margin>16</margin> good things." But not all obeyed the

<margin>18</margin> hearing through the word of God. But I say, have they not

and their words to the ends of the world." 
<margin>19</margin> But I say, did Israel not know? First 
Moses says, "I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation,

I became manifest to those who did not ask for me." 
<margin>21</margin> But to Israel he says, "All day long I have stretched out 
my hands to a disobedient and contrary people."

---

<margin>e</margin> Someone might have corrected Paul. Certainly, in the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible used by early Christians.</note> it is held, *and the one who rejoices does not do it.* <note>original: "καὶ ὁ χαιρει ουκ ποιειν αυτὸν"</note>
<margin>8</margin> **Everyone who believes in him will not be confounded** | <note>original: "καὶ καταισχυνθήσεται"</note> He frequently translates it this way, and commonly then, as it appears, people spoke thus, even though "to be confounded" properly means to be mixed up or disturbed. Those who are ashamed are said to be "suffused." Although sometimes a powerful sense of shame so disturbs a person that they are rendered like one who is raving. Furthermore, what is read in the Acts, *and he confounded the Jews*, is a different word, <note>original: "καταισχυν"</note> that is, he rendered them disturbed and perplexed in mind, so that they did not know which way to turn. The translator of Origen <note>An influential early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD).</note> translates the Greek word for "shamed" <note>original: "καταισχυνθήσεται"</note> here as "he shall blush," bringing forward the example of Adam, who blushed and hid himself after his sin. Truly, those whose hope has failed them also blush; for the shame of the righteous is the fear of disgrace. Thus the Jews insulted Christ as if all hope were frustrated: "if he is the Son of God, let him defend himself now from the cross."
<margin>9</margin> **Jew and Greek** | <note>original: "Ἰουδαίου τε καὶ Ἕλληνος"</note> Again, the doubled conjunction makes the speech more forceful, which we translate as *or*, expressing the same weight of meaning for the sentence.
<margin>10</margin> **Rich toward all** | In Greek it is a participle, <note>original: "πλουτῶν"</note> that is, abounding or overflowing in riches.
<margin>11</margin> **How they heard** | It could be translated as "of whom they had not heard." For thus it is in Greek, <note>original: "οὗ οὐκ ἤκουσαν"</note>.
<margin>12</margin> **How beautiful the feet** | Paul rendered this testimony according to the Hebrew truth, <note>Erasmus's term for the original Hebrew text of the Old Testament.</note> according to which it is read in Isaiah chapter fifty-two, as translated by Jerome: *How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger and the preacher of peace, and the messenger of good, the preacher of salvation.* For the Septuagint translated it as <note>original: "ὡς ὥρα"</note>: which word, if written with an aspiration, either signifies "time"—as there are twelve hours in a day—or a part of the year, which tempers the world with various seasons (hence they are called *horae*), or it signifies "beauty," from which they call a beautiful thing *agathos*. But if written without aspiration, <note>original: "ὦρα"</note>, it declares care and concern. Thus, according to the Septuagint, we read: *As an hour upon the mountains, so are the feet of the evangelist.* But Saint Jerome more approves of *How beautiful*; although this reading is not far from the Greek reading of the Septuagint, provided you take *horae* for beauty. For thus it is read: *As the pleasantness upon the mountains, so are the feet* and so on.
<margin>13</margin> **They obey the Gospel** | "They obeyed" is the Greek <note>original: "ὑπήκουσαν"</note>, a word in the past tense; unless by chance this word is among those which signify a continuing act, such as "I have become" or "I have feared," in which the past tense stands for the present. He who copied the book is no longer writing; but those who are said to have hoped in the Lord, according to the idiom of the Greek language, have not ceased to hope. And anyway, the present tense frequently fits all time.
<margin>14</margin> **Lord, who has believed our hearing** | He took this testimony from Isaiah chapter fifty-three, following the Septuagint Edition, who added the word *Lord* for the sake of clarifying the person, since it is not held in the Hebrew, but only, *Who has believed our report?* This same thing was observed by Origen. The reader should be warned that in this place "hearing" <note>Latin: "auditum"</note> is put for the speech itself which is heard; therefore it was clearer to say, *Who has believed our words?* or, *Who has believed what we have heard?* For the name "hearing" to the Latins sounds like nothing other than the power and sense of hearing. But if it sounds like nothing other than "the sense of hearing" to us, why here does the same Translator translate differently in Matthew 3, *and reports of wars*, <note>original: "ἀκοὰς πολέμων"</note> that is, "rumors of wars" rather than "hearings of wars"? And in the last chapter of Acts, *with hearing you shall hear*, <note>original: "ἀκοῇ ἀκούσετε"</note> why did he dare to translate "by hearing you shall hear"? I had counted this place among the manifest solecisms <note>A grammatical mistake or absurdity.</note>, adding this: Who speaking in Latin ever called the speech of the speaker a "hearing"? At this, a certain mocker becomes angry, boasting that he will declare what was said by me to be a mere falsehood, and that there is no fault of speech here. "Jerome," he says, "Augustine, and Ambrose knew Latin, and yet they speak thus." First, we do not count these authors in the number of those by whose authority a solecism can be excused. For they partly diminished the elegance of their speech for the ears of the unlearned multitude, to whom they were then both writing and speaking; partly the Roman speech itself at that time was degenerating from its genuine purity. Then, what wonder is it if, using testimonies from Scripture, they use the words of the same? But which of them, speaking in his own name, wrote, *Formerly it will repent you not to have listened to my hearing*, in place of what should have been, *not to have listened to my words?* Yet I did not deny that it was "Latin" for whoever spoke thus, but I denied that anyone speaking *Latine* <note>In the pure, classical Roman style.</note> spoke in that manner; if that were a mere falsehood, even one example ought to have been produced from approved authors. Has the Translator not been beautifully defended from a solecism, and has it not been magnificently declared that I spoke a mere falsehood? And those who publish such unlearned nonsense in books, rebuking with a strange haughtiness and insulting with strange pride and almost triumphing—they would do better if they learned the rudiments of Greek and Latin Grammar in the meantime.

<column-break/>

<margin>11</margin> [leads] to salvation. For the Scripture says, <margin>8</margin> "Everyone who trusts him will not be put to shame." For there is no distinction <margin>9</margin> either of Jew or of Greek: for the same Lord of all is <margin>10</margin> rich toward all who call upon him. For whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. How then will they <margin>11</margin> call upon him, in whom they have not believed? And how will they believe in him, of whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher? And how <margin>12</margin> will they preach, unless they are sent? As it is written, <margin>12</margin> "How beautiful are the feet of those announcing peace, of those announcing good things." But not all <margin>13</margin> obeyed the Gospel: for Isaiah says, <margin>14</margin> "Lord, who has believed our words?" Therefore faith is from hearing, but hearing <margin>15</margin> is through the word of God. But I say, did they not hear? <margin>18</margin> Indeed, their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. But I say, did <margin>19</margin> Israel not know? <margin>16</margin> First Moses says, <margin>17</margin> "I will provoke you to jealousy <margin>18</margin> by a nation that is not a nation, by a foolish nation I will stir you to anger." <margin>19</margin> But after him Isaiah dares, and says, <margin>20</margin> "I was found by those who were not seeking me, I was made visible to those who were not asking about me." <margin>21</margin> But against Israel he says, "All day long I stretched out my hands to a people not believing <margin>22</margin> and contradicting."

---

<margin>C</margin> [solecism.] For they partly diminished the elegance of their speech for the ears of the unlearned multitude, to whom they were then both writing and speaking; partly the Roman speech itself at that time was degenerating from its genuine purity. Then, what wonder is it if, using testimonies from Scripture, they use the words of the same? But which of them, speaking in his own name, wrote, *Formerly it will repent you not to have listened to my hearing*, in place of what should have been, *not to have listened to my words?* Yet I did not deny that it was "Latin" for whoever spoke thus, but I denied that anyone speaking *Latine* <note>In the pure, classical Roman style.</note> spoke in that manner; if that were a mere falsehood, even one example ought to have been produced from approved authors. Has the Translator not been beautifully defended from a solecism, and has it not been magnificently declared that I spoke a mere falsehood? And those who publish such unlearned nonsense in books, rebuking with a strange haughtiness and insulting with strange pride and almost triumphing—they would do better if they learned the rudiments of Greek and Latin Grammar in the meantime.
<margin>D</margin> <margin>15</margin> **Through the word of Christ** | <note>original: "διὰ ῥήματος Θεοῦ"</note>, of God, not of Christ. It is certain that Chrysostom <note>An early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople (c. 347–407 AD).</note> reads "of God," explaining this place so that it pertains even to the speech of the Prophets. Theophylact agrees with this, although the Translator rendered it differently than he read; both indicate the word of God was spoken in contrast to human speech, which could be despised. It is not very clear from the commentary what Ambrose read. The translator of Origen seems to have read "of Christ" instead of "of God." For the sense, it does not matter so much, except that the voice of "God" more exaggerates the dignity of the Apostolic speech, and the sense is broader. For the Prophet seems to place this complaint in his own name, which Paul fits as a prophecy to the heralds of the Gospel.
<margin>16</margin> **First Moses** | <note>original: "Πρῶτος Μωσῆς"</note>. Which the Greeks more often use in place of the comparative, "Prior Moses." For it refers to Isaiah, whom he cites shortly after, although Thomas Aquinas <note>A 13th-century theologian and philosopher.</note> brought forward another explanation, as if he were called "first" because he was the chief: or first, because he was the first among the others to say this; although that latter opinion does not shrink much from our own.
<margin>E</margin> <margin>17</margin> **To jealousy I will lead you** | <note>original: "παραζηλώσω"</note>, that is, I will provoke to emulating, and as if to pain by simulated envy. So says Ambrose.
<margin>18</margin> **In a non-nation** | <note>original: "ἐπ᾽ οὐκ ἔθνει"</note>, that is, in a non-nation: for in Greek it is the dative case. Likewise soon after, *in a foolish nation*. For he called a nation a "non-nation" which was most contemptible, and not worthy of any honor: which he adds when explaining, "in a foolish nation." Thus elsewhere he calls "things which are not" those which were held in no value.
<margin>F</margin> <margin>19</margin> **But Isaiah dares** | The conjunction <note>original: "δὲ"</note> connects this part with Moses who preceded, as we have shown. Nor is it simply "he dares" <note>original: "τολμᾷ"</note>, but "he is bold" <note>original: "ἀποτολμᾷ"</note>, as if confidence were taken from the one who had said it first.
<margin>20</margin> **I was found by those not seeking** | The place is in Isaiah chapter sixty-five; the sense is almost the same among the Hebrews and the Septuagint. The Hebrew truth holds thus: *They sought me who before were not asking me; they found me who did not seek me.* According to the Septuagint we read: *I appeared to those not seeking me, I was found by those who were not asking me.* Paul seems to have followed neither the Hebrew truth nor the Septuagint Edition anxiously, content to render the meaning.
<margin>21</margin> **But to Israel** | <note>original: "Πρὸς δὲ τὸν Ἰσραήλ"</note>. It can also be taken as "Against Israel": for he does not address Israel, but what was said works against the Jews. Since the preposition <note>original: "πρὸς"</note> is ambiguous to the Greeks. Thomas Aquinas also noted this. The testimony that Paul brings forward is in Isaiah chapter sixty-five. Origen indicates that in the copies of the Hebrews the little part *and contradicting me* is not added, but that it was added by the seventy elders (the Septuagint). And the translation of Jerome from the Hebrew truth declares that to be true, which holds thus: *I extended my hands all day long to an unbelieving people.* The Septuagint Edition holds thus: *I expanded my hands all day long to an unbelieving and contradicting people.*
<margin>22</margin> **And contradicting me** | <note>original: "ἀντιλέγοντα"</note>, "to me" has been added by us. "Contradicting" was enough, that is, rebellious and non-compliant, just as the Greeks read. And I found it was not added in the codex of Donatianus.

<summary>Erasmus provides a detailed linguistic analysis of Romans 10:11-21, emphasizing the nuances of "hearing" vs "speech" and comparing Paul's citations of Isaiah and Moses with the Hebrew and Greek sources. He also defends his philological corrections against critics who favor traditional Latin usage over grammatical purity.</summary>
