<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s philological analysis of the Epistle to the Romans, moving into Chapter 11. Following the previous discussion on the rejection of the word by some and its acceptance by others, Erasmus now addresses the question of whether God has entirely rejected the people of Israel, introducing the concept of the "remnant" saved by grace.</meta>

### TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER XI.

<margin>XI. 1</margin> I say then, has God cast away his people? Certainly not! For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.
<margin>2</margin> God has not cast away his people, whom he foreknew. Or do you not know what the Scripture says regarding Elijah? How he intercedes with God against Israel, saying:
<margin>3</margin> "Lord, they have killed your prophets and torn down your altars; I alone am left, and they are seeking my life."
<margin>4</margin> But what does the divine response say to him? "I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal."
<margin>5</margin> So then, at the present time also, there is a remnant according to the election of grace.
<margin>B</margin> <margin>6</margin> But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. But if it is from works, it is no longer grace; otherwise work is no longer work.
<margin>7</margin> What then? What Israel sought, it did not obtain; but the elect obtained it, and the rest were hardened.
<margin>8</margin> As it is written: "God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that they should not see and ears that they should not hear, down to this very day."
<margin>9</margin> And David says: "Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution to them.
<margin>10</margin> Let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs forever."
<margin>C</margin> <margin>11</margin> I say then, have they stumbled so as to fall? Certainly—

<column-break/>

<margin>D</margin> <margin>1</margin> **I say then, Has God]** In the Greek, there is only the particle <note>original: "Μὴ"</note> indicating a question: he asks himself and answers himself, a figure of speech that permeates all of Paul’s discourse. It brings a great deal of light and sharp focus, especially in argumentation. Some call this "reasoning."

<margin>2</margin> **Whom he foreknew]** <note>original: "προέγνω"</note>. It must be noted in this place that the word for "knowledge" <note>original: "γνῶσις"</note> among the Greeks does not always mean "to know" or "to recognize," but sometimes "to decree" or "to judge"; hence "opinions" <note>original: "γνῶμαι"</note> are so named. Even among the Latins we read "the people knew" <note>meaning "decreed"</note> and "the decrees of the people." However, "to pre-determine" <note>original: "προορίζειν"</note> seems to indicate something more than "to foreknow" <note>original: "προγνῶναι"</note>: the latter refers to a mental decree which an individual is free to change, while the former refers to a fixed pronouncement of judgment which is not within one's power to rescind. Hence, Nicholas of Lyra <note>A 14th-century Franciscan exegete</note> does not hesitate to explain "foreknew" in this place as "predestined"; and Augustine certainly interprets it this way in the second book of *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter eighteen. I have preferred to translate it as "whom he knew beforehand," according to the character of Divine Scripture, by which God is said to "know" those whom he favors and whom he embraces, as I previously noted based on the opinion of Origen. For it is not consistent that God rejected a people whom he previously so loved and embraced as his own. Chrysostom <note>An influential Early Church Father</note> thinks that the phrase "whom he foreknew" was added because of the chosen among the Jews, among whom Paul counts himself, and lest he seem alone, he adds the mention of the seven thousand men. For he does not simply say "his people," but "his people, whom he knew beforehand." Furthermore, the prefix "pre-" can refer to that eternal predestination which existed before the people of the Jews were born, or to the Gentiles called later to the grace of the Gospel, according to that Gospel saying: "The last shall be first, and the first shall be last."

<margin>3</margin> **How he intercedes]** Ambrose reads "pleads." In Greek it is <note>original: "ὡς ἐντυγχάνει"</note>.

<margin>4</margin> **Torn down]** <note>original: "κατέσκαψαν"</note>, which sometimes means "undermined" or "overthrown."

<margin>5</margin> **Divine response]** <note>original: "χρηματισμός"</note>, that is, an oracle. The Translator <note>referring to the Vulgate</note> explains this as "they were handed over."

<margin>6</margin> **Bowed the knee]** "Knee" is in the feminine among the Greeks <note>note: Erasmus is discussing the Greek grammatical gender of the word for knee here</note>. And "Baal" is in the dative case without a preposition before it, which the Latins add: and it is "to the Baal" <note>original: "τῇ Βάαλ"</note>, so that you understand the image, not the man himself. For among the Hebrews, "idol" especially sounds like *bosheth* <note>shame</note>: hence Beelphegor, "Idol of the corpse," and Beelzebub, "Idol of the flies."

<margin>7</margin> **Are made safe]** <note>original: "γέγονεν"</note>, that is, "have become." Some add "are rendered safe" or "remain of God"; but the text is simply: "So then, at the present time also, there is a remnant according to the election of grace." Paul is not arguing here whose grace it is, but rather opposes grace to the works of the law, and election to physical kinship. And yet, I do not know how it happened that in the Origenist commentary it reads "are now made safe," even if "of God" is not added. Although I have warned that the Translator took much liberty in his commentaries, certainly these words are not added in Chrysostom or Theophylact. It is no wonder if some, while explaining, remembered those who were saved, since Paul here calls "remnant according to the election of grace" those from the Jewish people who were predestined for salvation. Hence it is probable that those words we say "remain" were added by some studious person to make the speech clearer. Finally, while I examine the commentary of Origen, I find that he read just as Chrysostom reads. For he speaks thus, quoting Paul’s speech: "But because he says that the remnant was made according to grace, here the addition of 'election' seems to me superfluous." Here the genuine reading has remained, even if the reader changed the rest. For in the first context he added "somehow," though it is not added in the explanation. The diligence of those who "correct" quoted Scripture testimonies according to the Vulgate edition has corrupted many things in ancient authors.

<margin>8</margin> **But if by grace]** <note>original: "Εἰ δὲ χάριτι"</note>. "Grace" is in the ablative case, not the nominative.

<margin>9</margin> **Otherwise grace]** <note>original: "ἐπεὶ"</note>, that is, "since" or "seeing that." Although the translator rendered it correctly and clearly, among the Greeks "if it were otherwise" <note>original: "εἰ δὲ μὴ"</note> is understood, as we will soon indicate: "otherwise grace is no longer grace." The Greek manuscripts have somewhat more in this place than our Latin ones. For they repeat: "from works so that they are not works"; whereas our Latin texts only pronounce concerning grace in this manner: "But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works, since grace is no longer made grace; but if it is from works, it is no longer grace, since work is no longer work." <note>original: "Εἰ δὲ χάριτι, οὐκ ἔτι ἐξ ἔργων... εἰ δὲ ἐξ ἔργων, οὐκ ἔτι ἐστὶ χάρις, ἐπεὶ τὸ ἔργον οὐκ ἔτι ἐστὶ ἔργον"</note> And Theophylact certainly reads and interprets it thus. But since I do not find this addition in Origen, I doubt somewhat whether it is the genuine reading, especially since Chrysostom, in explaining this passage, reads only: "But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works, since grace is no longer made grace." He adds nothing to this. Furthermore, the flow of the speech seems inverted, and should rather be arranged in this order: "But if it is by grace, then not from works, since work is no longer work; but if from works, then not from grace, since grace is no longer grace." Unless there is a hidden exception in the law, as Paul has used this phrasing elsewhere. Thus the sense was: "If grace, therefore not from works; for if it were, grace would not be grace," that is, it would be falsely called grace. And yet, what makes me favor the Latin reading more is that Paul is not arguing here whether work is work, but is establishing grace, which the Jews were trying to expel. Nevertheless, the Aldine Edition, and also the Spanish one, agreed with what we find in the Greek manuscripts.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>10</margin> **As it is written]** It is uncertain whether this particle refers to what precedes or what follows. Origen confessed he had never read in the Divine Books: "He gave them a spirit of compunction." But he excuses it thus: that we should take Paul as explaining the meaning of Isaiah in his own words, and adding something of his own. This is made more probable by what he added at the end: "down to this very day." For the core of the thought is in Isaiah, chapter six: "Hearing you shall hear, and not understand; and seeing you shall see, and not perceive; blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest they see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and be converted and healed." This passage is also cited in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter twenty-eight, but according to the translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint</note>, who interpreted it so that the Lord predicts their blindness rather than commanding it: "With the ear you shall hear, and not understand..." In which place Jerome, explaining Isaiah, excuses Luke <note>as the author of Acts</note> for reporting Paul arguing with the Hebrews not according to the Hebrew text (which he knew was correct) but according to the Septuagint, because Paul knew Greek literature better than Hebrew, which is why his speech is more polished and reeks of secular eloquence.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>11</margin> **A spirit of compunction]** <note>original: "κατανύξεως"</note>, which signifies when someone is bitten and stung by pain: hence he said earlier, "they were pierced" <note>original: "κατανύγησαν"</note>.

<margin>12</margin> **Let their table become a snare]** The passage he brings forward exists in Psalm sixty-eight <note>Psalm 69 in English Bibles</note>. Even here Paul did not care to quote the prophetic testimony word for word. First, he omitted "before them"; then he added "into a trap"; which is found neither among the Hebrews nor among the Seventy, as Origen indicated before us.

<margin>13</margin> **Into a trap]** "Capture" <note>original: "captio"</note> here is not strictly a deception, which is why we call people "captious," but it is used for "hunting" <note>original: "venatu"</note>, by which we catch wild animals: as if to say, "let them be caught by their own table," at which they ought to relax their minds; for we do not fear an enemy during feasts. In Greek it is <note>original: "θήραν"</note>.

<margin>14</margin> **Have they stumbled so as to fall]** <note>original: "Μὴ ἔπταισαν, ἵνα πέσωσι;"</note> that is, "Did they slip so as to collapse," or "so as to fall," namely to the ground. For to "stumble" <note>original: "πταίειν"</note> is properly to strike against something: and to slip is lighter than to fall; just as to strike...

<meta>catchword: strike...</meta>

<summary>In this commentary on Romans 11:1–11, Erasmus explores the theological and philological nuances of God's "remnant" in Israel, debating the correct Greek readings of Paul's statements on grace versus works. He highlights Paul's rhetorical style and provides historical context on how the Apostle adapted Old Testament citations from Isaiah and the Psalms.</summary>

<keywords>Paul, Israel, Abraham, Benjamin, Elijah, Baal, David, Chrysostom, Origen, Nicholas of Lyra, Theophylact, Isaiah, Jerome, grace, election, predestination, compunction, capture, Septuagint, Greek translation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed commentary on Romans 11, focusing on the metaphorical relationship between the Jews (the natural branches) and the Gentiles (the grafted wild olive). Erasmus uses philological analysis of the Greek text to argue that the "stumbling" of the Jews was not a permanent or total "fall," but a divinely ordained event to bring salvation to the rest of the world.</meta>

<page-num>623</page-num>
# EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER XI.

11 ...[stumble]? Certainly not! But by their transgression salvation has come to the nations, so as to make them jealous. 12 But if their transgression is the riches of the world, and their loss the riches of the nations, how much more their fullness? 13 For I speak to you Gentiles, inasmuch as I am the apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry, 14 if somehow I may provoke my own flesh to jealousy and save some of them. 15 For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead? 16 If the firstfruit is holy, so is the dough; and if the root is holy, so are the branches. 17 But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, being a wild olive tree, were grafted in among them and became a sharer of the root and the richness of the olive tree, 18 do not boast against the branches; but if you boast, you do not support the root, but the root supports you. 19 You will say then, "Branches were broken off so that I..."

No one can describe this without completely collapsing. The Translator <note>original: "Interpres"; Erasmus refers to the author of the Latin Vulgate</note> added the word *so* on his own: *Did they so stumble, that they should fall?* And I would approve of the addition if the word "so" were placed here as an adverb to correspond to "to such a degree": as when we say, *He hates me so, that he does not even greet me*: he hates me to such an extent that he cannot speak. But the Greek word <term>μὴ</term> <note>mê; a negative particle used in questions expecting a 'no' answer</note> signifies something of a different nature from that which is <term>ὡς</term> <note>hôs; as</note> or <term>ὥστε</term> <note>hôste; so that</note>, which have varied meanings, just as "that" or "so" do for us. Yet Theodore Gaza <note>A 15th-century Greek grammarian</note> lists it among causal conjunctions and does not indicate it is used otherwise, even though he diligently notes its usage. For it does not matter here that it is sometimes an adverb of place. Therefore, the sense cannot be taken as, *Did they strike or stumble to such a degree that they fell?* Instead, it seems it should be referred to God: *Did God allow the Jews to slip for the purpose that they might fall entirely?* No; but so that for a time they might make room for the Gentiles, and that they themselves, provoked by the piety of the Gentiles, might repent and be saved. And the following fits this sense beautifully: *Certainly not: but by their offense salvation is for the Gentiles*; and the whole following discourse does not speak of the magnitude of the slip, but of the outcome. Chrysostom <note>An early Church Father and famed orator</note> explains it no differently, noting that Paul exaggerated the malice of the Jews fighting against the Gospel with testimonies from the Prophets, but offered consolation in his own name. Therefore, there is no doubt that they stumbled most seriously, but he consoles them with the outcome: *What then*, he says, *is the consolation? When the fullness*, he says, *of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved.* So far his view. And so, God turned the slip of the Jews into a good for the Gentiles, by whose emulation the Jews might eventually be provoked to salvation. Theophylact <note>A medieval Byzantine commentator</note> asserts nothing else, nor does Origen, except for what was added by learned scribes, nor does Ambrose: they all speak of the outcome, not the magnitude of the slip—except that the translator of Origen mixes in something about lighter sins, whereas Paul in this whole Epistle exaggerates the crime of unbelief. Whence I wonder why translators have wavered on whether they sinned or fell without hope of restoration, just as Lucifer fell. However, whatever words of the Prophets seemed to indicate an incurable evil, Paul mitigates that bitterness, showing that the sin was indeed very grave, but nevertheless the hope of the whole people was not taken away for that reason. **Otherwise Origen**. Origen, in the order of his discourse, clearly declares the genuine reading: *He says*, he says, *that the slip of Israel was such, not so that they should fall, but so that by their offense they might give salvation to the Gentiles.* Similarly Augustine, in the judgment he noted on this Epistle, admits the magnitude of the sin but indicates the good outcome of a very bad thing. His words are as follows: *Therefore did they sin, so as to fall? Far from it: but by their offense salvation is for the Gentiles: he does not say this because they did not fall, but because their fall was not in vain, since it profited the salvation of the Gentiles.* Therefore they did not sin so as to fall: that is, to fall only, as if for their punishment alone, but so that this very fact that they fell might benefit the Gentiles for salvation. These are his words: in which it is clear that he did not add *so*: which nevertheless was tolerable, if it is taken not as the atrocity of the slip, but as the manner and outcome. We have already frequently warned, on the authority of the Ancients, that final conjunctions of this kind sometimes pertain to the outcome rather than to the purpose or destination. The word <term>offenderunt</term> <note>they stumbled</note> was indeed elegantly used by the Translator: but "to offend" is also said of one who harms. Augustine, explaining some questions of this Epistle, reads *deliquerunt* <note>they failed/sinned</note> for "stumbled." And you might quite rightly call <term>πταίειν</term> <note>ptaiein; to trip or stumble</note> a "slip" or a "fault": but one cannot likewise use *delinquere* <note>to fail in duty</note> for "to strike against."

<margin>15</margin> <gloss>by their offense</gloss>] <term>τῷ αὐτῶν παραπτώματι</term> <note>tô autôn paraptômati</note>, that is, through their slip, rather than "offense." For he looked back to what he just said, *that the Jews stumbled*: for <term>παράπτωμα</term> is properly when someone slips through negligence, from <term>πίπτω</term> <note>piptô</note>, which means "I fall."

<margin>16</margin> <gloss>That they might emulate them</gloss>] <term>εἰς τὸ παραζηλῶσαι αὐτούς</term> <note>eis to parazêlôsai autous</note>. Which could more correctly be translated, "to provoke them": so that the action of the verb is referred to God, who in this way wished to stimulate the Jews through a certain envy and jealousy, when they saw that what had been promised to them had been transferred to the Gentiles. Whence we, to exclude ambiguity of speech, translated it, *so that he might provoke them to emulation*, <term>εἰς τὸ παραζηλῶσαι αὐτούς</term>. Nor was there any need for the "four-horse chariot" of interpretations which Thomas Aquinas brought into this place, not even touching the genuine meaning in this way: which is not at all to be imputed to him, but to the Translator. For who, ignorant of Greek, could perceive from these words what Paul meant? So also a little later Paul used this verb: <term>Εἴπως παραζηλώσω μου τὴν σάρκα</term> <note>If somehow I may provoke my own flesh to jealousy</note>. And in the next chapter: <term>Ἐγὼ παραζηλώσω ὑμᾶς ἐπ’ οὐκ ἔθνει</term> <note>I will provoke you to jealousy by those who are not a nation</note>. Yet the Translators have used this word elsewhere in a bad sense, as in Psalm 77: *and in their graven images...*

<column-break/>

<page-num>624</page-num>

...did they stumble, so that they should fall down? Far from it: but through 11 their slip salvation happened to the nations, for the purpose of provoking them to emulation. Now if their slip is the 12 riches of the world, and their reduction the riches of the nations, how much more their fullness? For I 13 speak to you Gentiles, insofar as I am indeed the Apostle to the Gentiles, I illustrate my ministry, if by 14 any means I may provoke my flesh to emulation, and render some of them safe. For if the rejection 15 of them is the reconciliation of the world, what will the acceptance be, but life from the dead? Now if the firstfruits are 16 holy, the mass is also holy: and if the root is holy, the branches will also be holy. Now if some branches were 17 broken off, and you, though you were a wild olive, were grafted into them, and were made a partaker of the root and the fatness of the olive tree, Do not boast against the branches: but if you boast, 18 you do not carry the root, but the root carries you. You will say therefore, branches were broken 19 off...

<margin>A</margin> <gloss>by their offenses... them.</gloss> Furthermore, he applies the word <term>παραζηλῶσαι</term> <note>parazêlôsai; to provoke to jealousy</note> to the Jews, so that *them* refers to the Gentiles. Nor did any Translator perceive this, except for I-know-not-what slight reasoning of the Greek speech; but he preferred to extort this sense rather than not to pluck at our annotation. Even if those who twist the words of the Translators here do not stop, they do so falsely: they indeed make mention of the Jews who will emulate their own nation. But what wonder, since <term>παραζηλῶ</term> means to irritate to envy and emulous zeal? I have shown several places in which <term>παραζηλοῦν</term> means "to provoke" either to anger or to emulous zeal: they would have profited us in one instance where it might be placed for "to emulate."

<margin>17</margin> <gloss>Inasmuch as I am the apostle to the Gentiles</gloss>] <term>ἐφ’ ὅσον μέν εἰμι</term> <note>eph’ hoson men eimi</note>. Origen seems to take <term>ἐφ’ ὅσον</term> for "as long as": so that he understands *as long as I live*: and he doubts whether it should be taken as "as long as I am in this life," and whether the emphasis pertains to the effect: just as we commonly say, *I will not desert you as long as I live*: or whether Paul would be an Apostle even more invisibly after death. But since that is a bit far-fetched, I would prefer to take <term>ἐφ’ ὅσον</term> for "insofar as," or "to the extent that." And so Theophylact seems to have felt, as much as one can gather from his interpretation. The Greek says the same things as Chrysostom, who clearly interprets it that Paul is compelled by his delegated office to provoke some Jews and thus save them. For he will save those provoked if he draws as many as possible from the Gentiles to the Gospel. For he does not speak of the measure of time, as if he were soon to abdicate the Apostolic office, but since he had been called <margin>B</margin> as Apostle to the Gentiles, it is allowed that by diligently performing the province committed to him, he may adorn and illustrate it. Nor does Ambrose mention anything about time; he speaks only of the office. Similarly, in Matthew 25, *as long as you did it to one of these least ones, etc.* in my opinion, he would have more correctly translated "insofar as" or "to the extent that."

<margin>18</margin> <gloss>I will honor</gloss>] <term>δοξάζω</term> <note>doxazô</note>, that is, "I glorify": thus Augustine cites this passage in several places, specifically in the ninth book against Faustus, chapter two. Lefèvre d'Étaples preferred *I estimate.* <note>Erasmus refers to his contemporary humanist rival</note> Although I do not know whether <term>δοξάζω</term> is found among the Greeks for "I estimate." And the sense fits well, if you take Paul to be making his ministry in the Gospel of the Gentiles celebrated, so that by emulation at least he might provoke the Jews to Christ. The translator of Origen translates <term>δοξάζω</term> as *I illustrate and adorn*, explaining this sense with many words.

<margin>C</margin> <gloss>For if the loss of them</gloss>] <term>ἀποβολὴ</term> <note>apobolê</note>, that is, "casting away" or "rejection," for he opposes this to "acceptance." Augustine cites *rejection* for *loss* <margin>D</margin> in the ninth book against Faustus, chapter two, according to the reliability of an ancient manuscript volume.

<margin>20</margin> <gloss>what acceptance</gloss>] <term>τίς ἡ πρόσληψις</term> <note>tis hê proslêmpsis</note>, that is, "assumption" or "taking up," by which we adopt someone as a companion to ourselves, that is, we join them. For he opposes "acceptance," as I said, to "rejection."

<margin>21</margin> <gloss>But if the first taste</gloss>] "Delibatio" <note>first taste/offering</note>, <term>ἀπαρχὴ</term> <note>aparchê</note>, that is, "firstfruits." Theophylact interprets <term>ἀπαρχήν</term> as <term>τὸν ζύμην</term> <note>ton zymên</note>, that is, "leaven": so that the mass corresponds to the tree, and the leaven to the root. It is more approved by me that we understand the grain itself, from which the "conspersio" <note>dough/lump</note> is taken. Moreover, you could not make a good dough from faulty wheat. But he said "firstfruits" because the most praised things are usually dedicated to the Divinity, whence it is called <term>ἀπαρχὴ</term>, as if the "chief part." Furthermore, I think the "conspersio" <note>lump</note> is not referred to flour tempered with moisture, but rather to the sacrificial cakes or rolls: that was flour sprinkled with oil, which were once sacrificed according to the rite of the Mosaic Law, whence he also calls it "holy." Chrysostom interprets the <term>ἀπαρχήν</term> <note>firstfruit</note> and <term>ῥίζαν</term> <note>root</note> as Abraham and the rest of the Patriarchs, and the <term>φύραμα</term> <note>dough</note> and <margin>E</margin> <term>κλάδους</term> <note>branches</note> as their <margin>F</margin> descendants. And "oleaster" <note>wild olive</note> is <term>ἀγριέλαιος</term> <note>agrielaios</note> for the Greeks; which sounds like a rustic or wild olive: to which corresponds <term>καλλιέλαιος</term> <note>kallielaios</note>, which is a fruitful olive.

<margin>22</margin> <gloss>You are grafted</gloss>] <term>ἐνεκεντρίσθης</term> <note>enekentristhês</note>, that is, "you are grafted": whenever a scion is inserted into a branch of a tree. For this is one kind of grafting. Although here it seems to signify more "inoculation," when a flower is inserted by boring through the bark where the bud has put itself forth. *You are grafted in them*, <term>ἐν αὐτοῖς</term>. It was clearer as "among them": that is, grafting gave to you what nature gave to them. But it is ridiculous that some interpret *in them* for what was "in their place." For since he understands the people of the Jews by "the olive," the changed number or gender is not offensive. According to the property of Hebrew speech, a preposition is frequently added superfluously, as in, *I will confess in me; I will confess in him; and He struck in the sword.*

<margin>23</margin> <gloss>Sharer of the root</gloss>] <term>συγκοινωνὸς</term> <note>synkoinônos</note>, that is, "partaker," or rather "at the same time a partaker," or "consort": that is, together with the other branches into which you were grafted.

24 <gloss>Well</gloss>

<summary>Erasmus provides a philological and theological commentary on Romans 11, arguing that the stumbling of the Jews was a purposeful act by God to include the Gentiles, using metaphors of firstfruits and grafted olive branches to illustrate the relationship between the two groups. He critiques earlier translations and interpretations, including those of the Vulgate and Thomas Aquinas, for failing to capture the nuance of the original Greek.</summary>

# TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER XI.

**Column 1**

<margin>A</margin> 20 **...I might be grafted in. Well; they were broken off because of unbelief, but you stand by faith; do not be high-minded, but fear.**
21 **For if God did not spare the natural branches, see to it that he does not also fail to spare you.**
22 **Behold therefore the goodness and severity of God: toward those who fell, severity; but toward you, goodness, if you remain in that goodness; otherwise you also will be cut off.**
23 **And even they, if they do not remain in their unbelief, shall be grafted in; for God is able to graft them in again.**
24 **For if you were cut out of the naturally wild olive tree, and were grafted contrary to nature into a good olive tree, how much more shall these, who are the natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree.**
<margin>B</margin> 25 **For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, so that you are not wise in your own conceits: that a hardening in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the nations has come in,**
26 **And so all Israel shall be saved; as it is written: There shall come out of Zion the Deliverer, and he shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob.**
27 **And this is my covenant with them, when I shall take away their sins.**
28 **According to the gospel, they are enemies for your sake; but according to the election, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers.**
29 **For the gifts and the calling of God are without repentance.**
30 **For just as you once were disobedient to God, but now have obtained mercy through their disobedience;**
31 **So these also have now been disobedient because of the mercy shown to you, so that they also may obtain mercy.**

---

**24** [Well] This should be separated so that it serves as a response to the previous point, "well" <note>original Greek: καλῶς</note>, and as an approval of what he had said under the persona of the Gentile: these words are to be read as a declaration. Indeed, Augustine distinguishes it this way in his Epistles when citing this passage.
**25** Do not be high-minded] <note>original Greek: μὴ ὑψηλοφρόνει</note>, that is, do not be proud, do not please yourself, do not be carried away in spirit. For here "to be minded" <note>original: sapere</note> refers to an affection of the mind, "to think" <note>original Greek: φρονεῖν</note>, which is elsewhere called "to think highly of oneself." For the issue here is not wisdom or folly, but arrogance and modesty.
**26** Lest perhaps neither to you] <note>original Greek: μὴ πως</note>. Either the filler conjunction should have been omitted, or it should have been translated as "lest in some way" or "lest by any means." For "perhaps" <note>original: forte</note> adds nothing to the meaning here.
**27** See therefore the goodness] in most Greek manuscripts it was <note>original Greek: ἴδε</note>, that is, "see." Though this affects the sense very little. "Goodness and severity" <note>original Greek: τὴν χρηστότητα καὶ τὴν ἀποτομίαν</note>. This "goodness" is what we previously translated as "benignity," following the opinion of Saint Jerome; it is a certain inclination of the mind toward deserving well of someone, which could not ineptly be translated as "indulgence," to which he opposes <note>original Greek: ἀποτομίαν</note>, which literally sounds like "cutting away." This occurs whenever a matter is driven to the quick, which you might also call "rigor."
**28** Otherwise] Again, <note>original Greek: ἐπεὶ</note>, that is, "since." Which the Translator <note>Erasmus refers to the author of the Vulgate</note> nonetheless correctly rendered.
**29** Into a good olive tree] <note>original Greek: καλλιέλαιον</note>, which is the opposite of <note>original Greek: ἀγριελαίῳ</note>, that is, the wild olive: as was just said.
**30** Brothers, this mystery] <note>original Greek: μυστήριον</note>. In this place, "mystery" sounds like nothing other than a secret matter known to a few, and not to be shared except with the initiated.
**31** Wise in yourselves] <note>original Greek: παρ' ἑαυτοῖς φρόνιμοι</note>, that is, "prudent in your own eyes": and "prudent" <note>original: φρόνιμος</note> refers more to an attitude than to practical wisdom. It means you should not be insolent or of an exalted mind; otherwise, one is "wise to oneself" who only looks out for his own advantages.
**32** May he rescue and turn away ungodliness] <note>original Greek: ἀσεβείας</note>, that is, "impieties." And "may he rescue," <note>original Greek: ὁ ῥυόμενος</note>, that is, "the one who delivers": as if you were to say, "the Deliverer." And "he will turn away," not "may he turn away," <note>original Greek: ἀποστρέψει</note>, a verb in the future tense. This testimony is brought from the fifty-ninth chapter of Isaiah, where we read as follows according to the Hebrew truth: *And they shall fear the name of the Lord from the west, and his glory from the rising of the sun, when he shall come like a violent river, which the spirit of the Lord drives, and there shall come to Zion a redeemer, and those who return from iniquity in Jacob, says the Lord: this is my covenant with them, says the Lord.* According to the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> it is this way: *And they from the west shall fear the name of the Lord, and they from the east his glorious name; for the wrath from the Lord shall come like a violent river, it shall come with fury, and there shall come for the sake of Zion the Deliverer, and he shall turn away impieties from Jacob, and this is the covenant from me with them, said the Lord.* From this it is clear that Paul cited this passage according to the Edition of the Seventy, except that he added from himself, *when I shall have taken away their sins*: which is found neither in the Hebrew nor in the Seventy, but he added it as if explaining the Prophet’s meaning. For "covenant" <note>original Greek: διαθήκη</note>, which is "testament" in Latin, is "alliance" or "pact" <note>original: fœdus</note> to the Hebrews. And what the Seventy translated as "out of Zion" <note>original Greek: ἐκ Σιὼν</note>, is "for the sake of Zion" for the Hebrews. Origen indicates the Hebrew is "for the sake of Zion." And it is indeed written that way in the Edition of the Seventy: I suspect it was corrupted by a scribe’s error, whereas it should have been written "near Zion." Jerome also interprets it in Greek as "approaching" <note>original Greek: ἐγγίζοντος</note>, that is, "near": unless someone argues that "for the sake of" was said instead of "near." Furthermore, what is read in Jerome as "the wrath of the Lord," is for them "wrath from the Lord" <note>original Greek: ὀργὴ παρὰ Κυρίου</note>.
**33** And this is my covenant with them] It is indeed <note>original Greek: διαθήκη</note> in Greek.

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

...the branches were broken off, that I might be grafted in. **24** You say well: because of unbelief they were broken off, but you have stood by faith:
**25** do not be carried away in spirit, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, see **26** that it does not happen that he does not spare you either.
**27** See therefore the goodness and severity of God: toward those indeed who fell, severity; but toward you, goodness, if you remain in that goodness: **28** otherwise you also will be cut off.
And they again, if they do not remain in unbelief, shall be grafted in: for God is able to graft them in again.
For if you were cut out of the naturally wild olive tree, and contrary to nature were grafted **29** into a true olive tree, how much more shall these who are natural, be grafted into their own olive tree?
For I do not want you to be ignorant, **30** brothers, of this mystery, so that you are not **31** exalted in spirit in your own eyes, that blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the nations has arrived,
And so all Israel shall be saved: as it is written, There shall arrive from Zion he who delivers, and he shall turn away impieties from Jacob. **32** And this is my covenant with them, when I shall have taken away their sins.
According to the Gospel indeed they are enemies for your sake, **34** but according to the election they are beloved for the sake of the Fathers.
For the gifts and the calling of God are such **35** that he cannot repent of them.
For just as you also were formerly unbelieving toward God, but now have obtained mercy **36** through their unbelief:
So also these have now been made unbelieving **37** because you have [obtained] mercy.

---

<margin>C</margin> Furthermore, Augustine also indicated this in the first book of *On the Locutions of Genesis*, that "testament" is frequently used in the sacred writings for "pact." Although the Greek word <term>διαθήκη</term> <note>diatheke; usually translated as "testament" or "covenant"</note> was not named from "witnessing" <note>original: a testando</note>, but from "ordering and arranging."
**34** But according to the election, most dear] <note>original Greek: ἀγαπητοὶ</note>, that is, "beloved": a word he often translates this way. Furthermore, the two nominative cases, "enemies" and "most dear," according to grammatical order have nothing to hang on unless you supply "they are": but it is more likely that the logic of the case was neglected by Paul; otherwise, he should have said "of the most dear" and "of enemies."
**35** Without repentance] <note>original Greek: ἀμεταμέλητα</note>, that is, things which he who gave or promised cannot repent of; as if you were to say, "un-repentable." Augustine somewhere reads "not to be repented of." Ambrose twists this to say that in baptism sin is forgiven freely, and neither mourning nor lamenting nor any other good work is required, but only a profession from the heart. This interpretation seems to me rather forced, and is not touched upon by Origen. Thomas [Aquinas] finally reached that opinion in the last place, as if not quite approving of it.
<margin>D</margin> **36** Because of their unbelief] <note>original Greek: τῇ τούτων ἀπειθείᾳ</note>, that is, "through" the unbelief of these, not "because of." For "because of" signifies a cause, while "through" signifies an instrument or manner: as far as the meaning goes, it matters little.
<margin>E</margin> **37** Into your mercy] <note>original Greek: τῷ ὑμετέρῳ ἐλέει</note>, "through the mercy of you." For this dative is similar to the one that precedes it, "through the unbelief of these." For the sense is: Just as their falling away created an entrance for you to the faith, so your faith, which you obtained by God’s mercy, will provoke them to change their minds and show themselves worthy to be received by God. Ambrose reads, "in your compassion": as if the Greek read <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ ὑμῷ ἐλέει</note>. If this reading were approved, there would be no difficulty. For the sense would be: While the Gentiles were called to life through God's mercy, the Jews persisted in unbelief. And perhaps the Translator read it as Ambrose did. I know some interpret "into your mercy" as meaning Christ. Thomas Aquinas explains "into your mercy" in three ways: as the grace of Christ; or they did not believe so that through this they might come into your mercy; or they did not believe, which occasionally resulted in your mercy. But to bring forth such comments without consulting the Greek, what else is it than to engage in guesswork? Chrysostom ignores this little phrase, "in your mercy." Theophylact brings a new commentary, as if arranging it thus: *So also these, having been disobedient, [will find] that by your mercy they also may receive mercy.* For his commentary has it: "But your mercy shall also be theirs, for they shall envy you." Nor is Chrysostom’s commentary far from this, teaching that both peoples were disobedient in turn, and in turn called to grace.
<margin>F</margin> For while the Gentiles persisted in unbelief, the Jews were called to the Law: soon, when the Gentiles were called to the Gospel, the Jews withdrew, persisting in unbelief, but were to be called back to faith by the example of the Gentiles. Thus, by certain turns, one group was saved through the other. Translators seem to have shrunk from saying that the Jews persisted in unbelief because of the occasion of the Gentiles: when, on the contrary, the unbelief of the Jews rather provided the occasion for the Gospel to pass to the Gentiles. However, if we remember that "so that" <note>original: ἵνα</note> here does not sound of purpose or intention, but of consequence or outcome, and in the other parts "occasion" is understood more truly than "cause," I do not see why this sense should frighten us, which the Greek speech, accepted most simply, expresses, consisting of opposites related to each other: moreover, he calls the faith of the Gentiles "mercy," lest they should please themselves being preferred to the Jews. For the grace of the Gospel seemed in a way to be owed to the Jews, either because it was specifically promised to them, or because of their observation of the Law and the worship of the one God. So...

<summary>Erasmus provides a detailed linguistic analysis of Romans 11:20-31, focusing on the Greek text to clarify the relationship between Gentile "mercy" and Jewish "unbelief." He argues that the displacement of the Jews was a providential occasion for Gentile salvation, which in turn serves to eventually provoke the Jews back to faith.</summary>

# EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER XII.

> 32 For God has shut up all into disobedience, that He might have mercy on all. 33 Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments, and His ways untraceable! 34 For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor? 35 Or who has first given to Him, and it shall be repaid to him? 36 For from Him, and through Him, and to Him are all things; to Him be glory forever. Amen.
> 
> XII. 1 I beseech you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your rational worship. 2 And do not be con-

---

<margin>B</margin> He speaks thus: <note>original: "Ὥσπερ γὰρ ὑμεῖς..."</note> *For just as you once were disobedient to God, but now have obtained mercy through their disobedience; so these also have now been disobedient through your mercy, that they also may obtain mercy.* That is, *Just as you were formerly unbelievers toward God, but now believe because of their unbelief: so also these now believe because of your belief, so that they too may return to belief.* The order which Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and Bible commentator</note> seems to follow is more forced, and it is no less harsh that in the first part the Greek dative indicates the occasion: *you obtained mercy by their disobedience*; while in the second part it indicates the acquisition: *they obtained mercy by your mercy*; just as we say, "To you are the riches," meaning "he was enriched by your good," because he shares his resources with you. For those who read it as "into your mercy" seem to have looked at this, because "by your mercy" seemed to be said too obscurely. That sudden change in the rhetorical pattern is somewhat harsh. To this is added another disadvantage: that according to their interpretation, the same thing is said twice, which the words "just as" and "so" do not allow. For what he had said—"you obtained mercy by their disobedience"—he repeats in the other part—"so that they too always by your mercy"—as if someone were to say, "just as the Princes grow rich by the poverty of the people, so the poverty of the people adds riches to the Princes." Furthermore, since the discourse here concerns the stubborn Jews who cried out "Crucify him," who persecuted the Apostles, who boasted in the works of the Law and were swollen with pride over their kinship with the Patriarchs (and for that reason cursed the other nations as dogs), it is not absurd to say that the faith of the Gentiles was a stumbling block to the Jews, alienating them from the Gospel. Peter, the chief of the Apostles, was forced to excuse himself among the brothers for baptizing Cornelius and his family; in Paul’s presence at a banquet, he withdrew from the table so as not to cause a scandal to the Jews by eating common foods. And in the Acts, the Jews murmur against the Gentiles because their women were received into the Apostolic ministry. How with great difficulty Paul obtained the freedom of the Gentiles from the burden of the Law! If these things happened among those who had embraced the Gospel faith, is it not probable that many Jews either held back or recoiled from the Gospel? This sense fits what he said shortly before: "according to the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake." While Origen <note>a 3rd-century Alexandrian scholar</note> interprets this, he says: "He says 'for your sake,' because they were jealous of your salvation when the Apostles spoke to the Gentiles, and they persecuted those who announce Christ." Does he not say that envy was the occasion for them not to believe the Gospel? The Gospel parable confirms this, in which the elder son refused to enter the house when he heard the prodigal son had been received with such joy. Therefore, I have followed this sense because it seemed simpler to me, though none of the other interpretations stray from piety.

**32** *For God has concluded all*] <note>original: "τοὺς πάντας"</note> that is, *all people*, not *all things*. The meaning is the same, except that "all things" is more emphatic. Furthermore, what follows—*incredulity*—can also be understood as *disobedience*. For it is <term>apeitheia</term> <note>literally "un-persuadableness" or "disobedience"</note>. And "into incredulity" is the Greek phrasing, as we say, "I will shut myself into a narrow space."

**33** *O the depth*] <note>original: "Ὢ βάθος"</note> that is, O the profundity. I wonder why it pleased the Translator <note>referring to the Vulgate</note> to use an ambiguous word <note>Latin "altitudo" can mean both height and depth</note>.

**40** *Of the riches of the wisdom*] The Greeks divide these two nouns with an inserted conjunction, *of the riches and of the wisdom* <note>original: "πλούτου καὶ σοφίας"</note>, according to every manuscript I have seen, even in Chrysostom: so that you may understand Paul to wonder at three things in God: *riches, wisdom, and knowledge*. Toward the Gentiles: *wisdom*, in that He imparted such wisdom to them; *knowledge*, in that He prudently disposes what is expedient for whom. Theophylact explains it in this way. Even if Chrysostom sometimes seems to read it differently, joining these two, "the depth of the riches," so that the remaining genitives do not depend on "depth" but on the combination of the two words, as if you said, "O the deep riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God." That he thinks this is gathered from the fact that he noted Paul used two words for the "epitaph" <note>likely meaning "epithet" or "description"</note> of wisdom to emphasize it: *depth* and *riches*. For "deep" has its own intensification, and "riches" sounds of abundance. It becomes a double amplification if you say, "the deep riches of wisdom." I prefer that it pertains to the whole dispensation of this plan, by which it happened that the Gentiles, formerly serving demons, are now suddenly called to the grace of the Gospel, and the Jews, to whom it seemed specifically promised, have fallen away from it.

**41** *Incomprehensible*] <note>original: "ἀνεξερεύνητα"</note> that is, *inscrutable*; and Jerome frequently cites it thus.

**42** *Unsearchable*] <note>original: "ἀνεξιχνίαστοι"</note> that is, *untraceable*; just as Saint Hilary reads it in the eighth book *On the Trinity*, according to the faith of the most ancient manuscripts—that is, "not trackable" or "un-investigable." For Chrysostom, and after him Theophylact, noted the emphasis of this word. He did not say "unfinished" or "unattainable," but *inscrutable* and *untraceable*. So great is the depth that it is not even lawful to search it out. Now, whether among the Greeks the same difference exists between *searching* <note>ereunan</note> and *tracking* <note>ichneuein</note> that exists among the Latins between *tracking* and *investigating* and *searching thoroughly* must be considered. Furthermore, Saint Jerome thinks Paul was referring to the passage in Isaiah chapter 11: "And there is no investigation of his way."

**43** *The sense of the Lord*] <note>original: "νοῦν"</note> that is, the *mind*, or *thought*.

<column-break/>

> 32 For God has shut up all under incredulity, that He might have mercy on all. 33 O the profundity of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God, how inscrutable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways! 34 For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor? 35 Or who first gave to Him, and it shall be repaid to him? 36 Because from Him, and through Him, and in Him are all things: to Him be glory forever. Amen.
> 
> XII. 1 I beseech you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, your rational worship: 2 And do not be con-

---

<margin>A</margin> ...attained, so that they too may obtain mercy.

**32** For God has shut up all under incredulity, that He might have mercy on all. **33** O the profundity of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God, **41** how inscrutable are His judgments, and **42** untraceable His ways! For who has known **43** the mind of the Lord? **34** Or who has been His counselor? Or who first gave to Him, **35** and it shall be repaid to him? **44** Because from Him, and through Him, and **36** in Him are all things: **45** to Him be glory forever. Amen. **1** I be- **XII.** seech you therefore, brothers, **2** by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, **4** your rational worship: **And do not** be con-

**44** *Because from Him and through Him*] In these three prepositions <margin>C</margin> the ancient Theologians philosophize. Thomas <note>Aquinas</note> interprets: *from Him* as from the first cause of all; *through Him* as the one working and administering; *in Him* as the end; although it does not escape me that these are discussed variously by them. It seems to differ much, however, from the opinion of Origen, who explains it thus: "When he says 'from Him,' it indicates our very being; 'through Him,' that we are dispensed in life by His providence; 'in Him,' however, because the perfection and end of all will be in Him, then when God will be all in all." Furthermore, a certain Thomas indicates that the preposition *de* <note>of/from</note> has almost the same power as *ex* <note>out of/from</note>, except that it adds a partnership of substance—following Augustine, as one may guess, who in the book he wrote *On the Nature of the Good* against the Manichaeans, discusses almost to that effect in the twenty-sixth chapter. Whether this is true among the Latins, others may see; certainly among the Greeks it is the same preposition. And when we say, "he speaks *of* (de) him," there is no significance of a shared essence. Ambrose seems to have read *into Him*, when he says all things look to the end.

**45** *Honor and glory*] In the Greek, only *glory* is written <note>original: "ἡ δόξα"</note>. *Honor* is not added. *Unto ages of ages*. "Of ages" was added by us; for in the Greek it is only "unto the ages" <note>original: "εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας"</note>; it is not added in Origen, nor in Theophylact, nor in Chrysostom.

**1** *I beseech you*] <note>original: "Παρακαλῶ"</note> This can also be taken as *I exhort*; for the Greek word is ambiguous, except that what follows soon after, "by the mercies," seems more like someone entreating and beseeching than exhorting.

**2** *By the mercy*] <note>original: "διὰ τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν"</note> that is, *through the mercies* (plural). Chrysostom and Theophylact agree in this reading. Origen also noted the significance of the plural number, thinking there was an emphasis in it on the immense mercy of God.

**3** *That you exhibit your bodies*] <note>original: "παραστῆσαι τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν"</note>. Let that be *exhibited* which was previously promised, or what is <margin>D</margin> brought forward for worship, or as contracts are "exhibited." It is frequently used in a bad sense, as "to exhibit trouble," meaning one who causes trouble. It is "presented" (praebetur) when it is supplied for use; thus we "present" our ears to one speaking, we "present" help for expenses. Chrysostom and Theophylact indicate that they are properly said to *present* <note>parastēsai</note> who provide war-horses to the emperor. Thus we translate it as "to present." If you look at what we abjured in baptism—the desires of the flesh—and that we dedicated ourselves to Christ, the word *exhibiting* fits, by which we are warned to provide what we professed. Again, if we consider the old custom of the burnt offering, in which the Priest placed the victim on the altar and God consumed it with fire sent from heaven, the word *exhibiting* fits well. For what is once dedicated to God ought not to be adapted to other uses; just as he who provides horses to the emperor for war thereafter has no business with them, nor recalls to private use what he has once handed over. Chrysostom also noted that he did not say "make" your bodies a sacrifice, but "present" <margin>E</margin> them—that is, hand them over, so that they cease to be under your right and begin to be under the divine right. He makes it so that once you have presented them to the Emperor God for fighting against the Devil, you do not again adapt them to the service of the Devil. At the same time, we are warned to take care to treat our bodies so that they are fit instruments for the divine will, and worthy to be presented before His eyes.

**4** *Reasonable service*] <note>original: "τὴν λογικὴν λατρείαν ὑμῶν"</note> that is, *your rational worship*, so that it adheres appositively to the preceding words. This is indicated by the Greek article <term>tēn</term>, which means "your worship which is rational and spiritual." It is as if he were to say: "If you kill and sacrifice to God in your spirit—that is, your bodily affections—not slaughtering brute and dead cattle as was previously done by the Jews, then finally you will present to Him an acceptable victim." And he calls it *rational* (or "logical"), not so you understand it as a "moderate" worship—that is, a moderate maceration of the body—as the <margin>F</margin> common crowd of Preachers nowadays is everywhere accustomed to cite (seemingly to themselves learnedly, but to those who know Greek, quite ridiculously), but a *living and rational* victim. For they think "rational" means what is agreeable to reason and tempered by reason. But Paul here calls the worship *rational* in the same way that in the first epistle of Peter it is called "spiritual milk" <note>original: "λογικὸν γάλα"</note>, that is, *rational milk and spiritual*. Truly, what can they do where the force of the sentence depends on a Greek idiom, and the Translator is entirely ignorant of that language? He placed "service" (obsequium) here for "sacrifice" or "worship," according to his custom. Furthermore, to show that the worship of Christians is unlike Jewish ceremonies in which they sacrificed brute beasts, he added *rational*—namely, the sentient human being himself, who is a rational victim, and for that reason more acceptable to God than the beasts of the Jews which the Lord abominates in Isaiah. And Saint Jerome openly cites it in this sense, both in several other places and truly in the Epistle to Pammachius, the beginning of which is "To the healed wound." Origen interprets it no differently, saying: "Because this worship formerly consisted in the bodies of dead beasts, let it now be offered in the body of a rational man, and your bodies rather than beasts..."

# TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER XII.

...be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, so that you may prove what is the will of God—the good, and acceptable, and perfect. For I say through the grace given to me, to everyone who is among you, not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think so as to be sober-minded, to each as God has distributed a measure of faith. For just as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function; so we, the many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another. But having gifts according to the grace given to us—differing, whether prophecy according to the proportion of faith, or ministry in the ministry, or he who teaches...

<column-break/>

...fit yourselves to the shape of this world, but be transformed <gloss>6</gloss> through the renewal of your mind, so that you may prove <gloss>7</gloss> what is the will of God, that which is good, and acceptable, and perfect. <gloss>8</gloss> For I say through the grace which is given to me, <gloss>9</gloss> to any of you among you, let no one think arrogantly of himself beyond what it is necessary to think of himself, but let him so think, <gloss>10</gloss> that he may be modest and sober, <gloss>11</gloss> as God has distributed to each a measure of faith. For just as in one body we have many members, yet not all members have the same function: so we many are one body in Christ: <gloss>12</gloss> but individually members one of another: but yet <gloss>13</gloss> having gifts according to the grace given to us <gloss>14</gloss> which are varied, whether prophecy <gloss>15</gloss> according to the portion of faith, or ministry...

---

<margin>A</margin> *or a sacrifice to God, and so forth*. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquent preaching</note> explains it no differently, indicating that it is called "rational" <note>original: "λογικὴν"</note> because it is a matter of the soul and spiritual: instead of a temple, there is the heart of man; instead of an animal, the body of man (that is, the impulses of the flesh); instead of fire, there is the love of God. And so far, it is the duty of Christian piety to imitate Christ, who sacrificed himself for us. Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian</note>, as is his custom, touches upon another interpretation: a "rational" worship is one for which a reason can be given, whereas a reason could not be given for the victims of the Jews. Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine commentator</note> also suggests something similar: that all our actions ought to be conducted by reason. While I confess this is truly said, it seems to wander away from the simplicity of the Apostle’s speech.

<margin>5 But be reformed</margin> <note>original: "μεταμορφοῦσθε"</note>, that is, *be transformed, or let yourselves be transformed*. For it can be taken in either way, either as a statement of fact or as a command.

<margin>6 In the novelty of sense</margin> <note>original: "τῇ ἀνακαινώσει τοῦ νοὸς"</note>, that is, *by the renewal of the mind*, specifically alluding to that "reprobate mind" into which they had been handed over before, when they offered honor to idols instead of God.

<margin>7 What is the will of God, good and well-pleasing and perfect</note> It is strange that Augustine, following some manuscript, reads it this way in the tenth book of *The City of God*, and likewise in his eighty-sixth letter: *To prove what is the will of God, that which is good and well-pleasing and perfect*: as if these three adjectives do not belong to the "will of God," but to the whole previous phrase: *Let us present our bodies*, and so forth, *and let us not be conformed to this world, but be reformed*, and so forth. The sense would be that we should obey not our own desires, as the Pagans do, but the divine will. If we do this, I say, the sacrifice would be good, pleasing, and legitimate to God. To make it possible to take it in this sense, the Greek article is added: *the* good, and *the* well-pleasing, and *the* perfect <note>original: "τὸ ἀγαθὸν, καὶ εὐάρεστον, καὶ τέλειον"</note>. For things are properly called "perfect" in which you can find nothing lacking in those things that pertain to the nature of a sacrifice and the rite of religion—and a little earlier, Paul had begun with a metaphor of sacrifices. The translator of Origen indicates that here the Latin versions differ somewhat from the Greek, but I do not quite understand what he means, since the Greek speech is ambiguous enough to allow both senses. Certainly, Ambrose agrees with Augustine. And what he reads, he *interprets* with these words, closing his commentary: *This will be to become conformed to spiritual things, renewed in spirit and faith, to know what pleases God, and that nothing else is good and perfect.* The added article creates the ambiguity of the speech; if he had said "what is the will of God [which is] good and well-pleasing," without the article, there would be no ambiguity. Now, because it is said "the good," the article can be taken two ways: either to distinguish one will from another, or to refer back to what preceded, "to know what is the will of God." The interpreters touch on both meanings. According to the first meaning, not only is the will of God distinguished from our own will, but even that same will of God is distinguished within itself. For that old Jewish worship and its observations was indeed the will of God, but not that "good" nor "well-pleasing" nor "perfect" will. For the will of God indulged them because of their weakness, just as He granted a King to the people when they demanded one. But the New Testament was this perfect will of God. So say Chrysostom and Origen. Ambrose explains this passage in such a way that he refers the articles not only to the immediate phrase, *that you may be able to know what is the will of God*, but to the whole speech which he embraces as a coherent whole: *that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, your rational service: and do not be conformed to this world, but be reformed in the newness of your sense, that you may prove what is the will of God, the doing of which is good, pleasing to God, and perfect.* Thus we understand it is the same thing to offer a living, holy sacrifice pleasing to God, and not to be conformed to this world (which is ignorant of what the will of God is, but still clings to the rites of idolaters or Mosaic ceremonies and lives by the judgment of its impulses), but to be reformed in the newness of sense, so that having renounced the will of the flesh, we can know what the will of God is. All of this is a worship that is good, well-pleasing, and perfect before God. Now, "be transformed," as I said a little earlier, can be either a command or a statement. If a command, it responds to what preceded, "do not be conformed." If a statement, you should understand that through those things said about rational worship, we *are* transformed: so that having been transformed, we can know what the will of God is. For unless we slaughter the desires of our flesh, we cannot be fit to understand in our actions what the will of God is; rather, whatever greatly appeals to our own senses, we interpret as being the will of God. He teaches something similar in Ephesians 5: *Proving what is well-pleasing to the Lord.* Also in the second chapter of this Epistle: *And you know the will, and prove the things that are better.*

<column-break/>

<margin>8 For I say through grace</margin> <note>original: "Λέγω"</note>. He said "I say" instead of "I command" or "I warn"; just as the Latins say "He bids you be well" or "He says hello," the Greeks say in a similar fashion, "I speak a good word." For this reason, <margin>B</margin> there is added "through the grace which is given to me": lest he should seem to command them arrogantly or warn them without authority. He commands as an Apostle, as one understanding what is pleasing to God, but he credits this very thing to divine favor. Unless you prefer to interpret the words such that Paul explains and clarifies what he had said above regarding the sacrificing of the body and the fleeing from the desires of this world: for he makes the matter clearer by adding examples. Arrogance, above all, must be slaughtered for God.

<margin>9 To all who are among you</margin> <note>original: "παντὶ τῷ ὄντι ἐν ὑμῖν"</note>. The translator of Origen thought it should be noted that the Greek does not have "to all who are among you," but "to every one who is among you." Since it is clear this makes no difference to the meaning, I wonder why he thought it necessary to point out. We preferred to translate it "to any" or "to whomever." <margin>C</margin> For some status seemed to be attributed to those who excelled in fortune or gifts. Paul, completely removing that choice of persons, declares that whoever he may be, provided he is found among Christians, he should not place himself before anyone, but should contribute whatever gift he has received from God to the convenience of his neighbor.

<margin>10 To think unto sobriety</margin> <note>original: "εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν"</note>. Saint Jerome, fighting in his first book against Jovinian, out of a zeal for defending virginity, thinks it should read "unto chastity" <note>original: "ad pudicitiam"</note>; and he condemns what the Church now reads, "to think unto sobriety." But the Greek <note>original: "σωφρονεῖν"</note> is to be temperate, modest, and sober; sometimes it also pertains to chastity, but certainly not in this place. Yet the translator of Origen in the Epistle to the Romans preferred "temperance" rather than "sobriety," because that virtue which the Greeks call *sophrosyne* is called "temperance" by learned Latins, which is the moderation of desires and actions. And it is in this way, clearly, that Augustine cites this passage in his forty-seventh Letter. Hilary, in the tenth book of *On the Trinity*, rendered the Greek word for "thinking too highly" <note>original: "ὑπερφρονεῖν"</note> as "super-thinking" or "over-wise." Although it is true <margin>D</margin> what Paul writes elsewhere—"Knowledge puffs up, unless charity is its companion"—here he is not properly speaking of academic knowledge. There is, however, a pleasant wordplay in the Greek speech which the Latin translator could not render: "thinking over," "thinking," and "thinking unto sobriety" <note>original: "ὑπερφρονεῖν, φρονεῖν, εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν"</note>. Nor in this place does "thinking" <note>original: "φρονεῖν"</note> (to be wise) pertain to erudition, but to thought and opinion, as when someone is carried away in spirit and thinks magnificently of himself, as we also warned above. Origen declares this is so, immediately indicating that this speech pertains to those who, being grafted from the wild olive into the olive tree, were becoming wild and proud against the branches broken off from the olive: and that what he said here has the same weight as what he said elsewhere, "Do not be proud." Furthermore, regarding what he brings from the sources of the philosophers about the habit of virtue being pulled back from two extremes, interpreting the matter with subtlety more according to someone else's opinion than his own—Chrysostom warns of the same thing: that here is indicated the mother of all good things, modesty, which is humility <note>original: "ταπεινοφροσύνην"</note>. Theophylact agrees with this. Ambrose reads it as we do, "unto sobriety," and his explanation makes no mention of chastity. Truly, in the heat of battle, the blessed Jerome allowed himself so much that what he approves elsewhere, he rejects here. For he cites the passage thus: "Not to think more than one ought to think, but to think unto chastity, not unto sobriety," claiming that "to think unto chastity" is wrongly read in the Latin manuscripts.

<margin>11 As God has divided to each</margin> <margin>E</margin> The Greek also has it this way: yet the old reading has nothing to which it refers. Thus it is necessary to admit that here too Paul looked at the sense more than the integrity of the speech, unless we prefer to order it thus: "that each may think as God has divided to each the measure of faith." Origen hints that something is to be understood when he says, "In order that the guarding of unity may happen, God divided the measure of faith."

<margin>12 Individually however members one of another</margin> <note>original: "ὁ δὲ καθ᾽ εἷς ἀλλήλων μέλη"</note>, that is, *each individually members of one another*: or, as we have translated it, *individually others members of others*. It signifies the mutual communion of the members among themselves.

<margin>13 Having gifts</margin> The translator, or as I rather think, the scribe, omitted the conjunction which most conveniently connected this part with the one above: *But having gifts* <note>original: "Ἔχοντες δὲ χαρίσματα"</note>. For when he had said, "we are individually members of one another," lest we imagine a confusion, he added, "we are indeed members of the same body, but having gifts." Otherwise, the speech was tangled; therefore someone, being offended and thinking this part did not depend on the previous ones, wiped out the conjunction. But certainly it is added <margin>F</margin> in Ambrose and in the Pauline manuscript, although "but" <note>original: "sed"</note> was more clear and appropriate than "however" <note>original: "autem"</note>; just as a little before: "for just as in one body we have many members, but not all members have the same function." "Gifts" <note>original: "charismata"</note>. He affects an abundance of words when there is no need, especially since "donations" <note>original: "donationes"</note> is a poorly chosen Latin word in this place.

<margin>14 Differing</margin> <note>original: "διάφορα"</note>, that is, "diverse," or rather "diverse gifts."

<margin>15 According to the ratio of faith</margin> <note>original: "κατὰ τὴν ἀναλογίαν"</note>, that is, *according to the proportion...*
