# PAUL’S EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER XII.

<margin>8</margin> ...or he who exhorts, in
<margin>9</margin> exhortation; he who gives, in simplicity; he who
<margin>10</margin> leads, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.
<margin>11</margin> Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhorring what is evil,
<margin>12</margin> clinging to what is good. In brotherly love, be affectionate
<margin>13</margin> toward one another. In honor, giving preference to one another.
<margin>14</margin> In diligence, not lagging. Fervent in spirit. Serving the
<margin>15</margin> opportunity <note>The author notes a variant here: "serving the time" rather than "serving the Lord."</note>. Rejoicing in hope. Patient in
<margin>16</margin> tribulation. Continuing steadfastly in prayer. Contributing
to the needs of the saints. Pursuing hospitality.
Bless those who persecute you; bless,
and do not curse. Rejoice with those who
rejoice, and weep with those who weep. Be
of the same mind toward one another. Do not
be haughty in mind...

<margin>A</margin> **Proportion:** so that you may understand that these are greater gifts to the extent that your faith is more intact. The translator of Origen indicates that "analogy" <note>original: *analogian*</note> was not very conveniently translated as "reason," but is rather a "fitting measure." Certainly, what Paul called "analogy" here, he called "measure" <note>original: *metron*</note> shortly before: here it was clearer to say "by proportion," or "according to the portion of faith." For an analogy is the congruence of a thing in relation to something else: as when we say, "A cicada has large wings, in proportion to its body"—for the wings are small if they are compared to the wings of butterflies.

<margin>B</margin> 16 **In ministering and in exhorting** ] These are nouns: "in the ministry," "in the exhortation." Although this does not change the Apostle's meaning. Origen thinks each part can be referred back to what precedes: "Whether having prophecy according to the measure of faith," so that no one thinks more highly than they ought, but works within that, and likewise for the rest.

17 **Abhorring evil** ] <note>original: *apostygountes*</note> that is, having a hatred for it. Although here it was elegantly "shuddering away from evil," to correspond to what follows, "clinging." Furthermore, "good" and "evil" here cannot refer to a person, since it is a neuter term <note>original: *to agathon*</note>; it must refer to a thing. He called "good" honesty, and "evil" baseness.

18 **Loving one another with brotherly love** ] There is another sense among the Greeks: "In brotherly love, be naturally affectionate toward one another." Plutarch wrote a booklet "On Brotherly Love" <note>original: *peri tēs adelphias*</note>, a word the Apostles frequently use for the zeal and love of Christians toward each other, from which the Greek word is composed. Ambrose reads, "In the love of brotherhood, be kind to one another." For among the Greeks, "naturally affectionate" <note>original: *philostorgos*</note> describes one who has a natural leaning of affection toward relatives or kin; conversely, those who are not touched by the affection of piety are called "without natural affection" <note>original: *astorgoi*</note>. Paul wants, by this name, a Christian to be dear to a Christian simply because he is a Christian. Chrysostom thinks "natural affection" <note>original: *storgēn*</note> is more than "friendship" <note>original: *philian*</note>. For we love our kin of our own accord, even if they have not provoked us with any service, and we endure and cherish them even if they are not very convenient, for the very reason that they are kin. It clearly smells to me like a scribe's error, where "love" was changed into "charity." "By the love of brotherhood"—that is, by the fraternal—loving one another; and the grammatical case for "love" corresponds to what follows, "outdoing one another in honor." For one is born from the other: beneficence from love.

19 **Outdoing one another in honor** ] The sense is entirely ambiguous in Greek. For "to lead the way in honor" means one who excels in honor. And yet the Greeks interpret "leading the way" <note>original: *proēgoumenoi*</note> here as "anticipating" or "preoccupying." If the scripture is free of error, it adds an accusative case to the participle, whereas a dative would have been more fitting due to the preposition "before." Furthermore, he calls the person who assists an "unskilled person" <note>original: *idiōtēn*</note>. For it suits brotherly love to run ahead of each other in a race to perform services. However, that other sense is not absurd—that we understand honor as being deferred. For where there is brotherly love, no one tries to snatch honor for himself, but rather yields to the other, judging each one more fit than himself out of modesty. Nor does the word "leading" contradict this sense. For "to lead" <note>original: *hēgeisthai*</note> sometimes sounds like "to consider": which the Latins imitate by saying "to lead" <note>original: *ducere*</note>, as in "to lead someone as worthy" <note>to consider them worthy</note>. Hence "to lead before" describes one who has a better opinion of another than of himself. "To lead" is also sometimes "to be a leader": hence "the leader" <note>original: *ho hēgoumenos*</note>, a "prince" or "president." Following this, the Translator rendered it "preventing" <note>in the sense of acting before someone else</note>; and no differently Theophylact, who explains "leading before" as "anticipating" or "getting ahead."

20 **Not lazy in diligence** ] "In diligence not shrinking" <note>original: *oknēroi*</note>. He calls "diligence" <note>original: *spoudēn*</note> the industriousness and zeal in performing a service; and "shrinking" <note>original: *oknēros*</note> describes one who does something with a heavy heart. Hence he commands that we should not only love and defer honor to one another, but also succor each other with eagerness and readiness.

21 **Serving the opportunity** ] Origen, or certainly his translator, indicates that in some copies it was written, "Serving the opportunity" <note>original: *Tempori servientes*</note>; and it can be taken as: one must diligently use the occasion of the time, since it is short. To me, it seems rightly understood that whatever inconvenience happens for the time being should be taken in good part: for that, I think, is to serve the time. This fits with what follows, "Rejoicing in hope." If someone demands a tribute, pay it; if a tax, settle it; if someone demands honor, give it; if someone afflicts you, endure it; and let that thing not break your strength, but let hope raise your spirit in evils. Also, what precedes: "Fervent in spirit." For fervor of spirit despises obstacles and seizes every opportunity to do good to a neighbor. Ambrose also testifies that it was originally in the Greek codices as "Serving the time" <note>original: *Tō kairō douleuontes*</note>. And in passing, I wonder, since he knew Greek, why he did not consult the Greek manuscripts himself. Indeed, the "Ordinary Gloss," as they call it, warns of a double reading, I believe on the authority of Bede. Saint Jerome, in a certain letter to Marcella, prefers this reading which we commonly use, yet gives no reason why he prefers it.

<meta>catchword: but</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>1</margin> ...in administration, or he who teaches in
<margin>2</margin> doctrine, or he who exhorts in exhortation, he who
<margin>3</margin> imparts in simplicity, he who presides in diligence, he who
<margin>4</margin> shows mercy in cheerfulness. Let love be without pretense. Be
<margin>5</margin> 17 pursuing with hatred that which is evil, clinging to that
<margin>6</margin> which is good. 18 Through brotherly love, be inclined to
<margin>7</margin> loving one another. 19 Anticipating one another
<margin>8</margin> in honor. 20 Not lazy in zeal. Fervent in spirit.
<margin>9</margin> 21 Serving the time. Rejoicing in hope. In affliction,
<margin>10</margin> patient. 22 Persevering in prayer. 23 Sharing in the
<margin>11</margin> needs of the saints. Pursuing hospitality.
<margin>12</margin> 24 Speak well of those who harass you; speak
<margin>13</margin> well, I say, and 25 do not pray for evil. 26 Rejoice
<margin>14</margin> with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep. 27 Of the
<margin>15</margin> same...

Let it be free for everyone to follow what they wish. To me, "Serving the time" is more pleasing. But that sentiment, because it was commonly circulated under the name of the Pagan Philosophers and seemed to prescribe a certain craftiness, someone more easily offended changed it to "Serving the Lord" <note>original: *Kyriō*</note>—not noticing sufficiently that "Serving the Lord" does not fit as well with the whole context of this discourse. Although in the Latin words "time" <note>original: *tempori*</note> and "Lord" <note>original: *Domino*</note> there is no affinity, yet in the Greek words there is some—*kairō* and *kyriō*—especially since scribes are accustomed to shortening syllables when writing. Chrysostom and Theophylact read and interpret it as "Serving the Lord," and they connect it thus: by loving, honoring, and cherishing one another, you will show a most pleasing worship to the Lord, because whatever service is paid to a neighbor reaches the Lord himself. Chrysostom notes an emphasis, or rather an intensification, in each word Paul used here. For he did not just say "impart," but "in simplicity," that is, generously and readily; nor did he say "preside," but adds "with zeal," that is, studiously; nor did he say "pity," but "with cheerfulness," that is, love, and that without pretense; nor was it said "abstain from evils," but "hating them," that is, have them in hatred; nor was it said "love virtue," but "be glued to the good" <note>original: *kollōmenoi*</note>; nor did he just say "be fond of," but added "naturally affectionate," that is, with a friend's affection; nor did he simply say "be careful," but added "not lazy," that is, not sluggishly; nor did he say "having the spirit," but "boiling in the spirit" <note>original: *pneumati zeontes*</note>.

22 **Persevering in prayer** ] <note>original: *proskarterountes*</note> which sounds like a constant persistence.

<margin>D</margin> 23 **Sharing in the needs of the saints** ] Ambrose reads, "Sharing in the *memories* of the saints" <note>original: *memoriis*</note>, and Origen's translator admits this is found in Latin copies. It is not at all unlikely that this was a mistake from "needs" <note>original: *chreiais*</note> made by some little-educated scribe, especially since "memories" seemed like a more religious sense. However, Paul seems to be doing this so that they would not only impart mutual love to those present, but also be mindful of those absent—just as Paul, warned by Peter, does in the Epistle to the Galatians, being mindful of the poor to collect donated money. Chrysostom and Theophylact read and explain it as "needs." For he said "needs," not "luxuries"; and he said "sharing," not "helping": because it is a commerce between the giver and the receiver, and the one who gives the benefit makes more profit than the one who receives. Yet it is not "in necessities" <note>original: *ankankais*</note>, but "needs" <note>original: *chreiais*</note>, which sounds more like "use" or "having a task." He suggested this because some think we ought not to help a neighbor except in extreme necessity.

<margin>E</margin> 24 **Bless those persecuting you** ] In Greek it is indeed "Bless," that is, "speak well of": which Origen’s translator explains as "pray well for," I think because there follows "do not curse." For commonly those who cannot avenge an injury tend to devote those who hurt them to the Furies. "To bless" <note>original: *Eulogein*</note> sometimes means "to praise," in which way it certainly cannot be taken here. For he does not command that they praise a harasser, but that we pray well for him, or that his error be corrected with kind words. Chrysostom seems to interpret it regarding insults: "Do not revile," he says. We translated it "speak well of those who persecute you" to indicate this sense as well. The disciples were spoken ill of among unbelievers, and he who is vituperated and he whom men curse is spoken ill of; so he speaks well of another who does not vituperate, and he prays well who prays for his enemies; he speaks well who teaches without insults, but from an affection of love.

<margin>F</margin> 25 **Do not curse** ] <note>original: *mē katarasthe*</note> that is, do not pray for evil; do not devote anyone to destruction. If Paul so insists that we should not pray for evil for anyone, where are those who think it holy to slit the throat of an enemy, or even someone who is not an enemy?

26 **To rejoice** ] <note>original: *Chairein*</note>. It is the custom of the Greeks to put the infinitive for the imperative: "to rejoice" for "rejoice," and "to weep" for "weep." I think they must imply a verb. A similar trope is found among Latin historians especially, "to hunt" <note>original: *venari*</note> for "he hunted," in which "he was accustomed" or "he began" is implied. But no Latin writer imitated this trope. Chrysostom noted the order of the words, thinking it is more "to rejoice with those who rejoice" than "to weep with those who weep," because calamity shakes out pity even from the unwilling, but prosperity moves envy. Here Chrysostom speaks as if what is most important is usually placed first.

27 **The same toward one another** ] <note>original: *To auto eis allēlous phronountes*</note> that is, "thinking the same thing for others as for yourselves," or "feeling the same about others." This also refers to a modest disposition of mind, by which no one thinks another is less than himself, but accommodates himself to everyone, thinking equally well of everyone. For Paul wants there to be a common feeling among Christians...

<margin>A</margin> ...aiming so that we measure everyone not by wealth, nor birth, nor learning, nor honors, but by Christ, who is equally common to all. Now the noble disdains the obscure, the rich man barely considers the poor man a human, the learned man despises the unlearned <term>idiotam</term> <note>original: *idiotam*, meaning a common or uneducated person, not "idiot" in the modern sense</note>, the Priest is puffed up over the layman, the monk hardly considers laypeople as Christians, holding all others as barbarians and almost despising and shuddering at them like cattle. The German hates the Frenchman, the Englishman the Scot: and from these and other types of the most foolish emotions, wars, lawsuits, and these turmoils of affairs, which we have seen now for some years, arise. But Paul wanted every Christian to be affected toward the other members just as the individual members of the body are affected toward the others, as he explains more clearly elsewhere, and he calls this "thinking the same thing" <note>original: *to auto phronein*</note>. Both Chrysostom and Theophylact <note>Greek Church Fathers who wrote influential commentaries</note> expound on this meaning, if authority moves anyone more than reason.

**28 High-minded** <note>original: *Alta sapientes*</note> ] This is the same participle as just now, "thinking" <note>original: *phronountes*</note>, that is, feeling or pondering: so that it refers to the affection of the mind. And this particle should be connected with the previous speech, which the Translator separated poorly. For Paul added this as if explaining what he had said, "Thinking the same thing toward one another." For where each person thinks magnificently of himself and his own, he must necessarily despise others.

**29 But accommodating yourselves to the humble** <note>original: *Sed humilibus consentientes*</note> ] "Associating with the humble" <note>original: *tois tapeinois synapagomenoi*</note>. He calls "humble" here not the modest, but people of low status, such as the poor, the ignoble, the unlearned, the commoners. And it is not "consenting," but rather "yielding and accommodating yourselves," so that as each person forgets their greatness, they descend to the feelings of the inferiors. Paul inculcates this with wonderful diligence in many places, not unaware that the greatest plagues of life gush from this source. Paulinus, in the letter to Augustine, reads "to be compatible with the humble."

**30 Do not be arrogant** <note>original: *Nolite esse prudentes*</note> ] "Prudent" <note>original: *phronimoi*</note>. He calls "prudent" not one who is wise, but one who thinks of himself with too little modesty, as we just advised; the Greek commentaries interpret it in that way. Otherwise, what is the affinity of prudence with vengeance? But arrogance is a vengeful thing, while each person thinks himself better than to have to yield to another.

**31 Providing good things** <note>original: *Providentes bona*</note> ] These words, "not only before God, but also," are not in the Greek, but only "providing good things in the presence..." <note>original: *pronooumenoi kala enōpion*</note>, that is, "before all men." Therefore, they are not added in Origen, nor in Chrysostom or Theophylact: it appears they were added by someone explaining Paul’s meaning. For Paul is not here opposing men to God, but comparing the perfect and imperfect, the good and the bad, to all of whom he wants us to be approved if possible. And this which follows, "If possible," in my opinion would be more correctly referred to the previous parts, since the following clause has its own "as much as is in you" <note>original: *to en hymin*</note>, which has the same power: although others follow a different distinction. He who added "not only before God" wanted to complete the sentence, lest Paul seem content with the praise of men. I do not indeed blame this, although it was better to leave the Scripture in its integrity, unless some necessity urges, which I see none of here: for he does not say "before all men" but "in the presence of <margin>E</margin> all men": that is, Jews and Gentiles, the strong and the weak. The phrase "not only before God" does not flow very gracefully into this sense.

**32 Vindicating** <note>original: *Defendentes*</note> ] "Vindicating" <note>original: *ekdikountes*</note>. For it is the participle of the same verb from which the noun "vengeance" <note>original: *ekdikēsis*</note> comes, which he translates as "punishment." And yet "to defend" is frequently used among Ecclesiastical writers for "to avenge." Otherwise, defense is permitted to Christians if "defending" means repelling injury, with the exception of blameless protection. "Dearly beloved" <note>original: *Charissimi / agapētoi*</note>, that is, beloved. He added this as if wishing to coax them: because it was hard to obey—having been provoked by an injury—to give up vengeance.

**33 Vengeance is mine** <note>original: *Mihi vindictam*</note> ] "Vengeance is mine" <note>original: *Emoi ekdikēsis*</note>, that is, mine is the vengeance or retribution: in the nominative case. And so Jerome cites it against Rufinus in the Letter whose beginning is "Having read the letters of your prudence." Therefore, it is explained more clearly in the thirty-second chapter of Deuteronomy, from where this place is taken: "Vengeance is mine": that is, it is mine to avenge, I who am the judge. Nor is it added in the Greek codices, "and I will repay," but "I will repay": without the conjunction, just as it was written in the very ancient Constantian manuscript.

**34 Feed him** <note>original: *Ciba illum*</note> ] "Feed" <note>original: *psōmize*</note>. Which indeed is not without emphasis. For "to feed" <note>original: *psōmizein*</note> is not simply to nourish, but to nourish indulgently, as if with bread soaked in bits, or food cut into small pieces: which happens among some toward those who are favored at banquets, while others meanwhile are allowed to go hungry.

**35 If he is thirsty, give him a drink** <note>original: *Si sitit, potum da illi*</note> ] This was not added in some Greek copies. It is not clear enough from Origen what he read: in Ambrose it is added, and likewise in the old copies...

<margin>B</margin> ...besides in Theophylact and Chrysostom. Although drink is also contained in the word "food" <note>original: *cibo*</note>.

**36 You will heap upon the head** <note>original: *Congeres super caput*</note> ] "You will heap up" <note>original: *sōreuseis*</note>, that is, you will accumulate or pile up. And "coals of fire," he said in a Hebrew figure for "burning coals," which Theophylact interprets this way: Do you wish to avenge yourself magnificently on your enemy? Accumulate benefits upon him. For so it will happen that he is punished more severely by God. To me, it seems more suited to Christian doctrine if we understand the enemy to be overwhelmed by benefits, so that he may finally come to his senses, and being conquered by our merits and gentleness, becomes a friend from an enemy.

**37 Do not be overcome by evil** <note>original: *Noli vinci a malo*</note> ] Good and evil here do not refer to a wicked or upright man, but signify the benefit or injury itself. He is overcome by evil, therefore, who, provoked by an injury, does not restrain his mind but is led to retaliate for the injury. <margin>C</margin> He overcomes evil with good who, repaying bad deeds with benefits, causes the enemy to come to his senses and become a friend. This precept, because it was hard for human feelings, he added with the authority of the Lord: "Says the Lord." And Christ commanded the same in the Gospel: and yet, I do not know how it happens that those who seem to themselves quite Christian not only neglect this doctrine but even openly mock it. People whose pious ears, forsooth, cannot bear even a superstitious word regarding the cult of Christopher, Barbara, or Erasmus, do not fear to raise a laugh at these most holy precepts of Christ. And what Socrates taught the Pagans before Christ, this—handed down by Christ himself and so often drummed in by the Apostles—Christians mock, though by this sign especially Christ distinguished his own from the world. But this lamentation does not belong here. And from this chapter Saint Augustine brings forth an example of speech that is both moderate and rhythmic <note>original: *modulatæ*</note>. Certainly, there is hardly another place in Paul more composed and, so to speak, more picturesque. To point out only the more notable features, what dignity that "distribution" has—as the Rhetoricians call it—whereby each thing is given to that <margin>D</margin> to which it fits: "Having gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy according to the proportion of faith, or ministry in ministering, or he who teaches in teaching, he who exhorts in exhorting, he who gives in simplicity, he who leads in diligence, he who shows mercy in cheerfulness"—and the rest which run down with similar rhythm and pleasantness even to the two-part period: "Not high-minded, but consenting to the humble." Meanwhile, there is no small grace in the same words repeated through "traduction" <term>traductionem</term> <note>a rhetorical device of repeating a word in different grammatical forms</note>, or similar ones through "pun" <term>adnominationem</term>, and likewise from contraries given to each other: of which kind are those, "Rejoicing with those who rejoice"; likewise, "Evil for evil"; "all of you" <note>original: *pan hymōn*</note>; in those it is, "Weeping with those who weep," "Rejoicing with those who rejoice"; likewise in those, "Bless, and do not curse"; likewise, "Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good"; likewise, "Not high-minded, but consenting to the humble." Furthermore, the whole speech is so rhythmic with balanced members and clauses, with similar cadences and endings, that no song could be more pleasant. But it is not my intention to dwell on pursuing these things, lest I both <margin>E</margin> weary the Reader and seem to depart from the subject undertaken.

**1 Every soul** <note>original: *Omnis anima*</note> ] he said, for "every human." For as to what Origen philosophizes here—that "soul" refers to the human according to the part lower than the spirit, just as "flesh" is said according to the worse part, and therefore "soul" is understood as the human who is not entirely pure from worldly things and thus rightly ought to obey those who manage worldly affairs—this seems to me more clever than true. I do not know if it happened by a mistake of the Librarians that in Ambrose we read it differently: "Be subject to all higher powers."

**2 Higher [powers]** <note>original: *Sublimioribus*</note> ] "Standing above" <note>original: *hyperechousais*</note>, that is, "pre-eminent": it is positive, not comparative. For he understands people endowed with public authority, such as Kings, Governors, and Magistrates. The comparative, which the Latin translator used, makes it possible <margin>F</margin> for someone to take this meaning: "One must obey Kings and Governors, but not inferior Magistrates." What he translates here as "higher," in 1 Peter 2:13 he translates as "pre-eminent," "to the kings as pre-eminent" <note>original: *tois basileusi hōs hyperechousi*</note>, or "to the king as pre-eminent."

**3 Those that are from God** <note>original: *Quæ autem sunt a Deo*</note> ] The Greeks divide this differently: "and the powers that exist are ordained by God" <note>original: *hai de ousai exousiai, hypo Theou tetagmenai eisin*</note>, that is, "but those that are powers, have been ordained by God": so that you place the comma after "powers": for he repeats what he had said above, "There is no power except from God." And so Ambrose reads and interprets: "Those that exist, have been ordained by God." Again, on Luke chapter 3: "Those that are," he says, "are ordained by God": not given, but ordained. And thus the oldest copies distinguish it, specifically the one provided by the College of the Church of Constantinople. Again, in my copy from the old printing press, and in the Constantian one, it was "ordained" <note>original: *ordinatæ*</note>, not "ordained" <note>original: *ordinata*</note>.

635 PAUL’S EPISTLE CHAPTER XIII. 636

...judgment; and those who resist will bring judgment upon themselves. <margin>2</margin> For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to evil. Do you wish then to not fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it; <margin>4</margin> for he is God’s servant to you for good. But if you do what is evil, be afraid; for he does not bear the sword in vain; for he is God’s servant, an avenger for wrath to the one who practices evil. <margin>5</margin> Therefore it is necessary to be subject, not only because of <margin>6</margin> wrath, but also because of conscience. For because of this you also pay taxes; for they are God’s ministers, attending to this very thing. <margin>7</margin> Render therefore to all their dues: taxes to whom taxes are due, customs to whom customs, fear to whom fear, honor to whom honor. <margin>8</margin> Owe no one anything except to love one another; for he who loves another has fulfilled the <margin>9</margin> law. For this: "You shall not commit adultery," "You shall not murder," "You shall not steal," "You shall not bear false witness," "You shall not covet," and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying, namely, "You shall love your <margin>10</margin> neighbor as yourself." <margin>2</margin> **born:** <note>original: *nata*</note> so that it appears this was avoided by the Scribes. Nor does Augustine distinguish differently, citing this testimony in his fifty-fourth *Letter to Macedonius*, except that he *did not include "powers"*: reading it thus, *For there is no power except from God: but those that exist, are ordained by God*: so that the punctuation <term>hypostigme</term> <note>a low dot used in ancient Greek punctuation, similar to a comma</note> follows the word *exist*. Theophylact does not repeat *powers*: *But those things which are from God, are ordained*: but in such a way that he wants it to be understood. In Chrysostom it is repeated. However, I do not find this entire clause in Origen, nor is any mention made of this matter in any interpretation. It could seem to have been added by some translator who, wishing to confirm that all power is from God, repeated the same sentiment as an assertion: "Therefore those who resist, resist God’s ordinance," leading into what follows soon after: even if Chrysostom and Theophylact, as I just said, punctuate according to our custom. Since Paul understood that some Christians, under the pretext of religion, were refusing the orders of Princes—and thus, with order disturbed, everything would be mixed up topsy-turvy—he commands that they obey whoever is endowed with public power, except in cases of faith and piety. They may indeed be Pagans and evil, but the order itself is good, and for this reason even evil Princes must sometimes be endured by godly men. Chrysostom noted the word "to be subject" <note>original: *ὑποτάσσεσθαι / hypotassesthai*</note>: for he did not say "to obey" <note>original: *πείθεσθαι / peithesthai*</note>, which is simply to comply, but *be subject*. For those who comply by persuasion are said to "obey," that is, they are listening to what is said—which the Greeks express with the single word <term>peitharchein</term> <note>to obey authority</note>—but "to be subject" applies even to servants. The Apostle therefore requires of Christians that they comply with and endure even Tyrants: just as when a Tyrant says, "Go to prison," they go; "Submit your neck," they submit. And the term "soul" is more significant than the word "man," lest anyone at all think himself exempt from the obedience of Princes, whether he be an Apostle or a Prophet. He also noted that he did not say all Princes are ordained by God, but the "power" <note>the office itself</note>: just as marriage is from God, but God does not join all spouses.

<margin>4</margin> **They acquire damnation** <note>original: *λήψονται / lepsontai*</note>, that is, they shall receive: as it is in the future tense. Furthermore, he translated <term>krima</term> <note>judgment</note>, that is, *judgment*, not poorly as *damnation*.

<margin>3</margin> **They are not for a terror to a good work** [In other Greek copies: *οὐκ εἰσὶ φόβος τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἔργων*], that is, they are not a terror or fear to good works. This means: They are not to be dreaded by those acting well. For they do not deter good deeds, but crimes.

<margin>6</margin> **For he is God’s minister]** <note>original: *διάκονός / diakonos*</note>, that is, a minister, an attendant. For he is speaking of the power. Although a magistrate is sometimes called a "man" performing a magistracy, so also the "power" is a man endowed with power. And the Greeks add the pronoun "to you" <note>original: *σοι / soi*</note>: he is God’s minister, but for *your* good: so there is less reason to fear or hate him.

<margin>7</margin> **And therefore be subject to necessity]** In other Greek copies the sense is: *Διὸ ἀνάγκη ὑποτάσσεσθαι*. Wherefore it is necessary [to be] subject. The translator seems to have read *ὑποτάσσεσθε* <note>subject yourselves (imperative)</note> with an *e-epsilon*, not with the *ai-diphthong* <note>to be subject (infinitive)</note>. Although if it were the imperative, the sense would be the same as the infinitive, since the infinitive verb is used in place of the indicative. Even if the word for "necessity" is not read in Ambrose at all. Origen, in his usual manner, twists that necessity only to those who are not yet purely spiritual. However, in my opinion, Princes are to be endured by others as well, lest they be provoked to a great and heavy ruin of the state, and this, unless I am mistaken, he calls necessity. Furthermore, following the Hebrew custom, he calls "wrath" the vengeance and punishment by which crimes are chastised. "Conscience" can be understood in two ways: either of the one who does not comply with him whom God wishes to be complied with, or of the one who, by your example, thinks he should despise the Magistrate whom he sees neglected by you, and wrongly imitates the one rightly neglecting. Augustine interprets "necessity" as the authority of Princes in taking the property of subjects. Nor shall it be concealed that in Theophylact and Chrysostom these words, "Wherefore it is necessary to be subject," are inserted so as to connect the preceding context with what follows: "He is God’s minister: it is therefore necessary to obey," just as I had begun to say at the start. Since, however, because of a rather long <term>hyperbaton</term> <note>a figure of speech where the natural word order is disrupted</note> these words, "not only because of wrath," and so on, were joined somewhat harshly with what preceded ("Let every soul be subject"), someone repeated what had preceded so that the flow of the speech would be smoother. He who inspects the manuscript will see that this is true...

<margin>2</margin> resists the ordinance: but those who have resisted will receive judgment for themselves. For princes are not a terror to those acting well, but to the evil. Do you wish then to not fear the power? Do that which is good, and you will have praise <margin>4</margin> from it: for he is God’s minister to you for good: but if you have done that which is evil, fear: for not in vain does he bear the sword: for he is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath to him who has done what is evil. Wherefore it is necessary to be subject, not only because of wrath, but also <margin>6</margin> because of conscience. For because of this you also pay taxes: since they are ministers of God, devoting themselves <margin>7</margin> to this very thing. Love works no evil to a neighbor: the fulfillment of the law, therefore, is love. Especially <margin>11</margin> since we know the time, that it is the season, that we

...very ancient and most diligently written, which the Dominican College of Basel showed to us, and the manuscript of Chrysostom, which served me as I was writing these things. I do not find fault, however, but praise what has been done.

<sig>D</sig> <margin>8</margin> **Serving in this very thing]** <note>original: *προσκαρτεροῦντες / proskarterountes*</note>. What he translated a little earlier as *standing by*, he now translates as *serving*: we more likely say *applying themselves*, that is, giving effort and striving. Augustine supports me, citing this passage in the fourth book of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter twenty, reading, *persevering in this very thing*.

<margin>9</margin> **Owe no one anything]** <note>original: *ὀφείλετε / opheilete*</note>. It is uncertain whether it is "you owe" (indicative) or "you should owe" (imperative). The sense of the Greek speech is ambiguous; for it can be understood thus: "Pay to each what you owe," and once paid, you cease to owe. It can also be understood as "to owe," but let it always be paid, and nevertheless always be owed, so that there is no end to doing good. Origen, Chrysostom, and Theophylact explain it in this way. It can also be understood so that the preceding parts refer to Pagan Magistrates, as we were taught above. What follows, "To no one anything," and so on, refers to Christians. Pay to those what you owe. Otherwise, a Christian owes nothing to Christians except mutual charity. And Ambrose embraced this sense, explaining it thus: "He wants us to have peace, if possible, with all: but love with the brothers." Augustine noted the grace of the distribution in the place mentioned, where individual things are appropriately rendered to individuals with a rhythmic flow of speech: *to whom tribute, tribute: to whom tax, tax: to whom fear, fear: to whom honor, honor*. And here, he says, let it flow limb by limb; they are even closed by the circuit itself when two members are connected: *Owe no one anything, except that you love one another*. Although there is much delight in this, from the balanced parts, the <term>asyndeton</term> <note>omission of conjunctions between parts of a sentence</note>, and such repetitions of words, and finally in the repetitions of the word at the start: *to whom, to whom, to whom, to whom*.

<margin>10</margin> **For he who loves his neighbor]** <note>original: *ὁ γὰρ ἀγαπῶν τὸν ἕτερον / ho gar agapon ton heteron*</note>, that is, for he who loves the other. The translator seems to have read "the neighbor" <note>original: *τὸν πλησίον / ton plesion*</note>. Although for the sense it has very little importance.

<margin>11</margin> **For you shall not commit adultery]** Just as before, so here too he did not render the force of the Greek article, *τὸ οὐ μοιχεύσεις* <note>the [commandment] "you shall not commit adultery"</note>, which we would have expressed as: "except this, that you love one another, And, The [saying], 'You shall not commit adultery'." For those [commandments], "You shall not commit adultery," and so on.

<margin>12</margin> **In this word it is restored** <note>original: *ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται / anakephalaioutai*</note>, that is, it is recapitulated, that is, it is contained summarily in this word. Augustine in a certain Letter translates it as *recapitulated*. It is taken from the Epilogues of Rhetoricians, in which the whole case is repeated summarily, which they call an <term>anakephalaiosis</term> <note>a summary or gathering together</note>. For "restored" <note>Latin: *instauratur*</note> means it is replaced according to the pattern of the former ones: so we say a collapsed building is "restored." For Ambrose reads *is consummated*. We more likely say *summarily comprehended*: doubting whether *recapitulari* <note>to recapitulate</note> is found among the Latins; he certainly found it by choice. Chrysostom noted the property of this word: he did not say *πληροῦται* <note>is fulfilled</note>, that is, it is filled up: but *ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται*: to express compendium and brevity.

<margin>13</margin> **Love of neighbor]** <note>original: *τῷ πλησίον / to plesion*</note>, that is, "to the neighbor," in the dative case, so that it refers to the verb *works*. For he confirms with a reason what he had said: that the Epilogue, that is, the compendium of the whole Law, is in charity. The Law with various mandates deters from harming a neighbor: "You shall not swear falsely, You shall not steal, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not speak false testimony, You shall not kill," and what not? But he who is endowed with Christian charity harms no mortal at all; he benefits everyone he can, both the good and the bad. Even if the other reading, "the neighbor" <note>in the dative case</note>, is sound; as Chrysostom reads, and also Theophylact, however the Translator treated it.

<margin>14</margin> **And knowing this time]** This pronoun among the Greeks does not refer to "time," since time for them is of the masculine gender. Rather, he speaks thus: *And this, or even when we know it, namely that it is the season*. So that "And this" has the force of emphasizing, as when we say, "You are a fornicator, and that in Lent": so that we understand that what he commanded is now especially to be performed in the Gospel Law, which requires something more above the Law of Moses and nature. *Time* in this place signifies opportunity and occasion <note>original: *καιρὸν / kairon*</note>, for which they used *hour* <note>original: *ὥρα / hora*</note>. An hour is part of a day, whence that saying, "And it changes by the hours." An hour is part of a year, like winter,
<meta>catchword: spring,</meta>

The commentary highlights the rhetorical structure of Paul's writing and distinguishes between simple obedience and structural subjection.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final verses of Romans 13 and the opening of Romans 14. Having established the believer’s duty to the state and the law of love, the author now focuses on the urgency of the Christian life—moving from the "night" of ignorance to the "day" of the Gospel—and how to treat those who are "weak in faith" regarding dietary laws.</meta>

TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER XIV.

**Column 1:**

> ...that we should already be awakened from sleep; for now our salvation is nearer than when we first believed.
> <margin>12</margin> The night is far spent, and the day is at hand; let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armor of light;
> <margin>13</margin> as in the day, let us walk becomingly, not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and wantonness, not in strife and jealousy;
> <margin>14</margin> But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to fulfill its lusts.
> <margin>XIV.</margin> But receive him who is weak in faith...

---

Spring, summer, autumn: each of which has its own actions: as with the same Poet, *And he tempers the world with varying hours.* <note>original: *Variisque mundum temperat horis.*</note> Whence the Greek term *horaios* <note>original: ὡραῖος</note> means *timely*, or *beautiful*: and *horais* refers to that which has already flowed past. Thus all of time is distinguished by its own specific hours: there was an hour before the Law, an hour under the Law, and an hour under the Gospel. The Gentiles lived in darkness, the Jews in shadows, and sleep was ignored. But as soon as the clearest light of the Gospel shone forth, it became shameful for anyone to remain asleep.

**11 To rise from sleep]** <note>original: *De somno surgere*</note> In Greek: *to be awakened from sleep.* <note>original: ἐξ ὕπνου ἐγερθῆναι.</note> The word *Egeiresthai* <note>original: Ἐγείρεσθαι</note> is used for one who was lying down or sitting; it refers to a structure that rises upward; *existasthai* refers to one who is standing up. In Genesis 49: *He rose up like a lion.* <note>original: Ἡγέρθη ὡς λέων.</note> Pharaoh was also "awakened." Regarding the temple of his body, the Lord said in the Gospel of John, "I will raise it up" <note>original: ἐγερῶ</note>; and in Isaiah 26, *Awake and sing*: the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translated this as *they shall be raised*, changing the tense and person. In Ephesians 5, *Awake, O sleeper* <note>original: Ἔγειραι ὁ καθεύδων</note> and *rise from the dead* <note>original: ἀνάστα</note>, which is a word with two meanings, much like *egeiresthai*. However, to signify the ending of sleep, the proper words are *egregorsis* (vigilance) and *exypnistheis* (having been woken up). But the Apostle calls a life spent in vice "sleep," as in 1 Thessalonians 5, offering a thought similar to this passage: *For you are all children of light and children of the day; we are not of the night or of the darkness. Therefore let us not sleep as others do, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night.* Looking to this, he translates "to wake up" instead of "to rise": and if there is any emphasis in "rising," the same remains in "waking up." For it is said that one is *experrectus* (awakened), as if "thoroughly set right" from sleep. If anyone thinks this passage pertains to the resurrection of the dead (who are said to "sleep" by the Apostle), the word "awaken" fits beautifully. It is trivial for some to argue about rising for good works and that those who have awakened fall back asleep. For even those who have risen return to their beds, and some rise while still drowsy. Therefore one is stirred from sleep so that we may truly rise.

**11 For now it is nearer]** <note>original: *Nunc enim propior est*</note> In Greek: *nearer to us.* <note>original: ἐγγύτερον ἡμῶν.</note> That is, it is closer to us, or it is less distant from us, so that "nearer" acts as an adverb and takes the case of the preposition from which it flowed. For the Greeks say *engys sou* <note>original: ἐγγὺς σοῦ</note>, that is, *near you.* Consequently, the comparative "nearer" <note>original: ἐγγύτερον</note> can take a double genitive case, one from the root and one from the comparison. This "of us" <note>original: ἡμῶν</note> is not the comparison, but the root. Just as in an old Latin phrase, if you say, "I am more abundant in money than you" <note>original: *Sum abundantior pecuniæ te*</note>: "money" is the root case, "you" is the comparison. Now, our Translator referred the genitive "of us" to "salvation," whereas it belongs to "nearer." For he means that the faith of the Gospel is closer now than it was then, when they trusted in philosophy and the works of the Law. Otherwise, if he had meant "our salvation," he would have said *our salvation* <note>original: ἡ σωτηρία ἡμῶν</note>. Instead, it is *to us, the salvation.* He speaks absolutely of the salvation approaching everyone.

**11 Than when we believed]** <note>original: *Quam quam credidimus*</note> In Greek: *than when we believed.* <note>original: ἢ ὅτε ἐπιστεύσαμεν.</note> Certainly it would be clearer, and in better Latin, to say: *than at the time when we were believing.* Indeed, in the Law of Moses, there was more an *opinion* of salvation than salvation itself—a shadow rather than the thing itself. Hence he calls it "night" while the sun is still far off, which gradually recedes as the light approaches.

**12 The night has passed]** <note>original: *Nox præceſſit*</note> In Greek: *has advanced* <note>original: προέκοψεν</note>, that is, it has gone forward and tends toward its end. This means the night is for the most part finished, and the day is pressing on as the Gospel gradually dawns. Cyprian, in his sermon on jealousy and envy, reads, *The night has passed over.* Origen’s translator in the twenty-fifth Homily reads, *The night has moved forward.* Thus there should be no doubt that through an error of the scribes, "preceded" <note>original: *præcessit*</note> was made out of "proceeded" <note>original: *processit*</note>. Chrysostom clearly interprets this as the coming night: *The day,* he says, *approaches.* Therefore, he says, if the night is ending and this day is approaching, let us perform the things that belong to the latter, not the former, just as is done in worldly matters. For when we see the night hastening toward the dawn and hear the swallow singing, we each rouse one another, even if it is still night. Furthermore, once the night has gone, we hasten to say to one another, *It is day*, and we do all things that belong to the day, dressing ourselves and casting aside dreams, shaking off sleep so that the day finds us prepared. Theophylact also says clearly, imagining for example's sake a night of twelve hours: after ten have passed, we say, *The night has advanced* <note>original: Ἡ νὺξ προέκοψεν</note>, that is, *it is near the end.* Nor would it be absurd for those who say the night has "passed" to speak thus, but that is not what *proekopsen* <note>the Greek verb</note> sounds like, a word that is consistently found in the Greek manuscripts. Finally, the verb "to precede" does not fit what follows: *the day approaches.* For once the night is finished, the day is no longer imminent—it is already day, and it is too late to wake men from sleep. It is not hidden from me that all interpret this passage as referring to the resurrection. If we accept that interpretation, the night has not entirely passed, nor is the day fully here; rather, we are in a kind of dawn of hope, awaiting the day of resurrection as something imminent. There is no doubt that "preceded" was corrupted by scribes from "proceeded," as they did not realize that "to proceed" does not always mean to go out in public, but sometimes to have made progress or to have advanced. They could have learned this from the first chapter of Luke, who writes that Zechariah and Elizabeth had "proceeded in their days," meaning they were advanced in age, though their life had not yet passed away but was nearing its end.

**12 Has approached]** <note>original: *Appropinquavit*</note> In Greek: *has drawn near.* <note>original: ἤγγικεν.</note> It is indeed in the past tense, but in Latin it is more properly rendered by a verb in the present tense...

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

> <margin>11</margin> ...it is time to awaken from sleep: <gloss>16</gloss> for now salvation is nearer <gloss>17</gloss> to us than when we believed. <gloss>18</gloss> The night <margin>12</margin> has <gloss>19</gloss> advanced, and the day approaches: let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us walk <gloss>20</gloss> becomingly as in the day, <gloss>21</gloss> not in <margin>13</margin> revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and wantonness, not in strife and jealousy. But put on the <margin>14</margin> Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh <gloss>22</gloss> to fulfill its lusts. Furthermore, <gloss>1</gloss> him who is weak in faith <gloss>2</gloss> <margin>XIV.</margin> accept...

---

<margin>A</margin> ...with the sense intact: "it approaches" or "it is nearby." I see that in many manuscripts it has been corrupted to "it will approach" <note>original: *appropinquabit*</note>. For he feels that the day of Christ's coming is already imminent, and the night of former ignorance is already tending toward its end.

<margin>B</margin> **20 Let us walk honestly]** <note>original: *Honeste ambulemus*</note> In Greek: *euschēmonōs* <note>original: εὐσχημόνως</note>, that is, in an orderly or modest fashion. Cyprian, in the place we just cited, translates it as "decently." For when the light has risen, people behave more bashfully out of shame and adapt their behavior to the judgment of others; for shame soon takes hold.

**21 Not in revelries]** <note>original: *Non in comessationibus*</note> In Greek the preposition "in" is absent: *not revelries* <note>original: μὴ κώμοις</note>; although the addition is not entirely displeasing. Among the Greeks, *Komos* <note>original: Κῶμος</note> is the God of drunkenness, and they use the same name for a bold and youthful banquet. Furthermore, the Greeks call wanton songs and dances *komoi*: which is where the word "comedy" comes from. And those who, crowned and well-drunk, burst into someone else's banquet (not without a flute player) are said "to revel" <note>original: κωμάζειν</note>; just as in Plato, Alcibiades bursts into Agathon's banquet. Athenaeus declares in several places that this was a custom among the Greeks.

<margin>C</margin> **22 In desires]** <note>original: *In desideriis*</note> In Greek: *unto lusts* <note>original: εἰς ἐπιθυμίας</note>; that is, for necessity, not for pleasure. For "care," he translates *pronoian* <note>original: πρόνοιαν</note>, that is, "providence" or "foresight": for this is how Origen reads it in his ninth Homily on Exodus. Likewise, Augustine, citing this passage in the fourth book of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter twenty: although he admits the rest of the speech is rhythmic and musical, he is offended by something in the final clause: *and do not make provision for the flesh in its desires.* For he would prefer this arrangement: *and for the flesh, providence in its desires do not make.* Let them go now and condemn my "melody-making" in the Holy Scriptures, when such tiny details were a concern for so great a Bishop! And yet, I cannot guess what it is that offended Augustine. Furthermore, "in lusts" is placed at the end not only to agree with the order of the Greek language, but also because it strikes the ears more forcefully there. For he does not forbid having care for the flesh; therefore he, as it were,

<margin>D</margin> inserts: "in lusts." Among the Greeks, the first part, *and for the flesh, providence* <note>original: καὶ τῆς σαρκὸς πρόνοιαν</note>, according to the system of accents (which we look at more in composition), is a "trochaic dimeter catalectic" <note>A specific poetic rhythm.</note>; the latter part is a "trochaic trimeter brachycatalectic." Augustine actually cites this passage as an example of the "moderate style," which he thinks is suitable for exhortation. Although many other beauties are present, such as "antithesis" and "rhyme" <note>original: *homoioteleuton*</note> in those words: *The night has preceded, the day has approached.* Likewise there is "exchange" <note>original: *enallagē*</note> in casting off and putting on, in light and darkness. To these is added a metaphor in the single phrase "armor of light." Again, a comparison: "as in the day." But the sound of the Greek words is more pleasant: *apothōmetha, endysōmetha, kōmois, phōtos.* In the verbs, there is full rhyme; in the nouns, there is partial "similarity of case" <note>original: *homoioptōton*</note>, whereas in our Latin there is none at all. There is also a grace of "misuse" <note>original: *katachrēseōs*</note> in the words "becomingly" and "let us walk." For neither is used in its strictly literal sense. I will say nothing for now of the elegance of the members, the articles, and the comparatives, which is nevertheless more evident in the things that follow. Although this entire speech can be seen as an allegory: *The night has preceded, the day has approached, let us cast off the works of darkness*, so that we may walk honestly as in the day. For no word here is used in its literal sense.

<margin>E</margin> There is a rhythmic modulation and a more musical flow in those words: *not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and impurities, not in strife and jealousy.* Each member is joined by a pair of related words, so that the translation might seem like a formal "schema"; nor is the repetition of the same word at the beginning of the members without grace. Add to these the almost equal length of the clauses and phrases, and then the similarity of case endings. Even if these do not always correspond in the Greek: for in *kōmois* and *methais* the count is equal, but the similarity of case is not as full as in the Latin. Again, in "contention and jealousy," we have similar case endings, but the Greeks by no means do: *eridi kai zēlō* <note>original: ἔριδι καὶ ζήλῳ</note>. In short, the rhetorical figures that rely on specific words do not always match the Greek reading. But those that rely on the *ideas* are common to all languages.

<margin>F</margin> **1 But the weak one]** <note>original: *Infirmum autem*</note> In Greek: *the one who is weak* <note>original: Τὸν δὲ ἀσθενοῦντα</note>. And it is not "in the faith," but "by faith," so that it refers back to the participle "weak," not to the following verb: "You who are stronger, receive him who is not yet firm in his faith." He calls the Jews "the weak," as they could not yet despise the choice of foods; and yet he turns his speech to the "firm" ones, so that he might more easily heal the feeble. So says Chrysostom.

**2 Receive]** <note>original: *Assumite*</note> In Greek: *proslambanesthe* <note>original: προσλαμβάνεσθε</note>, that is, join to yourselves, and receive into your fellowship. He who does not yet believe perfectly is not to be rejected (lest a smoking flax be extinguished), but is to be tolerated and nourished until he makes progress toward better things. It should be noted in passing that Paul attributes the abstinence from foods to a weakness of faith. He is not speaking of those who, having a more disciplined body, abstain from richer foods, but of those who, in the Jewish manner, avoid certain foods. And yet he wants these people to be tolerated, but with this hope: that they might grow in faith and come to neglect such ceremonies. But today we see Christians who are almost more superstitious in the choice of foods than was ever the case among the Jews. Nor are such things tolerated now; rather, they establish a kind of absolute piety in them. We fight for them with every kind of weapon; by these things we judge and turn away from others...

It also begins exploring Romans 14, where Paul counsels the "strong" in faith to patiently receive the "weak" (specifically Jews adhering to dietary laws), a point the author uses to critique modern Christian superstitions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the fourteenth chapter of the Epistle to the Romans. The author is meticulously comparing the Greek source text with the standard Latin Vulgate, focusing on the treatment of the "weak in faith"—specifically those who still adhered to Jewish dietary laws and sabbaths—and urging mutual tolerance among early Christians.</meta>

# EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER XIV.

<margin>2</margin> ...is weak, let him not be brought into disputes over his thoughts. * One believes he may eat all things; but he who is weak eats vegetables. <margin>3</margin> Let not him who eats despise him who does not eat; and let not him who does not eat judge him who eats; for God <margin>4</margin> has received him. Who are you to judge another’s servant? To his own master he stands or falls; but he shall stand, for God is able to make him <margin>5</margin> stand. * One man judges one day above another, while another judges every day alike; let each be fully convinced in his own mind. <margin>6</margin> He who observes the day, observes it for the Lord; and he who does not observe the day, does not observe it for the Lord. He who eats, eats for the Lord, for he gives thanks to God; and he who does not eat, does not eat for the Lord, and gives thanks to <margin>7</margin> God. For none of us lives to himself, and no one <margin>8</margin> dies to himself. For if we live, we live for the Lord; and if we die, we die for the Lord. Whether we live, therefore, or die, <margin>9</margin> we are the Lord’s. For to this end Christ both died and [rose...] <note>The Greek text ends abruptly at the word 'died' (apethane) due to the page break.</note>

---

<margin>a</margin>
We curse and execrate our neighbor as if they were barely a Christian; because of these outward things, we most foolishly please ourselves, while otherwise being infected with the most foul diseases of the soul: pride, anger, envy, and self-love.

<margin>3</margin>
**Not in disputes over thoughts**] <note>original: *μὴ εἰς διακρίσεις διαλογισμῶν* (mē eis diakriseis dialogismōn)</note> that is, not for the purpose of judging disputes. This means one should not engage in helpful disputes that might alienate the person who should instead be cherished with gentleness until they progress to more perfect things. Most writers apply this to the Gentiles; it seems to me to apply to both groups, so that we understand it refers to the mutual disputes that arise from distinctions between foods. Indeed, as Paul declares elsewhere, both groups were judging the others: those who ate called the abstinence of others "superstition," while those who did not eat judged those who did, as if they were using forbidden things. He does not want this kind of frivolous dispute to exist among Christians, but wants both to yield to the other for the sake of maintaining concord. It is strange, however, why the Translator preferred "thoughts" <note>original: *cogitationum*</note> rather than "discussions" <note>original: *disceptationum*</note>, unless perhaps he did not read *dialogismōn* (discussions) but *logismōn* (reasonings). Among the Greeks, *dialogismos* sometimes denotes an empty verbal contest over worthless matters. A thought can belong to one person; a dispute involves many. For they were judging one another; it does not matter whether they did so in silent thought or in speech. I will add this: "judgments of thoughts" is not phrased so that you understand the thoughts themselves are judged, but rather as an appositive, so you understand the judgments *are* the thoughts—as if he had said "silent judgments."

<margin>4</margin>
**To eat all things**] <note>original: *φαγεῖν καὶ ἐσθίειν* (phagein kai esthiein)</note> which both mean to eat or feed; here he constantly translates them as "manducare" <note>to chew/eat</note>, although "mandere" or "manducare" properly means to crush food with the teeth. Furthermore, he would have translated "all things" <note>original: *πάντα* (panta)</note> more significantly as "anything whatsoever," that is, any food without selection. For this is also what *pas* means. For who alone could eat "everything"? One minor point: "he believes to eat" <note>original: *credis manducare*</note> is a figure of speech new to both Greeks and Latins. To the Greeks, it sounds like "he thinks he eats all things," while the sense is: "He believes it is permitted for him to feed on any foods without distinction." Hence, it would have been more correct to translate the infinitive as a gerund: "he believes that he should feed on anything."

<margin>5</margin>
**But he who is weak**] <note>original: *ὁ δὲ ἀσθενῶν λάχανα ἐσθίει* (ho de asthenōn lachana esthiei)</note> that is, "but he who is weak eats vegetables." This is in the indicative mood, not the imperative. Jerome cites these exact words in his commentary on the second chapter of Ecclesiastes: For he does not command that he should eat vegetables—you would prefer him to be stronger and eat anything—but he shows what the weak do who comply with superstition. For when he says "weak," it is not to be referred to the health of the body, but to the superstition of the soul; this is why the Latins also call it "infirmity." Horace says in his *Satires*: "But I am a little weaker," <note>original: *At sum mi paulo infirmior*</note> meaning more superstitious. Chrysostom reads *esthiei*, "he eats," and thus interprets it, saying this happened because they eventually abstained from meat entirely so that it might look more like a fast rather than an observation of the Mosaic Law. There is no word in his commentaries that suggests this was commanded by Paul. Theophylactus agrees with Chrysostom in all points, relating the same opinion in almost the same words. Origen indicates nothing else; nor does Ambrose seem to have read anything else, though his commentary appears corrupted. He says: "He, however, who is weak, let him eat vegetables." Then, because he thinks this, namely that he should eat vegetables, he must be persuaded to eat meat. I think it should be read: "Therefore, because he thinks this, that he should eat vegetables, he must *not* be persuaded to eat meat." And it is true that "let him eat" <note>original: *edat*</note> can be taken as a permission, not a command; but the consistent reading and interpretation of the Greek manuscripts stand against this. Thus, it is probable that wherever "let him eat" <note>original: *manducet*</note> is read, either the reading is corrupted, or the interpreter did not consult the Greek. A similar comment is added in the Latin scholia, but it had previously indicated it should be read in the indicative. In some Greek copies, it was written *hos de asthenōn* <note>the one who is weak</note>. Paul often uses the postpositive article in place of the prepositive in such cases. It should have been translated: "One believes he should feed on all things, or anything; another again, who is weak, eats vegetables." Otherwise, the "one" <note>original: *alius*</note> that precedes in the first part of the division has nothing to correspond to it.

<margin>6</margin>
**Let him not despise**] <note>original: *ἐξουθενείτω* (exoutheneitō)</note> as if you were to say, "let him treat as nothing" or "consider of no value," as the Greek word is composed from the word for "nothing."

<margin>7</margin>
**To his own master he stands or falls**] "He will stand, however" <note>original: *σταθήσεται δέ*</note>. Cyprian, quoting this in the second letter of his fourth book, not unskillfully translates the next verb *stēsai* as "to make firm" or "to stabilize"; yet it means the same as the above: "for God is powerful to stabilize him."

<margin>8</margin>
**For one man judges**] <note>original: *Ὃς μὲν κρίνει ἡμέραν παρ' ἡμέραν· ὃς δὲ κρίνει πᾶσαν ἡμέραν· ἕκαστος &c.*</note> That is, some indeed judge

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
Receive him, and not for the purpose of judging disputes.
One indeed believes <term>vescendum esse quibuslibet</term> <note>that he should feed on anything whatsoever</note>: and another, however, who is weak, eats vegetables. He who feeds, let him not despise the one not feeding: and he who does not feed, let him not judge the one feeding: for God has received him. Who are you who judges another's servant? To his own master he stands, or falls, indeed he shall be propped up so that he stands: for God is powerful to make him stand. * This one indeed judges, comparing day to day; that one, however, judges the same concerning any day: * let each one’s own mind satisfy him. He who cares for the day, cares for the Lord: and he who does not care for the day, does not care for the Lord: he who feeds, feeds for the Lord, for he gives thanks to God: * and he who does not feed, does not feed for the Lord, and gives thanks to God. For none of us lives to himself, and none to himself dies. For whether we live, we live for the Lord, or whether we die, we die for the Lord: whether therefore we live, or whether we die, we are the Lord's. For in this Christ both [died...]

---

<margin>B</margin>
"day alongside day": but he judges every day: each one, etc. If it were permitted to render the sense in good faith while ignoring the superstition of words, it could be translated this way: "This man indeed thinks there is some difference between one day and another; but that man feels the same way about any day." Augustine, in his *Questions* on this Epistle, reads: "One indeed judges alternate days: but another judges every day." But I am ashamed of the commentary he adds in that same place, which he would never have written if he had either consulted the Greek or if a better translation had been available. I will transcribe his words, so no one distrusts me: "Setting aside for now," he says, "a better consideration, this does not seem to me to be said about human use of days, but about man and God. For he who judges alternate days is good: for he can judge one thing today and another tomorrow: that is, so that whomever he condemned today as evil, convicted and having confessed, he may find corrected tomorrow. But he who judges every day is God: because He knows what each person is. Let each one abound in his own understanding, he says: that is, let him dare to judge only as much as is granted to human understanding, or to each individual man. He who is wise regarding the day, he says, is wise for the Lord: that is, because he judges well regarding this present day, he is wise for the Lord. This, however, is to judge well for the day: that you know one must not despair of the future correction of a person whose manifest fault you have judged in the present." So far Augustine. I ask you, Reader, does he not seem to be living in another world when he writes these things? I would not want anyone to take this <margin>D</margin> as an insult to Augustine’s words—we admire his learning and venerate his holiness—but so that the lapse of such a great man may persuade us that the comparison of Greek volumes must not be neglected. Saint Jerome, in his second book against Jovinian, translates this passage in this way: "One judges a day more than a day: so that *para* <note>original: παρὰ</note> is taken for 'above' or 'beyond,' as is found several times among the Greeks." Although to the Greeks, *para* sometimes has a relational sense, as in their proverb: "Purple beside purple" <note>original: *Τί πορφύραν παρὰ πορφύραν* (Ti porphyran para porphyran)</note>. For he who compares thinks one is better than the other. To the Jews, one day was profane, another holy. But to Christians, any day is equally holy: not that feast days should not be observed—which the holy Fathers later instituted so that the Christian common people might more conveniently gather for the church assembly and divine worship—but only a few of them, namely the Lord’s Day, Easter, Pentecost, and several of this sort, which Jerome lists. Truly, I do not know if it is expedient to pile feasts upon feasts for any reasons whatsoever, <margin>E</margin> especially when we see that the customs of Christians have reached a point where, just as it was once conducive to piety to institute these things, it now seems equally beneficial to abolish them.

<margin>9</margin>
**In his own sense**] <note>original: *ἰδίῳ νοῒ πληροφορείσθω* (idiō noi plērophoreisthō)</note> that is, in his own mind or soul let him be certain, or let him have a certain persuasion; that is, let him rest in his own opinion. Ambrose interprets it as: "let each one be left to his own counsel." What Augustine interprets, we have just shown. Otherwise, "to abound in one's own sense" describes a headstrong person of obstinate mind.

<margin>10</margin>
**And he who does not eat, for the Lord he does not eat**] The Greeks add: "and he who does not regard the day, for the Lord he does not regard it" <note>original: *καὶ ὁ μὴ φρονῶν τὴν ἡμέραν, Κυρίῳ οὐ φρονεῖ*</note>. Then follows, "and he who eats, for the Lord he eats: for he gives thanks," and so on. Otherwise, there is nothing provided to contrast with the first part, "He who regards the day, for the Lord he regards it." Certainly, this clause is added in Theophylactus. But since there is great agreement among our [Latin] codices, and it is found <margin>F</margin> neither in Ambrose nor in Origen, it is possible that someone supplied from their own mind what was missing in Paul. And I do not know if "giving thanks" can be referred to the one who distinguishes the day. For he who eats and he who does not eat, both nevertheless consume food, and for their eating, though different, they equally give thanks. It should also be noted that Paul presents these parts of the "strong" and the "weak" in varying order: when he first says, "One believes he eats all things, but he who is weak eats vegetables," he put the strong first and the weak second. But soon he repeats it in the same order: "therefore he who eats, let him not despise the one not eating. He who does not eat, let him not judge the one eating." And a little later he inverts the order: "For one man judges a day among days, but another man judges every day"; here he put the weak man's part in the first place. Moreover, in the things that follow, he again inverts the order: for when he says, "He who regards the day, for the Lord he regards it," he put the weak man's part first. For "to regard" in this place is to care for and perceive a distinction between one day and another, which is a matter of Jewish superstition. And "not to regard" is to not care about the distinction of the day. And soon: "He who eats, for the Lord he eats: and he who does not eat, for the Lord he does not eat": which...
