# TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER XIV.

...died, and rose, and lived again, so that he might rule over both the dead and the living. <margin>10</margin> But why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ. <margin>11</margin> For it is written: As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God. <margin>12</margin> So then each of us shall give an account of himself to God. <margin>13</margin> Therefore let us no longer judge one another; but rather judge this: not to put a stumbling block or an occasion to fall in a brother's way. <margin>14</margin> I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, except to him who considers anything to be unclean; to him it is unclean. <margin>15</margin> But if your brother is grieved because of food, you are no longer walking according to love. Do not destroy with your food him for whom Christ died. <margin>16</margin> Therefore do not let your good be spoken of as evil. <margin>17</margin> For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. <margin>18</margin> For he who serves Christ in these things is acceptable to God and approved by men.

---

[The commentator] placed the stronger person first, and made the weaker person's position second. Unless one prefers to interpret "observing the day" in a different sense. Certainly Thomas Aquinas explains it so that he who "observes the day" is said to be the one who distinguishes between one day and another, even if he twists this to refer to our feast days and fast days, which he considers praiseworthy. If that interpretation were true, it would not be a sign of weakness to judge between one day and another, but of perfect piety; and to judge every day as the same would not be a sign of firm faith, but of impiety. Ambrose also twists this passage in some way, offering this as a commentary: *It is true, because he who always abstains thinks he is pleasing God; to always abstain is more perfect than to abstain sometimes and not others. But if he who judges every day always abstains, and yet he was previously considered weaker than the one who does not eat, how is he now, in turn, the stronger one, when he was previously held to be weaker?* 

But what Paul said regarding the choice of foods according to Jewish custom, and likewise the choice of days according to their rites, Ambrose and Thomas have deflected toward later times, in which feast days and specific fasts were ordained by Bishops—though fewer than we have now—none of which I believe existed yet in Paul’s age; I am speaking of those publicly decreed. Origen interprets <term>sapere diem</term> <note>original: "observing/valuing the day"</note> as the one who does not distinguish one day from another, linking the one who eats everything with the one who values every day equally. From this, it occurs to me that this phrase can refer to both: the one who distinguishes and the one who does not. Indeed, he who values the day—meaning he who feels the same about any given day—and he who values the day—meaning he who feels differently about one day versus another—has encompassed both parties in a general statement. He who values the day, whether he does it one way or the other, does so for his Lord, not for you, to whom it does not pertain. And this appears to be the reason why no contrary part was provided here, whereas "not eating" was opposed to "eating": certainly Chrysostom does not even touch upon this phrase in his narration. 

In this passage, we preferred to translate as *feeds upon* and *does not feed upon* <note>Latin: "vescitur" and "non vescitur"</note>: because he is not simply talking about eating or not eating, but about the *type* of food: that is, pork or meat sacrificed to idols. Furthermore, whenever we speak of a type of food, it is more elegant to use *vesci* <note>to feed/consume</note> than *edere* <note>to eat</note>. Additionally, instead of "values" <note>Latin: sapit</note>, we preferred "regards" <note>Latin: curat</note>, because the word <term>phronein</term> (φρονεῖν) among the Greeks is <term>polysemon</term> <note>has many meanings</note>; sometimes it is used for "to feel," sometimes "to know," sometimes "to think," and occasionally for "to be disposed toward." Sometimes the Latin language can hardly render what it intends with seriousness.

<margin>11 Died and rose again]</margin> Here the Greek codices add, <term>kai anezēsen</term> (καὶ ἀνέζησεν), that is, *and lived again*. Although Theophylact reads <term>ezēsen</term> (ἔζησεν), that is, *lived*, not *lived again*. If we follow this, the past tense should be understood as the present, as often happens with such words: in this he died, in this he rose, and in this he now lives, and so forth. Ambrose reads and interprets it thus: *For in this Christ both lived and died and rose again.* In the Pauline codex, which was worth many to me when I first edited these things, it was written in this manner: <term>For in this Christ both died and lived again</term>, and so on: certainly agreeing with the Greek copies in that it doubles the conjunction. That Origen read it this way is shown by his own interpretation, which begins: *He says Christ died by the dispensation of the passion, but lived through the mystery of the resurrection.* 

And this reading corresponds to what follows: <term>that he might be Lord of the dead and the living</term>. For this is the order read both among the Greeks and in Origen, who is indifferent to these words: *But perhaps it might move someone that the Apostle said he died and lived for this reason, to rule over the dead and the living: as if he meant that if he had not died, and if he had not lived again after death, he would not have held lordship over the living.* The order is the same in Ambrose, and the same in the very ancient manuscript I just cited: so that the dead precede and the living follow: for dying comes first, and living second—especially in Christ, regarding his human nature which was mortal. And yet in the previous verses, the living preceded: *Whether we live, we live to the Lord; whether we die, we die to the Lord.* In Chrysostom, it is only <term>apethanen, ezēsen</term> <note>died, lived</note>. Although the Verona Edition has three: <term>apethanen, anestē, ezēsen</term> <note>died, rose, lived</note>. That middle one, <term>anestē</term> <note>rose</note>, seems to have been added, because near the end of this commentary he speaks of <term>nekrōn kai zōntōn</term> <note>of the dead and of the living</note>. The Aldine Edition agrees with the Verona. Truly, I dwell on these things too much, since they contribute nothing or very little to the sense.

<margin>12 Or why do you despise]</margin> <term>ē kai sy ti exoutheneis</term> (ἢ καὶ σὺ τί ἐξουθενεῖς), that is, *or even you, why do you look down upon...*: so that the first "you" refers to the one not eating,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>9</margin> and died, and rose, and lived again, that he might rule over the dead and the living. But why do you judge your brother? <margin>10</margin> Or even you, why do you despise your brother? <margin>10</margin> For we shall all be stood before the judgment seat of Christ. For it is written: I live, says the Lord, <margin>11</margin> every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God. Therefore each one of us shall give an account of himself to God. Let us therefore no longer judge one another: <margin>13</margin> but judge this instead, that no stumbling block be placed before a brother, or an occasion for a fall. <margin>14</margin> For I know and am persuaded through the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, except to him who thinks something is unclean; to him it is unclean. But if <margin>15</margin> because of food your brother is grieved, you are no longer walking according to love: do not destroy him with your food, for whom Christ died. <margin>16</margin> Therefore do not let your good be subject to the slander of men. For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, <margin>17</margin> but justice, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. <margin>18</margin> For he who through these things serves Christ is accepted by God and approved by men.

---

and the second to the one eating: so that the conjunction <term>kai</term> <note>and/also</note> is not idle. For the one who does not eat judges the one eating out of superstition. Conversely, the one eating, out of knowledge, despises the weakness of the one not eating. Ambrose, adding a few words, reads it thus: *But you, why do you judge your brother for not eating? Or you, why do you despise your brother for eating?* Although I think he added "for eating" and "for not eating" on his own to explain the matter.

<margin>C</margin> <margin>13 For we shall all stand]</margin> <term>pantes gar parastēsometha tō bēmati tou Christou</term>. That is, *for we shall all be presented, or are to be presented, at the judgment seat of Christ.* For defendants, or those to be judged, are said to be "presented" for judgment when they are compelled to be present.

<margin>14 To me shall be bowed]</margin> <term>emoi kampsei</term>, that is, *to me shall bow: understanding 'itself' as the subject, every knee.* Certainly, in one or two very ancient manuscripts, we find it written as *shall bow*, not *shall be bowed*. The testimony exists in Isaiah, chapter forty-six, which Paul cited in such a way that it corresponds neither word-for-word to the Hebrew truth nor to the Septuagint Edition. Indeed, according to the latter, we read: *I swear by myself, unless justice goes out of my mouth, my words shall not be turned away, because every knee shall bend to me: and every tongue shall swear and confess, saying...* According to the Hebrew, Jerome translates it: *I have sworn in myself, the word of justice shall go out of my mouth and shall not return, because every knee shall be curved to me, and every tongue shall swear and confess to God.*

<margin>D</margin> <margin>15 But judge this rather]</margin> Ambrose reads, *and in this or regarding this judge more:* I know not which manuscript he followed. For both the Greek codices and our ancient ones disagree. Jerome, or whoever was the translator of Origen, indicates in the commentary that "judge" is used here not for condemnation, as before, but for a "decree" or "statute." For using "judgment" to mean "condemnation" is peculiar to the Hebrews. Among the Greeks, the word <term>krisis</term> (κρίσις) is <term>mesē</term> <note>neutral/middle</note>, which sometimes sounds like "to judge," and sometimes "to establish" or "to decree." But if anyone prefers the word "judge" to be taken as it was in the other instances, the sense could also be this: It is not fitting that any of you judge another, who, whether he acts rightly or otherwise, is reserved to be judged by his own Lord; but if anything is to be judged about anyone, he is rather to be judged who, for the sake of bodily food, refuses to avoid offending a brother, since he who even suspects that the other does not eat with a sincere conscience, or is provoked by his example to do that which he thinks is not done rightly.

<margin>16 I know and am confident]</margin> <term>oida kai pepeismai</term>, that is, *I know and am certain, or am persuaded.*

<margin>17 Nothing is common through itself]</margin> The translator seems to have read <term>di' autou</term> with a smooth breathing <note>referring to Christ</note>. And Ambrose reads it this way, interpreting that through the benefit of Christ nothing is unclean. But it is more correct as it is held, <term>di' hautou</term>, with the aspirated breathing, or <term>di' heautou</term>, that is, *through itself, or of itself:* because it follows, *but to him who considers it unclean, it is unclean.* Origen reads it this way, and Chrysostom and Theophylact agree with him, interpreting <term>di' hautou</term> as <term>tē physei</term>, that is, *by nature*.

<margin>18 Is grieved]</margin> <term>lypeitai</term>, that is, *grieves, or is affected by distress.*

<margin>19 Therefore let not your good be blasphemed]</margin> *Your* in the Greek is the second person plural, <term>hymōn to agathon</term>, that is, *your [plural] good.* Care must be taken so that what you do rightly does not provide someone with material for mocking. Or, "your good" refers to your correct opinion, by which you feel it is permissible to eat anything. Theophylact explains it in that way. Chrysostom likewise reads <term>hymōn</term>, interpreting it as the "concord of Christians." This phrasing seems similar to that: *your good order*; although it is more commonly said, *our good things*. But here <margin>F</margin> he calls it "good," not because it is simply good, but because it is good for the one who does it with a good intention: and for that reason, he distinguished it with an article. Although I won't fight over it if someone argues the form of speech is exactly the same.

<margin>20 Justice, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit]</margin> And here the preposition is used in the Hebrew manner for <term>dia</term>, that is, *through*: which Origen sufficiently indicates when discussing this passage. He opposes the Holy Spirit to the dispute about foods: the latter breeds anger, sadness, and injustice; the former [the Spirit] brings peace instead of anger, joy instead of sadness, and justice instead of offense and injury.

<margin>21 For he who in this serves Christ]</margin> The Greeks read "in these things" <note>plural</note>: which has the same power as if he had said, "through these things." <term>Ho gar en toutois douleuōn</term>. He referred to the feminine nouns <note>justice, peace, joy</note> using a neuter plural pronoun, so that you might simultaneously understand other things of the same kind.

# EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER XV.

<margin>A</margin> 19 to men. Therefore let us pursue the things of peace, and 
20 the things of building up one another. Do not, for the sake of 
food, destroy the work of God; all things indeed are 
clean, but it is evil for the man who eats through a 
21 stumbling block. It is good not to eat meat, 
nor to drink wine, nor anything in which your brother 
22 stumbles, or is offended, or is weakened. Do you have 
faith? Have it to yourself before God. 
23 Blessed is he who does not judge himself in what he approves. But he who 
doubts, if he eats, is condemned, because it is not from 
faith; and everything that is not from faith is sin. 
<margin>B</margin> XV. 1 We who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the 
2 weak, and not to please ourselves. For let 
each of us please his neighbor for his good 
3 toward building him up. For even Christ did not please himself, 
but as it is written: The reproaches of those who reproached 
4 you fell upon me. For whatever was written before, 
was written before for our instruction, so that 
through patience and the consolation of the scriptures 
5 we might have hope. Now may the God of patience and 
of

---

22 *And what things are for building up, let us keep for one another]* <note>original: "Et quæ ædificationis sunt, invicem custodiamus"</note> Greek: "and the things of building up toward one another" <note>original: "καὶ τὰ τῆς οἰκοδομῆς τῆς εἰς ἀλλήλους"</note>, that is, things that pertain to mutual building up, and "let us pursue" <note>original: "διώκωμεν"</note> is understood. Furthermore, Paul in his usual manner calls "to build up" to be "to be useful." Although "toward one another" <note>original: "τῆς εἰς ἀλλήλους"</note> does not prevent it from also referring to peace, so that you understand mutual peace and mutual help. Moreover, the word *let us keep* <note>original: "custodiamus"</note>, which I know not who added, is not found in the Greek codices, nor in Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching</note>, nor in Theophylact <note>Theophylact of Ohrid (c. 1055–1107), a Byzantine archbishop and biblical commentator</note>. Nor is it necessary, since *let us pursue* <note>original: "sectemur"</note> preceded it. Nor was it added in the very old Constantinopolitan codex, except that someone had written it between the lines in a barbaric hand.

23 *In which your brother is offended]* <note>original: "In quo frater tuus offenditur"</note> In Greek it is "stumbles" <note>original: "προσκόπτει"</note>, that is, strikes against. And in the codex of Donatianus it was written *offends*, not *is offended*. The very old Constantinopolitan copy agreed. As to the sense, it matters little, except that for the Latins, "is offended" <note>original: "offenditur"</note> refers to one who is provoked to anger: as a King is offended, but he does not "strike against" or trip. But he who, having seen a girl, feels lust, "offends" <note>trips into sin</note>, he is not "offended" <note>angered</note>. Chrysostom and Theophylact, speaking in Greek, correctly explain "stumbles" <note>original: "προσκόπτει"</note> through "is scandalized" <note>original: "σκανδαλίζεται"</note>.

24 *The faith you have]* <note>original: "Tu fidem quam habes"</note> Since the relative pronoun is absent among the Greeks: "You have faith, have it according to yourself" <note>original: "Σὺ πίστιν ἔχεις, κατὰ σαυτὸν ἔχε"</note>, that is, *You have faith, have it in yourself*, or *with yourself alone*. And I found it written así in the Pauline copy—if anyone gives little weight to the Greeks—even though Ambrose <note>Ambrose of Milan (c. 339–397), a prominent Latin doctor of the Church</note>, Chrysostom, and Theophylact agree with the Greeks. And the speech is altogether more vivid with the word *when* omitted. He added *Before God*, suppressing vain glory, which usually accompanies knowledge. Furthermore, Chrysostom indicates that "faith" here is not taken for faith in dogmas, but for the confidence of conscience, which is opposed to weakness and trembling. Some distinguish it thus: *Do you have faith in yourself? Have it before God*. That is harsher.

25 *But he who discerns]* <note>original: "Qui autem discernit"</note> Greek: "But he who wavers" <note>original: "Ὁ δὲ διακρινόμενος"</note>, that is, *but he who hesitates*. Although it is a middle participle, it could be taken as "he who is judged." *And he who is powerful*. This part up to *We ought, however*, some codices do not have at all, and some add it at the end of the Epistle. Chrysostom interprets it at the end. Theophylact interprets it in this place, although he who translated this man into Latin did not translate it here or at the end; which I think happened by chance. He omitted it here to agree with our codices; when he reached the end, he forgot and did not add it. We, since it did not seem to belong to this place, moved it to the end of this Epistle. Marcion <note>A 2nd-century heretic who rejected the Old Testament and believed the God of the New Testament was different from the God of the Law</note> ended the Epistle to the Romans here, claiming the remaining appendix was spurious.

**1** *We who are firmer]* <note>original: "Nos firmiores"</note> Greek: "we who are powerful to bear the weaknesses of the powerless" <note>original: "ἡμεῖς οἱ δυνατοὶ τὰ ἀσθενήματα τῶν ἀδυνάτων βαστάζειν"</note>, that is, *we who are powerful [should] carry the impotence of the weaker*. Laurentius <note>Lorenzo Valla (c. 1407–1457), an Italian humanist who critiqued the Vulgate</note> prefers, *strong, of the weak*. For thus is rendered the figure of opposition and naming <term>schema of opposition and paronomasia: a rhetorical device using contrasting but similar-sounding words</term>, which is in the Greek words. Which would have been equally possible if he had translated it, *firm, of the infirm*, or *valid, of the invalid*. For here, in place of *of the infirm*, Ambrose reads *of the invalid*.

**2** *Each one of us]* <note>original: "Unusquisque nostrum"</note> The Greeks and Latins vary here. Some have, "For each one of us" <note>original: "Ἕκαστος γὰρ ἡμῶν"</note>. Some do not add the conjunction "for" <note>original: "γὰρ"</note>. It is more tolerable that some have "but" <note>original: "δὲ"</note> in place of "for." Some of our [Latin] texts have *of you* instead of *of us*; although in Greek it is "of us" <note>original: "ἡμῶν"</note>, the first person. Nor is "his" added among them: it is only, "let him please the neighbor" <note>original: "τῷ πλησίον ἀρεσκέτω"</note>. Ambrose reads without the pronoun: *and let each one please the neighbor*. Moreover, *please* is placed here for *yield to* or to gratify. For Paul did not please everyone, and yet he says, *Even as I please all men in all things*. But in all things Paul accommodated himself to everyone so that he might win everyone, just as follows,

3 *Christ did not please himself]* Why would Christ, in himself, be displeasing to himself? But in this place *pleases himself* refers to one who serves his own convenience, and as he says, draws profit to himself: people of this kind are called by the Greeks "lovers of self" <note>original: "φίλαυτοι"</note>, not only on account of arrogance, but also

and joy. This is indeed how Theophylact reads and narrates, and Chrysostom reads it no differently, except that in his commentary he does not reveal what he read. But nevertheless, despite the disagreement of Ambrose, and the disagreement of Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253), a prolific early Christian scholar and theologian</note>, who in this refers back to the Holy Spirit, of whom mention was made a little before: as if you were to say, those serve Christ in the flesh who contend about foods; those serve in the spirit who, having despised those things, pursue only those things which are of peace and harmony: the ancient Latin codices also disagreeing.
<margin>C</margin> 4 *But as it is written, the reproaches and the rest]* And this speech is a little incomplete, but the contrary part must be understood: *Christ did not please himself, but displeased himself*, that is, he did not serve his own convenience, but consulted our convenience at his own inconvenience, just as it is written, etc.
<margin>D</margin> 5 *For whatever things were written]* It is not simply "written" <note>original: "scripta"</note> in the Greek, but in both cases "written before" <note>original: "προεγράφη"</note>, that is, *prescribed*, or *written beforehand*. And in that very way Augustine <note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430), a preeminent Latin Father</note> brings up this passage in Epistle 137: *For whatever things were written before, were written so that we might be taught*. Likewise against Faustus in the thirteenth book, the last chapter. For he felt that these things were written before they happened or were made known: and the promise precedes, the reality follows; the Scriptures promise what is later exhibited. Chrysostom and Theophylact agree in this reading. He used the same word in the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter three: *Before whose eyes Christ was portrayed* <note>Erasmus notes the Greek implies 'written before' or 'publicly displayed'</note>. Therefore it would not be absurd if we take *prescribed* <note>original: "præscripta"</note> to mean those things which are set forth to be imitated: whence we also call a "prescription" <note>original: "præscriptum"</note> a model set forth for imitation. Nor do I doubt that Origen and Ambrose read the same, the former of whom interprets the preposition "before" <note>original: "πρό"</note> in two ways: first regarding the figures of the Old Testament, which although they have now ceased, like shadows when the light has arisen, nevertheless were once produced in writing for our sake; the mysteries revealed in them provide salvific teaching, even from those things which seemed superfluous: of which kind are those, *You shall not muzzle the mouth of the ox while it treads*: and that Abraham had two sons, the first from a handmaid, the latter from a free woman: that the people in the desert ate manna, that they drank water from the rock. Of this kind are also those things which Paul commemorates in 1 Corinthians 10. Indeed, the history of the world's establishment itself teaches us many things, if we understand the allegory. All these things were written before the mystery was made known. Secondly, he explains it concerning the prophetic Scriptures: it was foretold to the Jews, *By hearing you shall hear, and shall not hear, seeing you shall see, and shall not understand*. Concerning us it was foretold, *Those to whom it was not announced concerning him, shall see*. When the Gospel exhibited all these things, we conceive confidence, and those things which were promised to us concerning the age to come will undoubtedly come to pass. Ambrose likewise mentions the promises. And Augustine interprets this place concerning the prophetic Scriptures, such as that which Paul just cited: *The reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me*. Which words, according to Chrysostom, are of the Father to the Son. For when the Jews cried out, *If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross*, through the Son they were also affecting the Father with insult. Moreover, just as Christ through tortures and ignominy arrived at eternal glory, so we ought to endure the injuries and insults of the wicked with a calm mind, so that we may be glorified together with Christ. <margin>F</margin> Therefore the preposition *before* <note>original: "πρό"</note> is not idle, declaring that those things which were written in the Old Testament are either exhibited or opened through the Gospel, lest the Gentiles believe those things did not pertain to them. Moreover, they were written not only so that we might believe them, but even so that we might imitate them: thus nothing forbids *prescribed* <note>original: "præscripta"</note> from being taken as those things which are set before the eyes: just as in Galatians 3 Paul says Christ was *portrayed* before their eyes. Two most trifling quibbles remain. Many crimes are written in the Old Testament which are not set forth for imitation, such as the parricide of Cain: likewise many miracles, such as the crossing of the Red Sea. We have already said that even in these there are things which, according to the mystical sense, are to be imitated by us, and the recounted crimes warn us to imitate the good. Therefore in these too there is an example for imitation. The other is: *Many things were written after they were done*. But here he was dealing with the prophetic Scriptures, from which he had brought the nearest testimony. But if anyone entirely wants it to be a general sentiment, since a mystical sense lies hidden in all things, they are rightly called *written before* under a veil, which were later unlocked through the Gospel. And it is plainly true that there is nothing in divine matters which does not pertain to our instruction. However, here Paul seems to speak properly of the prophetic things, which preceded and designated the Gospel and Christ. Someone might say these are minute points, and that it does not matter if the translator omitted a syllable. And yet if any such thing is committed by us, then in every single mark there lies a huge mystery, and the way is very easy to find.
<margin>E</margin> 6 *Through patience and consolation]* Ambrose for *consolation-*

# TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER XV.

<margin>

</margin>
...of encouragement, grant you to be of the same mind with one another according to Christ Jesus, *that with one accord and one mouth you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.* Therefore, receive one another, just as Christ also received us to the glory of God. For I say that Jesus Christ became a minister of the circumcision for the sake of the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the Fathers; and that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy; as it is written: For this cause I will confess to You among the Gentiles, and sing to Your name. And again it says: Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people. And again: Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and laud Him, all you peoples. And again Isaiah says: There shall be a root of Jesse, and He who shall rise to reign over the Gentiles; in Him the Gentiles shall hope. Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit. And I myself am persuaded, my brothers—

---

...does not read "exhortation." For the word <term>paraklesis <note>original: παράκλησις</note></term> is a term common to both meanings <note>The Greek can mean both "encouragement/consolation" and "exhortation."</note>. However, for the sense of this passage, it does not matter much which way it is read.

7 **the same thing** <note>original: *idipsum*</note>] *to auto* <note>original: τὸ αὐτὸ</note>, that is, the same: which is said more compactly as *tauto* <note>original: ταὐτό</note>. Since *to* <note>original: τὸ</note> is nothing other than a prepositive article, it is not rendered in Latin by a genuine pronoun. And *to ex allelois* <note>original: τὸ ἐξ ἀλλήλοις</note>, that is, "among yourselves mutually," or "one another": about which I have warned previously. Lorenzo Valla here charges the translator with a genuine solecism <note>a grammatical error</note>, which he nonetheless excuses thus: Ambrose and Augustine, men of fine Latin, spoke in that manner; nor are the Orations of Cicero to be scrutinized here, but rather we are dealing with the simplicity of the truth of Scripture. First, even if they were the most Latinate of men, what does it matter if they speak this way, using the words of Scripture, which even Cicero would have done? Now, to allege the "simplicity of Scripture" here, what else is it but to acknowledge the solecism?

8 **That with one mind** <note>original: *Ut unanimes*</note>] *hina homothymadon* <note>original: ἵνα ὁμοθυμαδὸν</note>, that is, "that unanimously." It seems the translators read *homothymoi* <note>original: ὁμόθυμοι</note>. It does not matter greatly for the sense.

9 **Receive one another** <note>original: *Suscipite invicem*</note>] *proslambanesthe allelous* <note>original: προσλαμβάνεσθε ἀλλήλους</note>, that is, "take one another to yourselves": that is, let one person join another to himself and help him: so that it corresponds to that earlier phrase, <term>receive the one who is weak in faith</term>.

10 **To the honor** <note>original: *In honorem*</note>] *eis doxan* <note>original: εἰς δόξαν</note>, that is, "to the glory." The translator fell short through an affectation of variety. For Paul intends that a brother should be supported so that this results in the glory of God, who is praised through the good deeds of those who profess Him. This is exactly how Chrysostom and Theophylact explain it. Moreover, this phrase, <term>to the honor of God</term>, can be attached to the phrase immediately preceding, as in "just as Christ received you, adopting you into the place of the sons of God, who is glorified by your concord among unbelievers": or with the earlier part, "receive one another to the honor of God": or even to both: "Just as it resulted in God's glory that Christ mercifully received you, so it will result in His glory if you receive one another." While it is true that sometimes it doesn't matter whether you say "honor" or "glory," it more often happens that only one is appropriate. "Honor must be held for a parent" <note>original: *Habendus est honor parentis*</note> is said in Latin. "Glory must be held" is not said in the same way. We provide "honor" by way of help, not "glory." And those who excel in dignity and authority are "in honor," not "in glory." A people grants "honors" to candidates, not "glories." And children defer "honor" to parents, not "glory." But Jerome is brought forth to us explaining the first chapter of Malachi, whose words I shall transcribe: <quote>As for our saying 'glory' or 'honor,' in Greek it is *doxa* <note>original: δόξα</note>, and in Hebrew it is *kabod* <note>original: כבוד</note>, which is one word: but we have placed 'honor' for the sake of the property of the Latin language.</quote> What does "for the sake of the property of the Latin language" mean? If "honor" and "glory" sound the same, what is that property which persuaded him that he preferred to translate *doxa* as "honor" rather than "glory"? That matter proves that among the Hebrews the voice is equally accommodated to *doxa* <note>glory</note> and *timē* <note>original: τιμὴν - honor</note>, but among the Latins there is some difference between honor and glory: just as among the Greeks there is some difference between *doxa* and *timē*. In Exodus 20, where it is "Honor your father and mother," it is not *doxason* <note>glorify</note>, but *tima* <note>original: τίμα - honor</note>: and in Leviticus 19, "Honor the face of the old man," it is *timēseis* <note>original: τιμήσεις - you shall honor</note>: and in Psalm 8 these two are joined, *doxē kai timē* <note>original: δόξῃ καὶ τιμῇ</note>, that is, "with glory and honor": and Jerome interprets these words distinctly: "glory," when the underworld shone at His descent; "honor," when He conquered death; "a crown," when He returned from hell triumphing, surrounded by a choir of saints. Nor do "to honor" <note>original: *honorare*</note> and "to make honorable" <note>original: *honorificare*</note> mean exactly the same, nor "to make bright" <note>original: *clarificare*</note> and "to honor." Among the Greeks, *doxa* sounds like a magnificent reputation: hence those who are powerful in authority are called *dokountes* <note>original: δοκοῦντες</note>: *timē* sounds like the payment of a duty owed, from *tiō* <note>to pay/value</note>, whence it is said, "Honor your parents rightly," which is not to celebrate their praises, but to exhibit every duty of piety, especially support in poverty. This is also the origin of that in 1 Timothy 5: "The elders who rule well are worthy of double honor": where it would be inept to place *doxa* instead of *timēs*. Finally, although in this place the word "honor" does not fit entirely badly, "glory" seems to me to signify something more magnificent. This saying corresponds to that Gospel passage in Matthew 5: "That they may see your good works and glorify your Father": and there the Translator renders it "glorify," not "honor," since it is *doxasōsi* <note>original: δοξάσωσι</note>.

11 **To confirm the promises of the fathers**] While the Translator turned one infinitive verb into a gerund and left the other as it was, he obscured the sentence, which is of this sort: Paul, as if having digressed slightly, returns to what he had established. "I say," he says—that is, "what we have said thus far tends toward this"—so that you may understand Christ to be the author of the New Testament, which he first admini-

<column-break/>

<margin>
A
5
6
7
8
9
10
11
B
12
13
14
15
</margin>
-stered to the Jews, to show that the Father is truthful, who had promised it to them through the Prophets. Moreover, He willed that this be common to the Gentiles, not from a promise—although it had been foretold about them too—but from mercy, and that this gift is more pleasing because it had happened to those not expecting it. He therefore opposes mercy to promises; for in the latter there is something that seems owed, while here it is pure favor. For he to whom you have made a promise has something to expect if you do not perform; and yet it brings more pleasure and praise because a good thing happened beyond all hope. Therefore, it could be translated clearly in this way: "Moreover, this is what I am saying: Jesus Christ performed this duty of His toward the Jews for the sake of the truth of God, so that He might confirm those things which had been promised to the fathers; but that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy, to whom nothing had been promised, and yet the same thing happened to them as to the others." Chrysostom shows nothing regarding the speech. There are those who think both infinitive verbs pertain to "I say" <note>original: *lego*</note>: and it is tolerable; if in the first part "I say" is taken as the voice of one interpreting, and in the second as the voice of one commanding. However, the infinitive *doxasai* <note>to glorify</note> can be taken for an imperative: but it does not matter that Theophylact and Origen in their commentary separate this part, "But the Gentiles," as if it contains it conjunctively. It is marvelous, however, with what skill Paul moderates his speech; in order that the Gentiles recognize God's clemency toward them, he calls it "mercy": again, lest the Jews should be terrified that the Gentiles were admitted to a common grace, he subjoins the testimonies of the Jews, by which he declares that it was promised to them as well, even if not so evidently.

12 **For this cause I will confess to you among the Gentiles, Lord**] This prophecy exists in the eighteenth Psalm.

13 **Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people**] *Euphranthēte ethnē meta tou laou autou* <note>original: Εὐφράνθητε ἔθνη μετὰ τοῦ λαοῦ αὐτοῦ</note>. This is referred to God, as being common to both peoples. For he called the Jews "the people of God." These things are found in the same words in the song of Deuteronomy. It is strange, however, why Thomas <note>Aquinas</note> cited this from Isaiah chapter thirty-five, whether by a slip of memory or because a similar argument is treated there. Again, it is strange that our edited versions of the Bible also disagree with Paul, having: "Praise, O Gentiles, His people." The Hebrews have, "Sing, O Gentiles, His people." But the Apostle in this place followed the Septuagint Edition, who translate: "Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people."

14 **And magnify Him**] *kai epainesate* <note>original: καὶ ἐπαινέσατε</note>, "and laud Him," as if giving back praise: such as is *epeuphemein* <note>to shout applause</note>. Ambrose likewise reads "magnify." Although "to magnify" is said for "to extol" and "to bring forth with praises," Origen warns in the Psalm that "laud together" <note>original: *collaudate*</note> was written instead of "magnify." From which it is clear that in his manuscript it was *hymnēsate* <note>original: υμνήσατε</note> instead of *epainesate*: unless perhaps the Latin Translator added this on his own. It seems, however, that Rufinus translated this work, who leaves nothing uncontaminated <note>Erasmus frequently criticized Rufinus for his loose translations of Origen</note>.

15 **There shall be that root of Jesse**] This testimony exists in Isaiah chapter eleven: which Paul nevertheless added according to the translation of the Septuagint, as he is accustomed to doing for most. According to the Septuagint we read thus: "And it shall be in that day the root of Jesse, he who arises to be a prince of the Gentiles, in him the Gentiles shall hope, and his rest shall be honor." According to the Hebrew truth <note>the Hebrew original</note> in this manner: "In that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for a sign to the peoples, him the Gentiles shall entreat, and his sepulcher shall be glorious." Jerome warns that for "his rest" <note>original: *requies*</note>, the Hebrew has *menuchatho* <note>original: מנוחתו</note>, on which word all Translators agree: which nonetheless Jerome translates as "his sepulcher" <note>original: *sepulchrum ejus*</note>: wishing to explain a sense that is otherwise somewhat obscure. For *menucha* sounds like rest, but properly that which we are accustomed to pray for the deceased. Thus, although the Septuagint and Jerome disagree in words, they nonetheless agree in meaning. Moreover, what he translates as "stand for a sign," for the Hebrews is *nes* <note>original: נס</note>. Furthermore, *nes* sounds like a banner, or a trophy, likewise a miracle attested by a thing: the sense is roughly the same, that the people act under the banner of a prince. Furthermore, "they shall entreat" for the Hebrews is *jidreschu* <note>original: ידרשו</note>, which is "they shall seek": for he who seeks, petitions, and those who run to someone, hope. I will add this: the small phrase, "and his rest shall be honor," although it is in Isaiah and in the context of Origen, nevertheless it does not appear to have been added by Paul, since it is not found among the Greeks, nor explained by Origen, nor written anywhere among our people.

16 **And he who arises**] *ho anistamenos* <note>original: ὁ ἀνιστάμενος</note>, "arising": although this is in the present tense, the Translator nonetheless not absurdly translated it into the future: because it adheres to the verb of the future tense, *estai* <note>original: ἔσται</note>, that is, "it shall be." Otherwise, it could also be translated thus, "for also *anistamenos archein* <note>original: ἀνιστάμενος ἄρχειν</note>, that is, 'he who may arise to reign.'"

17 **I am certain, however**] *pepeismai* <note>original: πέπεισμαι</note>, that is, "I have been persuaded."

# EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER XV.

### Romans 15:14–21

<margin>14</margin> I myself am persuaded concerning you, my brothers, that you also are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, <margin>19</margin> able also to admonish one another. <margin>15</margin> But I have <margin>20</margin> written to you more boldly, brothers, <margin>21</margin> in part, as though reminding you, because of the grace given to me by God, <margin>16</margin> that I might be a minister of Jesus Christ to the nations, <margin>22</margin> performing the sacred service of the Gospel of God, so that the offering of the nations might be <margin>23</margin> acceptable, sanctified in the Holy Spirit. <margin>17</margin> <margin>24</margin> Therefore I have a reason to boast in Christ Jesus <margin>25</margin> in those things which pertain to God. <margin>18</margin> <margin>26</margin> For I would not dare to speak of any of <margin>27</margin> those things which Christ has not worked through me, for the obedience of the nations, by word and deed, <margin>19</margin> in the power of signs and <margin>28</margin> wonders, in the power of the Spirit of God, so that from Jerusalem <margin>29</margin> and the surrounding regions as far as Illyricum <margin>30</margin> I have fulfilled the Gospel of Christ. <margin>20</margin> <margin>31</margin> And so I have striven to preach the Gospel, not where Christ was already named, so that I would not build on another’s foundation; <margin>21</margin> but as it is written: They to whom it was not announced concerning him shall see, and they who have not heard shall understand.

<column-break/>

**18 You are full of love** <note>original: *Pleni estis dilectione*</note>] The Greek is <term>agathosynes <note>original: ἀγαθωσύνης</note></term>, which means "goodness." Translators seem to have read it as "love" <note>original: ἀγαπήσεως</note>. However, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching.</note> reads and interprets it as "goodness," and Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop who summarized earlier patristic commentaries.</note> agrees with him. They indicate that this word describes a universal virtue. Although Origen <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253) whose commentaries were foundational but controversial.</note> reads "goodness" in his commentary, someone seems to have corrupted the text of the passage itself to "love"; the translator of Theophylact did the same thing in his usual manner. Here, "goodness" is the opposite of malice, rather than "kindness" <note>original: *benignitas*</note> which corresponds to the Greek <term>chrestoteti <note>original: χρηστότητι</note></term>.

**19 So that you can [admonish] one another**] The Greek is "able also to admonish others" <note>original: δυνάμενοι καὶ ἄλλους νουθετεῖν</note>, that is, *being capable of advising others as well*. Theophylact interprets it this way. It is not clear from Chrysostom's explanation what he read, except that the word "others" appears once and "one another" <note>original: ἀλλήλους</note> appears twice. It seems the translator read "one another" instead of "others"; and indeed, I prefer "one another." The sense is: You are so strong in knowledge and charity that, even without my advice, you could advise each other if necessary. Jerome's interpretation shows he read it this way too: *He did not say they should teach one another, but admonish.* The word "even" <note>original: καὶ</note> is not pointless here; in Greek, it often means "of one's own accord" or "spontaneously," as in Homer:
->Why do you urge me on when I am already hurrying?<-
<note>original: Τί με σπεύδοντα καὶ αὐτὸν ὀτρύνεις;</note>
This conjunction is not idle in Paul, any more than in Homer: it refers back to Paul's act of admonishing, as if to say: "Even if I were not admonishing you, you would be able to admonish each other."

**20 More boldly**] He said "more boldly" instead of "more familiarly" or "more freely." This refers back to the previous section: "You do not need my admonition since you can do it yourselves; nevertheless, relying on your goodness, I have not feared to write to you, more to remind you than to teach you." To make this clearer to the reader, I have translated it as *But yet more boldly*. Paul frequently uses this rhetorical figure to soften what might otherwise cause offense.

**21 In part**] <note>original: ἀπὸ μέρους</note>. He added this to mitigate the phrase "more boldly." it is the same as saying "to some extent." For he had mixed in some rather free speech regarding the foolishness of wisdom, idols, and perverted lusts; therefore, he says he spoke somewhat freely, not because he looked down on them, but because he trusted them as their own Apostle. We dare more with those we love most familiarly.

**22 Performing the sacred service of the Gospel of God** <note>Erasmus corrects the Vulgate's *sanctificans* (sanctifying).</note>] The Greek is <term>hierourgōn <note>original: ἱερουργῶν</note></term>. It is as if he is performing a sacred rite, which corresponds to <term>leitourgon <note>minister</note></term>, a word used for someone who administers sacred or public affairs. Augustine, in the book where he explains certain questions on Romans, reads "consecrating" instead of "sanctifying," which is closer to the Greek. Paul wanted the preaching of the Gospel to be seen as a primary sacred act, like a victim most pleasing to God, because it makes the nations worthy of Christ. He makes himself a sort of priest of this sacrifice. It is required of a sacrificial victim that it be pure, holy, and legitimate for divine matters—what Paul elsewhere calls "perfect." Origen's translator noted something about this. Chrysostom, however, carefully explains the emphasis of the Greek word. It is composed of *hieron* (sacred) and *ergon* (work); hence "to work at sacred things." From this follows the "offering" <note>original: προσφορά</note>.

**23 Acceptable and sanctified**] The "and" is redundant; it was not in the Constance manuscript. "Sanctified" refers to what follows immediately, "in the Holy Spirit," meaning "through the Holy Spirit." He shows that nothing is lacking in his sacrifice, as the Holy Spirit himself has consecrated it.

**24 Therefore I have glory**] The Greek <term>kauchēsin <note>original: καύχησιν</note></term> means "boasting"—that is, "I have something to boast about."

**25 Toward God**] <note>original: τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν</note>, that is, *in those things that pertain to God*. The translator omitted the article *ta* (the). While it does not change the meaning, the article has the power of distinguishing or excluding. We see this in the first chapter of this Epistle with the phrase *to kat' eme* (as far as lies in me). Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Origen’s translator all silently point this out when they warn that one should not boast in just anything—not in works or wisdom—but only in those things which are of divine grace.

**26 For I do not dare**] The Greek <term>tolmēsō <note>original: τολμήσω</note></term> means "I will dare" or "I would dare." With this little introduction, he both avoids the charge of arrogance and wins the reader's trust.

**27 Of those things which Christ has not worked through me**] Ambrose <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Milan and one of the four original Doctors of the Church.</note> interprets this as if Paul could not mention anything worthy of praise in his preaching that Christ had not already provided 

<column-break/>

for you, because you yourselves **18 are full of goodness**, filled with all knowledge, **19 able even to admonish one another**. But **20 yet I have written more boldly** to you, brothers, **21 in part**, as if reminding you, because of the grace given to me by God, that I might be a minister of Jesus Christ to the nations, **22 performing the sacred service** of the Gospel of God, so that the offering of the nations might be **23 acceptable**, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. **24 I have therefore reason to boast** through Christ Jesus **25 in those things which pertain to God**. **26 For I would not dare** to speak anything of **27 those things which Christ has not worked through me**, for the obedience of the nations, in word and deed, by the power of signs and **28 wonders**, by the power of the Spirit of God, so that from Jerusalem **29 and the surrounding regions** as far as Illyricum, **30 I have fulfilled** the Gospel of Christ. **31 So I have striven** to preach the Gospel, not where Christ was named, so that I would not build on another’s foundation: but as it is written, They to whom it was not announced concerning him shall see.

<margin>A</margin> by the help of God. I will include his words here: 
> *He says he has glory before God through Christ Jesus. For believing and serving Christ Jesus with a pure conscience, he earned merit with God the Father, to the extent that he says nothing is lacking that Christ has not worked through him for the exhortation of the nations.*

And shortly after:
> *For being in accord with Christ, he has glory toward God, to the extent that he has no need of any divine power that was not granted to him by the Lord through faith, because he was found fit to spread and achieve those things which lead to the conversion of the nations through the power of signs.*

Origen follows a different opinion, namely this:
> *I would not want to claim the praise of others' deeds for myself; I will only speak of those things which Christ worked through me personally.*

I will also include his words:
> *The things I speak of, he says, are not the words of another’s work, lest I become a praiser of others’ deeds: but I write to you here of the things Christ worked through me, which he fulfilled for the obedience of the nations by word and deed in me.*

<margin>B</margin> Origen’s interpretation is more pleasing to me, not only because it is more modest and more consistent with what follows, but <margin>C</margin> because this is how he preached the Gospel. (It was necessary to tell this part to the former, because there is a conflict between telling of deeds done by others and preaching in such a way that they never preached where others had.) Furthermore, <margin>D</margin> I do not see how the meaning Ambrose likes can be pulled from the Greek text, which reads: "For I will not dare to speak of any of those things which Christ has not worked through me." It is certain that "of those things" cannot refer to the other Apostles, but to the deeds themselves. There could also be a third sense: "I would not dare speak anything of my own deeds, but only of those Christ did through me." Truly, I give the prize to Origen's interpretation. The emphasis of the whole sentence is on the pronoun "me," which excludes the deeds of others. Chrysostom and Theophylact mix and embrace both views: "I do not boast of what I did not do; rather, what I did, I did not do, but Christ through me." And "has worked" is in the past tense, not the present: for he is recounting what he had already done.

**28 Of wonders in the power of the Holy Spirit**] In Greek it is "Spirit of God" <note>original: ἐν δυνάμει Πνεύματος Θεοῦ</note>. And indeed, this is how Origen, Chrysostom, and Theophylact read it. Although Ambrose and the old Latin copies have it differently. It is no wonder if Origen mentions the Holy Spirit in his explanation, <margin>E</margin> since the Spirit of God is the Holy Spirit. But the word "God" expresses the authority of miracles more strongly. Nor is there anything in Ambrose's commentary to suggest he read it as anything other than "Spirit of God." In this place, Chrysostom rightly seems to note certain Bishops who claim authority for themselves with miters, staffs, and robes, while Paul proves himself an Apostle with far more excellent arguments: the greatness of his miracles and the success of the Gospel teaching. Yet he claims none of this for himself, but credits all the glory to God—a man both most modest and grand-spoken, magnificently humble, proud in Christ but lowly in himself.

**29 In the circuit**] <note>original: καὶ κύκλῳ</note>, that is, in the surrounding area, or <margin>F</margin> on every side.

**30 I have fulfilled the Gospel of Christ**] The translator did not translate the pronoun "here," though he added "you" elsewhere rather harshly. Furthermore, he here calls the "preaching of the Gospel" the "Gospel," which he had performed in so many regions. Although "fulfilled" or "completed" <note>original: *impleverim* or *compleverim*</note> was more fitting than "replenished" <note>original: *repleverim*</note>. I think a similar figure is used in the Gospel: "Before you have finished all the cities," meaning "Before you have traveled through all the cities." Chrysostom noted that he did not say he "preached," but "fulfilled," meaning he left out nothing that pertained to a faithful and vigorous Evangelist.

**31 But so I have preached**] The Greek differs slightly from the Latin: "But thus striving to preach the Gospel" <note>original: Οὕτως δὲ φιλοτιμούμενον εὐαγγελίζεσθαι</note>. The word <term>philotimeisthai</term> means to seek something with a kind of ambition. Thus Paul, with a certain holy ambition, stayed away from those places where the other Apostles had preached, so that he himself might be the father and author of his own people. Chrysostom indicated the emphasis of the word *philotimoumenon* by saying the Apostle did this for the sake of glory, because he studiously avoided those who had already heard the Gospel. Ambrose explained it using the word for "striving." Moreover, the conjunction "but" <note>original: δὲ</note>, even if it could not be conveniently rendered, is by no means idle in the Greek: for it signifies that something of great importance is being added to greatly increase the matter, which we usually express with "indeed" or "furthermore."

<summary>Erasmus provides a detailed linguistic analysis of Romans 15:14-21, emphasizing Paul's humility and his unique mission to the Gentiles. He uses Greek philology to argue that Paul viewed his ministry as a sacred priestly service and a "holy ambition" to reach unreached regions.</summary>

# TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER XV.

<margin>A</margin> 22 For which reason also I have been often hindered from coming to you. 23 But now, having no more place in these regions, and having had a great desire for many years to come to you, 24 whenever I begin my journey into Spain, I will come to you. For I hope that, as I pass through, I shall see you, and be brought on my way there by you, if first I may be satisfied with your company in part. 25 But now I am going to Jerusalem, ministering to the saints. 26 For it has pleased those of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem. 27 For it has pleased them, and they are their debtors. For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in carnal <note>material or worldly</note> things. 28 When, therefore, I have performed this, and have sealed to them this fruit, I will return by way of you into Spain. 29 And I know that when I come to you, I shall come in the fullness of the blessing of the Gospel of Christ.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> will see, 32 and they who had not heard, shall understand. <margin>22</margin> 33 For which reason also I was often hindered from coming to you. Now, however, 34 since I no longer have a place <margin>23</margin> in these regions, but have had a desire for 35 many years now to come to you, 36 whenever I <margin>24</margin> set out on a journey into Spain, I will come to you: 37 for I hope it will be that, making my way through that area, I may see you, and be led there by you, if however I 38 shall first have been filled, in part, by your company. 39 But now I am setting out for <margin>25</margin> Jerusalem, ministering to the saints. 40 For it seemed good to <margin>26</margin> Macedonia and Achaia 41 to make some communication <note>sharing or contribution</note> for the poor saints who are in Jerusalem. For so it seemed good to them, and they are their debtors: 42 <margin>27</margin> for if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in carnal things. Therefore, 43 <margin>28</margin> when I have finished this, <margin>B</margin> 44 and have sealed this fruit for them, I will return through you into Spain. For I know 45 that when I come to you, I shall come with the fullness of the blessing... <margin>29</margin>

---

32 **And they who have not heard of him shall understand**] The phrase "of him" is redundant <note>unnecessary for the sense</note>. Although it is understood as being repeated from the previous section.

33 **On account of which I was hindered very much**] <note>original Greek: Διὸ καὶ ἐνεκοπτόμην τὰ πολλὰ τοῦ ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς</note>. That is, *for which reason I was also hindered many times from coming to you*. For the Greek phrase *ta polla* <note>original: τὰ πολλὰ</note> also signifies this, used in place of an adverb: and thus the Greek commentaries explain it, specifically and clearly Chrysostom and Theophylact: for he tried frequently, but business in which he was detained always stood in the way. Furthermore, that word "I was hindered" <note>original Greek: ἐνεκοπτόμην / enekoptomēn</note> signifies that a thing already begun is interrupted: so it would be more fitting to say "I was inhibited" or "I was prepedited" <note>obstructed in advance</note>: just as in the Acts, when he intended to set out for Bithynia, he was "prohibited" by the Holy Spirit.

34 **Not having a place**] <note>original Greek: μηκέτι τόπον ἔχων / mēketi topon echōn</note>, that is, *since I no longer have a place*. Moreover, he understands a "place" to be a vacuum, which he was looking for so that there might be more fruit, as he had said before.

35 **From many years now preceding**] <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ πολλῶν ἐτῶν / apo pollōn etōn</note>, that is, *from many years*, or *for many years now*. I do not see why the translator thought something should be added, since the speech cannot be understood as referring to future years.

36 **When I shall have begun to set out for Spain**] <note>original Greek: Ὡς ἐὰν πορεύωμαι εἰς τὴν Σπανίαν, ἐλεύσομαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς</note>. "As if I set out for Spain, I will come to you." Although some Greek codices had *isō* <note>original: ἴσω</note>, not *hōs* <note>original: ὡς</note>. If the punctuation is separated, it reads "As if"; if joined, it could be translated as "As soon as," to indicate a brief delay there. Furthermore, the Greek writers, following Paul, pronounce "Spain" with the first syllable of the region <note>original: "Spaniam prima regioni syllaba"</note>: though they are accustomed to add to such words, saying *espero* for *spero* <note>I hope</note>, or *exspecto* for *specto* <note>I look</note>: doing the same in this word as we Latins do in the word *Scariote* <note>Iscariot</note>.

37 **For I hope that passing through I may see you**] <note>original Greek: ἐλπίζω γὰρ διαπορευόμενος θεάσασθαι ὑμᾶς, καὶ ὑφ᾽ ὑμῶν προπεμφθῆναι ἐκεῖ</note>. Since I see this phrase offended Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>Erasmus's contemporary and rival scholar</note>, it could be translated into Latin thus: *for I hope it will happen that, making a journey through that place, I may see you, and be produced—or led—thither by you*. The word "passing through" <note>original Greek: διαπορευόμενος / diaporeuomenos</note> means "crossing through" or "making a journey in that place." Furthermore, those words "I will come to you" <note>original Greek: ἐλεύσομαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς</note> seem to be an addition, for this reason: Chrysostom does not touch upon them, even though they are added in Theophylact. Ambrose reads, *When I begin to set out for Spain, I will see you, and be promised thither by you*. If the passage is free of error, Ambrose organizes it thus: *Having a desire to come to you for many years now, when I begin to set out for Spain, and to be led thither by you*, so that both parts—coming and being led—pertain to the noun "desire." But the conjecture of writers is that the text is mutilated. If the Greek conjunction *gar* <note>for</note> is removed (which is not found among the Latins), the speech has no problem, so that "I hope" is referred jointly to what came before, in this manner: *Since I do not have a empty place in these regions, and I have been somewhat desirous for many years now to come to you, and at the same time I am setting out for Spain, I hope it will be that in passing I see you, and being led by you from there, I am escorted*. The translator usually renders words of the future tense with a verb of beginning. But here the Greeks read, *Whenever I journey*. Furthermore, whoever it was, he ineptly translated *propempthēnai* <note>original Greek: προπεμφθῆναι</note> as "to be sent ahead." For thus Ambrose reads, *Since it is a matter of duty to escort one who is setting out*. The translator of Origen organizes it differently, explaining: *When I set out for Spain, I hope that I am about to see you*. However, he does not add the conjunction. Now these words, *for I hope that passing through I may see you*, although they are in Chrysostom, are not added in Theophylact, neither in the context nor in the explanation, just as they are not in Ambrose. I see that the Ancients, in those things which did not seem to pertain much to Apostolic dogma, did not take too much liberty in changing the scripture. Hence that great variety in the Acts of the Apostles and the Apocalypse. And the Epistle to Philemon was hardly received among the Apostolic ones by the Greeks, because it seems to deal with human affairs. But I wish we had three hundred Epistles of that kind.

38 **I shall have been fruit**] <note>original Greek: ἐμπλησθῶ / emplēsthō</note>, that is, *I shall have been filled* <note>or satisfied</note>: which indeed is much more significant for explaining the huge desire of Paul. And so that he may increase the emphasis <note>term: emphasis / epitafin</note>, he adds "in part," signifying an insatiable desire.

39 **Now therefore I set out**] <note>original Greek: πορεύομαι / poreuomai</note>, that is, *I set out*: it is in the present tense, as is the participle which follows, *ministering* <note>original Greek: διακονῶν / diakonōn</note>: for he was already doing this. Indeed, we are said to do that which we are preparing to do. For the Apostle, by this saying, excuses the delay of his departure for Spain. For they could have said, "If there is nothing there to delay you, why do you put off visiting us?" "Now," he says, "I am setting out for Jerusalem": if he had said *I will set out*, he would have in-

<column-break/>

-creased the suspicion of a longer delay. Therefore the verb of the present tense is more consistent with the Apostolic meaning. I wonder, however, why the Translator changed the participle into an infinite verb, unless perhaps he read *diakonein* <note>to minister</note>.

<margin>C</margin> 40 **For the Macedonians have provided**] <note>original Greek: εὐδόκησαν / eudokēsan</note>, that is, *they approved, and so it seemed to them*. But he soon translates the same verb as "it pleased them": the translator thought it a sin to repeat the same verb, which however Paul himself was not afraid to do. Furthermore, *eudokēsan* does not only sound like "to approve," but to "approve from the soul": whenever a thing does not just please in any way, but pleases well and from the heart: so that we may understand that gifts of this kind, if they are offered voluntarily, should be accepted by those who have need, not demanded: since Paul himself preferred to labor with his hands rather than live on another's food.

41 **Contribution**] <note>original Greek: κοινωνίαν / koinōnian</note>, that is, *communion, or communication*. For so he calls the sent alms, using an overly civil term: as if it were not a "benefit" to help with money, but rather to impart to others, when there is need, the wealth which we hold in common with them. Moreover, as for his translation, "unto the poor of the saints," the Translator was clearly excessive, as one who expressed even the scheme and idiom of the Greek speech. Otherwise, it should have been said, "to the poor saints": lest anyone suspect that the saints had poor people who were not themselves holy. For since all Christians were then called "saints," there was no need for the genitive case to distinguish pagan poor from the faithful. It should be noted that Paul seems to join two conflicting things, "it pleased them" and "debtors." For he who offers spontaneously and with a good will of the soul does not seem to "owe": hence he calls divine beneficence toward men *eudokia* <note>original: εὐδοκίαν - good will</note>. And although he seemed to have added this more politely than from the heart, yet he approached this one <margin>D</margin> cause: that they had imparted spiritual things, so that anyone might owe something. But today none demand tithes more tyrannically than those who impart nothing spiritual. For so Paul calls the Evangelical doctrine.

42 **If the Gentiles were made partakers of their spiritual things**] The Greek reads thus: <note>original Greek: εἰ γὰρ τοῖς πνευματικοῖς αὐτῶν ἐκοινώνησαν τὰ ἔθνη</note>. Paul uses this verb *koinōnein* <note>original: κοινωνεῖν</note> ambiguously, so that it sometimes pertains to the giver, sometimes to the receiver. In Galatians chapter six: *Let him who is taught the word share with him who teaches*, he used it for "impart": here *koinōnēsai* seems to be taken for "they were partakers," so that it pertains to the receiver: unless you read *autōn* <note>of them</note> without the aspiration <note>smooth breathing mark</note>, and "the nations" in the accusative case. It does not matter to the sense which way you read it. For if we take it as said that the Law and the Gospel and Christ first arose from the Jews, as we owe to posterity for a benefit received from ancestors, so the descendants are said to have shared <margin>E</margin> with us that which came from their own progenitors. And soon Chrysostom uses *koinōnēsai* and *metadounai* <note>sharing and giving a share</note> in different ways, interpreting what Paul called "to minister" <note>original: λειτουργῆσαι / leitourgēsai</note>. Chrysostom also noted that he added "their" to "spiritual things," because those are each person's own proper goods, but he did not add "their" to "carnal things," because these resources belong not only to the possessor, but also to the needy.

43 **When I shall have consumed**] <note>original Greek: ἐπιτελέσας / epitelesas</note>, that is, *when I shall have finished*.

44 **And I shall have assigned**] <note>original Greek: σφραγισάμενος / sphragisamenos</note>, that is, *when I shall have sealed, or rendered it sealed*: for so money is usually delivered. For Paul feels that he wants to deliver this gift diligently and with certain faith. Because every handling of money is usually suspect, especially to the very greedy Jews: Theophylact also indicates something of the kind. **This fruit.** Chrysostom and Theophylact refer "fruit" not to the ones about to receive, but to those who had contributed: as if in the benefits of Christians, the profit lies with the giver, <margin>F</margin> not with the receiver. For if Paul had delivered that money integrally and safely, it was going to be that to the Macedonians and the others who had contributed, it would seem like a certain treasure stored up in one place. I have pointed this out so that the Reader may understand that the pronoun "to them" does not refer to the Saints, but to the Greeks.

45 **In the fullness of blessing and so forth**] <note>original Greek: ἐν πληρώματι εὐλογίας τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου τοῦ Χριστοῦ</note>, that is, *in the fullness of the blessing of the Gospel of Christ*. Paul several times calls almsgiving "a blessing." And here he seems modestly to signify that the Romans should also contribute. Although Chrysostom prefers this to be taken generally for every kind of virtues and duties, because "of the Gospel" is added. Yet that which is given in the name of the Gospel is the "blessing" of the Gospel. By a similar trope they called almsgiving a "blessing" <note>original: εὐλογίαν</note>, which was given with friendly words, just as the feast usually given to the poor was called "love" <note>original: ἀγάπην / agape</note>. Some read, "of the Gospel of Christ": which is read in the context in Chrysostom, but in explaining he declares he had read only "of the Gospel." It is also added in Theophylact, but in the context.

<summary>Erasmus analyzes Paul’s plans to visit Rome and Spain after delivering a collection to Jerusalem, providing philological nuances on the concepts of "fellowship," "blessing," and the "sealing" of financial gifts.</summary>

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER XVI.

30 I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers for me to God, 31 so that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service to Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints, 32 so that in joy I may come to you, by the will of God, and may find rest with you. 33 Now may the God of peace be with you all. Amen.

Greet those from the household of Aristobulus. 11 Greet Herodion my kinsman. Greet those from the household of Narcissus, who are in the Lord. 12 Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord. Greet Persis the beloved, who worked hard in the Lord. 13 Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine.

only in the text. Our Translator, following Ambrose, has only *in the blessing of Christ*: Ambrose explains it this way as well. Origen reads it similarly.

46 *I beseech you therefore*] <note>original: Παρακαλῶ δὲ ὑμᾶς</note>, that is, *I exhort you*. Although in this place *I beseech* does not fit badly, because of what follows: *by our Lord Jesus Christ*.

47 *By the charity of the Holy Spirit*] The word "Holy" is extra <note>original: διὰ τῆς ἀγάπης τοῦ Πνεύματος</note>, that is, *through the love of the Spirit*. <margin>D</margin>

48 *That you help me*] <note>original: συναγωνίσασθαί</note>, which means to bring help, or to strive and labor with someone. Origen noted this before us, though he twisted the meaning to suggest that in praying there is a struggle against wicked demons who wish to interrupt the prayers of the pious. However, Ambrose reads, *that you share in my anxiety*. In my opinion, the Translator expressed this more freshly than Ambrose. And he used "in prayers" for "through supplications," a form of speech that should be familiar to you by now.

49 *The offering of my service*] <note>original: καὶ ἵνα ἡ διακονία μου</note>, that is, *And that my ministry*. Ambrose, as if explaining, reads *that the offering of my gifts*. However, it seems to me he read something else, perhaps *prosphora* <note>offering</note>, a word he used before: especially since <margin>E</margin> a little earlier he used a sacrificial word, *leitourgēsai*, which the Translator rendered as *to minister*. We have added the pronoun, *that this ministry of mine*, because of the Greek article.

50 *May be acceptable in Jerusalem*] The Greeks read this somewhat differently. Some have it thus: *And that my ministry, which is in, or toward Jerusalem, may be acceptable to the saints*. One manuscript had, *my ministry which is at Jerusalem*. But Theophylact, neither reading nor interpreting it, adds this small part, just as Chrysostom does not. Furthermore, he modestly calls it a *ministry*, since he is merely the administrator of others' generosity.

1 *Who is in the ministry*] <note>original: οὖσαν διάκονον</note>, that is, who is a female minister. It is thought that this Phoebe delivered the Epistle to the Romans.

2 *Who is at Cenchreae*] In Greek it is *Kenchreais*, or as it is written in some, *Kenchreai*, a three-syllable word. We translated this as *Cenchrensian*. However, since there are several places of this name—namely a town in the Troad and another in Italy—<margin>F</margin> it is more likely that Paul means the Cenchreae that was the naval station of the Corinthians, since it is certain this Epistle was sent from Corinth. Origen also indicated this. For he speaks thus in the preface to his exposition of this Epistle: *For Cenchreae is said to be a place near Corinth, or rather the port of Corinth itself*.

3 *Worthily of the saints*] <note>original: ἀξίως τῶν ἁγίων</note>, it could be translated *as becomes saints*, or *as is worthy of saints*. He adds the case of the noun to the adverb.

4 *Prisca and Aquila*] Origen thinks Prisca is the same person whom Luke calls Priscilla in the eighteenth chapter of Acts; her husband was Aquila, a man of the Pontic race, but a Jew by origin and religion, a "fellow-craftsman" of Paul—that is, a maker of tents, or as Origen interprets it, a *shoemaker*. Origen is moved by how it was possible for Aquila to be in Rome when the Emperor Claudius had driven them

the coming of the Gospel of Christ. 46 But I <margin>A</margin>
beseech you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ, 47 and by the love of the Spirit, 48 that you help me in my labor with prayers for me to God, 31 that he may deliver me from the unbelievers in Judea, 49 and that this ministry of mine, which I offer in Jerusalem, may be acceptable to the saints, 32 that I may come to you with joy, by the will of God, and be refreshed together with you. 33 And may the God of peace be with you all. Amen. XVI. 1 Now I commmend to you Phoebe, our sister, who is a minister of the Church of Cenchreae, 2 that you receive her in Christ, in such a way as becomes the saints, and that you assist her in whatever business she may need from you: for she herself has assisted many, and even me myself. Greet Prisca <margin>B</margin> 3 and Aquila, my helpers in Christ Jesus, 4 who for my life laid down their own necks: to whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the nations, 5 likewise the congregation that is in their house. Greet Epaenetus my beloved, who is the firstfruits of Achaia in Christ. Greet Mary, 6 who has labored much toward us. Greet 10 7 Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen, and my fellow prisoners, 11 who are distinguished among the Apostles, who also were in Christ before me. Greet 12 Amplias 8 my beloved in the Lord. Greet Urbanus our helper in Christ, and Stachys 9 my beloved. 13 Greet Apelles, approved in <margin>C</margin> 10 Christ. Greet those who are of the household of Aristobulus. Greet Herodion my kinsman. 11 Greet those who are of the household of Narcissus, those who are in the Lord. Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, 12 who labor in the Lord. Greet Persis the beloved, who has labored much in the Lord. Greet 13 Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine.
