5 *Their own necks*] <note>original: τὸν ἑαυτῶν τράχηλον</note>, that is, *their very own neck*.

6 *And the domestic church*] <note>original: καὶ τὴν κατ’ οἶκον αὐτῶν ἐκκλησίαν</note>. He calls the Christian family, and any who had joined them, a "church." For this reason, we preferred to call it a *congregation*, because of certain unrefined people who think a "church" must be a physical temple. Nor should it seem unworthy if someone calls a gathering of Christians a *congregation*, since the Translator of the second chapter of Second Thessalonians calls the whole gathering of the faithful in Christ a *congregation*.

7 *Greet Epaenetus*] <note>original: Ἐπαίνετον</note>. It is pronounced Epaenetus, not Ephenetus: which in Latin sounds like *Praised* or *Praiseworthy*.

8 *Who is the firstfruits of the Church of Asia*] <note>original: ἀπαρχὴ</note>, that is, *firstfruits*. Either because he converted this first of the Greeks to Christ, or because he was the most prominent. For Ambrose seems to relate this to the dignity of the man, saying: *He does not keep silent about the present dignity of this Epaenetus, to show that more worthy men believe, and to invite the leading Romans to the faith*. So he says. For the best things are usually set aside as firstfruits. And shortly after, *The Church of Asia*: it is *of Achaia* in Greek, not *Asia*, although a very ancient Pauline manuscript disagrees. Chrysostom and Theophylact read *Achaia*. Origen reads *Asia*. Likewise Jerome cites it in several places. Those who changed *Asia* to *Achaia* seem to have been offended by the idea that it was unlikely Epaenetus was the first, either in dignity or conversion, of all Asia Minor, which is divided into many regions. However, it is established that whenever *Asia* is said on its own, it signifies that part of Asia Minor where Ephesus is. Nor is "of the Church" added among the Greeks, nor in ancient Latin copies, nor even in Ambrose. He adds, however, *in Christ*: obviously explaining why he called him the firstfruits.

9 *Who has labored much in you*] <note>original: εἰς ὑμᾶς</note>, that is, *toward you*. The same is gathered clearly enough from the interpretation of Origen, even more clearly from Ambrose’s, and most clearly from Theophylact’s. Though I am not unaware that in some Greek manuscripts it is written *en hymin* <note>in you</note>. Indeed, a slip of the pen is very easy for scribes in these matters. In Chrysostom, a scribe could have done either: from the commentary it was not clear what he had read, except that *you* (plural object) fits the first person better.

10 *Andronicus and Julia*] <note>original: Ἰουνίαν</note>, that is, *Junia*. For he mentions *Julia* later in that place. A very ancient manuscript provided from Constance agreed with the Greeks.

11 *Who are noble*] <note>original: ἐπίσημοι</note>, that is, *distinguished*. Lest anyone think he is speaking of their social rank or lineage.

12 *Ampliatus*] <note>original: Ἀμπλίαν</note>, that is, *Amplias*: unless perhaps the Roman voice corrupted the name toward a Hebrew pronunciation. And it is not "most beloved," but *beloved* (masculine).

13 *Greet Apelles*] Origen wonders whether this is Apollo of Alexandria, a man learned in the Scriptures, who is mentioned in the eighteenth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles.

14 *From the house of Aristobulus*] <note>original: τοὺς ἐκ τῶν Ἀριστοβούλου</note>, that is, those who belong to Aristobulus; the last syllable should be sounded with an acute accent...

### TO THE ROMANS. CHAPTER XVI.

<margin>14</margin> Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, <margin>15</margin> Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with <margin>16</margin> them. Greet one another with a holy kiss. <margin>17</margin> The churches of Christ greet you. Now I urge you, brothers, to watch out for those who create dissensions and obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have learned, and <margin>18</margin> turn away from them. For such people do not serve our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own bellies, and through smooth talk and flattery they deceive the <margin>19</margin> hearts of the simple. For your obedience has become known to everyone. Therefore I rejoice over you; but I want you to be wise in what is good, and <margin>20</margin> innocent in what is evil. And the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ <margin>21</margin> be with you. Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you, as do Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, <margin>22</margin> my kinsmen. I, Tertius, who wrote this epistle, greet <margin>23</margin> you in the Lord. Gaius, my host and the host of the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, greets you, and <margin>24</margin> our brother Quartus. The grace of our Lord Jesus <margin>25</margin> Christ be with you all. Amen. Amen.

<margin>14</margin> **it is a diphthong in Greek:** <note>original: "est enim Graecis diphthongus"</note> the name is derived from "excellent counsel." <gloss>The word "house" was not added in the manuscript provided by Constance. Similarly, Horace says, "We came to Vesta’s," where "temple" is understood. The Greeks say, "in Hades," understanding "house." It would not be absurd to say, "I will come to the Passover," understanding "the feast."</gloss>

<margin>15</margin> **Asyncritus, Phlegon]** It should be read as *Asyncritos, Phlegon* <note>Greek: Ἀσύγκριτον, Φλέγοντα</note>. *Asyncritos* means "incomparable," and *Phlegon* means "burning."

<margin>16</margin> **Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes]** These are different names: the first is *Hermas*; the other is *Hermes*, which in Latin sounds like *Mercurius*: and so we have translated it, lest someone might be <term>alienated</term> <note>original: "xenizetai" - to be surprised or find something foreign</note> by them. Origen, in his books *On First Principles*, thinks this *Hermes* is the author of the apocryphal book titled *The Shepherd*: from which he draws testimonies, and thinks it was written before the judgment, though he admits it is not accepted by many. There was a remarkable either credulity or kindness in these ancients, who attributed so much to books we have under the title of Clement, when in these there appears such a manifest deception by the man who wrote such things.

<margin>17</margin> **Olympias]** In Greek it is *Olympas* <note>Greek: Ὀλυμπᾶν</note>. For it is apparent they are men, not women, from the two Greek masculine articles *autoi* and *syn autois* (them and with them). One cannot make a man out of "Olympias."

<margin>18</margin> **All the churches of Christ greet you]** Origen disputes how Paul could offer greetings in the name of all churches, since it is not likely that all were present in Corinth when this Epistle was written. But since he knew the affection of everyone toward the Romans, he greets them in the name of all.

<margin>19</margin> **Through sweet words and blessings]** <note>Greek: διὰ τῆς χρηστολογίας καὶ εὐλογίας</note>. Lest anyone imagine these are the commonly called "blessings" of Bishops; in Greek there are two terms: *chrestologia*, which you might rightly call "smooth talk" or "fair-speaking": hence we have heard of certain Caesars who were kinder in speech than in deed, commonly called *chrestologoi*. And *eulogia* literally sounds like "benediction": however, here it is used for "praise" or "flattery." He repeated the same point out of a hatred for the vice of fawning.

<margin>20</margin> **Hearts of the innocent]** In Greek *akakōn*, which signifies "simple" and "least crafty" rather than "innocent." Indeed, in Latin one is called "innocent" who is free from any crime of life; *akakos* is one who is void of fraud and suspicion. Indeed, "innocence" is one of those words which Cicero says the Greeks lack.

<margin>21</margin> **For your obedience]** This was placed here: *For your obedience*. For it answers the silent question: Why did he say "hearts of the simple"? **For your [obedience], who are prudent, etc.**

<margin>22</margin> **Timothy my helper]** <note>Greek: ὁ συνεργός μου</note>, which signifies a partner and sharer in work for the Greeks, as you might say "colleague" or "co-worker." Ambrose translates it not inelegantly as *the sharer of my labors*.

<margin>23</margin> **I Tertius]** It should be read as *Tertius*, not *Terentius*. Although in some manuscripts it is held as Terentius. Ambrose reads "Tertius"; for he adds, "by name, not by number." And so read Chrysostom and the Greek interpreter Theophylact. For he is called "Tertius" here, just as among the Romans they were called Sextus, Quintus, and Decimus.

<margin>24</margin> **And the whole Church]** The Latin speech has an <term>amphibology</term> <note>a grammatical ambiguity</note>, because it is uncertain whether Gaius, the host of Paul, greets the Romans together with the whole congregation, or if he is to be understood as the host not only of Paul, but also of the whole Church. Among the Greeks, only the latter sense

<column-break/>

<margin>D</margin> can be accepted, and therefore we translated it, *my host and that of the whole Church*.

<margin>25</margin> **Treasurer of the city]** <note>Greek: ὁ οἰκονόμος</note>, that is, *dispensator*: hence we translated it as "treasurer of the treasury." Theophylact thinks he was a prefect, and indeed he was a prefect in that regard. I believe it signifies the one in charge of the treasury.

<margin>26</margin> **The grace of our Lord and so forth]** Since almost the same words were placed a little higher up, they are not found here in Ambrose and Origen, nor in the very ancient manuscript provided by the Library of Constance. In Chrysostom it is not added in the first place, neither in the text nor in the commentary, but only at the end after the doxology; and he notes it is fitting that our speech should begin from the grace of God and end in the commemoration of grace. Theophylact agrees with Chrysostom.

<margin>27</margin> **Now to him who is able]** This is a part which is not added in most Greek manuscripts. In some it is added in another place, namely at the end of the fourteenth chapter, as we indicated in that place. In some it is added at the end of the Epistle. We have done this as well, especially following the Latin manuscripts, even the ancient ones, and Ambrose, and with them Origen. Origen teaches that not only was this part cut away by Marcion—who rejected some Epistles inscribed to Paul entirely and truncated or mutilated others—but even all that follows from the point where Paul said, *But everything that is not from faith is sin*: that is, from the end of the fourteenth chapter, because the rest, occupied only with exhortations and greetings, seemed to correspond too little to Pauline <margin>E</margin> gravity. But what is the point of refuting his opinion, which was exploded by everyone long ago? It is strange, however, how it happened that this part was moved from its place. For if it was moved because it co-hered poorly with what preceded and followed, it does not even co-here here. I am less surprised that the order of the sentence did not hold together among the Greeks or us in Paul’s writing, among whom such inconveniences frequently occur. Even if we ignore the <term>hyperbaton</term> <note>a transposition of words</note>, where "honor and glory" is added at the end, the word "to whom" <note>original: "cui"</note> prevents it from being referred back to the beginning of the speech, "Now to him who, etc.," as Thomas [Aquinas] also noted, following Augustine. Augustine explains the other awkwardness of construction so that "through Jesus Christ" is not referred to "wise"—lest God the Father should seem to be wise through the Son—but to what follows, "be honor and glory": because he glorified the Father among men by his death. But what shall we do with the "to whom" (as that man Aquinas says)? It so constantly occupies all Greek and Latin manuscripts that it cannot be <margin>F</margin> erased except with the greatest impudence. If the location is defended, and neither what is above nor below co-heres, I myself certainly do not find what to devise here, unless one is willing to admit frankly that Paul, in his usual manner, uttered this speech in an incomplete way, so that we must understand "we give thanks," or something similar. Ambrose connects the earlier parts with the end, "be honor and glory," ignoring the difficulty of the construction, which nevertheless offended Thomas. But long before him, Augustine, in his third book against Maximinus the Arian Bishop, chapter thirteen, thinks it can be ordered thus: *To him be glory, to whom through Jesus Christ be glory*. Though he admits that if the word "to whom" were omitted, the speech would be more common. Furthermore, what we read as "through the scriptures of the prophets," in Greek is *dia te graphōn prophētikōn*, that is, "and through the prophetic scriptures": since there is nothing preceding to which the conjunction *te* (and) refers, nor is there a following *kai* (and) which is usually connected to this, unless the force of another conjunction is understood in *kata*: and we take this sense, that the mystery was manifested now through the Gospel and of old through the prophetic scriptures.

<margin>23 It was sent from Corinth</margin> We have added this from the Greek volumes, except that we have translated <note>original: "ἐγράφη"</note> *written* as *sent*: it was *sent* through Phoebe; otherwise it was written by the hand of Tertius, with Paul dictating. And meanwhile, it occurs to me to wonder what kind of messengers those truly greatest High Priests <note>Erasmus uses the term "Pontifices" (Popes/Bishops) here to refer to the Apostles, contrasting the simplicity of the early church with the grandeur of his own day.</note> used then, seeing as Paul wrote to the Romans—who were then still in their prime—concerning such difficult matters by means of a mere woman <note>Erasmus reflects the surprise of his era that a woman, Phoebe, was entrusted with such a foundational theological text.</note>. Next, one might laugh at the "new diligence" of Nicholas of Lyra <note>A famous 14th-century Franciscan biblical commentator.</note>, who, although Origen and Saint Jerome, and with them all the Ancient writers, confirm that this

Epistle was sent from Corinth, yet he himself wavers: specifically because Haymo <note>Haymo of Auxerre, a 9th-century theologian often cited in medieval glosses.</note> wrote that it was sent from Athens. But see with what dexterity this "marvelous craftsman" unties this more-than-Gordian knot: "Part," he says, "he wrote in Athens; what remained, he then added in Corinth; and thus he sent it to Rome." O, what a charming man! He would prefer, I think, for Paul to make however great a waste of travel, just so that the authority of Haymo might suffer no blow—as if that man could not have slipped up in one or two places.

# THE ARGUMENT
### of the
# FIRST EPISTLE
### to the
# C O R I N T H I A N S.

<note>original: "Υ Π Ο Θ Ε Σ Ι Σ" (Hypothesis). This was a standard summary often prefixed to biblical books in Greek manuscripts to give readers the historical context.</note>

He sends this letter from Ephesus in Asia, having already seen them and taught them, yet reminding them through this letter nonetheless. The occasion for the letter is this: the Corinthians, coming together out of rivalry, were divided in their opinions, and consequently there were schisms among them. Because of these schisms, they even overlooked a man who had taken his stepmother <note>A reference to the case of incest mentioned in 1 Corinthians 5:1.</note>. Others wanted to leave their own wives on the pretext of self-control. Some even ate in the temples of idols, as if things sacrificed to idols were a matter of indifference. Others looked down on some people but marveled at those who spoke in tongues. Finally, they were even deceived regarding the mystery of the resurrection, saying that this flesh is not raised. Since all these things were stirred up in Corinth, the people wrote to the Apostle. Consequently, he writes back addressing everything. First, he bears witness to their prudence and knowledge. However, he does not accept their creating schisms; rather, he advises them to consider virtue not in word, but in deed and power. Then, after rebuking the one who took his stepmother and urging them not to have lawsuits against one another, he answers the things they wrote about. Concerning marriage, he teaches that the union is meant to be unbroken, and that they should abstain only for a season for the sake of prayer. Because of their love for self-control, he writes about virginity, saying it should not be by necessity but by persuasion. Then, concerning things sacrificed to idols, he warns them not to abuse their knowledge but to conduct themselves with love. He forbids banquets in idol temples so that the "little ones" <note>Those with a weaker or more sensitive conscience.</note> are not scandalized. Then he writes about spiritual gifts, so that they do not differ over their gifts, nor prefer the one who has this gift over the one who has that. For he says all these things belong to the same Spirit. Finally, he teaches about the resurrection: that the flesh is raised—dying as something "soulish" or "fleshly," but rising incorruptible. He establishes this through the grace of God and the resurrection of Christ. He concludes the letter with words of exhortation regarding what he has written and gives instructions for the collection for the saints.

# INTRODUCTION
### TO THE
# FIRST EPISTLE
## TO THE CORINTHIANS
### BY
## DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring elaborate foliate patterns and scrolls.</image-desc>CORINTH was once the metropolis of Achaia <note>A province of the Roman Empire, covering much of modern-day Greece.</note>. Because of the convenience of its ports—for it is an Isthmus—it was the most famous and wealthiest trading center in all of Achaia. However, it usually happens that the morals of such cities are quite corrupt, because from every nation, vices rather than virtues tend to be imported, and the merchant class claims for itself a great license in living. Therefore, although the Corinthians had long ago received the Gospel teaching through the preaching of Paul, some traces and remains of their former nature and life still lingered. So much so, that there was a danger they might be alienated from the sincerity of Christ by philosophers—who looked down on the preaching of the cross as humble and unlearned—and by false apostles inviting them toward Judaism. It is a very difficult thing to be transformed into a different kind of person from the environment in which you were born and to which you have long been accustomed. Indeed, Saint Jerome, in the preface to the second book of his *Commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians*, testifies that even in his own age, remains of these things which Paul charges against the Corinthians still existed among the Greeks. Yet today, we think it is enough to be just dipped in a little water <note>A critique of those in Erasmus's day who viewed baptism as a mere ritual rather than a call to deep moral transformation.</note> to suddenly become a Christian.

Paul, therefore, knowing that it requires no less virtue to guard what has been won than to have won it, calls his children back to Christ with equal zeal. He had fathered them for Christ with great effort, having spent a year and a half among them. Now he speaks with Apostolic authority, correcting, rebuking, and finally threatening; now he coaxes and exhorts with fatherly affection, softening the sharpness of necessary reproof by mixing in praise. Following the example of wise physicians, he sweetens the bitter medicine of wormwood by coating it with honey, applying the appropriate remedies to each individual evil.

First, pride and ferocity are the usual companions of wealth; and among the fierce, factions generally arise, as no one wants to yield to another, and everyone considers himself superior. To these things, wealth adds luxury and a devotion to gluttony, and luxury brings lust as its companion. Furthermore, greed is the particular vice of merchants. Nor were they only swollen with wealth, but also with the arrogance of Greek philosophy, without which they despised others as barbarians. It was a sign of their pride that they puffed themselves up based on the status of the Apostles by whom they had been baptized. Hence those voices of discord: *I am of Apollos; I am of Cephas <note>The Aramaic name for the Apostle Peter.</note>; I am of Paul.* Furthermore, they could not even agree sufficiently in their formal meetings, since each person was pleased with himself regarding spiritual gifts; and while they refused to yield to one another in the exercise of those gifts, tumult and confusion arose—to the point that even women spoke and taught in the public assembly. Furthermore, luxury...

--- Page 410 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Argumentum" or scholarly introduction to the First Epistle to the Corinthians, likely written by Desiderius Erasmus. It transitions from a general summary of the Corinthian situation to a detailed analysis of the specific vices and theological errors Paul addresses in the letter, followed by a breakdown of the letter's structure and scholarly debates regarding its origin.</meta>

At the same time, there was a sense of pride <note>original: "tumor," literally a swelling, used here to mean arrogance or puffed-up ego</note> in the fact that whenever they gathered for the most holy supper, which Paul calls the Lord’s Supper, where it was most fitting to demonstrate Christian harmony, the wealthy would take their food without waiting for those of humbler means. They would gorge themselves even to the point of drunkenness while others went hungry. Thus, there was not only discord and lack of restraint there, but even a certain unbecoming inequality, which the Lord's Supper was never meant to know. Furthermore, it was partly a fault of pride and partly of worldly philosophy that some of them looked down on Paul as someone thin and humble, and moreover, as uneloquent and unskilled in speech. It was indeed a characteristic of their philosophy that they called into doubt the resurrection of the dead, which is the very foundation of our faith. It was a sign of luxury that they would eat indiscriminately those things which were then sacrificed to the idols of demons, failing to avoid the stumbling block this created for the weak. There was also a spirit of lust, which reigned nowhere more freely than in Corinth; among other things, one was found among them who contaminated himself through a shameful affair with his father’s wife—that is, his own stepmother. Nor did they expel the author of this outrage from their company; instead, they maintained fellowship with other flagrant Christians, as if they were favoring their vices. To this we may add that, contrary to what is proper, men wore their hair long, and women were not afraid to be seen with heads uncovered in the ecclesiastical assembly, displaying effeminate manners and a love of luxury by their very physical appearance. It was a sign of greed that they pursued lawsuits among themselves—not over their reputation or their lives, but over money—with such a growing passion for wealth that these Christians, who professed a contempt for such things, litigated before pagan and ungodly judges to the great disgrace of the Christian name. And so far were they from simply enduring the loss of a little money that they even went out of their way to cheat others in such business dealings. Finally, they disagreed among themselves regarding marriage, as some Christians were already asserting that one should abstain from marriage entirely, seeing that the Apostles themselves stayed away from their wives.

I have shown these ailments of the Corinthians—not of all of them, but of some—and Paul countered them with these remedies so that the contagion would not infect the entire flock. In the first place, having prefaced his words with confidence in their future constancy in the Gospel of Christ, he rebukes them more severely and teaches them: they should not boast in men through human contention, but should boast equally in Christ through harmony, to whom alone all things must be credited. In passing, he indicates that the source of such dissensions is pride of mind. Accordingly, he calls them back from the superstition of worldly philosophy to the humility of the cross, which, although it lacks outward show, nevertheless possesses power and energy. He also identifies the authors of this evil as the "False Apostles" <note>original: "Pseudapostoli," refers to rival teachers who undermined Paul's authority</note> who thrust themselves in after Paul’s departure. He declares that he laid a right foundation and warns that they should not build upon it something that would soon have to be demolished—that is, the Corinthians should not learn anything that they would soon have to unlearn. Then, like a father with his children, he reasons with them for having reached such a height of self-importance that they now despise their own founder as someone humble, even though he endures everything for the sake of the Gospel—the very reason they ought to favor him more. He exhorts his children not to fall away from their father, nor to surrender themselves willingly into slavery to "pedagogues" <note>A "paedagogus" was a slave who supervised children; here Paul contrasts his fatherly love with the strict, impersonal rule of other teachers.</note>. He deals with these matters primarily in chapters one, two, three, and four. Furthermore, the end of the fourth chapter seems to me to belong to the beginning of the fifth. Regarding the incest, he gave instructions and decreed by public counsel that the man’s company should be avoided—partly so that he might be corrected by shame and come to his senses, and partly so that others might not be infected by contact with him. He warns, however, that not only this man must be avoided, but also all who were infamous for manifest outrages while bearing the false title of "Christian." For flagrant pagans need not be avoided in the same way, either because it is not our concern what they are like, or because they are so numerous everywhere that anyone wishing to escape the flagrant would have to avoid everyone. He deals with this in chapter five. In the third place, he warns about lawsuits: if any such questions arose among them—though it seemed foul enough among Christians to contend over money, which ought to be of the least value to us—the matter should not proceed to the point of approaching pagan judges. Instead, they should settle the matter among themselves through any arbitrators whatsoever. He deals with this in chapter six, a large part of which, in my opinion, belongs to the seventh. Namely, from that place where he is about to treat marriage, he condemns among other vices: fornication, adultery, and homosexual acts <note>original: "masculam Venerem," literally "male Venus," a classical euphemism for male-male sexual relations</note>. He follows this up at the beginning of the next chapter: *Do you not know that your members are temples of Christ?* <note>original: "Nescitis quod membra vestra templa sunt Christi?"</note>. In the fourth place, he gives instructions on marriage, widowhood, unequal marriages <note>Marriages between a believer and a non-believer.</note>, divorce, and virginity—noting in passing that one’s state of life should not be changed simply because they have embraced the Christian faith. Throughout this entire discourse, he so encourages celibacy and continence that he does not, however, take away the remedy of marriage from those who need it. This is dealt with in chapter seven. In the fifth place, he teaches that meat sacrificed to idols differs in no way from other meat in reality; and yet, one must abstain from these if there is a danger that some pagan or some weaker Christian might think, because you eat, that you consent to the worship of idols. He deters them from these and similar vices by the example of the ancients. He deals with this in chapter eight, and again in chapter nine. For in the middle, he digresses into a commendation of himself, silently preferring himself to the other Apostles—even the greatest—as he alone of all of them imparted the evangelical doctrine to the Corinthians for free. In the sixth place, he teaches what ought to be observed in the public assembly of Christians: that men should not have long hair, that women should not have uncovered hair, and then that community and equality should be maintained in the Lord's feast. For the business of the belly is not to be conducted there (which is better done at home), but the Lord’s Supper is to be represented by mystical meals. Moreover, he warns that no one should be self-satisfied because of a spiritual gift <note>original: "dotem spiritualem," literally a spiritual dowry</note>, but each should contribute his own gift to the common good, following the example of the members of the body. He exhorts them to use the remaining gifts they have received correctly, yet above all to strive for charity <note>In this period, "charity" (caritas) was the standard translation for "love" (agape).</note>, without which the rest are of so little benefit that they even become harmful. Furthermore, since he gives the first place to charity, he gives the next to prophecy—for so he calls the explanation of the hidden meaning of Scripture. In this, he warns that tumult and confusion must be avoided. This will happen if only a few speak in turn, while the women are commanded to remain silent for the time being, to the extent that they are not even permitted to ask questions for the sake of learning in the assembly. He deals with this in chapters eleven, twelve, thirteen, and fourteen. In the seventh place, he establishes the resurrection of the dead with various arguments, declaring what it will be like and in what manner it will occur. And that is in chapter fifteen. In the final chapter, he adds some familiar matters concerning the collection of money for the support of the poor and regarding his return to the Corinthians. Finally, he commends Timothy and several others to them.

Saint Ambrose thinks this is not the first Epistle that Paul wrote to the Corinthians; he followed, I believe, this conjecture because in the fifth chapter, he says, *I wrote to you in a letter*, as if he had written to them previously in another letter on this matter. However, the Greek interpreters disagree. They think this was sent by Timothy, whom he mentions once or twice, and also by Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, whom he commends to them. Again, others think it was sent from Ephesus, because at the end he writes: *But I will remain at Ephesus until Pentecost.* Others say from Philippi, for the Greek manuscripts have this inscription. Nor can I guess what those who thought so were following, unless they conclude it was written during his journey because of what Paul writes: *I will come when I have passed through Macedonia, for I will pass through Macedonia.* And shortly after: *For I do not wish to see you now in passing.*

-># THE EPISTLE OF PAUL<-
->## TO THE<-
-># CORINTHIANS<-
->### THE FIRST.<-

<margin>1. 1.</margin> Paul, called to be an Apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother, <margin>2.</margin> To the Church of God which is at Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, <margin>3.</margin> in every place, both theirs and ours: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. <margin>4.</margin> I thank my God always concerning you, for the grace of God which was given to you in Christ Jesus; <margin>5.</margin> That in everything you were enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge; <margin>6.</margin> even as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you, <margin>7.</margin> so that you lack no spiritual gift, as you wait for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ; <margin>8.</margin> Who will also confirm you until the end, blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. <margin>9.</margin> God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of His Son, Jesus Christ our Lord. <margin>10.</margin> Now I plead with you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment. <margin>11.</margin> For it has been declared...

---

<margin>1</margin> **Called an Apostle & called to be saints**] <term>klētos</term> <note>original Greek: κλητὸς</note> and <term>klētois</term> <note>original Greek: κλητοῖς</note> are nouns, not participles, as we have advised above; they are called "saints" not because they are already holy, but because they have been called to holiness. As Ambrose <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Milan and influential theologian</note> also indicated: though formerly all Christians were called "saints" to distinguish them from the profane, and it was not a title of virtue, but of their profession.

<margin>2</margin> **Of theirs**] In more proper Latin this would be <term>suis</term> <note>their own</note>. However, the Greeks use a double conjunction, <term>autōn te kai hēmōn</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτῶν τε καὶ ἡμῶν</note>, that is, "theirs and ours." By itself, the sense is somewhat ambiguous. Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine commentator</note> thinks that "theirs" and "ours" could refer to the Lord, who is first our Lord, and then Paul repeats and adds that He is not only ours, but also the Lord of whoever invokes Him. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquence</note> arranges it in the same way in his Greek Commentaries—which are not yet translated—written on this Epistle, if the title does not deceive me. A copy of that manuscript was made available to us from the Library of the Preachers at Basel. Truly, this interpretation seems affected to me. In this Edition, as we now give the fifth, we have consulted other manuscripts of Chrysostom and found that he so tempers his explanation that "theirs and ours" can refer either to the Lord or to the place, because just as there is one Lord, so there is one Church. Some interpret it simply: whether in their own places where they live, or in those where we live. A third sense seems more acute to me and more suited to Paul’s feelings: that Paul considers every place his own where there are those who call upon the name of the Lord, because among Christians, charity makes all things common. Theophylact does not shrink from this view, indicating that Paul is about to rebuke the Corinthians for the discords that have arisen among them, using this preparation as if to say: "If the Church is one and the same for all who believe in Christ in any place, why do you, citizens of the same Republic, disagree among yourselves?" Ambrose seems to refer "theirs" to the lands of the Gentiles and "ours" to the Jews, for he writes: *He joins the Gentiles with the converted Jews.* Unless you prefer to invert it, so that the first belongs to the Jews and "ours" to the Gentiles: because the name of the Lord used to be invoked only in Judea, and Paul, as the Apostle to the Gentiles, said "ours." The addition by Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, followed by Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a medieval exegete</note>, is forced: that "theirs" refers to the Bishops of that place, to whom they were subject, though they were not thereby exempt from the jurisdiction of the Apostle. Certainly, the word "jurisdiction" <note>original Latin: "ditio"</note> was unheard of among the Apostles.

<margin>3</margin> **From God our Father and the Lord Jesus**] The sense is ambiguous among the Greeks because this genitive can refer back to the preposition <term>apo</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ, meaning "from"</note>, so the sense is that peace proceeds equally from the Father and from the Son. It can also refer to the noun "Father," so we understand the Father to be common to Christ and to us. Yet everyone follows the former sense.

<margin>4</margin> **In all things**] <term>en panti</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν παντὶ</note>, that is, "in every": that is, in whatever matter. Although that does not change the integrity of the meaning, the Translator rightly changed the number <note>from singular "every" to plural "all things"</note>.

<margin>5</margin> **Even as the testimony**] <term>Kathōs</term> <note>original Greek: Καθὼς</note>, that is, "just as": which refers to what preceded, namely, "by speech and knowledge." For the more they abounded in sacred gifts, the more the truth of the Gospel was made manifest. Theophylact interprets it exactly in this sense. Ambrose is not far from this view. Thomas introduces various opinions instead of one.

<margin>6</margin> **So that nothing is lacking to you**] <term>hōste hymas mē hystereisthai en mēdeni cha-</term> <note>original Greek: ὥστε ὑμᾶς μὴ ὑστερεῖσθαι ἐν μηδενὶ χα-</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>1. 1.</margin> PAUL, called to be an Apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Sosthenes the brother, to the Church <margin>2.</margin> of God which is at Corinth, to those sanctified through Christ Jesus, called to be saints, together with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, in whatever place, either theirs or ours: Grace to you and peace from God <margin>3.</margin> our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. I give thanks <margin>4.</margin> to my God always for you, for the grace of God which was given to you through Christ Jesus. Because in all things you were enriched through him, in every word and every knowledge: by which things the testimony of Jesus Christ was confirmed in you, so that you are not destitute <margin>7.</margin> in any gift, waiting for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ, Who will also confirm you until the end, blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. <margin>8.</margin> God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship <margin>9.</margin> of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord. I beseech <margin>10.</margin> you, however, brethren, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all speak the same thing, and let there be no dissensions among you, but be one whole body with the same mind and the same judgment. For it has been signified <margin>11.</margin> to me

---

<term>rismati</term> <note>original Greek: ρίσματι</note>, that is, "So that you are not destitute in any gift." And "so that" <note>original Greek: ὥστε</note> in this place does not denote an end, but a consequence, like "to the point that." Likewise, "gift" in this place is not <term>charis</term> <note>grace</note>, as it was a little above, but <term>charisma</term> <note>a specific spiritual gift</note>, which he frequently translates as "gift."

<margin>7</margin> **Without blame**] <term>anegklētous</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνεγκλήτους</note>, as if you were to say, "un-accusable" or "blameless": from <term>egkalein</term> <note>original Greek: ἐγκαλεῖν</note>, which is "to call into court"; and <term>egklēma</term> <note>original Greek: ἔγκλημα</note> is "crime" or "charge" to the Greeks, from which the word is derived. However, to be "un-accusable" is more perfect and expansive than being "innocent." For even innocence itself is sometimes not free from accusation.

<margin>8</margin> **God is faithful**] <term>pistos ho Theos</term> <note>original Greek: πιστὸς ὁ Θεός</note>. Paul uses this expression in various ways. Sometimes those who believe are called "faithful" <note>original Latin: "fidi"</note>, as the "unfaithful" <note>original Greek: apistoi</note> are unbelievers; at other times "faithful" refers to those who are of good faith, performing what they have received, as in this place, according to Theophylact, who interprets "faithful God" as "truth-telling" and "incapable of lying." Meanwhile, it refers to the "thing" itself, as in "a faithful word," for a certain and indubitable speech. Furthermore, Horace testifies that the word "faithful" also applies to a superior:
> He will make himself as useful to me, and as faithful.
For he speaks of one whom he certainly wished to seem superior.

<margin>9</margin> **Into fellowship**] <term>eis koinōnian</term> <note>original Greek: εἰς κοινωνίαν</note>, "into communion," or "partnership." The Translator rendered this correctly.

<margin>10</margin> **I beseech you**] <term>Parakalō</term> <note>original Greek: Παρακαλῶ</note>. It could have been "I exhort." Although "I beseech" fits well enough, or "I adjure": especially because there follows, "through the name of our Lord Jesus." For Theophylact also interprets it this way: that Paul adjures the Corinthians by that name which ought to be most sacred to all initiated into Christ.

<margin>11</margin> **That you speak that same thing**] <term>hina to auto legēte</term> <note>original Greek: ἵνα τὸ αὐτὸ λέγητε</note>, that is, "that you say the same thing": which is to say, that you agree. Writing to the Romans he said, "to be of the same mind" <note>original Greek: to auto phronein</note>, that is, "to feel the same," or, as he translates, "to savor the same thing": because these things are related—to disagree in heart and to differ in words. Theophylact also explains it in this way. But some people do not remember this precept: one of them tenaciously holds to the Scotist sect, another the Thomist, another the Ockhamist, another the Albertist. Some speak as Nominals, others as Reals, others as Junsperians, others as Theologians; then some as Transalpines, others as Cisalpines. <note>Erasmus is satirizing the many competing schools of Scholastic theology in his own day, contrasting their constant bickering with Paul's call for unity.</note>

<margin>12</margin> **Schisms**] He left the Greek word; he could have said "factions," or "dissensions," or "discords."

<margin>13</margin> **But that you be perfect**] <term>ēte de katērtismenoi</term> <note>original Greek: ἦτε δὲ κατηρτισμένοι</note>, or, as some had it, <term>apērtismenoi</term>: which signifies "perfect," like a body in which no member is mutilated, or maimed, or unequal; from <term>artios</term> and <term>artizein</term> <note>to fit together or make whole</note>. Hence, for the sake of explanation, we translated it "that you be one whole body." For when "perfect" is said, the common people understand absolute virtue, which Paul is not yet discussing with these seditious people. If I had translated it as "whole" <note>original Latin: "integri"</note>, I would have seemed to say "uncorrupted and honest." For Paul warns that they should not only be concordant in tongue, saying the same thing, but also that just as the members of a whole body are moved by the same spirit, so they should have the same mind. Furthermore, whatever is said to be "divided and scattered" is not whole and solid.

<margin>14</margin> **In the same sense**] <term>autō noï</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτῷ νοῒ</note>, that is, "with the same mind." The preposition "in" is placed for "through"; therefore, having omitted it, we rendered the sense of the same. "In the same judgment," <term>autē gnōmē</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτῇ γνώμῃ</note>, that is, "in the same opinion": this was either changed by scribes, or the Translator read <term>gnōsei</term> <note>knowledge</note>, as is found in the Aldine Edition, instead of <term>gnōmē</term> <note>judgment/opinion</note>. But this is less likely, since the Greek manuscripts agree, and in the most ancient Latin copies "judgment" is found instead of "knowledge," specifically in a Pauline manuscript of most proven faith which is worth many others; and again in that which the College of Canons of Constance provided to us. To these, Ambrose is found to have read "judgment," not "knowledge," if anyone observes closely.

<meta>This page continues the text of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, specifically moving from the introductory greetings into the first major conflict Paul addresses: the factions within the Corinthian church. # THE EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER I.

<margin>11</margin> For it has been declared to me concerning you, my brothers, by those of Chloe’s household, <margin>12</margin> that there are contentions among you. Now I say this, that each of you says, "I am of Paul," or "I am of Apollos," or "I am of Cephas <note>Cephas is the Aramaic name for Peter.</note>," or "I am of Christ." <margin>13</margin> Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized into the name of Paul? <margin>14</margin> I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, <margin>15</margin> lest anyone should say that I had baptized into my own name. <margin>16</margin> Yes, I also baptized the household of Stephanas; besides, I do not know whether I baptized any other. <margin>17</margin> For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel, not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of no effect. <margin>18</margin> For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. <margin>19</margin> For it is written, "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent." <margin>20</margin> Where is the wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the disputer of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? <margin>21</margin> For since, in the wisdom of God, the world through wisdom did not know God, it pleased God through the foolishness of the message preached to save those who believe. <margin>22</margin> For Jews request a sign, and Greeks seek after wisdom; <margin>23</margin> but we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling block and to the Greeks foolishness.

<column-break/>

...declared to me concerning you, my brothers, <margin>11</margin> by those of Chloe's household, that there are contentions among you. Now I say this, <margin>12</margin> that each of you says, "I indeed am of Paul," but "I of Apollos," but "I of Cephas," but "I of Christ." Is Christ divided? Was Paul cru- <margin>13</margin> cified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul? I give thanks to my God, that I bap- <margin>14</margin> tized none of you, except Crispus and Gaius, lest <margin>15</margin> anyone should say that I baptized in my own name. I <margin>16</margin> also baptized the household of Stephanas: furthermore, I do not know whether I baptized any other. For <margin>17</margin> Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel, not with learned speech, lest the cross of Christ be rendered empty. For the word of the cross, to those indeed who perish, <margin>18</margin> is foolishness, but to us who obtain salvation, it is the power of God. For it is written, I will de- <margin>19</margin> stroy the wisdom of the wise, and the intelligence of the intelligent I will reject. Where is the wise man? where is the scribe? where is the dis- <margin>20</margin> puter of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? For after that in the wisdom <margin>21</margin> of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it seemed good to God, through the foolishness of preaching, to save those who believe. Since both the Jews de- <margin>22</margin> mand a sign, and the Greeks seek wisdom. We however <margin>23</margin> preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed an offense...
<meta>Catchword: dicu-</meta>

---

...and those things which, by way of reminder, he will place below: *He wants them to be perfect in the same sense* <note>original Latin: "eodem sensu"</note>, which he had implanted in them, so that they might not disagree. For he calls them to the example of those whom he praised above, so that they might defend them. Thus far Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose, 4th-century Bishop of Milan.</note>. He refers "sense" to that which had been handed down to them by Paul, and "judgment" to its defense. For that which is brought forth and recited is generally called a "judgment" <note>original Latin: "sententia"</note>, while "sense" resides within us. Certainly, Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers.</note> plainly reads "judgment" for "judgment" in the commentary on Psalm 132. Again, Augustine, in the first book against the Donatists on Baptism, chapter ten, reads "judgment," not "knowledge." Likewise, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, the "Golden-Mouthed" preacher of Antioch.</note> and Theophylact read it this way, as anyone who weighs their interpretation more closely will discover. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> twists "sense" to mean the power of the soul by which we judge things to be done, and "judgment" to mean that by which we judge things to be known. This invention does not quite please me, since we judge things to be known with the mind instead. Nor can "sense" here be taken for the sense of a bodily organ, like sight or hearing. The handle for this error was provided from what was held a little earlier: <term>gnōsei</term> <note>original Greek: γνώσει — "knowledge"</note>, in "in every word and in all knowledge" <note>original Greek: παντὶ λόγῳ καὶ πάσῃ γνώσει</note>. Truly, there the Apostle was speaking of the abundance of science and learning; here he is dealing with consensus. But it is possible that knowledge is not the same, even when the mind is the same.

**15** *By those who are of Chloe’s*] Theophylact, the Greek interpreter, thinks Chloe is the name of a Corinthian family, so that you understand there were some of that kin who indicated to Paul the discord of the Corinthians. Just as when writing to the Romans he had said, <term>ek tōn Aristoboulou</term> <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῶν Ἀριστοβούλου — "those from Aristobulus"</note>, meaning his kinsmen and familiars. Thomas doubts whether he would rather make Chloe a village that belonged to the jurisdiction of the Corinthians, or a matron. Ambrose also doubts whether it refers to people, a place, or a woman. However, among the Greeks, a preposition is usually added to the names of places. For it is not accepted among them to say <term>tois apo Rōmēs</term> <note>original Greek: τοῖς ἀπὸ Ῥώμης — "those from Rome"</note> as we say "those who are at Rome," but they express it with an added preposition, <term>ek tēs Rōmēs</term> <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῆς Ῥώμης — "out of Rome"</note>. Certainly, in Horace’s Odes, *Chloe* is a woman's name:
> Now Chloe rules me,
> Learned in sweet measures, and skilled with the lyre.
Truly, with wonderful counsel, Paul expressed the name of the person for the sake of credibility, but again suppressed the names of the [contentious] people, lest he should stir up any envy against them.

**16** *My God*] "My" is not found among the Greeks, nor in Ambrose, nor in the ancient manuscripts, specifically in the Pauline and Constance versions. And it is absolute, so that He is the God of all. For regarding what he said a little earlier, *I give thanks to my God*, it was noted by Theophylact that he called the common God of all "his" God out of a certain supreme affection; he would have noted it here as well, if he had said "his God."

**17** *You were baptized in my name*] <term>ebaptisa</term> <note>original Greek: ἐβάπτισα</note>, that is, "I baptized," in the first person, although the Latin manuscripts constantly resist this; yet to the sense it makes no difference. From Theophylact’s commentaries, it is not entirely clear what he read, except that conjecture leans more toward him having read "I baptized" rather than "you were baptized": for he adds that Paul baptized many, but in the name of Christ, not his own. In this fifth edition, because a Greek codex was at hand, I found "I baptized" written both in Chrysostom and in Theophylact. The commentary of Chrysostom confirms the reading: *Why*, he says, *do you boast that I baptized, when I give thanks to God that I did not do it?* Certainly Augustine, elsewhere as well as in the third book against Cresconius, chapter eleven, reads *according to the Greeks*. But lest you err, Reader, in this often-repeated word: in the first place, "or were you baptized in the name of Paul," the Latin codices agree with the Greek; in the second place, "Lest anyone say that I baptized in my name," the Greeks agree [with "I baptized"], but the Latins disagree, because some read "you were baptized," others "to be baptized."

**18** *If any other of you*] <term>ei tina allon</term> <note>original Greek: εἴ τινα ἄλλον</note>, that is, "if any other." For "of you" is redundant; it is not added in Ambrose, nor in Chrysostom or Theophylact.

<column-break/>

**19** *Not in wisdom of word*] <term>en sophia logou</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν σοφίᾳ λόγου</note>, that is, in the learning of speech. For they call <term>sophian</term> <note>original Greek: σοφίαν — "wisdom"</note> not only that which is wise, but also whatever is elegant and learned. Moreover, learning pleased the Greeks, just as miracles and portents pleased the Jews. And the preposition "in" <note>Greek: "en"</note> is placed instead of "through" <note>Greek: "dia"</note>, and it is spoken in a Hebraic figure, "in the wisdom of speech," for that which was "with learned speech" or "through learned speech." Furthermore, since <term>logos</term> <note>original Greek: λόγος</note> signifies "speech" rather than "word" <note>Latin: "verbum"</note>, why in this place did it please [the translator] to misuse "word"? And presently in the same manner, "for the word of the cross," for here the Son of God is not signified. Where this also should be noted in passing: here a double article is added, <term>ho logos gar ho tou staurou</term> <note>original Greek: ὁ λόγος γὰρ ὁ τοῦ σταυροῦ — "for the word, the [one] of the cross"</note>: by which there is a more evident distinction between this simple and composed speech about the cross, fitting its own argument, and the painted and composed speech of philosophers and rhetoricians.

**20** *Lest it be made void*] <term>hina mē kenōthē</term> <note>original Greek: ἵνα μὴ κενωθῇ</note>, that is, lest it become empty. For that is called "empty" which is not solid, but charms with its appearance. You will note this very well, excellent Reader, how solicitously Saint Paul cared that the Gospel of Christ be most pure from all human supports, lest this world could claim anything for itself from it; so much so that he did not even wish to add eloquence or human learning. But in these times, while we adorn Christ with wealth, profane business, honors, empires, armies, pleasures, and what not? we execrate eloquence alone. And in this one part we even surpass the Apostles; for they spoke simply, but from the heart, without allurements, yet again without filth, without monstrosities; they spoke without affectation, but prudently: and to say it in few words, just as they were powerful and rich in another way, and noble and famous in another way, so were they in a different way both learned and eloquent.

**21** [*that is, to us*] Someone added <term>hēmin</term> <note>original Greek: ἡμῖν — "to us"</note>, I know not who, for in Greek it is <term>tois de sōzomenois hēmin</term> <note>original Greek: τοῖς δὲ σωζομένοις ἡμῖν</note>, that is, "but to us who obtain salvation." In Ambrose it is read thus: *But to those who are being saved, it is the power of God*, with "to us," *as it appears*, omitted.

**22** *Is the power of God*] <term>dynamis Theou</term> <note>original Greek: δύναμις Θεοῦ</note>. So that it may be opposed to weakness and impotence: because the Corinthians were insolent with riches, just as the Romans swelled with the glory of empire and military praise.

**23** *I will destroy the wisdom of the wise*] The testimony is in Isaiah, chapter twenty-nine, which he cited in his own manner, not according to the Hebrew truth, but according to the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>; although in sense there is no discrepancy. For thus the Hebrew truth has it: *For the wisdom shall perish from its wise men, and the understanding of its prudent ones shall be hidden*. The Seventy thus: *And I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the prudent I will hide*.

**24** *And the prudence*] <term>tēn synesin tōn synetōn</term> <note>original Greek: τὴν σύνεσιν τῶν συνετῶν</note>, that is, "the intelligence of the intelligent," if one renders it word for word.

**25** *Where is the scribe?*] <term>grammateus</term> <note>original Greek: γραμματεύς</note>. Theophylact thinks this refers to the Jews, among whom the profession of wisdom was in the hands of the Scribes; otherwise <term>grammatikos</term> <note>original Greek: γραμματικός</note> word for word sounds like "literary man": whence he is also called "literate." For among the Hebrews, a scribe is not simply called one who writes, but one who, being consulted about perplexed matters, responds from the oracles of the Holy Scriptures, as we noted in the Gospels. It appears to be taken from Isaiah chapter thirty-three, where according to the Hebrew truth, Jerome thus reads: *Where is the scribe? where is he who weighs the words of the Law? where is the teacher of the little ones?* According to the Seventy we read in this manner: <term>Pou eisin hoi grammatikoi? pou eisin hoi symboulueontes? pou estin ho arithmōn tous syntrephomenous mikron kai megan laon?</term> <note>original Greek: Ποῦ εἰσιν οἱ γραμματικοί; ποῦ εἰσιν οἱ συμβουλεύοντες; ποῦ ἐστιν ὁ ἀριθμῶν τοὺς συντρεφομένους μικρὸν καὶ μέγαν λαόν;</note> that is, *Where are the literary men? where are the counselors? where is he who numbers those who nourish the small and great people?*

**26** *Where is the inquisitor*] <term>syzētētēs</term> <note>original Greek: συζητητής</note>, that is, "disputer": word for word it sounds like "searcher": for <term>syzētein</term> <note>original Greek: συζητεῖν</note> is to dispute. And so Ambrose reads it. Thus I found it written in the Pauline and Constance manuscripts. We gave some warning about this word in the Gospels: "Where is the scribe? where is he who weighs the words of the Law? where is the teacher of the little ones?"

**27** *Has he not made foolish*] <term>Ouchi emōranen</term> <note>original Greek: Οὐχὶ ἐμώρανεν</note>, that is, "Has he not stultified," or "infatuated," if we may speak thus: for "fatuous" <note>meaning foolish/tasteless</note> and "sapid" <note>meaning wise/tasty</note> are in conflict with each other.

<meta>Catchword: 28 Gen-</meta>

The editor provides a detailed philological analysis of the Greek text, citing various Church Fathers and manuscript traditions to clarify the meaning of terms like "scribe," "wisdom," and "word."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary on the first and second chapters of the First Epistle to the Corinthians. Having addressed the divisions in the church, the author (Erasmus) now explores Paul's argument regarding the "foolishness" of the Gospel compared to worldly wisdom, specifically focusing on the choice of the Greek and Latin vocabulary used by the Church Fathers like Augustine and Ambrose.</meta>

-># TO THE CORINTHIANS I. CHAPTER II.<-

24 ...to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God. <margin>A</margin> 25 Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men. For see your calling, brothers, 26 that not many were wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many of noble birth; 27 But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; and God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong; <margin>B</margin> 28 And the base things of the world and the despised things God chose, and the things that are not, so that 29 he might bring to nothing the things that are; So that no flesh might boast in his presence. 30 But from him you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption; 31 So that, as it is written, "Let him who boasts, boast in the Lord." <margin>II. 1</margin> And I, when I came to you, brothers, came not with excellence of speech or wisdom, declaring to you the testimony of God. 2 For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. 3 And I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling. 4 And my speech, and my preaching, was not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of the spirit and of power, 5 so that your faith might not be in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.

---

**28 To the nations, however, foolishness** <note>original: "Gentibus autem stultitiam"</note>] Ἕλλησι δὲ <note>original Greek: "To the Greeks..."</note>, that is, "to the Greeks": by which name they were accustomed to include everyone who was not Jewish.

**29 But to the called themselves**] Αὐτοῖς δὲ τοῖς κλητοῖς. It would be clearer to say, "But to those same who are called": so that you understand the Christians of both nations, to whom Christ is proven equally. Since he is one thing for both, fulfilling what each nation required. What do you seek, O Jew? Signs: here is the power of God. What do you seek, O Greek? Wisdom: here is the wisdom of the eternal Father. For the Greek interpreters also testify that Paul felt this way.

**30 Because that which is foolish of God**] τὸ μωρὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ τὸ ἀσθενὲς τοῦ Θεοῦ, that is, the foolishness of God, and the weakness of God: so that the adjective placed in the neuter gender is understood in place of a noun. Augustine noted this passage in his work *On Christian Doctrine*, book two, chapter thirteen, showing that in this interpretation, although there is no grammatical error <term>solecism|An error in grammar or syntax</term>, there is nonetheless an <term>ambiguity|amphibologiam</term>, because it is uncertain whether "of men" <note>original: "hominibus"</note> is in the dative or the ablative case: as if you were to say, "it is foolish to you," or "he is a fool to this person." He thinks that inconvenience can be avoided if you translate it as "it is stronger *than* men," and "it is wiser *than* men." And he relates it in this way in the twelfth book of his work *Against Faustus*, chapter twenty-three. Otherwise, if the translator had translated literally "wiser and stronger of men," there would have been a double inconvenience: for not only would he have admitted a grammatical error, but also an ambiguity: because it could be perversely understood that "that which is foolish of men" is wiser than God's, and "the weak of men" is stronger than God's. Furthermore, he calls the preaching of the cross the "foolishness and weakness of God," either because that matter seemed foolish and weak to the impious, or because compared to that infinite divine wisdom and power, this too was in some way "foolish" and "weak." For just as all the righteousnesses of men before God are like a woman's menstrual cloth, so the entire wisdom of mortals, if compared to that unthinkable and heavenly wisdom, might be called a kind of foolishness. Nor should we shrink from this phrase, "the foolishness of God": which Augustine did not shudder at in his 102nd Letter, writing to Lucillus: "This foolishness of God, and the foolishness of preaching, draws many to salvation." If God lowered himself to our weakness to make us strong, is it anything new if he lowered himself to our foolishness to make the foolish wise?

<margin>C</margin> **31 For see**] Βλέπετε γάρ. Although the Greek word is ambiguous <note>original: "anceps"</note>, nevertheless "You see" [indicative] fits the sense better than the command "See" [imperative]. For he is not admonishing them to see what they already knew, but he is drawing what was already evident into an argument. Ambrose takes the ambiguous Greek word and explains it with a Latin one, reading, "For behold, brothers." Theophylact interprets it as a command, as does Chrysostom: yet the indicative mood fits this explanation better. For the Apostle cites the Corinthians themselves as witnesses to what he said. You yourselves see that among you those were chosen who, according to the world, are foolish and despised. Yet the meaning ends up the same.

<margin>D</margin> **32 That he might confound**] καταισχύνῃ, that is, "make ashamed," or "suffuse with shame," rather than "confound": for "confound" is usually said of one who is thrown into disorder. "That he might confound the wise." It is strange why Paul did not maintain the similarity of gender in both places. For against "foolish things" [neuter] he opposes "wise people" [masculine], not "wise things," and yet in the others he returns to the neuter gender: "strong things," and "things that are not."

<margin>E</margin> **33 And those things which were not**] καὶ τὰ μὴ ὄντα. Although he had said before "despised things," that is, things held for nothing, or reduced to nothing, he increased the effect with a Hebrew figure of speech, just as in the earlier part of the Epistle, he calls those things which are not as though they were: meaning that things which are most despised or utterly lost "are not." Hence we call a man of no value a "man of nothing."

<margin>F</margin> **34 That he might destroy those things which are**] καταργήσῃ, which is sometimes trans-

<column-break/>

the foolishness: 24 But to those same who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God. 25 Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men. 26 For you see your calling, brothers, that not many were wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many born of noble stock: 27 But what things were foolish according to the world, God chose, that he might shame the wise: and what things were weak in the world, God chose, that he might shame those things which are strong: 28 And what things were ignoble in the world and despised, God chose, and those things which were not, so that he might obliterate those things which are: 29 That no flesh might boast in his presence. 30 But from the same [God] you are in Christ Jesus, who was made for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption: 31 So that, as it is written, let him who boasts, boast in the Lord. <margin>II. 1.</margin> And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come with excellence of speech or wisdom, announcing to you the testimony of God. 2 For I did not judge myself to know anything among you, except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. 3 And I was among you in weakness, and with fear, and in much trembling. 4 And my speech, and my preaching, was not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of the spirit and of power, 5 So that your faith might not be in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.

---

lated as "make void." It means to make obsolete and, as it were, to obliterate: as we have already frequently pointed out.

**35 All flesh**] πᾶσα σάρξ. It would be smoother to say "any flesh." This too is spoken as a Hebrew figure of speech. For here he used "flesh" to mean "man," just as earlier he used "soul": "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers," and so forth. **In his sight.** In the Greek it is "of God," instead of "his." And indeed we find it written this way in Chrysostom and Theophylact. Although the Greek manuscripts vary. For there are those that have αὐτοῦ ["his"], instead of Θεοῦ ["of God"]: though this matters very little to the meaning.

**36 But from him**] Ἐξ αὐτοῦ δὲ, can be taken as, "For from the same": that is, neither from the rich, nor from the wise: but without distinction from the same. It would be smoother if the article "the same" <note>original: "τὸ αὐτὸ"</note> were added. Even if Ambrose refers it to the Father, as does Theophylact: so that the meaning is, "There is no reason for one to hate or despise another, you were all born from the same Father, namely as children of God: and that through Christ." In this place Theophylact clearly indicates that the preposition "from" <note>original: "ex"</note> is placed instead of "through" <note>original: "dia"</note>, which we have also indicated elsewhere.

**37 Who was made for us**] This sounds the same in Greek as if you said, "he began to be wisdom for us," or "he was made wisdom for us," ὃς ἐγενήθη ἡμῖν σοφία. Like that phrase, "he was made before me," that is, "he began to be before me." "Who was made for us wisdom." After "wisdom," the Greeks have ἀπὸ Θεοῦ, that is, "from God": which is not read in some of our manuscripts, though it is found in Ambrose and in the Pauline manuscript. Ambrose also interprets it, and Theophylact likewise indicates it was added not without cause, "from God." Let no one doubt that in our copies where it is missing, it was omitted through the negligence of scribes.

**38 So that as it is written**] There is no doubt but that it is from the ninth chapter of Jeremiah: "Thus says the Lord, Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, and let not the strong man boast in his strength, and let not the rich man boast in his riches: but in this let him boast who boasts, that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord who does mercy and judgment and justice on the earth; for these things please me, says the Lord."

**II. 1 In loftiness**] καθ' ὑπεροχὴν, that is, according to excellence: for Ambrose used this word. Nor is it "in" among the Greeks, but κατὰ, "according to," or something similar. Ambrose reads "with excellence." The Pauline codex had "through loftiness of speech."

**2 The testimony of Christ**] It is "of God" among the Greeks, not "of Christ": and this is clear from the interpretation of Theophylact: "Of God," he says, "about to pronounce the testimony to you, that is, the death of Christ." Ambrose reads, "preaching to you the mystery of God": nor does he only read it thus, but also interprets it. Thus he seems to have used a different Greek manuscript, since among them there is some affinity between the words *martyrion* [testimony] and *mysterion* [mystery].

**3 For I did not judge myself to know**] Οὐ γὰρ ἔκρινα τοῦ εἰδέναι τὶ, that is, "For I did not judge so as to know anything." Perhaps "I judged" refers to the plan for coming. Indeed, the Greek interpreters distribute the force of this article *tou*, which is placed before the infinitive verb. Or, what is more pleasing, he used "judged" for "estimated": as in the previous Epistle, "One man judges day from day." The sense, therefore, will be, "I did not estimate myself to be of any value, because of the fact that I knew something among you," and so forth. For where a cause is signified, the word *heneka* [for the sake of] is usually understood in these, so the sense is "for the sake of knowing." Certainly, Hilary, in the tenth book *On the Trinity*, citing this passage, does not add the pronoun "myself."

**4 Not in persuasive things**] ἐν πειθοῖς, that is, in suasive things, and those suited for persuading: and *kopia* [labor] often signifies doctrine, as we have already warned.

**5 In the demonstration of the spirit**] ἐν ἀποδείξει, which almost sounds like "display." For rhetoricians call *apodeixeis* those speeches which they recite to audiences for the sake of displaying their talent: of which kind some by Lucian and Apuleius exist. Mathematicians also use the term *apodeixeis* [proofs].
