<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed philological and theological commentary on Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians. Following the previous page’s discussion on the "foolishness" of the Cross, Erasmus now examines the nature of "hidden wisdom" and the distinction between worldly rulers and those enlightened by the Spirit.</meta>

# PAUL’S LETTER CHAPTER II.

->**THE BIBLE TEXT IN GREEK**<-

<margin>6</margin> <margin>v. 7</margin> <margin>v. 8</margin> <margin>v. 9</margin> <margin>v. 10</margin> <margin>v. 11</margin> <margin>v. 12</margin> <margin>v. 13</margin> Yet we speak wisdom among the mature <note>original Greek: "en tois teleiois"</note>; but a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing. But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom, which God predestined before the ages for our glory, which none of the rulers of this age knew; for if they had known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. But as it is written: "Things which eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and which have not entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love Him." But God revealed them to us through His Spirit; for the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him? Even so, no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. Now we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we might know the things freely given to us by God, which things we also speak, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in those taught by the Holy Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual.

---

**THE COMMENTARY OF ERASMUS**

<margin>A</margin> *Demonstration* <note>original: "deixē"</note>, is used where people show a thing with pictures; and Logicians call a syllogism that gathers a certain matter from first principles a "demonstration" <note>original: "apodeixin"</note>. Paul, however, calls "wisdom" that which he himself presents and declares as a "demonstration of the spirit."

6 **But wisdom.**] From this passage it appears what Paul meant when he attributed "foolishness" to God—namely, in comparison to this wisdom, which he spoke of among the "mature" <note>or "perfect"</note>. This is so that no one thinks that other sentiment we reviewed in the previous chapter should be entirely rejected.

7 **Nor of the Rulers of this age.**] *The Rulers* <note>original: "archontōn"</note>. Some have interpreted these as Demons, though Chrysostom and Theophylact both object to this. They instead explain them as Philosophers, Orators, and the learned who once governed the Republic. For Origen’s view <margin>B</margin> in his fourth Homily on Matthew—that the "Rulers of this age" are the Demons to whom the Father handed over the Son for the salvation of the human race, through whom He was then handed into the hands of wicked men—strikes me as a bit forced, even though that opinion pleased Ambrose. Furthermore, what the Orators and Philosophers were among the Pagans, the Scribes and Pharisees were among the Jews. The phrase *who are being destroyed* <note>original: "katargoumenōn"</note> seems to refer to both: that is, to the age and to the rulers who are abolished. Thus we understand that both are to be abolished: both this age and the Rulers of this age.

8 **In a mystery, which is hidden.**] In the Greek, the word *hidden* does not depend on the words immediately preceding it, as if he said "recondite in a mystery." Rather, he says: "We speak, not openly or everywhere, so as not to cause offense, but in secret; nor among just anyone, so as not to cast roses before swine, but among the mature. Nor do we speak just any wisdom which other Philosophers profess publicly, but that arcane and recondite, and, so to speak, ancient wisdom." This is proven by the Greek article added to the participle: *the hidden* <note>original: "tēn apokekrymmenēn"</note>. This seems to be how whoever translated Origen’s books *Against Celsus* read it. For he cites the testimony this way: *But we speak wisdom among the mature, yet a wisdom not of this age, nor of the Rulers of this world who are destroyed, but we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, which is hidden, which he predefined...* and so on. Augustine reads it no differently in Bede’s collections, except that in the Greek it is "which [wisdom] is hidden" (feminine), not "that which is hidden" (neuter). <margin>C</margin> <margin>D</margin> Jerome cites it the same way in his preface to the third Commentary on the Letter to the Galatians: *But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, which is hidden.* And I found it written this way in a very ancient Pauline manuscript. Both manuscripts supplied to us from Constance agreed. Ambrose cites this passage no differently in his third book *On the Faith*, chapter three. For it is fitting that things which are secret are not poured out openly, but communicated in secret to those who are worthy.

9 **Never the Lord of glory.**] The Greek says *not at all* <note>original: "ouk an"</note>. This could have seemed changed by the carelessness of scribes if there were not such great consensus among our manuscripts.

10 **As it is written.**] *But as it is written* <note>original: "Alla kathōs gegraptai"</note>. That is, "but as it is written," so that the conjunction connects the speech with what came before: "We do not speak the wisdom of this world, but we speak those things which neither eye has seen, nor ear," etc. Furthermore, what immediately precedes, *which God predefined* <note>original: "hēn proōrisen"</note>, is more correctly "prepared" or "pre-ordained"—namely, to be revealed in its own time, so they would not think the matter was a recent invention.

11 **What eye has not seen.**] Lorenzo Valla rightly advises that the singular verb *descended* <note>referring to "entered into the heart"</note> should have been translated as plural because of the neuter noun. And Saint Jerome cites it this way in several places, especially *Against Rufinus*: they *ascended* <note>original: "adscenderunt"</note>, not *it ascended* <note>original: "adscendit/anebē"</note>, and *the things which* <note>plural</note>, not *that which* <note>singular</note>. I found the same writing in another manuscript from Constantinople of wonderful antiquity. However, the relative pronoun *the things which* <note>original: "ha"</note> at the start of the sentence is more troublesome, for it renders the sentence incomplete in both Latin and Greek, unless it is understood as: "These are the sorts of things which you have prepared." Though similar constructions can be found elsewhere in Paul, unless the Translator read *that* <note>original: "hoti"</note> instead of *the things which*, or unless someone added the conjunction *that* on their own, or unless one prefers what we just indicated. Lefèvre d’Étaples seems to have read *which* <note>original: "han"</note> for *the things which* <note>original: "ha"</note>. But I see that *the things which* refers back to what precedes: "None of the rulers of this age knew it, but God revealed it to us." Furthermore, Paul took this testimony from the sixty-fourth chapter of Isaiah, expressing the truth of the meaning more than counting the words. For there, according to the Hebrew truth:

<column-break/>

6. <margin>v. 6</margin> of God. Moreover, we speak wisdom among the mature: yet a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are abolished:
7. <margin>v. 7</margin> But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, which is hidden, which God predefined before the ages for our glory,
8. <margin>v. 8</margin> Which none of the rulers of this age knew: for if they had known, they would by no means have crucified the Lord of glory.
9. <margin>v. 9</margin> But as it is written: The things which eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and have not ascended into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him.
10. <margin>v. 10</margin> But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit: for the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God.
11. <margin>v. 11</margin> For what man knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him? So also the things of God no one knows, except the Spirit of God.
12. <margin>v. 12</margin> Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things that are given to us by Christ,
13. <margin>v. 13</margin> Which things we also speak, not in words which human wisdom teaches, but which the Holy Spirit teaches, comparing spiritual things with spiritual.

---

<margin>A</margin> <margin>B</margin> ...it is read this way: *From the age they have not heard, nor perceived with ears. Eye has not seen, O God, besides you, what you have prepared for those who wait for you.* The Apostle seems to have read, *for those who love him* <note>Hebrew: "l’chakeh lo"</note>, using the letter *beth*, from the verb *chakah*, which means "to love vehemently." The Seventy <note>The Septuagint translators</note> however read it with the letter *caph*, from the verb *chakah*, meaning "to wait." Additionally, in the Hebrew there is the third-person pronoun *lo*, just as in the Apostle’s Greek *autō* <note>"for him/himself"</note>.

12 **To those who love him.**] *To those loving him* <note>original: "tois agapōsin auton"</note>, that is, to those who love him. In the Septuagint, not only are the words different, but the sense itself differs greatly from this; for it is read: *From the age we have not heard, nor have our eyes seen a God besides you, and your works, which you will do for those who await mercy.* Hilary cites it this way in the fifth book of *On the Trinity*. Because of this, some sought this passage in the Apocrypha of the Jews, but Jerome strongly disagrees. Indeed, this is one of the few passages Paul cited from the "Hebrew truth" <note>the original Hebrew text</note>, though he expressed the sense more than he matched the words.

13 **Even the deep things of God.**] *And the depths* <note>original: "kai ta bathē"</note>, that is, even the profundities. Though this matters little to the overall meaning.

14 **For who of men knows the things of a man.**] *The things of the man* <note>original: "ta tou anthrōpou"</note>. Augustine explained this elegantly in the first book of *The City of God*. It could be translated as *what is happening in a man*, or *the state of a man*, or *the affairs of a man*. <margin>C</margin> <margin>D</margin>

15 **But in the teaching of the Spirit.**] The Greek has it thus: *not in words taught by human wisdom, but in those taught by the Holy Spirit*, where you should understand "words" to be implied. In this passage, "taught" <note>original: "didaktois"</note> is an adjective, not a participle; and the possessive "of wisdom" refers more to "taught" than to "words." You might say, "not in the clever words of human wisdom, but in the words skilled in the Spirit"—that is, words that possess the teaching of the Spirit, which comes by divine inspiration. In a few Greek manuscripts, it was written "teaching-ly" <note>original: "didaktikōs"</note>; Paul uses this word elsewhere in an active sense, as in the second chapter of the second letter to Timothy: *ready and inclined toward teaching everyone*. You could read it the same way here: not in words that teach human wisdom, but in those that teach the Spirit of God. But it is more proven to me that we should understand the Apostles’ speech here as not consisting of human doctrine, but of divine inspiration. For such people are called *taught* <note>original: "didaktoi"</note>, that is, divinely taught. Although this is somewhat harsh outside of a compound word, John used it this way in the sixth chapter of his Gospel: *And they shall all be taught by God.* In that place, it is certain that those divinely inspired are meant. Ambrose expresses the sense more than he translates the words, reading it this way: *Not in the doctrine of the words of human wisdom, but in the doctrine of the Spirit.* Theophylact, following Chrysostom, feels that the things Paul said were from the Spirit. Augustine, expressing this, reads in his 150th letter: *Not in the taught words of human wisdom, but taught by the Spirit.* What will certain Theologians say here—those who, in their own eyes, sound like nothing but Aristotelian philosophy when delivering the Sacred Scriptures?

16 **Comparing spiritual things.**] *Comparing* <note>original: "synkrinontes"</note>, that is, conferring or composing; let no one take "comparing" to mean "preparing." For "spiritual things" does not refer to people, but to things: Paul thought it fitting to match spiritual eloquence to spiritual things, lest it seem absurd for that heavenly philosophy to be commended by human ornaments of words. As for Theophylact’s suggestion that this refers to comparing the sacraments of the Gospel with the sacraments of the Old Testament—while I admit that is true, I don't think it fits the meaning of this passage. Chrysostom’s writings are more appropriate here, confirming that the Gospel is not the work of human philosophy, but that Scripture is sufficient for itself. For example, to prove that Christ was born of a virgin or rose from the dead, one should not use the reasons of Philosophers, but either the oracles and types of the Old Testament, or miracles. He who created trees in paradise without seed, who created Adam from clay, Eve from the man’s rib, and the earth from nothing—it was easy for Him to create a human body from a virgin’s substance or return a dead man to life. For whatever is in the Scriptures is spiritual, because it was produced by the same Spirit.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s meticulous philological analysis of 1 Corinthians. # TO THE CORINTHIANS I. CAP. III.

<margin>14 17</margin> But the natural man <note>original Greek: "psychikos," referring to the person governed by the soul or human reason alone</note> does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he is not able to know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
<margin>15</margin> But he who is spiritual discerns all things, yet he himself is discerned by no one.
<margin>16</margin> For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct Him? But we have the mind of Christ.
<margin>III. 1</margin> And I, brothers, was not able to speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to carnal people, as to infants in Christ.
<margin>2</margin> I gave you milk to drink, and not solid food; for you were not yet able to receive it, nor are you even now able;
<margin>3</margin> For you are still carnal. For where there is jealousy among you, and strife, and divisions, are you not carnal, and walking according to the manner of men?
<margin>4</margin> For when one says, "I am of Paul," and another, "I am of Apollos," are you not carnal?
<margin>5 B</margin> Who then is Paul? and who is Apollos? But ministers through whom you believed, even as the Lord gave to each.
<margin>6</margin> I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase.
<margin>7</margin> So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.
<margin>8</margin> Now he who plants and he who waters are one; and each will receive his own reward according to his own labor.
<margin>9</margin> For we are God’s fellow-workers; you are God’s field, you are God’s building.
<margin>10</margin> According to the grace of God which was given to me, as a wise master builder I have laid the foundation, and another builds upon it. But let each one take heed how he builds upon it.
<margin>11</margin> For no other foundation can anyone lay than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.

<margin>17 C</margin> 17 **But the natural man**] <note>original Greek: "Psychikos"</note>. As if following the "soul," that is, human emotions. Indeed, since Paul divides man into three parts—flesh, soul, and spirit—he seems here to have used the word "soul" in place of "flesh."
18 **For it is foolishness to him**] In Greek, this should have been translated in the plural <note>meaning "they (the things of the Spirit) are foolishness"</note>, so that you understand that the things of the Spirit are foolishness to him. The Translator was deceived by a singular verb, which was used here in place of the plural.
19 **They are spiritually examined**] <note>original Greek: "anakrinetai"</note>, that is, they are judged or discerned. This word is translated more frequently as "judged" shortly thereafter. Again, here "examined" should have been said in the plural number, so that you understand the preceding subject: namely, the things that are of the spirit. Unless the word "that" <note>original Greek: "hoti"</note> is an article rather than a conjunction, in which case the sense would be: "He cannot understand that those things are spiritually discerned, since he is himself carnal." However, Ambrose accepts it in the singular number.
<margin>20 D</margin> 20 **As it is written, For who has known**] I do not find "As it is written" in the Greek codices, nor in the very ancient codex of Donatianus. Both codices were compared with the one sent from Constantinople. Furthermore, the testimony cited at the end is found in Isaiah, chapter forty. Though Paul expressed the sense rather than quoting the words exactly. Indeed, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament</note> translated it in this way, as Jerome points out: <gloss>Who has known the mind of the Lord, and who has been His counselor?</gloss> <note>original Greek: "Tis egnō noun Kyriou, kai tis autou symboulos egeneto"</note>. According to the Hebrew truth, Jerome translated it thus: <gloss>Who has aided the Spirit of the Lord? or who was His counselor?</gloss> and showed them one who might instruct and teach Him? Furthermore, where Paul says "shall instruct" <note>original Greek: "symbibasei"</note>, Theophylactus, following Chrysostom, interprets it as "shall teach" <note>original Greek: "didaxei"</note>, that is, shall correct or reprove; which I do not entirely approve of. Moreover, where Jerome translates "aided" and Paul "known," the Hebrew is <term>יָדַע</term> <note>yada - to know</note>. Where Jerome translates "Spirit" and Paul "mind," the Hebrew is <term>רוּחַ</term> <note>ruach - spirit/wind</note>.
<margin>21 E</margin> 21 **Or who has instructed him**] <note>original Greek: "hos symbibasei auton"</note>, that is, who shall instruct or teach him? The Donatian codex had "who may instruct him," not differing much from the Greek. Both of the Constantinian copies support this. Although it is ambiguous in Greek whether the pronoun "who" refers to the "mind" or to the "Lord." Yet I myself would prefer to read it in the sense that everyone else reads: <gloss>Who has known the mind of the Lord? Who is there to instruct Him?</gloss> To make this clearer, they explained it using a disjunctive conjunction. It might seem to refer to that sentiment in the ninth chapter of the Book of Wisdom: <gloss>For what man can know the counsel of God? or who can think what the will of God is?</gloss> and a little later, <gloss>And who shall know your sense?</gloss> except that among the Hebrews the Book of Wisdom is outside the canon. Therefore it is better, as we have shown, to refer the testimony to Isaiah.
22 **But we have the sense**] <note>original Greek: "noun"</note>, that is, the mind. "We hold" fits better than "we have," so that we may understand that the mind of the Lord is known to the perfect.
<margin>1 F</margin> **As if to spiritual people**] The Greek <note>original Greek: "hōs"</note> is used everywhere; which the translator sometimes renders as "as if" and sometimes as "as." It would have been better to translate it as "as" everywhere. Although here the speech is somewhat grammatically imperfect; it would have been complete if he had said, "I could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but I had to speak to you as to carnal people."
2 **As to little ones in Christ**] <note>original Greek: "hōs nēpiois"</note>. The word for "little one" <note>nēpios</note> signifies an infant who is still very small, foolish, and lacking in prudence, primarily due to age. He could therefore have said, "to infants in Christ." Furthermore, the dative here, "to little ones," belongs to what precedes, that is, to the "speaking," not to what follows, "I gave you milk to drink," as is clear from the Greek. And thus the distinction is preserved in the most ancient Latin...

<margin>14</margin> 17 The natural man, however, does not accept those things which are of the Spirit of God, 18 for they are foolishness to him, nor can he know them, because 19 they are spiritually discerned.
<margin>15</margin> But the spiritual person discerns all things, yet he himself is discerned by no one.
<margin>16</margin> 20 For who has known the mind of the Lord, 21 that he might give counsel to Him?
<margin>22</margin> But we hold the mind of Christ.
<margin>III. 1</margin> And I, brothers, could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but I had to speak to you as to carnal people, 2 as to infants in Christ. I fed you with a drink of milk, 3 and not with food; for you were not yet able, 4 indeed even now you are not yet able: For you are still carnal.
<margin>3</margin> Since there is among you jealousy, and strife, and factions, 6 are you not carnal, and walking according to the manner of man?

<margin>10</margin> 13 As a wise master builder I have laid the foundation, but another builds upon it; let each one see how he builds upon it.
<margin>11</margin> For no one can lay another foundation...

---

...copies of the Latin: <gloss>I could not speak to you as if to spiritual people, but as if to carnal people, as to infants in Christ.</gloss> If this distinction is preferred, the words "I had to speak" must be understood.
3 **Not meat** <note>or "not solid food"</note>] Either a misuse of terms <note>Greek: "akyrologia"</note> must be tolerated, or something must be understood. The Greek <gloss>I gave you milk to drink, and not food</gloss> <note>original Greek: "Gala hymas epotisa, kai ou brōma"</note> literally sounds like "I gave you milk to drink, and not food." But who gives a person food to drink? Hence Theophylactus, explaining this, adds the word "redundant" <note>original Greek: "perittton"</note>, so that this applies to the food. To avoid this absurdity of speech, we have translated it thus: *I fed you with a drink of milk, not with food*. In the older Constantinian codex it was simply, *I gave you milk, not food*.
4 **But not even now can you**] <note>original Greek: "all’ oute eti nyn dynasthe"</note>, that is, "nay, not even yet now are you able." Although this changes nothing of the meaning.
5 **Jealousy and strife**] The Greeks put it this way: <gloss>zeal and strife and divisions</gloss> <note>original Greek: "zēlos kai eris kai dichostasiai"</note>, that is, emulation, discord, and sedition.
6 **Are you not men**] And here, instead of "men," the Greeks have "carnal" <note>original Greek: "sarkikoi"</note>. Nevertheless, in our more corrected copies I find it written "carnal," as in the Paulinian codex, with both Constantinian codices agreeing. And it is cited this way by Augustine, frequently elsewhere and in the fourth chapter of his book *On Continence*, just as we read among the Greeks; Ambrose also agrees with the Greeks. For shortly after follows, *and you walk according to man*: a part that would fit poorly with the preceding *you are men*, as the same thing would be said twice. Yet a little later he does call them "men," wanting the same thing to be understood: *I am of Paul, and I am of Apollos, are you not men?*
7 **What then is Apollos**] In Greek it is "Who," not "What" <note>original Greek: "Tis"</note>; but all our Latin copies disagree. I do not know if the Greeks read it incorrectly, especially since it follows, *therefore neither he who plants is anything*. He used "What" <note>quid</note> to mean "of what importance," as elsewhere he says, *the things that are not*, for things of no value. His interpretation indicates that Chrysostom read it this way. And "Apollo" is in the nominative case <note>Erasmus notes the Greek form "Apollōs"</note>.
8 **And to each as the Lord gave**] <note>original Greek: "all’ ē diakonoi, di’ hōn episteusate"</note>, that is, *except ministers, through whom you believed*; that is, not the authors of your faith, but only ministers. And we find this reading in Chrysostom and Theophylactus. It matters little to the sense.
9 **And to each as the Lord gave**] This speech is somewhat incomplete unless you read, *just as the Lord gave to each*. We pointed out a similar case in the twelfth chapter of the Epistle to the Romans: <gloss>And to each as God divided the measure of faith.</gloss>
10 **They are one**] <note>original Greek: "hen eisin"</note>, that is, they are the same, and there is no distinction between them. Inasmuch as each is doing someone else's business, not his own, so that people should not take their names from them as authors, nor be divided by factions among themselves. But if Saint Paul is so indignant toward the Corinthians because they took the names of those from whom they received baptism and were first initiated into the mysteries of Christ, **what would he say of the factions of our own time**, who are divided among themselves by a thousand surnames, a thousand styles of dress, ceremonies, and rules—those who are called "the religious"? <note>Erasmus is attacking the various religious orders (Franciscans, Dominicans, etc.) whose partisan loyalties he felt undermined Christian unity.</note> I do not care to mention here how much Christian concord is born among us from such things.
11 **For we are God's helpers**] <note>original Greek: "synergoi"</note>. Augustine reads "fellow-workers." Ambrose reads "participants in the work," as if explaining the Greek word.
12 **God's agriculture**] <note>original Greek: "Theou geōrgion"</note>, that is, God's tilling or husbandry. Among the Greeks, the verb "you are" is only placed in the next part of the sentence, *you are God's building*. And Ambrose reads it this way.
13 **As a wise architect**] <note>original Greek: "architektōn"</note>, the one who is the leader and author of the construction. For in laying a foundation, the greatest effort is required. Here he clearly used "expert" to mean "learned and skillful."

<summary>Erasmus provides a detailed linguistic analysis of 1 Corinthians 2:14–3:11, focusing on the Greek terms for "natural" versus "spiritual" man and the metaphor of the Church as a building. Most notably, he uses Paul's critique of Apollos/Paul factions to launch a sharp attack on the divisive religious orders of the 16th century.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s philological and theological commentary on 1 Corinthians Chapter 3. Having established that Christ is the only foundation, Erasmus now examines Paul’s metaphor of building materials and the "testing fire," navigating through various patristic interpretations to determine if this passage refers to Purgatory, the quality of apostolic teaching, or moral conduct.</meta>

# EPISTLE OF PAUL CAP. III.
## PAGE 671

<margin>12</margin> [which is] laid, which is Jesus Christ. But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, <margin>13</margin> precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each one’s work will become manifest; for the Day will declare it, because it is revealed in fire; and the fire will test what sort each one's <margin>14</margin> work is. If anyone’s work which he built remains, he will receive a reward. <margin>15</margin> If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire. <margin>16</margin> Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells <margin>17</margin> in you? If anyone destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him; for the temple of God is holy, which you are. <margin>18</margin> Let no one deceive himself; if anyone among you thinks he is wise in this age, let him become a fool, so that he may become wise. <margin>19</margin> For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God; for it is written—

---

<margin>14 Hay, stubble]</margin> <note>original Greek: *kalamēn*</note>, that is, a stalk or straw. It should be noted in passing that he said *gold, silver, and precious stones* pertain to the pious, while *wood, hay, stubble* pertain to wicked deeds: as is clear from the first book of Jerome against Jovinian. For to the three things that will endure in fire, he opposed three that will perish if fire falls upon them. Origen likewise cited this in his sixth Homily on Exodus: *For the way of acting well,* he says, *is threefold. Nevertheless, something is driven toward the good either in action, or in thought, or in word. The Apostle also signifies this when he says, "But he who builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones," indicating a threefold way of good things: he likewise adds a threefold way of evil things when he says, "wood, hay, stubble."* He said these things because there are those who refer these not to bad and good works, but to degrees of good works. Nor is it particularly relevant to bring in a mention of purgatory here. Since the "day of the Lord" stands for a clear inspection of the work. For at night even things that are ugly can be pleasing, and things that are beautiful can be displeasing, but the judgments of the day are more certain. Furthermore, he used *fire* as a metaphor for an exact testing. Indeed, Ambrose also noted that it was not said, *he shall be saved through fire*, but *as if through fire* <note>original Latin: "quasi per ignem"</note>, so that you may understand it as a comparison, not the thing itself. Yet they say that in the lower regions there is true, material fire. Finally, this sense is not displeasing to Gregory—that by fire we should understand temporal affliction—following Saint Augustine, as it appears, who interprets *wood, hay, and stubble* as the love of temporal things remaining alongside sincere faith, and the fire as the distress of losing those things which they wrongly loved, making mention neither of Gehenna <note>Hell</note> nor of purgatory. Nor is it new in the Scriptures for fire to be taken as the affliction of this life, as in the Psalms: *We passed through fire and water, and you led us out into a place of refreshment.* But if anyone should insist that by fire one must understand the punishments of Gehenna or purgatory, how can those who built above with gold and precious stones be said to be tested by fire, as well as those who built above with wood, hay, and stubble? He is forced into this because some interpret wood, hay, and stubble as venial sins <note><term>venialia</term>: minor sins that do not cause the death of the soul</note>: so that stubble signifies the lightest of all faults, to which they oppose lead. But lead is less heavy than gold, and is purified by fire just as gold is. Now, since the Greek has <term>kalamēn</term>, that is, a stalk, what persuaded these men that a stalk is lighter than hay? Or how did it happen that, while in the order of good things the best holds the first place and the cheapest the last, in the order of evil things that which is least evil holds the extreme place? Therefore, by the word "fire," an exact judgment is signified, which, once it has revealed an error, is followed by the affliction of repentance. This sense agrees with the saying in the first chapter of the first Epistle of Peter, *That the testing of your faith may be more precious than gold, which is tested by fire.* Likewise the Gospel sentiment concerning those who believe for a time, but in the time of temptation fall away. Nor am I unaware that this place is twisted into various meanings by both ancient and modern writers, especially Thomas [Aquinas], all of which it is not my purpose to examine. To me, the simplest view is most pleasing: if we understand it as the doctrine of the Apostles succeeding Paul. He had laid a good foundation; let the others, he says, see what they build upon it. If the work is worthy of Christ, it will endure, even when viewed in the light: but if they have added Judaism, they will indeed deceive for a time, but their imposture will be laid bare as soon as they begin to be weighed by true judgment. And he who followed this will have wasted his effort, and will be forced, once what was built is destroyed, to build something else above. This is what happened among the Romans and Galatians, whom Paul again labored to bring forth for Christ. And Saint Ambrose follows this opinion, lest anyone suspect it to be my own dream: *The work,* he says, *which is said to burn, is bad doctrine.* Likewise, in the words that follow, he interprets the punishment of fire as the burning up and refutation of false doctrine. And a little later: *But when he says,* he says, *it is as if through fire, he shows that the man will indeed be saved, but will suffer the punishments of fire, so that being purified through fire he may be saved, and not like the faithless be tortured in eternal fire forever, so that in some part it may have been worthwhile to have believed in Christ. For he who sees that he has defended falsehood as truth must always be ashamed. And in a similar way, he always had confidence in God who, having cast aside the false, followed the truth.* From these points it is clear that Ambrose does not feel this refers to the fire of purgatory in the lower regions, but to the correction of this life, and to the shame that follows a recognized error. From Ambrose's commentary, the one whose notes exist on all the Pauline Epistles under the name of Jerome does not entirely disagree. Theophylactus interprets it regarding the degrees of good and evil works, suggesting that to others "wood" signifies commissions of lighter fault, "hay" more serious ones, and "stubble" the most serious—or to others, the reverse. In the order of good things he gave the first place to gold, the next to silver, the third to precious stones—for he was thinking of marbles

<column-break/>

## PAGE 672

<margin>A</margin> [can anyone] lay, besides that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. But if anyone builds upon <margin>12</margin> this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, <margin>13</margin> hay, stubble, each one's work will become manifest: <margin>14</margin> for the Day will declare it, because it is revealed in fire: and <margin>15</margin> the fire will test what sort each one's work is. If anyone's <margin>14</margin> work remains, which he built upon it, he will receive a reward. If anyone's work is burned up, he will suffer loss: <margin>15</margin> but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire. Do <margin>16</margin> you not know that you are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone profanes the temple of God, <margin>17</margin> God will destroy him: for the temple of God is holy, which you are. Let no one deceive himself: if anyone <margin>B</margin> seems to himself to be wise among you, let him become a fool in this age, that he may be made wise. For the wisdom of this <margin>19</margin> world is foolishness with God: for it is written, <margin>21</margin> He who

---

and such things, I believe, not regarding gems, with which no one constructs a building. It is consistent that the same order be preserved in those things which do not endure fire. So that doctrine departing slightly from the truth is "wood," that which is further away is "hay," and that which is furthest is "straw." John Chrysostom seizes the occasion from this passage of the Apostle to prove that Gehenna is eternal, because at that time it appears there were many who believed the punishments of Gehenna would have some end—an error they drank from the Origenists—and in this confidence they sinned more licentiously. To strike terror into them, he twists this discourse of the Apostle to mean that by the foundation we should understand faith, and by the superstructures good or evil works. Truly he does this with arguments lacking solidity, so that this commentary is scarcely likely to be Chrysostom's. He wants the Apostle by these words to pave the way for attacking the lusts of the Corinthians: and from <margin>C</margin> these same words he gathers the eternity of punishments, from which more recent writers gather the opposite sense. *"He himself will be saved, but so as if through fire."* How can they be pronounced as "going to be saved" who are handed over to eternal death, which is Gehenna? Here this ingenious man excuses it by saying that Scripture sometimes misuses words declaring evil in a good sense, just as we read of a "desirable captivity" and a "good mortification." Likewise, he wants it understood here that "saved through fire" means he will be tortured in fire, but will not be consumed by fire. Who does not see immediately that this commentary is harsh? For who speaks like this: *"He will be saved, but so as if through fire,"* in place of what should be: "he will be tortured by eternal fire, but he himself will not be consumed"? What, then, does that exception do—*"but so as if through fire"?* Or who in an entire discourse [uses the term "saved"] in some way or other, but not without torture? Furthermore, what does <term>dēlōsei</term> <note>will declare/reveal</note> mean, a word which declares a similarity, not a reality? It seems likely to me either that these things were added by another, or that Chrysostom misused this interpretation to terrify a stiff-necked people. Yet in the meantime, no mention of purgatory is made there. Moreover, to note this in passing, the Apostle seems to allude to a passage in Isaiah <margin>D</margin> chapter one: *And your strength shall be as the spark of tow, and your work as a spark, and they shall both burn.* Both signify that empty confidence will perish when the work in which one trusted is taken away.

<margin>15 For the Day of the Lord]</margin> "Of the Lord" was added by a scribe or by a translator wishing to make the speech clearer, since it is not among the Greeks, and thus it was not written in Paul's original copy, but some clever person had added it in the margin with a different hand. Theophylactus neither reads nor interprets it, even if the Latin translator added this on his own. The night of ignorance hides many things; the day uncovers them—namely, when the breaking and flashing truth declares itself by facts and the things themselves. But yet the article almost requires that it be understood as a certain day: *hē gar hēmera*, as if you were to say, "for *that* day."

<margin>16 It is revealed in fire]</margin> "Is revealed" <note>apokalyptetai</note> is in the present tense, so that the sense is absolute: every work is made clear by fire. For the two future-tense verbs correspond to each other: *"will declare and will test"*; however, *"is revealed"* is joined to the previous verb: <margin>E</margin> *"for that day will declare"*, that the work of this or that man is opened and made manifest for what it is through fire. Indeed, the Translator put "because" [quia] for "that" [quòd]: although among the Greeks it is not clear whether the conjunction is *hoti* [because/that], or a relative pronoun for *ho, ti* [whatever].

<margin>17 The work of each one]</margin> Here Ambrose reads: *"he who does this work shall be manifest"*: if indeed the manuscript is free of error.

<margin>18 He will suffer loss]</margin> <note>original Greek: *zēmiōthēsetai*</note>, that is, he will be affected by damage. They will obtain pardon somehow if they repent, but those who have wasted their labor will carry away no reward.

<margin>19 If anyone violates, God will destroy]</margin> <note>original Greek: *Phtheirei, phtherei*</note>, that is: he destroys, He will destroy—a pleasant wordplay [allusion]. And the Translator varied the same word, but rightly so, because the wordplay would not correspond among the Latins. For to the Greeks *phtheirei* is "I corrupt," as a virgin is corrupted, or a sacred thing; it is also "I destroy." For I would rather the wordplay perish than what Hilary translated in his commentary on Psalm 64: *"If anyone corrupts the temple of God, God will also corrupt him."* And Augustine testifies that this was the earlier reading in his book *Against the Epistle of Manichaeus*, chapter 39: but that the Reader, offended by the word "corrupt," changed it to "destroy," although he admits the Greeks have "corrupt."

<margin>20 Which you are]</margin> <note>original Greek: *hoitines este hymeis*</note>, that is, "who you are": just as a little above, "which is Christ Jesus," or "who is Christ Jesus": as I find in the oldest copies. However, this changes nothing of the sense. The testimony is brought from Job chapter five.

<margin>21 Let him become a fool that he may be wise]</margin> Since the Greek has *genesthō* and *ginetai*, perhaps both should have been translated with the same verb: *"let him become a fool, so that he may become wise"*; or *"let him become a fool, so that he might be wise."*

<summary>Erasmus provides a philological analysis of 1 Corinthians 3, debating whether the "testing fire" refers to Purgatory, as some contemporaries argued, or to the testing of apostolic doctrine and the shame of error, as he and several Church Fathers conclude.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s annotations on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, moving from the conclusion of Chapter 3 into the opening of Chapter 4. Having discussed the "foundation" of Christ and the "fire" of judgment, he now focuses on the humility required of teachers and the specific Greek idioms used by Saint Paul, which Erasmus often defends against those who demand classical purity from the biblical text.</meta>

# TO THE CORINTHIANS I. CHAPTER IV.
## PAGE 673, 674

<margin>20</margin> For it is written: He catches the wise in their <margin>21</margin> craftiness. And again: The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile. Therefore, let no one boast in men; for <margin>22</margin> all things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, <margin>23</margin> or things present, or things to come; all are yours, <margin>IV. 1</margin> and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s. Let a man <margin>2</margin> so account us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover, it is required <margin>3</margin> in stewards that one be found faithful. But to me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by a human day; indeed, I do not even judge <margin>4</margin> myself. For I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not justified by this; but He who judges me <margin>5</margin> is the Lord. Therefore, judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of the hearts; and then each one’s praise will come from God. <margin>6</margin> Now these things, brothers, I have figuratively applied to myself and Apollos for your sakes, that you may learn in us not to think beyond what is written, that none of you may be <margin>7</margin> puffed up on behalf of one against the other. For who distinguishes you? And what do you have that you did not receive? Now if you did receive it, why do you boast—

<column-break/>

<margin>A 19</margin> Who catches the wise in their own craftiness. <margin>20</margin> And again, The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain. Therefore let no one glory in <margin>21</margin> men: for all things are yours, whether Paul, or <margin>22</margin> Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come: all, I say, are <margin>23</margin> yours, and you are Christ’s, but Christ is God’s. <margin>B IV. 1</margin> Let a man so estimate us as ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God. <margin>2</margin> What remains, however, is that it is required in stewards that a man be found faithful. But to me it is for the least, that I should be judged <margin>3</margin> by you, or by human judgment; nay, I do not even judge myself. <margin>4</margin> For I am conscious to myself of nothing, but I am not justified by this: but he who judges <margin>5</margin> me is the Lord. Therefore do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both illuminate the secrets of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of hearts, and then praise shall be to every man from God. Now these things, <margin>6</margin> brethren, I have transferred in a figure to myself and to Apollos for your sakes, that in us you might learn, <margin>7</margin> that no one should think of himself above that which is written, so that you be not puffed up, this one in the name of that one, or that one in the name of this, one against another. <margin>8</margin> For who judges you? what have you, that you did not receive? but if you did receive it, why do you glory, as if [you had] not

---

<margin>22</margin> *I will catch*] <note>original Greek: Ho drassomenos</note>, that is, *The one who catches*. For <term>drassesthai</term> <note>to catch/clutch</note> means to overtake someone fleeing in a race and to grab them by laying a hand upon them. Ambrose reads "I will reprove," a word that is certainly elegant but ambiguous, for one who corrects also "reproves."

<margin>23</margin> *In their craftiness*] The word "their" refers back to the wise: thus it was more Latin to say *ipsorum* <note>of them themselves</note>, so that we understand the "foolishly wise" were captured and defeated by their very own craftiness, while they discover for themselves that their wisdom profited nothing toward true happiness.

<margin>24</margin> *For all things are yours*] The word "for" is not repeated in the second instance, and it obstructs the meaning. For this particle is repeated for the sake of confirmation, as if he were saying, "all things, I say, are yours." In this place, Ambrose agrees with the Greeks.

<margin>D 1</margin> *Stewards of the mysteries*] <note>original Greek: mysteriōn</note>, that is, *of the mysteries*, or secrets: all agree on this, even Thomas <note>Aquinas</note>, except for a few corrupted but very common manuscripts. And it was better to use *estimate* rather than "think" <note>Latin: aestimet vs. existimet</note>; for no one speaks in this way in Latin, "you think me as a king," but "you think me a king." Nor is this about "reputation" <note>existimatio</note>, but "valuation" <note>aestimatio</note>. For Paul does not want the Apostles to be valued more highly than those who manage someone else's property ought to be. And the stewards here are called <term>oeconomi</term> <note>household managers</note>, who indeed manage, but manage the property of another and must give an account.

<margin>2</margin> *Here now it is required*] <note>original Greek: Ho de loipon zēteitai</note>, that is, *But what remains is required*, or *furthermore*, or *hereafter it is required*. The translator seems to have read <note>original Greek: Hōde</note> <note>meaning "here"</note>, not <note>original Greek: Ho de</note> <note>meaning "but what/that which"</note>: but all the Greek manuscripts resist this with great consensus. Therefore, it is for the reader to choose which reading they prefer to follow. We have translated what we found in the Greek codices, so that the Latin would not disagree with the Greek. *Required* in this place means "looked for" or "demanded": for faithfulness is what is chiefly looked for in a steward; authority remains with the master. Furthermore, "in stewards" was more correct than "among stewards." For this is not something debated *among* managers, but *demanded* of them.

<margin>3</margin> *Or by a human day*] Jerome cites this passage somewhere to show that Paul was not particularly elegant in the Greek language, but spoke certain things in the manner of the Cilicians: for he was a Cilician, born in Tarsus. Here, although nothing insulting was said against Paul, someone [a critic of Erasmus] has stirred up great drama over this passage, declaring from this that I understand nothing at all of what I read in Jerome or other Doctors of the Church. Because of such slanders, I had appended Jerome's words from his *Letter to Algasia*, the tenth question: "That which we have frequently said," he says, "'though unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge' <note>2 Corinthians 11:6</note>: we still approve that Paul said this not out of humility, but from the truth of his conscience. For the tongue does not explain deep and hidden meanings. And since he himself senses what he is saying, he cannot transfer it to the ears of others in pure speech: though he is most eloquent in his native tongue—being a Hebrew of Hebrews and educated at the feet of Gamaliel, a man most learned in the Law—when he desires to interpret himself, he becomes entangled." Does Jerome not openly admit here that Paul was less skilled in the Greek language than in Hebrew, because he had learned one from his ancestors and a most learned teacher, and the other from trade with the Cilicians? Does he not confirm here what I have shown elsewhere, that Paul speaks unskillfully due to an ignorance of the Greek language? Furthermore, if one cannot express what he feels in pure speech, does he not express it somehow in speech that is lacks elegance and purity? And soon Jerome shows that he said many things from the <term>idiotism</term> <note>local dialect/slang</note> of the Cilicians: such as "from a human day" <note>original Greek: apo anthrōpinēs hēmeras</note> for "human judgment," and "I speak humanly" <note>original Greek: anthrōpinōs legō</note> when he says something more humbly than is perfect, and "I will be a burden to you" <note>original Greek: katanarkēsō hymas</note> when one hangs heavily over another, and "to deprive of a prize" <note>original Greek: katabrabeuein</note> where someone in a contest unjustly snatches the reward from another. Jerome wants these to be said by Paul in the same way that "wicked cold" <note>Latin: sceleratum frigus</note> was said by Virgil. Nor indeed does it escape me that these things are written by Jerome in various and clever ways, nor do I weigh how much these things he writes should matter to me. I only indicate that I did not point out the passage recklessly. If Paul cannot explain purely what he feels, either his own lack of skill was the cause, or the speech itself was insufficiently polished, or the subject matter itself. But

<column-break/>

<margin>C</margin> he explains the matter in the Hebrew language in which he was most eloquent; it remains that either the language of the Cilicians was less elegant, or Paul was less skilled in it. Jerome hints that both were true, since he both admits Paul was unskilled in Greek speech—not that he could not speak in the common way, but that pure and elegant speech was lacking to declare his mind—and he shows there are certain peculiarities of that nation in which he was born, which he used to explain however he could what he had felt. Nor does it go against me if Tarsus produced several learned men, such as Aratus and Oppian: as if Scythia did not also give us Anacharsis. It does not matter where you were born, but from whom you learned. Nor do those who write use everything that common speech possesses. For even in the age of Cicero, certain things were commonly said from which he himself abstained. But that Paul's speech was common, no one, I think, would deny. He would have spoken more eloquently, I suppose, if he had spent time in Athens with Demosthenes, Plato, and Isocrates, and he could have expressed what he felt more purely. <margin>D</margin> I wish God would give a better mind to those who, with such slanders, waste both their own leisure and that of others. Furthermore, just as a little earlier he used "day" for "judgment"—in the same way he often elsewhere calls the "day of the Lord"—so here he said "human day" for human judgment, for a "day" is set for those who are accused.

<margin>4</margin> *For I am conscious of nothing to myself*] Whether it is said correctly in Latin, "I am conscious of nothing" <note>Latin: nihil sum conscius</note>, just as it is said, "I am not ignorant of that," is not entirely clear to me; in Greek the word is, "conscious to myself" <note>original Greek: syneidōs emautō synoida</note>. So also Horace:

> *To be conscious of no wrong to oneself, to turn pale at no crime.*

<margin>5</margin> *Therefore do not*] <note>original Greek: Hōste mē pro kairou ti krinete</note>, that is, *Do not judge anything before the time*. Augustine reads, "Do not wish to judge anything before the time": both in several other places and when explaining Psalm 88: likewise to the widow Proba concerning praying to God.

<margin>6</margin> *I have transfigured into myself and Apollos*] <note>original Greek: meteschēmatisa</note>, that is, *I have transfigured*, which is to say, I have transferred the persona of others onto us two, <margin>E</margin> and under our own persona we have spoken about bad stewards, lest we should offend anyone. Likewise "Apollos" in this place ought to be taken in the accusative case, "into me and into Apollos." And here some Latin codices have *erroroneously*, "that in yourselves you may learn," in the second person, instead of "in us," in the first.

<margin>7</margin> *Not above that which is written*] The Greek is slightly different: <note>original Greek: mē hyper ho gegraptai phronein, hina mē heis hyper tou henos mē physiouthe kata tou heterou</note>, that is, *not to think above that which is written*, that is, to think concerning yourselves, as we have already frequently warned, lest one be puffed up for the sake of one against another. The speech is rather disordered, but it will be clearer if "one for one" pertains to individual disciples and teachers—so that this one is puffed up in the name of Apollos, that one in the name of Paul, another in the name of Cephas—and what follows, "against another," pertains to Christians disagreeing among themselves due to the foolishness of teachers, who are often prone to be contentious. Since "one for one" is placed for "one for another," or to say it better, "one concerning another or over another." This is new, <margin>F</margin> that the phrase "lest not" <note>original Greek: hina mē</note> is joined to the indicative mood, unless perhaps "you are puffed up" <note>original Greek: physiousthe</note> is a corruption of "you may be puffed up" <note>original Greek: physiousthe (subjunctive)</note>, or unless the rule of syntax varies here as well, as in several other instances. And in some Greek copies the "not" is doubled, while in some it is placed only once.

<margin>8</margin> *For who discerns you*] <note>original Greek: diakrinei</note>, that is, *judges between*. Saint Augustine, in his Letter to Valentinus, and again in the book to the same man *On Grace and Free Will*, and likewise in the book to Boniface *Against Two Epistles of the Pelagians*, chapter 7, interprets "discerns" as "separates from the mass of Adam" <note>i.e., the mass of fallen humanity</note>: which sense is indeed pious and true, although here Paul was not dealing with the sin of our first parents, but was disputing against those who preferred themselves to others because they had been baptized by the leading Apostles, when baptism is equal for all. So Saint Ambrose says. And Theophylact interprets "discerns" as "judges" <note>original Greek: dikazei</note>, adding that the judgments of men are deceptive. Chrysostom ignores this particle. Furthermore, <term>diakrinein</term> in the Holy Scriptures is sometimes used for "to doubt" or "to hesitate," and sometimes for "to prefer": just as <term>diakriseis</term> sometimes means "legal judgments."

8 ...and as if you had not received it? Already you are filled, already you have become rich, without us you have reigned; and I wish indeed that you did reign, so that we also might reign with 9 you. For I think that God has displayed us, the Apostles, as the last, as those sentenced to death; because we have become a spectacle to the world, and to angels, and to men. 10 We are fools for Christ's sake, but you are wise in Christ; we are weak, but you are strong; you are 11 honorable, but we are without honor. To this very hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are beaten with fists, and are homeless, 12 And we labor, working with our own hands; being reviled, we bless; suffering persecution, we 13 endure; Being slandered, we entreat; we have become as the filth of the world, the offscouring 14 of all things until now. I do not write these things to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved 15 children. For if you should have ten thousand guardians in Christ, yet you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus through the Gospel I 16 begot you. I exhort you therefore, be imitators 17 of me. For this reason I have sent to you Timothy, who is <gloss>the</gloss> my beloved child...

8 ...not received? Now you are filled, now you are enriched, without us you have obtained the kingdom; and I wish indeed you had obtained it, so that we also might reign together with you. 9 For I think that God has shown us, who are the last Apostles, as if appointed to death: since 10 we are made a spectacle to the world, and to angels, and to men. We are fools for Christ's sake, but you are prudent through Christ: we are weak, but you are strong: you are famous, 11 we are despised. Even unto this time we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted with blows, and wander with no certain 12 dwelling, And we labor, working with our own hands: hearing evil of ourselves, we bless: suffering 13 persecution, we endure: Affected by insults, we beseech: we are made as the excrement of the world, the refuse of all things unto this day. 14 I do not write these things that I may cover you with shame, but I warn you as my beloved sons. 15 For even if you have countless tutors in Christ, yet you do not have many fathers: since in Christ Jesus through the Gospel I have begotten 16 you. I therefore exhort you, that you be 17 imitators of me. For this cause I have sent to you Timothy...

---

<columns>1</columns>

<margin>A</margin>
...distinguishing <note>original: "διακρινων"</note>; for that which we prefer above others, we separate from the crowd. I advise this because here Paul seems to be speaking about the leaders, whom he does not allow to prefer themselves to anyone else, because if they have anything above the rest, they do not have it from themselves. If the letter <unclear>epsilon</unclear>, which is in the word "who" <note>original: "τις"</note>, were transferred to the end of the verb "distinguishes" <note>original: "διακρινει"</note>, the sense would be more convenient: "Why do you distinguish yourself?" that is, why do you segregate yourself from the common people as if you were superior?

<margin>B</margin>
9 **Without us you reign** <note>original: "Sine nobis regnatis"</note>] In Greek it is "you have reigned" <note>original: "εβασιλευσατε"</note>: and "I wish you reigned," which is also "you have reigned" <note>original: "εβασιλευσατε"</note>, meaning "I wish you had reigned." Although in cases like this, the Greeks never misuse the past tense for the present. It could be translated as "you have attained the kingdom," or "you have acquired it," and "may you be those who have attained it."

10 **As if destined for death** <note>original: "Tanquam morti destinatos"</note>] <note>original: "ως επιθανατιους"</note>, that is, liable to death. Although the Translator renders it nicely. For he is thinking of those who, according to Roman custom, were shut in cages and thrown to the beasts while the people watched.

11 **We are a spectacle** <note>original: "Spectaculum sumus"</note>] <note>original: "θεατρον"</note>, that is, a theater: which among the Greeks is named from the act of "beholding." And among the ancients, the punishment of the guilty was exhibited to the people in place of a show, such as a man set to fight a lion or a bear. Jerome used this Greek word 
<margin>C</margin>
when explaining the fourth chapter of the Epistle to the Galatians, while also mixing in a comparison to stage actors, whose sole concern is that the play pleases the people. *Paul*, he says, *was changing his voice, and in the likeness of actors, he was made a theater to the world and to Angels and to men: he turned his appearance into various figures and voices, not because he was what he pretended to be, but because he seemed to be only that which benefited others.* No one doubts that Jerome said this piously, but what slanders would some people stir up if Erasmus had said these things? Paul is compared to an actor <term>histrio - a stage performer, often viewed with suspicion in the ancient world</term> and is said to "pretend": but what an actor is, is not understood, and the slanderer builds a false accusation out of the word "pretending."

12 **Noble, ignoble** <note>original: "Nobiles, ignobiles"</note>] <note>original: "ενδοξοι, ατιμοι"</note>, that is, glorious and infamous, or famous and obscure, or held in value and despised. For "noble" here is not the same word as was used earlier, "well-born" and "low-born" <note>original: "ευγενης" and "αγενης"</note>. For those refer to lineage, while these refer to reputation and opinion. Nor is there in the Greek words that "battle of persons," noble and ignoble.

13 **We are unstable** <note>original: "Instabiles sumus"</note>] <note>original: "αστατουμεν"</note>, we do not have a fixed home. Whence we translate, "we wander with uncertain seats." It is also one of the tragic curses, to be without a steady hearth.

14 **We are cursed, and we bless** <note>original: "Maledicimur, & benedicimus"</note>] The Translator rendered the passive participles of the present 
<margin>D</margin>
tense through verbs, adding a conjunction: <note>original: "λοιδορουμενοι, διωκομενοι, βλασφημουμενοι"</note>, that is, while we are cursed, or affected by insults, while we suffer persecution, while we are blasphemed.

15 **The purgations of this world** <note>original: "Purgamenta hujus mundi"</note>] The pronoun "this" is not added among the Greeks.

16 **The offscouring of all** <note>original: "Omnium peripsema"</note>] <note>original: "παντων περιψημα"</note>. The Translator left the Greek word, which Laurentius <note>The humanist Lorenzo Valla</note> thinks could have been translated as "the dust of footprints." Greek commentaries say that *peripsema* is the cloth with which those sweating wipe themselves; others say it is the leather sewn under a shoe; others the dust we tread upon; others that which is thrown into the sea so that a ship may be safe. It seems altogether that *peripsema* among the Greeks is something like what we call "a trifle," "scraps," or "a dunghill." Suidas adds that a man liable to continual evils is usually called this. 
<margin>F</margin>
Theophylact thinks *perikatharma* <note>purgation/refuse</note> and *peripsema* <note>offscouring/scraping</note> are the same, namely <note>original: "αποσμηγμα"</note>, that is, that which is wiped away; for <note>original: "απεψηθη"</note> means to wipe off. Nor does Chrysostom make any distinction. Hesychius adds: Among the Greeks, the price by which a captive or someone's life is redeemed is called *perikatharmata*; finally, that which is trampled by everyone's feet. They are also called *antilytra* and *antipsycha*, that is, redemptions, when a life is redeemed by a life, just as we read concerning Admetus and Alcestis. Ambrose, explaining the Psalm "Blessed are the undefiled," in his eighth sermon, relates it in these words: *We are made as the lustrations of this world.* "Lustrations" <note>original: "lustramenta" - sacrificial purifications</note> of all even until now, because among the Latins, things by which people are cleansed are said to be "lustrated." Or shortly after, the same Ambrose interprets "lustrations" as "purgations." But "lustrations" are not simply called "purgations," but those things through which the expiation of others is performed. The commentator on Aristophanes's *Plutus* relates that formerly, men who were sacrificed to the Gods for the expiation of a city during a plague, famine, or any other evil that announced the wrath of the Deity, were usually called "catharma-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
-ta" <term>catharmata - human scapegoats sacrificed for communal cleansing</term>. He says this custom also prevailed among the Romans, meaning, I think, the Decii and Quintus Curtius <note>Historical figures who famously sacrificed themselves for Rome</note>. Servius, explaining Virgil's poem from the third book of the *Aeneid*:
> ...To what do you not drive mortal hearts,
> Accursed hunger for gold?
notes that "hunger for gold" was called "sacred" <note>The Latin 'sacra' can mean both 'holy' and 'accursed/devoted to a god for destruction'</note> according to the custom of the Gauls. For when the people of Marseilles were suffering from a plague, one of the poorer men would offer himself to be fed for an entire year on public and pure foods; afterward, adorned with sacred branches and garments, he was led around the city with curses, so that all the evils of the city might fall upon him, and thus he was cast out. He cites Petronius as the author of this history. Indeed, Suidas indicates it was an ancient custom that, if some evil 
<margin>C</margin>
pressed upon them, they would throw one person into the sea every year, as if sacrificing to Neptune, adding these words: <note>original: "περιψημα ημων γενου"</note>, "be our offscouring"; that is, our safety or redemption. But whether Paul meant any such thing, I do not know. Certainly, none of the ancient Translators touched upon this sense. Nor do I deny that Paul sometimes draws examples and comparisons from the things of the Pagans, such as from boxers, from racecourses, from military service—but these are public things and can be performed without serious sin. He never drew an example for good morals from robbers, sorcerers, or impious rituals. Now, whether he 
<margin>D</margin>
took upon himself all evils, he would seem to claim for himself what is proper to Christ: although in a pious sense it could be said that the deaths of the Martyrs were in a way a supplement to those things which Christ suffered for us, because Christ suffers in them. Paul also wishes to be an "anathema" <note>cursed/separated</note> for his brothers, and in the second Epistle he does not refuse to be "spent" for the Corinthians. There is another scruple: that Paul does not call himself *catharma* in the singular number, but *perikatharmata* <note>plural</note>, so that by comparison it refers to "cast-off things" rather than to a person. As for his calling himself the "refuse of the world" and the "offscouring of all," this pertains to not offending those to whom he writes, to whom he was most dear; but he preferred to impute what he suffered among them to the city and the public name. Chrysostom noted that. I have performed the duty of a commentator; let the judgment be with the reader. To me, Paul seems to signify by these words his extreme contempt among men not yet initiated into piety. Indeed, Pliny, in his thirty-second book, the last chapter, calls the things which the sea 
<margin>E</margin>
throws back onto the shore "purgamenta" <note>refuse/purgations</note>. For when he had spoken of fish, he says: *Besides these, there are some purgations unworthy of report, and to be numbered among seaweeds rather than animals.* These words do not lose their native meaning if they are sometimes transferred to men, just as a "buskin" <note>a tragic actor's boot</note> does not stop signifying a buskin if someone of slippery faith is called a "buskin." Although Paul also called himself "refuse" and "offscouring" not without a trope <term>trope - a figure of speech</term>; just as Terence called a filthy man a "dunghill."

17 **Not that I may confound** <note>original: "Non ut confundam"</note>] <note>original: "ουκ εντρεπων"</note>, that is, not confounding. Although "shaming" was better, or "shaming with a blush": for in Greek a person is said to be "turned in" <note>original: "εντρεπεσθαι"</note> when their own disgrace is thrust upon them so that they recognize themselves; for the word was named from this.

18 **Beloved** <note>original: "Charissimi"</note>] <note>original: "αγαπητα"</note>. Which he translates this way almost perpetually, 
<margin>F</margin>
even though it is "dearly loved": except that I suspect it was done on purpose, because that word signifies something more to the Greeks than "beloved" does to us.

19 **If ten thousand** <note>original: "Si decem millia"</note>] <note>original: "μυριους"</note>. Which sometimes signifies ten thousand, at other times a huge number: for which the Latins misuse the words "a thousand" or "six hundred"; he said "myriads," therefore, for "any number of many." And "pedagogues" <term>pedagogue - a slave who escorted and supervised children, distinct from a father</term> were servants to whom fathers entrusted the care of governing their children: whence the Greek word was named. But there is a great difference between a pedagogue and a father. A pedagogue is fierce for the sake of authority; a father even spends his life, if necessary.

20 **I ask therefore** <note>original: "Rogo ergo"</note>] <note>original: "Παρακαλω"</note>. Which he mostly translates as "I beseech." And so Ambrose reads it; sometimes "I exhort."

21 **Be imitators of me** <note>original: "Imitatores mei sitis"</note>] <note>original: "γινεσθε"</note>. Which could also be translated "become." For when he had said "I begot you," he added, "therefore imitate me," by which it becomes clear that you are truly my children, if you express me as your parent. For, as Horace elegantly says:
> Mothers are praised for a similar offspring.
But fathers are much more praised for a similar offspring. Just as I also [am of] Chri...

<summary>Erasmus provides an exhaustive philological and historical analysis of Paul's description of the Apostles as the "offscouring" and "refuse" of the world, linking these terms to ancient Greco-Roman rituals of human sacrifice and scapegoating. He contrasts the temporary, authoritative role of a 'pedagogue' with the life-giving, sacrificial role of a 'father' in the faith.</summary>
