->### TO THE CORINTHIANS I. CHAPTER V.<-

<margin>18</margin> ...who is also faithful in the Lord, who will remind you of <margin>19</margin> my ways, which are in Christ, just as I teach everywhere <margin>19</margin> in every Church. But as if I were not coming <margin>19</margin> to you, some have become puffed up. But I will come <margin>20</margin> to you quickly, if the Lord wills, and I will know not the word of those who are puffed up, but <margin>21</margin> the power. For the kingdom of God is not in word, <margin>21</margin> but in power. What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit <margin>V. 1</margin> of gentleness? It is reported everywhere that there is sexual immorality <note>original: πορνεία (porneia)</note> among you, and such sexual immorality as is not even mentioned among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father’s <margin>2 Ch.</margin> <margin>1</margin> wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that the one who has done this deed might be removed from your midst. <margin>2</margin> For I indeed, though absent in body, but present in spirit, <margin>3</margin> have already judged as though present the one who has so committed <margin>4</margin> this, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ—when you and my spirit are gathered together, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ— <margin>5</margin> to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day <margin>6</margin> of the Lord Jesus. Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? <margin>7</margin> Therefore clean out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, just as you are unleavened; for indeed Christ our Passover was sacrificed for us. <margin>8</margin> Therefore let us celebrate the feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, <margin>9</margin> but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. I wrote...

---

<margin>1</margin> This small part <note>referring to "as I am of Christ" in the previous chapter</note> is neither added among the Greeks, nor in the works of Ambrose <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Milan and influential theologian</note>. It is missing in the Pauline manuscript: it was noted below by hand in the margin, or added by someone else: although Thomas Aquinas reads and interprets it thus. It is not added in the Donatian codex, nor in the two of Constance. It seems to have been added from the eleventh chapter of this Epistle, *Be imitators of me:* and there it is added, *just as I also am of Christ.* Although it fits more aptly there, for it had been preceded by: *Be without offense to Jews and Gentiles and the Church of God, just as I also please everyone in all things, not seeking what is profitable for me, but what is profitable for many, so that they may be saved:* and to this corresponds what follows shortly after: *Be imitators of me, just as I also am of Christ.* He felt the same as he wrote to the Romans in the fifteenth chapter: *But we who are stronger ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves: let each of you please his neighbor for good unto edification. For even Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, "The reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me."* Otherwise, I do not know whether, just as it is said *to be reborn in Christ, or through Christ*, it might be read that *Christ has begotten us for God.* For so Aquinas interprets it.

<margin>22 my most dear son]</margin> <gloss>beloved</gloss> <note>original: ἀγαπητὸς</note>, about whom we just made mention.

<margin>23 As though I were not coming]</margin> <gloss>As if my not coming to you</gloss> <note>original: Ὡς μὴ ἐρχομένου μου πρὸς ὑμᾶς</note>, that is, "as if I am not coming to you," or "as if I shall not come." Although this word is found several times with a future meaning. And by a Hebrew idiom he said *in a rod*, for what would be more Latin to say, *with a rod*, or *by means of a rod*.

---

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>1 Truly sexual immorality...]</margin> To use the word *fornicari* <note>to fornicate</note> for practicing illicit lust, and *fornicatio* for debauchery, I have not yet found among suitable Authors, although I know *fornix* <note>an arch, often implying a brothel</note> is found for a den of vice. We sometimes translate it as *debauchery* <note>Latin: stuprum</note>, sometimes as *consorting with prostitutes* <note>Latin: scortatio</note>. Indeed, "scortatio" is derived from *scortum* <note>a prostitute</note>.

<margin>2 Such as is not even among the nations]</margin> Missing in the Latin manuscripts is <gloss>is named</gloss> <note>original: ὀνομάζεται</note>. Nor was the emphasis of this word idle, because this kind of lust was not only not committed among the Heathen, but was not even named: which Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator</note> also noted, even if it seems a somewhat shameless hyperbole, unless you prefer *named* to be placed simply for *heard of*. Although even so there is room for hyperbole, since among the Heathen even fouler things are heard of: unless Paul denies it is heard of because it is rare. It is certain that it is added neither in Ambrose, nor in Thomas, nor in Augustine, nor in the very old manuscripts: whence I think our reading is the pure one, even if the Greek versions do not differ in sense.

<margin>3 Absent in body, but present in spirit]</margin> Jerome <note>The 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> noted this in a certain place: that Paul, due to his lack of skill in the Greek language, sometimes does not render these conjunctions *men* and *de* <note>Greek particles used to contrast "on the one hand" and "on the other"</note>, through which the Greeks mostly connect parts of a sentence. It would have been smoother: *absent indeed in body, but present in spirit:* and yet in Greek Authors of proven elegance, one can find a similar form of speech.

<margin>4 Him who has so worked this]</margin> <gloss>the one who has so done this, or rather perpetrated it</gloss> <note>original: τὸν οὕτως τοῦτο κατεργασάμενον</note>. This is what he repeats shortly in the same manner. In several of the Greek manuscripts, the first part does not add *so* <note>original: οὕτως</note>, but the latter part does. Ambrose in the latter part reads: *I have already judged as present, the one who has so worked*, whereas in the former he reads: *who did this work:* from which one can guess that among the Greeks, something was added to both from both—*this* from the former, and *so* from the latter.

<margin>5 When you and my spirit are gathered]</margin> <gloss>when you and my spirit are called together, or gathered together</gloss> <note>original: συναχθέντων ὑμῶν καὶ τοῦ ἐμοῦ πνεύματος</note>. Our friend Faber Stapulensis <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, a prominent French humanist and reformer</note> changed this place, wishing to derive "gathered" from a word meaning "to suffer together," in which part

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Timothy, who is my beloved and faithful son in the Lord, who will lead you into the memory of my ways, which are in Christ, just as I teach everywhere in every Church. <margin>18</margin> Just as if I were not about to come to you, <margin>19</margin> some have been puffed up. <margin>20</margin> But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord wills, and I will know not the speech of those who are puffed up, but the power. <margin>21</margin> For the kingdom of God is not in speech, but in power. What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness? <margin>1</margin> It is reported everywhere that there is debauchery <note>Erasmus uses "stuprum" here</note> among you, and <margin>B</margin> such debauchery as is not even named among the nations, that someone should have his father’s wife. <margin>2</margin> And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that he who had perpetrated this deed might be taken from your midst. <margin>3</margin> For I indeed, as one absent in body, but present in spirit, have already decreed as if present, that he who has so committed this, <margin>4</margin> In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you and my spirit are gathered, together with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, <margin>5</margin> Be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be safe in the day of the Lord Jesus. <margin>6</margin> Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole batch? <margin>7</margin> Clean out therefore the old leaven, that you may be a new batch, just as you are unleavened: for even Christ our Passover has been sacrificed for us. <margin>8</margin> Therefore let us <margin>C</margin> celebrate the feast, not in old leaven, nor in the leaven of malice and craftiness, but in the bread that lacks leaven, that is, in sincerity and truth. <margin>9</margin> I wrote to you in an Epistle, not to mix with...

---

I do not readily agree with his judgment, though he is otherwise a most learned and diligent man, and other things, as well as the Greek commentaries, cry out against it. Furthermore, all the Interpreters whom I have seen testify that Paul said this for the purpose of showing that this so severe a sentence did not proceed from himself properly, but from the common consensus of the Church: for "to be gathered" is said here from the verb meaning *to bring together, or to call together.* Furthermore, he added *and my spirit*, because he himself was not present in body then, but was present in spirit at least in the pronouncing of that sentence.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>6 With the power of our Lord Jesus Christ]</margin> <gloss>with the power of the Lord</gloss> <note>original: σὺν τῇ δυνάμει τοῦ Κυρίου</note>. It is uncertain whether it refers back to the participle *gathered*, or to the delivering of the man to Satan. Ambrose seems to refer it to the participle: so that we may understand that council to consist of three things: from Paul’s decree, from the consensus of the multitude, and from the authority of Christ. Otherwise, the preposition *with* <note>Greek: σὺν</note> among the Greeks sometimes sounds not like a companion, but a favorer and helper, as in *with the Muses*, meaning *with the Muses helping:* or *with God*, meaning *God favoring.* Concerning "virtue," which here signifies authority or force, not moral probity, we have already given warning frequently.

<margin>7 For the day of our Lord Jesus Christ]</margin> <gloss>in the day of the Lord Jesus</gloss> <note>original: ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ</note>, that is, *in the day of the Lord Jesus*, and *Christ* is not added. Again, he calls the judgment "the day," as was indicated before.

<margin>8 Your boasting is not good]</margin> Augustine, in the third book of *Against the Epistle of Parmenian*, second chapter, indicates that in certain manuscripts, especially Latin ones, it was written, *your glory is good*, which he wants to be taken ironically. *It corrupts the whole mass.* Where he here translates *mass*, he shortly after translated as *batch* <note>Latin: conspersio</note>. In Greek it is <gloss>lump</gloss> <note>original: φύραμα</note>: that is flour sprinkled or tempered with water, from the verb *to mix*, just as when clay is softened by moisture, or flour by a liquid like water or oil, or something similar. In this sense *sprinkling* <note>conspersio</note> is found among approved Authors. Although we also read of *little masses* in Columella <note>A 1st-century writer on agriculture</note>. The Translator changed it, when there was no reason why variety should be sought.

<margin>9 A little leaven corrupts the whole mass]</margin> Jerome, in the third book of his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, taxes the Translator because he translated wrongly: citing this place and correcting it in this manner: *A little leaven leavens the whole batch.* But I would say more gently, *a tiny bit of leaven*, rather than *a little leaven*, because any part of leaven becomes leaven, just as any part of water is water. Now if we have the New Testament restored by Jerome, as some claim, how does he here tax what we read?

<margin>10 Our Passover]</margin> Missing is *for us*, <gloss>was sacrificed for us</gloss> <note>original: ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἐτύθη</note>, that is, *was immolated for us*, and so forth: but with all our books crying out against it, to which in this part, to speak frankly, I more agree.

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>11 Therefore let us feast]</margin> <gloss>let us keep the feast day</gloss> <note>original: ἑορτάζωμεν</note>: so indeed the Translator of Origen’s fifth *Homily on Leviticus* renders it. Those days are usually celebrated with solemn feasts.

<margin>12 And wickedness]</margin> <gloss>and of wickedness</gloss> <note>original: καὶ πονηρίας</note>. Which signifies both malice and craftiness. He proposed two, <gloss>malice and wickedness</gloss>, to which correspond those things that follow afterward, <gloss>sincerity and truth</gloss>: for to *malice* is opposed *sincerity*, and to *craftiness* is opposed *truth*, that is, simplicity: so also Ambrose. So that sincerity may make a clean life, and truth may exclude all judgment.

<margin>13 But in the unleavened bread]</margin> The word *Azymis*, which he leaves everywhere, he could have translated as *unleavened*, or *lacking leaven:* but I think *loaves* should be understood, *in unleavened loaves*. Then explaining what he meant by *unleavened*, he adds "of sincerity and truth," just as if he had said: this is to celebrate our Passover with unleavened things, to be of a sincere mind toward everyone.

<margin>14 Mix with fornicators]</margin> <gloss>prostitutes</gloss> <note>original: πόρνοις</note>, that is, whores: for it is...

<summary>Erasmus provides a philological analysis of Paul's rebuke to the Corinthians regarding their pride and their tolerance of a man committing incest. He disputes common Latin translations, preferring "stuprum" for sexual immorality and discussing the precise meaning of the "leaven" metaphor.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s annotations on 1 Corinthians Chapter 5, focusing on Paul’s instructions regarding social separation from sinners within the church. It transitions into the beginning of Chapter 6 regarding lawsuits between believers.</meta>

# PAUL’S EPISTLE CHAPTER VI.

<note>Note: Although the header says Chapter 6, the text begins by completing the discussion of Chapter 5.</note>

...to you in my letter, not to associate with sexually immoral people. I did not mean at all with the sexually immoral of this world, or with the greedy, or swindlers, or idolaters; for then you would be required to go out of the world. But now I have written to you not to associate: if anyone called a brother is sexually immoral, or greedy, or an idolater, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a swindler, do not even eat with such a person. For what is it to me to judge those who are outside? Do you not judge those who are inside? But God will judge those who are outside. And you shall remove the evil person from among yourselves. Does any of you, having a matter against another, dare to go to court...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...with sexually immoral people: 15 And not entirely with the sexually immoral of this world, or with the greedy, or with swindlers, or worshippers of idols: 16 otherwise you would have to leave the world. But now I have written to you, do not be mixed together: 17 if anyone, though he is called a brother, should be a sexually immoral person, or greedy, or a worshipper of idols, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a swindler, do not even take food with such a person. 18 For what does it concern me to judge also concerning those who are outside? Do you not judge concerning those who are within? But those who are outside, God judges. 19 Even drive out that one, who is evil, from among yourselves. *Does any of you sustain a matter*

---

For the word <note>original: πόρνος (pornos)</note> is a common term for any body for hire. Indeed, in Corinth, there were not only female prostitutes but also catamites <note>young men kept for sexual purposes</note>; although there are those who want *pornos* and *scortator* <note>sexually immoral man</note> to mean more than just a prostitute. They think the word is derived from *parnō*, which means "I sell," a term more fitting for prostitutes; and the Greeks call pimps *pornoboskous*, whom the Italians commonly call *ruffiani* <note>pimps or ruffians</note>. Furthermore, where he said "to be mixed together," the Greek is *συναναμίγνυσθαι* <note>synanamignysthai</note>, which can be understood as "to let ourselves be mixed together," implying they were accustomed to doing so before they were initiated into Christ. And "to be mixed" does not only mean to have sexual relations with them, but also to have social intimacy and trade. He emphasizes this when he adds: *not at all with the sexually immoral of this world*. It is very difficult to live among so many allurements in that region and not be enticed into sin. 

However, some do not deny the argument brought forward by many of the Ancient Fathers: namely, that Paul does not forbid having social contact with defiled Pagans—otherwise the whole of Greece would have to be abandoned—but rather that they should avoid any man who, having professed the Christian Religion, was of this sort. For when he said *of this world*, it is not to be understood as if there were another physical world. By *this world*, he means Greece, and especially Corinth, which was most corrupt with these kinds of pleasures. John Chrysostom <note>a 4th-century preacher</note> interprets it this way, provided that the Greek commentaries attributed to him are actually his, as does Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine commentator</note>, who arranges the passage like this: *I wrote to you a little while ago in this Epistle, not to mix with male or female prostitutes, when I said the old leaven must be purged. However, I would not want this to be taken as if I were ordering the avoidance of the company of all the prostitutes of this world. But if anyone called a brother be of this sort, he is to be avoided to such an extent that I would not even have you take food with him.* 

Nicholas of Lyra <note>a 14th-century Franciscan commentator</note> learnedly explains the "fornicators of this world" as those who are "commonly called ribalds." O, what a "grave" interpreter of Divine Scripture! If indeed this was written by him, and not rather added by some other idle fellow.

15 *Not at all]* <note>original: Καὶ οὐ πάντως (Kai ou pantōs)</note>. And *not entirely*, or *in total*: so that you understand one should abstain from all; or, as Ambrose <note>a 4th-century bishop</note> prefers in his explanation, one should not abstain from the fornicators of this world, but from the brothers—that is, from Christian fornicators. Among these was the one whom he orders to be handed over to Satan—that is, to be cast out from the fellowship of the other Christians, so that he might be corrected by shame. For there were perhaps those who believed only wicked Pagans were to be avoided, while Christians were not. Paul, on the contrary, orders the brothers to be avoided, while he does not forbid eating with Pagans. The words that follow support this sense: *For what is it to me to judge those who are outside?* Although, to be honest, this entire discourse seems somewhat disordered to me, requiring some "divine swimmer" <note>an idiom for a very skilled interpreter</note> to navigate it. Especially since he mentions *idolatry*, which it is not likely existed among Christians at that time. I think there is no need to remind anyone that "to be mixed" here does not refer to sexual intercourse, but to the social habits of life.

16 *Otherwise you would have had to, etc.]* <note>original: ἐπεί (epei)</note>, that is, "since" or "inasmuch as": which here he translates as *otherwise*, and sometimes *appropriately*, namely whenever there is a silent exception, as may be understood here. For if it is not possible for you to entirely abstain from all Greek prostitutes, and if you cannot do that, you must rather flee from all of Greece. Or: I do not forbid contact with the wicked entirely, otherwise if you tried that, you would have to flee from this world, since such people are everywhere. 

*You would have had to go out*, <note>original: ὀφείλετε (opheilete)</note>, that is, you ought: it is read among the Greeks with a small *e* <note>epsilon</note>, by a great consensus of the Greek manuscripts. Since you "ought to have gone out," or "to go out" from this world, when it is not fitting to mix with prostitutes. Ambrose's interpretation is a bit harsh—that it is better to die and depart from this world than to have anything to do with the wicked—even if the Greeks interpret it as leaving Greece, as has already been said often. If it is not possible by any other means to escape the trade of prostitutes and fornicators, it is better to leave that infested and pestilential region. Truly, he does not dare to demand this of them, though he might prefer it. Certainly, he demands this: that they do not "mix," that is, that they do not maintain a familiar social life with them, as if favoring their vices. And therefore it follows, *But now I have written to you*, that is, more mildly. It appears the Translator and Ambrose read *ōpheilete* with a long *o* <note>omega</note>. 

However, to add something of my own to the studies of my predecessors, it seems to me that *opheilete* in this place is a sign of a wish, used elegantly for *eithe*, that is, "would that," or "if only." Sometimes another small word is added, "would that you had" or "how you should have." When written with a small *o* <note>omicron</note>, *opheles* expresses a wish, without distinction of person or number. Otherwise, if you are not restrained from the company of such people, would that you had rather gone out from this world and gone into exile anywhere else. Thomas Aquinas produces many interpretations for this one sense, as ignorance is fertile: the first of which is, "otherwise you would have had to go out of this world," meaning if you want to avoid the company of all evil people, you would have to flee the world, since the world is filled with evil on all sides. Another is: There was no need to be reminded of this matter, since you have already been removed from the world by baptism. A third follows Ambrose: It was better to die than to have social contact with the wicked. Hugh of St. Cher <note>a 13th-century cardinal</note> adds...

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin>
...a fourth: You ought to have gone out of this world, that is, fled to "religion"—for that is what he calls the Monastic life. But the interpretation of Chrysostom pleases me most of all: that we understand Paul to be explaining what he meant when he ordered them in his letters to flee the commerce and company of the sexually immoral, the greedy, and those who sacrifice to idols. Since this, being misunderstood, seemed too harsh to the Corinthians, he says he did not order this so that they should abstain from wicked Pagans; for although that might be desirable, it could not be done, since everywhere all things were full of wicked men; but as far as possible, they should abstain from Christians of that sort. And therefore, as if in passing, he inserted: *otherwise you would have had to go out of this world*, meaning, "would that it were as I wish, that you could avoid such fellowships entirely." Now, since I wish in vain for what cannot be done, I write what I wrote before: that you should drive out from your fellowship Christians infamous for such foul vices, partly so that you do not seem to agree with their deeds, and partly so that they, being seized by shame, may repent.

<margin>C</margin>
17 *If he who is named a brother]* Here the Latins add of their own *among you*: these two words are not in the Greek manuscripts, nor in Saint Ambrose, nor in the Donatian manuscript, nor in either of the Ghent manuscripts. Now, although it does not matter much to the sense, in Greek it is *if anyone being named a brother*, or *when he is named a brother*, so that you may understand the substantive verb "be" or "has been." Unless we prefer to see the participle used in place of a verb, *named* for *is named*. For the very ancient Pauline Codex had it thus: "if any brother is named among you a fornicator, or greedy, or serving idols," and so on: so that "named" is joined to those things that follow—"sexually immoral, idolater, greedy." For the Greeks refer it to what precedes: so that we understand that he who is subject to such shameful things is a Christian in title only, since true Christianity is innocence of life. 

Furthermore, consider this, Reader: to which part should this phrase be referred, *if he who is named a brother*, etc.—to what precedes, or is it independent and belongs to what follows? If you refer it to what precedes, what follows remains in order: *not to take food with such a person*. But if to what follows, how does he correct what he had written—"that they should not mix"—if nothing is added to explain the general sentiment? Or shall we admit here too that Paul, either through lack of skill or neglect of the Greek language, explains what he feels in a somewhat disordered way, and *if anyone is named a brother* should be referred to what preceded: "I wrote to you not to be mixed, if anyone named a brother is a fornicator, or etc."; and then, the order of speech being neglected, it is added by way of emphasis <note>term: epitasis (a rhetorical increase in intensity)</note>, *not even to take food with such a one*, exactly as if he had said: "This I meant: if any Christian brother is infamous for such crimes, one ought so much not to have social contact with him that I would not even want the table to be shared." For it is in your interest that he be corrected, and there is a danger that he might corrupt others by his example, whereas in the case of a Pagan, the reasoning is not the same.

<margin>D</margin>
18 *For what to me]* <note>original: Τί γάρ μοι καὶ τοὺς ἔξω κρίνειν; (Ti gar moi kai tous exō krinein?)</note>; that is, "For what is it to me to judge even those who are outside?" This means: "What does it concern me, since it is troublesome enough to judge those who belong to our flock, that I should also pass judgment on those who are strangers to our fellowship?" He said *to judge* in place of *to hold as condemned*. But he who avoids the social habit of a man's life holds him as condemned. But if we avoid Pagans, how will they be converted to Christ? They must be endured in this world so that they may be healed. And if you do not mix in the salt, how will that which is tasteless be salted?

<margin>E</margin>
19 *Take away the evil]* <note>original: Καὶ ἐξαρεῖτε τὸν πονηρόν (Kai exareite ton ponēron)</note>, that is, "And remove that wicked man": so that it refers to the person, not the thing, because of the added article <note>the Greek "the" indicates a specific person</note>. This was also noted by Augustine in his *Questions on Deuteronomy*, reminding us that Holy Scripture is accustomed to use this style of speech whenever it orders the taking of capital punishment against a guilty person. He suggests Paul felt the same, but that excommunication among Christians is the equivalent of capital punishment. 

However, this passage seems to have twisted Saint Augustine quite a bit; he seemed to have such an abhorrence for killing the wicked that in frequent letters he beseeches and implores the Caesar's prefects not to inflict capital punishment on the Donatists <note>a schismatic Christian group in North Africa</note>, who not only most stubbornly segregated themselves from the fellowship of Christians, but also raged with the most cruel punishments against the Orthodox. Consequently, he fled to this interpretation: that we should understand Paul to be ordering each person to "strip off" the evil man from within themselves; according to what was said to the Ephesians, "Strip off the old man with his deeds." Likewise, against the *Letter of Parmenian*, book three, chapter one, he interprets "the evil" as "malice," as if it were written in the neuter gender. But both interpretations are forced, and they disregard both the reading and the commentary of the Ancients.

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>A</margin> *Does any of you dare]* <note>original: Τολμᾷ (Tolma)</note>. Sometimes it means "to sustain" or "to be able," when we signify a thing that is not dangerous (in which case we are properly said to "dare"), but something hard on our emotions and intolerable and unworthy. Thus Suetonius <note>a Roman historian</note>, in imitation of the Greeks, says in his *Life of Augustus*: "But after he finally took up the office of Chief Pontiff—which he had never *sustained* <note>dared/endured</note> taking away while Lepidus was alive—only after his death." The same author in the same work a little lower: "For although he least of all sought after inheritances, as one who never from the will of a stranger..."

<meta>catchword: mento (part of the word "testamento")</meta>

<summary>Erasmus provides a detailed linguistic and theological commentary on 1 Corinthians 5:9-13, clarifying that Paul’s instruction to "shun" sinners applies strictly to fellow Christians (to bring them to repentance) and not to the secular world. He also critiques previous commentators and begins discussing Paul's prohibition against believers taking one another to secular courts in Chapter 6.</summary>

# TO THE FIRST CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER VI.

<margin>1</margin>...dare to go to law before the unrighteous, and not before the <margin>2 saints?</margin>saints? 2 Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is judged among you, are you <margin>3 unworthy</margin>unworthy of the smallest judgments? 3 Do you not know <margin>4 that</margin>that we shall judge angels? How much more matters of this life? 4 If then you have judgments regarding matters of this life, <margin>5 I say this to</margin>appoint those who are least esteemed in the Church. 5 I say this to your shame. Is it so, that there is not a wise man among you, not even one, who will be able to judge between his brothers? 6 But brother <margin>6</margin>goes to law with brother, and that before <margin>22 7</margin>unbelievers. 7 Now therefore, it is altogether a failure among you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why not rather <margin>8</margin>suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? 8 But you yourselves do wrong and defraud, and that your brothers. <margin>28 9</margin>9 Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God?

---

1 *sustinuerit* <note>original: "dare" or "bring oneself to"</note> Although one might endure anything from a friend, one weighs the final judgments most peevishly. Again, regarding Caesar the Dictator: he never "brought himself" to harm Cornelius Phagita, even though he had barely escaped Phagita's nightly ambushes while sick and hiding to avoid being brought to Sulla, even after a bribe was given. Likewise, in several other places, one can find this word used to mean "he willed," or "he was able," or "he brought his mind to it." For us, it is enough to indicate one or two instances in this argument for the sake of a skeptical or difficult reader; for you will find this word used in the same sense in Seneca, Quintilian, and Lucan. Paul, therefore, indicating that this is a matter of great shame, wonders that there is any Christian who could bring his mind to contend for money before pagan judges.

2 *Before the unrighteous* <note>original: ἐπὶ τῶν ἀδίκων</note>. This sounds more like "under the unjust" and "under the saints," just as we say "under such a prince" or "under a judge"; as Horace says,
-> ---- and the lawsuit is still under the judge. <-
But since justice is especially required in a judge, Paul added the appropriate epithet: "under the unrighteous." Unless, according to the Hebrew custom, any kind of wickedness is called <term>iniquity</term> <note>original: iniquitas</note>.

3 *They will judge this world* <note>original: τὸν κόσμον κρινοῦσι</note>. That is, they will judge the world itself. This pronoun is not added in the Donatian codex nor the Constantinopolitan. He said the world "is judged" because it appears from the lives of the saints that worldly people are in error and act foolishly; and as if explaining this, he added, "if the world is judged in you." For "is judged" is in the present tense <note>original: κρίνεται (krinetai)</note>, not "will be judged" <note>original: κριθήσεται (krithesetai)</note>, as both the Greek copies and interpreters agree. This makes it clear he is speaking of the Christian way of life—which I wish were such today that the world might be judged by it! Now, we differ from pagans mostly in title and ceremonies rather than in our passions and lives. Furthermore, Ambrose's interpretation suggests he read "is judged," saying: "Then this world is judged in you, if the work of perfect men is found in you." Theophylact, like Chrysostom, both reads and interprets it as "they will judge"; and yet the translators consistently render it as "it shall be judged." Augustine, however, reads "it shall be judged," referring it to the final judgment where the saints will sit on twelve thrones to judge the twelve tribes of Israel. But nothing prevents this passage from belonging to both times. For even now the impious world is judged—that is, condemned—by the innocent life of the godly; and in the future, it will be condemned when all the works of the godly and impious are brought into the open. It should be noted in passing that <term>in you</term> is said here in the Hebrew manner for <term>through you</term>.

4 *Are you unworthy to judge of the smallest matters?* <note>original: ἀνάξιοί ἐστε κριτηρίων ἐλαχίστων</note>. That is, you are unworthy of the smallest judgments. For a <note>original: κριτήριον (kriterion)</note> is a place where causes are heard. Since capital cases are heard in some places, and lighter civil cases—about loans, things borrowed, or things bought—in others, he calls these matters that pertain to the use of life <term>smallest</term>. The Greeks understand this passage thus: "Since you are going to judge the world, it is unworthy for you to be judged in the courts of the Gentiles," which he calls "smallest" in comparison to that magnificent judgment by which the saints will judge the world and the angels. This is the view of Theophylact and Chrysostom, so that it is not a question implying a negative, but a strong assertion.

5 *How much more secular things* <note>original: μήτιγε βιωτικά (metige biotika)</note>. In Greek, this is not only things relating to food, but whatever pertains to livelihood, resources, or the use of life. For <note>original: βίος (bios)</note> in Greek signifies three things: life, livelihood, and the resources or substance by which we live. He means financial lawsuits. Since the common crowd is devoted to these things pertaining to livelihood—and the term "livelihood" encompasses clothes, housing, and other necessities of life—the Ancients called those devoted to the things of the world "biotikous." So it is in Suidas under the word *bios*, from Philo: "worldly men" <note>original: βιωτικῶν ἀνθρώπων</note>; and Chrysostom, in the third book of *On the Priesthood*, chapter 15, calls those eager for glory "worldly men" <note>original: ἀνθρώποις βιωτικοῖς</note>. Again, in the fourth book, chapter 1, he calls military service, trade, and farming "biotika." And Hesychius noted that *metige* in Greek has the same force as "all the more" <note>original: panto mallo / πάντων μᾶλλον</note>.

6 *Secular things therefore* <note>original: βιωτικά (biotika)</note>. Here too it is "biotika," as if pertaining to livelihood and domestic matters. There is a strange affectation of variety in this translator. What similarity is there between "secular" and "biotika"?

7 *Contemptible* <note>original: ἐξουθενημένους (exouthenemenous)</note>. That is, those who are despised and held as nothing.

8 *Appoint them to judge* <note>original: καθίζετε (kathizete)</note>. This word is ambiguous, as it could be translated "appoint" (as a command) or "you have appointed." The imperative mood does not displease me: that the Apostle orders that even the least of Christians 

<column-break/>

A...having a matter with another, to be judged ² under the unrighteous, and not rather under the saints? Or do you not know that the saints ² will judge the world? And if the world is judged through you, ⁴ are you unworthy of the smallest judgments? Do you not know that we shall judge angels, ⁵ not only those things which pertain to livelihood? Therefore, if you have judgments ⁶ concerning those things which pertain to the use of life, ⁷ those who are despised in the Church, ⁸ appoint them. ⁹ I say this to your shame: ¹⁰ is there so little a wise man among you, ¹¹ not even one, ¹² who can judge between his brother and his brother? ¹³ But brother strives with brother in judgment, ¹⁴ and that under ¹⁵ infidels. ¹⁵ Therefore there is now altogether a fault in you, that you have lawsuits among yourselves: why do you not rather suffer injury? why do you not rather ¹⁶ accept loss? Instead, you do injury, and cause loss, ¹⁷ and that to brothers. Or do you not know that the unrighteous [shall not inherit] the <margin>kingdom</margin>

---

should be delegated this task rather than going to pagan judges. Augustine, in the fifth book against Faustus, chapter 9, reads "place" instead of "name"; Ambrose also disagrees, explaining this passage differently, as if Paul were rebuking the Corinthians for appointing just anyone to judge such matters. The Greek commentaries, specifically Chrysostom and Theophylact, side with me, and it fits Paul’s meaning better. For he is not discussing who should be appointed as judges in the Church, but rather that Christians should not litigate before the impious; they should make anyone, even the most despised—provided he is a Christian—an arbiter of their cause rather than going to the tribunals of the impious. Not that he thinks it should be done this way (committing judgments to the lowest), but to declare how unbecoming the alternative is, he says this should sooner be committed to them. And therefore he immediately follows with: *I say this to your shame*, not because I think there are none among you who are wise, but to take away that false excuse from you. Saint Augustine, in the book *On the Work of Monks*, says he was forced by this passage of Paul to take up the judging of cases when he was a Bishop. Whether he felt rightly or wrongly is not for this place to examine. Nor does Paul here by the name "Church" specifically designate the Priests, but the assembly of Christian people, in which it was impossible that there would not be some fit to judge small matters. Augustine supports me in this: that Paul felt it was more tolerable for such humble causes to be delegated even to the lowest and most despised Christians than to be conducted before profane and impious judges. Finally, Paul seems to be speaking especially about choosing arbiters. If something is not right, let it be settled through arbiters, even those arbiters who are held as more contemptible among you. If this pleased Christians today, the most rapacious crowd of Advocates, Proctors, and Legal Consultants would grow cold. <term>Appoint</term> <note>original: καθίζετε</note>, that is, "place in a seat"; for *kathizein* is properly to "place in a seat," and it is the role of a judge to sit. He adds "those" <note>original: τούτους</note> marvelously, to show his hatred for the situation.

9 *To your shame* <note>original: Πρὸς ἐντροπὴν</note>. That is, "to your blushing" or "modesty," which is more fitting than "reverence"; a little earlier he translated it "to confusion." He added this to show he was not speaking from his heart (that he actually wanted the most despised to be chosen to judge), but that he judged even this more tolerable than what they were doing: Christians litigating before pagans.

10 *Is it so?* <note>original: Οὕτως</note>. In some Greek copies, this is joined with the preceding word "I say," not with what follows: so the sense is, "I speak thus, not because I want it done, but so you understand how unworthy is what you do." We, however, prefer the alternative reading, where "so" is used for "to such a degree," expressing indignation. It is a wonder where the translator of Theophylact reads "if" for "so," unless the text is faulty.

11 *Anyone wise* <note>original: οὐδὲ εἷς</note>. That is, "not even one," which is more emphatic since you are so many.

12 *Who can judge between his brother* <note>original: ἀνὰ μέσον τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ</note>. As if you said, "in the middle of the brother." And how is someone a judge between one person? Therefore, it was clearer and more Latin to say, "between brother and brother": that is, between Christian and Christian. It is noted in passing that great legal subtlety is not needed among Christians, among whom brotherly affection easily either forgives the offense or settles the matter.

13 *Brother contends in judgment with brother* <note>original: κρίνεται</note>. That is, "is judged." However, he translates this not inelegantly as "litigates," or as here, "contends in judgment."

14 *And this before the unrighteous* <note>original: ἐπὶ τῶν ἀδίκων</note>. That is, "under the unjust," as we just indicated, or as we read in most places, <note>original: ἐπὶ τῶν ἀπίστων</note>, that is, "under the unbelievers"; and thus Chrysostom and Ambrose read and interpret it. For the Apostle does not deter them from the judgments of the pagans because they are unjust, but because it is unseemly to run voluntarily to their tribunals for the most trivial causes.

15 *Now indeed it is altogether a fault* The Greek is not "wickedness," but <note>original: ἥττημα (hettema)</note>, which signifies that someone has been conquered and overcome. He seems conquered by anger or greed who moves a lawsuit against a brother over a bit of money. The Greek scholia explain it this way. Furthermore, "among you" the translator rendered better than Augustine reports in his book against the Manicheans, chapter 9: "That you have judgments with yourselves"; since the Greek is *meth' heauton*. In Latin we say, "he litigates with him"; but they do not likewise "litigate with themselves" to mean they "litigate among each other."

16 *Suffer fraud* <note>original: ἀποστερεῖσθε</note>. That is, you are affected by loss or defrauded. For "fraud" is sometimes used not for deceit, but for loss.

17 *And that to brothers* The translator could have translated this, while keeping the grammar intact, as: "you inflict injury and defraud, and that your brothers." There is no reason to change "and that" <note>original: καὶ ταῦτα</note> into "and by this"; as if by this way...

<summary>In this commentary on 1 Corinthians 6, Erasmus analyzes Paul's rebuke of Christians taking legal disputes to pagan courts, arguing that believers should settle matters internally, even if it requires the arbitration of the "least esteemed" members.</summary>

# EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER VI.

->Greek Text<-

...do you suppose? Do not be deceived; neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, <margin>10</margin> nor those who lie with men <note>Greek: *arsenokoitai*</note>, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers, will inherit <margin>11</margin> the kingdom of God. And such were some of you, but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and <margin>12</margin> in the Spirit of our God. "All things are lawful for me," but not all things are profitable; "all things are lawful for me," but I will not be dominated by anything. <margin>13</margin> Food is for the stomach, and the stomach for food; but God will destroy both this and these. Now the body is not for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord <margin>14</margin> for the body. And God both raised the Lord, <margin>15</margin> and will raise you through His power. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? <margin>16</margin> May it never be! Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute is one body with her? For "the two," He says, "shall become one flesh." <margin>17</margin> But he who is joined to the Lord is one <margin>18</margin> spirit with Him. Flee sexual immorality; every sin <margin>λυ</margin> that a man commits is outside the body, but the <margin>19</margin> fornicator sins against his own body. Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God, and you are not <margin>20</margin> your own? For you were bought with a price; glorify God, then, in your body and in your spirit, which are God's.

---

<margin>C</margin> ...assistance should be given to Latinity, as Stapulensis <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples (c. 1455–1536), a French humanist and theologian often critiqued or cited by Erasmus.</note> wishes: since the Latin language, when it adopts this form of speech, does not accept the plural number unless it is a noun of the same number, such as: *Many cattle [multa pecora] were driven away, and those [eaque] remarkable.* Even if Suetonius <note>Roman historian known for his biographies of the Caesars.</note> once seems to have expressed the Greek form of eloquence in *Tiberius Caesar*, chapter twenty-two: *Concerning which codicils it was doubtful whether Augustus had left them while dying, so as to remove the material for a riot after him, or whether Livia had dictated them in the name of Augustus, and those [ea] with Tiberius either knowing or ignorant, and so forth.* Unless you prefer to refer "and those" [*ea*] to Livia, instead of "and she" [*eaque*], just as we say "and he" [*is que*].

<margin>18 Will not possess]</margin> "will not inherit the kingdom of God" <note>original Greek: βασιλειαν Θευ ὐ κληρονομήσουσι</note>, that is, they will not obtain the lot or the inheritance of the kingdom of God: this means the kingdom of God will not fall to them.

<margin>19 Neither fornicators]</margin> "neither fornicators" <note>original Greek: οὔτε πόρνοι</note>, that is, harlots or whoremongers. I think the Translator <note>Referring to the author of the Vulgate, the standard Latin Bible.</note> consulted the modesty of ears, because "harlot" [*scortum*] among the Latins is a more obscene word, derived from "skins" [*pellibus*]. And presently, "those who lie with men" [ἀρσενοκοῖται], he signified a most foul thing in itself as least foully as he could. For those who sleep in the same bed also lie together, even if they do no sin. I wonder at this: why Faber Stapulensis preferred the word *cinaedus* <note>A term for a catamite or an effeminate man, often used in a derogatory or theatrical context.</note> in this place, which is not only obscene but also expresses something other than what Paul intended. For *cinaedi*, unless I am mistaken, are those who shamefully submit, formerly so called because they would gesture and dance with a masculine delay of the body in a theater, or because they moved the body effeminately to song, or because they irritated and moved the shameful parts of the body—from the Greek phrase "to move the genitals" <note>original Greek: παρὰ τὸ κινεῖν τὰ αἰδοῖα</note>—or because they were devoid of shame, as if "common genitals" <note>original Greek: κοινοὶ αἰδοῖα</note>. Certainly, it cannot be avoided that if *cinaedus* is not the proper term for catamites, it is at least common to both types of effeminacy.

<margin>20 And these things indeed once]</margin> "And such were some of you" <note>original Greek: Καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε</note>, that is, "And these things you were in part": so that you should understand that some of them were such, not all, as Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla (1407–1457), an Italian humanist who famously applied philological criticism to the New Testament.</note> noted. For it is not consistent that all were thieves, or adulterers, or those who lie with males, even if the vice of idolatry was common. For theft and adultery were punished among the Greeks even by laws. Unless we prefer "these things" [*ταῦτα*] placed for "these people" [*τούτοις*], and "some" [*τινες*] added according to the property of the Greek language, as it is often appended elsewhere, so that the sense is: "You were men of this kind." Although by great consensus the Latin manuscripts I have seen have written "indeed" [*quidem*], so that it is a conjunction. And so Augustine reads. Indeed, even Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop known for his concise biblical commentaries.</note> interprets it thus, as if he had read "indeed" [*μὲν*] instead of "some," as if this speech pertains to all, whereas in the context it is "some" [*τινες*], not "indeed" [*μὲν*]: unless we prefer to attribute this to the Translator. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), a famous early church father and orator.</note> reads "some" [*τινες*], but ignores this particle in his explanation. Ambrose <note>The 4th-century Bishop of Milan.</note>, however, seems to have read "certain ones" [*quidam*], which he writes in place of a commentary, lest he should seem to attribute this to everyone: *and certainly he would make all immune from these crimes if he remained silent.* For he seemed to have prohibited, not revealed, the crimes of his own people: therefore he says, *And these things indeed you were.* Thus far he. But how is it apparent from Paul's words that he does not attribute these things to everyone, unless we read "certain ones" [*quidam*]? Hence it is likely that by a librarian's error, "certain ones" [*quidam*] was changed to "indeed" [*quidem*]. Saint Irenaeus, in his fifth book, citing this passage once and again, reads "certain ones" [*quidam*]: which word had been corrupted by librarians in earlier books; because they saw the same thing repeated so often, they left it.

<margin>21 All things are lawful to me, but I under none]</margin> The translator could not preserve the pleasant allusion of the Greek words, *it is lawful* and *I shall be brought under power* <note>original Greek: ἔξεστι and ἐξουσιασθήσομαι</note>, that is, *it is permitted, and I shall be reduced to power.* We have rendered it however we could in this way: *I have power over all things, but I shall not be reduced under the power of any.*

<margin>22 Food for the stomach]</margin> "foods" [*escae*] should be said in the plural number, just as a little later, "the stomach for foods." Then "both this and these" should have been said. Jerome cites it almost this way in his Epistle to Amandus, and the Greek texts
<meta>catchword: have</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...will not inherit the inheritance of God? 19 Do not err: neither fornicators, nor worshippers of idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie <margin>10</margin> with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor the rapacious, will receive the inheritance of the kingdom of God. 20 And these things <margin>11</margin> some of you were, but you have been washed, but you have been sanctified, but you have been justified through the name of the Lord Jesus, and through the Spirit of our God. All things are lawful for me, but not all things are profitable: <margin>12</margin> I have power over all things, but I shall not be reduced under the power of any. 21 Foods are destined for the stomach, and <margin>13</margin> the stomach for foods: but God will abolish both this and those: The body, however, is not for debauchery, but for the Lord, and the Lord <margin>B</margin> for the body. God, moreover, both raised the Lord, and <margin>14</margin> will raise you through his power. 23 Or do you not know that <margin>15</margin> your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I therefore, taking the members of Christ, make them the members of a prostitute? Far be it. Or do you not know that 24 he who is joined to a prostitute is one <margin>16</margin> body? 25 For the two, he says, shall be reduced into <margin>17</margin> one flesh. But he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit. Flee prostitution: every sin, whatsoever a man shall commit, <margin>18</margin> is outside the body: but he who fornicates sins against his own body. Or do you not know that your body is the <margin>19</margin> temple of the Holy Spirit dwelling in you, whom you have from God, and you are not your own masters? 26 For you were bought <margin>20</margin> with a price: 27 glorify God now in your body and in your spirit, which are God's.

<sig>C</sig>

---

...have it, as he cites. The Donatian Codex had: *both this and these he will destroy.* Nor is this of such great importance, except that the plural number is more suitable in this place, since he is dealing with kinds of foods, not simply food. The Constance manuscript had written *both this and these* [**& hunc & has**]: as if it had read "foods" [βρώματα]. Moreover, some verb seems to be understood in "food for the stomach, and the stomach for food," just as a little later, *the body however not for fornication, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body*, surely "is destined" or "is dedicated." In a similar form of speech in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter seven, he signified a woman dedicated and proper to a man: *She shall be called an adulteress,* he says, *if she shall be for another man*: for so the Greek language has it, in which Paul wrote. And I do not know whether, according to the property of the Hebrew language, it is said to "be for someone" which pertains to him and is destined for his good.

<margin>23 Or do you not know that your members are a temple]</margin> In Greek it is not "members" [*membra*], but "bodies" [*σώματα*]. And so Chrysostom and Theophylact read and interpret it at the same time: thus Jerome cites it against Jovinian, in the second book, nor does Ambrose read otherwise. Our manuscripts with great consensus have in the former place: *do you not know that your bodies are of Christ*: in the latter, *Or do you not know that your members are a temple of the Holy Spirit.* Furthermore, where it says "temple," not "temples," either one number is placed for the other, or because he is speaking of the body of the Church collected together, "temple" was more fitting than "temples," as he also indicates.

<margin>24 He who adheres to a harlot]</margin> "he who adheres" <note>original Greek: ὁ κολλώμενος</note>. As if you were to say, "he who is glued to." And that fits neatly with what follows: "is made one body." There in the Greek it is "is" instead of "is made": which is more forceful.

<margin>E 25 For they shall be two in one flesh]</margin> "into one flesh" <note>original Greek: εἰς σάρκα μίαν</note>, that is, "into one flesh." And so Saint Jerome reads in his book to Gerontia on Monogamy: which is evident from what follows in his work, "not into two, nor into three." Furthermore, according to the property of the Hebrew language, "the two shall be in one flesh" is nothing other than "of those two, it shall become as if one man." It is cited in the same way in the books against Jovinian, and more than once in Tertullian <note>c. 155 – c. 220 AD, a prolific early Christian author from Carthage.</note>.

<margin>26 For you were bought with a great price]</margin> "Great" was added by our [translators], "For you were bought with a price" <note>original Greek: Ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς</note>, that is, "For you were bought at a value." For he is only arguing here that we are not our own masters, since they have been bought, and bought for a price, being already made the property of him by whom they were bought. And in that way Chrysostom introduces this place in his fifty-fifth Homily on Matthew. Nor does he read otherwise in his Commentaries. Although Theophylact proposes this reading, and in explaining it repeats it again and again, nevertheless the Translator <note>the Vulgate</note> everywhere insists on our common Edition, not to say the corruption of the Scribes. Yet it does not follow that if the Translator said "the price was great," the Apostle therefore wrote "great": here he finds "price," and does not add "great." Ambrose, bringing in this sentence from the chapter immediately following, in the second book of *Cain and Abel*, chapter three, does not add "great." Again, in the second book of Epistles, chapter two: and soon in the next chapter Paul repeats the same sentence in as many words, though in a reversed order, "You were bought at a price" <note>original Greek: Τιμῆς ἠγοράσθητε</note>. Nor does Origen <note>c. 184 – c. 253 AD, a highly influential early Christian scholar and theologian.</note> cite it differently in his sixth Homily on Exodus. However, concerning the greatness of the price, it appears to have been added from the first Epistle of Saint Peter, chapter one: *not with corruptible things like gold or silver, and so forth.* <margin>D</margin> Whoever changed the writing seems to have been offended by the absurdity of the speech, as if anything could be bought without a price, and that the word "price" was superfluous unless you added "great." But "with a price" being added emphasizes the Lord’s right, into whose jurisdiction we have entirely passed, having been redeemed from the right of the Devil, and that with a present price. However, when he found the same form of speech in the vicinity, he did not dare to change the writing.

<margin>F 27 Glorify, and bear God]</margin> In the Greek, "bear" is not added, but

<meta>This page transitions from the general warnings against sexual immorality in Chapter 6 to Paul’s specific responses to questions from the Corinthian church regarding marriage, celibacy, and conjugal rights. Erasmus continues his scholarly tradition of comparing the Greek source text with the Latin Vulgate and the writings of the Church Fathers.</meta>

### TO THE FIRST [EPISTLE TO THE] CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER VII.

->**Chapter VII.** 1 Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me: It is good for a man not to touch a woman. 2 But because of sexual immoralities, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. 3 Let the husband render the due benevolence to the wife, and likewise also the wife to the husband. 4 The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; and likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife. 5 Do not deprive one another, unless perhaps by agreement for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, so that Satan does not tempt you because of your lack of self-control. <margin>33</margin> 6 But I say this by way of concession, not by command.<-

<margin>A</margin> But it is added, which the Latin manuscripts do not have, *and in your spirit* <note>original: "καὶ ἐν τῷ πνεύματι ὑμῶν"</note>, that is, *and in your spirit*. Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and biblical commentator often cited by Erasmus.</note>, in explaining this passage, makes no mention of "bearing" <note>referring to the Latin Vulgate's "portate," meaning "bear/carry [God in your body]"</note>, but interprets the part about the spirit separately and sharply. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, the 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople, famous for his eloquent preaching.</note> does the same. Although in the Verona edition someone added "therefore take up" <note>original: "ἄρατε δή"</note>, the speech does not cohere. For it reads, "therefore glorify, and take up God." Likewise that phrase, *which are God’s* <note>original: "ἅτινά ἐστι τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note>, that is, *which are of God*: so that it refers at once to the body and the spirit, both of which are dedicated to God. Furthermore, both words, *body* and *spirit* <note>original: "σῶμα & πνεῦμα"</note>, are of the neuter gender in Greek. Theophylact also explains this small part; and Chrysostom both reads and interprets it in the same way. Nevertheless, both the Latin manuscripts and their interpreters disagree with great consensus.

<margin>D</margin> **Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me**] The speech is indeed incomplete, but this style of speaking is not unusual even among the Latins. For the sense is: "So that I may respond concerning these things which you wrote to me."
**2 It is good [for a man]...**] This is one place, I believe, in which it was appropriate to add the conjunction "that," which corresponds to "concerning." Truly, this is very frequent in Paul, from which argument Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> concludes that Paul did not perfectly master the Greek language.
**3 Not to touch a woman**] It would have been more correct here to say *wife*. Since the Greek word for "woman" <note>original: "γυναικός"</note> is ambiguous. Furthermore, "to touch" <note>original: "ἅπτεσθαι"</note>, according to the property of the Greek language, frequently signifies not touching with the hand, but having business or commerce with someone. Therefore, "not to touch a woman" sounds like nothing else than if you said, "it is good to abstain from a wife": that is, not to marry a wife. Even if Saint Jerome, in his work against Jovinian, zealously twists this word to mean simple physical contact, as if there were danger in the contact itself, and not only in sexual intercourse. This perhaps must be conceded in Holy Scripture whenever we are either exhorting, or consoling, or deterring, or rebuking. In a serious theological dispute, I would not want this to happen, even if Jerome permits this to himself especially, and defends having done so by the example of Paul, in whose writings he says testimonies fight which do not fight in their own places. Truly, there is danger meanwhile from those whose habit it is to pluck four or five words from any book and bring them forth as if from an oracle, not considering what preceded or what follows—as if in the thing itself—what is being done, to what end, and with what intent it was said. What of the fact that those things which follow clearly indicate this is the sense: *But because of fornication, etc.* It was best not to take a wife: but he who fears lest he fall into debauchery, let him rather marry, and have his own wife rather than another’s. Now this point, although not specific to this purpose, it will have been useful to advise in passing: that "good" is here taken for "expedient," rather than as the opposite of "vice," just as it is commonly said, "it was good for him that it profited him," and a man is called "bad" for war by Horace who is useless in war. For the question was not asked by the Corinthians, I believe, whether it was lawful to marry a wife, but whether it was expedient in that state of affairs to be bound by the chains of marriage. Jerome, however, fighting against those who attributed more than enough to marriage, reasons thus: "If it is good not to touch a wife, it is therefore bad to touch one; since bad is the contrary to good." Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo, the influential 5th-century Latin theologian.</note>, who had read Aristotle’s *Categories*, refutes this reasoning, saying that some things are "indifferent," which are neither good nor bad, such as blowing one's nose or spitting. For since he established three "goods" in marriage, he did not allow any mention of "bad," and therefore says "good" is here taken for "better": lest anyone think it disgraceful to marry a wife, as if "good" fought with "disgraceful." But if in Jerome’s words "bad" and "good" are taken similarly in both cases, his argument proceeds correctly according to the question proposed by the Corinthians. If it is expedient not to marry a wife because of the burdens of care and the bonds of kinship, it is therefore inexpedient to marry. Just as if someone asked whether it were good for him, about to enter upon a long journey subject to robberies, to carry money, and the answer was "it is good not to carry money," it would correctly follow that it is "bad" to carry it. For what is here opposed to "good," Paul a little later calls "tribulation" or "affliction of the flesh." Nor does he say simply, "it is good to remain thus as I am," but "it is good because of the present necessity." Therefore, what is good for a specific time and present circumstance is not immediately "good" in an absolute sense. In Paul’s age, when there were very few Christians among countless pagans, perhaps it was more convenient to abstain from marriage: now, with things changed, I do not know whether it might be more expedient to holily and purely cultivate holy marriage and an immaculate bed, even for Priests, if any do not remain continent, since their number is so vast everywhere, and again there is such a rarity of those living chastely. That Jerome twists these things somewhat must be granted to his desire for victory [in debate]: especially since he thinks it matters a great deal whether someone is to be taught or to be bound; to be instructed or to be ensnared. Furthermore, as for Augustine’s clever arguments here, though they may be true, they certainly do not seem to me to pertain properly to Paul’s meaning.
**4 Because of fornication**] <note>original: "διὰ δὲ τὰς πορνείας"</note>, that is, *because of*

<column-break/>

1 Furthermore, concerning the things about which you wrote to me; It is good for a man not to touch a wife. 2 Yet to avoid sexual immorality, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. 3 Let the husband render the due benevolence to the wife, and likewise the wife to the husband. 4 The wife does not have the right over her own body, but the husband: likewise also the husband does not have the right over his own body, but the wife. 5 Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps it be by consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to fasting and prayer: and come together again, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control. 6 But I say this by way of indulgence, not by way of command.
13 For

<margin>B</margin> *fornications*, or *acts of prostitution*. Although this matters nothing to the sense, unless perhaps by the plural number he hints at various species of lust.
**5 Let him have his own wife**] <note>original: "ἐχέτω"</note>: which word among the Greeks is clearly in the imperative mood. But there is no reason why it should not move them, nor is there reason why we should interpret "let him have" as "it is permitted to have": since this is said to those who cannot restrain themselves from the company of women—not to everyone. And to those, indeed, who would permit themselves prostitution, or some more foul kind of lust, he commands that they rather marry a wife. But if in this place he had wrongly translated *husband* <note>original: "maritum"</note> for "render" <note>original: "ἀποδιδότω"</note> and *wife* <note>original: "uxorem"</note> for "woman" <note>original: "γυναῖκα"</note>, a bit more light would have reached the speech. For the words among the Greeks are ambiguous. Let Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, the 15th-century humanist whose critiques of the Vulgate inspired Erasmus.</note> be scrutinized in this place concerning the pronouns *his own* and *her own*, which I did not think worth the effort to write down.
**6 Let the husband render the due benevolence to the wife**] In Greek it is thus, "Let the husband render the due benevolence to the wife" <note>original: "τῇ γυναικὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τὴν ὀφειλομένην εὔνοιαν ἀποδιδότω"</note>. That is, *let him render the due benevolence*: so that he might modestly note a matter that is not very modest. Although Ambrose and Jerome read it otherwise. It signifies their "all," and therefore he weaves into words what ought to be understood. In only one manuscript <margin>C</margin> instead of *benevolence* <note>original: "εὔνοιαν"</note>, I found written *honor* <note>original: "τιμὴν"</note>: with the commentaries attributed to Chrysostom explaining it in that way, but the title is suspect to me. Therefore, since the Greek writing varies, I am led to the conjecture that Paul wrote *the debt* <note>original: "τὴν ὀφειλὴν"</note>: which then, either by chance or so that the speech might be more modest, someone changed into "certain discoveries." Although Theophylact reads and interprets it in that way, making no mention of intercourse. Before I prepared this fifth edition, I obtained Greek manuscripts of better reliability. In these, the context has *the due honor* <note>original: "τὴν ὀφειλομένην τιμὴν"</note>, and likewise the commentary, but with the addition "attraction" <note>original: "ἐφολκίαν"</note> in the middle, which he says "on account of honor and shame he called the matter thus," that is, *and therefore he called this business a debt*. However, he makes no mention of honor. And Chrysostom turns the explanation in this direction, as if Paul by these words were commending conjugal fidelity and chastity, lest either this man or that woman grant the use of their body to anyone except the one to whom it is owed by the faith of marriage. And <margin>D</margin> while in other writings of both Testaments they attribute much authority to the man, in this he shows them equal: that the husband, just as much as the wife, cannot grant the use of his body to another; which indeed pertains to conjugal use. These things are indeed truly said, but even those things which follow declare the Apostle is thinking of conjugal intercourse: *Do not defraud one another, except by consent*. For if you interpret "Do not defraud" as "Do not grant the use of your body to another," how does what follows fit: "unless by consent"? Will it be permitted to commit adultery by consent? Therefore, in this place, the Latin edition is more corrected.
**7 Do not defraud**] <note>original: "Μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε"</note>, that is, *Do not deprive*. For we properly defraud when we withdraw a thing that is owed, just as we are frustrated in a thing hoped for.
**8 Unless perhaps by consent**] It is not "perhaps" in Greek, but *if not something indeed* <note>original: "εἰ μή τι ἄν"</note>. Truly, the translator wanted to express the filler conjunction *an*, <margin>E</margin> and that not inaptly: but it also diminishes it, unless something is done by consent. The Apostle sensed the Corinthians were more prone to lust and that it was not safe to live apart too often or too long, and therefore he binds this confession in many ways: *unless something is done by consent, and for the sake of prayer, and for a short time*.
**9 That you may devote yourselves to prayer**] The Greek adds *to fasting and to prayer* <note>original: "τῇ νηστείᾳ καὶ τῇ προσευχῇ"</note>: which two things Saint Jerome also joins: although Chrysostom, and Theophylact following him, in explaining this passage, make no mention of fasting: although *fasting* is added in the text, he would not have been silent if he had read it. The same noted the emphasis of this word *devote yourselves* <note>original: "σχολάζητε"</note>. For he did not say "you should pray," but "you should be at leisure for prayer": because that matter requires a mind free from all worldly cares. And yet the word "to be at leisure" does not fit fasting in the same way.
**10 Return to the same thing**] <note>original: "καὶ τὰ αὐτὸ συνέρχεσθε"</note>, that is, *to the same*, or *come together into one*, or *convene*, so that you understand them to have been previously separated in their bedchambers. For in Greek, those are said to "come into the same" <margin>F</margin> who meet in the same place, or who agree—that is, they go into the same opinion—as in the eleventh chapter of this Epistle: *When you come together into one*, <note>original: "συνέρχεσθαι ὑμᾶν εἰς τὸ αὐτό"</note>. What he translates here as *into the same*, he translated there as *into one*. It is strange, however, that Augustine, following a manuscript in his 199th Epistle, reads "and again be for that very thing." The same reading exists in the 50th Homily, on mixed arguments, and again in the fifth book against Faustus, the ninth chapter. Nay, and in Origen, it is cited thus in the 23rd Homily on Numbers. Perhaps they read *be ye* <note>original: "γίνεσθε"</note>.
**11 Because of incontinence**] <note>original: "διὰ τὴν ἀκρασίαν"</note>, that is, *because of lack of self-control*: although there is very little difference.
**12 According to indulgence**] Some Greek manuscripts have *according to concession* <note>original: "κατὰ συγγνώμην"</note>, that is, *according to acknowledgment* or *pardon*. Some have *according to opinion* <note>original: "κατὰ γνώμην"</note>, that is, *according to advice* or *judgment*...
