<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed commentary on 1 Corinthians Chapter 7. Having previously discussed Paul’s "concession" regarding marital relations, Erasmus now examines Paul’s specific instructions for the unmarried, widows, and those in "unequal" marriages between believers and unbelievers, while debating whether Paul himself was ever married.</meta>

<page-num>687</page-num>
# EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER VII.

<margin>A</margin> 7 by way of concession. For I wish all men to be even as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this manner and another in that. 8 But I say to the unmarried and to the widows: it is good for them if they remain even as I am. 9 But if they do not have self-control, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn. 10 Now to the married I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife not be separated from her husband. 11 But even if she is separated, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband; and let a husband not divorce his wife. 12 But to the rest I say, <margin>B</margin> 13 not the Lord: If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she is willing to live with him, let him not divorce her. 14 And a woman who has an unbelieving husband, and he is willing to live with her, let her not divorce him. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the husband; otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy. 15 But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart; the brother or the sister is not under bondage in such cases, but God has called us in peace. 16 For how do you know, O wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, O husband, whether you will save your wife? 17 Only as God has distributed to each, as the Lord has called each, so let him walk; and so I ordain in all the Churches.

---

*...opinion:* <note>Erasmus is finishing a thought from the previous page regarding Paul’s "opinion" or "judgment."</note> as if he were saying: "I speak my opinion, and what seems best to me to do, but I do not command it." Although the word "concession" <note>original: "συγγνώμην"</note> is more aptly translated as "pardon" or "allowance" rather than "command." A command demands; a pardon grants something beyond what is strictly required. For here Paul is indulgent toward their fragility. Augustine does not hesitate to assert from this passage that sexual intercourse with a wife initiated for the sake of quenching lust is not free from fault, even if it is "venial" <note>An "excusable" or minor sin in Catholic theology.</note>, with marriage serving as the excuse.

13 **For I wish you all to be as I myself am** In the Greek, they have "for" <note>original: "γὰρ"</note>, not "but" <note>original: "δὲ"</note>. For he is explaining what he meant by "according to indulgence": "otherwise I would wish," he says, "that all who have wives would abstain from them entirely." From this passage, one might even conjecture that Paul had a wife, since he makes mention of himself while discussing marriage.

14 **But I say to the unmarried** The Greek term is *unmarried* <note>original: "ἀγάμοις"</note>; "single" would have been clearer, or perhaps "marriageable" or "unjoined." For the [Greek] article indicates this is said to men—*to the unmarried men*—that is, those who are single. Although nothing prevents this from referring to both sexes. And Theophylact <note>An 11th-century commentator.</note> added the feminine article, "to the unmarried women," so that one term might refer to virgins and the other to widows. Those who are single can be called *unmarried*, but those who have already experienced marriage cannot. It appears this was done by some studious person to preserve Paul’s reputation for virginity. For Chrysostom <note>A 4th-century Church Father.</note> includes the feminine article; however, neither interpretation makes any mention of "virgins" or "virginity." The flow of the speech itself suggests that we should understand the Apostle here to be dealing with widowers and widows, or certainly with men who were single in any way, whether by the death of a spouse or because they had never attempted marriage. For a virtuous woman, if she is single, must be either a widow or a virgin. First, the Apostle exhorts the married that those who cannot abstain entirely should sometimes temper their union for the sake of prayer, but by mutual consent. From the married, he passes to the single who have experienced marriage, whom he exhorts not to seek marriage again. From here he returns to the married, giving many instructions about divorce and unequal marriage. After these things, he comes to female virgins. Finally, he discusses a mixture of widows, the married, and virgins. What remains is that the phrase "those who have wives," and so on, pertains to the married. "He who is without a wife," and so on, pertains to the single. "And the unmarried woman and the virgin" pertains to widows and virgins. What he previously called "widows," he here calls "unmarried"; just as he previously called the widowers "unmarried." And so he mixes the discussion of this chapter. Furthermore, he mentions himself in two places. For having exhorted the married to spontaneous continence, which he nevertheless does not dare to demand, he adds: *For I wish you all to be as I myself am.* Soon, having spoken of widowers and widows, he adds, *it is good for them if they remain even as I am.* It is not absurd for mention of the Apostle to be made in both places. For he exhorts all to his own example, who—whether he had a wife and had turned her into a "sister" <note>A common early Christian practice of "spiritual marriage" without sexual relations.</note> and held her as though not holding her, or whether she was already deceased—was in either case free from the anxiety of marriage. For what he says here, "I wish you all to be as I myself am," he later explains as, "I wish you to be without anxiety." Therefore, what he says to the married and the widows—"I wish you to be as I am"—does not necessarily mean we must assume the Apostle desires those who had married to become single; but rather that they should do as he perhaps had done: turn their wives into sisters, and by this means prepare for themselves leisure to serve the Lord. Nor does it follow that Paul was a widower simply because he desires them to be as he was. For even if Paul had not been a widower, he nevertheless possessed that freedom which widowers have. Exhorting them to maintain this, he warns them to persevere in their freedom. The example, therefore, to which Paul invites them is not found in the condition or state of life, but in the tranquility which continence provides. Moreover, where he speaks without controversy about virgins, he makes no mention of himself. For although he prefaced that he has no command from the Lord regarding virgins, he adds, *it is good for a man to be so*, but he does not refer to himself, but to the present state. And if he were to refer to himself, it would not immediately follow that he was a virgin—no more than it follows that he was married or a widower because he invites those people to imitate him. For what was in Paul could be common to the married, the widowed, and the virgins alike.

<column-break/>

<page-num>688</page-num>
13 For I would wish all men to be as I myself am: but each one has his own gift from God, one indeed in this way, another in that. 14 But I say to the unjoined and the widows, it is good for them if they remain as I also am. But if they do not restrain themselves, let them contract marriage: 15 for it is better to contract marriage than to be burned. 16 But to the married I command—not I, but rather the Lord—that a wife not be separated from her husband: But if she has been separated, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband; and let a husband not dismiss his wife. 17 But to the rest I say, not the Lord: If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she agrees to live with him, let him not dismiss her. And a woman who has an unbelieving husband, and he agrees to live with her, let him not dismiss him. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through the husband; otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy. But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart: a brother or sister is not subject to servitude in such matters, but God has called us in peace. For how do you know, woman, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, man, whether you will save your wife? 20 However it may be, as God has distributed to each, as the Lord has called each, so let them walk—

---

<margin>C</margin> Therefore, although it cannot be proven from this passage whether Paul was a husband, or a widower, or a virgin, it is more probably gathered that he was one of those first two than the third. However, the matter is not worth a dispute.

15 **It is better to marry than to burn** <note>original: "κρεῖσσον γάρ ἐστι γαμῆσαι ἢ πυροῦσθαι"</note> For the Greeks, the verb "to marry" <note>original: "γαμῆσαι"</note> is ambiguous, as it signifies both "to marry a man" and "to take a wife." For this sentiment pertains to both men and women. Therefore, what he said before—"to the unmarried and the widows"—is written in some Greek manuscripts as "to the unmarried men" <note>original: "τοῖς ἀγάμοις"</note> with the masculine article added. Yet it is written such that you understand both sexes under one gender; although, as was just said, some manuscripts have the feminine article, yet they soon return to the masculine gender: "it is good for them" <note>original: "καλὸν αὐτοῖς ἐστι"</note>. And the word for "better" <note>original: "κρεῖσσον"</note> is not strictly "better," but rather "more to be chosen." Furthermore, regarding "to burn" <note>original: "πυροῦσθαι"</note>, I wonder why some people, against the opinion of all the Ancients, explain this as referring to the fire of Hell <note>original: "gehennæ"</note>, when here he is clearly speaking about the fire of lust and the physical distress of one who is not self-controlled.

<margin>D</margin> 16 **But to those who are joined in marriage** For the Greeks, the word <note>original: "γεγαμηκόσι"</note> is masculine, but in such a way that it also embraces the feminine; this is declared by what follows. Therefore, we have translated it as "the married," so that it pertains to the husband and wife simultaneously. And indeed, in very old copies—specifically in the one provided by the Library of the College of Saint Paul in London—I found it written in the masculine gender: "To those who are joined in marriage." Then Augustine, explaining the Sermon on the Mount, cites it in the masculine: "To those who are in marriage, I command, not I, but the Lord."

17 **For to the rest I say** Augustine indicates this pertains to those joined in an unequal marriage <note>A marriage between a Christian and a non-Christian.</note>.

<margin>E</margin> 18 **Through the faithful wife, through the faithful husband** <note>original: "ἐν τῇ γυναικὶ, ἐν τῷ ἀνδρὶ"</note>, that is, "in the wife, in the husband." Although for the Greeks the word for "woman" signifies both "woman" and "wife." And in this place, the recent Translator changed the preposition, which he otherwise either fears or neglects to do. The adjective "faithful" was added by us in both places, since it is not added by the Greeks but is understood. Augustine, in the first book where he explains the Sermon on the Mount, reads it this way: "For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the faithful wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the faithful brother." And lest anyone think this happened by chance, or that the passage is corrupted, he himself brings forward the testimony of this place several times later in the same book, teaching that in Sacred Scripture a Christian is signified by the word "brother," though here he does not add "faithful." And he calls "sanctified" here "purified." For it follows, "otherwise your children were unclean."

19 **Called you** <note>original: "ἡμᾶς"</note>, that is, "us," in the first person, not the second, supported by the very ancient manuscript of the Pauline Library, and likewise of the Donation <note>A reference to another manuscript source Erasmus consulted.</note>.

<margin>F</margin> 20 **Unless to each as the Lord divided** Some Greek manuscripts have "unless" <note>original: "εἰ μὴ"</note>; some have "or not," so that it refers to the preceding part. But the Greek scholars want the punctuation to be placed after "unless": "whether you will save," or "not": because to some, the construction of the speech seems incomplete. For this punctuation, they cite a certain Severianus as the author. Theophylact also mentions a double attempt at this passage. The first is: "How do you know whether you, the wife, will save the husband, or not?" And soon, as if abruptly, it is interjected: "To each as the Lord divided." Then follows what responds to the first part: "How do you know, husband, whether you will save the wife, or not?" so that the phrase "to each as the Lord divided," since it is separated from both by the law of construction, might respond to both. The gifts of God are varied: perhaps it will happen that he or she is saved; therefore, whether it happens or does not happen, the marriage must not be dissolved. The other arrangement joins the two parts: "How do you know whether you will save the husband, or you will save the wife?" then follows as a new heading: "Unless to each as the Lord divided, let him so remain"; as if he were saying, let nothing else be attempted or changed because of an unbelieving wife: only that as each one's lot befell him, so let him remain. And he prefers this reading over the former. But if one labors over the punctuation, nothing prevents it from referring to the previous verb: "How can you know whether you are going to save—"
<meta>unless</meta>

<summary>Erasmus provides a philological analysis of 1 Corinthians 7:7-17, debating Paul’s marital status and clarifying that Paul’s advice on marriage is a "concession" to human weakness rather than a command. He also corrects common misinterpretations of "burning" as hellfire, arguing instead that it refers to the "fire of lust."</summary>

# TO THE CORINTHIANS I. CHAPTER VII.

<margin>A</margin> 18 I ordain in all the churches. Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not undo his circumcision. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised. 19 Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God. 20 Let each remain in that calling in which he was called. 21 Were you called as a slave? Do not let it concern you; but if you are also able to become free, rather make use of it. 22 For he who is called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman; likewise, he who is called as a free man is Christ’s slave. 23 You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men. 24 Let each one, brothers, <margin>B</margin> remain with God in that state in which he was called. 25 Now concerning virgins, I have no commandment from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful. 26 I think therefore that this is good because of the present necessity: that it is good for a man to remain as he is. 27 Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek a release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. 28 But <margin>C</margin> if you do marry, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. Yet such people will have tribulation in the flesh, and I would spare you. 29 But this I say, brothers, the time is short; it remains that even those who have wives should be as though they had none; 30 and those who weep as though they did not weep; and those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice; and those who buy as though they did not possess; 31 and those who use this world as though they did not use it fully; for the form of this world is passing away. 32 but I want you to be without care. The unmarried man cares for the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord. 33 But he who is married cares for the things of the world, how he may please his wife. 34 There is a difference also between a wife and a virgin.

---

*...unless each remains as he was when called?* <note>original: "nisi unusquisque sic permanserit, ut vocatus est?"</note> Truly, it pleases me more that the phrase <term>εἰ μὴ</term> <note>original: "ei mē," usually translated as "unless"</note> be read separately, so that it effectively means "anyhow" or "in short." We tend to use this form of speaking whenever we set aside uncertain matters and return to what is certain. Terence seems to have expressed this figure of Greek speech in his play *The Brothers*: *I was rejoicing. But behold, it starts anew; anyhow, I want to know whatever it is and meet the man.* He used it in several other places in the same manner. So Paul, because he had proposed a doubtful point regarding keeping an unbelieving husband or wife, says "anyhow," let each remain as God has distributed to him and as he was called, whatever the outcome of keeping the spouse may be. Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> also mentions something about a double reading of this passage, from which it appears he was aided by commentaries translated from the Greek which are no longer extant.

21 *I teach in all the Churches*] <term>διατάσσομαι</term> <note>original: "diatassomai"</note>, that is, *I ordain* or *I establish*.

22 *Let him not draw down the foreskin*] <term>μὴ ἐπισπάσθω</term> <note>original: "mē epispasthō"</note>, that is, *let him not procure it: understanding the foreskin*. Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator</note> suggests that a removed foreskin was often brought back using medicine. Cornelius Celsus <note>a Roman medical writer</note> indicates a certain technique for this in book seven, chapter twenty-five, regarding how the glans should be covered either naturally or when bared by amputation. But whether Paul meant this, I do not know. Certainly, Origen in the fourth book of *On First Principles* <note>original: "peri archōn"</note> thinks it is impossible for a foreskin once amputated to be restored in any way. However that may be, we preferred the word *procure* <note>original: "accercere"</note> rather than *draw down*, if only for the sake of modesty.

23 *Each in which he was called, brother*] <term>ἀδελφοί</term> <note>original: "adelphoi"</note>, that is, *brothers*, in the plural number, and only in this latter part. Furthermore, the word "in" is repeated superfluously here according to the property of Hebrew speech, just as a little earlier: *Each in which calling he was called, in that let him remain.*

24 *But I give my counsel*] <term>γνώμην δὲ δίδωμι</term> <note>original: "gnōmēn de didōmi"</note>, that is, *I give my opinion*, or I say that which seems best to me: that is, I put forward my own judgment on this matter. He who gives counsel opens up his own judgment. And lest he be despised, he adds that he obtained this through divine mercy, so that he might speak in good faith on the matter as an Apostle.

25 *Because of the imminent necessity*] <term>ἐνεστῶσαν</term> <note>original: "enestōsan"</note>. The Greeks call the present time <term>ἐνεστῶτα</term> <note>original: "enestōta"</note>, and Fabius <note>Quintilian</note>, imitating them, calls it *imminent*. Ambrose reads it as *because of the present necessity*, clearly understanding the present state of those times. For it is necessary to moderate counsels of this kind according to the conditions of the times. And this confirms what was said by us above.

26 *Do not seek a release*] <term>λῦσιν</term> <note>original: "lysin"</note>. For others, *divorce* is more pleasing than *release*, as it is for the Latins; but nevertheless, the grace of the opposites—*bound, released, and release*—is somewhat lost.

27 *Tribulation of the flesh*] In Greek it is <term>τῇ σαρκὶ</term> <note>original: "tē sarki"</note>, that is, *to the flesh*, or *in the flesh*. Nor is there reason for Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, humanist critic</note> to reject for this sake the exposition of Ambrose and all the others, who interpret "tribulation of the flesh" as the inconveniences of this world, such as disputes with relatives, the care of children, anxiety over household matters, and six hundred other things of that kind which accompany marriage. For Paul, in his usual manner, calls *flesh* that which is more coarse and thick, departing from that purity and simplicity of the divine Spirit. But it is said *to have tribulation in the flesh* just as we say *we are afflicted in mind* or *tormented in body*.

28 *The time*] <term>ὁ καιρὸς συνεσταλμένος</term> <note>original: "ho kairos synestalmēnos"</note>, that is, *the time is contracted*: which Jerome, against Jovinian, translates as *time in brief* <note>original: "tempus in collecto"</note>.

Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, 19 but the keeping of the commandments of God. Let each remain in that calling in which he was called. Were you called as a slave? Let it not be a care to you, but rather, if you can become free, use it. For he who is called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman; similarly, he who was called as a free man is Christ’s slave. You were bought with a price, do not become slaves of men. 23 Let each one, brothers, remain with God in that state in which he was called. <margin>D</margin> And what follows, *the rest* <note>original: "<term>τὸ λοιπὸν</term>"</note>, can be referred to what preceded, so that you read: *the time that remains is contracted*. And thus the Greeks seem to read it, specifically Theophylact, and in the same way Ambrose, as is gathered from his interpretation. If one chooses to follow this, the conjunction *that* <note>original: "<term>ἵνα</term>"</note> which follows will not be taken *causally*, but to declare a consequence, as in this speech: *All this life is short, so that even if marriage has any pleasure, it must be neglected, for the very reason that it will soon slip away.*

29 *As though they did not use it fully*] <term>ὡς μὴ καταχρώμενοι</term> <note>original: "hōs mē katachrōmenoi"</note>, that is, *as though not abusing*. Although this "abusing" is nothing other in my opinion than "using intensely." We "use" for good, we "abuse" for evil, and according to the legal experts, "abuse" <note>original: "abusus"</note> applies to wine, grain, and similar things which are consumed by use; "use" applies to a horse, or clothing, and the like; and we "use" a man with whom we have familiarity. Here "to abuse" seems to be said for "to use greatly," just as the Latins say *to tire and to weary out, to love and to love desperately, to lose and to lose utterly*. For "to abuse" does not always sound in a bad sense, just as <term>καταχρᾶσθαι</term> <note>original: "katachrasthai"</note> does not among the Greeks. For sometimes when we apply something in an unsuitable place or time, we are said "to abuse" it; whence even the Rhetoricians have *catachresis* <note>a figure of speech where a word is used in a new or "forced" way</note> among their figures, that is, ornaments of speech. Since the preposition among the Greeks can also sound as praise, <term>καταχρᾶσθαι</term> sounds more like a fault. Thus the Apostle says this: the time here is short, and there is no leisure to be devoted to a wife.

30 *For the figure passes away*] <term>παράγει</term> <note>original: "paragei"</note>. Faber Stapulensis <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, a French humanist</note> corrects it to *deceives*: because the word itself seems to sound like "to lead away," as if to *seduce, or lead away from the path*. But the compounds of this verb are frequently used as neuters <note>intransitive verbs</note>, such as *I go away, I go before*: which is placed more than once in the Gospel writings. *Go behind me.* And in John chapter nine, *And Jesus passing by*. And in the same author chapter ten, verse fourteen, *let us go hence*. Likewise in Matthew chapter four, *Jesus went about Galilee*, that is, he traveled through all Galilee. In the same author chapter twenty, *that Jesus passed by*, that is, that Jesus was passing. Again in chapter twenty-one, *they go before*, they precede. Likewise in chapter twenty-three, *you go about*. and so indeed it fits better with Paul's meaning, and the Greek notes explain it thus: *passes by, goes away*. Moreover, what he called <term>σχῆμα</term> <note>original: "schēma"</note>, that is, *figure*, is just as if you said *habit or state*. Theophylact also noted the emphasis of the noun, because this world has nothing solid in it, but only presents a certain appearance of good and evil. Chrysostom seems to be mutilated <note>missing text</note> in this place.

<margin>F</margin> 31 *He who is without a wife*] <term>ὁ ἄγαμος</term> <note>original: "ho agamos"</note>, that is, *he who is celibate*, or *unmarried*. It is a wonder why the Translator preferred a periphrasis <note>a roundabout way of speaking</note>, when a proper word is available to the Latins, which Cyprian certainly used in his second treatise on the dress of virgins: *The celibate thinks on the things which are of God, how he may please God: but he who has contracted marriage, and so forth.*

32 *How he may please God*] In the Greek it is *to the Lord*, not *to God*, <term>τῷ Κυρίῳ</term> <note>original: "tō Kyriō"</note>. She has no husband whom she may please, but she has a Lord, whose mind she ought to obey. Then follows, *that she may be holy both in body and spirit*, with a double conjunction.

33 *And she is divided*] There is a far different sense among the Greeks. Indeed, the verb <term>μεμέρισται</term> <note>original: "memeristai"</note> does not refer to what precedes, but to what follows. *The wife and the virgin are divided*, that is, *Divided are both the wife and the virgin*: that is, they are of a different life pursuit. Then he explains the distinction of life. Theophylact interprets it in that sense. This passage is cited correctly by Ver... <note>The text cuts off mid-name</note>

<header>THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER VII.</header>

34 ...the wife and the virgin. The unmarried woman cares for the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in both body and spirit; but the married woman cares for the things of the world, how she may please her husband.
35 This I say for your own benefit, not to cast a snare upon you, but for the sake of what is appropriate and for constant devotion to the Lord without distraction.
36 But if anyone thinks he is behaving improperly toward his virgin, if she is past her bloom <note>original: "hypērakmos"</note>, and so it must be: let him do what he wishes, he does not sin; let them marry.
37 But he who stands firm in his heart, having no necessity, but has power over his own will, and has decided this in his heart, to keep his virgin, does well.
38 So then, he who gives her in marriage does well; but he who does not give her in marriage does better.
39 A wife is bound by law for as long as her husband lives; but if her husband should fall asleep, she is free...

...against Helvidius, even if the books here also carry some errors. However, from the very continuity of the speech, it is clear that Jerome understands it as we interpret it—namely, as those who speak. See what great happiness it is for one who has even lost the name of her sex. Likewise, in the *Letter to Eustochium on Preserving Virginity*. But again, the same author in the first book *Against Jovinian* rejects this reading, which he admits is indeed in the Latin manuscripts and was explained by him according to the nature of the passage, yet he says it is not of Apostolic truth, by whom it was written thus: *He is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided.* Then, having finished this sentence, passing to virgins and the continent, he added, *The unmarried woman and the virgin think on the things of the Lord: and the face* <note>Erasmus is discussing a textual variant where "the virgin" might have been an explanatory gloss added later</note> of the interpretation was added as "virgin," lest we think that unmarried prostitutes could be included in this speech, or perhaps for the sake of elegance the same thing was said twice. From this, one may gather that the Greek copies in that age varied due to the times. Indeed, in the Greek manuscripts today we read in this manner: *But the married man cares for the things of the world, how he may please his wife. The woman and the virgin are divided* <note>original: "Memeristai hē gynē kai hē parthenos"</note>. That is, *But he who has taken a wife is anxious about these things which are of the world, how he may please his wife. Then, after a punctuation mark, it follows: The woman and the virgin are divided.* Therefore, what Jerome writes as being in the Latin manuscripts is found today in the Greek; and what he says is of Apostolic truth is read in the common Latin copies. But whichever way you read it, the meaning remains almost the same. Saint Ambrose reads it thus: *but he who is with a wife is anxious for the things of this world, how he may please his wife, and is divided: the woman and the virgin are divided.* And explaining this, he adds: *Divided not by nature, which they share, but by action: because we read in the book of Numbers that women were called virgins.* From these words it is clear that for Ambrose, Paul feels the pursuit of the woman and the virgin are different. Yet the same author in the booklet *On Widows* cites this place differently: *According to what is written,* he says, *both the unmarried woman and the virgin think on the things which are of the Lord, that she may be holy in body and spirit.* These things clearly prove that Ambrose's manuscripts also varied in this place. Similarly, Augustine cites it in the booklet *On the Good of Widowhood*, chapter two, adding there that an unmarried woman is called a widow. I will add this: certainly in this place it would have been more correct to translate <term>gynē</term> <note>the Greek word for woman or wife</note> as "wife" rather than "woman," even though that word signifies both. Jerome cites it in the same way, both in several other places and in the *Letter to Eustochium on Preserving Virginity*.

<margin>34 The virgin ponders</margin> 34 **The virgin ponders**] *merimna*, that is, she cares for, or is anxious about: just as he had translated above.

<margin>35 What is honorable, and what provides the means</margin> 35 **What is honorable, and what provides the means**] In Greek it has it thus: *alla pros to euschēmon kai euprosedron tō Kyriō aperispastōs*. These things would indeed be very difficult to translate word for word. But the meaning is roughly of this sort: *but toward that which is honorable and decorous, and so that you may always cling and adhere to the Lord without being pulled away.* Saint Jerome, in his work against Jovinian, testifying that the Greek property of the word cannot be rendered, explained the meaning of this passage in this manner: *But I say these things for your utility, not that I may cast a snare upon you, but that I may exhort you to that which is honorable, and which makes one serve the Lord intensely, without any distraction.* He adds that this sentence is not found in the Latin manuscripts at all, because of the difficulty of the translation. Certainly, in Ambrose, the conclusion of this speech is absent: for he reads it thus, *But I say this for your own utility, not that I may cast a snare upon you, but toward that which is honorable.* Thus he ends the speech, nor in his interpretation does he indicate that he read any more. Jerome translates *euschēmon* as "honorable," and rendered *to euprosedron tō Kyriō* as "which makes one serve the Lord intensely," and for *aperispastōs* he put "without any distraction." Plutarch used this word in his booklet *On Curiosity*, calling the pursuit of wisdom *aperispaston* when no business calls the mind away to other things. In the old manuscripts, even the printed ones, it is still held as "to be cast against the Lord" <note>original: "Domino objectandi"</note>; I do not think anyone ever spoke in Latin in such a way. The Donatian manuscript had "to be observed" <note>original: "observandi"</note>. In both of the Constance manuscripts it was also "to be observed." From these one might guess that the first writing was "to serve the Lord" <note>original: "Domino obferviendi"</note>, which one person turned into "to be cast against," leaving the dative case, and another into "to be observed," changing the case as well. Certainly, among the Greeks, there is no mention of "casting against."

<margin>36 He thinks himself to appear shameful</margin> 36 **He thinks himself to appear shameful**] *Ei de tis aschēmonein epi tēn parthenon hautou nomizei*, that is, if anyone thinks it shameful or indecorous regarding his virgin. Augustine, in his *Questions on the Numbers of the Pentateuch*, indicates that some interpret "virgin" in this place as "virginity." But he does not approve of their opinion, because nothing else similar is found in the Divine Books. For Paul is feeling out the situation of parents giving their daughters in marriage, without whose authority he did not think

34 The unmarried woman cares for those things which are the Lord's, that she may be holy in both body and spirit; on the other hand, she who is married cares for the things of the world, how she may be pleasing to her husband.
35 But I say this toward that which is conducive for you, not that I may cast a snare upon you, but so that you may follow what is honorable and decorous, and cling to the Lord without any distraction.
36 But if anyone thinks it indecorous for his virgin, if she should pass the time of marrying, and so it ought to be done: let him do what he wants, he does not sin, let them be joined in marriage.
37 But he who stands firm in his heart, not having necessity, but has power of his own will, and has decreed this in his heart, that he will keep his virgin, does well.
38 And so he who gives her in marriage does well; however, he who does not give her in marriage does better.
39 A wife is bound to marriage as long as her husband lives; but if her husband should sleep, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in...

marriage contracts were made. Would that this were also observed in these times, especially at that age which does not yet have enough established counsel or judgment, especially since it is so pleasing that a marriage once entered into by whatever agreement cannot be dissolved by anything other than death. However, that these words refer to the parent rather than to virginity itself is suggested by what follows: *therefore both he who joins his virgin in marriage* and so on. And indeed, Theophylact explains this passage in this way.

<margin>37 If she be past her prime</margin> 37 **If she be past her prime**] *hypērakmos*. For that refers to one past her bloom, whose flower has already passed. Which Ambrose renders thus: *if she be beyond puberty*; something which is commonly ridiculed when they call an old woman a virgin. Virgins who are quite grown up are also accustomed to be subject to infamy, as if they were fastidiously rejected by suitors.

<margin>38 He does not sin if she marries</margin> 38 **He does not sin if she marries**] *gameitōsan*, that is, let them marry. Although the verb *gamein* is common to the man taking a wife and the girl marrying a man. Whence suddenly Paul, having changed the number of the verb, looked to the groom and the bride, or certainly to him who places his daughter and the groom. Theophylact reads *gameitō* (let him/her marry); nor does he add "if," but "as," as in "he does not sin, let her marry": so that "he does not sin" pertains to the father, and "let her marry" to those between whom the marriage is coming together.

<margin>39 For he who has decided</margin> 39 **For he who has decided**] *Hos de estēken hedraios*, that is, but he who stands firm, except that the verb *istēmi* means both "I stand" and "I establish" for the Greeks. Certainly, he translated the same word in the Gospel of John as "stands." Here, surely, "stands firm" was more fitting, for the word "decreed" follows immediately. However, what he says here about standing firmly corresponds to what preceded, "he who thinks himself shameful," and so forth. He who does not fear for the daughter's chastity, nor is moved by common reproach because he keeps a marriageable virgin at home, let him do what he judges to be best.

<margin>40 But having power over himself</margin> 40 **But having power over himself**] *echei*, he has, not they have. Although here the manuscripts vary.

<margin>41 And this he judged</margin> 41 **And this he judged**] Better "decreed" or "established": in this place it is *kekriken*, which he elsewhere translates thus.

<margin>42 She is liberated from the law</margin> 42 **She is liberated from the law, but to whom she wishes, let her marry**] The Greek says it slightly differently: *eleuthera esti, hō thelei gamēthēnai*, that is, she is free to marry whom she wishes, or for marrying whom she wishes. The Donatian manuscript had it thus: *she is free, let her marry whom she wishes.* I suspect it was written by the translator as *ut cui vult nubat* ("that she may marry whom she wishes"), and the *ut* ("that") was corrupted into *autem* ("but"). Certainly, "but" is not in the old manuscripts, specifically those that were at Constance. However, as I testified once at the beginning of this work, it is right to keep it testified throughout the entire work that I nowhere wish to be the author of contentious dogma; I only wish, out of a desire to help, to advise the studious, always with the unshaken and steady judgment of the Holy Church and of those to whom a richer gift of erudition and wisdom has happened from Christ. Nevertheless, I testify to the same thing in this place specifically, because of certain people who are more captious in these matters, as if it truly becomes a Christian man. Furthermore, just as I do not think it is insulting to disagree with any author, however great or ancient, so I will not begrudgingly disagree with myself if anyone brings forward what is more correct, even if it is an uneducated person who teaches it. I know it is most accepted among Christians that once a marriage has come together, it can in no way be dissolved except by the death of the other. And I see that Chrysostom and the ancient Latins were of this opinion; without a doubt, Augustine was of it, and it was confirmed by the constitutions of the ancient Bishops and the authority of the decretal laws, and finally approved by the consensus of the Theological Schools. However, if this has always been in the hearts of good men—to change an opinion for the better, and it is fitting to adapt laws like medicines to the habit and reason of diseases—let us consider whether it is expedient for the same to be done here: and if it is expedient, whether it is permitted that certain marriages be dissolved, not rashly, but for grave reasons; and not by anyone at all, but by the prefects of the Church or legitimate judges; and so dissolved that it is free for either to be joined to whom they wish, or at least for the one who did not give cause for the <term>divortium</term> <note>divorce</note>. I know there are some things of that kind that it is a sin to call into dispute as if they were doubtful. Such kind are: whether Christ is God and the same man, whether born without the work of a man, whether souls survive the death of the body, whether these bodies are one day to live again. For these are so evidently handed down to us by the authority of Divine Scripture and the consensus of the whole Church that it is impious and dangerous to discourse in a different direction about them, unless by chance we fall in with the Ebionites. And yet I do not think one should be hatefully rejected who opens the scruple of his mind about these kinds of things also, as is the weakness of the human mind, doing nothing else than trying to believe more certainly what he believes anyway. But it must be seen whether the thing we are now acting upon is of this kind. Some things have been so received by the authority of the Church that they can be changed according to the circumstances. And just as it is not right to abrogate Divine Scripture, which we have as the most certain rule of life, so it is the part of a pious and prudent administrator to adapt it to public...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on 1 Corinthians 7. Here, he shifts from the virtues of virginity to the difficult practicalities of marriage, specifically exploring the views of the Early Church Fathers and later Canon law on divorce and remarriage in cases of adultery, crime, or abandonment.</meta>

<header>TO THE FIRST CORINTHIANS CHAPTER VII.</header>

...to accommodate public customs. But we shall say a bit more about this matter <margin>A</margin> elsewhere; for now, let us proceed quickly to our purpose. First, then, it is the mark of Apostolic piety to look out for the salvation of all as much as possible, and to provide help for even the lowest members of the Church through such care. We see thousands of people bound together in unhappy marriages to the destruction of both, who might otherwise be saved if they were separated. If this could be done without violating divine command, I believe it would be desired by all pious people; if not, I still consider the wish itself to be pious, especially since charity sometimes desires even what cannot be done. Moses desired to be blotted out of the book of life; Paul desired to be made anathema <note>original: "anathema", meaning cursed or separated from Christ</note> for the sake of his brothers. There have not been lacking those who thought that after a marriage was rightly dissolved, it was permissible to be joined to another. Let no one immediately think this proposition should be exploded as unheard of or in every way absurd, or unworthy of being called into debate. Indeed, Origen, in his *Seventh Homily on Matthew*, testifies that he knew certain bishops who permitted women who had divorced their husbands to marry other men. He admits this was done by them against the command of the Lord and Paul, <margin>B</margin> yet he does not altogether condemn the act, because he believes they were led by a probable cause to permit it—namely, to prevent something worse from happening. They were undoubtedly yielding to the "hardness of heart," just as Paul permitted second marriages to incontinent widows. Origen compares these examples, suggesting it seems harsher to permit new marriages to widows who desire a second husband for the sake of lust rather than children, than to permit a man to marry a more worthy woman after casting off an adulterous wife. Furthermore, he does not seem to doubt that a man is allowed the same right which the Gospel permits in repudiating a wife for adultery, nor does Paul command such a man to be reconciled to his wife.

<margin>B</margin> But Origen noted that this was also permitted to wives by the Bishops, which Paul seems specifically to forbid. For Origen does not there call a "Jewish man" one who divorces a wife because of adultery or a similar cause, but one who is moody and stubborn, preparing a divorce for any slight reason after the manner of the Jews. For such a Jewish man argues, while meditating on divorce: *"Moses permitted divorce for a shameful thing, and he uses adultery as an example of a shameful thing; therefore, it will be permitted to cast off a wife for other shameful things."* Origen rejects this argument, denying <margin>C</margin> that Moses meant adultery when he said "a shameful thing," since for adultery a bill of divorce was not given, but the wife was led away to be stoned. Rather, he called any fault of character or physical defect by which the husband was offended a "shameful thing." That Origen felt this way is shown by what follows: *"Afterwards, however,"* he says, *"the Lord did not permit a wife to be dismissed for any other fault except for the sole cause of fornication."* Under this, Origen raises another question: whether, just as it is permitted to divorce a wife for adultery, it might also be permitted for parricide <note>the murder of a parent or close relative</note>, poisoning, or theft. He remains perplexed here, seeing it as impious to act against the command of God, yet finding it unjust and inhumane to force a husband to endure those sins in a wife which are more grave than adultery. Finally, seeking a way out of this difficulty, he says: *"I argue, therefore, that he did not command by precept that no one should dismiss his wife except for the cause of fornication, but spoke as if explaining the matter: He who dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, causes her to commit adultery."* Origen felt, I believe, that the wife is pushed toward adultery when, having been rightfully rejected, she has no right to marry again, but <margin>D</margin> this is to be imputed to the woman, not to the repudiating husband. A little earlier, he had brought in a comparison to Christ, who repudiated the prophet-killing Synagogue and took the Church as his new bride. These are Origen’s words: *"It must be said that Christ did not dismiss his first wife—that is, the first Synagogue—according to the spiritual appearance, observing what was said: 'What God has joined, let no man separate,' except when that wife is an adulteress, corrupted by the adulterous enemy, by whose counsel she also plotted against her husband,"* and so forth. And soon after: *"And Christ the husband left his Father, with whom he was when he was in the form of God, for the sake of the Church; he also left his mother,"* and so forth. Thus far Origen. You hear, reader, of divorce; you hear of a new bride after divorce. From these it is clear enough that Origen was of the opinion that after an adulteress is repudiated, it is permissible to bring another wife home. Moreover, as to his saying those Bishops acted against Gospel doctrine by permitting marriage after divorce, Origen meant this regarding those who divorced their wives for other causes, following the Jewish example. Similarly, <margin>E</margin> what he writes must be understood this way: *"For by the same reasoning that a woman is an adulteress, even if she seems to marry legally while her husband is living; by that same reasoning, a man, although he seems to legally take a woman dismissed by another man, does not take her legally according to the judgment of Christ, but rather commits adultery, as if taking another's wife."* Here Origen is dealing with those who had divorced for other reasons which Christ did not except, or for light causes. Nor was he who did this punished by human laws; indeed, the marriage was considered legal. But Origen disputes whether it is legal according to Christ’s judgment, especially in the more atrocious crimes, such as attempted poisoning or murder. For he says: *"If he has a just excuse before God, he will deal with it."* And yet he confesses that he who dismisses her thus provides a cause for adultery, but perhaps before God this is to be imputed to the wife, not the husband.

<margin>F</margin> Nor does Tertullian seem to disagree with these in his fourth book *Against Marcion*, interpreting these words of Christ: *"If anyone dismisses his wife and marries another"*—as meaning one who repudiates with the intent of marrying a new one does not dismiss her rightly. For he dismisses her not from a just cause, but seeks a reason so that the one he has fashioned might seem to be dismissed justly. *"The marriage remains,"* he says, *"which has not been properly dissolved; while the marriage remains, to marry is adultery."* Thus, if he prohibited not dismissing a wife conditionally, he did not prohibit it entirely. And what he did not prohibit entirely, he permitted entirely. The same author a little later says: *"Therefore, the justice of divorce has a defender even in a Christian."* You will say Tertullian should not be heard, since he removed himself from the Church. Truly, in this part, he was not marked by any Orthodox writer; he certainly would have been marked if this opinion had differed from that which was then held by the Orthodox.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Of the same opinion was a certain Pollentius, a man, as it appears, grave and learned, against whom Augustine argues in two books—but he argues not as with a heretic leader, but as with an antagonist. Therefore, he refutes his opinion without intending a charge of heresy. Furthermore, Saint Ambrose—without controversy a man not only orthodox, but also of proven holiness—grants a man the right to marry another wife when he has repudiated the first for a fault committed. There is no doubt that if a Bishop practiced among his own people what he wrote could be done rightly and lawfully. He wrote while explaining the seventh chapter of the *First Epistle to the Corinthians* in this manner: *"And that a husband should not dismiss his wife—it is understood, however, except for the cause of fornication. And therefore he does not add, as he did regarding the woman, 'But if she departs, let her remain so,' because a man is permitted to marry a wife if he dismisses a sinning wife; because he is not so bound by the law as the woman. For the man is the head of the woman."* The same author a little earlier says: *"But if he cannot contain himself <margin>B</margin> because he does not wish to fight against the flesh, let him be reconciled to his husband. For it is not permitted for a woman to marry if she has dismissed her husband for the cause of fornication, or apostasy, or if he seeks the use of a wife while lust unlawfully impels him: because the inferior does not entirely use this law by which the superior is governed. If, however, the husband has apostatized, or seeks to invert the use of a wife, the woman can neither marry another nor return to him."* Here, when he says "the inferior does not entirely use this law by which the superior is governed," he seems silently to grant the husband the right to marry another. But a little later he also grants the wife the right to marry another while her first husband is living; for explaining Paul’s words, *"For a brother or sister is not subject to servitude in such cases,"* he says: *"That is, the reverence of marriage is not owed to one who abhors the author of marriage. For a marriage is not valid which is without devotion to God, and through this, it is not a sin if one who is dismissed for the sake of God joins themselves to another. For the insult to the Creator dissolves the right of marriage regarding the one who is left behind, lest the one joined to another be accused. But an unbeliever who departs is recognized to sin both against God and against the marriage, because he did not wish to have a union under devotion to God. Therefore, the loyalty of marriage is not to be kept for him who departed so that he might not hear that the God of the Christians is the author of marriage. For if your fathers dismissed infidel wives or husbands so that God might be favorable, and did not receive those born of them, but took others of their own kind—<margin>C</margin> for they were not commanded thus, that having sent those away they should by no means marry others—how much more, if an unbeliever departs, will the believer have free choice if they wish to marry a man of their own law?"* For that ought not to be imputed as a marriage which is outside the law of God. Thus far Ambrose. Nor do I think anyone can object here that Ambrose is talking about a woman who through ignorance married a Pagan husband whom she believed to be a Christian, since Paul permits the union if the unbeliever consents. For if an error of this kind intervened in contracting the marriage, by no law could she remain with him with whom she could not have contracted a marriage in the first place.

<margin>C</margin> Indeed, it is a cold argument that Peter Lombard brings in, citing that passage from Ambrose which we first reviewed, in the fourth book of his *Sentences*. He tries to dilute it by saying these words were inserted into the books of Ambrose by forgers, even though the style agrees perfectly and nothing there is ascribed as a commentary. It would be no trouble to dissolve any knot by that reasoning, if one accepts it. There are things in the books of Cyprian, Jerome, Augustine, and Thomas Aquinas which the Church rejects. Why do we not <margin>D</margin> use the same escape in all these, and immediately sing out: "They were substituted by forgers"? Now, if we examine the opinions of more recent authors, to whom both the courts and the schools have hitherto granted the most authority, we will find that among them also were those who thought marriage could be dissolved, or certainly who thought this argument was debatable. First, John Andreae <note>a famous 14th-century canon lawyer</note> maintained that a marriage, before it has been consummated by sexual union, can be dissolved—not only by the profession of Monastic life, but even by the sole authority of the Roman Pontiff. But if they grant me that such a marriage, contracted with legal words and mutual consent between suitable persons, is a true marriage, they will simultaneously grant that its power depends on divine law. Either, therefore, divine law did not mean what we interpret it to mean, or the Pope has the power to relax divine law. Again, the same John teaches that a marriage consummated by the intervention of sexual union cannot be dissolved. But for this distinction, I have yet to hear any sufficiently <margin>E</margin> grave reason. For the reasons which Hostiensis, Augustine, and Pope Leo bring forward—besides being human commentaries—do not explain why they dissolve a marriage against the doctrine of Christ and Paul, and why the right to remarry arises from divorce. Either, then, it must be denied that it is a marriage which a marital encounter did not confirm, or it must be admitted that a marriage is rightly dissolved. Otherwise, what God revealed to those Doctors that a profession of Monastic life and mutual worship according to human institution dissolves a marriage, even if the other spouse protests? It is "ratified," they say, but not "confirmed"—as if before the encounter it were not legal and perfect as far as the nature of marriage is concerned. What oracle revealed that falling into heresy dissolves a marriage, even a confirmed one, and dissolves it in such a way that the one who perseveres in the faith has the right to be joined to another? I will set aside for a moment that Pope Zachary, as reported in the fourth book of the *Sentences*, distinction thirty-four, dissolves a marriage because of a sexual act had with the sister of one's wife. His words <margin>F</margin> are as follows: *"You have slept with your wife's sister. If you have done this, have neither woman; and your wife, if she was not conscious of the crime and does not wish to remain continent, let her marry in the Lord whom she wishes. But you and the adulteress remain without hope of marriage, and do penance as long as you live."* Thus far Zachary. Now, it does not seem at all likely to me, the common explanation which Peter Lombard adds: what he says—namely, *"let her marry whom she wishes"*—is to be understood as *"after the death of her husband."* Was the Pope going to be silent on a matter of such importance if he had meant what this man interprets? What if the husband outlives the wife? Will not the punishment of the guilty and the innocent then be equal in this part? But however this may be; for someone is punished by the claim that it was not a marriage because it was contracted against the Pope's constitution. And yet, if that is true, why is the woman not set free?
But this question, as I said, let us not pursue for the present...

He also critiques medieval Canon lawyers like Peter Lombard and John Andreae for their inconsistent rules on the indissolubility of marriage.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s critical examination of marriage laws. Having previously discussed the views of the Early Church Fathers, he now moves into a comparison of contradictory Papal decrees and a deep rhetorical analysis of Christ's words in the Sermon on the Mount, questioning why the Church is more rigid regarding divorce than other divine prohibitions.</meta>

### TO THE FIRST CORINTHIANS CHAPTER VII.

<margin>A</margin> ...had decreed that the subdeacons of Sicily should abstain from the wives they had legally married before that constitution was made. This decree, as if it were unjust and at odds with the Gospel precept, was reconsidered and repealed by Gregory, the first of that name, who succeeded Pelagius. He established that in the future, no one should be admitted to that order unless they had vowed chastity. However, he deemed it harsh and unjust that a man who had not vowed chastity should be forced into it, nor had he committed any fault that deserved such compulsion. Yet, what seemed unjust to Gregory here did not seem unjust to Innocent III in the passage we just cited. Innocent responded to those who objected—arguing it seemed beyond equity for a deserted spouse to be deprived of their rights without fault—by saying it is more insulting to Christ when a baptized person falls back into heresy or Paganism than when a born Heathen refuses to convert to the profession of Christ. Furthermore, for some centuries, the Church of Modena held the view that if someone contracted a marriage with Barbara with legal words and sincere intent, but without sexual intercourse, and later contracted with Cornelia and included intercourse, he should be forced to leave the first and live with the second. This was openly rescinded by

<margin>B</margin> Innocent, the Roman Pontiff, who pronounced a diametrically opposite opinion: namely, that the first was the legitimate wife, and what was done with the second was adultery, not marriage. This is recorded in the fourth book of the *Decretal Epistles*, under the fourth title, the chapter beginning *Tua duclum*, and in the same title, the chapter *Licet*. Alexander III indicates in his rescript <note>A formal written reply to a legal question or petition.</note> that it had been established and defined at one time by his predecessors—that is, the Roman Pontiffs—precisely what Innocent condemned in the Church of Modena. How much more dangerous is this than a cause for divorce? And yet here, a Roman Pontiff changed the decrees of other Pontiffs. I shall not mention, in the meantime, how in a matter of faith the School of Paris once publicly disapproved of a Roman Pontiff's opinion and compelled him to recant <note>original: "palinodiam", a formal retraction.</note>, if there is any faith to be put in histories. Unless, perhaps, we think it a vain fable, what Jean Gerson reports in a certain Easter sermon concerning Pope John XXII, who decreed that before the Day of Judgment the souls of the wicked were not to be punished. The School of Paris publicly exploded this error, forcing the Pope to recant. Nor can it be said that this was a private error of the Pope; it must have been public, spread by writing or even by decree, since the matter moved the whole kingdom of France. But why do I speak of Pelagiuses, Alexanders, or Innocents, when Peter, the prince of the Apostles, was not ashamed to listen to his betters after he recognized his error through Paul’s admonition? At least if we embrace the opinion of Saint Aurelius Augustine on this matter.

<margin>C</margin> Now, even if we grant that marriage is of divine law, certainly most things treated concerning matrimonial causes belong to positive law <note>Human-made laws as opposed to natural or divine laws.</note>, such as degrees of kinship, impediments, and annulments. Nor did these decrees come down to us from famous Synods, but from the private responses of Pontiffs, who answered various consultations according to what seemed equitable at the time, sometimes even disagreeing with themselves. And this custom of which we now treat first began, I believe, with one or two Bishops, and then gradually spreading wider, it gained strength. Those men were human, and no one is ignorant of how much weight a custom carries once it is received. It is no wonder those Ancients were so hostile to divorce, since even among the Heathens it was always offensive, and they even admitted marriage itself with difficulty, and dignity with even more difficulty. We bring these things forward so that no one rejects a discussion about changing divorce laws as if it were an absurdity. But now, if you please, let us examine the passages of the divine volumes from which they seem to have been compelled to accept this law. Our Lord Christ, in the fifth chapter of Matthew, delivering that heavenly philosophy of his and prescribing an absolute model of the kind of people he wanted his followers to be, speaks in this manner:

> It was also said, ‘Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce.’ But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality <note>original: "fornicationis causa"</note>, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.

But since in that same place he teaches many things that are purely and genuinely Christian, why in all the others do we accept an interpretation, yet in this one matter of divorce are we so rigid that we bind Christ’s words even more tightly? For although he left the husband one cause for repudiating a spouse, we restrict it in many ways. First, one may only divorce such that he must afterwards live castrated and bereaved. Then, if he has had relations with his wife after a suspicion of adultery, he loses the right to repudiate her. Furthermore, if he himself has also been an adulterer, he is forced to remain with the adulteress. Finally, we twist the small clause of exception so that it does not give the husband a right to repudiate, but so that if he does repudiate, he will not be making her an adulteress, since she has already cast away her marriage through adultery. For if this is Augustine's interpretation—I call it "divorce" for now, the true kind, and the only kind that age knew, in which it was lawful to marry another after the repudiation of the first. For as for what we interpret as "divorce"—a separation of domestic living while the marriage bond remains—what ancient theologian or legal expert ever called that "divorce"? But more on this shortly. In this one part, therefore, we hold so tooth-and-nail to the "extreme law" <note>original: "summum jus", often used in the sense of "the letter of the law is the greatest injustice."</note>, while in others we readily accept interpretation. He forbids there, "Do not swear at all": he forbids it much more severely than divorce, and insists upon it with more words, and yet for the sake of three coins we swear everywhere, excusing ourselves by saying, "One must not swear rashly." Why do we not likewise say, "One must not divorce a wife rashly"? He forbids being angry; we immediately add, "Rashly." He forbids calling anyone by an insulting name; we even strike them with blows, finally we kill, and we excuse it by saying, "Not with the intent of hurting, but of punishing." He forbids us to offer a gift unless we have first reconciled with a brother; we excuse it, "If he asks to be forgiven, and if he makes satisfaction." He forbids going to judges for a debt, but orders the matter to be settled with the adversary. We, for the sake of a few

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> stolen coins, drive a man to the gallows, and excuse it by saying, "I am pursuing justice, not vengeance." He forbids resisting evil; we excuse it by saying it was "advice, not a command," and that it is nonetheless lawful to repel force with force. And so as not to pursue every instance, we are commanded to love our enemies, to do good to those who treat us ill, to pray for those who curse us; we excuse it, saying, "I will wish my enemies a better mind, but I am not bound to show signs of friendship." Finally, the common excuse of all is opposed to all: "These things are commanded to the perfect." Meanwhile, no one among so many who sell themselves under the title of "perfection" acknowledges the profession of perfect piety when a duty is required, so that those words of Christ were said almost in vain. Christ spoke these things not to the crowds, but to the disciples, and that on a mountain, depicting that purest part of his body which he calls the Kingdom of Heaven, which has no need of laws. For what need is there for the command,

<margin>B</margin> "Thou shalt not kill," where no one, even when hurt, is angry or speaks evil? Where even the one who has been affected by injury initiates reconciliation? Where everyone prefers to yield their rights rather than experience a trial before a judge? What need of a law that forbids adultery, where no one covets what belongs to another? To what purpose is an oath, where no one seeks to deceive, and no one distrusts? What need is there for the law to moderate the balance of retaliation <note>The *lex talionis*, or "eye for an eye."</note>, where even enemies are loved, where a bad deed is weighed against a benefit, and an insult against blessings? Thus there is no need for a certificate of divorce where no one is wicked; or if there is some human vice, it is either tolerated in turn or healed. Set up such a people as Christ desires, and there would be no need for divorce, nor for oaths. But if, because of the weak—of whom the Church has a great number—no one is forbidden by law to pursue their rights, no one is forbidden to ward off violence from their person, no one is forbidden to swear provided it is for a serious matter and they do not perjure themselves, and no one is forced to do good to those who treat them ill: why do we demand this one thing concerning divorce indiscriminately from everyone? If because of the "hardness of heart" it was permitted to the Jews to cast off a wife for any cause, lest they commit something more serious, and we see among Christians, besides

<margin>C</margin> constant quarrels in their unions, even more serious dangers—namely, murders, poisonings, and sorceries—why, when the disease is the same, is the same remedy not applied? Paul does not approve of second marriages <note>original: "digamiam", marrying again after a spouse's death or divorce.</note>, and yet because of incontinence <note>Lack of self-restraint.</note> he permits what he does not dare to demand, judging it "better to marry than to burn." And do we relax nothing at all of the rigor of divorce? What Moses had written about the certificate of divorce, the Jews interpreted as if husbands had the right to reject a spouse for any trivial cause, such as if she showed some ugliness in her body. For thus they ask Christ in the nineteenth chapter, *Is it lawful to divorce one’s wife for any cause?* Christ restricts this to the single cause of adultery: not because there are no other crimes more wicked than adultery, but because adultery is totally at odds with the very nature of marriage. Marriage makes one out of two; adultery cuts that bond apart. Therefore, Christ would grant his followers only one cause for divorce; he does not take away from the Jews what Moses granted because of their hardness of character, denying that it was so from the beginning. If man had

<margin>D</margin> persevered as he was created, there would have been no divorce among them. Christ, calling his people back to their original innocence, does not want divorces because he does not want them to be hard of heart; and yet Paul indulges human frailty, frequently relaxing the Lord's precept. Why could the Roman Pontiff not do the same? Furthermore, as to the objection from the same passage, *What God has joined, let no man separate*, it can be solved without great difficulty. God has joined that which is rightly joined; God dissolves that which is rightly dissolved. Among the Heathens, a marriage was not considered valid unless approved by the authority of parents or guardians; nor even among the Jews; and yet among both, a marriage could be dissolved in some way. Among Christians, a marriage is joined very easily, and once entered into, it can in no way be torn apart. Marriage is joined stealthily between boys and girls, through pimps and madams, among fools and the drunken, and what is so shamefully begun is indissoluble, and what is even more a novelty, what is so begun becomes a "sacrament." For the things we discuss about consent, and "words of the present," and "ratified" versus "not ratified," are human interpretations, not the oracles of God. I confess that without mutual consent

<margin>E</margin> a marriage does not come together, but I require a sober consent. A consent not extorted through snares and drunkenness. A consent applied with the advice of friends, as is proper in a matter that can never be rescinded, and which deserves to be numbered among the sacraments of the Church. Otherwise, where a Bishop or other legitimate judges dissolve a marriage of this kind after the facts are known, it is not "man" separating what "God joined," but rather what was badly glued together by childhood, by wine, by rashness, by ignorance—what the Devil had joined through his deacons, the pimps and madams—this, God rightly dissolves through his ministers.

Yet the Church, they say, approves of divorce: but only so far as both remain unmarried. I ask you, was this the divorce Christ meant? Asked by the Jews, he answers the Jews. But they knew no other divorce except that which took away the right to reclaim the dismissed woman and gave the right to marry another. Indeed, that it was lawful for the Jews, and even for the women, to marry another after a repudiation is proved by the fact that a Priest is forbidden to marry a divorced woman—a law that would have been superfluous if it were not lawful for any divorced woman to marry. Indeed,

<margin>F</margin> the certificate of divorce was given for this reason: so that there would be no right to take back the dismissed woman, and the second marriage would be firm. Indeed, this reasoning of Chrysostom seems more probable to me than that which Augustine brings in the nineteenth book against Faustus, the twenty-fifth chapter. But if Christ spoke of true divorce, where did we get this new kind of divorce, which is "divorce" in name rather than in reality? But let us imagine Christ meant this [limited] divorce; since he granted only one cause for repudiation, why does Augustine add idolatry and heresy, on no other title than that this is a "kind of fornication"? And yet by that reasoning, it seems every capital crime that alienates the soul from God could be called "a kind of fornication." Why have our laws added so many cases, almost innumerable, in which divorce is accepted? Jerome even pronounces that a wife may be freely rejected on suspicion of adultery: *Wherever*, he says, *there is fornication and the suspicion of fornication, the wife is dismissed freely.* If it is permissible to change anything in the precepts of Christ, why is it not done for the benefit of...

<summary>Erasmus argues that the Church's absolute prohibition of remarriage after divorce is a human interpretation that lacks the flexibility applied to other Gospel commands. He highlights historical contradictions in Papal decrees and suggests that marriages entered into through "rashness" or "drunkenness" might not be truly "joined by God."</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s critical inquiry into the indissolubility of marriage.
