Here, he pivots to challenge the logical consistency of current canon laws and the traditional interpretations of Church Fathers like Jerome and Augustine.</meta>

### EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER VII.

...how does this poorly align with salvation? If nothing is permitted, why have they dared to derive so many exceptions from a single cause? Papal laws allow a spouse to remarry if their partner converts to Christ and the other refuses to turn away from blasphemous impiety: Christ made an exception for sexual immorality <note>Greek: *porneia*</note>, but He did not make an exception for this case. And yet, here we dare to grant what we do not dare there. Remarriage is allowed after being dismissed from an impotent husband <note>original: *a frigido*</note>, but it is not allowed after being dismissed from a parent-killer <note>original: *a parricida*</note>. An "error of condition" <note>a legal mistake regarding a person's social status</note> voids a contract and a confirmed marriage—for instance, if a woman marries a slave whom she believed to be free-born. Yet an "error of quality" <note>a mistake about a person's character or traits</note> does not dissolve it. As if it were not more tolerable to be joined to a slave than to a poisoner, a sorcerer, a murderer, or even a parent-killer! What is lighter is not demanded; what is heavier is demanded. Someone will respond that here the marriage is not being dissolved, but rather it is simply being declared that it was never a true marriage to begin with. I hear you, but I ask this: by what authority do they pronounce that this cause is valid for dissolving a presumed marriage, while another equal cause, or one even much more serious, is not? Or why, by the same reasoning, is no relief given to those poorly joined—declaring it was never a true marriage—when it was contracted between boys and girls still under their parents' power, without parental authority, through violence or the snares of procurers?

<margin>B</margin> But now, if you please, let us examine the cases that led the Ancients not to allow remarriage, even for the crime of adultery. Jerome provides this reason: lest, if a man takes another wife, he seems to have changed his spouse not out of offense at her previous vice, but out of greed for a more beautiful one. Indeed, I will transcribe his own words: *And because it could happen,* he says, *that someone might bring a false charge against an innocent person, and pin a crime on the old wife for the sake of a second marriage, he is commanded to dismiss the first wife in such a way that he does not have a second while the first is living.* For what he says is this: if you dismiss your wife not because of lust but because of injury, why, having experienced unhappy first nuptials, do you thrust yourself into the danger of new ones? Nor is he who could "vomit up" one wife allowed to take another; by the same caution, a law of health is prescribed so that a wife also gives a divorce to her husband, lest she take a second man. And because a prostitute, and she who has once committed adultery, does not fear disgrace, a second command is given to the man: that if he takes such a woman, he himself is under the charge of adultery. So far, Jerome. But meanwhile, setting aside the authority of the Writings for a moment, let the reader weigh the matter with me: are these reasons grave enough why an innocent husband should either be bound to a wicked woman, or bear the misery of bereavement and the fire of lust throughout his whole life? Simply so he might not be considered "insufficiently prudent" by some for attempting a thing again that did not succeed the first time? As if it were a disgrace for someone who has once experienced a storm to repeat a voyage, or for one who has erred in choosing a friend to admit anyone else into friendship! Or as if he were intemperate or greedy because he wanted to change a character or a dowry, not just a wife. But I ask you, when the matter has been handled by Bishops, by proven and grave judges, and where a divorce has been approved by their authority, who then will harbor suspicion? The good or the wicked? Surely the wicked. But do we think it fair that, because of a few wickedly suspicious people, an innocent husband or an innocent woman should be crushed by such great calamity? Augustine provides almost identical reasons in his books *To Pollentius*: *Lest,* he says, *he seem to have preferred another in insult to the previous husband, or lest she seem to have departed not so much offended by the husband's vices as by a greed for a recent one, even mixing him in.* He denies that the Gospel ought to be subverted because of the complaints of the wicked. And yet, first of all, the Gospel does not forbid repeating a marriage where you have rightfully dismissed a wife. We shall speak of Paul's words soon. Secondly, since neither Christ nor Paul demands continence from those who cannot remain continent, why are they called "evil" who cannot remain continent, and have not bound themselves by a vow of continence? This is a defect of the body, not the soul. Why is a person forced to pay a penalty who has committed no fault? Nay, who has been afflicted.

Now, let us see the nature of what they claim regarding the "sacrament," by which they want every marriage, once contracted, to be indissoluble. For Augustine—who places three "goods" in marriage—when he calls the third a "sacrament," does not mean one of the Seven Sacraments. Peter Lombard seems to note this himself in his thirty-first distinction. In fact, I do not know if this "seventh sacrament" was even known to the Ancients. First, because Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential early Christian author</note>, listing each one by name and explaining their powers, rites, and ceremonies, makes no mention of marriage. For what some claim—that it is included under the sacrament of Orders—is the kind of argument made just to avoid seeming to have no answer when you refuse to remain silent. As if a priest were consecrated with the same ceremonies as a groom being joined to a bride! At the very least, he would have added the name in two words, especially since Paul wrote so much about it. Furthermore, although marriage has been treated in so many volumes by both the Greeks and the Latins, there is no place from which it is permitted to commemorate marriage among the seven sacraments, especially since Augustine, a supporter of marriage, diligently reviews and hammers home the "goods" of marriage. Even Jovinian, who favored marriage so intensely that he was judged a heretic for it, having shaken out all the books of both Testaments and twisting everything to the praise of marriage—even he did not produce this plausible and prize-winning argument: "Marriage is one of the seven sacraments of the Church, while virginity is not." Nor do I think Jerome would have vented his anger so freely against those who marry twice <note>original: *digamos*</note> if it had been established that it was one of the seven sacraments. But why do I review these things, since Durandus <note>Guillaume Durand, a 13th-century canonist</note> admits that marriage only finally began to be numbered among those things properly called "Sacraments of the Church" by more recent theologians? Furthermore, when the Ancients, following Paul, occasionally call marriage a "sacrament," they mean, I think, the union of husband and wife: because it is the closest friendship, representing a certain "type" <note>a symbolic foreshadowing</note> and image of Christ joining His bride, the Church, to Himself. And indeed, marriage rightly observed is an entirely holy and sacred thing; and yet a thing can be a "type" of a sacred matter without being holy in itself—such as Bathsheba being taken from Uriah and joined to David, or the adultery of the Prophet Hosea, or the story of Samson and Delilah, as Jerome openly testifies. And again, it is not necessary for a "type" to correspond in every detail. Otherwise, it

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> will not be a sacrament when someone has a sterile wife, or where a wife endures a husband who is a drunkard, infamous, or a gambler. Even if we grant for the moment that marriage is accepted here as a true sacrament, it will not be a sacrament where an old man marries an old woman, or a drunkard marries a drunkard—and yet the Church recognizes it as a sacrament. Six hundred other things could be cited in which the image does not correspond between human and mystical marriage. The sacrament of Baptism is not immediately wronged if some people lead an unwashed life. Nor is marriage immediately "not a sacrament" if the married couple are contaminated by certain vices. No injury will be done to the sacrament of Christ by our divorce, which we grant so easily. In some way, we "dissolve" the marriage, even though Christ adheres to His bride in every way. Finally, marriage ought not to be dissolved even by death if it were required that the "type" correspond in all respects. Indeed, if we push the "type," according to the interpretation of Origen, Christ divorced the Synagogue as the killer of His mother, whose voice said, *Take him, take him, crucify him!* <note>John 19:15</note>—and having divorced her, He joined the Church to Himself. According to this image, it would be permitted to cast off a woman who plotted the death of her husband and to marry another worthy of himself. As far as the congruence of the mystery is concerned, it is enough that one is always joined to one with the intent that no separation occurs, and that for most people, marriage is permanent. Certainly, it is strange that while so many ancient Greeks and Latins sought reasons why marriage is indissoluble, nothing of this sort occurred to their minds which seems indissoluble to us. No one contracts a marriage except with the intent that it be perpetual; nor does anyone here wish to predict a divorce. But if it should happen out of necessity, as human affairs go, let it not be an injury to the sacrament if the necessity of a few is relieved. For just as the privilege of a few does not void a general law, so the unhappiness of a few does not spoil the common sacrament. Finally, it would follow either that marriage was not a sacrament in the Old Testament, or that it should never have been dissolved—especially since the dangers of homicide could have been met by our practice of divorce.

<margin>C</margin> Chrysostom cites a double reason why, among the Jews, it was permitted as a vice to cast off a wife, provided a bill of divorce was given: *It is permitted,* he says, *to divorce, lest he kill the woman he hates.* Is it so, that among the Jews their malice should benefit their flagrant crime, but among us, a husband's innocence does not benefit him? He says a man is commanded to give a bill of divorce so that those he has divorced may be allowed to breathe; otherwise, there would be an infinite and foul confusion of adulteries. And yet this reason deters us from giving the husband the right to receive back the woman he divorced. And he thinks the reason is the same as to why it is permitted to cast off an adulteress: lest mutual adulteries be mixed everywhere. If this reason is true, why among us is no one compelled to divorce an adulteress—indeed, it is forbidden, unless he prefers to be castrated? Innocent III, in the chapter *Quanto* which we cited above, gives this reason why the wife of a husband who has fallen into heresy cannot renew her marriage with another: *Because,* he says, *out of hatred for their spouses, or when they were displeased with each other, if they could dismiss them in such a case, they would fake heresy so that they could spring away from the spouses they were marrying.* The Gloss <note>marginal legal commentary</note> cites the same sentiment in the chapter *Dixit Dominus*, cause thirty-two, question one, which we ourselves cited from Jerome a little earlier.

<margin>D</margin> And yet, if we accept this reason, it will not be permitted for a woman to marry who, through error, married Peter believing him to be John, or a slave believing him to be free—lest any woman who desires a divorce should fabricate such reasons. Even if the chapter cited by the Gloss does not seem to me to do much toward declaring a sentence. For it considers a husband who fakes being a heretic to deter his wife, and then, once she has joined another, fakes that he has repented. Likewise, he could fake being a slave if he were eager to drive away his wife. Indeed, the same things could be used as a pretext against our kind of divorce: a man whose wife is a nuisance at home will fake something to drive her from the house, thinking the reward for the simulation is great enough if he does not have to see the one he hates at home. But so much for these causes.

<margin>E</margin> Now, if it seems right, let us examine the passages of Paul, from which our Pontiffs seem chiefly to have drawn this difficulty in dissolving marriages. Paul, in the *seventh chapter of the Epistle to the Romans*, says: *Do you not know, brothers (for I speak to those who know the law), that the law has dominion over a man as long as he lives? For the woman who is under a husband is bound by the law to her husband as long as he lives; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband. Therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man. But if her husband dies, she is freed from the law of her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man.* Paul is not dealing with divorce here; rather, he is bringing an analogy to the Jews from their own law to teach and persuade them that, the Law of Moses now being made obsolete through the Gospel, they are no longer held by the ceremonies of the Law, since they have married Christ, the new spouse. It is not necessary for an analogy or a parable to match in every detail; otherwise, we would ridiculously demand this rule for parables about the thief digging through a house at night, the money owed to a moneylender, the unjust steward, the vine and the branches, the children playing in the marketplace, and countless others of that kind. It is enough if they agree so far as they declare the point for whose sake they are used. It is peculiar to Paul to twist everything toward the business of the Gospel with a pious and Christian shrewdness, turning himself into all things so that he may win all for Christ. Today, those who turn themselves into all things to call people away from Christ—so that they themselves may win wealth and honor—are very difficult. Otherwise, if one wanted to press this speech of Paul according to what the words sound like, it would not even be lawful to dismiss an adulteress, for he makes no exception. Again, Paul would not seem to be aptly citing the Mosaic Law to the Jews for this purpose, since the Law permits husbands to divorce for any reason, provided they give a bill of divorce. It is clear, therefore, that Paul is not here excluding divorce—which the Law itself openly allows and to which he brings testimony—but he is conducting his own business, ignoring that which did not serve his present case. Again, in the seventh chapter of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, he writes in almost the same way: *Therefore, he who joins his virgin in marriage does well; and he who does not join her does better. A woman is bound to the law as long as her husband lives. But if her husband sleeps [dies], she is freed from the law; let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. But she will be more blessed if she remains as she is, according to my counsel.* Not even here does Paul...

<summary>Erasmus critiques the legal and sacramental arguments for the absolute indissolubility of marriage, arguing that the Church Fathers' prohibitions were often based on preventing fraud rather than divine law. He further interprets Paul's metaphors in Romans and Corinthians as rhetorical devices about the Law of Moses, not as strict bans on divorce for the innocent.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s critical inquiry into the indissolubility of marriage. On the previous page, he highlighted inconsistencies in Papal decrees regarding subdeacons and the validity of marriage based on sexual consummation. Here, he pivots to challenge the logical consistency of current canon laws and the traditional interpretations of Church Fathers like Jerome and Augustine.</meta>

### TO THE CORINTHIANS I. CHAPTER VII.

...he treats the subject of divorce, but exhorts, given the state of those times, that those who are free from marriage, especially widows (for he seems to return to their case), should abstain from marriage so they might be freer from worldly business, then still dominated by the ungodly and idolaters, with whom they could not help but be entangled through family ties. And yet he does not demand this; he only decrees that those who have not married, if they wish to marry, should be joined to a Christian. Otherwise, he does not tear away a Christian already joined to a Heathen from her husband, unless the husband himself departs; for she does not sin if she marries when free. Furthermore, there is no need for a husband for one who already has a husband. I believe this is the principal key to understanding mystical Scripture: to perceive what the speaker is doing—especially in Paul, who is slippery in argument, now dashing here, now there, so that, as Origen <note>An early Christian scholar from Alexandria</note> says, the reader hardly understands where he started or where he is being led. There remains a most difficult passage which preceded in the same chapter, where, treating those who are married, he speaks thus: <margin>A</margin> *I say to the unmarried and to widows, it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn. But to those joined in marriage, I command—not I, but the Lord—that the wife should not depart from her husband. But if she departs, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband; and let the husband not put away his wife.*

These sayings seem to concern equal marriages, that is, between a Christian man and a likewise Christian woman. For regarding an unequal marriage, there follows: *But to the rest I say, not the Lord.* First, since Paul nowhere adds the Gospel exception <note>referring to Matthew 5:32 and 19:9 regarding "except for sexual immorality"</note>, Ambrose <note>Likely "Ambrosiaster," a 4th-century commentator Erasmus often mistook for St. Ambrose</note> reminds us that it must be supplied everywhere, lest the Apostle seem to fight against the commands of his Lord. Furthermore, Paul does not seem here to be dealing with grave outrages that might equal or even surpass the crime of adultery, but with lighter offenses, on account of which frequent divorces occurred, especially among the Greeks, according to that line from Juvenal’s Satire VI <note>A Roman poet known for his biting social critiques</note>:

---
-> --- *thus eight husbands are made / Within five autumns:* --- <-
---

This is gathered from what follows: *or be reconciled to her husband.* For those whom some human offense has separated return to favor. And she who caused the offense is reconciled, not she who was offended. But if she departed legally, why does he command her to be reconciled, when she was the one who needed to be appeased? If the offenses were mutual but minor, he forbids her from immediately joining herself to another man and blocking her return to the first, but she should remain unmarried in case a return to favor is granted to both. To this, the Apostle speaks here only of the woman, because among the Jews this sex had no right of repudiation. He only exhorts the husband not to cast away his wife for offenses of this kind. He does not add, however, that if he casts her away, he should remain celibate or be reconciled to his wife. For Ambrose noted this, even if Augustine wants the right to be equal for both wife and husband; which, as he asserts it strongly and constantly, he has no certain way to prove. Indeed, I do not know whether Paul attributed something in this part to his own law, which permits a man to change his wife for any cause and indulged a harsh remedy for the vice of jealousy, yet granted nothing of the kind to the wife. Furthermore, the Apostle in all his Epistles does not attribute much authority to wives, whom he subjects to the power of the husband, whom he does not allow to have an uncovered head, and whom he does not even permit to speak in the Church. It seems likely, therefore, that Paul meant the wife should not leave her husband for common offenses. If it were done, she should abstain from a second marriage, lest she be unable to return to the former one with a mind for reconciliation. For he does not approve that she remain unmarried while separated from her husband against his will, but he says this rather than having the old marriage abolished by a repeated new one.

But if such a case had been proposed to Paul—a fool has contracted with a fool, a boy with a girl, with a procuress intervening, wine, and rashness bringing it to a conclusion before it had even begun—and the world is full of such marriages, and infinite thousands of mortals are miserably ensraed. Marriage comes together with a nod, if only intercourse follows; indeed, even if it does not follow, nothing is agreed between the joined parties, so great is the dissimilarity of character and disposition: constant quarrels, incurable hatred, poison is feared, slaughter is feared, nothing but evils are expected; neither can live celibately; if they stay together, both perish twice over; if they change their marriage, there is hope that both will be safe. Perhaps, according to the circumstances of the case, the Apostle would respond differently and relax something of the rigor of his previous counsel, and would, I believe, interpret his own writings more kindly for us than we interpret them. Or if that noble Fabiola <note>A Roman noblewoman who divorced an abusive husband and remarried, later becoming a saint</note> had fled to Paul—she who was consecrated to the eternal memory of men by Jerome’s writings, who in hair-cloth and with bare feet performed public penance because, having left her first husband as a girl, she had married another (Jerome hints, however, that the husband had abused the wife in a way unbecoming a husband, when he reports that she was forced to suffer things from her husband that no maidservant would suffer from a master; since even slaves were given refuge at the statue of the Emperor if they were attempted with infamous injury by their masters)—and if she had addressed him with these words: "You will not demand, Paul, that I bear a husband of this kind, whom I cannot obey unless I become abominable. Indeed, you will not suffer me to bear such a one, even if I wish to, and I feel that state of body in myself that it is not safe to lack marriage. Nor do you demand so much from those to whom this has not yet happened divinely, you who command even wanton widows to marry." If Fabiola had told these things, and things of this kind, I believe she would have found the Apostle more civil than that Bishop, whoever he was, who drove an innocent girl to public punishment as if she had killed her mother as a poisoner—especially since she, as Jerome indicates, had taken another husband not out of contempt for Pontifical decree, but through imprudence. But if anyone urges that Paul is here dealing with the cause of adultery, why does he not make the exception the Lord made? Indeed, why did he add what the Lord did not add: *let her remain unmarried*? Why does he forbid the husband to dismiss her, whom Christ permits to dismiss an adulteress? Yet we do not say these things because we wish to open a window to frequent divorces; but where nothing has been attempted except in vain, I would desire that the safety of the unfortunate or the weak be consulted. Nor is there truly a danger that marriages will be everywhere dissolved, since even among the Heathens honor was sufficiently established for marriage, among whom there was a mutual right of divorce, yet not recklessly...

<column-break/>

...nevertheless. Do you want divorces to be rare? Why not see that marriages do not come together so easily? Let them come together by judgment; let them come together by the authority of parents, or those whom it concerns; just as among the Hebrews, Greeks, Romans, and Barbarians they used to come together. For who among Christians first brought forth this oracle: that marriage is contracted by consent alone, even against the will of those under whose power God willed children to be? This argument Thomas Aquinas <note>The influential 13th-century Scholastic philosopher and theologian</note> dismissed far too easily: "A daughter is not in the power of the father as a handmaid," he says, "but as a daughter." Why then was it not likewise permitted among the Jews to marry against the will of parents? And connecting the thresholds with thread, he adds: "Just as one can enter religion without the consent of parents, since they are a free person." That children, against the will of parents, should betake themselves to the profession of the Gospel, the Gospels themselves teach us. Here, however, they only neglect the authority of parents insofar as they are forced toward impiety. But that a girl or boy, having abandoned Christian <margin>B</margin> parents to whom they owe obedience on a double account, should devote themselves to the institute of the Benedictines or Dominicans—among whom perhaps they live more licentiously and with more impunity, though not more religiously—and emancipate themselves against public law from the power of those to whom both nature and human and divine laws willed them to be subject, and give themselves up to I-know-not-what human slavery, so that from free children they become fugitives from their parents and bondservants of other men—I do not see on what reason this rests. This decree seems to have proceeded from those same people who established that from a spouse legitimately wedded but not yet known <note>referring to a non-consummated marriage</note>, it is permitted to depart to a Monastic life, nor meanwhile is it lawful for the girl to marry another before the profession of the spouse is issued; and if before the profession he migrates to another Monastery, and from there again to another, so that now four years pass, the bride will nevertheless be forced to remain unmarried. Finally, if he never makes his profession but returns to the bride, she will be forced with the greatest infamy to have as a husband one who lived so many years in a cowl. Extraordinary equity. Exceptional favor of religion—to violate divine law for a human institution, <margin>C</margin> with injury to an innocent girl, and even with no small danger. And here "cold subtleties" are brought to us: "Monks are dead to the world. Death of the body dissolves marriage; much more does spiritual death." As if indeed all Christians did not profess this death in baptism, and were not buried with Christ in baptism; they boast of their "devotion," as if other Christians were not entirely devoted to Christ. Those who established these things either did not understand the vigor of divine law or attributed too much to human institutions. But to return to the matter. At least let this be granted among us to unhappy innocence, which among the Jews was granted to the perverse bitterness of husbands, and which Paul indulges to intemperate widows lest they commit something more criminal. For a woman who married a "frigid" <note>impotent</note> man, a silent condition comes to her aid, and the marriage is dissolved. But the quality of the mind is often more serious than a defect of the body; why is there no remedy here for so great a condition? Divorce, they say, is not approved among the Jews, but permitted. Public brothels are also permitted <margin>D</margin> among Christians, lest they commit something worse. But it does not seem likely to me that a Jew was in sin who had cast off a remarkably wicked wife and had taken another home, since the law openly permitted it, adding nothing about this being granted only for "hardness of heart," especially since from the sense of nature it cannot be known what we interpret. And if it is granted to hardness of heart, certainly it is allowed, because God allows it—especially if He declares by no sign that those who use the permission are sinning. But however these things may be, it is so granted that it is nonetheless unpunished for a husband to have let go whomever he wished, nor are they forbidden from marrying after repudiating either one. For sometimes that is said to be permitted which the law does not punish. But among us, the same is not only not tolerated, but is punished as an atrocious crime, and somewhat more gravely than adultery; although Augustine clearly pronounces it more wicked to be lustful outside of marriage than to live joined to a new husband after a divorce. Nor does he simply deny that she is the wife of this one, but rather that she belongs more to the one she left than to the one she married.

But let there now be a limit to this disputation, since it is a matter for a volume, not an annotation. <margin>E</margin> Nevertheless, I wished to taste these few things so that we might provide more abundant material for thought to the learned and studious. Nor do we in any way attempt to go before the judgment of our elders because of these things, much less that of the Catholic Church. Furthermore, since in the previous Edition I had hinted at our wish in this matter—whether prudent or imprudent, certainly pious—lest anyone interpret it otherwise than I had written, I thought it should be declared by what reasons we were led to desire such a thing, if it could in any way be done through Ecclesiastical authority. I felt pity for those whom I saw involved in such inextricable bonds, whom I knew to be very many, especially among the British, among whom I first drafted this work. I saw that men of formerly proven learning and holiness had not been deterred by the words of the Gospel and Paul from admitting divorce. I saw that certain things could be explained more skillfully than they have been explained thus far. I saw that this was attributed to the Roman Pontiff: that he may interpret, bind, loosen, dispense, and according to some, <margin>F</margin> even abrogate some parts of Evangelical and Apostolic doctrine. I see even today that marriage is dissolved on account of an error of person and condition even after intercourse is consummated; and that even one about which there could be no doubt it was a true marriage is dissolved on account of a lapse into heresy. I saw that on account of the profession of a human institute, on account of a changed cloak <note>the taking of monastic vows</note>, a legitimate bride is defrauded of her spouse. I saw that through the Roman Pontiff persons are rendered incapable whom neither nature nor divine law made incapable; and it can seem to be of the same power for a man’s authority to forbid a marriage from coming together and to cause a marriage to be dissolved. I saw that Scripture in this part, as in most, is perplexed and ambiguous. I saw that the most learned ancient interpreters disagree with the more recent ones. I saw how much authority was given to the Church by Christ, to whom He gave the keys to the kingdom of heaven. I thought the Church has for its spouse His Spirit, and that nothing can be wrongly established which is established for the salvation of men with Him as the author. I saw how great was the mercy of the Roman Pontiff, which succors even those in the underworld who are tormented without the danger of eternal destruction. I desired that succor also be given to those who, while...

He questions why legal "subtleties"—such as a husband entering a monastery—can dissolve a marriage, while the suffering of innocent spouses in abusive or toxic unions remains unaddressed.</summary>

# PAUL’S EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS CHAPTER VIII.

### PAGE 703
### PAGE 704

She has the right to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord. <margin>43</margin> But she is more blessed if she remains as she is, according to <margin>44</margin> my judgment; and I think that I too have the Spirit of God. <margin>VIII, 1</margin> Now concerning things offered to idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. <margin>2</margin> If anyone thinks he knows something, he does not yet know anything as he ought to know. <margin>3</margin> But if anyone loves God, this person is known by Him. <margin>4</margin> Therefore, concerning the eating of things offered to idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no other God but one. <margin>5</margin> For even if there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords— <margin>6</margin> yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we for him; and <margin>B</margin> one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him. <margin>7</margin> But not everyone has this knowledge; for some, through their habitual consciousness of the idol until now, eat food as if it were a sacrifice to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. <margin>8</margin> Food does not bring us close to God; for we are no better if we eat, nor worse if we do not eat. <margin>9</margin> But watch out, lest somehow this right of yours becomes a stumbling block to the weak. <margin>10</margin> For if someone sees you, who have knowledge, reclining in an idol's temple, will not his conscience, since he is weak, be "built up" <note>Erasmus notes the irony here: their conscience is encouraged to do something harmful</note> to eat things offered to idols?

---

<margin>A</margin> They were being tormented in this life by the peril of their eternal salvation, with no benefit. I saw that the objections raised could easily be dissolved without injury to our Religion. I saw that the reasons brought forward in this case by the Ancients and the Moderns were not so urgent as to drive the human race to such necessity. Moved by these things, Christian charity proposed to those who see more clearly than I do that they should discern whether there is any way the Gospel word and Paul’s dispensation could be managed for the salvation of the many—for whose sake all things were written for us, and for whose sake Paul sometimes even stretches the Sacred Scriptures. But if this which I desire cannot happen, certainly this much could be established: that marriages should not be entered into so easily—not to say so rashly—contrary to the custom of all the Ancients and contrary to natural equity. For if the Roman Pontiff can decree that a marriage between those joined in the third degree <note>Second cousins</note> is not a marriage, he can surely also decree that marriage is not valid among those who are under another's power <note>such as minors under parental control</note>, or among youths, girls, the drunk, or the ill-advised, who act without the counsel of their elders but rather by the impulse of pimps and madams, or rather by the counsel of folly. By this certain path, it would happen that so many would not be entangled in miserable bonds.

<margin>43 But she will be more blessed ] The Greek has "is" <note>original: "ἐστιν"</note>, in the present tense, not "will be." Even from this it appears that when he said earlier that it is "good for a man not to touch a woman," he was thinking not of vice, but of the convenience of life.</margin>

<margin>44 According to my advice ] <note>original: "κατὰ τὴν ἐμὴν γνώμην"</note>, that is, in my opinion, or by my judgment: meanwhile leaving each person's judgment free in this matter.</margin>

<margin>1 Knowledge puffs up, love builds up ] Some twist this passage to say that it is dangerous to touch "good letters" <note>The humanities or classical literature</note>, even though Paul himself said just before regarding himself, "We know that we all have knowledge," clearly speaking of himself and those like him. Therefore, Paul does not forbid us from embracing knowledge, but forbids that love be lacking from knowledge; otherwise, nothing puffs up quite as much as ignorance. Augustine treats this passage elegantly in the fifteenth book against Faustus, chapter eight.</margin>
**K**nowledge puffs up, love builds up.

<margin>2 If anyone thinks he knows ] <note>original: "Εἰ δέ τις δοκεῖ εἰδέναι τι"</note>. If anyone seems to know anything, or, If anyone seems to himself to know something; so that you may understand that all overconfidence in knowledge ought to be absent.</margin>

<margin>3 He has not yet known ] <note>original: "οὐδέπω οὐδὲν ἔγνωκε"</note>, that is, he has not yet known anything: so we may understand that this is the chief part of knowledge: to know the proper way of knowing. Now, although the doubling of the negation in Greek is an idiom of the language, it nevertheless adds some vehemence; otherwise, it would have to be translated literally as "he has not yet known nothing." Here again, I call upon those "anxiously religious" people who think absolutely nothing should be changed in the Divine Letters, not even a jot or a tittle: why did the Translator dare to omit the entire negation here? Or who will explain this passage, among those who contend that the rules of the Logicians are in all things sacred and <term>unmovable</term> <note>original: "ἀκινήτους"</note>?</margin>

<margin>4 Concerning food ] <note>original: "Περὶ δὲ τῆς βρώσεως τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων"</note>, that is, "Concerning the eating of those things which are sacrificed to idols": some translate it as "sacrificial meats." The Greek is translated harshly. For who is said to "sacrifice food"? Nor is ambiguity absent. For it can be understood that they eat the things that are sacrificed to idols. And I wonder that the word "food" <note>Latin: "escarum"</note> pleased the Translator here, since in Greek it could have been conveniently rendered as "concerning those things which are sacrificed to images."</margin>

<margin>5 Because an idol is nothing ] <note>original: "ὅτι οὐδέν"</note>. It can be read as "because there is no," or "that an idol is nothing": for he adds "in the world." But he would have translated better as "into something." Jerome <note>Erasmus likely refers to the Vulgate's source material</note> always reads "image" <note>Latin: "simulacrum"</note> for "idol": for "idol" is a Greek word, but now used by the Latins, and derived from "to sacrifice"; hence <term>idolothytes</term>, things sacrificed to images, for which the common version reads "idolothytum" in error, since in Paul’s codex it is written "idolothyta." Thomas Aquinas brings a new distinction between an "idol" and an "image": that an image is shaped into the likeness of some natural thing, whereas an idol is contrary—as if, he says,</margin>

<column-break/>

...in the Lord. <margin>43</margin> However, she is more blessed if she remains so, <margin>44</margin> according to my opinion: and I suppose that I too have the Spirit of God. Furthermore, concerning those things which are <margin>1 VIII.</margin> sacrificed to images, we know that we all have knowledge: knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up. But <margin>2</margin> if anyone seems to himself to know something, he has not yet known anything in the manner that he ought to know. But if anyone <margin>3</margin> loves God, he is known by Him. Therefore, concerning the eating <margin>4</margin> of those things which are sacrificed to images, we know that there is no image in the world, and that there is no other God but one. For even if there are those who are called <margin>5</margin> gods, whether in heaven or on earth, just as there are many gods and many lords: yet for us there is one <margin>6</margin> God, who is that Father, from whom are all things, and we in Him: and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through Him. But not in all is there knowledge: <margin>7</margin> for some, with consciousness of the image until now, eat it as something sacrificed to images, and their conscience, since it is weak, is defiled. <margin>10</margin> Yet food does not commend us to God: for neither if we eat <margin>8</margin> will anything remain for us, nor if we do not eat will anything be lacking to us. But see to it, lest by any <margin>9</margin> means this liberty of yours becomes a stumbling block to those who are weak. For if anyone sees you, who have knowledge, <margin>10</margin> reclining at a feast of images, will not the conscience of him who is weak be "built up" to eat...

---

<margin>C</margin> a horse's head were added to a human body. Whether this distinction is true or not, let others judge: to me, the dictionary they call the *Catholicum* <note>A popular medieval dictionary by Balbus</note> seems not unworthy of it. Certainly, Ambrose knew no distinction between an "idol" and an "image": nor do I see any, except that "image" <note>simulacrum</note> is a Latin word derived from "simulating," while "idol" is Greek, from "eidos" <note>species/form</note>, which puts forward an empty appearance and image when the truth is absent; hence what we call "ghosts," the Greeks call "idols."

<margin>6 There is no God but one ] <note>original: "ἕτερος θεὸς"</note>, that is, "another," is missing in our copies. And just as there is no God besides one, so there is no idol that represents any god.</margin>

<margin>7 Since there are gods ] <note>original: "ὥσπερ εἰσὶ θεοὶ πολλοὶ"</note>, that is, "just as there are many gods." Perhaps the Translator read "eiper" <note>if indeed</note>. "If indeed there are many gods and many lords." All of this is missing in Ambrose, so much so that he does not even indicate he read it. However, there will be no danger from this that we would believe in many gods, since he testifies clearly enough that those are not gods or lords simply, but are gods and lords to those by whom they were worshipped. <margin>D</margin> Just as Paul, writing to the Romans, says the god of the False Apostles is their belly. To this corresponds what follows, "But for us," and so forth. In the same place also concerning himself a little later: "Even if to others I am not an Apostle, yet to you I am." Again, he does not call them simply gods and lords, but says they are "called" gods and lords—namely in name, not in reality; and in opinion, not in power.</margin>

<margin>8 From whom all things, and we in Him ] The Greek is <note>original: "ἐξ οὗ τὰ πάντα"</note>; and so it was first written in the most corrected copy of all that I have seen, from the Pauline Library: which was nevertheless erased in such a way that a very evident trace still testifies to the original writing. Nor indeed am I unaware that the Greek preposition is to be understood, nor does it escape me what Ambrose and Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> interpret: yet "in Him" <note>Latin: "in illum"</note> seems more original to me: so that it corresponds to what precedes, "from whom all things," as if from the highest author, "and we in Him," to whom as a fountain all things are to be referred. <margin>E</margin> Or "all things indeed are from Him," who created the universe, yet "we" who have believed through faith are turned "into Him," and as if committed into one, as Theophylact <note>11th-century commentator</note> interprets.</margin>

<margin>9 And one Lord ] This passage supports what we have advised elsewhere, that Paul almost always attributes the word "God" to the Father and "Lord" to the Son, even though elsewhere the Father is called Lord and the Son is called God.</margin>

<margin>10 Food does not commend us to God ] <note>original: "ἡ παρίστησι τῷ Θεῷ"</note>, that is, makes us commended or pleasing to God. But if Paul said this truly, whence come so many precepts among Christians now concerning types of food? Whence such great superstition in observing these, that we are judged by no matter more than this?</margin>

<margin>11 We will fail ] <note>original: "ὑστερούμεθα"</note>, that is, we have less. Ambrose reads, "it will not be lacking to us." The sense is that what foods we eat has no importance for piety. Furthermore, for the Greeks, both verbs are in the present tense, <note>original: "περισσεύομεν"</note> and <note>original: "ὑστερούμεθα"</note>, "we have more" and "we have less." For Paul did not want to declare a calculation of time, but the nature of the thing: just as if someone were to say, "The poor are neglected everywhere."</margin>

<margin>12 Lest perhaps by this license ] <note>original: "ἡ ἐξουσία"</note>, that is, power or right. Nor is it "him," but "you": <note>original: "Ἐὰν γάρ τις ἴδῃ σὲ τὸν ἔχοντα γνῶσιν"</note>, that is, "For if someone sees you, who have knowledge." He used the second person according to the custom of speech in place of any person. <margin>F</margin></margin>

<margin>13 In an idol ] <note>original: "ἐν εἰδωλείῳ"</note>, that is, in an "idoleum," with the penultimate syllable lengthened. An "idoleum" is a place of images, or a table on which sacred meats were set out. And why not "accumbentem" <note>reclining at table</note> rather than "recumbentem" <note>lying down</note>: for those who "recumb" lie on their backs.</margin>

<margin>14 Will not his conscience, since it is weak ] <note>original: "ἡ συνείδησις αὐτοῦ ἀσθενοῦς ὄντος οἰκοδομηθήσεται"</note>, that is, "the conscience of him, who is weak, will be built up," and so forth. The Translator seems to have read "since he is weak" <note>original: "ἀσθενοῦς ὄντος"</note>.</margin>

<summary>Erasmus provides a philological and theological commentary on 1 Corinthians 7-8, critiquing the rigidity of contemporary marriage laws and food superstitions. He emphasizes that Christian charity and the salvation of the many should take precedence over strict legalism, while carefully analyzing Greek terms like "idol" and "knowledge."</summary>

# TO THE CORINTHIANS I. CHAPTER IX.

<margin>11</margin> ...to eat? <margin>A</margin> And the weak brother, for whom Christ died, will perish through <margin>12</margin> your knowledge. Thus, by sinning against the brothers and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against <margin>13</margin> Christ. Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat, so that I do not cause <margin>IX. 1</margin> my brother to stumble. Am I not an Apostle? Am I not free? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? Are <margin>2</margin> you not my work in the Lord? If to others I am not an Apostle, yet surely I am to you; for you are the seal of my <margin>3</margin> Apostleship in the Lord. My defense to those who <margin>4</margin> examine me is this: Do we not have the <margin>5</margin> right to eat and drink? <margin>B</margin> Do we not have the right to take along a sister-wife, as do the rest of the Apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and <margin>6</margin> Cephas <note>original: "Kephas," the Aramaic name for Peter</note>? Or is it only I and Barnabas who do not have <margin>7</margin> the right to refrain from working? Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Or who tends a flock and <margin>8</margin> does not eat of the milk of the flock? Do I say these things according to human standards? Or does not the law also say <margin>9</margin> these things? For in the law of Moses it is written, "You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain." Is it for oxen that God is concerned? <margin>10</margin> Or does he say it entirely for our sake? For it was written for our sake, that the plowman ought to plow in hope, and the <margin>11</margin> thresher ought to share in his hope. If we [sowed spiritual things] among you...

<margin>15 Idolotica]</margin> He left this word untranslated several times. It should actually be written as *Idolothyta*, which means "sacrificed to idols," from the Greek words *eidolon* (idol) and *thuo* (to sacrifice), as we just noted.

<margin>16 Sinning against Christ]</margin> In this place, I am unsure whether to agree with the opinion of Ambrose, who reads "in Christ" rather than "against Christ." For his interpretation suggests this. He argues that when people are not striving for the charity by which Christ freed us, they sin "in Christ," because to sin "against Christ" is to deny Him, whereas to sin "in Christ" refers to these matters which belong to Christ. Just as a person under the Law is said to sin "in the Law," so those under Christ are said to sin "in Christ." Certainly, the Greeks read it as "against Christ" <note>original: "eis Christon"</note>. While the phrasing may be ambiguous, Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret it as an injury committed against Christ, since it is committed against a member of Christ's body.

<margin>17 I will not eat meat]</note> <note>original: "ou me phago krea"</note>, that is, I do not eat, or I shall not feed upon meat. It is more emphatic in the present tense, though I do not deny that the Greeks sometimes use the present tense in place of the future, and a double negative adds nothing more than a single one, except perhaps a bit of intensity. It should be noted in passing that since nothing offends Paul regarding food sacrificed to idols except the stumbling of the weak—whom he wants to be supported only so that they might make progress—it is surprising why Augustine, in his 154th Letter to Publicola, declared it better for a Christian to reject food found in an idol's temple even if they were in danger of starving to death and no one else was present, provided they knew the food had been sacrificed to idols. I suspect he would have retracted this passage if he had been prompted to weigh the matter more closely. Now, regarding what Paul discusses here about avoiding scandal, I do not think it should be stretched to cover the avoidance of *every* kind of scandal. For the scandal of idolatry was huge, and in those times, suspicion was almost invincible. Yet Paul teaches that the weak person ought not to be offended and approves more of the knowledge of the strong; he only wants a concession to be made to weakness that cannot be overcome. But as for us, while we voluntarily follow whatever foolishness is commonly accepted, what else are we doing but nourishing the people's weakness? For we do not work so that they stop being weak, but so that we ourselves may be weak along with them. If the one who is stronger always complies with another's weakness, and if through such compliance stumbling blocks always sprout and increase, what end will there be to these obstacles? Or when will we have Christians who are strong and mature in Christ? Let us therefore distinguish between the causes of offense, and let us not nourish this kind of foolish weakness in certain people, but rather correct it.

<margin>1 <insert>C</insert></margin> <margin>1</margin> **Am I not an Apostle?]** It would be clearer as "Am I not an Apostle?" for the Greeks plainly read this as a question, which nonetheless affirms quite strongly, as if it would be impudent to contradict it. There is no reason to fear that these words might seem too arrogant coming from Paul. Nothing is more fitting for him than this kind of "holy boasting" and pious boldness, which he uses in other places as well.

<margin>2</margin> **You are the seal of my Apostleship]** <note>original: "he gar sphragis"</note>, that is, a "seal" or signet, by which certain faith is established regarding Apostolic authority. Just as in common proverbs, when we want something to be understood as extremely certain and beyond doubt, we say it is "attested by sealed letters."

<margin>3</margin> **Those who examine me]** <note>original: "tois eme anakrinousin"</note>, that is, those who judge or pass sentence on me. Although the sense could also be: "answer this to those who ask me"—that is, those who ask by what argument I prove I am an Apostle. The word is ambiguous, meaning both "to ask" and "to examine or investigate." Whoever wrote the commentaries on this Epistle that exist under the name of Jerome noted this. Chrysostom interprets it in various ways: those who want to know how it is clear that I am an Apostle; or those who turn it into a crime that I take money; or those who ask why I do *not* take it; or those who try to persuade others that I am not

<margin><insert>C</insert></margin> an Apostle; to all these I answer that I have declared among you that I am an Apostle, and I defend myself against them with those arguments I shall soon mention: "Do we not have the right to eat and drink," and so on.

<margin>4</margin> **Do I not have]** <note>original: "Me ouk echomen"</note>, that is, "Do we not have?"

<margin>5</margin> **A sister-woman]** <note>original: "adelphen gynaika"</note>, that is, "a sister-woman" <note>often translated as "believing wife"</note>; and so it is written in the most ancient manuscripts. Lorenzo Valla cavils at this point: since he had said "sister," what need was there to add "woman," as if there were a sister who was not a woman? From this, he concludes that the Apostles were accustomed to take their wives with them, but wives who were now in the place of sisters. Rather, he added "sister" so that you would understand she was a Christian, and for that reason she followed the Apostles. Ambrose reads "women" instead of "sister-woman." And Saint Jerome cites it this way against Jovinian in his second book, either because this reading better suited the case he was arguing there, or because he was unaware of the other reading; for the word *gyne* among the Greeks also signifies "wife," as we have frequently noted. Certainly, Clement, as Eusebius reports in the third book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, cites this passage to show that Paul had a wife, though he did not take her with him, conforming to Gospel liberty, while Peter and Philip did take theirs.

<margin>6</margin> **Or I only and Barnabas]** Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples corrects and hesitates over the word "Or" <note>Latin: "An"</note>. But "Or" <note>Latin: "Aut"</note> was correct, since "Me" <note>interrogative particle</note> preceded it; that is, "Whether," which is silently repeated here. For if it had been a new line of questioning, he would have said again, "Do we not?" <note>original: "Me ouk"</note> as he had begun.

<margin>7</margin> **Of this working]** This was added here. <note>original: "Ouk echomen exousian tou me ergazesthai"</note>, that is, "Do we not have the power of not working?" so that the word for working is used absolutely. The sense seems to be: "Is it not permitted for us alone to live in leisure while others supply our needs?" Thus both Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret "to not work" as "to lead a life in leisure," looking back to the fact that Paul and Barnabas earned their living through manual labor, whereas not only the other Apostles but even Cephas himself was supported by the kindness of others. Theophylact also noted this, suggesting that the more excellent a Bishop is, the less he ought to burden his flock. But today, what a burden it is to endure certain men—more truly tyrants than Bishops—who, the greater they are, the more heavily they loom over the people. But perhaps it is more correct to take it in the sense that everyone else interprets it: "Do we not have the power that it be permitted to us to do what everyone else does?" For among the Greeks, the two negatives are used as one. It was more polite to speak of doing what others do than to speak of "taking a woman along," especially since he had named Peter and the brothers of the Lord; Ambrose suggests this. But let the diligent reader weigh this more exactly.

<margin>8</margin> **Expense]** <note>original: "opsoniois"</note>. Regarding which we made mention above.

<margin>9</margin> **Does not the law also say these things]** Ambrose reads "these things" <note>Latin: "tauta"</note>, not "the same things" <note>Latin: "tauta" with a different accent</note>, and for that reason translates "the same," not "these."

<margin>10</margin> **Surely for us]** <note>original: "pantos"</note>. Again, as a little above, he translates "surely." It is an adverb of affirmation.

<margin>11</margin> **And he who threshes]** In Greek it is slightly different: <note>original: "kai ho aloōn tēs elpidos autou metechein ep’ elpidi"</note>, that is, "and he who threshes, to participate in his hope in hope." Although we have changed the Greek word order <note>term: "hyperbaton," a transposition of words</note>, following Ambrose and others. Furthermore, regarding what is added in our manuscripts, "of receiving fruit," it seems to have been done for the sake of explaining the matter. It is certain that this is not added among the Greeks. Moreover, "in hope," which is not added in our copies, is even specifically interpreted by Theophylact, noting that in the sentence "hope" is placed only once, and no mention is made of "participation" for the plowman, because the entire crop is only in the prayers of the one plowing. But the one who threshes already begins to be a partaker of hope and enjoys the things he wished for, while laboring in the meantime for another hope of the following year. Although I am not unaware that Theophylact refers this clause specifically to the Apostles, who did not teach just for the sake of food, but looked forward to a richer reward in the future: Theophylact drew these points from Chrysostom.

# EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER IX.

<margin>A</margin> ...If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things? If others share in this power over you, do we not have it even more? But we did not use this power; instead, we endure all things, so that we might not give any hindrance to the Gospel of Christ. Do you not know that those who work in the holy places eat from the temple? That those who wait upon the altar share in the offerings of the altar? So also the Lord ordained for those who proclaim the Gospel to live from the Gospel. But I have used none of these things. I have not written these things, however, so that it might be done so in my case. For it would be better for me to die than for anyone to make my boast empty. For if I preach the Gospel, I have nothing to boast about. For necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel! For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me. What then is my reward? That in preaching the Gospel, I may provide the Gospel of Christ free of charge, so as not to abuse my power in the Gospel. For though I am free from all, I have made myself a slave to all, that I might gain the more. And I became to the Jews as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews; to those under the law, as if under the law, that I might gain those under the law; to those without the law, as if without the law—though I am not without the law of God, but subject to the law of Christ—that I might gain those without the law. I became to the weak as if weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I might by all means save some. And I do this for the sake of the Gospel, that I might become a sharer in it. Do you not know that those who run in a race all run indeed, but only one receives the prize? So run, that you may

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin> ...is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things? <note>Referring to material support like food and money</note> If others are sharers of this power toward you, why not we rather? But we did not use that power, but we suffer all things, lest we give any stumbling block to the Gospel of Christ. Or do you not know, that those who work in sacred matters live from the sacrifice? Those who assist at the sanctuary take a part along with the sanctuary? So also the Lord ordained, that those who announce the Gospel should live from the Gospel. I however have used none of these things. Although I have not written these things so that it may be done so in my case. For it is better for me to die rather than that anyone should render my boasting void. For even if I should preach the Gospel, there is nothing for me to boast of. For necessity lies upon me. But woe is to me, unless I preach the Gospel. For if I do this willingly, I have a reward: but if unwillingly, a stewardship is committed to me. What therefore is my reward? That when I preach the Gospel, I may make the Gospel of Christ free of charge, in this, that I do not abuse my power in the Gospel. For since I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, so that I might gain more. And I became to the Jews as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews: to those who are under the law, as if I were under the law, that I might gain those who are under the law: To those who are without the law, as if I were without the law, though I am not <margin>C</margin> without the law of God, but subject to the law of Christ, that I might gain those who are without the law. Moreover, I do this because of the Gospel, so that I may become a partaker of it. Do you not know, that those who run in a race, all indeed run, but one receives the prize? So run, that you may

12 **If we reap your carnal things**] <note>original Greek: θερίσομεν</note>, that is, we shall reap: although this makes no difference to the sense.

13 **Of your power**] <note>original Greek: ἐξουσίας</note>: so that you understand not just any power, but the faculty of reaping, and of leading around wives or women, which they permitted to the other Apostles.

14 **Why not rather**] The Translator added "Why" <note>Latin: Quare</note> on his own: it was enough to say, "not rather us?" <note>original Greek: ἢ μᾶλλον ἡμεῖς;</note>

15 **But we sustain all things**] <note>original Greek: στέγομεν</note>: which properly refers to a vessel that contains all things.

16 **Lest we give any stumbling block to the Gospel**] In Greek it is not "scandal" <note>original Greek: σκάνδαλον</note>, which is translated here as "offense," but <note>original Greek: ἐγκοπήν</note>, which sounds like <term>interception</term> or <term>interruption</term>: <margin>D</margin> lest anything exist that brings any delay to the Gospel preaching. Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine Bible commentator</note> noted this before us.

17 **Those who work in the sanctuary**] It is a bit different among the Greeks: <note>original Greek: ὅτι οἱ τὰ ἱερὰ ἐργαζόμενοι, ἐκ τοῦ ἱεροῦ ἐσθίουσιν</note>, that is, "those who perform sacred acts eat from the sacred place or temple": for <note>original Greek: ἱερὸν</note> clearly signifies a temple as well.

18 **Who serve the altar**] <note>original Greek: τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ προσεδρεύοντες</note>, that is, "assisting or sitting by the sanctuary." Theophylact noted the emphasis of this word before us, and before him Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father</note>. For he does not say "Priests," but "those who sit by the altar": so that we may understand the constant service of sacred things. But today almost no one is further from the altar than those who are most participants in the altars' benefits. Nor does anyone more troublesome-ly demand tithes from the people than those who provide nothing to the people for whose sake the tithes had been given. Nor is it enough to sit by it, but one must work: nor is it enough for anyone to work, one must perform sacred work, and be constant in these things. Nor did he say they "receive" from the sacred place, but they "eat" from the sacred place: to remind us that a living is owed, not riches. And "they share with the sanctuary," they receive a part with the sanctuary. For the victim was divided between the Priests and the Levites. Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a 15th-century humanist who critiqued the Vulgate Bible</note> is indignant at this passage, perhaps a bit more freely than some ears can bear: but not entirely without reason against Remigius, who distinguished these two words "sanctuary" and "altar" so that "sanctuary" pertains to idols and "altar" to God, when the proper use of these words should have been sought rather from the Greeks. Then, carried further by the heat of his mind, Valla marvels at the impudence of certain theologians who, though the Pauline Epistles were written in Greek, dared to interpret them while being entirely ignorant of Greek letters. Nor does he refrain from the name of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> here; for they tell a certain story about him that, after finishing his commentaries on Paul, Paul appeared to him and ingenuously confessed that his <margin>F</margin> Epistles had been understood by no one before that time except by Thomas—Valla mocks this as a made-up and impudently fashioned fable: since it is not even possible for anyone to interpret exactly if they are ignorant of the language in which that which they are interpreting was written. For my part, while I cannot entirely refute what Valla writes, I think that some deference should be given to such men, especially those commended for their holiness. Regard must be had for the times in which they lived. Finally, it must be remembered they were men. Therefore, just as it is both noble and conducive to learning not to hide it if the Ancients slipped anywhere, so I think it the duty of an upright man to refrain from insults, and so to heal the evil that, as far as possible, you do not harm the man. Thomas in this place interprets "sanctuary" as the temple of the Jews or Gentiles; "altar" as the altar of the Jerusalem temple, or the temple itself: exposing, I think, the sense of the speech rather than the propriety of the words. Otherwise, just as a house is no more called "of the Gauls" than "of the Britons," so

<column-break/>

"sanctuary" and "altar" belong to any people. Except that <note>original Greek: θυσιαστήριον</note>, named from sacrificing, is the place where victims are slaughtered.

<margin>B</margin> 19 **Than that my glory**] <note>original Greek: ἢ τὸ καύχημα</note>, that is, "boasting." For just a little before, he boasted as if glorifying himself. And "make void" is <note>original Greek: κενώσῃ</note>, that is, "render useless or empty."

20 **And if I shall have preached the Gospel**] <note>original Greek: εὐαγγελίζωμαι</note> is in the present tense, "I preach" or "I should preach," as Ambrose <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note> reads.

21 **My reward**] Instead of "my," it is "to me" among the Greeks: <note>original Greek: Τίς οὖν μοί ἐστιν ὁ μισθός;</note> "what therefore to me is the reward?" It appears the Translator read "my" <note>Greek: μοῦ</note> instead of "to me" <note>Greek: μοί</note>.

22 **I put without expense**] <note>original Greek: ἀδάπανον θήσω</note>, that is, "I will make it free," as he pleasantly calls "without expense" that which is a cost to no one. Otherwise, even he who spends nothing does it without expense. Furthermore, the word "to put" <note>Greek: θήσω</note> is commonly found among the Greeks in place of "to make." And after "Gospel," the Greeks add "of Christ." O truly Apostolic glory! But one which no one now strives to emulate. Nothing now is free of charge, not even burial, even though Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo</note> in his sixty-fourth letter does not want funeral rites to be sold.

23 **As if I were without law**] The Greek adverb <note>original Greek: ὡς</note> is ambiguous: yet here "quasi" <note>as if</note> was more fitting: and so Saint Jerome reads it on Isaiah, and so Ambrose in many places. For an example is not being set, but a false appearance of the thing is being proposed. Theophylact reads, "without law to God" and "under law to Christ," which sounds harsh: <term>exlex</term> <note>out-law</note> of God and <term>sublex</term> <note>under-law</note> of Christ.

24 **Without the law of God**] It is "to God" in Greek, <note>original Greek: μὴ ὢν ἄνομος Θεῷ</note>, "when I am not without law with God." Although the Greek <margin>E</margin> manuscripts vary on this. Chrysostom reads, "without law of God" <note>Greek: Θεοῦ</note>.

25 **Weak to the weak**] <note>original Greek: ὡς ἀσθενής</note>, that is, "as if" or "quasi" weak.

26 **That I might make all saved**] In Greek it is otherwise: <note>original Greek: ἵνα πάντως τινὰς σώσω</note>, that is, "that I might by all means save some." Although here it appears the Greek manuscripts varied. Certainly Valla is somewhat offended that Theophylact changed the tense of the verb incorrectly, "that I might make all saved," as if <note>original Greek: σώσω</note> referred to the past, when the verb is of the future tense. Nor is the sense that he did this for my sake and now stops, but that he does it even now, and will do so. Furthermore, what is said here as "I shall save," the same must be understood regarding what preceded: "I shall gain" <note>Latin: lucrifaciam</note>, rather than "I was gaining."

27 **Moreover I do all things**] <note>original Greek: Τοῦτο δὲ ποιῶ</note>, that is, "Moreover I do this." And so Theophylact reads. Chrysostom has "all things," although from his explanation it is not clear what he read.

28 **One receives the prize**] Ambrose reads "palm" for "prize" <note>Latin: bravio</note>: likewise Cyprian <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage</note>, for it is <note>original Greek: βραβεῖον</note> in Greek. And it is indeed altogether a "brabium," a reward: but specifically that which is given to those contending and winning. For they think <note>original Greek: βραβεῖον</note> was said as if it were <note>original Greek: βραβείδιον</note>, with two letters changed and moved: because the judges of the contests would designate the victor with a palm branch <note>Greek: rhabdos</note> being given: hence they are called <note>original Greek: βραβευταὶ</note> by the Greeks, as if they were <note>original Greek: ῥαβδευταί</note>, those who announce the victor.

29 **That you may obtain**] <note>original Greek: ἵνα καταλάβητε</note>. Either he used "that" <note>Greek: hina</note> in place of "because" <note>Greek: hoti</note>: or the sense is, "Run with this mind, not only so that you may seem to have contended, but with the desire for victory," just as Theophylact plainly interprets. If this opinion is approved, then the adverb is not to be referred to the "that" which follows: as if you said, "Follow so that you may follow": but to the likeness which preceded. So,

# TO THE CORINTHIANS I. CAP. X.

<margin>25</margin> ...that you may lay hold of it. Every man who strives in a contest exercises self-control in all things; they indeed do it to receive a perishable crown, <margin>26</margin> but we an imperishable one. I therefore run in this way, not as if uncertainly; I box in this way, not as one <margin>27</margin> beating the air. But I treat my body roughly and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, having preached to others, I myself should become <margin>X. 1</margin> disqualified. For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, <margin>2</margin> and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; <margin>3</margin> and all ate the same spiritual food, <margin>4</margin> and all drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ. <margin>5</margin> But God was not well-pleased with most of them, for they were struck down in the desert. <margin>6</margin> Now these things became examples <note>original: "typoi"</note> for us, so that we should not be desirers of evil things, as they also desired. <margin>7</margin> Neither become idolaters, as some of them were, as it is written: "The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play." <margin>8</margin> Neither let us commit sexual immorality, as some of them committed it, and twenty-three thousand fell in one day. <margin>9</margin> Neither let us test Christ, as some of them tested Him, and were destroyed by serpents. <margin>10</margin> Neither grumble, as some of them grumbled, and were destroyed by the destroyer. <margin>11</margin> Now all these things happened to them as examples <note>original: "typoi"</note>; and they were written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. <margin>12</margin> Therefore, let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall. <margin>13</margin> No temptation has taken hold of you except what is common to man; but God is faithful, who will not allow you...

That is, run in your own race-course according to their example. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Archbishop and Church Father known for his eloquent preaching.</note> suggests the same with these words: <note>Greek: "And when he speaks thus, he teaches the pattern,"</note> that is, when he says "so," he also commemorates the form or example. It is a wonder where Cyprian <note>Bishop of Carthage (d. 258 AD).</note> reads here: "So run that you may seize all." Although, he who attains and goes before others does indeed "seize" correctly.

<margin>30</margin> **He who strives in a contest**] <note>Greek: "For every one who strives,"</note> that is, "For everyone who competes": but specifically in public contests, such as the wrestling school, or the Olympic, or Circensian games. For he soon mentions the race and the boxers.

<margin>31</margin> **Abstains from all things**] <note>Greek: "exercises self-control in all things,"</note> that is, he sustains or endures all things; or, as I prefer, he is temperate in all things. Cyprian reads, "is continent in all things." Indeed, athletes are prepared for contests even by a regime of diet.

<margin>32</margin> **But we an incorruptible**] <note>Greek: "perishable and imperishable."</note> I wonder why the translator varied the terms.

<margin>33</margin> **So I fight**] Not "I fight" in the sense of the Greek word for "to battle" <note>original: "machomai"</note>, but "I box" <note>original: "pykteuo"</note>, which means to practice the contest of a prize-fighter, and to fight with fists. The Translator alluded to fists, not to general battles. Ambrose reads "I strike with fists" for "I fight." And so he cites the passage in his book *On Paradise*, chapter twelve. Augustine, explaining Psalm 57, reads: "Not such a boxer as one beating the air." Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274 AD), the dominant medieval theologian.</note>, however, seems to interpret "fighting" as "waging war," first when he says, "Secondly, he puts his fight in victory," and soon after, "So I fight, he says, by battling against enemies against evil." This slip should be forgiven, unless some people were to press us too hard with that story about the little commentary of Paul approving of his work. <note>Erasmus is likely mocking a legend that Paul appeared to Aquinas to approve of his commentaries.</note>

<margin>34</margin> **Beating the air**] This was said as a proverbial figure, meaning to labor in vain and fruitlessly, just as a boxer accomplishes nothing unless he touches a body. Furthermore, this parable tends toward this point: that we understand it is not enough to perform our duty in just any way, unless we take care that we are seen to have conducted ourselves notably and beyond the others.

<margin>35</margin> **I chastise**] <note>Greek: "hypopiazo"</note>, that is, I restrain, or I curb and subject: for the Translator expressed the sense rather than rendering the Greek word literally. Paulinus expressed it more closely in his forty-eighth Epistle to Augustine: "I make my body livid [black and blue]," he says, "& I bring it into slavery." For to the Greeks, the word means to strike specifically under the eyes with the fist so as to cause a bruise or a bloody mark. The eyes they call <note>Greek: "opas"</note>, and such marks <note>Greek: "hypopia"</note>, according to the authors Hesychius and Suida. It appears the metaphor is taken from the contest of boxers, from which Paul is often wont to draw similarities. In these contests, he "supplanted" who threw his antagonist to the ground, and he "boxed" who had fixed a notable mark on the face.

<margin>1</margin> **For I would not**] <note>Greek: "I do not wish, however."</note> Ambrose reads "for," with the ancient manuscripts agreeing, so that these things might cohere with the preceding: if what he just taught the Corinthians, he now corroborates with the examples of the Jews. But if you prefer "however," it will be for the sake of digressing to other matters.

<margin>2</margin> **And all were baptized in Moses**] It is <note>Greek: "into Moses"</note> in Greek. Augustine, explaining Psalm 77, reads "through Moses." I think it is more correctly taken as "into Moses," meaning "into the Mosaic Law," for they were not yet in Christ, whose coming was far off; meanwhile Moses bore the "type" <note>term: Typology. The theological study of how Old Testament persons or events foreshadow New Testament realities.</note> of Christ, and Gospel realities were being shadowed forth in figures.

<margin>3</margin> **But they drank**] In the Greek it is "for." And so Augustine reports...

<margin>25</margin> ...that you may lay hold of it. 30 Every one who competes, 31 is temperate in all things: they indeed, therefore, that they may receive a perishable crown, 32 but we an eternal one. <margin>26</margin> I therefore so run, as not into uncertainty: <margin>27</margin> 33 I act as a boxer, not as 34 beating the air: But 35 I subject my body, and lead it into slavery, lest by any means it happen that, when I have preached to others, I myself should be made a castaway. <margin>A</margin> <margin>X. 1</margin> I would not, however, have you be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, <margin>2</margin> And all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea: And all ate the same <margin>B</margin> spiritual food, <margin>4</margin> And all drank the same spiritual drink: 3 for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them: but the rock was Christ. But with many of them 5 God was not pleased, for they were laid low in the desert. <margin>6</margin> Now these things were our figures, lest we be desirers of evil things, just as they also desired. <margin>7</margin> Neither be worshippers of idols, like some of them, as it is written: The people sat down to eat and drink, and they rose up to play. Neither <margin>8</margin> let us commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and there fell in one day twenty-three thousand. Neither <margin>9</margin> <margin>C</margin> let us tempt Christ, 8 as also some of them tempted him, and were destroyed by serpents. <margin>10</margin> Neither murmur, as also some of them murmured, and were slain by the destroyer.
