Therefore, he who thinks he stands, let him see that he does not fall. <margin>12</margin> 10 Temptation has not taken you, except what is human: but 13 God is faithful,

...in the twelfth book against Faustus, chapter twenty-nine, <margin>D</margin> following the faith of an ancient manuscript, where he also says in Greek, "following them." And elsewhere he speaks several times thus, "This is following that."

<margin>4</margin> **Following them**] <note>Greek: "akolouthouses"</note>, that is, following, or accompanying. He said "following," as if they were perpetual companions of the journey: for that is what the Greek implies rather than simply "passing by." Origen, in his fifth Homily on Exodus, refers the "following rock" to the cloud which preceded the Hebrew lawgivers, having shown, as it appears, the absurdity of the sense if a rock were said to "follow" those setting out. But it can be understood as the stream which, springing forth from the rock, followed them continually. And Augustine, in several other places as well as against the adversary of the Law and Prophets (Book 2, Chapter 6), interprets: "Christ was the rock," that is, the rock signified Christ. Nor does it hinder that he called this rock "spiritual." For whatever has a mystical sense is called spiritual. They drank water from the rock—not just any rock, but from the spiritual one, which signified that unique rock from which all believers draw salvation. Jerome, or whoever else it was, explaining Psalm 41, brings up this passage omitting the pronoun "them": since it is not in the Greek, it was added by the Translator so that the speech would be clearer, and we likewise have added it. Yet Ambrose does not add it, though he frequently brings up this passage in his books.

<margin>5</margin> **It was well-pleasing to God**] <note>Greek: "God was well-pleased."</note> Which Ambrose <margin>E</margin> renders "God felt well," but we more truly "approved." We have already frequently advised regarding this word.

<margin>6</margin> **In figure they were made of us**] "Figures," or "forms," is the Greek, in the plural number <note>Greek: "typoi"</note>: just as a little later, "Now all these things happened in figure" <note>Greek: "Now all these things happened as types"</note>, that is, he knows all things happened figuratively. In the collections of Bede, "figure" is read in the first place, though "our" had been corrupted into "your": which nevertheless is frequently encountered in the same way in the books of Augustine. And in the former place, the Greek adds "of us" <note>Greek: "hemon"</note>, so they read: "Now these things were figures of us." And in that manner Augustine cites this place, explaining Psalm 113. Again against Faustus in a fragment of the fourth book, and in several other places.

<margin>7</margin> **Neither be made an idolater**] I suspect that for "become" <note>Greek: "ginesthe"</note> it was changed to <note>Greek: "genesthe"</note>, that is, "Neither should we be made worshippers of idols": since in this too it is added, "as some of them," so that "become" might respond to "be." Otherwise, in two places he changed the person, in the idolaters and the grumblers. <margin>F</margin>

<margin>8</margin> **As some of them**] <note>Greek: "as also some of them tempted."</note> The Translator reads "him" <note>Latin: "eum"</note>; and so it is written in some manuscripts. It is not clear enough from Ambrose, nor from Chrysostom, nor from Theophylact what they read, except that in each the context has "him" <note>original: "auton"</note>. If we read "him," that is, "Him," the Divinity of Christ is declared from this place, whom he says was tempted by the Jews before He took on manhood. For regarding what preceded, "the rock however was Christ," someone could interpret it as "that rock designated Christ who was to be born later." But it is called "spiritual" because it had the type of the mystical rock. If we read "him" [God/Christ], the sense will be: lest we tempt Christ, as the Jews of old tempted God.

<margin>9</margin> **For our correction**] <note>Greek: "for our admonition," or "of us"</note>: which nevertheless is sometimes used for "correction."

<margin>10</margin> **Let temptation not seize you**] <note>Greek: "has taken,"</note> that is, has apprehended, in the past tense, or "began." For it suggests that the Corinthians already...

# PAUL’S EPISTLE CHAPTER X.

...you to be tempted beyond what you are able; but with the temptation he will also make the way out, so that you are able <margin>14</margin> to endure it. Therefore, my beloved, flee from <margin>15</margin> idolatry. I speak as to wise men; you judge <margin>16</margin> what I say. The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body <margin>17</margin> of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one <margin>18</margin> bread. Look at Israel according to the flesh. Are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the <margin>19</margin> altar? What then do I say? That an idol is anything? Or <margin>20</margin> that what is sacrificed to idols is anything? No, but that what the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons, and not to God. I do not want you to become participants with demons. <margin>21</margin> You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the <margin>22</margin> table of demons. Or do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? <margin>23</margin> Are we stronger than He? All things are permitted to me, but not all things are profitable; all things are permitted to me, but <margin>24</margin> not all things build up. Let no one seek his own good, but <margin>25</margin> each that of the other. Eat everything sold in the meat-market, asking no questions for the sake of conscience. <margin>26 27</margin> For the earth is the Lord's, and its fullness. If any of the unbelievers invites you, and you wish to go, eat everything set before you, asking no <margin>28</margin> questions for the sake of conscience. But if someone says to you, "This is sacrificed to idols," do not eat for the sake of the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience. For the... <meta>Ku-</meta>

---

...had already fallen into temptation, but "human" temptation, that is, tolerable and curable. And indeed, all the Greek manuscripts I have seen agree with this reading; although it appears that Ambrose read <note>original: "apprehendat"</note> "let it seize," based on these words which he adds: *However, he exhorts them so that human temptation might seize them.* Although what similarity is there between <note>original: "katalambanētai" (be overtaken)</note> and <note>original: "eilophen" (has taken)</note>? Unless perhaps Ambrose read <note>original: "eilēphen"</note>. But nothing seems more genuine to the sense of the Greek reading than Paul's intent, and it is also clear that this pleased Chrysostom and Theophylact. Previously he had terrified them with horrific examples; soon, lest they despair, he restores them, downplaying the fact that they had sinned up to this point, and saying it was a light thing compared to those more serious evils by which they had been tempted.

11 **Outcome** <note>original: "Proventum"</note>] <note>original: "tēn ekbasin"</note>, that is, the exit, or the event: that is, He who allows you to fall into temptation will likewise ensure that the temptation turns out well. Jerome, in his commentaries on Jonah, reads it in this way: *But he will make with the temptation also an exit.* And likewise Augustine when explaining the sixty-first Psalm. For "proventús" usually refers to sowings and things growing from the earth. Again, in the eighty-ninth Epistle. But lest anyone should think it was said thus, *but he will make with the temptation a result*, as if God were bargaining with the temptation regarding the outcome, we have translated it: *But he will make together with the temptation the event*: so the sense is, He who permitted the temptation to occur will also give a good exit.

12 **That you may be able to sustain**] In Greek, something more magnificent is said: <note>original: "hypenenkein"</note>, which is to bear it in such a way that you are above the burden and overcome it: just as he said to the Romans, "we are more than conquerors."

13 **Which we bless**] <note>original: "ho eulogoumen"</note>, that is, which we receive with thanksgiving. For this is how Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret it. Some more recent commentators interpret it as the blessing of the one consecrating.

14 **And the bread, which we break**] <note>original: "Ton arton, hon klōmen"</note>, that is, the bread, which we break. Why are those people not offended by this passage, who are offended by the fact that the Greeks, in the words with which the Latins consecrate the body of Christ, say: *This is my body, which is broken for you*? They are following, it appears, the authority of Paul, who in the next chapter recounts the words of Christ in this way. But if anyone should quibble that this passage has been corrupted in the manuscripts, certainly our codices agree in this place with the Greek reading, and yet there are those who think this refers to the consecrated bread and cup, or at least in a general sense, so that the passage can be accommodated to both meanings. For the early Christians held all bread to be sacred, as it were, in memory of the Lord's Supper, and passing the cup among themselves, they gave thanks to the Lord, even when a sacramental consecration did not always take place. It is noted here that he mentions the cup before the bread. In Luke, the cup is mentioned twice: the first while they were eating, the second after supper.

15 **Is it not a participation of the body**] <note>original: "koinōnia"</note>. Previously he had translated this as "communion," now he translates it as "participation": I do not see what this abundance of words contributes. Meanwhile, the reader ignorant of Greek vainly invents some distinction between *communication* and *participation*.

16 **One bread and one body**] The conjunction "and" is absent in the Greek: <note>original: "heis artos, hen sōma"</note>, that is, one bread, one body. This is how Chrysostom and Theophylact read it, and I found it written this way in the Pauline manuscript. Both of the Constantinople codices agreed. Someone might say, what does it matter if the conjunction "and" is added? Not much; however, the lack of a conjunction <note>term: "asyndeton" — a rhetorical figure where conjunctions are omitted for emphasis</note> better fits the sense brought by the Greeks. For they think we are to understand that bread which is the body of the Lord: since all Christians are members of Christ, it is as if he corrected what he had said before about "participating": for it is more to be one and the same thing than to be a participant.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...God, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able; indeed, He will make with the temptation an 11 event, so <margin>14</margin> that 12 you may be able to endure it. Wherefore, my beloved, flee from the worship of idols. I speak as to <margin>15</margin> prudent men; you judge for yourselves what I say. <margin>16</margin> The cup of blessing, 13 which we bless, is it not a communication of the blood of Christ? 14 The bread, <margin>17</margin> which we break, 15 is it not a communication of the body of Christ? Since 16 we being many are one <margin>17</margin> bread, one body: for we all participate in the same bread. 18 Look at Israel according to the flesh. Are <margin>18</margin> not those who eat the victims participants in the sanctuary? 19 What then do I say, that an idol is any- <margin>19</margin> thing? Or that what is sacrificed to idols is any-
<margin>B</margin> thing? No. 20 But I say this, that what the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons, and not to God. <margin>20</margin> 21 I would not have you be partners of demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of <margin>21</margin> demons. You cannot be participants in the table of the Lord and the table of demons. 22 Do we <margin>22</margin> provoke the Lord? Are we stronger than He? All things are permitted to me, but not all things are <margin>23</margin> profitable: all things are permitted to me, but not all things build up. Let no one seek what is his <margin>24</margin> own, 23 but each what is the other's. 24 Everything <margin>24</margin> that is sold in the meat-market eat, 25 asking no <margin>25</margin> questions for the sake of conscience. For the earth is the Lord's, and its fullness. But if any of the <margin>26 27</margin>
<margin>C</margin> unbelievers invites you, and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions for the sake of conscience. But if someone should <margin>28</margin> say to you, 27 "This is sacrificed to idols": do not eat for the sake of him 28 who informed you, and for the sake of... <meta>con-</meta>

---

17 **All who**] <note>original: "hoi gar pantes"</note>, that is, "for all," without the word "who." For we all participate in one bread. Ambrose also reads it this way. In a very ancient codex, I found written <note>original: "syneidomen" (we are conscious of)</note>: so it is likely that the "that" <note>Latin: "que"</note> was changed into "who" <note>Latin: "qui"</note>; although this variety of reading does not significantly change the sense. Furthermore, there is no mention of the cup either among the Greeks or in the codex of Donatianus. In the older Constantinople codex, there was no mention of the cup, but someone had added it in the space between the lines with a more recent hand. In some printed editions, I found "all indeed of one bread," and both Constantinople codices had it thus, so it is probable the Translator rendered the particle <note>original: "gar"</note> as an expletive conjunction.

18 **Look at Israel according to the flesh**] He added "according to the flesh" for the sake of distinction, to show there is another Israel according to the spirit: although the article is not repeated in the Greek.

19 **What then do I say**] Based on the Greek manuscripts, the passage should be punctuated like this: *What then do I say? That an idol is anything, or that what is sacrificed to idols is anything?* As if he were saying, "I am by no means saying this." And as if he had already denied that he felt that way—which would be absurd if said on its own—he adds what he actually thinks: *But what they sacrifice, etc.*: otherwise, what follows would connect harshly: *But what the nations sacrifice, etc.* Therefore, we have not feared to add a few words to make the speech clearer. The ancient Latin manuscripts also punctuate it in this manner.

20 **But what the nations sacrifice**] <note>original: "All' hoti ha thyei"</note>, that is, *But that those things which they sacrifice*: so that you understand, "But I say this, that what the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons, not to God."

21 **I do not wish you to become partners**] <note>original: "koinōnous"</note>, that is, participants, or communicants, or consorts.

22 **Do we emulate the Lord?**] <note>original: "parazēloumen"</note>, that is, we provoke and irritate: which he translated earlier as "provokes to emulation." And the Greek scholia interpret it in this way, specifically Theophylact: *we emulate or we provoke to anger*, that is, we test and irritate: for "emulate" <note>original: "zēloumen"</note> is also used in a positive sense, but "provoke" <note>original: "parazēloumen"</note> is almost never used except in a negative sense.

23 **But what is the other's**] <note>original: "alla to tou heterou hekastos"</note>, that is, "but each what is of the other."

24 **Everything that comes in the meat-market**] "Comes" in this place means "is sold" <note>original: "pōloumenon"</note>: and it should be read "in the market" <note>Latin: "in macello"</note>, not "into the market." Saint Augustine also indicates this against Adamantius; he says that Paul forbids asking questions when something is bought from the market. And a circumflex accent marked over the Greek word <note>original: "pōleitai"</note> could have removed this kind of ambiguity.

25 **Asking no questions**] <note>original: "mēden anakrinontes"</note>, that is, discerning nothing: which is the same word used a little further down. Ambrose reads, "discerning nothing." It is, moreover, the participle of that which he translated earlier as "asking."

26 **And its fullness**] "Its" refers to the earth, not to the Lord; that is, whatever the rich earth produces, it is all the Lord's.

27 **This is sacrificed to idols**] Ancient codices have: *This is an idol-offering.* And we read it thus in Ambrose. However, in Greek, it is the same word the Translator has left so many times: <note>original: "eidolothyton"</note>.

28 **Who judged**] <note>original: "ton mēnysanta"</note>, that is, "he indicated" or "informed," with an 'n' <note>nu</note>, not a 'r' <note>rho</note>. Although this is a small detail, because a slip into this kind of error is very easy, I thought it should be noted. For among the Greeks, this means to bring to light a thing previously hidden: although in Ambrose this little part is not added, "on account of him who indicated," perhaps through the negligence of scribes.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed philological notes and his own Latin translation of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, transitioning from Chapter 10 to Chapter 11. # TO THE CORINTHIANS I. CHAP. XI.

<margin>29</margin> The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness. <note>original: "Κυρίου ἡ γῆ, καὶ τὸ πλήρωμα αὐτῆς"</note> But I say "conscience," not one's own, but that of the other person. For why is my liberty judged by another's conscience?
<margin>30</margin> If I partake with thankfulness, why am I slandered for that for which I give thanks?
<margin>31</margin> Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
<margin>32</margin> Give no offense, either to Jews, or to Greeks, or to the Church of God.
<margin>33</margin> Just as I also please everyone in all things, not seeking my own advantage, but that of the many, so that they may be saved.

XI. 1 Be imitators of me, just as I am of Christ.
<margin>2</margin> <margin>B</margin> I praise you, brothers, because you remember me in everything, and you hold fast the traditions just as I delivered them to you.
<margin>3</margin> But I want you to know that the head of every man is Christ; and the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God.
<margin>4</margin> Every man praying or prophesying with his head covered <note>literally "having [something] down from the head"</note> disgraces his head.
<margin>5</margin> But every woman praying or prophesying with her head uncovered disgraces her head; for it is one and the same as if she were shaved.
<margin>6</margin> For if a woman is not covered, let her hair also be cut off. But if it is disgraceful for a woman to have her hair cut off or to be shaved, let her be covered.
<margin>7</margin> <margin>C</margin> For a man indeed ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of the man.
<margin>8</margin> For man is not from woman, but woman from man.
<margin>9</margin> For man was not created for the woman, but woman for the man.
<margin>10</margin> For this reason, the woman ought to have authority <note>meaning a symbol of authority, i.e., a veil</note> on her head, because of the angels.

---

<margin>29</margin> **I say conscience, not &c.]** Before this passage, the Greek manuscripts repeat: *For the earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness:* which was placed a little earlier. It fits well in both places. There, it means it does not matter what we eat, for all things belong to the Lord. And here, there is no reason to offend a brother by eating what was sacrificed to idols, since the rich world provides such a great abundance of food. However, in this later passage, it seems to be introduced from the perspective of another person, as if someone were objecting to Paul: "What is this 'conscience' you tell me about, when you yourself admit the earth and its fullness are the Lord's?" Therefore, Paul adds a distinction: your conscience says the earth is the Lord's, but the conscience of the other person does not say the same, as they think something belongs specifically to the idols and is not shared with God. We should not be too bothered that Laurentius <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous Renaissance humanist whose notes on the New Testament influenced Erasmus</note> argues here about the word "himself" or "that conscience." For when Paul says, *if because of conscience*, he explains what he had said before: otherwise, the person who heard he shouldn't eat because of the one who pointed it out might ask, "What does this have to do with him?" Paul answers: because of *his* conscience, which you wound by your action, even if your own is more firm. Then, when he says *my [liberty]*, he adopts a persona in his usual way; he often takes on the role of another to make the matter more visible to the eyes.

<margin>30</margin> *By another's conscience]* <note>original: "ὑπ’ ἄλλης συνειδήσεως"</note>, that is, by a different conscience. And so Ambrose <note>An influential 4th-century bishop and theologian</note> reads it, and it is seen written this way in the most ancient copies, specifically in both the Constantinopolitan ones. Though this makes little difference to the sense.

<margin>31</margin> *I partake with grace]* Ambrose reads, *I am a partaker by grace:* but I do not find "I partake with grace" <note>original: "μετέχω χάριτι"</note> unless it refers to a partner in communion, not to the thing you are partaking in. Hence I prefer *with grace*, meaning with thanksgiving. It can also be understood this way: that "grace" <note>original: "χάριτι"</note> here sounds like beneficence, acting as a "dative of instrument" or "manner." If I am a partaker of foods, and that not through an idol but by the benefit of God's generosity, why should I be spoken of badly? Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an early Church Father known for his preaching</note> and Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine commentator</note> interpret it in this sense, calling God's grace the "strength of the soul" that despises the idol, and God's goodness, which ensures His gifts are not polluted for the pure by the malice of the wicked.

<margin>32</margin> *For that which I give thanks]* <note>original: "ὑπὲρ οὗ ἐγὼ εὐχαριστῶ"</note>, that is, for the thing for which I give thanks. He contrasts these things as opposites: *to be slandered* and *to give thanks*.

<margin>33</margin> *Or anything else]* <note>original: "εἴτε τι"</note>, that is, "or something." The word "else" was added to explain the matter. Ambrose reads it this way, *or if you do anything:* just as it is found among the Greeks.

<margin>34</margin> *Be without offense]* In Greek it is more pleasant: *Aproskopoi*, meaning people such that no one is tripped up by you.

<margin>35</margin> *To Jews & Gentiles]* For "Gentiles" it is *Hellenesi*, that is, Greeks. But again, there is the conjunction "and" <note>original: "καὶ"</note> for each, so we translate it as *neither*.

<margin>36</margin> *Not seeking what is useful to me]* It was simpler and truer: *not seeking my own advantage*, <note>original: "μὴ ζητῶν τὸ ἐμαυτοῦ συμφέρον, ἀλλὰ τὸ τῶν πολλῶν"</note>.

<column-break/>

conscience. For the earth is the Lord's, and its fullness. <margin>29</margin> Moreover, I say conscience, not yours, but that of the other. For why is my liberty judged by another conscience? <margin>30</margin> But if I partake with thankfulness, why is evil said of me for that for which I give thanks? <margin>31</margin> Therefore, whether you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all for the glory of God. <margin>32</margin> Be such that you provide no stumbling block, neither to the Jews, nor to the Greeks, nor to the Church of God. <margin>33</margin> Just as I please everyone in all things, not seeking my own advantage, but that of the many, so that they may be saved.

XI. 1 Be imitators of me, just as I am of Christ. <margin>2</margin> I praise you, brothers, that you hold all my things in memory: and just as I delivered to you, you hold the institutions. <margin>3</margin> But I want you to know that the head of every man is Christ: the head of the woman, however, is the man: but the head of Christ is God. <margin>4</margin> Every man praying or prophesying, having anything on his head, brings shame upon his head. <margin>5</margin> But every woman, praying or prophesying with an unveiled head, dishonors her head: for it is exactly as if she were shaved. <margin>6</margin> For if a woman is not veiled, let her also be shorn. <margin>7</margin> But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her be veiled. <margin>8</margin> A man indeed ought not to veil his head, since he is the image and glory of God: but the woman is the glory of the man. <margin>9</margin> For man is not from woman, but woman from man. <margin>10</margin> Nor was man created for the sake of the woman, but woman for the sake of the man. <margin>11</margin> Because of this, the woman ought to have authority on her head, because of the angels.

---

<margin>1</margin> **Be imitators of me, just as &c.]** We gave a warning about this passage earlier in the fourth chapter of this Epistle: this is a voice worthy of those who claim the place of the Apostles for themselves. Paul sets himself as an example, conscious that he has nothing that should not be imitated; and yet he does not want this example to seem imitable to anyone unless it corresponds to the archetype of Christ. Nowadays, some who live according to their own whim—to say nothing more—think it is enough if they announce with threats whatever they have decided should be done by others, whether it is right or otherwise. There are others, superstitious rather than religious, who each call men to their own institution: the Franciscans say, *Be imitators of us.* On the other side, the Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note> cry out, *Be imitators of us.* In just as many words, the Carmelites cry out, then the Benedictines, then others and still others. And they cry out rightly, provided they can truly add with Paul, *as we also are of Jesus Christ.* Now they themselves—I speak of many—are imitators of men, yet they cry out, *Be imitators of us.*

<margin>2</margin> <margin>D</margin> *That you remember all my things]* <note>original: "ὅτι πάντα μου μέμνησθε"</note>, that is, that you have remembered all my things. And Ambrose accepts it in this sense: for he reads, *that you retain all my things in memory.* And the Greek scholia agree, specifically Theophylact. For he prepares them with praise for the following admonition: as if to say, "Just as you hold my precepts in other matters, so follow me in this too." This interpretation is surely no more pleasing than that of Ambrose. For he writes in this manner: *After he rebuked their morals and conversation, now he wants to correct the traditions. Therefore he does not confirm this, but to them doing it, because since he was their Apostle, they were unmindful of his traditions: nor did they follow what they had not yet learned from the tradition of other Churches, and through this he delivers it to them as if anew, saying.* Perhaps the Translator read "everything" <note>original: "πάντα"</note>, that is, *in all things*, or took it as a figure of speech. An older Constantinopolitan codex had, "you remember all my things." The preposition was omitted, which is also not present among the Greeks.

<margin>3</margin> <margin>E</margin> *And just as I delivered to you my precepts]* Here it appears there was a varied reading in the Greek codices. For Ambrose reads it this way: *and how everywhere I delivered my traditions you hold them:* which may also be gathered from the interpretation. For he interprets "everywhere" as meaning in all the Churches. But "everywhere" <note>original: "πανταχοῦ"</note>, which Ambrose seems to have read, we do not find in the Greek codices; nor do the interpreters I have seen mention it anywhere. The speech would have been smoother if he had placed *but* in the first part and *and* in the latter. "I praise you indeed, that in other things you hold all my ways: but you must be warned of this, which you seem to remember little." Or that first part notes a digression from the started discourse about things sacrificed to idols, and the latter has an adversarial force, as if he had commanded them. In a very old codex, for "you hold" was *katechete*. For the Greek word is ambiguous. Nor is "precepts" used in Greek, but a more modest and slightly more dignified word, *paradoseis*, that is, *traditions:* which we can call "institutions." For "tradition" is lighter than "precept."

<margin>4</margin> <margin>F</margin> *With covered head]* In Greek it is *kata kephales echon*, that is, "having on the head": so that you understand it not only of a hat, but even of hair, which itself covers the head: and so the Greek scholia note, specifically Theophylact. And soon he mentions shearing, arguing thus: If a woman imitates a man in this, that she uncovers her head, let her also be imitated in this, that he is shorn.

<margin>5</margin> *Defiles his head]* <note>original: "καταισχύνει"</note>, that is, disgraces, or makes ashamed, or dishonors.

<margin>6</margin> *For it is one]* <note>original: "ἓν γάρ ἐστι καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ"</note>, that is, "for it is one and the same": this means, it makes no difference at all. Ambrose reads somewhat differently, *but this has no weight as to the sense.*

<margin>7</margin> *But if she is made bald]* <note>original: "τῇ ἐξυρημένῃ"</note>, that is, with her being shaved or shorn: that is, it is the same as if she were shaved. Ambrose reads, *for it is one and that very thing to be made bald.* Perhaps the Translator favored this word "decalvare" <note>to make bald</note> as more hateful, since baldness is considered offensive for women.

<margin>8</margin> *Let her be shorn]* <note>original: "καὶ κειράσθω"</note>, that is, let her also be shorn. In the Pauline and Donatian manuscripts it was written, *if a woman is not veiled, also let her be shorn.* Both Constantinopolitan ones agreed. For the conjunction is not idle; it is the same as saying, "By the same token let her be shorn, since she uncovers her head."

<margin>9</margin> *Or to be made bald]* <note>original: "ἢ ξυρᾶσθαι"</note>, that is, to be shaved: which we just mentioned.

<margin>10</margin> *Let her veil her head]* <note>original: "κατακαλυπτέσθω"</note>, that is, let her be veiled: nor is anything else added among the Greeks. Ambrose reads, *let her veil the head.*

<margin>11</margin> *To have a veil]* <note>original: "ἐξουσίαν ἔχειν"</note>, that is, to have authority.

---

Furthermore, Ambrose and the Greek scholia <note>Ancient explanatory notes found in the margins of Greek manuscripts.</note> indicate that *authority* <note>original: "potestatem"</note> in this place is understood as a veil: because a plain veil compels her to cast down her eyes, and signifies that she is under the authority of another. Laurentius indicates that in several Latin codices <note>Handwritten books/manuscripts.</note> it was written as *authority* instead of *veil*. This was also noted by Thomas Aquinas: and we found it written thus in our manuscript of Paul, supported by both manuscripts from Constance.

12 *Judge among yourselves*] <note>original: "Ἐν ὑμῖν αὐτοῖς κρίνατε"</note>, that is, Among yourselves, or *Judge in yourselves*: that is, each in his own mind.

13 *Does not nature itself teach*] <note>original: "Ἢ οὐδὲ αὐτὴ ἡ φύσις διδάσκει ὑμᾶς;"</note>, that is, *Does not even nature itself teach you?* Although in Latin the word "neither" is sometimes used for "not even." The translator does not seem to have read the "or" [original: "ἤ"], which we see today present in the Greek codices.

<margin>D</margin> 14 *Wear long hair*] <note>original: "κομᾷ"</note>, that is, he is long-haired. "Coma" means hair, but hair that is grown long and cared for.

15 *Heads*] <note>original: "ἡ κόμη"</note>, that is, *hair*. Why did the translator, who just now translated it as "hair," now change it to "locks of hair"?

16 *Nor the church of God*] "Church" in the plural number, <note>original: "αἱ ἐκκλησίαι"</note>, as supported by the Latin manuscript we just cited. There are also worldly gatherings full of litigation and quarrels. Furthermore, the assembly of Christians ought to be free from such vices.

<margin>E</margin> 17 *Now in giving this instruction I do not praise*] <note>original: "Τοῦτο δὲ παραγγέλλων οὐκ ἐπαινῶ"</note>, that is, *But giving this instruction or denunciation, I do not praise*. He had praised them before for holding to all things; now he does not praise them in this, that he is forced to give instructions about concord: as if to say, "I do not praise this thing about which I am instructing." For you ought to have held and done what is right of your own accord. Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine commentator.</note> is of this opinion, as was Chrysostom before him in the Homily translated for us by Girolamo Donato. Also in his Commentary. For the Greeks misuse participles for infinitive verbs. The translator and Ambrose seem to have read: *Now I instruct, not praising*. This sense can also be taken: "Previously I praised them because they remembered and held to all things Paul had ordered; here they are rebuked because they did not observe everything they held in memory."

18 *In part*] <note>original: "μέρος τι"</note>, that is, in some part, or some portion. And he left the word *heresies* [original: "αἱρέσεις"], though he could have conveniently said "sects." Saint Chrysostom, in the one homily translated by Girolamo Donato, asserts with great effort and many words that *heresies* here does not refer to opinions, but to dissensions of the mind: and he proves this by two arguments especially. One is that unless you take heresies as dissensions, what follows does not fit: *When you come together into one place, it is not to eat the Lord's supper*, and so on. Now he calls it the "Lord's supper" because in it, as if among fellow servants of the same Lord, all things are common. The other reason is that Paul speaks more sharply than he does here against the authors of heretical opinions, whom he calls both dogs and evil workers, saying that not even an Angel speaking from heaven should be heard if he teaches differently from what Paul taught. The same is found in the Greek Commentaries. Now, although it is true that those who are approved are made manifest through heresies of opinion, nevertheless in this place Paul is not acting specifically regarding such people as he would have taught should not be received into the church.

19 *Schisms*] <note>original: "σχίσματα"</note>. Where he usually leaves this word as it is, here "factions" or "dissensions" would fit better. Furthermore, "among you" is not added in the ancient Latin codices, though it appears in the Greek <note>original: "ἐν ὑμῖν"</note>.

20 *So that those who are approved*] <note>original: "ἵνα οἱ δόκιμοι"</note>, that is, so that the upright may be opposed to the reprobate. And the conjunction *ina* [that/so that] does not signify the cause, but the result: which Chrysostom carefully noted.

21 *For eating*] <note>original: "ἐν τῷ φαγεῖν"</note>, that is, in the act of eating; and Saint Ambrose reads it thus. Nor is the conjunction of the word idle

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Otherwise, neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without <margin>11</margin>

the *pro* in *prolambanei* <note>the Greek word for "takes beforehand"</note>, which we translate as "occupies." For "presumes" sounds different to Latin ears. For they were coming before the others, and without waiting for them, each was eating his own supper: and because of this, he immediately adds, "wait for one another."

22 *Do you not have houses*] Do you not have houses? or, *Have you no houses?*

23 *And you confound*] <note>original: "καταισχύνετε"</note>, that is, you make them ashamed. Although Jerome, on the fourth chapter of the Epistle to the Galatians, thinks there is no difference between "shame" [aischyne] and "confusion" [synchysis], even though it is found to be otherwise among reliable Authors. Indeed, he who is vehemently ashamed is also troubled, that is, he is confused in mind: but not everyone who is confused is ashamed. And *aporia* [perplexity/want], from which *aporein* comes, does not always mean to be in need, but sometimes to be at a loss for counsel and perplexed in mind, so that it does not quite match "to be shamed" [kataischynesthai], but rather "to be confused" [syncheesthai].

24 *I praise you etc.*] *Shall I praise you in this? I do not praise.* <note>original: "Ἐπαινέσω ὑμᾶς ἐν τούτῳ; οὐκ ἐπαινῶ."</note> This is how the Greek codices punctuate it. For he could have said simply, "I do not praise you in it": but the preceding question makes the speech more passionate. Although I see Theophylact interpreting it so that this little part, "I praise you," is sounded not as a question but as a statement. Lest he irritate the wealthy too much, he says he would praise their service in other matters, but in this he denies he can praise them. But the other distinction also works well: "Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise": so that to the question there is subjoined, "I praise in other things."

25 *For our Lord Jesus Christ*] "Our" is not added among the Greeks. Latin codices vary. The speech is more direct without the pronoun added.

26 *And giving thanks*] <note>original: "καὶ εὐχαριστήσας"</note>, that is, having given thanks, or when he had given thanks.

27 *Take and eat*] <note>original: "Λάβετε, φάγετε"</note>, that is, Take, eat: without a conjunction placed between them. Furthermore, because these two words, "Take, eat," are not added in the later edition of Ambrose, I suspect it was committed by a scribal error. Although they were added in the older manuscript from Constance, they had been added in the margin by a more recent hand.

28 *This is my body*] <note>original: "τοῦτο μου ἐστὶν"</note>, that is, *this my body*, without the substantive verb "is" [est]: although I find it added in some. Thomas [Aquinas] admits there were those who said Christ consecrated the bread with other words before reaching it out to the Disciples and saying, *This is my body*. And there are those who deny that the Incarnate Word had need of other words to consecrate. In all things we must yield to the judgment of the Church, although this speech seems to be of one reaching out bread already consecrated. For unless one rests in the decrees of the Church, it would be most difficult to prove by human sense with what words a Priest consecrates. For even if we grant that Christ consecrated with such words, how is it established that this pact was made with us, so that by reciting the words of another, we ourselves might consecrate? But here, as Paul says, the human intellect must be taken captive in obedience to faith, so that the merit of faith may be greater, the less human reason can attain it.

29 *Which shall be delivered for you*] <note>original: "τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν κλώμενον"</note>, that is, which is broken for you. And in this, the consensus of the Greek codices is so great that it appears the variation arose among us, or the writing was changed on purpose, because it seemed absurd for the body to be broken—not that it is truly broken, but that, as Saint Augustine says, it is received in parts: because formerly that same sacred bread, cut into many parts, was distributed to all as the body of Christ. Just as Christ, eaten by individuals, lives and is not torn apart again, so in this way I have said, it is bro-

# 717 TO THE FIRST CORINTHIANS CHAP. XII. 718

XII. 1 Now concerning spiritual things, brothers, I do not want you to be ignorant. 
2 You know that when you were Gentiles, you were led away to mute idols, however you were led. 
3 Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, "Jesus is accursed" <note>original: "ἀνάθημα" (anathema)</note>...

<margin>A</margin> [The body] is not torn into pieces. Certainly the divine Ambrose reads *is broken*, agreeing with the Greeks, and was not at all offended by that reading. Nor does Bede cite it otherwise when explaining the Gospel of Luke. Furthermore, if it is offensive that it is first said he "broke" the bread, and shortly after added *which is broken*, I suppose that either he first began to break the bread perhaps into two or three parts, then as it was distributed to each person, he broke smaller pieces from the larger fragments; or, *is broken* is used without a specific sense of time, just as something is said to happen when it is accustomed or necessary to happen, even if it is not happening at that very moment—likewise something is "loosened" which ought to be loosened, even if it is often not. 

Moreover, the interpreter Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Archbishop of Bulgaria known for his influential biblical commentaries.</note> indicates that to be "broken" here is nothing other than to be *distributed*. He says: *His own body, which he destines for death by distributing it equally to all. He himself, however, anticipating the time for taking food, neither puts this common and dietary bread in the middle, nor breaks the same so that it may be given to many, but reserves it for himself.* And it is clear from the Greek manuscripts that Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), the Archbishop of Constantinople famous for his eloquence.</note> read the same thing as Theophylact. This is clear from the explanation itself, regardless of the intention with which Jerome Donatus rendered into Latin what our Vulgate reading has. 

Finally, it is not sufficiently clear from the ancient commentaries whether Paul is treating the priestly consecration of the Lord's body and blood here. Indeed, the Apostle's speech began with the feasts of idolaters and Christians. After he had shown that it is not fitting for Christians to mix themselves with the religious or rather superstitious feasts of the Gentiles, he proceeded to show what the truly religious feasts of Christians ought to be, and with what great concord and communion of all things they should be conducted. The Apostle's entire discourse seems to revolve around this: to correct the criticized inequality of the feast and recall them to the original model <note>original: "archetypum exemplum"</note> of Christ and the Apostles. 

For in the beginning of the adolescent Church, all things were common. From this highest state of charity, the minds of the Greeks gradually ebbed away, though some vestige of the former communion was preserved; they would meet together on certain days, especially festivals, and the rich would provide the preparations for the feast while the poor were present. At last, even that was corrupted by some; meetings were held, but with the poor excluded, each would feast with his own people, even to the point of drunkenness, so that not only were the poor not refreshed, but they were even mocked for their humble condition. 

Therefore Paul, as Chrysostom and Theophylact explain, brings in the mention of the Lord's Supper so that by the record of that most sacred feast they might be recalled to sobriety and fraternal communion, which the Lord displayed among his own by the distribution of his own body. For the Lord did not always consecrate his body whenever he is read to have broken bread after giving thanks; indeed, he blessed and broke bread while providing a meal for many thousands of men. And in Emmaus, he blesses, breaks, and offers the bread. Again, whenever mention is made of broken bread in the Sacred Books, it must not immediately be understood that the body and blood of the Lord were consecrated among the disciples, just as in the second chapter of Acts, mention is made twice of the "breaking of bread" which was prepared daily in individual homes. 

<margin>B</margin> Likewise Paul, in the twenty-seventh chapter of Acts, blesses and breaks bread during a voyage, inviting others to take food and, as is likely, offering the broken bread. In these solemn Christian feasts, there was some commemoration of the Lord's Supper, even when the body and blood of the Lord were not being consecrated. Indeed, even today in many places, after the sacred rite is finished, a small piece of bread is given to individuals as a sign of the Lord's body, so that, mindful of that mystery, they may conduct their feast more frugally at home, by no means unmindful of the poor. Perhaps the feasts of the Corinthians were of such a kind, and Paul is annoyed that they are conducted indecently. 

And I do not know whether they might have sometimes called that bread and cup, which the Christians brought among themselves with thanksgiving and as a sign of mutual charity, the "body and cup of the Lord" because they were signs of them. Certainly Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret "the Lord's supper" not as the consecration of the Lord's body and blood there, but as the communion of food and drink. Although at the end they add something about the unworthy reception of the body

and blood, but more obscurely. For my part, it pleases me more that this passage also pertains to the consecration; nevertheless, it seemed good to advise the reader so that he might examine it more diligently. Furthermore, the word *breaking* agrees quite well with the Lord's body: wheaten bread is broken so that it may grant life to many; the Lord's body is also said to be broken because it grants life equally to all who receive it worthily. The same bread distributed among many is a symbol of concord; the same body sacrificed for all is a sign of friendship.

<margin>D</margin> 30 *In remembrance of me*] <note>original: "εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν"</note>, that is, in memory of me, or in my commemoration, as Ambrose reads. Although the Greek word can hardly be rendered conveniently unless you use a circumlocution: "to renew the memory of me."

31 *Likewise also the chalice*] Ambrose reads *cup* <note>Latin: "poculum"</note>, expressing more closely the Greek word <note>original: "ποτήριον"</note>, named from "drinking," just as *poculum* is used among us. For a *calix* [chalice] is a type of cup. A *poculum* is that from which one drinks, whether it be a ladle, a chalice, or a pitcher.

32 *You shall proclaim*] <note>original: "καταγγέλλετε"</note>, that is, proclaim! (imperative), or you proclaim (indicative). In these words, I see the Pastors and Apostles misuse the tense, as in those things which immediately preceded: *as often as you drink.* Ambrose reads *proclaiming*, having left out some words in the middle—I suspect due to the error of scribes. For we read in his text: *Do this as often as you will drink in remembrance of me, proclaiming the Lord's death until he comes.* I will not argue with one who prefers *you proclaim* in the indicative mood, yet I think both readings stand: and he who reads *you shall proclaim* seems to speak in an imperative sense.

33 *The bread etc.*] <note>original: "τὸν ἄρτον τοῦτον"</note>, that is, this bread. Here he openly calls the consecrated body "bread," not because it is still bread in the way it was, but because it is living bread and granting true life.

34 *Let him eat of that bread*] "That" <note>Latin: "illo"</note> is not added in this place among the Greeks, but the Translator explained the force of the article, which he also does many other times. Ambrose reads *let him eat of the bread*.

<margin>E</margin> 35 *Unworthily*] <note>original: "ἀναξίως τοῦ Κυρίου"</note>, that is, unworthily of the Lord. Chrysostom reads it in that way, adding the name of the Lord in both places. Ambrose likewise repeats the name of the Lord: *Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily of the Lord*, although in the next place he does not add "of the Lord": *for he who eats and drinks unworthily, eats judgment to himself.* Although in some Greek codices it is read, <note>original: "τοῦ Κυρίου ἀναξίως"</note>, so that "of the Lord" can be referred to either way: the bread of the Lord, or unworthily of the Lord.

36 *For if*] <note>original: "Εἰ γὰρ"</note>, that is, "If indeed," not *Ei di* [But if].

37 *So that not with the world*] "With the world" <note>original: "σὺν τῷ κόσμῳ"</note> was sufficient. Nor could the not unpleasant wordplay of the Greek words be preserved here: *krinomenoi* [being judged] and *katakrithomen* [let us not be condemned].

38 *So that you do not meet for judgment*] <note>original: "εἰς κρίμα"</note>. It was clearer as "to condemnation" <note>Latin: "ad condemnationem"</note>, so that no one takes it to mean going before judges.

<margin>F</margin> **N**ow concerning spiritual things] <note>original: "Περὶ δὲ τῶν πνευματικῶν"</note>. It is uncertain whether he means the gifts of the Spirit, as the divine Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Ambrose interpret it, or concerning the "singing spirit" <note>original: "psallendo spiritu"</note>, about which there seems to have been some question.

2 *When you were Gentiles*] The Greeks have this slightly differently: <note>original: "ὅτι ἔθνη ἦτε, πρὸς τὰ εἴδωλα τὰ ἄφωνα ὡς ἂν ἤγεσθε ἀπαγόμενοι"</note>, "because you were nations [Gentiles], you were led away to mute idols however you were led," or led away, or, as I would prefer, *following*. For if you read "when," the sentence would hang, unless you like the participle being put in place of a verb, *apagomenoi* for *apegesthe*. For the participle *apagomenoi* does not simply stick to the noun *ethne* [nations]. Furthermore, I do not disapprove of the Translator's paraphrase. Ambrose reads: *When you were Gentiles, going in the form of idols, according as you were led.* Although here I think the conjunction "when" is superfluous, which is nearly clear from his interpretation; I will subscribe his words if anyone should perhaps ask: *Being about to hand down spiritual things to them,* he says, *he mentions the example of their prior conversation, so that, just as they were worshippers of idols in the form of idols, and were led by the leading of the will of demons, so also [they should be] worshipped.*

He argues that "breaking bread" in the early church often referred to communal charity and distribution rather than just a sacramental rite, and analyzes Greek nuances missed by the Latin Vulgate.</summary>

# 719 THE EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER XII. 720

<margin>A</margin> ...Jesus is accursed; and no one can say "Jesus is Lord," except by the Holy Spirit. Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit. And there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord. And there are varieties of workings, but it is the same God who works all things in everyone. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the same Spirit; to another <margin>B</margin> the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discerning of spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, and to another the interpretation of tongues. All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each one individually just as he wills. For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body— <margin>C</margin> whether Jews or Greeks, slaves or free—and all were made to drink of one Spirit. For the body does not consist of one member but of many. If the foot should say, "Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body," would that make it any less a part of the body? And if the ear should say, "Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body," would that make it any less a part of the body? If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing? If the whole body were an ear, where would be the sense of smell? But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose. If all were a single member, where would the body be? As it is, there are many parts, yet one body. The eye cannot say to the hand, "I have no need of you," nor again the head...

<margin>D</margin> *...worshipping God, without the form of the Lord’s law.* Thus far that author <note>Erasmus is likely referring to a commentary by Ambrose or a similar authority</note>. For he recalls to their memory that they were once Gentiles, and he warns them that since they have ceased to be such, they must live by other customs. Augustine, in the twenty-first book against Faustus, chapter eight, relates this passage thus: *Do you know when you were Gentiles, how you went up to voiceless idols, having been led?* It is clear enough that this Translator read "before when" <note>original: "πρὸ ὅτε"</note>, etc. And I do not know whether *incedebatis* (you walked) was written instead of *adscendebatis* (you went up). Furthermore, since he translates it as "led away," he seems to have read "being led away" <note>original: "ἀπαγόμενοι" (apagomenoi)</note> instead of "being led up" <note>original: "ἀναγόμενοι" (anagomenoi)</note>.

3 **He says Jesus is accursed]** <note>original: "λέγει ἀνάθεμα Ἰησοῦν"</note>, that is, he says Jesus is anathema, using the accusative case, meaning he says *Jesus is an accursed thing*, which is to say, he curses and execrates Jesus. It is probable that Ambrose also read it this way, for this reason: that the next part remained uncorrupted in that case. *No one can say "Jesus is Lord."* Certainly, Hilary relates it this way in the eighth book of *On the Trinity*, following the sense of a very old manuscript.

4 **And no one can say "Lord":]** Jerome, in his commentary on Joel, reads *Dominum Jesum* (the Lord Jesus), and Hilary likewise in the second book of *On the Trinity*. Again, Ambrose, in the second book of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, chapter two. And again, in his *Commentaries* explaining this very passage, he cites it thus. Likewise in the first book of *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter ten. Similarly, Origen in his seventeenth *Homily on Genesis*, just as it is read today in all the Greek manuscripts: "can say 'Jesus is Lord'" <note>original: "δύναται εἰπεῖν Κύριον Ἰησοῦν"</note>: so that it stands in opposition to what he said above, "he says Jesus is anathema," that is, he calls him accursed. Nor, conversely, does anyone call him *Lord*, except, etc. For the ancients spoke this way: "Let him be Anathema," whenever they meant a person was to be avoided. From this chapter and the next, one may learn what the gifts of that ancient Christian Church were, before it was burdened with so many ceremonies, riches, powers, troops, wars, and other things of that kind. Now, almost all these noble functions have been reduced to a single power—that is, a tyranny cloaked with the title of Christ. For what is power to others, unless an Apostolic spirit be present?

5 **Divisions of graces]** <note>original: "χαρισμάτων"</note>, that is, of gifts: so Jerome translates in his *Epistles* and other places. Augustine, in his booklet *On the Presence of God to Dardanus*, reads *divisions of donations*. But a "charisma" is a free gift, for it takes its name from *charis*, meaning grace.

6 **Divisions of operations]** <note>original: "ἐνεργημάτων"</note>. This does not simply mean an action, but a certain force and efficacy by which God acts in us. For it follows soon after: "working all things," and a little later "he works," which the Translator renders as *operatur*. Although, as I said, it sounds like something else to the Greeks. It means "to act" more than "to work."

7 **For utility]** <note>original: "πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον"</note>, that is, for that which is expedient: so Jerome translates in *Questions to Hedibia*, and again in the second book *Against Jovinian*. However, literally it sounds more like "for that which contributes": even if the Translator rendered it correctly.

8 **Grace of healings]** <note>original: "χαρίσματα ἰαμάτων"</note>, that is, gifts of healings. "In one Spirit" <note>original: "ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ Πνεύματι"</note>, that is, in the same Spirit, or rather *through* the same Spirit.

9 **Operation of virtues]** <note>original: "ἐνεργήματα δυνάμεων"</note>, that is, operations, and more so, as was said, efficacy.

10 **Discretion of spirits]** <note>original: "διακρίσεις πνευμάτων"</note>. The Translator reads "discerning" in the singular, although it makes no difference to the sense.

11 **To another interpretation of speeches]** <note>original: "γλωσσῶν"</note>. This word he had just translated as "tongues," but now he translates as "speeches." For the Greeks find

---

the same word in both places: "tongues" <note>original: "γλωσσῶν"</note>. *To some kinds of tongues, to others the interpretation of tongues.* This is how Augustine cites this passage in the twelfth book of *Against Faustus*, chapter eight, from ancient manuscripts written by a faithful hand. Certainly, Theophylact read it this way, as is clear from his own interpretation, when he says: *For the grace of teaching is far more excellent, and the simple gift of speaking in various tongues is far surpassed by the interpretation of tongues.* Although a little later, repeating the gifts of the Spirit in order, he lists kinds of tongues and interpretations of speeches in the last place. It may be that this latter wording was only added there among the Latins.

12 **But all these things he works]** <note>original: "ἐνεργεῖ"</note>. It means "effects" more than "works." And he effects it through a hidden power within us. Saint Hilary, in trying to express the Greek word, sometimes translates it as *is inspired*, specifically in the eighth book of *On the Trinity*.

13 **One and the same]** <note>original: "τὸ ἓν καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ"</note>. The added article makes us understand it refers to a specific Spirit. Therefore, we translate it: *that one same Spirit*.

<margin>E</margin>
14 **Dividing to individuals]** <note>original: "διαιροῦν ἰδίᾳ ἑκάστῳ"</note>, that is, dividing privately or uniquely to each one: which Jerome, in the first *Dialogue against the Pelagians*, translates as *to their own*, or *proper things. Dividing to individuals, as he wills.* The Greek speech has an ambiguity: "dividing individually, as he wills" <note>original: "διαιροῦν ἰδίᾳ, καθὼς βούλεται"</note>. For the verb "wills" can be referred to the Spirit who divides, and to the person to whom it is divided, as in Latin you might say, *imparting to each, as he wills.* For it is unclear whether it is as He Himself wills, or as each person wills. And Origen, explaining the *Epistle to the Romans*, twists this passage toward this latter sense in some places, suggesting it is situated within us how much grace God might impart to us. Furthermore, among the Greeks, the word *idia* (uniquely/privately) is added, which the Translator did not render. If you want it to have the force of an adverb, it should be translated as *dividing peculiarly, or privately*. But if you prefer it to be a noun, it should be translated as *dividing to each their own things, or his own to each*. And indeed, Augustine cites it this way in the eighth chapter of the book *On the Trinity and Unity of God*: *dividing proper things to each, as he wills.* Moreover, this whole discourse of Paul is florid with distributions, repetitions of the same words—now at the beginning, now in the middle, now at the end—with clauses that are cut, balanced, and falling or ending similarly, and with rounded periods.

<margin>F</margin>
15 **Whether Gentiles]** <note>original: "εἴτε Ἕλληνες"</note>, that is, *whether Greeks*: as Ambrose reads, about which we have already frequently reminded the reader.

16 **In one Spirit we have been watered]** In Greek it is, *into one Spirit we have been watered* <note>or "made to drink"</note>: just as he translated above "into one body" <note>original: "εἰς ἓν σῶμα"</note>. Ambrose reads in the same way, following the Greek copies. However, a little further up he mixed different prepositions, "into" and "in" <note>original: "εἰς" and "ἐν"</note>. *For indeed in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body*, that is, *Indeed in one Spirit, or through one Spirit, we were all baptized into one body.* If you read this as a whole, the sense will be: We were all made one body by baptism, and that through the Spirit imparting Himself commonly to all. But if you read it separately, the substantive verb "are" must be understood: *For indeed in one Spirit are we all.* But the first reading pleases me more. *We have been watered* <note>original: "potati sumus"</note>, etc. The Greek is indeed *epotisthemen*, that is, *we have been drunk, or been watered*, but in the sense that "watered" is understood as one to whom drink has been given. Ambrose elegantly expressed the sense, reading: *and we have all drunk of one Spirit.* Augustine reads it the same way. For *potizein* is said by the Greeks of that which is irrigated; however, whatever is liquid is drunk up. There-

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s meticulous philological analysis of 1 Corinthians 12, transitioning into the famous "Hymn to Love" in Chapter 13. # 721 TO THE CORINTHIANS I. CHAPTER XIII. 722

<margin>A</margin> ...the head to the feet, "I have no need of you." On the contrary, the members of the body that seem to be **22** weaker are all the more necessary; and those parts of the body that we think less honorable, upon these we bestow greater honor; and our unpresentable parts are treated with **23** greater modesty. But our presentable parts have no such need. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it, so that there may be no **24** division <note>original: "schisma"</note> in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another. If one member **25** suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is honored <note>original: "glorificatur"</note>, all the members rejoice with it. Now you are the body of Christ and **26** members in particular. And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, **27** helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues. Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all **28** speak in tongues? Do all interpret? But earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more **29** excellent way.
**XIII.** 1 If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I have become a noisy gong or a **30** clanging cymbal.

<column-break/>

...the head to the feet, "I have no need of you." No, much rather, those **22** members of the body which seem to be weaker are **23** necessary: And those which we think to be less honorable parts of the body, upon these we bestow more abundant honor: and our uncomely parts have more abundant comeliness. For our comely parts **24** have no need: but God has tempered the body together, giving more abundant honor to that part which lacked, **25** That there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another. And whether one member suffer, all the members **26** suffer with it; or one member be honored, all the members rejoice with it. Now ye are the body of Christ, and members **27** in particular. And God hath set some in the church, first **28** apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers, after that miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, diversities of tongues. Are all apostles? are all prophets? **29** are all teachers? are all workers of miracles? Have all the gifts of healing? do all speak with tongues? do all **30** interpret? But covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet **31** shew I unto you a more excellent way. Though I **1 XIII.** speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.

---

...so that we might be clearer, we have seen, *we have drunk of the same Spirit*. In some copies, I found the word for "we were made to drink" <note>Latin: *potati sumus*</note> corrupted into "we were called" <note>Latin: *vocati sumus*</note>. Such is the audacity of the scribes.

**17** *I have no need of you*] <note>Greek: Χρείαν ὑμῶν οὐκ ἔχω</note>. Which he had just translated as *I do not require your service*.

**18** *Are necessary*] <note>Greek: ἀναγκαῖα</note>, that is, *necessary*, using the positive form, not the comparative; for the comparison is rendered by the word "more." Certainly, following the Greek manuscripts, Augustine cites this in his fifty-third sermon: *And those parts of ours which are dishonorable are more necessary*. Again, he says the same against Faustus in book twenty-one, chapter eight. Likewise Ambrose in the book he titled *On Noah and the Ark*, chapter eight. Although "rather" <note>Greek: μᾶλλον</note> can be taken for "more," so that it corrects more truly than it compares: and the sense becomes, those members which are thought dishonorable are commended by necessity and use. For it does not appear that Paul intends this—that the "shameful members," as they are called, are more necessary than the others—if it is enough that they are necessary to the body so as not to be thought negligible.

**19** *And those which we think more ignoble*] The Translator did not render the playful wordplay <note>Greek: ἀτιμότερα and τιμὴν</note>, that is, *the unhonored and the honor*. Instead of *unhonored*, Augustine reads "viler."

**20** *And our uncomely parts*] <note>Greek: ἀσχήμονα and εὐσχημοσύνην</note>, that is, *unbecoming, or uncomely, and modesty, or comeliness*. Ambrose reads, *and those things which are inferior to us have more abundant reverence*. Truly, I do not know if that passage is faulty.

**21** *They lack nothing*] <note>Greek: οὐ χρείαν ἔχει</note>, that is, *they have no need: that you might stand firm, with that honor added*.

**22** *He has tempered*] <note>Greek: συνεκέρασε</note>, that is, *he has blended together*: this means he moderated and mixed the members in a certain "temperature" <note>meaning a balanced mixture</note> so that they might be a mutual help to one another.

**23** *To that which lacked*] <note>Greek: τῷ ὑστεροῦντι</note>, which usually translates as "fails": but here he has rendered it quite well.

**24** *That there be no schism in the body*] He left the Greek word *schisma*, though he could have translated it as "dissension."

**25** *But for the same thing*] <note>Greek: ἀλλὰ τὸ αὐτὸ ὑπὲρ ἀλλήλων μεριμνῶσι τὰ μέλη</note>, *but let the members care for the same thing mutually*: so that "the same" indicates an equal concern for all members.

**26** *Whether it boasts*] <note>Greek: δοξάζεται</note>, that is, *is glorified*: that is, it is treated with honor. The Translator seems to have said "boasts" <note>Latin: *gloriatur*</note> instead of "is affected with glory." Thomas Aquinas interprets "boasts" as "thrives": so that you can sense he was somewhat troubled by this passage. Certainly, Ambrose reads "is glorified" in agreement with the Greeks. And Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine exegete</note> interprets it in that sense. In the same way, Augustine reads it in his third tractate on the Epistle of John; he doesn't just read it that way, but actually interprets it as "glorification." Again, against Faustus, book twenty-one, chapter eight; and again in Epistle 144. Furthermore, Possidonius (or Possidius) in his *Life of Augustine*, chapter seven.

**27** *Members of a member*] <note>Greek: μέλη ἐκ μέρους</note>, *members in part*. He says this because the Corinthians were not all the members of the body, but some part of the members. Although Ambrose seems to have read *ek melous* <note>meaning "from a member"</note>. However, a slip in these letters is easy because of the similarity of the words *melous* <note>member</note> and *merous* <note>part</note>, especially if a "labdacism" <note>a speech error or scribal swap of 'l' and 'r'</note> occurred. In the same way, Saint Thomas reads it, explaining this passage in three ways. Otherwise, that sense is less forced: that we understand "members from a member," meaning one member depends on another by mutual connection. But Theophylact follows the former reading; some had published this verse in Latin under the completely false title of Athanasius. And they deny that this was done through the recklessness of scribes, but rather by the cunning and zeal of Christopher Persona himself, who translated this work. This is also evidenced by that manuscript which Christopher presented, beautifully illustrated, to Pope Sixtus IV. He had prefixed the title *Athanasius* in large red letters, while in the preface he makes no mention of either Athanasius or Theophylact. It seems, therefore, that he deceived the Pope. Those who have seen the manuscript kept in the Papal Library write these things. Origen, in his seventh homily on Leviticus, cites this passage according to what is read in the Greek manuscripts.

<margin>B</margin> **28** *And some indeed*] <note>Greek: Καὶ οὕς μὲν</note>. Paul sometimes uses the post-positive article for the pre-positive in distributions. But here it has nothing to correspond to, which is common with this Apostle. For what Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>a French humanist and contemporary of Erasmus</note> thinks—that "certain ones" is used as "his own"—is not probable, especially in prose, mostly since no noun is attached to the pronoun; otherwise, he would have said *tous autou*. The awkwardness of the <term>anapodotis</term> <note>a grammatical break where the second part of a sentence doesn't match the first</note> could be avoided if you read the first part of this division together, in this way: *And those whom God placed in the church, first Apostles*: so that all this makes one order: then *second, Prophets*, so that what he began to say with "those whom," he later says with "second" and "third," having changed the phrasing. It could be expressed more clearly thus: *And others indeed he appointed in the first place, namely Apostles; others in the second, namely Prophets; others in the third, namely Teachers; and likewise for the rest*.

<margin>C</margin> **29** *Helps*] <note>Greek: ἀντιλήψεις</note>, that is, *assistances, or subsidies*: which elsewhere he translates as "to receive": but *antilambanesthai* is to help someone who is struggling by reaching out a hand. *Interpretations of speeches*. All of this is not read among the Greeks in this place, nor even in the old Latin manuscripts, specifically those shown to us by the College of Saint Donatian in Bruges, nor in two shown in this edition by the College of Constance. For it seems to be the same as that which he just listed, "kinds of tongues." I suspect "interpretations of speeches" was added by some translator, or what those people call a "postillator" <note>a writer of marginal notes or glosses</note>, which was later brought into the main text; especially since no mention of this small part is found in any Greek interpreter. Although, to hide nothing, Ambrose reads it just as we commonly do, and he not only reads it but interprets it. Then, a little later, repeating these ranks, he renders two here, not one: *Are all speaking in tongues, are all interpreting?* Unless perhaps he placed these two as one because they are related: though we might ignore that he now translates the word as *fanations* <note>meaning "temple-gifts," likely a typo in the Latin edition Erasmus is critiquing</note> instead of *sanations* <note>healings</note>; for *iamata* among the Greeks means nothing but "healing."

<margin>D</margin> **30** *But be zealous for the gifts*] <note>Greek: Ζηλοῦτε τὰ κρείττονα χαρίσματα</note>, that is, *Be zealous for the better gifts*: that is, strive for those gifts of the Spirit which are outstanding. He did not say *meizona*, that is, "greater," but *kreittona*, that is, "better," or "more useful for the public good." Here he left the Greek word *charismata*: Saint Jerome, in his second book against Jovinian, translates it as "gifts," preferring to speak in Latin rather than Greek. Nor is the conjunction "but" <note>Latin: *si*</note> idle, for it separates love from the crowd of outward gifts. Different gifts fall to different people, but you should seek those which are better.

**31** *A more excellent way*] <note>Greek: καθ’ ὑπερβολὴν ὁδὸν</note>, that is, *an excellent way, or an extraordinary and outstanding way*. Ambrose seems to have read *eti mallon*, for he translates it "more more-excellent" <note>a double comparative</note>. Furthermore, that our Translator rendered it through the comparative "still" <note>Latin: *eti*</note>, that is, "furthermore," was because it sometimes takes the form of a comparative.

<margin>E</margin> **1** *I am as it were sounding brass*] "As it were" is redundant: <note>Greek: γέγονα χαλκὸς ἠχῶν</note>, that is, *I have become sounding brass, or tinkling, or clattering*. Nor is the adverb "as" added among the Greeks; but someone else added it from his own.

<margin>F</margin> **2** *Or a tinkling cymbal*] <note>Greek: ἢ κύμβαλον ἀλαλάζον</note>. Which they elsewhere translate as "to shout for joy." But *alalazein* is properly *to make a noise and tinkle with a continuous sound*, as the Greek etymologists explain, with sound following sound, as happens in the "cauldrons of Dodona" <note>ancient bronze vessels used in oracles that rang for a long time when struck</note>. I have spoken more copiously about this in my *Adages* <note>Erasmus's famous collection of Greek and Latin proverbs</note>. I do not think I need to refute those here who think an Evangelical preacher is compared to sounding brass because he benefits others with his ringing, yet does not consume himself. Since he calls the preachers "Prophets" here: but those who merely speak with the tongue, being useless in themselves, he compares to tinkling cymbals. This pertains more to those who sing or recite sacred words in churches without understanding them.

He also includes a sharp critique of a contemporary translator, Christopher Persona, for misattributing Greek commentaries to Athanasius to gain papal favor.</summary>
