<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed commentary on 1 Corinthians 13. Having established the diversity of the "body of Christ" in the previous chapter, he now moves into the famous "Hymn to Love," focusing on the rhetorical structure of Paul’s argument. He specifically addresses the relationship between spiritual gifts (like prophecy and faith) and the virtue of love, using linguistic analysis to explain why Paul uses hypothetical "if" statements.</meta>

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>2</margin> And if I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing. <note>original Greek: "Καὶ ἐὰν ἔχω προφητείαν..."</note>

<margin>3</margin> **And if I should know all mysteries]** mysteries <note>original: "mysteria"</note>. Augustine, both elsewhere and frequently in his small book *On Leisure* with Emeritus, reads "sacraments" instead of "mysteries." You should know that in that context, a "sacrament" <term>sacramentum: here used in its older sense of a sacred secret or mystery, rather than a church ritual</term> is sometimes said to be that which is hidden away.

<margin>4</margin> **If I have not love]** Augustine, in the second book of *To Simplician*, admits that this passage does not strictly teach that prophecy or faith can exist without love. He argues that this form of speech does not make an assertion, but rather creates a "fiction" <term>fiction: a rhetorical device (hypothetical) where a speaker assumes something is true for the sake of argument, even if it is impossible</term>. It is like saying, "If a body has a shape but lacks color, it cannot be seen." It does not follow that a body actually lacks color; it is merely imagined to lack it, and if it did, it could not be seen. Similarly, Basil the Great, in his *Epistle to the Neocaesareans*, referring to this passage of the Apostle, adds: "Not that each of these things we have mentioned can be found without love, but that Saint Paul wanted to confirm by testimony that the command of love is infinitely more excellent than all the rest."

As for the word "fiction" or "imagining," there are some who think that to "imagine" is nothing other than to lie. They should know that whenever they hear in the "Disputations of the Theologians" the phrases "a case being granted" or "given that," these men are saying the same thing as others who say "imagine," "suppose," or "make it so." Rhetoricians teach that the method of both arguing and amplifying a point can come from such a "fiction." Although the word "imagining" in this specific sense is not in Holy Scripture, the thing itself is frequent. Nothing is more common than this figure of speech. We hear it every time someone says: "If you were my son, I could not have acted more lovingly toward you." Or: "If you had a body of iron, you would not have survived these labors." Or: "If you had been born among the Scythians <note>Scythians: an ancient people often used as a shorthand for "uncivilized" or "harsh" people</note>, you could not have been more bitter in your manners." Or: "If I had a hundred tongues, I could not recount everything."

The Lord argues this way: "If I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?" And: "If you believed Moses, you would surely believe me." The Apostle argues through this same kind of fiction in 1 Corinthians 15: "If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain, and your faith is in vain." And soon after: "If the dead are not raised, then Christ has not been raised." Again: "If in this life only we have hoped in Christ," and so on. The Prophet David used such a fiction in Psalm 138 <note>Psalm 139 in modern numbering</note>: "If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings at dawn and dwell in the furthest parts of the sea, even there your hand will lead me," and so on. No living human can ascend into heaven, or descend to the underworld, or take wings and fly far away. But the Prophet mentions these through a "fiction" to better assert that no one can escape the hands of God.

Blessed Paul speaks with a similar figure: "Even if I am unskilled in speech, yet I am not so in knowledge." Paul was not actually unskilled in speech, for he boasts to the Corinthians that he speaks in tongues more than all of them. Another similar example: "For though you might have ten thousand guardians in Christ, yet you do not have many fathers." At that time, few among the Corinthians believed, so it was impossible for them to have ten thousand teachers in the doctrine of faith; for that is what he calls "guardians." Of the same form is what he says here: "And if I speak in the tongues of men and of angels." Angels do not have a tongue, but this is added through a fiction for the sake of exaggeration. Add to this that among the gifts of the Spirit mentioned here is the "episcopacy" <note>the office of a bishop or overseer</note>; and in Romans 12 we read, "He who gives, let him do so in simplicity; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness."

<margin>5</margin> And yet, through this fiction, Paul in this place separates things that cannot be separated: "If I distribute all my goods to feed the poor," and "If I deliver my body to be burned," and so on. For Paul does not mean those who, out of vainglory, lavish their goods on the poor or deliver their body to the fire—as we read that Peregrinus did <note>Peregrinus Proteus: a Cynic philosopher who famously committed public suicide by self-immolation at the Olympic Games in 165 AD</note>; otherwise, he would be coldly comparing a sinful action with the gifts of the Spirit. Rather, he speaks of those who are prepared for these things out of the abundance of Gospel love. What then does this "fiction" achieve? Not that we should understand that this can happen without love, but that it might be clear that God estimates our actions not by the measure of liberality, nor by the difficulty of the action, but by the magnitude of love. Hence it happens that one who gives a small copper coin sometimes pleases God more than one who gives ten thousand ducats.

The same must be felt concerning all spiritual functions, which love for one's neighbor commends to God. Lest anyone think I am inventing this out of my own head, let them know that Saint Chrysostom and his imitator Theophylact discuss it this way. They remind us that the Apostle is looking back at those two things which the Lord proposed as proofs of the highest love for one's neighbor: one being when he says to the young man, "If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all you have and give to the poor"; the other being when he says to the Disciples, "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends." How is it fitting, then, that things which declare perfect love should be done without love?

They also add that Paul, in many places, for the sake of either exaggerating or confirming a point, "fictionalizes" that something is what it is not, nor could it be. For example, when he writes to the Galatians: "But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel other than the one you received, let him be accursed." If he is speaking of evil angels, the speech is not only cold but absurd; if of good angels, it does not apply to them to preach falsehoods or to fall under the curse of anathema. They also bring up that passage in Romans 8, when he says that neither angels, nor principalities, nor powers can separate us from the love which is in Christ Jesus. Yet the role of angels is to draw us toward the love of God, not to tear us away. He adds: "nor any other creature," when there is no other creature—for he has already encompassed the entire creation: visible and invisible, highest, middle, and lowest. But for the certainty of his assertion, he "fictionalizes" that this is so, even though it cannot be.

It also seems worth noting what he says: "And if I have the gift of prophecy and know all mysteries." For to no man, except Christ, was it given to know all mysteries—perhaps not even to any of the angels. Finally, it is established that the "if" is conditional; however, its use is in reasoning

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> and in amplifying. The word Paul uses here, *eite* <note>original: "εἴτε"</note>, is no less conditional: "whether prophecies, they will be done away; whether tongues, they will cease; whether knowledge, it will be destroyed." Although neither Saint Basil nor Augustine asserts that the other gifts of the Spirit cannot be found without love, they rightly feel that it cannot be evidently proven from this passage that prophecy or faith are found without love.

I am of the opinion, however, that the Apostle is speaking here not of just any faith or prophecy, but of the gifts of the Spirit after the Lord’s ascension. Otherwise, Balaam’s donkey had the gift of tongues, and Balaam himself was a prophet, and Caiaphas uttered a prophecy, though he did not <margin>B</margin> understand it himself. And at the final judgment, some will say, "Lord, did we not prophesy in your name?" but they will hear, "I never knew you." But we do not find this kind of prophetic gift mentioned as a gift of the Spirit in Holy Scripture after Christ was taken up into heaven.

Furthermore, that the Apostle is not speaking here of just any faith or prophecy is shown by those words: "And if I had prophecy, so that I knew all mysteries." Again: "And if I had all faith, so as to remove mountains." How could such prophecy occur without love, since it is written: "Wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul"? And since true faith encompasses many things—a certain assent to all things delivered to us as necessary for eternal salvation, and a certain trust in the mercy of the Lord and in his promises, to be fulfilled either in this life or in the age to come—how could such a gift fall into a mind devoid of love?

Now I make use of the opinion of those who interpret "all faith" as "perfect faith." I think no one will deny that Paul is speaking here of love—not just any love, but true and Gospel love. If you compare it <margin>C</margin> with other "dead" gifts, the rhetorical amplification falls flat. For what great thing would it be if true love were preferred to the kind of prophecy that Balaam had, or to the kind of faith that even the demons have? That would surely be like someone wanting to exaggerate the strength of a bull by comparing it to a lion that is either dead or stripped of its claws and teeth. It is probable, therefore, that Paul, for the sake of amplification, compares true and Gospel love with the true and perfect gifts of the Spirit, separating by "fiction" those things which are actually joined together.

It is beyond controversy that whenever the Lord or the Apostles speak of faith, they speak of a "living faith." Such are: "Your faith has made you well," and "If you have faith as small as a mustard seed." And when blessed Paul teaches that Abraham earned the title of righteousness because of his faith, and in countless other places; for throughout all his Epistles he emphasizes nothing more than grace and faith, and that a man is <margin>D</margin> justified by faith, and stands by faith, and that those who are of faith will obtain the blessing, and that Christ dwells in us through faith. Finally, with the Hebrews, he extensively sings the praise of faith. Likewise, Peter in the Acts: "Purifying their hearts by faith." Again, when in his Epistle he commands us to resist the Devil, "strong in faith." Likewise, when John writes that we "overcome the world through faith."

If someone joins the inseparable companion, Love, to this Faith that is so often preached in the volumes of the New Testament, I ask you, what sin does he commit? Since faith gives birth to the works of love, just as the Apostle writes to the Romans, "Whatever is not of faith is sin," and to the Galatians he describes the "faith that works through love," the works of love must be attributed to faith. How is it fitting, then, to separate love from faith—that is, the root from the branches?

But it offends some if one says that "by faith alone" <term>Sola Fide: a central theological point of the Reformation, arguing that salvation comes through faith rather than deeds</term> righteousness—that is, the remission of sins—comes to a man. These people, it seems to me, either do not know or do not remember that these words—"alone," "singular," and "only"—are frequently used by both the Pagans and the Orthodox to declare not "solitude" <note>solitude: being entirely by itself</note>, but "eminence." For instance, when the Satirist says in Satire VIII:

---
-> Virtue is the one and only nobility, <-

<margin>E</margin> he means that the highest and most excellent kind of nobility is the fame of a name won by one's own virtue. And he who says a man is endowed with "singular" prudence does not strip him of the other virtues, but attributes to him an "exquisite" prudence. Again, when someone in a Comedy says, "He alone is a friend who is a friend," he does not mean that besides him no one else is a friend to anyone, but that this person is a friend in an excellent way. Similarly, when blessed Jerome, exhorting Heliodorus to despise the affections of his parents for the sake of religious love, says, "The only kind of piety is to be cruel in this matter," he does not mean that there is no piety in other matters, but that this is the "chief" piety: if one despises natural affections for the love of Christ.

Furthermore, even if these examples carried little weight, one must weigh from the very tone of the speech what is being excluded by such words. When David says, "One thing I have asked of the Lord," and so on, he does not mean that he asks for nothing else from the Lord—since so many times in the Psalms he asks for remission of sins, help against enemies, understanding of the Law, the stability of his kingdom, the prosperity of the <margin>F</margin> city of Jerusalem—but he means that he desires that one thing *above all*. Likewise, when the Law says, "You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve," it does not exclude the veneration and honor due to Kings and parents, or to the Saints, I think; nor the obedience that servants owe to their masters; but it shows that the "highest" honor and the "highest" worship are due to God.

Moreover, when Christ, speaking to the Father, says, "That they may know you, the only true God," and so on, he does not exclude himself and the Holy Spirit from the fellowship of the Divinity, but he excludes the Gods of the Nations. Again, when he says, "God alone is good," he does not remove all angels and men from the name of "good," since in the Parables he calls servants "good," and fish "good" (using this metaphor to designate good men), but he attributes the "highest" and "native" goodness to God. Likewise, when he says to the ruler of the synagogue, "Only believe, all things are possible to the one who believes," the word "only" does not exclude other virtues, but rather excludes anxiety about an incurable disease or the death of a daughter. In the same figure <note>original: "schemate"</note>, Paul calls God "only wise and immortal," not excluding the Angels and Prophets, since in the Gospel the five virgins are called "prudent" <note>prudent: here meaning wise</note>.

<meta>The catchword "tes" at the bottom of page 724 indicates the start of the next word on the following page (likely "prudentes"). Erasmus concludes this section by arguing that theological terms like "alone" or "only" should be understood as highlights of importance rather than as exclusions of all other factors—a key argument in his moderate approach to the "Faith Alone" controversy.</meta>

<summary>Erasmus provides a rhetorical and philological analysis of 1 Corinthians 13, arguing that Paul uses "fictions" or hypothetical scenarios to emphasize the supreme importance of love. He also addresses the "Sola Fide" (Faith Alone) controversy, suggesting that "alone" often signifies preeminence rather than the total exclusion of other virtues like love.</summary>

# 725 TO THE FIRST CORINTHIANS. CHAPTER XIII. 726

3 ...if I have not love, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my goods to feed the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may be burned, but have not love, it profits me nothing.
4 Love is patient, it is kind; love does not envy; love is not boastful, it is not puffed up,
5 It does not act unbecomingly, it does not seek its own, it is not provoked, it does not think evil,
6 it does not rejoice in injustice, but rejoices with the truth,
7 It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.
8 Love never fails; but whether prophecies will be abolished, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be abolished.
9 For we know in part, and we prophesy in part.
10 But when that which is perfect comes, then that which is in part will be abolished.
11 When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I put away the things of a child.
12 For we see now through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then I shall know just as I have been known.
13 And now remain faith, hope, love, these three; but the greatest of these is love.

<margin>A</margin> ...and besides Solomon, many are proclaimed by the name of "wisdom" in the canonical scriptures: but it is attributed to God that these titles uniquely apply to Him. In the same way, Jesus is called the "only-begotten" and "unique" Son of God—not because He is the only son, but because He is the Son in an extraordinary way. Similarly, in Luke chapter nine, when we read, *Jesus was found alone*, the three Disciples are not excluded, but rather Moses and Elijah, who were previously speaking with him. Soon in the same chapter, it says, *When he was praying alone*. Yet the Disciples were also with him. The word *alone* <note>original Latin: "solus"</note> excludes the crowd that is usually present. Finally, when Blessed Thomas Aquinas says in the Prologue, *To strengthen a sincere heart, faith alone suffices*, by the word *alone* <note>original: "sola"</note> he does not exclude love and other virtues, but only human reason and the experience of the senses. Since the Sacred Volumes, the books of the Orthodox fathers, and the daily speech of men are full of such expressions—for example, when we say, "He hungers for nothing, thirsts for nothing here but gold"—bread and wine are not literally excluded, but his remarkable greed is highlighted. Likewise, we say "The King walks alone," even if he is accompanied by one or two people, but we say "alone" meaning he is not surrounded by his usual retinue. We say Anchorites <term>Anchorites: religious hermits who live in total isolation</term> live alone in the woods, though various kinds of animals and sometimes a servant are present. Therefore, one who says that men are justified by faith alone does not entirely exclude love, nor the works of love, but rather human philosophy, or ceremonies and legalistic works, or a life lived before baptism, or something similar that is gathered from the context of the speech. In Paul’s writing, the word *alone* is not actually added. What does it matter? Since in so many places he drives home the point that Abraham was pronounced righteous without works. We are all justified through faith, and not from works, for if it were from works, grace would already be abolished. All of Paul's Epistles overflow with this kind of language. Yet he never separates love from purifying faith, and so often exhorts us to works of love. But we have lingered long enough on this "contribution" <note>original: "symbolam," a metaphor for a shared feast or contribution to a debate</note>, as the nature of the argument allows.

<margin>B</margin> **5 Distribute to feed the poor]** In Greek it is one word, *psōmisō* <note>original: ψωμίσω</note>. And "all my resources," *eis ta panta mou* <note>original: εἰς τὰ πάντα μου</note>, that is, all my things. In some copies, however, we read, *ta panta hyparchonta mou* <note>original: τὰ πάντα ὑπάρχοντά μου</note>.

**6 So that I may burn]** The word "so" <note>original: "ita"</note> is redundant. Nor was it added in two of the Constantian manuscripts: *hina kauthesomai* <note>original: ἵνα καυθήσωμαι</note>, that is, "that I may be burned," or "for burning." Saint Jerome, writing on the Epistle to the Galatians chapter five, says that in Latin codices the reading is *so that I may glory*, and he calls that reading an error, but adds that the Greek copies are also diverse. There is no doubt that the error arose from the change of a letter, *kauchesomai* <note>to boast</note> instead of *kauthesomai* <note>to be burned</note>. Theophylact, and before him Chrysostom, read and interpret "to be burned" along with us. And that reading seems to me to be the genuine one. Although the Spanish Edition had "that I may glory." He does a great thing who spends all his resources on feeding the poor: but he does a greater thing who hands his body over to the flames, which Peregrinus <note>Peregrinus Proteus, a 2nd-century philosopher who famously burned himself to death at the Olympic Games</note> is recorded to have done. He who wrote the scholia <term>scholia: ancient explanatory notes written in the margins of manuscripts</term> on all the Epistles of Paul mentions something about "glory." Jerome's title is as if he read, "that I may glory." Basil, in a certain letter to the Neocaesareans, reads "that they may burn," so that "the body" is understood.

**7 Love is patient]** *makrothymei* <note>original: μακροθυμεῖ</note>, that is, is long-suffering, or is of a gentle mind. And so Ambrose reads it. Although in common codices they changed "long-suffering" <note>original: "longanima"</note> to "magnanimous." Even if in Cyprian love is sometimes called "magnanimous" based on this passage of Paul, because *makron* means both "long" and "great." To me, neither "long-suffering" nor "magnanimous" seems to express the force of the Greek word well enough. For we Latin speakers do not say "long mind" in the same way we say "great mind": rather, we use "gentle" instead of "long," that is, not headlong into anger or revenge.

<margin>C</margin> **8 Is kind]** *chresteuetai* <note>original: χρηστεύεται</note>, for which Ambrose reads "is pleasant." It signifies a courtesy and sweetness of manners, which is opposed to harshness, difficulty, or moodiness. True piety does not know how to be haughty; feigned holiness is heavy with harshness of manners. To the Latins, "benignity" mostly refers to beneficence. For just as a bad person is called "malignant," a good person is called "benign." Thomas Aquinas brings forward a new etymology: "Benignity," he says, is called as if it were "good fieriness" <note>original: "bona igneitas"</note>, because just as fire makes things flow out, so does love. And he teaches this by the testimony of Solomon in Proverbs chapter five, *Let your fountains be dispersed abroad*. A man unworthy <note>Erasmus is famously critical of Aquinas's linguistic skills</note> to have mixed such unlearned nonsense into sacred Commentaries. For it is clear enough that if anything pertains to the explanation of words or testimonies of the Sacred Volumes, he sought it almost never from the 

<column-break/>

but if I have not love, I am nothing. 3 And if I spend all my resources on food, and if I hand over my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing of use. 7 Love is patient, it is kind: love does not envy: love is not insolent, is not puffed up, 10 Is not fastidious, does not seek what is its own, is not provoked, 11 does not think evil, Does not rejoice in injustice, but rejoices with the truth, 12 Bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, sustains all things. 13 Love never fails: whether prophecies will be abolished, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be abolished. 15 For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect comes, then that which is in part will be abolished. 16 When I was a boy, I spoke as a boy, I felt as a boy, I thought as a boy: but when I became a man, 17 I abolished boyish things. For we see now through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face: now I know in part, but then I shall know just as I have been known. sources themselves, but from the collections and indexes of others.

<margin>D</margin> **9 Does not act perversely]** *perpereuetai* <note>original: περπερεύεται</note>. Love is repeated in this place among the Greeks. And the Greek scholia interpret this word in various ways. Some think *peripereuesthai* is the same as "to flatter," others that it means "to be extolled" and "to show oneself off," from the name *perperos*, which they want to be said as if it were *peripetros*. Hesychius seems to have felt this too. Others interpret it as "to babble," from *perperos*, which they say is like *periperos*, being one who is carried around by words, because chatterboxes are annoying with their long-winded speeches. There are those who interpret it as "headlong and reckless," and *perperon-bian* as being a headlong force. Theophylact interprets it as "inconstant and light." To me, the word seems to be fashioned from the *Perperis* brothers, who were also called *Cercopes* <note>mischievous forest spirits in Greek myth</term>, whose insolence and wickedness were made famous even in fables. We have related more about them in the proverb, *Lest you fall in with the Black-Buttocks* <note>referring to a story about Hercules and the Cercopes</note>, if anyone cares to know. We translate it as "is not procacious" <note>bold or insolent</note>: which interpretation Theophylact also records. Otherwise, in Latin, one "acts perversely" who deliberately acts otherwise than he should. And thus Aquinas interprets it, "perversely," that is, "wickedly."

**10 Is not ambitious]** *ou physioutai* <note>original: οὐ φυσιοῦται</note>, that is, does not act insolently, or "swollen." I wonder where the word "ambitious" crept in here, since *aschēmosynē* <note>indecency</note> and *philotimia* <note>ambition</note> have no affinity, unless perhaps because "not being puffed up" excels, which seems to belong to ambition. Although the Greek scholia interpret it this way: *hōs aschēmonei*, that is, it thinks nothing is unbecoming to itself, however humble the office, provided it is useful. And Theophylact explains it in the same way, though not concealing the other interpretation as well. Nothing could be gathered from Ambrose, since he, content with explaining the gist of this passage, neglects to follow the individual words. Augustine in *On Grace and Free Will* to Valentinus, chapter seventeen, reads, "is not dishonored."

**11 Does not think evil]** *ou logizetai to kakon* <note>original: οὐ λογίζεται τὸ κακόν</note>, that is, does not impute evil to anyone, nor think evil of anyone, as Valla notes; either because love measures all by its own mind, or because it does not plot revenge.

<margin>E</margin> **12 Bears all things]** *Panta stegei* <note>original: Πάντα στέγει</note>, that is, "Is burdened by nothing." It is a metaphor taken from beams supporting an imposed weight, or from vessels receiving what is poured in. Cyprian, in the third treatise of *On the Simplicity of Prelates*, instead of "bears all things," reads "loves all things." From this one may guess his codex had *Panta stergei* <note>original: Πάντα στέργει</note>, adding a little letter to the word *stegei*. Both senses are tolerable, though the one our Edition has is more approved by me, because all these things piled together seem to pertain to the same point: "bears all things," "believes all things," "hopes all things," "endures all things." For indeed, he who believes receives what is handed over, and he who believes hopes, and he who hopes endures, that is, lasts through time so that the promises may appear: for that is what *hypomenein* properly sounds like, different from the *stegei* that precedes it.

**13 Love never fails]** *oudepote ekpiptei* <note>original: οὐδέποτε ἐκπίπτει</note>, that is, "never ceases," is useful everywhere, is of use everywhere, indeed it grows daily. Even if *ekpiptein* in Greek is "to go away shaken out and ejected." Thus the sense will be: There is never not a place for love.

**14 Whether prophecies will be vanished]** The Greeks add *de*. And so Saint Ambrose reads, "But whether prophecies will be vanished." Then, what follows:

<margin>F</margin> **15 For we know in part]** *Ek merous de* <note>original: Ἐκ μέρους δὲ</note>. Some Greek codices had "but" instead of "for," *de* instead of *gar*.

**16 When I was a little one]** *Nēpios* <note>original: Νήπιος</note>. Which signifies both "boy" or "infant," and "not very prudent," because that age, due to lack of experience in things, knows little, as we have already frequently reminded.

**17 I vanished the things of a little one]** Which Ambrose reads, "those things which were of a little one I destroyed." And in this place, it seems to me the Greek codices are corrupted, in which I find it written thus, with the Aldine Edition also agreeing: *katērgēka kata ta nēpiou*. But I suspect it was written by Paul as *katērgēka ta tou nēpiou*, or *katērgēka ta tō nēpiō*. Theophylact reads *katērgēka*, as does Chrysostom.

**18 But the greatest of these]** *meizōn de toutōn hē agapē* <note>original: μείζων δὲ τούτων ἡ ἀγάπη</note>, that is, the "greatest" of these is love. Although the Latins, following the example of the Greeks, sometimes use the comparative for the superlative. As in that line of Catullus:
->Hesperus, what fire shines more pleasantly in the sky?<-
And Quintus Curtius said "the two greater of all ships." And the Greeks never fail to use comparatives in place of superlatives. And so indeed Theophylact explains it: "Among those things that remain, Love is right..."

## Commentary

We prefer to use the ablative case <note>i.e., a grammatical construction in Latin that indicates separation or instrumentality</note> to avoid the awkwardness of saying "hers" or "his" with these nouns. In the Donatian codex <note>a manuscript from the collection of Donatus, used by Erasmus for textual comparison</note> the reading was *"but the greatest of these is love"* — which is an absurd formulation, since love cannot be greater than itself. This difficulty would have been avoided by adding a preposition: *"the greatest among these"* or *"the highest of these,"* so that a proper distribution of meaning is understood.

Another difficulty arises here: what does the adverb *"now"* indicate — the present life, in which we walk by faith, or the early days of the Church? The latter cannot be accepted, since it would follow that the Church Militant could exist without faith, hope, and love. If we understand these three as enduring in this life — as though they will cease in the life to come — there would be reason to argue this of faith and hope, but the Apostle has already declared earlier that even if all other gifts of the Spirit were removed, love would never fail.

The Apostle Peter himself acknowledges that Paul wrote certain things that are difficult to understand, <note>cf. 2 Peter 3:16</note> and some of the most learned among the Ancients who were deeply trained in Sacred Scripture admit that Paul in his argumentation is, as they put it, slippery and shifting — that he touches on certain matters in passing, as though forgetting what he had set out to say, and sometimes uses the same word in different senses, and now and then suddenly slides into a different argument altogether. The word "law" recurs frequently in Paul but not always with the same meaning. Perhaps something of that kind is impeding our understanding here as well.

For certain gifts that were necessary for the Church's infancy have now ceased — such as the gift of tongues, healings, foreknowledge of future events, and the other miracles that are superfluous for those already confirmed in faith, since signs were given for unbelievers, not for believers. <note>cf. 1 Corinthians 14:22</note> Paul seems to hint at something of this kind when he says *"when I was a child"* and the rest — as though certain gifts had been given for a time to the Church in its early growth, destined to cease once that Church had advanced to the full measure of the stature of Christ. <note>cf. Ephesians 4:13</note> But from this state of perfection Paul seems to move further, toward a greater perfection that will come in the future life. For those words — *"then we shall see face to face, and then we shall know even as we are known"* — do not fit the Church Militant here on earth.

If we accept that the Apostle has here digressed somewhat by way of opportunity — as he sometimes does elsewhere — perhaps it would not be unreasonable to take the passage in this sense: *Even if all other gifts should cease in the Church, faith, hope, and love will never cease* — for without these there is no Church of Christ, only a Synagogue of Satan. In the heavenly life, however, neither faith, nor hope, nor love as we now exercise them will remain. For faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. <note>cf. Hebrews 11:1</note> And *"what a man sees, why does he still hope for it?"* <note>cf. Romans 8:24</note>

Yet it seems absurd to say that love ceases among the blessed, where there will be perfect charity among all. But — saving the judgment of others — it seems to me that the Apostle here is speaking not of love in its entirety, by which we love God above all things and our neighbour for God's sake, but only of *one particular function of love*: the earnest desire to benefit our neighbour. This is indicated by the whole tenor of the discussion, in which there is no mention of love toward God, but the entire argument points toward this: that whatever gift one has received from God should be used for the benefit of one's neighbour. True love of neighbour is not, of course, separable from love of God — from which it is born; perhaps they are even one and the same thing. And this is why Paul wishes anyone who speaks in tongues to remain silent in the assembly unless there is an interpreter; he approves of no interpreter unless a prophet is present to explain the deeper meaning; and he approves of no prophet unless what the Spirit has prompted is offered for the edification of the church, without quarrelling and division. This *function* of love will cease among the blessed, for there no one will need the assistance of another's service — whereas in this life no one exists who does not need the help of a neighbour.

Perhaps someone will also be troubled by this: given that both the Lord in the Gospels and Paul in his Epistles so prominently commend faith, how can Paul here say that love is the greatest? For just as no gift is pleasing to God without love, so no gift is received without faith — indeed, no gift is even given without faith. For faith is, so to speak, the hands of the soul, by which we receive and embrace the generosity of the Spirit, without which even works of love are not pleasing to God. Moreover, faith is by nature prior to love, for through faith we come to know God, and nothing is loved unless it is first known. And what generates seems more excellent than what is generated.

Add to this: if it is true that even when love is extinguished, the seed of faith can still remain in a person, that is a great commendation of faith — that faith can rekindle love once extinguished, whereas love cannot do the same in return. And finally, Paul everywhere attributes a person's salvation to faith rather than to love. If love is the greatest of gifts, then in the preceding chapter, where the gifts of the Spirit are listed, love ought to have been given first place. As it stands there, faith is given some place; love is not even named.

To this one may respond: although love is not named there, many of love's *functions* are enumerated — such as the word of wisdom, the word of knowledge, the grace of healings, the working of miracles, prophecy, the discernment of spirits, helps, forms of governance, the interpretation of utterances, and the rest. For through these works love expresses itself. One who displays the branches and the fruit has sufficiently commended the root. And since this whole passage urges us toward the benefit of our neighbour, by this logic those gifts that are more useful to more people are called the better gifts, and love is called the greatest, because it directs all things toward the benefit of the Church. Nothing prevents the same thing from being, under different aspects, both superior and inferior to another.

Perhaps — beyond all this — someone will be troubled by the following: since no gift of the Spirit comes without faith, and since no grace at all comes without faith, how does Paul list faith as though it were present in some members of the mystical body but not in others? For he speaks thus: <note>original: "Divisiones gratiarum sunt..."</note> *"There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of workings, but it is the same God who works all things in all."* <margin>B</margin> *"To each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing in the one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits,"* and so on.

But Theophylact <note>Theophylact of Ohrid (c. 1055–1107), Byzantine archbishop and biblical commentator whose annotations were well known to Erasmus</note> has removed this difficulty, indicating that here the word "faith" does not refer to that belief and trust in God through which all graces are given, but only to that particular faith which works miracles — which is not given to all, nor is it necessary for salvation. And the Apostle clearly seems to have this in mind when he says, *"And if I have all faith, so as to move mountains."* <note>cf. 1 Corinthians 13:2</note> For just as, following the Lord's example, he set forth the ultimate example of love as the willingness to hand over one's body to be burned — that is, to a terrible death — so also, following the Lord's example, he set forth the supreme example of faith as the ability to move mountains. <margin>C</margin> And this too can be called perfect faith in its own kind, though it is not simply perfect with respect to all powers. For the root and source of all spiritual gifts — including love itself — is this foundational faith.

But it is love's role to direct whatever good comes to a person — whether spiritual, moral, natural, or fortuitous — toward the benefit of one's neighbour. I have argued these matters in this way not to assert anything dogmatically, but wishing to offer the wise an occasion to perceive better things.

---

### Verse Annotations

<margin>1</margin> **"Pursue love, eagerly desire spiritual gifts."** Most Greek manuscripts also add the conjunction *"but"* <note>original Greek: "δὲ"</note> in the second clause: <note>original: "Διώκετε τὴν ἀγάπην, ζηλοῦτε δὲ τὰ πνευματικά"</note> *"Pursue love, but eagerly desire spiritual things."* Without it, Paul seems to be urging both equally. As it stands, he first wants us to strive with all effort to do good — for this is what he calls "love." Then, lest anyone should be offended, he adds that the rest are not to be scorned either: these he calls "spiritual gifts," because they are sometimes given by the breath of the Spirit even to the wicked. Among these, however, he assigns the first place to prophecy. <margin>D</margin> In this passage Paul uses the word "prophecy" not to mean prediction of future events, but the interpretation of Holy Scripture. Similarly, Plato distinguished between diviners <note>original Latin: "vates"</note> and prophets: diviners, seized by divine power, do not themselves understand what they are saying; prudent interpreters explain it to others. Furthermore, the verb *"pursue"* <note>original Greek: "διώκετε"</note> is stronger than *"desire earnestly"* <note>original Greek: "ζηλοῦτε"</note>: *"to desire"* refers to those things we merely approve and admire; *"to pursue"* means to strive with great eagerness until you obtain them. We are to wish that those other gifts may come to us — but the things that belong to love must be sought with every effort of our will, not merely wished for.

<margin>2</margin> **"In the spirit, however, he speaks."** <note>original Greek: "πνεύματι δὲ λαλεῖ"</note> That is, *"he speaks in the spirit"* or *"he speaks by the spirit"* — corresponding to what preceded (*"he does not speak to men, but to God"*) and what follows (*"he speaks to men"*) — meaning, he speaks by his own soul's voice. Ambrose <note>Ambrose of Milan (c. 340–397), bishop and theologian, whose text of Paul's letters Erasmus frequently consulted</note> reads *"in the spirit"* in the ablative case, <margin>E</margin> which he glosses as: *"he speaks in the spirit, not in understanding, because he does not know what he is saying."* And this reading is still to be found in the most ancient and at the same time most carefully corrected codex of the Pauline letters, confirmed likewise by the most ancient Donatian codex, and by both the Constance codices. <note>Erasmus here names specific manuscripts he consulted: a "Pauline codex," the "Donatian codex," and two manuscripts from Constance — reflecting his rigorous textual method</note> And indeed, if one looks more attentively, one will find that this is also how blessed Augustine read the passage in his *Commentary on Genesis in the Literal Sense*, <note>original: "libro de Genesi ad literam" — Augustine's detailed commentary on the early chapters of Genesis</note> even though in many manuscripts *"in the spirit"* was changed to *"the Spirit"*; for when he cited this passage he immediately followed it with another similar one: *"If you bless in the spirit, who fills the place of the layman?"* — as if to say that *"to bless in the spirit"* there corresponds to *"to speak in the spirit"* here. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the great Scholastic theologian, whose commentary on Paul Erasmus cites here</note> plainly states that he read *"the Spirit,"* explaining it as meaning that it is God who speaks through them. But one must consider how this fits the purpose of diminishing this gift — for Paul's aim is to show that speaking in tongues is far inferior to prophecy. In Greek, as I said, the expression is ambiguous: the dative <note>original Greek: "πνεύματι"</note> can be instrumental — which is rendered in Latin by the ablative case — and it can equally be a dative of relation, as if one were to say *"speaks to the tongue"* and *"speaks to you."* Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), Archbishop of Constantinople, a leading patristic commentator on Paul</note> and Theophylact discuss this passage in such a way as to make clear they read *"Spirit"* rather than *"in the spirit."* When Chrysostom says, <margin>F</margin> *"That is, they do not tell men things easy and open, but in the Holy Spirit they speak mysteries"* — and Theophylact, when he says, *"Paul attributes both gifts to the Spirit"* — their reading is apparent. I myself am more drawn to Ambrose's view: that *"spirit"* here means voice or breath. Although in several other short works Ambrose cites the verse *"I will sing with the spirit, I will sing with the mind also"* in a way that takes *"spirit"* to mean the Holy Spirit. But such slips are not uncommon in Ambrose.

<margin>3</margin> **"For he who prophesies."** <note>original Greek: "Ὁ δὲ προφητεύων"</note> That is, *"But he who prophesies."*

<margin>4</margin> **"He speaks to men for edification."** In Greek the preposition is absent: <note>original Greek: "λαλεῖ οἰκοδομὴν"</note> *"he speaks edification."* Latin usage allows the same construction, as when we say *"you tell me pleasure"* meaning *"you tell me things that are a pleasure to me."* I suspect from the translation that Ambrose read it the same way.

<margin>5</margin> **"He edifies the church of God."** The word *"of God"* is not added in the Greek manuscripts, nor in the most ancient Donatian codex, nor even in the Constance codex.

<margin>6</margin> **"Unless perhaps he interprets."** The word *"perhaps"* was added by the Translator on his own authority. <note>Erasmus criticizes the Vulgate translator for inserting a word not found in the Greek</note> It is not present in the Greek, nor in Ambrose, and I do not see what it contributes to the meaning.

<summary>This page presents Erasmus's parallel Greek and Latin text of 1 Corinthians 14:1–6, accompanied by his detailed philological and theological commentary on the closing verse of Chapter 13 (concerning faith, hope, and love) and the opening verses of Chapter 14 (concerning tongues and prophecy). Erasmus engages with manuscript variants, patristic authorities (Ambrose, Augustine, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Thomas Aquinas), and the precise meaning of Greek grammatical constructions to argue for a more nuanced and contextually grounded reading of Paul's text than the standard Vulgate provides.</summary>

<margin>7</margin> Likewise, even inanimate things that give a sound, whether a flute or a harp, if they do not give a distinction in the notes, how will what is fluted or what is harped be known?

<margin>7</margin> **Even those things without a soul**] <note>original Greek: Ὅμως τὰ ἄψυχα</note>. Some interpret "Even" as "Likewise" or "In the same way," as if the manuscripts had <note>original: Ὁμοίως</note>. At first glance, this seems to fit the sense better. Writers easily slip into such errors. However, I do not approve of this opinion; first, because both the Latin and Greek copies argue against it. Second, it does not seem to fit the sharpness of Paul's sentiment, especially since we find this form of speech elsewhere in Paul, as in the third chapter of Galatians: **nevertheless, a man’s confirmed testament** <note>original: ὅμως ἀνθρώπω κεκυρωμένην διαθήκην</note>, which will be discussed in its own place. Paul feels that empty noise among Christians is so unapproachable that even things lacking a soul—prepared for nothing but to ring and tinkle—are of no use unless they give a distinct and meaningful sound. Hence, it could be translated: *Even the inanimate,* or *Inanimate though they be,* or *Nay, even the inanimate.* Both Chrysostom and Theophylact <note>Greek Church Fathers who wrote early commentaries</note> explain it in this sense. For "things without a soul," he could have more simply said *inanimate* or *soulless.* In ancient times, the common people recognized the type of sentiment from the harmony of flutes, and even today a soldier understands what the commander wants by the different calls of the trumpet; likewise in hunting, those far from the beast understand the state of the hunt by the sound of the horn.

<margin>8</margin> **Of the sounds**] <note>original Greek: τοῖς φθόγγοις</note>, that is, "by the sounds." It is likely that Ambrose read it this way, as his text still reads "by the sounds" rather than "of the sounds." And "he gave" <note>original: δῷ</note> could be "they gave," referring to the "inanimate things."

<margin>9</margin> **What is played**] <note>original: τὸ αὐλούμενον ἢ τὸ κιθαριζόμενον</note>, that is, "what is played on the flute or harp." Ambrose reads: "what is played through the flute."

<margin>10</margin> **Who will prepare [himself]**] <note>original: τίς παρασκευάσεται</note>, that is, "who will be made ready?" The translator frequently and rightly uses this active/passive phrasing.

<margin>11</margin> **A clear word**] <note>original: εὔσημον</note>, that is, "significant" or "meaningful." Saint Ambrose reads it this way in his Commentaries. Though both readings are fine.

<margin>12</margin> **For instance**] <note>original: εἰ τύχοι</note>, that is, "for example," used when we invent or pose an example.

<margin>13</margin> **Kinds of tongues**] <note>original: φωνῶν</note>, that is, "of voices." Chrysostom and Theophylact read and interpret it this way. For he is speaking of all kinds of voices, not just languages. Although Ambrose reads "of tongues" for "of voices," that is, <note>original: γλωσσῶν</note>. It is possible the Apostle misused the word "tongue" just as he misused the word <term>voice</term> <note>meaning the sound itself</note>. There are indeed nations that use a whistle or a hiss as speech.

<margin>14</margin> **In this world**] Again, <note>original: ἐν κόσμῳ</note>, that is, "in the world," without the pronoun.

<margin>15</margin> **And nothing [without voice]**] <note>original: καὶ οὐδὲν αὐτῶν ἄφωνον</note>, that is, "and none of these" (meaning the "kinds") "is voiceless," that is, "lacking voice or mute." And yet a Greek does not understand a Scythian. Therefore, voice alone is not enough.

<margin>16</margin> **I shall be to him to whom I speak**] <note>original: ἔσομαι τῷ λαλοῦντι βάρβαρος</note>, that is, "I shall be a barbarian to the one speaking"; I won't understand you, and you won't understand me. For the ancients called any foreigner by this name.

<margin>17</margin> **And he who speaks to me**] <note>original: ὁ λαλῶν</note>, that is, "is in me" <note>original Greek: ἐv</note>, meaning "to me," or "in my judgment, in my mind." Even if the speaker is most eloquent in himself, in my mind he is a barbarian. Furthermore, as I just said, the ancients called anything foreign a <term>barbarian</term>; later the word was twisted to mean the absurdity of a voice or speech. For foreign speech makes people appear ignorant, even if it is more refined than our own tongue. Finally, it began to be applied to wild and harsh manners. In the past, those first Greeks called "Hellene" referred to everyone else as barbarians. Homer calls the Carians "barbarian-voiced" <note>original: βαρβαροφώνους</note> because of the foreign and absurd sound of their language. And Ovid, living among the Getae, said: "Here I am the barbarian, because I am understood by no one." <note>original: "Barbarus hic ego sum, quia non intelligor ulli."</note> And Plautus said he had translated a Greek play "barbarously" when he had merely turned it into Latin. There is also the famous saying of Anachar-

->But<-
-sis, the wise Scythian philosopher: "The Scythians are barbarians to the Athenians, but the Athenians are likewise barbarians to the Scythians." Furthermore, regarding what is read here about "barbarians," there is a note in the commentaries of Aquinas that is written more than "barbarously." I suspect it was added by someone else who wished to sprinkle Aquinas's books with a few "flowery" thoughts. Otherwise, who could believe such a man would want to pronounce so arrogantly on a matter he completely failed to understand? But it is worth transcribing the words themselves—not for the reader to laugh, but so that they do not trust such magical interpretations in the future, and suspect them in other matters after catching them pronouncing with such authority on things they do not know: <note>Erasmus is mocking a Scholastic definition of "barbarian."</note> *Note,* he says, *that according to some, Barbarians are those whose language differs entirely from Latin. Others say that any foreigner is a Barbarian to every other foreigner, namely when he is not understood by him. But this is not true, because according to Isidore, Barbaria is a specific nation. Furthermore, thirdly: In Christ Jesus there is neither Barbarian nor Scythian. But as was said before, Barbarians are properly called those who do not flourish in virtue, who fail in the power of reason, and are as if outside the laws, without the governance of justice. And Aristotle seems to agree with this in his Politics.* Thus far his "beautiful" annotation. These things might be laughed at, if the authors of such trifles had not prescribed laws for the Christian world—and indeed continue to prescribe them—and if there were not those who want their authority to be almost equal to the Gospel. I would not want these things said against Thomas himself; I am convinced this commentary was sewn on by someone else.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>18</margin> **So also you, since you are emulators of spirits**] Theophylact indicates that some punctuate this passage so that the phrase "So also you" refers to what precedes: "So also you, speaking in tongues, are not understood; you will seem like barbarians to those listening." Then they start a new sentence: "You are emulators, etc."

<margin>F</margin> But he rejects this punctuation on the authority of Basil, who punctuated it as we commonly do. I do not see what that first punctuation accomplishes unless the word "since" <note>original: ἐπεὶ</note> is removed, or unless we translate "be ye" instead of "you are." Chrysostom punctuates it as we do.

<margin>19</margin> **My spirit prays, but the mind**] He calls the "voice of the tongue" the *spirit*, and the "affection or sense of the soul" the *mind*: <note>original: πνεῦμα & νοῦς</note>. "My spirit prays" means nothing other than "my tongue sounds pious words," so that you understand this benefits neither others nor the one making the sound. Theophylact cites Basil as the author of this opinion.

<margin>20</margin> **If you bless**] <note>original: εὐλογήσῃς</note>. It is a single word, meaning to praise and celebrate God, and to speak words of good omen. *Bless with the spirit.* "With the spirit" was absent in most Greek copies; we added it from others, both because it helps the sense and because Ambrose, Augustine, Chrysostom, and Theophylact read it that way.

<margin>21</margin> **Who fills the place of the unlearned**] <note>original: ὁ ἀναπληρῶν τὸν τόπον τοῦ ἰδιώτου</note>, that is, "who fills the place of the layman," or acts in the stead of the unlearned. It is still written this way in a very ancient manuscript of the Pauline library. The word *Idiota* is Greek, meaning a private person (one not holding office) or an unlearned person. Here it could be translated as *commoner* or *unlearned.* This custom—the common people responding in church—lasted until the time of Jerome in Rome, as he testifies in his preface to the second book of his Commentaries on Galatians: "Where," he asks, "does the 'Amen' roar like heavenly thunder in this way?"

<margin>22</margin> **Upon your blessing**] <note>original: ἐπὶ τῇ σῇ εὐχαριστίᾳ</note>, that is, "upon your giving of thanks." We gather from this place that there is very little difference between *blessing* and *giving thanks*, as both pertain to the praise of God.

<margin>23</margin> **I speak in tongues more than all of you**] The Greek has a different sense: <note>original: Εὐχαριστῶ τῷ Θεῷ μου, πάντων ὑμῶν μᾶλλον γλώσσαις λαλῶν</note>, "I give thanks to my God, speaking in tongues more than all of you."

<summary>Erasmus argues that the gift of tongues is useless without interpretation, comparing it to musical instruments played without distinct notes. He critiques a narrow Scholastic definition of "barbarian," asserting that barbarism is simply mutual unintelligibility rather than a lack of Latin or virtue.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed commentary on 1 Corinthians 14. On the previous page, Erasmus argued that intelligible speech is superior to speaking in tongues for the edification of the church. Here, he focuses on verse 19—Paul’s preference for "five words" of understanding over "ten thousand" in a tongue—using it as a platform for a famous and biting critique of contemporary 16th-century church music and scholastic theology.</meta>

# EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER XIV.
### PAGE 731–732

19 ...good. But in the church I would rather speak five words with my mind <note>original: *dia tou noos mou*</note>, so that I might also instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.
20 Brothers, do not be children in your thinking, but be infants in regard to evil, and be mature in your thinking.
21 In the law it is written: "By people of strange tongues and by the lips of others I will speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me," says the Lord.
22 Therefore, tongues are for a sign, not for those who believe, but for unbelievers; whereas prophecy is not for unbelievers, but for those who believe.
23 If, therefore, the whole church comes together and everyone speaks in tongues, and unlearned people or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your minds?
24 But if everyone prophesies, and an unbeliever or unlearned person enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all;
25 and so...

---

->B<-

19 **that is, that I speak in tongues more than all of you.** Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Early Church Father known for his preaching</note> interprets it in this sense. Jerome refers the comparison "more" to the other Apostles, so that you should understand that Paul spoke in the languages of everyone more than the rest of the Apostles did. See the exposition of the ninth question to Hedibia, where he cites this passage more than once differently than our edition has it: although I see that the reading which the Vulgate Edition <note>The standard Latin Bible of the time</note> has pleases Ambrose.

24 **Five words** <note>original: *pente logous*</note>, that is, five speeches or sayings; for he does not count the individual words. And "five" is used for "very few," just as "ten thousand" is used for "very many." For who would not immediately see how "cold" <note>uninspired or pedantic</note> the argument is that Aquinas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic theologian</note> brings in here—drawn from I know not where—that "five" was said because a perfect sentence ought to have five parts: **the subject, the predicate, the verbal copula, the qualification of the subject, and the qualification of the predicate.** But if this opinion is not pleasing enough, he adds another similar to it: he teaches, he says, that one ought to teach five things: things to be believed, things to be done, things to be avoided, things to be hoped for, and things to be feared. It would have been less "cold" if he had said the five books of the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible</note>. Whoever wrote the scholia <note>brief explanatory notes</note> on all the Epistles, whoever he was, quite wittily mocks this kind of curiosity regarding numbers. "Some," he says, "certainly ask why there are five words, and on the contrary, one should ask why there are ten thousand." Chrysostom explains it thus: **so that I may bring it about that others understand my meaning**, through my mind, that is, through my intellect.

25 **So that I might also instruct others** <note>original: *katēchēsō*</note>, that is, I might educate: a word Paul likes to use, as does Luke. This properly means to institute and teach by the living voice: hence they are called **Catechumens** <note>converts receiving basic religious instruction</note>, to whom the mysteries of our faith were entrusted not by writing, but by the ministry of the voice.

26 **Than ten thousand**] The word **rather** should have been added, so that the place would fit this conjunction **than**. Among the Greeks, it is frequently understood <note>implied but not written</note>, but among the Latins, that is unusual. In this matter, it is a marvel how much the custom of the Church has changed. Paul preferred five words in the sense <note>meaningful understanding</note> than ten thousand in the spirit. But now in some regions, people sing "in the spirit" all day long—there is no limit or end to the songs—while a wholesome sermon exhorting true piety is hardly heard once in six months: for that is what Paul calls **speaking in the sense**. I will omit for now that this kind of music has been introduced into divine worship such that it is impossible to clearly perceive a single word. Nor do those who are chanting have the leisure to attend to what they are singing. Only the tinkling of voices strikes the ears, and soothes them with a little delight that is soon to perish. This might be bearable, if the common crowd of Priests and Monks did not place the summit of piety in such things, disagreeing greatly from Paul. Why does the Church hesitate to follow such a great author? Indeed, why does it dare to disagree with him? What else is heard in Monasteries, in Colleges, in almost all Temples, than a noise of voices? And yet in Paul's age, there was no singing, but only pronunciation. Singing was scarcely received by later generations, and even then it was such that it was nothing other than a distinct and modulated pronunciation, of the kind that still remains among us when we sound the Lord's Prayer in the sacred canon: and the common people, still mixed together, understood the language in which these things were sung, responding "Amen." Now, what do the common people hear but voices signifying nothing? And the pronunciation is usually such that the words are not even heard; only the sound strikes the ears. And these things, first received under the appearance of piety, have gradually proceeded to the point where there is neither limit nor end to Psalms, songs, sacred rites, and manuals, because we feel that something is added to our revenues from this. And what is more serious, Priests are bound to perform these things with almost tighter chains than those things which Christ commands. The people are forced to hear these things, driven away from the work by which they support their children and wife—and what can be more holy than that task? Let the temples certainly have solemn songs, but let them be moderate. We are forced to do the same things privately when occupied, and we carry a public choir with us in ships, in wagons, and in inns. By observing or neglecting these things, we are judged pious or impious. Someone may be greedier than Crassus <note>Marcus Licinius Crassus, famously wealthy and greedy Roman</note>, more slanderous than Zoilus <note>a Greek critic known for bitter cynicism</note>, yet he is considered a pious man because he sounds those little prayers with a loud voice, even if he understands nothing. I ask you, what do they think of Christ, who believe He is delighted by this kind of noise of voices? Not content with this, we have introduced a certain laborious and theatrical music into the sacred rites: a tumultuous chattering of different voices, such as I do not think was ever heard in the theaters of the Greeks or Romans. Everything rings with trumpets, clarions, pipes, and harps, and human voices compete with these. Filthy and amorous songs are heard, to which prostitutes and mimes dance. People run to the sacred house as if to a theater to soothe their ears. And for this use, organ builders and flocks of boys are maintained with large salaries, whose entire lives are consumed in learning this kind of "yelping," while they learn nothing good in the meantime. A rabble of sordid and frivolous men is maintained—as most of these Dionysiacs <note>musicians or performers, named for the god of theater and wine</note> are—and the Church is burdened with such great expenses for a thing that is pestilential

->C<-

as well. I ask you to calculate: how many poor people in danger of their lives could be fed with the salaries of the singers? These things are so pleasing that the Monks do nothing else, especially among the British; and those whose singing ought to have been mourning, believe God is appeased by lewd whinnying and a flexible throat. For this use, even in the Colleges of the Benedictines among the British, youths and boys and voice-artists are maintained, who every morning chirp a modulation of voices and decant the sacred rite with musical organs to the Virgin Mother. Bishops are forced to maintain such choirs at home. And being occupied with these things, they neither touch good literature, nor do they hear in what things true religion is situated. Now, those who are too coarse to be able to learn the art of music do not think the feast day is satisfied unless they employ a certain depraved kind of singing, which they call **Bardurdum** <note>a style of drone or crude polyphony</note>. It neither renders the prescribed theme nor observes the harmonies of the art. To this, although sober music was received into the Church for the purpose of making the sense of the words flow more effectively into the minds of the listeners, it also seems beautiful to some if one or another singer, mixed with the others, makes it so that not a single word can be perceived by means of a huge bellowing of the voice. In this, the whims of fools are indulged, and the belly is consulted. Why do only those things please us which Paul specifically condemned as the infancy of little children—indeed, which he would have tolerated in no way? For he is speaking of sacred reading, not of theatrical little songs. Let us sing in the spirit, but let us sing as Christians; let us sing sparingly, but more so let us sing with the mind. Let us speak in tongues, but let us pursue the prophet's work more zealously. Let the voice of the Prophet be heard above all, which may rebuke the conscience of the impious, which may comfort the downcast, which may stir those who are drowsy, which may bring forth the mysteries of the divine Spirit: and let the tender age be instructed for this use instead. But I think it is better to pursue what has been begun than to deplore these things—I know not if in vain.

->D<-

27 **Do not become children in your senses**] <note>original: *mē ginesthe*</note>, which sounds more like **be not**. And then, **senses** <note>original: *phresi*</note>, which Augustine reads as "minds," and in my judgment more correctly.

28 **But in malice be little ones**] <note>original: *nēpiazete*</note>, a single word, as if you were to say "be child-like" or "act like children." Although, as I have often warned, **nēpioi** refers to children of that age at which they cannot yet be wise. Hence, for "little ones," Augustine’s old version of Psalm 130 reads "infants."

->E<-

29 **In other tongues**] <note>original: *en heteroglōssois*</note>, that is, in those who are of different languages: as if you were to say in a composite word, "diverse-tongued": this can be taken so that we understand the variety of tongues which the Apostles used, or a new tongue different from that former one, that is, a tongue different among themselves, or different from others. The passage he cites is in Isaiah, chapter twenty-eight: "For in the speech of the lip, and in another tongue he will speak to this people," to whom he spoke. For so Jerome rendered the Hebrew. For according to the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> we still read it this way: **Because of the mockery of the lips, through another tongue, because they will speak to this people**, saying to them. Paul brings the testimony according to the Hebrew truth, whereas the Seventy and the rest of the Interpreters read far differently in this place, but in such a way again that he expressed the sense more than the words: a point which Saint Jerome also mentions when explaining this passage. Now those words, **and not even so will they hear me, says the Lord**, are found neither among the Hebrews nor among the Greek Interpreters, but yet a little later it follows in the prophecy, "and they would not hear," which Paul seems to have woven in. For this clause, **says the Lord**, is customarily added solemnly in prophecies, like an epiphonema <note>a concluding exclamation</note>. Unless perhaps this testimony was taken from elsewhere. Indeed, Jerome does not dare to affirm it, but says it seems so to him, that it was taken from that place.

->F<-

30 **To the faithful**] <note>original: *pisteuousi*</note>, that is, to believers.

31 **Unlearned or unbelievers**] "Unbelievers" is not added in the first place in Ambrose, I know not whether by the fault of the Scribes. For nothing is clear from the commentary. Certainly, it is added among the Greeks.

32 **That you are mad**] <note>original: *hoti mainesthe*</note>, that is, because you are insane. For he would not ask *why* they were mad, but would affirm that they *are* mad. That it was written "because you are mad" appears in the Pauline manuscript, and likewise in the Constantian. Nor does Ambrose read it otherwise, in whose work it is "because you are insane," which makes it more evident that it was changed into "why." The same man, in the third book on the Holy Spirit, chapter nineteen, reads, **will they not say that you are insane?** And likewise, I found it written in the codex of Donatianus. Therefore, lest any scruple remain, we have translated it: **will they not say you are mad?** Just as Theophylact and Chrysostom most clearly interpret it.

33 **For the secrets**] <note>original: *Kai houtōs ta krypta tēs kardias*</note>, that is, **And so the secrets of the heart**: as a little later, **and so falling**, <note>original: *kai houtōs pesōn*</note>. Ambrose does not add "for," nor do the Greeks. Nor yet does he add "so," except that in the second part he puts "then" for "so," "and then falling on his face," and the rest.

<margin>34 *Has a revelation*]</margin> Although he <note>the previous Latin translator</note> previously translated this as "revelationem," he has now left the Greek word *apokalypsin*. I do not see why he preferred that. Ambrose <note>a 4th-century Church Father</note> also reads "revelationem" here. And a little before, where he says "Psalm," in Latin he could have said "song" (*canticum*).

<margin>35 *By twos, or at most threes*]</margin> <note>original: *kata dyo, ē to pleiston treis*</note>. The word "let it be" must be understood, for it preceded: "let all things be done for edification," so if anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be done "for edification." But it should be done so that in individual meetings only two speak, or at most three, and even then, not all speaking at once, but in turn—one remaining silent while the other speaks. Furthermore, what kind of stylistic phrasing is this which the Translator used: "according to two, or according to three" <note>a literalistic rendering of the Greek</note>? Or what is the relevance of what Aquinas <note>Thomas Aquinas, 13th-century theologian</note> brings up here regarding "in the mouth of two or three witnesses"? For Paul does not want more to prophesy in the same assembly simply to avoid confusion. *To pleiston* means "at the most."

<margin>36 *By parts*]</margin> <note>original: *ana meros*</note>, that is, "in turn." What does "by parts" mean? Ambrose reads "piece by piece" (*particulatim*).

<margin>37 *By individuals*]</margin> <note>original: *kath' ena*</note>, that is, "one by one" or "singly."

<margin>38 *The spirits of the prophets*]</margin> <note>original: *pneumata*</note>. In the Greek it is in the plural number: just as Jerome <note>translator of the Vulgate, c. 347–420</note> cites in the Prologue to Isaiah: "The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets." And "are subject" <note>original: *hypotassetai*</note> is a verb in the present tense: let us not think this is said about the Holy Spirit himself, but about the gift of the Spirit: which was given to individuals in such a way that it was in their own judgment to use it or not use it; this is not the case for those who are possessed or frantic <note>original: *lymphaticis*, referring to pagan ecstatic states</note>.

<margin>39 *For God is not a God of dissension*]</margin> <note>original: *akatastasias*</note>: that which more clearly sounds like "confusion, sedition, and a disordered state of affairs." Ambrose reads "a matter of dissension, not a God of dissension." And he published it thus: "Because therefore it is a matter of peace—as the Savior said, 'My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you'—no one should stop another from speaking. Unless perhaps 'of a matter' (*rei*) was changed to 'of a thing' (*res*)."

<margin>40 *As in all the churches of the saints*]</margin> In this place, the word "I teach" seems to have been added by our people <note>Latin scribes</note>. For it is not found among the Greeks. In the Verona edition of Chrysostom it is added, but in his commentary he does not touch upon it; hence it seems to be an addition. It is not added in the Aldine edition. Nor indeed did Paul "teach" in all the Churches, but in all the Churches of the saints business was conducted in order and without tumult. Something must be understood here, however: "Just as in all the Churches there is peace and concord." For he exhorts the Corinthians by the example of all, that they should do likewise: although Ambrose seems to have added something, since he wrote: "By this saying he exhorts them to do what he commanded, because he testifies that he preaches similarly in the Churches of the saints." And Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine commentator</note> twists this saying of Paul to apply to all Churches, even of the Jews and Gentiles: since unseemly dissension occurs in no Churches, you should be ashamed of these tumults in yours. Furthermore, he calls the gatherings and meetings of people "Churches." Indeed, even among the Pagans, it was considered unseemly to have a tumult in a banquet or in a council. That Latin Scholiast <note>an anonymous commentator</note> seems to read it with the Greeks, because he added this comment: "So it is everywhere, lest you think I am commanding you something new."

<margin>41 *It is permitted*]</margin> <note>original: *epitetraptai*</note>, that is, "it has been permitted." The Translator and Ambrose seem to have read *epitrepetai* <note>a slightly different Greek verb form</note>. Although the Greek word is ambiguous, sometimes meaning to permit, and sometimes to command or commit. Since this somehow follows among the ancients: "but that they should be subject to their husbands." Furthermore, for "in the church," he would have said more clearly in Latin "in the congregation" or "in the assembly."

<margin>42 *He is ignorant, he shall be ignored*]</margin> <note>original: *agnoei, agnoeitō*</note>, that is, "he is ignorant, let him be ignorant," which means: if anyone does not want to know these things, let him not know them at his own peril. However, Ambrose explains it as "he shall be ignored," citing that verse from the Gospel: "Amen I say to you, I do not know you." For I think he read *agnoeitai*. But the Greek scholia take it differently, specifically Chrysostom and Theophylact: "he is ignorant, let him be ignorant": by which figure of speech it is said, "he who is in filth, let him still be filthy."

<margin>43 *Let them be done in you*]</margin> "In you" is not found among the Greeks.

<column-break/>

<margin>1</margin> *By what reason I preached*] <note>original: *tini logō*</note>. It appears the order here is: "If you hold by what reason I preached to you." Theophylact explains it almost this way, as if Paul had indeed preached the future resurrection to the Corinthians, but had handed down nothing regarding the manner or reason of rising again. In Ambrose, we read: "that which we announced to you by word, you ought to hold." Perhaps Ambrose had written "by which word."

<margin>2</margin> *If you hold*] This passage seems to have varied in the Greek manuscripts. Ambrose reads "you ought to hold." Unless perhaps instead of *ei katechete* (if you hold), it is "certainly you hold," or *ē katechete*, as if he had woven in "surely you hold." For the Grammarians teach that *ē* also sounds like that to the Greeks. If that is not pleasing, something must be understood: "If you hold—and you certainly do hold—unless you believed in vain." We have demonstrated things of this kind elsewhere in the Pauline writings.

<margin>3</margin> *And after these the eleven*] The Greek codices have *eita tois dōdeka*, that is, "then to those twelve." But the Greek scholia struggle here, and they doubt whether by a slip of the scribe "twelve" is held instead of "eleven": or whether we should understand that Christ appeared to Matthias also, not yet indeed chosen into the Apostolic order, but nevertheless already destined by God. Theophylact says almost the same. In which place I surely wonder at the drowsiness of the Translator by whose labor the Latin Theophylact exists, who, when he sees the question raised about "twelve," nevertheless in the context translated it as "eleven," according to the Vulgate edition. One may frequently detect this kind of thoughtlessness in him, unless perhaps we prefer to blame the scribes. Ambrose reads "eleven," but he also rendered the article: *tois hendeka*, that is, "to those eleven," he says. Regarding the placed article, Augustine <note>354–430, influential North African bishop</note> also carefully notes the question in the first book of *On the Old Instrument*: *tois dōdeka*, that is, "those twelve": so that it cannot be taken as any twelve in number, but only those whom the Lord Jesus had designated. Furthermore, he unties the knot by saying that in rendering a larger number, no account is taken of some small missing part. And to this form he draws several similar passages, which he contends were spoken *kata synekdochēn* <note>by synecdoche, where the whole stands for a part</note>. The same Augustine discusses this matter in the third book of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, suspecting that the same is read erroneously by some, and adding that the number twelve was consecrated by Christ, and remained even in the eleven: especially by soon substituting Matthias in the place of Judas.
