4 **By more than five hundred brothers**] <note>original: "Plus quam quingentis fratribus"</note> Greek: <greek>ἐπάνω πεντακοσίοις ἀδελφοῖς</greek>. The term <term>Epano</term> <note>meaning "above" or "more than"</note> cannot be referred to the dative case "five hundred brothers": since among the Greeks it takes the genitive case if it is used in place of a preposition, unless I am mistaken. And yet Theophylact <note>a prominent 11th-century biblical commentator</note> admits that some interpret it in this sense, according to which our Translator <note>referring to the Vulgate</note> has rendered it. Others again take <term>epano</term> to mean *from above*, or *from heaven*, because Christ showed himself to all not on the ground, but from on high. So Chrysostom interprets <term>epano</term> as "from above" <note>original: "ἄνωθεν"</note>, denying it can be understood otherwise. This would have happened by a display of power when he was ascending into heaven. The other sense is tolerable if <term>epano</term> is an adverb and "than" <note>original: "quam"</note> is understood; just as we say, "more than a thousand." Among the Greeks, <term>epano</term> is bounded by <term>epana</term>, that is, *once*. Though the meaning is nearly the same.

5 **Of whom many**] <note>original: "Ex quibus multi"</note> Greek: <greek>πλείους</greek>, that is, *more*, or *several*. Although this is a minor point.

6 **They fell asleep**] <note>original: "Dormierunt"</note> If anyone wishes to quibble over the nature of the language, those who have "slept" are those who have awakened. Therefore, it should have been translated either as *they sleep*, or *they fell asleep*: so that it comes from "falling asleep," although I do not know if the specific word <term>obdormio</term> <note>to fall asleep in death</note> is found in standard usage.

7 **I am not worthy**] <note>original: "Non sum dignus"</note> Greek: <greek>ἱκανὸς καλεῖσθαι</greek>, that is, fit or suitable to be called.

8 **And his grace in me**] <note>original: "Et gratia ejus in me"</note> Greek: <greek>καὶ ἡ χάρις αὐτοῦ ἡ εἰς ἐμὲ</greek>, that is, *and his grace toward me, or the favor which he showed in me*. And why not rather *void* <note>original: "inanis"</note> than *empty* <note>original: "vacua"</note>? Finally, a certain author, Ambrose, read it so that he translated it as *poor* instead of empty; though in Greek it is <greek>κενὴ</greek>. Unless perhaps, according to the idiom of the Hebrew language, the poor are called "empty": as in that passage, "he has sent the rich away empty." For he opposed the empty to the rich. Here he calls "empty" that which is sterile and unfruitful.

9 **Yet not I, but the grace of God with me**] <note>original: "Non ego autem, sed gratia Dei mecum"</note> Greek: <greek>ἀλλ’ ἡ χάρις τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἡ σὺν ἐμοί</greek>, that is, *but the grace of God, which is with me*. For Paul corrects what he had just said, that he had labored more than all. "On the contrary," he says, "I am not the one who did this, but rather the grace of God, which was present with me": so that we may understand this whole thing is to be credited to God. Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo Valla, whose work inspired Erasmus</note> in this place rejects those who, from these words, assert a grace which they call *cooperating*, among whom is Aquinas, and before him Augustine. Nor do I see what this passage does against them: for the Greek conjunction <term>syn</term> <note>meaning "with"</note> signifies favor and help; and help does not exclude the work of the one who is being helped: "the [grace] with me," that is, *which is with me*, or rather *which is a help to me*. We translate, *which is present to me*: because, as I said, the preposition <term>syn</term> sometimes signifies assistance, as in "with the Muses." Jerome, writing against the Pelagians, reads, *the grace of God, which is with me*, explaining the force of the article.

10 **So we preached**] <note>original: "Sic prædicavimus"</note> Greek: <greek>οὕτως κηρύσσομεν</greek>, that is, "so we preach," in the present tense. Ambrose also reads it this way, supported by a very ancient Pauline manuscript. And Augustine likewise reports this passage in the second book against Faustus the Manichæan, chapter two, according to the reliability of the old handwritten copies.

11 **For you are still**] <note>original: "Adhuc enim estis"</note> The word "for" is redundant. For these things are referred to the previous argument: "If Christ did not rise, then you are still in your sins." It should be noted that in Ambrose, in the latter place, the phrase *your faith is vain* is not repeated. For he reads it thus: *But if Christ did not rise, you are still in your sins, and those who fell asleep in Christ have perished.* But both the reading and the commentary of Theophylact agree with ours.

12 **If in this life only we are hoping in Christ**] <note>original: "Si in hac vita tantum in Christo sperantes simus"</note> Greek: <greek>Εἰ ἐν τῇ ζωῇ ταύτῃ ἠλπικότες ἐσμὲν ἐν Χριστῷ μόνον</greek>. The meaning of the pre-

<gloss>p</gloss> But if Christ is preached that he rose from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? <margin>12</margin>
Furthermore, if there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ did not rise either. <margin>13</margin>
<margin>B</margin> <gloss>q</gloss> But if Christ did not rise, then our preaching is clearly in vain, and your faith is also in vain. <margin>14</margin>
And we are found also to be false witnesses of God, because we have testified concerning God that he raised up Christ, whom he did not raise up, if indeed the dead do not rise. <margin>15</margin>
For if the dead do not rise, then Christ did not rise either. <margin>16</margin>
<gloss>r</gloss> But if Christ did not rise, your faith is useless: you are still in your sins. <margin>17</margin>
<gloss>s</gloss> Therefore also those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. <margin>18</margin>
<gloss>t</gloss> If in this life we have our hope fixed only in Christ, we are the most miserable of all men. <margin>19</margin>
<margin>C</margin> <gloss>u</gloss> But now Christ has risen from the dead, he was the firstfruits of those who have slept. <margin>20</margin>
<gloss>x</gloss> For since death was through a man, the resurrection of the dead was also through a man. <margin>21</margin>
<gloss>y</gloss> For just as through Adam all die, so also through Christ shall all be made alive. <margin>22</margin>
<gloss>z</gloss> But each one in <margin>23</margin>

---

<margin>D</margin> 13 **We are more miserable than all**] <note>original: "Miserabiliores simus omnibus"</note> Greek: <greek>ἐλεεινότεροι πάντων</greek>. It appears that among the Greeks the comparative is put in place of the superlative, *most miserable of all*. Although Aulus Gellius <note>a 2nd-century Roman grammarian</note> also speaks in this manner. Otherwise, the difficulty could have been avoided if one had translated, *we are more miserable than any men*: since in this type of speech *all* and *any* fall into the same sense.

14 **Firstfruits of those sleeping**] <note>original: "Primitiæ dormientium"</note> In the Greek manuscripts the verb <greek>ἐγένετο</greek> <note>meaning "became" or "was"</note> is consistently added, that is, *he was made*, or *he was*: although it is connected somewhat awkwardly with what precedes. Hence it seems to have been added by scribes among the Greeks. Ambrose translates <term>aparchen</term> <note>firstfruits</note> as *beginning*: because he was the first of all.

15 **Since indeed by man came death**] <note>original: "Quandoquidem per hominem mors"</note> In the Greek codices that I have seen, it is held thus: <greek>Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ δι’ ἀνθρώπου ὁ θάνατος, καὶ δι’ ἀνθρώπου ἡ ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν</greek>. That is, *For after death [came] through man, also through man [came] the resurrection of the dead*. For the conjunction <term>kai</term> <note>meaning "and" or "also"</note> has a hidden force of inference. Since it is established that death arose through one man, it was a consequence that through a man the resurrection of the dead should arise. Theophylact explains in this sense.

<margin>E</margin> 16 **Just as in Adam all**] <note>original: "Sicut in Adam omnes"</note> Greek: <greek>Ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐν τῷ Ἀδάμ</greek>, that is, *For just as in Adam*, or *through Adam: as follows presently, through Christ*. The "for" <note>original: "enim"</note> was missing in our manuscripts. And according to the custom of the Greeks, he reads "of man" <note>original: "ἀνθρώπου"</note>: for Paul connects the proof with that which he puts forward: Since death had crept in through one man, it is fitting that life be given to all through one man: *for just as through Adam etc*.

<margin>F</margin> 17 **In Christ all shall be made alive**] <note>original: "In Christo omnes vivificabuntur"</note> Cyprian—or rather Rufinus—explaining the creed <note>original: "symbolum fidei"</note>, reads *are made alive*: so that it corresponds to the earlier word *die*. And this reading would be far more approved by me, if the manuscripts did not oppose it. Otherwise, if *are made alive* offends us because the resurrection is to be in the future, then by the same effort the word *die* should offend us, because once many were made to die in Adam. Paul here did not have regard for time, but felt just as if he had said: "Just as through Adam there is death, so through Christ there is resurrection." Hitherto in my labors I have cited the exposition of the creed under the name of Cyprian, although the character of the speech showed something else, and in some places the talk is more wordy than is typical of Cyprian: nevertheless I did not dare to pronounce on it, nor had I focused my mind here. And I had tasted Rufinus's creed rather than read it through. But the learned show by many arguments that this work is by Rufinus, not Cyprian. First, because it is written to Gaudentius, to whom Rufinus dedicated certain other of his labors, such as the "Itinerary of Peter." Furthermore, because Heretics are mentioned there whom it is certain were not yet born in the age of Cyprian, such as Arius, Mani, Eunomius, Donatus, Photinus, and several others, some of whom were later than Cyprian by whole centuries. They add also that argument of no small weight, that Rufinus, in the first book of his invectives against Jerome, writes in this manner: *But for the greater reliability of the matter I add something more, and compelled by the necessity of slanderers, I reveal the singular and chief mystery of our Church. For since all Churches in the matter of the sacraments...* <note>Erasmus frequently uses his annotations to perform "higher criticism," such as correcting the authorship of traditional texts like those of the Church Fathers.</note>

He spends significant effort correcting the Vulgate's Latin grammar against the Greek source and debates the authorship of a creed commentary formerly attributed to Cyprian.</summary>

# TO THE CORINTHIANS I. CHAPTER XV.
### Aaa
<meta>catchword: things</meta>

<margin>23</margin> Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ’s at his coming.
<margin>24</margin> Then the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God and the Father, when he shall have abolished all rule and all authority and power.
<margin>25</margin> For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet.
<margin>26</margin> The last enemy to be abolished is death.
<margin>27</margin> For he has put all things under his feet. But when he says that all things are put under him, it is manifest that he is excluded who put all things under him.
<margin>28</margin> And when all things shall be subjected to him, then shall the Son also himself be subjected to him who put all things under him, so that God may be all in all.
<margin>29</margin> Otherwise, what shall they do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all? Why then are they baptized for the dead?
<margin>30</margin> And why do we stand in danger every hour?
<margin>31</margin> I die daily by our glorying <note>original: "καύχησιν," meaning boasting or pride in a person or work</note>, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord.
<margin>32</margin> If, according to the manner of men, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what does it profit me if the dead do not rise? Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.
<margin>33</margin> Do not be deceived. Bad company corrupts good morals.

<margin>35</margin> But someone will say: How are the dead raised? And with what body do they come?

<margin>C</margin> ...they hand down the Creed <note>The Apostles' Creed</note> in such a way that, after they have spoken of the "remission of sins," they add the "resurrection of the flesh." We say, the "resurrection of *this* flesh." So says Ruffinus <note>Tyrannius Ruffinus, a 4th-century monk and translator</note>. To this, he adds an admonition in the Creed, and in two places: at the beginning, where he teaches that the Creed is not held to be identical in every respect in all Churches; and again at the end, when treating this part of the Creed. In the former place, he specifically names the Church of Aquileia: "We, however," he says, "follow that order which we received in the Church of Aquileia for the grace of the washing <note>Baptism</note>." It is well-established that Ruffinus was baptized at Aquileia and held the office of Priest there; whereas Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian, 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage</note> was an African, first a Priest and later Bishop of Carthage. Furthermore, Gennadius <note>Gennadius of Massilia, a 5th-century priest and historian</note>, among those works which Ruffinus did not translate from the Greek but composed by his own effort, mentions with great praise the *Exposition of the Apostles' Creed*. However, it is certain from irrefutable arguments that both works—the one joined to the works of Jerome under the name of Ruffinus, and the one read under the name of Cyprian—are the same and by the same author. This makes it all the more surprising what that person intended who varied the Scripture in countless places, especially in the wording. For if he did this (as do craftsmen who add gilding to cups or attach new handles so that they do not appear to belong to another) to deceive the reader, he ought to have rewritten the preface and erased those speeches and names which do not allow the work to seem as if it were written by Cyprian. Moreover, he should have rewoven a good part of the discourse. Now, omitting the necessary signs I have mentioned, the agreement is so great that they cannot be seen as two works by two authors; yet there is such a discrepancy in words that it cannot be attributed to a slip of the pen. I did not want this to be hidden from the reader, because in many other places, but especially in the exposition of the Creed, I cite this book under the name of Cyprian.

<margin>18</margin> 18 *Those who believed at his coming*] <note>original Greek: "οἱ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ αὐτοῦ"</note>, that is, "those who are Christ’s, at his coming." And Saint Ambrose reads it thus, so that we may understand those whom Christ shall find as his own when he arrives. For he is speaking here of the resurrection of the godly.

<margin>D 19</margin> 19 *When he shall have abolished all rule*] Ambrose reads this place thus: *When he shall have delivered the kingdom to God and the Father, when he shall have removed all rule and all power and all strength and all dominion.* Indeed, he translates the Greek word <note>original: "καταργήσῃ"</note> as "removed," though it could also be translated as "abolished" or "made obsolete."

<margin>E 20</margin> 20 *And last the enemy*] "Last" is a noun here, not the adverb "lastly"; as if you were to say: "Death, the last of all, shall be destroyed." The word is <note>original: "καταργεῖται"</note>, that is, "is destroyed" or "is abolished," in the present tense. Saint Jerome, in his commentaries on Isaiah, cites this more than once in this way: *Death, the last enemy, shall be destroyed*; as if to say, the final foe of all shall be destroyed, namely death. For, as Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a pioneering Renaissance humanist</note> elegantly taught in this place, a person can be an "enemy" without being a "foe" <note>distinguishing between 'inimicus' (personal enemy) and 'hostis' (public foe)</note>. Furthermore, in Greek, "death" is of the masculine gender. Augustine also, in explaining Psalm 51, reads "last" as a noun, not an adverb. He does the same elsewhere, and specifically in his third sermon on the words of the Apostle. Again, quite frequently in the books he wrote against Faustus the Manichean. And it is seen written this way even now in the Pauline manuscript. The manuscripts of Constance agreed. Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers</note>, following I know not what, when bringing forward this passage several times in his books on the Trinity, reads: *The last enemy, death, has been conquered.*

<margin>21</margin> 21 *Without doubt except him*] <note>original Greek: "δηλονότι"</note>. This should have been rendered more fully: for as it stands, the sentence is incomplete. Yet when it says all things are subjected, it is clear that he is excepted who subjected all things to him.

<margin>22</margin> 22 *By your glorying*] It is not here <note>original: "δόξα"</note>, "glory" or "honor," but <note>original: "καύχησις"</note>, "glorying" or "boasting": <note>original: "νὴ τὴν ἡμετέραν καύχησιν"</note>, that is, "by our glorying." "By" in this place is the preposition of one swearing an oath. And since he has already boasted with a certain holy pride regarding the progress of his Gospel, he now swears by that glory with which he glories in Christ, as if by something sacred and most dear to him. Augustine also cites this passage in his eighty-ninth Epistle. Again, more fully in his twenty-eighth sermon on the words of the Apostle, showing that Paul swore in this place, and that this is permissible according to the Greek manuscripts. Nor is there any reason for people to dodge the issue and deny the Apostle swore, when in many other places he clearly swears.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...in his own order: the firstfruits Christ, then those who are Christ’s at his coming. Then the end, when he <margin>24</margin> shall have delivered the kingdom to God and the Father, when he shall have abolished all rule and all power and strength. For he must reign until he has put all <margin>25</margin> enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be abolished <margin>26</margin> is death. For he has subjected all things under his feet. But <margin>27</margin> when he says that all things are subjected, it is clear that he who subjected all things to him is to be excepted. And when <margin>28</margin> all things have been subjected to him, then also the Son himself shall be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all. Otherwise what will they do who are baptized <margin>29</margin> for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all? Why then are they <margin>B</margin> baptized for the dead? Why also do we stand in danger <margin>30</margin> at every moment? Daily I die by our glorying, <margin>31</margin> which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord. If according to the manner of men I fought with beasts at <margin>32</margin> Ephesus, what use is it to me, if the dead do not rise? Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. Do not be <margin>33</margin> deceived. Bad conversations corrupt good morals. Awake to righteousness, and do not sin; for <margin>34</margin> some have ignorance of God; I speak this to your shame. But someone will say, How do the dead rise? <margin>35</margin>

---

<margin>23</margin> 23 *I fought with beasts*] <note>original Greek: "ἐθηριομάχησα"</note>: a compound word in Greek. For in ancient times, those condemned were often thrown to the beasts. It is strange that no mention of this matter is made in the Acts of the Apostles. For it does not quite satisfy me that the Greek interpreters, among whom is Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator</note>, twist this to refer to the riot stirred up by Demetrius the silversmith on account of Diana of the Ephesians.

<margin>24</margin> 24 *Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die*] This is the voice of those who distrust and despair of God's promises. "For tomorrow we die" <note>original: "ἀποθνήσκομεν"</note>, that is, "we are dying." Lorenzo <note>Valla</note> reminds us that this was a Laconian <note>Spartan</note> proverb. However, it exists in Isaiah chapter 22, in the very same words as Paul cited. Although in Hebrew the verb is in the future tense <note>original Hebrew: "נמות"</note>. Truly, this matters little to the sense: and I do not know whether Paul wrote <note>original Greek: "ἀποθανούμεθα"</note> (we shall die); especially since here, in other respects, the Seventy <note>the Septuagint, Greek Old Testament</note> do not disagree with the Hebrew. Certainly, in the Septuagint it is read: *Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.*

<margin>25</margin> 25 *Corrupt morals*] <note>original Greek: "Φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί"</note>. This is a six-foot verse <note>senarius</note> of Menander <note>the famous 4th-century BC Greek playwright</note>, as Saint Jerome indicates, and it stands on its own feet if the apostrophe is preserved:
->Bad company corrupts good morals.<-
We have rendered it in verse:
->Good morals are corrupted by evil talk.<-

<margin>F 26</margin> 26 *Awake to righteousness*] <note>original Greek: "Ἐκνήψατε δικαίως"</note>, that is, "be sober justly," or "awake justly": so that "justly" is an adverb: that is, as is fitting and right. For some are awake even for injustice: a point which Theophylact also noted. Otherwise, what was the point of commanding the "just" to be awake and not to sin, when if they do so, they are not just? Secondly, how is it fitting to call them "just" when he is rebuking them, and of whom he immediately adds, "some have ignorance of God"? Because Ambrose also—as one may gather from his interpretation—reads it just as it is found among the Greeks: "He commanded them," he says, "to be just": as if "Awake justly" were equivalent to saying "Awake unto justice." Yet those who use the word "just" as a title do not command them to be just, even if in common manuscripts it is written, *Awake, be ye just*. In the older manuscript of Constance, the genuine reading remained, *Awake justly*: lest anyone should despise the consensus of the Greeks.

<margin>27</margin> 27 *To your shame*] <note>original Greek: "πρὸς ἐντροπὴν"</note>, that is, to a blushing, and to shame.

<margin>G 28</margin> 28 *How do they rise*] <note>original Greek: "ἐγείρονται"</note>, that is, "they are raised." And they "come" <note>original: "ἔρχονται"</note>; it would be more fittingly translated as "they come," to match the preceding verb. For he is not speaking here of the time, but of the manner.

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER XV.

36 You fool! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies. 37 And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain. 38 But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body. 39 Not all flesh is the same: but there is one kind for humans, another for animals, another for fish, <margin>Other versions: for birds</margin> 40 and another for birds. There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is one thing, and the glory of the earthly is another. 41 There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. 42 So it is with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. 43 It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. 44 It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body. 45 Thus it is written, “The first man Adam became a living soul”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. 46 But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual. 47 The first man was from the earth, made of dust; the second man, the Lord from heaven. 48 As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven. 49 Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven. 50 I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. 51 Listen, I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed,

---

...as is usually done with words in the present tense, as if you were to say: "Such is the resurrection," or "Such is the coming." For then the action of the thing is declared without specifying a particular time. Augustine, in his work *Against Faustus*, book eleven, chapter three, reads "they come" <note>original Greek: ερχεται</note>, although the Greek word is ambiguous.

29 **Foolish** <note>original Latin: Insipiens</note>] <note>original Greek: Ἄφρον</note>, that is, Stupid, Mindless, or Foolish. The word is derived from *phren* (mind), with a negative particle added. *Foolish you*. A punctuation mark should have been placed after "Foolish": *Foolish one, you, what you sow*, that is, *Stupid man, that which you sow*. For he distinguishes by the pronoun the person of the man from the person of God: "If what you sow comes forth much more excellent, how much more abundantly will God achieve this in the resurrection, of which he is properly the author."

30 **Unless it first dies**] Why was it necessary to add "first," since the Greek is <note>original: ἐὰν μὴ ἀποθανῃ</note>, which means "unless it shall have died"? Augustine, citing this passage in his third book *To the Catechumens*, chapter ten, does not add the adverb "first."

31 **As it happens**] <note>original Greek: εἰ τύχοι</note>. He translates it this way here and a little earlier, as is the custom of someone providing an example. Augustine, in his 146th Epistle, translates <note>original Greek: εἰ τύχοι</note> as "perhaps." He does the same in his literal commentary on *Genesis*, book five, chapter twenty.

32 **As he wills**] <note>original Greek: καθὼς ἠθέλησεν</note>, that is, *as he shall have willed*; so that it is in the subjunctive mood. And indeed, Augustine cites it this way in the passage we just mentioned.

33 **Not all flesh**] <note>original Greek: Οὐ πᾶσα σὰρξ</note>, that is, *Not just any flesh*.

34 **Celestial and terrestrial bodies**] <note>original Greek: ἐπουράνια & ἐπίγεια</note>, which sounds as if you were to say "those things that dwell in heaven" and "those things that dwell on earth," so that we do not understand it to mean the heavens themselves, or the material of heaven or earth.

35 **Another brightness**] <note>original Greek: δόξα</note>. The same word that he had just translated as "glory," he now translates as "brightness." Perhaps because he thought it absurd to speak of the "glory" of the sun, or of the moon, or of the stars. On the contrary, "glory" seems to signify something greater—dignity, majesty—than "brightness." Elsewhere, the Translator renders <note>original: δόξα</note> as "majesty." Finally, since Paul used the same word throughout, what was the point of the Translator offering different Latin words when the sense did not require it?

36 **For star differs from star**] <note>original Greek: ἀστὴρ γὰρ ἀστέρος διαφέρει</note>, that is, *for one star excels another*. For that is also what <note>original Greek: διαφέρειν</note> signifies to the Greeks.

37 **Sown in ignobility**] Ambrose reads "ignominy," and more correctly, for <note>original Greek: ἀτιμίᾳ</note>.

38 **If there is a natural body**] The "if" is redundant: <note>original Greek: ἔστι σῶμα</note>, that is, *it is a body*. However, Ambrose does not touch upon this particle in his reading or explanation, nor do the commentators. Theophylact <note>an 11th-century biblical exegete</note>, however, interprets it. It might seem to have been repeated here from above, and what the commentator added was perhaps moved into the main text by a careless scribe.

39 **The first man Adam was made**] Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>a French humanist scholar</note> advises that the word "man" is superfluous. Although in most of the Greek codices I have managed to see, I found it written as <note>original Greek: ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος Adam</note>, that is, *the first man Adam*. Nevertheless, from Ambrose’s interpretation, one can suspect that he read simply "Adam," omitting the word "man," since he says the Apostle establishes two "Adams." Furthermore, in the second part of the verse, Adam is found alone without the mention of "man": *the last Adam into a life-giving spirit*. It is likely that "man" was added by some translator who wanted to explain what "Adam" meant among the Hebrews—namely, "man." Consequently, in Genesis, as often as the word for man is repeated, <term>Adam <note>original Hebrew: אָדָם</note></term> is placed there.

<meta>catchword: Adam po-</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>36</margin> Foolish one, what you
sow is not brought to life, unless it has died. And this
<margin>17</margin> which you sow, you do not sow the body that will be born, but
a bare grain, for example, of wheat, or of some
of the others. But God gives it a body, as he willed, and
<margin>38</margin> to each of the seeds its own body. Not all flesh is
<margin>39</margin> the same flesh: but there is one flesh of men, another
flesh of beasts, another of fish, another of

<margin>40</margin> heavenly bodies, and there are earthly

<margin>41</margin> another glory of the stars: for star differs from star

<margin>43</margin> sown in ignominy, it rises in glory: it is sown in

The first man Adam was made into a living

<margin>46</margin> the spiritual was not first, but the natural,

us—

---

And a little later, omitting "Adam," he repeats only "man": *The first man from the earth*, and so on. Cyprian, in his sermon on jealousy and envy, quite well added the pronoun "that": *such as that one from the mud, such are they who are from the mud*, as if expressing the force of the article, which I wish the Translator had done elsewhere: *That first man from the earth, earthly* <note>original Greek: ὁ πρῶτος</note>.

<margin>D</margin> 40 **Into a living soul**] Now, Reader, I think you recognize the idiom of this phrasing, having been warned so often; it is said *he was made into a living soul* instead of *he was made a living soul*, just as it is said, *Be to me as a protector God*.

41 **The second man from heaven, heavenly**] The Greeks have a reading different from ours. And they do so consistently, with Chrysostom and Theophylact interpreting it in the same way: <note>original Greek: ὁ δεύτερος άνθρωπος, ὁ Κύριος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ</note>, that is, *the second man, the Lord himself from heaven*. Although, to speak frankly, I prefer what is written in our codices, especially since Jerome and Ambrose read it that way; it responds better to what preceded: *from the earth, earthly*. Therefore, I think "the Lord" <note>original Greek: ὁ Κύριος</note> was added by some studious person who wanted to make the speech clearer; nonetheless, we have rendered it so that the Greek and Latin would not fail to correspond.

42 **Let us also bear the image of the heavenly**] *We shall bear* <note>original Latin: Portabimus</note> is in the future tense in the Greek: <note>original: φορέσομεν</note>. Although some codices have <note>original: φορέσωμεν</note>, that is, *let us bear*; it does not matter much to the meaning, except that the future tense was more fitting for this place, in which Paul <margin>E</margin> deals with the future resurrection. We have carried the image of the earthly Adam by sinning and dying; we shall carry the image of the later one by living innocently, and we will imitate his immortality in a certain way, since here is the beginning and a kind of meditation on it. The exhortation "let us bear" could also be tolerated. Theophylact points out both readings: "we shall bear," as it predicts future immortality; and "let us bear," as it exhorts to purity of life. The latter fits well with what follows: "flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God." Ambrose reads "let us bear," not "we shall bear." Nor is there any danger if we read "we shall bear" that we might seem to agree with the Arians, who denied that we would have flesh after the resurrection: we will have flesh, and the same flesh, but not in all respects the same kind. Saint Ambrose also touches on this meaning.

43 **They cannot possess**] <note>original Greek: κληρονομῆσαι</note>, that is, *to receive by inheritance*. And a little later, *it will possess* <note>original Greek: κληρονομεῖ</note>, that is, *you receive by inheritance*, using a word in the present tense, even though the Latin <margin>F</margin> copies protest. Theophylact reminds us that Basil interpreted these things in such a way as to say that Paul wished to exhort the Corinthians to innocence of life with these words. If this opinion is pleasing, the present tense verb was gentler, but it notes the fact of the matter rather than a distinction of time. And the commentary itself shows that Chrysostom read it this way. I ask you, Reader, to compare Ambrose's commentaries in this place with those that are falsely circulated under the name of Jerome; you will find the same words, and you will find this in many other places. In this spot, many agree word-for-word. I have some doubt, however, whether these were transcribed here from Ambrose's commentaries, or whether they were from other commentaries but substituted for Ambrose's. For what does the boldness of scribes not permit themselves then?

44 **We shall all indeed rise**] The Greek says this: <note>original: Πάντες μὲν οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα, πάντες δὲ ἀλλαγησόμεθα</note>, that is, *We shall not all indeed sleep, but we shall all be changed*. But Saint Jerome, in his letter to Minerva and Alexander, shows that this passage is read in two ways among the Greeks: both in this way that I have indicated here, and in the way the common edition [the Vulgate] has it. And indeed, in this place, it is surprising how they pour—

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed philological defense of his translation of 1 Corinthians 15:51. He is specifically addressing the controversy over whether the text should read "We shall not all sleep [die], but we shall all be changed" (the Greek reading) or "We shall all rise, but not all be changed" (the common Latin reading).</meta>

# TO THE CORINTHIANS I. CHAPTER XV.

The Greek commentaries provide evidence for this. Theophylact and Chrysostom <note>Theophylact (c. 1050–1107) and John Chrysostom (c. 347–407) were influential Byzantine biblical commentators.</note> read and interpret the passage exactly as we read and translate it from the Greek manuscripts. Chrysostom likewise cites it while explaining the eleventh chapter of the Epistle to the Romans, such that the meaning is: *Not all will die, but all must nevertheless be changed.* Furthermore, if anyone wishes to doubt our citation, let them know that Chrysostom and Theophylact are held in the Dominican Library at Basel, from which many volumes were made available. Anyone who knows Greek will be able, upon examining the passage, to either confirm or refute me. Tertullian reads it no differently in his book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*. This is clearly detected from his interpretation, even though a scribe corrupted the words of the Apostle he recited. For he adds: *For who will not desire, while he is in the flesh, to put on immortality, and to continue a life sacrificed by death through a substitute transformation*, and so on. Saint Jerome also cites this passage in his *Letter to Marcella*, in the third question; he explains the passage in 1 Thessalonians 4 according to this sentiment and mentions no other. Origen also cites this passage in this sense in the second book of *Against Celsus*.

But I think it better, for the sake of those who are distrustful, to add his actual words: *The trumpet,* he says, *will give the signal, and the dead will rise incorruptible.* Regarding the changing of the living and the separate rising of the dead, he writes: *And we shall be changed*; which he certainly said after he had first said, *The dead shall rise.* Moreover, even in the first Epistle to the Thessalonians, presenting the same distinction in other words—affirming that some are sleeping and others are living—he says: *For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again,* and so forth. From these things it is clear enough what Origen felt: namely, that all the godly are to be changed—both those who will rise and those who are found alive—the latter will not die, but they must nevertheless be changed along with those who had died. And for this reason, he had said at the beginning that all were to be changed, even if not all were to rise.

Paul places himself among those whom the coming of the Lord would find alive because Christ willed that day to be hidden from everyone. It appears from other passages that Paul always wanted that day to be expected, although I am aware it can be understood as Paul using the first person to designate whoever the coming of the Lord happens to find, as in *We who are alive*, and so on. If the coming of the Lord should happen now, what would happen to us would happen to whoever is there. Saint Ambrose seems to follow that reading which we commonly hear <note>The Latin Vulgate reading: "We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed."</note>, so that we feel not everyone is changed for glory, even though everyone will rise to life. However, even he adds another interpretation in which he indicates there will be some who do not die, and for that reason do not rise, yet they are changed. For no one "rises" unless they have died.

A little further down, explaining the passage *at the last trumpet, for the trumpet shall sound*, and so on, he partly mentions this view: *The dead,* he says, *are to be understood either as sinners, who even while living are said to be dead, or certainly he says simply that all the dead rise, and only the saints, who were found living and righteous, are changed into glory.* Truly, what Paul writes to the Thessalonians agrees more with what the Greeks read: *For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so God will bring with Him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus. For this we say to you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep, for the Lord Himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the Archangel, and with the trumpet of God: and the dead in Christ will rise first: then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord.*

That passage in 2 Corinthians 5 is also referred to this same sense: *because we do not want to be unclothed, but further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life*; that is, that immortality might be granted without death. From these things it is clear that not everyone will sleep, but some will be remaining at the coming of Christ. There are those who say that even those who remain will die and live again suddenly in a moment; Augustine records this opinion in the twentieth book of *The City of God*, chapter twenty, but only as a conjecture that should not be entirely rejected, not as a settled opinion or decree. He also declares in the same place that the Latin manuscripts varied. In some it was written, *We shall all indeed rise*; in others, *We shall all indeed sleep.* He indicates the same in the booklet on the *Eight Questions of Dulcitius*, question three. Furthermore, he argues that from either reading it follows that all die, because no one "rises" unless they are dead. <margin>See Jerome, Letter to Minervius and Alexander.</margin> However, Jerome, in his *Letter to Minervius*, denies that this reading *We shall all indeed rise*—which Ambrose follows—is found in the Greek codices.

Moreover, the person who collected the brief commentaries on all the Pauline Epistles (which some think are Jerome’s, but falsely, as the preface itself sufficiently testifies—though I think the preface is by a different hand than the collection of commentaries itself, which appear to be by some studious and not unlearned person drawing a compendium from various commentaries of the Ancients). For whoever it was who added the little preface, though he is unlearned and inarticulate <note>Original Latin: "infans ac balbus," literally "an infant and a stammerer."</note>, he nevertheless impudently pretended to be Jerome. But as I began to say, whoever was the compiler <note>Original Latin: "rhaphodus," a stitcher of texts.</note> of that work, he indicates a triple reading of this passage: First, *We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed*: so that "to be changed" is proper to one passing into the blessed life; and of this reading he makes this sense: *We shall all rise who are found dead; we shall not all be changed who are found living in the body*; because only the godly are to be changed, but many ungodly are to be found alive. Second, *We shall all indeed sleep, but we shall not all be changed*: so that we accept that everyone will die, but not everyone will be changed for glory. Third, *We shall all indeed not sleep, but we shall all be changed*: so that you understand not everyone will die, yet everyone will be transformed for that same glory. Indeed, this whole discourse does not pertain to all men in common, but properly to the righteous. And he especially approves of this last reading as most congruent with the Apostle's meaning. Nor did Aquinas keep silent about this triple reading, disapproving of none, although Jerome, having followed it, prefers this common one—but in such a way that he denies a different version

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> conflicts with the faith or has a heretical meaning. Furthermore, as for the fact that some are offended because it seems hardly true when it is written, *It is appointed for all men once to die* <note>Hebrews 9:27</note>, if we say some will not die, this is easily solved: the prerogative of a few does not obstruct the common law, as Origen reminds us several times. For it is not therefore untrue what Paul wrote, that *all die in Adam, and all have sinned in Adam*, even if Mary was immune from all sin. Nor is it immediately false what the Prophet wrote, that there is no one free from sin, not even an infant of one day, if we say that Jeremiah and John the Baptist were both born and lived without any sin.

But why do we use these arguments? Since Jerome himself, whom we cited before, writing to Marcella in the third question, openly affirms that there would be those who, while living, would be transformed to the glory of immortality. I would add his words, were they not reviewed in this place by the *Gloss*, as they call the ordinary one. And here is the one snag that moved Augustine and some others to shrink from the Greek reading. Indeed, <margin>B</margin> this also offended Augustine: *in Christ all shall be made alive*, especially since he adds, *that which you sow is not made alive unless it first dies.* And by these words of Paul, he thinks we are urged to believe that the living will suddenly die and live again in the very act of being "caught up": although, in my opinion, there is no necessity for this if we accommodate Paul's present discourse to those who had fallen asleep before the coming of Christ. For Paul is not laboring here to persuade us that everyone must die (which is by no means difficult to believe), but to persuade us that those who are buried will live again in the manner of a seed committed to the earth.

And yet the same Augustine, in the book *On Church Dogmas* (even if that book does not seem to be by the same author), clearly pronounces that those who follow the Greek reading—which is the only one they now have—are equally Catholic. For when he had recounted the opinion of those who did not want anyone to be exempt from the common law of dying, he adds: *But because there are also other equally Catholic and learned men who believe that those found alive at the coming of the Lord are to be changed to incorruption and immortality while the soul remains in the body, and that this serves for them instead of a resurrection from the dead—that they lay aside mortality by transformation, not by death—* whoever acquiesces to this, <margin>C</margin> is not a heretic, unless he becomes a heretic out of contentiousness. For it suffices in the Church to believe that the resurrection of the flesh will occur from death according to the law.

Augustine, or whoever was the author of that work, equates both readings; and that sense which the Greek codices we see today follow seems to establish the resurrection no less effectively than the other. For since in some versions the same bodies are said to be changed to the glory of immortality, the error of those who denied the same bodies would rise is more effectively defeated. If that [denial] were true, there would now be inequality among the blessed, with some possessing their own body and others having some other which they did not have before. Furthermore, regarding the fact that Augustine, in the twentieth book of *The City of God*, chapter twenty, twists that saying of Paul to the Corinthians—*what you sow is not brought to life unless it dies*—Paul is not acting there to teach that there is no one who will not die, but rather so that no one might despair of rising from death, since even a rotted seed in a furrow rises into a plant.

Therefore, which reading is most to be embraced, the learned reader will see. I have not taken up the business of pronouncing on such matters, <margin>D</margin> except that, as I said, the Greek reading is more consistent with the other passage in Thessalonians. And whenever the Ancients admit that a reading is diverse, the one that seems more absurd at first glance usually becomes more *suspect* to me <note>Erasmus's marginal note: *Read: more true*</note>; so that it is plausible that a reader, either unlearned or inattentive, being offended by the perceived absurdity, changed the scripture. Although I know, as I said, in Jerome's booklet to Alexander and Minervius, both readings having been mentioned and explained, this one we now commonly use is preferred.

Furthermore, I suspect this was the occasion for varying the scripture: he who read *We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed*, not noticing that Paul is here speaking properly of the resurrection of the godly, thought the word *changed* did not apply to all, since the ungodly are not to be changed. For he calls the transition to a happy immortality "change" here. And soon after, when he adds, *And the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed*, he shows the mind of an inattentive reader: for what purpose, having said before concerning the godly *we shall all be changed*, would he now, as if repeating what he had said redundantly, <margin>E</margin> say, *And the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed*? He did not notice that Paul here separated the godly dead from the godly living: for when he says, *And the dead shall rise incorruptible*, he means the godly who had already fallen asleep in Christ before Christ's coming; when he adds, *and we shall be changed*, he explains that which he had begun to say a little before: *We shall indeed not all sleep, but we shall all be changed.* And yet this snag alone moved Jerome to prefer the reading common among us.

Furthermore, Paul, as I said, numbers himself among those whom that day would find alive, whether he truly thought this or for the sake of teaching transfers to the first person what could be said under any person. That he speaks here of the godly is declared both by what precedes and what follows this passage. For before, teaching that we must meditate on the immortality of that life, he says: *But this I say, brothers, that flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God, nor shall corruption <margin>F</margin> possess incorruption.* And soon he returns to the same: *For it is necessary for this corruptible* and so forth. And again, *Where, O death, is your sting*, and so forth. All these things certainly fit the godly, but not the ungodly. Since, therefore, most people held the opinion that Christ would come suddenly as He had promised in the Gospel, and they had already learned from Paul that the dead would rise and be presented for divine judgment, they asked what would happen to those whom that day struck while living. He responds that these too, even if they do not "rise" because they have not died, are to be transferred to the same reward of immortality, and in all things made equal and joined to those who had lived again. You see, excellent reader, how there is nothing here for which I should be reproved. For because I follow that reading which alone is now found in the Greek books, which the Greeks translate, it was not...

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER XVI.

52 In an atom <note>original: "en atomo," an indivisible moment</note>, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised 53 incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For it is necessary that this corruptible body put on incorruption, and this mortal body put on 54 immortality. But when this corruptible body has put on incorruption, and this mortal body has put on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: 55 Death is swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your sting? 56 Where, O grave, is your victory? The sting of death is sin; and the power 57 of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through 58 our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing XVI, 1 that your labor is not in vain in the Lord. Now concerning the collection for the saints, as I have directed the churches of Galatia, 2 so you also should do. On the first day of the week, let each of you put something aside by himself, storing up whatever he may prosper in, 3 so that when I come, no collections need to be made. And when I arrive, whomever you approve by your letters, these I will send to carry...

---

...it was not right to do otherwise. And yet, from this passage, two certain men—though they call themselves Theologians—have convinced themselves that the entire Church would collapse unless they propped it up with their own shoulders. One of them even shines with the dignity of a Bishop, and both are professors of that religion which has rendered the profession of baptism almost irreligious. They have constructed an atrocious calumny against me. The first one, in a crowded circle of noble and learned men at the courts of great Princes, attacked me on the grounds that I was "abolishing the resurrection," simply because I allowed (though did not assert) that some might not die at the coming of the Lord. The other, in his public and ordinary lectures, attacked me for "heresy," because I brought in a <term>reading that contradicts</term> <note>original: "antilogiam"</note> the one the Church follows. 

First, even if we grant there is a true <term>contradiction</term> <note>original: "antilogian"</note> here—granting that the Church approves this reading so as to condemn the other, and granting there is a heretical sense—still, no crime could be imputed to one who professes nothing other than to be a translator. Unless, perhaps, Jerome bound himself to heresy when he faithfully translated Origen’s books *On First Principles*; Jerome would have been more deserving of blame if he had *not* rendered what Origen had written. Now, we have shown that so many orthodox men recognize both readings, and they are so far from condemning the alternative as heresy that Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> specifically warns that in the version Jerome does not reject (but which he places after the one Latins hold today), there is no heretical sense. Furthermore, we have shown that the reason Jerome preferred this reading is of no weight; likewise, we have shown that the reasons moving Augustine can be dismissed. 

Indeed, Peter Lombard in his fourth book, distinction forty-three, reporting Augustine’s words from the twentieth book of *The City of God*, annexed this as if it were his own—deceived, if I am not mistaken, by the third of the eight questions to Dulcitius. But I would rather hear the more learned on these matters. Was Lombard so dull that he did not see the heresy and <term>contradiction</term> <note>original: "antilogian"</note> that these men see? Certainly, even schoolboys know how many things are required for a true contradiction to exist. For Ambrose makes the sense of this proclamation—*We shall not all rise*—the same as this one—*We shall all rise*. For if you speak of those who died before Christ’s coming, the statement *We shall all rise* will be true; if you speak indiscriminately of those who died before and those whom that day finds alive, it will be equally true to say, *We shall not all rise*. This is no more strange than if two people both spoke the truth when one pronounced that "all Theologians are sincere" (meaning those from Louvain), while the other said "not all Theologians are sincere" (meaning the group in general). It is no wonder if Paul includes himself in both groups, since for the sake of teaching he uses the first person to stand for anyone. 

Since these things have been noted partly by us, are held partly by famous authors, and are partly so clear that they would be apparent even to a blind man, as they say—what is this madness in such men who wish to be seen as the lights of the world? I wish them a sounder mind, and better patrons for the Church. For these men clearly do not seek the things of Jesus Christ, but under another title, more than the Pharisees, they serve their own glory and their bellies. They love the <term>first seats</term> <note>original: "protokathedrias"</note> in the Schools, they rejoice in them at sumptuous banquets, they love to be called "Rabbi," they hunt for mitres and Abbeys, and by flattering men, they adulterate the word of God. By their traditions, they obscure and overwhelm the spark of Gospel charity. They do this so openly that, distrusting the defenses with which Theologians ought to be armed, they flee to violence—as if the human mind could be forced to believe something other than what it perceives. May Christ eventually wake up and free his people from this Judaism and this tyranny. Unless, perhaps, he redeemed us with his blood so that we might serve monsters of this kind.

<margin>
45 **In a moment**] <term>in an atom</term> <note>original: "en atomo"</note>, that is, an indivisible point of time, from "temno" (to cut) and the private particle "a." **In the twinkling of an eye**, that is, in a strike of the eye. Jerome, writing to Minervius, indicates that both are found: *rhipe*, meaning a "strike," and *rhope*, meaning "movement." The first is translated from the strike of a weapon or lightning; the second from the movement of a scale or balance. One comes from "rhipto" (to throw), the other from "rhepo" (to tilt). Laurentius <note>Lorenzo Valla</note> suspects the Translator wrote not "strike" but "movement" of the eye.
</margin>
<margin>
46 **For the trumpet shall sound**] <note>original: "salpisei gar"</note>, that is, for it shall sound; the word "trumpet" is understood from what preceded. Unless you prefer to say, "it shall be trumpeted," or as someone turned it in Origen’s thirtieth Homily on Matthew, "it shall trumpet," which is explanatory rather than good Latin; unless you prefer to understand an Angel, though no mention is made of one here.
</margin>

In the Ambrosian Commentaries, these words—*for the trumpet shall sound*—are not added; this clearly appears to be omitted through the fault of scribes, even if he does not indicate in his interpretation that he read them. In the Codex of Donatian, it was written: *it shall sound, and the dead shall rise*.
<insert>C</insert> 47 **But when this mortal has put on**] In the Greek, both parts are repeated: *But when this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality*. <note>original Greek: "Hotan de to phtharton touto endysētai aphtharsian, kai to thnēton touto endysētai athanasian."</note> This is despite the Latin manuscripts resisting it. Augustine, however, cites this passage according to the Greek in his forty-third sermon on John, and again in his second and third sermons on the words of the Apostle.
<insert>D</insert> 48 **In victory**] Ambrose reads *in contention*: for "neikos" <note>original: "νεῖκος"</note>, if written with a diphthong, sounds like "contention"; if otherwise, it signifies "victory" <note>original: "νῖκος"</note>. And Jerome reads it this way in some places in his Epistle against John, Bishop of Jerusalem. Again, in the Commentary on Hosea, he reads *contention*; and for *stimulus* he reads *sting* <note>original: "aculeum"</note>. For that is a mixture where either the Translator or the Scribe changed the order of the Greek speech: *Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O grave, is your victory?* <note>original Greek: "Pou sou thanate to kentron, Pou sou adē to nikos?"</note> Furthermore, the testimony he brings is taken from the thirteenth chapter of Hosea; and that more according to the Septuagint than according to the Hebrew Truth, although it has in Jerome's translation: *I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell.* According to the Septuagint, we read it this way: *Where is your case <note>or "vengeance"</note>, O death? Where is your sting, O hell?* <note>original Greek: "Pou hē dikē sou thanate? Pou to kentron sou adē?"</note> Jerome translates this as "I will be your death." Symmachus interpreted it as "I will be your plague." The Fifth Edition and Aquila have "Where are your words?" In Hebrew, the word is <term>dabar</term> <note>original Hebrew: "דבר"</note>; if written with two cametz vowels <note>original: "דָּבָר"</note> it sounds like "word"; if with six points <note>original: "דֶּבֶר"</note> it sounds like "death" or "pestilence," according to what we read in Isaiah: "The Lord sent death into Jacob, and it came into Israel." Jerome translates it as "He sent a word into Jacob." Moreover, for "sting," which Jerome preferred to translate as "bite," Symmachus translated it as "occurrence" <note>original Greek: "akentēma"</note>; Theodotion and the Fifth Edition interpreted it as "plague."
49 **But thanks be to God**] <note>original: "Tō de Theō charis"</note>, that is, *But to God be grace*: so that you understand "is" or "be," as the Latins also speak.
50 **Be stable and immovable**] <note>original: "hedraioi ginesthe, ametakinētoi"</note>. The conjunction is redundant. They are called "stable" who hold a firm and certain faith; "immovable," who cannot be moved or led away from one place to another.

<insert>E</insert> 1 **Concerning the collections**] <note>original: "Peri de tēs logias"</note>, that is, *Concerning the collect* or collection: a new word for Paul, derived from "collecting" or "gathering." It appears to be a metaphor taken from the fruits of trees or the earth, which are said to be "gathered" <note>original: "legi"</note>; from which the word "legumes" also comes. He could have translated it as "contribution," unless this word "collecta" was then, I believe, more widely accepted by the common people.
<insert>F</insert> 2 **On the first of the sabbath**] <note>original: "kata mian"</note>, that is, of the sabbaths. Theophylact warns that "one" is used for "first," meaning the Lord's Day; Chrysostom agrees in this.
3 **Storing up**] <note>original: "thēsaurizōn"</note>, that is, "treasuring up": which he finally translates into Latin, having been accustomed before to leave the Greek word.
4 **Whatever he may prosper in**] <note>original: "ho ti an euodōtai"</note>. Laurentius thinks it should be translated as *whatever is easy or light*, or *what turns out well*. To me, it seems more correctly translated as *whatever shall be convenient*, and whatever happens by God's prosperity. He added this, lest perhaps one be ashamed of a gift that is not very magnificent. The Translator seems to have read "euodōtai" for "euodōtai." Certainly, Theophylact sides with us, explaining it thus: *whatever God prospers and enriches, and what you have in abundance*. Chrysostom noted it was not said "whatever you have profited," but whatever happens readily: so they might understand that resources are supplied by God, so that from them the needy might be relieved. It is not clear from Ambrose what he read.
5 **To carry your grace**] <note>original: "tēn charin hymōn"</note>. Here he clearly placed "grace" for "benefit," but a benefit freely contributed.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed textual analysis and translation of 1 Corinthians 16. The previous page ended with Paul's plan to collect money for the saints in Jerusalem. # TO THE FIRST TO THE CORINTHIANS. CHAPTER XVI.

4 ...to carry your gift to Jerusalem. And if it is worthy for me to go also, they shall go with me. 5 But I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia; for I am passing through Macedonia. 6 And perhaps I will stay with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me on my way wherever I go. 7 For I do not wish to see you now in passing, but I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits. 8 But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost. 9 For a great and effective door has opened for me, and there are many adversaries. 10 Now if Timothy comes, see that he is with you without fear; for he works the work of the Lord, as I also do. 11 Therefore, let no one despise him; but send him on in peace, so that he may come to me; for I am expecting him with the brothers. 12 Now concerning our brother Apollos, I strongly urged him to come to you with the brothers; and it was certainly not his will to come now; but he will come when he has the opportunity. 13 Watch, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. 14 Let all your things be done in love. 15 I urge you, brothers—you know the house of Stephanas, that it is the first-fruits of Achaia, and they have appointed themselves to the ministry of the saints— 16 that you also submit to such people, and to everyone who works and labors with them. 17 I rejoice at the presence of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they have supplied what was lacking on your part. 18 For they refreshed my spirit and yours; therefore, recognize such people. 19 The churches of Asia greet you. Aquila and Priscilla greet you much in the Lord, with the church that is in their house. 20 All the brothers greet you. Greet one another with a kiss.

***

⁶ **And if it be worthy** ] <note>original: "Ἐὰν δὲ ᾖ ἄξιον"</note>. Among the Greeks, this word is sometimes used somewhat differently than among us, meaning "it is worth it": hence we translate, *And if it be worth the effort*, that is, if the matter be of such importance.

⁷ **For I shall pass through Macedonia** ] It makes no difference to the meaning, even though <unclear>you distinguish</unclear> it; it is ambiguous regarding both tenses: hence it is not wrongly translated as *I shall pass through*.

⁸ **Or even I will winter** ] Although the verb for "wintering" <note>original: "hyemandi"</note> in Suetonius’s *Life of Augustus* seems to be used as if it meant to be afflicted by the discomfort of winter, and in Sallust—as Seneca notes—the phrase *the sea winters* <note>original: "hyemare mare"</note> was a new way of saying the sea is troubled by a storm; nevertheless, the same verb is frequently found in Caesar’s *Commentaries* in place of *to hibernate* <note>original: "hybernare"</note>, that is, to spend the winter. In Suetonius, however, the sense itself suggests that we should understand Augustus was accustomed to being bothered by the winter cold in Rome. The words of Suetonius are as follows: *And for more than forty years he stayed in the same bedroom in winter and summer, although he found the city poorly suited to his health, and he wintered in the city constantly.* These are his words. Since Suetonius is presenting an argument to show that Augustus had little care for his health, and both parts of the sentence depend on the word *although*, what does it matter that he spent the winter in Rome constantly—not to mention that it is doubtful whether it is correctly said *to winter constantly* to mean "always." Rather, he means that Augustus was constantly in a worse state at Rome because of the cold: and this latter part proves the former, which says Rome was inconvenient for his health because he was always in danger there in winter. I would not have added these things, had there not been someone who built a false accusation from this.

⁹ **to see in passing** ] <note>original: "ἐν παρόδῳ"</note>, that is, in passing, and as if hurrying elsewhere.

¹⁰ **Until Pentecost** ] <note>original: "ἕως τῆς Πεντηκοστῆς"</note>, and until the fiftieth: as you might understand the word "day": for I do not think he is speaking of the festival. And I do not know whether the festival of Pentecost was known to the ears of the Gentiles at that time, especially since Paul, in the Epistle to the Romans (which it is established was written after this one), removes all distinction of days and calls those "weak" who compare one day with another. Certainly, none of the ancient Interpreters, as far as I remember, makes mention of that festival. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> explains this rather coldly, writing: "Perhaps this Epistle was sent in winter, or in spring, and then after Pentecost he was supposed to go into Macedonia, and stay there until winter, and then go to Corinth and winter there." Theophylact interprets it without controversy as "until the fiftieth day," noting that this is a sign of a remarkably loving spirit, that he even prescribed the measure of time. Chrysostom writes things not dissimilar to these, although it is not equally clear whether he understood it as the Jewish feast day or the span of the delay. Likewise, Ambrose interprets that he must stay longer in Ephesus because he had many adversaries there, and the fruit would be great. Neither makes a word of the festival. Although in Acts chapter twenty, when he says, *the day of Pentecost* <note>original: "τὴν ἡμέραν τῆς Πεντηκοστῆς"</note>, he seems to signify a certain festival to the Jews. Even if Bede, in the *Ordinary Gloss*, thinks that the festival of Easter and Pentecost was celebrated by the Christian rite even in the times of the Apostles. This, I think, is a fiction invented by them so that Paul would not be believed to observe Jewish feast days, which he had taught were to be neglected. Among those Ancients, there was a great dispute about the time and rite of celebrating the festival of Easter; if fifty days are counted from that day, there will be the same controversy about the day of Pentecost, about which, however, there was no controversy. But in this matter, let each enjoy his own judgment while preserving charity.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...they may carry your generosity to Jerusalem. ⁶ And if it is worth the effort that I also go, they shall go with me. ⁵ But I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia: ⁷ for I am about to pass through Macedonia. ⁶ But perhaps I will stay with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may escort me wherever I go. ⁷ For I do not wish to see you now ⁹ in passing, but I hope I will stay with you for some time, if the Lord permits. ⁸ But I will stay in Ephesus until the fiftieth day. ⁹ For a <margin>B</margin> door has been opened for me, ¹¹ great and effective, ¹² and there are many adversaries. ¹⁰ But if Timothy comes, see that he is without fear among you: for he works the work of the Lord, just as I do. ¹¹ Therefore, let no one despise him, but follow him with peace, so that he may come to me: for I expect him with the brothers. ¹² Furthermore, concerning brother Apollos, I strongly urged him to go to you with the brothers: and it was altogether not his will to go now: but he will come ¹³ when he has found an opportunity. ¹³ Watch, stand in the faith, act manfully, be strong. ¹⁴ Let all things be done among you with love. ¹⁵ And I urge you, brothers, ¹⁷ you know the household of Stephanas: that they are the first-fruits of Achaia, and that they have appointed themselves to the service of the saints, ¹⁶ That you also be subject to such people, and to everyone who helps and labors. ¹⁷ Indeed, I rejoice at the arrival of Stephanas, and Fortunatus, and Achaicus, since ¹⁸ that which was lacking to me from you, ¹⁹ these men have supplied: ¹⁸ For they have refreshed <margin>C</margin> my spirit and yours: therefore, recognize such as these. ¹⁹ The churches of Asia greet you. Aquila and ²⁰ Priscilla greet you much in the Lord, ²¹ with that church which is in their house. All the brothers greet you. ²⁰ Greet...

***

<margin>A</margin> ¹¹ **Great and evident** ] <note>original: "μεγάλη καὶ ἐνεργής"</note>, that is, *great and effective*. For it is written with an *epsilon* <note>ε</note>, not an *alpha* <note>α</note>. The Translator seems to have read *enarges* <note>ἐναργής</note> with an *alpha*: and that sounds to the Greeks as *evident*: and thus Ambrose reads it, though Chrysostom and Theophylact do otherwise.

¹² **And many adversaries** ] Certain Greek manuscripts agree with our Vulgate edition. Although otherwise what Jerome brings forward in his commentaries explaining Joel seemed more fitting: *A door is opened to me, great and evident, but there are many adversaries*: so that you understand the hope of fruit is abundant, but not without trouble, because of those who would try to hinder it.

<margin>B</margin> <margin>D</margin> ¹³ **But concerning brother Apollos** ] "to warn the brothers" and "I make known to you"—I do not find these words in the Greek manuscripts: I find "brother" in some. But this omission is familiar in the Epistles, so that one understands "he replied," or "know," or something similar: for example, "Regarding the books you thought were lost, they are safe with my son-in-law." Therefore, for the sake of the simple reader, the Translator seems to have added, *I make known to you*.

¹⁴ **And certainly** ] <note>original: "πάντως"</note>, in his usual way he translates *utique* <note>certainly</note> for "altogether." *It was not his will*, <note>original: "ἦν θέλημα"</note>, that is, it was not the will. And the Translator added this for the sake of explanation. Theophylact refers it to the will of God, to whom it had seemed thus. Chrysostom reads as Theophylact does: he is silent about the will of God.

¹⁵ **When he has leisure** ] <note>original: "ὅταν εὐκαιρήσῃ"</note>, that is, when it will be opportune: although *vacat* <note>he is free</note> produces the same effect: and he translates it thus in the Acts of the Apostles, *The Athenians had leisure for nothing else* <note>original: "εὐκαίρουν"</note>. This particle supports Theophylact's commentary. For if he was going to come as soon as he was free, it was not his will that was lacking, but the opportunity. <margin>E</margin>

¹⁶ **For all your** ] "For" in this place is completely superfluous. Nor is it anywhere among the Greeks, but *all of yours* <note>original: "πάντα ὑμῶν"</note>: nor is it added in Ambrose, and not even in the Paulist manuscript or the Constance manuscript. For he explains what he meant by "be strengthened." Superstition makes people weak, charity makes them strong.

¹⁷ **You know the house of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus** ] The Greek manuscripts do not have Fortunatus and Achaicus in this place, but only Stephanas, though these three are joined together a little later. In the Constance manuscript, Fortunatus was added, but Achaicus not at all. And in this place "house" signifies the "family," which he calls the first-fruits of Achaia because it was the first to receive Christ. Furthermore, because *oidate* <note>οἴδατε</note> is translated as *you know*, he thinks it should be understood as *you should know*, so that he orders those who have served well to be recognized, especially <margin>F</margin> because a little later, speaking of the same men, he says, *recognize, therefore, such as these*. Ambrose interprets "recognize" as "to hold in honor," with Theophylact also agreeing. From this place, those who changed "first-fruits of Asia" to "first-fruits of Achaia" in the last chapter of the Epistle to the Romans seem to have snatched an opportunity.

¹⁸ **What was lacking to you** ] <note>original: "τὸ ὑμῶν ὑστέρημα"</note>, that is, your deficiency: namely, because they had come to Paul on behalf of everyone. Thus "what was lacking," that is, what Paul desired in the Corinthians—certainly their presence—these men supplied by their arrival. Faber <note>Lefèvre d'Étaples</note> reads, *because my deficiency* <note>original: "ὅτι τὸ ἐμῶν"</note>; but that matters very little to the sense. And a little earlier, for *presence* <note>original: "παρουσίᾳ"</note>, he could have translated *in the arrival*. Ambrose, being uncertain in this place, touches on both meanings, discussing it thus: "Because they are present with you, and in them you can have great progress, or because they came to me to perform the duty of charity on your behalf."

¹⁹ **they themselves supplied** ] <note>original: "οὗτοι"</note>, that is, "these men." The Translator seems to have read *autoi* <note>αὐτοὶ</note>.

²⁰ **Prisca** ] In Greek, *Priscilla*: just as above.

²¹ **With their domestic church** ] He translates correctly indeed, but not...

<margin>22</margin> If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema, maranatha <note>The first is Greek for "cursed" and the second is an Aramaic phrase likely meaning "Our Lord has come" or "Our Lord, come!"</note>.

## THE END OF THE
### FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS.

---

<margin>A</margin>
*Word for word, as Ambrose has it, "with the church that is in their house," <term>σὺν τῇ κατ’ οἶκον αὐτῶν ἐκκλησίᾳ</term> <note>original: "with the church in their house"</note>. Truly, I would have preferred "congregation" here rather than "church," since it signifies a Christian family. "With whom I also stay." I do not find this added in the Greek manuscripts, although Ambrose reads it this way.*
<margin>22 By my hand, Paul's</margin> "My" is in the ablative case <note>A grammatical note explaining that the word "My" refers specifically to the person of Paul acting as the writer</note>. "By my hand," namely, Paul’s.
<margin>23 Let him be Anathema</margin> With this word, Paul is accustomed to signify extreme destruction, which the Hebrews call <term>חרם</term> <note>herem — something devoted to destruction or banned</note>. Furthermore, *Maran atha*, Ambrose thinks is a Syrian <note>Aramaic</note> phrase rather than Hebrew, although there is some affinity between these languages; among them, it sounds like, *Our Lord has come*. However, among Hebrew words which are passed down without a certain author, I find *Maran atha* explained as *at the coming of our Lord*: so that it may cohere with what comes before, *let him be accursed at the coming of our Lord*: just as it recalls the end of Malachi <note>referring to the final verse of the Old Testament</note>, *Lest I come and strike the earth with a curse*. Theophylact interprets it according to Ambrose's opinion, *The Lord has come*; and he wants it to be seen as a kind of oath, by which he confirms that the Lord will arrive.

<margin>23</margin> The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
<margin>24</margin> My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen.

## THE END
### OF THE FIRST
### EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS.

<margin>B</margin>
Saint Jerome wrote much the same in a certain Epistle to Marcella, whose words on this matter I will not be burdened to write down: "*Maran atha* is more Syrian than Hebrew: although from the proximity of both languages it also sounds somewhat like Hebrew: and it is interpreted <term>מרן אתא</term> <note>Aramaic: Maran atha</note> *Our Lord has come*: so that the sense is, If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be accursed: and with that completed, it is then brought in, *Our Lord has come*. For it would be superfluous to wish to contend with stubborn hatred against him whom it is established has already come." Thus far Jerome. Augustine wrote things not dissimilar to these. That point must be advised, that in *Our Lord has come*, the word *come* is in the past tense; for it is <term>ἦλθε</term> <note>elthe — Greek for "he came"</note>: as the Greek Interpreters declare, if it were not clear enough from Jerome’s interpretation. Again, the Reader must be warned by me, that these words, which I just related from Jerome—*Maran atha is more Syrian than Hebrew, although from the proximity of both languages it also sounds somewhat like Hebrew, and it is interpreted, Our Lord has come*—are held to be the same in the Commentaries of Ambrose, and in those notes which are carried under the title of Jerome.
