<meta>The previous page concluded Erasmus's annotations on 1 Corinthians, discussing the final greetings and the meaning of "Anathema Maranatha." This page marks the transition to the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, providing both the traditional Greek "Hypothesis" (an ancient introductory summary) and Erasmus’s own "Argumentum" (summary) for the letter.</meta>

# THE ARGUMENT
->of the<-
# SECOND EPISTLE
->TO THE CORINTHIANS.<-

**H**e sends this letter from Macedonia; and the reason for the letter is this. When the Corinthians received the first epistle, they were pierced with compunction because of the sin of the man who had taken his stepmother, and they were grieved because they had previously overlooked such a transgression. Furthermore, they were being led astray by certain individuals—the very ones who were creating causes for division—so that they might cling to the letter of the law <note>original: "γράμματι τοῦ νόμου" — referring to the literal adherence to Mosaic Law over the spirit of the Gospel</note>, consider the grace of Christ to be of no consequence, and instead pay more attention to those who boast in outward appearance. However, they were also properly concerned with the collection of funds for the saints. The Apostle, therefore, writes back in response to these matters. First, he accepts those who had cast out the lawbreaker; then, he pleads with them as they have requested, and commands that the man be received back since he has repented. In this same letter, he teaches about the Law, distinguishing the "letter" of the Law; he shows that one must not merely take the literal words of the Law, but must search for the meaning within those words. For the Law is not merely a spoken word, but the mind of the Spirit exists within its utterances. Furthermore, he explains that because Christ has come, a new creation has occurred, and one must no longer live according to the old way, but be renewed in all things as in a new creation—and that circumcision is thereafter of no effect. He also commends them regarding their service <note>original: "διακονίας" — here referring to the charitable collection for the poor in Jerusalem</note> and encourages them to abound in it even more. Rebuking those who boast in outward appearance, he lists all the things he has suffered for the sake of the Lord; he also recounts the visions he saw, how he was caught up into Paradise and the third heaven. Then, after instructing those who sin not to continue in it, but to repent with thanksgiving, he completes the letter. Additionally, the entire discourse in the letter concerns himself, the Corinthians, and the false apostles. From this summary, it is clear that the letter pertains to the grace of God and to a good way of life—guided by a clear conscience, perseverance, a lack of greed, the virtue of generosity, and a warning against the arrogance and wickedness of false apostles.

---

# ON THE SECOND EPISTLE
# TO THE CORINTHIANS
->*An Argument by*<-
# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a person, likely a scholar or the Apostle Paul, seated at a desk or table within a landscape setting.</image-desc>
**F**irst, he gives reasons to the Corinthians why he did not visit them again as he had promised in the previous Epistle: after first speaking briefly about his afflictions, which he was enduring for the Gospel of Christ, he shows that in such great evils God had been his comfort. Soon after, he reconciles to the Corinthians that man whom he had ordered to be delivered to Satan in the previous Epistle, so that they might lovingly receive him now that he has been corrected, whom they had cast out when he was sinning. These matters are handled roughly in chapters one and two. Next, he proclaims his zeal in preaching the Gospel, passing judgment on and noting the other false apostles <note>original: "pseudapostolos"</note> who, serving their own gain and striving for their own glory, never ceased to entice people toward the Mosaic Law; they attempted to mix this with Christ as if without this addition there were no hope of salvation. Therefore, he prefers the light of the Gospel to the shadows of the Mosaic Law: repeatedly exhorting them not toward the ceremonies of the Law, but toward a conscience and a life worthy of Christ. Meanwhile, he testifies with what sincerity he preached the Gospel of Christ, and how many evils he suffered for its sake in the hope of a heavenly reward. To these points, he indicates in which things Christian piety is chiefly situated. These matters are treated at the end of chapter two, and in chapters three, four, five, and the beginning of six. For in the remaining part of this chapter, and at the start of the next, he exhorts them that—recognizing the dignity and holiness of their profession—they should by all means abstain from the defilements of the heathens, with whom they should have nothing in common. In the fourth place, he softens the bitterness of his previous rebuke, praising their obedience because they had obeyed his Epistle in all things, even though it was a reprimand. He rejoices that this temporary sorrow produced the greatest joy for both parties, just as when the most pleasant health follows a bitter medicine. In the fifth place, using both the example of the Macedonians and various arguments and testimonies of the Scriptures, he challenges each person to contribute something—according to their own ability and inclination of mind—to the aid of the saints who were living in Jerusalem; he remembers that this was commanded to him by Peter. For this business, Titus was sent with another colleague (whom most think was Luke), and he commends them to the Corinthians. This is dealt with in chapters eight and nine. Sixthly, he openly attacks the false apostles whom he previously criticized indirectly; these men displayed Apostolic dignity and majesty with pride and disdain, calling Paul contemptible and humble, as one who practiced a manual trade <note>original: "cerdonicam" — the work of a 'cerdo' or low-level artisan/cobbler; a slur against Paul's tent-making</note>, and as one unskilled and speechless <note>original: "infantem" — literally "unspeaking," implying he lacked the polished rhetoric of the Greek orators</note>, and furthermore as one so often beaten and harassed by insults. Against these men, he asserts his authority among the Corinthians, testifying that he never lacked Apostolic authority and power, but that he refused to use it to burden others as the rest did, using it instead only for the benefit of his people and the glory of which Christ. Then, having asked pardon for his "folly" because he was forced to say certain boastful things about himself, he first equals himself to the highest Apostles, and then even places himself above them—and that on many counts: either because he spread the teaching of the Gospel more widely, or because he alone delivered it freely, burdening the Achaeans neither through himself nor his companions, or because he suffered more for the sake of the Gospel than any of them. He turns those very things into glory for himself which made him seem more contemptible to some. Furthermore, acknowledging a lack of skill in speech for the sake of modesty, he claims knowledge of reality for himself, so that they might not find him lacking even here. Finally, since the false apostles were selling themselves to the simple-minded with fabricated visions of Angels, Paul brings forward a true and remarkable vision: that he was caught up even to the third heaven, and there was taught things that exceed human understanding. These things are handled roughly in chapters ten, eleven, and twelve. Seventhly, lest they slide back into their former vices through the false apostles, he testifies that he intends to visit them. He threatens them with authority, lest he find them in such a state that he is forced to act like his true self—or lest, just as he was forced to be harsh in his Letter, he be forced to be harsh in person as well, something he has not done before, even though he could have by his own right. These matters he deals with at the end of chapter twelve and in chapter thirteen. The Greek inscriptions testify that this Epistle was sent from Philippi through Titus and Luke. However, the summaries (which are found in the Latin codices without an author but with convenient brevity) testify that it was sent through the same men from Troas, for he mentions this place in the second chapter.

THE SECOND EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS.

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL
### TO THE
# CORINTHIANS
### THE SECOND.

<margin>1. a.</margin> PAUL, an Apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the church of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints who
<margin>2</margin> are in all Achaia: Grace be to you and peace from
<margin>3</margin> God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father
<margin>4</margin> of mercies, and the God of all comfort, Who comforts us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort those who are in any trouble, by the
<margin>5</margin> comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted by God. For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our comfort also abounds through Christ. And whether
<margin>6</margin> we be afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation, which is effective in the enduring of the same sufferings which we also suffer; or whether we be comforted, it is for your
<margin>7</margin> comfort and salvation; and our hope of you is steadfast, knowing that as you are partakers of the sufferings, so shall you be also of the comfort. <margin>b</margin> For we would not,
<margin>8</margin> brethren, have you ignorant of our trouble which came to us in Asia, that we were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life.
<margin>9</margin> But we had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in
<margin>10</margin> God who raises the dead, Who delivered us from so great a death...

---

<margin>C</margin> <insert>1 <image-desc>Decorative initial "I" featuring a landscape with a figure and a tree</image-desc> **In all Achaia]** <note>original: "ἐν ὅλῃ"</note>, that is, in the whole: namely, the remaining parts: for Corinth itself is in Achaia, and is its capital city.</insert>

<margin>2</margin> **From God our Father and the Lord]** It is a slight matter that Lorenzo <note>Erasmus refers to Lorenzo Valla (c. 1407–1457), a humanist whose philological notes on the New Testament heavily influenced Erasmus.</note> warns about concerning ambiguity, as if it could be read, *from God the Father of us and of the Lord Jesus Christ*. For it is characteristic of Paul to call God "Father" and Christ "Lord." I have also warned elsewhere that the Greek phrasing is ambiguous: for it can be understood such that grace proceeds from the Father and from the Son, or that it proceeds from the Father, who is common to both Christ and us. Furthermore, as for the fact that Ambrose <note>Likely "Ambrosiaster," a 4th-century commentator whose work was long attributed to St. Ambrose of Milan.</note> reads only *from God*, and does not add *our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ*, that perhaps happened by the fault of the scribes.

<margin>3</margin> **Blessed be God and Father]** <note>original: "ὁ Θεὸς καὶ Πατήρ"</note>. A single article among the Greeks makes *God* and *Father* refer to the same person, whereas among the Latins two could be understood, *God* and *Father*. It would have been the same among the Greeks if he had said, <note>original: "ὁ Θεὸς καὶ ὁ Πατήρ"</note>. It could be rendered more expressly as, *he who is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ*.

<margin>4</margin> **Of all consolation]** "Every consolation" fits better here. And Jerome refers to it in this way in his Commentaries on Isaiah. Some explain it as *perfect consolation*. And in this Epistle, Reader, if it does not bother you to compare the Commentaries of Ambrose with the notes that circulate under the name of Jerome, you will see a wondrous confusion. This study would not be entirely condemned if what was done in the *Golden Chain* <note>The "Aurea Catena," a famous commentary on the Gospels compiled by Thomas Aquinas from the writings of the Church Fathers.</note> had been done here. Now <margin>D</margin> we have a mutilated Ambrose, indeed a confused one, nor do we have these works in their entirety.

<margin>5</margin> **Through exhortation]** <note>original: "διὰ τῆς παρακλήσεως"</note>, that is, through comfort. It is the same word which he had just translated as *consolation*. Where we exhort even ourselves, <note>original: "παρακαλούμεθα"</note>, that is, we are comforted. What an untimely affectation of variety <note>Erasmus critiques translators who use different words for the same Greek word to make the Latin sound more elegant, which he feels obscures the author's intent.</note>. The translator reads, <note>original: "καὶ αὐτοὶ"</note>, that is, *and themselves*: although the conjunction *and* <note>original: "καὶ"</note> is not added among the Greeks, nor does it displease me to have it added: Just as we are strong in harsh circumstances with God comforting us, so it is fitting that by our strength the hearts of others be strengthened in turn, either by example or by exhortation. And "we are comforted" in this place is passive: whence Ambrose reads, *we obtain exhortation*. Since there are two parts of the sentence, "whether... or...", both of which correspond to one clause—namely this one, "and our hope is firm for you"—which is added to the latter part by us, it is placed in the middle by the Greeks: from whom, however, we disagree here. Furthermore, I wonder why Aquinas, following a certain copy, makes three parts out of two: *Whether we are troubled for your exhortation, or we are comforted for your consolation, or we are exhorted for your exhortation*. But both the Greek and Latin copies cry out against this, even the ancient ones, specifically the Paulinian and Donatian codices; in addition to both Constantinopolitan ones. Nor do I see what place there could be here for a third part, since "to comfort" and "to exhort" are the same word to the Greeks: and yet he even interprets it in that way, not just reads it. For in Ambrose, I believe the same thought is repeated in other words, which he reads thus: *But whether we suffer narrowness, it is for your exhortation and salvation*: and soon, with a little commentary inserted: *But whether we suffer pressure for your exhortation and salvation, or we obtain exhortation for your exhortation, which works, and so forth*. Likewise in the translated Theophylact <note>Theophylact of Ohrid (c. 1055–1107), a Byzantine archbishop and biblical commentator.</note>, concerning...

<margin>1.</margin> PAUL, an Apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy the brother, to the gathering of God which is at Corinth, together with all the saints who are in
<margin>2</margin> all Achaia: Grace to you and peace from God our Father,
<margin>3</margin> and the Lord Jesus Christ. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the Father of mercies, and the God of every comfort, Comforting us
<margin>4</margin> in all our affliction, to this end that we might be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort by which God comforts us ourselves. Since as the
<margin>5</margin> afflictions of Christ abound in us, so through Christ also abounds our comfort. But whether we are afflicted,
<margin>6</margin> that is done for your comfort and salvation, which works in the endurance of the same afflictions which we also suffer: or whether we receive comfort, it is for your
<margin>7</margin> <margin>B</margin> comfort and salvation: our hope also is firm for you, since we know that just as you are sharers of the afflictions, so shall you be of the comfort also.
<margin>8</margin> For we do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning our affliction which happened to us in Asia, because we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so much so that we despaired even of life. Rather, we ourselves in ourselves
<margin>9</margin> had received the sentence of death, so that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead to life, Who
<margin>10</margin> from...

<meta>catchword: from</meta>

---

<margin>6</margin> **As the passions of Christ abound]** <note>original: "περισσεύει"</note>, which can be understood as stated absolutely. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), Archbishop of Constantinople and famous preacher.</note> indicates it can also be referred to Christ, as if they endured more than Christ did.

<margin>7</margin> **For your exhortation]** Again it is <note>original: "παρακλήσεως"</note>: that is, *of comfort*: although in Ambrose I see these confused, as if there were no difference at all between *exhortation* and *comfort*, because whoever comforts, exhorts one to be of good courage.

<margin>8</margin> **Which works endurance]** <note>original: "τῆς ἐνεργουμένης"</note>, or, as some have it, <note>original: "ἐνηργουμένης ἐν ὑπομονῇ πολλῇ"</note>, that is, that which works in much endurance. Now "works" means it acts, and unfolds and opens its own power. Even if Chrysostom thinks <note>original: "ἐνεργουμένης"</note> should be read passively, not <note>original: "ἐνεργούσης"</note> [actively], so that there is a place for the grace of God, to whom the chief praise of our salvation is owed, and he interprets <note>original: "ἐνεργεῖσθαι"</note> as "to be acquired," "to grow," "to be intensified," that is, it is shown, it grows, and it is stretched, and becomes greater.

<margin>9</margin> **Of the same passions]** <note>original: "τῶν αὐτῶν παθημάτων"</note>, that is, of the same evils, or pains, or of the same afflictions. And a little later, *you are sharers of the passions*, that is, sharers of the evils, or afflictions: for the word "passion" is harsh to Latin ears <note>In Erasmus's time, "passio" was becoming a technical theological term, but he preferred words that sounded like natural, classical Latin.</note>.

<margin>10</margin> **So shall you be of the comfort]** "You shall be" has been added. It seems, however, that "you are" should be understood rather than "you shall be": for it is not added among the Greeks. For he perceives here also that both are common: the affliction of evils and the comfort of God. And Theophylact interprets in this sense, following Chrysostom in his usual manner. Indeed, Ambrose reads, *so that we despaired that we even lived*: and interprets that the afflictions proceeded even unto the death that was brought upon them. <margin>E</margin>

<margin>11</margin> **Which was made in Asia]** The Greeks add "to us," <note>original: "τῆς γενομένης ἡμῖν ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ"</note>, that is, which happened to us in Asia.

<margin>12</margin> **So that it wearied us even to live]** <note>original: "ὥστε ἐξαπορηθῆναι ἡμᾶς καὶ τοῦ ζῇν"</note>, it could be taken as "so that we despaired even of life." And St. Ambrose takes it in this sense, and Theophylact agreeing with him: nor does Chrysostom disagree.

<margin>13</margin> **The answer of death]** <note>original: "ἀπόκριμα"</note>: as if the dangers themselves were announcing nothing else but death.

<margin>14</margin> **From such great dangers]** <note>original: "ἐκ τηλικούτου θανάτου"</note>, that is, from such a great death. For <note>original: "τηλικοῦτος"</note> is a word that signifies quantity rather than quality. Ambrose, coming closer to the Greek truth, reads, *from such great deaths*: just as Chrysostom reads, showing by hyperboles that the immense dangers were called "deaths."

# TO THE CORINTHIANS II. CHAPTER I.

---

deaths. Our Translator <note>Erasmus refers to the author of the Vulgate, the standard Latin Bible</note> was satisfied to have rendered the general meaning: for he perceives "deaths" to mean "afflictions very close to death." If nothing is allowed to be changed, why did the Translator dare this?

<margin>A</margin>
*15 Rescued and will rescue]* <note>original: "ἐῤῥύσατο καὶ ῥύεται"</note>, that is, he rescued and he rescues. It is the same verb in Greek, except the latter is in the present tense. Otherwise, if we read "will rescue" here, how does it fit with what follows immediately: "in whom we hope that he will *still* rescue"? In Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose, 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note>, the present tense verb in the middle is not added, but was omitted, I believe, by the carelessness of scribes.

*16 In whom we hope]* <note>original: "εἰς ὃν ἠλπίκαμεν"</note>, that is, in whom we have hoped. In verbs of this sort, they often use the past tense for the present, as in "I know" or "it is written": for that "we have hoped" sounds as if you were to say, "we have fixed our hope."

*17 That from the persons of many faces]* The Greek has it thus: <note>original: "ἵνα ἐκ πολλῶν προσώπων, τὸ εἰς ἡμᾶς χάρισμα, διὰ πολλῶν εὐχαριστηθῇ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν"</note>, that is, so that from many persons, concerning the gift bestowed on us, thanks may be given in many ways on our behalf. Instead of "from many persons," Ambrose has "in the face of many": so that we may understand thanks are to be given publicly. For *prosōpon* <term>πρόσωπον - literally "face" or "mask," but also "person"</term> among the Greeks sounds not only like "person," but also "aspect" and "face." And "through many" will be "through many [men]": with "men" being understood. It can also be taken this way: "from many persons," that is, in many ways: since we call the appearance of a thing its "face." Nor can I quite guess what our Translator read, since the same word in Greek signifies both "face" and "person": unless perhaps some slightly skilled Greek added "of faces," wanting to interpret what *prosōpon* meant to the Greeks. For the older Constance manuscript had an erasure; the first writing seems to have been "from the face of many." "Persons" was written in the margin. Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo Valla, a pioneer of humanist biblical criticism</note> devised a different meaning, namely this: so that for the grace in me from many persons, or bestowed in respect of many, thanks may be given through many because of you. This invention does not displease me, except that the article being placed somewhat awkwardly pushes back against this meaning. For it would have been more convenient if it were: "so that the gift toward us which is from many persons," or as Ambrose translates, "the gift bestowed on us." And "on our behalf" <note>original: "ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν"</note>, as Theophylact <note>11th-century Byzantine commentator</note> and Ambrose have it, "for us," in the first person. In some Greek copies it is "on your behalf" <note>original: "ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν"</note>, and Valla seems to have read it thus. Either is tolerable: let thanks be given on your behalf (by whose prayers and for whose good I was saved), and on our behalf (who were saved). Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople</note> disagrees with Theophylact and reads "that from many persons the gift toward us may be thanked for through many on our behalf." Although even here "from many persons" can be taken as "in many ways." Nor is it absurd if we understand it as "in a great crowd of people," or "with many witnesses." Or if one prefers this to refer to the frequency of those giving thanks, "through many" could be referred to the manifold afflictions from which he had been freed. Furthermore, he used "be thanked" <note>original: "εὐχαριστηθῇ"</note> passively, just as the Latins say "to be congratulated for a safe return." Ambrose paraphrased it as "celebrated in the giving of thanks." Our Translator was more obscure: "the thanks of that donation," instead of "for that donation" or rather "gift." There are those who are annoyed that I sometimes note that this Translator affects an abundance of words without cause. But I ask you, Reader, what use is there in changing the word here? He calls "salvation" here "safety," because he emerged safe and alive from such great evils.

*18 For our glorying]* <note>original: "καύχησις"</note>, that is, boasting: although we read "glories" for "boasting," it is usually in a bad sense; hence the "glorious" are called braggarts.

*19 In simplicity of heart]* "Of heart" is absent in the Greek codices; it is not added in Ambrose, nor in Chrysostom, nor in the Greek Theophylact, even if the Translator added it of his own accord, and it was not added in either of the Constance manuscripts.

*20 More abundantly toward you]* <note>original: "πρὸς ὑμᾶς"</note>, that is, among you, or toward you, in the second person.

*21 You have read and known]* Both verbs in the Greek are in the present tense: "you read," "you acknowledge." And that Ambrose read it thus can be gathered from his own exposition: "Those things," he says, "he says he writes, which they would not only discern in letters, but also have manifest in his works." But some slightly learned Reader, because the speech seemed absurd at first glance—"We write no other things to you than what you read"—changed the writing: because nothing seems to be read except what is written. But Paul expressed this thought in his own way. "We write no other things to you than those which you not only read as written by us, but even acknowledge as expressed by us in deed and fact." The Greeks add a conjunction, "or even acknowledge": for we acknowledge what we have seen. But I suspect the article "which" <note>original: "ἃ"</note> was changed into "or" <note>original: "ἢ"</note>. The Donatian codex had "which you acknowledge," certainly preserving the integrity of the old writing in the other verb.

<margin>B</margin>
*22 In the day of our Lord Jesus Christ]* The Greek has "in the day of the Lord Jesus" <note>original: "ἐν ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ"</note>, and does not add "Christ." Furthermore, he calls the Judgment "his day" according to custom. Although by the judgment of the common people there is no cause for me to boast of you, or you of me, yet before Christ there is reason for both of us to boast of each other.

*23 That a second grace]* <note>original: "δευτέραν χάριν"</note>, which could be translated as a "repeated benefit" or a "double benefit," namely first through the Letter, later through his own presence. The Greek scholia and Chrysostom advise that "grace" <note>original: "χάριν"</note> was put for "joy" <note>original: "χαράν"</note>. For among the Latins also, those things which delight are said to "have grace."

<margin>D</margin>
*24 When I had willed this]* <note>original: "Τοῦτο οὖν βουλευόμενος"</note>, that is, "When I was deliberating this," or "deciding." The same verb follows soon after, "the things I purpose" <note>original: "ἃ βουλεύομαι"</note>, which the Translator renders "what I think": the Translator permits himself to change whatever he likes in any way he likes. Ambrose reads "thinking." Theophylact the Translator sufficiently indicates that it should be understood as a plan or decree. Similarly Chrysostom, although in the earlier parts he reads "I was willing." It matters very little to the sense. Nor is there an "and" in this place, but "therefore" <note>original: "οὖν"</note>: and Ambrose reads "therefore," even if "but" <note>original: "δὲ"</note> does not displease me, which is an adversative. For he seems to wash away what they would easily have objected: "if you had decided to come, why did you change your mind?"

*25 I used levity]* <note>original: "τῇ ἐλαφρίᾳ"</note>, a word derived from *elaphros* <note>light, nimble</note>, on account of the speed of changing a plan. And here "I used levity," he said in a more Latin way in Greek, instead of "I behaved lightly or inconstantly."

*26 I think according to the flesh]* Here an answer must be understood: "I do not think," or "By no means": so that what follows may fit aptly, "so that with me it should be, etc." And this sense fits better if we read as the Latins read, "so that with me it should be, 'it is' and 'it is not'." For immediately a different reading renders a different sense. Although even if the reading is agreed upon, the speech still has some obscurity. For at first glance this sense offers itself: I am neither inconstant nor <margin>E</margin> deceitful in the manner of men, who either change their purpose or deceitfully promise what they have no mind to perform. Now from Chrysostom's interpretation, Paul seems to mean something else: namely this, "That I delayed my promised return is not because of a changed opinion: for I wanted it then, and I still want it: but what I turn over in my mind, I do not so turn it over according to the flesh, that is, according to the will of men, who in conducting affairs follow their own mind, so that with me there is 'Yes, Yes' and 'No, No'": that is, that whatever I want, I do, and whatever I don't want, I avoid. Rather, I am subject to the Spirit of God, by whom I am sometimes forbidden to do what I want, and commanded to do what I did not want. Therefore, it was through Him that I did not come. For with Him is "Yes, Yes" and "No, No," and this is why I did not fulfill what I promised: but yet, although my word frustrated you in this part, nevertheless in the preaching of the Gospel I have not deceived you, but with God helping, whatever I taught is firm and undoubted.

<margin>F</margin>
*27 That there be with me 'it is']* This passage is confused among us; among the Greeks it has it thus: <note>original: "ἵνα ᾖ παρ’ ἐμοὶ τὸ ναὶ, ναὶ, καὶ τὸ οὒ, οὒ"</note>, that is, "so that there should be with us what is 'Yes, Yes' and what is 'No, No'." Certainly Ambrose reads, "is, is, no, no." And a very old Pauline manuscript showed manifest traces of erasure. Furthermore, among the Greeks "nai" is the word of one affirming, and "ou" of one denying. Therefore, for those who do not do what they say they will not do, their "no" is "no," and those who do what they affirm they will do, their "yes" is "yes." Furthermore, as to why Lorenzo <note>Valla</note> does not want "in him" and "in the same" to refer to Christ, I do not see what moved the man. For it is extremely ridiculous that Valla wants "not Christ" to be understood in "in himself": on the contrary, Paul attributes the happy outcome of promises to God and to Christ, through whom this is commanded, lest he should seem to claim anything by his own strength: a thing which the conclusion of this speech also testifies, "to the glory of God through us." God is the author, Christ the obtainer, we are merely their ministers. It was clearer and more Latin to say "in my power" rather than "with me" <note>original: "παρ’ ἐμοὶ"</note>. I do not, he says, think this according to the flesh: this

# 755 EPISTOLA PAULI CAP. II. 756

...purpose? That with me there should be "Yes, Yes" and "No, No"? <margin>18</margin> But as God is faithful, our word toward you was not "Yes and No." <margin>19</margin> For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us—by me, Silvanus, and Timothy—was not "Yes and No," but in him it has been "Yes." <margin>20</margin> For however many are the promises of God, in him they are "Yes," and in him "Amen," to the glory of God through us. <margin>21</margin> Now he who establishes us with you in Christ and has anointed us is God, <margin>22</margin> who also has sealed us and given us the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts. <margin>23</margin> Moreover, I call God as a witness against my soul, that to spare you I came no more to Corinth. <margin>24</margin> Not that we have dominion over your faith, but we are fellow-workers for your joy; for by faith you stand. <margin>II. 1</margin> But I determined this within myself, that I would not come again to you in sorrow. <margin>2</margin> For if I make you sorry, who is he then who makes me glad, but the same who is made sorry by me? <margin>3</margin> And I wrote this very thing to you, lest, when I came, I should have sorrow from those of whom I ought to rejoice; having confidence in you all, that my joy is the joy of you all. <margin>4</margin> For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you, with many tears, not that you should be grieved, but that you might know the love which I have more abundantly toward you. <margin>5</margin> But if anyone has caused grief, he has not grieved me, but in part—lest I overcharge you all. <margin>6</margin> Sufficient for such a man... <meta>catchword: such a man...</meta>

<meta>continued from previous page</meta> I do not claim it for myself, as if it were in my power to provide whatever I wish. However, Paul acknowledges in some way the fault of not keeping his word, but only in terms of human purpose, provided his faith remains constant in the preaching of the Gospel.

<margin>28</margin> **But God is faithful**] He rightly used *fidelis* <note>faithful</note> in the sense of "trustworthy," whereas otherwise this noun is more commonly used for "one who believes." Lest he should seem to arrogance to himself what he said, he added, *But God is faithful*, by whose authority and help I provide what I provide. This speech can also be punctuated thus: *For the things I purpose, do I purpose according to the flesh, so that with me there is both "Yes, Yes" and "No, No"?* treating it as a question. Then, as if answering that he by no means speaks according to carnal affection so as to claim credit for himself, he adds: *On the contrary, God is faithful*, who through me provides whatever He willed. Ambrose <note>a 4th-century Church Father</note> punctuates it this way. And so the adversative distinction has the force of a correction, in place of which could be put "rather" or "nay."

<margin>29</margin> *Which was toward you*] <note>original: "ὁ πρὸς ὑμᾶς"</note>, that is, which I spoke to you. For he refers, if I am not mistaken, to those things he promised in the first Epistle.

<margin>30</margin> *Was not in Him "Yes" and "No"*] <note>original: "οὐκ ἐγένετο ναὶ καὶ οὐ"</note>, that is, *was not "Yes" and "No"*. Furthermore, these words, *but it is in Him*, are not read in the Greek manuscripts in this place, although they are added immediately in the next sentence, supported by a very ancient Pauline manuscript, in which is seen written: *But God is faithful, because our word, which was toward you, is not in Him "Yes" and "No": for the Son of God, etc.*

<margin>31</margin> *By me and Silvanus*] Jerome <note>the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note> advises that "Silas" should be read, not "Silvanus," of whom frequent mention is made in the Acts of the Apostles; but the Greek manuscripts I have seen disagree.

<margin>32</margin> *Was not in Him "Yes" and "No," but in Him it was "Yes"*] <note>original: "οὐκ ἐγένετο ναὶ καὶ οὐ, ἀλλὰ ναὶ ἐν αὐτῷ γέγονεν"</note>, that is, *was not "Yes" and "No," but in Him it was "Yes"*. When he says "Yes" <note>original: "ναὶ"</note> and "No" <note>original: "οὐ"</note>, he refers to the freedom of doing what you wish. When he says "Yes" and "Yes," he signifies a slippery faith—that is, falsehood. When he says "No," he signifies frustrated hope and a vain promise. When he says "Yes" or "is," he signifies inviolable truth. However, in adding *in him*, he uses the preposition in place of "through"—*through Him*—lest he should claim anything for himself.

<margin>33</margin> *For however many*] <note>original: "Ὅσαι γὰρ ἐπαγγελίαι Θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ τὸ ναὶ, καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ τὸ ἀμὴν"</note>, that is, *For however many are the promises of God, in Him or through Him is the "Yes," and in Him is the "Amen."* For among the Hebrews, *Amen* is a word of confirmation, just as among the Greeks "Yes" is.

<margin>34</margin> *Therefore through Him*] "Therefore" should be removed, <note>original: "καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ τὸ ἀμὴν"</note>, that is, *and in the same is the "Amen."* Here again, *Amen* has its own article <note>original: "τὸ"</note>, just as "Yes" and "No" did above: so that you may understand the certainty he wished to signify through *Amen*. And "in Him, Amen to God" signifies that all things God has promised are certain and ratified. The translator rendered <note>original: "ἐν αὐτῷ"</note> as *through Him*, which is strange since he did not choose to do the same in the other instances.

<margin>35</margin> *And who has sealed us*] <note>original: "καὶ σφραγισάμενος"</note>: a word he usually uses to signify the certainty of a thing, just as when we seal a legal document or a jar; and he explains this shortly after, indicating that a pledge was given so the promise might be more certain. I thought this should be noted because I see more recent interpreters <note>referring to medieval Scholastic theologians</note> philosophizing at length here about "cooperating grace," which is not particularly relevant to the matter.

<margin>36</margin> *The pledge of the Spirit*] <note>original: "τὸν ἀῤῥαβῶνα"</note>, that is, a <term>pledge (arrhabon)</term><note>A legal or commercial term for a down payment or deposit that guarantees a full contract will be fulfilled.</note>, which gives faith that the entire promise will be performed.

<margin>37</margin> *I came no more to Corinth*] "Not yet" would fit better than "no more": for it is <note>original: "οὐκ ἔτι ἦλθον"</note>, that is, "I have not yet come." For he felt he had delayed his return, unless you prefer to take <note>original: "ἔτι"</note> as "again." Furthermore, Ambrose interprets it as a delayed return, as do Chrysostom and Theophylact.

<margin>38</margin> *We have dominion over your faith*] See whether this sense could be accepted: *we have dominion over you because of your faith*, or *for the sake of faith*. As is the Greek custom, one might understand <note>original: "ἕνεκα"</note> <note>for the sake of</note>. The Greek reads: <note>original: "Οὐχ ὅτι κυριεύομεν ὑμῶν τῆς πίστεως"</note>. And that I should sense it this way is caused by the article <meta>catchword: after</meta>

<column-break/>

after <note>original: "ὑμῶν"</note> <note>your</note> rather; otherwise it would be more fitting to say <note>original: "τῆς ὑμῶν πίστεως"</note> <note>of your faith</note>. Although Chrysostom is not at all offended by the article. Now he says these things because he had previously said "sparing," like someone about to show favor. But there is no dominion unless there has been sin somewhere; however, they had not yet sinned in faith, in which they stood firm; they had sinned in lust, contention, and discord. He therefore softens the word in this way. Chrysostom is of this opinion. Theophylact, agreeing with me in other points, raises no scruple about the transposed article, although the other sense also holds well: *Faith is free, dominion belongs to necessity*, as Ambrose interprets it. These things must be noticed by us, who abuse the title of faith and religion for tyranny. Perhaps we desire the world to be reduced to the profession of Christ with no other zeal than that we ourselves may rule more widely.

<margin>39</margin> *By faith you stand*] <note>original: "ἑστήκατε"</note>, that is, *we stand* or *we consist*. Although the Greek manuscripts vary here. And "you stand" fits better, lest they seem to be rebuked in every way. Thus Chrysostom reads. <margin>D</margin>

> <insert>**Unless he who is made sad by me**] <note>original: "ὁ λυπούμενος ἐξ ἐμοῦ"</note>. He uses "to be made sad" in his own way for "to be affected by grief," whereas it sounds like something else to Latins. He feels that this very thing is a pleasure to him: that having been warned, they feel pain, because that is evidence of a repenting mind; thus, in turn, joy is born from sorrow.
>
> <margin>2</margin> **Sorrow upon sorrow**] *Lest coming I should have sorrow upon sorrow*. Truly that was transferred here from elsewhere, namely from the Epistle to the Philippians chapter two. Certainly in Ambrose it is not added, and his interpretation agrees with this reading. Theophylact also agrees with Ambrose, although the translator added it in the context of his own accord, following the Vulgate Edition. Someone indicates that in one particular manuscript a Greek reading is found agreeing with our translation, <note>original: "ἵνα μὴ ἐλθὼν λύπην ἐπὶ λύπῃ σχῶ"</note>. He says this was sent from Rhodes to the Reverend Father Francisco Ximenes <note>Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros, 1436–1517, founder of the University of Alcalá and sponsor of the Complutensian Polyglot Bible</note>, formerly Cardinal of Toledo, for whose memory I indeed have a pious regard, because he himself favored piety and all good studies. <margin>E</margin> But since Ambrose agrees with us, and since so many manuscripts support this reading which we indicate, it is possible that the Rhodian book was corrupted—especially since we have indicated the cause of corruption—or it is possible that it was emended to match the Latin manuscripts, especially since it is from Rhodes. For it is known that this was done in some cases: that after concord was entered with the Roman Church, they should also agree in this part. Furthermore, manuscripts of that kind are nothing more than a "white ruler on a white stone" <note>An ancient proverb meaning a useless or unreliable standard of measurement</note>. Nor indeed would I wish to assemble our translation on the faith of a manuscript that agreed in all points with our own. Yet the matter is not worthy of any contention; the sense is pious and sound.
>
> <margin>3</margin> **Anguish of heart**] <note>original: "συνοχῆς"</note>, by constriction or anxiety. For "narrowness of heart" is faintheartedness and sounds like a vice.
>
> <margin>4</margin> <margin>F</margin> **That you may know what love**] In Greek it is, *that you may know the love which I have more abundantly in you*: as Ambrose also reads. And "toward you" is more correct than "in you." For it is <note>original: "εἰς ὑμᾶς"</note>, or *toward you*.
>
> <margin>5</margin> **But if anyone has made me sad**] "Me" is not found among the Greeks, nor in Chrysostom or Theophylact, <note>original: "Εἰ δέ τις λελύπηκεν"</note>, that is, *If anyone has caused grief*: so that you may understand whatever is convenient—someone, or you, or me. Likewise Saint Ambrose does not add the pronoun but reads according to the Greeks: *but if anyone has caused sorrow, he has not caused me sorrow*. For he burdens the sinner who has made everyone sad, not just Paul, but all good people at Corinth. For what he says afterward, *he has not made me sad*, is as if he said: he has not made me specifically and alone sad, but only in part, as one for whom this grief is common with all of you. Chrysostom, unless the title deceives, seems to punctuate it differently, so that *everyone* refers not to the word *burden*, but to the previous *made sad*: *he has not made me sad, but in part*

# SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. CHAPTER II.

7 so that on the contrary you should rather forgive and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one be swallowed up by excessive sorrow.
8 Therefore I urge you to reaffirm your love toward him.
9 For to this end I also wrote, that I might know the proof of you, whether you are obedient in all things.
10 To whom you forgive anything, I also forgive; for if I indeed have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it for your sakes in the presence of Christ,
11 lest we should be taken advantage of by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his devices.
12 Furthermore, when I came to Troas for the Gospel of Christ, and a door was opened to me by the Lord,
13 I had no rest in my spirit, because I did not find Titus my brother; but taking my leave of them, I departed for Macedonia.
14 Now thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ, and through us diffuses the fragrance of His knowledge in every place.
15 For we are to God the fragrance of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing.
16 To the one we are the aroma of death leading to death, and to the other the aroma of life leading to life. And who is sufficient for these things?
17 For we are not, as so many, peddling the word of God; but as of sincerity, but as from God, we speak in the sight of God in Christ.

<column-break/>

---

*part (lest I be a burden) to all.* <note>Original Latin: "parte (ne gravem) omnes."</note> For it was harsh to say, *he did not only grieve me, but all of you with me*; therefore he lightens the burden of the one who had sinned, adding *in part*, as if softening what he had said. *In part*, that is, in some way. Theophylact interprets this more clearly as <note>Greek: "ἀπὸ μέρος, ὀλίγον τι"</note>, that is, a very little bit: although the previous Translator did not understand this passage of Theophylact. Yet the interpretation of Ambrose is not absurd, though he follows a different sense. Finally, it is not simply *to burden*, but <note>Greek: "ἐπιβαρῶ"</note> *to weigh down*: that is, I add a burden to one already burdened.

*6 This rebuke which is made]* <note>Greek: "ἐπιτιμία"</note>, which he usually translates as *reproof*. And *which is made by the many*, <note>Greek: "ἢ ὑπὸ πλειόνων"</note>, could be translated as *which was done by the majority*.

*7 So that on the contrary you rather give]* <note>Greek: "Ὥστε τοὐναντίον μᾶλλον ὑμᾶς χαρίσασθαι καὶ παρακαλέσαι"</note>, *So that on the contrary you ought rather to forgive and console*. For there seems to be a synecdoche <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole or vice versa.</note> in these words, or if you prefer, an ellipsis <note>The omission of a word needed for grammatical completeness.</note>, so that *it is necessary* or something similar is understood.

*8 That you confirm toward him]* <note>Greek: "κυρῶσαι"</note>. Which almost means as if you said: "Cause your love for him to have weight and authority." For he speaks as if to judges and an assembly, by whose votes he wishes the man to be acquitted, who had been handed over to Satan. For <note>Greek: "κυρία"</note> [kyria] signifies an assembly in which magistrates are created—what the Latins call the *comitia*—and a day appointed for some cause, and a certain right of acting. Furthermore, the Greeks call an authentic document <note>Greek: "κύριοι"</note>, according to the authorities Hesychius and Suidas. It seems to me that the opinion which had prevailed in the voting was also called *kyria*, whence the proverb, *this is the authoritative one*. Therefore it likewise signifies the effective proof or weight and authority of a sentence, which is called <note>Greek: "κύρωσις"</note>. Aristotle, in the first book of the *Rhetoric*, calls prior agreements *invalid* <note>Greek: "ἄκυρα"</note> and subsequent ones *authoritative* <note>Greek: "κύρια"</note>, because a prior agreement is rendered void and ineffective by a later one: from which is derived <note>Greek: "κυρόω"</note>, as in, "I approve by vote and make valid." Some here corruptly read *in him* instead of *toward him*.

*9 What I have forgiven]* <note>Greek: "καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ εἴ τι κεχάρισμαι, ᾧ κεχάρισμαι"</note>, that is, *for I also if I have forgiven anything, to whom I forgave*: or, *if I have granted grace for any matter*. For by *to give* he means *to forgive a fault*. Then, with *to whom I forgave*, the verb *forgave* must be understood again, so that *forgave* is repeated three times: the speech will be somewhat incomplete: *for I also if I have forgiven anything, to whom I forgave, for your sake I forgave*. Chrysostom indicates this, supplying from his own words <note>Greek: "ἐποίησα"</note>, that is, *I did*. However, it should be noted that while Paul delivered few to Satan, and with what affection he commends this man to his people, we excommunicate <note>Literally "strike with lightning."</note> people everywhere for the sake of three drachmas <note>A small silver coin; Erasmus is satirizing the Church's quickness to excommunicate for minor financial debts.</note>. Nor did he deliver this man to Satan by his own private authority, but by the public judgment of all—a man who, among us, would be thrown straight into the fire. And in the condemnation itself, he mixes in a sign of charity, *for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit etc.* So great is his mercy toward the wicked, though he himself was subject to no sins, while we, who are so poorly conscious of our own state, rage in such an un-Christian way against other offenders.

*10 In the person]* <note>Greek: "ἐν προσώπῳ"</note>, which is *either in the person*, or *in the face*, or *sight*. For the Greek word is ambiguous, and the commentaries explain it in various ways. Chrysostom interprets it as *either according to God, or for the glory of Christ, or as if Christ were commanding this*. Theophylact says, *in the person of Christ*, that is, *in the sight of God, and as if He were commanding this, and as if acting in His place* <note>Greek: "καὶ ὡς ἀντιπρόσωπος ἐκείνου"</note>. Although the translator of Theophylact only rendered it here as, *This is, no differently than if Christ himself had forgiven*. By what chance or zeal that was done, I do not know. Ambrose interprets it as *in the person of Christ*, meaning *in the place of Christ*.

*11 That we not be circumvented by Satan]* <note>Greek: "ἵνα μὴ πλεονεκτηθῶμεν"</note>, that is, *lest we be occupied and used, as if by an unjust possessor, Satan*. Ambrose reads, *that we not be possessed*: and expresses the Greek word more closely. For <note>Greek: "πλεονεκτεῖν"</note> is to occupy what is not yours, as the greedy and usurpers of others' property do. Chrysostom and Theophylact carefully explain the emphasis of the Greek word.

*12 I have no rest for my spirit]* He rendered the Greek dative with too much "good faith," when it should have been translated into the ablative case. For

<column-break/>

while they express the instrument and manner of action with the dative case, we use the ablative. Ambrose comes closer to the Greek: for he reads, *I had no rest in my spirit*, <note>Greek: "Οὐκ ἔσχηκα ἄνεσιν τῷ πνεύματί μου"</note>, that is, *I did not rest in my mind*. This is that Titus whom Paul is thought by some to have missed for the reason that he was more skilled in that language <note>i.e., Greek.</note>. Theophylact is among these. Even Saint Jerome, in his eleventh question to Hedibia, did not fear to write that Paul, though he had knowledge of the Scriptures and spoke in various languages, was nevertheless unable to explain the majesty of divine meanings in the worthy eloquence of the Greek language, and for that reason Titus was his interpreter, just as Mark was the interpreter for Peter. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> also mentions this interpretation, but rejects it, lest he strip the Apostles of the gift of tongues. But even from this, it can be gathered that he was helped by Commentaries translated from the Greek, since Ambrose touches on nothing of this sort.

*13 But saying farewell]* <note>Greek: "ἀποταξάμενος"</note>, that is, *the brothers having been dismissed*, or *renouncing with a 'farewell'*. Ambrose reads, *but I said farewell to those, and set out*, and so forth.

*14 But thanks be to God]* In Greek it is *grace*, <note>Greek: "χάρις"</note>. And so, if I am not mistaken, the Translator rendered it.

*15 Who always triumphs over us]* <note>Greek: "τῷ πάντοτε θριαμβεύοντι ἡμᾶς"</note>. Saint Jerome, in the eleventh question to Hedibia, explains, *triumphs over us*, that is, *concerning us*, or *leads his triumph through us*. Ambrose likewise, *triumphs over us, makes us victors*, with faith conquering perfidy. In Latin, those are said *to be triumphed* over who are led as the conquered in a triumph. Thus a soldier also, who has done good work in war, is said to be in the triumph for the sake of honor, so that he is a participant with his leader. *In Christ* can be understood as *through Christ*, or *in Christ*, in whom our glory lies. Theophylact noted these things.

*16 A good odor/smoke to God]* <note>Greek: "εὐωδία"</note>, that is, *fragrance*, or *goodwill*, to translate literally: for in Greek it is a compound word. And he again calls God *Father* in his custom. For as often as he uses this word absolutely, he almost always understands God the Father, especially if the mention of the Son is joined.

*17 To some indeed]* He would have translated more elegantly as, *to these and to those*.

*18 So fit]* <note>Greek: "Τίς ἱκανός"</note> is not read among the Greeks, nor in Ambrose, nor in Augustine, who cites this passage when explaining the seventh Psalm and reads, *And who is fit for these things?* Origen likewise brings this up in his thirteenth Homily on Genesis. Perhaps the Translator had added *profit* <note>Latin: "quaestum"</note> on his own. That was turned into *who so*. But the response is understood: *Very few*, or something similar. For he understands that the matter is exceedingly difficult, and one that cannot be performed by just anyone, unless you prefer to refer it by hyperbaton <note>A relocation of words from their natural order.</note> to that which follows a little after: *Who is fit for these things?* And after he increased the magnitude of the deed by delaying the response, he then answers: *But such confidence we have*, and so forth.

*19 Like the many]* <note>Greek: "ὡς οἱ πολλοὶ"</note>, that is, *like the rest*. Others have, <note>Greek: "ὡς οἱ πολλοὶ"</note>, that is, *like the many*, or *most*.

*20 Adulterating]* <note>Greek: "καπηλεύοντες"</note>, that is, *huckstering* or *peddling*. Jerome, in the eleventh question to Hedibia, translated it as *selling off* and *vending*. For <note>Greek: "καπηλεύειν"</note> is to misuse some thing for profit, which Peter applied even to men themselves, *peddling you*. Ennius used this word in Cicero's *Offices*: *Not peddling war, but waging it*. The Translator rendered *adulterating* for *corrupting*: and Ambrose followed that, not ungracefully. For the Ancients called whatever was insincere and spoiled by trickery and fraud <note>Greek: "κάπηλον"</note>, as Aeschylus—cited by whoever it was that compiled the Greek Etymologies—says, <note>Greek: "κάπηλα προσφέρων τεχνήματα"</note>, that is, *offering huckster's arts*: because this class of men is mostly insincere, measuring everything by profit. The Greek word properly fits those who sell food or drink: whose chief study is to sell spoiled things as if they were pure.

*21 But from sincerity]* <note>Greek: "ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ἐξ εἰλικρινείας, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ἐκ Θεοῦ"</note>, but as if from sincerity, but as if from God: with the adverbs added. And yet, unless you understand something, the speech will be incomplete: *not adulterating, but as if preaching from sincerity*.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s critical edition and commentary on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, transitioning from Chapter 2 to Chapter 3. Here, Erasmus focuses on Paul’s defense of his apostolic authority, the contrast between the "letter" of the Law and the "Spirit" of the New Covenant, and the imagery of the veil over Moses’s face.</meta>

# EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER III.

<margin>1 III.</margin> we speak in Christ. Do we begin again to commend ourselves? or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or letters of recommendation from you? <margin>2</margin> You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all men; <margin>3</margin> clearly showing that you are a letter of Christ, delivered by us, written not with ink but by the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on fleshy tablets of the heart. <margin>4</margin> And such trust we have through Christ toward God; <margin>5</margin> not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think of anything as being from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God; <margin>6</margin> who also made us sufficient as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the spirit; for the letter kills, but the spirit gives life. <margin>7</margin> But if the ministry of death, in letters engraved on stones, was in glory, so that the children of Israel could not look steadily at the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance, which glory was passing away; <margin>8</margin> how will the ministry of the spirit not be more glorious? <margin>9</margin> For if the ministry of condemnation had glory, much more does the ministry of righteousness exceed in glory. <margin>10</margin> For even what was made glorious has no glory in this respect, because of the glory that excels. <margin>11</margin> For if what is passing away was glorious, much more that which remains is in glory. <margin>12</margin> Having therefore such a hope, we use great boldness of speech; <margin>13</margin> and not as Moses, who put a veil over his face, so that the children of Israel could not look steadily at the end of what was passing away. <margin>14</margin> But their minds were blinded; for until this day the same veil remains at the reading of the old cove—

<column-break/>

<margin>1 III.</margin> of God through Christ we speak. Do we begin again to commend ourselves? or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or from you? <margin>2</margin> You are our letter, written in our hearts, which is understood and read by all men: <margin>3</margin> while you declare that you are a letter of Christ, ministered by us, inscribed not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone, but on fleshy tablets of the heart. <margin>4</margin> Such confidence we have through Christ toward God: <margin>5</margin> not that we are fit of ourselves to think anything as if from ourselves: <margin>B</margin> but if we are fit for anything, it is from God: <margin>6</margin> who also made us fit ministers of a new Testament, not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter kills, but the spirit gives life. <margin>7</margin> But if the ministry of death in letters, shaped in stone, was in glory, so that the children of Israel could not fix their eyes on the face of Moses, because of the glory of his countenance, which is passing away: <margin>8</margin> why shall not the ministry of the spirit rather be in glory? <margin>9</margin> For if the ministry of condemnation is glory, much more does the ministry of righteousness excel in glory. <margin>10</margin> Since indeed even that which was glorified was not glorified in this part, on account of the excellent glory. <margin>11</margin> For if that which is done away was in glory, much more that which remains is in glory. <margin>12</margin> Therefore, since we have such hope, let us use much freedom: <margin>C</margin> <margin>13</margin> And not as Moses put a veil on his face, so that the children of Israel would not look into the end of that which was being done away. <margin>14</margin> But their senses were blinded: for until this day the same veil in the reading of the old Testament <meta>catchword: Te-</meta>

---

<margin>1</margin> *We begin again to commend ourselves*] <term>to commend</term> <note>original: "συνιστάνειν"</note>, which does not simply mean *to praise*, as the common people think, but to introduce oneself into the favor of another.

<margin>2</margin> *To you, or from you*] The Greek text repeats the word <term>recommendatory</term> <note>original: "συστατικῶν"</note>, even though the Latin copies I have seen all disagree; yet it is not repeated without reason. *Recommendatory letters to you*, that is, letters coming from others that recommend us to you, or coming from you to recommend us to others. For Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Bulgarian archbishop and biblical commentator</note> reads and interprets it in this same way.

<margin>3</margin> *Our letter*] He calls it "his," not because he wrote it, but because it is what recommends him. His zeal for their love and salvation was the proof and served in place of a letter. However, he said *our* either for the sake of modesty, instead of *my*, or because certain other colleagues of Paul shared the same zeal.

<margin>4</margin> *Which is read and read*] The translator did not capture the beauty of the Greek phrasing, <term>known and read</term> <note>original: "γινωσκομένη καὶ ἀναγινωσκομένη"</note>, that is, what is understood and what is read aloud. <note>Erasmus is pointing out a wordplay in Greek: 'ginoskomene' (known) and 'anaginoskomene' (read).</note>

<margin>5</margin> *Manifested, because you are a letter*] <term>being manifested</term> <note>original: "φανερούμενοι"</note>. This is a middle-voice verb, which could be conveniently translated as *While you are manifest as being a letter*, etc. Or, *While you are made manifest, that you are a letter*, etc.

<margin>6</margin> *And written not with ink*] In the Greek, the word *and* is not added; nor is it in Ambrose <note>a 4th-century Church Father</note>. Nor is it *written*, but *inscribed* <note>original: "ἐγγεγραμμένη"</note>.

<margin>7</margin> *On fleshy tablets of the heart*] <term>fleshy</term> <note>original: "σαρκίναις"</note>, that is, made of flesh, so that you understand the material, not the quality, which is what they mean when they say *carnal*. For what we read elsewhere as "carnal things" is <term>σαρκικοῖς</term> (sarkikois) in Greek. <insert>Some manuscripts have "that is, hearts," but I think this is in error. Those who read it this way wanted it to be an apposition: "on fleshy tablets—namely, the hearts themselves."</insert>

<margin>8</margin> *But our sufficiency*] <term>the sufficiency</term> <note>original: "ἡ ἱκανότης"</note>, or "fitness," so to speak.

<margin>9</margin> *Who also made us fit ministers*] <term>Who also made us sufficient as ministers of a new covenant</term> <note>original: "ዸς καὶ ἱκάνωσεν ἡμᾶς διακόνους καινῆς διαθήκης"</note>, that is, *Who made us fit to be ministers of a new Testament*: as if you were to say, "He empowered us." Moreover, the verb comes from the noun which he just translated as *sufficient* and *sufficiency*.

<margin>10</margin> *Not the letter, but the spirit*] In Greek, this is in the genitive case, *not of the letter, but of the spirit*: so that you refer it to the ministers, and understand the "New Testament" as Scripture and the "Old" as the letter. But the Apostles were chosen to administer the spirit, not merely the ceremonies and precepts of the Law, which Paul in his usual way calls the "letter." For the spirit was not given through Moses in the way it was through the Apostles. From Ambrose's interpretation, it cannot be determined for certain what he read, and in terms of meaning, it really doesn't matter much. For what offended Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a humanist who previously critiqued the Vulgate</note> could be avoided thus: *Who made us to be fit ministers of a new Testament, which is spiritual, not literal like the old*: so that the letter and spirit refer to the Testament, or to the ministers of the New Testament—that is, not of the letter, but of the spirit. And lest anyone think we are bringing something new, both codices from Constance agreed with the Greek, and the passage had no erasure. Augustine cites it no differently in his book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 179: although in the 14th chapter of the same work a scribe corrupted the passage; seeing that the writing was consistent, he did not dare to change everything.

<margin>11</margin> *Letter deformed*] Some interpret *deformed* <note>Latin: "deformata"</note> as *shamefully formed*. To make us believe this more, Carrensis <note>Hugo de Sancto Caro, a 13th-century commentator</note> adds, *Just as a woman is said to be deformed*. O, what a pillar of Theology! As if truly only a woman is called "deformed." Then, after some trifles of that sort, he adds another invention, in case this one isn't approved: *Deformed, that is, very well formed*: as if Paul’s point were to understand...

<column-break/>

<margin>D</margin> they understand that Law to be "very well formed," which he wants to be held in lower regard compared to the Gospel. But is it worth attacking these people? Since, on the whole, this entire thing is most impudent: to want to interpret the New Testament written in Greek by the Apostles, if you are entirely ignorant of Greek. Paul wrote <term>inscribed</term> <note>original: "ἐντετυπωμένη"</note>, that is, *informed*, to translate it word-for-word, which means "engraved." Although the Translator elegantly said *deformata* for *formata*. For here the prefix *de-* does not increase the meaning, any more than in *deambulare* (to walk) or *deosculari* (to kiss). And Quintilian says, *marbles first "deformed" [sketched out] by the hand*. Ambrose reads *formed*, not *deformed*.

<margin>12</margin> *Of condemnation is in glory*] The "is" is extra: <term>glory</term> <note>original: "δόξα"</note>. And so Ambrose reads it. He said "glory" after the manner of the Hebrews, instead of "glorious": though this does not change the sense much. The Greek codices vary. And shortly after, it is *through glory*, where he said *for in glory*.

<margin>13</margin> *For neither was that glorified which shone*] <term>For even what was glorified was not glorified</term> <note>original: "Καὶ γὰρ οὐδὲ δεδόξασται τὸ δεδοξασμένον"</note>, that is, *Indeed, not even that which was glorified has been glorified*: meaning, that which was then being glorified lost its glory when the glory of the Gospel arrived. And therefore he added, *in this part*: that is, by comparison. This is how the Greek scholia <note>ancient marginal notes</note> explain it.

<margin>14</margin> *Much confidence*] <term>much boldness</term> <note>original: "πολλῇ παῤῥησίᾳ"</note>: a word which among the Greeks signifies freedom of speech, when one speaks openly what one feels. He refers this to Moses, who did not dare to speak openly and clearly, but with a veiled face. And <term>we use</term> <note>original: "χρώμεθα"</note> can also be translated as *let us use*. And indeed Ambrose reads it this way, so that it is an exhortation to a purely Christian freedom.

<margin>15</margin> *Into the face*] <term>unto the end</term> <note>original: "εἰς τὸ τέλος"</note>. This undoubtedly happened through an error of the scribes. Certainly Ambrose reads, *even to the end of that which is evacuated*, and interprets it in that way. He meant that Moses’s face was covered and not to be looked upon until that which was to be abolished vanished before the brightness of the Gospel, and thus he spoke of looking at Moses’s face. Both Chrysostom and Theophylact read and interpret it as *end* <note>telos</note>. The thick-headed people could not grasp that the Law would have an end. Furthermore, for this speech to be complete, something must be understood, such as: "we do not act like Moses, who put," etc. And yet in some Greek codices we found it written <term>into the face</term> <note>eis to prosōpon</note>, just as we read in the Latin. But I suspect these were corrected to match the Latin reading. Where he here translates *look steadily*, the Greek is <term>to gaze</term> <note>original: "ἀτενίσαι"</note>, that is, to fix the eyes, and to look with unmoving eyes: just as lovers do, or those who listen attentively to a speaker. They could look at him, but they could not look with fixed eyes for a long time. Hence, when the business was done and Moses spoke to the people, he covered his face with a veil, *unto the end*, namely, so that they would not rest their gaze there. <margin>F</margin> And, *that which is evacuated*, sounds as if you were to say, *of him who is evacuated or abolished*, referring to Moses who was to die. Moses was mortal, Christ is immortal. Moses's Law was established for a time; Christ’s Law knows no end. Or *absolutely, to the end of the thing which is passing away*. And "is evacuated" here is <term>is abolished</term> <note>original: "καταργουμένον"</note>, that is, what is done away with and rendered void. Theophylact also noted this. Although the Law is not "abolished" in the strict sense, rather the figures give way to the truth.

<margin>16</margin> *They are dulled*] <term>they were blinded</term> <note>original: "ἐπωρώθη"</note>. And "thoughts" rather than "senses," <term>thoughts</term> <note>original: "νοήματα"</note>, which he translated a little earlier as "reflections." As for how it was translated, *But whenever it shall turn* <note>original: "Ἡνίκα δ᾿ ἂν ἐπιστρέψῃ"</note>, I think "Israel" must be understood for "the Israelite." Augustine, in the 12th book against Faustus, chapter 4, reads, *But when you shall have passed over*: so that <term>ἐπιστρέψῃ</term> is from a middle verb and is the second person, used for any person: unless perhaps we prefer to think "you pass over" was written by a scribe's error for "it shall have passed over." Although he also cites this passage in the same words elsewhere, such as in the 39th chapter of the same book.
