<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s annotations on Paul’s Second Letter to the Corinthians. Having discussed the "veil" over the Old Testament, he now concludes Chapter 3 and begins Chapter 4, focusing on the clarity of the Gospel and the identity of "the god of this world."</meta>

### SECOND LETTER TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER IV.

of the covenant remains, not being lifted, because it is abolished in Christ. <margin>15</margin> But even to this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies upon their heart. <margin>16</margin> But whenever one turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. <margin>17</margin> Now the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. <margin>18</margin> And we all, with unveiled face, beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, just as by the Spirit of the Lord. <margin>IV. 1</margin> Therefore, since we have this ministry, as we have received mercy, we do not faint. <margin>2</margin> But we have renounced the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness nor handling the word of God deceitfully, but by the manifestation of the truth, commending ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God. <margin>3</margin> But even if our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing; <margin>4</margin> in whom the god of this world has blinded the minds of those who do not believe, so that the light of the Gospel should not shine upon them.

---

<margin>17 Remains unrevealed</margin> <note>original: "Manet non revelatum"</note> It remains unrevealed, and it is not removed: so that the sense may be more open.

<margin>18 But when they shall have turned to the Lord</margin> <note>original: "Quum autem conversi fuerint ad Dominum"</note> Since the Greek word is *epistrepse* <note>original: "ἐπιστρέψῃ"</note>, if you prefer the middle voice, it would be *when you have been turned*, in the second person; this is how Augustine repeatedly cites this passage, specifically in the books he wrote against Faustus <note>Faustus was a prominent Manichaean teacher whom Augustine famously debated</note>, "When you pass over to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away." However, if it is the active verb, it would be *when he has turned*, in the third person: so that you understand "Israel" is the subject. And so Saint Ambrose reads it: "But when he shall have turned to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away." He used the same verb in the chapter that immediately follows. Yet it does not hinder the meaning that our translator changed the number. For it does not matter whether you say, "The horse carries its load for ten months," or "Horses carry for ten months." Origen, citing this place in his twelfth homily on Exodus, reads: "Where anyone has turned, the veil shall be taken away." He does the same in his second homily on Leviticus.

<margin>19 Now the Lord is the Spirit</margin> He does not simply say that the Lord is spirit and deny that he has a body, but he added the article *to pneuma* <note>original: "τὸ πνεῦμα"</note>, that is, *that* spirit—namely, the spirit of the Law. It is as if Moses were the flesh, being mortal, weak, and thick, according to the type he represents, while Christ is the spirit, as he is effective and immortal.

<margin>20 Beholding as in a mirror</margin> *Katoptrizomenoi* <note>original: "κατοπτριζόμενοι"</note>, that is, "mirroring": in this place, the word is derived from a mirror, not from a lookout point. You should understand that the glory of God is received and reflected by purified souls as if by a mirror. For the Greek commentaries <note>The "scholia" or marginal notes found in Greek manuscripts</note> explain it in this sense, so that "mirroring" means expressing and reflecting as a mirror does. Augustine also noted the emphasis of the Greek word in the fifteenth book of *The Trinity*, chapter eight. And regarding the addition "into the same image," the preposition is absent in the Greek, *tēn autēn eikona* <note>original: "τὴν αὐτὴν εἰκόνα"</note>, that is, "according to the same image": so that you must understand the word "according to" <note>original: "κατά"</note> is implied.

<margin>21 From brightness to brightness</margin> "From glory to glory," <note>original: "ἀπὸ δόξης εἰς δόξαν"</note>: for he translates this word in different ways at times. But this variety in translating sometimes provides Latin expositors with an occasion for error, as they think Paul is saying two different things, "brightness and glory," when in his text it is the same word.

<margin>22 By the Spirit of the Lord</margin> This passage can be understood in three ways among the Greeks: "by the Spirit of the Lord," or "by the Lord who is the Spirit," or "from the Lord, the Spirit," so that we understand the Lord himself to be the Spirit. However, the middle reading—"from the Lord of the Spirit"—is not highly approved. Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine biblical commentator</note> seems to follow the first, as does Ambrose. Nazianzen follows the last in a work titled after Chrysostom's epistle, using it against the Arians <note>Heretics who denied the full divinity of Christ</note>. Likewise, Saint Basil in his work *On the Holy Spirit* to Amphilochius, chapter twenty-one. It is strange what Augustine followed in the twenty-second book of *The City of God*, chapter twenty-nine, where he reads, "as if to the Spirit of the Lord," if the manuscript is not faulty. Furthermore, "Spirit" here does not sound like "spiritual," but "heavenly," as in "from the Spirit of the Lord": so that you understand the exceptional dignity which is conferred by the Spirit of the Lord. A similar passage is in John: "as of the only-begotten from the Father."

<margin>1</margin> **According to** the mercy we have obtained] *Kathōs ēleēthēmen* <note>original: "καθὼς ἠλεήθημεν"</note>. The translator seems to have read *kai* <note>meaning "and"</note> instead of *kathōs* <note>meaning "as"</note>. Moreover, he said "we have obtained mercy" in his usual modest way, instead of saying "we have been chosen for the Apostolic office."

<margin>2 Let us not fail</margin> *Ouk ekkakoumen* <note>original: "οὐκ ἐκκακοῦμεν"</note>, that is, "we do not fail," or "we do not grow sluggish," or "degenerate." For among the Greeks, *kakos* <note>bad/evil</note> sometimes signifies one who is idle or weak, as has been pointed out elsewhere. Ambrose reads "let us not fail" and "let us renounce": so that both are words of exhortation, as if he read *mē ekkakōmen* and *apeipōmetha*. To me, it seems better that they be read in the indicative mood, referring to Paul’s own person, who, having despised the ceremonies of Moses, was freely preaching the philosophy of Christ.

<margin>3 But we renounce</margin> *Apeipametha* <note>original: "ἀπειπάμεθα"</note>, that is, "we have abdicated," or "denied," or "rejected." Ambrose reads "let us renounce," as if they were words of invitation. But Chrysostom and Theophylact read and interpret all these in the indicative mood. For the Apostle is not prescribing to them what they ought to do, but showing them the nature of his own office, while in passing censuring the false apostles who were throwing up smoke screens before the disciples, just as today the Jews boast of their Talmudic and Kabbalistic mysteries.

<margin>4 The hidden things of shame</margin> *Ta krypta tēs aischynēs* <note>original: "τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς αἰσχύνης"</note>. "Of disgrace" or "of dishonor" is more fitting than "of modesty." For he did not say *aidous* <note>modesty/reverence</note>, but *aischynēs* <note>shame/disgrace</note>. And so Ambrose reads it. For he opposes disgrace to the glory which he attributes to the Gospel. Furthermore, he said "hidden things" instead of "evasions," for foulness loves lurking places.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> of the Testament remains, nor is the veil removed, which is abolished through Christ. But until this very day, when Moses is <margin>15</margin> read, a veil is placed upon their hearts. <margin>16</margin> <margin>18</margin> But when they shall have turned to the Lord, the veil will be taken away. 19 Now the Lord is the Spirit: and where the <margin>17</margin> Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. But we all, with un- <margin>18</margin> covered face, 20 representing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image 21 from glory to glory, as 22 by the Spirit of the Lord. Therefore, <margin>IV. 1</margin> since we have this ministry, as God has had mercy on us, 2 we do not degenerate: But we have rejected 3 the hidden <margin>2</margin> <margin>B</margin> things of disgrace, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God with deceit, but by the manifestation of the truth, commending ourselves to every man's conscience, in the sight of God. But if our Gospel is still <margin>3</margin> veiled, it is veiled in those who perish: In whom 7 the god <margin>4</margin> of this world has blinded the senses of the unbelieving, lest the 8 light of the Gospel should shine upon them.

---

<margin>5 Nor adulterating</margin> *mēde dolountes* <note>original: "μηδὲ δολοῦντες"</note>, that is, using deceit, or handling deceitfully. The word here is not *kapēleuontes* <note>huckstering/peddling</note>, which he previously translated as "adulterating": but *dolountes*, as if you were to say, "falsifying." Nor is it "in the manifestation," but "by the manifestation": so that it refers back to "commending": that is, not capturing men's favors by deceit, but by the sincerity <margin>C</margin> of preaching.

<margin>6 It is covered</margin> *kekalymmenon* <note>original: "κεκαλυμμένον"</note>. What he translated as "veiled" until now, he now changes to "covered," even though the word is the same in Greek.

<margin>7 The god of this world</margin> *ho Theos tou aiōnos toutou* <note>original: "ὁ Θεὸς τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου"</note>, that is, "the God of this age." Theophylact and the Greek scholia think this can be read by hyperbaton <note>a figure of speech where word order is transposed for emphasis</note> in this way: "In whom [God] blinded the thoughts of the unbelievers of this world": so that we understand the true God, the avenger of crimes, blinds the minds of the infidels of this world. And indeed this sense could be accepted if "God" is separated by a sub-punctuation <note>hypostigme</note> from those words which follow, in this manner: "in whom God, has blinded the minds of the infidels of this world": that is, in whom God blinded the minds of the unbelievers belonging to this world. Augustine testifies in the twenty-first book against Faustus, chapter two, that this reading pleased many of our people, because the Manichaeans made two Gods: one true, and another from whom evils flowed, whom they called *Hyle* <note>Greek for "matter"; the Manichaeans believed matter was inherently evil</note>. But a little later, the same Augustine denies that it should seem absurd if the Devil is called the "god of this world," just as it <margin>D</margin> was said by Paul, "whose God is their belly." Likewise in the Psalm, "The gods of the Heathen are demons." He repeats the same against the adversary of the Law and the Prophets, book two, chapter seven. Ambrose explains it according to this sentiment. Therefore, what we said in the first place from the Greek scholia seems affected and forced. It is simpler and truer that we understand the "god of this world" to be Satan, as Cyril thinks, citing the Greek scholia. Nor should it bother anyone that the title of "God" is attributed to him. For the Devil is not simply <margin>E</margin> God, but "is God" to those who put him before Christ. Just as for the greedy, money or Mammon is God; for the gluttonous, the gullet is God; and "man is a god to man," according to the proverb. Certainly, Ambrose does not fear to interpret the "god of this world" as the Devil of the wicked. For in the Divine Scriptures, the name of God and Lord is found with a threefold distinction: according to nature and truth, thus God alone is called God and Lord; according to adoption, "I said, you are gods"; and according to opinion, in First Corinthians eight, "For even if there are those who are called gods in heaven or on earth." Chrysostom zealously resists the idea that the Devil should be called God, out of hatred for Marcion and Manichaeus <note>early heretics who believed in an evil creator god</note>, and wants this passage to be understood as referring to the true God: and he points out the word order which I showed before. Soon, having dismissed this escape, he nevertheless urges the same sense and removes a double scruple: first, how the God of heaven and earth can be called "god of this world"; and second, how He can be said to blind. He excuses the first by the custom of mystical Scripture, which calls God "the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob." Likewise "the God of Israel," or again "the God of heaven," even though He is the God of all things. He resolves the second according to the custom of mystical speech: God is frequently said to *do* what He *permits* to happen; just as in the Letter to the Romans it is said He "gave the philosophers over to a reprobate mind," and in Exodus it is said He "hardened the heart of Pharaoh." Chrysostom speaks piously indeed, although I think the other opinion is the genuine one. But I do not see what these evasions pertain to, since Paul elsewhere clearly attributes the name of God to those who <margin>F</margin> are not truly gods but are held as gods, as in First Corinthians eight: "Just as there are many gods and many lords": and in Ephesians six, he calls wicked spirits *kosmokratoras* <note>original: "κοσμοκράτορας"</note>, that is, the rulers of the world: taking "the world" to mean the wicked: just as he uses the word "age" <note>seculi</note> here. Shall the Manichaeans triumph immediately if Satan is called the "god of this world" here? And shall we flee to forced little defenses rather than to the genuine interpretation? I will add this: the Commentaries which circulate under Chrysostom's name on this Epistle are not his, but belong to some chatterbox.

<margin>8 The illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ</margin> The heap of genitives <note>A grammatical structure where many "of" phrases are linked together</note> makes the speech ambiguous. For it can be taken thus: lest the "illustration of the Gospel"—that is, the preaching of the glory of Christ—should shine on them; or, lest the "light of the glory of the Gospel of Christ" should shine; or, lest the "light of the Gospel, which is the glory of Christ," should shine. I wonder, however, what Ambrose read in the Greek, since he translates this place: "in whom the God of this world blinded the senses of the infidels, so that they do not see through the light of the Gospel of the glory of Christ": unless perhaps for *autois* <note>them</note> he read *autas* <note>them/feminine things</note> in this way, "so as not to shine upon *them* [the senses] the illumination." For on the authority of Hesychius, *augazō* and *augazomai* <note>to shine/behold</note> for the Greeks is "to see" and "to look at." Then, in the *Glossary* it properly sounds as "illumi-"

<summary>Erasmus provides a detailed philological and patristic analysis of 2 Corinthians 3:14–4:4, focusing on the metaphorical "veil" of the Law and the controversial identification of the "god of this world." He argues against strained interpretations intended to combat heresy, preferring a direct reading that identifies Satan as the "god" of those who reject Christ.</summary>

### PAUL'S EPISTLE CHAPTER IV.
763, 764

...of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God. For we do not preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus' sake. For it is God, who commanded light to shine out of darkness, who has shone in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. 

But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the excellence of the power may be of God and not from us. In all things we are pressed, but not crushed; we are at a loss, but not in utter despair; persecuted, but not abandoned; cast down, but not destroyed. Always carrying about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our body. For we who live are always being delivered to death for Jesus' sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh. So then, death is at work in us, but life in you. But since we have the same spirit of faith, according to what is written, "I believed, and therefore I spoke," we also believe, and therefore we speak, knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us through Jesus and will place us with you.

<column-break/>

...of the gospel of the glory of Christ, 9 who is the image of God. For we do not preach ourselves, 10 but Christ Jesus the Lord, 11 and ourselves as your servants for the sake of Jesus. Because: it is God, 12 who commanded light to shine out of the darkness, 13 who has shone in our hearts, for the illumination 14 of the knowledge of the glory of God 15 in the face of Jesus Christ. But we have this treasure 16 in clay vessels, 17 so that the excellence of the power may be of God, and not from us: While 18 we are pressed in all things, we are not rendered anxious: 19 we labor, but we are not forsaken: we suffer persecution, 20 but we are not abandoned in it: we are cast down, but we do not perish: 21 always carrying the dying of the Lord Jesus in the body, so that the 22 life of Jesus may be manifested in our body. For we who live are always delivered to death for the sake of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may be manifested in our mortal flesh. 23 And so death indeed acts in us, but life in you. But since we have the same spirit of faith, 24 according to that which is written, 25 "I believed, and therefore I spoke": we also believe, and for that reason we speak, 26 knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also through Jesus, 27 and will establish us with you.

---

<term>Illumination</term> <note>original: "illuminationem"</note> or illustration: which Ambrose translates as "light." But when "light" is brought forth, the Greek word is *phōtismos* <note>original: "φωτισμός"</note>. Chrysostom and Theophylact, in agreement with him, interpret it as *augēn* <note>original: "αὔγην"</note>, meaning a brilliance and a sort of taste of future glory, just as the Spirit is called a "pledge": a light that is ineffable, which is revealed afterward.

9 **Who is the image of God** <note>original: "Qui est imago Dei"</note> In the Aldine Edition <note>A famous early printed edition of the Greek New Testament</note>, the word "invisible" is added, which is not in our Latin texts. However, it seems to have been added by some studious person from the first chapter of the Epistle to the Colossians, especially since it is not found in other Greek manuscripts, and neither Chrysostom nor Theophylact read or interpret it. In fact, neither of the two Constance manuscripts contained the word "invisible."

10 **But Christ Jesus our Lord** <note>original: "Sed Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum"</note> The word "our" is redundant. It was not found in Theophylact or Chrysostom, nor in the older Constance manuscript, though it was added in the margin by a more recent hand. It is more complete as it is, so that we may understand Him to be the Lord of all. Furthermore, Paul distinguishes his own person from the person of Christ; he himself is a minister doing someone else's work, while Christ is the Lord, to whose glory everything the servant does must be referred.

<margin>D</margin> 11 **And ourselves your servants through Jesus** <note>original: "Nos autem servos vestros per Jesum"</note> It should be read as "for the sake of Jesus" <note>original: "propter Jesum; διὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν"</note>. And this is how Saint Ambrose reads it.

12 **Who said** <note>original: "Qui dixit"</note> The Greek is *ho eipōn* <note>original: "ὁ εἰπὼν"</note>. It was more fittingly translated as "who commanded," and a substantive verb should have been added: "It is God who commanded light to shine," and so forth. Next:

13 **He himself has shone** <note>original: "ipse illuxit"</note> Instead of "he himself," the Greek has "who" <note>original: "ὃς"</note>. For he who commanded is the one who shone. Moreover, the Greek words are *lampsai* and *elampse*, which Augustine, in his work against the slanderer of the Mosaic Law, reads as "to become bright" and "it became bright." He does so again when disputing against Faustus in book twenty-two, chapter eight.

14 **Of the knowledge of the brightness** <note>original: "Scientiæ claritatis"</note> The Greek is *tēs gnōseōs tēs doxēs*, meaning "of the knowledge of the glory." For some interpret "illumination" as the knowledge of the glory of Jesus. Also, instead of "of God," Ambrose reads "His own" <note>original: "suæ"</note>—unto the illumination of His own glory—because "God" preceded it.

<margin>E</margin> 15 **In the face of Christ Jesus** <note>original: "In facie Christi Jesu"</note> The Greek is *en prosōpō Iēsou Christou*. Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples <note>Erasmus refers to him as "Faber"</note> prefers to read "covered" here instead of "face," following Lorenzo Valla, I believe. But to me, it seems to fit Paul's meaning much better if we read "in the countenance" or "in the face." For he is alluding to the face of Moses which was covered by a veil, whereas in the face of Christ the glory of God the Father shone clearly, as if in a most perfect image. Chrysostom and Theophylact are roughly of this opinion.

16 **In earthen vessels** <note>original: "in vasis fictilibus"</note> The Greek is *ostrakinois*, meaning "made of clay/shards," though the sense is the same.

17 **That the sublimity** <note>original: "Ut sublimitas"</note> The Greek is "that the excellence of the power may be of God, and not from us." Here the Greeks consistently differ from the Latins. For Ambrose not only reads what our translation has, but also interprets it. He speaks thus: "That the eminence of his power may appear through human preachers," etc. Although here "power" is understood not as opposed to vice, but to weakness. Accordingly, Jerome, in his Dialogues against Pelagius, cites this passage in these words: "That the abundance of our strength may be from God." However, that word for "power" refers to us, not to God; so the sense is: "That our power, though so extraordinary, is not attributed to us, but to God." Furthermore, it is not "sublimity," but *hē hyperbolē*, meaning "excess," or "excellence," or, as Ambrose says, "eminence." Augustine several times reads "eminence," a most fitting word, and joins "eminence" with "power," so that "the eminence of power may be of God," both in his commentary on the Psalms and elsewhere. Also in Letter 153, and again in his fifteenth sermon on the words of the Apostle.

18 **In all things we suffer tribulation** <note>original: "in omnibus tribulationem patimur"</note> The translator has neither clearly rendered Paul’s meaning nor the pleasantness of the rhetorical figure. The Greek is *En panti thlibomenoi, all' ou stenochōroumenoi*, which means "Everywhere pressed or afflicted, but not hemmed in," or "not rendered anxious." Otherwise, it follows that those who are pressed are driven into a narrow space. Ambrose rendered

<column-break/>

the Greek more closely in this way: "In all things having suffered pressure, but not being crushed."

<margin>A</margin> 19 **We are at a loss, but not forsaken** <note>original: "Aporiamur, sed non destituimur"</note> There is a pleasant wordplay in the Greek: *aporoumenoi, all’ ouk exaporoumenoi*. One of these means to be stuck, lacking counsel and perplexed; the other means to be plainly despairing and overcome by weariness. Although *aporeisthai* can also mean to be in want, but in an anxious way, which the translator followed. Ambrose translates it as "having suffered want." The word restored here is a participle of the same verb that he translated a little earlier as "to be weary," *exaporeisthai*, as in "we were weary of living." The Greeks interpret it such that *aporeisthai* is to be reduced to extreme narrowness and want, but *exaporoumenoi* is to be conquered and overwhelmed by evils.

20 **But not abandoned** <note>original: "Sed non derelinquimur"</note> The Greek is *Diōkomenoi, all’ ouk egkataleipomenoi*. The latter sounds like being failed or destitute in danger, because of the added preposition *en*. "We are humbled, but not confounded." These words are found neither in the Greek manuscripts, nor in Ambrose’s reading, nor in the very ancient manuscript of Saint Donatian, nor in either of the Constance manuscripts; I wonder from where they crept in. Chrysostom and Theophylact neither read nor interpret them, nor even the one whose short commentary is falsely attributed to Jerome. And yet they would fit Paul’s meaning well enough, as confusion is very close to humiliation. Where the translator here uses verbs, the Greeks use participles. Ambrose reads it this way: "In all things having suffered pressure, but not crushed; having suffered want, but not destitute." But because the tense of the participle did not fit, the translator preferred to render them as verbs.

<margin>B</margin> 21 **Always the dying of Jesus Christ** <note>original: "Semper mortificationem Jesu Christi"</note> The Greek is "of the Lord Jesus," *nekrōsin tou Kyriou Iēsou*. But someone will object: what do these things matter to the sense, whether it be "of the Lord Jesus" or "of Jesus Christ"? First, I think it is a sin in Holy Scripture to change even one tiny stroke knowingly and willingly. But if anyone looks closer, they will see that even this variation in Paul is not idle, for in him nothing at all is idle. He added the title "Lord" so that the servants would not be reluctant to suffer similar things; likewise, lest the name of "death" should bring contempt to Christ, he added the title of "Lord." Ambrose, instead of "mortification" <note>the process of dying or putting to death</note>, reads simply "death," not absurdly in my opinion.

<margin>E</margin> 22 **The life of Jesus may be manifested in our bodies** <note>original: "Vita Jesu manifestetur in corporibus nostris"</note> The Greek is *en tō sōmati hēmōn*, that is, "in our body" (singular). Ambrose reads it this way as well, agreeing with the Greeks, so that you do not look at your body or my body, but that which is opposed to the spirit.

<margin>C</margin> 23 **Therefore death works in us** <note>original: "Ergo mors in nobis operatur"</note> The Greek is *Hōste ho men thanatos en hēmin energeitai*, which is "And so death indeed acts in us." Although it is "acts" <note>original: "agit"</note> rather than "works" <note>original: "operatur"</note>, about which enough has already been said.

24 **As it is written** <note>original: "Sicut scriptum est"</note> The Greek is *kata to gegrammenon*. Lefèvre d'Étaples thinks it could be read "by whom it is written." But the logic of the Greek language in no way allows this, so I wonder if he had a different manuscript, or certainly what came into the mind of such a learned man.

25 **I believed, because of which I spoke** <note>original: "Credidi propter quod loquutus"</note> This passage is in Psalm 115 <note>Psalm 116 in modern bibles</note>. The Greek phrasing is ambiguous: if you read it together, the sense is "I believed those things which I spoke"; if separately, the sense will be "I believed, and therefore I spoke." According to the first distinction, he would not have believed unless he had spoken; according to the latter, he would not have spoken unless he had believed. *Dio* means "wherefore" or "because of that."

<margin>F</margin> 26 **Knowing that he who raised Jesus** <note>original: "Scientes, quoniam qui suscitavit Jesum"</note> The Greeks read "the Lord Jesus." Furthermore, regarding the word *hoti*, sometimes it means "because" and sometimes "how"; it occurs too frequently to be worth correcting every time. For in Latin one could say, "Knowing that the one who raised Jesus would also raise us through Jesus." Or, "knowing that he who raised Jesus is the one who will raise us through Jesus."

27 **And will establish us with you** <note>original: "Et constituet vobiscum"</note> The Greek is *kai parastēsei syn hymin*. It means "and will present or join to himself together with you"; that is, not only us Jews, but also you Gentiles. Again, the phrase "with Jesus" is "through Jesus" in Greek (*dia Iēsou*). For it is not "with Jesus," who already rose long ago, but "through him," whose members we have become, and through whom he has given us all things. Even if Ambrose reads "with Jesus," he is not looking at the time, but at the common resurrection of the Head and the members.

He highlights subtle wordplays in the Greek describing the apostles' perseverance through suffering.</summary>

# SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER V.

15 <margin>15</margin> For all things are for your sakes, so that grace, having abounded <note>original: "πλεονάσασα"</note>, through the many might cause thanksgiving to overflow <note>original: "περισσεύσῃ"</note> to the glory of God.
16 <margin>16</margin> Therefore we do not lose heart; but even if our outer man is decaying, yet the inner man is being renewed day by day.
17 <margin>17</margin> For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, is working for us a far more exceeding <note>original: "καθ’ ὑπερβολὴν εἰς ὑπερβολὴν," literally "from excess unto excess"</note> and eternal weight of glory,
18 <margin>18</margin> While we do not look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen; for the things which are seen are temporary, but the things which are not seen are eternal.

### Chapter 5.

1 <margin>1</margin> For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle <note>A <term>tabernacle</term> refers to a tent, a temporary structure for travelers or soldiers.</note> is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
2 <margin>2</margin> For indeed in this we groan, longing to be clothed over <note>original: "ἐπενδύσασθαι"</note> with our dwelling which is from heaven.
3 <margin>3</margin> If indeed, having been clothed <margin>Otherwise: having been unclothed</margin>, we shall not be found naked.
4 <margin>4</margin> For indeed we who are in the tabernacle groan, being burdened; since we do not want to be unclothed, but clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.
5 <margin>5</margin> Now He who has prepared us for this very thing is God; who also has given us the down payment <note>original: "ἀῤῥαβῶνα," a technical term for earnest money or a deposit.</note> of the Spirit.
6 <margin>6</margin> Therefore being always of good courage, and knowing that while we are at home in the body, we are away from the home of the Lord.
7 <margin>7</margin> For we walk by faith, not by sight.
8 <margin>8</margin> We are of good courage and well-pleased rather to be away from the home of the body and to be at home with the Lord.

---

<margin>28 So that grace abounding through many, in the giving of thanks, may abound to the glory of God]</margin> <note>original: "ἵνα ἡ χάρις πλεονάσασα, διὰ τῶν πλειόνων τὴν εὐχαριστίαν περισσεύσῃ εἰς τὴν δόξαν τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note> That is, so that grace overflowing, or redundant, or by which it overflowed, on account of the thanksgiving of many, might abound to the glory of God. For the Greek word <note>original: "διὰ"</note> here means "on account of," not "through," unless you refer "through" to "the many," but then you have nothing to which to refer "thanksgiving." It seems Paul occasionally misused this preposition. And <term>Ambrose</term> <note>A 4th-century Church Father often cited by Erasmus.</note> reads it as follows: *through the thanksgiving of many*, meaning, if more people give thanks, it yields to the glory of God. The verb "abound" <note>original: "περισσεύσῃ"</note> can also be taken transitively, linked to the word "thanksgiving," so that we distinguish it thus: *so that grace, having abounded through the many*—here we place a comma—*might make thanksgiving overflow*. That is, that grace which overflowed through many people causes the giving of thanks to also overflow to God's glory. Lest this seem entirely accidental, in an older <term>Constantinopolitan manuscript</term> it was held thus: *so that grace abounding through many, thanksgiving may abound to the glory of God*. Another manuscript agreed in this: that "thanksgivings" was separated from the preceding words by a colon and a capital letter. As if to say: as grace overflows through many, likewise thanksgiving should overflow through many to the glory of God. In this case, the first noun is used absolutely instead of a possessive, and "through the many" refers to both parts: "having abounded" and "overflow."

<margin>29 We do not fail]</margin> <note>original: "οὐκ ἐκκακοῦμεν"</note>. Just as it was mentioned above: we do not become sluggish, we are not exhausted.

<margin>30 For momentary and light]</margin> <note>original: "Τὸ γὰρ παραυτίκα ἐλαφρὸν"</note>, that is, for that which is light in a moment. The word "present" is not in the Greek, except that the translator wanted to render the adverb <note>original: "τὸ παραυτίκα"</note>. He could have translated it this way: "For the momentary lightness of our affliction, remarkably, beyond measure, works or effects for us an eternal weight of glory." Here "lightness" <note>original: "τὸ ἐλαφρὸν"</note> is used as a noun, and "momentary" acts as an adjective, which is very common in Greek. Paul opposed "lightness" to "weight," which is certainly a noun. Nor is it called "light" here because it was easy to endure, but because it passes quickly; just as "weight" is not said because it burdens, but because it is solid and remains. Indeed, those who possess dignity are said to have "gravity" or weight. Now that phrase, *beyond measure unto measure* <note>original: "καθ’ ὑπερβολὴν εἰς ὑπερβολὴν"</note>, which is found consistently in all Greek manuscripts and repeated in the commentaries, means nothing other than a remarkable and ineffable excellence. As if you were to say "extraordinarily extraordinary," so he said "beyond measure" twice. For the two Greek phrases mean the same thing. I have noted elsewhere that the Hebrews express emphasis through this kind of doubling. It is not common in Greek, but it is for us, even without the preposition. <term>Chrysostom</term> and <term>Theophylact</term> <note>Prominent Greek commentators on the New Testament.</note> noted this repetition. Our Latin translator rendered one part as *beyond measure* and the other as *in sublimity*. Because certain more recent scholars, such as <term>Thomas Aquinas</term> and <term>Nicholas of Lyra</term>, were ignorant of this, they philosophized rather inappropriately here about the "manner and proportion" of rewards to merits and the "sublimity" of heavenly life. I will mention this, however: the adjective "eternal" can refer to both the "excess" that precedes it and the "weight" that follows. This whole speech is painted with contrasting relations, which Chrysostom also pointed out. For to "glory" he opposes "affliction," to "light" he opposes "weight," and to "momentary" he opposes "eternal." Again, he sets against each other "things seen" and "things not seen," and "temporary" versus "eternal." Regarding what he said a little earlier, "from day to day," the Greek is not "daily," but "day and day" <note>original: "ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ"</note>, so that you understand the progressive increase of renewal, just as the body fails more and more every day, especially in the elderly. This speech of Paul tastes of the Hebrew dialect, like the phrase "to generation and generation" instead of "to all generations."

<margin>31 Temporary]</margin> <note>original: "πρόσκαιρα"</note>, that is, lasting for a time. This is the same word the Evangelist used for the seed that soon withers away.

<column-break/>

15 <margin>15</margin> For everything is for your sake, <margin>A</margin> so that the benefit which has overflowed, as many give thanks, may abound to the glory of God.
16 <margin>16</margin> Therefore we are not exhausted, but although our outer man is corrupted, yet the inner is renewed every single day.
17 <margin>17</margin> For the momentary lightness of our affliction produces for us, in a marvelous way beyond measure, an eternal weight of glory,
18 <margin>18</margin> While we do not look at those things which are seen, but those which are not seen; for the things that are seen are temporary, but those not seen are eternal.

### V.

1 <margin>1</margin> For we know that if our earthly home of this tabernacle is destroyed, we have a building from God, a home not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
2 <margin>2</margin> For in this we groan, <margin>B</margin> desiring to be clothed over with our home which is from heaven.
3 <margin>3</margin> If indeed, being clothed, we shall not be found naked.
4 <margin>4</margin> For truly we who are in this tabernacle groan, being burdened: because we do not wish to be stripped, but to be clothed over, so that mortality may be swallowed up by life.
5 <margin>5</margin> Furthermore, He who prepared us for this very thing is God: who also gave us the down payment of the Spirit.
6 <margin>6</margin> Therefore we are always of good courage, and know that as long as we are at home in the body, we are wandering away from God.
7 <margin>7</margin> For we walk by faith, not by sight.
8 <margin>8</margin> We are confident and rather approve being away from the body and being present with God.

---

<margin>1 For we know, that]</margin> <margin>C</margin> The Greeks read it this way: *For we know that if our earthly house of the tabernacle be dissolved*. The word "this" is not added, except that the Greek article indicates a specific tabernacle. He adds "of the tabernacle" to show that this dwelling is not permanent, but prepared for a few days, as tents <note>original: "tabernacula"</note> are.

<margin>2 Not made with hands]</margin> It is more pleasant in the Greek compound word, <note>original: "ἀχειροποίητον"</note>, which distinguishes it from those things built and destroyed by manual labor.

<margin>3 For in this we groan]</margin> <note>original: "Καὶ γὰρ ἐν τούτῳ στενάζομεν"</note>. It is uncertain whether the pronoun "this" refers to the "tabernacle of the body," or if it is used absolutely to mean *on account of this* we groan, *because we desire to be clothed over*. Or, as <term>Lorenzo Valla</term> <note>A famous humanist critic whose work Erasmus edited.</note> prefers, "to be clothed over, to be clothed over." This refers to an outer garment, like a toga or a cloak. The following verse supports this: *If however, being clothed, and not found naked*. For one cannot be "clothed over" unless one is already clothed.

<margin>4 Our habitation]</margin> <note>original: "τὸ οἰκητήριον ἡμῶν"</note>, that is, our domicile. It refers to the verb "to be clothed over." For the body is the domicile of the soul, and Ambrose reads "in the domicile." Furthermore, regarding what he adds, "which is from heaven," I believe it refers to Christ's body, <margin>D</margin> to which our own are conformed in the fellowship of immortality.

<margin>5 If however clothed, and we be not found naked]</margin> Ambrose indicates a different reading in some manuscripts: *If indeed being stripped, we be not found naked*; that is, if having been stripped of this body, we are not found naked, but clothed in Christ. The Greek commentaries note the same: some have "having unclothed ourselves" <note>original: "ἐκδυσάμενοι"</note>, and others "having clothed ourselves" <note>original: "ἐνδυσάμενοι"</note>. The participle is active: "when we have stripped off" or "when we have put on." For he speaks of the body as if it were a garment.

<margin>6 In this tabernacle]</margin> <note>original: "ἐν τῷ σκήνει"</note>. Chrysostom noted the emphasis of these words. He calls the mortal body a "tabernacle" <note>original: "σκῆνος"</note>, but the immortalized body a "house" or "domicile." The tabernacle belongs to a traveler or soldier and is therefore temporary; the house belongs to one who dwells and remains permanently.

<margin>7 So that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life]</margin> <note>original: "τὸ θνητόν"</note>. Why not "mortality" rather than "what is mortal," to better correspond to "life"? In this way, the Greeks use neuter adjectives as nouns.

<margin>8 But He who works us for this very thing]</margin> <note>original: "Ὁ δὲ κατεργασάμενος ἡμᾶς εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο, Θεός"</note>, that is, "He who has made or prepared us for this very thing, God." It implies God is the guarantor. God will renew us in the resurrection, <margin>E</margin> having created us for this very purpose. Ambrose reads "perfected" instead of "worked." I do not see how "affected," which <term>Faber Stapulensis</term> <note>A French humanist and rival/colleague of Erasmus.</note> adds, corresponds to the Greek.

<margin>9 Pledge]</margin> <note>original: "ἀῤῥαβῶνα"</note>. It is not just "who gave," but "who also gave" <note>original: "ὁ καὶ δούς"</note>, referring to the one who prepared us for this and afterwards also gave the pledge of His Spirit, so that we might hope more surely.

<margin>10 Therefore daring]</margin> <note>original: "Θαῤῥοῦντες"</note>, that is, being confident or trusting. In this place, Paul seems to use the participle instead of a verb, <margin>F</margin> which happens more frequently in Greek than in Latin. Unless you prefer to arrange the speech so that the phrase *For we walk by faith* is interjected as a parenthesis. Then, as if returning to the point, he goes back to the interrupted speech: *We are confident and well-pleased*. He had begun with the participle "being confident," so the sense is: "Therefore, being always confident, and knowing that while we dwell in the body, we are away from the Lord (for we walk by faith, not by sight), yet we remain confident, I say, and not only confident, but so minded that we prefer to be away from the body, that we might be present with God."

<margin>11 But we dare]</margin> Again, "we are confident" <note>original: "Θαῤῥοῦμεν"</note>. And "we have a good will" <note>original: "εὐδοκοῦμεν"</note>. Ambrose translates this as "we agree"; I preferred "we approve." For that which pleases us is what we approve.

<margin>12 While we are in this body]</margin> Being "at home" <note>original: "ἐνδημοῦντες"</note>, being "away from home" <note>original: "ἐκδημοῦντες"</note>. He opposed these...

<meta>The catchword at the bottom is "posuit," referring to the continuation of the word "opposed" (opposuit) on the next page.</meta>

He emphasizes the rhetorical contrasts between the momentary sufferings of this life and the eternal weight of glory in the next.</summary>

On this page, he focuses on the motivations of the apostles: their desire to please God, the upcoming judgment, and the transformative power of Christ’s love which creates a "new creature."</meta>

# EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER V.

9 Therefore we also strive, whether present or absent, to be pleasing to Him. 10 For we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive the things done through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil. 11 Knowing, therefore, the fear of the Lord, we persuade men, but we have been made manifest to God; and I hope we have been made manifest also in your consciences. 12 For we are not commending ourselves to you again, but giving you an occasion to boast on our behalf, so that you may have something to say to those who boast in outward appearance and not in heart. 13 For whether we were beside ourselves, it was for God; or whether we are of sound mind, it is for you. 14 15 For the love of Christ compels us, having judged this: that if one died for all, then all died; and He died for all, so that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died for them and was raised. 16 So that from now on we know no one according to the flesh; and even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know Him thus no longer. 17 So that if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old things have passed away, behold, all things have become new. 18 And all things are from God, who has reconciled us to Himself through Jesus Christ, and has given to us the ministry of reconciliation. 19 Namely, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world to Himself, not imputing their trespasses to them, and having placed in us the word of reconciliation. 20 Therefore, we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us, we implore on behalf of Christ, be recon—
<meta>catchword: ciled</meta>

---

it can be rendered in words that the Latin Translator <note>Erasmus refers to the traditional translator of the Vulgate, often identified as St. Jerome.</note> could not conveniently render, unless you say, *while we are present, we are absent*. Indeed, in the Greek words, the complex opposition <note>original: "ἐναντιότης" (enantiotēs)</note> has a double grace, because it resides both in the sounds and in the subjects: *being at home* <note>original: "ἐνδημοῦντες" (endēmounte)</note> is to act abroad, that is, not to be at home; *being away from home* <note>original: "ἐκδημοῦντες" (ekdēmounte)</note> is to act at home. The Translator rendered this in various ways, according to his custom. Tertullian, in the eighth book of *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, translates it as *whether traveling or staying*.

13 *And therefore we contend*] <note>original: "φιλοτιμούμεθα" (philotimoumetha)</note>, that is, we strive and are ambitious. Ambrose reads *we endeavor*; although *we contend* fits well, provided it is well understood by us. For to "act with ambition" is to contend for something eagerly, such that you do not allow yourself to be surpassed by another.

14 *Whether absent or present*] These are participles of those verbs which he previously translated as *we travel*. It could be translated as *whether acting abroad or at home*. For he is thinking of the dwelling of the body, in which when we are at home, we are then abroad, separated from the Lord. Ambrose has *whether present or traveling*. The Translator almost rendered the grace of the figure of speech, which the opposition and the play on words <note>original: "παρονομασία" (paronomasia)</note> add to the Greek words.

15 *The things of the body*] In Greek it is <note>original: "τὰ διὰ τοῦ σώματος"</note>, that is, the things which are done through the body. The Translator seems to have read *the proper things of the body*. And Ambrose reads it this way. Theophylact reads and interprets it as *the things through the body*. Tertullian reads "through," suggesting an ambiguity in the speech. For the sense can be that each one carries back through the body, or the things he did through the body.

16 *According to what he did*] <note>original: "πρὸς ἃ ἔπραξε"</note>, that is, according to those things he did, which is to say, in proportion and part to the things he did in the body. A certain manuscript had *according to that which he did* (singular).

17 *But we are manifest to God*] In the Greek it is not "manifest" as a noun, but *we have been made manifest*, a verb <note>original: "πεφανερώμεθα"</note>. And likewise soon after, *that we are made manifest in your consciences* <note>original: "πεφανερώσθαι"</note>. Whether this was changed by scribes or placed by the Translator, it does not matter much to Paul's meaning.

18 *We give occasion*] In Greek it is *giving* <note>original: "διδόντες"</note>. But the Translator rightly changed the participle into a verb.

19 *That you may have toward those*] <note>original: "πρὸς τοὺς"</note>, that is, against those. And "you may have" is used for "you may be able to boast."

20 *We exceed*] <note>original: "ἐξέστημεν"</note>: as if you were to say, we are snatched outside of ourselves; what they call an "excess of mind" or a "rapture" <note>This refers to a state of spiritual ecstasy where the soul feels separate from the body.</note>. Perhaps it was written just after, *that we are made manifest in your consciences*, which is to say, whether we are insane or whether we are sane, whether we are wise or whether we are foolish. This explains more clearly what follows next.

21 *Whether we are sober*] <note>original: "εἴτε σωφρονοῦμεν"</note>, that is, whether we are of sound mind. Ambrose reads *whether we are wise in a healthy way*, so that it refers back to *we exceed in mind*. For that is also what "being sober" sometimes signifies. And the Greek commentaries warn that it is characteristic of the insane to speak grand things, as if forgetting themselves. Ambrose indicates the same. Augustine, in many other places as well as in explaining the thirtieth Psalm, refers this "excess" to ecstasy; and in many places he reads "excess" rather than "we exceed," observing the tense of the Greek verb. Although in things pertaining to the affections of the mind, the past tense is often used for the present. And in the twelfth book against Faustus, chapter twenty-six, instead of *we are sober*, he reads *we are temperate*. Theophylact added a triple commentary: when we speak of great things, he calls it *ecstasy*; again, *whether we seem to be insane* or *to be sober*; finally, he attributes to Paul a madness, but an *erotic* one, that is, one of love. For Plato teaches a threefold frenzy—that of prophets, of poets, and of lovers—of which he thinks the last is the most blessed. Theophylact attributes such a frenzy to Paul, who lived not in himself but in Christ, just as the soul of a lover is not where it gives life, but where it loves, and who for his brothers...
<meta>catchword: brothers</meta>

<column-break/>

<sig>A</sig> 13 Wherefore we contend, 14 whether present at home, 9
or acting as travelers abroad, that we may please him. For 10
it is necessary for us all to be made manifest before the tribunal of Christ, that each one may carry back 15 those things which are done through the body, 16 according to that which he has done, whether good or evil. Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men, 17 but to God we are manifest: and I hope that we are manifest also in your consciences. For 12
we do not commend ourselves to you again, 18 but we give you an occasion of boasting about us, 19 so that you may have something against those who boast in appearance, and not in heart. 20 For whether we are out of our mind, we are out of our mind for God, 21 or 13 whether we are of sound mind, we are of sound mind for you. For the charity of Christ 14
<sig>B</sig> 22 constrains us, Judging this, 23 that if one died for all, then all were dead: and he died for all, so that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and rose again. Therefore we 24 from now on know no one according to the flesh: furthermore, even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer. 25 Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature: the old things have passed away, behold all things have been made new. But all things are from God, who has reconciled us 18
<sig>C</sig> to himself through Jesus Christ, and has given to us the ministry of reconciliation. 26 Since God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, 27 not imputing to them their sins, and he placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore in the name of Christ 28 we perform the office of ambassadors, 29 20 as if God were beseeching you through us, we pray on behalf of Christ...
<meta>catchword: Christ</meta>

---

<sig>D</sig> ...it is necessary to become anathema from Christ. It should be noted that unless you repeat both verbs, the speech seems incomplete: *For whether we exceed in mind, we exceed for God; or whether we are of sound mind, we are sane for you*. For if Paul boasts of anything, it pertains not to his own glory, but to the glory of God. If he speaks of modest things, he attributes that to the weaker ones, to whose affections and capacity he accommodates himself. A similar figure was used in that saying to the Romans: *For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh, and so on*, as we indicated there.

22 *Urges us*] <note>original: "συνέχει" (synechei)</note>, that is, constrains, or compels; although *urges* sounds well. And shortly after, it is not *estimating*, but <note>original: "κριναντας" (krinantas)</note>, that is, *judging*, or we who have judged and determined that. Augustine reads *judging* in the eleventh book against Faustus, chapter eight, as does Ambrose.

23 *Since if one for all*] The "if" is not found in some Greek manuscripts. Certainly it is not added in Theophylact, nor in Ambrose, although it is clear from his interpretation. For he separates this from what follows with an intervening commentary: *Therefore all were dead, and so on*. Paul assumes what is beyond doubt—that Christ died for all—and then brings in what follows from this. Truly, it matters very little to the sense, except that what the Greeks read is more assertive: *Christ died, there is no disputing this; and for that reason he says "having judged."* It follows, therefore, that all were dead.

24 *From this*] <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν" (apo tou nyn)</note>, that is, *hereafter*: which he usually translates here as "from this point." Ambrose reads, *from this time*. In Quintus <sig>E</sig> Curtius, we read *for the rest*.

25 *If any then in Christ a new creature*] Ambrose interprets: *If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature*: so that the substantive verb is understood twice, even if the words of the context are corrupted in the Ambrosian manuscripts. But the same man, bringing forward this passage of Paul in the second book of Epistles, the eighth letter, clearly indicates what he read, writing thus: *And therefore he added, If anyone in Christ, a new creature: that is, he who is perfect in Christ is a new creature*. The interpreter Theophylact agreed in all things with Ambrose, even if in his interpreter also the words of the context were held to be corrupted in the Roman Edition, which ascribed it to Athanasius under a false title, when it was by Theophylact, Archbishop of Bulgaria. What of the fact that Origen brings this passage to the same sense in his twelfth Homily on Leviticus? *Every man therefore*, he says, *according to the Apostle, who is in Christ, is a new creature*. For Origen explains "if anyone" as "whoever." Finally, Chrysostom explains it thus: *If anyone has believed in him, he says, he has come into another creation; for indeed he was born from above through the Spirit*. The <sig>F</sig> same notes the intensity <note>original: "epitafin" (epitasin)</note>, because he called a violent change a *new creation* <note>original: "καινὴν κτίσιν" (kainēn ktisin)</note>.

26 *Since God was in Christ*] <note>original: "Ὡς ὅτι" (Hōs hoti)</note>. It sounds almost like *So because*, to show the manner in which God reconciled us to himself. So the Greek commentaries seem to indicate, and even more clearly Theophylact: *He reconciled: how? by not imputing sins*.

27 *Not reputing*] <note>original: "μὴ λογιζόμενος" (mē logizomenos)</note>. Better, *not imputing*.

28 *We perform the office of ambassadors*] <note>original: "πρεσβεύομεν" (presbeuomenom)</note>: which also signifies *we pray*. Although they are also called *oratores* (spokesmen) who demand something in the name of another.

29 *As if God were exhorting through us*] <note>original: "παρακαλοῦντος" (parakalountos)</note>. I know the Greek voice is ambiguous. Nor would I fight it if "exhorting" pleases someone more. Yet I am not moved by the scruple of those who think it indecorous for God to "beseech." Certainly, he soon prays through Paul: *we beg* <note>original: "δέομεθα" (deometha)</note>. Chrysostom writes thus on this passage: *Do you see how before...*

# SECOND LETTER TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER VI.

<column-break/>

<margin>21</margin> ...and word to God. For He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in Him. <note>original Greek: "δικαιοσύνη Θεοῦ" (dikaiosyne Theou)</note>
<margin>VI. 1</margin> Working together with Him, we also exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain. <margin>2</margin> For He says, "In an acceptable time I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you." <note>Quoting Isaiah 49:8</note> Behold, now is the highly acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. <margin>3</margin> Giving no offense in anything, so that the ministry may not be blamed, <margin>4</margin> but in everything commending ourselves as ministers of God: in much patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses, <margin>5</margin> in stripes, in imprisonments, in turmoils, in labors, in sleeplessness, in fastings; <margin>6</margin> in purity, in knowledge, in longsuffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in sincere love, <margin>7</margin> in the word of truth, in the power of God; through the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, <margin>8</margin> through glory and dishonor, through evil report and good report; as deceivers, and yet true; <margin>9</margin> as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; <margin>10</margin> as disciplined, and not put to death; as sor—

---

<margin>21</margin> **The matter at hand** is that he places this plea to introduce Christ—or rather, not only Christ but also the Father. That is, you see how he has heightened the matter, bringing in Christ performing this supplication; indeed, he makes it Christ, but also the Father Himself.
<margin>30</margin> **Him who knew no sin, He made sin]** The first "sin" mentioned is the transgression committed; the second refers to the victim destined for the expiation of sin. It is a wonder why Faber <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples (c. 1455–1536), a French humanist and theologian</note> is so anxious lest anyone think Christ actually sinned, since that meaning cannot be taken from these words in any way, as it says "He who had known no sin, He made sin for us." For he did not say "He made Him a sinner," but "sin." That is, He willed Him to suffer punishment just as if He had committed all sins, though He alone had sinned in nothing. You should understand "sin" as the victim usually sacrificed for the expiation of sin, just as we read, "they shall eat the sins of the people." <note>Hosea 4:8</note> This is generally how the Greek commentaries <note>The "scholia" or ancient marginal notes</note> explain it. Finally, he called Christ "sin" in this place just as he called us "the righteousness of God" a little earlier; and elsewhere he called Christ "a curse." Augustine does not shrink from this manner of speaking in his fourteenth book against Faustus. Even if in some places he explains this sentence as if the word "made" refers to Christ rather than the Father.
<margin>31</margin> **The righteousness of God]** In the Hebrew idiom, he said "righteousness" for "righteous people," and added "of God" to exclude reliance on and the pride of our own works. So says Chrysostom. One should note the literary figure <term>schema</term> <note>a rhetorical pattern</note> in the transition from "sin" to "sin," and likewise in the contrast <note>antithesis</note> between "sin" and "righteousness."

<margin>A</margin> **And helping, we exhort]** Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274)</note> twists himself in this place, first interpreting it twofold: "Helping you," as if referring to the Corinthians, and then "Helping God." But since it seems absurd for God to be helped by a human, he applies a tiny distinction which would have been unnecessary had he consulted the Greek, which has "Working together" <note>original: Συνεργοῦντες (synergountes)</note>, that is, "Cooperating." For why should we dread this phrasing, since in the third chapter of the previous Epistle we read, "For we are God's helpers"? <note>1 Corinthians 3:9</note> Chrysostom, however, retains the former meaning, as does Theophylact. But the second meaning fits better with what precedes and follows: the Father is the author of the business, Christ is the chief of the embassy, and the Apostles are the ministers. The Father works in Christ, and Christ in the Apostles. Nor is the conjunction lacking in emphasis: "and we exhort." It was a great thing to have preached the Gospel to them and to have suffered so much, and yet to this he even adds an entreaty. Next, where it follows "we exhort," the Greek is <gloss>parakaloumen</gloss>, which, as has been said frequently, means both "we beseech" and "we comfort." Just as a little earlier, it was "as though God were exhorting through us." In both places the word for "beseeching" fits well, especially since "I beg" <note>original: δέομαι (deomai)</note> follows, which the Translator renders as "I beseech." One should note how much so great an Apostle humbles himself, even before those who had sinned; whereas now, those far unlike him, with wondrous pride, croak out nothing but commands, threats, excommunications, and anathemas. He asks twice: first in the name of Christ, whose place he takes, then in his own, as His co-worker, as if this also pertained somewhat to himself. Finally, he calls the "grace of God" the "benefit of God."

<margin>B</margin> **In an acceptable time I heard you]** When he says "He says," the "Lord" or "Scripture" is to be understood. This form of speech is not infrequent in Paul. The passage he cites is in Isaiah, chapter forty-nine. Saint Jerome rendered the Hebrew thus: "In a pleasing time I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you." The Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament</note> do not differ from this: "In an opportune time I heard you..." I wonder, meanwhile, how it happened that we read "of you" <note>Latin: tui</note> for "to you" <note>Latin: tibi</note>, since in Greek it is the dative: "I helped you" <note>original: ἐβοήθησά σοι (eboethesa soi)</note>. However, this is more "to be a help to you" than what is translated here as "I aided."

<margin>C</margin> **Giving no offense to anyone]** The Translator seems to have read, "Giving not even one [offense] to anyone," whereas in the Greek manuscripts I have been able to see, it was written, "Not even one in anything," that is, "not any, anywhere," or "in any matter." This is how Theophylact and Chrysostom read it. Augustine likewise cites it in the eighth book of *On the Trinity*, chapter nine: "Giving no offense in anything," so that "anyone/anything" <note>original: μηδενὶ (medeni)</note> refers to the thing, not the person.

<margin>D</margin> **Our ministry]** The word "our" is not added among the Greeks; and it is better not to add it, so that the meaning may be fuller: Salvation is the gift of God, and it is administered through us. Thus, let the one who administers conduct himself so that the gift itself is not despised by the fault of the minister. The Translator wanted to express the force of the article: "the ministry" <note>original: ἡ διακονία (he diakonia)</note>.

<margin>E</margin> **Let us exhibit]** <gloss>commending ourselves</gloss>; and thus Saint Ambrose reads it, and Augustine agrees in the fourth book of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter twenty. It is uncertain whether it should be "let us exhibit" or "we exhibit." For soon he enters into praises of himself. For he calls this "commendation," which wins favor and authority by the deeds themselves. It is not "as ministers of God," but "as ministers of God" <note>Erasmus is correcting the Latin case ending here</note>, as if to say "we are"; just as in "giving no offense," and the rest; unless one prefers to refer it back to "we exhort." Then, after many things are interjected, the answer is "we are giving." Thus all these things will pertain to the person of Paul, and that is more consistent. Finally, Ambrose reads "as ministers of God," not "to the ministers."

<column-break/>

<margin>21</margin> (By Christ, be reconciled to God. <margin>20</margin> For Him, who knew no sin, He made sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God through Him.
<margin>VI. 1</margin> Moreover, as helpers we beseech you, that you receive not the grace of God in vain. For He says, <margin>2</margin> In an acceptable time I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you. Behold now is the acceptable time, behold now is the day of salvation. <margin>3</margin> That we give no offense in anything, lest the ministry be blamed, <margin>4</margin> but in all things let us commend ourselves as ministers of God, in much endurance, in afflictions, in necessities, in anxieties, <margin>5</margin> in beatings, in prisons, in seditions, in labors, in watchings, in fastings, <margin>6</margin> in purity, in knowledge, in gentleness of spirit, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in love unfeigned, <margin>7</margin> in the word of truth, in the power of God, by the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, <margin>8</margin> by glory and shame, by insults and praises: <margin>14</margin> as impostors, and yet truthful: as unknown, and yet known: as dying, and behold <margin>9</margin> we live: as chastened, and not killed: <margin>16</margin> as grieving...

---

<margin>6</margin> **In much patience]** In this enumeration of things, the copies vary somewhat, which usually happens whenever such short lists are copied, I suppose, from memory by a scribe. Then the preposition "in," repeated so many times, seems almost to be used by misuse for "through."

<margin>7</margin> **In sweetness]** <note>original: ἐν χρηστότητι (en chrestoteti)</note>, that is, in kindness, or goodness, and affability, which is opposed to pride and harshness of manners.

<margin>8</margin> **In unfeigned love]** The compound word is more pleasant in Greek, <gloss>unhypocritical</gloss>, that is, which is free from pretense. Ambrose reads "not simulated."

<margin>9</margin> **In the power of God]** <note>original: ἐν δυνάμει Θεοῦ (en dynamei Theou)</note>. This should be understood as referring to signs and miracles, as Ambrose also interprets it.

<margin>10</margin> **On the right and on the left]** Faber Stapulensis <note>Lefèvre d'Étaples</note> in this place changes "right and left" to "favorable and adverse things." I do not understand at all what he means by this. For first, "left and right" is far different from "adverse and favorable." Although I do not even see how the weapons we carry on our back can be called "favorable," and those on our chest "adverse." But even if we grant this to be so, he should not have said "of favorable and adverse things," but "favorable and adverse [weapons]": for these epithets refer to the weapons, unless I am mistaken. But Faber, I suppose, wanted to interpret "right and left" as if by the right hand favorable things are signified, and by the left, adverse things. Yet that is the duty of one writing a commentary, not a translator. Nor is it absurd that he calls "right-hand weapons" those which protect us on the right against the indulgence of fortune, and "left-hand weapons" those by which we are shielded on the left against the attack of evils and afflictions. Although it seems simpler to me that we take "from the right and left" as if to say "armed on all sides against everything"; for the proverbial figure of speech achieves this. Certainly, Saint Aurelius Augustine, both elsewhere and in his Commentaries on the ninety-second Psalm, reads "through the weapons of righteousness on the right and left." He cites it the same way in the eighth book of *On the Trinity*, chapter nine.

<margin>11</margin> **Through glory and ignobility]** <note>original: διὰ δόξης καὶ ἀτιμίας (dia doxes kai atimias)</note>, that is, through glory and ignominy, or contempt.

<margin>12</margin> **Through infamy and good fame]** <note>original: διὰ δυσφημίας καὶ εὐφημίας (dia dysphemias kai euphemias)</note>. As if you were to say "speaking ill" and "speaking well."

<margin>13</margin> **As seducers]** <note>original: ὡς πλάνοι (hos planoi)</note>, that is, as impostors, or rather "as if," as he translates soon after. Although it was necessary to translate it consistently this way, since <gloss>hos</gloss> is everywhere. But the Translator was strangely pleased with his own variety, sometimes translating "as," sometimes "as if," sometimes "just as," sometimes "like," just as if there were no difference among all these words in Latin. Even if we grant there is no difference, certainly the iteration of the same word contributes not only to the beauty of the speech but also to its force. For this whole discourse is varied, rolled, and rotated through contraries, through members, through pairs, through similar endings, through repetition <term>anadiplosis</term>, and other such figures, so that nothing could be more elegant or more ardent. Whence Saint Augustine produces this passage in his books *On Christian Doctrine* as an example of grandiloquent style. For as if snatched into an ecstasy, he finally adds, "Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians."

<margin>14</margin> **Just as those who are unknown, and recognized]** <note>original: Ὡς ἀγνοούμενοι, καὶ ἐπιγνωσκόμενοι (hos agnooumenoi kai epignoskomenoi)</note>. Augustine, in the fourth book of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter twenty, having preserved the logic of the whole, reads, "As those who are ignored, and are known." In which place he noted the heat and harmony of this tone of speech, if anyone wishes to know.

<margin>15</margin> **As if chastened, not put to death]** <note>original: ὡς παιδευόμενοι (hos paideuomenoi)</note>. Which Augustine, both elsewhere and in the eleventh book of *The City of God*, reads as "as restrained, and not put to death." The Greek participle is in the present tense, which could be expressed as "as those who are being corrected, not being killed." For it signifies that the godly are corrected by God, but like sons by a father, who chastens and amends with a whip, but does not kill.

<margin>16</margin> **As if sad]** <note>original: Ὡς λυπούμενοι (hos lypoumenoi)</note>, that is, "grieving," rather.
