# EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER VII.

...sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things. <margin>11</margin> Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our <margin>12</margin> heart is enlarged. You are not restricted in us, but you are restricted in your own affections <note>original: "σπλάγχνοις" (splangchnois), literally "bowels," a term used for the seat of deep emotion or mercy</note>. <margin>13</margin> For the same reward (I speak as to children), be enlarged yourselves also. <margin>14</margin> Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? or what fellowship has light with darkness? <margin>15</margin> What accord has Christ with Belial? or what portion has a believer with an unbeliever? What <margin>16</margin> agreement has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God, as God said: "I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people." <margin>17</margin> "Therefore come out from their midst and be separate," says the Lord; "and touch no unclean thing, and I will receive you. <margin>18</margin> And I will be a father to you, and you shall be my sons and daughters," says the Lord Almighty. <margin>VII. 1</margin> Therefore, having these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from all defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God. <margin>2</margin> Make room for us; we have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have defrauded no one. <margin>3</margin> I do not say this to condemn you; for I have said before...

---

<margin>C</margin> <margin>10</margin> 10 *As having nothing, and possessing all things*] Perhaps in this place, some allowance should be given to the Translator for not rendering the grace of the Greek structure: <note>original: "ὡς μηδὲν ἔχοντες, καὶ πάντα κατέχοντες" (hōs mēden echontes, kai panta katechontes)</note>, which is as if you were to say, *as holding nothing, and containing all things*. It would have been clearer to say: *as if having nothing, though we possess all things*.

<margin>11</margin> 11 *You are not restricted in us*] <note>original: "Οὐ στενοχωρεῖσθε" (Ou stenochōreisthe)</note>. First, the reader should be advised that "restricted" here is not in the imperative mood (as a command), but in the indicative (stating a fact); for the Greek does not say *mē* <note>the Greek particle for "not" used with commands</note>, but *ou* <note>the particle for "not" used with facts</note>. Yet the Translator is accustomed to render this type of speech in the form: *Do not be restricted*, just as he does a little later with: *Do not draw the yoke with unbelievers*. Furthermore, those who are pressed into narrow spaces are said to be "restricted" <note>original: "στενοχωρεῖσθε" (stenochōreisthe)</note>. Paul feels, therefore, that he has a very large and open heart in Christ. However, he says they are narrow, not because of Paul, but because of their own feelings, which he calls "bowels." And soon he exhorts them to cease being narrow. Indeed, in this place, he calls "narrowness" not affliction or mental distress, but the anxious observation of the ceremonies of the Mosaic Law, or human traditions. For he previously argued concerning food offered to idols. Unless you prefer to refer this to the grief they felt because of the man Paul had ordered to be handed over to Satan <note>a reference to the excommunicated man in 1 Corinthians 5</note>.

<margin>13</margin> 13 *But having the same reward*] The word "having" is not found in the Greek copies, so it seems the preposition "according to" <note>Greek: "κατὰ" (kata)</note> should be understood: that is, *be enlarged yourselves also according to the same reward*. Theophylact <note>an 11th-century biblical commentator</note> supplies the verb "acknowledge" <note>Greek: "γινώσκετε" (ginōskete)</note>, meaning *assert it*. Although Ambrose reads "the reward of payment," to express the Greek word *antimisthian* <note>meaning a recompense or return</note>. He also distinguishes it so that the participle "having" pertains to "you are restricted": *You suffer restriction not through me, who am of an open heart and mouth toward you, but in your own souls, although you have the same payment of reward as the rest and as I do*. Then he adds: *I speak as to children*, be enlarged yourselves also, so that you might respond to your parent. But from Chrysostom <note>a 4th-century Church Father known for his preaching</note> we learn the reading of this passage, such that there is no need for a preposition nor a verb summoned from elsewhere. What Paul calls "enlargement" is extraordinary charity; what he calls "narrowness" is a charity that does not respond equally. He complains to the Corinthians, therefore, that he is loved less by them than he himself loves. When he said, therefore, *you are restricted in your own affections*, it is as if the Corinthians had asked, "Whose fault is that?" He responds: "I do not demand anything difficult from you, nor do I demand back my merit with interest; I only ask this as a father from his children—that you respond in love. I will consider everything paid if I am loved in return." This will be the reward of my duties toward you. Thus, "I say" is like explaining what he had said more obscurely: *You are not restricted in me, but in your own affections*, just as we are accustomed to say, "I am talking about a stepmother." I say these things as if to children, demanding mutual love from them. I will write down Chrysostom's words: <note>Erasmus provides a lengthy quote from Chrysostom's Homily 13 on 2 Corinthians, where the Father explains that Paul isn't being harsh but is pleading for the natural love a child owes a father, even if the father loved first.</note> From these words of Chrysostom, it appears that the word "say" <note>Greek: "λόγον" (logon), though Erasmus likely means "λέγω" (legō)</note> does not refer to the following speech, *Be enlarged yourselves also*, but to the reward.

<margin>14</margin> 14 *Do not draw the yoke*] The Translator has rendered the sense correctly. Although the Greek speech is more significant: <note>original: "Μὴ γίνεσθε ἑτεροζυγοῦντες ἀπίστοις" (Mē ginesthe heterozygountes apistois)</note>, that is, *Do not be joined under the same yoke with unbelievers*.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...rejoicing: as poor, yet making many rich: as having nothing, and yet possessing all things. Our mouth is open toward you, Corin- <margin>11</margin> thians: our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted <margin>12</margin> in us, but you are restricted in your own affections. For the <margin>13</margin> same reward (I speak as to children), be enlarged also yourselves. Do not draw the yoke with unbelievers. For <margin>14</margin> what partnership has righteousness with injustice? or what fellowship has light with darkness? Or what harmony has Christ <margin>15</margin> <margin>B</margin> with Belial? or what part has a believer with an infidel? Or <margin>16</margin> what agreement has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God, <margin>22</margin> as God said: I will dwell in them, <margin>23</margin> and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. Wherefore <margin>17</margin> come out from their midst, and be separate from them, says the Lord: and touch not the unclean thing, and I will receive you, and I will be to you in the place of a father, and you shall be to me <margin>18</margin> in the place of sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty. Since we have these promises, most beloved, <margin>VII. 1</margin> let us cleanse ourselves from all defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness with the fear of God. <margin>1</margin> Make room for us: we have harmed no one, we have <margin>2</margin> corrupted no one, <margin>2</margin> we have defrauded no one. I do not say this for <margin>3</margin> condemnation...

---

<margin>D</margin> For if a Christian marries a Pagan, or if a Christian is a colleague with a Pagan in holding a magistracy, he is said to be "unequally yoked" <note>original: "ἑτεροζυγεῖν" (heterozygein)</note>. Jerome calls marriages of this kind "impious." The word *heteros* among the Greeks sometimes means "the other" of two, and sometimes "different," whether of two or many: a "one-eyed person" <note>Greek: "ἑτερόφθαλμος" (heterophthalmos)</note> is one who lacks the other eye; a "heterodox person" <note>Greek: "ἑτερόδοξος" (heterodoxos)</note> is one of a different opinion. Hence it is uncertain whether Paul says "unequally yoked" of those who bear the other part of a yoke, or those who draw a yoke with a man of a different condition, just as if you were to pair a horse and an ox in a yoke. The latter is more probable from what follows: *for what participation has justice with iniquity?* etc.

<margin>21</margin> 21 *Harmony*] <note>original: "συμφώνησις" (symphonēsis)</note>, that is, *agreement* or *concord*. Of Christ with Belial. The Greeks read *Beliar*, *Beliar*, for the reason, unless I am mistaken, that no Greek noun ends in the letter *lambda* (l). Greek notes indicate that for the Hebrews, Belial signifies "the Deserter," that is, Lucifer. But that excellent man Johann Reuchlin <note>a famous German humanist and Hebrew scholar, 1455–1522</note>—a man most learned in every respect, and the second glory and ornament of our Germany after Rodolphus Agricola—teaches in his Lexicon that *Belial* among the Hebrews signifies *evil and unjust*, or even a *harmful Demon*, which fits well enough. For Christ did all things to be of benefit; on the contrary, Belial, even when he helps, helps only to harm.

<margin>22</margin> 22 *As God said*] Saint Thomas Aquinas thinks this testimony is taken from the twenty-sixth chapter of Leviticus, where we read in this manner: *I will set my tabernacle in your midst, and my soul shall not cast you away. I will walk among you, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people*. But Carrensis, following Didymus, refers it to the thirty-seventh chapter of Ezekiel, where we read: *And my tabernacle shall be in them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And the nations shall know that I am the sanctifier of Israel, when my sanctification shall be in their midst forever*. And yet Paul's citation does not match either of these places in every detail. Therefore, let the reader know that this testimony was not brought forth from <margin>E</margin> a single place, but fused from many, which we have shown happened elsewhere as well. Indeed, the first part seems taken from Leviticus. Then what follows, *Wherefore come out from their midst*, etc., is excerpted from Isaiah, where you read in chapter 52: *Depart, depart, go out from there, touch no polluted thing, go out from the midst of her: be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord*. Finally, what he added, *And I will be to you a father*, etc., can be seen as taken from the thirty-first chapter of Jeremiah: *Because I have become a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn*.

<margin>23</margin> 23 *And I will walk among them*] "Among them" is not in the Greek, but the Translator nonetheless tried to express the verb *emperipatēso* <note>original: "ἐμπεριπατήσω"</note>, which signifies *to walk in something*. For "to walk in" <note>Latin: "inambulare"</note> for the Latins is nothing else sometimes than "to walk about"; however, it was better to say "in them" than "among them," unless we think that in both cases the preposition "in" is put for "among." Ambrose wrote both, reading it thus: *I will dwell in them, and among them I will walk*.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>1</margin> 1 *Receive us*] <note>original: "Χωρήσατε ἡμᾶς" (Chōrēsate hēmas)</note>. Because he said before "you are restricted." Nor is "Receive" <note>Latin: "Capite"</note> here used for "understand," but just as a vessel or a place "contains" or "receives" something. Ambrose explained it nearly the same way, reading, *Be capable of containing us*, which we have followed. For he rubs again what he said before: *Be enlarged yourselves also*.

<margin>2</margin> 2 *We have defrauded*] <note>original: "ἐπλεονεκτήσαμεν" (epleonektēsamen)</note>. Which he also translates elsewhere in the same way: *Lest we be defrauded by Satan*. It properly means to have taken away by fraud what was not owed by right. Ambrose reads in this place, *we have harmed no one, we have burdened no one, we have defrauded no one*; and he explains it thus: The false apostles do harm when they corrupt the senses of their own people, and they burden their purses by the fraud of serpentine cunning. The Greek says, <note>original: "οὐδένα ἠδικήσαμεν, οὐδένα ἐφθείραμεν, οὐδένα ἐπλεονεκτήσαμεν" (oudena ēdikēsamen, oudena ephtheiramen, oudena epleonektēsamen)</note>, that is, *we have treated no one with injury, we have corrupted no one, we have defrauded no one*; that is, we have occupied no one's property against what is right, and turned it to our own advantage. He "does injury" <note>original: "ἀδικεῖ" (adikei)</note> who exercises tyranny; he "corrupts" <note>original: "φθείρει" (phtheirei)</note> who teaches false things; he "defrauds" <note>original: "πλεονεκτεῖ" (pleonektei)</note> who usurps the property of others by guile. For in this way he obliquely attacks the false apostles. Otherwise, it would not have been a great praise that Paul had not done these things. O truly priestly glory—and would that all Bishops were truly permitted to glory in the same way!

<summary>In this commentary on 2 Corinthians 6-7, Erasmus explores Paul's emotional plea for the Corinthians to open their hearts and separate themselves from pagan influences. He uses philological analysis to show how Paul blends multiple Old Testament passages and defends the apostle against the greed and corruption typified by false teachers.</summary>
<keywords>enlargement of heart, Belial, unequal yoke, temple of God, Johann Reuchlin, false apostles, Greek philology, patristic commentary</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the text of 2 Corinthians Chapter 7. The previous page ended with Paul appealing to the Corinthians to "make room" for the apostles in their hearts. This page contains the biblical text in both Greek and Latin, followed by Erasmus’s detailed philological notes on the vocabulary and grammar of the passage, particularly focusing on the nature of "godly sorrow" and repentance.</meta>

# TO THE SECOND CORINTHIANS. CHAPTER VII.

<margin>κ</margin> For I have said before, that you are in our hearts to die together and to live together. Great is my boldness of speech toward you, great is my glorying on your behalf: I am filled with comfort, I exceedingly abound with joy <margin>6</margin> in all our tribulation. For even when we had come into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we were troubled on every side: without were fightings, within were fears. But God, who comforts the humble, comforted us by the coming of Titus. And not only by his coming, but also by the comfort wherewith he was comforted in you, when he told us your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that <margin>9</margin> I rejoiced the more. For though I made you sorry with a letter, I do not repent, though I did repent: for I perceive that the same letter, though but for a time, made you sorry. Now I rejoice, not that you were made sorry, but that you sorrowed to repentance: for you were made sorry <margin>10</margin> according to God <note>original: "κατὰ Θεὸν" (kata Theon), often translated as "godly sorrow"</note>, so that you might suffer loss by us in nothing. For the sorrow that is according to God works repentance unto salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world <margin>11</margin> works death. For behold this selfsame thing, that you sorrowed according to God, what great diligence it wrought in you, what clearing of yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what revenge: in everything you have shown yourselves to be pure in this matter. Therefore, though I wrote to you, I did it not for his sake that had done the wrong, nor for his sake that suffered wrong, but that our care for you in the sight of God might be made manifest—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> I do not say this to condemn you: for I have said before, that you are in our hearts to die together and to live together. Great is my confidence toward you, <margin>4</margin> great is my glorying of you: I am filled with comfort, I exceedingly overflow with joy in all our affliction. For when we were come into Macedonia, our flesh had no relief, <margin>5</margin> but we were afflicted in all things: without were battles, within were terrors. <margin>B</margin> But He who comforts the humble, <margin>6</margin> God, comforted us by the arrival of Titus. Not only by his arrival, but also by the comfort which <margin>7</margin> he received from you, when he announced to us your desire, your weeping, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced the more. For even if I saddened you by my letter, I do not regret it, even <margin>8</margin> if I had regretted it: for I see that that letter, although only for a time, made you sad. Now I rejoice, not <margin>9</margin> that you were made sad, but that you were made sad unto repentance: for you were saddened according to God, <margin>10</margin> so that in no thing were you affected by loss through us. <margin>C</margin> For the grief that is according to God produces a repentance <margin>10</margin> toward salvation not to be regretted: on the other hand, the grief of the world brings death. For behold this very thing, <margin>11</margin> that you were saddened according to God, what great anxiety it produced in you, rather what satisfaction, rather what indignation, rather what fear, what longing, what emulation, what vengeance: indeed everywhere <margin>C</margin> you commended yourselves, that you are pure in that business. <margin>12</margin> Therefore although I wrote to you, I did it not for the sake of him— <margin>12</margin>

---

3 **For we said before**] <note>original: "προείρηκα γὰρ" (proeirēka gar)</note>, that is, *for I have said before*: and this is how Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose, 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note> reads it.

4 **To die together and live together**] <note>original: "εἰς τὸ συναποθανεῖν καὶ συζῇν" (eis to synapothanein kai syzēn)</note>. Among the ancients, there was a type of friendship where, if a friend happened to die, the other would voluntarily take his own life: Horace indicates he had this kind of friendship with Maecenas. Hence they were called **those who die together** <note>original: "συναποθνήσκοντες" (synapothnēskontes)</note>. Not that Paul intends anything of this sort, such as we read once existed among the Pagans, but in this way he wished to indicate the closest possible friendship.

5 **Glorying for you**] <note>original: "καύχησις ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν" (kauchēsis hyper hymōn)</note>. It is better translated here as *concerning you*, that is, in your name.

6 **I superabound with joy**] <note>original: "ὑπερπερισσεύομαι" (hyperperisseuomai)</note>. Which means I abound beyond measure or vehemently, or rather, I overflow. The addition of "super" in Latin does not achieve the same effect as "hyper" or "peri" does in Greek composition. Therefore, it was appropriate to explain it with different Latin adjectives.

7 **But we suffered every tribulation**] <note>original: "ἀλλὰ ἐν παντὶ θλιβόμενοι" (alla en panti thlibomenoi)</note>, that is, *but in all things afflicted*, so that the word "were" is understood. For it is frequently familiar to the Hebrews and Greeks to leave the verb "to be" implied.

8 **Wherewith he was comforted in you**] "Comforted" here must be taken in the passive sense <note>original: "ᾗ παρεκλήθη" (hē pareklēthē)</note>.

9 **Even if I repented**] <note>original: "εἰ καὶ μετεμελόμην" (ei kai metemelomēn)</note>, that is, *even if I had repented*. You should take this to mean that Paul does not actually admit to regret for having caused them sorrow before, but now he rejoices so much because he learned from Titus that the matter turned out well, that even if any regret had held him for his prior action, he would now cast it aside. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople</note> notes this carefully. For he did not say, "I repented before, now I do not repent," but "I do not repent, even if I had repented." We speak this way when mistakes turn out happily: and it refers to what came before, not what follows. For "for" follows in Greek <note>original: "βλέπω γὰρ" (blepō gar)</note>, that is, *for I see*. Although it does not escape me that it is punctuated differently by Ambrose, who orders it thus: *Even if I repented, I see etc.* and does not add "for." In this he certainly agrees with the Greeks, that he reads "I see" <note>original: "βλέπω"</note>, not "seeing" <note>original: "βλέπων"</note>. But whether we read *I see* or *seeing*, we are forced to admit that one part of the speech is incomplete, unless we accept the first reading we indicated. The difficulty could be removed this way: Although that Epistle made you sad for a time, yet now I rejoice, not that I made you sad, but that I see you were made sad unto repentance.

10 **That in nothing you might suffer detriment**] <note>original: "ἵνα ἐν μηδενὶ ζημιωθῆτε" (hina en mēdeni zēmiōthēte)</note>, that is, *lest you should suffer loss in any matter*, unless perhaps Paul misused this word "that" <note>Greek: "ἵνα" (hina)</note> instead of "so that" <note>Greek: "ὥστε" (hōste)</note>, which he seems to do sometimes.

11 **Stable**] <note>original: "ἀμεταμέλητον" (ametameleton)</note>, that is, *not to be repented of*. Augustine reads it as "un-repentable" in the fourteenth book of *The City of God*, chapter eight, according to the reliability of a very ancient Lombard manuscript. It refers, I believe, to "repentance," not to "salvation," **repentance not to be repented of** <note>original: "μετάνοιαν ἀμεταμέλητον" (metanoian ametameleton)</note>, with opposites most elegantly joined together, as if you were to say, **unregrettable regret**. Although Ambrose seems to refer the adjective to "salvation," not to "repentance." It is a type of sentence and a rhetorical figure woven from opposites: the world and God, death and salvation, repentance not to be repented of. Quintilian <note>Fabius Maximus, Roman rhetorician</note> thinks that pithy saying belongs to this class: *Compliance breeds friends, truth breeds hatred.* From Chrysostom and Theophylact <note>11th-century Byzantine commentator</note> it is not clear to which they referred the word "unrepentable." Either way works well: it makes a repentance not to be repented of—for we often repent of our penance—or it makes a repentance that leads to salvation, which knows no regret but has perpetual thanksgiving. Lorenzo Valla noted that two Greek words, **repentance** <note>original: "μετάνοια" (metanoia)</note> and **regret** <note>original: "μεταμέλεια" (metameleia)</note>, correspond to the same Latin word *pœnitentia*, where—

<column-break/>

<margin>D</margin> —the former is named from "re-thinking" a feeling, the latter from "changing care" for the better. And just as Cicero judges the Latin word **banquet** <note>Latin: "convivium"</note> to be more appropriate than the Greek **drinking party** <note>Greek: "συμπόσιον" (symposion)</note>, so Valla thinks the Greek words are more elegant here than the Latin, because *pœnitentia* signifies the sadness of what was committed, while the Greek words signify a correction of the mind. For "to repent" <note>Latin: "pœnitere"</note> is to be vexed and weary. Therefore, those who use this passage to bring in a "three-fold penance"—one consisting of contrition, the second of confession, and the third of satisfaction—achieve nothing. Our friend Valla is mostly of this opinion. Although I do not entirely agree with him that "to repent" <note>Latin: "pœnitere"</note> is derived from "punishment" <note>Latin: "pœna"</note>, but I rather think it is said from "holding back almost" <note>Latin: "pœne tenendo"</note>, that is, from understanding after the fact, which is why it is called "change of mind" <note>Greek: "μετάνοια" (metanoia)</note> by the Greeks. And from this, when we speak, we remove neither contrition, nor confession, nor satisfaction, but we show the force of the Evangelical word. For those three things accompany true repentance: grief, confession (which in my judgment is a part of satisfaction), and satisfaction, which weighs bad deeds against good deeds. For I judge this type of satisfaction to be the best: when labors are undertaken to help one's neighbors, rather than when tortures are summoned, which are heavy for the one bearing them but otherwise useful to no one, like those in the underworld.

12 **But the sorrow of the age works death**] Elsewhere he translates "age" <note>Greek: "αἰὼν" (aiōn)</note> as "world" <note>Latin: "saeculum"</note>, but here he uses "cosmos" <note>Greek: "κόσμος" (kosmos)</note>, that is, **world** <note>Latin: "mundum"</note>. Ambrose reads *of this world*.

13 **To be saddened according to God**] <note>original: "τὸ κατὰ Θεὸν λυπηθῆναι ὑμᾶς" (to kata Theon lypēthēnai hymas)</note>, that is, *that you were saddened according to God*.

14 **But defense, but indignation**] Ambrose reads it thus: *but excuse, but fear, but desire, but emulation, but vengeance.* The Greek has it so: <note>original: "ἀλλὰ ἀπολογίαν, ἀλλὰ ἀγανάκτησιν, ἀλλὰ φόβον, ἀλλὰ ἐπιπόθησιν, ἀλλὰ ζῆλον, ἀλλὰ ἐκδίκησιν"</note>, that is, *but excuse or cleansing, but indignation, but fear, but longing, but zeal, but vengeance.* The Greek scholia <note>ancient commentaries</note> warn that **but** <note>Greek: "ἀλλὰ" (alla)</note> is placed here for **and** <note>Greek: "καὶ" (kai)</note>, though in my opinion it is used for **nay more** or **furthermore**. For it increases and, as it were, corrects what he had called "the same diligence," nay more, something extra, even to the point of punishing the shameful act. In this list, one part is missing in Ambrose, which he does not mention even in his commentary. For he does not mention **indignation**, by whatever chance that may have happened.

15 **In all things you have shown yourselves**] <note>original: "συνεστήσατε" (synestēsate)</note>, that is, *you have commended*. Although here *you have proven* would not fit badly. And **in all things** <note>original: "ἐν παντὶ" (en panti)</note>, which was also translated above, is better rendered as "everywhere." Again, that phrase **in the business**. The added Greek article, <margin>F</margin> <note>original: "ἐν τῷ πράγματι" (en tō pragmati)</note>, signifies that he is speaking not of just any thing, but of a certain specific business—namely, that of which he had written in the former Epistle, that someone had had an affair with his father's wife. In that business they showed themselves to be pure, having cast out and punished such a man, whereas Paul had previously imputed something to them there: saying, *And you are puffed up.*

16 **Therefore though I wrote**] "I wrote" must be understood twice: *Though I wrote, I wrote*. Although in Greek it is placed only once. *Though I wrote to you, I wrote not for his sake etc.* Just as he says elsewhere, *And if I have forgiven anything, I did it for your sakes.* The Greek commentaries advise that here the negation has a comparative force. For he had certainly written also for the sake of those who had sinned. For he perceived these: him who did the injury and him who suffered it, but this was not the chief cause. This is similar to that saying: *I want mercy, and not sacrifice*. And, *God does not eat the meat of bulls.*

17 **Not for the sake of him who did the injury**] Ambrose reads it thus: *Not for the sake of him who behaved wickedly, but neither for the sake of him who was treated wickedly.*

Erasmus provides extensive notes on the Greek vocabulary for repentance, distinguishing "godly sorrow" from "worldly sorrow" and challenging contemporary scholastic views on penance.</summary>

Here, Paul expresses his relief at their response and introduces the collection for the poor in Jerusalem, using the Macedonians as an example of generosity.</meta>

# PAULINE EPISTLE PAGE VIII.

<margin>12</margin> ...our earnest care for us <note>original: "ὑμῶν τὴν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν" (your care for us); Erasmus notes some manuscripts swap "us" and "you" here</note> toward you in the sight of God. Therefore we were comforted in your comfort: and we rejoiced <margin>13</margin> exceedingly more for the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all. <margin>14</margin> For if I have boasted anything to him on your behalf, I was not put to shame; but as we spoke all things to you in truth, even so our boasting, which I made before Titus, was found to be the truth. <margin>15</margin> And his inward affection is more abundant toward you, whilst he remembers the obedience of you all, how with fear and trembling you received him. <margin>16</margin> I rejoice that I have confidence in you in everything.

<margin>VIII.1</margin> Moreover, brothers, we make known to you the grace of God bestowed on the churches of Macedonia; <margin>2</margin> how in a great trial of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality <note>original: "ἁπλότητος" (haplotētos), meaning simplicity or sincerity, often used for generous giving</note>. <margin>3</margin> For to their power, I bear witness, and even beyond their power, they were willing of themselves; <margin>4</margin> praying us with much entreaty that we would receive the grace <note>meaning the gift or favor</note> and the fellowship of the ministering to the saints. <margin>5</margin> And this they did, not as we hoped, but first gave their own selves to the Lord, and unto us by the will of God. <margin>6</margin> Insomuch that we urged Titus, that as he had begun, so he would also finish in you this same grace also. <margin>7</margin> Therefore, as you abound in everything, in faith, and utterance, and know-
<meta>catchword: ledge</meta>

---

<margin>18</margin> *To manifest our care, which we have for you]* Ambrose reads this in the same sense: *But that our care, which we have for you before God, might be manifested*, obviously having the pronouns "your" and "our" <note>original: "ὑμῶν & ἡμῶν"</note> swapped, a mistake easily made by a scribe's forgetfulness. But the Greek reads: *to reveal your earnestness for us before God*. From these words, it appears Paul meant that he rejoiced because that sorrow resulted in it becoming clear how much affection the Corinthians had for him. The phrase *among you* can be taken as referring to the verb *revealed*, meaning Paul acted so that the false apostles among the Corinthians might understand the affection the whole church had for him. Furthermore, when he adds *among you before God*, it is like an oath, calling both them and God to witness. He mentioned their zeal earlier, which he learned from Titus. However, Theophylactus <note>a Byzantine commentator</note> reads and interprets this the same way as Ambrose.

<margin>19</margin> *More abundantly]* He either joined two comparative words to express greater emphasis, or "more" should be translated as *rather*. In Greek, *mallon* <note>original: "μᾶλλον"</note>, like our word *rather*, sometimes corrects a statement, suggesting he received much comfort from the corrected Corinthians, but even more truly from the joy of Titus. Ambrose reads *more and more* instead of *more abundantly*. We should not hide the fact that the Greek punctuation here differs greatly from the Latin. The common Latin Bible and Ambrose have: *And therefore we were comforted. But in our comfort we rejoiced more abundantly*. The Greek reads: *Therefore we were comforted in your comfort, but more abundantly*, etc. Ambrose follows our Latin division, cutting through with a small commentary what the Greek joins together.

<margin>20</margin> *His spirit was refreshed]* *Anapepautai* <note>original: "ἀναπέπαυται"</note>, that is, *was revived*, which is specifically said of someone who has worked and been exhausted and is later revived by rest. Ambrose reads this differently, likely having found a different manuscript: *because*, he says, *his spirit rested in all of you*.

<margin>21</margin> *I am not put to shame]* *Ou katēschynthēn* <note>original: "οὐ κατῃσχύνθην"</note>, meaning I was not made to feel ashamed.

<margin>22</margin> *More abundantly in you]* *Eis hymas* <note>original: "εἰς ὑμᾶς"</note>, that is, *toward you*.

<margin>23</margin> *Remembering]* *Anamimnēskomenou* <note>original: "ἀναμιμνησκομένου"</note>, that is, *recalling* or *bringing to memory*.

<margin>24</margin> *That in all things I trust in you]* The word "in" is not in the Greek manuscripts, which say *I trust you* <note>original: "θαῤῥῶ ὑμῖν"</note>. However, some had *I trust in you* <note>original: "θαῤῥῶ ἐν ὑμῖν"</note>; that is how Theophylactus reads it. In these syllables, it is very easy for scribes to slip up by inserting the word "in" <note>original: "ἐν"</note>.

---

<margin>F</margin> <margin>1</margin> **And** that in much] The "And" is redundant; it is not in the Greek codices, nor added by Ambrose, nor even in our more corrected versions. *In much trial*, that is, in much testing. Saint Ambrose reads it this way.

<margin>2</margin> *Abundance of joy]* *Hē perisseia* <note>original: "ἡ περισσεία"</note>. But Ambrose rightly changed the noun into a verb, reading, *joy abounds*.

<margin>3</margin> *Deepest poverty]* *Hē kata bathous ptōcheia* <note>original: "ἡ κατὰ βάθους πτωχεία"</note>. Ambrose reads *profound poverty*. It seems to be an image taken from a jar or chest already exhausted to the very bottom. This relates to what Hesiod wrote: *thrift comes too late when you reach the bottom*. Therefore, the Translator did not do a bad job. Paul contrasts opposites: *profound poverty* (the most exhausted state) and *abounded*. That which is empty does not "abound," and poverty usually fights against riches.

<margin>4</margin> *Into the riches of simplicity]* *Eis ton plouton haplotētos* <note>original: "εἰς τὸν πλοῦτον ἁπλότητος"</note>, that is, *into the wealth of simplicity*. He is "simpler" <note>in the sense of single-minded or sincere</note> who gives freely, and

<column-break/>

<margin>12</margin> ...not for the sake of him who did the wrong, nor for the sake of him who suffered the wrong, but so that your care for us might be made clear among you in the sight of God. Therefore we took comfort <margin>13</margin> from your comfort: but even more abundantly we rejoiced because of the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by you all. For if I boasted <margin>14</margin> anything about you to him, I was not put to shame; but as we spoke all things to you in truth, so also our boasting, which I used before Titus, was found to be the truth. And his heart is more <margin>15</margin> greatly moved toward you as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling. I rejoice that in all things I have <margin>16</margin> confidence in you. I make known to you, brothers, <margin>1 VIII.</margin> the grace of God which was given in the churches of Macedonia: <margin>B</margin> how through much testing of affliction <margin>2</margin> their joy abounded, and their deep poverty overflowed into the riches of their simplicity. For <margin>3</margin> according to their power, I testify, and even beyond their power, they were ready of their own will, begging us with much entreaty that we would <margin>4</margin> accept the gift and the fellowship of the service to the saints. And not merely as we hoped, but they <margin>5</margin> even gave themselves first to the Lord, and then to us by the will of God, so that we urged Titus, <margin>6</margin> that as he had begun before, so he would also finish this work of generosity toward you. Indeed, just as you abound everywhere in faith, and in <margin>7</margin> <margin>C</margin> speech...

---

he is made richer in the good of the heart and kindness the more his money is diminished.

<margin>5</margin> *Because according to virtue]* *Hoti kata dynamin* <note>original: "Ὅτι κατὰ δύναμιν"</note>, that is, *Because according to their power* or *strength*. Saint Ambrose reads it this way so that no one here takes "virtue" as the opposite of vice <note>Erasmus is clarifying that "virtus" here means physical or financial "power/strength," not moral "virtue"</note>.

<margin>6</margin> *Above virtue]* *kai hyper dynamin* <note>original: "καὶ ὑπὲρ δύναμιν"</note>, that is, *even beyond their strength*. Ambrose reads it this way, just as above, *according to their strength*. Although it would be clearer to say *even beyond their strength*. From Ambrose, the word *testify* <note>original: "μαρτυρῶ"</note> is almost missing, which he translates as *I am a witness to them*, inserting it in a parenthesis: *since according to their strength, I witness, even beyond their strength they were willing to give*.

<margin>7</margin> *Voluntary]* *authairetoi* <note>original: "αὐθαίρετοι"</note>, that is, *spontaneous*, implying they "were" so—meaning they were not asked or provoked.

<margin>8</margin> *With much exhortation entreating us]* The Greeks read it differently: *With much entreaty begging of us, the grace and the fellowship of the ministry, which is toward the saints, that we would receive*.

<margin>9</margin> *And not as we hoped]* *Kai ou kathōs ēlpisamen* <note>original: "Καὶ οὐ καθὼς ἠλπίσαμεν"</note>, that is, *Much more than we dared to hope*, lest we think this happened to Paul unexpectedly. Therefore we translated it as *inasmuch as*. In this place, a ridiculous thing happened in the "Corsendoncenfi" manuscript—a codex otherwise very elegant, but more beautiful than accurate. The reader, as can easily be guessed, had found something noted by some scholar in the margin; believing it had been left out by the Scribe, he moved the note into the middle of the text like this: *begging us, in many of the original copies it is found thus, And not as we hoped*. Indeed, that scholar, indicating that the word "us" <note>original: "ἡμᾶς"</note> is not added in most copies but is added in others, had written this: *in most manuscripts it is found thus*. The unlearned Scribe mixed those words into the middle of Paul’s speech! Something similar happened in a letter from Paulinus to Augustine, number 58. In the middle of the letter's context, because Apostles and Prophets had been mentioned, an unlearned Scribe mixed in a long dream about the etymology of the words "Apostle" and "Prophet," which some idle person had perhaps written in the margin: *For as*, he says, *I may proceed from the force of the term, Apostle in Greek is said from 'apos,' which denotes increase or preeminence, and 'stolon,' which is mission, as if sent preeminently for the increase of the catholic faith. And soon after: Prophet, he says, is from 'pro,' that is, 'from afar,' and 'for, faris,' as if about to speak things that are, will be, or have been*. That fake Paulinus had babbled many other things of that kind in the middle of a letter by a man as eloquent as he was learned. And since many such things are detected by the learned in books read with authority, what do we think will happen if we choose to accept, without judgment or censorship, whatever has been smeared into books in any way? By this occasion, we have found that innumerable passages have been corrupted.

<margin>10</margin> *So that we urged Titus]* *Eis to parakalesai hēmas Titon* <note>original: "Εἰς τὸ παρακαλέσαι ἡμᾶς Τίτον"</note>, that is, *Toward this, that we should exhort Titus*.

<margin>11</margin> *So also let him complete in you, etc.]* *eis hymas* <note>original: "εἰς ὑμᾶς"</note>, that is, *toward you* or *for you*. Again, he translates *charis* as "grace," though he would have been more accurate to translate it as "benefit" or "munificence," or as we translated, *beneficence*. Cicero frequently used this name, including in the first book of *On Duties*, lest anyone should find fault. Then why not *toward you* rather than *in you*, since in Greek it is *eis hymas*, especially since Ambrose reads: *that as he began, so he may complete also toward you this grace*. He interprets it to mean that just as you began to imitate the generosity of others at the urging of Titus, so by that same urging you should finish it. There is a double conjunction *kai* <note>original: "καὶ"</note> in Greek, the first of which refers to the beginning, and the second to the other gifts in which the Corinthians were strong. Let the one who began also complete it, so that just as you are approved in other virtues, you may also earn praise in this one. Like a great artist, he mixed praise with exhortation, according to the rules of Rhetoric.

<meta>The previous page concluded Chapter 7 of 2 Corinthians, where Paul rejoiced over the Corinthians' repentance following his stern letter. This page begins the commentary on Chapter 8, where Paul transitions to the collection of funds for the poor Christians in Jerusalem, holding up the Macedonian churches as an example of generosity and discussing the theological basis for giving.</meta>

# SECOND LETTER TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER 8.

<margin>A</margin>
...in knowledge, and in all diligence, and in your love for us, see that you abound in this grace also. 8 I speak not by commandment, but by the diligence of others, and to prove the sincerity of your love. 9 For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might be rich. <margin>B</margin> 10 And herein I give my advice: for this is expedient for you, who have begun before, not only to do, but also to be willing a year ago. 11 Now therefore perform the doing of it; that as there was a readiness to will, so there may be a performance also out of that which you have. 12 For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man has, and not according to that he has not. 13 For I mean not that other men be eased, and you burdened, but by an equality. At this present time your abundance may be a supply for their want, 14 that their abundance also may be a supply for your want, that there may be equality: As it is written, He that had gathered much had nothing over; 15 and he that had gathered little had no lack. But thanks be to God, who put the same earnest care for you into the heart of Titus, for he accepted the exhortation; but being more forward, he went...

---

<margin>C</margin>
12 **Moreover and in charity** <note>original: "Insuper & charitate"</note>] *and in the love from you in us* <note>original: "καὶ τῇ ἐξ ὑμῶν ἐν ἡμῖν ἀγάπῃ"</note>, that is, the charity which is in us because of you. For the phrase "from you," the Translator <note>The Vulgate translator</note> renders as "your," which is not bad. However, "moreover" <note>original: "insuper"</note> is not found in the Greek, not even in the oldest Pauline manuscripts, nor in the Constantinopolitan ones, though it appears in Ambrose. It seems that "in us" was said instead of "toward you." Theophylactus and the Greek scholars interpret this as the charity of the Corinthians toward Paul. Ambrose seems to invert the pronouns: *that charity which is from us in you*, meaning you abound in that charity which you learned from us. Even in the common books, it was held as "and to you" instead of "in you"; I believe it should be corrected to "from you in us."

13 **And in this grace you may abound**] "Grace" in this place is understood as a benefit or an alms, as it was a little earlier. For he is speaking about helping the holy ones through liberality. The word "I exhort" or "give effort" must be understood, otherwise the sentence will not be complete.

<margin>D</margin>
14 **Not as if commanding**] *Not according to a command* <note>original: "Οὐ κατ' ἐπιταγὴν"</note>, that is, not according to authority, or not as one commanding. Ambrose reads, "Not according to imperial command."

15 **But through the solicitude of others**] In Greek it is "through," not "because of." The sense is that your charity might become more proven by the duty of others toward us, not that I am demanding anything from you; although the Greek phrasing has a double meaning. It can be taken to mean that your charity, like that of others, is made more proven and notable if the poverty of the saints is relieved by your concern. Or it can mean that your charity might be more approved and praised by me if, provoked by the example of others, you do not yield to the rest in this kind of beneficence, since you are not inferior in other things.

16 **The good nature of your charity** <note>original: "Vestrae charitatis ingenium bonum"</note>] The Greek has it differently: *and the sincerity of your love* <note>original: "καὶ τὸ τῆς ὑμετέρας ἀγάπης γνήσιον"</note>, that is, the "ingenuousness" or "sincerity" of your charity. "Ingenuous" is said for "ingenuity"; they call "genuine" <note>original: "γνήσιον"</note> that which is true, authentic, noble, and not at all painted or adulterated. Ambrose reads "good," omitting "nature" <note>original: "ingenio"</note>. Indeed, I suspect that in our manuscripts it was once written "ingenuous" <note>original: "ingenuum"</note>, not "nature" <note>original: "ingenium"</note>, and that, being poorly understood by someone, it was corrupted. Now, is it worth mentioning what a certain recent theologian <note>Likely Thomas Aquinas</note> dreams up here? They are indeed more impudent as they are more unlearned, since Thomas philosophizes at length on this word "nature" <note>original: "ingenium"</note>. For he also read it that way, following his own manuscript. What else could he do, being ignorant of Greek literature? And here, the more studiously he labors, the more he must err; just as if someone has once wandered from the path, the more vehemently he runs, the more he must wander. However, I think he should be pardoned, as I see nothing was lacking in him except a knowledge of languages. But it would have been better to be somewhat less Aristotelian than to lack this tool. He whose notes are circulated under the false title of Jerome seems to have read "nature" as if it meant "innate." For he adds: "For piety is so innate to you that you have no need to learn it from others."

<margin>E</margin>
17 **Since for your sakes he was made needy**] "Since" or "because" would have been better translated as "that." In this place, Faber changes "you" (second person) into "us" (first person), claiming it is found thus in the original sources. But the Greek manuscripts that I have seen constantly disagree, as do the Latin ones; and "you" fits better because he is excelling in deeds, and "you might be rich" follows. By this speech, he strives to elicit the liberality of the Corinthians, although it makes little difference to the sense whether you read "us" or "you." But that phrase, "he was made needy," is in Greek *he became a pauper* <note>original: "ἐπτώχευσε"</note>, or rather, *he begged*; from this, those who enjoy attributing their own begging to Christ as the author might take an argument. The Translator did not preserve the wordplay between *he became a pauper* and *poverty* <note>original: "ἐπτώχευσε, πτωχείᾳ"</note>. It is a wonder why he confused it as if on purpose, when it could have been rendered without any trouble.

<margin>F</margin>
18 **And I give advice in this**] *And I give my judgment in this* <note>original: "Καὶ γνώμην ἐν τούτῳ δίδωμι"</note>. Here he clearly seems to take "judgment" for "advice." Furthermore, "in this" means in this matter; lest anyone err here thinking "this" is in the accusative case.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
(in speech, and knowledge, and all diligence, 12 and in that charity which is from you toward us, 13 see that you abound in this beneficence also. 14 I speak not according to command, 15 but through the concern for others, 16 also approving the sincerity of your love. 17 For you know the beneficence of our Lord Jesus Christ, 17 that for your sakes he was made a pauper, though he was rich, so that you might become rich by his poverty. 17 And I give advice in this: for this is profitable for you, who indeed not only to do, 19 but also to will have already begun 20 a year ago. <margin>B</margin> Now therefore, also complete that which you began to do: 21 so that just as the will was prompt, 22 so you may also complete it out of that which you are able. 23 For if there is first a promptness of mind, 24 it is accepted according to whatever it is that someone possesses, not according to that which he does not possess. For it is not 25 that there should be relief for others, 26 and distress for you, but that from equality in the present time 27 your abundance should succor their need, and their abundance succor your need, that there may be equality, just as it is written: 28 He who had much, had nothing left over; and he who had little, 29 nevertheless had enough. 30 But thanks be to God, who gave 31 the same concern for you in the heart of Titus, 32 who accepted the exhortation...

---

<margin>C</margin>
19 **But also to will**] The sense is ambiguous: whether they began both to will and to do a year ago, so that you understand this benefit was not recently started; or whether they began not only to do, but even to do it voluntarily and of their own accord, for that is more than just doing. Indeed, it is the genuine praise of the Corinthians that they not only began to give to the poor of their own will, not provoked by the examples of others, but they even took up this purpose of mind voluntarily without being urged. And the Translators follow this second sense.

20 **From the prior year**] *From last year* <note>original: "ἀπὸ πέρυσι"</note>, that is, from the preceding year.

21 **Mind of the will**] *Just as the readiness of the will* <note>original: "καθάπερ ἡ προθυμία τοῦ θέλειν"</note>, that is, just as the mind is prompt to will, or for willing.

22 **So let it be also of completing from that which you have**] *So also let there be the completing, out of having* <note>original: "οὕτως καὶ τὸ ἐπιτελέσαι, ἐκ τοῦ ἔχειν"</note>, that is, so let the completion be from having, meaning from the fact that you have, or because you are able. Indeed <margin>D</margin> "to have" seems to be used loosely for "to be able." *To will belongs to a prompt mind; to provide what you will belongs to one's resources.*

23 **For if the will is prompt**] *For if the readiness of mind is present first* <note>original: "Εἰ γὰρ ἡ προθυμία πρόκειται"</note>, that is, if there is a prior promptness of mind, or if promptness of mind has gone before, as the foundation of beneficence.

24 **According to that which he has**] *According to what someone may have* <note>original: "καθὸ ἐὰν ἔχῃ τις"</note>. Here I take "has" in the Greek manner to mean "is able." Saint Ambrose implies this, reading "according to ability." And it is rather "according to whatever it is that one is able, so that 'to give' is understood." Although this does not change Paul's meaning much.

25 **That there be remission for others**] *Relief* <note>original: "ἄνεσις"</note>, that is, ease, remission, and relaxation of labor. Accordingly, Ambrose translates it as "refreshment."

26 **But for you, tribulation**] *Distress* <note>original: "θλῖψις"</note>. In this place, it is better rendered by Ambrose as "straits" <note>original: "angustia"</note>; for we speak of "straits" in family affairs. Relief is given to those for whom family affairs are less of a strain; and here something must be understood to make the sentence complete. For <margin>E</margin> it is not to be given so that others [are relieved], etc.

27 **Your abundance**] Here "supplied" is added, since the Greek has it thus: *your abundance for their lack, that also their abundance might be for your lack*. The word "might be" <note>original: "γένηται"</note> applies to both parts. It could be rendered this way: *that your abundance [might supply] their lack, and their abundance your lack*. For the Greek speech is figured by opposites and the repetition of the word "their." Indeed, there is a hidden "is present" <note>original: "ἐνυπάρχει"</note> in "your" and "their."

28 **He who much**] *He [who had] much* <note>original: "Ὁ πολὺ"</note>. Even in Greek, the participle "was" or "had" is understood.

29 **Did not diminish**] *He did not have less* <note>original: "οὐκ ἠλαττόνησε"</note>, that is, he was not inferior, or he did not have less. Furthermore, the testimony he brings is from Exodus chapter sixteen. According to the Hebrew truth, Saint Jerome translates it this way: *Neither did he who had collected more have more, nor did he who had prepared less find less.* It was said <margin>F</margin> regarding the gathering of manna, which Paul turned toward his own business. In Theophylactus I found such a reading: *He of the much did not exceed, and the little did not diminish*, as if to say, in abundance nothing was left over, and in poverty nothing was lacking. In explaining, he adds the word "having."

30 **But I give thanks to God**] *But thanks be to God* <note>original: "Χάρις δὲ τῷ Θεῷ"</note>, so that you understand "may there be" or "let there be."

31 **The same solicitude**] What he has now frequently translated as "solicitude," in Greek is *zeal* <note>original: "σπουδὴ"</note>, that is, study or care. Both the Translator and Ambrose read "the same" <note>original: "τὴν αὐτὴν"</note>, or as Ambrose renders it, "this very." Likewise Augustine, who reads "the same study." And so it is read in some Greek manuscripts, while in others, instead of "the same," it is "such" <note>original: "τοιαύτην"</note>. Chrysostom reads "the same."

32 **Since indeed the exhortation**] Ambrose reads "consolation," but our Translator better reads "exhortation." For it signifies that he came because he was asked, yet he was nonetheless leaning toward it and eager of his own accord. Theophylactus holds this view.

<summary>Erasmus provides a detailed philological commentary on 2 Corinthians 8, focusing on the Greek text to correct Latin mistranslations regarding Christian charity and the poverty of Christ. He famously critiques Thomas Aquinas for over-analyzing a mistranslated word ("ingenium") and explains the theological principle of "equality" in giving based on the Old Testament example of manna.</summary>

# THE LETTER OF PAUL, CHAPTER 9.

18 We have sent with him the brother whose praise is in the Gospel throughout all the churches. 19 And not only that, but he was also chosen by the churches to be our traveling companion with this grace, which is administered by us to the glory of the Lord himself and to show your ready mind. 20 We avoid this: that any man should blame us in this abundance which is administered by us. 21 Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men. 22 And we have sent with them our brother, whom we have often proved diligent in many things, but now much more diligent, because of the great confidence I have in you. 23 Whether any do inquire of Titus, he is my partner and fellow helper concerning you; or our brothers be inquired of, they are the messengers of the churches, and the glory of Christ. 24 Therefore show to them, and before the churches, the proof of your love, and of our boasting on your behalf.
->IX.<-
1 For as touching the ministering to the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you. 2 For I know the forwardness of your mind, for which I boast of you to them of Macedonia, that Achaia was ready a year ago,

<column-break/>

<margin>33 18</margin> he accepted, 33 but rather as he was more diligent, 34 he went to you of his own accord. We have sent with <margin>35</margin> him that brother, 36 whose praise is in the Gospel throughout all the churches. And not only that, 37 but he <margin>19</margin> was also chosen by the churches as a companion of our journey, 38 with this benevolence, which is administered by us 39 to the glory of the same Lord and 40 the readiness of your mind: 41 Avoiding this, lest anyone should find fault <margin>20</margin> with us 42 in this abundance, 43 which is administered by us, 44 Providing honest things, not only before the Lord, <margin>21</margin> but also before men. And we have sent with <margin>22</margin> them our brother, whom we have proven 45 many times in many things 46 to be diligent, but now much more diligent, 47 because of the great confidence which <margin>23</margin> I have toward you. Whether in the name of Titus, who is my partner, 48 and a helper toward you, or the others, who are our brothers and the legates of the churches, 49 the glory of Christ. <margin>50 24</margin> Therefore, show the proof of your charity, and of our boasting about you, toward them, even 51 in the sight of the churches. For concerning the assistance <margin>IX.</margin> which is made for the saints, 1 it is superfluous for me to write <margin>1</margin> to you. For I know 2 the readiness of your mind, <margin>3</margin> which
<meta>catchword: which</meta>

---

<margin>33 But as he was more solicitous</margin> <note>original: σπουδαιότερος (spoudaioteros)</note>, that is, *more studious, diligent, and eager*. And in this place, the conjunction *but* <note>original: δὲ (de)</note> has a corrective force, so that it could not absurdly be translated as *rather*. For what he had just said—that Titus had undertaken the business being moved by Paul’s prayers—he now changes, saying *rather*, that he did not do this by Paul's impulse, but since he was prompted by his own accord, he became even more eager and diligent at Paul's request, just as when we urge on someone who is already running of their own will.

<margin>34 Of his own will</margin> <note>original: αὐθαίρετος (authairetos)</note>, that is, *spontaneous, or voluntary*. Ambrose reads *voluntary*.

<margin>35 With him our brother</margin> The word *our* is not in the Greek, which has only "the brother" <note>original: τὸν ἀδελφὸν</note>. Nor was it added in the Donationico codex <note>A specific manuscript Erasmus consulted</note>. For this is how he calls a Christian. However, the added article makes us understand a certain designated person whose name he intentionally suppressed, preferring to describe him by praise rather than by name. Therefore, it should be translated: *We sent with him that brother, whose praise is in the Gospel throughout all the churches*. But a little further down, *our* is added: *We sent together with them also our brother, whom we have proven in many things*.

<margin>36 Whose praise is in the Gospel</margin> The phrase seems ambiguous. For it appears it could be taken to mean his praise is written in the Gospel <note>as in a book</note>. But what it actually says is that he, whoever he is (for this is uncertain), was so active in the preaching of Christ, which he here calls the "Gospel," that he is praised by the testimony of all the churches. Yet this does not prevent it from being understood as referring to Luke, which Jerome seems to have thought, while others think Barnabas is meant, and still others, Apollos. But I wanted to advise that here the words are more about preaching than about a written Gospel, because of what follows: *throughout all the churches*. Furthermore, it is uncertain whether at the time Paul wrote this, Luke had already written his Gospel. Now, the phrase *Not only that*, should be translated as *Neither that alone*, so we understand he was not only esteemed for preaching the Gospel, but was also chosen as a companion for Paul.

<margin>37 But he was also ordained</margin> <note>original: χειροτονηθεὶς (cheirotonētheis)</note>, that is, *chosen, or created by vote*, which is what the Greek word properly signifies <note>literally "stretching out the hand" to vote</note>. And *traveling companion* <note>original: συνέκδημος (synekdemos)</note> is correct, except that "companion" is less than "colleague or partner," implying an equal rather than a follower.

<margin>38 in this grace</margin> The Greeks have <note>original: σὺν τῇ χάριτι ταύτῃ</note>, that is, *with this grace*. Although "grace" in this place sounds like *benefit* or *benevolence*.

<margin>39 To the glory of the Lord</margin> <note>original: πρὸς τὴν αὐτοῦ τοῦ Κυρίου δόξαν</note>, that is, *to the glory of the same Lord*.

<margin>40 Destined will</margin> <note>original: καὶ προθυμίαν</note>, that is, *readiness of mind*. Ambrose reads *solicitude*: I think this is an error of the scribes, who changed *readiness* to *solicitude*. Thomas Aquinas interprets *destined will* as that which is predestined by God, who predestined from eternity that you should have such a will. I do not wish to attack such a learned and famous man with insults. I would rather attribute whatever error there is to the age he lived in, provided the reader understands that not even the most learned can interpret Divine Literature without the danger of error if they lack skill in the languages. They should realize that what Thomas introduced here is entirely far from Paul’s meaning. For Paul means that this benefit is administered by him for the glory of the Lord, and at the same time to promote and declare the readiness of mind of those who were giving of their own accord. Just as Ambrose read *solicitude* for *readiness*, so he read the first person *our* instead of the second person *your*, but the Greek commentaries and Theophylact interpret it differently.

<margin>41 Avoiding this</margin> <note>original: Στελλόμενοι τοῦτο</note>, that is, *Guarding against that*. This is a term taken from sailors, who by a winding course avoid a rock or danger.

<margin>42 in this plenitude</margin> <note>original: ἐν τῇ ἁδρότητι</note>, that is, *abundance, or exuberance*. For a large amount of money is usually subject to the suspicion of fraud.

<margin>43 Which is administered by us to the glory of the Lord</margin> The phrase *to the glory of the Lord* is not repeated in this place among the Greeks.

<margin>44 For providing</margin> <note>original: Προνοούμενοι</note>, that is, *Providing*; the word *for* is absent and depends on what came before, *We have sent*. Although this does not change the sense. And the word for *good* <note>original: καλὰ</note> sounds more like *honorable* than simply *good*.

<margin>45 many times in many things</note> The translator could have rendered the charm of the Greek figure of speech, *in many things many times* <note>original: ἐν πολλοῖς πολλάκις</note>, as if to speak in that way.

<margin>46 To be solicitous</margin> <note>original: σπουδαῖον ὄντα</note>, that is, *diligent, or prompt, or even upright*. For the word also signifies *upright*.

<margin>47 Much confidence in you</margin> <note>original: πεποιθήσει πολλῇ τῇ εἰς ὑμᾶς</note>, that is, *on account of the great confidence they have toward you*. The Greek is ambiguous. For "confidence" could refer to Paul, who trusts that the man will now be more diligent because he hopes the Corinthians will treat him well. But he trusts not only in this, but also in Titus. Why? Because he is his partner and a helper in assisting the Corinthians. Likewise regarding the others, because they are Paul’s brothers and sent by the churches, as he said before. Therefore, we prefer to translate *apostles* <note>original: ἀποστόλους</note> here as *legates* or *messengers*.

<margin>48 And a helper in you</margin> <note>original: καὶ εἰς ὑμᾶς συνεργὸς</note>, that is, *and toward you a cooperator, or colleague*. Furthermore, these nominatives are awkwardly placed. It would have been simpler to say "for Titus my partner, and a cooperator or helper toward you."

<margin>49 The glory of Christ</margin> <note>original: δόξα Χριστοῦ</note>, so that you understand the Apostles themselves are the glory of Christ. Although this whole passage is read in various ways. Ambrose reads it thus: *Whether through Titus, who is my partner and helper among you, or through our brothers the apostles of the churches, the glory of Christ*. The Greek has it thus: *Whether concerning Titus, my partner and fellow worker toward you, or our brothers, messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ*. The commentaries explain it this way: *Whether of Titus (as if something remains to be said), this I can say: that he is my partner etc.* Or if something must be said of the others: *I say this, that they are the messengers of the churches and the glory of Christ*, through whose preaching and life the Gospel of Christ becomes more illustrious. All these things are intended to commend those he is sending to the Corinthians. It does not escape me what Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples wrote here, but I do not subscribe to his opinion in this part, especially as it is opposed by the Greek commentaries, namely Chrysostom and Theophylact, and finally Ambrose himself. Furthermore, I do not care to report what Thomas and more recent writers bring to this passage. Although Aquinas sensed something when reading *glory*, he nevertheless interpreted it as *for glory*, as if glory were in the dative case, whereas in Greek it is the nominative. Chrysostom and Theophylact touch upon another meaning, namely: in whatever name you receive them, whatever duties you perform for them, it will be the glory of Christ. For whatever is spent on the ministers of the Gospel redounds to Him. It can also be taken this way: Whatever these men I praise are, it pertains to the glory of Christ.

<margin>50 The showing therefore which is of your charity</margin> In Greek it is simply, *the showing of your charity*. Ambrose reads it no differently. And *of our glory* is again *of boasting* <note>original: καυχήσεως</note>, which Ambrose translates in this place as *exultation*.

<margin>51 In the face of the churches of God</margin> <note>original: εἰς πρόσωπον τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν</note>. "Of God" is not added in the Greek, nor in Ambrose. Furthermore, the phrase *in the face* better fits the "person" of the churches. For the honor shown to those whom the churches sent redounds to the person of the churches. So says Theophylact. Although I also approve of the other sense, namely: that the other churches may also see your charity, about which I am accustomed to boast to them, so that *in the face* means *in the sight*.

### I.

<margin>1</margin> **I**t is from an abundance] <note>original: περισσόν μοι</note>, that is, *it is superfluous*. And so Ambrose reads, *it is superfluous*. I ask, what was the need to bring in a paraphrase here? Unless the Translator simply wished to play around.

<margin>2 Your prompt mind</margin> <note>original: τὴν προθυμίαν ὑμῶν</note>, that is, *the readiness of your mind*, or, as Ambrose reads, *your prompt will*. This is the same word in Greek which he just translated as "destined will," upon which Thomas was philosophizing.

<margin>3 For which of you</margin> <note>original: ἣν ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν καυχῶμαι Μακεδόσιν</note>, that is, *which I boast of you to the Macedonians*, or among the Macedonians. For he said, *of which I glory*, just as we say, "I congratulate you on your return to your country."

<margin>4 Whi-</margin>
<meta>catchword: Whi-</meta>

<summary>Erasmus provides a philological commentary on Paul’s delegation to Corinth, identifying "the brother" as likely being Luke and critiquing medieval scholastic interpretations (especially Thomas Aquinas) for lacking Greek linguistic precision.</summary>
