<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed commentary on 2 Corinthians Chapter 9. Having previously discussed the delegation sent to Corinth, Erasmus now focuses on Paul’s rhetorical strategies for encouraging the collection for the poor in Jerusalem, specifically the concepts of "blessing" (generosity) versus "greed" and the spiritual rewards of giving.</meta>

# TO THE SECOND CORINTHIANS. CHAPTER IX.

<page-num>781</page-num>

<margin>3</margin> and your zeal has stirred up most of them. But I have sent the brothers, so that our boasting about you should not be in vain in this matter; so that, as
<margin>4</margin> I was saying, you may be prepared; lest perhaps, if the Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we—not to say you—should be put to shame 
<margin>5</margin> in this confidence of boasting. Therefore I thought it necessary to exhort the brothers to go ahead to you and arrange beforehand your previously promised blessing, so that it might be ready as a blessing and not as 
<margin>6</margin> greed. But this I say: he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly; and he who sows with blessings will 
<margin>7</margin> also reap with blessings. Each one should give as he has decided in his heart, not out of regret or necessity; for 
<margin>8</margin> God loves a cheerful giver. And God is able to make every grace abound toward you, so that in everything, always having all sufficiency, you may abound in every 
<margin>9</margin> good work; as it is written: He has scattered, he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains 
<margin>10</margin> forever. Now may he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, supply and multiply your seed, and increase the fruits of your righteous—

---

<margin>C</margin> 4 *Since also Achaia* <note>original: "Quoniam & Achaja"</note>] The conjunction "and" is redundant here, and it is not added in the works of Ambrose. Furthermore, perhaps it would have been more fitting to translate the Greek *epi* <note>original: "ἐπὶ"</note> as "that." For this was indeed what Paul was boasting about.

5 *From the past year* <note>original: "Ab anno praeterito"</note>] In Greek, *apo perysi* <note>original: "ἀπὸ πέρυσι"</note>, which means "from the previous year." Ambrose reads it as "from the prior year."

6 *And your emulation* <note>original: "Et vestra aemulatio"</note>] In Greek, *kai ho ex hymon zelos* <note>original: "καὶ ὁ ἐξ ὑμῶν ζῆλος"</note>, which means the emulation or zeal arising from you; that is, your example. Although "zeal" (*zelos*) also carries the sense of devotion and fervor.

7 *Provoked very many* <note>original: "Provocavit plurimos"</note>] The Translator used "very many" for "many," just as priests commonly read "from very many martyrs" for "from several martyrs" in their hourly prayers. In Greek it is *pleionas* <note>original: "πλείονας"</note>, meaning "more" or "quite a few." The Greeks also misuse this comparative form in place of a positive noun. Ambrose reads "more," not "very many." Though this might seem to have happened through a scribe’s error.

8 *But we have sent* <note>original: "Misimus autem"</note>] In Greek, *Epempsa de* <note>original: "Ἔπεμψα δὲ"</note>, meaning "But I sent." But in this place, "brothers" (*tous adelphous*) should be read in the accusative case, not the nominative or vocative. Paul makes excuses for speaking so many words about administering the alms to the saints, yet he thought the brothers absolutely must be sent, lest they be caught off guard and take offense. That is, he does not doubt they will willingly help the poor, but he thought they should be forewarned so they might contribute in time what they wish to give, lest they seem to give less willingly than the other churches.

9 *Lest we say you in this substance* <note>original: "Ut non dicamus vos in hac substantia"</note>] Meaning, "so that we do not say you in this substance of boasting." Ambrose reads: "lest I say all in this part." Truly the manuscripts agree: and it is beautifully phrased so we may understand it this way: "Lest we then be ashamed—we who will seem foolish if you do not provide what we said you would provide." Then, through a rhetorical anticipation, he adds "not to say you," signifying that the shame would belong to them most of all if they failed their pious decree of mind. But he preferred to let that be understood rather than explaining it, so as not to offend the minds of the Corinthians. Afterward, what follows—"in this substance of boasting"—must refer back to the earlier part, "we may be ashamed," namely, being put to shame in this matter of my boasting, by which I have boasted about you. Or, "not in all things in which I rightly boast, but also in this part," so there is nothing in which I do not seem to have rightly boasted of you. He used "substance" (*hypostasin*) to mean the subject-matter and that upon which the credibility of the speech rests.

10 *To ask the brothers* <note>original: "Rogare fratres"</note>] Again, "brothers" should be read in the accusative case, not the vocative.

11 *That they may go before* <note>original: "Ut praeveniant"</note>] Meaning that they should come earlier, or "precede," as Ambrose reads.

12 *The promised blessing* <note>original: "Repromissam benedictionem"</note>] In Greek, *prokatengelmene* <note>original: "προκατηγγελμένην"</note>, meaning "promised beforehand." Furthermore, by "blessing" in this place, he wants "beneficence" to be understood, not a gesture of the hand. For earlier he called them *logias* <note>original: "λογίας"</note>, that is, collections; here he calls the same things "blessings" (*eulogias*), not from *logos* (reason), but from *lego* (to collect). What he adds shortly after fits this meaning: *He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows in blessings will also reap in blessings.* For he opposed "blessing" to "parsimony," as if it were named from a good and kind collection. Therefore, it seems it would not be absurd if "blessing" (*eulogia*) could be translated as "munificence" or "generosity": *he who sows sparingly, reaps sparingly; he who sows generously, likewise reaps generously.* Unless you prefer to twist it this way: that a benefit should be given eagerly and with kind words, and for that reason he called it a "blessing." For this is how it goes among the greedy: that as little as possible is given, and if they are forced to give anything, they give it with ill-omened words. But a benefit should be given with such a mind and face as if you were making a profit by giving. The Greek commentaries explain it in this sense. And "your" should be added, which is absent in our codices, though it is added in Ambrose.

13 *To be ready* <note>original: "Paratam esse"</note>] To translate the Greek as a nominative: "that this your previously promised blessing be ready," that is, that you give eagerly what you previously promised to give.

14 *As a blessing* <note>original: "Quasi benedictionem"</note>] In Greek, *houtos hos eulogian, kai me hosper pleonexian* <note>original: "οὕτως ὡς εὐλογίαν, καὶ μὴ ὥσπερ πλεονεξίαν"</note>, that is, "thus as it were a blessing, and not as it were greed." For beneficence ought to be eager, whereas the greedy person gives sadly. Nothing forbids us from interpreting "greed" (*pleonexia*) as usurpation, occupation, cheating, or extortion. For these are given by those who are unwilling, and with such an omen as that used by the shepherd in Virgil:
> *We send these kids to him—and may it not turn out well.* <note>original: "Hos illi, quod nec bene vertat, mittimus haedos."</note>
Ambrose reads "circumvention" for "greed." For such are generally the "blessings" of the people, which a new Bishop exacts from sacred and profane alike—"prayers," as they call them, or first-fruits. Furthermore, here "greed" seems to refer to those who receive, so it would not have been badly translated as "plunder."

<column-break/>

<page-num>782</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> ...which I boast about you among the Macedonians, 4 that Achaia has been ready 5 from the previous year, 6 and your example 7 has stirred up many. 8 Nevertheless, I have sent these brothers, so that our glory, which I boast of concerning you, should not become empty in this part; so that, just as I was saying, you may be ready: lest in any way it happens that, if the Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we should be covered in shame— 9 not to say you—in this matter of boasting. Therefore I thought it necessary 10 to exhort the brothers 11 that they should go to you first, and prepare now 12 your previously promised good collection, 13 so that it may be ready, 14 just like a good 
<margin>B</margin> collection, and not like an extortion. 15 But this I say: he who does the sowing sparingly, he shall reap sparingly; and he who does the sowing 16 willingly and generously by bestowing, shall reap abundantly. Each one 17 according to the purpose of his heart, not out of annoyance or 18 necessity: for God loves a cheerful giver. And 8 God is able 19 to bring it about that every benefit may overflow toward you: 20 so that in all things, always having all sufficiency, you may overflow into every good work: as it is written, He has scattered, he has given to the poor: his righteousness remains 21 forever. 22 Moreover, he who supplies seed to the sower—

---

<margin>D</margin> 15 *But this I say* <note>original: "Hoc autem dico"</note>] "I say" is not expressed in the Greek manuscripts, it is only "But this" (*touto de*), and the rest is understood; evidently the verb was added by the Latins for the sake of explaining the matter. Another verb could also be understood, such as "remember," or whatever else is more pleasing. Paul does not force anyone to give, nor does he prescribe how much should be given to each; he only warns that the measure of the reward will be according to the measure of the generosity.

16 *Of blessings* <note>original: "De benedictionibus"</note>] "In blessings." For in both places it is *ep' eulogiais* <note>original: "ἐπ' εὐλογίαις"</note>. The Translator changed it at his own discretion, even though in Ambrose it is "in" in both places—a preposition not equally familiar to the Latins in this sense. Again, he recognizes here a type of sentence composed of opposites: "sparingly and generously, sows and reaps." They add beauty by the repetition of the same word, which we called "transition"; then two members divided into two phrases, and again another section similarly cut, to which is added one simple member, like an epiphonema <note>term: epiphonema — a concluding exclamation or summary statement</note>: "God loves a cheerful giver." It would be superfluous to note these everywhere, but it will be useful to have pointed them out a few times so that Paul’s speech may be more pleasant and clear.

17 *As he has purposed* <note>original: "Ut destinavit"</note>] In Greek, *proaireitai* <note>original: "προαιρεῖται"</note>, meaning "he proposes," in the present tense. And Ambrose reads, "according to the purpose of the heart"; and "his" or "of his own" is not added, so the sense is more absolute. For he is not talking about this or that person’s mind. He only indicates that what is given should be given willingly and from the heart. Not even a preposition is added, but it is "purposes in his heart."

18 *From necessity* <note>original: "Ex necessitate"</note>] In Greek, *ex anankes* <note>original: "ἐξ ἀνάγκης"</note>. Lorenzo <note>note: Likely Lorenzo Valla, a humanist scholar whom Erasmus admired</note> thinks that "necessity" in this place should be taken as "poverty," not as "compulsion," with which I do not <margin>E</margin> agree in this place. For he opposed this phrase, "from necessity," to the one that preceded it, "by purpose," that is, as he has decided of his own accord. And he who gives because he is forced, gives sadly, which is why he cited that "God loves a cheerful giver." All the Interpreters, Greek and Latin alike, side with me.

19 *To make abound in you* <note>original: "Abundare facere in vobis"</note>] Meaning "toward you" (*eis hymas*), and he took the verb "to abound" (*perisseusai*) transitively, which elsewhere he usually uses neutrally; just as with us, "to supply" is sometimes "to be available" and sometimes "to provide." And here also he calls beneficence "grace." For he feels it should be given willingly, because God is able to bring it about that whatever they contribute to his saints will return to them with much interest, lest that very thing deter them from giving—the fear that generosity might seem to exhaust the family estate.

20 *So that in all things always* <note>original: "Ut in omnibus semper"</note>] Meaning "so that having all sufficiency in all things." Now *autarkeia* <note>term: autarkeia — a state of self-sufficiency or being content with what one has</note> is when someone is content with his own things and his own lot, and <margin>F</margin> does not desire anything from elsewhere. The Translator and Ambrose—if the manuscripts are free of error—seem to have read it this way: *hina en panti pantote charan*, "so that in all things I might always pray." But there is a pleasant repetition of the same sound in "all," "always," and "every" <note>original: "παντὶ, πάντοτε, & πᾶν"</note>.

21 *Forever and ever* <note>original: "In seculum seculi"</note>] In Greek it is only "for the age" (*eis ton aiona*), meaning "forever."

22 *But he who supplies* <note>original: "Qui autem subministrat"</note>] In Greek, *Ho de epichoregon*. This passage is held slightly differently among the Greeks: *Now may he who supplies seed to the sower also supply bread for food, and multiply your seed, and increase the fruits of your righteousness.* Thus, "supply," "multiply," and "increase" <note>original: "χορηγήσαι, πληθύναι, αὐξήσαι"</note> seem to be infinitives that should be translated instead through the imperative mood: "let him supply, let him fill, let him increase." Unless perhaps the word "is going to" (*mellei*) is understood, which when added to infinitives creates a future tense. For in so many words, it is not likely the tense was changed by chance, so that you would read "he will supply, he will multiply, he will increase," even though Ambrose reads it in this sense.

<summary>Erasmus analyzes Paul’s appeal to the Corinthians to complete their charitable collection, focusing on the Greek terminology for "blessing" versus "greed" and the rhetorical structure of Paul's encouragement toward cheerful, voluntary giving.</summary>

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER X.

<page-num>783</page-num>
<page-num>784</page-num>

11 ...without your awareness, being enriched in every way toward all sincerity, which produces through us thanksgiving to God. 12 For the ministry of this service not only supplies the needs of the saints, but also overflows through many <margin>Alternatively: *age*</margin> thanksgivings to God. 13 Through the testing of this ministry, <margin>13 in the obedience</margin> they glorify God for the obedience of <margin>of this confession.</margin> your confession to the Gospel of Christ, and for the sincerity of your fellowship toward them and toward all, 14 and by their prayer for you, as they long for you because of the surpassing grace of God upon you. 15 Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift.

<margin>X. 1</margin> Now I, Paul myself, urge you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ—I who am humble in person when among you, but bold toward you when absent. 2 I beg of you that when I am present I may not have to be bold with that confidence with which I intend to dare to oppose some who consider us as walking according to the flesh. 3 For though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. 4 For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful in God for the pulling down of strongholds, pulling down reasonings, 5 and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ.

<margin>A</margin> **Ambrose.** Certainly the Greek commentaries interpret <term>to supply</term> <note>original: χορηγῆσαι (*chorēgēsai*)</note> as <term>may he supply</term> <note>original: χορηγήσειεν (*chorēgēseien*)</note>, that is, *may he provide*. Specifically, Theophylact indicates that this is the speech of one wishing for physical provisions.

<margin>23 He will increase the growth of the fruits</margin> <term>the products of righteousness</term> <note>original: γεννήματα τῆς δικαιοσύνης (*gennēmata tēs dikaiosynēs*)</note>, that is, the *produce* or *harvest of justice*. Nor is it without grace that the translation added the word <term>own</term> to the verb. Where it translates here as <term>increments of fruits</term>, Ambrose translates as <term>of the fruits</term>.

<margin>24 In all things be enriched</margin> Paul, in his usual manner, occasionally overuses participles; hence it is correctly translated from the participle <term>being enriched</term> <note>original: πλουτιζόμενοι (*ploutizomenoi*)</note> into a verb. Lorenzo Valla thinks this should refer back to the preceding phrase, "that you may abound" in every good work.

<margin>25 Which works through us</margin> Instead of <term>which</term> <note>original: ἥτις (*hētis*)</note>, Ambrose reads <term>if anyone</term> <note>original: εἴτις (*eitis*)</note>, and his commentaries agree with this reading. The Greeks read <term>which</term>.

<margin>26 The ministry of this office</margin> <term>the service of this liturgy</term> <note>original: διακονία τῆς λειτουργίας ταύτης (*diakonia tēs leitourgias tautēs*)</note>, that is, the administration of this ministry. For this is what he calls the duty of supplying money. But <term>liturgy</term> <note>original: λειτουργία (*leitourgia*)</note> sometimes signifies a sacrifice to the Greeks, performed according to their rite, so that you may understand the money to be offered to God as if it were a victim, of which Paul is the minister, just as priests perform a sacred rite.

<margin>27 Through many thanksgivings in the Lord</margin> <term>through many thanksgivings to God</term> <note>original: διὰ πολλῶν εὐχαριστιῶν τῷ Θεῷ</note>, that is, by the fact that many give thanks to God. Although in some copies I found it written <term>thanksgiving of many</term> <note>original: διὰ πολλῶν εὐχαριστίας</note>. This seems to be how the Translator read it. Yet let us follow what I previously found among the Greeks: the participle <term>overflowing</term> <note>original: περισσεύουσα (*perisseuousa*)</note> must be taken transitively, so that the infinitive "thanksgivings" depends on it. The sense is: "But it also brings it about that thanks are copiously given to God by many." The Greek commentaries interpret it in this sense. Theophylact reads it this way: "which works thanksgiving to God through you." Chrysostom reads similarly, except he has "through us," that is, through us in the first person, and he interprets what he reads.

<margin>28 And in the obedience of confession</margin> Faber [Stapulensis] wants there to be a reversal of terms (hypallage), so that we understand it as "in the confession of your obedience." But I see no reason to flee to such a reversal when the manuscripts and interpretations cry out against it. For <term>obedience of confession</term> can be understood to mean that by being obedient to the Gospel in giving alms, they declared that they truly and from the heart confess the Gospel. But if you prefer <term>obedience</term> <note>original: ὑπαταγὴν (*hypatagēn*)</note> to mean *assent*, he is praising their obedience because they did not resist him when he persuaded and admonished them. Ambrose reads <term>subjection</term> instead of <term>obedience</term>, which more closely expresses the Greek word <term>hypotagēn</term>. However, <term>confession</term> <note>original: ὁμολογία (*homologia*)</note> signifies not only confession but also agreement, so that you may understand the future result to be that many will give thanks to God when they see the Corinthians obeying Paul with such great consensus. And so he silently warns that everyone should contribute according to his own will and means. Furthermore, when he adds "into the Gospel of Christ," he means that this pertains to the business of the Gospel if all Christians agree among themselves in doing good. And the Gospel admonishes that alms must be given, promising that all things will be clean.

<margin>29 Longing for you</margin> <term>longing for you</term> <note>original: ἐπιποθούντων ὑμᾶς (*epipothountōn hymas*)</note>. Ambrose added, "longing to see you," either because he had a different manuscript or because he wanted to explain the sense, which the Greek commentaries also interpret this way. Although in this place <term>grace</term> could be translated as <term>benefit</term>: so that you understand they are eager to see the Corinthians, in whom God had bestowed such great beneficence upon them.

<margin>30 I give thanks to God</margin> Again it is <term>But grace to God</term> <note>original: Χάρις δὲ τῷ Θεῷ</note>, that is, *But thanks be to God*: so that it is a matter of trust.

<margin>1 I Paul myself</margin> <term>But I Paul myself</term> <note>original: Αὐτὸς δὲ ἐγὼ Παῦλος</note>. Paul remarkably separated his own person from the other Apostles using three words: "Paul," "himself," and "I," because previously he acted on the business of others, but now he speaks from his own feeling.

<margin>2 And modesty</margin> <term>and the gentleness</term> <note>original: καὶ τὴν ἐπιεικείαν (*kai tēn epieikeian*)</note>, which sounds more like courtesy and ease or humanity than "modesty," which is the opposite of arrogance.

<margin>3 In the face</margin> <term>according to the face</term> <note>original: κατὰ πρόσωπον (*kata prosōpon*)</note>, that is, according to appearance, for that which is in outward show. However, the Greeks interpret this as Paul's presence: "when I am present in person," I seem humble. Some think this is irony.

<column-break/>

...threatens, may he both supply bread for food, and multiply your seed, 23 and increase the harvest of your righteousness, 24 so that in all things you may be enriched toward all simplicity, 25 which through us causes thanks to be given 12 to God. 26 For the performance of this ministry not only supplies those things which the saints lack, but also overflows in 27 this: that through many, thanks are given to God, who through the 13 testing of this ministry glorify God 28 for the obedience of your confession toward the Gospel of Christ, and for the simplicity of your sharing toward them and toward all, and in their prayer for you, 29 who 14 long for you because of the excellent grace of God in you. 15 But thanks be to God for his unspeakable gift.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, I Paul myself beseech you by the mildness 2 and 1 gentleness of Christ, who 3 according to the face am indeed humble among you, 4 but when absent am bold toward you. But I ask you, that when present I may not dare with that confidence 2 by which I intend to be bold against certain ones, 5 who think we walk as if according to the flesh: For walking in the flesh 3 we do not wage war according to the flesh. For 4 the weapons of our warfare 6 are not carnal, 7 but powerful to God, for the destruction of fortifications, by which 8 we destroy plans, and every height 9 that is raised 5 against the knowledge of God, and we lead captive 10 every thought.

<margin>C</margin> ...irony. <margin>But I ask you.</margin> Since he previously said he was observing, he did not add what he was observing. Hence the beginning of this chapter can be referred to both: to what came before, so the sense is, "I ask that you also freely contribute this money in my name"; or to what follows, as we just said. And so he repeats <term>I beg</term> <note>original: δέομαι (*deomai*)</note>, which had been said as <term>I urge</term> <note>original: παρακαλῶ (*parakalō*)</note>, like someone returning to what he had begun, as if he had said, "I ask, I say." Ambrose suggests this when he says, *The sense is the same, which he repeats to make it clear.*

4 <margin>But absent I trust in you</margin> <term>I am bold toward you</term> <note>original: θαῤῥῶ εἰς ὑμᾶς (*tharrō eis hymas*)</note>. The Greek is indeed ambiguous, but it is more fitting that we understand it as <term>I am bold or confident toward you</term>, just as he says elsewhere, *His letters are strong, but his presence is weak.* Although the Greek commentaries do not explain it in the same way. Theophylact, following Chrysostom (to whom irony is not displeasing), takes it as if Paul is referring this to the person of others: "When present he carries himself abjectly; when absent he writes truly threatening letters." Although they also indicate the sense of "trust" without irony. I personally see no reason why we should flee to irony. Now, as for the fact that the Translator renders <term>I reckon</term> <note>original: λογίζομαι (*logizomai*)</note> as "I am thought of," this does not fit the exposition of the ancients. For Chrysostom shows that this is the speech of a threatening Apostle; because they thought he walked according to the flesh (that is, did not have the Spirit of Christ), they despised him, as if they could sin with impunity. Wanting to terrify them, Paul asks the Corinthians not to be forced to use that boldness (for so he calls his power, which they said was in his letters) while present. Furthermore, <term>softening the threats</term>, he does not say "which I have decreed" or "wish to use," but "which I intend," still inviting them to repentance. This is clearly a sign of the greatest kindness in Paul, who did not establish or decree a punishment upon those who deserved it—which he could have inflicted by his authority and should have because of their stubbornness—but only says he is thinking about the matter, as if he would gladly change his mind if they were willing to return to a better mindset of their own accord. Theophylact explains <term>I reckon</term> with two words, <term>I suppose & I aim</term> <note>original: ὑπολαμβάνω & στοχάζομαι (*hypolambanō & stochazomai*)</note>, that is, I suspect and I intend. For suspicion belongs to one whose thought is not yet certain, and one who intends and directs his eye to the target has not yet released the weapon from his hands, but as it were threatens that he will send it, looking around to see at whom he should send it and how.

<margin>D</margin> 5 <margin>Who think us as if</margin> <term>those who reckon</term> <note>original: τοὺς λογιζομένους (*tous logizomenous*)</note>, that is, those who think or estimate, or who hold us to be, as if walking according to the flesh.

6 <margin>Not carnal</margin> <term>not fleshly</term> <note>original: οὐ σαρκικά (*ou sarkika*)</note>. This is different from the word <term>fleshy</term> <note>original: σάρκινα (*sarkina*)</note>, which the Latin rendered with the same word, as we warned above.

<margin>E</margin> 7 <margin>But powerful to God</margin> In Greek it is <term>powerful to God</term> <note>original: δυνατὰ τῷ Θεῷ (*dynata tō Theō*)</note>. Ambrose reads <term>strong for God</term>. Lorenzo Valla prefers <term>valid for God</term>. Furthermore, that "to God" in Greek is a dative of instrument, and it is effective just as if you were to say, <term>strong through God, and divine works</term>. I wish it were permitted for all Bishops—and especially those who have succeeded to Paul's place—to use this word as truly and by their own right as Paul himself used it: <term>The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but strong through God; not for the demolition of towns and citadels, but of impious thoughts.</term> These are the weapons, these the wars, these the fights, this the victory, these the triumphs worthy of the successors of the Apostles. Now one can see some who, when the situation demands, have troops, have swords, spears, and cannons—in short, whatever is worthy of a brave warrior. However, when the battle-line of vices must be demolished by the sword of the divine word, they have neither tongue nor hands.

<margin>F</margin> 8 <margin>Destroying plans</margin> <term>reasonings</term> <note>original: λογισμούς (*logismous*)</note>, that is, thoughts. And again he added a participle which is not referred to anywhere else, <term>pulling down</term> <note>original: καθαιροῦντες (*kathairountes*)</note>, that is, by which weapons we destroy. Furthermore, since he mentioned weapons, he wonderfully added metaphors of fortifications, some of which are impregnable by skill, others by height. We, to make the sense clearer, translated it in this way: <term>But powerful through God for the demolition of fortifications, by which we demolish thoughts, and every high thing that is raised up against knowledge.</term>

9 <margin>Exalting itself</margin> <term>being raised up</term> <note>original: ἐπαιρόμενον (*epairomenon*)</note>, that is, insurgent, or that which is extolled. For there was a kind of machine of this sort, which, suddenly raised on high, would hurl the enemy from the walls.

10 <margin>Every intellect</margin> <term>every thought</term> <note>original: πᾶν νόημα (*pan noēma*)</note>, every reasoning.

<summary>In this passage, Erasmus provides a linguistic and theological commentary on Paul's defense of his ministry, famously contrasting the 'carnal' weapons of worldly power (including a critique of contemporary militant bishops) with the 'spiritual' weapons of the Gospel. He emphasizes Paul's humility and his rhetorical strategy of using 'gentleness' to bring stubborn believers back to the faith.</summary>
<keywords>Apostolic authority, weapons of warfare, carnal vs spiritual, critique of bishops, humility of Paul, Greek philology, Ambrose, Theophylact, Chrysostom, benevolence</keywords>

# TO THE SECOND CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER X.

6 And having readiness to avenge all disobedience, <gloss>11</gloss> when your obedience is fulfilled.
7 <gloss>12</gloss> Do you look at what is before your face? <gloss>13</gloss> If anyone is confident in himself that he is Christ’s, let him consider this again for himself: that just as he is Christ’s, so also are we Christ’s.
8 For even if I should boast somewhat more about our authority, which the Lord gave us for building up and <gloss>15</gloss> not for your destruction, I shall not be ashamed,
9 lest I should seem as if I were trying to terrify you through my letters.
10 For his letters, <gloss>14</gloss> he says, are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and <gloss>17</gloss> his speech is contemptible.
11 Let such a person consider this: that what we are in word through letters when absent, such we are also in deed when present.
12 <gloss>18</gloss> For we do not dare to classify or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves; <gloss>19</gloss> but they, measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves with themselves, do not understand.
13 But we will not boast beyond measure, but <gloss>20</gloss> according to the measure of the rule which God has assigned to us, a measure to reach even as far as you.
14 For we are not overextending ourselves, as though we did not reach you; for we came even as far as you in the Gospel of Christ,
15 not boasting beyond measure in the labors of others, but having hope that, <gloss>21</gloss> as your faith grows among you, <gloss>22</gloss> we shall be magnified according to our rule unto abundance.

---

<margin>C</margin>
11 <gloss>Into the obedience of Christ</gloss>] <note>original: εἰς ὑπακοὴν (*eis hypakoēn*)</note>, that is, into obedience, as it has always been translated before, but it was clearer to say "for obeying Christ." Captives go under the yoke. But happy are those who are so captured and led that they stand firm for Christ. Would that Bishops would seek after triumphs of this kind.

12 <gloss>Do you look at what is according to the face</gloss>] The Greek manuscripts, following the opinion of Theodoret <note>A 5th-century bishop and influential commentator</note>, read this as a question: "Do you see?" or "Do you not see?" as if he is imagining what is happening in order to rebuke it. Do you perceive those things that are according to the face? That is, things that are seen outwardly and involve ostentation rather than efficacy. For he remembers that he said he was humble among them according to the face, that is, appearing contemptible, while others acted as Apostles with great pride. Ambrose <note>The 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note> reads "according to the face" to mean things that are in plain sight and open, so that it pertains to what follows: *If anyone is confident that he is a servant of Christ*. It is as if he wants the things he is about to say to seem very clear and easily judged. Others interpret "according to the face" as referring to evident signs by which false apostles can be detected—such as if someone is rich, or arrogant, or boastful, or masked with a false image of virtue. Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop</note> thinks it is a rebuke because they were judging a man by his wealth and fashionable dress rather than by the goods of his soul; I agree with this more. Gennadius also supports Theophylact, as cited in the Greek scholia <note>Ancient marginal commentaries</note>. Moreover, it is a rebuke phrased as a question. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, the "Golden-Mouthed" preacher</note> likewise thinks this is the speech of one rebuking them because they judged a man by external things.

13 <gloss>Let him think again within himself</gloss>] <note>original: ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ (*aph’ heautou*)</note>, that is, from himself, surely not waiting for our rebuke.

14 <gloss>So also we</gloss>] The Greek added "of Christ": *that just as he is Christ’s, so also we are Christ’s*. However, this may seem to have been added among the Greeks for the sake of explaining the matter. Furthermore, "of Christ" is in the genitive case, not the nominative. For Ambrose also interprets it in this sense, as if Paul so far makes himself equal to them—that he himself is not a stranger to Christ—if they think they are servants of Christ; thus he may later show how much he excels the others.

15 <gloss>Not for destruction</gloss>] <note>original: οὐκ εἰς καθαίρεσιν ὑμῶν (*ouk eis kathairesin hymōn*)</note>, for destroying you. Furthermore, in his usual manner, he calls "to build up" to be of benefit, and "to destroy" to cause harm. This passage should be noted by those who lift up the authority of the Supreme Pontiff <note>the Pope</note> to an immeasurable height, asserting that the entire body of the Christian Church stands or falls by one man, so much so that if he were to lead all souls down to hell, there would be no right to resist him. Paul had received Apostolic authority from Christ himself, not from Peter (with whom he later conferred, but in such a way as to say he gained nothing from him), and yet he frankly confesses that whatever power this is, it was given to be useful, not to cause harm. As for those who now attribute such great power to the Roman Pontiff, I wish they could also attribute to him the other pontifical gifts: wisdom, purity, charity, and contempt for all worldly things. The Greeks interpret this "destruction" as referring to the punishment of false apostles.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...every thought into obedience to Christ. And 6
we have in readiness vengeance against all disobedience, when your obedience has been fulfilled.
<gloss>12</gloss> Do you look at what is in your sight? If anyone 7
is confident in himself that he is Christ's, <gloss>13</gloss> let him consider that again
from himself, that just as he is Christ's, so also we are Christ's. For if I should boast even somewhat more 8
about our power, which the Lord gave us for building up, <gloss>15</gloss> and not for your destruction, I shall not be shamed, lest I should seem as if trying to terrify you through letters.
For his letters, <gloss>14</gloss> he says, are weighty and 10
strong, but his bodily presence is weak, <gloss>17</gloss> and his speech
contemptible. Let such a person reflect, that what 11
<margin>B</margin>
we are in word through letters when we are absent, such
we are also in deed when we are present. For we do not endure 12
<gloss>18</gloss> to insert or compare ourselves with certain people who
commend themselves: <gloss>19</gloss> but these men do not understand that
they are measuring themselves among themselves, and comparing themselves
to themselves. But we will not boast beyond measure, but 13
according to the measure of the rule, <gloss>20</gloss> by which God has distributed to us
a measure of reaching even as far as you. For not as though 14
we did not reach as far as you, do we extend ourselves
beyond limit: for we reached even as far as you in the
Gospel of Christ, not boasting beyond measure 15
over the labors of others, hoping that it will be that, <gloss>21</gloss> as your faith grows in you, <gloss>22</gloss> we may be magnified according to our rule...

---

...that is, they themselves measuring themselves in themselves, and comparing themselves to themselves, do not understand, etc. And thus the Greek scholia explain it, so that we understand those arrogant men measure themselves from their own mind, and are great in their own eyes, and are praised by one another in a kind of mutual exchange. And Saint Augustine followed this sense in his work *On Christian Doctrine*, when he says: *And let it be to them what the Apostle says: For comparing themselves to themselves, they do not understand.* Again, explaining Psalm 34: *And comparing, says the Apostle, themselves to themselves, they do not understand, neither what they say, nor about what they affirm.* Again on Psalm 118. Again on Psalm 141: *They themselves measuring themselves from themselves.* Likewise against Faustus, book 22, chapter 27, interpreting also according to the opinion of the Greeks. Theophylact, a not-unskilled interpreter of the Pauline Epistles, interprets it in the same way. Although Ambrose seems to have followed a different <margin>D</margin> manuscript, and makes the speech continuous by removing these words, *they do not understand*, in this way: *But we, measuring ourselves in ourselves, and comparing ourselves to ourselves, will not boast beyond measure, etc.* Furthermore, as for the addition, *they do not understand*, the Greek interpreters think the speech is incomplete, as if you should understand, *how much they are to be laughed at by others*. But it seems to me that in this place a participle is used instead of an infinitive verb, which is not uncommon among the Greeks. And then this will be the sense: *But they themselves do not understand that they are measuring and comparing themselves among themselves, and not rather with those who are better than they*, nor according to the rule of Christ. And this sense fits better with what follows. For what Theophylact wants to be understood—*they do not understand how ridiculous they are to others*—seems forced to me. Even if some Greek scholia seem to divide this speech so that the first part pertains to Paul: *But we, measuring and comparing ourselves in ourselves: so that we understand Paul does not measure himself by the opinion or praise of others, but by his own virtues and the power handed down from Christ.* Then what follows pertains to the false apostles, <note>original: ἑαυτοῖς ἑαυτοὺς ἐν ἑαυτοῖς (*heautois heautous en heautois*)</note>, that is, *themselves by themselves*, understand *comparing, they do not understand:* that is, while a false apostle is compared to a false apostle, and the wicked praise each other, they do not understand that they appear ridiculous. Otherwise, he calls a "rule" <note>original: *regula*</note> a "measure" here, taking a metaphor from the rules of builders. Let no one dream of such a thing as when we say "the Rule of Saint Francis" or "Saint Benedict" <note>Erasmus clarifies that Paul means a physical measuring line, not a monastic code of conduct</note>.

20 <gloss>By which he has measured</gloss>] <note>original: οὗ ἐμέρισεν ἡμῖν ὁ Θεὸς μέτρον (*hou emerisen hēmin ho Theos metron*)</note>, that is, <margin>E</margin> by the measure which God has distributed to us, as if you were to say "by that measure also, insofar as we boast as far as you." Nor is it simply "to you," but "even as far as you," <note>original: ἄχρι καὶ ὑμῶν (*achri kai hymōn*)</note>: so that we understand it is no small thing to reach the standard of the Corinthians. It corresponds to what follows shortly: *for we have come even as far as you*. In the same way that ambitious Princes are accustomed to boast if they have extended their empire very far, so Paul, the leader for Christ, boasts that he has propagated the domain of his Prince that far, hoping that he will bring the empire even further. The translator seems to have read *hypermetron* [beyond measure] instead of *emerisen* [he distributed].

21 <gloss>Of increasing faith</gloss>] <note>original: αὐξανομένης τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν (*auxanomenēs tēs pisteōs hymōn*)</note>, that is, with your faith growing, or increasing; among the Greeks this is a genitive absolute.

22 <gloss>To be magnified according to the rule</gloss>] It would have been more correct to translate these infinitives in another way: <margin>F</margin> *having hope that, as your faith grows more in you, according to our rule in abundance, for evangelizing those things which are beyond you, not so that we may boast in a rule not our own in those things which are already prepared.* He means he hopes that as the faith of the Corinthians grows daily, he himself may also grow and become greater and greater, so that his preaching may now be extended further, even to those who are beyond the Corinthians, and this according to his own rule, not another's—that is, by his own exertion—lest he seem to boast of those things which are already prepared and labored over by others, as the false apostles were doing.

He emphasizes that spiritual authority is intended for building up the church rather than destruction, while critiquing excessive claims of papal power.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed philological and theological commentary on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians. Having finished Chapter 10, he transitions into Chapter 11, where Paul defends his apostolic authority against "false apostles" by comparing his own conduct and hardships to theirs.</meta>

# PAUL’S LETTER TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER XI.

16 To preach the gospel in the regions beyond you, not to boast in another man’s rule regarding things already made ready.
17 18 But he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord. For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.
XI. 1 Would that you could bear with me in a little of my folly; but indeed, do bear with me.
2 For I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy; for I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.
3 But I fear that somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness, so your minds might be corrupted from the simplicity that is toward Christ.
4 For if he who comes preaches another Jesus whom we did not preach, or if you receive a different Spirit which you did not receive, or a different Gospel which you did not accept, you might well bear with him.
5 For I consider myself to be in no way inferior to those "super-apostles."
6 Even if I am unskilled in speech, I am not so in knowledge; indeed, in every way we have been made manifest among all of you.

->H<-

**23 Also to preach the gospel in those regions which are beyond you**] <note>original: "Εἰς τὰ ὑπερέκεινα ὑμῶν"</note>. Lefèvre d’Étaples <note>Erasmus refers to him as "Faber," a contemporary humanist scholar</note> reads this passage as "In those things which are above yours." But he is mistaken, in my judgment. For "beyond" <note>original: "ὑπερέκεινα"</note> is an adverb to which an article is added to make it an epithet, meaning "further than you," that is, "farther away," and among other peoples. This is how it is interpreted not only by Chrysostom, Theophylact, and the other Greek fathers, but also by Saint Ambrose. Therefore, I wonder why Lefèvre, even changing the text itself, wished to disagree with so many authors, especially since there is nothing here that gives offense or suggests we should seek another meaning. But sometimes even the "good Homer nods" <note>A famous Latin idiom from Horace meaning even the greatest experts make mistakes</note>. Nor do we refuse to forgive others, while asking for the same indulgence for ourselves in return.

**1 Would that you sustained a little**] <note>original: "Ὄφελον ἀνείχεσθέ μου μικρόν τι τῇ ἀφροσύνῃ"</note>, that is, "Would that you suffered me for a little while in my foolishness." And it is "would that you had sustained" rather than "would you sustain." Furthermore, what came into Lorenzo Valla’s mind—that he thought "sustineretis" (bear with) should be changed to "suspiceretis" (look up to)—to speak frankly, I simply do not understand. Unless perhaps he dreamed of "receive" <note>original: "ἀναδέχεσθε"</note> instead of "bear with" <note>original: "ἀνείχεσθε"</note>. For the Greek "to bear with" could not be more literally rendered than by saying "sustain." Otherwise, let him show that "to bear with" sometimes has the same force as "to receive," as in "take up my cause." Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Greek lexicographer</note> notes that "to bear with" sometimes means "to endure," which, even if we grant it is true elsewhere, certainly does not fit here. He rightly notes that in the Greek phrase, the word for "in" is missing before "a little." And the Translator <note>referring to the Vulgate</note> used "modicum" (a little) in his usual way for "pusillo" (a tiny bit). We have translated it as "for a little while" <note>original: "paulisiper"</note> so that it refers to time, as it does in other warnings, such as: "Yet a little light is in you," and "A little while and you shall not see me."

**2 Support me**] <note>original: "ἀνείχεσθε"</note>. The Greek word is ambiguous <note>it can be imperative "bear with me!" or indicative "you are bearing with me"</note>. But it fits better as the indicative: "you are bearing with me." For he corrects what he had said: "Would that you were bearing with me," nay, he says, "you are bearing with me," and "what I wish were done, you are doing." The Greek commentaries explain it in this sense.

**3 For I am jealous of you**] <note>original: "Ζηλῶ γὰρ ὑμᾶς"</note>. Ambrose used the Greek word <note>zelus</note>, I think, because he could not find a way to explain the force of the word. For here he calls "zeal" a great and, so to speak, immoderate love, as if he were courting them, so that he might be first with them, and cannot bear other apostles to be admitted into a share of that love. Indeed, he is dealing here with certain apostles who wanted to be held in higher esteem by the Corinthians than Paul was. He adds, however, "with the zeal of God," lest anyone think he was moved by the loss of his own glory. We translated it, "we are jealous lovers toward you." Why should one fear to understand Paul this way, when Origen—unquestionably the prince of theologians in his time—interprets it the same way regarding God: that He is called "jealous," like a jealous lover of ours who will suffer no rival in love?

**4 For I have betrothed**] <note>original: "ἡρμοσάμην"</note>, that is, "I have adapted" or "joined." Ambrose reads "I have prepared," which Erasmus suspects he read as <note>original: "ἠτοιμασάμην"</note>. Jerome, in his commentary on Amos, reads "I have established," but he slipped, I think, in his memory. Augustine, writing against the Manichaeans on Genesis, reads "I have fitted you to one man." For in Greek, "to join" <note>original: "ἁρμόζειν"</note> properly means "I apply fitly and neatly," like things joined by glue or soldering.

**5 By his craftiness**] The Greek adds "in" <note>original: "ἐν"</note>, "in his craftiness," following the property of the Hebrew language where "in" stands for "by means of." And while the Translator rightly omitted it here, I do not know why he chooses to add it elsewhere.

**6 Minds be corrupted**] <note>original: "Φθαρῇ"</note>. He used a word appropriate to the mention of a virgin. And "senses" <note>original: "sensus"</note> in Greek is not "physical senses" <note>original: "αἰσθήσεις"</note>, such as sight or hearing, but "thoughts" <note>original: "νοήματα"</note>, which properly pertains to the mind and soul. Certainly, Augustine reads "minds" instead of "senses" in the passage we will soon cite. For he adapts the allegory: Eve's eyes were deceived, but the Corinthians had to fear for their minds. Furthermore, that word "fall away" is neither in the Greek nor in Ambrose. Therefore, it seems to have been added by the Translator, because otherwise it would seem harsh to say "be corrupted from simplicity." For simplicity does not corrupt the mind, but a corrupted mind degenerates from simplicity. Just as Virgil said,

---
-> "How changed from that [Hector]," <-
---

not that Hector had changed himself, but that he had been made unlike his former self. And Paul appropriately attributes "simplicity" to a virgin, mindful of his allegory, although Ambrose seems to have read "purity" <note>original: "ἁγνότητι"</note>, since he reads "chastity" instead of "simplicity." Augustine cites it no differently in several other 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> our gluttony into excess: 16 So that I may preach the gospel to those regions also that are beyond you, not according to another man’s rule, so as to boast of things already prepared. But he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord. For not he who commends himself is approved, but he whom the Lord commends. Would that you had tolerated me for a little while in my foolishness: nay, and do bear with me. 1 For I am a jealous lover toward you with the zeal of God: 2 for I joined you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear lest by any means, as the serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that was toward Christ. For if he who comes preaches another Jesus whom we have not preached, or if you receive another Spirit which you did not receive, or another Gospel which you did not accept, you would have rightly sustained him. For I think I was in no way inferior to the eminent Apostles. <margin>B</margin> 5 But although I am unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge: 13 but everywhere...

---

places, both in the fifteenth book of *Against Faustus*, chapter three, and again in the twenty-second book, chapter forty-nine. Except that here he joins both: "lest your minds be corrupted from the simplicity and chastity which is in Christ Jesus." Finally, it is not simply "lest," but "lest somehow" <note>original: "μήπως"</note>, which we translate as "lest by any means." For it is more emphatic with the addition of the filler conjunction. Indeed, it should be noted that as he is about to rebuke the Corinthians, he first relieves them of blame, shifting all the ill-will onto the corrupter.

<margin>A</margin> **7 Which is in Christ Jesus**] <note>original: "τῆς εἰς τὸν Χριστόν"</note>, that is, which is "toward Christ" or "into Christ," because we obey him purely and simply.

<margin>B</margin> **8 Another Christ**] <note>original: "ἄλλον Ἰησοῦν"</note>, that is, "another or a second Jesus." Thus the Greek manuscripts that I have seen agree. And so Theophylact reads and interprets it, with the commentaries in agreement. Ambrose reads "Christ" with us. It should be noted in passing that what Paul warns the Corinthians about, we too must greatly guard against: lest we summon or rather invent for ourselves "another Jesus"—one burdened with riches, burdened with power, dominion, pleasures, and whatever deceptions this world has—and moreover, one encrusted with ceremonies more than Jewish, when that true Jesus was most pure from all these things.

<margin>C</margin> **9 You would rightly obey**] Why not "sustained" here as well? <note>original: "ἀνείχεσθε"</note>. He seems to be saying to them: If those false apostles taught anything that we did not teach, why would you tolerate them now when they bring nothing regarding Christ that we have not already taught?

<margin>D</margin> **10 I have done nothing less**] <note>original: "μηδὲν ὑστερηκέναι τῶν ὑπὲρ λίαν Ἀποστόλων"</note>, that is, "to have been in no way inferior to the excellent Apostles." And Ambrose reads it in this sense: "For I estimate that in nothing was I inferior to those who are 'very much' Apostles." For he means Peter, James, and John, who were considered the chiefest, as the Greek commentaries indicate, with Chrysostom and Theophylact agreeing. But it is strange how the preceding and following words fit them. More recent scholars excuse this, saying it was not said of the true Apostles, but of those who pretended to be sent by Peter and the others. Furthermore, the Greek "beyond very much" sounds like something more than "excellent" because of the added preposition "beyond" <note>original: "ὑπὲρ"</note>; as if you were to say, "the apostles who are excellent beyond measure," which seems to be said with a bit of a sarcastic "stomach" <note>bitterness or resentment</note>.

<margin>E</margin> **11 For if**] <note>original: "Εἰ δὲ καί"</note>. Here the Translator frequently renders "but" <note>original: "δὲ"</note> as "for" <note>original: "nam"</note>. Furthermore, "although unskilled," for it contrasts with the previous part where he boasted that he was in no way inferior to the greatest Apostles.

<margin>F</margin> **12 But not in knowledge**] Why not rather, more Latinately and simply: "but not in knowledge" or "cognition"? Lorenzo Valla rightly laughs at some who, from this passage, mistakenly conclude that Paul was some kind of stutterer with an impeded tongue; as if there were no difference between an "impeded" man and an "unskilled" one. He says Paul was a man truly impeded in speech, and even in knowledge—since in Greek it is "idiota," a word which to them means both a private citizen and an unlearned person. Jerome is inconsistent on this matter, shouting in several places that Paul was ignorant of the more elegant Greek speech—which might happen sometimes because he uses certain words native to Cilicia <note>Paul’s home region</note>, and sometimes he does not provide the matching "but" for a "indeed" <note>original: "μὲν... δὲ"</note>. Additionally, he is sometimes troublesome with the twists of his "hyperbaton" <note>disrupted word order</note>, and occasionally leaves a sentence unfinished. Yet elsewhere Jerome declaims in the opposite direction, pushing far away those who think Paul said this from his heart, since he knew all the properties of language beautifully and was perfectly skilled in all the tricks of argumentation. Even Saint Augustine, in his work *On Christian Doctrine*, cites many rhetorical schemes from Paul’s Epistles. The same author notes elsewhere that in this passage Paul is not confessing a fault, but rather conceding a point: as if you were to say, "grant that I am unskilled in speech, I am certainly not unskilled in knowledge." Furthermore, as far as the meaning is concerned, nothing can be more divine than Paul; but his speech, while free of the "solecisms" <note>grammatical errors</note> that the Translator added to him, still cannot be called "polished" in the human sense. Greek interpreters are everywhere twisted by the awkwardness of his speech, which would not have happened if he had spoken to us in the language of Socrates or Lucian.

<margin>G</margin> **13 But in all things I am manifest to you**, or **as the ancient manuscripts have it, we have been made manifest**] The Greek reads differently: <note>original: "ἀλλ᾿ ἐν παντὶ φανερωθέντες ἐν πᾶσιν εἰς ὑμᾶς"</note>. Which literally sounds like: "but in everything having been manifested in all things toward you." But the sense is this: We are not like the false apostles, who are disguised and masked, imposing on you with a pretense of holiness; but in every matter and among all people we have been declared, and it is apparent what kind of men we are toward you. And that "in everything" can refer to the matter, and "among all" to the persons, unless you prefer to see it as a repetition for the sake of emphasis.

<summary>Erasmus provides a linguistic and theological defense of Paul's authority in 2 Corinthians 11, arguing that Paul's "unskilled" speech is a mark of his sincerity compared to the polished but deceptive rhetoric of his rivals. He analyzes key Greek terms to clarify that Paul considers himself equal to the highest apostles and warns against a "false Jesus" based on worldly power.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s examination of Second Corinthians 11. Having just asserted his equality with the "super-apostles," Paul now addresses the specific criticism regarding his refusal to accept financial support from the Corinthians, a choice he uses to distinguish himself from his opponents.</meta>

# SECOND LETTER TO THE CORINTHIANS. CHAPTER XI.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>7</margin> ^14 Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached the Gospel of God to you for free? <margin>8</margin> ^15 I robbed other churches, taking wages from them to serve you. <margin>9</margin> And when I was present with you and in need, ^17 I ^18 was not a burden to anyone. ^19 For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I lacked. In everything, I kept myself from being a burden to you, and I will continue to do so. <margin>10</margin> As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting will not be silenced <note>original: "φραγήσεται", literally "fenced in" or "blocked"</note> regarding me in the regions of Achaia. <margin>11</margin> Why? ^22 Because I do not love you? God knows I do! <margin>B</margin> ^23 But what I am doing, I will continue to do, so that I may cut off the opportunity from those who desire an opportunity to be regarded as our equals in the things they boast about. <margin>13</margin> For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into apostles of Christ. <margin>14</margin> And no wonder! For Satan himself transforms into an angel of light. <margin>15</margin> Therefore, it is no great thing if his ministers also transform themselves as ministers of righteousness, whose end will be according to their works. <margin>16</margin> I say again, let no one think me a fool. But if you do, then at least receive me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. <margin>17</margin> What I am saying, ^29 I do not say according to the Lord, but as if in foolishness, in this matter of boasting. <margin>18</margin> <margin>C</margin> ^30 Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast. <margin>19</margin> For you gladly bear with fools, being so wise yourselves! For you bear it if someone makes slaves of you, if someone devours you, if someone takes from you, if someone exalts himself, if <margin>21</margin> someone strikes you in the face. I speak to my shame, as though we had been weak. ^33 But in whatever anyone else dares—I am speaking in foolishness—I dare also. <margin>22</margin> Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they the seed of Abraham? So am I. <margin>23</margin> Are they ministers of Christ? I am speaking as if I were out of my mind—I am more so! In labors more abundant...

***

<margin>14</margin> **Or did I commit a sin]** <margin>D</margin> The Greek text says, *Or did I commit a sin*, or *Did I sin*. The Greeks do not distinguish between the particles "or" and "whether" in this context. Among the Latins, there is a great difference, and what was the point of adding "that" <note>the word "quòd" in the Vulgate</note> when the Greek language does not have it?

<margin>15</margin> **I robbed other churches]** <note>original: "ἐσύλησα"</note>, that is, I plundered them. Paul is quite fond of using military metaphors, as we see shortly with the phrase *receiving a soldier’s wage*. <note>Erasmus highlights Paul's use of "depraedatus sum" (plundered) and "stipendium" (soldier's pay) to show the intensity of his language regarding support from other churches.</note>

<margin>16</margin> **To serve you]** The Greek uses *eis* or, as in some copies, *pros*, meaning "toward your service." This was done so that I might serve you without you having to pay for it, while I received my wages in the meantime from others.

<margin>17</margin> **And was in need]** <note>original: "καὶ ὑστερηθεὶς"</note>, that is, *and being destitute*, or "when things were lacking." In my opinion, the conjunction "and" is not just simple here, but carries an emphasis <note term="epitasis">an intensification of the argument</note> in this passage, so the meaning is: "I burdened you so little that I was unwilling to do it even when I was in dire need."

<margin>18</margin> **I was a burden]** <note>original: "κατενάρκησα"</note>. This word is derived from *narkē*, meaning "idleness" or "torpor." It describes those who weigh down and hang over others from whom they seek something. It is composed of *narkaō*, which means "to be numb" or "torpid"—the source of the name for the *torpedo* fish <note>the electric ray, which numbs its prey</note>—and the preposition *kata*, which often carries a negative sense, as in "condemn" or "despise." This is especially true here since it is paired with a grammatical case suggesting a target: "I was not a 'dead-weight' upon anyone." Jerome, in his book to Algasia, mentions that this word was peculiar to the people of Cilicia <note>Paul's home region</note>. But if Paul, who worked so hard, was unwilling to be a burden to anyone, with what nerve do certain people today fleece the common folk when they themselves are of no use to anyone?

<margin>19</margin> **In all things without burden]** <note>original: "ἀβαρῆ"</note>, meaning "not at all heavy."

<margin>20</margin> **The truth of Christ is in me]** He adds this as a sort of oath to confirm what he has said. Ambrose hints at this when he says, "under the testimony of Christ."

<margin>21</margin> **Will not be silenced]** <note>original: "οὐ φραγήσεται"</note>. The Greek commentaries explain this as "will not be interrupted" or "will not fail." By this, they say he means he will not accept anything from them in the future either, so that this occasion for boasting—that he taught the Gospel for free—will not be blocked off from him. For something is "interrupted" if it is not continuous. But he swears that this glory will be perpetual for him, so that he would not be heavy upon anyone. The word is derived from "fencing off," as we are often excluded by obstacles placed in our way. Furthermore, the Greek is not "in me" in a local sense, but "against me" <note>original: "εἰς ἐμὲ"</note>, as if to say, "in opposition to me."

<margin>22</margin> **Because I do not love you]** It was clearly meant to be, "Is it because I do not love you?" He changed the mood of the verb, for the Greeks often ignore such distinctions.

<margin>23</margin> **But what I do and will do]** The translator does not seem to have noticed the elegance of the conjunction "and" <note>original: "καὶ"</note> which it holds in this and similar places among the Greeks: *what I do, I will also do*, that is, "What I am doing now, I am also going to do in the future." Furthermore, although the Greeks have a single conjunction *kai* that corresponds to several Latin words (*but, yet, indeed, further, conversely, etc.*), it makes a difference for us which one you place where. Here, "but" was more appropriate than "however." "Is it because I do not love you? God knows. *But* what I do, etc."

<margin>24</margin> **So that in what they boast]** <note>original: "ἵνα ἐν ᾧ καυχῶνται"</note>. Ambrose came closer to the Greek: "so that in that which they boast, they may be found even as we." That is, if they boast that they preach for free, they will not be better than us in this, since I myself teach for free even while in need.

<column-break/>

<page-num>790</page-num>

In everything we have been made manifest in all things toward you. <margin>Num 7</margin>
^14 Did I commit that sin, that I humbled myself so that you might be exalted? That I preached the Gospel of God to you for free? <margin>8</margin> ^15 I plundered other churches, having accepted a wage from them, <margin>16</margin> in order to serve you: and when I was with you and in need, I was not <margin>18</margin> a burden to anyone: For the brothers who had come from Macedonia supplied what was lacking to me: and in all things I so kept myself, <margin>19</margin> that I would be a burden to no one, and so I will keep myself. <margin>9</margin>
<margin>10</margin> ^20 The truth of Christ is in me, that this boasting <margin>21</margin> shall not be interrupted against me in the regions of Achaia. Why? <margin>22</margin> Is it because I do not love you? God knows. ^23 <margin>11</margin>
But what I do, I will also do, that I may cut off the opportunity for those who desire an opportunity, <margin>24</margin> so that in the matter in <margin>12</margin> which they boast, they may be found just as we are.
^25 For such false apostles are deceitful workers, having put on the persona of the Apostles of Christ. And <margin>13</margin> it is no wonder: since Satan himself is transformed <margin>14</margin> into an angel of light. It is no great thing therefore, <margin>15</margin> ^26 if his ministers also take this persona upon themselves, as if they were ministers of righteousness, whose end will be according to their works. I say again, let no one think me to be a fool, otherwise even now receive me as a fool, ^28 so that <margin>16</margin> I too may boast a little something. What I say, I do not say ^29 according to the Lord, but as if through foolishness, <margin>17</margin> ^30 in this matter of boasting. Since <margin>18</margin> many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast. For you gladly endure fools, since you are wise. <margin>19</margin> For you endure it if someone drives you into slavery, if someone devours you, ^31 if someone takes from you, if someone lifts himself up, if someone strikes you in the face: ^32 I speak according to <margin>20</margin> the dishonor, just as ^33 if we had been weak: <margin>21</margin>
^34 indeed, in whatever anyone else dares, ^35 I speak through foolishness, I dare also. Are they Hebrews? I am too. Are they <margin>22</margin> Israelites? I am too. Are they the seed of Abraham? I am too. ^36 Are they ministers of Christ? I speak as one out of my mind, I am more <margin>23</margin> abundantly so...

***

<margin>25</margin> **Such false apostles]** This should be "pseudapostoli," a compound word, just as it is in the Greek; it cannot be divided into two. In Latin, it sounds like "Apostles by a false title." For an Apostle does the business of the one who sent him; these men serve their own interests.

<margin>26</margin> **If his ministers]** <note>original: "εἰ καὶ οἱ διάκονοι"</note>, that is, "if also the ministers"; and this is how Ambrose reads it. And they "transform themselves"—the Greek uses a passive form, "they are transformed" <note>original: "μετασχηματίζονται"</note>.

<margin>27</margin> **Otherwise as a fool]** <note>original: "εἰ δὲ μήγε"</note>, that is, "but if otherwise." That is: if I cannot persuade you that I am not a fool—since I proclaim these things about myself not for empty glory but compelled by necessity—nevertheless tolerate me boasting as a fool. "Receive me even as a fool" <note>original: "κἂν ὡς ἄφρονα"</note>, that is, "even as a fool." Perhaps the Translator turned *kai* into "or" <note>Latin: "vel"</note>; we have poorly joined those conjunctions.

<margin>28</margin> **A little something]** <margin>E</margin> <note>original: "μικρόν τι"</note>, that is, "a little bit," or "for a little while."

<margin>29</margin> **According to the Lord]** <note>original: "κατὰ Κύριον"</note>. This is just as he wrote in the previous Letter, "I, not the Lord," and "of the Lord, not I." He means something human and perhaps less than perfectly serious, which he says is not "according to the Lord."

<margin>30</margin> **In this substance of glory]** <note>original: "ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ ὑποστάσει τῆς καυχήσεως"</note>, that is, in this part or "matter" of boasting. Saint Ambrose also reads it this way: "the substance of boasting."

<margin>31</margin> **If someone takes]** <note>original: "εἴ τις λαμβάνει"</note>. The preceding word, "devours," seems to refer to the food they were taking from the disciples; this refers to gifts. Theophylact thinks the same thing is said twice—devours and takes—so that we might understand the insatiable greed for taking in the false apostles, joined with the highest arrogance.

<margin>32</margin> **I speak according to ignobility]** <note>original: "Κατὰ ἀτιμίαν"</note>. "According to the insult" or "contumely" would fit better. For he is explaining those harsh things: "if someone devours you, if someone strikes you in the face, etc." He is saying: not that you suffer these things from the false apostles, but that as far as the account of insult goes, you suffer no lighter things from them than if you were actually suffering those physical blows.

<margin>33</margin> **As if we had been weak in this part]** <margin>F</margin> I do not find "in this part" in the Greek codices that I have seen.

<margin>34</margin> **In what anyone dares]** <note>original: "ἐν ᾧ δ᾽ ἄν τις τολμᾷ"</note>, that is, "in whatever indeed someone dares." For he is correcting what he just said, as if we were less capable in "this part," that is, in the argument for boasting. But this is so far from the truth that I am equal to them in all these things, and in some, even superior. Therefore, we translate it using "indeed" <note>Latin: "imo"</note>, which makes the correction more evident.

<margin>35</margin> **I speak in foolishness]** He inserts this as a parenthesis, mindful of what he said before: "I do not speak according to the Lord, but as if in foolishness."

<margin>36</margin> **Are they ministers of Christ?]** After this part, "so am I" is not repeated in the Greek. In fact, adding it subverts the whole meaning. It should be read like this: "Are they ministers of Christ? I am more." Then the phrase "I speak as a fool" is inserted as a parenthesis, as I just noted. This agrees with the Greek copies...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on Second Corinthians 11 and 12.
