# THE EPISTOLA OF PAUL. CHAPTER XII.

<margin>24</margin> Five times from the Jews I received forty lashes minus one; <note>original: "ὑπὸ Ἰουδαίων πεντάκις τεσσαράκοντα παρὰ μίαν ἔλαβον"</note>
<margin>25</margin> Thrice I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck; a night and a day I have spent in the deep; <note>original: "Τρὶς ἐρραβδίσθην, ἅπαξ ἐλιθάσθην, τρὶς ἐναυάγησα· νυχθήμερον ἐν τῷ βυθῷ πεποίηκα"</note>
<margin>26</margin> In journeys often, in dangers of rivers, in dangers of robbers, in dangers from my own nation, in dangers from the Gentiles, in dangers in the city, in dangers in the wilderness, in dangers in the sea, in dangers among false brothers; <note>original: "Ὁδοιπορίαις πολλάκις... κινδύνοις ἐν ψευδαδέλφοις"</note>
<margin>27</margin> in labor and hardship, in many watchings, in hunger and thirst, in many fastings, in cold and nakedness; <note>original: "ἐν κόπῳ καὶ μόχθῳ..."</note>
<margin>28</margin> besides those things that are without, my daily pressure, the care for all the Churches. <note>original: "χωρὶς τῶν παρεκτὸς, ἡ ἐπισύστασίς μου..."</note>
<margin>29</margin> Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is offended, and I do not burn?
<margin>30</margin> If I must boast, I will boast of the things that concern my weakness.
<margin>31</margin> The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever, knows that I do not lie.
<margin>32</margin> In Damascus, the governor <note><term>ethnarch</term>: a local ruler or tribal leader</note> under King Aretas guarded the city of the Damascenes, wishing to seize me;
<margin>33</margin> and through a window I was let down in a basket through the wall, and I escaped his hands.
XII. 1. It is not indeed profitable for me to boast, for I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord.

---

<margin>A</margin> Ambrose reads this more extensively, in this manner: *They are ministers of Christ (I speak as a fool), I am more.* For in other matters he made himself equal to the other Apostles, but in that which is proper to the Apostles, he places himself before them, not merely equal. Truly, because that might have seemed a rather arrogant thing to say, he fortifies it with the pretext of "folly," just as he did at the beginning. But even if it were read this way—*They are ministers of Christ, and I*—meaning "I speak as one less wise, I am more," there was no necessity to introduce the sense which Nicolaus (surnamed de Lyra) introduced following the opinion of Aquinas. Lyra makes a new sentence starting from this point, *I speak as one less wise, I am more*, and explains it this way: *If I seem foolish to you by equaling myself to the false apostles, I shall seem even less wise to you by preferring myself to them.* For that phrase, *I am more*, could have been added as a correction, following a softening of the insolence, in this way: *They are ministers of Christ, and so am I. But what did I say, "and I"? Nay, to speak in the manner of fools, more gloriously, I am more.* However, it is not our purpose here to discuss what such writers thought, as it is well known that, being ignorant of ancient literature, they treated the Sacred Letters with a hodgepodge of glosses patched together from here and there in a disorganized study. Our business is rather with the Ancients. Furthermore, for those who wish to know more fully about the ornaments of speech and the rhetorical schemes with which this entire discourse is painted and tuned, let them read the fourth chapter of the fourth book of *On Christian Doctrine* <note>A famous work on rhetoric and hermeneutics by St. Augustine.</note>.

<margin>37 In labors many]</margin> <note>original: "ἐν κόποις περισσοτέρως"</note>, that is, *in labors more abundantly*. Perhaps the Translator rendered it *more* <note>Latin: "pluribus"</note>, which is tolerable. However, among the Greeks the order is different: *in labors more abundantly, in stripes above measure, in prisons more abundantly*. For what the Translator rendered in two ways, the Greeks have as a single adverb <note>original: "περισσοτέρως"</note>, even though the comparative is used in place of the superlative.

<margin>38 Above measure]</margin> <note>original: "ὑπερβαλλόντως"</note>, that is, exceedingly, and so to speak, excessively, and beyond what can be believed; so that those who interpret it as "above the measure of human virtue" do not quite hit the mark.

<margin>39 Forty]</margin> <note>original: "τεσσαράκοντα"</note>, that is, forty, although he translates it correctly, indicating that he was beaten five times, and at each time he was struck with forty stripes—if indeed that is true, which is certainly very likely, especially since he was beaten among the Jews. For Saint Ambrose thinks so, adding that the commandment in the book of Deuteronomy was that those who deserved it should be corrected with thirty-nine stripes. For we read in the twenty-fifth chapter of Deuteronomy: *According to the measure of the sin shall be the measure of the stripes: provided that they do not exceed the number of forty, lest your brother depart foully torn before your eyes.* Therefore, it is probable that for the sake of humanity, one stripe was usually omitted, so that they might stop short of the prescribed number. From where they drew this, I do not know, but Lyra and the so-called Ordinary Gloss indicate it. Valla prefers: *five times I received thirty-nine*, though "stripes" must undoubtedly be understood.

<margin>40 Thrice I suffered shipwreck]</margin> <note>original: "τρὶς ἐναυάγησα"</note>, as if you were to say *I was shipwrecked*. He translates into Latin as *naufragium feci* <note>literally: "I made shipwreck"</note> for *I suffered shipwreck*. Just as Terence said: "he broke the ship at Andros," concerning one whose ship was broken by a storm.

<margin>41 Night and day]</margin> <note>original: "νυχθήμερον ἐν τῷ βυθῷ πεποίηκα"</note>, that is, *I have spent a night and a day in the deep*. Nor is "of the sea" added, even though Ambrose and also Theophylact interpret it as the sea; however, "the deep" <note>original: "βύθος"</note> can also be said of the depth of another thing, such as a prison.

<margin>42 Dangers from my nation]</margin> He does not strictly mean from his kinsmen, but calls the nation of the Jews his "nation" <note>original: "genus"</note>, which he immediately contrasts with the Gentiles.

<margin>43 In false brothers]</margin> In Greek there is a single word <note>original: "ψευδαδέλφοις"</note>, that is, false Christians, who pretend to be disciples of Christ when they are not. For as I have often warned, all Christians were called "brothers" in an absolute sense. That title is now occupied by only a few, as if Christianity had fallen to them alone, and it is held almost in contempt by the common people, though there is no other name of charity more worthy of praise.

<margin>44 In labor and hardship]</note> <note>original: "κόπῳ καὶ μόχθῳ"</note>. He has said almost the same thing twice. For *mochthos* <note>hardship</note> is also labor, but one that has diffi-

<column-break/>

-culty joined to it. Hence the Greeks call the calamitous *mochtheroi*. From this, Ambrose reads *trouble* instead of *hardship*.

<margin>45 In many watchings]</margin> Instead of "many," the Greek is *often* <note>original: "πολλάκις"</note>. Likewise, it is *in fastings often*, not *in many fastings*.

<margin>46 Besides those things that are without]</margin> <note>original: "Χωρὶς τῶν παρεκτὸς"</note>, that is, besides those things that happen outwardly and from the outside. Most people explain it in that way. However, Chrysostom, and Theophylact following him, take *parektos* to mean "except," as if to say, *besides those things which I omit*: so the sense is that Paul has listed only a few things in this catalog of his evils and not everything. The Greek scholia agree. But which opinion is more to be approved, I leave to the prudent reader to weigh.

<margin>47 My daily pressure]</margin> This is separate from the above, *my daily accumulation* <note>original: "ἡ ἐπισύστασίς μου ἡ καθ’ ἡμέραν"</note>. Although this particle *daily* can refer to both the "pressure" and the "daily anxiety." Chrysostom and Theophylact refer it to what preceded, the *epistasis* <note>pressure/accumulation</note>. For with a commentary inserted, they subjoin "the anxiety for all the Churches." The Greek scholia interpret *epistasis* not as care or diligence, but as a conspiracy against Paul: so that you understand that besides those persecutions that were from without (that is, from the Pagans), there were almost daily ambushes and insults from the crowds and cities stirring up sedition against the Gospel. However, Ambrose interprets it as the urgent cares of all the Churches which were looming over Paul. And Augustine, explaining the ninety-eighth Psalm, was certainly led to this opinion: *the daily incursion upon me, the anxiety for all the Churches*, so that he joins *epistasis* and *merimnan* <note>anxiety</note> by apposition. And in this sense it could be conveniently translated: *the daily anxiety for the Churches pressing upon me.*

<margin>48 And Father of our Lord Jesus Christ]</margin> "Our" is not added in several Greek copies. And He is called "the Lord" simply and absolutely, as He who is Lord of all, unless some other addition suggests otherwise.

<margin>49 The governor of Damascus]</margin> The genitive *of Damascus* <note>original: "Δαμασκῷ"</note> is adverbial here, for "governor" refers to his ruling: *the ethnarch of King Aretas*. King Aretas was the father-in-law of Herod the Tetrarch, since he was the King of Arabia Petraea and the ruler of the city of Damascus, which is near Arabia, as Josephus teaches in the eighteenth book of *Jewish Antiquities*. He means, therefore, the man whom King Aretas had placed over Damascus.

<margin>50 To seize me]</margin> <note>original: "πιάσαι με θέλων"</note>, that is, wishing to seize me.

<margin>51 And so I escaped his hands]</margin> "So" is not in the Greek, but only *and I escaped the hands*. It was not added in the Donatian codex, nor even in the Constantian one.

<margin>XII.</margin> **1** **It is necessary to boast]** The Greek has it thus: *To boast indeed is not profitable for me.* Although Laurentius reads "it is not necessary" in most codices, so that the sense is: *Truly, to boast is not expedient for me.* Chrysostom also interprets it this way, and his imitator Theophylact, advising that this is a transition to the mention of those things which have even more glory. But if "it is necessary" <note>Latin: "dei" / "oportet"</note> is preferred, it should be read as a question: *Must one boast?* Then he answers himself: *it is not expedient.* Ambrose reads it in this sense. But the former reading is much more approved by me, because it appears that this passage was changed from the one above, where he had said: *If I must boast, I will boast in the things that concern my weakness*, for there is less danger in that. However, when he comes to revelations, he pulls back, denying that one should boast—even if the things he is about to say are true—because these are more subject to the suspicion of bragging than the former things. Now, just as the scribes erred between *dei* <note>it is necessary</note> and *de* <note>indeed</note>, or *de* <note>but</note>, due to the similarity of both the letters and the sounds, so it is likely they erred between *me* <note>not</note> and *moi* <note>to me</note>. For the Greeks do not read "it is not expedient indeed," but "it is not expedient for me" <note>original: "οὐ συμφέρει μοι"</note>. And that is suited to Paul's meaning, so the sense is: It is indeed expedient for *you* to know what kind of Apostle you have—far different from those haughty ones. But it is not expedient for *me* to tell it, as one for whom it is not safe, either because of the risk of vain glory, or because of the suspicion of men, to whom I will seem to be bragging about these things.
<meta>Catchword: bragging</meta>

<summary>In this passage, Erasmus provides a detailed commentary on Paul’s "catalogue of sufferings," including the famous thirty-nine lashes and his escape from Damascus. He also begins discussing the textual variants of Chapter 12 regarding the necessity and risk of boasting about spiritual revelations.</summary>
<keywords>2 Corinthians 11, Paul's tribulations, thirty-nine lashes, Damascus, King Aretas, boasting, spiritual revelations, Greek New Testament, textual criticism, Erasmus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from the previous account of Paul’s physical sufferings. Having listed his earthly trials (lashes, shipwrecks, and escapes), Paul now transitions to his spiritual credentials: his heavenly visions and the mysterious "thorn in the flesh" that keeps him humble. Erasmus provides a parallel Greek and Latin text along with extensive philological notes comparing the readings of Church Fathers like Ambrose and Augustine.</meta>

# TO THE CORINTHIANS II. CHAPTER XII.

2 <margin>A</margin> ...of the Lord. I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago—whether in the body I do not know, or whether out of the body I do not know, God knows—such a person was caught up to the
3 third heaven. And I know such a
4 man—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows—that he was caught up into
5 paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not permitted for a man to speak. On behalf of such a one I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except in my
6 weaknesses. For if I should wish to boast, I will not be a fool, for I will speak the truth; but I refrain, <margin>B</margin> lest anyone should credit me with more than what he sees in me or hears
7 anything from me. And lest I should be exalted by the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, to buffet me, lest I should be exalted.
8 Concerning this, I pleaded with the Lord three times that it might depart from me.
9 And He said to me, "My grace is sufficient for you; for my power is perfected in weakness." Most gladly, therefore, I will rather boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell upon me.
10 Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in insults, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ’s sake; for when
11 I am weak, then I am strong. I have become a fool in boasting; you compelled me; for I ought to have been commended by you; for I was in no way inferior to those <margin>C</margin> super-eminent <note>original: "ὑπερλίαν"</note> apostles...

---

...for the sake of substance, as many are accustomed to do. And Ambrose reads nothing here, nor does he add, *If it is necessary to boast, but it is not expedient for me.* Now, what follows coheres much more aptly with the preceding parts; for I shall come to visions, as if giving a reason why he said it was not expedient for him to boast over these things. Nor is the word "but" <note>Greek: δέ (de)</note> in the Greek at this place, but "for" <note>Greek: γάρ (gar)</note>, with the manuscripts in wonderful agreement.

2 *I know a man*] It should be noted in this place that the Greek article is not added, lest it should seem to designate a specific certain man; instead, he spoke of a man in general, *Oida anthropon* <note>original: "Οἶδα ἄνθρωπον"</note>.

3 *Whether in the body*] After this phrase is added *eite oida*, that is, *I do not know*, which is likewise repeated after the other: *whether in the body, I do not know, whether outside the body, I do not know.* The Donatian manuscript agreed with the Greek, which had it written thus: *whether in the body, I do not know, whether outside the body, I do not know.* The Constantinian manuscript had the same reading. And for the word *eite*, a more Latin rendering would have been *an* <note>meaning "whether" or "if"</note>.

4 *Unspeakable words*] *arrheta rhemata* <note>original: "ἄῤῥητα ῥήματα"</note>. That is, *words not to be spoken* or *ineffable words*. There is a hidden grace in the related and contrary Greek sounds, as if you said in Latin *indicenda dicta* for *non dicenda dicta* <note>a play on words: "un-spoken sayings"</note>.

5 *On behalf of such a one I boast*] *Hyper tou toioutou* <note>original: "Ὑπὲρ τοῦ τοιούτου"</note>. And it seems to pertain more to the person than to the event. For Paul tells this thing as if it were about someone else whom he nevertheless knew: *Therefore about myself*, he says, *I will not boast.* But I will boast of this sort of man whom I know, as if disguising that he himself is the one of whom he speaks. Theophylact <note>a prominent 11th-century Byzantine commentator</note> argues much the same.

6 *On my own behalf nothing*] *hyper de emautou ou kauchesomai*, that is, *but concerning myself I will not boast*.

7 *Lest anyone think of me*] *me tis eis eme logisetai, hyper ho blepei me, e akouei ti ex emou*, that is, *lest anyone should reckon in me above that which he sees me, or hears something from me.* That "in me" is just as if you said, "think of me" or "attribute to me." Ambrose reads "he sees me," rendering the speech word-for-word; and both Constantinian manuscripts had the same.

8 *And lest the greatness*] In Greek it has it thus: *Kai te hyperbole ton apokalypseon hina me hyperairomai, edothe moi skolops te sarki, angelos Satan*, that is, *And lest I be exalted by the excellence of revelations, there was given to me a thorn to the flesh (or in the flesh), a messenger of Satan.* And Ambrose reads it almost exactly so. Augustine, in his *Questions on the Book of Judges*, reads, *And in the magnitude of revelations lest I be exalted*, as if he had read *en te hyperbole*. Furthermore, the word here is not *kentron* <note>a sting</note>, as in Acts, but *skolops* <note><term>skolops</term>: a Greek word for a sharpened stake or a splinter</note>, which sounds like a sharpened pale. Some interpret this "thorn" as the stirrings and impulses of lust, which <margin>D</margin> I wonder should please any learned theologian. For what is more absurd than to think so great an Apostle, now an old man, was still troubled by the itch of lust, and so troubled that he was forced by this grace to appeal to the Lord three times? The mention of "flesh" moves these people, and they immediately think the words refer to Venus <note>sexual desire</note>, just as Augustine almost always interprets the word "concupiscence" as the impulse for coitus, whereas Paul is accustomed to call "flesh" every human affection that does not proceed from the Spirit of God. But likewise he calls external troubles, which human life brings with it, "flesh," as when speaking of the married he says, "nevertheless such shall have tribulation of the flesh." That he means weakness in this place, not a disease of the body but affliction brought by enemies, is testified by what follows: *Gladly will I boast in my infirmities, etc.* Soon he explains what he calls infirmities: *Because of which, he says, I am pleased in my infirmities, in insults, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ.* And in the previous chapter he prefaced: *If it is necessary to boast, I will boast of the things that are of my weakness.* Saint Jerome, in the Commentaries he published on the Epistle to the Galatians, reports that some felt this *thorn* was the body's ill health, because Paul was often accustomed to be afflicted by a headache. Theophylact reports this too. Thomas Aquinas, following I know not whom, says he was subject to "iliac disease" <note>likely intestinal pain or colic</note>. Chrysostom, in his sixth Homily on the praises of Paul, interprets it as contempt of the body... <margin>F</margin>

<column-break/>

2 of the Lord. I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago, whether in the body, I do not know, or outside the body, I do not know, God knows, such a one was caught up even to the
3 third heaven. And I know such a man, whether in the body, or outside the body, I do not know, God knows,
4 that he was caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not permitted for a man to speak.
5 On behalf of such a one I will boast, but of myself I will not boast, except in my
6 weaknesses. For if I wish to boast, I will not be a fool, for I will speak the truth: but I spare you, lest anyone should think of me above what he sees me to be, or
7 what he hears from me. And lest I be puffed up beyond measure by the excellence of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn through the flesh, a messenger of Satan,
8 to strike me with fists, lest I be puffed up beyond measure.
9 Concerning this I asked the Lord three times, that it might depart from me. And He said to me, "My grace is sufficient for you:
10 for my power is perfected through weakness."
11 Most willingly therefore will I rather boast over my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may dwell in me.
13 Wherefore I am pleased in my weaknesses, in insults, in necessities, in persecutions, in anxieties for Christ: for when I am weak, then I am strong.
14 I have become a fool by boasting: you have compelled me: for I ought to have been commended by you:
15 for in no matter was I inferior to those highest Apostles, even if...

---

...pain. But to me, the closest view seems to be what Ambrose says: that the harassment of evil men, which constantly made trouble for him, is called a "thorn." For he says: *either therefore a remedy was given to the Apostle so that, pressed by the injuries of adversaries, he could not be puffed up in spirit.* Indeed, in this regard even enemies are sometimes useful, teaching us sobriety and modesty. Theophylact indicates that some interpret *hyperairomai* as "I am exalted," that is, being glorified beyond measure by men, but he rejects this fabrication. However, he raises the question: since Paul suffered many adversaries—Hermogenes, Phygellus, Alexander—why did he call the false apostles "Satan," and why does he call this one an "angel"?

9 *To buffet me* <note>original: "hina me kolaphize"</note>] *hina me*, that is, *me*. And so Ambrose reads. Although "which" is sometimes put for "that it might." *To buffet me.* After these words I find repeated again, *hina me hyperairomai*, that is, *lest I be exalted*. And so Ambrose reads. Although the Greek word sounds like more than just "exalted"—rather "carried away beyond measure," as if you said "excessively over-exalted."

10 *Concerning this*] *Hyper toutou*, that is, *About this, or For this*, and it refers to the preceding things, not to what follows.

11 *For power*] In Greek it is *my power*, *he dynamis mou*. For these are the words of the Lord responding to Paul. Nor is "power" *arete* <note>virtue</note>, as if opposed to vice, but *dynamis* <note>strength/power</note>, as opposed to weakness. For he perceives that divine power and potency are declared in a far different way than the power of the world. For while the latter becomes known by strengths and force, the former, on the contrary, by enduring. Another sense can be taken here: Divine power is most clearly illustrated when he through whom it acts, being conscious of his own weakness, claims nothing for himself but attributes all praise to God alone. Ambrose seems to follow a different opinion, which however does not quite satisfy me. Although Theophylact constrains it to the same. And Augustine, in the third book to Bishop Boniface, chapter seven, refers it to the virtue of man, which will be perfected in the future age, whereas here it is not *arete* but *dynamis*. For Ambrose adds that devotion, while not broken by the pressure of encroaching weakness, may be seen as proven, so that it responds to what follows: *for when I am weakened, then I am powerful.* Furthermore, he elegantly related two opposing things: *dynamis* and *astheneia* <note>power and weakness</note>.

12 *Gladly*] *Hedista*, that is, *Most gladly*. And it is not simply "I will boast," but *mallon kauchesomai*, that is, *more or rather I will boast*. Nor does the comparative conflict here with the superlative, since "rather" pertains not to the manner of boasting, but to the argument and matter of boasting. Ambrose joined both together. But in this place, I would prefer "than more."

13 *Wherefore I am pleased*] *Dio eudoko*, that is, *Wherefore I am pleased*, or *it is pleasing to me*: with the more correct Latin versions agreeing. Nor is "my" added; it is only *in weaknesses*. The Constantinian manuscript agreed, for he soon explains what he calls weaknesses.

14 *I have become a fool*] *Gegona aphron kauchomenos*. It can also be taken in this sense: *I was a fool boasting*, or *by boasting*.

15 *I have done nothing less*] In what way that ought to be translated, we showed above: *I was in no way inferior*. Ambrose reads: *for I have done nothing less*.

16 *Above the measure of an Apostle*] *ton hyper lian Apostolon*, that is, *the most excellent Apostles*. Ambrose reads: *than those very great Apostles*. For he doubled the adverb for emphasis <note>term: "epitasis"</note>, so that the speech might be more vehement. Since in this place *hyper* is an adverb, not a preposition, declaring excellence; and he did not say this out of a bitter stomach—not because they were such, but because they wished to be held as such—lest he should seem to have felt this about Peter and James.

17 *Even if I am nothing*] *ei kai ouden eimi*. This particle must be referred to the preceding, to mitigate what might have seemed too arrogant: "I am in no way inferior to the highest Apostles." For the closest speech has *eis*, which prohibits reading it as Ambrose did, who added "nevertheless" in one place. For he reads in this manner: *for I have done nothing less than those very great Apostles. And having inserted a commentary he adds, as if the beginning of another speech: And if I am nothing, nevertheless the signs of an Apostle, etc.*

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER XIII. <note>The header indicates the transition toward the final chapter of 2 Corinthians.</note>

<margin>12</margin> ...I am in no way inferior <note>original: ὑστέρησα (hysteresa)</note>, even though I am nothing. <margin>A</margin> Indeed, the signs of an Apostle were performed among you with all patience, with signs, wonders, and mighty deeds. <margin>13</margin> For what is there in which you were treated as inferior to the rest of the Churches, except that I myself was not a burden to you? Forgive me this wrong. <margin>14</margin> Behold, for the third time I am ready to come to you, and I will not be a burden to you; for I do not seek what is yours, but you. For children ought not to save up for their parents, but parents for their children. <margin>15</margin> But I will most gladly spend and be utterly spent for your souls; even if, the more abundantly I love you, the less I am loved. <margin>16</margin> But be that as it may, I did not weigh you down; yet, being crafty, I caught you with guile. <margin>17</margin> Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? <margin>B</margin> <margin>18</margin> I urged Titus to go, and I sent the brother with him. Did Titus take any advantage of you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did we not walk in the same footsteps? <margin>19</margin> Again, do you think that we are making an excuse to you? We speak in the sight of God in Christ; but all things, beloved, are for your edification. <margin>20</margin> For I fear that perhaps, when I come, I may not find you such as I wish, and that I may be found by you such as you do not wish; lest perhaps there be strife, jealousy, anger, selfish ambitions, slanders, whisperings, conceits, and disorders. <margin>21</margin> Lest, when I come again, my God may humble me before you, and I should mourn many of those who have sinned before and have not repented of the impurity, fornication, and lewdness which they have practiced.

<margin>XIII. 1</margin> This is the third time I am coming to you. <margin>C</margin> By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall be established. <margin>2</margin> I have said before, and I say it in advance—as I did when present the second time, so now being absent I write to those who sinned before and to all the rest—that if I come again, I will not spare them. <margin>3</margin> Since you seek a proof of Christ speaking in me, who is not weak toward you, but is powerful in you. <margin>4</margin> For even if he was crucified out of weakness, yet he lives by the power of God; for we also are weak in him, but we shall live with him by the power of God toward you.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> although I am nothing. <margin>12</margin> The signs indeed of the Apostle were performed among you in all patience, and in signs and wonders and mighty deeds. <margin>13</margin> For what is it in which you were inferior to the other Churches, except that I myself was not burdensome to you? <margin>13</margin> Forgive me this injustice. <margin>14</margin> Behold, I am inclined in my heart for a third time to come to you, and I will not be burdensome to you: for I do not seek the things that are yours, but you: for children ought not to store up for their parents, but parents for their children. <margin>15</margin> But I most willingly will spend, and be spent for your souls: although loving you more, I am loved less. <margin>16</margin> But so be it, I did not burden you: but, since I was crafty, I caught you with guile. <margin>B</margin> <margin>17</margin> Did I fleece you through any of those whom I sent to you? <margin>18</margin> I requested Titus, and together with him I sent a brother. <margin>18</margin> Did Titus extort anything from you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? In the same footsteps? <margin>19</margin> Do you think again that we are excusing ourselves to you? In the sight of God in Christ we speak: all things, most dearly beloved, are for your building up. <margin>20</margin> For I fear lest it might happen that, if I come, I shall not find you such as I would wish, and I shall be found by you such as you would not wish: lest in any way there be contentions, envies, angers, brawls, detractions, whisperings, puffings-up, seditions. <margin>21</margin> Lest again when I come, my God should humble me among you, and I should mourn many of those who sinned before, and did not repent of the uncleanness and lust and lewdness which they committed.

<margin>XIII. 1</margin> <margin>C</margin> This will be my third arrival to you. In the mouth of two witnesses or three shall every word be established. <margin>2</margin> I have said before and I say it now, as when I was present a second time, so also being absent I now write to those who sinned before, and to all the rest: that if I come again, I will not spare. <margin>3</margin> Since you seek a test of Christ speaking in me, who is not weak toward you, but is powerful in you. <margin>4</margin> For although he was crucified out of weakness, yet he lives by the power of God: for indeed we are weak in him, but we shall live with him by the power of God toward you.

---

<margin>12 Signs of Apostleship]</margin> In <term>Greek</term> <foreign xml:lang="grc">σημεῖα τοῦ Ἀποστόλου</foreign>, <gloss>note that it is "Signs of the Apostle," not "of apostleship."</gloss> Nor is the <term>Greek</term> conjunction <foreign xml:lang="grc">μὲν</foreign> (men) entirely pointless, for it softens the tone, as if one were saying *at least* or *certainly*.
<margin>13 Were done over you]</margin> <foreign xml:lang="grc">ἐν ὑμῖν</foreign>, <gloss>that is, "among you,"</gloss> as <term>Ambrose</term> <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Milan and influential theologian.</note> reads, or rather <term>among you</term>, <gloss>as used here, meaning "before your eyes." The Latin translator seems to have read it as "over you" (eph' hymon).</gloss>
<margin>And with powers]</margin> <foreign xml:lang="grc">δυνάμεσι</foreign>. <gloss>So that you may understand the power of miracles.</gloss>
<margin>You had less than the other Churches]</margin> <foreign xml:lang="grc">ὃ ἡττήθητε ὑπὲρ τὰς λοιπὰς Ἐκκλησίας</foreign>, <gloss>that is, in which you were inferior to the other Churches.</gloss>
<margin>Grant me this injury]</margin> <foreign xml:lang="grc">Χαρίσασθέ μοι τὴν ἀδικίαν ταύτην</foreign>, <gloss>which I would have preferred to translate as "Forgive," or, to better express the Greek word, "Grant me a favor regarding this wrong." Indeed, this figure of speech is frequent in Suetonius and Sallust. Saint Augustine reminds us in the first book of *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets* that this was not said simply by Paul, but rather as an irony of one reproaching them, similar to that phrase in Genesis: "Behold, Adam has become like one of us." For why would he ask to be forgiven for a service that was beneficial?</gloss>
<margin>14 Behold this third]</margin> <gloss>The word "this" is not in the Greek.</gloss> <foreign xml:lang="grc">Ἰδοὺ τρίτον ἑτοίμως ἔχω ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς</foreign>, <gloss>that is, "Behold, I am ready to come to you for the third time." The translator and Ambrose seem to have read "this third" (triton touto), that is, "this third time," as it appears a little later.</gloss>
<margin>I myself shall be spent over you]</margin> <foreign xml:lang="grc">Ἐγὼ δὲ ἥδιστα δαπανήσω καὶ ἐκδαπανηθήσομαι</foreign>. <gloss>Even if Ambrose reads it this way, from which it can be inferred that the manuscripts varied.</gloss>
<margin>16 But so be it, I did not burden you]</margin> In <term>Greek</term> it is <foreign xml:lang="grc">ἐγὼ οὐ κατεβάρησα ὑμᾶς</foreign>, <gloss>with our more corrected manuscripts supporting this, and also Ambrose, who reads "But so be it, I did not burden you." It would be clearer if the translator had used "himself" (ipse) so that Paul's person could be distinguished from the false apostles.</gloss>
<margin>17 Was it through any of them]</margin> In <term>Greek</term> it is <foreign xml:lang="grc">Μή τινα ὧν ἀπέσταλκα πρὸς ὑμᾶς, δι' αὐτοῦ ἐπλεονέκτησα ὑμᾶς</foreign>, <gloss>that is, "Was there anyone whom I sent to you through whom I circumvented you, or defrauded you?" But in this place the grammatical order is a bit lacking; for since "anyone" (metina) came first, it seems he was about to add something else, which he changed indirectly, especially since the case does not match. Otherwise, it might seem from the Hebrew idiom that he repeated "through him" after "through anyone." The unlearned reader should also be warned that the relative article does not agree with its verb "I sent," but with the preceding noun "anyone."</gloss>
<margin>Did Titus circumvent you]</margin> <foreign xml:lang="grc">ἐπλεονέκτησεν</foreign>. <gloss>Which Paul sometimes uses transitively to mean "to extort through greed," or "to occupy more than is proper." Ambrose does not read this poorly as "Was Titus greedy toward you?" We have translated it as "Did he extort from you?"</gloss>
<margin>19 Formerly you think]</margin> <gloss>It is not "formerly" (olim), but "again" (palin), that is, "again" or "once more." The translator perhaps read, or surely dreamed, "palai," which means "formerly." Ambrose reads "again," that is, "palin," because it seems Paul had been seen to be commending himself before.</gloss>
<margin>20 For all things]</margin> <gloss>But all things: <foreign xml:lang="grc">& ἀγαπητοὶ</foreign>, that is, "beloved."</gloss>
<margin>21 And I be found by you]</margin> <gloss>The word "by" (a) is superfluous according to the Greek manuscripts. For it was enough to say "found to you."</gloss>

<column-break/>

<margin>21 Animosities]</margin> <foreign xml:lang="grc">θυμοὶ</foreign> (thymoi), <gloss>that is, "angers," even if *thymos* sounds like the impulse of a boiling mind. For to the Greeks, *thymos* is that part of the soul which Plato places in the heart and which obeys reason, to which he assigns a seat in the brain. Elsewhere the translator renders it as "fury," as in "Lord, not in your fury" (in thymo sou). "Let there be among you." These words, since they are not found in the Greek manuscripts I have read, I suspect were added to make the speech clearer. Furthermore, in Greek it is not simply "lest" (me), but "lest somehow" (mepos), which could be rendered as "lest in any way." For the connective word diminishes the verb in such a way that it increases the meaning. Paul wants there to be no discord whatsoever among them. "Dissensions" (eritheiai), that is, contentions or struggles.</gloss>
<margin>22 And they did not do penance]</margin> <foreign xml:lang="grc">μὴ μετανοησάντων</foreign>, <gloss>that is, they did not repent, or those who did not regret. Although elsewhere we have warned that "to do penance" (agere poenitentiam) is the same to the Latins as "to repent," just as "to lead a life" is the same as "to live": but it is harsher unless you add the grammatical case indicating what it is we repent of.</gloss>
<margin>XIII. 1</margin> <margin>C</margin> <margin>Behold the third]</margin> <foreign xml:lang="grc">Τρίτον τοῦτο ἔρχομαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς</foreign>, <gloss>that is, "On this third occasion I come to you." For "third" (triton) is an adverb here, not a noun. Nor is "behold" added in this place, either among the Greeks or in Ambrose. But it was carried over here from the earlier passage, just as the pronoun "this" was moved there from this place.</gloss>
<margin>2 That in the mouth of two]</margin> <gloss>The "that" (ut) is redundant; it is simply "in the mouth of two or three every word shall stand." It is read this way also in Ambrose.</gloss>
<margin>3 For I said before and I say in advance]</margin> <gloss>The "for" (enim) is redundant, though it is added in Ambrose's commentaries. However, it is not clear in the commentaries what he actually read.</gloss>
<margin>4 As present to you]</margin> <term>Greek</term> <gloss>reads thus:</gloss> <foreign xml:lang="grc">ὡς παρὼν τὸ δεύτερον, καὶ ἀπὼν νῦν γράφω</foreign>, <gloss>that is, "as being present a second time, and now being absent I write," so that you may understand that he foretold it when he was present the second time, which he now foretells a third time while writing in his absence. Ambrose translates "the second time" (to deuteron) as "in his second arrival," so that it refers to the participle "being present" and not to the following "and being absent now I write," so that we understand he was in Corinth twice. And Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator.</note> also explains it in this sense.</gloss>
<margin>5 Do you seek an experiment]</margin> <gloss>It is not "Whether" (An), but "Since/Because" (Epei). And he would have translated more correctly as "of Christ speaking in me," that is, whether Christ speaks in me. In Ambrose it is read as "How" (Quomodo), from which he seems to have read "Pos": "How do you seek a proof," etc. But I think it was written "Since" (Quoniam) or "When" (Quando): for it hangs on the preceding words, "I will not spare," since you seek a test of whether Christ also speaks in me, just as in the other Apostles—that is, whether my commands have proceeded from a human spirit or from God's. Now, why was it necessary for the Translator to add "of him, of him who speaks in me, Christ"? First, this is not in the Greek, and second, it was added to the sentence with a grammatical error (solecism). Lorenzo Valla <note>A famous 15th-century humanist and critic of the Vulgate.</note> prefers "document" or "specimen" for the Greek "dokime" (proof). Where "experiment" is used here, Ambrose reads "probation."</gloss>
<margin>6 Who is not weakened in you]</margin> <foreign xml:lang="grc">ὃς εἰς ὑμᾶς</foreign>, <gloss>this is, "toward you." and likewise a little later.</gloss>

*7 In the power of God toward you* ] <note>original: εἰς ὑμᾶς (eis hymas)</note>, that is, *toward you*. And so Ambrose <note>Ambrose of Milan, a 4th-century bishop and theologian</note> reads it.

*8 Unless perhaps you are reprobates* ] <note>original: εἰ μή τι (ei me ti)</note>, that is, *unless in some respect*. Ambrose omits *perhaps* <note>original: forte</note>, for that word is sometimes added more for the sake of elegance than for necessity.

*9 Which you know* ] <note>original: ὅτι γνώσεσθε (hoti gnosesthe)</note>, that is, *you shall know*. Ambrose reads, *But I hope you will know*.

*10 But we pray to God* ] <note>original: Εὔχομαι δὲ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν (Euchomai de pros ton Theon)</note>, that is, *I pray indeed before God*, in the singular number. And soon after, this "we pray," <note>original: τοῦτο δὲ καὶ εὐχόμεθα (touto de kai euchometha)</note>, that is, *this also we even pray for*, so far are we from being grieved. Ambrose reads *into your consummation*, though I know not if the text is corrupted. For among the Greeks, *into* is not added. Both the Constance manuscripts <note>Manuscripts Erasmus consulted in the city of Constance</note> agreed with the Greeks. For this is the very thing he prays for, namely, their perfection.

*11 For we rejoice because we are weak, but you are powerful* ] It is clear here that *when* <note>original: quando</note> has been changed into *because* <note>original: quoniam</note>, seeing as. Ambrose reads, *when we are weakened, but you are strong*. The Constance manuscript had *when* <note>original: ὅταν (hotan)</note> in both places, not *because*. And the Greek reads thus, *when we are weak, and you are strong*, <note>original: ὅταν ἡμεῖς ἀσθενῶμεν, ὑμεῖς δὲ δυνατοὶ ἦτε</note>, when we shall have been weak, but you shall have been strong. For he does not affirm it to be so, but says he rejoices if it were so. And here the Apostle omitted the other conjunction *indeed* <note>original: μὲν (men)</note>, which Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note> elsewhere attributes to a lack of skill in the Greek language. Again, *we pray* could be translated as *we boast that you are such*. He calls himself weak because he has no power against the innocent; and they are powerful who do not sin. For they have nothing to fear from the Apostle.

*12 I shall act more harshly* ] <note>original: ἀποτόμως (apotomos)</note>, that is, *precisely or exactly*, what the Latins call *to the quick*, as we advised above. The Greek

speech sounds word-for-word as *lest I use rigidly*, that is, *lest I behave severely*.

*13 For the rest* ] <note>original: Λοιπὸν (Loipon)</note>, that is, *As for what remains*. And *farewell* <note>original: χαίρετε (chairete)</note>, which also means *rejoice*, was rather to be translated in this manner here.

*14 Be perfect* ] <note>original: καταρτίζεσθε (katartizesthe)</note>. This word is appropriate whenever we mend and refit a torn thing. He notes the disagreements of the Corinthians with this word.

*15 Be exhorted* ] <note>original: παρακαλεῖσθε (parakaleisthe)</note>. More correctly in this place, *be comforted*, provided you take it in the passive sense.

*16 think the same thing* ] <note>original: τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖτε (to auto phroneite)</note>, that is, *feel the same way*. Ambrose reads *savor the same thing*. It was clearer to say, *be harmonious or unanimous*. For this is what Paul means. For he is not discussing opinions, but the affection of their minds.

*17 Have peace* ] <note>original: εἰρηνεύετε (eireneuete)</note>, that is, *live in peace*. <margin>D</margin> Ambrose correctly reads, *act in peace*. Just as a truly Apostolic man begins with peace, so he ends in peace. For he explains what he had said: *feel the same thing, be harmonious, and be joined together in peace*; he says this because of the contentious people.

*18 In a kiss* ] "In" is added according to the property of the Hebrew language.

*19 The grace of the Lord* ] In his custom, he calls God "Father," and the Son "Lord." And he attributes "communion" to the Spirit, while he attributed "grace" to the Son and "love" to the Father. The redemption of the human race took its beginning from the Father, who so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son unto death; through the Son came grace, who redeemed us when we deserved nothing by his death; the distribution of gifts was made through the Holy Spirit. From this passage, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching</note> refutes those who denied that the Holy Spirit is of the same nature as the Father and the Son, because Paul, in the introductions of his Epistles, always joins the Father and the Son, omitting mention of the Spirit <note>Erasmus suggests this final benediction proves the Trinity by including the Spirit</note>.

<meta>Continuity note: This page marks the transition from the Second Epistle to the Corinthians to the Epistle to the Galatians. The previous page ended with the closing of 2 Corinthians and a catchword "E P I-" indicating the start of the next section, the Epistles.</meta>

# SUMMARY
->of the<-
## EPISTLE TO THE
### GALATIANS BY PAUL.

He sends this letter from Rome <note>original: Ῥώμης (Rhōmēs)</note>, having already seen them and taught them. This is the occasion for the letter: The Galatians had been well-taught by the Apostle and had sincerely believed in Christ, but after the Apostle's departure, they were misled by certain people into being circumcised. Therefore, upon learning of this, the Apostle writes to them. First, he bears witness to the faith they held and their sincere devotion to Christ. He rebukes them, however, for acting foolishly and for changing their minds. Then he discusses the law and the faith associated with Abraham, demonstrating from the law and from Abraham's wives—treating them as an allegory—that the "shadow" <note>the ceremonial law</note> and circumcision were given only for a time, and are now obsolete through the presence of Christ. Having proven this, he further instructs them no longer to pay attention to those who deceived them, but rather to hold fast to the faith in Christ, and to know that the grace in Christ nullifies circumcision according to the flesh. And thus, having once more exhorted and taught them concerning moral conduct, he completes the letter.

---

## PREFACE TO THE EPISTLE TO THE
## G A L A T I A N S
->Argument by<-
### DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'G' with elaborate scrolling foliage and floral motifs inside a square border.</image-desc>
**G**alatians are Greeks, but descended from the Gauls: hence, according to Saint Jerome, they reflected the nature of their origin with great sluggishness; for indeed even Hilary, himself a Gaul, in a verse of his Hymns, calls the Gauls "unteachable." And Paul, rebuking them, calls them <term>ἀνοήτους</term> <note>original: anoētous; meaning "senseless" or "foolish"</note>. Tempering his speech to their nature, he chastises them more sharply than any others in his remaining Epistles, and rebukes them more than he teaches them, so that he might use authority to recall those whom reason could not persuade. He argues in this Epistle what he argues everywhere: he invites them from the slavery of the Mosaic Law to the grace of the Gospel. He does the same in the Epistle to the Romans, for the same error had befallen both groups, though for different reasons. The Romans were first led into Judaism and later came to their senses; the Galatians, rightly instructed by the Apostle, were dragged back into Judaism by the work of false apostles. That the Romans were wrongly instructed was due to simplicity; that they came to their senses once warned was due to prudence. On the contrary, that the Galatians embraced Christ was due to ease of mind; that they immediately relapsed into Judaism was due to fickleness and folly. False apostles had come to these people, pretending to be sent by Peter and James, the chief Apostles; they undermined Paul's authority with slanders, denying that faith should be placed in one who was inconsistent—now using the ceremonies of the Law, undertaking vows, shaving his head, and circumcising Timothy, and now neglecting and condemning the Law when among the Gentiles. They argued that those who had lived with Peter and James and who had seen the Lord Jesus should be heard instead, since Paul had neither seen Christ and was merely a disciple of disciples, not of Christ. Consequently, Paul, in a vehement and sharp speech—for no Epistle is more stirred with emotion—and with a healthy austerity and merciful severity, simultaneously heals the error of the Galatians, asserts his own authority, and exposes the fraudulence of the false apostles. At the very threshold of the Epistle, he testifies that he is equal to, or even superior to, the highest Apostles in this: that he had received the authority for preaching the Gospel from the immortal Christ from heaven. Relying on this Author, he had preached Christ for some time in Arabia and Damascus before he had conferred with any of the Apostles. Later, in Jerusalem, he did indeed see Peter and James for a few days, yet he was not helped by them in any way. Following this, he acted as a herald of Christ in Syria and Cilicia for fourteen years, until, being divinely warned, he returned to Jerusalem together with Barnaba and Titus, and compared his Gospel with the primary Apostles. He did this not because he had come to doubt his many years of preaching, but so that by the approval of those whose authority was greatest among all, others might be more fully confirmed. Yet he conferred with Peter in such a way that he received nothing from him regarding the matter of the Gospel. And he was so far from being compelled by Peter to impose the burden of the Law on the Gentiles, that at Antioch, he openly rebuked Peter to his face when Peter, who had been eating common foods, withdrew himself from the banquet for fear of the arriving Jews. Paul taught that Gospel salvation comes from faith, not from the observation of the Law which was now outdated. Having begun to say this to Peter, as it were, he proceeds more broadly toward the Galatians, demonstrating that the Mosaic Law was given only for a time, and that all those things looked toward Christ alone. In the Law was the flesh, in the Gospel the spirit; in the Law shadows, in the Gospel light; in the Law images, in the Gospel truth; in the Law slavery, in the Gospel freedom. It is indeed a sign of madness, having tasted the better things, to fall back voluntarily into the worse. He deals with these matters in chapters one, two, three, and four. Then, having gravely threatened them lest, by accepting circumcision, they should basely surrender themselves to the slavery of the Law, he shows that Christian liberty is not a license for sinning, but the voluntary performance of the duties of piety, which are performed at the dictate of charity, not at the command of the law. Finally, he exhorts them to Christian harmony, to the lifting up of the weak or those who have fallen, and to doing good for those who taught us the faith. Eternal rewards are owed to deeds of this kind, since they are of the spirit, whereas temporary glory belongs to temporary ceremonies. In passing, he brings the false apostles into hatred, who were eager for the Galatians to be circumcised for no other reason than to glory in this as the authors of the deed. Those who today devise new forms of worship and extraordinarily distinguished rituals are related to this disease, so that it may be said, "That man founded this class of people." As it appears, Paul wrote this entire Epistle with his own hand to testify to his singular affection toward the Galatians, whereas in others he is usually accustomed only to sign his name. Our arguments testify that it was written from the city of Ephesus; the inscriptions of the Greeks say it was from the city of Rome.

->THE EPISTLE OF PAUL<-
->THE APOSTLE TO THE<-
# GALATIANS.

<margin>1:1</margin> PAUL, an Apostle—not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the <margin>2</margin> Father, who raised him from the dead—and all the brothers who are with me, to the churches of Galatia: <margin>3</margin> Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord <margin>4</margin> Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins, so that he might rescue us from the present wicked age, according to the will of our God and <margin>5</margin> Father, to whom be glory forever and ever. <margin>6</margin> Amen. I marvel that you are so quickly turning away from the one who called you in the grace of Christ, to another <margin>7</margin> Gospel, <margin>Otherwise: to God <note>original: "Alias Θεῷ"</note></margin> which is not really another, except that there are some who are troubling you and wanting to subvert the Gospel of <margin>8</margin> Christ. But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach a gospel to you other than what we preached to <margin>9</margin> you, let him be accursed <note>original: "anathema"</note>. As we have said before, and now I say again, if anyone preaches a gospel to you other than what you received, <margin>10</margin> let him be accursed. For am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God?

---

<margin>C</margin> <margin>1</margin> **PAUL the Apostle**] Jerome indicates that "Apostle" is a term specific to the Hebrews, called by them *Silae* <note>Erasmus likely refers to the Hebrew 'Shaliah,' meaning 'one who is sent'</note>, which in Latin means "sent" or "delegate." And as if he had said "sent," he adds, *not from men*: "not from men" as if they were the authors, *nor through men* as if they were recommending or approving him.

<margin>2</margin> **From God our Father**] The word *our* should be referred to "Lord," not to "Father," or rather <term>perhaps</term> <note>original Greek: ἴσως (isōs)</note> it signifies both. However, there are some who read it this way, and likewise two agreeing Greek manuscripts.

<margin>3</margin> **From the present age**] *in <term>the present</term>* <note>original Greek: τῷ ἐνεστῶτι (tō enestōti)</note>, that is, *out of the immediate*. Although the Greeks sometimes call this "the present." What is translated here as *wicked*, Ambrose and Augustine read as *malignant*, and Jerome as *evil*; in Greek it is <term>wicked</term> <note>original Greek: πονηροῦ (ponērou)</note>, which signifies both "shrewd" and "miserable" or "full of labor." He calls this age "evil" in comparison to the age to come. Augustine, instead of *rescue*, reads *exempt* in his commentaries on this Epistle.

<margin>4</margin> **To whom is glory**] The word "is" is not in the Greek, but only, *to whom glory*: so that it expresses a wish.

<margin>5</margin> **That so very quickly**] <term>so quickly</term> <note>original Greek: οὕτως ταχέως (houtōs tacheōs)</note>. It is not *so very*, but *so quickly*, or *thus quickly*: for <term>so</term> <note>original Greek: οὕτως (houtōs)</note> signifies both. It is strange that this reading—which is otherwise deviant and discordant from the Greek copies—has become so established that it is found in Ambrose, Augustine, and Tertullian. However, from the commentaries of Saint Jerome, one can sense that the adverb *so* was not added by him. Truly, since in some manuscripts there was *very* and in others *so*, which some studious person had noted in the margin, an inattentive scribe brought it into the main text.

<margin>6</margin> **You are transferred from him**] <term>you are being changed/transferred</term> <note>original Greek: μετατίθεσθε (metatithesthe)</note>. If you render this word for word, it sounds like "you are being transposed": the Translator changed it correctly. It is likely, as Jerome suggested, that Paul alluded to the Hebrew word *Galata*, which to them means "translated" or "led away," an analogy taken from wheels or round objects that are easily rolled from one place to another.

<margin>7</margin> **Into the grace of Christ**] <term>in grace</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν χάριτι (en chariti)</note>, that is, *in grace*. Augustine, explaining this passage, reads *into glory* instead of *into grace*, as evidenced by his own exposition. Certainly, it is clear that Jerome read *in grace* using the ablative case, which is easily shown from his own words. For he writes thus in his Commentaries: *The passage itself contains a transposition of words (hyperbaton), which can be read in its own order as follows: I marvel that you are so quickly transferred from Christ Jesus, who called you in grace, saying, I have not come to call the righteous, and so forth.* However, here again another problem of ambiguity arises: *who called you through grace into another Gospel*. For it can be understood that Christ called them into another Gospel, as Ambrose arranges it. Therefore, we have changed the order and translated it thus: *I marvel that you are so quickly being transferred from Christ, who called you in grace or through grace, into another Gospel*. Furthermore, in what follows immediately: *But even if we, or an Angel from heaven, preach a gospel to you, other than what we have preached to you*. Jerome indicates that this speech can be taken as hyperbole—not that an Angel or Paul was going to preach another Gospel, but that one must by no means withdraw from the Gospel once received. But if someone rejects tropes and figures of speech in the Sacred Scriptures, he will often either remain perplexed or be forced to explain himself with very weak reasoning. Further, regarding what he adds, *this will be*, so that the authority of Peter and John would not be considered greater, since it was not permitted for them to preach another Gospel either, I think it should be understood this way: if Peter or John were to mix Judaism with Christ (which the false apostles were attempting to do using their names as authority), Paul might otherwise seem to be placing his own authority above Peter's. And "of Christ" can either refer to *grace* or to the preposition *from*, so that for us it is the ablative case *from Christ*, or rather *from God*. I would prefer the ablative. And some manuscripts have *God* instead of *Christ*. For Paul always makes God the one who calls, but through Christ. And in the Gospel, it is the Father who draws his people to Christ.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>1</margin> **PAUL** an Apostle, not from men, nor
through man, but through Jesus Christ and God
the Father, who raised him from the dead, and all <margin>2</margin>
the brothers who are with me, to the churches of
Galatia: Grace to you and peace from God the <margin>3</margin>
Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave
himself for our sins, so that he might rescue <margin>4</margin>
us from the present evil age, according to the
will of our God and Father, to whom be glory <margin>5</margin>
forever and ever. Amen. I marvel that you are <margin>6</margin>
so quickly being transferred from Christ, who
called you through grace, into another Gospel,
which is not another, except that there are some <margin>7</margin>
who trouble you, and want to subvert the Gospel
of Christ. But even if we, or an Angel from heaven, <margin>8</margin>
should preach a Gospel to you other than what
we preached to you, let him be accursed. Just as <margin>9</margin>
we said before, and now I say again, if anyone
preaches a Gospel to you other than what you
received, let him be accursed. <margin>10</margin> <margin>B</margin> For am I now
persuading men, or God?

---

->Furthermore, he said "in grace" for that which is "through grace."<-

<margin>D</margin> <margin>8</margin> **Into another Gospel, which is not another**] I see that the ancients followed different readings, one after another. Jerome, as is clear from his own explanation, reads it thus: *That you are so quickly transferred into another Gospel, which is not*, so that "another" is understood. Or if you prefer that the noun "another" was added by him: here he adds a point of clarification, so the sense is that he wonders at the inconstancy of those who are transferred; then, that they are transferred so quickly; finally, that they go into "another Gospel" which is so far from being better than the one they received that it is actually nothing at all. The Apostle wonders at the cause of this. But lest he seem to condemn the Gallic character <note>Erasmus links the Galatians to the Gauls of France</note>, he casts the blame for the act upon the "Apostles" (those Judaizers you know well), saying, "unless there are," and so forth. For so Jerome reads. Chrysostom and Theophylact agree in sense with Jerome, except that he adds *another*, and that which follows, *unless that*, he separates from the preceding words. Ambrose reads in this manner: *From him, who called you into the grace of Christ, into another Gospel: nor did he add, "which is not another."* Nor can it be gathered from his explanation that he read it otherwise. He, referring this phrase *into another Gospel* not to the verb *you are transferred*, but to *he called*, arranges the speech in this way: *I marvel that you are so quickly transferred from him who called you into another Gospel, that is, into another and different one from that which the false apostles preach to you, recalling you to Judaism.* What we say will be clear if one unrolls the Commentaries of Ambrose. Furthermore, as for the suspicion that Jerome read *which is not* without adding *another*, the reason is what he adds: *because everything that is false does not subsist, and what is contrary to the truth is not*. Like that phrase: *Do not hand over, O Lord, your scepter to those who are not*. And, *God called those things which were not.* And soon after in the same place: *If this is said of those who believed in the same God and had the same Scriptures, that they were transferred into another Gospel, which is not a Gospel, what of Marcion and the other heretics, and so forth.* But Ambrose separates *unless there are some*, and so forth, from the preceding words by an inserted commentary, so that *unless there are* does not refer to *which is not another*, but to *they wonder*. Tertullian, in the fourth book against Marcion, if the manuscripts are free of error, seems to add *another*, but in such a way that the sense is the same as we have said.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>9</margin> **And they want to convert the Gospel**] Indeed, I would prefer *to subvert* <note>original: "invertere"</note>, even though Ambrose, Augustine, and likewise Jerome consistently read it this way <note>as "convert"</note>. However, the Greek word is <term>to distort/subvert</term> <note>original: μεταστρέψαι (metastrepsai)</note>, which means to twist toward something else, or to twist in a different direction. For us, the word "subvert" or "invert" is more appealing, and Jerome’s own interpretation supports this; I will transcribe his very words: *Everyone who interprets the Gospel with a different spirit and mind than it was written, troubles the believers and "converts" the Gospel of Christ, so that what is in the front, he puts behind the back, and those things which are behind the back, he turns to the front. If anyone acquiesces to the interpretations of the Jews, he casts behind his back those things which by their nature are placed in the front.* Thus far Jerome. But "to subvert" properly describes turning something in a different and backward way. Christ delivered a doctrine of such a kind that there should be as much piety as possible and as few ceremonies as possible. Those men, on the contrary, wanted there to be the most ceremonies and the least piety.

<margin>10</margin> **Other than that which**] <term>besides what</term> <note>original: παρ’ ὅ (par' ho)</note>, that is, "besides that which": and so it will be more fitting.

<margin>11</margin> **Let him be accursed**] Saint Jerome advises that *anathema* is a word specific to the Jews, by which they are accustomed to signify extreme detestation.

<margin>12</margin> **For do I now persuade men**] <term>For am I now persuading men, or God?</term> <note>original: Ἄρτι γὰρ ἀνθρώπους πείθω, ἢ τὸν Θεόν;</note> that is, "For do I now persuade men, or God?" This means: "Do I advocate for human things, or divine things?" And indeed Theophylact interprets it in this sense. Although "I persuade men" can be tolerated, since <term>persuade</term> <note>original: πείθω (peithō)</note> among the Greeks sometimes takes the accusative case in this sense, though not when it means "to trust," or...

or <note>catchword: aut</note>

<header>THE EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER I.</header>

<margin>A</margin> 10 God? Or do I seek to please men? For if I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ. 11 But I make known to you, brothers, that the Gospel which was preached by me is not according to man. 12 For I neither received it from man, nor was I taught it, but it came through a revelation of Jesus Christ. 13 For you have heard of my former way of life in Judaism, how I persecuted the Church of God beyond measure and tried to destroy it. 14 And I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries among my people, being far more a zealous advocate for the traditions of my fathers. <margin>B</margin> 15 But when it pleased God—who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me by His grace—16 to reveal His Son in me, so that I might preach Him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately consult with flesh and blood, 17 nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were Apostles before me; but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus. 18 Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and I stayed with him for fifteen days. 19 But I saw none of the other Apostles except James, the Lord’s brother. 20 Now regarding the things I am writing to you, behold, before God, I am not lying. 21 Afterward I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. 22 And I was unknown by face to the Churches of Judea which were in Christ. <margin>C</margin> 23 But they were only hearing it said: "He who...

---

...either to believe, or to behave in a certain way, as our colleague Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>original: "Faber Stapulensis," a French humanist and theologian</note> seems to think. Although I know that Jerome, Augustine, and Ambrose follow a different opinion. Furthermore, the word *now* <note>original: "modo"</note> is used for the present time, signifying that after he became an Apostle, he looked for nothing else than what pertains to the honor of God, whereas formerly in Judaism he felt differently.

<margin>13</margin> *If still* ] <note>original: "εἰ γὰρ ἔτι" (ei gar eti)</note>, that is, *for still*.

<margin>14</margin> *I received it, nor was I taught* ] <note>original: "παρέλαβον αὐτὸ, οὔτε ἐδιδάχθην" (parelabon auto, oute edidachthen)</note>. Jerome distinguishes between "receiving" and "learning." We "receive" what is not ours but handed down by another. We "learn" that whose mystery is opened to us. Even so, the Greek does not say "I learned," but "I was taught" <note>original: "doctus sum"</note>. This could be understood either absolutely—meaning "I was not taught, but inspired"—or simply that "I was not taught by a human." Next, Jerome denies that the word *revelation* <note>original: "ἀποκάλυψις" (apokalypsis)</note> is found anywhere among the pagan Greek writers; rather, he thinks this word, like many others, was a new term coined by the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> to more suitably explain the new mysteries of God.

<margin>15</margin> *And I was destroying it* ] <note>original: "καὶ ἐπόρθουν" (kai eporthoun)</note>. This word is specifically used for those who pillage and tear down cities captured by force of arms. I do not see why Lorenzo Valla <note>An Italian humanist who critiqued the Vulgate translation</note> gets upset here, as if it were an insult to the Church of God to say it was "destroyed" by Paul; he prefers the word "attacked" <note>Latin: "oppugnabam"</note> rather than "destroyed" <note>Latin: "expugnabam"</note>. I do not deny that in Latin "to take by storm" <note>expugnare</note> is one thing, and "to assault" <note>oppugnare</note> is another, just as "to persuade" is more than "to suggest." But what can you do when the Greek word *porthein* means nothing other than "to destroy" or "to overthrow"? Furthermore, he calls the "Church" that congregation of Christians which he was utterly destroying, as much as lay in his power. For this was Paul’s goal. Therefore, when he says "I was destroying," it refers not to the final outcome of the event, but to his intent and efforts. However, the reading found in the commentaries of Jerome and Augustine—"I was devastating" <note>Latin: "devastabam" or "vastabam"</note>—is more fitting, used in the manner of an enemy or a wild beast laying waste to everything. And a little further down: "He who once persecuted us, now preaches the faith which he once laid waste." Grammarians think the word is derived from the Greek for "fire" <note>original: "πύρ" (pyr)</note>, because a victorious enemy devastates with fire. Others prefer a derivation meaning "to run around," because that also happens in a captured city.

<margin>16</margin> *Contemporaries* ] I wish this word were more accepted among Latin speakers. In Greek he said <note>original: "συνηλικιώτας" (sunelikiotas)</note>, that is, "those of the same age." However, both terms are ambiguous. For people are called "of the same age" if they lived in the same century, and they are called "equals" if they are equal in wealth or learning. *In my nation* <note>original: "in genere meo"</note>. By "nation" <note>genus</note>, he refers to the Jewish people, just as in the next Epistle he speaks of "dangers from my own nation."

<margin>17</margin> *Zealot* ] <note>original: "ζηλωτής" (zelotes)</note>. He calls himself a "zealot" because of his immoderate and superstitious devotion and love. *Of my paternal traditions* <note>original: "πατρικῶν" (patrikon)</note>, things handed down from fathers and ancestors. He adds "my," not because he considered them strictly his own (as Thomas Aquinas interprets it), but to make his error seem more excusable, as he was a born Pharisee following the institutions of his ancestors—institutions he did not hesitate to leave once he was taught better things.

<margin>18</margin> *But when it pleased Him* ] <note>original: "Ὅτε δὲ εὐδόκησεν ὁ Θεὸς" (Hote de eudokesen ho Theos)</note>, that is, "But when it seemed good to God."

<margin>19</margin> *I did not yield* ] <note>original: "ἢ προσανεθέμην σαρκὶ καὶ αἵματι" (he prosanethemen sarki kai haimati)</note>, that is, "I did not consult with flesh and blood." For this is how Jerome translates the Greek in his commentaries, and the Greek scholars agree. The Translator <note>The author of the Vulgate</note> himself translates it this way a little later. It means: "I did not share my Gospel with any man, but I had commerce with God." Some readings have "I consulted beforehand." Thus, it is clear that Thomas Aquinas and Hugh of Saint-Cher <note>original: "Carrensem"</note> are off the mark when they interpret "flesh and blood" as carnal vices, for we never read that Paul was subject to such things; even if Thomas adds a second explanation, interpreting "flesh and blood" as affection toward relatives. But Paul did not mean that either. Rather, the Translator...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> 10 ...to God? Or do I seek to please men? For if I had hitherto pleased men, I would by no means be a servant of Christ. 11 But I make known to you, brothers, that the Gospel which was preached by me is not according to man. 12 For I neither received it from man, nor was I taught it, but it came through a revelation of Jesus Christ. 13 For you have heard of my former conversation in Judaism, how beyond measure I persecuted the Church of God, 14 and was laying it waste. And I advanced in Judaism beyond many equals in my nation, since I was a vehement student of the institutions handed down by my ancestors. <margin>B</margin> 15 But when it seemed good to God—who had set me apart from my mother's womb and called me by His grace for this purpose—16 to reveal His Son through me, so that I might preach Him among the nations, I did not immediately consult with flesh and blood, 17 nor did I return to Jerusalem to those who were Apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and turned back again to Damascus. 18 Then after three years I returned to Jerusalem to see Peter, and I stayed with him for fifteen days. 19 But I did not see any other of the Apostles, except James the brother of the Lord. 20 Furthermore, the things I am writing to you, behold, before God, I am not lying. 21 Afterward I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. 22 And I was unknown by face to the Churches of Judea which were in Christ. 23 But only this rumor was among them: "He who once persecuted...

---

<margin>D</margin> ...gave occasion for this error, for he translated <note>original: "προσανεθέμην" (prosanethemen)</note> as "I yielded," when it should have been translated as "I consulted" or "I communicated" with "flesh and blood." Although Saint Jerome labored greatly in this place, wishing to untie this knot—namely, that Paul might seem insulting by calling Peter, John, and James "flesh and blood," especially since the philosopher Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist critic of Christianity</note> uses this to claim Paul was arrogant because he did not deign to compare his Gospel with the other Apostles. In short, Jerome struggles with the idea that Paul, who previously did not consult with flesh and blood, later did consult them, as if he lacked confidence in his revelation after the fact. Trapped by these difficulties, Jerome takes the adverb "immediately" <note>original: "continuo"</note> and applies it to what follows—"I did not return to Jerusalem"—so that the sense is: Paul was so ready to preach that he did not waste time visiting the Apostles first, but immediately attacked the duty of preaching as he was commanded. The Greek commentaries also vary here. But to discuss these things further is not the purpose of this work. We note what seems to pertain to the method of reading. Therefore, it is no small task to reconcile Paul’s narrative here with the account in Luke's Acts of the Apostles, chapter nine, as Jerome explains quite diligently in his own commentaries.

<margin>20</margin> *I came to Jerusalem* ] <note>original: "ἀνῆλθον" (anelthon)</note>, that is, "I returned" or "I went up."

<margin>21</margin> *To the Apostles my predecessors* ] <note>original: "πρὸς τοὺς πρὸ ἐμοῦ Ἀποστόλους" (pros tous pro emou Apostolous)</note>, that is, to those who were Apostles before me, and who for this reason seemed greater to some, because they were called first.

<margin>22</margin> *To see Peter* ] <note>original: "ἱστορῆσαι" (historesai)</note>: This word in Greek signifies something more than just "to see"; namely, to see for the purpose of inquiring and learning, as Jerome notes.

<margin>23</margin> *James the brother* ] In his commentary on Galatians, Jerome notes the error of those who think this James was one of the twelve Apostles (the brother of John mentioned in the Gospel), since that James is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles as having shed his blood for the Lord shortly after Stephen's death. Instead, he affirms this is James surnamed "the Just," the son of Mary who was the sister of Mary the mother of Jesus. For these are also called "brothers" according to the Jewish custom. Theophylact <note>A Byzantine cathedral archdeacon and commentator</note> indicates he was called "brother of the Lord" as a title of honor. He was ordained the first Bishop of Jerusalem, and most judge the Epistle we read today under the name of James to be his. He is called an "Apostle" in the same way all others are called Apostles who preached Christ after seeing Him in the flesh.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>24</margin> *Because I do not lie* ] Here the word "that" <note>original: "ὅτι" (hoti)</note> could be omitted; it has the force of an assertion, but primarily among the Greeks—unless you prefer to add: "Behold, before God I testify that I do not lie." For it is added as if by one taking an oath, which Jerome does not deny. But his addition that <note>original: "ἀπομαγίζειν" (apomagizein)</note> means "things are before God," that is, "worthy of God’s sight," seems to me somewhat forced. However, the Ancients allow themselves some liberty in these matters, as they also do with the interpretation of names like Arabia, Cilicia, Damascus, and so on. Ambrose and Theophylact both agree this is the language of one making an assertion.

<margin>25</margin> *Of Cilicia* ] <note>original: "Κιλικίας" (Kilikias)</note>. For "parts," the word is <note>original: "κλίματα" (klimata)</note>, that is, regions or tracts of land.

<margin>26</margin> *Which were in Christ* ] Why not rather "which are in Christ" <note>original: "ταῖς ἐν Χριστῷ"</note>?

<margin>27</margin> *They had heard* ] <note>original: "ἀκούοντες ἦσαν" (akouontes esan)</note>, that is, "they had heard." Literally, "they were hearing," meaning "the rumor was among them." It would be very good Latin to say "it was heard by them" or "this rumor was among them," because the participle is in the present tense. It was not necessary to translate "that" <note>original: "ὅτι"</note> here either, as the pronoun "us" forbids it.

The commentary provides a detailed linguistic analysis of the Greek text, critiquing earlier medieval interpretations and addressing historical questions about the identity of "James the brother of the Lord."</summary>
