<header>TO THE GALATIANS CH. II.</header>

<margin>A</margin> That he who once persecuted us now preaches the faith which he once tried to destroy. And they glorified God in me. 
<margin>II. 1</margin> Then after fourteen years, I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me also. 
<margin>2</margin> I went up by revelation, and I laid out <note>original: "ἀνεθέμην"</note> before them the Gospel which I preach among the Gentiles—but privately to those of reputation <note>original: "τοῖς δοκοῦσι"</note>—lest by any means I might be running, or had run, in vain. 
<margin>3</margin> But not even Titus, who was with me, though he was a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised. 
<margin>B</margin> <margin>4</margin> And this was because of the false brothers secretly brought in, who sneaked in to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into bondage. 
<margin>5</margin> To them we did not yield in subjection even for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you. 
<margin>6</margin> But from those who seemed to be something <note>original: "τῶν δοκούντων"</note>—whatever they were, it makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality to man—for those of reputation added nothing to me.

---

<margin>28</margin> *Which he once tried to destroy* | <note>original: "ἐπόρθει"</note>. He used this word again, as he did above, just as we noted. 
<margin>29</margin> *They glorified God* | <note>original: "ἐδόξαζον"</note>, that is, they gave glory. Saint Jerome reads it this way; *Ambrose* uses "magnified." 
<margin>C</margin> <margin>I</margin> **A**fter years | <note>original: "διὰ δεκατεσσάρων ἐτῶν"</note>, that is, throughout fourteen years. However, the Translator has rendered the sense correctly. 
<margin>2</margin> *And I conferred with them* | <note>original: "ἀνεθέμην"</note>. Saint Jerome denies that this Greek word properly means "to confer," but rather to expose those things we know into the lap of a friend and to bring them into the open, so that by common counsel they may be either approved or disapproved. Hence, the word we had earlier, *prosanethemen* <note>original: "προσανεθέμην"</note>, means "I further conferred with someone," specifically after Christ's call. Or if you read it as "I conferred beforehand," it refers to when he went into Arabia. In this, Paul seems not to have mistrusted his calling, and in this matter, he did not seem to need the advice of others to teach Christ in Arabia. Furthermore, regarding Jerome’s warning about the property of the word *anethemen*, I believe it refers to this: in Greek, *anatithesthai* <note>original: "ἀνατίθεσθαι"</note> is said both of one who takes up a burden and one who imposes it on another. Truly, he who confers with others lays his pack in the middle, as if weighting down those whom he makes judges of his deeds, ready to accept it if they take anything away or add to the pack. From this, we also call those things that are set aside or hung up high "offerings" <note>original: "ἀναθήματα," anathema</note>. Euripides in *Iphigenia at Aulis* used *anathemen* for the same thing, as if to say "to bring in together." Thus Clytemnestra says to Agamemnon, "I submit to the oath" <note>original: "ἀνατίθεμαι δ’ ὅρκον"</note>. 
<margin>3</margin> *Who seemed to be something* | <note>original: "τοῖς δοκοῦσι"</note>, that is, those who were seen [as leaders], as Augustine reads it, or "the approved." Furthermore, the word "something" <note>original: "τι"</note> was added by someone who thought the phrase seemed incomplete. Therefore, those who read "who seemed to be something" read it incorrectly; but worse are those who read "who thought themselves to be something," among whom is Ambrose (provided the manuscripts are free of error). For it was insulting to say "who thought themselves to be something," as if they were of no value but only something in their own opinion, when the term refers more to the estimation of others. For in Greek, those "who seem" <note>original: "δοκοῦσι"</note> are spoken of absolutely as those who are of great authority, just as the "unregarded" <note>original: "ἀδοξοῦντες"</note> are those whose authority is slight. Thus Euripides in *Hecuba*: "For a speech coming from the unregarded and from those of reputation, though the same, does not have the same power." In Greek, in the first and third instances, the word "something" <note>original: "τι"</note> is not added; however, it is added in the middle instance. "From those who seemed to be something." I suspect this might have been added by someone who thought it should be understood, although the manuscripts agree surprisingly well. Since even Ambrose reads, "who were thought to be something." It seems probable to me, as Valla conjectures, that it is an addition. And from Jerome's interpretation, it is almost clear that he did not read "who seemed to be something," but only "who seemed," when he writes: "He was anxious to find out only what it was that they said, those who seemed; but now he has freed me from all doubt, adding: 'those who seemed to be pillars.'" And in the Paulist manuscript, in the first instance, it is only "those who seemed." Since Paul feels they were held in high regard—which he soon explains clearly by "those who seemed to be pillars"—how does "who seemed to be something" fit here? For we speak that way about things to which we wish to attribute almost nothing. However, although Jerome stands with me so far in not adding "something," he does not seem to have sufficiently weighed the force of the Greek participle *dokountes*. Therefore, we have translated it as "those who were in high standing." Yet, so as not to hide anything from the reader, since the "something" <note>original: "τι"</note> is added once here in the Greek, it is possible he placed "something" here in the same sense that Luke in Acts chapter five used "someone" for "someone great": "For before these days Theudas rose up, saying he was someone." Ambrose indicates in passing here something that should have been noted more in Acts. For where we read in the fifteenth chapter of that book a decree for the Gentiles to abstain from four things—from things sacrificed to idols, from fornication, from blood, and from things strangled—he warns that only three were prescribed by the Apostles, and the fourth was added by the Greeks. Indeed, he closes the discussion thus: "Which the Greek sophists, not understanding, but taking it that one must abstain from blood, corrupted the scripture, adding a fourth commandment, 'and from what is strangled'—which I think they now understand by God's will, because it was already said above what they added." And he interprets the abstinence from blood not as refraining from murder (which was also forbidden by the laws of the pagans), but from eating meat with blood, in the manner of Noah, according to the dogma of Pythagoras. However, those who interpreted the forbidden blood otherwise added the restriction on "strangled meat" from the ceremonies of the Jews.

<column-break/>

...once persecuted us, now preaches the faith, <margin>28</margin> which he once tried to destroy, <margin>29</margin> and they glorified God in me. Then <margin>II. 1</margin> after fourteen years, I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me also. I went up according to revelation, <margin>2</margin> and I conferred with them the Gospel which I preach among the Gentiles, but privately with those who were in high standing, lest by any means I might be running, or had run, in vain. But <margin>3</margin> not even Titus, who was with me, <margin>A</margin> though he was a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised, <margin>4</margin> because of the false brothers who sneaked in, who entered by the way to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, <margin>B</margin> to drive us into slavery. To whom not even for a time <margin>5</margin> did we yield by subjection, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you. From those however who <margin>6</margin> seemed to be something, whatever they once were, it makes no difference to me. God does not accept the person of man; for to me, those who seemed to be in high standing <margin>10</margin> conferred nothing.

---

regarding strangled meat. Furthermore, they fear in vain lest we eat a strangled beast, when we are commanded to abstain from eating all meat, according to the opinion of Ambrose. How much weight should be given to him, others may see; certainly Irenaeus refers several times to the passage from Acts, and does not add mention of strangled things, specifically in the third book against Heretics, <margin>C</margin> chapter twelve. 
<margin>4</margin> *Since he was a Gentile* | <note>original: "Ἕλλην ὤν"</note>, that is, though he was a Greek, which he uses however for "Heathen." 
<margin>5</margin> *But because of the introduced false brothers* | <note>original: "παρεισάκτους"</note>, as if you were to say, "those who entered by the way." For *para* <note>original: "παρὰ"</note> among the Greeks usually signifies something in a bad sense, and it is a noun, not a participle: such as *pareisaktos*, that is, Christians in name only, about which he added above, "sub-introduced brothers"; thus also shortly after, "who sneaked in" <note>original: "παρεισῆλθον"</note>, that is, who entered by the way while we were doing something else—the sort of thing spies and those plotting traps usually do. Now *false brothers*, <note>original: "ψευδαδέλφους"</note>, that is, Christians by a false name, as we warned above. Saint Jerome thinks the conjunction "but" or "and" is superfluous in this place and should be cast out; partly because if it is placed there, it has no part that responds to it (for in Greek *de* <note>original: "δὲ"</note> always responds to *men* <note>original: "μὲν"</note>), and partly because it strongly conflicts with the sense of this Epistle. For Saint Jerome understands that Paul could not be compelled by any force to circumcise Titus, since he was a Gentile, and that this pertained to the truth of the Gospel. And so what follows, *Because of the secretly brought in false brothers*, <margin>D</margin> coheres with the preceding: "he was not compelled to be circumcised because of the false brothers," and so on. Augustine interprets in this sense, although Ambrose reads it differently. 
<margin>6</margin> *We yielded in subjection* | The word is indeed a dative in Greek <note>original: "ὑποταγῇ"</note>, but it should be translated as an ablative, "by subjection": that is, so that we might be subjected to them. And in the Paulist manuscript, it had been written in the first hand as "by subjection," in the ablative case. Jerome indicates that in some Latin codices the word "to whom" <note>original: "οἷς"</note> is not present, which would lead you to understand that Titus yielded for a time; but in the Greek it is added, so that the sense is that he yielded in no way. But if it were read that he "yielded for a time," Jerome still does not think this refers to the circumcision of Titus, but only to the fact that he returned to Jerusalem to satisfy them. And yet what Jerome denies being in the Latin codices is now seen written in all Latin manuscripts, except in Ambrose, who also arranges the sentence differently than we do, namely in this manner: *But because of the secretly brought in false brothers, who <margin>E</margin> sneaked in to explore our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, to subject us to slavery, for a time we yielded to subjection.* And he declares he read it thus by the scope of his interpretation of the pronoun "to whom," which if added seems to make the speech incomplete, unless we arrange it this way: *Titus was not compelled to be circumcised because of the Apostles, to whom we yielded to some extent, but because of the secretly brought in brothers, to whom we did not yield even a little.* But how did he not yield, he who was forced to circumcise Timothy? Ambrose argues at length on this point. I do not see how the passage can be explained unless we admit that Paul’s speech is imperfect <note>term: anacoluthon: a sentence that changes grammatical structure mid-stream</note>, so that we understand it in this way: "The Apostles did not compel us, but because of the false brothers it seemed we might be compelled, because they insisted more hatefully; yet we did not yield to them for the time so far as to circumcise anyone from the Gentiles." 
<margin>7</margin> *With you* | <note>original: "πρὸς ὑμᾶς"</note>, that is, toward you. 
<margin>8</margin> *But from those who seemed* | Again Paul does not finish the sentence he began because he interjects certain things; then, having changed the form of the speech, he returns to what he had started. For it seemed <margin>F</margin> he was going to add, "From those who were held in high standing, I was aided in nothing." Then, as if he had interjected a parenthesis, "whatever they once were, it does not matter to me: God does not accept the person of man"—for that seems to have come to his mind in passing, from the fact that he had said, "those who now seem to be great"—he soon returns to what he began, but with a different sentence structure: "For to me, those who seemed to be something conferred nothing." 
<margin>9</margin> *But to me those who seemed to be something* | Again in this third instance "to be something" is not there, but only "those who seemed" <note>original: "οἱ δοκοῦντες"</note>: that is, those held in high regard, whom the common people call "reputed." 
<margin>10</margin> *Conferred nothing* | <note>original: "οὐδὲν προσανέθεντο"</note>, that is, they communicated nothing; the same word which he often translates as "acquiesced," as Saint Jerome also notes. Paul had conferred his Gospel with them; they, in turn, did not confer theirs, but only approved Paul's Gospel. Therefore, in this place, "conferred" does not mean the same as "added," as some think, but rather that. <note>meta: catchword: lud (beginning of "illud")</note>

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER II.
<page-num>808</page-num>

<margin>7</margin> But on the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the Gospel to the uncircumcised <note>the Gentiles</note>, just as Peter had been to the <margin>8</margin> circumcised <note>the Jews</note>. For he who worked effectively in Peter for the apostleship to the circumcised, worked effectively also in me toward <margin>9</margin> the Gentiles. And when they recognized the grace given to me, James and Cephas <note>Peter</note> and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the <margin>10</margin> circumcised. Only they asked that we should remember the poor; which very thing I was also eager to do. <margin>11</margin> But when Peter came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face...

<margin>A</margin> ...this follows from here. For what could they have added to Paul, who did not even share anything of their own concerning the Gospel? They could receive something from Paul, but they could add nothing. Saint Jerome thinks there is a *hyperbaton* <note>a transposition of words for effect</note> here, so that if we remove the many intervening phrases, we should read it this way: *For to me, those who seemed to be something contributed nothing, but on the contrary gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship.* However, following the sense above, we can read it such that Paul, without boasting, secretly indicated that nothing was contributed to him by them, but rather by him to them. This follows more truly from the facts, as we just said, than is signified by the words. For here is that same word *prosanethento* <note>original: "προσανέθεντο"</note>, which means to communicate concerning some matter for the sake of consulting. In this place, Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous 15th-century humanist scholar</note> was not attentive enough, as he thinks that "to contribute" is the same as "they added."

11 **When they had seen that it was entrusted** | <note>original: "ὅτι πεπίστευμαι τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον"</note>, that is, that the Gospel was entrusted or committed to me. For this is how the Greeks speak: "I was entrusted with this thing" and "I was committed with this thing." The word "that" <note>original: "ὅτι"</note> should either be omitted or translated as "because."

12 **For he who worked in Peter** | It was closer to the Greek reading to say "in Peter" and "in me" <note>original: "ἐνεργήσας Πέτρῳ, ἐνήργησε καὶ ἐμοί"</note>. Indeed, the preposition is within the compound verb. It does not simply mean "worked," but was "effective" and "showed his power." For Origen, in his *Epistle to the Romans*, thinks that "to manifest" and "to work effectively" have the same force—that is, the act and power that moves the instrument from within. For he feels that whatever was accomplished through Peter was perfected not by his own strength, but with God as the author. Aided by whose help and protection, Paul himself performed no less among the uncircumcised than Peter did among the circumcised. And here again, a parenthesis is needed, so that we read in this manner: *But on the contrary, when they had seen that the Gospel of the uncircumcision was committed to me, just as that of the circumcision was to Peter (then let what follows be separated by a parenthesis: For he who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision, worked also in me toward the Gentiles). Soon, let what follows be connected with what came before: And when they had known the grace given to me, etc.*

13 **They gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship** | Either the word "were" must be understood, or, following the Hebrew idiom, he said "right hands of fellowship" (like "the kiss of peace") instead of "social right hands," if we may speak that way.

14 **Among the Gentiles** | <note>original: "εἰς τὰ ἔθνη"</note>, that is, "into the nations," as Ambrose reads it. Elsewhere he cites "to the nations" or "toward the nations," to correspond to what preceded: "for the apostleship of the circumcision." Just as "we into the nations, they however..." Here the speech is not complete, but it must be understood as "should perform the apostolic duty." For "into" is used for "toward." And he calls the Jewish nation itself "the circumcision," which he opposes to the Gentiles, whom he sometimes calls "the uncircumcision."

15 **Only that the poor** | The word "only" <note>original: "tantum"</note> is adversative and refers to what follows, not what precedes. I note this because some people punctuate it differently. Something must be understood here, such as "they only warned or commanded."

16 **I resisted him to his face** | <note>original: "κατὰ πρόσωπον αὐτῷ ἀντέστην"</note>, that is, I stood against him according to his face, or certainly "in the face," not "into the face." This means openly and in the sight of all; for "into the face" would be insulting. The Greek is not "into the face" <note>original: "κατὰ πρόσωπον"</note>, but "to the face" <note>original: "κατὰ πρόσωπον"</note>. Both the Greek commentaries and Ambrose agree with this, interpreting "in the face" as openly and in person. Saint Jerome, however, takes it as "according to the face," meaning not from the heart, but so that he might show a display of rebuke to those present, whereby Peter’s pretense—which Paul saw would be harmful to the Gentiles—might be corrected by a pretended rebuke. He calls this hypocrisy on both their parts a "dispensation" <note>a tactical maneuver for the good of the church</note>. However, according to this sense, it would be rather weak that Paul would deter the Galatians from Judaism with this argument: that he rightly resisted Cephas to his face, even though Cephas had not sinned, but Paul merely sought an opportunity for a verbal lashing. Nevertheless, this interpretation by some Greeks is not approved by Augustine for another reason; and from this was born that magnificent dispute between them concerning lying, since it involves "pretense" and "dissimulation" rather than a lie. Jerome is so far from shrinking from this word that he is not afraid to attribute such hypocrisy to the Prophets and even to Christ himself. For Peter, when the Jews arrived, rising from the table, pretended that he did not eat common foods <note>foods forbidden by Jewish law</note>, lest they be offended, since they could not be persuaded that it was permitted, even though he knew it was permitted. And again, when Paul perceived that from this dissimulation—by which Peter had sought to heal the Jews—a grave offense was born, such that he feared for Barnabas as well, he opposed him with a sharp rebuke, but "according to the face," that is, in appearance and through pretense. Not because he believed Peter had sinned in his dissimulation, but because he saw that what Peter had done as a remedy for his own nation was turning into a destruction for the Gentiles, for whom Paul was caring. Augustine, explaining this Epistle quite harshly in my opinion, treats Peter in this way, speaking of him in these words: *But Peter, when he had come to Antioch, was rebuked by Paul, not because he observed the custom of the Jews, in which he was born and raised (though among the Gentiles he no longer observed it), but he was rebuked because he wanted to impose it on the Gentiles.* Thus far Augustine. For it seems to smack of a certain perversity if someone tries to impose a burden on others that he does not judge should be taken up. But

contributed. But on the contrary, when they had seen that the Gospel of <margin>7</margin> the uncircumcision was committed to me, just as that of the circumcision was to Peter. 12 For he who was effective in Peter for the apostleship <margin>8</margin> of the circumcision, was effective also in me toward the Gentiles. And when they had known the grace given to me, <margin>9</margin> James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave the right hands of fellowship to me and Barnabas, so that we <margin>14</margin> should perform our apostleship to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision. 15 Only that we should be mindful of the poor; <margin>10</margin> in which I was also diligent to do this very thing. But when Peter had come to Antioch, 16 <margin>11</margin>

<insert>pa-</insert>
his voice is in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter fifteen: *Now therefore why do you tempt God, to put a yoke upon the necks of the disciples, which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?* How is it consistent that he is said to tempt God here, who would want to impose the yoke of the Law on the <margin>B</margin> Gentiles, yet himself tried so hard to impose it that he used pretense for that purpose? Again, Augustine in his book *On the Christian Struggle*, chapter 30, calls this act of Peter a "superstitious pretense," and mixes it with his other sins—of distrust, fighting, and denial—and indeed a little later in the same chapter he calls it a "depraved pretense": *These,* he says, *the motherly bosom of the Catholic Church receives, just as it did Peter after the weeping of his denial, warned by the cock’s crow, or just as it did him after his depraved pretense, corrected by the voice of Paul.* But it is worth the effort to see how far Jerome is from Augustine’s opinion. Augustine is not afraid to charge Peter, the Prince of the Apostles, even after receiving the heavenly Spirit, with "depraved pretense"; Jerome cannot bear even an error to be attributed to Peter. For thus he speaks in the Preface to the Commentaries he published on this Epistle: *Wherefore, he walks so cautiously between the two // that he neither betrays the grace of the Gospel, entirely by the weight and authority of the elders, nor does injury to his predecessors while he is the defender of grace.* <margin>C</margin> Indirectly // as if walking through tunnels, he walks so as to teach Peter to act for the sake of the people of the circumcision committed to him, lest, suddenly falling away from their ancient way of living, they—being scandalized—might not believe the harsh message; and to teach himself, to whom the preaching of the Gentiles was entrusted, that it was right to defend for the sake of truth what Peter otherwise pretended for the sake of a "dispensation" <note>tactical flexibility</note>. Eunomius, not understanding this at all, and that wicked Porphyry <note>a famous Neoplatonist philosopher and critic of Christianity</note>, in the first book of his work against us, claimed that Peter was rebuked by Paul because he did not walk with a "right foot" in evangelizing—wishing to brand Peter with the stain of error and Paul with procacity <note>boldness/insolence</note>, and to accuse the lie of a shared fictional dogma, while the princes of the Churches disagreed among themselves. Thus far we have related Jerome's words. Indeed, some, while they cannot extricate themselves from these difficulties, have invented a story that this "Cephas" whom Paul resisted to his face was not Peter the Apostle, but someone else. The Greek commentaries cite Eusebius as the author of this opinion in his *Ecclesiastical History*, who made the matter more probable with an argument: <margin>D</margin> *For what need was there,* he says, *for Peter to withdraw from the table because of the arrival of the Jews, when much earlier he had satisfied everyone who complained that he had shared fellowship with the uncircumcised Cornelius? He satisfied them so well that when they knew the business, they harmoniously gave thanks to God—especially since no mention of this matter is made in the Acts of the Apostles?* But Jerome strongly rejects this opinion as common and "chilly," since the matter itself shows that this entire speech pertains to Peter and his colleagues. He denies that any Cephas is known to us besides the Apostle, who is called "Cephas" in the Syrian language, because Cephas sounds the same to them as "Petros" does to the Greeks and to us. Furthermore, it is not surprising if Luke omitted this, by whom so many other things were passed over—such as that Peter first sat at Antioch, then transferred his seat to Rome. Finally, the sycophant Porphyry ought not be so important to us that we should invent a new "Cephas" for his sake. Otherwise, if we try to erase from the Scriptures whatever becomes subject to the slanders of Heretics, many other things would have to be erased. Thomas Aquinas has not unsuccessfully contracted into a compendium the very wordy dispute which turns on this matter between Jerome and <margin>E</margin> Augustine, indicating that the sum of the controversy is situated chiefly in four things. First, in time: that Jerome distinguished it into two parts, and Augustine into three. Thus, the legal rites were "living" before the Gospel; soon after the death of Christ, they were "dead" but not "deadly" <note>mortifera</note>, to Jews only, provided they placed no hope of salvation in them; finally, once the Gospel was widely spread, those same things became deadly to everyone. While Augustine distinguished this truly, Jerome thinks the Gospel was already sufficiently spread when it was shown to Peter by a vision that nothing is "common" <note>unclean</note>, when he satisfied the complaining Jews on this matter, and when he himself testified in a public assembly that the yoke of the Law should be imposed on no one, which neither they nor their ancestors could bear. And shall we deny that the grace of the Gospel was spread, when everywhere among the nations so many thousands of men held the Gospel? Especially since Christ himself had said openly long before, *The Law and the Prophets were until John*, and when the veil of the temple had been torn from top to bottom. Nor was injury done to the Law in this, if, insofar as it was a <margin>F</margin> shadow, it yielded to the truth. Nor, I think, was so much honor owed to the Synagogue when Christ repudiated it as a murderer of her husband—especially since from that honor so much danger was imminent that it nearly happened that the Gentiles also were dragged back into Judaism. Nor would there be no distinction between the sacrifices of the Gentiles and the Jews; for while the former were always to be detested, the latter held a fixed honor for a time. Now, that boundary which Augustine introduces between two times—by what mark shall we determine it? Is it until there are those who cannot ignore them? But there are many of this kind, even in our times, among Christians. Although all of this, which Augustine brings forward concerning the "dead but not deadly," concerning the middle time, and concerning the Synagogue being buried with honor at the tomb, is supported more by human reason than by the testimonies of Divine Scripture. For what sane person would want to observe those things from which...

Erasmus explores the famous theological debate between Jerome and Augustine regarding whether Peter actually sinned or if the conflict was a "staged" tactical move to manage Jewish and Gentile converts.</summary>

<meta>Continuity note: This page continues the deep dive into the incident at Antioch described in Galatians 2:11-16. Erasmus is navigating the famous patristic debate between Saint Jerome (who argued the conflict was a staged "simulation" to teach the faithful) and Saint Augustine (who argued Peter genuinely erred and Paul genuinely corrected him). Erasmus also critiques the later Scholastic interpretations of Thomas Aquinas and the harsh censures of the Parisian theologians.</meta>

<page-num>809</page-num>
<page-num>810</page-num>
### TO THE GALATIANS. CHAPTER II.

<margin>12</margin> I resisted him <note>original: "τῷ ἀντίστην"</note>, because he stood condemned. For before certain men came from James, he used to eat with the Gentiles; but when they came, he began to draw back and separate himself, fearing those of the circumcision. <margin>13</margin> And the rest of the Jews also acted hypocritically along with him, so that even Barnabas was led away by their <margin>14</margin> hypocrisy. But when I saw that they were not walking uprightly <note>original: "ὀρθοποδοῦσι"</note> toward the truth of the Gospel, I said to Peter in the presence of everyone, "If you, being a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, why do you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews <note>original: "ἰουδαΐζειν"</note>?" <margin>15</margin> We who are Jews by nature, and not sinners from among the Gentiles, <margin>16</margin> knowing that a person is not justified by the works of the law, except through faith in Jesus Christ...

...from which he could expect no fruit? But if the Jews observed the legal ceremonies with this intention—as being neither useful nor useless—why do they demand them of Paul? Indeed, why of the Gentiles? Surely those who did these things thought it mattered to the cause. Why did the Apostles not rebuke them? But if there was no fruit from them, they certainly should have been avoided for this reason: that those who observed them gave the appearance of being weak, as if the Gospel were not sufficient without these things. And from this source was born the heresy of the Ebionites <note>A group of early Jewish Christians who insisted on the necessity of following Jewish Law</note>, among several others, which mixed Christ with Moses, whereas He wished to be most pure.

Now, in the second point of disagreement, he says that according to Jerome's opinion, the Apostles did not observe the legal ceremonies but sometimes simulated doing so for a time, yet for specific reasons: for instance, whoever abstained from work on the Sabbath did so not out of superstition but for rest; or they abstained from certain foods, not as if they were forbidden, but because they were considered abominations. For these points, unless I am mistaken, Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> added on his own. As if indeed the same things are not permitted now, or as if someone would be sinning if, exhausted from a journey, he rested on the Sabbath, or if he loathed rancid bacon when a capon was served. Or as if it were fitting for the Apostles to serve an abomination of that kind of superstition such as we see in foolish little women. 

But according to Augustine, he says, the Apostles did observe the legal ceremonies, and with that intention, yet not placing their hope in them. And this was permitted to them as Jews, if this was only a concession to the weakness of some. But what is this to the Apostles, through whom alone the weakness of others was to be driven out? Furthermore, what is the difference between one who observes them under compulsion so as not to offend anyone, and one who, for whatever reason, observes a thing as if it were useless? And what does the person who does this intend? Or does he intend nothing, he who observes them in simulation so as not to alienate anyone from the Gospel?

In the third place, they disagree in this: Jerome frees both from any sin, since each was doing his own business—that is, the business of the Gospel. Augustine burdens Peter with sin, but only a venial one. And yet from these words of Augustine which we have just cited, it does not appear that this sin seemed venial to him. Furthermore, the opinion that frees both Apostles from sin is initially more favorable than the one that burdens one of them; but more will be said on this soon. 

Now, as for what Thomas brings forward concerning the "weight of authors," it seems to me to be a matter of voting. Out of the seven Doctors on whose testimony Jerome relies, Thomas rejects four—the Laodicean <note>Apollinaris</note>, Alexander, Origen, and Didymus—as if they were infamous for heresy. But for my part, in the interpretation of Scripture, I would prefer Origen alone to ten "orthodox" ones, certain dogmas of faith excepted. But if those in whose books heretical things are found are to be rejected, perhaps both Cyprian and Ambrose will also be rejected. 

Furthermore, what kind of thing is it to produce Paul, whose very writings are the subject of the controversy, in the number of witnesses? This is done so that three would not be opposed by three; but meanwhile, nothing is said about lying. For simulation or dissimulation, if the intent is established, cannot be called a lie in such a way that it is always joined with vice. Moreover, what was said by Paul—*they were not walking rightly toward the Gospel*—seems to be said of the others, not of Peter. There remains, therefore, one scruple: that Cephas <note>Peter</note> is called "reprehensible" by Paul. For either that was said truly, and it follows that Peter sinned; or it was said falsely, and Paul is held liable for a lie. But we will soon show from the interpretation of the Ancients how this knot can be untied.

In the fourth place, not to pursue every single point, Thomas mentions among other things that Peter sinned because a scandal was born from his simulation; Paul did not sin, because no offense arose from his rebuke. But how could Peter have known that those who were reclining at the table would be offended, since they knew that Peter was perhaps making this concession to the Jews who were weak or hasty? If they knew it was permitted for a Jew to eat or not to eat, why should they be offended if he does for a time what he thinks is best? It was more likely that the Jews would be offended than the Gentiles. But if he had not simulated, he would have sinned more seriously again, because he would have more seriously offended his own people, to whom he was more closely joined. 

And yet, not every scandal is joined with vice. On the contrary, a grave offense could have been born from so sharp a rebuke from Paul. First, they could have suspected that some rancor existed between the chief Apostles, since Paul so attacked Peter to his face over a trivial matter. Furthermore, there was a danger that Peter’s authority among the faithful might be diminished, which ought to have been sacrosanct. I have seen fit to add these things because the common crowd of theologians thinks that Augustine fought beautifully and that Thomas explained the matter well. Certainly, the passage is quite obscure, and one that greatly tormented the most learned men of Greece. I do not see why, out of a hatred for lying, we should treat Peter as harshly as Augustine treated him. Even more harshly do the *Articles of Paris* <note>The censures of the Faculty of Theology at the University of Paris</note> speak, which say that Peter erred in faith. We read that a dissension occurred between Paul and Barnabas. But to say that the Apostles, after receiving the heavenly Spirit who would lead them into all truth, erred in the dogmas of faith, seems to me an impious thing to say. I think, however, that Paul grew incensed because that wavering of "Judaizing" had not yet been removed from among the Christians; and that is what Paul means when he says *that he was blamed*, because...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>11</margin> ...I resisted him openly, <gloss>17</gloss> because he was blamed.
<margin>12</margin> For before certain men had come from James, he took food together with the Gentiles: but when they had come, he withdrew and separated himself from them, fearing those who were of the circumcision: <margin>13</margin> <gloss>18</gloss> And the <gloss>19</gloss> other Jews also simulated together with him, so that even Barnabas was led away with them into their simulation. <margin>14</gloss> <gloss>20</gloss> But when I had seen that they were not <gloss>21</gloss> walking with a straight foot toward the truth of the Gospel, <gloss>22</gloss> I said to Peter in front of everyone: If you, although you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, why do you force the Gentiles to live like Jews? <margin>15</margin> We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from the Gentiles: <margin>16</gloss> <gloss>23</gloss> Since we know that a man is not justified by the works of the law, <gloss>24</gloss> except through faith in Jesus Christ,

<margin>B</margin> ...it belongs to those who limp. For it was now right, all superstition having been exploded, to profess Christ freely before everyone. But if Paul desired some strength in this part from Peter, it does not immediately follow that Peter sinned, since that "limping" proceeded from nowhere else than a zeal for piety. Therefore, Paul’s reprimand was nothing other than a confirmation of those who were as yet not very consistent in themselves. These things I have brought forward according to my ability, being ready to receive better views if anyone offers them.

<margin>C</margin> <gloss>17 Because he was reprehensible</gloss> <note>original: "ὅτι κατεγνωσμένος ἦν"</note>, that is, because he was blamed and condemned by those who judged him poorly, even if he was not "reprehensible" in himself. And here the Greek scholia agree. Ambrose likewise reads "blamed," not "reprehensible." And he adds "blamed": From where? Surely on account of the evangelical truth, which this deed opposed—here he disagrees with the Greeks and agrees with Augustine. The Greek scholia offer this and another sense: "I was given an opportunity," says Paul, "to openly resist Peter, because he had previously been blamed by the Apostles in Jerusalem, because he had taken food with a tribute-payer in Antioch." But if he had not been rebuked before, he would not have withdrawn now; but fearing lest some tumult should arise again, he was preparing to withdraw from the banquet. Furthermore, Paul, having found the opportunity, rebukes him openly, not because he was angry with him, but to strengthen others who were wavering. For if Peter had truly sinned in anything, and Paul had been angry with him from his heart, he would have expostulated in private, not before everyone. Nor does Paul narrate these things boastfully, but so that he might consult the salvation of the Galatians. Finally, it plainly seems to me that James and his followers were of this opinion: that they believed the Mosaic Law, even after the Gospel was published, was to be observed by the Jews even regarding ceremonies, as we noted in Acts chapter twenty-one; not because they believed that without these things the grace of the Gospel was not sufficient for salvation, but because they thought it expedient, on account of the invincible superstition of some, that it not be entirely neglected.

<margin>D</margin> <gloss>18 And they consented to his simulation</gloss> <note>original: "συνυπεκρίθησαν αὐτῷ"</note>, that is, they simulated together with him, and so Saint Ambrose reads.

<gloss>19 The rest of the Jews</gloss> And there should be added, "and the rest," or "the rest also."

<gloss>20 By them into that simulation</gloss> In Greek it is thus: "so that even they in their hypocrisy," that is, he was likewise led away into their simulation, or by their simulation. Fabri <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples</note> reads *led away together*, but this is neither found in the Greek codices nor read by anyone, nor do I think he will find the word anywhere.

<gloss>21 They walked rightly</gloss> The Greek is a single word, *orthopodousi* <note>walking straight-footedly</note>. Whence Saint Jerome against Pelagius, and also in his Commentaries, translates it as *they did not walk with a straight foot*: but that refers to the others, not to Peter. For these others simulated in one way, Peter in another. Peter was dissimulating rather than simulating, lest he offend his own people. The others were dissimulating, suspecting something had been allowed against good morals. Certainly Augustine, in the letters in which he struggles with Jerome over this passage, reads it in many ways, and similarly cites it in the last chapter *To Consensus* on lying. Likewise Ambrose: *they walk in the right way*. Again, it is not "to not walk rightly," that is, to wander from the way, but to limp and waver, because they were not firm in that which was to be freely defended, leaning now this way, now that. And since the Mosaic Law was in the borderland, it could be that Peter also somewhat doubted whether the Law should be openly neglected. But this itself was to waver, not however to commit a crime, since neither Paul nor Peter judged the observation of the Law to be required for salvation, although Paul was also forced to circumcise Timothy and shave his head—not out of superstition, but out of compliance. Hitherto, certainly, there is no mention of a lie. Nor does anyone deny that a pious man may sometimes rightly simulate and dissimulate. And we have shown from this place that there is no necessity to bring in a "lie." Nor was Peter forcing the Gentiles to live as Jews as if he were trying to draw them into Judaism, but because some seized this handle from his dissimulation.

<margin>E</margin> <gloss>22 I said to Cephas</gloss> The Greeks read "to Peter." Nor does it matter to the sense. For what sounds like "Petros" to the Greeks, sounds like "Cephas" to the Hebrews and Syrians, on the authority of Jerome. *Before everyone.* Here he explains what he said before, "to his face," that is, in the sight of everyone, for whose sake these things are said.

<gloss>23 But knowing</gloss> I do not find the conjunction "but" <note>autem</note> in the Greek copies, nor is it necessary, unless you understand the verb "we are" in the preceding part, so that we read: "We are born Jews, sprung from holy fathers, born under a holy law, not however Gentiles, who were produced without the law from impious and profane ancestors. And yet we, thus born, are forced, distrusting our law, to flee to the faith of Christ if we wish to be saved; how much less should the Gentiles be persuaded to hope for salvation from the Law of Moses." Furthermore, he said "Jews by nature" to distinguish them from proselytes.

<gloss>24 Except through the faith of Jesus</gloss> <note>original: "ἐὰν μὴ"</note>, that is, "if not." It is, however...

He challenges the strict censures of the Parisian theologians and balances the competing interpretations of Jerome, Augustine, and Thomas Aquinas regarding the persistence of Mosaic Law.</summary>

<meta>Continuity note: This page continues Erasmus’s detailed linguistic and patristic analysis of Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians. Having finished the historical account of the dispute between Peter and Paul at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14), Erasmus now moves into Paul's theological argument regarding justification by faith versus the works of the Law (2:16–21) and the sharp rhetorical transition in Chapter 3, where Paul addresses the "foolish Galatians."</meta>

# 811 EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER III. 812

[In Christ], and we have believed in Christ Jesus, so that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law; because no flesh shall be justified by the works of the law. 
17 But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves were found to be sinners, is Christ then a minister of sin? 
18 Heaven forbid. For if I build up again the things I destroyed, I prove myself a transgressor. 19 For I through the law died to the law, so that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ. 20 It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me; and the life I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me. 21 I do not set aside the grace of God; for if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing.
III. 1 O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you, that you should not obey the truth? Before whose eyes Jesus Christ was clearly portrayed, among you, as crucified.

---

<note>Erasmus is commenting on the Greek phrasing of Galatians 2:16</note> ...a new form of expression; in common speech it should have been said: "he is not justified by the works of the law, but only through faith."

<margin>A</margin> 25 **In Jesus Christ we have believed** <note>original: "ἐπιστεύσαμεν"</note>, that is, "we believed," in the past tense. And Jerome reads it this way.

26 **Because of which from**] "Because that," if he had wanted to speak in proper Latin, for <note>original: "διότι"</note>.

<margin>B</margin> 27 **I build up again**] <note>original: "οἰκοδομῶ"</note>, that is, "I build," for it is preceded by "again" <note>original: "πάλιν"</note>, that is, "a second time."

<margin>C</margin> 28 **I have died**] <note>original: "ἀπέθανον"</note>, that is, "I was dead," in the past tense; this means that through the law of faith I ceased to be subject to the Mosaic law.

<margin>D</margin> 29 **I am fastened to the cross**] <note>original: "Χριστῷ συνεσταύρωμαι"</note>, that is, "I am fastened together with Christ," or "I am crucified with Christ."

<margin>E</margin> 30 **But that I now live**] Again, he used "which" <note>original: "ὃ"</note> for "that" <note>original: "ὅτι"</note>, just as we pointed out in the Epistle to the Romans: "For that he lives, he lives to God."

<margin>F</margin> 31 **In the faith I live of the Son of God**] <note>original: "ἐν πίστει ζῶ τῇ τοῦ Υἱοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note>. The added article distinguishes the faith of Christ from other faith, which could be expressed as "I live in faith—that specific faith, I say, of the Son of God." It is strange, however, that having left the narrative, as if forgetting himself, he pursues the matter in such a way that it is not clear where he stopped rebuking Peter. Even though Jerome thinks Paul's correction continues until the end of this chapter—following Theophylact, who ends his commentary on this chapter thus: "But if you yourself asserted this, you see to what extent of impiety the blasphemy would progress." Yet there are things in this discourse that would better suit a teacher toward a disciple than Paul toward Peter. Hence it is more probable that Paul said the rest to those who had brought [the false teachings]: or, having dropped what he had begun, he secretly turned his speech toward the Galatians. Otherwise, it was too abrupt to say, "O senseless Galatians." From Ambrose, nothing was sufficiently clear.

32 **I do not cast away**] <note>original: "Οὐκ ἀθετῶ"</note>, that is, "I do not reject, I do not repel, I do not despise." Ambrose reads: "I am not ungrateful for the grace of God." Augustine: "I do not make void the grace of God." He would seem to despise Christ's grace if he had accepted the law of Moses as necessary for salvation.

33 **Christ died for nothing**] <note>original: "δωρεὰν ἀπέθανεν"</note>, which also sounds like "gratuitously." This is an argument from the impossible: for if no one is so insane as to say that Christ died for nothing, then salvation does not come from the observation of the Mosaic law.

<column-break/>

[The faith] of Jesus Christ, and we have believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: 16 because by the works of the law no flesh will be justified. But if, while we seek to be justified through Christ, we ourselves are also found to be sinners, is Christ then a minister of sin? Heaven forbid. For if the things I destroyed, those 17 I build up again, I establish myself as a transgressor. For I through the law 18 died to the law, that I might live to God. I am 19 crucified together with Christ. Nevertheless I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me: 20 but the life which I now live in the flesh, 21 I live through the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me. 22 I do not despise the grace of God: for if justice is through the law, then 23 Christ died in vain. O foolish Galatians, 24 who has bewitched you, that you should not believe the truth? 25 before whose eyes Jesus Christ [was portrayed]...

---

<margin>G</margin> **O Senseless** <note>original: "Ὦ ἀνόητοι"</note>, that is, "foolish." And so Augustine reads in the Commentary he published on this Epistle; otherwise "senseless" is a harsher and more insulting word. The Greek word sounds more like "unrefined" or "lacking in sense," especially since the Galatians originated from the fiercer parts of Gaul. Hilary himself, a Gaul, in his Book of Hymns, calls the Gauls "unteachable." Jerome adds that Ancyra, the capital of Galatia, seemed to him to retain great traces of ancient rudeness, and from their borders arose monstrous heresies—the Ophites, Borborites, and Manichaeans. Furthermore, he notes that their language (except for Greek, which almost the entire East used at that time) was nearly the same as that of the Treveri <note>A tribe in what is now Germany/Luxembourg</note> in his day. For Jerome spent time among them. And I do not know whether the language that is now used by the Germans was formerly that of the Gauls. The Translator, where he here renders "senseless," soon renders it as "foolish," playing with his usual abundance of synonyms.

2 **Who has bewitched you**] To "bewitch" <note>Latin: "fascinare"</note> is said by the Latins of those who harm with a malicious look, but among the Greeks <note>original: "ἐβάσκανε"</note>, the word Paul used here, also means "to envy," so that you may understand that some, moved by envy, wanted to call the Galatians back to the slavery of the law. But Paul seems to have used this word in place of "enchanted," as if he had deceived their eyes with a trick: for "bewitching" <note>original: "βασκαίνειν"</note> is called a "stage-front" <note>original: "προσκήνιον"</note> by the Greeks because the bewitcher harms through the eyes. Furthermore, the words that follow immediately testify that Paul is thinking of dazed eyes: "before whose eyes Christ Jesus was prescribed, and crucified among you." It is plainly a kind of trick, so that you do not see what you perceive right before you, and then you think you see what is not there. Though Demosthenes used that word for "to slander" or "to accuse" in his Oration for Ctesiphon. Hesychius adds it is properly said of an ungrateful person. "Fascination" <note>bewitchment</note> was believed to harm children most of all, and for this reason he calls them "foolish," though it does not contradict the Gospel sentence: "Whoever says to his brother, 'You fool,' shall be in danger of hellfire." For this is not a cry of indignation, but of charitable rebuke. And yet he overlooks their admission, since he attributes such great blindness to bewitchment, shifting a large part of the blame onto others.

3 **To not believe the truth**] "To not obey," <note>original: "τῇ ἀληθείᾳ μὴ πείθεσθαι"</note>, that is, lest you should comply with the truth. However, this particle is entirely omitted by Jerome, because he denies it is found in the copies of Adamantius <note>Origen</note>. In the very ancient and most correct copy of the Pauline Library, it was not added in the main text, but I know not who had noted it down in a later hand far in the bottom margin. In the more recent Constance manuscript it was not held at all; in the older one it read, "who has bewitched you not to obey," and "the truth" was not added. They added the same particle in another place below, where [Greek] was changed to [Greek]. This is one place out of many which proves that this Edition <note>the Vulgate</note> is not entirely Jerome’s. For while he testifies that he omitted this particle because it was not found in Adamantius’s codices, it is consistently held in our copies; and what the Translator says he rendered in this place in the fifth chapter of the Epistle, "not to believe the truth," our codices have "not to obey the truth." Chrysostom reads nothing other than "who has bewitched you?" Nor does Theophylact, even though the Translator follows our reading in his usual way, since in the explanation there is not a single syllable that explains this particle.

4 **Before whose eyes**] <note>original: "προεγράφη"</note>, that is, "under whose gaze Christ Jesus was publicly displayed." I wonder why he translated it "prescribed" <note>Latin: "praescriptus"</note>, since that word means something quite different to the Latins, unless because the Greeks also use <note>original: "προγράφειν"</note> for a kind of condemnation among the Romans called "proscriptions" <note>Latin: "proscriptio"</note>. But the sense can be twofold. Either the Galatians were so demented that they did not perceive what was most manifest and exposed to their eyes because they were blinded; or they saw so little that they believed Christ had perished by proscription and was crucified in the common manner. Augustine and Ambrose follow the latter sense. To me, the former is more pleasing as being simpler and less forced. Although Augustine seems to read "prescribed," not "proscribed," as if speaking of the "prescription" of possessions, which is transferred to the right of another through occupation. If anyone should require his words, I will add them: "Before whose eyes," he says, "Jesus Christ, proscribed, was crucified: that is, while they were watching, Jesus Christ lost his heritage and possession, these people taking it away even then and expelling the Lord from there; those who were calling back the believers to the works of the law were taking away from Christ the possession of the nations, which he holds through the grace of faith." And a little lower: "So that he might move them most from this, when they considered at what price he bought the possession which he was losing in them, as if it were not enough that he died for nothing (as he said above); for that sounds as if he did not arrive at the possession for which he gave his blood, but by proscription even that which he was holding is taken away. But this proscription does not hinder Christ, who even so is Lord of all through his divinity, but rather the possession itself, which through this lack of grace remains uncultivated." Thus far Augustine. From these words, I think it is clear enough that he is treating the legal "prescription" of right, and in this whole discourse the "pro" is placed in the position of "pre" in the word "proscription." But Ambrose reads "proscribed," making mention of condemnation. I will not find it troublesome to bring his words also for the lazy or distrustful reader: "because in the eyes of fools," he says, "Christ seems proscribed, that is, his right is condemned; but in the eyes of the prudent and knowing, he seems not only not condemned, but to have himself condemned death by his cross." And soon after: "But because these people had begun to think unworthily, having transferred to the law, therefore he complains that Christ seems condemned in their minds." So says the most recent Ambrosian text. Theophylact reads "prescribed," that is, depicted as if before the eyes. For in Greek <note>original: "γράφειν"</note> also means "to paint." By this hyperbola, he notes their most certain faith—that those who believed Christ had freed the human race by his death believed more certainly than those who had watched him being raised on the cross in person. And for this very reason, he is more indignant that they slide back into Judaism as if failing Christ. Jerome seems to have read "prescribed," that is, written before: "crucified in you," before you read it in the Gospel—namely, to those reading and believing the prophecies of the Prophets, who had predicted long before that it would be so. It should be advised that the Greek word <note>original: "προγραφήν"</note> is common to both writing and painting. If that first opinion pleases, which is certainly more approved by me, and the Greek scholia agree, it will fit better as "depicted before the eyes" than "prescribed." For they had so believed in Christ crucified as if he were present to their eyes. The Donatianus codex had "prescribed," and both Constance codices had it with no trace of erasure. However, this discourse should be read together: "before whose eyes Christ was prescribed crucified in you," as if to say, he was exhibited to your eyes as if depicted hanging on the cross. For he was not crucified among the Galatians, but he was represented as crucified to them through faith. Chrysostom silently suggests this, touching nothing regarding the preposition in the word <note>original: "προεγράφη"</note>, which Paul seems to have used for "publicly displayed." Among the Latins, the preposition "pro" sometimes signifies that something is made public, as in "pro-duce," "pro-mulgate," "pro-ffer," "pro-nounce," "pro-fess." And formerly the names of condemned persons were publicly posted in the forum, from which this type of condemnation was called "proscription."

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s philological notes on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians. Following the rebuke of the "foolish Galatians" in verse 1, Erasmus now examines Paul’s appeal to their own experience of the Holy Spirit and his scriptural defense of justification by faith using the example of Abraham. Erasmus compares the Greek text with the Latin Vulgate and various patristic commentaries (Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine).</meta>

# TO THE GALATIANS. CHAPTER III.

<margin>2</margin> This only I want to learn from you: Did you receive the Spirit from the works of the law, or from the hearing of faith?
<margin>3</margin> Are you so foolish? Having begun with the spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?
<margin>4</margin> Have you suffered so many things in vain? If indeed it really was in vain.
<margin>5</margin> Does he, therefore, who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you, do so from the works of the law or from the hearing of faith?
<margin>6</margin> Just as Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.
<margin>7</margin> Know then that those who are of faith, these are the sons of Abraham.
<margin>8</margin> And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, foretold the good news to Abraham, saying: "In you shall all the nations be blessed."
<margin>9</margin> <margin>B</margin> So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with the faithful Abraham.
<margin>10</margin> For as many as are of the works of the law are under a curse; for it is written: "Cursed is everyone who does not abide by all the things written in the book of the law, to do them."
<margin>11</margin> Now, that no one is justified by the law before God is evident, because "the righteous shall live by faith."
<margin>12</margin> But the law is not of faith; rather, "the man who has done these things shall live by them."
<margin>13</margin> Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us; for it is written: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree."
<margin>14</margin> So that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

---

<margin>1</margin> *And crucified among you*] The "and" is redundant. "Among you" can be understood as "in your midst," if the first interpretation we reviewed is preferred. It does not mean Christ was literally crucified among them, but that he was so well known and preached there that they knew and believed it no less than if the event had taken place in their very presence.

<margin>6</margin> *From the works of the law*] The word "and" is redundant here; it is not added by Saint Jerome or Augustine, nor is it found in the ancient manuscripts. For Paul does not simply ask which of the two it is, but first proposes the one as if it were absurd to say, and then by way of correction introduces what is true. It is as if he said, "Did you receive the Spirit from the works of the law—or rather from hearing?" Now, that phrase *from the hearing of faith*, although understood by us, is unusual to Latin ears. Romans do not use the word "hearing" <note>original: "ἀκοὴν" / "akoe"</note> to mean "fame" or "rumor" in the same way the Greeks do. Therefore, it would be clearer to say "from the preaching of faith," that is, from the faith which you heard from us, not what you learned from the law. For who could tolerate someone saying, "The hearing of the slain King dismayed the people," instead of "The rumor of the slain King"? We have therefore translated "hearing" as "preaching."

<margin>7</margin> *That with the spirit*] The word "that" is not in the Greek; rather, it says *having begun with the spirit, you are now perfected by the flesh* <note>original: "ἐναρξάμενοι πνεύματι, νῦν σαρκὶ ἐπιτελεῖσθε"</note>, except that there is a preposition in the compound verb. For example, Horace says:

->------ with sacks piled high on every side<-
->gaping at them helplessly ------<-

Likewise, Virgil:

->To doubt my own strength ------<-

And this very "in" is placed there to mean "through." Thus, "by spirit and flesh" fits better. Chrysostom noted that the Apostle did not say "perfected" <note>original: "τελεῖσθε"</note>, but "completed afterward" <note>original: "ἐπιτελεῖσθε"</note>, as if to say you are finishing your course by moving away from your original principles.

<margin>8</margin> *Without cause*] <note>original: "εἰκῇ" / "eike"</note>, that is, "in vain," or "to no purpose."

<margin>9</margin> *He gives to you*] <note>original: "ἐπιχορηγῶν" / "epichoregon"</note>, that is, "supplying" or "ministering." Both "supplying" and "working" could be in the past tense—that is, "he who was supplying" and "he who was working"—so that one might then understand a verb in the past tense, like "he gave," or something similar. However, Jerome advises that the present tense verb is more correctly read, because the Spirit has not ceased to supply his gifts; and indeed, Ambrose reads it this way. Peter Lombard, in the first book of his *Sentences* (distinction 14), following Augustine’s opinion, thinks that "he who provided for you" refers to the person of Paul. However, Jerome and Theophylact refer it to God, which is clear from their interpretation.

<margin>10</margin> *And works miracles*] "Works" refers not to the Spirit, but to the one who supplies the Spirit. This speech contains an ellipsis <note>A grammatical omission where the meaning is implied</note>, for it is understood that "He does this." This is a Hebrew idiom, as we have indicated many times already.

<margin>11</margin> *As it is written*] "It is written" is redundant. Jerome reads, *Just as Abraham believed God*. It does not appear that Ambrose read it differently, as he adds: "He shows by the example of Abraham, who is the father of faith, etc." He therefore brought forward an example, not a testimony of Scripture. Both of the Constance manuscripts supported this original reading.

<margin>12</margin> *Know therefore*] <note>original: "Γινώσκετε ἄρα" / "Ginoskete ara"</note>, that is, "You know therefore." Saint Jerome reads it this way: "You recognize therefore," and Ambrose agrees; the Greek word can be taken as either an instruction or a statement of fact.

<margin>13</margin> *He foretold to Abraham*] <note>original: "προευηγγελίσατο" / "proeuangelisato"</note>, that is, "pre-evangelized," if we may speak this way for the sake of explanation. For *evangelion* in Greek sounds like "good and joyful news." Even in Homer, Ulysses asks for an *evangelium*—that is, a reward usually given to those who are the first to bring joyful news. Therefore, what was displayed in the Gospel of Christ was promised long before the Gospel to Abraham, which he calls here "pre-evangelized."

<margin>14</margin> *Therefore those who are of faith are blessed*] <note>original: "εὐλογοῦνται" / "eulogountai"</note>, that is, "are blessed," in the present tense. In the promise, the word was in the fu-
<meta>catchword: -ture</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>1</margin> <margin>A</margin> Christ was previously depicted and crucified among you.
<margin>2</margin> This only I desire to learn from you: Did you receive the Spirit from the works of the law, or from the preaching of faith?
<margin>3</margin> Are you so foolish that, having begun with the spirit, you are now perfected by the flesh?
<margin>4</margin> Have you suffered so many things in vain? If indeed it is in vain.
<margin>5</margin> He, therefore, who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you, does he do this from the works of the law or from the preaching of faith?
<margin>6</margin> Just as Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.
<margin>7</margin> You know, therefore, that those who are of faith, these are the sons of Abraham.
<margin>8</margin> Moreover, the Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the nations by faith, previously announced the joyful news to Abraham, saying: "In you all nations shall be blessed."
<margin>9</margin> <margin>B</margin> Therefore, those who are of faith are blessed with the faithful Abraham.
<margin>10</margin> For as many as are of the works of the law are subject to a curse: for it is written, "Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them."
<margin>11</margin> But that no one is justified in the law before God is evident, since "the just shall live by faith."
<margin>12</margin> Now the law is not of faith, but "the man who does those things shall live in them."
<margin>13</margin> Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law while he was made a curse for you: for it is written, "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree":
<margin>14</margin> So that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations through Christ Jesus, so that the prom-
<meta>catchword: -ise</meta>

---

ture tense, but here it is "they are blessed" <note>original: "εὐλογοῦνται"</note> in the present. I know it is hardly good Latin to say "they will be blessed" and "they are blessed" <note>original: "benedicentur & benedicuntur"</note>, but certain things of this kind simply cannot be avoided. One could say, "they obtain the blessing," but even so, the vice of wordiness is not avoided. One might guess that Ambrose read it this way too, although the passage is corrupted. Certainly, the Greek commentaries agree with their own text. This present-tense verb agrees with what follows.

<margin>15</margin> <margin>C</margin> *Are under a curse*] <note>original: "ὑπὸ κατάραν εἰσὶ"</note>, that is, "they are under a curse or an execration." It could also be rendered as "they are liable to a curse."

<margin>16</margin> *Cursed is everyone*] This passage is from Deuteronomy chapter 27. According to the Septuagint, it reads: "Cursed is every man who does not remain in all the words of this law, to do them, and all the people shall say, let it be so." In Aquila's version, it is: "Cursed is he who has not established the words of this law, to do them, and all the people shall say, truly." Symmachus translates it this way: "Cursed is he who has not confirmed the words of this law, to do them, and all the people shall say, amen." Theodotio translated it thus: "Cursed is he who has not raised up the words of this law to do them, and all the people shall say, amen." <margin>D</margin> Jerome adds regarding this testimony, as with others, that the Apostle was more concerned with rendering the sense than the exact words. Furthermore, regarding the words "every man" and "in all," since they are found only in the Septuagint, they were either added by the Septuagint translators or erased by the Jews—especially since Jerome found them in the Hebrew volumes of the Samaritans. But I do not see a very weighty reason why any Jew would want to erase things that work in favor of the Jews rather than against them. For they wished for the entire human race to be made subject to their law. And they so desired that everything belonging to the law should be observed that they even added many things. "Who does not remain" <note>original: "ὃς οὐκ ἐμμένει"</note>, that is, "he who does not abide," even if it changes nothing of the sense.

<margin>17</margin> *But since*] <note>original: "Ὅτι δὲ" / "Hoti de"</note>, that is, "But that." And Ambrose reads it this way, for "since" does not fit here.

<margin>18</margin> <margin>E</margin> *Lives by faith*] "Shall live" <note>original: "ζήσεται" / "zesetai"</note>, as we previously noted in the Epistle to the Romans. Jerome indicates it can also be punctuated this way: "The righteous [man] from faith," and then understand "shall live," so the sense is: "He who is truly righteous, not by the works of the law but by faith, he is the one who will live." From his interpretation, it is clear he read "shall live" <note>future</note>, not "lives" <note>present</note>. Furthermore, how this passage is handled differently among the Greek interpreters was discussed in the Epistle to the Romans.

<margin>19</margin> *And the curse of the law*] <note>original: "ἐκ τῆς κατάρας" / "ek tes kataras"</note>, that is, "from the curse," as Jerome reads in the second dialogue against the Pelagians, or "from the detestation." And again, "made a curse for you," <note>original: "κατάρα" / "katara"</note>, that is, an "execration." I wonder why the word "malediction" was preferred here, since to Latin ears that word means something else entirely, namely "an insult."

<margin>20</margin> <margin>F</margin> *Made cursed for you*] <note>original: "κατάρα" / "katara"</note>, that is, "a curse," as it is found in the ancient manuscripts—either "malediction" or "execration." Just as we call a pestilent man "a pest."

<margin>21</margin> *Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree*] This passage is from Deuteronomy chapter 21. Paul, acting wisely and knowingly, I believe, omitted the mention of God in this testimony. For Aquila and Theodotio translated it "is the curse of God"; the Septuagint, "cursed by God"; Symmachus, "is suspended for the blasphemy of God." Ebion the Heresiarch, who was half-Jew and half-Christian, interpreted it in this way: "that he who hangs is an injury or an insult to God." Jerome adds that in the *Disputation of Jason and Papiscus* (which was written in Greek), he found: "he who hangs is a reproach to God." To these, the Jew Barhanina (the teacher Jerome used at night) added that it could also be read: "because God was hung insultingly." I wonder, however, why Jerome labors so much here to avoid saying Christ was "cursed," when Paul says the same Christ was "made sin." Surely, just as Christ was "sin," so he was also "a curse." He is called "sin" by a figure of speech <note>metonymy</note>, and "curse" by a figure of speech.
