<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed philological notes on the third chapter of Paul’s Letter to the Galatians. Having established that justification comes through faith rather than the law, Erasmus now examines Paul’s legal analogy of a "testament" or "covenant" and the significance of the "seed" of Abraham, specifically addressing the 430-year gap between the promise and the Mosaic law.</meta>

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER III.

...in Christ Jesus, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. Brothers, I speak in human terms: though it is only a man’s covenant, once it has been ratified, no one sets it aside or adds to it. Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. It does not say, "and to seeds," as referring to many, but as referring to one, "and to your seed," who is Christ. What I mean is this: the law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, does not revoke a covenant previously ratified by God so as to nullify the promise. For if the inheritance comes from the law, it is no longer from a promise; but God has graciously given it to Abraham through a promise. Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made, having been ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not for one party only; but God is one. Is the law then against the promises of God? May it never be! For if a law had been given that was able to impart life, then righteousness would certainly have come from the law. But the scripture has imprisoned all things under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe. Now before faith came, we were kept under guard by the law, imprisoned until the faith that was to be revealed. So the law became our tutor <note>original: "paidagogos"</note> leading us to Christ, so that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a tutor. For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is no male and female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus. And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, and...

---

22 **Even a man’s ratified testament** <note>original: "Tamen hominis confirmatum testamentum"</note>] The Greek is *homōs anthrōpou diathēkēn*, which could be rendered as *although it is a man’s testament*, so that you immediately understand the implication: how much more ought this to be the case with God. I also see it can be connected with what precedes, *I speak in human terms*, that is, I will bring forward an example from human affairs, which are in no way to be compared with divine matters; and yet in a human testament no one rescinds or changes anything, so great is the weight of a human decree and decision.

23 **No one despises a ratified testament**] The Greek is *kekyrōmenēn diathēkēn oudeis athetei*, that is, *no one rejects or rescinds a confirmed or approved testament*. For a little earlier, he translated this verb *athetei* as "rejects." *Ambrose reads, "confirmed by authority."* The opposite of this is *akyroun*, which means to make void or rescind. It is a participle from the verb we mentioned in the previous Epistle, *Confirm your love toward him*.

24 **Or adds to it**] *ē epidiatassetai*, that is, *he joins and ordains something besides it*; that is, he neither takes away, nor adds, nor detracts, nor claims.

25 **As of many**] *hōs epi pollōn*. It would fit better here to use *as if*. Saint Jerome notes that Paul used this argument somewhat loosely among the "dense" Galatians, knowing that it would not be approved by the prudent or the learned, and for that reason he warned the prudent reader: *Brothers, I speak in human terms*. For he denies that the word "seed" is ever used in the plural in Holy Scripture <note>Jerome argues that "seed" is a collective noun like "wheat," which is singular even when referring to many grains.</note>. And yet the Apostle twists this as an argument to teach that this promise applies to Christ alone. It seems more likely to others that he testified he was speaking in a human manner because he was going to draw a comparison from human affairs to divine things for the sake of teaching. Thus also Virgil says:
-> ——— if one may compare small things with great. <-
By now it ought to be known, even without a teacher, that the preposition *en* is used in place of *per* [through], as in *in your seed*, meaning *through your seed*. By *seed*, moreover, he means posterity.

26 **A testament ratified by God**] *diathēkēn prokekyrōmenēn hypo tou Theou eis Christon*, that is, *a testament previously ratified by God in Christ*. "In Christ" is added in the Greek, and likewise in Ambrose. Saint Jerome advises in this place that if anyone diligently weighs the Hebrew volumes, whenever the Seventy [the Septuagint] translated *diathēkēn*, that is, *testamentum*, the Hebrew word is *berit*, which sounds more like "pact" than "testament." For in pacts, good faith is required. However, Paul did not think he had to act with such precision among the "dense" Galatians. So says Jerome. As if Paul did not also follow the Septuagint version in many other places! Now, regarding the number of years, whether they sufficiently agree with the narrative of Genesis, Saint Augustine discusses this acutely in the *City of God*, book 16, chapter 24, lest we burden this project more than enough with such appendices.

27 **Does not make void**] *ouk akyroi*, which is the opposite of *kyroō*; the latter means not just "to approve," but "to decree with authority and to legally settle a matter, so that what has been done is thereafter ratified."

28 **Through the promise God gave it**] *kecharistai*, a verb from *charis*, meaning *by grace*, which Paul everywhere opposes to the works of the Mosaic Law.

29 **What then is the law? Because of transgressions**] Augustine in his Commentaries insists it be punctuated thus: *What then?* followed by the response, *the law was added because of transgressors*. And this distinction was held in both Constantius codices. But he retracts this and thinks it better to punctuate as we have: *What then is the law?* and then Paul answers himself, *it was added because of transgressions*. He learned this distinction, as

<column-break/>

<page-num>816</page-num>
<header>THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER III.</header>

...we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. Brothers, I speak in human terms: 22 though it is only a man’s testament, 23 yet if it be ratified, no one rejects it 24 or adds anything. Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and 16 to his seed. It does not say, "and to seeds," 25 as if of many, but as of one, "and in your seed," who is Christ. Now I say this, 26 a testament previously ratified by God toward Christ, the law which began four hundred and thirty years later, 27 does not make void so as to abolish the promise. For if the inheritance is from the law, it is no longer from a promise. But to Abraham 28 through a promise God gave it. 29 What then is the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made, ordained through angels 32 in the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not of one, 20 but God is one. Is the law therefore against the promises of God? Far from it. For if a law had been given which could give life, truly righteousness would be from the law. But the scripture has enclosed all things under sin, so that the promise from faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe. But before faith came, we were guarded under the law, enclosed for that faith which was to be revealed. Therefore the law 33 was our tutor toward Christ, 34 so that we might be justified by faith. But after faith came, we are no longer under a tutor. For you are all children of God because you have believed in Christ Jesus. For as many of you as were baptized, you have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; 35 there is no male and female; 36 for you are all one in Christ Jesus. 37 And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed...

---

I believe, from the Greeks: for so says Theophylact, *Ti an ho nomos*.

30 **Was placed** <note>original: "Posita est"</note>] *prosetethē*, that is, *was added*, or *was set alongside*, unless you read *prosethē*. But Theophylact reads *prosetitē* and explains it with care. For he did not say it was "placed," but "added," lest anyone should think this was the primary thing, but rather something joined incidentally between the first promise and the Gospel.

31 **To whom he had promised**] In a certain codex I read *hō epēngeltai*, that is, *which was promised*. In others it was *hō* [to whom]. For I do not think that among the Greeks the same thing happens in the nominative as happens in these oblique cases, where the relative article agrees with the antecedent rather than its own verb, except that among the Greeks those to whom news is brought are said to be "evangelized." By this trope, the sense will be the same *whether you read "to whom" or "which"*. Theophylact reads *hō*.

32 **In the hand of a mediator**] *mesitou*. Perhaps this is one of those words, peculiar to divine Scripture, which we cannot change, unless "reconciler" or "intercessor" is preferred. Here Jerome mentions a *hyperbaton* <note>A figure of speech where the natural order of words is shifted for emphasis.</note> and restores the confused order of the speech in this way: *The law was placed through angels in the hand of a mediator, ordained because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made*.

33 **Our tutor was in Christ**] Better here, *toward Christ*, or *to Christ*, *eis Christon*. And so Jerome reads in his second dialogue against Pelagius. For a *paidagogos* among the Greeks is a servant to whom the care of a boy is committed for a time, lest he commit some fault due to his age; named from "leading the boy," which fits better with what follows: *to Christ*.

34 **That we might be justified by faith**] Ambrose reads *justificaremur, hina dikaiōthōmen*.

35 **There is no male nor female**] In the other pairs he used the conjunction *neque* [neither], but in this last pair he used *kai tō* [and the]; yet the conjunction has the same force: *male and female*. Jerome advises here that *Hellēna*, that is, *Greek*, is used for "Gentile."

36 **For you are all one**] Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine seem to read "one" in the neuter [*unum*], except that it is suspected Ambrose read "one" in the masculine [*unus*] from what he writes: *For with God there is no distinction of persons, except merit and life, so that men of one faith are distinguished by merits, not persons*. However, the Greeks read "one" in the masculine gender, *eis este*, and Theophylact interprets it: either because we have now put on the form of Christ, or because we are one body under one head, Christ. Chrysostom indeed reads *unus*, but his interpretation is such that it fits even if you read *unum*. And certainly, our reading is more approved by me, except that the Greek copies disagree with it by great consensus. Yet I do not see why we should shrink from this trope by which many are called "one" [masculine], just as they are called "one" [neuter] without a trope, or "unanimous."

37 **If however you are Christ’s**] In this place, I see the ancients read in three ways. Saint Jerome reads it in the way we find written in the Greek copies, *ei de hymeis Christou*, that is, *But if you are Christ’s*. Saint Augustine reads it this way: *You are all one in Christ Jesus*; then he adds, *But if...* so that with a sub-distinction interposed here, it is understood: *you are one in Christ*, and then it is inferred, *therefore you are Abraham’s seed*. Furthermore, what Augustine thinks should be understood, Ambrose makes explicit, reading in this manner: *If therefore you are one in Christ Jesus, therefore you are Abraham’s seed*. Jerome noted that whenever Christ is mentioned, the promises are placed in the singular number, as there: *Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed, that is, Christ*. Again, where it speaks of those who are Abraham’s through Christ, it is in the singular number, as in this place: *and heirs according to the promise*.

1 **I say...**

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s philological and theological commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians. Following the discussion in Chapter 3 regarding the Law as a "tutor," Erasmus now moves into Chapter 4, where Paul uses the legal metaphor of a minor heir to explain the transition from the old religious "elements" to the freedom of sonship in Christ.</meta>

# TO THE GALATIANS, CHAPTER IV.

IV. 1 ...heirs according to the promise. Now I say, as long as the heir is a child <note>Greek: *nepios*</note>, he does not differ at all from a slave, though he is the master of everything. 2 But he is under guardians and managers until the time set by the father. 3 So also we, when we were children, were enslaved under the basic elements <note>Greek: *stoicheia*</note> of the world. 4 But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, 5 to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. 6 And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, "Abba, Father!" 7 So you are no longer a slave, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ. 8 But at that time, when you did not know God, you served those who by nature are not gods. 9 But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how is it that you are turning back again to the weak and miserable elements, to which you want to be enslaved all over again? 10 You observe days and months and seasons and years. 11 I fear for you, lest I have labored for you in vain. 12 Become as I am, for I also became as you are, brothers, I beg you. You have done me no wrong. 13 You know that it was because of a physical infirmity <note>Greek: *astheneian tes sarkos*</note> that I preached the gospel to you the first time. 14 And though my condition in the flesh was a trial to you, you did not despise or loathe me, but welcomed me as an angel of God...

---

1 **Now I say** <note>Latin: *Dico autem*</note>] Paul is accustomed to speak in this manner whenever he enters into an interpretation of what he had previously said. Therefore, it would be clearer to say, "what I mean is this," or "this is what I am saying."

2 **The heir is a child** <note>Latin: *Hæres parvulus est*</note>] The Greek word *nepios* <note>νήπιος</note> refers to a boy or an infant, and specifically to that age which does not yet have legal discretion. However, the Latin Translator renders it as "child."

3 **He differs nothing from a slave** <note>Latin: *Nihil differt a servo*</note>] The Greek word *diapherei* <note>διαφέρει</note> is ambiguous. For it can mean "to differ" or "to excel." But in this passage, it means he is no different; indeed, he is subject to a slave.

4 **Under guardians and managers** <note>Latin: *Tutoribus & actoribus*</note>] The Greek terms are *epitropois* <note>ἐπιτρόποις</note> and *oikonomois* <note>οἰκονόμοις</note>, which mean curators and dispensers—that is, those who manage family property. Although Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine read "under actors" for the Greek *oikonomois*, referring to those who administer the affairs of minors. Furthermore, "tutors" were given to young wards, while "curators" were given to the mentally ill or adolescents to manage their affairs, though I believe these were also called "actors." "Actor" is an ambiguous word; the first Greek term implies an office of permitted judgment or right, the latter implies the management of domestic affairs.

5 **The pre-set time** <note>Latin: *Præfinitum tempus*</note>] The Greek is *prothesmias* <note>προθεσμίας</note>. This word signifies a prescribed limit until which a person's legal right lasts, beyond which they may no longer act; such is the legal status of tutors.

6 **Children** <note>Latin: *Parvuli*</note>] The Greek *nepioi* <note>νήπιοι</note>. I have already commented on this frequently.

7 **We were serving under the elements of the world** <note>Latin: *Sub elementis mundi eramus servientes*</note>] The Greek is *dedoulomenoi* <note>δεδουλωμένοι</note>, meaning "brought into slavery." Ambrose reads this as "subjected," and it should be referred back to "under the elements" <note>Greek: *hypo ta stoicheia*</note>, as if to say, "reduced to slavery under the elements." The Latin word "element" is ambiguous, just like the Greek *stoicheion* <note>στοιχεῖον</note>, which can mean the beginning or origin of a growing thing, or even the letters of the alphabet. For Aristotle, in his *Physics*, lists *stoicheia* (elements) among the things from which knowledge of things is born, placing them under principles and causes. And Justinian calls the books of the *Institutes* the "Elements of Law," like basic instructions. Paul used the same word in the Letter to the Colossians: "See that no one plunders you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world" <note>Greek: *stoicheia tou kosmou*</note>. And again in the same letter: "If you have died with Christ from the elements" <note>Greek: *apo ton stoicheion*</note>. I do not see why Saint Jerome wants "element" in this passage to Galatians to be one thing, and "element" in the Letter to the Colossians to be another. Certainly, in both places, Paul is dealing with Jewish ceremonies and human institutions, which were given as beginnings to people who were still unrefined and not yet capable of Evangelical teaching. This is no different from what he writes to the Hebrews: "And when you ought to be teachers because of the time, you have need again to be taught what the elements of the beginning of the words of God are" <note>Greek: *tina ta stoicheia tes arches*</note>. This sense seems genuine to me; the others, in my judgment, show off the learning or wit of the interpreter more than they show the mind of Paul. Nor is there any reason to be troubled that Paul added "of the world." For he calls "world" whatever is visible and fleeting. In such things is placed the superstition of ceremonies: "do not taste, do not touch, do not handle."

8 **God sent his Son** <note>Latin: *Misit Deus Filium*</note>] The Greek is *exapesteilen* <note>ἐξαπέστειλεν</note>, meaning "sent out," or rather "sent as an envoy," specifically with commands. For that is what the Greek word properly sounds like; it is different from the simple "to send" <note>Greek: *pemphein*</note>.

9 **Made from a woman** <note>Latin: *Factum ex muliere*</note>] The first "made" in Greek is *genomenon* <note>γενόμενον</note>, and the second is *genomenos* <note>γενόμενος</note>, so that you might translate the first as "born" and the second as "made." Although not all Greek manuscripts make this distinction. Certainly, Theophylactus reads *genomenon* in both places. But Augustine, in his book *On the Trinity and the Unity of God*, chapter 11, reports it this way: "God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law." And soon after in chapter 6 of the same work: "Made" here means nothing else than "subjected to the law," just as a person who has turned pale is said to be "made pale," lest anyone here should fruitlessly philosophize about the Son being a "creature."

10 **He might redeem** <note>Latin: *Redimeret*</note>] The Greek is *exagorase* <note>ἐξαγοράσῃ</note>, which literally sounds like "to buy out of the market"—that is, by paying a price, to assert into liberty, or as you might say, to release.

11 **That adoption** <note>Latin: *Ut adoptionem*</note>] The Greeks have a single word, *huiothesian* <note>υἱοθεσίαν</note>. The Translator, to express it more fully, used a paraphrase, because "adoption" might seem to have a broader meaning. "We might receive back" <note>Latin: *Reciperemus*; Greek: *apolabomen*</note>. Augustine notes that it says "receive back," not merely "receive," so that we might understand

that which was lost is being restored. This would have more standing if the Greek had said *apolabomen* <note>Erasmus is debating the nuance of the Greek prefix *apo-*, which implies a "return" to a previous state</note>.

12 **Because you are sons of God** <note>Latin: *Quoniam autem estis filii Dei*</note>] The word "God" is redundant according to the consistent Greek reading, nor does it add much to the sense; Paul is simply discussing the status of free children. All the Latin authors I have seen disagree, except for a very ancient manuscript of Donatianus.

13 **Into your hearts** <note>Latin: *In corda vestra*</note>] The Greek is *hemon* <note>ἡμῶν</note>, meaning "our," which is consistent with the Greek in both the Constantinensian manuscripts, as well as Ambrose and Jerome. However, because the word "you are" <note>Latin: *estis*</note> preceded it, an inattentive reader corrupted the text. And as was shown above, "Abba, Father" <note>Greek: *Abba ho Pater*</note> is not a repetition <note>term: *anadiplosis*—a rhetorical repetition</note> according to Jerome, Augustine, and if I am not mistaken, Ambrose. Rather, "Abba" is a foreign word, common to the Hebrews and Syrians; it is interpreted by the addition of the Greek word. This is a peculiar custom of Holy Scripture, like "Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus" in the Gospel; "Aser, riches"; "Tabitha, Dorcas" in Acts; and in Genesis "Mesech, house-born," and other similar examples.

14 **He is no longer a slave** <note>Latin: *Jam non est servus*</note>] It is "You are" <note>Latin: *Es*</note>, in the second person, not the third person "is." In some copies, the verb is not added at all. It is simply "no longer a slave" <note>Greek: *ouk eti doulos*</note>, so that "you are" <note>Greek: *ei*</note> is understood. And the Translator is too fond of his "now" <note>Latin: *jam*</note>, sometimes delighting in untimely variety; the Greek is *ouk eti ei*, which means "you are not henceforth" or "you are no longer."

15 **And an heir through God** <note>Latin: *Et hæres per Deum*</note>] "And an heir of God through Christ" <note>Greek: *kai kleronomos Theou dia Christou*</note>. Jerome reads, "And an heir through Christ," omitting the mention of God. Ambrose and Augustine read as our Edition has it. Jerome's reading is more pleasing to me. Furthermore, "of God" seems to have been added by some translator. For "heir" was complete enough if you add nothing else, as it stands in opposition to "slave." Finally, in adding "through Christ," Paul acted according to his custom; he wants all God's benefits to proceed to us from the Father in such a way that they come to us through Christ the Son, as if grafted into Christ. Through him, by adoption, we are both sons and heirs. In this place, Theophylactus has more, reading: "if a son then an heir, an heir indeed of God, but a co-heir of Christ." He interprets it just as he reads it. But what is extra here appears to have been transcribed from the eighth chapter of the Letter to the Romans.

16 **When you have known** <note>Latin: *Cum cognoveritis*</note>] The Greek is *Nyn de gnontes Theon*, meaning "But now, after you have known God."

17 **Or rather have been known** <note>Latin: *Imo cogniti sitis*</note>] The Greek is *mallon de*, meaning "but rather." Jerome reads it thus. Although "rather" in this place serves more as a correction than a comparison.

18 **To which again** <note>Latin: *Quibus denuo*</note>] Instead of "again" <note>Latin: *denuo*</note>, the Greeks have *palin anothen*, meaning "again from the beginning." This repetition <note>term: *anadiplosis*</note> adds to the intensity. We translate it as "again from the start."

19 **And seasons** <note>Latin: *Et tempora*</note>] The Greek is *kairous*, meaning "opportunities" or "appointed times." It is not merely "time" <note>Greek: *chronos*</note>. These refer to the festival days of the Jews, on which this or that was permitted or forbidden.

20 **I fear lest** <note>Latin: *Times ne*</note>] The Greek is *Phoboumai hymas*, meaning "I fear you." Ambrose and Augustine read it this way, and it is found thus in ancient manuscripts. It could be translated as "I fear for you."

21 **Brothers, I beg you** <note>Latin: *Fratres, obsecro vos*</note>] The Greek is *deomai hymon*, meaning "I ask you." Saint Jerome wants these words to refer to what preceded in this manner: "Brothers, I beg you, be as I am, since I am as you are"—that is, cast off the Jewish superstition, which you see I have cast off. Or, advance to my perfection, since I have inclined myself to your weakness. For as Valla prefers "how" instead of "as," not only here but also in the following passage.

22 **Long ago** <note>Latin: *Jam pridem*</note>] The Greek is "previously" <note>Greek: *proteron*</note>.

23 **Your trial** <note>Latin: *Tentationem vestram*</note>] The Greek is *peirasmon mou*, meaning "my trial" or "the trial of me"—rather "my trial," so that you understand Paul tried the Galatians with his humble and unpolished speech. Although the Greek phrasing is ambiguous, and Jerome explains it in various ways. Certainly, the trial of the Galatians was that a humble man, subject to human ills, while preaching Christ crucified and nothing else magnificent, nevertheless promised immortality. Or certainly, he suffered from ill health there, and when they saw his little body afflicted with disease...

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, specifically focusing on the transition from the physical Law to spiritual promise. Erasmus here analyzes the Greek vocabulary of Paul’s emotional appeals and his famous allegory of the two covenants represented by Hagar and Sarah.</meta>

## PAUL'S EPISTLE CHAPTER IV.

**15** ...as an angel of God you received me, even as Christ Jesus. Where then was your sense of blessing? For I bear you witness that, if possible, you would have plucked out your own eyes and given them to me. **16** Have I therefore become your enemy because I tell you the truth? **17** They are zealous for you, but not for good; rather, they wish to shut you out, so that you might be zealous for them. **18** But it is good to be zealous in a good thing always, and not only when I am present with you. **19** My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you. **20** I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, for I am perplexed by you. **21** Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not hear the law? **22** For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. **23** But the one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, **24** while the one by the free woman was through the promise. These things are spoken as an allegory; for these are two covenants, one from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery, which is Hagar. **25** For Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, and it corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.

---

**15** *Since, however, they believed the one preaching immortality.* There are those who think Paul was vexed by frequent headaches, and that he called this his "thorn from Satan." Or, what is closer to the truth, they saw their Apostle loaded with insults, driven by persecutions, beaten with whips, and overwhelmed by stones. These things could have alienated them from their admiration of him. However, we do not read that the Lord himself or the Apostles suffered from any disease.

**24** *Where is it then?* <note>original: "Tís oûn ên"</note>, that is, "what then was it." This is how Ambrose reads it. Furthermore, "blessedness" is not <term>makariotes</term> <note>a state of bliss</note>, but <term>makarismos</term> <note>the act of being pronounced blessed</note>, which sounds more like *beatification*, from the verb <term>makarizein</term>, which means to call or judge someone blessed. Saint Jerome <note>A 4th-century scholar and Bible translator</note> clearly indicates this with these words: *You ask, he says, at that time when you received the Gospel according to the flesh, should I call you blessed because you were fervent at the start? Yet now, because I do not see the roof placed upon the building, and the foundations almost laid in vain, I am forced to say: where is your blessedness, by which I previously praised you, judging you blessed?* Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine commentator</note> explains it the same way, namely as the praise by which they were proclaimed by everyone because they were "lovers of teaching" <note>original: "philodidaskaloi"</note>.

**25** *They are zealous for you]* <note>original: "Zeloûsin hymâs"</note>. Although this word has various uses among the Greeks, in this place it is rightly translated as "They love," or "They affect," or "They court," and they suffer from a kind of jealousy toward you, as Jerome notes at the end. For he is dealing with certain people who, under the pretext of love and devotion toward the Galatians, were acting to drag them back into the slavery of the Mosaic Law.

**26** *But to exclude you]* The Greek is <term>ekkleisai</term>, which means to shut out. Although the Greek manuscripts vary here—some having <term>ekkleisai</term> (to exclude), others <term>enkleisai</term> (to include or involve)—it means to exclude them from the liberty of Christ. Theophylact reads and interprets it as "to exclude." For he is excluded who is not admitted, and he is excluded who is cast out. Would that today there were no one among Christians to whom this complaint of Paul applies.

**27** *That you might be zealous for them]* <note>original: "hína autoùs zeloûte"</note>, that you might be zealous for them, or for themselves.

**28** *It is good to be zealous in a good thing]* <note>original: "Kalòn dè tò zeloûsthai en kalô"</note>, that is, it is always good to be zealous in a good matter. It is good to want to imitate others, but not in just any matter, only in a good one. Augustine reads it this way: *It is good, he says, to be zealous in a good thing always.* The translators seem to have read <term>zeloûsthe</term>, so the last syllable ends in "e" <note>epsilon</note>. In the Greek sound, one cannot distinguish between "to be zealous" and "be you zealous." Indeed, the infinitive could be taken for an imperative, were the article not added. However, "to be zealous" means one thing in the first instance and another in the following two, where it does not simply mean "to imitate," but to imitate with admiration and a desire to follow. For this is what he says more clearly a little later: *that they may glory in your flesh.*

**29** *When I am present with you]* Although everyone agrees, the Greek phrasing is ambiguous and could also have this sense: <note>original: "mê mónon en tô pareînaí me pròs hymâs"</note>, not only in the fact that I am present with you, because he said "in a good thing" before. For what is honorable must always be followed, even if the one who delivered it is absent. He implies that his absence was the reason they slipped away elsewhere.

**30** *I wish I could be with you now]* "Now" <note>Latin: "modo"</note> in this place stands for <term>arti</term> <note>at this moment</note>. And it is not "to be," but <term>pareînai</term>, that is, "to be present."

**31** *Because I am confounded in you]* <note>original: "aporoûmai"</note>, that is, I am perplexed or I am at a loss, for so Saint Jerome explains it. Although among the Greeks <term>aporeîsthai</term> sometimes means to be without resources or counsel. Paul was so affected that he did not know what to do with the Galatians, whom he saw tending entirely toward the slavery of the law, and this because great Apostles (as it was thought) were calling them there. Furthermore, the common people make no distinction between "confusion," which the Greeks call <term>synchysis</term>, and "shame" or "blushing," which is <term>aischynê</term> or <term>entropê</term>. But it is one thing to be ashamed and blush, and another to be troubled in mind so that you do not know what should be done. Even if it is sometimes twisted to mean a powerful shame that usually disturbs the mind and pours darkness over it, as in Euripides: *what an unworthy name for misfortune is confusion.* Although here too "perplexed" can be understood more than "shamed." There was no reason for the word "confounded" to be used here, unless the Translator elsewhere willingly and frequently used it for "to blush"; otherwise, it beautifully explained the Greek word <term>aporoûmai</term>.

<column-break/>

**15** ...nor did you reject me, but you received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus. <margin>A</margin> **24** What then is your blessedness? For I bear witness to you that, if it could have been done, you would have plucked out your eyes and given them to me. **16** Have I then become an enemy to you by speaking the truth to you? **17** They court you not for good, **26** rather they wish to exclude you, **27** so that you might be zealous for them. **28** But it is good to be zealous in a good thing always, and not only **29** when I am present with you. My little children, for whom I labor again, until Christ is formed in you. **20** I wish I could be present with you now, and change my voice, **31** because I am at a loss regarding you. **21** Tell me, you who wish to be under the law, **32** do you not hear the law itself? **22** For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. <margin>B</margin> **23** But he who was born of the slave woman was born according to the flesh; but he of the free woman was through the promise. **33** These things are said through allegory: **34** for these are two testaments, **35** one indeed from Mount Sinai, bearing children into slavery, which is Hagar. For Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, **36** and it borders on that which is now called Jerusalem, and she is in slavery with her children...

---

<margin>A</margin> **32** *You have not read the Law]* In Greek it is "you hear" <note>original: "akoúete"</note>. Jerome reads "you have heard," unless there is an error. For I believe it was written "you have heard." This figure of speech <note>trope</note> has its own grace, as if the law itself were speaking, forbidding that it be observed hereafter. Therefore, by the very fact that they affected to observe the law, they were rebelling against the law.

**33** *Spoken through allegory]* <note>original: "allêgoroúmena"</note>, that is, things which are being said through allegory. <margin>C</margin> An allegory is when one thing is said and another is signified. Augustine, in the fifteenth book of *On the Trinity*, chapter nine, testifies that he read "which are in allegory." And since "allegory" is a Greek word, some Latin translators rendered it "those which signify one thing from another." Chrysostom <note>A famous 4th-century preacher</note> warns that Paul misused this word "allegory" to mean a "type" or "figure." For an allegory is properly a sustained metaphor. But the Apostle here refers to a true history which is a type of another thing.

**34** *For these are two testaments]* Chrysostom asks what the word "these" <note>original: "haûtai"</note> refers to. It refers to the two mothers, the slave Hagar and the free Sarah, who were mentioned before. This is smoother in the Greek language, in which "testament" <note>original: "diathêkê"</note> is of the feminine gender. And again, the word "are" is used to mean "signify."

**35** *One indeed on the mountain]* In Greek it is "From the mountain" <note>original: "apò órous"</note>. And both Jerome and Ambrose read it this way. Nor was the Donatian codex any different. In the other Constantiensian codex—the older one—the genuine writing remained, while in the other, it was erased by the work of a corrupter. However, this passage has been corrupted in many ways. <margin>D</margin> Furthermore, the Greek has it thus: *from Mount Sinai, bearing children into slavery, which is Hagar. For Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, it is joined to the one which is now Jerusalem, and she serves with her children. But the Jerusalem above is free, which is the mother of us all.* The Greek scholia <note>ancient marginal notes</note>, and with them Theophylact, advise that Mount Sinai is called "Hagar" in the language of the Arabs. It is the same mountain, but with different names. Yet Jerome mentions nothing of this sort in his commentaries on this Epistle. Augustine and Ambrose read "which [neuter] is Hagar," not "who [feminine] is Hagar." Although both readings express the same sense, because a relative pronoun placed between <margin>E</margin> two nouns usually agrees with either one; for "testaments" preceded it, and the name of the woman "Hagar" follows. Except that when we read "who is Hagar," it is ambiguous whether "who" refers to the slavery, even if by this reading the sense ends up being almost the same. Indeed, the word "is" in this place stands for "signifies," as in that type "the rock was Christ," as Augustine notes in several places. It matters very little whether Hagar is a type of the testament bearing children into the slavery of the law, or of the slavery itself which the testament possessed. Furthermore, that word "bearing children" must necessarily refer to the testament, which he intends to be signified in the type of Hagar. Then, what is said—"For the [neuter] Hagar"—pertains not to the slave woman but to the mountain, which is detected even from the gender itself, because "mountain" among the Greeks is neuter. Ambrose seems to have retained the Greek gender <margin>F</margin> when he says "bearing children into slavery, which [neuter] is Hagar," unless one prefers the relative word to pertain to the context of the speech—that is, "which is to say, to generate into slavery." For Hagar, whether as the slave woman or the mountain having received its name from the slave woman, bore the type of this thing. Furthermore, what he adds—"which is now Jerusalem"—pertains to the fact that this city was formerly called by other names: first Jebus, then Salem, then Jerusalem (as if a name composed from both), and finally Aelia. It should not seem strange if common usage said Jerusalem for Jebusalem, since it turned Salem into Solyma, and Jerusalem into Hierosolyma.

**36** *Which is joined to that which is now Jerusalem]* <note>original: "systoicheî dè tê nûn Hierousalêm"</note>. For "is joined to," we translate "is bordering on." For Saint Jerome used this word when explaining this passage. Nor does it matter that Mount Sinai is separated by a journey of many days from Mount Sion. For Paul here is not measuring the distance of the journey, but is comparing the similarity of the allegory. For things which correspond to each other by some similarity are called "neighboring" and "bordering," which Paul said in Greek as <term>systoichei</term>, as if you were to say they are "in the same series." From this, grammarians also call letters <term>systoichia</term> because they are joined to each other in a certain series. Philosophers call the elements of things <term>stoicheia</term>...

<meta>Catchword: cant [they can]</meta>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, specifically focusing on the transition from the physical Law to spiritual promise. Erasmus here analyzes the Greek vocabulary of Paul’s emotional appeals and his famous allegory of the two covenants represented by Hagar and Sarah.</meta>

# TO THE GALATIANS. CHAPTER V.

**26** But the Jerusalem above is free, which is the mother of us all. **27** For it is written: *Rejoice, you barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry out, you who are not in labor; for the children of the desolate are many, more than those of her who has a husband.* <note>Erasmus is quoting Paul, who is in turn quoting Isaiah 54:1, comparing the Church (the "barren woman" who becomes fruitful) to the Jewish Synagogue.</note> **28** But we, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise. **29** But just as then the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the spirit, so it is now. **30** But what does the scripture say? *Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.* **31** Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman, but of the free woman.

**V. 1** In the freedom, therefore, with which Christ has made us free, stand fast, and do not be entangled again in a yoke of slavery. **2** Look, I, Paul, say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will benefit you nothing. **3** And I testify again to every man being circumcised that he is a debtor to keep the whole law. **4** You have been severed from Christ, you who are justified in the law; you have fallen from grace. **5** For we through the Spirit by faith wait for the hope of righteousness. **6** For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision is of any force, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love. **7** You were running well; who cut you off from obeying the truth? **8** This persuasion is not from him who...

---

...they speak of, for example, earth, water, air, and fire, because each of these stands in its own order. Likewise, verses are called *stichoi* <note>Greek: στίχοι</note>, and battle lines arranged in order are called *stichoi*, which words and others like them are derived from the verb *steichein* <note>Greek: στείχειν</note>, which means to go forward in order, or to stand in a series. Moreover, Mount Sinai, although separated by a long distance from Jerusalem, is nevertheless contiguous to it by this similarity: just as the law was first brought forth on Sinai with great terrors, so in Mount Sion the same law was promulgated and even propagated to foreigners, according to the prophecy: *Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.* 

However, the Apostle says this in this place to show that the law without grace strikes terror with threats and precepts, and to be driven by fear is a slavish thing. Thus the Jews, who were empty of charity and observed the law according to the letter and external rites, even though they had moved from Mount Sinai to Jerusalem, they did not degenerate from their slavish condition, being as it were children of Hagar, not Sarah. The word *systoichein* <note>Greek: συστοιχεῖν, meaning "to correspond" or "stand in the same row"</note> is found in this sense among approved Greek authors, notably in Theophrastus *On Causes*, and Aristotle in his *Metaphysics*. Nor is Suidas silent about this word in his entry for *stoicheia* <note>Greek: στοιχεια, meaning "elements" or "principles"</note>, for here things are called such when they are of the same order and lot. And these elements are placed in a series of similar things, just as if you place the letters p, k, t together, they would be one *systoichia* <note>Greek: συστοιχία</note>, for they agree in that they are thin sounds. 

Another is opposed to this, containing ph, ch, th. And these elements compared among themselves are *systoicha* <note>Greek: σύστοιχα, "parallel"</note>, but compared to the upper series, they are *antistoicha* <note>Greek: ἀντίστοιχα, "opposite"</note>. Saint Chrysostom interprets *systoichei* as "neighbors and touches" <note>Greek original: γειτνιάζει καὶ ἅπτεται</note>, that is, it is near and contiguous. Theophylact interprets the same more clearly, adding that this vicinity is not of place, but of similarity. And the *Gloss*, which is called "Ordinary," explains it by the word "joined" as "similar." But Aquinas rejects this interpretation because he thinks this was not the mind of Paul, and soon says Mount Sinai was called joined to Jerusalem because the Israelites traveled from there to here; so that we understand the mountain of Arabia to be bordering Jerusalem, not by proximity of site, but by the continuation of a journey. 

This commentary is opposed by the word *systoichein* being in the present tense, which Ambrose translates as "who is joined." But the journey had preceded by many centuries. He who collected the scholia on all Paul's Epistles writes thus on this place: *From the qualities of places he wants the diversity of testaments to be understood.* This man, whoever he was, seems to have felt that Sinai is a type of the Old Testament, Jerusalem of the New. If we accept this, how are they said to *systoichein*? To me, Paul seems to equate the Arab and Jerusalem Jews, because both equally served the law and belonged to the Synagogue, not to the Church. But to the earthly Jerusalem, which he does not distinguish from Mount Sinai, he opposes the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the Church. It is strange, however, that neither Jerome nor Ambrose touch upon this difficulty regarding the vicinity.

**37** *Rejoice, you barren woman who does not bear;* He brings forth testimony from Isaiah chapter 54. Jerome rendered the Hebrew thus: *Praise, you barren woman who does not bear, sing praise and neigh, you who did not travail, for many are the children of the deserted more than of her who has a husband.* But according to the Septuagint <note>The early Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> we read in this manner: *Rejoice, you barren woman who does not bear, break out and cry, you who are not in labor, because many are the children of the desert more than of her who has a husband.* Symmachus translates it thus: *Rejoice, you barren woman, who did not give birth, rejoice in exultation and neigh, you who did not travail, for more are the children of the dissipated one more than of her who was under a husband.* Theodotion and Aquila do not differ from this, except in a few words. From this it is clear that in this place Paul used the words of the Septuagint, because in everything the sense agrees with the Hebrew truth.

**38** *With the son of the free woman;* Jerome reads, *with my son Isaac.* And indeed it is read thus in Genesis chapter twenty-one. Ambrose reads in the same way. All the more I wonder from where this scripture invaded the Greek and our codices. It is not clear enough from the interpretation of Theophylact what he read, though his context agrees with our common reading. Chrysostom reads as the Latins do and does not refer to the sense; the Apostle substituted the person of Scripture for the person of Sarah...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...Jerusalem, but she is in slavery with her children. But the Jerusalem 26 that is above is free, which is the mother of us all. For it is written, 27 *Rejoice, you barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry, you who do not travail, because many are the children of the desolate more than of her who has a husband.* 28 But we, brothers, are children of promise according to Isaac. 29 But just as then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the spirit, so also now. 30 But what does the scripture say? *Cast out the slave woman and her son: for the son of the slave woman shall not be an heir with the son of the free woman.* Therefore, 31 <margin>B</margin> brothers, we are not children of the slave woman, but of the free woman. In the liberty, therefore, V. 1. with which Christ has set us free, stand fast, and do not be entangled again in the yoke of slavery. Behold, I, Paul, say 2 to you, that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing. And I testify to every man who is 3 circumcised, that he is a debtor to keep the whole law. Christ 4 has become useless to you, whoever of you are justified by the law, you have fallen from grace. For we by the spirit from 5 faith wait for the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Je- 6 sus neither circumcision prevails for anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith which works through love. You were running 7 well, who hindered you, that you should not believe the truth? 8 <margin>C</margin> Surely this persuasion is not from him who calls you.

---

...to the person of Scripture, so that there would be more weight, and he rendered the sense conveniently to the cause he is treating. In this testimony, Paul followed neither the Hebrew authority nor the Septuagint, content to render the sense of the Scripture in his own words. *By what liberty Christ, etc.* The Greek has it thus: *In the freedom, therefore, with which Christ has made us free, stand, and not,* that is, so that "liberty" belongs to the following words, not the preceding ones. Although Jerome translates otherwise, and Ambrose and Augustine read otherwise, beginning a new head of the speech here: *Stand therefore, etc.* Chrysostom and Theophylact clearly agree with me, separating <note>unclear: even by the word</note> the commentary itself from those things which follow; nor could the Translator change this. It does not matter much to the sense.

<margin>D</margin> **1** *Entangled* <note>Greek: μὴ ἐνέχεσθε</note>, that is, do not be liable, or be involved, or be pressed down by those things.

**2** *Circumcised* <note>Greek: ἢ περιτεμνομένη</note>, that is, he who is circumcised.

**3** *You are evacuated from Christ* <note>Greek: Κατηργήθητε ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ</note>. The Translator constantly renders this word thus, since it signifies something being abolished and becoming void and idle, and as if obsolete. It is the same as what he said a little above: *Christ will profit you nothing:* if you add yourselves to the law of Moses, Christ is for you obsolete and idle. Jerome indicates that this word *katargeisthai* <note>Greek: καταργεῖσθαι</note> is not correctly translated by the Translator, since it is rather to cease from work: for *argos* <note>Greek: αργὸς</note> is idle, as if *a-ergos* [without work]: from which *katargeisthai* was said.

**4** *Works through charity;* Again here, "working" does not signify what the common people dream, but that which exercises its hidden power in us, which is proper to the Spirit. For the power is felt, though it itself appears nowhere. For he wants the law to seem little effective, but faith effective: *energoumenē* <note>Greek: ἐνεργουμένη</note>, which could have been more correctly translated as "acting."

<margin>E</margin> **5** *Who has bewitched you;* <note>Greek: ἐβάσκανεν</note>. Which Jerome and Ambrose translate as *hindered.* And the Ordinary Gloss indicates that in the Latin codices there was a double reading, while among the Greeks there is only one. Certainly, in the codex of Donatianus I found it written as *bewitched.* From this place it seems to have been added, *to not believe the truth*, about which we warned above in chapter III. And what he translated there as *to not believe*, here he translates as *to not obey*. Indeed, Jerome warns here that all of this—*to not obey the truth*—is not found in the ancient codices: even if the Greek codices are confused by this error. Although in this place there is no difference between the Greek and Latin codices, except that the former read *hindered*, not *bewitched*, nevertheless not even here does that little part matter much to the sense. For the sense was full: *You were running well, who interrupted your course?* 

Again, another argument that this Edition is not purely Jerome's: for he, with the Greeks, reads *hindered*. *You should consent to no one.* And Jerome passes over this little part as if it were an addition, since it is found neither in the Greek codices, nor among any of those who wrote commentaries on Paul. Even if the translator of Theophylact added it from his own in the context, since it is neither among the Greeks nor is there any mention made in the interpretation. Certainly it was not added in the codex of Donatianus, nor in either of the Constantian ones. And yet one might almost dare to say that Ambrose added this part, but did not add the earlier one, *to not believe the truth*, for he explains it thus: *He testifies that their exercise in the work of faith was good, but that they were detained by the wickedness of evil men, lest they should finish their course with persevering duty: whence he exhorts them to repent, believing none of those for the rest, who, to persuade them that the works of the law were to be kept, allowed them not to obey the Evangelical truth.* Certainly in the context of Ambrose this part is not added, "consent to no one," nor even in Augustine.

<margin>F</margin> **6** *The persuasion is not here, etc.* In the Greek there is neither *this*, nor *yours*, as Augustine reads, but only *The Persuasion* <note>Greek: Ἡ πεισμονὴ</note>. Although it does not clash much, except that here it signifies persuasion, not obedience, so that it refers to the earlier question: *who hindered you while running well?* Surely the persuasion of some calling you away to Mosaic ceremonies, which persuasion did not proceed from Christ, who called you to another thing, namely to spiritual things.

<summary>Erasmus provides a detailed philological analysis of Galatians 4 and 5, focusing on the Greek term "systoichein" to explain the relationship between the Law and the Gospel, while critiquing various manuscript traditions and the interpretations of the Church Fathers.</summary>

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER V.

<margin>9</margin> ...calls you. A little leaven leavens the whole <margin>10</margin> batch of dough. I have confidence in you in the Lord, that you will think nothing else. But the one who troubles you will bear the <margin>11</margin> judgment, whoever he may be. But I, brothers, if I still preach circumcision, why am I still persecuted? In that case, the stumbling block of the cross <margin>12</margin> has been abolished. I wish that those who upset <margin>13</margin> you would even cut themselves off! For you were called to freedom, brothers; only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love <margin>14</margin> serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word, in this: You shall love your neighbor <margin>15</margin> as yourself. But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another. <margin>16</margin> But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will <margin>17</margin> not carry out the desire of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to each other, so that you do not do whatever you <margin>18</margin> want. But if you are led by the Spirit, <margin>19</margin> you are not under the law. Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are: adultery, fornication, uncleanness, <margin>20</margin> lewdness, Idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousies, outbursts of anger, selfish ambitions, dissensions, <margin>21</margin> heresies, Envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these, of which I tell you beforehand, just as I also told you before, that those who practice such things will not <margin>22</margin> inherit the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the Spirit is: love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, <margin>23</margin> goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control. Against such...

<column-break/>

<margin>9</margin> ...of you, Paul, [does a little] leaven [leaven] the whole batch? I trust in you in the Lord, <margin>A 10</margin> that you will feel nothing else. But he who disturbs you shall bear his judgment, whoever he may be. I, however, brothers, if <margin>11</margin> I still preach circumcision, why do I still suffer persecution? The stumbling block of the <margin>12</margin> cross is therefore abolished. I wish that those who undermine you would even be cut off. For you have been called into freedom, brothers: <margin>13</margin> only do not give freedom as an occasion to the flesh, but through charity serve one another. For the whole <margin>14</margin> law is completed in one word, namely this: You shall love <margin>15</margin> your neighbor as yourself. But if you in turn bite and devour one another, see that you are not in turn consumed <margin>B 16</margin> by one another. I say, however, walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the lust of the flesh. For <margin>17</margin> the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh: for these are mutually opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever things you might wish. But if you are led by the spirit, you are not under the law. Furthermore, <margin>18 19</margin> the works of the flesh are manifest, which are these: adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, <margin>20</margin> worship of idols, sorcery, enmities, strife, emulations, wraths, contentions, seditions, sects, Envy, murders, <margin>21</margin> drunkenness, revelries, and things like these, concerning which I forewarn you, just as I have already forewarned you, that those who do such things shall not be heirs of the kingdom of God. On the contrary, the <margin>22</margin> fruit of the Spirit is: charity, joy, peace, gentleness, kindness, goodness, faith, mildness, temperance. <margin>C 23</margin> Against...

---

<margin>7</margin> **Corrupts the whole mass** <note>original: *Totam massam corrumpit*</note>] *Leavens the whole batch of dough* <note>original: ὅλον τὸ φύραμα ζυμοῖ</note>, that is, it ferments the whole mixture; for Saint Jerome translates it thus in his Commentaries, openly condemning and rejecting the word "mass" <note>original: *massae*</note>. Yet he does not give a reason why he rejects it, nor does he refrain from using the condemned word in his interpretation. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that *massa* is a Latin word, even if *conspersio* (mixture/batch) is found in this sense in Columella <note>A Roman writer on agriculture</note> and more accurately expresses the Greek word *phyrama*. This very passage argues that the common translation is not Jerome's, as it contains a phrasing which he himself testifies to have corrected. Instead of "corrupts," Jerome reads "leavens" <note>original: *fermentat*</note>. For the Greek is *zymoi*. Indeed, something is not immediately "corrupted" just because it is affected by leaven. For Christ compares his doctrine to leaven hidden in flour.

<margin>8</margin> **You will be of no other mind** <note>original: *Nihil aliud sapietis*</note>] *Phronēsete*. Ambrose translates this better as "you will feel" <note>original: *sentietis*</note>, meaning you will not be of a different opinion, and you will not think about innovating your way of life. For "nothing else" means nothing different, nothing new. Just as we say, "something other than that."

<margin>9</margin> **Whoever he is** <note>original: *Quicumque est ille*</note>] *Hostis an ē*, that is, "whoever he might be" or "whoever he is." And so Saint Ambrose reads it.

<margin>10</margin> **Therefore the stumbling block is made void** <note>original: *Ergo evacuatum est scandalum*</note>] *Ara katērgētai*, that is, "Therefore it has ceased." Saint Jerome explains this quite elegantly as what is commonly called "annulled" <note>original: *cassatum*</note>. He notes here also that the Greek word expresses Paul’s mind more correctly than the Latin. For something is "annulled" when it has ceased to have force.

<margin>11</margin> **I wish they were cut off** <note>original: *Utinam abscindantur*</note>] *I wish they would even be cut off* <note>original: καὶ ἀποκόψονται</note>, with the conjunction added, that is, "may they even be amputated" or "cut away." There is some emphasis in the conjunction: not only should they be judged, but they should even be made anathema, utterly cut off from your fellowship. Or, those who want you to be circumcised, let them be completely cut off <note>Erasmus is hinting at castration here, as circumcision is a partial cutting</note>, so that Paul imprecates the cutting off of the whole member against those who teach circumcision. Ambrose touches on this meaning, as does Theophylactus following Chrysostom, but the former seems to me more worthy of Apostolic gravity. Augustine turns a curse into a blessing, interpreting it thus: *As if Paul prays for the false apostles, not that they be circumcised, but cut off*, that is, *that they become eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven: for thus it would happen that they cease preaching Jewish circumcision*. He preferred to embrace this clever interpretation rather than attribute a curse to Paul.

<margin>12</margin> **Who trouble you** <note>original: *Qui vos conturbant*</note>] *Hoi anastatountes hymas*, that is, those who move you from your position. Hence Ambrose reads, "these who subvert you." We have translated it as "those who undermine you." For he was referring to what he had said, "you stand fast." That which is moved from its state is "undermined." Theophylactus carefully notes the emphasis of this word, following Chrysostom.

<margin>13</margin> **Give for an occasion to the flesh** <note>original: *in occasionem detis carni*</note>] The verb "give" is not found in the Greek. And "to the flesh" is produced in the dative case, not the genitive "of the flesh." And one must understand "give," as Saint Jerome advises, or something more suitable. It appears that Valla refers the accusative "freedom" to the verb that follows, "serve," as if to say, "do not serve your freedom to the flesh." But that, besides being far from everyone's opinion, is somewhat harsh and forced. Theophylactus thinks we should understand *echoimen*, that is, "that we might have." Certainly, as I just said, Jerome testifies that the word "give" was added by the Translator, not placed there by Paul. I do not know what peculiar grace this "aposiopesis" <note>A rhetorical device where a sentence is broken off and left unfinished</note> has in deterring those whom you would not wish to offend.

<margin>14</margin> **But through the charity of the spirit** <note>original: *Sed per charitatem spiritus*</note>] "Spirit" is not found in the Greek manuscripts, nor in Jerome, nor in Augustine; I only remember reading it in Ambrose, who also interprets it so that it is what he opposes to the flesh.

<margin>15</margin> **You shall love your neighbor** <note>original: *Diliges proximum tuum*</note>] The Greeks have: *namely in this, You shall love your neighbor*, etc. Hence we also translate it thus. Augustine notes with many words that the love of God is silent here because it can be feigned, whereas love of neighbor can more easily be

<column-break/>

proven. And it follows that he who treats his neighbor harshly does not love God either. Ambrose suggests the same, though more obscurely. I thought this should be noted lest anyone add on his own what was omitted, as if it were left out by Paul.

<margin>16</margin> **You bite and eat** <note>original: *Mordetis & comeditis*</note>] Instead of "eat," Ambrose reads "slander" <note>original: *criminatis*</note>, if indeed the manuscript is free of error. I wonder if his copy had *ekballete*, that is, "you calumniate."

<margin>17</margin> **I say, however, in Christ** <note>original: *Dico autem in Christo*</note>] "In Christ" is not added among the Greeks, nor in Jerome, nor in Ambrose, not even in the oldest Pauline manuscript; both codices of the Church of Constance agree; it is only, *I say, however, walk by the Spirit*. For thus he indicates where this whole discourse is heading.

<margin>18</margin> **And the desires** <note>original: *Et desideria*</note>] In Greek it is "desire" <note>singular: *epithymian*</note>. Ambrose <margin>D</margin> reads "you shall not fulfill the concupiscence of the flesh," though these differ nothing in meaning.

<margin>19</margin> **For these [are] to each other** <note>original: *Hæc enim sibi invicem*</note>] Among the Greeks, instead of "for" <note>enim</note> it is "but" <note>de/autem</note>. Although that matters little to the sense.

<margin>20</margin> **Which are** <note>original: *Quæ sunt*] In reviewing most lists of this kind, the Latin differs somewhat from the Greek, I believe through the forgetfulness of scribes. In Greek, they are: *adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousies, wraths, contentions, dissensions, sects, envies, murders, drunkenness, revelries*. This is also how Chrysostom reads it, except that in the first place he reports "fornication." Saint Jerome reads it thus: *Which are fornication, uncleanness, impudicity, service of idols, sorceries, enmities, contentions, emulations, wraths, brawls, dissensions, heresies, envies, drunkennness, revelries*. <margin>E</margin> Ambrose reads it in this manner: *Adultery, fornication, impurity, obscenity, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, contentions, simulations, wraths, simultaneous feuds, dissensions, heresies, envies, drunkenness, revelries*. If anyone wishes to be more fully informed about each of these, let him read Saint Jerome’s Commentaries on this passage. We have already noted in the Epistle to the Romans that in *phthonoi* (envies) and *phonoi* (murders) there is a pleasant wordplay <note>allusion of voices</note> which the Translator was not even able to render. Nor are the "asyndeton" <note>omission of conjunctions</note> and "homoeoptota" <note>words with similar endings</note> without their own charm.

<margin>21</margin> **They will not obtain** <note>original: *Non consequentur*] *They will not inherit* <note>original: οὐ κληρονομήσουσιν</note>: for which Jerome <margin>F</margin> puts "they will possess." And more expressively Ambrose: "they will not obtain the inheritance of the kingdom of God."

<margin>22</margin> **Patience** <note>original: *Patientia*] *Makrothymia*, that is, "long-suffering," or mildness of mind, which the Translator, in his usual way, almost always renders as "patience," which is more frequently said of the body than the mind. Even if Saint Jerome thinks it makes no difference. Ambrose translates it as "gentleness." And this catalog of the fruits of the Spirit in Greek is: *love, joy, peace, long-suffering, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control*. Saint Jerome, writing against Jovinian, reads it así: *charity, joy, peace, long-suffering, kindness, goodness, faith, mildness, continence*. Ambrose reads it in this way: *charity, joy, peace, long-suffering, kindness, hope, gentleness, continence, chastity, goodness, etc.* Accordingly, I do not think the anxious diligence of some is much to be approved, who in catalogs of this kind usually labor over the number, and are superstitiously tortured in distinguishing each one, when it is probable that Paul produced a certain heap of evils and goods that usually follow, not because these are the only ones, but because the sum of them is in these.

<margin>23</margin> **Against**...

He focuses on the nuances of Paul's list of "works of the flesh" and "fruit of the Spirit," arguing that Paul's list is a general summary of character rather than an exhaustive or technical legal catalog.</summary>
