<meta>This page continues Erasmus's philological and theological commentary on the final chapters of the Epistle to the Galatians. He focuses on the "fruit of the Spirit" and the practical ethics of the early Christian community, particularly the restoration of sinners and the support of teachers. He draws heavily on the Greek text to correct or clarify the Latin Vulgate, referencing various Church Fathers to weigh different interpretations.</meta>

### TO THE GALATIANS. CHAPTER VI.

24 Against such things there is no law. And those who belong to Christ have crucified the 25 flesh with its passions and desires. If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. 26 Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another. <margin>VI. 1</margin> Brothers, even if a person is overtaken in some trespass, you who are spiritual, restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, 2 considering yourself, lest you also be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and in this way fulfill the law 3 of Christ. For if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, 4 he deceives himself. But let each one examine his own work, and then he will have his reason for boasting in himself alone, 5 and not in another. For each one 6 will bear his own load. Let the one who is taught the word share in all good things with the one who teaches. 7 Do not be deceived, God is not mocked. For whatever 8 a man sows, this he will also reap. Because the one who sows into his own flesh, from the flesh will reap corruption...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> 23 ...against such things there is no law. Those who truly belong to Christ have crucified the flesh 24 with its affections and lusts. 25 If we live by the spirit, 25 let us also walk by the spirit. 26 Let us not be made greedy for empty glory, provoking one another, envying one another. Brothers, even if <margin>VI. 1</margin> a man should be occupied in some fault, you who are spiritual, 2 restore such a one in a spirit of mildness, 3 considering yourself, lest you also be tempted. Carry one another’s burdens, 3 and thus fulfill the law of Christ. For if anyone seems to himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceives his own mind. But let each one prove his own work, 7 and then he will have glorying in himself alone, 8 and not in another. For each one shall carry his own pack. 9 <margin>B</margin> Let him who is instructed in the word communicate to him who instructs him in all good things. Do not err, God 10 is not mocked. 11 For whatever a man has sown, this he shall also reap. For he who sows 12 through his flesh, from the flesh 13 shall reap <meta>cor-</meta> <note>Note: The text cuts off here at "corruption" due to the page break.</note>

---

<margin>23 But those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh.]</margin> In this place, Origen <note>A 3rd-century scholar and theologian from Alexandria.</note>, omitting one conjunction <note>original: "δὲ" (de), meaning "but" or "and"</note>, varies the entire meaning, reading it in this way: *Against such things there is no law—those of Christ who have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires* <note>original Greek: "Κατὰ τῶν τοιούτων οὐκ ἔστι νόμος, οἱ τοῦ Χριστοῦ τὴν σάρκα ἐσταύρωσαν σὺν τοῖς παθήμασι καὶ ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις"</note>. This would imply that it is not that "those who belong to Christ have crucified their own flesh," but rather that "there is no law against those who have crucified the flesh of Christ within themselves along with their vices." He suggests that the "flesh of Christ" is crucified in a praiseworthy way in pious people when their carnal affections are tamed, but it is "recrucified" <note>term: <gloss>anastaurousthai</gloss> — to crucify again or anew</note> in a bad sense by those who return to their former life after having once accepted Christ. However, the Greek manuscripts resist this reading, even if Jerome <note>A 4th-century Father and translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> approves of Origen's opinion. Ambrose <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Milan.</note> seems to have read it this way: *the christs*, <note>original: "οἱ δὲ χριστοῦ"</note> taking "christs" as a plural noun in the nominative case, not a possessive singular. He adds that those who are devoted to Christ are called "christs," that is, "anointed ones."

<margin>24 With vices and desires]</margin> <note>original: "παθήματα" (pathēmata)</note>, that is, *passions*, or as Augustine <note>Bishop of Hippo, 4th-5th century.</note> reads it, *affections*. In his work *Against the Manichaeans on Genesis*, he uses *disturbances* instead of *affections*. In Letter 39, he reads it as *with passions and longings*, although that letter seems to be by Paulinus. However, every torment or disease, even of the body, can be called a *passion*, and therefore he added *desires*, which is specific to the longings of the mind, as Jerome also pointed out.

<margin>25 By the Spirit let us walk]</note> <note>original: "καὶ στοιχῶμεν" (kai stoichōmen)</note>, which Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a 15th-century humanist critic.</note> corrects to *let us be content*. Truly, this fits Paul's meaning more than the Greek word *stoichōmen*, which means "to walk in one's order." This suggests we should contain ourselves within the Spirit and not look back to the Law. Action is a kind of movement, like that of a living being. But movement proceeds from the same source as life; so if life has come to us from the Gospel Spirit and not from the Law, let us act according to that same Spirit. I do not see what moved Valla, unless perhaps he read *stergōmen* <note>meaning "to love" or "be satisfied"</note> instead of *stoichōmen*. Though it is not unknown to me that Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine commentator.</note> interprets it according to Valla’s view, saying *stoichōmen* is used instead of *let us be satisfied*. Saint Augustine reads, *We live by the Spirit, let us also follow the Spirit*, and he interprets it exactly as he reads it. Whoever translated it that way either read, or certainly dreamed up, *stochazō*, which means "to aim the eye at a target." Otherwise, this word *stoichōmen* is multi-faceted <note>term: <gloss>polysēmon</gloss> — having many meanings</note> among the Greeks, but it is derived from "order" and a "direct course," from which come *stoichoi* (rows or verses) and *stoicheia* (elements or letters). From the same root comes *systoichos* <note>meaning "in the same row" or "corresponding"</note>.

<margin>26 Greedy for empty glory]</margin> In Greek, this is one word: <note>original: "κενόδοξοι" (kenodoxoi)</note>, that is, "vainly glorious," or as Ambrose reads, "seeking empty glory."

<margin>1 If overtaken]</margin> <note>original: "προληφθῇ" (prolēphthē)</note>, that is, "caught" or "surprised" before one could take care. By these words, Paul entirely excludes deliberate malice and the willful intent to sin.

<margin>2 Restore such a one]</margin> <note>original: "καταρτίζετε" (katartizete)</note>, that is, "reinstate," "repair," or "mend." I suspect the translator likely used "reinstate" and a scribe turned it into "instruct." Erasmus, in his commentary on Ezekiel 16, translates it as "perfect such a person." Ambrose reads it as "with humility," if the text is free of error, which I strongly suspect. For from his interpretation, one cannot perceive what he read—or if anything can be gathered, he read "correct," when he says, "they are to be provoked with gentleness toward reforming themselves." We hardly remember what Paul and the holy Doctors advise here. If something needs correcting, we immediately make a noise with such arrogance and such cruelty. This practice has alienated many excellent men from the communion of the Church, as Jerome openly recorded regarding Tertullian <note>A 2nd-century Christian author who eventually joined a schismatic sect.</note>.

<margin>3 Considering yourself]</margin> He has suddenly changed the number in a wonderful way, from "you all" to <note>original: "σκοπῶν σεαυτὸν" (skopōn seauton)</note> "you" (singular), looking more to the sense than to the grammatical order. From this passage, Saint Jerome concludes it was truly said by Paul that he was "unskilled in speech," not just out of modesty. But to me, it seems he changed the number suddenly for a reason: the singular number is more suitable for addressing the conscience of each individual. Furthermore, it was harsher to say to everyone, "consider yourselves, lest you all be tempted." Paul always acts with wonderful caution so as not to offend those he seeks to correct. Theophylact notes that the word "you" <note>original: "σὺ" (sy)</note> was added to remind them of human fragility. Indeed, this saying does not only pertain to the Galatians but calls out to every mortal individually. For this reason, the number was changed, as we have noted Paul doing elsewhere.

<margin>4 Each other's burdens]</margin> <note>original: "Ἀλλήλων τὰ βάρη βαστάζετε"</note>. The Latin translator, Ambrose, and likewise Augustine in his 21st sermon on the Words of the Lord, rendered it as *carry your burdens for one another*, both of them citing it this way elsewhere as well. It could also be translated as: *Let some carry the burdens of others in turn*. For in Latin, "one another" <note>original: "alter alterius"</note> is usually said of two people.

<margin>5 And thus you will fulfill]</margin> <note>original: "καὶ οὕτως ἀναπληρώσατε" (kai outōs anaplērōsate)</note>, that is, "and so fulfill" (as a command). The translator read it as "you will fulfill" (as a future promise), but it does not greatly change the sense. He returns here to the plural number. Although the Greek word sounds more like "re-fulfill," as if to say: what was diminished in the observation of the law by another's fault, let the charity of others mend it. Chrysostom <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople famed for his preaching.</note> diligently noted the emphasis of this word.

<margin>C</margin> <margin>6 If anyone thinks himself to be]</margin> The Greek is slightly different: *For if someone seems to be something* <note>original: "Εἰ γὰρ δοκεῖ τις εἶναί τι"</note>, implying "someone." And the word for self-deception in Greek is a compound word: <note>original: "φρεναπατᾷ" (phrenapata)</note>, that is, "he seduces the mind" or "he deceives his own mind," as Saint Jerome explains. It is the most dangerous kind of deception when one imposes upon oneself. Augustine, in the second chapter of his book *On the Singularity of Clerics*, reads *he leads himself astray* <note>original: "seipsum implanat"</note>, and as if interpreting the Greek word, he adds, "but surely the one who leads himself astray deceives his own soul." The word *planus* is found among the Latins for an "imposter," but whether the verb *implanare* (to lead astray) is found, I do not know.

<margin>7 And so in himself]</margin> <note>original: "καὶ τότε" (kai tote)</note>, that is, "and then," as Ambrose reads. The word "only" is not added in most Greek texts, though it is added in some <note>original: "μόνον" (monon)</note>. Furthermore, where the Greek says <note>original: "εἰς ἑαυτὸν"</note>, that is, "in himself," and soon after <note>original: "καὶ οὐκ εἰς τὸν ἕτερον"</note>, that is, "and not in another," it might have been more correctly translated as "with himself, and not with another." Though it does not escape me that the nature of this preposition is ambiguous. Chrysostom interprets it as "against himself" rather than "against another."

<margin>8 For each will carry his own pack]</margin> <note>original: "φορτίον" (phortion)</note>. Ambrose reads this as "pack" <note>original: "sarcinam"</note>. And "will carry" is <note>original: "βαστάσει" (bastasei)</note>, which is specific to porters.

<margin>D</margin> <margin>9 Let him who is taught communicate]</margin> In Greek, it is not "by the word" but "the word" in the accusative case <note>original: "τὸν λόγον"</note>. Though it can be understood through a figure of speech <note>term: <gloss>synecdoche</gloss> — where a part represents the whole or vice versa</note>, as if the preposition "according to" were understood. Or he said it as "he is catechized the word," just as we say "he is taught grammar." Ambrose weighs the Greek word this way: <note>original: "ὁ κατηχούμενος τὸν λόγον"</note>, that is, "the one who is a hearer of the word of God." For "to catechize" is to hand down the mysteries of the Christian religion. However, the phrase "in all good things" should be referred to "sharing," not to "teaching." Marcion <note>A famous 2nd-century heretic who rejected the Old Testament.</note>, as Jerome indicates, refers the accusative "word" to the instruction to "share the word," understanding that the faithful and the students should pray together, and the teacher should share in prayer with the disciples—feeling especially bolstered by the fact that "in all good things" follows. Yet, if the discussion was about prayer, the instruction should not have been given to the student, but to the teacher. However, the things that follow reject this interpretation: "Whatever a man sows, these things he will also reap." Here Lorenzo Valla is somewhat annoyed that the translator left the Greek word as it was, when he translates it differently; and thus Valla thinks it should be translated: "Let him who is taught the word communicate with him who teaches him in all good things." I will add from my own side that "word" <note>original: "λόγον" (logon)</note> could be taken in this place for "account": so we may understand Paul to be advising that an account of giving and receiving be established between the one who handed down the religion and the one who received it—but only if the one who handed it down did so sincerely. Otherwise, it would be an unfair exchange if a benefit is returned for a falsely handed-down religious doctrine. And he even added "in all good things," repeating what he said above: "It is good to be zealous in a good thing always." Against those who were insincerely handing down Christ for glory and gain, he objects with what follows: "God is not mocked." Ambrose seems to have felt this, writing, "especially among those who disagree, so that the law may be our guide rather than a man." Theophylact interprets this as the generosity of students toward their teachers, and Jerome agrees with this.

<margin>10 Is not mocked]</margin> <note>original: "οὐ μυκτηρίζεται" (ou myktērizetai)</note>. This properly means to laugh with a sneer and to mock, and "to hang from the nose." Indeed, the Greeks call the nose <note>original: "μυκτῆρα" (myktēra)</note>.

<margin>11 For what things he has sown]</margin> In Greek, it is in the singular: "For what a man sows, this he will also reap." This is how Ambrose and Saint Augustine read it.

<margin>12 In the flesh]</margin> In Greek it is <note>original: "εἰς σάρκα"</note>, that is, "into the flesh": just as shortly after, <note>original: "εἰς τὸ πνεῦμα"</note>, that is, "into the spirit": even though the preposition *eis* is used in various ways.

<margin>13 Will reap corruption]</margin> <note>original: "θερίσει φθοράν"</note>, that is, "will reap decay," meaning a fruit that will perish, for he opposes this to eternal life. The mortal flesh has likewise mortal fruits; the Spirit has eternal ones.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>D</margin> ...fruit has immortal qualities. <note>Erasmus is commenting on the word "corruption" vs "incorruption" in verse 8.</note> Indeed, in other places he also translates *aphtharton* <note>Greek: ἄφθαρτον</note> as "immortal," and *aphtharsian* <note>Greek: ἀφθαρσίαν</note> as "immortality."

*14 Let us grow weary, and growing weary* ] In the Greek, these are different words. For "let us grow weary" is *ekkakomen* <note>Greek: ἐκκακῶμεν</note>, while "growing weary" is *eklyomenoi* <note>Greek: ἐκλυόμενοι</note>, that is, "being exhausted." Ambrose <note>A 4th-century Bishop and Church Father.</note> reads "infatigable" (unwearied), as if to capture the timing of the participle as well. Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage.</note> reads "lest it become tedious" instead of "lest we grow weary."

*15 To all* ] Why not rather, *toward* all? <note>Erasmus is debating the choice of the Latin preposition "ad" vs "erga".</note>

*16 With what letters* ] *Pelikois* <note>Greek: πηλίκοις</note>, that is, "with what kind," but in a way that signifies magnitude and wonder. Here it refers more to Paul’s appearance <note>or "regard"</note>; this matter was so close to his heart that he did not find it a burden to write about it with his own hand. Saint Jerome <note>The primary translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> thinks the rest of the Epistle was written by someone else's hand, but that Paul, to exclude any suspicion of a forged letter, wrote the remainder of the Epistle with his own hand. But why not rather—if I may speak with Jerome's permission—conjecture from this very passage that this entire Epistle was traced by Paul's own fingers? Jerome admits that the Greek word *pelikois* signifies magnitude rather than quality. Hilary noted the same regarding the Psalms, following Origen, I believe. For the Greek word sounds of "magnitude," but the Latin does not. Although Saint Hilary refers the magnitude not to the shape of the characters, but to the sublimity of the meanings, which seems to me quite forced. Furthermore, Saint Jerome struggles to explain how these letters are "large," as if Paul meant that this Epistle was written with physically large letterforms. On the contrary, the Greeks use "letters" in the plural to refer to a single Epistle, just as we do. Therefore, to show how much this matter was at his heart, the Apostle says: "You see what a great Epistle I have written with my own hand," for he had already finished the Epistle. In his other letters, he usually only signs his name: "by my hand, Paul." There is no reason for anyone to be offended by the dative case *grammasin* <note>Greek: γράμμασιν</note> instead of the accusative. Just as we say "in many words" and "many things," so we write "with a few" or "a few things." Ambrose agrees with me, concluding from this passage that this Epistle is an autograph <note>written entirely by the author</note>. And yet I wonder why he reads "Know" instead of "See" or "You see," unless perhaps he had the Greek *eidete* <note>a variant spelling</note> in his text. Augustine reads, "You see with what letters I have written to you," as if Paul is reminding them of his recognized handwriting so they would not be deceived by letters faked by others. Theophylact, following Chrysostom, admits it can be gathered from this passage that the Epistle was written by Paul's hand. However, regarding the word "what kind," he says it pertains not to the size of the letters, but to their ugliness, suggesting that Paul...

<margin>10</margin> good <margin>A</margin> toward all, but especially toward those of the household of faith. ->T H E   E N D.<-

...wished to appear unskilled in writing, and yet was not burdened to write out the whole Epistle with his own hand regardless.

*17 They wish to please in the flesh* ] *euprosopesai* <note>Greek: εὐπροσωπῆσαι</note>, that is, "to please according to the face" <note>to put on a good outward appearance</note>. For the Greek word is composed of this, and "this in the flesh."

*18 Only so that they may not [suffer] the persecution of the cross of Christ* ] The Greek has it thus: *monon hina me to stauro tou Christou diokontai* <note>Greek: μόνον ἵνα μὴ τῷ σταυρῷ τοῦ Χριστοῦ διώκωνται</note>, that is, "lest they be persecuted by the cross of Christ." You should take "be persecuted" in the passive sense, meaning "lest the cross of Christ bring persecution upon them." In Ambrose's text, the word "only" is not added, even if it is added in Augustine. Something must be supplied to make the speech more complete. They only do this so that they may flee the hatred directed at the cross of Christ.

<margin>E</margin> *19 They keep the law* ] *autoi* <note>Greek: αὐτοὶ - themselves</note> is missing, which Ambrose also adds. Jerome reads "these," as if he read *outoi* <note>Greek: οὗτοι</note> in the Greek.

*20 Far be it to glory* ] "Far be it that I should glory," or "may it not happen that I glory."

*21 And whoever shall have followed this rule* ] *Kai osoi to kanoni touto stoichesousin* <note>Greek: Καὶ ὅσοι τῷ κανόνι τούτῳ στοιχήσουσιν</note>. It is the same verb used above, "we walk" (*stoichoumen*), that is, whoever shall walk according to this rule.

*22 And upon the Israel of God* ] *ton Israhel* <note>Greek: τὸν Ἰσραὴλ</note>, so that you understand either the man or the people. And he adds "of God," because of the "Synagogue of Satan."

*23 For the rest* ] *Tou loipou* <note>Greek: Τοῦ λοιποῦ</note>. It is not *To loipon*, which in other places translates to "It remains," or "What is left." Indeed, here he seems to be speaking more about questions <note>disputes</note> than about time, as if you should understand the preposition *peri* ("concerning"). I have delivered whatever was to be delivered; I want this to be firm, nor will I allow it to be called into doubt again.

*24 Let no one be troublesome to me* ] *kopous moi medeis parecheto* <note>Greek: κόπους μοι μηδεὶς παρεχέτω</note>, that is, let no one exhibit labors to me. And in this manner Saint Jerome translates and explains it. Augustine reads, "let no one provide labor for me," although not concealing that in most manuscripts it is written "let no one be troublesome to me," in his book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, at the very beginning.

*25 Marks* ] The Greek word is *stigmata*. It signifies a branded mark. Slaves are usually marked by their masters so that no stranger can claim them as his own. He feels, therefore, that he has certain marks proving he is a servant of Jesus Christ, for whom he had suffered so many things. So often beaten with rods, so often stoned, so often cast to beasts, so often thrown into chains: from all these he prepares his authority against the false apostles. They boasted in the scars of the circumcised; Paul carried around the marks of the cross of Christ on his own body. Such a teacher, therefore, is more to be believed than those delicate masters who boast in someone else's wound.

<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of the Epistle to the Galatians to the introductory material for the Epistle to the Ephesians. # PREFACE
### to the
# EPISTLE OF PAUL
## TO THE EPHESIANS.

He sends this letter from Rome, though he had not yet seen them himself, but had only heard about them. The occasion for the letter is as follows: the Ephesians, having believed in our Lord Jesus Christ, held a genuine faith in him and love toward all the saints, and they wished to be confirmed in this by Paul. Therefore, having learned of this, the Apostle writes this letter to them as a form of instruction <note>original Greek: "katēchētikēn", meaning foundational or catechetical teaching</note>. First, he demonstrates that our mystery is not a new thing, but rather that it was God's good pleasure from the beginning—even before the foundation of the world—that Christ should suffer for us and that we should be saved. Next, he discusses the calling of the Gentiles to show that they have believed worthily. He demonstrates that their calling came not through men, but through Jesus Christ, who is the Son of God; from this they might learn that they have not become "man-worshipers" by believing in Christ, but true worshipers of God. He also indicates that he himself was sent for this purpose, to preach the Gospel, and that he has been concerned for them. Then, he places in the letter words of exhortation for husbands and wives, parents and children, and masters and slaves. Finally, he prepares everyone for the struggle against the devil and his demons, saying that our wrestling is against them. And like a good trainer <note>original Greek: "aleiptēs", an athletic trainer who oils and prepares wrestlers for a match</note> who has anointed everyone with his words against the influence of the devil, he thus concludes the letter.

---

# ON THE EPISTLE TO THE
# EPHESIANS
### Argument by
## DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring a scholar or saint seated at a writing desk within a classical architectural setting, looking towards a landscape visible through an arched opening.</image-desc>
Ephesus was once the metropolis of Asia Minor, a city devoted to superstition and the worship of demons, and especially to Diana. For this reason, in the Acts of the Apostles, it is called the <term>temple-keeper</term> <note>original Greek: "neōkoros"</note> of Diana—not that huntress to whom the poets attribute arrows and weapons, but the "many-breasted" one <note>original Greek: "polymasion"</note> whom the Greeks call <term>Polymastos</term>, and whom they intended to represent as the nurturer of all living creatures, as Jerome has indicated. Indeed, even pagan writers frequently mention the temple of Ephesian Diana, which was celebrated throughout the whole world. The people here were gripped by a devotion to "curious arts" <note>a common biblical term for magic or the occult</note>. Thus we read that, upon the preaching of the Apostles, their books of magic were brought together and committed to the fire; when the price was calculated, it was found to be fifty thousand pieces of silver, as is recorded in Acts chapter 19. Therefore, to lead them away from such great errors, Paul spent three years among them, doing nothing in the meantime that did not lead toward their salvation. He did this while many people protested and clamored loudly against him, as he himself testifies elsewhere—where he was even "thrown to the beasts," as he states in the second Epistle to the Corinthians. Upon his departure, he ordered Timothy to remain with them. 

Furthermore, just as that city was full of people devoted to magic and curiosity, it also abounded with very learned men. Consequently, Paul—who adapts himself to the customs and character of all people—frequently mentions demons and spirits, indicating the difference between the good and the evil ones. In addition to this, he reveals certain hidden matters. Indeed, there is no other Epistle that contains such deep and hidden meanings; it seems it was because of this letter in particular that Peter wrote:

> *Just as our most dear brother Paul, according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you, speaking of these things in all his Epistles. In them are certain things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort, as they do the other scriptures, to their own destruction.*

The difficulty, however, lies not so much in the words—though nowhere else is his phrasing more complex—as it does in the meanings <note>original Latin: "sensibus", referring to the theological depths</note>, as Saint Jerome also acknowledges in the Preface to his Commentaries. We have recounted all these things for this reason: to show why the Apostle, in this Epistle above all others, compiled obscure meanings and "sacraments" <note>mysteries or divine secrets</note> unknown to previous ages. Since they had persevered in the faith, he exhorts them to continue and to advance toward perfection. He reminds them of what they were like when they served wicked spirits as slaves to vice, and what they have now become, having been grafted into Christ. Meanwhile, he teaches that the grace of the Gospel was spread to the Gentiles according to God's plan—even though it had been promised to the Jews—and that he himself was appointed by God as a minister of this gift. Because he wrote from prison, he exhorts them not to be discouraged by his afflictions, but rather to consider them a source of glory for themselves. He deals with these matters in the first and second chapters. In the remaining three, he prescribes a form of life for them, demonstrating what should be followed and what should be avoided: what the duties of husbands are toward wives and wives toward husbands; of parents toward children and children toward parents; of masters toward slaves and slaves toward masters. The Epistle was written from the city of Rome by Tychicus the deacon, whom he mentions at the end, calling him a faithful minister. Ambrose adds that it was written from prison while Paul, having been brought from Jerusalem to Rome, lived outside the military camp in his own rented lodging under the care of a guarantor.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial "E" containing a seated scholar writing at a desk with a landscape visible through a window.</image-desc>
THERE IS the same fervor in this Epistle of Paul, the same depth, and entirely the same spirit and heart; yet nowhere else is the speech more troubled by <term>hyperbaton</term> <note>a figure of speech where the natural order of words is disrupted</note>, <term>anapodotis</term> <note>a sentence where the second part does not grammatically follow the first</note>, and other inconveniences. Whether this was the fault of the translator he used in this instance, or whether the skill of the language could not keep up with the sublimity of the thoughts, is unclear. Certainly, the style differs so much from Paul’s other Epistles that it might seem to belong to another, were it not that the heart and character of the Pauline mind claimed this entirely for itself.

1 *Who are at Ephesus*] <note>original Greek: "tois ousin en Ephesō"</note>. This can also be read in the second person: *who are you at Ephesus*. Now, Ephesus is the metropolis of Asia, which is specifically called "Minor."

2 *Grace to you and peace*] Jerome reminds us that grace and peace are equally referred to both—namely, the Father and the Son—yet it can be understood such that *grace* refers to the Father and *peace* to the Son. Thus, the grace of the Father is understood in the fact that he deigned to send the Son for our salvation, while the peace of the Son is found in the fact that through him we are reconciled to the Father. Jerome found the occasion for this thought in what soon follows: *To the praise of the glory of his grace, in which he graced us in the beloved*. For it is certain that this passage pertains to the Father.

3 *Blessed be God*] This can be distinguished in two ways: *Blessed be God*, with a pause <note>Erasmus uses the Greek term "diastole" for a punctuation mark or pause</note> here, and then separately adding, *and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ*. Or it can be joined: *God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ*. He is "Father" because he begot him, and "God" of Jesus according to the humanity he assumed. Jerome noted this.

4 *In the heavenly places in Christ*] <note>original Greek: "en tois epouraniois Christō"</note>, that is, *in the heavenly things, or above the heavenly things for Christ*: so that "Christ" is in the dative case <note>indicating for or to Christ</note>. Ambrose omitted this little part, *in Christ*. Jerome reads *in Christ*. If you read, *he blessed us for Christ*, the sense will be: *He blessed us for the glory of Christ*. If *in Christ*, the sense will be: *That this blessing is conferred upon us through faith in Christ*. Theophylact <note>an 11th-century biblical commentator</note> interprets it in this sense—whom they recently and falsely claimed was Athanasius. For he reads "in Christ."

5 *Before the foundation of the world*] <note>original Greek: "pro katabolēs kosmou"</note>. This phrase sounds as if you were to say, *before the foundations of the world were cast*. Saint Jerome also notes this using many of the same words.

6 *And immaculate*] <note>original Greek: "amōmous"</note>. This signifies "unblamed" or "irreproachable" rather than "immaculate" (spotless). For among the Greeks, *mōmos* means "reproach," or "blame before God."

7 *In charity*] These words can be referred to what precedes them, so that you understand us to be irreproachable and chosen in love; or to what follows, so that you understand us to be predestined in love. However, the Greek codices link these to what precedes. Jerome also noted this.

8 *Who predestined us*] <note>original Greek: "Proorisas"</note>. Jerome and Ambrose read, *predestining us in charity*. But that "predestining" in Greek is in the past tense, as if (if the type of verb could be changed) he had said *having been predestined* or *pre-defined*. And in this place, truly, is the verb for *predestining*, which we touched upon somewhat in the Epistle to the Romans. St. Jerome thinks the difference between <term>horizein</term> <note>to limit or define</note> and <term>proorizein</term> <note>to pre-limit or pre-destine</note> is that the former is attributed to things that have always existed, while the latter to things that, though they did not exist at one time, then began to be. If something was decreed or thought regarding these things before they existed, it is predestination. Conversely, if something concerns the Lord Jesus Christ, who never was not with the Father, and whose existence was never preceded by a paternal will that he should come into being, it is "destination." Hence, in the Epistle to the Romans, speaking of the Son of God, he said *horisthentos* <note>having been defined/determined</note>, not *prooristhentos* <note>having been predestined</note>.

9 *Into the adoption of sons*] In Greek, this is one word, <note>original Greek: "huiothesian"</note>, by which they signify that adoption by which someone is adopted into the place of a son, as we noted above. For grandsons and granddaughters are also adopted.

10 *Into himself*] <note>original Greek: "eis hauton"</note>, that is, *into his own self*, so that there is a return to the Father; although it can also be referred to Christ, though more forcefully. For through adoption we are made brothers of Jesus Christ, not sons, according to the property of mystical speech; rather, we are sons of God the Father, as if grafted into the body of Christ and made one with him.

<column-break/>

<margin>C</margin>
11 *According to the purpose*] <note>original Greek: "kata tēn eudokian"</note>, that is, *according to the pleasure*, or rather *according to the good pleasure*. Jerome thinks the word is new and was coined by the Seventy <note>the translators of the Septuagint</note> so they could explain what is found among the Hebrews as <note>Hebrew: "rason", meaning favor or goodwill</note>. Furthermore, *eudokia* is properly said when something not only pleases, but has pleased rightly. For things can please even when they do not please rightly. Ambrose reads, *according to the pleasure of his will*.

12 *To the praise of the glory of his grace*] Certain manuscripts incorrectly add a conjunction, *of the glory and of his grace*, since it is <note>original Greek: "doxēs tēs charitos autou"</note>, that is, *of the glory of his grace*, so that you understand the glory of divine grace is being praised. And Jerome certainly reads it this way. Ambrose reads, *to the praise of his brightness*, omitting the mention of grace. For in place of "glory" he rendered it "brightness," yet in explaining it he mentions "grace." He usually translates *doxa* as "majesty," and majesty is more suited to power, but here he attributes it to grace. For God appeared more wonderful in redeeming man than in creating him. Everywhere here the Apostle extols grace, diminishing trust in human works. Nowadays, there are those who sin in both directions. The middle way is the safest. But if one must deviate, it is safer to deviate toward the side of grace, by which Christ is glorified, than toward our works, by which men are glorified.

13 *In which he graced*] <note>original Greek: "en hē echaritōsen"</note>. And "he graced" here means *he made acceptable or dear*. From *echaritōsen* comes the participle used for Mary, "highly favored" <note>original Greek: "kecharitōmenē Maria"</note>. If in that place it was to be translated "full of grace," then here he ought to have translated it "he filled with grace." For "to grace" <note>Latin: "gratificare"</note> is a word unfamiliar to Latin ears; "to be gracious" <note>Latin: "gratificari"</note> means to do something for the sake of another’s favor.

14 *In his beloved Son*] *His Son* is not added in the Greek or in Jerome; it is <note>original Greek: "en tō ēgapēmenō"</note>, that is, *in him who is beloved*. For the word here is not *agapētos* <note>beloved as a title</note>. Ambrose reads as the Vulgate edition has it, and certainly understands it to mean the Son. But the Apostle preferred to designate him by the name "the Beloved," so that you would understand that we are loved by God not because of our merits, but because of the love with which the Father pursues the Son, to whom he willed us to be brothers. Jerome noted this carefully: it was not said "to the beloved Son"—for what is so great if a father loves a son?—nor "to the beloved on behalf of all," but absolutely "to the beloved in all things," and before all things, and without whom no one else is loved.

15 *Unto the remission of sins*] The preposition "unto" is not present in the Greek, nor in Ambrose, nor in Jerome, but it is necessary to link the accusative case by apposition as an explanation. For in explaining what that redemption is, he adds *the remission of sins*. For this is the slavery from which Christ redeemed us. Both of the Constance manuscripts supported this.

<margin>16</margin>
16 *In us*] <note>original Greek: "eis hēmas"</note>, that is, *toward us*.

17 *In all wisdom and prudence*] These can either be referred to what precedes or to what follows, so that the sense is: *Which he poured out abundantly upon us in all wisdom and prudence*, or *Making known to us the mystery in all wisdom and prudence*. Jerome follows this latter distinction.

18 *That he might make known*] <note>original Greek: "Gnōrisas hēmin to mystērion"</note>, that is, *Revealing*, or *The mystery having been notified to us*. The translator and Ambrose, I believe, read it as an infinitive. Jerome reads, *Making known*, so that you understand it is a participle, although it is in the past tense. What I shall say, even if it does not greatly pertain to the sense, should not in my judgment be neglected. It seems to me the others have noticed too little what is read in the Greek codices: for they have it in this manner: *Which he made to abound toward us in all wisdom and prudence, having made known to us...* The verb *made to abound* <note>original Greek: "eperisseusen"</note> is placed here transitively—that is, *he caused to overflow*. Otherwise, the participle *having made known* has nothing to hang upon. It could be translated in this way: *Of which he shared with us abundantly, the mystery having been revealed to us, etc.* Certainly, it is clear that Chrysostom and Theophylact felt this way; for in interpreting "he made to abound," he adds, "he poured out the unspeakable [grace]," that is, *he poured it out amply*. He increased the magnitude of grace with a double increase, since he names it "riches" and adds not "he gave," but "he made to abound."

19 **Sacrament**] <note>original: "Sacramentum"</note> In this place it signifies "mystery," <note>original: "μυστήριον"</note>
and Ambrose uses the Greek word. Among the Greeks, a *mystery* 
is called a secret matter, not to be uttered to the common people. 
This was later transferred to sacred things, which we especially 
venerate with silence. Here he means that the divine will concerning 
the calling of the Gentiles to the faith was unknown to the world 
in previous ages—with the Jews thinking this promise belonged 
properly to themselves—but now that which was hidden has 
become known.

20 **According to his good pleasure**] <note>original: "Secundum beneplacitum ejus"</note> Jerome reads, *according 
to his good pleasure, or according to his liking*, <note>original: "κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν αὐτοῦ"</note>.

21 **Which he purposed in him**] <note>original: "Quod proposuit in eo"</note> If you read *in himself* <note>original: "ἐν αὐτῷ"</note> with the "alpha" aspirated, 
it signifies *in himself*. If you prefer *in him* <note>original: "αὐτῷ"</note> with the first vowel smooth, it refers 
to the Son, in whom the Father purposed to show us favor. And 
the Interpreters follow this opinion with great consensus. Jerome 
indicates the difference between *purpose* <note>original: "πρόθεσιν"</note> and *foreknowledge* <note>original: "πρόγνωσιν"</note>, that is, 
between predestination and a proposal or purpose: the former 
pertains to those things which we determine in the mind long before they happen; 
the latter, when the plan is already near, so that the effect almost follows the thought.

22 **In the dispensation**] <note>original: "In dispensatione"</note> <note>original: "εἰς οἰκονομίαν"</note>, that is, *unto the dispen-
sation* <note>or "administration"</note>.

23 **To restore**] <note>original: "Instaurare"</note> <note>original: "ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι"</note>, that is, to be recapitulated, 
which means that they are gathered into a sum. For Orators call it a 
*recapitulation* <note>original: "ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν"</note> when those things which were said 
scattered and at length are repeated briefly and renewed for the judge 
all at once. Saint Jerome reads *to recapitulate*, and thinks this 
word can rightly be used by the Latins; he wonders why in the 
Latin manuscripts *to restore* is found more often than *to recapitulate*. 
There are some, including Theophylact and Chrysostom, who inter-
pret *recapitulation* as Christ becoming the head of both Angels and men, 
and of Jews and Gentiles. This agrees with what follows shortly after: 
*and gave him to be the head*. Indeed, the Greek word sounds 
as if you were to say *to recall to the head*.

24 **Which are on earth**] <note>original: "Quæ in terra sunt"</note> <note>original: "τά τε ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς, καὶ τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς"</note>, that is, both those in the heavens and those on the earth. That which 
is added in the Greek codices, *in him* <note>original: "ἐν αὐτῷ"</note>, I find neither 
in Ambrose nor in Jerome; not even in Theophylact 
or Chrysostom, at least regarding their commentary. 
For in the text itself, it is present in Theophylact. And 
it fits better to say "in the same" than *in him*: for the Greek word is 
ambiguous, so that you may understand all things as comprised in one 
and the same, and the entire sum of all things is recalled to the one 
Christ, and that in one person exists at once what was previously sought 
in parts from many. Unless you prefer "through the same," so that it 
corresponds to what follows, *In whom* etc. or *Through whom*, so 
that the sense is: All things were restored through the same person 
through whom we also were admitted into the lot and 
fellowship. Now, where we read *all things in Christ*, in 
Theophylact it was read *all things which are in Christ*. 
However, I think this was done by a scribe's error.

25 **We were called by lot**] <note>original: "Sorte vocati sumus"</note> <note>original: "ἐκληρώθημεν"</note>, that is, we were 
admitted by lot. Jerome indicates that this word is said partly from 
"lot" <note>chance</note> and partly from "inheritance," because the Greek word 
*kleros* <note>original: "κλῆρος"</note> is ambiguous. Ambrose reads, *we have obtained a lot*, 
that is, we were admitted into the lot and into a part of the inheri-
tance. In his small book *To the Virgins*, he reads, *we were established by lot*.

26 **According to the purpose**] <note>original: "Secundum propositum"</note> In the Greek it is not "of good pleasure" <note>original: "εὐδοκίας"</note>, but *purpose* <note>original: "πρόθεσιν"</note>.

27 **Who works all things**] <note>original: "Qui operatur omnia"</note> <note>original: "τοῦ τὰ πάντα ἐνεργοῦντος"</note>. Ambrose 
reads, *of him who created all things*, if the writing is free from 
error. But the Greek word sounds more like, *of him by whose power 
and virtue all things are done*, that is, of one acting upon and 
governing all things, as we have already often advised; and in this 
way we have translated it.

28 **Who hoped before**] <note>original: "Qui ante speravimus"</note> <note>original: "προηλπικότας"</note>, that is, who hoped 
beforehand. Saint Jerome refers this to divine foreknowledge, 
in which we hoped even before the world was founded, obviously 
moved by this preposition *pre-* <note>original: "πρό"</note>. Theophylact refers it elsewhere. 
We hope even now for the things that happen to us in the future age; 
or we began to hope long ago when we believed in Christ. Ambrose 
diverts this so that it pertains to the Apostles, who, while still 
living in Judaism, nevertheless had hope in Christ, whom they 
expected from the oracles of the Prophets. Tertullian follows this in 
his fifth book against Marcion, reading *pre-hoped* instead of 
*hoped before*.

29 **In whom also you, when you had heard**] <note>original: "In quo & vos cum audissetis"</note> <note>original: "ἐν ᾧ καὶ ὑμεῖς ἀκούσαντες τὸν λόγον"</note>, that is, in whom also you who heard the word. Saint 
Jerome reads, not elegantly, *in whom also you, the word of 
truth having been heard*. It must be noted that among the Greeks 
in some codices the first person is used ("we"), not the second person ("you"). 
Although Ambrose and Jerome seem to have read it otherwise, as can be

<meta>catchword: which</meta>

guessed from their interpretation. <margin>C</margin> Theophylact, in his commentary, 
does not declare what he read, though the text has *you* and *your*. The 
Aldine edition had *we* and *our* with mixed persons; the Spanish 
edition has the second person in both places. Others make a 
distinction from this point: first, those who *hoped before in Christ*; 
then they add a separation, *in whom also you*; so that the former 
refers to the Apostles or Jews, the latter to the Ephesians or 
Gentiles. But it seems to me that Paul suddenly changed the person 
in this place, attending more to the sense than to the laws of 
speech. For when he had said, *That we should be to the praise 
of his glory*, as if explaining whom he meant by "we," lest anyone 
should think he was speaking only of the Jews, he immediately added 
*those who hoped before*, as if to say: When I say "we," I mean all 
who hoped in Christ, among whom we also are. And he says *we* in 
such a way that he joins his own person with the person of the 
Gentiles, since he is the Teacher of the Gentiles. Truly, the Greek 
preposition *pre-* <note>original: "πρό"</note>, meaning "before," somewhat obstructs this 
sense. For if it is understood of all who had believed in Christ, who 
were those who believed *before*? Unless one wishes to follow the 
sense of Jerome, whom Ruffinus falsely accuses of savoring 
something of Origen. Furthermore, if it is pleasing to change the 
person, and we read, *in whom you also hoped*, just as Jerome 
reads (which is clear from his interpretation), there is nothing 
to offend us in the preposition. Since "before" refers 
to the Jews, who were called first to the faith, and first 
believed in Christ; then the Gentiles followed. But if the first 
person is entirely preferred, as some Greeks read, then the 
preposition "before" could refer to others who would believe 
later: for those were the first among the Gentiles to believe. Unless 
you prefer to understand a vague hope, which the healable Pagans 
held even before the Gospel was preached; <margin>D</margin> although they did 
not yet know Christ, they nevertheless hoped in some way for 
salvation, as if through a dream.

30 **Of the Gospel of salvation**] <note>original: "Evangelii salutis"</note> In the Greek, "the Gospel" 
is added by apposition, <note>original: "ἀκούσαντες τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον τῆς σωτηρίας"</note>, that is, you who heard the word of truth, which is the 
Gospel of salvation. As if others promise nothing of truth, who 
teach anything besides the Gospel.

31 **In whom also believing**] <note>original: "In quo & credentes"</note> "Believing," among the 
Greeks, is in the past tense, <note>original: "πιστεύσαντες"</note>, that is, after you believed, 
or because you believed, or having received the faith, or 
having been made faithful.

32 **You were signed**] <note>original: "Signati estis"</note> <note>original: "ἐσφραγίσθητε"</note>. Which signifies 
"you were sealed," just as we seal tablets in contracts: because 
afterwards he speaks of the guarantee <note>earnest money</note>, to show that 
hope is certain. Didymus cites this passage in his book on the Holy 
Spirit, reasoning from here that the Holy Spirit is holy and good 
not by participation in another, but by his own nature, because in 
a seal, by which a character is imprinted, there is an archetype 
of the good: *For if, he says, some are formed by the Holy <margin>E</margin> 
Spirit, assuming his form and likeness, it is from this that the Spirit is 
holy, by which they are held and do not have, those who have him 
being imprinted with his seal*. Writing also the same thing to the 
Corinthians: *Do not, he says, grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom you 
were sealed*, testifying that they were sealed who received 
the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. We have brought these things forward 
so that the Reader may understand that I have not without cause 
noted the Greek word for "sealing," nor should he who wishes to 
philosophize in Divine Letters run "outside his own territory," as 
the saying goes, being ignorant of Greek literature.

33 **Which is a pledge**] <note>original: "Qui est pignus"</note> <note>original: "ἀῤῥαβὼν"</note>, that is, a guarantee 
<note>arrhabo</note>. And so Saint Jerome wishes it to be read, thinking that 
"guarantee" and "pledge" <note>pignus</note> do not sound the same to the Latins: 
because a pledge is usually given to a creditor until the owed money 
is paid; a guarantee is as a sign and obligation of future possession. 
A pledge is given in a loan, a guarantee in a contract of selling 
and buying, by which the obligation is confirmed. If the earnest 
which God gives to his own is so great, how great will be the thing 
itself, which he will provide in his own time? And both the Greeks 
call it *arrhabona*, and a pledge *enechyron*, or a hypothesis. 
And "who" <note>the relative pronoun</note> refers not to Christ, but to the Spirit, 
that is, which Spirit is the guarantee.

34 **Unto the redemption of the acquisition**] <note>original: "In redemptionem acquisitionis"</note> <note>original: "εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν τῆς περιποιήσεως"</note>, that is, unto the redemption of the acquisition or possession, <margin>F</margin> 
as Jerome reads, emending the Vulgate Edition, which had *unto the 
redemption of adoption*. From which one may guess that even this 
version which we commonly use was not the same as that which 
Jerome then had. But that person, whoever he was, seems to me 
to have wished to interpret a word that was otherwise ambiguous 
concerning "acquisition." For the sense is: the Holy Spirit was given 
by God to the faithful as a guarantee, by which they would know 
for certain that they would one day claim for themselves their 
possession, which he had acquired by redemption. Therefore we 
have translated it, *unto the redemption of the acquired possession*. 
For the thing that was being acquired and prepared, he calls 
"acquisition," just as we call the thing possessed "possession."

35 **Hearing the faith**] <note>original: "Audiens fidem"</note> <note>original: "ἀκούσας τὴν καθ’ ὑμᾶς πίστιν"</note>, that is, 
your faith having been heard.

<margin>A</margin>
36 **I do not cease giving thanks**] <note>original: "Cesso gratias agens"</note> This follows the Greek phrasing. In Latin one should say, "I do not cease to give thanks" <note>original: "Non cesso gratias agere"</note>; and this is how Jerome reads it. Ambrose reads "by giving thanks" <note>original: "gratias agendo"</note>.

37 **Memory of you**] <note>original: "Memoriam vestri"</note> Why not "mention of you," <note>original: "μνείαν ὑμῶν" (mneian hymon)</note>, since when we pray we are speaking with God?

38 **The God of our Lord**] <note>original: "Ὁ Θεὸς τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν"</note> Here it is openly stated that the Father is called the God of Jesus Christ, which in other passages was ambiguous.

39 **In knowledge**] <note>original: "ἐν ἐπιγνώσει" (en epignosei)</note>, that is, in the acknowledgment <note>original: "in agnitione"</note>; just as Ambrose and Jerome read it. Jerome notes the emphasis on the word "acknowledgment" <note>original: "agnitio"</note>, by which we recognize things once known but which we had ceased to notice for a time; whereas "knowledge" <note>original: "gnosis"</note> refers to things we begin to know that were previously unknown. He hints here at something like a Platonic idea, following Origen's opinion (if I am not mistaken), regarding the Father being known previously, whom we begin to remember again through the revelation of the Spirit. Truly, there was no need for a Platonic fable here. The philosophers knew God, but they did not *acknowledge* Him—that is, they did not embrace Him. Similarly, a son might know his father but not acknowledge him as such. And here the following words agree: "the enlightened eyes of the heart." For though they saw before, they did not truly see.

40 **The enlightened eyes**] The entire context of this speech is somewhat incoherent. I marvel that Jerome labored so much to defend Paul against those who accused him of being unskilled in the Greek language and full of grammatical errors <note>original: "solecisms"</note>. Elsewhere, Paul himself frequently admits he was "unskilled in speech," and Jerome defends this against those who refuse to attribute Paul’s writing style to modesty but rather to a true confession of his limits. Jerome thinks the order of the reading can be restored this way: "Hearing of your faith... and seeing the excellence of your faith... I do not cease giving thanks... so that the God and Father... may give you the Spirit of wisdom." Furthermore, he thinks the part that follows, "the enlightened eyes of your heart," can be rendered through a "hyperbaton" <note>term: hyperbaton: a figure of speech where the natural word order is disrupted for emphasis or due to complex thought</note>. But Ambrose refers "enlightened eyes" to the verb "may give." He adds from his own "faith," that it has enlightened eyes. It is strange why Chrysostom and Theophylact felt no difficulty here, or if they did, they concealed it.

41 **Of your heart**] <note>original: "διανοίας ὑμῶν" (dianoias hymon)</note>, that is, "of your mind."

42 **Surpassing greatness**] <note>original: "τὸ ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος" (to hyperballon megethos)</note>, that is, "sublime greatness," as Jerome has it. "Lofty greatness," as Ambrose reads it.

43 **The operation of the power of his virtue**] <note>original: "κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν τοῦ κράτους τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ" (kata ten energeian tou kratous tes ischyos autou)</note>, that is, according to the efficacy or force of the power of his fortitude or strength; for the word is *energeia*. And shortly after he repeats "he exercised" <note>original: "ἐνήργησεν" (energesen)</note>: which we have translated more truly as "exercised," not as we wished (as they say), but as we were able.

44 **Raising him up**] <note>original: "ἐγείρας αὐτόν" (egeiras auton)</note>, that is, "him having been raised."

45 **And appointing**] <note>original: "καὶ ἐκάθισε" (kai ekathise)</note>, that is, "and he made him sit." Jerome reads, "making him sit." Ambrose has "placed him." For the Greek word sometimes has a neutral and sometimes a transitive meaning.

46 **Both virtue and dominion**] "Virtue" here is <note>original: "δύναμις" (dynamis)</note>, not "moral virtue" <note>original: "ἀρετή" (arete)</note>; and "dominion" is <note>original: "κυριότητος" (kyriotetos)</note>, which suggests authority and the right of an owner. This is expressed better in Latin as *dominium* <note>term: dominium: legal ownership or right of control</note> than as *dominatio* <note>term: dominatio: the act of ruling or dominating</note>. For he is not speaking only of Angels, but of all things in general.

47 **Under his feet**] <note>original: "ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας" (hypo tous podas)</note>, that is, "beneath his feet."

48 **Over the whole church**] <note>original: "ὑπὲρ πάντα τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ" (hyper panta te Ekklesia)</note>, that is, "above all things for the Church": so that "Church" is in the dative case, not the genitive. This means He gave Him to be the head of the Church, set over all things. Jerome reads it this way in his *Commentaries*, agreeing with the Greeks, even if Ambrose seems to have read it otherwise. Theophylact, in his explanation, clearly shows he read it as we have edited it, adding that Christ is the head of the Church in such a way that He not only excels His own members, but also all created things in heaven and on earth. Chrysostom holds the same sense, but in two ways regarding "over

<column-break/>

<margin>C</margin>
all things": simply, that we should understand Christ is superior to all visible and intelligible creatures; or that this is "above all things" that the Father did for us, that He gave such a head to the Church. An older manuscript from Constance agreed with us, in which—with no trace of erasure—it was written "above all things for the Church."

49 **And the fullness**] The conjunction "And" is not in the Greek codices. Nor was it added in the very ancient manuscript of St. Donatian, and both manuscripts from Constance supported this. And the word "fullness" <note>original: "τὸ πλήρωμα" (to pleroma)</note> seems to be read in the accusative case, so that it refers to Christ. The things that follow support this.

50 **Who fills all things in all**] <note>original: "τὸ πλήρωμα τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσι πληρουμένου" (to pleroma ta panta en pasi pleroumenou)</note>, that is, the fullness or completion of him who fills, or is filled, with all in all; for the participle comes from a "middle" verb <note>term: middle verb: a Greek grammatical form where the subject acts upon or for themselves, sitting between active and passive</note>. Saint Jerome seems to interpret it both ways: that the body (that is, the faithful) is the consummation of Christ himself, who is the head, who is so fulfilled that he is all in all; or that he so fills all that he is all to all—things which are now scattered, some in some people, others in others. But if you take "being filled" <note>original: "πληρουμένου" (pleroumenou)</note> passively, <margin>D</margin> then "all things" <note>original: "τὰ πάντα" (ta panta)</note> can be understood as "in all things," as if the preposition "according to" <note>original: "κατά" (kata)</note> were implied. The sense would be that Christ is fulfilled in all the members of his body collected together. Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret it in this sense, so that the "fullness" is the Church, and the verb is placed passively.

<margin>E</margin> 1 **And he quickened you**] I do not find the word "co-quickened" <note>original: "convivificavit"; meaning to bring to life together with Christ</note> in this place in the Greek codex, nor in Jerome, nor Ambrose, nor in the ancient codex of St. Donatian, nor in either of the Constance manuscripts. Thus, I wonder how it crept into the common books—unless perhaps it was taken from the commentary of Thomas Aquinas or Jerome. Jerome, arranging the speech of this passage, thinks "co-quickened" should be understood as if placed twice, because of the long hyperbaton. For he speaks thus: "And you, when you were dead in your faults and sins, God co-quickened with Christ... who is rich in mercy... and when we were dead in faults... he co-quickened us with Christ." So Jerome thinks it is understood "in common," as if said twice. Therefore, something that was meant to be understood, someone added into the text. The Apostle himself corrected the circuit of the long hyperbaton by saying, "But God, who is rich," etc. Furthermore, the accusative "you" could refer to the earlier verb "he gave": "he gave him as head, [and gave] you as members." But it is more likely it should be repeated here from the hyperbaton, which we will discuss a little further down.

2 **When you were dead in faults and sins**] It could be doubted whether these are dative or ablative—as if he were saying, "They are dead to you." However, Saint Jerome seems to take it as the Greek "dative of instrument," that is, "dead *by means of* sin." What is read here as "fault" is <note>original: "παράπτωμα" (paraptoma)</note> in Greek, which Jerome thinks is that first slip into sinning. For "sin" in Greek is <note>original: "ἁμαρτία" (hamartia)</note>, which he thinks is more serious, as it refers to the deed itself. "In your sins": the word "your" is redundant according to the Greek manuscripts. For he is speaking generally of sins that bring death to all. He used a new expression "dead to sins," whereas elsewhere he calls them "dead to sin," meaning sin is extinguished in them. Here they are called "dead to sins" whom sin has killed. Furthermore, the pronoun "your" which follows is even more redundant: "in which you once walked."

3 **Of the spirit of the power of this air**] <note>original: "κατὰ τὸν ἄρχοντα τῆς ἐξουσίας τοῦ ἀέρος τοῦ πνεύματος" (kata ton archonta tes exousias tou aeros tou pneumatos)</note>. This can be understood in two ways: so that "air" and "spirit" are linked by apposition—"The power of the air, which is indeed the spirit." The Greek article "the" <note>original: "τοῦ" (tou)</note> invites us to take it this way. For the Greeks usually interpret things using the article. But what follows—"of the one working"—stands somewhat in the way. For this "air" does not do anything in the children of disobedience; rather, it is the instigation of the Devil. Therefore, it is better to read it thus: "according to the prince, whose power is of the air, and his spirit works in the children of distrust." You should understand the "air" to be this lowest part of the world, in which he alone reigns—not as a lord, since Christ is Lord of all, but...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed philological and theological commentary on the second chapter of Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians. # TO THE EPHESIANS. CHAPTER II.

<margin>3</margin> [of the] air, of the spirit, now working in the children of unbelief. <margin>A</margin> Among whom we all also lived at one time in the desires of our flesh, doing the wills of the flesh and of the thoughts, <margin>4</margin> and we were by nature children of wrath, even as the others. But God, being rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, <margin>5</margin> even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ, (by grace you have been saved,) <margin>6</margin> and raised us up together, and seated us together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus. <margin>7</margin> so that he might show in the ages to come the surpassing riches of his grace, in kindness toward us <margin>8</margin> in Christ Jesus. For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God. <margin>9 10</margin> <margin>B</margin> Not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, so that we should walk in them. <margin>11</margin> Therefore remember, that you were once Gentiles in the flesh, who are called the "uncircumcision" by those called "the circumcision" in the flesh made by hands. <margin>12</margin> That you were at that time without Christ, being alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of the promise, having no hope, and without God.

---

<margin>3</margin> ...but like a tyrant, and powerful only by our own fault. Next, you should take *spirit* to mean a worldly disposition, distinct from that heavenly *spirit* of Christ, which loves nothing but heavenly things. You should refer both genitives, *of the air* and *of the spirit*, back to the third preceding word, *power*. This is not the Greek word <term>dynamis</term> <note>meaning inherent power or strength</note>, but <term>exousia</term> <note>meaning authority or legal right</note>, so that we understand it as a right and authority. Furthermore, the translator adds the pronoun *among* on his own, as it is not found in the Greek, nor even in Jerome’s text, although *of this world* <note>original Greek: "kosmou toutou"</note> preceded it.

<margin>4 In the children of unbelief] <note>original: "en hyiois apeitheias"</note></margin>, that is, in the children of disobedience, or those who are unyielding, or as Cyprian <note>an early Christian bishop and martyr</note> translates it, *stubborn*. For it is the property of children to be obedient and compliant to their parents. I have warned many times now about this figure of speech: *children of disobedience* is used for *disobedient children*, just as a little earlier *Father of glory* was used for *glorious Father*. In some manuscripts, the text was corrupted to read *unbelief into the children*.

<margin>5 Doing the will] <note>original: "thelemata"</note></margin>, that is, "the wills," for there are various types of desires. However, in many manuscripts, people had corrupted the text to read *pleasures* <note>Latin: "voluptates"</note> instead of *wills* <note>Latin: "voluntates"</note>.

<margin>6 And of the thoughts] <note>original: "kai ton dianoion"</note></margin>. Jerome seems to approve more of the translation *and of the minds*, distinguishing between the sins of the flesh and the sins of the mind, because the former are more coarse, such as lust, gluttony, and drunkenness, while the latter belong more to the soul, such as heresy. Ambrose <note>the 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note> reads it as *of the counsels*.

<margin>7 By nature children of wrath] <note>original: "physei"</note></margin>. For this, some had translated *altogether*, as Jerome indicates, because the Greek word is ambiguous. And Theophylact <note>a medieval Byzantine commentator</note> advises that *by nature* is put for *truly and properly*. In the same way, we say a man is "by nature" wretched who is so devoted to misery that he would not wish to escape it if he could. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, the "Golden-Mouthed" preacher</note> adds: *just as one born of a human is nothing other than a human, so we were nothing other than children of wrath*. It seems to me that Paul opposed "nature" to "grace," because a little later it follows, *by grace you have been saved*. Wrath belonged to our nature or our birth; salvation belonged to grace, and for that reason is to be attributed to Christ, not to ourselves.

<margin>8 Because of the great] <note>original: "dia pollen"</note></margin>, that is, "on account of much." This is how Jerome and Ambrose read it. Otherwise, the Latin word for *too much* <note>Latin: "nimium"</note> refers to something that is immoderate.

<margin>9 And when we were] <note>original: "kai ontas hemas"</note></margin>, that is, *Even when we were*. Thus the conjunction, which has a double force in both Latin and Greek, does not simply join the sentence but adds emphasis.

<margin>10 Dead in sins]</margin> He would have avoided ambiguity if he had said *dead through sins*. For sometimes Paul calls those *dead to sin* who no longer commit sin, as I noted just a little while ago. <margin>E</margin> Ambrose did not add *in sins* in this passage, but only read *when we were dead*.

<margin>11 But God who is rich]</margin> Jerome warns that in the phrase *But God*, the conjunction was either added by unlearned people or was added redundantly by Paul himself through his lack of skill in the Greek language. It interrupts the flow of the speech. But I wonder why Jerome calls "but" a causal conjunction. Perhaps he read *for* <note>Latin: "enim"</note> instead of *but* <note>Latin: "autem"</note>. The contrastive conjunction was not useless here; it is opposed to the calamity which the Apostle had exaggerated with many words: for great evils required an abundant mercy. If you read *nevertheless* instead of *but*, the flow of the speech is not hindered.

<margin>12 He made us alive together in Christ]</margin> Neither the pronoun *us* nor the preposition *in* is in the Greek manuscripts; it is simply <note>original: "synezoopoiese to Christo"</note>, that is, *he made [us] alive with Christ*, so that you understand we have come back to life together with Christ. This is how Augustine reports it in the eleventh book against Faustus, chapter eight, in handwritten books. A very old manuscript from Constance retained the genuine reading, with two words, *us* and *whose*, having been deleted by a hand that was not recent. For the preposition *in* was added in neither.

<margin>13 By whose grace] <note>original: "chariti"</note></margin> The word "whose" was added, but it is only <note>original: "chariti este sesosmenoi"</note>, that is, *by grace you have been saved*. And Saint Jerome reads it this way, so that this little part is inserted as if through a parenthesis, as Theophylact clearly advised. The Latins added the word *for*, but incorrectly. Furthermore, because the order of the speech in this place seems disturbed, Jerome restored it in this manner: *And you, when you were dead in your offenses and sins, God, who is rich in mercy, made you alive with Christ, because of the great love with which he loved us, he had mercy on us, so that when we were...*

<column-break/>

<margin>3</margin> ...the power of the air, and of the spirit now working in the children of stubbornness, among whom we all also lived at one time in the desires of our flesh, doing what pleased the flesh and the mind, and we were by nature children of wrath, just like the rest. <margin>4</margin> But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, <margin>5</margin> even when we were dead through offenses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you are saved—<margin>6</margin> and raised us up together with him, and made us sit together with him among the heavenly ones in Christ Jesus, <margin>7</margin> so that he might show in the coming ages the outstanding wealth of his grace, by his kindness toward us through Christ Jesus. <margin>8</margin> For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God, <margin>9 10</margin> not of works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his work, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we should walk in them. <margin>11</margin> Therefore remember, that you, formerly Gentiles in the flesh, were called the "uncircumcision" by that which is called "the circumcision" in the flesh, which circumcision is made by hands. <margin>12</margin> That you were, I say, at that time without Christ, alienated from the republic of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope, and lacking God.

---

<margin>C</margin> *...dead in offenses, in which we once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air of the spirit, who now works in the children of unbelief, in which we all also lived at one time in the desires of our flesh, doing the wills of the flesh and of the minds, and were by nature children of wrath, he made us alive with Christ:* so that you repeat *he made us alive* twice, and remove the causal conjunction, *For God*. For Jerome seems to have read it this way, <note>original Greek: "Ho gar Theos"</note>, because he thinks this was either added by unlearned scribes or by Paul himself because of his lack of skill in the Greek language, since in most manuscripts it is <note>original Greek: "de"</note>, that is, *but*. Although either conjunction prevents the earlier part of the speech, *When you were etc.*, from being completed. But I think Paul added the contrastive conjunction to provide the opposite part to the preceding words—that is, having been made alive, as opposed to being dead in sins. And because he had mixed in many things, he added the preposition as if starting a new head of the speech. It would have been better if the *Translator* had said, *nevertheless God made [us] alive*. It should also be noted that in this speech Paul frequently changes the person, sometimes addressing them in the second person, sometimes including himself with them. One must also add that in Ambrose there is a different reading than the one we have, though I do not know if it was introduced by scribes. It is written in this manner: *But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love, had mercy on us*.

<margin>14 And he raised us up together] <note>original: "kai synegeire"</note></margin>. <margin>D</margin> <note>original: "kai synegeire, kai synekathisen"</note>, that is, *And equally with him he raised up, and at the same time with him he made to sit*.

<margin>15 In goodness] <note>original: "en chrestoteti"</note></margin>. Which Augustine, in the eleventh book against Faustus, translates as *in benignity*. For it signifies God’s clemency and gentleness toward us.

<margin>16 For by grace] For by grace</margin> is not added in some Greek manuscripts, nor is the phrase a little further down, *For it is the gift of God*. "For" is not added, although Ambrose reads it that way.

<margin>17 For we are his workmanship] <note>original: "poiema"</note></margin>. Ambrose reads *figmentum* <note>meaning a thing fashioned or formed</note>, like something made out of material. And so we had translated it that way, because the word *factura* <note>fashioning</note> seemed insufficiently Latin, but having been advised by learned friends, we changed *figmentum* to *opus* <note>work</note>. For they feared lest the word *figmentum* might offend some unlearned person <note>as it can imply a fiction or a lie in Latin</note>. Yet if one decided to avoid all such offenses with similar zeal, nothing at all should be changed. However, in this part, we followed the will of our friends rather than our own judgment.

<margin>18 In good works] <note>original: "epi ergois agathois"</note></margin>, that is, *toward good works*.

<margin>19 Which God prepared]</margin> <note>original Greek: "hois"</note>, that is, *to which*, I think should be referred to the people. Although according to the property of the Greek language it can also be referred to the works, so that the Greek dative is turned into an accusative, as Ambrose reads it, *which God prepared*, and likewise Jerome.

<margin>20 By that which is called circumcision] <note>original: "hypo tes legomenes peritomes"</note></margin>, that is, by the Jews themselves, for the Greek words are clearer. The people of the Hebrews, on account of the cut genital member, were called "circumcision"; the rest were called "uncircumcision," but only by the Jews, to whom that nickname was honorable, while this one was ignominious. And *made by hands* refers to the circumcision, not to the flesh.

<margin>21 Who were]</margin> It should be read, *Because you were*, or *Since*, as Ambrose (agreeing with the Greek) and Jerome read, <margin>F</margin> with the support of both Constance manuscripts. <note>original Greek: "Hoti ete"</note>, so that it is a repeated conjunction, as if he had put, *Because, I say, you were*.

<margin>22 Alienated from the conversation] <note>original: "tes politeias tou Israel"</note></margin>, that is, *from the city*, or *from the republic of Israel, or of the Israelis*.

<margin>23 And guests of the covenants] <note>original: "kai xenoi ton diathekon"</note></margin>, that is, foreigners, or outsiders, *from the agreements or testaments*. For he alludes to the republic which he just mentioned; hence he calls them guests, who are alienated from the rights of citizens. And he says *covenants of the promise* according to the Hebrew idiom. Furthermore, Ambrose adds a pronoun: *of the law, of their promise*.

<margin>24 And without God] <note>original: "atheoi"</note></margin>. Those who believe there is no God; and <term>atheism</term>, which Plutarch shows is a lesser evil than *superstition* <note>Greek: "deisidaimonia"</note>, because the latter imagines the Gods to be moody and vengeful, whereas God is by nature beneficent. *In this wor...*

# PAUL'S EPISTLE CHAPTER III.
