<margin>C</margin> <note>original: "do]"</note> This is redundant: except that I think the Translator <note>Erasmus refers to the author of the Vulgate Latin Bible</note> wanted to render the force of the article "the" <note>Greek: "tō"</note>.

25 *And dissolving the middle wall of the partition, the enmities*] The Greeks distinguish this so that the accusative "enmities" refers to the lower participle "abolishing." Although it can be referred to both: to "dissolving" which precedes, and to "abolishing" which follows, so that "enmity" coheres appositively with "the middle wall," or with "the Law of commandments." And it is a wonder why, since he turned "the one who made" into a verb, he did not also change the other "dissolving," that is, "who dissolved," or "with the wall being dissolved." Again, in Greek it is "the middle-wall of the fence," as if you were to say, the space between a barrier or a hedge. And in the Comic poet, "to dissolve the wall" <note>Greek: "lyein maceriam"</note> means for a wall to be pulled down so that it becomes one house. And therefore, that which separates the houses, he calls a "middle-wall." Nor does the Translator translate poorly, except that the speech does not lack ambiguity. For he strikes the "middle wall" who hits the middle part.

<margin>D</margin> 26 *Abolishing in decrees*] The preposition "in" being omitted subverts the whole sense, as if he abolished the law *by* decrees: rather, he abolished the law *consisting* in precepts and decrees. A certain edition, which Jerome cites, had "in dogmas," using the Greek word. Ambrose reads "in decrees": elsewhere he cites "edicts": in the second book of *Abraham the Patriarch*, chapter six. If the article had been added to the Greek, "the law of commandments which are in decrees," no doubt would remain: now the speech has ambiguity: for "in decrees" can apply to what precedes and what follows simultaneously. If to what precedes, the sense will be: "he abrogated the law of precepts situated in decrees." If to what follows, the sense will be: "he invalidated the law of ceremonial precepts through Evangelical dogmas," so that the preposition "in" is placed in the stead of "through." This is what the Translator seems to have followed, who omitted the preposition as if it were superfluous to us. I find this interpretation in Theophylact alone, who seems to have followed Chrysostom; he thinks the "dogmas" are the faith by which we are saved, or Evangelical precepts, such as: "But I say to you, do not be angry at all." Ambrose follows a different view, whose words I will subscribe here: "Because the law, which was given to the Jews in circumcision, and in new moons, and in foods, and in sacrifices, and in sabbaths, he abolished, that is, he commanded it to cease now, because the era had arrived, and thus he made peace." Hence Peter the Apostle says in the Acts of the Apostles: "Why do you place a yoke upon the neck of the brothers, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?" In these words of Ambrose, no mention is made of "decrees" through which the law was invalidated. Ambrose indicates, however, that circumcision and similar observations of the law became obsolete, so that it might be consistent between the Gentiles and Jews. These things therefore having been invalidated through Christ, we are reconciled by faith, which confers salvation to both Jews and Gentiles without the observation of the law. Jerome puts it this way: "The law of commandments was also subverted in dogmas, after circumcision, and the sabbath-keeping which is left to the people of God, and Passover, and Pentecost, and not appearing empty in the sight of God, are understood otherwise than they sound, departing from the killing letter and following its vivifying Spirit." From these words of Jerome it is clear that he feels the law was abrogated not by "decrees," but by the spiritual understanding of those things which it decreed. Nor is the commentary of the Scholiast <note>A term for an ancient commentator</note>, who goes by the name of Jerome, inconsistent with these things. He says, "Justifying through faith alone, they shall decree moral things only." Now, Paul also elsewhere calls the prescriptions of the law "dogmas," as in Colossians 2: "The handwriting of the decree that was against us": in which place the Greeks read "to the dogmas" for that which is "in dogmas." For the preposition is added from the idiom of the Hebrew language. Again elsewhere: "Why are you still making dogmas?" <note>Colossians 2:20</note>. Furthermore, we never read in Paul that the precepts of the Gospel are called "dogmas." Therefore, that doubt about the article must be set aside. To me, it seems to have been omitted because of the pile-up of articles, if he had said "the law of the commandments of the ones in the dogmas." For to me, "in decrees" seems to adhere more to the nearest word; otherwise the same thing seemed to be said twice: "the law of the commandments of the ones in the dogmas." Now showing the law to be overbearing, he calls it "of commandments," as if you were to say "imperative," that is, commanding. How? Not by persuasion and gentleness or promises, but by prescriptions, which he calls dogmas; the Latins call them "placita" <note>Formal decrees or opinions</note>. For if you ask why God commanded us to <margin>E</margin> abstain from such and such foods, the Jew would respond: "Because it so 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> 13 lacking in the world. But now through Christ Jesus you, who once were far off, have been made near through the blood of Christ. For he is our peace, <margin>14</margin> who made one from both, <gloss>25</gloss> and destroyed the space of the partition, the enmity through his flesh, <gloss>26</gloss> the Law of commandments situated in decrees abrogating, <gloss>27</gloss> so that he might create the two in himself <gloss>28</gloss> into one new man, making peace, and that he might reconcile both in one body <margin>16</margin> to God through the cross, <gloss>29</gloss> having slain the enmity through it, and coming he preached peace to you, who were far away, <gloss>30</gloss> and to those who were near. Because however through <margin>18</margin> him <gloss>31</gloss> we have access both in one Spirit to the Father. Now therefore you are not <gloss>32</gloss> guests and inhabitants, <gloss>33</gloss> <margin>19</margin> but fellow-citizens of the saints and members of the household of God, <gloss>34</gloss> built <margin>20</margin> <margin>B</margin> upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, <gloss>35</gloss> with the highest cornerstone being Jesus Christ himself, in whom whatever structure <gloss>36</gloss> is joined together, it grows into a holy temple in the Lord, in whom you also <margin>22</margin> are built together into a dwelling of God <gloss>37</gloss> through the Spirit. For the <margin>1 III.</margin> sake of this thing I, Paul, <gloss>1</gloss> am a prisoner of Christ Jesus <gloss>2</gloss> <margin>2</margin> for you Gentiles. If indeed you heard <gloss>3</gloss> the stewardship of the grace of God, <gloss>4</gloss> which was given to me toward you, that according to revelation <gloss>5</gloss> he made known the mystery to me, <margin>3</margin> <gloss>6</gloss> as—

pleased God." And "abolishing" is in the past tense, as if you were to say, "the law having been invalidated."

27 *And he may create the two*] This is "might create" or "might prepare," <note>Greek: "ktisē"</note> as if explaining the thought.

28 *In one new man*] "Into one new man" is the Greek, <note>Greek: "eis ena kainon anthrōpon"</note>. And thus Augustine relates it in the book *Against Faustus*, book 22, chapter 89. Both the Constance manuscripts supported this. Furthermore, where the Greek is "might reconcile" <note>Greek: "apokatallaxē"</note>, the Latin version has "reconciliet." Augustine translates it "might change" <note>Latin: "commutaret"</note>. He who translates it thus seems to have read "allaxē."

29 *Enmities in himself*] "In himself," Jerome reads "in it" <note>the cross</note>, so that it refers to the cross, not to Christ. Indeed, even "cross" <note>stauros</note> among the Greeks is of the masculine gender. But if it were reflexive, he would mean "in his own self" <note>Greek: "en hautō"</note>. Although not even that is observed by Greek writers. Finally, Ambrose reads otherwise.

30 *And peace to those who are near*] "And peace" is not repeated by the Greeks.

31 *We have access*] <note>Greek: "prosagōgēn"</note>, that is, an approach or an introduction: as when someone is introduced into the sight of a Prince.

32 *Guests and strangers*] <note>Greek: "xenoi kai paroikoi"</note>, that is, foreigners and inhabitants, or neighbors, that is, those who have migrated from elsewhere into another's city. Augustine several times reads "tenants" <note>Latin: "inquilini"</note> instead of "stranger."

33 *But you are citizens*] <note>Greek: "alla sympolitai"</note>, that is, "but fellow-citizens," so that word is rendered by word.

34 *Built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets*] The Marcionites <note>A second-century Christian sect that rejected the Old Testament</note> erased this particle, "and Prophets," undoubtedly out of hatred for the Old Testament.

35 *Cornerstone*] In Greek it is a single word, <note>Greek: "akrogōniaiou"</note>, by which is signified the highest stone in the corner of a building, which is usually the strongest. Moreover, it is an ablative absolute, as if you were to say, "In which structure the highest stone is in the corner." And for this reason Augustine, bringing up this passage in his commentary on Psalm 81, adds "existing," more clearly in Latin. Again *Against Faustus*, book twelve, chapter twenty-four: "In the very highest cornerstone, Christ Jesus." And here the ablative is placed absolutely, as if you were to say, "with Christ as leader," <note>Greek: "ontos akrogōniaiou hautou Iēsou Christou"</note>, that is, with Jesus Christ himself being the highest cornerstone.

36 *Construction*] In Greek it is more significant, <note>Greek: "synarmologoumenē"</note>, that is, "joined together," or "fastened," or "fitted." Jerome reads "compacted." Ambrose "compacted." Nor does it mean every structure is compacted by this cornerstone, but whatever is connected by that stone, it rises into a temple of the Lord. For it is a present participle, "being joined together." Although "every building" <note>Greek: "pasa hē oikodomē"</note> could be translated "the whole structure," so that you do not understand just any structure, but the whole one. And thus Theophylact interprets it.

37 *In the holy Spirit*] "Holy" is redundant according to the Greek and Ambrose, and also Jerome, whose interpretation also declares what they read. For he opposes the "Spirit" to the carnal affection of the Jews, which Paul never ceases to attack.

<margin>F</margin> 1 *Prisoner of Christ Jesus*] "Prisoner" is the noun in Greek <note>Greek: "desmios"</note>: and for this reason it coheres more smoothly with the genitive "of Jesus Christ."

2 *For you Gentiles*] I think it is a mistake that "for you brothers" is read in the Ambrosian codices.

3 *Stewardship of grace*] <note>Greek: "oikonomian"</note>, that is, stewardship, or administration.

4 *Is given to me in you*] <note>Greek: "en hymin"</note>, that is, "toward you." Jerome also renders this place ungrammatically in this way: "For the sake of this thing I, Paul, prisoner of Jesus Christ, and prisoner for you in you, who are from the Gentiles, have known the mystery, so that I might hand it over to you: just as I spoke a little before in this same Epistle. But with many things deleted, 'the stewardship of the grace of God, which was given to me in you, who are from the Gentiles, for whom I am also a prisoner of Jesus Christ'." Although he thinks it is simple to admit that Paul "stuttered" in a foreign language, and was more concerned with the sense than the words. The inconvenience of the imperfect speech could also be removed in this way, if you understand the substantive verb "sum" <note>I am</note>: "I, Paul, am a prisoner of Jesus Christ."

5 *It was made known to me*] <note>Greek: "egnōrise moi to mystērion"</note>, that is, he made known to me the mystery, which the Translator again turned into "Sacrament."

6 **Just as I wrote before** <note>original: *Sicut supra scripsi*</note>] <note>original Greek: *kathos proegrapsa*</note>, that is, "just as I wrote before," as Ambrose has it. Saint Jerome reads it as "I have prescribed."

7 **In brief** <note>original: *In brevi*</note>] <note>original Greek: *en oligo*</note>, that is, "in a small amount," as Jerome and Ambrose read it. For it signifies that he wrote a few things about these matters, as the Greek commentaries <note>The "scholia" or marginal notes in Greek manuscripts.</note> explain. The sense could also be: "just as I wrote a little while ago." For he mentions those who were far off, meaning the Gentiles. Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and Bible commentator.</note> takes it in this sense.

8 **In the ministry of Christ** <note>original: *In ministerio Christi*</note>] <note>original Greek: *en to mysterio*</note>, that is, "in the mystery," which is usually translated as *Sacramentum* <note>Erasmus often notes that the Latin "sacrament" comes from the Greek word for "mystery."</note>.

9 **In other generations** <note>original: *Aliis generationibus*</note>] It is clearer as Ambrose reads it: "in other ages." For he is speaking of eras of time, not of nations. "It was not known" <note>original Greek: *hos egnoristhe*</note>, that is, not made known, or revealed.

10 **In the Spirit** <note>original: *In Spiritu*</note>] In the Greek, "holy" is added. Not only is the reading different, but also the phrasing. Theophylact arranges the sentence like this: "as it is now revealed to his holy Apostles in the Holy Spirit," so that we understand this was revealed to them through the Holy Spirit. Ambrose, on the other hand, connects "Spirit" with what follows: "As it has now been revealed to his holy Apostles and Prophets, that by the Spirit the Gentiles are co-heirs." This is clearly proven by his own interpretation, saying the Gentiles are co-heirs not by the ceremonies of the Mosaic Law, but by the Spirit—that is, by Gospel doctrine. Saint Jerome follows the Greek phrasing. To me, Ambrose's way is more approved.

11 **That the nations are** <note>original: *Esse gentes*</note>] <note>original Greek: *Einai ta ethne*</note>, that is, "that the nations might be."

12 **Of the same body** <note>original: *Concorporales*</note>] <note>original Greek: *syssoma*</note>, as if you were to say "of one body." In this place, a heap of conjunctions offends Jerome’s ears as being, in his view, awkward: "co-heirs and of the same body and fellow-partakers." It is surprising that he is offended by such a small thing—he who so often claims Paul was unskilled in the Greek language, even though he admits Paul was not unskilled in knowledge. Furthermore, while he admits here that "fellow-partakers" should be read in a positive sense, in the fifth chapter of this same Epistle he denies this word is ever used in Holy Scripture except in a negative sense. But more will be said on that matter there.

13 **Of the promise in Christ Jesus** <note>original: *Promissionis in Christo Jesu*</note>] Our Latin text lacks "his" <note>original Greek: *autou*</note>, which refers to the Spirit, as Ambrose seems to have felt when he wrote: "This is what he says: that by the Spirit the Gentiles are co-heirs and of the same body and partakers of his promise in Christ. For whoever worships God in spirit has no need for the works of the Law."

14 **Of all the saints** <note>original: *Omnium sanctorum*</note>] In some Greek copies, "of men" was added, but incorrectly, if I am not mistaken. And "the very least" <note>original Greek: *elachistotero*</note>, that is, the lowest, as Jerome translates it. But Paul, to diminish himself even more, coined a comparative form from a superlative—as if you were to say "leaster" instead of "least," or "the most-lastest."

15 **Unsearchable** <note>original: *Investigabiles*</note>] <note>original Greek: *anexichniaston plouton*</note>, that is, the "un-trackable" riches. For where Ambrose reads "un-flammable," I suspect it is an error by the scribe; he certainly interprets it as "incomprehensible."

16 **And to enlighten** <note>original: *Et illuminare*</note>] <note>original Greek: *Kai photisai pantas*</note>. Ambrose does not add "all," and the sentence is more natural. Nor is there any mention of this added noun in Jerome; he has only "to enlighten." Yet Paul does not "enlighten" men himself; rather, he brings into the light and makes clear to everyone what had previously been hidden.

17 **What is the dispensation** <note>original: *Quae sit dispensatio*</note>] Some read "what are the riches" <note>original Greek: *plethos*</note>. Again, he translates "mystery" as "Sacrament."

18 **Who created all things** <note>original: *Qui omnia creavit*</note>] "Through Jesus Christ" <note>original Greek: *dia Iesou Christou*</note> is added in this place in the Greek copies, though Jerome does not have it, nor Ambrose, nor the old Latin manuscripts.

19 **So that it might be known** <note>original: *Ut innotescat*</note>] <note>original Greek: *Hina gnoristhe nyn*</note>, that is, "so that it may be known now." Jerome also reads it with the "and" conjunction added, provided the manuscript is free of error.

20 **To the powers in the heavenly places** <note>original: *Potestatibus in caelestibus*</note>] <note>original Greek: *en tois epouraniois*</note>, that is, "in the heavenlies."

21 **Through the Church** <note>original: *Per Ecclesiam*</note>] <note>original Greek: *dia tes Ekklesias*</note>. The preposition "through" in this place signifies the instrument, as if you were to say "by the work of the Church." Though, to speak candidly, the Greek phrasing would be quite ambiguous if the article "the" <note>original Greek: *tes*</note> had not been added; without it, the sense would have been "on account of the congregations, or churches."

22 **Manifold wisdom** <note>original: *Multiformis sapientia*</note>] <note>original Greek: *polypoikilos*</note>, or elsewhere "all-varied," that is, greatly diverse, and varied in every way. For the "poly-" prefix in the composition adds intensity.

23 **According to the pre-definition** <note>original: *Secundum praefinitionem*</note>] <note>original Greek: *Kata prothesin*</note>, that is, "according to the purpose," as Jerome reads it.

24 **Which he made** <note>original: *Quam fecit*</note>] <note>original Greek: *hen epoiesen*</note>. The Greek phrasing is ambiguous. For the Greek article can refer back to the wisdom, the church, or the pre-definition (which Ambrose and Jerome call the "purpose"). If it refers to the "purpose," the sense is: "according to the time he had purposed or pre-defined in Christ." If to the "church," the sense would be: "the Church made in Christ Jesus." If to the "wisdom," you understand the wisdom to have been made—that is, created—in Christ. This last sense is most approved by Jerome. And "confidence" is <note>original Greek: *parrhesia*</note>, which Ambrose translates as "liberty." It is, however, the boldness of speaking freely. Furthermore, there is none of this spirit in those with a guilty conscience, just as nothing is more confident than innocence.

25 **In my tribulations for you** <note>original: *In tribulationibus meis pro vobis*</note>] <note>original Greek: *athymein hyp' emauto*</note>. Saint Jerome warns that the Greek phrase is ambiguous, because the verb "to fail" <note>original Greek: *ekkakein*</note> can be applied to any person: that *I* might not fail, that *you* might not fail, or that *they* might not fail. Jerome certainly interprets it according to the first and second sense: "I ask that I might not fail, lest the bitter power of those attacking me from all sides overcome me."

26 **Which is glory** <note>original: *Quae est gloria*</note>] In some Greek codices it was held as "which will be." In this place, Jerome twists himself quite a bit, and I don't quite understand why he struggles so much, thinking the logic of this phrasing cannot hold unless he admits Paul spoke unskillfully. He complains that Paul used a singular relative pronoun ("which is glory") for the plural "tribulations." As if grammar does not teach us that it is actually more correct to speak this way than to say "in the tribulations, which are your glory." He finds this so awkward that he tries to use a "transposition" <note>term: hyperbaton - a figure of speech where the natural word order is disrupted for emphasis</note> to twist this phrase "which is your glory" back to what came before: "in whom we have confidence and access and faith," and so on—"which confidence, power, and faith is your glory." But since he saw this was too forced, he prefers to make Paul "unskilled in speaking." But meanwhile, what will they do with Jerome, who wanted the Apostles to have received the knowledge of all languages by the gift of the Holy Spirit, and for that gift to have been perpetual for them? Thomas Aquinas seems to be of that number in his commentary on Galatians. Yet Jerome is not afraid to so often accuse Paul of ignorance of the Greek language. Though in this specific place, I don't see what could be seen as "unskilled," except perhaps that he spoke in a more Hebrew than Greek fashion by saying "in tribulations" instead of "because of tribulations."

27 **To the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ** <note>original: *Ad Patrem Domini nostri Jesu Christi*</note>] Saint Jerome indicates that in the Latin manuscripts, four words were added—"of our Lord Jesus Christ"—whereas in the Greek, the original writing remains. For he is not speaking here specifically of the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ, but in a general sense he bows his knees to that Father whom all rational creatures recognize as their founder and author. And yet, it is strange that what Jerome writes was added in the Latin manuscripts is now found in the Greek. However, Chrysostom and Theophylact, in explaining the passage, do not touch upon this phrase; from which it must be guessed either that it was added to the Greek from our Latin copies, or that the Greek manuscripts varied even in antiquity.

28 **Every paternity** <note>original: *Omnis paternitas*</note>] <note>original Greek: *pasa patria*</note>, that is, "every family," as Saint Jerome also indicates in his Commentaries. The same Jerome, writing against Helvidius, admits that the Latins use the word "paternitas" for what the Greeks call "patrias"—the great multitude of a lineage that spreads out from one root. But in the Greek, the wordplay remains <note>A pun on "Father" (*pater*) and "family/lineage" (*patria*)</note>, which the Latin translator tried to preserve. Now, as for those questions raised in this place by Thomas Aquinas—whether because paternity exists in heaven, and whether every paternity on heaven and earth is derived from that paternity which is in the divine—since they pertain aptly to this place, let the Theologians look to them; since the word from which...

...strengthened through his Spirit in the inner man, that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, being rooted and grounded in love; <margin>18</margin> that you may have the strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and depth and height, <margin>19</margin> and to know the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. <margin>20</margin> Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly beyond all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us, <margin>21</margin> to him be glory in the Church in Christ Jesus to all generations forever and ever. <margin>IV. 1</margin> Amen. I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you were called, <margin>2</margin> with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, <margin>3</margin> eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. <margin>4</margin> There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling. <margin>5</margin> One Lord, one faith, one baptism, <margin>6</margin> one God and Father of all, who is over...
<meta>catchword: all-</meta>

---

<margin>A</margin> <note>Referring to the word "paternitas" (fatherhood) from the previous page.</note> This choice draws out every possible question; the translator did not understand it. Certainly, elsewhere the Translator renders it as *family*, such as in the Psalm, *All the families of the nations* <note>original Greek: πατριαί (patriai)</note>. Likewise in Luke, *of the house and family of David*. The translator of Origen’s second Homily on Numbers noted this; Chrysostom explains it as *tribes* <note>original: φυλὰς (phylas)</note>. Truly the Translator, as I began to say, strove to reflect the linguistic relationship between the words *father* and *fatherhood* <note>original: pater and paternitas</note>. But that was not so important that the meaning should be lost for its sake. *Kindred* <note>original: parentela</note> explained the matter well enough, if only the word were considered proper Latin. And yet Jerome testifies that this word was commonly used in his own age, making it more tolerable than "fatherhood," especially since the grammatical analogy supports it here. For just as *clientela* (clientage) comes from *cliens* (client), so *parentela* (kindred) comes from *parens* (parent). I have rendered it with a workaround as best I could.

*29 Strengthened by power*] <note>original: δυνάμει (dynamei)</note>, that is, by power. The sense would be clearer if the Greek infinitive were translated with a subjunctive verb, *so that you might be strengthened*.

*30 Height and depth*] <note>original: καὶ βάθος καὶ ὕψος (kai bathos kai hypsos)</note>, that is, both depth and height. Jerome says, both the deep and the altitude.

*31 To know also*] This is not the start of a new sentence where "also" is needed: *To know and* <note>original: Γνῶναί τε (gnōnai te)</note>, that is, *And to know*, or *And that you might know*.

<margin>B</margin> *32 The love of Christ which surpasses knowledge*] In our Latin text, it is uncertain whether *knowledge* is in the dative or genitive case: so that you might understand either the love of Christ is known, which is too great to be fully grasped; or according to Ambrose, that it stands above our knowledge; or that you understand it as the exceptional love of shared understanding. But the latter sense fits the Greek speech better. Jerome follows this. Furthermore, that Ambrose felt as I said is shown by these words of his: *after the infinite and incomprehensible knowledge of God the Father, and his unspeakable mercy, he wishes us to also recognize the love of Christ, which stands above knowledge, and is understood as human, so that the love of Christ is held above the knowledge of men. For who can grasp the reason for this love in the mystery, that God should be born a man for the sake of man? etc.* However, I suspect there is a mistake in this manuscript. For in the context we have, *And to know the surpassing knowledge of the love of Christ*, which is how Augustine quotes it in his 120th Epistle: this reading sounds very different from the Greek. Moreover, regarding what is in the commentary, *it is of surpassing knowledge*, I suspect he himself wrote, *knowledge is surpassing*. Furthermore, what Jerome discusses in this place seems to me somewhat harsh. He does not refer this word *knowledge* to *surpassing*, but to *love*. Certainly Theophylact interprets it in the same sense as Ambrose. And Augustine agrees with Ambrose, citing this passage in his book *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 19: likewise, he says, *when the Apostle speaks of the love of Christ surpassing knowledge, what is more insane than to think knowledge comes from God—which must be subject to love—and that love, which surpasses knowledge, comes from men?* There would be no doubt, however, if the word *surpassing* <note>original: ὑπερβάλλουσα (hyperballousa)</note> were allowed to be joined to the case of the father <note>the genitive case</note>, just as occurs with words like *to outlast*, *to praise excessively*, and *to exceed*, which means the same as *to surpass*. For I do not wish to retreat to the claim that Paul misused the case because of a neglect or ignorance of the Greek language. Theophylact explains it in this way: *So that you might be able,* he says, *to know the love of Christ, which excels all knowledge. How shall we know it? First indeed you say this excels knowledge, surely human knowledge, but you will know this not through human knowledge, but through the Spirit.* Then he did not say, *You will know how great it is*, but this very thing, *that it is great, and that it exceeds all knowledge. This I pray that you may say by the Spirit. And who,* he says, *does not know this? All, even those who take offense at what happens daily, and those who prefer Mammon to God. But if we knew this, we would by no means grumble against divine providence, or devote our souls to present things, falling away from God, who loved us so. But attend to this: If love excels all knowledge, how much more does his very substance.* Thus far Theophylact: from which it appears he felt that love was more excellent than knowledge. Chrysostom does not touch on this difficulty.

*33 And to him, who is able to do all things*] In Greek it is <note>original: τῷ δὲ δυνάμενῳ ποιῆσαι (tō de dynamenō poiēsai)</note>, that is, *to do above all things*. And so Ambrose and Jerome read it: but in such a way that *above* seems to be an adverb, not a preposition, carrying the force of, as if you were to say, *excellently*. Certainly in the 
<meta>catchword: next</meta>

<column-break/>

the riches of his glory, that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner man, That Christ may <margin>17</margin> dwell through faith in your hearts, with roots fixed in love and the foundation laid: That you may be able <margin>18</margin> to grasp with all the saints, what is the breadth and length and depth and height, || And to know <insert>32</insert> the love of <margin>19</margin> Christ which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled into all the fullness of God. ---

<margin>C</margin> next place when it is repeated, *far more abundantly* <note>original: ὑπὲρ ἐκπερισσοῦ (hyper ekperissou)</note>, it can be nothing other than an adverb. It is moreover a double emphasis <note>term: epitafis — a rhetorical addition for emphasis</note>, as Chrysostom and Theophylact noted. God can do all things, which no man can, and he can provide most abundantly whatever he wills, and beyond what we ask. Now, Reader, you will notice even without being told that this is a kind of "coronis" <note>term: coronis — a concluding summary or flourish</note>, such as Paul sometimes attaches to his arguments as if he were carried away and inspired.

*34 More abundantly than we ask*] <note>original: ὑπὲρ ἐκπερισσοῦ ὧν αἰτούμεθα (hyper ekperissou hōn aitoumetha)</note>, that is, from an abundance above those things which we ask. *Than we ask* we understand as, *what we ask or think*. For so Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo Valla, a pioneer of New Testament scholarship</note> corrects it: though that does not matter so much to the sense. The unlearned Reader should only be reminded that the relative *of which* <note>original: ὧν (hōn)</note> agrees with the preceding word, though it differs from its own verb, and this is due to a property of the Greek language.

*35 In the Church and in Christ*] The conjunction *and* is redundant. Ambrose reads it in a different order, *in Christ Jesus and in the Church*. And he interprets it according to this order. In the first place, the preposition is used simply, *in the Church*, as if you said "in the Assembly"; in the other, it follows the property of Hebrew speech. For he prays that the Father be glorified in the congregation of the saints through the Son Jesus Christ, and in this sense the use of the preposition was intended.

<margin>D</margin> <insert>1</insert> *Worthy of the calling*] <note>original: ἀξίως τῆς κλήσεως (axiōs tēs klēseōs)</note>. He added the case of a noun to an adverb, as if you said, "similarly to you." And again the article corresponds to the preceding noun, though it disagrees with its own verb. Otherwise one would have to say, *by which you were called*.

*2 With all humility*] <note>original: ταπεινοφροσύνη (tapeinophrosyne)</note>. Which signifies a habit of the soul contrary to arrogance: for "humility," which is *tapeinosis* <note>lower state or humiliation</note>, signifies something else. And for that reason Ambrose adds *humility of the soul*, lest we should take it for the humility of one's fortune or social status.

*3 With patience*] <note>original: μακροθυμίας (makrothymias)</note>, that is, with long-suffering, if one renders it word-for-word. Ambrose reads it thus: *with all humility of mind and modesty, with magnanimity*: translating *makrothymia* as "magnanimity," though it sounds more like mildness and moderation of the mind, by which it happens that we are not easily moved, nor carried away to a desire for revenge. *Long-suffering* expresses the Greek word more closely than *magnanimity*: and yet a "long mind" is different from being mild and slow to anger. *Patience* was held correctly, except that it is ambiguous, and more often pertains to the endurance of the body than to the mildness of the soul.

<margin>E</margin> *4 Eager to keep*] <note>original: Σπουδάζοντες (Spoudazontes)</note>, that is, *Striving*. Which Augustine, in the second book against the *Letters of Petilian*, chapter 69, translates as *Acting solicitously*. And soon in chapter 78 he translates it as, *Striving to keep*: just as we have translated it. Ambrose has, *Solicitously keeping*.

*5 In the bond of peace*] <note>original: ἐν τῷ συνδέσμῳ (en tō syndesmō)</note>. As if you said, in a binding together and a linking. Augustine in the same place translates it as *conjunction*. For a "bond" <note>Latin: vinculum</note> can be said of one thing: a *syndesmos* is that by which one thing is connected to another.

*6 Who is over all and through all*] It was better to persevere in the same gender, and not mix things with people: *over all things and through all things*, or *over all people and through all people*; for among the Greeks the gender is uncertain. Jerome seems to embrace the neuter gender more, bringing in that line from Virgil,
<margin>F</margin> > ------ For God goes through all 
> lands, and the reaches of the sea, and the deep heaven.
At any rate, the scribes inserted *all [people]* <note>masculine plural</note>, but against the sense. For Jerome explains it thus: *For God the Father is over all: because he is the author of all. The Son is through all: because he runs through all things and goes through all. The Holy Spirit is in all: because nothing is without him.* These are his words. In the first part, since "of all" could be of any gender, it is not clear whether it refers to all men or all things that exist. In the second part, when he adds this reason, *because he runs through all things and goes through all*, he declares that he read not *through all people*, but *through all things*. In *in all*, it is again ambiguous: but what is subjoined, *because without him nothing is*, declares that *in all* is said in the neuter gender. Otherwise he would have said, *without him no one is*. This is supported by the question which Jerome soon adds: *Nor indeed should it be thought,* he says, *that there is one God and Father of all in a common way, so that for instance the name of Father could be applied to irrational beasts, and the rest.* This doubt is raised in vain if he reads that he is *Father over all [people]*. To the same point belongs what he adds: *Zeno with his Stoics suspected something of the sort regarding creatures and God:* for the opinion regarding the doctrine...

...of all, and through all, and in all you. 7 But to each one of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift. 
8 Therefore he says: "When he ascended on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men." <note>original: Ἀναβὰς εἰς ὕψος, ᾐχμαλώτευσεν αἰχμαλωσίαν, καὶ ἔδωκε δόματα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις.</note>
9 Now this "he ascended," what is it but that he also first descended into the lower parts of the earth? 
10 He who descended is the same also who ascended far above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things. 
11 And he gave some as Apostles, some as Prophets, some as Evangelists, some as Pastors and Teachers, 
12 For the restoration of the saints for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, 
13 Until we all arrive at the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, into a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ, 
14 So that we may no longer be infants, tossed by waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine, in the trickery <note>original: κυβείᾳ (kybeia), literally "dice-playing."</note>

<margin>A</margin> Of Zeno, which Laertius reports thus: <note>original: Θιὸν δὲ εἶναι ζῶον ἀθάνατον... (the Greek passage below)</note> "That God is an immortal animal, rational, or perfect, whose happiness is not subject to any evil, taking providential care of the world and the things in the world. However, he is not merely human in form, but is the creator of all things, just as he is the Father of all; both in a general sense and in that part of him which extends through all things, which is called by many names according to his powers. For they call him *Dia*, because through him are all things, and they call him *Zena*, insofar as he is the cause of life," and so forth. *That is, God is an immortal animal, rational, or an intellect, happy because he is capable of no evil, having providential care both of the world and those things that are in the world. Yet he is not of human appearance, but is the craftsman of all things, just as he is also the Father of all, indeed in common, but in such a way that he is a part of the world itself, by which, or because, he penetrates through all things, which is called by various surnames according to different powers.* *Dia*, *that is, they call him Jove, because through him all things exist; Zena, that is, they call him Jove, because he is the author of life.* So says Laertius. In his words, I suspect there is a mistake which the Interpreter seems to have followed; instead of what is written, "through whom all things," I think it should be written "extending through all things," so that "animal" is understood, or "showing all things," or certainly "by means of whom are all things." For "on account of whom all things" does not sound like "through whom all things," but "because of whom all things." Therefore, looking back at this opinion of Zeno, Jerome adds: *Whom Virgil followed when he said:*
> For God goes through all
> The lands, and the tracts of the sea, and the deep sky.
<margin>And,</margin>
> In the beginning, the sky and the lands, and so forth.
These testimonies do not match unless we read "through all things." This is also supported by what he adds: *Some think this phrase—over all, through all, and in all—should be referred to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in this way: "over all" belongs to the Father, because he is the greatest of all; "through all" to the Son, because through the Son all things were created; "in all" to the Spirit, for he is given to believers, and we are the temple of the Holy Spirit, and the Father and Son dwell in us.* Here again you see "all things" <note>neuter: omnia</note> placed in the interpretation, not "all people" <note>masculine: omnes</note>, except for the last part. Although "all things" may fit there too, as the testimony of the Psalm suggests: *The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and he who contains all things has knowledge of the voice.* Likewise, at the beginning of Genesis: *The Spirit of the Lord was spread over the waters.* However, what great thing would the Apostle be saying if he said God the Father was "over all men," since the Angels are more excellent than the human race? The doubt raised by Jerome could be removed in another way: since all things are simply from God the Father, he is not absurdly called the *Father of all* by a general use of the paternal name, just as the Devil is called the father of lies because he first taught how to lie. Such academic debates would not burden the reader, had not certain people with great arrogance rebuked me for saying that Jerome's explanation seems to embrace the neuter gender more. Chrysostom, explaining this passage, advises: "over all, through all, and in all." The dignity of God excels not only men, but the entire creation. Then, when he explains "through all" regarding the governance of God, he surely governs all things. In Chrysostom's explanation, a pronoun is added in the third place: "in all you" <note>original: ἐν πᾶσιν ὑμῖν</note>, that is, *in all of you*. Yet in the context, it is not added. Ambrose prefers the masculine gender: *over all, through all, and in all you:* the last of which cannot be anything but masculine. Theophylact refers both to us in the masculine gender.

7 *And in all you*] For which Ambrose reads *in all believers*. In Jerome, "you" is not added, it is only *in all*. Nor can anything else be gathered from his interpretation. From this passage, the Greeks refute the Heretics who make the Son less than the Father and the Holy Spirit less than both, because they say the preposition "through" <note>original: διὰ</note> properly applies to the Son, and "in" <note>original: ἐν</note> to the Holy Spirit, while "over" <note>original: ἐπὶ</note> is attributed to the Father. Here, both prepositions are attributed to the Father: "through" and "in." Yet they do not have the power of diminishing his status.

8 *Ascending on high*] <note>original: Ἀναβὰς εἰς ὕψος</note>, that is, After he had ascended on high, in the past tense. Now the testimony he brings is from the sixty-seventh Psalm. The Seventy <note>The Septuagint</note> translated it in this way: *You ascended on high, you led captivity captive, you received gifts among men.* Paul, knowingly and deliberately, changed a single word from the Hebrew, as Jerome indicates while explaining this passage. For while among them it is read, *he received gifts among men*, here he changed it to *he gave gifts among men*. Nor does that variation hinder the meaning at all, since in the Psalm a future event is promised which had not yet happened, and for that reason he is said to have "received" gifts which he would later distribute. Here, because the Apostle describes what had already

who is over all, and through all, 7 and in all you. But to each one of us was given grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ. Wherefore he says, <margin>7</margin> <margin>8</margin> When he had ascended on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men. 9 But that word "he ascended," what is it, except that he had also descended first <margin>9</margin> into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same one <margin>10</margin> who also ascended above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things. And the same one gave some indeed as Apostles, but others as Prophets, others as Evangelists, but others as Pastors and Teachers, 11 For the restoration of the saints into the work of administration, into the building up <margin>12</margin> of the body of Christ, Until we all arrive at the unity of faith and of the recognition of the Son of God, into a perfect man, into the measure of the full adult age of Christ, So that <margin>13</margin> we may no longer be children, who fluctuate and are carried about by any wind of doctrine, 14 through the trickery of men—

<margin>B</margin> happened, with Churches established everywhere throughout the world, he is written to have "given," not "received."

<margin>C</margin> 9 *But that he ascended*] <note>original: Τὸ δὲ ἀνέβη, τί ἐστι</note>, that is, *But that which is said, "he ascended," what is it?* and so forth.

<margin>10</margin> *Others moreover Pastors and Teachers*] Jerome noted, and Augustine followed him in his fifty-ninth Letter, that while he distinguished the types of offices in the others, here he joined two; for he does not say "some Pastors, some Teachers," but "others Pastors and Teachers," because whoever are Pastors ought to be the same as the Teachers. Ambrose, not noticing this, I believe, takes them separately, as if Pastors and Masters were different. Again, he seems to have observed little that among the Greeks, instead of Masters, it is *Didaskalous*, that is, Teachers. For he interprets "Masters" as Exorcists, who restrain and beat the restless in the Church. Although Theophylact, having proposed the sense we have shown, also touches on this regarding Deacons.

11 *For the consummation of the saints*] <note>original: Πρὸς τὸν καταρτισμόν</note>. Jerome reads, *for the instruction*. It signifies also the refreshing or the repairing or the restoration of a collapsed thing. For Teachers come to the aid of the fallen and cast down. But what is most approved is that Ambrose agrees with us: *for the consummation of the saints*; for this is also what *katartizesthai* sounds like to the Greeks. Thus what follows fits perfectly: *for the building up of the body of Christ*; namely, so that the body might be perfect in every part.

<margin>D</margin> 12 *Into the recognition of the Son of God*] *And of the knowledge of the Son of God*, <note>original: καὶ τῆς ἐπιγνώσεως</note>: for it depends on "unity," just as "faith" does. And so reads Saint Jerome, who also reminds us that what was previously known is properly "recognized" <note>agnosci</note>.

13 *And we are carried about*] In the Greek it is a participle, <note>original: περιφερόμενοι</note>, that is, *being driven around*. Augustine reads "to be carried about." The rest is convenient, if the tense corresponded. *And little ones* is *nepioi*, which signifies a child in such a way that it also signifies one lacking in wisdom. And *every wind*, it was more correct to say *any wind*. For the Greek word *panti* is ambiguous.

14 *In the wickedness of men*] <note>original: ἐν κυβείᾳ (en kybeia)</note>. This word is derived from the game of dice <note>original: tesserae</note>, in which he who can, cheats and circumvents the other. Even if Faber, in his first Edition, changed "wickedness" for "confusion and perturbation," he was deceived, it seems, by the similarity of the shape, which might look like a *kappa*; thus he read *kinesei* <note>movement</note> for *kybeia*, because of the *beta*. And he indeed changed this passage in a later Edition, but in such a way that even there he does not support the man. Concerning which <margin>E</margin> he touched on nothing in his notes to that Apology. Moreover, the word seems to be fashioned from *kybos*, which means "I play with dice," because in games of this sort there is need for art, and everyone strives to circumvent his fellow player if he can, looking only to his own advantage; so that you might call *kybeias* "dicing," that is, craftiness and deceptive artifice, or rather a crafty deception. Hesychius also testifies that *kybeuein*, among other things, signifies "to wander" or "to mock or sneer." And Jerome refers this to the cleverness and insidious traps of the Dialecticians. Having followed this conjecture of our mind, although it is greatly probable, and having committed it to writing, we found the Commentaries of Bishop Theophylact on the Pauline Epistles—by no means to be despised—and discovered that he also thinks as we do. I will not be burdened to write down his words, as far as this matter pertains: <note>original: Κυβείαν λέγονται... (Greek passage below)</note> "They are called *Cybeutae* who use dice; such are the false teachers, moving the simpler people around like dice-men, as they wish." For my part, my conjecture satisfied me, being so consistent with the truth. However, since some are more <margin>F</margin> moved by authority than by the thing itself, we have added the support of the Greek Interpreter. Theophylact followed Chrysostom, as he usually does. It is a wonder that neither puts a difference between *kybeias* and *panourgias*, that is, *between dice and villainy*; except that in both there is a place for fraud. Jerome warns that this passage, if one reads the Greek, is more manifest; but while it is rendered word for word to the Latins, it becomes more obscure in the finish. He could have explained it by Paraphrase in this manner: *Until we all reach that point where the faith of all is the same, and the Son of God is equally known or recognized; that is, that we reach a perfect, solid, and manly age, namely to that measure of age which makes us fully adult in Christ, so that hereafter we may not be infants, who are driven and carried about by any wind of doctrine, through the craftiness of men imposing upon us, doing this not to teach us Christ sincerely, but to ensnare and capture us by clever arts. Rather, having neglected those things, and following those which are true and worthy of Christ, let us grow up in all things into him who is the head of all. He, however, is* Christi—

<header>847 EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER IV.</header>

<margin>14</margin> ...by the trickery of men, in craftiness toward the deceitful <margin>15</margin> scheme. But speaking the truth in love, let us grow into him in all things, who is the head, <margin>16</margin> Christ, from whom the whole body, being fitted and held together through every joint of supply, according to the working in the measure of each individual part, causes the growth of the body for its building <margin>17</margin> up in love. This I say therefore and testify in the Lord, that you no longer walk as the rest of the nations walk in the vanity of <margin>18</margin> their mind, having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, through the <margin>19</margin> hardness of their heart; who, having become callous, gave themselves over to licentiousness, for the practice of every uncleanness <margin>20</margin> in greed. But you did not so learn Christ; <margin>21</margin> if indeed you heard him, and in him were <margin>22</margin> taught, as truth is in Jesus, to lay aside, according to the former conduct, the old man...

---

Christ, not Moses: for the latter is merely a member, not the head. Jerome reads, "in the fallacy of men, in craftiness," and so on.
<margin>15</margin> **Toward circumvention** ] <note>original: ἐν μεθοδείᾳ (en methodeia)</note>. Now, *methodeia* refers to attacking a person from an ambush. And "of error," <note>original: τῆς πλάνης (tēs planēs)</note>. It would have been better translated as "of imposture." For *planē* refers to the one deceiving, whereas "error" refers to the one deceived. It is a wonder what Ambrose followed when he read, *as a remedy for error*: unless perhaps he wrote "method" and someone transformed it into "remedy." Augustine has *machination*.
<margin>16</margin> **But doing the truth** ] It would be clearer as "but rather," or "on the contrary," for it corrects what preceded. "Doing the truth" <note>original: Ἀληθεύοντες (Alētheuontes)</note>, that is, "pursuing the truth." For *alētheuein* means either to fulfill what you have said or to speak true things. For this is the opposite of "the error and the trickery," that is, the craftiness and imposture.
<margin>17</margin> **Let us grow in him** ] <note>original: αὐξήσωμεν εἰς αὐτὸν τὰ πάντα (auxēsōmen eis auton ta panta)</note>, that is, "let us be increased into him in all things." This is how Lorenzo <note>Valla</note> corrects it. I certainly think it can be rightly translated as "let us grow into him through all things," so that one understands the preposition *kata* <note>according to/through</note> before "all things." Even so, Jerome reads "that we may grow all things in him." And likewise Ambrose, if indeed the manuscripts are correct. Theophylact does not disagree with these, interpreting it to mean that everything in us must be increased—both our life and our doctrines. Chrysostom interprets it more somberly: first, so we understand that the body achieves growth while the Spirit works in individual members according to each one's capacity. In a second way, so we understand the tongue or members receive growth from the supply of the Spirit. Third, so we understand the Spirit is increased while, flowing from the head, it travels through all members, touching and connecting each one. Furthermore, a reflexive pronoun can be understood in the transitive verb, even if "growth" <note>original: αὔξησις (auxēsis)</note> among the Greeks has a neutral meaning; I do not recall finding it with another meaning. Therefore, let the reader follow what they most approve of, even if our reading hardly differs from their interpretation, especially since "the growth of the body" follows immediately.
<margin>18</margin> **Fitted** ] <note>original: συναρμολογούμενον (synarmologoumenon)</note>. Which he had previously translated as "constructed."
<margin>19</margin> **Connected** ] <note>original: συμβιβαζόμενον (symbibazomenon)</note>, that is, "cemented together." Jerome reads "glued together."
<margin>20</margin> **Through every joint** ] <note>original: ἁφῆς (haphēs)</note>. I could not translate this more clearly than as "seam" or "joint." For *haphē* is a joining, such that each part touches the other mutually, just as a member is connected to a member. Accordingly, Augustine in his commentary on Psalm 10 reads "through every touch." The same author, in *The City of God*, Book 22, Chapter 18, cites this passage in these words: > *He who descended is the same also who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. And he gave some as Apostles, some as Prophets, some as Evangelists, some as Pastors and Teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all meet in the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, into a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ, that we may no longer be children, tossed and carried about by every wind of doctrine, in the mockery of men, in craftiness, for the machination of error: but doing the truth in charity, let us grow in him through all things, who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, connected and fitted, through every touch of supply, according to the operation in the measure of each individual part, makes the increase of the body, for the building up of itself in charity.*
<margin>21</margin> **According to the operation** ] <note>original: κατ’ ἐνέργειαν (kat' energeian)</note>. Again, there is that noun so frequently encountered, which signifies "act" and "hidden power." He is speaking of the vital spirit which, proceeding from the head, imparts its power—not equally to all, but insofar as it benefits the whole body. Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret it in this way, so that "energy" (which he translates here as "operation") pertains to the act of Christ’s Spirit in his members, not to our works, as Lyranus explains. Thomas <note>Aquinas</note> tempers his interpretation so that he seems to have perceived both meanings.
<margin>22</margin> **Into the measure** ] <note>original: ἐν μέτρῳ (en metrō)</note>, that is, "in measure," even if the Latin manuscripts disagree; so that you understand that in the body, the life and nourishment of the body are imparted to each member according to its own proportion. For he said "in measure" as if he had said "by measure" or "according to the manner." Of each member: <note>original: μέρους (merous)</note>, that is, "of the part." Although for the Greeks there is little difference between *melos* <note>member</note> and *meros* <note>part</note>; Chrysostom reads "member."
<margin>23</margin> **For the building up of itself** ] <note>original: ἑαυτοῦ (heautou)</note>, that is, "of its very self."
<margin>24</margin> **In the Lord** ] Certain Greek manuscripts have "before God" <note>original: ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ (enōpion tou Theou)</note>.

<margin>A</margin> ...of men, through craftiness, <margin>15</margin> by which they attack us to deceive us. <margin>16</margin> But pursuing the truth in charity, <margin>17</margin> let us grow into him through all things, who is the head, namely Christ. In whom the whole body, <margin>18</margin> if it be joined and fastened together <margin>16</margin> through every joint of supply, <margin>21</margin> according to the act <margin>22</margin> in the measure of each individual part, makes the increase of the body, <margin>23</margin> for the building up of itself through charity. This therefore <margin>17</margin> I say and testify <margin>24</margin> through the Lord, that from now on you do not walk as the rest of the nations walk <margin>26</margin> in the vanity of their mind, <margin>27</margin> while they have a mind <margin>18</margin> darkened, <margin>28</margin> alienated from the life of God, <margin>29</margin> because of the ignorance that is in them, <margin>30</margin> and the blindness of <margin>B</margin> their heart; <margin>31</margin> who, after they arrived at the point where they ceased <margin>19</margin> to feel pain, gave themselves over to lasciviousness, for the <margin>32</margin> committing of all uncleanness <margin>33</margin> with greed. You, <margin>20</margin> however, did not so learn Christ: <margin>34</margin> if indeed you <margin>21</margin> heard him, and were taught in him, just as the truth is in Jesus, <margin>35</margin> to lay aside according to your former conduct...

---

<margin>25</margin> **Just as also the nations** ] Some manuscripts have "just as also the rest of the nations" <note>original: τὰ λοιπὰ ἔθνη (ta loipa ethnē)</note>.
<margin>26</margin> **In the vanity of sense** ] <note>original: ματαιότητι τοῦ νοὸς (mataiotēti tou noos)</note>, that is, of the "mind" rather than the "sense." And in that manner the Translator soon renders: *Be renewed in the spirit of your mind*. Valla rightly rebukes those who interpret "sense" as "sensuality," since for the Greeks *nous* is that part of the soul most removed from the matter of the body, which alone is thought to act without bodily organs.
<margin>27</margin> <margin>C</margin> **Having the intellect obscured** ] <note>original: Ἐσκοτισμένοι τῇ διανοίᾳ (Eskotismenoi tē dianoia)</note>, that is, "darkened in thought" or "in soul." Jerome reads "darkened in mind." Ambrose "darkened in intellect." But our Translator certainly expressed it more clearly in this place as "darkened."
<margin>28**Alienated from life** ] "Abalienated," <note>original: ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι (apēllotriōmenoi)</note>. And so Saint Jerome reads, "from the life of God." Some manuscripts erroneously have "from the way of God." For it is "from life" <note>original: τῆς ζωῆς (tēs zōēs)</note>. Ambrose reads "from the faith of God." This could also be the meaning: "from life, which is God." For the articles placed on both sides indicate this: *tēs zōēs tou Theou*, "from the true life, which is God."
<margin>29</margin> **Through ignorance** ] <note>original: διὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν (dia tēn agnoian)</note>, "because of ignorance."
<margin>30</margin> **Because of blindness** ] <note>original: πώρωσιν (pōrōsin)</note>. Which sounds more like "callousness" or "blinding." It is a wonder why Ambrose reads "hardness" instead of "blindness," unless perhaps his manuscript had *sklērōsis* <note>hardness</note> instead of *pōrōsin*.
<margin>31</margin> <margin>D</margin> **Who despairing of themselves** ] <note>original: Οἵτινες ἀπηλγηκότες, ἑαυτοὺς παρέδωκαν (Hoitines apēlgēkotes, heautous paredōkan)</note>, that is, "who after they had ceased to feel pain, handed themselves over," according to the emendation by Valla. But Saint Jerome thinks it can be rightly translated as "unfeeling" instead of "despairing," because the Greek word seems to be derived from when someone is free from pain and the sense of their own evil, and because of that stupor is carried into every vice. The Greek scholia interpret it in the same way. Indeed, Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> misuses the word "indolence," but desiring somehow to explain the Greek *analgēsia*. For *algein* to the Greeks means to feel pain; *apēlgēkōs* is said of one who, so to speak, has "finished grieving," or as the comic poet says, "grieved it out," and who has reached such hardness that they have hardened against every sense of evil—just as *deferbuisse* <note>to have cooled down</note> is said in Latin of one who has ceased to boil, and *desipere* <note>to be foolish</note> of one who has ceased to be wise. I do not know whether the Translator read *apēlpikotes* <note>having despaired</note>. The slip of a single letter is very easy. Even Ambrose reads and interprets it as "despairing." Chrysostom interprets it as "having given up on themselves," even if the context has *apēlgēkotes*, and in his commentary he mentions *analgēsia*; because these two are connected: despair and lack of feeling. In my opinion, "despairing" fits the flow of the sentence better. For those who despair that there is life after the death of the body seize the pleasures of this life most greedily and gorge themselves on them, as if they will have nothing pleasant once these are lost. Nor do I think the Greeks speak this way: "having ceased to feel pain for themselves."
<margin>32</margin> <margin>E</margin> **The uncleanness of all into avarice** ] Avarice seems to have nothing in common with uncleanness or lust; and for that reason, Jerome warns that for the Greeks it is not *philargyria* <note>love of money</note>, which refers to the greed for money, but *pleonexia*, named from "having more than is fair." Furthermore, one who is vehemently greedy for pleasures is not content with his own wife, but also defiles another's, and then invades another's, to avoid a satiety of pleasure. In this way, he thinks that passage of Paul's in the First Epistle to the Thessalonians, chapter four, should also be taken: *For this is the will of God, your sanctification, that you abstain from fornication, that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God; that no one overstep and cheat his brother in the matter, because the Lord is an avenger of all these things.* For there also, what the Translator renders as "circumvent" is *pleonektein* <note>to take advantage of/be greedy</note>. It seems to me it could also be taken such that "in avarice" was said for "greedily." Theophylact refers it to every immoderate concupiscence. For this drags men into blindness of mind. Chrysostom refers it to avarice.
<margin>33</margin> **Into avarice** ] In avarice, <note>original: ἐν πλεονεξίᾳ (en pleonexia)</note>, as if you were to say, through greed or the desire for what belongs to another.
<margin>34</margin> <margin>F</margin> **If however him** ] <note>original: Εἴγε (Eige)</note>, that is, "since," or "if indeed." Theophylact warns that it is not the word of one doubting, but of one confirming. And yet, the addition makes the speech sound doubtful.
<margin>35**Lay aside** ] In Greek it is thus: *To have laid aside the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error, and to have been renewed in spirit, and to have put on the new man.* Or as Saint Jerome reads, "That you lay aside," so that it refers to "you learned"; but then the pronoun "you" should have been omitted. For he arranges it in this manner: *But you...*
<meta>The text cuts off with the catchword "nem" (part of "conversionem"), indicating the discussion of "former conduct" (priorem conversationem) continues on the next page.</meta>

# TO THE EPHESIANS. CHAPTER V.

God was created in righteousness and holiness of
<margin>25</margin> truth. Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak the 
truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are
<margin>26</margin> members of one another. Be angry, and do not sin; let
<margin>27</margin> not the sun go down on your provocation, nor
<margin>28</margin> give place to the devil. Let the thief no longer 
steal, but rather let him labor, working what is good

<margin>29</margin> one who has need. Let no foul word proceed

building up of a need, that it may give grace to those who 
<margin>30</margin> hear. And do not

---

<margin>C</margin>
*but you did not so learn Christ, if indeed you heard him, and were taught in him, to lay aside, according to the former conduct, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error.* <note>Erasmus is quoting Ephesians 4:20-22</note> Ambrose reads in this way: *That you should lay aside, according to the prior conversation, the old man*; but he soon turns the infinitives into imperatives: *be renewed, put on*. Theophylact thinks the infinitives can be referred either to that which was said, *you were taught*, or to this, *as is the truth*: as if he were asking, what were you taught? namely, to lay aside the old man. Or what is the truth? namely, to lay aside, and so forth. Chrysostom follows the latter sense: so that, he says, life may agree with the doctrines.

<margin>36</margin> **According to the desires of error**] Hilary, in the twelfth book *On the Trinity*, adds a pronoun, *according to the lusts of his deception*: perhaps desiring to express the force of the article, <note>original: τῆς ἀπάτης (tēs apatēs)</note>.

<margin>37</margin> **Be renewed however**] Here too there are infinitives, as we have advised, which can likewise be referred to the same thing, "if you have learned."

<margin>38</margin> **And in holiness of truth**] <note>original: ἐν ὁσιότητι τῆς ἀληθείας (en hosiotēti tēs alētheias)</note>. Ambrose reads, *in truth and justice*: it could be translated as "in the religion of truth." For Greek grammarians think *hosia* <note>holiness</note> was said as if it were *ania*, from the verb *azo*, which is to worship the divine power with sacrifices.

<margin>39</margin> **With the neighbor**] <note>original: μετὰ τοῦ πλησίον (meta tou plēsion)</note>, that is, toward the neighbor. Although the Translator <note>the Vulgate</note> translates correctly. For we are said to speak *with* him to whom we speak: just as we say to fight *with* him against whom we fight.

<margin>40</margin> **Be angry, and do not sin**] Just as this is taken from the Psalm, so he expressed it according to the form of Hebrew speech. For the meaning is: If it happens that you are angry, nevertheless do not sin; that is, restrain your anger. For Paul does not command us to be angry, but he does not want the anger to be long-lasting, nor to proceed as far as injury. Nor is the Greek word for "anger" <note>original: παροργισμῷ (parorgismō)</note> one that signifies a vice of nature or a certain habit of a mind easily angered (as the Latin words sometimes do), but rather an "irritation," that is, anger, or commotion, or provocation: so that we may understand that for him who has been provoked by an injury, even if he feels some pain, that pain ought to be brief, and among Christians, it ought to stop short of retaliating for the injury. Next, concerning the "devil," I do not know whether here it could be taken as "slanderer": *Be harmonious*, he says, *lest even if you take vengeance justly, you provide a handle for slandering to the Pagans, to whom you will seem greedy for revenge.* For the Devil also slanders through his instruments. Nor does anything forbid the Devil himself to be called a slanderer in Latin. Since even in this place, as rendered by me, the Devil is not lacking. Chrysostom touches upon both meanings. Discord gives a place to the enemy—to Satan and to the slandering man.

<margin>41</margin> **Do not give**] <note>original: Μήτε δίδοτε (Mēte didote)</note>, that is, "And do not give."

<margin>42</margin> **With his hands**] <note>original: ταῖς ἰδίαις χερσίν (tais idiais chersin)</note>, that is, with his own hands. Although here he has habitually translated *idiais* and *heautou* with the same pronoun, *suus* <note>his/his own</note>. Certain manuscripts do not add "his own": as neither does Ambrose. **What is good**. It can be read as a parenthesis, *which is a good thing*, because the thing is good, or let him perform a good work: that is, let him not seek a living from a shameful trade, but an honorable one.

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>43</margin> **To one suffering necessity**] <note>original: τῷ χρείαν ἔχοντι (tō chreian echonti)</note>, that is, to one having need. He advises this because of certain people who teach that we are not obliged to help a neighbor except in "necessity." Now we call "necessity" that which one lacks. And yet they think that this very thing which has been given in this way can be rightfully reclaimed if the one who received it is able to return it. To these narrow straits we have thrust that most ample Evangelical charity. Jerome reads, *to him who is in want*. And it is *hina echē metadidonai*, that is, so that he might be able to impart. For *echō* <note>to have</note> joined to infinitive verbs is sometimes used for "I am able."

<margin>44</margin> **Bad speech**] <note>original: λόγος σαπρὸς (logos sapros)</note>, that is, filthy or vicious speech. For he does not mean, I think, light or superfluous speech, but obscene or pestilential speech. Theophylact noted the emphasis of the Greek word: although in the Gospels, when speaking of the "bad tree," the Evangelist used the same word.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>45</margin> **Edification of faith**] In the Greek manuscripts I read *tēs chreias*, that is, of utility, not "of faith." Jerome testifies that he corrected it to *for the building up of opportunity*: but in the Latin manuscripts, instead of "opportunity," "faith" was read for the sake of euphony <note>harmonious sound</note>. And so Saint Ambrose reads. Theophylact also advises concerning the word *chreias*. Chrysostom likewise reads *chreias*. Yet I do not see what cacophony <note>harsh sound</note> is in "opportunity," or, as I would prefer, "utility." For *opportunitas* <note>opportunity</note> sounds differently to Latins than *chreia* <note>need/use</note>: nor does *opportunitas* correspond to the verb *oportet* <note>it is necessary</note>. From this place one may gather that Jerome follows in this Epistle what he himself had corrected, and yet in no other Epistle are there more things that disagree with the common reading. Where are they then, who throw heaven and earth into confusion because they doubt whether the common Edition <note>the Vulgate</note> is Jerome’s? Moreover, that he wrote these Commentaries after he had corrected the New Testament is proved by his own book *On Illustrious Men*, in which he mentions the Commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians, to Titus, and to Philemon. Furthermore, since the corrected New Testament makes no mention of this work, he surely would have done so unless he had written these Commentaries after the catalog of *Illustrious Men* was published. Here certainly someone will perhaps answer that forgetfulness was the cause, or that the Spirit did not want this.

<margin>46</margin> **In the day**] <note>original: εἰς ἡμέραν (eis hēmeran)</note>, that is, unto the day.

<margin>47</margin> **Anger and indignation**] <note>original: θυμὸς καὶ ὀργή (thymos kai orgē)</note>, that is, ferocity and anger: *thymos* is properly the impulse of a mind boiling and excited.

<margin>48</margin> **Kind to one another**] <note>original: χρηστοί (chrēstoi)</note>. Jerome thinks "sweetness" is more rightly translated than "kindness," so that it may be opposed to bitterness and harshness of manners: for those who are exceedingly companionable and charming are also usually called *chrēstologoi*. For "kindness" properly pertains to giving, that is, to liberality.

<margin>49</margin> **Merciful**] <note>original: εὔσπλαγχνοι (eusplanchnoi)</note>. Which pertains not only to mercy, but to every affection of piety, as if you were to say, "of good bowels." For the Divine Scriptures use "bowels" for "affections."

<margin>50</margin> **Giving to one another**] <note>original: χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς (charizomenoi heautois)</note>, that is, giving to your own selves, so that you may understand that whatever good you do to others is done for your own good and profit no less than for his who receives it. So says Jerome. For "giving" here is not used for "forgiving" or "pardoning," I can say: but *charizomenoi*, that is, bestowing, or giving freely. Ambrose reads and interprets it as giving, pardoning, and remitting sin. And indeed Paul used the same word *charizesthai* in the second Epistle to the Corinthians: "And I to whom I have given anything," etc. Which indeed Chrysostom and Theophylact followed here too. Therefore, if this sense is pleasing—which is more agreeable to me—we should have translated it "to one another": so that we mutually pardon each other's errors: for this too pertains to mercy.

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>51</margin> **Gave to you**] <note>original: ἡμῖν (hēmin)</note>, that is, "to us," first person. Although the Greek manuscripts vary.

<margin>1</margin> **For an odor of sweetness**] <note>original: εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας (eis osmēn euōdias)</note>, that is, for an odor of fragrance or good scent. Jerome, in the Preface to Zechariah, renders it "an odor of good fragrance."

<margin>2</margin> **Nor be named**] <note>original: μηδὲ ὀνομαζέσθω (mēde onomazesthō)</note>, that is, let it not even be named.

<margin>3</margin> **Or filthiness, or foolish talking**] In the Greek, "or" is not repeated in this place, but "and"; and yet I praise the fact that the Translator changed it. For although the meaning is the same, nevertheless the speech is more convenient. But if it is correctly done in several places, as often as the Translator pleased, what forbids the same being done as often as reason demands?

<margin>4</margin> **Or scurrility**] <note>original: εὐτραπελία (eutrapelia)</note>, that is, facetiousness, or wit. For it is taken in a good sense among the Philosophers. But he means a scurrilous wit unworthy of a grave man. Although Jerome thinks even jokes of that kind, which are told only for the sake of laughter, are unworthy of true Christians, citing from the Hebrew Gospel: *Never be glad except when you have seen your brother in charity*. For my part, while I tolerate jokes in any case, provided they are learned and witty...
