<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed philological annotations on the fifth chapter of the Letter to the Ephesians. Erasmus is focusing on the transition from the "works of darkness" to the "fruit of the light," comparing the original Greek terminology with the Latin Vulgate and the interpretations of early Church Fathers like Jerome and Ambrose.</meta>

# EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER V.

<margin>5</margin> ...rather thanksgiving. For you know this for certain: 
that no fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous man, who 
is an idolater, has an inheritance in the king- 
dom of Christ and God. Let no one deceive you with emp- 
ty words; for because of these things the wrath of 
<margin>7</margin> God comes upon the sons of disobedience. Therefore, do not be- 
<margin>8</margin> come partners with them. For you were once darkness, but 
now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light. 
<margin>9</margin> For the fruit of the Spirit is in all good- 
ness and righteousness and truth. Discerning what 
<margin>10</margin> is pleasing to the Lord. And do not participate in the 
<margin>11</margin> unfruitful works of darkness, but instead even ex- 
<margin>12</margin> pose them. For it is shameful even to speak of the things 
<margin>13</margin> done by them in secret. But all things exposed by the 
light are made manifest; for everything that is made manifest 
<margin>14</margin> is light. Therefore he says: "Wake up, O sleeper, and arise 
from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you." See 
<margin>15</margin> then how accurately you walk, not as unwise, but as 
wise,

---

...well-seasoned: likewise, I cannot bear those who, whenever they wish to appear sophisticated, twist something from the Divine Scriptures to suit their own follies. I see that this offensive type of "wit" is immensely popular with certain monks and even some priests; if they desire to attack someone, they take the song of Mary commonly called the *Magnificat*, or the song commonly called the *Te Deum*, and by changing a few words, they twist it into a poisonous slur. Jests of this kind rightly please those who enjoy the *Catholicum* <note>A 13th-century Latin dictionary by John of Genoa, often criticized by humanists for its poor Latinity</note>, the *Mammotrectus* <note>A popular medieval guide to the Bible's vocabulary, often mocked by Erasmus for its simplistic nature</note>, and that sort of most tasteless glosses, which delight in the coldest little questions. They are always consistent with themselves: no less ridiculous when they are joking—that is, when the "camel dances"—than when they are handling serious matters. 

As for what follows, "thanksgiving," in Greek it is <term>thanksgiving</term> <note>original: εὐχαριστία (eucharistia)</note>. Saint Jerome interprets this word as "gratificitas" <note>favor or pleasantness</note> or "grace," because among the Hebrews "gracious" and "giving thanks" are expressed by the same word. For he thinks it is written thus in Proverbs: <term>A gracious woman raises up glory for her husband</term> <note>original: Γυνὴ εὐχάριστος ἐγείρει ἀνδρὶ δόξαν</note>. Indeed, the other interpreters, Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus, translated it as <term>chariesta</term> <note>graceful/pleasant</note>, not "eucharistos." These things tend toward the point that the speech of Christians should be free from scurrilous jokes, but seasoned with its own particular grace. But I leave this to the reader to weigh. For my part, I do not entirely approve of Jerome’s commentary in this place, especially since the Greek does not support it. Ambrose interprets <term>thanksgiving</term> as "speech made to the praise of God."

**5** *Which are not to the purpose* ] <term>the things not fitting</term> <note>original: τὰ οὐκ ἀνήκοντα</note>, that is, not convenient, or things that are not suitable: just as he translates elsewhere so as to refer to the person. One kind of speech was fitting for them, another for a servant of Christ. And if one must joke, a decorous joke ought to be employed. We see that certain jokes passed even between Paul the Hermit and Anthony, and that Hilarion said many witty things. Truly, jests of this kind do not excite foolish laughter, but sound the praise of God.

**6** *Know this, understanding* ] <term>know, knowing</term> <note>original: ἴστε γινώσκοντες</note>, that is, "you know by recognizing." Although some manuscripts have "este," that is, "be ye," so that the doubling emphasizes the point. Ambrose and Jerome follow the first reading. <term>Covetous</term> <note>original: Πλεονέκτης (pleonektēs)</note>, which Cyprian translates as "defrauder"; we read it as "greedy." Concerning the word <term>covetous</term>, Saint Jerome notes it is derived from <term>to have more</term> <note>original: πλέον ἔχειν</note>, used when someone occupies what belongs to another. Hence, a little earlier, regarding the phrase "let no one circumvent his brother in business," he interpreted it as adultery; and here he thinks <term>covetousness</term> <note>original: πλεονεξίαν (pleonexian)</note> can be understood as debauchery.

**7** *Which is the service of idols* ] <term>who is an idol-worshiper</term> <note>original: ὅς ἐστιν εἰδωλολάτρης</note>. Jerome reads, "that is, serving idols." Here the translator renders <term>latreia</term> <note>worship/service</note> sometimes as "cult," sometimes as "homage," and sometimes as "servitude." Augustine, in the tenth book of *The City of God*, notes that "servitude," where one is not their own master, is called <term>douleia</term>. However, that cult by which we most often worship God is called <term>latreia</term> in the Sacred Scriptures.

**8** *In the kingdom of Christ and God* ] In this way he seems to call the Father "God," as if Christ were not God. But we have noted elsewhere that the Father is signified by the custom of Apostolic speech whenever he names "God" absolutely, since it is clear from many places that Christ is also called "God" by them.

**9** *The wrath comes* ] <term>it comes</term> <note>original: ἔρχεται</note>. "Comes" in this place is in the present tense, or certainly the future, for it cannot be the past. I think it is more rightly taken in the present tense, so that we understand that because of these things, divine wrath is accustomed to rage against sons who are ill-behaved and less obedient to what is said.

**10** *Upon the children of unbelief* ] <term>of disobedience</term> <note>original: ἀπειθείας</note>, that is, of disobedience or incredulity, as we mentioned before. Jerome thinks it is more rightly translated as "unpersuadability," those whom we call "intractable." It is strange, however, that the word "unpersuadability" pleased Jerome, as it is unheard of to Latin ears. Cyprian, in the Epistle to Epictetus, reads "upon the children of contumacy." Furthermore, concerning the style of Hebrew speech, in which they call a rebellious son a "son of rebellion," we have already noted this frequently.

**11** *Partakers of them* ] <term>fellow-sharers</term> <note>original: συμμέτοχοι</note>, that is, partakers: that is, "do not be sharers of evils with them." For he is speaking of the fruits of impiety, of which he does not want them to be partakers with the impious, so that one part of the communion pertains to the thing, the other to the person. Jerome noted this carefully and with many words. To me, whoever is a "partaker" must be a partaker of some thing and a partaker with someone. Jerome adds that in Divine Scripture "partaker" is used in a good sense, and "co-partaker" in a bad sense; whether this is always true, I do not know. Certainly in the third chapter of this Epistle, he used it in a good sense when speaking of the Gentiles converted to Christ: <term>co-sharers of the promise</term> <note>original: συμμέτοχα τῆς ἐπαγγελίας</note>. One should not attack a holy man, but nevertheless, this is a notable lapse of memory. First, he orders this distinction to be observed diligently, and denies...

...that the feminine word for "co-partaker" is ever read in Divine Scripture except with a bad meaning, even though in the third chapter of this very Epistle he carefully indicates that the preposition added to these words—<term>concorporal and co-sharers</term>—sounds harsh to Latin ears, but nevertheless should not be omitted, because in Divine Scripture neither marks nor points <margin>C</margin> lack mystery. It seemed right to mention these things so that, in the case of those who strive to be useful, we might bear human lapses more moderately, since such a thing happened to a man so practiced in the Divine volumes.

**12** *For the fruit of the light* ] In Greek it is, *For the fruit of the Spirit*, <term>The fruit of the Spirit</term> <note>original: Ὁ γὰρ καρπὸς τοῦ Πνεύματος</note>. Although the Latin manuscripts, the consensus of the Interpreters, and the order of the discourse itself contradict this reading. For a mention of light preceded: "but now light in the Lord, walk as children of light." However, Theophylact reads and interprets "fruit of the light." Chrysostom seems to have read "Spirit." Likewise, there follows: "And do not communicate in the unfruitful works of darkness."

**13** *Well-pleasing to God* ] In Greek it is "to the Lord."

**14** *But rather reprove* ] The conjunction <term>but</term> <note>original: δέ (de)</note> was omitted. And "reprove" <note>redarguite</note> instead of "expose" <note>arguite</note>. Ambrose reads "rebuke"; but "expose" <note>original: ἐλέγχετε (elenchyete)</note> was more appropriate. Indeed, light itself exposes the good things of life and reveals the shameful deeds of darkness, even if you rebuke nothing. Mindful of the metaphor, he therefore adds, "but rather expose." For he exposes who reprehends and overcomes, and he exposes who reveals. And the speech that follows, "But all things are manifested by the light," requires more that <margin>D</margin> we read "expose" in the sense of "reveal" rather than "rebuke." Although here too Ambrose reads "are rebuked," just as he previously read and explained "rebuke." Theophylact agrees with me so far.

**15** *For everything that* ] <term>the thing being manifested</term> <note>original: τὸ φανερούμενον (to phaneroumenon)</note>. Since the participle is in the middle voice, it makes the sentence ambiguous. For the sense can be, "whatever is manifested, is light," or "whatever manifests, is light." It appears, however, that it should be read actively rather than passively. Were it not for the article being attached to the participle and not the noun, I would interpret it in this way: "that which manifests all things is light," <term>the thing manifesting all things is light</term> <note>original: τὸ πάντα φανερώμενον, φῶς ἐστιν</note>. For whatever night and gloom hide, the light uncovers and opens. From the holy life of the pious and from the preached truth, all things that differ from it become clear. But now we have: <term>for everything manifested is light</term>. And Theophylact, with Chrysostom, interprets "manifested" passively, explaining that "a sin, as soon as it has been revealed and uncovered, is turned from darkness into light." And this we have followed. Jerome reads "reproved," but the Interpreter is better, who also expressed the logic of the tense: again, from this place and the next, it is clear that the common translation is not <margin>E</margin> Jerome's.

**16** *Rise you who sleep* ] That which Paul cites, Jerome denies is found anywhere in Divine Scripture, but thinks it was either taken from apocryphal writings or brought forth by Paul himself through a prophetic spirit. It is strange, however, that this difficulty is ignored by the Greeks.

**17** *And he will enlighten you* ] <term>and Christ will shine upon you</term> <note>original: καὶ ἐπιφαύσει σοι ὁ Χριστός</note>, that is, "and Christ will illuminate you," or "Christ will rise upon you," as Saint Jerome translates and emends. As for what the same man mentions—that it is read by some not as "will shine" <note>epiphausei</note> but as "will touch" <note>epipsausei</note>, wishing this to seem spoken by Christ hanging on the cross to Adam buried there, who, touched by the blood of the Redeemer, received life—this is more forced and tastes of Jewish fables. And yet Jerome testifies that he was present at a sermon in which this invention was received with wonderful applause by the people. Just as I myself have heard about the letter *Shin* <note>original: Syn</note>, which in the British tongue sounds like "sin," being in the middle of the Hebrew name *Jesus*; likewise about the three inflections, *Jesus, Jesu, Jesum*, which someone interpreted from the last letters as "highest, last, and <margin>F</margin> middle." Although I see that Ambrose read it almost that way, he was nonetheless somewhat more diligent than our reading elsewhere. For he reads in this way: "And rise from the dead, and you will touch Christ." Augustine likewise, explaining the third Psalm, reads: "and Christ will touch you." The Greek commentaries, which circulate under the title of Chrysostom, mention both readings, although they more approve of the one we follow: and indeed it fits better with what precedes: "Do not communicate with the unfruitful works of darkness," etc., "Everything that is manifested, is light." However, it is not improbable what Blessed Thomas mentions: that the Apostle neither took this place from apocrypha nor brought it forth in a prophetic manner, but as if explaining the passage in Isaiah 60 with some of his own added: "Rise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you." Those who sleep are ordered to rise, and those who are buried and cannot see the light of the world are ordered to rise up.

**18** *See therefore brethren* ] "Brethren" is not among the Greeks. *Walk cautiously*, <term>accurately</term> <note>original: ἀκριβῶς (akribōs)</note>, that is, diligently and precisely, surely in such great...

...by such great light. Wherefore he rightly said, *To see*, because in darkness it is not possible to discern.

19 *Redeeming the time* ] <note>original: "Redimentes tempus"</note> The Greek is *Exagorazomenoi*, signifying as if "marketing" and "buying up." And "time" here sounds like "occasion" or "opportunity," which he wishes to be purchased at the expense of other things.

20 *They are evil* ] <note>original: "Mali sunt"</note> The Greek is *ponērai*. This very word is ambiguous, meaning either "afflicted" or "wicked," as it is derived from *ponos* meaning "labor." Indeed, it is a laborious and deceptive thing.

<margin>E</margin> 21 *The will of God* ] <note>original: "Voluntas Dei"</note> For the Greeks, it is "of the Lord," *tō Kyriō*.

22 *In which is luxury* ] <note>original: "In quo est luxuria"</note> The Greek is *asōtia*, that is, excess or wastefulness. I have advised on this lest anyone take "luxury" here for "lust," <note>Erasmus is distinguishing between *luxuria* (extravagance/riotous living) and *libido* (sexual lust).</note> as the common people do. Nor do I see why Faber <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, a contemporary scholar.</note> prefers "unhealthiness" instead of "luxury," as if Paul were acting like a Physician, so that we might have healthy bodies by refraining from drunkenness. For even if we grant that *asōtia* is derived from the word "to be saved" (*sōzesthai*), with the privative "a" added, it still cannot signify "unhealthiness," nor is it ever found used in this sense among Greek writers. Rather, the "Prodigal" people <note>original: "Asotorum"</note> were so called by the Greeks because they were destroyed by luxury—the ancients were so overflowing in their revelries that they never saw the sun rise or set, as Plato and countless others mention. From this is derived the verb *asōteuesthai*, to overflow with luxury, which Athenaeus used in the eighth book of the *Deipnosophists*. Now, the relative "in which," in my opinion, does not simply refer to the wine, but to the entire preceding clause. "Do not be drunk with wine," in which thing—that is, in the intoxication of wine—is excess. Furthermore, what he calls *asōtia* here, he calls *aselgeian* (licentiousness) elsewhere. It would not be entirely absurd if someone were to occasionally misuse "luxury" for the vice of lust, because of the kinship between these types of vices: feasting, drunkenness, dancing, and lust. However, it seems shameless to me what Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the medieval scholastic theologian.</note> tries to extort: that "luxury" is properly said of the immoderate use of sexual matters, to the point that he even rejects his own Augustine here. For Augustine wrote in the books titled *Confessions*: "Luxury desires to be called by the names of satiety and abundance." Thomas solves this knot with this artifice: "that just as temperance is principally and properly about the pleasures of touch, but is said by a certain similarity in other matters; so luxury is principally in sexual pleasures, which most of all dissolve the mind of man, and secondarily in any other things pertaining to excess." Thus far we have recounted Thomas’s words. Now, without being too harsh—since he so easily recedes from the opinion of Augustine, who knew the propriety of the Roman language better than most—who ever said temperance was chiefly concerned with the pleasures of touch, when it is the moderation of all passions? Even if lust is the most powerless passion, is the chief part of this evil located in touch, and not rather in the eyes, in speech, and in the soul? Secondly, is "luxury" transferred to *any* excess? Is one who loves money immoderately called luxurious? Is one who is frugal beyond measure called luxurious? And yet these are excesses. Finally, if Euclio <note>A miserly character from the plays of Plautus.</note> loves money and gives nothing, is he called luxurious? Yet Thomas confirms this opinion by the authority of the Gloss <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, a standard medieval biblical commentary.</note> on Galatians chapter 5, which says "that luxury is any kind of superfluity." And it is a wonder he did not bring up this passage of Paul, since he cites a passage from Proverbs: "Wine is a luxurious thing, but the use of wine pertains to drink, therefore etc." But he explains this knot quite successfully. The third difficult knot is: "Luxury," he says, "is called a lustful appetite for pleasure, etc." Here, since he cites no author, he imagines "lustful pleasure" is taken for sexual pleasure. Yet Augustine testifies that "lust" (*libido*) is frequently taken for any passion that does not obey reason. If a prince kills a threatening man, it is "lust." And yet, as Augustine confesses, common usage sometimes accommodates this word properly to sexual matters, which no upright author ever wrote concerning "luxury." But even more clever is what he inserted among the antitheses: It says in the book *On True Religion* regarding the luxurious: "he who sows in the flesh, shall from the

First, I appeal to the sober reader, whether Paul there meant sexual pleasure, and not rather the Mosaic Law, and if he did mean that, whether he meant it "properly." If he meant the impious love of all visible things, how does this help Thomas, who wants "luxury" to properly suit sexual pleasure? After this, he brings Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, 7th-century encyclopedist.</note> to us, who thinks *luxuria* is so called as if it were "dissolved" (*solutum*). I suspect it comes from "dislocating" (*luxando*) or "loosening" (*laxando*), but since "Venus" <note>Metonymy for sexual love/lust.</note> most of all dissolves the soul, therefore luxury pertains here. But this was not what Thomas had proposed, but rather whether the *word* itself belonged here. Finally, <margin>D</margin> what is Thomas doing here but dealing with a fault of the vocabulary? Furthermore, where should vocabulary be sought if not from Latin authors? Why was there a need to twist "luxury" into this, when "lust" (*libido*) and "unchastity" (*impudicitia*) were well-known Latin words? And yet, as if the matter were won, he carves up "luxury" into all species of lusts. I do not attack Thomas, but I plainly pity those who learn nothing else: and I am less displeased with myself for not having consumed as much of my life in writers of this kind.

23 *Be filled with the holy Spirit* ] In Greek it is, "but be filled with the Spirit," and "holy" is not added, neither among the Greeks, nor in Ambrose, nor in Jerome, nor in the old copies; both [manuscripts] of Constance agree. It is simply "with the Spirit," *en Pneumati*. He opposes this to the intoxication of wine—a subtle thing opposed to a coarse one.

24 *In psalms* ] *en psalmois* and *hymnois*. It is not "in your hearts" (plural), but "in the heart" (singular). Moreover, both "psalms" and "hymns" are Greek. The former signifies "singing," the latter "praise," but properly of God. And he opposes these to drunken songs.

25 *In the fear of Christ* ] I have frequently advised that "in fear" is the same as if he said "through fear." Jerome thinks this particle can be taken as if it were a general category which is soon divided into its parts, namely: wives subject to husbands, servants to masters, children to parents.

26 *Be subject* ] <note>original: "Subditæ sint"</note> "Be ye subject," *hypotassesthe*. Jerome denies that this word is added in the Greek codices, "be subject," but that this sentence hangs from the previous heading, "Subject to one another in the fear of God." Namely, "women [subject] to men," etc. And yet today it is found added in the Greek codices, appearing as though it were added so that the sense might be clearer and the chapter could be read separately if necessary.

27 *He is the savior of the body* ] <note>original: "Ipse salvator corporis"</note> *kai autos esti sōtēr tou sōmatos*, that is, "and he is the preserver of the body." And the pronoun "his" is not added among the Greeks, nor in Ambrose, nor in Jerome.

28 *In the word of life* ] <note>original: "In verbo vitæ"</note> "Of life" is not added among the Greeks, nor in Ambrose, nor in Jerome.

29 *That he might present* ] <note>original: "Ut exhiberet"</note> *Hina parastēsē autos heautō*, that is, "That he might join her to himself." And immediately there is added "glorious," *endoxon*, then *tēn Ekklēsian*, that is, "namely the Church."

30 *Holy and immaculate* ] <note>original: "Sancta & immaculata"</note> *kai amōmos*, that is, "and blameless." Though I do not condemn "immaculate."
31 *So also men* ] And the conjunction is redundant.
32 *As their own bodies* ] *hōs ta heautōn sōmata*, that is, "as their own bodies."
33 *Of his body* ] It can be read "of the same," for "his," *autou*.
34 *For this reason he shall leave* ] <note>original: "Propter hoc relinquet"</note> *Anti toutou*, that is, "In place of this," or "In place of that." Which indeed Saint Jerome also noted, that *anti toutou* was said by Paul instead of *epi kai toutō*, which almost means "in place of father and mother." He took the testimony from Genesis chapter two, but in his own way plucking what seemed convenient for the present passage. For omitting the pronouns "his" and "her," he only put "father and mother." Then, he omitted what was in the middle, "and shall cleave to his wife," and annexed what follows, "and the two shall become one flesh," because that is more effective than "cleaving," namely that from two, one person is made.
35 *And shall cleave* ] <note>original: "Et adhærebit"</note> *kai proskollēthēsetai*, that is, "he shall be glued."

# EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER VI.

<margin>31</margin> ...and he shall be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh. <note>Original: καὶ προσκολληθήσεται πρὸς τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν.</note>
<margin>32</margin> This mystery is great; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church. <note>Original: Τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν· ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω εἰς Χριστὸν καὶ εἰς τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν.</note>
<margin>33</margin> Nevertheless, let each one of you in particular so love his own wife as himself; and let the wife see that she reverences her husband. <note>Original: Πλὴν καὶ ὑμεῖς οἱ καθ’ ἕνα, ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα οὕτως ἀγαπάτω ὡς ἑαυτόν· ἡ δὲ γυνὴ ἵνα φοβῆται τὸν ἄνδρα. The Greek 'phobetai' literally means 'fears', but Erasmus interprets it as reverence.</note>
<margin>VI. 1</margin> Children, obey your parents in the Lord; for this is right. <note>Original: Τὰ τέκνα, ὑπακούετε τοῖς γονεῦσιν ὑμῶν ἐν Κυρίῳ· τοῦτο γάρ ἐστι δίκαιον.</note>
<margin>2</margin> Honor your father and your mother, which is the first commandment with a promise, <note>Original: Τίμα τὸν πατέρα σου καὶ τὴν μητέρα, ἥτις ἐστὶν ἐντολὴ πρώτη ἐν ἐπαγγελίᾳ.</note>
<margin>3</margin> that it may be well with you and you may live long on the earth. <note>Original: ἵνα εὖ σοι γένηται καὶ ἔσῃ μακροχρόνιος ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς.</note>
<margin>4</margin> Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up...

*be joined*, a word which is not lacking in emphasis. *Nor is it "to his wife," but "unto his wife."*

<margin>A</margin> **36 in one flesh]** <note>Original: εἰς σάρκα μίαν</note>, that is, "into one flesh," which means that from two, one person is made, according to the idiom of the Hebrew language, which sometimes calls the whole person "flesh," and sometimes calls people "souls." Likewise among the Greeks, you will often find <gloss>body</gloss> <note>Original: σῶμα</note> used to mean a person. Truly, we have spoken of this elsewhere: and also regarding the figure of speech by which those who are "one flesh" are said to be "into one flesh."

**37 This Sacrament]** <note>Original: μυστήριον</note>, that is, "mystery." I did not want those who make marriage one of the seven Sacraments based on this passage—according to a specific and exact reasoning for this word—to be unaware of this. Not that this point should be doubted, since it is probable that this tradition has come down to us from the Apostles or certainly the holy Fathers. Even if this was doubted in the past by orthodox Scholastic thinkers, indeed, a different opinion was even upheld. For it is objected by some that Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian theologian</note>, who treats the Ecclesiastical Sacraments as a profession and explains the rites and ceremonies of each one diligently, makes no mention of marriage. Furthermore, in all the volumes in which Jerome discusses marriage, it is nowhere called a "Sacrament"; indeed, not even by Augustine, who was more inclined toward Jerome’s view on this and even wrote on the *Good of Marriage*, grants it this name. And what might seem even more strange than these is that even in Jovinian <note>An opponent of asceticism whom Jerome criticized</note>, who was a champion of marriage, there is no mention anywhere of the word "Sacrament." For if it had been made, that passage would have been addressed by Jerome when he was refuting Jovinian's books, especially since he does so so accurately. Yet this weapon was precisely what Jovinian needed when he was equating marriage to celibacy. Indeed, he could have argued: if marriage is a Sacrament, and virginity is not a Sacrament, then the dignity of marriage wins out by that very logic. These points, I say, and others like them, are easily resolved by the learned. Therefore, I would not say these things as if calling into doubt whether marriage is a Sacrament—for I favor its dignity in a great way—but because it does not seem to be very effectively gathered from these words of the Apostle. Since the adversative particle, *but I*, sufficiently indicates that this "great mystery" pertains to Christ and the Church, not to the husband and the wife. For it is not a "great Sacrament" in this: if a man is joined to a wife, which is also customary among the Heathens. This is the opinion, unless I am mistaken, of Saint Augustine when discussing Psalm 118. *They shall be*, he says, *two in one flesh: which great Sacrament the Apostle Paul explains, saying, "I speak in Christ and in the Church."* Although he explains the same thing clearly in his book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* to Valerius: *Which the Apostle called a "great Sacrament" in Christ and in the Church. What is therefore great in Christ and in the Church, this is least in individual husbands and wives, but is nevertheless a Sacrament of inseparable union.* Paul used a similar coloring in the first Epistle to the Corinthians. And for the sake of conscience, soon to exclude error, he adds: *But I say conscience, not yours, but the other's.* Then, as I had begun to say, in this passage the Greek word does not properly signify a "Sacrament" of the kind the Church calls the seven, but a "secret" or "hidden thing" <note>Erasmus is distinguishing between a mystical ritual and a generic secret</note>, which word Paul used frequently concerning other things that are far removed from the nature of Sacraments. Indeed, writing to the Thessalonians, he calls it the "mystery of iniquity." Again, in the first chapter of Corinthians XIII, where we read, *even if I knew all mysteries*. Augustine, writing to Valentinus *On Grace and Free Will*, reads, *even if I knew all sacraments*, as if there were no difference between "mystery" and "sacrament." The ancients called an oath a "sacrament," or a religious obligation, I suppose because these were performed with certain secret ceremonies. And this passage was treated by two certain men, one of whom we answered, in such a way that he is unworthy of being answered. For I do not deny that marriage is a Sacrament, but I want it to be examined whether it can be properly called a Sacrament from this passage in the same way that Baptism is so called.

<margin>B</margin> **38 In Christ]** Both "into Christ" and "unto the Church." Although I am not ignorant that the accusative case among the Greeks sometimes has the same power as another case. It can, however, be understood as "concerning Christ" and "concerning the Church." For it is used in this sense by the Greeks, <gloss>unto Emmaus</gloss> and <gloss>unto Apollo</gloss>, in titles.

**39 And you individually, let each one love his own wife as himself]** This speech is consistent with the rules of grammar neither among the Greeks nor among us. However, it would not be difficult to heal it in this manner: *Nevertheless, you also perform this individually, so that each may love his own wife as himself.*

**40 But let the wife fear]** In Greek it is, "so that she may fear," <gloss>ἵνα φοβῆται</gloss>, that is, "so that she may reverence." For Saint Jerome thinks the word <gloss>to fear</gloss> can be understood in this sense.

**1 In the Lord]** This particle is not added in Ambrose, nor in the Commentaries; I do not know if it was omitted by chance. Jerome indicates a double distinction: for this clause, *in the Lord*, can be referred either to the verb *obey*, or to the noun *parents*: parents "in the Lord" are those who have begotten us for Christ through sacred doctrine. But they "obey their parents in the Lord" who comply with them out of the love of Christ, provided they do not command impious things:

<column-break/>

<margin>31</margin> [be joined] to his wife, and from two shall become one flesh.
<margin>32</margin> This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and the Church.
<margin>33</margin> Nevertheless, you also perform this individually, so that each may love his own wife just as himself, and the wife so that she may reverence the man.
<margin>VI. 1</margin> Sons, obey your parents in the Lord, for that is just.
<margin>2</margin> Honor your father and mother: which is the first commandment with a promise,
<margin>3</margin> That it may be well with you and you may be long-lived on the earth.
<margin>4</margin> Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up through instruction

<margin>C</margin> for those who obey [impious things], do not obey "in the Lord." The first distinction, which Jerome reports, would be more probable if the article had been added <gloss>to those in the Lord</gloss> <note>Original: τοῖς ἐν Κυρίῳ</note>: but then it would exclude natural parents, of whom Paul is undoubtedly speaking here.

<margin>D</margin> **2 in the promise]** Some read this together, *first in the promise*: first, not simply, because in the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> the law about honoring parents holds the fourth place, but *first in the promise*, because to this one alone is a reward added, *That it may be well with you and you may be long-lived*. Jerome does not sufficiently approve of this solution, because a promise is also attached to the second commandment, *showing mercy to thousands*, and he suggests another: that we take "first commandment" to mean the whole Decalogue, because this law was first brought to the Hebrews after leaving Egypt. Even this device does not satisfy them, for it would follow that a promise was attached to all the precepts. But Paul attributes this to this precept as if it were unique. Nor is what more recent writers bring forward much more solid: that this precept is the first on the "second table" <note>The commandments regarding human relationships, as opposed to the first table regarding God</note>. In the first table, those things are commanded which relate to the worship of God, and they are four; in the second, those which pertain to neighbors, and in this order, the commandment about honoring parents holds the chief place. Truly, this distinction is not founded in Holy Scripture, but is a device of more recent Theologians. In my opinion, it could be said that a promise is added to this one commandment—not that general promise which is frequently made to those observing God's commandments, but a proper and specific one: for it is fitting that he who is dutiful toward those from whom he received life should enjoy that life happily and for a long time. To the second commandment, however, both threats and mercy are added; the mercy which is promised pertains generally to all the precepts of the law. The words of the Decalogue go like this: *For I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, who returns the sins of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation to those who hate me, and showing mercy to thousands to those who love me and keep my commandments.* Thus the Decalogue. Here, furthermore, the speech is general: "who keep my commandments." In the other precept, the promise is specific, and as if spoken to one person, "that it may be well with you." Jerome also points out that the Apostle omitted the final words of the testimony which he quotes from Exodus: *for there it is held, "that you may be long-lived upon the land, which the Lord your God is going to give to you."* From these, the Apostle intentionally omitted the last words, lest the Jews believe that another land was to be expected by them through the Messiah: for when Moses brought that law, they had not yet arrived at the land flowing with milk and honey. We see, however, that Scripture everywhere feeds a coarse people with earthly promises, the chief of which was the promise of a most fertile land. Whence what the Apostle says here, that this commandment was the first in promise, can be understood so that we perceive not just any promise, but that one by which the Jews were most especially led. Mention of this is first made in this commandment. Nor is it necessary that we flee with Jerome to allegory: since Augustine teaches that even for the impious, temporary rewards are paid by God for certain good deeds, such as for piety toward parents. If a happy longevity in this world does not happen to all who have cultivated piety toward parents, there is no necessity for every single exception to be included under a general statement: although Paul did not say, *so that it will be well with you and you will be long-lived*, but *so that it may be well with you and you may be long-lived* <note>Erasmus notes the use of the subjunctive mood here</note>. For by such duties God is provoked to give prosperity of things and life; He is not obligated.

<margin>E</margin> Chrysostom, and Theophylact agreeing with him, indicate the same thing was called "first in promise" because in Exodus 20 the other commandments only forbid evils: *You shall not worship foreign Gods. You shall not take the name of your God in vain. You shall do no work on the Sabbath. You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not speak false witness against your neighbor. You shall not covet the thing, nor the wife, etc.* But he who abstains from forbidden things escapes punishment, but earns no reward. However, when he says, *Honor father and mother*, he does not forbid doing evil, but commands doing well, for which a reward is due. According to this interpretation, the commandment about honoring parents is not only the first in promise, but also the only one. They correctly noted that the promise is suited for young children, because that age, more than others, desires to live long and pleasantly.

<margin>F</margin> **3 And you may be long-lived]** <note>Original: καὶ ἔσῃ</note>, that is, "and you will be." Although in this passage it is ambiguous. For it can be referred to *hina* [so that], or it can be read absolutely, so that *the conjunction "and" sounds like the consequence of the event*: "If you do this, you will be."

**4 And you fathers]** The "you" is redundant, for it is understood by the Greeks.

**5 In discipline and correction]** <note>Original: ἐν παιδείᾳ καὶ νουθεσίᾳ</note>, that is, in instruction or training and admonition. For that word is more pleasing to Saint Jerome, being softer than "correction," which Ambrose used. Although I do not quite understand from where the word "conversation" crept into the books first printed by our Froben, in which it is read, *in the discipline and conversation of the Lord*. Furthermore, both words are ambiguous to the Greeks. <gloss>Paideia</gloss> signifies both instruction and chastisement, derived from the word for "child" <note>pais</note>. <gloss>Nouthesia</gloss> means admonition and rebuke or correction, named from the fact that you place and urge into someone's mind what ought to be done or ought to have been done.

He also examines the ethical duties of children to parents, explaining the historical and theological context of the "first commandment with a promise."</summary>

# TO THE EPHESIANS. CHAPTER VI.

<margin>5</margin> ...bring them up in the discipline and admonition of the Lord. Slaves, obey those who are your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, <note>original: ἐν παιδείᾳ καὶ νουθεσίᾳ Κυρίου. Οἱ δοῦλοι, ὑπακούετε τοῖς κυρίοις κατὰ σάρκα, μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου</note>
<margin>6</margin> in the simplicity of your heart, as to Christ; not by way of eye-service as men-pleasers, but as slaves of <note>original: ἐν ἁπλότητι τῆς καρδίας ὑμῶν, ὡς τῷ Χριστῷ, Μὴ κατ' ὀφθαλμοδουλείαν ὡς ἀνθρωπάρεσκοι, ἀλλ' ὡς δοῦλοι</note>
<margin>7</margin> Christ, doing the will of God from the soul, serving with <note>original: Χριστοῦ, ποιοῦντες τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐκ ψυχῆς, μετ' εὐ-</note>
<margin>8</margin> goodwill to the Lord, and not to men, knowing <note>original: νοίας δουλεύοντες τῷ Κυρίῳ, καὶ οὐκ ἀνθρώποις, Εἰδότες</note>
that whatever good thing each one does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a slave or free. And you masters, <note>original: ὅτι ὃ ἐάν τι ἕκαστος ποιήσῃ ἀγαθόν, τοῦτο κομιεῖται παρὰ τοῦ Κυρίου, εἴτε δοῦλος, εἴτε ἐλεύθερος. Καὶ οἱ κύριοι</note>

<margin>10</margin> there is no partiality with him. For the rest, my brothers, be strengthened in the Lord, and in the power of his <note>original: προσωποληψία οὐκ ἔστι παρ' αὐτῷ. Τὸ λοιπόν, ἀδελφοί μου, ἐνδυναμοῦσθε ἐν Κυρίῳ, καὶ ἐν τῷ κράτει τῆς ἰσχύος</note>

---

<margin>6 To masters according to the flesh]</margin> <note>original: τοῖς κυρίοις κατὰ σάρκα</note>, that is, the master according to the flesh. Truly he changed this correctly to avoid ambiguity, so that no one might refer "according to the flesh" to the act of serving.

<margin>7 Not serving to the eye]</margin> In Greek, the word is a compound, <note>original: μὴ κατ' ὀφθαλμοδουλείαν</note>. It is as if you were to say, "Not according to eye-service," if one strives to render the word for word.

<margin>8 Men-pleasers]</margin> And here the word is a compound, <note>original: ἀνθρωπάρεσκοι</note>, which is much more pleasant than the Latin paraphrase, but the Translator could not render it. it sounds as if you were to say, "man-pleasing," those who strive to be approved by men rather than by God.

<margin>9 With good will]</margin> <note>original: Μετ' εὐνοίας</note>, that is, with benevolence. It is a wonder why the Translator thought this should be changed. It does not at all please me what Augustine gathers from this saying: that slaves ought not to demand freedom from Christian masters, even though the Mosaic Law willed that all slaves be set free every seventh year. I would not deny that what he said is true, since Paul here is acting even regarding Ethnic <note>pagan</note> masters, not only Christians. For he wants the Christian slave to serve his master faithfully out of love for Christ, just as he wants Christian citizens to obey a Prince who commands as an idolater. And if it is not lawful for slaves to demand freedom, nevertheless it seems hardly Christian that Christian masters do not grant to their slaves what that Law, which was far less merciful than Christianity, indulged to its own. Indeed, it seems shameful that among Christians the name of "lord" or "slave" is heard at all; for since Baptism makes all men brothers, how is it fitting for a brother to be called the slave of a brother? Let this be the rule for those who favor Imperial law; let it not be the rule of Gospel law, according to which the slave obeys the master from the heart, and the master, in turn, treats the slave as a brother in Christ.

<margin>10 Serving as to the Lord]</margin> The adverb "as" is redundant and is not added by Ambrose. For he feels that this obedience, which is paid to impious or difficult masters, is not paid to men, but to Christ, out of whose love the slave bears the man's tyranny, lest he place any stumbling block before the Gospel. In Chrysostom, the "as" <note>original: ὡς</note> is added, but from his explanation it is not clear what he read. The commentary of Theophylact indicates more clearly that "as" was not added, otherwise it would have had to say, "serving as to the Lord, and not as to men." And we are said to serve Him from whom we expect a reward, and therefore the Apostle immediately adds: "each one, whatever good he has done, will receive from the Lord."

<margin>11 Giving up threats]</margin> <note>original: ἀνιέντες τὴν ἀπειλήν</note>, that is, relaxing threats; that is, being less fierce and less threatening. For he wants them to be less domineering than the pagans are toward their own.

<margin>12 Because both their and your Lord]</margin> <note>original: εἰδότες ὅτι καὶ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν ὁ Κύριός ἐστιν ἐν οὐρανοῖς</note>, that is, knowing that your own Lord is in the heavens: so the sense is, since you know that you also have a Lord in the heavens whom you ought to fear. Ambrose and Jerome seem to have read, <note>original: ὑμῶν τε καὶ αὐτῶν</note>, that is, "yours and theirs at the same time," so that you understand a Lord common to both.

<margin>13 Brothers]</margin> The pronoun "my" is added among the Greeks, <note>original: ἀδελφοί μου</note>. Furthermore, neither Jerome nor Ambrose adds "brothers." Moreover, he would have translated <note>original: Τὸ λοιπὸν</note> better as "What remains."

<margin>14 Put on the armor of God]</margin> <note>original: πανοπλίαν</note>. This word signifies everything that pertains to arming a soldier for battle. As if you were to say, all the weapons together that pertain to a man. Hence, a little further down, Saint Jerome warns that it should have been translated not as "arms" (which the Greeks call <note>original: ὅπλα</note>), but as "universal arms," <note>original: πανοπλίαν</note>. And Ambrose reads "the universality of arms"; Cyprian in some places translates "total arms."

<margin>15 Against the wiles]</margin> <note>original: μεθοδείας</note>, the same as what he had previously translated as "circumvention." Ambrose reads "against nations," but in a corrupted manuscript, I suppose; perhaps "nations" was written <note>note: Latin 'nationes' vs 'machinationes' or similar error</note>. For "method" <note>original: μέθοδος</note> is a rational way of doing something, but here it is for attacking something. However, it is a "wile" <note>original: μεθοδεία</note> if someone attacks another from ambush. Jerome reads and interprets it as "against the craftiness of the devil." Although he could have translated it here as "the slanderer."

<margin>16 Wrestling]</margin> <note>original: ἡ πάλη</note>, that is, a struggle or wrestling match.

<margin>17 Rulers of the world]</margin> <note>original: κοσμοκράτορας</note>, that is, the masters of the world:

<header>TO THE EPHESIANS. CHAPTER VI.</header>

<margin>A</margin> ...and the correction of the Lord. Slaves, obey those who are masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, with the simplicity of your heart, as to Christ,
<margin>6</margin> Not serving to the eye, as if striving to please men, but as slaves of Christ, doing what
<margin>7</margin> God wills from the soul, serving with goodwill
<margin>8</margin> the Lord, and not men, knowing this, that whatever good each one does, this he will receive back from the Lord,
<margin>9</margin> whether he was a slave or free. And you masters, do the same things toward them, giving up threats, knowing that your own Lord is in the heavens, and there is no
<margin>B</margin> <margin>10</margin> respect of persons with him. Finally, my brothers, be strong through the Lord, and through the power of his
<margin>11</margin> strength. Put on the whole armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the craftiness of the devil.
<margin>12</margin> Since there is not for us a struggle against blood and flesh, but against principalities, against powers, against the masters of the world, the rulers of the darkness of this age, against spiritual craftiness in the heavenly places.
<margin>13</margin> Therefore take up the universal armor of God, so that you may be able to resist in the evil day, and having perfected all things, to stand.
<margin>14</margin> Stand therefore, with your loins girded with the belt of truth,
<margin>15</margin> and put on the breastplate of righteousness, and your feet shod, that you may be ready for the Gospel of peace.
<margin>16</margin> Above all, having taken up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming
<margin>C</margin> <margin>17</margin> darts of that evil one. And receive the helmet of salvation, and...

<meta>catchword: gla-</meta>

---

...which word is plainly new, and not found anywhere else. Saint Jerome thinks it was first coined by Paul, so that he might adapt new vocabulary to explain new things. Moreover, it is a compound word in Greek, and therefore the genitive "of this darkness" fits more conveniently. Tertullian, in the fifth book against Marcion, translates <note>original: κοσμοκράτορας</note> as "world-holders." Hilary, in the Psalms, translates it as "world-powers," a compound word not inelegantly formed.

<margin>18 Of this darkness]</margin> In Greek it is <note>original: τοῦ σκότους τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου</note>, that is, of the darkness of this age.

<margin>D</margin> <margin>19</margin> Against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places] As for what Faber advises—that "in the heavenly places" could be taken for "against the heavenly beings"—the logic of the Greek language in no way allows this, in my judgment. Now, as for his heavily venting his anger against superstitious Astrologers and prognosticators, though it was not done without cause, it certainly was not done in its proper place. Furthermore, he said "spiritual things of wickedness" for "spiritual wickednesses," or rather "craftinesses," for the Greek is <note>original: πονηρίας</note>. Ambrose, in the book *On Paradise*, chapter twelve, inverts it thus to explain the sense: "against the wickedness of spiritual beings, which are in the heavenly places."

<margin>E</margin> <margin>20</margin> And in all things being perfect, to stand] The Greeks read it thus, <note>original: καὶ ἅπαντα κατεργασάμενοι στῆναι</note>, that is, "and having finished or perfected all things, to stand," that is, after you have perfected all things, to stand. Jerome reads and explains it as "having worked all things, to stand." Cyprian likewise in the fourth Epistle of the sixth book says, "so that when you have perfected all things, you may stand with your loins girded, etc." Just as a soldier does everything he can so that he might resist the enemy and protect his life, so we must do all things with spirits who are constantly struggling. Now, while I judge that pointing these things out is not a matter of great difficulty, I do not think it safe to be either ignorant of or to neglect these small details. For what if a Theologian here, in a long and elaborate sermon, philosophizes much about those who stand perfectly or those who stand imperfectly, and soon moves those skilled in Greek to laughter? Nor indeed would that be undeserved. Chrysostom warns that it was not said simply <note>original: ἐργασάμενοι</note>, that is, "after you have done," but <note>original: ἅπαντα κατεργασάμενοι</note>, that is, "after you have perfected all things." The Apostle, however, persists in the metaphor of war. There are many duties for soldiers: to surround the trench, to raise the rampart, to fortify the camp with palisades, to ready the weapons, to drive back the enemy. After all these things have been diligently accomplished, it remains for them to stand, always ready for battle. For to many, victory brings security and leisure; security, by a change of fortunes, turns victors into the vanquished. That the Apostle felt this regarding military vigilance is declared by what immediately follows: "Stand therefore girded, etc." Thomas <note>Aquinas</note> interprets "in all things" as in prosperity and in adversity; and taking the opportunity of this word "perfect," he makes a double perfection, one according to the mode of the traveler, the other according to the fullness of the homeland, which I confess are rightly said, but hardly in their proper place. I suspect the Latin manuscripts here were corrupted, and the Translator rendered it "that you may be able to stand in all perfected things." For I do not think he read <note>original: κατεργασάμενοι</note>.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>21</margin> Stand therefore girded] <note>original: περιζωσάμενοι</note>, that is, accincted, or girt about, that is, fortified. For that part of the body is usually covered in war by a belt thickened with metal plates, to which the Apostle now alludes. And Saint Jerome, explaining this place, mentions a "leathern zone," with which John the Baptist is read to have been girded; and soon he mentions a "spiritual belt." Indeed, even that proverb is taken from military service: "He lost his belt." Both the feet and shins are fortified for the sake of protection; even though legal scholars deny that footwear is included under the name of "arms." Ambrose indicates a double use of the belt: both that the garment being tucked up makes a man unencumbered, and that it protects the soft parts of the middle body. It seemed good to add this, because I understand that the word "loin-cloth" <note>original: subligaculum</note> is more approved by the learned than "belt" <note>original: balthei</note>.

<margin>22</margin> Darts of the most wicked] <note>original: βέλη τοῦ πονηροῦ</note>, the darts of the evil one, or of that scoundrel.

<margin>23</margin> Helmet of salvation] <note>original: τὸ σωτήριον</note>, that is, of the savior or salutary. And so Jerome reads in the Commentaries. Nor is it an "assumption," but "receive," <note>original: δέξασθε</note>.

859 THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE EPHESIANS. CHAPTER VI. 860

...and receive the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which <margin>18</margin> is the word of God, praying at all times in the Spirit with every prayer and supplication. To this end, keep <margin>24</margin> alert with all <margin>25</margin> perseverance and supplication for all the saints, <margin>19</margin> and for me, so that a message may be given to me when I open my mouth, to make known with <margin>26</margin> boldness the <margin>20</margin> mystery of the Gospel, for which I serve as an ambassador in <margin>27</margin> chains, that <margin>21</margin> in it I may <margin>28</margin> speak boldly, as I ought to speak. But so that you also may know my affairs and what I am doing, Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful <margin>22</margin> minister in the Lord, will make everything known to you. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that <margin>23</margin> you may know our circumstances and that he may encourage your hearts. Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the <margin>24</margin> Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with incorruptible love. Amen.

->It was written from Rome to the Ephesians by Tychicus.<-

### OF THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE EPHESIANS
->T H E  E N D.<-

<margin>24</margin> **And watching in this same thing** <note>original: "Et in ipso vigilantes"</note>] *and watching for this very purpose* <note>original: καὶ εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἀγρυπνοῦντες</note>, that is, and being vigilant toward this very thing, just as Ambrose reads it. It is uncertain among the Greeks whether this refers back to "the spirit" or to the matter at hand, because "spirit" <note>original: πνεῦμα</note> is a neuter noun in their language.

<margin>25</margin> **In all persistence** <note>original: "In omni instantia"</note>] *in all perseverance* <note>original: ἐν πάσῃ προσκαρτερήσει</note>. Concerning this, see above. Ambrose reads "perseverance."

<margin>26</margin> **With confidence** <note>original: "Cum fiducia"</note>] *with boldness* <note>original: ἐν παρρησίᾳ</note>. This properly refers to freedom and audacity in speaking. Ambrose translates this as "clearly." Regarding the phrase "To make known": why not rather "that I might make known"?

<margin>27</margin> **In this chain** <note>original: "In catena ista"</note>] The word "this" <note>original: ista</note> is redundant. It is found neither in Ambrose nor in Jerome, nor even in the most ancient manuscript copies—specifically the Pauline and Donatian codices—and is supported by both manuscripts from Constance. <note>Erasmus frequently cites specific local manuscripts he consulted during his travels.</note>

<margin>28</margin> **I may dare in it** <note>original: "in ipso audeam"</note>] *that I may speak boldly* <note>original: ἵνα παρρησιάσωμαι</note>. Explaining this word, Ambrose says, "that in it I may speak with clear liberty, as it behoves me to speak." It is not exactly like that, but rather *hina parrēsiasōmai*, which means "that I may dare" or "speak freely."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God, praying in every <margin>18</margin> prayer and supplication at all times in the spirit, and watching for this very thing <margin>24</margin> with all <margin>18</margin> diligence <margin>25</margin> and supplication for all the saints, and for <margin>19</margin> me, so that speech may be given to me in the opening of my mouth <margin>26</margin> with liberty, that I may make known the mystery of my Gospel, <margin>20</margin> for which I act as an ambassador <margin>27</margin> in a chain, <margin>28</margin> so that in it I may speak freely, as I ought to speak. But so that you <margin>21</margin> also may know the things that pertain to me and what I am doing, Tychicus, the <margin>29</margin> beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make you certain of all things. I have sent him to you for this <margin>22</margin> very purpose, <margin>30</margin> so that you might know about our affairs and he might <margin>23</margin> comfort your hearts. Peace to the brothers and charity with <margin>B 23</margin> faith <margin>31</margin> from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace be <margin>24</margin> with all those who love our Lord Jesus Christ <margin>32</margin> with sincerity. Amen.

->It was sent from Rome to the Ephesians through Tychicus.<-

### OF THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE EPHESIANS
->F I N I S.<-

<margin>C 29</margin> **Our most dear brother** <note>original: "Charissimus frater noster"</note>] *beloved* <note>original: ἀγαπητὸς</note>, that is, "dear." Jerome reads it this way, although here he almost always translates it as "most dear" as if by habit.

<margin>30</margin> **That you may know what is around us** <note>original: "Ut cognoscatis quae circa nos sunt"</note>] *the things concerning us* <note>original: τὰ περὶ ἡμῶν</note>, that is, the things that involve us—meaning our affairs and our status.

<margin>31</margin> **From God our Father** <note>original: "A Deo Patre nostro"</note>] The word "our" is not added in the Greek, nor in Jerome, nor even in the Pauline manuscript. Both Constance manuscripts agree with this omission.

<margin>32</margin> **In incorruption** <note>original: "In incorruptione"</note>] *in incorruptibility* <note>original: ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ</note>. While elsewhere this is usually rightly translated as "immortality," here it sounds like integrity and sincerity of mind, free from all corruption of vices. Jerome does not approve of those who apply "incorruptibility" <note>original: ἀφθαρσίαν</note> specifically to bodily chastity. We are supported by Chrysostom and the interpreter Theophylact, who also advise that the preposition "in" <note>original: ἐν</note> here has the same force as "through" <note>original: διὰ</note>. For Christ is loved in this way: if we keep ourselves uncontaminated by this world. In Ambrose, "Amen" is not added at the end of this Epistle, nor can it be gathered from his commentaries what he read.

# THE ARGUMENT
<note>original: Υ Π Ο Θ Ε Σ Ι Σ (Hypothesis); a scholarly summary or introductory argument common in Greek manuscripts.</note>
-> of the <-
## EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE PHILIPPIANS.
-> <-

He sends this letter from Rome, having previously seen them and taught them. The occasion for the Epistle is this: the Philippians had sent aid to Paul <note>The Philippians were known for their financial support of Paul's ministry.</note>, and certain people were going about corrupting the hearing of the simple-hearted under the pretext of the "shadow of the Law" <note>A reference to Jewish rituals viewed as precursors to Christ.</note> and circumcision, claiming that without these one cannot be justified. Having learned of this, the Apostle writes to the Philippians. First, he commends their faith and indicates that he remembers them. Then he recounts how he made his defense in Rome, and that some have become a burden to him, stirring up envy against him while he is in bonds. Next, he exhorts them to love one another, explaining the Savior’s love for humanity—that being God, He became man for our sake. Then, dealing with circumcision and the old Law, he proves thereafter that circumcision has become obsolete, using himself as the example and saying, "I have counted all these things as loss for the sake of Christ." Therefore, having rebuked those teaching in favor of circumcision and wanting to deceive them—calling them enemies of Christ—he commends the Philippians for the gift of fellowship they sent to him. And having exhorted them once more regarding their moral conduct, he completes the Epistle.

---

### ON THE EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS
-> An Argument by <-
## DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'P' featuring a landscape scene within an ornate square border.</image-desc>
The Philippians are located in the first part of Macedonia, as is narrated in the sixteenth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles. They are a colony originating from the city of Philippi, named after its founder, Philip <note>Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great.</note>. Their metropolitan city is Thessalonica. Because they persisted in the faith once they had received it, and did not admit the false apostles to whom the Corinthians and Galatians had listened, they are deservedly praised by the Apostle. Paul, having set out to them at the prompting of the Spirit, spent several days among them, though not without trouble. For it was here that Paul was beaten with lashes and thrown into prison with Silas. At that time, the keeper of the prison was baptized with his entire family. Here also was Lydia, the seller of purple, who was the first convert and received Paul with hospitality. Here too, the soldiers, upon learning that he was a Roman citizen, voluntarily asked that he go wherever he wished, and the name of Christ became famous under very favorable circumstances. 

Furthermore, when Paul was living in chains at Rome, they sent him those things which were necessary for his life's needs via Epaphroditus; they had also done this previously when he was staying in Thessalonica, as he himself testifies in this Epistle. Having praised them, he therefore exhorts them to persevere and make progress, showing that one must boast even in afflictions that serve to highlight the Gospel of Christ. He himself does not dread death; indeed, he even desires it, if it should happen by the will of Christ. Then, he especially exhorts them to mutual harmony, which cannot exist among the proud. To make them more encouraged, he promises that Timothy and even he himself will return to them shortly; in the meantime, he has sent Epaphroditus, who had recovered from a most dangerous illness. 

He deals with these matters in the first two chapters. In the third, he strengthens their minds against the false apostles who are everywhere soliciting people toward Judaism <note>Often called "Judaizers," these were early Christians who insisted that converts must follow Mosaic Law, including circumcision.</note>. He calls these men "dogs," "workers of iniquity," and "enemies of the cross of Christ," saying they worship their bellies in place of God; never is he more openly angry with them than here. The fourth chapter is occupied with commendations and greetings, except that he mixes in certain warnings in passing and gives thanks to the Philippians for their generosity toward him. He wrote this from the city of Rome by way of Epaphroditus while he was in prison for the second time. For after his first defense, he was led back into prison, a fact he himself mentions in the Epistle to Timothy.

<summary>This page provides two introductory summaries (one Greek, one by Erasmus) for the Epistle to the Philippians, highlighting the city's history, Paul's imprisonment there, and the Philippians' unique financial support for his ministry.</summary>
<keywords>Philippians, Paul the Apostle, Erasmus, Macedonia, Lydia the purpuraria, Epaphroditus, Rome, circumcision, Judaizers, Christian generosity</keywords>

<header>THE EPISTLE OF THE APOSTLE PAUL TO THE PHILIPPIANS.</header>

# THE EPISTLE OF THE APOSTLE PAUL TO THE PHILIPPIANS.

<margin>1. 1</margin> Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are in Philippi, <margin>2</margin> with the bishops and deacons: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. <margin>3</margin> I give thanks to my God upon every remembrance of you, <margin>4</margin> always in every prayer of mine for you all, making my prayer with joy, <margin>5</margin> for your fellowship in the Gospel from the first day until now, <margin>6</margin> being confident of this very thing: that He who began a good work in you will perfect it until the day of Jesus Christ. <margin>7</margin> Even as it is right for me to think this of you all, because I have you in my heart, both in my bonds and in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel, you all being partakers of my grace. <margin>8</margin> For God is my witness, how I long for you all in the bowels <note>A common biblical idiom for deep affection or the "heart" of one's emotions.</note> of Jesus Christ. <margin>9</margin> And this I pray: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and in all judgment, <margin>10</margin> that you may approve the things that are excellent, that you may be sincere and without offense until the day of Christ, <margin>11</margin> being filled with the fruits of righteousness, which are through Jesus Christ, <margin>12</margin> to the glory and praise of God. But I want you to know, brothers, that the things which happened to me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the Gospel, <margin>13</margin> so that my bonds in Christ have become manifest in all the palace <note>original: πραιτωρίῳ (praitorio); referring to the Roman Praetorium or the Emperor’s guard.</note> and in all other places, <margin>14</margin> and many of the brothers in the Lord, growing confident by my bonds, are much more bold to speak the word without fear. <margin>15</margin> Some indeed preach Christ even out of envy and strife, but some also out of goodwill. <margin>16</margin> The former preach Christ out of contention, not sincerely, thinking to add affliction to my bonds.

---

<margin>1</margin> **Timothy** Although it does not affect Paul's meaning, I thought it necessary to advise that "Timothy" <note>original: Timotheum</note> should be pronounced with the accent on the third-to-last syllable, whether you follow the Greek or Latin rule; yet the opposite is currently done in all the churches. And while one might wish this were the most serious error in Christian life, it is nonetheless shameful that we perpetually err in public in such a manifest matter. Yet there exists one who thinks it a religious duty not to change even lapses of this kind, as if they were handed down from the fathers—as if this excuse could not be used to prevent the deletion of anything, however it was received. And yet, what he says carries some weight if the language is becoming familiar to the common people. Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Archbishop of Bulgaria and biblical commentator.</note> placed this Epistle after the one to the Colossians.

<margin>2</margin> **With the bishops** In some Greek codices, it is a single word: <term>synepiscopis</term> <note>original: συνεπισκόποις; meaning "fellow-bishops"</note>. It is as if Paul shared his office with their elders. However, the Greek copies vary here, and in some it was written <term>syn episkopois</term> <note>original: σὺν ἐπισκόποις</note>, that is, "together with the bishops." Ambrose <note>The 4th-century Bishop of Milan.</note> follows the latter reading, and we do not wish to differ from him. Theophylact both reads and interprets it as joined. For out of honor, Paul calls the elders "Bishops." For, as Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, the 4th-century "Golden-Mouthed" preacher.</note> indicates, there were not multiple Bishops of a single city. It is clear that Timothy was a Bishop from what Paul writes to him: "Lay hands suddenly on no man." And formerly, Bishops were called Deacons, as elsewhere: "Fulfill your ministry."

<margin>3</margin> **And deacons** <term>diakonois</term> <note>original: διακόνοις</note>, that is, "ministers," as it often occurs. If the Greek word is preferred, one should say *diaconis*, not *diaconibus*. Yet this word is found several times in the books of Augustine using the third declension <note>A grammatical point regarding Latin endings.</note>, I suppose because it was commonly used that way, just as "baptism" is used in the neuter gender.

<margin>4</margin> **In every remembrance of you** <term>epi pasē mneia hymōn, meta charas tēn deēsin poioumenos</term> <note>original: ἐπὶ πάσῃ μνείᾳ ὑμῶν, μετὰ χαρᾶς τὴν δέησιν ποιούμενος</note>, that is, "in every memory of you, making supplication with joy." Ambrose reads it this way: "Upon every memory of you, always in every prayer of mine for all of you, making prayer with joy, upon your communication"—so that you refer the "joy" to the "communication" as the cause of the joy.

<margin>5</margin> **In all prayers** <term>en pasē deēsei</term> <note>original: ἐν πάσῃ δεήσει</note>, "in every supplication."

<margin>6</margin> **Confident in this very thing** <term>pepoithōs auto touto</term> <note>original: Πεποιθὼς αὐτὸ τοῦτο</note>, that is, "having been persuaded of this very thing."

<margin>7</margin> **Partners of joy** In the Greek it is "of grace" <note>original: χάριτος (charitos)</note>, but it is an easy slip between "grace" and "joy" <note>original: χαρᾶς (charas)</note>. Elsewhere we have shown the one is used for the other. Ambrose reads "of joy"; Chrysostom and Theophylact read "of grace." Where he said "partners," in Greek it is <term>synkoinōnos</term> <note>original: συγκοινωνὸς</note>, as if you said, "equal participants." "That you all are" <note>original: ὄντας (ontas)</note>. It would have been more correctly translated "since you are partners of grace" <note>original: συγκοινωνοί (synkoinōnoi)</note>.

<margin>8</margin> **That you are in the bowels** This is redundant; it is simply "in the bowels of Jesus Christ." He added this lest anyone suspect there was any human affection here in why he loved them so much. He calls the affection of the mind "bowels." He added "of Jesus Christ" to declare that this affection belongs to piety, not human nature.

<column-break/>

->A<-
<margin>1. 1</margin> Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, <margin>2</margin> together with the bishops and deacons: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. I give <margin>3</margin> thanks to my God in every remembrance of you, always in <margin>4</margin> every prayer of mine for all of you, making my prayer with joy, because you have come into the <margin>5</margin> fellowship of the Gospel, from the first day until this time, having been persuaded of this very thing: that He who began in <margin>6</margin> you a good work will perfect it until the day of Jesus Christ. Even as it is right for me to think this of all of <margin>7</margin> you, because I have you in my heart, and in my bonds, and in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel, since you are all my partners in grace. For <margin>8</margin> God is my witness, how I long for you all in ->B<- the bowels of Jesus Christ. And this I pray: that your love <margin>9</margin> may still more and more abound in knowledge and every understanding, that you may approve the things that are excellent, <margin>10</margin> that you may be sincere and such that you are a stumbling block to no one until the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness, which comes <margin>11</margin> through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God. Now I want you to know, brothers, that the things which happened <margin>12</margin> to me have turned out more for the progress of the Gospel, so that my bonds have become manifest in Christ <margin>13</margin> in the whole palace and to all the rest, and that <margin>14</margin> many of the brothers in the Lord, relying on my bonds, have dared more abundantly to speak the word without fear. Some <margin>15</margin> indeed preach Christ through envy and strife, but some ->C<- also because of goodwill. Others indeed announce <margin>16</margin> Christ out of contention

---

<margin>9</margin> **More and more** <term>eti mallon</term> <note>original: ἔτι μᾶλλον</note>, that is, "still more."

<margin>10</margin> **Better things** <term>ta diapheronta</term> <note>original: τὰ διαφέροντα</note>, that is, "excellent things." Ambrose reads "useful things." I suspect his codex had written <term>sympheronta</term> instead of <term>diapheronta</term>; unless we say <term>diapherein</term>, that is, "to differ," refers to things that pertain to our business. Theophylact, without controversy, interprets <term>diapheronta</term> as "useful things" <note>original: συμφέροντα</note>. Chrysostom does not touch upon this word. In Romans chapter 11, the translator renders <term>diapheronta</term> as "more useful things." Things that are "indifferent" <note>original: ἀδιάφορα (adiaphora)</note> do not matter whether you do them or not. By contrast, "excellent things" <note>original: διαφέροντα</note> are relevant to the matter.

<margin>11</margin> **And without offense** Ambrose reads "un-offended," as if you were to say "sturdy," those who cannot be offended or who never stumble. Although the Greek word is ambiguous—<term>aproskopoi</term> <note>original: ἀπρόσκοποι</note>—it is as if you said, "such that you are a stumbling block to no one." And the Greek scholia interpret it in this sense.

<margin>12</margin> **Through Jesus Christ** <term>tōn dia Iēsou Christou</term> <note>original: τῶν διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ</note>, that is, [the fruit] which is or happens "through Jesus Christ," as the Greek article distinguishes this fruit from others.

->D<-
<margin>13</margin> **In all the palace** <term>en holō tō praitōriō</term> <note>original: ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ πραιτωρίῳ</note>, that is, "in the whole palace." Let no one take this to mean Paul was led through all the palaces [plural], since he himself says something else: namely, that the prisoner's preaching reached even the court of Nero itself, and from there was spread through the entire city. For Theophylact refers "palace" to Nero's household, and "to all the rest" to the remaining citizens, following Chrysostom and noting that the houses of Emperors were commonly called *praetoria* at that time, a Latin word used by the Greeks. Ambrose, somewhat harshly, refers "palace" to Judaism and "all the rest" to the Churches of the Gentiles. The translator, however, not infrequently misuses "every" <note>Latin: omnis</note> for "whole" <note>Latin: totus</note>.

<margin>14</margin> **And in all other places** This is redundant: whether it should be understood as "to others," I leave for others to weigh. Nor does he refer "others" to other palaces, as if the meaning were that the Gospel was known in other palaces too, but rather to others of that city who did not live in the palace. Thus Theophylact says. Therefore, the conjunction had no use, nor was it added by Ambrose.

<margin>15</margin> **They dared more abundantly** Ambrose explained the Greek figure of speech in Latin: "they began to dare more." For in the phrase "to dare worthily" <note>original: ἀξίως τολμᾷν</note> there seems to be a synecdoche, or if you prefer, an ellipsis, which Flaccus <note>The Roman poet Horace.</note> nevertheless dared to imitate in his Odes:
->That whatever shall be, it is better to endure.<-
So that you might understand "is able" or "you begin," or a similar verb suited to the meaning.

<margin>16</margin> **Because of goodwill** <term>di’ eudokian</term> <note>original: δι’ εὐδοκίαν</note>. Which is usually translated as "good pleasure." The order of this passage is different among the Latins and the Greeks. The Greek text has it thus: "Some indeed preach Christ out of contention, not purely, thinking to add pressure to my bonds. Others truly out of love, knowing that I am placed for the defense of the Gospel." Our reading is thus: "Some indeed preach Christ because of envy and strife, but some also because of goodwill."
