<meta>This page continues the text of the first chapter of Paul's Epistle to the Philippians. It contains the Greek source text for verses 17 through 30, followed by Erasmus's detailed philological commentary and his own revised Latin translation in parallel columns.</meta>

<header>TO THE PHILIPPIANS. CHAPTER I.</header>

<margin>17</margin> in my bonds. But others out of love, knowing that <margin>18</margin> I am appointed for the defense of the Gospel. For what then? Nevertheless, in every way, whether in pretext or in truth, Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice, and <margin>19</margin> indeed I will continue to rejoice. For I know that this will turn out for my salvation, through your prayer and the supply <margin>20</margin> of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, according to my earnest expectation <note>original: "apokaradokian"</note> and hope, that in nothing I shall be put to shame, but with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether through life or through death. <margin>21</margin> For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain. <margin>22</margin> But if living in the flesh is the fruit of my work, then what I shall choose, I do not know. <margin>23</margin> For I am hard-pressed between the two, having a desire to depart <note>original: "analysai"</note> and to be with Christ, which is far, far better. <margin>24</margin> But to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake. <margin>25</margin> And having this confidence, I know that I shall remain and continue with you all, for your progress and joy of faith, <margin>26</margin> that your glorying may abound in Christ Jesus through me, by my presence with you again. <margin>27</margin> Only conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the Gospel of Christ, so that whether I come and see you or am absent, I may hear of your affairs, that you stand fast in one spirit, with one soul, striving together for the faith of the Gospel, <margin>28</margin> and not being terrified in any way by the adversaries, which to them is a proof of perdition, but to you of salvation, and that from God. <margin>29</margin> For to you it has been granted on behalf of Christ, not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer for His sake, <margin>30</margin> having the same struggle which you saw in me, and now hear to be in me.

***

<margin>A</margin> *...others out of love, knowing, etc.* Among the Greeks, the word for "contention" appears twice: in the first instance as *eris* <note>quarrel or strife</note>, and in the second as *eritheia* <note>ambition or self-seeking</note>. 
<margin>17</margin> **Not sincerely**] In Greek, *ouch hagnos*, which is to say, "not purely." This is how Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine biblical commentator</note> reads it. Ambrose <note>a 4th-century Church Father</note> reads it as "not simply." Perhaps his manuscript had *ouch haplos* <note>not simply</note>; in such a close similarity of words, a slip of the pen is very easy. Augustine, in the eleventh book against Petilianus, reads it as "not chastely."
<margin>18</margin> **While in every way, whether by occasion**] The Greek reading is slightly different: *What then? Nevertheless, in whatever way, whether by pretext or in truth, Christ is announced.* That is to say: what does it matter? At any rate, in whatever manner, whether by an occasion or truly, Christ is preached. For he does not command that this should be done—that someone should preach Christ insincerely—but from those things which were not being done rightly, he extracts that which is good. He disregards their hatred toward him, provided that in whatever way they benefit the Gospel. This is roughly the view of Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, the "Golden-Mouthed" preacher of the 4th century</note> in his booklet on the progress of the Gospel, and of Theophylact in his commentaries. Therefore, "in every way" is more correctly translated as "in whatever way." Nor is Paul speaking here of those who would teach heretically, but of those who teach Christ correctly, even if with a less than sincere heart. He does not approve of them, but he says you should not have to debate the spirit in which they do it, provided they are of benefit. Furthermore, what is translated here as "occasion" is *prophasis* in Greek, which also sounds like "pretext," for it is contrasted with "truth." Tertullian <note>an early North African theologian</note>, in his fifth book against Marcion, reads "causation" for *prophasis*, thinking, I suppose, that they were pretending to act on Christ's behalf while serving their own interests.
<margin>B</margin> <margin>19</margin> **According to expectation**] The Greek is *kata ten apokaradokian*. This signifies something more than simple expectation; namely, a vehement desire of the heart. The term is a compound word implying that something is expected with the whole soul. For he did not say *prosdokian* <note>ordinary expectation</note>, but *apokaradokian*, from a gesture of those who gape vehemently with the head stretched out; hence the Greek compound. I wonder what Ambrose read in the Greek that led him to translate it as "according to my contemplation," unless perhaps this was mixed up by the carelessness of scribes. However, *karadokein* among the Greeks can also mean to contemplate with a bent head. That, I think, is what Ambrose wanted to express.
<margin>20</margin> **That in nothing**] *In nothing* <note>original: "en oudeni"</note>. And again, "confidence" <note>original: "parrhesia"</note>.
<margin>21</margin> **As always now**] "And now" should be read.
<margin>22</margin> **And what I shall choose I know not**] The conjunction "and" makes the sentence more obscure. For this is what Paul felt: "If I live, I live for Christ's sake; if I die, I die for my own benefit." But if my preaching proceeds and I benefit the Church, I do not prefer my own benefit to your good—so much so that I even doubt which I should choose. The word "and" <note>original: "kai"</note> has a peculiar and hidden power here of excluding what was different. It could also be read as, "But if living," assuming the word "happens" or "will be" is understood, and then adding "this is the fruit of my work." In that way, the conjunction joins what follows in the usual manner. However, the first reading is more approved, and Theophylact follows it. Augustine cites this passage as an example of ambiguous punctuation in the third book of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter two. For it can be read this way: "I am hard-pressed by two things, having a desire," meaning he is tormented by the desire for both life and death. Or it can be done this way: "I am hard-pressed by two things," and here a break is placed, followed by "having a desire to be dissolved." Truly, from what follows—"but to be dissolved is much, far better"—it is gathered that "having a desire" refers to what follows. Although Augustine reads "best" instead of "better."
<margin>23</margin> **For I am hard-pressed by two things**] *Synechomai*. As if he were saying, "from both sides!"

<column-break/>

not purely, thinking to add affliction to my bonds. Others again out of love, knowing that <margin>18</margin> I am appointed for the defense of the Gospel. For what then? Nevertheless, in whatever way, whether by occasion or by truth, Christ is nonetheless proclaimed; and in this I rejoice, and indeed I will rejoice. <margin>19</margin> For I know that this will turn out for my salvation, through your prayer and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, <margin>20</margin> according to my expectation and hope, that in nothing I shall be put to shame, but with all freedom, as always, so now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether through life or through death. For to me life is Christ, <margin>21</margin> and death is gain. But if it happens that I live in the <margin>22</margin> flesh, that thing is the fruit of my work to me, and what I shall choose, I do not know. For I am hard-pressed by these two, desiring <margin>23</margin> to be dissolved and to be with Christ, which is much and by far the better. But to remain in the flesh is more <margin>24</margin> necessary for your sake. And this I know for certain, that I <margin>25</margin> shall remain and continue with all of you, for your progress and the joy of faith, so that your <margin>26</margin> glorying may overflow through Christ Jesus in me, by my return to you. Only conduct yourselves as is <margin>27</margin> worthy of the Gospel of Christ, so that whether I come and see you or am absent, I may hear about your affairs—that you stand in one spirit, with one soul, helping the struggling faith of the Gospel, and that you are in no way <margin>28</margin> terrified by the adversaries, which to them is a cause of destruction, but to you of salvation, and this from God. Because it has been given to you for Christ, not only that <margin>29</margin> you should believe in Him, but also that you should suffer for Him, having the same struggle as you saw in me, and <margin>30</margin> now

***

<margin>C</margin> I am held. Ambrose reads "from these two," as if expressing the force of the Greek article *ton dyo*. Indeed, he speaks of death and life: in both of which there is something that invites and something that deters.
<margin>24</margin> **Much more better**] Ambrose reads "for much better." But Paul elsewhere also doubles the comparative for emphasis, to signify the greatest excellence, following the idiom of the Hebrew language. Therefore, we have translated it as "much and by far the better." Furthermore, what is translated here as "to be dissolved" is *analysai* in Greek. Saint Jerome, in his work against Rufinus, more than once suggested it meant "to return." Tertullian, in his book *On Patience*, translates it as "to be received." I do not see how it can be read as "to be dissolved" unless the Greek were *analyesthai* <note>the passive form</note>, and if we interpret him as being "dissolved" who is dismissed so that he may return. As it stands, *analysai* is an active verb; whether it can be found in a neutral sense (just as among the Latins a sailor who departs is said to "loosen" <note>solvere</note>), let the learned reader consider. The word for a "lodging" is *katalyma* in Luke chapter 11 and 22. From this, just as those who settle into a lodging are said *katalyein* <note>to unloose/rest</note>, so those who move their baggage and change their lodging are said *analyein* <note>to unloose/depart</note>. This was also borrowed from sailors who "loosen" the ropes; the ropes of tents are also loosened. The sense is the same, but the Greek word is more expressive. Chrysostom translates *analysai* as "migration," that is, to emigrate or change one's seat.
<margin>25</margin> **Necessary for your sake**] *Anagkaioteron*, that is, "more necessary."
<margin>26</margin> **And having this confidence I know**] *Pepoit hos oida*, that is, "I know for certain," or "I know being persuaded."
<margin>27</margin> **That I shall remain and continue**] *hoti meno kai symparameno pasin hymin*, that is, "that I shall remain and shall continue together with all of you." Although some manuscripts have *meno*, meaning "I remain" or "I may remain."
<margin>28</margin> **That your rejoicing**] *to kauchema*, that is, "boasting." Which the Translator usually renders as "glory."
<margin>E</margin> <margin>29</margin> **In me**] *en emoi*, used in the ablative case.
<margin>30</margin> **I may hear of you**] *akouso ta peri hymon, hoti stekete*, that is, "that I may hear about you," or rather "those things which concern you, that you stand, etc."
<margin>31</margin> **Of one mind**] *mia psyche*, that is, "with one soul," namely in one spirit, in one soul.
<margin>F</margin> <margin>32</margin> **Collaborating**] *synathlountes*, that is, "striving together," which is to say, helping us in this struggle. Ambrose explains it thus: "striving equally with the faith of the Gospel." For "to collaborate" in the flesh might perhaps be approved in a poem, but "to concert" implies those who strive against each other. But here Paul felt that the faith was in danger and, as it were, engaged in a contest, which it will win if there are those who take up the same struggle alongside it. Although there is ambiguity in Ambrose's words too, for it can be taken as "striving with the faith of the Gospel," meaning striving against the faith, or striving by means of the faith of the Gospel. Therefore, we have translated it as "helping the struggling faith of the Gospel."
<margin>33</margin> **Be terrified**] *me ptyromenoi*, that is, "not troubled" or "not in a tumult." Ambrose reads "not trembling," which makes no difference to the sense.
<margin>34</margin> **Which is to them a cause**] The Greek is "to them indeed an *endeixis*," that is, a "showing" or "indication." And so Ambrose reads, "an ostentation of destruction." Yet the Translator did not change it incorrectly, since in Greek *endeixis* or *apodeixis* is also said of the one who does it. Thus also elsewhere in Paul: "he showed me many evils" instead of "he did many evils to me."
<margin>35</margin> **And now you heard**] *akouete*, that is, "you hear." Regarding "of me," the Greek is *en emoi*, meaning "in me." But I do not know if our reading is more true.

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL. CHAPTER II.

->**THE TEXT**<-

<margin>II. 1</margin> If there is therefore any encouragement in Christ, if any comfort of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any affection and mercy, 2 complete my joy: that you be of the same mind, having the same love, being in one accord, thinking the one thing. 3 Do nothing out of selfish ambition or conceit, 5 but in humility let each count others better than themselves. 7 Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others. 9 For let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus: 6 Who, being in the form of God, did not consider being equal to God something to be seized <note>original: "harpagmon"</note>, 10 but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men; and being found in fashion as a man, 8 He humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death.

->**THE COMMENTARY**<-

1 <gloss>If there is therefore any encouragement]</gloss> <term>paraklesis</term> <note>original Greek: "παράκλησις"</note>. Saint Ambrose reads it as *If there is any exhortation*, so as not to say <term>consolation</term> <note>original: "consolationem"</note> twice. Yet nothing prevents a teacher from using repetition for <term>emphasis</term> <note>original: "epifasin"</note>. For he feels the consolation which the Philippians owed to Paul, who was afflicted by so many evils. This entire duty tends toward this: that they might be in harmony among themselves because of all these things.

2 <gloss>If any bowels of mercy]</gloss> In Greek it is <term>if any bowels and mercies</term> <note>original Greek: "εἴ τινα σπλάγχνα καὶ οἰκτιρμοί"</note>. And so Ambrose reads it, supported by the preservation of the Latin manuscripts. For in that codex provided by the Library of St. Paul in London, a clear erasure testified that a conjunction had been deleted, and <term>mercies</term> <note>original: "miserationes"</note> was still written in the nominative case, with a letter marked out by a pen. An even clearer trace of the genuine reading remained in both the Constance manuscripts. Otherwise, in the Greek codices, I do not find <term>any bowels</term> <note>original: "tina splangchna"</note> written, but <term>if anyone is bowels</term> <note>original Greek: "εἴ τις σπλάγχνα"</note>, that is, *if anyone has the heart/bowels*. Since this is found in the corrected written copies, I wonder that none of the translators pointed out this reading. Unless perhaps he called the man himself "bowels" as one endowed with the affection of mercy, and Paul looked more at the reality than the specific word. Certainly Chrysostom and Theophylact read it as <term>if anyone is bowels</term>, yet it causes no difficulty; nor can the verb "has" be understood, because of the nominative case that follows immediately, <term>mercies</term> <note>original: "oiktirmoi"</note>.

3 <gloss>That you be of the same mind]</gloss> May you feel, <term>phronete</term> <note>original Greek: "φρονῆτε"</note>, that is, may you be in harmony.

4 <gloss>Thinking the same thing]</gloss> <term>to hen phronountes</term> <note>original Greek: "τὸ ἓν φρονοῦντες"</note>, that is, thinking one or the same thing. It is a participle of the same verb he just translated as "to be of a mind."

5 <gloss>Nothing through contention]</gloss> <term>kata eritheian</term> <note>original Greek: "κατὰ ἐρίθειαν"</note>. Ambrose reads this as *irritation*, that is, for the purpose of provoking others.

6 <gloss>In humility]</gloss> The Greek has it thus: *but in humility, considering one another superior to themselves*, <term>alla te tapeinophrosyne allelous hegoumenoi hyperechontas heauton</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ τῇ ταπεινοφροσύνῃ ἀλλήλους ἡγούμενοι ὑπερέχοντας ἑαυτῶν"</note>. And again, he calls humility "modesty of the soul," by which one claims nothing for oneself.

7 <gloss>Considering]</gloss> <term>skopeite</term> <note>original Greek: "σκοπεῖτε"</note>, that is, *consider or look at*. For we look at what we desire; hence the word <term>scopus</term> <note>meaning "goal" or "target"</note> is derived. Ambrose reads it as *contemplating*.

8 <gloss>The things of others]</gloss> The Greeks add <term>ekastos</term> <note>original Greek: "ἕκαστος"</note>, that is, *each*. They also add the conjunction <term>kai</term> <note>original: "and"</note>, in this manner: <term>but also the things of others</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ ἑτέρων"</note>. However, the translators do not touch upon this. Therefore, it has the force, I believe, as if you were to say, *nay: rather, even more the things of others*.

9 <gloss>For let this mind be in you]</gloss> <term>phroneistho</term> <note>original Greek: "φρονείσθω"</note>, that is, *let it be felt*, so that each one understands what just preceded, *or let it be sensed*. Although the Translator rightly rendered it "feel" <note>original: "sentite"</note>, that is: let that sense, that affection be in you which was in Christ Jesus. Or: Be so affected toward one another in turn as Christ was affected toward you.

10 <gloss>That he was equal to God]</gloss> <term>to einai isa Theo</term> <note>original Greek: "τὸ εἶναι ἴσα Θεῷ"</note>, that is, *to be on an equality with God*. For <term>isa</term> <note>original: "equal"</note> is a noun used in place of an adverb. For he speaks of Christ insofar as he was man. Nor is the article among the Greeks useless here, surely explaining what he had called "a robbery"—undoubtedly this very thing, *to be equal to God*. He did not snatch at equality with God for himself but cast himself down. Furthermore, "form" here is <term>morphe</term> <note>original Greek: "μορφή"</note>, which sounds like "outward appearance" or "figure," which in the Epistle to the Hebrews he calls the <term>character</term> <note>the exact representation</note>. As to whether "form" here is that which Aristotle discusses in his books on Natural Philosophy <note>the *Physics*</note>, which corresponds to "matter," let those who bring such disputations into this passage see to it—especially since Paul himself immediately adds, <term>taking the form of a servant</term>. Certainly, according to the opinion of Chrysostom, Christ is not called a servant, but a Son. Although Saint Jerome, in his commentary on Paul's Epistle to Titus, thinks that what is said in Isaiah chapter 49, "It is a great thing for you to be called my child," is said by the Father to the Son; and that <term>paida</term> <note>child/servant</note>, which the Seventy <note>the Septuagint</note> translated, is the Hebrew עבד <note>Hebrew: "ebed"</note>, which signifies nothing but "my servant." Saint Ambrose interprets "form" as a *specimen or example*, which, while walking about in a human body, nevertheless gave evidence of Divinity. "For the form of God," he says, "what is it but the example by which God appears, while he raises the dead, makes the deaf hear, and cleanses the lepers?" Now, that he took the *form of a servant* does not seem to refer properly to the assumed human nature, but to the appearance and likeness of a guilty man, whose persona he took for us while he was scourged, condemned, and crucified. "Servants," he says, "are made from sin, like Ham the son of Noah, who first deservedly received the name of servant." For it does not seem to me, as it does to some, that he took the "form of a servant" simply by being born a man. Furthermore, regarding what he says here, *he did not think it a robbery*, Ambrose, as if explaining, says: *He did not defend his equality for himself—that is, he did not claim it for himself—so that he might show us an example of humility, but he subjected himself, so that he might be exalted by the Father*. Indeed, for an example, Paul brought forward Christ here, who was spontaneously humbled and exalted by the Father's authority. Yet it is not lost on me that this passage is explained quite differently by almost all the Ancients regarding certain points; I do not wish to prejudice their opinion, but I bring forward for the reader's consideration what seemed necessary to add. I know that great authors, like Hilary

<column-break/>

<margin>1. 11</margin> and now you hear in me. If there is therefore any encouragement in Christ, <margin>1</margin> if any solace of love, if any fellowship of the spirit, <margin>2</margin> if any bowels and mercies, Complete my <margin>a</margin> joy, <margin>3</margin> that you be similarly affected, having the same charity, being of one mind, <margin>b</margin> thinking the same thing, <margin>4</margin> Let nothing be done through contention or through empty glory, <margin>5</margin> but through humility of mind let each count another more excellent than himself. Let not each of you <margin>7</margin> look to his own things, but each one <margin>4</margin> to <margin>8</margin> the things of others. <margin>9</margin> For let that affection be in you, <margin>5</margin> which was also in Christ Jesus: <margin>10</margin> Who, when he was in the form <margin>6</margin> of God, did not think it a robbery, <margin>10</margin> that he was equal to God, <margin>11</margin> But emptied himself, taking the <margin>7</margin> form of a servant, being established in the likeness of men, and found in figure as a man, <margin>12</margin> He showed himself humble, <margin>8</margin> made

<sig>B</sig>

and Augustine, to say nothing of others, interpret it thus: *He did not think it robbery that he was equal to God*, for what belonged to his nature could not be a matter of robbery. When he was in the form of God, that is, when he was truly God. And they hold this as the chief nail with which to strike the Arians <note>a heretical group that denied Christ's full divinity</note>, who want only the Father to be truly God. Yet, if we may speak the truth, what greatness does Paul attribute to Christ if, since he was God by nature, he simply understood that this was not robbery—that is, he merely knew himself? It is a known fact that no greater violence is done to the Holy Scriptures than when we distort everything to achieve victory while debating with heretics. Although I do not see what this passage specifically does against the Arians, who did not deny that the Son of God was God—nay, they even confessed him to be the Great God and God blessed above all things—but they thought that the Father was called God in some peculiar way in which the Son or the Holy Spirit was not. Paul is not acting here to define *what* Christ was, but *how he conducted himself*, namely, by giving us an example. He was God, and he was man. He hid the God and displayed the man all the way to the tomb; for other pious men have also been famous for miracles. And yet, if he showed any sparks of his divine nature in passing, he always referred them back to the Father as the author, claiming nothing for himself. Therefore, this whole passage seems to me to be rather violently distorted when applied to Christ's nature, whereas Paul is discussing the appearance he exhibited to us. With this understanding, what follows fits perfectly: *Because of which God exalted him*. What does "he humbled" mean? He showed the appearance of a servant and a despised man. What does "he exalted" mean? He declared the appearance of one who was raised up, though he was supreme of himself. Now, as for what a certain learned friend argued to me in his letters—that these words, *Who, being in the form of God, did not think that he was equal to God*, do not apply to Christ insofar as he is man, since according to that nature it truly would have been robbery if he had made himself equal to God—I believe this is spontaneously cleared up by this <margin>D</margin> interpretation: Christ could not have acted as a lowly man, a condemned man, unless he had been a man. Nor should anyone overwhelm me with the great names of authors; indeed, I would not have mentioned this unless I knew it had pleased writers of great name. Nevertheless, I would not deny that the Greek can be taken thus: *Who, although he had been in the form of God*, that is, who although he had been God from eternity, by no means thought it a robbery if he had conducted himself as God; yet having been made man, he did not display what he always was: he did not show off how great he was, but how humble he was, how mild, how obedient, showing us this way to reach the heights. Now, where it translates as "likeness," the Greek is <term>homoiomati</term> <note>original Greek: "ὁμοιώματι"</note>, which sounds more like *assimilation*; and where it says "habit" <note>or "fashion"</note>, they have <term>schemati</term> <note>original Greek: "σχήματι"</note>, which sounds more like *figure*. I thought these few things should be indicated so that it might appear that what Thomas <note>Aquinas</note> brings forward regarding "habit"—according to the custom of the Dialecticians <note>logicians</note>, which Aristotle calls <term>hexis</term> <note>original Greek: "ἕξις"</note>—does not quite fit Paul's meaning. The Latins also call this "habit," distinct from that which is called <term>diathesis</term> <note>disposition</note>. For a quality turned as <margin>E</margin> it were into nature is called <term>hexis</term> by the Greeks, from "having"; on the contrary, that which is easily removed is <term>diathesis</term>, which in Latin is called *possession*. He places these in the first type of quality, but he reviews <term>schema</term> <note>figure</note> and <term>morphe</term> <note>form</note> in the fourth type, and he reviews them as if there were either no difference or the very least difference between these two words. There is also a substantial form, which he calls <term>entelecheia</term> <note>actualization</note>, sometimes <term>eidos</term> <note>species/form</note>, and occasionally <term>morphe</term> <note>form</note>, although these last two are frequently used for the external appearance of the body. Nor did the Translator render it badly, for "habit" <note>original: "habitus"</note> among the Latins is sometimes referred to the appearance of the body, though not so among the Greeks. Furthermore, he said "found" <note>original: "inventus"</note> for "discovered," <term>heuretheis</term> <note>original Greek: "εὑρεθείς"</note>, surely by the most certain proofs. For in Latin, "found" is said of that which happens to be sought; thus it is also said, "she was found to be with child." And "as a man" can be taken to mean "as any other man," which he was not, even if he was truly man as far as the nature of man is concerned; or "in the appearance of a man," namely <margin>F</margin> displaying that which he was, as Theophylact indicates. Cyprian, citing this passage in his second book against the Jews, chapter thirteen, reads: *Who, when he was in the figure of God*. Chrysostom treats this passage more extensively, fighting from it against all heresies that have thought wrongly about Christ's divine nature. Although these Commentaries seem to me to be <unclear>bastard</unclear> <note>original Greek: "nothoi", meaning spurious or not actually by Chrysostom</note>. Whoever the author was, he surpasses Chrysostom's <term>wordiness</term> <note>original Greek: "polylalias"</note> but has not achieved his sharp insight.

11 <gloss>He emptied himself]</gloss> <term>ekenosen heauton</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐκένωσεν ἑαυτόν"</note>, that is, *he made himself void*. For Quintus Curtius, in his fourth book, used "to empty" <note>original: "exinanire"</note> for "to exhaust": *So that they might not be surrounded if they stood too close, nor yet empty out the center of the battle line*. Here <term>ekenose</term> seems to be said for "he made himself most humble and of no account," so that those who contend that Christ was diminished just a little bit from God, according to the human nature he assumed, achieve nothing. Certainly, one who is only a little bit less would not be called "emptied." Furthermore, how he might be said to be diminished or emptied is not the purpose of this work to pursue.

12 <gloss>He humbled himself]</gloss> There are those who think "to humble" <note>original: "humiliare"</note> is a poor Latin word. I certainly think it is desirable, even if it has not yet happened to be found in a suitable Author. In Latin, it could have been rendered as "submitted" or "cast down."

<summary>Erasmus provides a detailed philological and theological analysis of Philippians 2:1-12, focusing on the Greek terminology of Christ’s self-emptying (Kenosis). He argues that the passage is intended primarily as an ethical example of humility rather than a purely metaphysical proof against Arianism.</summary>

...became obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Wherefore also <margin>13</margin> God raised him up to the highest sublimity, and gave him a name, which is above every name, That in the name of Jesus <margin>14</margin> every knee should bow, of those in heaven, and those on earth, <margin>15</margin> and those below, And every tongue should confess that the Lord is Jesus Christ <margin>16</margin> to the glory of God the Father. Therefore my beloved, just as you have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, with fear and trembling <margin>17</margin> work out your own salvation. <margin>18</margin> For it is God who acts in you, both <margin>19</margin> that you may will and that you may perform, <margin>20</margin> according to the good purpose of the mind. Do all things <margin>21</margin> without grumblings <margin>22</margin> and disagreements, <margin>23</margin> so that no one can complain of you, <margin>24</margin> and sincerely, as <margin>25</margin> irreproachable children of God in the midst of a <margin>26</margin> wicked and crooked nation, <margin>27</margin> among whom shine as <margin>28</margin> lights in the world, sustaining the word of life, <margin>29</margin> so that I may boast <margin>30</margin> in the day of Christ, that I have not run in vain, nor labored in vain. Furthermore, if I am sacrificed <margin>31</margin> upon the victim and sacrifice of your faith, I rejoice and <margin>32</margin> rejoice with you all. For this same reason you also rejoice and <margin>33</margin> rejoice with me. But I hope in the Lord Jesus that I will send Timothy to you shortly, so that <margin>34</margin> I may be of a cheerful mind, <margin>35</margin> having learned of your state. For I have no one <margin>36</margin> endowed with a mind equal to my own, <margin>37</margin> who will sincerely care for your affairs. For all seek what is their own, not what is Christ Jesus's. Furthermore <margin>38</margin> you know his proof, <margin>39</margin> that as a son with me, as if with a father, he has served in the Gospel.
<meta>catchword: This</meta>

---

<margin>13 God exalted him]</margin> The Greek word <term>hyperypsose</term> <note>original: "ὑπερύψωσε"</note> explains more; it means he exalted him vehemently, or remarkably. Hence Ambrose reads it as *superexaltavit* <note>meaning "highly exalted" or "exalted above"</note>, striving to express the Greek voice.

<margin>14 Every knee should bow]</margin> <note>original Greek: "πᾶν γόνυ κάμψῃ"</note>, that is, every knee should bend, so that "itself" is understood. Matthew, or rather his translator, wrote in a similar form: *lest they should return to Herod* <note>original: "μὴ ἀνακάμψαι πρὸς Ἡρῴδην"</note>. And in Latin, we say *praecipitare* <note>to hurl headlong</note> instead of "to plunge oneself."

<margin>15 And those below]</margin> <term>katachthonion</term> <note>original: "καταχθονίων"</note>, that is, those who are underground.

<margin>16 in glory]</margin> <note>original: "εἰς δόξαν"</note>, that is, into glory: *that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father*, so that you understand that every tongue confesses this—that Jesus Christ is Lord, and that this is to the glory of God the Father. Although that phrase "into the glory of God the Father" can be referred back to the word "confess" which precedes it, meaning that all tongues confess to the glory of God.

<margin>17 your salvation]</margin> <note>original: "τὴν ἑαυτῶν"</note>, that is, of your own selves. Although, as I have warned, these compound pronouns are almost always used in place of simple ones.

<margin>18 Work out your salvation]</margin> And soon after, *For it is God who works in you*. The first verb is <term>katergazesthe</term> <note>original: "κατεργάζεσθε", meaning to achieve or work out</note>; the second is <term>energein</term> <note>original: "ἐνεργεῖν"</note>, which we have translated as "who acts," so that no one would err in this. And that phrase "in you" is <term>hymin</term> in some manuscripts, and <term>en hymin</term> in others. However, this makes no difference to the meaning.

<margin>19 And to perform]</margin> <note>original: "καὶ ἐνεργεῖν"</note>, that is, to do or to work. It is the infinitive of the participle that just preceded it, *the one working* <note>original: "ὁ ἐνεργῶν"</note>, that is, "he who works." Let no one think there is a new mystery in the word "perform," as if it meant "to lead to the end." Ambrose reads it as "to work."

<margin>20 For good will]</margin> <note>original: "ὑπὲρ τῆς εὐδοκίας"</note>. The speech is ambiguous; it can be understood as the good will of either God or the Philippians. Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Bulgarian archbishop and commentator</note> refers it to God; Ambrose refers it to men.

<margin>21 Without grumblings]</margin> Some Greek codices have "without anger" <note>original: "χωρὶς ὀργῆς"</note>. Others have "grumblings" <note>original: "γογγυσμῶν"</note>.

<margin>22 And hesitations]</margin> <note>original: "καὶ διαλογισμῶν"</note>, that is, disputations. He sometimes translates this as "thoughts." For a person who lacks confidence disputes and argues.

<margin>23 Without complaint]</margin> <term>amemptoi</term> <note>original: "ἄμεμπτοι"</note>, that is, those about whom no one can complain or find fault; otherwise "without complaint" refers to one who complains about no one.

<margin>24 And simple]</margin> <note>original: "καὶ ἀκέραιοι"</note>, that is, sincere, without pretense <note>literally "without dye" or "unmixed"</note>.

<margin>25 Without reproach]</margin> <note>original: "τέκνα Θεοῦ ἀμώμητα"</note>, that is, irreproachable children of God, or blameless, which is frequently translated as "immaculate."

<margin>26 Crooked]</margin> <term>skolias</term> <note>original: "σκολιᾶς"</note>. This does not simply mean "wicked" (that is, bad), as people commonly think, but "tortuous" and "rough," so that it corresponds to what he placed above, "simple" <note>original: "ἀκέραιοι"</note>. He explains this as if interpreting it, adding "and perverse" <note>original: "καὶ διεστραμμένης"</note>, meaning "distorted." Augustine, in his commentary on Psalm 146, reads "tortuous" instead of "wicked."

<margin>27 Among whom you shine]</margin> <term>phainesthe</term> <note>original: "φαίνεσθε"</note>. It is ambiguous whether this is the imperative mood ("Shine!") or the indicative ("You are shining"). Certainly, Cyprian <note>a 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage</note> reads it as "Shine!" in the imperative in his Letter to Rogatian the Priest. And Ambrose explains it this way, declaring that these things are not pronounced by Paul as happening, but are commanded to happen: "He warns them," he says, "that being mindful of their profession they should respond, so that they appear so bright among the dissenters—in life, conversation, and character—just as the sun and moon are sublime in splendor among the stars." Furthermore, *phainesthai* does not simply mean "to shine," but to be in plain sight so that it is apparent to all, like a light placed on a high point.

<margin>28 Lights]</margin> <term>phosteres</term> <note>original: "φωστήρες"</note>. Like a raised structure that is lifted high, sustaining a light. Whence he adds, "sustaining the word of life," that is, holding it at the summit.

<margin>29 To glory]</margin> <note>original: "εἰς καύχημα"</note>, about which we have already warned several times. And it is "to glory for me" <note>original: "εἰς καύχημα ἐμοὶ"</note>. And so Saint Ambrose reads it. It was clearer as: "so that I may be able to boast in the day of Christ, that

<column-break/>

I have not run in vain." For that "boasting" <note>original: "καύχημα"</note> is referred to here, so that he can boast in the presence of Christ, with them assisting this glory. Thus Theophylact surely has it.

30 <margin>In the day]</margin> <note>original: "εἰς ἡμέραν"</note>, that is, unto the day.

31 <margin>Upon the sacrifice]</margin> <note>original: "ἐπὶ τῇ θυσίᾳ καὶ λειτουργίᾳ τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν"</note>, that is, *upon the victim and sacrifice of your faith*. He feels that his own death and chains are a kind of sacrificial victim, of which he himself is the minister and sacrificer, immolating himself for their faith, and he rejoices in this name. Not that I deny that this can sometimes sound like an "addition" in Greek, but in my opinion, it does not fit Paul’s meaning here. For he makes, as it were, two victims: one is their faith, which he has offered to Christ, of which he makes himself the minister and <term>leitourgon</term> <note>a public servant or ritual minister</note>; the other is himself, if while he strives to duly present that victim to God, he himself is slaughtered and becomes a victim. Indeed, he does not refuse this, provided he achieves the goal of presenting them as worthy to God. Both Ambrose and the "Pseudo-Jerome" <note>an anonymous commentator once confused with St. Jerome</note> interpret in this sense, as does Theophylact in agreement. Some more recent scholars mistakenly use the word "heart" <note>original: "Laimi"</note> for what in Greek is "to serve" <note>original: "λατρεύειν"</note>, which Paul expressed in Greek words.

32 <margin>I congratulate]</margin> <term>synchairo</term> <note>original: "συγχαίρω"</note>, that is, I rejoice with.

33 <margin>Congratulate me]</margin> <term>synchairete</term> <note>original: "συγχαίρετε"</note>, that is, rejoice with me. It can be read in the indicative mood, "you rejoice and you rejoice with me," which indeed pleases me more.

34 <margin>That I may be of good heart]</margin> <term>eupsycho</term> <note>original: "εὐψυχῶ"</note>. In Greek, this is a compound word, and it means more "to be well-affected in soul" than "to be of good heart." Since they say "to be of heart" <note>original: "Laimi"</note> after being made more certain about you; according to that form by which we say "those from Plato" to mean Plato himself. Thus the Translator soon renders it "the things concerning you" <note>original: "τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν"</note>.

36 <margin>So like-minded]</margin> The "so" is redundant; it is just <term>isopsychon</term> <note>original: "ἰσόψυχον"</note>, that is, of an equal soul. Augustine did not add "so" when citing this passage in the second book against Petilian, chapter 76. But the Translator, offended by the sense, added "so," lest Paul should seem to praise Timothy while condemning the rest. It is a newly compounded Greek word, which signifies a mind equal and the same in all things, in the way Pythagoras used to signify the highest and perfect friendship. Paul did not have such a person at that time who would handle the Gospel with equal sincerity. But those who are offended by this passage ought to be more offended by the words that follow soon after: *All seek what is their own, not what is Jesus Christ's.*

37 <margin>who with sincere affection]</margin> <note>original: "ὅστις γνησίως"</note>, that is, who truly and naturally, as Augustine reads in Letter 137; or as he translates elsewhere, "ingenuously." *Let him be solicitous for you.* In Greek it is thus: <note>original: "τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν μεριμνήσει"</note>, that is, "he will care for your affairs," to render the meaning more than the words.

38 <margin>you know his [proof]]</margin> <term>ginoskete</term> <note>original: "γινώσκετε"</note>. The Greek word is indeed ambiguous <note>it can be a command "Know!" or a statement "You know"</note>, yet in this place it is more correctly translated as "you know," as the things that follow soon after declare: "because as a father etc." "You know," that is, you have heard, or "know from me." Theophylact reads "you know," explaining it as if Paul is citing the Philippians as witnesses to how much sincerity Timothy showed in the Gospel.

39 <margin>Because as to a father]</margin> It should have been translated: "because as a son with a father he served with me"; or "as a son to a father he served with me." Since the Greek has it thus: <note>original: "ὅτι ὡς πατρὶ τέκνον σὺν ἐμοὶ ἐδούλευσεν"</note>. Paul served the Gospel, seeking nothing for his own advantage, and Timothy gave himself as a companion to him, moved by an equal sincerity.

40 <margin>And I hope to send]</margin> Why not rather "that I will send." For infinitives are sometimes used this way.

# THE LETTER OF PAUL, CHAPTER III.

41. **What concerns me** ] The Greeks add "having seen" <term>idonti</term>, that is, "forthwith" or "immediately," which the Translator here seems to have earned. But that "soon" should rather be referred to the verb "to send."

42. **I will come to you** ] "To you" is redundant. Rather, in Greek, it is "that I myself will also come quickly." And this is how Ambrose reads it.

43. **And he was sorrowful** ] <term>kai adēmonōn</term> <note>distressed or troubled</note>. Ambrose translates this as "and he was with impatient anxiety." For "to be distressed" <note>Greek: adēmonein</note> is to be faint-hearted and fail because of grief.

44. **Even unto death** ] <term>paraplēsion thanatō</term>, that is, "very near to death," or "so as to be a neighbor to death." Ambrose reads, "near death."

45. **More hurriedly** ] <term>Spoudaioterōs</term>. It could also be translated as "more zealously." Ambrose reads "more solicitously," even if "solicitously" is a corrupted reading; however, I do not dislike what the Translator has provided.

46. **That I may be without sadness** ] <term>alypoteros ō</term>. Ambrose translates, "that I may be of better mind." The Greek word sounds as if you were to say, "that I might be freer from all pain," or "that I might grieve less."

47. **Hold in honor** ] <term>entimous echete</term>, that is, "hold in value."

48. **Handing over his life** ] <term>parabouleusamenos</term>. Ambrose expressed the Greek word more closely: "handing over his life unto destruction." To "take bad counsel" <note>Greek: parabouleuesthai</note> is to take poor advice and have no regard for oneself—not, as some think, to hand over willingly and deliberately. For Paul feels that the man was saved by divine help; otherwise, he would have cast himself headlong into the destruction of his life.

49. **What was lacking from you** ] <term>to hymōn hysterēma</term>, that is, "your deficiency." **Toward my service**, <term>tēs pros me leitourgias</term>. Ambrose reads, "regarding my duty." Although this does not explain what the Greek words mean, the sense is this: so that what was diminished in your service toward me, you might supply through those whom I send to you, and what you did less for me, you might compensate in such men. But some manuscripts have "he might fulfill" <note>Greek: plērōsē</note>, not "you might fulfill" <note>Greek: plērōsēte</note>, so that the verb refers to Epaphroditus, not to the Philippians. Then the meaning would be that *he* might supply what was diminished in your duty toward me. Although Ambrose reads "that he might supply," that which Paul had delivered less clearly. Although the Ambrosian speech is obscure. For he speaks thus: "that he might supply what was lacking to the people in the tradition according to the tradition of the Apostle." Theophylact, while reading the same as Ambrose, interprets it differently: namely, that since the Philippians were not at Rome, Epaphroditus brought their generosity to him, and in this way filled up what the separation of places seemed to have taken away from their duty toward Paul. Chrysostom interprets in the same way. It is not to be doubted that Theophylact read the same as Chrysostom, but the Translator, in his usual way, forced in the common Latin reading, "regarding my duty," which I do not think belongs to the Translator, but to a corrupter. For while in Latin it might be called "the service or duty or ministry of him to whom it is paid," the Greek, which does not vary—"the service toward me"—declares nothing else than "duty regarding me, or rather toward me." From this it is clear that in Ambrose it is read corruptly as "regarding my duty," and in the Vulgate Edition as "toward my service," instead of "duty regarding me" and "service toward me." It is a wonder, however, how that word "my" took over all the Latin manuscripts. Chrysostom noted that Paul called the Philippians' generosity a "service" <note>Greek: leitourgian</note> so that they would not be too pleased with themselves. And it is not "near," but "to fill up by addition" <note>Greek: anaplērōsōsin</note>, which is to fulfill by adding what was lacking to a perfect fullness.

<margin>D</margin> 1. **Finally** ] <term>To loipon</term>, that is, "As for what remains." And "rejoice" <note>Greek: chairete</note> can be read as "farewell."

2. **Indeed not troublesome to me** ] <term>emoi men ouk oknēron</term>, <term>hymin de to asphales</term>. Word for word it could be rendered, "to me indeed not sluggish, but to you safe." But it would be more lucid and more Latin to say, "it does not trouble me, and for you it is safe." The sense is: I do not grudge this labor of repeating the same things often, so that frequent admonition may make you safer, lest you slip. For from this

my affairs. But I trust in the Lord that 24.
I myself will come **shortly** 42. But I thought it worthwhile 25.

**eighth** 

---

the word "safe" <note>Greek: asphales</note> is properly used. This speech of the Apostle aims at ensuring the Philippians are not offended by so many repeated warnings. Someone could say, "Do you have so much leisure, Paul, that you have time to warn us so often?" "The love," he says, "with which I embrace you, makes it so that I feel no weariness in this matter." Again, someone could say, "Do you think us so forgetful that we must be warned so many times?" He responds: even if my warning were not necessary for you, yet no disadvantage comes to you from it; rather, it provides cautions against the snares of evil men. This diligence of mine makes you safer. At least my persistence brings you this fruit. And for this reason, he added the article, "but for you **the** safety," that is, "yours is the security." Even though the Roman language does not have a word that properly expresses "safety" <note>Greek: asphaleian</note>. It is a wonder why Ambrose reads with us, "for your... necessary." For he also interprets it thus, unless the Greeks call "safe" that which cannot be avoided.

<margin>D</margin> 3. **See the mutilation** ] He distinguished "mutilation" from "circumcision"—<term>katatomēn</term>, <term>peritomēn</term>. For that which is torn apart and completely distracted is "mutilated" <note>cut down</note>. That which is polished, with the superfluous parts rejected, is "circumcised." Saint Jerome noted this in his *Commentaries on Micah*. Furthermore, the article prefixed to each of these names indicates that he is speaking of certain specific people whom they know: "the dogs," "the evil ones," "the mutilation." And he used "see" for "beware," just as several times in the Gospel they use "behold" <note>Greek: horate</note> or "look out" <note>Greek: blepete</note>. For Ambrose cited this passage in his book to the devoted virgin as: "Avoid the dogs, avoid the evil workers."

4. **Who serve God in spirit** ] In Greek it is: "who serve by the Spirit of God," <term>hoi pneumati Theou latreuontes</term>. Furthermore, he said "we serve" for the fact that we "worship with religion." And yet in some manuscripts it was held as "serving God" <note>Greek: Theō latreuontes</note>, that is, "we serve God." Ambrose indicates in his second book on the Holy Spirit, chapter 6, that this passage in the Latin manuscripts <margin>E</margin> was varied by the treachery of falsifiers, and that for this reason one must stand by the authority of the Greek copies, in which it was held: "who serve by the Spirit of God." And from this he concludes that the Spirit is also God, to whom worship is due; which, however, does not necessarily follow from the Greek words. Since the dative "spirit" <note>Greek: pneumati</note> can indicate the *manner*, so that the verb "to serve" is placed absolutely: "we are religious." In what way? Not in the flesh, but in the spirit. Or "to God" is understood: "we serve God, by the spirit of God." And indeed the Greek commentaries explain it in this sense, and even Chrysostom himself, interpreting "in spirit" as "spiritually." Theophylact: "serving spiritually; and through these," that is, "spiritually" <note>Theophylact</note> "and worshipping God with the mind, not with bodily ceremonies," in the manner of the Jews, who amputated the member while having an impure mind. Furthermore, that "spirit" is taken here not for the Holy Spirit is argued also by the fact that the article is not placed before "spirit." Augustine indicates a triple reading of this passage in his third book to Boniface, chapter 7. <margin>F</margin> Again in his first book on the Trinity, chapter 6. Whether you read "God" or "of God," the words do not force us to confess from here that the Holy Spirit is God. For either reading has an ambiguous sense, but besides the omitted article, which we have mentioned, the very tenor of the speech cries out against Ambrose: for the Apostle is not dealing with the divine Persons, but with circumcision—that is, spiritual and carnal Judaism—of which the Lord speaks: "Those who worship the Father, worship him in spirit."

5. **Having confidence in the flesh** ] The Greek has, "and in the flesh," <term>kai en sarki</term>. And this is how Ambrose reads it. And indeed the word "having trusted" <note>Greek: pepoithōs</note> is a verb of the past tense, but we misuse those for verbs of the present tense. Wherefore both Ambrose and the Translator rightly read, "I may have confidence," and "to have confidence."

6. **Circumcised on the eighth day** ] The Greek has it thus: <term>peritomē oktaēmeros</term>, that is, "a circumcision of the eighth day." He calls himself "circumcised," just as he often calls other nations "the uncircumcision" <note>literally: the foreskin</note>. In the Ambrosian manuscripts, writers who were not very attentive had corrupted this place, reading "the circumcision of the eighth day."

Here, he continues that list before explaining why he has abandoned those advantages for the sake of Christ.</meta>

# TO THE PHILIPPIANS. CHAPTER III.

<margin>5</margin> ...circumcised on the eighth day, of the race of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; according to the law, a Pharisee; <margin>6</margin> according to zeal, persecuting the Church; according to the righteousness which is in the law, having become blameless. <margin>7</margin> But what things were gain to me, these I have counted as loss for the sake of Christ. <margin>8</margin> More than that, I even count all things as loss because of the surpassing excellence of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord, for whose sake I have suffered the loss of all things, and count them as refuse <note>original: "skubala"</note>, so that I may gain Christ, <margin>9</margin> and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God based on faith, <margin>10</margin> to know him and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being conformed to his death, <margin>11</margin> if somehow I may attain to the resurrection from the dead. <margin>12</margin> Not that I have already obtained it, or am already perfected; but I press on, if I might also lay hold of that for which I was also laid hold of by Christ Jesus. <margin>13</margin> Brothers, I do not yet consider myself to have laid hold of it; but one thing I do: forgetting the things that are behind and reaching forward to the things that are ahead, <margin>14</margin> I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus. <margin>15</margin> Therefore, let those of us who are mature think this way; and if you think otherwise in anything, God will reveal this also to you. <margin>16</margin> Nevertheless, to the point we have reached, let us walk by the same rule.

---

7 **Of the race of Israel**] <note>original: "en genous Israēl"</note>. *Israel* here can be a nominative case, not a genitive. For just as he just now called himself "the circumcision" in place of "a Jew," so here he names himself "Israel" in place of "an Israelite." In the same way, "Israel" is frequently used elsewhere to mean the Israelites. However, he added *from the race* to distinguish himself from proselytes <note>converts to Judaism</note>, who were indeed Israelites by adoption, but not by biological race.
8 **Having become blameless**] <note>original: "genomenos amemptos"</note>, that is, I became or was the kind of person about whom no one could complain. Though the Translator <note>referring to the Vulgate</note> renders this not badly as "conversing without complaint."
9 **Losses**] <note>original: "zēmian"</note>, that is, detriment or damage.
10 **Because of the eminent knowledge**] <note>original: "dia to hyperechon tēs gnōseōs"</note>, that is, because of the eminence of the cognition, where the neuter participle is used in place of a substantive noun.
11 **As refuse**] <note>original: "kai hēgoumai skubala einai"</note>, that is, I judge them to be dung, or I regard them as filth. To the Greeks, *skubalon* refers to that which is cast out from the intestines of animals to the dogs, derived from the phrase "to be thrown to the dogs" <note>original: "apo tou tois kusi ballesthai"</note>. Although Saint Ambrose, in his eighth sermon on Psalm 118, reads it as *I am esteemed as refuse*, as if Paul suffered himself to be held as nothing so that he might gain Christ. However, the same author interprets it differently—and in my opinion more correctly—in the Commentaries he wrote on this Epistle. This is especially supported by the Greek, according to which Paul utterly neglects the Law, which was once held in great veneration, as being useless compared to the Gospel of Christ, even though he was born into it. Chrysostom brings this passage to this same meaning in his 35th Homily on the Advent. Likewise, Augustine does so in the third book against Boniface, chapter seven; though he explains it differently when writing to Jerome regarding Peter being rebuked by Paul (at a time, I believe, before he was a Bishop). Yet I am not sure whether that phrase, "I have suffered the loss of all things" <note>original: "ta panta ezēmiōthēn"</note>, should have been translated as *I have been affected by all detriments*. Ambrose translates it, *I have led all things as loss*, and Augustine agrees with him. Theophylact interprets it in this sense, so that we understand "I have suffered loss" in the same way we speak of sharing in "Communion" or "piety." Chrysostom’s commentary does not shrink from this sense either. Yet the same Ambrose, explaining the Psalm *Blessed are the undefiled*, in his eighth sermon, translates it differently: *for whose sake I have suffered the loss of all things*, somewhat disagreeing with himself.
12 **Is from faith**] <note>original: "dia pisteōs"</note>, that is, through faith.
13 **Which is from God**] He adds *righteousness* <note>original: "tēn ek Theou dikaiosunēn"</note>, so that the word "righteousness" is repeated. For this is how Ambrose reads it: *Righteousness, I say, which consists of faith, not the works of the Law.* Also, *in faith to know him.* The Greeks punctuate it this way so that you understand he is known through faith.
14 **The fellowship of his suffering**] <note>original: "pathēmatōn"</note>, that is, of sufferings, or evils, or afflictions. Ambrose reads "communication" instead of "fellowship."
15 **If by any means**] <note>original: "Eipōs"</note>, if in any way.
16 **Which is from the dead**] <note>original: "tōn nekrōn"</note>, that is, of the dead. I wonder why he chose a paraphrase here, unless I suspect that this translator, and likewise Ambrose, read it as *the resurrection of the dead*.
17 **But I follow**] <note>original: "diōkō"</note>, that is, I pursue, and I desire to attain. The Translator used the word *sequor* (follow) in a very Latin sense; therefore, I have given warning lest anyone should err. For while it is common to "follow" someone who precedes us, or to "follow" what we imitate, it is rarer to "follow" that which we simply desire to reach.
18 **If in any way**] <note>original: "ei kai katalabō"</note>, that is, if it might be that I take hold. The Translator seems to have read it as "even as."
19 **In which also I was apprehended**] <note>original: "eph' hō"</note>, that is, in that which. In this context, "in which" and "because of which" produce the same meaning. Therefore, the sense seems to me to be: If in any way I may attain that for which Christ chose me and ordered me to compete in this stadium.
20 **I do not judge**] The Laurentian manuscript had *nondum* <note>original: "oupō"</note>, that is, "not yet"; my own and several others have *not yet*. And Saint Ambrose reads it this way.
21 **But one thing**] <note>original: "hen de"</note>, the word "I do" <note>original: "ago"</note> must be understood, as if he were saying, "I do this thing alone, and I am entirely in this." This is how Augustine interprets it in the third book to Boniface, chapter seven. However, it is simpler to see "one thing" used here to mean "only."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>5</margin> On the eighth day, of the race of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, according to the law a Pharisee, <margin>6</margin> According to zeal persecuting the Church, according to the righteousness which is in the law, made blameless. <margin>7</margin> But the things that were gains to me, those I have considered loss for Christ's sake. <margin>8</margin> Furthermore, I consider all things to be loss because of the excellence of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord, for whose sake I have led all things as losses, and I hold them as refuse, so that I may gain Christ, <margin>B</margin> <margin>9</margin> and so that I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, which is from God, a righteousness based on faith, <margin>10</margin> so that I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his afflictions, while I am made conformable to his death, <margin>11</margin> if by any means I may reach the resurrection of the <margin>12</margin> dead. <margin>13</margin> Not that I have already apprehended, or am already perfect, but I pursue, if it might be that I take hold, in that for which I have also been taken hold of by Christ Jesus. Brothers, I <margin>13</margin> do not yet judge myself to have attained: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and stretching forward to those things which are in front, <margin>14</margin> <margin>C</margin> I follow toward the established mark for the palm <note>the prize leaf</note> of the heavenly <margin>14</margin> calling of God through Christ Jesus. Therefore, as many of us <margin>15</margin> as are perfect, let us feel this way: and if you feel otherwise in anything, God will reveal this also to you. Nevertheless, <margin>16</margin> toward that which we have attained, let us proceed by the same rule.

---

<margin>D</margin> 22 **Those things which are behind**] <note>original: "ta opisō"</note>, that is, the things at one's back, which is to say, things that are past and left behind. For he takes a metaphor from runners, who do not pay attention to nor look back at the distance they have already crossed, but at what remains. Augustine, explaining Psalm 38, interprets *the things that are behind* as the former life stained by vices; whereas in my opinion, Paul is speaking about the degrees of piety, where lower stages are passed over as one strives toward the more difficult heights of perfection. For he also showed the Corinthians a more excellent life toward which they should progress, neglecting the lesser gifts of the virtues.
23 **The things prior**] <note>original: "tois de emprosthen"</note>, that is, the things which are in front.
24 **Toward the mark**] <note>original: "Kata skopon"</note>, that is, according to the goal, or the target set before one. The Translator did not render this so much badly as obscurely. Jerome advises that the Greek word is more significant. For *skopos* is properly the target set up for archers. Hence, whatever we intend and set before our minds is a "scope" or goal. Augustine, in many places as well as on Psalm 38, reads it as *according to the intention* for *kata skopon*. Cyprian, in *On the Life of Clerics* (if indeed that work should be seen as his), reads *I follow according to the rule*. Tertullian, in his book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, reads *I follow toward the palm according to the goal*.
25 **Let us think this**] Jerome, in the first dialogue against Pelagius, indicates that the Greek manuscripts varied in this place: in some was written *we think* <note>original: "phronoumen"</note> in the indicative mood, in others *let us think* <note>original: "phronōmen"</note> in the subjunctive.
<margin>E</margin> 26 **You think otherwise**] <note>original: "phroneite"</note>, that is, you feel or judge. And "he will reveal" <note>original: "apokalupsei"</note> ought to be in the future tense; but the ancient Latin manuscripts cry out against this, as does Ambrose himself, who not only reads it otherwise but also interprets it so; likewise Augustine in several places, including the second book against Cresconius, chapter 31. Again in Epistle 48, unless there is an error in the writing. For in his 15th Sermon on the Words of the Apostle, it is found written as *he will reveal*. Again in the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 1. For I think "otherwise" is said for that which is somewhat different than it ought to be. Therefore, if the correct reading is *he has revealed* <note>original: "apokalupse"</note>, I suspect it was written by Paul as such. Either sense is tolerable. Indeed, I think Paul is speaking of Jews converted to the Religion of Christ, who were not yet able to give up the observation of their ancestral law. Paul, however, has just taught that righteousness consists of faith. But nevertheless, he says, if anyone among you has felt differently and attributed something to the Law, there is no reason for that to break the concord which is peculiar to Christians; rather, let each person interpret it thus: "What does it matter to me if God has revealed this to him? I shall nonetheless follow what my conscience dictates to me." Another sense here is: if anyone has felt differently, that is, attributed something to the Law, let him be borne with until he makes progress. For it will happen perhaps that God will breathe this perfection into him as well, so that eventually <margin>F</margin> he may despise those things which he cannot yet despise. Although it is not hidden from me that Ambrose interprets this differently. Theophylact offers this sense: If you feel anything otherwise about seeking victory, you do not feel rightly; but nevertheless, God will change that mind of yours for the better. Chrysostom interprets it to mean that God will inspire someone if they have not yet attained something; he does not want this said regarding the dogmas of faith, but regarding the perfection of life. Hilary, in the eleventh book on the Trinity, reads *he will reveal* in the future tense, and interprets it to mean that for those who have not yet attained the absolute truth, the revelation of God must be expected, who grants the full knowledge of the truth and corrects whatever was previously erred.
27 **Nevertheless**] The Greek is slightly different, namely in this manner: *Nevertheless, in that to which we have reached, to walk in the same rule, to think the same thing.* <note>original: "Plēn eis ho ephthasamen, tō autō stoichein, ta auta phronein"</note>. Although these infinitives seem to be put in place of imperatives. Hilary, in the eleventh book on the Trinity, translates it in this manner: *Truly, in that which we have hastened, let us enter into the same.* He seems to have understood the Greek speech very little.

# THE LETTER OF PAUL. CHAPTERS III–IV.

<note>The following is the Greek source text of the New Testament provided by the author for analysis.</note>

17 Join in imitating me, brothers, and keep your eyes on those who walk according to the 18 example you have in us. For many walk, of whom I have often told you, and now tell you even with weeping, as enemies of the cross of Christ. 19 Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame, those who set 20 their minds on earthly things. For our citizenship <note>original: "politeuma"</note> exists in the heavens, from which also we 21 await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform <margin>Alternative: "generation."</margin> our humble body, to become conformed to his glorious body, according to the working of his power to subject all things to himself.

<margin>IV. 1</margin> Therefore, my brothers, beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, stand firm in the Lord in this way, beloved. 2 I urge Euodia and I urge Syntyche to think the same way in the Lord. 3 Yes, I ask you also, true yoke-fellow <note>original: "syzyge gnēsie"</note>, help these women, who have struggled together with me in the Gospel, along with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life. 4 Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice. 5 Let your gentleness <note>original: "to epieikes"</note> be known to all people; the Lord is near. 6 Be anxious for nothing, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. 7 And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus. 8 Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are...

---

<margin>28 Join in imitating me ]</margin> <note>original: "Symmimētai mou"</note>, that is, *Be my joint-imitators*. Either this means: "Imitate me together with the others who imitate me." Or: "Let there be agreement among you, even if there is disagreement in other things, so that you are imitators of me." Accordingly, we have translated it as: *Be likewise imitators of me*. Ambrose <note>A 4th-century Church Father and commentator.</note> gives no indication of this "joint" prefix.

<margin>29 And observe ]</margin> <note>original: "kai skopeite"</note>, that is, *and consider*. And this is how Ambrose reads it.

<margin>30 Our form ]</margin> <note>original: "typon hēmas"</note>, that is, *us as a model*, spoken as a direct comparison.

<margin>31 Of whom I often told you ]</margin> It appears Paul did not finish the sentence he began. "For many walk,"—one must understand—"not as I do, but in the flesh and in pride and ceremonies, and for that reason they are enemies of the cross."

<margin>32 They mind earthly things ]</margin> <note>original: "Phronountes"</note>, they *care for*, or *feel*, meaning those who have earthly affections. He used a participle in place of a verb.

<margin>33 Our indeed ]</margin> *For our*.

<margin>34 From whence ]</margin> <note>original: "ex hou"</note>, that is, *from which place, namely heaven*. It does not matter that "heavens" <note>original: "ouranois"</note> preceded it in the plural; the "place" is understood, just as "time" is often understood when time, not place, is signified. However, time could be understood here, so that we understand "from that time" in which we began to hope for heavenly life with Christ, we belong to the heavenly city, not the earthly one.

<margin>35 Body of humility ]</margin> <note>original: "to sōma tēs tapeinōseōs"</note>, that is, the *humble* and *lowly body*. He spoke according to the characteristic of Hebrew speech.

<margin>36 Conformed to the body ]</margin> The Greek reads thus: <note>original: "eis to genesthai auto symmorphon tō sōmati"</note>, that is, *so that it may become conformed to the body, etc.*

<margin>37 According to the operation of power ]</margin> And this is read in the Greek in this manner: <note>original: "kata tēn energeian tou dynasthai auton kai hypotaxai heautō ta panta"</note>, that is, *according to the working, or force, or efficacy, so that he is able even to subject all things to himself*. Ambrose reads, *by which he is able even to subject all things to himself*. The Donatian Codex had, *according to the working, by which he is also able*.

<margin>C</margin> <margin>1 Dearly beloved and longed for ]</margin> <note>original: "agapētoi kai epipothētoi"</note>, that is, *beloved and desired*, or *lovable and desirable*.

<margin>2 And Syntyche I beseech ]</margin> To "ask" and to "beseech" are the same word in Greek. Therefore, the translator inopportunely sought variety in this passage, since the repetition <note>term: "anadiplosis" (the repetition of a word for emphasis)</note> of that word serves to signify the vehemence of the emotion.

<margin>3 That they mind the same thing ]</margin> <note>original: "to auto phronein"</note>, that is, *to feel the same*, which means to be in harmony. Though Ambrose interprets this as examining one's prudence.

<margin>4 Indeed ]</margin> Here a word of affirmation: <note>original: "nai"</note>. And "I ask" <note>original: "erōtō"</note>, which means *I interrogate*, he placed here for *I pray*. Unless perhaps "to ask" is ambiguous among the Greeks, just as *rogo* is among the Latins.

<margin>5 True yoke-fellow ]</margin> <note>original: "syzyge gnēsie"</note>. They are called "yoke-fellows" as if they are leading a yoke together. He translates "True" here as what he had translated earlier as "sincere affection," from the word <note>original: "gnēsios"</note>. Some refer this to Paul's wife. For the Greek can be taken in the feminine gender: <note>original: "syzyge gnēsie"</note>, that is, "true wife" or "sincere spouse." There are great authors among the Greeks who think Paul had a wife. And it is consistent here that women are commended to women. Furthermore, what he adds—"true" or "genuine"—beautifully fits her who herself would embrace Christ together with her husband. For when there is consensus, not only in living together but also in the profession of faith, in the pursuit of piety, and in the similarity of life, then finally it is a true marriage. Otherwise, it is called an unequal marriage whenever people are held in the yoke of matrimony by different religions. Saint Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, 2nd-century theologian.</note>, in the third book of *Ecclesiastical History* as reported by Eusebius, cites this passage to show that Paul had a wife, whom he nevertheless did not lead around with him (following Peter’s example) so that he might be more unhindered for the work of the Gospel. Indeed, he also writes that Philip had a wife and that the Apostles gave their daughters in marriage, so far...

<meta>catchword: as</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...as it was from them to condemn marriage. The holy martyr Ignatius, in his *Letter to the Philadelphians*, frankly confesses that not only Peter and Paul, but also the other Apostles had wives, and were not held in less esteem by him for it, since the Patriarchs and Prophets lived in marriage, not for the sake of lust but for the sake of offspring. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> admits there were those who thought Paul was calling his wife here, but he disagrees, nor does he give a reason why he disagrees. But to whom is it more reasonable to yield: to Clement and Ignatius, of whom the former was a companion of Peter and the latter a disciple of Mark the Evangelist, or to Chrysostom, who was separated from the times of the Apostles by such a great interval? Theophylactus, however, sharply argues against us attributing a wife to Paul, as if there were some danger in this. Lest that happen, he prefers that this person was either a brother or husband to one of the women, or perhaps the prison guard. Yet he admits there were those who thought Paul wrote this to his wife, whom he refutes with no other argument than a single word, which Paul placed in the masculine gender, whereas it would likely be feminine if he were speaking of a wife. He is thinking, I believe, of the word "true" <note>original: "gnēsie"</note>. For as for "yoke-fellow" <note>original: "syzyge"</note>, everyone knows it is of common gender <note>note: can be used for male or female</note>. But those who thought it was said of a wife were, unless I am mistaken, Greeks, whom nothing offended that offended Theophylactus; they surely understood that in words of this kind, according to Attic custom, the masculine gender is frequently used for the feminine. Just as Homer said "famous" <note>original: "klytos"</note> for a woman, and Euripides used "noble" <note>original: "gennaios"</note> for a female. Finally, since Theophylactus, in his commentary on Titus Chapter 2, reads "saving" <note>original: "sōtērios" (masculine)</note> instead of "saving" <note>original: "sōtēria" (feminine)</note> and interprets it accordingly, I wonder why he was offended here by "true" <note>original: "gnēsios"</note>. Therefore, while I do not think this opinion is absurd, I confess the other can also stand. He only shows that he joins a man or companion to the women, contrary to his usual custom. Then, whoever that prison guard might be, whom Paul would deign with such honor as to call him a "true yoke-fellow" and prefer the women to him? Paul was accustomed to calling sharers in the Gospel labor "fellow workers" <note>original: "synergous"</note>; "yoke-fellow" <note>original: "syzygon"</note> more properly fits a pair of people whom the same yoke joins, from which the Latins also derived the word for "marriage" <note>original: "conjugium"</note>. Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a medieval commentator.</note> suggests that "Germanus" is a proper name, as if to add nothing of his own, which he seems to have drawn from the Commentaries that circulate under the false title of Jerome on all the Epistles of Paul. Furthermore, since this Epistle was written to all the holy bishops and deacons with no specific name expressed, I do not see who could be understood here.

<margin>6 Help those women ]</margin> <note>original: "syllambanou autais"</note>, *assist them*, and lend a hand.

<margin>7 They labored with me ]</margin> <note>original: "synēthlēsan moi"</note>, that is, *they struggled together with me*.

<margin>8 Rejoice in the Lord ]</margin> <note>original: "Chairete"</note>. It can also mean *Farewell*.

<margin>9 Gentleness ]</margin> <note>original: "epieikes"</note>, that is, *humanity, or equity*. Ambrose explains it as *reasonable conversation*, when one does not contend for the utmost letter of the law, but one yields to another as the time requires, following what humanity demands.

<margin>10 For the Lord ]</margin> "For" is redundant, and is not added in Ambrose's text.

<margin>11 But in every ]</margin> "Every" is not an adjective for "prayer," <note>original: "en panti"</note>, that is, *in every thing*, or *in all things*.

<margin>12 Every sense ]</margin> <note>original: "noun"</note>, that is, *mind, or intellect*, lest anyone twist it toward the physical senses. Certainly Ambrose reads *mind*, explaining this Epistle, and cites it thus in his sixth chapter of the book *On Jacob and the Happy Life*.

<margin>13 Shall guard ]</margin> <note>original: "phrourēsei"</note>, that is, *will guard*, in the future tense. For he is not wishing this for them, but encouraging them with this confidence. You may gather that Ambrose read it this way from his own interpretation, if you weigh it carefully.

<margin>14 For the rest, brothers ]</margin> <note>original: "To loipon"</note>, that is, *What remains*. It is the word of one continuing after some digression.

<margin>15 Whatever things are modest ]</margin> <note>original: "semna"</note>. Which Ambrose reads as *magnificent*. He could have translated it as *grave, severe, honest, or reverent*. For the Greek word "semna" signifies all these things.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed philological analysis of the fourth chapter of Paul’s Letter to the Philippians. Having previously discussed Paul’s appeal for unity, Erasmus now turns to the famous "whatever is true" passage (Phil 4:8) and Paul’s gratitude for the financial support sent by the Philippians through Epaphroditus. Erasmus continues to weigh the Greek original against the Latin Vulgate and the interpretations of Church Fathers.</meta>

### TO THE PHILIPPIANS. CHAPTER IV.
