Nevertheless, you have done well, sharing in my affliction. <margin>15</margin> And you yourselves know ^15, Philippians, that in the beginning of the Gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church shared with me in the matter of giving and receiving, except you only. <margin>16</margin> For even in Thessalonica ^30, you sent once and twice ^31 for my need ^32. <margin>17</margin> Not that ^33 I seek the gift, but I seek ^34 the fruit that increases ^35 to your account. <margin>18</margin> I have received ^36 all, and I abound: I am filled, having received ^37 from Epaphroditus the things from you, an odor of sweetness ^38, a sacrifice acceptable and well-pleasing to God. <margin>19</margin> And my God shall supply your every need ^39 according to his riches, in glory, in Christ

->Jesus.<-

***

16 **Whatever is holy**] <note>original: "hagna"</note>, that is, pure, or chaste.

17 **Lovely**] <note>original: "prosphilē"</note>. This is what Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> used in his work against Jovinian, referring to things pertaining to chastity, but he was twisting it, I believe, to fit his own argument. Unless perhaps he rendered *ad castitatem pertinentia* (pertaining to chastity) for *hagna* (pure), but it is more probable that this error belongs to the scribes. For since it was permissible to say "whatever is chaste," what need was there for the long-winded phrasing that was necessary for "lovely"? Indeed, unless we take "modest" to mean "shamefast," he would be repeating the same idea of chastity twice, in both *semna* (venerable) and *hagna* (pure); thus I suspect this passage in Jerome is not free from error: perhaps he had written "whatever is chaste, whatever pertains to friendship."

18 **Of good fame**] <note>original: "euphēma"</note>, that is, well-spoken of, or of good omen. Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), Bishop of Milan.</note> translates this as "praiseworthy." Jerome rendered this whole passage as follows: "Whatever things therefore are true, whatever things are modest, whatever things are just, whatever things pertain to chastity," etc.

<margin>D</margin> 19 **If there be any praise of discipline**] The word "discipline" is redundant according to the Greek codices. Nor does it appear from Ambrose's commentaries that he read it differently than the Greeks. And "virtue" here is <note>original: "aretē"</note>, which is the opposite of vice, not <note>original: "dynamis"</note>, which is the opposite of weakness.

20 **Think on these things and do them**] "Think on" is extra; in the Greek it is only <note>original: "tauta prassete"</note>, that is, "do these things." And this is how Ambrose read it. A certain person <note>Likely referring to one of Erasmus's many theological critics, such as Edward Lee or Diego López de Zúñiga.</note> attacked this passage with great laughter and insults, claiming I was not in my right mind when I wrote this. But I soon discovered the man's error. For while I had noted the reading of the latter part—"do these things, and the God of peace etc."—he dreamed that I was speaking about the earlier part—"if there be any praise of discipline, think on these things, which you have learned." But he will ask: why was I making a note at all, since the text of this passage was perfectly fine in both the Greek and Latin codices? I am not so stupid that I would make a note without cause. Indeed, when I was writing this, I consulted a very ancient—even the first, if I am not mistaken—edition of a codex which has the Ordinary and Interlinear Glosses attached; it was provided by the Carthusian Monastery near the city of Brussels, close to the College of Anderlecht, where I was then staying in the country for the sake of my health. In it, the text was written as follows: *think on these things, which you have learned, and received, and heard, and seen in me: think on these things and do them, and the God of peace shall be with you.* And the Gloss in the interlinear verse said: "He says not only think, but also fulfill in action." Here my corrector will shout that the text was corrupted and that the word "think" was repeated from the verse above. I admit it, and that is why I gave the warning—so that this reading, which had already occupied countless codices, would not spread further. May the Lord grant such sycophants the grace to eventually come to their senses.

21 **Because at last finally**] <note>original: "hoti ēdē pote"</note>, that is, because now at last. "You have flourished again to feel for me" <note>original: "anethalete to hyper emou phronein"</note>, that is, you have revived in your thinking about me; you should understand this as "regarding your thinking," meaning that love, concern, and zeal for me have revived in you, even though you have not sent anything until now, because the opportunity for sending was lacking to you, not the will.

22 **As also you were thinking**] <note>original: "eph’ hō ephroneite"</note>, that is, "in that which you were thinking."

23 **But you were occupied**] <note>original: "ēkaireisthe de"</note>, that is, but you lacked the opportunity. For that is what the Greek word seems to mean.

<margin>E</margin> 24 **Not as if**] <note>original: "ouch hoti"</note>, that is, Not that. "According to penury" <note>original: "kath’ hysterēsin"</note>, that is, according to lack.

25 **To be sufficient**] <note>original: "autarkēs einai"</note>, that is, to be content. It was clear: "For I have learned to be content in those things in which I am" <note>original: "en hois eimi autarkēs einai"</note>, that is, I have learned to make the best of what is present.

26 **I know also how to abound**] <note>original: "perisseuein"</note>. What he here translates as "abound"

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>8</margin> whatever is honorable, whatever is just, ^16 whatever is pure, ^17 whatever is suitable, ^18 whatever is of good omen, if there be any virtue, and ^19 if there be any praise, think on these things. ^9 Which you have both learned, and received, and heard, and seen in me: ^20 do these things, and the God of peace will be with you. <margin>10</margin> But I ^21 rejoiced in the Lord greatly, that now at last your concern for me has revived, ^22 in which also you were concerned, ^23 but opportunity was lacking. <margin>11</margin> ^24 Not that I speak according to penury: for I have learned, in those things in which I am, to be ^25 content. <margin>12</margin> I know how to be humble, ^26 I know also how to excel: ^27 in every place and in all things I have been instructed, both to be full and to be hungry, ^28 both to abound and to suffer penury. <margin>13</margin> I can do all things through Christ, who <margin>B</margin> strengthens me. <margin>14</margin> Nevertheless you did rightly, that you shared in my affliction. <margin>15</margin> And you also know, ^15 Philippians, that in the beginning of the Gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church shared with me in the matter of giving and receiving, except you only. <margin>16</margin> For even ^30 in Thessalonica when I was there, ^31 once and ^16 <note>Note: Source likely intended 32</note> again you sent ^32 that which was necessary for me. <margin>17</margin> ^33 Not that I require a gift, ^34 but I require fruit ^35 abounding to your account. <margin>18</margin> ^36 However, I have received all things, and ^18 I abound: ^37 I have been filled, after I received from Epaphroditus those things which were sent by you, ^38 an odor of good fragrance, a sacrifice accepted and pleasing to God. <margin>19</margin> And my God will supply ^39 whatever is necessary for you,

<margin>C</margin> <meta>catchword: fecund-</meta>

***

not only refers to an abundance of things, but to every kind of excellence, so that it is opposed to what preceded it: "to be humbled." For he mentions abundance and lack shortly thereafter. Though Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and biblical commentator often cited by Erasmus.</note> explains it differently.

27 **Everywhere and in all things**] <note>original: "en panti kai en pasi"</note>, that is, in every thing and in all things. And this is how Ambrose read it. Although the Translator <note>The Vulgate translator.</note> translates well here, so that you take "everywhere" for "in every matter." Theophylact explains the first part "in every thing" in two ways: either "at every time," so you understand long experience, or "in every business," so you understand experience in very many things; "in all things," however, refers to things that happen by the way. **I have been instructed**] <note>original: "memuēmai"</note>, which Ambrose translates as "I have been imbued." Properly, it means to be initiated into mysteries. Furthermore, mysteries are first learned, then practiced.

28 **To abound and to suffer penury**] <note>original: "perisseuein kai hystereisthai"</note>, which is to say, so to speak: to suffer having more than enough, and to suffer having less than enough.

29 **Who comforts me**] <note>original: "en tō endynamounti"</note>. It is not "comforts," as if he consoles and refreshes, but he strengthens, that is, he makes one powerful and strong: *corroborat* (corroborates/strengthens) would be more Latin.

30 **Unto Thessalonica**] <note>original: "en Thessalonikē"</note>, that is, in Thessalonica. For they did not send "unto Thessalonica," but they sent to Paul, who was there at that time. Unless perhaps the Apostle ignored the rules of Grammar.

31 **Once and twice**] <note>original: "hapax kai dis"</note>. If someone wanted to render this in Latin, they should say "once and again" <note>original: "semel atque iterum"</note>. Ambrose reads "once and again." Otherwise "once and twice" sounds like nothing other than "thrice." For what is said well in Greek is not immediately suitable in Latin.

32 **For use**] <note>original: "eis tēn chreian"</note>, that is, for want, or for necessity. Although "for use" is not absurd, provided you understand it as "for use," meaning when there was a need. I have been instructed: "you sent for my uses."

33 **Not because I seek a gift**] <note>original: "ouch hoti epizētō to doma"</note>, that is, Not that I am looking for the gift itself. Ambrose reads, "Not because I seek a reward."

34 **But I require fruit**] That word "I seek" and this "I require" are the same word in Greek, <note>original: "epizētō"</note>; let no one wonder in vain at the Translator's variety of vocabulary.

35 **Abounding to your account**] Here he would have translated better if he had turned the Greek participle <note>original: "pleonazonta"</note> into a verb: "which may redound to your benefit" rather than mine.

<margin>F</margin> 36 **But I have all things**] <note>original: "apechō"</note>. Ambrose reads, "But I have received all things." For *apechein* is to receive from someone like a tax or a return from the fields. And in that manner he translates in the Gospels, "they have received their reward," <note>original: "apechousi"</note>. Feeling this, Theophylact suggests that it means to receive something given as if it were a debt.

37 **I am filled with things received**] <note>original: "peplērōmai dexamenos"</note>, that is, I have been filled receiving, except that the participle is in the past tense. He would have translated more conveniently in this way: "I was satisfied after I received from Epaphroditus the things sent by you, an odor, etc."

38 **Unto an odor of sweetness**] <note>original: "osmēn euōdias"</note>. As we indicated above. It is not "unto an odor," but "odor" placed in apposition, supported by the Greek Donatian codex <note>A manuscript from the Church of St. Donatian in Bruges.</note>. Both of the Constance codices also supported this. Ambrose reads "an odor of good sweetness," but changing the case from ablative to accusative, as I also do. Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian (c. 210–258 AD), Bishop of Carthage.</note>, explaining the Lord's Prayer, cites it in this way: "I am saturated," he says, "receiving from Epaphroditus those things which were sent by you, with an odor of sweetness, a sacrifice accepted and pleasing to God." Moreover, he indicates that what he called a sweet odor is taken from sacred rites, in which incense was scattered, pleasing to the nostrils of the gods.

39 **Every desire**] <note>original: "pasan chreian"</note>, that is, every necessity,

# ARGUMENT
<note>original: "ΥΠΟΘΕΣΙΣ" / Hypothesis; a traditional summary of a book's contents often found in Byzantine manuscripts.</note>
->of the<-
## EPISTLE OF PAUL
### TO THE COLOSSIANS.

<image-desc>Decorative square woodcut initial T with vine and leaf patterns.</image-desc>
He sends this letter from Rome, though he had not seen them in person, but had heard reports about them. The occasion for the Epistle is as follows: certain people wished to deceive the Colossians with Greek sophistries <note>clever but fallacious arguments intended to deceive</note> directed against their faith in Jesus, and concerning the dietary laws of the Torah and circumcision. Therefore, having learned of these things, the Apostle writes this Epistle to them as a form of instruction. First, in giving thanks to God, he indicates from what darkness they have moved into the light of truth, and that Christ, in whom they have believed, is the image of God and the Word through whom all things were made. Furthermore, it was fitting that He, being the Creator, should become the firstborn of all creation and the firstborn from the dead, so that He might join both together and give life to all things. He exhorts them to remain in the faith, pointing out that Paul himself is a servant of the Gospel in which they were instructed. Then he explains about the Law, the foods mentioned within it, and about feast days and years, demonstrating that these ancient things and circumcision have now become void. He advises them not to be led astray by those who use clever arguments and wish to deceive them. Finally, after offering exhortations to parents and children, husbands and wives, slaves and masters, and giving other advice regarding moral character, he completes the Epistle.

---

# ON THE EPISTLE TO THE
## COLOSSIANS
->*The Argument by*<-
### DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

<image-desc>Decorative square woodcut initial C with floral scrollwork.</image-desc>
The Colossians are in Asia Minor <note>modern-day Turkey</note>, neighbors to the Laodiceans. The Apostle had not seen them personally. For they were converted to Christ by the preaching of Archippus or, as Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397), an influential Latin Church Father</note> adds, Epaphras, to whom this duty had been delegated. False Apostles <note>original: "Pseudapostoli"</note> were pressuring them vehemently, attempting to lead them into a most perverse doctrine. These teachers taught that the Son of God was not the author of salvation, but that the way to the Father lay open through the angels. They claimed that the Son of God had neither come into this world, nor would he come, since in the Old Testament all things were administered by angels. Furthermore, they mixed Judaism and the superstitions of Philosophy with the teaching of Christ, observing certain institutions of the Law and superstitiously watching the sun, moon, stars, and the elements of this world, to which they taught we were subject. Paul therefore reminds them of their profession of faith, showing that whatever they have attained so far they owe not to angels, but to Christ, the creator of angels. He teaches that Christ alone is the head of the Church, and that salvation must not be sought from anyone else. Meanwhile, he asserts his own authority. He diligently warns them not to allow themselves to be deceived by the pompous speech of the False Apostles and their fabricated visions of angels, lest they slide back into either Judaism or philosophical superstition. He deals with these matters in the first two chapters. In the remainder, he exhorts them to the duties of piety, specifically prescribing how a wife should act toward her husband, a husband toward his wife, a parent toward children, children toward parents, servants toward masters, and masters toward servants. The final part is occupied with greetings, except that he reminds Archippus of his duty. He wrote this from prison in Ephesus <note>Erasmus notes a tradition here, though he immediately provides the counter-evidence</note> by means of Tychicus, as he himself openly testifies in the fourth chapter of this Epistle, to whom he had given Onesimus as a companion. The inscriptions in the Greek manuscripts testify that it was sent from the city of Rome. Certainly, it was from there that he sent back Onesimus, whom he had begotten for Christ while in chains.

<vocab>HYPOTHESIS, Colossians, Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam, Paul, Epistle, Colossae, Tychicus, Onesimus, False Apostles</vocab>

<margin>C</margin>
First, I cannot help but wonder what was in the minds of those who say that the Colossians, to whom Paul writes this Epistle, are the people of Rhodes <note>Rhodienses</note>, because of that famous Colossus which is numbered among the seven wonders of the world. For while every writer mentions the statue, not even those who have most diligently recorded the history of the whole island have said a single word about a city of this name. Rather, Colossae is a city of Phrygia, which is in Asia Minor, not so far from Hierapolis and Laodicea, both of which Paul mentions in this Epistle: *at Laodicea*, when he says: *For I want you to know what kind of conflict I have for you, and for those who are at Laodicea.* And again at the end: *See that it is read in the Church of the Laodiceans, and that you also read the one sent from Laodicea.* And a little earlier: *For I have much zeal for you, and for those who are at Laodicea, and those who are at Hierapolis.* It is well established that Hierapolis and Laodicea are in Phrygia, or certainly on the border, according to Ptolemy. Furthermore, Herodotus in Book VII calls Colossae a great city of Phrygia, which has the river Lycus; this river, casting itself into a chasm in the earth, disappears, and later breaks out again after fifty stadia. In addition to this, Pliny in Book V, chapter 31, specifically lists Colossae in his description of Phrygia, which is bordered on its northern part by Galatia, on the south by Lycaonia, Pisidia, and Mygdonia, and touches Cappadocia to the east. The most celebrated towns are Ancyra, Andria, Celena, Colossae, Carina, Cotiaion, Cerana, Iconium, and Midaium. The same author in Book XXXI, chapter 2, recorded that there is a river of Colossae into which if bricks are thrown, they are pulled out as stones. Furthermore, Strabo in Book X of his *Geography* also makes mention of Colossae among the places neighboring Laodicea. Now, even Theophylact <note>A 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and biblical commentator often cited by Erasmus.</note>, the Greek interpreter, has handed down this concerning the Colossians: *Colossae is a city of Phrygia, now called Chonae. And this is clear from the fact that it is near Laodicea.* <note>original: "Πόλις Φρυγίας αἱ Κολοσσαί, αἱ νῦν λεγόμεναι Χῶναι. Καὶ δῆλον ἐκ τῶν τὴν Λαοδίκειαν εἶναι πλησίον."</note> These things are abundantly sufficient, I believe, to refute those who transfer the Colossians to Rhodes. Nor does Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>Erasmus refers to him as Faber Stapulensis, a contemporary French humanist.</note> disagree with our opinion. As for what we read in Suidas, that the Rhodians and Lindians were called *Colossians* because of the remarkable Colossus they erected to the Sun—even if that be true, it does not mean this Epistle was written to the Rhodians. Furthermore, as for our reading **Colossaeis** in Greek manuscripts written with an "alpha" <note>Colassaeis</note> in the second syllable, I suspect it happened through the carelessness of scribes, especially since Theophylact, explaining the site of the city, writes *Colossae*, not *Colassae*. Moreover, we say *Colossa, Colossarum*, just as we say *Athenae, Athenarum*.

1. **From God our Father** Theophylact notes, following John Chrysostom as he usually does, that the mention of Christ is not added here, though it is customary in almost all the other Epistles. And yet we see this added in the Greek manuscripts, no doubt by the error of scribes adding it from their own memory of what usually appears. Certainly, Theophylact does not add it. In the edition published in Verona, it is added in the text, though the commentary argues against it. Latin manuscripts vary.
2. **Which has come to you, as it is also in the whole world, and**
<margin>E</margin>

<column-break/>

**it bears fruit and grows** *Just as also in all the world and it is fruit-bearing*, <note>original: "καθὼς καὶ ἐν παντὶ τῷ κόσμῳ καὶ ἔστι καρποφορούμενον"</note> although in some copies the latter *and* is not added before *is*. However, that conjunction does not seem idle to me. For the former refers to the adverb, just as the latter refers to what is implied: *it has come to you*, just as it is in the whole world, and it is so in such a way that it is not only preached, but also bears fruit and grows. I have not read these words in the Greek, yet Lefèvre indicates that *growing* <note>original: "αὐξανόμενον"</note> is added in certain copies; and indeed, Ambrose, Theophylact, and Chrysostom read it thus. And a little later below, these two participles are joined again: *in every good work*, etc.
3. **Just as in you** *Just as also in you*, adds the conjunction, <note>original: "καθὼς καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν"</note>. And thus Ambrose reads it.
4. **Our fellow-servant** In Greek it is *for*, you. Although the books vary here, and our first person fits better, so that we understand him as an assistant to Paul and a minister to them.
<margin>D</margin>
5. **Praying and asking** These participles ought to be translated as infinitive verbs: *to pray and to ask*, <note>original: "προσευχόμενοι καὶ αἰτούμενοι"</note>.
6. **That you may be filled with the knowledge** <note>original: "ἵνα πληρωθῆτε τὴν ἐπίγνωσιν"</note>. Either the preposition *according to* <note>original: "κατά"</note> must be understood, after the manner of the Greeks, as if by synecdoche <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole or vice-versa.</note>, or *be filled* must be taken actively, that is, *that you may fill*. Nevertheless, I approve more of the former sense. And Theophylact follows it along with Chrysostom.
7. **Worthily of God** It is *the Lord* in the Greek: <note>original: "ἀξίως τῷ Κυρίῳ"</note>.
8. **Pleasing in all things** <note>original: "εἰς πᾶσαν ἀρέσκειαν"</note>. As if you were to say, *into all pleasingness*. Ambrose reads, *unto every pleasure*.
9. **Strengthened in all virtue** The Greek speech is more pleasant: <note>original: "Ἐν πάσῃ δυνάμει δυναμούμενοι"</note>, that is, *being made powerful in all power*, or *growing strong in strength*. For it is a present participle.
10. **Of brightness** <note>original: "δόξης"</note>, that is, *of glory*.
11. **To God and the Father** In Greek it is only *the Father*, just as Ambrose reads. In the Venetian edition, it was *God*. The translator of Theophylact always insists on the reading common to the Latins. *Who made worthy*: <note>original: "τῷ ἱκανώσαντι ἡμᾶς"</note>, that is, *who made us fit*.
12. **The Son of His love** Now, we have warned more than once that this form of speech is peculiar to the Hebrews: *vessel of election* for *chosen vessel*, and *son of perdition* for *lost son*. Likewise here, *Son of love* for *beloved Son*, <note>original: "τῷ Υἱῷ τῆς ἀγάπης αὐτοῦ"</note>.
13. **Redemption and remission** The Greek manuscripts have here: *the redemption through his blood, the remission of sins*, <note>original: "τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ, τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν"</note>. Ambrose seems likewise to have read this, except that he does not have *here* the phrase *through his blood*. Furthermore, the fact that he joined *redemption and remission* with no intervening conjunction, but by apposition <note>Placing two nouns side by side where one explains the other.</note>, indicates that he adds a distinction: *For the remission of sins makes men free*. For Paul, explaining what he meant by *redemption*, added *remission of sins*.
14. **Image of the invisible God** *Invisible* does not refer to the *image*, but to God <note>original: "ἀοράτου"</note>, that is, of God. For just as the Father alone is called immortal and wise, so He alone is called invisible—not because the Son is visible according to His divine nature, but because from the Fa-

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the first chapter of Colossians, specifically focusing on the Christological hymn in verses 15–24. Erasmus provides a philological and theological analysis of Christ’s role in creation and the Church, comparing Greek manuscripts with the Latin Vulgate and the writings of Church Fathers like Ambrose, Chrysostom, and Jerome.</meta>

# TO THE COLOSSIANS. CHAPTER I.

16 **The firstborn of every creature**, *For in him all things were created*, both those in the heavens and those on the earth, the visible and the invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created 17 through him and for him. And he is before all things, and in 18 him all things hold together; And he is the head of the body, the Church, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that in all things he might 19 hold the primacy; *Because in him it pleased all the fullness to 20 dwell*, And through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross—through him, whether those on the earth or those in the 21 heavens. And you, who were once alienated and enemies in your mind in wicked works, 22 He has now reconciled in the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and blameless and 23 irreproachable before him. If indeed you remain grounded and steadfast in the faith, and not moved away from the hope of the Gospel which you heard, which was preached in all creation under heaven, of which I, 24 Paul, became a minister. Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and I fill up what is lacking of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh, for his body,

---

<margin>A</margin> ...nature has an invisible character. Therefore, the Father remains invisible as the source. However, through the image, the Son in some way brings Himself forth, while through Him He established this world, and while through Him, having become man, He becomes known to us.

15 *Firstborn of every creature*] Since he said *creature* <note>original: "creaturae"</note> here, why did he shortly after change it to *established* <note>original: "conditae"</note>, since in the Greek the words *ktisis* and *ektisthē* are of the same origin? From this it can be gathered that there is no difference between *creating* and *establishing*. The sense here can be: He who was begotten before every creature. This is to prevent anyone, following Arius, from making the Son of God a creature. Ambrose discusses this view. But if you read it with a change in accent as *prōtotókos* <note>Erasmus notes that changing the Greek accent from the firstborn (passive) to the first-procurer (active) changes the meaning.</note> of every creature, the sense will be that He first produced all things, and every creature was born from Him. The following part, *that in Him all things were created*, etc., fits this sense well. Whether you prefer one sense or the other, I do not see how it matters enough to bring in Platonic ideas here, as Aquinas does. Since, according to the property of Hebrew speech, Paul said "in Him" instead of "through Him," as we have frequently pointed out. He declares this by repeating the thought; what he had said here as *en autō* (in Him), he changes to *di’ autou* (through Him). Theophylact, following Chrysostom, agrees with our view in explaining this passage. Furthermore, what follows, *eis auton*, should not have been translated as "in Him," lest he seem to say the same thing twice, but "into Him" or "for Him," so that you understand these things were not established through Christ as through a servant, but as through a partner in rule. Therefore, he added "into Him," upon whom all things depend for governance. This is how the Greek Paul wrote sounds, and Theophylact, among others, interprets it this way. Now, I think it is clear in itself that what Thomas Aquinas explains regarding this as a "formal cause" <note>An Aristotelian term used by Aquinas to explain Christ as the pattern of creation.</note> does not much pertain to the matter, though it is fair to blame the Translator who translated it differently than the Apostle wrote.

16 *In heaven and on earth*] *ta en tois ouranois kai epi tēs gēs*, that is, *the things in the heavens and those on the earth*.

17 *And he is before all*] It fits better as *before all things*, *pro pantōn*. For he spoke of the universe, and it follows immediately, *and all things*. Tertullian, however, in his fifth book against Marcion, reads "before all [people]," concluding that one cannot be called "before all people" unless he is before all things. Hilary reads it the same way in the ninth book on the Trinity.

18 *And all things consist in him*] *kai ta panta en autō synestēke*, that is, *and all things consist* or *have consisted in Him*: although the Translator correctly changed the tense of the Greek verb. Furthermore, "to consist" is said to mean "to be preserved."

19 *Who is the beginning, the firstborn*] *hos estin archē prōtotokos*. Since no article is added to either word, this sense can also be taken: That Christ is the firstborn beginning from the dead, as if you said the first principle, because He is the source of all resurrection: so that "firstborn" is an epithet for "beginning." For Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Ambrose adapt it to this, saying Christ is called the beginning here because He is the leader and author of the resurrection.

20 *Holding the primacy*] *prōteuōn*, that is, *holding the first place*, although in Greek it is a single word.

21 *In him it pleased*] *eudokēse*. If this refers to the Father, whose will and decree it was, the interpretation will be more suitable than if it refers to the Son. And this is how Theophylact felt. For when he argued that the fullness of the Deity is in the Son by nature, he added that no cause is brought for this matter, except that it so seemed good to God. Therefore, we have added "to the Father" on our own <note>Erasmus added "Patri" (to the Father) to the Latin text for clarity, as it is implied in the Greek.</note>.

22 *All the fullness of Divinity*] I do not find "of Divinity" in the Greek in this place; it is only "the fullness" (*to plērōma*), nor is it added in Ambrose's text, though he adds it in his explanation for the sake of clarity. Nor does Hilary add it when citing this place in the eighth book on the Trinity in more than one location. The situation is similar with Chrysostom and Theophylact. If anyone examines the interpretation of Saint Thomas, they will find that not even he added "of Divinity." Both manuscripts from Constance supported this. And I do not know if it is in that translator at all. Therefore, I wonder from where that word crept into certain Latin copies, unless it was added here from the next chapter of this Epistle by some studious person.

<column-break/>

15 **the firstborn of all creation**, That through him 16 all things were created, which are in the heavens, and which are on the earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created through him and for him, 17 And he is before all things, 17 and 18 all things consist through him: And he is the head 18 of the body of the Church, 19 who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he himself might be 20 holding the first place in all things: Because 21 it pleased the Father 22 that 19 all fullness should dwell in him, 23 And through him to re- 20 concile all things toward himself, 24 having made peace 25 through the blood of his cross, through the same, whether those things which are on the earth, or those which are in the heavens. And you were once alien- 21 ated, and 26 enemies in mind in evil works, Yet now 22 he has reconciled in the body of 27 his flesh through death, to present you holy 28 and irreproachable 29 and blameless in his sight. If indeed you remain 23 grounded and stable in the faith, and are not moved from the hope of the Gospel, which you heard, 30 which was preached in all creation, which is under heaven, of which I, Paul, was made a minister. 31 Now I rejoice over my afflic- 24 tions for you, 32 and I supply what was lacking of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh, for his body, which

---

<margin>D</margin> 23 *Through him to reconcile all things into himself*] Why did he not also previously translate "into himself," when the Greek words are the same, *eis auton*: although "to reconcile" (*apokatallaxai*), an active verb, was more correct. And "toward himself" <note>original: "erga se"</note> is better than "into himself."

24 *Making peace*] *eirēnopoiēsas hōste ta en tois gēs, eite ta en tois ouranois*, that is, *peace having been made for those things on earth and those in the heavens*. Otherwise, the speech will not lack a solecism <note>A grammatical error.</note>. For just as the Greek says *eudokēsen eirēnopoiēsas*, it does not please the Latins to say "making peace" in that way.

25 *Through the blood in his cross*] The Greek is different: *dia tou haimatos tou staurou autou*, that is, *through the blood of his cross, through him*, or *through the same*: so that it may refer to the Father, and these pronouns pertain to Christ.

26 *Enemies in mind*] *echthrous tē dianoia*, that is, *enemies in mind*, or *in thought*. Furthermore, the speech is ambiguous to the Greeks, for the dative *dianoia* can be taken either instrumentally, that is, *through the sense, or mind*: or relatively, *enemies, but namely in mind*. For he who serves the flesh fights against reason. Ambrose and Jerome refer "in the [mind]" not to the sinning man, but to God, so that you understand the mind of God, not of man. For the former reads it thus, *And you, since they established you as alienated and his enemies in iniquitous works*, etc. The latter in this way, in the Epistle to John, Bishop of Jerusalem, *When you were alienated, and enemies of his sense*: though I would certainly prefer "foes" <note>original: "hostes"</note> rather than "enemies" <note>original: "inimici"</note>. Theophylact refers "mind" to the Colossians, lest they think they were to be excused if they had been enemies of God by fate or nature. Therefore he added "mind," so they would understand they were enemies by their own will. Chrysostom brings the same sense, though it is not clear to what he refers *dianoia*.

27 *Of his flesh*] *Insuæ sua* <note>Erasmus is likely correcting a Latin textual variant here.</note>.

28 *And immaculate*] *amōmous*, that is, *irreprehensible*. Which Tertullian somewhere translates not inelegantly as *unvituperable*. For from this comes the god Momus <note>The Greek god of mockery and criticism.</note>, because he would carp at the deeds of others.

29 *And irreproachable*] *anegklētous*, that is, *incriminable*, or *blameless*.

<margin>E</margin> 30 *Which was preached in all creation*] *en pasē ktisei*. Aquinas is somewhat tortured here, thinking "was preached" is put for "will be preached": rather, it is a hyperbole, by which he signifies that the Gospel of Christ is already common everywhere, so the Colossians would not think of changing the faith, which had already been received by all. However, it is more magnificent and ardent to say "in every creature" than "among all men." But if someone does not accept hyperbole in Divine Letters, let him, if he wishes, quarrel with Jerome, Origen, Chrysostom, and Augustine, who frequently note this figure. They foolishly shudder at a lie, because hyperbole exceeds the belief of truth. But it is not a lie where no one is deceived, nor is the will to deceive present. Hyperbole seeks an increase, and the listener understands nothing else.

31 *Who now I rejoice*] I do not find "Who" among the Greeks, but only, "Now I rejoice," *Nyn chairō*. And among the Greeks it is *en pathēmasi mou*, that is, *in my afflictions*. To which "for you," *hyper hymōn*, adheres continually, although in these words too there is some ambiguity <margin>F</margin> of sense: "I rejoice for you," that is, "I congratulate your protection," and "I rejoice that I am afflicted for your sake."

32 *And I fill up those things which are lacking of the passions*] *kai antanaplērō ta hysterēmata tōn thlipseōn*. He could have translated more conveniently: *and I supply what is lacking to the afflictions of Christ*. Ambrose thus: *and I supply the remains of the pressures*. Furthermore, the verb *antanaplērō* is composed of three parts: from *anti*, which signifies "in turn," when someone does something in another's place; and *ana*, which among Latins sometimes has the force of "re-"; and *plērō*, as if "I refill" in the place of Christ, that which is diminished in his afflictions. Ambrose seems to have wanted to explain Paul’s meaning when he says "remains," so that we understand Christ’s passion was not diminished for the salvation of men, but that the passion of Christ and of the martyrs is one, that is, of the head and the members. Theophylact does not disagree with this opinion, interpreting that Christ still suffers in the Apostles for his body, not because anything is lacking, but because his charity toward us is so immense. Chrysostom notes similar things, saying that the Apostle, for the sake of modesty, calls his own afflictions, which he endures for the Church, the afflictions of Christ. That Latin Scholiast adds another commentary: So much so that I am not weary of affli-

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL Chapter II.

<note>The following Greek text represents the source passage Erasmus is analyzing, covering Colossians 1:25 through 2:10.</note>

25 ...of which I became a minister according to the stewardship of God, which was given to me for 26 you, to fulfill the word of God, the mystery which has been hidden from the ages and from the generations; 27 but now it has been revealed to His saints, to whom God willed to make known what are the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the 28 hope of glory. Him we proclaim, warning every man and teaching every man in all wisdom, that we may present every 29 man perfect in Christ Jesus; for which I also labor, striving according to His working, which works II. 1 in me in power. For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you, and for those in Laodicea, and for as many as have not seen my face in 2 the flesh, that their hearts may be encouraged, being knit together in love, and attaining to all the riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the knowledge of the mystery 3 of God, both of the Father and of Christ, in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and of knowledge 4 hidden. Now this I say lest anyone should delude 5 you with persuasive words. For though I am absent in the flesh, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order and the firmness of your 6 faith in Christ. As you therefore have received Christ 7 Jesus the Lord, walk in Him, rooted and built up in Him and established in the faith, as you have been taught, abounding in it with 8 thanksgiving. Beware lest anyone cheat you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the basic principles of the world, 9 and not according to Christ. For in Him dwells all 10 the fullness of the Godhead bodily, and you are in Him...

---

### Annotations

33 **Of which I was made a minister**] This refers to the Church, not the "body." Ambrose seems to refer it to the Gospel; I do not see where that is repeated from, though it is certainly a small matter. Truly, great theologians sometimes stumble over these very tiny details if they do not know Greek. It is said twice, *Of which I am a minister*: in the first instance, it refers to the Gospel without controversy; in the latter, it refers to the Church, and it can be nothing else, since in Greek <note>original: "ἐκφωνητικὴ generis"</note> the pronoun indicates the gender. Accordingly, we have translated it, *Of which Church*.

34 **The Word of God, a mystery**] Since Paul here calls the Word of God a "mystery"—which the Latin often translates as "Sacrament"—why do they not add an eighth Sacrament from this? There are those who, whenever the word "Sacrament" is mentioned in the Scriptures, want it to be understood as one of those seven <note>The seven sacraments of the Catholic Church</note>, even though "mystery" in this place sounds like a secret or something hidden, as indicated by what follows: *but now it has been revealed*.

35 **To make known the riches**] In Greek it is <note>original: "γνωρίσαι τίς ὁ πλοῦτος"</note>, that is, *to make known what the riches are*. And so Ambrose reads it.

36 **Of the Sacrament**] <note>original: "μυστηρίῳ"</note>, that is, *of the mystery*, meaning of the secret.

37 **Which is Christ**] <note>original: "ὅς ἐστι Χριστὸς"</note>, that is, *who is Christ*. Although Laurentius Valla thinks it should be translated *which is Christ* <note>using the feminine relative pronoun in Latin</note> to refer to "riches" <note>original: "πλοῦτον"</note>, which is a masculine noun in Greek and singular in number. And indeed, the Greek scholia explain it this way. Ambrose says otherwise. Theophylact varies.

38 **In you**] <note>original: "ἐν ὑμῖν"</note>, that is, *among you*. And so Ambrose reads it, as it is in the more corrected Greek codices, although in some Greek codices it was written <note>original: "ἐν ἡμῖν"</note>, *in us*.

39 **Correcting**] <note>original: "νουθετοῦντες"</note>, that is, *admonishing*, and so Ambrose has it. For the Greek word is ambiguous; they sometimes translate it as "to rebuke."

40 **And teaching**] Here the Greeks repeat "every man" <note>original: "πάντα ἄνθρωπον"</note>. And so it was written in the codex of Donatian. Both manuscripts from Constance supported this.

41 **In which etc.**] <note>original: "Εἰς ὃ"</note>, *unto which*, or *unto which thing*, so that you do not refer it to Christ, but to their perfection. Nor is it simply *I labor by contending*, but <note>original: "κοπιῶ ἀγωνιζόμενος"</note>, which pertains to danger. For an *agon* is sometimes a contest, sometimes a danger.

42 **Which works**] <note>original: "τὴν ἐνέργειαν"</note>, that is, *the efficacy which works*. And so Ambrose reads. And the "operation" is the *energeian*, so that you understand an active force in Paul. And "by power" is <note>original: "δυνάμει"</note>, which fights against weakness.

1 **What great care**] <note>original: "ἡλίκον ἀγῶνα"</note>, that is, *how great a struggle*, or *danger*. Nor is it "for" you, but "concerning" you <note>original: "περὶ ὑμῶν"</note>: although *agon* sounds like labor, it is linked with difficulty and danger.

2 **My face**] <note>original: "τὸ πρόσωπόν μου"</note>: which plainly refers to the face. For to have seen a "unique person" is not, I think, good Latin, even if that appeals more to someone else.

3 **Constructed**] <note>original: "συμβιβασθέντων"</note>, that is, *compacted* or *knit together*. Some have "instructed." Ambrose reads, *when they shall have been instructed in charity*, Hilary reads *instituted*. Furthermore, this is the same word that was previously translated as "constructed"; it signifies being compacted and con-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...which is the Church, 33 of which Church I have been made a minister according to the 25 stewardship of God, which was given to me toward you, to fulfill 34 the word of God, the mystery which 26 was hidden from ages and from generations: but now is made manifest to His saints, to whom God willed 27 35 to make known what are the riches of the glory of 36 this mystery among the Gentiles, 37 who is Christ 38 in you, the hope of glory: whom we announce, 39 admonishing 28 every man, 40 and teaching every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man <margin>B</margin> perfect in Christ Jesus: 41 for which also I strive, 29 contending according to His efficacy, 42 acting in me through power. For I want you to know 1 how great a II. 1 concern I have concerning you, and those who are at Laodicea, and as many as have not seen 2 my face in the 2 flesh, that their hearts may receive consolation, 3 when they have been knit together in charity, and unto all the 4 riches of the certain persuasion of understanding, into the acknowledgment of the mystery 5 of God and the Father and of Christ, in whom are all 3 the treasures of wisdom and of knowledge 6 hidden. Now this 4 I say, lest anyone should impose upon you 7 with probability of speech. For 8 although I am absent in flesh, 5 yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order and 9 the solidness of your faith in Christ. As 6 <margin>C</margin> therefore you have received Christ Jesus 10 the Lord, so walk in Him, so that you have roots fixed in Him, 7 11 and be built up in Him, and confirmed through faith, as you have been taught, abounding in it with thanksgiving. See 12 that there be no one who makes a prey of 8 you through philosophy and empty deception, according to the constitution of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ. For in Him dwells 9 all the fullness 13 of the Godhead bodily, and you are in 10 Him...

---

*nected, in the manner of the members of one body clinging fitly together.*

<margin>D</margin> 4 **Riches of fullness**] <note>original: "πληροφορίας" (plerophorias)</note>. It is not *pleromatos*, which itself also translates as "fullness." For *plerophoria* sounds more like *certain persuasion*, as when someone has full faith so that he no longer doubts at all, just as we noted at the beginning of the Gospel of Luke. For he wishes for them a certain knowledge of the mystery, so that they do not hesitate at all. Theophylact interprets it in this way: "so as in no way to doubt." Therefore, what more recent interpreters bring to this place cannot very well fit Paul's sense.

5 **Of God the Father and of Christ**] The Greeks add the conjunction *and* <note>original: "καὶ"</note>, *of the God and Father, and of the Christ*: just as he speaks in other places, as if you were to say, *of Him who is God and Father, and of Him who is the Anointed*.

6 **Hidden**] <note>original: "ἀπόκρυφοι"</note>, that is, *hidden*. Here it is a noun, not a participle, meaning *occult or secret things*.

7 **In sublimity of speech**] <note>original: "ἐν πιθανολογίᾳ"</note>, that is, *in persuasive oratory, or persuasiveness, or probability*. <margin>E</margin> Ambrose reads, *in sublimity of speech*, twisting this passage against the Sophists. He perhaps read it as <note>original: "λεπτολογίᾳ" (subtle speech)</note>. Augustine in Letter 60 reads, *in plausible speech*.

8 **Even if in body**] <note>original: "σαρκὶ"</note>, that is, *in flesh*: which he opposes to the spirit, which follows immediately.

9 **Firmament**] <note>original: "τὸ στερέωμα τῆς εἰς Χριστὸν πίστεως ὑμῶν"</note>, that is, *the solidness of your faith in Christ*. I wonder why Saint Ambrose added in this place: *for he reads in this way, seeing your order*, and supplying *that which is lacking to the utility of your faith*. For it appears he read it thus in the Greek codices, *and filling up what is lacking of your faith*. Otherwise, the Translator added "his" from his own, which was not needed because of the pronoun "your" which follows.

10 **Our Lord**] "Our" is redundant in our version. In the Greek it is only *Christ Jesus the Lord*. The manuscripts from Constance agreed. He is absolutely called simply *the Lord*: just as in the Gospel, *the Lord has need of it*.

<margin>F</margin> 11 **And built up**] <note>original: "ἐποικοδομούμενοι"</note> is in the present tense, so that you are being built up while Christ remains the root and foundation, or so that you grow in Him, or so that you may be restored from having somewhat collapsed. For Theophylact follows this last sense.

12 **Lest anyone deceive you**] <note>original: "μὴ τις ὑμᾶς ἔσται ὁ συλαγωγῶν"</note>, that is, *lest there be one who plunders you, or carries you off as prey*. Ambrose translates "plunder" <note>original: "depraedetur"</note>: and likewise Jerome in his book *Commentary on Hosea*. Again in the *Commentaries* he published on the Epistle to the Galatians. The Greek word properly sounds like *to carry off as booty*. Hence the Greeks called those *hierosyloi* who plunder sacred things. For it is sacrilege to drive away what has been consecrated to God. Cyprian reads in a similar way in his sermon *On the Benefit of Patience*. Hilary in his book *On the Trinity*, book 12, reads: *See that no one spoils you*: and he repeats what he reads as the sermon progresses. Therefore I wonder where this "deceive" of ours came to us from. He means we must beware lest someone, having attacked with hidden snares, leads them away from the right path of faith into error, ruin, and the servitude of the Mosaic Law.

13 **Of the divinity bodily**] <note>original: "Θεότητος"</note>, that is, *of the Deity*. And he added...

<summary>In this passage, Erasmus provides a philological analysis of Colossians 1:25–2:10, correcting the Latin Vulgate's translation of terms like "mystery," "fullness," and "plunder." He emphasizes that Paul's warning against philosophy refers to being "plundered" or "carried off as prey" rather than merely being "deceived."</summary>
<keywords>Colossians, Paul, Christ, Church, mystery, sacrament, fullness, deity, plundering, philosophy, Erasmus, Theophylact, Ambrose</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed philological and theological commentary on the Epistle to the Colossians. In this section, he moves into the core of Chapter 2, focusing on the sufficiency of Christ over the requirements of the Mosaic Law, specifically addressing the metaphors of "bodily" fullness, spiritual circumcision, and the "handwritten bond" of debt canceled at the Cross.</meta>

### TO THE COLOSSIANS. CHAPTER II.

...in him you are filled, who is the head of all principality <margin>11</margin> and power, In whom also you were circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands, in the stripping off of the body of the sins <margin>12</margin> of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ, Buried with him in baptism, in which also you rose again through faith in the working of God, who raised <margin>13</margin> him from the dead. And you, when you were dead in your sins and the uncircumcision of your flesh, he brought to life together with him, forgiving us all <margin>14</margin> our sins, Blotting out the handwriting against us in its decrees, which was contrary to us, and he took it out of the way, nailing it to the <margin>15</margin> cross; Stripping the principalities and the powers, he made a public example of them, triumphing over them <margin>16</margin> in himself. Let no one therefore judge you in food, or in <margin>17</margin> drink, or in respect of a festival, or of the new moon, or of the sabbaths, which are a shadow...

---

...given "corporally" <gloss>original: σωματικῶς</gloss>, *corporaliter*, so that he might exclude the shadows of the Mosaic Law. For the "Body" is opposed to the "shadow," so that there is no need here for a complex explanation about the Deity, which remained joined to the body during the three days of death even though the soul was separated. This is despite the fact that Theophylact <note>A 12th-century Byzantine exegete often cited by Erasmus</note> offers a double exposition different from ours: "corporally," that is, according to nature and substance, not just according to effect (as it was in the Prophets); or because the Deity was never separated from the body of Christ. Where Theophylact drew these ideas from, I do not know. Everyone is entitled to their own judgment. To me, a simpler explanation seems more consistent with the topic at hand—the one found in the *Ordinary Gloss* <note>The standard medieval commentary on the Bible</note>, concerning the shadows of the Law and the truth of the Gospel; for it follows, "but the body is of Christ." Augustine interprets it in this sense in Letter 59. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father known for his preaching</note> is even more subtle: in Christ dwells the whole fullness of the Godhead, and that corporally, "as in a head." And through Him, it dwells in His body, which is the Church; for the head and the body are one. And it follows, "And you are complete in him." For Paul always does this: he makes us close to Christ, as when he says, "He raised us up together with Him and made us sit with Him." And, "If we suffer with Him, we shall also reign with Him." Also, "He will give us all things with Him." Again, while he calls us co-heirs with Christ. What Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> writes about the divine nature personally united to the flesh of Christ is very true; however, Paul is not dealing with that matter here. Rather, he is striving to persuade them that whoever is grafted into the body of Christ through faith does not need the protection of the Mosaic Law, circumcision, and similar things, since in Christ all things are present truly and effectively.

<margin>14 Not handmade</margin> <gloss>original: ἀχειροποιήτῳ</gloss>: this is a compound word, meaning that which is made without hands.

<margin>15 Of the body of the flesh</margin> In Greek it reads thus, <gloss>original: τοῦ σώματος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τῆς σαρκός</gloss>, that is, of the body of the sins of the flesh: this refers to that which is liable to carnal sins. Augustine, in Letter 59 to Paulinus, testifies that it was written this way in some Latin copies, lest anyone should entirely despise them, being too hostile to the Greeks.

<margin>16 But in the circumcision</margin> The word "But" is redundant here.

<margin>17 In which you also rose again</margin> <gloss>original: συνηγέρθητε</gloss>, that is, you rose together. And this is how Ambrose reads it.

<margin>18 And you, when you were</margin> In Chrysostom and Theophylact, the pronoun is everywhere in the first person, "us" and "our" <gloss>original: ἡμᾶς & ἡμῶν</gloss>. Likewise in what follows.

<margin>19 Forgiving you</margin> "To us" is the first person in the Greek, and this is how Ambrose reads it. For Paul is discussing the "uncircumcision" of the Jews, which they held in their souls.

<margin>20 Blotting out what was against</margin> It would have been better to say, "the handwriting being blotted out which was against us." And so Ambrose reads it, <gloss>original: Ἐξαλείψας τὸ καθ' ἡμῶν χειρόγραφον</gloss>.

<margin>21 The handwriting of the decree</margin> In Greek it is "by the decrees" <gloss>original: τοῖς δόγμασιν</gloss>. The Greek manuscripts distinguish it so that you understand the handwriting was blotted out—the bond that was contrary to us through the decrees of the Mosaic Law, or through the decrees of the divine Law. Certainly, Saint Augustine in Letter 59 to Paulinus reads, "the handwriting in the decrees." Theophylact, following Chrysostom, interprets it as the "handwriting of the Mosaic profession," or the obligation to God, who said to Adam and Eve, "In whatever day you eat, you shall die," which was removed and made obsolete by the decree of Gospel faith. The metaphor is drawn from legal obligations. A signed contract <gloss>original: αὐτόγραφος</gloss>—that is, one you have written with your own hand—is a more powerful obligation; the Greeks call this a <term>chirographum</term> <note>A handwritten bond or "I.O.U."</note>. This is rendered void either by crossing it out (canceling it with transverse lines), by erasing it (using a sponge on bark or a stylus on wax tablets), or by tearing it up. In the crossing out, traces of the writing remain; in the erasure, they do not. Paul, therefore, to emphasize God's mercy toward us, first declares that we were so bound that there was no room for denial. For the profession of the Law was like a "handwriting," and the matter itself, and even our conscience, proved us to be transgressors of the Law. What then remained but the penalty owed by the pact—that is, from our own handwriting? Here God's kindness overflowed: if He had condemned us, we could not complain. If He had relaxed part of the debt and left part, much thanks would be owed. If He had simply crossed out the bond, traces of the old obligation would remain; now He has blotted and obliterated it once and for all, covering whatever was contrary to us and from which a legal action could be reborn. Not content with this, He tore and mangled the bond, taking it out of the way and nailing it to the cross, where what we owed hung for us, and He turned the obligation of death into a covenant of eternal salvation. Saint Chrysostom noted something of this sort in a certain Homily, and also in his Commentaries. Nor is it useless to philosophize on the emphasis of these words, especially in the writings of blessed Paul, whose speech overflows everywhere with figures and metaphors. The Scholiast on all Paul's Epistles indicates there are some who interpret the "handwriting" as the memory of God, who preserves our sins; according to that saying, "Are these things not stored up <column-break/> <page-num>890</page-num> with me, and sealed in my treasures?" And what Jeremiah says, "The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron and the point of a diamond." All these things are correct. Nevertheless, it seems to me less fitting to join this with those who interpret "decrees" <gloss>original: δόγματα</gloss> as "faith," since the word *dogma* is never found used in that sense by the Apostles. Since in this very chapter, following what he says about avoiding the prescriptions of the Jews, he says those who either prescribe external things or are urged toward superstition by such prescriptions are "subject to decrees" <gloss>original: δογματίζεσθαι</gloss>, such as: "Touch not, taste not, handle not." Therefore, it seems more probable, following the flow of this speech, that <term>dogmata</term> <note>decrees or ordinances</note> here refers to the Jewish prescriptions, the head of which was circumcision.

<margin>22 He led them away</margin> <gloss>original: ἐδειγμάτισεν</gloss>. Which Ambrose translates as "he put on display." Augustine in Letter 59 to Paulinus reads "stripping," expressing the Greek word more faithfully than elegantly. He brought it up in the same way in his book *On the Christian Struggle*, chapter 2. It is a wonder, however, why he subsequently brings up this passage with these words: "Stripping himself of the flesh, he made an example of the principalities and powers," as if Paul meant that the principalities are only conquered if the victor strips off his flesh. For so also does the translator and author of the book *Against Faustus*, book 15, chapter 29. So he relates it in the book *On Merit and the Forgiveness of Sins*, book 1, chapter 27. Indeed, Hilary in book 9 of *On the Trinity* relates this passage: "Blotting out the handwriting that was against us in sentences, which was contrary to us, he took it from the middle, nailing it to the cross, having stripped off the flesh, and made the powers an object of display." And lest anyone think this happened through a corruption of the scripture, he repeats the mention of "flesh" in his explanation. The commentary of the Scholiast notes something similar. It seems he took "stripping" <gloss>original: ἀπεκδυσάμενος</gloss> reflexively, as "stripping himself," just as wrestlers throw off their clothes to be more agile; so Christ threw off his flesh. Thus, those who prepare themselves for a fight or a contest are said to be "stripping off" <gloss>original: ἀπεκδυόμενοι</gloss>, so they cannot be grabbed. Theophylact points out this interpretation, which in my judgment is genuine. And the Greek manuscripts distinguish "having stripped" <gloss>original: ἀπεκδυσάμενος</gloss> from what follows, so we would not take it that the principalities were the ones stripped. Rather, Christ in the fight threw off his flesh as a garment, and led his enemies away in a triumph. But to the point: here the Latin translator renders the same word for "speaking boldly" <gloss>original: παῤῥησιάζεσθαι</gloss>—that is, to translate or lead—at the beginning of Matthew; and in this place "he made a show of them" <gloss>original: ἐδειγμάτισεν</gloss>. While the former means to turn into an example, this latter means to put on display and propose for all to see. For it alludes to the custom of those celebrating a triumph, who carried their trophies around and displayed the monuments of victory to the people, and so forth. If Thomas [Aquinas] could have consulted the Greek interpreters, there would have been no need here for two interpretations instead of one: "He led," he says, "the saints into heaven." Or he led, that is, he expelled the demons from man. Origen, in his 4th Homily on Exodus, or certainly his translator, explains the force of this word: "Those whom Christ is said to have led away at his coming—that is, led as captives—and triumphed over on the wood of the cross."

<margin>23 Confidently in public</margin> In "boldness" <gloss>original: παῤῥησίᾳ</gloss>: which Ambrose reads as "in authority." Origen in his 8th Homily on Joshua reads, "so he shone freely triumphing." Now, <italic>parrhesia</italic> is when someone dares things openly, especially in speaking, although Paul sometimes uses it for other things. "Publicly triumphing"—it should be noted in passing that "stripping" and "triumphing" and the other participles in this place are in the past tense. "Triumphing over them in himself"—the translator of Origen’s Homily on Joshua 8 indicates that in some manuscripts it is read "in himself." However, today the Greek copies agree in this very place with ours. There are those who are troubled by this point of grammar—whether it is correct Latin to say "triumphing them" <note>using "triumph" as a transitive verb with a direct object</note>; certainly, Virgil spoke of "triumphed nations." Nor is this color of speech rare among historians. To "triumph a woman" is rarer, though it is found in Trebellius Pollio. "In himself" <gloss>original: ἐν αὐτῷ</gloss> can be taken as "by himself," that is, by his own defenses.

<margin>24 Judge in food or in drink</margin> There is a pleasant affinity of words in the Greek which the translator did not attempt: "in eating or in drinking" <gloss>original: ἐν βρώσει, ἢ ἐν πόσει</gloss>. You could say "in edibles or in drinkables." For this figure, besides its pleasantness, carries a sense of contempt and disdain. It is like the phrase "these daily forms." What will those people say to this, who judge their neighbor by nothing more than food, drink, and clothing?

<margin>25 New Moon</margin> <gloss>original: νουμηνίας</gloss>, that is, "of the new moon": from <italic>neos</italic> (new) and <italic>mēn</italic> (moon or month). For the Greeks do not start the month from the calends, but from the beginning of the new moon.

<margin>26 Which are a shadow of things to come</margin> Augustine, in his 6th book *Against Faustus*, cites from handwritten books "which is a shadow." Perhaps someone semi-skilled in Greek changed "which [plural]" <gloss>original: ἅ</gloss> into "which [singular]" <gloss>original: ὅ</gloss>, thinking the plural relative pronoun did not agree with the singular verb "is" <gloss>original: ἐστί</gloss>.
