<summary>Erasmus provides a linguistic and theological breakdown of Colossians 2:9-17, focusing on the metaphor of Christ as the "body" that replaces the "shadows" of the Old Testament Law. He explores the legal metaphor of the 'chirographum' (debt-bond) and the imagery of a Roman triumph to explain Christ's victory on the cross.</summary>
<keywords>Colossians, handwriting of debt, decrees, circumcision, triumph, new moon, shadow of things to come, Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Ambrose, Augustine, Origen</keywords>

--- Page 526 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s philological and theological commentary on the second chapter of the Epistle to the Colossians. Having just discussed the "shadows" of the Old Law, Erasmus now moves into the specifics of Paul's warnings against the worship of angels, false humility, and the burdensome human traditions that mimic the "elements of the world."</meta>

# EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER II.

<margin>18</margin> <margin>A</margin> …a shadow of things to come, but the body belongs to Christ. Let no one defraud you of your prize, delighting in humility and the worship of angels, intruding into things he has not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind,
<margin>19</margin> and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together by joints and ligaments, grows with the growth of God.
<margin>20</margin> If therefore you died with Christ from the elements of the world, why, as though living in the world, do you submit to 
<margin>21 22</margin> decrees? "Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle," which all perish with the using, according to the commandments <margin>B</margin> and doctrines of men.

---

27 **But the body is of Christ**] The Greek scholia <note>interpretive comments from Byzantine scholars</note>, specifically Theophylact, indicate that this passage can be read in two ways. First, as: *those things are a shadow, but the body itself*, that is, *the truth, belongs to Christ* <note>original: τὸ δὲ σῶμα τοῦ Χριστοῦ</note>. Alternatively: *the body of Christ*, let no one deceive you—so that you refer "body" to the faithful, who are the members of Christ. The sense would then be: "You, who are the body of Christ, let no one turn you away from the prize you began to earn by believing in Him." This second sense is approved by Augustine in his *Letter to Paulinus*. However, the first reading seems more fitting to me, as it is less forced. Ambrose seems to seize upon a third meaning, as if both "shadow" and "body" refer back to the preceding list: *food, drink, feast, new moon, sabbaths*. All these things would be shadows of things to come, yet also the body of Christ. For he concludes: *All these things are the body of Christ*, because names of elements are based on their effects. But in my opinion, the Apostle calls those things the "body of Christ" because whatever was foreshadowed in them was fully exhibited in Christ, so that now those shadows should be neglected. When the body itself is absent, we feed on shadows as best we can; when the body is present, even the shadow is a nuisance. And this sense, as I mentioned, is followed by Augustine in *Letter 59* to Paulinus.

<margin>D</margin> 28 **Let no one seduce you**] The Greek is <term>katabrabeuetō</term> <note>original: καταβραβευέτω</note>, that is, *to cheat someone out of the prize or reward*. Jerome interprets it this way in his *Questions to Algasia*, Question 10: *Let no one take the prize against you*. For when someone is in a contest and, through the unfairness of the judge or the plots of the masters, loses the prize and the palm of victory owed to him, he is said to be <term>katabrabeuesthai</term>. Jerome suggests this word might be peculiar to the Cilicians <note>The Roman province where Paul was born</note>. The Greek scholia warn that <term>katabrabeuein</term> is used whenever the victory belongs to one person, but the prize is given to another. Ambrose reads, *let no one conquer you*. Augustine in *Letter 59* reads, *let no one convict you*. From these, it is clear enough how far the opinion of Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>A contemporary French humanist scholar, often called Stapulensis</note>—otherwise a learned man—is from the truth in his first edition. He was led into this error by Valla, who thinks <term>katabrabeuein</term> means *to call out to the prize* or *to show off the prize*. It is perhaps a small point, but I should mention in passing that the Latin should be *brabium*, not *bravium*—written with a ‘b’, the second letter of the alphabet, not a ‘v’. Furthermore, the second-to-last syllable should be sharp or circumflexed, as it is in Greek: <term>brabíon</term> or <term>brabēum</term>. Those who write on the etymology of Greek words believe *brabeion* is derived from *a-brabeion*, with some letters changed and transposed, meaning a *rod* or *scepter*. Thus, those who carry royal scepters are called <term>brabeutai</term> <note>judges of a contest</note>, because it was their role to award the prize to the victor in contests to prevent riots among the competitors. Martial indicates something similar in a preface when he says, "the rod against the net-fighter." Some think a small palm branch was traditionally given to the victor as a symbol, and that rod was called a *brabeion*. Therefore, *katabrabeuein* means to intercept the prize, not to summon someone toward it. Hesychius indicates that *parabrabeuein* means the same thing. Nor is it proven that this word is exclusively Cilician, as Aristotle uses it in the first book of his *Rhetoric* when he says that a judge of court cases is a "just prize-giver" <note>original: βραβευτὴς</note>. Aristotle has nothing barbaric in his speech; he is pure and Attic. Furthermore, when Paul adds the word "willing" <note>original: θέλων</note>, it is not meant to contrast with "unwilling," but acts as if you said *on purpose* or *with deliberate effort*, to show that those people were maliciously plotting against the Colossians. Although Augustine, in his letter to Paulinus, does not attach "willing" to the verb "seduce," but to what follows: "in humility." *Willing in humility*, as if you said, "An affector of humility," just as we say *ethelodoulos* <note>a "willing slave" or voluntary servant</note>. The Greeks distinguish it in the same way. From Ambrose, it is gathered that they wanted to cast down men's minds through a studied humility, so that they would not lift themselves up to heavenly things. Theophylact does not disagree, separating the participle "willing" from the previous words and interpreting it as the false apostles forcing the worship of certain Angels, so that through them a path might be opened for men to a Father who was otherwise inaccessible. But Paul, relying on Christ, breathes something far above the Angels.

<margin>E</margin> 29 **In humility**] In Greek: <term>tapeinophrosunē</term> <note>original: ταπεινοφροσύνῃ</note>. This refers to modesty of the mind, which is why Ambrose rendered it *in humility of mind*, distinguishing it from the humility of condition or social status, which is called *tapeinōsis*. And yet, in the meantime, he seems to have used "humility of mind" in a bad sense. For those who boast of visions of Angels seek out coarse and abject minds that they can easily deceive; otherwise, someone with a sharp nose <note>meaning someone discerning</note> would immediately smell the fraud. Unless, following Augustine's opinion, you prefer to take it as the simulated modesty of the False Apostles.

30 **And the religion of Angels**] In Greek: <term>thrēskeia</term> <note>original: θρησκείᾳ</note>. This sounds like "religion," sometimes used in a good sense, but often meaning a foreign or superstitious one. The word, as people think, is derived from the Thracians, because among them Orpheus invented many things about the Gods, handing down ceremonies by which they should be worshiped.

<margin>F</margin> 31 **Walking**] In Greek: *intruding into those things which he has not seen* <note>original: ἃ μὴ ἑώρακεν ἐμβατεύων</note>. Although Jerome, in the same place, interprets *embateuōn* as *walking haughtily*. It is a wonder why Saint Augustine reads *insisting on things he has not seen*—as if he had read *embateuōn* with a ‘p’ <note>likely confusing it with a word for treading upon</note>. Ambrose reads: *behold, extolling the things he sees*. Hesychius indicates that *embateusai* sometimes means the same as *to occupy*, such as a place, a house, or an entire inheritance. But Jerome's—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...shadow of things to come, <margin>17</margin> but the body is Christ's. <margin>18</margin> <margin>18</margin> Let no one snatch away your palm of victory by deliberate effort <margin>29</margin> through humility <margin>30</margin> and the superstition of angels, <margin>31</margin> walking haughtily in the things he has not seen, vainly puffed up <margin>32</margin> by the mind of his flesh, <margin>19</margin> and not holding the Head, from which the whole body through <margin>19</margin> joints and ligaments, supplied and knit together, <margin>33</margin> grows with the growth of God. Therefore if you are dead <margin>20</margin> with Christ <margin>34</margin> from the elements of the world, <margin>35</margin> why, as though living in the world, <margin>36</margin> are you held by decrees? <margin>21</margin> Do not <margin>21</margin> touch, <margin>37</margin> do not taste, and do not handle; all of which <margin>22</margin> perish by their very <margin>38</margin> misuse, according to the precepts and doctrines of <margin>22</margin> men.

---

<margin>B</margin> opinion is bolder. I think the metaphor is drawn from the buskins <note>platform boots</note> of tragic actors, since this type is called *embades*, because those who play a King or a God walk sublimely in them. Augustine indicates to Paulinus that in some Latin manuscripts it was written "things he has seen," just as Ambrose also reads "things he has seen" in some, and "has not seen" in others. But it is strange that while Paul seems to be speaking of visions of Angels, Augustine interprets it as sacrifices—which someone values highly because he has seen them observed somewhere, or because he hasn't seen that they should be done, but is led by popular opinion. It is no less strange that Ambrose twists this to refer to the study of Astrology and Philosophy.

32 **By the sense of his flesh**] In Greek: <term>hypo tou noos</term> <note>original: ὑπὸ τοῦ νοὸς</note>, that is, *by the mind*, as Saint Ambrose reads it. For that is what he calls the disposition of an ungodly man.

33 **Grows into the increase**] In Greek: <term>auxei tēn auxēsin</term> <note>original: αὔξει τὴν αὔξησιν</note>. This is a Greek figure of speech, as if you said "he lives a life" or "he rejoices a joy." So in this place: "he grows a growth."

34 **From the elements of this world**] The word "this" is redundant; it is simply *from the elements of the world*. For he calls "the world" whatever is seen.

<margin>C</margin> 35 **Why yet as though**] The word "yet" is redundant. Nor is "why as though" <note>original: τί ὡς</note> added in Ambrose, and so on. *Living in the world*. "In the world" is in the Greek, and that is how Ambrose reads it.

36 **By decrees**] In Greek: <term>dogmatizesthe</term> <note>original: δογματίζεσθε</note>, that is, *you are decreed*. Although the word "decreed" does not fully explain what Paul meant. He means that they are being led by the decrees and constitutions of men, as if they were subjects, and this is what *dogmatizesthe* marks—to be "dogmatized." For in Greek, a *dogma* is a decree, which Paul almost always takes in a negative sense, for laws prescribed by the will of men rather than God. This is just as we call the decrees of Popes "decretals," distinguishing them from Divine Law. For those precepts about the choice of foods, the observation of days, and sacrifices began to belong to men once they had vanished in the eyes of God. The Greek scholia warn that Paul did not say *dogmatizete* <note>you make decrees</note> but *dogmatizesthe* <note>you are burdened with decrees</note>. Theophylact noted the same, though the Latin translator brought out a very different meaning. The Greek says: "See also how it has the accusative *dogmati*, *dogmatizesthe*: for the laws punish those children who have just begun to learn, being dogmatized and shaped as to what must be done." And the translator rendered it: "Notice how you argue them of folly and rebuke them when you decree," he says: "as if you say, no differently than children are accustomed to in play, you act as dictators, you who were born yesterday and were recently instructed; for you have come into the assembly to bring forth opinions on dogma, having been sanctioned as to what is necessary to do." But the meaning of the Greek speech is this: "Look at that as well, how he silently taxes them by saying *dogmatizesthe*." Since, like children, he says, who have just begun to learn, you are shaped, and it is dictated and prescribed to you what is necessary to do. I have warned you of this, Reader, so that you may understand the reliability of a translator of a foreign tongue. Therefore, I do not approve of Jacques Lefèvre's opinion here, who translates it as "you seek decrees." The common translator and Ambrose seem to have read *dogmatizete*. Tertullian seems to have read the same in his book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: "How," he says, "do some of you bring a sentence as though living in the world?" It is a wonder, however, what Cyprian was following in his third book *To Quirinus* when he reads, "Why, as though living in the world, do you follow vain things?" Unless perhaps because the word *dogma* comes from the verb *dokein* <note>to seem or to think</note>, he calls the opinions on human matters "vain."

<margin>E</margin> 37 **Do not have tasted**] These three words in the Greek are in the singular number: <note>original: μὴ ἅψῃ, μηδὲ γεύσῃ, μηδὲ θίγῃς</note>, that is, *Do not touch, nor taste, nor handle*. And these seem to be said by Paul <term>mimētikōs</term>, that is, through imitation—which some list among the rhetorical figures. For thus spoke those who burdened Christians with their decrees: "Do not taste this, do not touch that, do not handle this." And with these ceremonies, they subjected those whom Christ wanted to be free to a kind of tyranny. And would that in these times certain Priests did not do the same thing! Omitting those things that pertain more closely to piety, they heap constitutions upon constitutions, acting only to make the common people as entangled as possible, rendering them beholden to themselves and serving their own tyranny and profit. It should not, therefore, be taken as if Paul is forbidding the touching or tasting of anything, but he is rebuking the arrogance of those who were forbidding these things with great pride. Saint Augustine clearly indicates the same in *Letter 59* to Paulinus. And yet <margin>F</margin> Ambrose interprets it as if Paul is deterring us from all hope of worldly things—in my opinion, not attentively enough, if I may say so with respect to such a great man. He cites the same in the same sense in his commentary on Psalm 118, Sermon 18. Again in the book on the *Patriarch Abraham*, chapters 2 and 6, and several other places. Tertullian brings up this passage of Paul in the fifth book *Against Marcion*. And Theophylact, with Chrysostom, stands with us. Even more evidently, the *Glossa Ordinaria* <note>The standard medieval commentary on the Bible</note>.

38 **By the use itself**] In Greek: <term>tē apochrēsei</term> <note>original: τῇ ἀποχρήσει</note>, that is, *by the misuse* or *consumption*. And Ambrose reads, *through the using up*. For he is discussing food and drink, which are consumed by use and excreted into the latrine. For one is properly said to "use up" those things which are consumed by use, as the writings of the legal experts also teach us.

<summary>In this passage, Erasmus provides a philological critique of Colossians 2:18-22, focusing on the Greek term for being "cheated of a prize" and rebuking the "dogmatizing" of believers. He uses the text to launch a contemporary critique of the clergy who use complex human traditions and ceremonies to exercise tyranny over the laity.</summary>

# 893 TO THE COLOSSIANS. CHAPTER III. 894

<margin>A</margin>
**23** ...according to the commandments and teachings of men? These things indeed have an appearance of wisdom in self-imposed worship, false humility, and severity to the body, but are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh.

**III, 1** If then you were raised with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God.
**2** Set your mind on things above, not on things on the earth.
**3** For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
**4** When Christ who is our life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.
**5** Therefore put to death your members which are on the earth: fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, <margin>B</margin>
**6** which is idolatry. Because of these things the wrath of God is coming upon the sons of disobedience,
**7** in which you yourselves once walked when you lived in them.
**8** But now you yourselves must put off all these: anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy language out of your mouth.
**9** Do not lie to one another, since you have put off the old man with his deeds,
**10** and have put on the new man who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of Him who created him,
**11** where there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcised nor uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all.
**12** Therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, put on tender mercies, kindness, humility, <margin>C</margin>
**13** meekness, longsuffering; bearing with one another, and forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another; even as Christ forgave you, so you also must do.
**14** But above all these things put on love, which is the bond of perfection.
**15** And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called...
<meta>catchword: and</meta>

---

39 **Indeed having the appearance of wisdom**] <margin>and</margin> Here, the word <term>reason</term> <note>original: Λόγον / logon</note> is interpreted as "appearance." Because Thomas Aquinas felt this was a bit harsh, he connects it to what follows—"in superstition"—so that we understand this "reason for wisdom" exists not simply, but in relation to superstition. But to me, the sentence seems incomplete. Paul began with the particle "on the one hand" <note>original: μὲν / men</note> and did not provide the "on the other hand" <note>original: δὲ / de</note> that should respond to it. Therefore, it seems to me that <term>logos</term> in this place sounds like "speech" or "words," as opposed to the actual reality. If he had finished the sentence, he would have said, "but in this manner..." These things all seem learned and magnificent in word—evidently having come from Angels, as they tell it. However, in reality, they are far removed from the religion of Christ, which is situated neither in superstition nor in that abasement of mind where men are led around like cattle at the whim of some little fellow, nor in the harming of the body. God intended the body to be honored with food, not tortured with starvation; the true religion lies in purity of life and charity. Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine commentator</note> openly agrees with us. Furthermore, he calls the "honor" of the body "sustenance" <note>original: subsidium</note> here, following the style of Hebrew speech, just as in other places: "honor widows," and "Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor."

40 **In superstition**] <note>original: ἐν ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ / en ethelothreskeia</note>. This is false religion, according to Jerome's interpretation in the passage I just cited. For superstition is called <term>ethelothreskeia</term>. Ambrose reads it as "superstition." Furthermore, the Greek word sounds as if you were to say "spontaneous religion," which is when someone invents a religion for themselves of their own accord. For the word for religion, <term>threskeia</term>, comes from the Thracians, among whom Orpheus first began to talk nonsense about the Gods (as was just mentioned), and <term>ethelo</term> means "I will" or "I want." This fits perfectly with ceremonies devised by petty men.

41 **And humility**] <note>original: ταπεινοφροσύνῃ / tapeinophrosyne</note>. Saint Jerome also notes this word, as it is used improperly in this place; while elsewhere it usually signifies a virtue, here it signifies a vice—one by which a person thinks lowly and earthly things and is of such an abject mind that he allows himself to be led by the nose like an ox by the precepts of men.

42 **Not to spare the body**] <note>original: καὶ ἀφειδίᾳ σώματος / kai apheidia somatos</note>, which literally sounds like "un-sparingness," that is, when one does not spare a certain thing. For <term>pheidomai</term> means "I spare," and the "a" is a negating particle. Ambrose reads it as "to the vexation of the body." Augustine also indicates this reading in his *Letter to Paulinus*, which we have often mentioned. He is thinking of those who, out of superstition, used to slash or mutilate their own bodies, or exhaust themselves with immoderate fasting. Some remnants of this practice remain today among the "Flagellants" in Italy, many examples of which Apuleius mentions in his *The Golden Ass*.

1 **Those things which are above**] <note>original: τὰ ἄνω / ta ano</note>. Why not rather "heavenly things"? And for "set your mind on" <note>original: φρονεῖτε / phroneite</note>, "care for" is better than "savor."

2 **Your life**] The Greeks read "our," <note>original: ἡμῶν / hemon</note>, that is, "our," in the first person.

3 **Lust**] <note>original: πάθος / pathos</note>. You may translate this as "disease," or rather "softness" <note>original: mollitiem</note>, so that you understand it to refer to the effeminate and the "pathic" <note>passive partners in male-male intercourse</note>. For otherwise, what was the point of adding "lust" when he had already said "fornication"? A genus is not typically added after a species. Furthermore, Horace calls "softness" a disease in his *Odes*: "...with a herd of shameful men, diseased."

4 **On account of which comes**] <note>original: Δι' ἃ ἔρχεται / Di ha erchetai</note>. That is, "Because of which [the wrath of God] comes." Here "comes" is in the present tense; understand that divine wrath is *accustomed* to come because of these things. For this is what he calls "vengeance."

5 **Sons of unbelief**] What he had translated above as "mistrust," <note>original: ἀπειθείας / apeitheias</note>, also means "disobedience." Although in this place Ambrose does not add "upon the sons of mistrust." He only reads, "Because of which the wrath of God comes." We have spoken more than once about the Hebrew form of this expression <note>i.e., "sons of..."</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...of men, 39 which in word indeed have a show of wisdom 40 through superstition 41 and humility of mind 42 and harming of the body, not through any honor, but for the filling of the flesh. Therefore, if you have risen III. 1 together with Christ, seek the heavenly things, where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God. 2 Care for heavenly things, not earthly ones. For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. Whenever Christ is manifested, 4 who is our life, then you also will be manifested with him in glory. Put to death therefore your earthly members: 3 debauchery, uncleanness, softness, evil desire, and greed, which is the worship of idols. 4 Because of which the wrath of God is accustomed to come 5 upon the unmanageable sons, 6 among whom you once walked, when you lived in these things. But now you also put away everything: anger, indignation, malice, slandering, 7 foul language from your mouth. 8 Do not lie one against another, 9 after you have stripped off the old man with his deeds, and have put on the new man, who is renewed 10 to knowledge and the image of him who created him, where there is not 11 Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, 12 barbarian, Scythian, slave, free: but Christ is all in all. Therefore, be clothed, as the elect of God, holy and 13 beloved, with bowels of mercies, courtesy, 14 modesty, 15 mildness, 16 gentleness, bearing with one another, and 13 forgiving one another mutually, if anyone has a complaint against another: just as Christ forgave you, so also you. Above all these things, however, 14 17 have charity, 18 which is the bond of perfection. And let the peace of God 19 bear the palm in your hearts, 15

---

6 **In which you also**] <note>original: 'Ἐν οἷς / En hois</note>. The Greek phrasing is ambiguous, because the pronoun could refer either to the "disobedient sons" among whom the Colossians once were, or to the "vices" which he mentioned just before. Certainly, what follows immediately—"when you lived in them"—pertains to the vices.

7 **Filthy speech**] <note>original: αἰσχρολογίαν / aischrologian</note>, that is, "foul-talking."

8 **Do not lie to one another**] <note>original: Μὴ ψεύδεσθε εἰς ἀλλήλους / Me pseuthesthe eis allelous</note>. That is, "Let not one lie against the other." For what is "lie to one another," as the Translator <note>the Vulgate</note> renders it, if not "to lie in turn"? He adds an accusative case to the Greek verb.

9 **Stripping off**] <note>original: ἀπεκδυσάμενοι / apekdysamenoi</note>, that is, "unclothing," meaning "after you have stripped off," for it is in the past tense. The Translator repeatedly renders this word as "despoiling." It alludes to what he said before: "Christ conquered by stripping off the flesh."

10 **Into the knowledge of God**] The word "of God" is redundant, according to the Greek manuscripts. Ambrose does not add it. Nor was it added in the Donatian manuscript. Both Canterbury manuscripts agreed with these. "Male and female." I do not find these words among the Greeks. Nor does Theophylact touch upon them. Chrysostom does not even read them, nor does Ambrose. But it seems to have been added here from the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 3. Both Canterbury codices supported this as well.

11 **Gentile and Jew**] <note>original: Ἕλλην / Hellen</note>, that is, "Greek," for which he translates "Gentile."

12 **Barbarian**] After this word, the Greeks omit the conjunction, and the speech becomes more fiery. For first, he joined Jew with Greek and circumcision with uncircumcision in pairs; then, without a conjunction, he couples Barbarian with Scythian, and slave with free. Furthermore, he opposed "Scythian" to "Barbarian," not because the Scythian is not a barbarian, but because compared to him, other barbarians are not considered barbarians <note>Scythians were viewed as the most extreme examples of uncivilized people</note>.

13 **Beloved, bowels of mercy**] "Beloved" <note>original: ἠγαπημένοι / agapemenoi</note> here is a participle, not a noun. And it is not "of mercy" in the singular, but <note>original: οἰκτιρμῶν / oiktirmon</note>, that is, "of mercies," in the plural.

14 **Humility**] <note>original: ταπεινοφροσύνην / tapeinophrosynen</note>. Ambrose translates this as "humility of sense." We preferred "modesty." For "modesty" is closer to what the Greeks call <term>tapeinophrosyne</term>. "Humility of sense" sounds more like a vice, such as "abject in mind." Even though the Greek word signifies something more than "modesty." For a modest person is one who is not arrogant; but a <term>tapeinophron</term> is one who attributes less to himself than he deserves.

15 **Modesty**] <note>original: πραΰτητα / prayteta</note>, that is, "meekness" or "gentleness."

16 **Patience**] <note>original: μακροθυμίαν / makrothymian</note>, literally "long-suffering," or gentleness of mind, or moderation of mind, by which one is not easily provoked.

17 **Have charity**] I do not find "Have" among the Greeks, nor in Ambrose; the accusative "charity" must be referred back to the previous verb, "be clothed."

18 **Which is the bond of perfection**] <note>original: σύνδεσμος τελειότητος / syndesmos teleiotetos</note>, that is, "the bond of integrity." For he was looking toward the body, in which the spirit binds and connects all the members, which would otherwise fall apart. Although I am not unaware that many interpret it otherwise. Furthermore, it is "the peace of God" in both the Greeks and Ambrose, not "the peace of Christ."

19 **Exults**] <note>original: βραβευέτω / brabeueto</note>. That is, "let it be given in place of a prize," or "let it happen," or "let it bear the palm." This means: let not anger judge in you, or envy, or pride, but let peace carry the palm <note>the prize of victory</note>, so that one thinks he has conquered if he has preserved peace at the cost of other things. For this, finally, is the peace of God. Otherwise, the peace of the world is born from vengeance. Theophylact interprets it almost in this sense. Now indeed...

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER IV.

<margin>16</margin> in one body, and be thankful. Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with grace <margin>17</margin> singing in your heart to the Lord. And whatever you do in word or in deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father through <margin>18</margin> him. Wives, be subject to your own husbands, <margin>19</margin> as is fitting in the Lord. Husbands, love your <margin>20</margin> wives, and do not be bitter toward them. Children, obey your parents in all things; for this <margin>21</margin> is well-pleasing to the Lord. Fathers, do not provoke your children, so that they do not lose <margin>22</margin> heart. Slaves, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh, not with eye-service as men-pleasers, but in sincerity of heart, fearing God. <margin>23</margin> And whatever you do, work from the soul, <margin>24</margin> as for the Lord, and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance, <margin>25</margin> for you serve the Lord Christ. But he who does wrong <margin>IV. 1</margin> will receive back what he did wrong, and there is no partiality. Masters, provide justice and equality to your slaves, knowing that you also have a Lord in heaven. <margin>2</margin> Persevere in prayer, being watchful in it with <margin>3</margin> thanksgiving, praying also for us at the same time, that God may open a door for the word to us, to speak the mystery of Christ, because of which I am also bound, <margin>4</margin> that I may manifest <margin>5</margin> it as I ought to speak. Walk in wisdom toward <margin>6</margin> those outside, redeeming the time. Let your word always be with grace, seasoned with salt, to know how it is necessary <margin>7</margin> for you to answer each one. Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord, will make known to you all things concerning me. <margin>8</margin> I have sent him to you for this very reason, that he might know your circumstances and comfort <margin>9</margin> your hearts, together with Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you; they will make <margin>10</margin> known to you everything that is happening here. Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you, and Mark the cousin of Barnabas, concerning whom you received instructions: if he comes to you, receive him.

---

Is it relevant to review what recent theologians have commented on this place, following the word "rejoicing"?

<margin>A</margin> 20 *in which* ] Or "into which," thus the Greek *en* <note>original: "ἐν"</note>, or "unto which."
21 *And be thankful* ] Greek: *kai eucharistoi ginesthe* <note>original: "καὶ εὐχάριστοι γίνεσθε"</note>. We previously noted, according to Jerome's opinion, that *eucharistos* <note>original: "εὐχάριστος"</note> in the Divine Scriptures is taken to mean "gracious and lovely," which I believe is how it should be understood here. Indeed, he added this as if indicating the reason why peace can remain among them: if they are companionable and kind toward everyone, inclined to do good for all. <term>Chrysostom</term> <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching.</note> interprets it in this sense, so that the "thankful" person is one who shows himself to his fellow servants as he has experienced God to be toward himself. <term>Theophylact</term> <note>Theophylact of Ohrid (c. 1050–1108), a Byzantine commentator who summarized earlier Patristic thought.</note> interprets it as being thankful toward God—that is, mindful of how He has been toward us, so that we in turn may be merciful toward our fellow servants. Truly, this second exposition seems more forced to me.

<margin>B</margin> 22 *Abundantly* ] Greek: *plousiōs* <note>original: "πλουσίως"</note>, as if you were to say "opulently," and in the manner of the wealthy. For Paul delighted in this word whenever he wanted to signify the exuberance of anything.
23 *Teaching and admonishing* ] Either he misused the participle in place of a verb, according to the custom of the Hebrew language, or these things refer back to what precedes, "be thankful": then, as if inserting a few words by parenthesis, "teaching and admonishing" is subjoined; so that this is Christian kindness: to teach and admonish. Furthermore, "yourselves," which in Greek is *heautous* <note>original: "ἑαυτοὺς"</note>, would have been better translated as "one another." For who teaches himself?
24 *In psalms* ] The "In" is redundant in our version; it is not found among the Greeks, nor in <term>Ambrose</term> <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), Bishop of Milan and a key Latin Doctor of the Church.</note>.
25 *in hearts* ] In the heart [singular]. And it is "to the Lord," not "to God." Then for "whatever," the Greeks add a conjunction.
26 *To God and the Father* ] Greek: *tō Theō kai Patri* <note>original: "τῷ Θεῷ καὶ Πατρί"</note>. The article being placed only once makes the title of "God and Father" belong to one person, him who is God and Father. "God" because of his authority; "Father" because of his extraordinary love toward us.

<margin>C</margin> 27 *Toward them* ] Greek: *pros autas* <note>original: "πρὸς αὐτάς"</note>, that is, "toward them," or "against them."
28 *It is pleasing in the Lord* ] The "in" is redundant; Greek: *euareston tō Kyriō* <note>original: "εὐάρεστον τῷ Κυρίῳ"</note>, "pleasing" or "acceptable to the Lord."
29 *to indignation* ] Greek: *mē erethizete* <note>original: "μή ἐρεθίζετε"</note>, that is, "do not provoke." "To indignation" was added by some interpreter. Ambrose, however, reads "to provoke to wrath."
30 *With a small spirit* ] Greek: *mē athymōsin* <note>original: "μὴ ἀθυμῶσιν"</note>, that is, "lest they lose heart," and be dejected in spirit.
31 *Serving to the eye* ] Again he used those two nouns, *en ophthalmodouleiais* <note>original: "ἐν ὀφθαλμοδουλείαις"</note> and *anthrōpareskoi* <note>original: "ἀνθρωπάρεσκοι"</note>, which we noted before.

<margin>D</margin> 32 *Fearing the Lord* ] The Greeks read *Theon* <note>original: "Θεὸν"</note>, that is, "God," instead of "Lord"; lest anyone should think a man is to be feared.
33 *As in the Lord* ] Greek: *hōs tō Kyriō* <note>original: "ὡς τῷ Κυρίῳ"</note>, "as to the Lord," that is, to God.

<column-break/>

20 into which you were also called in one body, ²¹ and be thankful. Let the word of Christ dwell in you ²² opulently with <margin>16</margin> all wisdom: ²³ teaching and admonishing one another, ²⁴ in spiritual songs and praises and chants with grace singing ²⁵ in your heart to the <margin>17</margin> Lord. And whatever you do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks ²⁶ to God and the Father through him. Wives, be subject to your own hus- <margin>18</margin> bands, as is fitting in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives, <margin>19</margin> and be not bitter ²⁷ toward them. Children, obey your <margin>20</margin> parents in all things, for this ²⁸ is well-pleasing to the Lord. Fathers, ²⁹ do not provoke your children, ³⁰ lest they <margin>21</margin> lose heart. Slaves, obey in all things those who are your <margin>22</margin> masters according to the flesh, not with ³¹ service exhibited to the eye as if striving to please men, but with simplicity of heart, ³² fearing God. And whatever you do, do it from the soul, ³³ as to the <margin>23</margin> Lord, and not to men, Knowing that from the Lord <margin>24</margin> you will receive the reward of the inheritance, ³⁴ for you serve the Lord Christ. ³⁵ But he who sins will receive back <margin>25</margin> his sin, and there is no ³⁶ respect of persons. You masters, exhibit justice ¹ and equity to your slaves, <margin>1 IV.</margin> knowing that you also have a Lord in heaven. Persevere in prayer, watching in it with <margin>2</margin> thanksgiving, Praying at the same time for us also, that God <margin>3</margin> may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which also I am bound, That I may <margin>4</margin> manifest it, as it is necessary for me to speak. Walk wisely <margin>5</margin> toward those outside, redeeming the opportunity. Let your speech always be with grace ² seasoned with salt, <margin>6</margin> that you may know how it is necessary for you to answer each one. Concerning all my affairs, <margin>7</margin> Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord, will make you certain, Whom I have sent to you for this very thing, that he may <margin>8</margin> know how you are doing, and comfort your hearts, Together <margin>9</margin> with Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you; they will explain to you everything that is being done here. <margin>10</margin> Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you, and Mark the cousin of Barnabas, ³ concerning whom you received instructions:

---

34 *Serve Christ* ] Greek: *tō gar Kyriō Christō douleuete* <note>original: "τῷ γὰρ Κυρίῳ Χριστῷ δουλεύετε"</note>, that is, "For you serve the Lord Christ." Although the Greek word *douleuete* is ambiguous [could be indicative "you serve" or imperative "serve!"]. Ambrose reads it this way: "you shall receive the retribution of the inheritance of the Lord Christ, whom you serve."
35 *For he who does injury* ] Greek: *Ho de adikōn* <note>original: "Ὁ δὲ ἀδικῶν"</note>, that is, "But he who does injury," or "he who does not act rightly." Ambrose reads: "For he who acts unjustly will bear that which he did unjustly": which preserves the affinity of the Greek words *adikōn* <note>original: "ἀδικῶν"</note> and *ēdikēse* <note>original: "ἠδίκησε"</note>, which we have rendered as: "He who sins will receive back his sin." <term>Augustine</term>, in his book *On the Nature of the Good against the Manichaeans*, following I know not what, cites this testimony in these words: "For that which harms, it will receive that which it harmed."
36 *Acceptance* ] Greek: *prosōpolēpsia* <note>original: "προσωποληψία"</note>, that is, "respect of person, or distinction." I do not find "With God" in the Greek codices. Nor is this properly about the respect of persons with God, but about equal sins.

<margin>E</margin> 1 **E**quality ] Greek: *tēn isotēta* <note>original: "τὴν ἰσότητα"</note>, that is, "equality," or rather "equity." And he calls "just" that which is owed to slaves by masters. "Equity" means they should not hold one in delight and treat another unjustly, a thing which makes slavery intolerable. Furthermore, the Interpreter added the pronoun "you" on his own; Greek: *Hoi kyrioi* <note>original: "Οἱ κύριοι"</note>. Ambrose did not add it.
2 *Be seasoned with salt* ] Greek: *halati ērtymenos* <note>original: "ἅλατι ἠρτυμένος"</note>. Ambrose reads, "always be seasoned in the salt of grace," as if it were said: Let your speech be witty, seasoned by grace. Although the Greek means just as if you were to say: Let your speech always have grace, being seasoned with salt: so that we understand pleasantness and modesty in the conversations of Christians with Pagans, but that joined with wisdom. This can be applied to us when we must deal with great men, lest we provoke them with untimely insults and bitterness and make them worse than they are, but rather by prudent moderation of speech, lead them gradually to better things if they are going astray.

<margin>F</margin> 3 *He will make known* ] The Greeks read in the plural number: *panta hymin gnōriousi ta hōde* <note>original: "πάντα ὑμῖν γνωριοῦσι τὰ ὧδε"</note>, that is, "they will make known to you all things that are here." For he speaks of two, Tychicus and Onesimus. Nor do they add the pronoun "who," neither in the Greek nor in Ambrose.
4 *Concerning whom you received instructions* ] The Latin speech could seem ambiguous, and be understood that something was commanded to the Colossians through Barnabas. I am surprised that Theophylact interprets it thus. But the Greeks lack this ambiguity: *peri hou* <note>original: "περὶ οὗ"</note> [concerning whom]. Again, it is doubtful whether the Greek article refers to Barnabas or Mark. Here again the reader must be warned how unsafe it is to trust books translated into another language. In previous editions I added two words, relying on the Interpreter, because perhaps then a Greek codex was not at hand. In this fourth edition I consulted the Greek codex, and I find something much different than what the Interpreter handed down to us: for the Greek has it thus: *Markos ho anepsios Barnaba (peri hou elabete tas entolas, ean dexētai auton pros hymas)* <note>original: "Μάρκος ὁ ἀνεψιὸς Βαρνάβα (περὶ οὗ ἐλάβετε τὰς ἐντολάς, ἐὰν δέξηται αὐτὸν πρὸς ὑμᾶς)"</note>... [Erasmus begins a complex grammatical argument about the phrasing of the Greek instructions].

### THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE COLOSSIANS

# T H E  E N D.

<margin>A</margin>
...to read from another beginning, the matters concerning the material before you, O Colossians, receive him honorably. That is, they had perhaps received a command from Barnabas <note>The Greek text here mentions "παρὰ Βαρνάβα" or "concerning Barnabas"</note> to receive him with honor. Indeed, a period can be placed after these words, *you have received commands*; then read from a new start: *if he comes to you, O Colossians, receive him honorably.* What is read in Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator</note> as "from Barnabas," he either used "from" <note>Greek: παρά</note> instead of "concerning" <note>Greek: περί</note>, or, as is more likely, the scribe corrupted the text. Theophylact indicates that if you read it as one phrase, you should say "to receive" <note>Greek: δέξασθαι</note> in the infinitive mood, as Ambrose reads it; but if read separately, "receive" <note>Greek: δέξασθε</note> in the imperative mood.

5 **Who is called Justus** ] "Justus" here is a Latin name <note>Greek: Ἰοῦστος</note>, even though Paul testifies that the man was a Jew.

6 **Always anxious** ] <note>Greek: ἀγωνιζόμενος</note>, that is, striving, or working, or rather, working with great effort.

7 **That you may stand perfect** ] "That you may be" <note>Greek: ἵνα ἧτε</note>. And so Ambrose reads it. It appears the translator read "stand" <note>Greek: στῆτε</note> instead of "be."

8 **Much labor** ] <note>Greek: ζῆλον πολὺν</note>, that is, much zeal, or much emulation.

9 **Luke the physician** ] <note>Greek: Λουκᾶς ὁ ἰατρός</note>. The article <note>the</note> added for the sake of distinction suggests more strongly that this refers to a specific Luke; for interpreters are uncertain.

10 **And the church which is in his house** ] <note>Greek: καὶ τὴν κατ' οἶκον αὐτῶν ἐκκλησίαν</note>, that is, "and his domestic church." Ambrose, unless the manuscripts deceive us, thinks Nymphas was a "devout woman," as they say; but the pronoun "his" <note>Greek: αὐτοῦ</note> added by the Greeks signifies that it was a man named Nymphas. Furthermore, regarding the addition "and the church in his house," I believe "church" is understood here not as the entire assembly, but as the rest of the family who were already Christian. For the Greek interpreters think he must have been a man of high rank because he hosted a church in his home.

<margin>B</margin>
11 **And when it has been read** ] On the occasion of this passage, certain people forged an Epistle as if written by Paul to the Laodiceans, but it contains nothing of Paul's except for a few little words begged from his other Epistles. Although Faber <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, a French humanist</note>—a learned man, but sometimes overly trusting—carefully included it among the Epistles, the Greek commentaries deny that this letter Paul mentions was written *to* the Laodiceans. For he did not say "the one written to the Laodiceans," but "the one written *from* Laodicea." Consequently, it was likely an Epistle that someone in Laodicea had written to Paul, which nevertheless contained matters pertaining to the Colossians. Theophylact indicates there were those who thought this was the First Epistle to Timothy, because Paul wrote it from Laodicea. Tertullian, in his book against Marcion, claims...

<column-break/>

11 ...if he comes to you, receive him, and Jesus who is called Justus, who are of the circumcision: these alone are my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, who have been a comfort to me. 12 Epaphras greets you, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, always laboring anxiously for you in prayers, 7 that you may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God. 13 For I bear witness to him, that he has 8 much zeal for you, and those who are at Laodicea, and those at Hierapolis. 14 9 Luke the beloved physician greets you, and Demas. 15 Greet the brothers who are at Laodicea, and Nymphas, 10 and the congregation that is in his house. 16 11 And when the Epistle has been recited by you, cause it to be recited also in the church of the Laodiceans, and that you also read the one 12 written from Laodicea. 17 And say to Archippus, "See to the ministry which you received in the Lord, that you fulfill it." 18 The salutation is by my own hand—Paul. Be mindful of my bonds. 13 Grace be with you. Amen.

->Sent from Rome by Tychicus and Onesimus.<-

### THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE COLOSSIANS

# T H E  E N D.

<margin>C</margin>
...that the letter we know as the one to the Ephesians was actually addressed to the Laodiceans. But while I make no pronouncement on that matter, I am not afraid to assert that the one Stapulensis <note>Faber Stapulensis</note> added is not by Paul. It is not within every man's power to imitate the heart of Paul; Paul thunders, he lightens, he speaks pure flames. But this letter, besides being incredibly brief, how cold it is, how lifeless! It is even foolish, as well as impudent, that whoever forged it collected most of its content from this very Epistle to the Colossians. If everything in the "Laodicean" letter is found in this one (and much more copiously), what was the point of commanding that it be read here too? Finally, how is it that this Epistle exists among the Latins, while there is no trace of it among the Greeks—not even among the ancients who might testify to having read it? Though why bother arguing? Let whoever wishes read the letter; it is found in the commentaries of Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples. No argument <margin>D</margin> will more effectively persuade you that it is not Paul's than the letter itself. And if I have any sense of smell at all, it is the work of the same craftsman who has contaminated, defiled, and ruined all the writings of the ancient theologians with his nonsense—especially those of the one who least deserved such an insult, namely Saint Jerome. For we have almost nothing left of Jerome, besides the Commentaries on the Prophets and a few Epistles, that has not been deliberately mutilated, adulterated, or foully contaminated by this scoundrel <note>Latin: furcifero</note>; to say nothing of the many tasteless volumes that same madman published under Jerome's name. I would gladly imitate my friend Faber's kindness, if I did not see that by humoring a few unlearned people in this way, we allow insults to be cast not only upon those heroes who left us their beautiful monuments, but also upon promising young minds who might be deterred from literature by this imposture if they suspect it, or infected by it if they do not. With similar "kindness," Faber added to his Psalter a letter in Jerome's name <margin>E</margin> addressed to Pope Damasus, in which he asks that at the end of every Psalm the "Gloria Patri" be added. Yet nothing could be imagined more childish, unlearned, or tasteless than this. It is far from being the work of Jerome—a man endowed with inimitable learning and eloquence.

12 **Be read by you** ] <note>Greek: ἵνα καὶ ὑμεῖς ἀναγνῶτε</note>, that is, "so that you also may read it": for it precedes it.

13 **The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ** ] I do not find all of this among the Greeks. And Ambrose reads it exactly as it is found in the Greek manuscripts: <note>Greek: Ἡ χάρις μεθ' ὑμῶν</note>, that is, *Grace be with you*. In the Donatian manuscript it was written, *The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you*. Both manuscripts provided from Constance agreed with the Greek: *Grace be with you. Amen.*

# ARGUMENT
### of the
# FIRST EPISTLE TO THE
# THESSALONIANS.

He sends this letter from Athens, having seen them previously and spent time among them. The occasion for the Epistle is as follows: The Apostle, having suffered many afflictions in Beroea and in Philippi of Macedonia and in Corinth, and knowing what he also suffered in Thessalonica, feared that the Thessalonians, hearing what he suffered in the aforementioned cities, might be tempted by the tempter and stumble. Having learned that they were also deeply grieved over those who die, he sends Timothy to them with this Epistle. First, he strengthens them in the faith, so they are not shaken by their afflictions, and so they realize they have suffered nothing strange at the hands of the Jews—the very ones who killed the Lord; for he said it is characteristic of Christians to be afflicted in this life. After exhorting them much to live as they had received from him, he writes about those who pass away, comforting them and teaching them not to take it heavily; for death is not destruction, but a path to resurrection. Then he also teaches about its timing, so that knowing the day is uncertain, they may always be ready and pay no attention to anyone making announcements about it. For he says the Presence <note>original: "παρουσίαν" (parousian), a term used for the Second Coming of Christ</note> will be such that those left behind and found on that day will not precede those raised from the dead; for he teaches that the transformation of all happens at once. In addition, he urges them to improve in their character, and he urges them to always rejoice in hope, to pray, and to always give thanks to the Lord, adjuring them to read this Epistle to all the brothers. And thus he completes the Epistle.

---

### ARGUMENT FOR THE
# FIRST EPISTLE TO THE
# THESSALONIANS
### by
## DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'T' within a square frame, depicting a classical or biblical scene with several figures in a courtyard setting.</image-desc>
Thessalonica is the metropolis of Macedonia, from which the inhabitants of the region are called Thessalonians. These people persisted in the faith, once received, with such constancy that, following Paul's example, they bore the persecutions of their fellow citizens with an unbroken and eager spirit; nor could they be turned away from the Gospel's instruction by any persuasion of the false apostles <note>original: "Pseudapostolorum"</note>. Fearing this, Paul—to whom the wickedness of the false apostles was not hidden—since he was not permitted to visit them himself, sent Timothy. When Timothy returned and Paul learned of their constancy, he praises them highly, giving thanks to God. This occupies the first and second chapters. In the remaining chapters <note>Erasmus's Latin says "duobus" (two), though the Epistle has five chapters; he likely views the remaining section as a single thematic block</note>, he instructs them in various duties of piety, indicating that there were some among them not yet entirely pure from all lust, and that there were some who, devoted to idleness, were a burden to others; likewise, there were restless individuals who disturbed the peace of the Church, whom he orders to be rebuked. Furthermore, he instructs and strengthens those whose opinion regarding the resurrection was not yet sufficiently firm, since they mourned the deceased as if they had perished rather than migrated to a better state. Again, others had disputed about the day of the Lord's coming, as if it could be known or predicted in advance, whereas it is uncertain to all. But he says it will be sudden and arrive beyond everyone's expectation, so that we might be more prepared at every moment. He wrote from Athens by the minister Tychicus, according to the Greek inscription; to whom our common arguments (which are read from an uncertain author in the standard copies) add Onesimus as a colleague.

# THE FIRST EPISTLE OF PAUL THE APOSTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS.

->Lll 2<-

<margin>I. 1</margin> PAUL and Silvanus and Timothy, to the Church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
<margin>2</margin> We give thanks to God always for all of you, making mention of you in our prayers, unceasingly
<margin>3</margin> Remembering your work of faith and labor of love, and the endurance of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ before
<margin>4</margin> our God and Father, Knowing, brothers beloved by God, your election;
<margin>5</margin> Because our Gospel did not come to you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit, and in much certainty, just as you know what kind of men we were among you for your sake.
<margin>6</margin> And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, having received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit;
<margin>7</margin> So that you became examples to all those who believe in Macedonia and Achaia.
<margin>8</margin> For from you the word of the Lord has resounded, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith toward God has gone forth,
<margin>9</margin> so that we have no need to say anything. For they themselves report concerning us what kind of entrance we had to you, and how you turned to God from idols,
<margin>10</margin> to serve the living and true God, and to await his Son from the heavens, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus,
<margin>II. 1</margin> who delivers us from the coming wrath. For you yourselves know, brothers, our entrance to you,
<margin>2</margin> that it was not in vain, but even after suffering before and being outlandishly treated, as you know, in Philippi, we were bold in our God...

---

<margin>A</margin> 1 **Peace**] In this place, the Greeks add those almost solemn words, *from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ*: though Ambrosiaster <note>A name given to the unknown author of a famous 4th-century commentary on Paul’s letters, once attributed to St. Ambrose.</note> reads, *grace to you and peace*: following our own Latin manuscripts.
2 **Mindful of the work**] It can also be understood this way, *mindful of you because of the work of faith*, so that the Greek word *heneka* <note>meaning "because of" or "on account of"</note> is understood.

<margin>B</margin> 3 **Endurance**] *hypomonēs tēs elpidos*, that is, *tolerance, or the patience of hope*: this means that you patiently persevered in hope. Ambrose reads *expectation, instead of endurance*.
4 **Before God**] *emprosthen tou Theou*, that is, *in the presence of God*.
5 **Knowing, brothers**] The rules of grammar were not strictly observed by the Greeks in this speech, though we have avoided that inconvenience in our translation. I am aware that Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and biblical commentator.</note> refers the word *Knowing* to Paul and Paul’s colleagues. However, I am not sure if the Translator has passed down his own ideas to us here, even though Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching.</note> says almost the same things, albeit more obscurely, and they interpret *election* as *excellence*. Truly, the things that follow, *Because our Gospel*, do not fit this sense very well. To me, *Knowing* seems to be put for *You know*, which he repeats a little later, *as you know*. For Paul’s aim is that those who are humble and afflicted may testify that the Gospel they received was not human, but from God who calls them. He proves this with a double argument: both that it transformed them so, and that those who preached—though they were humble and afflicted—nevertheless performed all things by the signs and power of the Spirit.
6 **Not in word only**] In the last Epistle, we warned that "word" is opposed to truth and efficacy; for which the Translator there had rendered *appearance*. Likewise here, he feels his preaching was confirmed by miracles.
7 **In fullness**] *en plērophoria*, about which we warned above, that is, in certainty, and sure persuasion. For a person who only teaches does not create a certain faith; rather, it is the one who persuades by miracles and the endurance of evils who truly persuades, which the "false apostles" did not do. Theophylact, however, refers this last part to the afflictions endured, arguing it is not likely anyone would want to suffer such evils for a vain doctrine. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the prominent medieval theologian.</note> brings forward two interpretations, but neither hits the mark: *In fullness*, he says, *lest they think they received less than the Jews. Or, In fullness*, because Paul handed down to them nothing of those things pertaining to the faith. Ambrose paraphrased the Greek word this way: *not in fantasy, but in the truth of fullness*.

<margin>C</margin> 8 **Receiving the word**] *dexamenoi ton logon*. Better, *having received the word*, or *speech*: or you who accepted the word of the Lord. Just as Paul delivered it not without persecution, so they received it not without affliction and the pursuit of evils. Furthermore, in this place, either the participle *having received* is put in place of a verb, or it must be punctuated as Theophylact punctuates it: *you became imitators of me and of the Lord*, so that the break is here, then follows *receiving the word*: so the sense is, you imitated me and Christ himself in that you willingly suffered affliction for the sake of the Gospel. Ambrose reads, *you were made imitators of us and of the Lord himself, looking up to the word*.

<column-break/>

<margin>I. 1</margin> PAUL and Silvanus and Timothy to the Church of the Thessalonians, in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
<margin>2</margin> We give thanks to God always for all of you, making mention of you in our prayers, unceasingly
<margin>3</margin> Mindful of you because of the work of faith and labor of charity, and because you remained in the hope of our Lord Jesus Christ before our God and Father,
<margin>4</margin> Knowing, beloved brothers, your election by God:
<margin>5</margin> Because our Gospel was toward you not through speech alone, but also through power, and through the Holy Spirit, and through much certainty, just as you know what kind of men we were among you for your sake.
<margin>6</margin> And you were made imitators of us, and of the Lord, receiving the speech with much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit:
<margin>7</margin> So that you were an example to all believers in Macedonia and Achaia.
<margin>8</margin> For from you the speech of the Lord resounded, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith, which is toward God, flowed forth, so that it is not necessary for us to say anything.
<margin>9</margin> For they themselves announce concerning you what kind of entrance we had to you, and how you were converted to God from idols, to serve the living and true God,
<margin>10</margin> And to await his Son from the heavens, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus, who delivers us from the coming wrath.
<margin>II. 1</margin> For you yourselves know, brothers, our entrance to you, that it was not in vain,
<margin>2</margin> But that having been previously afflicted with evils and affected by insults, just as you know, at Philippi, we acted boldly in our Lord to speak the Gospel of God among you in much struggle.

---

<margin>D</margin> 9 **Form**] *typoi*, that is, *forms*: which Ambrose translates, *as an example*, and rightly so.
10 **It was defamed** <note>Erasmus is discussing the Latin word "diffamatus est" used in some translations.</note>] *exēchētai*, that is, *it thundered out, or was trumpeted forth*, as Laurentius <note>Lorenzo Valla (c. 1407–1457), a famous humanist scholar who critiqued the Vulgate translation.</note> points out. He rightly mocks Remigius <note>Remigius of Auxerre (c. 841–908), a Carolingian scholar.</note> for this, who noted that Paul was as if committing a grammatical error because he used this word *diffamare* <note>original: "to defame" or "to spread a bad report"</note> in a good sense—as if Paul had written in Latin, and not rather in Greek! Or as if Paul were responsible for whatever some translator chose to render. It is as if Remigius translated *retem* <note>net</note> as *to be drunk*, and then Paul was to be called to court on the charge of violating the Latin language. Furthermore, it is plainly false that all words composed this way in Latin signify something in a bad sense, unless perhaps *disperse, disjoin, dissolve*, and six hundred others of that kind are to be taken in a bad sense. In Greek, this kind of prefix added to nouns and verbs makes them difficult or ill-named, but it is not so in Latin. Certainly Augustine uses *diffamare* to mean "to divulge," when a rumor is spread far and wide. Forgiveness can be given for ignorance, but who can bear such arrogance joined with ignorance? Indeed, who would not laugh at such remarkable folly, that he attributes to Paul writing in Greek what was actually committed by a Latin translator? Unless perhaps Remigius believed that Paul wrote to the Greeks in Latin. Finally, it is possible that this commentary was added to Remigius’s writings by someone else.
11 **It has gone forth**] *exelēlythen*, that is, *it flowed out, or reached*, or rather *spread forth*. For he did not say, *into every place*, but *in every place*, so that you may understand that what was previously whispered in secret has now begun to be publicly proclaimed.
12 **Who rescued**] *ton rhyomenon hēmas*, that is, *who rescues us*: a present participle.

<margin>E</margin> 1 **But having suffered much before**] Someone or other added "many things" out of his own head. For it is not in the Greek, nor in Ambrose, nor in the ancient manuscripts, specifically the Donatian one; both of the Constantian ones agreed, *kai propathontes, kai hybristhentes*, that is, *both having suffered before, and having been affected by insults*. Furthermore, he used "suffered" in the Greek manner for "afflicted," for whom both *pathos* and *pathēma* mean "affliction."
2 **We had confidence**] *eparrēsiasametha*. Which Ambrose paraphrases as, *with exerted liberty we dared*. Now *parrēsiazesthai* means to say what must be said openly and fearlessly, as we have already often warned.
3 **In much anxiety**] *en pollō agōni*, that is, *in much struggle, or labor, or danger*: which he nevertheless often translates in this way. Ambrose reads *struggle*.

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER II.

->n<-

<margin>2</margin> ...in our God to speak to you the Gospel of God in much struggle. <margin>3</margin> For our exhortation was not from error, nor from impurity, nor in deceit, <margin>4</margin> But just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the Gospel, so we speak, not as pleasing men, but <margin>5</margin> God, who tests our hearts. <margin>6</margin> For we never came with words of flattery, as you know, nor with a pretext of greed—God is witness— <margin>7</margin> Nor seeking glory from men, neither from you nor from others; though we could have held authority <note>or "been a burden"</note> as Apostles of Christ, but we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherishes [her children].

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>4</margin> *Not from error*] <note>original: "ἐκ πλάνης"</note>. "Error" among us refers only to one who is deceived, but for the Greeks, *planē* <note>original: "πλάνη"</note> also refers to the one who deceives: thus I would have preferred to translate it as *imposture*. The Greek commentaries interpret it in this sense. For someone who strives to deceive others puts himself into danger, but rather indulges in sins and looks after his own business.
<margin>5</margin> *Nor from impurity*] <note>original: "ἐξ ἀκαθαρσίας"</note>, that is, out of uncleanness: which the Greek scholia <note>brief explanatory notes</note> explain as "wicked and abominable arts," which they call impurity because it is done through impure and sordid methods to deceive the simple-minded, as magicians and impostors are prone to do when faking miracles.
<margin>6</margin> *That it might be believed by us*] <note>Erasmus notes the Latin Vulgate wording</note> so that it might be redundant: that is, so that the Gospel might be entrusted to us <note>original: "πιστευθῆναι τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον"</note>.
<margin>7</margin> *Though we could have been a burden to you*] <note>original: "ἐν βάρει εἶναι"</note>, that is, to be in burden, or in weight. The Greek scholia read this in two ways. Either "in burden" <note>original: "ἐν βάρει"</note>, meaning in weight and authority: since it was preceded by, *Not seeking glory*, and is followed by, *but we became little ones*. To this, Ambrose <note>Likely "Ambrosiaster," an anonymous 4th-century commentator</note> seems to interpret it as being about honor, not about being a weight. Finally, what he added immediately after fits this sense: *as Apostles of Christ*. For it is not the way of Apostles to weigh anyone down with their arrogance. Or "in burden" could mean that he received nothing from them, and was nowhere a cost or a burden. The first interpretation pleases me more.
<margin>8</margin> *But we became little ones*] The Translator and Ambrose seem to have read "infants" <note>original: "νήπιοι"</note>, that is, little ones or boys. However, the Greek manuscripts have "gentle" <note>original: "ἤπιοι"</note>, that is, mild and not at all harsh. Either is tolerable. But the latter is closer to Paul’s meaning, as it is opposed to "being in weight/authority": so that you may understand that he did not use pride and arrogance among them, as the False Apostles did, but rather mildness and gentleness. Theophylact <note>a Byzantine commentator</note> indicates both readings. Ambrose reads "honor" rather than "burden," and thus he wrote: *To suppress those*, he says, *who had neither the means nor the shame, and yet fed themselves on honor. For they wished themselves to be commended rather than the doctrine of God. But the Apostle, who sought glory not for the present but for the future, made himself humble so that the preaching of God might be exalted.* These are the words of Ambrose. Now, even if we grant that in the context "honor" was written for "burden," it is certainly clear that Ambrose embraces the opinion that is more powerful for us. I would more willingly subscribe to this, not only because it fits the meaning of this passage more aptly and agrees beautifully with many other points in this same place, but also because among so many excellent gifts with which a Prince and especially a Bishop ought to be endowed, there is no other by which he is either more decently adorned or more effectively commended than gentleness and mildness of character and mind, which usually both accompany and prove exceptional integrity and remarkable wisdom. Common or even fake integrity has its own pride, its own arrogance, and indulging itself more than is fair, just as it is a spiteful judge of others' virtues, so it is a bitter persecutor of others' vices. Although the primary glory of this praise, after Christ, belongs to our Paul—who, though he far surpassed all others in both Apostolic gifts and duties, yet wished to be as one of the Apostles in his humility, carrying himself more submissively the greater he was—nevertheless, in these times I know no one who approaches closer to this praise than my own (nay, not mine, but all of Britain's) Maecenas <note>A classic Roman name for a generous patron</note>, William Warham, Archbishop of Canterbury. In him, while there is nothing that you would not judge to be exceptional and greatest in every human perfection, yet he usually seems greater in no other thing than that, being in every way the greatest, he himself does not acknowledge his own greatness. Thus it happens that while he surpasses even the greatest in other virtues, by this one title he surpasses even himself: that he is not great to himself. If anyone were to weigh the height of his dignity, the mass and amplitude of his business, his almost divine judgment, his incomparable force of mind, his absolutely complete learning, the purity of his life, and the splendor of his fortune (which he tolerates out of duty and the custom of the region rather than possesses for himself), you will find no one, even among the highest, whom you would dare compare with him. Again, he is so accessible and open to all that you would hardly find even among the common people, among men of the lowest rank, someone whom he does not surpass in courtesy, ease, and gentleness. O truly heroic mind worthy of an Apostolic man, since you have transcended human measure, yet you bring yourself back into the ranks and do not look down upon even the lowest of men! For others, a little bit of learning raises their crests. For others, the splendor of their ancestry elates their spirits. There are those for whom a rarer life brings on a frown. Nor are there lacking those whom even a mediocre breeze of fortune puffs up, not allowing them to remember themselves. This man has always held the highest place in every kind of learning, as one who added indefatigable study to the far-happier genius that fell to him as a gift from nature and God. Then, for so many times and so many years, he has been involved in the gravest as well as the most splendid affairs of the kingdom, and that not without the highest praise for both piety and prudence. Now, finally—behold, a truly marvelous Geryon <note>a triple-bodied giant from myth</note>—he presents himself as a triple-threat hero to all Britain: Archbishop and Primate, Chancellor, and Patron. Archbishop for religion, Chancellor for justice and the republic, Patron for studies. Who is endowed with such strength of soul

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
struggle. For our exhortation was not from imposture, nor from impurity, nor with deceit, <margin>4</margin> But just as we had been approved by God, so that the Gospel might be entrusted to us, so we speak, not as pleasing men, but God, who proves our hearts. <margin>5</margin> For we never conducted ourselves through the speech of flattery, as you know, nor through the opportunity of greed—God is witness— <margin>6</margin> Nor seeking glory from men, neither from you, nor from others: <margin>7</margin> Although we could have been in authority, as Apostles of Christ, but we were gentle in your midst, just as if a nurse

<margin>C</margin>
who would not pant and gasp under any one of these burdens? Yet this man alone sustains them all, especially since he thoroughly understands what each title demands. Indeed, the title of Archbishop and Primate—which that most holy man Thomas <note>Thomas Becket</note> made more venerable by his martyrdom—requires that what the Roman Pontiff owes to the whole world, he should provide to all Britain. Now, the office of Chancellor requires the highest and uncorrupted judge of the entire kingdom, and one to whom there is access for all, Laity and Clergy alike, from whom there is no further appeal. Who do you think could sustain such a mass of business, such waves of legal cases, in one man? Let me not mention meanwhile the neither few nor mediocre weights of care that come from royal business, and let me pass over domestic anxieties, which it is agreed are not small in such a large household. And yet that one heart is not only sufficient for attending to so many things, but even has room to spare. In such an immense line of roaring business, there is enough left over to devote to religion, to the private affections of friends, and to the unfolding of books—which he does not despise, but rather talks with no friends more willingly whenever he can steal a little leisure from public functions. No doubt a certain admirable felicity of nature and an incredible dexterity of mind grants him this, as does a judgment no less sharp than it is prompt and ready, a long experience of affairs, and above all a certain perpetual sobriety and vigilance of life. Not even the smallest portion of disorder <note>original: "ἀταξίας"</note> is given to dice, none to pleasures, none to banquets, none to sleep; indeed, he even takes something away from nature so that nothing is withheld from the service of his country. By this means, both his time and his now somewhat advanced age, and his health, are sufficient for attending to, sustaining, and exhausting so many and such great affairs, for which not even ten others could be equal. Now, it cannot be helped that in such a varied crowd of business, there arise things that are not only difficult but also annoying and dangerous. Since it was not said lightly that not even Jove pleases everyone. Yet no one has seen this man sad, no one moved to anger, no one grim-faced: such is the force and constancy of his untiring heart. Then his equity and sweetness are so great that even those defeated by him depart with more balanced minds than <margin>D</margin> some are accustomed to feel when they are the victors. He is perpetually tranquil for himself, and courteous and cheerful for others. Now, indeed, he so guards and sustains the persona of Patron, which he took up voluntarily, that this island—always powerful in men and resources, once noble in religion—has now also flourished in the best literature and disciplines, chiefly through his work, so that it should yield to no region, whether you seek skill in Greek and Latin literature, or look at the strength of eloquence, or the sharpness of mathematicians, or the rest of the knowledge of philosophy, or the mysteries of sacred letters. He alone nourishes many, promotes most, favors, cherishes, adorns, and protects all, not only the exceptional but also the mediocre, and not only his own countrymen but even foreigners and those born under any sky. Among their number, his kindness wished me also to be, as small as I am. To his beneficence, although otherwise profuse and overflowing, this adds a double grace: that he hardly ever allows himself to be reminded of it, and never to be asked. Nay, when someone gives thanks, <margin>E</margin> he soon interrupts, as if it were too much for the one who has been affected by a great benefit to acknowledge in words what he has received. He thinks himself abundantly repaid if his support has profited studies, if it has turned out well for all that he contributed from his own private resources. And just as he does not boast if his kindness results in success, so he neglects and as if forgets it if ever it turns out otherwise. Since it cannot be that this does not happen sometimes to one who is inclined toward deserving well of everyone. He learns by judgment whom he wishes to cherish, but with a judgment certainly more candid and friendly than severe. Moreover, those whom he has once embraced, he cherishes most constantly, nor can he be alienated by any detractions of the envious. If he is ever forced to hear these, he marvels at how he can ignore them, also striving so that they do not even reach the person they target, lest his mind be saddened in any way. If such a Patron had fallen to me in those first years, perhaps I could have been something in good literature. Now, born in a less-than-happy age, when barbarism reigned everywhere with impunity, especially among our people—among whom it was then even a crime to have touched anything of good literature, so far was it from honor nourishing men’s studies, in that region which was then more truly <margin>F</margin> dedicated to Bacchus and Ceres <note>the gods of wine and grain/food</note> than to the Muses—what, I ask, could I do, endowed with a barely mediocre talent? For envious death snatched away that most illustrious man Henry of Bergen, Bishop of Cambrai, the first Patron of my study. Encroaching upon the next, William Mountjoy, the renowned Primate of England, were the business of the court and the tumults of war. Although, to speak truly, I was lacking to him rather than he to me. Finally, through him, I happened upon that greatest man of Canterbury, but already at a more advanced age and verging on my fortieth year. And yet, awakened by his kindness, I have as if turned green again and revived in the studies of literature: and what neither nature nor my country had given, his kindness gave. This is the nature of mortal geniuses; this is the nature of the study of letters: they require some president and leader who may supply leisure, who may add spirit, who may protect against the hydra of envy, which follows the glory of learning no differently than a shadow follows a body. Finally, someone by whose judgment they may measure their strength and to whom they may bring their late-night labors. Prudent antiquity, I believe, saw this, when it placed its own Apollo in charge of the virgin Muses. Therefore, as it is truly said

# 905 TO THE THESSALONIANS I. CHAPTER II. 906

8 ...her own children, so being affectionately desirous of you, we were well-pleased to impart to you not only the Gospel of God, but also our own souls, because you have become beloved to us. 9 For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil; for working night and day so as not to be a burden to any of you, we preached to you the Gospel of God. 10 You are witnesses, and God also, how holily and justly and blamelessly we behaved toward you who believe. 11 As you know how we [exhorted] each one of you, as a father does his own children, 12 encouraging you, and comforting you, and testifying, so that you would walk worthily of God, who calls you into His own kingdom and glory.
