<margin>D</margin>
8 <note>Erasmus begins with a literary digression before returning to the biblical text.</note> There is a Greek proverb: "The year produces the harvest, not the field," meaning that the mercy of the heavens contributes more to the crop’s success than the goodness of the soil. In the same way, the kindness of Princes is what makes men of talent. No region is so barbaric, so far removed from the "horses of the Sun" <note>A poetic reference to the heat of the tropics, citing Virgil's *Aeneid* (Maro)</note>, that it does not possess very dexterous minds which might seem born in the middle of Greece, if only Patrons <note>original: "Maecenates", referring to Gaius Maecenas, the famous Roman patron of the arts</note> were not lacking. But while I am held by the thought of these things, I know not how I have almost forgotten the work I started, lingering longer than is right on a digression. Therefore, I must return to the matter at hand.

9 **Desiring you greedily**] <note>original: "οὕτως ἱμειρόμενοι ὑμῶν"</note>. He attempted to explain the emphasis of the word, for it signifies being held by a desire and mutual affection for someone, just like parents or friends. Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine commentator</note> indicates a double reading among the Greeks: for some read *homeiromenoi*, that is, "glued to and clinging to," from *homou* (together) and *eirō* (to connect); others read *imeiromenoi*, which sounds like "desiring with affection." For *himeros* sounds like desire, and *imeiromai* means "I desire or am touched." The word seems composed of *hiēmi ienai*, which is "I send" or "I stretch," and *erōs* (love or longing), as if you were to say, "I am carried away by longing."

10 **We were willing**] <note>original: "εὐδοκῶμεν"</note>. This word also carries affection, as if you were to say, "the soul exults," although the Greek word can be in the present tense.

11 **Because you are most dear**] <note>original: "διότι ἀγαπητοὶ"</note>, that is, because you are beloved, etc.

12 **For you are made mindful**] <note>original: "Μνημονεύετε γὰρ"</note>, that is, "For you remember." And so Ambrose <note>referring to Ambrosiaster, a 4th-century commentator</note> reads it.

13 **Of our labor**] <note>original: "κόπον καὶ μόχθον"</note>. He signified the same thing with two words, except that *mochthos* is labor joined with difficulty, as if you were to say, an "effort" or "toiling": and therefore they translated it as "fatigue." In the Greek words, the similarity of the sound is more pleasant.

14 **Night and day**] <note>original: "νυκτὸς γὰρ καὶ ἡμέρας"</note>, that is, for by night and by day.

15 **How holily**] <note>original: "ὡς ὁσίως"</note>, that is, that, or because, in a holy manner. Although the Translator also renders it correctly. Theophylact notes the emphasis of this word *hosiōs*, which for the Greeks sounds of religion and reverence for the Deity. This is present in him who remembers that he is doing the business of God. For what he adds, "justly" <note>original: "δικαίως"</note>, refers to men, to none of whom he did injury.

16 **And without complaint**] <note>original: "ἀμέμπτως"</note>, that is, so that no one could complain about us; that is, blamelessly.

17 **We were present**] <note>original: "ἐγενήθημεν"</note>, that is, we were.

18 **How [we were toward] each one of you**] Here, unless one understands the word "embraced," or something similar, the speech will be imperfect. But this ought not to be a new thing in Paul; it would be easy to fix, were it not that *hōs* <note>meaning "as"</note> was repeated: and when he had said before "each one of you," he added again, "exhorting you." Truly, this is the **stammering of Apostolic charity**, which, as if intoxicated, does not explain itself in human words. <note>Erasmus beautifully suggests that Paul's grammar breaks down because his love for the Thessalonians is so overwhelming.</note>

19 **And we have testified**] <note>original: "καὶ μαρτυρούμενοι"</note>, that is, and testifying, or rather, calling to witness.

20 **The word of the hearing of God**] <note>original: "ἀκοῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note>, that is, the speech concerning God, or the speech by which you learned of God.

21 **You accepted it not as the word &c.**] I do not find "as" <note>original: "ut"</note> in certain Greek copies, [it reads] "not the speech of men" <note>original: "οὐ λόγον ἀνθρώπων"</note>: even though the Greek codices vary somewhat here, and

<column-break/>

<margin>D</margin>
it appears from the Greek scholia that the adverb "as" was not added in the first part, but rather, *you received the word of God*: which is more effective than *as the word of God*. Certainly, in Chrysostom and Theophylact it is not included, although they explain it as if they had read *hōs* <note>as</note>. In the later part, *kathōs* <note>just as</note> is added, but *estin alēthōs* <note>it truly is</note> is also added. Therefore, since *hōs* is sometimes said even of those things which truly are, it helped to add it in the first part; what should have been added to follow was, *just as in reality it is not*. Although that earlier word, "of God," belongs to the preceding part, "when you received from us the word of the hearing of God," that is, the word which God was speaking to you through us. But I would prefer, "when you were receiving," rather than "when you had received": otherwise how were they receiving what they had already received?

22 **Who works**] <note>original: "ὃ ἐνεργεῖται"</note> which among the Greeks can be referred either to the Word or to God, but more to the Word: and so Ambrose [reads], because "which" (*ὃ*) works, with the conjunction "and" (*καὶ*) also added, agreeing with the Greeks in this. For Paul feels that the seed, as it were, of the divine word acts in the Thessalonians, while they declare the power of the Gospel speech by their very deeds. Theophylact reads and interprets it in this way.

23 **To you who have believed**] <note>original: "πιστεύουσιν"</note>, that is, to you who believe: and so Ambrose reads it, or certainly, "to you who were believing," because of the past tense verb to which it is attached.

24 **To your fellow-countrymen**] In Greek it is "to your own fellow-countrymen" <note>original: "ὑπὸ τῶν ἰδίων συμφυλετῶν"</note>; although it signifies of the same nation rather than the same tribe.
<margin>E</margin>
25 **Just as also they**] Understand "us" <note>referring to the Apostles</note>.

26 **And the Prophets**] In Greek it is "and their own Prophets" <note>original: "καὶ τοὺς ἰδίους Προφήτας"</note>.

27 **But the wrath of God has reached them**] "Of God" is not added here in the Greek, it says: "but the wrath has reached them" <note>original: "ἔφθασε δὲ ἐπ’ αὐτοὺς ἡ ὀργὴ"</note>, that is, the vengeance. And the ancient codices, specifically two from Constance, had "anticipated" <note>original: "praevenit"</note>, which is how Ambrose also reads it. But "anticipated" is said for "seized upon," while they hesitate to repent. Theophylact noted the added article *hē orgē* <note>the wrath</note>, by which that inevitable vengeance would be signified, which was predicted to hang over them by Christ and the Prophets. Furthermore, he said *eis telos* <note>to the end</note>, for that which is the "extremes," or "to the extreme," that is, the implacable wrath of God.

28 **Desolated**] <note>original: "ἀπορφανισθέντες"</note>, that is, made as if orphans, and bereaved of you as if of children.
<margin>F</margin>
29 **To the time of an hour**] <note>original: "πρὸς καιρὸν ὥρας"</note>. Why not rather, "to the opportunity," or "occasion," or certainly "a point of time," that is, for a short time? Since *hōra* <note>hour</note> is "time" to the Greeks, and *kairos* is a "brief time." We translate it, "for a space of time." Theophylact thinks there is a diminutive emphasis in both words, for *kairos* is a point of time, and *hōra* is the smallest part of the day. Certainly the Apostle thus thinned out his absence, which he neither wants to be understood as perpetual, when he says "for a time" (*pros kairon*), nor long-lasting, when he says "of an hour" (*hōras*).

30 **In sight, not in heart**] <note>original: "προσώπῳ, οὐ καρδίᾳ"</note>, that is, in face, not in heart. And so Ambrose reads it, but what the Translator renders is more pleasing.

31 **More abundantly we have hastened**] <note>original: "περισσοτέρως"</note>, which signifies both "we have studied" and "we have cared for." And "more abundantly" is said for "more," or "more vehemently."

32 **Both once and again**] <note>original: "καὶ ἅπαξ καὶ δὶς"</note>, that is, "and twice": but the Translator renders it in Latin.

# EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER IV.

...of boasting, or is it not even you before our Lord Jesus Christ, at his coming? For you are our glory and joy.
<margin>III. 1</margin> Therefore, when we could no longer bear it, we were well-pleased to be left in Athens alone,
<margin>2</margin> and we sent Timothy, our brother and minister of God, and our fellow-worker in the Gospel of Christ, to strengthen you and to encourage you concerning your faith,
<margin>3</margin> so that no one might be shaken <note>original Greek: σαίνεσθαι (sainesthai), literally "to be wagged" like a dog's tail, used here for being unsettled by trials</note> by these afflictions; for you yourselves know that we are appointed to this.
<margin>4</margin> For even when we were with you, we told you beforehand that we were going to suffer affliction, just as it happened, as you know.
<margin>5</margin> For this reason, when I could no longer bear it, I sent to know your faith, lest by some means the tempter had tempted you, and our labor might be in vain.
<margin>6</margin> But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and brought us good news of your faith and love, and that you always have good memories of us, longing to see us, just as we also long to see you.
<margin>7</margin> For this reason, brothers, we were comforted over you in all our affliction and distress, through your faith.
<margin>8</margin> For now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord.
<margin>9</margin> For what thanksgiving can we return to God concerning you, for all the joy with which we rejoice because of you before our God,
<margin>10</margin> night and day praying exceedingly that we might see your face and supply what is lacking in your faith?
<margin>11</margin> Now may God himself, our Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way to you.
<margin>12</margin> And may the Lord make you increase and abound in love toward one another and toward all, just as we do toward you,
<margin>13</margin> so as to establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints.
<margin>IV. 1</margin> Finally then, brothers, we ask you and exhort you in the Lord Jesus, that as you received from us how you ought to walk and please God, so you would abound more and more.
<margin>2</margin> For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus.
<margin>3</margin> For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you should abstain from sexual immorality;
<margin>4</margin> that each one of you know how to possess his own vessel <note>The "vessel" here is often interpreted as either one's own body or one's wife</note> in sanctification and honor,
<margin>5</margin> not in the passion of lust, like the Gentiles who do not know God;
<margin>6</margin> that no one overstep and defraud his brother in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, as we also told you before and solemnly testified.
<margin>7</margin> For God did not call us to impurity, but in sanctification.
<margin>8</margin> Therefore he who rejects this, rejects not man but God.

<margin>33</margin> **Is it not even you before the Lord**] In the Greek, the conjunction "and" <note>original: καὶ (kai)</note> is added: "is it not *also* you." Theophylactus <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and Bible commentator</note> noted the emphasis of this. For he feels that not only we, but also the others whom he converted to Christ, are his crown and glory. "Before the Lord" <note>original: ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ Κυρίου (emprosthen tou Kyriou)</note>, that is, in the presence of the Lord, or in the sight of the Lord.

<margin>1</margin> **No longer bearing it**] <note>original: στέγοντες (stegontes)</note>, that is, not enduring, or being impatient with the desire to see you. "We were well-pleased" <note>original: εὐδοκήσαμεν (eudokēsamen)</note>. To explain this, Ambrose <note>The 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note> translated it as "we thought it best." Saint Jerome thinks the word is a new one coined by the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> to explain a specific property of the Hebrew language.

<margin>2</margin> **To remain**] <note>original: καταλειφθῆναι (kataleiphthēnai)</note>, or as others have it, to be left behind. Ambrose reads, "that we should be left alone at Athens."

<margin>3</margin> **Minister of God**] The Greek adds, "and our fellow-worker" <note>original: καὶ συνεργὸν ἡμῶν (kai synergon hēmōn)</note>, that is, our co-operator. Thus Ambrose also has "and a sharer in the work of God," for that is how he renders "fellow-worker."

<margin>4</margin> **Lest anyone be moved**] <note>original: σαίνεσθαι (sainesthai)</note>. The Greek commentaries explain this as "to be disturbed" or "terrified." The metaphor is taken from dogs wagging their tails, a point which Theophylactus also mentioned.

<margin>5</margin> **Coming and bringing news**] In the Greek, both are in the past tense <note>original: ἐλθόντος, καὶ εὐαγγελισαμένου (elthontos kai euangelisamenou)</note>, that is, "when he had come and had brought news," as Ambrose reads it.

<margin>6</margin> **Just as we also**] <note>original: καθάπερ καὶ ἡμεῖς ὑμᾶς (kathaper kai hēmeis hymas)</note>, that is, "just as we also [long to see] you." Either the conjunction "also" should have been omitted, or "and."

<margin>7</margin> **Praying more abundantly**] <note>original: ὑπὲρ ἐκ περισσοῦ δεόμενοι (hyper ek perissou deomenoi)</note>. Expressing the intensity of the words <note>term: intensity (epitasion)</note>, Ambrose reads, "praying most abundantly." For Paul doubled the vehemence of the feeling: "hyper" meaning "exceedingly," and "ek perissou" meaning "out of abundance" or "out of superfluity," as if to say, beyond measure and more than is necessary.

<margin>8</margin> **And make you abound**] Here he uses both verbs transitively: "to make to increase" and "to make to abound." We mentioned one of these above; since it is rare, we thought it should be noted.

<margin>9</margin> **And we in you**] <note>original: εἰς ὑμᾶς (eis hymas)</note>, that is, "toward you."

<margin>10</margin> **Without reproach**] <note>original: ἀμέμπτους (amemptous)</note>, that is, "blameless," as Ambrose reads. For it refers to "hearts," which Paul wishes to be such that no complaint can be made against them.

<column-break/>

...boasting, 33 is it not also you in the sight of our Lord Jesus Christ, at his coming? For you are <margin>20</margin> our glory and joy. Therefore <margin>1 III</margin> when we could no longer bear it, it seemed good to us to remain at Athens <margin>2</margin> alone, and we sent Timothy our brother, <margin>2</margin> and 3 minister of God, and a helper in our work in the Gospel of Christ, to strengthen you and comfort you concerning our faith, <margin>4</margin> Lest anyone should be disturbed in these <margin>3</margin> afflictions: for you yourselves know that we are placed for this purpose. <margin>B</margin> For even when we were with you, we told <margin>4</margin> you beforehand that we would suffer affliction, just as it even happened, as you know. Wherefore I also, no longer <margin>5</margin> bearing it, sent for this purpose, that I might know your faith, lest by some means he who tempts had tempted you, and our labor had become in vain. But recently <margin>5</margin> when <margin>6</margin> Timothy had come to us from you, and had brought us news of your faith and love, and that you have a good memory of us always, desiring to see us, 6 just as we also you. Therefore we <margin>7</margin> received consolation, brothers, through you in all our affliction and necessity, through your faith. Since now we live, if you stand in the Lord. <margin>8</margin> For what thanksgiving can we <margin>9</margin> repay to God concerning you for all the joy which we rejoice because of you in the sight of our God, night and day <margin>7 10</margin> praying beyond measure, that we may see your face, and supply the things that are lacking in your faith? Now may God <margin>11</margin> himself and our Father and our Lord Jesus Christ direct our way to you. And may the Lord <margin>8 12</margin> make you increase and overflow with mutual charity among yourselves and toward all, just as 9 we also toward you, That he may confirm your hearts 10 blameless <margin>13</margin> in holiness before God and our Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, with all his saints. As for the rest then, brothers, we ask you and <margin>1 IV.</margin> exhort you through the Lord Jesus, 1 as you received from us, how you ought to conduct yourselves and please God, 2 that you may abound more. For you know what <margin>2</margin> instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus. For <margin>3</margin> this is the will of God, your sanctification, that you should abstain from fornication, And that each one of you should know <margin>4</margin> how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, Not with the passion of lust, just as also the <margin>5</margin> nations, who have not known God, 3 Lest anyone oppress <margin>6</margin> and defraud his brother in business: 4 because the Lord is the avenger of all these things, 5 as we also previously said to you, and testified. For <margin>7</margin> God did not call us for the sake of 6 uncleanness, but to sanctification. Therefore 7 he who rejects, does not reject a man, <margin>8</margin>

---

<margin>F</margin> **As you received**] The "as" is redundant. For this conjunction follows.

<margin>2</margin> **So that you may also abound**] <note>original: ἵνα περισσεύητε μᾶλλον (hina perisseuēte mallon)</note>, that is, "so that you may abound more." The remaining words, "just as you also walk," are redundant. They seem to have been added for the sake of explaining the thought. Ambrose, however, adds, "just as you also walk." And we find it written this way in the ancient Latin copies. It does not appear from the commentaries of Theophylactus that it was added; certainly it is absent in the context, as it is in Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, the 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople famous for his preaching</note>.

<margin>3</margin> **Lest anyone overstep or circumvent his brother in business**] In the Epistle to the Ephesians, chapter 5, we indicated on the authority of Jerome that the word used here, "pleonektein" <note>to take advantage of or defraud</note>, does not properly pertain to greed for money, but to the fraud by which we wrongfully seize the wives of others; otherwise, he thinks it is inconsistent to join greed with lust, especially since it is followed immediately by: "For God did not call us to uncleanness." And indeed, Theophylactus interprets it this way in this place, following Chrysostom. He for whom his own wife is not enough is one who "defrauds" <note>original: πλεονεκτεῖ (pleonektei)</note>.

<margin>4</margin> **Because he is the avenger**] "Because he is the punisher, or avenger," etc. he said.

<margin>5</margin> **Just as we told you before**] "Just as we *also* told you before." And so Ambrose reads, adding the conjunction, so that this appears to be a repetition of a former warning which they ought to have remembered.

<margin>6</margin> **To uncleanness**] <note>original: ἐπὶ ἀκαθαρσίᾳ (epi akatharsia)</note>. This has the same force as if you were to say, "He did not call us on this condition, that we should be unclean." For the cause and condition of the calling was that we should cease to be what we were. For the preposition "epi" <note>meaning "upon" or "toward"</note> sometimes has this force when attached to the dative case. Though in what follows immediately, he misused "in" <note>Latin: in</note> for "toward" <note>Greek: epi</note>.

<margin>7</margin> **He who despises these**] The "these" is redundant. <note>original: ὁ ἀθετῶν (ho athetōn)</note>, that is, "he who rejects." The Translator added the pronoun "these" for the sake of explaining the matter. However, I wonder why it seemed right to Jerome to translate "athetein" <note>to reject or set aside</note> as "to transgress" <note>Latin: praevaricari</note>; for in the third book of Didymus *On the Holy Spirit*, adding something of his own, he writes in this way: "For God did not call us to uncleanness, but to sanctification. Therefore he who despises, or," as is better in the Greek, "he who transgresses, not a man..."

<summary>This page contains Paul's account of sending Timothy to the Thessalonians to strengthen them during trials and Erasmus's philological notes on Chapter 3 and the start of Chapter 4. Erasmus explores the nuances of Greek terms for "abounding" and "defrauding," noting that the latter might refer specifically to marital infidelity rather than general greed.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on Paul's First Epistle to the Thessalonians. # FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS, CHAPTER V.

<note>The top of the page presents the original Greek text of 1 Thessalonians 4:8 through 5:3.</note>

...the one giving his Holy Spirit to you. 
<margin>9</margin> Now concerning brotherly love, you have no need for me to write to you; for you yourselves are taught by God to love one another. 
<margin>10</margin> For indeed you do this for all the brothers who are in all Macedonia. But we exhort you, brothers, to excel even more, 
<margin>11</margin> and to aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you, 
<margin>12</margin> so that you may walk properly toward those on the outside, and have need of nothing. 
<margin>13</margin> But I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who have fallen asleep, so that you do not grieve as the others do who have no hope. 
<margin>14</margin> <margin>A</margin> For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with Him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus. 
<margin>B</margin> <margin>15</margin> For this we say to you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive and remain until the coming of the Lord will by no means precede those who have fallen asleep. 
<margin>16</margin> For the Lord Himself, with a shout, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven, and the dead in Christ will rise first. 
<margin>17</margin> Then we who are alive and remain will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord. 
<margin>18</margin> Therefore comfort one another with these words. 
<margin>V. 1</margin> Now concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need for anything to be written to you. 
<margin>2</margin> For you yourselves know accurately that the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night. 
<margin>C</margin> <margin>3</margin> For when they say, "Peace and safety," then sudden destruction comes upon them, just as...

---

8 **Who also** <note>original: "Qui etiam"</note>] The word "also" is not in the Greek; it says *ton didonta*, which means "the one who gives." Ambrose reads it this way as well.

9 **in you** <note>original: "in vobis"</note>] The Greek is *eis hymas*, which means "into you."

10 **Concerning brotherly love** <note>original: "De charitate fraternitatis"</note>] The Greek is *philadelphia*, meaning "brotherly love." Ambrose translates it as "brotherly affection." Indeed, with this word—composed of "love" and "brother"—the Apostles usually signify the mutual love of Christians among themselves; they do this following the custom of the Hebrews, who call all members of their nation "brothers."

11 **We have need** <note>original: "Necesse habuimus"</note>] The Greek is *chreian echete*, meaning "you have need"—that is, it is not necessary for me to write to you. The translator seems to have read *eichomen* <note>meaning "we had"</note>.

12 **You have been taught by God** <note>original: "A Deo didicistis"</note>] The Greek is *theodidaktoi*. Where this appears here as a compound word, John elsewhere uses two separate words, *didaktoi Theou* <note>"taught of God"</note>. While that is translated as "teachable by God," here it signifies those taught by God and inspired through divine instinct.

13 **And give effort** <note>original: "Et operam detis"</note>] The Greek is *philotimeisthai*, which means "to strive ambitiously." Ambrose translates it as "to exert oneself"; we translate it as "apply yourselves to this."

14 **To mind your own business** <note>original: "Ut vestrum negotium agatis"</note>] That is, that you attend to your own affairs. For he deters them from seeking after the affairs of others and from idleness, toward which many were already leaning under the pretext of religion. Now the world is filled everywhere with this kind of person—as if food were owed to everyone who "lives well" (which is common to all Christians), and as if those who labor with their hands or prove themselves in some other duty were not living well. They say they pray; but this is the duty of all Christians, and labor does not hinder prayer. I will say nothing of the many who live most wickedly under a holy persona, showing off their garments, belts, and fancy shoes in place of holy character. Furthermore, some ridiculously interpret this as "taking care of the business of one's own salvation."

15 **And desire nothing from anyone** <note>original: "Et nullius aliquid desideretis"</note>] The Greek is *kai mēdenos chreian echēte*, that is, "and that you have need of nothing." This "nothing" can refer to a person or a thing. Take care that you lack nothing, or take care that you do not have to beg for help from others.

16 **Concerning those sleeping** <note>original: "De dormientibus"</note>] The Greek is *tōn kekoimēmenōn*. It is like saying "those lulled to sleep" or "slumbering," derived from a word for falling asleep rather than just sleeping.

17 **For if we believe that Jesus died**] Chrysostom, citing this passage in his first Homily on 2 Corinthians, adds a third verb: "died, rose, and lived." The same reading is in the Commentaries, but in his explanation he does not touch upon the third word, just as Theophylact does not; therefore I suspect it was an addition.

18 **He will bring with him**] The Greek is *syn autō*, meaning "with himself" or "with him"—that is, with the Son. This latter view is more approved by me.

19 **In the coming** <note>original: "In adventu"</note>] Or "into the coming," *eis tēn parousian*. "We who are left and remain" are reserved for that coming; for the Greek article was not added without reason.

20 **We will not precede those who have slept** <note>original: "Non praeveniemus eos qui dormierunt"</note>] It would be more accurate to say "those who are sleeping" or "who fell asleep," for those who are already awake are usually said to "have slept." Furthermore, the Greek word sounds like "those lulled to sleep." Augustine, in several places including *The City of God*, Book 20, reads "those who slept before." From this, it appears that in some Greek codices it was written as *prokoimēthentas* <note>"those who slept before"</note>.

21 **With a shout** <note>original: "In jussu"</note>] The Greek is *en keleusmati*. It is not a simple command, but that cry with which sailors or soldiers encourage one another to perform a task vigorously.

22 **With a shout and with**] The preposition "with" is redundant; it is *en phōnē*, that is, "with a voice." It is as if he had said "with the command of a voice," similar to the poetic phrasing "a mass and mountains" instead of "a mass of mountains."

<column-break/>

...man, but God, 8 who gave his Holy Spirit into you. 10 Concerning brotherly love, 11 you have no <margin>9</margin> need for me to write to you: for you yourselves 12 are taught by God to love one another. For indeed you <margin>10</margin> do this toward all the brothers who are in all Macedonia. But we beseech you, brothers, that you abound more, 13 and that you apply yourselves to be quiet, 14 and <margin>11</margin> attend to your own affairs, and work with your own hands, just as we commanded you, so that you may behave honorably <margin>12</margin> toward outsiders, 15 and that you may have need of nothing. Furthermore, I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, 16 concerning those who have fallen <margin>13</margin> asleep, lest you grieve as the rest who have no hope. 17 For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, <margin>14</margin> so also God will bring those who have fallen asleep through Jesus 18 with him. For this we say to you <margin>15</margin> in the word of the Lord, that we who live and are left 19 until the coming of the Lord, 20 shall by no means precede those who are sleeping: Because the Lord himself, 21 with a shout of encouragement, 22 and with the <margin>16</margin> voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven, and the dead in Christ will rise 23 first. Then 24 we who live, who are left, <margin>17</margin> together with them shall be caught up in the clouds 25 to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord. Therefore comfort one another 26 with these <margin>18</margin> words. Furthermore, concerning the times and the points <margin>1 V.</margin> of time, brothers, there is no need for me to write to you. For you 2 yourselves <margin>2</margin> clearly know that the day of the Lord, like a thief in the night, so shall it come. For when they shall say, peace and <margin>3</margin> all is safe, then sudden 4 destruction threatens them, just as...

---

23 **First** <note>original: "Primi"</note>] The Greek is *prōton*, meaning "first" or "sooner."

<margin>D</margin> 24 **We who live**] Paul seems to speak as if the resurrection were going to happen in the age in which he was writing. However, since the use of a participle follows the tense of the verb it is attached to, it could be translated in the future: "Then we who shall be living and shall remain, together with them shall be caught up." It is remarkable how much Augustine and more recent writers sweat here while they desire to explain how Paul plainly says in this place that some who are living are to be caught up to immortality. But since that is not the purpose of this work, I will not pursue it at present; I have spoken elsewhere on this matter in the notes on *1 Corinthians, Chapter 15*. Certainly, Saint Ambrose, in his book *On the Faith of the Resurrection*, Chapter 9, brings up this passage in such a way that he seems to feel that those remaining at the coming of Christ will be caught up to him without having tasted death. He says: "For them, life is sweeter after rest. For the living, though the shortcut is heavy, the remedy remains unknown." For if I am not mistaken, he calls death the "remedy" there. But as I write this, the suspicion arises that Ambrose wrote "the remedy is unwelcome" rather than "the remedy is unknown," even though both editions consistently had "unknown." Therefore, I think it is safer to follow what is more correct, especially since elsewhere he seems to feel the same when explaining this very passage. He thinks that even those who remain will taste death in the very act of being caught up and in the transition. Theophylact, however, although he admits Paul is not included in this speech, nevertheless interprets that the pious, whom the Lord finds alive at his coming, will be caught up into the air together with those who have been raised, and he makes no mention of a momentary death in the catching up itself. Nor is what the Latin Scholastic says on this passage absurd: that the Apostle always makes that day "suspected," as if he might perhaps find those to whom he was writing still alive. But how do we know for certain that Paul was sure he would die before the Lord's coming? 1. In the [Second] Epistle to the Thessalonians, Chapter 2, he warns them not to be disturbed by a letter <margin>E</margin> as if written by him, suggesting that the day of the Lord is already at hand. He insists that it is near, and insists that it already presses; however, that whole passage is so entangled that it is as if Paul did not want to be understood. Elsewhere he says openly, "The Lord is near."

25 **To meet Christ** <note>original: "Obviam Christo"</note>] The Greek is *eis apantēsin tou Kyriou*, that is, "into the meeting of the Lord." And so he reads it, whoever he was, who wrote the second Epistle to the virgin Demetrias. For there are those who think that letter is not by Jerome, but by Julian.

26 **In these words** <note>original: "In verbis istis"</note>] That is, "in these words of comfort/spirit." In some Greek codices I found "of the spirit" added, but I do not know if it is an error, especially since I do not read it that way in Jerome or Ambrose, nor even in Theophylact.

<margin>F</margin> 1 **And moments** <note>original: "Et momentis"</note>] The Greek is *kai kairōn*. Perhaps it would have been better to translate "points of time" or "opportunities." For *chronos* simply signifies "time," such as a year or a month. But *kairos* means a "point of time" when a thing is to be done. Tertullian, in his book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, translates it as "concerning times and the spaces of times."

2 **You know diligently** <note>original: "Diligenter scitis"</note>] The Greek is *akribōs oidate*, meaning "you know exactly" or "you know to the full."

3 **And security** <note>original: "Et securitas"</note>] The Greek is *asphaleia*, that is, "when the matter is safe" and there is no danger. For this reason, Ambrose translates it as "firmness."

4 **Destruction will come upon** <note>original: "Superveniet interitus" </note>] The Greek is *ephistatai olethros*, which means "destruction stands over" or "threatens," using a verb in the present tense to express more effectively the unexpected onset of evil. And it is not "they will escape," but "they might escape," *ekphygōsin*, that is, "they would not be able to escape."

<summary>This page provides a Greek and Latin parallel of 1 Thessalonians 4:8–5:3 with extensive philological notes. It focuses on the linguistic nuances of "brotherly love," the necessity of manual labor, and the nature of the Second Coming and the resurrection.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on the First Epistle to the Thessalonians. It transitions from the discussion of the "day of the Lord" coming like a thief in the night to the final exhortations regarding church order, the three-part nature of the human person (spirit, soul, and body), and Paul's closing greetings. # THE FIRST EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE THESSALONIANS, CHAPTER V.

Just as labor pains come upon a woman with child, and they shall by no means escape. But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that the day should overtake you like a thief. You are all sons of light and sons of the day; we are not of the night, nor of darkness. Therefore, let us not sleep as others do, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, get drunk at night. But let us, being of the day, be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet, the hope of salvation. For God did not appoint us to wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that whether we wake or sleep, we should live together with him. Therefore, comfort one another and edify one another, just as you are doing. We ask you, brothers, to recognize those who labor among you, and are over you in the Lord and admonish you, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves. Now we exhort you, brothers, warn the unruly, comfort the faint-hearted, uphold the weak, be patient toward all. See that no one renders evil for evil to anyone, but always pursue what is good both for yourselves and for all. Rejoice always. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you. Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies. Test all things; hold fast to what is good. Abstain from every form of evil. Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely; and may your whole spirit, soul, and body be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. He who calls you is faithful, who also will do it. Brothers, pray for us. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I charge you by the Lord that this epistle be read to all the holy brothers. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.

-> The first to the Thessalonians was written from Athens. <-

## END OF THE FIRST EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE THESSALONIANS.

***

<gloss>5 In the womb having]</gloss> <note>original: "τῇ ἐν γαστρὶ ἐχούσῃ"</note>, that is, "to the one having in the womb," in the dative case. Moreover, here <note>original: "ὠδίν"</note> refers to pain, but specifically the pain of those in labor. Thus, Ambrose expressed it as "just as the pain of birth to the pregnant woman": so the sense is that the sudden day of judgment looms over them just as the pangs and pain of birth rush upon a pregnant woman.

<gloss>6 You are not of the night, nor of darkness]</gloss> Valla reads <note>original: "ἐσμὲν"</note>, that is, "we are," rather than "you are." Although as far as the meaning is concerned, it makes no difference, for he is speaking of all Christians. Ambrose reads, "you are not of the night."

<gloss>7 The breastplate of faith]</gloss> <note>original: "θώρακα"</note>. Among physicians, that part of the body is the thorax which encompasses the chest, shoulders, and shoulder blades down to the location of the stomach. From this, the garment or armor protecting this area is called a "thorax" <note>breastplate</note>. And he called "hope" a helmet by way of apposition. We, so that the speech might be clearer, translated it as "for a helmet, the hope of salvation."

<gloss>8 And edify one another]</gloss> <note>original: "εἷς τὸν ἕνα"</note>, that is, "one the one," which means "each other in turn."

<gloss>9 That you may have them more abundantly in love]</gloss> The Greek reads thus: <note>original: "Καὶ ἡγεῖσθε αὐτοὺς ὑπὲρ ἐκ περισσοῦ ἐν ἀγάπῃ"</note>. The meaning could be rendered as: "That you hold them in the highest value through love." Ambrose reads it as: "That you hold them in the highest honor in love," etc. Moreover, he doubled the expression "super-abundantly" <note>original: "ὑπὲρ ἐκ περισσοῦ"</note>, about which we gave warning above.

<gloss>10 Because of their work]</gloss> <note>original: "διὰ τὸ ἔργον αὐτῶν"</note>. This sounds just as if you said, "because of their deeds." Bishops ought to note this place diligently, who demand the highest honor from their people while they themselves do not care to perform their duty. Paul commands them to be held in the highest honor, but "because of their work," not because of an empty title; that is, because they are laboring, presiding in the Lord (not dominating with pride), admonishing, teaching, and consoling—which is the proper duty of Bishops.

<gloss>11 And have peace with them]</gloss> <note>original: "εἰρηνεύετε ἐν αὐτοῖς"</note>, that is, be peaceful enough among them. Although the Translator rendered the sense correctly enough. Other Greek manuscripts had <note>original: "ἐν ἑαυτοῖς"</note>, that is, "among yourselves." And so Ambrose reads it.

<gloss>12 Correct the restless]</gloss> <note>original: "νουθετεῖτε τοὺς ἀτάκτους"</note>, that is, "admonish the unordered" or "the disorderly." He means those who are unmanageable, who refuse to obey, and because of this disturb the common peace.

<gloss>13 Support the weak]</gloss> <note>original: "ἀντέχεσθε τῶν ἀσθενῶν"</note>, that is, "lift up"

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...just as the pain of birth to a pregnant woman, and they shall not escape. But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that the <margin>4</margin> day should seize you like a thief. You are all sons of light, and <margin>5</margin> sons of the day; <gloss>6</gloss> we are not of the night, nor of darkness. Therefore <margin>6</margin> let us not sleep, as the others do, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night; and <margin>7</margin> those who are drunk, are drunk at night. But we who are <margin>8</margin> of the day, let us be sober, having put on <gloss>7</gloss> the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation. Since <margin>9</margin> God did not appoint us to stir up wrath for ourselves, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that, whether we watch or <margin>10</margin> sleep, we may live together with him. Therefore <margin>11</margin> exhort one another, <gloss>8</gloss> and edify one another, individually, just as you are doing. We ask you, however, brothers, <margin>12</margin> to acknowledge those who labor among you, and who are over you in the Lord, and who admonish you, <gloss>9</gloss> so that you may hold them in the highest value through love <gloss>10</gloss> because of <margin>13</margin> their work; <gloss>11</gloss> have peace with them. We beseech <margin>14</margin> you, brothers, <gloss>12</gloss> warn the disorderly, comfort the faint-hearted, support <gloss>13</gloss> the weak, <gloss>14</gloss> be patient toward all. See that no one returns evil for evil <margin>15</margin> to anyone, but always pursue what is good, both toward one another and toward all. Always <margin>16</margin> rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In all things give <margin>17 18</margin> thanks: for this is the will of God through Christ Jesus toward you. Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise <margin>19 20</margin> prophecies. <gloss>16</gloss> Test all things, hold fast to what is good. <margin>21</margin> <margin>C</margin> Abstain from every evil appearance <gloss>17</gloss>. And may the <margin>22 23</margin> God of peace himself <gloss>18</gloss> sanctify you entirely: and may your whole spirit, and soul, and body, <gloss>19</gloss> so that you cannot be blamed in anything, be preserved at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Faithful is he who called you, who will also do it. <margin>24 25</margin> Brothers, pray for us. Greet all the brothers with a <margin>26</margin> holy kiss. I adjure you by the Lord, that <margin>20 27</margin> this Epistle be read to all the holy brothers. The grace of our Lord <margin>28</margin> Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.

## THE END OF THE FIRST EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE THESSALONIANS.

***

<margin>D</margin> and prop up the weak: as Ambrose reads, "bring help to the weak": for <note>original: "ἀντέχεσθαι"</note> properly means to assist one who is struggling.

<gloss>14 Be patient]</gloss> <note>original: "μακροθυμεῖτε"</note>, that is, "be slow to anger."

<gloss>15 We find 'to you']</gloss> <note>original: "εἰς ὑμᾶς"</note>, that is, "toward you."

<gloss>16 But test all things]</gloss> "But" is not added among the Greeks, nor does it affect the matter. Furthermore, <note>original: "δοκιμάζειν"</note> is an ambiguous word for the Greeks as well, just as "to prove" <note>Latin: probare</note> is for the Latins; it sometimes means "to approve" and sometimes "to explore" what kind of thing it is. Theophylact interprets it in this place as: "test, judge." Just as elsewhere, "Test the spirits, whether they be from God." Prophets are to be heard, but with judgment. I wonder which manuscript Augustine followed, for he reads in this way in his book against Adamantius, chapter 15: "Do not throw down the Spirit, do not quench prophecy, read all things, hold fast what is good"; unless I think an error happened to the scribe which Augustine followed, for what follows shows he read it that way. He likewise cites it in the book on *Nature and Grace*, chapter 9. Or perhaps he accommodated the sense of Paul to his own purpose. Tertullian, in his book *On the Prescription of Heretics*, says: "Examine all things, hold fast what is good."

<gloss>17 Abstain yourselves]</gloss> <note>original: "ἀπέχεσθε"</note>, that is, "abstain." "Yourselves" is not added.

<margin>E</margin> <gloss>18 May he sanctify you through all things]</gloss> <note>original: "ἁγιάσαι ὑμᾶς ὁλοτελεῖς· καὶ ὁλόκληρον ὑμῶν τὸ πνεῦμα, καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ"</note>, etc., that is, "may he sanctify you whole: and your whole spirit, and soul," etc., as Tertullian records in the book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*. Jerome, in his *Questions to Hedibia*, cites this place thus: "May the God of peace therefore sanctify you through all things, or full in all things, or perfect"; for this is what <note>original: "ὁλοτελεῖς"</note> sounds like more. Therefore the sense is, "may he sanctify you as perfect through all things," that is, in spirit, in soul, and in body. For Paul divides man into these parts. Furthermore, <note>original: "ὁλόκληρον"</note> sounds like "complete," not what we call complete as in "uncorrupted," but that which consists of all its numbers and parts. This is what Didymus indicated in his work *On the Holy Spirit*. Indeed, gathering from this place that "spirit" cannot be understood as the Divine Spirit, he says, "It is incredible and blasphemous for the Apostle to pray that the Holy Spirit be preserved whole, who can neither receive change nor progress."

<gloss>19 Without complaint]</gloss> <note>original: "ἀμέμπτως"</note>, that is, "blamelessly."

<gloss>20 This Epistle]</gloss> "This" is redundant for us. It was added, however, to explain the force of the article, "the" <note>original: "τὴν"</note>.

<meta>This page transitions from the text of the First Epistle to the Thessalonians to the introductory materials (the "Argument") for the Second Epistle. The previous page ended with Paul's closing exhortations and the beginning of his final blessing in 1 Thessalonians.</meta>

# THE INTRODUCTION
#### to the
# SECOND EPISTLE
### TO THE THESSALONIANS.

He sends this from Rome. The occasion for the Letter is as follows: Certain idle and disorderly people from Thessalonica were wandering about and unsettling the brothers, claiming that the presence of the Lord was already at hand. They deceived those who heard them, pretending that the Apostle had declared this or that it had been heard through the Spirit. When the Apostle learned these things, he wrote the Letter. First, he commends their growing faith and the fact that he boasted of them because they bravely endured tribulations for the sake of Christ. He also comforts them with the thought that there will be a reckoning from God against those who persecute them. Then, he teaches concerning the coming of the Savior, telling them not to believe anyone or be troubled—neither by a spirit, nor by a claim that he had written it—nor to think at all that it has already arrived. For it will not happen until the falling away <note>original: "ἀποστασία" (apostasia); often interpreted as a Great Revolt or spiritual defection.</note> comes first, and after it the Antichrist, the son of perdition, whose coming he indicates will be accompanied by signs and false wonders through the working of Satan. Next, having exhorted them to stand bravely and hold to the traditions <note>original: "παραδόσεις" (paradoseis); referring to the oral and written teachings passed down by the apostles.</note> which they were taught by him, he commands them to have no fellowship with the disorderly, but to reject them; for he revealed such people to be meddlers and deceivers. He gave a general command that anyone not obeying his words should be excluded from the assembly <note>original: "ἀποσυνάγωγον" (aposynagogon); literally "put out of the synagogue" or congregation.</note>. Finally, having prayed for peace for them, he completes the Letter, writing the greeting with his own hand, which he declared to be the sign of every Letter.

---

### ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO
# THE THESSALONIANS.
#### Introduction by
## DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop-cap 'Q' featuring a landscape scene with a prominent tree in the foreground and a small house or chapel in the distant background.</image-desc> Since Paul did not have the opportunity to revisit the Thessalonians, he strengthens their minds through this Letter, so that they might bravely bear the afflictions brought upon them for Christ’s sake, knowing that they will not lack a reward, nor will their enemies lack punishment. Furthermore, regarding the day of the Lord’s coming—which he had touched upon somewhat in the previous Letter—he warns them not to be disturbed by the words of certain people who were asserting that it was already imminent. He indicates that first the Roman Empire <note>original: "Romanum Imperium"</note> must be abolished, and then the Antichrist will come. He even more carefully emphasizes that those who disturb public peace and order with their idleness and meddling must be restrained and compelled to work, since Paul himself labored with his own hands while among them. He wrote this from Athens by the same messengers through whom he sent the first Letter, as our introductions show.

# THE SECOND EPISTLE
## OF THE APOSTLE
### PAUL TO THE THESSALONIANS.

<margin>A</margin> 1 **P**AUL and Silvanus and Timothy, to the Church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: 2 Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. 3 We are bound to give thanks to God always for you, brothers, as is fitting, because your faith grows exceedingly, and the love of every one of you all toward each other abounds, 4 So that we ourselves boast of you in the Churches of God for your patience and faith in all your persecutions and the tribulations that you endure, 5 A clear evidence of the righteous judgment of God, so that you may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you also suffer. 6 Since it is a righteous thing with God to repay tribulation to those who trouble you, 7 And to you who are troubled, rest with us, at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from <margin>B</margin> heaven with his mighty angels, 8 In flaming fire, taking vengeance on those who do not know God, and on those who do not obey the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. 9 These shall pay the penalty of eternal destruction from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his power, 10 When he comes to be glorified in his saints and to be wondered at in all those who believe, because our testimony among you was believed in that day. 11 To which end we also pray always for you, that our God would count you worthy of this calling, and fulfill all the good pleasure of his goodness and the work of faith with power, 12 That the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God II. 1 and the Lord Jesus Christ. Now we beseech you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together unto him, 2 That you be not quickly shaken from your mind, nor be troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by

---

<margin>C</margin>
1 *As is fitting* <note>original: "dignum est"</note>] This is indeed found among the Latin writers, but it is more common and more characteristically Latin to say "as is right" <note>original: "ut par est," translating the Greek "καθὼς ἄξιόν ἐστιν" (kathos axion estin)</note>.
2 *Your faith grows exceedingly*] The Greek word <term>hyperauxanei</term> contains a prefix that implies intensification. Otherwise, in Latin, one might say "it grows into" <note>original: "insercrefcit"</note>, which suggests something growing into another thing or overwhelming others by its growth.
3 *Of every one of you*] The Greek adds "of all" <note>original: "πάντων" (panton)</note> for emphasis. Ambrose also reads, "of every one of all of you."
4 *As an evidence*] The word is not <term>paradeigma</term> (an example to be followed), but <term>endeigma</term>, which means a proof, a showing, a specimen, or a declaration. For an "exemplar" is set forth for the sake of imitation, while an "evidence" declares what was hidden. Then God’s justice will become clear, when those who here endlessly torment the godly are given over to eternal tortures, and those who here suffered dire things in the hope of promised happiness take possession of the heavenly kingdom. The preposition "in" is redundant here, or it functions in the nominative case as "a showing," referring to those who are afflicted—meaning, "You are the proof, and you show that the judgment of God is right when he rewards those who have suffered so much with his kingdom."
5 *In the kingdom of God*] The preposition "in" is redundant; Ambrose does not include it.
6 *Since indeed it is just*] Ambrose reads "siquidem" (since) rather than "si" (if). Aquinas noted that in some copies it was written "siquidem" instead of "si tamen" (if however). Greek commentaries explain that in this passage <term>eiper</term> is used for <term>epeidēper</term>, meaning "since" or "inasmuch as"; for it expresses affirmation, not doubt. Even if it were translated as "if," it would affirm it all the more, as if introducing a truth that it would be wrong to doubt. It is a wonder why the Translator thought "however" <note>original: "tamen"</note> should be added.
7 *To repay retribution*] The Greek is "to repay tribulation to those who trouble you." Ambrose says, "to repay pressure to those who depress you." Therefore, it seems the common Latin copies were corrupted by the error of scribes <note>note: Erasmus suggests a copyist wrote "retributionem" (retribution) instead of "tribulationem" (tribulation)</note>, especially since in the very ancient manuscript of the Pauline Library it stands as "to repay tribulation"; I have found it written this way in several other printed editions as well. Indeed, the very structure of the sentence, composed of opposites, indicates the genuine reading. He opposes those who afflict to those who are afflicted, and affliction to rest, which in Greek is <term>anesis</term>, meaning "relaxation"; for <term>thlipsis</term> properly means "pressure."
8 *Of his power*] <term>Dynameōs</term>, that is, of his might.
9 *In a flame of fire*] That is, in a conflagration or the fire of a flame. Ambrose reads it this way.
10 *Giving vengeance*] The word "giving" <note>original: "dantis"</note> refers to the Lord, not to the flame. Although the speech is ambiguous in Latin, it is not so in Greek.
11 *They shall pay the penalty*] That is, they shall suffer or weigh out the punishment.
12 *In destruction*] The "in" is redundant; it should be "eternal destruction," added appositively so we understand it is not just any punishment, but an eternal one.

<margin>D</margin>
13 *The glory of his virtue*] <term>Ischyos</term>, that is, of his strength or power; let no one take it for <term>aretē</term>, that is, "virtue" as the opposite of vice, as we have often warned.
14 *To become wonderful*] <term>Thaumasthēnai</term>, which Ambrose expressed as "to be made marvelous." For in Greek it is a passive verb, used when someone is rendered an object of wonder to others.
15 *Because our testimony was believed*] Ambrose, to avoid ambiguity, explains it thus: "because our testimony found faith." But it could be more Latin to say, "that faith was given to our testimony."
16 *In that day*] Ambrose adds here, "of the Lord's coming."
17 *In which also we pray*] That is, "To which end we pray," or "For which." If you refer this to what precedes, the sense is that this prayer is made among the first things—that is, before all else. Chrysostom explains it in this way. But if referred to what follows, the sense is that prayers should be made by everyone.
18 *And may he deign*] <term>Axiōsē</term>. Ambrose translates this as "may he count worthy."
19 *By his calling*] <term>Tēs klēseōs</term>, that is, by the calling. The word "his" is not added in the Greek, though the presence of the article has almost the same effect; therefore we added "that calling."
20 *All the will*] <term>Eudokian</term>, that is, "good pleasure" or "good purpose." I wonder what Ambrose was following when he read "in every pleasure of goodness," unless he understood a hidden "according to"—as in, "may he perfect you according to his good will." Again, this is a word by which Paul and the Evangelists typically exclude human merits.
21 *Of his goodness*] <term>Agathōsynēs</term>. Again, "his" is redundant.
22 *And the work of faith*] Here too Ambrose reads "in the work," to correspond with "pleasure."
23 *In virtue*] <term>En dynamei</term>, that is, in power and strength.
24 *May be glorified*] <term>Endoxasthē</term>, that is, may become celebrated, or ennobled, or glorified.

<margin>E</margin>
1 *By the coming*] The Greek says: "concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and our gathering together unto him." The meaning could be rendered as "in the name of the coming... and in the name of our gathering." The Greek commentaries interpret it in this sense. For he adjures them not only by this name—that Christ is to appear in his power—but also because the faithful themselves will be present there and joined to Christ. The word "him" <note>original: "αὐτόν" (auton)</note> refers not to the Lord, but to the "coming" <note>original: "παρουσίαν" (parousian)</note>. Ambrose seems to have read it as "in it" <note>original: "in idipso"</note>, if the manuscript is free of error.
2 *Be quickly moved*] <term>Tacheōs saleuthēnai</term>. This properly refers to something wavering or being displaced.
3 *From your sense*] <term>Noos</term>, that is, from your mind or intellect.

# TO THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS, CHAPTER 2

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>2</margin> ...by a letter as if from us, as though the day of Christ were at hand. <margin>3</margin> Let no one deceive you in any way, for that day will not come unless the rebellion <note>original: "ἡ ἀποστασία" (hē apostasia)</note> comes first, and the man of sin is revealed, the son of <margin>4</margin> destruction, who opposes and exalts himself against everything called God or an object of worship, so that he sits in the temple of God as God, showing himself <margin>5</margin> that he is God. Do you not remember that when I was still with you, <margin>6</margin> I told you these things? And now you know what is restraining him, <margin>7</margin> so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of lawlessness <note>original: "τῆς ἀνομίας" (tēs anomias)</note> is already at work; only he who <margin>B</margin> <margin>8</margin> restrains it now will do so until he is out of the way. And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord will consume with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the appearing <margin>9</margin> of his coming. The coming of the lawless one is according to the working of Satan, with all power and signs <margin>10</margin> and lying wonders, and with every deception of unrighteousness among those who are perishing, because they did not receive the love of the truth, <margin>11</margin> that they might be saved. And for this reason, God will send them a strong delusion, so that they <margin>12</margin> believe the lie, that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but took pleasure in <margin>C</margin> <margin>13</margin> unrighteousness. But we are bound to give thanks to God always for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you from the beginning for salvation through sanctification of the spirit and belief in the truth, <margin>14</margin> to which he called you through our Gospel, to the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. <margin>15</margin> So then, brothers, stand firm...

<margin>D</margin>
...nor by letter, <margin>4</margin> as if we were the authors, as if the <margin>5</margin> day of Christ were at hand. Let no one deceive you in any way, for the Lord will not come <margin>6</margin> unless the rebellion comes first, and <margin>7</margin> that wicked man is revealed, the lost son, <margin>8</margin> who is the adversary, and is exalted <margin>8</margin> against everyone who is called God, or a divinity, so that he sits in the temple of God as if he were God, <margin>9</margin> showing himself to be God. <margin>10</margin> Do you not remember that when I was still <margin>5</margin> with you, <margin>11</margin> I said these things to you? And now you know what <margin>6</margin> holds him back, namely <margin>12</margin> so that he may be revealed in his own time. <margin>13</margin> For the mystery of iniquity now works; <margin>14</margin> only let him who holds, hold for the present, <margin>7</margin> until he is taken out of the way. And then that wicked one will be revealed, whom the Lord <margin>15</margin> will finish off with the breath of his mouth, and will abolish with the <margin>16</margin> brightness <margin>E</margin> of his coming. His coming <margin>9</margin> is according to the operation of Satan, with all power, and signs, <margin>17</margin> and lying wonders, and with every deception of <margin>10</margin> injustice, <margin>18</margin> in those who perish, because <margin>19</margin> they did not receive the love of truth, so that they might be saved. <margin>20</margin> And therefore God will send them <margin>21</margin> the efficacy of illusion, <margin>11</margin> so that they believe a lie, that all may be judged who <margin>12</margin> did not believe the truth, <margin>22</margin> but approved of injustice. But we must give thanks to God always <margin>13</margin> for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, <margin>23</margin> because God chose you <margin>24</margin> from the beginning for salvation through the sanctification of the spirit and faith of the truth, <margin>25</margin> to which he called <margin>14</margin> you through our Gospel, for the acquisition of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, brothers, stand firm, <margin>15</margin> etc.

---

**4** *As if sent by us]* <note>original: "ὡς δἰ ἡμῶν"</note>, that is, "as if through us." The word "sent" was added for the sake of explanation, even if it changes the sense somewhat. For Paul does not want them to be troubled, neither by a spirit (as if coming from Paul), nor by a word (brought in Paul’s name), nor by a letter (written by his command or name); and this is what the Greek words sound like.

**5** *Day of the Lord]* For "Lord," the Greek has "Christ."

**6** *Unless the falling away comes]* <note>original: "ἡ ἀποστασία"</note>. Ambrose translates this as "falling away" <note>original: "defectionem"</note>: specifically when someone falls away from their author or prince. The added article <note>the "the" in Greek</note> signifies that famous and previously predicted falling away.

**7** *Man of sin]* <note>original: "ὁ ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἁμαρτίας"</note>. Saint Ambrose, to explain the force of the article, read it as "that man," so that we would understand it was spoken regarding a specific man.

**8** *Above everything that is called]* The translators seem to have read "above everything that is called." But the Greek manuscripts have it thus: "against everyone called God, or an object of worship," that is, *above, or against everyone who is called God, or a cult, or a veneration.* And we find it written this way in Origen. Augustine, in the last chapter of book 12 *Against the Adversary of the Law and Prophets*, reads, "above every God and that which is worshipped," but he was using a faulty manuscript, which happened to him frequently. Jerome, in *Against Jovinian*, cites it in this way: "against everything that is called God or religion," coming closer to the Greek words. Although I see that some read "all" <note>original: "πᾶν"</note> instead of "everyone" <note>original: "πάντα"</note>, meaning "against everything called God or religion." For "object of worship" <note>original: "σέβασμα" (sebasma)</note> is properly said of that which we adore and venerate with the highest reverence, and which excels in majesty: and it can be translated as "divinity" <note>original: "numen"</note>. Theophylact, reading "everyone," explains the passage so that "everyone" seems to refer to all the demons or men who were held to be gods, and "object of worship" to statues, groves, or temples. If we read "everything," which I think was the original writing, the participle "called" must refer to both: that which is called "God," or that which is called a "sebasma." For just as those were not true gods, so neither were they true "sebasmata" which they venerated. For how could he prefer himself to the true God, whom he did not know?

**9** *As if he were God]* <note>original: "ὥστε εἰς τὸν ναὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὡς Θεὸν καθίσαι"</note>, that is, showing himself off to be God, when he is not. Paul does not finish the order of his speech, but as if forgetting what he had begun, he throws in what comes to mind. For he seemed about to add: "because unless the falling away comes, etc., the day of the Lord will not come."

**10** *You do not retain]* <note>original: "Οὐ μνημονεύετε"</note>, that is, "You do not remember." Oh, what a new affectation of abundance, even to the injury of the sense! Is this, I ask you, to translate the Divine Letters, or rather to play games in a serious matter? When a simple, well-known, and proper word was available <note>the word "remember"</note>, he preferred "retain." "Hold" would have been more tolerable, even if it were ambiguous. But it is one thing to "retain" and another to "hold": he holds who remembers or even understands; he retains who calls back what is otherwise about to leave. And in this place, a certain person rages against me like a tragic actor, saying I am utterly ignorant of the Latin language, apparently not understanding that "retain" is said in Latin for "remember," since Seneca wrote this way in a certain letter he wrote to Paul, and the same Translator translated it thus in Acts chapter 20. As if any learned person believes those letters are by the people whose names they bear! Or as if it follows that "retain" was said correctly here for "hold" just because it was said the same way elsewhere. And he who conducts the matter with such sharp logic—while producing no passage from approved Latin authors—calls me utterly ignorant of Latin, calling me unrefined and of a dull, thick wit. But it bothers the man that I criticized the Translator whom he had undertaken to defend; yet meanwhile, he leaves his guilty party abandoned in so many places where he doesn't mutter a word in his defense, which is itself more modest than defending his cause so clumsily.

<column-break/>

**11** *These things I said to you]* Ambrose, unless the manuscript is faulty, reads it this way: "Do you not remember that while I was still doing these things among you, these things were said to you."

**12** *That he might be revealed in his own]* The word "he" <note>original: "αὐτὸν" (auton)</note> is missing in the Latin: "so that he may be revealed." He, I say, the adversary of whom we just spoke.

**13** *The mystery of iniquity is already at work]* "Mystery" is the same word which elsewhere he translates as "sacrament." Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples thinks "works" is taken passively here for "is performed." Though this is not necessary, as it is a middle verb. And "to work" <note>original: "ἐνεργεῖν"</note> is not properly "to perform" or "to do," but "to act," that is, to exercise its power: just as the Spirit is said to "work" in us when he shows his power and efficacy. So now Paul says Antichrist has not yet appeared, but nevertheless his spirit already prevails secretly and acts in those who persecute Christians. The Greek interpreters think this was said regarding Nero.

**14** *Only that he who holds now]* <note>original: "μόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι ἕως"</note>. It seems something is missing in the Greek manuscript: "let him who now holds, hold, until, etc.," unless we prefer it to be an "aposiopesis" <note>a sudden breaking off in speech</note>, which signifies more by staying silent than if the word were explained. They explain this passage as referring to the Roman Empire, upon the dissolution of which Antichrist will come. Some say it refers to Nero, whom they think will either rise again or be the future Antichrist, or that a fable is being kept about this so he may come forth in his own time; some say it refers to the Christian faith. Augustine discusses these things more accurately in *The City of God*, book 20, chapter 19.

**15** *He will slay]* <note>original: "ἀναλώσει"</note>, that is, "he will consume."

**16** *By the illustration of his coming]* <note>original: "τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ"</note>, that is, "by the appearance," even if Ambrose reads "by the illustration of his presence." Augustine reads "by the illumination of his presence," so that you may understand that the Antichrist will be obscured by the brightness of the coming Christ.

**17** *And lying wonders]* <note>original: "ψεύδους"</note>, that is, "of a lie": Ambrose also reads it this way. Although if the Translator translated it this way on purpose, he translated elegantly; if by chance, then luckily.

**18** *In those who perish]* In Greek it is "among those," even if the Latin manuscripts object.

**19** *The charity of truth]* <note>original: "τὴν ἀγάπην τῆς ἀληθείας οὐκ ἐδέξαντο"</note>, that is, "they did not receive the love of the truth." And thus Saint Ambrose reads it. For "charity" <note>original: "charitas"</note> coheres rather harshly with the genitive case of "truth"; for he meant the love of the true, or true charity, or if we believe Theophylact, Christ himself, who was both charity and truth.

**20** *Therefore he will send]* <note>original: "Καὶ διὰ τοῦτο"</note>, that is, "And therefore." For we are missing the conjunction "and."

**21** *The operation of error]* <note>original: "ἐνέργειαν πλάνης"</note>, that is, "the efficacy of seduction," or "imposture," so that it refers to the wonders which Antichrist is going to do, specifically with the unclean spirit acting in him. Furthermore, Saint Jerome thinks Paul took this passage from Isaiah, who writes: "The Lord will send them a spirit of error." Moreover, a spirit is to act, like fire.

**22** *But they consented]* <note>original: "ἀλλ’ εὐδοκήσαντες ἐν τῇ ἀδικίᾳ"</note>. This could be translated as "but to whom iniquity was pleasing." Or, "but they approved of iniquity," as "eudokein" <note>to take pleasure in</note> is used elsewhere.

**23** *Because he chose us]* <note>original: "ὅτι εἵλετο ὑμᾶς"</note>, that is, "he chose you."

**24** *First fruits unto salvation]* <note>original: "ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς εἰς σωτηρίαν"</note>, that is, "from the beginning unto salvation." And Ambrose reads "from the principle." It appears the Translator read "first fruits" <note>original: "ἀπαρχὰς"</note>, so that the sense is that they were among the first called from the Thessalonians. But if you read "from the beginning," it pertains to divine predestination. Although from the same words this sense can also be taken: "God snatched us from the empire." Theophylact in his commentary reads "from the beginning" and interprets it as predestination, yet it is not entirely clear if he read "first fruits."

**25** *In which also he called]* <note>original: "Εἰς ὃ"</note>, that is, "Unto which." And this can...

### PAUL’S EPISTLE CHAPTER III.

<margin>15</margin> ...stand firm, and hold to the traditions that you were taught, <margin>16</margin> whether by word or by our letter. Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, <margin>17</margin> who loved us and gave us eternal comfort and good hope through grace, comfort your hearts and establish you in every good word and <margin>III. 1</margin> work. Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified, just as it is <margin>2</margin> among you, and that we may be delivered from absurd and <margin>3</margin> wicked men; for not everyone has faith. But the Lord is faithful, who will establish you and guard you from the evil one. <margin>4</margin> And we have confidence in the Lord concerning you, that the things we command <margin>5</margin> you, you both do and will do. And may the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and <margin>6</margin> into the patience of Christ. Now we command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks in a disordered way <margin>7</margin> and not according to the tradition which they received from us. For you yourselves know how it is necessary to imitate us; because <margin>8</margin> we were not disordered among you, nor did we eat anyone’s bread for free, but worked with labor and toil night and day, so as not to be a burden <margin>9</margin> to any of you. Not because we do not have the authority, but so that we might give ourselves as an example to you to imitate us. <margin>10</margin> For even when we were with you, we commanded this to you: that if anyone does not want to work, let him <margin>11</margin> not eat. For we hear that some are walking among you in a disordered way, doing no work, but being busybodies. <margin>12</margin> To such people we command and exhort through our Lord Jesus Christ, that by working with quietness they <margin>13</margin> may eat their own bread. But you, brothers, <margin>14</margin> do not grow weary in doing good. And if anyone does not obey our word, through this letter...
