<margin>A</margin> This may be taken absolutely, or referred to the spirit, so that you say, "into which": and so the Greek commentaries <note>The "Scholia" or marginal notes found in ancient manuscripts.</note> indicate. The ancient codices have <term>in which</term> <note>original: "in quam"</note>, as Ambrose <note>Likely referring to Ambrosiaster, a 4th-century commentator often confused with St. Ambrose.</note> reads. From these one may guess that the first writing was <term>into whom</term> <note>original: "in quem"</note>, namely the spirit. This seemed harsher to the reader, and for that reason someone changed it to <term>in which</term>, so that it might refer more smoothly to the nearest word, "faith." However, it pleases me more that it be taken absolutely.

<margin>26 Which you were taught</margin> <note>original: "ἃς ἐδιδάχθητε"</note>, that is, which you were instructed in, so that he might more incidentally commend his own duty.

<margin>27 God and our Father</margin> The Greek speech is smoother, <note>original: "ὁ Θεὸς καὶ Πατὴρ ἡμῶν"</note>, that is, <term>He who is God and likewise our Father</term>. For if he had said "the God and the Father," he would have seemed to designate two persons, of whom one was God and the other was Father. Ambrose did not add the conjunction; I do not know if this was a fault of the scribes.

<margin>28 Comfort your hearts</margin> <note>original: "Παρακαλέσαι ὑμῶν τὰς καρδίας"</note>, that is, <term>Console your hearts</term>. Although the verb *parakalein* is ambiguous: and among the Greeks, "speech" precedes "work," but in our language the order is different. In handing down piety, it is more important to teach than to act; in the disciplines, speech comes before work. For first one must learn what is fitting to do.

<margin>1</margin> <margin>A</margin> <term>From troublesome men</term> <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῶν ἀτόπων"</note>. This sounds more like <term>from the absurd and monstrous</term>. Ambrose reads, <term>from the unjust</term>. *Atopos* in Greek is said of one who fits into "no place," such as heretics.

<margin>2 But God is faithful</margin> In Greek it is <term>Lord</term> <note>original: "Πιστὸς δέ ἐστιν ὁ Κύριος"</note>.

<margin>3 Since whatever</margin> <note>original: "ὅτι"</note>, "because." There is a strange confusion of conjunctions. The Greek speech has an ambiguity. For the sense can be taken here: "We trust in you, and that relying on the protection of the Lord, that you are keeping our precepts now, and will keep them in the future." Or it can be taken: "We trust in you, that those things which we commanded you are both being kept and will be kept in the future." In the first sense, the conjunction <term>and</term> <note>original: "καὶ"</note> connects these two words, <term>we commanded and you do</term>; in the second, the repeated conjunction connects both parts—<term>both you do and you will do</term>—equally with the verb "we trust." Theophylact <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and Bible commentator.</note> seems to follow the first sense, Ambrose the latter. In the first sense, the first <term>and</term> simply couples the words, and the second stands for <term>also</term>, which is a Greek idiom.

<margin>4 In charity</margin> <note>original: "εἰς τὴν ἀγάπην"</note>, that is, <term>into love</term>.

<margin>5 And the patience of Christ</margin> <note>original: "καὶ εἰς τὴν ὑπομονὴν τοῦ Χριστοῦ"</note>, that is, <term>into the expectation of Christ</term>. So Ambrose reads, and rightly so. Furthermore, *hypomonē* sounds like <term>perseverance</term> in some matter, not without trouble, but again with the expectation of a reward, or certainly the end of an evil thing.

<margin>6 But we denounce</margin> It is the same word that he had translated as <term>we command</term> <note>original: "Παραγγέλλομεν"</note>.

<margin>7 Walking inordinately</margin> <note>original: "ἀτάκτως"</note>, either "disordered," or "turbulently." Now it is nothing new that he said <term>walk</term> instead of <term>conduct oneself</term>.

<margin>8 Which they received</margin> The translator seems to have read <note>original: "παρέλαβον"</note> (plural), but the Greeks read <note>original: "παρέλαβεν"</note>, that is, <term>he received</term> (singular).

<margin>9 We were not restless</margin> <note>original: "οὐκ ἠτακτήσαμεν"</note>, that is, <term>we were not disordered</term>, or <term>we were not unruly</term>. Ambrose translates, <term>we did not live intemperately among you</term>: and he likewise translates the word for disordered as <term>intemperately</term>. These are strange choices by this translator, who at one point translates the word as <term>disordered</term>, and now translates the verb form as <term>we were restless</term>, although both words have the same origin. Ambrose translates correctly, provided he felt that <term>intemperately</term> was the same as <term>turbulently</term> and <term>unsteadily</term>. Indeed, in Latin, those are said to be <term>driven into order</term> who are bound by common law and do not differ in any way from the rest. The opposite of this is if anyone,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> and hold the institutions, <margin>26</margin> which you learned, whether through word or through our letter. But may the <margin>16</margin> Lord himself, our Jesus Christ, and God and our Father, who loved us, and gave eternal consolation and good hope through grace, <margin>27</margin> console your hearts, <margin>17</margin> and establish you in every word and good work. What <margin>III. 1</margin> remains, pray, brothers, for us, that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified just as it is among you, and that we may be <margin>2</margin> snatched away from absurd and perverse men: for faith is not of all. <margin>2</margin> But the Lord is faithful, who will <margin>3</margin> establish you and guard you from evil. But we trust through <margin>4</margin> the Lord concerning you, <margin>3</margin> that what we command you, you both <margin>B</margin> do and will do. Furthermore, may the Lord direct your <margin>5</margin> hearts into the love of God and into the expectation of Christ. <margin>4</margin> But we command you, brothers, through the <margin>6</margin> name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you withdraw yourselves from every brother who conducts himself in a disordered way, and not according to the institution <margin>8</margin> which he received from us. For you yourselves know <margin>7</margin> how it is necessary to imitate us: since we did not conduct ourselves in a disordered way among you, <margin>10</margin> nor did we <margin>8</margin> receive bread for free from anyone, but with labor and sweat night and day doing work, for this purpose: that we might not be a burden to any of you. Not <margin>12</margin> that this is not permitted to us, but <margin>9</margin> <margin>C</margin> that we might show ourselves as a model to you for imitating us. For even when we were among you, this we <margin>13</margin> commanded <margin>10</margin> you: that if anyone was unwilling to work, let him not eat. <margin>14</margin> For we hear that some <margin>15</margin> are conducting themselves among <margin>11</margin> you in a disordered way, <margin>16</margin> doing no work, but acting meddlesomely. To those who are of this sort, <margin>17</margin> we command <margin>12</margin> and beseech <margin>18</margin> through our Lord Jesus Christ, that working with quietness they <margin>19</margin> may eat their own bread. But you, brothers, do not be weary in <margin>13</margin> doing well. But if anyone does not obey our word, <margin>14</margin>

---

despising public laws, lives by his own will. For Paul calls this *ataktein*, to live "out of order." The metaphor is taken from military service, where it is not permitted to desert the rank, which they call *ataktein*.

<margin>10 Nor did we eat bread for free</margin> Ambrose reads <term>we ate</term> <note>original: "edimus"</note>, so it appears he read "we ate" <note>original: "ἐφάγομεν"</note> instead of "we received" <note>original: "ἐλάβομεν"</note>. Furthermore, "we received," which is now held in the Greek codices, fits better with what follows: <term>from anyone</term>.

<margin>11 In labor and fatigue</margin> <note>original: "κόπῳ καὶ μόχθῳ"</note>. Of which we made mention above: both come in the same way: <term>kopos</term> is labor, <term>mochthos</term> is troublesome labor.

<margin>12 As if we did not have</margin> <note>original: "ὅτι οὐκ ἔχομεν"</note>, that is, <term>that we might not have</term>. And we give, <term>we would not give</term>, <term>we have</term>, this is, <term>that this was not permitted for us to do</term>. By which saying he at once both excuses others who were taking support, and exaggerates his own temperance, who required nothing beyond his right, so that he did not even receive what had been just.

<margin>13 We were denouncing</margin> <note>original: "παρηγγέλλομεν"</note>, that is, <term>we were commanding</term>. I wish the translator had successfully affected a variety of words here, as I easily conclude. Plutarch gave a title to his book, *Marriage Precepts* <note>original: "γαμικὰ παραγγέλματα"</note>: who would dare to translate this as <term>connubial denunciations</term>? Among the legal experts I read, <term>denunciation of a new work</term>. Furthermore, whether they always "denounce" who command and prescribe, I do not know. Indeed, if it is not permitted in every place to put "mortals" for "men," I think much less should one put "to denounce" for "to command" in every place.

<margin>14 For we heard</margin> <note>original: "Ἀκούομεν γὰρ"</note>, that is, <term>For we hear</term>, so that it is the present tense.

<margin>15 To walk restlessly</margin> <note>original: "ἀτάκτως"</note>. Which a little above he translated as <term>inordinately</term>, now he translates as <term>restlessly</term>. Again Ambrose uses <term>intemperantly</term>. And in this place, "walking restlessly" is <term>walking about</term>, that is, <term>wandering around, which is the native meaning of this word</term>.

<margin>16 Doing no work, but &c.</margin> The translator did not preserve the elegance of the Greek figure of speech, <note>original: "μηδὲν ἐργαζομένους, ἀλλὰ περιεργαζομένους"</note>, that is, <term>doing nothing, but being busybodies</term>. For there is such a thing in these words of Paul's as Marcus Tullius [Cicero] points out in a saying of Domitius Afer, who said <term>his friend Manlius, because he was in a turmoil in his acting, was not acting, but over-acting</term> <note>original: "non agere, sed satagere"</note>. Now there is a double grace here: the first is in the affinity of the words, which kind is: <term>one must linger on embassies, not loiter</term>; the other is in the corruption of the word, such as is in <term>to act and to over-act</term>. For he "acts" who performs his duty; he "over-acts" who struggles vehemently but in vain. "Working" <note>original: "ἐργαζομένοι"</note> is a matter of praise; "being busybodies" <note>original: "περιεργαζόμενοι"</note> is blameworthy, and yet "being busybodies" seems to be more than "working." There is also a not unpleasant irony: "to work" is he who works fruitfully; "to be a busybody" is he who works unfruitfully. Although that "being a busybody" also signifies <term>doing superfluous and useless things</term>, which are called "perierga," as if pertaining to nothing. From this it certainly appears that "working" and "meddling" are different things, though both are usually rendered by the same word.

<margin>17 We denounce and beseech</margin> <note>original: "παρακαλοῦμεν"</note>, which could be <term>we exhort</term>, but better is <term>we obtest</term> <note>To appeal to or call to witness.</note>, so that he may soften the authority of the one commanding. "And he royally adds prayers to threats," as they say. Paul, on the contrary, adds prayers to threats, and, lest either authority or prayers should be despised, he adds, <term>in the Lord Jesus</term>.

<margin>18 In the Lord Jesus Christ</margin> <note>original: "διὰ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν"</note>, that is, <term>through our Lord</term>.

<margin>19 Their own bread</margin> <note>original: "τὸν ἑαυτῶν ἄρτον"</note>, that is, <term>their very own bread</term>, and that more emphatically: as if you were to say, not someone else’s, but their own.

### THE SECOND EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE THESSALONIANS
### T H E  E N D.

---

<margin>20 Through this letter ]</margin> This is "this" <note>original: "hunc"</note> in Greek, not "this" <note>original: "hanc"</note>; that is, it is in the masculine gender, not the feminine, just as it is found in the more corrected Latin copies, specifically in both Constance manuscripts. Theophylact indicates that among the Greeks there was a double reading. One was: "But if anyone does not obey our word through the letter" <note>original: "Εἰ δέ τις οὐχ ὑπακούει τῷ λόγῳ ἡμῶν διὰ τῆς ἐπιστολῆς"</note>, so that you understand Paul is speaking to the Thessalonians through the Letter. He testifies that another reading pleased John Chrysostom: that instead of "our" <note>original: "ἡμῶν"</note> in the first person, "your" <note>original: "ὑμῶν"</note> in the second person is used. The sense would then be: "If anyone does not obey you when you propose what I command from this my Letter, mark this man." What is "mark" <note>original: "σημειοῦσθε"</note> to the Greeks means he should be noted by you so that you might avoid him, just as we mark oxen that strike with their horns so they may be avoided. In the Greek wording, it is doubtful whether "mark" refers to "through the letter," but the consensus of the interpreters refers it to the "word" <note>original: "λόγῳ"</note>.

<margin>21 So that he may be confounded ]</margin> <note>original: "ἵνα ἐντραπῇ"</note>, that is, so that he may be ashamed and covered in a blush when he sees himself avoided by everyone. One who is otherwise disturbed is also "confounded." Therefore, Saint Ambrose, to explain the force of the Greek word, translated it as "confounded by reverence."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>14</margin> [our word], <gloss>20</gloss> mark him through this letter, and have no commerce with him, <gloss>21</gloss> so that he may be covered in shame.
<margin>15</margin> Neither <gloss>22</gloss> regard him as an enemy, but <gloss>23</gloss> admonish him as a brother.
<margin>16</margin> Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace <gloss>24</gloss> always in every way. <gloss>25</gloss> The Lord be with all of you.
<margin>17</margin> <gloss>26</gloss> The greeting is by my own hand, Paul’s, which is the sign in every letter: so I write.
<margin>18</gloss> The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you. Amen.

<margin>B</margin> ->It was sent from Athens.<-

### THE SECOND EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE THESSALONIANS
### T H E  E N D.

---

<margin>C</margin> <margin>22 As an enemy ]</margin> <note>original: "ὡς ἐχθρὸν"</note>, that is, like an enemy. Notice the marvelous gentleness of the Apostle, who does not wish even an unmanageable person to be held as an enemy.

<margin>23 Admonish as a brother ]</margin> <note>original: "νουθετεῖτε"</note>. Ambrose translates this as "warn with counsel," preferring a gentler word.

<margin>24 Always ]</margin> <note>original: "διὰ παντὸς"</note>, that is, forever or perpetually. <margin>In every place,</margin> <note>original: "ἐν παντὶ τρόπῳ"</note>, that is, in every manner. Although the Translator seems to have read "place" <note>original: "τόπῳ"</note> instead of "way" <note>original: "τρόπῳ"</note>, and Ambrose reads it the same way, even if the Greek notes read "way" <note>original: "τρόπῳ"</note>. Theophylact refers "always" to time, and "in every way" to business—that is, in opinions, in words, and in deeds. In Chrysostom's text, it is "in every way," but the commentary suggests he read "in every place," for he explains it as "everywhere" <note>original: "πανταχοῦ"</note>, that is, even among those foreign to the Christian religion. It is not clear from Ambrose's commentary what he read. Yet the sense is not absurd: "at all times and in every place," both "always and everywhere," as a proverbial expression.

<margin>25 God be with all ]</margin> It is "Lord," not "God," and that is how Ambrose reads it.

<margin>26 And my greeting ]</margin> "My" is in the ablative case and refers to "hand." By my hand, Paul's.

---

### DESIDERIUM ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

# THE ARGUMENT
#### of the
# FIRST EPISTLE
### T O  T I M O T H Y.

He sends this from Macedonia. The occasion of the Letter is this: In Ephesus, certain people who were "Judaizing" <note>Those who insisted that Christian converts must follow the ceremonial laws of Moses.</note> were attempting to teach different doctrines and to deceive the simple-hearted under the pretext of the Law. Having learned of this, the Apostle encourages Timothy to remain there for their correction. He writes the Letter and first reminds Timothy—who already knows the faith in Christ—to restrain, by teaching about the Law, those who speak against sound doctrine, and to rebuke them. For he himself handed over Hymenaeus and Alexander to Satan <note>A form of excommunication or spiritual discipline intended to lead the offender to repentance.</note>, so that they might be disciplined not to blaspheme. Having reminded him of these things, he then lays down for him ecclesiastical canons <term>canons: established rules or standards for church conduct</term> regarding prayer: how, where, and for whom one ought to pray. He writes concerning women keeping silence in the church, and rather that they should learn and not teach; concerning bishops, elders, and deacons: how and what sort of men those being appointed ought to be; concerning the widows in the church: from what age they should be enrolled, what sort they must be, and how one must care for them; concerning the need for younger women to be self-controlled and rather to marry, so as not to live in a way that brings reproach. He writes regarding the instructions for the rich: not to be high-minded, nor to hope in wealth. Having set out these regulations, he encourages Timothy to teach these things, and no longer to drink only water, but to attend to himself and to his teaching, knowing that times will come in which some will depart from the faith. After teaching that even foods are pure, and instructing him to turn away from contentious disputes as profane—in which some, by boasting, have turned aside from the faith—he thus concludes the Letter.

---

# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO
# T I M O T H Y.
### The Argument by
### DESIDERIUS ERASMUM OF ROTTERDAM.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial letter 'T' set within a square frame featuring a classical architectural background with figures.</image-desc>
Timothy—born of a Jewish mother (who was also a Christian) and a Greek father—had been adopted by Paul into the ministry. He was a young man of honest character and well-learned in the Sacred Scriptures, whom Paul nevertheless felt compelled to circumcise on account of the Jews <note>Timothy’s father was Greek, but his mother was Jewish; Paul performed the rite so that Timothy could minister in Jewish settings without creating a legal scandal.</note>. Since Paul had delegated the care of the churches to him, just as he had to Titus, because he could not visit them himself, he instructed him in the Episcopal function <term>Episcopal: relating to the office and duties of a bishop or overseer</term> and in the discipline of the Church. He does not advise him as a student, but as a son and a colleague. To ensure this is done with greater authority, he frequently asserts his own Apostolic authority. He warns that, having rejected those who would introduce "Jewish fables," Timothy should teach those things which belong to faith and charity. Furthermore, he teaches that the authority of Princes—even if they are Pagans—is not to be despised by Christians, since the order of the city and the tranquility of the public state depend upon it; indeed, he commands that prayers be offered for them. He prescribes what is fitting for men in the ecclesiastical assembly and what is fitting for women. He portrays the Bishop along with his household. These matters occupy roughly three chapters. Then he warns Timothy not to accept Jewish fables concerning the choice of foods or the avoidance of marriage. Presently, he teaches how Timothy ought to conduct himself toward older men, toward youths, toward old women, toward young girls, and toward widows—both the wealthy and the poor who are to be supported by the church's collection—and toward those who are younger and of a suspect age. To these things he adds instructions on what should be commanded to masters, to servants, and to the rich: warning that in every way, the contentious questions of the sophists <note>Scholars or debaters who use clever but fallacious arguments to sell a false appearance of wisdom.</note>, who hawk themselves with an empty show of doctrine, must be rejected. He writes from Laodicea by way of Tychicus the deacon.

<header>THE FIRST EPISTLE OF PAUL THE APOSTLE TO TIMOTHY.</header>

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL
## THE APOSTLE TO
# TIMOTHY I.

<margin>1:1. A</margin>
1 **P**aul, an Apostle of Jesus Christ by the command <note>original: "κατ' ἐπιταγὴν"</note> of God our Savior and the Lord Jesus Christ, 2 our hope, to Timothy, my true child <note>original: "γνησίῳ τέκνῳ"</note> in the faith: grace, mercy, and peace from God our Father and 3 the Lord Jesus Christ our Lord. As I urged you to remain in Ephesus when I was going into Macedonia, so that you might command certain people not to 4 teach different doctrines <note>original: "ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν"</note>, nor to pay attention to myths and endless genealogies, which provide questions rather than 5 the stewardship of God, which is in faith. But the end of the command is love from a pure heart, and a good 6 conscience, and a sincere faith. From which 
<margin>B</margin>
some, having missed the mark, have turned aside into vain 7 talking, wanting to be teachers of the law, not understanding what they say, nor the things about which they make assertions. 8 But we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully.

---

1 *According to the command* <note>original: "Secundum imperium"</note>] In Greek, *kat’ epitagen*. It would be clearer here to say "according to the injunction" or "delegation." For *epitattein* means to enjoin or command something. He is thinking of his Apostolic office, which he did not claim for himself, but was delegated to him by Christ himself. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching.</note> noted this, indicating that being an Apostle by delegation and command is more significant than merely being "called." For when writing to the Romans, he says *klētos*, that is, "called."
2 *Of God our Savior*] Here, certainly, no one can evade the fact that the Father is called "Savior." This refutes those who, regarding the passage in the Epistle to Titus—*The kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared*—want to refer "Savior" to no one other than the Son.
3 *And of Christ Jesus our hope*] In Greek, *tēs elpidos hēmōn*. It would be clearer as: *Jesus Christ, who is our hope*. For the article *tēs* has an explanatory force. He makes the Father the author of salvation and calls the Son "hope." Chrysostom, Ambrose, and Theophylact interpret it in this sense. However, whether we correctly attribute to the Virgin Mother or other saints what Paul here attributes to Christ, I leave for others to examine.
4 *To my beloved son*] In Greek, *gnēsiō teknō*, that is, "to my legitimate or true son." This is how Ambrose reads it, and even Chrysostom (or whoever was the author of that work), even though the Latin translator everywhere thrusts in his own word "dearest," just as the translator of Theophylact reads "beloved." Since Paul uses so many words regarding the likeness of a son reflecting his father, he clearly indicates he read "true/genuine" <note>original: "γνησίῳ"</note>, not "beloved" <note>original: "ἀγαπητῷ"</note>. He calls him "genuine," meaning true and noble, not a bastard, because Timothy responded in all things to his spiritual father, Paul; it is the nature of sons to reflect the parent and not degenerate. But this word has been discussed elsewhere. "Son" is a name of either age or affection. Since Paul calls all Christians "brothers," why would he otherwise call a Bishop "son" unless he was thinking of his age?
5 *Grace and mercy*] The Greeks do not add conjunctions in this place, but say: *grace, mercy, peace*. This is exactly how Ambrose reads it. Chrysostom noted that when writing to this one man, Paul remembered "mercy," whereas in others he mentions "peace and grace." Origen noted the same in the Epistle to the Romans.
6 *In Christ Jesus our Lord*] The Greek manuscripts repeat the title of Lord: *and of the Lord Jesus Christ our Lord*. That is, from the Lord Jesus Christ, who is our Lord. It is as if he is the Lord of all in one way, and the Lord of the faithful in another, as he possesses them uniquely. Though Ambrose and the Vulgate edition disagree, Theophylact, on the other hand, sides with us. We have not changed the Greek reading, but have left it so the reader is free to follow whichever they wish. This repetition seems by no means idle; it is a great comfort to Christians to uniquely have such a Lord who cares for them. Chrysostom and Theophylact noted this, albeit obscurely.
7 *As I asked you* <note>original: "Sicut rogavi te"</note>] In Greek, *parekalesa se*. Although the Greek word is ambiguous, "I exhorted" or "I urged" fits better here, as Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla (c. 1407–1457), a humanist who pioneered the philological study of the New Testament.</note> prefers; yet Paul sometimes used that word even toward common people. Indeed, Chrysostom specifically noted this (and Theophylact, rejoicing to follow him), that so great an Apostle used a word so humble and so gentle toward his disciple. Furthermore, as for what Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>original: "Stapulensis"</note> advises—that it should have been translated "thus" rather than "as"—I do not understand at all what he means. For I do not think *kalōs* can be taken for *houtōs* ("thus").
8 *That you remain at Ephesus*] The speech is fuller in Greek than in Latin, because *prosmeinai* ("to remain") can be either in the infinitive or the imperative mood, as far as the sense is concerned: "As I asked you to remain, *remain*." Ambrose seems to have read it this way, as he reads "that you might denounce," which would not fit unless "remain" or a similar verb was understood. Furthermore, as for the phrase we added, "so do" <note>original: "ita facito"</note>, I will not beg pardon for admitting this "easy-reading," unless the Translator frequently does the same, and unless necessity frequently compels it. I did not mean that "to remain" should be taken as an imperative in the first part of the sentence, but that it is understood in the latter part; however, it is not necessary that the exact same word be understood. I would not add these things to burden the reader, were it not that certain people have attacked this passage in published books with as much ignorance as venom.

<column-break/>

<margin>1:1. A</margin>
1 **P**aul, an Apostle of Jesus Christ according to the delegation of God our Savior and 2 our Lord Jesus Christ, who is our hope, to Timothy, his 4 true son in the faith: 5 grace, mercy, peace from God our Father 6 and the Lord Jesus Christ our Lord. 7 As I asked you 8 to remain in Ephesus when I set out for Macedonia, so do, that you may 3 command certain people 9 not to follow a different doctrine, nor to attend to 4 fables and genealogies 10 that never end, which provide questions rather than the edification of God, which is through faith. 5 Furthermore, the end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith. 6 From which things because 11 some have strayed, 12 they have deflected 13 to vain talking, wanting 7 
<margin>B</margin>
to be doctors of the law, not understanding what they speak, nor the things about which they assert. But we know that 8 the law is good.

---

<margin>C</margin>
9 *Lest they teach otherwise*] In Greek, *mē heterodidaskalein*, that is, lest they teach different things, or rather, lest they use different doctrines. It is a compound word from *heteros* ("another") and *didaskalein* ("to teach"), implying following now these, now those teachers. However, Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret it as "introducing a different doctrine," referring to the False Apostles. We have translated it ambiguously as "lest they follow a different doctrine," which applies to both those teaching and those speaking different things. Paul used the same word in chapter 6 of this Epistle. Ambrose agrees with the interpretation of the Ancients.
10 *Endless*] In Greek, *aperantois*, that is, things which have no end. Of this sort are some of the questions, opinions, and difficulties of common theologians <note>Erasmus is criticizing the Scholastic theologians of his own day.</note>. For the more there are of these petty questions, the more it obscures the truth; and with such things that never end—of which you could produce a million—even more will remain. Where impiety is absent, nonetheless this difficulty of questions calls one away from those things which pertain more closely to the matter. Chrysostom thinks this passage should not be taken as referring to the history of the Old Testament. But Ambrose clearly seems to interpret it that way when he says: *Lest they be delighted by the fables which the Jews are accustomed to tell about the generation of their origins, about Abraham and Isaac and the rest of the Patriarchs, and about circumcision...* And to me, indeed, not even those people seem to contribute much to true Christian piety who dispute about the genealogy of Christ so anxiously and, I might almost say, in such a Jewish fashion. On the whole, I would rather see certain things picked out from the books of the Old Testament for their usefulness, than to see their authority equaled to the majesty of the Gospel—indeed, almost preferred. For what else is read in the churches now? We even receive into our canon those books of the Jews which they themselves refused to receive into theirs; Christians have a greater leaning toward Jewish books than the Jews themselves. Furthermore, where the Translator here says "endless" <note>original: "interminatis"</note>, Ambrose says "infinite."
<margin>D</margin>
11 *Straying*] In Greek, *astochesantes*, that is, having strayed. It is a word specifically used for those who miss a target. Chrysostom also hints at this.
12 *They have turned aside*] In Greek, *exetrapēsan*. I would prefer "deflected." It explains the Greek word better, as when someone missing the mark deflects themselves elsewhere.
13 *Into vain talking*] In Greek, *eis mataiologian*. As far as pronunciation goes, "mataeology" is not far from "Theology," though the things themselves differ greatly. Therefore, we too must be careful lest we follow Theology in such a way that we fall into "mataeology," fighting without end over frivolous trifles. Let us rather treat those things which transform us into Christ and make us worthy of heaven. For what does it matter to fight over how many ways "sin" can be understood—whether it is only a privation or a stain clinging to the soul? The Theologian should rather act so that all may shudder at and hate sin. For whole centuries we dispute whether the grace by which God loves and draws us, and by which we in turn love him, is the same grace, and whether it is something created or uncreated. Let us rather act, through pure prayers, innocence of life, and pious deeds, so that God may deem us worthy of that gift. We fight without end over what distinguishes the Father from the Son, and both 
<margin>E</margin>
from the Holy Spirit—whether it is a "thing" or a "relation"—and how it stands that three are spoken of, none of whom is the other, while they are one essence. How much more does it pertain to the matter to act in every way so that we may piously and holily worship and adore that Trinity whose majesty it is not permitted to scrutinize, and express its ineffable concord through our own concord as much as we are able, so that we might eventually attain a share in its company. We dispute how it can be that the fire which will torture the souls of the ungodly, since it is material, can act on an incorporeal thing. How much more relevant it would be to strive with all our might so that that fire, whatever it may be, finds nothing in us to burn? And if these things were done for the sake of relaxing the mind or in certain debates, they could be borne. But now, for some, an entire lifetime is consumed in such questions, and the matter proceeds all the way to shouting, to insults, to abuse, and sometimes even to fisticuffs. What swarms of questions...

<meta>catchword: swarms</meta>

<summary>In this opening to 1 Timothy, Erasmus provides a new Latin translation and detailed notes, using the Apostle's warning against "endless genealogies" and "vain talking" to launch a sharp critique of the Scholastic theological disputes of his own time.</summary>

<meta>Continuity note: This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on the first chapter of 1 Timothy, moving from the initial greeting to a scathing critique of Scholastic theology and its obsession with "vain questions" over the simplicity of the Gospel.</meta>

<page-num>927</page-num> <header>EPISTLE OF PAUL CH. I.</header> <page-num>928</page-num>

<margin>
...uses it lawfully, 9 Knowing this, that the law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners, for the unholy and profane, for those who kill their fathers and those who kill their mothers, for murderers, 10 for the sexually immoral, for those who practice homosexuality, for kidnappers, for liars, for perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine... <note>original: Greek text of 1 Timothy 1:8-10</note>
</margin>
We perform constant examinations regarding baptism, the assembly, and the sacrament of penance; some of these are of such a kind that it does not greatly matter to know them, and even if they are asserted, they can neither be refuted nor proven. It would be more to the point to focus on this, and to exhort one another to this: that we respond to the sacrament of baptism with a life worthy of Christ, that we approach those sacred feasts frequently and purely, and that there be little on our journey that needs to be burned away by the cautery of penance. But what shall I say now of those little questions—not only unnecessary but, I might almost say, impious—which we raise about the power of God and the power of the Roman Pontiff? Whether God could command any evil, even the hatred of Himself, and forbid every good, even the love and worship of Himself. Whether He could produce an actual infinite in every dimension. Whether He could have made this world better than He did, even from eternity. Whether He could produce a human being who could in no way sin. Whether He could reveal to someone their own future sin or damnation. Whether He could understand some things distinctly if He did not have distinct concepts of them in His reason. Whether He can produce a relation without a foundation or a term. Whether He can produce and preserve a universal nature without individuals. Whether He can be contained within any category. Whether He can communicate the power of creation to a creature. Whether He can make what is done undone, and through this, make a virgin out of a harlot. Whether any divine person could assume any nature, just as the Word <note>The Logos, or the Second Person of the Trinity</note> assumed a human one. Whether three persons could simultaneously assume the same nature. Whether one created "supposit" <note>A technical term in Scholasticism for an individual substance</note> could assume another created nature. Whether this proposition, "God is a beetle," or "a pumpkin," is as possible as this one, "God is a man." Whether God assumed a human individual or a species. Whether it is more fitting to say that God cannot do the impossible, or that the impossible cannot be done by God. Whether it is more fitting for God to have the power to produce first, or for the creature to have the capacity to be produced. Whether the ideas of all things are in the divine mind, and whether they are practical or speculative. Whether it is consistent with Aristotelian doctrine and natural reason; finally, whether the matter itself forces one to confess that there is some "relation" absolutely distinct from all things. Whether God is "one" by something distinct from Himself. Whether the divine persons are called "three" by a true number. Whether the number of persons in the divine nature belongs to the substance or the relation. And whether it belongs to the "first intention" or the "second," <note>Terms from medieval logic regarding how we categorize concepts</note> and whether they are distinguished and constituted by relations. Whether the Father produces the Son and the Holy Spirit by reason of intellect or will. Likewise, whether by reason of essence or attribute, naturally or freely. Whether the essence in the Father is the generative principle of the Son, and whether it is the "term" of the Father’s generation. Whether God generates God. Whether the Father produces the Holy Spirit by origin before the Son does. Whether in God there is an "active" and "possible" intellect. Whether the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, comes from one principle or two. Whether this proposition is possible: "God the Father hates God the Son." Whether the soul of Christ could be deceived, or deceive, or lie.

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, the power of the Roman Pontiff is now disputed almost more busily than the power of God, while we inquire about his twofold power, and whether he can abrogate what was decreed in the Apostolic writings. Whether he can establish something that conflicts with Gospel doctrine. Whether he can create a new article in the creed. Whether he has greater power than Peter, or equal. Whether he can command the Angels. Whether he can abolish the whole of Purgatory, as they call it. Whether he is a mere man, or as it were a God, or participates in both natures with Christ. Whether he is more merciful than Christ was, since Christ is not read to have recalled anyone from the pains of Purgatory. <margin>B</margin> Whether he alone of all men cannot err. Six hundred things of this kind are disputed in ever more published volumes, and that by great Theologians, especially those distinguished by their religious profession. And these things are done not without a manifest suspicion of flattery, nor without injury to Christ, compared to whom Princes—however great they may be—are nothing but little worms. Do they think these things please Leo <note>Pope Leo X, to whom Erasmus dedicated the New Testament</note>, our brother and the true vicar of Christ, who as a true shepherd holds nothing more ancient than the safety of the Christian flock, and as a true vicar of Christ holds nothing dearer than the glory of his Prince, Christ? <margin>C</margin> And yet the schools of certain Theologians are seriously occupied with these sorts of petty questions. Upon these things the age of Christian affairs is spent. Why then, putting aside unnecessary things, do we not rather look to those things which Christ wanted us to know, which the Apostles handed down, which properly lead to charity: from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith—the one thing Paul calls the end and perfection of the whole Law. <margin>D</margin> For so many years now we have been quibbling in the Schools about what words we should use to speak of Christ. Whether this proposition is true: "Christ was from eternity"; whether He is rightly said to be "composed" of both natures, or to "consist" of them, or "compounded," or "mixed," or "glued together," or "joined," or "welded," or "coupled." None of these please them; only "unity" pleases them—a new word, though it signifies nothing less than that for which it was invented to signify. Furthermore, if it were asked whether we speak piously in saying the human nature is united to the divine, they admit it is piously said. Again, they hesitate whether it is piously said that the divine is united to the human. If these were the afternoon conversations of Christians, I would approve of such talk for excluding foolish stories. <margin>E</margin> Now these things seem to be the defenses of our faith. We seek those things which we can neither know nor are commanded to know. We neglect those things which alone should have been meditated upon. Some things are even pernicious for the very reason that they delay and weary the mind with their obscurity, when it should be occupied with better things. Such, I believe, was the philosophy of Pytha-

<column-break/>

the law is made, if anyone uses it lawfully, 14 knowing this: that the law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the unjust and the disobedient, the impious and sinners, the irreverent and the profane, for killers of fathers and killers of mothers, 17 for murderers, for fornicators, for those who lie with males, 18 for kidnappers, for liars, for perjurers, and whatever else is [contrary] to sound doctrine.

<margin>A</margin> goras. And for this reason, even the books of Heraclitus are criticized by the Pagans; Socrates used to joke that one needed a "Delian diver" <note>Someone who could dive to the depths without drowning; a metaphor for a profound reader</note> to understand them. Certainly, for this reason Chrysostom condemns the philosophy of Plato, because it is wrapped in numbers and riddles—no less harmful than a story, however elegant, that would delay a soldier fleeing from battle. Yet such are nearly all the things handed down by those who boast of their knowledge of a more "subtle" Theology: even if they preached truths, they explain them in words that are not only sordid but so obscure and involved that it is not worth the effort to learn them. <margin>B</margin> Of this kind are their disputes about the "four instances of nature." Likewise when they distinguish that a "person" does not signify a relation of origin, neither common nor specific, but a "double negation of communicability" within a genus, not outside a genus, and connotes something positive, and is a name of "first intention," not "second." Likewise when they say that the persons in the Godhead are in one another through *circumincessio* <term>Circumincessio: a Latin term for the Greek 'perichoresis', describing the mutual indwelling of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit</term>, and they define *circumincessio*, a new word, in a new way: "Circumincessio," they say, "is the mutual assistance of presence of one subsisting thing in another subsisting thing that is really distinct, within the same essence." <margin>C</margin> Again, they define: "personal or hypostatic union is a relation of real disparity in one extreme, to which no real reason corresponds in the other." Likewise: "the union of the Word in Christ is a relation arriving from without, terminated in the Word and founded in the assumed humanity, and that relation does not depend on an efficient cause, but on the sustainer to the sustained." Everything among these people is full of such tangles. And in this Theology, which is so far from simple, those who profess the simple and Apostolic life consume their entire existence. And those who, by their very title, profess the greatest modesty, raise their crests high through the profession of this kind of philosophy. How does the profession of an Apostolic life fit with such a great and curious study of Pagan philosophy? The mouth is consecrated to the Gospel, yet it sounds of nothing but Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle</note> and Aristotle. The touch of money is dreaded, yet an entire lifetime is spent on the books of a blasphemous Philosopher. The ancients, who learned such things in Paganism or through the ignorance of their age, plucked certain things from them for Christian education. Now, those who profess the simplicity of Christ and are fed by preaching the Gospel are forced to learn such things. <margin>D</margin> I know a certain Theologian who denied that nine years were enough to understand what Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a highly complex Scholastic philosopher</note> wrote merely in the preface to Peter Lombard. I heard of another who preached that it was impossible for anyone to understand a single proposition in all of Scotus unless he held his entire Metaphysics in his memory. With such labyrinths did Basilides, Valentinus, and Marcion <note>Early Gnostic heretics</note> capture the minds of the simple. Finally, let us imagine these things are fruitful; how great a battle of opinions occurs here! Imagine again that everyone agrees; how many things are sought in vain, how many things are defined rashly? And they pretend that these subtleties are necessary for refuting Pagans and Heretics, when they are of no use anywhere except among the members of the same School. <margin>E</margin> These remarks are not intended to suggest that Logic and Philosophy as taught in the Schools should be condemned; I disapprove only of immoderate study of frivolous things. No less do those sin who thrust upon us the smoke of the Kabbalah and the Talmud. Similar is the study of those who reduced all Philosophy to numbers. *The time is short*, says Paul, and a great business is at hand; why do these wastes of time please us? Let the best things be handed down, and as much as possible in summary; let the superfluous be cut away. I wish the Jurists would do the same. Let us rather act in such a way that we may be transformed into Christ. This will happen if we meditate with all our strength on His innocence, abstaining from every crime; if, as much as lies in us, we emulate His charity, deserving well of all; if we imitate His patience, so far from retaliating an injury that we even repay evil deeds with good.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
<margin>E</margin>
<margin>F</margin>

<margin>
14 Knowing this] *Eidos*, that is, *Knowing* (singular). Paul, however, occasionally changes the number in other places. Though "Knowing" could refer to the verb "uses," that is, "let him use." Certainly, Ambrose reads "Holding for certain" instead of "Knowing," in the singular number; both the Constance manuscripts support "if anyone uses it lawfully." The wordplay <note>paronomasia</note> in the Greek words is more evident: *nomos*, *nomimos*—law and lawfully.
</margin>
<margin>
15 and for the disobedient] *anhypotaktois*, that is, those who do not wish to be subject, nor bear authority. Ambrose translates it as "unsubmissive."
</margin>
<margin>
16 For the polluted] *bebelois*, that is, profane and to be kept away from sacred things. Furthermore, those polluted by some crime are usually barred from sacred rites. The Greek *anosiois* sounds almost the same in sense, for *hosios* is derived from *hazomai*, "I revere." Thus they call *anosioi* those who fear neither Gods nor men. And therefore he added "profane," who are strangers to sacred things.
</margin>
<margin>
17 Murderers] *androphonois*, that is, "man-killers," if one translates word for word.
</margin>
<margin>
18 Kidnappers] *andrapodistais*, that is, those who steal away the slaves of others by theft; this kind of theft is called *plagium* among Jurists. Just as those who steal sacred things are "sacrilegious"; those who steal from the public or the Prince’s treasury are "embezzlers"; those who drive away another's cattle are "rustlers." So those who steal the children or slaves of others are "plagiaries." Since this term exists not only among Jurists but in nearly all good authors, who would not marvel at the ignorance of [Nicholas of] Lyra—or whoever else added this commentary—who was either ignorant of this, or too lazy to investigate it, or so impudent that he interpreted it so loosely? He says "plagiaries" are those accustomed to inflicting blows [*plagas*] and lashes on others. And Carranza followed him, saying "plagiaries" are those who inflict blows of any kind on their neighbors. Aquinas, while explaining almost everything else, wisely ignores "plagiaries," confessing by his very silence that the word was little understood by him. The Greek word is derived from "slave" [*mancipium*], for *andrapodon* is a slave; *andrapodistes* is, as you might say, a "slave-thief." It should be noted that the Apostle, hating [sin]...
</margin>

<summary>Erasmus provides a sharp critique of Scholastic theology, arguing that complex metaphysical questions about God's power and the Pope's authority distract from the simple, transformative charity of the Gospel. He also provides philological corrections to the Latin Vulgate, specifically regarding the Greek term for kidnappers, which medieval commentators had misinterpreted as "those who beat others."</summary>

<meta>Continuity note: This page continues Erasmus’s detailed philological and theological commentary on the first chapter of 1 Timothy. Having previously criticized the "vain questions" of the Scholastic theologians, Erasmus here focuses on the text of Paul's personal testimony and his doxology to God, while defending his own translation choices against contemporary critics like Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples (Faber).</meta>

# TO FIRST TIMOTHY CHAPTER I.

<column-break/>

[A] ...is contrary to sound doctrine, 19 **according to the Gospel of the glory** [11] **of the blessed God**, 20 **which was entrusted to me.** And 21 **I give thanks** [12] **to him who has made me powerful, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to the ministry**, 23 **who was formerly a blasphemer, and a persecutor**, [13] 24 **and a violent man,** 25 **but I also obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.** 26 **And the grace of our Lord overflowed** [14] **beyond measure with the faith and love which is through Christ Jesus.** 27 **This is a certain word, and worthy to be embraced in every way,** [15] **that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first.** [B] **Truly for this reason I obtained mercy, that** 28 **in me** [16] **first Jesus Christ might show** 29 **all his clemency** 30 **to set forth an example for those who were to believe in him, unto eternal life. Now to the King of the ages,** [17] **immortal, invisible,** 32 **the only wise God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen. This commandment** [18]...

<column-break/>

<margin>
In his catalog of vices, Paul proceeds in pairs—as if an army were joining together—and omits the conjunctions: *the lawless and disobedient, the ungodly and sinners, the unholy and profane, those who kill fathers and those who kill mothers.* So far he moves in pairs; *then he mentions the ungrateful, murderers, the sexually immoral, those who sleep with men, and kidnappers.* To these he again adds a pair, *liars and perjurers*, so that the sequence is concluded there. <note>original: "per juga... conjunctionem omittit"</note>
</margin>

19 *Which is according to the Gospel* ] <margin>C</margin> These two words, *which is*, I do not find in the Greek manuscripts. However, they are rightly added for the sake of explanation. Ambrose and the Vulgate translator seem to have read the text with the article added, *tēi kata to euangelion* <note>original: "τῇ κατὰ τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον"</note>, that is, *which is according to the Gospel*. One cannot gather what they read from the commentaries of Chrysostom or Ambrose. Theophylact reads it without the article but advises that the article should be supplied, just as the Latins do. The translator seems to have read it with the article. The meaning, however, is no less ambiguous among the Greeks than among us. For it can be understood as the *Gospel of the glory of the blessed God*, because it proclaims the glory of God; or the *Gospel of glory*, that is, the "glorious" Gospel, to contrast it with the Mosaic Law, which has no glory compared to the splendor of the Gospel. This is because the Gospel moves toward eternal glory in the world to come, or because it was itself glorious to suffer for Christ on account of the Gospel, which seemed like foolishness to the Gentiles. And for this reason, he added *blessed* <note>original: "μακαρίου"</note>, because true happiness is found even in these hardships.

20 *Which was entrusted to me* ] <margin>D</margin> "Entrusted" in this place must mean "committed," *ho episteuthēn egō* <note>original: "ὃ ἐπιστεύθην ἐγώ"</note>. "Was concredited" would be clearer. As God is my witness, I am reluctant to disagree with men whom I venerate in my heart, but the concern for public benefit must come first, especially if an error can be admitted without insult. Faber <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, a rival scholar</note>, instead of what the Translator rendered as *which was entrusted*, translated it as *to whom I was entrusted*, not noticing the idiom of the Greek language, as we also noted in our *Apologia*. Furthermore, as for what he adds in his examination—that "to whom I was entrusted" and "which was entrusted to me" amount to the same thing—who does not see that they are far apart? Unless, perhaps, it makes no difference whether you say, "Your son was committed to me," or "I was committed to your son."

21 *I give thanks* ] *Kai charin echō* <note>original: "Καὶ χάριν ἔχω"</note>, that is, *And I have gratitude*.

22 *Who has strengthened me in Christ Jesus* ] The "in" is redundant; it is not found in Chrysostom, nor in Ambrose, nor in the ancient manuscripts—specifically in the older Constantiense manuscript. It reads *tō endynamōsanti me Christō* <note>original: "τῷ ἐνδυναμώσαντί με Χριστῷ"</note>, that is, *who made me powerful for Christ*, so that "Christ" is in the dative case. You should understand that Paul was strong and powerful for the glory of Christ, not his own. This can also be the sense: I have gratitude to Jesus Christ, by whose protection I am powerful.

23 *Who before was* ] *Ton proteron onta* <note>original: "Τὸν πρότερον ὄντα"</note>. It can also be rendered, *though I was formerly*, or *Since I had been formerly*.

24 *And a violent man* ] *hybristēn* <note>original: "ὑβριστήν"</note>, which more significantly means one who uses force—that is, an oppressor or a violent person. For this should not be referred here to lust. Indeed, it appears that Paul is exaggerating his sin by certain degrees. Even a sin committed out of pious zeal through error must be called a sin. The first degree is to speak evil. The second is to persecute. The third is to apply force. For persecution can exist without physical violence.

25 *But mercy* ] *alla kai* <note>original: "ἀλλὰ καὶ"</note>, that is, *but even*; as if he were to say: "Not only did I obtain pardon, being such a man, but even mercy, so that I might become an Apostle." For elsewhere, when downplaying himself, he calls the authority handed to him the "mercy of God," as in the first Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 7: *But I give my counsel as one who has obtained mercy*. Although the interpretation of Ambrose does not shrink from this annotation of ours, it cannot be clearly gathered whether the conjunction "and" <note>original: "καὶ"</note> was added by him or by Chrysostom. Certainly, in Theophylact, "and" is not added. *In unbelief* <note>original: "ἐν ἀπιστίᾳ"</note>, that is, *not yet believing*, as Ambrose translates, or *through incredulity*.

26 *A faithful saying* ] Paul is accustomed to using this as a little preface when he is about to say something certain and indubitable, so that "faithful" refers to the matter as being beyond doubt. Jerome, in his Epistle to Marcella, testifies that some read *A human saying*, following, I believe, some Greek manuscripts that had *koinos* <note>meaning "common" or "human"</note> instead of *pistos* <note>meaning "faithful"</note>. And for "acceptance," the Greeks have *apodoxēs*, which also sounds like "approbation." For that which is approved is not rejected.

27 *Into this world* ] "This" is redundant.

28 *In me first* ] *en emoi prōtō* <note>original: "ἐν ἐμοὶ πρώτῳ"</note>. "First" here is a noun <note>meaning the "foremost" sinner</note>, not an adverb.

29 *All patience* ] *makrothymian* <note>original: "μακροθυμίαν"</note>, that is, *long-suffering*, if one renders it word-for-word. Ambrose used two words for this one: *magnanimity and patience*. It is a quality of a great...

<column-break/>

...and gentle and moderate soul. For vengeance belongs to a small mind. He added *all*, exaggerating his own sin, whence he also called himself *first*—not in time, but in the magnitude of his crimes.

30 *To set forth a pattern for them* ] *pros hypotypōsin* <note>original: "πρὸς ὑποτύπωσιν"</note>. This is what Ambrose translates as *for an example*. For a *hypotypōsis* is when a matter is expressed and placed before the eyes. In Paul, therefore, God proposed a sort of model of what they ought to hope for themselves—whoever, having left their former ways, have believed in Christ. *Unto eternal life*: it is strange that this is touched upon neither by Ambrose, nor by Chrysostom, nor by Theophylact, at least not in their commentaries. Yet it is included in the text by all of them. It seems to have been added as an appositive, so that this might result for them in eternal life.

31 *Immortal, invisible* ] *aphthartō* <note>original: "ἀφθάρτῳ"</note>, that is, he who cannot be corrupted, which he rightly translates as "immortal," especially since he is speaking of a living being. And in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 1, we translated *aphthartou* as immortality, to avoid interruption, lest anyone should take it as referring to lust.

32 *To the only God* ] *monō sophō Theō* <note>original: "μόνῳ σοφῷ Θεῷ"</note>, that is, *to the only wise God*: so that you join "wise" with "only," and "God" refers to everything. This word *wise*, placed between *only* and *God*, separates them so they are not taken together, which might give an opening to those who agree with the Arians <note>a heretical group that denied Christ was fully God, often arguing that only the Father is truly "the only God"</note>. And indeed, Chrysostom reads it in this way, and Theophylact followed him, unless the manuscripts deceive us. However, I do not find it in Ambrose, nor in Jerome, nor in any other ancient writer. Indeed, Ambrose explains this passage with these words: *These things pertain to the person of God the Father, whom he calls immortal and invisible for this reason: because all immortality is from him.* And shortly after: *In a similar way we read in the Gospel the Lord saying: No one is good, he said, except the one God. And again he says: A good man brings forth good things from a good treasure; yet no one is good except the one God, because he is the fountain of goodness, from which others drink.* Honor and glory, therefore, he pronounces to God the Father in truth, by whose piety and providence Christ delivered sinners from death. So far we have reviewed the words of Ambrose. From these, I think it is clear enough that *wise* was not added in his copies. Augustine brings forward the testimony of this passage against Adamantus and did not add *wise*. Again, in explaining Psalm 67, and again Psalm 119. Although it is not clear enough from Chrysostom's interpretation that *wise* was added by him. For when he argues thus: *Behold, he said "to the only God"; is the Son, therefore, not God? and "to the only immortal"; is the Son, therefore, not immortal?*—it is more probable that he did not read *to the only wise*, but *to the only God*. However, at the end of the Epistle to the Romans, *wise* is added, and the Ambrosian interpretation does not hide this. And Theophylact adds it in this place, and even interprets it, saying that the Father alone is properly called wise because he is the fountain of wisdom. But there is no reason for us to be anxiously tormented by these things, since the Arian heresy is so radically dead that not even a trace remains. For whether you refer the word *only* not to "God" but to the epithets *immortal, invisible*, the impious reader will still find something to carp at—saying that only the Father is invisible, or certainly not the only immortal one. Whether you take it together with "God" or separately, he will seize more of an opportunity for slander. But for us, the fact that he added *only* does not exclude the Son or the Holy Spirit from the fellowship of the Father, but from the fellowship of false gods, who were gods only in the most false opinion of men. Or, according to Saint Ambrose, he calls the Father "only immortal" because he is the fountain of all immortality. By this reasoning, the Son also has immortality from the Father, from whom he has it that he is God. Nor, in my opinion, would he be thinking impiously who says the Father is *the only God* in the sense that he is the sole principle of the entire Deity, as Augustine speaks in the fourth book of *On the Trinity*. If, according to Ambrose, the Father is rightly called "only immortal" because he alone is the fountain of immortality for all, and "only wise" because he is the fountain of all wisdom divine and human, why could he not in some sense be called "only God," from whom the Son has his being as God, and the Holy Spirit likewise? But so it happens in human affairs: once the battle of studies has grown hot, no one acts for the sake of concord, but for the sake of victory. Chrysostom and Theophylact labor to show that all these things are common to the Son with the Father. Truly, it is rare in the Apostolic writings to attribute the title of *God* to Christ or the Holy Spirit—either to avoid offending certain people, or because they reserved that for its own time. For Christ was not preached as God or Son immediately by the Apostles...

<summary>Erasmus provides a detailed philological analysis of 1 Timothy 1:11-18, focusing on the accuracy of translations regarding Paul's past sins and the nature of God. He notably defends the Trinitarian orthodoxy of the phrase "the only God" against potential Arian misinterpretations, arguing that the Father is the "fountain" of the Godhead.</summary>

### PAUL’S EPISTLE CHAPTER II.

18 ...the prophecies that went before concerning you, so that by them you might 19 **wage the good warfare, having faith and a good conscience, which some, having rejected,** 20 **have made shipwreck concerning the faith. Of whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have delivered to Satan, so that** II. 1 **they may learn not to blaspheme. I exhort therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions,** 2 **and giving of thanks be made for all men; for kings and all who are in authority, that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all** 3 **godliness and honesty. For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior, who** 4 **desires all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and one** 5 **mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all, the** 6 **testimony in its own times, for which I was appointed a herald** 7 **and an apostle—I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie—a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth. I desire therefore that men pray** 8 **in every place, lifting up holy hands, without** 9 **anger and doubting. In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefastness and sobriety, not with braided hair, or** 10 **gold, or pearls, or costly clothing, but (as becomes women professing** 11 **godliness) through good works. Let a woman learn in silence**

---

<margin>C</margin>
*Son of God.* <note>original: "Filius Dei"</note> For Peter calls him a "man" in the Acts, <term>approved by God</term>. And Paul, speaking before the Athenians, calls him a "man" in whom God had ordained, etc. Indeed, not even in the Creed, which the common people call the "Apostles' Creed," is the title of "God" explicitly attached to the Son or the Holy Spirit. And in Matthew chapter 10, when Christ himself first sends his followers to preach, he commands nothing else than that they should preach repentance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. Again, in chapter 16, after they had already confessed him to be the Christ, he forbids them to tell anyone that he himself was the Christ. In that very place, Origen points out exactly what we have just said. Chrysostom points out the same. For the truth is not to be spoken by just anyone, at any time, or among any people.

<margin>D</margin>
33 *According to the preceding prophecies concerning you* <note>original: "Secundum praecedentes in te prophetias"</note>] <gloss>according to the prophecies leading the way toward you</gloss>, <note>original: "κατὰ τὰς προαγούσας ἐπί σε προφητείας"</note> that is, according to the prophecies that came before regarding you or directed to you. And indeed, the Greek commentaries <note>original: "scholia"</note> refer this to what follows, *that you might wage the good warfare*. But it can also be referred to what precedes, *This commandment I entrust to you*, meaning: just as I made you a Bishop being warned by the spirit of prophecy, so now I command you, according to that same prophecy, to wage war and to respond to that prophecy. Chrysostom is roughly of this opinion, and Ambrose does not disagree.

34 *In them* <note>original: "In illis"</note>] We must understand *prophecies*; nothing else can be understood in the Greek, meaning: wage war according to them and responding to them. A certain Hugo de Sancto Charo <note>A 13th-century Dominican cardinal and theologian.</note> ridiculously explains this as referring to "explaining the Prophets." But what is the point of noting one or two errors in this type of author, when it is easier to find mistakes in this class of writers than to avoid them? And yet there are those who take it poorly if anything in their writings is criticized. Regarding the man from Saint-Cher, because he was a Cardinal, or rather because he belonged to the order of preachers <note>The Dominicans.</note>. Regarding Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a famous Franciscan commentator.</note>, for no other reason than that he was a Minorite <note>A Franciscan.</note>. They want so much respect given to their titles and their habits, even while they calmly allow us to disagree with Cyprian, Jerome, or Cyril.

35 *Which some, rejecting* <note>original: "Quam quidam repellentes"</note>] This is in the past tense, <gloss>which some having thrust away</gloss>, <note>original: "ἥν τινες ἀπωσάμενοι"</note> that is, by which rejection some—that is, having despised their conscience—fell away.

36 *Have made shipwreck concerning the faith* <note>original: "Circa fidem naufragaverunt"</note>] <note>original: "ἐναυάγησαν"</note> that is, they suffered shipwreck. For who has ever used the Latin verb *naufragare* <note>Erasmus is critiquing the non-standard Latin grammar of the Vulgate here.</note>?

37 *Of whom is* <note>original: "Ex quibus est"</note>] <note>original: "ὧν ἐστι"</note> that is, from whose number is.

<margin>E</margin>
1 *I beseech therefore* <note>original: "Obsecro igitur"</note>] <note>original: "Παρακαλῶ"</note>. Which indeed in this place would be more rightly translated as *I exhort that there be made*. Ambrose reads *Exhort*, in the second person; perhaps he read <note>original: "Παρακάλει"</note>.

2 *First of all* <note>original: "Primum omnium"</note>] It is uncertain whether *of all* refers to *first* or to *the supplications*, and both senses are tolerable. If you refer it to what precedes, the sense is that the prayer should be made among the first things, that is, before all things. Both Chrysostom and Ambrose explain it in this way, namely, at dawn. But if you refer it to what follows, the sense is that prayers should be made by everyone.

3 *Supplications, prayers, intercessions* <note>original: "Obsecrationes, orationes, postulationes"</note>] <note>original: "δεήσεις"</note>. Ambrose translates as *deprecations*, and more rightly so. What is translated here as *postulations*, <note>original: "ἐντεύξεις"</note>, is commonly called *intercessions*. And that is what the Greek word sounds like. Although the Translator renders this word in various ways. The Greek commentary distinguishes these three thus: it says a *deesis* is what we call upon when we ask to be freed from evils—if this is true, Ambrose most elegantly translated it as *deprecations*. A *proseuche* is what we pray that good things may happen to us. An *enteuxis* is when we complain about those who harm us—if this is true, he would have aptly translated it as *interpellations*. But Augustine discusses these matters more diffusely in Letter 59 to Paulinus, if anyone requires more copious instruction.

4 *In high place* <note>original: "In sublimitate"</note>] <gloss>of those who are in authority</gloss>, <note>original: "τῶν ἐν ὑπεροχῇ"</note> that is, those who are in a position of dignity. Ambrose reads, *those who are placed in a more sublime place*.

5 *Quiet and peaceable* <note>original: "Quietam & tranquillam"</note>] <note>original: "ἤρεμον καὶ ἡσύχιον"</note>, that is, placid and quiet, etc.

<column-break/>

I entrust this 33 commandment to you, son Timothy, according to the prophecies which went before concerning you, that you might wage 34 in them a good warfare, Having faith and a good conscience, 35 19 which some 36 having rejected, have made shipwreck concerning the faith, 37 From whose number is Hymenaeus and Alexander, 20 whom I have delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to speak evil. I exhort therefore, that before all things there be made 1 II. 1 deprecations, supplications, interpellations, and thanksgivings for all men, For kings and all 4 established in eminence, that 5 we may lead a placid and quiet life with all godliness 6 and honesty. For this is good and accepted before our Savior God, Who wants all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, one also 7 conciliator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, Who gave 8 himself as the price of redemption for all, so that it might be 9 a testimony in its own times, In which I have been placed as 10 a herald and apostle, 11 I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, a teacher of the nations in faith and truth. I desire therefore that men pray in every place, lifting up 12 pure hands, without anger 13 and dispute. Likewise also women 14 in modest dress, with shamefastness and chastity 15 to adorn themselves, not 16 with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, 17 or sumptuous clothing, But what becomes women 18 professing godliness through good works. Let a woman learn in silence with all subjection. 11

---

6 *And honesty* <note>original: "Et castitate"</note>] <note>original: "καὶ σεμνότητι"</note>. Which word has a wider scope, namely to all gravity and honesty of manners.

7 *Mediator of God and men* <note>original: "Mediator Dei & hominum"</note>] In Greek it is <note>original: "μεσίτης"</note>, which we have translated as *conciliator*. Tertullian, in his book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, translates it as *sequester* <note>A legal term for a neutral third party or trustee.</note>.

8 *Himself a redemption* <note>original: "Semetipsum redemptionem"</note>] <note>original: "ἀντίλυτρον"</note>. This signifies the price by which captives are redeemed from enemies in war, or from pirates. For what are commonly called *ransoms* <note>original: "ranson"</note>, the Greeks call *lytra*. Furthermore, the prefix *anti* more fully explains the exchange made by Christ, who exchanged himself for all of us; he added *antilytron*, where a head is redeemed by a head, and a life by a life.

9 *Of which the testimony* <note>original: "Cujus testimonium"</note>] The pronoun *whose*, which is not in the Greek codices, and it is confirmed that it is not among the Greeks, was added by some Translator for the sake of explaining the meaning. For the Greek reads: *the testimony in its own times, for which I was placed*, that is, <note>original: "testimonium temporibus suis, in quod positus sum ego"</note>. Although Ambrose reads in the same way, agreeing with the Vulgate Edition. Both the Constance codices agreed with the Greek reading thus: *for all, a testimony in its own times in which I was placed*. However, "testimony" is added appositively, because he gave himself as an *antilytron*; it was a testimony of the prophetic promise, and a confirmation of divine charity toward the human race. Theophylact and Chrysostom agree with this. Moreover, the added article is not idle, *the testimony* <note>original: "τὸ μαρτύριον"</note>, that is, that which was that testimony about which no one ought to doubt. For he does not deceive who gives proof by his own death.

10 *Preacher* <note>original: "Praedicator"</note>] <note>original: "κήρυξ"</note>, that is, a herald or messenger, rather than a preacher.

11 *I speak the truth* <note>original: "Veritatem dico"</note>] The phrase *in Christ* <note>original: "ἐν Χριστῷ"</note> is missing in our Latin version. Yet it is not added in Ambrose, nor in Chrysostom, nor in Theophylact.

12 *Pure hands* <note>original: "Puras manus"</note>] <note>original: "ὁσίους"</note>. Which Ambrose translates as *holy*. Although the Translator in this place rendered it well as *pure*, because in sacred matters all things ought to be pure. However, by "pure" here he did not mean "washed" in the manner of the Jews, but pure from plunder, pure from lust, pure from fights and blood.

13 *And dispute* <note>original: "Et disceptatione"</note>] <note>original: "διαλογισμοῦ"</note>. Which Lorenzo Valla preferred to translate as *hesitation*, and the Greek commentaries agree with this sense. Although Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>original: "Stapulensis"</note> not absurdly pulls it toward a mind that is not at peace with its neighbor, and Chrysostom errs toward this sense, even though the Translator frequently renders the same word as *thought*.

<margin>F</margin>
14 *In adorned habit* <note>original: "In habitu ornato"</note>] <note>original: "ἐν καταστολῇ κοσμίῳ"</note>. It is not quite safe to prescribe this to little women, especially British or even Italian ones, who are already quite fond of decking themselves out of their own accord. Indeed, Paul commands women to use modest dress, so that they are covered on all sides, and their habit of life might testify to their integrity and womanly shamefastness—for that is what <note>original: "κόσμιον"</note> sounds like. For what is the point of warning little women not to use filthy dress? It appears Aquinas was somewhat offended here, and for that reason they philosophize about the interior adornment of the mind, which is required of women because they are otherwise less strong in body and soul. Those who are offended that some interpret *gnōsē* <note>Greek for "knowledge"</note> regarding a woman, why are they not offended by this speech, "in well-ordered dress"?

15 *Adorning themselves* <note>original: "Ornantes se"</note>] <note>original: "κοσμεῖν ἑαυτάς"</note>, that is, to adorn themselves.

16 *In braided hair* <note>original: "In tortis crinibus"</note>] <note>original: "ἐν πλέγμασιν"</note>. He rendered the meaning by paraphrase.

17 *Or precious clothing* <note>original: "Vel veste pretiosa" </note>] <note>original: "ἢ ἱματισμῷ πολυτελεῖ"</note>, that is, or sumptuous dress.

18 *Promising* <note>original: "Promittentes"</note>] <note>original: "ἐπαγγελλομέναις"</note>, that is, *professing*, as Ambrose translates. And "professing" here is in the accusative case; that is, they should use that dress which becomes a woman who displays godliness by the thing itself: for it is not for women to teach, but those who teach are called "professors." Furthermore, godliness, which he here calls *theosebeia*, sounds like the worship of God; let it not be taken as piety toward children. She [shows] it by her deeds...
