# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY, CHAPTER III.

<margin>12</margin> to learn in all submission. But I do not permit a woman to teach, nor to exercise 
authority over a man, but to be in silence. <margin>13</margin> For Adam was formed first, 
then Eve. <margin>14</margin> And Adam was not deceived, but the woman, 
having been deceived, fell into transgression. <margin>15</margin> Nevertheless, she will be saved 
through childbearing, if they remain in faith, love, and holiness with 
sobriety. <margin>III. 1</margin> The saying is faithful: if anyone aspires to the office of a bishop, 
he desires a good work. It is necessary, then, for a bishop to be 
blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, modest, hospitable, 
<margin>3</margin> able to teach; Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy for 
filthy lucre, but gentle, not a brawler, not covetous; 
<margin>4</margin> One who rules his own house well, having his children in subjection

---

wants it to be provided, not merely promised by a religious habit, as those do today whom they call "Nuns."
<margin>19</margin> **To rule over the man** <note>original: *Dominari in virum*</note>] *authentein andros* <note>original: αὐθεντεῖν ἀνδρὸς</note>, as if you were to say, *to use authority over men*, and to compel them to one’s own will. From this word comes the term *Authentica* <note>referring to authoritative or original documents</note>.
<margin>20</margin> **The woman being seduced was in transgression** <note>original: *Mulier seducta in praevaricatione fuit*</note>] The word "was" <note>Latin: *fuit*</note> should not be referred to the participle "deceived," but to the phrase that immediately follows, *in praevaricatione fuit*, which means, she stepped across the line, or was made liable to the transgression. The Greek phrasing <note>hypodigme</note> makes this sense: *but the woman having been deceived, began to transgress the commandment.*
<margin>21</margin> **If they remain** <note>original: *Si permanserint*</note>] *ean meinosin* <note>original: ἐὰν μείνωσιν</note>, that is, "if they shall have stayed," in the plural number, so that it refers to the children. Jerome clearly testifies to this when explaining this passage against Jovinian, and again in his Letter to Laeta. Chrysostom argues very clearly in the same way, that a woman can be saved by this means: if she has borne children and taken care to diligently instruct them in the faith of Christ and in chaste morals. Theophylact agrees with this reading and interpretation. Nor does Ambrose dissent from this reading and interpretation. Even Augustine, in book 12, chapter 7 of *On the Trinity*, cites this passage in such a way that the reading "if she remains" (in the singular) cannot stand. However, I do not approve of the commentary he brings there, interpreting "children" as a man's good works. Furthermore, I am ashamed even to mention what Thomas Aquinas <note>the famous Medieval Scholastic philosopher</note> comments on these words of Paul; how he twists himself, how many cracks <note>logical loopholes</note> he seeks through which he might slip away. Whoever wishes may compare for himself, and he will understand what it means to write commentaries on the New Testament without consulting the Greek manuscripts. "She will be saved," says Thomas, "as to the health of the body, because she will not be deprived of her Jesus and the faculty of generating. She will be saved as to the health of the soul, because she will not be deprived of grace. And soon after mixing in an allegory, in which he does not have much faith, he returns to a literal exposition: that 'through' does not declare a cause, but a contrast, making the sense: 'a woman will be saved even if she walks through childbearing, that is, if she marries.'" It loathes me to report the rest. Let those who, despising the Ancients, attribute everything to these moderns <note>the Scholastics</note>, tell me: what could those men have done in explaining the sacred volumes if they had been required to finish the business by their own "Mars" <note>an idiom for "by their own strength"</note>? Deprived of the help of the Ancients—from whom they have drawn almost everything they have that is worth reading—they nevertheless hardly ever acknowledge them as the authors. With what spirit they have done this, let others judge. In this place, I would certainly like an answer from those who are exceedingly pleased by that oft-repeated fable about Thomas: where was that Paul then, who is said to have confessed that his Epistles were understood by no one until Aquinas illuminated them with his commentaries? Theophylact indicates that some interpret that passage, "But she will be saved through the generation of children," as referring to the Virgin Mother, as if through her all women were saved because she bore the Redeemer. For the Greek word *teknogonia* <note>childbearing</note> can be said of a single son or daughter. But he rejects this commentary as not fitting at all with what precedes and follows.
<margin>22</margin> **With sobriety** <note>original: *Cum sobrietate*</note>] *meta sophrosynes* <note>original: μετὰ σωφροσύνης</note>, which Jerome, writing against Jovinian, wanted to be translated as "chastity" rather than "sobriety." And here the Translator <note>referring to the Vulgate</note> sometimes translates it as "chastity," and Ambrose reads it thus as well. Although the Greek word is ambiguous, it sounds more like "sobriety" and "health of mind" than "chastity." But, as has been said, Jerome is acting as the patron of virginity there.
<margin>1</margin> **A faithful saying** <note>original: *Fidelis sermo*</note>] *Pistos ho logos* <note>original: Πιστὸς ὁ λόγος</note>. And in this place Saint Ambrose translates it as "A human saying" <note>original: *Humanus sermo*</note>, from which one may guess that he read *chrestos* <note>kind/human</note> instead of *pistos* <note>faithful</note>. Chrysostom and Theophylact refer this back to the previous statements, which Paul wanted to be beyond doubt: namely, what he said about the woman being saved by bearing and rightly instructing children.
<margin>2</margin> **If anyone desires the office of a bishop** <note>original: *Si quis Episcopatum desiderat*</note>] *oregetai* <note>original: ὀρέγεται</note>, that is, "appetites" or "seeks after." And it is a *noble* work rather than just a *good* one, *kala erga* <note>original: καλὰ ἔργα</note>. That was true in that century. But in these times, he who seeks the office of a bishop seeks a noble income, he seeks a noble empire—as many bishops are today. However, he called it a "work," because *episkope* <note>the Greek word for the office</note> is named by the Greeks from "inspecting" and "providing." Furthermore, although the Translator used "desires" twice, in Greek there are two different words: *oregetai* and *epithymei*. He makes up for this in other places by rendering the same word in different ways.
<margin>3</margin> **For it behooves** <note>original: *Oportet enim*</note>] *Dei oun* <note>original: Δεῖ οὖν</note>, that is, "It behooves therefore."
<margin>4</margin> **The husband of one wife** <note>original: *Unius uxoris virum*</note>] *mias gynaikos andra* <note>original: μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα</note>. Nowadays people twist this too harshly, not to say ridiculously, to refer to "one Church." Does a bishop not have many churches? But Chrysostom interprets it as the single wife a bishop should have, though adding that there are some who explain it thus: the husband of one wife means one who has been married only once. And Chrysostom is at risk of making it seem that Paul requires a bishop to have a wife, or (following the example of the Jews) to have several at once. But now, not only is chastity <note>celibacy</note> required of so many priests, but even marriages contracted by Subdeacons are dissolved. Indeed, they also strictly enforce what Paul established as a rule for bishops in that century—when there was an extreme scarcity of priests—that a man twice-married <term>digamous; one who married again after a first wife died</term> should not enter this honor. For now, when there are so many thousands of priests everywhere, men are excluded from the priesthood who perhaps unknowingly married a woman who wasn't a virgin, or even one who had a wife before baptism and married another after baptism when the first had died—he is barred from the priesthood, even though Jerome vigorously protested against this. Indeed, it is even more strange that while Paul requires so many excellent qualities in a bishop, all the others are overlooked, and only the matter of a wife is considered. Incest is admitted, a murderer is admitted, a pirate is admitted, a Sodomite, a sacrilegious man, a parricide—finally, who is *not*? Only the twice-married man is excluded from this honor, who alone has committed no crime. It is a wonder how we polish some things and hold onto them more than "with our teeth" <note>an idiom for stubbornness</note>, while being completely blind to others. If anyone considers the current state of the times—what a portion of men the herds of Monks occupy, what a portion the colleges of Priests and Clerics; then considers how few from such a number truly keep a life of chastity, and then into what kinds of lusts innumerable men fall, and with what disgrace many are openly incestuous and impure—perhaps he will judge it more expedient that for those who are entirely unable to contain themselves, the right of public marriage be granted, which they might observe purely and holily without a bad reputation, rather than lusting unhappily and shamefully. Now the world has as many celibates as possible, but very few who are chaste; although he is not chaste who does not touch sex only because it is not permitted. But again and again I fear that ecclesiastical revenues are what make Clerics "chaste" today more truly than piety does, while we fear that what we hold might be intercepted, or certainly that nothing would be added to it. But these things are not for this current project.

<column-break/>

A | Furthermore, I do not permit a woman to teach, nor 19 to <margin>12</margin>
usurp authority over men, but to be in silence. For Adam <margin>13</margin>
was formed first, then Eve: And Adam was not <margin>14</margin>
deceived, but 20 the woman being seduced was made liable
to transgression: Nevertheless, she will be made safe through the 
procreation of <margin>15</margin> children, 21 if they remain in faith and love and 
sanctification 22 with chastity. | An indubitable saying: 1 <margin>III.</margin>
if anyone seeks the office of a bishop, he desires a 
respectable work. 3 It behooves therefore a bishop to be 
irreproachable, <margin>2</margin> 4 the husband of one wife, vigilant, 5 
sober, 6 modest, 7 hospitable, 8 fit for teaching, 9
B Not given to wine, not a striker, not greedily desirous of <margin>3</margin>
shameful gain, but fair, 10 far from fights, 11 far 
from avarice, 12 One who presides well over his own house, 
who has children <margin>4</margin>...

---

<margin>5</margin> **Prudent** <note>original: *Prudentem*</note>] *sophrona* <note>original: σώφρονα</note>; in this place Ambrose translates it as "chaste," which greatly pleases Jerome, though it sounds more like "sober and of sound mind." For *nephalion* <note>original: νηφάλιον</note>, which precedes it, sounds like both "vigilant" and "abstaining from wine," from which come the *nephalia*, sacrifices in which water was offered instead of wine. The etymology of the word is given variously among the Greeks. Vigilance and sobriety are companions to each other. It does not befit a watchman, vigilant for the safety of all, to be drowsy; nor can he stay awake who indulges in luxury.
<margin>6</margin> **Adorned** <note>original: *Ornatum*</note>] *kosmion* <note>original: κόσμιον</note>, that is, "composed," or well-mannered, or "modest." This is the same word that he translates elsewhere as "in respectable apparel."
<margin>7</margin> **Hospitable** <note>original: *Hospitalem*</note>] *philoxenon* <note>original: φιλόξενον</note>, kind to strangers and newcomers. Theophylact noted the emphasis of the Greek word. Nowadays they call it "hospitality" when they receive Satraps and Kings with great luxury and send them away with gifts.
<margin>8</margin> **Teacher** <note>original: *Doctorem*</note>] *didaktikon* <note>original: διδακτικὸν</note>, that is, "teachable," or "fit for teaching." For that is what Paul meant, and that is the chief duty of a bishop. For the other things listed are required even of those under his authority. But teaching the people, exhorting, comforting, warning, and E rebuking is the closest and most splendid function of Bishops, which many today gladly hand off to others, no matter how low-status. Where it has become accepted that Bishops handle secular rule, they should at least on the chief feasts grace the duty of evangelical preaching by speaking before the people. Jerome, writing against the Pelagians in book 1, rebuked the common edition <note>the Vulgate</note> of those times, which had *docibilem* <note>teachable</note>, calling it Latin simplicity, and translated it as "one who can teach." For "teachable" <note>docilis</note> is one who learns easily.
<margin>9</margin> **Not given to wine** <note>original: *Non vinolentum*</note>] *paroinon* <note>original: πάροινον</note>. Which Ambrose translates as "liable to wine"; he could have said "wine-bibbing." Chrysostom and with him Theophylact deny that this should be taken as referring to a drunkard, but rather to one who is fierce, arrogant, and ready for violence, such as those who rage when drunk with wine. Gentleness especially befits a father.
<margin>10</margin> **Not litigious** <note>original: *Non litigiosum*</note>] *amachon* <note>original: ἄμαχον</note>, that is, "far from fighting," which Jerome translates against Pelagius as "without brawling." And that phrase, "not a striker" <note>original: *non percussorem*</note>, *me plekten* <note>original: μὴ πλήκτην</note>, does not pertain to the violence of the hands, but to the bitterness of the tongue, lest he be a cruel and wicked rebuker. Saint Jerome noted this as well. For what great thing would it be if a Bishop merely restrained his hands? Chrysostom subscribes to Jerome's opinion. Ambrose translates "striker" as "one who lashes out." And in Horace we read of "lashes with tongues." Likewise in Cicero, "Tyro is lashed," referring to a silent rebuke of one's reputation.
<margin>11</margin> **Not greedy** <note>original: *Non cupidum*</note>] *aphilargyron* <note>original: ἀφιλάργυρον</note>, that is, far from the desire for silver. Jerome, writing against Pelagius, translates it as "not avaricious." He added this either because one who is avaricious cannot be hospitable, or because, as Theophylact says, some people amass treasures out of their "hospitality."
<margin>12</margin> **Well-presiding over his own house** <note>original: *Domui suae bene praepositum*</note>] *kalos proistamenon* <note>original: καλῶς προϊστάμενον</note>, that is, one who rules well, as he translates shortly after, "he who knows not how to rule over his own house," *proistasthai*. And again concerning Deacons, "presiding well over their children," *teknois kalos proistamenoi*. For Valla <note>the Italian humanist Lorenzo Valla</note> shrewdly points out that to be "well-presided over" is not a praise of the Bishop, but of him who committed the office of Bishop to him.

<summary>Erasmus provides a detailed philological and social critique of the qualifications for bishops in 1 Timothy 3, arguing for a return to the original Greek meanings and apostolic practices. He famously uses this passage to criticize the mandatory celibacy of the clergy and the perceived corruption and ignorance of Scholastic theologians like Thomas Aquinas.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s annotations on 1 Timothy 3, moving from the qualifications of a bishop to those of deacons and their families, concluding with the famous passage on the "mystery of godliness" and the nature of the Church.</meta>

# PAUL'S EPISTLE CHAPTER III.

<margin>5</margin> ...one who rules his own house well, having his children in subjection with all reverence.
<margin>6</margin> For if a man does not know how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?
<margin>7</margin> Not a novice <note>original: *neophytos*</note>, lest being puffed up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the slanderer <note>original: *diabolou*</note>. Moreover, he must have a good testimony from those who are outside, lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the slanderer.
<margin>8</margin> Deacons likewise must be reverent, not double-tongued, not given to much wine, not greedy for filthy lucre,
<margin>9</margin> holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience.
<margin>10</margin> And let these also first be tested; then let them serve as deacons, being found blameless.
<margin>11</margin> Even so must their wives <note>original: *gynaikas*</note> be reverent, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things.
<margin>12</margin> Let the deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well.
<margin>13</margin> For those who have served well as deacons gain for themselves a good standing and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus.
<margin>14</margin> These things I write to you, hoping to come to you shortly;
<margin>15</margin> but if I am delayed, that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
<margin>16</margin> And without controversy, great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached...

<margin>A</margin> *13 With all chastity]* The word here is not *semnotēs* in the sense that sometimes means <term>pudicitiam</term> <note>sexual purity/chastity</note>, and at other times <term>sobrietatem</term> <note>sobriety</note> and <term>modestiam</term> <note>modesty</note>, of which I spoke a little earlier. Rather, it is *semnotēs* in the sense that signifies many things among the Greeks: a noble shame of *subjection*, *gravity*, and *reverence*. Jerome, while seeking every defense to protect and adorn the state of virginity, translated it here as *pudicitiam* <note>chastity</note>. <margin>C</margin> But we prefer "reverence," because "subjection" precedes it, so that you may understand children who are obedient to their father and modest with a noble shame. Chrysostom seems to have felt the same. Otherwise, what does "with all chastity" mean? Furthermore, there are various readings here. First, the Greek text has it thus: *Not given to wine, no striker, and not greedy for filthy lucre, but gentle, not a brawler, not covetous*, etc. Not <term>vinosum</term> <note>addicted to wine</note>, not <term>percussorem</term> <note>a violent man</note>, and not <term>turpi lucro deditum</term> <note>devoted to shameful gain</note>, but <term>humanum</term> <note>kind/gentle</note>, <term>abhorrentem a pugnis</term> <note>shrinking from fights</note>, <term>alienum ab avaritia</term> <note>a stranger to greed</note>. Ambrose reads it this way: *Not subject to wine, not a striker, but modest, not litigious, not harsh*. I have frequently warned that the writing varies in lists of this kind. Furthermore, where the Greek says *aischrokerdē*, Saint Jerome in his Epistle to Heliodorus translates it as *turpilucrum* <note>filthy lucre</note>, imitating the Greek compound. Even so, it is no secret to me that this passage, like countless others in the common copies of Jerome, has been corrupted.

<margin>B</margin> *14 He will have diligence]* *epimelēsetai*, that is, *he will take care*, or *he will manage*. For who speaks like this: "he has no diligence for me"? *Of the church of God*. It cannot be gathered from Ambrose or Chrysostom that they added the word <term>Dei</term> <note>of God</note>. For "church" is contrasted with "house." And the church is a great house. Certainly, in Ambrose, it is not added in the text, nor does Theophylact touch upon it in his commentary.
*15 Not a neophyte]* *neophytos*, meaning *newly born* or *newly planted*. For Paul calls a recently baptized person this because they were newly joined to Christianity through baptism. Furthermore, in this place, the word for "devil" might perhaps not be poorly translated as <term>calumniatoris</term> <note>of a slanderer</note>. For Paul requires from a Bishop not only that he himself be free from all fault, but also that he not be subject to slanders or suspicion. Therefore, he wants his character and life in Christianity to be so well-regarded that no one is even able to slander him. However, even in Jerome’s time, this was so little observed that it was then considered a Bishop's highest recommendation if he were snatched away to this honor immediately after baptism. Ambrose interprets this as referring not to an unblemished reputation, but to pride and the swelling of the soul. Certainly, since the Greek speech is ambiguous, I do not think it absurd if someone abounds in his own sense here, as Paul says. Indeed, it works in my favor that mox, repeating the same speech, he writes in this manner: *But it behooves him also to have a good testimony from those who are without, so that he does not fall into reproach and the snare of the Slanderer*. For he indicates a double danger: that a novice might behave insolently in a new honor and thus be subject to slander. For a Bishop ought to be far from all pride and swelling of heart, and he ought to have a reputation not subject to disgrace or slanders. The meaning here stands, whether you take "Devil" as Satan, who contaminates the reputation of good men through malicious tongues, or as a human slanderer. For "neophyte," we have used "novice."
*16 Bilingues]* *dilogous*, that is, <term>double in speech</term>, and inconsistent in what they say.
*17 And so let them minister]* *eita*, that is, *then*.
*18 Having no crime]* *anegklētoi ontes*, that is, of such a kind that no one can accuse them. This is what Jerome indicates against Pelagius. For *egkalein* is to call into court and to charge with a crime. And *egklēma* is a heinous injury for which someone can be called into court. Furthermore, a person is called *anegklētos* if no crime can be fixed upon them, not merely one who has no crime—for the modesty of many has been infamous. Even Cato's innocence was not *anegklētos*, since it is read that he was frequently called into court, though always acquitted.
*19 Women likewise modest]* Since the tenor of the speech itself openly declares that he is speaking about the wives of Bishops and Deacons, in my opinion, it would have been more correctly translated as *wives* than *women*, since the Greek is *gynaikas*. For Paul is not instructing the whole people here, but the Bishop with his family and dependents, all of whom he wants to be unblemished. Nor does it strongly contradict my opinion that Chrysostom interprets this passage as referring to the women whose ministry the Church used; for these could have been the wives of Deacons and Bishops. Certainly, concerning the widows whom the Church had supported, he gives instructions later in their own place. Nor do I see why we should shrink from the name "wives" here, since it is well known that marriage was permitted to Greek priests. Furthermore, for "reverent" (*semnas*), he uses the same word he used when requiring reverence and modesty in the Bishop's children.

<column-break/>

<margin>4</margin> have his children in subjection with all reverence.
<margin>5</margin> But if any man knows not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the Church of God?
<margin>6</margin> Not a novice, lest being puffed up he fall into the condemnation of the slanderer.
<margin>7</margin> Moreover, he must have a good testimony from those who are without, lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the slanderer.
<margin>8</margin> Ministers likewise composed, not double-tongued, not given to much wine, not greedily desirous of shameful gain,
<margin>9</margin> Holding the mystery of the faith with a pure conscience.
<margin>10</margin> And let these also be proved first, then let them minister, so that no one can accuse them.
<margin>11</margin> Wives likewise modest, not slanderous, sober, faithful in all things.
<margin>12</margin> Let the deacons be the husbands of one wife, who rule their children and their own households rightly.
<margin>13</margin> For they that have ministered well gain for themselves a good degree, and much liberty in the faith which is in Christ Jesus.
<margin>14</margin> These things I write to you, hoping that I shall come to you soon.
<margin>15</margin> But if I tarry longer, that you may know how you ought to behave in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and stay of the truth.
<margin>16</margin> And without controversy, great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached to the nations, faith...

<margin>D</margin> *20 Not detracting]* *mē diabolous*, that is, <term>not slanderers</term>, which Ambrose translates as <term>not striving for discord</term>. For *diabolos* is named from *diaballein*, which is to spread a rumor, but against a person. For that sex is almost naturally inclined to this vice.
*21 Deacons]* *diakonoi*, that is, <term>ministers</term>, and <term>Deacons</term>, not *Diacones*.
*22 They acquire]* *peripoiountai*, that is, *they acquire*, in the present tense.
*23 These things I write to you, son Timothy]* These two words, *son Timothy*, I do not find in certain Greek manuscripts, nor does Ambrose add them, nor even Chrysostom in his actual Commentaries; it is merely *Tauta soi graphō* <note>These things I write to you</note>. For the rest was added by someone from the Vulgate Edition. Theophylact does not even have it in the text. Both copies of the Library of Constance agreed with the Greek.
<margin>E</margin> *24 Pillar and foundation of the truth]* *stylos kai hedraiōma tēs alētheias*. These things are to be referred to the Church, not to Timothy, as some think; for he calls her the pillar and base and seat of the true. And Augustine cites this passage in that very sense, explaining Psalm 47. He calls the Church the *house of God* to distinguish it from the Synagogue of Moses, and the *pillar and foundation of the truth* because of the inviolable certainty of its dogmas, while the Jews occupy themselves in shadows.
*25 And manifestly]* *homologoumenōs*, that is, <term>confessedly</term>, or *without controversy*. Ambrose explained it thus as *periphanōs* <note>clearly/manifestly</note>, "And indeed by the confession of all, great is the mystery," etc. Likewise, <term>sacramentum</term> <note>sacrament</note> here is <term>mysterium</term>, that is, <term>a secret</term>.
*26 Mystery of faith]* Some interpret this as the dogmas of the faith, but it can also be understood as silence, so that ministers do not divulge—as they are prone to do—those things which happen at home.
<margin>F</margin> *27 Which was manifested in the flesh]* In Greek it is different: *Theos ephanerōthē en sarki*, that is, *God was manifested in the flesh*; and the things that follow are to be referred to God. Ambrose and the Vulgate translator read *ho* <note>which/that</note> instead of *Theos* <note>God</note>. Chrysostom and Theophylact read it differently, and if we wish to follow them, the genders of the participles must be changed: *justified*, *preached*, *believed*, *taken up*. However, I am somewhat uncertain which reading is truer. Lawrence shows how a mystery is said to be *taken up into glory*; but why does he not show even more that God is said to be *justified*? That is something that does not seem to fit Christ at first glance, even though Ambrose interprets it as being about Christ. I suspect that "God" was added against the Arian heretics. However, in my opinion, the simplest interpretation would be if one understands "mystery" to be the preaching of the Gospel, which he elsewhere often calls a "mystery"—previously hidden and unknown, but now manifested to the whole world. For he is already acting against those who were trying to introduce the ceremonies of the Mosaic Law instead of the grace of Christ, and would not receive the Gentiles on any other condition. Therefore, he calls the law of Christ "godliness," being void of ceremonies, the mystery of which is great, but which is now made manifest through Christ’s humanity; which was *justified in spirit* and the power of God, namely through miracles. Moreover, he says *justified* because of the power of justifying given to Christ, through faith without the Mosaic Law; which was *seen by Angels*, who sang, "Glory to God in the highest"; which was *preached to the nations*, when only the Jews were waiting; which was *believed* not only by the Jews, but by the whole world; finally, after the resurrection, it was received into heaven, from whence it had proceeded. Accordingly, in this very place, our reading pleases me more, especially since there is a great consensus of the ancient copies. For Chrysostom's interpretation in this place is more forced and harsh, if one weighs it carefully.
*28 He appeared to Angels]* *ōphthē*. Why not rather *was seen* or *was beheld*? And, *it was believed in the world*. The Greek speech, *episteuthē*...

# TO TIMOTHY I. CHAPTER IV.

...was preached among the nations, was believed on in the world, was taken up <margin>1V.</margin> in glory. <margin>1</margin> Now the Spirit expressly says that in the latter times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceiving spirits and doctrines of demons, <margin>2</margin> <margin>2</margin> through the hypocrisy of speakers of lies, having their own conscience seared with a brand, <margin>3</margin> <margin>3</margin> forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth. <margin>4</margin> For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving; <margin>5</margin> for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. If you point these things out to the brethren, you will be a good minister of Jesus Christ, nourished in the words of faith and of the good doctrine which you have followed. <margin>7</margin> But reject profane and old wives' fables, and exercise yourself toward godliness. <margin>8</margin> For bodily exercise profits a little, but godliness is profitable for all things, having promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come. <margin>9</margin> This is a faithful word and worthy of all acceptance. <margin>10</margin> For to this end we both labor and suffer reproach, because we have hoped in the living God, who is the Savior of all men, especially of those who believe. <margin>11</margin> Command and teach these things. <margin>12</margin> Let no one despise your youth, but be an example to the believers in word, in conduct, in love, in spirit, in faith, in purity. <margin>13</margin> Until I come, give attention to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine. <margin>14</margin> Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you by prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the eldership. <margin>15</margin> Meditate on these things, in...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...faith was had of him in the world, he was received in glory. <margin>1</margin>
But the Spirit clearly speaks, that in later <margin>1 IV.</margin> times some will fall away <margin>2</margin> from the faith, attending <margin>3</margin> to impostor spirits and doctrines of demons, <margin>4</margin> <margin>5</margin> Through the simulation <margin>6</margin> of speakers of falsehood, having their conscience marked with a brand, <margin>7</margin> forbidding to contract marriage, commanding to abstain from foods which God created to be taken with thanksgiving by the faithful and those who have known the truth: That whatever God created is good, and nothing is to be rejected, if it is taken with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified through <margin>B</margin> the word of God and prayer. If you have reminded <margin>8</margin> the brothers of these things, you will be a good minister of Jesus Christ, <margin>9</margin> nourished in the words of faith and of good doctrine, <margin>10</margin> which you have followed throughout. Otherwise, reject profane <margin>11</margin> and old wives' fables, <margin>12</margin> but rather exercise yourself toward godliness. For bodily exercise has a little utility, but godliness is useful for all things, as that which has promises of the present and future life. <margin>13</margin> An <margin>14</margin> indubitable word, and worthy to be approved in every way. For in this we both labor <margin>15</margin> and are affected by reproaches, <margin>16</margin> because we have fixed hope <margin>17</margin> in the living God, who is the savior of all men, especially the faithful. <margin>C</margin> Command these things and teach. Until I come, attend to reading, exhortation, <margin>13</margin> doctrine. Do not neglect the gift that is in you, <margin>21</margin> <margin>14</margin> which was given to you through prophecy, with the laying on <margin>22</margin> of hands, by the authority of the priesthood. <margin>D</margin> *In the world: there is no lack of ambiguity here, for it can be understood in either way. Either this mystery was committed to the world through the authority of preaching given to the Apostles and Bishops; or, faith in Him was held and men in the world were persuaded of that which seemed incredible according to the order of nature. Chrysostom follows the latter sense.*

1 *But the Spirit manifestly says* ] <note>original: "ῥητῶς"</note>, as if you were to say "expressly," or "precisely and certainly," not obscurely and in a roundabout way, as he is accustomed to speak in the Prophets. For the Greeks call things <term>rheta</term> which are certainly prescribed and defined.
2 *In the latest times* ] <note>original: "ὑστέροις"</note>, that is, "later" or "following." For it is not <note>original: "ἐσχάτοις"</note> (last).
3 *They will fall away* ] <note>original: "ἀποστήσονται"</note>, that is, they will fail or defect.
4 *To spirits of error* ] <note>original: "πνεύμασι πλάνοις"</note>, that is, to seducing or deceiving spirits, or fallacious ones: as Ambrose translates. Likewise Hilary in book 10 of *On the Trinity*. Furthermore, Augustine in his book 15 against Faustus, chapter 10, reads "seducing spirits." But the Translator seems to have read <term>planois</term> (wandering) as a noun rather than an adjective, a matter of a Greek letter change. However, in terms of the sense, it has no weight.
5 *Doctrines of demons* ] <note>original: "δαιμονίων"</note>. In this place, the word could be an adjective meaning "of the divine/demonic": because of what follows—"branded," and so on—which does not fit demons but rather those "diviners" who pretend to have commerce with Spirits. Therefore he added, "in the simulation of speakers of falsehood." If we read "of demons" in the sense of "diviners," the genitives always refer to the same thing. But if we read "of demons" as "devils"—for <margin>E</margin> Theophylact and Chrysostom read <note>original: "δαιμόνιος"</note>—the sense will be that there will be those who, turned away from Evangelical doctrine, listen to false doctrine which deceptive demons will invent through men who insinuate lies under the appearance of piety.
6 *In hypocrisy* ] <note>original: "Ἐν ὑποκρίσει"</note>, that is, in simulation, as Ambrose has it, or in fiction. It is a wonder that Christians are so delighted by this Greek word. And for "speakers of falsehood" <note>original: "ψευδολόγων"</note>, Ambrose more elegantly translates it "false-speakers," a compound word just as it is in the Greek. Augustine uses "lie-speakers." Likewise Hilary in *On the Trinity* rendered the Greek word as "lie-speakers"; we have translated it "false-speakers."
7 *Having been cauterized* ] <note>original: "κεκαυτηριασμένους τὴν ἰδίαν συνείδησιν"</note>, that is, those whose conscience is marked with a branding iron. For criminals used to be marked with a glowing iron, with stigmas impressed upon the skin. But these men have a "stigmatized" soul rather than a body, on account of the disgraces of their life of which they themselves are conscious. Augustine reads "cauterizing" instead of "having been cauterized," but I do not know if that is a scribe's error.
8 *Proposing these things* ] <note>original: "ὑποτιθέμενος"</note>, that is, suggesting or admonishing.
9 *Nourished by the words* ] This can also be read actively: "educating them in the words of faith." For the participle is in the middle present tense, <note>original: "ἐντρεφόμενος"</note>. This fits with what follows immediately: "which you have followed"—that is, pass on to others what you have learned from us.
10 *Which you have followed* ] <note>original: "ᾗ παρηκολούθηκας"</note>, that is, which you have followed throughout. For "followed" <note>original: "assequutus"</note> here is not to be taken in the sense used by rhetoricians (to attain a goal). The Greek commentaries support this, explaining it as: "of which you are a pupil, that is, in which you have been educated and involved since youth." In Latin, because of the difficulty of a task, if men do not reach what they aim for, they are said "not to have attained" <note>original: "assequi"</note>, which the Greeks call <note>original: "ἐφικνεῖσθαι"</note> or <note>original: "ἐπιτυχεῖν"</note> (to hit the mark), the opposite of which is "to miss" <note>original: "ἀτυχέειν"</note>. But those who follow the whole sequence of a matter in order and pass over nothing are said to <term>parakolouthein</term>. Luke used it this way in the preface to his Gospel History: "It seemed good to me also, having followed all things from the beginning," meaning no part of the life was passed over that he had not investigated. And Athenaeus in book <margin>F</margin>...

1. *The Spirit expressly says and the rest, having followed pleasures*: namely, noting those who had been addicted to pleasures through their whole life. Furthermore, it would be ridiculous if someone wanted to interpret it as "having attained" pleasures. Chrysostom and Theophylact support our view, speaking of the constant study of Divine Letters in which Timothy had been involved from a boy.
11 *But the inept* ] <note>original: "βέβηλος"</note>, that is, profane.
12 *Avoid* ] <note>original: "παραιτοῦ"</note>, which Ambrose translates as "refuse," but it means to "reject," "pray against," and "not admit."
13 *Which now is and is to come* ] <note>original: "τῆς νῦν καὶ τῆς μελλούσης"</note>: which Ambrose says more clearly as "present and future." Hence "promises" <note>original: "ἐπαγγελίας"</note> fits well, as the Greeks have it.
14 *Faithful saying* ] <note>original: "πιστὸς"</note>, for "trustworthy." Not without a trope, as he attributes to the "saying" what belongs to a person. Furthermore, for the Greeks <term>apodoxe</term> is more frequently "to embrace with approval." For we receive what we do not reject, and this little part confirms what he had just said about the promises of both lives.
15 *For in this we labor* ] In Greek it is: "and we labor." For he said "to labor" instead of "to be affected by troubles": by which argument he confirms the faith of the promise. For who would labor for vain promises?
16 *And we are cursed* ] <note>original: "ὀνειδιζόμεθα"</note>, that is, we are affected by reproaches. Ambrose reads "we suffer persecutions"; I wonder what manuscript he followed.
17 *Because we hope* ] <note>original: "ὅτι ἠλπίκαμεν"</note>, that is, that we have hoped. Except that in verbs of affection such as this, the Greeks sometimes use the past tense for the present. It could be translated: "in whom we have fixed our hope." And it is not "unto God," but "in God."
18 *No one [despise] youth* ] Although in Greek it is <note>original: "νἑοτης"</note>, it would have been more correctly translated "youthhood." For Timothy was not an adolescent, but did not yet have the old age worthy of a Bishop. He warns, therefore, that what is lacking in age, he should make up for in integrity of character.
19 *But be an example* ] <note>original: "τύπος"</note>, which he sometimes translates as "form."
20 *In charity* ] The Greeks have it thus: "in word, in conduct, in love, in spirit, in faith, in purity." Namely, "in spirit" is redundant according to the Latins. However, Chrysostom does not touch on this in his Commentaries, though Theophylact reads and interprets it. Nor is there need to warn that "in word" is said for "through word."
21 *To neglect grace* ] <note>original: "χαρίσματος"</note>, that is, "the gift."
22 *Of the hands of the presbytery* ] Thus some manuscripts have it. But the Ancients agree with the Greeks, among whom it is <note>original: "πρεσβυτερίου"</note>, that is, "of the eldership," not "of the elder." And so Ambrose reads it. But he says this: You have not only the gift of prophecy, but also the efficacy of giving the spirit to others by the laying on of hands, and that by the office of your eldership—namely, as a Bishop. For in antiquity there was no difference between a Presbyter, a Priest, and a Bishop, as Saint Jerome also testifies. Later, one was chosen as Bishop to prevent schisms. Furthermore, the Greek preposition <term>meta</term> (with) stands in the way of the sense that "the eldership" is what you received; <term>meta</term> signifies a companion, not an instrument. Otherwise, it would fit well with what he said in the next Epistle: "Stir up the gift of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands." And I do not know whether here too it must be admitted that Paul neglected the elegance of Greek speech, especially since Chrysostom interprets it in this sense: that prophecy is the gift and authority of teaching, and then through the laying on of hands he was made a Bishop.
23 *Meditate on these things* ] <note>original: "Ταῦτα μελέτα"</note>. Which the Translator renders elegantly. But Cardinal Hugo, not understanding this word, at this...

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER V.

<margin>A</margin> Be diligent in these things, so that your progress may be manifest to all. Take heed to yourself and to the doctrine; persevere in them; for in doing this, you will save both yourself and <margin>V. 1</margin> those who hear you. Do not rebuke an elder <note>original: "Πρεσβυτέρῳ," referring here to an older man rather than just the office of "priest"</note> harshly, but exhort him as a father, and younger men as broth-<margin>2</margin>ers, older women as mothers, and younger women as sis-<margin>3</margin>ters, in all purity. Honor widows who are truly <margin>4</margin> widows. But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show piety to their own household and to make a return to their parents; for this is good <margin>5</margin> and acceptable before God. Now she who is truly a widow and left alone has set her hope on God, and continues in supplications and prayers night <margin>6 7</margin> and day. But she who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives. And <margin>8</margin> command these things, so that they may be blameless. But if anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. Let a widow be <margin>9</margin> enrolled only if she is not less than sixty years old, having been the wife of one husband, and having a reputation for <margin>10</margin> good works—if she has brought up children, if she has shown hospitality, if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has assisted those in trouble, if she has diligently followed every good <margin>11</margin> work. But refuse younger widows; for when they begin to grow wanton against Christ, they desire to marry,

---

<margin>B</margin> He explains this manner: *Turn it over in the heart through constant memory.* Although Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian</note> does not shrink from this interpretation, I wonder why he did not at least consult Ambrose <note>The 4th-century Bishop of Milan</note>. However, "to meditate" means to be practiced in any matter. Ambrose makes this clear enough, interpreting it as the practice of sacred doctrine, so that one's life also demonstrates what one teaches. And in these books <note>likely referring to his own editions or the "Glossa Ordinaria"</note> which have the standard gloss in the space between the verses, this comment is added: <gloss>Execute these things with persistent action.</gloss> Chrysostom and Theophylact <note>Greek Church Fathers</note> interpret it as constant and vehement zeal, which can be referred to either the soul or the body. For no one denies that meditation of the soul is possible, just as when someone is about to speak before a judge, he meditates with himself on how and what he is going to say. But I noted this because I had observed that for some, "meditation" meant nothing other than "thought."

<margin>24</margin> *Be manifest to all*] <insert>in all things</insert> <note>original: "ἐν πᾶσιν"</note>, that is, in all respects.
<margin>C</margin> *Do not rebuke an elder*] <insert>Do not strike an elder</insert> <note>original: "Πρεσβυτέρῳ μὴ ἐπιπλήξῃς"</note>. Here *elder* refers to age, because the mention of *younger men* follows; and I think the comparative forms are used in place of the positive. Furthermore, the word is not simply "rebuke," but <insert>to strike a blow</insert> <note>original: "ἐπιπλήξῃς"</note>, which signifies inflicting a wound, and is transferred to the meaning of scolding harshly and fiercely. Thus Flaccus <note>the Roman poet Horace</note> says in his Odes:
> —— fearing the lashes of an uncle's tongue.
And earlier, Paul did not want a Bishop to be a <insert>striker</insert> <note>original: "πλήκτην"</note>, that is, a sharp scolder.

<margin>2</margin> *but entreat him as a father*] Valla <note>humanist scholar Lorenzo Valla</note> prefers in this place "exhort," because the Greek word <insert>exhort/entreat</insert> <note>original: "παρακάλει"</note> can mean to stir up, to urge, to entreat, or to comfort, all of which are closely related. But it seemed to him a little beneath the dignity of a Bishop if he "entreats," especially one who is sinning, and most especially a younger man or a mere youth. Certainly, Ambrose reads it as "exhort." And Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret it in that sense.

<margin>3</margin> *In all castity*] <insert>with all purity</insert> <note>original: "ἐν πάσῃ ἁγνείᾳ"</note>; though the word "chastity" is not displeasing. For I see Chrysostom interprets it this way, so that any suspicion of impurity is absent, properly referring this clause to what immediately preceded. Ambrose speaks of chastity in such a way that he does not seem to have read this part. In my opinion, it could refer to all the preceding parts, so that whether he deals with elders, younger men, or girls, he may be pure from every appearance of either cruelty, defiance, greed, or hatred.

<margin>4</margin> *Who are truly widows*] That is, abandoned and desolate. For <insert>widow</insert> <note>original: "χήρα"</note> is called by the Greeks from a word meaning "bereft" or "destitute" <note>original: "χῆρος"</note>. Whence also among the Latins, *vidua* (widow) is said from *viduando*, that is, to be bereaved; hence "widowhood" signifies desolation and solitude. Paul clearly alludes to the etymology of the Greek word, which he explains more clearly a little further down: <insert>The one who is truly a widow and left alone</insert>, that is, *the one who is a true widow and desolate.* Now we have frequently noted that the word "to honor," according to the custom of the Hebrews, carries the meaning of providing support.

<margin>5</margin> *Let them first learn their own house*] <insert>let them learn</insert> <note>original: "μανθανέτωσαν"</note>, in the plural number: so that this precept pertains to the children and grandchildren, who are to be so instructed by the mother or grandmother that they are pious toward their parents. For this he calls <insert>to be pious</insert> <note>original: "εὐσεβεῖν"</note>, which Theophylact interprets as <insert>graciously</insert>, and which the Greeks also call <insert>care for the aged</insert> <note>original: "γηροβοσκία"</note>. Ambrose seems to refer it more to the widow herself, perhaps reading <insert>let her learn</insert> <note>original: "μανθανέτω"</note> in the singular. Chrysostom also seems at first glance to have read the singular when he adds that this must be repaid in the grandchildren, since the widow cannot do so for deceased parents. But looking closer, he does not mean this: for he speaks of the widow's children, now mothers or fathers, whom he calls "grandchildren" with respect to the parents who are already dead. Theophylact without controversy reads the plural, following the first interpretation.

<margin>6</margin> *To rule their own house*] <insert>to treat piously</insert> <note>original: "εὐσεβεῖν"</note>: as Saint Ambrose translates it. And likewise Augustine in Question 43 on Deuteronomy. "Mutual return," <insert>requital</insert> <note>original: "ἀμοιβάς"</note>, as if you were to say, "repayment in kind." He alludes to <insert>stork-like gratitude</insert> <note>original: "ἀντιπελάργησιν," a Greek term for children caring for parents, based on the belief that storks fed their elders</note>.

<margin>7</margin> *This is acceptable*] In Greek it is, *good and acceptable*, <insert>honest and welcome</insert> <note>original: "καλὸν καὶ ἀποδεκτὸν"</note>.

<margin>8</margin> *Let her hope in God*] <insert>she has hoped</insert> <note>original: "ἤλπικεν"</note>, that is, she has hoped or she hopes: as Ambrose also reads, in the indicative mood, not the imperative. For in words of this kind, the past tense is sometimes used for the present.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> be in these things, so that your progress <margin>24</margin> may be manifest in all things. Attend to yourself and to the doctrine: persist in these: for <margin>16</margin> if you do this, you will save yourself and those who hear you. <margin>1 V.</margin> Do not <margin>1</margin> harshly scold an elder, but exhort him as a father, younger men as brothers, women older in birth <margin>2</margin> as mothers, younger women as sisters, <margin>3</margin> with all chastity. Honor widows <margin>4</margin> who are truly widows. But if any <margin>3 4</margin> widow has children or grandchildren, <margin>5</margin> let them first learn to treat their own house piously and to repay their elders: <margin>7</margin> for this is honorable and acceptable before God. Furthermore, she who is truly a widow and desolate <margin>8</margin> hopes in God, <margin>9</margin> and perseveres in supplications and prayers night and day. But <margin>10</margin> she who lives in luxury is dead while living. And command these things, so that they may be blameless. <margin>11</margin> But if anyone for his own, and especially for his <margin>12</margin> family, does not provide, <margin>13</margin> he has denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel. A widow is enrolled, not less than sixty years <margin>9</margin> old, who was the wife of one husband, proven by the testimony of men in good works, <margin>14</margin> if she has brought up children, if she was hospitable, if she washed the feet of the saints, if she ministered to those <margin>15</margin> afflicted, if she was constant in every good work. But younger widows <margin>17</margin> reject: <margin>18</margin> for when <margin>11</margin> they have begun to grow wanton against Christ, they wish to marry,

---

And Paul here does not prescribe what he wants widows to do, but explains <margin>C</margin> by description whom he would call true widows. Moreover, there was no reason for the timing of the verbs to offend Valla. Certainly, the codex of Saint Donatian has supported us thus far. Both codices of Constance also supported it.

<margin>9</margin> *And let her persist*] *And she persists*, in Greek it is <insert>and she remains</insert> <note>original: "καὶ προσμένει"</note>, that is, she perseveres, or is constant. Ambrose reads "and she perseveres" in the indicative mood, and the two Constance codices agreed here too.

<margin>10</margin> *She who is in luxury*] The Greeks distinguish this so that they join two contraries: *living, she is dead* <note>original: "ζῶσα τέθνηκεν"</note>, as if you would say, though living she does not live. Although the participle can be referred to either side. But the sense is smoother according to the Greek distinction. Add to this that this reading is much more elegant, which Chrysostom also read and published. Hilary says it more clearly in his commentary on Psalm 67, following Origen's opinion, I believe: *And the Apostle, he says, knows that some who are dead still live: that is, while they live they are already dead.* Augustine likewise in Question 43 on Deuteronomy relates it <margin>D</margin> in this way: *But she who acts in luxury, living is dead:* supported by very ancient Latin copies, in which a punctuation mark was added under the word "is," separating that part of the speech from the one that follows: "But she who is in luxury, *living is dead*." Jerome distinguishes it in the same way in his Epistle; the beginning of which is, *You entreat by letters*.

<margin>11</margin> *If anyone however of his own*] <insert>But if anyone</insert> <note>original: "Εἰ δέ τις"</note>. More correctly, "If anyone." For Paul says these things about the widow. The Greek scholia <note>ancient marginal commentaries</note> also advise this. Therefore Ambrose interprets it as being about the widow. Certainly Theophylact specifically interprets it as the widow who, living in luxury, has care for no one but herself. Nor does it matter that "worse than an unbeliever" follows, since this word in Greek is always of common gender <note>meaning it can refer to a man or a woman</note>.

<margin>12</margin> *Does not have care*] <insert>does not provide</insert> <note>original: "οὐ προνοεῖ"</note>, that is, does not look forward or provide.

<margin>13</margin> *He has denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel*] This seems to be a harsh saying, and because of that Aquinas explains the difficulty with a distinction. For he explains what Paul said, "He has denied the faith," <margin>E</margin> as "he is false." Aquinas is indeed right. For he who does not perform what the Christian faith dictates—which does not abolish the teaching of nature but perfects it—has in this part fallen away from the faith. Nor is he simply "worse than an unbeliever," but he is worse in this specific part: he does not perform this duty for his own people, to whom he is joined by the bond of nature, which even the Pagans perform by the instinct of nature. Yet today, in the judgment of some, it is considered the height of piety if someone, having left children and wife at home, or even elderly parents, either goes off to Jerusalem or hides himself in a Monastery, to live for himself, or perhaps even for his belly.

<margin>14</margin> *If she has brought up children*] In Greek it is more pleasant with a compound word, <insert>if she has child-reared</insert> <note>original: "εἰ ἐτεκνοτρόφησεν"</note>, so that you might include daughters as well. Likewise, what follows, "received with hospitality," is a compound word, <insert>she has guest-received</insert> <note>original: "ἐξενοδόχησεν"</note>, which we translate, *if she was hospitable*.

<margin>15</margin> *If she has followed every good work*] <insert>if she has followed after every good work</insert> <note>original: "εἰ παντὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ ἐπηκολούθησεν"</note>. It signifies a woman who was missing from no good work, and was always present for all duties of piety. Jerome on Zechariah, instead of "followed," said "pursued." We translate it, *if she was constant in every good work.* Let the one who philosophizes about "following," as if she follows because she thinks she has caught up, read if there is any "Lover of Angles" <note>original: "Φιλεγγελος," likely a pun or obscure reference to scholastic hair-splitting</note>.

<margin>16</margin> *The younger however*] <insert>But the younger</insert> <note>original: "Νεωτέρας δὲ"</note>. I would prefer *Juniores*. For it is not a comparative used in place of a positive, but it refers to what he had just said: "not less than sixty years": but those who are below these years, reject—at least so far as they should not be fed by the food of the Church while being idle.

<margin>17</margin> *Avoid*] <insert>reject</insert> <note>original: "παραιτοῦ"</note>. Of which was spoken above, that is, *reject* and *refuse*: that is, do not receive them to be supported. For he does not mean they should be barred from conversation.

<margin>18</margin> *For when they have become luxurious in Christ*] <insert>for when they grow wanton against Christ</insert> <note>original: "ὅταν γὰρ καταστρηνιάσωσι τοῦ Χριστοῦ"</note>. Jerome interprets this in his Epistle to Geruntia: "For these reasons," he says, "therefore they have committed fornication to the injury of their husband, Christ." For this is what the Greek speech <insert>to grow wanton</insert> <note>original: "καταστρηνιάσωσι"</note> signifies. For <insert>to be wanton</insert> <note>original: "στρηνιᾶν"</note> signifies to be lascivious or to be fierce, which they think is derived from the word "to deprive" <note>original: "στερεῖν"</note>, as a metaphor taken from beasts of burden, which when they have been fed with fodder, tear away the reins and are carried along by their own will.

<summary>This page contains Paul’s instructions to Timothy regarding the respectful treatment of different age groups and the specific qualifications for the church's order of widows. Erasmus uses the text to critique contemporaries who abandon family duties for religious pilgrimages or monastic life, arguing that natural familial duty is a core part of the faith.</summary>

# TO TIMOTHY I. CHAPTER V.

12 **Having condemnation, because they have set aside their first faith.** 13 **And at the same time they also learn to be idle, going about from house to house; and not only idle, but also gossips and busybodies, speaking things they ought not.** 14 **I desire therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, manage the household, and give no occasion to the adversary for the sake of reproach.** 15 **For already some have turned aside after Satan.** 16 **If any faithful man or faithful woman has widows, let them assist them, and let the Church not be burdened, so that it may assist those who are truly widows.** 17 **Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and doctrine.** 18 **For the scripture says: You shall not muzzle the ox while it treads out the grain; and: The laborer is worthy of his wages.** 19 **Do not receive an accusation against an elder, except on the evidence of two or three witnesses.** 20 **Those who sin, rebuke in the presence of all, so that the rest also may have fear.** 21 **I charge you in the sight of God and the Lord Jesus Christ and the elect angels, that you observe these things...**

<column-break/>

...they desire, 19 **Having condemnation, because they have rejected their first faith.** 12 13 **And at the same time they also learn to be idle, going about from house to house: indeed, not only idle, but also gossips and busybodies, speaking what is not proper.** 14 **I desire therefore that the younger marry, bear children, manage the house, and give no occasion to the adversary to have a cause for speaking evil.** 15 **For already some have turned aside, following Satan.** 16 **But if any faithful person has widows, let them supply their needs, and let not the Church be burdened, so that it may supply those who are truly widows.** 17 **Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and teaching.** 18 **For the scripture says: You shall not muzzle the ox as it treads: and, The laborer is worthy of his wages.** 19 **Against an elder do not admit an accusation, unless under two or three witnesses.** 20 **Rebuke those who sin before everyone, so that the others also may have fear.** 21 **I solemnly charge you in the sight of God and the Lord Jesus Christ and the elect angels, that you keep these things.**

---

<margin>A</margin> Some again think the word is derived from *scheuo*, which means "hard." Hence Hesychius interprets "to shout harshly" as "to cry out sternly," that is, to shout harshly or fiercely. For among the Greeks, *sprenos* <note>Erasmus is discussing the Greek word *strenos*, meaning "wantonness" or "luxury," which appears in verse 11.</note> sounds like "seizing, strong, rough, choking, shameless"—that is, manifest, powerful, assertive, hateful, and stubborn—finally being the same as *skrinos*. Furthermore, he interprets *spreniontes* <note>meaning "growing wanton"</note> in this way: "struck, twisted," adding sometimes it has the same value as *tryphan*, which means "to act fiercely because of wealth" and "to bear heavily," that is, to be indignant. Sophilus, in Athenaeus's third book, seems to use it for being delicate or *acting wantonly*: "There will be a lavish stuffing of the belly, I see the prologue: I shall be filled with all good things, by Bacchus, men, I now grow wanton." If one were to translate these words literally, they have this manner: "The gluttony will be sumptuous, I see the opening; I shall be satisfied with all good things, by Bacchus, men, I am already behaving wantonly." Rufus in the same book says, "I was acting wantonly after devouring food, perhaps as much as four elephants." Hence, those are said *katasprenian* <note>to grow wanton against someone</note> who are already hearing threats. Theophylact interprets the word as "being unwilling to obey and living in luxury"; the former word being taken from the character of a most petulant woman named Acco, as we explained in our *Chiliads* <note>A reference to Erasmus's own collection of proverbs and adages.</note>. The same word is found in Revelation chapter 18: "As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury"; for which the Latin translator rendered "and was in delights." And shortly after there, "and having lived in luxury." Furthermore, the preposition *kata* signifies "against" and in a bad sense when it takes the genitive case. Therefore, "to grow wanton against Christ" is to behave wantonly to the injury of Christ. For this is how I have chosen to interpret it. Both Chrysostom and Theophylact lean toward this opinion. Indeed, a widow who is taken in to be supported in some way devotes herself to Christ as her spouse, and it is to his insult that she thinks again of a new husband.

I do not fully understand what Faber <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, a contemporary scholar with whom Erasmus often disagreed.</note> intends in this passage. First, he wants Paul's reference to "younger widows" to be understood as "inconstancy of character," even though a little earlier Paul clearly and expressly stated "sixty years" for the older ones and ordered those younger than this age to be rejected. Secondly, those whom Paul forbids to be taken in to be supported by the Church's alms, Faber adds should be pushed back into a monastery by the Bishop, even against their will, if their parents allow it. Beyond this, he wonders if "to live luxuriously" signifies anything other than "to commit fornication." And because of this, he says tastelessly, "she has lived luxuriously to Christ"; whereas one should say, "she has lived delicately to Christ." Yet if Paul is dealing here with vicious delights—as it is certain he is—how is it less tasteless to say "delighted to Christ" than "luxuriated to Christ"? Or what does "delighted to Christ" mean at all? Although in corrected copies it is held as "luxuriated *in* Christ." But if any manuscripts are found in which the punctuation separates the words "in Christ" from what precedes and connects them to what follows, certainly none of the Interpreters of any weight interprets it in that way. Jerome distinguishes it one way, Ambrose another, and Thomas Aquinas another. Truly, I cannot help but wonder what happened to that man—who is, I believe, both pious and learned—that he wished to act so wantonly with Paul's letters, as if he were dealing with a trivial matter, especially after so many excellent and approved Interpreters. Finally, he treats these things as if he does not doubt, but prescribes mere decrees to us. I suggest these things unwillingly, but the authority of the Divine Scriptures demands it, and public utility demands it, that the consideration of a friend should be slight for a moment, especially when he is helped rather than harmed. Nor do I refuse a similar critique in return, provided there is no insolence. If advised, I will candidly confess my error and change it, if I am unable to defend it; indeed, I will even be grateful. But we have spoken about these things a little more accurately in the notes we wrote on the Epistles of Saint Jerome. Ambrose reads, "when they have lived in delights." And Thomas indicates that luxury here is not the specific vice of lust, but the immoderate use and abundance of any things whatsoever. This is correct, but he is not correct regarding the same matter in his arguments.

<margin>19 Having condemnation</margin> *krima*, that is, *judgment*. Although the Translator correctly expressed the sense.

<margin>20 They have rejected</margin> *ēthetēsan*, that is, they have pushed away, or rejected, or despised. Nevertheless, it also signifies what the Translator rendered. For we reject what has ceased to have value for us.

<margin>21 Not only idle</margin> Something is missing: "not only however, *ei monon de*": and the conjunction suits the letters; the word "indeed" explains it more clearly.

<margin>22 Gossipy</margin> *phlyaroi*, that is, *triflers, or foolishly talkative*. Again he gives a masculine epithet to women.

<margin>23 Speaking what</margin> *lalousai*: which sometimes means to chatter. Hence that phrase "best at chattering," and the Greeks call those who are talkative *laloi*.

<margin>24 I desire however</margin> I desire therefore, *Boulomai oun*.

<margin>25 To be mothers of families</margin> *oikodespotein*, that is, to manage the family: 

<column-break/>

<margin>B</margin> lest anyone should take it as being about bearing children (about which he had just spoken), but about the governing of the household: which the Greek word declares more clearly, being derived from *doma* (house) and *despotēs* (master). And what immediately preceded, "to bear children," is more elegantly said in Greek with a compound word than in Latin, "to procreate sons or children."

<margin>26 Back after Satan</margin> *opisō tou Satana*, that is, *after Satan*: and there is no need for "back." Next, what he translates here as "have turned aside," Ambrose reads as "have wandered away": *exetrapēsan*, that is, "they have turned aside," which we mentioned above. The sense, however, is that they have defected from Christ and followed Satan: for he calls it "going after Satan" to follow him as leader, having deserted Christ.

<margin>C</margin> 27 **If any faithful man** In Greek it is, "If any faithful man or faithful woman, *Ei tis pistos ē pistē*." And so Ambrose reads it. I believe the genuine writing was "If any faithful woman," so that we might understand that the care of women is commended to women—for instance, if any mother has a widowed daughter. And both of the Constance manuscripts had this reading. But because men seemed to be excluded from this care for relatives, someone added "If any man." And in Theophylact, "faithful man or faithful woman" is indeed added in the text: but in explaining the passage, he touches on no such thing. You will find the same in Chrysostom, who, in repeating the Apostle's words in his explanation, says simply "if any woman," not "if any faithful man." From this it appears clearly enough that "faithful man" is an addition, since both noted the emphasis of this word *eparkeitō*, which declares that what is sufficient for necessity should be supplied, not what leads to luxury. Moreover, it is the same word that follows shortly after, *eparkesē*. He translates the first as "administer support," the latter as "it may suffice": for the first is taken actively, to supply; the latter neutrally, to be available, among the Latins. Unless you prefer to supply "the Church" in the latter part: "lest the Church be burdened, so that it may be enough for those who are truly widows." For the other widows, who are not desolate, he provides only so far as they are not alienated from their unbelieving relatives, but Christian women by Christian relatives. He wants only the desolate ones to be supported at the Church's expense.

<margin>D</margin> 28 **That it be not burdened** And "let it not be burdened," *kai mē bareisthō*, that is, let them support them at their own expense, and not burden the Church.

29 **The elders who rule well** "Elder" <term>presbyter</term> here is a title of office (Bishop), not of age. And "honor" signifies support: not that common honor of moving out of the way, uncovering the head, or bending the knee—as Saint Jerome noted in more than one place. Indeed, in other cases it is called alms, but for those whom age, or dignity, or merit makes venerable, the duty performed is called "honor." And the Latins call it an "honorary gift."

30 **You shall not muzzle the ox** *ou phimōseis*. Which Ambrose translates as "you shall not bridle." Moreover, the passage he cites exists in Deuteronomy chapter 25. Now it is the custom among some to do the threshing by driving a beast around, whereas among our people they beat it out with flails. This passage should be noted against those who, with such great shouting and such great tyranny, extort tithes and more than tithes even from the poorest laity, yet do not understand that the law forbids anyone from muzzling the ox, but specifically the *treading* ox—that is, the one teaching, warning, exhorting, sacrificing, and performing other priestly duties. But what is this to those certain people who spend their whole lives not only in idleness, but in <term>Sardanapalic luxuries</term> <note>Sardanapalus was a legendary Assyrian king famous for extreme decadence and self-indulgence.</note>? And I say these things not so that the laity might be slower in their beneficence toward their Priests—to whom, if they are good, no equal thanks can be repaid—but so that we, in turn, may remember our own duty.

<margin>E</margin> 31 **Against an Elder** It is uncertain whether he speaks of an older person or a Bishop. Chrysostom refers it to age, Ambrose to dignity. Saint Jerome, in a certain letter to Marcella, indicates that some read something else here, "at least this," "Against an elder do not receive an accusation," but he prefers this reading which we use. and yet what Jerome condemns, Ambrose follows, interpreting it conveniently: that against an Elder, because of the dignity of his order, an accusation should not be easily received, nor should there be any mention of two or three witnesses. For what need is there to command this for an Elder, which must be observed for everyone? Chrysostom excuses this by saying it must be observed *especially* in the case of elders. And I do not know whether some slightly-learned reader, offended by the first appearance of the speech, changed it, as if wishing to explain what the Apostle meant. Again, what follows, "Rebuke those who sin before everyone," if you refer the previous parts to Elders, this must pertain to the same: so the sense is that a charge should not be easily accepted unless there are suitable witnesses. But if the crime is proven, they are to be rebuked openly as an example to all. Chrysostom and Theophylact explain both parts as referring to the elderly.
