# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER VI.

<margin>21</margin> [I charge you before...] the angels, that you observe these things without prejudice, <margin>22</margin> doing nothing according to partiality. Do not lay hands <margin>23</margin> hastily on anyone, nor share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure. <margin>24</margin> No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and <margin>25</margin> your frequent illnesses. The sins of some people are clearly evident, leading the way to judgment, but for others, they also follow after. <margin>25</margin> Likewise also good works are clearly evident, and those that are otherwise cannot be hidden.

### VI.
<margin>1</margin> Let as many as are under the yoke of slavery consider their own masters worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be blasphemed. <margin>2</margin> Those who have believing masters, let them not despise them because they are brothers; but rather let them serve, because those who receive the benefit are faithful and beloved. These things teach and exhort. <margin>3</margin> If anyone teaches otherwise and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching which is according to godliness, <margin>4</margin> he is puffed up, knowing nothing, but is sick with questions and word-fights, from which come envy, strife, blasphemies, evil suspicions, <margin>5</margin> useless disputes of men corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth, thinking that godliness is a means of gain. Withdraw from such people. <margin>6</margin> But godliness with contentment is great gain. <margin>7</margin> For we brought nothing into the world, and it is clear that we can carry nothing out. <margin>8</margin> But having food and clothing, with these we shall be content. <margin>9</margin> But those wanting to be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and many foolish desires...

---

**32 Without prejudice** ] <note>original: "χωρὶς προκρίματος"</note>, *without prejudice.* In this context, "prejudice" does not mean what it does to legal scholars—a matter already judged—but rather a "precipitated judgment," when something is done based on a rashly conceived opinion, and we judge for ourselves before we have the facts. The Greek commentaries interpret it in this manner.

**33 By inclining to the other side** ] <note>original: "κατὰ πρόσκλισιν"</note>. The translator seems to have read it as *prosklesin* (invitation/calling), with an *iota* not an *isi* <note>Erasmus is discussing a Greek spelling variation</note>, from the verb *proskalo* (to call), not *prosklino* (to incline). This is how Saint Ambrose reads it, in whose work it says "declining to another part." Saint Basil also reads it this way in the beginning of his work on Proverbs, as cited by the Greek commentaries. Chrysostom and Theophylact read and interpret it no differently. However, Clement reads it as the Greek copies now have it, though it seems to me it should be read as *prosklesin* (provocation), not *prosklisin* (inclination), if one prefers the sense of "attacking" someone.

**34 No longer drink water** ] <note>original: "Μηκέτι ὑδροπότει"</note>, that is, *Do not drink water after this.* It implies that he had been a water-drinker up to that time, as Saint Jerome reasons; in Greek, this is a single word: *hydropoto*.

**35 Your frequent infirmities** ] <note>original: "πυκνὰς ἀσθενείας"</note>. By infirmities, he does not mean major diseases or serious sicknesses, but a general frailty of the body.

**36 Are manifest** ] <note>original: "πρόδηλοί"</note>, that is, "pre-manifest": things that are evident in themselves even before they are condemned by anyone's judgment. For that prefix *pro-* (before) refers to external judgment. He is speaking of those who are openly evil or openly good, and conversely those whose evil or good is hidden.

**37 Preceding to judgment** ] <note>original: "προάγουσαι εἰς κρίσιν"</note>. For those sins have already been condemned before the one who committed them is brought to trial.

**38 But of some** ] <note>original: "τισὶ δὲ καὶ ἐπακολουθοῦσιν"</note> is the Greek: and so Ambrose reads it, that is, *but some they also follow after*; both manuscripts from Constance support this.

<margin>E</margin> **1 Lest the name of the Lord** ] The Greek says "the name of God," <note>original: "τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note>. Chrysostom reads it this way, and Ambrose as well, as can be gathered from his interpretation.

**2 Because they are partakers of the benefit** ] <note>original: "οἱ τῆς εὐεργεσίας ἀντιλαμβανόμενοι"</note>, that is, *those who are partakers of beneficence,* or *those who are helped by beneficence.* In the ancient codices I found, it does not say "because." This refers to the slaves, not the masters. Although Theophylact explains it two ways, Chrysostom, though he speaks ambiguously, seems to follow this sense: that Christian masters should be served more diligently because service is placed upon those who have moved from the arrogance of masters into the affection of parents, and have begun to be loved as allies. For he says, *let them not despise them because they are brothers: but rather let them serve, since they are faithful and beloved, who receive the benefit.* Ambrose interprets it in the same sense.

**3 If anyone teaches otherwise** ] <note>original: "ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖ"</note>, that is, *teaches different things,* or *follows a different doctrine.* For it seems to apply to those who, having loathed the Gospel teaching, were devoted to empty little questions. Among the Greeks, this is a single compound word, about which we warned above.

**4 And does not acquiesce** ] <note>original: "προσέρχεται"</note>, that is, *approaches* or *comes to*: so the Greek sounds, and the Latin responds appropriately. Perhaps the translator read *prosechetai*, which means *adheres to.*

<margin>F</margin> **5 He is proud** ] <note>original: "Τετύφωται"</note>, that is, *he is puffed up.* Ambrose reads, "He is arrogant." Cyprian in a certain Epistle reads, "Elated with stupor." I suspect he actually wrote "Elated with tumor" <note>meaning a swelling or puffiness of pride</note>.

**6 But languishing** ] <note>original: "νοσῶν"</note>, that is, *sick*: a word which among the Greeks is often referred to the mind, so that those who are foolish or raving are said to "be sick," that is, laboring under a disease of the mind. This word fits marvelously

<column-break/>

<page-num>944</page-num>
<header>THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER VI.</header>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>32</margin> observe, so that without precipitation of judgment, you do nothing <margin>33</margin> according to the leaning of the mind. Do not lay hands <margin>22</margin> quickly on anyone, nor share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure. <margin>34</margin> No longer drink water, but use a <margin>23</margin> little wine for the sake of your stomach <margin>35</margin> and your frequent illnesses. The sins of some men are <margin>24</margin> <margin>36</margin> manifest beforehand, <margin>37</margin> preceding to judgment; <margin>38</margin> but for some, they also follow after. Likewise also good <margin>25</margin> works are manifest beforehand, and those which are otherwise cannot be hidden. Whoever are slaves under the yoke <margin>VI. 1</margin> should consider their masters worthy of all honor, <margin>1</margin> lest the name of God and the doctrine be spoken of poorly. Those who <margin>2</margin> have believing masters should not despise them because they are brothers: <margin>B</margin> but rather serve them, because they are faithful and beloved, <margin>2</margin> who are partakers of the benefit. These things teach and exhort. <margin>3</margin> If anyone follows a different doctrine and does not <margin>3</margin> approach the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the doctrine which is according to godliness, <margin>4</margin> he is puffed up, <margin>4</margin> knowing nothing, but is insane regarding questions and battles of words, <margin>7</margin> from which is born envy, contention, evil-speaking, bad suspicions, <margin>8</margin> useless conflicts of <margin>5</margin> men of corrupt minds <margin>9</margin> and those from whom truth has been taken away, who think that <margin>10</margin> godliness is a source of gain. Separate yourself from those who are like this. But godliness is a great gain, <margin>11</margin> with a mind content with <margin>6</margin> its lot. For we brought nothing <margin>12</margin> into the world, <margin>13</margin> and it is clear we can carry nothing out: But having <margin>8</margin> <margin>C</margin> <margin>14</margin> food and things to cover us, <margin>15</margin> with these we shall be content. But those who wish to be rich fall into temptation, <margin>16</margin> and a snare, and many foolish <margin>17</margin> desires...

---

*against those Scholastic theologians, who, not content with the things that are necessary to learn, waste their entire lives, poor wretches, in their most foolish subtleties and labyrinths of nothingness. However, do not take this as an insult to their order, as some are wont to do; it is said of the few who are unworthy of a most honorable order, who go about with a perpetual itch for frivolous questions and do absolutely nothing else through their whole lives. And would that theologians might so temper their studies that there would be no one of whom these things could truly be said. Paul elegantly used a single word for "battles of words,"* <note>original: "λογομαχίας"</note>, *while those men boast that they are entirely focused on "realities."*

**7 From which arise** ] Paul put "envy" and "contention" in the singular number, and Ambrose did the same.

<margin>D</margin> **8 Evil conflicts** ] <note>original: "Παραδιατριβαί"</note>. The Greeks refer "evil" to the "suspicions." And Theophylact, in his commentary, separates this particle from the things that follow: for the word that follows, *paradiatribai*, sounds negative in itself because of the prefix *para-*, which often has that effect, as in "being out of one's mind" (*paraphronein*), "being delivered over" (*paradidosthai*), or "being paralyzed" (*paralyein*). The Greeks called the meetings and discussions of philosophers "diatribes," which Paul here makes useless and irrelevant to the matter by adding the prefix. The Greek scholia suggest a metaphor taken from mangy sheep, which communicate their disease by mutual friction and contact. So too Theophylact says: *Paradiatribai, that is, useless schools; for it is the custom to call schools diatribes; or because just as mangy sheep, by rubbing against a healthy one, transmit the disease to it; so also these men, by rubbing against others, corrupt them.* Almost the same words are found in Chrysostom. In some copies, it was written *diaparatribai*. The Greeks here interpret "evil suspicions" as false and invented opinions, which fits with the empty conflicts.

**9 [They are] deprived of the truth** ] <note>original: "ἀπεστερημένων τῆς ἀληθείας"</note>. Ambrose reads, "and who have lacked the truth." The Greek sounds more forceful: "from whom the truth has been snatched away," according to that saying of Publilius: *By too much wrangling, the truth is lost.* Regarding "piety" (*Eusebeian*), Ambrose, after saying "piety," adds as if interpreting: "the culture of God."

**10 That godliness is a source of gain** ] After these words, I found among the Greeks: *Withdraw from such people,* <note>original: "Ἀφίστασο ἀπὸ τῶν τοιούτων"</note>. Ambrose also says, "Depart from such as these." Yet this is not found in the common Latin copies. Nevertheless, Theophylact reads and interprets it, following Chrysostom.

**11 With sufficiency** ] <note>original: "μετ᾿ αὐταρκείας"</note>. That word means when someone is content with his lot and desires nothing else.

**12 Into this world** ] He adds "this" in his usual way, which is not in the Greek.

**13 No doubt that** ] <note>original: "δηλονότι"</note>. This is an affirmative. He would have more fully rendered the affinity of the Greek words "clear" (*clarum*) and "evident" (*eudelon*) if he had used "bring in" and "carry out."

**14 And food** ] <note>original: "διατροφάς"</note>. Cyprian, explaining the Lord's Prayer, translates this as "exhibition" <note>term: exhibition - in a legal or ecclesiastical sense, a maintenance allowance or stipend</note>, that is, what they call a "prebend," coming closer to Paul's sense than the one who translates it as "food."

**15 With these let us be content** ] <note>original: "ἀρκεσθησόμεθα"</note>, that is, *we shall be content.* The translator read *arkesthesometha* <note>Erasmus notes a grammatical tense/mood variation in the Greek</note>.

**16 And into the snare of the Devil** ] "Of the Devil" is not in the Greek, nor is it added in Ambrose. Hence it is likely it was added by someone from the preceding verses who wished to interpret this passage.

**17 And by snares** ] The conjunction is redundant and is not uselessly present among the Greeks.

<summary>In this passage, Paul advises Timothy on personal health and social conduct, notably instructing slaves to honor their masters. Erasmus uses the text to launch a sharp critique of Scholastic theologians, comparing their pointless debates to mangy sheep spreading disease.</summary>
<keywords>Timothy, wine for the stomach, slavery, contentment, Scholasticism, battles of words, greed, greed for gain, mangy sheep metaphor, Greek vs Latin translation</keywords>

# TO TIMOTHY I. CHAPTER VI.

<margin>9</margin> ...foolish and harmful [desires], which drown men <margin>10</margin> in ruin and destruction. For the love of money is the root of all evils; which some, reaching after, have wandered away from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows. <margin>11</margin> But you, O man of God, flee these things; and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, and gentleness. <margin>12</margin> Fight the good fight of faith; lay hold of eternal life, to which you were also called, and have confessed the good confession before many witnesses. <margin>13</margin> I charge you in the sight of God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who witnessed the good confession under Pontius Pilate, <margin>14</margin> that you keep the commandment without spot and blameless until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, <margin>15</margin> which he will show in his own time—he who is the blessed and only Potentate, the King of kings and Lord of lords, <margin>16</margin> who alone has immortality, dwelling in unapproachable light, whom no man has seen nor can see, to whom be honor and eternal power. Amen. <margin>17</margin> Charge those who are rich in this present age not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who provides us richly with all things to enjoy; <margin>18</margin> to do good, to be rich in good works, to be ready to distribute, <margin>19</margin> willing to share, storing up for themselves a foundation...

---

<margin>A</margin> **Harmful** ] <note>original: "βλαβεράς"</note>, that is, foolish: although the Translator <note>The Vulgate</note> seems to have read <note>original: "ἀνοήτους"</note> <gloss>senseless</gloss>, as did Ambrose.
18 **Which drown** ] <note>original: "βυθίζουσι"</note>, that is, they submerge into the depths.
19 **And greed** ] <note>original: "ἡ φιλαργυρία"</note>, that is, the pursuit of money. Ambrose reads "avarice." Otherwise, greed can also be for other things, such as glory, power, pleasure, or revenge.
20 **Which some, reaching after** ] Here Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a Renaissance humanist</note> raises a subtle point: what does the word "which" refer to? Does it refer to greed? For who is said to "reach after" greed? Rather, they reach for money, which is included in this word <note>original: "φιλαργυρίας"</note> <gloss>love of money</gloss>. Indeed, among the Latins, there is no word here that has "money" included within it; we must accept what Lorenzo indicates regarding the Greek. But in "love of money," what is included? Is it silver or money? How then does the feminine article <note>original: "ἧς"</note> <gloss>of which</gloss> agree? Here, Lorenzo has surely made a human error. However, those who devote themselves to it are said to "reach after" the pursuit of money.
21 **Wandered from the faith** ] <note>original: "ἀπεπλανήθησαν"</note>, that is, they strayed away.
22 **Patience, gentleness** ] <note>original: "πρᾳότητα"</note>. Ambrose translates this as "tranquility of mind."
23 **Of faith** ] It seemed cold or redundant if Paul were to command "faith" to the man he had made a Bishop—that is, a teacher of the faith. Therefore, Theophylact suggests that by the word "faith," Paul excludes quarrelsome questions which he wants Timothy to reject. For faith does not require human subtelty.
24 **To which you were called** ] To which: <note>original: "εἰς ἥν"</note>. Ambrose uses "Toward which." The Greeks add "and": "to which you **also** were called," though "also" is not added in Theophylact's version.
25 **Without spot** ] <note>original: "ἄσπιλον"</note>, that is, immaculate; and this refers to Timothy himself, not to the commandment—meaning, that you keep the commandment while being yourself immaculate and irreproachable. Ambrose, however, refers it to the commandment, provided his manuscript is free of error; Chrysostom does the same, though the phrasing of the context disagreed with his commentary. Although the Greek language does not forbid the adjective from being referred to the "precept" <note>the commandment</note>. Even if you refer "without spot" and "blameless" to the commandment, there remains some ambiguity. For if you refer it to the one *keeping* it, the sense is "do not stain the commandment by your own fault." If you refer it to the commandment itself, it means "keep the commandment which knows no stain or reproach," unlike the precepts of the false apostles. Yet the lack of a Greek article speaks against this sense; it should rather have said, "the commandment, the one without spot."
26 **Until the appearing** ] <note>original: "μέχρι τῆς ἐπιφανείας"</note>, that is, until the manifestation or the shining forth. I would certainly prefer this, because it follows: "Which he will show." What will he show? Surely the glory of his Son, which he had previously exhibited in humility.
27 **Which in his own times** ] "Which" refers to the "appearing," not to Christ; this is clear from the Greek.
28 **Blessed and only Potentate** ] <note>original: "ὁ μακάριος"</note>. The Greek article carries an emphasis which we have rendered by adding a pronoun: "that blessed one." The Greek word is derived from immunity to corruption, which Homer also attributes to the gods: <note>original: "μακάρεσιοι θεοῖσι"</note> <gloss>the blessed gods</gloss>. Nor is <note>original: "δυνάστης"</note> simply "powerful," but rather a substantive title meaning "governor and prince of the state." The Apostle, as if explaining this word, adds "King of kings and Lord of lords." Those who hold the state by power are called "Potentates" <note>original: "Δυνάται"</note>, which is proper to God, who is subject to no laws. "King" <note>original: "Βασιλεὺς"</note> is said to come from providence, as if <note>original: "πάνυ λεύων"</note> <gloss>all-watching</gloss>, because he looks out for everyone. And this uniquely suits God. "Lord" <note>original: "Κύριος"</note> is a name of authority. For no one can rescind what has pleased God.
29 **King of Kings** ] In Greek it is "of those reigning": <note>original: "τῶν βασιλευόντων"</note>. For some "act as kings" rather than truly being Kings. Theophylact applies all these things to the person of the Son; but Ambrose, in my opinion, more correctly applies them to the Father. This is clear from these words: "Not because the Son is a different light, since it is written in the Psalm, 'And in your light we shall see light.'" This means the light of the Father is in the Son; but because no one sees the Father, he therefore "dwells in unapproachable light." For there is no order for anyone seeing the Father except for Christ, who is from God; he has seen God. The Son, 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...foolish and harmful, 18 which drown men in destruction and ruin. Since the root of all evils <margin>10</margin> is 19 the pursuit of money, 20 which some, while they reach for it, 21 have wandered from the faith, and entangled themselves in many sorrows. But you, man of God, flee these things: pursue <margin>11</margin> righteousness, godliness, faith, charity, 22 patience, gentleness. Fight the good fight <margin>12</margin> 23 of faith: lay hold of eternal life, 24 to which you were also called, and have professed the good profession before many witnesses. I charge you in the sight of God, who <margin>13</margin> gives life to all things, and Jesus Christ, who bore witness under <margin>B</margin> Pontius Pilate to the good profession, That you keep the precept <margin>14</margin> 25 immaculate and irreproachable, 26 until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, 27 Which <margin>15</margin> in his own times 28 that blessed and only Prince will show, 29 King of those reigning, and Lord of those dominating, Who alone has immortality, inhabit-<margin>16</margin> ing unapproachable light, whom no man has seen, nor can see, to whom be honor and 30 everlasting power. Amen. 31 Charge those who are rich in the present age, <margin>17</margin> 32 not to be high-minded, nor to place their hope 33 in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who provides 34 us with all things abundantly for our enjoyment, 35 That they do good, <margin>18</margin> <margin>C</margin> that they be rich in good works, 36 that they be ready to distribute, willingly sharing, 37 Storing <margin>19</margin> up...

---

...however, because he himself performs all things, is said both to appear and to be seen. That other quality, therefore, is peculiar to the Father, as was said above. What Chrysostom wrote is uncertain; certainly his verses seem to contradict themselves at first glance. For in the beginning he asks: of whom are these things said? Of the Father, or of the Son? Of the Son, of course, whom He—the Father—will show, he says, in his times, etc. And a little later, as if having forgotten himself, he moves another question: "Who alone," he says, "has immortality." What then? Does the Son not have it? From these words it is plain that Chrysostom applied what was said to the Father; otherwise the question would be absurd. But more closely, Chrysostom hints in the first question not at who is *showing*, but who is to be *shown*. The Father shows, the Son is shown. <margin>D</margin> Theophylact admits that Chrysostom attributes these things principally to the Father, although they are common to both the Son and the Holy Spirit. Thomas Aquinas follows this and explains it as the Trinity. I do not dispute the truth of the theological opinion, but rather the custom of Gospel and Apostolic speech. For when in other places such things are attributed to the Father as if proper to him, without insult to the Son or Holy Spirit, why do we twist them here to refer to the Trinity? For the Son is not therefore *not* eternal because eternity is attributed to the Father as a peculiar notion; nor is the Father therefore *not* wise because wisdom is ascribed to the Son; nor is the Son therefore *not* good because goodness is attributed to the Holy Spirit. But in Holy Scripture, they have their own certain way of speaking. All things are referred to the Father as the author: from him is immortality, life, and light. Now, at the beginning of this discourse, a distinction of persons was made: "I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who rendered testimony," etc. <margin>E</margin> He pursues this: for what he says—"until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ"—pertains to the Son; and what immediately follows—"Which coming he will show," that is, he will illuminate—pertains to the Father. Since the Father is invisible, he shows his majesty in the Son. In the first coming, the Son obeyed the Father even unto death, and under Pontius Pilate made the good profession; in the second coming, the Father will exhibit him as glorious and equal to himself. And in the doxology of the Mass, the Son is said to be "in the glory of God the Father." And in the Gospel, "No one has seen or known God except the Son." Similarly, in the appendix to the Epistle to the Romans, God is called "the only wise God," even while mention is made there of the Son, the "preaching of Jesus Christ," and immediately after, "through Jesus Christ." Finally, since Paul so many times by name calls the Father "God" and the Son only "Lord," and no one is offended, why do we tremble here at the custom of mystical speech? <margin>F</margin> Here I am forced to long for the candor of Christian charity in some; we hear with fair ears that the Father alone is immortal, yet we attack it if anyone says, in a pious sense, that only Christ was entirely foreign to every contagion of sin.
30 **Everlasting** ] <note>original: "in sempiternum"</note> in the superscript. And <note>original: "κράτος"</note> also signifies power or empire. Hence Ambrose reads "power" instead of "empire."
31 **To the rich of this age** ] <note>original: "τοῖς πλουσίοις ἐν τῷ νῦν αἰῶνι"</note>, that is, to those who are wealthy in the present world.
32 **Not to be high-minded** ] <note>original: "ὑψηλοφρονεῖν"</note>: which Ambrose translates as "to think proudly." It means to be of an elated mind and to think arrogantly of oneself.
33 **In the uncertainty of riches** ] <note>original: "ἐπὶ πλούτῳ ἀδηλότητι"</note>, that is, in the instability of wealth.
34 **Us all things abundantly** ] <note>original: "πλουσίως"</note>. Again, the Translator failed to render the playfulness found in the affinity of the words: <note>original: "πλούτῳ"</note> <gloss>wealth</gloss> and <note>original: "πλουσίως"</note> <gloss>wealthily</gloss>, as if you were to say "by riches and richly," or "by opulence and opulently."
35 **To do good** ] <note>original: "Ἀγαθοεργεῖν"</note>, the word is composed of "good" and "work," as if you said, "To work well." I wonder what Saint Ambrose read, who rendered this passage in this way: "in the will of good works," unless perhaps he read <note>original: "θελήσει ἔργων"</note>.
36 **To give easily** ] <note>original: "εὐμεταδότους εἶναι"</note>, that is, to be easy in imparting. So Ambrose reads, except that he omitted "to be."
37 **To treasure up** ] <note>original: "Ἀποθησαυρίζοντας ἑαυτοῖς"</note>, that is, laying up or storing up for themselves.

<margin>C</margin>
38 **And the true path** ] <note>original: *Et veram viam*</note> In the Greek it is "eternal life" <note>original: *æternam vitam*</note>. Ambrose <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Milan and influential theologian.</note>, however, reads and interprets it as "true life" <note>original: *veram vitam*</note>. On the other hand, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an early Church Father known for his preaching.</note> reads "eternal," yet adds nothing in his interpretation from which it might be certain what he actually read. Theophylact <note>A Byzantine archbishop and biblical commentator.</note> without controversy reads "of eternal life" <note>original: *τῆς αἰωνίου ζωῆς*</note>; even if he does not touch upon it while explaining, it does not matter much, since there is no other true life except immortal life. For the life of the wicked is death, and this life, which must soon end, is a course toward death.

39 **Guard the deposit** ] <note>original: *παρακαταθήκην*</note>, that is, that which has been committed to you. He means this doctrine, which he had also commended to him in the beginning. And so the Greek scholia <note>Ancient marginal comments or explanatory notes in manuscripts.</note> explain it. For he does not want anything added to what was handed down.

40 **Novelties of words** ] <note>original: *κενοφωνίας*</note>, that is, vanities of words. Ambrose and the Translator seem to have read "novelties of words" <note>original: *καινοφωνίας*, meaning 'new sounds' rather than 'empty sounds'.</note>. Although the Greek scholia read it with an *e* <note>meaning *kenophonias* or 'empty sounds'.</note>. For he is not dealing here with the inventing of new words, but with useless disputations. It is not clear from Chrysostom’s interpretation what he read. Theophylact reads and interprets "empty sounds" <note>original: *κενοφωνίας*</note>, that is, "foolish talk" <note>original: *ματαιολογίας*</note>; yet he does not hide the fact that Chrysostom

<column-break/>

seems to have read "novelties" <note>original: *καινοφωνίας*</note> with the *ai* diphthong. He adds "seems," because, as we have said, it is not clear from his explanation what he read.

41 **Of a false name** ] <note>original: *ψευδωνύμου γνώσεως*</note>, as if you were to say, "of knowledge falsely named." For it is not knowledge where faith is not present. And all these things fit marvelously well with certain "thorny" theologians <note>Erasmus’s frequent nickname for the Scholastic theologians of his day, whom he accused of over-complicating simple faith with logic-chopping.</note>. For I do not speak of everyone, and perhaps none of them will be like that. And he aptly said "oppositions" <note>original: *ἀντιθέσεις*</note>: because among those men, there is a marvelous sword-fight <note>Metaphorical for fierce academic debate.</note> over every single matter.

42 **Promising** ] <note>original: *ἐπαγγελλόμενοι*</note>. Why not rather "professing" <note>original: *profitentes*</note>?

43 **Regarding the faith they have fallen away** ] <note>original: *ἠστόχησαν*</note>, that is, "they have wandered" <note>original: *aberraverunt*</note>: just as he translated it before. It refers to those who stray from the target. Jerome <note>The translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note>, in the second dialogue against the Pelagians, translates it as "they have erred."

44 **Grace be with you** ] Paul wrote this with his own hand, as Ambrose believes.

<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of the First Epistle to Timothy to the introductory materials for the Second Epistle. It includes a traditional Greek summary (Hypothesis) followed by a Latin preface (Argumentum) authored by the Renaissance humanist Erasmus of Rotterdam.</meta>

# SUMMARY <note>original: ΥΠΟΘΕΣΙΣ; a traditional introductory summary common in ancient manuscripts.</note>
->of the<-
## SECOND EPISTLE
### TO TIMOTHY.

Paul sends this letter again from Rome. The occasion for the Epistle is as follows: Since those who were traveling with Paul had abandoned him, and the Apostle himself wished for Timothy to come to him, he writes this Epistle. First, he indicates that he remembers Timothy's piety and the faith of his ancestors. Then, he makes it clear that those from Asia, including Phygellus and Hermogenes, turned away from him when they saw his chains. He testifies only to the diligence of Onesiphorus, whom he welcomed after he arrived in Rome and remained with him. Paul instructs Timothy to avoid foolish disputes, as they only give birth to battles. Indeed, Hymenaeus and Philetus, having turned aside in this way, transgressed the truth by claiming the resurrection has already happened, thereby subverting the faith of some. Therefore, Paul exhorts Timothy to pay close attention to himself and to his teaching, and to realize that in the last times men will be lovers of self and lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God. Foreseeing these things, Timothy is to secure the people so that none of them may be deceived, both in their personal character and in the accuracy of their doctrine. After encouraging him in many matters and signaling that the time of his departure <note>original: *analyseos*; a euphemism for death or "loosing the anchor."</note> is at hand—meaning he is about to be poured out as a sacrifice and bear witness as a martyr—he commanded Timothy to come to him quickly, bringing his cloak and his books. He also warned him to guard against Alexander the coppersmith, who had shown much malice toward him; and with this, he concludes the Epistle.

---

->ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO<-
# T I M O T H Y  II.
->*Preface by*<-
## DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'Q' with floral and foliate motifs inside a square border.</image-desc>

Since in the previous Epistle Paul had given Timothy (who was then serving among the Ephesians) hope of his return, but the opportunity to fulfill it was not granted because he was held in chains at Rome, he strengthens him with this letter. He does this so Timothy might not be cast down by the storms of persecution, but might instead prepare his soul for martyrdom following Paul's own example. For he warns that dangerous times are pressing in because of certain people who, under a pretext of godliness, subvert true piety—boasting as if the Christian religion consists in mere words, rather than in the purity of the mind. Then, having testified that the day of his death is imminent and that he has now been abandoned by most, he orders that Timothy, together with Mark, should come to him in Rome in haste. He wrote this at Rome when he was presented a second time before the tribunal of Nero <note>The Roman Emperor notorious for the first state-led persecution of Christians; Paul's "second" appearance suggests a period of release between two Roman imprisonments.</note>.

<vocab>Hypothesis, Preface, Timothy, Paul, Erasmus, Rome, Nero, Ephesus, Phygellus, Hermogenes, Onesiphorus, Hymenaeus, Philetus, Alexander the coppersmith</vocab>

# THE SECOND EPISTLE OF PAUL THE APOSTLE TO TIMOTHY.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>1</margin> PAUL, an Apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, according to the promise of life which is in
<margin>2</margin> Christ Jesus, to Timothy, my beloved child: grace, mercy, peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. <margin>3</margin> I have gratitude toward God, whom I serve from my ancestors with a pure conscience, as I have unceasing remembrance of you in my prayers night and day, <margin>4</margin> Longing to see you, mindful of your tears, so that I may be filled with joy,
<margin>B</margin>
<margin>5</margin> Taking a reminder of the unfeigned faith in you, which dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice; and I am persuaded that it is in you also. <margin>6</margin> For which cause I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands. <margin>7</margin> For God did not give us a spirit of cowardice, but of power, and of love, and of self-control. <margin>8</margin> Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner, but suffer hardship with the Gospel according to the power of God, <margin>9</margin> Who saved us, and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times,
<margin>10</margin> But has now been made manifest through the appearance of our Savior Jesus Christ, who indeed abolished death, and brought life and immortality to light through the Gospel, <margin>11</margin> To which I was appointed a herald and apostle, and a teacher of the nations; <margin>12</margin> For which cause I also suffer these things, but I am not ashamed; for I know whom I have be-

---

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' showing a seated figure with a book.</image-desc>

<margin>1</margin> <gloss>To Timothy my most dear son</gloss> <note>original: "Timotheo charißimo filio"</note>] Here the Greek is not "genuine" <note>original: γνησίῳ (*gnēsiō*)</note> as in the previous letter, but "beloved" <note>original: ἀγαπητῷ (*agapētō*)</note>, that is, "dearly loved."
<margin>2</margin> <gloss>Grace and mercy</gloss>] In the Greek manuscripts the conjunctions are absent; it is simply "grace, mercy, peace."
<margin>3</margin> <gloss>I give thanks</gloss>] The Greek is "I have grace" <note>original: Χάριν ἔχω (*charin echō*)</note>. For Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla (c. 1407–1457), a humanist who pioneered the philological study of the New Testament.</note> prefers it this way. And Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397), an influential Bishop of Milan and Church Father.</note> reads it in that manner. However, Valla not unreasonably doubts whether anyone is said to "have grace toward God" before. For a person is said to "have grace" who has the intention of returning a favor. But one "gives thanks" even if they do not think of returning it, simply declaring a grateful and mindful soul.
<margin>4</margin> <gloss>From my ancestors</gloss>] The Greek is "from ancestors" <note>original: ἀπὸ προγόνων (*apo progonōn*)</note>, that is, from progenitors or forefathers. Ambrose reads "from great-grandfathers" <note>original: "a proavis"</note>. Paul signifies that he was born of those who, in a long series going back, were worshippers of God. The pronoun "my" is redundant in our version, added for the sake of clarifying the matter. The word "progenitors," moreover, encompasses not only parents but also higher ancestors whose names are lost. And "I serve" is not the word for a slave <note>original: δουλεύω (*douleuō*)</note>, but the word for religious service <note>original: λατρεύω (*latreuō*)</note>, that is, "whom I worship." For this too is the meaning of the Greek. He worshipped Him also in Judaism, but with an impure conscience.
<margin>5</margin> <gloss>Recordationem</gloss> <note>meaning "recollection" or "remembrance"</note>] The Greek is "a reminder" <note>original: ὑπόμνησιν (*hypomnēsin*)</note>, that is, a calling to mind, when something is suggested to the memory so that it does not fall into oblivion.
<margin>6</margin> <gloss>Of the faith which is in you not feigned</gloss>] Ambrose says it better: "of the sincere faith which is in you."
<margin>7</margin> <gloss>Your mother Ethnice</gloss>] Eunice, as is found in our most ancient manuscripts, or rather Eunica, a name derived from "victory" <note>From the Greek *nikē*.</note>. It is, however, the name of a little prostitute in Theocritus <note>An ancient Greek poet.</note>. A diligent man named Carnensis interprets "Ethnica" as sounding like "Fortunate" to the Greeks. The one who first translated this read "Euryche," or dreamt up something else <note>Erasmus is criticizing a corruption in the standard Latin Vulgate of his day, which had corrupted the name Eunice into "Ethnice."</note>.
<margin>8</margin> <gloss>I am certain, however, that also in you</gloss>] The Greek is: "I have been persuaded, however, that also in you" <note>original: πέπεισμαι δὲ, ὅτι καὶ ἐν σοί (*pepeismai de, hoti kai en soi*)</note>, namely, that this faith exists. "That also in you." Here in Greek there is a colon, so that you should understand "it dwells."
<margin>9</margin> <gloss>I admonish you</gloss>] The Greek is "I remind you" <note>original: ἀναμιμνήσκω (*anamimnēskō*)</note>, that is, I bring it to your attention, or rather, I bring it back into your memory.
<margin>10</margin> <gloss>Refuscites</gloss> <note>meaning "re-kindle" or "fan into flame"</note>] The Greek is "to stir into fire" <note>original: ἀναζωπυρεῖν (*anazōpyrein*)</note>, which properly means to rouse a fire that is already buried and dormant. Ambrose reads "that you might recreate the gift of God." "The grace of God" is "the gift" <note>original: χάρισμα (*charisma*)</note>. And so Ambrose has it. It is strange that Ambrose, following the Greek manuscript, reads "Do not therefore blush in the testimony of our Lord, nor in me his prisoner." And his interpretation almost declares that it was read this way, in which it is held, "For there is no reason for you to blush in it." Even if we read in the Gospel, "whoever confesses in me, etc." but it is strange that this form of speech was affected here, since it is not found among the Greeks.
<margin>11</margin> <gloss>But of power</gloss>] The Greek is "of power" <note>original: δυνάμεως (*dynameōs*)</note>, that is, of potency, strength, and fortitude. And what he just translated as "fear," in Greek is "cowardice" <note>original: δειλίας (*deilias*)</note>, which also sounds like "laziness" and weakness of soul. Furthermore, for "sobriety" <note>original: σωφρονισμοῦ (*sōphronismou*)</note>, Augustine in *To Boniface* Book IV, Chapter V, reads "continence," and elsewhere often translates it as "chastity." "Sobriety" how-

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>1</margin> PAUL, an Apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, according to the promise of life, which is in Christ Jesus, <margin>2</margin> to Timothy, my beloved child: grace, mercy, peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. <margin>3</margin> I have gratitude toward God, whom I serve from my ancestors with a pure conscience, because without any intermission I make mention of you in my prayers night and day, <margin>4</margin> Longing to see you, mindful of your tears, so that I may be filled with joy, <margin>5</margin> When I shall have been reminded of the unfeigned faith which is in you, which dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice: <margin>B</margin> and I know for certain that it is in you also. <margin>6</margin> For which cause I remind you to stir up the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands. <margin>7</margin> For God did not give us a spirit of timidity, but of power, and of love, and of sobriety. <margin>8</margin> Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor be ashamed of me, who am his prisoner, but be a sharer in the afflictions of the Gospel according to the power of God, <margin>9</margin> Who saved us, and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which indeed was given to us through Christ Jesus before eternal times, <margin>10</margin> But has now been made manifest through the appearance of our Savior Jesus Christ, who indeed abolished death, and brought life to light and immortality through the Gospel, <margin>11</margin> In which I was placed as a herald and apostle, and a teacher of the nations: <margin>C</margin> For which cause I also suffer these things, yet I do not blush: for I know for cer-

---

<margin>C</margin> ever, encompasses more things. For a person is not sane who is held by luxury, sleep, love, hate, or similar emotions.
<margin>12</margin> <gloss>Collabora</gloss> <note>meaning "work together" or "suffer together"</note>] The Greek is "be afflicted together with the Gospel" <note>original: συγκακοπάθησον τῷ Εὐαγγελίῳ (*sygkakopathēson tō Euangeliō*)</note>, that is, be afflicted at the same time as the Gospel, and be a sharer in the afflictions that accompany the preaching of the Gospel.
<margin>13</margin> <gloss>Who delivered us</gloss>] The Greek is "Who saved us" <note>original: Τοῦ σώσαντος ἡμᾶς (*Tou sōsantos hēmas*)</note>, that is, Who made us safe or preserved us. So too Ambrose.
<margin>14</margin> <gloss>By his calling</gloss>] "His" is not in the Greek manuscripts, nor even in several ancient copies, nor in Ambrose, nor in Chrysostom's interpretation: it is simply "with a holy calling." In both copies from Constance "his" was present, without "holy." But "according to works": Ambrose reads "merits" instead of "works."
<margin>15</margin> <gloss>Before secular times</gloss>] The Greek is "eternal" <note>original: αἰωνίων (*aiōniōn*)</note>. For thus he denotes the whole of time which began from the creation of the world. It is a wonder what author Aquinas followed when he said a "secular age" <note>original: *seculum*</note> is a thousand years, since the "Secular Games" were customarily renewed every hundredth year. And he adds that a thousand years is the age of a man, because a man is said to live as long as his memory lasts, but that memory does not stretch beyond a thousand years. But how many thousands of men are there whose memory is more famous now than their life was a thousand years ago? And how rare is the person whose memory lasts even to two hundred years? Moreover, what was the point of mentioning years here, since he is speaking of eternal predestination, which knows no time? How often Paul excludes reliance on works, commending the grace of God: and yet today there are those who, shrinking from this kind of speech, boast of their own good works, not bringing praise to grace or faith with sufficiently fair ears.
<margin>16</margin> <gloss>Through illumination</gloss>] The Greek is "through the appearance" <note>original: διὰ τῆς ἐπιφανείας (*dia tēs epiphaneias*)</note>, which earlier he translated as "advent." Although *epiphaneia* sometimes sounds like "illustration" or "shining forth," just as *epiphainō* means "to illustrate." Yet the Translator did not render the relationship of the Greek words *phōtisantos* <note>"having brought to light"</note> and *epiphaneias* <note>"appearance/shining forth"</note>, as if one were to say, "it was illustrated through the illustration of Jesus Christ."
<margin>17</margin> <gloss>He indeed destroyed death, but illuminated life</gloss>] The Greek is "abolished" <note>original: καταργήσαντος (*katargēsantos*)</note>, that is, who did away with and blotted out; and "brought to light" <note>original: φωτίσαντος (*phōtisantos*)</note>. For he composed these two as if they were in conflict. Death was reigning; its kingdom was revoked. Life lay hidden;
<margin>E</margin> it flashed forth through Christ.
<margin>18</margin> <gloss>In which</gloss>] The Greek is "Into which" <note>original: Εἰς ὃ (*Eis ho*)</note>: namely, the Gospel.
<margin>19</margin> <gloss>Preacher</gloss>] The Greek is "herald" <note>original: κήρυξ (*kēryx*)</note>, rather than "preacher."
<margin>20</margin> <gloss>Master of the nations</gloss>] The Greek is "teacher" <note>original: διδάσκαλος (*didaskalos*)</note>. He claims three things for himself: The Herald publicly announces; the Apostle executes what has been committed to him, concealing nothing; the Teacher gives the reason, so that he may persuade. He attributes this authority to God—"in which I was placed"—and confirms it with the argument, "For which cause also I suffer these things." Now many are teachers by disputing, not by suffering.
<margin>21</margin> <gloss>I will not be confounded</gloss>] The Greek is "do not be ashamed," or "it does not shame me."
<margin>22</margin> <gloss>For I know whom I have believed</gloss>] This is not the sense of the Greek speech—that Paul is not ignorant of whom he has trusted. Rather, this is the meaning: "I know that he, in whom I have believed, is powerful to keep my deposit," I know...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s scholarly examination of the Second Epistle to Timothy. On the previous page, Paul was encouraging Timothy to remain steadfast in the face of suffering. Here, the text concludes Chapter 1 and begins Chapter 2, where Paul uses the metaphors of the soldier, the athlete, and the farmer to describe the Christian life.</meta>

# ON TIMOTHY CHAPTER II.

<margin>13</margin> ...whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able to guard my deposit until 그 day. <margin>13</margin> Have a pattern <note>Greek: *hypotyposin*</note> of sound words, which you heard from me in faith and love, which is in Christ Jesus. <margin>14</margin> <margin>Another hand for 13: "in the indwelling..."</margin> Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit, who dwells in us. <margin>15</margin> You know this, that all those in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Phygellus and Hermogenes. <margin>16</margin> May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain. <margin>17</margin> But when he was in Rome, he sought me out more diligently and found me. <margin>18</margin> May the Lord grant to him to find mercy from the Lord on that day; and how much he served in Ephesus, you know better than I. <margin>II. 1</margin> You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus, <margin>2</margin> and what you heard from me through many witnesses, commit these things to faithful men, who will be capable of teaching others as well. <margin>3</margin> You therefore suffer hardship, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ. <margin>4</margin> No one serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of life, so that he may please the one who enlisted him. <margin>5</margin> And if anyone competes as an athlete, he is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules. <margin>6</margin> It is necessary for the laboring farmer to be the first to partake of the fruits. <margin>7</margin> Think on what I say; for may the Lord give you understanding in all things. <margin>8</margin> Remember Jesus Christ risen from the dead, of the seed of David, according to my Gospel; <margin>9</margin> in which I suffer hardship even to chains, like an evildoer; but the word of God is not bound. <margin>10</margin> Therefore I endure all things for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory. <margin>11</margin> The word is faithful: for if we have died together...

---

...for whom I have believed, and I am persuaded that he is able. <note>original: *γὰρ ᾧ πεπίστευκα, καὶ πέπεισμαι, ὅτι δυνατός ἐστι*</note> For if the former sense were intended, he would not say "to whom" <note>Greek: *ᾧ*</note>, but "whom" <note>Greek: *ὅν*</note>. Although this sense is also possible: "I know him whom I have trusted, and I am certain that he is powerful." Since I have rendered this same sentiment more clearly than the previous Translator <note>referring to the Vulgate</note>, I wonder why a certain person thought this passage should be attacked with great insults, as if I did not understand what Paul meant. Although in the first edition, due to a printer's error, a conjunction was carelessly left behind; in the second place, where we now have "because." In short, whether you read, "I know him whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is powerful," and so on; or joined together, "I know and am certain that he to whom I have believed is powerful," and so on: the meaning remains nearly the same.

<margin>23 Hold the pattern</margin> *Hypotyposin eche*, that is, "Have a form," or "Have a model," which is to say, set a pattern of pious living for others. The Ambrosian reading <note>a reference to commentaries attributed to St. Ambrose</note> in this place differs somewhat from both our version and the Greek: for it reads, "Having the form of sound words, which you heard from me in faith and love, which is in Christ Jesus. Guard the excellent deposit through the Holy Spirit, who dwells in us." And it fits beautifully, just as if "having" were said instead of "guard."

<margin>24 Of sound words</margin> *hygiainontōn*. Whatever the Greeks approve of, they call "healthy" <note>Greek: *hygies*</note>; hence the proverb, "nothing healthy" <note>Greek: *hygiēs ouden hen*</note>, when everything is displeasing. Conversely, when a matter is joined with a fault, they say, "everything is diseased" <note>Greek: *ta panta nosei*</note>: and we bid those in whom we desire a sound mind to "be healthy" <note>Greek: *hygiainein*</note>.

<margin>25 For even this]</margin> The "for" is redundant.

<margin>26 Have turned away from me]</margin> *apestraphēsan me*, that is, they loathed me, or they despised me. Ambrosius reads "loathed," not "turned away." And no one says "he loathed from me": hence I suspect the preposition "from" was added by a scribe.

<margin>27 All who are in Asia]</margin> *pantes hoi en tē Asia*. It can also be read as "were," for the tense is not explicitly expressed in the Greek verbs.

<margin>28 Philetus]</margin> *Phygellos*, that is, Phygellus, and so it is read in very ancient Latin copies, and thus it is cited by Saint Jerome in his Epistle on the vestments of Aaron. And so Ambrosius reads it.

<margin>29 When he had come to Rome]</margin> *genomenos en Rhōmē*, that is, when he was in Rome. And so Ambrosius reads it.

<margin>30 Diligently]</margin> *spoudaioteron*, that is, more studiously. Ambrosius points out a play on words <note>Greek: *prospoiomasia*</note> in "happened" and "struck": he who sought him in afflictions found him; may he who showed mercy also find mercy on the day of judgment.

<margin>31 And how many things at Ephesus]</margin> *kai hosa*, that is, "And in what ways," or "whatever," or rather "in whatever things."

**B**e strengthened] *endynamou*, that is, be strong or robust, or be reinforced. For some deny that the word "confortare" <note>the Vulgate's word</note> is proper Latin.

<margin>2 Labor as]</margin> *Sy oun kakopathēson*, that is, "You therefore bear afflictions": for this is what *kakopathein* means, as we just advised.

<margin>3 No one militating for God]</margin> "For God" is redundant: although it is added in Ambrosius, it is not in the interpretation. In Chrysostom's primary text "for God" is not added, nor does it appear from his commentary that he added it. For Paul uses this simile taken from soldiers, none of whom cares for domestic matters after being bound by the military oath, but carries out the business of his commander. It is much more fitting for him to do so who militates for the Gospel. Furthermore, that these are used as parables is most clearly testified by the interpreter Chrysostom. Theophylactus certainly reads with us "entangles," not "may entangle," and does not add "for God," even if the Translator added it on his own.

<margin>4 Entangles himself]</margin> *empleketai*, that is, is implicated. Although passives of this kind are frequently used with reciprocal pronouns. But those who read "may entangle" in the imperative mood are more corrupt. For he does not command that they should not entangle themselves, but denies that those who involve themselves are militating for God.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> [and am certain, that he to whom I have believed is powerful to guard my deposit until that day. <margin>23</margin> Hold the pattern of sound sermons, which you heard from me with faith and charity, which is in Christ Jesus. Guard the excellent deposit through the Holy Spirit, who dwells in us. <margin>25</margin> You know this, that <margin>26</margin> all who are in Asia have loathed me, among whom is <margin>28</margin> Phygellus and Hermogenes. May the Lord give mercy to the family of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me, and did not blush at my chain: But <margin>29</margin> when he was in Rome, <margin>30</margin> he sought me more studiously, and found me. May the Lord grant him, <margin>B</margin> that he may find mercy with the Lord on that day: <margin>31</margin> and in how many things he ministered at Ephesus, you know better. You therefore, my son, <margin>1</margin> be strong in the grace which is through Christ Jesus, and in these things which you heard from me through many witnesses, commit these to faithful men, who will be fit to teach others also. <margin>2</margin> You therefore bear affliction, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ. <margin>3</margin> No one who militates, <margin>4</margin> is entangled in the businesses of life, so that he may please him who chose him for military service. <margin>5</margin> But if someone also competes, <margin>8</margin> he is not crowned unless he has competed legitimately. <margin>9</margin> It is necessary for the laboring farmer to first receive of the fruits. Think on what I say: <margin>10</margin> for may the Lord give you understanding in all things. Remember that Jesus <margin>C</margin> Christ rose from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my Gospel, <margin>11</margin> in which I am afflicted with evils, <margin>12</margin> like a criminal, even unto chains: but the word of God <margin>13</margin> was not bound. Therefore I suffer all things for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain salvation, which is in Christ Jesus, <margin>14</margin> with eternal glory. <margin>15</margin> A certain word:

<margin>D</margin> <margin>5 In secular businesses]</margin> *tais tou biou pragmateiais*, that is, in the negotiations or occupations of life. Furthermore, *biou* sounds more like "livelihood" than "life." And among Legal Experts, the name "livelihood" includes both food and clothing. He who militates is not anxious about his livelihood; he acts for the sake of victory; the commander provides for the livelihood.

<margin>6 That he may please him to whom he proved himself]</margin> *hina tō stratologēsanti aresē*, that is, so that he may please him who chose him as a soldier; that is, him by whose spirit he was chosen and enrolled into this military service. Perhaps the Translator rendered it "to whom he proved himself," even though Ambrosius reads and even interprets it as "to whom he pledged himself," meaning, as it appears, to whom he bound himself. The interpreter of Chrysostom reads, "who chose him."

<margin>7 For also he who competes in a contest]</margin> *Ean de kai athlē tis*, that is, "But if anyone also competes." This is the verb from which "athletes" are named: for he also draws a simile from them.

<margin>8 He is not crowned]</margin> *ou stephanoutai*, that is, he is not crowned—Ambrosius supporting this—which means it is not enough to compete in any way whatsoever, but one must compete so that you win. The very ancient Codex Constantiensis supported this.

<margin>9 The laboring farmer]</margin> I see that the Greek Interpreters also hesitate somewhat in this place, but in my opinion, the slightly disturbed order of the language has brought obscurity to the speech. This will be removed if "laboring" <note>Greek: *kopiōnta*</note> is in the past tense, and the adverb "first" <note>Greek: *prōton*</note>—that is, "previously"—depends on it, and not on the infinite verb which follows, "to receive." So that we may arrange the meaning in this order: "It is necessary for the farmer to receive the fruits, but if he has labored first." For he used three parables: the soldier, the athlete, and the farmer, each of whom, having set aside other cares, diligently performs his duty. Nor is the reward lacking, if each has first performed his office. Indeed, I think Paul meant this, although Ambrosius follows a different opinion, interpreting it to mean that he who is first ought to receive first, and then distribute to the rest. Chrysostom interprets it in two ways. Other athletes do not receive the prize unless victory is won. The farmer, even while he tills the earth, perceives some fruit in the meantime, while expecting a more bounteous harvest in the future. Or for the farmer, since he has commerce with rich and faithful earth, his reward is not withheld; he who cultivates is the first to receive it.

<margin>10 For the Lord will give to you]</margin> In Greek it is not "will give," but *dōē*, that is, "may he give," which is the word of one praying. Chrysostom explains this place openly in that manner, saying that Paul, with paternal affection, does not cease to pray for good things for Timothy, as if fearing for his most dear son. Although the translator of Chrysostom, following our Edition, renders it <margin>F</margin> "will give" instead of "may he give."

<margin>11 In which I labor]</margin> *kakopathō*, that is, I am afflicted, which he almost always translates as "labor" according to his custom. Although I am not unaware that even among the Latins "to labor" is sometimes taken to mean the same as being occupied in difficult circumstances.

<margin>12 As one doing evil]</margin> *hōs kakourgos*, that is, as a malefactor or a criminal. I wonder what example Ambrosius followed when he rendered it "as a thief." For there is nothing similar in *kakourgos* and *lēstēs* <note>thief/brigand</note>, which sounds more like a criminal. Although in the Gospel this Translator constantly renders *kakourgos* as "thieves," as we indicated there.

<margin>13 It is not bound]</margin> *ou dedetai*, that is, it was not bound. There is, moreover, a playful allusion in the Greek words *desmois* <note>chains</note> and *dedetai* <note>has been bound</note>, that is, chains and "it was bound."

<margin>14 With heavenly glory]</margin> *aiōniou*, that is, eternal. The Translator and Ambrosius seem to have read *ouraniou* <note>heavenly</note>.

<margin>15 A faithful word]</margin> Again it is "A faithful word" <note>Greek: *Pistos ho logos*</note>. Paul, according to his custom, puts these words first when he is about to say something certain and indubitable, or he adds them, as if confirming what he said with an assertion. Although they are not added in Ambrosius in this place.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s annotations on the Second Epistle to Timothy. On the previous page, Paul encouraged Timothy to endure hardship like a soldier. This page focuses on Chapter 2, verses 11–19, where Paul warns against "word-battles" and "profane babblings," urging Timothy instead to "rightly divide" the word of truth. Erasmus uses these verses to critique the overly complex and aggressive theological disputes of his own time.</meta>

# EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER II.

11. ...we died with him, we shall also live with him;
12. If we endure, we shall also reign with him; if we deny him, he also will deny us;
13. If we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself.
14. Remind them of these things, testifying before the Lord, not to engage in word-battles <note>Greek: *logomachein*</note>, which is useful for nothing, but leads to the ruin of the listeners.
15. Be diligent to present yourself approved to God, a worker who does not need to be ashamed, rightly handling <note>Greek: *orthotomounta*, literally "cutting straight"</note> the word of truth.
16. But avoid profane and empty babblings; for they will progress to even more ungodliness,
17. And their talk will spread like gangrene; of whom are Hymenæus and Philetus,
18. Who have strayed concerning the truth, saying that the resurrection has already happened, and they subvert the faith of some.
19. Nevertheless, the solid foundation of God stands, having this seal: "The Lord knows those who are his," and, "Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity."

---

16 **If we have denied**] <note>original: "εἱ ἀρνήσαμεθα"</note> that is, *if we deny*, which is the same mood he used in the preceding phrases.
17 **If we do not believe, he is faithful**] In this place, the affinity of the Greek words was not preserved: <note>original: "ἀπιστοῦμεν, πιστὸς"</note>, that is, *we are untrusting, he is faithful*, or *trustworthy*.
18 **Do not contend in words**] <note>original: "λογομαχεῖν"</note>, a compound word, that is, *to fight with words*: a word related to the noun he previously translated as *word-fights*.
19 **For it is useful for nothing**] <note>original: "εἰς οὐδὲν χρήσιμον"</note>, that is, *to no utility*. By now it should not be new that an adjective is used in place of a noun, unless you prefer to think of this little phrase as being inserted as a parenthesis.
20 **Except to the subversion**] And "except" is redundant: and *to the subversion* refers back to that higher phrase, *do not fight with words*, or as Apuleius says, to be beaten with words; so that the phrase *useful for nothing* is inserted as a parenthesis, if the substantive verb "is" is understood. Although the Translator and Ambrose, to make the sense clearer, added one or two words of their own. The speech should be ordered thus: *Remind them of these things, testifying before the Lord, that they should not follow word-battles, which have no utility, to the subversion of those listening.* Furthermore, as for the infinitive, which the Translator renders as addressed to Timothy, I suspect it might more correctly be applied to everyone else: so that this is the very thing he warns them about through Timothy, that they should not fight among themselves over frivolous little questions, since Christian philosophy is not a sophistical disputation, but a pure life worthy of Christ. Indeed, Paul did not fear this disease in Timothy, but encourages him to despise those who were gripped by such a sickness.
21 **Be diligently careful**] <note>original: "Σπούδασον σεαυτὸν"</note>, that is, *Study yourself*, etc. Augustine reads, *Do enough*, instead of *Study*. And the word "yourself" is not found in the Greek, nor in Ambrose.
22 **To exhibit yourself approved**] <note>original: "δόκιμον"</note>, that is, *approved, or upright*.
23 **A worker who cannot be confounded**] <note>original: "ἀνεπαίσχυντον"</note>, that is, *one who is not put to shame, or does not blush*. Although Ambrose reads, *not un-shamed*. Furthermore, he calls those *un-shamed* who strive in contentions; as if this pertains to contentious disputations, which he calls "word-fights," because in these no one wishes to yield, but each defends his own view with persistence and refutes the other. Augustine, in Book 3 against Cresconius, Chapter 11, reads *not blushing* instead of *unconfoundable*.
24 **Rightly handling**] <note>original: "ὀρθοτομοῦντα"</note>. It sounds as if you would say, *rightly cutting*. And the Greek commentaries advise that the metaphor is taken from an axe or a sword, with which useless and superfluous things are cut away. There is a proverb about the "Tenedian axe" <note>A Greek proverb referring to a swift, harsh judgment or a clean cut</note>, which if anyone reads, he will better understand the sense of this passage. For the speech of truth is cut into when, in such disputations, the truth is lost and becomes entangled in certain thorns. While the ancient orthodox writers interpret it this way with great consensus, it seemed to someone that we should use "cutting" instead of "handling," not at all rebuking what the Translator had used, but explaining more clearly what Paul wrote and felt. Whether *rightly handling* sounds like the Greek *orthotomein* I will not dispute for now; perhaps the Translator had no other words with which to render the Greek. Certainly, no one will understand Ambrose's interpretation unless he grasps the emphasis of the Greek word. I will subscribe his commentary here, since it seems to me useful for more than just this purpose: *Since there are some who say that worldy contention is profitable, the Apostle, knowing it is rather harmful, commands this: that each person should take care that, having despised altercation, he makes himself approved, calling those who strive in contentions "un-shamed." For it is necessary that contention wrings out something, indeed many things, which are said against conscience, so that a man loses within his soul while appearing the victor without. For no one allows himself to be conquered, even if he knows the things he hears are true. But he handles rightly and with a good conscience who speaks to those who are willing and peaceful.* Therefore, there should be a conferring between the servants of God, not an altercation. Thus far Ambrose. What he advises here, Chrysostom advises in many places. As for how far they are from this rule who today tear each other apart with venomous books and tongues—as impiously cruel toward their neighbor as they are shamefully flattering toward Princes—let them see to it themselves. It is certainly clear that Ambrose interprets what it is to *cut rightly*: he who prunes away contentious things and leaves what is peaceful and useful, cuts rightly, having surely amputated those things which are harmful. Chrysostom writes in this manner: *For many people tear the word apart from every side and scatter it, mixing in many harmful sprouts. He does not say "directing," but "rightly handling," as if to say: Ampute whatever adulterated things arise, and other such things; apply yourself with the greatest vehemence so they may be rejected. And just as with straps and thongs, cut away everything superfluous and alien to the proclamation with the sword of the spirit.* Thus far Chrysostom. Theophylact harmonizes with him: *Rightly handling the word of truth: Although, he says, many...*
<meta>catchword: many</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> 11. ...for if we have died together, we will also live together:
12. If we suffer together, we will also reign together: if we deny, he also will deny us:
13. If we are unfaithful, he remains faithful, he cannot deny himself.
14. Remind them of these things, testifying before the Lord, that they should not follow word-battles, to no utility, to the subversion of those hearing.
15. Study to exhibit yourself approved to God, a worker not to be blushed at, rightly cutting the word of truth.
16. But pass over profane vanities of words: for they will progress to greater ungodliness,
<margin>B</margin> 17. And their speech will have a spreading like a cancerous disease: in whose number is Hymenæus and Philetus,
18. Who have strayed concerning the truth, saying the resurrection has already happened, and they subvert the faith of some.
19. Nevertheless the solid foundation of God stands, having this seal, The Lord knows who are his: and, Let everyone who names depart from iniquity...

---

<margin>C</margin> ...vary that word and translate it elsewhere, you nevertheless handle that very thing rightly. Or "handle," he says, that is, direct, and prune around all useless things, and remove with the sword of the word those things which are alien to the preaching of the Gospel.* Nor does the <term>Gloss</term> <note>The "Glossa Ordinaria," a standard medieval commentary on the Bible</note> shrink from this, which is inserted in the Rhapsody (which for I know not what reason they call "ordinary") in the space separating the verses; it reads thus, perhaps extracted from Bede’s Commentaries: *According to the suitability of each individual, just as you distribute spiritual things to the mature, distribute milk to the little ones.* We see that everyone explains the emphasis of the Greek word, which is said to come from "cutting," although to none of the Latins does "to handle" mean "to cut." But Greek volumes are called *Tomoi*, which the Latins call *Tractatus* (Treatises). I admit this, but *Tomoi* are named from "cutting," because formerly they were written on skins, trimmed for this purpose so they could be rolled onto a rod. But those things which are disputed in words are also "handled."
25 **But profane**] <note>original: "βεβήλους"</note>. Which word he translated above as *unsuitable*. And *empty talk*. The conjunction "and" is redundant: <note>original: "κενοφωνίας"</note>, that is, *empty voices*: the same word which he translated above as *novelties of voices*. And in this place also Ambrose reads *novelties* for "empty voices," with Chrysostom also agreeing. Furthermore, *kenophonias* could be translated as *empty-speech*. Indeed, here the Translator translated it well. Two manuscripts from Constance and others less corrupted still retain the genuine reading.
<margin>D</margin> 26 **Avoid**] <note>original: "περιΐστασο"</note>. Although this might mean *cut off*, nevertheless since the Greek preposition is of a dual nature, you would better translate it in this place as *stay away from*, or *pass over*. The Greek commentaries explain it two ways: either *reject*, or *press on vehemently so that they are coerced*. For it is opposed to what he had just said, *orthotomounta*, rightly cutting and judging, with superfluous altercations rejected and cut back—those by which lawsuits are not finished, but nourished and increased. And Ambrose warns that the disputations of Christians ought to be conferrings, not altercations. And Chrysostom is everywhere annoyed with this race of men; and yet he had not yet heard our disputations about <term>filiations</term>, about <term>relations</term>, about <term>instants</term> <note>Technical terms used in Scholastic logic and theology which Erasmus found overly pedantic</note>—not to add anything that could be said more justly, but more dangerously.
<margin>E</margin> 27 **They will progress to ungodliness**] <note>original: "προκόψουσιν"</note>, that is, *they will progress*, in the future tense, and so Ambrose reads it, supported by ancient copies: nor is it so much "much" as "more." Furthermore, when he says *empty-speech progresses to ungodliness*, Paul does not entirely mean what the Latin words perhaps sound like—that these kinds of discussions lead us to ungodliness. Rather, he means that the more these kinds of discussions are admitted, the more they crawl and grow toward a greater ungodliness, with contentions of the wavering person spreading daily: <note>original: "ἐπὶ πλεῖον ἀσεβείας"</note>, that is, *toward greater ungodliness*. And in this way the Greek commentaries interpret it, and those things which follow agree perfectly.
28 **Will creep like a cancer**] Cancer in this place is the disease <note>original: "γάγγραινα"</note> (gangrene). Let no one think of the animal in this place. "It creeps," <note>original: "νομὴν ἕξει"</note>, that is, *it will have a spreading*, so that it agrees with the verb "it will progress," which is in the future tense. Furthermore, that disease consumes the place it has occupied, whence it must be fended off immediately.
29 **Who have fallen away from the truth**] <note>original: "περὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἠστόχησαν"</note>, that is, *they have wandered concerning the truth*, about which verb we warned above. For one "misses the mark" <note>Greek: *astochei*</note> who does not reach what he intended to reach, such as a target or something similar.
30 **And they subvert**] <note>original: "ἀνατρέπουσι"</note>, that is, *they subvert*. For they were still persisting in their perverse zeal. So Augustine cites it in Book 13 against Faustus, Chapter 11, according to the text of an ancient hand-written volume which the honorable College of Canons of St. Martin at Leuven showed us.
<margin>F</margin> 31 **The Lord knew**] This appears to be added as an example of a seal, which Chrysostom clearly declares, and Theophylact, gladly agreeing with him, explains this passage. Whence it fits less well what is read in the Ambrosian codices, *For the Lord knew*. Although Augustine relates it in the same way in the book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, Chapter 11. And Chrysostom thinks this testimony is taken from the book of Deuteronomy, which however does nothing to hinder our annotation. *Those who are his*, <note>original: "τοὺς ὄντας αὑτοῦ"</note>, that is, *those who are his own*. And so Saint Jerome cites it in his commentary on Zechariah. It is tolerable that Ambrose reads in the *First Epistle*, *The Lord knew those who are his*: which himself comes very close to the nature of a reciprocal pronoun.
32 **And departs**] *Let him depart*, <note>original: "Ἀποστήτω"</note>. And so Ambrose reads, and even Aquinas himself, with the ancient copies agreeing.
33 **Who calls upon the name**] <note>original: "ὁ ὀνομάζων τὸ ὄνομα"</note>, that is, *he who names the name*, just as the ancient codices also have. Indeed, in the Pauline manuscript, an evident erasure testifies that something else had been written.
<meta>catchword: And</meta>

<summary>In this section of his annotations, Erasmus examines Paul's instructions to Timothy regarding the "handling" of truth and the avoidance of "empty babblings." He argues that the Greek term for "rightly dividing" implies cutting away superfluous and contentious arguments to reach a pure Christian life, a point he uses to critique the pedantic Scholastic theology of his own day.</summary>
