<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s annotations on the Second Epistle to Timothy. On the previous page, Paul encouraged Timothy to avoid "word-battles" and "profane babblings." Here, Erasmus examines the metaphor of "vessels" in a great house and the specific vices Paul warns will appear in the "last days," using linguistic analysis to sharpen the moral distinctions in the text.</meta>

# TO TIMOTHY II. CAP. II. III.

<margin>20</margin> names the name of the Lord. In a large house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay; some for honor, and some for <margin>21</margin> dishonor. If anyone therefore cleanses himself from these, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, useful to the master, prepared for every good <margin>22</margin> work. Flee youthful lusts; but pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, with those who call upon the Lord from a pure heart. But refuse <margin>23</margin> foolish and unlearned questions, knowing that they breed strife. <margin>24</margin> And the servant of the Lord must not fight, but be gentle toward <margin>25</margin> all, apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those who oppose him, if perhaps God may give them repentance to the knowledge <margin>26</margin> of the truth, and that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, having been taken captive by him for <margin>III. 1</margin> his will. But know this: that in the last days perilous times will <margin>2</margin> come. For men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, <margin>3</margin> unholy, without natural affection, truce-breakers, slanderers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of <margin>4</margin> good, traitors, headstrong, puffed up, lovers of pleasure rather <margin>5</margin> than lovers of God, having a form of godliness, but denying its power. And from these—

---

And in the Donatian manuscript it was written without erasure, "who names the name of the <term>Lord</term>." <note>original: "Domini"</note> Constantine supports both readings. Theophylactus <note>A 12th-century Byzantine archbishop known for his biblical commentaries.</note> both reads and explains the name <term>names</term>, although the Latin Translator has consistently inserted <term>invokes</term> for <term>names</term>. Augustine, in the passage we just cited, records "who invokes the name of the <term>Lord</term>." Although in certain Greek copies <term>of Christ</term> <note>original: "Χριστοῦ"</note> had been added, and Chrysostom reads it thus, unless it is an error. For Theophylactus reads <term>of the Lord</term>, which I find more probable. For no one acknowledges <term>lordship</term> <note>original: "dominium"</note> except his servant. In other words, the Apostle referred to the sentiment found in 1 Corinthians chapter 12: <term>No one can say "Jesus is Lord" except in the Holy Spirit</term>.

34 <term>And some indeed unto honor</term>] It was clearer to say, <term>those indeed unto honor</term>, but these unto ignominy: so that "these" refers to the nearest items, namely the wooden and clay vessels, and "those" to the gold and silver. For the Greeks are careful with the specificity of such pronouns. If the Translator had wanted to render the beauty of the figure, he should have said, <term>for grace and disgrace</term> <note>original: "τιμὴν, ἀτιμίαν"</note>.

35 <term>If anyone therefore cleanses himself</term>] <note>original: "ἐκκαθάρῃ"</note>. Chrysostom notes the preposition of the word, as if *thoroughly cleansing* <note>original: "ἐκκαθάρῃ"</note> is more than simply *cleansing* <note>original: "κάθῃ"</note>.

36 <term>And useful to the master</term>] "And" is redundant: <note>original: "εὔχρηστον τῷ δεσπότῃ"</note>, which means <term>well-suited for the master's uses</term>.

37 <term>Prepared for every good work</term>] <term>Prepared</term> in this place is a participle <note>original: "ἡτοιμασμένον"</note>. So you may understand it not as merely "ready," but as something made ready by the Lord for this use.

38 <term>Faith, hope</term>] <term>Hope</term> is neither in the Greek, nor in the ancient Latin manuscripts, nor in Ambrose, nor in Theophylactus, nor in Chrysostom—whether you look at the context or examine the interpretation. It is not even in the Donatian manuscript, which we consulted for the third Edition. Nor in the two sent from Constance. Ambrose, with the Greeks, places only three: <term>faith, charity, and peace</term>. Faith excludes ambitious disputes, charity does not seek its own, and from these, peace is nourished. And "peace." Here the conjunction "and" is also redundant.

39 <term>Questions without discipline</term>] <note>original: "ἀπαιδεύτους ζητήσεις"</note>, that is, unlearned questions. And thus Ambrose translates it. And again, "avoid" is <note>original: "παραιτοῦ"</note>, in which it is strange the translator did not remember his own abundance of vocabulary. It means <term>reject, and despise, and do not admit</term>.

40 <term>They generate strifes</term>] <note>original: "μάχας"</note>, that is, battles. He elegantly calls such contentious disputes <term>quarrelsome battles</term>.

41 <term>It does not behoove to strive</term>] <note>original: "μάχεσθαι"</note>, that is, to fight. And again a little later, he translates "fighting" as "to strive." Although the meaning is not greatly changed, the emphasis of the metaphor is lost.

42 <term>Apt to teach</term>] <note>original: "διδακτικὸν"</note>, that is, fit and ready for teaching, rather than being imperious. Nowadays some of us prefer to compel rather than to teach. Cyprian, in his Epistle to Stephen, Bishop of the city of Rome, interprets it as <term>docile</term>, meaning one who is ready to learn; the Greek word speaks against this sentiment, although it is not refuted by Augustine in book 5, chapter 26 of *On Baptism against the Donatists*. What is here called <term>apt to teach</term> <note>original: "διδακτικὸν"</note>, Plato in the *Gorgias* calls <term>instructional</term> <note>original: "διδασκαλικόν"</note>.

43 <term>Patient</term>] <note>original: "ἀνεξίκακον"</note>, that is, tolerant of evil people or evil things. For the Greek word signifies more than just "tolerant."

44 <term>With modesty</term>] <note>original: "Ἐν πραότητι"</note>, that is, in gentleness or mildness. For it can be referred to either side: either to what precedes, <term>tolerant of evil in mildness</term>, or to what follows, <term>instructing in mildness</term>. Although I do not deny that <term>to instruct</term> <note>original: "παιδεύειν"</note> sometimes means "to rebuke."

45 <term>Who resist the truth</term>] "The truth" is redundant and is not found in Ambrose. For he indeed reads in this manner: <term>correcting those who think differently</term>.

46 <term>Lest perhaps he gives</term>] <note>original: "μή ποτε δῷ"</note>, lest at any time he gives. Although, if the Translator had wished to speak in Latin, he would have said, <term>if ever</term>: because *me* <note>original: "μὴ"</note> among the Greeks is not always negating or prohibiting, but sometimes doubting, like our words <term>whether</term> or <term>if</term>. Augustine felt the awkwardness of the phrasing; therefore, in the book he titled *On the Singularity of Clerics*, chapter 14, he interprets <term>lest at any time he gives</term> as <term>so that at some time he may give</term>.

47 <term>And they may recover themselves</term>] <note>original: "ἀνανήψωσιν"</note>, that is, they may return to sobriety, or wake up: for <term>to be sober</term> <note>original: "νήφειν"</note> signifies both. "From the snares of the devil." In the Greek it is <term>snare</term>, in the singular number.

48 <term>By whom they are held captive</term>] <note>original: "ἐζωγρημένοι ὑπ' αὐτοῦ"</note>: it properly signifies being taken alive in war. For here the Greek word is a compound, as we have advised elsewhere.

1 <term>There shall be</term>] For there shall be, <note>original: "Ἔσονται γὰρ"</note>.

<margin>E</margin> 2 <term>Lovers of themselves</term>] <note>original: "φίλαυτοι"</note>, that is, loving themselves, and pleasing themselves, that is, striving for their own advantages. Whence the term <term>philautia</term> <note>Self-love.</note> is derived; "dear," as Flaccus says, "is the love of oneself." Ambrose rendered it thus: <term>Men will be lovers of themselves only</term>. We have discussed this word <term>philautoi</term> more copiously in our *Adages* <note>Erasmus refers to his *Chiliades Adagiorum*, a massive collection of Greek and Latin proverbs.</note>. Hugo de Saint-Cher explained this word in a purely "theological" manner, and I will subscribe his words in all their "flower": <term>"Just as," he says, "a rascal is said of a rogue, who, when it is very cold, hugs himself with his arms to warm himself in whatever way, and it is said mockingly: 'this rascal loves himself much, who thus embraces himself with his arms.'"</term> Shall I call it a crime or a folly <margin>D</margin> to trifle thus with sacred letters, and so unlearnedly, not just impiously? And yet these things are read by those in authority, who can hardly bear the "play of Folly" <note>A reference to Erasmus's own satirical work, *The Praise of Folly* (*Moriae Encomium*).</note>. At least let those who so intensely favor Saint-Cher deny these things were written by him, but were added by his less-than-sober companions.

3 <term>Covetous</term>] <note>original: "Φιλάργυροι"</note>, that is, greedy for money: Ambrose reads "avaricious."

4 <term>Elated</term>] <note>original: "ἀλαζόνες"</note>, that is, vainglorious, as Plautus himself interpreted it. Ambrose reads <term>insolent</term>. Jerome, on Micah, reads <term>disdainful</term>. But I suspect it was written as <term>haughty</term>. I do not condemn what the Translator rendered, yet one can be elated without being a "boaster" <note>original: "ἀλαζὼν"</note>, who tosses and sells himself with pride, even when he is empty of good qualities.

5 <term>Not obedient to parents</term>] <note>original: "ἀπειθεῖς"</note>, that is, unmanageable, or intractable.

6 <term>Wicked</term>] <note>original: "ἀνόσιοι"</note>. Which Ambrose more correctly translates as <term>impious</term>. They can also be called impure.

7 <term>Without affection</term>] <note>original: "Ἄστοργοι"</note>. Which properly signifies those who have no affection for their own—say, children, or servants, or a wife. <margin>E</margin> For they are most deplorable in whom even the natural affections have withered away.

8 <term>Without peace</term>] <note>original: "ἄσπονδοι"</note>. Which Ambrose translates as <term>without faith</term>: *spondē* signifies a treaty and friendship, which refers to strangers, and not members of the household, with whom good men are joined by treaties and the bonds of friendship, to whom they are not joined by nature. For he touched upon several degrees: unmanageable to parents, which is a species of impiety; impious toward God, <note>original: "ἀνόσιοι"</note>; ungrateful toward the well-deserving; without natural affection <note>original: "ἄστοργοι"</note> toward relatives; truce-breakers <note>original: "ἄσπονδοι"</note> toward those joined by a treaty of friendship.

9 <term>Accusers</term>] <note>original: "διάβολοι"</note>, that is, slanderers, or informers.

10 <term>Without benignity</term>] <note>original: "ἀφιλάγαθοι"</note>. Which sounds as if you were to say, "not friends of the good." Thus the Greek commentaries interpret it. Ambrose translates, <term>enemies of the good</term>. Cyprian, <term>not loving what is good</term>.

11 <term>Traitors</term>] <note>original: "Προδόται"</note>, that is, Deserters of friendship and fellowship.

12 <term>Proterve</term>] <note>original: "προπετεῖς"</note>, that is, headlong, or rash.

13 <term>Tumid</term>] <note>original: "τετυφωμένοι"</note>, that is, puffed up. Although the Translator did not <margin>F</margin> render it badly: <term>we call the same people turgid</term>. I suspect it is the same word that Cyprian several times renders as <term>elated by stupor</term>. Others read "blind," which is neither in the Greek nor in the ancient Latin copies, nor in Chrysostom, nor in Ambrose. I think this word crept in because some clever fellow wrote in the margin, as if correcting, "blinded" <note>original: "τυφλωμένοις"</note> instead of "puffed up" <note>original: "τετυφωμένοις"</note>. Of which the former means <term>elated</term>, the latter <term>blind</term>.

14 <term>Lovers of pleasures</term>] <note>original: "φιλήδονοι μᾶλλον ἢ φιλόθεοι"</note>. He said it far more gracefully in Greek, with compound words, that is, <term>pleasure-lovers rather than God-lovers</term>. Cyprian reads, <term>loving pleasure more than God</term>. Such a great army of vices follows self-love <note>philautia</note>. This plague is rendered more incurable by the addition of the simulation of godliness.

15 <term>Appearance of godliness</term>] <note>original: "μόρφωσιν"</note>, as if you were to say "formation." For he notes those who know how to prescribe to others in words how they ought to live piously, while they themselves follow the opposite. Cyprian reads, <term>deformation of religion</term>.

16 <term>But the virtue</term>] <note>original: "δύναμιν"</note>. He would have translated "force" or "power" better here, as it...

<summary>In this commentary on 2 Timothy 2 and 3, Erasmus uses philological analysis to distinguish between various types of moral character and the specific vices of the "last days." He notably critiques medieval scholastic interpretations, such as those of Hugo de Saint-Cher, while emphasizing the importance of natural affection and the dangers of self-love disguised as piety.</summary>

# EPISTLE OF PAUL. CAP. IV.

6 <margin>6</margin> For of this sort are those who creep into houses and make captives of silly women weighed down with sins, led away by various lusts,
7 <margin>7</margin> always learning and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.
8 <margin>8</margin> Now just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth: men of corrupt minds, disapproved concerning the faith.
9 <margin>9</margin> But they will progress no further, for their folly will be manifest to all, as theirs also was.
10 <margin>10</margin> But you have carefully followed my doctrine, manner of life, purpose, faith, longsuffering, love, perseverance,
11 <margin>11</margin> persecutions, and afflictions, which happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium, at Lystra—what persecutions I endured. And out of them all the Lord delivered me.
12 <margin>12</margin> Yes, and all who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution.
13 <margin>13</margin> But evil men and impostors will grow worse and worse, deceiving and being deceived.
14 <margin>14</margin> But you must continue in the things which you have learned and been assured of, knowing from whom you have learned them,
15 <margin>15</margin> and that from childhood you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
16 <margin>16</margin> All Scripture is God-breathed, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness,
17 <margin>17</margin> that the man of God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.

### CAP. IV.
<margin>IV.</margin> <margin>1</margin> I charge you therefore before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead at His appearing and His kingdom:
2 <margin>2</margin> Preach the word! Be ready in season and out of season. Convince, rebuke, exhort, with all longsuffering and teaching.
3 <margin>3</margin> For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires, because they have itching ears, they will heap up for themselves teachers;
4 <margin>4</margin> and they will turn their ears away from the truth...

---

<margin>17</margin> <term>opposed to appearance</term>. *Denying*, <term>arnoumenoi</term> <note>original Greek: "αρνουμενοι"</note>, that is, having denied; for it is in the past tense, meaning those who have already denied.
<margin>18</margin> *And avoid these*] <term>apotrepou</term> <note>original Greek: "αποτρεπου"</note>, that is, turn away from, which is stronger than just "avoid"; for it is not the word <term>paraitou</term> <note>original Greek: "παραιτου"</note>, which is usually translated as "avoid."
<margin>18</margin> *Who penetrate*] <term>endyndontes</term> <note>original Greek: "ενδυνοντες"</note>, that is, those who enter in stealthily. Ambrose reads, *who creep in*; but the Translator does not render this poorly.
<margin>19</margin> *Burdened with sins*] <term>sesōreumena</term> <note>original Greek: "σεσωρευμενα"</note>, as if you were to say piled up, or overwhelmed by a heap of sins.
<margin>20</margin> *Coming to the knowledge of the truth*] <term>elthein dynamena</term> <note>original Greek: "ελθειν δυναμενα"</note>, that is, being able to come.
<margin>21</margin> *Jannes & Jambres*] <term>Iannēs kai Iambrēs</term> <note>original Greek: "Ιαννης και Ιαμβρης"</note>, that is, Jannes and Jambres, whom Chrysostom says were two Egyptian magicians who competed with Moses by performing portents. Although their names are not added in Exodus, Paul likely received them from Jewish tradition, which they call <term>agrapha</term> <note>unwritten tradition</note>, or certainly from the Holy Spirit. As if it really mattered so much to know the names of the magicians. In the interpretation of Hebrew names, we read both Mambres and Jambres; they are similarly called <term>antistatai</term> <note>resisters</note>, as if it makes no difference whether it sounds like Jambres or Mambres. Whether this is written correctly or otherwise, the risk lies with the author rather than the indexer.
<margin>22</margin> *But they will progress no further*] <term>ou prokopsousin epi pleion</term> <note>original Greek: "ου προκοψουσιν επι πλειον"</note>. Ambrose reads, *they will not progress more*. Where our translator uses <term>insipience</term> <note>folly</note>, Ambrose uses <term>ignorance</term>; however, <term>anoia</term> <note>original Greek: "ανοια"</note> more properly means <term>mindlessness</term> or <term>dementia</term>, and the translator of Chrysostom renders it thus.
<margin>23</margin> *You have attained*] <term>parēkolouthēkas</term> <note>original Greek: "παρηκολουθηκας"</note>. This does not strictly mean "attained" in the sense of "acquired." Otherwise, how would it fit what follows: *persecutions and sufferings*? For no one is said to "acquire" these. Thus it is better understood as: you were present from the beginning to the end and are a witness of all things. For that is what <term>parakolouthein</term> <note>original Greek: "παρακολουθειν"</note> signifies, as we have noted elsewhere. Theophylact interprets it in this sense, which is why we translated it as *you have followed*.
<margin>24</margin> *What things happened to me*] <term>hoia moi</term> <note>original Greek: "οια μοι"</note>, that is, which things to me; for the Greeks customarily use <term>hoia</term> for <term>ha</term>. *In Antioch*, <term>en Antiocheia</term> <note>original Greek: "εν Αντιοχεια"</note>, that is, in Antioch—unless he is speaking of the city, and I believe it should be understood as the city.
<margin>25</margin> *Seducers*] <term>goētes</term> <note>original Greek: "γοητες"</note>, that is, impostors or sorcerers. Ambrose reads *deceivers*.
<margin>26</margin> *Erring and into error etc.*] <term>planōntes kai planōmenoi</term> <note>original Greek: "πλανωντες και πλανωμενοι"</note>, that is, leading astray and being led astray. Ambrose rendered or explained this more truly as: *themselves erring, and involving others in errors*.
<margin>27</margin> *Which can instruct you*] <term>sophisai</term> <note>original Greek: "σοφισαι"</note>, that is, to erudite or to make wise.
<margin>28</margin> *Through faith which is in Christ Jesus*] This is missing in Ambrose, but I think that happened by accident.
<margin>29</margin> *Divinely inspired*] <term>theopneustos</term> <note>original Greek: "θεοπνευστος"</note>, which Paul said more pleasantly with a compound word.
<margin>30</margin> *Is useful*] *Useful*, with the conjunction added, <term>kai ōphelimos</term> <note>original Greek: "και ωφελιμος"</note>. A subtle, hidden power of argument appears in the conjunction. Scripture, as it is divinely inspired, is also effective for many things, whereas human doctrine is ineffective. Or: Scripture is divinely inspired, and the same is useful etc., so that "all" refers specifically to canonical Scripture.
<margin>31</margin> *For reproving*] <term>pros epanorthōsin</term> <note>original Greek: "προς επανορθωσιν"</note>, that is, for correc-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>17</margin> they have denied. 17 And turn away from those. For of these are <margin>18</margin> those who enter stealthily into families, and lead captive silly women <margin>19</margin> burdened with sins, who are led by various lusts, always learning, and never <margin>20</margin> able to come to the knowledge of the truth. But just as <margin>B</margin> <margin>21</margin> Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth: men corrupt in mind, reprobate concerning the faith. <margin>22</margin> But they will progress no more: for the dementia of these will be evident to all, just as theirs was. But you <margin>23</margin> have followed my doctrine, training, purpose, faith, gentleness, charity, patience, Persecutions, afflictions, <margin>24</margin> which happened to me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra; what persecutions I endured: and out of all the Lord rescued me. But indeed all who wish to live piously in Christ <margin>B</margin> Jesus will suffer persecution. Furthermore, evil men <margin>25</margin> and impostors will progress toward the worse, <margin>26</margin> while they both lead into error and err themselves. But you persist in those things <margin>14</margin> which you have learned, and which have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you learned them, and that from a child you have known the sacred letters, <margin>15</margin> <margin>27</margin> which can render you erudite unto salvation <margin>28</margin> through faith which is in Christ Jesus. All scripture <margin>29</margin> di- <margin>16</margin> vinely inspired, <margin>30</margin> is also useful for doctrine, for reproof, <margin>31</margin> for correction, for training which is in justice, <margin>32</margin> that the man of God may be whole, <margin>17</margin> prepared for every good work <margin>33</margin>. I charge you therefore <margin>1</margin> <margin>IV.</margin> <margin>C</margin> <margin>2</margin> before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who is to judge <margin>3</margin> the living and the dead <margin>4</margin> in his appearing and in his kingdom. Preach the word, be urgent in season and out of season: reprove, rebuke, exhort <margin>6</margin> with all gentleness and doctrine. For the time will be when they will not endure sound doctrine: but according to their own lusts they will heap up for themselves <margin>7</margin> teachers, those whose ears itch, and they will turn away their ears from the truth, but unto fables... <margin>4</margin>

---

-tion. In this place Saint Ambrose, for <term>pros epanorthōsin</term> <note>original Greek: "προς επανορθωσιν"</note>, translates *for redintegration* <note>restoration to a whole state</note>, for which our manuscripts have *for reproving*. But I do not know if the translator wrote *for correcting*. And regarding the word "divine" in the fourth edition, I found in the Constance manuscripts, *for correcting*. For the Greek word sounds like straightening that which was curved. Unless perhaps <term>elenchon</term> <note>reproof</note> and <term>epanorthōsin</term> <note>correction</note> pertain to the same <margin>D</margin> thing. For Ambrose, in explaining both sentiments, seems to embrace them together. For he writes thus: *It is manifest that all Scripture, since God is shown to be the author, is useful. For it was given for this: that it might benefit the unskillful, and restore the deformed, drawing the unworthy to justice, so that the man of God might be perfect in every good work.* Thus far he speaks. Now, where Paul said "for doctrine," he explains it as "benefiting the unskillful"; where he says "for reproof and correction," he says "to restore the deformed"; finally, what is "for instruction, which is in justice," he interprets as "drawing the unworthy to justice."
<margin>32</margin> *That the man may be perfect*] <term>hina artios ē ho tou Theou anthrōpos</term> <note>original Greek: "ινα αρτιος η ο του Θεου ανθρωπος"</note>, that is, that he who is a man of God may be perfect or sound.
<margin>33</margin> *Equipped*] <term>exērtismenos</term> <note>original Greek: "εξηρτισμενος"</note>, that is, consummated and perfected. And thus Ambrose reads, and the interpretation of the Greeks agrees.
<margin>1</margin> <term>E</term> *I charge therefore*] <term>Diamartyromai oun egō</term> <note>original Greek: "Διαμαρτυρομαι ουν εγω"</note>, that is, I testify therefore, or *I charge*.
<margin>2</margin> *God and Jesus Christ*] He said "God" for the Father, but among the Greeks, since the word <term>Despota</term> <note>Master/Lord</note> is not added, the speech becomes ambiguous. For if you read it as a complex whole, the sense is that Jesus Christ is called both God and Judge; but if you read it separately, the name "God" pertains to the Father, and "Judge" to Christ. In the previous Epistle, chapter 6, he separated them: *I charge you before God who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus etc.* Nor is the title "Lord" added here, and thus it coheres more aptly with the relative pronoun that follows, <term>tou</term> <note>of the [one who]</note>.
<margin>3</margin> *Living and dead*] Either this is said as a proverbial figure for everyone, or he meant the pious and the impious, or those deceased before the day of judgment and those whom that day finds still living. With what great solicitude Paul charges his Timothy. In the former Epistle he had said *I command*, here he says *I charge*, which is more vehement; and he adds what is more terrible: *who is to judge the living and the dead*. Would that all Bishops would consider here that this charge is delivered to each one individually, as it truly is. But what does he require <margin>F</margin> with such a religious charge? That you keep the commandment without spot and blameless, until the coming of the Lord. Preach the word. What shall we pastors answer Paul when we come to the judgment of which he reminds us?
<margin>4</margin> *And by His appearing*] <term>kata tēn epiphaneian</term> <note>original Greek: "κατα την επιφανειαν"</note>, that is, in the appearing, or according to the appearing. For it refers back to the participle, *who is to judge at His appearing*. The Translator seems to have read "and before according to." Furthermore, the word here is not <term>parousia</term> <note>presence/arrival</note>, but <term>epiphaneia</term> <note>appearing</note>, which sounds more like an "illustration" or "making manifest," for the mention of the *kingdom* follows.
<margin>5</margin> *In season, out of season*] <term>eukairōs, akairōs</term> <note>original Greek: "ευκαιρως, ακαιρως"</note>, that is, timely and untimely; and this is said as a proverbial figure for "assiduously" and "instantly."
<margin>6</margin> *In all patience*] <term>makrothymia</term> <note>original Greek: "μακροθυμια"</note>, that is, longsuffering, or, if this word seems insufficiently Latin, gentleness. For among the Greeks, this is the virtue opposed to <term>oxythymia</term> <note>quickness to anger/sharp temper</note>.
<margin>7</margin> *Itching teachers*] <term>didaskalous, knēthomenoi</term> <note>original Greek: "διδασκαλους, κνηθομενοι"</note>, that is, teachers: and *itching*...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on Paul’s Second Epistle to Timothy. Having discussed the dangers of false teachers in Chapter 3, the text now moves to the final chapter, where Paul gives his farewell charge to Timothy, reflects on his own approaching death, and provides personal instructions regarding his companions and belongings.</meta>

# TO TIMOTHY II. CHAPTER IV.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>5</margin> ...they will turn their hearing away from the truth, and will be turned aside to myths. But you, be sober in all things, endure hardship, do the work of an Evangelist, fulfill your ministry. For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Finally, there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give to me on that day, and not only to me, but also to all those who have loved his appearing. <margin>10</margin> Make every effort to come to me quickly: for Demas has forsaken me, having loved this present world, <margin>B</margin> and has gone to Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me. Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for ministry. I have sent Tychicus to Ephesus. When you come, bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus, and the books, especially the parchments. Alexander the coppersmith did me much harm; may the Lord reward him according to his works. <margin>15</margin> You also should be on guard against him, for he has greatly resisted our words. In my first defense no one stood with me, but everyone forsook me: may it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled, and all the Gentiles might hear; and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion. And the Lord will deliver me from every evil work, and will preserve me for his heavenly kingdom; to whom be glory forever <margin>C</margin> <margin>19</margin> and ever. Amen. Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus. <margin>20</margin> Erastus stayed in Corinth. I left Trophimus <margin>21</margin> at Miletus sick. Make every effort to come before winter. Eubulus greets you, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers. <margin>22</margin> The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Grace be with you. Amen.

# THE END OF THE SECOND EPISTLE OF PAUL TO TIMOTHY.
### T H E  E N D.

---

The word "itching" <note>original: "prurientes"</note> here is to be taken in the nominative case, "itching" <note>original: "κνηθόμενοι" (knēthomenoi)</note>, that is, those who feel a tickling or itch in their hearing. From this they seek out those who might scratch their ears with the pleasure of a speech, rather than those who might scrape them with the truth.
<margin>8 But you be sober]</margin> Be sober <note>original: "νῆφε" (nēphe)</note>, that is, be moderate or keep watch.
<margin>9 Labor]</margin> Endure hardship <note>original: "κακοπάθησον" (kakopathēson)</note>, that is, bear afflictions, or, as we have translated it, be hardened in afflictions.
<margin>10 Fulfill your ministry]</margin> Fully perform <note>original: "πληροφορήσον" (plērophorēson)</note>. We have frequently commented on this word elsewhere. It means to give full proof of your preaching. This will happen if people see that your life corresponds to your teaching, and that you do not hunt for your own profit, but rather bear even the most cruel afflictions cheerfully for the love of Christ. "Be sober." In this place, though some ancient manuscripts have "be watchful," I do not find this in the Greek manuscripts, nor in Ambrose, nor in Chrysostom, nor even in the most reliable manuscript of the Pauline Library. I suspect it crept in because the Greek word <note>original: "νῆφε" (nēphe)</note> signifies both "be sober" and "be watchful." Thus, it is possible that what a learned person noted as "be sober" was later pulled into the main text.
<margin>E</margin> <margin>11 I am now poured out]</margin> I am being sacrificed <note>original: "σπένδομαι" (spendomai)</note>, that is, offered up. Ambrose reads "I am poured out," but in his commentary he declares there is no difference between being poured out and being sacrificed. Chrysostom and Theophylact say the difference is that a sacrifice <note>original: "θυσία" (thysia)</note>, that is, a victim, is not entirely left to God, whereas a libation <note>original: "σπονδὴ" (spondē)</note> is entirely left. I leave it to others to examine what this means.
12 And the time of my departure] Departure <note>original: "ἀναλύσεως" (analyseōs)</note>. Cyprian, in a certain Epistle, seems to have read "of my taking up" <note>original: "assumptionis meae"</note> when citing this passage: "I am already being sacrificed, and the time of my taking up is near." The translator of Origen, both elsewhere and in the Homilies on Numbers, indicates there were two readings for this place: "departure" <note>original: "resolutionis"</note> and "return" <note>original: "regressionis"</note>. I do not fully understand what the word "return" implies, except that in Greek the word "dissolution" <note>original: "ἀνάλυσις" (analysis)</note> sounds like both "resolution" and "return": for just as one who departs is said to "loosen" <note>original: "solvere"</note>, so a return is a "re-loosening" <note>original: "resolutio"</note>, in Greek "analysis."
<margin>F</margin> <margin>13 Good fight]</margin> The good <note>original: "τὸν καλὸν" (ton kalon)</note>. This does not simply mean "good," but "illustrious" and "excellent." And the definite article indicates that specific Gospel struggle.
14 Henceforth] <note>original: "Λοιπὸν" (Loipon)</note>, that is, "As for what remains"; and so Ambrose translates it. Our usual translator is accustomed to translate this as "For the rest."
15 But also to those] <note>original: "ἀλλὰ καὶ πᾶσι" (alla kai pasi)</note>, that is, "but also to all." "Who love" <note>original: "τοῖς ἠγαπηκόσι" (tois ēgapēkosi)</note>, that is, "who have loved": although the Greeks often use past tenses for verbs of affection.
<margin>16 Hasten to me]</margin> <note>original: "Σπούδασον" (Spoudason)</note>, that is, "Strive" or "Give your attention." Otherwise, the figure of speech "Hasten quickly" is a redundancy <note>original: "σχῆμα καὶ κατάχρησις" (schēma kai katachrēsis)</note>, just as Aristophanes jokes.
<margin>17 Loving this world]</margin> <note>original: "ἀγαπήσας τὸν νῦν αἰῶνα" (agapēsas ton nyn aiōna)</note>, that is, "after he loved the present age," or "having embraced the present age."
<margin>18 Crescens into Galatia]</margin> <note>original: "Κρήσκης" (Krēskēs)</note>, that is, Crescens, but the Greek speech adapted the Latin name, just as "Poudes" <note>original: "Πούδης"</note> is used for Pudens.
<margin>19 In ministry]</margin> <note>original: "εἰς διακονίαν" (eis diakonian)</note>, that is, "for ministry."
<margin>20 Cloak]</margin> In Greek <note>original: "φαινόλην" (phainolēn)</note>. This is a type of cloak, not a consular one as some think, but one we use for protection from the rain, made of leather, as Hesychius thinks. <column-break/> <page-num>962</page-num> <margin>D</margin> they will be turned. <sup>8</sup> But you, be sober in all things, <sup>9</sup> endure afflictions, perform the work of an Evangelist, <sup>10</sup> render your ministry fully proven. For I myself <margin>5</margin> <sup>11</sup> am now being sacrificed, and <sup>12</sup> the time of my departure is at hand. <sup>13</sup> I have fought a good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. <sup>14</sup> As for what remains, there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, who is a just judge, will render to me on that day: and not only to me, <sup>15</sup> but also to all who love his coming. <sup>16</sup> Give your attention to coming to me quickly: for Demas has <margin>10</margin> forsaken me, <sup>17</sup> having embraced the present age, and has set out for Thessalonica, <sup>18</sup> Crescens for Galatia, Titus for Dalmatia, Luke alone is with me. Bring Mark along with you: for he is very useful to me <sup>19</sup> for ministry. Furthermore, I have sent Tychicus to Ephesus. <sup>20</sup> The cloak which I left at Troas with Carpus, bring it when you come, and the books, but especially the parchments. <sup>22</sup> Alexander the coppersmith <sup>23</sup> did me much harm, <sup>24</sup> may the Lord reward him according to his deeds: <sup>25</sup> whom you also must avoid: for he has vehemently <sup>26</sup> resisted our words. In my first defense no one was present with me, but all deserted me: may it not be imputed to them: but the Lord was present with me and strengthened me, so that through me <sup>27</sup> the preaching might be fulfilled, and all nations might hear, and <sup>28</sup> I was snatched from the mouth of the lion: and the Lord will snatch me from every evil deed, and will preserve me for his heavenly kingdom: <sup>29</sup> to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. Greet Prisca, and Aquila, and the family of Onesiphorus. Erastus stayed at Corinth. I left Trophimus at Miletus weak. Give your attention to coming before winter. <sup>30</sup> Eubulus greets you, and <sup>31</sup> Pudens, and Linus, and Claudia, <sup>32</sup> and all the brothers. The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. <sup>33</sup> Grace be with you. Amen.

# THE SECOND EPISTLE OF PAUL TO TIMOTHY
### T H E  E N D.

---

Although the same author [Hesychius] wonders whether it might be a small case for reeds; others think it is a box for books. So say the Greek commentaries. Jerome, in the third dialogue of his epistle against the Pelagians, calls it a "lantern" or a "cloak." Though in most manuscripts "lantern" <note>original: "lucerna"</note> was corrupted from "cloak" <note>original: "penula"</note> by some candle-lighter.
<margin>21 And the parchments]</margin> The "and" is redundant; <note>original: "μεμβράνας" (membranas)</note>. Here Paul used a Latin word. Oh, Apostolic furniture! A cloak to protect against the rain, and a few books, undoubtedly sacred. Now, look at how many horses, how many cannons, how many other things there are, which I do not care to list.
<margin>22 Coppersmith]</margin> <note>original: "χαλκεὺς" (chalkeus)</note>, that is, a blacksmith or worker in copper, lest anyone take it to mean a treasurer or a guardian of money, as some have interpreted it.
23 He showed me much evil] <note>original: "πολλά μοι κακὰ ἐνεδείξατο" (polla moi kaka enedeixato)</note>, that is, he afflicted me with many evils. Augustine also noted in his book on the expressions of Genesis that in the Holy Scriptures "to show" is frequently used for "to do."
<margin>24 May the Lord reward him]</margin> In Greek it is "may he reward" <note>original: "ἀποδώῃ" (apodōēi)</note>, as in a prayer or imprecation. Although Augustine, in his explanation of the Sermon on the Mount, seems to have read "he will reward" in the future tense, thus resolving a question he posed: that Paul was not calling down evil on the one who hurt him, but predicting what would happen. He treats the same thing in the book against Faustus, chapter 22, in which very place it is written "he will reward" in the common copies. Yet shortly after in the same place he cites that word of Paul, "I wish they would even cut themselves off who disturb you," which certainly cannot be a prediction. Furthermore, what need was there to excuse why imprecations are found in Holy Scripture if these were spoken in the future tense, agreeing with the Latin copies? Chrysostom reads "may he reward," but in his commentary he does not raise this difficulty. Theophylact frankly confesses that he read "may he reward," but says it was put there for "he will reward." But we have spoken about these things more accurately in Acts chapter 23, where Paul, having been struck by a slap, says to the High Priest: "God strike you, you whitewashed wall."
<margin>25 And you avoid]</margin> <note>original: "Φυλάσσου" (phylassou)</note>, that is, watch out for, or beware.
<margin>26 Resisted]</margin> <note>original: "ἀνθέστηκε" (anthestēke)</note>.
27 Preaching may be fulfilled] <note>original: "πληροφορηθῇ" (plērophorēthē)</note>, that is, might be fully poured out, and have a certain faith.
28 He delivered] <note>original: "ἐῤῥύσθη" (errusthē)</note>, that is, "he will deliver," in the future tense, supported by both manuscripts from Constance. For there follows, "and he will save."
29 To whom be glory] The Greek manuscript added, "to whom be power and might."
<margin>30 Eubulus]</margin> <note>original: "Εὔβουλος" (Euboulos)</note>, Eubulus with the second to last syllable lengthened, a name derived from "good counsel."
31 And Pudens] <note>original: "καὶ Πούδης" (kai Poudēs)</note>. Ambrose and the ancient manuscripts have "Pudens," again a Latin name somewhat distorted by the Greeks.
32 And his brothers] Not "his," but "all," is found among the Greeks, and so Saint Ambrose reads, with Chrysostom agreeing; and finally the Pauline manuscript, as well as both from Constance. For having named some of his own, he embraces the rest with a general name.
<margin>33 Grace be with you]</margin> Instead of this, for some unknown reason, "Farewell" is read in the Ambrosian manuscripts. And yet from his commentaries it is possible to guess that he read as we do.

### THE END OF THE ANNOTATIONS ON THE SECOND EPISTLE OF PAUL TO TIMOTHY, BY DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

# PREFACE
### to the
# EPISTLE OF PAUL TO TITUS.

Paul sends this from Nicopolis <note>A city in Epirus, Greece</note>, for he spent the winter there. The occasion for the Epistle is this: He left Titus in Crete so that he might appoint clergy throughout the cities. Since many people there were attempting to deceive the people under the pretext of the Law <note>The Mosaic Law of the Old Testament</note>, Paul, having learned of this, wrote to him. First, giving thanks to God for Titus's piety, he indicates that faith in Christ is not a recent innovation, but has been prepared and promised by God from eternity. Next, he teaches about the appointment of clergy and about these men—what kind of people they ought to be. He also commands Titus to rebuke those who speak against the sound faith, especially those "of the circumcision" <note>Jewish converts who insisted on the necessity of Jewish rituals</note>. He notes that the Cretans are known to be lazy and are in need of censure. Having taught that all foods are clean to those who are clean, and describing the character required of older women who must encourage the younger women to be sensible, he advises how slaves also ought to serve their own masters. Finally, having reminded him that the Savior's grace justified us not by works but by his own love for humanity, and having commanded that legalistic battles be avoided as being useless, he makes it clear to him that after he sends Artemas to him, Titus should come to join him. He also gave him instructions regarding teaching and being a leader in good works; and thus he concludes the Epistle.

---

# ON THE EPISTLE TO TITUS
### *The Argument by*
## DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter T featuring a scene with several figures, possibly a landscape or interior with classical or biblical figures in a woodcut frame.</image-desc>
Titus, his disciple and held in the place of a son, was placed in charge of the most noble island of Crete by the Apostle on account of his exceptional gifts; and departing from there, Paul had consecrated him as Archbishop <note>original: "Archiepiscopum"</note>. He writes to him from the city of Nicopolis, which is on the Actian coast, while matters were—as it appears—still quite peaceful, since there is no mention of afflictions or persecutions. Moreover, he advises that he should complete and finish what Paul himself had begun among the Cretans: that he should establish Bishops <term>Episcopos — from the Greek for "overseers," here used for high-ranking church leaders</term> throughout the individual cities—which that island is famously said to have had a hundred of—whom he also calls Elders <term>Presbyteros — the Greek term for "elders," from which the word "priest" is derived</term>, prescribing the form of a fit Bishop. And since "False Apostles" <note>original: "Pseudapostoli"</note> had also penetrated this place, who were forcing their version of Judaism upon everyone, he encourages Titus to reject and refute them boldly. Then he prescribes the duties for various persons and age groups, just as he prescribes to Timothy. He adds this instruction: that no one, under the pretext of the Christian Religion, should resist Princes and Magistrates performing their duty, even if they are strangers to the faith of Christ; rather, they are to be borne gently, in the hope that perhaps eventually, by God's will, they too might come to their senses. Finally, he orders Titus to come to him at Nicopolis, but only after Paul has sent Artemas or Tychicus there, so that the Cretans would not seem to be deprived of the comfort of a Bishop.

# THE EPISTLE OF THE APOSTLE PAUL TO TITUS

<margin>1</margin> PAUL, a servant of God, and an Apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of the elect of God and the knowledge of the truth which is according to godliness, <gloss>1</gloss>
<margin>2</margin> In the hope of eternal life, which the God who does not lie promised before eternal times, <gloss>2 3 4 5</gloss>
<margin>3</margin> But manifested in His own seasons His word in preaching, which was entrusted to me according to the command of our Savior God; <gloss>6 7 8</gloss>
<margin>4</margin> To Titus, a true child according to the common faith: grace, mercy, peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ our Savior. <gloss>9</gloss>
<margin>5</margin> For this reason I left you in Crete, that you might set in order the things that are lacking, and appoint in every city <note>original: κατὰ πόλιν</note>
<margin>6</margin> Elders, as I directed you. If any is blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not under accusation of riot, or <note>original: ἀνυπότακτα</note>
<margin>7</margin> unruly. For it is necessary for the Bishop to be blameless, as a steward of God, not self-willed, not quick-tempered, not given to wine, not a striker, not greedy for shameful gain,

---

1 **Paul, but]** <note>original: Paulus autem</note> He noted here something about the form of the greeting; he added "but" <note>autem</note>, even though "indeed" <note>quidem</note> did not precede it. Jerome elsewhere attributes this to a lack of skill in the Greek language, as if this usage were not found among the Greeks. However, the Grammarians note that the Greek word *de* <note>δὲ</note> is frequently used as a simple connective conjunction, which clearly happened in this passage.

2 **According to the faith of the elect of God]** Saint Jerome here again attacks the lack of skill in Greek phrasing. He says, "He did not speak according to humility, as most think, but truly, when he said 'if I am unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge,' etc." I do not see the reason why Jerome does this, unless perhaps because Paul said, "the elect of God," just as he had said before, "servant of God," and shortly after "which God promised." Paul was a servant of God not according to the Mosaic Law, but according to the faith of the elect; and an Apostle of Jesus Christ according to the acknowledgment of Gospel truth, which the Jews might grasp as shadows. And he opposed "piety" <note>godliness</note> to ceremonies. Furthermore, the word used is "acknowledgment" <note>ἐπίγνωσις</note>, not merely "knowledge" <note>γνῶσις</note>—more truly a recognition or "acknowledgment," a distinction I have often mentioned.

3 **In hope]** <note>original: Ἐπ' ἐλπίδι</note> That is, "In hope," or "Under hope."

4 **Who does not lie]** <note>original: ὁ ἀψευδής</note> As if you were to say "un-lying," or "truthful," and far removed from falsehood. Ambrose reads "True"; Jerome reads "Not a liar."

5 **Before eternal times]** <note>original: πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων</note> That is, before everlasting ages. Jerome reads it this way. Augustine, in his work against the Pelagians and in several other places, especially against the Manichaeans on Genesis, also reads "before eternal times." However, they are called "eternal" not because they had no beginning (since the creation of the world has a beginning), but because there were no times before them. Thomas Aquinas makes no mention here of the "thousand years," and notes that another manuscript had "for secular, eternal; that is, ancient." I do not know what he means by this, unless perhaps some Greek manuscript had "ancient" <note>ἀρχαῖα</note> instead of "eternal" <note>αἰώνια</note>. For in Acts 15, "from ancient days" seems to be said for "from eternity."

6 **But manifested]** Here too, the Greek "indeed" <note>μὲν</note> did not precede the "but" <note>δὲ</note>. The Greek word for "his" is *idiois* <note>ἰδίοις</note>, referring to the thing itself, not to God. Every thing has its own proper time. To us, something is said to happen not in its own time or in an alien time when it happens unseasonably. And some interpret "the word" <note>τὸν λόγον</note> as the word of promise, while others interpret it as the Son himself.

7 **Which was entrusted to me]** <note>original: ὃ ἐπιστεύθην ἐγώ</note> Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>Faber Stapulensis</note> translates this as "to whom I was committed," as if it makes no difference whether you say "your son was committed to me" or "I was committed to your son." I marvel that such a deep sleep crept over so great a man that he did not recognize the Greek figure of speech, in which they say "I was committed this thing" whenever they mean "this thing was committed to me," especially since this formula is so common in Paul. But I think I can guess what drove our friend Lefèvre: namely, the relative pronoun *ho* <note>ὃ</note> was placed in the dative case, when the accusative would be more fitting. But this was done because of the preceding noun in the same case, "preaching" <note>κηρύγματι</note>, with which the "which" <note>ὃ</note> agrees according to the Greek idiom, even while disagreeing with its own verb. For so it is read, I confess, in several copies, though in the more corrected ones it is "which I was entrusted" <note>ὃ ἐπιστεύθην</note>, and indeed Lefèvre himself writes it thus in his own examination.

8 **According to the command]** Again, the Greek is *kata epitagēn* <note>κατὰ ἐπιταγὴν</note>, that is, according to the injunction. We translate it "delegation." For he feels this duty of preaching was delegated to him by the Lord, so that he is not allowed to refuse.

9 **To Titus, a beloved son]** <note>original: γνησίῳ τέκνῳ</note> That is, a true, legitimate, proper, and natural son. And so Ambrose reads it, as if you would say, truly a son and not a bastard, nor one degenerating from his father. Saint Jerome also notes the elegance of this word when discussing this passage, adding that the specific property of the Greek voice cannot be fully expressed in Latin, though "true," "natural," or "honorable" might nearly explain it. For "natural" <note>γνήσιος</note> and "bastard" <note>νόθος</note> (that is, adulterous) are opposites. And Pliny, in Book 10, Chapter 3, calls the fifth kind of eagles "natural" <note>γνήσιον</note>, and interprets it as the only true eagle of uncorrupted origin. Ambrose in this place reads "natural son," as he does in the first epistle to Timothy.

<column-break/>

1 <gloss>1</gloss> PAUL, servant of God, <gloss>2</gloss> but Apostle of Jesus Christ, <gloss>3</gloss> according to the faith of the elect of God and the acknowledgment of the truth, which is according to godliness, 2 <gloss>4</gloss> In hope of eternal life, <gloss>5</gloss> which He promised, <gloss>6</gloss> who does not know how to lie, God, <gloss>7</gloss> before eternal times, 3 <gloss>8</gloss> But He manifested His word in His own times through preaching, <gloss>9</gloss> which was committed to me <gloss>8</gloss> according to the delegation of our Savior God: 4 <gloss>10</gloss> To Titus, a natural son according to the common faith, <gloss>11</gloss> grace, mercy, peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ our Savior. 5 <gloss>12</gloss> For the sake of this matter <gloss>13</gloss> I left you in Crete, <gloss>14</gloss> so that you might proceed to correct what is lacking, and appoint <gloss>15</gloss> elders town by town, as I had ordained for you. 6 <gloss>16</gloss> If anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, <gloss>17</gloss> not subject to the crime of luxury, or who are not unmanageable. 7 For it is necessary for a Bishop to be blameless, <gloss>16</gloss> as God’s steward, <gloss>17</gloss> not stubborn, not prone to anger, not fond of wine, <gloss>18</gloss> not a striker, <gloss>19</gloss> not devoted to shameful gain,

---

10 **Grace and peace]** <note>original: χάρις, ἔλεος, εἰρήνη</note> That is: grace, mercy, peace. However, neither Jerome nor Ambrose adds "mercy." Certainly, Chrysostom and Theophylact read it as the Greek manuscripts have it, the latter of whom even touches upon it in his commentary. But it appears "mercy" was added among the Greeks, not only because the consensus of Latin manuscripts argues against it, but also because Origen, noting and distinguishing the forms of greetings used by Paul in each Epistle in his work on the Epistle to the Romans, speaks in this manner: "In the first and second to Timothy: grace, mercy, and peace, etc. But to Titus: grace and peace from God the Father."

11 **I left you in Crete]** <note>original: ἐν Κρήτῃ</note> That is, in Crete. The Greeks also add a preposition to the names of cities, which is very rare among the Latins. But the Translator removed the Greek preposition from the name of the island, which is quite intolerable, especially since it is present in the Greek.

12 **That you might correct what is lacking]** <note>original: ἐπιδιορθώσῃ</note> That is, "super-correct," to speak thus for the sake of explanation. Paul perceived that he had corrected certain things previously, but since they were not yet fully corrected, he orders them to be corrected by Titus. Jerome noted the emphasis of the Greek word when explaining this passage. And Chrysostom clearly interprets it in the same sense, whose translator renders it "you should super-correct." Therefore, we translate it "proceed to correct."

13 **Through the cities]** <note>original: κατὰ πόλιν</note> That is, in the city, or through the city; meaning in each individual city, or town by town. This island was once called "the hundred-citied" <note>ἑκατόμπολις</note> because it had a hundred towns.

14 **Without crime]** <note>original: ἀνέγκλητος</note> This does not sound as if you were saying someone is free from all fault, but someone whom no one can accuse, or charge, and call into court for some crime. For so Chrysostom also interprets it. To be "unaccusable" <note>ἀνέγκλητος</note> is more than to be free from fault, because integrity is not rarely subject to accusation due to a plausible appearance of fault. But Paul does not allow even this in a Priest: for "to charge" <note>ἐγκαλεῖν</note> is to call into court with an intended crime. And a "charge" <note>ἔγκλημα</note> is a committed act for which someone could be dragged into court; "unaccusable" is one who cannot be accused in this way. And he repeats the same thing shortly after: "It is necessary for the Bishop to be without crime." Augustine, writing to Boniface, concludes that if "without crime" were the same as "without sin," no one could be admitted to the ecclesiastical ministry.

15 **In the accusation of luxury]** <note>original: ἀσωτίας</note> That is, of excess. Do not take "luxury" as referring only to lust, which Nicholas of Lyra seems to do when he mentions the sons of Eli. But what does "in the accusation of luxury" sound like to Latin ears? For Paul means those who are sober and not infamous for riotous living.

16 **As God’s steward]** The word "as" <note>ὡς</note> here does not signify a likeness, but a congruence. Therefore, "as" or "in the capacity of" <note>tanquam or ut</note> was more suitable than "just like" <note>sicut</note>.

17 **Not proud]** <note>original: μὴ αὐθάδη</note> That is, not stubborn <note>praefractum</note>, which Jerome and Ambrose read as "not forward" <note>protervum</note>, and rightly so. We translate "stubborn" <note>praefractum</note>, meaning hard and holding too tightly to one's own opinion. A certain man, who considers himself intensely learned, says he does not understand what this word means, even though it appears several times in Cicero, who writes in the third book of *Duties*: "I even disagreed with my friend Cato: he seemed to me too stubborn <note>praefractum</note> in defending the treasury so vigilantly and denying everything to the tax collectors." A similar example exists from Cicero's *Hortensius* in Nonius Marcellus: "But Aristotimus was the opposite—stubborn, iron-willed, thinking nothing good except what is right and honorable." Even from this Grammarian one could learn what "stubborn" was: namely "hard," he says, "and inflexible."

18 **Not a striker]** <note>original: μὴ πλήκτην</note> Jerome thinks this does not refer to fists, but to an abusive and quarrelsome tongue. Whence also Horace in his Odes:
<- — — — the lashes of a father's tongue. ->
As was also noted in the preceding sections.

19 **Not greedy for shameful gain]** <note>original: μὴ αἰσχροκερδῆ</note> The Translator used three words to describe this single Greek word, as if you were to say "shameful-gain-seeker." Paul means, however, that every pursuit of profit is foul for a Priest.

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER 2

...[greedy for filthy] lucre, but hospitable, a lover of good, sober, just, holy, temperate, holding fast the faithful word according to the teaching; that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to convict those who contradict. For there are many unruly men, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision, whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert whole houses, teaching things they ought not, for the sake of shameful gain. One of them, their own prophet, said: "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, slow bellies." This testimony is true; for which cause rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith, not giving heed to Jewish fables and commandments of men who turn away from the truth. All things indeed are pure to the pure: but to those who are defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure: but both their mind and their conscience are defiled. They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient, and to every good work reprobate.

<margin>II. 1 2</margin>
But you, speak the things which befit sound doctrine: that the aged men be sober,

<column-break/>

[greedy for filthy] gain, but hospitable, <gloss>20</gloss> a lover of good things, <gloss>21</gloss> sober, <gloss>22</gloss> just, pious, <gloss>23</gloss> temperate, <gloss>24</gloss> holding fast to that which is according to doctrine, <gloss>25</gloss> the faithful word: that he may be able also to exhort by sound doctrine, and to convince the gainsayers. For there are many <gloss>27</gloss> unruly, and vain talkers, and <gloss>28</gloss> deceivers of minds, especially those who are of the circumcision, <gloss>29</gloss> whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for shameful gain's sake. One of them said, <gloss>30</gloss> their own prophet: <gloss>31</gloss> "The Cretans are always liars, <gloss>31</gloss> evil beasts, <gloss>32</gloss> slow bellies." This testimony is true: for which cause <gloss>33</gloss> rebuke them sharply, <gloss>34</gloss> that they may be sound in the faith, not attending to Jewish fables and the precepts of men <gloss>35</gloss> who turn away from the truth. All things indeed are pure to the pure: <gloss>36</gloss> but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure: but both their mind and conscience are defiled. They profess that they know God, but in their deeds they deny him, <gloss>37</gloss> since they are abominable, and disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate. But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine. That the aged men be sober,

---

<note>Erasmus begins by discussing "shameful gain." He notes that Hugo de Sancto Caro wittily interpreted this as "dregs," as if there were another kind of ecclesiastical profit that was honorable. Erasmus uses this to launch a critique against the corruption of the clergy in his own time, mentioning the pursuit of inheritances and the fleecing of the elderly.</note>

<margin>A</margin>
20 **A lover of good** <note>original: φιλάγαθον / philagathon</note>, as if you were to say, *studious of good things*, or *a lover of good men*. Earlier he used the term "not a lover of good." Jerome in this place reads it as "a lover of good works." Theophylact explains it as *humane*, *modest*, and *least envious*.

21 **Sober** <note>original: σώφρονα / sophrona</note>, which Jerome translates as *chaste*, and Ambrose as *prudent*. Indeed, the word *sophron* signifies all these things, or rather, it encompasses almost everything. However, Saint Jerome notes that the ancient Translator <note>referring to the Vulgate</note>, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, translated "prudent" instead of "chaste." Yet, to offer some defense for the Translator, if the Greek word is ambiguous—meaning both *prudent* and *chaste*—how was he "deceived" by choosing "prudent"? Is prudence not fitting for a Bishop? But, as I have warned elsewhere, Saint Jerome, in his zeal for defending virginity, gathers and enlists support from everywhere, pulling whatever he can into his own ranks. Nevertheless, to the Greeks, it does not so much mean *prudent* as *sober and of sound mind*, meaning one whose mind is present and not intoxicated by any desires. Indeed, Euripides joins these two ideas in *Iphigenia in Aulis*:
-> For you do not wish to be sober, but not to think. <-
Theophylact interprets *sophrona* as *pure*, *just* toward men, and *holy* without offense in matters toward God.

22 **Just, holy** <note>original: δίκαιον, ὅσιον / dikaion, hosion</note>. Jerome interprets this to mean a holiness mixed with piety, which is referred to God. For *hagios* and *hosios* both mean "holy," pure from vices; but *hosios* specifically means "pious toward God."

23 **Temperate** <note>original: ἐγκρατῆ / enkrate</note>, that is, *holding oneself back*. As Saint Jerome indicates, some wrongly refer this only to lust, whereas it pertains to all passions—anger, greed, ambition, envy, fear—so that a Bishop should be superior to all of these. Paul saw this marvelously: one cannot be of use to others if he is himself a slave to his passions. I see no hope for public affairs unless a Prince happens to be free from all the common desires of the crowd. But today, I do not know if any class of men serves all passions more than Princes, whether you look at the secular ones or the sacred. This one thing is what has miserably corrupted the laws of the Emperors, the laws of the Popes, the Theological Schools, and church sermons; so much so that, if you weigh it up, nothing will be considered more "heretical" than if someone teaches Christian truth sincerely and purely.

24 **Holding fast** <note>original: Ἀντεχόμενον / Antechomenon</note>, which Ambrose translates as *tenacious*, and Saint Jerome as *obtaining*. Ambrose expresses the Greek word more elegantly. For *antechesthai* is properly said of one who clings to something, as if fixed with claws, and does not allow himself to be torn away.

25 **The faithful word** <note>original: πιστοῦ λόγου / pistou logou</note>, which elsewhere Ambrose translates as "human speech." It signifies speech that is certain and beyond doubt, so that one answers with certainty and presents the very face of truth.

26 **That he may be able to exhort**. In Greek it is *and to exhort* <note>original: καὶ παρακαλεῖν / kai parakalein</note>. Jerome translates it as "to console." And "in doctrine" is used for *through doctrine*. Doctrine is useful for a Bishop not only for teaching the unlearned but also for consoling the afflicted or exhorting and prodding those who are idling.

27 **Unruly** <note>original: ἀνυπότακτοι / anypotaktoi</note>, which Saint Jerome reads as "not subject." It sounds like you are saying "those who cannot be forced into order."

28 **Deceivers** <note>original: φρεναπάται / phrenapatai</note>. In Greek, this is a compound word that sounds just as if you said "deceivers of minds." Saint Jerome interprets it in this way. Now, the worst and most destructive kind of deception is when someone infects the mind—the source of all actions—with depraved opinions. For in this way, it happens that we are not only not ashamed of evil deeds, but we even hope for praise from them. Furthermore, "vain talkers" in Greek is *mataiologoi*, which does not mean a liar, but one speaking empty and frivolous things. For "vain" <note>vanus</note> is properly called a "liar" in Latin.

29 **Whose mouths must be stopped** <note>original: ἐπιστομίζειν / epistomizein</note>, that is, *to close or plug the mouth*. Jerome reads "silence should be imposed." From this passage, it is clear that Laurentius <note>Lorenzo Valla</note> read, or certainly dreamed, *epistomizein* for *apostomatizein* in Luke’s Gospel, about which we spoke there. Here it should be noted in passing that profit is always noted where it urges and infects ceremonies.

<margin>B</margin>
30 **Their own prophet** <note>original: ἴδιος αὐτῶν προφήτης / idios auton prophetes</note>. He calls a Poet a "prophet," as if he had sensed the future. He calls him "their own" because he was a Cretan himself who wrote these things about Cretans; or because he called him a prophet ironically, as if such Christians deserved such prophets; or because that book of <term>Epimenides</term> from which this verse is believed to be taken is titled "On Oracles." Though there are some who refer this testimony to <term>Callimachus of Cyrene</term>, in whose work the beginning of this poem is found: "Cretans are always liars," because they fabricated that the tomb of Jove <note>Jupiter</note> was among them, even though he, according to common opinion, was immortal. Jerome indicates it was also tossed about as a proverb among the Greeks. There exists the phrase "to act the Cretan" <note>original: πρὸς τὸ Κρῆτα</note>, witnessing to the vanity of the Cretans. To "Cretanize," one should read the *Miscellanea* of Angelo Poliziano, or our own *Adages* <note>the Chiliades</note>. For here, since we are writing annotations, we must strive for brevity as much as possible. The Greek scholia also testify to the occasion of this poem. The full verse is a <term>heroic verse</term> in Epimenides the Cretan. I am truly surprised that <term>Lefèvre d'Étaples</term> labored to render the poem into verse in this way: "The Gnosian is ever loquacious, an evil beast, slow guts." For being "loquacious" is not the same as being "a liar," nor do we call a man dedicated to food "guts" in the same way we call him a "belly": though meanwhile, we might grant that "Gnosian" is correctly placed for "Cretan," and "ever" for "always."

<margin>C</margin>
31 **Evil beasts** <note>original: θηρία / theria</note>. This does not simply mean animals, but wild and venomous beasts. The title of <term>Nicander's</term> work indicates this, as he wrote the *Theriaca*; for you would not correctly call a sheep a *therion*. Even today, the Germans sound out "Sau" <note>sow/pig</note> for such an animal.

<margin>D</margin>
32 **Slow bellies** <note>original: γαστέρες ἀργαί / gasteres argai</note>. One should read "bellies." For he calls those men dedicated to the paunch "bellies." Just as Lucilius calls those dedicated to the belly "bellies." And Terence in *Phormio* says: "Stuff it into that fat belly," referring to a parasite. A more recent manuscript from Constance preserved the genuine reading. In an older one, I discovered something ridiculous. Some learned person had noted in the margin, "The poet Memetu used this verse," which Callimachus later usurped. An unrefined scribe inserted this into the main text and put "Memetu" instead of "Epimenides." Someone might say: why delay the reader with such trifles? So that I may be believed if ever I point out a passage corrupted in a similar way—which I wish happened less frequently, especially in sacred volumes.

<margin>E</margin>
33 **Rebuke them** <note>original: ἔλεγχε αὐτούς / elenche autous</note>, that is, *to the quick and severely*. It is not just "rebuke," but "refute" or "convict."

34 **That they may be sound** <note>original: ἵνα ὑγιαίνωσιν / hina hygiainosin</note>. The reader should be advised that Paul frequently used this word, by which the Greeks signify whatever is to be approved. Hence the phrase "nothing sound," meaning everything is displeasing. Here, "that they may be sound" is nothing other than that they behave correctly. Conversely, "to be sick" <note>nosein</note> is said by them of one who is not rightly disposed.

35 **Turning away from the truth** <note>original: ἀποστρεφομένων τὴν ἀλήθειαν / apostrephomenon ten aletheian</note>, that is, "loathing the truth." For what the Greek has is more vehement.

<margin>F</margin>
36 **To the defiled** <note>original: μεμιασμένοις / memiasmenois</note>. This sounds more like those who are made impious and profaned by some ritual pollution, such as those who should be kept from sacred things. Furthermore, "All things are clean to the clean" was more correctly "All things are pure to the pure." Since they use these words when dealing with the chastity of sacred rites. For a law exists in Seneca: "Let the priestess be chaste among the chaste, pure among the pure." You see how Paul burns against none more fiercely than those who sought to abolish Christ with Mosaic ceremonies, and under this pretext seized tyranny over the Christian people.

37 **Abominable and incredulous** <note>original: βδελυκτοὶ ὄντες καὶ ἀπειθεῖς / bdelyktoi ontes kai apeitheis</note>, that is, "since they are abominable and unbelieving." Ambrose and Jerome read "execrable and disobedient," for which "intractable" or "unpersuadable" fits well. Furthermore, "profess" was more fitting here than "confess," meaning "they profess themselves to know." For *homologein* signifies this as well.

38 **Sober** <note>original: νηφάλιος / nephalios</note>, which word Jerome warns is ambiguous, signifying both *sober* (not drunk) and *watchful*. Since the verb *nephein* is also twofold.
