# TO TITUS. CHAPTER II.

<margin>A</margin> ...[That the] aged men be sober, grave, temperate, sound in faith, in love, in patience. <margin>3</margin> The aged women likewise, that they be in behavior as becomes holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things; <margin>4</margin> that they may train the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children, <margin>5</margin> to be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed. <margin>6</margin> Young men likewise exhort to be sober-minded. <margin>7</margin> In all things showing yourself a pattern of good works: in doctrine showing integrity, gravity, <margin>8</margin> sound speech, that cannot be condemned; that he who is of the contrary part may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say of us. <margin>9</margin> Exhort servants to be obedient to their own masters, and to please them well in all things; <margin>10</margin> not answering again; <margin>B</margin> not stealing <note>original: "νοσφιζομένους," meaning to embezzle or skim off the top</note>, but showing all good fidelity; that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior in all things. <margin>11</margin> For the grace of God that brings salvation has appeared to all men, <margin>12</margin> teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present world.

---

<margin>2</margin> **Grave** <note>original: "Pudicos"</note>] The Greek is *semnous* <note>σεμνούς</note>, which Ambrose more aptly translates as *graves*, meaning serious and carrying themselves with dignity.

<margin>3</margin> **Prudent**] The Greek is *sōphronas* <note>σώφρονας</note>, meaning moderate or modest. Saint Jerome, in his usual manner, translates this as *pudicos* (chaste). To ensure it does not seem absurd to command chastity to the elderly, he adds: "lest in their later years they seem to shamefully indulge in lust." Thus, even in the holiest men, one may find a trace of human weakness. Chrysostom <note>a 4th-century Church Father known for his preaching</note> interprets *sōphronas* as referring to mental moderation, because that age, due to mental frailty, tends to flare up immoderately. Just as he commands them to be "sober" because the elderly are often drowsy and cold; then he wants them to be "grave" because they often act foolishly as they enter their second childhood. Finally, he commands them to be "sound," because the common run of old men often lose their wits.

<margin>4</margin> **In holy behavior**] The Greek is *en katastēmati hieroprepeis* <note>ἐν καταστήματι ἱεροπρεπεῖς</note>, which is effectively saying: in that dress, gait, and bodily movement which befits holy matrons dedicated to God. Ambrose translates this as *in a state worthy of religion*, as if explaining the compound word *hieroprepeis*; he refers *katastēma* (behavior/state) not only to clothing but to the entire habit and gesture of the body. Saint Jerome explains it the same way.

<margin>5</margin> **Not false accusers**] The Greek is *mē diabolous* <note>μὴ διαβόλους</note>, meaning not slanderers or informers. In Jerome we read *incentrices* (inciters), though I suspect the text might be corrupted, even if he also explains it as "accusers."

<margin>6</margin> **Not given to much wine**] That is, not addicted to much wine. Older women are often prone to this vice.

<margin>7</margin> **Teachers of good things**] The Greek is *kalodidaskalous* <note>καλοδιδασκάλους</note>, meaning those who teach honorable things. I believe this is mentioned because some women of those years act as madams, serving the wickedness of others.

<margin>8</margin> **That they may teach prudence**] The Greek is *hina sōphronizōsi* <note>ἵνα σωφρονίζωσι</note>, meaning to make them sober or modest. Jerome reads this as "that they may train them to chastity," twisting everything he can toward virginity (which he favored) in his usual way—not without suspicion or criticism. Ambrose reads "that they may instruct."

<margin>9</margin> **Young women**] The Greeks refer this object to the verb "to train." Understand that the older matrons are commanded to teach the young girls to love their husbands.

<margin>10</margin> **Prudent**] The Greek is *sōphronas* <note>σώφρονας</note>, which Jerome again reads as "chaste." But because "chaste" or "pure" (*hagnas*) follows immediately after, perhaps "sober" or "prudent" would fit better here.

<margin>11</margin> **Keepers at home**] The Greek is *oikourous* <note>οἰκουρούς</note>, which sounds like "guardians of the house," implying they stay at home and care for household matters, which is the chief praise of women. Hence the Ancients, on the authority of Plutarch, used to paint Venus standing on a tortoise, because that animal never leaves its home—a symbol of the upright mistress of a family.

<margin>12</margin> **That it be not blasphemed**] This is thought to be added because of those who might have a pagan or Jewish husband.

<margin>13</margin> **That they be sober**] Jerome here reads "chaste," consistent with his style.

<margin>14</margin> **Show yourself**] The Greek is *parechomenos* <note>παρεχόμενος</note>. Ambrose reads it this way, agreeing with the Greeks. "A pattern" (*typon*) means a form or a model rather than just an "example."

<margin>15</margin> **In doctrine, in integrity**] The Greeks have it: *in doctrine, integrity, gravity, incorruption, sound speech*. Chrysostom reads it almost this way, though it is unclear where he got the word for "abundance" unless he found *euporian* written instead of *adiaphthorian* (integrity). His translator says: *In doctrine, he says, abundance, honesty, sound speech, irreproachable,* yet I find no such thing in the Greek Chrysostom. Furthermore, in some codices, "integrity" is added twice. There is nothing corresponding to the first instance in Ambrose, Jerome, or Chrysostom. Theophylact does not touch upon "integrity" <note>adiaphthorian</note>. Jerome also twists this word "integrity" toward virginity, whereas in my opinion it more clearly describes a mind that is uncorrupted by desires—not by anger, ambition, or greed. Saint Hilary refers to this passage differently: *showing yourself in all things a pattern of good deeds, teaching the sound word with veneration.* What is "gravity" in Greek, Hilary seems to have translated as "with veneration." "Sound word" is *logon hygiē*. Saint Jerome notes that the things following could refer to the integrity of doctrine, but "sound speech" stands in the way. But to me, there seems to be no reason 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> [that they] be, 2 grave, 3 modest, sound in faith, charity, and patience. The aged women likewise, 4 that they be in behavior that becomes religion, 5 not slanderers, not 6 given to much wine, 7 that they may teach honorable things, 8 that they might make the 9 young women modest, to love their husbands, to love their children, 10 to be sober, pure, 11 guardians of the home, good, subject to their husbands: 12 lest the word of God be spoken of ill. Young men likewise exhort, 13 that they be sober. In all things 14 presenting yourself as a model of good works 15 in doctrine, integrity, gravity, sound speech, 16 irreproachable: so that he who opposes 17 may be filled with shame, 18 having nothing evil to say of you. Exhort servants, 19 that they <margin>B</margin> obey their masters, and please them in all things, 20 not talking back, 21 not stealing, 22 but showing all good faith, so that they may adorn the doctrine of our Savior God in all things. 23 For the grace 24 of God has shone forth, bringing salvation to all men, 25 instructing us, 26 that having denied impiety and 27 worldly lusts, 28 we should live soberly and justly and piously in the present age.

---

to be offended by this. For although no one teaches without speaking, it matters a great deal *how* one speaks.

<margin>16</margin> **Irreproachable**] The Greek is *akatagnōston*. This can also mean something that cannot be looked down upon; that is, teaching with authority.

<margin>17</margin> **Are ashamed**] The Greek is *entrapē*, meaning "to feel shame," which is often translated as "to be confounded." Ambrose and Jerome read "revere."

<margin>18</margin> **Having nothing to say**] This means having no power to say anything, or having no grounds for what he says. For "to have" <note>echein</note> with an infinitive verb signifies "to be able" among the Greeks.

<margin>C</margin> <margin>19</margin> **To be subject**] Saint Jerome warns that this passage can be read in two ways. One way is to take it as "servants ought to be subject to masters in all things," where the phrase "in all things" refers to the preceding verb. The other way is to understand it as "servants ought to be pleasing in all things," following the Greek word order. Modern Greek manuscripts follow this second way. Furthermore, Jerome interprets "pleasing" <note>euarestous</note> not as those who satisfy and please their masters, but as those who do not displease themselves and are content with their lot, whatever it may be. I do not know if this interpretation is forced; it certainly differs from the Greek interpretation and does not fit with what follows: "not talking back." Earlier, Paul used "pleasing" to mean that which is acceptable and pleasing. It is strange that Ambrose read "the best" <note>optimos</note>, unless there is a mistake in the text or his manuscript had *exairetous*. Certainly, "pleasing" here refers to those who strive to please in every way, which <margin>D</margin> fits better with "not talking back."

<margin>20</margin> **Not talking back**] The Greek is *mē antilegontas*. Ambrose elegantly renders this as "responsatores" (those who snap back).

<margin>21</margin> **Not stealing**] The Greek is *mē nosphizomenous*. Jerome reads "stealing." Indeed, *nosphizein* is to pluck something away and take it by stealth when you do not dare to take the whole thing—as servants often do.

<margin>22</margin> **But in all things**] "But all fidelity." Jerome and Ambrose both read "all fidelity."

<margin>23</margin> **For it has appeared**] The Greek is *epephanē*. Jerome and Ambrose translate this as "shone forth." For "appears" refers to what is seen, even if it is not truly there. But "shines forth" <note>epiphainetai</note> describes that which becomes conspicuous and illustrious. For previously, the grace was seen hiding in a narrow corner among the Jews, and even there it was obscured by trust in legalistic works; now it has been made illustrious even to the class of servants. Yet at that time, the grace of the Gospel had not become known to *every* single human being, but no *kind* of human being was excluded.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>24</margin> **Of God and Savior**] The Greek is different: "the saving grace of God." Jerome and Ambrose read it otherwise. However, in the very ancient Greek manuscript of Chrysostom, we read *sōtērios* (saving/salutary). Theophylact certainly reads *sōtērios*. In the more corrected Latin texts, the conjunction "and" is not added. The article "the" <note>hē</note> before "saving" is not idle; it declares that there is no salvation except through God's grace. As for "Savior," it can be understood as either the Father or the Son. Jerome says either Christ himself is the living and subsisting grace of God the Father, or this is the grace of Christ the God-Savior, and we are not saved by our own merit. The same applies to the next phrase: "adorn the doctrine of God our Savior." There is very little difference between "Savior" (*sōtēros*) and "Saving" (*sōtērios*).

<margin>25</margin> **Instructing us**] The Greek is not *didaskousa* (teaching), but *paideuousa*, a word derived from "children." This implies either that grace gently teaches us as if we were unlearned, or that it maternally <margin>F</margin> corrects us when we have fallen through ignorance.

<margin>26</margin> **Denying**] This is a past participle. It could be translated as "worldly desires having been denied," as Ambrose reads: "impiety and worldly desires having been denied." This passage should be noted by those who, wrongly trusting in grace, neglect good works, whereas grace frees us from sins for this very reason: so that we may hereafter devote ourselves to pious works.

<margin>27</margin> **Worldly lusts**] That is, mundane desires. In Latin, "secular" sometimes refers to things that happen every hundred years, like "secular games." But here it is connected to the phrase "in this present age."

<margin>28</margin> **Soberly**] The Greek is *sōphronōs*. Here too Jerome translates it as "chastely" <note>pudice</note>, in his usual manner, so as not to appear inconsistent.

<meta>This page continues the translation of the commentary on the Epistle to Titus. It moves from Chapter 2 to the beginning of Chapter 3, focusing on the theological nature of Christ's appearance and the moral duties of believers toward authorities.</meta>

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER III.

<margin>A</margin> 13 ...looking for the blessed hope and the appearance of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ,
14 who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify for himself a peculiar people <note>original: "περιούσιον," meaning a special or treasured possession</note>, zealous for good works. Speak these things, and exhort, and rebuke with all authority.
<margin>III.</margin> 15 Let no one despise you. Remind them to be subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates, to be ready for every good work,
2 to speak evil of no one, to be no brawlers, but gentle, showing all meekness toward all men.
<margin>B</margin> 3 For we ourselves were also once foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving various lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another.
4 But when the kindness and love of God our Savior toward man appeared, not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to His mercy He saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit,
6 whom He poured out on us abundantly through Jesus.

---

<margin>C</margin> 29 *And the coming*] <note>original: "ἐπιφάνειαν"</note>, that is, the apparition or the shedding of light, as it is translated elsewhere. Although the same word also signifies "coming," it implies a coming with splendor, just as when the sun emerges.
30 *Of the great God and Savior*] <note>original: "τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ καὶ Σωτῆρος"</note>. This can be read in such a way that both titles refer to Christ (as God and Savior), or the first refers to the Father and the second to Christ. John Chrysostom and Theophylact attribute both to Christ, as does Jerome, who exults against the Arians <note>A 4th-century group who denied the full divinity of Christ</note> as if he were the victor, though the speech is plainly ambiguous. Indeed, it might seem to favor the Arians more than us. First, it cannot be denied that the Greek phrasing is ambiguous and can equally support either meaning. Why would you fight a heretic using a passage that is completely uncertain? If one presses them with the consensus of interpreters, certainly Ambrose—a most eminent man and orthodox Bishop—takes them separately, so that "great God" refers to the Father and "Savior" to Christ. I will transcribe his own words: *He says these things are the blessed hope of believers, who expect the coming of the glory of the great God, which is to be revealed with Christ as judge, in whom the power and glory of God the Father will be seen, so that they may receive the reward of their faith. For Christ redeemed us for this purpose: that pursuing a pure life with good works, we might be heirs of the kingdom of God.* Does he not here openly say the Father will reveal His glory with Christ as the judge? Yet in Holy Scripture, "the coming" is usually attributed not to the Father, but to the Son. Nor is it simply called the coming of the Father here, but the coming of his glory, which we expect while situated in humility. Then our majesty will appear, when the glory of the great God the Father and our Savior Jesus is revealed. Why do we fear the Arians here, when Paul in so many places attributes the name of "God" to the Father and calls the Son "Lord"? If the Son were only called "God" as clearly as he is in the beginning of the Gospel of John, would that not suffice against all Arians? Finally, some Arians also accept this passage as referring to the Son, and yet they do not believe what we believe. For they confess him as a "great God," but deny he is the "true God," and this is their impiety. Although the omission of the article in the Greek books lends some weight to the other opinion: "of the great God and Savior." He would have distinguished the person more clearly if he had said "and *the* Savior" <note>original: "καὶ τοῦ Σωτῆρος"</note>. I wonder what that Scholar <note>likely referring to a medieval commentator like Peter Lombard</note> was following when he interpreted "great God" as the Holy Spirit. Perhaps he was looking for a passage where the Holy Spirit was explicitly called God. As for Thomas <note>Aquinas</note> attributing the "appearance of grace" to the Holy Spirit (to whom the office of Christ's conception is peculiarly ascribed), I do not think this passage can be twisted to fit that.

<margin>D</margin> 31 *An acceptable people*] <note>original: "περιούσιον"</note>, that is, "peculiar" or "special." Saint Jerome, in his commentaries on this passage, denies that he could learn from any secular man skilled in letters what *periousios* meant; but he gathered from Deuteronomy (from where Paul seems to have taken this phrase) that it meant a people chosen as a special treasure out of all peoples. Again, in Psalm 24, "The Lord has chosen for Himself a possession," the Septuagint and Theodotion translated this as "a wealth of possession," while Aquila and the Fifth Edition used *periousion*, changing the syllable but not the sense. Symmachus, instead of the Greek *periousion*, used *exaureton* for the Hebrew *segullah*, meaning "excellent" or "distinguished," because in another volume using the Latin tongue, he translated it as "peculiar." For Jerome thinks there is very little difference between *periousion* and *epiousion* <note>The word used for "daily" in the Lord's Prayer</note>. Furthermore, this variety arises from the ambiguity of the prepositions *peri* and *epi*. For those who translate it as "possession" and "peculiar" looked to the fact that *ousia* signifies substance (that is, resources and possession) and *peri* means "around"—just as we call "peculiar" that which is among our goods and, as they say, "in our own coin." Conversely, those who translated it as "excellent" looked to the fact that *peri* sometimes signifies eminence and *ousia* signifies essence; as if you were to say, "surpassing other substances." He thinks that the phrase in the Lord's Prayer, "our *epiousion* bread," can be taken in the same sense: that is, not common bread, but that extraordinary bread sent from heaven (a matter we have touched upon in its own place). Furthermore, regarding what Faber <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, a contemporary humanist</note> adds—that to Jerome *periousion* and *geneon* are the same—I wonder where he got that, unless perhaps he thinks "peculiar" is the same as "noble" or "true." Just as Symmachus, as I said, translated "peculiar." Augustine, in his *Letter Against the Letter of the Pelagian*, chapter 13, reads it as "an abundant people."
32 *follower*] <note>original: "ζηλωτὴν"</note>, that is, an "emulator." And so does Ambrose.
33 *With all authority*] <note>original: "μετὰ πάσης ἐπιταγῆς"</note>. Not that he orders him to be overbearing, but that he wants these things to be diligently commanded and enjoined upon the people.

<column-break/>

13 Waiting for that blessed hope and the 29 shedding of light of the glory of 30 the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ,
14 who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify for himself 31 a peculiar people, 32 a follower of good works. These things speak, and exhort, and rebuke 33 with all diligence in commanding.
<margin>III.</margin> 1 Let no one despise you. Admonish them to be subject to princes and powers, to obey magistrates, to be ready for every good work,
2 to speak evil of no one, not to be fighters, but humane, showing all gentleness toward all men. For we were also once foolish, unbelieving, wandering, serving various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, pursuing each other with hatred. But after the goodness and love toward men of our Savior God appeared,
5 not by works which are in righteousness, which we were doing, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us richly, through Jesus.
<meta>catchword: Jesus</meta>

---

34 *Let no one despise you*] <note>original: "Μηδείς σου περιφρονείτω"</note>. Saint Jerome notes that this is not the same word Paul used when writing to Timothy: "Let no one despise your youth." There the word is *kataphroneitō*. For *kataphronein* is said of one who looks down on something and makes nothing of it, which can even be taken in a good sense—as if someone were to despise torture or death for Christ. But *periphronein* is said of one who, out of pride, seems to himself better and wiser than another. He cites (without naming the author) a line from Aristophanes' *The Clouds*, where Socrates is introduced saying: *I walk the air and look down upon the sun* <note>original: "Αεροβατῶ καὶ περιφρονῶ τὸν ἥλιον"</note>, interpreting it this way: "I climb through the air, and I know myself to be of more value than the sun." Paul therefore wants Titus to live in such a way that no one can seem better to himself than Titus, even though Titus is a Bishop.
1 <insert>to obey the word</insert> <note>original: "πειθαρχεῖν"</note>. This properly means to obey magistrates.
2 *Not litigious*] <note>original: "ἀμάχους"</note>, that is, "not brawlers," which means not quarrelsome and contentious.
3 *unbelieving*] <note>original: "ἀπειθεῖς"</note>. Ambrose translates as "disobedient"; Jerome reads it as "unobeying."
<margin>E</margin> 4 *And humanity*] <note>original: "καὶ ἡ φιλανθρωπία"</note>, that is, "and love toward men," not "humanness" <note>original: "ἀνθρωπότης"</note>. For some in this place interpret "humanity" as the incarnation of Christ, among whose number is Thomas [Aquinas], who nevertheless adds a second interpretation. Furthermore, what Theophylact explains regarding the "assumed human nature" is not to be understood as if the Father assumed it, but that the Father so loved the human race that out of a desire to save it, He sent His only Son to earth, so that having become man He might draw us to Himself. But Paul here speaks of the Father of Jesus. What is here translated "humanity," Jerome interprets as "clemency" in his Commentaries. And for "appeared" <note>original: "ἐπεφάνη"</note>, Jerome translates as "shone forth," that is, it was made manifest through the incarnate Son. For the distinction of Thomas which he introduces here has no place, because the Greek word Paul used can signify nothing other than "eagerness and love toward men," the opposite of which is *misanthropia* <note>hatred of humans</note>. And the fact that he calls God "Savior" seems to refer more to the Father than to the Son. Certainly both Ambrose and Jerome interpret it as the Father. No one has yet interpreted it as the Son. Furthermore, Jerome clearly stands in the way of this being taken as the whole Trinity, as he demonstrates that in this chapter the three persons are distinctly expressed, working together in the business of human salvation. These are his words in the Commentaries: *Let us attend diligently,* he says, *and we will find in the present chapter the most manifest Trinity. For the benignity and clemency of our Savior God—none other than God the Father—through the washing of regeneration and the renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom He poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ, etc.* Ambrose is less evident, but writes the same thing: *For He gave,* he says, *by His mercy He saved us through Christ, by whose grace being reborn we have received the Holy Spirit.* You see, Reader, how he distinguishes three persons here. I would not burden the Reader with these things, except that this passage, although clear, has been frequently attacked by slander. We see here, however, that the Father is called "Savior," just as in the previous chapter.
<margin>F</margin> 5 *Not by works of righteousness*] <note>original: "Οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων τῶν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ"</note>, that is, "not from works which are in righteousness." He means the works of the Mosaic Law, about which he writes much to the Romans. Although the orthodox interpret this as referring to *all* works of men. Those who cry out that my voice is the "deceiver of thousands" whenever we extol the grace of God by downplaying our merits—why do they not protest against Paul? He so often rejects our works and so often insists upon the grace and mercy of the Lord. Why do they not summon to court Chrysostom, Theophylact, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome—briefly, all the Ancients, who filled their books with such words?
6 *And the renewing of the Holy Spirit*] The Greek phrasing is ambiguous because "through" <note>original: "διὰ"</note> requires the genitive case. It can be read as "and the renewing of the Holy Spirit" (repeating the preposition), or "through the renewing of the Holy Spirit." And so indeed Jerome reads it, arranging this passage in his Commentaries. Chrysostom interprets it no differently, repeating it thus: *For this is what he says: through the renewal of the Holy Spirit.*
7 *Abundantly*] <note>original: "πλουσίως"</note>. Which Jerome translates as "richly." Augustine, writing to Valentinus, reads it as "most wealthily." Similarly in his book *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, Book 1, chapter 27.

<sig>8</sig> <meta>catchword: I will</meta>

The commentator defends a reading that emphasizes God the Father's love and mercy as the source of salvation, rather than human works or merit.</summary>

# TO TITUS CHAP. III.

<margin>A</margin> 7 ...of Jesus Christ our Savior, that having been justified by His grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life. <note>original Greek: Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν, Ἵνα δικαιωθέντες...</note>
8 This is a faithful saying; and concerning these things I want you to affirm constantly, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable to men. <note>original Greek: Πιστὸς ὁ λόγος...</note>
9 But avoid foolish disputes, genealogies, contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and useless. <note>original Greek: Μωρὰς δὲ ζητήσεις...</note>
10 Reject a divisive person <note>original Greek: Αἱρετικὸν ἄνθρωπον, a "heretical" or factious man</note> after the first and second admonition,
11 knowing that such a person is warped and sinning, being self-condemned. <note>original Greek: αὐτοκατάκριτος</note>
12 When I send Artemas to you, or Tychicus, be diligent to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there.
13 Send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey diligently, that they may lack nothing.
<margin>B</margin> 14 And let our people also learn to maintain good works, to meet urgent needs, that they may not be unfruitful.
15 All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with you all. Amen.

->It was written from Nicopolis of Macedonia.<-

->THE END OF THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO TITUS.<-

<column-break/>

7 Jesus Christ our Savior, that having been justified by His grace, we might be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life. <note>This is Erasmus's Latin translation of the preceding Greek verses.</note>
8 This is an indubitable saying: I want you to confirm these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to be foremost in good works; for these are honest and useful to men.
9 But omit foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and legal battles: for they are useless and superfluous.
10 Flee from a sectarian author <note>original Latin: "Sectarium auctorem," referring to a heretic</note> after one and another admonition,
11 knowing that he who is of this sort is subverted, and he sins being condemned by himself.
12 But when I send Artemas to you or Tychicus, do your best to come to me at Nicopolis: for I have decided to winter there.
13 Lead forth Zenas the legal expert and Apollos studiously, lest anything be lacking to them.
<margin>B</margin> 14 And let our people also learn to be foremost in good works for necessary uses, so that they are not unfruitful.
15 All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in faith. Grace be with all of you. Amen.

->Written from Nicopolis of Macedonia.<-

->THE END OF THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO TITUS.<-

---

<margin>8</margin> **I want you to confirm**] <note>original Greek: διαβεβαιοῦσθαι</note>, which is an ambiguous word: for it can also mean "to be confirmed."
<margin>9</margin> **That they may be careful to be foremost in good works**] <note>original Greek: ἵνα φροντίζωσι καλῶν ἔργων προΐστασθαι</note>. Ambrose rendered it thus: "that they may be solicitous toward the effect of good works." Those things are especially to be urged which lead to a life of piety. *In good works* [bonis operibus] is in the dative case here, not the ablative, and corresponds to the prefix "pre-" [in "praeesse"]. For "to be foremost in good works" is said in the same way one is called "prefect of the grain supply" or "prefect of the military."
<margin>10</margin> **Who believe**] <note>original Greek: οἱ πεπιστευκότες</note>, that is, "those who have believed." This is how Ambrose reads it.
<margin>11</margin> **And genealogies**] <note>original Greek: γενεαλογίας</note>. Which Ambrose renders as "enumerations of origins." And "admonition" is better than "correction," as the same author indicates. Furthermore, he calls someone a "heretic," if I am not mistaken, not because they disagree with any particular opinions of the doctors, but because they are factious—though he who is the author of a heresy is indeed factious. This is how Chrysostom interprets the passage in 1 Corinthians chapter 11: *There must be heresies.* Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret this regarding perverse dogmas.
<margin>12</margin> **Legal battles**] <note>original Greek: μάχας νομικάς</note>, that is, legal fights, which Jerome explains as "those which come from the Law." *Avoid* <note>original Greek: περιΐστασο</note>, about which we have spoken above.
<margin>13</margin> **After a first and second**] It was more Latinate to say "after one and another." And this is how Jerome reads it. Ambrose reads "after the first," interpreting that they should be warned only once, lest, if it happens too often, they become hardened in their evil; rather, they should be avoided so that, left to themselves, they might either grow cold with no one opposing them, or perish alone. We follow the Ambrosian reading today, we who do not avoid one once convicted of heresy if he relapses, but rather we burn him. Tertullian, in his book *On the Prescription of Heretics*, reports it the same way as Ambrose.
<margin>14</margin> **Avoid**] <note>original Greek: παραιτοῦ</note>, that is, reject: it is not the same as the word for "avoid" used just above <note>original Greek: περιΐστασο</note>. This is the passage which a certain elderly theologian, and a particularly severe one, produced in a Council. When the question arose whether there was any place in the canonical scriptures which ordered a heretic to be punished with the death penalty, he said, "*Devita, devita!*" [Avoid, avoid!], thinking that in Latin "to avoid" [*devitare*] meant "to take from life" [*de vita tollere*]. <note>This is a famous Erasmus pun: the monk confused the verb "devitare" (avoid) with the phrase "de vita" (from life/execution).</note> Lest anyone suspect this is my own invention, I received it from John Colet, a man

<column-break/>

<margin>C</margin> of proven integrity, under whose presidency the matter was conducted. Let us go now and deny that there is danger in erring over words. In this way, legal experts might hang a thief because the law orders a "brigand" to be punished by the head [capital punishment], and the common people of the Gauls call a thief a "brigand." In this way, physicians frequently err, at great risk to our heads, while through ignorance of vocabulary they offer poison instead of a remedy.
<margin>15</margin> **Condemned by his own judgment**] <note>original Greek: αὐτοκατάκριτος</note>, a compound word, meaning "condemned by himself," who stubbornly disagrees with everyone. Cyprian, in the third epistle of the first book, reads "damned by his own self." It was more correctly "condemned by himself," that is, condemned even if no judge pronounces on him, just as we say "self-taught" <note>original Greek: αὐτοδίδακτος</note>. Furthermore, that phrase "he is subverted" is <note>original Greek: ἐξέστραπται</note> in Greek, which can also be understood as "he has fallen away from life" or "turned aside." And it can never be translated as "he errs," but rather he errs in such a way that he is self-condemned, even if no one condemns him, as one who, having been warned once and again, refused to repent.
<margin>16</margin> **Hasten**] <note>original Greek: σπούδασον</note>, that is, "be eager" or "take care." Nicopolis is a city of Thrace, as Chrysostom supposes. Theophylact wrote that it sits upon the river Ister [the Danube]. Jerome thinks it is the one which received this name because of the victory by which Caesar Augustus defeated Antony and Cleopatra. But it is well established that this victory took place at the promontory of Actium in Epirus. Hence Suetonius calls it the "Actian victory." And Jerome, in his preface to these Commentaries, clearly declares that he thinks Paul was speaking of Nicopolis in Epirus.
<margin>17</margin> **Expert in the law**] <note>original Greek: νομικόν</note>. Jerome reads, "teacher of the law."
<margin>18</margin> **Carefully send forward**] <note>original Greek: σπουδαίως</note>. Or rather, "escort" or "accompany," an office we usually perform for guests. And Saint Jerome interprets it in this sense.
<margin>20</margin> **Grace be with you**] The Greeks read, "Grace be with all of you." Jerome approves of this reading, testifying that in some manuscripts two words were added, "of our Lord." Ambrose reads, "The grace of God be with all of you." The Constance manuscript had, "The grace of God be with all of you. Amen."

# ARGUMENT
->of the<-
# EPISTLE OF PAUL
->TO PHILEMON.<-

He sends this letter from Rome. The reason for the Letter is as follows: Onesimus, the servant of Philemon, fled, and after coming to the Apostle, he was instructed in the faith by him and became useful to him in ministry. Therefore, Paul writes to Philemon regarding him, commending Onesimus to him so that he might look upon him with sincerity and no longer hold him as a slave, but as a brother. He also urged him to prepare lodging for him, so that if he comes, he might find a place to stay. And thus he concludes the Letter.

---

# ON THE EPISTLE TO
# P H I L E M O N
->*The Argument by*<-
# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

The Greeks record that this Philemon was a Phrygian <term>Phrygian: a person from Phrygia, an ancient region in modern-day Turkey</term> by birth. That nation was considered so unmanageable and servile that it was even boasted of in a Greek proverb: *A Phrygian is improved by blows* <note>original Latin: *Phryx plagis emendatur*</note>. Nevertheless, Paul held Philemon among his closest friends because of his piety and his services to the holy people. His servant, Onesimus, had fled to Rome, and not without committing a theft, as servants are often prone to do. There, having heard Paul—who was then in chains—he embraced the Gospel doctrine and served Paul in prison. However, lest the master be tormented in his mind by the flight of his servant, Paul sends him back. Yet, with wonderful zeal and wonderful courtesy, he reconciles the servant—both a fugitive and a thief—to his master. He offers himself in the meantime as a guarantor, ready to provide a defense if the servant had stolen anything during his flight. For he writes from his chains through the said Onesimus, whom he even calls his son.

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL
## THE APOSTLE TO
### PHILEMON.

1 Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, to Philemon our beloved and fellow-laborer,
2 and to our beloved Apphia, and to Archippus our fellow-soldier, and to the church in your house:
3 Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
4 I thank my God, always making mention of you in my prayers,
5 hearing of your love and faith, which you have toward the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints,
6 so that the sharing of your faith may become effective in the knowledge of every good thing which is in you toward Christ Jesus.
7 For we have great joy and consolation in your love, because the hearts <note>original: "σπλάγχνα" (splangchna), literally "bowels" or "entrails," used in the Bible to refer to the seat of deep emotion or the "heart."</note> of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother.
8 Therefore, though I might have much boldness in Christ to command you what is fitting,
9 yet for love’s sake I rather appeal to you—being such a one as Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.
10 I appeal to you for my son, whom I have begotten in my chains, Onesimus,
11 who once was unprofitable to you, but now is profitable to you and to me, whom I have sent back.
12 You therefore receive him, that is, my own heart.
13 Whom I wished to keep with me, that on your behalf he might minister to me in the chains of the Gospel;
14 but without your consent I wanted to do nothing, so that your good deed might not be as it were by necessity, but voluntary.
15 For perhaps he departed for a while for this reason, that you might receive him... <note>The text continues on the next page.</note>

---

<margin>1</margin> **TO OUR BELOVED** helper] <note>original Greek: ἀγαπητῷ καὶ συνεργῷ (agapētō kai synergō)</note> that is, *to the beloved and helper, or co-worker*. And so it is read in the ancient Latin codices, in Jerome, Ambrose, and Chrysostom. Of these, Ambrose paraphrases it as "a sharer in our labors." For "beloved" here is a noun, not a participle, which Jerome also notes in his commentaries explaining this Epistle. He considers that the Greek term *agapētō* sounds more like "worthy of love" than merely "loved." He argues there is a real difference: a person might be "loved" <note>Greek: ἀγαπημένος (agapēmenos)</note> without being "worthy of love" <note>Greek: ἀγαπητός (agapētos)</note>. For example, when we love our enemies by Christ's command, they are indeed "loved" by us, but they are not "worthy of love." See how Jerome did not consider it a small matter to note even in his accurate commentaries, yet to some I seem to be pointing out nothing at all.

<margin>2</margin> *And to Apphia our dearest sister*] <note>Greek: Καὶ Ἀπφίᾳ τῇ ἀγαπητῇ</note> that is, *And to Apphia the beloved*. Chrysostom believes she was the wife of Philemon. Chrysostom notes Paul’s strategy here: he brings in many people so that he might more easily persuade. He joins Timothy, whom he calls "brother" (though he usually calls him "son"), because the title of brother suited his authority here. Then he gives Philemon twin titles, "beloved" and "co-worker," so that he might agree, and to him he joins Apphia, whom he calls "beloved." Again, he adds Archippus, whom he calls a "fellow-soldier" <note>Greek: συστρατιώτην (systratiōtēn)</note>. To the same purpose, he calls himself a "prisoner of Jesus Christ." It is quite inhumane to deny a prisoner. Such was the Apostle's concern to reconcile one lowly fugitive.

<margin>3</margin> *Which is the church in your house*] <note>Greek: καὶ τῇ κατ' οἶκόν σου ἐκκλησίᾳ</note>. He refers to the household, I believe. Therefore, we translate it as "congregation." Chrysostom indicates this clearly enough when explaining this passage. However, since this Epistle is written to several people, it was uncertain to whom the pronoun "your" referred—to Philemon, or to Archippus, who immediately preceded him in the list—unless one considers that he soon turns the entire discourse to Philemon alone. Jerome indicated this before us.

<margin>4</margin> *Always making mention of you*] The adverb "always" <note>Greek: ἀεὶ (aei)</note> can be referred to either the preceding part or the following part. It does not matter much to the sense whether we understand him as always giving thanks, or always being mindful in his prayers to God. Jerome also noted this, lest anyone complain that I am bringing up frivolous matters.

<margin>5</margin> *In the Lord Jesus, and toward all the saints*] It is strange why the Latin translator changed the grammatical case, since in the Greek it is the accusative case in both instances: *toward the Lord Jesus, and toward all the saints*. This is how Ambrose and Chrysostom read it.

<margin>6</margin> *May become evident*] The Greeks read *energēs*, which means "effective" or "active." If it were *enargēs* (with an alpha), it would mean "evident." It seems the Translator read it this way. Jerome warns that in Greek it is better held as *energēs*, which he explains as "effective" or "working," so that we understand faith to be proven and validated by deeds. Chrysostom and Theophylact <term>Theophylact: an 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and Bible commentator</term> explain it in this sense. It is strange, however, what Ambrose followed when he read "accepted" instead of "evident" or "effective."

<margin>7</margin> *Of every good work*] The word "work" is redundant; it is not found in either the Greek or the ancient Latin codices. Furthermore, it is not found in Jerome, Ambrose, Chrysostom, or Theophylact; it is simply "of every good thing."

<column-break/>

1 PAUL, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy the brother, to Philemon the beloved and our colleague,
2 And to Apphia the beloved, and to Archippus our fellow-soldier, and to the congregation which is in your house:
3 Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
4 I give thanks to my God, always making mention of you in my prayers,
5 Since I hear of your charity and faith, which you have toward the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints,
6 That the communication of your faith may become effective in the recognition of every good thing which is in you toward Christ Jesus.
7 For we have much joy and consolation in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother.
8 Wherefore, although I have much confidence in Christ to enjoin upon you that which was your duty:
9 Yet for love's sake I rather appeal, being such a one as Paul the old man, but now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.
10 I appeal to you for my son, whom I begot in my chains, Onesimus,
11 Who was once useless to you, but now is very useful to you and to me, whom I have sent back.
12 But you receive him, that is, my own heart,
13 Whom I desired to retain with me, so that on your behalf he might minister to me in the chains of the Gospel:
14 But without your opinion I wished to do nothing, lest your good should be as if of necessity, but spontaneous.
15 For perhaps for this reason he withdrew for a...

---

<margin>8</margin> *In Christ Jesus*] Before these words, I find in the Greek codices, "that which is in you." And this is read in Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Jerome. Ambrose reads "which is in us," referring it to the "recognition" rather than the "good." And it is clearer to say "toward Christ Jesus," so that this phrase refers to "faith": *that the communication of your faith may be effective toward or in Christ Jesus*, to whose glory the communication of your faith looks. Indeed, in most Greek codices I find written, "unto Christ Jesus" <note>Greek: εἰς Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν</note>. But if we read "in Christ Jesus," it should be translated "through Christ Jesus," so that you understand the recognition of good, or the good itself, to be in us by the benefit of Christ, not by our own merit. However, although Theophylact interprets this as living and working faith in us, the Translator, either not perceiving this or ignoring it, always inserts his word "evident," though it does not fit the explanation.

<margin>9</margin> *For I had great joy and consolation*] In Greek it is, *We have much grace in your love*. The Translator read "joy" <note>Greek: charan</note> instead of "grace" <note>Greek: charin</note>, and Jerome and Ambrose seem to have followed that reading, along with Chrysostom. I think it is the original and true reading, because we often find scribes slipping in these types of similar-sounding words. And yet, I have noted elsewhere that "grace" is sometimes used for "joy" in Paul's writing. Theophylact reads "grace" but interprets it as "joy."

<margin>10</margin> *They have rested*] <note>Greek: ἀναπέπαυται (anapepautai)</note> that is, *they have been refreshed or revived*.

<margin>11</margin> *Much confidence*] <note>Greek: παῤῥησίαν (parrēsian)</note>. I have noted this word frequently.

<margin>12</margin> *That which pertains to the matter*] <note>Greek: τὸ ἀνῆκον (to anēkon)</note> that is, *fitting or convenient*. For he feels that it is Philemon's duty, yet he asks it of him as if it were a favor or beyond duty.

<margin>13</margin> *Since you are such as Paul*] The Greek has it thus: *rather I appeal, being such a one as Paul the aged*. For he feels that, while as Paul, an old man, and finally a prisoner of Jesus Christ, he could by his own right command Philemon what was fair, he preferred instead to use appeals, mindful of love rather than authority. Ambrose reads, "since *you* are such a one." But here the logic of grammar clearly protests, unless perhaps one likes to think Paul committed a solecism <term>solecism: a grammatical mistake or intentional break from standard syntax</term>, or that the nominative case was used for the dative, and the pronoun "to you" is understood—a form of speech occasionally found among the Greeks. Jerome seems to interpret it according to the Greek when he says, "The great authority of the petitioner having been proposed, through which he was both an Apostle and an old man and a prisoner of Jesus Christ." We, therefore, have preferred to follow this, yet in such a way that everyone is free to enjoy their own judgment.

<margin>14</margin> *Him as my own heart*] <note>Greek: αὐτὸν, τουτέστι, τὰ ἐμὰ σπλάγχνα</note> that is, *him, that is, my own bowels (inner heart)*. Furthermore, what is added in most Latin versions, "my dearest son," is not added among the Greeks. Nor is there anything in Jerome's commentaries from which you might guess he read "dearest son." Perhaps this was added by someone who wanted to explain what "that is, my heart" meant.

<margin>15</margin> *Without counsel*] <note>Greek: Χωρὶς δὲ τῆς σῆς γνώμης</note> that is, *Without your opinion or consent*.

<margin>16</margin> *For an hour*] <note>Greek: πρὸς ὥραν (pros hōran)</note>. Jerome rightly noted here that "hour" is put for "time," except that "hour" indicates a very brief time. Although the Greeks use "hour" for time in general, the Roman poet Horace followed this almost exactly:
->...to purge the bile at the hour of the springtime.<- <note>A quote from Horace’s *Ars Poetica*, illustrating that "hour" can mean "season" or "time."</note>

Volume VI. Qqq

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO PHILEMON.
## PART TWO

16 ...that you might have him forever, no longer as a slave, but more than a slave—a beloved brother, especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord? 17 If then you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me. 18 But if he has wronged you in any way, or owes you anything, charge that to my account. 19 I, Paul, have written this with my own hand: I will repay it—not to mention to you that you owe me even your own self besides. 20 Yes, brother, let me have joy <note>original: "ὀναίμην" (onaimen). This is a wordplay on the name Onesimus, which means "useful" or "profitable." Paul is essentially saying "Let me have 'Onesimus-like' profit from you."</note> from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in the Lord. 21 Having confidence in your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. 22 But meanwhile, also prepare a guest room for me, for I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you. 23 Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you, 24 as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow laborers. 25 The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.

-> Written from Rome by Onesimus the servant. <-

### THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO PHILEMON

-> T H E   E N D. <-

---

<margin>17 That forever</margin> <term>αἰώνιον</term> (aionion), that is, eternal; this means he is now not just a temporary servant, but one who will live with you perpetually. This is how Ambrose reads it, as does Jerome; and both the manuscripts from Constance agreed with the Greek reading.

<margin>18 But as a servant</margin> In Greek it is <term>ὑπὲρ δοῦλον</term> (hyper doulon), that is, "above a slave." Some seem to have read it as "on behalf of a slave." Although "in place of a slave" <note>original: "ἀντὶ δούλου" (anti doulou)</note> might have fit better here. Certainly, Jerome read: *Now not as a slave, but more than a slave*; although the Latin versions had, *better than a slave*. And both Constance manuscripts held this as well.

<margin>19 I will repay</margin> <term>ἀποτίσω</term> (apotiso), that is, I will pay out, or I will discharge the debt. This is the language of someone acting as a legal guarantor for Onesimus, binding himself in his place. Saint Jerome reasons from this passage that Onesimus did not flee from his master without first committing a theft. Theodoret testifies to the same in the Greek commentaries. In those same commentaries, I find that Philemon was a Phrygian. Among the Phrygians, there was a massive production of slaves, which gave rise to the proverb: *A Phrygian is improved by lashes* <note>An ancient, derogatory stereotype suggesting that people from Phrygia were stubborn and only learned through corporal punishment.</note>. And yet, they record that this same Onesimus later earned the crown of martyrdom at Rome.

<margin>20 Even so, brother</margin> "Even so" here is the adverb of affirmation, <term>ναί</term> (nai, meaning "Yes" or "Truly"). Ambrose adds it like this: *Even so, brother, thus let me enjoy you in the Lord.* It is the voice of one entreating a brother or a son, whom we wish to be a source of pleasure to us, as if nothing were sweeter to us than enjoying his company. Through this, therefore,

<column-break/>

For a time, 17 that you might receive him forever, 16 no longer as a slave, 18 but above a slave, namely a beloved brother, especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord? 17 If therefore you hold me as a partner, receive him as me. 18 But if he has hurt you in any way, or owes you, impute this to me. 19 I, Paul, have written with my own hand, 19 I will pay it back: so as not to say to you, that you even owe your own self to me besides. 20 Even so, brother. I shall enjoy you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in the Lord. 21 Trusting in your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even beyond what I say. 22 But at the same time also prepare a lodging for me. For I hope that by the help of your prayers 21 I shall be given to you. 23 Epaphras, my fellow captive in Christ Jesus, greets you, 24 Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, Luke, my helpers. 25 The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen. <margin>B</margin>

-> It was sent from Rome through Onesimus the servant. <-

### THE EPISTLES OF PAUL TO PHILEMON

-> T H E   E N D. <-

---

<margin>C</margin> he adjures Philemon. Jerome wants <term>ναί</term> (nai) to be the word of one who is coaxing or flattering, just as among the Hebrews it is <term>ana</term> <note>A Hebrew particle of entreaty, often translated as "I beseech you."</note>. Moreover, there is an allusion to the name of the servant whom he commends. For <term>Onesimus</term> in Greek means *useful* or *profitable*, which he alluded to earlier when he said: *Who was once useless to you, but is now useful both to me and to you*; that is, he is now exactly what he is called: <term>Onesimus</term>. This Epistle, however short it may be, declares that Paul was a man endowed with a singular humanity, who with such great zeal commended a runaway slave, and commended him by pleading and entreating a man whom he could have commanded by his own authority and by his merits. Furthermore, what could be said with more wit or charm, even by Cicero <note>Erasmus uses the name "Tullius," referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero, the gold standard of Roman eloquence.</note> himself, on such a subject? 

Except that some people—Christians in name only, but in spirit most hostile to Christ—think nothing is learned or elegant unless it is also Pagan. They think the entire flower of speech has perished if anything about Christ is mixed in that tastes of His doctrine, even though the primary part of eloquence is to adapt the speech to the subject matter. For this reason, I wonder even more that any have doubted whether this Epistle belongs to Paul, since, given the nature and style of the argument, nothing could be more "Pauline."

<margin>21 To be given to you</margin> <term>χαρισθήσομαι ὑμῖν</term> (charisthesomai hymin), that is, I shall be given to you. And this is how Ambrose reads it.

---

# THE ARGUMENT <note>original: ΥΠΟΘΕΣΙΣ (Hypothesis)</note>

->of the<-

# EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE HEBREWS.

He sends this letter from Italy. The occasion for the Epistle is as follows: Since the Jews clung to the Law and its shadows <note>original: σκιαῖς (skiais) – symbolic ceremonies or rituals that prefigured Christ</note>, for this reason the Apostle Paul, having become a teacher of the nations and having been sent to the nations <note>The "nations" or "Gentiles" (non-Jewish people)</note>, proclaims the Gospel. Having written to all the nations, he finally writes also to the Hebrews who believed from the circumcision <note>Jewish converts to Christianity</note> this demonstrative Epistle concerning the presence of Christ, and the cessation of the shadow of the Law. And first, he demonstrates that the Prophets were sent in order that they might announce the Savior, and after them He Himself came; he shows that the prophets were the heralds and messengers of His presence, and that Christ Himself is the Son of God, through whom all things were made. And he shows that it was necessary for the Son of God to become man, so that through the sacrifice of His body He might destroy death; for salvation would come to men not through the blood of calves or goats, but through the blood of Christ. He demonstrates that the Law made no one perfect, but held only a shadow of the good things to come. And though the people rested <note>in the land of Israel</note>, a common day of rest still remains for us all. Again, he demonstrates that the priestly service was transferred from Aaron to Christ, of whom Melchizedek was a type <note>original: τύπος (typos) – a person in the Old Testament who foreshadows a future person, in this case, Christ.</note>. Therefore, he signifies that the fathers were justified by faith from the line of Levi, and not by the works of the Law. Then, having exhorted them toward moral conduct and having commended their endurance for the sake of Christ, and having persuaded them to honor their elders, he concludes the Epistle.

---

# ON THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

->*The Argument by*<-

## DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial N depicting a seated figure in a landscape, surrounded by ornamental foliage.</image-desc>
No nation resisted the Gospel of Christ with more stubborn minds than that of the Jews, who were also particularly hostile toward Paul because he declared himself the Apostle to the Gentiles—whom the Jews detested as profane and impious. They also hated him because he seemed to nullify the Mosaic Law, which they held as sacrosanct and desired to see spread throughout the whole world in place of the Gospel. Indeed, there were even some among those who had received the teaching of Christ who thought that the observation of the Law should be mixed with the Gospel. Therefore, those in Jerusalem who had believed were afflicted with various calamities by those who resisted the Gospel, for public authority was in the hands of the latter. They were cast into chains, beaten, and their goods were plundered. Paul, therefore, consoles them, partly by the example of the ancient saints—most of whom were tested by similar or even more severe calamities so that their virtue might be more thoroughly examined and admired—and especially by the example of Christ, and partly by the hope of a heavenly reward. Then he declares that, with the Gospel of Christ now shining forth, the shadows of the Law of Moses have ceased, repeating many things from the Old Testament and applying them to Christ. He teaches that salvation is not to be hoped for from the observation of the Law (which was given only for a time and was imperfect), but from faith, by which even those ancient men of proven holiness, whose memory was sacred to the Jews, had most pleased God. In the end, he hands down certain precepts pertaining to Christian conduct.

# THE EPISTLE OF THE APOSTLE PAUL TO THE HEBREWS.

# 1.

<margin>1.</margin> God, who in many parts and in many ways spoke of old to the fathers in the prophets, <margin>2.</margin> In these last days has spoken to us in a Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages; <margin>3.</margin> Who, being the radiance of his glory and the exact expression of his substance, and upholding all things by the word of his power, having through himself made purification for our sins, <margin>4.</margin> sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high; Having become so much better than the angels, as he has inherited a more excellent <margin>5.</margin> name than they. For to which of the angels did he ever say: You are my Son, today I have begotten you? And again: I will be to him a father, and he <margin>6.</margin> shall be to me a son? And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says: And let all the angels of God worship <margin>7.</margin> him. And of the angels indeed he says: Who makes his angels spirits, and his <margin>8.</margin> ministers a flame of fire. But to the Son: Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; a scepter of righteousness is <margin>9.</margin> the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you <margin>10.</margin> with the oil of gladness above your companions. And: You, Lord, in the beginning laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the works <margin>11.</margin> of your hands; They shall perish, but you <margin>12.</margin> remain; and they all shall grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will fold them up, and they shall be changed; <margin>13.</margin> but you are the same, and your years shall not fail. But to which of the angels has he ever said: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet?

<column-break/>

<margin>1.</margin> God, who of old spoke many times and in many ways to the fathers through the prophets, in these last <margin>2.</margin> days has spoken to us through the Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he created the worlds: <margin>3.</margin> Who, since he is the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his substance, and governs all things by the word of his power, having made purification for our sins through himself, sat at the right hand of majesty in the highest: <margin>4.</margin> Having been made so much more excellent than the angels, by as much as he has obtained a more excellent name than they. For to which of the angels did he ever say: You are my Son, <margin>5.</margin> today I have begotten you? And again, I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. <margin>6.</margin> And again, when he introduces the firstborn into the world, he says: And let all the angels of God worship him. <margin>7.</margin> And to the angels indeed he says: Who creates his angels as spirits, and his ministers as a flame of fire. <margin>8.</margin> But to the Son: Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever, a scepter of rectitude, the scepter of your kingdom. <margin>9.</margin> You have loved justice, and hated iniquity, therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of exultation beyond your peers. <margin>10.</margin> And you in the beginning, Lord, laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands: <margin>11.</margin> They shall perish, but you remain, and they all shall grow old like a garment, <margin>12.</margin> and like a cloak you will roll them up, and they shall be changed: but you are the same, and your years shall not fail. <margin>13.</margin> To which of the angels has he ever said? Sit at my right hand, until I have placed your enemies as a footstool for your feet.

---

->Is it not<-

<image-desc>A decorative square initial 'M' showing a figure (possibly a prophet or scholar) in a landscape with buildings in the background.</image-desc>

> **M**ANY TIMES and in many ways] <note>original: Πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως (Polymerōs kai polytropōs)</note>. The first word refers to "parts," and the second to the "manner." If there is a difference, the former can refer to the various parts of human redemption, and the latter to the variety of figures and oracles: the parts being the birth of the Savior, his teaching, miracles, cross, resurrection, ascension, and so on. Just as these individual parts were prefigured by different types <note>historical symbols or characters</note>, so they were foretold by the different oracles of the Prophets.

<margin>2 Speaking] <note>original: λαλήσας (lalēsas)</note>.</margin> That is, "having spoken," in the past tense; just as he spoke in the Prophets, in these recent times he has spoken to us in the Son. The Latin translator <note>Erasmus refers to the author of the Vulgate</note> seems to have avoided this so as not to say "spoken" twice, although Paul uses the word in both places—"having spoken" and "he spoke"—and there is even a certain grace in this arrangement of the words.

<margin>3 In the Prophets, in the Son]</margin> Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople</note> also notes that the preposition "in" is placed here instead of "through."

<margin>4 Radiance of glory]</margin> <note>original: ἀπαύγασμα (apaugasma)</note>, that is, a refulgence or reflection, which shines out from another source. For the Son is light from light.

<margin>5 And the figure]</margin> <note>original: χαρακτήρ (charaktēr)</note>, which you might call a form expressed from another, or a mark impressed on something, such as in wax. The word comes from the verb *charatto*, which means to engrave or to impress a mark. Augustine, in his book *On the Incarnation of the Word*, occasionally uses "expressed figure" for *character*. Jerome, citing this passage in his commentary on Isaiah, reads "form" instead of *character*. Nothing, however, expresses the archetype more closely than an image impressed by a seal. And "of his substance," <note>original: ὑποστάσεως (hypostaseōs)</note>, not *ousias* <note>essence</note>, which Quintilian translates as "essence": *hypostasis* is derived from "subsisting," and among the Greeks it is sometimes taken to mean "person." From this word arose a great struggle <note>original: gladiatio (sword-fight/clash)</note>, because the Arians <note>a 4th-century group who argued the Son was not co-eternal with the Father</note> demanded three *hypostases* and would not accept the word *homoousion* <note>of the same substance</note>.

<margin>6 And upholding all things by the word of his power]</margin> <note>original: φέρων τε τὰ πάντα (pherōn te ta panta)</note>. In my judgment, *pherōn* in this place does not mean the same as "carrying" or "bearing a burden," but rather "acting" or "moving and governing." For the Greeks use the term *pheromena* for things that are driven by a certain impulse; hence they call impulses *phoras*. And one who governs someone at his own will is said to "lead and carry" <note>original: ἄγεται καὶ φέρεται (agetai kai pheretai)</note> them. For Paul, or whoever was the author of the Epistle, feels that this world was not only founded through the Son—as he just said, "through whom he also made the ages"—but was established to be ruled and administered: and that not through zeal, care, or industry as humans administer things, but by a "word," that is, by the nod of his power. For what a word is to a Prince, by which he orders something to be done, "to will" is to Him. Chrysostom interprets it in this sense as well, noting the emphasis of this participle *pherōn*. For someone governs with effort; but he "carries" who moves things wherever he wishes without effort. Therefore, we find "acts and governs" more likely. Although Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> did not perceive the emphasis of this word, he did not stray far from the target.

<margin>7 Making purification of sins]</margin> The Greeks add "through himself" <note>original: δι’ ἑαυτοῦ (di’ heautou)</note>. And "making," among the Greeks, is in the past tense: from which he could have translated "purification of sins having been made," so that he does not seem to be purifying while sitting. For he first purified by his death, then he sat down.

<margin>8 He sits]</margin> "He sits" is in the past tense among the Greeks, *ekathisen*, as if you were to say, "he sat down." The translator of Chrysostom translates it "he made him to sit." And both the commentary of Chrysostom and that of Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator</note> agree with this reading; it is no wonder they were not offended by the participle "becoming," unless perhaps they had read "having become." And indeed, the Greek word is ambiguous, but the participle that follows, "he has inherited," stands in the way. However, Chrysostom has no such thing. It is true that "to sit" <note>original: καθίζειν (kathizein)</note> is used by the Greeks both neutrally and transitively. "At the right hand" etc. The Greek copies sometimes have it differently: "at the right hand of the throne of majesty." Although here the Greek manuscripts vary, and no mention of the "throne" is added in Chrysostom or Theophylact. And here it truly is "majesty," not "glory" <note>original: δόξα (doxa)</note>.

<margin>9 Being made so much better than the Angels]</margin> In Greek, it is not "greater" <note>original: μείζων (meizōn)</note> but "better" <note>original: κρείττων (kreittōn)</note>, which sounds like "more powerful" or "more potent." Let those who contend that Christ was in no way inferior to the angels explain this passage. How shall he be said to have been "made better" or "more powerful" who was never "lesser"? Unless perhaps, in the manner of the Sophists, one wishes to argue that he was made "greater" from a state of being "equal." Nor does "better" here refer to morals, but to excellence, dignity, and power.

<margin>10 More differently]</margin> <note>original: διαφορώτερον (diaphorōteron)</note>, that is, "more excellently": because the Greek *diapherō* means two things: "to differ" and "to excel." "He inherited," <note>original: κεκληρονόμηκεν (keklēronomēken)</note>, that is, he received by inheritance, or he obtained by lot.

<margin>11 I will be to him for a father]</margin> Although it otherwise fit the place of the papyrus and the style, I stayed with "I will be to them a father, he to me a son," lest anyone imagine an adoption.

<margin>12 And when again]</margin> <note>original: Ὅταν δὲ πάλιν (Hotan de palin)</note>, that is, "But when again."

<margin>13 And to his Angels indeed]</margin> The word "his" is extra. It is not added in the more corrected Latin versions.

<margin>14 A flame of fire]</margin> <note>original: πυρὸς φλόγα (pyros phloga)</note>, that is, "a flame of fire," meaning a fiery flame.

<margin>15 Your throne, O God]</margin> <note>original: Ὁ θρόνος σου, ὁ Θεὸς, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος</note>. It is uncertain whether the sense here is, "O God, your seat is for ever and ever," or this: "God himself is your throne for ever and ever." For the Greek speech is ambiguous. But the Translators follow the former. Chrysostom noted that the article "the" <note>original: ὁ (ho)</note> was added here before "God"; I do not see what place this observation has, unless we take "the God" as being said to the Son. For Chrysostom implies that the article signifies the "True God." As for the Father, even the Arians do not doubt that He is "the God."

<margin>16 They shall perish, but you shall remain]</margin> In the Greek, the words are in the present tense: "they perish, and you remain" <note>original: ἀπολοῦνται, διαμένεις (apolountai, diameneis)</note>. Although "they perish" is ambiguous, and in "you remain," only the accent makes it the future tense "you shall remain."

<margin>17 You shall change them]</margin> <note>original: ἑλίξεις αὐτοὺς (helixeis autous)</note>, that is, "you shall roll up or turn them." And that word fits better for the heavens, or even for a garment. The translator seems to have read "you shall change." And among the Hebrews there is a second transitive form from the word *chalaph* <note>Erasmus uses the Hebrew characters</note>, which is "he changed," just as a cloak is changed. From which also "changes of clothing" are named, as noted by our friend Capnion <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a famous humanist and Hebraist</note>. The Greeks consistently read "you shall roll up," not "you shall change." And so Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret it. Therefore, I leave what should be read for the learned to weigh.

Erasmus explores the nuances of Christ's superiority over angels and provides a critical comparison of the Greek vocabulary against the Latin Vulgate.</summary>
