--- Page 573 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews, moving from the end of Chapter 1 into the beginning of Chapter 2. The author (Erasmus) is engaged in a detailed scholarly debate regarding the translation of Psalm 8 as quoted in Hebrews, specifically whether Christ was made "lower than the angels" or "lower than God," while also defending himself against criticisms from his contemporary, Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples.</meta>

# TO THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER II.

14 Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?

II. 1 Therefore we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away. 2 For if the message declared through angels was firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just penalty, 3 How shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? It was declared at first through the Lord, and it was attested to us by those who heard him, 4 While God also added his testimony by signs and wonders and various miracles, and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will. 5 For he did not subject the world to come, about which we are speaking, to angels. 6 But someone has testified somewhere, saying, "What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you care for him? 7 You made him for a little while lower than the angels; you have crowned him with glory and honor, and set him over the works of your hands. 8 You have put all things in subjection under his feet." Now in putting all things in subjection to him, he left nothing outside his control. At present, however, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him.

---

<margin>14</margin> 14 *Sent into service*] "Sent" <note>original: "Missi"</note> in the Greek is the present participle, "being sent" <note>original: "apostollomena"</note>, that is, those who are currently being sent. For they are sent even today. And they "will inherit" <note>original: "capient"</note>, not "they inherit," meaning in the future, not the present.

<margin>1</margin> 1 *We drift away*] Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a humanist scholar</note> prefers "we flow past" <note>original: "praeterfluximus"</note>, following the Greek "drift away" <note>original: "pararryomen"</note>. Chrysostom interprets this as "to perish utterly," and thinks it is taken from the Proverbs of Solomon: *My son, do not drift away* <note>original: "pararryes"</note>. For that which slips away perishes completely and irreparably. In this same manner, the woman spoke in 2 Samuel chapter 14: *we all must die, and are like water spilled on the ground.*

<margin>2</margin> 2 *Which, having begun to be declared*] The word "declared" <note>original: "enarrari"</note> is read in the ancient manuscripts, specifically in the Pauline ones; in Greek it is "to be spoken" <note>original: "laleisthai"</note>, that is, that which was first spoken by the Lord.

<margin>3</margin> 3 *Of which we speak*] This refers to the world, not to God. This is clear from the Greek.

<margin>4</margin> 4 *Someone saying*] Means "a certain person."

<margin>5</margin> 5 *You made him a little lower than the angels*] In this place, Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>Faber Stapulensis</note> reminds us that in the Hebrew it says, *you made him a little lower than God*. And Jerome indicated exactly this (or whoever wrote the commentary on Psalm 8) stating that for the word *Angels*, which are called *Malachim* <note>Hebrew: מַלְאָכִים</note> there, the original has *Elohim* <note>Hebrew: אֱלֹהִים</note>. Thomas Aquinas refers this passage to the human nature of Christ, who was made lower than the angels not in his soul, but in the body he assumed, through which he was mortal and subject to pains, whereas angels can be touched by no evils. I do not reject his opinion, except that it must be understood carefully when he says Christ was not inferior to angels according to his human soul. For if no sense of pain belonged to that part of the soul, there could not have been that most bitter pain in Christ, which Thomas himself argues was close to the torments of the damned in hell. And if he is called "lesser" because he had a body subject to pain, he would be called even more "lesser" because he had a soul subject to weariness and sorrow. But Lefèvre, disagreeing with Thomas here, argues with many proofs that we should read "lower than God," not "lower than the angels." It would be too long to review these, and not entirely necessary, since his book is available in print. However, whether you read "God" or "Angels," the same difficulty seems to remain. For if you understand this of the "assumed man" <note>Christ's humanity</note>, as is necessary, he was not just "a little" diminished from God, but indeed placed below even the most lowly of men, as he testifies of himself in the Psalms: *But I am a worm, and no man, a reproach of men, and despised by the people.* For there is no proportion between human nature and Divinity. He was not even "a little" diminished from the Angels, he who descended all the way to hunger, to lashes, to the cross, and finally to death. Therefore, it seems to me that the phrase "a little," which in Greek is *brachy ti*, should not refer to the *degree* of diminished dignity, but to the *amount of time* Christ spent on earth—as if you said, *for a short time he was made lower than the angels*. This is how Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret it. Nor does the following phrase contradict this sense: *you crowned him with glory and honor, you subjected all things under his feet, sheep and oxen, etc.* For the first part pertains to Jesus' life on earth and his passion, while the latter pertains to his glorification, to which he was raised as a man. Nor did Aquinas entirely miss the mark here, as he indicates "a little" can be taken in two ways: either pertaining to quantity (as he puts it) or pertaining to duration. Lefèvre d'Étaples calls the Translator of the Epistle to account <note>critiques the translation</note>, though it is uncertain who that translator was. Since it is considered unlikely by some that the Epistle was written by Paul himself, there are those who think Luke was the translator. If we accept this opinion, that Translator cannot be blamed, especially since in Hebrew the word *Elohim* is considered "polysemous" <note>having many meanings</note>, as it can declare "God" or "gods" in either the singular or plural, and sometimes refers to "Angels," or even "men worthy of admiration." Sometimes it means "Princes" or "Judges," as in: *you shall not curse the prince of your people.* And in Exodus chapter 21: *Let his master bring him to the gods <note>Elohim</note>, and he shall be brought to the door.* In that place, the Hebrews interpret "gods" as "judges." And the Chaldean translation rendered it as: *Let his master bring him to the judge*, as our friend Reuchlin <note>Capnion</note> noted in his *Rudiments of Hebrew*. But these things do not properly belong to the present purpose, except as the logic of the reading requires. Therefore, it is enough to have pointed them out briefly.

<column-break/>

->A<- Are they not all ministering spirits, <margin>14</margin> who are sent out into service for the sake of those who will be heirs of salvation? Therefore it is necessary for us to <margin>1</margin> attend more vehemently to those things which have been said to us, lest we should ever drift away. For if the <margin>2</margin> word which was spoken through angels was firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just repayment of reward, How <margin>3</margin> shall we escape, if we neglect such great salvation? which, when it first began to be declared through the Lord himself, was confirmed unto us by those who heard him, God attesting to it with signs and wonders <margin>4</margin> ->B<- and various miracles, and distributions of the Holy Spirit, according to his own will. For he did not subject the world <margin>5</margin> to come, of which we speak, to angels. But <margin>6</margin> someone has testified in a certain place, saying, What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him? You made him for a little while lower than the angels, with glory and <margin>7</margin> honor you have crowned him, and you have set him over the works of your hands. You have subjected all things under his feet. <margin>8</margin> For in that he subjected all things to him, he left nothing not subject to him. But we do not yet see all things subject to him.

---

->C<- Otherwise, there were many things in this Epistle to be examined more diligently, which cannot be explained except by a wordy dispute. I will add this one thing: Jerome seems not to have entirely approved of these things being properly attributed to Christ, when in explaining this Psalm he says, *The Apostle in the Epistle to the Hebrews interprets this place as being about Christ.* And there was such doubt about its author that it was only late received by the Roman Church: indeed, Ambrose wrote no commentary on this one alone out of all of them. And Jerome says it was not received by some because certain things were cited in it which are not found among the Hebrews. From this passage, Lefèvre d'Étaples, a man of the highest integrity and learning, took the opportunity to pick a fight with me—whether he did so at the prompting of another, or to test my spirit, or from some human emotion (as no man has yet existed who was wise at all hours). But since his attack is read scattered throughout his commentaries, and it did not seem convenient to stuff our defense (which responds to him more fully) into this place, I will only note the main points for the Reader.

->D<- First, as for his making me out to be rejecting his opinion and the Hieronymian <note>Jerome's</note> interpretation, the reality is far different, as I review both, rejecting neither this one nor that one, but only pointing out a difficulty <note>original: "scrupulum," literally a small sharp stone</note> that seems to disrupt both readings, and I try to remove it, thereby even helping Lefèvre's side. For that difficulty was more troublesome if we read "diminished a little from God" than "from the Angels."

Next, his calling this dispute undertaken with me a "defense of prophetic understanding" certainly does not apply to me, since I assist prophetic understanding with all my might and do not oppose it. Nor does he here, without insult, make me an adversary of prophetic understanding, even if it were certain the Prophet meant what he wants, since I do not oppose Lefèvre, and I even specifically bring forward Jerome's annotation.

Next, regarding my saying that he disagrees in this part with Thomas Aquinas: he defends this as if I had brought it up as a crime, when there is nothing of the sort in my writings. Jerome alone gave the warning about the word *Elohim*; all others, both Greek and Latin, read "from the Angels." Thomas agrees with these, except that he adds a distinction about the body and soul of Christ; because he had that unique view, I mentioned him by name. For what great thing would it be if I had said Lefèvre disagrees with Thomas here, where he disagrees with all the orthodox—indeed, with Paul himself (whom he thinks is the author of this Epistle) and with the public reading of the Church, received and approved for so many centuries?

->E<- In the fourth place, he argues with me as if it were already established and settled that we must read "from God" and not "from the Angels," when that is the very question at hand. Indeed, that which he assumes as certain and confessed—whether we should read "from God"—is a matter of great doubt, as Jerome noted it only once, and in few words, without rejecting the received reading, and in other places citing this Psalm according to the way we commonly read it.

->F<- In the fifth place, he rejects and refutes as if it were an impious statement that I wrote in passing that what is read in the Psalm, *you diminished him a little less than the Angels*, should be understood of the "assumed man." It is as if by these words I had pulled apart the person of Christ <note>the hypostatic union</note>, or as if I used the name of Christ for only one nature, when my speech contains nothing of the sort. My words do not shrink from the custom of the Latin language, nor from the writings of the Ancients, nor from Holy Scripture, unless you wish to slander me openly. That Christ is said to be "diminished" certainly pertains to the human nature he assumed, according to which he was diminished. And yet I show, though it is extra detail, that something can be stated without absurdity about one of the natures in Christ that properly applies to the other. But these things are discussed more fully in my *Apology*, where they cannot be noted in just a few words.

Sixth, whereas he curses as an absurdity the idea that the name of Christ could be taken for only one nature, I demonstrate that it is rightly understood according to the common Scholastic opinion—namely, for the divine nature united to the human—even if I deny that I did so myself, and I teach this with the clearest arguments.

Seventh, that which he hammers home so many times—that the "assumed man" was diminished from God—is clearly Lefèvre's own phrasing, not mine.

Eighth, regarding the point that the divine Christ did not only descend below the Angels, but even below the most abject of men: Lefèvre fiercely refutes that statement as if it were impious and most unworthy of Christ and God, as if it were opposing the spirit and the letter that kills...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s rebuttal of Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples (Faber) regarding the interpretation of Hebrews 2:7 and Psalm 8:5. The core of the dispute is whether Christ was made "a little lower" than the angels (in rank) or "for a little while lower" (in time), and how His human humiliation relates to His divine nature.</meta>

# EPISTLE OF PAUL [TO THE HEBREWS] CHAPTER II.

<margin>A</margin> clinging to it as if it were contradicting the Prophet. I have demonstrated in many ways that this discourse is, above all, pious, containing the oracles of the Prophets, consistent with the interpretation of the orthodox fathers, and especially in agreement with the words of Paul; particularly if we judge the manner of His lowering <note>The Latin *dejectio* refers to Christ’s "casting down" or humiliation in the Incarnation.</note> not only according to the human nature He assumed, but also according to the many injuries of our corrupted nature. Most importantly, it is according to the appearance of a guilty man, which He took on for a time for our sake, according to which He was crucified between two criminals, as if He himself were condemned for His own crimes. For it is according to this sense that Ambrose especially prefers to understand what Paul writes to the Philippians: *He emptied himself* <note>original: "exinanivit semetipsum"</note>, etc.

Ninth, regarding the argument Faber makes there: "If He was diminished a little by God because of the human nature He assumed, since He continued to be God, it is not consistent for Him to have been cast down below the lowest of men." It is obvious to everyone that Faber is not arguing logically <note>original: "dialectice"</note> when he assumes against me that "a little" <note>original: *βραχύ τι* (brachy ti)</note> refers here to a degree of dignity (as the opposite of "much"), whereas I teach that it refers to time (as the opposite of "for a long time"). Nor is there a conflict between being *diminished by a small amount* and being *diminished for a short time*.

Tenth, regarding what is added in the same article—that I intend the Prophet’s meaning to be that Christ was not just a little diminished below the angels, and even less so by God; and that it follows from this that He was diminished much more by God if He was diminished much by the angels; and thus finally the Prophet’s meaning is undermined either way, whether we read "by God" or "by the angels"—I think it is clear enough from what I said above that this was said against me not only without cause, but without sense. That concluding phrase is of the same sort: *Wherefore this discourse destroys itself, and reveals itself to be false in every part.* For there is no conflict in my discourse; all this conflict exists only in the things Faber devises out of his own head.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, regarding the eleventh point he adds: that the discourse does not hold up where I write that Christ was not even a little bit diminished below the angels, He who descended even to the death of the cross. Anyone can see this was said as if he had not considered what he was saying himself, or as if he wished to mock a friend. "If He was not diminished a little by the angels," he says, "how is it approved that we should read in the Prophet, 'You made him a little lower than the angels'?" Do "a little less" and "not a little less" conflict? Do "a little" and "not a little" conflict? Faber does not notice that this statement, *He was not diminished even a little by the angels*, is affirmative, not negative; it signifies He was diminished, but not just a little—rather, a great deal. It would be different if I had said, "He was not diminished at all." It is clear, therefore, that there is nothing here that contradicts itself.

Twelfth, the things we brought forward from the Psalms—*I am a worm and no man*—and similar passages testifying to Christ’s humility, he denies apply truly to Christ, but only according to the estimation of the wicked. Yet since these are attributed to Christ by the interpreter Augustine, and indeed by all the Ancients, because of the human nature assumed and the injuries of our nature, and finally because of the afflictions He suffered as a guilty man, would even these not truly apply to Him? Indeed, because Christ’s lowering <note>original: *dejectio*</note> prescribes for us an example of humility, I think it more fitting that we believe this example to be as true as it is supreme. If the name "worm" also applies to the members of Christ <note>Meaning the followers of Christ, his "body."</note>, it does not immediately follow that it does not apply to Him.

Thirteenth, regarding his point that Mary the mother of Jesus, the beloved disciple, Magdalene, and the rest wept for Christ with much compassion: this actually supports my case. For if there was nothing in Him that was not magnificent and happy, why were they weeping over Him?

Fourteenth, he asks: how is it fitting for Him to be called a worm, who is the firstborn of all creation and superior to all creatures? In turn, I will ask him: how was it fitting for Christ to be called God and man, mortal and immortal, Son of Man and Son of God, dead and living? For who does not see that very different things apply to the same person because of the diversity of natures which the same person <note><term>hypostasis</term>: The technical theological term for the person of Christ, who is one person with two natures (divine and human).</term></note> encompasses?

<margin>C</margin> Fifteenth, what he says—that Jesus was so much a man that He was the most truly man of all—pertains nothing to me. It is enough for me that He himself calls Himself "not a man." For no one is so insane as to think He was not truly a man. But just as those things which are most despised are said "not to be," so we call the most cast-down men "not men." Furthermore, whether Christ was "more" of a man than others, I leave to the Logicians <note>original: *Dialecticis*</note> to dispute, who deny that "more" and "less" apply to substance. I profess that Christ was man; thus I would not dare to affirm He was "more" of a man than all others.

Sixteenth, regarding the fact that Christ, as He says in the Gospel, does not assign the name of "worm" to Himself, but rather those things that belong to dignity: first, it is enough for me that He called Himself a worm in the Prophet. Nor do the things in Holy Scripture that testify to Christ’s dignity detract from His assumed humility; just as, conversely, those things that declare His humility do not detract from His highness.

<margin>D</margin> Seventeenth, he denies that Christ can be called a worm because He is not earthly, but according to Paul, heavenly. Indeed, He was both heavenly and earthly. According to the former, He is called Son of God; according to the latter, Son of Man, or of Adam. Furthermore, regarding what he adds about the proportion of identity or equality—whether any such thing exists—let him see to that himself. But if he places only this in Christ, He would not be diminished by God in any way, which Faber nevertheless admits. But if He is said to be inferior to God the Father according to the assumed nature, let him bring forward any proportion he knows between a creator and a created thing.

Eighteenth, his reasoning that even the Seraphim, compared to the Deity, could be called worms, pertains nothing to me. For I do not argue this way: "there is no proportion between man and God, therefore man is a worm." Rather, I conclude this: Christ calls Himself a worm and not a man, the reproach and rejection of the people; therefore He was not diminished from the angels just a little, but a great deal, even below the common crowd of men.

Nineteenth, he raises the question of whether Christ was diminished in Himself because of the injuries He undertook. Let him explain what he means by "in Himself," and it would be no trouble to answer him. Nor does reason forbid that Christ, by the more things

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> He suffered, became greater in merit, and yet meanwhile was truly cast down. I will overlook here that he makes me his adversary while I am actually supporting him; that he links my discourse with the opinion of the Jews (by which Christ was much diminished); and that he announces "danger" if one stubbornly clings to your words. I, however, will easily recant my words if Paul first recants what he wrote: *He emptied himself*.

Twentieth, he denies that the death of Christ should be called a humiliation, but rather an exaltation, since He Himself says: *When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself.* By that same reasoning, the thieves could be said to have been exalted. Indeed, Paul himself interprets Christ's passion as a "diminution" in this very Epistle, and "exaltation" as the glory of resurrection and immortality. And in this place, Faber seems to be inconsistent with himself. For while Faber uses every tool to ensure Christ is not said to have been truly humiliated, he concludes thus: His passion should not be called a humiliation in a "bad sense." He admits, therefore, that it is a <margin>B</margin> humiliation in a "good sense." But we attribute it to Him in the "best sense." For who would attribute it to Christ otherwise, unless they were utterly impious?

Twenty-first, he says that when Christ suffered those things, He was nonetheless the King of Angels, as if it were absurd to say He was below the angels by humiliation when He is the King of Angels. But by that reasoning, He was not inferior to God, since He was God. And yet Faber certainly grants this.

Twenty-second, he says: "But He had to suffer all these things for us miserable ones according to the oracles, and appear wonderful above all, and appear rejected and humiliated." He is clearly implying that one who is afflicted undeservedly is not humiliated. On the contrary, He lowered Himself all the more because, being more innocent, He was willing to suffer those things for the unworthy. And, unless I am mistaken, just as He truly appeared wonderful, so He truly appeared rejected and humiliated—not in a simple sense, but (which is enough for me) in a certain way.

<margin>C</margin> Twenty-third, what he proposes about the martyrs supports my case. They are humiliated when they offer their necks to the executioner; they are exalted by both the memory and the reward of a glorious death.

Twenty-four, he denies that "a little" <note>original: *βραχύ τι*</note> can refer to the amount of time Christ spent on earth, since all the angels are soon commanded to adore Him. It would be a wonder indeed if they were not commanded to adore Him who is God. Yet it does not follow from this that He who was mortal was not in some part lower than those who are immortal.

Twenty-fifth, he strongly denies that among the Hebrews the word *Me-at* <note>Hebrew: מְעָט</note> sounds like a span of time, but rather quantity or magnitude. By producing a few passages, he thinks he has settled the matter—as if it follows that if *Me-at* is used elsewhere among the Hebrews not to declare brevity of time, it can never be adapted to a temporal meaning. Certainly, in Psalm 37: *Yet a little while and the sinner shall not be.* In Hebrew it is *Me-at*. Likewise in Psalm 109: *Let his days be few*, it is again *Me-atim*. Again in Psalm 2: *When his wrath is kindled in a short time*, it is *Bime-at*. I do not doubt that a hundred passages could be produced <margin>D</margin> if someone were to do the work. See what it is to assert a doubtful thing as if it were fully explored.

Twenty-sixth, who does not see that the rule he teaches is irrelevant—that these words "much" and "small" and the like, whenever they are joined to words designating increase or decrease, are never accustomed to signify time, but "a little less" is joined to the verb "you have diminished." For the issue here is not whether the Latin translator translated correctly, but what the Greek word *βραχύ τι* declares. For what Latin speaker ever said "a little less" <note>original: *paulominus*</note> for "a little bit" <note>original: *paululum*</note>? That sounds more like "nearly." If *βραχύ τι* refers to time for the Greeks, it should not have been translated as "a little less" or "a little bit," but as "for a little while." Nor does anything forbid speaking this way: "You increased my wealth for a little while," or "You were cast down for a little while."

Twenty-seventh, he tries to prove by the authority of the Greeks that *βραχύ τι* cannot refer to time, because Eustathius, the interpreter of Homer, speaking of talents <note>A unit of currency or weight.</note>, used *βραχύ τι*, indicating not time, but magnitude or value. First, I think more credit should be given to Athanasius, Chrysostom, and Origen—men skilled in Greek even to <margin>E</margin> the miracle of eloquence—than to Eustathius, a collector of other people's commentaries. Besides, what follows from this: "Eustathius adapted *βραχύ τι* to magnitude, therefore it cannot pertain to a measure of time"? Just as, because we speak of a "short path," it would not be permitted to say "a short time."

Twenty-eighth, he teaches that if anyone wants to signify time, one must say "in a little" <note>original: *ἐν ὀλίγῳ*</note> or "a small [thing]" <note>original: *μικρῷ*</note>; the latter is found in John. These do not signify time unless the word "time" <note>original: *χρόνῳ*</note> is understood—just as "donkey" is signified if "ass" is understood. The same thing happens with *βραχύ τι* when we say "in a little," meaning "in a short time."

Twenty-ninth, he teaches that if the Seventy Translators <note>The Septuagint authors.</note> had wanted time to be understood, they would have said, "You diminished him a small bit <note>original: *mikron ti*</note> from the angels," and that it should have been translated into Latin as "You diminished him quickly from the angels." But who speaks like that—"he lived quickly" instead of "he lived not for long"? Although "he died quickly" might be aptly said of one who did not live long. Christ was "quickly" exalted because He was not humiliated for long.

<margin>F</margin> Thirtieth, he makes Vulgarius and Athanasius two different people, whereas the Commentaries on the Epistles of Paul which are circulated as translated by a certain Prior of St. Balbina are by Vulgarius—or rather, by Theophylact, the Bulgarian Bishop—not Athanasius. This will be immediately discovered by anyone who compares the Greek.

Thirty-first, although Faber asserts that this reading is impious and even heretical if anyone tries to defend it—*diminished for a little while from the angels*—nevertheless he excuses Chrysostom and all the other orthodox writers only on the grounds that they were deceived by the Seventy (who translated "from the angels"), thinking it was so in the Hebrew; and, constrained by the difficulty of the passage, they fled to this refuge of twisting *βραχύ τι* to a measure of time, but falsely. I would have preferred him to have spoken a little more civilly about such great pillars of the Church, especially since there is no one who does not agree with them on this point. Finally, Jerome himself agrees with them, as we showed before, and that in a work not under suspicion; for the Commentaries we have on the Psalms are either not Jerome's, or certainly are contaminated in many places by foreign additions—not to mention that for so many centuries this reading has been held with great consensus.

<summary>Erasmus continues his detailed point-by-point rebuttal of Faber, defending the interpretation that Christ was humiliated "for a short time" (βραχύ τι) rather than just "a little bit" in rank. He uses linguistic analysis of Hebrew and Greek and appeals to Church Fathers like Chrysostom to argue that Christ's temporary lowering during the Incarnation was a profound act of humility, not a minor change in status.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s rebuttal of Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples (referred to here as Faber) concerning the interpretation of Hebrews 2:7 and Psalm 8:5. Erasmus is defending his view that "a little" (*brachy ti*) refers to a duration of time (Christ was lower than angels for a short while during His earthly life) rather than a degree of dignity (Christ being only slightly less than God).</meta>

# TO THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER II.

<margin>A</margin> This is what the Church sings and teaches; since she could hardly fail in this, she certainly would not have embraced this critical sense for so many ages.

Thirty-second: the points he brings forward from the Gospel concerning the dignity of Christ do not work against me. I attribute to Him a humility assumed for a time in such a way that I do not detract from His dignity. He is said to be "less than the Father" <note>John 14:28</note> in one sense; this is true, yet He was equal to that same Father. Thus, according to one aspect He was inferior to the Angels, but not simply inferior in His nature.

Thirty-third: with many words, he strives to teach that the one man was so united to the Divinity and exalted above all things that he was only "diminished a little from God." And yet, what Faber calls "exaltation" here, Paul calls "emptying" <note>original: "exinanitionem"; refers to the concept of *kenosis* in Philippians 2:7.</note>. He adds, *taking the form of a servant*, which Faber himself earlier interpreted as human nature. Certainly, Faber places an inequality in Christ according to a certain respect; but if this is taken as a comparison between the divine and human natures, how can He be said to be "diminished a little" in that regard?

Thirty-fourth: he wanders into a wide-open field, gathering many points about the excellence of Christ. I take nothing away from these; indeed, compared to His true dignity, they seem to me to be stated meagerly and sparingly. But, as demonstrated before, these do not obstruct what has been said about His humility according to the nature He assumed.

<margin>B</margin> Thirty-fifth: since Faber holds so stubbornly to the idea that Christ was only diminished a little bit from God, he should explain in what sense Paul says He "emptied himself." Does "to empty" mean to be diminished by just a little bit? To us, the word sounds almost like "to reduce to nothing." It is as if you said, "he eviscerated the man," and you interpreted it to mean, "he moved him slightly."

Thirty-sixth: he does not defend Thomas Aquinas <note>original: "Aquinati"</note> very kindly. Aquinas, being ignorant of Greek and Hebrew, followed the error of others. Yet if Christ was in no way inferior to the Angels, it is manifest blasphemy to make Him inferior to them. Thomas, who was not an entirely stupid man, could certainly have sensed this even without skill in the original languages.

<margin>C</margin> Thirty-seventh: since Faber shifts all blame onto the Translator <note>The unknown person who translated Hebrews from Hebrew/Aramaic into Greek, or the Latin translator.</note>, he argues thus: if Luke is the translator of this Epistle, he should not be held guilty. Faber says: "We do not accept this, since everyone feels it was translated by an unknown author." On the contrary, whoever wrote the argument <note>A traditional preface or summary found in manuscript traditions.</note> to this Epistle testifies that Luke was more than just a translator; that he, mindful of the sense and order after Paul’s death, wrote it down in Greek from his own memory. Faber says the author "does not assert it, but testifies that many felt this way." But if the Translator is entirely unknown, as he admits, how can Faber so certainly deny that it was Luke?

Thirty-eighth: he now adds at the end: "Furthermore, it is not the authority of the writer, whoever he was, that should prevail, but the truth." If that is true, why does Faber follow a single annotation by Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymi"</note> so strictly and pronounce so confidently on such a great matter? Then, what if Luke *is* the author—for I have assumed that—should he not be deferred to in some way?

<margin>D</margin> Thirty-ninth: he admits that the word *Elohim* <note>original: "Eloim"</note> is polysemous <term>polysemous: having multiple meanings</term> to the Hebrews and corresponds to two Latin words, *Deus* (God) and *Dii* (gods). What he admits is true and cannot be denied; however, this should have been added: it is well known that *Elohim* does not only mean "gods," but also "leaders," "judges," and finally "Angels."

Fortieth: he says the difference is that *Elohim*, whenever it is placed without a mark of plurality, means "God," and thus the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX) translators.</note> always translated it; conversely, whenever it means "gods," the word *kol* <note>original: "col"; likely referring to a Hebrew quantifier or grammatical marker</note> (a mark of plurality) is added. There is no need to refute this with arguments sought from elsewhere, since the very discourse <unclear>syndesmos</unclear> <note>original: "σύνδεσμος" - connection or syntax</note> refutes itself. In this Psalm, *kol* is not added, and yet they did not translate it as "God." Again, in Exodus 22: *You shall not revile the gods* <note>Exodus 22:28</note>, *kol* is not added, and yet they translated it as "gods."

Forty-first: he lashes out at the Translator of this Epistle because in the Psalm he did not translate *me-Elohim* as "from God," even though the Seventy did the same thing—and they were the ones most suited to be blamed for this.

<margin>E</margin> Forty-second: a certain Spanish Hebrew scholar—a man, in my opinion, uncommonly practiced in his own literature—says the difference between *Elohim* and *Malachim* <note>original: "Malachim"; Hebrew for messengers/angels</term> is this: Angels are called *Elohim* when dignity is the subject, because they shine back the light of God; they are called *Malachim* when the subject is their function, that is, when they are sent on a mission. But here, the comparison is one of dignity.

Forty-third: he dismisses the Chaldean paraphrase <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, which, like the Septuagint translation, has *Malachim* (that is, Angels) for *Elohim*. In this part, I think not a little weight should be given to it, especially since it agrees with the authority of the Septuagint, which the Apostles usually follow.

Forty-fourth: like a severe censor, he rebukes me and accuses me of madness because I wrote that Jerome does not seem to have entirely approved of this Psalm being properly attributed to Christ. He twists this as if I had said "truly," when in Latin, as I believe, I meant "properly attributed" in the sense that it is attributed in a way that fits no one else. There are many things in the Psalms that we have in common with Christ. Therefore, there is nothing in these words of mine that should have been attacked so sharply.

Forty-fifth: he rejects my conjecture that Jerome didn't quite approve of these things being properly attributed to Christ because Jerome wrote: "The Apostle in the Epistle to the Hebrews interprets this place as being about Christ." I admit Paul is a weighty author, but first, it is uncertain whether he is the author of this Epistle. Second, Jerome admits that the author sometimes "twists" the Scriptures for the sake of winning an argument <note>original: "ad victoriam detorquere"</note>. Finally, I do not see how this entire Psalm can be accommodated to Christ. We are accustomed to shift the responsibility onto the author if we do not wish to guarantee the truth of the statements ourselves. But since this cannot be noted in a few words, whoever wishes may seek the rest from my *Apology*. I affirm nothing here; I only point out how it appears to another.

Forty-sixth: the fact that Christ in the Gospel cites a verse from this Psalm—*Out of the mouths of babes and nursing infants you have perfected praise* <note>Matthew 21:16; Psalm 8:2</note>—does not necessarily prove that this Psalm properly applies to Christ; rather, the statement he brings forward can be a general one.

Forty-seventh: he charges me with folly for writing that the author of this Epistle was so doubted that it was only late-

<column-break/>

ly received by the Romans, as if this has nothing to do with the matter at hand. It certainly was relevant to this extent: if it is not by Paul, his authority weighs less upon us.

Forty-eighth: he denies it is established that the Romans received this late. It would not be established to me either, had Jerome not recorded it in writing, testifying that in his age the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> was not received by the Greeks, nor the Epistle to the Hebrews by the Latins. For the Greeks received this one more willingly out of hatred for the Arians <note>A fourth-century heretical group that denied the full divinity of Christ.</note>. Anyone who reads the *Letter to Dardanus* concerning the Promised Land will find this is not my dream; there Jerome admits it was not received by the Latins, though he very much wished it were. Let him read Jerome's *Commentaries on Isaiah*, chapter 6; again on chapter 8 even more clearly; and again on Matthew, chapter 26.

<margin>A</margin> Forty-ninth: he argues it was received by the Romans long ago because this translation predates the time of Jerome. Even if we grant this is true, nothing else can be concluded from it except that this Epistle was translated before Jerome's time. For a thing is not received immediately just because it has been translated.

<margin>B</margin> Fiftieth: he thinks it is a most evident argument that this Epistle was received by the Romans because Jerome uses its testimony against Jovinian. If it was received because he uses its testimony, then Pythagoras was also received, for he uses his testimony against the same man!

Fifty-first: he pleasantly mocks my argument as being hardly logical: "It was received late because Ambrose wrote no commentary on it." As if it follows by equal reasoning that whatever book Ambrose did not write commentaries on was received late by the Roman Church. He truly proclaims that this enthymeme <term>enthymeme: a logical argument with an unstated premise</term> is worthy of multiple doses of hellebore <note>original: "Anticyris"; a reference to Anticyra, a place famous for hellebore, used to treat madness.</note> if one assembles it in that way. But I used a "collection of conjectures" <note>original: "synathræsmo"</note> in a matter of speculation. First, that it was received late, according to Jerome; then, that certain things are cited in it from Hebrew volumes that are not found there. <margin>C</margin> I add to the heap of conjectures that Ambrose, while he wrote on all the others, did not write on this one. There were other conjectures too, which I did not think needed to be recounted here, as if I were doing something else. It is not necessary for a certain conclusion to be born from each individual conjecture. It is enough if a probable suspicion is forged from many gathered arguments.

Fifty-second: he considers it an irrefutable argument that this Epistle was received because Ambrose and Jerome use its testimony in their books. That is an argument that it was received in the sense that it was already being read by many as if it were Paul's, but not that it had been received by public authority as a part of canonical Scripture that one was not permitted to doubt.

Fifty-third: now to the argument he brings from Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite.</note>, who cites the testimony of this Epistle in his books *On the Divine Names*. I respond that since that Dionysius is of uncertain date, it is possible he was somewhat later than Ambrose.

<margin>D</margin> Fifty-fourth: he strongly asserts that no one ever doubted this Epistle except the Ebionites, Marcionites, and similar heretics. But if I show that Jerome and Augustine doubted this Epistle—as we shall show shortly and at the end of this Epistle—it will follow from Faber’s rule that they are heretics; yet they are certainly orthodox to us, and I do not doubt they are to Faber as well.

Fifty-fifth: he says that when Jerome states certain things are cited there that do not appear among the Hebrews, he is reciting the slanders of heretics, not his own opinion. What Jerome thought about this Epistle is not entirely clear to me; for he is subtle <note>original: "vafet"</note>, and was of the opinion that one’s private thoughts should not be entirely made public, just as Christ spoke to the crowds in parables while opening the mystery of the kingdom only to the Disciples. If those things are found among the Hebrews, why does Jerome not point them out?

Fifty-sixth: at the end, he concludes that there should be no doubt about this, since the most holy Synods and Canons have approved it. I am not certain about the approval of the Synods. Now <margin>E</margin> it is certainly established as received. In what spirit it was received is not yet clear to me—whether as Paul’s, or as something owed equal authority with the rest. Under whatever laws it was received, I accept it. I will only say this: if the Apocalypse had not been received into the Canon, the Christian faith could nevertheless have stood. Furthermore, if a most holy Synod approved the Epistle to the Hebrews, why does Faber dare to mark a passage in it as "impious and unworthy of Christ"? Unless perhaps the Synod had a corrected copy, and immediately after the approval, all the manuscripts of the whole world, Greek and Latin alike, were suddenly corrupted, so that no one could know what that Synod had read.

Fifty-seventh: whatever is inconvenient or a stumbling block, he shifts onto the Translator. But in my judgment, he does this with little shame, given such consensus among Greek and Latin manuscripts, especially since none of the Ancients used this softening explanation, and it is uncertain whether Luke is the Translator. But I contend nothing on this matter; I only advise the reader in a few words to provide him with material for thinking and searching, which was most appropriate for this argument, in which we profess to offer annotations, not definitions.

<margin>F</margin> We have noted the main points for the fastidious Reader. Whoever wishes to know the matter more fully may read our *Apology* in which we respond to Faber. I will easily acknowledge the charge of ignorance; but a charge of impiety against Christ I neither should nor can acknowledge. I confess that all glory is owed to Him alone—far greater than any human proclamation could attribute to Him. Nor is it an insult that we attribute humility to Him, whose cross and whose scourges we reverently adore, and whose ignominy is our glory. And I wish that Faber, while measuring his own opinion, had not attacked a simple and sincere friend with so many hateful sayings; that would have been worthy of the man, even if I had opposed him in some way. And yet, as far as the insult is concerned, I easily either ignore it, or grant it to friendship, or finally forgive the man—especially since whatever crime or error he charges me with, I hold in common with the most approved Doctors of the Church, and indeed with the public judgment of the whole Church. However, I do not think so much should be granted to a friend that, for his sake, you would wish to be considered blasphemous and impious toward Christ where you are not. And yet this...

<margin>6 But him who was [made lower] than the angels <note>original: "Τὸν δὲ βραχύ τι παρ’ ἀγγέλους ἐλαττωμένον"</note>, that is, "But him who was diminished a little bit compared to the angels," if one renders it word for word; but if one prefers the sense, "But him who was diminished for a short while before the angels."</note></margin>
> I have pushed back against the slander in such a way that, as far as was possible, I did not wound the reputation of my friend: so that no one can doubt that it was a matter of necessity that I defended myself, and of Christian modesty that I refrained from retaliation.

<margin>7 By the grace of God] This is in the ablative case <note>original: "χάριτι Θεοῦ"</note>, that is, through the grace of God, which means by divine favor.</margin>
<margin>8 For everyone] <note>original: "ὑπὲρ παντὸς"</note>, that is, for the whole world, or for every person, or anyone at all.</margin>
<margin>9 For it was fitting for him] This refers to the Father, not the Son. Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and Bible commentator</note> struggles with this so that the preposition "through" does not seem to diminish authority. For all things are said to be made through him, by whom all things are made. Hence, it is not only said of the Son that all things were created through him, but also of the Father. Therefore, "to make perfect" <note>original: "τελειῶσαι"</note> should be read in the active voice, not the passive. Certainly, in the manuscript provided to us by the Pauline Library in London <note>the library of St. Paul's Cathedral School</note>, it is seen written as "to make perfect," although some corruptor has marked it out with a pen. A very old manuscript from Constance supported this. The sense here is: It was fitting for him, namely the Father, who wished to lead not just one Son (Jesus) but many into glory, to make him—who was the leader and captain of the salvation of the rest—legitimate and perfect through various afflictions. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father known for his preaching</note> reads and interprets it in this way. Consequently, by an error of the scribes, "to be made perfect" is found written as a passive verb in some manuscripts. However, I find that reading in the commentaries of Faber <note>Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples, a French humanist and rival to Erasmus</note>.</margin>
<margin>10 Author of salvation] <note>original: "ἀρχηγὸν τῆς σωτηρίας"</note>, that is, the leader and captain of salvation. For authority rests more with the Father, according to Saint Hilary, even if Christ is also the author.</margin>
<margin>11 I will praise you] <note>original: "ὑμνήσω σε"</note>, I will celebrate you with hymns.</margin>
<margin>12 Trusting in him] In the same place, <note>original: "πεποιθὼς ἐπ' αὐτῷ"</note>.</margin>
<margin>13 And my children] "My" is implied, <note>original: "τὰ παιδία, ἅ μοι"</note>, that is, the children, whom [he gave] to me.</margin>
<margin>14 For he never takes hold of angels] <note>original: "Οὐ γὰρ δήπου"</note>, that is, "For not indeed." Although the Greek particle *de* adds some emphasis. And *pō* is sometimes translated as "anywhere," making the sense: "I have nowhere read in Divine Scripture that God assumed an angelic nature." If this is approved, it should be translated: "For he surely does not anywhere take hold of angels." The present tense verb also supports this sense. I wonder, however, what the translator of Chrysostom was doing when he read, "For he does not take hold of any of the angels," unless perhaps he thought a "certain one" was implied in the genitive "of angels," but the genitive belongs to the verb. Certainly, the Greek context does not differ from our reading. Now, Chrysostom himself notes that the metaphor is taken

> from those who, following in a race, seize and pull back a fugitive. Christ did not redeem the fallen angels, nor did he assume their nature. He "takes hold of" angels. "Takes hold," in the present tense, <note>original: "ἐπιλαμβάνεται"</note>, that is, he assumes and puts on, just as it says shortly after, he "takes hold of" the seed of Abraham. Although elsewhere Paul uses this verb to mean "to attain."

<margin>15 And a faithful High Priest] <note>original: "Ἀρχιερεύς"</note>, that is, High Priest: though he [the Vulgate translator] often translates it this way.</margin>
<margin>16 To God] <note>original: "τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν"</note>, that is, in those things which pertain to God, or which are performed before God.</margin>
<margin>17 For in that] <note>original: "Ἐν ᾧ γὰρ"</note>, that is, For in that which, which means, For the reason that.</margin>
<margin>18 He who is tempted] And the conjunction is redundant, nor is it read in the ancient Latin manuscripts. These two are connected adjectives, <note>original: "πειρασθεὶς πειραζομένοις"</note>, that is, because it happened to him to be tempted, so that the participle is placed in the position of an infinitive verb.</margin>
<margin>19 To those who are tempted] Here also the conjunction "and" is redundant. In an older Constance manuscript, it had been added in the margin.</margin>

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>1 The High Priest of our confession] The Greeks read "our" <note>original: "ἡμῶν"</note>; and so does Chrysostom, supported by the very ancient and simultaneously most faithful Pauline manuscript. Both Constance manuscripts agreed. And again it is "High Priest" <note>original: "Ἀρχιερέα"</note>. Furthermore, he could have translated "Apostle" as "Legate." To me, "profession" seems a more accurate square [translation] than "confession," since the Greek word is ambiguous.</margin>
<margin>2 In all the house] <note>original: "ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ οἴκῳ"</note>, that is, in the whole house.</margin>
<margin>3 For by more glory] The translator follows the Greek speech; he translates the genitive instead of the ablative. It should have been said, "worthy of more glory."</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
<margin>4 The house has] Again here he translated the genitive for the ablative: for it should have been said, "greater than the house," or "greater than that of the house." Lorenzo [Valla] indicates that the translator Remigius slipped here, not finding a way out of the sentence, and blames the Latin translator. Thomas [Aquinas], and the more recent ones, take it as the honor of the house, or glory in the house, or concerning the house, while Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret it differently, wanting the people of God to be designated by the name "house." Moses administered the people; Christ founded them. We, so that the sense might be more clear, expressed it in this way: "For this man has been considered worthy of so much greater glory than Moses, by as much as the one who built the house has more honor than the house itself."</margin>
<margin>5 which house] <note>original: "ὗ οἴκος"</note>, that is, whose house, so that "whose" may refer either to God or to Christ.</margin>
<margin>6 confidence] <note>original: "παῤῥησίαν"</note>, as if you were to say, boldness.</margin>
<margin>7 And glory] <note>original: "καύχημα"</note> adds something more, if we not only trust, but also glory, and as it were, boast of our lot.</margin>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed philological notes on the Epistle to the Hebrews. Having established the superiority of Christ over Moses in the previous section, Erasmus now examines the warning against unbelief, using the Israelites’ failure in the wilderness as a cautionary example. He focuses heavily on the linguistic nuances between the Greek original and the Latin Vulgate, particularly concerning the concepts of "rest" and the "hardening" of the heart.</meta>

# TO THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER IV.

<note>This section begins with the Greek text of Hebrews 3:8 through 4:3, which serves as the basis for the commentary below.</note>

...during the day of testing in the desert, 9 where your fathers tested me, tried me, 10 and saw my works for forty years. Therefore I was angry with that generation, and I said, "They always go astray in their heart, and they have not known my ways," 11 as I swore in my anger, "They shall not enter into my rest." 12 See to it, brothers, that there never be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, in falling away from the living God, 13 but encourage one another every day, as long as it is called "Today," so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. 14 For we have become partners of Christ, if indeed we hold the beginning of our conviction firm until the end. 15 While it is said: "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the rebellion." 16 For some, when they heard, rebelled; but not all who came out of Egypt through Moses. 17 And with whom was he angry for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the desert? 18 And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, if not to those who were disobedient? 19 And we see that they were not able to enter because of unbelief. IV. 1 Therefore, let us fear, lest while a promise of entering his rest remains, any of you should seem to have fallen short. 2 For indeed we have had the good news preached to us, just as they did. But the word of hearing did not benefit them, because it was not mixed with faith in those who heard it. 3 For we enter...

8 **They tested]** The Greeks add "me" <note>original: με (*me*) </note>.
9 **Forty years]** The Greeks, by their punctuation, refer this to the preceding phrase: *they saw my works for forty years*. But that reading is clearly refuted by what follows: *With whom was he angry for forty years?*
10 **I was offended by the generation]** <note>original: προσώχθισα (*prosochthisa*)</note>. Laurentius <note>Valla, a 15th-century humanist</note> prefers "incensed" rather than "offended," because, if I am not mistaken, "offended" sits awkwardly with the dative case "by that generation." However, we read in Suetonius "more offended by repentance" meaning "somewhat angry." Furthermore, for the Greeks, <term>prosochthisa</term> <note>to be weary or disgusted</note> means to take weariness or trouble from something. Finally, for the Hebrews it is <term>קוץ</term> <note>quts</note>, which carries the sense of weariness and trouble. From this, Saint Jerome translated: *For forty years that generation displeased me*, that is, I endured them always rebelling, and that not without my own weariness. For God in the Holy Scriptures often speaks in the manner of men. The Greek word seems to be composed from <term>bank</term> <note>original: ὄχθη (*ochthē*)</note> or shore, or a rough place against which ships strike.
11 **To this generation]** In Greek it is <term>that</term> <note>original: ἐκείνῃ (*ekeinē*)</note>, that is, "to that one"; and Jerome translated it as "that one," as was just indicated.
12 **And I said always]** The Greeks punctuate this so that the adverb "always" refers to the verb "they err," and the pronoun "they" is not added.
13 **To whom I swore]** <term>As I swore</term> <note>original: Ὡς ὤμοσα (*hōs ōmosa*)</note>, that is, "Just as I swore." The translator seems to have read <term>if</term> <note>original: εἰ (*ei*)</note>. Furthermore, that phrase, *if they shall enter*, is the language of one taking an oath, so that it effectively means: *I swore they would not enter into my rest*. We sometimes add, "may I die if I do it," or "may I perish if it wasn't for the best."
14 **Lest perhaps]** <term>lest at any time</term> <note>original: μή ποτε (*mē pote*)</note>.
15 **Of departing from the living God]** <term>in falling away</term> <note>original: ἐν τῷ ἀποστῆναι (*en tō apostēnai*)</note>, that is, in defecting or by defecting.
16 **Today it is named]** <term>it is called today</term> <note>original: τὸ σήμερον καλεῖται (*to sēmeron kaleitai*)</note>. For this whole time until the end of life is called "today."
17 **That he be not hardened]** <term>lest he be hardened</term> <note>original: ἵνα μὴ σκληρυνθῇ (*hina mē sklērynthē*)</note>, that is, so that not.
18 **Today if his voice]** In the repetition of this speech, some Greek manuscripts had "my voice" <note>original: Φωνῆς με (*phōnēs me*)</note>. Others again had "his" <note>original: αὐτοῦ (*autou*)</note>. Chrysostom indicates there is a transposition <note>an inversion of natural word order</note> here, in the phrase *his voice, etc.* For the whole speech in the middle depends on the beginning of the next chapter. Therefore, "I" was added to correct a rather long transposition. Likewise, a transposition can be seen in what preceded: *As the Holy Spirit says, Today etc.* up to the word *See, brothers*. For in the middle there is no verb to complete the sentence.
19 **In that provocation]** The article <term>the</term> <note>original: τῷ (*tō*)</note> is redundant, except that it was added for the sake of explaining the matter.
20 **For some hearing]** <term>having heard</term> <note>original: ἀκούσαντες (*akousantes*)</note> is in the past tense, meaning "when they had heard."
21 **Whose corpses]** <term>whose limbs</term> <note>original: ὧν τὰ κῶλα (*hōn ta kōla*)</note>. The translator seems to have read "fallen bodies" <note>original: πτώματα (*ptōmata*)</note>, unless he preferred to express the sense; for "limbs" are also spoken of the living.
22 **Not to enter]** <term>that they would not enter</term> <note>original: μὴ εἰσελεύσεσθαι (*mē eiseleusesthai*)</note>.
23 **Because they could not enter]** In this place, the words that are added—"into his rest"—I do not find in the Greek copies, nor even in the ancient Latin ones. But it is clear from the preceding parts that they were added.
IV. 1 **Lest perhaps]** <term>lest at any time</term> <note>original: μή ποτε (*mē pote*)</note>.
2 **Someone from you to be lacking]** <term>to have fallen short</term> <note>original: ὑστερηκέναι (*hysterēkenai*)</note>, that is, not to have attained.
3 **And to us]** "And" is redundant. <term>We have been evangelized</term> <note>original: εὐηγγελισμένοι ἐσμὲν (*euēngelismenoi esmen*)</note>, rendered word for word: *we have been brought good news*, that is, the Gospel has been preached to us. So elsewhere the poor *are evangelized*.
4 **Not mixed]** <term>not tempered with</term> <note>original: μὴ συγκεκερασμένος (*mē synkekerasmenos*)</note>, that is, not combined, or not previously joined or united in mind to the body by a tempering, such as faith is to hearing.
5 **From those which they heard]** <term>by those who heard</term> <note>original: τοῖς ἀκούσασιν (*tois akousasin*)</note>. Furthermore, this dative case belongs to the participle "mixed." I find a great deal of

Therefore, I will transcribe the Greek of Theophylact as it stands: <note>Erasmus provides a long Greek quote from Theophylact discussing the "mixing" of faith. The summary follows.</note> That is, *“Not mixed by faith with those who had heard, that is, not united, not in agreement concerning faith with those who heard, but torn away from them. He did not say ‘not consenting,’ but ‘not mixed,’ to declare the highest unity. By ‘those who heard,’ he means those who believed: for these can truly be said to have heard the word. Furthermore, Saint John [Chrysostom] understood Caleb and Joshua as those ‘not mixed’; for these remained un-submissive to the rebellion, and were not mixed with the others who were rioting and who all held one mind; they did not rise up together, nor were they joined together. But to which ones? To those who heard and received no benefit. This was spoken by that saint according to his great and deep wisdom, but to me, unworthy as I am, he did not give the understanding of how he said this.”* This is from Theophylact,
<margin>E</margin>
though in the Latin translation some things are different and some are missing. For there, mention is made of *Basil*, not *John* [Chrysostom], and the last lines are omitted. From these I gather either that there was a double reading among the Greeks, or that the reading among us is corrupted. For if the Greeks correctly read <term>mixed</term> <note>original: συγκεκραμένους (*synkekramenous* - plural)</note>, we must read "to those mixed," not "not mixed" <note>singular</note>. And in a very old manuscript from the [monastery of] Cunitz, it was held as <term>admixtis</term> <note>mixed (plural/dative)</note>, without any trace of erasure or alteration. I do not doubt that the same reading can be found in many copies, if one were to examine old libraries. Indeed, while I am writing this, I consult the Spanish Edition <note>The Complutensian Polyglot</note>, and I find <term>admixtis</term>, not <term>admixtus</term>, and in Greek <term>συγκεκερασμένους</term> <note>mixed (plural)</note>, not <term>συγκεκερασμένος</term> <note>mixed (singular)</note>. From this it appears that among the Greeks there was a double reading. For even in Theophylact it was written <term>mixed</term> ending in *omega* <note>plural</note>, which someone had corrected by noting a diphthong; and the Aldine Edition had the singular, agreeing with the copies we followed. But in both readings there is some difficulty. For if you read the plural, Chrysostom’s interpretation—applying the passage to Caleb and Joshua—does not stand; for the word clearly
<margin>F</margin>
profited them, who did not mix themselves in the sedition because they believed the divine word. If you read the singular, the two dative cases "with faith" and "with those who heard" fit together harshly. Then, how can the word be said not to have been heard by those who heard? But this last difficulty is easily shaken off from the Greek words, in which "hearing" is a noun <note>original: ἀκοῆς (*akoēs*)</note>, not a participle, sounding just as if you said, "the word of report" or "of promise." For some interpret this as being about the scouts reporting what they had seen. Now, if you read the singular, the sense will be that the hearing of that same word concerning the promised land did not profit the unbelievers, because through faith they were not mixed with those who had "heard," that is, who had obeyed. In this way, you take the first "hearing" as simple listening, and the second as belief—as if you said, "they had heard and yet not heard." And for this meaning, one should not read "of faith," but "by faith"; so that the Greek dative declares the manner, similar to an instrumental case. How do you say they were not mixed with the others? Because they did not believe as the others did. In this way, the two datives do not clash, as one indicates the manner and the other responds to the preposition "with" <note>original: σύν (*syn*)</note>. If you read the plural, you will understand that the word was not...

He debates whether the failure to enter "rest" resulted from an internal lack of faith or a refusal to join with the faithful minority, such as Caleb and Joshua.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s philological analysis of the Epistle to the Hebrews. The previous page concluded the warning against hardening one’s heart, drawing parallels between the Israelites in the desert and the current readers. Here, Erasmus explores the nature of God’s "rest" and the piercing power of the Word of God, transitioning into the role of Christ as the Great High Priest. Note that while the header indicates Chapter 5, the text covers the conclusion of Chapter 4 and the very beginning of Chapter 5.</meta>

# EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER V.

For we who have believed enter into that rest, as he has said, "As I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter into my rest," although the works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he has spoken somewhere about the seventh day in this way, "And God rested on the seventh day from all his works." And in this place again, "They shall not enter into my rest." Since therefore it remains for some to enter into it, and those who formerly received the good news did not enter because of disobedience, he again defines a certain day, "Today," saying through David after so long a time, as it has been said, "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts." For if Joshua had given them rest, he would not have spoken later about another day. So then, a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God. For whoever has entered his rest has also rested from his works, just as God did from his own. Let us therefore strive to enter into that rest, so that no one may fall by the same example of disobedience. For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. And no creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give an account. Since then we have a great High Priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast to our confession. For we do not have a High Priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin. Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need. For every High Priest chosen from among men is appointed on behalf of men—

---

The word heard was not mixed with faith in those who had heard it. For just as wine does not benefit a person unless it is mixed into the body, so the word heard does not benefit unless faith transfers it into the inward parts of the soul. And in this sense, the dative case of *faith* <note>original: "fidei"</note> responds to the preposition *with* <note>original: "cum"</note>, and in the phrase *in those who had heard*, the dative is one of acquisition, so that you might understand "in" to be implied: "in those who had heard." And "heard" will mean nothing other than "drank in with their ears." Although this passage is also rather confused in Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquent preaching.</note>, if indeed these Commentaries are his. For the title, indicating they were published after his death, provides no small suspicion to the reader. In these, however, I have caught a double reading. For when he says, "but the word of hearing did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in those who heard," he declares clearly enough that he read "the word mixed with faith in those who had heard." Again, in the progress of his discourse, he seems to have read something else: *“What he says is like this: They also heard just as we hear, but it was of no benefit to them. Therefore, do not think that you will benefit from hearing the preaching, since they also heard, but gained nothing because they did not believe. But those around Caleb and Joshua, because they were not mixed with those who were disobedient, escaped the punishment brought upon them.”* And see how wonderful it is—he did not say "they did not agree," but "they were not mixed," being displeased by that unholy rebellion, while all the others held one and the same mind. *“Here he seems to me to hint at the order of the rebellion.”* That is to say: "What he says is such. They also heard just as we hear, but no utility returned to them from it. Therefore, do not think that the hearing of the preaching will be profitable to you, since they also had heard, but perceived no fruit from it, because they did not believe. Therefore, Caleb and Joshua, because they did not consent to those who did not believe, escaped the vengeance inflicted on them." And see something marvelous: he did not say "they did not consent," but "they were not mixed," that is, they withdrew themselves from the sedition, while all those others held one and the same mind. Here he seems to me to silently signify the sedition. From these things, it seems that whoever wrote this read *synkekramenous* <note>original: συγκεκραμένους, the plural form "those mixed."</note>, namely when he says, "they did not agree, but they were not mixed"; and he applies this to Caleb and Joshua, who abstained from the conspiracy, obeying the voice of God. But this sense does not even hold up, since it is denied that the word profited those who had *not* mixed themselves. Therefore, I suspect this commentary is a rhapsody of diverse opinions. To me, the simpler reading seems to be *synkekramenos* <note>original: συγκεκραμένος, the singular form "the word being mixed."</note>. The preposition remains, and "who" should be read, not "which."

<margin>6</margin> *Who believe*] <note>original: οἱ πιστεύσαντες</note>, that is, we who have believed.
<margin>7</margin> *And indeed from the works*] <note>original: καίτοι</note>, that is, "although": so you may understand that He swore they would not enter into rest when the rest was already prepared, namely, the works of the world having been finished, which being completed, God rested on the seventh day; although the other reading can also be tolerated.
<margin>8</margin> *To whom formerly*] "Formerly" is first, in Greek <note>original: πρότερον</note>.
<margin>9</margin> *He limits a day*] <note>original: ὁρίζει</note>, that is, he designates, or defines, or pre-defines. The word "certain" is not added among the Greeks: although the manuscripts vary in this place.
<margin>10</margin> *He would speak of another day thereafter*] <note>original: περὶ ἄλλης ἐλάλει μετὰ ταῦτα ἡμέρας</note>, that is, he would have spoken of another day after this. Unless you take *posthac* <note>hereafter/thereafter</note> adverbially. For he perceives some other Sabbath day which would follow that first one.
<margin>11</margin> *Into that very thing someone*] It was better, *into the same example*, <note>original: αὐτῷ ὑποδείγματι</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For we enter into rest, ⁶ we who have believed, just as he said: "As I swore in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest," ⁷ although the works were perfected from the foundations of the world being laid. For he said in a certain place concerning the ⁺ seventh day thus: "And God rested on the seventh day from all his works." And in this again: "If they shall enter ⁸ into my rest." Since therefore it ⁶ remains that some enter into it, and ⁸ they to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief. Again he ⁹ predefines a certain day, "Today," ⁷ saying in David, after so much time, just as it has been said: "Today, if you hear his voice, do not ⁹ harden your hearts." For if Joshua <note>The Latin 'Iesus' here refers to Joshua, son of Nun, as is common in older translations.</note> had provided <margin>B</margin> rest for them, he would by no means ¹⁰ have spoken thereafter of another day. Therefore, a Sabbath rest is left for the people of God. For he who has ⁹ ¹⁰ entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, just as God did from his own. Let us strive ¹¹ therefore to enter into that rest, lest anyone ¹¹ fall by the same example of unbelief. For the word of God is living, ¹² and effective, ¹³ and more piercing than any ¹⁴ sword that cuts on both sides, and reaching even to the division of the soul as well as the spirit, and of the joints ¹⁵ and marrows, ¹⁶ and a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart. Nor is ¹⁷ there any creature that is not ¹³ manifest in his sight. But all things are naked ¹⁸ and laid bare to his eyes, to whom our speech is directed. ¹⁴ Having therefore a great High Priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast to ¹⁹ our profession. For ¹⁵ we do not have a High Priest ²⁰ who cannot be affected by the feeling of our infirmities, ²¹ but one tempted in all things according to likeness, without sin. Let us approach ¹⁶ therefore with confidence ²³ to the throne of grace, so that we may obtain mercy and find grace ²⁴ for timely help. For every High Priest, who ¹ V. is taken from among men, is appointed for men—

---

<margin>C</margin> And to me indeed the meaning of the Greek words seems to be this: "Lest anyone fall, as they fell into ruin, by the same example of unbelief and disobedience." And thus he makes it that they fell because of unbelief, as the Psalmist says, so these would perish in like manner, sinning in like manner. The Greek scholia <note>Ancient marginal commentaries on a text.</note> agree with this sense. The Greeks have it thus: "lest anyone fall in the same example of disobedience."
<margin>D</margin> <margin>12</margin> *And effective*] <note>original: ἐνεργής</note>. Jerome <note>The 4th-century translator of the Vulgate.</note> elsewhere translates this as "evident," specifically commenting on Isaiah chapter 66, because, as I think, he read *energes* <note>meaning "visible" or "clear" in a different context</note>. But in this place, "effective" certainly fits better.
<margin>13</margin> *And more penetrable*] <note>original: τομώτερος</note>, that is, sharper, or more cutting—if it is permitted to speak thus in Latin—from the verb *temno*, to cut or incise.
<margin>14</margin> *With a two-edged sword*] <note>original: δίστομος</note>, that is, cutting on both sides, or sharp on both sides: which Jerome in several places translates as "two-headed" <note>original: bicipiti</note>. The Greeks call the edge of a sword the "mouth" <note>original: στόμα</note>, because it bites from that part.
<margin>15</margin> *And of marrows*] <note>original: καὶ μυελῶν</note>. Although some Greek manuscripts have *melon* <note>original: μελῶν</note>, that is, of members. Theophylactus <note>An 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator.</note> reads "marrows," together with Chrysostom.
<margin>16</margin> *And a discerner*] <note>original: κριτικός</note>, that is, a judge, or one who is able to judge: from which the term "Critics" comes to the Latins. The Greeks here explain *kriton* as *etazon*, that is, examining, although the Translator translates it beautifully.
<margin>17</margin> *Any invisible creature*] <note>original: οὐκ ἔστι κτίσις ἀφανὴς</note>, that is, there is no creature not manifest, or hidden.
<margin>E</margin> <margin>18</margin> *And open*] <note>original: καὶ τετραχηλισμένα</note>. Which sounds just as if you were to say "necked." The Greeks think the metaphor is taken from sheep whose skin is pulled back from the neck when they are flayed, or from those who bend the neck when they submit themselves and acknowledge that they are inferior. So also Juvenal <note>A Roman satirist.</note> says of one bending everything: "...he lays back the neck of his friend."
<margin>19</margin> *The confession of our hope*] "Of our hope" I do not find among the Greeks: nor is it added in the Pauline manuscript, nor in the Donasian, nor in Chrysostom. It seems to me the article was added to explain what profession he means, namely that of which he spoke a little before, "Jesus, the Apostle of our confession." In the older Constantian manuscript it was written: "let us hold fast his confession." Another more recent one agreed.
<margin>20</margin> *Who cannot sympathize*] <note>original: συμπαθῆσαι</note>. The word for sympathizing <note>original: compatiendi</note> is indeed as much received by the best Latin authors as *sympathein* is by the Greeks, and has the same power. Therefore, we have expressed the matter by being forced into a paraphrase. For to sympathize is to be affected and moved by the feeling of another's misfortune.
<margin>F</margin> <margin>21</margin> *Tempted however*] It was better, *but tempted*. The force of both conjunctions is the same, but not all of them fit everywhere for us.
<margin>22</margin> *According to likeness*] <note>original: καθ' ὁμοιότητα</note>, that is, according to likeness. Which is not to be understood as if Christ were either not truly man, or had not truly suffered, but that he himself, immune from sin, took on the evils of the nature of sinful flesh, and thus paid the penalties as if he himself had sinned.
<margin>23</margin> *To the throne of his grace*] "His" is redundant, nor is it in the ancient manuscripts: "to the throne of grace." For he opposes grace to the severity of the Mosaic Law.
<margin>24</margin> *In timely help*] <note>original: εἰς εὔκαιρον βοήθειαν</note>, that is, in opportune or timely help.
<margin>1</margin> *Taken from men, is appointed for men*] Either the conjunction "and" <note>original: &</note> should have been added, or the relative pronoun "who": which I would prefer later, even if it is not added to the Greek participle.

<summary>This page analyzes Hebrews 4, focusing on the linguistic distinction between "the word" being mixed with faith versus the "hearers" being mixed with it. Erasmus also provides a famous philological explanation for the "piercing" nature of God's Word and the vulnerability of all creatures before Him.</summary>
