<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on Christ as the Great High Priest. Here, Erasmus focuses on the qualifications of a High Priest—specifically their ability to empathize with human weakness—and contrasts the priesthood of Aaron with the eternal priesthood of Melchizedek. He also begins a stern rebuke of the audience for their lack of spiritual progress, comparing them to infants who still need milk instead of solid food.</meta>

# TO THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER VI.

<column-break/>

[Hebrews 5:1-14]
...is appointed in things pertaining to God, to offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins. **2** He is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and going astray, since he himself is also subject to weakness. **3** Because of this, he is obligated to offer sacrifices for sins, just as he does for the people, so also for himself. **4** And no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was. **5** So also Christ did not glorify himself to become a High Priest, but was appointed by the one who said to him, "You are my Son, today I have begotten you." **6** As he says also in another place, "You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." **7** In the days of his flesh, he offered up both prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears to the one who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence. **8** Although he was a son, he learned obedience from what he suffered. **9** And having been made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him, **10** designated by God as a High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek. **11** Concerning this we have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become dull of hearing. **12** For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the basic elements of the oracles of God; you have come to need milk and not solid food. **13** For everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is an infant. **14** But solid food is for the mature, for those who through practice have their senses trained to distinguish good from evil. [Hebrews 6:1] **1** Therefore, leaving behind the elementary doctrine of Christ, let us be carried along toward perfection, not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God, **2** of instruction about baptisms, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. **3** And this we will do, if God permits. **4** For it is impossible...

<column-break/>

<margin>D</margin> *he adds the article* "the" [note: original Greek: ὁ]. For these things are not said specifically of Christ our High Priest, but are applied for the sake of drawing a comparison, even though in some Latin copies the correct reading remains.

<margin>2 Who can condole</margin> ] <term>moderate feeling</term> <note>original: μετριοπαθεῖν</note>: which sounds as if you were to say, to bear moderately, that is, not to be heavily provoked to anger. Although the Greek commentaries explain <term>moderate feeling</term> as <term>compassion</term> <note>original: συμπαθεῖν</note>, that is, to suffer with, the word itself does not strictly imply this. Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and biblical commentator</note> renders many words for this single one: to be commensurate, to condole, to condescend, to forgive—that is, to agree with, to suffer with, to accommodate oneself, to pardon. The Greek word, however, is derived from "moderate affections." For one who is uncontrollably angry when hurt does not easily forgive. I am indeed surprised that this was not even noticed by Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous 15th-century humanist</note>, who thinks it could have been rightly translated as *who is able to be a partaker of passions*. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father</note> noted that this speech denotes the excellence of Christ over the other priests; for this reason, if I am not mistaken, because he alone was free from all sin, yet he grieved for the sins of others. But now, with what loathing, with what arrogance do we despise the errors of others! How fiercely we rage against the fallen, though we ourselves are subject to even graver vices.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>3 Just as Aaron</margin> ] <note>original: καθάπερ καὶ ὁ Ἀαρὼν</note>, that is, "just as also Aaron," with the conjunction added.

<margin>4 He glorified himself</margin> ] <note>original: ἐδόξασε</note>, that is, he gave glory to.

<margin>5 Because of his reverence</margin> ] <note>original: ἀπὸ τῆς εὐλαβείας</note>, that is, "from reverence." The word "his" was added for the sake of explanation, although "of him" would have been more fitting. And that it was written thus in the Pauline codex is still evidenced by a trace of an erasure. It should also be noted that "reverence" <note>original: εὐλαβείαν</note> signifies not only respect, but also piety. This sense of the word fits quite well in this place, since it speaks of the Father and the Son.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>6 And indeed though he was a son</margin> ] <note>original: Καὶπερ ὢν υἱὸς</note>. The translator separated these things, whose order is linked together, because of the Greek participles. The sense, however, is of this sort: *Who in the days of his flesh, when he had offered prayers and supplications to him who was able to save him from death, with a strong cry and tears, and was heard because of his reverence: although he was a son, he learned obedience from those things which he suffered*. It could be rendered through participles in this manner: *Who in the days of his flesh, prayers and supplications having been offered to him who could save him from death, with a strong cry and tears, and heard because of his reverence, although he was a son, nevertheless from those things which he suffered, he learned obedience*. "Son of God." "Of God" is not in the Greek, nor in the translator Chrysostom, nor in Theophylact. Though he was a son, not a slave, he was nevertheless afflicted like a guilty slave.

<margin>7 High Priest from God</margin> ] <note>original: Ἀρχιερεὺς</note>, that is, Chief Priest; although here he almost constantly translates <term>Archhiereus</term> this way.

<margin>8 Large speech</margin> ] <note>original: πολὺς ὁ λόγος</note>, that is, a much or copious discourse.

<margin>9 And interpretable for speaking</margin> ] I suspect the translator meant to translate *uninterpretable*, just as above, *unsearchable*. For in Greek it is "a difficult-to-interpret speech" <note>original: δυσερμήνευτος λόγος</note>, that is, difficult to interpret and explain. At this point, I somewhat marvel at Thomas [Aquinas], who thought this word, "interpretable," could be explained in two ways: either that the "in-" has a negative force (one which no one can interpret), or affirmatively "interpretable" (one that needs interpretation). First, if it is negative, as in "unlearned" or "impious," what does it mean that follows: "you have become dull"?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...is [appointed] in those things which are done before God, so that he may offer gifts and victims for sins, <margin>2</margin> who is able to be placable to those who are ignorant and erring, since he himself is also surrounded by infirmity. And because of this he ought, <margin>3</margin> just as for the people, so also for himself, to sacrifice for sins. No one usurps this honor for himself, <margin>4</margin> but he who is called even by God, <margin>5</margin> just as Aaron was. So also Christ did <margin>4</margin> not glorify himself so that he might become High Priest, but he who had said to him, "You are my Son, today I have begotten you." As he says also elsewhere, <margin>6</margin> "You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." Who in the days of his flesh, when he had offered both <margin>7</margin> prayers and supplications to him who could <margin>B</margin>save him from death, with a strong cry and tears, and had been heard because of his reverence, <margin>6</margin> although <margin>8</margin> he was a son, nevertheless learned obedience from those things which he suffered, and having been made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who <margin>9</margin> obey him, designated <margin>7</margin> <margin>10</margin> by God as High Priest according to the ordering of Melchizedek. Concerning whom <margin>8</margin> many things would have to be said by us, <margin>9</margin> and those <margin>11</margin> difficult to explain, since <margin>10</margin> you have become sluggish in your ears. For indeed, since you ought to be teachers according to the ratio of time, you have need again that we teach you <margin>C</margin>what are the elements of the beginning of the oracles of God, and you have become those who have need of milk, and not solid food. For <margin>13</margin> whoever is a partaker of milk is <margin>11</margin> unskilled in the word of justice, <margin>12</margin> for he is an infant. Furthermore, solid food is for the perfect, namely these who <margin>13</margin> because of habit have their senses exercised to the discerning of good as well as evil. [VI.] Wherefore, omitting the discourse which begins the unlearned in Christ, let us be carried to perfection, not again laying a foundation of repentance from dead works, and <margin>2</margin> of faith in God, <margin>3</margin> of baptisms, of doctrine, and of the imposition of hands, and of the resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment. And this we will do, if indeed God permits. For it is impossible that...

---

<meta>catchword: who</meta>
Although, in which words is this preposition usually added when it has a negative sense? Is it permissible to say *inamare* for "not to love," in the same way as *inamabilis* [unlovable], or *impudere* for "not to be ashamed," in the same way as *impudens* [impudent]? For "interpreter" is not composed from *in-* and *interpretor*, but from *inter* and a word no longer in use, or rather a noun. Then, if we take it affirmatively, who will grant him that "interpretable" means the same thing as "needing interpretation"? As if "healable" were said of someone who needs healing. Is it not a sign of a certain remarkable impudence to teach these things with authority without consulting the Greeks, without whom these things cannot be determined? Whether it was written by that man [Aquinas] or someone else mixed it in. For the Greek word altogether rejects this distinction of Aquinas, which can declare nothing other than "difficult to interpret"—that is, that which no one could easily interpret, or rather, narrate. For the philosophers also translate <term>hermeneuein</term> as "enunciation."

<margin>10 you have become weak for hearing</margin> ] <note>original: νωθροὶ ταῖς ἀκοαῖς</note>, that is, "sluggish in the ears," as he himself translates a little later.

<margin>11 He is void of the word</margin> ] <note>original: ἄπειρος</note>, that is, inexperienced, or unskilled. For he is not entirely without speech, but has not yet grown up in it. "Void" [expers] corresponded to "partaker" [particeps], and this deceived the translator, or certainly the scribe. "Of the words of God" [note: original: λογίων], that is, of the oracles, according to Valla.

<margin>12 For he is a little one</margin> ] <note>original: νήπιος</note>. Why not rather "infant," since he is speaking of milk? Especially since the Greek word does not properly mean "little one," but a child, or one with little wisdom, particularly due to age.

<margin>13 Because of custom</margin> ] <note>original: διὰ τὴν ἕξιν</note>, that is, because of "habit": although the translator explained the matter not badly, if it is said for "custom" or "disposition." For "habit" in this sense is a word peculiar to the philosophers. But the "senses" are <note>original: αἰσθητήρια</note>: which sounds more like the "organs of sensing," lest anyone think it is the "habit" [hexis] that he has translated in that way here and there.

<margin>Q</margin> Wherefore intermittent ] <note>original: ἀφέντες</note>, that is, omitting, or rather "the discourse having been omitted," the "beginning." He would have translated it better as "the first principles," or "of the start," just as he translated it a little before as "exordium" [note: original: ἀρχῆς]. He means those words by which the unlearned are still being initiated and instructed in Christ, namely the catechumens.

<margin>2 Of faith toward God</margin> ] <note>original: ἐπὶ Θεὸν</note>, that is, "into God."

<margin>3 Of the doctrine of baptisms</margin> ] Some read this conjunctively, so the sense is "of the doctrine which is about baptizing." But the Greek commentaries interpret it such that it should be read separately. "Omitting that discourse by which the unlearned are first instructed in Christ, namely that which is about repentance": this will be, first they are warned to leave their former life, to be reborn in Christ; then they learn in faith concerning Christ what is to be believed; then, these things having been handed down, baptism follows, whose mysteries are then finally opened. After these things, they are taught about the sacraments of our faith and are prepared for receiving the Holy Spirit. Although if you prefer to read it more conjunctively, nothing prevents you from understanding it as the primary instruction and doctrine which is usually handed down to those to be baptized, that is, the catechumens. If this is pleasing, each of the things that follow can also be referred to doctrine: that which is about the imposition of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. And Chrysostom seems to me to follow this sense, so that all this which he recounted—concerning repentance, faith, baptisms, the imposition...

<summary>This page contains Erasmus's commentary on Hebrews 5 and 6, where he argues for a precise understanding of Christ's empathy as High Priest and critiques medieval misinterpretations of the Greek text. He also explains the transition from basic "catechumenal" teachings to spiritual maturity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Apostle Paul's exhortation to the Hebrews. In the previous section, the author rebuked the readers for their spiritual immaturity, comparing them to infants who still require milk. Here, he moves into a stern warning about the impossibility of re-baptism and the necessity of moving toward spiritual perfection, ultimately grounding his argument in the unshakeable promise God made to Abraham.</meta>

# EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER VI.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>4</margin> 4 For those who were once enlightened, and have tasted the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy <margin>5</margin> 5 Spirit, and have tasted the good word of God, <margin>6</margin> 6 and the powers of the world to come, and then have fallen away, it is impossible to renew them again to repentance, since they crucify the Son of God again for themselves, and hold <margin>7</margin> 7 him up to contempt. For the earth, which drinks in the rain that often comes upon it, and brings forth herbs useful for those <margin>8</margin> 8 for whom it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God. But that which bears thorns and briars is rejected, and is near to a <margin>9</margin> 9 curse, whose end is to be burned. But we are persuaded concerning you, beloved, of better things and those that accompany <margin>B</margin> <margin>10</margin> 10 salvation, even though we speak in this way. For God is not unjust to forget your work and the labor of love which you have shown toward his name, in that you have ministered to the saints, and do <margin>11</margin> 11 minister. And we desire that every one of you show the same diligence to the full assurance of hope until the <margin>12</margin> 12 end, that you be not sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the <margin>13</margin> 13 promises. For when God made a promise to Abraham, because he could swear by no one greater, he <margin>14</margin> 14 swore by himself, saying: Surely blessing I will bless <margin>15</margin> 15 you, and multiplying I will multiply you. And so, after he had <margin>16</margin> 16 patiently endured, he obtained the promise. For men indeed swear by one greater than themselves, and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of <margin>C</margin> <margin>17</margin> 17 all dispute. Wherein God, willing more abundantly to show to the heirs of the promise the immutability of his <margin>18</margin> 18 counsel, interposed an oath, so that by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before <margin>19</margin> 19 us; which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and...

---

laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment—this is the foundation of Christian doctrine, without which no one becomes a Christian. Furthermore, to grow up in these things, and to progress from virtue to virtue, belongs to perfection.

4 <term>They also tasted</term>] In Greek it is <note>original: "γευσαμένους τε"</note>, "and having tasted." Let us not think this is a new chapter here.

5 <term>They nevertheless tasted</term>] He again explains the force of the conjunction: for in Greek it is "and having tasted."

6 <term>And the powers of the world to come</term>] <note>original: "δυνάμεις"</note>, so that you may understand that there is weakness here, but there power appears, which even now begins in the godly, as a pledge of future immortality. He warns that this was seen so that no one might interpret it as the virtues that are opposed to vices.

7 <term>To be renewed again</term>] <note>original: "ἀνακαινίζειν"</note>, that is, to renew, an active verb, with "themselves" being understood. This passage was also the reason why this Epistle was not thought by some to be by Paul, because it seems to assert what was defended by certain Heretics <note>likely the Novatians, who denied readmission to the church for those who committed serious sins after baptism</note>: that if anyone, after baptism, fell back into a deadly sin—that is, into murder, or adultery, or the like—they could not be restored by penance. But they explain this difficulty in two ways. First, that we should take "impossible" to mean that which he wanted to be understood as extremely difficult. Such exaggeration is timely for the purpose of deterring someone. For it seems to me a way of escape is provided here if we say that it is "impossible" in terms of our own strength. Secondly, so that we may join penance with baptism. Since through baptism former sins die. Furthermore, it has long been accepted by the authority of the Fathers that baptism is not to be repeated. The things that follow support this view: *crucifying again for themselves the Son of God*, because elsewhere Paul calls baptism being crucified together with Christ, dying together, and being buried together. Therefore, just as He died only once, so it is not fitting for baptism to be repeated. The word for "renewing" pertains to the same thing. For in the penance we use, we are not so much renewed as we are patched up; baptism alone renews. Chrysostom <note>a 4th-century Church Father known for his preaching</note> argues roughly in this way. It appears, however, that there were those then who, with a Jewish mindset, thought the ceremonies of the sacraments were enough, and in this confidence they sinned more freely, because they thought they could repeatedly return to those remedies. Therefore, Paul diligently removes this error in this place.

8 <term>To repentance</term>] <note>original: "εἰς μετάνοιαν"</note>. Chrysostom notes that the preposition *eis* (into) is used in place of *en* (in), and is positioned in place of *dia* (through), according to the Hebrew custom.

9 <term>Crucifying again</term>] <note>original: "ἀνασταυροῦντας"</note>: which Jerome in a certain place translates as "recrucifying," expressing the Greek word.

10 <term>And holding them up to contempt</term>] <note>original: "παραδειγματίζοντας"</note>: which he translates in Matthew as "to expose to public disgrace." It could be translated as "defaming" or "exposing to mockery." For they somehow make Christ infamous and make him a mockery; those who, since he died once to live forever, by their own way cause him to have to die more often—namely, by repeating that for which he underwent death.

11 <term>By whom it is cultivated</term>] <note>original: "δι’ οὓς καὶ γεωργεῖται"</note>, that is, "through whom it is tilled": so that we understand the fruit must be returned, not to just anyone, but to those by whose labor the earth was cultivated. For that is what the added conjunction does, which the translator omitted.

12 <term>Nearer to salvation</term>] <note>original: "ἐχόμενα σωτηρίας"</note>, that is, close to salvation, or clinging to salvation. Certainly Augustine, in his third book against Cresconius, chapter 74, cites "better things and those clinging to salvation." But the Translator, because a comparative had preceded it, likewise added a comparative.

13 <term>And of love</term>] In Greek it is <note>original: "καὶ τοῦ κόπου τῆς ἀγάπης"</note>, that is, "and the labor of love," namely the labor which they undertook out of charity in helping their neighbors.

<margin>D</margin>
14 <term>To show</term>] <note>original: "ἐνδείκνυσθαι"</note>, that is, to show, or to point out, to exhibit, to perform. For "to make a show of" (*ostentare*) always has a negative connotation.

15 <term>To the fulfillment of hope</term>] <note>original: "πρὸς τὴν πληροφορίαν"</note>. As if you were to say "certification." For the confidence of the most certain hope is born from godly works rather than from logic puzzles; and he who hopes coldly, languishes in godly works. For *plerophoria* is the term used when faith in something is established by the most certain arguments.

16 <term>Even unto the end</term>] <note>original: "ἄχρι τέλους"</note>. This can be taken not only as perseverance until the end of life, but much more as the perfection of hope, which grows and matures in us as piety increases at the same time, until we become a perfect man. For Paul began this discussion here so that they might grow large in Christ.

17 <term>That you be not sluggish</term>] <note>original: "ἵνα μὴ νωθροὶ"</note>, that is, "Lest you be lazy or sluggish." This is what he translated a little earlier as "weak."

18 <term>And patience</term>] <note>original: "μακροθυμίας"</note>, that is, "long-suffering," if one were to express it word-for-word. But the Apostle spoke more expressively than the *translator*, who said "through faith and patience."

<margin>E</margin>
19 <term>They shall inherit</term>] <note>original: "κληρονομούντων"</note>, that is, "they take by inheritance," and it is in the present tense, not the future.

20 <term>To Abraham namely</term>] He put "namely" (*nempe*) for "certainly" (*quippe*), <note>original: "Τῷ γὰρ Ἀβραὰμ"</note>. But in some manuscripts it is correctly held as "for truly" (*namque*), as in the Pauline copy, and in other more corrected ones likewise.

21 <term>Unless blessing I shall bless</term>] It is not <note>original: "εἰ μὴ"</note> ("unless") in Greek, but <note>original: "ἦ μὴν"</note>, which, as Theophylact <note>an 11th-century Byzantine commentator</note> indicates, is an adverb of confirmation in this place. An oath is nothing other than a vehement confirmation. The same word is found in the Septuagint <note>the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> of Genesis 22, which Jerome nevertheless did not render into Latin because it often cannot be rendered conveniently. However, since Scripture frequently uses the syllable *ei* when it denies by swearing, and *ei me* when it affirms, the Translator here correctly put "unless" for *e men*. Nor is this contrary to the custom of the Latins.

22 <term>I will multiply</term>] Why not rather "I shall have multiplied" (*multiplicavero*), <note>original: "πληθυνῶ"</note>.

23 <term>By a greater of himself</term>] Having forgotten again, he left the Greek case. In Latin it should have been said, "greater than himself" (*majorem se*). Although among the Greeks no pronoun is added, but it is only "by the greater."

<margin>F</margin>
24 <term>And the end of all controversy</term>] The Greeks read this as "for them" (*autois*), not "of them" (*auton*), so that you should take it as: "to them," namely to men, an oath is the end of all controversy.

25 <term>The oath is for confirmation</term>] It appears here too that *eis* (into) is placed for "through." The controversy is ended by the confirmation of the oath.

26 <term>Immobility</term>] <note>original: "τὸ ἀμετάθετον"</note>, that is, immutability, or firmness. For the testaments and pacts of men are usually rescinded, but not so with God's.

27 <term>In which it is impossible</term>] In Greek it is <note>original: "ἐν οἷς"</note>, "in which." And it is not "the strongest," but "strong" <note>original: "ἰσχυρὰν"</note>, that is, valid.

28 <term>As an anchor</term>] <note>original: "ὡς ἄγκυραν"</note>, that is, "just like an anchor." Ancient Latin manuscripts have "like an anchor."

<meta>This page continues the transition from the end of Hebrews Chapter 6 into the detailed theological exposition of Chapter 7. The previous page concluded God’s promise to Abraham, established by an oath. Here, the author connects that promise to Jesus, who functions as a high priest in the line of the mysterious figure Melchizedek, whose superiority to the traditional Jewish priesthood (the Levites) is the primary focus of this section.</meta>

# TO THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER VII.

...and firm, and entering into the inner part of the veil, where the forerunner has entered on our behalf, Jesus, having become a High Priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. <margin>VII. 1</margin> For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, <margin>2</margin> to whom also Abraham divided a tenth part of all; being first, by interpretation, King of Righteousness, and after that also King of Salem, which is, King of Peace; <margin>3</margin> without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God, he remains a priest perpetually. <margin>4</margin> Now consider how great this man was, to whom even the Patriarch Abraham gave a tenth of the choice spoils? <margin>5</margin> And indeed, those of the sons of Levi who receive the priesthood have a commandment to take tithes from the people according to the law, that is, from their brothers, though they have come from the loins of Abraham. <margin>6</margin> But he whose genealogy is not counted from them received tithes from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises. <margin>7</margin> And without any contradiction, the lesser is blessed by the greater. <margin>8</margin> And here, mortal men receive tithes; but there, he receives them of whom it is witnessed that he lives. <margin>9</margin> And, so to speak, even Levi, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham. <margin>10</margin> For he was still in the loins of his father when Melchizedek met him. <margin>11</margin> If therefore perfection were through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people received the law), what further need was there for another priest to rise according to the order of Melchizedek, and not be called according to the order of Aaron? <margin>12</margin> For when the priesthood is changed, there is of necessity a change of the law also. <margin>13</margin> For he of whom these things are spoken belongs to another tribe, from which no one has officiated at the altar. <margin>14</margin> For it is evident that our Lord arose out of Judah, a tribe about which Moses spoke nothing concerning the priesthood. <margin>15</margin> And it is yet far more evident if, according to the likeness of Melchizedek, another priest arises, <margin>16</margin> who has become so, not according to the law of a fleshly commandment, but according to the power of an indestructible life. <margin>17</margin> For he testifies: "You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." <margin>18</margin> For there is a setting aside of the preceding commandment because of its weakness and uselessness. <margin>19</margin> For the law made nothing perfect, but...

---

<margin>29</margin> **To the inner parts of the veil**] <note>original Greek: καταπετάσματος (katapetasmatos)</note>. This properly signifies something stretched out and drawn over, which blocks the view.

<margin>1</margin> **First interpreted King of Righteousness**] For Melchizedek among the Hebrews sounds like "King of Righteousness." Since among them <term>Malci-zedek</term> <note>Hebrew: מלכי־צדק</note> "Malci" is called "my King." In the compound word, the letter *i* is added for the sake of euphony [pleasant sound], and <term>zedec</term> <note>Hebrew: צדק</note> means "righteousness." <term>Shalom</term> <note>Hebrew: שלום</note> however, sounds like "peace": some think this name was given by Melchizedek to the city of Jerusalem. From this passage, an error in interpretation can be detected in a small book circulated under an uncertain title, added to the volumes of both Testaments, concerning Hebrew names. It appears that work is nothing other than a disorganized collection by more than one man, even if Saint Jerome testifies that he published a book on these matters. For there, Melchizedek is explained in this manner: "Melchizedek, the Just King, or King of Righteousness, or King of Peace, or Peace-bringer." Yet in this name "Melchizedek," there is no word that signifies peace. Nor does Paul say that "Melchizedek" sounds like "King of Peace," but rather that "Melchij-salem" <note>Hebrew: מלך שלום (Melek Shalom)</note> expresses "King of Peace." Jerome, in his names for this Epistle, explains Melchizedek as "Just King."

<margin>2</margin> **Without father, without mother**] <note>original Greek: ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ (apatōr, amētōr)</note>. These are compound words among the Greeks. And "without genealogy" among them is <note>original Greek: ἀγενεαλόγητος (agenealogētos)</note>, which sounds almost as if you were to say, one whose family origin cannot be rendered.

<margin>3</margin> **Now consider**] <note>original Greek: θεωρεῖτε (theōreite)</note>, "You consider," or "You see." Although it can also be taken as "Consider!" [as an imperative].

<margin>4</margin> **From the choice spoils**] <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῶν ἀκροθινίων (ek tōn akrothiniōn)</note>. This usually signifies the firstfruits of the crops. The translator read "from the victors," but the Greek word signifies the "choicest parts." Truly, in this place he used "akrothinia" for the spoils or clothing stripped from the enemy, as interpreted by the Greek commentaries and Chrysostom himself. It is found with this meaning in the writings of Philostratus the Sophist. The translator seems to have followed the idea that the "choicest things" are usually placed at the peak of a heap. It is somewhat ridiculous that the translator of Chrysostom, when he had turned "akrothinia" into "choicest things" following our edition, added "the choice things are called spoils," apparently forgetting how to speak in Latin rather than Greek. Although even among the Latins, the best spoils were called "egregia" [excellent], being those taken from the enemy leaders. The Greek word is derived either from "touching the tops" (from which we get *akrothiganein* and *akrothigōs*) or from *akros*, which is "top," and *thinos*, a heap of grain or barley.

<column-break/>

...both sure and firm, and entering even <margin>20</margin> into those things which are within the veil, where the forerunner has entered for us, Jesus, having been made a High Priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. <margin>A</margin> For this was Melchizedek, king of Salem, <margin>VII. 1</margin> priest of the most high God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, and blessed him, to whom also Abraham <margin>2</margin> shared a tenth of all: who first, by interpretation, is called King of Righteousness, and then indeed also King of Salem, which is King of Peace, of unknown <margin>3</margin> father, unknown mother, unknown lineage, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but being likened to the Son of God, he remains a priest forever. <margin>B</margin> Consider <margin>4</margin> indeed, how great this man was, to whom even Abraham the Patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils? And those indeed, who <margin>5</margin> because they are of the number of the sons of Levi, take up the office of the priesthood, have a commandment that they should receive tithes from the people according to the law, that is, from their brothers, though they have come out of the loins of Abraham. But he, whose <margin>6</margin> lineage is not reckoned from them, received tithes from Abraham, and blessed him who held the promises. Furthermore, <margin>7</margin> no one denies that the one who is less receives a blessing from the one who is greater. And here indeed <margin>8</margin> men who die receive tithes; but there he does, of whom it is witnessed that he lives. And, so to <margin>9</margin> speak, in Abraham even Levi himself was tithed, who is accustomed to receive tithes. For he was still in the <margin>10</margin> loins of his father when Melchizedek met Abraham. Therefore, if perfection were through the Levitical <margin>11</margin> priesthood, for through this the people had received the law, what need was there further for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek, and not be called according to the order of Aaron? For <margin>12</margin> when the priesthood is transferred, it is necessary that a transfer of the law also take place. <margin>C</margin> For he, concerning whom these things are said, <margin>13</margin> belongs to another tribe, from which no one has stood at the altar. For it is plain that our Lord <margin>14</margin> has arisen from the tribe of Judah: but regarding this tribe, Moses spoke nothing concerning the priesthood. And this is <margin>15</margin> even more clear, since according to the likeness of Melchizedek another priest arises, <margin>D</margin> who has been made so, not according to a law <margin>16</margin> of a fleshly commandment, but according to the power of an indissoluble life. For he testifies in this manner: "You are <margin>17</margin> a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." For the commandment which preceded is <margin>18</margin> abolished because of its weakness and uselessness. For the law brought nothing to <margin>19</margin> perfection...

---

<margin>5</margin> **As if they themselves had come out**] The Latin phrase is ambiguous as to whether these words refer to the Levites receiving tithes or to the brothers giving them. However, since the Greek is <note>original: ἐξεληλυθότας (exelēlythotas)</note>, it can refer to nothing other than the brothers.

<margin>6</margin> **But of whose lineage, etc.**] <note>original Greek: Ὁ δὲ μὴ γενεαλογούμενος ἐξ αὐτῶν, δεδεκάτωκε τὸν Ἀβραὰμ</note>, that is, "He who is not numbered from their generation took tithes from Abraham."

<margin>7</margin> **Without any contradiction**] <note>original Greek: Χωρὶς δὲ πάσης ἀντιλογίας</note>, that is, "Without any true contradiction," which he just now translated as "controversy."

<margin>8</margin> **But there he is witnessed**] Witnessing, <note>original Greek: μαρτυρούμενος (martyroumenos)</note>, that is, of whom it is witnessed that he lived. For it was pronounced of him that he would be a Priest forever. Since the participle "martyroumenos" is in the middle voice. The Greek commentaries interpret it in this sense.

<margin>9</margin> **As it might be said**] <note>original Greek: ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν (hōs epos eipein)</note>, that is, "as I might say." Word for word it sounds like "as to say a word." The Greeks say the same thing as "to speak in a figure" [hōs typō eipein]: you will find this type of speech nowhere else in Paul.

<margin>10</margin> **And Levi who**] "And" in this place is not to be taken simply as a connecting word, but rather for "even" or "also," so that the sense is: not only did Abraham give tithes to Melchizedek, but even in Abraham—the author of the race—Levi himself, to whom the right of tithes belongs, paid tithes. Furthermore, what he explains with a figurative speech, saying "so to speak," follows shortly: "For he was still in the loins of his father," that is, Levi was not yet born, yet I say he was in a certain way tithed in his father.

<margin>11</margin> **He received tithes**] <note>original Greek: ὁ δεκάτας λαμβάνων (ho dekatas lambanōn)</note>, that is, "he who receives tithes," or "is accustomed to receive," using the present participle. For he is speaking not of Melchizedek, but of the Levites of his own time, who were accustomed to receive tithes.

<margin>12</margin> **Under it**] Understand "under the Levitical priesthood," lest anyone refer it to a man.

<margin>13</margin> **In whom for**] <note>original Greek: Ἐφ' ὃν γὰρ (Eph' hon gar)</note>, that is, "for unto whom," or "concerning whom."

<margin>14</margin> **Is of another tribe**] <note>original Greek: Φυλῆς ἑτέρας μετέσχηκεν (Phylēs heteras meteschēken)</note>, that is, he was a partaker of another nation or tribe.

<margin>15</margin> **In which tribe**] <note>original Greek: εἰς ἣν φυλὴν (eis hēn phylēn)</note>, that is, "concerning which tribe," or "to which tribe."

...but the introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to <margin>20</margin> God. **18** *And inasmuch as it is not without an oath*] <note>original: "Καὶ καθ᾿ ὅσον" (Kai kath’ hoson)</note>. **19** *He has an eternal priesthood*] <note>original: "ἀπαράβατον" (aparabaton)</note>, that is, a priesthood that cannot pass to another; it does not migrate from one person to another by succession, as was necessary in the Mosaic priesthood.
**20** *He is able forever*] <note>original: "εἰς τὸ παντελὲς" (eis to panteles)</note>, which sounds more like *to the full*, or *perfectly*; that is, as the Greek commentaries <note>The author refers to "scholia," which are ancient marginal grammatical or explanatory notes.</note> explain, not only here, but also there. **22** *To intercede for us*] <note>original: "ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν" (hyper auton)</note>, that is, for them.
**23** *Innocent*] <note>original: "ἄκακος" (akakos)</note>, free from guile. This is also how Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching.</note> interprets it. For "innocent" in Greek cannot be rendered exactly into Latin, if we believe Cicero.
**24** *Which is after the law*] In Greek it is <note>original: "τῆς μετὰ τὸν νόμον" (tes meta ton nomon)</note>, that is, that which is after the law. However, the Greek preposition *meta* is ambiguous. For it can also be read as *above the law*. If you read it as *after the law*, understand it as being after the law was established—namely, in the Psalms. Or if you prefer *above the law*, it is understood that there was more weight in the divine voice than in the precept of Moses. For a later decree annuls a prior one; and that which proceeds from a greater author annuls what a lesser one had instituted.
**25** *perfected forever*] <note>original: "τετελειωμένον" (teteleiomenon)</note>. As if to say, made always suitable and legitimate; for a priest is not always or everywhere suitable for performing a sacred rite.

---

priesthood for others. Hence what we commonly call an "office" <note>original: "officium"</note>, the Greeks call a "liturgy" <note>original: "λειτουργίαν" (leitourgian)</note>. They think it is named from *leiton*—which they used to call the *prytaneion*, that is, a public place in which magistrates were occupied—and *ergon* or "work"; hence, with a few letters changed, it is called a "liturgy" for those who served in the places of the magistrates. Furthermore, the genitive "of the holy things" can refer either to people or to the holy objects themselves, as in "administering holy things for us as a priest." Although the Greek commentaries prefer to take it as referring to people, that which follows immediately after suggests more strongly that we should take it as referring to holy things: *minister of holy things* and *of the true tabernacle*, so that "true" also refers to the holy things. For just as this tabernacle, namely heaven, is a true tabernacle, so the holy of holies which they administer there are true holy things. Theophylact <note>A 11th-century Archbishop of Ohrid and prominent biblical commentator.</note> and Chrysostom follow the latter opinion, although Theophylact mentions both.
**4** *If therefore he were*] <note>original: "Εἰ μὲν γὰρ" (Ei men gar)</note>, that is, "For if indeed."
**5** *Neither would he be a priest*] <note>original: "οὐδ᾿ ἂν ἦν ἱερεὺς" (oud' an en hiereus)</note>, that is, "he would not even be a priest," as one who offered nothing such as the law had prescribed.
**6** *When he completed*] <note>original: "μέλλων ἐπιτελεῖν" (mellon epitelein)</note>, that is, "when he was about to complete."
**7** *But now better*] <note>original: "διαφορωτέρας" (diaphoroteras)</note>, that is, "more excellent"; though in some copies it is written *diapheroteras*.
**8** *By how much*] The Latin translator ought to have added "by so much" <note>original: "tanto"</note> to correspond with "by how much" <note>original: "quanto"</note>. For the Greeks are permitted to omit it.
**9** *That first one*] <note>original: "ἡ πρώτη ἐκείνη" (he prote ekeine)</note>, that is, "that first [thing]." Except that the Greeks sometimes use this superlative in place of a comparative.
**10** *Had been free of fault*] <note>original: "ἦν ἄμεμπτος" (en amemptos)</note>, that is, "had been irreproachable," or something about which you could not complain, or in which nothing could be desired. However, Chrysostom twists this so that *amemptos* is taken to mean not that the covenant itself is blameworthy, but that it makes people blameless—so that the fault belongs to the men, not the Testament. Yet Paul admits to the Romans that the law was weak and could not confer perfect salvation; and Luke affirms the same in Acts. And Peter calls it a burden unbearable for all. And God, through the Prophet, calls them "statutes that were not good." All these must be understood according to Chrysostom's view: for nothing proceeds from God that is not good. And Paul elsewhere calls the law holy and good.
**11** *A place would be sought*] <note>original: "ἐζητεῖτο τόπος" (ezeteito topos)</note>, that is, "a place would have been sought."
**12** *For blaming*] <note>original: "Μεμφόμενος γὰρ" (Memphomenos gar)</note>, this is the verb from which the word "faultless" <note>original: "ἄμεμπτος" (amemptos)</note> was derived; he proves it was not without reproach, since God Himself complains about it.
**13** *Behold the days will come*] He has brought this testimony from the <meta>catchword: chapter</meta> of Jeremiah.

<margin>chapter xxxi. and he cited it in such a way that it appears the Septuagint <note>The Septuagint is the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Old Testament.</note> version is followed in all things, but it varies very little from the Hebrew truth. First, <term>they shall come</term>, for which Jerome has <term>they shall come</term>, in Greek is <term>erchontai</term>, which pertains to both times. <margin>F</margin> 1 **Had** indeed also the first] <term>Eiche men oun</term>, that is, "It had indeed therefore." And "the first" is a noun, and refers to the testament. Nor is it <term>formerly</term> in Greek, but <term>the first</term>.
2 <term>Regulations of worship</term>] The speech is ambiguous: for it can be read distinctly as <term>regulations, of worship</term>, but it is more correctly read together: for he calls the rites of sacrifices <term>worship</term>.
3 <term>And a worldly sanctuary</term>] <term>to te agion kosmikon</term>, that is, a mundane holy place, because even proselytes and Gentiles were admitted into that part, which the commentaries of Chrysostom and Theophylact on this passage indicate.
4 <term>Lampstands</term>] <term>hē te lychnia</term>, that is, "the lampstand," in the singular number. We translate it as <term>lamps</term>, because that same lampstand supports many individual lamps.
5 <term>Which is called Holy</term>] "Holy" in this place is plural in number and neuter in gender, <term>ētis legetai agia</term>, which are called <term>the holy things</term>, so that it responds to that which follows soon after, <term>the holy of holies</term>. Saint Augustine is quite tormented in his "Questions on Leviticus," Question 53, regarding in what sense <term>holy</term> should be understood, and thinks it is said <term>ta agia tōn agiōn</term>, just as if you were to say clearly <term>the holy of the holy ones</term>, that is, <term>the Holy Spirit of the Holy God</term>, although it is established that this doubling, according to the idiom of the Hebrew speech, has the effect of an epithet of sanctity. Indeed, he calls the first part merely <term>holy</term>, the other as eminently holy, <term>the holy of holies</term>.

# PAUL’S EPISTLE CHAPTER IX. & X.

<margin>A</margin> 11 [But Christ being come as high priest] of good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not 12 made with hands, that is to say, not of this creation, neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered once for all into the holy place, having 13 obtained eternal redemption. For if the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkling those who are defiled, sanctifies for the purification of the flesh, 14 how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse your conscience from dead works to 15 serve the living God? <margin>B</margin> And for this reason he is the mediator of a new testament <note>original: "διαθήκης" (diathēkēs), which can mean both a covenant/agreement or a last will/testament</note>, so that a death having occurred for the redemption of the transgressions under the first testament, those who are called may receive the promise of the eternal 16 inheritance. For where there is a testament, it is necessary that the death 17 of the testator be brought forward. For a testament is firm over the dead, since it never has strength while the testator is living. 18 Wherefore not even the first was inaugurated without blood. 19 For when every commandment according to the law had been spoken by Moses to all the people, taking the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, he sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, 20 saying, "This is the blood of the testament which <margin>C</margin> 21 God has commanded to you." And likewise he sprinkled with blood both the tabernacle and all the vessels of the ministry. 22 And almost all things are cleansed with blood according to the law, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. 23 It was necessary therefore that the patterns of the things in the heavens should be cleansed with these; but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than 24 these. For Christ did not enter into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for 25 us. Nor was it that he should offer himself often, as the High Priest enters into the holy place every year 26 with the blood of others; for then he would have had to suffer often since the foundation of the world; but now once at the consummation of the ages, for the putting away of sin by his <margin>D</margin> 27 sacrifice, he has been manifested. And as it is appointed for men once to die, and after this 28 the judgment: so also Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, shall appear a second time without sin to those who await him <margin>X. 1</margin> <margin>E</margin> 1 for salvation. For the law, having a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things, can never, by the same sacrifices which they offer year after year continually, make those who approach 2 perfect. For then would they not have ceased to be offered, because the worshipers, having been once 3 cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins? But in those sacrifices there is a reminder of sins...

...closely connects to what follows: *he entered into the holy place*. For *how can one enter who was already present?*
19 *Through the greater*] These are two words, <note>original: "διὰ τῆς μείζονος"</note>, meaning through that which was larger or more significant.
20 *Not made with hands*] <note>original: "οὐ χειροποιήτου"</note>, a compound word.
21 *Who through the Holy Spirit*] <note>original: "διὰ Πνεύματος αἰωνίου"</note>, that is, through the eternal Spirit. This is how Chrysostom <note>a 4th-century Church Father known for his preaching</note> reads and interprets it.
22 *Death interceding*] <note>original: "θανάτου γενομένου"</note>, that is, *death having occurred*. However, the Translator has rendered the sense well.
<margin>F</margin> 23 *For where there is a testament, the death &c.*] But Saint Jerome <note>the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin</note> pointed out that the word which the Translators turned into *testament* sounds more like a "pact" or "covenant" <note>original Hebrew: "בְּרִית" (berit)</note> to the Hebrews. If this is true, it appears this Epistle was written by someone who did not know Hebrew, which seems not at all unlikely. Certainly, Saint Jerome consistently translates it as "pact." Now, for the Greeks, *diatheke* means a *disposition* or *arrangement* more than a *testament*. Among the Hebrews, *berit* is derived from "witnesses," because pacts which we wish to be ratified are usually sanctioned before witnesses. Therefore, the Seventy <note>the authors of the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament</note> seem to have followed this when they translated it as *testament*. But if anyone prefers to follow the word itself rather than common usage and property of language, whatever is done with witnesses will be a testament. And it is not "confirmed," but <note>original: "βεβαία"</note>, that is, *ratified* or *firm*, with "is" being understood.
24 *For when it was read*] <note>original: "λαληθείσης γάρ"</note>, that is, *For when it was spoken*. Regarding the mandate of the law, the Greek reads differently: <note>original Greek: "λαληθείσης γὰρ πάσης ἐντολῆς κατὰ νόμον ὑπὸ Μωϋσέως παντὶ τῷ λαῷ"</note>, that is, *For when every mandate had been spoken or recited according to the law by Moses to all the people*.
25 *And scarlet wool*] <note>original: "καὶ ἐρίου κοκκίνου"</note>, that is, *and scarlet wool, from the "coccus" [insect/dye] which is used for dyeing purple.*
26 *This is the blood of the testament*] Christ seems to have alluded to this at the Supper: *This is the blood of the new testament*, representing his own sacrifice in a similar way.

<column-break/>

of good things to come, 19 through the larger and more perfect tabernacle, 20 not made with hands, that is, not of this structure; neither through the blood of goats and calves, <margin>12</margin> but through his own blood he entered once into the holy place, having found eternal redemption. For if the blood <margin>13</margin> of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a young cow, sprinkling the defiled, sanctifies for the purification of the flesh, how <margin>14</margin> much more the blood of Christ, 21 who through the eternal Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, shall purge your conscience from dead works, to serve the living God. And for this reason he is the mediator <margin>15</margin> of a new testament, so that 22 death interceding, for the redemption of those transgressions which were under the first testament, those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance. 23 For indeed where a testament <margin>16</margin> is, the death of the testator must intercede. For a testament <margin>17</margin> is ratified over the dead, since it is not yet valid while the testator lives. Wherefore not even that first one <margin>18</margin> was dedicated without blood. 24 For when <margin>19</margin> Moses had set forth every precept according to the law to all the people, having taken the blood of calves and goats, with water 25 and scarlet wool and hyssop, he sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying, <margin>20</margin> 26 This is the blood of the testament, which God has commanded to you. Moreover, he likewise sprinkled both the tabernacle and all the <margin>21</margin> vessels of the ministry with blood. And <margin>22</margin> almost all things are purified with blood according to the law, and 27 without the shedding of blood there is no remission. Therefore <margin>23</margin> it is necessary that the examples of those things which are in the heavens be purified with these things; but the heavenly things themselves be cleansed with better victims than these are. <margin>24</margin> For Christ did not enter into holy places made with hands, 28 copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, that he might appear now in the sight of God for us, not that <margin>25</margin> he should offer himself more often, as the High Priest enters into the holy place every year with the blood of another. Otherwise he would have had to suffer more often <margin>26</margin> since the founding of the world. But now once at the consummation of the ages, for the destruction of sin, through the sacrifice of himself he appeared. And insofar as it <margin>27</margin> remains for men to die once, and after this the judgment: so also Christ was offered once, to <margin>28</margin> take away the sins of many; he shall be seen again without sin by those who look for him unto salvation. For the law, <margin>1. x.</margin> possessing a shadow of good things to come, 1 not the very image of the things, can never make those who approach perfect by these victims, which they offer the same ones <margin>2</margin> continually every year. 2 Otherwise would they not have ceased to be offered? because the worshipers, once they had sacrificed and been purified once, would have no further consciousness of sins. 3 But in these a reminder of sins is made... <margin>3</margin>

---

...every year.
27 *Without the shedding of blood*] In Greek this is a compound word, <note>original: "αἱματεκχυσίας" (haimatekchysias)</note>. This passage seems to taste somewhat of Origen’s <note>an early Christian theologian known for allegorical interpretation</note> style, if you read what follows and if one interprets it too literally. Therefore, Chrysostom treats the matter as an allegory. The Synagogue was the earth, the Church is heaven. Their holy place he called "worldly" a little earlier; ours are heavenly, since we ourselves are heavenly.
28 *For not in those made with hands*] In Greek it is <note>original: "εἰς χειροποίητα ἅγια"</note>, and our more corrected manuscripts agree.
29 *Copies of the true things*] In Greek it is not <note>original: "ὑποδείγματα" (patterns)</note>, as it was a little earlier, but <note>original: "ἀντίτυπα" (antitypes)</note>, as if giving back the likeness of the true things. Nor does it seem absurd to me to call those old things "patterns" which outlined and, as it were, foreshadowed the Gospel History. Certainly they were patterns for us, even if they were not for God. Whoever wrote this Epistle thought there was no difference between *pattern* and *antitype*.
30 *In the consummation*] <note>original: "ἐπὶ συντελείᾳ"</note>, at the consummation, or as the consummation is imminent. For that preposition sometimes has that force if joined to the dative case.
1 *Not the very image*] <note>original: "οὐκ αὐτὴν τὴν εἰκόνα"</note>. He used "very" for "true and expressed," which represents the whole thing as it is. Hence he also calls Christ the image of God. But a shadow <note>term: "skia" (shadow) vs. "eikon" (image)</note> represents nothing except the outer outlines of a body, from which the rough painting of the Ancients began.
2 *Otherwise they would have ceased to be offered*] The Greek commentaries advise that this should be read as a question: *would they not have ceased to be offered?* The Translator seems to have read <note>original: "ἐπεὶ ἐπαύσαντο ἂν προσφερόμεναι"</note>. Theophylactus <note>an 11th-century Byzantine archbishop and commentator</note> supports our view. Certainly, either the negation should have been omitted, or it should be read as a question, which carries the force of a negation. Furthermore, here the Translator elegantly turned the participle into an infinitive verb, *they ceased to be offered* for *to be offered*, which elsewhere he left less elegantly.
3 *But in them a reminder*] "In the sacrifices" or "victims" must be understood. For he is speaking of repeated acts.

# TO THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER X.

<margin>4</margin> <note>original: "κατ' ἐνιαυτὸν" (yearly)</note> For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins. <margin>5</margin> Therefore, when he comes into the world, he says: "Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body <margin>6</margin> you have prepared for me; In burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin you had no pleasure." <margin>7</margin> Then I said, "Behold, I have come—in the volume of the book it is written of me—to do your will, O God." <margin>8</margin> Above, when he says, "Sacrifice and offering, burnt offerings, and sacrifices for sin you did not desire, nor had pleasure in them" (which are offered according to the law), <margin>9</margin> then he said, "Behold, I have come to do your will, O God." He takes away the first that he may establish the second. <margin>10</margin> By that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. <margin>11</margin> And every priest stands ministering daily and offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. <margin>12</margin> But this Man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins forever, sat down at the right hand of God, <margin>13</margin> from that time waiting till his enemies are made his footstool. <margin>14</margin> For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified. <margin>15</margin> But the Holy Spirit also witnesses to us; for after he had said before, <margin>16</margin> "This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their hearts, and in their minds I will write them," <margin>17</margin> then he adds, "Their sins and their lawless deeds I will remember no more." <margin>18</margin> Now where there is remission of these, there is no longer an offering for sin. <margin>19</margin> Therefore, brethren, having boldness to enter the Holiest by the blood of Jesus, <margin>20</margin> by a new and living way which he consecrated for us, through the veil, that is, his flesh, <margin>21</margin> and having a High Priest over the house of God, <margin>22</margin> let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience and <margin>23</margin> our bodies washed with pure water. Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful. <margin>24</margin> And let us consider one another in order to stir up love and good works, <margin>25</margin> not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as is the manner of some, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching. <margin>26</margin> For if we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, <margin>27</margin> but a certain fearful expectation of judgment, and fiery indignation which will devour the adversaries.

---

<margin>4 *Sacrifice and offering you did not desire* </margin> Whoever wrote this Epistle differs very little from the Septuagint <note>The Septuagint is the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> version when citing testimonies from the Old Testament. According to them, we read: "Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you have prepared for me. Burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin you did not seek. Then I said, Behold, I come. In the volume of the book it is written of me, to do your will, O my God." Where "body" is placed instead of "ears," and this is how Augustine read it when explaining Psalm 39. But Saint Jerome, following the Hebrew truth, translated it this way: "Victim and offering you do not need, but you have pierced ears for me. Burnt offering and for sin you did not ask. Then I said, Behold, I come." <note>original: "aures autem perfodisti mihi"</note> Furthermore, where it says "you have pierced ears for me," it indicates the obedience of faith, which God already required from his worshippers, having grown weary of animal sacrifices.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>5 *That I may do, O God* </margin> This refers back to what preceded it: "Behold, I come to do, etc.," as noted in the Greek commentaries, and it is clear from what follows.

<margin>6 *Then I said, Behold, I come* </margin> Where these words are repeated, the Greek says *tote eireken* <note>original: "τότε εἴρηκεν"</note>, meaning "then he said." It is strange why the Latin translator changed the person <note>from "I said" to "he said"</note>, since it refers to the words placed above. Nevertheless, traces of an erasure in a very ancient Pauline codex indicate it was written that way. Chrysostom seems to have read it no differently, given that he raises a question about whom this is said of. For if he had read "then I said"—that is, if the speaker said it of himself—it would not be appropriate to ask whom it was said about. Later, I consulted a Greek manuscript and found *eireken* (he said) in the second instance, though in Theophylact it was *eipon* (I said). The Latin manuscripts also vary.

<margin>7 *That he may establish the second* </margin> <note>original: "τὸ δεύτερον"</note>, meaning the second thing, or the latter thing.

<margin>8 *The priest is present daily* </margin> <note>original: "Ἱερεὺς ἕστηκε"</note>, meaning "the priest stands," to render it word for word. There is no reason the sense of time should bother us, as in words of this kind the past tense is often used for the present. I mention this because I noticed some were needlessly troubled by it, including our friend Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>referred to here as "Stapulensis"</note>. Otherwise, if you read "he stood," it would hardly fit what follows: "which can never take away sins." Although in Greek it is "they are never able" <note>original: "οὐδέποτε δύνανται"</note>; and I found it written this way in the Pauline manuscript, and likewise in the one from Constance.

<margin>9 *Offering a sacrifice for sins* </margin> <note>original: "προσενέγκας θυσίαν"</note> is a past participle; therefore, by changing the voice, one could translate it as "a sacrifice having been offered."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>4</margin> yearly. For it is not possible for the blood of bulls and <margin>5</margin> goats to take away sins. Therefore, when entering the world, he says: Sacrifice and offering you did not want, but a body you fitted for me. Burnt offerings and <margin>6</margin> for sin you did not approve. <margin>7</margin> Then I said, Behold, I am present; in the heading of the book it is written of me, that I should do, <margin>8</margin> O God, your will. Above when he says: Sacrifice and offering and burnt offerings and for sin you did not want, nor did you approve, which are offered according to the law; <margin>9</margin> Then he said: Behold, I am present to do, O God, your will. He removes the first, that he may establish the latter. <margin>B</margin> <margin>10</margin> By which will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ, performed once. <margin>11</margin> And every priest indeed stands daily performing sacred rites, and often offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. <margin>12</margin> But this man, one victim having been offered for sins, sits forever at the right hand of God; <margin>13</margin> waiting for what remains, until his enemies are made a stool for his feet. <margin>14</margin> For by a single offering he has made perfect forever those who are being sanctified. <margin>15</margin> Moreover, the Holy Spirit himself also testifies to us, namely when he foretold: <margin>16</margin> This is the testament which I will establish with them after those days, says the Lord; I will give my laws in their heart, and in their minds I will write them, <margin>17</margin> and of their sins and iniquities I will no longer remember. <margin>18</margin> Furthermore, where there is remission of these, there is no longer an offering for <margin>C</margin> sin. <margin>19</margin> Since therefore, brothers, we have the liberty of entering into the holy places through the blood of Jesus, <margin>20</margin> by that way which he dedicated for us, fresh and living, through the veil, that is, through his flesh, <margin>21</margin> and since we have a great priest set over the house of God, <margin>22</margin> let us approach with a true heart in the certainty of faith, sprinkled in our hearts, and with an evil conscience driven away, <margin>23</margin> and washed in body with pure water, let us hold the confession of hope without wavering; for he is faithful who promised. <margin>24</margin> And let us consider one another in this: that we may provoke unto charity and good works, <margin>25</margin> not deserting our mutual gathering, as is the custom for some, but exhorting one another, and this all the more, because you see the day approaching. <margin>26</margin> For if we sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of the truth, <margin>D</margin> there is no longer a sacrifice left for sins, <margin>27</margin> but a certain terrible expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire, which is about to devour the adversaries.

---

<margin>10 *Sanctified* </margin> <note>original: "τοὺς ἁγιαζομένους"</note>, that is, those who are being sanctified <note>Erasmus notes the present tense implies an ongoing process</note>.

<margin>11 *I will give laws* </margin> <note>original: "διδὼς νόμους"</note>, that is, "giving laws." The Donatian manuscript had "by giving" instead of "I will give"; the Constance manuscript agreed.

<margin>12 *In the entrance* </margin> Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous humanist critic</note> corrects this to "into the entrance," as if we are confident that we will enter the holy places in the future. Indeed, the Greek phrase *eis ten eisodon* is ambiguous. But I do not see why it cannot rightly be taken as us having confidence in the entrance by which Christ the High Priest entered the sanctuary for us. Even if the other reading is not rejected, it fits better with what follows: "Let us approach with a true heart, etc."

<margin>13 *He initiated* </margin> <note>original: "ἐνεκαίνισεν"</note>, that is, "he renewed" or "he dedicated," from which we get the word *encaenia* <note>the Feast of Dedication</note>.

<margin>14 *A new way* </margin> <note>original: "ὁδὸν πρόσφατον"</note>, that is, a "recent" or "fresh" way.

<margin>15 *Let us approach* </margin> <note>original: "προσερχώμεθα"</note>, that is, "we approach." Although the Greek manuscripts vary here. And "in fullness" is *en plerophoria*, about which I have already often warned. The Greek commentaries attributed to Chrysostom interpret this as the certainty of confidence.

<margin>16 *A confession that does not decline* </margin> <note>original: "ἀκλινῆ"</note>, that is, not wavering, nor nodding here and there, but firm and unmoved. Otherwise, "indeclinable" refers to something that cannot be avoided.

<margin>17 *Into a provocation of charity* </margin> <note>original: "εἰς παροξυσμὸν"</note>. Which Luke in Acts uses for "a sharp disagreement" in a negative sense; here it is used in a positive sense, for "stimulation" or "incitement."

<margin>18 *Our collection* </margin> <note>original: "ἐπισυναγωγὴν"</note>, that is, "gathering together," as if they had arrived or were summoned afterward.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>19 *How much you see* </margin> <note>original: "ὅσῳ βλέπετε"</note>, that is, by as much as you see.

<margin>20 *But terrible* </margin> It was better to say "But a certain terrible..." Though these conjunctions signify the same thing, it sometimes matters where you place them.

<margin>21 *And jealousy of fire* </margin> <note>original: "ζῆλος"</note>, he attributes a kind of sense to the fire. For he calls the impulse of avenging "zeal."

<margin>22 *Which is going to consume* </margin> <note>original: "ἐσθίειν μέλλοντος"</note>, that is, which is about to eat up or devour. And this passage openly takes away hope from Christians who have relapsed into sin, unless we conveniently interpret it according to the reasoning I indicated above from the opinion of Chrysostom, and also Theophylact: that baptism, which represents Christ's death, cannot be repeated. Theophylact specifically testifies that this speech of Paul was distorted by some to interpret it as meaning no place for pardon is given to those who fall back into vice after baptism. Because...
