<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews. Having previously discussed the finality of Christ's sacrifice, the author now addresses the severe consequences of rejecting this grace and begins the famous discourse on the nature of faith in Chapter 11.</meta>

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL, CHAPTER XI. <note>The header indicates Chapter 11, though the text begins with the conclusion of Chapter 10.</note>

<margin>28</margin> ...the adversaries. Anyone who set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three <margin>29</margin> witnesses. Of how much worse punishment, do you think, will he be counted worthy who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has considered the blood of the covenant, by which he was sanctified, a common thing, and has insulted the Spirit of <margin>30</margin> grace? For we know him who said, "Vengeance is mine, I will repay," says the Lord. <margin>31</margin> And again, "The Lord will judge his people." <margin>32</margin> It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. But call to mind the former days, in which, after being enlightened, you endured a great struggle of sufferings: <margin>33</margin> partly while you were made a spectacle <note>The Greek term suggests being put on display in a theater for public mockery.</note> both by reproaches and afflictions, and partly while you became companions of those who were so <margin>34</margin> treated. For you also had compassion on my chains, and accepted the seizure of your goods with joy, knowing that you have for yourselves a better possession in <margin>35</margin> heaven, and one that lasts. Therefore do not cast away your confidence, which has a <margin>36</margin> great reward. For you have need of patience, so that, having done the will of God, you may receive the <margin>37</margin> promise. For yet a very, very little while, and he <margin>38</margin> who is coming will come, and will not tarry. But the just shall live by faith; and if he draws back, <margin>39</margin> my soul has no pleasure in him. But we are not of those who draw back to destruction, but of faith for the <margin>XI. 1</margin> preservation of the soul. Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. <margin>2</margin> For by it the elders obtained a good testimony. <margin>3</margin> By faith we understand that the worlds were prepared by the word of God...

---

<margin>A</margin> Since those things that follow—"But a fearful expectation of judgment"—seem to conflict with this interpretation (for otherwise he would have said, "but repentance follows"), it could also be explained that Paul uses <term>hypopheri</term> <note>original: "ὑποφέρη" — a rhetorical strategy of bringing up an objection or a terrifying possibility</note> in order to further deter them from sinning. There are similar passages in the Epistle of John; or we might understand this as referring to those who fall away from the law of Christ, whom he calls "adversaries."

<margin>23</margin> **Making void** ] <term>Athetesas tis nomon</term> <note>original: "Ἀθετήσας τις νόμον"</note>, that is, anyone who has made the law void or set it aside.

<margin>24</margin> **To deserve punishments** ] <term>axiōthesetai</term> <note>original: "ἀξιωθήσεται"</note>, that is, he will merit, or be held worthy of.

<margin>25</margin> **Considered it polluted** ] <term>koinon</term> <note>original: "κοινὸν"</note>, that is, common. For this is how the Jews refer to what is profane and abominable. Furthermore, "considered" is used in place of "judged" or "held."

<margin>26</margin> **Vengeance is mine** ] In Greek, "vengeance" is in the nominative case, <term>Emoi ekdikēsis</term> <note>original: "Ἐμοὶ ἐκδίκησις"</note>, as we noted before. It has the same force as saying, "Vengeance belongs to me," and "It is mine to avenge, not yours." And "I will repay" is added for emphasis, as the Constance manuscript <note>A reference to a specific ancient codex likely from the Diocese of Constance.</note> agrees.

<margin>27</margin> **Because he will judge** ] The word "Because" is not found in the Greek. Furthermore, that phrase, "In one part indeed by reproaches," could have been translated more clearly as "now and then," or "partly and partly," or "not only... but also." *Partly indeed while, being affected by both insults and pressures, you were a spectacle to everyone; and partly while you became companions of those living in such a way.* The sense is that they are praised on two counts: not only did they themselves endure persecution for the faith of Christ, but they also stood by and shared with others suffering these things. Furthermore, the opinion held by Laurentius <note>Laurentius Valla (1407–1457), a humanist scholar who questioned traditional authorship of biblical books.</note>—that this specific little word "my chains" proves this is Paul's Epistle—is trivial, if not ridiculous, as if almost all the successors and helpers of the Apostles were not also in chains.

<margin>B</margin> <margin>28</margin> **Made a spectacle** ] <term>theatrizomenoi</term> <note>original: "θεατριζόμενοι"</note>. <term>Theatron</term> to the Greeks is a spectacle. Hence those who are brought out into a theater to be a spectacle for all are called "those being theatricized."

<margin>29</margin> **For also in chains** ] In Greek it is <term>tois desmois emou</term> <note>original: "τοῖς δεσμοῖς ἐμοῦ"</note>, that is, "my chains." The translator seems to have read <term>desmiois</term> <note>meaning "prisoners"</note>. Theophylact <note>A prominent Byzantine commentator on the Bible.</note> reads "my chains." Both readings offer a sound meaning.

<margin>30</margin> **Knowing yourselves** ] The Greeks read it thus: <term>ginōskontes echein en heautois kreittona hyparxin en ouranois kai menousan</term> <note>original: "γινώσκοντες ἔχειν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς κρείττονα ὕπαρξιν ἐν οὐρανοῖς καὶ μένουσαν"</note>, that is, "knowing that you have in yourselves a better substance in heaven and one that remains." Some manuscripts have "in heaven" instead of "in yourselves." Some had it this way: "to have for yourselves a better substance in heaven."

<margin>31</margin> **Do not therefore cast away** ] <term>Mē apobalēte oun</term> <note>original: "Μὴ ἀποβάλητε οὖν"</note>, that is, "Therefore do not throw away."

<margin>32</margin> **For patience is necessary for you** ] <term>Hypomonēs gar echete chreian</term> <note>original: "Ὑπομονῆς γὰρ ἔχετε χρείαν"</note>. This does not simply mean "patience" by which we tolerate evils, but a "patient expectation," where we endure in evils with the hope of a reward and preserve ourselves for better things.

<margin>C</margin> <margin>33</margin> **For yet a very little while** ] <term>Eti gar mikron, hoson, hoson</term> <note>original: "Ἔτι γὰρ μικρὸν, ὅσον, ὅσον"</note>. Which could be translated: "For yet a very, very tiny, or extremely small time"; for the doubling of the word in the Greek language creates an emphasis <note>term: "epitafis" — a rhetorical intensification</note> on the brevity of time, following the idiom of the Hebrew language, which explains intensity by repeating the same word. An example of this is in Jeremiah: "figs good, good" and "figs bad, bad." Again in the same: "the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord." Likewise Isaiah in chapter 10: "For yet a very little while, and my indignation shall be finished."

<margin>34</margin> **Lives by faith** ] <term>zēsetai</term> <note>original: "ζήσεται"</note>, that is, "he will live," or "he is going to live."

<column-break/>

<margin>28</margin> He who has spurned the law of Moses dies without mercy under two or three witnesses. How <margin>29</margin> much worse punishments do you think he will be afflicted with, who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, and has held the blood of the covenant as a profane thing, through which he had been sanctified, and has insulted the Spirit of grace? For we <margin>30</margin> know him who said: "Vengeance is mine, I will repay," says the Lord. And again: "The Lord <margin>31</margin> will judge his people." It is a horrendous thing to <margin>32</margin> fall into the hands of the living God. But let the former days come back to your memory, in which, once illuminated, you sustained a great struggle of afflictions: Partim indeed while, being affected by <margin>33</margin> both insults and pressures, you were a spectacle to everyone; and partly while you became companions of those living in such a way. For indeed, <margin>34</margin> you were participants in the afflictions that arose from my chains, and you accepted the plundering of your goods with joy, knowing that you have in yourselves a better and lasting substance in the heavens. Do not, therefore, throw away your confi- <margin>35</margin> dence, which has a great repayment of reward. For <margin>36</margin> you have need of patience, so that, when you have performed the will of God, you may carry off the promise. For yet a very tiny amount of time, <margin>37</margin> and he who is to come will come, and will not delay. But the just man is going to live by faith; <margin>38</margin> and if he withdraws himself, he will not be approved by my soul. But we are not those who withdraw <margin>39</margin> ourselves into perdition, but we belong to faith for the acquisition of the soul. Now faith is the <margin>XI. 1</margin> substance of those things which are hoped for, the evidence of those which are not seen. For by this <margin>2</margin> <margin>3</margin> the elders earned a testimony. By faith we understand that the ages were perfected by the word of God...

---

<margin>35</margin> **Because if** ] Ancient manuscripts have "but if." The Greeks have <term>kai ean</term> <note>original: "καὶ ἐὰν"</note>, that is, "and if."

<margin>36</margin> **Will not please my soul** ] <term>ouk eudokei hē psychē mou en autō</term> <note>original: "οὐκ εὐδοκεῖ ἡ ψυχή μου ἐν αὐτῷ"</note>, that is, "my soul is not well-pleased in him." Although Saint Jerome thinks this should be read as referring to the *vision*, not to the *man*: for it is preceded in Habakkuk (from where this passage is taken), "Write the vision," etc. And that phrase, "if he withdraws himself," he refers to Christ delaying, not to a man despairing. Anyone who wishes to be more fully instructed on this should read his commentary on the second chapter of Habakkuk.

<margin>37</margin> **Sons of withdrawal** ] I do not find "Sons" in the Greek manuscripts, nor even in the Pauline exemplar, unless someone had written "sons" in the space between the lines with a more recent hand. The very ancient Constance manuscript supports us here. Furthermore, when he said, "we are not of withdrawal," it is as if he said, "we are not withdrawers," that is, those who flee and refuse to obey: but "we are of faith," that is, faithful, as if you were to say, "we are of God." And it is not "let us be," but "we are," in the indicative mood, not the imperative.

<margin>D</margin> <margin>1</margin> **Substance of things to be hoped for** ] <term>Hypostasis</term> <note>original: "Ὑπόστασις"</note>, that is, things which are hoped for, so that the name "of things to be hoped for" is a gerundive, not a participle. <term>Hypostasis</term> indicates certainty, and that upon which something leans and is supported. Augustine, explaining the 14th chapter of the Gospel according to John, cites it thus: "Now faith is the substance of those who hope," so that <term>hypostasis</term> is taken actively (as much as it is a middle-voice verb), as if faith is that upon which believers lean. He cites it likewise in his book *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, Book 2, chapter 31. In the same place he translates <term>elenchos</term> <note>original: "ἔλεγχος"</note> as "conviction," but harshly. Here certain people argue about this "definition," as they call it, when it is rather a praise of faith than a logical definition. Although Jerome and Theophylact call it a definition, because it has some appearance of a definition—the kind by which Logicians explain the nature of a thing. Indeed, with this little introduction he enters into the praise of faith, soon showing by examples how much power faith has. Unless, perhaps, they think it is a "definition" wherever they read the word "is." For example, if I say, "Letters are a solace in adversity, an ornament in prosperity," they might think this little praise of learning must be judged by the laws of a formal definition. And there are those who, having set aside this definition as too Apostolic and not "scholarly" enough, substitute another sophisticated one that reeks of Aristotle's logic, namely: "Faith is a voluntary certainty of things absent, situated below knowledge and above opinion." A very common commentary <note>term: "Gloss" — referring to the Glossa Ordinaria or similar medieval scholastic commentaries.</note> on the chapter concerning the High Trinity and the Catholic faith blathers other things of this sort. Among them is this: "Symbol [Creed] is said to come from *syn*, which is 'together,' and *bolus*, 'a morsel': because each of the Apostles brought his own little morsel." I will add this: in this place "faith" is not used properly for that by which we believe what must be believed, but for that by which we hope, that is, "trust" itself. An old commentary indicates this is said by synecdoche <note>A figure of speech where a part represents the whole.</note>, since faith concerns things past, present, and future.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>2</margin> **Argument** ] <term>elenchos</term> <note>original: "ἔλεγχος"</note>, that is, an indication or evidence; for that is what "argument" means in this place. The translator of Chrysostom renders it "conviction." Even if in common books it is everywhere corrupted to "conjunction." Although he repeats that word so many times, no one noticed the error, not even in the latest edition. Certainly, the sense itself could have warned the reader of this. For when he says, "Conviction is indeed in things that are quite manifest," it is clear that "conjunction" does not fit here.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>3</margin> **Of things not appearing** ] The Greek is <term>ou blepomenōn</term> <note>original: "οὐ βλεπομένων"</note>, that is, "which are not seen." And it is not "old men," but "elders," <term>hoi presbyteroi</term> <note>original: "οἱ πρεσβύτεροι"</note>. And <term>emartyrēthēsan</term> <note>original: "ἐμαρτυρήθησαν"</note>, which he translates here as "obtained a testimony," could be translated as "were approved by testimony," or "earned a testimony."

<summary>This page concludes the warnings against apostasy in Hebrews 10 and begins the famous "Hall of Faith" in Chapter 11, providing a scholarly linguistic analysis of terms like "substance" and "evidence." The author critiques medieval scholastic definitions of faith in favor of a more biblical, trust-based understanding.</summary>

# TO THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER XI.

...so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible. **4** By faith Abel offered to God a more excellent sacrifice <note>original: "πλείονα θυσίαν" (pleiona thysian), meaning a more abundant or superior offering</note> than Cain, through which he was testified to be righteous, God testifying over his gifts; and through it, though he died, he still speaks. **5** By faith Enoch was translated so as not to see death, and he was not found, because God had translated him; for before his translation he was testified to have pleased God. **6** But without faith it is impossible to please him; for he who approaches God must believe that he exists, and that he becomes a rewarder to those who seek him. **7** By faith Noah, having been warned by an oracle about things not yet seen, being moved with fear, prepared an ark for the salvation of his house, through which he condemned the world, and became an heir of the righteousness which is according to faith. **8** By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out into the place which he was to receive for an inheritance, and he went out, not knowing where he was going. **9** By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, the fellow-heirs of the same promise. **10** For he was waiting for the city which has foundations, whose craftsman and builder is God. **11** By faith even Sarah herself received power for the foundation of seed, and she gave birth past the time of her age, since she considered him faithful who had promised. **12** Therefore even from one man there were born—and him as good as dead—descendants as numerous as the stars of heaven in multitude, and as the sand by the shore of the sea, which is innumerable. **13** According to faith these all died, not having received the promises, but seeing them from afar, and being persuaded, and greeting them, and confessing that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. **14** For those who say such things make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. **15** And if indeed they had been mindful of that land from which they went out, they would have had opportunity to return. **16** But now they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed of them, to be called their God; for he has prepared a city for them. **17** By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the...

**4** *From invisible things, visible things*] <note>original: "Ex invisibilibus visibilia"</note> In the Greek, "so that what is seen was not made out of things that appear" <note>original: "εἰς τὸ μὴ ἐκ φαινομένων τὰ βλεπόμενα γεγονέναι"</note>. It means that from those things which are not apparent, those which are seen were made.
**5** *A very great sacrifice*] <note>original: "Plurimam hostiam"</note> In Greek, "a more excellent sacrifice" <note>original: "πλείονα θυσίαν"</note>, that is, a more abundant sacrifice, or more sacrifices. The translator, to avoid saying "a more sacrifice," changed the comparative into a superlative.
**6** *To be righteous*] In Greek this was said more elegantly than in Latin: <note>original: "ἐμαρτυρήθη εἶναι δίκαιος"</note>, which means "he was declared by testimony to be righteous," or "he earned the testimony that he was righteous."
**7** *Over his gifts*] Concerning the gifts in Greek is <note>original: "ἐπὶ τοῖς δώροις"</note>, that is, concerning the offerings.
**8** *Without faith, however, it is impossible to please God*] "God" in this place is not repeated among the Greeks whose texts I have seen, but is understood from the preceding words. Certainly, it is added neither in the works of the Greek Father Chrysostom nor in those of Theophylact.
**9** *Fearing*] <note>original: "εὐλαβηθείς"</note>, that is, being cautious or showing reverence.
**10** *By faith he who is called Abraham*] <note>original: "Πίστει καλούμενος Ἀβραάμ"</note>. The translator did not look to the past tense verb, "he obeyed." Therefore, it should have been translated, "By faith, Abraham, having been called, obeyed": or, "By faith, when Abraham was called, he obeyed," so that "by faith" pertains to the verb "obeyed." But it is more correctly applied to both: "Abraham was called through faith, and he obeyed through faith." Indeed, he earned through faith the enlargement of his name. For it was not increased before it was said of him, "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness." Theophylact interprets it such that "called" does not refer to the naming of his name, but to the command of God; for he was called twice by God: once when he was ordered to leave his native land, and again when he was called to the mountain to sacrifice his son. And according to this sense, the speech should be arranged: "Abraham, when he was called by God, obeyed through faith."
**11** *To go out into a place*] This too in Greek is "obeyed to go out"; it could be in Latin "obeyed, or complied, by going out, or so that he might go out."
**12** *In little huts*] <note>original: "ἐν σκηναῖς"</note>, that is, in tents.
**13** *Sarah the barren*] I do not find the epithet "barren" <note>original: "sterilis"</note> in the Greek, although it is written in our oldest Latin manuscripts. From the commentary of Chrysostom and Theophylact, it is not clear whether the translator added it on his own or took it from here.
**14** *For the conception of seed*] <note>original: "εἰς καταβολὴν σπέρματος"</note>. The translator rendered the meaning of the Greek speech honestly and modestly. For the weakness of the body prevents the seed from settling and adhering in the womb, because the power of attracting and retaining is diminished. For he sometimes translates "katabole" <note>the Greek word for "laying down" or "foundation"</note> as "foundation." Accordingly, Chrysostom explains the restored power as the ability to receive and retain the seed. However, I wonder why Faber <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, a contemporary humanist scholar</note> preferred "for succession" instead of "for conception," unless he studied to express it even more modestly than the translator, or—what I suspect more—through the carelessness of scribes, "succession" was substituted for "reception." Theophylact indicates that some are of the

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **4** ...so that from those things which were not appearing, those which are seen were made. By faith Abel offered a more abundant sacrifice to God than Cain: through which he earned <gloss>testimony</gloss> that he was righteous, God bearing witness <gloss>concerning the offerings</gloss> of that man, and through this, though dead, he still speaks. **5** By faith Enoch was translated, so that he would not see death, nor was he found, because God had translated him: for before he was translated, he had earned the testimony that he had pleased God. **6** But without faith, it cannot happen that anyone should please him: for he who approaches God, this man must believe that God exists, and that he is a <margin>B</margin> rewarder to those seeking him. **7** By faith Noah, having been warned by a divine oracle concerning those things which were not yet seen, fearing, prepared an ark for the salvation of his house, through which ark he condemned the world, and he was made heir of that righteousness which is according to faith. **8** By faith he who was called Abraham obeyed, so that he might go out into the place which he was to receive as an inheritance, and he went out, not knowing where he was going to come. **9** By faith he migrated into the land of promise, as if into a foreign land, when he lived in tents with Isaac and Jacob, co-heirs of the same promise. **10** For he had expected the city having foundations, whose maker and <margin>C</margin> founder is God. **11** By faith Sarah herself also received power <gloss>for</gloss> conceiving and retaining seed, <gloss>and</gloss> she gave birth beyond the rule of her age, because she judged him faithful who had promised. **12** Wherefore even from one man descendants were born, <gloss>and that man already worn out by years</gloss>, in as great a number as are the stars of heaven, and as the sand which is by the shore of the sea, innumerable. **13** According to faith all these died, when they had not received the promises, but had seen them from afar, and had believed, <gloss>and had greeted them</gloss>, and had confessed themselves to be guests and strangers on the land. For those who say these things declare that they seek a homeland. **15** And if indeed they had been mindful of that place from which they had set out, they had the <margin>D</margin> opportunity of returning. **16** But now they seek a better one, that is, a heavenly one. Wherefore God himself is not ashamed to be called their God: for he had prepared a city for them. **17** By faith Abraham offered Isaac, when he was tested, and he offered his only-begotten son, in whom...

<margin>E</margin> opinion that seed also exists in women, and that this passage can be adapted to that.
**15** *Even beyond the time of age*] In Greek it is thus: <note>original: "καὶ παρὰ καιρὸν ἡλικίας ἔτεκεν"</note>, that is, "and beyond the seasonableness of age she gave birth," which is to say, at an unseasonable age.
**16** *Are sprung*] <note>original: "ἐγεννήθησαν"</note>, that is, were born or begotten. Because of which from one they are sprung. <note>original: "Διὸ καὶ ἀφ᾿ ἑνὸς ἐγεννήθησαν, καὶ ταῦτα νενεκρωμένου"</note>, that is, "Wherefore from one they were born, or out of one, and that one deadened, or that man being deadened."
**17** *And this man as good as dead*] <note>original: "καὶ ταῦτα νενεκρωμένου"</note>. Let no one think that Abraham, having already departed this life, begot sons. For someone translates it thus, "from one they were born, and he himself since he was dead." Rather, the Greek speech signifies that he was already of a worn-out and failing body, just as in the Epistle to the Romans he said, "the deadness of the womb and body." Furthermore, "and these things" <note>original: "καὶ ταῦτα"</note>, according to the custom of Greek speech, serves for emphasis, which the Latins are accustomed to render as "and that, and indeed," and in other similar ways. So that not even Laurentius <note>Lorenzo Valla</note> ought to have been particularly offended by the number of the pronoun.
**18** *Looking at*] Regarding "and this man as good as dead" just before, in order to preserve the account of time, why does he not do the same in this participle? For he could have said, "not having received, but having seen and greeted and confessed from a distance or from afar."
**19** *And greeting*] Before these words I find in the Greek codices <note>original: "καὶ πεισθέντες"</note>, that is, "and being persuaded."
**20** *If indeed they had been mindful of that*] <note>original: "Καὶ εἰ μὲν ἐκείνης ἐμνημόνευον, ἀφ᾿ ἧς ἐξῆλθον, εἶχον ἂν καιρὸν ἀνακάμψαι"</note>, that is, "And if indeed they had been mindful of that land from which they had set out, they would have had time to return." For I do not agree in this part with Laurentius Valla, who thought it should have been translated in this manner: "And if indeed they were recording that land from which they had gone out, they would have time for returning," as if he were speaking of the present, not of the past. But it is far otherwise. For he speaks of Abraham and those like him, for whom it was free to return to their homeland, if a longing for their homeland had held them. But the present tense verb that soon follows, "But now they seek a better one," offended Laurentius. As if indeed a change of tense of this kind were not known. What of the fact that as it follows, so also a present tense verb precedes, "they declare"? Certainly what is added a little lower, "God is not confounded to be called their God," cannot be adapted except to the Patriarchs. For he is called the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob. Now, whether it can be said in Latin, "he is ashamed to be called good," just as we say, "he desires to be seen as good," Laurentius may have seen, who denies this, since nothing stands in the way of our speaking thus.
**21** *In whom he had received*] <note>original: "ὁ τὰς ἐπαγγελίας ἀναδεξάμενος"</note>, that is, he who had received the promises.

# EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER XI.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the one who had received the promises, to whom it was said, **19** "Through Isaac shall your offspring be named," having considered <note>original: "λογισάμενος" (logisamenos), meaning to calculate or reason through</note> that God was able to raise him even from the dead; from which he also received him back in a figure <note>original: "ἐν παραβολῇ" (en parabolē), often translated as a "type" or symbolic representation of the resurrection</note>. **20** By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come. **21** By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, and worshiped, leaning on the top of his staff. **22** By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the departure of the sons of Israel and gave instructions concerning his bones. **23** By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw the child was beautiful; and they were not afraid of the king’s edict. <margin>D</margin> **24** By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, **25** choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin, **26** considering the reproach of Christ to be greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt; for he was looking toward the reward. **27** By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the anger of the king; for he persevered as one seeing him who is invisible. **28** By faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch them. **29** By faith they crossed the Red Sea as if on dry land, which the Egyptians, when they attempted it, were swallowed up. **30** By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days. **31** By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had received the scouts in peace. <margin>C</margin> **32** And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets, <margin>E</margin> **33** who through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, obtained promises, shut the mouths of lions, **34** quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, <margin>F</margin> put foreign armies to flight. **35** Women received...

<column-break/>

...had received the promises, to whom it had been said, "In **19** Isaac shall your seed be called," <margin>A</margin> since he had considered within himself that God could raise even from the dead, whence he also brought him back as a type of the resurrection. By faith **20** Isaac blessed his sons Jacob and Esau concerning future things. By faith **21** Jacob, dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, and worshiped the height of his staff. By faith **22** Joseph, dying, remembered the departure of the children of Israel, and gave orders concerning his bones. By faith, when **23** Moses was born, he was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw a refined little boy, and they did not fear the king's decree. <margin>B</margin> By faith **24** Moses, now grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, rather choosing to be afflicted with the people of God **25** than to enjoy the temporary advantages of sin, judging **26** the reproach of Christ to be greater riches <margin>C</margin> than the treasures of the Egyptians: for he had respect for the reward. By faith he left Egypt, not **27** fearing the ferocity of the king: for he endured as if he saw him who is invisible. By faith he performed **28** the Passover and the pouring out of blood, lest he who destroyed the firstborn should touch them. By faith they passed through **29** the Red Sea as if through dry land, which when the Egyptians attempted, they were swallowed up. By **30** faith the walls of Jericho fell, <margin>E</margin> having been surrounded for seven days. By faith Rahab the harlot did not perish along with **31** those who were disobedient, since she had welcomed the scouts peacefully. <margin>C</margin> And what more do I say? **32** For time will fail me, recounting about Gideon, about Barak, and Samson, and Jephthah, as well as David, and Samuel, and the Prophets, who through faith **33** conquered kingdoms, worked justice, attained promises, closed the mouths of lions, extinguished **34** the force of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made strong from weakness, were made robust in war, <margin>F</margin> turned back the incursions of foreigners. Women **35** received...

---

**22** *Considering* <note>original: "Arbitrans"</note>] *Logisamenos*, that is, *Weighing*, even if it is a past participle.

**23** *He received in a figure* <note>original: "In parabolam accepit"</note>] *En parabolē ekomisato*, that is, he brought him back in a likeness; that is, in a "type" of Christ who was to be sacrificed. Indeed, that "him" refers to Isaac, whom he brought back home alive.

**24** *And he worshiped the top of his staff* <note>original: "Et adoravit fastigium virgæ illius"</note>] <margin>D</margin> Jerome, in his *Hebraic Questions*, notes that the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translated this as *he worshiped toward the top of his staff*, while among the Hebrews it is held as *and he worshiped at the head of the bed*. If that is true, what shall we do with the author of this Epistle, whoever he is? Or how shall we defend Jerome? Furthermore, since Jerome admits the Hebrew word is ambiguous <note>In Hebrew, the letters for "staff" (matteh) and "bed" (mittah) are the same without vowel points</note>, as it truly is if written without points, why does he assert one sense is false and hold so stubbornly to the other—even adding something of his own in his interpretation? He says, *He worshiped the Lord, turning toward the head of the bed*. At that time, they so shrank from worshiping any created things, reserving this honor for God alone; yet today it has been discovered through "supernatural philosophy" <note>A sarcastic jab at Scholastic theology</note> that a wooden statue may be worshiped with the same adoration with which the eternal Trinity is worshiped. Nor is there anyone whose ears are offended by this author's speech here, even though they produce so many things everywhere else that are offensive to pious ears. Moreover, when we read in several places in the sacred volumes that Kings were worshiped <note>original: "adoratos," meaning to bow down or show deep respect</note>, what was the danger if a father worshiped his son who was a prince? As in 2 Samuel chapter 9 and 1 Kings chapter 1. Solomon is even worshiped by David his father, as it seems. Some escape the difficulty as if he worshiped not Joseph’s staff, but the kingdom of Christ, which he understood to be figured by that scepter. Augustine opens another "crack" <note>an interpretive loophole</note>, suggesting we read *autou* (his own) instead of *autou* (his), with the same letters but a different breathing mark, so we understand the old man leaning on *his own* staff worshiped the Lord. It must not be hidden that in the Greek it is not *he worshiped the top of the staff*, but *at the top*: since our translator left out the preposition as if it were idle. Indeed, we seem to worship that toward which we incline ourselves with a prone body. The Greek word used by the Seventy, *prosekynēsen*, properly signifies the gesture of a bowed head, like when we lower the head after moving a hat from the forehead. Furthermore, since Symmachus <note>An ancient translator of the Old Testament</note> translated it as *he worshiped at the head of the bed* (which Jerome approves), it is a wonder why the author made no mention of this to better confirm his opinion; certainly elsewhere he frequently brings in the testimony of Symmachus. Moreover, when we hear of a "bed," we should not imagine that Jacob reclined on German feathers <note>Down-filled mattresses popular in the 16th century but unknown in antiquity</note>, but the "bed" was a type of seat on which several could sit, a type still seen among the Italians. In the afternoon hours, they rest with legs stretched out and the rest of the body upright. Thus it is probable that Jacob, at his son's entrance, sat on the bed with feet down, just as in the next chapter he is said to be *strengthened*, that is, he gathered his strength to speak his final words to Joseph and the rest of his sons. And just as after his final commands it is written he gathered his feet into the bed and expired, so here, after the command concerning his burial, he did not gather his feet, but out of weariness inclined his body toward the head of the bed. But if anyone prefers to read "staff" instead of "bed," the weariness of the elderly and now failing little body is figured in another way. The question about "worshiping the Lord" whose essence he might have seen at the head of the bed seems to be born from Hebrew commentaries.

<column-break/>

**25** *Concerning the departure* <note>original: "De profectione"</note>] *Peri tēs exodou*, that is, *concerning the exit*.

**26** *By faith Moses, having become great, denied he was the son...*] <margin>B</margin> Before this place, there is added in the Donatian codex, but in a more recent hand: *By faith Moses, having become great, killed the Egyptian, considering the grief of his brothers.*

**27** *Temporary sin*] ...that is, than to have the temporary enjoyment of sin.

**28** *Treasure of the Egyptians*] ...that is, the treasures which were in Egypt.

**29** *He looked toward* <note>original: "Adpiciebat"</note>] <margin>C</margin> ...that is, he looked back toward, or watched, or took account of the retribution.

**30** *The animosity of the king*] ...that is, the wrath or ferocity.

**31** *As if seeing*] *hōs horōn*, It was better: "just as if he saw."

**32** *First things* <note>original: "Primitiva"</note>] *prōtotoka*, that is, the firstborn.

**33** *Which having tried*] ...that is, of which (namely the sea) when the Egyptians had taken the trial.

**34** *In a circuit of seven days*] <margin>E</margin> ...that is, surrounded for seven days. Otherwise, in my opinion, he did not sufficiently express the meaning. For he did not mean the walls were overcome by a seven-day siege, but after the Levites carrying the ark had gone around the city each day, on the seventh day at the blast of the trumpets the walls fell.

**35** *Receiving the scouts*] And this is a past participle, *dexamenē tous kataskopous*, "the scouts having been received."

**36** *What shall I yet say*] *legō*, that is, I say.

**37** *Jephthah*] Which the Greeks write as four syllables, *Iephthae*. This place in the Epistle was noted by several, as Chrysostom warns, because it counts Jephthah (the son of a harlot and the killer of his innocent daughter) in the catalog of saints, likewise Barak and Samson.

**38** *The attack of fire*] *dynamin*, that is, the force.

**39** *The edge of the sword*] <margin>F</margin> *stoma machairas*, that is, the "mouth" of the sword, or "mouths" in the plural, which the Greeks use for the "edge," because it bites on that part. Though there are some among the Greeks who think *stoma* (mouth) is named from *toma* (a cut), because we cut and grind food with the mouth. Hence a "two-mouthed sword" <note>original: "machaera distomos"</note> is called a sword that cuts on both sides.

**40** *They grew strong from infirmity*] ...that is, they were rendered powerful out of weakness, lest anyone dream they recovered from a disease. Chrysostom interprets this as those returning from the Babylonian exile, in which they had been dejected and like the dead, but were later restored to their former vigor. Theophylact, touching on this interpretation, also mentions Hezekiah, who recovered from a disease. Thomas [Aquinas] follows the latter.

**41** *They turned the camps of foreigners*] *parembolas eklinan*, that is, they turned the incursions or pressures into flight. For an "inclined line of battle" is said when it prepares for flight and gives way in war. Nor does the Translator turn it badly, if only one understands what it means to "turn" in this place, that is, to drive to flight. I wonder why Lefèvre d'Étaples preferred "overturn" <note>original: "evertere"</note> rather than "turn" <note>original: "vertere"</note>. For "to turn" was much more apt. Certainly "to overturn," I do not see how it can be tolerated here.

The commentary notably debates the translation of "worshiping the top of the staff" versus "the head of the bed" and discusses the inclusion of morally complex figures like Jephthah in the list of saints.</summary>

# TO THE HEBREWS CHAPTER XII.

<margin>36</margin> Women received their dead back by resurrection. Others were tortured <note>original: "ἐτυμπανίσθησαν" (etympanisthēsan), referring to being beaten to death or stretched on a drum-like rack</note>, not accepting release, so that they might obtain a better resurrection. Others suffered mocking and scourging, and even chains and imprisonment. <margin>37</margin> They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were tempted, they were killed by the edge of the sword. They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, <margin>38</margin> mistreated—of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts and mountains, and in caves and holes in the ground. <margin>39</margin> And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised, <margin>40</margin> since God had provided something better for us, so that apart from us they should not be made perfect. <margin>XII. 1</margin> Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and the sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us, <margin>2</margin> looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God. <margin>3</margin> For consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted. <margin>4</margin> In your struggle against sin you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood. <margin>5</margin> And you have forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons: "My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him. <margin>6</margin> For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives." <margin>7</margin> If you endure discipline, God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? <margin>8</margin> If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons. <margin>9</margin> Furthermore, we have had earthly fathers who disciplined us and we respected them. Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live? <margin>10</margin> For they indeed...
<meta>catchword: for a short time (ὀλί-)</meta>

---

...profane place. A little lower down, "women," in Greek is <gloss>γυναῖκες</gloss> (gynaikes), a word that signifies both the female sex and a "wife." But in this passage, "their dead" should be understood as referring to their children.

<margin>42</margin> **They were stretched out**] <gloss>ἐτυμπανίσθησαν</gloss> (etympanisthēsan). This term is derived from the hide stretched over a drum [<term>tympanum</term>]. However, the Greek commentaries <note>original: "scholia," marginal notes in ancient manuscripts</note> interpret this as those who died from being beaten with clubs, for a drum is struck with frequent blows.

<margin>43</margin> **They were sawn in two**] Which <term>Jerome</term> elsewhere translates as *serrati sunt*, so as to match the traditional martyrdom of the prophet Isaiah.

<margin>44</margin> **They were tempted**] I do not know by what accident it happened that neither in <term>Chrysostom</term> nor in <term>Theophylact</term> <note>two influential early Christian commentators</note> is any mention made of this small phrase *they were tempted*, especially since it seems weaker than the terms it is mixed with. For "they were sawn in two" precedes it, and "they were killed by the sword" follows it. To me, it seems like an interpolation. I suspect some minor scholar wanted to change "they were sawn" [<gloss>ἐπρίσθησαν</gloss>] to "they were tempted" [<gloss>ἐπειράσθησαν</gloss>], and thus both words were pulled into the main text when one had merely been written in the margin.

<margin>45</margin> **In sheepskins**] <gloss>ἐν μηλωταῖς</gloss> (en melōtais), that is, in sheepskins. Just as a lion’s skin is called a *leontē*. Truly, I cannot laugh at a man who is otherwise great, <term>Thomas Aquinas</term>, yet I feel pity and shame on his behalf for such a foul slip—even though I admit these things do not strictly pertain to matters of faith, nor is there danger of being judged a heretic for such a hallucination. But the danger is that those who have learned good literature, when they read this, will judge his other works by it. "A melota," he says, "is a garment made of camel hair, as some say. Or *melos*, which is a rock that has a hairy skin, from which the garment is made." Now, how much more foolishly, indeed impudently, does the author of that most unlearned of all works, the <term>Catholicon</term> <note>a popular medieval dictionary</note>, rave about this word! Let those who defend their own ignorance under the pretext of "Apostolic simplicity" celebrate a triumph here. Such men surpass even the Apostles themselves! For none of the Apostles was so ignorant of words or things as to turn a sheep into a camel, or into a new animal named after a tree. Although I can hardly be brought to believe that these things were written by Aquinas—an Italian, and so vigilant in other matters. I suspect a good part of this error should be blamed on the Translator <note>referring to the Vulgate translator</note>, who translated one of the two Greek words and left the other as it was. For regarding "goat skins," the Greek is <gloss>αἰγείοις</gloss>. But why did he avoid translating <gloss>μηλωταῖς</gloss> in the same way as "sheep skins"? Except that, in his usual manner, he shrank from saying "skins" twice. Although a *melōtē* does not signify a sheep's skin so much as a hide, that is, a skin removed from the body with the wool still on it.

<margin>46</margin> **Destitute**] <gloss>ὑστερούμενοι</gloss> (hysteroumenoi), that is, deprived of necessary things. However, the Translator rendered this well.

<margin>47</margin> **Commended through the testimony of faith**] <gloss>μαρτυρηθέντες διὰ τῆς πίστεως</gloss>, that is, they were proven by testimony through faith.

<margin>48</margin> **Providing**] This is a past participle in Greek, <gloss>προβλεψαμένου</gloss>, meaning that God had foreseen something better for us. <term>Augustine</term> cites this differently in his book *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*. His manuscript had a different word, and he punctuated it differently, relating "to God" to the promises rather than the following participle.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...received their dead back from resurrection. But others <margin>42</margin> were **stretched out**, scorning redemption, so that they might obtain a better resurrection. Others again were tested by mockings and <margin>36</margin> floggings, and moreover by chains and prison. They were <margin>37</margin> stoned, <margin>43</margin> **sawn in two**, <margin>44</margin> **tempted**, they died by the slaughter of the sword, they wandered about <margin>45</margin> **in sheepskins** and goatskins, <margin>46</margin> **destitute**, oppressed, afflicted; of whom the <margin>38</margin> world was unworthy, wandering in deserts, and mountains, and caves, and the caverns of the earth. And all these, having <margin>39</margin> **merited a testimony** through faith, had not received the promise, because God had <margin>48</margin> **provided** something better for us, <margin>40</margin> lest they should be made perfect without us. There- <margin>XII. 1</margin> fore we also, since we are surrounded by so great a <margin>B</margin> cloud of witnesses, laying aside every <margin>2</margin> **burden**, and the <margin>3</margin> **tenaciously clinging** sin, let us run with patience in the race set before us, looking to the <margin>4</margin> **leader and perfecter of faith**, <margin>2</margin> Jesus, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, having <margin>5</margin> **despised the shame**, <margin>6</margin> and <margin>7</margin> **sat down** at the right hand of the throne of God. For consider that he <margin>3</margin> endured such contradiction from sinners against himself, lest you be weary, failing in your souls. You have not yet <margin>4</margin> resisted unto blood, struggling against sin, and you have forgotten the <margin>8</margin> **exhortation**, which speaks to you <margin>5</margin> <margin>9</margin> **as to sons**, saying: "My son, do not neglect the correction of the Lord, <margin>10</margin> **nor faint** when you are rebuked by him. For whom the Lord loves, he corrects; and <margin>11</margin> **he scourges** every son whom he receives." <margin>6</margin> <margin>12</margin> **Endure in discipline**; God offers himself to you as to sons. <margin>7</margin> <margin>C</margin> For what son is there whom a father does not correct? But if you are without correction, in which all have shared, <margin>8</margin> <margin>13</margin> **then you are bastards**, not sons. Furthermore, since we <margin>9</margin> have had the fathers of our flesh as <margin>14</margin> **teachers**, and we revered them, shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live? And they indeed for a <margin>10</margin>
<meta>catchword: short (pau-)</meta>

---

<margin>1</margin> **Encompassing cloud**] <gloss>περικείμενον</gloss> (perikeimenon), that is, placed around, or surrounding, and encircling us on all sides. He calls the huge multitude and crowd of witnesses a "cloud."
<margin>D</margin> <margin>2</margin> **Weight**] <gloss>ὄγκον</gloss> (onkon), that is, a burden or baggage.
<margin>3</margin> **Standing around us**] This is not in the Greek codices; the word is <gloss>εὐπερίστατον</gloss> (euperistaton), that is, that which easily stands around, and sticks and clings, as if refusing to be cast off. Hence we translated it "the tenaciously clinging sin." Whether the interpretation of Aquinas—who explains "standing around sin" as the *opportunity* for sinning—is fitting, I leave to others to discuss.
<margin>4</margin> **The author and finisher of faith**] <gloss>ἀρχηγὸν καὶ τελειωτὴν</gloss>. The Translator does not capture the force and elegance of the Greek speech, which consists of words that are opposites; the former is composed of "beginning," the latter derived from "end." It is as if you said the "initiator" and "finisher," so that the same Christ is the author of both the beginning and the end.
<margin>E</margin> <margin>5</margin> **Despising the confusion**] <gloss>καταισχύνῃ</gloss>, in his usual way, he approves and calls it "ignominy" <note>disgrace</note>, while in Greek it is simply <gloss>αἰσχύνη</gloss> (aischynē).
<margin>6</margin> **And at the right hand**] In Greek it is, "at the right hand of the throne of God."
<margin>7</margin> **Sits**] <gloss>ἐκάθισεν</gloss>, that is, he sat, or took his seat. Although, as I said, in these cases the past tense is used for the present.
<margin>8</margin> **Of consolation**] <gloss>παρακλήσεως</gloss> (paraklēseōs). Here "exhortation" fits better. Indeed, both are fine. Although <term>Theophylact</term> interprets it as exhortation.
<margin>9</margin> **Speaks as to sons, saying**] The word "saying" is not in the Greek.
<margin>10**Nor be weary**] <gloss>ἐκλύου</gloss>, that is, fail, or be exhausted.
<margin>11</margin> **He scourges every son**] <gloss>μαστιγοῖ</gloss>. Which Jerome in Hosea translates as "corrects," a word which, by changing a little letter, seems to have been derived from the Greek. To be beaten with whips was a more servile punishment among the Romans. Furthermore, that word "receives" is placed there to mean "approves," and does not disown or reject.
<margin>12</margin> **Persevere in discipline**] The Greek codex has it differently: <gloss>Εἰ παιδείαν ὑπομένετε</gloss>, that is, "If you endure correction," in agreement with the Greek commentators. For a little before, what was "discipline" [<gloss>παιδείας</gloss>] he translated as "corrects," and from that he translated "discipline" [<gloss>παιδείαν</gloss>]. Some following him call "discipline" a "correction," which <term>Valla</term> <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous Renaissance humanist critic</note> does not quite approve. <margin>F</margin> Although "discipline" can be found in reputable authors, especially <term>Suetonius</term>, to mean a stricter training and governance, of the kind usually applied in early years. <term>Augustine</term>, explaining Psalm 118, interprets discipline as when someone is instructed through troubles. Furthermore, where the Greek is <gloss>προσφέρεται</gloss>, and the Translator rendered "offers himself," Augustine reads "God approaches you as sons." For Paul is doing this so they do not dread the hand of the correcting God; for, he says, He does not move His hand against you as an enemy against an enemy, but as a father toward sons, intending to mend, not to destroy.
<margin>13</margin> **Therefore adulterers**] I think the Translator meant "adulterated" or "illegitimate" for "bastards." The Greeks and Latins alike call these <gloss>νόθους</gloss> (nothous), which is the word Paul used.
<margin>14**We had instructors**] <gloss>παιδευτὰς</gloss>, from the same verb <gloss>παιδεύειν</gloss>, which means to instruct as a child, because blows and rebukes are sometimes necessary.
<margin>15</margin> **In the time of a few days**] <gloss>πρὸς ὀλίγας ἡμέρας</gloss>, that is, for a few days.

# EPISTLE OF PAUL CHAPTER XII.

<column-break/>

<margin>10</margin> for a few days, according to what seemed good to them, they disciplined us; <margin>11</margin> but He does so for our benefit, so that we may share in <margin>12</margin> His holiness. Now, all discipline for <margin>13</margin> the present does not seem to be a matter of joy, but of pain; <margin>14</margin> but afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been <margin>15</margin> trained by it. Therefore, lift up your <margin>16</margin> drooping hands and your weakened knees, <margin>17</margin> and make straight paths for your <margin>18</margin> feet, so that the lame limb may not be turned aside, but rather <margin>19</margin> be healed. Pursue peace with everyone, and that <margin>20</margin> holiness without which no one will see the Lord. <margin>21</margin> See to it that no one falls short of the grace of <margin>22</margin> God; that no root of bitterness springing up causes trouble, <margin>23</margin> and through it many become defiled; that no one is sexually immoral <margin>24</margin> or profane like Esau, who for a single meal <margin>25</margin> sold his birthright. For you know that even <margin>26</margin> afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was <margin>27</margin> rejected; for he found no place for repentance, though <margin>28</margin> he sought it with tears. For you have not <margin>29</margin> come to a mountain that can be touched, and to a burning fire, and <margin>30</margin> to gloom, and darkness, and a storm, and to a <margin>31</margin> trumpet’s blast, and a voice of words, which those who <margin>32</margin> heard begged that no further word be spoken to them. For <margin>33</margin> they could not bear the command: "If even a beast touches <margin>34</margin> the mountain, it shall be stoned, or struck through with a dart." <margin>35</margin> And so terrifying was the vision that <margin>36</margin> Moses said, "I am terrified and trembling." But <margin>37</margin> you have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, <margin>38</margin> the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels in <margin>39</margin> festive gathering, and to the assembly of the firstborn enrolled in <margin>40</margin> heaven, and to God the judge of all, and <margin>41</margin> to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and to the <margin>42</margin> mediator of a new covenant, Jesus, and to the blood of sprinkling, which <margin>43</margin> speaks better than the blood of Abel. See that you do not <margin>44</margin> refuse the one who is speaking; for if those <margin>45</margin> did not escape who refused him who warned them on earth...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>10</margin> for a few days, <gloss>16</gloss> according to their own will, they were educating us; but he, <margin>11</margin> however, for our advantage, for this purpose <gloss>17</gloss> that he may impart <margin>12</margin> his holiness to us. Now, every punishment <margin>13</margin> for the present indeed does not seem to be of joy, but <margin>14</margin> of trouble: but afterward it <gloss>18</gloss> returns the tranquil fruit of justice <margin>15</margin> to those who have been exercised by it. Therefore, <margin>16</margin> lift up the hanging hands and the loosened knees, <gloss>19</gloss> and <margin>17</margin> make sure the steps are straight for your feet, <gloss>20</gloss> lest the <margin>18</margin> lameness wander from the way, but rather let it be healed. Follow peace <margin>B</margin> <margin>19</margin> with all, and holiness, without which <margin>20</margin> no one will see the Lord, <gloss>21</gloss> taking care, <gloss>22</gloss> lest there be anyone <margin>21</margin> who fails from the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness <margin>22</margin> sprout up and disturb, and through this <margin>23</margin> many be defiled, <gloss>23</gloss> lest there be any fornicator or profane person like Esau, <margin>24</margin> who for a single dish <gloss>24</gloss> exchanged his right of the firstborn. <gloss>25</gloss> <margin>25</margin> For you know that even afterward when he wished <gloss>26</gloss> by hereditary <margin>26</margin> right to obtain the blessing, he was rejected: for he <margin>27</margin> did not find a place for repentance, although with <margin>28</margin> tears he had sought it. For you have not approached <gloss>27</gloss> a <margin>29</margin> mountain that can be touched, <gloss>28</gloss> and a burning fire, and a whirlwind, <margin>C</margin> <margin>30</margin> and gloom, and a storm, and the sound of a trumpet, and the <margin>31</margin> voice of words, which those who heard <gloss>29</gloss> pleaded <margin>32</margin> that the speech not be joined to them. <gloss>30</gloss> For they did not bear what <margin>33</margin> was being proclaimed, <gloss>31</gloss> "If a beast touches the mountain, it shall be <margin>34</margin> stoned, or pierced with a spear." And, so terrible was the <margin>35</margin> sight that appeared, <gloss>32</gloss> Moses said, "I am <margin>36</margin> terrified and trembling." But you have approached Mount <margin>37</margin> Zion, and the city of the living God, the <margin>38</margin> heavenly Jerusalem, <gloss>35</gloss> and the assembly of innumerable angels, <margin>39</margin> and the gathering of the firstborn who are enrolled <margin>40</margin> in the heavens, <gloss>36</gloss> and God the judge of all, <margin>D</margin> <margin>41</margin> and the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and the <margin>42</margin> mediator of the new covenant, Jesus, <gloss>38</gloss> and the blood of <margin>43</margin> sprinkling, <gloss>39</gloss> speaking better things than the <margin>44</margin> blood of Abel spoke. See that you do not despise him who <margin>45</margin> speaks: for if they did not escape, who rejected him...

<meta>Catchword: and</meta>

***

<margin>16</margin> **According to their own will]** <note>original: "κατὰ τὸ δοκοῦν αὐτοῖς" (kata to dokoun autois)</note>, that is, *in what seemed good to them*, which is to say, at their own discretion. Sometimes even beyond what was deserved.
<margin>17</margin> **in receiving]** <note>original: "εἰς τὸ μεταλαβεῖν" (eis to metalabein)</note>, that is, *so that we may be participants.*
<margin>18</margin> **Most peaceful]** <note>original: "εἰρηνικὸν" (eirēnikon)</note>, that is, *peace-making, or calmed.*
<margin>19</margin> **And make straight steps]** <note>original: "τροχιὰς" (trochias)</note>. As Theophylact <note>a 12th-century Byzantine archbishop and Bible commentator</note> indicates, this is either the track of a wheel's course pressed into the ground, or the earth itself trodden down by the feet of those running.
<margin>20</margin> **Lest any limping person stray]** <note>original: "ἵνα μὴ τὸ χωλὸν ἐκτραπῇ" (hina mē to chōlon ektrapē)</note>, that is, *lest that which is lame wander away*, which is to say, lest the lameness lead one off the path, especially since it is narrow. Therefore, there is a need for swifter and non-staggering feet on this path.
<margin>21</margin> **Contemplating]** <note>original: "Ἐπισκοποῦντες" (Episkopountes)</note>, that is, *Considering, and taking care.* This is a metaphor taken from an army making a long journey. For here, a few men are usually delegated the task of looking ahead to ensure supplies are not lacking.
<margin>22</margin> **Lest anyone lack the grace of God]** <note>original: "μὴ τις ὑστερῶν ἀπὸ τῆς χάριτος τοῦ Θεοῦ" (mē tis hysterōn apo tēs charitos tou Theou)</note>, that is, *lest anyone be failing or destitute of the grace of God*, which is to say, one who cannot attain it, just as those on a journey who fail/fall behind.
<margin>23</margin> **Hinder]** <note>original: "ἐνοχλῇ" (enochlē)</note>, that is, *obstruct, or disturb.* Augustine, in his 16th Sermon on the words of the Apostle, reads *disturbs* instead of *hinders*.
<margin>24</margin> **Sold]** <note>original: "ἀπέδοτο" (apedoto)</note>, that is, *gave back*, which is to say, gave in exchange for another thing. For he who sells or barters, in exchange for what he receives, gives something back. And it is not "firstfruits," but <note>original: "πρωτοτόκια" (prōtotokia)</note>, that is, *birthrights*, to speak thus for the sake of teaching; that is, the right of the firstborn.
<margin>25</margin> **Know ye]** <note>original: "Ἴστε γὰρ" (Iste gar)</note>, that is, *for you know.*
<margin>26</margin> **By inheritance]** <note>original: "κληρονομῆσαι" (klēronomēsai)</note>, that is, *to receive by inheritance.*
<margin>27</margin> **To the touchable mountain]** The word "Mountain" is absent in many Latin manuscripts. Neither Theophylact nor Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, early Church Father known for his preaching</note> add "mountain." <note>original: "ψηλαφωμένῳ ὄρει" (psēlaphōmenō orei)</note>, that is, *to a mountain touched*, or one that was being touched, but not to be touched without destruction. For he alluded to Mount Sinai and that passage in the Psalm: *Touch the mountains, and they shall smoke.*
<margin>28</margin> **And the accessible fire]** <note>original: "καὶ κεκαυμένῳ πυρὶ" (kai kekaumenō pyri)</note>, that is, *and an enkindled fire.* Origen, in his third Homily on Numbers, does not add "mountain," and for "accessible" he reads *burning*: *For you have not approached a burning and touchable fire.* It is a wonder, however, what the same author follows when he reads, "and a multitude of Angels praising together." And Augustine, in the first book of *Questions on Genesis, Question 168*, reads it this way: *But you have approached Mount Zion, and the city of God Jerusalem, and to thousands of exulting Angels*, since nothing of the sort exists among the Greeks.
<margin>29</margin> **They excused themselves]** <note>original: "παρῃτήσαντο" (parētēsanto)</note>, that is, *they entreated against it, or refused.*
<margin>30</margin> **Lest the word be made to them]** <note>original: "μὴ προσθεῖναι αὐτοῖς λόγον" (mē prostheinai autois logon)</note>, that is, *lest the speech be entrusted to them, or lest the speech be added to them.* Doubtless, after such preludes, they were expecting a harsh discourse. Although the Greek speech has some ambiguity, because "to them" <note>original: "αὐτοῖς" (autois)</note> can refer to the people, and to the wonders which had preceded, so the sense is: *lest speech be added to such monstrosities already seen*; or lest the speech should threaten them, which they were expecting to be bitter.
<margin>31</margin> **For they did not carry it]** <note>original: "Οὐκ ἔφερον γὰρ" (Ouk epheron gar)</note>, that is, *for they did not bear, they did not tolerate.* That which was said, <note>original: "τὸ διαστελλόμενον" (to diastellomenon)</note>, that is, *that which was distinguished*, for *commanded*. For he expressed a Hebrew

<column-break/>

<margin>D</margin> figure of speech, according to which it was also said: *He distinguished with his lips.*
<margin>32</margin> **If a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned]** Here some Greek codices add, <note>original: "ἢ βολίδι κατατοξευθήσεται" (ē bolidi katatoxeuthēsetai)</note>, that is, *or pierced by a dart.*
<margin>33</margin> **What was seen]** <note>original: "τὸ Φανταζόμενον" (to Phantazomenon)</note> is not simply "what was seen," but what "seemed to be seen," just as phantoms, visions, or dreams are seen.
<margin>34</margin> **Moses however said]** I suspect this is the passage Jerome <note>translator of the Vulgate</note> meant when he said that this Epistle is not ascribed to Paul by some because certain things are cited in it, as if from the Old Testament, which are not found among the Hebrews. Indeed, in Exodus Chapter 19, where the history of the giving of the Law is narrated, Moses says nothing of this sort; nor even in the third chapter of the same volume, when he sees the Lord in the bush. For the place of Adama <note>referring to a specific interpretive tradition or text</note> twists him toward this. And because he felt that this was not very solid, he added: *he said what was done by the deed*; nor did he alone add to this commentary. Or perhaps the Apostle uses another text which we do not have. But does he use an apocryphal one, or an approved one? If apocryphal, Jerome denies elsewhere that it is the custom of the Apostles to use the testimonies of the Apocrypha. If approved, it is clear that something of the approved Edition is missing from our copies.
<margin>35</margin> **And the festive gathering of many thousands of Angels]** <note>original: "καὶ μυριάσιν ἀγγέλων πανηγύρει" (kai myriasin angelōn panēgyrei)</note>. He strangely joined "myriads" and "festive gathering," since we sometimes call a "myriad" an innumerable crowd. Otherwise, a "myriad" to the Greeks is a number comprising ten thousand; and so indeed Ambrose <note>bishop of Milan</note> cites it in the second book of *Cain and Abel*, chapter 11. And a <term>panēgyris</term> <note>festive assembly</note> is so called whenever the whole people are gathered on feast days or for public assemblies.
<margin>36</margin> **And God the judge of all]** <note>original: "καὶ κριτῇ Θεῷ πάντων" (kai kritē Theō pantōn)</note>, that is, *and to the judge God of all.*
<margin>37</margin> **And of the spirits]** <note>original: "καὶ πνεύμασι" (kai pneumasi)</note>, that is, *and to the spirits.* It is wonderful to say how vigilant Aquinas <note>Thomas Aquinas, 13th-century theologian</note> was here, indicating that there is a triple reading of this passage. The first is that of the Greeks, *and of the spirits of the righteous made perfect*, so the sense is: *You have approached the Holy Spirit, who makes them perfect in justice.* The second is this: *and of the spirits of the righteous made perfect*, so the sense is: *You have approached God, who is the judge of all, but is as if the inheritance of the spirits of the righteous made perfect.* The third: *and the spirits of the righteous made perfect*, that we might receive for ourselves a partnership with the spirits of the saints who are perfect. But he approves the first because it is, as he says, clearer; then because it is from the Greeks, since the last one agrees with the Greeks, according to which Chrysostom interprets "the souls of the pious." No one is angry with Thomas, who although he did not know Greek, nevertheless indicates a varying reading, and that supported by no authority. They are angry with me, who, equipped with so many resources for this task, indicate not what I dream up, but what the ancient and approved writers of both languages have read.
<margin>F</margin> <margin>38</margin> **And the sprinkling of blood]** <note>original: "καὶ αἵματι ῥαντισμοῦ" (kai aimati rhantismou)</note>, that is, *and of the blood of sprinkling*, the blood which is sprinkled, in the Hebrew manner.
<margin>39</margin> **Speaking better than Abel]** <note>original: "κρείττονα λαλοῦντι παρὰ τὸν Ἄβελ" (kreittona lalounti para ton Abel)</note>, that is, *speaking better things than the blood of Abel.* For the article "the" <note>original: "τὸ" (to)</note> openly demands this. For the blood of Abel is said to speak from the ground.

<margin>40 Speaking]</margin> <gloss>warning/delivering an oracle</gloss>, that is, he was returning oracles. For it is not simply <gloss>he says</gloss>, but to *respond* from an oracle.

Jerome rendered the Hebrew this way, and the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> do not disagree: *Yet one little while, and I will move the heaven and the earth.*

<margin>42 I will move]</margin> <gloss>I shake</gloss>, that is, I strike together; it is in the present tense.

<insert>C</insert> *Brotherly love*] <note>original: "Ἡ φιλαδελφία"</note>, that is, Brotherly love, which is the mutual love of Christians among themselves. "In you" is not added among the Greeks, nor in the Codex of Donatianus. Likewise, the conjunction <gloss>the</gloss> which follows is not found among them.

<margin>2 Some have pleased &c.]</margin> <gloss>some were unaware while entertaining angels</gloss>, that is, some were hidden, receiving angels with hospitality. For it could be translated word for word in this way. Furthermore, the sense is this: *certain people, being imprudent or unknowing, received angels as guests*. The translator <note>referring to the Vulgate translator</note> poorly followed a Greek figure of speech which Latin does not admit. Moreover, as to why our manuscripts have "pleased" written there, it is most likely introduced by an error of the scribes, who, since they did not understand "were hidden"—for that phrasing signifies nothing to Latins <note>The Latin 'latuerunt' (they were hidden) makes poor sense in the Vulgate's literal context compared to 'placuerunt' (they pleased)</note>—they changed the writing and made it "pleased." This is made more probable by the fact that in ancient Christian writers we see the Greek figure frequently used in speech, as in Irenaeus (or his translator) and Tertullian. For example, instead of saying in Latin, "unknowingly he passed the house," they say, "hidden he passed the house." To me, what Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo Valla, a pioneer of New Testament textual criticism</note> translates here does not entirely satisfy: *through this, it was hidden to some* that they had received angels into hospitality. For Paul did not mean to attribute it to hospitality that they were ignorant of whom they had received, but rather that they received angels when they thought they were receiving men. But much less satisfactory is the commentary on this passage by Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, who thinks "to have been hidden" is the same as being "concealed and not seen," writing in this manner: "They were hidden to the discordant, not pleased. For it was hidden from Lot and his family that they had taken angels into hospitality, when the Sodomites wanted to attack him and break down the doors, immediately being struck with blindness by the angels." Truly, Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret it otherwise, explaining the Greek figure, which is not unknown even to those moderately skilled in Greek. And Theophylact applies this praise to Abraham and Lot together. Chrysostom attributes it so much to Abraham that he doubts whether it ought to be shared with Lot. Chrysostom refers to the same sense in his 11th Sermon on Lazarus. For in this lies the excellence

of his praise: that being unaware they were angels, he showed such great humanity to his guests. For it was nothing great to provide this to angels if they were recognized. Augustine, in his *Questions on Genesis*, book one, citing this testimony, says: *For through this, some, being ignorant, received angels into hospitality*. And concerning Lot, there is no doubt that he received the angels while ignorant, thinking they were men. However, concerning Abraham, one might doubt somewhat because he worshipped and called Him "Lord" when he saw the three. On the other hand, when he offers food and the washing of feet, as if to those weary from a journey, he seems to believe they are men. Thomas <note>Aquinas</note>, using a *Tenedian axe* <note>A Greek proverb for a sharp, decisive solution to a difficult problem</note>, cuts the knot by saying that Abraham first took them for honorable men, and on account of the duties of humanity shown—although he worshipped them with the worship of <gloss>service</gloss>—he soon recognized them as angels in whom God was speaking. The same author reminds us of the genuine reading. For besides this one which we commonly have, he reads: *through this some, being ignorant, received angels*, and yet he does not deign to indicate any author of this reading to us. Now, since so many arguments work in our favor, since there is such great consensus among all the Greeks, since orthodox writers indicate the Greek phrasing, since the true reading is found in Augustine, and since the matter itself rejects the word "pleased," nevertheless some will defend "pleased" with great shouting for no other reason than that this was introduced by scribes into the common manuscripts. What can you do with those who neither wish to learn nor are able to teach?

<margin>3 Of those suffering]</margin> <gloss>of those being mistreated</gloss>, that is, the afflicted.

<margin>4 As if you yourselves were dwelling in the body]</margin> <gloss>as even themselves being in the body</gloss>, that is, just *as if* you yourselves were in the body. Lorenzo thinks "of them" should be understood, as if you were in the body of the afflicted, which I do not approve of at all. For he refers to the body and its being subject to similar evils. So too Theophylact.

<margin>5 Honorable marriage in all]</margin> <gloss>among all</gloss>, which Theophylact explains in various ways. "In all," so that you understand "in all ways," or "in all ages," or "at all times," and finally "among all." This last one is most approved by me. Since even among the Pagans honor was held for marriages for the sake of public benefit. Even if these things are not proclaimed in praise of marriage, but are commanded, so that it is understood to be so. For he seems to want marriage to be avoided by those who defile it with adulteries. Moreover, where he translates "bed" here, in Greek it is <gloss>κοίτη</gloss>. He translates that voice in the Epistle to the Romans as "intercourse" when dealing with Isaac and Rebecca; although <gloss>κοίτη</gloss> does not properly signify intercourse, but the bed/couch.

<margin>6 I will not leave you nor forsake you]</margin> * <gloss>leave, forsake</gloss>, that is, I *relinquish* and *abandon*, in the present tense. The passage is from Joshua chapter 1. Even if Jerome translates it, "I will not dismiss nor abandon you."
