# EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER XIII.

<note>original Greek text of Hebrews 13:16–25</note>
Do not forget to do good and to share; for with such sacrifices God is well pleased. Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over your souls as those who will give an account, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning—for that would be of no advantage to you. Pray for us; for we are confident that we have a good conscience, desiring to conduct ourselves honorably in all things. But I especially urge you to do this, so that I may be restored to you the sooner. Now may the God of peace, who brought up from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you in every good work to do His will, performing in you what is pleasing in His sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. And I urge you, brothers, bear with this word of exhortation, for I have written to you in few words. Know that our brother Timothy has been released, with whom, if he comes shortly, I will see you. Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those from Italy greet you. Grace be with you all. Amen.

->Written from Italy by Timothy.<-

->THE END OF THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE HEBREWS.<-

***

9 *God is won over*] <note>original: "εὐαρεστεῖται ὁ Θεὸς"</note> God is well-pleased, that is, God is reconciled, or it is pleasing to God. Although the translator used "merits" <note>Latin: "promeretur"</note>, it stands for "earns favor" and "is reconciled."
10 *And be subject to them*] <note>original: "καὶ ὑπείκετε"</note> that is, concede and yield. The word "to them" is redundant in the Latin.
11 *They keep watch*] <note>original: "ἀγρυπνοῦσιν"</note> that is, they are vigilant.
12 *As those who will give an account*] <note>original: "ὡς λόγον ἀποδώσοντες"</note> that is, as if they are to render an account.
13 *For this is not profitable*] <note>original: "ἀλυσιτελὲς γὰρ"</note> that is, for it is useless.
14 *May he equip you*] <note>original: "καταρτίσαι"</note> that is, may he make perfect. And the Greeks read, "in every good work."
15 *Word of comfort*] <note>original: "παρακλήσεως"</note>. Why not rather "of exhortation" in this place?
16 *I have written in very few words*] <note>original: "διὰ βραχέων"</note> that is, through few things, or in brief. For there are two words in Greek.
17 *Know our brother*] <note>original: "Γινώσκετε"</note> is ambiguous. For it can be taken as "You know," and it makes little difference to the sense.
18 *Brothers from Italy*] <note>original: "οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰταλίας"</note> that is, the Italians. The word "brothers" is not found among the Greeks. 

Excellent Reader, I would wish this Epistle to be of no less value to you simply because many have doubted whether it was Paul's or someone else's. Certainly, whoever's it is, it is worthy for many reasons to be read by Christians. And just as it differs far and wide from Paul's style regarding phrasing, so it approaches the Pauline spirit and heart very closely. But since it cannot be proven by certain arguments whose it is—as it bears no inscription of a name—so it can be gathered from several indications (if not certain ones, then surely probable ones) that it was written by someone other than Paul. 

First, because it alone of all the epistles does not display Paul's name, although it does not escape me that this is explained away by Jerome, but in such a way that he blunts the opponent's weapon rather than proving his defense. He says: "If it is not Paul's because it does not show Paul's name, then it belongs to no one, since it shows no one's title." But hear the counter-argument: "If every book ought to be believed to belong to this or that person because it displays their title, then the apocryphal Gospel of Peter should be attributed to Peter, because it displays Peter's name." 

Next, for so many years, namely up to the age of Jerome, it was not received by the Latins, as he himself testifies in his letters. Adding to this conjecture is that Ambrose, though he interpreted all of Paul's Epistles, wrote nothing on this one. Furthermore, Jerome recounted in his commentary on Isaiah chapter 6 that certain testimonies are cited in this epistle from the Old Testament which are not found in the Hebrew volumes, about which we touched upon in chapter 11 of this Epistle. Add to this that while no one cites the testimonies of Scripture more clearly or aptly than Paul, nevertheless this author refers to a passage from Psalm 8 in a contrary sense, gathering from it that Christ was cast down, when the entire Psalm extols the dignity of the human condition. 

I will not mention for now that there are some passages which at first glance seem to support the dogmas of certain heretics: such as where the author interprets the veil separating the Holy of Holies as heaven; and much more, that he openly seems to take away hope from those who have relapsed into sin after baptism, and that not in only one place—whereas Paul even received back into the communion of saints the man who had slept with his father's wife. Add to this that Saint Jerome, in several other places, cites testimonies from this Epistle in such a way that he seems to doubt the author; for instance, explaining Jeremiah chapter 31, he says, "The Apostle Paul, or whoever else wrote the Epistle, used this testimony to the Hebrews." Again, on Isaiah chapter 50: "It is said also in the Epistle which is carried under the name 'To the Hebrews'"; and in almost countless other places, sometimes saying it does not matter whose it is, provided it teaches healthy things. Likewise in chapter 6: "Wherefore also the Apostle Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which Latin custom does not receive." Again, explaining Isaiah chapter 8, citing a testimony from this Epistle, he says, "In the Epistle which is inscribed 'To the Hebrews,' he teaches, although the custom of the Latins does not receive it among the canonical Scriptures." Likewise, explaining Matthew chapter 26, he says: "Although many of the Latins doubt it." Likewise on Zechariah chapter 8, citing it, he adds: "If, however, the Latin tongue does not reject the authority of the Greeks in receiving this Epistle." Likewise in the *Letter to Paulinus*: "The eighth [letter], to the Hebrews, is placed by most people outside the number [of Paul's letters]."

<column-break/>

Do not forget to do good: for with such victims <margin>17</margin> God is pleased. Obey those who preside over you and yield: since they watch for your souls, as those who will give an account, so that they may do this with joy and not groaning: for that is useless for you. Pray for us: for we trust that we <margin>18</margin> have a good conscience, desiring to live honestly among all people. But I more greatly beseech you <margin>19</margin> to do this, that I may be restored to you the more quickly. Now may the God of peace, who <margin>20</margin> brought back from the dead that great shepherd of the sheep through the blood of the eternal testament, our Lord Jesus, render you perfected in <margin>21</margin> every good work, to do his will, effecting that what you do may be accepted in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. I beseech you, brothers, bear with the <margin>22</margin> word of exhortation: for I have written to you in <margin>B</margin> few words. Know that our brother Timothy <margin>23</margin> has been set free, with whom, if he comes quickly, I will see you. Greet all who preside <margin>24</margin> over you, and all the saints. They greet you from Italy. Grace be with you all. Amen. <margin>25</margin>

->Sent from Italy by Timothy.<-

# THE END OF THE EPISTLE OF PAUL TO THE HEBREWS.

<margin>C</margin> Likewise, in his *Catalog of Illustrious Men*, Jerome reports that Gaius was of the opinion that only thirteen Epistles should be ascribed to Paul, and denied that the one to the Hebrews was his. Then Jerome adds in his own name, "But among the Romans even until today it is not held to be Paul's." In a similar manner, Origen in his 26th Homily on Matthew, when he brings forward a testimony from this Epistle, does not dare to demand from his adversary that it be seen as Paul's, and almost dismisses the matter, as happens in that place regarding the book entitled *The Secrets of Isaiah*. And Augustine, about to cite a testimony from this Epistle in *The City of God*, book 16, chapter 22, prefixes it in this way: "Regarding which, in the Epistle inscribed 'To the Hebrews,' which many say is the Apostle Paul's, but some deny, many and great things have been written." Indeed, frequently elsewhere when bringing forward a testimony from this Epistle, he says, "It is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews," omitting Paul's name. So it was understood in the Epistle to the Hebrews, etc. Also regarding that matter, it is read in the Epistle which is inscribed "To the Hebrews." Since these and similar instances occur more than a hundred times, he nowhere (so far as I can recall) cites it by Paul's name, whereas in other citations he was accustomed to freely add Paul's title. Ambrose, although he did not publish commentaries on this one alone, nevertheless uses its testimonies not infrequently, and seems to attribute it to Paul.

<margin>D</margin> Indeed, Origen (as recorded in Eusebius) testifies that it was doubted by many whether this Epistle was the legitimate work of Paul, especially because of the dissonance of the style, although he himself strongly asserts it for Paul: the passage is in the *Ecclesiastical History*, book 6, chapter 17. Again, in chapter 15 of the same book, he relates that among the Latins this Epistle was not attributed to the Apostle Paul. There remains now that argument than which none is more certain: the style itself and the character of the speech, which has no affinity with Paul's phrasing. For as to what some bring forward here—that Paul himself wrote in Hebrew, but Luke explained the subject of the Epistle (which he held in memory) in his own words—let others see how much weight that carries. For the difference is not only in words or figures, but it disagrees in all its markers. And just as Paul, writing in Greek, left much of the Hebrew idiom in his speech, so also in this one, which (as those people want) he wrote in Hebrew, some traces of that language would remain. What of the fact that not even Luke himself in the *Acts of the Apostles*—that is, in a subject matter that easily receives the ornaments of speech—comes close to the eloquence of this Epistle? 

Truly, I will not interpose my own opinion here. However, it is very probable what Saint Jerome suggested in his *Catalog of Illustrious Men*: that Clement, the Roman Pontiff fourth from Peter, was the author of this Epistle. For Paul mentions Clement, and here the author mentions Timothy. But it is better, I think, to write down Jerome's own words on this matter: <margin>E</margin> "He wrote," he says, "namely Clement, in the persona of the Roman Church, to the Church of the Corinthians, a very useful Epistle, which is also read publicly in some places, which seems to me to agree with the character of the Epistle which is carried under Paul's name to the Hebrews. But he uses many things from the same Epistle, not only in sense but according to the order of words. There is a great similarity in both." Thus far Saint Jerome, indicating civilly enough to a prudent and learned Reader what he himself suspects. 

The same Jerome, in his *Letter to Dardanus*, testifies that this was not received by the Latins, but received by many Greek writers only insofar as they believed it was by an ecclesiastical man, yet denied it was Paul's; rather, they attributed it to Barnabas or Clement, or according to some, to Luke—which Jerome also diligently noted in his *Catalog of Paul*. From these things it is clear that in the age of Jerome, the Roman Church had not yet received the authority of this Epistle; and the Greeks who did receive it judged it not to be Paul's. Finally, Jerome tells Dardanus that it does not matter whose it is, since it belongs to an ecclesiastical man. And yet today there are those who think it is more than heretical if anyone doubts the author of the Epistle, for no other reason than because Paul's title is added in the churches. If the Church certainly defines it to be Paul's, I willingly take my intellect captive in obedience to the faith; as far as my own feeling is concerned, it does not seem to be his, for the reasons which I have presented here. And if I knew for certain it was not Paul's, the matter is unworthy of a sword-fight. Nor would I make such a fuss over a matter of words, unless some people were stirring up such great tumults over nothing.

# THE ARGUMENT
#### of the Catholic Epistle of Saint
# J A M E S.

This he addresses to those from the twelve tribes scattered abroad, who have believed in our Lord Jesus Christ. He writes the Epistle in a teaching style, instructing them about the different kinds of trials: which kind comes from God, and which comes from the human heart itself. He teaches that faith must be shown not by words alone, but also by deeds, and that it is not the hearers of the law, but the doers of it who are justified. Regarding the wealthy, he instructs that the rich should not be preferred over the poor in the churches, but rather should be rebuked as being prideful. Finally, having comforted those who are wronged and urged them to be patient until the coming of the Judge, and having taught about the benefit of patience using Job as an example, he instructs them to call for the elders over the sick, and to be diligent in turning those who have wandered back to the truth—for there is a reward for this from the Lord, the forgiveness of sins. And thus he concludes the Epistle.

James, because he was the Bishop of Jerusalem, writes to the rest of the Jews who lived scattered throughout all nations, forming and instructing their lives with various precepts.

<margin>1</margin>
**JAMES the Apostle**] The word "Apostle" is not added in the [Greek] books that I have seen, nor in the corrected Latin versions. It is possible that a name shared with an Apostle provided the occasion for this Epistle to be ascribed to James the Apostle, though it may have belonged to another James. For there has been some doubt concerning this as well. The same thing happened with the two later Epistles [of John], which are attributed to John the Apostle because of the shared name, even though they belong to someone else, according to Jerome. Jerome denies that this James is the Apostle from the number of the twelve who are listed in the Gospel, but says he is another man surnamed "the Just," the son of Mary, the sister of the Mother of the Lord, who was the first ordained Bishop of Jerusalem by the Apostles. It is no obstacle that he is elsewhere called an *Apostle*, since in Paul’s writing, disciples preaching Christ are called *Apostles*. Indeed, some even asserted that this Epistle did not originate from this James either, although, as the same Jerome says, it gradually gained authority over time. And Jerome, in his *Catalog of Illustrious Men*, says this is the same man with whom Paul communicated in Jerusalem and who is mentioned so often in the Acts of the Apostles. Ruffus, in explaining Chapter 18 of Isaiah, says the same. Also in explaining Chapter 

<column-break/>

<margin>C</margin>
1 of the Epistle to the Galatians, he says that those people are greatly mistaken who believe that the James whom Paul saw was one of the twelve Apostles. However, I think it is unnecessary to fight anxiously over the author; let us rather embrace the matter itself and kiss the hand of the Holy Spirit as the author.
2 **Have its perfect work**] <note>original Greek: ἐχέτω</note>, that is, "let it have." And so it is read in the corrected Latin copies.
3 **And complete**] <note>original Greek: καὶ ὁλόκληροι</note>. This is used in opposition to things that are mutilated. For things are <unclear>divided and pulled apart</unclear> so that a body is no longer whole.
4 **Lacks wisdom**] <note>original Greek: Εἰ δέ τις ὑμῶν λείπεται σοφίας</note>, that is, "But if indeed wisdom is missing for any of you."
5 **Let him ask of God who gives**] <note>original Greek: αἰτείτω ἀπὸ τοῦ διδόντος Θεοῦ</note>, that is, let him ask of the one who gives, namely God, so that you may understand that wisdom is not to be sought from elsewhere.
6 **Abundantly**] <note>original Greek: ἁπλῶς</note>, that is, simply and purely. For that is how the following phrase is interpreted: *and does not reproach*.
7 **And does not reproach**] <note>original Latin: et non improperat</note> There are those who deny that "improberat" is proper Latin in this sense, and it is true that in the writings of Pliny, *improperare* was said for "to hasten inward." Nevertheless, I cannot be persuaded that the word is a total invention, since it is so frequently encountered in the Sacred Books, both as the verb "to reproach" and the noun "reproach" <note>Latin: "improperare" and "improperium"</note>.
8 **Nothing hesitating**] <note>original Greek: μηδὲν διακρινόμενος</note>, that is, not judging between two opinions.

<note original="caus. Quanquam hæc affinia sunt..."> Erasmus notes that while "driven" and "tossed" are closely related, both terms are used to describe the motion of the waves.</note>
9 **And is tossed** ] <note original="καὶ ῥιπιζομένῳ">*kai rhipizomeno*</note>, that is, *and who is thrown about, or swept away.*
10 **For let not think** ] <note original="Μὴ γὰρ">*Me gar*</note>, that is, *For let him not.*
11 **That he shall receive** ] <note original="ὅτι λήψεταί τι">*hoti lepsetai ti*</note>, that is, *that he will receive, or is about to receive.*
12 **A man double-minded** ] <note original="δίψυχος">*dipsychos*</note>. As if you were to say, *two-souled*, just as we say *two-tongued* <note>Erasmus is explaining the literal Greek "two-souled" to describe someone wavering in faith.</note>.
13 **In exaltation** ] <note original="ἐν τῷ ὕψει">*en to hypsei*</note>, that is, *in loftiness.* For he sets opposing things against one another. It seems the Translator read, *in his height.*
14 **In humility** ] <note original="ἐν ταπεινώσει">*en tapeinosei*</note>, that is, *in humiliation, or being cast down.*
15 **The beauty of its face** ] This is a somewhat harsh metaphor which attributes a "face" to a plant. For here the word is <note original="χόρτος">*chortos*</note>, *which is sometimes translated as hay*, sometimes *grass*, and more rarely *herb.* Therefore the Reader should know the Greek is <note original="εὐπρέπεια τοῦ προσώπου αὐτοῦ">*euprepeia tou prosopou autou*</note>, that is, *the beauty of its look, or appearance.*
16 **The rich in his ways** ] <note original="πορείαις">*poreiais*</note>. From which it might be read as "abundance." Certainly, that would seem more fitting to the sense.
17 **God has promised** ] The Greeks read *the Lord*, instead of *God.* Nor should anyone suspect some mystery because he said "repromised" instead of "promised." For in Greek it is <note original="ἐπηγγείλατο">*epeingeilato*</note>. The same word is used similarly in Suetonius’s lives of Otho, Tiberius, and Claudius Caesar. For the prefix *re-* here does not signify a repetition of the act, but a relationship: as one "receives," not who takes twice, but who takes what is owed from another; and "retains," not who holds twice, but who holds one who wishes to leave.
18 **Because he is tempted by God** ] <note original="ὅτι ἀπὸ Θεοῦ πειράζομαι">*hoti apo Theou peirazomai*</note>, that is, that *I am tempted by God.* Although the Latin language does not accept this phrasing unless you omit the conjunction "that."
19 **He is an untempter** ] <note original="ἀπείραστός ἐστι κακῶν">*apeirastos esti kakon*</note>, that is, *he is inexperienced in evils*, or *he cannot be tempted by evils.* It means that God is neither tempted by evils himself, nor does he tempt anyone; as if you were to say, *untemptable.* I wonder, however, that the Translators did not explain this word with a longer phrase. For in Latin an *intentator* is one who inflicts something evil. If *apeirastos* is taken actively, he has said the same thing twice. And the conjunction "but" <note original="δὲ">*de*</note> speaks against this sense.
20 **Is drawn away and enticed** ] <note original="ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος">*exelkomenos kai deleazomenos*</note>, that is, *lured and baited.* Although these participles are in the present tense, that is, *while he is being lured and baited.*
21 **Generates death** ] <note original="ἀποκύει">*apokyei*</note>. A metaphor taken from pregnant women. As if you would say *labors to bring forth.*
22 **Most beloved** ] <note original="ἀγαπητοὶ">*agapetoi*</note>, that is, *beloved.*
23 **Best gift** ] <note original="δόσις ἀγαθὴ">*dosis agathe*</note>, that is, *a good gift*, or *a good giving.* Jerome reads, *Every perfect giving*, in a passage I will soon cite.

24 **There is no change** ] <note original="παραλλαγή">*parallage*</note>. Which Jerome, in his first commentary *Against Jovinian*, translates as *difference.* Augustine, in the book *The City of God XI*, reads: *with whom there is no change, nor shadow of a moment.* Again, in *Against the Manichaeans on the Nature of the Good, chapter XXIV.* Hilary, in *On the Trinity, Book IV*, reads: *with whom there is no mutation.*
25 **Nor** ] <note original="ἤ">*e*</note>, that is, *or, used for nor.* **Shadow of turning**, <note original="τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα">*tropes aposkiasma*</note>, that is, *shadow of conversion.* It signifies that from this light a shadow is cast, and that our sun increases and decreases at the solstices. Saint Jerome says almost the same in the place we just cited.
26 **For voluntarily etc.** ] <note original="Βουληθεὶς ἀπεκύησεν ἡμᾶς λόγῳ ἀληθείας, εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἡμᾶς ἀπαρχήν τινα τῶν αὐτοῦ κτισμάτων">"Having willed it, he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we might be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures."</note> Bede indicates this passage is read by some as *that we might be the firstfruits of his creatures*, as if understanding that we are more excellent than other created things, because formerly
<margin>F</margin>
the firstfruits of individual things were offered—that is, the best of each. Furthermore, where our Translator renders "us" as "something" <note original="aliquid">meaning 'some thing'</note>, according to this sense it would be more correctly translated as *a certain thing, or certain firstfruits*, so that with the noun added, we understand the speech to contain a metaphor.
27 **You know, my brothers** ] <note original="Ὥστε ἀδελφοί μου">*Hoste adelphoi mou*</note>, that is, *Therefore, my brothers.* The Translator seems to have read <note original="ἴστε">*iste* (you know)</note> instead of <note original="ὥστε">*hoste* (therefore)</note>. For "For you know," which is in our [Latin] manuscripts, I do not find in the Greek ones.
28 **But let there be** ] "But" is redundant.
29 **All filthiness** ] <note original="ῥυπαρίαν">*rhyparian*</note>, that is, *dirtiness.*
30 **Abundance** ] <note original="περισσείαν">*perisseian*</note>, that is, *superfluity.* For he alludes to the filth and superfluities of the body. Even if there are some who deny that *superfluity* is a Latin word. Yet I do not see why it is less permitted to say *superfluity* from *superfluous* than *scantiness* from *scanty*, *assiduity* from *assiduous*, or *perpetuity* from *perpetual.*
31 **And not hearers only** ] I do not find "only" <note original="tantum">in Latin</note> among the Greeks, not even in the Aldine edition. But someone indicates it is in the Rhodian manuscript. The matter is safe. But I truly fear that this manuscript was corrected according to our [Latin] ones. In fact, not even in the more corrected Latin ones is "only" added, but it seems to have been added by someone to whom it seemed absurd that we should be commanded not to be hearers of the word; as if interpreting the writer's mind, he added "hearers only."
32 **Has looked into** ] <note original="παρακύψας">*parakypsas*</note>, that is, *one who has looked forward*, from the gesture of one tilting the head out of a desire to see. **Into the perfect law**, <note original="εἰς νόμον τέλειον">*eis nomon teleion*</note>, that is, *into the perfect law.* The Donatian manuscript had *in the perfect law.*
33 **Of liberty** ] <note original="τὴν τῆς ἐλευθερίας">*ten tes eleutherias*</note>, that is, *which is of liberty*, or *namely, of liberty.*
34 **Has remained in it** ] <note original="καὶ παραμείνας οὕτως">*kai parameinas houtos*</note>, that is, *and has remained thus.*
35 **To be religious** ] The Greeks add *among you*, that is, *between you.*

4 have you not judged <gloss>8</gloss> within yourselves, and become judges of wicked thoughts? <gloss>9</gloss>
5 Listen, my beloved brothers: has not God chosen the poor of this world <gloss>10</gloss> to be rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he promises to those by whom he is loved?
6 But you have held the poor man in contempt. Do not the rich <gloss>11</gloss> exercise tyranny over you, and do they not drag you to the tribunals? <gloss>14</gloss>
7 and do they not speak evil of the good name which has been invoked over you?
8 If you indeed fulfill the law of kings according to the scripture, "You shall love your neighbor as yourself," you do well.
9 But if you respect the person, you commit sin, and are refuted by the law <gloss>15</gloss> as if you were transgressors. <gloss>16</gloss>
<margin>C</margin>

12 So speak, and so act, as those who are to be judged by the law of liberty. <gloss>18</gloss>

### Translator's Annotations

36 **But seduces his own heart**] From a wandering and unstable heart is born the petulance of the tongue; hence we translate it, *but allows his heart to go astray*. For the Greek word is *apaton* <note>original: ἀπατῶν, meaning "deceiving"</note>.

37 **From this age**] *apo tou kosmou* <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ κόσμου</note>, that is, *from the world*.

1 **...of Christ of glory**] Following the character of Hebrew speech, this is the same as saying *glorious*, *Iēsou Christou tēs doxēs* <note>original: Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τῆς δόξης</note>. See, Reader, whether the word *doxa* here might signify not "glory," but "opinion" <note>Greek *doxa* can mean both fame/glory and a personal opinion/judgment</note>, so that it refers back to "respect of persons." The sense would be: do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ based on a distinction of persons, such that each man judges someone according to his own opinion—not based on whether the person is a Christian, but whether they seem great or humble to us because of family ties or wealth.

2 **Into your assembly**] *eis tēn synagōgēn hymōn* <note>original: εἰς τὴν συναγωγὴν ὑμῶν</note>, that is, *into your congregation* or *gathering*. It is clear here that "synagogue" refers to any gathering or assembly of people.

3 **Having a gold ring**] *chrysodaktylios* <note>original: χρυσοδακτύλιος</note>. The author used a compound word to describe someone wearing gold rings, as if you were to say, "gold-ringed."

4 **In a white robe**] *en esthēti lampra* <note>original: ἐν ἐσθῆτι λαμπρᾷ</note>, that is, *in a splendid robe*, though in ancient times white garments were the mark of the magnificent and the royal.

5 **In this seat**] *ē kathou hōde* <note>original: ἢ κάθου ὧδε</note>. The Translator <note>referring to the Vulgate</note> varied his wording, though the Greek word is the same.

6 **Who is dressed in excellent clothing**] *epi ton phorounta tēn esthēta tēn lampran* <note>original: ἐπὶ τὸν φοροῦντα τὴν ἐσθῆτα τὴν λαμπρὰν</note>, that is, *toward him who wears the splendid robe*. It is the same word that the Translator just rendered as "white"—he is an excessive seeker of variety.

7 **Or sit under**] *ē kathou hypo* <note>original: ἢ κάθου ὑπὸ</note>, that is, *or sit here*.

8 **You have not judged**] *ou diekrithēte en heautois* <note>original: οὐ διεκρίθητε ἐν ἑαυτοῖς</note>, that is, *you have not been judged within yourselves*. For it can be understood this way, and it fits better with what follows. Furthermore, the conjunction *de* <note>original: δὲ, meaning "but" or "and"</note> which is added in the Greek serves only for emphasis and emotion: *And have you not made distinctions*, as if to say, "Have you not indeed?"

9 **Of wicked thoughts**] *ponērōn* <note>original: πονηρῶν</note>, that is, *evil*.

10 **In this world**] *tou kosmou* <note>original: τοῦ κόσμου</note>, that is, *of the world*. The Translator, for some strange reason, always adds a demonstrative pronoun like "this," even though it is added here in only a few Greek manuscripts.

11 **But the rich**] The "but" is redundant and fights against the sense. The Translator seems to have read *plousious de*, as if the text previously said "we are poor indeed in this world, *but* rich in faith."

12 **You have dishonored**] *ētimasate* <note>original: ἠτιμάσατε</note>, that is, *you have treated with ignominy* or *held in contempt*.

13 **Oppress by power**] What the Greeks say with the single verb *katadynasteuousin* <note>original: καταδυναστεύουσιν</note>, which is to say, "they abuse their magistracy and power to your harm."

14 **To judgments**] *eis kritēria* <note>original: εἰς κριτήρια</note>, that is, *to the tribunals*.

15 **Argued against by the law**] *elenchomenoi* <note>original: ἐλεγχόμενοι</note>. This would have been better translated as *you are refuted* or *convicted*, so that the tense matches the context.

16 **As if transgressors**] *hōs parabatai* <note>original: ὡς παραβάται</note>, that is, *as transgressors*.

17 **Whoever however**] The Greek has "For" (*gar*), not "however" (*autem*).
<margin>E</margin>
18 **Beginning to be judged**] *mellontes krinesthai* <note>original: μέλλοντες κρίνεσθαι</note>, that is, *who are to be judged*. The Translator frequently translated this way, but here it was truly intolerable.

19 **Who does not do**] *tō poiēsanti* <note>original: τῷ ποιήσαντι</note>, that is, *who has not done*.

20 **Mercy however exalts itself**] *kai katakauchatai eleos kriseōs* <note>original: καὶ κατακαυχᾶται ἔλεος κρίσεως</note>. I think the Translator rendered it "superexult" <note>original: *superexultat*</note>, that is, "to boast over." The meaning is that mercy boasts against judgment as a victor. Therefore, the five explanations of Hugo of Saint Cher <note>a 13th-century theologian</note> are irrelevant; he brings in whole wagon-loads of commentary for this one place, making an "examination of interpretations" instead of a single true interpretation. Such is the fertility of ignorance, while the speech of truth is simple. James uses the same verb in the same way a little further down: *do not boast and lie against the truth*. It appears that Augustine also read it as "superexult." This can be gathered from his words explaining Psalm 118. Likewise, in *The City of God* (Book 21, Ch. 27), he interprets it as "superexults, overcomes," saying that when it comes to judgment, mercy will be the winner; he is not far from the mark regarding the sense. It appears Augustine read "superexult" even if it is corrupted to "super-exalt" in common manuscripts; for it is the victor's role to exult. Rufus, in his *Questions on Exodus*, reads "mercy superexalts in judgment." From this, a clearer suspicion arises that he read "superexult." Again, in his Letter to Jerome (29), he treats this passage such that the word "superexult" does not fit; for the conquered "superexalts" the conqueror rather than vice versa. Also, in Letter 89, it was written "superexalts in judgment," from which one must further guess that it was written "superexult." Certainly, from the commentaries of Bede, it is plain that he read "superexult." I will write his words: "Mercy superexults over judgment, because just as the one who did not show mercy will grieve being condemned in God's judgment, so he who did show it will exult and rejoice when rewarded." Otherwise, "mercy superexalts judgment." It did not say "mercy conquered judgment." For it is not an enemy to judgment, but he who gathers more through mercy "superexalts." From these things, it is clear that Bede read "superexult" according to the Greek manuscripts, although the scribe corrupted the word almost everywhere. There remains a small doubt about the preposition. For he who translated "superexult" seems to have read *hyperkauchatai*. Indeed, *katakauchasthai* sounds more like boasting *against* someone.
<margin>F</margin>
21 **And sister**] The Greek has "Or," not "And."

22 **Be you warmed**] *thermainesthe* <note>original: θερμαίνεσθε</note>, that is, *may you be warmed* or *warm yourselves*. For what was "be you warmed"? Or why not rather change the form to "warm yourselves," just as the Translator rendered the participle of this verb more than once in the Gospel: *thermainomenos*, "he was warming himself." But grammarians cite the form "be warmed" from obsolete authors, so let us grant it to them—though they seem to prefer using obsolete and doubtful forms when common and certain ones are available.

The extensive annotations provide a philological critique of the Latin Vulgate's translation choices compared to the original Greek.</summary>

### E P I S T L E   C H A P T E R   I I I.

17 Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself.
18 But someone will say, "You have faith, and I have works." Show me your faith from your works, and I will show you my faith from my works. 19 You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and tremble. 20 But do you want to know, O foolish man, that faith without works is dead? 21 Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar? 22 Do you see that faith was working together with his works, and by works faith was made perfect? 23 And the Scripture was fulfilled which says, "Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness," and he was called the friend of God. 24 You see then that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only. 25 Likewise, was not Rahab the harlot also justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out another way? 26 For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.

III. 1 My brothers, let not many of you become teachers, knowing that we shall receive a stricter judgment. 2 For we all stumble in many things. If anyone does not stumble in word, he is a perfect man, able also to bridle the whole body. 3 Indeed, we put bits in horses' mouths that they may obey us, and we turn their whole body around. 4 Look also at ships: although they are so large and are driven by fierce winds, they are turned by a very small rudder wherever the pilot desires. 5 Even so the tongue is a little member and boasts great things. See how great a forest a little fire kindles! 6 And the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity. The tongue is so set among our members that it defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature; and it is set on fire by hell. 7 For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and creature of the sea, is tamed and has been tamed by mankind. 8 But no man can tame the tongue. It is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison. 9 With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in the similitude of God. 10 Out of the same mouth proceed blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so. 11 Does a spring send forth fresh and bitter water from the same opening?

***

23 **In itself**] <note>original: "καθ᾿ ἑαυτήν" (kath’ heautēn)</note>, that is, by itself, or alone.

24 **Without works**] <note>original: "ἐκ τῶν ἔργων σου" (ek tōn ergōn sou)</note>, that is, "from your works." The Translator <note>The "Translator" usually refers to the author of the Latin Vulgate, traditionally St. Jerome.</note> seems to have read <note>original: "ἐκτὸς τῶν ἔργων" (ektos tōn ergōn)</note> ["outside of" or "apart from" works]: for there is a very small difference in the words, though the whole meaning is contested. But if you read "without works," as the Translator does, I do not see how the sense holds up: for faith cannot be demonstrated except by deeds. Whoever this James was, his meaning is: "Demonstrate your faith which you claim to have by joining it to deeds, so that you possess both; and I will declare by my deeds alone that I lack neither." The Greek phrasing seems somewhat clearer. Indeed, to teach that neither faith without works nor works without faith are valid, James presents two people speaking: one, relying on his faith, neglects works. To him it is said: "You have faith; let that be enough for you." Again, the other, trusting in works but neglecting faith, answers him: "And I have deeds; that is enough for me." James refutes the speech of both. "In fact," he says, "what either of them has is not sufficient for salvation. But you who boast of your faith, show by your very deeds that you have faith—which is certainly not an idle thing. And I will declare by my very deeds that I lack neither." For it is not fitting that these words, "you have faith," should belong to the person of the Apostle, who rejects faith that lacks deeds.

25 **Abraham believed God**] The very same testimony that Paul brings forward in the Epistle to the Romans against a reliance on works, James brings here to the commendation of works. However, Paul there calls "works" the observance of the <term>Mosaic Law</term> <note>The ritual laws of the Old Testament</note>, while here James refers to the duties of piety and charity.

26 **You see, that**] <note>original: "Ὁρᾶτε τοίνυν, ὅτι" (Horate toinun, hoti)</note>, that is, "You see therefore, that."

1 **Many teachers**] <note>original: "πολλοὶ" (polloi)</note>, that is, "many."

2 **We shall receive**] <note>original: "ληψόμεθα" (lēpsometha)</note>, that is, "we shall take," or as Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla (1407–1457), a pioneering humanist scholar who critiqued the Vulgate.</note> prefers, "we shall receive." For we do not "take" unless we are willing, but we "receive" even if unwilling; thus we rightly say someone "received a wound," but not that he "took a wound." And what follows—"we all offend"—is in the present tense, not the past: <note>original: "πταίομεν" (ptaiomen)</note>, that is, "we stumble," so that you understand everyone stumbles daily. Likewise, what follows—"If anyone does not offend in word"—is in the present tense.

3 **Can also by a bridle**] <note>original: "δυνατὸς χαλιναγωγῆσαι καὶ ὅλον τὸ σῶμα" (dynatos chalinagōgēsai kai holon to sōma)</note>, that is, "able by a bridle to control also the whole body."

4 **If however bits**] In the Greek it is not "If however," but "Behold" <note>original: "Ἰδοὺ" (Idou)</note>. The Translator read <note>original: "Εἰ δὲ" (Ei de)</note>. Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (672–735), an English monk and scholar.</note> indicates that in some copies it was written, "As however the horses," etc.

5 **To obey**] <note>original: "πρὸς τὸ πείθεσθαι αὐτοὺς ἡμῖν" (pros to peithesthai autous hēmin)</note>, that is, "so that they may obey us," or "submit to us."

6 **The whole body**] The Greek reads "If the whole body," but it was necessary to discard the conjunction once it said "If however." But if we accept "Behold," this will be the sense: he who can control a horse with a bridle will, by that same effort, turn the horse's whole body wherever he wishes.

For every nature <gloss>16</gloss> of beasts and 7
<margin>D</margin> birds, and of serpents <gloss>17</gloss> and sea-creatures, is tamed and has been tamed <gloss>18</gloss> by human nature. But the tongue 8 no man can tame, <gloss>19</gloss> an uncontrollable evil, full of deadly poison. 7 **And behold ships**] <note>original: "Ἰδοὺ καὶ τὰ πλοῖα" (Idou kai ta ploia)</note>, that is, "Behold also the ships," or "the ships too."

8 **Though they are large**] <note>original: "τηλικαῦτα ὄντα" (tēlikauta onta)</note>, that is, "though they are so great."

9 **By fierce winds**] <note>original: "σκληρῶν" (sklērōn)</note>, that is, "harsh": but the Translator seems to have read something else. *Are driven*: <note>original: "ἐλαυνόμενα" (elaunomena)</note>, that is, they are driven or carried.

10 **They are turned about however**] "However" is redundant.

11 **A little indeed**] "Indeed" is superfluous and hinders the sense.

12 **And exults in great things**] <note>original: "καὶ μεγαλαυχεῖ" (kai megalauchei)</note>. Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a Franciscan teacher whose biblical commentaries were highly influential.</note> reads "exalts," and explains it as "exalting great evils" or "provoking" them. I believe the Translator wrote "exults," that is, "boasts," which is what the Greek word sounds like. Nor does Bede hide that in certain codices it was written "exults in great things." We found it written this way in the very ancient Codex of Donatianus. In Greek, the speech is more pleasant with the compound word <note>original: "μεγαλαυχεῖ" (megalauchei)</note>, which means to boast or brag with a mix of things—that is, it magnificently boasts of itself.

13 **Behold how great a fire**] I think the Translator should have rendered it "how tiny a fire," that is, how small. For in Greek it is <note>original: "ὀλίγον πῦρ" (oligon pyr)</note>, that is, "a meager fire." Jerome, in chapter 57 of Isaiah, cites it thus: "A small fire, how great a mass of material it burns." Bede also testifies that in several copies it was written, "Behold a modest fire," etc. I added this so that no one thinks the Greek codices were corrupted. And "forest" <note>original: "sylvam"</note> in this place would be more correctly translated as "matter" or "material" <note>original: "materiam"</note>.

14 **The universe of iniquity**] <note>original: "ὁ κόσμος τῆς ἀδικίας" (ho kosmos tēs adikias)</note>, that is, "the world of iniquity." Sometimes <term>mundus</term> <note>Latin for "world"</note> refers to a heap of things stored together. Hence we speak of a "woman's world" <note>referring to her collection of ornaments or toiletries</note>.

15 **The tongue is placed**] "Thus the tongue," the Greeks read: <note>original: "Οὕτως ἡ γλῶσσα" (Houtōs hē glōssa)</note>.

16 **Of beasts**] <note>original: "θηρίων" (thēriōn)</note>, that is, of wild beasts, or harmful brutes. For that is what the word properly signifies.

17 **And of the others**] <note>original: "καὶ ἐναλίων" (kai enaliōn)</note>, that is, "and of sea-creatures." The Translator seems to have read <note>original: "ἄλλων" (allōn)</note> ["others"], or at least wrote "of the others," which itself still appears in several codices. A sleepy scribe changed it to "of the others": for even sea creatures, such as dolphins, can become tame.

18 **By human nature**] <note>original: "τῇ φύσει τῇ ἀνθρωπίνῃ" (tē physei tē anthrōpinē)</note>, that is, by human ingenuity or human nature. Although this makes little difference to the sense.

19 **A restless evil**] <note>original: "ἀκατάσχετον" (akatasketon)</note>, that is, "uncontrollable" or "unrestrainable." Jerome, in his second Dialogue against the Pelagians, translated it as "an incontinent evil."

20 **We bless God and the Father**] In Latin, one who speaks at a banquet curses; does he not immediately bless the man whom he praises?

21 **From the very mouth**] <note>original: "Ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ στόματος" (Ek tou autou stomatos)</note>, that is, "From the same mouth."

22 **It flows out**] <note>original: "βρύει" (bryei)</note>, that is, it sends forth from a spring. If, however, it is said in Latin "it flows out water": I know it was said by Virgil...

# JAMES CHAPTER IV.
Tom. VI. Ttt 3

<margin>A</margin>
12 Can a fig tree, my brothers, produce olives, or a vine produce figs? In the same way, no spring can produce both salt and sweet 13 water. Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show his works by his good conduct in the 14 gentleness of wisdom. But if you have bitter jealousy and contention in your heart, do not boast and lie 15 against the truth. This is not the wisdom coming down 16 from above, but is earthly, animal, demonic. For where there is jealousy and contention, there is instability and every 17 evil thing. But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, modest, easy to be entreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without judging, and without 18 hypocrisy. And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

<margin>IV. 1</margin>
Where do wars and brawls among you come from? Is it not from here, from your pleasures, which war in your members? 2 You desire, and do not have; you kill and are jealous, and cannot obtain; you brawl and war; you do not have 3 because you do not ask. 4 You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, so that you may 4 spend it on your pleasures. Adulterers and adulteresses, do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Whoever wishes to be a friend of the world 5 is constituted an enemy of God. Or do you think the Scripture speaks in vain, 5 "The spirit that dwells in 6 us yearns toward envy"? But he gives greater grace. Therefore, submit to God; resist the devil, and he will flee from 8 you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your 9 hearts, you double-minded. Be afflicted, and mourn, and weep; let your laughter be turned into mourning 10 and your joy into gloom. Humble yourselves 11 before the Lord, and he will lift you up. Do not speak against one another, brothers. He who speaks against a brother and judges his brother, speaks against the law and judges the law; but if you judge the law, you are not <unclear>a doer</unclear>...

---

<margin>D</margin>
> And the hard oaks shall sweat dewy honey. <note>original: *Et dura quercus sudabunt roscida mella* — a quote from Virgil’s Eclogues 4.30, used here to illustrate poetic descriptions of flowing substances.</note>

To flow with water was considered more gentle. It is said to flow "with liquid" or "the liquid itself," referring to what it emits, though the liquid itself emanates. And in Pliny, certain trees are said to "flow" with pitch and resin. "Sweet and bitter" <note>original: *αμαυὸν, τὸ γλυκὺ καὶ τὸ πικρὸν*</note>, that is, sweet and bitter, as in the law of <unclear>Claudianus</unclear>.

23 **Fig trees making grapes**] <note>original: *συκῆ ἐλαίας ποιῆσαι*</note>, that is, for a fig tree to produce olives. Indeed, he opposed the fig to the olive, because the latter is of a sharp and harsh flavor, unlike the fig. Though he soon mentions the vine.

24 **So neither can salt water make sweet**] <note>original: *Οὕτως οὐδεμία πηγὴ ἁλυκὸν καὶ γλυκὺ ποιῆσαι ὕδωρ*</note>, that is, "So no spring can make sweet and bitter water."

25 **And disciplined**] <note>original: *ἐπιστήμων*</note>; that is, knowing, or endowed with knowledge, which more recent writers call "scientific" <note>term: *scientificus* — here used in the older sense of "producing knowledge" or "knowledge-based."</note>.

26 **His operation**] <note>original: *τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ*</note>, that is, his works.

27 **And contention**] In Greek only *eris*, "and contention" <note>original: *καὶ ἐριθείαν*</note>. And it follows immediately, "in your heart."

28 **Descending from above**] That which is added here, "from the Father of lights," is not found in the Greek Codices, but appears to have been added here from the first chapter. Nor is it touched upon by Bede.

29 **Animal, diabolical**] "Animal" here is derived from the soul <note>original: *ψυχική* — psychikē</note>. For so he sometimes calls human affection when it is opposed to the spirit. Currensis thinks it is said of animals, because it belongs to brutes to be led by pleasures; while Bede specifically warns of what we are saying, citing Greek authority, which however is held too cheaply by our contemporaries. Nor is it "diabolical," but "demonic" <note>original: *δαιμονιώδης*</note>, that is, not from the spirit of Christ, but from the spirit of this world. And "Demons" are called by the Greeks as if they were <note>original: *δαήμονες*</note>, that is, "the knowing ones," and the Ancients attributed the invention of human arts to them.

30 **There inconstancy**] <note>original: *ἀκαταστασία*</note>. Which sounds more like tumult and sedition.

31 **Chaste**] <note>original: *ἁγνὴ*</note>, that is, pure or chaste. And "modest," in Greek is <note>original: *ἐπιεικής*</note>, that is, humane or equitable. For the wisdom of the world makes people morose.

32 **Suadible**] <note>original: *εὐπειθὴς*</note>, that is, tractable, or compliant, and one who is easily persuaded. "Consenting to the good." These are not found in the Greek codices that I have seen, nor even in the very ancient codex of Donatianus, even if Bede reads and interprets them.

33 **Judging without simulation**] In Greek it is <note>original: *ἀδιάκριτος καὶ ἀνυπόκριτος*</note>, that is, discerning nothing and feigning nothing. Or "without partiality, without simulation." And yet that word "judging" is found even in ancient codices. I wonder, however, what Augustine was following when, instead of "undiscriminating" <note>original: *ἀδιάκριτος*</note>, he read "inestimable." For so he has it in his book *On Grace and Free Will to Valentinus*, the last chapter: *But the wisdom which is from above is first pure, then peaceable, modest, easy to be entreated, full of mercy and good fruits, inestimable, without simulation.* He who translated it thus seems to have used the word *adiakritos*—for it is ambiguous—in a passive sense.

1 **Strife**] <note>original: *καὶ μάχαι*</note>, that is, and fights: although he calls contentions "fights."

2 **Is it not in concupiscence**] We lack what is found among the Greeks, <note>original: *Οὐκ ἐντεῦθεν*</note>, that is, "Is it not from here?" Nor is it "in concupiscence," but <note>original: *ἐκ τῶν ἡδονῶν ὑμῶν*</note>, that is, "from your pleasures," or lusts, since we follow that which is not right in itself, but what pleases the mind.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
12 Can a fig tree, my brothers, 23 produce olives, or a vine produce figs? 24 So no spring can yield salt and sweet water. Who is wise 25 and endowed with knowledge among you? Let him show by his good conduct 26 his works with the gentleness of wisdom. But if you have 14 (bitter) jealousy 27 and contention in your heart, do not boast, and be liars against the truth. For that is not the wisdom 28 descending from above, 15 but earthly, 29 animal, demonic. For where there is 16 jealousy and contention, 30 there is instability and every evil work. But the wisdom from above is 17 indeed 31 chaste, then peaceable, modest, 32 tractable, full of mercy and good fruits, 33 without
<margin>B</margin>
partiality, and without simulation. And the fruit 18 of righteousness is sown in peace for those who make peace. Whence 1 IV. come wars and brawls among you? 2 Is it not from here, namely from your pleasures, which war in your members? You lust, and do not have: 3 you envy and are 2 jealous, and cannot obtain: 4 you fight and war: you do not have, 5 because you do not ask. You ask, 3 and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, 6 so that you may consume it on your pleasures. 7 Adulterers and adulteresses, do you 4 not know that 8 friendship with the world 9 is enmity with
<margin>C</margin>
God? Whoever therefore wishes to be 10 a friend of the world, is constituted an enemy of God. Or do you think that 5 the Scripture says in vain? 11 The spirit yearns toward envy, 12 which has dwelt in us. 13 But he gives greater 6 grace. Therefore be subject to God, but resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw 8 near to you. Cleanse your hands, O sinners, and purify your hearts, 14 double-minded. 15 Be afflicted, and 9 mourn, and weep: let your laughter be turned into mourning, and your joy into sorrow. Humble yourselves 10 in the sight of the Lord, and he will lift you up. Do not speak against 11 one 16 another, brothers. He who speaks against a brother, and who judges his brother, 17 speaks against the law, and judges the law:

---

<margin>D</margin>
3 **You kill and are jealous**] <note>original: *φονεύετε καὶ ζηλοῦτε*</note>. I do not see what that word, "you kill," contributes to the sense. Perhaps it was written, <note>original: *φθονεῖτε*</note> (you envy) and you are jealous, and you cannot obtain: so that a sleepy scribe wrote "you kill" <note>original: *φονεύετε*</note> instead of "you envy," especially since there follows, "The spirit yearns toward envy." Certainly Bede does not touch upon these words, "you lust and do not have, you kill and are jealous."

4 **You quarrel and war**] <note>original: *μάχεσθε καὶ πολεμεῖτε*</note>, that is, you fight and war.

5 **Because you do not**] <note>original: *διὰ τὸ μὴ αἰτεῖσθαι ὑμᾶς*</note>, that is, for the reason that you do not ask.

6 **That in your concupiscences**] Again in this place it is, "in your pleasures" <note>original: *ἐν ταῖς ἡδοναῖς*</note>.

7 **Adulterers, do you not know**] In Greek it is, <note>original: *Μοιχοὶ καὶ μοιχαλίδες, οὐκ οἴδατε*</note>, that is, "Adulterers and adulteresses, do you not know?"

8 **Friendship of this world**] <note>original: *ἡ φιλία τοῦ κόσμου*</note>, that is, "of the world": and he added "this" in his own manner.

9 **Is an enemy to God**] <note>original: *ἔχθρα τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐστιν*</note>, that is, is enmity of God, or rather "with God," as we noted in Paul. And so it is read in the more corrected Latin copies, even those which were printed. Nor does Bede recount it otherwise, except that he reads "enemy" instead of "enmity." The difference is in the accent: *échthra* is enmity, *echthrá* is enemy.

10 **To be a friend of the age**] <note>original: *κόσμου*</note>, that is, "of the world."

11 **Toward envy the spirit yearns**] Upon this passage, modern theologians have brought wagon-loads of interpretations; if they are ever deprived of the commentaries of the Ancients—which the Rhetorical and Grammatical writers, as they call them, left to us—they are quite helpless. To me, this sense is most approved: The spirit of man, devoted to the world, envies itself, but God imparts his grace more copiously than we ourselves might desire. However, it is not clear where this is found written. Bede brings forward a threefold sense.

12 **Which dwells**] <note>original: *ὃ κατώκησεν*</note>, that is, which dwelt, or established its seat.

13 **But he gives greater**] Before these words, in some Greek copies, certain things are added, which as it were complete the speech: "Therefore he says, The Lord opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble." Truly I suspect these were added here by some studious person in the marginal space, from the First Epistle of Peter, and then transferred into the text by an insufficiently learned scribe. For in most it is only, "But he gives greater grace." In this place the words which seemed added to me are subjoined, which I nevertheless found in the Aldine Edition: "Therefore he says, The Lord opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble." To the humble, <note>original: *ταπεινοῖς*</note>. Which pertains more to condition than to the mind.

14 **Double-minded**] <note>original: *δίψυχοι*</note>, that is, double in their souls.

15 **Be wretched**] <note>original: *Ταλαπωρήσατε*</note>. A word derived from "tolerance" or "enduring hardship."

16 **One another**] <note>original: *ἀλλήλων*</note>, that is, in turn, or some to others.

17 **Speaks against the law**] <note>original: *καταλαλεῖ*</note>, that is, speaks against, as also above, "he who speaks against," that is, he who speaks against or disparages.

# EPISTLE CHAPTER V.

11 ...you are a maker of the law, but a judge. 12 There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy. Who are you, who judges the other? 13 Come now, you who say, "Today and tomorrow let us go into such and such a city, and let us spend one year there, and trade, and make a profit." 14 You who do not know what tomorrow will bring. For what is your life? For it is a vapor, appearing for a little while, and then disappearing. 15 Instead of you saying, "If the Lord wills, we shall both live and do this or that." 16 But now you boast in your arrogance. All such boasting is evil. 17 Therefore, to him who knows to do good and does not do it, to him it is sin. V. 1 Come now, you rich men, weep and howl over your miseries that are coming upon you. 2 Your riches have rotted, and your garments have become moth-eaten. 3 Your gold and silver are rusted, and their rust will be a witness against you, and will eat your flesh like fire. You have heaped up treasure in the last days. 4 Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which were kept back by you, cry out; and the cries of the harvesters have entered into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth <note>Sabaoth is a Hebrew term meaning "of hosts" or "of armies," referring to God's power.</note>. 5 You have lived in luxury on the earth and been lived in pleasure; you have fattened your hearts as in a day of slaughter. 6 You have condemned, you have murdered the righteous man; he does not resist you. 7 Be patient therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it, until it receives the early and late rain. 8 You also be patient; establish your hearts, because the coming of the Lord has drawn near. 9 Do not groan against one another, brothers, so that you may not be condemned. Behold, the judge stands before the doors. 10 Take as an example of suffering, my brothers, and of patience, the Prophets, who spoke in the name of the Lord. 11 Behold, we count as blessed those who endure. You have heard of the endurance of Job, and you have seen the end of the Lord <note>The "end" or "outcome" the Lord brought about for Job.</note>, that the Lord is very compassionate and merciful. 12 But above all things, my brothers, do not swear, neither by heaven, nor by the earth, nor by any other oath; but let your "yes" be yes, and your "no" be no; so that you do not fall into hypocrisy...

<margin>E</margin>
18 *For there is one*] The word "for" is redundant and does nothing for the meaning. "And judge": I do not find these two words in the Greek.
19 *To destroy and to liberate*] <note>original: σῶσαι καὶ ἀπολέσαι</note>, that is, to save and to destroy.
20 *But you*] The Greeks do not add "but."
21 *Who judges your neighbor*] <note>original: τὸν ἕτερον</note>, that is, the other, or the fellow man.
22 *Behold now who*] <note>original: Ἄγε νῦν</note>, that is, "Come now."
23 *Today or tomorrow*] The Greek says, "Today and tomorrow" <note>original: Σήμερον καὶ αὔριον</note>. Nor is it "into that one," but "into this" <note>original: εἰς τήνδε</note>.
24 *there indeed*] "indeed" is redundant according to the Greek manuscripts. "A year": The Greeks have "one year" <note>original: ἐνιαυτὸν ἕνα</note>.
25 *What will be on the morrow*] <note>original: τὸ τῆς αὔριον</note>, that is, what the fortune of the next day might be.
26 *They appear for a little while*] It is strange why he wanted to speak so poetically here, saying *parens* instead of *apparens* <note>Erasmus is criticizing the Vulgate for using a shortened, more "poetic" Latin form of "appearing."</note>, when the Greek is <note>original: φαινομένη</note>.
27 *And thereafter it shall be exterminated*] <note>original: ἀφανιζομένη</note>, that is, vanishing, or no longer appearing, if he had wanted to render the affinity of the words.
28 *Instead of that you say*] <note>original: Ἀντὶ τοῦ λέγειν ὑμᾶς</note>, "In place of," or "In the place of that which you ought to have said." It could be rendered: "Since this is what you should rather say."
29 *If the Lord wills*] The Greek has it thus: <note>original: Ἐὰν ὁ Κύριος θελήσῃ, καὶ ζήσωμεν, καὶ ποιήσωμεν τοῦτο ἢ ἐκεῖνο</note>, that is, "If the Lord wills, and we live, and we do this or that." But I suspect the Greek may be corrupted in this place, and should read <note>original: καὶ ζήσομεν, καὶ ποιήσομεν</note>, that is, "if we shall live, and we shall do": so that you understand that they will neither live nor do anything unless the Lord wills it. Unless we prefer to take it as a command, "let us live and let us do."

<margin>F</margin>
1 *Have been eaten by moths*] <note>original: σητόβρωτα γέγονεν</note>, that is, they have become moth-eaten, or subject to moths, or such that they are gnawed by moths.
2 *And it shall eat*] It can be in the present tense <note>original: φάγεται</note>, "it devours" or "it eats," although the Greek word is ambiguous as to either tense.
3 *You have hoarded wrath for yourselves*] <note>original: Ἐθησαυρίσατε ἐν ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις</note>, that is, you have hoarded in the last days. "Wrath for yourselves" is not added. The very ancient Donatian codex agreed with the Greek.
4 *Which has been defrauded by you*] <note>original: ὁ ἀπεστερημένος</note>, that is, which by fraud has not been paid back. It refers to the wages owed to the laborers.
5 *And their cry*] <note>original: καὶ αἱ βοαὶ τῶν θερισάντων</note>, that is, and the cries of those who have harvested.
6 *You have feasted*] <note>original: Ἐτρυφήσατε</note>, that is, you have lived in luxury.
7 *And in luxuries you have nourished your hearts*] The Greek says:

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> the law: but if you judge the law, you are not an observer of the law, but a judge. 18 There is one legislator, who can save and destroy. 21 Who are you, 21 who judges another? 22 Come now, you who say: 23 Today and tomorrow let us go into this city, 24 and let us spend one year there, and let us trade, and make a profit; you who do not know 25 what the next day will bring. For what is your life? For it is a vapor, which 26 for a small time appears, 27 and then vanishes. 28 Instead of what you ought to say: 29 If the Lord wills, and if we live, let us do <margin>B</margin> this or that. But now you exult in your arrogance. All such exultation is evil. Therefore, he who knows how to do right, and does not do it, is held by sin. Come now, rich men, weep, howling over your miseries which shall come upon you. Your riches have rotted, your clothes have become subject to moths. Your gold and silver have been corrupted by rust, and their rust will be a testimony to you, and will eat your flesh like fire. 3 You have gathered treasure in the last days. Behold, the wages of the workmen who harvested your fields, 4 which by fraud was not paid by you, cries out; and the cries of those who harvested have entered into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth. 6 You have lived in delights upon the earth, 7 and in wantonness you have nourished <margin>C</margin> your hearts, 8 as in a day of slaughter. 9 You condemn and have killed the just man, and 10 he does not resist you. Therefore, be patient, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, patiently waiting for it, 11 until he receives the early and late rain. Therefore, be patient yourselves, and strengthen your hearts, because the coming of the Lord approaches. Do not groan one against another, brothers, so that you are not condemned. Behold, the judge stands before the door. Take as an example, my brothers, 14 of affliction and patience, the Prophets, who spoke in the name of the Lord. Behold, 15 we count them blessed who endure. 16 You have heard of the tolerance of Job, and you have seen the end of the Lord, 17 that the Lord is very <margin>D</margin> merciful and compassionate. But before all things, my brothers, do not swear, neither by heaven, nor by the earth, nor by any other oath whatever: let your speech be 18 "yes, yes," and "no, no": so that...

---

lived in luxury on the earth, and you have been wanton, and you have nourished your hearts.
8 *In the day of slaughter*] <note>original: ὡς ἐν ἡμέρᾳ σφαγῆς</note>, that is, as in a day of butchering, which is to say, a feast day, on which victims are usually butchered for a banquet.
9 *You have led away*] <note>original: Κατεδικάσατε</note>, that is, you have condemned. Perhaps the translator had rendered it "you have led away" instead of "you have condemned." A scribe, either inattentive or poorly educated, turned it into "you have led away" <note>The Latin words "adduxistis" (led away) and "condemnastis" (condemned) are being compared</note>. Certainly "adduxistis" was written in the very old Donatian codex.
10 *He does not resist*] <note>original: ἀντιτάσσεται</note>, that is, "he resists," in the present tense. And so Bede reads it.
11 *until he receives the early and late*] The Greeks read, <note>original: ὑετὸν πρώϊμον καὶ ὄψιμον</note>, that is, the morning and evening rain, or if you prefer, the early and late rain. For Augustine, in his book on the idioms of the Old Testament, thinks the word *serotinum* <note>late/evening</note> is not very good Latin, citing this place from Deuteronomy: "And he will give rain to your land in its time, early and late." Furthermore, these words signify the parts of the year when the farmer desires some rain at the very sowing, and again in summer, so that the crops may grow and be nourished. And so James seems to have borrowed this phrase from that very place.
12 *Be you*] "And you," the Greek reads.
13 *The coming of the Lord will approach*] <note>original: ἤγγικε</note>, that is, "has approached," in the past tense, or certainly in the present: "it is at hand."
14 *Evil outcome*] <note>original: τῆς κακοπαθείας</note>, that is, "of affliction." Furthermore, these words, "evil outcome" and "long-suffering," seem to have been added from a different interpretation. For they were not contained in two very old copies of the Donatian codex. For whereas someone had translated *kakopatheias* and *makrothymias* as "evil outcome" and "long-suffering," another seems to have translated it as "labor and patience"; a clever scribe joined both together.
15 *We beatify*] <note>original: μακαρίζομεν</note>, that is, we judge blessed, or we call blessed. And it is not "those who have endured," but "those who are enduring" <note>original: τοὺς ὑπομένοντας</note>.
16 *Sufferance*] <note>original: τὴν ὑπομονὴν</note>, that is, tolerance or patience. "You have seen the end of the Lord." He calls it the "end" because through afflictions he emerged into the highest glory.
17 *Because the Lord is merciful*] <note>original: πολυεύσπλαγχνός</note>, that is, very merciful.
18 *Yes yes, no no*] <note>original: τὸ ναὶ, ναὶ, καὶ τὸ οὒ, οὐ</note>, that is, that which is "yes, yes," and that which is "no, no." And it is not "your speech," but "let your yes be yes, and your no be no": that is, what you affirm, affirm truly, and what you deny, deny truly, as we advised in the Gospels.

# JAMES. CHAPTER V.

<margin>13</margin> Is any among you suffering? Let him pray. <margin>14</margin> Is any cheerful? Let him sing psalms. Is any among you sick? Let him call for the elders <note>The Greek term is *presbyteros*, which refers to leaders or elders of the community.</note> of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil <margin>15</margin> in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the sick man, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven. <margin>16</margin> Confess your faults to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be healed. The <margin>17</margin> effective prayer of a righteous man is very powerful. Elijah was a man with a nature just like ours, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain; and it did not rain on the earth for three years <margin>18</margin> and six months. And he prayed again, and the heaven gave rain, and the earth brought forth its fruit. <margin>19</margin> Brothers, if any among you wanders from the truth, and someone turns him back, <margin>20</margin> let him know that he who turns a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death, and will cover a multitude of sins.

-> THE EPISTLE OF JAMES <-

-> T H E   E N D . <-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...lest you fall into hypocrisy. <margin>13</margin> Is anyone among you afflicted? Let him pray. Is anyone of a composed mind? Let him sing. <margin>14</margin> Is anyone weak among you? Let him summon the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. <margin>15</margin> And the petition of faith will restore the one who is laboring, and the Lord will lift him up: and if he be in sins, they shall be forgiven him. <margin>16</margin> Confess <margin>B</margin> your faults to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healthy. For the effective prayer of the righteous man avails much. <margin>17</margin> Elijah was a man subject to the same passions as we are, and he prayed with a prayer that it might not rain: and it did not rain upon the earth for three years and six months. <margin>18</margin> And again he prayed, and heaven gave rain, and the earth produced its fruit. <margin>19</margin> Brothers, if anyone among you has wandered from the truth, and someone has converted him, <margin>20</margin> let him know, that he who has caused a sinner to be converted from the error of his way, will save a soul from death, and will cover a multitude of sins.

-> THE EPISTLE OF JAMES <-

-> T H E   E N D . <-

---

<margin>19 He is sad however]</margin> <note>original: "Κακοπαθεῖ"</note> That is, *he is afflicted*.
<margin>20 Pray with a calm mind and sing]</margin> I do not know if some scribe has corrupted this passage, for the Greek reads far differently: <note>original: "Κακοπαθεῖ τίς ἐν ὑμῖν; προσευχέσθω· εὐθυμεῖ τίς; ψαλλέτω"</note>, that is, *Is anyone among you afflicted? Let him pray: is anyone of a calm mind? Let him sing*. Surely the point is that in times of trouble we should seek help from God, and in prosperous times we should give thanks to God. For that is what he calls "singing" <note>original: "psallere"</note>. However, Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, an 8th-century English monk and scholar.</note> both reads and interprets this differently.
<margin>21 Anointing him with oil]</margin> This was left over from the Gospel precept, by which Christ commanded his followers that into whichever houses they entered, they should heal the sick, anointing them with oil. For it is consistent that what we read was done by the Apostles was done by the command of the Lord, even if we do not read that they were specifically ordered to do it. This is now done at the final crisis of life <note>Erasmus is referring to the sacrament of Extreme Unction, or Anointing of the Sick.</note>.
<margin>22 He will save the infirm]</margin> <note>original: "τὸν κάμνοντα"</note>, that is, *the one laboring*. For he is referring to the sick person.
<margin>23 Your sins]</margin> The word "your" <note>original: "vestra"</note> is not found among the Greeks, though it is understood. And the word is more "errors" than "sins," <note>original: "παραπτώματα"</note>, as if you were to say "lapses." For he is thinking of the daily offenses of Christians among themselves, whom he wishes to be continually reconciled. Otherwise, if he had meant the confession which we call a part of the sacrament of penance, he would not have added "to one another," <note>original: "ἀλλήλοις"</note>, but "to the priests." The interpretation of Bede does not disagree with this view. And he cites it openly in the commentaries he wrote on the fifth chapter of the Epistle of John.
<margin>24 That you may be saved]</margin> <note>original: "ὅπως ἰαθῆτε"</note>, that is, *that you may be healed*.
<margin>25 Constant [prayer] of the righteous]</margin> <note>original: "ἐνεργουμένη"</note>, that is, *working*, or *while it acts*, so that you understand it to be effective, poured out from the soul. Perhaps the translator, by rendering it as "constant," meant intent and persistent, so that it attains what it seeks.
<margin>26 Like unto us]</margin> <note>original: "ὁμοιοπαθής"</note>, that is, *similarly affected*, or *subject to similar passions*.
<margin>27 The earth gave fruit]</margin> <note>original: "ἐβλάστησε"</note>, that is, *it germinated* or *sprouted*.

<column-break/>

<margin>C</margin> <margin>28 If any of you]</margin> <note>original: "ἐν ὑμῖν"</note>, that is, *in you*, or *among you*.
<margin>29 Will save his soul]</margin> The Greeks do not add "his" <note>original: "ejus"</note>, only "him."
<margin>30 And will cover]</margin> <note>original: "καὶ καλύψει"</note>, that is, *and will cover*. Bede indicates that in the Latin codices there is a double reading, "will save his soul" and "will save its own soul," adding that the Greek speech is ambiguous. That would be true if a pronoun were added. For if it were written <note>original: "αὐτοῦ"</note> with a smooth breathing, it would mean "his," but if <note>original: "αὑτοῦ"</note> with a rough breathing, it would mean "his own." As it stands, the pronoun is not added among the Greeks, at least in those codices I have happened to see.
<margin>D</margin> Regarding this Epistle, although it is full of healthy precepts, there was doubt in the past as to who its author was, as I began to say at the beginning. For it does not seem to reflect that Apostolic majesty and gravity in every respect. Nor are there as many Hebraisms <note>Linguistic structures or idioms typical of the Hebrew language.</note> as would be expected from James, who was the Bishop of Jerusalem. Saint Jerome, in his *Catalog of Illustrious Writers*, indicates on the authority of Hegesippus that there were many disciples of this name. And the author himself, in the title of the Epistle, does not call himself an Apostle—although the title "Apostle" has been added in our versions—but the Greek copies protest this with great consensus. Furthermore, Jerome, in the book I just cited, writes in these very words: "He wrote only one Epistle, which is among the seven canonical ones, and which is asserted by some to have been published by another under his name, although it has gradually gained authority as time progressed." Thus far Jerome. Saint Jerome indicates clearly enough what he thought about the author of this Epistle. However, I will not fight with anyone over this matter. I approve of the Epistle and embrace it. It is a wonder that no one asserts these matters more hatefully and constantly than those who cannot even explain in which language it was written, Hebrew or Greek, or by which translator it was made into Latin. Jerome, so great a man, was doubtful, and prudently indicates what he felt. We, the less we know, the more boldly we affirm.
