<meta>This page follows the conclusion of the Epistle of James and introduces the First Epistle of Peter. It includes a traditional Greek summary (Hypothesis) followed by a formal introduction (Argumentum) by Erasmus of Rotterdam.</meta>

# T H E M E
-> of the first Epistle of the holy Apostle <-
# P E T E R

The blessed Peter sends this letter to the Jews who are in the Diaspora <note>original: "διασπορᾷ" (diaspora) – the dispersion of Jews outside the ancestral land of Israel</note> and have become Christians. He writes the Epistle as a teaching, strengthening them, because they came to faith from among the Jews. First, he explains and demonstrates that faith in Christ was proclaimed by the Prophets, and through them the redemption through His blood was revealed. He shows that all things were preached to them and to the nations—things which even angels desire to look into.

Then, having advised them to conduct themselves in a manner worthy of the one who called them, he exhorts them to honor even kings. He proclaims harmony to both wives and husbands. After offering a few exhortations regarding morals, he signifies that the preaching of salvation and resurrection was also performed by the Lord in Hades <note>This refers to the "Harrowing of Hell," a traditional belief that Christ preached to the souls of the dead between his crucifixion and resurrection</note>; this was so that those who died before might also rise, being judged indeed in the body, but remaining alive through the grace of the resurrection. He concludes by stating that the end of all things is near, and everyone ought to be ready, as those who must give an account to the judge. And thus he finishes the Epistle.

---

# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE
# OF PETER
-> *Introduction by* <-
# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

Peter, just as James did, writes to the Jews living scattered throughout the regions of the Pagans <note>original: "Gentium" – the non-Jewish nations</note>. This Epistle is truly worthy of the prince of the Apostles: it is full of authority and Apostolic majesty, spare in its words but packed with profound meaning. He encourages the readers to tolerate the evils they were suffering due to the hatred of the Gospel, holding out the hope of future rewards. To this he adds a warning: since they have been called freely to such great dignity according to the oracles of the prophets, they should lead a life worthy of their profession. For Christianity consists not in a title or in baptism alone, but in the innocence of one's character. Otherwise, their affliction by evils will not bring glory to Christ if it appears they are merely paying the penalty for their own wrongdoings.

Furthermore, he warns that they should not use Christianity as an excuse to refuse obedience to Magistrates, even if they are Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicis" – those of the traditional Greco-Roman religions</note>, lest the rulers be provoked and neither turn to Christ nor cease their fierce cruelty. Likewise, he instructs that servants should not deny their duty to their masters, even if they are Pagans. It is the mark of Christian goodness to endure all things. In the same way, Christian women should not despise their husbands, even if they are Pagans, but should strive to win them over to better things through their own conduct. He warns husbands to yield to their wives and to sometimes abstain from sexual union <note>original: "coïtu"</note> so that they may have more time for prayer.

Then, using the example of Christ, he calls for the tolerance of evils, urging them not to try to repay injury with injury, but to strive to overcome those who treat them poorly with gentleness and good deeds. He handles these matters in the first three chapters and the beginning of the fourth. After this, he encourages a newness of life, discouraging the vices of the Pagans. He invites them to sobriety, to vigilance, to constant prayers, and especially to mutual love, to hospitality, to mutual duties, and again to patience during the persecutions brought on for the name of Christ.

Next, he instructs the Bishops <note>original: "Episcopos" – literally "overseers"</note> and the people subject to them. at the conclusion, he testifies that he himself wrote another letter to the same people through Silvanus, which has since been lost <note>Erasmus likely refers to the mention of Silvanus in 1 Peter 5:12, though scholars today debate if he meant a literal lost letter or the relationship between 1 and 2 Peter</note>. It appears this was written from Babylon, for he bids them greetings in the name of the Church there—unless one does not approve of the common fiction that "Babylon" refers to Rome <note>Erasmus expresses his characteristic scholarly skepticism regarding the traditional Roman Catholic view that "Babylon" was a coded reference to the city of Rome</note>.

<summary>This page provides two introductory summaries of the First Epistle of Peter: a traditional Greek synopsis and a detailed scholarly introduction by Erasmus, focusing on Peter's exhortations to endurance, social order, and moral purity.</summary>
<keywords>Apostle Peter, Erasmus, Diaspora, Babylon, Persecution, Christian Conduct, Silvanus, New Testament Introduction</keywords>

# THE FIRST EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PETER.

<margin>A</margin> <margin>1</margin> <image-desc>Decorative initial P with floral motifs</image-desc> PETER, an Apostle of Jesus Christ, to the chosen strangers of the dispersion <note>original: "διασπορᾶς" (diasporas) — the scattering of Jews throughout the Roman world</note> in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, <margin>2</margin> according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus <margin>3</margin> Christ: may grace and peace be multiplied to you. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has fathered us again into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus <margin>4</margin> Christ from the dead, into an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that does not fade away, preserved in <margin>5</margin> heaven for you, who are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation, which is ready to <margin>6</margin> be revealed in the last time; in which you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while, if it is necessary, you are grieved <margin>7</margin> in various trials, so that the testing of your faith, much more precious than gold which perishes, though it is tested by fire, might be found unto praise and glory and honor at the revelation <margin>8</margin> of Jesus Christ; whom, having not seen, you love; in whom, though now you do not see him, yet believing, you rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory, <margin>9</margin> receiving the end of your faith, even the salvation <margin>10</margin> of souls. Concerning which salvation the Prophets have inquired and searched diligently, who prophesied of the grace that should come <margin>11</margin> to you, searching into what time or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the <margin>12</margin> glories that should follow; to whom it was revealed, that not for themselves, but for you...

<column-break/>

<margin>1</margin> <image-desc>Decorative initial P with floral motifs</image-desc> PETER, an Apostle of Jesus Christ, <gloss>to the guests living here and there</gloss> in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, chosen <margin>2</margin> according to the pre-definition of God the Father, through the sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ: may grace and peace be multiplied to you. Praise is due to <margin>3</margin> God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his abundant mercy has fathered us again into a living hope, by the fact that Jesus Christ rose from the dead, <margin>4</margin> into an immortal inheritance, and one that is unstained and unfading, preserved in the heavens <margin>5</margin> toward you, who are guarded by the strength of God through faith for salvation, which is prepared in this way, to be made open in the final time: <margin>6</margin> In which you exult, <gloss>now for a short time afflicted</gloss> in various trials, if there is need, so that the testing of your faith, <margin>7</margin> much more precious than gold which perishes, and yet is proved by fire, may be found unto praise and glory and honor, at the time when Jesus Christ shall be revealed: Whom, though you have not <margin>8</margin> seen, you love: <gloss>in whom at present, though you do not see him, yet believing, you exult with joy inexpressible and glorified,</gloss> bringing back the goal of your faith, <margin>9</margin> the salvation of souls: <margin>B</margin> Concerning which salvation the <margin>10</margin> Prophets inquired and searched, who prophesied about the grace to come unto you, searching for what or what <margin>11</margin> kind of moment of time the Spirit of Christ who was in them signified: who, before they happened, testified to the afflictions coming upon Christ, and the glories that would follow: <margin>C</margin> To whom it was <margin>12</margin> revealed...

---

<margin>D</margin> **1** *To the guests of the dispersion in Pontus, etc.*] In Greek, the word is not "proselytes" <note>original: "προσήλυτοις"</note>, which is the term usually used for those who converted from Paganism to the Mosaic Law, but "strangers" <note>original: "παρεπιδήμοις" (parepidēmois) — literally 'sojourners' or temporary residents</note>. Therefore, Nicholas of Lyra <note>A 14th-century Franciscan exegete</note> says nothing of value when he thinks this was written specifically to the prophets. He seems to have followed Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, 7th-century English monk</note>, who suggests in his commentaries that "Latin guests" refers to those the Greeks call "proselytes," implying the Epistle was for them because Peter was the Apostle to the circumcised <note>i.e., the Jews</note>.

**2** *Cappadocia, Asia*] Others should consider whether "Pontus" is a specific region while "Asia" is a general category, unless perhaps he means the Ephesians, which is specifically called "Asia Minor." For it does not seem it can be understood as "Greater Asia," since he immediately adds Bithynia, which is part of Asia Minor.

**3** *According to foreknowledge*] <note>original Greek: "Κατὰ πρόγνωσιν" (Kata prognōsin)</note>, meaning "According to predestination" or "pre-definition." Even Lyra admits that in this passage "foreknowledge" is taken for "predestination." Nor does Thomas Aquinas deny that predestination is sometimes used for foreknowledge. Truly, I have spoken about this matter at some length in my Annotations on Paul. Indeed, even among the Latins, "decrees" are called "known things" <note>original: "scita"</note>, and judges are called "those who know" <note>original: "cognitores"</note>. Furthermore, this phrase, "according to foreknowledge," seems to refer to the word that precedes it, *chosen*, so that we understand they were chosen not randomly or by chance, but by the determined decree and counsel of God. Otherwise, I do not see what it pertains to. Bede, an author not to be despised, agrees with me.

<margin>E</margin> **4** *In sanctification*] <note>original Greek: "Ἐν ἁγιασμῷ Πνεύματος"</note>, that is, in sanctification, which means "through the sanctification of the Spirit," according to the characteristic of Hebrew speech. For in what follows, *unto obedience*, the Greeks use a different preposition, <note>original Greek: "εἰς ὑπακοὴν" (eis hypakoēn)</note>. Whether this should be understood as they being chosen *for* obedience, or chosen *through* obedience, I leave for the reader to discuss. To me, the first sense is more appealing. For he means that they owe this very thing to God: that they were chosen for the grace of faith (which he calls "obedience" here), so that through this they might be cleansed from sins by the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus. Furthermore, he opposed the "sanctification of the Spirit" to the "works of the Mosaic Law," from which trust he wishes to lead them away.

**5** *God and Father*] This can be read together as one title, or separately, as I have indicated elsewhere.

**6** *Through resurrection*] <note>original Greek: "δι' ἀναστάσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐκ νεκρῶν"</note>. Here he seems to use "resurrection" almost ambiguously, both neutrally and actively; regarding Christ, neutrally <note>Christ being raised</note>, and regarding us, actively <note>Christ raising us</note>. Thomas Aquinas noted this in the Epistle to the Romans.

**7** *Into an inheritance*] This refers back to the word "fathered again" <note>or "re-begotten"</note>. He fathered us again by a heavenly birth into a heavenly inheritance. For the Jews were expecting a very different kingdom through their Messiah.

**8** *In you*] <note>original Greek: "εἰς ὑμας"</note>, that is, "into you," or "toward you": so that it refers to the inheritance being "preserved." In the phrase "In power," "by power" was sufficient.

**9** *In which you exult*] It can also be read as "Exult!" in the imperative mood <note>original Greek: "ἀγαλλιᾶσθε"</note>, as it is below. If the indicative mood <note>statement of fact</note> is preferred, he seems to be using the present tense for the future.

<column-break/>

**10** *A little now, if it is necessary*] <note>original Greek: "ὀλίγον ἄρτι, εἰ δέον ἐστὶ"</note>. For the sake of clarity, it was better translated as "now for a short time afflicted, if it be necessary."

**11** *Much more precious let it be than gold*] The word "let it be" is redundant. Furthermore, the Greek reading goes like this: <note>original Greek: "πολυτιμιώτερον χρυσίου τοῦ ἀπολλυμένου, διὰ πυρὸς δὲ δοκιμαζομένου"</note>, that is, "much more precious than gold, which is lost (or perishes), and yet is tested by fire," or "than lost and ruinous gold." You should understand that a cheap and perishable thing is tested by fire; how much more appropriate is it for our faith to be explored, so that it might be found sincere.

**12** *In the revelation of Jesus Christ*] He could have avoided ambiguity if he had translated it as "when Jesus Christ shall be revealed." For what is elsewhere called "in glory" and "the presence," he here called "revelation" <note>original Greek: "ἀποκάλυψις" (apokalypsis)</note>. Bede reads this somewhat differently.

**13** *In whom now also, etc.*] The Greek is slightly different: <note>original Greek: "εἰς ὃν ἄρτι μὴ ὁρῶντες, πιστεύοντες δὲ"</note>, that is, "in whom now not seeing, yet believing," or, "in whom now since you do not see, and yet you believe."

**14** *You shall exult*] <note>original Greek: "ἀγαλλιᾶσθε"</note>, that is, "you exult," a verb in the present tense, as agreed by the second Donatian manuscript; even though it can be "Exult!" as a command, since the Greek word is ambiguous. Certainly, Augustine cites it this way in Book 11 to the Catechumens, chapter 6: "Believing in him whom you do not see, rejoice with unutterable joy."

<margin>F</margin> **15** *Who concerning the future grace in you*] The Translator added "future" on his own, for the Greek has: <note>original Greek: "οἱ περὶ τῆς εἰς ὑμᾶς χάριτος προφητεύσαντες"</note>. I would have preferred to express it this way: "who prophesied of the grace to come unto you." Nor is it "time," which the Greeks call *chronos* <note>general time</note>, but *kairos* <note>a specific, appointed moment</note>, which we translate as "moment" <note>original: "articulum"</note>. For it is more specific than "time," as has been indicated elsewhere. It is likely that Peter is referring to the passage in Daniel, chapter 9, where through the "mystical weeks" he indicates the time at which Christ was to be killed.

**16** *The Spirit in them signified*] <note>original Greek: "τὸ ἐν αὐτοῖς Πνεῦμα"</note>, that is, "the Spirit who was in them," so that we understand the prophetic Spirit, which he calls the same as the Spirit "of Christ."

**17** *Foretelling*] <note>original Greek: "προμαρτυρόμενον"</note>, that is, "testifying beforehand." Furthermore, where the text here translates *passiones* as "passions," I would prefer "afflictions."

**18** *And the later glories*] <note>original Greek: "καὶ τὰς μετὰ ταῦτα δόξας"</note>, that is, "and the glories that were to follow those things." For he means the glory which he attained after the shame of the cross. Even if Jerome translates "glories" as "decrees" in some places, as I will soon show—unless perhaps "fitting things" <note>original: "decora"</note> was written instead of "decrees" <note>original: "decreta"</note>. For that book was printed from a copy not sufficiently corrected. Surely it is established that *doxas* <note>original Greek: "δόξας"</note> signifies to the Greeks both "glory" and "opinion." Therefore, it is probable that in Jerome's case, "opinions" became "decrees."

**19** *To whom it was revealed*] <note>original Greek: "Οἷς ἀπεκαλύφθη"</note>. The Greek speech is ambiguous; for the sense can be taken as: "testifying the sufferings and glories of Christ to those to whom the Spirit revealed them," namely the Prophets. Or it can be: "the sufferings and glories through which Christ was revealed to the world, who before had been unknown." Nor should the Greek article "the" <note>original Greek: "τὰς"</note> bother anyone, since "sufferings" preceded it. Although the former sense is simpler in my judgment: that the article refers to the Christians, who...

<meta>This page continues the scholarly examination of the First Epistle of Peter, moving from the introduction into the specific verses of Chapter 1 (verses 12–25) and the beginning of Chapter 2. # THE EPISTLE OF PETER, CHAPTER II.

<column-break/>

...but they were ministering those very things to us, which have now been announced to you through those who preached the gospel to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven—things into which <margin>13</margin> angels long to look. Therefore, girding up the loins of your mind and being sober, hope perfectly in the grace that is brought to you at the <margin>14</margin> revelation of Jesus Christ. As children of obedience, do not be conformed to the former lusts you had in <margin>15</margin> your ignorance, but according to the Holy One who called you, be holy yourselves in <margin>16</margin> all your conduct; because it is written, "Be holy, for I am holy." <margin>17</margin> And if you call upon the Father, who judges without respect of persons according to each one's work, conduct yourselves in fear during the time of <margin>18</margin> your stay here. Knowing that you were not redeemed with corruptible things like silver or gold from your futile conduct handed down <margin>19</margin> from your fathers, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb <margin>20</margin> without blemish and without spot. He was indeed foreknown before the foundation of the world, but was manifested in <margin>21</margin> these last times for your sake, you who through him believe in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that <margin>22</margin> your faith and hope might be in God. Having purified your souls in obedience to the truth through the Spirit for sincere brotherly love, love one another fervently from a <margin>23</margin> pure heart, having been born again, not of corruptible seed but of incorruptible, through the <margin>24</margin> word of the living God which remains forever. For "all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withers, <margin>25</margin> and its flower falls away; but the word of the Lord remains forever." And this is the word <margin>II. 1</margin> that was preached as good news to you. Therefore, laying aside all malice, and all deceit, and hypocrisy, and envy, and all slander, <margin>2</margin> like newborn infants, long for the pure, rational milk...
<meta>catchword: epi- (longing)</meta>

---

<margin>D</margin> **20. To you however** <note>original: "Vobis autem"</note> This refers to those who saw what the Spirit had foretold concerning Christ. For he feels that the glory of Christ became known to the world through these deep affections. A third meaning can also be taken here: it was revealed to the Prophets that they were preparing these things they foretold not for themselves, but for you, since they knew these events would not happen in their own times. A fourth meaning can even be accepted: the Prophets foretold both the death of Christ and the enlightenment gained through that death; both are true, as is known to those to whom these things were shown.

But "to you" was also in the Latin versions, and it would be clearer, or rather not suspicious, to say <term>indeed to you</term>, or <term>whoever suggests</term>, or <term>but also</term>. From this it is certainly clear that it matters a great deal which conjunction you place in which spot. Jerome, translating Didymus’s second book *On the Holy Spirit*, rendered this entire passage of Peter in this way: *Searching and inquiring into what, or what manner of time, the Spirit of Christ within them was signifying, testifying to the sufferings in Christ. And those decrees that were to follow afterward were revealed to those to whom it was shown that they were ministering not for themselves, but for us, those things which have now been announced to you through the Holy Spirit.*

**21. Who preached the gospel to you** <note>original: "Qui evangelicaverunt vobis"</note> The Greek says "You" [as an object] rather than "to you," although this does not change the sense at all.

**22. Holy Spirit** <note>original: "Spiritu sancto"</note> The word <term>in</term> is missing in the Latin, but the Greek says <note>original: "ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ"</note>, that is, "in the Holy Spirit," which means "through the Holy Spirit" according to the Hebrew idiom.

**23. Into which they desire** <note>original: "In quem desiderant"</note> The Greek is <note>original: "εἰς ἃ"</note>, which means "into which things"—namely, those things foretold by the Prophets and then preached by the Apostles. It is an easy corruption to change <note>original: "εἰς ἃ"</note> (into which things) into <note>original: "εἰς ὅν"</note> (into whom). He is not referring to the Spirit of the Prophets (into whom it would be no wonder if angels wished to look), but rather the majesty of the Gospel, which even angels venerate. Bede interprets this as referring to the glorified Christ, though he indicates shortly after that it can be taken as the Spirit sent to earth. However, Irenaeus, in *Against Heresies* Book 4, Chapter 67, feels it refers to the promises of the Prophets which Christ made manifest upon his arrival. Certainly, we find it written this way in a fragment of Origen which we have translated into Latin.

**24. Hope perfectly** <note>original: "Perfacti sperate"</note> The Greek <note>original: "τελείως"</note> (perfectly) is an adverb, indicating a hope that perseveres right to the end. The older Donatianus codex had it this way. It is not "unto revelation," as some read, but "in revelation" <note>original: "ἐν ἀποκαλύψει"</note>, meaning through the revelation. He is referring to the mystery of the Gospel now made public, through which Christ became known, or to the second coming of Christ.

**25. As children** <note>original: "Quasi filii"</note> The Greek is <note>original: "Ὡς τέκνα"</note>, which means "like children" or "as children." We usually use "as if" <note>original: "quasi"</note> for things that appear to be what they are not. Furthermore, he said "children of obedience" according to the Hebrew property of speech, meaning "obedient children."

**26. Not conformed** <note>original: "Non configurati"</note> The Greek <note>original: "μὴ συσχηματιζόμενοι ταῖς πρότερον ἐπιθυμίαις"</note> means "not adapting yourselves to your former desires." That is the meaning of <note>original: "συσχηματίζεσθαι"</note>. It is not "desires of ignorance," but "the desires [that were] formerly in your ignorance." We have expressed this more clearly than a word-for-word translation: <term>so that you do not adapt yourselves to those former desires by which you were driven while you were still ignorant of Christ.</term>

<column-break/>

<page-num>1044</page-num>
<margin>A</margin> ...it was revealed that they were ministering these things not for themselves, but rather for us—those things which have now been announced to you by those who preached the Gospel to you, through the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, into which things angels desire to look. Therefore, having girded the loins of your mind, being perfectly sober, hope in the grace that is offered to you as Jesus Christ is revealed to you. <margin>14</margin> As obedient children, do not adapt yourselves to the former desires by which you were driven while you were still <margin>15</margin> ignorant of Christ; but just as he who called you is holy, so you also should become holy in all your conduct. Because <margin>16</margin> it is written: "Be holy, for I am holy." <margin>17</margin> And if you invoke the Father, who judges according to each man's work without respect of persons, see that you spend the time of your pilgrimage living in fear. <margin>18</margin> For you know that you were redeemed from your vain conduct, which you received from the tradition of your fathers, not with perishable things like silver and gold, <margin>19</margin> but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb spotless and undefiled. <margin>20</margin> He was indeed foreordained before the world was founded, but was made manifest in the final times for your sake. <margin>21</margin> Through him you believe in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that you might have faith and hope toward God. <margin>22</margin> Since you have purified your souls by obeying the truth through the Spirit, with brotherly love free from all pretense, love one another intensely from a pure heart. <margin>23</margin> You have been born again, not from mortal seed but from immortal, through the word of the living God which remains forever. For "all flesh becomes as grass, <margin>24</margin> and all the glory of man is like the flower of the grass. The grass has withered, and the flower has fallen; but the word <margin>25</margin> of the Lord remains forever." Now this is the word that was brought to you through the Gospel. <margin>II. 1</margin> Therefore, having laid aside all malice, and all deceit, and pretenses, and envies, and all slanders, like newborn infants, [desire] that milk which is not of the body, but of the soul...
<meta>catchword: ani- (soul/rational)</meta>

---

**27. But according to him who called you holy** <note>original: "Sed secundum eum qui vocavit vos sanctum"</note> The Greek says <note>original: "Ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸν καλέσαντα ὑμᾶς ἅγιον, καὶ αὐτοὶ ἅγιοι γενήθητε"</note>, which means "but just as he who called you is holy, so you also should be made holy."

**28. That you might be holy** <note>original: "Sancti fitis"</note> The Greek <note>original: "γενήθητε"</note> means "be made" or "become." It is not <note>original: "γίνεσθε"</note>, which could be ambiguous.

**29. And if you call the Father** <note>original: "Et si Patrem vocatis"</note> The Greek <note>original: "ἐπικαλεῖσθε"</note> means you invoke, implore, or name, as the Greek word has multiple senses. Also, the phrase "without respect of persons" is written much more elegantly in Greek as <note>original: "ἀπροσωπολήπτως"</note>, a compound word meaning "without selecting or respecting a persona." This note seems to be missing in the commentaries of Bede and the *Glossa Ordinaria*, nor does Lyra mention it.

**30. Paternal tradition** <note>original: "Paterna traditione"</note> There is a single word for this in Greek: <note>original: "πατροπαραδότου"</note>. It is an epithet for "conduct," as if to say "handed down from the fathers." Saint Jerome records it this way in his commentaries on Isaiah, as does Augustine on Psalm 146.

**31. As of a lamb** <note>original: "Quasi agni"</note> The Greek <note>original: "ὡς ἀμνοῦ"</note> means "just like a lamb" or "as if a lamb."

**32. Foreknown indeed** <note>original: "Praecogniti quidem"</note> The Greek <note>original: "Προεγνωσμένου"</note> means foreknown or <margin>E</margin> pre-decreed. In this context, it clearly seems to be used for what they call "predestination," and Lyra interprets it as "foreordination."

**33. You are faithful in God** <note>original: "Fideles estis in Deo"</note> The Greek <note>original: "τοὺς πιστεύοντας εἰς Θεὸν"</note> means "you who have believed in God." However, the [Latin] translator shrank from using the past tense, lest those who once believed might seem to have now stopped believing.

**34. In the obedience of charity** <note>original: "In obedientia charitatis"</note> The Greek is <note>original: "ἐν τῇ ὑπακοῇ τῆς ἀληθείας"</note>, meaning "in the obedience of truth." Furthermore, the Greek codices add <note>original: "διὰ Πνεύματος"</note> here, meaning "through the Spirit," a phrase not found in the Latin copies.

**35. In brotherly love, simple, from the heart** <note>original: "In fraternatis amore simplici ex corde"</note> The Greek <note>original: "εἰς φιλαδελφίαν ἀνυπόκριτον, ἐκ καθαρᾶς καρδίας"</note> means "into a brotherly love that is not feigned, from a pure heart." He uses the word <note>original: "φιλαδελφίαν"</note> to describe the mutual love and benevolence among Christians. Moreover, the phrase "from a pure heart" should be linked to what follows: "love one another from a pure heart."

<margin>F</margin> **36. More earnestly** <note>original: "Astentius"</note> The Greek <note>original: "ἐκτενῶς"</note> means vehemently or powerfully, or if you wish for a more literal translation, "intensely."

**37. All its glory** <note>original: "Omnis gloria ejus"</note> The Greek says "of man" <note>original: "ἀνθρώπου"</note>, for he is explaining what he just said about "flesh."

**38. Which was preached among you** <note>original: "Quod evangelizatum est in vos"</note> The Greek <note>original: "τὸ εὐαγγελισθὲν εἰς ὑμᾶς"</note> means that which was brought to you through the Gospel, or what was preached among you.

<margin>I</margin> **Reasonable milk without deceit** <note>original: "Rationabile sine dolo lac"</note> The Greek <note>original: "τὸ λογικὸν, ἄδολον γάλα"</note> means "rational milk, expert of deceit." He calls the milk "logical" <note>original: "logicum"</note> to distinguish it from physical milk. Jerome, in his commentary on Isaiah chapter 55, cites this passage so that "milk" refers to "rational," not to "infants," even if he does not add "without deceit." However, in Isaiah chapter 60, he cites it this way: *Like newborn little ones, desire the rational milk that is without deceit, so that it is clear that "without deceit" must be joined to the "milk."* He says this again when explaining Zechariah chapter 10. Likewise, Augustine in his 20th Homily on the Epistle of Peter records it this way: *Therefore, having laid aside all malice, and all deceit, and flattery, and envy, and...*
<meta>catchword: sta- (slander)</meta>

<meta>This page continues the textual analysis of the First Epistle of Peter. Having concluded the first chapter on the previous page, the author—the scholar Erasmus—now focuses on Chapter 2, verses 3 through 14. He specifically examines the metaphors of "spiritual milk" and the "living stone," comparing the Greek source text with the Latin Vulgate and the interpretations of medieval theologians like Nicholas of Lyra and the Church Father Bede.</meta>

# THE SECOND CHAPTER OF PETER.

<margin>3</margin> ...long for it, so that by it you may grow. <margin>4</margin> If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is kind. Drawing near to him, a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God and <margin>5</margin> precious; you yourselves also, as living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God <margin>6</margin> through Jesus Christ. Therefore it is also contained in the scripture: "Behold, I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen, precious; and he who believes on <margin>7</margin> him shall not be put to shame." To you therefore who believe is the honor; but to those who are disobedient, "the stone which the builders rejected, this has become the <margin>8</margin> head of the corner," and "a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense." They stumble at the word, being disobedient, to which they were also <margin>9</margin> appointed. But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his <margin>10</margin> marvelous light; who once were not a people, but now are the people of God; who had not obtained mercy, but now have <margin>11</margin> obtained mercy. Beloved, I beseech you as aliens and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the <margin>12</margin> soul, having your conduct honorable among the Gentiles, so that in that which they speak against you as evildoers, they may, by seeing your good works, glorify God in the day of visitation. <margin>13</margin> Therefore be subject to every human creature for the <margin>14</margin> Lord’s sake, whether to the king, as supreme, or to governors, as sent by him for the punishment...

<column-break/>

**A** ...of the soul which knows no guile, crave it, so that by it you <gloss>2</gloss> may <margin>3</margin> grow. If indeed you have tasted, 3 that the Lord is kind, to whom drawing near, who is the living stone, <margin>4</margin> rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God and precious: you yourselves also as living stones <margin>5</margin> be built up, a spiritual house, 6 a holy priesthood 7 for the offering of spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God 8 through Jesus Christ. 9 Wherefore it also <margin>6</margin> contains in scripture, 10 Behold, I place in Zion a stone, 11 to be placed at the highest corner, chosen, precious: and he who believes in him shall not be put to shame. 12 To you therefore <margin>7</margin> he is precious, you who believe: but to those who do not **B** believe, the stone which the builders rejected, this has come to be the head of the corner: and 13 a stone over which one strikes, <margin>8</margin> and a rock at which they stumble, namely to those 14 who strike against the word, nor do they believe 15 in that for which they were also appointed. But you are a chosen race, a royal <margin>9</margin> priesthood, a holy nation, 16 a people who have come into gain, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light: 17 Who <margin>10</margin> once were not a people, now the people of God: who once had not obtained mercy, now have obtained mercy. Beloved, I beseech you as <margin>11</margin> strangers and pilgrims, abstain from carnal desires, which war against the soul, and 18 have your **C** conduct honest among the nations, <margin>12</margin> so that in this which they disparage you as evildoers, judging you by your good works, they may glorify God 19 in the day of visitation. 20 Therefore be subject to every hu- <margin>13</margin> man creature for the Lord's sake, whether to the king, as excelling, 21 Or to governors, as those who are <margin>14</margin> sent through him...

---

*1 <note>original: "lac concupiscite"</note> ...crave the rational and innocent milk, as newborn babes, so that in it you may grow into salvation.* Even Bede reads and interprets this just as the Greeks read it. The manuscript from the Library of the Monastery of the Antwerpish, which served me while writing this, will be witness. Another manuscript of Donatianus also supported this somewhat, in which it was written, *rational without guile.* Therefore, what more recent theologians bring to this place concerning "rational infants" contributes nothing to the Apostle's meaning. Desiring also to express the Greek article, we translated it in this way: *As newborn babes, crave that milk—not of the body, but of the soul—which knows no guile.* For the "infancy" of Christ is to be far from all craftiness and the desire to harm. The stages of age are the progress of virtues.

*2 Grow into salvation]* These two words, *into salvation*, I do not find in the Greek copies, nor do they particularly fit the proposed metaphor. For infants are already safe: but let them grow up by this milk into a perfect man in Christ.

*3 Since the Lord is sweet]* <note>original: "ὅτι χρηστὸς ὁ Κύριος"</note>, that is, that the Lord is kind. Elsewhere it is translated "good." It sounds humane, and not at all austere or hard.

*4 And honored]* These two words are redundant. Furthermore, <note>original: "ἔντιμον εστὶ"</note>, with no preposition intervening, means *precious*, or rather held in high price: which the Translator, I think, translated as *honorificatum* (honored).

*5 A spiritual house]* <note>original: "οἶκος πνευματικός"</note>, that is, *spiritual house*: so that it is a nominative case added by apposition. Lyra, offended by a manifest solecism, interprets *house* as "into houses." And Augustine reads *into a house*, both elsewhere and when explaining Psalm 86. The same in the booklet *On the Presence of God* to Dardanus reads, *be built as spiritual houses*. And indeed I do not know whether it was first written *spiritualibus* (by spiritual things), and then the scripture, corrupted by the half-learned, makes this conjecture more probable, because elsewhere, as if explaining, he reads "into a house" for "house." Bede indicates a double reading of this place: *spiritual houses* in the plural, *spiritual house* in the singular, and *into a spiritual house*, just as Augustine reads in some places.

*6 Into a priesthood]* <note>original: "ἱεράτευμα ἅγιον"</note>, that is, *holy priesthood*: it is an appositive nominative, just like *house*: for he calls the faithful themselves the *priesthood*. However, he calls the function and administration of sacred things in the spiritual house a *priesthood*, that is, in the temple of the Holy Spirit, which we ourselves are.

*7 Offering]* <note>original: "ἀνενέγκαι"</note>, that is, *to offer*.

*8 Through Jesus Christ]* This can refer to that which is closest, *acceptable*, or to all the preceding things.

*9 Because the Scripture contains]* <note>original: "Διὸ καὶ περιέχει ἐν τῇ γραφῇ"</note>, that is, *Wherefore also it contains in the Scripture*: so that the sense is, by this argument that stone is the chief one, because according to the testimony of Isaiah it was placed in the corner, by which, embracing and containing both walls, it might support the whole building. For that is *periechei*, to embrace and hold from all sides, unless perhaps he used *periechei* neutrally. It can be taken for *to excel*: whence also that stone *excels*, or is eminent in the Scripture: to which the things that follow, "chief cornerstone" etc., agree aptly enough.

*10 Behold I will place]* <note>original: "Ἰδοὺ τίθημι"</note>, that is, *Behold I place*. The passage is in Isaiah chapter 28. Peter expressed the meaning in good faith, he did not count the words. However, in that "whoever believes in him shall not be confounded," he followed the Seventy (Septuagint). Otherwise the Hebrew truth has, *whoever believes, let him not hasten*: but we have spoken of this elsewhere. And again *shall not be confounded*, in Greek is <note>original: "αἰσχυνθῇ"</note>, that is, *shall be put to shame*, or *it will shame*, *it is doubtful*.

*11 Highest angular]* In Greek it is a single word, <note>original: "ἀκρογωνιαῖον"</note>, as if you were to say, *top-corner-stone*.

*12 To you therefore who believe, honor]* Lyra and Carrensis interpret this place all too childishly: *To you there will be honor in the heavens*, since Peter is thinking of the stone previously rejected by the Jews, and then honored and held in high price. For he previously called it *precious*, now mindful of that he says, <note>original: "Ὑμῖν οὖν ἡ τιμὴ τοῖς πιστεύουσιν"</note>, that is, *To you therefore he is precious, you who have believed in him*; to the Jews and non-believers he is vile. Bede differs from us slightly in words, but agrees in matter. Therefore, lest the Reader stumble in a similar way, we translated, *To you therefore he is precious, you who believe.* Laurentius preferred *honorific* rather than *precious stone*. For here it is not a question of the price of the stone, but of the estimation. Although "dear" is sometimes said of what costs a great deal, and sometimes of what is greatly valued: so also *precious* is said of what is of great price, or what is held in high regard. For the "precious stone" is opposed here to the "rejected stone," just as a little above, *rejected indeed by men, but chosen and honored by God*: to "rejected" he opposes "precious" and truly "honored."

*13 Rock of scandal]* He spoke in a Hebrew manner rather than a Greek one, <note>original: "λίθος προσκόμματος, καὶ πέτρα σκανδάλου"</note>. In Latin it could be translated, *a stone against which one strikes, and a rock at which men stumble*.

*14 Who stumble at the word]* <note>original: "οἳ προσκόπτουσι τῷ λόγῳ"</note>, that is, who strike against the word, that is, those whom the Gospel offends, and to whom it provides an occasion for impiety.

*15 In which]* <note>original: "εις ο"</note>, that is, *unto which*. For Judaism was prepared for this: that Christ should be believed in, whom the Mosaic Law prefigured. Bede reads *unto which*, warning however that in some manuscripts it was written *in which*.

*16 People of acquisition]* <note>original: "λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν"</note>. And here there must be a Hebrew figure of speech. For he means a people who have come into gain, adopted and grafted into the people of God. Ambrose, explaining the Psalm *Blessed are the undefiled*, in the sixth sermon reads, *a people for adoption*.

*17 Who once were not the people of God]* In this first part the genitive, *of God*, is not to be added: <note>original: "Οἱ ποτὲ οὐ λαὸς, νῦν δὲ λαὸς Θεοῦ"</note>, that is, *who once were not a people, but now the people of God*. And according to this reading the sense is not a little more subtle: they who once were not a people—that is, a most abject people and held for nothing—they are now not only a people, but the people of God. Our more corrected books also agree with the Greek copies.

*18 Having your conduct good]* <note>original: "καλήν"</note>, that is, honest/honorable, so that it pertains also to the dignity that follows virtue according to the Stoics. And a little later, "they were disparaging," in Greek is <note>original: "καταλαλοῦσιν ὑμῶν"</note>, that is, *that they speak evil of you, or disparage you.*

*19 In the day of visitation]* <note>original: "ἐπισκοπῆς"</note>, that is, *of inspection*. Although the Greek word is ambiguous, as it can be derived from *episkeptomai* (to inspect/visit). However, *episkepsis* is more common from this. In Hebrew it is *pekudah*, which for them sounds like a certain prefecture and administration. For he who has been entrusted with the care of a business occasionally visits and inspects what is being done. Thus Peter calls that time in which God deigns to draw a man by his inspiration to better things.

*20 Be subject]* <note>original: "Ὑποτάγητε οὖν"</note>, that is, *Therefore be subject*. And by an extension of meaning he called man a "creature."

*21 Or to leaders, as sent by him]* <note>original: "ἡγεμόσιν"</note>, which he now frequently translates as "governors." For Peter is not here dealing with war, but with those who act in the Roman provinces, which were administered by governors in the name of the Caesars. Since he is here dealing with ethnic magistrates, he said to be "subject," meaning to tolerate certain things which they seem to do by their own right when they exact tax, when they take a census: but this...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed philological analysis of the First Epistle of Peter, specifically moving from the end of Chapter 2 into the beginning of Chapter 3. On the previous page, Erasmus discussed the role of governors and the call to submission; here, he examines the specific duties of servants and wives, the suffering of Christ as a model for endurance, and the nature of inner beauty. He continues to contrast the Greek source text with the Latin Vulgate and the interpretations of medieval scholars like Bede and Hugo of Saint-Cher.</meta>

# EPISTLE CHAPTER III.

<margin>15</margin> ...to those who do evil, but for the praise of those who do good. For <margin>16</margin> this is the will of God, that by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish men. As free people, not using your freedom <margin>17</margin> as a covering for malice, but as servants of God. Honor all people, love the brotherhood, fear God, honor the king. <margin>18</margin> Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the crooked <note>original: "skoliois," meaning perverse or harsh</note>. <margin>19</margin> For this is grace, if for the sake of conscience toward God one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly. <margin>20</margin> For what glory is it if, when you sin and are beaten, you endure it? But if when you do good and suffer, you endure it, this is grace before <margin>21</margin> God. For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that you should follow in his steps. <margin>22</margin> He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. <margin>23</margin> When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but committed himself to him who judges <margin>24</margin> justly. He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, so that we, having died to sins, might live for righteousness; by his <margin>25</margin> wounds <note>original: "mōlōpi," a bruise or stripe from a lash</note> you were healed. For you were like sheep going astray, but you have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer <term>Bishop<gloss>The Greek word "episkopos" literally means an overseer or one who watches over</gloss></term> of your souls. <margin>III. 1</margin> Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won over without a word <margin>2</margin> by the conduct of their wives, as they observe your chaste conduct <margin>3</margin> coupled with fear. Your adornment should not be the external kind—the braiding of hair, the wearing of gold, or the putting on of <margin>4</margin> fine clothing—but rather the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious in the <margin>5</margin> sight of God. For in this way formerly the holy women, who hoped in God, also [adorned themselves]...
<sig>D</sig>
<meta>catchword: adorned</meta>

---

<margin>A</margin> *...belonged to those times. Yet it does not mean "one who is sent,"* <note>original Greek: "phepomenoisin"</note> *that is, those who are being sent: so that you understand the action without a specific time. "As if by him,"* <note>original Greek: "hōs ap' autou"</note> *that is, as if through him, namely the King, or through him, meaning God.*

<margin>22</margin> **Praise indeed of the good]** <note>original Greek: "agathopoiōn"</note> that is, of those who will do good, or of those who are doing good. Furthermore, among the Ancients—as Plato taught in his *Republic*—laws did not only threaten punishment to those acting badly, but also invited people to their duties with rewards. Now, bad deeds are punished sharply enough, but no thanks are given to those who deserve well. In the first part of the phrase, the word "indeed" <note>original Greek: "men"</note> is used, *for the punishment indeed*, so that it corresponds to the following "but" <note>original Greek: "de"</note>. And bad deeds are called crimes or offenses by the Latins; I do not know if the word "malefactor" is found in pure Latin. "Maleficus" <note>evildoer/sorcerer</note> is an ambiguous word. For "malefici" is almost always used for those who practice the dark arts, and so we translate it as *of the guilty*. For in Greek it is "kakopoiōn," that is, *those who do evil.*

<margin>23</margin> **That you may cause the ignorance of foolish men to be silenced]** Because the Heathen spoke ill of good people, attributing it partly to laziness and partly to ignorance; the Apostle wants this met with excellent obedience toward magistrates, lest Christians seem to be justly punished as transgressors of public discipline.

<margin>24</margin> **Honor all]** <note>original Greek: "Pantas timēsate"</note> that is, give honor to whomsoever it is due, even to Heathen who are endowed with dignity. However, "love the brotherhood" <note>original Greek: "adelphotēta agapate"</note> refers specifically to Christians. Those officials demand honor, pay it; but love is owed to fellow Christians.

<margin>25</margin> **In all fear]** <note>original Greek: "en panti phobō"</note> that is, with all reverence. For Jerome interprets this word in this way in some places. Nor is the Greek "epieikesin" used for those who are "not arrogant," but rather for those who are fair and kind, not overly rigid.

<margin>26</margin> **But also to the perverse]** <note>original Greek: "alla kai tois skoliois"</note> that is, even to the crooked or harsh. It is a wonder what came into the Translator's mind, that he rendered a Greek word with another Greek word: for "dyskolos" sounds like "difficult" to the Greeks. Hugo of Saint-Cher <note>Carrensis</note> interprets *dyscolis* as "unlearned" or "unrefined," because they have not spent time in the *Scholiis* <note>Schools</note>. But he also notes that in some copies, instead of *dyscolis*, it was written *difficultatibus* <note>difficulties</note>. It is even more marvelous that Bede hallucinated here in the same way (if indeed this commentary is his), who thinks *dyscolus* is derived from *Schola* <note>School</note>, citing that verse from the Psalm, "Be still and see," where for "be still" the Greek has "scholazete." He also notes soon after that Saint Fulgentius in his works cites this passage as: *Serving with fear, not only the good and modest, but also the more difficult.*

<margin>27</margin> **One endures sorrows]** <note>original Greek: "lypas"</note> that is, troubles.

<margin>28</margin> **For what is the grace]** <note>original Greek: "Poion gar kleos?"</note> that is, what is the glory, or what is the praise? An ancient manuscript from Donatianus supported this, though only one. Another from the Library of the University of Basel also supported it. Both manuscripts from Constantinople agreed.

<margin>29</margin> **If doing good, you suffer patiently]** <note>original Greek: "ei agathopoiountes kai paschontes hypomeneite"</note> that is, if when you are doing well, and yet you are afflicted, you endure it.

<margin>30</margin> **For us, you]** <note>original Latin: "pro nobis, vobis"</note> In the Greek, both are "hēmin," that is, *for us*, in the first person: even if some manuscripts vary.

<margin>31</margin> **Who when he was cursed, did not curse back]** <note>original Greek: "Hos loidoroumenos, ouk anteloidorei"</note> that is, he who when attacked with curses, did not curse in return, or throw back the insults.

<column-break/>

They should be sent for the punishment indeed of the guilty, <margin>15</margin> but for the praise of those acting rightly. Because such is the will of God, that by doing well <margin>23</margin> you should stop the mouths of foolish and ignorant men. As free people, and not as if <margin>16</margin> having freedom as a pretext for malice, but as servants of God. <margin>24</margin> Honor all, love the brotherhood, <margin>17</margin> fear God, honor the king. Servants, be subject <margin>18</margin> with fear to your masters, not only to the good and kind, <margin>26</margin> but also to the perverse. For this is grace, if <margin>19</margin> anyone for the sake of conscience toward God <margin>27</margin> endures troubles, having been affected by evils beyond what they deserve. <margin>28</margin> For what is the praise, <margin>20</margin> if when sinning you are struck with blows and you endure it? <margin>29</margin> But if when you do good, and yet are affected by evils, you endure. For this is grace before God. Since to <margin>21</margin> this you were called, because Christ also was afflicted <margin>30</margin> for us, leaving us an example, so that you should follow his footsteps: Who had committed no sin, nor <margin>22</margin> was deceit found in his mouth: <margin>31</margin> who when he was attacked with <margin>23</margin> insults, did not throw back insults: when he was affected by evils, he did not threaten: <margin>32</margin> but handed over vengeance to him who judges justly: Who himself bore our sins <margin>24</margin> in his body upon the tree, <margin>33</margin> whereby having died to sins, we might live for righteousness: <margin>34</margin> by whose same wound <note>original: "vibice," the mark of a lash</note> you were healed: For you were like wandering sheep, but you have been <margin>25</margin> turned back now <margin>35</margin> to the shepherd and curator of your souls. Likewise, wives, be subject to your husbands, <margin>III. 1</margin> so that even those who do not obey the word, <margin>1</margin> may be won over without a word through the conduct of the wives: While <margin>2</margin> they observe your chaste conduct joined with reverence, <margin>2</margin> Whose adornment should not be ex- <margin>3</margin> ternal, which is located in the braiding of hair, and the addition of gold, or in the wearing of cloaks, But the hid- <margin>4</margin> den man of the heart, if he lacks all cor- <margin>4</margin> ruption, so that the spirit is gentle and quiet, which spirit in the eyes of God <margin>5</margin> is a magnificent and sumptuous thing. For in that manner formerly also those holy wo- <margin>5</margin>
<meta>catchword: men,</meta>

---

<margin>32</margin> **But he handed himself over to one judging him unjustly]** The Greek is different: <note>original Greek: "paredidou de tō krinonti dikaiōs"</note> that is, *but he committed it to him who judges justly.* It signifies that Christ handed over vengeance to God, rather than taking it for himself. Augustine renders the Greek reading in his 81st tractate on John: *When he received injury,* he says, *he did not threaten, but commended it to him who judges justly.* Hugo of Saint-Cher, I know not from where, dreamed up something else about this reading.

<margin>33</margin> **That having died to sins]** <note>original Greek: "apogenomenoi"</note> that is, extinguished, as if they had already ceased to be. Ambrose translates it as "separated" in his first book on the Holy Spirit, chapter 8.

<margin>34</margin> **By whose stripe]** <note>original Greek: "tō mōlōpi"</note> a lash-mark. For he refers to what is in Isaiah chapter 53: *And by his stripe we are healed.* For a "livor" <note>bruise/stripe</note> is the mark of a blow on the skin. Hugo of Saint-Cher, a man of many words, interprets this in three ways: by the "stripe," that is, by immoderate love which had drawn paleness upon him, according to that line of Ovid <note>Naso</note>:
> Let every lover grow pale, for this is the color suited to a lover:
or by the "stripe," that is, by the flesh made black and blue from blows: or by the "stripe," that is, by the envy of the Jews. But certainly in this place the Greek word allows for only one interpretation, even if for the Latins "livor" has many meanings. Indeed, among the Hebrews it is "chabburah," a word which for them signifies a swelling hardened from a blow. In the Psalms it translates as "scar": *My scars have appeared.* Ambrose, in the place we just cited, reads: *By whose wound of blows we are healed.*

<margin>35</margin> **And the bishop of souls]** <note>original Greek: "poimena kai episkopon"</note> shepherd and curator. For they are called Bishops who look out for necessary things. Bede reads, *and the visitor of your souls*, citing that verse: *Because the Dayspring from on high has visited us.*

<margin>E</margin> <margin>1</margin> **Through the conduct of the women]** <note>original Greek: "dia tēs tōn gunaikōn anastrophēs"</note> Why not rather *through the conduct of the wives?* And certainly in this place "en phobō" <note>in fear</note> would have been more correctly translated as *with reverence*. Furthermore, it is not "holy conduct," but "agnēn," that is, pure or chaste. The manuscript from the Basel University Library had "chaste," and both manuscripts from Constantinople agreed.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>2</margin> *Whose hair-styling should not be outward, or the encircling of gold, or the display of clothing attire]* The Greek speech is clearer: <note>original Greek: "Hōn estō, ouch ho exōthen ek plokēs trichōn, kai peritheseōs chrysiōn, ē endyseōs imatiōn kosmos"</note> that is, to render the sense rather than the words: *Whose adornment should be, not the external kind, which is located in the curling or weaving of hair, or the pinning on of gold, or the wearing of clothes or cloaks.*

<margin>3</margin> **The man of the heart]** Ambrose, in the third book of his Letters, Letter 11, notes this is a novel expression, *man of the heart*, for the internal and hidden man: therefore we have explained the matter through a paraphrase.

<margin>4</margin> **Quiet and modest]** <note>original Greek: "tou praeos kai hēsychiou"</note> that is, mild and quiet, or silent. For he does not want women to be fierce toward their husbands.

<margin>5</margin> **Rich]** <note>original Greek: "polyteles"</note> It is worth noting for a Glossary that some write *locuplex* with an 'x' instead of *locuples* with an 's'. Although in Greek it is "polyteles," that is, sumptuous and splendid. It seems to refer back to the quiet spirit: for it is of the neuter gender, just as "spirit" is among the Greeks. Or certainly to the whole part of the speech which...

Erasmus corrects several Vulgate errors, notably the claim that Christ committed himself to an "unjust" judge, showing the Greek specifies a "just" judge (God).</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on the First Epistle of Peter, Chapter 3. Having previously discussed the general submission of Christians to authorities, Erasmus here turns to the specific conduct of wives and husbands, the call to a peaceful life, and the readiness to defend the faith. He continues his method of comparing the Greek source text with various Latin manuscripts and the interpretations of Church Fathers like Jerome and Augustine.</meta>

### PETER I. CHAPTER III.

<margin>u</margin> ...adorned themselves, being submissive to their own husbands, <margin>6</margin> as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord; of whom you have become children by doing good, and not fearing any terror. <margin>7</margin> Husbands, likewise, dwelling together according to knowledge, as to a weaker vessel, the feminine, assigning honor, as also being fellow-heirs of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered. <margin>8</margin> Finally, be all of one mind, sympathetic, loving the brethren, tenderhearted, friendly. <margin>9</margin> Not returning evil for evil, or railing for railing, but on the contrary blessing, knowing that to this you were called, so that you might inherit a blessing. <margin>10</margin> For he who wishes to love life and see good days, let him stop his tongue from evil, and his lips from speaking deceit. <margin>11</margin> Let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it. <margin>12</margin> For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil. <margin>13</margin> And who is he who will harm you, if you become imitators of the good? <margin>14</margin> But even if you should suffer for the sake of righteousness, you are blessed. And do not fear their fear, nor be troubled. <margin>15</margin> But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. And be always ready for a defense to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the hope that is in you, <margin>16</margin> with gentleness and fear, having a good conscience, so that in that which they speak against you as evildoers, those who revile your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame. <margin>17</margin> For it is better, if the will of God wills it, to suffer while doing good than while doing evil. <margin>18</margin> Because Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God, being put to death...

---

...preceded this, namely that having a spirit of this kind is a magnificent and splendid adornment for a woman in the eyes of God. Certainly, in both of the Donatian manuscripts <note>Erasmus refers to manuscripts from the library of St. Donatian in Bruges</note> it is written, *which is rich in the sight of God*.

<margin>6</margin> *Of whom you are daughters* ] <note>original: "hēs"</note> in the Greek necessarily refers to Sarah, and not Abraham. For in our Latin version, it could be referred to Abraham.

<margin>7</margin> *Pertaining to any disturbance* ] <note>original: "mē phoboumenai mēdemian ptoēsin"</note>, that is, not terrified by any fear. You should know, Reader, that this accusative "disturbance," which the Vulgate edition has, is not transitive but reciprocal, according to the property of the Attic writers, who speak thus: *to rejoice a joy, to rage a rage, to fear a fear*. For here *terror* <note>original: "ptoēsin"</note> signifies that feminine fear by which they are usually frightened out of their wits over nothing, which ought to be absent from holy women. If certain Interpreters of great name had understood this, they would, I think, have explained this passage differently; however, out of respect, I do not name them at present.

<margin>8</margin> *Imparting honor* ] Saint Jerome interprets *Honor* not as bowing the knee to them, or being burdened with gems and gold, or being given the first seat—which we now see done most foolishly in many regions—but as abstinence from sexual intercourse. For in this way honor is held for the feminine vessel, if it is not defiled by lust. And this is indicated by what follows: *so that your prayers may not be interrupted*. Again, I do not care to report here what Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a medieval commentator</note> and many similar Interpreters interpret "explaining honor" to mean: that it proceeds from food and clothing, and that being honorable according to their status and own resources. Then, concerning the hindering of prayers, he interprets it as prayers not being heard unless the husband and wife are in good harmony.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>9</margin> *As fellow-heirs* ] <note>original: "hōs kai sygklēronomoi"</note>, that is, *as also fellow-heirs*. For he adds this as if it were a second and more effective argument; hence the conjunction is not even idle. Furthermore, he calls the woman herself a "weaker vessel" on account of the frailty of the sex. To what purpose, you will say, did it pertain to advise this, which no one was ignorant of? Indeed, a certain man who was very wise in his own judgment attacked this with strange insults, because he saw "feminine vessel" being taken for the shameful member, or the nature of the woman. But yet, to speak frankly, Jerome's interpretation seems to me to be more forced. The general sentiment pleases me more: that husbands should defer some honor to their wives, and not hold them as concubines or handmaids. For he brings forward dual causes why he wants honor to be deferred to wives: either on account of the frailty of the sex, just as we hold the less honorable members of the body in more honor; or on account of the dignity of God, who made the woman equal to the man in the promises of the Gospel. *Of the grace of life*, <note>original: "charitos zōēs"</note>, that is, *of the living grace*; although in this place the Greek manuscripts vary. But if you read *of life*, it is necessary that you take grace for a benefit.

<margin>10</margin> *In the end, however* ] <note>original: "To de telos"</note>, that is, *in summary*. How great a field for disputing is opened here to certain moderns concerning faith, and in how many ways it is taken, when Peter wrote nothing of this kind, nor intended it. Now, where it translates here as *compassionate*, in Greek it is <note>original: "sympatheis"</note>, that is, those who are touched by a mutual affection. For there are those whom the troubles of others do not move even a little. Although Bede interprets it as *in faith*, according to the common Latin reading.

<margin>11</margin> *Lovers of the brotherhood* ] <note>original: "Philadelphoi"</note>, that is, *lovers of brothers, or loving fraternally*.

<margin>12</margin> *Modest* ] <note>original: "Philophrones"</note>: which sounds more like being affable and humane, and easy and accommodating to the custom of life. Furthermore, as to what is added in our versions, *humble*, I think it was added by one who wanted

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>6</margin> ...women hoping in God, adorned themselves, and were subject to their husbands, just as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord, whose daughters you have become while you do good, and are not terrified by any fear. <margin>7</margin> Husbands similarly cohabit according to knowledge, imparting honor as to a weaker feminine vessel, as also fellow-heirs of the grace of life, lest your prayers be interrupted. <margin>8</margin> In summary, let all be of one mind, similarly affected, endowed with brotherly charity, merciful, affable, <margin>9</margin> Not retaliating evil for evil, or insult for insult, but on the contrary blessing, knowing you were called to this, that you might possess a blessing by inheritance. <margin>10</margin> For he who wishes to love life, and see good days, let him restrain his tongue from evil, and his lips lest they speak deceit. <margin>11</margin> Let him turn away from evil, and do good: let him seek peace, and pursue it. <margin>12</margin> Because the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears toward their prayer. Again, the gaze of the Lord is upon those who do evil things. <margin>13</margin> And who is he who would afflict you, if you were emulators of goodness? <margin>14</margin> Indeed, if anything inconvenient even happens on account of justice, you are nevertheless blessed. But do not be terrified by their terror, nor troubled, <margin>15</margin> But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. But be always ready to respond to anyone asking, that you may speak of the hope that is in you, <margin>16</margin> With gentleness and reverence, having a good conscience, so that in this which they disparage you as criminals, those who attack your good conduct in Christ may be shamed. <margin>17</margin> For it is better that you, doing well, if the will of God so wills, be affected by evils, than doing evil. <margin>18</margin> Since Christ also suffered once for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might lead us to God, put to death indeed in the flesh, but quickened in the spi-

---

to interpret modesty: for it was not added in either Donatian manuscript.

<margin>13</margin> *And his lips* ] <note>original: "kai cheilē autou"</note>, that is, *and his own lips*. Thus Valla also preferred, nor do I see for what reason. "His own" was more fitting. For here there is not a true reciprocation, as in the former part.

<margin>14</margin> *That you be not troubled* ] <note>original: "mēde tarachthēte"</note>, that is, *neither be troubled*.

<margin>15</margin> *But the Lord Christ* ] It is *God* in Greek, not *Christ*. And *sanctify* appears to be placed for *glorify*. Which is like that phrase, *Hallowed be thy name*.

<margin>16</margin> *To satisfaction* ] <note>original: "pros apologian"</note>, that is, *to an excuse, or defense*.

<margin>17</margin> *Which is in you (hope and faith)* ] In Greek it is only <note>original: "peri tēs en hymin elpidos"</note>, that is, *concerning the hope that is in you*.

<margin>18</margin> *With modesty and fear* ] <note>original: "Meta praÿtētos kai phobou"</note>, that is, *With gentleness and reverence*. For he speaks of those who respond calmly and reverently when questioned by anyone concerning the faith of Christ.

<margin>19</margin> *In which they detract from you* ] The Greeks read, <note>original: "hina en hō katalalousin hymōn hōs kakopoiōn"</note>, that is, *so that in that which they disparage you as evildoers*. We have noted before concerning the word *evildoers*.

<margin>20</margin> *They calumniate* ] <note>original: "hoi epēreazontes"</note>, those who rail, or who attack, or persecute.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>21</margin> *For it is better that doing good, if the will of God wills* ] The Greek manuscripts indeed agree with our Edition; however, it is a wonder what Augustine followed in book 22, chapter 20 of *Against Faustus*, where he relates this passage in these words: *It is better that doing good, if the spirit of God wills, you suffer, than doing evil*. Unless perhaps instead of *will* <note>original: "thelēma"</note>, *spirit* <note>original: "pneuma"</note> was written in some copies, and then a scribe changed it back to *spirit*.

<margin>22</margin> *Put to death indeed in the flesh* ] <note>original: "thanatōtheis"</note>, that is, *put to death*. Likewise *quickened*, not *quickened ones* <note>making a grammatical distinction between singular and plural</note>, <note>original: "zōopoiētheis"</note>. And thus Saint Jerome cites it in *Ephesians* chapter 4. And also Augustine in *Letter 99 to Evodius*. Again, in the *Sermon on the words of the Apostle 14*. It was said of Christ, he says, *put to death indeed in the flesh, but quickened in the spirit*. Thus it can be said of a man, *wasted in the flesh, quickened in the spirit*: so that you understand Christ died according to the frailty of the body, but rose again by the power of the spirit. Now, what does it pertain to review in this place what those who are ignorant of Greek dream up regarding this sentence, following only what a scribe corrupted rather than what Peter wrote? They could attack the overly arrogant ignorance of those men with insults at every point, who pronounce as if from an oracle whatever they have dreamed about these things, which cannot even be read correctly without skill in languages. For if you read *put to death and quickened* (plural), how will what follows, *in which*, cohere? Bede reads and interprets it as *quickened and put to death* (plural), and brings in Athanasius *Against the Arians*. But a little later he also indicates this reading, which the Greeks have. Both Donatian manuscripts agreed, except that in one a corrupter had turned *us* into *os* <note>referring to Latin endings</note>, the letter *u* being closed at the top. A manuscript from the library of the Academy of Basel also supported this. And this passage must be read cautiously, lest we feel anything such as some people do concerning the soul of Christ suffering among those below. Regarding which matter Bede touches on something, but with the author's name silenced, signifying, if I am not mistaken, Origen.

He focuses on the conduct of spouses, the definition of "honor," and the theological significance of Christ's suffering and resurrection.</summary>

### THE EPISTLE CHAPTER IV.

**Column 1 (1051)**

<page-num>1051</page-num>

<margin>19</margin> revealed in the flesh, but made alive by the spirit, in which he also went and preached to the spirits in prison, <margin>20</margin> who were once disobedient; when once the patience of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared, in which a few, that is, <margin>21</margin> eight souls, were saved through water. This, as a corresponding type, now saves us—baptism; not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience toward God, through the resurrection of Jesus <margin>22</margin> Christ, who is at the right hand of God, having gone into heaven, with angels and authorities and powers having been subjected to him. <margin>IV. 1</margin> Since Christ, therefore, has suffered for us in the flesh, you also arm yourselves with the same thought, because he who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from <margin>2</margin> sin; so as to live the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for the lusts of men, but for the will <margin>3</margin> of God. For the time of life that has passed is sufficient for you to have worked out the will of the Gentiles, having walked in unrestrained lusts, desires, wine-drinking, revelries, drinking bouts, and <margin>4</margin> lawless idol-worship. In this they are surprised, that you do not run with them into the same flood of profligacy, <margin>5</margin> blaspheming. They will give an account to him who is ready to judge the living and the <margin>6</margin> dead. For to this end the Gospel was preached also to the dead, so that they might be judged indeed according to men in the flesh, but live <margin>7</margin> according to God in the spirit. But the end of all things has drawn near. Therefore be of sound mind and be sober for <margin>8</margin> prayers. Above all things, have fervent love for one another; for love will cover a multi-<margin>9</margin>tude of sins. Be hospitable to one another without <margin>10</margin> grumbling. As each has received a gift, minister it to one another, as good stew- ->ards.<-

23 <margin>A</margin> *They were in prison in spirit*] <note>original: "τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ πνεύμασιν"</note> *that is, to those who were spirits in prison*. Jerome reads it this way in the place we just cited: *he was put to death in the flesh, made alive in the spirit, and preached to the spirits established in prison*. Hugo of Saint-Cher <note>Erasmus refers to him as "Carrenis"</note> warns that in some copies "in the flesh" was written instead of "in prison." Truly, Bede pointed this out before him. In both Constantiensian manuscripts it was written *spiritually* instead of *by the spirit*.
24 *Who had been unbelieving formerly*] <note>original: "ἀπειθήσασι ποτε"</note> *that is, to those who were once disobedient*.
25 *When they expected the patience of God*] <note>original: "ὅτε ἀπεξεδέχετο ἡ τοῦ Θεοῦ μακροθυμία"</note> *that is, when the leniency of God was being waited for*; even if some codices had *ote* <note>when</note>. In the second Constantiensian manuscript it was, *the patience of God was expected, just as the Greek reads*. Again, in many it was, *once he expected*, instead of *he was expecting*. I suspect it should have been read, *once he expected*. Augustine, in Letter 99, reads *he expected*. For the verb is middle-voiced.
26 *While it was being fabricated*] <note>original: "κατασκευαζομένης"</note> *that is, while it was being prepared*.
27 <margin>E</margin> *Which also now saves you, baptism, in a similar form*] The Greek words have more light: <note>original: "Ὃ καὶ ἀντίτυπον νῦν καὶ ἡμᾶς σώζει βάπτισμα"</note> *that is, to which now a similar, or responding, baptism also saves us*. For <term>sōzei</term> <note>saves</note> is in the present tense, *it preserves*. Furthermore, the word "which" <note>original: "ὃ"</note> responds harshly, whether you refer it to the water or to the baptism; perhaps it was written "to which" <note>original: "ᾧ"</note>.
28 *Who is at the right hand of God*] In this place, the following words are missing in the Greek codices: *Swallowing death, so that we might be made heirs of eternal life*. But skipping these, there follows: <note>original: "πορευθεὶς εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν"</note> *that is, having set out into heaven*.
1 <margin>B</margin> *To the one having suffered in the flesh and you*] <note>original: "παθόντος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν σαρκὶ, καὶ ὑμεῖς"</note> *that is, since he suffered for us in the flesh, you also, etc.*
2 *Be armed with the same thought*] <note>original: "τὴν αὐτὴν ἔννοιαν ὁπλίσασθε"</note> *that is, put on the same thought, as if arming yourselves, or arm yourselves according to the same thought*. Augustine, in Letter 99, reads *knowledge* instead of *thought*.
3 *For the past time is sufficient to have finished the pleasure of the Gentiles*] The Greek is more clear than the Latin: <note>original: "Ἀρκετὸς γὰρ ὑμῖν ὁ παρεληλυθὼς χρόνος τοῦ βίου, τὸ θέλημα τῶν ἐθνῶν κατειργάσασθαι"</note> *that is, For the past time of life is sufficient for us to have perfected the will of the nations; that is, it is enough to have lived impiously until now*. Augustine brings this sense forward in his Homily on the Epistle of Peter XX: *For the past time is sufficient to have finished the wills of the nations*.
4 *In luxury*] <note>original: "ἐν ἀσελγείαις"</note> *that is, in wantonness*. For they do not have "in drunkenness" among the Greeks, nor in either of Donatian's codices, with which all the ancient codices agreed. For what need was there to say "in drunkenness," when he immediately adds "revelries and drinking bouts"?
5 *In the unlawful cults of idols*] <note>original: "ἀθεμίτοις"</note> *that is, nefarious, which is more atrocious than simply unlawful*.
6 <margin>C</margin> *In which they wonder*] <note>original: "ἐν ᾧ ξενίζονται"</note> literally sounds like *in which they act as foreigners*. Furthermore, among the Greeks, those to whom something seems new or absurd are said "to be surprised" <note>original: "ξενίζεσθαι"</note>. This pertains to what follows. Augustine, in Letter 99, brings this passage forward in these words: *For the past time is sufficient to have finished the will of men, walking in lusts, and desires, and drunkenness, revelries, drinking bouts, and unlawful slaveries to idols, in which they are stunned that you do not run together into that confusion of luxury, blaspheming*.
