7 <margin>D</margin> *The confusion of luxury*] <note>original: "ἀσωτίας ἀνάχυσιν"</note> which sounds more like *a refusion, just as when the surging sea pours itself back*.
8 *The end will approach*] <note>original: "ἤγγικε"</note> *that is, it has approached, in the past tense. Or certainly, it presses on and is imminent*.
9 *Be therefore prudent*] <note>original: "Σωφρονήσατε"</note> *that is, Be temperate, or sober*. *And watch*, <note>original: "καὶ νήψατε"</note> *that is, and be sober, or watch; for the force of <term>nēphein</term> signifies both. It is peculiar to the Apostles to join these three: sobriety, watchfulness, and prayer, so that sobriety is opposed to luxury and excess, and watchfulness to sleepiness and laziness*. I have heard those who, in sacred sermons to the people, when they proposed a theme from this place, heaped up many things from Aristotle’s *Ethics*, or rather from his literary *Sophistical Refutations*, concerning "prudence." Likewise concerning "charity" which they say arises from ourselves and only then flows out to others—namely, running "outside the olive trees" <note>a Greek proverb meaning to wander off-topic</note>. Not that I think such slips should be hounded with insults, but I do not think they should be ignored—even if, to speak without trickery, it seems foul in itself that one who has undertaken to teach everyone in a crowded assembly of the people, and an ecclesiastical one at that, does not understand the very thing he wants to be seen as the base and foundation of his entire speech. And yet some of these people insolently tear apart our admonition; what would they do if they were provoked by an injury, when they return such "thanks" to one who deserves well? If some rich man were to receive them <margin>F</margin> with a more elegant insult, or give them a little money, they would almost adore him—those "Greeks"—and call it alms; and they impart in turn their own benefits, with which they abound, of course. But they pursue with every kind of insult the one who affects them with so much better services. For some time later, a certain <term>koryphaios</term> <note>leader or headman</note> of that flock, to whom, I believe, someone had recounted that I had lamented among friends that they lacked this understanding (even though otherwise what was said had pleased me), in a public sermon while I was present, twisted two sins committed against the Holy Spirit—obliquely, or rather quite openly—against me: "presumption," for so they call it, because I had not feared to correct the *Our Father* and the *Magnificat*; likewise "attacking the known truth," because I had denied that sacred preachers understood their own theme, which had been drawn from sacred letters by sacred men. As if, indeed, the ignorance of those who wrongly interpret what is in those letters were not even more foul. Those who have so hardened their faces, did they not deserve to be exposed by name? I, however, spare both names and their order.
10 *In yourselves*] <note>original: "εἰς ἑαυτοὺς"</note> *that is, toward yourselves, or rather toward one another mutually*. This will perhaps seem like a trivial point to some, and yet I heard a man who, in a public sermon, diligently philosophized from this place on how charity first proceeds from ourselves, and how it is poured into hearts, and many things of that sort, touching neither heaven nor earth. And yet these are the ones who despise this labor of ours as vain and fruitless; they are the ones who would need it most if they were wise—or rather, because they are not wise, they are truly useless men, and most deservedly to be rejected into that third class of Hesiod’s, who neither are wise by themselves, nor believe one who warns them rightly. *Continuous*, <note>original: "ἐκτενῆ"</note> *which previously appeared as "attentively," here he could have said "propense" or "vehement."*
11 *Because charity covers*] <note>original: "καλύψει"</note> *that is, will cover, or will hide, a verb in the future tense, so that it pertains to the day of judgment*.
12 *Received grace*] <note>original: "χάρισμα"</note> *that is, a gift*.
13 *Administering it*] <note>original: "αὐτὸ διακονοῦντες"</note> *that is, ministering by it, or through it, namely the grace. Although in some* <meta>catchword: Greek</meta>

# FIRST EPISTLE OF PETER CHAPTER 5
### Pages 1053, 1054

<margin>A</margin> 11 ...of the manifold grace of God. If anyone speaks, let him speak as the oracles of God; if anyone ministers, let him do so as by the strength which God supplies, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom is the glory and the dominion forever and ever, amen. 12 Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial among you, which comes upon you for your testing, as though something strange were happening to you. 13 But insofar as you share in the sufferings of Christ, rejoice, so that also at the revelation of his glory you may rejoice with exultation. 14 If you are reproached in the name of Christ, you are blessed; because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you. On their part he is blasphemed, but on your part he is glorified.

<margin>B</margin> 15 For let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or an evildoer, or as a <term>busybody in other men's matters</term> <note>original: "allotrioepiskopos"</note>. 16 But if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in this matter. 17 For it is the time for judgment to begin from the house of God; and if it begins first from us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel of God? 18 And if the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear? 19 Therefore, let those who suffer according to the will of God commit their souls to a faithful Creator in doing good.

<margin>V. 1</margin> 1 The elders who are among you I exhort, I who am a fellow-elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, who am also a partaker of the glory that is to be revealed:

<margin>V. 2</margin> 2 Shepherd the flock of Christ which is among you, exercising oversight...

<note>In the Greek copies it was written "it," referring to the gift to be administered. And regarding the phrase "in one another," a word the Translator often uses very carelessly, the Greek is "among yourselves," which has the same meaning as what was just said, "to one another," that is, one toward the other.</note>

<margin>C</margin> <note>14 *Of the manifold grace of God*] <note>original: "poikilēs"</note>: Which the Translator expressed not poorly, since the Greek word signifies "various," so that we may understand the diverse forms of gifts.</note>
<note>15 *As the oracles*] <note>original: "hōs logia"</note>, that is, as the divine utterances.</note>
<note>16 *By the strength*] <note>original: "ex ischyos"</note>, that is, out of power or robustness, so that the authority remains with God, not with man. Which he supplies, <note>original: "hēs choregei"</note>, that is, which he provides or furnishes. For he "administers" who performs the management of a thing committed to him; he "supplies" who offers and grants what is needed. Thus Peter attributes "ministering" to man, and "supplying" to God.</note>
<note>17 *Be honored*] <note>original: "doxazētai"</note>, that is, be glorified.</note>

<margin>D</margin> <note>18 *Do not be surprised*] <note>original: "mē xenizesthe"</note>. That word for being a "stranger" or "foreigner" means to the Greeks to be moved or disturbed, as if by something new and unusual; for a little later "stranger" <note>original: "xenou"</note> becomes "new thing." And <term>Bede</term> <note>An 8th-century English monk and scholar</note> advises that in some manuscripts it was written, *do not wonder*. At this point, I prudently pass over the absurd interpretations of certain "great" theologians, as they seem to be. For what purpose is served by filling volumes with the errors of others?</note>
<note>19 *In the heat*] <note>original: "tē en hymin pyrōsei"</note>, that is, the burning, or the testing through fire. For he again refers to gold, which is tested by fire. Therefore, we translate it: *do not be disturbed as by a new thing while you are being tested through fire*.</note>
<note>20 *Which is to you*] "Comes to be" is the Greek <note>original: "ginomenē"</note>.</note>
<note>21 *But communicating*] <note>original: "Alla katho koinōneite"</note>, that is, "But in this that you share," or "insofar as you share." <term>Cyprian</term> <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage</note> in the fourth Letter of the sixth book renders this passage in this manner: *Dearest ones, do not wonder at the heat happening to you, which occurs for your temptation, lest you fall away, as if something new happens to you, but as often as you share in Christ's passions, rejoice through all things, so that also in the revelation made of his brightness you may rejoice exulting*. If you are reproached in the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the name of the majesty and power of the Lord rests in you. Thus far we have recounted his words. First, he correctly translates *to be a stranger* as *to wonder*. Furthermore, *heat* could have been more aptly translated as *conflagration*. Although here he rendered the Greek more confusingly. Then he seems to have put "lest you fall away" for "to wonder greatly" or "to be stunned," as if expressing the Greek word *existate*, just as elsewhere in Paul, or "boiling over for God." Furthermore, I do not know what he means by "the name of the majesty and power of the Lord," unless perhaps "light" came in place of "spirit," or he read "will" <note>original: "nōma"</note> instead of "spirit" <note>original: "pneuma"</note>. He brings forward this same testimony in the same words in his exposition of the Creed.</note>

<margin>E</margin> <note>22 *You shall be blessed*] "You shall be" is not added among the Greeks; it is simply "blessed" <note>original: "makarioi"</note>. It is more correct to understand "you are" than "you shall be."</note>
<note>23 *Which is of honor, glory, and power*] The Greek has it thus: <note>original: "to tēs doxēs, kai to tou Theou Pneuma"</note>, that is, "that which is of glory, and the Spirit of God." However, you should take "Spirit" in the nominative case, not the genitive. This passage can be taken in two ways; one, so that "that of glory" is read separately for "glory," as our Translator did; the other, so that the nominative "the Spirit" applies equally to two genitives: "the Spirit of glory and of God," as if interpreting what he had called the "Spirit of glory" by adding "and of God." "Of power" is not in the Greek.</note>
<note>24 *Shall rest*] <note>original: "anapauetai"</note>, that is, "rests," in the present tense, or "is refreshed."</note>
<note>25 *But let none of you suffer*] Before these words, the Greeks have text which I do not find in the Latin manuscripts. They have these words: *According to them indeed he is blasphemed, but according to you he is glorified*.</note>

<margin>C</margin> <note>...fied. Which things, however, are not absent in that passage which we just showed in Cyprian, for he reads: *Which indeed according to them is blasphemed, but according to you is honored*. So that the two words refer to the Spirit, or the glory of God, which was being dishonored by the judgment of impious men through the punishment and affliction of those present; but in their own opinion, in this way the glory of God was made more illustrious. Nor does Bede touch upon this part in his Commentaries. For that which we read as "suffer," <note>original: "paschetō"</note>, in both the Constance manuscripts it was held as "deceive" <note>original: "uemoseisthō"</note>. I think that was committed through the fault of the scribes.</note>
<note>26 *But none of you*] <note>original: "Mē gar tis hymōn"</note>, "For let not any of you."</note>
<note>27 *Or a thief*] <term>Valla</term> <note>Lorenzo Valla, a 15th-century humanist whose work on the NT inspired Erasmus</note> prefers "as a thief, as a murderer." So he soon translates, "But if as a Christian." Yet he truly was a Christian, he was not a murderer. But the speech must be referred to the opinion of the one afflicting, not the one afflicted. "Or an evildoer," <note>original: "ē kakopoios"</note>, that is, or a criminal.</note>

<margin>D</margin> <note>28 *A craver of others' things*] <note>original: "allotrioepiskopos"</note>, that is, an inspector or curator of others' things. A composite word, from "other's" and "bishop" <note>overseer</note>, that is, an inspector, because he who craves something, inspects it. Augustine, in his incomplete exposition of the Epistle to the Romans, reads: *or acting in others' cares*.</note>
<note>29 *In this name*] <note>original: "en tō merei toutō"</note>, that is, in this part. He divides the affliction into the torment of the body and the cause. One must not glory in torments, but one must glory in the other part: that we suffer for Christ.</note>
<note>30 *Begin from the house of God*] <note>original: "apo tou oikou tou Theou"</note>, that is, from the house of God.</note>
<note>31 *And if indeed the righteous man will scarcely be saved*] Bede advises this is taken from Proverbs according to the old translation. Otherwise, according to our version it has: *If the righteous man receives on earth, how much more the ungodly and the sinner?* But what Bede says is in the old translation is read among the Greeks from the Septuagint translation: "If the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?" Nor is it "will be saved," but <note>original: "sōzetai"</note>, "is saved."</note>

<margin>E</margin> <note>32 *To the faithful creator*] <note>original: "hōs pistō ktistē"</note>, that is, as to a faithful or trusty founder, or possessor.</note>
<note>33 *In good deeds*] <note>original: "en agathopoiia"</note>, that is, in beneficence, or in doing good.</note>
<note>1 *More earnestly therefore*] "Therefore" is not among the Greeks. "Fellow-elder." He would have more correctly said *the elders, fellow-elder*. And Jerome translates it so, as I will soon show. Although here also the Greek name is somewhat offended by the addition of the Latin conjunction. And I do not know whether anyone is a "happy fellow-elder."</note>
<note>2 *Which is to be revealed in the future*] There was no need for these words "in the future," <note>original: "tēs mellousēs doxēs apokalyptesthai"</note>. It was enough to say, *will be revealed*.</note>

<margin>F</margin> <note>3 *Shepherd*] To the Greeks it is <note>original: "Poimanate"</note>, which is "Shepherd," just as shepherds shepherd. It is the same word in Psalm 2: *Rule them with a rod of iron*, that is, rule them in a shepherdly way, to use Hilary's words. And Homer repeatedly calls a king <note>original: "poimena laōn"</note>, that is, the shepherd of the people.</note>
<note>4 *Which is among you*] <note>original: "to en hymin poimnion"</note>. The Greek speech is indeed ambiguous in itself. To me, however, the more genuine sense seems to be: *Shepherd, as much as is in you, the flock of Christ*. For the Greek manuscripts have "of Christ," not "of God." For he calls himself a shepherd in the Gospel writings. But if this sense does not please anyone, let him know that "in you" was said for "among you," or "at your place," so that you understand that each person must care for his own flock.</note>
<note>5 *Providing*] <note>original: "episkopountes"</note>, that is, attending to, or acting as a bishop. Saint Jerome notes this word in a certain letter to Evagrius, the beginning of which is, "We read in Isaiah," and he brings it out as "to look into," but he adds that the meaning is stated in Greek. For in Latin he "inspects" who desires to learn what a thing is; to the Greeks, he <note>original: "episkopei"</note> who takes care and provides for necessary things. Furthermore, this whole place...</note>

# THE EPISTLE OF PETER CHAPTER V.
### Pages 1055, 1056

<margin>1</margin> ...acting as overseers, not by compulsion, but willingly; not for <margin>2</margin> shameful gain, but eagerly. Nor as <margin>3</margin> lording it over the <term>allotments</term> <note>original: "kleron," often translated as "clergy," but here meaning those entrusted to a pastor's care</note>, but being examples to the <margin>4</margin> flock. And when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive <margin>5</margin> the unfading crown of glory. Likewise, you younger <margin>6</margin> men, be subject to the elders; and all of you <margin>7</margin> being subject to one another, <term>clothe yourselves</term> <note>original: "egkombosasthe," literally meaning to tie or knot a garment on</note> with humility, <margin>8</margin> for God resists the proud, but gives grace to the <margin>9</margin> humble. Humble yourselves, therefore, under the <margin>10</margin> mighty hand of God, so that He may exalt you in due time, <margin>11</margin> casting all your care upon Him, <margin>12</margin> because He cares for you. Be sober, be vigilant, <margin>13</margin> because your adversary the devil walks about as a roaring lion, <margin>14</margin> seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in the faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world. But the God of all grace, who called us to His eternal glory in Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little, will Himself restore you, support, strengthen, and establish you. To Him be the glory and the power forever and ever, amen. By Sylvanus, a faithful brother to you, as I consider him, I have written in few words, exhorting and testifying that this is the true grace of God, in which you stand. She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, greets you, and so does Mark my son.
<meta>catchword: Greetings-</meta>

---

The Epistle which I just cited proceeds in this manner: "I, a fellow-elder and witness of the sufferings of Christ, and a partaker of the glory that is to be revealed, exhort the elders among you to shepherd the flock of Christ, overseeing it not out of necessity, but willingly according to God."

6 **Spontaneously according to God**] The phrase "according to God" is not added in the Greek manuscripts.

7 **But willingly**] <note>original: "prothymos"</note>, that is, promptly, or with ready minds.

8 **Not lording it over the clergy**] In Greek it is: "Neither as exercising lordship against the allotments." <note>original: "kleron"</note>. He calls "allotments" not the Deacons or Priests, but the flock which happened to fall to each person's governance; let no one think that Bishops are permitted lordship over the clergy while being forbidden it over others. And here he calls the "Elders" <note>Presbyteros</note> "Bishops." For the crowd of Priests had not yet grown large; rather, as many as there were Elders, there were just as many Bishops. This precept of the Prince of the Apostles ought to be inscribed in every Bishop’s hall, even in letters of gold: "Feed the flock," he says, "do not oppress it, do not fleece it." And do this not by compulsion, as if merely performing a duty, but from sincere affection, like fathers; and not for the sake of shameful gain, as if the hide of the present Church were destined to come from there. Finally, do not rule in the manner of Kings, but feed them by example, and conquer them through good deeds. Nowadays, the common crowd of Bishops hears of nothing except learned warriors, lordships, jurisdictions, swords, keys, and powers; hence arises a pride in some that is more than royal, and a cruelty more than tyrannical.

9 **But being made a pattern**] <note>original: "typoi ginomenoi"</note>, that is, made into forms or examples. Though the change in grammatical number does not vary the sense, there is little doubt the Interpreter translated it as "forms" in the plural, as that reading stands in the older Constance manuscript. In another, a corrupter changed it from "fecerat." It also appeared in the copy provided by the Library of the Basel School. Regarding the phrase "from the heart" <note>Ex animo</note>: the Greeks do not add this.

10 **For all [be subject] to one another in humility**] In Greek: "being subject to one another," that is, in turn, one to the other. In some ancient copies, it is not "for" but "however." Although the Interpreter translates "to one another" for the Greek term, I found this reading in old copies, except that in the Constance manuscript, a corrupter had erased the preposition.

11 **Insinuated**] <note>original: "egkombosasthe"</note>. This sounds as if you were to say, "knot it on." He means that humility should be kept in the soul with skill, as if bound with knots, so that it cannot be knocked out by any occasion, as frequently happens to the weaker sort. And the word here is not *tapeinotes* [lowliness], but *tapeinophrosyne*, which sounds like humility of mind, or rather, modesty.

12 **To the humble**] <note>original: "tapeinois"</note>. Here it certainly refers to modesty of the soul's feeling.

13 **In the time of visitation**] "Of visitation" is redundant according to the Greek codices. It is simply "in due time." For "in due time" <note>en kairo</note> sounds as if you said "in its own time," or "when it is opportune." It is not *chrono*, which signifies a duration or span of time, whereas *kairos* signifies opportunity. A "span" is when we say "three years"; a "season" is when we say "in winter" or "in summer"; *kairos* is when we say "before the day" or "late." And since some doubt whether "humiliare" [to humble] is a proper Latin word, it could have been translated: "Submit yourselves under the powerful hand of God." For so the Greek has it: "under the mighty hand."

14 **Seeking whom he may devour**] <note>original: "Zeton tina katapie"</note>, that is, seeking someone to swallow down. In others again, it was held as "seeking to devour someone," just as the Interpreter read. The Interpreter followed by Augustine seems to have read "seeking what" <note>zeton ti</note>. For so he cites this passage in the thirty-fifth Homily: "Your adversary the Devil, like a roaring lion, seeking something to devour, goes about." But I do not know if that happened through the fault of the scribes, for in Homily 46 of the same work, he reads, "seeking someone to devour." Though Cyprian cites it in the same way in his book on jealousy and envy...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>1</margin> ...acting as overseers not by compulsion, but willingly; not greedily <margin>2</margin> seeking shameful gain, but with a ready mind. <margin>3</margin> Neither as exercising lordship against the allotments, but <margin>4</margin> in such a way that you are examples to the flock. And when that <margin>5</margin> chief of pastors appears, you will carry back the unfading <margin>6</margin> crown of glory. Similarly, you younger men, be subject to the <margin>7</margin> elders, so that all of you may be subject to one another in turn: keep humility of mind fixed within you, <margin>8</margin> because God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. Be humbled therefore under the mighty <margin>B</margin> hand of God, so that He may lift you up when the time is opportune. All your care being cast upon Him, for He has a care for you. Be sober, watch, because your adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion, <margin>9</margin> seeking someone to devour. Resist him, solid in faith, knowing that these same afflictions are being completed in your <margin>10</margin> brotherhood which is in the world. But the God of all grace, who called us to His eternal glory through Christ Jesus, after you have been afflicted a little while, <margin>11</margin> may He Himself restore, support, strengthen, and establish you. To Him be glory and empire <margin>12</margin> forever and ever, amen. By Sylvanus, a faithful brother to you, as I judge, I have written in few words, exhorting and testifying that this is the true grace of God, in <margin>C</margin> <margin>13</margin> which you stand. She who is in Babylon, the partner of your election, greets you, as does Mark my son.
<meta>catchword: Greet-</meta>

---

...and "seeking something to devour," so that it appears the codices varied among both the Greeks and the Latins.

15 **Resist strongly**] <note>original: "stereoi"</note>, that is, firm and solid.

16 **The same passion**] <note>original: "ta auta ton pathematon"</note>, that is, the same sufferings, or rather afflictions.

17 **To your brotherhood**] <note>original: "epiteleisthai"</note>, that is, to be perfected or fulfilled.

<margin>B</margin> 18 **He will perfect, confirm, solidify**] In Greek it is: "May he himself perfect you, support you, with confirmation and foundation." Although I am not unaware that these three can be taken as verbs in the future tense: "he will support, he will confirm, he will found." In some Greek copies, these were optative forms: "may he confirm, may he strengthen, may he found."

<margin>D</margin> 19 **By Sylvanus**] The phrase is ambiguous, whether Sylvanus wrote at Peter's command, or if Peter gave the letter to Sylvanus to be delivered.

20 **I have written briefly**] <note>original: "di' oligon egrapsa"</note>, that is, I have written in few words.

<margin>C</margin> 21 **Collected in Babylon**] <note>original: "he en Babyloni syneklekte"</note>, that is, she who is chosen together in Babylon, meaning the partner of your election. And Jerome cites it almost this way in the *Catalog of Illustrious Men* regarding Mark. Though there, neither Jerome’s Latin nor Sophronius’s Greek were entirely free of errors. Bede, explaining this passage, reads "co-elect," which the scribe corrupted into "collected." In two very ancient copies of Donatianus, it was written as "con-elect." There are those who interpret "Babylon" here as Rome, which does not entirely convince me. I think it more likely that Peter truly lived in Babylon at that time. But Papias, as cited by Eusebius, indicated that Peter designated Rome by the name of Babylon. Yet the same Eusebius elsewhere rejects the authority of Papias, because he records certain things as if heard from the Apostles; he does not dare to say things he had not heard, but things he had not <margin>E</margin> understood, preferring to deprive him of intelligence rather than of faith. If anyone does not believe this, let him read the final chapter of the third book, where he frankly pronounces that from Papias's little works which he wrote, it is clear that he was a man of meager intellect and less capacity, whose ignorance gave occasion to the error of the Chiliasts <note>believers in a literal 1,000-year earthly reign of Christ</note>. Nor has it escaped me that Saint Jerome, following Papias in a certain letter, designated Rome by the name of Babylon, but he was serving his own resentment because he had been unworthily treated there. But what reason could there be why Blessed Peter preferred to say Babylon rather than Rome? Was it because idols were worshiped at Rome? At that time, that was done everywhere, except in the region of the Jews. Or did he not want it known where he was active when he wrote this letter? For since he writes to Jews dispersed through all nations, how could they, being far removed, divine that he was writing from the city of Rome when they read the title "of Babylon"? Add to this that nothing is contained in this Epistle that could offend the Romans, unless perhaps <margin>F</margin> that there were some there who embraced the Gospel faith. But whence this great timidity in the Prince of the Apostles? By similar reasoning, he ought not to have named so many regions in the salutation in which he reveals there are Christians. It is truly frivolous what some quibble: that the primacy of the Roman see wavers if Peter wrote this letter from Babylon—as if it could not be that Peter, while writing these things, was active in Babylon and afterward sat at Rome. Nor is it difficult to believe what Ecclesiastical History relates: that Peter preached the Gospel in those regions which he names in the preface. Therefore, it could have happened that while active in Babylon, he confirmed by letter those he had instructed, and to console them, added that even in Babylon there were those who had received the word of God. Nor is it established at what time he wrote this letter. For the fact that he calls himself a "fellow-elder" while addressing the elders does not prove Peter’s old age. For he calls "Elders" the Bishops and pastors, with whom he equals himself out of his modesty. In the Second Epistle, however, he declares that he is already near death; therefore, nothing forbids us from believing that the first Epistle was written before he came to Rome. But if the primacy of the Roman see is taken from the location, it is established that Peter sat first at Antioch, and it is known...
<meta>catchword: known</meta>

He also offers a critical historical analysis of whether "Babylon" refers to Rome or the literal city in Mesopotamia, questioning the reliability of the early church writer Papias.</summary>

# PREFACE
->to the second Catholic Epistle of the holy Apostle<-

# PETER.
The same Peter writes this again to those who already believe. This Epistle is a reminder of the first things; for knowing that the dissolution of his body would be swift <note>a reference to his impending martyrdom</note>, he was eager to remind everyone of the teaching in which they were instructed. And first, he shows that it was proclaimed by the Prophets, and that the prophecies concerning the Savior are not of human origin, but were spoken concerning God. Then he commands them not to pay attention to those who deceive, saying that their destruction will come, just as it happened to the angels who transgressed. He foretells in the Epistle that days will come in which mockers will walk about, wishing to deceive some, saying that the coming of the Savior is spoken of by us in vain, because everything continues as it was and He has not yet arrived. He therefore commands them to keep away from these people especially, teaching them not to be discouraged by the passage of time; for all time is nothing before the Lord, because one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. He confirms and demonstrates that the day of the Lord will come quickly, and he commands everyone to be ready for it through good works, and to love the things written by the Apostle Paul, and not to pay attention to those who slander them, for those people slander all the divine scriptures. Thus, having reminded and taught everyone to foresee these matters, he exhorts them not to fall from the goal of faith, and so he completes the Epistle.

---

### ON THE EPISTLE OF
# PETER II.
->Argument by<-
### DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.
This, as it appears, he wrote when he was quite old and now close to death, since he mentions his own passing. He writes generally to all Christians, exhorting them to purity of life, and—using the examples of the ancients and the terror of the final judgment—deterring them from disturbances. He vehemently attacks those who would corrupt the minds of the simple with perverse doctrine, denying that Christ will return.

---

<header>EPISTLE CHAPTER I.</header>

<margin>1</margin> [Seeing that] his divine power has given to us all things that pertain to life <margin>2</margin> and godliness, through the knowledge of <margin>3</margin> him who called us by glory and virtue, <margin>4</margin> through which he has given us <margin>4</margin> precious and very great promises, <margin>5</margin> so that through these you might become partakers of the divine nature, having <margin>6</margin> escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust. <margin>5</margin> And <margin>7</margin> for this very reason, applying all diligence, <margin>8</margin> supply in your faith virtue, and in <margin>9</margin> virtue knowledge, <margin>6</margin> and in knowledge <margin>10</margin> self-control, and in self-control patience, and <margin>11</margin> in patience godliness, <margin>7</margin> and in godliness <margin>12</margin> brotherly affection, and in brotherly affection <margin>13</margin> love. <margin>8</margin> For if these things are yours and abound, <margin>14</margin> they make you neither idle nor unfruitful in the <margin>15</margin> knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. <margin>9</margin> For he who <margin>16</margin> lacks these things is blind, shortsighted, having forgotten <margin>17</margin> the cleansing of his old sins. <margin>10</margin> Therefore the more, <margin>18</margin> brothers, be diligent to make your <margin>19</margin> calling and election sure; for by doing these things, you <margin>20</margin> will never stumble. <margin>11</margin> For in this way there will be richly <margin>21</margin> supplied to you the entrance into the eternal kingdom of <margin>22</margin> our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. <margin>12</margin> Therefore I will not <margin>23</margin> neglect to remind you always about these things, <margin>24</margin> although you know them and are established in the present <margin>25</margin> truth. <margin>13</margin> I think it right, as long as I am in <margin>26</margin> this tabernacle <note>a metaphor for the physical body</note>, to stir you up by a <margin>27</margin> reminder, <margin>14</margin> knowing that the laying aside of my <margin>28</margin> tabernacle is swift, just as our Lord Jesus Christ <margin>29</margin> has revealed to me. <margin>15</margin> Moreover, I will be diligent so that at every opportunity <margin>30</margin> after my departure you may be able to remember these things. <margin>31</margin> <margin>16</margin> For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made <margin>32</margin> known to you the power of our Lord Jesus Christ...

<column-break/>

Divine power has bestowed all things upon us which pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us <gloss>6</gloss> by glory and virtue. <gloss>7</gloss> Through which precious <margin>4</margin> and very great promises <gloss>8</gloss> have been given to us, <gloss>9</gloss> so that through these you might be made sharers of the divine nature, <gloss>10</gloss> if you flee from the corruption which is in the world <gloss>11</gloss> through lust. <gloss>12</gloss> But for this very purpose, having applied all study, <margin>5</margin> supply <gloss>13</gloss> in your faith virtue, and in virtue indeed knowledge, <gloss>14</gloss> and in knowledge indeed temperance, in <margin>6</margin> temperance indeed patience, again in patience godliness, and in godliness <gloss>15</gloss> brotherly charity, and in <margin>7</margin> brotherly charity love. For when these <margin>8</gloss> are present <gloss>16</gloss> and abound in you, they make you neither idle nor working in vain toward the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. For he to whom these are not present <margin>9</margin> is blind, <gloss>17</gloss> and groping for the way with his hand, having forgotten that he was purged from his old sins. For in this manner <margin>11</margin> there will be abundantly supplied to you the entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. <gloss>20</gloss> Wherefore I will not neglect to <margin>12</margin> always remind you of these things, <gloss>21</gloss> although you know them, and are confirmed <gloss>22</gloss> in the present truth. Indeed, <margin>15</margin> I will <gloss>23</gloss> always give effort, so that you <gloss>24</gloss> after my departure <gloss>25</gloss> may be able to make mention of these things. <gloss>26</gloss> For <margin>16</margin> not having followed artfully composed fables, have we made known to you...

<columns>2</columns>

<insert>All things that his divine power, etc.</insert> <note>original: τὰ ἡμῖν τῆς θείας δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ, κτλ.</note> that is, *As his divine power has bestowed all things upon us, which pertain to life and godliness.* and shortly after, *through the recognition* <note>original: agnitionem</note> would be more aptly "knowledge," <note>original: ἐπιγνώσεως</note>. <unclear>For knowledge</unclear> <unclear>primarily</unclear> can be a genitive absolute, and can refer back to "recognition," so that the sense here is: Through the recognition of God and Christ Jesus our Lord, as all things pertaining to salvation have been bestowed upon us by his divine power. Some incorrectly make the start of a new sentence from the word *as* <note>original: quemadmodum</note>, when this depends on what came before. Thus the grace of God is fulfilled as all things are given by him. Bede distinguishes this differently, but in this way, *as* has nothing to respond to. He also warns that in the Latin manuscripts there was a double reading; in some it was written, *which was given for life and godliness:* in others, *which things were given for life and godliness.*

<gloss>6 By his own glory and virtue</gloss>] <note>original: διὰ δόξης καὶ ἀρετῆς</note>, that is, *through glory and virtue.* At this point the reader must be warned that "virtue" is not "power" <note>original: δύναμιν</note>, which he frequently reads elsewhere, but "excellence" <note>original: ἀρετὴν</note>, which is the opposite of vice. It seemed necessary to advise this because Bede interprets "virtue" as *divine*. This is clear from his words: *Rather, seeing us weak and inglorious, he recovered us by his own virtue and glory.* He feels that Peter means that while we were bound by vices, God imparted his justice to us, and when we were cast down, he bestowed his glory upon us.

<gloss>7 Through whom the greatest and precious</gloss>] <note>original: Δι' ὧν τὰ τίμια ἡμῖν καὶ μέγιστα ἐπαγγέλματα</note>, that is, *Through which precious to us and greatest promises.* Although the Greek speech has some ambiguity, because the article "through which" <note>original: δι' ὧν</note> can refer back to "glory and virtue," or to the "all things" that preceded a little earlier.

<gloss>8 Given</gloss>] <note>original: δεδώρηται</note>, that is, *have been given.*

<gloss>9 So that through this</gloss>] <note>original: ἵνα διὰ τούτων</note>, that is, *so that through these.* Both manuscripts of the Donatiani <note>a reference to a specific set of codices Erasmus consulted</note> agree.

<gloss>10 Fleeing</gloss>] <note>original: ἀποφυγόντες</note>, that is, *escaping,* or rather, *if you shall have fled.* For it is in the past tense.

<gloss>11 In lust</gloss>] <note>original: ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ</note>, that is, *in concupiscence.*

<gloss>12 You moreover all care</gloss>] <note>original: Καὶ αὐτὸ τοῦτο δὲ σπουδὴν πᾶσαν παρεισενέγκαντες ἐπιχορηγήσατε</note>, that is, *And in this very thing moreover, bringing in all care, minister.* However, the Translator did not express the added preposition in "bringing in" <note>original: παρεισενέγκαντες</note>, that is, *bringing in incidentally or besides,* so that our care is added to the gift of which he spoke. Likewise "supply" <note>original: ἐπιχορηγήσατε</note>, that is, *additionally provide:* and this sounds like a certain addition.

<gloss>13 In your faith virtue</gloss>] It is not "power" <note>original: δύναμιν</note>, which sounds like potency or a miracle, but "excellence" <note>original: ἀρετὴν</note>, which refers to the goodness of character that accompanies faith. Bede also noted this.

<gloss>14 In knowledge abstinence</gloss>] <note>original: ἐγκράτειαν</note>, that is, *temperance.*

<gloss>15 Love of the brotherhood</gloss>] <note>original: φιλαδελφίαν</note>, that is, *fraternal love,* as I have now often advised. Furthermore, because he subjects "love" <note>original: ἀγάπην</note> to "fraternal charity," he either said the same thing twice, or added it as something more general and broader: so that "fraternal love" refers to the mutual love of Christians among themselves, since the Apostles call us brothers; "love" <note>original: dilectio</note> to all people, even the Pagans: or "agape" is something more intense than "philia": or "brotherly love" refers to affection, "love" to the action. But the middle opinion pleases me more.

<gloss>16 Be present and abound</gloss>] Since it is "abounding" <note>original: πλεονάζοντα</note>, what Bede ascribes here cannot have a place, "if they have prevailed with better virtue against the wars of vices." For "to overcome" is not transitive in this place, but neuter, having the same force as *to abound.* Lorenzo <note>likely Lorenzo Valla, the humanist critic</note> finds fault

<sig>F</sig>

<column-break/>

with the inelegance of the phrase, "if it be present with you" <note>original: si vobiscum adsit</note>. But this was committed not by the fault of the Translator, but the Scribe. For it should be "these things when they are present and abound in you": then a reader, not paying enough attention, finding the conjunction written "with you" <note>original: vobiscum</note>, thinking something was missing, added "is" <note>original: fit</note>. When I had guessed this, I found the genuine reading in both Constantiensi manuscripts. What he calls "are present" is in Greek <note>original: ὑπάρχοντα</note>, which sounds like "are at hand." Now, what is "at hand" is what is sufficient for use. Since that word seemed more frugal, he added "and abounding" <note>original: καὶ πλεονάζοντα</note>, a word of abundance. For shortly after is "fruits" <note>original: κάρποι</note>, which comes quite elegantly, especially.

<gloss>17 And groping with the hand</gloss>] <note>original: μυωπάζων</note>. It is certain that the word is composite. It seems, moreover, to be a metaphor derived from mice <note>original: μυὸς / mus</note>, which are accustomed to follow a wall, or a board, or whatever else is in the way, until they find a hole. Although it is read as "of a mouse," and a type of fly that infests the eyes of cattle, from which the verb "to be shortsighted" <note>original: μυωπάζειν</note> might seem to be said. The Apostle added this to express profound blindness. For those with dim sight see large bodies, so that the guidance of the hands is not necessary.

<gloss>18 Busy yourselves more</gloss>] <note>original: σπουδάσατε</note>, that is, *give effort, or study.* Nor is it "busy yourselves more," but "rather brothers busy yourselves," so that "rather" <note>original: magis</note> is for correcting, not for increasing: as if you said, "Rather busy yourselves, rather than these things be lacking to you, give effort that you may attain them." And in this place I would certainly prefer "given effort," or "be admitted," than "be busy."

<gloss>19 That through good works</gloss>] "Through good works" I do not find added among the Greeks. "Your certain calling," <note>original: βεβαίαν</note>, that is, firm, or ratified. "Of you" <note>original: vestri</note> is better than "your" <note>original: vestram</note>.

<gloss>20 Because of which I will begin</gloss>] It is far different in Greek, <note>original: διὸ οὐκ ἀμελήσω</note>, that is, *I will not neglect, or I will not omit:* even if Bede reads and interprets it as *I will begin.* What of the fact that the speech itself displays absurdity? For who says they "always begin" what they do constantly? Perhaps the Translator, if indeed he turned it this way, looked at "I will be about to" <note>original: μελλήσω</note>, and turned a double negative into an affirmation. And I do not know whether he read "if I shall be about to" <note>original: αἰ μελλήσω</note>, that is, "I will not delay."

<gloss>21 Indeed knowing</gloss>] <note>original: καίπερ</note>, that is, *although, or even though.* For in this way he softens the admonition.

<gloss>22 In the present truth</gloss>] Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra, a 14th-century commentator</note> indicates that in some manuscripts "I wish" <note>original: volo</note> is added here, and must be supplied entirely, not noticing that the accusative case depends on the verb that preceded, "to remind," when we say, *I will remind you though you are mindful.*

<gloss>23 Frequently</gloss>] <note>original: ἑκάστοτε</note>, that is, *always, that is, I shall not cease as long as I live.*

<gloss>24 After death</gloss>] <note>original: ἔξοδον</note>, that is, *exit* <note>the word "Exodus"</note>, for he had mentioned the tabernacle.

<gloss>25 So that of all these</gloss>] "All" is redundant. Nor was it added in either manuscript of the Donatiani. Three very ancient manuscripts, which were present to me in the fourth Edition, supported this. The context of this speech is somewhat more disturbed, and because of that, more obscure. For they could be composed in Greek as, *I will give effort also at every opportunity, to have you make mention of these after my exit,* that is, *Indeed I will always give effort, whereby you may be able to make mention of these after my exit.* For "to have" <note>original: ἔχειν</note> is placed in the stead of "to do" <note>original: ποιεῖν</note> for "to be able," and refers to the infinite verb "to make" <note>original: ποιεῖσθαι</note>. It is moreover the same verb which he translated a little earlier as *busy yourselves.*

<gloss>26 For not following introduced fables</gloss>] <note>original: σεσοφισμένοις μύθοις</note>, that is, *artfully fashioned fables.* And I do not know whether the Translator turned it as "learned fables," which Peter opposes to the simple and rustic truth. Such were formerly the cleverness of the Philosophers rather than healthy disputes...

And many will follow 2 their ruin, through whom the way of truth will be affected by curses. And through 3 avarice they will trade in you with made-up words; for whom judgment has not been slow for a long time, and their perdition does not sleep. For if God 4 did not spare the angels who sinned, but delivered them into Tartarus, cast down in chains of night, saved for judgment; and did not spare the ancient world, but 5 saved Noah, the eighth herald of justice, when a flood was brought into the world of the impious; and condemned the cities of Sodom and 6 Gomorrah to ashes by an overthrow, and made them 12 an example to those who would act impiously; and rescued just Lot, who was oppressed by 7 lawless men through their lustful conversation. 14 For 8 that just man, in sight and hearing, while he lived among them, tormented his just soul daily with their iniquitous deeds.

---

[The following are Erasmus's notes on the text above]

**27 Power and presence]** <note>original: *δύναμιν καὶ παρουσίαν* (dynamin kai parousian)</note>, that is, virtue, or power, and arrival. For he frequently translates *parousian* this way. It appears, however, that "presence" <note>original: *praesentiam*</note> was once written: for he sometimes translates *parousian* that way too; then, by a scribe's error, it was changed to "foreknowledge" <note>original: *praescientiam*</note>. And yet, from that scribe’s drowsiness, great theologians—among whose number is Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a major medieval biblical commentator</note>—gave birth to a huge mystery. Not that I would mock those who provided what they could, but I think those who were forced to handle the Sacred Scriptures without being sufficiently instructed in literature—without which these things cannot be handled as they deserve—are to be pitied. In the older and more reliable Donatian codex, "presence" was written. And old manuscripts support this. For Peter says the same thing here as Paul does elsewhere: that he did not preach the coming of Christ with the wisdom of the word, but by the power <note>original: *virtute*</note> of the spirit.

**28 Of his magnitude]** "His" <note>original: *illius*</note> here is masculine and refers to God, not to the magnitude.

**29 In whom I am well pleased]** Since he here professes that he was one of those who heard the voice of the Father on the mountain when the Lord was transfigured, it is a wonder that some have doubted whether this Epistle was Peter's. For if it is not Peter's, it must necessarily be John's or James's, or that voice was produced on the mountain at another time, or someone falsely usurped the title of Peter for himself—none of which are likely, and the last is even vehemently absurd. And yet the Ancients, who doubted the author of this Epistle, were not ignorant that this was written in this Epistle. It is clear there is an evident difference in style between this and the first.

**30 And we have a firmer]** <note>original: *Καὶ ἔχομεν βεβαιότερον* (Kai echomen bebaioteron)</note>. In this place, the moderns sweat profusely trying to explain how Peter could say the speech of the Prophets is "firmer" than his own or that of the Father. But it is the custom of the Greeks to occasionally use the comparative for the positive. Augustine seems to have felt this, citing this passage in his *Fifty-seventh Homily*, being not at all offended by the comparative "more certain" <note>original: *certiorem*</note>; for that is how he read it, instead of "firmer" <note>original: *firmiorem*</note>. Furthermore, he did not simply say the speech of the Prophets was firmer, but that what was already said was "more certain," with the voice of the Father attesting to their words. Finally, the Father himself was in a way the prophet and herald of his own Son, foretelling openly all things that would please him, which the Son was going to say or do. And hence the prophetic word was firmer than the speech of the Prophets whom they [the Jews] venerated; which Peter does not disapprove of, provided they understand those prophecies are to be interpreted spiritually, not in the Jewish manner. I think this last sense is the true one of Peter, though I would not argue if someone prefers Augustine's commentary on the words of the Lord in *Sermon 27*, noting that the prophetic word was called "more certain," not "truer" or "better," because detractors could attribute a voice brought down from heaven to magical tricks, which they could not do regarding the prophetic word, which had preceded it.

**31 Private interpretation]** <note>original: *ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως οὐ γίνεται* (idias epilyseos ou ginetai)</note>, that is, it does not become of one's own interpretation. The Greek word is derived from "loosening" <note>original: *solvendo*</note>, which fits intricate things; or from "approaching," which fits better what follows. For they did not approach the publishing of prophecies by their own will, but were approached by the impulse of the Spirit.

**32 Inspired by the Holy Spirit]** <note>original: *ὑπὸ Πνεύματος ἁγίου φερόμενοι* (hypo Pneumatos hagiou pheromenoi)</note>, that is, snatched, or agitated, or impelled by the Holy Spirit.

**1 Denying the God who bought them]** <note>original: *καὶ τὸν ἀγοράσαντα αὐτοὺς δεσπότην ἀρνούμενοι*</note>, that is, and denying the Master <note>original: *Dominum*</note> who traded for them.

**2 Their luxuries]** <note>original: *ἀπωλείαις* (apoleiais)</note>, that is, destructions or ruins. The translators seem to have read *aselgeiais* <note>sensualities</note> or *aselgeion*. Although the Greek manuscripts that I have seen agree [on *apoleiais*].

**3 They will trade in you]** <note>original: *ὑμᾶς ἐμπορεύσονται* (hymas emporeusontai)</note>, they will hawk you like tavern-keepers and use you for profit. How well Peter depicted what we see today, where by many priests nothing is handled that is not for profit?

**4 Does not cease]** <note>original: *οὐκ ἀργεῖ* (ouk argei)</note>, that is, it is not slow. Not noticing this, Bede interprets it as "does not cease, that is, does not stop."

**5 For if God did not spare the sinning Angels]** Bede thinks there is a transposition <term>hyperbaton: a figure of speech where the natural order of words is changed</term> here, and finally it is resolved there: "The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation." "Sinning angels" <note>original: *ἁμαρτήσασιν*</note>, that is, those who had sinned.

**6 But with cables]** <note>original: *σειραῖς* (seirais)</note>, that is, chains. The Translator [of the Vulgate] said "cables" <note>original: *rudentes*</note>, meaning huge ropes like those used by sailors. Augustine in some places reads "prisons" instead of cables. Bede interprets "cables" in a forced way, since the Greek word sounds like "chains." He adds that in some codices "roaring" <note>original: *rugientibus*</note> is found instead of "cables," which he certainly would have rejected if he had known Greek and consulted Greek manuscripts. "Hell" <note>original: *ζόφου* (zophou)</note>, that is, of darkness. Although *zophou* in Greek signifies a "Tartarean cave," and darkness, and the setting of the sun.

**7 Delivered into Tartarus]** <note>original: *ταρταρώσας παρέδωκεν* (tartarōsas paredōken)</note>, that is, having thrust them into Tartarus, he delivered them to chains.

**8 To be tortured for judgment]** <note>original: *εἰς κρίσιν τηρουμένους* (eis krisin tēroumenous)</note>, that is, saved or to be saved for judgment. Even if some Greek codices have "having been saved" <note>original: *τετηρημένους*</note>.

**9 The original world]** <note>original: *ἀρχαίου κόσμου*</note>, that is, the ancient world. He means the early world as recently established.

**10 Herald of justice]** The Aldine Edition has "the herald" <note>original: *τὸν κήρυκα*</note>, but it should be "preaching" <note>original: *κήρυγμα*</note>, to refer to what follows, "example."

**11 He guarded]** <note>original: *ἐφύλαξεν*</note>, that is, he saved.

**12 Example]** Here it is not *paradeigma*, but *hypodeigma*, so that you understand an example not to be imitated, but one that warns what is to be avoided.

**13 From the injury and lustful conversation of the lawless]** In Greek it is: "by the conduct of the lawless in sensuality," that is, from those who were lawless through their lascivious lifestyle.

**14 For in sight and hearing]** The Greek differs somewhat from the Latin: "For in sight and hearing the just man, dwelling among them, day after day tormented his just soul with lawless deeds," or tested it. For it means that since he had holy eyes and holy ears that abhorred all filth, he was gravely tormented because, living among them, he was forced daily to see and hear what he did not want to. Bede does not touch this passage. Indeed, the corruption between "he tormented" <note>original: *ἐβασάνιζεν*</note> and "they tormented" <note>original: *ἐβασάνισεν*</note> is easy. But there is a huge consensus in the Greek codices, and if you read "they tormented," it contradicts the rules of grammar, unless you take the nominative words for genitives absolute.

<summary>This page contains Erasmus's commentary on 2 Peter 1:16–2:8, where he defends the authenticity of the epistle and discusses the precise Greek vocabulary regarding the Transfiguration, prophecy, and the judgment of the ungodly. He famously critiques scribal errors in the Vulgate, such as the confusion between "chains" and "cables" or "roaring" in the description of Tartarus.</summary>
<keywords>Transfiguration, prophetic word, private interpretation, Tartarus, Noah, Sodom and Gomorrah, Lot, philology, Vulgate errors, Bede, Augustine</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s philological annotations on the Second Epistle of Peter. Having concluded Chapter 1 on the previous page, he now moves into Chapter 2, providing the Greek text alongside the Latin Vulgate and his detailed scholarly critiques of the translation. He focuses on the descriptions of false teachers and the judgment awaiting them.</meta>

# EPISTLE CHAPTER II.

<margin>9</margin> 9 The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, and to keep the unrighteous for the day of judgment while they are being punished, <margin>10</margin> 10 Especially those who go after the flesh in the desire of pollution, and despise authority; daring and self-willed, they do not tremble as they blaspheme against glories. <margin>11</margin> 11 Whereas angels, who are greater in strength and power, do not bring a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord. <margin>12</margin> 12 But these, like irrational animals, naturally born for capture and destruction, blaspheming in matters they do not understand, shall perish in their own corruption, <margin>13</margin> 13 Receiving the reward of unrighteousness; counting as pleasure the luxury of the day; they are spots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions, feasting with <margin>14</margin> you, 14 Having eyes full of an adulteress, and unceasing from sin, enticing unstable souls; having a heart trained in greed; children of a curse. <margin>15</margin> 15 Leaving the straight path, they have gone astray, following the way of Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the reward of unrighteousness, <margin>16</margin> 16 But was rebuked for his own lawlessness: a mute beast of burden, speaking with a human voice, restrained the madness of the Prophet. <margin>17</margin> 17 These are waterless springs, mists driven by a storm, for whom the gloom of darkness is reserved forever. <margin>18</margin> 18 For speaking swelling words of vanity, they entice with the desires of the flesh and with debaucheries those who had truly escaped from those living in error, <margin>19</margin> 19 Promising them freedom, while they themselves are slaves of corruption: for by whatever a man is overcome

<column-break/>

15 The Lord knows how to rescue the pious from temptation, <margin>9</margin> but to keep the unjust to be punished on the day of judgment, 17 especially those who, following the flesh, walk in the <margin>10</margin> lust of pollution, 18 and despise lordship; bold, 19 stubborn, 20 who, though they excel in glory, do not fear to attack with insults. Whereas <margin>11</margin> the angels themselves, who are greater in strength and power, 21 do not bring against themselves before the Lord 22 a cursed judgment. But these, like 23 brute beasts, by nature 24 born to be captured and destroyed, speaking evil in things they do <margin>12</margin> not understand, shall perish in their own destruction, <margin>B</margin> receiving the reward of unrighteousness, 25 counting it a pleasure to enjoy delights for a day, 26 stains and blemishes, who, banqueting 27 in their errors 28 insult <margin>13</margin> you, having eyes 29 full of an adulteress, and 30 who <margin>14</margin> do not know how to cease from sinning, 31 enticing unstable souls, having a heart practiced in greed, accursed children, who, having left the right path, have gone astray, following the way of Balaam 32 the son of Bosor, who loved the reward of iniquity, but was rebuked 33 for his iniquity: a mute <margin>15</margin> beast of burden, speaking with a human voice, prohibited the <margin>16</margin> madness of the Prophet. These are springs lacking water, clouds which 34 are carried by a storm, for whom the mist 35 of darkness is reserved forever. 36 For where <margin>17</margin> <margin>C</margin> the haughty words of vanity have sounded loudly, 37 they <margin>18</margin> entice men through the lusts of the flesh with pleasures, 38 those who have truly fled from those who live in error, while they promise them liberty, although <margin>19</margin> they themselves are the slaves of corruption: for by whom anyone is overcome

---

15 **The Lord knows]** <note>original: "Novit Deus"</note> The Greek says *Kyrios*, that is, "the Lord." Though in these words, scribes often use one for the other.

16 **To keep them to be tormented]** <note>original: "Servare cruciandos"</note> The Greek is *kolazomenous*. You should understand that they are punished in the meantime while they are being kept. The translator seems to have read it as *kolasthesomenous* <note>the future tense: "those who will be punished"</note>. And it seems Origen <note>an early Christian scholar from Alexandria</note> read it this way, for he thought the wicked demons were not to be subjected to the fire before the final day of judgment. Supporting Origen's opinion is the fact that in the Gospel, the demons cry out, "Have you come to torment us before the time?" But here, Peter is not strictly discussing demons, but the souls of the ungodly.

17 **But especially those]** <note>original: "Magis autem eos"</note> The Greek is *Malista*, that is, "Maxime" <note>most of all</note>, unless perhaps the superlative is used in place of the comparative, which happens frequently in the Greek language.

18 **And lordship]** <note>original: "Dominationemque"</note> The Greek is *kai kyriotetos*, that is, "and authority," meaning those endowed with legitimate power: for *kyrios* often means not simply "master," but one who possesses authority and has the right of prescribing rules.

19 **Self-pleasing]** <note>original: "Sibi placentes"</note> The Greek is *authadeis*, that is, stubborn, or what is commonly called "a law unto themselves" or "their own masters."

20 **They do not fear sects]** <note>original: "Sectas non metuunt"</note> The Greek is *doxas ou tremousi*, that is, "they do not tremble at opinions." Although in this place, "tremble" is used for "fear." To me, the sense seems far different from what the common crowd of theologians interprets, if I may say so with everyone's peace. For Peter is dealing with the stubborn and intractable, who do not obey their superiors and bishops: whom he calls *authadeis* and *tolmetas* <note>bold</note>, and "despisers of authority." Not content with this, they do not fear even to attack with insults men endowed with glory and majesty. For these, unless I am mistaken, he calls *doxas* <note>glories/dignities</note>, just as a little earlier Paul calls them *kyriotetas* <note>lordships</note>. Furthermore, the participle "blaspheming" <note>original: "blasphemoūntes"</note>, according to the property of the Greek speech, is put in place of an infinitive verb: "they do not fear blaspheming," instead of "they do not fear to blaspheme." It seems, however, that "lordships" is something less than "glories." For any master has lordship over a slave, but not immediately "glory." But a Prince or a Magistrate has "glory," whence one who violates that majesty is usually accused of treason. Jude uses the same words and in the same sense in his Epistle: "they reject lordship, but they blaspheme glories." Now, as for that word "to introduce," you should know it is a later addition, as it is found neither in the Greek codices nor in the ancient copies. For in both the Constance and Basel manuscripts, it was written "they do not fear blaspheming sects," and there was no trace of an insertion or erasure. Therefore, a reader offended by the absurdity of the Latin phrase added "to introduce."

21 **They do not carry]** <note>original: "Non portant"</note> The Greek is *ou pherousi*, that is, "they do not bear." It is a wonder why the word "carrying" was preferred here. *Against themselves.* After these words, the Greeks add *para Kyrio*, that is, "before the Lord."

<margin>F</margin> 22 **Execrable judgment]** <note>original: "Execrabile judicium"</note> The Greek is *blasphemon krisin*, that is, a blasphemous judgment, as if it were abominable and of ill omen. For he seems to have used "blasphemous" for "evil-speaking."

23 **Irrational beasts]** <note>original: "Irrationabilia pecora"</note> The Greek is *aloga zoa*, that is, mute living creatures; for he is not speaking only of sheep. Certainly, in the Epistle of Jude, he translates it "animals": *alogon*, however, means both that which lacks speech and that which is devoid of reason.

24 **Naturally]** <note>original: "Naturaliter"</note> The Greek is *gegennemena*, that is, "born." Although it seems to me that *gegennemena* was added by the Greeks in place of a <term>scholium</term> <note>a marginal explanatory note in a manuscript</note> by someone who wanted to interpret what *physika* <note>natural</note> meant, and someone else moved it into the text: for he said, "natural for capture," just as we say "born to learn," meaning "composed by nature." Then "natural things" was translated elsewhere as "naturally." Otherwise, what animals are *not* natural? Is man not a natural animal? Furthermore, "capture" <note>original: "captio"</note> here does not sound like fraud, but servitude. For it is *eis halosin* <note>for capture</note>, not *theran* <note>hunting</note>, which is in Psalm 133: "And he did not give us into capture." Again in Psalm 34: "And the capture which he hid," *he thera*.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, what is translated here as "destruction," in the Greek is *phthora*, which word signifies both ruin and destruction. He translates the same word soon after as "corruption."

25 **The delights of the day]** <note>original: "Diei delicias"</note> The Greek is *ten en hemera tryphen*, that is, "daytime luxuries." Bede <note>the Venerable Bede, an 8th-century monk</note> mentions that some distinguish it this way: "receiving the reward of unrighteousness as a pleasure," so that their foul pleasure is even their punishment, according to the saying, "he gave them over to a reprobate mind." But he prefers to follow the distinction which he says he found in the works of the blessed Pope Gregory. Yet if the first reading is accepted, the word "thinking" <note>original: "existimantes"</note> has no object. As for what he said, "the luxury in the day," it either means that they live for the day, unconcerned about the future, or he wants their luxury to seem more shameful because they feast even during the day, whereas according to Paul, those who are drunk are drunk at night. And concerning one who is lustful at night and sober in the morning, Prudentius <note>a Roman Christian poet</note> says, "And the trifler tastes of the chaste."

26 **Of defilement and spots]** <note>original: "Coinquinationis & maculæ"</note> The Greek is *spiloi kai momoi*. Both should be read in the nominative case <note>the subject case</note>, not the genitive <note>the possessive case</note>. For he calls the men themselves "spots" and "stains," which makes the speech more forceful.

27 **In their banquets]** <note>original: "In conviviis suis"</note> The Greek is *en tais apatais auton*, that is, "in their deceptions." The translator seems to have read *agapais* <note>love-feasts</note> instead of *apatais*. Furthermore, since the scribe did not understand *agape*, which in Greek sounds like "charity" and is sometimes used for a banquet, suspecting the place was faulty, he corrected it to *apatais*. Jude used the same word in his Epistle, about which we will say something there.

28 **Reveling with you]** <note>original: "Luxuriantes vobiscum"</note> The Greek is *syneuochoúmenoi hymin*, that is, "feasting with you." Although another sense can be drawn from these words, so that <margin>E</margin> the dative "with you" <note>original: "hymin"</note> refers to the participle "insulting" <note>original: "entryphontes"</note>, and "feasting together" to the phrase "like irrational beasts," so that this would be the sum of the meaning: "Insulting you and speaking evil in their errors, while they feast among themselves."

29 **Full of adultery]** <note>original: "Plenos adulterii"</note> The Greek is *mestous moichalidos*, that is, "full of an adulteress," so that you understand them to be lewd and impudent. Cyprian <note>a 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage</note>, explaining the Creed, reads "full of adulteries," if the text does not deceive.

30 **Unceasing of sin]** <note>original: "Incessabiles delicti"</note> The Greek is *akatapaustous hamartias*, that is, those who cannot be restrained from sinning.

31 **Enticing]** <note>original: "Pellicientes"</note> The Greek is *deleazontes*, that is, "baiting with food": for *delear* means "bait."

32 **From Bosor]** <note>original: "Ex Bosor"</note> The Greek is *tou Bosor*, that is, "the son of Bosor."

33 **Of his own madness]** <note>original: "Suæ vesaniæ"</note> The Greek is *idias paranonias*, that is, "of his own iniquity." I suspect the translator read *paraphorias*, which word sounds like intemperance from excessive drinking.

34 **By whirlwinds]** <note>original: "Turbinibus"</note> The Greek is *hypo lailapos*, that is, "by a whirlwind" or "by a storm." "Driven" is *elaunomenai*, that is, "which are carried," or "driven," or "impelled."

35 **Of darkness is reserved]** <note>original: "Tenebrarum reservatur"</note> The Greek is *eis aiona teteretai*, that is, "is kept for an age" or "forever."

36 **For the pride of vanity]** <note>original: "Superbia enim vanitatis"</note> The Greek is *Hyperonka gar tes mataiotetos phthenxamenoi*. I think the translator wrote "proud things" <note>original: "superba"</note> to correspond to *hyperonka*, and that it was changed to "pride" <note>original: "superbia"</note> by a scribe's error. And that this conjecture is not vain is indicated by that older codex of Donatianus, which was supported by the Constance copy. It could be translated in this way: "For having spoken exceedingly haughty words of vanity, they entice in the lust of the flesh with debaucheries." The meaning does not differ from that of Juvenal <note>a Roman satiric poet</note>:
> — — — — but they are worse, who attack such things 
> with the words of Hercules, and having spoken of virtue, etc.

37 **They entice in desires]** <note>original: "Pelliciunt in desideriis"</note> The Greek is *deleazousin*, that is, "they bait." However, the translator translated correctly. "Of luxury" is *aselgeiais*, that is, "with debaucheries."

38 **Those who flee a little]** <note>original: "Qui paululum effugiunt"</note> The Greek is *tous ontos apophygontas*, that is, "those who have truly fled." Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a pioneer of Renaissance philology</note> suspects the translator translated it as "entirely" <note>original: "plane"</note>, and that it was corrupted into "a little" <note>original: "paululum"</note>. To me, it seems more probable that for *ontos* <note>truly</note>, the translator's copy had *oligos* <note>a little</note>, or certainly *oligon*. For this adverb frequently has a diminishing force, as noted by the Ancients.

<summary>Erasmus provides a detailed philological commentary on 2 Peter 2:9-19, correcting the Latin Vulgate's translation of terms describing false teachers, such as their "haughty words" and their "baiting" of unstable souls. He argues that the text refers to those who disrespect church authority and bishops, rather than just abstract doctrinal sects.</summary>
