<meta>This page concludes the annotations on Chapter 2 of the Second Epistle of Peter and begins the commentary on Chapter 3. Erasmus continues his rigorous comparison between the Greek source text and the Latin Vulgate, focusing on the vivid metaphors of moral backsliding (the dog and the sow) and the prophetic warnings regarding the end of the world and the "day of the Lord."</meta>

# SECOND EPISTLE OF PETER CHAPTER III.

<margin>20</margin> <margin>A</margin> ...whatever someone is overcome by, to that he is also enslaved. For if, having escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first. <margin>21</margin> For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than having known it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. <margin>22</margin> But what the true proverb says has happened to them: "A dog returns to its own vomit," and, "A sow, after washing, returns to wallowing in the mire."
<margin>III. 1</margin> <margin>B</margin> This is now, beloved, the second letter I am writing to you, in both of which I stir up your pure mind by way of a reminder, <margin>2</margin> to remember the words spoken beforehand by the holy Prophets, and the commandment of us, your Apostles, from the Lord and Savior. <margin>3</margin> Knowing this first, that in the last days scoffers will come, walking according to their own desires, <margin>4</margin> and saying, "Where is the promise of his coming? For since the fathers fell asleep, all things remain as they were from the beginning of creation." <margin>5</margin> For they willfully ignore this, that the heavens existed long ago and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God, <margin>6</margin> <margin>C</margin> through which the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished. <margin>7</margin> But by the same word, the present heavens and earth are being reserved for fire, kept for the day of judgment and the destruction of ungodly men. <margin>8</margin> But do not let this one thing escape your notice, beloved, that with the Lord one day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like one day. <margin>9</margin> The Lord is not slow about his promise, as some count slowness, but is patient toward us, not wishing for any to perish, but for all to come to repentance. <margin>10</margin> But the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night, in which the heavens will pass away with a loud noise, and the elements will be dissolved by burning heat, and the earth and the works in it will be burned up. <margin>11</margin> Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in holy conduct and godliness, <margin>12</margin> <margin>D</margin> looking for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be dissolved by fire, and the elements will melt with burning heat. <margin>13</margin> But according to his promise we look for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells.

---

...is. In the Gospel of John, it says, *Jesus sat thus over the well* <note>original: "Sedebat Jesus sic super puteum"</note>. Those who *thus fled* <note>original: "sic aufugerunt"</note>, that is, who fled in whatever way. For it is certain that Jerome read *a little* <note>original: "paullulum"</note>, in his books against Jovinian, when he says, *as those who have fled a little from sins, return to their error*. However, this passage is also twisted by other difficulties. For our Latin manuscripts begin a new sentence here: *Those who live in error* <note>original: "Qui in errore conversantur"</note>. We might take this to mean those who entice others to luxury are themselves in error because they promise liberty to others while being slaves to filth. But the Greek phrasing does not allow this sense at all, which says: "they entice those who had clearly escaped from those living in error" <note>original: "δελεάζουσι τοὺς ἐν ἐπιγνώσει σαφῶς ἀποφεύγοντας τοὺς ἐν πλάνῃ ἀναστρεφομένους"</note>. Indeed, if this sense <margin>E</margin> which we follow were intended, it would have to read "living in error" <note>original: "ἐν πλάνῃ ἀναστρεφόμενοι"</note> in a different case; as it stands, both the case of the participle and the added article reject this interpretation. Even with this removed, another difficulty remains: whether this phrase, "those living in error," refers to the enticers or the enticed. If to the enticed, a conjunction seems to be missing, such as "and those in error." This would be tolerable. I would prefer it to refer to the enticers, so that the phrase "those in error" depends on the participle "fleeing," provided it allows an accusative case. Thus the sense will be: "They entice those lured by pleasure, who had begun to flee even a little from those very people who are erring in this: that they, being slaves of filth, promise liberty to others." Furthermore, where the translation here says *of corruption* <note>original: "corruptionis"</note>, the Greek is *phthoras* <note>original: "φθορᾶς"</note>, which was previously translated as *destruction*; here, a more Latin term would have been *of debauchery* <note>original: "corruptelæ"</note>.

<margin>39 Of whom he is also the slave</margin> <note>original: "τούτῳ καὶ δεδούλωται"</note>, that is, to this one he is also handed over into slavery.
<margin>40 The things have become for them &c.</margin> <note>original: "τὰ ἔσχατα χείρονα τῶν πρώτων"</note>, that is, the last things are worse than the first.
<margin>41 To not know</margin> <note>original: "μὴ ἐπεγνωκέναι"</note>, that is, not to have known.
<margin>42 In the wallowing-place of mud</margin> <note>original: "εἰς κύλισμα βορβόρου"</note>, that is, at the rolling in filth, with the word "returned" being understood. Jerome, in his Letter to Furia, says *to the wallowing-place* <note>original: "ad volutabrum"</note>. And Ambrose, to the devoted Virgin, says *Like a sow washed, returning to the wallowing*. An older manuscript from Constance held *velligium* as the sister reading, but it was erased and changed from *volutabrum* to *volutabro*.

<margin>1 Behold this</margin> <note>original: "Ταύτην ἤδη"</note>, that is, *This now*. The translator seems to have read "already" <note>original: "ἤδη"</note>.
<margin>2 In which</margin> <note>original: "ἐν αἷς"</note>. It is strange that Lorenzo Valla was not offended by this phrasing, *Epistle, in which (plural)*. Bede sensed something was off, and thus writes, "in these letters," or, "in those to whom he writes." But this latter point does not hold up, since the Greek *ais* is feminine. Therefore, the article must refer to "Epistle," but the number disagrees. This little doubt is easily settled. For when he says, *the second Epistle*, he mentions two: the word thus refers to both: *The Epistle, both the former and the latter*.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...overcome, <margin>39</margin> he is also handed over into slavery to this one.
For if, after they have fled from the defilements <margin>20</margin> of the world through the recognition of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are nevertheless again entangled in these and overcome, <margin>40</margin> the last things have become worse for them than the first. For it would have been better <margin>21</margin> for them <margin>41</margin> not to have known the way of justice, than, once they knew it, to turn back from that holy precept which was delivered to them. But it has happened to them what <margin>22</margin> the true proverb is accustomed to say: "The dog returned to his own vomit," and, "The sow that was washed returned <margin>42</margin> to the wallowing-place of filth."
<margin>III. 1</margin> <margin>B</margin> These now are the second letters I am writing to you, most dear ones, <margin>2</margin> in which I stir up your <margin>3</margin> sincere mind through a reminder, so that you may be mindful <margin>4</margin> of the words which were foretold by the holy Prophets, and <margin>5</margin> of our commandment, we who are the Apostles of the Lord and Savior; knowing this first, that in the last <margin>3</margin> days scoffers will come, who walk according to their own desires, and say, "Where is the promise of his coming? <margin>4</margin> For since the day the fathers fell asleep, all things remain <margin>6</margin> as they were from the beginning of creation." For they <margin>5</margin> ignore this willfully, that <margin>8</margin> the heavens existed long ago and the earth, consisting out of water and through water by the word of God, through <margin>6</margin> which <margin>9</margin> that world which then existed perished, flooded by water.
<margin>C</margin> But the heavens and earth which now exist, have been <margin>7</margin> stored up by the same word, and are being kept for fire on the day of judgment and the destruction of ungodly men. But let this one thing not <margin>8</margin> be hidden from you, beloved, that one day with the Lord is just as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord does not delay his promise, as <margin>9</margin> some judge it to be slowness; but <margin>10</margin> he is patient toward us, since he does not want any to perish, but all <margin>11</margin> to be received to repentance. But the day of the Lord will come <margin>12</margin> <margin>10</margin> like a thief in the night, on which the heavens will pass away with a whistling sound, the elements indeed being burned will be dissolved, and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up. Since <margin>11</margin> all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in holy conduct and piety, looking for and <margin>12</margin> <margin>D</margin> <margin>14</margin> hastening the coming of the day of God, <margin>15</margin> through which the burning heavens will be dissolved, and the <margin>16</margin> elements will melt with heat. But new heavens and a new earth <margin>17</margin> according to his promise <margin>13</margin> we look for, <margin>18</margin> in which righteousness dwells.

<margin>3 In reminder</margin> Some manuscripts have "in knowledge" <note>original: "ἐν ἐπιγνώσει"</note>.
<margin>4 Which words I foretold</margin> <note>original: "τῶν προειρημένων ῥημάτων ὑπὸ τῶν ἁγίων Προφητῶν"</note>, that is, the foretold words, or the words which were foretold by the holy Prophets.
<margin>5 Of your commandments</margin> <note>original: "ἐντολῆς"</note>, that is, "of the commandment," in the singular number. However, the sense can be twofold, though one differs very little from the other: "of the commandment of us who are the Apostles of the Lord and Savior," or "of the commandment of the Lord and Savior, which you received through us his Apostles." Thus you should understand that "of the Lord" was added for the authority of the commandment. For an Apostle reports in another’s name what he reports. I call upon your conscience, Reader: who was going to perceive the writer's mind from this Latin version <margin>E</margin>? *That you may be mindful of those things I foretold, of the words by the holy Prophets and of your Apostles' commandments of the Lord and Savior*. I do not read the word for "deception" in the Greek.
<margin>6 From the beginning of the creature</margin> <note>original: "κτίσεως"</note>, that is, of the creation or founding.

<margin>9 That world then</margin> <note>original: "ὁ τότε κόσμος"</note>, that is, the world which was then, or the world of those times.

It seems to be directed toward us, who await new heavens and a new earth, if we live justly, so that we may deserve to enjoy the novelty of creation.
19 **Without spot and blemish** <note>original: "Immaculati & inviolati"</note>] In Greek, *aspiloi kai amōmētoi*, that is, unspotted and irreproachable, or uncontaminated. I wonder where the word "inviolate" <note>original: "inviolati"</note> came into the Translator's mind here. Except perhaps that a virgin is called "inviolate" when she is uncorrupted.
20 **They distort** <note>original: "Depravant"</note>] In Greek, *strebloousin*, that is, they twist or turn away.
21 **Take care** <note>original: "Custodite"</note>] In Greek, *phylassesthe*, that is, observe, or beware.
<margin>C</margin> 22 **Lest by the error of the foolish etc.** <note>original: "Ne insipientium &c."</note>] In Greek, *tē tōn athesmōn planē synapachthentes*, that is, led away by the error of the wicked <note>Erasmus prefers "wicked" or "lawless" over the Vulgate’s "foolish."</note>. I wonder what the Translator read who rendered it "foolishness" <note>Latin: "insipientiam"</note>. Nor is it simply "led away," but *synapachthentes*, which means "led away together" with others. Augustine, in book 20, chapter 18 of *The City of God*, brings forth almost this entire chapter in this manner: <note>Erasmus provides Augustine’s version to show how the Latin text varied in the early Church.</note> "In the last of days mockers will come with mockery, going according to their own desires, and saying, 'Where is the promise of his presence? For since the fathers fell asleep, all things have continued as they were from the beginning of creation.' Thus far we have related the words of Peter the Apostle, partly so that the meaning might be clearer from the comparison, and partly so that it might appear how much Augustine’s reading differs from our Edition <note>Referring to the Vulgate Bible common in Erasmus's time.</note>. Regarding this second Epistle of Peter, there was a controversy as to whose it was. Jerome testifies to this in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Writers* <note>Also known as *De Viris Illustribus*.</note> in these words: "He wrote two Epistles which are called canonical, the second of which is denied by most to be his, because of the discrepancy of the style with the first." But the same Jerome elsewhere varies, sometimes wishing it to be Peter's and blaming the difference in style on the Interpreter <note>A secretary or translator.</note> whom Peter then used; at other times denying it is his because the style cries out against it. Eusebius, in book 3, chapter 2 <note>of his *Ecclesiastical History*</note>, testifies thus regarding this Epistle: "Truly Peter the Apostle left us very few monuments of his preaching. For there is one Epistle of his about which no one at all doubts. For concerning the second, it is uncertain to many, yet among most it is accepted as something that should be read." The difference in style both in words and in sense is clearer than can be hidden. Furthermore, since the author here testifies that he was a spectator of the vision on the mountain <note>The Transfiguration</note>, then makes mention of the previous Epistle, and finally calls Paul a brother, I am not displeased with what Jerome suggests about an Interpreter. For in the Gospel they record that Mark was the Interpreter of Peter. Otherwise, we would be forced to suspect that someone studiously inserted these marks so that he might claim it for Peter the Apostle—just as he did who wrote many things under the title of Clement. <note>Referring to the "Clementine" literature, early Christian writings falsely attributed to Pope Clement I.</note>

## THE ARGUMENT
->of the first catholic Epistle of the holy Apostle and Evangelist<-
# JOHN
### THE THEOLOGIAN.

John himself, who wrote the Gospel, sends this letter as a reminder to those who have already believed in the Lord. And first, just as he does in the Gospel, so also in this Epistle he speaks theologically <note>The Greek term *theologei* refers to a deep discourse on the nature and divinity of God.</note> about the Word, demonstrating that He is always in God, and teaching that the Father is Light, so that we may thus understand the Word to be the radiance emanating from Him. While speaking of divine things, he explains that our mystery is not something recent, but has existed from the beginning and for all time, and has now been made manifest in the Lord, who is eternal life and true God. He also sets forth the reason for His presence and His appearance, saying it was for this: to destroy the works of the devil, so that we might be freed from death and know the Father and the Son Himself, our Lord Jesus Christ. 

He writes to people of every age—to children, to young men, and to the elderly—noting that God has been made known and the devil’s power has henceforth been conquered through the abolition of death. Then, throughout the rest of the Epistle, he teaches about love, desiring that we love one another, since Christ also loved us. He explains the difference between fear and love, between the children of God and the children of the devil, and concerning sin that leads to death versus sin that does not, as well as the distinction between spirits. Furthermore, he distinguishes which spirit is from God and which is of error, and when we are recognized as children of God versus children of the devil. He clarifies for which sins we ought to pray for those who stumble and for which we should not, and warns that he who does not love his neighbor is not worthy of the calling, nor can he be called Christ’s. 

He also demonstrates the unity of the Son with the Father, and that he who denies the Son does not possess the Father either. He makes a further distinction in this Epistle by describing the characteristic of the antichrist: which is to say that the Son is not Himself the Christ, so that, by denying Him, that liar might claim to be the Christ himself. Throughout the entire Epistle, he exhorts those who believe in the Lord not to be discouraged if they are hated by the world, but rather to rejoice; for the hatred of the world shows that the believers have passed out of this world and belong instead to the heavenly citizenship <term>politeia</term> <note>original: "politeia" — a term referring to one's conduct as a citizen of a specific commonwealth, here the Kingdom of Heaven.</note>. Finally, at the end of the Epistle, he reminds them once more that the Son of God is eternal life and true Light, and that we should serve Him and keep ourselves from idols.

## ON THE FIRST EPISTLE
# OF JOHN
->Summary by<-
### DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial letter 'H' featuring an ornate pattern of foliage and scrolling designs.</image-desc>

Even the character of the speech itself argues that this is the Epistle of John the Apostle, who wrote the Gospel. He is frequent in his mention of light and darkness, life and death, hatred and charity, and in the repetition of words as if they were caught up from the immediately preceding sentence. This style is of a kind that may be made clearer by an example: *"Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, because everything that is in the world,"* and so forth. And soon after: *"It is not of the Father, but is of the world. And the world passes away."* How many times is "world" repeated here? Finally, throughout his entire discourse, there is something less restricted and more diffuse <note>original: "fusius" — Erasmus suggests John's style is more flowing or expansive compared to the more concise or structured prose of Paul or Peter.</note> than in the speech of the other Apostles. However, the Epistle is too clear to require much of a summary—just like the two following ones, which are attributed to a certain John the Presbyter, rather than the Apostle.

1. <image-desc>Small ornamental initial 'Q'</image-desc>**THAT which was** <note>original: "QUOD fuit"</note>] <note>original Greek: "Ὃ ἦν"</note>, *that which was*, just as he had translated in the Gospel: *in the beginning was the Word*.
2. <margin>E</margin> **Have handled** <note>original: "Contrectaverunt"</note>] <note>original Greek: "ἐψηλάφησαν"</note>. Saint Jerome usually quotes this as *palpaverunt* <note>Both Latin words mean to touch or feel, but "contrectaverunt" implies a more thorough handling or examination.</note>. He translates the same word as *handle and see* in Luke 24. This sentence can be divided in three ways: First, so that the main clause follows this part: *and our hands have handled, etc.* That which was from the beginning, and which we have heard and seen and peered into concerning the word of life, the same we also handled with our hands. A second way is that, after a grammatical delay <term>hyperbaton</term>, it returns to what he had intended to say: *that which we have seen, I say, and heard, we announce to you*. The third way is that the main clause sits after *we have seen*, so that the sense is: *the word which was from the beginning, just as we heard with our ears and saw with our eyes—and we did not simply see, but lived with him for a long time as witnesses—indeed, we even handled the word of life with our hands; for our life, which was previously hidden, was exposed to the senses of the body, and thus it was possible to see it.* Therefore, what we have discovered in so many ways, we also testify and announce to you. Then, in his usual manner, he repeats what he had said: *That which we have seen and heard, we announce to you*. The context of the speech almost matches the Gospel; *That which was from the beginning*, he repeated at the end of the period, <margin>F</margin> *which was with the Father*. The reader who is ignorant of the Greek language should be warned that in the first and third instances "we have seen" is <note>original Greek: "ἐωράκαμεν"</note>, while in the middle it is <note>original Greek: "ἐθεασάμεθα"</note>. The former means simply *to see*, while the latter means *to behold and contemplate*, as if displayed for viewing.
3. **And our fellowship may be**] <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἡ κοινωνία δὲ ἡ ἡμετέρα"</note>, that is, *and indeed our fellowship*. The word "may be" is not added in the Greek; it would be more appropriate to understand it as "is."
4. **That you may rejoice**] In Greek it is only, *that your joy may be full*, or *fulfilled*. An older manuscript from Constance supported the Greek, in which I have more confidence because the scribe was too unlearned to corrupt anything. Augustine and Bede cite it no differently in their *Commentaries*. Though Augustine reads *our joy*, not *your*, he is contradicted by the Greek books, which...

<margin>1. 1</margin> <image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'Q' depicting a figure kneeling in prayer or contemplation before a vision or light.</image-desc>THAT which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have peered into, and our hands have handled concerning the word of life,
<margin>2</margin> And the life was manifested, and we have seen, and we bear witness, and we announce to you the eternal life, which was with the Father, and was manifested to us.
<margin>3</margin> <margin>A</margin> That which we have seen and heard, we announce to you, so that you also may have fellowship with us, and our fellowship may be with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.
<margin>4</margin> <margin>B</margin> And these things we write to you, so that your joy may be full.
<margin>5</margin> And this is the promise which we have heard from him and announce to you, that God is light, and in him there are no darknesses at all.
<margin>6</margin> If we say that we have fellowship with him and walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.
<margin>7</margin> But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have mutual fellowship among ourselves, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanses us from all sin.
<margin>8</margin> If we say, "We have no sin," we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
<margin>9</margin> <margin>C</margin> If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all iniquity.
<margin>10</margin> If we say, "We have not sinned," we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
<margin>II. 1</margin> <margin>D</margin> My little children, these things I write to you so that you may not sin: and if anyone has sinned, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.
<margin>2</margin> And he is the propitiation for our sins: not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world.
<margin>3</margin> And in this we know that we have known him, if we observe his commands.
<margin>4</margin> He who says, "I know him," and does not keep his precepts, is a liar, and in him the truth is not.
<margin>5</margin> But he who keeps his word, truly in this man the love of God is perfected. By this we know that we are in him.
<margin>6</margin> He who says he abides in him ought to walk just as he walked.
<margin>7</margin> Brethren, I write no new precept to you, but an old precept which you had from the beginning. The old precept is the word which you heard from the beginning.
<margin>8</margin> Again, I write a new precept to you, which is true in him, the same truth...

---

...I have indeed seen until now. Otherwise, the pronoun of the first person [our joy] would not displease me.
5. <margin>H</margin> **And this is the announcement which we have heard**] In Greek it is <note>original: "ἐπαγγελία"</note> (*epangelia*), which sounds more like *promise*, although the word <note>original: "ἐπαγγέλλω"</note> is ambiguous. Among the Greeks there are four different words which the Translator rendered in the same way. The first is *katangellomen*, the second *epangeliamen*, the third *anangellomen*, all of which he translates as "we announce"; the fourth is *epangelia*, which he translates as "announcement." To me, the word *promise* is not unpleasing, except that the things that follow do not fit well: *that God is light, and in him there are no darknesses at all*. No mention is made of a promise here, unless you twist the meaning. But what the Son announced from the Father, this the Apostle, having received it from the Son, reports back to us. For that is what *anangellō* properly sounds like. Indeed, the word "that" <note>original Greek: "ὅτι"</note> here is not a causal conjunction [because], but explanatory [noting what]. What are you announcing? That God is light. Furthermore, in many places in this chapter he renders *hoti* as "since" or "because."
<margin>1</margin> **We have an advocate**] <note>original Greek: "παράκλητον ἔχομεν"</note>, that is, *we have a patron*. Although here the Greek manuscripts vary: the older manuscript from Constance agreed with the Greek reading.
<margin>2</margin> **He who says he knows God**] <note>original Greek: "Ὁ λέγων, Ἔγνωκα αὐτόν"</note>, that is, *he who says, "I have known him."*
<margin>3</margin> **To abide in Christ**] In Greek it is *in him*. The Constance manuscript and Augustine agreed. And shortly after, instead of "Dearly beloved," the Greek has *Brethren*.
<margin>4</margin> **Which you heard**] The Greeks add <note>original: "ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς"</note>, that is, *from the beginning*, in the latter part.
<margin>5</margin> **Again a new commandment**] *Palin* could have been aptly rendered as *On the other hand* or *Conversely*. For the Greek word declares both opposition and repetition. Here, however, it is a declaration of opposition, not repetition.
<margin>6</margin> **Both in him and in you**] The first "and" is redundant. *Which is true, [original Greek: "Ὅ ἐστιν ἀληθὲς ἐν αὐτῷ, καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν"]*, that is, *which is true in him, the same is true also in you*. For in the Greek, "which" cannot be referred back to the "commandment" [due to grammatical gender].

# THE FIRST EPISTLE OF JOHN. CHAPTER II.

[The Greek text translates as follows:]

He who loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no cause for stumbling in him. 11. But he who hates his brother is in the darkness, and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes. 
<margin>A</margin>
12. I write to you, little children <note>Greek: *teknia*</note>, because your sins are forgiven you for his name’s sake. 13. I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. 14. I write to you, children <note>Greek: *paidia*</note>, because you have known the Father. I have written to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. I have written to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God remains in you,

and you have overcome the evil one. 15. Do not love the world, nor the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. 16. For all that is in the world—the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life—is not from the Father but is from the world. 17. And the world is passing away, and its lust; but he who does the will of God remains forever. 18. Little children,

<margin>D</margin>

[The Latin Vulgate text translates as follows:]

He who loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no stumbling block in him. 11. But he who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and knows not where he goes, because darkness has blinded his eyes. 12. I write to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven you for his name's sake. 13. I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you have overcome that evil one. 14. I write to you, little children, because you have known the Father. I have written to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. I have written to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God remains in you, and you have overcome that evil one. 15. Love not the world, nor those things which are in the world. If any man love the world, the charity of the Father is not in him. 16. I have not written to you as to those ignorant of the truth, but as to those knowing it: and that every lie is not of the truth. 22. Who is a liar, but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son. 23. Whosoever denies the Son, the same has not the Father. 24. You therefore, let that which you have heard from the beginning remain in you. If that remain in you which you have heard from the beginning, you also shall remain in the Son and the Father. 25. And this is the promise, which he himself has promised us, life eternal. 26. These things have I written to you concerning them that seduce you. 27. And the unction, which you have received from him, remains in you. And you have no need...

---

7. **The darkness has passed away** <note>Latin: *Tenebrae transierunt*</note>] The Greek is *paragetai*, that is, *they pass away*.

8. **I write to you, infants** <note>Latin: *Scribo vobis infantes*</note>] The Greek is *paidia*, that is, boys, or "little sons," but "boys" is better.

9. **I write to you, fathers** <note>Latin: *Scribo vobis patres*</note>] Here the Greek has *egraphsa*, that is, *I have written*. It is strange that this same phrase, pertaining to the fathers, is repeated in the exact same words, while none of the others are repeated. However, modern manuscripts vary on this. In the very ancient Cambridge manuscript <note>Latin: *vetustissimo Cantabrigiensi*</note>, it was held thus: *I write to you little sons, because your sins are forgiven you for his name's sake. I write to you fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. I write to you young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you infants, because you have known the Father. I write to you fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. I write to you young men, because you are strong, and the word of God remains in you, and you have overcome the evil one.* In this reading, the same phrase is placed twice: *I write to you fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning.* The Basle copy agreed, except that in the last place it did not have "adolescents" <note>Latin: *adolescentes*</note> but "youths" <note>Latin: *juvenes*</note>. But in the other Cambridge manuscript, "adolescents" was also here, except that some "eraser-man" <note>Latin: *rasor ille*; Erasmus refers to a scribe who scraped the parchment to make a correction</note> had turned "adolescents" into "youths." Yet the repeated phrase about the fathers was absent—though it is consistently found in the Greek manuscripts and is recited by Augustine, who does not hide the repetition, for he notes it, commends it, and repeats it. It was right to mention this because in many common editions, reckless editors have removed this phrase. It should be noted that Augustine reads "youths" instead of "adolescents." Although most Latin manuscripts have "adolescents" in the first place and "youths" in the second, in the Greek it is the same word: *neaniskoi*. Perhaps some grumpy person will mutter that these are pointless trifles <note>Greek: *akyros*</note>. On the contrary, even an eagle-eyed theologian ignorant of Greek letters might stumble here. For when he adds, "because you are strong," it seems to suggest a more robust age than that of adolescents. I would have philosophized on this myself, had the Greek reading not taught me that there is no new meaning, but simply an emphasis on the previous one. Furthermore, regarding the diminutive *teknia* for "sons" or "children," it is a common usage. In the first part, "little sons" is not *paidia* but *teknia*. Again, where the Latin has "infants," the Greek has *paidia*, whereas "infant" in Greek is usually *brephos* or *nēpios*. Therefore, he distinguishes three ages: boys, youths, and old men, and he addresses each twice, except that in the case of the boys he changes the word, while in the case of the fathers and youths he does not. He attributes to each what is fitting. Boys slip up through ignorance, therefore their sins are forgiven; also, due to their age, they sometimes do not even recognize their own parents, so he congratulates them that they know the Heavenly Father. Old men remember ancient and long-past things; and nothing is more ancient than that Father. Youths, eating solid food, are strong in vigor; therefore they are said to overcome the Devil and to have the word of God remaining in them, for from this food comes the strength of the Gospel youth. Now, as for the fact that in the last section the Greek has...

<column-break/>

...*egraphsa* <note>"I have written"</note> while in the others it has *graphō* <note>"I write"</note>, I think it changes nothing of the sense. We should also not overlook that in the conjunction *hoti* <note>"because" or "that"</note> there is some ambiguity, as the sense can be taken as: "Therefore I write to you, *because* your sins are forgiven," or: "I write this very thing to you, *that* your sins are forgiven."

10. **You have overcome the evil one** <note>Latin: *Vicistis malignum*</note>] The Greek is *ton ponēron*, that is, "that evil one," namely Satan. For in Latin, "malignant" often refers to someone who is envious or lacks sincerity. 
<margin>E</margin>

11. **All that is in the world** <note>Latin: *Omne quod in mundo est*</note>] The Greeks punctuate this differently than we do, although the meaning is the same: *For all that is in the world, [namely] the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father.* The translator <note>the author of the Vulgate</note> tried to make it clearer but made it more obscure. For when he says, "which is not from the Father," it seems as if only the "pride of life" is not from the Father. But according to Saint Augustine, he mentions three things which are not from the Father: the first seems to pertain to pleasures, the second to the ostentation of images and nobility, the third to worldly dignities.

12. **Pride of life** <note>Latin: *Superbia vitae*</note>] The Greek is *hē alazoneia tou biou*, that is, the "arrogance" or "uproar" of life, or of resources; for *bios* signifies both. For this is not *zōē*, the word that describes the life by which we breathe; *bios* signifies one's livelihood and all resources pertaining to the use of life, as well as a way of life, and life itself (hence the word *makrobios* or "long-lived"). Paul also calls those things *biōtika* which pertain to the support of the body.
<margin>F</margin>

13. **Antichrist comes** <note>Latin: *Antichristus venit*</note>] *Venit* <note>comes</note> is in the present tense, *erchetai*, or certainly the future.

14. **Now Antichrists** <note>Latin: *Nunc Antichristi*</note>] *Kai nyn*, that is, "and now," meaning even now there are many in place of one. And it is not "are," but *gegonasi*, that is, "they have been made," or "they have begun to be."

15. **Last hour** <note>Latin: *Novissima hora*</note>] The Greeks sometimes use "hour" to mean "time."

16. **They went out from us** <note>Latin: *Ex nobis prodierunt*</note>] *Exēlthon*, that is, "they had gone out." When a defection from a community is signified, rather than an origin, "went out" <note>Latin: *prodierunt*</note> does not fit aptly. Augustine reads "externally."

17. **As if to those who do not know** <note>Latin: *Quasi ignorantibus*</note>] *Hoti ouk oidate*, that is, "because you have not known."

18. **And because every lie** <note>Latin: *Et quoniam omne mendacium*</note>] In the Greek, this is not separate but depends on what goes before: "I have written to you not as to those ignorant of the truth, but as to those knowing it, and that no lie is from the truth"—that is, knowing this also, that no lie comes from the truth. *He who confesses has the Son and the Father.* I do not find these [last words] in the Greek manuscript, nor even in the Aldine edition.

19. **Which he himself promised us** <note>Latin: *Quam ipse pollicitus est nobis*</note>] It would be more correct to say, "by which he promised us eternal life." For it is an Attic idiom <note>a style of Greek from Athens</note>: "he promised a promise."

# THE EPISTLE OF JOHN CHAPTER III.

<note>The Greek text actually begins here at the end of Chapter 2, verse 27.</note>

...which remains in you. And you have no need that anyone teach you; but as the same anointing teaches you about all things, and is true, and is not a lie. And just as it taught you, you will remain in him.
<margin>28</margin> And now, little children, remain in him, so that when he appears, we may have confidence and not be ashamed before him at his coming.
<margin>29</margin> If you know that he is righteous, know that everyone who practices righteousness is born of him.
<margin>III. 1</margin> See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God. Because of this, the world does not know you, because it did not know him.
<margin>2</margin> Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be. We know that when he is revealed, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.
<margin>3</margin> And everyone who has this hope in him purifies himself, just as he is pure.
<margin>4</margin> Everyone who commits sin also commits lawlessness; and sin is lawlessness.
<margin>5</margin> And you know that he was revealed to take away our sins, and in him there is no sin.
<margin>6</margin> Everyone who remains in him does not sin; everyone who sins has not seen him nor known him.
<margin>7</margin> Little children, let no one deceive you. He who practices righteousness is righteous, just as he is righteous.
<margin>8</margin> He who commits sin is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. To this end the Son of God was revealed, to destroy the works of the devil.
<margin>9</margin> Everyone born of God does not commit sin, for his seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he is born of God.
<margin>10</margin> In this the children of God and the children of the devil are manifest. Everyone who does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is he who does not love his brother.
<margin>11</margin> For this is the message you heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.
<margin>12</margin> Not as Cain, who was of the evil one and slaughtered his brother. And for what reason did he slaughter him? Because his works were evil, but those of his brother were righteous.
<margin>13</margin> Do not wonder, my brothers, if the world hates you.
<margin>14</margin> We know that we have passed from death to life because we love the brothers. He who does not love his brother remains in death.
<margin>15</margin> Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in him.
<margin>16</margin> In this we have known love, because he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
<margin>17</margin> But whoever has the world's goods <note>literally: "the life/substance of the world"</note>, and sees his brother in need, and closes his heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him?
<margin>18</margin> My little children, let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth.
<margin>19</margin> And in this we know that we are of the truth, and we shall persuade our hearts before him.
<margin>20</margin> For if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart and knows all things.
<margin>21</margin> Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God.
<margin>22</margin> And whatever we ask, we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what is pleasing before him.
<margin>23</margin> And this is his commandment: that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, as he gave commandment.
<margin>24</margin> And he who keeps his commandments remains in him, and he in him. And in this we know that he remains in us, from the Spirit.

---

**20** *Just as his anointing*] <note>original: "Sicut unctio ejus"</note> The Greek says "as the same anointing," that is, as the anointing itself. Augustine certainly read it as "remain in it," referring to the anointing, though here it is read as "his anointing."
**21** *Remain in him*] <note>original: "Manete in eo"</note> Augustine reads "in it," referring it back to the anointing. The Greek manuscripts have *menete*, meaning "remain" <note>an imperative command</note>, though it can also be read as "you will remain." The Spanish edition <note>The Complutensian Polyglot</note> and the Aldine edition <note>published by Aldus Manutius in Venice</note> agreed with my copies.
**22** *Let us not be confounded by him*] <note>original: "Non confundamur ab illo"</note> The meaning can be that he might not be ashamed of us.
**1** *See what kind*] <note>original: "Videte qualem"</note> The Greek *idete* is ambiguous; it could be "you see" or "see!" <note>a command</note>, but it does not change the meaning much.
**2** *May be named and be*] <note>original: "Nominemur & simus"</note> "And be" is not added in the Greek. It seems to have been added so that no one would think it is a small thing to merely be "named" <note>called</note> children, which Augustine indicates when he writes: "For those who are called and are not, what does the name profit them?" But here the text speaks of a name granted by God, where there is no difference between being called and being.
**3** *Does not know us*] <note>original: "Non novit nos"</note> The Greek says *hymas*, meaning "you" in the second person plural.
**4** *Sanctifies himself just as*] <note>original: "Sanctificat se sicut"</note> The Greek *hagnizei* means "purifies." Just as he is "holy" (*hagnos*), which means pure and chaste.
**5** *And commits iniquity*] <note>original: "Et iniquitatem facit"</note> "And" is used here for "also," so the sense is: "Whoever commits sin, that same person also commits lawlessness."
**6** *Has not seen him nor known him*] <note>original: "Non vidit eum nec cognovit"</note> The Greek *egnoken* means "nor has known." This Greek word signifies a lasting state, as if you were to say "to have as a known thing." For just as one who sees knows, one who has learned has not ceased to know; but it is worse that some versions have "he knew him" <note>in a simple past sense</note>.

<column-break/>

you have no need that anyone teach you; but as the same anointing teaches you about all things, and is true, and is not a lie. And just as it taught you, **21** remain in it.
<margin>And 28</margin> And now, little children, remain in him, so that when he appears, we may have confidence and **22** not be put to shame by him at his coming.

<margin>3</margin> And everyone who has this hope in him **4** purifies himself, just as he is pure.
<margin>4</margin> Everyone who commits sin also **5** commits iniquity: and sin is iniquity <note>or lawlessness</note>.
<margin>5</margin> And you know that he appeared to take away our sins, and sin is not in him.
<margin>6</margin> Everyone who remains in him does not sin: everyone who sins **6** has not seen him, nor known him.
<margin>7</margin> Little children, let no one lead you astray. He who practices righteousness is righteous, just as he is righteous.
<margin>8</margin> He who commits sin is of the devil: because from the beginning the devil sins.
<margin>7</margin> To this end the Son of God appeared, that he might destroy the works of the devil.
<margin>9</margin> <margin>C</margin> Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin: because his seed remains in him, and he cannot sin, because he is born of God.
<margin>10</margin> In this the children of God and the children of the devil are manifest. **8** Everyone who does not practice righteousness is not of God, and he who does not love his brother:
<margin>11</margin> Because this is the message you heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.
<margin>12</margin> Not like Cain, who was of that evil one and killed his brother. And for what reason did he kill him? Because his works were evil, **9** but those of his brother were righteous.
<margin>13</margin> Do not wonder, my brothers, if the world hates you.
<margin>14</margin> We know that we have been moved from death to life, because we love the brothers. He who does not love his brother remains in death.
<margin>15</margin> Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer has eternal life **D** remaining in him.
<margin>16</margin> **10** By this we have known love, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
<margin>17</margin> But whoever has the goods of the world and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his heart from him, how does the love of God remain in him?

<margin>19</margin> By this we know that we are of the truth, and in his sight **11** we will persuade our hearts.
<margin>20</margin> Because **12** if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart and knows all things.
<margin>21</margin> Beloved, **13** if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God:
<margin>22</margin> <margin>E</margin> And whatever we ask, we receive from him: because we keep his commandments and do those things that are pleasing in his sight.
<margin>23</margin> And this is his commandment: that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another, just as he gave commandment.
<margin>24</margin> And he who keeps his commandments remains in him, and he in him. And by this we know that he remains in us **14** by the Spirit, whom he [gave] us.

---

<margin>F</margin>
**7** *In this*] <note>original: "In hoc"</note> The Greek *Eis touto* means "To this end," or "For this purpose," rather than just "In this."
**8** *Everyone who is not righteous*] <note>original: "Omnis qui non est justus"</note> The Greek says "Everyone who does not practice righteousness."
**9** *But those of his brother*] <note>original: "Fratris autem ejus"</note> One must understand the word "works" here, as in "but the works of his brother."
**10** *In this we have known the love of God*] <note>original: "In hoc cognovimus charitatem Dei"</note> The word "of God" is redundant according to the Greek manuscript, although it is added a little further down.
**11** *We will persuade our hearts*] <note>original: "Suadebimus corda nostra"</note> Augustine reads "we shall persuade our heart," as if to say, we satisfy our conscience. For "heart" is interpreted as "conscience." The Greek word *peitho*, which means to bend by persuasion, sometimes takes the accusative case, though when it means "to obey," it takes the dative. Paul used this word similarly in Galatians 1: "Am I now persuading men or God?" One ancient manuscript had "we keep" instead of "we will persuade." Another from Constance agreed.
**12** *If our heart reproves us*] <note>original: "Si reprehenderit nos cor nostrum"</note> The Greek *kataginosko* can be taken as "if our heart condemns us."
**13** *If our heart does not reprove us*] <note>original: "Si cor nostrum non reprehenderit nos"</note> It is a wonder what Augustine followed here when he reads "if the heart has not felt badly," for he interprets it this way as well.
**14** *Of the Spirit*] <note>original: "De Spiritu"</note> The Greek *ek tou Pneumatos* means "out of the Spirit." This is spoken in the same way we might say, "drink of your wine," instead of simply "drink your wine."

# FIRST EPISTLE OF JOHN CHAPTER IV.

<margin>IV. 1</margin> ...of the Spirit, whom he gave to us. Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world. <margin>2</margin> By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ having come in the flesh is from <margin>3</margin> God. And every spirit that does not confess Jesus Christ having come in the flesh is not from God. And this is the spirit of the antichrist, which you have heard is coming, and <margin>4</margin> now is already in the world. You are from God, little children, and have overcome them; because he who is in you is greater than he who is in the <margin>5</margin> world. They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world’s perspective, and the world listens to them. <margin>6</margin> We are from God. He who knows God listens to us; he who is not from God does not listen to us. From this we know the spirit of <margin>7</margin> truth and the spirit of error. Beloved, let us love one another; for love is from God. And everyone who loves has been born of God and knows <margin>8</margin> God. In this the love of God was revealed among us, that God has sent his only-begotten Son into the world, so that we might live through him. <margin>10</margin> In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as an atonement <note>original: "hilasmon," often translated as propitiation or a sacrifice that makes amends</note> for <margin>11</margin> our sins. Beloved, if God so loved us, <margin>12</margin> we also ought to love one another. No one has ever seen God. If we love one another, God remains in us, <margin>13</margin> and his love is perfected in us. In <margin>9</margin> this appeared the love of God in us, because God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him. Be- <margin>11</margin> loved, <margin>11</margin> if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another. No man has seen God at any time. If we <margin>12</margin> <margin>C</margin> love one another, God dwells in us, and his love is perfected in us. <margin>12</margin> By this we know <margin>13</margin> that we dwell in him, and he in us, because <margin>13</margin> he has given us of his Spirit. ---

<margin>1</margin> *To an evil spirit]* In more proper Latin, it would be *to any spirit*, that is, without selection. And *si* <note>original: "if"</note> is put for *an* or *num* <note>original: "whether"</note>, as in *whether they be of God*.

<margin>2</margin> *In this is known]* The Greek is *ginōskete*, that is, *you know*, or *know ye*. The translator seems to have read *ginōsketai* <note>meaning "is known"</note>.

<margin>3</margin> *And every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not of God]* I do not find this phrase <note>original: "solvit Jesum," meaning to dissolve or separate Jesus's natures</note> in the Greek manuscripts that I have seen; instead, it is held thus: *And every spirit that does not confess Jesus having come in the flesh, is not of God*. The *Tripartite History* <note>a famous 6th-century church history</note> indicates that this passage was corrupted by heretics. I suspect rather that this phrase <note>"dissolves Jesus"</note> was added against heretics: some of whom attributed human nature to Christ in such a way as to take away the divine, while others attributed the divine in such a way as to take away the human. Others wanted him to be a half-man, attributing a human body but denying he had a human soul. Certainly, what the Greek reads agrees more with the phrasing of John the Apostle, whose peculiarity is to echo a contrary sentiment to the prior one, the better to fix what was said in the mind. Such as these: *He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony of God in himself. But he who does not believe the Son, etc.* And shortly: *He who has the Son of God has life; he who has not the Son of God has not life. He who confesses is of God; he who does not confess is not of God.* The whole of his discourse abounds with figures of this kind. Cyprian, in book 2 against the Jews, chapter 7, reports this passage according to the Greek reading: *Every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ to have come in the flesh is of God. But he who denies him to have come in the flesh is not of God, but is of the spirit of Antichrist.* In Augustine's Homilies, in which he explains this Epistle, in the context presented in the commentary, this passage is cited just as the Greeks and Cyprian read it. And yet at the end he also interprets this: *Every spirit that dissolves Christ is not of God*, so it appears that this phrase was a third one in his manuscript, as if he read: *everyone who confesses, everyone who does not confess, everyone who dissolves*; or certainly that the ecclesiastical reading varied so much in that time, and Augustine did not wish to pass over either. It was not added in either of the Constance manuscripts. But let everyone have their own free judgment on this matter; I hand down what I found in the Greek manuscripts, neither approving nor disapproving of the differing reading.

<margin>4</margin> *And this is Antichrist]* The Greek is *kai touto esti to tou antichristou*, that is, *and this is that of the antichrist*, so that you understand the word *spirit*. Cyprian, whom we cited a moment ago, agrees with me.

<margin>5</margin> *Of whom you heard when he comes]* The Greek is *hon akēkoate*, that is, *that he is coming*. So Augustine reads it.

<margin>6</margin> *And you have overcome him]* The Greek is *autous* <note>them</note>. Both Constance manuscripts supported the Greek reading, except that in the more recent one, traces of a corruptor testified that *eos* <note>them</note> had been changed to *eum* <note>him</note>. Augustine reads *him* and interprets it. Otherwise, *them* refers to two things: *the Antichrist and the world*.

<margin>7</margin> *They speak of the world]* The Greek is *ek tou kosmou lalousi*, that is, *they speak out of the world*. For it is not *eis* <note>about</note>, as in speaking *about* the world, but speaking from the disposition of the world, to which they belong. Just as it is noted in the Gospels, *He who is of the earth, speaks of the earth*.

<margin>8</margin> *In this we know]* The Greek is *Ek toutou*, that is, *From this*.

<margin>9</margin> *Since he himself first]* "First" is not in the Greek manuscript. The older Constance copy agreed with this, except that some more recent person had written *prior* <note>first</note> in the margin, as if in place of a note. Augustine also sides with us.

<margin>10</margin> *An atonement for our sins]* Bede notes—and I believe Augustine does too—that in some copies, instead of this word *propitiationem* <note>atonement/propitiation</note>, it is *litatorem* <note>one who offers a pleasing sacrifice</note>. Now, one who "litates" is one who appeases by sacrifice. Augustine interprets it as *sacrificationem* <note>sacrifice</note>.

<margin>11</margin> *If God loved us]* The Greek is *ei outōs ho Theos ēgapēsen hēmas*, that is, *if God so loved us*.

<margin>12</margin> *In this we know that we remain in him, and he in us, because]* The Greek *hoti* <note>that/because</note> is placed in both spots. Through this we know we remain in him, and he in us, because he gave us of his Spirit.

<margin>13</margin> *Of his Holy Spirit]* The word "Holy" is redundant <note>it is not in the Greek</note>. Both Constance volumes agreed.

<margin>14</margin> *And we believed the love]* The Greek is *the love* <note>in the accusative case</note>.

<margin>15</margin> *Fear has punishment]* The Greek is *kolasin*, that is, *punishment*, or rather *retribution* or *torment*. Augustine reads *tormentum*: for where there is fear, there is no quiet conscience.

<margin>16</margin> *Let us therefore love God]* The Greek is *auton*, that is, *him*, not *God*.

<margin>17</margin> *Because God first]* The Greek is *hoti autos prōtos*, that is, *because he himself first*, or *primary*.

<margin>18</margin> *Whom he sees, God whom he does not see]* In both places the Greek has *heōrake*, that is, *he has seen*. For it is not necessary to see in order to love; it is enough to have seen in order to know. Nothing is loved unless it is known. Unless you take the Greek verb to signify an inherent act.

<margin>19</margin> *We have from God]* The Greek is *ap’ autou*, that is, *from him*.

# THE EPISTLE OF JOHN CHAPTER V.

<margin>V. 1</margin> ...the one who loves God, also loves his brother. |
**Everyone** who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God. And everyone who loves the one who gave birth, also loves the one who has been born of him. <margin>2</margin> By this we know that we love the children of God: whenever we love God and keep his <margin>3</margin> commandments. For this is the love of God: that we keep his commandments; and his commandments are not <margin>4</margin> burdensome. Because everything that is born of God overcomes the world; and this is the victory that has overcome the world: <margin>5</margin> our faith. Who is it that overcomes the world, if not the one who believes <margin>6</margin> that Jesus is the Son of God? This is the one who came through water and blood: Jesus Christ; not in the water only, but in the water and the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, <margin>7</margin> because the Spirit is the truth. Because there are three who bear witness

<sig>A</sig>

<margin>1</margin> *When we love God*] Or "Since we have loved God." And "let us do his commandments," <note>original: "τηρῶμεν" (tērōmen)</note>, that is, we have observed or should observe them.
<margin>2</margin> *Because the Spirit is truth*] <note>original: "ὅτι τὸ Πνεῦμά ἐστιν ἡ ἀλήθεια"</note>, that is, because the Spirit is truth itself. It is "truth," spoken in the Hebrew manner, instead of saying it is "true." The flesh is deceptive, but the Spirit does not know how to lie. In visible things there is a focal point; in eternal things, there is truth.
<margin>3</margin> *There are three who give testimony in heaven*] In the Greek manuscript, I find only this concerning the threefold testimony: <note>original: "Ὅτι τρεῖς εἰσιν οἱ μαρτυροῦντες, τὸ πνεῦμα, καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ, καὶ τὸ αἷμα"</note>, that is, *Because there are three who testify: the spirit, and the water, and the blood.* Saint Jerome, in his prologue to the Canonical Epistles, suspects that this passage was corrupted by Latin translators and that the testimony of the Father, Word, and Holy Spirit was omitted by some. And yet, according to our Edition, Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century Church Father</note> cites this passage in his work titled *On the Treasure*, Book 14: "Again," he says, "John in the same Epistle says: *Who is he who overcomes the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? This is he who came through water, blood, and spirit: Jesus Christ, not in water alone, but in water and blood. And it is the Spirit who bears testimony. For the Spirit is truth. Because there are three who bear testimony: the spirit, water, and blood, and these three are one. If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater*," etc. Thus far Cyril, a man who was, if I am not mistaken, orthodox. Since he was fighting against the Arians <note>Arians were early Christians who argued that Jesus was a created being and not fully equal to God the Father</note> and gathered many testimonies against them from the divine books, it is not probable that he would have omitted a weapon he could have relied on so heavily, if he had either found it or believed it had been written by the Apostle. Furthermore, Cyril concludes that the Holy Spirit is God, not from the addition of *and these three are one*, but from what follows: *if we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater*, which he refers to the Spirit mentioned just before. 

Now Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, an 8th-century English monk</note>, carefully explaining this passage and accurately expounding the triple testimony on earth with many words, made no mention of the testimony in heaven of the Father, Word, and Spirit. This man did not lack knowledge of languages, nor diligence in examining ancient copies. Indeed, he does not even add this in the text of the manuscript; he only reads, *There are three who give testimony.* In a manuscript that was sent to me from the Library of the Minorites in Antwerp, a note was written in the margin about the testimony of the Father, Word, and Spirit, but in a more recent hand; so it is likely this was added by some scholar who did not want this small part to be left out, especially since no mention of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit exists in the Badian Edition. 

Bede followed Augustine, who in the books he wrote against Maximinus the Arian, leaves no stone unturned to prove from Canonical Scripture that the Holy Spirit is God and that all the Persons are of one substance <note>original: "ὁμοουσίους" (homoousious)</note>, yet he does not bring forward this testimony, even though he cites this passage more than once elsewhere. Specifically, in Book 3, Chapter 22, he shows that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are signified through the *spirit, blood, and water*. For that reason, he emphasizes the rule that nothing is called "one" unless they are of the same substance. If this rule is as true as he wishes it to seem, this passage would have offered a certain victory, proving not only the Son but also the Holy Spirit is of one substance with the Father. It is therefore sufficiently clear that Augustine did not read this specific phrase in his copies; if he had read it and not used it, he might seem to be colluding with his adversary, which he never does. 

But I am pressed by the authority of Jerome, which I would not wish to dismiss lightly, although he is often forceful, somewhat bold, and frequently inconsistent. However, I do not quite see what Jerome means in this place. I will provide his words below: "but," he says, "just as we previously corrected the Evangelists according to the line of truth, so we have restored these to their proper order with God's help. For there is the first of James, two of Peter, three of John, and one of Jude. If these were faithfully translated into the Latin language by interpreters as they were arranged by the authors, they would neither cause ambiguity for readers nor would the variety of words conflict, especially in that place where we read about the unity of the Trinity in the first Epistle of John; in which we find much error from the truth of the faith by unfaithful translators, who put only three words in their Edition—namely water, blood, and spirit—and omit the testimony of the Father, the Word, and the Spirit, by which the Catholic faith is especially strengthened and the single essence of the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is proven." So far we have cited Jerome's words, from which it is clear that Jerome complains nothing about the Greek manuscripts, but only about those who translated the Greek into Latin. But now, in the Greek manuscripts, the very thing he complains was omitted is missing, while it is found in Latin manuscripts, though not all of them. But from where did Jerome correct the error of the interpreters? Surely from the Greek copies. But those copies either had what we see now, or they varied. If they varied, just as the Latin ones did,

<column-break/>

<margin>V.</margin> let him who loves God also love his brother. | **Everyone**
who believes Jesus is the Christ, is born of God. And
everyone who loves him who gave birth, loves also him who
was born of him. By this we know that we love the <margin>2</margin>
children of God: when we love God and keep his
commandments. For this is the love of God: that we <margin>3</margin>
keep his commandments, and his commandments are not burdensome. Be- <margin>4</margin>
cause everything that is born of God overcomes the
world: and this is the victory that has overcome the world,
our faith. Who is it that overcomes the world, except the one who believes <margin>5</margin>
that Jesus is the Son of God? This is he who came through water <margin>6</margin>
and blood, Jesus Christ: not through water only,
but through water and blood. And it is the Spirit who
testifies, because the Spirit is the truth. Because <margin>7</margin>
there are three

<sig>B</sig> by what argument does he show which is more correct, or which was written by the Apostle? Especially since what he criticizes was then part of the public use of the Church? If it had not been, I do not see how the following could have any place: "But you, Eustochium, virgin of Christ, while you seek the truth of Scripture from me more earnestly, you expose my old age to be gnawed by the teeth of the envious, who pronounce me a forger and a corrupter of the sacred Scriptures." Who would have called him a forger unless he had changed the public reading? But if Cyril read among the Greeks what the Greek manuscripts now have, and if among us Augustine and Bede either read only this or read both, I do not see what argument Jerome brings to show that the reading he hands down to us is the genuine one. 

But someone will say: This was an effective weapon against the Arians. First, since it is established that the reading varied long ago among both Greeks and Latins, this weapon will have no power against those who, without doubt, claimed the reading that favored them with equal right. But imagine the reading is not controversial: since what is said about the testimony of the water, blood, and spirit—"they are one"—refers not to the same nature, but to the agreement of their testimony, do we think the Arians would be so stupid as not to interpret the Father, Word, and Spirit in the same way in this passage? 

<sig>C</sig> Especially since in a similar place, orthodox men interpret it this way in the Gospels, and Augustine does not reject this interpretation when debating with the Arian Maximinus. Indeed, a fragment of the *Ordinary Gloss* <note>The standard medieval commentary on the Bible</note> interprets this very place this way, in a note added between the lines: "They are one," it says, "that is, testifying about the same thing." This is not to confirm the faith, but to make it suspect, if we flatter ourselves with such pedigrees. Perhaps it would be better to strive through pious study to make ourselves one with God, than to fight with curious studies over how the Son differs from the Father or the Spirit from both. Certainly, I do not see that what the Arians deny can be taught except by reasoning. Finally, since this whole passage is obscure, it cannot be very effective for refuting heretics. But we respond more fully to this matter in our apology to the slanderer. I will add this: since my friend Stunica so often boasts of the Rhodian manuscript, to which he attributes so much authority, it is strange he did not bring forward its oracle here, 

<sig>D</sig> especially since it usually clashes with our manuscripts like a "Lesbian rule" <note>An ancient metaphor for a flexible or unreliable standard</note>. Nevertheless, so as not to conceal anything, a single Greek manuscript was found in England in which what is missing in the common ones is present. For it is written in this manner: "For there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit, and these three are one. And there are three who bear witness on earth: the spirit, water, and blood, for the testimony of men." <note>original Greek: "Ὅτι τρεῖς εἰσιν οἱ μαρτυροῦντες ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ, Πατὴρ, Λόγος, καὶ Πνεῦμα, καὶ οὗτοι οἱ τρεῖς ἕν εἰσιν. Καὶ τρεῖς εἰσιν οἱ μαρτυροῦντες ἐν τῇ γῇ, πνεῦμα, ὕδωρ, καὶ αἷμα εἰς τὴν μαρτυρίαν τῶν ἀνθρώπων."</note> Although I do not know if it happened by chance that in this place it does not repeat what is in our Greek manuscripts: "and these three are unto one." From this British manuscript, therefore, we have restored what was said to be missing in ours, lest anyone have a handle for slandering us. However, I suspect that manuscript was "corrected" to match ours <note>Erasmus implies the manuscript might have been back-translated from Latin to support the inclusion of the verse</note>. 

I consulted two Latin manuscripts of marvelous antiquity in the Library of Saint Donatian in Bruges. Neither had the testimony of the Father, Word, and Spirit. Not even the phrase "on earth" was added in either. It was only, *And there are three who give testimony: the spirit, water, and blood.* In both copies from Constance, after the testimony of the water, blood, and spirit, the testimony of the Father, Word, and Spirit was added in these words: *Just as in heaven there are three: Father, Word, and Spirit, and the three are one.* The phrase "bear witness" was not added, nor the pronoun "these." In the manuscript provided by the public library of the School of Basel, the testimony of the spirit, water, and blood was not even held. Furthermore, Paolo Bombasio, a learned and upright man, at my request described this passage word-for-word from a very ancient manuscript in the Vatican Library, in which the testimony of the Father, Word, and Spirit was not present. If the authority of antiquity moves you, that book was a most ancient one belonging to the Supreme Pontiff; the evidence was sought from his library. The Aldine Edition agrees with this reading. What Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo Valla, a pioneering humanist scholar</note> read is not quite clear. Meanwhile, the Spanish Edition <note>The Complutensian Polyglot</note> reached us, which differed from all others. For it has it in this way: "For there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, and the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and the three are unto one. And there are three who bear witness on the earth: the spirit, and the water, and the blood." 

<sig>F</sig> First, the copy followed by the Spanish—sought from the same library, if I am not mistaken—differs from the British copy because here articles are added: "the" Father, "the" Word, "the" Spirit, which were not added in the British one. Secondly, the British one had "these three," while the Spanish only had "and the three," which is the same for the spirit, water, and blood. Furthermore, the British one had "are one," the Spanish "are unto one." Finally, the British one also added in the testimony of the earth, "and the three are unto one," which was not added here in the Spanish Edition. I indeed think that the phrase "unto one" comes from the idiom of the Hebrew language. "I will be to him for a father" cannot mean anything else than "I will be a father to him." Now, the Spanish Edition had added a scholarly note from the Decretals, which is attributed to Saint Thomas. It declares that according to the manuscripts...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s detailed philological and theological examination of the First Epistle of John, Chapter 5.
