# THE FIRST EPISTLE OF JOHN CH. V.

<margin>7</margin> For there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy <margin>8</margin> Spirit; and these three are one. And there are three who bear witness on earth: the spirit, and the water, and the blood; <margin>9</margin> and these three are in one. <note>original: "εἰς τὸ ἕν" (eis to hen) — literally "unto the one" or "for the one [purpose]"</note> If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater; for this is the testimony of God which he has testified concerning his Son. <margin>10</margin> The one who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. The one who does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that <margin>11</margin> God has testified concerning his Son. And this is the testimony: that God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his <margin>12</margin> Son. The one who has the Son has life; the one who does not <margin>13</margin> have the Son of God does not have life. I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life, and that you may believe <margin>14</margin> in the name of the Son of God. And this is the confidence that we have toward him: that if we ask anything according to <margin>15</margin> his will, he hears us. And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the <margin>16</margin> requests that we have asked from him. If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and he will give him life—for those whose sin is not leading to death. There is a sin leading to death; I do not say <margin>17</margin> that he should pray about that. All unrighteousness is sin, and <margin>18</margin> there is sin not leading to death. We know that everyone who has been born of God does not sin; but the one who was born of God keeps himself, and the evil one does not touch <margin>19</margin> him. We know that we are of God, and the whole world <margin>20</margin> lies in the power of the evil one. And we know that the Son of God has come...

---

...that corrected manuscripts do not add "and these three are one" to the testimony of the spirit, water, and blood, but rather that this seems to have been added by those who favored the Arian heresy. <note>The Arians believed Jesus was a created being, not co-equal with God the Father.</note> For if it were added here, it could only be interpreted as a consensus of testimony, since by their nature spirit, water, and blood cannot be called "one" substance. From this it would follow that what precedes concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—"and these three are one"—could also be taken as a consensus of love and testimony. Now, by these words, John has asserted the same essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. In principle, what they conclude is most true: that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have the same most simple and indivisible nature. Unless this were so, the Son would not truly be born of the Father, nor would the Holy Spirit truly proceed from the Father and the Son, as God from the substance of God.

<margin>D</margin> We are dealing only with the collection of evidence. It is clear that the topic here is the faith of testimony, not the substance of the persons. If in many other places this word "one" (*unum*) sounds like consensus rather than a unity of an individual being, what would be the harm if we interpreted it similarly here? How often do we read in both Testaments of "one heart, one spirit and soul, one mouth, one mind," where agreement and mutual love are signified? Since this figure of speech is so familiar in the divine volumes, what prevents it from being taken similarly here? The Lord says in John 10: *I and the Father are one.* How shall an Arian be defeated by this testimony unless you teach that "one" in Holy Scripture is never used except for things of the same substance? Since there are innumerable places that teach it is understood as consensus and mutual goodwill, they are effective for confirming the opinion of the Orthodox, but I do not see how much they avail for refuting the stubbornness of the Heretic. Moreover, that Christ speaks there of the concord he has with the Father is gathered by probable conjecture, because Christ does not respond to the fact that he said he was one with the Father, but that he called God his Father and called himself the Son of God in a singular way. And in John 17: *Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given to me, so that they may be one even as we are.* And again, *that they all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us.* This entire passage treats of the consensus of love and testimony, and whether we like it or not, we are forced to interpret that "one" differently regarding ourselves than regarding the divine persons. Therefore, this passage does not shatter the Arian position, but the authority of the Orthodox and the prescription of the Church compel us, teaching that this passage cannot be explained otherwise. It is pious to always submit our sense to the judgment of the Church as soon as we hear its clear opinion. Nor, meanwhile, is it a sin to search for the truth without contention, as God reveals different things to different people.

But to return to the business of the reading: from what we have mentioned, it is clear that both Latin and Greek codices vary, and in my opinion, there is no danger in whichever reading you embrace. For what Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> says about a particle added by heretics—first, he does not affirm it, but says "it is said." Otherwise, the Catholic Church throughout the world would be embracing what had been adulterated by heretics. This will trouble the Grammarians: how it is said of the spirit, water, and blood, "there are three who" (masculine), and "these are one," especially since "spirit," "water," and "blood" are neuter gender in Greek. <note>Erasmus notes the grammatical mismatch: John uses masculine adjectives for neuter nouns.</note> Truly, the Apostle looked more to the sense than the words; in place of three witnesses, as if three persons, he substituted three things: spirit, water, and blood. It is the same as if one said, regarding what kind of craftsman someone is, "the craftsmanship itself is a witness."

<margin>4</margin> 4 *And these three are one*] "These" is redundant, except that the translator added it for the sake of explaining the meaning. Nor is it "one," but "into one" (*in unum*), <note>original: "εἰς τὸ ἕν"</note>, in certain manuscripts.
<margin>5</margin> 5 *This is the testimony of God which is greater*] The word "which" (*ὅ*) is extra in this place, according to the Greek codices.
<margin>6</margin> 6 *Because he has testified*] <note>original: "ἣ μεμαρτύρηκε"</note>, that is, "which he has testified."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...there are three who give testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit: <gloss>4</gloss> and these three are one. <margin>8</margin> And there are three who give testimony on earth: the spirit, and the water, and the blood: and these three are one. <margin>9</margin> If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater: since this is the testimony of God, <gloss>6</gloss> which he has testified concerning his Son. <margin>10</margin> The one who believes in the Son of God, <gloss>7</gloss> has the testimony in himself. <margin>9</margin> <gloss>8</gloss> The one who does not believe God makes him a liar: <gloss>10</gloss> because he does not believe in the testimony that God has testified concerning his Son. <margin>11</margin> And this is the testimony, that God has given us eternal life: <margin>B</margin> and this life is in his Son. <margin>12</margin> The one who has the Son has life; the one who does not have the Son of God does not have life. <margin>13</margin> <gloss>11</gloss> These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life, and that you may believe in the name of the Son of God. <margin>14</margin> And this is the confidence that we have toward God, that if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us. <margin>15</margin> And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests <gloss>12</gloss> which we have asked from him. <margin>16</margin> <gloss>13</gloss> If anyone sees his brother sinning a sin not unto death, <gloss>14</gloss> he shall ask, and he will give him life, for those sinning not unto death. There is a sin unto death; <gloss>15</gloss> I do not <margin>C</margin> say concerning that one that he should ask. <margin>17</margin> <gloss>16</gloss> All unrighteousness is sin. And there is a sin not unto death. <margin>18</margin> We know that everyone who is born of God does not sin: <gloss>17</gloss> but the one who is begotten of God keeps himself, and that evil one <gloss>18</gloss> does not touch him. <margin>19</margin> We know that we are of God, and the whole world is set in the evil one. <margin>20</margin> We know, however, that the Son of God...

---

<margin>7</margin> 7 *Has the testimony of God in himself*] "Of God" is redundant here. However, the [Greek] article has emphasis, so that you understand it as the testimony of God.
<margin>8</margin> 8 *The one who does not believe the Son*] In Greek it is "does not believe God" <note>original: "τῷ Θεῷ"</note>.
<margin>9</margin> 9 *Makes a liar*] In Greek it is "has made" <note>original: "πεποίηκεν"</note>.
<margin>10</margin> 10 *Because he does not believe*] <note>original: "ὅτι οὐ πεπίστευκεν"</note>, that is, "because he has not believed."
<margin>11</margin> 11 *These things I have described*] <note>original: "Ταῦτα ἔγραψα"</note>, that is, "These things I have written." In this place, the Greek differs from the Latin, but I fear they have been rashly corrupted. [The Greek says]: "I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life, and that you may believe in the name of the Son of God." Certainly, the Greek copies are consistent.
<margin>12</margin> 12 *Which we have asked*] <note>original: "ἃ ᾐτήκαμεν"</note>, that is, "the things we have asked," in the past tense.
<margin>13</margin> 13 *The one who (sees a brother)*] <note>original: "Ἐάν τις ἴδῃ"</note>, that is, "If anyone knows/sees."
<margin>14</margin> 14 *Let him ask and life shall be given to him sinning not unto death*] <note>original: "αἰτήσει, καὶ δώσει αὐτῷ ζωὴν, τοῖς ἁμαρτάνουσι μὴ πρὸς θάνατον"</note>, that is, "he will ask, and he will give him life, to those who sin not unto death." This rightly troubles the Grammarians: how "to those sinning" (plural) follows "to him" (singular). However, if Bede reads "to the one sinning," he agrees with our edition. Truly, this change in number does not change the sense, since the pronoun "him" is used generally; just as if you say, "it is harder to fight with a man than with a woman," it has the same force as saying "with men than with women." There is another difficulty: who does the verb "he will give" refer to—God, or the one who asks? For the one who obtains [the request] also, in a way, gives to the other.
<margin>E</margin> 15 *Not for that one*] <note>original: "οὐ περὶ ἐκείνης"</note>. "That one" should refer to the sin, not to the man. This passage appears on the surface to take away hope of pardon for those who have relapsed into grave fault. It is not hidden from me by what arguments theologians extricate themselves from this. But it seems to me another exit can be opened. Venial faults, without which one does not live, are blotted out by daily prayer, "Forgive us our debts," as Augustine also interprets. However, atrocious crimes are not healed in the same way; in the past, they were cast out from the fellowship of the Church and handed over to Satan, nor were they received back unless the fault was blotted out by fasting, tears, and many hard remedies. Bede thinks there is absolutely some sin for which pardon should not be sought, because it would be sought in vain; following Augustine, who felt this in his books on the *Sermon on the Mount*. This was also the opinion of Origen, Theognostus, and Athanasius. Truly, Augustine sings a retraction of this opinion in his first book of *Retractations*, adding that this is true only if one perseveres in a perverse disposition until death. Bede touches on this opinion, but judges the former one to be better, because what follows—"All unrighteousness is sin," etc.—hardly agrees with it. I suspect, however, that Augustine’s commentary is mutilated, with the part that offended the reader cut off, which Bede nonetheless seems to have read. His imitation of Augustine, as in other things, argues for this.
<margin>F</margin> 16 *All unrighteousness is sin... Is a sin unto death*] The Greeks read, "is [a sin] *not* unto death." The Ordinary Gloss explains it in this sense. Although elsewhere the speech has an ambiguity; for the sense can be taken as: "All unrighteousness is sin," and indeed unto death, so that the word "sin" is more general and "unrighteousness" more specific. Another [sense] is also possible: "All unrighteousness is sin," and there is some kind of sin that surpasses all unrighteousness, and for that reason is not forgiven.
<margin>17</margin> 17 *But the begotten of God*] <note>original: "ἀλλ’ ὁ γεννηθεὶς ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ τηρεῖ ἑαυτὸν"</note>, that is, "but the one begotten of God keeps himself." The Greek copies agree, and the Latin ones are no less constantly different. If "him" (*αὐτὸν*) were written instead of "himself" (*ἑαυτὸν*), "the one begotten" could refer to the Son of God, who preserves the children of God.
<margin>18</margin> 18 *Shall not touch*] <note>original: "οὐχ ἅπτεται"</note>, that is, "does not touch," in the present tense.

### S U M M A R Y
#### of the second catholic Epistle of Saint
## J O H N
#### T H E  T H E O L O G I A N.

The elder writes this to the Lady and her children. The occasion of the Epistle is this: Seeing her children walking well in the faith, and many deceivers going about and saying that the coming of Christ in the flesh did not occur, he writes this Epistle. And first, he accepts her children. Then, teaching that our mystery is not something new, he exhorts them again concerning love, and that they should remain in the teaching delivered to them; further, he teaches that anyone who says Christ has not come in the flesh is an antichrist. He instructs them not to receive such people into their house, nor to say "greetings" to such people. And thus he completes the Epistle.

<margin>A</margin>
*who*, which, if it were absent, would without controversy refer to what came before. Nor is there anything that should offend us in the change of number, since when he says *Antichrist* [in the singular], he understands all who resist Christ. By this figure of speech, we say "the Gaul" for "the Gauls," or "the soldier" for "the soldiers." Furthermore, *coming* <note>original: "ἐρχόμενον" (erchomenon)</note> can be understood as being in the imperfect tense—"who was coming"—or it can be understood as the future, so that we understand it as referring to the final judgment.
<margin>8</margin> *May you receive a full reward*] *Apolabōmen* <note>original: "ἀπολάβωμεν"</note>, that is, "let us receive."
<margin>9</margin> *Who recedes*, *ho parabainōn* <note>original: "ὁ παραβαίνων"</note>, that is, who passes by or transgresses: and where it says "remains," the Greek is *menōn* <note>original: "μένων"</note>, he stays. The translator was eager to express the <term>invariable</term> <note>the use of consistent words for "recede" and "stay"</note> nature of the phrase. Ancient manuscripts had "precedes," not "recedes." Our version changed both the word and the number, for it said "precedes" instead of "passes by."

<margin>7</margin> *Nor say "hail" to him*] *Chairein autō mē legete* <note>original: "χαίρειν αὐτῷ μὴ λέγετε"</note>, that is, do not say a greeting to him, or do not bid him be well. *Behold, I have foretold this to you, so that on the day of the Lord you may not be put to shame.* I do not find these [last] words in the Greek manuscript.
<margin>8</margin> *I hope that I shall be with you*] If the Greek had been *genesthai* <note>original: "γενέσθαι"</note>, he might seem to have followed that form; but since it is *elthein* <note>original: "ἐλθεῖν"</note>, that is, "to come," I wonder why "shall be" pleased him, especially since "to you" follows. For in the Greek there is a synecdoche, and *kata* <note>original: "κατά" (meaning "according to" or "at")</note> is understood. We have expressed it as "the present [person] speaking to the present [persons]." He closes the following Epistle with a similar style of speech.

# I N T R O D U C T I O N <note>original: "Υ Π Ο Θ Ε Σ Ι Σ"</note>
#### to the third catholic Epistle of Saint
# J O H N
#### T H E  T H E O L O G I A N.

This Epistle is about hospitality. And first, he accepts Gaius, who is well-reported by all for his hospitality. And he urges him to remain in that same purpose and to welcome the brothers. Again, he himself accepts the offering. But he blames Diotrephes, as one who neither provides for the poor himself, but also hinders others, and talks much nonsense. He says such people are strangers to the truth and do not even know God. He recommends Demetrius, bearing witness to his excellent qualities.

---

# J O H N
### T H E  T H E O L O G I A N.

Why, I ask, is this affectation of variety useful?

<margin>C</margin> *to be received [faithfully/hospitably], you make it safe, or you place it in safety. Or here: you do a Christian thing.* <note>original: "fus accipi, tutum reddis..." The prefix 'fus' likely refers to 'fidus' or 'fideliter' (faithfully) from verse 5.</note>

4 *And this to strangers*] This is redundant, according to the Greek codices.
5 *May we be fellow-workers for the truth*] <note>original: τῇ ἀληθείᾳ</note>, that is, for the truth.
6 *I would perhaps have written*] In Greek <note>original: Ἔγραψα</note>, that is, "I wrote." The word "perhaps" <note>original: "forsitan"</note> was not added. I suspect some corrector added "I would have written" in the margin instead of "I wrote," and added "perhaps" so as not to seem too arrogant; then, by an unskillful scribe, both were transferred into the main text. The Translator did not translate badly if he indeed read <note>original: Ἔγραψά ἄν</note> [I would have written]. Otherwise, the other sense stands: "I wrote to the Church, but in vain, since Diotrephes stands in the way."
7 *And as if those things were not enough for him*] <note>original: καὶ μὴ ἀρκούμενος ἐπὶ τούτοις</note>, that is, "and not content with these."
8 *And those who receive*] <note>original: καὶ τοὺς βουλομένους</note>, that is, "and those who wish," so that one understands "to receive."

-> OF THE THIRD EPISTLE OF JOHN. <-
-> T H E  E N D. <-

---

9 *Testimony is rendered*] <note>original: μεμαρτύρηται</note>, that is, testimony has been provided. It is established among Authors that the first Epistle of John belongs to that John whom Jesus loved most. However, John the Presbyter wrote the two later ones, not John the Apostle. Regarding this matter, Jerome reported in his *Catalog of Illustrious Writers* in these very words: "He wrote also one Epistle, whose beginning is 'That which was from the beginning' etc., which is approved by all ecclesiastical and learned men. But the remaining two, whose beginning is 'The Elder to the chosen Lady' and 'The Elder to the most dear Gaius,' are asserted to be by John the Presbyter, whose other tomb is shown at Ephesus to this day." The same Jerome demonstrates in Papias that John the Elder was distinct from John the Apostle and Evangelist: and that the two later Epistles are ascribed to the Elder, not the Apostle: see Eusebius, book 3, chapter 99.

<column-break/>

# T H E  H Y P O T H E S I S  O F
# T H E  E P I S T L E
## O F  J U D E.

He writes this Epistle to those who have already believed. The occasion is this: certain people having crept in and teaching that faith is a matter of indifference, and denying the Lord, he had a necessity to write and secure the brethren. And first, he exhorts them to contend for and remain in the faith delivered to them. Then he denounces such people as deceivers; and he commands them to have no fellowship with such, knowing that it is not enough only to be called, unless we also walk worthily of the calling. For God, having led the former people out of Egypt, destroyed those who did not remain in the faith; and he did not spare the angels who did not keep their own order. It is necessary, therefore, to withdraw from such people. For even Michael the Archangel did not bring a blasphemous judgment against the devil; and he teaches that their destruction will be like that of Sodom. Then he gives exhortation regarding character. And having prayed for them to have stability of faith from the Lord, he completes the Epistle.

---

# O N  T H E  E P I S T L E
# O F  J U D E
## Argument by
## DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

With many words, he expresses his indignation <note>term: "destomachatur" - literally to vent one's stomach or spleen; to be greatly annoyed</note> against those who, blinded by their own desires, were opposing the Gospel. Yet this should not seem new, since they were destined for this long ago, and it was predicted by the Apostles that this kind of men would creep into the flock of Christians. Against these he so arms the believers that they should strive to restrain those men by rebuke, or save them by admonishing. But if they cannot, they should certainly prepare themselves for the coming of Christ.

# THE EPISTLE
### OF THE CATHOLIC BLESSED
# JUDE
### THE APOSTLE.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>1</margin> JUDE, a servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James, to those who are sanctified in God the Father, and preserved in Jesus Christ, and called:
<margin>2</margin> Mercy unto you, and peace, and love, be multiplied.
<margin>3</margin> Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
<margin>B</margin>
<margin>4</margin> For there are certain men crept in unawares, who were before of old ordained to this condemnation, ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and denying the only Master God, and our Lord Jesus Christ.
<margin>5</margin> I will therefore put you in remembrance, though ye once knew this, how that the Lord, having saved the people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed them that believed not.
<margin>6</margin> And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day.
<margin>C</margin>
<margin>7</margin> Even as Sodom and Gomorrah, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire.
<margin>8</margin> Likewise also these filthy dreamers defile the flesh, despise dominion, and speak evil of dignities.
<margin>9</margin> Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee.
<margin>10</margin> But these speak evil of those things which they know not: but what they know naturally, as brute beasts, in those things they corrupt themselves.
<margin>11</margin> Woe unto them! for they have gone in the way of Cain, and ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward, and perished in the gainsaying of Korah.

---

<margin>D</margin>1 *Beloved in God the Father* ] <note>original: "In Deo Patre dilectis"</note> The Greek is *hēgiasmenois*, which means "sanctified." The translator seems to have read *ēgapēmenois* <note>meaning "beloved"</note>.
2 *And called* ] <note>original: "Et vocatis"</note> The conjunction "and" is redundant here. Furthermore, "called" is used as a noun here, not a participle.
3 *Be fulfilled* ] <note>original: "Adimpleatur"</note> The Greek is *plēthuntheiē*, meaning "be multiplied." The translator seems to have read *plērōtheiē* <note>meaning "be filled"</note>.
4 *All solicitude* ] <note>original: "Omnem sollicitudinem"</note> "Making all haste to write to you concerning our common salvation, I found it necessary to write to you." This passage can be understood in two ways. The first sense is: not only did I have the greatest desire to write to you about our common salvation, but it was also a necessity to write because of the enemies of Christ. The second is: since I had a wonderful desire to write to you about our common salvation, I could not help but write; that is, I could not but obey the longing of my soul.
5 *Exhorting [to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered]* ] <note>original: "Deprecans [supercertare semel traditæ fidei]"</note> The Greek is *parakalōn epagōnizesthai tē hapax paradotheisē toīs hagiois pistei*. If one wishes to translate the sense, it could be: "exhorting you to labor for the faith, which was once delivered to the saints." Some Latin manuscripts had "for the saints" instead of "to the saints," but this was in error. Others had "the faith delivered of the saints," but the Greek words do not allow this reading. According to the Greek copies, it is "the faith once delivered to the saints." Certainly, the first edition of the volume containing the *Ordinary Gloss* <note>a standard medieval collection of biblical commentaries</note> agrees with this order, reading "the faith once delivered to the saints." The text was changed because the reader did not realize that the dative case "to the saints" <note>Greek: toīs hagiois</note> refers to the verb "to labor for" (just as we say, "you labor for him"), but instead attached it to the previous word "delivered." It is not "handed over," but "given." Thus the sense is: that through the faith once given, you may be a help to the saints, so that they may profit more in the faith. However, since we found the other reading—matching ours—in the Spanish and Aldine editions, we have followed it, as we did before.
6 *The Master and Lord* ] <note>original: "Dominatorem & Dominum"</note> The Greek is *despotēn Theon kai Kyrion hēmōn*, that is, "the Master God and our Lord." If there is a difference, *despotēs* is a name of private right <note>like a homeowner or master of slaves</note>, while *kyrios* is a title of honor and authority. For even mothers of families are called *oikodespotai* <note>house-masters</note>, but not *kyriai* <note>ladies/rulers</note>.
7 *Knowing once all things* ] <note>original: "Scientes semel omnia"</note> In Greek, it is not "all things," but *touto*, meaning "this."
8 *Since Jesus* ] <note>original: "Quoniam Jesus"</note> The Greek says *hoti ho Kyrios*, that is, "that the Lord."
9 *Saving, a second time those &c.* ] <note>original: "Salvans, secundo eos &c."</note> The Greek is *sōsas, to deuteron apōlesen*, meaning "having saved them, he afterward destroyed them."
10 *Their own principality* ] <note>original: "Suum principatum"</note> The Greek is *tēn heautōn archēn*, that is, their own origin

<margin>1</margin> JUDE, a servant of Jesus Christ, brother of James, to those who are sanctified in God the Father, and who are preserved for Jesus Christ, being called.
<margin>2</margin> Mercy unto you, and peace, and love, be multiplied.
<margin>3</margin> Beloved, so great was my desire to write to you concerning our common salvation, that I could not help but write to you, beseeching that by your labors you might be an aid to the faith which was once given to the saints.
<margin>4</margin> For certain ungodly men have crept in by the way, who were previously described for this judgment, who turn the grace of our God into lewdness, and deny God, who is the only Master, and our Lord Jesus Christ.
<margin>5</margin> But I wish to remind you, since you once knew this, that the Lord, after he had led the people safe out of Egypt, again destroyed those who did not believe.
<margin>6</margin> And the angels, who did not keep their own origin, but had left their own dwelling, he has kept in eternal chains under darkness for the judgment of that great day.
<margin>7</margin> Just as Sodom and Gomorrah, and the neighboring cities, which in a similar manner to them had been defiled with fornications and had followed after strange flesh, are set forth as an example, enduring the punishment of eternal fire.
<margin>8</margin> In like manner surely these also, deluded by dreams, indeed pollute the flesh, but they despise masters, and heap curses upon those endowed with power.
<margin>9</margin> But Michael the archangel, when contending against the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, did not dare to cast upon him a mark of a curse, but said, The Lord rebuke you.
<margin>10</margin> But these men infect with curses those things they do not know; but what things they know by nature, like animals devoid of reason, in these they are corrupted.
<margin>11</margin> Woe to them, for they have entered the way of Cain, and in the decep-

tion.
<margin>E</margin> or beginning. It signifies that first nature in which they were created.
11 *In the judgment of the great God* ] <note>original: "In judicium magni Dei"</note> The Greek is *megalēs hēmeras*, meaning "of the great day." And so it is cited by Jerome in his *Epistle against John, Bishop of Jerusalem*, as attested by very ancient copies. No interpretation argues against this, even though a corruption had already crept into many manuscripts.
12 *They are made an example* ] <note>original: "Facit sunt exemplum"</note> The Greek is *prokeintai deigma*, that is, "they are set forth as an example."
13 *And these who [defile] the flesh* ] <note>original: "Et hi qui carnem"</note> The Greek says *kai outoi enypniazomenoi*. The Greeks do not simply have "these," but add "dreaming," or "deluded in dreams." The Greek manuscripts agree, but the Latin ones constantly differ. What "dreaming" <note>Greek: enypniazomenoi</note> exactly means here, I cannot quite guess, unless perhaps it refers to the obscene dreams of those living intemperately, or because all lust is carried out as if in a dream when reason is asleep.
14 *But majesty* ] <note>original: "Majestatem autem"</note> The Greek is *doxas de*, that is, "but glories." This is the same thing he calls "dominion" <note>Greek: kyriotēta</note>. Jerome, in his work *Against Jovinian*, translates this as "dominations," since the name implies authority. Furthermore, he calls those "masters" who have rights over subjects, and "glories" he calls Princes endowed with public power—as we noted before in the Epistle of Peter. For he calls men held in public esteem "glories" <note>Greek: doxas</note>, just as Suetonius, in his life of Claudius Caesar, calls those who perform a magistracy "powers": "He entrusted the powers throughout the provinces."
15 *Michael the archangel* ] <note>original: "Michael archangelus"</note> The Greek is *ho de Michaēl*, that is, "But Michael."
16 *May God command you* ] <note>original: "Imperet tibi Deus"</note> The Greek is *Epitimēsai soi Kyrios*, meaning "May the Lord rebuke you." Jerome, in his work *Against Ruffinus*, reads "The Lord rebuke you," imitating the Greek phrasing. A similar passage is found in the Prophet Zechariah, chapter 3: "The Lord rebuke you, Satan; even the Lord who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you." Furthermore, the passage which <margin>F</margin> Jude cites here is taken from the Apocrypha of the Hebrews; and as Saint Jerome indicates in his *Commentaries on the Epistle to Titus*, it is from the book titled *Enoch*. Because of this, the Epistle itself was not free from suspicion, as it seemed to some to be un-Apostolic to cite anything from the Apocrypha. However, Origen in the third book of *On First Principles*, citing a passage from that little book, suggests it was written about the *Ascension of Moses*, though titled *Enoch*; he cites it again in book four.
17 *Who in the way* ] <note>original: "Qui in viam"</note> The Greek is *hoti*, meaning "because" or "for." "They went in the way of Cain" <note>Greek: tē hodō tou Kain eporeuthēsan</note>, that is, they entered the way of Cain. It is translated similarly in the Psalm: "who walked not in the counsel." It means they enter through the path of Cain.
18 *They are poured out for reward* ] <note>original: "Mercede effusi sunt"</note> The Greek is *misthō exechythēsan*. The sense is somewhat obscure: "and in the error of Balaam they were poured out for reward." Otherwise, the Greek order—

<header>THE EPISTLE OF JUDE.</header>

<margin>12</margin> These are spots in your love feasts <note>original: "agapais"</note>, when they feast with you, feeding themselves without fear; they are clouds without water, carried about by winds; trees of late autumn, fruitless, twice dead, plucked up by the roots; 
<margin>13</margin> Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness forever. 
<margin>14</margin> And Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these, saying: "Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his saints, 
<margin>15</margin> To execute judgment upon all, and to convict all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all the hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against him." 
<margin>16</margin> These are murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts; and their mouth speaks great swelling words, admiring people's persons for the sake of profit. 
<margin>17</margin> But, beloved, remember the words which were spoken before by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ; 
<margin>18</margin> How they told you that there should be mockers in the last time, who should walk after their own ungodly lusts. 
<margin>19</margin> These are they who separate themselves, worldly <note>original: "psychikoi," literally 'soulish' or 'natural'</note>, having not the Spirit. 
<margin>20</margin> But you, beloved, building up yourselves on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit, 
<margin>21</margin> Keep yourselves in the love of God, looking for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life. 
<margin>22</margin> And of some have compassion, making a distinction; 
<margin>23</margin> And others save with fear, pulling them out of the fire; hating even the garment spotted by the flesh. 
<margin>24</margin> Now unto him that is able to keep them from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy, 
<margin>25</margin> To the only wise God our Savior, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and ever. Amen.

## THE EPISTLE OF JUDE
## T H E  E N D.

---

The word in the text is as follows: *and they poured themselves out into the error of Balaam’s reward* <note>Greek: "kai exechythēsan tē planē tou misthou Balaam"</note>, that is, they have rushed headlong into the deception of profit. He calls them "poured out" because they are led into every crime and have fallen away, no longer restraining themselves or abstaining from any wickedness. Furthermore, he calls the "deception of reward" that corruption by which Balaam was hired for a fee to curse the people of Israel.

**19** *In their feasts*] <note>Greek: "en agapais hymōn"</note>, that is, in your charities, or among your expressions of love. Just as the term *eulogiai* <note>blessings</note> began to be used by Christians for small gifts sent out of an affection of charity, so the banquets provided for the refreshment of the poor were called *agapai* <note>love feasts</note>. I suspect that the feasts of the Corinthians, about which Paul complains much in his letters, were of this kind. Faustus—not an orthodox man, yet not an inelegant speaker—uses this word in this sense in Book 20, chapter 4. It is also found in several places in the decrees. If Jude meant such feasts here, and we accept the Greek reading, the sense is: the foulness of their luxury is all the more notable because, amidst honest examples of charity and frugality, they shamefully indulge in the lust of drunkenness. Otherwise, what our Latin manuscripts have—*in their feasts*—hardly fits, unless perhaps for the Greeks every banquet to which several friends are invited is called an *agape*. Indeed, this custom persists among some even today, where friends invite each other in turn so that the vigor of friendship does not perish through disuse. Tertullian, in the book he wrote *Against the Nations*, seems to feel that this term was peculiar to Christian banquets: "Our supper," he says, "shows its nature by its name; it is called *agape*, which among the Greeks means love."

**20** *Without fear*] *Without fear* is an adverb in Greek, *aphobōs*, that is, intrepidly or securely, and it refers to the participle *feeding*.

**21** *Feeding*] <note>Greek: "poimainontes"</note>, that is, *shepherding*, meaning they act as their own leaders and guides in the manner of shepherds, being shepherds unto themselves. He means that they obey no one’s command but live according to their own will.

<margin>F</margin> **22** *Autumnal trees*] <note>Greek: "dendra phthinopōrina"</note>. This sounds almost as if you were to say, *trees withering in autumn*, or with withered fruit, or as the Translator seems to have intended, *trees of late autumn*. For some trees are accustomed to bloom at the very end of autumn, contrary to the season's logic, and this indicates to farmers that they are soon to die.

**23** *Wild waves of the sea*] "Wild" is the epithet for the waves, not the sea <note>Greek: "kymata agria thalassēs"</note>.

**24** *To whom the storm*] <note>Greek: "ho zophos tou skotous"</note>, the gloom of darkness, or the *cavern of darkness*.

**25** *Enoch saying*] This is brought in from the Apocrypha, just as was the earlier reference to Michael.

**26** *Behold he will come*] <note>Greek: "Idou ēlthe Kyrios"</note>, that is, *Behold the Lord has come*, in the past tense.

**27** *In which impiously*] <note>Greek: "hōn ēsebēsan"</note>, which they have impiously committed.

->THE END OF THE ANNOTATIONS ON THE EPISTLE OF JUDE, BY DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.<-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...reward, by which Balaam was deceived, they have been poured out, and they have perished in the rebellion of Korah. These are <margin>12 19-</margin> spots among your charities, feasting together, living without any fear under their own guidance and will; clouds having no water, which are driven about by winds, <margin>22</margin> trees withering in autumn, fruitless, twice dead, and uprooted; <margin>23</margin> fierce waves <margin>13</margin> of the sea, foaming out their own disgraces; wandering stars, <margin>24</margin> for whom the gloom of darkness is reserved forever. But Enoch, the seventh from <margin>14</margin> Adam, prophesied of these before, saying, <margin>26</margin> "Behold, the Lord comes with his holy thousands, to execute judgment against <margin>15</margin> all, and to rebuke all those among them who are ungodly, for all the <margin>B</margin> deeds <margin>27</margin> which they have impiously committed, and for all the hard things which <margin>28</margin> ungodly sinners have spoken against him." These are murmurers, complainers, walking according to <margin>16</margin> their own lusts, 29 and their mouth speaks swelling things, admiring persons <margin>31</margin> for the sake of utility. But <margin>17</margin> you, beloved, be mindful of the words which were spoken before by the Apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ, <margin>32</margin> for they told you that in the last time there would be <margin>18</margin> mockers, who would walk according to their 33 ungodly desires. These are 34 those who separate themselves, worldly men, not having <margin>19</margin> the Spirit. But you, beloved, 35 building yourselves up on your most holy faith, praying through the Holy Spirit, keep one another in the love of God, <margin>21</margin> awaiting the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life. <margin>36</margin> And indeed have compassion on these <margin>22</margin> <margin>C</margin> while you are being judged; but 38 save those through fear, 39 snatching them from the fire, pursuing with hatred even 40 that garment which is spotted in the flesh. To him <margin>24</margin> who is able to keep them immune from sin, and to set them in the sight of his glory unblemished with exultation, 42 to the only wise God our Savior, be glory and magnificence and empire and power, now and for all ages. Amen.

## THE END
## OF THE EPISTLE OF JUDE.

<margin>D</margin> **28** *Against God*] <note>Greek: "kat' autou"</note>, that is, *against him*. This is supported by the ancient manuscripts.

**29** *And the mouth*] <note>Greek: "ta stomata"</note>, that is, *mouths*. Although here the Greek manuscripts vary.

**30** *Pride*] <note>Greek: "hyperonka"</note>, that is, *proud things*. One ancient codex had "pride," in another the writing was similar, but someone had marked the letter 's' with a subscript dot. A third had "proudly." The variety suggests a corruption, since the Greek does not vary at all.

**31** *For the sake of gain*] <note>Greek: "ōpheleias charin"</note>, that is, *for the sake of utility*.

**32** *Who was saying*] <note>Greek: "Hoti elegon"</note>, that is, *Because he said*. Or, *Because they said*.

**33** *And ungodliness*] <note>Greek: "tōn asebeiōn"</note>, that is, *of ungodlinesses*. The conjunction "and" is redundant.

**34** *They separate themselves*] In Greek it is simply, *those who separate* <note>Greek: "apodiorizontes"</note>.

**35** *Of our faith*] <note>Greek: "hymōn pistei"</note>, that is, *of your faith*.

**36** *And indeed rebuke these*] <note>Greek: "eleeite"</note>, that is, *have compassion*.

**37** *Judging*] <note>Greek: "diakrinomenoi"</note>, that is, *discerning*, or *when you are being judged*; the word is ambiguous for the Greeks.

<margin>E</margin> **38** *Save from the fire*] <note>Greek: "en phobō sōzete"</note>, that is, *keep in fear*, or *through fear*.

**39** *They should snatch from the fire*] <note>Greek: "ek pyros"</note>, that is, *out of the blaze*. This whole passage is somewhat different from the Greek manuscripts. They read: "And on some have compassion, making a distinction; others save in fear, snatching them from the fire, hating even..." and so on. Furthermore, the sense here is otherwise somewhat obscure: that they should draw some to Christ with gentleness, taking into account the persons, while deterring others from sinning through fear; and they should hate not the men themselves, but the foul affections, which he here calls "the garment spotted by the flesh." Unless you prefer to interpret it in this sense: hating not only the foul deeds of the flesh themselves, but even the garment contaminated by the flesh—that is, whatever pertains in any way to foulness. The Greek conjunction "and" <note>kai</note> supports this interpretation, yet the former fits better with what follows: "To him who is able." To hate the vices, not the men, and to not usurp the glory for yourselves, but to attribute it to God, who is able to turn them from evil into good.

**40** *Which is carnal*] <note>Greek: "ton apo sarkos espilōmenon chitōna"</note>, that is, *the tunic soiled by the flesh*.

**41** *Unblemished*] <note>Greek: "amōmous"</note>, that is, *beyond reproach*. The phrase "at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ" is not read in the Greek codices. Nor was it in the older Constance codex.

**42** *To the only God*] <note>Greek: "Monō sophō Theō"</note>, that is, *To the only wise God*. "Through Jesus Christ our Lord"—these words are also not found in the Greek codices. "Before all ages" is also absent from the Greek books.

He specifically explores the etymology of "agape" (love feasts) and clarifies that Christians should hate the sin, represented by the "spotted garment," rather than the person.</summary>

<margin>D</margin> **A**POCALYPSIS <note>original: "Apocalypsis"</note>] Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a pioneering humanist scholar</note> wonders why the Translator <note>the author of the Vulgate</note> left the Greek word here, since he had often translated it before. For the Greek word is *apocalypsis*, which in Latin you could call *revelatio* <note>revelation</note>. We have indicated elsewhere, on the authority of Saint Jerome, that this new word was found by the Seventy <note>the translators of the Septuagint</note> to express the property of the Hebrew speech. Indeed, they use "to apocalypse" <note>original: "apokalyptein"</note> whenever a thing previously hidden is opened. Whoever was the author of this work, he began the book according to the custom of the Hebrews, namely, from the title.

<margin>2</margin> *To make manifest* <note>original: "Palam faceret"</note>] *deixai* <note>Greek: "to show"</note>, that is, *so that he might show*, or *demonstrate*, and it refers to what follows, *so that through this revelation of Jesus, his servant might show what is soon to happen*. Valla suspects it was written by the Translator as *to make plain* <note>original: "planum facere"</note>, instead of *to explain*, which is appropriate for obscure things. For if *to make manifest* is used for "to publish," the Latin speech certainly does not lack ambiguity. Indeed, he makes manifest who does something in public.

<margin>3</margin> *Sending by his Angel* <note>original: "Mittens per Angelum"</note>] *aposteilas dia tou angelou* <note>Greek</note>, that is, with the command having been sent. Otherwise, since he sent the Angel, what was it that he was sending *through* the Angel? Or, *commanding through the Angel*.

<margin>4</margin> *Who bore witness to the word of God, and the testimony of Jesus Christ*] *Hos emartyrēse ton logon tou Theou, kai tēn martyrian Iēsou Christou* <note>Greek</note>, that is, *who testified the word of God, and the testimony of Jesus Christ*. For in Greek, *word* and *testimony* are in the same case. He said "to testify" instead of "to preach publicly."

<margin>5</margin> *Whatever he saw* <note>original: "Quæcunque vidit"</note>] The Translator ought to have added, *and whatever he saw, hosa te eide* <note>Greek</note>, so that this is the third accusative, depending on the verb *testified*. Indeed, in this place I find something added in the Greek codices <note>manuscripts</note> which is not found in the Latin ones at all, *kai hatina eisi, kai hatina chrē genesthai meta tauta* <note>Greek</note>, that is, *and whatever things are, and whatever things must happen after these*.

<margin>6</margin> *Blessed is he who reads and hears*] In Greek the number is different, *Makarios ho anaginōskōn kai hoi akouontes tous logous tēs prophēteias* <note>Greek</note>, that is, *Blessed is he who shall read and those who shall hear the words of the prophecy*: for some unknown person added "of this" <note>hujus</note> from his own, wanting, I suppose, to express the force of the Greek article.

<margin>7</margin> *From him who is, who was, and who is to come*] It must be frankly admitted that the Greek speech signifies nothing at all, however you read it, *apo tou ho ōn, kai ho ēn, kai ho erchomenos* <note>Greek: "from the he-who-is..."</note>. For imagine it being placed as if absolute; *ho esomenos* <note>he who shall be</note> is tolerable, but what on earth does *ho ēn* <note>the 'he was'</note> signify? Literally it sounds like this, if it can even be expressed: *from ens* <note>being</note>, *from that which was, and from him who is to come*. Valla thinks that by this novelty of speech, the immutable property in God is signified, especially since he inflected the case for the spirits, *kai apo tōn hepta pneumatōn* <note>and from the seven spirits</note>. Furthermore, that *erchomenos* <note>coming</note> is a participle of the verb, which is ambiguous as to both times. But in this place, the future was certainly more appropriate, since two times had preceded. In the Spanish Edition <note>the Complutensian Polyglot</note> the article *apo tou* was omitted, whether by chance or by design I do not know.

<margin>8</margin> *Who loved us*] *tō agapēsanti hēmas* <note>Greek</note>, that is, *to him who loved us*, so that it refers to the Father, and thus the sense is, *that Christ was a faithful witness to the Father, who loved us, and washed us from sins through his blood*. For *me* should have been translated as *his* <note>ipsius</note>, not *his* <note>ejus</note>, if it pertained to Christ. Although soon it is necessary to change the person: *and made us kings and priests*. For thus it is in the Greek copies, *basileis kai hiereis*, that is, *kings and priests*, even if the Spanish copy had *basileian*, that is, *a kingdom, instead of kings*.

<margin>9</margin> *And every eye shall see him*] The *Glossa Ordinaria* <note>a standard medieval collection of biblical glosses</note> indicates a reading somewhat different from this: *and all the earth shall see such a one*.

<margin>10</margin> *Even so amen*] *nai amēn* <note>Greek/Hebrew</note>, "Even so" is not a conjunction, but an adverb of confirming, so that there is a double confirmation, one Greek, the other Hebrew.

<margin>11</margin> *I am alpha and omega*] *to A kai to Ō* <note>Greek</note>. He who is first in anything is called *alpha* even by a Greek proverb, as in Martial <note>a Roman poet</note>, *the alpha of cloak-wearers*, and *omega* is the last in the order of letters. Regarding this matter, we have spoken somewhat more copiously in our *Chiliades* <note>Erasmus's collection of proverbs, the *Adagia*</note>. Furthermore, *the beginning and the end* was not in the Spanish edition. And again, *who is, who was, and who is to come* is written here in Greek with just as many syllables as a little before.

<margin>12</margin> *Clothed with a long robe* <note>original: "podere"</note>] *Podere* must be pronounced with the penultimate syllable lengthened. For it is a Greek word *podērēs*, which signifies *a garment let down all the way to the feet*, from "foot" <note>pes</note>, says Lyranus <note>Nicholas of Lyra</note>, *which is 'pes', and 'hære' 'hæres', because such a thing 'sticks' to the feet*. Rather, it is from *airō*, which is to adapt, because it fits all the way to the feet. To what end did it belong to the same word

### ANNOTATIONS BY DESIDERIUS ERASMUS ###

...to forge a voice from Greek and Latin? Although there are some who prefer to call it *podērēs* [a long garment reaching the feet] in the same manner as *triērēs*.

13 **His feet like aurichalcum** <note>fine brass</note>] In Greek it is *chalcolibanō*. A word composed of copper and frankincense. Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> indicates it is a type of amber more precious than gold: he says it is fused from glass and stone, witnessing that the holy table of the "Great Church" (as he calls it) was of this temperament. Pliny, in his *Natural History* book 34, chapter 11, witnesses it is a kind of copper, which is dug from the veins of the earth, once held in high value.

14 **As in a burning furnace**] We did not have an equal abundance of copies <note>manuscripts</note> for this work, because the Apocalypse is hardly found added in any of the volumes of the Greeks. In those codes which I have seen, it was written, *hōs en kaminō pepyrōmenoi*, that is, just as burning in a furnace, or ignited, so that the participle pertains to the feet.

15 **And his face**] *kai hē opsis*, that is, the sight or appearance.

**And you found them liars**] In this place I found added in a very ancient codex *kai ebaptisas*, that is, "and you baptized," but erroneously, if I am not mistaken, since in the Greek commentaries there was nothing that pertained to baptism. Later, from other copies I found it should read *epeirasas*, that is, "you bore," or

<column-break/>

tolerated. Although in the Latin codices the order is inverted, "you have patience" precedes, "you have borne" follows.

2 **But if not**] *ei de mē*, otherwise. A little later it transitioned to, "if by any less": he could have translated it "otherwise."

3 **To the angel of the Church of Smyrna**] It is "of the Smyrneans" in Greek, *Smyrnaiōn*. And likewise a little later, "And to the Angel of the Church of Pergamum," in Greek is "of the Pergamene Church," *tēs en Pergamō*, as a little above, "of the Ephesian Church."

4 **The doctrine of Balaam, who taught in Balak**] Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, the humanist scholar</note> rightly advises that a little before "there" was said for "in that place." For the Greeks lack this difference in pronouns. Furthermore, the history of King Balak and the Prophet Balaam, you have in Numbers chapters 22, 23, and 24.

5 **A white pebble**] *psēphon leukēn*. In ancient times they cast votes with pebbles <note>calculi</note>. From this, those things which are approved are said to be marked with a white stone, and those condemned with a black one. And in the voting of assemblies, the name of him who was favored was inscribed on the pebble.

6 **Thyatira Church**] *Thuateirōn*, that is, of the Thyatirensis.

7 **His feet like aurichalcum**] Again it is *chalcolibanō*, about which we have just spoken.

# THE REVELATION OF JOHN. CHAPTER III. #

[I know] your faith, and your patience, and your works, and that your last works are more than the first. But I have a few things against you, because you allow the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit sexual immorality and to eat things sacrificed to idols. And I gave her time so that she might repent of her immorality; but she did not repent. Behold, I will cast her into a bed, and those who commit adultery with her into great affliction, unless they repent of their deeds. And I will kill her children with death; and all the Churches shall know that I am he who searches the kidneys <note>original: "nephrous" - in ancient thought, the kidneys were considered the seat of emotions and conscience</note> and hearts, and I will give to each of you according to your works. But to you I say, and to the rest in Thyatira, as many as do not have this teaching, and who have not known the depths of Satan (as they say), I will put no other burden upon you. However, that which you have, hold fast until I come. And he who overcomes, and who keeps my works until the end, to him I will give power over the nations, and he shall rule them with a rod of iron; as the vessels of a potter are broken to pieces. Just as I also received from my Father, I will give him the morning star. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.

<margin>8</margin> *And to eat of things sacrificed to idols*] It should be read as "idolothytis," that is, things sacrificed to an image <note>Erasmus is correcting the spelling of the Latin term for food sacrificed to pagan idols</note>.
<margin>9</margin> *That she might perform penance*] <note>original: "ἵνα μετανοήσῃ"</note> that is, "that she might come to her senses" <note>original: "resipisceret"</note>, which he almost always translates in this manner. Truly, we have already warned about this frequently <note>Erasmus preferred "resipiscere" (to change one's mind) over the Vulgate's "poenitentiam agere" (to do penance) to emphasize internal change over external ritual</note>.
<margin>10</margin> *Like a vessel of a potter*] <note>original: "ὡς τὰ σκεύη τὰ κεραμικὰ"</note> that is, like earthenware vessels.

<margin>1</margin> *† to the angel of the Church of Sardis*] <note>original: "τῆς ἐν Σάρδεσιν"</note> that is, of the Sardian Church. And likewise a little lower, *to the angel of Philadelphia*, <note>original: "τῆς ἐν Φιλαδελφείᾳ"</note> that is, of the Philadelphian Church.
<margin>2</margin> *Who opens, and no one shuts*] Lorenzo <note>referring to the humanist scholar Lorenzo Valla</note> reads, *he will shut and you shall open*, in the future tense. And he adds, *no one will shut except he who opens*. Truly our manuscript agreed with our Edition. With Valla’s reading, the

<column-break/>

<margin>F</margin> Spanish edition agreed. But let no one despise ours; it was of such great antiquity that it could seem to have been written in the age of the Apostles.
<margin>3</margin> *To the angel of the Laodicea Church*] <note>original: "τῆς Ἐκκλησίας Λαοδικέων"</note> that is, the Church of the Laodiceans.
<margin>4</margin> *Neither are you cold, nor hot*] <note>original: "οὔτε ζεσὸς"</note> that is, neither fervent, from the word *zeo*, to boil or glow.
<margin>5</margin> *I will begin to vomit you out*] <note>original: "μέλλω σε ἐμέσαι"</note> that is, I will vomit you. Yet the Translator enjoys turning it in this manner at times.
<margin>6</margin> *You say that I am rich*] From these words no other sense can be perceived, except that he says Christ is rich. Therefore the conjunction *that* <note>original: "quod"</note> should have been omitted, which in this place has no use for those speaking Latin <note>Erasmus is criticizing the clunky grammar of the older Latin translation</note>.
<margin>7</margin> *Gold ignited and tested*] The Greek is otherwise: <note>original: "πεπυρωμένον ἐκ πυρός"</note> that is, ignited from fire. The Greek scholia interpret it in almost the same way. Perhaps the Translator read *pepyromenon*, from which he might have added "tested" <note>original: "probatum"</note>.

<margin>8 *The shame of your nakedness*] <note>original: "aischyne"</note> that is, *filthiness, or disgrace, or shame.* It is a wonder how the word *confusio* <note>confusion</note> crept into Christian usage.</margin>
<margin>9 *Anoint your eyes with eye-salve*] <note>original: "kollyrion"</note> This word is thought to be named from *ius* <note>broth or juice</note> because they have a docked tail. In this passage, it refers to a type of medicine.</margin>
<margin>10 *I, those whom I love*] <note>original: "hosous ean philo"</note> that is, *whomever I love.*</margin>
<margin>2 *Similar in appearance to jasper*] <note>original: "homoios horasei litho iaspidi"</note> that is, *similar in appearance to a jasper stone:* so that the first dative case indicates the manner, and the second indicates the relation.</margin>
<margin>2 *Similar in appearance to emerald*] that is, *similar in emerald appearance, so that you may understand "stone" as implied.* For he just said <note>original: "sardino"</note>, that is, *a sardine stone.*</margin>
<margin>3 *Twenty-four elders*] Since among the Greeks "sitting elders" are in the accusative case, "clothed" connects poorly; but in several manuscripts the word *vidi* ("I saw") is not added, but *esan* ("they were") is understood. Therefore, the translator seems to have read <note>original: "kathemenoi"</note> <note>the nominative form</note>.</margin>

<margin>5 *Holy, holy, holy*] In the Laurentian manuscripts <note>The Laurentian Library in Florence, containing the Medici collection.</note>, as he himself indicates, *holy* is repeated nine times. But in my manuscripts it was placed only three times, and nowhere is there greater variety than in this book, because among the Greeks this book was held almost among the Apocrypha <note>Meaning it was not always accepted as part of the official biblical canon in the Eastern Church.</note>. The Spanish copy <note>original: "exemplar Hispaniense" — likely a reference to the Complutensian Polyglot Bible.</note> agreed with the Laurentian reading.</margin>
<margin>6 *Who was & who is*] These are the same words about which I have already spoken before.</margin>
<margin>7 *And when those living creatures gave*] In the Greek manuscripts it is <note>original: "dosousi"</note>, that is, *they shall give*, unless perhaps it was written <note>original: "dososi"</note>, and it was changed, that is, *they fall down*.</margin>
<margin>8 *Worthy are you Lord to receive*] The Spanish copy has a few more words here, <note>original: "Axios ei ho Kyrios kai Theos hēmon ho hagios labein"</note>, that is, *Worthy are you, Lord and our holy God, to receive*.</margin>
<margin>9 *Because of your will they were*] In Greek it is <note>original: "ēsan"</note>, *they are, not they were*.</margin>
<margin>1 *Inside and outside*] <note>original: "esōthen kai exōthen"</note>, that is, *inside and on the back*, that is, on both sides of the parchment.</margin>
<margin>2 *The Lion of the tribe of Judah*] <note>original: "ho leōn ho ōn ek tēs phylēs Iouda"</note>, that is, *the lion, the one who is from the tribe of Judah*.</margin>
<margin>3 *And they were singing a song*] <note>original: "kai adousin"</note>, that is, and *they sing*.</margin>

<note>4 *And you have made us*] <note>original Greek: "ἡμᾶς"</note>. Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous 15th-century scholar of Latin and Greek</note> reads *autous*, that is, "them." Furthermore, it is not "kingdom," but *Basileis*, "kings," as we indicated above.</note>
<note>5 *And their number was thousands of thousands*] Lorenzo reads "myriads of myriads, thousands of thousands." A "myriad" signifies ten thousand, a "chiliad" signifies a thousand. Our manuscript agrees more with the common Latin edition, while the Spanish edition <note>Refers to the Complutensian Polyglot Bible</note> agrees with what Lorenzo reads.</note>
<note>1 *Come and see*] <margin>And I heard one of the four animals as it were a voice of thunder</margin>] Valla reads, "come together." Our manuscripts had "Voice." Otherwise, we would have had to say *demus* instead of *dicentem*, which Valla seems to have read. However, I do not know what his note means in this place; it is either faulty or confused.</note>
<note>2 *A measure of wheat*] In Greek it is *Choenix*, which is a measure of wheat or legumes sufficient for a day's food. Our friend Budé <note>Guillaume Budé, a French humanist scholar</note> in his fifth book *On the As* thinks a *choenix* weighs four pounds; Pollux <note>A Greek grammarian</note> thinks only three. And it is valued at a denarius, without adding "one."</note>
<note>3 *Pale horse*] In Greek it is *chloros*. It also means green, and he translates it that way a little later as "all green grass."</note>
<note>4 *Souls of the slain*] The Spanish edition adds "of the marked men."</note>
<note>5 *As a fig tree casts its unripe figs*] <note>original: "βάλλει"</note>, that is, "throws away." And the "unripe fig" is *olynthos*. This refers to immature figs.</note>
<note>6 *Like a rolled-up book*] <note>original Greek: "ὡς βιβλίον εἱλισσόμενον"</note>, that is, like a book that is rolled or curled up. This same word is used in the Psalms regarding the changing heavens.</note>

<margin>1</margin> <term>Twelve thousand sealed</term> <note>original: "Uodecim millia signati"</note>] In the Greek, the word "sealed" is not repeated except at the beginning and the end. It is not added for each individual tribe, as <note>Lorenzo Valla was a famous Renaissance scholar who looked for errors in the Latin Bible by comparing it to Greek manuscripts.</note> Valla points out, although it was added in our Latin copies. And "sealed" is a participle from the verb to seal, as if you were to say "marked with a signet" or "closed with a seal."

<margin>2</margin> <term>Salvation to our God who sits</term> <note>original: "Salus Deo nostro qui sedet"</note>] In Greek: <note>original: "Σωτηρία" (Sōtēria)</note>. This more strongly signifies the act of saving. Otherwise, what need was there to pray for "safety" or "health" for Christ? <note>The translator is exploring the nuance of the word "Salus," which in Latin can mean health, safety, or salvation.</note>

<margin>3</margin> <term>And they washed their robes</term> <note>original: "Et laverunt stolas suas"</note>] In Greek: <note>original: "καὶ ἐπλάτυναν τὰς στολὰς αὐτῶν"</note>, that is, "and they expanded their robes." The Latin translator seems to have read <note>original: "ἔπλυναν" (eplunan)</note>, meaning "they washed." My guess did not fail me; for I found it written this way in the Spanish Edition <note>Referring to the Complutensian Polyglot, a massive multilingual Bible printed in Spain in the early 1500s.</note>.

->**Notes on the Greek and Latin Text**<-

...might be possible, as if you were to say *apishon* <note>Referring to a previous discussion on the word "Wormwood"</note>. For it deals with the waters being turned into bitterness.

<margin>4 Woe, woe, woe]</margin> The Laurentian manuscript added "thrice," that is, three times; my own had "thrice," and had the word "woe" only twice.
<margin>1</margin> *They had breastplates]* The Greek is *Thorakas*, that is, thoraxes; whether *lorica* <note>a Latin leather or metal cuirass</note> has exactly the same value, I do not know.
<margin>2 Whose name in Hebrew is Abaddon]*</margin> <note>original: "אבדון"</note> In Hebrew, it is from the word <note>original: "אבד"</note> meaning "to perish," hence *Abaddon* as if you were to say "perdition" or "one who destroys." In Latin, the name is *Exterminans* <note>The Exterminator</note>. The Translator added this on his own. Since John—or whoever else it was—wrote in Greek, he was content to be understood by those who knew Greek. However, there is no reason for Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous 15th-century humanist scholar</note> to be so angry if the Translator wanted the Latins also to know what "Apollyon" means.
<margin>3 Twenty thousand times ten thousand]*</margin> <note>original: "δύο μυριάδες μυριάδων"</note> That is, two myriads of myriads, which is twenty thousand myriads. A myriad, as we just said, comprises ten thousand.
<margin>4 Fiery breastplates]*</margin> <note>original: "Θώρακας"</note> That is, thoraxes. It is the part of the body from below the neck down to the stomach, encompassing the ribs and the rest from both back and front; hence the garment or armor covering that part is called a "thorax."
<margin>5 His feet like pillars of fire]*</margin> <note>original: "ὡς στύλοι"</note> That is, like columns.
<margin>2 He had in his hand a little scroll]*</margin> Some manuscripts had *biblaridion*, others *biblidarion*, and others again *biblidakion* <note>These are all Greek diminutive forms for a "little book"</note>.
<margin>3 Just as when a lion roars]*</margin> In Greek it is *mykatai*, which technically means "lows" or "bellows" (like an ox); perhaps because the Greeks do not maintain that distinction between *mykasthai* <note>bellowing</note> and *ryasthai* <note>roaring</note> that the Latins do between *rugire* and *mugire*.
<margin>4 Seal the things spoken by the seven]*</margin> <note>original: "Σφράγισον"</note> That is, "Sign it shut" as if they are things to be hidden.

> <margin>1</margin> *through His servants the Prophets* ] Some Greek manuscripts had <note>original: ὡς εὐηγγέλισατο τοῖς δοῦλοις αὐτοῦ τοὺς Προφήτας</note> "as He announced to His servants the Prophets." Someone, offended by the use of the accusative case [the direct object] with the verb "to announce," added the preposition "through."

> <margin>1</margin> *like a rod, and it was said to me* ] <note>original: λέγων</note> "saying," as if the reed itself were speaking. Unless the nominative is placed here absolutely in place of the genitive. In the Spanish manuscript there was another reading, <note>original: καὶ εἱστήκει ὁ ἄγγελος λέγων</note> that is, *and the angel stood saying.*

> <margin>2</margin> *The court however which is outside the temple cast out* ] My manuscript had <note>original: ἔσωθεν</note>, that is, *inside*. The Spanish edition had <note>original: ἔξωθεν</note>, that is, *outside*, which agrees with our reading; this reading is more approved by me, and yet neither is absurd.

> <margin>3</margin> *And You have received Your great power and have reigned* ] <note>original: ἐβασίλευσας</note>. It would have been more aptly translated here as *and you have obtained the kingdom.* For in Latin, "reigned" (*regnavit*) can imply someone who has ceased to reign, just as "they have lived" (*vixerunt*) implies those who have ceased to live. Among the Greeks, it is otherwise, at least in these specific verbs <note>meaning the Greek verb implies the beginning of a state of being</note>.

The scholarly notes discuss grammatical variations in the Greek manuscripts, particularly regarding the measuring of the temple and the nuances of the Greek verb for "reigned."</summary>

<margin>1</margin> **A**nd she cried out in labor } <note>original: κράζει [krazei]</note>, that is, she cries. This is argued by what follows immediately: "and she is tormented to give birth." Now, how aptly these things fit the divine Mary, mother of Jesus, is for those to see who distort what was said about the Church to apply to her. Indeed, they distort what was said about Wisdom—that is, about Christ—to Mary, contrary to the interpretation of all the Ancients. And here we stir up atrocious tragedies, as if it were pleasing to her that conflict be committed for her sake among Christians, for whose reconciliation her Son died.

<margin>2</margin> So that he might cause her to be carried away by the river } <note>original: ἵνα ποταμοφόρητον ποιήσῃ [hina potamophorēton poiēsē]</note>, that is, so that he might bring it about that the river would take her away, or that she would be snatched by the river. In Greek, it is said more pleasantly with a compound word.

<margin>1</margin> And the whole earth wondered after the beast } <note>original: καὶ ἐθαυμάσθη ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ γῇ ὀπίσω τοῦ θηρίου [kai ethaumasthē en holē tē gē opisō tou thēriou]</note>, that is, and there was admiration in the whole earth after the beast.

<insert>
1. "He goes into captivity": <note>original Greek: εἰς αἰχμαλωσίαν ὑπάγει</note> that is, he who leads others into captivity, goes into captivity himself. Laurentius reads this differently.
3. "The mark in the right hand": <note>original Greek: χάραγμα</note> that is, an imprinted mark or an insignia.
1. "Which is mixed pure": <note>original Greek: τὸ κεκερασμένον ἀκράτου</note> so that "pure" is in the ablative case and refers to "wine." Among the Greeks, the word for "mixed" is used for what is poured into a cup for drinking, even if it is not diluted with water or another type of drink.
2. "From now on, says the Spirit": The Greeks punctuate this so that "from now on" is the end of the sentence, meaning they will be blessed hereafter who have died in the Lord. Then follows: "and says the Spirit" <note>original Greek: καὶ λέγει τὸ Πνεῦμα</note>. And here also is a confirmation.

<margin>1</margin> *Into the winepress of God’s wrath* ] The Greek is <note>original: "εἰς ληνὸν"</note>, which is a *winepress* <note>original: "lacus"</note>, into which the juice of the grapes is pressed.
<margin>'Q'</margin> *Because you alone are pious* ] The Greek is <note>original: "ὅσιος"</note> [hosios]. Laurentius and the Spanish Edition read <note>original: "ἅγιος"</note> [hagios], that is, *holy*.
<margin>2</margin> *Clothed in pure and white stone* ] In Greek, it is <note>original: "εἶτ’ λῖνον καθαρόν"</note>, that is, *in pure linen*. The Translator seems to have read <note>original: "λίθον"</note> [lithon, meaning stone]. The former word differs from "stone" by only a single letter. And "splendid" <note>original: "λαμπρῷ"</note> is more accurate than "white."
<margin>1</margin> *A sore, cruel and very bad* ] In Greek, <note>original: "κακὸν καὶ πονηρόν"</note>, that is, *bad and bad*. For in Greek, it says the same thing twice. Unless you prefer *miserable and bad*.
<margin>2</margin> *who is, and who was* ] Although the Translator changed the person, yet it is said with just as many syllables as above: *he who is, who was, who is to come*, <note>original: "ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, ὁ ἐρχόμενος"</note>.
<margin>3</margin> *Even so, Lord* ] In Greek, <note>original: "Ναὶ Κύριε"</note>. "Even so" <note>original: "Etiam"</note> is a word of confirmation.

1 *And lived in luxury* <note>original: "Et in deliciis fuit"</note>] <note>original: "καὶ ἐστρηνίασε"</note>. This is the same word used by Paul in the first Epistle to Timothy, chapter five: *But when they have lived luxuriously against Christ, they want to marry.* This was discussed at greater length in that place. Also, a little later, <note>original: "καὶ στρηνιῶντες"</note>, that is, "and *they lived wantonly*."

2 *Thyine wood* <note>original: "Lignum thyinum"</note>] <note>original: "ξύλον θύϊνον"</note>, from the thyine tree, of which mention is made in 1 Kings chapter 10.

3 *And fine flour* <note>original: "Et simila"</note>] <note>original: "καὶ σεμίδαλιν"</note>. Some interpret this as winter wheat <note>original: "siliginem"</note>.

4 *A great millstone* <note>original: "Lapidem molarem magnum"</note>] <note>original: "λίθον ὡς μύλον"</note>, that is, a stone like a mill.

5 *With this force it shall be thrown* <note>original: "Hoc impetu mittetur"</note>] <note>original: "Οὕτως ὁρμήματι βληθήσεται"</note>, that is, "Thus with force it shall be thrown."

*As it were a great voice of many crowds* <note>original: "Quasi vocem magnam turbarum multarum"</note>] <note>original: "ἤκουσα φωνὴν ὄχλου πολλοῦ"</note>, that is, "I heard a voice of a vast multitude." Therefore, it follows that the Translator wrote "of crowds" [plural] rather than "of a crowd" [singular].

*Hallelujah* <note>original: "Alleluia"</note>] Which for the Hebrews sounds like "Praise the Lord." Indeed, *Hallelu* <note>original: "הλלו"</note> is "Praise," and *Yah* <note>original: "יה"</note> is "the Lord." This expression is frequent in the Psalms: "Praise the Lord."

<margin>
**Gog & Magog** — Both are in the accusative case and of the masculine gender, as the Greek article declares, <note>original: "τὸν Γὼγ καὶ τὸν Μαγὼγ"</note>, whether they are to be understood as men or as a lineage. Nor is it "he will gather," but <note>original: "συναγαγεῖν αὐτοὺς"</note>, that is, "to gather them," or "so that he might gather them." Furthermore, "them" does not refer to the corners or the nations, but to Gog and Magog.

### XXI.

1 And I saw a new heaven and a new earth; for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more.
<margin>B</margin>
2 And I, John, saw the holy city, the New Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
3 And I heard a loud voice from heaven, saying: "Behold, the tabernacle <note>original: "σκηνὴ"; a dwelling place or tent, reminiscent of the portable sanctuary used by the Israelites.</note> of God is with men, and he will dwell with them; and they shall be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God."
4 And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes; and death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor pain shall be anymore, for the former things have passed away.
5 And he who sat upon the throne said: "Behold, I make all things new." And he said to me: "Write, for these words are true and faithful."
6 And he said to me: "It is done. I am the Alpha <note>original: "Α"; the first letter of the Greek alphabet.</note> and the Omega <note>original: "Ω"; the last letter of the Greek alphabet, signifying the beginning and the end.</note>, the beginning and the end. I will give to the thirsty from the fountain of the water of life freely."
7 He who overcomes shall inherit all things, and I will be his God, and he shall be my son.
<margin>C</margin>
8 But for the cowardly, the unbelieving, the abominable, the murderers, the sexually immoral, the sorcerers, the idolaters, and all liars, their portion shall be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death.
9 And there came to me one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues, and he spoke with me, saying: "Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb."
10 And he carried me away in the spirit to a great and high mountain, and showed me the great city, the holy Jerusalem, descending out of heaven from God,
11 Having the glory of God; and her radiance was like a most precious stone, like a jasper stone, clear as crystal.
12 It had a great and high wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names written on them, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel.
<margin>D</margin>
13 On the east were three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates.
14 And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and in them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.
15 And he who spoke with me had a golden reed <note>A measuring rod made of a stalk or cane.</note> to measure the city, and its gates, and its wall.
16 And the city lies foursquare, and its length is as large as its breadth; and he measured the city with the reed at twelve thousand stadia <note>A stadium was approximately 185 meters; 12,000 stadia is roughly 1,400 miles.</note>; its length, breadth, and height are equal.
17 And he measured its wall, one hundred and forty-four cubits, according to the measure of a man, which is that of an angel.
<margin>E</margin>
18 And the structure of its wall was of jasper; and the city was pure gold, like clear glass.

20 The fifth sardonyx, the sixth sardius, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh hyacinth, the twelfth amethyst.

<margin>F</margin>
22 And I saw no temple in it; for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple.

24 And the nations of those who are saved shall walk in its light, and the kings of the earth bring their glory and honor into it.
25 And its gates shall not be shut at all by day; for there shall be no night there.
26 And they shall bring the glory and honor of the nations into it.
